## Volume front matter

### Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library**, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts; most carefully corrected; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by others possessing some authority with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which it is readily possible for the reader to discover which Fathers have commented on the individual texts of each biblical book, and in which passages of their works. An extremely accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself: a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# [The Book of the Pastoral Rule]

[Col. 0009]

## Preface to the Book of the Pastoral Rule

### I

After the exegetical works on Sacred Scripture contained in the first volume, in this second volume we have gathered the remaining works unquestionably by Gregory, free from every interpolation, whatever their kind: whether apologetic, in defense of the burden of pastoral care that he had declined; historical, namely the *Dialogues*; or dogmatic and canonical, that is, the Register of Letters, which contains almost the whole of canon law. There were many reasons for beginning this second volume with the apologetic book, the *Pastoral Rule*, especially the antiquity, excellence, and usefulness of the little work.

First, that it was written before the *Dialogues* and the Register of Letters, at the very beginning of his pontificate, is clearly attested by the holy Doctor himself in what was formerly Letter 46, now Letter 48 of Book I.

Second, of all Saint Gregory’s writings, none is more excellent, whether one considers the order and arrangement of the whole work or the abundance and weight of its statements.

Third, there is nothing in that wholly golden little book that does not confer the greatest benefit—not only upon bishops and other shepherds and governors of souls, but also upon all Christians individually, especially those entrusted with the care of a household.

### II

Hence it was eagerly desired by all, both Greeks and Latins, and received with great applause. Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, kissed it when it was sent to him by his friend Gregory and published it throughout all the churches of Spain. The Emperor Maurice, having obtained it from the deacon Anatolius and being greatly pleased with it, entrusted it to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, to translate into Greek and publish. This displeased the holy Doctor, who was no less distinguished for humility than for learning.

[**Note:** We mourn the loss of the Greek version. We infer that no memory of it survived into the ninth century from the fact that Photius, who in his *Bibliotheca* highly praises the *Dialogues* translated into Greek by Zacharias, is completely silent about a Greek translation of the *Pastoral Rule*, Codex 252.]

The English have always held it in the highest esteem, having received it from the first preachers of the Gospel, disciples of our Gregory. But lest only those who knew Latin should be nourished by the fruits of this book, Alfred, the wisest king of the West Saxons and founder of Oxford University, translated it into Saxon and, after prefacing it with an introduction, offered it as a most welcome gift to his people. Copies of this translation survive both in the library of the Most Holy Trinity at Cambridge and in the Cottonian Library.

### III

Yet nowhere did esteem for this work shine forth more brightly than in our Gauls and in the neighboring provinces then subject to the Franks, as is clear from almost innumerable ancient monuments, a few of which we shall mention here.

At the Council of Mainz in the year 813, after the holy Gospel, the Epistles and Acts of the Apostles, and the canons, this book was brought forward so that the bishops might examine by what means they could, with God’s gracious assistance, establish and preserve the condition of God’s Church and the progress of the Christian people, secure in sound doctrine and examples of justice, as is read in the preface of that council.

At the Second Council of Rheims, held in the same year, canon 10:

> The statements of the *Pastoral Book* of blessed Gregory were read, so that the pastors of the Church might understand how they themselves ought to live and in what manner they ought to admonish those subject to them; for, as the same blessed Gregory testifies, prelates must be admonished in one way and subjects in another.

At the Third Council of Tours, held about the same time, canon 3 was promulgated:

> No bishop may be ignorant, if it can be avoided, of the canons or of the *Pastoral Book* by blessed Pope Gregory. In these each person ought continually to examine himself as in a mirror.

The first canon of the Second Council of Chalon decrees that bishops should understand the canons and the book of blessed Pope Gregory on pastoral care, and should both live and preach according to the rule established there.

Finally, at the Council of Aachen in the year 836, chapter 1, on the life of bishops, the same book is commended in canons 7, 9, and 10; and chapter 2, on the teaching of bishops, commends it in canons 3, 5, and 6.

To this may be added the testimony of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims (*Preface to Opusculum 55 of the Capitula*), from which we understand that it was then customary for a bishop who was to be ordained and consecrated to receive before the altar, together with the book of the sacred Canons, the *Pastoral Rule* of blessed Gregory in his hand, with this charge: that he should preserve it in living, teaching, and judging exactly as it was set forth there.

And so that the most perfect and refined rules for life proposed in this book might benefit more people among our Gauls, a French translation of it was recently published at Paris by André Pralard in 1694. If it had been based on handwritten codices rather than printed editions, it could rightly be called complete in every respect.

### IV

Before it was published, the holy Doctor labored long in bringing forth this most excellent work. Certainly he was already carrying it conceived in his mind when he was composing the thirtieth book of the *Moralia*, as becomes clear when one compares the subjects of the admonitions in the third part with chapter formerly 4, now number 13, of that book, where we read:

> Men must be admonished in one way, women in another. Young men in one way, old men in another, and so forth.

He concludes:

> Indeed, we ought subtly to have indicated what order of admonition belongs to each individual case; but we are hindered by fear of the length of our speech. Yet, with God as author, my mind desires to complete this in another work, if any time still remains to me in this laborious life.

### V

He happily fulfilled this intention at the very beginning of his pontifical office, in answer to John, bishop of Ravenna, who complained as a friend that Gregory had wished to escape the burdens of pastoral care by hiding himself. Such complaints are now rare, but once they were frequent, since almost all devout men, when called to pastoral office, pleaded against so great a burden out of lowliness of spirit and the greatest modesty.

For the same reason, another Gregory—much older and surnamed “the Theologian”—was compelled to answer his friends’ protests in his *Apologetic*, or first Oration, in which he explains the reasons for his flight in order to avoid the episcopate (Volume I). After rebuking the madness of those who seek the episcopate, he discusses the difficulties of pastoral office: in governing souls, in distributing and preaching the divine word, and in attaining Christian perfection.

> For it is the fault of a bishop, he says, not to be as good as possible.

This is truly an outstanding work, and one from which our Gregory may reasonably be judged to have drawn much, especially the statement:

> The art of arts and the science of sciences is the governance of a human being,

which is found in chapter 31 of Gregory Nazianzen’s *Apologetic* and in Part I, chapter 1, of the *Pastoral Rule*.

[Col. 0011]

John Chrysostom likewise wrote, on the same subject and on a similar occasion, six books *On the Priesthood*. Among the many outstanding works of the holy Doctor, Suidas rightly gives these the first place, because of both the sublimity and the clarity and elegance of their style.

But let us now return to the *Book of the Pastoral Rule* itself and show what we have accomplished in publishing it.

### VI

In most works composed by the holy Pontiff, the division into chapters and the headings of those chapters do not belong to him. But in this work they are recognized as his by both the division of the entire *Pastoral Book* into four parts and the division of the parts into various chapters, as well as by the titles prefixed to the individual chapters.

Our principal concern was to present a text purified from all errors and corruptions, whether those of antiquaries or of printers. We trust that this has been accomplished, at least for the greater part, with the aid of numerous and indeed excellent manuscripts.

The beautiful work had indeed been shamefully disfigured even in the latest printed editions, so that its meaning often either came to a halt, disappeared altogether, or—worse—was turned toward error. It is worthwhile to demonstrate this with a few examples, not to bring discredit upon other editors or win favor for ourselves, but to make the need for a more carefully corrected edition increasingly clear.

### VII

In Part III, chapter 1, admonition 22, column 1106 of Gussanville’s edition, one reads:

> Lest, when they neglect to bear the fruit of a good work, they be utterly dried up from the present life, as though by the dryness of the root;

where the sequence of the sentence and the manuscript books require us to read:

> As though they were cut off by the greenness of the root.

This agrees perfectly with what immediately precedes:

> Let them foresee the blow of the axe that is near;

and it undoubtedly refers to John’s rebuke quoted from Luke:

> The axe has already been laid to the root of the tree (Luke III).

In admonition 23, column 1108, the passage from Matthew is mutilated in this form:

> What do you think: that I have come to bring peace on earth? Certainly not, but a sword (Matthew X);

whereas the manuscripts read:

> Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace on earth—or, in the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.

In admonition 24, column 1110:

> Hence it is that the divine voice says to blessed Job concerning the vessels of that condemned one, namely, the preachers of Antichrist.

But the manuscripts have:

> Concerning the vessels of that condemned one, namely, Antichrist;

which agrees with Gregory’s meaning, since he customarily calls Antichrist the devil’s vessel. See *Moralia*, Book XXXII, number 22.

In admonition 36, column 1112:

> And differently [must those be admonished] who do good and conceal.

The meaning is lacking, but it is restored by supplying the word *which* and reading:

> Who conceal the good things which they do.

In chapter 2 of the same Part III, column 1139, what appears in our edition as chapter 63 reads:

> Good things must be preached in such a way that evil things may be commanded from the side;

where it should read:

> So that evil things may be assisted from the side,

as all the manuscripts have. The holy Doctor’s intention is evident from what immediately follows:

> Thus, he says, generosity in giving should be poured into the miserly, while the reins of extravagance should in no way be slackened for the prodigal.

Finally, in chapter 4, which is chapter 38 in our edition, column 1129:

> For by granting the small, he withdraws the sharper things, so that, since the mind would not rise at once to abandon all things, while it is familiarly left in something of its own, it might be tolerated without labor by something of its own.

If there is any meaning in these words, they sound exceedingly bad: namely, that the mind should be left in certain minor vices so that it may be tolerated and remain at rest in greater ones. Far be this from the mind of so great a Doctor. It should therefore be read from the manuscripts:

> For by granting the mild—or light—things, he withdrew the sharper ones; so that, since the mind would not rise at once to abandon all things, while it is familiarly left in some one of its own vices—or in one of its own vices—it might be lifted from one of its own vices without pain.

These readings are clear and sound.

### VIII

Because errors of this kind, and many more besides, disfigured the beautiful work, we applied every effort to gather a large collection of the older and better manuscripts against which the text could be compared and by whose aid it could easily be cleansed. Here is a list of them.

1. The ancient manuscript of Troyes, written in uncial and large capital letters, probably not long after the death of Saint Gregory. In this codex the sources from which the testimonies of Sacred Scripture are drawn are elegantly and accurately noted. When passages are cited according to the Septuagint, this is indicated. But this precious book was corrupted by some idle reader, especially in the biblical passages. It was nevertheless not difficult to determine what had been written before the corruption, and that is what we have followed. This very ancient codex was lent to us by the Reverend Fathers of the Oratory of Troyes, with the consent and support of the most reverend Father de la Tour, most worthy superior general of the Congregation of the Oratory.

2. The Corbie codex, marked 93, is more than eight hundred years old.

3. That of the Church of Chartres, of approximately the same antiquity.

4. That of Saint Peter of Chartres, scarcely less ancient.

5. Another of the same monastery, marked D, approximately six hundred years old.

6. That of Saint Peter of Beauvais. This codex was written while Hugh was governing the Church of Beauvais as bishop, in the middle of the tenth century or shortly thereafter, as we can infer from verses concerning the bishop’s recent death, written in the same hand at the end of the volume.

7. That of the Church of Laon.

8, 9, and 10. Three codices of Saint Peter of Jumièges, the oldest of which claims an age of seven hundred years.

11, 12, and 13. Three of Saint-Ouen of Rouen. The first is scarcely six hundred years old.

14. That of the primatial Church of Rouen, six hundred years old.

15. That of the monastery of Notre-Dame de Lyre.

16 and 17. Two codices of Saint-Thierry near Rheims, entirely agreeing with one another.

18. That of the Cistercian monastery of Vallis Clara.

19. That of the monastery of Longpont, of the same order.

20. Eight English codices, to be listed at number twenty: one from the public library at Oxford, another from Merton College, and the others from St John the Baptist’s College or from the library of Winchester Cathedral. On these, consult Thomas James in *Gregory Restored*.

21. We also consulted and used, for the more important passages, two codices of Saint-Germain, which we kept especially before our eyes while this excellent work was being sent to press.

We also used various editions, especially two Parisian editions, one of 1518 and another of 1571; the Roman or Vatican edition prepared by order of Pope Sixtus V; and others either nearly contemporary or more recent, especially the Paris edition of 1668, which came from the Leonardine press through the work of a Parisian theologian. We observed that the various readings collected by him with great care from older manuscripts almost everywhere agree with ours.

May God grant that, just as Gregory, by continually reading and consulting this book, governed the universal Church with such charity, piety, humility, gentleness, and diligence, so those who are placed over individual Churches may properly fulfill their pastoral office with his counsels and admonitions shining before them, and may govern others in such a way that they benefit both them and themselves.

[Col. 0013]

# The Book of the Pastoral Rule of Saint Gregory the Great, Roman Pontiff,

[**Note:** Thus the Corbie, Beauvais, and other ancient manuscripts. We preferred this title because it is read in Letter formerly 46, in another arrangement Book IV, now Book V, Letter 49: “the book of the Pastoral Rule which I wrote at the beginning of my episcopate.” In more recent manuscripts one reads, “the book of Pastoral Care,” and many printed editions agree with them. The title may perhaps have been suggested by the beginning of the book: “The burdens of pastoral care upon me,” and so forth. The title is absent from the Troyes manuscript.]

## Addressed to John, Bishop of the City of Ravenna

(C, S)

# Part One

[Col. 0013A]

## 1. To the most reverend and holy brother John, fellow bishop, Gregory

[**Note:** The third Jumièges manuscript adds: “greetings.”]

You reproach me, dearest brother, with kindly and humble intent, because I wished to avoid the burdens of pastoral care by concealing myself. Since these burdens might appear light to some, I set down in the style of this book all that I consider concerning their weight, so that one who is free from them may not carelessly seek them, and one who has carelessly sought them may fear that he has obtained them.

[**Note:** This persuaded the editors to divide the book into four parts, although there are no traces of this division in the ancient manuscripts. Yet Gregory, in Part III, chapter 26, admonition 27, refers to things already said by him in the first part: “as we have already said,” he says, “in the earlier part of this volume.” Hence it is not unreasonable to understand Gregory himself as the author of this division of the book. The division into four parts is found in the very ancient codices of Troyes, Beauvais, Jumièges, and Saint-Thierry.]

This book is divided into a fourfold discussion, so that it may advance toward the mind of its reader by orderly arguments, as by certain steps. For when circumstances require it, one must carefully consider how anyone comes to the summit of government; and, having reached it properly, how he should live; and, living well, how he should teach; and, teaching rightly, with what careful reflection he should recognize his own weakness every day, lest humility avoid the office, life contradict the attainment, life be deprived of teaching, or presumption exalt teaching.

[**Note:** This was absent from Corbie, but was added by a later hand. The first Chartres manuscript likewise lacks “or life be deprived of teaching.” Troyes and the others preserve these words.]

[**Note:** Troyes, Beauvais, and two ancient Chartres manuscripts have “by connections.”]

### 2

Therefore, let fear first restrain desire; afterward, let life commend the office of teaching that is received without having been sought; and then it is necessary that the good of the shepherd, shown by living, be spread also by speaking.

[**Note:** Corbie reads “by seeing.”]

Finally, it remains that reflection upon one’s own weakness should humble every perfect work, lest the swelling of pride extinguish it before the eyes of the hidden Judge.

[**Note:** Laon and Troyes have “before the eyes of arbiters.”]

But since there are many like me in ignorance, who, because they do not know how to measure themselves, desire to teach what they have not learned; who judge the burden of teaching to be so much lighter because they do not know its greatness, let them be reproved from the very beginning of this book. Since the unlearned and rash desire to hold the citadel of teaching, let them be driven back from the audacity of their rashness at the very gate of our discourse.

# Chapter One

[**Note:** This heading is found in the index of the Troyes codex, but it is not prefixed to the first chapter, which begins simply: “No art …” The first line is written in red. In the margin it is marked 1, and the remaining chapters are marked 2, 3, 4, and so forth. In this respect the Jumièges manuscripts agree with this one.]

## Those who are inexperienced should not dare to undertake the office of teaching

No art is presumed to be taught unless it is first learned through attentive reflection.

[**Note:** Corbie, Laon, and Longpont read: “Therefore pastoral office is received by inexperienced shepherds with great rashness, since the governance of souls is the art of arts.”]

With what rashness, then, is pastoral teaching undertaken by the inexperienced, when the governance of souls is the art of arts? Who does not know that the wounds of thoughts are more hidden than wounds of the body’s inner organs? And yet those who have never learned spiritual precepts do not fear to proclaim themselves physicians of the heart, while those who do not know the power of medicines are ashamed to appear physicians of the flesh.

But because, by God’s providence, every position of honor in the present age now bows before the reverence of religion, there are some who, within the holy Church, seek the glory of honor under the appearance of rule. They desire to appear teachers, long to surpass others, and, as Truth itself testifies, seek the first greetings in the marketplace, the first couches at banquets, and the first seats in assemblies (Matthew XXIII, 6–7).

The more they have reached the office of pastoral care through sheer pride, the less able they are to administer it worthily. For the tongue itself is confounded in teaching when one thing is learned and another taught.

Against such men the Lord complains through the prophet, saying:

> They have reigned, but not from me; they have become princes, and I did not know it (Hosea VIII, 4).

Those who are supported by no virtues and have not been divinely called, but are inflamed by their own desire, reign from themselves and not by the will of the supreme Ruler; they seize the summit of government rather than attain it.

Yet the inner Judge both raises them up and does not know them, because those whom he tolerates by permitting them he certainly does not know through the judgment of rejection. Hence he says even to certain people who come to him after performing miracles:

> Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are (Luke XIII, 27).

The inexperience of shepherds is rebuked by the voice of Truth when it is said through the Prophet:

> The shepherds themselves did not know understanding (Isaiah LVI, 11).

Again the Lord detests them, saying:

> Those who hold the law did not know me (Jeremiah II, 8).

Thus Truth complains that it is not known by them, and declares that it does not know the rule of those who do not know. For those who do not know the things that belong to the Lord are not known by the Lord, as Paul testifies when he says:

> But if anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored (1 Corinthians XIV, 38).

This inexperience of shepherds often corresponds to the merits of those subject to them. For although they do not possess the light of knowledge because their own fault demands its removal, strict judgment nevertheless brings it about that, through their ignorance, even those who follow them stumble.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit (Matthew XV, 14).

Hence the Psalmist, not with the spirit of one who wishes evil, but in the ministry of prophecy, announces:

[**Note:** The first two Jumièges manuscripts, the second Saint-Ouen manuscript, Lyre, and Rouen read “in mystery.”]

> Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and continually bend their backs (Psalm LXVIII, 24).

The eyes are those who, placed at the very face of supreme honor, have undertaken the duty of providing a path; those who cling to them from behind are called their backs. When the eyes are darkened, therefore, the back is bent, because when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are inevitably bent beneath the burdens of sins.

# Chapter II

## Those who do not perfect in living what they have learned through reflection should not assume the office of government

[Col. 0015C]

There are some who diligently investigate spiritual precepts, but trample in their lives what they penetrate by understanding. Suddenly they teach what they have learned not through practice but through reflection, and oppose by their conduct what they preach in words.

[**Note:** The third Chartres manuscript, Rouen, the second Audomarus manuscript, Lyra, Longpont, and Vallis Clara read “by reading.” The error may perhaps have entered through the writing practice of the ancients, who used *understanding*, as in Troyes.]

The result is that when the shepherd walks over precipices, the flock follows toward the abyss. Hence the Lord complains through the prophet against the contemptible knowledge of shepherds, saying:

> While you drank the clearest water, you disturbed the rest with your feet; and my sheep ate what had been trampled by your feet, and they drank what your feet had disturbed (Ezekiel XXXIV, 18–19).

Shepherds drink the clearest water when they rightly understand and draw in the streams of truth. But to disturb that same water with their feet is to corrupt the pursuits of holy meditation by evil living.

Sheep drink their water disturbed by the shepherds’ feet when those subject to them do not follow the words they hear, but imitate only the examples of depravity that they see.

[**Note:** Corbie has “the works they observe.”]

When they thirst for the words but are perverted by the works, they take mud in their drink as though from polluted springs.

Again it is written through the prophet:

> Evil priests are a snare causing the ruin of my people (Hosea V, 1; IX, 8).

Again the Lord says through the prophet concerning priests:

> They became a stumbling-block of iniquity to the house of Israel.

No one (Distinction 83, chapter *Nemo quippe*) harms the Church more than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares to rebuke this delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when a sinner is honored because of the reverence due to his rank.

Those who are unworthy would flee the burden of so great a guilt if they carefully listened with the ear of the heart to the sentence of Truth:

> Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be plunged into the depths of the sea (Matthew XVIII, 6).

[**Note:** Most Norman manuscripts have: “it would have been better for him.”]

The millstone expresses the circuit and labor of secular life, while the depths of the sea signify final damnation. Therefore, when one raised to the appearance of holiness destroys others either by word or by example, it would certainly have been better if earthly actions, under an external appearance, had bound him to death, than that sacred offices should display him to others as an example to imitate in guilt.

For if he alone had fallen, the punishment of hell would in some way have tormented him more tolerably.

# Chapter III

## On the burden of government; and that every adversity should be despised and prosperity feared

We have said these things briefly in order to show how great is the burden of government, so that no one unequal to it may dare to profane sacred authority and, through desire for high office, undertake the leadership of perdition.

Hence James piously forbids this, saying:

> Do not become many teachers, my brothers (James III, 1).

Hence the Mediator of God and human beings himself avoided receiving a kingdom on earth, although he reigns in heaven before the ages, surpassing even the knowledge and understanding of the heavenly spirits.

For it is written:

> When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come and seize him to make him king, he fled again alone to the mountain (John VI, 15).

[**Note:** The first Saint-Ouen manuscript and three Jumièges manuscripts read: “They came to seize him and appoint him king for themselves; when Jesus learned this, he fled and hid himself again alone on the mountain.” Other Norman manuscripts read: “When Jesus learned this, he fled and hid himself.”]

Who could have ruled human beings with such innocence as the one who would rule those whom he himself had created?

But because he had come in the flesh not only to redeem us through his passion but also to teach us through his way of life, offering himself as an example to those who follow him, he did not wish to become king. Instead, he willingly approached the gallows of the cross. He fled the offered glory of high office and desired the punishment of a shameful death.

He did this so that his members might learn to flee the world’s favors, fear its terrors not at all, love adversity for the sake of truth, and avoid prosperity through fear. For prosperity often stains the heart through pride, while adversity cleanses it through pain.

In prosperity the mind raises itself; in adversity, even if it raises itself at times, it is cast down. In prosperity a person often forgets himself; in adversity he is recalled to the memory of himself, even unwillingly and under compulsion. In prosperity, past good deeds often perish; in adversity, even sins committed long ago are wiped away.

For commonly the heart is pressed under discipline by the instruction of adversity. But if it breaks through to the summit of government, it is immediately changed into exaltation by the habit of glory.

Thus Saul, who had first fled while considering himself unworthy, swelled with pride as soon as he took up the reins of the kingdom (1 Samuel X, 22; XV, 17, 30). Desiring to be honored before the people, and refusing to be publicly rebuked, he tore apart the very man who had anointed him for the kingdom (Acts XIII, 22).

[**Note:** This is found in almost all the manuscripts, “in the kingdom.” The printed editions have “as king.”]

Thus David, pleasing the judgment of his Maker in almost all his actions, as soon as he was relieved of the burden of oppression, broke out into the swelling of a wound (2 Samuel XI, 3 and following). In the death of a man he became cruelly harsh, although in his desire for a woman he had been weakly indulgent;

[**Note:** Almost all printed editions read “in the death of Uriah,” against the English manuscripts and ours.] and he who had previously known how to spare the wicked piously afterward learned to rush without restraint toward the death even of the good (ibid., 15).

Previously he had refused to strike the discovered persecutor; afterward, even at the cost of the army’s exhausting labor, he destroyed a devoted soldier.

His guilt would have dragged him far from the number of the elect had not scourges recalled him to forgiveness.

# Chapter IV

## That the occupation of government commonly dissipates the mind’s steadfastness
Often the responsibility of governance, once undertaken, cleaves the heart in different directions, and each person is found unequal to individual tasks while, with a confused mind, being divided among many. Hence a certain wise man prudently forbids this, saying: “My son, let not your activities be many” (Ecclus. 11:10), because the mind is by no means gathered fully into the purpose of any one undertaking when it is divided among various things.

[Note: Recent Vulgate editions read “admonet” (“he admonishes”), to which the manuscripts are opposed. Besides, it is Gregory’s customary practice to call the author of Ecclesiasticus “a certain wise man,” as is clear from Moral. VII, 45; XX, 51; XXVII, 53, and elsewhere. See also below, Part II, chapter 6. He similarly designates the writer of the Book of Wisdom throughout. See Moral. XIV, 26.]

When the mind is drawn outward by excessive concern, it is deprived of the firmness of inward fear. It becomes anxious in arranging external matters while ignorant only of itself; it knows how to think about many things without knowing itself. For when it entangles itself in external affairs more than necessary, it forgets, as though occupied along the road, where it was heading. Thus, estranged from the pursuit of self-examination, it does not even consider the losses it suffers and remains unaware of the extent of its offenses.

Hezekiah, for example, did not think he was sinning when he showed the chambers of spices to the foreigners who came to him (2 Kings 20:13); yet he incurred the judge’s anger, which was to fall upon his descendants, because he had judged that he might do this freely (Isa. 39:4).

[Col. 0017D]  
[Note: In the first Aud., “disputatione” (“by argument”).]

Often, when many resources are available and many things can be done—things at which subordinates may marvel because they have been accomplished—the mind exalts itself in thought and fully provokes the judge’s anger, although it does not break out externally through wicked deeds.

6 For there is one who judges within, and there is that which is judged within. When, therefore, we sin in the heart, what we do within ourselves is hidden from human beings; nevertheless, with the judge himself as witness, we sin.

For the king of Babylon did not become guilty of arrogance only when he reached the words of arrogance (Dan. 4:16 ff.). Indeed, although he had previously kept silent in his pride, he heard the sentence of condemnation through the prophetic mouth.

[Note: In Trecensis, the first Aud. and the first two Gemet. manuscripts: “the king of Babylon, by the success of his power,” with the other words omitted.]

He had already wiped away the guilt of the pride he had committed when he proclaimed to all the nations subject to him the almighty God whom he had discovered he had offended. But afterward, lifted up by the success of his power, while rejoicing that he had accomplished great things, he first preferred himself to all others in his thought, and then, still swollen with pride, said:

“Is this not great Babylon, which I have built as a royal dwelling by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Dan. 4:27).

[Note: Corb., “when he reached arrogance.”]

This utterance openly bore the vengeance of that anger which hidden arrogance had kindled.

[Note: Carnotensis I: “Yet he silently heard the words of his silent arrogance, because he immediately reproved them by striking him.” The reading of the second Carnot. and the third Aud. does not differ greatly.]

For the strict judge first saw invisibly what he afterward reproved publicly by striking him. Therefore he turned him into an irrational animal, separated him from human society, and joined him, with his mind changed, to the beasts of the field, so that by a strict and just judgment the man who had thought himself great beyond other human beings might lose even the status of being human.

In saying these things, we do not criticize authority; rather, we protect the weakness of that heart from the desire for authority, lest the imperfect dare to seize the summit of governance and those who stumble while standing on level ground place their foot on a precipice.

[Note: In Corb., “who stumble on level ground,” with “while standing” omitted. “While standing” is found in Trecensis.]

## CHAPTER V. On those who can benefit others by the example of their virtues at the summit of governance, but avoid it by pursuing their own peace

[Col. 0018C]

There are some who receive exceptional gifts of virtue and are exalted with great responsibilities for the training of others. They are pure through devotion to chastity, strong through the power of abstinence, filled with the nourishment of doctrine, humble through long endurance in patience, upright through the strength of authority, kind through the grace of compassion, and strict through the severity of justice.

If such people, when called, refuse to accept the summit of governance, they often deprive themselves of the very gifts that they received not for themselves alone but also for others. When they think only of their own gains and not those of others, they deprive themselves of the goods they desire to possess privately.

Therefore Truth says to the disciples: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matt. 5:14–15).

[Col. 0019A]

Likewise he says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21:15–17).

[Note: In most Norman manuscripts, “Peter, do you love me?”—a reading formerly found in Trecensis.]

When Peter immediately replied that he loved him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” If pastoral care is therefore the testimony of love, whoever, though endowed with virtues, refuses to feed God’s flock is shown not to love the chief Shepherd.

Paul says: “If Christ died for all, then all have died. And if he died for all, it follows that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and rose again” (2 Cor. 5:15).

[Note: The particle “if” is absent from Corb. III, Gemet. II, Aud. and Lyr.]

Moses commanded that the surviving brother should take as wife the wife of a brother who had died childless and raise children in his brother’s name (Deut. 25:5). If he should happen to refuse to take her, the woman was to spit in his face, his nearest relative was to remove one of his sandals, and his house was to be called “the house of the barefooted man.”

[Note: All the manuscripts require this reading, although the printed editions, with good sense, read “the house of the unshod man.”]

7 That dead brother is the one who, appearing after the glory of the resurrection, said: “Go and tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10). He died, as it were, without children, because the number of his elect had not yet been completed.

His surviving brother is commanded to take his wife because it is plainly fitting that responsibility for the holy Church should be imposed upon one who is able to govern it well. The woman spits in the face of the unwilling man because whoever does not care to benefit others through the gifts he has received is reproached by holy Church for those very gifts, and she casts saliva into his face, as it were.

His sandal is removed from one foot so that his house may be called the house of the barefooted man. For it is written: “With your feet shod in readiness for the gospel of peace” (Eph. 6:15). If, therefore, we care for the concerns of our neighbor as for our own, we protect both feet with sandals. But whoever, thinking of his own advantage, neglects the concerns of others loses, in disgrace, the sandal of one foot.

There are therefore some who, enriched with great gifts, as we have said, burn with zeal for contemplation alone. They avoid contributing to the benefit of their neighbors through preaching; they love the privacy of peace and seek the withdrawal of contemplation. If they are judged strictly, they are surely guilty in proportion to the extent to which they could have benefited others by coming into public life.

For with what state of mind does one who might shine for the benefit of his neighbors prefer his own withdrawal to the benefit of others, when the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father himself, in order to benefit many, went forth from the Father’s bosom into our public life?

## CHAPTER VI. That those who flee the burden of governance out of humility are truly humble when they do not resist divine judgments

[Col. 0019D]

There are some who withdraw solely out of humility, lest they be preferred to those to whom they consider themselves unequal. Their humility is certainly genuine before God—provided it is joined to the other virtues—when it is not obstinate in rejecting what they are commanded to undertake for the benefit of others.

For he is not truly humble who understands that the will of the heavenly summons requires him to preside, yet refuses to preside. Rather, subject to divine arrangements and free from the vice of obstinacy, when the summit of governance is commanded to him, if he has already been endowed with gifts by which he may benefit others, he ought both to flee it from his heart and to obey unwillingly.

[Note: Longip. reads “to benefit, and nevertheless to benefit.” This manuscript divides the chapters differently from the others, so that chapter 7 is attached to chapter 5.]

## CHAPTER VII. That some rightly desire the office of preaching, while others are rightly compelled and drawn into it

Although some rightly desire the office of preaching and others are rightly compelled and drawn into it, this becomes clear if we weigh the actions of two prophets. One of them offered himself willingly to be sent to preach, while the other refused with fear to proceed.

[Note: Rothomag. and Aud. I read “of whom nevertheless.”]

Isaiah, when the Lord asked whom he should send, offered himself without hesitation, saying: “Here am I; send me” (Isa. 6:8). Jeremiah, however, was sent, yet humbly resisted lest he be sent, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jer. 1:6).

Externally, a different utterance came from each of them, but it did not flow from a different source of love. There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Isaiah, therefore, desiring through the active life to benefit his neighbors, seeks the office of preaching. Jeremiah, desiring through the contemplative life to cling diligently to love of the Creator, objects lest he be sent to preach.

What one laudably desired, the other laudably feared: the latter lest he should lose the gains of silent contemplation by speaking, the former lest he should suffer the losses of diligent work by remaining silent.

But in both cases something must be observed with subtle care: the one who refused did not resist completely, and the one who wished to be sent first saw himself cleansed by the coal from the altar.

[Note: Gemet., Aud. II, Lyr. III, Carnot. and Longip. read “sacred mysteries.”]

Thus no one should dare approach sacred ministry without purification, nor should anyone whom heavenly grace has chosen proudly contradict it under the appearance of humility. Since it is extremely difficult for anyone to know that he has been purified, the office of preaching is more safely avoided. Yet, as we have said, it must not be avoided obstinately when heavenly will is recognized as calling one to undertake it.

Moses fulfilled both requirements in a remarkable way: he neither wished to preside over so great a multitude nor refused to obey. He would perhaps have been proud if he had accepted the leadership of an innumerable people without trembling; but he would again have been proud if he had refused to obey the Creator’s command.

In both respects, therefore, he was humble and subject: measuring himself, he did not wish to preside over peoples; yet, relying upon the strength of the one who commanded, he consented.

Let all rash persons learn from this how great their guilt is when, out of personal ambition, they do not fear being preferred to others, if holy men feared to undertake leadership of peoples even when God commanded it. Moses trembles when the Lord urges him, while the weak person pants to receive the burden of honor. One who is already driven toward ruin by what is his own willingly offers his shoulders to be crushed by burdens that belong to others: he cannot bear what he has undertaken, and he increases what he must carry.

## CHAPTER VIII. On those who desire to preside and seize the Apostle’s words as an instrument for their own desire

Often those who desire to preside seize the Apostle’s words as an instrument for their own desire, where he says: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). Yet, while praising the desire, he immediately turns what he has praised into fear when he adds: “Now a bishop must be blameless” (ibid., 3:2).

[Note: Aud. II substitutes “rule” for “desire.”]

As he subsequently enumerates the virtues that are necessary, he makes clear what blamelessness itself is. Thus he encourages through desire and terrifies through command, as though he were openly saying: “I praise what you seek, but first learn what you are seeking, lest, by neglecting to measure yourselves, your blameworthiness appear all the more disgraceful because it hastens to be seen by everyone at the summit of honor.”

9 The great master of governance drives his hearers forward by encouragement and draws them back by fear, so that, by describing the summit of blamelessness, he may restrain them from pride and, by praising the office that is sought, shape them for a life of virtue.

[Note: Corb., Bellov. and Carnot. II read “by strictness”; others, especially Trecensis, “by describing.”]

It should also be noted that this was said at a time when whoever presided over a people was led first to the torments of martyrdom. It was therefore praiseworthy to seek the episcopate when it was beyond doubt that through it one would reach more severe punishments.

Hence the episcopal office itself is defined by the expression “good work,” when it is said: “If anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). He is therefore his own witness that he does not desire the episcopate if he seeks through it not the ministry of good work but the glory of honor.

He does not truly love the sacred office at all—and does not even know it—if, panting for the summit of governance, he feeds in the hidden meditation of his thoughts upon the submission of others, rejoices in his own praise, lifts his heart toward honor, and exults in an abundance of worldly possessions. Thus he seeks worldly gain under the appearance of an honor through which the gains of the world ought to have been destroyed. When the mind takes hold of the summit of humility in order to turn it toward exaltation, it inwardly changes what it outwardly desires.

## CHAPTER IX. That the mind of those who wish to preside often flatters itself with a fabricated promise of good works

[Col. 0021D]

Often those who desire to undertake pastoral leadership also propose certain good works to themselves.

[Note: Carnot. II reads “to undertake,” and Aud. II “temporal” for “pastoral.”] Although they desire it with an intention of pride, they nevertheless consider themselves about to perform great deeds.

[Note: Carnot. I reads “they propose.”]

Thus one intention suppresses another in the depths, while the surface of thought displays something else to the mind that is considering the matter.

[Note: Aud. I reads “in the depths.”]

The mind often lies to itself about itself. It pretends to love, on account of a good work, what it does not love, and not to love, on account of worldly glory, what it does love. Desiring to rule, it becomes fearful while seeking it, but bold once it has attained it.

[Note: This is the reading of Corb. and other Gallic, English, Norman, and other manuscripts. The Trecensis manuscript is mutilated here and continues only at chapter 15, “let the ruler be discerning in silence,” etc. The printed editions have “Timene enim,” an obvious error not corrected in any of the Vulgate editions.]

While striving toward it, a person fears that he may not attain it; but, suddenly attaining it, he thinks that he has a rightful claim to what he has reached. Once he begins to enjoy the office of the authority he has received in a worldly fashion, he readily forgets whatever he had considered religiously.

Therefore, when thought is carried beyond practical use, the mind’s eye must immediately be recalled to past actions. Let each person weigh what he did when subordinate, and he will suddenly recognize whether, as a superior, he can do the good things he had proposed. For no one can learn humility at the summit who, placed below, did not cease to be proud. He does not know how to flee praise when it is available who learned to pant after it when it was absent. Nor can he conquer avarice when he is directed toward supporting many, if his possessions were not sufficient even for himself alone.

Let each person therefore discover himself from his former life, lest the image of his thoughts deceive him in his desire for the summit.

Yet often, in the occupation of governance, even the practice of good work that was maintained in tranquility is lost.

[Note: Aud. I reads “in himself also.”] In calm seas even an inexperienced man properly steers a ship; but when it is disturbed by the waves of a storm, even a skilled sailor becomes confused.

[Note: Corb. and Carnot. I read “disturbed”; the earlier manuscript, with Aud. I, reads “when disturbed.”]

10 For what is the power of the summit except a storm of the mind? In it, the ship of the heart is always shaken by the tempests of thoughts and driven incessantly this way and that, so that through sudden excesses of speech and action it is shattered, as though against opposing rocks.

Amid these things, what must be followed and held fast except this: let the person strong in virtues come to governance when compelled; let the person lacking in virtues not approach it even when compelled.

If the former resists completely, let him beware lest, binding the money he received in a handkerchief, he be judged for hiding it (Matt. 25:18). To bind money in a handkerchief is to hide received gifts in the inactivity of sluggish torpor.

The latter, however, when he desires governance, must beware lest, by the example of wicked conduct, he become an obstacle to those seeking entrance into the kingdom, after the manner of the Pharisees, who, according to the Teacher’s word, “neither enter themselves nor allow those who are entering to enter” (Matt. 23:13).

He must also consider that when an elected bishop assumes responsibility for a people, he approaches as a physician approaches a sick person.

[Note: Corb., Val. Cl., Theod., Carnot. II, Norm., Longip. and Laud. read “we follow the manuscripts,” not the printed editions, which have “when they undertake pastoral care.”]

If the diseases are still alive in his own conduct, with what presumption does he hasten to heal one who has been struck, when he carries a wound on his own face?

[Note: The printed editions read “in his own body,” against nearly all the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER X. What sort of person should come to governance

[Col. 0023A]

That person, then—he above all—must be drawn to governance as an example of living who, having died spiritually to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually; who has placed worldly prosperity beneath him; who fears no adversity; who desires only inward things.

In harmony with this intention, his body should neither resist entirely through weakness nor his spirit offer excessive resistance through contempt.

[Note: The editors, at least the more recent ones, preferred “obstinacy,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.]

He is not led to desire what belongs to others but gives away what belongs to himself.

[Note: Gemet., supported by Lyr. and Aud. II, reads “to seize what belongs to others.”]

Through the compassion of his heart he is quickly moved to forgive, yet, by never forgiving more than is proper, he does not bend from the fortress of uprightness. He commits no unlawful acts, but mourns as his own the acts committed by others. Out of heartfelt affection he sympathizes with another’s weakness, and he rejoices in the good of his neighbor as in his own advancement.

He so presents himself as worthy of imitation by others in everything he does that among them he has nothing for which even concerning past actions he need be ashamed.

He strives to live in such a way that he can irrigate the parched hearts of his neighbors with the streams of doctrine.

Through the practice and experience of prayer he has already learned that he can obtain from the Lord what he asks. To him, through the effects of his prayer, the saying is addressed almost personally: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isa. 58:9).

[Note: In many printed editions this marks the beginning of chapter 11. The manuscripts disagree.]

If someone should perhaps come to ask us to intercede for him with some powerful man who is angry with him but unknown to us, we immediately reply: “We cannot come to intercede, because we do not know him through familiarity.”

If, then, a human being is ashamed to act as intercessor with someone whom he scarcely knows, with what frame of mind does one seize the place of intercession with God on behalf of a people when he does not know, through the merit of his life, that he is familiar with God’s grace?

11 Or how can he ask forgiveness from God for others when he does not know whether God is pleased with him?

In this matter, something else must be feared even more anxiously: lest the one who is thought able to appease anger should himself, because of his own guilt, deserve to provoke it (Dist. 49, beginning and chapter 1). For we all clearly know that when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the angry person’s mind is provoked to worse things.

Therefore, whoever is still bound by earthly desires must beware lest, by aggravating the anger of the strict judge, he become an author of ruin to his subjects while delighting in the glory of his position.

## CHAPTER XI. What sort of person should not come to governance

[Note: In Longip. this chapter still belongs to chapter 7.]

Let each person therefore measure himself carefully, lest he dare assume a place of governance while a damnable vice still reigns within him, lest one whom his own crime corrupts desire to become an intercessor for the sins of others.

[Note: At these words chapter 11 begins in two Corb. manuscripts, the first Carnot. and three Gemet. manuscripts.]

For this reason the heavenly voice says to Moses concerning Aaron: “Speak to Aaron: None of your descendants throughout your generations who has a blemish shall offer the bread of his God, nor shall he approach his ministry” (Lev. 21:17).

It immediately adds: “If he is blind, or lame, or has a small or large and crooked nose, or a broken foot or hand, or is humpbacked, or bleary-eyed, or has a white spot in his eye, or a continual scab, or a skin disease on his body, or is burdened” (ibid., 18).

A blind person is one who does not know the light of heavenly contemplation. Oppressed by the darkness of the present life, he does not see the light to come because he does not love it, and he does not know where to direct the steps of his actions.

[Note: Aud. I reads “where to direct . . . to place”; Laud. reads “where to direct the step of the body.”]

For this reason Anna says in prophecy: “He will guard the feet of his holy ones, and the wicked will be silent in darkness” (1 Sam. 2:9).

A lame person is one who sees where he ought to go but, through weakness of mind, cannot perfectly keep to the way of life that he sees. Since his unstable habit is not raised to the state of virtue, his active steps do not effectively follow where his desire leans.

[Note: The printed editions read “while unstable habit,” against all the manuscripts.]

Hence Paul says: “Strengthen the drooping hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be turned aside but rather be healed” (Heb. 12:12–13).

A person with a small nose is one who is not capable of maintaining the measure of discernment. We distinguish odors and stinks through the nose. Properly, therefore, discernment is expressed by the nose, since through discernment we choose virtues and reject sins.

Hence it is said in praise of the bride: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song 7:4), because holy Church observes through discernment what kinds of temptations arise from individual causes and detects from above the wars of vices that are to come.

But there are some who, unwilling to be considered dull, often exercise themselves in certain investigations more than necessary and are deceived by excessive subtlety. Hence it is added here: “Or one who has a large and crooked nose.”

A large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment. When it grows beyond what is fitting, it itself confuses the uprightness of one’s action.

A person with a broken foot or hand is one who is entirely unable to travel along God’s way and is wholly deprived of and empty of good works. He does not retain these things even as a lame person does, with weakness, but is altogether alienated from them.

A humpbacked person is one whom the weight of earthly concern depresses, so that he never looks toward heavenly things but attends only to what is trodden underfoot in the lowest places. Even if he should sometimes hear something about the good of the heavenly homeland, he does not lift the face of his heart toward it, weighed down by the burden of perverse habit. He cannot raise the posture of his thoughts because earthly concern keeps him bent down through habitual preoccupation.

The Psalmist speaks of such people when he says: “I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly” (Ps. 38:8, according to the Septuagint).

[Note: Corb. omits “and humbled.”]

Truth itself also reproves their guilt, saying: “The seed that fell among thorns—these are those who have heard the word, but as they go on their way are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and they bear no fruit” (Luke 8:14).

A bleary-eyed person is one whose natural intelligence shines toward knowledge of the truth, but whose carnal actions obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are healthy, but the eyelids swell from the fluid that flows down; because they are repeatedly irritated by this discharge, the sharpness of the pupils is also impaired.

[Note: Here the manuscripts vary remarkably: Laud. reads “the weaknesses of the eyelid”; the first two Gemet. manuscripts, “the weakening eyelid”; Corb., Bellov., Carnot. II, and two Theod. manuscripts, “weakening eyelids”; Carnot. I and Aud. I, “eyelids causing weakness.”]

There are some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of a carnal life. They could see what is right with subtle intelligence, but they grow dim through the practice of wicked deeds. A bleary-eyed person, therefore, is one whose nature sharpens his understanding but whose corrupt way of life confuses it.

To such a person the angel rightly says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. 3:18). We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when we assist the sharpness of our understanding, through the medicine of good works, in recognizing the brightness of the true light.

A person has a white spot in his eye when he is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or justice. The pupil of the eye, being black, sees; when it suffers a white spot, it sees nothing. Thus, if the understanding of human thought recognizes itself as foolish and sinful, it grasps the knowledge of inward brightness. But if it attributes to itself the whiteness of justice or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of knowledge.

[Note: The Gemet. manuscripts read “of thought.”]

It penetrates the brightness of the true light no further precisely because it exalts itself before itself through arrogance. As it is said of certain people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:22).

A person has a continual scab when the wantonness of the flesh continually dominates him. In a scab, the heat of the inner organs is drawn toward the skin; lust is rightly signified by this, because if the temptation of the heart leaps into action, the inward heat bursts out as far as the scab of the skin. It already wounds the body externally, because when pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also dominates in action.

Paul sought, as it were, to wipe away the itching of the skin when he said: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13). He was saying openly, as it were: “Let temptation not seize you except as human; to suffer temptation in the heart is human, but to be overcome in the struggle with temptation and in action is demonic.”

Whoever is ravaged in mind by avarice also has a skin disease on his body. If avarice is not restrained in small matters, it surely spreads without measure. A skin disease occupies the body without pain and, growing without causing distress to its victim, disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So avarice, while seeming to delight the captive mind, wounds it; while presenting to thought whatever is to be acquired, it inflames the mind toward hostility. It causes no pain in the wound because it promises abundance to the mind that burns with desire.

Yet the beauty of the limbs is lost because through avarice the beauty of the other virtues is also corrupted. It irritates the whole body, as it were, because through every vice it undermines the mind, as Paul testifies when he says:

[Note: Laud. reads “wounds.”] “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10).

A burdened person is one who does not practice shameful conduct in action but is nevertheless weighed down in mind by continual thoughts of it without restraint. He is not dragged all the way to the wicked deed, but his mind delights in the pleasure of lust without any opposing goad of resistance.

[Note: The printed editions read “obstacle of resistance,” which is found in none of our manuscripts.]

The condition of being burdened is illustrated when the humor of the inner organs descends to the genitals, which swell with the discomfort of shameful arousal. A burdened person, therefore, is one who, flowing toward lust with all his thoughts, carries the weight of shame in his heart.

[Note: Carnot. I and Aud. I–II read “in the body.”]

Although he does not practice wicked things in action, he is not torn away from them in mind. Nor can he rise openly to the practice of good works, because the shameful weight hidden within him weighs him down.

Whoever is subjugated by any one of these vices is forbidden to offer bread to the Lord, since one who is still devastated by his own sins cannot cleanse the sins of others.

[Note: Carnot. I reads “is subjoined”; Bellov. and others, “is subjugated.”]

Since we have shown briefly who is worthy to come to pastoral leadership and how the unworthy person should fear it, let us now demonstrate how the person who has come to it worthily ought to live within it.

[Note: Here the chapter ends in Longip.]

## PART TWO. ON THE LIFE OF THE PASTOR

[Note: This title is not found in the ancient manuscripts, except perhaps as an addition by a later hand, as seems to be the case in Gemet. II. In the manuscripts, chapter 12 follows in an uninterrupted sequence. Longip. has only chapter 9. Since this heading agrees with the division proposed by the holy Doctor, as is clear from the preceding words with which chapter 11 ends, we have retained it.]

[Col. 0025]

## CHAPTER ONE [also XII]. How the person who has come rightly to governance ought to conduct himself in governance

[Col. 0025D]

The conduct of a ruler ought to surpass the conduct of the people by as much as the life of a shepherd ordinarily differs from that of the flock.

[Col. 0026D]

For he must diligently strive to measure the extent of the necessity that binds him to maintain uprightness, since under his judgment the people are called a flock.

He must therefore be pure in thought, outstanding in action, discerning in silence, useful in speech, near to each person through compassion, lifted above all others in contemplation, a companion through humility to those who act well, raised up against the vices of sinners by zeal for justice, not diminishing his care for inward things amid external occupation, nor abandoning his provision for external matters amid concern for inward things.

But these points, which we have briefly touched upon in enumeration, let us now discuss by repeating them at somewhat greater length.

## CHAPTER TWO [also XIII]. That the ruler should be pure in thought
## Chapter II [Alternatively XIII]. That the ruler should be pure in thought

The ruler should always be pure in thought, so that no impurity defiles him who has undertaken the office of wiping away stains of pollution even from the hearts of others. For the hand that undertakes to wash away filth must necessarily strive to be clean, lest whatever it touches be made dirtier if, while following the mud, it is itself filthy. [Note: [Col. 0027D] The Vatican manuscript, following the Paris 1518 edition, Gilot, and other editions, reads: “if a mind, filthy in itself.” The Angers manuscript and our manuscripts disagree.] [Note: [Col. 0027D] The second Chartres manuscript reads: “remains.”] [Col. 0027B] Hence it is said through the prophet: “Cleanse yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11). For they carry the Lord’s vessels who, in the faithfulness of their way of life, take upon themselves the souls of their neighbors, to lead them to the eternal sanctuaries. Let them therefore observe how much they must cleanse themselves, since they carry living vessels toward the temple of eternity in the bosom of their own commitment.

Hence, by the divine voice, it is prescribed (Exodus 28:15) that “the breastpiece of judgment” be fastened upon Aaron’s breast with binding cords, so that the priestly heart may in no way be possessed by wandering thoughts, but may be held together by reason alone. Nor should one who has been appointed as an example to others think anything indiscriminate or useless; rather, by the gravity of his life he should always show how much reason he carries in his breast. [Note: [Col. 0027D] In Corbie, “the breastpiece of judgment.”]

To this breastpiece it is also carefully added that the names of the twelve patriarchs be inscribed. To carry the fathers whose names have been written there always upon one’s breast is to contemplate without interruption the life of the ancients. For then the priest walks irreproachably when he continually looks upon the examples of the fathers who came before, when he unceasingly considers the footsteps of the saints, and suppresses illicit thoughts lest his foot in action extend beyond the boundary of his order. [Note: [Col. 0027D] In the first Anchin manuscript, “place.”]

This is rightly also called “the breastpiece of judgment,” because the ruler must always distinguish good from evil by a subtle examination, and diligently consider what is suitable, to whom, when, and in what manner. He must seek nothing for himself, but regard his own advantages as the goods of his neighbors.

Hence it is written there: “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth, which shall be upon Aaron’s breast when he enters before the Lord; and he shall carry the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast always in the sight of the Lord” (ibid., 30). For the priest to carry the judgment of the children of Israel upon his breast before the sight of the Lord is to examine the cases of his subjects solely with the intention of the inner Judge, so that no human consideration may mingle with what he administers in the place of God. Thus private grief must not embitter the zeal for correction. [Note: [Col. 0027D] In the first Chartres manuscript and the first Audomari manuscript, “zeal.”]

When he shows himself zealous against the vices of others, let him pursue what belongs to him, lest the tranquillity of judgment be stained by hidden envy or disturbed by rash anger. But since the terror of him who presides over all things—the inner Judge, that is—must be considered, subjects should not be governed without great fear. This fear, while it humbles the ruler’s mind, also purifies it, lest presumption lift it up, bodily pleasure defile it, or the importunity of earthly desire obscure it with the dust of polluted thought. [Note: [Col. 0027D] The manuscripts differ here. Corbie has “the desire of polluted, dusty thought.” The second Chartres manuscript has “the desire of polluted thought,” omitting “dusty.” The two earlier Gembloux manuscripts read: “desire obstructed by dusty thought.”]

Such thoughts cannot fail to knock at the ruler’s mind; but he must hasten to conquer them by resistance, lest the vice that attempts him through suggestion subdue him by the softness of delight. And when this is driven slowly from the mind, let the sword of consent slay it. [Note: [Col. 0028D] The first Chartres manuscript: “the malice of love.” The first Audomari manuscript: “the malice of delight.”] [Note: [Col. 0028D] The second Chartres manuscript and Beauvais: “I fear that consent may follow.”]

## Chapter III [Alternatively XIV]. That the ruler should always be preeminent in action

Let the ruler be distinguished in action, so that by living he may proclaim the way of life to his subjects, and the flock, which follows the shepherd’s voice and conduct, may proceed more effectively by examples than by words. For the one who is compelled by the necessity of his position to speak of the highest things is compelled by that same necessity to display the highest things. That voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more willingly which the speaker’s life commends, because what he commands by speaking, he assists by showing so that it may be done.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isaiah 40:9). Thus the one who employs heavenly preaching, having already abandoned the low things of earthly works, may be seen to stand upon the summit of things; and he may draw his subjects toward better things all the more easily because, through the merit of his life, he cries out from above. [Note: [Col. 0028D] The first Audomari manuscript: “of heavenly things.”]

Hence, in the divine law, the priest receives the right shoulder as a sacrifice, separately (Exodus 29:22), so that his action may be not only useful but also singular. He must not merely do what is right among the wicked; he must also surpass subjects who act well in the virtue of their conduct, just as he surpasses them in the honor of his office. [Note: [Col. 0028D] The second Audomari manuscript omits the word “of the office.”]

He is also given the breast with the shoulder as food, so that from what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice he may learn what to offer from himself to the Creator. And he should not merely think what is right in his breast; he should also invite those who observe him to the lofty instruments of action. [Note: [Col. 0028D] This passage is read without the word “breast” in the first Audomari manuscript and the first Chartres manuscript.]

He should desire none of the prosperity of the present life and fear none of its adversities. He should despise the world’s flatteries in view of the inner terror, and, considering the attraction of inner sweetness, disregard its terrors. Hence also, by the command of the heavenly voice (Exodus 29:5), the priest is bound at both shoulders with the covering of the ephod, so that he may always be fortified by the adornment of the virtues against adversity and prosperity. Thus, in accordance with Paul’s words (2 Corinthians 6:7), he proceeds by the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, and, while striving only for the things that are inward, he is not bent to either side by any low delight. [Note: [Col. 0029D] So Corbie, three Chartres manuscripts, Beauvais, the first Audomari manuscript, and three Gembloux manuscripts. The editions nevertheless read “the things that are before.”] [Note: [Col. 0029D] The first Chartres manuscript: “of love”; Corbie: “lest low delights bend him to either side.”]

Prosperity must not exalt him, adversity must not disturb him, pleasant things must not charm him into compliance, and harsh things must not press him into despair. Thus, while he does not lower the intention of his mind before any passions, he shows by how great a beauty of the ephod he is covered on both shoulders.

It is rightly also prescribed that the ephod be made of gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen (Exodus 28:8), so that the extent to which the priest ought to shine with a diversity of virtues might be demonstrated. In the priest’s vesture, gold shines above all, so that the understanding of wisdom may principally gleam in him. Hyacinth, which glows with an azure color, is added to it, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding, he may rise not toward lowly approval but toward love of heavenly things, lest, heedlessly captivated by his own praises, he be emptied even of his understanding of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0029D] In most manuscripts: “with gold also, and linen, and hyacinth.” “And linen” should be omitted, since linen is mentioned below.]

Purple is mingled with gold and hyacinth, so that the priestly heart, while hoping for the highest things that it preaches, may also restrain within itself the suggestions of vices and oppose them as though by royal authority. Thus it may always regard the nobility of its inner regeneration and defend for itself, by its conduct, the character of the heavenly kingdom.

Peter speaks of this nobility of the spirit: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). John’s voice also strengthens us concerning this power, because we subdue vices: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become the sons of God” (John 1:12). The Psalmist considers this dignity of strength when he says: “Your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored; their principality has been exceedingly strengthened” (Psalm 138:17). For the minds of the saints are raised principally to the highest things when they are seen outwardly to endure what is lowly.

To the gold, hyacinth, and purple, twice-dyed scarlet is added, so that all the good works of the virtues may be adorned before the eyes of the inner Judge, and everything that shines before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Arbiter by the flame of inner love. [Note: [Col. 0030D] The first Chartres manuscript, Laon, and Beauvais: “of the hidden Arbiter.”]

This love, because it loves God and neighbor simultaneously, shines as though from a double dye. Therefore, whoever longs so for the likeness of the Creator that he neglects the care of his neighbors, or carries out the care of his neighbors in such a way that he grows cold toward divine love, neglects one of these two things and does not know how to possess scarlet dyed twice in the adornment of the ephod.

But when the mind is directed toward the commandments of love, it remains undoubtedly necessary that the flesh be disciplined through abstinence. Hence twisted linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet. For linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance. And what is signified by linen except bodily chastity, glowing with the beauty of purity? It is twisted and fastened to the beauty of the ephod because chastity is led to the perfect brightness of purity when the flesh is wearied by abstinence. And when the merit of afflicted flesh also advances among the other virtues, twisted linen gleams as though in the varied beauty of the ephod.

## Chapter IV [Alternatively XV]. That the ruler should be discerning in silence and useful in speech

Let the ruler be discerning in silence and useful in speech, so that he neither utter what ought to be withheld nor withhold what ought to be uttered (Distinction 43, “Let the ruler”). For just as careless speech leads into error, so indiscreet silence leaves in error those who could have been instructed.

Often imprudent rulers, fearing the loss of human favor, dread speaking freely what is right. In accordance with the voice of Truth (John 10:12), they no longer serve the guarding of the flock with the care of shepherds, but act as hirelings, because when the wolf comes they flee by hiding themselves in silence. Hence the Lord rebukes them through the prophet, saying: “Mute dogs that are unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10). Again he complains, saying: “You have not gone up to oppose them, nor set yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5).

To go up in opposition is to confront the powers of this world with a free voice in defense of the flock. To stand in battle on the day of the Lord is to resist those who fight wickedly, out of love for righteousness. For what else is it for a shepherd to fear speaking what is right than to offer his back by keeping silent? When he places himself before the flock, he sets a wall against the enemies for the house of Israel.

Again it is said to the sinful people: “Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not reveal your iniquity, to provoke you to repentance” (Lamentations 2:14). [Note: [Col. 0030D] The first Chartres and first Audomari manuscripts read: “they reproved.”] In sacred discourse, prophets are sometimes called teachers, because, by showing that present things are fleeting, they reveal what is to come. Divine speech rebukes them for seeing false things, because, while they fear reproving faults, they flatter sinners with a false security. They do not reveal the iniquity of sinners because they fall silent instead of speaking words of rebuke.

The word of correction is the key of opening, because by rebuking it exposes a fault that often remains unknown even to the one who committed it. [Note: [Col. 0030D] Three Gembloux manuscripts, the second and third Audomari manuscripts, Lyré, and Corbie read: “rebuke.”] Hence Paul says: “So that he may be able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9). Hence it is said through Malachi: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).
