Hence through Isaiah the Lord admonishes, saying: “Cry out; do not cease; lift up your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1).

Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, so that, before the Judge who follows in terror, he himself may go forward crying out. If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice of proclamation will a mute herald give? Hence the Holy Spirit settled upon the first shepherds in the form of tongues (Acts 2:3), because those whom he fills he immediately makes speak about him.

Hence Moses is commanded that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he be surrounded by bells (Exodus 28:33), so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Observer through silence. For it is written: “So that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary in the sight of the Lord, and he may not die” (ibid., 35). The priest entering or leaving dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge if he walks without the sound of preaching.

The bells are appropriately described as inserted into his garments. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than right actions? The prophet bears witness, saying: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 132:9). Thus bells cling to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may cry out, together with the sound of his tongue, the way of life.

But when the ruler prepares himself to speak, let him consider with how much caution he should speak, lest, if he is carried away disorderly into speech, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error, and, when he perhaps desires to seem wise, he foolishly sever the bond of unity. Hence Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Salt signifies the wisdom of speech. [Note: [Col. 0031D] Laon reads: “the word of wisdom.”] Therefore, whoever strives to speak wisely must greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be disrupted by his eloquence.

Hence Paul says: “Do not be wiser than you ought to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Romans 12:3). Hence, in the priest’s vesture, according to the divine word, pomegranates are joined to the bells (Exodus 28:34). For what is signified by pomegranates except the unity of faith? Just as, within a single external rind, many seeds are protected inside a pomegranate, so the unity of faith covers the innumerable peoples of the holy Church, whom diversity of merits holds within.

Therefore, lest the ruler rush heedlessly into speech, Truth itself cries out to the disciples in the words already mentioned: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). It is as though he said figuratively through the priest’s vesture: “Join pomegranates to the bells, so that in everything you say you may preserve the unity of faith with careful observance.” [Note: [Col. 0031D] Three Gembloux manuscripts, the first and second Chartres manuscripts, and Beauvais read: “under one … rind.” Lyré reads: “all.”]

The rulers must also carefully and attentively ensure that not only do they never utter anything wicked, but that they do not even utter what is right excessively or disorderly. For often the power of what is said is lost when it is worn smooth against the hearts of hearers by the careless intrusiveness of loquacity; and this same loquacity pollutes its author because it does not know how to serve hearers for their improvement.

Hence it is rightly said through Moses: “A man who suffers a discharge of semen shall be unclean” (Leviticus 15:2). In the minds of hearers, the seed of subsequent thought is the quality of the speech heard, because when speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind. Hence the outstanding preacher was called “a seed-sower of words” by the wise men of this world (Acts 17:18).

Thus the one who suffers a discharge of semen is declared unclean, because a person subject to excessive speech pollutes himself with what, if he brought it forth in an orderly manner, could produce offspring of right thought in the hearts of his hearers. But when he flows out carelessly through loquacity, he pours forth seed not for the use of generation but for uncleanness.

Hence Paul, when admonishing his disciple about the urgency of preaching, says: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, by his coming and his kingdom: preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:1). Before saying “out of season,” he placed “in season,” because, plainly, his own speech destroys itself in the mind of the hearer by its very worthlessness if its untimeliness does not know how to find an appropriate occasion. [Note: [Col. 0031D] Three Gembloux manuscripts, the third Chartres manuscript, Val-Dieu, the second Audomari manuscript, and Lyré: “subtlety.” But two Theodulf manuscripts, Laon, and others have “usefulness.”]

## Chapter V [Alternatively XVI]. That the ruler should be near to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation

Let the ruler be near to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation, so that through the inward organs of pity he may transfer the weakness of others into himself, and through the height of contemplation may transcend even himself by seeking invisible things. Let him not despise the weakness of his neighbors while seeking lofty things, nor, while accommodating himself to the weakness of his neighbors, abandon the pursuit of lofty things (2 Corinthians 12:3).

Hence Paul is taken up into paradise and examines the secrets of the third heaven; yet, suspended in that contemplation of invisible things, he turns the gaze of his mind back to the bed of the carnal and regulates how they should conduct themselves in their hidden affairs, saying: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:2). A little later he says: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you” (ibid., 5).

Behold, he is already admitted to heavenly secrets, yet through the inward organs of condescension he searches the bed of the carnal. Though lifted up to invisible things, he mercifully directs the eye of his heart toward the hidden matters of the weak. [Note: [Col. 0032D] Longpont and most manuscripts read: “mercifully.”] He transcends heaven through contemplation, yet does not abandon the bed of the carnal through concern, because, joined by the bond of love to the highest and the lowest alike, he is powerfully snatched upward in himself by the strength of the spirit, and is made weak with equanimity in others. [Note: [Col. 0032D] The Troyes, Corbie, Norman, Beauvais, Laon, and other manuscripts support this wording; all editors, departing far from them, print “the state of the carnal.”]

Hence he says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). Again he says: “I became to the Jews as a Jew” (1 Corinthians 9:20). He did this without abandoning the faith but by extending compassion, transforming the person of unbelievers into himself so that from his own experience he might learn how he ought to have mercy on others, and might offer them what he would rightly have wished to receive himself, had he been in their condition. [Note: [Col. 0033D] We follow Troyes, Laon, the Gembloux manuscripts, and the two Chartres manuscripts. The first Chartres manuscript and the first Audomari manuscript have “but by desiring.” The printed editions disagree, reading “but by showing.”]

Again he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5:13), because he knew both how to transcend himself in contemplation and how to temper that same self for his hearers by condescension.

Hence Jacob saw angels ascending and descending, with the Lord resting above and the stone anointed below (Genesis 28:12). For truly upright preachers not only seek upward, by contemplation, the holy Head of the Church, namely the Lord; they also descend downward in compassion toward his members.

Hence Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle. The one who is carried away into contemplation within is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; outside, he carries the burdens of the carnal. When he is uncertain about matters, he always returns to the tabernacle and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant. He thus undoubtedly provides an example for rulers: when they are uncertain outside about what they should decide, they should always return to the mind as though to a tabernacle; and, as though before the ark of the covenant, they should consult the Lord, seeking within themselves the pages of sacred Scripture concerning the matters about which they are uncertain.

Hence Truth himself, revealed to us through the assumption of our humanity, remains devoted to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles in the cities (Luke 6:12). He thereby lays out the way of imitation for good rulers, so that, although they seek the highest things through contemplation, they may nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion. For love rises wonderfully to the heights when it mercifully draws itself down toward the lowly of its neighbors; and to the extent that it kindly descends to the weak, it returns forcefully to the highest things.

Let those who preside present themselves as such, so that their subjects are not ashamed to disclose even their hidden matters to them. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Laon reads: “all their hidden matters.”] Thus, when the little ones endure the waves of temptations, they may return to the shepherd’s mind as to a mother’s breast; and what they foresee will be defiled by the filth of the fault that assails them, they may wash away through the consolation of his exhortation and the tears of prayer.

Hence, before the doors of the temple, twelve oxen carry the bronze sea—that is, the basin—for washing the hands of those who enter (1 Kings 7:23 ff.). Their faces project outward, but what lies behind them is hidden. What is signified by the twelve oxen except the entire order of shepherds? Concerning them, as Paul explains, the law says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (1 Corinthians 9:9; from Deuteronomy 25:4).

We see their outward works clearly, but we do not know what awaits them afterward, in hidden recompense, before the strict Judge. Yet when they prepare the patience of their condescension for washing away the confessions of their neighbors, they carry the basin as though before the doors of the temple, so that whoever strives to enter the gate of eternity may disclose his temptations to the shepherd’s mind and wash the hands of thought or action, as it were, in the basin of the oxen.

It often happens, however, that while the ruler’s spirit learns about the temptations of others by condescending to them, he himself is also assailed when he hears of their temptations, because the same water of the basin by which the multitude of the people is washed is undoubtedly defiled. For while it receives the filth of those being washed, it seems to lose the serenity of its own purity.

But the shepherd must not fear this, because, with God weighing all things subtly, he is freed from his own temptation all the more easily the more mercifully he is wearied by the temptation of another.

## Chapter VI [Alternatively XVII]. That the ruler should be the companion of those who act well through humility and stand upright against the vices of those who offend through zeal for justice

Let the ruler be the companion of those who act well through humility and stand upright against the vices of those who offend through zeal for justice, so that he does not place himself above the good in any respect, yet, when the fault of the wicked demands it, immediately recognizes the authority of his precedence. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Troyes and most manuscripts read thus; the first Chartres and first Audomari manuscripts read: “the authority of his primacy.”] Thus, while suppressing his honor, he should regard himself as equal to subjects who live well, and should not fear to exercise the rights of rectitude against the perverse.

For, as I remember saying in the books of the *Moralia* (Book XXI, chapter 10, now no. 22), it is clear that nature brought forth all human beings equal, but that, through the varying order of merits, guilt places some below others. The very inequality that arose from vice is dispensed by divine judgment, so that, because every human being cannot stand equally, one is governed by another.

Therefore, all who preside should consider not the power of rank in themselves but the equality of their condition; nor should they rejoice that they preside over human beings, but that they are of benefit to them. [Note: [Col. 0034D] This appears to have been drawn from chapter 64 of the Rule of St Benedict, where it reads: “and let the abbot know that he ought rather to be of benefit than to preside.” This is unsurprising, since Gregory had been accustomed to the observance of that Rule.] For our ancient fathers are remembered as having been shepherds not of human beings but of flocks. And when the Lord said to Noah and his sons, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 9:21, as printed), he immediately added: “And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth.” Since their terror and dread are commanded to be over the animals of the earth, it is plainly forbidden that they be over human beings.

Human beings are naturally superior to brute animals, but not to other human beings. Therefore, it is said that human beings should be feared by animals and not by other human beings, because it is contrary to nature to be proud and desire to be feared by an equal.

Nevertheless, rulers must be feared by their subjects when they discover that their subjects scarcely fear God, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may at least fear to sin because of human fear. Superiors do not become proud through the fear they seek in this way, since they seek not their own glory but the justice of their subjects. In demanding fear from those who live perversely, they dominate not human beings but, as it were, animals, because to the extent that their subjects are beastlike, to that extent they should also lie subject to fear. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Three Gembloux manuscripts: “to strength.”]

But often the ruler swells with pride of thought precisely because he surpasses others. While everything lies subject to his use, while commands are swiftly fulfilled at his desire, while all his subjects raise to the skies whatever has been done well but oppose nothing that has been done badly with any authority, and while they often praise even what they ought to condemn, his mind, seduced by the things available below, is lifted above itself. While he is surrounded outwardly by immense favor, inwardly he is emptied of truth. Forgetful of himself, he pours himself out into the voices of others and believes himself to be what he hears outwardly, not what he ought to discern inwardly.

He despises his subjects and does not recognize them as his equals by the order of nature. Those whom he has surpassed by the lot of power, he believes he has also surpassed in the merits of life. He judges himself wiser than all those over whom he sees himself to have greater power. He sets himself upon a certain height in his own estimation; and although he is bound by the same natural condition as the rest, he scorns to regard others as equals. Thus he is led toward the likeness of the one of whom it is written: “He sees every high thing; he is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25).

Desiring a singular summit and despising the communal life of the angels, he says: “I will set my throne toward the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13). Thus, by a marvelous judgment, he finds inwardly a pit of humiliation while exalting himself outwardly on the summit of power. He becomes like the apostate angel when, as a human being, he scorns to be like other human beings.

Thus Saul, after the merit of humility, grew through the summit of power into a swelling of pride: through humility he was raised up, through pride he was rejected. The Lord bears witness to this, saying: “Were you not little in your own eyes when I made you head over the tribes of Israel?” (1 Samuel 15:17). At first he had seen himself as little in his own eyes; but, supported by temporal power, he no longer saw himself as little. Preferring himself to others because he had greater power than all, he considered himself greater than everyone.

In a marvelous way, when he was little in his own estimation, he was great before God; but when he appeared great in his own estimation, he was little before God. Often, when the mind is inflated by the abundance of its subjects, it is corrupted into a flood of pride, with the very height of power acting as its seductress. [Note: [Col. 0035D] Troyes, Chartres, Gembloux, Laon, Val-Dieu, and others, as well as the old Gilot edition and recent editions, read: “into a flood.”] One governs this power well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows how to rise above faults through it and how to join himself to others in equality through it. For the human mind often becomes exalted even when supported by no power; how much more does it raise itself up when power is also joined to it?

That power is rightly administered by one who carefully knows how to take from it what helps, to overcome what tempts, to see himself as equal to others despite possessing it, and nevertheless to place himself above sinners through zeal for punishment.

We recognize this discernment more fully if we observe the examples of the first shepherd. Peter, holding the primacy of the holy Church by God’s authority, refused to be excessively venerated by Cornelius, who humbly prostrated himself before him, and recognized himself as Cornelius’s equal, saying: “Rise; do not do this. I myself am also a human being” (Acts 10:26).

But when he discovered the fault of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:5), he immediately showed how greatly he had grown in power over the others. By his word he struck down their life, which he had detected by searching with the spirit; and he recalled that he was supreme within the Church against sins, a fact that he had not acknowledged before brothers who were acting well, despite the great honor shown to him. There, the holiness of conduct merited the fellowship of equality; here, zeal for punishment disclosed the right of authority. [Note: [Col. 0036D] The first Audomari manuscript: “rebuked.”]

Paul did not know himself to be placed above brothers who acted well when he said: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are helpers of your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:23, as printed). He immediately added: “For you stand by faith.” As though explaining what he had said, he continued: “For this reason we do not lord it over your faith, because you stand by faith; we are equal to you in that in which we recognize that you stand.”

He likewise did not know himself to be placed above his brothers when he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7). [Note: [Col. 0036D] Three Gembloux manuscripts: “like little ones.”] Again he says: “But we are your servants through Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5). But when he found a fault that ought to be corrected, he immediately recalled that he was a teacher, saying: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4:21).

The highest office is rightly governed when the one who presides rules over vices rather than over the brethren. But when superiors correct delinquent subjects, it remains necessary that they carefully attend to this: while by the authority of their office they justly strike faults as discipline requires [Note: [Col. 0036D] The first two Gemetensis manuscripts read *meritum*, “merit,”], they should recognize, by guarding humility, that they are equals of the very brethren whom they correct—although it is often also fitting that, in silent thought, we should place above ourselves those whom we correct. For their vices are struck through us with the force of discipline, whereas in the matters we ourselves commit, we are not wounded by so much as a word of rebuke from anyone. We are therefore all the more bound before the Lord, the more freely we sin before human beings without punishment. [Col. 0036D] Yet our discipline makes our subjects all the freer before divine judgment, inasmuch as here it does not leave their faults unpunished.

Humility must therefore be preserved in the heart, and discipline in action. Amid these things one must carefully watch lest, while the virtue of humility is guarded beyond measure, the rights of governance be dissolved; and lest, while each superior humbles himself more than is fitting, he become unable to restrain the lives of his subjects under the bond of discipline. Let rulers hold outwardly what they undertake for the benefit of others; inwardly let them preserve [Col. 0037A] what they fear concerning their own estimation. Yet through certain signs appropriately breaking forth, let their subjects also discern that they are humble within themselves, so that in their authority they may see what they should fear, and in their humility recognize what they should imitate.

Let those who preside therefore strive without interruption that, to the extent that their power is seen to be great outwardly, it may be humbled within them, [Note: [Col. 0037D] The first Carnotensis has *ne cogitatione tumeant*, “lest they swell in thought.” The first Audomaropolitan has *ne cogitatione timeant*, “lest they fear in thought.”] lest it conquer their thought, lest it carry their spirit away into self-delight, lest the mind, now placed beneath it, be unable to govern the power which it submits to through the desire to rule.

Lest the mind of one who presides be carried away by delight into exalting its own power, it is rightly said by a certain wise man: “They have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them” (Ecclus. XXXII, 1). Hence Peter also says: “Not lording it over the clergy, but becoming a pattern of the flock” (I Pet. V, 3). [Note: [Col. 0037D] Three Gemetensis manuscripts read *gregi*, “of the flock.”] [Col. 0037B] Hence Truth itself, summoning us toward higher attainments of virtue, says: “You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who are greater exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you; but whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant, just as the Son of Man came not to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. XX, 25 ff.).

Hence he indicates what punishments await the servant exalted by the rule he has undertaken, saying: “But if that wicked servant says in his heart, ‘My master is delaying his coming,’ and begins to strike his fellow servants, while he eats and drinks with drunkards, the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him asunder and appoint his portion with the hypocrites” (Matt. XXIV, 48 ff.). [Col. 0037C] He is rightly numbered among the hypocrites who, under the pretense of discipline, turns the ministry of governance into an exercise of domination.

Nevertheless, at times the fault is more gravely committed if equality is preserved among the perverse rather than discipline. Because Eli, overcome by false compassion, was unwilling to strike his delinquent sons, he struck himself together with his sons before the strict Judge with a cruel condemnation (I Sam. IV, 17–18). Hence the divine voice says to him: “You honored your sons more than me” (ibid., II, 29). Hence he rebukes the shepherds through the prophet, saying: “You have not bound up what was broken, and you have not brought back what was cast away” (Ezek. XXXIV, 4). One who has been cast away is brought back when someone who has fallen into guilt is recalled to the state of righteousness through the force of pastoral solicitude. A fracture, however, is bound when discipline suppresses guilt, lest the wound run on to destruction if the severity of strictness does not constrict it.

But a fracture is often broken worse when it is bound carelessly, so that it feels the tear more severely if the bindings constrict it beyond measure. Therefore, when the wound of sin in subjects is tightened through correction, [Col. 0038A] the strictness itself must also be moderated with great care, [Note: [Col. 0037D] In the printed editions: either *districtior* or *districtor ipse*. All the manuscripts resist these readings.] so that it exercises the rights of discipline against delinquents in such a way that it does not lose the compassion of mercy. It must surely be ensured that compassion presents the ruler to his subjects as a mother and discipline as a father.

Amid these things one must provide with vigilant circumspection lest either strictness be rigid or compassion lax. For, as we have already said in the *Books of Morals* (Book XX of the *Morals*, no. 14, ch. 8, and Epistle 25, Book I), discipline or mercy is greatly weakened if either is maintained without the other. But toward their subjects rulers ought to possess both merciful compassion that rightly consoles [Note: [Col. 0037D] In the majority of printed editions, both *Morals* and *Pastoral*, the reading is *consolans*, “consoling.” In Gratian and in the manuscripts, it is *consulens*, “counseling.”] and discipline that piously strikes.

Hence, when Truth teaches (Luke X, 34), the half-dead man is brought into an inn through the Samaritan’s care, and wine and oil are applied to his wounds, so that through the wine the wounds may be bitten, and through the oil they may be soothed. Whoever is in charge of healing wounds must necessarily apply to them the bite of pain in wine and the gentleness of compassion in oil, so that through the wine the putrid parts may be cleansed [Note: [Col. 0038D] Three Gemetenses, Lyranus, and the second Audomaropolitan have “may be made to bite.” Trecensis, Vallis Claræ, and others have “may be cleansed.”] and through the oil those needing healing may be soothed.

Gentleness must therefore be mixed with severity; a certain tempering must be formed from both, so that subjects are neither ulcerated by excessive harshness [Note: [Col. 0038D] Corbeiensis reads *nimia*, “excessive.” We follow Trecensis and many others.] nor loosened by excessive kindness. This is well signified, according to Paul’s statement (Hebr. IX, 4), by the ark of the tabernacle, in which, together with the tablets, there were both the rod and the manna: for when knowledge of Sacred Scripture is in the heart of a good ruler, there should be both the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness. Hence David says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII, 4). We are struck by the rod and supported by the staff. If, therefore, there is the strictness of the rod that strikes, there should also be the consolation of the staff that supports.

Let there be love, but not love that softens; [Note: [Col. 0038D] The printed editions have “let there be rigor.” All the manuscripts resist this reading.] let there be vigor, but not vigor that exasperates; let there be zeal, but not zeal that rages beyond measure; let there be compassion, but not compassion that spares more than is expedient. Thus, while justice and clemency mingle in the citadel of governance [Note: [Col. 0038D] The first Carnotensis reads *in arte*, “in the art.”], the one who presides may both soothe the hearts of his subjects by terrifying them and, by soothing them, nevertheless bind them to reverence for that terror.

## CHAPTER VII [Alternative XVIII]. That a ruler should not diminish his care for inward things amid his occupation with outward matters, nor abandon his provision for outward things amid his concern for inward matters

Let a ruler not diminish his care for inward things amid his occupation with outward matters, nor abandon his provision for outward things amid his concern for inward matters; lest [Note: [Col. 0038D] Corbeiensis and the third Gemetensis read: “lest either, devoted solely to outward things,”] devoted to outward things, he fall away from inward ones, or, occupied solely with inward things, fail to provide for his neighbors what he ought to provide outwardly. For often some, as though forgetting that they have been set over their brethren for the sake of their souls, devote all the effort of their hearts to worldly concerns. When these concerns are present, they rejoice to engage in them; when they are absent, they pant day and night amid the storms of troubled thought after them. [Col. 0039A] And when, perhaps because opportunity has ceased, they are at rest from these things [Note: [Col. 0039D] Here the manuscripts differ: some English manuscripts read *importunitate*, others *inopportunitate*; the latter is found in Corbeiensis, Belvacensis, and the second Carnotensis. We follow Trecensis, with which the Norman manuscripts and all the vulgate editions agree.], they are worn out still more by that very rest. They regard it as pleasure when they are weighed down by activities and count it as labor when they do not labor in earthly affairs.

Thus it comes about that, while they rejoice to be pressed by worldly disturbances [Note: [Col. 0039D] Corbeiensis reads *urgere se*, “to press themselves”; Trecensis reads *dum se urgueri*, “while they are pressed.”], they remain ignorant of the inward things they ought to have taught others. Consequently, without doubt, the life of their subjects also grows sluggish [Note: [Col. 0039D] Corbeiensis reads *vita turpescit*, “the life grows base.”], because when it desires to advance spiritually, it stumbles against the example of the one set over it as against an obstacle in the road. When the head languishes, the limbs are vigorous in vain; and an army follows its route swiftly to no purpose if it is led astray by the very commander of the journey. No exhortation lifts the minds of the subjects, and no rebuke chastises their faults, because while the office of an earthly judge is exercised by the ruler of souls, the shepherd’s care is absent from guarding the flock. The subjects cannot grasp the light of truth, because while the shepherd’s mind is occupied with earthly pursuits, dust driven by the wind of temptation blinds the eyes of the Church.

Against this, the Redeemer of the human race rightly added, when he was restraining us from the greed of the belly by saying, “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with drunkenness and gluttony” (Luke XXI, 34): “or with the cares of this life.” Immediately adding a warning, he says: “Lest that day come upon you suddenly” (ibid.). He also declares the nature of its coming, saying: “For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (ibid., 35). Again he says: “No one can serve two masters” (Luke XVI, 13). [Col. 0039C]

Hence Paul, solemnly warning—or rather admonishing—the minds of religious people away from association with the world, says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II, 4). Hence he both commands the rulers of the Church to devote themselves to leisure for spiritual things and shows them remedies for providing counsel [Note: [Col. 0039D] The first Carnotensis reads *consolandi*, “of consoling.”], saying: “If, then, you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are of little account in the Church” (I Cor. VI, 4). [Note: [Col. 0039D] The Carnotenses have “secular affairs.”] That is, let those serve in earthly administrations who are not adorned with spiritual gifts. As though he were saying more plainly: “Since they cannot penetrate inward things, let them at least perform the necessary tasks outwardly.”

Hence Moses, who speaks with God (Exod. XVIII, 17–18), is judged by the rebuke of Jethro, a foreigner, because he foolishly devotes himself to the earthly affairs of the people; and counsel is immediately given him, that he should appoint others in his place to settle disputes, while he himself might more freely learn the mysteries of spiritual things in order to instruct the people.

The lower tasks should therefore be carried out by subjects, while rulers should contemplate higher things, so that the eye which stands above to foresee the steps may not be obscured by concern for dust. All who preside are the head of their subjects; and, so that the feet may be able to take the right paths, the head must undoubtedly provide this from above, lest the feet grow sluggish on the road of their progress when the head, with the body’s uprightness bent, inclines itself toward the earth.

But with what mind does a ruler of souls make use of pastoral honor among others if he himself is engaged in earthly affairs that he ought to rebuke in others? This is what the Lord threatens through the prophet in the anger of just retribution, saying: “And it shall be as with the people, so with the priest” (Hosea IV, 9). The priest is as the people when the one who performs a spiritual office does what those do who are still judged by their carnal pursuits.

The prophet Jeremiah, seeing this with great grief of charity, laments it as though under the destruction of the Temple, saying: “How the gold has become dim, the finest color has been changed, the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. IV, 1). What is signified by gold, which surpasses the other metals, except the excellence of holiness? What by the finest color, except the reverence of religion beloved by all? What by the stones of the sanctuary, except persons of the sacred orders? What by the name of streets, except the breadth of the present life?

Because *πλάτος* (*platos*) in Greek means “breadth,” streets are clearly so called from their breadth. Truth himself says: “Broad and spacious is the way that leads to destruction” (Matt. VII, 13). Gold therefore becomes dim when the life of holiness is polluted by earthly actions. The finest color is changed when the former reputation of some who were believed to live religiously is diminished. For when anyone, after assuming the habit of holiness, inserts himself into earthly actions, his reverence, as though its color had been changed, grows pale and despised before human eyes.

The stones of the sanctuary are also scattered into the streets when those who ought to be free for the adornment of the Church through its inward mysteries, as though in the secrets of the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0039D; 0040D] The printed editions have “in the secrets of the sanctuary.” The multitude and authority of the manuscripts compelled us to print “of the tabernacle.” In Trecensis the reading is now *sanctuarii*, “of the sanctuary,” but it was written by a second hand.], seek the broad outward paths of secular affairs. For this purpose the stones of the sanctuary were made: that they might appear within the Holy of Holies in the vestment of the high priest.

But when ministers of religion do not demand from their subjects the honor of their Redeemer on the basis of the merit of their life, the stones of the sanctuary are not in the ornament of the pontiff. Those stones of the sanctuary lie scattered through the streets when persons of the sacred orders, devoted to the breadth of their pleasures [Note: [Col. 0040D] More recent printed editions have *libidini*, “to lust,” against all the manuscripts. Furthermore, by “persons of the sacred orders,” here and slightly above, Gregory principally understands bishops, without excluding priests and deacons. See below, “men of the sacred orders.”], cling to earthly affairs. It should be noted that he says they are scattered not merely in the streets but at the head of the streets, because even when they engage in earthly matters they desire to appear supreme: they occupy the broad roads through the pleasure of delight [Note: [Col. 0040D; 0041D] Three Gemetensis manuscripts, the second Lyranus, Audomaropolitanus, and Longipontanus read *ex voluntate*, “of their own will.” We follow Trecensis, Corbeiensis, and the others printed by all editors.], yet remain at the head of the streets because of the honor of holiness.

Nor does it hinder us if we understand the stones of the sanctuary as those very stones from which the sanctuary had been built—stones that lie scattered at the head of the streets when men of the sacred orders serve earthly activities out of desire, although the glory of holiness had previously appeared to stand through their office.

Secular business may therefore sometimes be tolerated out of compassion, but it should never be sought out of love, lest, when it weighs down the mind of one who pursues it, it plunge that mind, overcome by its own weight, from heavenly things into the depths.

On the other hand, some undertake the care of the flock but desire to devote themselves so completely to spiritual matters that they are in no way occupied with outward affairs. When they entirely neglect the care of bodily needs, they do not at all come to the aid of their subjects’ necessities. [Note: [Col. 0041D] The first Audomaropolitan, in a more refined sense, has “come to meet.”] Their preaching is often despised, because while they rebuke the deeds of delinquents, they do not provide them with the necessities of the present life, and therefore are not willingly heard. The word of teaching does not penetrate the mind of the needy if the hand of mercy does not commend it to his heart. The seed of the word germinates easily when the compassion of the preacher waters it in the breast of the hearer.

Therefore, the ruler must provide for outward things also, with an innocent intention, so that he may be able to pour inward things into others. Let shepherds therefore burn with zeal for the inward pursuits of their subjects in such a way that they do not abandon in them the provision for outward life as well. For, as we have said, the mind of the flock is rightly broken off from receiving preaching if the shepherd neglects care for outward support.

Hence the first shepherd carefully admonishes, saying: “The elders who are among you I beseech, as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and one who shares in the glory that is to be revealed in the future: feed the flock of God that is among you” (I Pet. V, 1). He made clear in this passage whether he was urging the feeding of the heart or of the body when he immediately added: “Providing care, not under compulsion but willingly according to God, neither for the sake of shameful gain but voluntarily.” [Note: [Col. 0041D] Corb., Belv., and the second Carnotensis have “not under compulsion.” The first Carnotensis has “not compelled, but voluntary.”]

By these words shepherds are piously warned not to kill themselves with the sword of ambition while they satisfy the poverty of their subjects; lest, when their neighbors are refreshed through them with bodily support, they themselves remain hungry for the bread of righteousness. [Note: [Col. 0041D] The second Carnotensis adds: “Hence the concern of shepherds.”]

Paul stirs up this solicitude of shepherds, saying: “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V, 8). Amid these things one must always fear and watch vigilantly lest, while outward care is carried on by them, they be overwhelmed away from inward intention. For often, as we have said above, when the hearts of rulers heed temporal concerns carelessly, they grow cold toward inward love; and, because their attention is poured outward, they do not fear forgetting that they have undertaken the governance of souls.

The solicitude expended outwardly upon subjects must therefore necessarily be held within a definite measure. Hence it is rightly said to Ezekiel: “The priests shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long, but they shall clip the hair of their heads” (Ezek. XLIV, 20). Those who preside are rightly called priests, because they provide sacred leadership to the faithful. The hairs on the head signify outward thoughts in the mind. Since they grow imperceptibly above the brain, they designate the cares of the present life; because they sometimes emerge from a negligent sense at inopportune times, they proceed as though without our noticing.

Since all who preside ought indeed to have outward concerns, but must not devote themselves to them too intensely, priests are rightly forbidden both to shave the head and to grow the hair long: so that they neither cut off entirely from themselves thoughts concerning the bodily life of their subjects, nor again allow them to grow without restraint. Here too it is rightly said: “Let them clip the hair of their heads” (ibid.), [Note: [Col. 0041D] Corb., with some others, has “the concerns of temporal care.” Laudensis has “temporal cares of care.”] so that the concerns of temporal solicitude may emerge as far as necessary, yet be cut back quickly, lest they grow beyond measure.

Thus, while the life of bodies is protected through administered outward provision, and is not obstructed by a moderate intention of the heart, the hairs on the priest’s head are both preserved to cover the skin and cut back lest they cover the eyes. [Note: [Col. 0042D] The Paris edition of 1518, Gilot, and many others have “through immoderate [care].” Many manuscripts support this, namely the three Carnotenses, the two Audomaropolitan manuscripts, Lyranus, and the third Gemetensis. Others differ, especially Trecensis, whom we have never found to err except where he was corrupted by a recent hand.]

## CHAPTER VIII [Alternative XIX]. That a ruler should not seek to please human beings as his aim, but should nevertheless direct himself toward that for which he ought to please them

Amid these things the ruler must also watch carefully lest the desire to please human beings drive him on; lest, while he diligently penetrates inward things and prudently supplies outward things, he seek to be loved by his subjects more than he seeks the truth; lest, when supported by good works, he is seen to be alien from the world, his own love make him alien to the Creator.

For he is an enemy of the Redeemer who, through the good works he performs, desires to be loved by the Church in the Redeemer’s place. He is guilty of adulterous thought if the servant seeks to please the eyes of the bride through whom the Bridegroom has sent his gifts. When this self-love has seized the ruler’s mind, it sometimes drags it disorderly toward softness and sometimes toward harshness.

The ruler’s mind is turned toward softness by self-love because, when he sees his subjects sinning, he does not dare to rebuke them, lest their affection for him grow cold. Sometimes, however, he soothes the errors of his subjects, which he ought to rebuke, with flatteries. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hands and make pillows under the head of people of every age, to capture souls” (Ezek. XIII, 18). [Note: [Col. 0042D] The first two Gemetenses here and below have *cubitu*, “elbow,” agreeing with Lyranus and the second Audomaropolitan.]

To place cushions under every elbow of the hands is to comfort with flattering indulgence souls that have fallen from their uprightness and recline in the delight of this world’s pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0042D] The first two Gemetensis manuscripts read *dilectione*, “love.”] For an elbow is received by a cushion, and the head of one lying down by pillows, when the harshness of correction is withdrawn from the sinner and the softness of favor is offered him, so that he may lie comfortably in error, untouched by any harshness of contradiction.

Rulers who love themselves undoubtedly provide these things for those whom they fear may harm them in their pursuit of temporal glory. But those whom they see as having no power against them they continually press with the harshness of severe rebuke; they never admonish them kindly but, forgetting pastoral gentleness, terrify them by the right of domination. Divine speech rightly rebukes such rulers through the prophet, saying: “But you ruled them with harshness and with power” (Ezek. XXXIV, 4).

Those who love themselves more than their Creator raise themselves boastfully against their subjects and attend not to what they ought to do but to what they are able to do. They fear nothing concerning the judgment to come and shamefully glory in temporal power. They desire to do unlawful things freely, with no subject contradicting them. Whoever therefore both strives to act perversely and nevertheless wants others to remain silent about it bears witness against himself: he desires to be loved more than the truth, since he does not want anyone to defend the truth against him.

No one lives in such a way that he does not sin to some degree. He therefore desires truth to be loved more than he himself does who wants no one to spare him against the truth. Hence Peter willingly accepted Paul’s rebuke (Gal. II, 11); hence David humbly listened to the rebuke of a subject (II Sam. XII, 7). Good rulers, because they do not know how to love themselves with private affection, believe that the word of free purity from their subjects is an act of humble obedience.

Amid these things the care of governance must be tempered with such skill of moderation that, when the mind of subjects is able to think certain things rightly, it may come forth in freedom of speech, yet without allowing freedom to burst into pride; lest, perhaps, while excessive liberty of speech is granted them, they lose humility of life.

It must also be known that good rulers ought to seek to please human beings, but in order to draw their neighbors, through the sweetness of their reputation, into affection for the truth—not in order to be loved themselves, but in order to make their love like a road by which they may lead the hearts of their hearers into love of the Creator. It is difficult for a preacher who is not loved, however rightly he announces the truth, to be heard willingly.

The one who presides should therefore strive to be loved, so that he may be heard; yet he should not seek love for his own sake, lest he be found to resist, through the hidden tyranny of thought, the one whom he is seen to serve through his office. Paul aptly suggests this when he reveals to us the hidden purpose of his conduct, saying: “Just as I please all people in all things” (I Cor. X, 33). Yet again he says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. I, 10). Paul therefore pleases and does not please: in what he seeks to please, he seeks not to please himself through human beings, but the truth through himself.

## CHAPTER IX [Alternative XX]. That the ruler ought carefully to know that vices often pretend to be virtues

[Col. 0044A]

The ruler must also know that vices often pretend to be virtues. Frequently avarice disguises itself under the name of frugality, while extravagance conceals itself under the title of generosity. Often disordered laxity is believed to be compassion, and unrestrained anger is regarded as the virtue of spiritual zeal. Often rash action is thought to be the effectiveness of speed, while slowness in acting is considered the prudence of gravity.

Therefore the ruler of souls must distinguish virtues and vices with watchful care, lest either avarice occupy the heart and he rejoice to appear frugal in his distributions; or, when something is squandered extravagantly [Note: [Col. 0043D] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read *quid impenditur*, “when something is expended.”], he boast of being generous as though out of compassion; or, by sparing what he ought to have struck, he drag his subjects toward eternal punishments; or, by striking savagely what has been done wrong, he himself commit a graver wrong; or, by prematurely anticipating what could have been done rightly and seriously, he make it trivial; or, by delaying the merit of a good action, turn it toward worse things. [Note: [Col. 0044D] Laudensis has “he will permit,” against the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER X [Alternative XXI]. What discrimination the ruler’s correction and concealment, fervor and gentleness ought to possess

It must also be known that sometimes the vices of subjects should prudently be concealed, but, because they are concealed, they should be pointed out; sometimes, although openly known, they should be tolerated at the proper time; sometimes they should be investigated subtly and secretly [Note: [Col. 0044D] The first Carnotensis and the second Audomaropolitan have “and secretly.”]; sometimes they should be reproved gently, and sometimes rebuked vehemently.

Some things, as we have said, should prudently be concealed, but, because they are concealed, they should be pointed out: so that when the delinquent knows that he has been detected and knows that he is being tolerated, he may be ashamed to increase the faults which he sees are silently endured in him; and he may punish himself as his own judge, while the ruler’s patience kindly excuses him before himself.

By such concealment the Lord rightly rebukes Judah when he says through the prophet: “You have lied and have not remembered me, nor considered it in your heart, because I was silent and as though not seeing” (Isa. LVII, 11). [Note: [Col. 0044D] The first Carnotensis, with the first two Gemetensis manuscripts, reads *non audiens*, “not hearing.”] He therefore concealed the faults and made them known: he both remained silent against the sinner and nevertheless declared that he had remained silent.

Some things, although openly known, must be tolerated at the proper time, when circumstances are in no way suitable for correcting them openly. For wounds cut prematurely become inflamed more severely; and unless remedies are applied at the right time, it is beyond doubt that they lose their power to heal. But when time is sought for correcting subjects, the superior’s patience is exercised by having to bear the faults themselves. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. CXXVIII, 3). We bear burdens on our back. He therefore complains that sinners have built upon his back, as though he were saying openly: “Those whom I cannot correct, I carry as a burden laid upon me.”

Some hidden things must be investigated subtly, [Col. 0045A] so that, when certain signs break forth, the ruler may discover in the mind of his subjects whatever lies concealed, and, when the moment for correction intervenes, may recognize greater things from the smallest signs.

Hence it is rightly said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, dig through the wall” (Ezek. VIII, 8). [Note: [Col. 0045D] Three Gemetenses have “dig for yourself,” a reading formerly found in Trecensis.] The same prophet immediately adds: “And when I had dug through the wall, one door appeared. And he said to me: ‘Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here.’ And I entered and saw; and behold, every likeness of creeping things, and the abomination of animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall” (ibid., 9–10).

Through Ezekiel the person of superiors is signified; through the wall, the hardness of subjects. And what is it to dig through the wall except to open the hardness of the heart by sharp inquiries? When he had dug through it, a door appeared, because when the hardness of the heart is split either by diligent questioning or by timely correction, a kind of door is displayed through which all the inner thoughts of the one being corrected may be seen.

Hence it also follows there: “Enter and see the most detestable abominations that these people commit here” (ibid.). One enters, as it were, to see abominations when, after examining certain outward signs that appear, one penetrates the hearts of subjects so that everything illicitly thought there becomes known to him. Hence he adds: “And I entered and saw; and behold, every likeness of creeping things, and the abomination of animals” (ibid.).

In creeping things are signified thoughts that are altogether earthly; in animals, thoughts already somewhat raised above the earth, but still seeking the rewards of earthly gain. Creeping things cling to the earth with their entire bodies, whereas animals are suspended above the earth with a large part of their bodies but, through the appetite of the stomach, are always inclined toward the earth. Thus creeping things are within the wall when thoughts revolve in the mind that are never lifted from earthly desires. Animals are also within the wall when, although some things already just and honorable are being thought, they nevertheless serve the pursuit of temporal gains and honors. In themselves they are already raised above the earth, as it were, but through ambition, like the desire of the stomach, they still lower themselves to the depths. [Note: [Col. 0045D] The second Audomaropolitan has “they suspend themselves toward the depths.”]

Hence it is rightly added: “And all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall” (Ezek. VIII, 10). For it is written: “And avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. III, 5). Idols are therefore rightly described after the animals, because although some people already raise themselves above the earth through honorable action, they nevertheless lower themselves to the earth through dishonorable ambition.

It is rightly said, “They were depicted,” because when the forms of outward things are drawn inward, whatever is contemplated through fictitious images is, as it were, painted in the heart.

It must therefore be noted that first a hole in the wall is seen, then a door, and finally the hidden abomination is revealed. For with every sin, outward signs appear first; then the door of iniquity opened by inquiry [Note: [Col. 0046D] Longipontanus has “of investigation.”] is shown; and finally all the evil lying within is disclosed.

Some things, however, should be reproved gently. For when one sins not through malice but through ignorance or weakness alone, the correction of the offense must certainly be tempered with great moderation. As long as we remain in this mortal flesh, all of us are subject to the weaknesses of our corruption. Each person should therefore gather from himself how he ought to show mercy toward another’s weakness, lest, when he is carried too fervently toward the voice of rebuke against his neighbor’s weakness, he appear to have forgotten himself.

Hence Paul aptly admonishes us, saying: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted” (Gal. VI, 1). As though he were saying openly: “When what you see displeases you because of another’s weakness, consider what you are, so that the spirit may restrain itself in its zeal for rebuking, while it fears that the same thing it rebukes may also be found in itself.”

Some things, however, must be rebuked vehemently, [Note: [Col. 0046D] Laudensis has “by the agent,” rather than “by the author.”] so that, when the offender does not recognize the weight of the fault, he may feel from the mouth of the rebuker how grave it is. And when someone makes light of the evil he has committed, he should fear it seriously because of the harshness of the one correcting him.

It is the ruler’s duty to display the glory of the heavenly homeland through the voice of preaching, to disclose how many temptations of the ancient enemy lie hidden along the road of this life, and to correct with great severity of zeal the evils of subjects that should not be tolerated gently; lest, if he is insufficiently inflamed against faults, he himself be held guilty of all faults.

Hence it is rightly said to Ezekiel: “Take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and depict upon it the city of Jerusalem” (Ezek. IV, 1). Immediately it is added: “And you shall arrange a siege against it, and build fortifications, and pile up a rampart, and set camps against it, and place battering rams around it.” And for its fortification it is immediately further said: “And you shall take an iron pan for yourself, and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.” [Note: [Col. 0046D] The second Carnotensis has “against you.” The manuscript reading is evidently corrupt: *eanimurum*; the sense is “you shall place it as an iron wall.”]

For whom does the prophet Ezekiel represent except the figure of teachers? To whom is it said: “Take a brick for yourself, and place it before you, and depict upon it the city of Jerusalem.”

The holy teachers take up a brick when they grasp the earthly heart of their hearers in order to instruct them. They place this brick before themselves, because they guard it with the full attention of their minds. They are commanded to draw the city of Jerusalem upon it, because by preaching they take the greatest care to show earthly hearts what the vision of heavenly peace is. But because the glory of the heavenly homeland is recognized to no purpose unless one also strives to understand how many assaults of the crafty enemy break in here, it is appropriately added: “And you shall lay siege against it, and build fortifications.” The holy preachers arrange a siege around the brick on which the city of Jerusalem has been drawn when they show an earthly mind—already seeking the heavenly homeland—how greatly the hostility of vices attacks it during the time of this life. For whenever it is shown how each sin lies in wait for those who are making progress, a siege is, as it were, arranged around the city of Jerusalem by the preacher’s voice.

But because it is necessary not only to make known how vices attack, but also how virtues, when guarded, strengthen us, it is rightly added: “And you shall build fortifications.” The holy preacher builds fortifications when he demonstrates which virtues resist which vices. And because, as virtue increases, the battles of temptation are often enlarged, it is rightly added: “And you shall bring up a mound, and place camps against it, and set up battering rams all around.” Each preacher brings up a mound when he declares the mass of the temptation that is increasing. He raises camps against Jerusalem when he foretells to the right intention of his hearers the crafty enemy’s carefully contrived and, as it were, elusive ambushes.

[Note: Gemeticensis and the third Carnotensis: “unwatchful.” This reading was adopted by Gilot, Vaticanus, and the other printed editions, except Gussanville, whom we follow, in accordance with the English manuscripts, Trecensis, Corbeiensis, and others.]

And he sets up battering rams all around when he makes known the stings of temptations that surround us on every side in this life and pierce the wall of virtues.

[Note: The second Carnotensis: “and the strength of the wall.”]

But although the rector subtly conveys all these things, unless he burns with the spirit of zeal against the offenses of individuals, he prepares no lasting absolution for himself. Hence it is rightly added there:

“32 And you shall take for yourself an iron pan, and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.”

By the pan, the frying of the mind is signified; by the iron, the strength of correction. What fries and tortures the teacher’s mind more intensely than zeal for God? Hence Paul was burned by the frying of this pan when he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29.)

And because whoever is inflamed with zeal for God is fortified by an enduring and powerful guard, lest he be condemned through negligence, it is rightly said: “You shall place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city.” An iron pan is placed as an iron wall between the prophet and the city because, when rectors now display strong zeal, that same zeal afterward remains a strong defense between them and their hearers, so that they may not then be left defenseless for punishment if now they have been lax in correction.

But amid these matters we must understand that, when the teacher’s mind hardens itself for correction, it is very difficult for it not at some time to break out into something that it ought not to say. It often happens that, while the fault of subjects is rebuked with great vehemence, the teacher’s tongue is drawn on to words of excess. And when correction is kindled beyond measure, the hearts of the guilty are cast down into despair. Therefore it is necessary that the rector, once angered, should always return to repentance when he considers that he has struck the minds of his subjects more severely than he ought, so that by lamentation he may obtain pardon in the sight of Truth even for the fact that he sins through the exertion of his zeal.

The Lord figuratively prescribes this through Moses, saying: “If anyone goes with his neighbor simply into the forest to cut wood, and the wood slips from the hand of the axe, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes and kills his neighbor, he shall flee to one of the aforementioned cities and live; lest perhaps the nearest relative of the man whose blood has been shed pursue and overtake him, and strike his life” (Deuteronomy 19:4–5).

[Note: Three Gemeticenses and the first Audomarensis: “the hand lets it slip.”]

[Note: Another reading: “let him flee,” as in the three Gemeticenses.]

We go into the forest with a neighbor whenever we turn our attention to examining the offenses of our subjects. We cut wood simply when we cut away the vices of those who sin with a devout intention. But the axe slips from the hand when correction drags itself into harshness more than necessary.

[Note: Corbeiensis with Normanus: “the hand lets it slip.”]

The iron leaps from the handle when a harsher word goes beyond what correction requires. It strikes and kills the neighbor because, through an insult that has been uttered, it destroys its hearer’s spirit of love. For the mind of the person corrected suddenly plunges into hatred if immoderate correction subjects it more than it ought.

But the one who carelessly strikes the wood and extinguishes his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that he may live, protected, in one of them. For if, turning to the lamentation of repentance, he hides within the unity of the sacrament under hope and charity, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed. The nearest relative of the one killed does not kill him when he finds him, because when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through sharing our nature—he will plainly not demand the guilt of the offense from the person whom faith, hope, and charity have hidden beneath His pardon.

**33 CHAPTER XI [Another reading: XXII]. How intent the rector ought to be upon meditation on sacred law**

But all this is rightly carried out by the rector if, filled with the spirit of heavenly fear and love, he diligently meditates every day upon the commandments of sacred speech, so that the words of divine admonition may restore in him the force of solicitude and the prudent watchfulness directed toward heavenly life—qualities that the practice of human society continually destroys—and so that the one who is led toward the old age of life through association with secular people may always be renewed toward love of the spiritual homeland by the aspiration of compunction.

[Note: The third Carnotensis: “may be renewed by harshness.” Longipontanus: “may be recalled.”]

For the heart flows downward greatly amid human words; and since it is certainly established that, driven by the external tumult of occupations, the heart falls away from itself, it ought to strive without ceasing to rise again through the pursuit of instruction. Hence Paul admonishes the disciple placed over the flock, saying: “Until I come, attend to reading” (1 Timothy 4:13). Hence David says: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; all day long it is my meditation” (Psalm 118:97).

Hence the Lord commanded Moses concerning the carrying of the ark, saying: “You shall make four golden rings, which you shall place at the four corners of the ark; and you shall make poles of setim wood, cover them with gold, and insert them through the rings that are on the sides of the ark, so that it may be carried by them. They shall always be in the rings and shall never be removed from them” (Exodus 25:12 ff.).

What is represented by the ark if not the holy Church? It is commanded that four golden rings be attached to its four corners, because, as it extends throughout the four regions of the world, it is plainly proclaimed as girded with the four books of the holy Gospel. The poles are made of setim wood and inserted into those same rings for carrying, because strong and persevering teachers, like incorruptible wood, are to be sought—teachers who, always cleaving to the instruction of the sacred volumes, should proclaim the unity of the holy Church and, as though inserted into the rings, carry the ark.

[Note: Thus Trecensis, Laudunensis, Gemeticensis, and others. In the printed editions: “having been inserted,” contrary to the sense of sacred Scripture.]

To carry the ark with poles is for good teachers, by preaching, to lead the holy Church toward the untrained minds of unbelievers.

[Note: The second Carnotensis: “of the faithful.”]

They are also commanded to be covered with gold, so that while their words resound in the ears of others, they themselves may also shine with the splendor of their life. Concerning them it is aptly added: “They shall always be in the rings and shall never be removed from them.” For it is necessary that those who keep watch over the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading.

The poles are commanded always to remain in the rings for this reason: when the need to carry the ark arises, no delay in inserting the poles for carrying should occur. For when something spiritual is sought from subjects, it is profoundly disgraceful if the pastor then seeks to learn what he ought to explain when the question must be resolved. Let the poles therefore remain attached to the rings, so that teachers, always meditating on sacred utterances in their hearts, may without delay lift the ark of the covenant and immediately teach whatever is necessary.

Hence the first shepherd of the Church rightly admonishes the other shepherds, saying: “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3:15).

[Note: Trecensis, Theodoricus, and Corbeiensis: “the hope that is in you.”]

As though he were saying plainly: So that no delay may impede the carrying of the ark, let the poles never leave the rings.

[Note: In Trecensis, Corbeiensis, and many old manuscripts this title is absent, and what follows constitutes chapter 23. In Longipontanus it reads: “The first book ends; the second book begins. Chapter 20.”]

**PART THREE. HOW A RECTOR WHO LIVES WELL OUGHT TO TEACH AND ADMONISH HIS SUBJECTS**

**PROLOGUE [Another reading: chapter XXIII]**

[Col. 0049C]

Since, then, we have shown what sort of person a shepherd ought to be, let us now demonstrate how he should teach. For, as Gregory of Nazianzus, of revered memory, taught long before our time (Oration 1), the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, because not everyone is bound by the same character. Often what benefits some harms others. Herbs that nourish certain animals sometimes kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but excites puppies. A medicine that reduces one person’s illness gives strength to another; and bread that strengthens the life of the strong kills the little ones.

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it corresponds to each person’s condition while never departing from the art of common edification. For what are the attentive minds of hearers, if I may put it this way, but a kind of arrangement of stretched strings spread across a lyre? The skilled player strikes them differently so that he may produce a melody not unlike itself; and therefore the strings produce harmonious modulation because they are struck by one plectrum, but not with one and the same stroke. Thus every teacher, in order to build all people up in the one virtue of charity, ought to touch the hearts of his hearers with one teaching but not with one identical exhortation.

**CHAPTER I [Another reading: XXIV]. How great the diversity ought to be in the art of preaching**

[Col. 0050C]

Men must be admonished in one way and women in another; young people in one way and the elderly in another; the poor in one way and the rich in another; the joyful in one way and the sorrowful in another; subjects in one way and superiors in another; servants in one way and masters in another; the wise of this world in one way and the dull in another; the shameless in one way and the modest in another; the insolent in one way and the fainthearted in another; the impatient in one way and the patient in another; the benevolent in one way and the envious in another; the simple in one way and the impure in another.

[Col. 0050D]

The healthy must be admonished in one way and the sick in another; those who fear punishments and therefore live innocently in one way, and those who have become so hardened in iniquity that they are not corrected even by punishments in another. The excessively silent must be admonished in one way and those who indulge in much speaking in another; the sluggish in one way and the rash in another; the gentle in one way and the angry in another; the humble in one way and the arrogant in another; the obstinate in one way and the fickle in another; those devoted to gluttony in one way and the abstinent in another.

[Col. 0051A]

Those who mercifully give away what is theirs must be admonished in one way, and those who strive to seize what belongs to others in another. Those who neither seize what belongs to others nor give away what is theirs must be admonished in one way; those who both give away what they possess and nevertheless do not cease to seize what belongs to others in another.

[Note: Corbeiensis: “those who desire what belongs to others.” The common editions have “desire” instead of “seize.”]

The quarrelsome must be admonished in one way and the peaceful in another; those who sow disputes in one way and peacemakers in another. Those who do not correctly understand the words of sacred law must be admonished in one way, and those who understand them correctly but do not speak them humbly in another. Those who, although able to preach worthily, are afraid through excessive humility must be admonished in one way; those whom lack of maturity or age prevents from preaching, yet whom rashness drives forward, in another.

Those who prosper in what they desire temporally must be admonished in one way, and those who indeed desire the things of the world but are nevertheless wearied by the labor of adversity in another. Those bound by marriage must be admonished in one way and those free from the bonds of marriage in another.

[Note: The printed editions: “those conscious of sins of the flesh in one way, and those unaware of them in another.” None of our manuscripts has this.]

Those who have experienced sexual intercourse must be admonished in one way and those who have not in another. Those who mourn sins of action in one way and those who mourn sins of thought in another. Those who lament the sins they have committed but do not abandon them must be admonished in one way, and those who abandon them but do not lament them in another. Those who even praise the unlawful things they do must be admonished in one way, and those who condemn wrongdoing but nevertheless do not avoid it in another.

Those who are overcome by sudden desire must be admonished in one way, and those who are bound in guilt by deliberate resolve in another. Those who frequently commit unlawful acts, even if minor ones, must be admonished in one way; those who guard themselves from small offenses but sometimes sink into graver ones in another.

[Note: Trecensis and Corbeiensis: “into serious offenses.”]

Those who do not even begin good works must be admonished in one way, and those who fail to complete what they have begun in another. Those who do evil secretly and good publicly must be admonished in one way, and those who conceal the good they do while nevertheless allowing others, through certain actions, to form a public bad opinion of them in another.

[Note: From these words through “Admonition 1,” nothing is read in Corbeiensis except the summaries of the chapters of this third and fourth part that follow the admonitions. Immediately afterward comes: “The second book begins.” In the Codex Regius, the Pastoral Rule is divided into only two books. The same division is found in the three Gemeticenses and in Longipontanus. In Trecensis there is no division either of books or of parts.]

But what benefit is there in running through all these matters in a collected enumeration if we do not also disclose, with as much brevity as we can, the forms of admonition appropriate to each?

[Note: In the common editions the following is appended: “Let us therefore, beginning with the principal matter, discuss these things more fully and in order, one by one.” This addition is unknown in the English manuscripts and in ours. It is otherwise unnecessary after the words “But what benefit,” etc., which are found in Trecensis and others except Corbeiensis.]

**[Another reading: chapter XXIV] (Admonition 1.)**

[Note: In Trecensis and other manuscripts, chapter 24, and so thereafter, counting each admonition as a separate chapter.]

Men must therefore be admonished in one way and women in another, because more serious duties should be imposed upon the former and lighter ones upon the latter, so that great things may exercise the men, while gentle things, by soothing them, may turn the women toward the better.

[Col. 0051D]

**[Another reading: chapter XXV] (Admonition 2.)**

Young people must be admonished in one way and the elderly in another, because severity of admonition generally directs the young toward progress, while gentle entreaty brings the elderly to better works. For it is written: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father” (1 Timothy 5:1).

**CHAPTER II [Another reading: XXVI]. How the poor and the rich should be admonished**

**(Admonition 3.)**

The poor must be admonished in one way and the rich in another: to the former we ought to offer the comfort of consolation against tribulation, while to the latter we ought to bring fear against pride. To the poor person the Lord says through the prophet: “Do not fear, for you shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 54:4). A little later, addressing her tenderly, he says: “O poor one, shaken by the storm” (Isaiah 54:11). Again he consoles her, saying: “I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty” (Isaiah 48:10).

But to the disciple concerning the rich Paul says: “Command the rich in this present age not to be high-minded, nor to place their hope in the uncertainty of their riches” (1 Timothy 6:17). Here it is especially noteworthy that the teacher of humility, when speaking of the rich, does not say “Ask,” but “Command,” because although compassion must be shown to weakness, honor is not owed to arrogance. What is rightly said to such people is commanded all the more rightly insofar as they swell with lofty thoughts over transitory possessions.

In the Gospel the Lord says of them: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have received your consolation” (Luke 6:24). Because they do not know the joys that are eternal, they are consoled by the abundance of the present life. Consolation must therefore be offered to those whom the furnace of poverty burns away; fear must be brought to those whom the consolation of temporal glory exalts, so that the former may learn that they possess riches they do not see, while the latter may recognize that they can by no means retain the riches they do see.

[Note: This should be read in accordance with the manuscripts Trecensis, Carnotensis, Vallis Clarae, Theodoricianus, Bellovacensis, Gemeticensis, and others: “the riches they do not see,” not “the riches they do not desire,” which is found in the third Gilot edition and later printed editions. Shortly afterward, the same printed editions, contrary to all the manuscripts, read “the riches they desire.”]

Often, however, the order of persons is altered by the quality of their character, so that the rich person is humble and the poor person arrogant. Therefore the preacher’s tongue should immediately be brought into harmony with the life of the hearer, so that it may strike the arrogance of the poor with greater strictness insofar as neither the poverty inflicted upon him bends it, and may soothe the humility of the rich more gently insofar as neither the abundance that raises them up exalts them.

[Note: The second Carnotensis: “may burn against the arrogance of the poor.”]

[Note: Laudunensis: “insofar as the swelling of arrogance harasses him, and the poverty inflicted upon him does not humble him.”]

Sometimes, however, even an arrogant rich person must be placated by the soothing of exhortation, because hard wounds often soften through gentle fomentations, and the rage of the insane is often brought back to health when the physician speaks soothingly. When one accommodates oneself to them with sweetness, the sickness of madness is calmed.

For it must not be overlooked carelessly that, when an evil spirit attacked Saul, David took up the harp and calmed his madness (1 Samuel 18:10). What is indicated by Saul if not the arrogance of the powerful, and what by David if not the humble life of the saints? When, therefore, Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David plays, because when the understanding of the powerful is turned into frenzy by arrogance, it is fitting that it be recalled to mental health, as though by the sweetness of a harp, through the tranquility of our speech.

Sometimes, when the powerful of this world are rebuked, they should first be questioned through certain comparisons as though concerning another person’s business. When they have pronounced a correct judgment as though against someone else, they should then be struck, in appropriate ways, concerning their own guilt. Thus a mind swollen with temporal power may not rise up against the one correcting it, since it has trampled the neck of its own pride by its own judgment, and may not exert itself in defending itself against a sentence by which its own mouth has bound it.
