This is why the prophet Nathan came to rebuke the king and sought a judgment, as it were, concerning a poor man against a rich man (2 Samuel 12:4–5 and following), so that the king might first pronounce the sentence and afterward hear his own guilt, lest he contradict the justice that he himself had pronounced against himself. Thus the holy man, considering both the sinner and the king, wisely sought first to bind the bold culprit through confession and afterward to cut him through denunciation.

He concealed for a little while the person whom he had sought, but suddenly struck the one whom he had held.

[Note: The printed editions: “the person whom he sought.” All our manuscripts read “the one whom,” with excellent sense.]

He might perhaps have been wounded more slowly if Nathan had wished to attack the fault openly from the very beginning of his speech; but, having first presented a comparison, he sharpened the rebuke that he had kept hidden. A physician had come to a sick man and saw the wound that needed to be cut, but was uncertain about the patient’s endurance. He therefore hid the healing iron beneath his garment; then, suddenly drawing it out, he drove it into the wound, so that the patient might feel the cutting blade before seeing it. If he had seen it beforehand, he might have refused to endure it.

**CHAPTER III [Another reading: XXVII]. How the joyful and the sorrowful should be admonished**

**(Admonition 4.)**

The joyful must be admonished in one way and the sorrowful in another. To the joyful, the sorrows that follow from punishment must be brought; to the sorrowful, the joys that are promised from the kingdom. Let the joyful learn from the harshness of threats what they ought to fear; let the sorrowful hear of the joys of rewards in which they may place their hope. To the former it is said: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn” (Luke 6:25); the latter hear from the same teacher: “I shall see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16:22).

Some people, however, are not made joyful or sorrowful by circumstances but exist in accordance with their natural constitution.

[Note: By *conspersiones* Gregory here and elsewhere understands disposition, nature, the constitution and condition of body and soul, as is sufficiently clear. See below, chapter 38 according to the recent edition, and chapter 61 in the manuscripts.]

They must certainly be told that certain vices are closely associated with certain constitutions. The joyful have lust near at hand; the sorrowful, anger. Therefore each person must consider not only what he suffers from his own constitution, but also what worse thing presses him from nearby, lest, while he does not fight against what he endures, he succumb to the vice from which he thinks himself free.

**CHAPTER IV [Another reading: XXVIII]. How subjects and superiors should be admonished**

**(Admonition 5.)**

Subjects must be admonished in one way and superiors in another: the former, so that subjection may not crush them; the latter, so that their superior position may not exalt them. The former must be admonished not to fulfill less than what is commanded; the latter, not to command more than is right to be fulfilled.

[Note: Laudunensis and Corbeiensis: “than can be fulfilled.”]

The former must be admonished to submit humbly; the latter, to preside with restraint. In a sense that can also be understood figuratively, it is said to the former: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord”; to the latter it is commanded: “And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger” (Colossians 3:20–21).

They should learn how to order their inner selves before the eyes of the hidden Judge; the others, how to provide externally to those entrusted to them examples of good living.

[Note: Laudunensis and Trecensis: “before the eyes of the hidden Judge.”]

For superiors must know that, if they ever commit wrongdoing, they are deserving of as many deaths as the examples of perdition they transmit to their subjects.

[Note: Gemeticensis and many others: “of as many punishments.”]

Therefore they must guard themselves from guilt with all the greater caution because, through the wrongs they commit, they do not die alone.

[Note: Trecensis, Corbeiensis, and Laudunensis lack this parenthesis. It is found in the Gemeticenses and in the first Audomarensis.]

They are also guilty of the souls of others whom they have destroyed by their bad examples.

Therefore the former must be admonished lest they be punished more strictly if they cannot be found absolved even concerning themselves; the latter, lest they be judged concerning the errors of their subjects, even though they now find themselves secure concerning themselves.

The former must be admonished so that they may live around themselves with all the greater care insofar as they are not involved in the care of others; the latter, so that they may fulfill the cares of others in such a way that they do not cease to attend to their own, and may burn with concern for themselves in such a way that they do not grow sluggish in guarding those entrusted to them.

To the person who is free to attend to himself it is said: “Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider its ways and learn wisdom” (Proverbs 6:6). But the superior is sternly admonished when it is said: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have struck hands with a stranger, you are ensnared by the words of your mouth, and captured by your own speech” (ibid., 1).

To become surety for a friend is to take responsibility for another soul at the peril of one’s own conduct. Therefore his hand is struck with a stranger, because his mind is bound to a care of solicitude that had previously been absent. He is ensnared by the words of his mouth and captured by his own speech because, when he is compelled to speak good things to those entrusted to him, he must first guard what he has said himself.

He is therefore ensnared by the words of his mouth when, as reason demands, he is constrained not to let his life relax into anything other than what he admonishes. Before the strict Judge he is compelled to carry out in his deeds as much as he is known to have commanded others by his voice.

And there the exhortation is rightly added immediately: “Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into the hands of your neighbor; run, hasten, rouse your friend. Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Proverbs 6:3).

Whoever is placed before others as an example for living is admonished not only to keep watch himself but also to awaken his friend. For it is not enough for him to keep watch by living well if he does not also separate the person over whom he presides from the torpor of sin.

It is rightly said: “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (ibid., 4). To give sleep to one’s eyes is, when attention has ceased, to neglect altogether the care of one’s subjects. The eyelids slumber when our thoughts, overcome by sluggishness, conceal the things in our subjects that they recognize must be rebuked.

To sleep fully is neither to know nor to correct the actions of those entrusted to one. Not to sleep but to slumber is to recognize what ought to be reproved and yet, because of weariness of mind, not to correct it with fitting rebukes. Through slumbering, the eye is led to complete sleep because, when the person in charge often fails to cut away the evil he knows, he eventually reaches, through the merit of his negligence, the point where he does not even recognize what is being done wrong by his subjects.

Those who preside must therefore be admonished to have, through diligent watchfulness, vigilant eyes within and all around, and to strive to become the heavenly creatures.

(See Ezekiel 1:18.)

For the heavenly creatures are described as full of eyes all around and within (Revelation 4:6). It is fitting that all who preside should have eyes within and all around, so that they may strive to please the inner Judge in themselves and, by offering examples of life outwardly, also detect what in others must be corrected.

Subjects must be admonished not rashly to judge the life of their superiors if they happen to see them doing something blameworthy, lest, in the very matter by which they rightly condemn evil, they plunge themselves into deeper evils through the impulse of pride. They must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they observe their faults, but, if some things in them are very wrong, to judge them within themselves in such a way that, nevertheless, bound by divine fear, they do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them.

We can show this more clearly if we bring forward David’s action (1 Samuel 24:4 and following). Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve himself; David was there with his men, having already endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for so long. When his men urged him to strike Saul, he restrained them by his replies, because he ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Nevertheless, he rose secretly and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak.

What is signified by Saul if not bad rectors, and what by David if not good subjects? Saul’s relieving himself therefore signifies wicked superiors extending the evil conceived in their hearts into deeds of foul odor, and displaying, by carrying out in external acts the harmful things they have thought within themselves.

Yet David feared to strike him, because devout minds among subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction, strike the lives of their superiors with no sword of the tongue, even when they criticize their imperfections. If at times, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves from speaking of certain extreme and external evils of their superiors, though humbly, they secretly cut off something like the edge of the cloak.

[Note: Corbeiensis, Laudunensis, and Longipontanus: “so that they do not speak of extreme matters.”]

For when they detract, at least harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity placed over them, they are, as it were, defiling the garment of the king who is set above them. Yet they return to themselves and reproach themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word.

[Note: The common editions: “they cut the garment,” apparently by conjecture rather than from the manuscripts, all of which disagree.]

Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David’s heart struck him, because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (ibid., 6). The deeds of superiors must not be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of criticism. But if the tongue slips against them even in the smallest matters, the heart must be weighed down through the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself and, having offended against the authority placed over it, may fear the judgment against itself of the one by whom that authority was placed above it.

For when we offend against superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who placed them over us. Hence Moses too, when he learned that the people had complained against him and Aaron, said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against the Lord” (Exodus 16:8).

**40 CHAPTER V [Another reading: XXIX]. How servants and masters should be admonished**

[Col. 0056C]

**(Admonition 6.)**

Servants must be admonished in one way and masters in another. Servants should always look upon the humility of their condition within themselves; masters should not lose the remembrance of their nature, by which they were created equal to their servants.

Servants must be admonished not to despise their masters, lest they offend God by proudly contradicting His ordering. Masters too must be admonished, because they grow proud against God concerning His gift if they do not recognize those whom they hold subject by condition as their equals through participation in the same nature.

The former must be admonished to know that they are servants of masters; the latter, to recognize that they are fellow servants of servants. To the former it is said: “Servants, obey your masters according to the flesh” (Colossians 3:22). And again: “Let all who are under the yoke of slavery consider their masters worthy of all honor” (1 Timothy 6:1).

[Note: The second Carnotensis: “who are under the yoke of slavery.”]

To the latter it is said: “And you masters, do the same to them, giving up threats, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven” (Ephesians 6:2).

**CHAPTER VI [Another reading: XXX]. How the wise and the dull should be admonished**

**(Admonition 7.)**

The wise of this world must be admonished in one way and the dull in another. The wise must be admonished to cease knowing what they know; the dull must be admonished to desire to know what they do not know.

[Note: This reading is required by the manuscripts Trecensis, the Carnotenses, Vallis Clarae, two old Gemeticenses, and two Audomarenses: “to cease knowing.” The printed editions have “to know how to lose,” supported by Codex Bellovacensis. In the third Gemeticensis it reads: “lest they lose the ability to know.”]

In the former, the first thing that must be destroyed is their belief that they are wise; in the latter, whatever is known of heavenly wisdom must now be built up, because, since they are not proud, they have prepared their hearts as though to receive a building.

With the former we must labor so that they may become foolish in a wiser way, abandon foolish wisdom, and learn the wise foolishness of God. To the latter it must be preached that they may pass more closely from what is considered foolishness to true wisdom.

To the former it is said: “If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish, so that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18); to the latter it is said: “Not many are wise according to the flesh” (ibid., 1:22). And again: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (ibid., 27).

Arguments of reasoning generally benefit the former, while examples sometimes convert the latter more effectively. It is useful for the former to lie defeated in their own arguments; for the latter it is sometimes enough to learn of the praiseworthy deeds of others.

Hence the distinguished teacher, debtor both to the wise and to the foolish (Romans 1:14), when admonishing certain Hebrews who were wise and others who were slower, spoke to the former about the completion of the Old Testament and overcame their wisdom by an argument, saying: “What is becoming old and aging is near to disappearance” (Hebrews 8:13).

But when he saw that some had to be drawn by examples alone, he added in the same Epistle: “The saints experienced mockings and beatings, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were cut in two, they were tested, they died by the slaughter of the sword” (ibid., 11:36–37). And again: “Remember your superiors, who spoke the word of God to you; observing the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (ibid., 13:7), so that victorious reason might break the former, while gentle imitation might urge the latter to climb toward greater things.

**41 CHAPTER VII [Another reading: XXXI]. How the shameless and the modest should be admonished**
### (Admonition 8)

The shameless are to be admonished in one way, and the bashful in another. The former are restrained from the vice of shamelessness only by harsh reproof; the latter are generally brought to a better state by moderate exhortation. The former do not recognize that they are sinning unless they are rebuked by many; for the latter, it is often enough for their conversion that a teacher gently recalls their sins to their memory. He corrects the shameless more effectively who rebukes them with invective; but the bashful make greater progress if what is censured in them is touched, as it were, obliquely.

Thus, openly rebuking the shameless people of the Jews, the Lord says: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. III, 3). And again, comforting one who is ashamed, he says: “You shall forget the shame of your youth, and shall remember no more the reproach of your widowhood, because he who made you shall rule over you” (Isa. LIV, 4).

Paul likewise openly rebukes the shamelessly sinning Galatians, saying: “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Gal. III, 1). And again: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed by the flesh?” (Ibid. 3). But he reproves the faults of the bashful as though sympathizing with them, saying: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because at last you have revived in your concern for me, as you were concerned before; for you were occupied” (Phil. IV, 10). Thus harsh reproof might expose the faults of the former, while gentler speech veiled the negligence of the latter.

[Note: Corb. reads “might wipe away” (*detergeret*). “Might expose” (*detegeret*) should be read because of its antithesis with “veiled”; this is the reading of Trec., Gemet., Aud., and others, with *harsh* omitted.]

## CHAPTER VIII [formerly XXXII]. How the arrogant and the fainthearted are to be admonished

### (Admonition 9)

The arrogant are to be admonished in one way, and the fainthearted in another. The former, because they presume greatly upon themselves, disdain others by reproaching them; the latter, because they are excessively conscious of their weakness, often fall into despair. The former consider everything they do to be supremely important; the latter regard what they do as utterly insignificant and are therefore crushed by despair. The works of the arrogant must therefore be examined subtly by the one who reproves them, so that they may be shown that what pleases them displeases God.

We correct the arrogant more effectively when we show that the things they believe they have done well were done badly, so that from the very source from which they are thought to have gained glory, useful shame may follow. Sometimes, however, when they recognize that they are not committing the vice of arrogance at all, they come more quickly to correction if, by obliquely seeking out some more obvious fault, they are put to shame by reproach.

[Note: Rothomag. and Longip. read: “they are put to shame in their own fault.”]

They may thereby recognize that, although unable to defend one charge, they are obstinately maintaining what they do defend. Thus, when Paul saw that the Corinthians were arrogantly puffed up against one another, one saying that he belonged to Paul, another to Apollos, another to Cephas, and another to Christ (I Cor. I, 12; III, 4), he brought forward an incestuous offense which had both been committed among them and remained uncorrected, saying:

> “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not found even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (I Cor. V, 1–2).

It is as though he said openly: “Why do you arrogantly claim to belong to this or that person, when by the dissolution of your negligence you show that you belong to no one?”

[Note: Manuscripts differ remarkably at this point. Corb. and Belv. read: “Why do you, through arrogance?” The first two Gemet. read: “Why do you arrogantly?” The first Carnot. and Laud. read: “Why do you show this arrogance?” The third Carnot., Rothomag., the first Aud., Lyr., Longip., and the third Gemet. read: “Why are you arrogant?” Our reading, found in Cod. Trec. and the printed editions, is clear in meaning.]

The fainthearted, on the other hand, are more suitably brought back to the path of good conduct if some of their good qualities are sought out obliquely. Thus, while correcting some things in them by reproving them, we praise others by embracing them, so that the praise they hear may nourish their sensitivity, while the reproof of their fault chastens them.

We often make better progress with them if we also recall their good deeds. If they have done anything disorderly, we should no longer rebuke them as though it had already been committed, but should prohibit it as though it were still to be avoided. In this way, the favor shown to what we approve may increase it, while modest exhortation may become more effective with the fainthearted against what we censure.

Thus Paul, recognizing that the Thessalonians, who persevered in the preaching they had received, were troubled by a certain faintheartedness concerning the nearness of the world’s end, first praises in them what he sees to be strong, and then, by cautiously admonishing them, strengthens what is weak. For he says:

> “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing exceedingly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, so that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God for your endurance and faith” (II Thess. I, 3–4).

After prefacing this gentle praise of their life, he adds shortly afterward:

> “But we ask you, brothers, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our gathering together to him, that you not be quickly shaken from your understanding or alarmed, either by a spirit, or by a word, or by a letter supposedly sent by us, as though the day of the Lord were imminent” (Ibid. II, 1).

The true teacher acted so that they would first hear praise for what they recognized in themselves, and afterward exhortation concerning what they were to pursue. Thus the praise that preceded it might strengthen their minds, lest the admonition that followed disturb them. Since he knew that they had been shaken by the suspicion of the end’s nearness, he did not rebuke them as already shaken, but, as though unaware of what had happened, prohibited them from being shaken further. In this way, while they believed that their teacher did not know about the very instability of their agitation, they would become more liable to reproach insofar as they feared that he might know them.

[Note: The third Carn. reads “the lightness of the admonition”; Belv. reads “the lightness of the agitation”; Laud. reads “the lightness of the movement.”]

## CHAPTER IX [formerly XXXIII]. How the impatient and the patient are to be admonished

### (Admonition 10)

The impatient are to be admonished in one way, and the patient in another. The impatient must be told that, because they neglect to restrain their spirit, they are swept into many precipices of wrongdoing, even into things they do not desire. For anger drives the mind where desire does not lead it, and in its agitation it acts as though unaware of what it will afterward, knowingly, regret.

The impatient must also be told that, when driven headlong by the impulse of agitation, they perform certain acts as though beside themselves, and scarcely recognize their own evils after they have been committed. Because they do not resist their disturbance, they even confuse whatever they may previously have done well with a tranquil mind, and by an unforeseen impulse destroy whatever they perhaps built through long and careful labor.

Through the vice of impatience, the virtue that is the mother and guardian of all virtues—charity—is itself lost. For it is written: “Charity is patient” (I Cor. XIII, 4). Therefore, where there is no patience, there is no charity. Through this vice of impatience, the teaching that nourishes the virtues is also scattered. For it is written: “A man’s instruction is known by his patience” (Prov. XIX, 14). The less patient someone is shown to be, therefore, the less learned he proves to be. For he cannot genuinely impart good instruction if, in his conduct, he does not know how to tolerate the faults of others with equanimity.

Through this vice of impatience, the fault of arrogance also often pierces the mind. For when a person cannot endure being despised in this world, he tries to display whatever good qualities are hidden within him; and so, through impatience, he is led even to arrogance. Since he cannot bear contempt, he glories in displaying himself.

Hence it is written: “The patient is better than the arrogant” (Eccl. VII, 9). The patient chooses to endure any evil rather than have his hidden good qualities become known through the vice of ostentation. The arrogant, on the other hand, chooses to have even false good qualities proclaimed about him rather than endure the slightest evil.

Since, when patience is abandoned, even the other good deeds already performed are destroyed, it is rightly commanded that a trench be made in the altar of God, so that the holocausts placed upon it may be preserved there (Ezek. XLIII, 13). For if there were no trench in the altar, the breeze that came upon it would scatter every sacrifice it found there.

What, then, do we understand by the altar of God except the soul of the righteous, which places upon itself, before his eyes, as many sacrifices as it has performed good deeds? And what is the trench of the altar except the patience of the good? By humbling the mind so that it may endure adversity, patience shows it as though placed at the bottom, in the manner of a pit.

Let a trench therefore be made in the altar, lest the sacrifice placed upon it be scattered by the breeze—that is, let the mind of the elect guard patience, lest, shaken by the wind of impatience, it lose even what it has done well. This same trench is rightly shown to be one cubit in measure (Ibid.), because, when patience is not abandoned, the measure of unity is preserved.

Hence Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 2). The law of Christ is the charity of unity, which is fulfilled only by those who, even when burdened, do not go beyond the bounds of charity.

Let the impatient hear what is written: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. XVI, 32). The victory over cities is less, because what is subdued lies outside; but what is conquered through patience is far greater, because the mind itself is overcome and subjects itself to itself when patience compels it to restrain itself within.

[Note: The first two Gem. read: “Better is the patient.” Laud., Belv., and the second Carnot. read “to be restrained” (*frenari*).]

Let the impatient hear what Truth says to his elect: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19). We have been wonderfully constituted in this way: reason possesses the soul, and the soul possesses the body. But the soul’s authority is driven from possession of the body if the soul is not first possessed by reason.

The Lord therefore showed that patience is the guardian of our constitution, since through it he taught us to possess ourselves. We thus recognize how great the fault of impatience is, since through it we lose even the possession of what we are.

Let the impatient hear what is again said through Solomon: “The fool pours out his whole spirit, but the wise person delays and reserves it for later” (Prov. XXIX, 11). When impatience drives him, a person acts so that his entire spirit is poured outward. Agitation expels it more quickly because no discipline of wisdom encloses it within. But the wise person delays and reserves it for later. When injured, he does not wish to avenge himself immediately, because, even while enduring, he desires to spare; nevertheless, he knows that all things will be justly avenged at the final judgment.

[Note: The first and third Carnot. read “to be judged.”]

The patient, on the other hand, must be admonished not to suffer inwardly from what they bear outwardly, lest they corrupt within by the plague of malice the sacrifice of so great a virtue which they offer outwardly intact. Even when their fault is not recognized by human beings, they still sin under divine scrutiny; and their fault of inward grief becomes worse insofar as they claim before human beings the appearance of virtue.

The patient must therefore be told to strive to love those whom they must endure. Otherwise, if love does not follow patience, the virtue displayed may turn into the more serious fault of hatred. Hence, when Paul said, “Charity is patient,” he immediately added, “It is kind” (I Cor. XIII, 4), showing that those whom charity tolerates through patience, it does not cease to love through kindness.

Thus the same distinguished teacher, when urging patience upon his disciples, says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be removed from you” (Eph. IV, 31). Then, as though he had already arranged everything outwardly well, he turns to the interior and adds: “Along with all malice” (Ibid.). For indignation, clamor, and blasphemy are removed from outward conduct in vain if malice, the mother of vices, rules within; and wickedness is cut away from the branches outwardly to no purpose if it is preserved inwardly in the root, where it will spring up more abundantly.

[Note: Trec., Laud., Rothom., Lyr., and the first two Gemet. read “if it is about to spring up more abundantly” (*si surrectura multiplicius*).]

Hence Truth himself also says: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Luke VI, 27). It is a virtue before human beings to tolerate adversaries; but it is a virtue before God to love them. For God accepts only that sacrifice which the flame of charity kindles before his eyes upon the altar of good works.

This is why he again says to certain people who were patient but did not love: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye but do not see the beam in your own eye?” (Matt. VII, 3; Luke VI, 41). The disturbance of impatience is the speck; malice in the heart is the beam in the eye. The former is stirred by the breeze of temptation, while the latter is borne almost immovably by consummate wickedness.

[Note: The first Carnot. reads “of the impatient.”]

The text rightly continues: “Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your eye, and then you will see to cast the speck out of your brother’s eye” (Ibid.). It is as though it were said to the wicked mind that suffers inwardly while displaying itself outwardly as holy through patience: “First shake the mass of malice from yourself, and then reproach others for the lightness of their impatience. Otherwise, because you do not strive to overcome your hypocrisy, it will be worse for you to tolerate the wickedness of another.”

It also often happens to the patient that, at the very time when they are suffering adversity or hearing insults, they are not troubled by pain at all. They display patience and do not fail to guard the innocence of their heart. But shortly afterward, when they recall what they have endured, they inflame themselves with the fire of pain, seek grounds for revenge, and, reconsidering the gentleness they displayed while enduring, turn it into malice.

A preacher can come to their aid more quickly if the cause of this change is disclosed. The crafty adversary wages war against two people: he inflames one so that he may first inflict insults, and provokes the other so that the injured person may return them. But often, after becoming victor over the one whom he has persuaded to inflict the injury, he is defeated by the one who bears the injury inflicted upon him with equanimity.

Having conquered one person by stirring him up and subduing him, the enemy rises with all his strength against the other. He grieves to see him resist stoutly and prevail. Since he could not move him during the very exchange of insults, he temporarily rests from open combat, harasses his thoughts by secret suggestion, and seeks a suitable time for deception.

For since he has lost the public battle, he burns to conduct an ambush in secret.

[Note: The first Carn. reads “because he did not lose the battle.” The better reading in the other manuscripts is “he lost,” that is, he was defeated, gave way, or fell from his purpose. The verb is often used absolutely in this sense, as in the preface to *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter III, no. 1, and in the preface to book XXVIII.]

During a time of quiet, he returns to the mind of the victor and recalls either losses of property or the weapons of insults. He greatly magnifies everything inflicted upon him and presents it as intolerable. He so disturbs the mind with grief that often the patient man, after his victory, is ashamed to have endured those things with equanimity, regrets not having returned the insults, and seeks an opportunity to repay them with worse ones.

To whom, then, are such people like except those who are victorious in the field through courage but are afterward captured within the walls of the city through negligence? To whom are they like except those whom a sudden grave illness does not remove from life, but whom a gently returning fever kills?

[Note: Longip. reads “a recurrent fever.”]

The patient must therefore be admonished to fortify the heart after victory, to watch the enemy defeated in public battle as he lays ambush within the walls of the mind, and to fear the illness that creeps back more greatly, lest the crafty enemy afterward rejoice with greater exultation in the deception, insofar as he tramples the stiff necks of those who had previously conquered him.

[Note: In Gemet., after correction: “to lay ambush in their minds.” Rothom., Lyr., and three Gemet. manuscripts read “returning” (*repetentem*) for “creeping back” (*reserpentem*).]

## CHAPTER X [formerly XXXIV]. How the kindly and the envious are to be admonished

### (Admonition 11)

The kindly are to be admonished in one way, and the envious in another. The kindly should rejoice in the good of others in such a way that they may desire to possess good of their own. They should praise the deeds of their neighbors with love in such a way that they may also multiply them by imitation. Otherwise, if in the arena of this present life they stand as devoted supporters but lazy spectators of another’s contest, they will remain without a prize after the contest because they do not labor in the contest now; and then, afflicted, they will behold the victory-palms of those in whose labors they now persist idly.

We commit a serious sin if we do not love the good deeds of others. But we earn no reward if we do not imitate, as far as we can, the things we love. The kindly must therefore be told that if they do not hasten to imitate the good things which they approve by praising them, then the holiness of the virtues pleases them in the same way that the vanity of theatrical arts pleases fools who merely watch.

Such people extol the performances of charioteers and actors with applause, yet do not wish to be like those whom they see and praise.

[Note: Rothom. and Lyr. read “with praises” (*laudibus*).] They admire that those performers have done what pleases them, but avoid pleasing others in the same way.

The kindly should be told that, when they see the deeds of their neighbors, they should return to their own heart and not presume upon the actions of others, lest they praise good deeds while refusing to perform them. Those who take pleasure in what they refuse to imitate will be struck by a more severe final punishment.

The envious must consider how great their blindness is: they are weakened by another’s advancement and wither away at another’s rejoicing.

[Note: Trec., Laud., Belvac., three Carnot. manuscripts, Theod., and the first two Gemet., agreeing with the old editions, read “rejoicing” (*exsultatione*). Gilot and newer editions read “exaltation” (*exaltatione*).] How miserable are those who become worse through the improvement of their neighbor, and who, when they see another’s prosperity increasing, are anxiously afflicted within themselves and die from the disease of their own heart. What could be more miserable than those whom another’s observed happiness afflicts and whom punishment makes more wicked?

If they loved the good things of others which they cannot possess, they would make them their own. All who stand in the faith are like many members in one body. Their functions are different, but through their mutual harmony they become one. Thus the foot sees through the eye, the eyes walk through the feet, hearing serves the mouth through the ears, and the tongue of the mouth joins with the ears for their use; the stomach is supported by the hands, and the hands work for the stomach.

In the very arrangement of the body, therefore, we understand what we should preserve in our conduct. It is exceedingly shameful not to imitate what we are. The things we love in others are truly ours, even if we cannot imitate them; and whatever we love becomes ours through our love.

Let the envious therefore consider how great a virtue charity is: it makes the works of another’s labor ours without labor on our part.

The envious must be told that, by failing to guard themselves against jealousy, they sink into the ancient wickedness of the crafty enemy. For it is written of him: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. II, 24). Because he himself lost heaven, he envied the human being who had been created, and, though already ruined, he increased his own condemnation by ruining others as well.

The envious must be admonished to recognize how many falls await the ruin that grows within them. For when they do not cast jealousy from their heart, they descend into open wickedness of conduct. If Cain had not envied his brother’s accepted sacrifice, he would never have gone so far as to extinguish his life.

Thus it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look. Cain was exceedingly angry, and his face fell” (Gen. IV, 4). Jealousy of the sacrifice was therefore the seedbed of fratricide. Cain grieved that the one whom he cut off was better than he, so that he might not exist at all.

[Note: The first two Gem. read “he tried.” Trec. and the others read “he cut off,” which, though difficult, we follow.]

The envious must be told that, while they consume themselves inwardly with this plague, they also destroy whatever other good they appear to possess. Hence it is written: “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. XIV, 30).

What is signified by flesh except certain weak and tender things, and what by bones except strong deeds? It often happens that some people, while innocent in heart, appear weak in several of their actions; others already perform certain deeds that appear strong before human eyes, yet inwardly waste away from the disease of envy toward the good of others.

It is therefore rightly said: “The health of the heart is the life of the flesh,” because, if innocence of mind is guarded, even things that are outwardly weak may eventually be strengthened. And rightly it is added: “Envy is the rottenness of the bones,” because through the vice of jealousy even what appears strong before human eyes perishes before the eyes of God. For bones rotting through envy means that even certain strong deeds are destroyed.

## CHAPTER XI [formerly XXXV]. How the simple and the devious are to be admonished

### (Admonition 12)

The simple are to be admonished in one way, and the impure in another. The simple should be praised because they strive never to speak falsely, but they must be admonished to understand that they should sometimes keep the truth silent. For just as falsehood always harms the one who speaks it, so truths that are heard sometimes harm certain people.

[Note: The same Gemet. manuscripts read “provokes” (*lacessit*).]

Hence, tempering his speech with silence before his disciples, the Lord says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John XVI, 12). The simple must therefore be admonished that, just as they always usefully avoid falsehood, so they should always usefully speak the truth.

They should be admonished to join prudence to the virtue of simplicity, so that they may possess the security of simplicity without losing the vigilance of prudence. Hence the teacher of the Gentiles says: “I want you to be wise in what is good and simple in what is evil” (Rom. XVI, 19). Hence Truth himself admonishes his elect, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. X, 16).

In the hearts of the elect, the craft of the serpent should sharpen the dove’s simplicity, and the dove’s simplicity should temper the serpent’s craft, so that they may neither become cunning through prudence nor grow sluggish in the pursuit of understanding through simplicity.

[Note: Corb., Carnot., Belv., Rothom., the first Aud., and Lyr. read “may become skilled in novel things through prudence” (*per prudentiam novi calleant*). Longip. reads *per prudentiam nova cal.* We follow Trec., Gemet., and others.]

The impure, on the other hand, must be admonished to recognize how great is the burden of duplicity which they endure along with their guilt. Because they fear being discovered, they are always seeking wicked defenses and are constantly harassed by fearful suspicions. Nothing is safer for defense than purity, and nothing easier for speech than truth. But when someone is compelled to protect his deception, his heart is exhausted by harsh labor.

[Note: Printed editions before Guss. read “falsehood” (*falsitatem*), against the English, Trec., Norman, and other manuscripts. Guss. and most printed editions read “tries” or “try” (*conatur* or *conantur*) for “is compelled” (*cogitur*), which is the reading of Corb., Trec., Laud., and others.]

Hence it is written: “The labor of their lips shall cover them” (Ps. CXXXIX, 10). What he now fills, he will then cover: what now wears out his mind through flattering agitation will then weigh upon it through harsh retribution.

[Note: Five English manuscripts read “now entangles,” with none of our manuscripts agreeing.]

Hence Jeremiah says: “They have taught their tongue to speak lies; they have labored to act wickedly” (Jer. IX, 5). It is as though it were said openly: Those who could have been friends of the truth without labor labor in order to sin; and, because they refuse to live simply, they impose labors upon themselves in order to die.

Often, when caught in guilt, they refuse to be recognized for what they are.

[Note: Trec., Carnot., and Belvac. read “they avoid knowing” (*cognoscere fugiunt*).] They hide themselves beneath a veil of deception and try to excuse what they are doing and what is already plainly visible. Thus the person who strives to rebuke their faults is often so misled by the clouds of falsehood they have spread that he nearly believes he has lost what he had already held as certain about them.

Hence, under the figure of Judea, the prophet rightly says against the soul that sins and excuses itself: “There the hedgehog had its den” (Isa. XXXIV, 15).

The hedgehog signifies the duplicity of an impure mind that cunningly defends itself. When a hedgehog is seized, its head, feet, and entire body can be seen; but as soon as it is caught, it gathers itself into a sphere, withdraws its feet inward, hides its head, and within the hands of the one holding it, everything that had previously been seen all at once disappears.

[Note: Trec., Belvac., and other ancient witnesses read “into a sphere” (*in speram*); we have already noted that *sphaeram* is so written in older codices.]

So, indeed, so are impure minds when they are caught in their transgressions. The hedgehog’s head is seen because the beginning by which the sinner approached his fault is visible. Its feet are seen because the tracks by which the wickedness was committed are recognized. Yet, when excuses are suddenly produced, the impure mind draws its feet inward, as it were, because it conceals every trace of its iniquity.

It withdraws its head because, through astonishing defenses, it does not even allow that it began some evil. And it remains like a sphere in the hand of the one holding it, because the person who rebukes, suddenly losing everything he had already understood, holds the sinner wrapped within his conscience; and he who had seen the whole matter by detecting it now knows nothing of it, deceived by the perverse evasions of the defense.

The hedgehog therefore has its den among the reprobate, because the duplicity of the malicious mind gathers itself within itself and hides in the darkness of its defense.

[Note: The first Carnot. reads “the duplicity of the doubled malicious mind.”]

Let the impure hear what is written: “He who walks simply walks securely” (Prov. X, 9). Simplicity of conduct is the confidence of great security. Let them hear what is said by the mouth of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. I, 5). Let them hear what Scripture again bears witness to: “With the simple is his conversation” (Prov. III, 32).

For God’s conversation means that, through the illumination of his presence, he reveals hidden things to human minds. He is said to converse with the simple because he illuminates with the ray of his visitation the minds of those whom no shadow of duplicity obscures.

Duplicity has a special evil: while deceiving others through perverse and double-dealing conduct, the duplicitous boast that they are wiser than everyone else; and because they do not consider the strictness of retribution, the wretched exult in their own ruin.

Let them hear how the prophet Zephaniah directs the force of divine judgment against them, saying:

> “Behold, the great and terrible day of the Lord is coming, a day of wrath, that day; a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and storm, a day of trumpet and blast against all fortified cities and against all the lofty corners” (Zeph. I, 14–15).

What is represented by fortified cities except suspicious minds, always surrounded by deceptive defenses, which, whenever their fault is rebuked, do not admit the darts of truth? And what is signified by lofty corners—for a corner always has two walls—except impure hearts? When they flee the simplicity of truth, they fold back upon themselves, as it were, through the perversity of duplicity; and, what is worse, in their own thoughts they exalt themselves in the pride of wisdom because of the very fault of their impurity.

The day of the Lord, therefore, full of vengeance and judgment, comes against fortified cities and lofty corners, because the anger of the final judgment destroys human hearts closed against the truth by their defenses and dissolves those wrapped in duplicity. Then the fortified cities fall, because minds impervious to God will be condemned.

[Note: This is the reading of Trec., Rothom., and other Norm. The third Carnot. reads “the unrepentant.” Almost all printed editions read “suspicious.”]

Then the lofty corners collapse, because hearts that raise themselves up through the prudence of impurity are cast down by the sentence of justice.

## CHAPTER XII [formerly XXXVI]. How the healthy and the sick are to be admonished

### (Admonition 13)

The healthy are to be admonished in one way, and the sick in another. The healthy should use the health of the body for the health of the mind, lest, if they incline the grace of the health they have received toward the use of wickedness, they become worse through the gift and afterward deserve heavier punishments, insofar as they now do not fear misusing God’s more abundant blessings.

The healthy must be admonished not to despise the opportunity of earning salvation forever. For it is written: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). They must be admonished lest, when they can please God, they refuse to do so, and then, when they wish to do so, be unable because it is too late.

Hence Wisdom abandons those whom she first called for a long time while they refused her, saying: “I called, and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was no one who looked; you despised all my counsel and neglected my reproofs. I too will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared comes upon you” (Prov. I, 24 ff.). And again: “Then they will call upon me, and I will not answer; they will rise early, and will not find me” (Ibid. 28).

How great a gift the health of the body is becomes known when, having been received for good works, it is despised and lost. What was not usefully possessed at the proper time is sought at the end, but without profit.

Hence Solomon again says: “Do not give your honor to strangers, nor your years to the cruel, lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your labors be in another’s house, and you groan at the end, when your flesh and body have been consumed” (Ibid. V, 9 ff.).

Who are those who are strangers to us except the evil spirits, who have been separated from a share in the heavenly homeland? And who is the cruel one except that apostate angel who, through his pride, struck himself with the punishment of death and, though ruined, did not spare the human race from bringing death upon it?

He therefore gives his honor to strangers who, having been created in the image and likeness of God, devote the time of his life to the pleasures of the evil spirits.

[Note: Gilot. and other recent editions, the sense seemingly requiring it, read “to the will of the evil spirits,” whereas the old edition and nearly all our manuscripts—namely Trec., Laud., Belv., Corb., Carnot., and the first two Gemet.—have “to the pleasures.” He calls “the pleasures of the evil spirits” those things which they suggest and offer. Shortly afterward Laud., Corb., Belvac., and the second Carnot. also read “to pleasure”; Trec. and the others differ. “Pleasure” may also be understood as “good pleasure” or “will,” which seems to be the same as “voluntas.”]

He also gives his years to the cruel one who spends the time of life granted to him according to the will of his wicked ruler and adversary.

The text rightly adds: “Lest strangers be filled with your strength, and your labors be in another’s house.” Whoever, through the health of body granted to him and the wisdom of mind bestowed upon him, labors not to exercise virtues but to commit vices, does not increase his own house by his own strength, but the dwelling places of strangers—that is, those made by unclean spirits. He acts either through lust or through pride, so that, by adding himself, he increases the number of the lost.

The text rightly adds: “And you groan at the end, when your flesh and body have been consumed.” Often the health of the flesh that has been received is spent in vices; but when it is suddenly taken away, when the flesh is worn down by afflictions, and when the soul is already being forced to depart, the health that was long possessed badly is sought, now lost, as a means of living well.

[Note: The second Carnot. reads “is extended.”]

Then people groan because they refused to serve God, when by serving him they can no longer recover the losses caused by their negligence. Hence it is said elsewhere: “When he slew them, then they sought him” (Ps. LXXVII, 34).

On the other hand, the sick are to be admonished to recognize themselves as sons of God precisely insofar as the scourges of discipline chastise them. For unless he intended to give an inheritance to those whom he corrects, he would not take care to instruct them through afflictions. Hence the Lord says to John through the angel: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise” (Apoc. 3:19; Prov. 3:11). Again, it is written: “My son, do not neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him. For the Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:5–6). Hence the Psalmist says: “Many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from all these” (Ps. 33:20).

[Note: The Trecaine, Gemeticensis, Vallicellian, Theodulphian, and many other excellent manuscripts do not have the final part of this verse.]

Blessed Job too, crying out in his pain, says: “If I am righteous, I will not lift up my head, being filled with affliction and misery” (Job 10:15). The sick should be told that, if they believe the heavenly homeland to be theirs, they must necessarily suffer hardships in this life as in a foreign land. This is why stones were hewn outside, so that they might be set into the construction of the Lord’s temple without the sound of a hammer: for now we are hewn outside by scourges, so that afterward we may be fitted inside—[Note: Laudian manuscript: “in the temple.”]—into the temple of God without the blows of discipline. Thus whatever is superfluous in us may now be cut away by the blows, and then only the harmony of charity may bind us together in the building.

The sick should be admonished to consider how harshly the scourges of discipline chastise bodily children for the sake of receiving earthly inheritances. [Note: The first Carnotian manuscript: “Ask us, therefore.”] What punishment of divine correction, then, can be severe for us, when through it an inheritance that can never be lost is obtained and punishments that will endure forever are avoided? Hence Paul says: “We had the fathers of our flesh as instructors, and we revered them; shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits, and live? For they indeed instructed us for a few days according to their own will, but he does so for what is useful, so that we may receive his sanctification” (Heb. 12:9–10). [Note: The printed editions read “shall we not much more”; Troyes, Beauvais, Chartres, and many others, with the same sense, simply read “not much more.”]

[Col. 0068C]

The sick should be admonished to consider how great a salvation of the heart bodily affliction is: it recalls the mind to self-knowledge, and restores the memory of the weakness that good health very often drives away, so that the soul, which is led outside itself into pride, may remember from the stricken flesh it endures to what condition it is subject. [Note: Thus read Troyes, the Chartres manuscripts, and others. All the editors, reading *memoria* (“memory”), corrupted the sense. The bodily affliction is said to restore the memory of weakness which very good health often drives away.]

This is aptly signified by Balaam—provided, that is, that he had been willing to obey by following God’s voice—in the very delaying of his journey (Num. 22:23 ff.). Balaam is striving to reach his intended goal, but his purpose is impeded by the animal over which he presides. For while the she-ass lingers because of the prohibition, it sees the angel whom the human mind does not see. Thus often the flesh, delayed by afflictions, makes God known to the mind through its scourge, although the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, had not seen him. In this way it impedes the anxiety of the spirit that desires to advance in this world, as though journeying along a road, until the invisible one who confronts it becomes known to it.

Hence Peter rightly says: “He received correction for his madness: a dumb beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s folly” (2 Pet. 2:15). A madman is rebuked by a dumb beast of burden when the afflicted flesh reminds the proud mind of the good of humility that it ought to possess. But Balaam did not obtain the gift of this correction because, while proceeding to pronounce a curse, he changed his voice, not his mind.

The sick should be admonished to consider how great a gift bodily affliction is: it both washes away sins already committed and restrains those that might have been committed; taken from outward blows, it inflicts the wounds of repentance upon the shaken mind. Hence it is written: “The bruise of a wound wipes away evils, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. 20:30). [Note: The Gemeticensis has “and a blow.”]

The bruise of a wound wipes away evils because the pain of scourging cleanses either contemplated or perpetrated wickedness. The belly commonly signifies the mind, for just as the belly consumes food, so the mind, by pondering, digests its cares. That the belly signifies the mind is taught by the saying: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of man, searching all the hidden parts of the belly” (ibid.). It is as though he said: When the illumination of divine inspiration enters the human mind, it illuminates it for itself and shows it what, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, it had been able to carry but did not know how to weigh.

Therefore, “the bruise of a wound wipes away evils, and blows reach the innermost parts of the belly”: when we are struck outwardly, we are silently and sorrowfully recalled to the memory of our sins; we bring before our eyes all the things we have done wrongly; and through what we suffer outwardly, we grieve more deeply within over what we have done. Thus, amid the visible wounds of the body, the hidden wound of the belly cleanses us more thoroughly, because the secret wound of sorrow heals the wickedness of evil deeds.

The sick should be admonished to preserve the virtue of patience, continually considering how many evils our Redeemer endured from those whom he had created: how many rejected insults and disgraces he bore; how, daily snatching captive souls from the hand of the ancient enemy, he received the blows of those who mocked him; how, washing us with the water of salvation, he did not hide his face from the spittle of the faithless; how, freeing us from eternal punishments by his advocacy, he silently endured scourges; [Note: All printed editions, against the English and our manuscripts, read “by his calling.” The point is that, as John teaches, Christ is our advocate with the Father.] how, granting us everlasting honors among the choirs of angels, he endured blows on the cheek; how, saving us from the pricks of sins, he did not refuse to submit his head to thorns; how, intoxicating us with eternal sweetness, he accepted the bitterness of gall in his thirst; how he, who worshiped the Father for us, although equal to him in divinity, remained silent when worshiped in mockery; how, preparing life for the dead, he himself, Life, went even unto death.

Why, then, is it thought harsh that a human being should endure scourges from God for evil deeds, if God endured such evils from human beings for the sake of good? Or who, with sound understanding, could be ungrateful for being struck, if he did not leave this life without scourging—the one who lived here without sin?

## CHAPTER XIII [Elsewhere XXXVII]

### How those who fear scourges and those who despise them are to be admonished

[Col. 0070A]

**Admonition 14.** Those who fear scourges and therefore live innocently are to be admonished in one way, and those who have persisted in iniquity so that they are not corrected even by scourges in another. Those who fear scourges should be told neither to desire temporal goods as something very great—for they see that even the wicked possess them—nor to flee present evils as though they were intolerable, since they know that even the good here are often afflicted by them.

They should be admonished that, if they truly desire to be free from evils, they must dread eternal punishments; yet they must not remain in this fear of punishment, but grow toward the grace of love through the nourishment of charity. For it is written: “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Again it is written: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15). Hence the same teacher says again: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

If, therefore, punishment still prevents someone from a wrongful action through fear, plainly no freedom of the spirit possesses the soul of the one who fears. For if he did not fear the punishment, he would undoubtedly commit the sin. The mind therefore does not know the grace of freedom when it is bound by the slavery of fear. Good things are to be loved for their own sake, not performed under compulsion from punishments. For one who does good because he fears the evils of torments wishes that there were nothing for him to fear, so that he might boldly commit unlawful acts. Thus it is clearer than daylight that innocence is lost before God, before whose eyes sin is committed in desire.

On the other hand, those whom not even scourges restrain from iniquities are to be struck with all the sharper denunciation, the more deeply they have hardened through their insensibility. Often they must be despised without contempt, and despaired of without despair—that is, in such a way that the expressed despair may instill fear, while the admonition that follows may restore them to hope.

Strict divine judgments must therefore be pronounced against them, so that, by considering eternal punishment, they may be recalled to self-knowledge. Let them hear that what is written has been fulfilled in them: “Though you pound a fool in a mortar, as though pounding grain with a pestle, his folly will not depart from him” (Prov. 27:22).

Against such people the prophet complains to the Lord, saying: “You have struck them, and they refused to receive discipline” (Jer. 5:3). Hence the Lord says: “I struck and destroyed this people, yet they did not return from their ways” (Isa. 9:13). Again he says: “The people did not return to the one who struck them” (Jer. 15:6). Through the voice of those who scourge, the prophet complains, saying: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9).

Babylon is treated, yet is not restored to health, when a mind confused in wrongful action hears words of correction and receives the scourges of correction, yet refuses to return to the right paths of salvation.

Hence the Lord reproaches the captive Israelite people, who nevertheless had not turned away from iniquity, saying: “The house of Israel has become dross to me; all these are bronze, tin, and iron, and lead in the midst of the furnace” (Ezek. 22:18). [Note: Here and below Troyes, Corbie, Laudian, and Gemeticensis consistently read *stagnum* (“tin”), in place of *stannum* (“tin”).]

It is as though he plainly said: “I wished to purify them through the fire of tribulation, and sought to make them silver or gold; but in the furnace they have become bronze, tin, iron, and lead to me, because even in tribulation they broke out not into virtue but into vices.”

When bronze is struck, it makes a louder sound than the other metals. Whoever, therefore, while placed in the blows, bursts into the sound of grumbling has become bronze in the midst of the furnace. Tin, when fashioned by art, imitates the appearance of silver. Whoever in tribulation is not free from the vice of hypocrisy has become tin in the furnace. One who lies in wait for his neighbor’s life uses iron. Iron in the furnace, therefore, is the person who does not abandon his malicious desire to harm in tribulation. Lead is heavier than the other metals. Lead is therefore found in the furnace in the one so weighed down by the burden of his sin that, even while in tribulation, he is not lifted from earthly desires. [Note: The Gemeticensis and other Norman manuscripts, together with the third Carnotian manuscript, read: “is not lifted toward eternal desires.”]

Again it is written: “Much labor was expended upon it, yet its excessive rust did not come out of it, not even through the fire” (Ezek. 24:12). [Note: Corbie reads “from it”; Laudian reads “from the furnace.”] He applies to us the fire of tribulation so that the rust of vices may be purified in us; but we do not lose our rust through the fire when, even amid scourges, we remain burdened by vice. [Note: The Trecaine, Corbie, Laudian, Gemeticensis, and other Norman manuscripts read: “so that he may purify in us.”] Hence the Prophet says again: “The smelter has smelted in vain; their wickednesses have not been consumed” (Jer. 6:29).

[Col. 0071C]

It must be understood, however, that sometimes, when people remain uncorrected amid the harshness of scourges, they should be soothed by gentle admonition. Those whom sufferings do not correct are sometimes restrained from wrongful actions by gentle blandishments. For often the sick whom a strong potion of [Note: The first Carnotian manuscript reads *purgamentorum* (“of purgatives”); were we not compelled by Troyes and the other manuscripts to prefer *pigmentorum* (“of medicinal compounds”), we would follow that reading.] medicines could not cure have been restored to their former health by tepid water; and some wounds that cannot be cured by incision are healed by applications of oil.

The adamant stone [Note: The Trecaine, the two earlier Gemeticensis manuscripts, and the oldest manuscript read “adamant.” The Laudian has “does not receive at all”; an excellent reading, namely, that adamant does not tolerate even the slightest incision of iron.] does not receive an incision from iron at all, but softens under the gentle blood of goats.

## CHAPTER XIV [Elsewhere XXXVIII]

### How the taciturn and the talkative are to be admonished

**Admonition 15.** Those who are excessively taciturn are to be admonished in one way, and those who devote themselves to excessive talk in another.

The excessively taciturn should be made to understand that, while they carelessly avoid certain vices, they become secretly entangled in worse ones. Often, because they restrain their tongue too severely, they endure more grievous loquacity in their hearts. Their thoughts burn more intensely in the mind because violent custody constricts them within indiscreet silence. These thoughts usually spread all the more widely because they consider themselves safer, since they are not seen outwardly by those who might rebuke them.

Thus the mind sometimes becomes inflated with pride and despises those whom it hears speaking as though they were weak. When it closes the mouth of the body, it does not recognize how widely it opens itself to vices through pride. It presses down the tongue and raises up the mind; and, since it gives no consideration to its own wickedness, it accuses everyone else all the more freely—and secretly.

The excessively taciturn should therefore be admonished to take careful pains to know not only what sort of people they appear outwardly, but also what sort of people they ought to show themselves inwardly, so that they may fear the hidden judgment of their thoughts more than the reproach of their neighbors’ words. For it is written: “My son, attend to my wisdom and incline your ear to my prudence, so that you may guard your thoughts” (Prov. 5:1).

Nothing in us is more fleeting than the heart, which departs from us as often as it flows away through evil thoughts. Hence the Psalmist says: “My heart has forsaken me” (Ps. 39:13). Returning to himself, he says: “Your servant has found his heart, that he might pray to you” (2 Sam. 7:27). When thought is restrained by vigilance, therefore, the heart that was accustomed to flee is found.

Often, when the excessively taciturn suffer some injustices, they fall into sharper pain because they do not speak of what they endure. For if the tongue calmly expressed the troubles inflicted, the pain would flow out of the conscience. [Note: Corbie, Laudian, Beauvais, and the second Chartres manuscript read: “the mind would remain free from the pain of conscience.” Beauvais and the second Chartres manuscript have *maneret* for *manaret*, through a scribal error. We follow Troyes and the other manuscripts.] Wounds cause more torment when they are closed. When the corruption that seethes within is expelled, pain is opened toward healing.

Those who are more silent than is fitting should therefore know that, amid the troubles they endure, they may increase the force of their pain by holding back their tongue. They should be admonished that, if they love their neighbors as themselves, they should not remain silent about the matters for which they rightly rebuke them. By the medicine of the voice, the welfare of both is advanced: the wrongful action is restrained in the one who commits it, and the heat of pain is moderated through an opened wound in the one who suffers it.

Those who see the evils of their neighbors yet press down their tongue in silence are like people who, after seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine. They become the authors of death precisely because they refuse to cure the disease they could have healed. The tongue must therefore be restrained with discretion, not bound with an unbreakable fetter. For it is written: “The wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclus. 20:7), so that, when he recognizes the appropriate moment, setting aside the discipline of silence, he may devote himself to useful service by speaking what is fitting.

Again it is written: “A time to be silent, and a time to speak” (Eccl. 3:7). The times of alternation must be weighed with discretion, lest the tongue flow uselessly in words when it ought to be restrained, or sluggishly restrain itself when it can speak profitably. Considering this well, the Psalmist says: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door around my lips” (Ps. 140:3). He does not ask that a wall be placed over his mouth, but a door, which can be opened and closed. We too must therefore learn carefully that a discreet mouth should be opened by speech at the proper time and closed again by silence at the proper time.

On the other hand, those who devote themselves to excessive talk should vigilantly observe how far they decline from the state of uprightness while they dissipate themselves through many words. The human mind, like confined water, gathers itself upward because it returns to the place from which it descended; but when released, it wastes away because it spreads itself uselessly through the lowest places. [Note: The English manuscripts read “like enclosed water.” Troyes, Beauvais, the three Chartres manuscripts, Rouen, and Lyre support the reading followed here.]

As many superfluous words as dissipate it from the discipline of silence, so many streams carry it outside itself. Hence it cannot sufficiently return inward to self-knowledge, because, scattered through excessive talk, it excludes itself from the secret interior of contemplation. It exposes itself wholly to the wounds of the ambushing enemy because it surrounds itself with no defensive guard. Therefore it is written: “Like an open city without a circuit of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28).

Because it lacks the wall of silence, the city of the mind lies open to the enemy’s arrows; and when it casts itself outside itself through words, it reveals itself as open to its adversary. The enemy conquers it with as little effort as the one being overcome fights against itself through excessive talk.

Often, because the slothful mind is driven into a fall through various stages, while we neglect to avoid idle words we reach harmful ones. First we take pleasure in speaking about other people; then we wound the lives of those about whom we speak through detraction; finally the tongue bursts out into open insults. From this come the sowing of goads, the rise of quarrels, the kindling of hatred’s torches, and the extinguishing of peace in hearts.

Hence Solomon rightly says: “He who releases water is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. 17:14). To release water is to loosen the tongue into a flow of speech. Conversely, in a good sense it is said again: “Deep water is the word from a man’s mouth” (ibid. 18:4). He who releases water is the beginning of quarrels because one who does not bridle the tongue destroys harmony.

Conversely, it is written: “He who imposes silence on a fool calms anger” (ibid. 26:10). [Note: Beauvais and the two earlier Chartres manuscripts read: “it will happen that one serving excessive talk will be unable to bridle his tongue, so as to maintain the rectitude,” etc.] That one who serves excessive talk cannot maintain the rectitude of justice is attested by the Prophet, who says: “The man of a talkative tongue will not be established upon the earth” (Ps. 139:12). Solomon also says again: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 10:19). Isaiah says: “The service of justice is silence” (Isa. 32:17), indicating that the justice of the mind is laid waste when immoderate speech is not restrained.

James says: “If anyone thinks that he is religious, yet does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, his religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26). Again he says: “Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak” (ibid. 1:19). Again, defining the power of the tongue, he adds: “An unquiet evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 2:8).

Truth itself admonishes us, saying: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). An idle word is one that lacks either the reason of just necessity or the intention of devout usefulness. If an account is demanded even for idle speech, let us consider what punishment awaits excessive talk, in which sin is also committed through harmful words.

## CHAPTER XV [Elsewhere XXXIX]

### How the sluggish and the hasty are to be admonished

[Col. 0074B]

**Admonition 16.** The sluggish are to be admonished in one way, and the hasty in another. The sluggish must be persuaded not to lose the good things they ought to do by delaying them; the hasty must be warned not to alter the merit of good deeds by carelessly anticipating their proper time.

The sluggish should therefore be told that often, while we refuse to do at the proper time what we can do, shortly afterward, when we wish to do it, we are unable. The sloth of the mind, when it is not kindled with appropriate fervor, is secretly slaughtered by increasing torpor and completely removed from the desire for good things. Hence Solomon plainly says: “Sloth sends sleep” (Prov. 19:15).

The sluggish person is awake, as it were, through right thinking, although he grows numb by doing nothing. Yet sloth is said to send sleep because, when one ceases from the pursuit of good action, even the vigilance of right thinking is gradually lost. [Note: The Belvacian, Corbie, Theodulphian, and the two earlier Carnotian manuscripts read “through thinking rightly.” This reading does not conflict with the correct sense if it is read as follows: “because, while ceasing from doing good, even the vigilance of thinking rightly is lost.” It is not enough to think rightly unless we do good; when this is neglected, vigilance is lost. The reading we follow is found in the Trecaine, Gemeticensis, and others.]

The text rightly adds: “And the slack soul will hunger” (ibid.). Because it does not direct itself upward by constraining itself, it spreads itself downward through desires once it has been neglected; and, because it is not restrained by the strength of lofty pursuits, it is wounded by the hunger of low desire. Thus, to the extent that it refuses to bind itself through discipline, it spreads itself hungrily through the desires of pleasure. [Note: The Laudian and first Carnotian manuscripts read “wounded by the sharpness of feeble hunger.” The Belvacian and second Carnotian have, in addition, “by the sharpness,” followed by the words “or its hunger is increased.”]

Again Solomon writes: “The idle person is entirely given to desires” (Prov. 21:26). Again, when Truth itself preaches (Matt. 12:44–45), a house is said to be clean when one spirit has gone out, but to be occupied more fully when it lies empty.

Often, while the sluggish person neglects to do what is necessary, he puts certain difficulties before himself and heedlessly fears others. When he seems to find something that he may justly fear, he shows that he is not unjustly growing numb in idleness. Solomon rightly says to him: “Because of the cold the sluggard would not plow; therefore he will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him” (Prov. 20:4).

Because of the cold the sluggard does not plow when, bound by the torpor of sloth, he refuses to do the good things he ought to do. [Note: The Norman and Carnotian manuscripts read: “when, bound by the sloth and torpor.”] Because of the cold the sluggard does not plow when he fears minor evils on the way and neglects to undertake great works.

It is rightly added: “He will beg in summer, and nothing will be given to him.” One who does not sweat now in good works will beg in summer, when the sun of judgment appears with greater heat, asking in vain for entry into the kingdom and receiving nothing.

Again Solomon rightly says to him: “He who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap” (Eccl. 11:4). What is signified by the wind except the temptation of evil spirits? And what is signified by the clouds moved by the wind except the adversities of wicked people? [Note: That is, the assaults and attacks of hostile wicked people. For the meaning of this expression in Gregory, see Book II of the Moralia, no. 51.]

The clouds are driven by the winds because wicked people are stirred up by the breath of unclean spirits. Therefore, “he who watches the wind will not sow, and he who considers the clouds will never reap”: whoever fears the temptation of evil spirits and whoever fears the persecution of wicked people neither sows the seeds of good work now nor cuts the sheaves of holy recompense then.

On the other hand, the hasty, by anticipating the proper time of good actions, pervert their merit; and they often fall into evils because they do not properly distinguish good things. They do not examine what they should do and when they should do it, but often recognize only afterward that they ought not to have acted as they did.

To them, under the figure of a hearer, Solomon rightly says: [Note: Here the holy doctor expressly attributes the book of Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, though elsewhere he often calls its author merely a certain wise man. See *Moralia* VII, no. 45; XX, no. 51; XXVII, no. 53; XXXIII, no. 23. Below, in Admonition 22, Solomon is, according to some excellent manuscripts, named as the writer of this sacred book. See the note there.] “My son, do nothing without counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” (Ecclus. 32:24). Again: “Let your eyelids go before your steps” (Prov. 4:25). The eyelids go before the steps when right counsels precede our action. Whoever neglects to foresee through consideration what he is doing advances with closed eyes; he completes the journey by proceeding, but does not go before himself through foresight. Therefore he falls more quickly, because he does not attend through the eyelid of counsel to where he ought to place the foot of his action.

## CHAPTER XVI [Elsewhere XL]

### How the gentle and the angry are to be admonished

**Admonition 17.** The gentle are to be admonished in one way, and the angry in another. Sometimes, when the gentle are placed in authority, they suffer the torpor of sloth, which lies close beside them, as it were. Often, through an excessive relaxation of gentleness, they soften the strength of strictness beyond what is necessary.

On the other hand, when angry people receive positions of authority, the farther anger drives them into madness of mind, the more they disturb the lives of their subjects by destroying the tranquillity of peace.
