When fury drives them headlong, they do not know what they do in anger, nor do they know what they suffer from themselves while angry. Sometimes, and this is more serious, they regard the goad of their anger as zeal for justice. When vice is believed to be virtue, guilt accumulates without fear.

The gentle therefore often grow numb through the weariness of laxity; the angry are often deceived by what they take to be zeal for uprightness. A vice is secretly joined to the virtue of the former, while to the latter their own vice appears like a fervent virtue.

The gentle should therefore be admonished to flee what lies beside them; the angry should attend to what lies within them. The gentle should discern what they lack, and the angry should embrace what they possess. [Note: The second Carnotian, Corbie, Longpont, Rouen, Lyre, and third Gemeticensis manuscripts read: “Let these embrace what they possess.” The gentle should condemn their torpor through vigilance, and the angry their disturbance. The first Carnotian likewise has “what they possess,” with *ut* added before “torpor.” The Laudian, Belvacian, and third Carnotian read: “Let the gentle discern what they possess, and the angry embrace what they lack. Let the gentle condemn their torpor through vigilance.” The two earlier Gemeticensis manuscripts read: “Let the gentle condemn torpor instead of vigilance.” We follow the Trecaine together with all the printed editions.]

Let the gentle embrace vigilance, and let the angry condemn disturbance. The gentle should be admonished to cultivate zeal for justice as well; the angry should be admonished to join gentleness to the zeal they believe themselves to possess. For this reason the Holy Spirit has been shown to us both in a dove and in fire: he makes all whom he fills gentle with the simplicity of a dove and burning with the fire of zeal.

No one, therefore, is filled with the Holy Spirit who either abandons the fervor of zeal in the tranquillity of gentleness or again loses the virtue of gentleness in the ardor of zeal.

Perhaps we can show this more clearly by bringing forward Paul’s teaching. Although he possessed two disciples endowed with the same charity, he gave them different forms of instruction. Advising Timothy, he says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. 4:2). He also admonishes Titus, saying: “Speak these things, exhort, and rebuke with all authority” (Tit. 2:15).

Why does he distribute his teaching with such skill that, in presenting it, [Note: Beauvais and the second Chartres manuscript read “in order to exhibit these things.”] he proposes authority to one and patience to the other, unless he saw Titus to possess the gentler spirit and Timothy the somewhat more fervent one? He inflames the former through zeal, and moderates the latter through the gentleness of patience. He joins to one what he lacks and takes away from the other what he has in excess. He attempts to drive one forward with a goad and restrains the other with a bridle.

He is truly the great cultivator of the Church he has undertaken: he waters some branches so that they may grow; when he sees others growing more than is proper, he cuts them back, lest either, by not growing, they fail to bear fruit, or, by growing excessively, they lose what they have produced.

But one kind of anger is that which creeps in under the appearance of zeal, and another is that which confuses the disturbed heart without any pretext of justice. The former extends itself disorderly in what it ought to do; the latter is always inflamed by what it ought not to do.

It must be understood that angry people differ from the impatient in this respect: the impatient do not tolerate what is inflicted upon them by others, whereas the angry inflict even what should be tolerated. For angry people often pursue even those who withdraw from them, provoke occasions for quarrels, and take pleasure in the labor of contention. Yet we correct them better if, during the very disturbance of their anger, we withdraw from them.

When disturbed, they do not know what they are hearing; but once they have returned to themselves, they receive words of exhortation more freely because they are ashamed that they were tolerated so calmly. [Note: Gemeticensis and many Norman manuscripts read “all the more willingly.”] To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears wrong. Thus Abigail commendably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and commendably spoke of it when the wine had passed (1 Sam. 25:37). He was able to recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard of it while drunk.

When angry people attack others in such a way that they cannot be avoided at all, they must be struck not by open reproach but with a certain caution, sparing them out of reverence.

We can show this more clearly by bringing forward the deed of Abner. When Asahel attacked him with the force of reckless haste, it is written: “Abner spoke to Asahel, saying: ‘Withdraw; do not pursue me, lest I be forced to strike you down to the ground.’ But he scorned listening and refused to withdraw. Therefore Abner struck him with the back of his spear in the groin, pierced him through, and he died” (2 Sam. 2:22–23).

Whom did Asahel typify except those whom violent fury seizes and drives headlong? They must be avoided in the same impulse of fury with as much caution as they are madly carried away.

Hence Abner—whose name in our language is said to mean “lamp of the father”—fled. The tongue of teachers, which points out the light from above, when it sees someone’s mind being carried through the precipices of fury, and when it refrains from returning the darts of words against the angry person, does not wish to strike the one who pursues it.

But when angry people do not moderate themselves through any reflection and, like Asahel, do not cease pursuing and raging, those who strive to restrain them must not raise themselves up in anger but must display whatever tranquillity they possess. They should bring forward certain subtle remarks by which, indirectly, they may prick the mind of the raging person.

Thus, when Abner stood against his pursuer, he did not pierce him with the point of the spear but with its reverse. To strike with the point of the spear is to meet someone with the force of open rebuke. To strike a pursuer with the back of the spear is to touch the raging person calmly in certain ways and, as though sparing him, to overcome him.

Asahel immediately fell, because disturbed minds, while they sense that they are being spared and yet are touched inwardly under tranquillity by the reasoning of the replies, fall at once from what they had raised up. Those who recoil from the force of their fury under a blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron. [Note: The printed editions read “from the impulse of their fury,” against both the English manuscripts and ours; the manuscripts read “from the impulse of their fervor.”]

## CHAPTER XVII [Elsewhere XLI]

### How the humble and the proud are to be admonished
(Admonition 18.) The humble must be admonished in one way, and the proud in another. To the humble it should be made clear how genuine is the excellence they hold by hope; to the proud, how worthless is temporal glory, which they embrace but do not possess. Let the humble hear how enduring are the things they seek, and how fleeting those they despise; let the proud hear how fleeting are the things they pursue, and how enduring those they lose. Let the humble hear from the authoritative voice of Truth: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14); let the proud hear: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (ibid.). Let the humble hear: “Humility precedes glory”; let the proud hear: “The spirit is exalted before a fall” (Prov. 15:33; 16:18). Let the humble hear: “Upon whom shall I look, unless upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2); let the proud hear: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Sir. 10:9). Let the humble hear: “God regards the lowly”; let the proud hear: “But the lofty he knows from afar” (Ps. 137:6). Let the humble hear that “the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20:28); let the proud hear that “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sir. 10:15). Let the humble hear that “our Redeemer humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8); let the proud hear what is written of their head: “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25).

Thus the occasion of our destruction was the devil’s pride, while the means of our redemption was found in God’s humility. For our enemy, created among all things, wished to appear exalted above all things; but our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become little among all things.

[Note: On this manner of expression, familiar to Gregory, see Moral. XV.20; XVI.37, and elsewhere.]

Let the humble therefore be told that, by casting themselves down, they rise to the likeness of God; let the proud be told that, by raising themselves up, they fall in imitation of the apostate angel. For what is more abject than pride, which, by reaching above itself, is separated from the height of true exaltation? And what is more exalted than humility, which, by lowering itself into the depths, joins itself to its Creator, who remains above all things?

Yet another matter must be carefully weighed in their case, because some are often deceived by the appearance of humility, while others are misled by their ignorance of their own pride. For often, in certain people who seem humble to themselves, there is joined to humility a fear that ought not to be shown toward human beings; while the proud are often accompanied by an assertion expressed in an unrestrained voice. When certain faults ought to be rebuked, the former remain silent out of fear, yet think that they are silent out of humility; the latter speak through the impatience of pride, yet believe that they speak through the freedom of uprightness. In the former, guilt born of fear suppresses them under the appearance of humility, lest they rebuke what is wrong; in the latter, the unbridled impulse of arrogance drives them, under the guise of freedom, to rebuke what they ought not to rebuke, or to rebuke more severely than they ought.

[Note: Gratian, citing this passage, gives not the words but the sense.]

Accordingly, the proud must be admonished (II, question 7, chapter “Admonendi”) not to be freer than is proper, and the humble must be admonished not to be more submissive than is useful. Otherwise the former may turn the defense of justice into an exercise of pride, while the latter, by striving to submit themselves to people more than is necessary, may be compelled even to revere their vices.

It must also be considered that we often correct the proud more effectively if we mingle with their reproofs certain incentives of praise. We should mention either other good qualities that are in them, or at least what they could possess if they do not; and only then should we cut away the evils that displease us, once the good things that please them have first made their minds receptive to listening. We first touch untamed horses with a gentle hand, so that afterward, even through blows, we may bring them more fully under control. Honey is added to a bitter medicinal draught, so that what will contribute to health may not be felt as harshly bitter at the moment of tasting; while the taste is deceived by sweetness, the deadly liquid is expelled through bitterness.

[Note: Laudunensis and the second manuscript of Gemeticum read “deadly moisture.” The same is also found in the first Gemeticum, but by a second hand.]

Thus the opening words of an attack upon the proud should be tempered by mingled praise, so that, while they admit the approval they love, they may also accept the corrections they hate.

We can often persuade the proud of what is useful more effectively if we say that their improvement will benefit us rather than themselves, and if we ask that their betterment be undertaken for our sake more than for theirs.

[Note: Laudunensis, Longipontanus, Vallis Clara, the first two Gemetica, and the third Carnotensis read “moderation.”]

Pride is easily bent toward what is good if its being bent is believed to benefit others as well. Thus Moses, who, under God’s direction, was traveling through the wilderness with the aerial pillar as his guide, wished to lead his kinsman Hobab away from the company of the Gentiles and subject him to the dominion of almighty God:

“We are setting out for the place that the Lord will give us; come with us, and we will do you good, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel.”

When Hobab replied to him, “I will not go with you, but I will return to my own land, in which I was born,” Moses immediately added:

“Do not leave us; for you know in what places in the wilderness we ought to camp, and you will be our guide” (Num. 10:29 ff.).

[Note: Some copies read “Jethro.” The Corbie manuscript has both readings.]

Moses was not distressed by ignorance of the route: knowledge of God had expanded him to prophetic understanding; the column went before him outwardly; and inwardly, through his constant fellowship with God, familiar speech instructed him concerning everything. Rather, this prudent man, speaking to a proud listener, asked for assistance so that he might give it; he sought a guide on the road so that the other might become a guide to him unto life. He therefore acted so that the proud listener might become all the more devoted to the voice persuading him toward better things because he was thought necessary; and so that, from believing himself to precede his exhorter, he might instead bow beneath the words of the one exhorting him.

[Note: Laudunensis, Rotomagensis, and Lyra read “to prophetic knowledge.” In Trecensis, Corbeiensis, and most manuscripts the reading is “whom,” referring to Moses’s mind, rather than “which.”]

CHAPTER XXIII [Elsewhere XLII]. How the obstinate and the fickle are to be admonished

[Admonition 19.] The obstinate must be admonished in one way, and the fickle in another. The former must be told that they think more highly of themselves than they are, and therefore do not accept the advice of others; the latter must be made to understand that, because they despise themselves excessively, they neglect themselves, and therefore are bent from their own judgment from moment to moment by the fickleness of their thoughts. The former must be told that, unless they considered themselves better than others, they would never place the counsels of all others below their own deliberation; the latter must be told that, if they paid some attention to what they are, the wind of change would never toss them about along so many shores of variation.

[Note: Most printed editions have “the shores of variety,” a reading whose source in the manuscripts is unknown. Shortly afterward they read “the fruits of his vineyard” instead of “the fruits of his way.” The Hebrew text, its versions, and the manuscripts of Saint Gregory require the reading “the fruits of his way.”]

Paul says of the obstinate: “Do not be wise in your own estimation” (Rom. 12:16); while the fickle hear: “Let us not be carried about by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. 4:14). Of the former it is said through Solomon: “They shall eat the fruit of their way and be filled with their own counsels” (Prov. 1:31); but of the latter he writes again: “The heart of fools will be unlike itself” (ibid., 15:7). The heart of the wise is always like itself, because, while it accepts upright counsels, it steadily directs itself toward good works. But the heart of fools is unlike itself, because, by displaying itself as varied through changeability, it never remains what it had been.

And because certain vices, just as they generate others from themselves, also arise from others, it must be recognized with the greatest care that we correct them more effectively when we dry them up from the very source of their bitterness. Obstinacy is generated from pride, while fickleness is generated from levity.

The obstinate must therefore be admonished to recognize the arrogance of their thinking and to strive to conquer themselves, lest, while they disdain being overcome outwardly by the sound persuasion of others, they remain inwardly captive to pride. They must be admonished to observe carefully that the Son of Man, whose will is always one with the Father’s, gives us an example for breaking our own will when he says: “I do not seek my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 5:30). To commend this virtue still further, he declared beforehand that he would preserve it at the final judgment, saying: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge” (ibid.).

[Note: Laudunensis reads “steadfastness.”]

With what conscience, then, does a human being disdain obeying another’s will, when the Son of God and of Man, coming to display the glory of his power, testifies that he does not judge from himself?

But the fickle must be admonished to strengthen their minds with seriousness. They dry up the shoots of changeability within themselves when they first cut away from their hearts the root of levity; for a strong structure is built only when a solid place is first prepared on which the foundation may be laid. Unless levity of mind is guarded against beforehand, the fickleness of one’s thoughts cannot be overcome. Paul declared himself free from such people when he said: “Have I acted with levity? Or are the things I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there is both ‘yes’ and ‘no’?” (1 Cor. 1:17). As if he were saying plainly: “I am not moved by the wind of change because I do not succumb to the fault of levity.”

CHAPTER XIX [Elsewhere XLIII]. How those who use food too intemperately and those who use it sparingly are to be admonished

[Admonition 20.] Those devoted to gluttony must be admonished in one way, and those who abstain in another. The former are often accompanied by excessive speech, fickleness in action, and lust; the latter by the fault sometimes of impatience and sometimes of pride. If immoderate loquacity did not carry away those devoted to gluttony, that rich man who is said to have feasted splendidly every day would not burn more grievously in his tongue, saying: “Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame” (Luke 16:24).

These words plainly show that he had sinned frequently with his tongue while feasting every day, since, although his whole body was burning, he especially sought relief for his tongue. Again, because fickleness of action immediately follows those devoted to gluttony, sacred authority testifies, saying: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6). Excessive eating often drags them as far as lust, because, when the belly is distended by satiety, the goads of desire are aroused. Hence the divine voice says to the crafty enemy who opened the mind of the first human being to desire for the fruit, but then bound it in the snare of sin: “You shall crawl upon your breast and belly” (Gen. 3:14); as if it were said plainly to him: “By thought and gluttony you will rule over human hearts.”

Because lust follows those devoted to gluttony, the prophet testifies, revealing hidden things while narrating what is manifest, saying: “The commander of the cooks destroyed the walls of Jerusalem” (Jer. 39:9; 2 Kings 25:10, according to the Septuagint). For the commander of the cooks is the belly, to which the cooks devote great care so that it may be filled pleasurably with food. The walls of Jerusalem are the virtues of the soul, raised toward the desire for heavenly peace. The commander of the cooks therefore throws down the walls of Jerusalem, because, when the belly is distended by gluttony, the virtues of the soul are destroyed through lust.

Yet if impatience did not often drive the minds of those who abstain from the shelter of tranquility, Peter would not have said: “In your faith supply virtue, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge abstinence” (2 Pet. 1:5), immediately adding attentively: “And in abstinence, patience.” He foresaw that patience might be lacking in those who abstain, and admonished them so that it might be present in them.

Again, if the thoughts of those who abstain were not sometimes pierced by the fault of pride, Paul would not have said: “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats” (Rom. 14:3). Speaking again to others, while criticizing the precepts of those who glory in abstinence, he added: “These things indeed have an appearance of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, but they are not of any honor for satisfying the flesh” (Col. 2:23).

Here it must be noted that in his argument the excellent preacher joins the appearance of humility to superstition. When the flesh is worn down through abstinence more than necessary, humility is displayed outwardly, but inwardly one becomes gravely proud of that very humility. And if the mind of those who abstain sometimes became swollen with pride over the virtue of abstinence, the arrogant Pharisee would never have deliberately counted it among his great merits, saying: “I fast twice on the Sabbath” (Luke 18:12).

Those devoted to gluttony must therefore be admonished not to transfix themselves with the sword of lust by surrendering to the pleasure of food. They should consider how much loquacity and how much fickleness of mind lie in wait for them through eating, lest, while they serve the belly softly, they be cruelly bound in the snares of vice. For one recedes that much farther from the second parent the more, through immoderate use, the hand is extended toward food and the fall of the first parent is repeated.

But those who abstain must be admonished always to watch carefully lest, while they flee the vice of gluttony, sharper vices arise in them as though from virtue; lest, while they discipline the flesh, the spirit break out into impatience. There is no longer any virtue in conquering the flesh if the spirit is conquered by anger. Sometimes, while the mind of those who abstain restrains itself from anger, an alien joy comes upon it and corrupts it; thus the good of abstinence is diminished because it does not guard itself from spiritual vices. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “On the days of your fasts your own desires are found” (Isa. 58:3, according to the Septuagint). And shortly afterward: “You fast for judgments and quarrels, and you strike with your fists” (ibid.).

[Note: Trecensis, the first Carnotensis, and Belvacensis, by a first hand, read “pleasure.” We have retained “desire,” which corresponds to the passage in Isaiah, where “your desires” is read. In Trecensis, however, we read “pleasures.” In the Hebrew source and in the translation of the Septuagint, from which the quoted words are taken, the reading is “desire” or “desires.” In the Syriac and Arabic versions one finds “you indulge your desires” or “you seek your desires.” Here, however, “desires” cannot mean “pleasures,” but means one’s own will.]

“Desire” pertains to joy, and “fist” to anger. The body is therefore worn down by abstinence in vain if the mind, abandoned to disordered impulses, is scattered among vices.

Again, those who abstain must be admonished to maintain their abstinence carefully and without diminution, yet never to consider it before the hidden Judge an extraordinary virtue. Otherwise, if it is believed to constitute great merit, the heart may be lifted up in pride. Hence the prophet says: “Is this the kind of fast that I have chosen? Rather, break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house” (ibid., 5).

In this matter it must be considered how little the virtue of abstinence is regarded when it is commended only through other virtues. Hence Joel says: “Sanctify a fast.” To sanctify a fast is to show abstinence from food as worthy of God when other good works are joined to it.

Those who abstain must know that they offer God abstinence pleasing to him when they give to the needy what they withdraw from themselves in food. They must listen carefully to what the Lord rebukes through the prophet, saying: “When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months during these seventy years, did you fast for me? And when you ate and drank, did you not eat for yourselves and drink for yourselves?” (Zech. 7:5 ff.).

[Note: Laudunensis, Vallis Clara, Corbeiensis, and the Gemetica read “when you ate and drank.” Trecensis reads “when you ate” and “when you drank.”]

For a person fasts not for God but for himself if he does not give to the needy what he temporarily withdraws from his belly, but keeps it to offer to his belly later.

Therefore, lest appetite for food cast the former down from the state of their minds, or afflicted flesh overthrow the latter through pride, let the former hear from the mouth of Truth: “Take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness and the cares of this world” (Luke 21:34). A useful fear is added there: “And that day come upon you suddenly. For it will come like a snare upon all who sit upon the face of the whole earth” (ibid., 35).

Let the latter hear: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. 15:11). Let the former hear: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13).

[Note: Laudunensis, Trecensis, and the first two Gemetica read “both it and these.”]

And again: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” (Rom. 13:13). And again: “Food does not commend us to God” (1 Cor. 8:8). Let the latter hear: “To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus 1:15). Let the former hear: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3:19). Let the latter hear: “Some will depart from the faith” (1 Tim. 4:1, 3), and shortly afterward: “Forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods that God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth.” Let the former hear: “It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, or anything by which your brother is offended” (Rom. 14:21). Let the latter hear: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Tim. 5:23). Thus the former may learn not to desire the foods of the flesh disorderly, and the latter may not dare to condemn the creature of God that they themselves do not desire.

CHAPTER XX [Elsewhere XLIV]. How those who distribute their own possessions and those who seize what belongs to others are to be admonished

[Admonition 21.] Those who already give their own possessions mercifully must be admonished in one way, and those who still strive to seize what belongs to others in another. Those who already give their own possessions mercifully must be admonished not to raise themselves up in proud thought above those to whom they distribute earthly goods, nor to consider themselves better simply because they see others sustained through them.

The master of an earthly household, distributing the ranks and duties of his servants, appoints some to rule and others to be ruled by others. He commands some to provide what is necessary for others, and others to receive what is supplied by others. Yet often those who rule offend, while those who are ruled remain in the favor of the master of the household. Those who are stewards incur anger, while those who subsist on another’s administration remain without offense.

Those who already distribute mercifully what they possess must therefore be admonished to recognize that they have been appointed by the heavenly Lord as stewards of temporal resources, and to provide them humbly in proportion as they understand that what they administer is not their own. When they consider that they have been placed in the service of those to whom they distribute what they have received, their minds must not be lifted up by pride, but weighed down by fear.

Hence they must carefully consider: do not distribute what has been entrusted to you unworthily; do not give some things to those who need nothing, nor nothing to those who need something; do not give much to those who need little, nor little to those to whom you ought to have given much; do not scatter what you give uselessly through haste; do not cruelly torment those who ask by delaying; do not allow an intention of receiving repayment here to creep in; do not let the light of giving be extinguished by the desire for passing praise; do not let sadness accompany the gift offered; do not let the mind rejoice beyond what is proper in a gift well offered; and, after fulfilling everything correctly, do not attribute anything to yourselves, lest you lose everything at once after accomplishing it all.

Lest they attribute the virtue of their generosity to themselves, let them hear what is written: “If anyone serves, let him do so as from the strength that God supplies” (1 Pet. 4:11). Lest they rejoice excessively in their good deeds, let them hear what is written: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do’” (Luke 17:10).

[Note: The first Audomarensis reads “we did not do.”]

Lest sadness corrupt their generosity, let them hear what is written: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Lest they seek passing praise from the gift they have made, let them hear what is written: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6:3). That is, the glory of the present life must in no way mingle with a pious administration; the desire for praise must not accompany the work of uprightness.

[Note: Printed editions read “the desire for praise.” We are compelled to follow the large number of manuscripts, including the best—Trecensis, Laudunensis, Corbeiensis, and the first two Carnotenses—which read “the desire of favor.”]

Lest they seek repayment for the favor they have shown, let them hear what is written: “When you give a dinner or a supper, do not invite your friends, your brothers, your relatives, or rich neighbors, lest they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the weak, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you” (Luke 14:12 ff.).

[Note: Corbeiensis, Trecensis, Laudunensis, and the Gemetica agree in reading “because they have nothing with which to repay you.” The old edition of 1518 also agrees. Other copies read “from which they may repay you.”]

Lest what ought to be given promptly be given late, let them hear what is written: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come again, and tomorrow I will give you,’ when you can give immediately” (Prov. 3:28). Lest they uselessly scatter what they possess under the pretext of generosity, let them hear what is written: “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand.”

[Note: Laudunensis and some others read “under the pretext of piety.”]

Lest they give little when much is necessary, let them hear what is written: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6). Lest, when little is appropriate, they give very much and afterward, unable to endure want, break out into impatience, let them hear what is written: “Not that there should be relief for others and affliction for you, but that by equality your abundance should supply their need, and their abundance should supply your need” (ibid. 8:13–14).

For when the mind of the giver does not know how to endure want, if he takes much away from himself, he seeks an occasion for impatience against himself. The mind must first be prepared for patience, and only then should much or everything be given, lest, when the want that follows is borne with insufficient equanimity, the reward of the previous generosity perish and the murmuring that follows further destroy the mind.

Lest they give absolutely nothing to those to whom they ought to contribute something small, let them hear what is written: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30). Lest they give even something to those to whom they ought to contribute nothing at all, let them hear what is written: “Give to the good, and do not receive the sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the wicked” (Sir. 12:4). And again: “Set out your bread and wine upon the burial of the just, and do not eat or drink of it with sinners” (Tob. 4:17).

For one gives his bread and wine to sinners who provides assistance to the wicked because they are wicked. Hence some rich people of this world, while Christ’s poor are tormented by hunger, nourish actors with lavish gifts. But whoever gives his bread even to a needy sinner, not because he is a sinner but because he is a human being, plainly nourishes not a sinner but a just poor person, because in him he loves not guilt but nature.

Those who already give their own possessions mercifully must also be admonished to guard carefully lest, while they redeem sins already committed through almsgiving, they continue to commit sins that still need redemption. They must not suppose that God’s justice is for sale, imagining that, by taking care to give money for their sins, they can sin with impunity. “The soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing” (Matt. 6:25; Luke 12:23). Whoever therefore gives food or clothing to the poor but is nevertheless polluted by iniquity of soul or body has offered to God what is lesser in justice and what is greater in guilt: he has given his possessions to God, but himself to the devil.

But those who still strive to seize what belongs to others must be admonished to listen carefully to what the Lord will say when he comes to judgment. For he says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25:35–36). He also announces to them beforehand: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

Behold, they do not hear that they committed robberies or any other acts of violence, and yet they are handed over to the eternal fires of Gehenna.

[Note: Corbeiensis, Belvacensis, and the first two Carnotenses read “because they committed robberies.”]

From this it must be inferred how great a condemnation awaits those who seize what belongs to others, if those who kept their own possessions indiscriminately are struck with such severity. Let them consider by what guilt the thing seized binds them, if a thing not given over to another subjects its owner to such punishment. Let them consider what the injustice inflicted deserves, if kindness not bestowed is worthy of such punishment.

When they intend to seize what belongs to others, let them hear what is written: “Woe to him who multiplies what is not his own! How long will he load himself with thick mud against himself?” (Hab. 2:6). For an avaricious person to heap thick mud against himself is to pile up earthly gains together with the weight of sin.

When they desire to multiply the spaces of their dwellings greatly, let them hear what is written: “Woe to you who join house to house and add field to field, until there is no place left. Will you alone dwell in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. 5:8). As if it were said plainly: “How far do you extend yourselves, when you cannot bear to have fellow inhabitants in the common world?”

[Note: Trecensis, the three Gemetica, Rotomagensis, Audomarensis, and Lyra read: “when you cannot in the least have fellow inhabitants in the common world.” Perhaps “in the least” does not have a negative force here, but means: “you do not even allow the smallest portion of the world to be inhabited by others.” See above, chapter 13, note e.]

You oppress those who are joined to you, yet you always find others against whom you can extend yourselves. When they pant after increasing their money, let them hear what is written: “The greedy person is not satisfied with money, and whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them” (Eccl. 5:9). He would gain fruit from them if, without loving them, he wished to distribute them well. But whoever retains them because he loves them will certainly leave this life without fruit.

When they burn with desire to be filled with all riches at once, let them hear what is written: “Whoever hastens to become rich will not be innocent” (Prov. 28:20). For plainly, whoever seeks to increase his wealth neglects to avoid sin; and, caught like a bird, when he eagerly looks upon the bait of earthly things, he does not recognize the snare of sin by which he will be strangled.

When they desire every profit of the present world and are ignorant of the losses they will suffer in the future, let them hear what is written: “An inheritance to which one hastens at the beginning will lack blessing at the end” (Prov. 20:21).

[Note: The printed editions erroneously read “the losses of the future.”]

We begin from this life so that at the end we may come to the lot of blessing. Those, therefore, who hasten to inherit at the beginning cut off from themselves the lot of blessing at the end, because, while they desire to multiply their possessions here through the wickedness of avarice, there they become disinherited from the eternal patrimony.

[Note: Gussanville, with an equally serious error, reads “with blessing.”]

When they either covet very many things or are able to obtain everything they have coveted, let them hear what is written: “What does it profit a person to gain the whole world but suffer the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16:26). As if Truth plainly said: “What does it profit a person to gather everything outside himself, if he condemns the one thing that he himself is?”

But the avarice of those who seize things is often corrected more quickly if the one admonishing them shows in his words how fleeting the present life is; if he brings to their attention the memory of those who strove for a long time to become rich in this world, yet could not remain long in the riches they acquired. Sudden and premature death took from them all at once whatever their wickedness had gathered neither all at once nor suddenly. They left behind not only what they had seized here, but also carried the causes of their seizure with them to judgment.

Let them hear the examples of these people, whom they themselves undoubtedly condemn in their words, so that, when they return to their hearts after these words, they may at least be ashamed to imitate those whom they judge.

CHAPTER XXI [Elsewhere XLV]. How those who do not desire what belongs to others but retain what is their own, and those who give their own possessions yet still seize what belongs to others, are to be admonished

[Admonition 22.] Those who neither desire what belongs to others nor give away what is their own must be admonished in one way, and those who give what they have yet do not cease to seize what belongs to others in another.

Those who neither desire what belongs to others nor distribute what is their own must carefully understand that the earth from which they were taken is common to all human beings, and therefore produces its nourishment for all in common. They therefore think themselves innocent in vain when they claim as private for themselves the common gift of God; when they do not give what they have received, they perpetrate the death of their neighbors, because they kill almost as many each day as the number of poor people whose means of support they conceal within their possession.

For when we provide whatever is necessary to the needy, we return to them what is theirs; we do not give them what is ours. We pay the debt of justice rather than fulfill a work of mercy. Hence Truth itself, speaking cautiously about the exercise of mercy, says: “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people” (Matt. 6:1). The Psalmist, agreeing with this statement, says: “He distributed and gave to the poor; his righteousness remains forever” (Ps. 111:9). Although he had first mentioned generosity bestowed upon the poor, he preferred not to call it mercy but righteousness, because what is given by the common Lord is plainly justly used in common by all who receive it.

Hence Solomon also says: “The righteous person gives and does not cease” (Prov. 21:26). They must also carefully observe that the fig tree which bore no fruit is accused by the strict husbandman of occupying even the ground.

A fruitless fig tree occupies the ground when the mind of the miser uselessly preserves what could have benefited many. A fruitless fig tree occupies the ground when a foolish person burdens with the shadow of idleness a place that someone else could have cultivated through the sunlight of good works.

[Note: The first Carnotensis reads “through the offspring of a good work.” The others disagree, and the contrast with “shadow” supports reading “sun,” namely, “through the sun of a good work.”]

Such people sometimes say: “We use what has been granted to us; we do not seek what belongs to others. And if we do not perform acts worthy of mercy’s reward, nevertheless we commit no wrong.” They think this because they close the ear of their heart to heavenly words. For the rich man in the Gospel, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day (Luke 16:19 ff.), is not said to have seized what belonged to others, but to have used his own possessions fruitlessly; and avenging Gehenna received him after this life, not because he had done anything unlawful, but because through immoderate use he had surrendered himself entirely to what was lawful.

The miserly must be admonished to know that they first inflict an injury upon God, because, although he gives them everything, they return to him no offering of mercy. Hence the Psalmist says: “He shall not give God his propitiation, nor the price of the redemption of his soul” (Ps. 49:8). To give the price of redemption is to return a good work to the grace that precedes us.

Hence John cries out: “The axe is already laid at the root of the tree. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Luke 3:9). Those who consider themselves blameless because they do not seize what belongs to others should foresee the blow of the nearby axe and abandon the torpor of their heedless security, lest, by neglecting to bear the fruit of good works, they be cut away completely from the present life, as it were from the greenness of the root.

[Note: Gussanville corruptly reads: “as though they might dry up through the aridity of the root.” Our reading is supported by the two Saint-Germain manuscripts and the others. Reason also supports it, since “be cut away” most appropriately refers to what immediately precedes, namely, “the blow of the nearby axe.”]

On the other hand, those must be admonished who both give away what they possess and do not cease to seize what belongs to others [Note: [Col. 0087D] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read: “lest, while they desire to appear very generous, they become worse in respect of the good.”], lest they desire to appear excessively generous and become worse through the appearance of goodness. For these people, indiscriminately giving away their own possessions, not only—as we have already said above—rush into murmuring born of impatience; but, when poverty compels them, they sink even into avarice. What, then, is more wretched than the mind of those in whom avarice is born from generosity, and a harvest of sins is sown as though from virtue?

They must therefore first be admonished to know how to retain their own possessions reasonably, and only then not to covet what belongs to others. For if the root of the fault is not burned away in the very act of lavish expenditure, the thorn of avarice, growing luxuriantly through its branches, is never dried up [Note: [Col. 0088D] The second Carnot manuscript reads: “is cut down.”]. The opportunity for seizing is therefore removed if the right of possessing is first properly ordered [Col. 0088C]. Then, once admonished, let them hear how they should distribute what they possess mercifully—namely, when they have learned not to corrupt the goods of mercy by the intervening wickedness of robbery.

For they violently demand what they distribute mercifully. But it is one thing to show mercy for the sake of sins, and another to sin for the sake of showing mercy. The latter can no longer be called mercy, because that which grows bitter through the poison of a pestilential root does not advance toward sweet fruit. Hence the Lord also rejects sacrifices through the prophet, saying: “I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery in the burnt offering” (Isaiah 61:8). Again he said: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, which are offered from crime” (Proverbs 21:27). Such people often also take away from the needy what they offer to God.

But with what great severity the Lord rejects them [Note: [Col. 0088D] The first two Gemet manuscripts read: “through Solomon.” In Trecensis one reads: “a certain wise man.” But the margin, in the same hand, notes: “Aput Salomonem,” that is, “with Solomon”; for in old manuscripts *t* is customarily used for *d*. The same note occurs below in this codex at Admonition 31, where another passage from Ecclesiasticus is cited.] he demonstrates through a certain wise man, saying: “Whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclesiasticus 34:24). What could be more unbearable than the death of a son before the eyes of his father? It is therefore shown with what anger this sacrifice is regarded, since it is compared with the grief of a bereaved father.

And yet they often weigh how much they give, while pretending not to consider how much they seize. They count their rewards, but refuse to assess their sins. Let them therefore hear what is written: “Whoever gathered wages has put them into a bag with holes” (Haggai 1:6). Money is seen when it is put into a bag with holes, but when it is lost, it is not seen. Those, therefore, who look at how much they give but do not consider how much they seize put their wages into a bag with holes, because they gather them, clearly, while looking toward the hope of their own confidence, but lose them because they do not look [Note: [Col. 0089D] Laudun and the first Aud manuscript read: “in the appearance of their own confidence.”].

## CHAPTER XXIII [Otherwise XLVI]. How those who are quarrelsome and those who are peaceable should be admonished

[Col. 0089B] (Admonition 23.) The quarrelsome must be admonished in one way, and the peaceable in another. The quarrelsome must be admonished to know with complete certainty that, however many virtues they may possess, they can in no way become spiritual if they neglect to be united in concord with their neighbors. For it is written: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace” (Galatians 5:22). Whoever therefore does not take care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit.

Hence Paul says: “While there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal?” (1 Corinthians 3:3). Again he says: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:14). Again, admonishing them, he says: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body and one Spirit, just as you were called in one hope of your calling” (Ephesians 4:3–4 [Col. 0089C]). One cannot reach the single hope of the calling unless one runs toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors.

Yet often some people, because they receive certain gifts in a special way, lose through pride the gift of concord, which is greater. Thus, if someone perhaps subdues the flesh more than others by restraining his appetite, he may despise those whom he surpasses in abstinence and refuse to live in concord with them. But whoever separates abstinence from concord should consider what the Psalmist admonishes. He says: “Praise him with the tambourine and choir” (Psalm 150:4). On the tambourine, a dry skin resounds when struck; in the choir, voices agree through their fellowship [Note: [Col. 0089D] The editors preferred “joined voices,” against all our manuscripts.].

Whoever therefore afflicts his body but abandons concord praises God on the tambourine, but does not praise him in the choir. Often, too, when greater knowledge raises certain people up, it separates them from the fellowship of others; and, as though the more they know, the more they become foolish concerning the virtue of concord. Let such people hear what Truth itself says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but evidence of condemnation. For the better someone understands, the worse he sins; and therefore he will deservedly receive punishment without excuse, because, if he had wished to do so prudently, he could have avoided sin [Note: [Col. 0089D] Laudun reads: “the more seriously he sins, abandoning concord.”].

To such people James rightly says: “If you have bitter jealousy and contentions in your heart, do not boast and be liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, but earthly, natural, demonic. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable” (James 3:14–15, 17). It is pure because it understands chastely; it is peaceable because, through pride, it does not separate itself from the fellowship of its neighbors [Note: [Col. 0089D] Corbie reads: “because of preeminence.”].

Those who are at variance must be admonished to know that, as long as they disagree with the love of their neighbors, they offer God no sacrifice of good work. For it is written: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24 [Col. 0090B]). From this command we must consider whose offering is rejected and how intolerable a fault is revealed.

For since all evils are washed away by the good deeds that follow, let us consider how great are the evils of discord, which, unless they have been completely extinguished, do not allow a good deed to follow. Those who are quarrelsome must be admonished that, if they turn their ears away from heavenly commands, they should open the eyes of their minds to consider what takes place below. Often birds of one and the same kind do not abandon one another as they fly together, and irrational animals feed in herds [Note: [Col. 0090D] Corbie reads: “do not turn away.”]. If we look carefully, irrational nature, by living in concord with itself, shows how great an evil rational nature commits through discord, since the latter has lost by the exercise of reason what the former preserves by natural impulse [Note: [Col. 0090D] Laudun and Vallicelliana read: “with the exercise of reason.” This indeed gives the better sense. Nevertheless, we are compelled to follow Trecensis and the other manuscripts, both handwritten and printed.].

[Col. 0090C] On the other hand, those who are peaceable must be admonished lest, by loving the peace they possess more than is necessary, they fail to desire to attain perpetual peace. For tranquility in worldly affairs often tests the mind’s purpose more severely: because the things they possess are not troublesome, the things that call them become less desirable; and because present things delight them, they do not seek eternal things.

Hence Truth itself, speaking and distinguishing earthly peace from heavenly peace, and calling the disciples from the present toward what was to come, said: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace” (John 14:27). “I leave,” that is, a passing peace; “I give,” an abiding one. If the heart is fixed in the peace that has been left behind, it never reaches the peace that is to be given.

The peace of the present must therefore be held in such a way that it is both loved and despised, lest, if it is loved immoderately, the mind of the one who loves it be caught in guilt. Hence those who are peaceable must also be admonished not, while desiring human peace too greatly, to refrain from rebuking the wicked ways of people; and, by consenting to the perverse, to separate themselves from the peace of their Creator. Let them not, while fearing outward human quarrels, be struck by the rupture of the inward covenant [Note: [Col. 0090D] Belvacensis and the two older Carnot manuscripts read: “by the dissolution.”].

For what is passing peace except a kind of footprint of eternal peace? What, then, could be more foolish than to love footprints impressed in dust but not to love the one by whom they were impressed? Hence David, when he bound himself entirely to the covenants of inward peace, testifies that he did not maintain concord with the wicked, saying: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and waste away because of your enemies? I hate them with perfect hatred; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 139:21–22).

To hate the enemies of God with perfect hatred is both to love what they were made to be and to rebuke what they do: to restrain the ways of the weak and to benefit their lives.

We must therefore consider, when rebuke is withheld, how great a fault it is to maintain peace with the worst of people, if so great a prophet offered this as a sacrifice to God—as it were, that he aroused against himself, for the Lord’s sake, the hostility of the wicked. Hence the tribe of Levi, taking up swords and passing through the middle of the camp, because it refused to spare the sinners who were to be struck down, is said to have consecrated its hands to God (Exodus 32:27 and following).

Hence Phinehas, scorning the favor of his sinful fellow citizens, struck down those who were joining themselves to the Midianites, and, angered by the Lord’s anger, appeased it (Numbers 25:9). Hence Truth itself says: “Do not suppose that I have come to send peace upon the earth. I have not come to send peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34) [Note: [Col. 0091D] Here we restore the Gospel text, which is largely mutilated in the printed editions, using two German manuscripts, Beauvais, Trecensis, and others.].

For when we carelessly join ourselves to friendships with the wicked, we are bound to their faults. Thus Jehoshaphat, who is praised with so many commendations for his former life, is rebuked as nearly ruined by his friendship with King Ahab. The Lord says to him through the prophet: “You give help to the ungodly, and you join yourself in friendship with those who hate the Lord; and therefore you deserved the Lord’s wrath. Nevertheless, good works have been found in you, because you removed the sacred groves from the land of Judah” (2 Chronicles 19:2–3 [Col. 0091C]).

Our life already departs from the One who is supremely righteous precisely insofar as it agrees with the friendships of the perverse.

Those who are peaceable must be admonished not to fear disturbing their temporal peace if they step forward with words of correction. They must again be admonished to preserve inwardly, with undivided love, that same peace which they disturb outwardly through forceful speech. David testifies that he carefully maintained both, saying: “I was peaceable with those who hated peace; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Psalm 120:7).

Behold: while speaking, he was attacked; yet, though attacked, he was peaceable, because he neither ceased rebuking those who raged nor neglected to love those whom he had rebuked. Hence Paul also says: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12:18 [Col. 0091D]). For, when he was about to exhort the disciples to have peace with everyone, he first said, “If it is possible,” and then added, “insofar as it depends on you.”

It was difficult, if they corrected evil deeds, for them to be able to live at peace with everyone. But when temporal peace is disturbed in the hearts of the wicked by our rebuke, it is necessary that peace remain inviolate in our own hearts. He therefore rightly says, “insofar as it depends on you,” as though he were saying: Since peace subsists through the agreement of two parties, if it is driven away by those who are being corrected, let it nevertheless be preserved intact in the minds of you who correct them.

Again, the same apostle admonishes the disciples, saying: “If anyone does not obey our word through this letter, mark that person and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed” (2 Thessalonians 3:14). And immediately he adds: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother” (ibid., 15). It is as though he were saying: Break outward peace with him, but guard inward peace toward him from the depths of your heart, so that your discord may strike the mind of the sinner in such a way that peace does not depart from your hearts, denied or abandoned.

## CHAPTER XXIII [Otherwise XLVII]. How those who sow quarrels and those who make peace should be admonished

(Admonition 24.) Those who sow quarrels must be admonished in one way, and those who make peace in another. Those who sow quarrels must be admonished to recognize whose followers they are. For it is written concerning the apostate angel, when weeds had been sown among the good crop [Note: [Col. 0091D] In Laudun and the third Gemet manuscript, “weeds had been inserted.” [Col. 0092D] Trecensis and others use “weed” in the singular.]: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew 13:28).

Of one who is also a member of that enemy, Solomon says: “An apostate man, a worthless man, walks with a perverse mouth; he winks with his eyes, signals with his foot, speaks with his finger; he devises evil with a depraved heart and sows quarrels at all times” (Proverbs 6:12–14). Observe that, when he wanted to describe one who sows quarrels, he first called him an apostate, because unless, following the example of the proud angel, he had first fallen inwardly from the sight of his Creator through the aversion of his mind, he would not afterward have gone outward as far as sowing quarrels.

He is rightly described as winking with his eyes, speaking with his finger, and signaling with his foot. For inward discipline is what orders and preserves the external members [Note: [Col. 0092D] The first Carnot manuscript and Theodulf read: “which adorns.”]. Whoever therefore has lost the stability of his mind subsequently flows outward into instability of movement and, through external restlessness, shows that he has no inner root.

Let those who sow quarrels hear what is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). From this opposite statement let them infer that, if those who make peace are called sons of God, without doubt those who cause confusion are sons of Satan.

All who are separated through discord from the greenness of love wither. Even if they produce the fruits of good works in their actions, they are certainly nothing, because those works do not arise from the unity of charity [Note: [Col. 0092D] Laudun reads: “from the virtue of charity.”]. Let those who sow quarrels therefore consider how many ways they sin: while committing one wickedness, they uproot all virtues from human hearts at once. In one evil they accomplish countless evils, because, by sowing discord, they extinguish charity, which is the mother of all virtues.

Since nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love, and nothing more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity, whoever destroys the love of his neighbors by sowing quarrels serves God’s enemy with particular intimacy. For the devil fell when he lost that love, whereas this person, withdrawing it from wounded hearts, cuts off their path of ascent.

On the other hand, those who make peace must be admonished not to diminish the weight of so great an action by failing to discern among whom peace ought to be established. For just as it causes great harm if unity is absent among the good, so it is very harmful if it is not absent among the wicked. If, therefore, the wicked are joined together in peace, their evil deeds are strengthened, because the more they agree with one another in wickedness, the more forcefully they inflict themselves upon the affliction of the good.

Hence, against the vessels of that condemned one—that is, the preachers of Antichrist—the divine voice says to blessed Job: “The members of his flesh cling to one another” (Job 41:14) [Note: [Col. 0093D] Gilot and other recent editors, against the manuscripts of Trecensis, Germanus, Beauvais, and others—and indeed against the holy Doctor himself, who habitually calls Antichrist the devil’s vessel—read: “against the vessels of that condemned man.” See Book 32 of the Moralia, section 22. These editors prefer to call sinners “vessels of Antichrist” [Col. 0094D].].

Again, under the image of scales, it is said of his followers: “One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes between them” (ibid., 7). The more his followers are not divided from one another by any opposition of discord, the more densely they gather together for the destruction of the good. Whoever therefore unites the wicked in peace supplies strength to wickedness, because they oppress the good more severely when they persecute them with one mind.

For this reason the outstanding preacher, having been caught amid the intense persecution of the Pharisees and Sadducees, sought to divide among themselves those whom he saw united against him with great force. He cried out, saying: “Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of Pharisees; concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged” (Acts 23:6). Since the Sadducees denied that there was a hope and resurrection of the dead, while the Pharisees believed this according to the teaching of sacred Scripture, dissension arose within the unanimity of the persecutors; and the crowd that had previously pressed Paul savagely while united was divided, allowing him to leave unharmed.

Those who devote themselves to the work of making peace must therefore be admonished first to pour the love of inward peace into the minds of the wicked, so that outward peace may subsequently benefit them. Their hearts must be suspended in the knowledge of that peace, so that they may not be carried away into wickedness by their acceptance of this earthly peace [Note: [Col. 0094D] The two older Gemet manuscripts read: “in thought.”]; and, while they look toward heavenly peace, may in no way bend earthly peace to the use of their own deterioration [Note: [Col. 0094D] Corbie and the third Gemet manuscript read: “the heavenly … the earthly”; “the heavenly,” that is, peace, is very appropriate.].

But when the perverse are of such a kind that they cannot harm the good, even if they desire to do so, earthly peace should certainly be established among them before they are able to know heavenly peace. Thus those whom the wickedness of their impiety provokes against the love of God may at least be softened by love of their neighbor; and, as though from a neighboring point, may pass toward what is better, so that they may ascend to the peace of their Creator, which is far from them.

## CHAPTER XXIV [Otherwise XLVIII]. How the unlearned in sacred doctrine, and the learned but not humble, should be admonished

[Col. 0093D]

(Admonition 25.) Those who do not correctly understand the words of sacred law must be admonished in one way, and those who do understand them correctly but do not speak them humbly in another [Note: [Col. 0094D] Laudun and Corbie read: “For some must be admonished in one way.”].

Those who do not correctly understand the words of sacred law must be admonished to consider that they turn the most health-giving drink of wine into a cup of poison for themselves and strike themselves with a mortal wound through medicinal iron, since by the very means through which they ought to have healthfully cut away what was wounded, they destroy what was sound within them.

They must be admonished to consider that sacred Scripture has been placed for us in the night of the present life like a certain lamp; but when they do not correctly understand its words, they become darkened by the light. A perverse intention would not drag them toward a distorted understanding unless pride had first inflated them.

For, while they consider themselves wiser than others, they disdain to follow those who understand things better. And, so that they may force the name of learning from the ignorant crowd, they devote themselves with the utmost zeal both to destroying what others have understood correctly and to strengthening their own perverse opinions.

Hence it is well said through the prophet: “They cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their boundary” (Amos 1:13). Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony.” Since the entire congregation of the Church, through confession, serves as a testimony to the truth, Gilead appropriately signifies the Church, which through the mouths of all the faithful bears witness to whatever is true concerning God.

The pregnant women signify souls that conceive an understanding of the word through divine love and, if they reach the proper time, are destined to give birth to the understanding they have conceived by displaying it in their works. To enlarge one’s boundary is to extend the reputation of one’s opinion.

Therefore, “they cut open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their boundary,” because heretics destroy through perverse preaching the minds of the faithful that have already conceived something of the understanding of truth, and extend the reputation of their own learning. They cut the hearts of little ones, already pregnant with the conception of the word, with the sword of error, and thus make a reputation for themselves as teachers.

When we try to instruct such people so that they may not hold perverse opinions, we must first admonish them not to seek empty glory. For if the root of pride is cut away, the branches of perverse assertion consequently wither.

They must also be admonished not, by generating errors and discord, to turn the law of God—which was given precisely to forbid sacrifices to Satan—into a sacrifice to Satan itself. Hence the Lord complains through the prophet, saying: “I gave them grain, wine, and oil, and I multiplied silver and gold for them, which they made into Baal” (Hosea 2:8).

We receive grain from the Lord when, in sayings that are more obscure, the covering of the letter having been withdrawn, we perceive the inner things of the law through the marrow of the Spirit. The Lord gives us his wine when he intoxicates us with the lofty proclamation of his Scripture. He also gives us his oil when, through more open commands, he orders our life with gentle kindness. He multiplies silver when he supplies us with sayings full of the light of truth. He enriches us with gold when he illuminates our heart with understanding of the highest splendor.

Heretics offer all these things to Baal, because, by understanding everything corruptly, they pervert all things in the hearts of their hearers. They offer a sacrifice to Satan from God’s grain, wine, oil, silver, and gold, because they bend words of peace toward the error of discord. They must therefore be admonished to consider that, while with a perverse mind they make discord out of commands of peace, by God’s just judgment they themselves die through the words of life.

On the other hand, those who correctly understand the words of the law but do not speak them humbly must be admonished, before they bring them forth to others in divine discourse, to examine themselves, lest, while pursuing the deeds of others, they abandon themselves. Even when they think everything correctly concerning sacred Scripture, they must not fail to attend to that one thing which Scripture says against the proud.

An evil and unskilled physician is one who desires to heal another but does not know the wound from which he himself suffers. Those who do not speak the words of God humbly must therefore be admonished that, when they apply medicines to the sick, they should first examine the poison of their own disease, lest, while healing others, they themselves die [Note: [Col. 0095D] Trecensis and the other manuscripts unanimously read this way; later editors changed it to: “while healing others.”].

They must be admonished to consider whether the quality of their speech is at variance with the virtue of what they say [Note: [Col. 0095D] With the same freedom, disregarding the manuscripts, Gilot and other recent editors read: “whether they are at variance with the virtue of their speech in the quality of their life,” or “with the virtue of what they say in their life,” and so forth.], lest, by saying one thing and displaying another, they preach contrary messages.

Let them hear what is written: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Peter 4:11). If, then, they do not possess from themselves the words they utter, why do they swell as though they possessed them from themselves?

Let them hear what is written: “As from God, before God, we speak in Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:17). One speaks from God before God who understands both that he has received the word of preaching from God and that through it he must seek to please God, not human beings.

Let them hear what is written: “Everyone who is arrogant is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 16:5). For, while seeking his own glory in the word of God, he invades the right of the giver and does not fear to put the one from whom he received the very thing for which he is praised after his own praise.

Let them hear what is said to the preacher through Solomon: “Drink water from your own cistern, and flowing water from your own well. Let your springs flow out, and distribute your waters in the streets. Have them alone, and let strangers not share them with you” (Proverbs 5:15–17).

The preacher drinks water from his own cistern when, returning to his own heart, he first hears within himself what he says to others. He drinks from the streams of his own well when he is infused by the watering of his own words. The text rightly continues: “Let your springs flow out, and distribute your waters in the streets” (ibid., 18). It is right that he should first drink himself and then, by preaching, flow into others.

To let one’s springs flow outward is to pour the power of preaching into others externally. To distribute waters in the streets is to dispense divine words among the great multitude of hearers according to the quality of each person.

And because the desire for empty glory often creeps in when the word of God runs out to the knowledge of many, after it has been said, “Distribute your waters in the streets,” it rightly continues: “Have them alone, and let strangers not share them with you” (ibid.). By “strangers” he calls the malicious spirits, of whom it is said through the prophet in the voice of a tempted man: “Strangers have risen up against me, and the powerful have sought my soul” (Psalm 54:5).

He therefore says: Distribute your waters in the streets, and yet possess them alone. As though he were saying more plainly: You must serve preaching outwardly in such a way that you do not join yourself through pride to unclean spirits, lest, in the ministry of the divine word, you admit your enemies as sharers with you.

We therefore distribute our waters in the streets and yet possess them alone when we spread preaching widely outwardly, while not seeking through it to obtain human praise.

## CHAPTER XXV [Otherwise XLIX]. How those who refuse the office of preaching through excessive humility, and those who seize it through rash haste, should be admonished

(Admonition 26.) Those who are genuinely able to preach worthily but fear to do so because of excessive humility must be admonished in one way; those whom imperfection or age prevents from preaching but whom rashness drives toward it must be admonished in another.

Those who can preach usefully but nevertheless shrink back through immoderate humility must be admonished to infer from a lesser consideration how much they abandon in greater matters. If they hid from needy neighbors the money they possessed, they would certainly be accomplices in calamity. Let them therefore consider by what guilt they are bound when, by withholding the word of preaching from their sinful brothers, they hide remedies of life from minds that are dying.

Hence a certain wise man rightly says: “Wisdom hidden and a treasure unseen—what benefit is there in either?” (Ecclesiasticus 20:32) [Note: [Col. 0096D] The first Carnot manuscript and the first Aud manuscript read: “a hidden treasure.”]. If hunger were wearing down a people and they themselves kept hidden grain, they would certainly be authors of death [Note: [Col. 0096D] The Gemet manuscript and many Norman manuscripts read: “exactors.”]. Let them therefore consider by what punishment they will be chastised when souls perish from hunger for the word and they do not distribute the bread of the grace they have received.

Hence it is well said through Solomon: “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples” (Proverbs 11:26). To hide grain is to keep the words of holy preaching to oneself. Such a person is cursed among the peoples because, through the guilt of silence alone, he is condemned for the punishment of many whom he could have corrected.

If those who were not ignorant of the medical art saw a wound that needed to be cut but nevertheless refused to cut it, they would certainly commit the sin of fraternal death through their mere negligence. Let those who recognize the wounds of minds but neglect to heal them by the incision of words consider how great a guilt entangles them.

Hence it is well said through the prophet: “Cursed is the one who withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah 48:10). To withhold one’s sword from blood is to hold back the word of preaching from the destruction of carnal life. Again it is said of this sword: “And my sword shall devour flesh” (Deuteronomy 32:42) [Note: [Col. 0096D] Gemet, together with the first Aud manuscript, reads: “shall eat.”].

When such people conceal the word of preaching within themselves, let them hear the divine judgments against them with terror, so that fear may drive fear from their hearts. Let them hear how the man who refused to distribute his talent lost it together with the sentence of condemnation (Matthew 25:24 and following).

Let them hear how Paul believed himself clean from the blood of his neighbors precisely because he did not spare their vices when they had to be struck, saying: “I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27).

Let them hear how John is admonished by an angelic voice when it is said: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Revelation 22:17). The one to whom the inward voice makes itself known must draw others there by crying out, where he himself is being drawn, lest, even when called, he find the doors closed if he approaches the one calling while empty.

Let them hear how Isaiah, because he had been silent concerning the ministry of the word, after being illumined by heavenly light rebuked himself loudly in repentance, saying: “Woe is me, for I was silent” (Isaiah 6:5).

Let them hear how, through Solomon, an increase in the knowledge of preaching is promised to the one who is not held back by the fault of sluggishness from using what he has already obtained. For he says: “The soul that blesses shall be made fat, and the one who intoxicates shall himself also be intoxicated” (Proverbs 11:25). Whoever blesses outwardly by preaching receives the richness of inward growth; and, while he does not cease to intoxicate the minds of his hearers with the wine of the word, he himself grows intoxicated and increases through the drink of multiplied grace [Note: [Col. 0097D] Corbie and others seen by Gussanville read: “while he intoxicates the minds of his hearers with divine speech.”].

Let them hear how David offered this to God as a gift: that he did not hide the grace of preaching which he had received, saying: “Behold, I will not restrain my lips; Lord, you know it. I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken of your truth and your salvation” (Psalm 40:10–11).

Let them hear what is said from the bridegroom to the bride: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen; let me hear your voice” (Song of Songs 8:13). The Church dwells in gardens, preserving cultivated plantings of virtues for inward greenness. That her friends listen to her voice means that the elect desire her word of preaching. The bridegroom desires to hear this voice because, through the souls of his elect, he longs for her preaching.

Let them hear how Moses, when he saw God angry with the people and commanding that a sword be taken up for vengeance, declared that those who struck the crimes of the guilty without hesitation stood on God’s side, saying: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me. Let each man put his sword upon his thigh; go back and forth from gate to gate through the middle of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (Exodus 32:27).

To put the sword upon the thigh is to place zeal for preaching before the pleasures of the flesh, so that whoever strives to speak holy things must necessarily take care to subdue unlawful suggestions. To go from gate to gate is to move reprovingly from vice to vice, through which death enters the mind. To pass through the middle of the camp is to live within the Church with such impartiality that the one who rebukes the faults of the guilty must not incline in favor of anyone.

Hence it rightly continues: “Let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” He kills a brother, friend, and neighbor when, upon finding things that must be punished, he does not spare even those whom he loves through kinship from the sword of rebuke.

If, then, the one who is stirred by zeal for divine love to strike down vices is called God’s own, clearly the one who refuses, as far as he is able, to rebuke the life of carnal people denies that he belongs to God.

But, on the other hand, those who are prevented from the ministry of preaching either by immaturity or by age, yet are driven on by rashness, must be admonished lest, while in their rashness they arrogate to themselves so great a burden of office, they cut off for themselves the path of subsequent improvement; and lest, when they prematurely seize what they are unable to accomplish, they also lose what, at the proper time, they might have been able to fulfill; and lest, because they attempt to display their knowledge incongruously, they should justly be shown to have lost it.
