They must be admonished to consider that if young birds desire to fly before their feathers are fully grown, from the very height to which they wish to rise they plunge into the depths. They must be admonished to consider that, if the weight of beams is placed upon recent structures whose foundations have not yet hardened, not a dwelling but a collapse is built. [Note: Corb. reads “if the weight of timbers.”] They must be admonished to consider that if women bring forth their conceived offspring before they are fully formed, they fill not houses but tombs.

For this reason the Truth himself, who could have strengthened those whom he wished immediately, gave an example to those who would follow, so that the imperfect would not presume to preach. After he had fully instructed the disciples in the virtue of preaching, he immediately added: [Note: Laudunensis reads “concerning the preaching of virtue.”] զբաղ “But you, remain seated in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). We remain seated in the city if we restrain ourselves within the enclosures of our minds, lest by speaking we wander outward; so that, when we have been perfectly clothed with divine power, we may then go forth, as it were, from ourselves, instructing others also.

Hence a certain wise man says: “Young man, speak scarcely in your own cause; and if you have been questioned twice, let your answer begin” (Ecclus. 32:10). Hence also our same Redeemer, although he is the Creator in heaven and by the manifestation of his power always the teacher of angels, did not wish to become the teacher of human beings on earth before the age of thirty, in order to instill the force of salutary fear into the rash: even he who could not fall preached the grace of perfect life only at a perfect age.

For it is written: “When he was twelve years old, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem” (Luke 2:42). When his parents sought him, the text shortly afterward adds: “They found him sitting in the temple in the midst of the teachers, listening to them and questioning them” (ibid., 46). We must therefore weigh with vigilant consideration the fact that when Jesus is said to be twelve years old and sitting in the midst of the teachers, he is found not teaching but questioning. By this example it is shown that no weak person should dare to teach, if that boy wished to be taught by questioning who, through the power of his divinity, supplied the word of knowledge to those very teachers of his.

But when Paul says to his disciple, “Command and teach these things; let no one despise your youth” (1 Tim. 4:12), we must understand that in sacred speech “adolescence” is sometimes called “youth.” This is shown more quickly if Solomon’s words are brought forward. He says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccles. 11:9). For if he did not judge the two to be one, he would not have called “young man” the one whom he was admonishing in his youth.

## CHAPTER XXVI [Al. L]

### How those who succeed in everything according to their wishes, and those who succeed in nothing, are to be admonished

**Admonition 27.**

Those who prosper in what they desire temporally must be admonished in one way, and those who desire the things of the world but are nevertheless wearied by the labor of adversity in another.

Those who prosper in what they desire temporally must be admonished lest, when everything is supplied according to their wishes, they neglect to seek the giver, but fix their minds upon the gifts. [Note: Gemeticensis reads: “but let them fix their minds upon him by whom they are given.” Other manuscripts of Normandy, together with the third Carnotensis, read: “if in those things which are given,” and so forth.] Let them not love their exile as their homeland; let them not turn the provisions for their journey into obstacles to reaching their destination; let them not, delighted by the moon’s nocturnal light, shrink from seeing the brightness of the sun.

They must therefore be admonished to believe that whatever they obtain in this world is consolation amid affliction, not rewards of recompense; and, against the world’s favors, to raise their minds, lest they succumb to them with the full delight of their hearts. Whoever does not restrain the prosperity he enjoys, in the judgment of his heart, through love of a better life, turns the favor of a passing life into an occasion of eternal death.

For this reason, under the figure of the Idumeans—who abandoned themselves to their prosperity to be overcome, rejoicing in the successes of this world—they are rebuked when it is said: “They gave my land to themselves as an inheritance, with joy, with all their heart, and with their whole soul” (Ezek. 36:5). [Note: Corb., Belv., and the first two Carnotenses read “abandoned themselves to their prosperity.”] From these words it may be understood that they are struck by strict rebuke not merely because they rejoice, but because they rejoice with all their heart and soul.

Hence Solomon says: “The turning away of the simple will kill them, and the prosperity of fools will destroy them” (Prov. 1:32). Hence Paul admonishes, saying: “Those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it” (1 Cor. 7:30). Thus the things supplied to us should serve us outwardly in such a way that they do not bend our minds away from the pursuit of heavenly delight, lest they temper for us the grief of our inner exile and provide assistance to us placed in exile; and lest, as though happy in transitory things, we rejoice while we see ourselves meanwhile wretched in relation to eternal things. [Note: Belv., the first and third Carnotensis, Rothomagensis, Lyranus, and Vallicellianus read “of love.”] [Note: The printed editions read “that we may be destroyed”; Trecensis, Belv., Corb., Laudunensis, and the first two Carnotenses have “that we may be inwardly wretched”; the third has “that we may be inwardly.”]

Hence, in the voice of the elect, the Church says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6). It placed God’s left hand—that is, the prosperity of the present life—as though beneath its head, pressing it down with the intention of supreme love. God’s right hand, however, embraces it, because it is held wholly and devotedly beneath his eternal blessedness.

Again, through Solomon it is said: “Length of days is in his right hand; in his left hand are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16). By mentioning riches and glory as placed in the left hand, he taught how they are to be held. Hence the Psalmist says: “Save me by your right hand” (Ps. 107:7). He did not say “by your hand,” but “by your right hand,” so that by saying “right hand” he might indicate that he was seeking eternal salvation.

Again it is written: “Your right hand, Lord, has shattered the enemies” (Exod. 15:6, according to the Septuagint). The enemies of God, although they prosper in his left hand, are shattered by his right, because the present life often raises up the wicked, but the coming of eternal blessedness condemns them.

Those who prosper in this world must be admonished to consider carefully that the prosperity of the present life is sometimes given to summon them to a better life, and sometimes to condemn them more fully for eternity. For this reason the land of Canaan was promised to the Israelite people, so that they might at some time be summoned to hope for eternal things. That inexperienced people would not have believed God’s promises for the distant future if they had not also received something nearby from the one who made the promise. Thus, to strengthen them more securely in faith in eternal things, they are drawn not only by hope toward realities, but also by realities toward hope.

The Psalmist clearly testifies to this, saying: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the peoples, so that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law” (Ps. 104:44). But when the human mind does not follow God, who gives generously, with the response of a good work, it is more justly condemned by the very source from which it is believed to have been piously nourished. [Note: The editors thought it appropriate to print “repayment” instead of “response,” although “response” is read in all our manuscripts.]

Hence the Psalmist says again: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). For when the reprobate do not repay divine gifts with upright works, when they abandon themselves entirely here and give themselves over to overflowing prosperity, from the very place where they advance outwardly they fall inwardly.

Hence it is said to the rich man being tormented in hell: “You received good things during your life” (Luke 16:25). The wicked man received good things here precisely so that he might receive evils there more fully, because here he had not been converted even by good things.

But, on the other hand, those who desire the things of the world but are wearied by the labor of adversity must carefully consider how great a grace the Creator and disposer of all things watches over them, since he does not abandon them to their desires. [Note: The same editors changed “disposer,” the reading of all the manuscripts, to “steward.”] When a physician despairs of a sick person, he allows him to receive everything he desires. But one whom he believes can be healed is forbidden many things he craves. We take money away from children for whom we reserve entire patrimonies as heirs.

Therefore, let those whom the adversity of temporal life humbles draw joy from the hope of an eternal inheritance, because if divine providence did not see that they were to be saved forever, it would not restrain them under the discipline of instruction. Those who are wearied by adversity while desiring the things of this life must carefully consider that temporal power often even lifts up the just as though it were a snare, and ensnares them in guilt.

As we have already said in the earlier part of this work (Part I, ch. 3), David, beloved of God, was more upright in servitude than when he attained the kingdom (1 Sam. 24:18). As a servant, through love of justice, he feared to strike an enemy who had been discovered; as king, persuaded by lust, he destroyed even a devoted soldier through a deliberate scheme (2 Sam. 11:17). Who, then, can seek wealth, power, or glory innocently, if these things proved harmful even to one who possessed them without having sought them? Who can be saved amid these things without the labor of great danger, if one who had been prepared for them by God’s choice was disturbed by guilt when he possessed them?

They must consider that Solomon, who is described as having fallen from such great wisdom all the way into idolatry, is not recorded to have experienced any adversity in this world before his fall; but the wisdom granted to him entirely deserted the heart that no discipline of even the smallest tribulation had guarded (1 Kings 11:4).

## CHAPTER XXVII [Al. LI]

### How married and celibate persons are to be admonished

**Admonition 28.**

Those bound by marriage must be admonished in one way, and those free from the bonds of marriage in another.

Those bound by marriage must be admonished that, while each considers what belongs to the other, each should strive to please the spouse in such a way as not to displease the Creator; that they should engage in the affairs of this world in such a way that they do not cease to desire the things of God; that they should rejoice in present goods in such a way that they nevertheless fear eternal evils with watchful attention; and that they should grieve over temporal evils in such a way that they nevertheless fix their hope firmly upon lasting goods through undiminished consolation.

Thus, while they recognize that what they are doing belongs to transience, they should desire what belongs to permanence. [Note: We removed “they should know,” which the editors added without justification, to the detriment of the meaning itself.] Let the evils of the world not break their hearts, since the hope of heavenly goods strengthens them; nor let the goods of the present life deceive them, since the evils of the coming judgment make them apprehensive.

Thus the mind of Christian spouses, both weak and faithful—unable wholly to despise temporal things, yet able through desire to join itself to eternal things—although for a time it lies in the pleasure of the flesh, should grow strong through the refreshment of heavenly hope. If it possesses the things of the world for use on the journey, it should hope for the things of God as the fruit of arrival. It should not devote itself entirely to what it is doing, lest it fall completely away from what it ought vigorously to hope for.

Paul expresses this well and briefly, saying: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice” (1 Cor. 7:29–30). A man has a wife as though he did not have one when he uses her for bodily consolation in such a way that, through love for her, he is never bent away from the uprightness of a better intention toward evil works. He has a wife as though he did not have one when, seeing that all things are transitory, he endures care for the flesh out of necessity, but awaits the eternal joys of the spirit with desire. [Note: Laudunensis reads “with the desire of the spirit.”] To weep without weeping is to lament outward adversities in such a way that one nevertheless knows how to rejoice in the consolation of eternal hope. Again, to rejoice without rejoicing is to lift the mind above lowly things in such a way that one never ceases to fear what is supreme.

A little later he appropriately adds: “For the form of this world is passing away” (ibid., 31). It is as though he were saying plainly: Do not love the world steadfastly, since even the world you love cannot stand. In vain do you fix your heart as though you were remaining, while what you love itself is fleeing.

Spouses must be admonished to tolerate patiently whatever sometimes displeases them in one another, and to save one another by mutual exhortation. For it is written: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). The law of Christ is charity, because he both generously bestowed his good things upon us and bore our evils with equanimity. [Note: We restored the reading of all the manuscripts; the editions previously read “because he is ours.”] We fulfill the law of Christ by imitation when we kindly confer our good things and piously endure the evils of our own people. [Note: The first Carnotensis reads “by meditating.”]

They must also be admonished that each should attend not so much to what he tolerates from the other as to what is tolerated from him. For if he considers what is endured on his account, he bears more lightly what he endures from the other.

Spouses must be admonished to remember that they were joined for the sake of receiving offspring; and when, serving immoderate intercourse, they turn the occasion of procreation into an instrument of pleasure, they must consider that, although they do not go outside the bounds of marriage, within marriage itself they nevertheless transgress the rights of marriage.

Therefore they must erase by frequent prayers what they defile by mingling pleasure with the beautiful appearance of union. [Note: Trecensis, Laudunensis, Gemeticensis, and others read “by frequent prayers.” The editions read “by frequent exhortations,” against the sense.] For this reason the Apostle, learned in heavenly medicine, did not so much instruct the healthy as show medicines to the weak, saying: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. 7:1 and following, etc.).

For by placing the fear of fornication first, he clearly did not give a command to those who were standing firm; rather, lest they perhaps fall to the ground, he showed a bed to those who were falling. Hence he added to the weak: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (ibid.). While granting something of pleasure within the great honor of marriage, he added: “But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command” (ibid.).

What is said to be conceded is thereby indicated to be a fault; yet it is relaxed all the more quickly because through it something illicit is not done, but what is licit is not maintained under proper restraint.

Lot expresses this well in himself: he fled from burning Sodom, but, after finding Zoar, did not immediately climb into the mountains (Gen. 19:30). To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the illicit fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is the purity of those who practice continence. Or certainly, those who cling even to carnal union are as though on a mountain, provided that outside the proper union for receiving offspring they are not released into any carnal pleasure. [Note: The sense is problematic in the editions, where one reads: “For what is it to stand on the mountain except not to seek the fruit of offspring in the flesh?” This conflicts with what precedes: “They are on the mountain who also cling to carnal union, yet outside the proper union for receiving offspring they are not released into any carnal pleasure.” We have followed especially the manuscripts of Trecensis, in which “except not to seek the fruit of offspring” has the same meaning as “to seek nothing but the fruit of offspring.”]

To stand on the mountain is not to seek in the flesh anything but the fruit of offspring. To stand on the mountain is not to cling carnally to the flesh. But because there are many who indeed abandon the crimes of the flesh, yet, being married, do not preserve the rights of the proper use alone, Lot did leave Sodom but did not immediately reach the mountains: a life already deserving condemnation is abandoned, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet observed with precision. [Note: The first Laudunensis, Audomarensis, and some others read “sublimely”; Trecensis and the others read “subtly.”]

In between there is the city of Zoar, which saves the fugitive who is weak: that is, when spouses unite with each other through incontinence, they flee the falls of sin and yet are saved by pardon. They find, as it were, a small city in which they are defended from the fires, because this conjugal life is not remarkable for virtues, but is nevertheless safe from punishments.

Hence Lot says to the angel: “There is a city here nearby, to which I can flee, a small one, and I shall be saved in it. Is it not a little one, and my soul shall live in it?” (Gen. 19:20). It is therefore called nearby and yet is declared safe for salvation, because conjugal life is neither far removed from the world nor alien from the joy of salvation.

But spouses preserve their life in this conduct as though in a small city when they intercede for one another with continual prayers. Hence the angel rightly says to the same Lot: “Behold, I have also accepted your prayers in this matter, so that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken” (ibid., 21). [Note: The relevant column reference is 103C.] When prayer is poured out, such a conjugal life is by no means condemned by God. Concerning this prayer Paul also admonishes, saying: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Cor. 7:5).

But, on the other hand, those who are not bound by marriage must be admonished to serve the heavenly commandments all the more rightly, since the yoke of carnal union does not incline them toward worldly cares; so that those whom the lawful burden of marriage does not weigh down may not be pressed by the unlawful burden of earthly anxiety. Let the final day find them all the more ready because it finds them more free; lest, because they can do better things while unoccupied but neglect them, they thereby deserve worse punishments.

Let them hear that when the Apostle was instructing certain people toward the grace of celibacy, he did not despise marriage but rejected the worldly cares arising from marriage, saying: “I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honorable and what gives opportunity to serve the Lord without impediment” (ibid., 35). [Note: Trecensis, Laudunensis, Vallicellianus, and three Gemeticenses read “to serve the Lord”; Corb. reads “to serve the Lord,” with a second hand giving “to entreat the Lord.”]

For earthly cares arise from marriage, and therefore the teacher of the nations persuaded his hearers toward better things, so that they would not be bound by earthly anxiety. Any celibate person whom the impediment of worldly cares hinders has not submitted to marriage, yet has not escaped the burdens of marriage.

Celibate persons must be admonished not to think that they may freely mingle with unmarried women without the judgment of condemnation. When Paul inserted the vice of fornication among so many abominable crimes, he indicated its guilt, saying: “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10). And again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers” (Heb. 13:4).

They must therefore be admonished that, if they endure the storms of temptation with difficulty and at the risk of salvation, they should seek the harbor of marriage. For it is written: “It is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:9). They come to marriage without guilt, provided they have not yet vowed themselves to better things. For whoever has resolved to undertake the greater good has made the lesser good, though permitted, illicit for himself.

For it is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62). Whoever, therefore, had devoted himself to a stronger pursuit is shown to be looking back if, abandoning greater goods, he is turned back toward lesser ones. [Note: Laudunensis, Theodorus, and Vallicellianus read “putting his hand to the plow.”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Al. LII]

### How those who have experienced sins of the flesh, and those who have not, are to be admonished

**Admonition 29.**

Those conscious of sins of the flesh must be admonished in one way, and those unfamiliar with them in another.

Those who have experienced sins of the flesh must be admonished to fear the sea even after shipwreck, and at least to dread the dangers of their ruin once they have come to know them; lest those who have been mercifully preserved after committing evil should die by wickedly repeating it.

Hence it is said to the soul that sins and never ceases from sin: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3). They must therefore strive that, if they were unwilling to preserve intact the good things they received from nature, they may at least repair what has been torn.

They must surely consider how, among so great a number of the faithful, many both preserve themselves undefiled and convert others from error. What, then, will these people say if, while others stand in integrity, they do not recover even after their losses? What will they say if, while many bring others with them into the kingdom, they do not even lead themselves back to the Lord who awaits them?

They must be admonished to consider their past offenses and avoid those that threaten. Hence, under the figure of Judah, the Lord through the prophet recalls to corrupt minds the sins they have committed, so that they may be ashamed to pollute themselves in the future, saying: “They fornicated in Egypt; in their youth they fornicated there; their breasts were pressed, and the breasts of their puberty were broken” (Ezek. 23:3).

In Egypt breasts are pressed when the will of the human mind is subjected to the shameful desire of this world. In Egypt the breasts of puberty are broken when natural senses, still intact in themselves, are corrupted by the assault of desire.

Those who have experienced sins of the flesh must carefully observe how benevolently God opens the lap of his mercy to us when, after our offenses, we return to him, since through the prophet he says: “If a man divorces his wife, and she, departing from him, marries another man, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? But you have fornicated with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3:1).

Behold, an argument from justice is proposed concerning a fornicating and abandoned woman, and yet when we return after our fall, not justice but mercy is shown to us. From this we may gather how greatly we sin through our wickedness if, when we offend, we are spared with such mercy, yet do not return after our offense; and what pardon there will be for the wicked from him who does not cease to call them after their guilt.

This mercy of the call after sin is well expressed through the prophet when it is said to the turned-away person: “Your eyes will see your teacher, and your ears will hear the word of one admonishing you behind your back” (Isa. 30:20). The Lord admonished the human race face to face when, after creating humanity and establishing it in free choice in paradise, he prescribed what it ought and ought not to do.

But the human being turned his back upon God’s face when, in his pride, he despised his commands. Yet God did not abandon the proud person: to call humanity back, he gave the law, sent exhorting angels, and himself appeared in the flesh of our mortality. [Note: The first Gemeticensis reads “having exhorted” (exhortatus).] Thus he admonished us while standing behind us, since even after being despised he called us back to the recovery of grace.

What could therefore be said generally of all must necessarily be understood particularly of each individual. Each person receives the words of God’s admonition as though placed before God, when, before committing sins, he learns the commands of his will. To stand still before his face is not yet to despise him by sinning. But when, abandoning the good of innocence and choosing iniquity, a person desires it, he already turns his back upon God’s face.

Yet behold, God still follows behind and admonishes the person who has turned away, persuading him to return to him even after his guilt. He calls back the one who has turned away, does not regard the offenses committed, and opens the lap of his mercy to the one who returns.

We hear the voice of one admonishing behind us if, even after our sins, we return to the Lord who invites us. We ought therefore to be ashamed of the mercy of the one who calls if we are unwilling to fear his justice, because his mercy is despised with all the graver wickedness when he does not disdain to continue calling even those who have despised him.

But, on the other hand, those unfamiliar with sins of the flesh must be admonished to fear a precipitous fall all the more carefully the higher they stand. They must be admonished to know that the more prominently they stand, the more frequently they are attacked by the arrows of the ambusher.

The enemy is accustomed to rise all the more fiercely the more strongly he sees himself defeated; and he resents being defeated all the more intolerably the more he sees the camps of weak flesh, kept undefiled, arrayed against him.

They must be admonished continually to keep the rewards before them, and they will undoubtedly tread willingly upon the labors of the temptations they endure. For if the happiness attained without passing away is considered, what is endured in passing becomes light.

Let them hear what is said through the prophet: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I have willed, and hold fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isa. 56:4–5).

Eunuchs are those who, restraining the movements of the flesh, cut off within themselves the inclination toward evil action. The place they hold with the Father is shown by the fact that in the Father’s house—that is, in the eternal dwelling—they are even preferred to sons.

Let them hear what is said through John: “These are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14:4). They sing a song which no one can sing except those one hundred forty-four thousand. To sing the Lamb’s song uniquely is to rejoice with him forever, above all the faithful, even in the incorruption of the flesh.

The other elect, however, can hear this song, although they cannot sing it, because through charity they rejoice in the exaltation of those persons, even though they do not rise to their rewards.

Those unfamiliar with sins of the flesh should hear what the Truth himself says concerning this integrity: “Not all receive this word” (Matt. 19:11). He made it known to be supreme by denying it to all; and while declaring that it is difficult to receive, he indicated to his hearers with what care it must be held once received. [Note: Corb. reads “what was begun.”]

Those unfamiliar with sins of the flesh must therefore be admonished to know that virginity is superior to marriage, yet not to exalt themselves above married persons; so that, while they prefer virginity and place themselves below others, they may neither abandon what they judge to be better nor fail to guard themselves because they exalt themselves vainly. [Note: The first Carnotensis reads “those whom they vainly.”]

They must be admonished to consider that often the life of the continent is put to shame by the conduct of worldly people, when the latter undertake works beyond their profession while the former do not rouse their hearts in accordance with their own order.

Hence it is well said through the prophet: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23:4). Sidon is brought to shame, as it were, by the voice of the sea when, by comparison with the life of worldly people and of those tossed about in this world, the life of one who appears fortified and stable, as it were, is condemned.

Often some who return to the Lord after sins of the flesh display themselves all the more ardently in good works because they see themselves to be more deserving of condemnation for their evils. And often some who persevere in bodily integrity, seeing that they have less to mourn, think their innocence of life fully sufficient for them and kindle themselves with no goads of ardor toward spiritual fervor.

Thus it often happens that a life burning with love after guilt is more pleasing to God than innocence growing sluggish through security. Hence the voice of the judge says: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). And: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:10).

We gather this more readily from ordinary experience if we weigh the judgments of our own minds. We love more the earth that, after thorns have been plowed, produces abundant fruits than the earth that had no thorns but, once cultivated, produces a barren crop.

Those unfamiliar with sins of the flesh must be admonished not to place themselves above others because of the eminence of their order, since they do not know how much better those of lower rank may act. In the assessment of the righteous judge, the merits of ranks are changed by the quality of actions. [Note: The same manuscript reads “the merits of hearts.”]

Who, when considering the very images of things, does not know that among precious stones the carbuncle is preferred to the hyacinth? Yet the hyacinth, with its blue color, is preferred to the pale carbuncle, because beauty of appearance adds to the one what the order of nature withholds, while the quality of color disfigures the one whom the natural order had preferred.

So, in the human race, some are worse in a better order, and some are better in a worse one: the latter transcend the lot of their lowly condition by living well, while the former diminish the merit of their higher position by failing to carry it out in their conduct. [Note: The same Codex reads “by failing to follow it.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX [Al. LIII]

### How those who mourn sins of action, and those who mourn only sins of thought, are to be admonished

**Admonition 30.**

Those who mourn sins of action must be admonished in one way, and those who mourn sins of thought in another.

Those who mourn sins of action must be admonished to wash away completed evils with complete lamentation, lest they be bound more tightly by the debt of the deed committed and pay less through tears of satisfaction. [Note: Laudunensis reads “if they pay less.”] For it is written: “You gave us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 79:6), so that each person’s mind may drink through repentance as many tears of compunction as it remembers having withered away from God through its sins.

They must be admonished continually to bring their offenses back before their eyes and, by living rightly, to act so that they may not have to be seen by the strict judge. Hence David, when he asked, saying, “Turn your eyes away from my sins” (Ps. 50:11), had said a little earlier: “My sin is always before me” (ibid., 5). It is as though he were saying: I ask you not to look upon my sin, because I myself never cease to look upon it. [Note: Corb. and Carnotensis read “against me.”]

Hence through the prophet the Lord says: “I will not remember your sins; but you, remember them” (Isa. 43:25–26). They must be admonished to consider each offense individually and, while mourning the defilement of their error in each one, to cleanse themselves entirely through tears.

Hence it is well said through Jeremiah, when the individual sins of Judah were being weighed: “My eye brought down divisions of waters” (Lam. 3:48). We bring down divided waters from our eyes when we give tears apportioned to individual sins. For the mind does not grieve equally over all things at one and the same time; but as it is more sharply touched now by the memory of this guilt, now of that, it is moved in each case concerning all of them together and is cleansed.

85. They should be admonished to take confidence from the mercy they seek, lest they perish through excessive severity of affliction. For the Lord would not piously place before the eyes of sinners the sins that ought to be mourned, if he had wished to strike them down strictly by himself. It is clear that he wished to hide from his judgment those whom, by mercifully anticipating them, he made judges of themselves. Hence it is written: “Let us come before the face of the Lord in confession” [Col. 0108B] (Ps. 94:2). Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:31).

Again, they should be admonished to possess confidence in hope in such a way that they do not grow sluggish through careless security. For often the cunning enemy, when he sees a mind which he has overthrown through sin afflicted by its ruin [Note: Belv., Corb., and the first Carnot. read “finds”], deceives it with the baneful flatteries of security. This is expressed figuratively in the account of Dinah. For it is written:

“Dinah went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and slept with her, violently oppressing the virgin; and his soul was joined to her, and he soothed her sadness with flatteries” (Gen. 34:1–3).

Dinah goes out to see the women of a foreign region when each mind, neglecting its own pursuits and concerning itself with the activities of others, wanders outside its own character and proper order [Col. 0108C]. Shechem, the prince of the land, overpowers her because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it occupied with external concerns. “And his soul was joined to her” (ibid.), because he sees her united to himself through iniquity. And because, when the mind recovers from its fault, it is brought back to itself [Note: The Vulgate manuscripts, contradicting one another, read “is brought back to himself.” This expression is familiar to our Gregory; he uses *addicitur* in this sense in *Moralia* II.15, and also IX.32 and XXII.22–23.], and tries to mourn what it has done, the corrupter recalls empty hopes and assurances before its eyes, so as to deprive it of the benefit of sorrow. Therefore the text rightly adds: “And he soothed her sadness with flatteries” (ibid.).

At one moment he speaks of the graver deeds of others; at another, of how insignificant the deed committed was; at another, of the mercifulness of God; at another, he promises that there will still be time for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these things, it is held back from its intention of repentance, so that it then receives no good because now no evils distress it; and it is then more completely overwhelmed by punishments because even now it rejoices in its sins [Note: Bellov., first hand, reads “rejoices in pleasures.”].

On the other hand, those who mourn sins of thought should be admonished carefully to examine, within the hidden recesses of the mind, whether they have sinned by delight alone or also by consent. Often the heart is tempted [Note: Thus the manuscripts; alternatively, “the tempted heart.” Guss. reads “the heart by temptation.”], takes delight in the wickedness of the flesh, and yet resists that same wickedness through reason, so that in the secrecy of thought it both grieves over what it desires and desires what it grieves over. Sometimes, however, the mind is so swallowed up by the abyss of temptation that it offers no resistance at all; rather, it deliberately follows that by which it is assailed through pleasure, and, if external opportunity is available, immediately completes its inward desires through outward deeds.

If the strict judgment of the just judge takes this into account, it is no longer merely the guilt of thought but of deed; for even if the delay of outward circumstances postpones the sin externally, the will has fulfilled it inwardly through the act of consent.

From our first parent we have learned that we commit every kind of wickedness in three ways: by suggestion, by delight, and by consent. 86 The first is perpetrated through the enemy, the second through the flesh, and the third through the spirit. The ambusher suggests evil [Note: The first Carnot. reads “suggests evil things”]; the flesh submits itself to delight; and finally the spirit, overcome by delight, consents. Thus the serpent suggested evil; Eve, as flesh, submitted herself to delight; and Adam, as spirit, overcome by suggestion and delight, assented [Note: Trec., the two earlier Carnot., the two earlier Gemet., and Bellov., by correction, read “and there the serpent.”].

By suggestion, therefore, we recognize sin; by delight, we are overcome; and by consent, we are also bound. Accordingly, those who mourn the wickedness of thought should be admonished carefully to consider the degree of sin into which their mind has fallen, so that, in proportion to the ruin they inwardly feel within themselves, they may also rise through a corresponding measure of lamentation. Otherwise, if imagined evils torment them too little, they may be led on to the commission of actual deeds.

Yet they should be so terrified in these matters that they are not completely broken. Often the merciful God washes away sins of the heart all the more quickly because he does not permit them to pass into deeds; and wickedness of thought is released more readily because it is not bound more strictly by the effect of an act. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: “I said, ‘I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my heart” (Ps. 31:3).

By saying that he had placed the iniquity of his heart before God, he indicated that he wished to declare the injustices of his thoughts. And when he says, “I said, ‘I will declare,’” and immediately adds, “And you forgave,” he shows how readily forgiveness is granted in such matters. While he still promises that he will ask, he obtained what he was promising to ask for [Note: Laud., Val. Cl., the third Gemet., and the third Carnot. read “he obtained by repenting what he was promising to ask for.”]. Thus, because the guilt had not reached the deed, the repentance did not reach torment; rather, the affliction of thought cleansed the mind which iniquity of thought alone had defiled [Note: The two earlier Gemet. manuscripts read “agitated.”].

## CHAPTER XXX [Al. LIV]. How those who do not cease from the sins they mourn, and those who cease but do not mourn, should be admonished

(Admonition 31.) Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them should be admonished in one way, and those who abandon them but do not mourn them in another. Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them should be admonished to understand carefully that they cleanse themselves uselessly by weeping if they defile themselves wickedly by living—washing themselves with tears only to return, once clean, to filth.

Hence it is written: “A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (Prov. 26:11; 2 Pet. 2:22). When a dog vomits, it certainly casts out the food that weighed down its breast; but when it returns to its vomit, it is again burdened by what had relieved it. Likewise, those who mourn their sins cast out through confession the wickedness with which they had been badly sated and which weighed down the innermost recesses of the mind; but when they repeat it after confession, they take it up again.

A sow, when washed in a muddy wallow, is made dirtier. Likewise, whoever mourns a sin but does not abandon it subjects himself to the punishment of a graver sin [Note: Bellov. and the second Carnot. read “subjects himself to a guilt all the graver in proportion as he …”] (the same distinction, canon 14, “Whoever mourns a sin”); for he both despises the forgiveness he could obtain by weeping and rolls himself, as it were, in muddy water. Since he removes the purity of life through his tears, he makes those very tears filthy before the eyes of God.

Again it is written: “Do not repeat a word in your prayer” (Sir. 7:15). To repeat a word in prayer is to commit, after weeping, what will again make it necessary to weep. Hence Isaiah says: “Wash yourselves” (Isa. 1:16), “be clean” (the same distinction, canon 15, “Wash yourselves”). Whoever neglects to remain clean after washing, that is, whoever does not preserve innocence of life after tears, remains unclean.

Thus those who do not cease mourning the sins they have committed, but commit again what must be mourned, are washed but by no means clean. Hence a certain wise man says [Note: In the Trecensis manuscript, a marginal note at this passage reads: “In Solomon.” This proves that the Book of Ecclesiasticus was then attributed to Solomon.]: “He who is baptized because of a dead person and again touches him, what benefit does his washing provide?” (Sir. 34:30). He is baptized because of a dead person (the same distinction, canon 16, “He is baptized”) who is cleansed from sin by tears; but after baptism he touches the dead person who returns to his fault after weeping.

Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them should be admonished to recognize that, before the eyes of the strict judge, they resemble those who approach certain people and flatter them with great submission, but, once they depart, inflict upon them as fiercely as they can the enmities and harms they are able to cause.

For what is it to mourn a fault except to display to God the humility of one’s devotion? And what is it to do evil after weeping except to exercise hostile behavior against the one before whom one had pleaded in submission? James bears witness, saying: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4).

Those who mourn their sins but do not abandon them should carefully consider that the wicked are often uselessly pierced toward righteousness just as the good are often innocently tempted toward guilt. Through the mysterious measure of an inner disposition corresponding to their merits, it comes about that the former, while doing something good which they nevertheless do not complete, become proud amid the evils they perpetrate most fully; while the latter, when tempted by evil to which they give no consent, fix the steps of their heart more truly in righteousness through humility precisely where they stumble through weakness.

Balaam, looking upon the tents of the righteous, said: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs” (Num. 23:10). But when the time of compunction had passed, he gave counsel against the life of those whose likeness he had asked to share even in death; and when he found an opportunity through avarice, he immediately forgot whatever he had desired for himself concerning innocence (ibid., 24:14).

The teacher and preacher of the nations, Paul, says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23). He is certainly tempted for this reason: so that, through knowledge of his own weakness, he may be strengthened more firmly in goodness [Note: The first Carnot. reads “through the thought of his weakness.”].

What, then, is the reason that one is pierced with compunction and yet does not draw near to righteousness, while another is tempted and yet is not defiled by guilt? It is this, which is plainly demonstrated: imperfect good does not help the wicked, nor does unfinished evil condemn the good.

On the other hand, those who abandon their sins but do not mourn them should be admonished not to regard as loosened the faults which, although they do not multiply them by committing them, they nevertheless cleanse with no tears. For a writer does not erase what he has written merely by ceasing to write, since he adds nothing else; nor does one who has uttered insults make satisfaction merely by becoming silent, since it is necessary to oppose the words of the preceding pride with words of subsequent humility; nor is a debtor released merely because he does not increase his debt, unless he also pays what had bound him.

So too, when we sin against God, we do not make satisfaction merely by ceasing from iniquity, unless we also pursue, with lamentation set against them, the pleasures that we loved. For even if no guilt of deeds had stained us in this life, our innocence alone would not suffice for our security while we still lived here, since many unlawful things would assail the mind. With what confidence, then, can the person live securely who, after committing iniquities, is himself a witness to himself that he is not innocent?

God is not nourished by our torments; rather, he cures the diseases of sins [Note: The same manuscript reads “diseases.”] with medicines opposed to them. Thus those who departed delighted by pleasures return embittered by tears; those who fell by flowing into unlawful things rise by restraining themselves even from lawful things; the heart that had been infused with unhealthy joy is burned by wholesome sorrow; and what the exaltation of pride had wounded is healed by the humility of a lowly life.

Hence it is written: “I said to the wicked, ‘Do not act wickedly’; and to sinners, ‘Do not exalt your horn’” (Ps. 75:5). Sinners exalt their horn when they do not humble themselves to repentance through knowledge of their iniquity. Again it is said: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 51:19). Whoever mourns his sins but does not abandon them does indeed crush his heart, but refuses to humble it. Whoever has already abandoned his sins but does not mourn them does indeed humble himself, but refuses to crush his heart.

Paul says: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (1 Cor. 6:11) [Note: Guss. omits “but you were washed.”]. For the more reformed life sanctifies those whom the affliction of tears, washing them through repentance, cleanses.

When Peter saw certain people terrified by consideration of their evils, he admonished them, saying: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (Acts 2:38). Since he was about to speak of baptism, he first set forth the lamentations of repentance, so that they might first pour over themselves the water of their affliction and afterward be washed by the sacrament of baptism.

With what confidence, then, do those who neglect to mourn past sins live secure in forgiveness, when the chief Shepherd of the Church believed that repentance must be added even to this sacrament, which principally extinguishes sins?

## CHAPTER XXXI [Al. LV]. How those who praise the unlawful things of which they are conscious, and those who condemn them but nevertheless do not avoid them, should be admonished

(Admonition 32.) Those who even praise the unlawful things they do should be admonished in one way, and those who condemn wicked deeds but nevertheless do not avoid them in another.

Those who praise the unlawful things they do should be admonished to consider that they often sin more by mouth than by deed. By deed they themselves alone perpetrate wickedness; by mouth, however, they display iniquity through as many persons as there are minds of listeners whom, by praising evil, they teach.

They should therefore be admonished that, if they pretend not to uproot evils, they should at least fear to sow them. They should be admonished to let their private destruction be enough for them. Again, they should be admonished that, if they do not fear being evil, they should at least be ashamed to be seen as what they are.

Often a fault is driven away when it is hidden, because, while the mind is ashamed to be seen as what it nevertheless does not fear to be, it eventually becomes ashamed to be what it flees being seen as. But when someone wickedly makes himself known without shame, the more freely he perpetrates every crime, the more he regards it as permissible; and what he supposes permissible he undoubtedly plunges into more deeply.

Hence it is written: “They proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and did not hide it” (Isa. 3:9). If Sodom had hidden its sin, it would still have sinned under fear. But it had utterly lost the reins of fear, since it did not seek even darkness for its guilt. Hence it is written again: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has been multiplied” (Gen. 18:20). Sin with a voice is guilt in action; but sin even with a cry is guilt with license.

On the other hand, those who accuse wicked deeds but do not avoid them should carefully consider what they will say in their defense at the strict judgment of God, since they are not acquitted even before themselves, who have become judges of their own crimes.

What else are such people but heralds of themselves? They utter words against faults, yet by their deeds drag themselves forward as guilty. They should be admonished to see that it is already a matter of the hidden retribution of judgment that their mind is enlightened to see the evil it commits but does not strive to overcome it—so that the better it sees, the worse it perishes, because it receives the light of understanding while not abandoning the darkness of wicked action.

When they neglect the knowledge granted for their assistance, they turn it into testimony against themselves. They increase their punishments through the light of understanding which they had received precisely so that they might be able to erase their sins. When their wickedness does what it judges evil, it already tastes the coming judgment here, so that, while it is reserved for eternal punishments as guilty, it is not acquitted here by its own judgment; and it receives more grievous torments there because here it does not abandon the evil which it itself condemns [Note: Laud. reads “innocent.”].

Hence the Truth says: “The servant who knew the will of his lord, and did not prepare himself and did not act according to his will, will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47) [Note: Gemet. reads “will be beaten with many blows.”]. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let them descend alive into hell” (Ps. 55:16). The living know and feel what is happening around them; the dead can feel nothing. The dead would descend into hell if they committed evil without knowing it. But when they know the evil and nevertheless do it, these wretched people descend alive and feeling into the hell of iniquity [Note: Laud. reads “knowing and feeling.”].

## CHAPTER XXXII [Al. LVI]. How those who sin through sudden impulse and those who sin deliberately should be admonished

(Admonition 33.) Those who are overcome by sudden desire should be admonished in one way, and those who are bound in guilt through deliberation in another.

Those whom sudden desire overcomes should be admonished to recognize that they are placed daily in the warfare of the present life. They should cover the heart that cannot foresee its wounds with the shield of vigilant fear [Note: The ancient Trec., Bellov., and Gemet. manuscripts read “foresee.”], so that they may dread the hidden arrows of the ambushing enemy and continually fortify themselves within the camp of the mind through constant attentiveness.

For if the heart is deprived of the vigilance of watchfulness, it is opened to wounds, because the cunning enemy strikes the breast more freely the more he finds it bare of the armor of foresight.

Those who are overcome by sudden desire should be admonished to cease from caring excessively for earthly things. While they involve their attention too immoderately in transient matters, they do not know by what arrows of guilt they are pierced.

Hence Solomon expresses the voice of one who has been struck and is sleeping, saying: “They struck me, but I did not suffer; they dragged me, and I did not feel it. When shall I awake and again find wine?” (Prov. 23:35) [Note: Corb. reads “they pierced me.” This is evidence of a correction made in Trec., where it seems once to have been read so. Otherwise there is no foundation or trace of this reading either in the Hebrew text or in its various translations. Nor did Gregory read it so, since he later says, in explaining the passage: “He is dragged, and does not feel it.”].

A mind sleeping in concern for its own vigilance is struck and does not suffer, because just as it does not foresee the evils that threaten, so it does not recognize those it has committed. It is dragged and does not feel, because it is led along by the allurements of vices and is nevertheless not awakened to guard itself.

It wishes to awaken in order to find wine again, because although it is oppressed by the sleep of sluggishness and neglects its own protection, it nevertheless strives to awaken to the concerns of the world, so that it may always be drunk with pleasures. While it sleeps with respect to what it ought carefully to watch over, it desires to watch over something else—something regarding which it could laudably sleep.

Hence it was written earlier: “You will be like one sleeping in the middle of the sea, and like a drowsy helmsman who has lost the rudder” (ibid., 23:34). He sleeps in the middle of the sea who, placed amid the temptations of this world, neglects to foresee the movements of invading vices, like heaps of waves threatening him.

He loses the rudder like a helmsman when the mind loses its diligent concern for steering the vessel of the body. To lose the rudder at sea is not to maintain prudent attention amid the storms of this world.

If a helmsman holds the rudder carefully, sometimes he directs the ship against the waves, sometimes he treads down the waves while overcoming them, sometimes he avoids one thing while taking precautions against another, and sometimes he cuts through the force of the winds obliquely [Note: Corb., Carnot., Belv., Laud., Longip., Val. Cl., and Theod. read: “sometimes he directs the ship against the waves, sometimes he treads down the waves while overcoming them, sometimes he avoids one thing while taking precautions against another, and sometimes he cuts through the force of the winds obliquely.” Trec., Gemet., and the later Carnot. manuscripts support this reading.].

So too, when the mind governs the soul vigilantly, sometimes it overcomes one thing and tramples it down, sometimes it avoids another by taking precautions; thus, by laboring, it subjects present things, and by foreseeing future struggles, it grows strong against them [Note: Recent editions read “the vigilant soul.” The manuscripts contradict them. The sense proposed by the holy Doctor is against that reading.].

Again, concerning the strong warriors of the heavenly homeland, it is said: “Each one’s sword is upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3:8). The sword is placed upon the thigh when evil suggestion of the flesh is subdued by the sharpness of holy preaching.

Night expresses the blindness of our weakness, because whatever adversity threatens in the night cannot be seen. Thus each one’s sword is placed upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night [Note: Many editions add “because of the temptations or terrors of the night.” This is a gloss.], since holy men, fearing what they do not see, always stand prepared for the struggle.

Again, it is said to the bride: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song 7:4). Often we foresee by smell what we do not perceive with our eyes. Through the nose, too, we distinguish fragrances and foul odors. What, then, is signified by the nose of the Church except the prudent discernment of the saints? It is also said to be like the tower that is in Lebanon, because their discerning foresight is situated on high, so that it sees the struggles of temptation before they come and stands fortified against them when they arrive.

What is foreseen as future becomes weaker when it is present; for when someone is made readier to withstand the blow, the enemy who believed he would be unexpected is weakened by the very fact that he has been foreseen [Note: That is, the blows are weaker; perhaps editors who did not understand this changed *virtutis* (“of strength”) to *timoris* (“of fear”), contrary to all the manuscripts.].

On the other hand, those who are bound in guilt through deliberation should carefully consider that, while they do evil after judgment and deliberation, they kindle a stricter judgment against themselves; the sentence strikes them more harshly in proportion as the bonds of deliberation bind them more tightly in guilt.

They might perhaps wash away their sins more quickly through repentance if they had fallen into them through mere impulsiveness. For a sin that is strengthened by deliberation is released more slowly. Unless the mind in every way despised eternal things, it would not perish in guilt through deliberate judgment.

Those who perish through deliberation differ from those who fall through impulsiveness in this respect: when the latter fall from the state of righteousness through sinning, they often fall at the same time into the snare of despair [Note: The printed editions read: “Those who have fallen through this impulsiveness and those who perish through deliberation differ …,” but the sense is defective. It should be read as in Trec., Corb., Theod., Val. Cl., Laud., Norm., and others: “Those who perish through deliberation differ from those who fall through impulsiveness.” Older manuscripts have *labsis* for *lapsis*; Theod. reads “those who have fallen from impulsiveness.” Below: “sins committed through deliberation differ from other sins.”].

Hence, through the prophet, the Lord censures not so much the wickedness of impulsive acts as the deliberate pursuit of sins, saying: “Lest my indignation go forth like fire, and burn, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your pursuits” (Jer. 4:4). Again, in anger he says: “I will visit upon you according to the fruit of your pursuits” (ibid. 23:2).

Since sins committed through deliberation differ from other sins, the Lord pursues not so much wicked acts as the deliberate pursuit of wickedness. In acts, one sins often through weakness and often through negligence; but in deliberate pursuits one always sins through a malicious intention.

Against this, the blessed man is rightly described by the Prophet: “He did not sit in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1). The seat is customarily that of a judge or one presiding. To sit in the seat of pestilence is to commit wicked deeds after judgment; to sit in the seat of pestilence is to discern evil through reason and nevertheless perpetrate it through deliberation.

He sits, as it were, in the seat of perverse counsel who is raised up by such an exaltation of iniquity that he attempts to fulfill evil even through deliberation. And just as those supported by the honor of the seat preside over the attending crowds, so the sins of those who fall through impulsiveness are surpassed by the sins chosen through deliberate pursuit.

They should therefore be admonished to infer from this what vengeance will eventually strike those who now bind themselves in guilt even through deliberation—those who are not merely companions but leaders of the wicked [Note: The manuscripts more correctly read “leaders” than the printed editions, which have “princes.”].

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Al. LVII]. How those who commit minor but frequent offenses, and those who avoid minor offenses but sometimes become submerged in serious ones, should be admonished

[Col. 0115D] (Admonition 34.) Those who commit unlawful acts that are minor but frequent should be admonished in one way, and those who guard themselves from small faults but sometimes become submerged in serious ones in another.

Those who frequently transgress in minor matters should be admonished to consider not what kind of things they commit, but how many. If they despise their deeds when weighing them, they should fear them when counting them.

Small but numberless drops of rain fill the deep channels of rivers. The bilge that secretly grows does what a raging storm does openly. The wounds that break out on the limbs through an itch are small, but when their multitude occupies the body beyond counting, they destroy bodily life just as a single grave wound inflicted in the chest does.

Hence it is written:

“He who despises small things will gradually fall” (Sir. 19:1).

Whoever neglects to mourn and avoid the smallest sins falls completely from the state of righteousness—not suddenly, but little by little.

Those who frequently transgress in small matters should carefully consider that one sometimes sins more seriously in a small fault than in a greater one. A greater fault is recognized as a fault more quickly and is therefore corrected more quickly; a lesser fault, because it is believed to be almost nothing, is retained in practice all the more harmfully because it is retained with greater security.

Thus it often happens that a mind accustomed to minor evils does not dread even serious ones, and, nourished through faults, reaches a kind of authority in wickedness. The more it has learned not to fear sinning in small matters, the more it disdains fearing larger ones.

On the other hand, those who guard themselves from small faults but sometimes become submerged in serious ones should carefully detect what happens to them: while their hearts are lifted up by the small things they have guarded, they are swallowed up by the very abyss of their pride into the commission of graver things [Note: Trec., supported by the more recent editions, reads “their heart is swallowed up.”].

While they subject small things to themselves outwardly but swell inwardly through empty glory, they cast outwardly into greater evils the mind that has been inwardly overcome by the sickness of pride.

Those who guard themselves from small faults but sometimes become submerged in serious ones should therefore be admonished not to fall inwardly where they suppose themselves to stand outwardly, and not to allow, according to the retribution of the strict judge, the pride of lesser righteousness to become a path toward the pit of graver guilt.

Those who, vainly exalted, attribute the guarding of small goodness to their own powers [Note: Corruptly in Guss.: “attribute their guarding to their own powers.”] are justly abandoned and overwhelmed by greater faults. By falling, they learn that what made them stand was not their own possession, so that immense evils may restrain the heart which small goods exalt.

They should be admonished to consider that they bind themselves by deep guilt even in more serious sins, and yet often sin more grievously in the small things they guard, because they do evil in the former and, through the latter, conceal from human beings the fact that they are wicked.

Thus, when they perpetrate greater evils before God, there is open iniquity; and when they guard small goods before human beings, there is feigned holiness. Hence it is said to the Pharisees: “You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (Matt. 23:24). As if it were said plainly: “You distinguish minor evils, but swallow greater ones.”

Again, they are rebuked by the mouth of the Truth when they hear: “You tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith.” We should not hear carelessly that, when he spoke of tithing small things, he chose the finest herbs, though fragrant, to mention. By this he plainly showed that hypocrites, while guarding small things, seek to spread from themselves the fragrance of a holy reputation [Note: The printed editions read “to display themselves.” All the manuscripts oppose this reading, and we judge that they should be followed.]. Although they neglect to fulfill what is greatest, they observe those small things which, in human judgment, give off a fragrance far and wide.

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Al. LVIII]. How those who do not even begin good works, and those who do not complete what they have begun, should be admonished

(Admonition 35.) Those who do not even begin good works should be admonished in one way, and those who fail entirely to complete what they have begun in another.

Those who do not even begin good works should not first be taught to build the things they may love profitably, but to destroy the things in which they wickedly occupy themselves. They do not follow what they hear as unfamiliar unless they first recognize how harmful are the things with which they are familiar. For no one desires to be lifted up if he does not know even that he has fallen; and whoever does not feel the pain of a wound does not seek remedies for health.

What they love must therefore first be shown to be empty, and only then should they be told attentively how useful are the things they neglect. Let them first see that what they love must be fled; afterward, without difficulty, they will recognize that what they flee ought to be loved [Note: The second Carnot. reads “they will recognize.”]. They receive unfamiliar things better if they truly understand whatever discussion they hear concerning familiar things.

Then they learn with full desire to seek true goods, when they have discerned with certain judgment that they have held false things in vain. Let them hear, therefore, that present goods both pass away swiftly from delight and nevertheless remain without passing away as the cause of punishment: what pleases is taken away from the unwilling now, while what causes pain is reserved for the unwilling then as punishment.

Thus they should be profitably terrified by the very things in which they take harmful delight. When the stricken mind, seeing the deep losses of its ruin, recognizes that it has reached the precipice, let it draw its step back; and, fearing what it had loved, let it learn to love what it had despised.

Hence it is said to Jeremiah, sent to preach: “Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10). For unless he first destroyed what was perverse, he could not usefully build what was right; unless he uprooted the thorns of vain love from the hearts of his hearers, he would plainly plant the words of holy preaching in them to no purpose. Hence Peter first overturns, so that afterward he may build. He did not admonish the Jews about what they should now do, but rebuked them for what they had done, saying:

“Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you by mighty works, wonders, and signs that God worked through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, delivered up by the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you killed by the hands of lawless men, nailing him to the cross” (Acts 2:22–24).

Thus, destroyed by knowledge of their own cruelty, they would seek the building of holy preaching with all the more anxiety and hear it all the more profitably. Therefore they immediately reply: “What then shall we do, men and brothers?” They are at once told: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized” (ibid., 37–38). They would surely have despised these words of building unless they had first profitably discovered the ruin brought about by their own destruction.

Hence, when Saul was suddenly illumined by a light sent from heaven, he heard not what he ought rightly to do, but what he had done perversely. For when, prostrate, he asked, “Who are you, Lord?” the answer came immediately: “I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute” (Acts 9:4ff.; 22:8ff.). And when he at once added, “Lord, what do you command me to do?” (ibid.), he was immediately told: “Rise, enter the city, and there it will be told you what you must do” (ibid.).

Behold, the Lord speaking from heaven rebuked the deeds of his persecutor, yet did not immediately show him what he was to do. Behold, the whole structure of his pride had already collapsed, and after his ruin he humbly sought to be built up; yet, though pride is destroyed, the words of building are retained. Thus the monstrous persecutor might lie long in ruin, and afterward rise more firmly in good works, in proportion as he had first been utterly overthrown and had fallen from his former error.

Those, therefore, who have not yet begun to do any good works must first be overturned from the rigidity of their former wickedness by the hand of correction, so that afterward they may be raised to the condition of right action. For this is why we cut down a tall tree of the forest: so that we may raise it up as a covering for a building. Yet it is not immediately placed in the structure, since its defective greenness must first dry out; and the more its moisture is boiled away below, the more solidly it is raised to the heights.

On the other hand, those who do not at all bring to completion the good works they have begun must be admonished to consider carefully that, when they do not fulfill what they have undertaken, they also tear down what they had begun. For if what appears to be done does not grow through diligent intention, even what had been well done diminishes.

In this world the human soul is like a ship ascending against the force of a river. It is not permitted to remain in one place, because it slips downward unless it strives upward. If, therefore, the strong hand of the worker does not raise begun good works to perfection, the very slackness of his work fights against what has been accomplished.

Hence Solomon says: “He who is slack and negligent in his work is a brother to him who destroys his own works” (Prov. 18:9). For whoever does not rigorously carry out the good he has begun imitates, through negligent dissolution, the hand of one who destroys.

Hence it is said by the angel to the church of Sardis: “Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die, for I do not find your works full before my God” (Rev. 3:2).

Because its works had not been found full before God, he foretold that even the remaining works already performed were about to die. For if what is dead in us is not kindled into life, even what is held as though still alive is extinguished.

They must be admonished to weigh the fact that it would have been more tolerable not to take up the way of righteousness than to turn back after having taken it up. For unless they looked backward, they would not grow sluggish through any torpor with respect to the undertaking they had begun.

Let them hear what is written: “It would have been better for them not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2:21). Let them hear what is written: “Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth” (Rev. 3:15).

The hot person is one who both undertakes good endeavors and brings them to completion; the cold person is one who does not even begin what must be completed. And just as one passes from cold through lukewarmness to heat, so from heat one returns through lukewarmness to cold.

Whoever, therefore, lives after losing the coldness of unbelief, but does not, after overcoming lukewarmness, grow until he burns, undoubtedly causes himself to grow cold through having despaired of heat, while lingering in harmful lukewarmness.

But just as before lukewarmness there is coldness under hope, so after coldness there is lukewarmness in despair. For the person who is still in sins does not lose hope of conversion. But the person who has grown lukewarm after conversion has removed from himself the hope that could have existed for the sinner.

Everyone is therefore required to be either hot or cold, lest he be vomited out as lukewarm: either, not yet converted, still giving others hope of his conversion, or, already converted, burning in the virtues. Otherwise he is vomited out as lukewarm—one who returns through torpor to harmful cold after turning away from the warmth he had resolved upon.

## CHAPTER XXXV [Elsewhere LIX]

### How those who do evil secretly and good publicly are to be admonished, and likewise those who do the opposite

(Admonition 36)

Those who do evil secretly and good publicly must be admonished in one way; those who conceal the good they do and nevertheless allow others, by certain actions, to form a bad opinion of them must be admonished in another.

Those who do evil secretly and good publicly must be admonished to consider how swiftly human judgments fly away, but how immovably divine judgments endure. They must be admonished to fix the eyes of their minds upon the end of all things, because the testimony of human praise passes away, while the heavenly sentence—which penetrates hidden things—grows strong for eternal recompense.

While they set their hidden evils before divine judgments but their upright deeds before human eyes, the good they do publicly is without a witness, while what they commit secretly is not without an eternal witness. Thus, by concealing their sins from human beings while displaying their virtues, they both expose what ought to be punished and conceal what might have been rewarded.

The Truth rightly calls them “whitewashed tombs, beautiful on the outside, but full of the bones of the dead” (Matt. 23:27), because within they conceal the evils of their vices, while before human eyes they flatter themselves by displaying certain works and showing only the outward color of righteousness.

They must therefore be admonished not to despise the upright things they do, but to believe them worthy of a better reward. For they greatly devalue their good deeds when they suppose that human favor is sufficient payment for them. When transient praise is sought for an upright deed, something worthy of eternal reward is sold for a worthless price. Concerning this price, once received, the Truth says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:2, 5).

They must be admonished to consider that, while they show themselves wicked in secret but publicly provide examples of good works, they display as worthy of imitation what they avoid, proclaim as worthy of love what they hate, and finally live for others while dying to themselves.

On the other hand, those who do good secretly but nevertheless allow others, through certain actions, to form a bad opinion of them must be admonished lest, while they bring themselves to life through the virtue of right action, they kill others through themselves, by the example of a perverse estimation; lest they love their neighbors less than themselves; and lest, while they themselves sip a healthy drink of wine, they pour a poisonous cup of venom into minds intent upon considering them.

Such people help the life of their neighbors less in one respect and burden it greatly in another, since they strive both to do what is right secretly and, through certain actions, to sow in others a wicked example of themselves.

Whoever is already able to trample down the desire for praise commits a fraud against edification if he hides the good he does. He is like someone who deprives seed, already scattered, of roots by which it might germinate, since he does not display the work that ought to be imitated.

Hence the Truth says in the Gospel: “Let your good works be seen, and let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). There, too, the statement is put forward which seems to command something quite different: “Take care not to perform your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1).

What then does it mean that our work is to be done so that it is not seen, and yet is commanded to be seen, except that what we do must be concealed lest we ourselves be praised, and yet displayed so that the praise of our heavenly Father may increase?

For when the Lord forbade us to perform our righteousness before people, he immediately added: “In order to be seen by them.” And when he again commanded that our good works be seen by people, he immediately added: “So that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

He showed, then, by the conclusion of these statements, how they were to be seen and how they were not to be seen: the mind of the one doing the work was not to seek that his work be seen for his own sake, yet was not to conceal it for the glory of his heavenly Father.

Consequently, it often happens that a good work is hidden even when it is done publicly, and is public even when it is done secretly. For whoever seeks not his own glory but that of the heavenly Father in a public good work conceals what he has done, because he had only that one as witness whom he took care to please.

And whoever, in his private good work, desires to be discovered and praised—even if no one happened to see what he presented—nevertheless did it before human beings, because he brought with him into the good work as many witnesses as the human praises he sought in his heart.

But when, insofar as this can be done without sin, a bad opinion is not removed from the minds of those who observe, an occasion of guilt is offered by example to all who believe the person bad.
