Hence it often happens that those who carelessly allow others to form a bad opinion of them themselves do nothing wicked, yet through those who imitate them they sin in greater numbers.

Hence Paul says to those who eat certain unclean things without pollution, but by this eating cause the scandal of temptation to the weak: “See to it that perhaps this liberty of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak” (1 Cor. 8:9). And again: “The weak person will perish through your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, by sinning against your brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ” (ibid., 11–12).

Hence, when Moses said, “You shall not curse the deaf,” he immediately added, “Nor shall you place a stumbling block before the blind” (Lev. 19:14). To curse the deaf is to disparage someone absent and unable to hear; to place a stumbling block before the blind is to do something in itself discerning, yet to offer an occasion of scandal to one who lacks the light of discernment.

## CHAPTER XXXVI [Elsewhere LX]

### On exhortation to be offered to many, so that it may assist the virtues of individuals without allowing vices contrary to those virtues to grow

[Column 0121C]

These are the things that the shepherd of souls must observe amid the diversity of preaching, so that, being attentive, he may apply suitable remedies to the wounds of individuals. Yet although it requires great effort to serve each person with an exhortation suited to each one, and although it is very laborious to instruct each individual concerning his own matters with the proper administration of consideration, it is far more laborious to address countless hearers suffering from diverse passions with one and the same voice at one and the same time.

The voice must be so skillfully modulated that, although the vices of the hearers are diverse and an appropriate remedy is found for each, the voice itself is not thereby divided against itself; so that it passes through the midst of the passions in a single course, yet, like a two-edged sword, strikes the swellings of carnal thoughts from opposite sides.

Thus humility must be preached to the proud without increasing the fear of the timid; authority must be infused into the timid without increasing the unrestrainedness of the proud. Concern for good works must be preached to the idle and sluggish without increasing the license for immoderate activity in the restless. Restraint must be imposed upon the restless without producing a secure torpor in the idle.

Anger must be extinguished in the impatient without increasing negligence in the lax and gentle. The gentle must be stirred to zeal without adding fuel to the anger of the irascible. Generosity in giving must be infused into the miserly without loosening the reins of outpouring for the prodigal. Frugality must be preached to the prodigal without increasing in the miserly the guarding of things destined to perish.

Marriage must be praised to the incontinent without recalling those already continent to luxury. Bodily virginity must be praised to the continent without making the fruitfulness of the flesh despised among married people.

Good things must be preached in such a way that evils are not thereby strengthened. The highest goods must be praised in such a way that the lowest are not despaired of. The lowest goods must be nourished in such a way that, while they are believed sufficient, no one strives toward the highest.

## CHAPTER XXXVII [Elsewhere LXI]

### On the exhortation to be addressed to one person suffering from contrary passions

It is indeed a heavy labor for a preacher, amid the common voice of preaching, to remain vigilant for the hidden movements and causes of individuals and, like a wrestler, to turn with skill toward opposing sides. Yet he is wearied by a much sharper labor when compelled to preach to one person subject to contrary vices.

Often someone is excessively cheerful in temperament, yet is suddenly and terribly weighed down when sadness arises. The preacher must therefore take care to wipe away the sadness that has come from circumstances without increasing the cheerfulness supplied by temperament, and to restrain the cheerfulness that comes from temperament without allowing the circumstantial sadness to grow.

One person is burdened by a habit of immoderate haste, yet is sometimes held back by the force of a sudden fear from doing what must be done quickly. Another is burdened by a habit of immoderate fear, yet is sometimes driven by rash haste toward what he desires.

In the first, sudden fear must be restrained without allowing the haste long nourished in him to grow; in the second, sudden haste must be restrained without allowing the fear impressed by temperament to gain strength.

What is surprising, then, if physicians of souls observe these things, when those who heal not hearts but bodies regulate themselves with such great skill?

Often a weak body is oppressed by a terrible illness. That illness must indeed be met with strong remedies, yet a weak body cannot bear a strong remedy. The physician therefore strives to remove the disease that has arisen without allowing the underlying weakness of the body to increase, lest perhaps the illness end together with life.

He composes the remedy with such discretion that at the same time he both confronts the illness and attends to the weakness. If, then, medicine applied undividedly to the body can serve in a divided manner—for it is truly medicine when it so confronts the disease present that it also serves the underlying weakness—why should not the medicine of the mind, applied through one and the same preaching, confront diseases of character in different ways, since it is administered with all the greater subtlety because it deals with invisible things?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII [Elsewhere LXII]

### That sometimes lesser vices must be left alone so that more serious ones may be removed

Since it often happens that, when the weakness of two vices attacks someone, one presses more lightly and the other perhaps more heavily, the vice by which the person is hastening more quickly toward destruction must rightly be helped first and more rapidly.

And if he cannot be restrained from approaching death unless the contrary vice also grows, the preacher must tolerate this, so that through his exhortation he may allow one vice to grow by artful moderation in order to hold the other back from approaching death. When he does this, he does not aggravate the disease; rather, he preserves the life of the wounded person to whom he is applying the remedy, so that he may find a suitable time for seeking health.

Often someone does not at all restrain himself from gluttony in food and is already being pressed almost to the point of collapse by the goads of lust, which is gaining the upper hand. Terrified by the danger of this struggle, while he tries to restrain himself through abstinence, he is harassed by the temptation of empty glory. In such a person one vice cannot be extinguished unless the other is nourished.

Which plague, then, must be pursued more ardently than the one that presses more dangerously? It must never be tolerated that, through the virtue of abstinence, arrogance should meanwhile grow against the person who is struggling, lest lust utterly destroy him from life through gluttony.

Hence Paul, perceiving that his weak hearer either still wished to do evil or rejoiced in human praise as the reward of right action, says: “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13:3).

Good deeds are not to be done so that no authority of this world is feared, nor so that the glory of passing praise may be gained through them. But when the excellent preacher judged that the weak mind could not rise to such strength as to avoid both wickedness and praise at once, he offered it something through admonition and took something away. By granting what was milder, he removed what was harsher, so that, because the mind could not rise to abandon everything at once, while it was left familiarly with one of its vices, it might be removed from another without difficulty.

## 99 CHAPTER XXXIX [Elsewhere LXIII]

### That lofty matters should by no means be preached to weak minds

The preacher must know that he should not draw the mind of his hearer beyond its strength, lest, so to speak, while it is stretched farther than it can bear, the cord of the mind should break.

Every lofty matter must be concealed from many hearers and opened only with difficulty to a few. Hence the Truth itself says: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the master appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matt. 24:45; Luke 12:42).

By the measure of wheat the proper measure of the word is expressed, lest, when something incapable of being contained is given to a narrow heart, it spill outside.

Hence Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal—as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1).

Hence Moses, coming out from the secret presence of God, veils his shining face before the people (Exod. 34:33), because he does not reveal to the crowds the secrets of inner brightness.

Hence, by divine command through him, it is prescribed that if someone digs a cistern and neglects to cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, he must pay its price (Exod. 21:33). For when someone who has reached the lofty streams of knowledge does not cover them before the brutish hearts of his hearers, he is condemned as guilty of punishment if, through his words, a mind—whether pure or impure—is caught in scandal.

Hence it is said to blessed Job: “Who gave understanding to the rooster?” (Job 38:36). For while the holy preacher cries out in this dark age, he sings like a rooster in the night when he says: “It is already the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13:11), and again: “Awake, righteous people, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15:34).

The rooster customarily gives forth loud cries during the deeper hours of the night. But when morning is already near, it makes short and faint sounds. So, plainly, one who preaches rightly cries out openly to hearts still obscure, but says nothing about hidden mysteries, so that they may hear the more subtle things concerning heaven when they draw near the light of truth.

## CHAPTER XL

### On the work and voice of preaching

Amid these matters, let us turn back through love to what we have already said above, so that every preacher may resound more through his actions than through his words and, by living well, impress upon his followers the footprints by which they should walk, rather than show them through speech alone.

For this rooster, which the Lord adopts in his speech to portray the character of a good preacher, when it is preparing to sing, first shakes its wings and strikes itself, making itself more watchful. Thus those who move the words of holy preaching must first awaken through devotion to good action, lest, while sluggish in themselves through their works, they rouse others with their voice.

They must first shake themselves through exalted deeds and then make others concerned to live well. They must first strike themselves with the wings of their thoughts, discover through careful investigation whatever in them is uselessly sluggish, correct it through strict examination, and only then order the lives of others by speaking.

They must first take care to punish their own faults with tears, and then announce what must be punished in others. Before the words of exhortation resound, they must proclaim through their works everything they are about to say.

## FOURTH PART

### How the preacher, after everything has been rightly accomplished, should return to himself, lest either his life or his preaching exalt him

Since, however, while preaching is often poured forth abundantly in fitting ways, the mind of the speaker is secretly lifted up by joy at displaying himself, he must take great care to bite himself with the wound of fear, lest one who restores others to health by healing their wounds should himself swell through neglect of his own salvation; lest, while helping his neighbors, he abandon himself; lest, while raising others, he fall.

For greatness of virtue has often been an occasion of destruction for some, so that, when they are inordinately secure through confidence in their strength, they unexpectedly perish through negligence.

When virtue resists vices, the mind flatters itself with a certain pleasure in that virtue. It happens that the mind of one who acts well casts aside fear of careful self-examination and rests securely in confidence in itself. Then the crafty seducer counts up everything it has done well and exalts it in the swelling of its thoughts as though it were superior to all others.

Thus the memory of virtue becomes a pit for the mind before the eyes of the just Judge. For in recalling what it has done, it raises itself up before itself and falls before the author of humility.

Hence the soul that grows proud is told: “Because you are more beautiful, descend and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. 32:19). As though it were plainly said: “Because you raise yourself up through the beauty of your virtues, you are driven by that very beauty to fall.”

Hence the soul growing proud through virtue is condemned under the figure of Jerusalem, when it is said: “You were perfect in my beauty, which I had placed upon you, says the Lord; but, trusting in your beauty, you prostituted yourself in your own name” (Ezek. 16:14–15).

The mind is lifted up by confidence in its own beauty when it rejoices in the security it feels concerning the merits of its virtues. But through this same confidence it is led into prostitution, because, when its mind has been intercepted, its own thoughts deceive it, and the evil spirit corrupts it by seducing it into countless vices.

It must be noted that he says, “You prostituted yourself because of your reputation.” For when the mind abandons regard for its heavenly ruler, it immediately seeks private praise and begins to claim for itself every good that it received in order to serve as a proclamation of the giver. It desires to spread the glory of its own reputation and strives to become known to all as admirable.

She therefore prostitutes herself in her own name who, abandoning the marriage of the lawful bed, submits herself to the corrupting spirit in the desire for praise.

Hence David says: “He delivered their virtue into captivity, and their beauty into the hand of the enemy” (Ps. 77:61). Virtue is delivered into captivity, and beauty into the hand of the enemy, when the ancient adversary rules a deceived mind through the exaltation of good work.

This exaltation of virtue, although it does not completely overcome the mind, nevertheless often tests even the minds of the elect. But when one who has been lifted up is cast down, the one who has been cast down is recalled to fear.

Hence David says again: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall not be moved forever’” (Ps. 29:7). But because he swelled with confidence in his virtue, he added shortly afterward what he suffered: “You turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (ibid., 8). As though he were plainly saying: “I believed myself strong among the virtues, but I came to know how great my weakness was when I was abandoned.”

Again he says: “I swore and resolved to keep the judgments of your righteousness” (Ps. 118:106). But because it was not within his strength to remain in the observance he had sworn to keep, he immediately discovered, in his troubled state, his weakness.

Therefore he suddenly turned to the help of prayer, saying: “I have been humbled exceedingly, Lord; give me life according to your word” (ibid., 107).

Sometimes, however, heavenly governance recalls the memory of weakness to the mind before advancing it through gifts, lest it swell with the virtues it has received. Hence, whenever the prophet Ezekiel is led to contemplate heavenly things, he is first called “son of man.” As though the Lord were plainly admonishing him: “Do not lift your heart in exaltation because of what you see; carefully consider what you are, so that, when you penetrate the highest things, you may recognize that you are a human being. Thus, while you are carried beyond yourself, you may be brought back attentively to yourself by the rein of your weakness.”

Therefore, when an abundance of virtues flatters us, the eye of the mind must return to its weaknesses and healthfully press itself downward. It must look not at the upright things it has done, but at those it has neglected to do. Thus, while the heart is worn down by the memory of its weakness, it is established more firmly in virtue before the author of humility.

For often Almighty God perfects the minds of rulers in large part, yet leaves them imperfect in some small part, so that, while they shine with remarkable virtues, they may waste away from weariness over their imperfection and may not lift themselves up because of great things while they still struggle against small ones. Since they cannot conquer the lowest matters, they should not dare to grow proud of their chief actions.

Behold, good man: compelled by the necessity of my criticism, while I am intent on showing what a pastor ought to be, I, an ugly painter, have depicted a beautiful man; and I direct others to the shore of perfection while I am still tossed about in the waves of sins. But I ask you: in the shipwreck of this life, sustain me with the plank of your prayer, so that, because my own burden weighs me down, the hand of your merit may lift me up.

## [THE BOOKS OF THE DIALOGUES]

## ARGUMENT TO THE FOUR BOOKS OF THE DIALOGUES OF SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT

From the Roman edition of the year 1591.

## 103

The most holy and learned pontiff Gregory set before himself the purpose of expressing truly and solidly, through the examples of the bishops in Italy—bishops flourishing both in holiness of life and in the discipline of episcopal virtue—whatever institutions and precepts concerning pastoral care he had committed to writing.

It therefore seems to have been done with the greatest justification that we added to the book of the *Pastoral Rule* those distinguished books of the *Dialogues* concerning the life and miracles of the Italian Fathers, both Latin and Greek, gathered in the Vatican library and corrected with the utmost fidelity according to the evidence of ancient copies.

Ancient Greece valued these books so highly that, because of their excellence, it called Gregory by the name “Dialogues.” And when some dispute was undertaken against the Greeks themselves, many Greeks—not only those worthy of that ancient Greece but also men recent to our own age—took from these very books weapons of argument against their own people, as is clearly shown in the final part of this argument.

These books are written with such sweetness and clarity that anyone can easily recognize their author as Gregory the Great. When he introduces Peter the Deacon as his interlocutor, he opens for himself both an entrance and a path toward those illustrious and divine answers and toward the explanation of great questions that are difficult to explain.

The second book, indeed, is full of miracles and examples from the life of Saint Benedict the Abbot. The remaining three are variously scattered with teachings and examples of other perfect and approved men, especially bishops: Paulinus of Nola, Marcellinus of Ancona, Boniface of Ferentium, Fortunatus of Todi, Constantius of Aquino, Fulgentius of Otricoli, Herculanus of Perugia, and many others whom it would be too tedious to enumerate one by one.

There is therefore good reason for all to read them with the greater eagerness, since they are richer both in teachings and in examples by which the practice of holy life may be shaped in every respect.

[Editorial notes and textual apparatus: At Acts 2:22–24, Guff. wrongly reads *affligentes*, “afflicting,” for *affigentes*, “nailing.” At Acts 22, more recent Vulgate editions read, “What do you want me to do?”; printed editions read “Rise and enter”; the text here has “Rising, enter the city.” In the ship comparison, editions before Guss. most corruptly read *condescendentis*; the text is emended from English manuscripts and from our own witnesses to *conscendentis*, “ascending.” At Revelation 3:2, Corb. reads *inveni* (“I find”); this was the earlier reading in Trec. The wording “lives after losing the coldness of unbelief” includes *vivit*, supplied from English and French manuscripts; the editors’ *exardescit* (“blazes”) is preferred to *excrescit* (“grows”), found in all manuscripts, or *crescit*.

For Chapter XXXVI, Corb. numbers this chapter 37, and Longip. 57. Printed editions read *apponat* (“apply”), but the manuscripts support *opponat* (“set in opposition”). Belv. and the first Carn. read *innumeris ac diversis* (“countless and diverse”); Trec. and the rest support the received reading. The first two Gem. manuscripts read *levibus* here and *leves* below. The correct reading is *juventur* (“are aided”), attested by the German, Beauvais, Trec., Norman, and other manuscripts, not the printed *jubeantur* (“are commanded”): old manuscripts wrote *jubentur* for *juventur*, using *b* for *v*, and later editors altered it further. Editors preferred *despiciantur* (“are despised”) by mere conjecture, rejecting *desperentur* (“are despaired of”).

For Chapter XXXVII, the word *conspersio* (“temperament/constitution”) has already been discussed in Admonition 4, or chapter 3. In the medical comparison, *occurritur* (“is met”) might be preferred from the first Carn. manuscript, but Trec. and other, even better, witnesses read *succurritur* (“is assisted”); Corb., Laud., Theod., and the first Carn. read *opposita* (“applied/set against”).

For Chapter XXXVIII, Corb., Belv., and the first two Carn. manuscripts read *curandum* (“must be dealt with”), while Trec. and others read *tolerandum* (“must be tolerated”); the first Carn. reads *superatis* (“overcome”). Gem., Trec., Belv., Corb., Norman, and others read *tolleretur* (“might be removed”), whereas more recent editors print *toleretur* (“might be tolerated”), against the manuscripts and the sense of the whole passage. Gregory therefore teaches that believers may be tolerated for a time in lesser vices, so that they may more readily be raised and freed from greater ones.

For Chapter XXXIX, Rothom., Lyr., and the third Gem. read *studendum* (“effort must be made”); the first Carn. has *occurritur* (“is met”), while Trec. and other stronger witnesses have *succurritur* (“is assisted”); Corb., Laud., Theod., and the first Carn. read *opposita* (“applied/set against”).

For Chapter XL, Guss. omits *potius* (“rather”); other witnesses read: “impress [their footsteps], so that rather by acting than by speaking ….” All manuscript codices read *monent* (“admonish”), omitted by editors in favor of *movent* (“move”).

In the Fourth Part, the Gemeticensis manuscripts read *suspectionis* (“suspicion/self-distrust”). Gilot’s edition and some others insert *ante stulti judicis* (“before the foolish judge”), a reading that may aptly refer to a mind foolishly presuming on its own virtues; the manuscripts are followed. Corb. reads “Arise, you who sleep, with the uncircumcised”; Lyr. reads *consideratione* (“by consideration”).]

To the Latin Dialogues we have appended the Greek, because, in the judgment and example of learned men, it seems an excellent practice to join Greek with Latin. This ought especially to have been done in the edition of these Dialogues, which, harassed by the perverse zeal of certain heretics who rashly attack everything, are henceforth fortified by the strongest defense: the ancient Greek translation, made by so learned a pontiff as Zacharias. Nothing could have been said or expressed more excellently in it, whether for discerning the truth, for the importance of the matters discussed, for purity of language, for the weight of the arguments, or for the significance of the doctrines.

How useful—or rather necessary—this edition is in every respect may readily be understood from many considerations, but especially from the fact that not only at the Council of Lyons, held by Gregory X, but also at the Council of Florence, these Greek Dialogues were not merely sought together with other monuments of the ancient Greek Fathers; they had already been carried away from Greece for the purpose of blunting the boldness of the Greeks themselves, who obstinately dissented from the Latins. Thus it happened that whenever any disputation was undertaken against the Greeks, many Greeks themselves took weapons of argument against their own people from these very Dialogues.

This may be observed in many others, but especially in Manuel Calecas, who, instructed by the doctrines of these Dialogues, conducted outstanding disputations against his own people at the Council of Lyons; and in Gennadius Scholarius, patriarch of Constantinople, who at the ecumenical Synod of Florence overcame the Greeks, who had long been disputing with the Latin Church concerning certain decrees of the Catholic faith, by means of the arguments and doctrines that he took from the authority of these Greek Dialogues—an authority which both ancient and modern Greece has always held in the highest esteem.

The matter is obvious and does not require fuller explanation here. Therefore, in order to serve the common good, we judged it worthwhile to append to the Latin Dialogues of the most holy Pope Gregory those Dialogues which the equally learned pontiff Zacharias rendered into Greek with divine skill. Since there may be several other reasons, and very weighty ones, why we have issued this Greek translation of the Dialogues from the Vatican Press, we leave them to the judgment of learned men who think rightly concerning the Catholic commonwealth.

[Col. 0127]

Nevertheless, we cannot deny that in this very edition, especially in the third book, six chapters are missing:[Note: [Col. 0127] Those six chapters of Book III, which were absent from the first edition of the Greek Dialogues, were restored in later editions from volume III of Henry Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*. They are likewise found in the Royal manuscript codex, from which several other passages were restored, as will be stated in the notes to the Dialogues. (Notice of Peter Gussanvillaeus).] namely, chapter 27, “Concerning the forty husbandmen who were unwilling to eat polluted food and were beheaded by the Lombards”; then the immediately following chapter, 28, “Concerning the captives who were unwilling to worship the head of a goat and were slaughtered”; afterward, the third chapter, 29, “Concerning an Arian bishop who was blinded”; next, the fourth chapter, marked with the letter 30, “Concerning the church of Saint Agatha at Subura”; then the following chapter, 31, “Concerning Hermenegild, a former Arian king, who, because he embraced the orthodox faith, was slain by his own father”; and finally the sixth chapter, 32, “Concerning the bishops from Africa who, on account of the orthodox faith, had their tongues cut out and afterward spoke again.”

These six chapters, numbered in order, are absent from this Vatican Edition—not through deceit or fraud, but because, despite the most careful investigation, they are not found in either of the two very ancient copies, one of which is Vatican and the other belonging to the most noble Library of Grottaferrata.

Nor, if these chapters are missing, should this edition of the Greek Dialogues for that reason be neglected, since the remaining chapters, rendered into Greek, can be exceedingly useful in every respect for the benefit of the Catholic commonwealth. As for the six that are missing, they are so beautifully and fully written in the Gregorian Latin exemplar and in the other Latin monuments that, even if they had not been erased in our own time through the antiquity of the centuries or through human negligence, no loss should be thought to have resulted from their absence here.

[Col. 0129]

# Vindication of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great, by Peter Gussanvillaeus

105 [Note: Indeed, very many of our own scholars had already done this, especially Benedict Haeftenus in the prolegomena to the *Life of Saint Benedict*, and J. Mabillon in the preface to volume I of the *Acta*, § 2.] No one, so far as I know, has hitherto undertaken to vindicate the Dialogues of Pope Gregory I, who is also called the Great, both because the consistent agreement of many centuries affirmed them to be the work of their author and because the class of critics, restricting the boundaries of its investigations within certain limits, had not yet dared to assail every truth with the instruments of its doubts.

At last, in our own age, certain men have appeared who either reject these Dialogues altogether or at least deny them to Saint Gregory, led, as I think, by slight conjectures. I intend to refute them, lest, if a new error is neglected, it spread more widely and infect the minds of the careless. Charity commands us to guard against this, and the nature of the task we undertook in publishing Gregory requires it.

To accomplish this effectively, first Gregory himself will appear vindicating his own Dialogues; second, there will follow numerous authors from almost every age after Gregory; third, countless handwritten codices, and codices of better quality, will lend their support; fourth, we shall finally disperse the principal arguments of these critics.

When Saint Gregory was asked by his friends to describe, following the example of Jerome, Theodoret, and Cassian, the more distinguished deeds of the Fathers who had recently flourished in Italy, he agreed and, in letters sent to his friends, earnestly requested that they transmit without delay whatever they knew pertaining to the matter. Read Letter 50 of Book II, Indiction 11, to Maximian:

> “My brothers who live with me in close familiarity continually urge me to write briefly something about the miracles of the Fathers that we have heard took place in Italy. For this purpose I greatly need the assistance of your charity, so that you may briefly indicate to me whatever returns to your memory and whatever you have happened to learn. For I remember that you told me something about the abbot Nonnosus, who was with Lord Anastasius of Pentumas, but I have consigned it to oblivion. I ask you, therefore, to have this and anything else of the kind impressed upon your letters and sent to me quickly.”

That Maximian replied is clear from chapter 7 of Book I of the Dialogues, where, speaking of Nonnosus, Gregory testifies that he learned all these things from Maximian, whom he also calls a bishop and indicates to have still been alive. It was the fourth year of Gregory’s pontificate when he wrote this, that is, A.D. 594. Maximian died in 596, according to the historians of Sicily. Gregory also mentions him in Book III of the Dialogues, chapter 36, and Book IV, chapter 32, as well as in Homily 34 on the Gospels; in these passages he calls him bishop of Syracuse and father of his monastery. Several letters in the Register are also addressed to him.

The reader will note that the same histories are found in the Homilies and in the Dialogues, expressed in nearly the same words and as though related by the same person. Thus, in Book III of the Dialogues, chapter 6, and Book IV, chapter 56, Gregory speaks of Cassius, bishop of Narni, whom he also mentions in Homily 37 on the Gospels.

In the same Book IV, chapter 14, speaking of Servulus, whom the ancient Martyrologies remember on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, he says that he spoke of him in the Homilies; this may be seen in Homily 15 on the Gospels. Likewise, in chapter 15 of the same book, Gregory speaks of Romula, concerning whom he testifies that he had spoken in the Homilies, namely in Homily 30 on the Gospels.

The same must be said of chapter 16, concerning Tarsilla, whom he discusses in Homily 38, chapter 19; of Stephen, in Homily 39, chapter 27; of Theophanius, in Homily 36, chapter 37; of Theodore the boy, in Homily 38, chapter 38; and of Chrysaorius, in Homily 12. In the same chapter 38 he speaks of Athanasius, a presbyter of Isauria, whom he often mentions in his letters.

Chapter 57 speaks of Agatho, bishop of Panormus, who, as the histories establish, lived in the time of Pelagius II, Gregory’s predecessor, as Gregory himself says. He also speaks explicitly of that predecessor Pelagius in Book III, chapter 16, and mentions him frequently elsewhere.

In chapter 19 he speaks of Autharith, king of the Lombards, whom he mentions in Book I of the Letters, letter 17, and elsewhere. But to whom other than Gregory’s own age could the history of Hermenegild be referred, since Gregory himself says that he learned it from his friend Leander, bishop of Seville, who had been present at the events? He recounts the matter at length in chapter 31 of the same book.

In chapters 32, 36, and 37 he also reports his own embassy to Constantinople, when he was apocrisiarius of Pelagius II. Who, moreover, does not know that Leander, who was then serving in Constantinople as ambassador for the king of the Visigoths, was an especially close friend of Gregory? Gregory dedicated to him the books of the Moralia, which he composed at Leander’s urging, and addressed several letters to him.

Finally, when Gregory begins to write the Life of Saint Benedict at the beginning of Book II of the Dialogues, he says that he received what he is about to relate from four disciples of that saint, two of whom were still alive.

From all this it is clearer than midday that those who assigned these Dialogues to Gregory II, who was 150 years younger than our Gregory, went seriously astray; no sane person could affirm or judge that all the matters we have related fit anyone other than Gregory I.

Among the authors who lived after Gregory, I first present Paterius, his close associate and disciple, notary and secundicerius of the Holy Roman Church, who is also mentioned in the Register. He published a book of Testimonies collected from all Gregory’s works, at the urging of the holy Father, as he himself says in the Preface. In it he cites more than twenty testimonies from the Dialogues, in precisely the same words, as the notes placed in the margin will indicate to the diligent reader.

[Note: In the Gussanvillaean Edition no notes identify testimonies excerpted from the Dialogues by Paterius. Some, however, are inserted into his Collection—for example, in the book of Numbers, chapter 4, and the book of Joshua, chapter 1. But they are far fewer than Gussanvillaeus claims, because the collection published under Paterius’s name is not Paterius’s collection of the New Testament, as we shall demonstrate in its proper place.]

Paterius’s book is appended to Gregory’s works.

Taius, or Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, who lived around the year 650, published a notable work entitled *Collectaneum from the Works of Saint Gregory*, as he himself testifies in the preface. He divided it into five books and dedicated it to Quiricus, bishop of Toledo, a man of great renown. In this work he offers several testimonies from Gregory’s Dialogues, which I omit for the sake of brevity; the reader can see them in a distinguished manuscript codex preserved in the Thuanean Library.

[Col. 0131] Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, who died in 667, mentions the Dialogues of our Gregory in chapter 1 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in these words:

> “He [Gregory] also published four books on the lives of the Fathers living throughout Italy, which he joined together in a single volume; and he preferred to call this codex the Dialogues.”

Julian, also bishop of Toledo, in 680 published a work entitled *Prognosticon of the Future Age*, which he dedicated to Idalius, bishop of Barcelona. In it he quotes several passages from the Dialogues, in Book II, chapters 8, 12, 19, 24, and 25, and elsewhere.

Bede the presbyter, who flourished around the year 730, says the following in Book II of his *History*, chapter 1, while recounting Gregory’s deeds:

> “He also composed four books of Dialogues, etc.”

A little earlier he introduces Saint Gregory lamenting the burden of pastoral office in these words, which occur at the beginning of the Dialogues:

> “My unhappy soul, etc.”

Paul the Deacon, who lived around the year 780, speaks as follows in the Life of Gregory that we placed at the beginning of his works:

> “He also published four books of Dialogues, in which, at the request of his deacon Peter, he related the virtues of the saints, etc.”

A little earlier he quotes the following words from the Preface to the Dialogues:

> “What his life was like in the monastery, and with what praiseworthy devotion he lived, we can gather from his own words, which, already established in the pontificate, he used while speaking with his deacon Peter and weeping: ‘My unhappy soul, etc.’”

Finally, in the history that he entitled *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, he mentions the Dialogues in Book IV, chapter 5, as follows:

> “The wisest and most blessed pope of the city of Rome, after writing many other things for the benefit of the holy Church, also composed four books concerning the lives of the saints. He called this volume the Dialogues, that is, ‘the conversation of two,’ because he published it as a conversation between himself and his deacon Peter. This pope therefore sent these books to Queen Theodelinda, whom he knew to be both devoted to the faith of Christ and outstanding in good works.”

Already above, in Book I, chapter 26, he had spoken of these Dialogues, where, discussing Saint Benedict, he says:

> “In those days also the most blessed Benedict, etc., whose life, as is well known, the most blessed Pope Gregory composed in his Dialogues in a graceful style.”

John the Deacon, who flourished around the year 875 and wrote Gregory’s life with the greatest care, diligently examined all the archives of the Roman Church and mentions the Dialogues published by Gregory in many places.

In Book I, chapter 7, he recounts the recovery of health through the prayers of the monk Eleutherius, concerning whom Book III of the Dialogues, chapter 37, speaks, and he repeatedly relates many other stories of the same kind that are contained in the work of the Dialogues.

In Book II, chapter 11, he says:

> “Among his most prudent counselors and friends he chose Peter the Deacon, his contemporary, with whom he later composed four books of Dialogues in conversation.”

And in Book IV, chapter 75:

> “Gregory, interrupting his deeper study of exposition, distinguished by the mere notation of names the miracles of the holy Fathers that he had brought forth with his deacon Peter through inquiry and response, and arranged them into four books, etc.”

Pope Hadrian I, in the year 787, cites Book I of the Dialogues, chapter 9, in his letter to Charlemagne on behalf of the seventh synod, session 5, chapter 16, in these words:

> “Saint Gregory, in his Dialogues, mentions Saint Boniface, etc.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in the Life of Pope Zacharias, says that Zacharias translated the four books of Saint Gregory’s Dialogues from Latin into Greek. Anastasius died in 887.

Alcuin, Bede’s disciple and Charlemagne’s teacher, at the end of his book *On the Divine Offices*, where he discusses the third, seventh, and thirtieth days for the dead, cites testimony on that subject from chapter 55 of Book IV of the Dialogues. He flourished around the year 790.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, who flourished around the year 860, cites very many testimonies from Gregory’s Dialogues in his works, for example in volume I, pages 106, 422, 460, 524, 537, 548, and elsewhere. It would be tedious to list them.

Paschasius Ratbertus, a monk of Corbie, around the year 850, cites chapter 58 of Book IV of the Dialogues in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, in 845 wrote a book *On Predestination* against John Scotus Eriugena, in which he offers several testimonies from Gregory’s Dialogues, for example in chapter 17, number 10, chapter 19, number 2, and elsewhere.

Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, around the year 870, in his *Bibliotheca*, codex 252, after praising Gregory and discussing the four books of Dialogues written by him and translated into Greek by Pope Zacharias, speaks as follows:

> “He also arranged into four Dialogues the lives of those who had flourished in Italy, adding salutary narratives. For 165 years those who did not know the Latin language were deprived of the sole benefit of this work. But Zacharias, who was the successor of this holy man after that period, translated so great a work, confined within Italy, into Greek and generously offered its common benefit to the whole world. I say nothing of the many other Greeks—John of Damascus, Euthymius, and others—who, because of the Dialogues written by Gregory, called Gregory ‘the Dialogist.’”

Regino, abbot of Prüm, who died in the year 904, recounts in Book II *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, chapter 198, the story found in Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 32, concerning a man who had violated his own little daughter.

The Council of Tribur, under Formosus, in the year 895, chapter 17, concerning the prohibition of burial in a church, cites from Book I of the Dialogues, chapter 53, the story of a certain Valentinus who was buried in a church and then expelled from it by demons.

Berno, abbot of Reichenau, around the year 1020, in his short work *On Certain Matters Concerning the Mass*, chapter 12, recounts what Blessed Gregory wrote about the deacon Paschasius in Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 40.

Burchard, bishop of Worms, cites many testimonies from the Dialogues in his *Decrees*. He lived around the year 1000.

Alger, a monk of Cluny, who flourished around the year 1050, cites in Book II *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 31, a passage from Book III of Gregory’s Dialogues.

Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, around the year 1080, takes his argument in chapters 14 and 20 of his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* from chapter 58 of Book IV of the same Dialogues.

Durand, abbot of Troarn, who flourished around the year 1075, does the same in Part VI of his book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*; so does Guitmund, archbishop of Aversa, around the year 1070, in his book *On the Truth of the Eucharist*.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca, who died in 1086, in Book V, chapter 24, of his *Collection of Canons*, cites nearly the entire chapter 30 of Book III of the Dialogues. In Book II, chapter 159, he cites testimony concerning purgatory from Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 39, as well as several other passages.

Alulfus, a monk of Tournai, who flourished around the year 1090, followed Paterius’s example but produced a much larger and remarkable book composed from all Gregory’s works, which he therefore entitled *Gregorial*. In it he collected testimonies on the twelve prophets and on certain other passages of Holy Scripture that Paterius had omitted.

Accordingly, in his excerpts on both the Old and the New Testament he offers innumerable passages from various books of Gregory’s Dialogues.

[Col. 0133] This work of Alulfus exists in three volumes, written in an ancient hand and elegant script, in the monastery of Longpont, of the Cistercian order and diocese of Soissons.

[Note: Alulfus’s work on the New Testament, published under the name of Paterius, appeared separately at Rome in 1553 and among the works of Saint Gregory in 1591, and thereafter in various Gregorian editions. We shall demonstrate the error when we present below the complete and genuine Paterius.]

We could cite very many distinguished men who approved those Dialogues: Sigebert of Gembloux, Ivo of Chartres, Honorius of Autun, Rupert of Deutz, Bernard of Clairvaux, Gratian [Note: We took care to mark in the margin every testimony from the Dialogues inserted into Gratian’s *Decretum* that occurred; Gussanvillaeus neglected this.], Peter Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences, William of Champeaux, founder of the canons of Saint Victor in Paris and later bishop of Châlons, Peter of Cluny, Albert the Great, Thomas Aquinas, Bonaventure, and others who flourished down to our own age. But, lest we become tedious, we refer the reader to them.

Nor is it worthwhile to enumerate the manuscript codices of Gregory’s Dialogues, since they are found almost everywhere in virtually infinite numbers, and scarcely any ancient monastery exists in which two or three copies of Gregory’s Dialogues are not found.

I do not see how our opponents can break the strength of so many witnesses and testimonies. It remains for us to dissolve the arguments that they derive from reason. They raise three principal objections.

First, they derive one from the style, which they say is altogether different, uneven, and inelegant in the Dialogues, filled with barbarous and corrupt expressions, and utterly unworthy of Gregory’s genius and majesty.

Second, they are astonished by many things in them that are entirely unbelievable.

Third, certain teachings appear contrary to Gregory’s doctrine, as in Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 29, where the fire of hell is said to be corporeal, whereas Gregory plainly says in Book XV of the *Moralia*, chapter 17, that such fire is incorporeal.

As for the style, I acknowledge some difference, though not an absolute one. Who does not know that nearly the same thing is observed in all the works of the holy Fathers, and that style varies according to the variety of treatises and subjects? Who in his right mind would assert that the style of sermons, letters, histories, dialogues, and so forth is identical?

Although in these Dialogues there are many passages that recall the style, force, elegance, and even depth of learning found in Gregory’s other works, as is evident to the reader, still the difference in style itself will not surprise anyone who has observed Gregory’s own frank admission that he was unable to maintain a uniform style even in the single work of the *Moralia*. Thus he says in Book XI of the *Moralia*, chapter 1:

> “Although variability of style ought not to be blameworthy in a lengthy work, etc.”

And shortly afterward:

> “My reader, receive the alteration of style with equanimity, because even for those who eat the same foods often, variety in their preparation is pleasing.”

As for barbarous phrases and expressions, who does not know that many such things are found in the treatises of the holy Fathers, who devoted themselves not so much to elegance and purity of language as to truth and simplicity?

Gregory himself admits that he did this deliberately in the letter to Leander prefixed to the *Moralia*, where he says in chapter 5:

> “I have disregarded the very art of speaking that the instruction of external learning teaches. For, as the tenor of this letter itself declares, I do not avoid the collision of repeated *m* sounds, nor do I shun the confusion of barbarisms; I do not care to preserve the position and movement of prepositions or the grammatical cases, because I consider it exceedingly unworthy to restrain the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus. For none of these things has been observed by any interpreters in the authority of Sacred Scripture.”

The same may be said of the barbarous expressions that the barbarism of the Lombards and other peoples had introduced into Italy, with the result that the purity of the Latin language was almost entirely polluted by this mud.

Indeed, Gregory himself declares in the Preface to the Dialogues that even those somewhat more rustic expressions, so to speak, are not his own but belong to others:

> “I want you to know that in some passages I retain only the meaning, while in others I retain both the words and the meaning; for if I had wished to preserve the precise words spoken by every person, the style of the writer would not fittingly receive expressions uttered in rustic usage.”

Concerning the histories contained in the Dialogues, I have nothing to say except that, by reporting them as he had learned them from others, Gregory freed himself from responsibility for their truth. There are few that he says he saw himself or in which he personally participated.

He did what many of the holy Fathers did in numerous histories that will certainly seem unbelievable if weighed on the scales of human reason. But since they are miracles—that is, events exceeding human faith—who can doubt that they ought not to be measured by human judgment?

He thought that public reports should be accepted, since eyewitnesses were unavailable, especially because the piety of the faithful could thereby be increased, and no appearance of error or falsehood arose from any other source.

Theodoret, in the Preface to his *History of the Holy Fathers*, speaks excellently and appropriately to our subject:

> “My narrative will proceed by relating events, not using the rules of panegyric, but reporting a few things truthfully. I ask those who encounter this religious history, or this account of monastic discipline—for let anyone call this work whatever he wishes[Note: In Theodoret one reads τὸ σύγγραμμα, meaning “this writing,” or, as the translator has it, “this work,” not “this body.” In the other passages of ancient writers cited here or elsewhere by Gussanvillaeus, we by no means undertake to vouch for the wording.], not to believe less in what is said if they hear something that surpasses their powers, nor to measure the virtue of those men by their own standard. Rather, let them know plainly that God measures out from above the gifts of the most holy Spirit to pious minds and grants greater gifts to those who are more perfect.
>
> “I have said this for those who have not been carefully initiated into the mysteries of divine things. For the initiates of the Spirit’s sanctuaries know the glory of the Spirit and the miracles that he performs through human beings and within human beings, drawing unbelievers to knowledge of God.
>
> “Whoever will not believe what I am about to say clearly does not believe even those things recorded as true that were performed through Moses, Jesus, Elijah, and Elisha, and he also regards as fables the miracles performed by the holy apostles. But if he testifies that those events were true, let him also believe that these are free from falsehood. For the grace that worked in those men performed through these men also the deeds that it performed. Grace is everlasting, and choosing those who are worthy, it pours forth through them, as through channels, the streams of its activity.
>
> “Of the things I am about to relate, I myself saw some; those I did not see I heard from men who had seen them—men who loved virtue and were considered worthy both to see such persons and to benefit from their teaching.
>
> “The writers of evangelical doctrine who are worthy of belief are not only Matthew and John, great and foremost among the evangelists, who saw the Lord’s miracles, but also Luke and Mark, whom those who had seen from the beginning and had been ministers of the Word carefully instructed not only concerning what the Lord suffered and did, but also concerning what he continually taught.
>
> “Blessed Luke himself had not seen these things; at the beginning of his work he says that he is relating matters about which he had been informed. Therefore, even though we hear that he did not see what he narrates but received this teaching from others, we believe him and Mark no less than Matthew and John. Each is worthy of belief in his narrative, since he learned from those who had seen.
>
> “We too shall relate some things as having been seen by us, and other things as men who have believed those who saw them and who imitated their lives. I have used a more extended discourse concerning these matters because I wish to persuade my readers that I shall relate the truth.”

Finally, it is certain that the holy Father’s judgment is the same in the Dialogues as in his other works. The claim that his teaching concerning the fire of hell is different, indeed wholly contrary, is frivolous. In the Dialogues he openly professes that the fire is corporeal, namely in Book IV, chapter 29. The words are:

> “If therefore the devil and his angel, although incorporeal, are to be tormented by corporeal fire, what is surprising if souls, even before they receive bodies, can experience corporeal torments?”

But, in Book XV of the *Moralia*, chapter 17 [Note: Now number 35, where nevertheless *corporeus* is read], he is said to declare most plainly that the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal, while explaining the words in Job, chapter 20: “A fire that is not kindled shall devour him.” He speaks as follows:

> “In a marvelous way the fire of Gehenna has been expressed in a few words. For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, requires corporeal fuel. When it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood; it cannot exist unless kindled and unless replenished.
>
> “But, by contrast, since the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal and burns corporeally the reprobate cast into it, it is neither kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood. Once created, it endures unquenchable; it does not require kindling and does not lack heat.”

I admit that this is how the passage is read in certain editions and even in some manuscript codices. Yet no one will fail to judge it an error of careless copyists and unlearned scribes after seeing the countless ancient and highly authoritative manuscript codices, some of which we ourselves have examined.

These include the manuscript codices of the *Moralia* in the Vatican Library, numbers 574, 575, 578, 579, and 582; the very ancient codex of the Barberini Library; another manuscript codex, in large folio on extremely old parchment, which was brought to Rome from the Urbino Library during the time of Alexander VII; and two codices of the Chigi Library. All these codices read *corporeus* (“corporeal”). Although two other manuscripts, numbers 576 and 580, read *incorporeus* (“incorporeal”), it nevertheless plainly appears that the syllable *in-* was added above the line by a later hand.

The old Italian translation of the *Moralia*, published at Florence in 1486, likewise renders the passage in this way:

> “But the fire of hell is altogether the contrary. For since it is corporeal and burns the wretched damned corporeally, etc.”

All the foregoing evidence was sent to me by the eminent Cardinal Bona, who, out of his exceptional kindness toward learned men, took the trouble to examine it.

The Gallican codices also read in the same way: the Sorbonne codex, more than 600 years old; that of the cathedral of Saint Mary of Reims, 600 years old; two codices of Saint Remigius of Reims, one 800 and the other 600 years old; that of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, nearly 800 years old; the very ancient and excellent codex of the Church of Bayeux; the codex of the library of the distinguished and learned Claude Joly, cantor of Paris, 700 years old; that of the Royal Monastery of the Cistercian order, 600 years old; that of the Library of the Church of Beauvais, 700 years old; two codices of Saint-Corneille at Compiègne, one more than 800 years old and the other 300 years old; the Royal Codex, 400 years old; the codex in the Library of the Church of Chartres, 400 years old; the codex in the library of the distinguished Emeric Bigot, 400 years old; and the codex in the monastery of Cluny, written by Bertramus the monk at the command of Saint Majolus, abbot, who died in the year 994 after having presided for forty years.

It is also clear that the editors of the older and more accurate editions read the passage in this way. I cite the Venetian edition of 1480, considered the first of the editions of Saint Gregory, prepared by Bartholomew of Cremona, a canon regular. In it, Book XV, chapter 50, reads *corporeus*. The same is true of another Venetian edition of 1496 and of the Paris editions of 1495, 1518, 1521, and others, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

Those who abridged Gregory’s books of the *Moralia* also read it in the same way. One such witness is the Corbie manuscript codex from the time of Abbot Adalard, around the year 750, preserved in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. After the letters numbered 54 of Saint Gregory, sent by the deacon Paul to the same Adalard, there is a book entitled:

> “Here begins the excerpt written by Lathen, son of Bath, from the *Moralia on Job*, which Gregory composed.”

There, in Book XV, near the end, one reads:

> “And a fire that is not kindled shall devour him. Since the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, it burns corporeally the reprobate cast into it, etc.”

The rest follows as in Saint Gregory.

Odo, abbot of Cluny, who flourished around the year 940, has the following in chapter 20, number 26, of his *Epitome of Saint Gregory’s Moralia*:

> “But, by contrast, since the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, etc.”

Garnerus, a canon regular of Saint Victor in Paris, under Abbot Hilduin, around the year 1140, in the work he entitled *Gregorian*, Book XI, chapter 1, reads the passage in precisely the same way as above.

The same reading is also found in a manuscript codex preserved in the Library of the Celestines in Paris, called *Remediarium of the Converts*, which was compiled from passages of Saint Gregory’s *Moralia*. In its third part, Book VI, chapter 7, the heading reads:

> “That the bodies and souls of the damned will be tormented together by corporeal and unquenchable fire, Book XV of the *Moralia*.”

In the body of the chapter one reads:

> “In the reprobate, conscience burns through desire, and outside them the fire of Gehenna torments them. Since it is corporeal and burns corporeally the reprobate cast into it, etc.”

Some attribute this work without its author’s name to Peter of Blois, namely in the *Catalogue of Manuscript Codices of England*. Pits, however, in his book *On the Writers of England*, attributes it to a certain Peter, archdeacon of London, somewhat later.

Finally, it is clear that this is the reading that must be adopted from the common teaching of theologians. After the Master of the Sentences, in Book IV, Distinction 50, and Saint Thomas, in Book IV, Distinction 44, Question 2, Article 3, they assert that the fire of hell is corporeal and rely chiefly upon two testimonies, namely those of Saint Augustine and Saint Gregory.

Saint Augustine, in Book XXI of *The City of God*, chapter 10, speaks as follows:

> “Why, then, should we not say that, although in ways that are indeed real yet marvelous, even incorporeal spirits can be afflicted by the punishment of corporeal fire?”

A little later:

> “Therefore, if the spirits of demons—or rather, the demonic spirits—have no bodies, they will cling to the fires; although incorporeal, they are nevertheless to be tormented by corporeal fires.”

And finally he concludes:

> “But that hell will be a corporeal fire, and it will burn the bodies of the damned—both of human beings and of demons: the solid bodies of human beings and the aerial bodies of demons, and so forth.”

Saint Gregory, who scarcely ever departs from the opinion of Saint Augustine, teaches the same thing in the two passages that we cited, namely Book XV of the *Moralia*, chapter 17, and Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 29 (now numbered 35), where he expressly states that the fire of hell is corporeal.

That this was indeed his teaching is demonstrated most clearly by Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, who lived around the year 850. For in his response to John Scotus Eriugena he says:

> “First, your opinion is shown to be false in that it falsely claims that Augustine called that fire corporeal, whereas Gregory called it incorporeal. Both of them, without contradiction, acknowledge it to be corporeal. And since you yourself have admitted this concerning Augustine, we have judged it unnecessary to set forth his opinion. But regarding Gregory’s position, lest it come into anyone’s doubt, although a little earlier we have quoted his opinion concerning this same fire in the *Moralia*, where he acknowledges it to be corporeal, it nevertheless seems worthwhile to bring forward another opinion of his from another of his works.”

For, as that book of his which is entitled *Dialogues* reports, when Deacon Peter, while asking about the aforementioned fire among other matters, began as follows—[the printed text has *suscitans*; read *sciscitans*, “inquiring”]—and he quotes the words of Book IV, chapter 29, of the *Dialogues*. Then he concludes:

> “[Col. 0137] Behold: while we present certain testimonies concerning that corporeal fire, the truth of the response is thereby demonstrated regarding nearly everything that you had asserted in your aforementioned opinion. For on the authority of so great a teacher, not only is that fire affirmed to be corporeal, but it is also credibly taught that human souls and apostate spirits are sensibly tormented in it.”

The opinion of Florus, master and deacon of the Church of Lyons, a contemporary of Prudentius, was the same. In the work that he published in the name of the Church of Lyons against that same Scotus Eriugena, chapter 17, he proves that the fire of hell is corporeal, citing Gregory’s testimony in this form:

> “Since the fire of hell is corporeal,”

and the remainder, as it appears in Saint Gregory, at the cited place in the *Moralia*.

These materials are taken from the book entitled *Vindications of Predestination and Grace*, by the distinguished scholar Dom Guillelmus Mauguinus. Sextus of Siena also elucidated the whole matter very well in Book V, Annotation 141, of the *Sacred Library*. After quoting Saint Gregory’s testimony from Book XV of the *Moralia*, he says:

> “It seems to follow from these words that the fire of hell is incorporeal and different in kind from our fire, and so forth. Nevertheless, that Gregory did not think this is plainly demonstrated in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 29, and so on.”

Then he concludes elegantly:

> “Accordingly, it must be understood that these words of Gregory are corruptly read in all the Lyon manuscripts of Hugh of the Gate, and in certain manuscript copies, where they have: ‘Since the fire of hell is incorporeal, and so forth.’ The syllable *in* ought to have been deleted, so that instead of *incorporeus* one would read *corporeus*. For the following words plainly show this.”

And in this form Saint Thomas cites the passage in the volume of the *Sentences*, Book IV, Distinction 44, Question 2, and so forth. From these facts it is evident that he recognized the corruption of certain copies, both manuscript and printed. We have set against them a very large number of manuscripts of the finest quality, in addition to copies of the older and more reliable editions, which retained the word *corporeus*. For that reason we restored the passage in Book XV of the *Moralia*, chapter 17, although the word *incorporeus* appeared in later editions. But enough, and more than enough, on this subject.

From the foregoing, it can plainly—if I am not mistaken—be understood and inferred that the four books of the *Dialogues* ought to be attributed to no one other than Pope Gregory, the first of that name. He was a Roman, distinguished by birth and wealth, and committed to writing the miracles of the Fathers who had flourished in Italy shortly before his time. In the same period Gregory, bishop of Tours, composed a book on the lives of the holy Fathers, or of certain men—if I may use his own expression—who had distinguished themselves in Gaul by holiness and miracles, including bishops and priests as well as abbots and recluses. But I could not easily say which of the two wrote first, or which was anticipated by the other in this subject matter.

Having established that the *Dialogues* belong to Gregory the Great, it remains for us briefly to inform the reader what has been accomplished in this edition.

First, we have corrected the Latin text, which was corrupt in many places, against the evidence of numerous manuscript copies. It would be superfluous to append their list here, since we supplied it sufficiently at the beginning of the entire Gregorian work, where we compiled a catalogue of all the manuscripts that we used in correcting the work as a whole.

Next, as regards the Greek version: its author is said to have been Pope Zachary, the successor of Gregory the Great 175 years later. Since he was Greek by nationality, he either translated those *Dialogues* into Greek out of love for his own people, or arranged for them to be translated, so that those who did not know Latin would not be deprived of the benefit of so great a work, as Photius says in the *Bibliotheca*, Codex 252.

This is also demonstrated by the anonymous author of the Greek preface that we prefixed to the *Dialogues* in our Latin translation. It was taken from a manuscript in the library of the Most Christian King. Because a copyist had corrupted it in many places, we corrected it from another manuscript in the Ambrosian Library at Milan. The distinguished scholar Petrus Paulus Boscha, doctor of theology and prefect of that library, kindly sent me a copy of this Greek preface. He also supplied several variant readings from the same Greek *Dialogues*, by means of which I corrected some errors—*σφάλματα*, “mistakes”—in the Royal Manuscript. I therefore acknowledge that I owe the learned and exceptionally cultivated man the greatest gratitude for so great a service.

Nor do I feel any less indebted to the learned Dom Emericus Bigotius, well known to all men of letters. Through his extraordinarily learned and judicious conjectures concerning the Greek text, and through the collation that he made, with the greatest labor, of Book II against the Ingolstadt copy, he assisted me greatly.

It should furthermore be noted that the author of this Greek version of the *Dialogues* did not always adhere to Saint Gregory’s meaning. He often employed paraphrases and additions, and in translating the words departed from Gregory’s sense, as will be shown in the notes. There are also many barbarous words, as might be expected of a period when both the Greek and Latin languages were beginning to deteriorate. A great many Greco-Latin words are likewise found, a list of which we shall append below.

Moreover, this Greek version is not everywhere identical in the printed editions and in the Royal Manuscript; indeed, it differs in very many places, so that complete sentences are sometimes found in the manuscript that do not appear in the editions. If conjecture may be used, I would believe that this happened because Zachary perhaps translated the *Dialogues* twice. Socrates reports that the same thing happened to him in Book II, chapter 1, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, where he says that what he had reported less accurately in the first edition he rendered more clearly and carefully in the second.

Although we corrected the Greek in many places with the help of the Royal Manuscript, we would have done this more accurately if more copies had been available. Add to this that not a few blemishes entered that Royal Manuscript through the copyist’s incompetence or negligence.

Finally, we added notes, though only a few and only on the more difficult passages, drawing on learned men. I had originally intended to provide notes only for the Epistles; nevertheless, the reader will receive these, such as they are, with a favorable mind and read them with a kindly eye, while more extensive and more elaborate studies are being prepared by learned scholars.

[Col. 0137]

# Preface to the Books of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory, Pope

**I.** Since we are about to publish the *Dialogues* that bear the name of Saint Gregory, Pope, we ought at least briefly to offer a preface concerning both their author and their work. Although both subjects have already been discussed at great length and with great learning, we would nevertheless like to add a few observations, as briefly as possible, so that still more light may be shed on the controversies that have arisen concerning this matter and so that they may more easily be settled.

**II.** Cedrenus, a Greek and a stranger to Latin literature, denied that Gregory, the first Roman pontiff of that name, was the author of these *Dialogues*. Huldricus Coccius, Chemnitz, Andreas Rivetus, and not a few others among the heterodox expressed doubts about the matter.

On our side, however, Benedict Haeften, provost of the monastery of Affligem, asserted it and demonstrated it by irrefutable arguments in the *Monastic Investigations*, Prolegomenon 2 and following, to the *Life of Saint Benedict*. So too did Jean Mabillon, in Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict* [Col. 0139], in the preface, numbers 17–30.

Petrus Gussanvillaeus later accomplished the same task no less vigorously in the *Vindications* that we have judged should be prefixed to this work. Above all our fellow religious, who translated the celebrated *Dialogues* from Latin into French and published them in 1689, reconsidered this subject with the greatest fullness and elegance in the preface with which he furnished that outstanding work. We shall here encompass and conclude the matter in something like a single syllogism.

**III.** Whoever the author of the *Dialogues* soon to be published may be, he repeatedly professes that he became a monk, and indeed in a monastery that he himself had founded at Rome: namely, in the very prologue of the *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 33; Book IV, chapters 21, 38, 47, 55, and elsewhere.

From the passages cited, especially Book IV, chapter 55, it is clear that he presided over the monastery that he had built. It is established from Book III, chapter 36, that he served as apocrisiarius at Constantinople. That he was later made Roman pontiff is evident from chapter 16 of the same book, where he calls Pope Pelagius II his predecessor, and from Book IV, chapter 57, where he still mentions that same predecessor.

While seated at Rome, he delivered the *Homilies on the Gospels* to the people, as he very frequently testifies, especially in Book IV, chapters 14, 15, 16, 19, and 27. In the cited *Homilies* he in turn speaks of the *Dialogues* that he himself composed, especially Homily 38 of Book I. Chapter 7 of the *Dialogues* concerns Nonnosus the abbot, and Gregory states that he received what he relates about him from Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

Furthermore, in Book III—otherwise Book II—Indiction 11, Letter formerly 50, now 51, Gregory asks that same Maximianus to communicate to him by letter what he knows about Nonnosus the abbot and about the miracles of the Italian Fathers, since his brothers were compelling him to write about this subject. This is precisely what is treated in the *Dialogues*, as can be understood clearly enough from their title.

**IV.** What sane person could suppose that even one of all these features, as it were the outlines by which his life is perfectly expressed, could belong to anyone other than our Gregory? Certainly they agree perfectly with what we have learned about that most holy Father from his indisputably authentic works: namely, from the *Moralia*, especially the preliminary letter to Saint Leander; from the *Register of Letters*; from the *Homilies*; and so forth.

**V.** “But,” you will say, “the author of the *Dialogues*, who wished to conceal himself beneath Gregory’s identity, learned the history of the holy Father precisely through constant reading of his works and tried to portray and adorn himself with those colors.”

As though someone to whom our opponents everywhere attribute excessive simplicity in believing and recounting miracles could have been so skillful an artist of deception! Besides, how could such a fraud have escaped all those who wrote about Gregory, whether they lived near his time or were even his contemporaries? How could it have deceived his notary and secretary, Paterius?

Indeed, we would be wasting time by lingering any longer over matters so certain and clearer than midday light. Having therefore vindicated the *Dialogues* for our Gregory, we must now vindicate him from his detractors, who accuse him of excessive credulity, or rather of crude and foolish simplicity, complaining that he relates old-wives’ tales to us.

**VI.** First, however, I ask those dour and sharp-eyed critics whether they sincerely believe the miracles narrated in both the Old and the New Testament, even though they lack all probability: Eve’s conversation with the serpent, Genesis 3; Lot’s wife being changed into a pillar of salt, Genesis 19; the she-donkey on which Balaam was riding speaking with him most wisely in human fashion—indeed, beyond the capacity and custom of most human beings—Numbers 22; water springing from a molar tooth of a jawbone of an ass to quench the thirst of Samson alone, Judges 15; a stater found in the mouth of a fish recently caught on a hook, Matthew 17; Peter walking upon the waters, Matthew 14; a legion of demons driven by Christ from one man and sent into swine, which threw themselves headlong into the sea and perished, Mark 5; and very many similar events.

Second, may we ask those who thus deride the miracles reported by Gregory whether they place unquestioning faith in Christ even when he solemnly affirms, John 14:12:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these.”

Third, let those critics of such keen discernment concede that the time was especially suitable for such signs and miracles to be published, when barbarians wholly deprived of the true religion and knowledge of God were being called to the faith. For, as the Apostle testifies, 1 Corinthians 14:22:

> “Tongues”—and say the same about the other miracles—“are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, whereas prophecy is not for unbelievers but for believers.”

Thus the Jews, to whom prophecies were granted as believers, were generally denied the signs that were reserved and appointed for the Gentiles, who were entirely alien to the faith.

**VII.** Once these points have been granted, it is hardly astonishing that, as the fifth century was passing away and almost the whole of the sixth century was running its course—the period encompassed by Gregory in his *Dialogues*—so many and such great miracles were brought about by God.

At that time nearly the whole world lay miserably either in the darkness of idolatry or in the dense gloom of abominable heresies. Indeed, scarcely one ruler then reigned, especially in the West, who worshiped the true God according to the proper rite.

Italy was either occupied by the Ostrogoths, who had embraced Arian perfidy, or later had been handed over to the Lombards, who followed the errors of the Arians just as zealously or, worse still, served idolatry. Gaul obeyed the Franks, worshipers of idols or only recently and imperfectly recalled from that worship, or else the Visigoths and other barbarians hostile to the Catholic faith. Spain had fallen to the same Visigoths and to the Suebi, who were likewise Arians. The island of Britain, subjected to new settlers, namely the Angles, lamented that the worship of idols had been restored in its temples. The Vandals, having gained control of Africa, declared a most savage war against the Catholics in order to establish the Arian doctrine.

**VIII.** Was it therefore contrary to God’s goodness and providence that so many and such great miracles should then take place, by which unbelievers might be drawn toward the light of truth? The result proves that it was not. For within a few years the Lombards renounced their Arian impiety; the Goths in Spain embraced the Catholic faith under the leadership and exhortation of King Reccared; the Angles gave their allegiance to Christ; and finally all were received into the unity of the Christian and orthodox faith.

**IX.** As regards the Lombards, who at that time possessed a large part of Italy, the Gregorian *Dialogues* contributed substantially to their conversion. For, as Paul the Deacon relates, Queen Theodelinda used the *Dialogues*, which Gregory had sent to her, to persuade both the king and his people and subjects to embrace the Catholic faith.

Indeed, many miracles are related in this history (*History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 5), performed in the very sight of the Lombard army. If they had not been certain and confirmed by the unanimous judgment of all, the Lombards—whom Gregory depicts as resembling bears more than human beings because of their ferocity—would have mocked them and burned with even greater hatred than before against the Catholic faith and the Roman Church.

The opposite, however, occurred, as Paul the Deacon reports from that same people in Book IV, chapter 4, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*: namely, that King Agilulf, with almost all the others following his example, embraced the Catholic faith, restored the property taken from the churches, and paid bishops the honor due to them.

**X.** In addition to the remnants of idolatry that still survived and openly flourished here and there in Italy and elsewhere, pernicious errors were then secretly creeping in and being disseminated even among those who were called Catholics—errors concerning the immortality of souls and the resurrection of bodies.

Gregory himself humbly admits that he had once been uncertain about the resurrection, in Homily 26 on the Gospels:

> “For many doubt the resurrection, just as we ourselves once did.”

See also Book II of the *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 8, formerly numbered 20, and Book XIV of the *Moralia*, no. 70.

Gregory of Tours, [Col. 0141] Book X of his *History*, chapters 13 and 14, testifies that a certain priest of his church taught that there would be no future resurrection; Gregory himself defeated him. He also reports that Theodulf, a deacon of the city of Paris, who seemed to himself to possess some learning, repeatedly raised disputes with him on this subject.

Let us hear Deacon Peter speaking with Gregory, Book III, chapter 38:

> “Because I perceive that many who are established within the bosom of the holy Church doubt the life of the soul after the death of the flesh.”

Concerned for their salvation, Gregory, after asserting these articles of faith with arguments that could not be refuted, adds a great many miracles and marvels, by which the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the flesh might be proved more effectively to the less educated.

**XI.** Of the events that Gregory reports, some he witnessed himself, while others he received from trustworthy witnesses—namely, from most holy bishops entirely free of deceit, from monks or superiors of monasteries whose lives were completely blameless, and from noble and freeborn men. He wrote nothing from the rumors of an ignorant mob.

Why, then, is he charged with guilt, when it is established that he observed the laws of history with such care and religious scrupulousness in writing?

**XII.** Nevertheless, I would not for that reason assert that nothing false has crept into the details and circumstances of the events narrated.
