Indeed, I cannot deny that some things reported about Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, conflict with historical truth—namely, that he was carried off to Africa by Vandals devastating Campania, although the Vandals occupied Africa and ravaged Italy only long after Saint Paulinus’s death.

Yet no insoluble difficulties arise from this passage. For it can be said that “Vandals” are used here for the Goths. As Chiffletius observes after Procopius in his *Pauline Illustrated* (*The Vandalic War*, chapter 2; Chiffletius, p. 187), they originated from the same people, used the same laws and the same language, called Gothic, and were devoted to the same heresy.

All writers agree that Nola was captured by the Goths around the year 410 of Christ. At that time Paulinus, bound by the barbarians and ordered to reveal where he had hidden his wealth, prayed to God as Augustine reports in Book I, chapter 10, of *The City of God*:

> “Lord, let me not be tortured on account of gold and silver; for you know where all my possessions are.”

It seems probable that the captives, including Paulinus, were taken with the Gothic army from Italy into Gaul, and three years later into Spain, and were sold to the Vandals, who had invaded Spain from the year 409 onward.

See Dissertation 7 appended to the works and life of Saint Paulinus in the new edition, namely that of the year 1685. Once this difficulty has been resolved, everything in the *Dialogues* is straightforward, both historically and chronologically.

**XIII.** If miracles are described that are in no way consistent with reason, similar events are found in Ambrose, Augustine—especially in the books *On the City of God*—Jerome, and Sulpicius Severus among the Latin Fathers. I say nothing for the moment of Gregory of Tours, Fortunatus of Poitiers, and Nicetius of Trier; nor, among the Greeks, of Theodoret in his *Religious History*, Gregory of Nyssa in the *Life of Gregory, Bishop of Neocaesarea, called the Wonderworker*, or Athanasius himself in the *Life of Saint Antony*, which our scholars rightly attribute to him in the latest edition of the works of the holy Doctor.

Accordingly, lest faith be denied to the miracles narrated by Gregory merely because of their extraordinary character, we have strengthened the less credible ones with similar examples drawn from elsewhere, as can be seen in Book I, chapters 1, 3, 4, and so forth; and Book III, chapter 3 and following.

As for those whom the pious Doctor testifies to have prophesied future events when they were near death, as in Book IV, chapter 26, this can be illuminated by Augustine, Book XII, chapter 17, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, where similar examples are presented; consult that passage. See also the very learned Petitus, Book I, *On the Sibyls*, where he cites Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 53, and uses the testimony of Cicero, Book I, *On Divination*, who asserts that a certain man from the island of Rhodes foretold the deaths of six other men.

**XIV.** As for those who do not approve of miracles so readily, they are free, while passing over these matters, to select the remarkable examples of virtue presented here. Without doubt, as the holy Doctor himself warns in Book II, the final chapter, these ought to be preferred to all miracles.

To remain with a single example, who could fail to be astonished by the humility, patience, and charity of the priest Sanctulus, as they are portrayed in Book III, chapter 37?

Many doctrines of the faith are also expounded and defended in these *Dialogues*. This perhaps aroused the hatred of the heterodox against them more than the long succession of miracles did. To learn what Gregory thought about the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, see Book II, chapters 24 and 37, and Book IV throughout. On the viaticum administered to those near death, see Book II, chapter 37, and Book IV, chapters 15 and 35. On the most holy sacrifice of the New Law, to be offered for the living and the dead, consult Book IV, chapter 55 and following. Purgatory is discussed in the same book, chapters 39, 55, and elsewhere. Predestination is explained with great learning in Book I, chapter 8. The immortality of the soul, and the eternity of punishments assigned to the reprobate and rewards assigned to the just, are defended with the strongest arguments in Book IV, chapter 4 and following. Theologically, the vision of God is discussed in Book II, chapter 35. On the blessedness of the just before the resurrection, read Book IV, chapter 25.

To touch upon something from mystical theology: nowhere is it explained more clearly what compunction is, how many kinds there are, what its effects are, and so forth, than in Book III, chapter 34.

But let us now put an end to our vindication of the *Dialogues*, so that we may briefly complete what remains to be observed about them.

**XV.** From what has been said above it is established that Saint Gregory is the author of the *Dialogues*. Yet since at least two persons converse in the *Dialogues*, it must be asked who the person is who engages in conversation with the most holy teacher.

Gregory himself informs us at the beginning of the *Dialogues*:

> “My dearest son, Deacon Peter, was present. From the earliest flower of his youth he has been bound to me by intimate friendship and has been my companion in the investigation of the sacred word.”

This testimony concerning Peter persuaded many that he had been a monk in the monastery of Saint Andrew and had been formed under the discipline of Gregory, who was then abbot. John the Deacon, however, in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book II, chapter 11, counts Peter among the clergy rather than among the monks living in the holy Father’s household.

There is nothing to prevent our conjecturing that he was the same Peter the Subdeacon to whom Gregory often wrote, and with particular intimacy. In the first year of Gregory’s pontificate he administered the ecclesiastical patrimony in Sicily, and in the second year in Campania. After completing his service in those provinces, he could have been promoted to the diaconate and thereafter remained at the side of the supreme pontiff.

See Letters 1 and 2 of Book I, and Book II, Letter 32, formerly Book XII, Letter 30. For his historical eulogy, see Volume I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 497.

**XVI.** This literary form, in which conversations are imagined between two persons, was employed by the holy Fathers not only to treat polemical subjects—as Jerome did both against the Luciferians and against the Pelagians, and Theodoret in the first three books of the treatise called *Eranistes*—but also to relate the deeds of saints.

Thus Palladius wrote the life of John, surnamed Chrysostom, and Sulpicius Severus, in three *Dialogues*, treated the virtues of the Eastern monks and of Saint Martin.

**XVII.** Gregory himself explains the occasion and purpose of writing the *Dialogues* in his letter to Maximianus of Syracuse:

> “My brothers who live familiarly with me compel me in every way to write briefly about certain miracles of the Fathers that we have heard took place in Italy. For this task I greatly need the assistance of your charity, so that you may briefly indicate to me what comes back to your mind and what you have happened to learn” (Book III, otherwise Book II, Indiction 11, Letter formerly 50, now 51), and so forth.

That Gregory intended to speak only about saints who flourished in Italy is clear from Book III, chapter 14, where he says of Saint Isaac:

> “This venerable Isaac was not born in Italy, but I relate those miracles of his that he performed while living in Italy.”

Here Gregory asks to be excused for treating Isaac, who was not born in Italy.

By “the miracles of the Fathers” we may understand both astonishing works of virtue and signs and marvels. Saint Gregory rightly teaches that the latter must be placed after good works, Book II, final chapter. He therefore observed the former no less carefully than the latter.

**XVIII.** The time at which the *Dialogues* were written seems capable of being established from Book III, chapter 19, where we read:

> “Almost five years ago, when the Tiber, near this Roman city, overflowed its channel,”

and so forth.

This overflowing of the Tiber was soon followed by a plague, which carried off Pope Pelagius. After Pelagius’s death, Gregory was appointed in his place in September of the year 590.

Accordingly, beginning with the flood that Gregory of Tours relates as having occurred in the ninth month—that is, November of the year 589—and counting five years (Book X of the *History*, chapter 1), we arrive at the year 594 as the time when the *Dialogues* were written.

Yet in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 26, our Gregory counts only three years as having passed since the final plague that devastated Rome:

> “Also during that mortality which three years ago ravaged this city with the most violent destruction,”

and so forth.

We can reconcile these apparently conflicting statements by saying that in the first passage Gregory is not speaking, but John the Tribune, whose words he reports. Further, John does not specify a full five-year period, but “almost five years.” In addition, John counts from the flood, whereas Gregory counts from the plague. The plague began somewhat after the flood, but raged long afterward and for more than a full year, as is clearly established by Homily 1 on the Gospels:

> “We are suffering plagues without cessation,”

says Gregory, already made supreme pontiff. For this homily, which is said to have been delivered on the Second Sunday of Advent, could not have been pronounced before a full year had elapsed since the flood.

Finally, John may perhaps be speaking of years that had merely begun, whereas Gregory speaks of completed years. We therefore agree with those who hold that Gregory composed the *Dialogues* in the year 593 or 594.

**XIX.** In order to devote himself more peacefully to this work, he did indeed seek a retreat, since he was especially devoted to the solitary life, as we read at the beginning of the *Dialogues*. Nevertheless, he did not leave Rome. In the previously cited Book IV, chapter 26, referring to Rome, he says:

> “Also during that mortality which three years ago devastated this city . . .”

He often speaks in the same way, especially in Book III, chapters 19 and 33, and Book IV, chapter 52. This clearly proves that he was then in Rome.

Nor would it have been fitting for so vigilant a shepherd to abandon his flock for long while so many dangers threatened and so many wolves surrounded it. From an ancient inscription published by our Mabillon in Volume IV of the *Analecta*, p. 497, it is understood that Gregory withdrew to the monastery of Saint Andrew in order to compose the *Dialogues*.

**XX.** As soon as the *Dialogues* were published, they were received throughout the Christian world with the greatest rejoicing, especially in Italy. Even among the Lombards, and particularly through the favor of Queen Theodelinda, as we have already said, they were held in the highest esteem.

The almost innumerable manuscript copies written by hand prove how highly our predecessors valued them. In some they are preserved complete, while in others they have been reduced to an epitome. Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, devoted himself above all to making such abridgements.

We found a compendium of this kind in a six-hundred-year-old manuscript at Utica; whether it is Odo’s or someone else’s, we do not know. (See Volume XVII of the *Library of the Fathers of the Church of Lyons*.)

**XXI.** The high opinion formed of these works is also confirmed by the fact that they were translated into so many languages.

Besides the Greek version, which we shall discuss shortly, there is an Arabic version preserved in the Colbert Library. It was made in the year 779 from the Greek, not from the Latin text itself. Concerning it, consult the preface to the new French translation, p. 106 and following.

In the same place, read what is recalled concerning the Saxon translation made at the command of King Alfred toward the end of the ninth century, or even prepared by Alfred himself, as William Cave asserts in his *Literary History*; concerning the French translation preserved in the library of John, Duke of Berry, who was the third son of King John and which had once been purchased at a high price; and concerning many others.

While examining the library of the monastery of Lyre in the diocese of Évreux, we encountered Manuscript D, containing these *Dialogues* translated into French and rendered in verse. They also exist in the library at Jumièges, written in concise Latin prose.

Of all these translations we present only one, namely the Greek. We shall explain what we have accomplished in publishing it after first making certain observations about this new edition of the Latin text. As for the other earlier editions, it will suffice to read the *Vindications of the Dialogues* by Petrus Gussanvillaeus, printed above, where he lists very many of the editions of which he had copies. Below, too, after the manuscript copies that we consulted have been listed, this information will be supplied.

**XXII.**

1. We have retained the arguments, or chapter titles, because they occur in almost all the manuscripts and may reasonably be believed to have originated with Gregory himself.

2. We have added brief notes below the columns. In them we either insert variant readings, explain the basis of restorations we have made, elucidate what Saint Gregory narrates, or address certain difficulties and remove doubts.

Of these notes, we borrowed a few from Gussanvillaeus and Mabillon, caring little whether we gave our own or another’s, provided that the latter were better than ours. We have written at the foot of the page the names of those from whom we borrowed them.

**XXIII.** 3. Nothing was more important to us than to restore the entire work to its former soundness and integrity with the help of manuscript copies. Here is their list:

1. A manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, at least eight hundred years old, marked on the back with the number 162, which for the sake of brevity we call *German*.

2. Two other manuscripts of a later period preserved in the library of the same monastery, which we shall call *Sangerm*.

3. Three manuscripts of Saint Peter of Chartres: one written in the ninth century, another in the eleventh, and a third in the thirteenth.

4. Two manuscripts of Saint-Thierry near Rheims, marked 58 and 59, which frequently disagree with one another.

5. A manuscript of the monastery of Compiègne, Saint-Corneille, marked on the back with the number 30.

6. A manuscript of the monastery of Longpont, of the Cistercian order.

7. A copy of the finest quality from the monastery of Clairvaux, of the same order.

8. Two manuscripts from the monastery of Saint Peter at Jumièges, the older of which approaches seven hundred years of age.

9. A manuscript of the monastery of Préaux, nearly equal in age and antiquity to the preceding.

10. Two manuscripts of the monastery of Saint-Ouen in the city of Rouen, not less than six hundred years old.

11. An equal number from Bec, though sometimes mutilated.

12. Manuscript D of the Bigot Library at Rouen, at least [the number of] years old.

13. A manuscript of the monastery of Lyre.

14. The series of Gallican manuscripts is closed by the distinguished manuscript of the Royal Library, written around the ninth century but copied from a far older source, as can be conjectured from its title, in which Gregory is by no means called a saint. It reads:

> “Here begins the book of the *Dialogues* of Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, concerning various beautiful miracles.”

And later:

> “Number 4 of the *Dialogues* of Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, concerning the miracles of the Fathers of Italy.”

15. In addition to all these are four manuscript copies against which the *Dialogues* were collated in England; their variant readings were published by Thomas James.

16. We also used the more distinguished editions: the Paris edition of 1518, prepared by Master Berthold Rembolt and Jean Petit; the Gilot edition published at Paris in 1571; the Vatican edition reprinted at Paris in 1605; and finally the Gussanvillaeus edition of 1675.

**XXIV.** We do not regret the great labor involved in examining so many manuscripts, since with their help we not only discovered the grounds for many of Gussanvillaeus’s restorations, which he himself concealed, but also corrected and restored very many passages that remained corrupt in all the printed editions. We shall now briefly demonstrate this with several examples as they arise.

[Col. 0145]

In Book I, chapter 9, concerning Saint Boniface, the printed editions read:

> “He held the office of bishop; he fulfilled it in his conduct.”

But the manuscripts read more elegantly, because of the antithesis:

> “He held the bishopric in the exercise of his office; he fulfilled it in his conduct.”

In the same book, chapter 11, the printed editions have:

> “Unbaked loaves are customarily marked with a sign.”

But the manuscripts, which we have judged should be followed, read:

> “They are customarily marked with wood.”

For otherwise, what meaning does *signo signari*—“marked with a sign”—have? What does it sound like?

## Book II, chapter 1

In Gussanville’s edition:

“But Benedict, desiring rather to endure the evils of the world than to seek praise from men” [118]. We have excised the last three words, which he added on his own initiative, without the guidance of any manuscript; once they are rejected, the sentence is more satisfactory.

A little earlier, the printed editions corruptly read: *omnes agnoscerent, a quanta Benedictus puer conversationis gratia perfectione coepisset* (“that all might recognize from what great perfection Benedict the boy had begun, for the sake of the grace of his way of life”). Instead read: *omnes agnoscerent, Benedictus puer conversationis gratiam, a quanta perfectione coepisset* (“that all might recognize the grace of Benedict the boy’s way of life, from what great perfection it had begun”).

In Book III, chapter 2, “Justinian the elder emperor” has crept into the printed editions instead of “Justin the elder,” which must be read from the manuscripts; historical truth does not permit any other reading.

In the same book, chapter 37, concerning Sanctulus, the published editions read: “as he was pleasant both in face and in spirit,” whereas the manuscripts have: “as he was joyful both in face and in countenance.” Saint Gregory means that Sanctulus was always cheerful in spirit and appearance, and therefore adds: “He greeted the laboring Lombards with a cheerful face.” A little later he says: “To them”—namely, to the Lombards by whom he had been harassed with injuries—“the man of God replied with an even more cheerful face.”

In Book IV, chapter 35, the printed editions read: “A certain Stephen, who was called by another name Optio.” In Gussanville’s edition the following is added in the margin: “whose surname was Optio.” We have restored the reading from the manuscripts: “A certain Stephen, who was an Optio in rank.” The error began with the first editors, who perhaps did not know what this rank was or what “Optio” meant. The notes to this passage will explain both matters.

In the same book, chapter 47:

“In the same monastery there was also another man named John, a young man of great ability, who passed his age in understanding and gravity.”

Thus the printed books have it, barbarously and contrary to the sense. But light has shone from the manuscripts, where one reads *transibat* (“was passing through”), which we have preferred. But enough concerning these matters and the Latin Dialogues. I now wish to give the reader a brief preliminary account of the Greek translation printed here together with them.

## XXV

That Zacharias was the translator of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory is attested by Anastasius the Librarian (*In Zachariam*), John the Deacon (Book IV, chapter 95), and Photius (*Codex* 252); no one denies it.

John the Deacon and Photius, however, are mistaken in assigning the time when this translation appeared. John states that it was made approximately 175 years later, in the time of the emperor Constantine—namely, Constantine Copronymus. Photius, followed by the anonymous author of the Greek preface placed before the Greek translation, asserts that 165 years elapsed between the composition of the Dialogues by Gregory and their rendering into Greek by Zacharias.

But it is established that Saint Zacharias began to sit as pope in the year 741 and ruled the Church for no more than ten years and a few months. Therefore, from the year 593, before which the Dialogues cannot have been composed, to the end of Zacharias’s pontificate there are only 158 years. Both writers must consequently have erred in their chronology.

As for the translation itself, anyone who reads it will see that it differs from the authentic Latin, both in the titles and summaries of the chapters and in many other respects, as we have noted in several places. As regards its diction, it teems with barbarous words, which provided a rich harvest for the most learned Cange when he compiled his *Glossary of the Greco-Barbarous Language*.

## XXVI

The complaint that this translation was corrupted is an ancient one, made by John the Deacon and other orthodox writers, particularly in the last chapter of Book II. Where the Latin reads:

“Since it is established that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son,”

the Greek translator—or rather interpolator—renders it:

“It is manifest that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.”

John the Deacon complains that this was done through the deception of Greeks who opposed the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. I strongly suspect that Photius was the author of this corruption, being highly skilled in such acts of alteration, especially because he praises Zacharias’s work and the Dialogues of Gregory so greatly. From these interpolated passages he was already forging weapons and preparing engines for himself or his supporters against the procession of the Holy Spirit.

For the rest, it is easy to prove how far Gregory is from the error of the Greeks, both from the creed that he issued at the beginning of his pontificate, where he teaches that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal and proceeding from the Father and the Son, and from many passages in the *Moralia*. Thus, in Book I, no. 30, formerly chapter 7, he says:

“While he considers the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from himself”—that is, from the Son.

And in Book V, no. 65:

“Who, proceeding from the Father and receiving from that which belongs to the Son.”

Still more clearly, in Homily 26 on the Gospels, near the beginning:

“He proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

## XXVII

It remains for me briefly to explain how much labor we expended in preparing a more accurate edition of this Greek translation.

We cannot conceal that, while reviewing Gussanville’s edition, we encountered extremely serious *σφάλματα* (“errors”). When we compared it with the Vatican printed editions, we realized that Gussanville had transferred into his own edition almost all the typographical errors found in those books, including the more serious ones. Whether this resulted from reverence for Roman types or from carelessness, let others judge.

So that this may not be thought an empty boast on our part, it must be confirmed by bringing forward several examples.

In Gussanville’s edition, Book III, chapter 21, column 178, the readings are **ἐκθλιβῆναι, ἐκβληθῆναι** (“to be pressed out, to be cast out”). The Vatican edition has the same text.

Chapter 26, column 187: in both editions the punctuation is faulty in the following manner: **καὶ τὰ μὴ ὑποστελλόμενα, ξίφος τὴν** etc. The comma must be transposed, and one should read: **ὑποστελλόμενα ξίφος, τὴν** etc.

On column 188 of the same chapter, the final word is incorrectly printed in both editions as **πειράσωμαι**, instead of **πειράσομαι**.

Chapter 28, column 190: in both editions **καθώπερ**, instead of **καθάπερ**.

Chapter 34, column 203: near the beginning both editions omit almost the following words: **θρηνῶνται ὅθεν ἐκ προσώπου τῶν μετανοούντων Ἰερ**. In the same place, approximately fifteen lines below, they have **οἱ συμμετοχή** instead of **ἡ συμ**.

Chapter 37, column 215, near the end: **οὕ τὸ**, instead of **οὕτως**.

In Book IV, in the title of chapter 4, column 226, one reads **Ἐκκλησιαστίκου**, instead of **Ἐκκλησιαστοῦ**.

In the final part of this chapter, column 230, two complete lines have been omitted.

At the beginning of the following chapter, three words are missing in the same place.

Chapter 15, shortly after the beginning, column 246: the sense is entirely lost through the omission of two lines.

Chapter 38, not far from the beginning, reads **καλεῖς**, instead of **λαλεῖς**. Near the end it has **δρόμου**, instead of **τρόμου**.

Chapter 42, approximately midway through, has **ὑπερκάτω**, instead of **ὑποκάτω**.

Before column 178 we observed no similar errors—not because the earlier portions are purer or more carefully corrected, but because we had already prepared almost the entire edition of the Dialogues before it occurred to us to make these observations.

To purge Zacharias’s translation of these errors common to both editions, as well as of many others, two Greek manuscripts were available to us, the Regius and the Colbertinus; the latter, however, ends at chapter 13 of Book II.

Nor were we satisfied merely to correct errors with their assistance. We also added certain notes to passages that were already sound and pure, in order to lighten the reader’s labor—something we ask him to regard favorably—and we refused no task.

[Col. 0147]

# Preface

[Note: Absent from the Latin manuscripts and from the Vatican edition. It exists in Greek in Regius manuscript 2934 and Colbertinus 2500.]

## Preface to the Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great, by an Anonymous Author

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: In the Benedictine edition, a Greek-Latin series of chapter lists is set out here; we deliberately omit it, since the same lists are printed before each individual chapter. — Editor.]

### Latin text

[Col. 0148A] 121

The followers of virtue are rightly celebrated with the praises of all. For they do not acquire gain for themselves alone; they also leave to those devoted to living rightly after them, as it were, a living image and animated statue of their deeds.

But those are judged worthy of far greater praise who, after performing works of virtue, devoted all their effort to leaving writings for the world that could train and exercise in virtue those who read them with affection. For the greatest path toward discovering what is honorable is meditation on the divine Scriptures. In them are found precepts for action, and the lives of holy men, handed down in writing, are set before us as living images of a godly way of life, proposed for the imitation of good works, as certain of our holy Fathers have philosophized on the matter.

Moreover, although many diligent men have arisen in both the Old and the New Testament who left the world writings containing histories of past events and predictions of future things, as well as lives of holy and virtuous men who excelled in the monastic life in the East and Egypt, our most holy Father Gregory—moved by the Holy Spirit, superior to all praise, pope of the renowned city of Rome—along with many other books distinguished by beauty of expression and profundity of meaning, also wrote in four books, in the Latin language, the lives of the holy men who shone forth in Italy, and the times and places in which they flourished.

When 165 years had already passed [Note: John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 75, counts 175 years. We have shown in the preface that both writers erred in their chronology], and no one among all men had been found willing to undertake their translation from Latin into Greek, Zacharias—chosen by divine providence as shepherd and chief of shepherds, leader of the orthodox faith, successor of Peter, chief of the apostles, thrice-blessed and equal to the angels, apostolic and ecumenical pope—because he possessed a soul devoted to God and to noble things and had consecrated his whole self to future recompense, diligently occupied himself with the divine Scriptures among his many splendid achievements, according to the Lord’s command:

“Search the Scriptures, because in them you think you have eternal life” (John 5:19).

Remembering the life and conduct of the holy Fathers and monks who had lived in the East, he conceived the excellent plan of translating into Greek both those books written in Latin by the men mentioned above and those containing the virtues of the holy Fathers who had flourished in Italy, desiring to distribute abundantly to all the spiritual wealth proceeding from them.

Bringing this work to completion, he left an unfailing treasure to those who would read these books diligently; for himself he acquired the reward reserved for faithful and prudent stewards.

The contents of the books set out below are as follows.

### Greek text

[Col. 0147A] 120

The followers of virtue are rightly praised by everyone. For they do not share in the profit alone; they also leave to those who afterwards choose to live rightly, through their memory, as it were, a living image and animated monument [Note: Colbertinus reads *βιοῦν*, “living”].

But far more worthy of praise are those who, after attaining virtue, devote all their zeal to leaving writings for the world, writings capable of training in virtue those who approach them with longing.

For the greatest path toward discovering what is right is the study of the divine Scriptures [Basil, Letter 1 to Gregory of Nazianzus]. In them are found both the principles of conduct and the written lives of blessed men, handed down as living images of the life according to God and set before us for imitation in good works, just as some of our holy Fathers have philosophized concerning this [Note: The manuscripts read *καί τινι τῶν . . . πεφιλοσόφηται*, “and one of our holy Fathers has philosophized …”].

Since many earnest men in the Old and New Covenants have left writings containing histories of past events and prophecies of things to come, as well as the lives of holy and virtuous men who distinguished themselves in ascetic practice in the East and Egypt, Gregory—our holy Father, superior to every praise, most blessed, pope of the renowned city of Rome—moved by the Holy Spirit, together with many other books shining with beauty of language and depth of meaning, wrote in four books, in the language of the Romans, the lives of the holy men who had distinguished themselves in Italy, according to the times and places in which they had lived [the manuscripts read “according to whatever times”; Colbertinus reads “in Rome” instead of “in the language of the Romans”].

When approximately 165 years had passed and no one at all had undertaken to translate these works from the Roman language into Greek, Zacharias—appointed from above as shepherd and chief shepherd, guide of orthodox faith, successor of Peter, foremost of the apostles, thrice-blessed, equal to the angels, apostolic and ecumenical pope—being devoted to God and to noble things in soul, and having dedicated his entire self to future recompense, diligently attending to the divine Scriptures amid all his good achievements, in accordance with the Lord’s command:

“Search the Scriptures, for in them you think that you have eternal life”—

remembering the life and conduct of the holy Fathers and ascetics who had lived in the East, conceived an excellent plan: to translate into Greek both the same books written in the Roman language by the authors mentioned above [Colbertinus: “the same four books written by our aforementioned and unforgettable Father Gregory”] and those containing the virtues of the holy Fathers who had distinguished themselves in Italy, wishing to provide everyone generously with the spiritual wealth derived from them.

Having brought this to completion, he left an inexhaustible treasure to those who approached the books with longing, while he secured for himself the reward laid up for faithful and prudent stewards.

[Note: The following is absent from Colbertinus.]

The contents of the books set out below are as follows.

[Col. 0149]

# The Four Books of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory, Pope, concerning the Life and Miracles of the Italian Fathers and the Eternity of Souls

[Note: This title is found in most manuscripts. It is absent, however, from the Italian manuscripts, Gemetensis, and Audomarensis. Saint Gregory sufficiently indicates that he intended to speak about the Italian Fathers. See the preface. By “Fathers” we should understand elders, or saints, of an earlier age. He therefore does not designate only monks here, in the sense in which one speaks of the *Life of the Fathers*. Although the holy Doctor commonly calls monks “Fathers” (see Book IV, formerly Book III, Letter 46, elsewhere 44), and we read that ancient monks were called abbots—that is, Fathers.]

Gregory, the most holy and apostolic pope of elder Rome: Historical Dialogues, addressed to Peter the deacon, concerning the conduct of various Fathers who flourished in Italy.

[Note: The words “and apostolic” are absent from the Colbertinus manuscripts.]

[Note: Seguntinus reads “dialogue.”]

[Note: The manuscripts read “archdeacon.” Below, he is simply called “deacon,” both in the Latin text and in the Greek translation.]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0149]

# Book One

## Chapter 1

### Concerning Honoratus, abbot of the monastery at Fundi

[Note: The Roman Martyrology mentions him on 16 January.]

[Col. 0153C]

[Note: This appears to be the man whose encomium is found in Cassiodorus, Book IX, Letter 23.]

There was once a villa belonging to the patrician Venantius in the region of Samnium [Note: Most manuscripts read “Samnia”; Pratellensis and Germanensis have “Samnia” here and later “Samnium”]. In it his tenant had a son named Honoratus [Roman Martyrology, 16 January], who from childhood burned with love for his heavenly homeland through abstinence.

As he advanced in a life of great discipline, restrained himself even from idle speech, and, as I have said, greatly subdued his flesh through abstinence, one day his parents prepared a banquet for their neighbors. Meat was set out for eating. When he refused to touch it, out of love for abstinence, his parents began to ridicule him and say:

“Eat! Are we supposed to bring you fish in these mountains?”

Fish were accustomed to be heard in that place, but never seen. While Honoratus was being mocked with these words, the water needed for the banquet suddenly ran out. A servant went to the spring with a wooden bucket, as was customary there.

[Note: Numerous miracles performed in commendation of abstinence are reported. See a nearly similar instance in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 3, on the virtues of Saint Martin, chapter 13: at the first cast of a very small net a deacon drew out an enormous *esox*, to be served to Martin, who abstained from meat even during the Easter festival days.]

As he drew water, a fish entered the bucket. The servant returned and poured out the fish together with the water before the faces of those reclining at table. It was large enough to have supplied Honoratus with food for the entire day.

Everyone was astonished, and all the ridicule of his parents ceased. They began to honor in Honoratus the abstinence that they had previously mocked. Thus the fish from the mountain wiped away from the man of God the disgrace of their mockery [some printed editions read “the fish from the spring”].

As he grew in great virtues, he was granted his freedom by the master mentioned above. At the place called Fundi he built a monastery, in which he became the father of approximately two hundred monks. There his life gave all around examples of outstanding discipline [Gemetensis and Pratellensis read: “who was called Flundis.” Fundi is now an episcopal city in Latium].

For one day a massive rock was torn from the mountain that rises high above his monastery. Rolling down the steep slope of the mountain, it threatened the destruction of the entire monastery and the death of all the brothers.

When the holy man saw it coming from above, he repeatedly invoked the name of Christ, immediately stretched out his right hand, and opposed to it the sign of the cross. He halted it as it fell along the slope of the mountain, as the religious man Laurence relates.

Because there was no place where it could have adhered, it can still be seen by those looking at the mountain: it appears that the rock, about to fall, is hanging there.

### Latin dialogue

**Peter:** Do we suppose that this distinguished man, who later became a teacher of disciples, first had a teacher?

**Gregory:** I have never heard that he was anyone’s disciple. The gift of the Holy Spirit is not confined by a law.

It is indeed the custom of right conduct that no one should dare to preside who has not learned to obey, nor command obedience to those subject to him when he has not known how to render it to his superiors.

Yet there are some who are taught inwardly through the instruction of the Spirit, so that, even if they lack the discipline of human teaching externally, they do not lack the judgment of an inner teacher.

Nevertheless, the freedom of such people’s lives must not be made an example for the weak, lest, while someone presumes himself similarly filled with the Holy Spirit, he disdain becoming a disciple of a human being and become instead a teacher of error.

A mind filled with the divine Spirit has its signs most clearly—namely, virtues and humility. If both are perfectly united in one mind, it is evident that they bear witness to the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Thus John the Baptist is not read to have had a teacher. Nor did Truth itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who taught the apostles through his bodily presence, gather John bodily among the disciples; rather, while teaching him inwardly, he left him outwardly in his freedom.

So Moses, taught in the wilderness, learned from an angel a commandment that he had not learned through a human being (Exodus 23).

But these things, as we have said, are to be revered by those who are weak, not imitated.

[Note: The manuscripts read *evidentissime* (“most plainly”), not the printed editions’ *evidentissima signa sua* (“his most evident signs”). Heterodox writers invoke the latter wording to argue that a person must certainly believe not only that he is just but also that he is elect; they are answered by Theodore Petreius the Carthusian, *Confession of Gregory*, Book II, chapter 4, no. 7.]

**Peter:** I approve what you say, but I ask you to tell me whether this great Father left behind any disciple as an imitator of himself.

### Greek text

[Col. 0154C]

## Chapter 1

### Concerning Honoratus, superior of the monastery called Fundi

There was a country estate belonging to Venantius, at that time a patrician, in the region of Samnium. In it his farmer had a son named Honoratus, who from the earliest age of childhood was inflamed with longing for the heavenly homeland through self-control [Regius reads “kingdom,” and shortly afterward “through purity and conduct”; in Colbertinus only the phrase “through conduct” is found, which better represents the Latin text].

As he advanced in such pure conduct, he restrained himself even from untimely speech and, as I have said, sufficiently subdued his flesh through self-control. One day, therefore, his parents held a banquet for their neighbors, at which meat was served for eating [the manuscripts read “meats”]. He completely refused to eat or even touch it, out of longing for self-control.

His parents began to mock him and say:

“Eat! Surely we do not have fish to set before you in these mountains” [Regius reads “in these regions”].

In that place fish were heard, but could not at all be found or seen. While Honoratus was being mocked with these words, the water needed for the banquet failed. With a wooden bucket—as was customary there—the servant went to the spring [Regius reads “buckets”; Colbertinus reads “pails”].

As he drew the water, a fish entered the vessel. The man carrying the water returned and poured out the fish with the water before the faces of those reclining at table. It was sufficient to provide Honoratus with food for the whole day.

When everyone was astonished [the printed editions read “and everyone was astonished”], all that mockery by his parents ceased. They began to revere Honoratus’s self-control, which they had previously ridiculed. Thus the fish from the mountain wiped away the insult of mockery from the man of God.

As he advanced in the greatest powers [Regius: “As he advanced in the greatest miracles, and after receiving freedom from the parents mentioned above …”], he obtained his freedom from his aforementioned master and built a monastery in that place called Fundi. In it he became father of two hundred monks.

There his life gave everywhere examples of wondrous conduct [Regius: “Throughout his life he displayed examples of wondrous conduct”; Colbertinus has “gave” instead of “has given”].

One day a huge stone was cut away from the same mountain on whose heights his monastery stood. Coming down its slope, it threatened the collapse of the monastery and the destruction of all the brothers.

When that holy man saw it coming from above, he repeatedly invoked the name of Christ, stretched out his right hand, and placed upon it the sign of the honorable cross. At once he stopped it as it descended on the mountain’s cliff, as the devout man Laurence says [Regius reads “descent”].

Since there was no place where the stone could fasten itself, it is still visible to everyone: one can see how, torn away from the mountain, it hangs there, having been stopped by the saint through the power of Christ.

### Greek dialogue

**Peter:** I inquire, venerable Father: did this distinguished man, who later became a teacher of disciples, previously have a teacher?

**Gregory:** I have never heard that he was anyone’s disciple; but the gift of the Holy Spirit is not confined by law.

Nevertheless, it is the custom of right conduct that no one should dare to preside who has not learned to submit, nor entrust obedience to those subject to him when he himself has not learned to render it to his superiors.

Yet there are some who are taught inwardly by the instruction of the Spirit, so that, even if they lack the knowledge of human teaching externally, they do not lack the wisdom of an inner teacher.

This occurs in perfect men, whose freedom of life cannot fall into the example of the weaker, lest someone, thinking himself likewise filled with the Holy Spirit, refuse to become a human being’s disciple and become a teacher of error.

A mind filled with the divine Spirit has its signs most clearly: power and humility. If both come together completely in a single mind, they plainly bear witness to the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Thus John the Baptist is read to have had no teacher. Nor did Truth itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, after teaching the apostles through bodily presence, gather him bodily among them; rather, while teaching him inwardly, he left him outwardly in freedom [the manuscripts read “he left him”].

Thus Moses, guided by an angel in the wilderness, learned a commandment that he had not learned through a human being.

But these things, as we have said, are to be revered by those who are weaker, not imitated.

**Peter:** I approve what you say, but I ask you to tell me whether this great Father left behind any disciple from among his students as an imitator of himself.

[Notes on the Greek dialogue: In Peter’s opening speech the manuscripts read *δυνάμεσι διαλάμψασαν* (“had shone in powers”), whereas the printed editions have *διαλαμψάντων*, which corresponds less well to the Latin; the printed *ἀνάπτεται* (“is kindled”) is senseless in context. Regius reads *μικρά* (“small”) for “substantial edification”; the manuscripts read *οὐρανίου πατρίδος* (“heavenly homeland”) and *ἤπερ* (“than”), while Regius has *ὑπέρ* and the printed editions *εἴπερ*. Regius reads *ἐπάρω* for *παρεπάρω* (“I remove”) in Gregory’s statement about removing the ground of unbelief. In the account of spiritual instruction, the manuscripts read *ἐκ τῶν ὑποδειγμάτων* (“from the examples”) for the expression concerning the weak; and, at the conclusion, the same manuscripts read *σαβάσμια εἰσί* (“they are venerable”) for *σεβαστέα εἰσί* (“they are to be revered”).]

## Chapter 2

### Concerning Libertinus, superior of the same monastery

[Gemetensis adds: “how he was thrown from his horse.”]

### Latin text

[Col. 0157A]

**Gregory:** The most reverend man Libertinus, who was superior of the same monastery at Fundi during the reign of Totila, king of the Goths [the words “of the Goths” are absent from three Chartres manuscripts, Germanensis, Normanensis, and many others; they are also absent from the Greek translation], lived and was instructed as Honoratus’s disciple.

Although the reliable reports of many people spread accounts of numerous virtues of his, the religious man Laurence mentioned above—who is still alive and was very close to Libertinus during his lifetime—was accustomed to tell me many things about him. I shall relate a few of those that I remember.

In the same province of Samnium that I mentioned above, this same man was traveling for the benefit of the monastery. When Darida, the leader of the Goths [Chartres, Longipontanus, and the first Theodorus read “the Gothic Count,” as does the Greek; the second Theodorus has “king of the Goths”], arrived at the same place with his army, the servant of God was thrown from the horse on which he was riding by Darida’s men.

He bore the loss of the animal cheerfully and even offered the whip he was holding to those who were robbing him, saying:

“Take it, so that you may have something with which to drive this animal.”

After saying this, he immediately devoted himself to prayer.

The army of the aforesaid leader, moving rapidly, reached a river called the Volturnus. There each man began to beat his horse with spears and wound it with spurs. Yet although the horses could be wearied by the blows and wounded by the spurs, they could not be moved; they feared to touch the river’s water as though it were a deadly precipice.

After the individual riders had long exhausted themselves by beating the horses, one of them suggested that they were suffering this delay on their journey because of the offense they had committed against the servant of God.

They immediately turned back and found Libertinus lying prostrate in prayer. When they said to him:

“Rise and take your horse,”

he replied:

“Go in peace. I have no need of a horse.”

They dismounted and, against his will, lifted him onto the horse from which they had thrown him, and immediately departed.

Their horses then crossed at such speed the river that earlier they had been unable to cross, as though its bed contained no water at all. Thus it happened that, when one horse was restored to the servant of God, every man received his own horse back.

At the same time Buccellinus came into the region of Campania with the Franks [a leader of King Theudebert of the Franks, concerning whom see Gregory of Tours, Book III of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 32].

A rumor had spread concerning the monastery of the aforesaid servant of God that he possessed a great deal of money. The Franks entered the oratory and began, raging, to seek Libertinus, shouting “Libertinus!” He was lying there prostrate in prayer.

A very remarkable thing occurred: as the Franks searched and raged, they entered and stumbled against him, yet they could not see him. Thus, frustrated by their blindness, they returned from the monastery empty-handed.

[The supplied source ends here.]

At another time, on monastery business, he was traveling to Ravenna at the command of the abbot who had succeeded his master Honoratus. Because of his love for that same venerable Honoratus, wherever Libertinus went he was accustomed always to carry Honoratus’s little *caligula* [Note: Gemetian, Audoenian, and Pratellian manuscripts read *calliculam*; Lyr reads *galliculam*. *Caligae* are counted among the footwear or garments of monks at the beginning of the Rule of Saint Pachomius and in its prologue, as well as in chapter 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Jerome, in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, writes: “The Tabennesiots have nothing in their cells except a mat … a linen belt, caligae, and a staff.” The first Theodulf manuscript has *caligam*, the second *ligulam*.] in his bosom.

As he was traveling, it happened that a woman was carrying the little body of her dead son. When she caught sight of the servant of God, inflamed by love for her son, she seized his animal by the bridle and said under oath: “You shall by no means go away unless you raise my son.” He, having no experience of such a miracle, was terrified by the oath attached to her request. He wished to turn away from the woman, but, unable to do so, remained inwardly torn. It is worth considering what a great struggle there was in his heart. There humility arising from his manner of life and the mother’s compassion were contending with one another: fear lest he presume upon something unprecedented, and grief lest he fail to help a bereaved woman. But, for the greater glory of God, compassion conquered in that courageous heart—the heart was courageous because it was conquered; for it would not have been a courageous heart if compassion had not prevailed. [Note: Bigot reads, “the mother’s compassion.”]

Accordingly, he dismounted, bent his knees, stretched his hands toward heaven, drew the little *caligula* from his bosom, and placed it upon the chest of the dead boy. As he prayed, the boy’s soul returned to his body. Libertinus took him by the hand, returned him alive to his weeping mother, and completed the journey he had begun. [Note: Lyr, Bigot, and Prat read “he proceeds.”]

[Col. 0161A]

PETER. What are we to say this means? Was it the merit of Honoratus that brought about the power of so great a miracle, or Libertinus’s petition?

GREGORY. In the manifestation of so wondrous a sign, the power of both converged with the woman’s faith. For that reason I believe that Libertinus was able to do these things because he had learned to trust much more in his master’s power than in his own. For the one whose little *caligula* he placed upon the chest of the dead body, he naturally believed would obtain for him what he asked.

Elisha likewise carried his master’s mantle and, coming to the Jordan, struck it once, but the waters were not divided. Then, suddenly saying, “Where is the God of Elijah, even now?” (2 Kings 2:14), he struck the river with his master’s mantle and made a path through the waters. Do you perceive, Peter, how much humility avails in the performance of mighty deeds? He was able to display his master’s power when he recalled his master’s name. For when, through humility, he returned to his master, he himself did what his master had done.

PETER. What you say pleases me. But, I ask you, is there anything else that you can still tell us about him for our edification?

GREGORY. Certainly—if there is anyone who wishes to imitate him. [Note: Audoen and Lyr add, “I do not know.”] I believe the power of patience to be greater than signs and miracles.

One day the man who, after the death of the venerable Honoratus, held the governance of the monastery became fiercely angry with the same venerable Libertinus, to the point of striking him with his hands. Since he could not find a rod with which to beat him, he seized a footstool and battered his head and face with it, making his whole face swollen and bruised. Severely beaten, Libertinus withdrew silently to his own bed.

The next day, however, monastery business had been arranged. After the morning hymns had been completed, Libertinus went to the abbot’s bed and humbly asked for his blessing. The abbot knew how highly everyone honored and loved Libertinus, and thought that, because of the insult he had inflicted upon him, Libertinus intended to leave the monastery. He therefore asked him, saying: “Where do you wish to go?”

Libertinus replied: “The monastery’s business has been arranged, Father, and I cannot avoid it. Yesterday I promised that I would go there today, and I have decided to go.” [Note: Audoen and Lyr read, “the matter having been arranged, he was about to depart.”]

Then, considering from the depths of his heart his own harshness and hardness, and Libertinus’s humility and gentleness, the abbot sprang from his bed, took hold of Libertinus’s feet, and confessed that he had sinned and was guilty for having dared to inflict so cruel an insult upon so great and distinguished a man. Libertinus, on the contrary, prostrated himself on the ground and, falling at the abbot’s feet, declared that what he had suffered was the result of his own fault, not of the abbot’s violence.

Thus the Father was led to great gentleness, and the disciple’s humility became the teacher of his master. When he had gone out on the monastery’s business, many prominent and noble men who greatly honored him were deeply astonished and anxiously asked what had happened to him, since his face was so swollen and bruised. He told them: “Yesterday evening, through my sins, I stumbled against a footstool and suffered this.”

Thus the holy man, preserving in his heart the honor of truth and of his master, neither exposed the Father’s fault nor fell into the sin of falsehood.

PETER. Do you suppose that this venerable man Libertinus, about whom you have related so many signs and miracles, left imitators of his virtues in so large a congregation?

## Chapter II. Concerning Libertinus, the second-in-command [Note: That is, the man who held the second position in the monastery. He is called the *praepositus*, especially in chapter 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Yet what is related here about Libertinus seems rather to outline the duties of a steward than of a *praepositus*. Perhaps Libertinus held both offices, that of *praepositus* and that of cellarer or steward. In the Council of Constantinople under Mena, session 1, we read: “Flavian, presbyter and *deuterarios*”; and below: “Anastasius, presbyter and *deuterarios*.” There is no contradiction in this title designating also a steward or cellarer, who may be called second after the abbot: for just as spiritual matters are entrusted to the abbot, temporal matters are entrusted to the cellarer. Hence chapter 31 of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “Let the cellarer … be like a father to the whole congregation.”]

of the same monastery.

[Col. 0158B]

GREGORY. During the reign of Totila, a most devout man named Libertinus was the *deuterarios* of that same monastery of Fundis, having lived under the discipline and instruction of this holy man. Many accounts have securely reported the numerous miracles concerning him, especially the most devout man Lawrence mentioned earlier, who is still alive and who was exceptionally intimate with that very man. [Note: Colbertinus reads *parrēsiōtatos*, “most outspoken”; Reginensis, *paraplēsios*, “close” or “similar.”] He has often told me many things about him; therefore, from what I remember, I shall relate a few.

In the previously mentioned region of Samnium, the same most devout man Libertinus was traveling on monastery business. Dardas, count of the Goths, encountered the servant of God with an army. [Note: Colbertinus reads *oun*, “therefore.” The printed editions read *hypantēsas*, “having met,” against the manuscripts and the sense.] Some of Dardas’s men beat him down from the horse on which he was sitting and took the horse away. Libertinus willingly endured the loss of the horse that had been taken from him and gave them the whip he was holding, saying: “Take this, so that you may have something with which to drive this animal.” [Note: The manuscripts read *phragellion*, “whip.”]

After saying this, he immediately devoted himself to prayer. At the swiftest pace, the army of the aforementioned commander reached the river called the Vulturnus. [Note: The same manuscripts read *ērxato*, “began.”] Each man began striking his own horse with the sword [Note: The manuscripts read, “with a spear, and striking with their spurs”] and beating it with his heels. The horses, beaten and struck for a long time, endured exhaustion but could not move; for they were as afraid to approach the river’s water as they would have been to approach a deadly precipice.

When they had flogged the horses for a long while and everyone had become exhausted, one of them said: “Because of the offense that we committed against the servant of God on the road, we are suffering these blows of pain.” They immediately turned back [Note: Reginensis reads *straphetes*, “having turned.”] and found Libertinus lying in prayer. They said to him: “Rise and take your horse.”

He replied: “Go in peace; I have no need of a horse.”

They dismounted, forcibly lifted him onto the horse from which they had taken him, and immediately departed. Their horses then crossed at such speed the river that previously they had been unable to cross, as though the riverbed had no water at all. Thus it happened that, once the servant of God’s horse had been returned, all the others crossed without difficulty. [Note: The manuscripts read: “This therefore happened so that the horse might be returned to the servant …”]

At the same time, Buccellinus came with the Franks into the region of Campania. A rumor spread that much money was stored in the monastery of the aforementioned servant of God, Honoratus. The Franks entered the oratory and began searching for Libertinus with the greatest fury, shouting his name: “Libertinus!” He was lying there stretched out in prayer.

A truly marvelous thing occurred. As the Franks entered, searching for him and raging [Note: Reginensis reads *zygomachountes*], they stumbled against him [Note: The manuscripts read *proekopton*, “they struck against” or “stumbled upon.”] but could not see him. Thus, punished by their own blindness, they left the monastery empty-handed. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “unsuccessful.” The translator very often uses the word *sabourus* to mean “empty.” See below, chapter 7, and consult Du Cange’s Greek Glossary, where he thinks the word derives from *saburra*, or sand, since ships loaded only with ballast are called “empty.”]

At another time, on monastery business and at the command of the abbot who had been appointed as the successor of his teacher Honoratus, he was departing for Ravenna. Because of the affection he had for that holy Honoratus, wherever Libertinus went he was accustomed to carry his *caligula* in his own bosom. [Note: Reginensis reads *kalēgion*; later, however, it has *kalygion*. Colbertinus reads *kallēgion*.] As he was departing for Ravenna, as has been said, it happened that a woman was carrying the body of her dead son. When she saw Libertinus and believed him to be a servant of God, burning with longing for her deceased son, she seized his horse by the bridle [Note: The manuscripts read “by the bit”] and swore that she would absolutely not allow him to go away unless he raised her son.

He had no experience of such a miracle and was astonished at the oath attached to her request. He wished to turn away from the woman, but could not in any way do so [Note: Reginensis reads *ekolythē*; perhaps *ekōlythē*, “he was prevented.”], for compassion bound him inwardly. One may therefore consider what kind and what degree of struggle he had within himself. As I think, a battle arose between the humility of his way of life and the mother’s compassion. Fear and grief accompanied it [Note: Reginensis reads *parēptonto phobos automolēsai*, “fear of deserting …”; Colbertinus, *pareiponto phobos automolēsai*, “fear accompanied [him] of deserting …”]: fear because such a miracle was unprecedented, and grief lest he fail to show compassion toward the afflicted mother.

But, for the greatest glory of God, compassion prevailed. This resolve could not have prevailed unless it had first been defeated by compassion. He therefore dismounted, bent his knee, stretched out his hands toward heaven [Note: Reginensis reads *exenenkōn*, “having brought forth.”], drew from his bosom the *caligula* he was carrying, and placed it upon the chest of the dead child. As he prayed, the child’s soul returned to its body, and he immediately rose. Libertinus took him by the hand, gave him alive to his weeping mother, and then continued along the road he had begun.

[Col. 0162A]

PETER. What are we to say this means? Did the holiness of Honoratus produce the power of so great a miracle, or Libertinus’s petition?

GREGORY. In the display of this wondrous sign [Note: Reginensis reads “of the miracle and sign”; Colbertinus is mutilated here.], the power of both came together with the woman’s faith. Therefore I believe that Libertinus was able to do these things because he trusted much more in his teacher’s power than in his own. For he believed that the soul of the man whose *caligula* he placed upon the dead child’s chest would certainly obey and obtain what he asked.

Elisha too, carrying his teacher’s mantle and coming to the Jordan, struck the water once, but the waters were not divided. When he immediately said, “Where is the God of Elijah?” he struck the river again with his teacher’s mantle and made a path through the waters. Do you understand, Peter, how powerful humility is in the performance of mighty deeds? He was able to perform the same power as his teacher when he brought his teacher’s name to mind. When, through humility, he returned to his teacher, he himself did what his teacher had done.

PETER. I like what you say. But, I ask you, venerable Father, is there anything else about him that you ought to relate for our edification?

GREGORY. There is indeed, if there is anyone who wishes to imitate him. I believe the power of endurance to be greater than miracles and signs.

One day [Note: Reginensis reads “on one of those days, that man …”] the man who, after the death of the most devout Honoratus, held the pastoral governance of the monastery became fiercely angry against the godly Libertinus, so that he laid his hands upon him. Since he could not find a rod with which to beat him, he seized a footstool and struck his head and face with it [Note: Reginensis reads “struck his face with it.”], making his whole face black and swollen. Severely beaten, Libertinus went away to his own bed and remained quiet.

There was, however, business arranged for the monastery’s care on the following day. After the morning hymns had been completed, Libertinus went to the abbot’s bed and asked for his blessing with complete humility. The abbot knew how highly Libertinus was honored and loved by everyone. He thought that, because of the insult he had inflicted upon him, Libertinus wished to withdraw from the monastery, and asked him: “Where do you wish to go?”

He replied: “There is monastery business arranged, Father, which I cannot possibly leave undone. Yesterday I arranged that I should be there today.”

Then the abbot sighed from the depths of his heart and considered his own exceedingly harsh hardness, as well as Libertinus’s humility and gentleness. He rose from his bed, seized Libertinus’s feet, and confessed that he had sinned and was condemned because he had dared to inflict so brutal a punishment upon so great and distinguished a man. [Note: The Reginensis manuscript reads “he wished”; the Colbertinus, “he fled.”]

Libertinus, on the contrary, spread himself upon the ground and, crawling at the abbot’s feet, said that what he had endured had happened because of his own fault, not because of the abbot’s weakness.

When this had taken place, the Father returned to great gentleness, and the disciple’s humility became the guide of his teacher. When he went to the arranged business on account of the monastery, many noble and well-known men who greatly honored him were deeply astonished and carefully asked how it had happened that he had such a swollen and black face. [Note: Colbertinus reads *melanomenon*, “being blackened.”] He replied: “Yesterday toward evening, because of my sins, I stumbled against the footstool and suffered this.”

Thus the holy man, preserving within himself the honor of truth, neither made public the Father’s fault nor fell into the sin of falsehood.

PETER. I should like to know, venerable Father, whether this most devout man Libertinus, about whom you have related so many signs and wonders, left imitators of himself in his community in the performance of mighty deeds. [Note: The Reginensis reads “in miracles.”]

## Chapter III. Concerning a monk who was gardener of the same monastery [Note: Colbertinus reads “concerning a certain monk.”]

[Col. 0164B]

GREGORY. The venerable abbot Felix, called Curvus (in the Greek, *Cecyphus*, that is, “hunchbacked”) [Note: The printed Greek editions add “in his own [monastery].”] [Note: German, two Chartres manuscripts, the second Theodulf, Compendian, and Longipontan manuscripts read *Corvus*. This is not how Pope Zachary read it.], whom you yourself know well and who was recently *praepositus* of that monastery, related many remarkable things to me about the brothers of the same monastery. I suppress some of them that come to mind because I am hurrying on to other matters. But I shall tell one, which I do not think should be omitted in any way.

In that monastery there was a monk of exemplary life who was the gardener. A thief used to come, climb over the fence, and secretly carry away vegetables. Since the gardener planted many things but found fewer of them, and saw some trampled underfoot and others torn away, he walked around the entire garden and found the path by which the thief used to come.

While walking through the same garden, he also found a serpent. He commanded it, saying: “Follow me.” When he reached the thief’s entrance, he ordered the serpent: “In the name of Jesus I command you to guard this entrance and not allow the thief to enter here.” Immediately the serpent stretched itself across the path [Note: Colbertinus reads “blocked the entrance.”] and the monk returned to his cell. [Note: Saint Benedict mentions the midday rest in chapter 48 of his Rule; see the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 55.]

At midday, when all the brothers were resting, the thief came as usual and climbed over the fence. As he lowered his foot into the garden, he suddenly saw that the extended serpent had blocked the way. Terrified, he fell backward, and his foot caught by the shoe on a spike of the fence. Thus he hung head downward until the gardener returned. [Note: Reginensis reads *ekremeto*, “was hanging.” It then repeats: “When the gardener came and found the thief hanging on the fence, he said to the serpent: ‘Thanks be to God, because you have fulfilled what you were commanded; withdraw now.’ It immediately withdrew.” Gemetensis reads “by the heel.” A similar miracle performed by Saint Spyridon, bishop of Cyprus, is related by Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, book 1, chapter 12: thieves secretly entered his sheepfold at night and tried to lead away the sheep. But God, who guarded the shepherd himself, also preserved his sheep; the thieves were held fast by some invisible power. He later released them and gave them a ram, adding jokingly: “So that you may not seem to have kept watch for nothing.” An even closer parallel occurs in Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 14.]

At the customary hour the gardener came and found the thief hanging on the fence. He said to the serpent: “Thanks be to God, you have fulfilled what I commanded; now withdraw.” [Note: The Reginensis reads “which he commanded you.”] The serpent immediately withdrew.

Approaching the thief, the gardener said: “What is it, brother? God has handed you over to me. Why have you dared so often to steal from the labor of the monks?” Saying this, he freed the man’s foot from the fence in which it had been caught and lowered him without injury. He said to him: “Follow me.”

He led the thief, who followed him, to the entrance of the garden and, with great kindness, gave him the vegetables he had been trying to steal [Note: Reginensis reads *labein*, “to take.”], saying: “Go, and do not steal any longer. When you have need, come in here to me, and whatever you struggle to take secretly and sinfully, I will gladly give you.”

PETER. As I now see, until this moment I had mistakenly thought that there had been no miracle-working fathers in Italy.

## Chapter IV. Concerning Equitius, abbot of the province of Valeria [Note: Valeria was a region of Latium near Lake Fucinus, where the cities of Valeria or the Marsi, Amiternum, Reate, and others were situated.]

[Col. 0165B]

GREGORY. I learned what I am about to relate from Fortunatus, the venerable abbot of the monastery called Cicero’s Bath [Note: Either at Puteoli or in the Tusculan territory, where Cicero possessed villas and elegant houses.], and also from the reports of other venerable men.

The most holy man named Equitius (in the Martyrology, 11 August), in the region of the province of Valeria, was held by everyone there in great admiration because of the merit of his life. The same Fortunatus was well acquainted with him. Because of the greatness of his holiness, Equitius became the Father of many monasteries in that province.

When, in his youth, the incitements of the flesh wearied him through fierce struggle, the very distress of his temptation made him more diligent in the practice of prayer. As he sought a remedy from almighty God in this matter through continual prayers, one night he saw an angel standing beside him and saw in the vision that the angel castrated him, cutting away every movement from his genital members. From that time onward he was so free from temptation that it was as though he had no sex in his body.

Relying on this virtue through the help of almighty God, he later began to preside over women just as he had previously presided over men. Nevertheless, he never ceased warning his disciples not to assume easily, on the basis of his example, that they could do the same, and thereby attempt to obtain a gift they had not received.

At the time when magicians were being discovered in this city of Rome [Note: On this Basil, see Cassiodorus, book 4, letters 22 and 23, where judges are assigned to him when he is accused of magical arts; see also Baronius, under the year 504.], Basil, who was foremost in magical practices, fled in the garb of a monk and went to Valeria. He went to the most reverend man Castorius, bishop of the city of Amiternum [Note: This city is now destroyed; it belonged to the province of Valeria.], and asked him to entrust him to Abbot Equitius and commend him to that monastery for healing.

The bishop then came to the monastery, bringing Basil the monk with him, and asked Equitius, the servant of God, to receive that monk into the community. The holy man immediately looked at him and said: “Father, the man whom you commend to me does not appear to me to be a monk, but a devil.”

The bishop replied: “You are looking for an excuse not to do what I ask.” The servant of God immediately said to him: “I declare him to be what I see him to be. Nevertheless, do not suppose that I am unwilling to obey you; I shall do what you command.”

He was therefore received into the monastery.

Not many days later, the same servant of God went somewhat farther from his cell in order to exhort the faithful to desire heavenly things. During his absence [Note: Gemetensis reads “as he departed.”], it happened that in the monastery of virgins over which the same Father watched, one of the women, who appeared beautiful according to the flesh’s corruptible condition, began to suffer from fever. She became greatly distressed and began to cry out—not now in loud words, but with shrieks: “I am about to die unless the monk Basil comes and, through his healing efforts, restores me to health.”

But in the absence of so great a Father, none of the monks dared to enter the community of the virgins, much less the newcomer, whose life the brotherhood did not yet know. A messenger was immediately sent to the servant of God Equitius and reported that the nun was burning with an immense fever and anxiously seeking a visit from the monk Basil.

When the holy man heard this, he smiled scornfully and said: “Did I not say that this man was a devil, not a monk? Go and drive him out of his cell. As for the handmaid of God who is being tormented by the anguish of fever, do not be concerned, for from this hour she will neither suffer from fever nor seek Basil.”

The monk returned and learned that the virgin of God had been restored to health at the very hour when the servant of God Equitius, far away, had said that she would be saved. [Note: Pratellian and Bigotian manuscripts read “that she had been saved.”] In this miracle he was following the example of the Master, who, when invited to the son of a royal official (John 4:46), restored him to health by a single word, so that when the father returned he learned that his son had been restored to life at the very hour when he had heard from the mouth of Truth that the child would live.

All the monks fulfilled their Father’s command and expelled Basil from the monastery’s dwelling. After being expelled, Basil said that he had frequently suspended Equitius’s cell in the air by magical arts, yet had been unable to harm anyone in it. Not long afterward, when zeal for the Christian people had flared up in this city of Rome, he was burned in the fire.

One day a handmaid of God from the same monastery of virgins entered the garden. Seeing a lettuce, she desired it and, forgetting to bless it with the sign of the cross, greedily bit into it. But she was immediately seized by the devil and fell.

When she was being tormented, word was quickly sent to Father Equitius that he should come swiftly and help her by prayer. [Note: The second Theodulf reads “protect her”; most manuscripts read “come running.” The miracle recorded here can be confirmed from Origen, *Against Celsus*, book 8, pages 399 and 401, concerning those who are handed over to the devil for punishment because of forbidden foods; and from Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, concerning a little girl who had tasted food sacrificed to idols and, as though compelled by a torturer, confessed her consciousness of the deed. In the same work, concerning another woman: “After the wicked food had been consumed, a madness armed for her destruction seized her mouth.”]

As soon as that Father entered the garden [Note: Compendian and German manuscripts read “the gate”; neither is found in the Greek version.], the devil who had seized her began to cry out from her mouth, as though making his defense: “What have I done? What have I done? I was sitting on the lettuce; she came and bit me.” [Note: Thus it is read in the manuscripts. The printed editions have “I was sitting there.” A similar way of speaking occurs in Bernard, Sermon 61 on the Song of Songs, no. 61: “I shall go to those well-stocked storerooms”; and Sermon 10 on Psalm 90: “I shall run to them”; and the sermon on Saint Martin: “I shall go for myself.” The first two Chartres manuscripts read, “I was sitting on my lettuce.”]

With stern indignation the man of God commanded him to depart and have no place in the handmaid of almighty God. He immediately departed and could no longer touch her.

A certain nobleman named Felix, from the province of Nursia, the father of Castorius [Note: He was almost certainly Castorius, master of the soldiers, who assisted Gregory greatly during the siege of Rome. See the letter formerly numbered 31 in book 4, now 40 in book 5.] who now resides with us in the city of Rome, noticed that the venerable Equitius did not possess a sacred order, yet went about from place to place and preached diligently. One day, taking advantage of their familiarity, he approached him and said:

“How do you dare to preach when you do not possess a sacred order and have not received permission to preach from the Roman pontiff under whom you live?”

Compelled by this question, the holy man explained how he had received permission to preach. He said:

“What you are saying to me, I too consider within myself. But one night a handsome young man appeared to me in a vision and placed a medical instrument—a phlebotome—in my tongue, saying: ‘Behold, I have placed my words in your mouth; go forth to preach.’ From that day onward, even when I wish to do so, I cannot remain silent about God.”

PETER. I should also like to learn of this Father’s works, since he is said to have received such gifts. [Note: We have removed “from God,” which the editors inserted against the manuscripts. It is likewise not expressed in the Greek, although it must always be understood.]

GREGORY. The work, Peter, comes from the gift; the gift does not come from the work, for otherwise grace would no longer be grace. Works are always preceded by gifts, although the gifts themselves increase through subsequent works. But lest you be deprived of knowledge of his life, the most reverend man Albinus, bishop of the Church of Reate, knew him well, and many still survive who were able to know him.

But why do you seek further evidence of his works, when purity of life was in harmony with his devotion to preaching? Such zeal for gathering souls for God burned within him that, while presiding over monasteries, he traveled throughout the churches, the fortified settlements, the villages, and even the houses of individual believers, stirring the hearts of his hearers to love their heavenly homeland.

He was extremely poor in clothing and so despised in appearance that, if someone happened not to know him, he would disdain even to return his greeting. Whenever he was traveling to other places, he used to ride an animal that could scarcely have been found in a stable more contemptible than all other animals. He used a halter for a bridle and sheepskins for a saddle. [Note: Most printed editions read “he sat upon the animal”; this is also found in a few manuscripts. We have already discussed this expression, familiar to Gregory and contemporary or earlier writers, in the note to book 1 of the *Moralia*, no. 22. See also book 2 on Ezekiel, homily 5, no. 2.]

He carried the sacred books himself in leather bags on his right and left sides. Wherever he arrived, he opened the fountain of Scripture and watered the meadows of people’s minds. [Note: The printed editions read “by himself”; we follow the manuscripts, including German, Norman, Theodulf, Valerian, Longipontan, and Compendian witnesses.]
