The reputation of his preaching also reached the notice of the city of Rome. At that time, clerics flatteringly complained to the bishop of this apostolic see—such is the tongue of flatterers, which kills the soul of its hearer by embracing it—saying:

“Who is this rustic man, who has seized for himself the authority to preach and, though unlearned, presumes to usurp the office of our apostolic lord? If it pleases you, let someone be sent to bring him here, so that he may learn what ecclesiastical authority is.”

As it is customary for flattery to insinuate itself into a mind occupied with many matters if it is not quickly driven back from the heart’s door, the pontiff, persuaded by the clerics, agreed that Equitius should be brought to Rome, so that he might discover what his capacity was.

He nevertheless sent Julian, then a defender and later bishop of the Sabine Church, with instructions to bring Equitius with great honor and ensure that the servant of God suffered no insult from this summons.

Julian hurried to the monastery, eager to comply with the clerics’ wishes. In Equitius’s absence he found monks writing books. [Note: We have already observed, in the French life of Cassiodorus, book 3, chapter 3, section 6, that copying manuscripts especially suits monks. See Cassiodorus himself, *Institutions*, chapter 30, and Sulpicius Severus, *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 7, where, praising the discipline established by Saint Martin in the monastery, he says: “No craft was practiced there except that of the copyists.” In the *Life of Saint Epiphanius*, by one of his disciples, no. 5: “A certain Christian man named Lucianus, admirable and learned, met him. He practiced the monastic life and possessed the elegant art of the scribe, by which he diligently earned his daily bread.” The example of Melania the Younger proves that nuns too worked at copying sacred books.]

Julian asked where the abbot was. They replied: “In the valley below the monastery, cutting hay.”

Julian had a very proud and stubborn boy who could scarcely be controlled even by Julian himself. He sent this boy to bring Equitius to him as quickly as possible.

The boy went, entered the meadow rapidly in a defiant spirit, and, seeing everyone there cutting hay, asked which one was Equitius. As soon as he heard who Equitius was, he saw him still at a distance. He was suddenly seized by immense fear, began to tremble and grow weak, and could scarcely carry himself with unsteady steps.

Trembling, he reached the man of God, humbly embraced and kissed his knees, and told him that his master had summoned him. Equitius returned his greeting and ordered him:

“Cut green hay and carry fodder for the animals on which you came. I shall follow you when I have finished, for little remains.”

Julian, the defender who had sent him, was greatly surprised at the boy’s delay. Then he saw the boy returning with hay carried on his neck. He became extremely angry and began shouting:

“What is this? I sent you to bring the man, not to carry hay.”

The boy replied: “The man you seek is following.”

Then the man of God appeared, wearing nailed sandals and carrying a hay scythe on his neck. The boy, while Equitius was still some distance away, pointed him out to his master as the one he sought.

As soon as Julian saw the servant of God, he despised him because of his appearance and prepared in his arrogant mind how he ought to address him. But as soon as the servant of God came near, unbearable fear seized Julian’s mind. He trembled, and his tongue could scarcely manage to explain the purpose for which he had come. [Note: This is how it should be read from the manuscripts. The printed editions, by way of explanation, read: “to explain the very matter for which he had come.” Bigot reads, “to explain the very matter to which he had come.”]

He immediately humbled himself, ran to Equitius’s knees, asked him to pray for him, and informed him that his father, the apostolic pontiff, wished to see him. [Note: By this name the Roman pontiff was already designated in the sixth century, and the usage has continued to our own time. Thus, in public litanies, we pray “that the apostolic lord,” and so forth. The custom was also received among the Greeks. Thus Theodore the Studite, book 1, letter 34, to Pope Leo: “To you, first of all, our apostolic head”; and book 2, letter 35: “I sent two letters to the apostolic one.” The term “pope” is also used shortly afterward for the supreme pontiff.]

The venerable Equitius began to give immense thanks to almighty God, declaring that heavenly grace had visited him through the supreme pontiff. He immediately summoned the brothers and ordered the animals to be prepared at once. Then he began pressing his escort insistently to depart immediately.

Julian said to him: “This cannot possibly be done, because I am exhausted from the journey and cannot leave today.”

Equitius replied: “You distress me, my son, for if we do not leave today, we shall no longer leave tomorrow.”

Thus the servant of God, compelled by the weariness of his escort, remained that night in his monastery. But at daybreak the following day, a boy arrived at Julian’s place, his horse having been driven to exhaustion, carrying a letter in which the pontiff ordered him not to dare to touch the servant of God or remove him from the monastery.

When Julian asked why the decision had been changed, he learned that on that very night in which the escort had been sent there, the pontiff had been violently terrified in a vision because he had presumed to send for the man of God.

Julian immediately rose and, commending himself to the venerable man’s prayers, said: “Our Father asks that you not be wearied.” [Note: Most manuscripts read “your Father.”]

When the servant of God heard this, he was saddened and said: “Did I not tell you yesterday that if we did not set out immediately, we would no longer be permitted to set out?”

Then, as an expression of charity, he detained his escort for a short time in the cell and, though Julian resisted, compelled him to accept the compensation for his labor. [Note: Here *commodum* means payment, remuneration, or reward for labor; in Greek, “the wage of toil.” Gregory often uses the word for any kind of compensation, as in book 1, letter formerly numbered 42, now 44.]

Understand, therefore, Peter, under what great protection of God those are placed who know how to despise themselves in this life. Within, they are counted among the citizens held in honor; outwardly, they are not ashamed to be despised by human beings. Conversely, those who swell with the desire for empty glory lie low in God’s eyes, even when they are honored by their own people and by the eyes of their neighbors.

Therefore Truth says to certain people: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16:15).

PETER. I am greatly astonished that so great a pontiff could have been deceived about such a man.

Gregory. Why are you surprised, Peter, that we human beings are deceived? Has it slipped your mind that David, who was accustomed to possess the spirit of prophecy, passed judgment against Jonathan’s innocent son when he heard the words of a lying boy? Since this was nevertheless done through David, we believe it just by God’s hidden judgment, although by human reasoning we do not see how it was just. What wonder, then, if we who are not prophets are sometimes led astray by the mouths of liars? Moreover, great is the density of cares that ravages the mind of each bishop. When the mind is divided among many things, it becomes less capable of each one; and the more broadly it is occupied with many matters, the more it is taken away from any single one.

Peter. What you say is entirely true.

Gregory. I ought not to keep silent about what I learned from Valentine, my once most revered abbot. He said that, while his body was buried in the oratory of the blessed martyr Lawrence, a certain farmer placed a chest of grain over his tomb, without taking care to consider or revere what sort of man lay there. Suddenly a whirlwind arose from heaven; while everything else there remained fixed in its place, the chest that had been placed over his tomb was lifted up and thrown far away, so that everyone might plainly understand how great was the merit of the man whose body lay there.

I also learned the following from the account of the aforementioned venerable man Fortunatus, who is especially pleasing to me in age, conduct, and simplicity. When the Lombards entered the province of Valeria, monks from the monastery of the most revered man Equitius fled to his tomb in the aforementioned oratory. When the enraged Lombards entered the oratory, they began dragging the monks outside, intending either to examine them by torture or to kill them with swords. One of them groaned and, moved by acute anguish, cried out:

“Alas, alas, holy Equitius! Are you pleased that we are being dragged away, and do you not defend us?”

Immediately, at his words, an unclean spirit entered the savage Lombards. They fell to the ground and were tormented until all the Lombards who were outside also learned of it, so that thereafter they did not dare to profane that holy place. Thus the holy man, while defending his disciples, also provided a remedy for many who later fled there for refuge.

#### Apparatus to the preceding Latin recension

[Note: [Col. 0176D] At the judgment concerning Jonathan’s son, the first two Carnot manuscripts, both Audoenus manuscripts, Bigot, and Lyra read: “and we believe it a just and hidden judgment of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0176D] At “my former abbot Valentine,” Bigot, both Audoenus manuscripts, Longipontanus with the German manuscript, and the Valentionensis have *Valentino*; the three Carnot manuscripts, Gemet, the first Audoenus, Pratensis, and Lyra have *Valentione*. The editor adds: “Here note that Gregory embraced the monastic life.”]

## Chapter IV. Concerning Equitius, abbot in the province of Valeria

### Greek recension

### Gregory

I learned the story I am about to tell from Fortunatus, a most devout man who became abbot of the monastery called the Bath of Cicero, and from other devout men. There was a man named Equitius, distinguished by holiness in the regions of the province of Valeria. Because of his virtuous life, he was held in honor by everyone there. The aforementioned Fortunatus was especially dear to him. Because of his virtuous way of life, Equitius became the father and spiritual leader of many monasteries in that same region.

When, in the time of his youth, he was being severely buffeted by temptations of the flesh, this pressure of temptation made him more earnest in the struggle of prayer. He therefore earnestly asked almighty God to grant him relief from his temptations. One night he saw an angel standing beside him and thought that the angel had castrated him; the angel cut away every movement of the flesh from all his members. From that day onward he was so freed from temptation that he thought he no longer possessed a body.

Thus, fortified by the help of almighty God, he who had previously presided over men began thereafter also to preside over women. He did not cease instructing his disciples, so that they would not easily entrust themselves to an undertaking of this kind in equal measure, lest they should fall through temptation.

At that time, when magicians were being persecuted in this Roman city, Basil, who had been foremost in magical practices, fled in the guise of a monk and came to the regions of Valeria. He went to the most devout man Castorius, bishop of the city of Amiternum, and begged him to introduce him to Equitius the abbot, so that Equitius might receive him into his monastery through the bishop’s recommendation.

The bishop therefore came to the monastery, bringing the monk Basil with him, and asked the servant of God Equitius to receive him into his company. When that holy man saw him, he said:

“This man whom you are commending to me, venerable father, I do not see to be a monk, but a devil.”

The bishop replied:

“You are making an excuse because you do not wish to obey our request.”

The servant of God said:

“I report him to be what I see him to be. But, so that you may not think that I am unwilling to obey, I will do what you command.”

He therefore received him into the monastery.

After not many days, the same servant of God Equitius went out a little way from the monastery to edify by a word of instruction those who longed for heavenly blessedness. While he was away, it happened that, in the monastery of virgins whose careful supervision the same father had undertaken, one of the women—very beautiful in bodily appearance—was burning with a severe fever and began uttering cries, saying:

“I am certainly dying at once unless the monk Basil comes and, through the assistance of his medical treatment, gives me healing.”

No brother dared approach the community of virgins even in the absence of their own father; how much less the newly arrived man, whose way of life was still unknown to the sisters. They therefore immediately sent word to the servant of God Equitius that a certain nun was burning with a violent fever and, in her distress, was urgently asking for a visit from the monk Basil.

When this righteous man heard it, he became indignant and, smiling slightly, said:

“Did I not say that this man is a devil and not a monk? Go, then, and throw him out of his cell. As for the servant of God who is burning with the onset of fever, do not worry about her. From this moment she will neither suffer from the fever nor ask for Basil.”

When the monk returned, he found that the virgin of God had received healing at the very hour when the servant of God Equitius, although far away, had spoken.

Following the example of his teacher, he accomplished the power of this miracle. For our Lord Jesus Christ, when the royal official pleaded with him, granted his son healing by a single word, as we find in the Gospels. When the official returned to his house, he found at that very hour that his son had received healing—the hour at which he had heard this from the mouth of Truth.

All the monks, fulfilling the command of their father, drove the same Basil from the monastery’s dwelling. While he was being driven away, he often said that by his magical arts he would cause the cell of Equitius to hang suspended in the air, but he was utterly unable to harm it in any way. Not long afterward, in this Roman city, when the zeal of the most Christian people for God had been kindled, they had him burned by fire.

One day, from the same monastery of virgins, a nun entered the garden and, seeing a *maroulion*—a lettuce—desired it. Forgetting to make the sign of the cross, she ate it greedily. Immediately seized by the devil, she fell and collapsed. Those present saw this and hastily reported it to Father Equitius, so that he might come quickly and, by his prayer, show compassion to the woman in danger.

As soon as the father entered the garden, the devil who had struck her began, as though to make the matter clear, to cry out through her mouth:

“What have I done? While I was sitting on that lettuce, she came and bit me!”

The man of God rebuked him angrily, ordering him to withdraw from the servant of God and never again to have a place in her. At once, in accordance with his command, the unclean spirit departed and thereafter did not dare approach her at all.

A most noble man named Felix, originally from the region of Nursia, was the father of Castorius, who now lives with us in this Roman city. Knowing that this most devout man Equitius did not possess priestly rank, yet seeing him earnestly travel from place to place for the sake of teaching, Felix one day took courage to question him openly:

“You possess no priestly rank, nor have you received authorization to preach from the patriarch of the Romans, under whose authority you stand. How do you dare to do this?”

The holy man replied:

“These are the very things you are telling me that I too have considered within myself. But I will make clear to you how I received the authority to preach. One night, in a vision, a very young and exceedingly handsome man appeared to me. He placed in my mouth a medical instrument—that is, a lancet—and said to me: ‘Behold, I have placed my words in your mouth. Go out and preach.’ From that day onward, even if I wish to remain silent, I cannot, because God compels me to this.”

Peter. I should like to understand the work of this father, who is said to have received such gifts.

Gregory. The work proceeds from the gift, not the gift from the work; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. The gifts anticipate each person’s work, and through the work that follows, the gifts increase. But so that you may not be deprived of knowledge of his way of life, the most devout man Albinus, bishop of the church of Reate, understood it very well, as did many others who still live to the present.

What greater work do you seek, when the purity of his way of life agreed with the earnestness of his preaching? Such a longing to offer souls to God burned within him that, although he presided over monasteries, he never ceased traveling through churches, cities, marketplaces, and every place where believers were found, awakening the hearts of his hearers to longing for eternal life.

He wore extremely humble clothing, so that those who did not know him, seeing people bow to him, would shrink from bowing in return. When he traveled to other places, it was his custom to ride the most wretched of all the monastery’s horses. Instead of a bridle he used a halter, and instead of a saddle, sheepskins. He carried the sacred books in a leather double bag, and wherever he went, opening the spring of Scripture, he watered the soil of human understanding.

The fame of his preaching reached even the city of Rome. As flatterers customarily do—drawing a listener’s soul toward themselves through their own tongue in order to destroy it—the clergy of that apostolic see, at that time speaking idly to their superior, said:

“Who is this rustic man, who claims for himself the authority to preach and has transferred to himself the ministry of your holiness, my lord, behaving like an utterly ignorant runaway? Let someone be sent, if it pleases you, to bring him here, so that he may learn what the order of the Church is.”

Just as often happens when the soul is occupied with many matters, allowing flattery to gain a place within it unless it is driven out by vigilant watchfulness, so it happened then that the patriarch consented to the clergy who were enticing him and ordered that the same most holy man Equitius be brought to the city of Rome, so that he might learn what his own limits were.

He sent Julian, who at that time was a *defensor* and later governed the episcopal see of the church in Sabina, commanding him to bring Equitius with the greatest honor, so that the servant of God might not suffer insult in any way.

Wishing to appear adequate in this matter to the clergy, Julian hastened to the monastery. Not finding Equitius there, he saw the leading brothers of the community writing beautifully and began to ask where the abbot was.

They replied:

“He is mowing hay in this valley belonging to the monastery.”

Julian had a very spirited and proud son, whom even he himself could scarcely control. He therefore sent the boy to bring Equitius quickly.

The boy went out, entered the meadow abruptly, looked over all those who were mowing the hay, and asked which one was Equitius. When he learned from them who he was, he saw him from a distance coming toward him and was struck by immeasurable fear. He began to tremble and be distressed, and could scarcely walk by moving his feet.

Fearfully approaching the man of God, he fell at his feet with complete humility, embraced them, and announced his master’s presence at the monastery.

The servant of God addressed him and ordered him to carry fresh hay for the animals with which they had come, saying:

“Go, my child. When I have finished the little work that remains, I will come immediately.”

The defensor Julian was greatly astonished at the boy’s delay. When he saw him returning with hay from the meadow on his shoulder, he became angry and began to shout:

“What is this? I sent you to bring a man, not to carry hay.”

The boy replied:

“Behold, the man you seek is coming behind me.”

The man of God immediately put on and fastened his shoes and came, carrying on his shoulder the sickle with which he had cut the hay. When the boy saw him approaching from a distance, he announced to his master:

“He whom you seek is the man himself.”

When Julian saw the servant of God approaching, he despised him from his very appearance. He was preparing to speak to him forcefully; but when the man of God came near, an unbearable fear entered Julian’s soul. Trembling, he could scarcely explain why he had come.

His pride humbled, he ran to the saint’s knees and asked him to pray for him. He also said that “our father the apostolic patriarch longs to see you, and he sent me for this reason.”

The most devout man Equitius began to offer hymns of thanksgiving to almighty God and said:

“The grace from above has visited me through the most exalted patriarch.”

He immediately summoned the brothers and ordered them to prepare the animals at that very hour. He began urging his mount to be brought out, so that they might set off at once.

Julian said to him:

“I am exhausted from the journey, father, and cannot leave today.”

The servant of God replied:

“You are troubling me, my child. For if we do not travel today, tomorrow it will no longer be possible for us to go.”

Compelled by Julian, he remained that night in the monastery. At dawn the following day, a boy arrived at great speed on horseback with a letter for Julian. The letter instructed him not to dare move the servant of God from his monastery.

When Julian questioned the messenger about why the decision had been changed, he learned that on that very night, the night on which Julian had been sent, the patriarch had been terrified by a vision because of the person whom he had dared to send to bring the man of God.

The patriarch immediately rose, commended himself to the prayers of the holy man, and said to Equitius:

“Our father the patriarch asks you not to be wearied.”

When the man of God heard this, he was deeply saddened and said:

“Did I not tell you yesterday that, if we did not travel immediately, it would not turn out for us to leave at all?”

Then, as an act of kindness, he detained the same defensor for a short while and, although the man was unwilling, gave him some payment for his trouble before sending him away.

Know, then, Peter, in what honor before God are those who have chosen to be despised in this present life. They are numbered among the citizens of their heavenly homeland, who are not ashamed to be despised by human beings. But those who justify themselves before their neighbors through arrogance and puff themselves up through empty glory lie on the opposite side in the eyes of God. Therefore the word of teaching, exposing them, says:

“You are those who justify yourselves before human beings, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among human beings is an abomination before God.”

Peter. I am greatly surprised that they were able to mislead the patriarch concerning such a man.

Gregory. Why are you surprised, Peter, if the human mind was deceived? We are human beings and therefore go astray. David likewise experienced this, although he is attested to have possessed the spirit of prophecy: when he heard the words of the lying boy, he passed judgment against Jonathan’s innocent son. We believe that what happened through David was just by God’s hidden judgment, though by human understanding we do not know how it was just. What wonder, then, if we, who are not prophets, are led elsewhere by the words of liars? It is no great wonder if the mind of each patriarch is ravaged by the tangled succession of cares. When the soul is divided among many things, it becomes smaller in each one; and while it is spread broadly through occupation with many matters, it is gathered up in each single matter.

Peter. What you say is very true.

Gregory. I do not think it right to keep silent about what I heard from Valentine, the most devout man who was then my abbot, when he was recounting this holy man’s story. He said that his body had been buried in the oratory of the blessed martyr Lawrence. A farmer placed a chest over the tomb, without understanding what sort of man lay there. Suddenly a disturbance arose from heaven. While everything remained in its own position, the chest placed over the tomb was lifted up and thrown far away, so that all might know how much honor from God had been granted to the man whose body lay there.

I learned the events I now add to this narrative from the account of the aforementioned most devout man Fortunatus. I am very fond of him for his old age, his deeds, and his innocence. He said that when the Lombards entered that same province of Valeria, monks from the monastery of the most devout man Equitius fled to his tomb in the aforementioned oratory.

The Lombards, enraged, entered the oratory and began dragging the monks outside, intending either to torture them with punishments or to kill them with the sword. One of them groaned and, moved by the extremity of his anguish, cried:

“Alas, holy Equitius! Are you pleased that we are being dragged away, and do you not avenge us?”

Immediately, at his words, an unclean spirit entered the savage Lombards. They fell to the ground and were so grievously tormented that all the Lombards outside learned of it; thereafter they did not dare set foot in that holy place. Thus the holy man, having then avenged his disciples, also provided protection for many who later fled there.

## Chapter V. Concerning Constantius, mansionarius of the church of Saint Stephen

### Latin recension

I learned the story I am about to tell from one of my fellow bishops, who lived for many years in the city of Ancona in the monastic habit and there led a life of no ordinary religious devotion. Some of our own people, now advanced in age and from those same regions, also attest to this.

Near that city stands the church of the blessed first martyr Stephen. In it a man of venerable life named Constantius served in the office of mansionarius. The reputation of his holiness had spread far and wide among people, because this man utterly despised earthly things and, with the whole effort of his mind, burned only for heavenly things.

One day the church ran out of oil, and the aforementioned servant of God had absolutely nothing with which to light the lamps.

He filled all the church’s lamps with water, placed papyrus in the middle as usual, and, bringing fire, lit them. Thus the water burned in the lamps as though it were oil.

Consider, then, Peter, how great this man’s merit was: compelled by necessity, he changed the nature of an element.

Peter. What I hear is exceedingly wondrous; but I should like to know how humble inwardly this man could have been, since outwardly he was of such excellence.

Gregory. You rightly ask what kind of spirit he possessed among his virtues, for the marvelous things performed outwardly greatly test and trouble the mind inwardly. But if you hear of one thing done by this venerable Constantius, you will quickly recognize how humble he was.

Peter. Since you have related such a miracle concerning his deed, it remains for you also to edify me concerning the humility of his mind.

Gregory. Because the reputation of his holiness had grown greatly, many people from various provinces eagerly desired to see him. One day a farmer came from a distant place to see him. At that very hour it happened that the holy man was standing on wooden steps, attending to the lamps.

He was extremely short, thin in bodily build, and unattractive in appearance. The farmer who had come to see him asked insistently who Constantius was and begged that he be shown to him. Those who knew him pointed him out.

But, as foolish people measure a man’s merits by his bodily appearance, when the farmer saw that he was small and unimpressive, he absolutely refused to believe that this was the man. In the farmer’s mind there arose a kind of quarrel between what he had heard and what he saw. He thought that one so short in appearance could not be the man whom reputation had made so great.

When several people had assured him that this was indeed the man, he despised him and began to ridicule him, saying:

“I expected to see a great man, but this fellow has nothing of a man about him.”

When the man of God Constantius heard this, he immediately left the lamps he was repairing, hurried down, ran to embrace the farmer, and began to clasp him in his arms with great affection and kiss him. He gave him abundant thanks for having formed such an opinion of him, saying:

“You alone had open eyes where I am concerned.”

From this we must consider how humble he was in his own estimation: he loved the farmer who despised him all the more. An insult reveals what kind of person someone secretly is. For just as the proud rejoice in honors, so the humble generally rejoice in being despised. When they see themselves regarded as worthless even in the eyes of others, they rejoice because they understand that this confirms the judgment they themselves have held about themselves.

Peter. As I understand it, this man was great outwardly in miracles, but greater inwardly in humility of heart.

#### Apparatus to the Latin recension

[Note: [Col. 0177D] At the lamps of Saint Stephen’s church, the German manuscript reads “all the candles”; the first Audoenus manuscript and Lyra read “all the cups.” The Greek recension has *κανδήλας, κανδήλαις*, which Cangius shows can mean oil lamps.]

[Note: [Col. 0177D] The “papyrus” placed in the lamps means a wick. Gregory of Tours likewise says, “neither papyrus was added nor a drop of oil poured in”; Paulinus speaks of fragrant lights burning with waxed papyrus. Here papyrus means fibers of the marsh plant, used for paper, ropes, mats, garments, and other purposes; Ennodius also describes papyrus borne by water as food for flame.]

[Note: [Col. 0180D] At the farmer’s foolish judgment, Pratensis, Bigot, Lyra, the first Audoenus, Gemet, and one Carnot manuscript read *stultae mentes hominis* or *hominum*, “the foolish mind(s) of a man/men.”]

[Note: [Col. 0180D] Where the humble are said to rejoice in contempt, Audoenus and Lyra read *gloriantur*, “they glory.”]

## Chapter VI. Concerning Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Ancona

### Latin recension

Gregory. The same church of the city of Ancona also had a bishop named Marcellinus, a man of very devout life. The disease of gout had contracted his feet so severely that he could not move, and whenever he needed to go somewhere, his attendants carried him in their arms.

One day, through someone’s negligent carelessness, the same city of Ancona caught fire. As the fire raged violently, everyone ran together to extinguish it. But while they threw water upon it in competition, the flames grew so much that they now seemed to threaten the destruction of the entire city.

As the fire seized the places nearest to it and had already consumed no small part of the city, while no one could withstand it, the bishop was carried there in his attendants’ arms. Compelled by the extreme danger, he ordered those carrying him:

“Place me opposite the fire.”

This was done, and he was set down where the full force of the flames appeared to be bearing down. The fire began, in a marvelous manner, to turn back upon itself, as though by the recoil of its own force it were crying out that it could not pass the bishop. Thus the blaze, restrained at that boundary, cooled within itself and thereafter dared not touch any building.

Do you understand, Peter, how great was the holiness of a sick man who, sitting down, suppressed the flames by prayer?

Peter. I understand it, and I am utterly amazed.

#### Apparatus to the Latin recension

[Note: [Col. 0181D] Of Marcellinus’s disability, Gemet reads: “whose gait excessive pain had contracted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0181D] The Venerable Bede retells this example in *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 14.]

## Chapter VII. Concerning Nonnosus, prior of the monastery on Mount Soracte

### Latin recension

Gregory. I will now tell you something from a nearby place, which I learned from the accounts of the venerable bishop Maximian and Laurio, the old monk whom you know; both are still alive. Laurio was brought up by the most holy man Anastasius in the monastery called Suppentonia, situated near the city of Nepi.

That Anastasius was closely associated with Nonnosus, the prior of the monastery situated on Mount Soracte, both because of the nearness of the places and because of the great excellence of their character and their zeal for virtue.

Nonnosus lived under the harshest abbot of his monastery, but he always endured the man’s harsh character with remarkable patience. Thus he presided over the brothers in gentleness, just as he frequently softened the anger of his abbot through humility.

Since his monastery stood at the very summit of the mountain, there was no level ground where the brothers could cultivate even a small garden. A narrow place had grown on the mountainside, but it was occupied by a massive natural outcropping of rock.

One day the venerable Nonnosus considered that the place could at least be suitable for growing herbs for seasoning, if the great mass of rock did not occupy it. Yet fifty pairs of oxen could not have moved that mass. When human labor had proved hopeless, he turned to divine assistance and devoted himself to prayer there in the silence of night.

When morning came and the brothers went to the same place, they found that the enormous rock had withdrawn a considerable distance from its former position, and by its retreat had given the brothers ample space for a garden.

On another occasion, while the same venerable man was washing glass lamps in the oratory, one fell from his hands and shattered into countless pieces. Fearing the furious anger of the monastery’s abbot, he immediately gathered all the fragments of the lamp and placed them before the altar, then devoted himself to prayer with a heavy sigh.

When he lifted his head from prayer, he found the lamp whole—the very lamp whose fragments he had gathered in fear.

Thus, in two miracles, he imitated the virtues of two fathers: in the matter of the rock, the deed of Gregory the Wonderworker, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, who moved a mountain; and in restoring the lamp, the power of Donatus, bishop of Arezzo in Etruria, honored as a martyr on 7 August, who restored a broken chalice to its former wholeness.

Peter. As I see, we have new miracles corresponding to ancient examples.

Gregory. Would you like to learn of something in Nonnosus’s conduct that also imitates Elisha?

Peter. I wish to, and I desire it eagerly.

Gregory. One day the monastery ran out of old oil, and the time for gathering olives had arrived, but no fruit appeared on the olive trees. The monastery’s abbot therefore decided that the brothers should go around to those who possessed olive trees and gather olives for them, so that they might bring a little oil to the monastery from the wages of their labor.

The man of God Nonnosus prevented this with great humility, lest the brothers, leaving the monastery to seek the profit of oil, should suffer loss of soul. Since a few olives seemed to be present on the monastery’s own trees, he ordered that they be gathered and put into the press, and that whatever small quantity of oil might come out be brought to him.

This was done. The brothers brought the oil they had received in a very small vessel to Nonnosus, the servant of God. He immediately placed it before the altar. After everyone had gone out, he remained alone inside the church and gave himself to prayer.

Afterward he summoned the brothers and ordered them to take the oil they had brought him and distribute it among all the monastery’s vessels, pouring it out little by little, so that all the vessels might appear to have been filled through the blessing of that oil. He immediately had the vessels, which were empty, sealed.

The next day, when they were opened, all were found to be full.

Peter. We see fulfilled every day the words of Truth:

“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

#### Apparatus to the Latin recension

[Note: [Col. 0181D] Mount Soracte was celebrated by the poets: Virgil says, “They possess the citadels of Soracte” (*Aeneid* VII), and Horace, “You see how Soracte stands white with deep snow” (*Odes* I.9). The mountain is now named for Saint Sylvester, said to have hidden there; in Gregory’s time its older name remained, evidence that the later story of Sylvester, Constantine’s proposed infanticide, and Constantine’s Roman baptism had not yet spread.]

[Note: [Col. 0182D] The bishop Maximian meant here is the Syracusan who often appears in Gregory’s letters.]

[Note: [Col. 0182D] For the monastery near Nepi, see the notes to the following chapter (column 185).]

[Note: [Col. 0182D] Gregory mentions Nonnosus in the letter formerly numbered Book II, indiction 11, letter 50, now Book III, letter 51.]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Older editions printed “five hundred” pairs of oxen. The reading is corrected here to “fifty” from both English and French manuscripts and from the Greek recension.]

[Note: [Col. 0184D] Against the manuscript evidence, the editions add *ad excolendum hortum*, “for cultivating a garden.”]

[Note: [Col. 0184D] At the shattered lamp, the German, Compendiense, and one Theodore manuscript read *qui vehementissime*, “who most vehemently.”]

[Note: [Col. 0184D] The Gregory compared here is Gregory the Wonderworker, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus; Gregory of Nyssa’s *Life* of him tells this miracle.]

[Note: [Col. 0184D] The Donatus compared here was bishop of Arezzo in Etruria and is venerated as a martyr on 7 August.]

[Note: [Col. 0185D] For the small amount of oil, the German manuscript reads *parum oleum* and the Norman manuscript *parvum oleum*, both meaning “a little oil.”]

### Greek recension: Concerning Nonnosus, second-in-command of the monastery on Mount Seraphthe

Gregory. I will now tell you something from a nearby place, which I learned from the accounts of the venerable bishop Maximian and Laurio, the old monk whom you know; both are still alive. Laurio was brought up by the most holy man Anastasius in the monastery called Suppentonia, situated near the city of Nepi.

That Anastasius was closely associated with Nonnosus, the prior of the monastery situated on Mount Soracte, both because of the nearness of the places and because of the great excellence of their character and their zeal for virtue.

Nonnosus lived under the harshest abbot of his monastery, but he always endured the man’s harsh character with remarkable patience. Thus he presided over the brothers in gentleness, just as he frequently softened the anger of his abbot through humility.

Since his monastery stood at the very summit of the mountain, there was no level ground where the brothers could cultivate even a small garden. A narrow place had grown on the mountainside, but it was occupied by a massive natural outcropping of rock.

One day the venerable Nonnosus considered that the place could at least be suitable for growing herbs for seasoning, if the great mass of rock did not occupy it. Yet fifty pairs of oxen could not have moved that mass. When human labor had proved hopeless, he turned to divine assistance and devoted himself to prayer there in the silence of night.

When morning came and the brothers went to the same place, they found that the enormous rock had withdrawn a considerable distance from its former position, and by its retreat had given the brothers ample space for a garden.

On another occasion, while the same venerable man was washing glass lamps in the oratory, one fell from his hands and shattered into countless pieces. Fearing the furious anger of the monastery’s abbot, he immediately gathered all the fragments of the lamp and placed them before the altar, then devoted himself to prayer with a heavy sigh.

When he lifted his head from prayer, he found the lamp whole—the very lamp whose fragments he had gathered in fear.

Thus, in two miracles, he imitated the virtues of two fathers: in the matter of the rock, the deed of Gregory the Wonderworker, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, who moved a mountain; and in restoring the lamp, the power of Donatus, bishop of Arezzo in Etruria, honored as a martyr on 7 August, who restored a broken chalice to its former wholeness.

Peter. As I see, we have new miracles corresponding to ancient examples.

Gregory. Would you like to learn of something in Nonnosus’s conduct that also imitates Elisha?

Peter. I wish to, and I desire it eagerly.

Gregory. One day the monastery ran out of old oil, and the time for gathering olives had arrived, but no fruit appeared on the olive trees. The monastery’s abbot therefore decided that the brothers should go around to those who possessed olive trees and gather olives for them, so that they might bring a little oil to the monastery from the wages of their labor.

The man of God Nonnosus prevented this with great humility, lest the brothers, leaving the monastery to seek the profit of oil, should suffer loss of soul. Since a few olives seemed to be present on the monastery’s own trees, he ordered that they be gathered and put into the press, and that whatever small quantity of oil might come out be brought to him.

This was done. The brothers brought the oil they had received in a very small vessel to Nonnosus, the servant of God. He immediately placed it before the altar. After everyone had gone out, he remained alone inside the church and gave himself to prayer.

Afterward he summoned the brothers and ordered them to take the oil they had brought him and distribute it among all the monastery’s vessels, pouring it out little by little, so that all the vessels might appear to have been filled through the blessing of that oil. He immediately had the vessels, which were empty, sealed.

The next day, when they were opened, all were found to be full.

Peter. We see fulfilled every day the words of Truth:

“My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17).

#### Apparatus to the Greek recension

[Note: [Col. 0182D] For the city near the monastery, Regius reads *Νεμεσίας* and Colbert *Νεσπεσίας*, variant forms of the place-name corresponding to Nepi/Suppentonia.]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] For the narrow plot, Colbert still has *σεμνός*, “venerable,” in place of *στενός*, “narrow”; Regius has *μικρός*, “small.”]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] After saying that fifty yoke of oxen could not move the rock, Regius adds *δι’ ἀνθρωπίνων χειρῶν*, “by human hands.”]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] Where the rock was found to have moved far away and made broad space, Colbert reads *μηκόθεν* (“from afar/at a distance”) and shortly afterward *πλατυσμὸν γεγονότα πρός …*, “a broadening made toward …”.]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] For the restoration of the lamp, both Regius and Colbert read *ἀνακτήσει*, “restoration/recovery.”]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] When Gregory asks whether Peter wishes to understand the likeness to Elisha, Colbert reads *νοῆσαι*, “to understand.”]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] At the abbot’s plan concerning the olive harvest, the manuscripts read *βουλὴ δή* (or *οὖν*) *τῷ πατρί*, “the father then/therefore formed a plan.”]

[Note: [Col. 0183D] For the brothers’ proposed journey to neighboring olive owners, Regius reads *ἅπως*, “so that.”]

[Note: [Col. 0185D] For the expected yield, Regius reads *ἴσως ὀλίγον ἔλαιον*, “perhaps a little oil.”]

[Note: [Col. 0185D] For the vessel, Colbert reads *σεμνοτάτῳ ἀγγείῳ* and Regius *μικροτάτῳ*, “in a very small vessel.” The editor notes that Zacharias repeatedly uses *σεμνός* in the sense “small, slight,” including *σεμνοῦ παιδαρίου* below in chapter 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0186D] Where the brothers brought the oil to Nonnosus, Regius reads *ἀπήγαγον* (“they led/took away”), a transmitted form the editor marks “so written.”]

## Chapter VIII. Concerning Anastasius, abbot of the monastery called Suppentonia

### Latin recension

Gregory. At the same time the venerable man Anastasius, whom I mentioned above in Chapter 7, was a notary of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority I serve. Desiring to devote himself to God alone, he left the chancery, chose the monastic life, and in the place I mentioned, called Suppentonia, lived for many years in holy conduct and governed that monastery with diligent care.

At that place a great cliff rises above, while a deep precipice opens below. This is why the place is called in Greek *Hypokrēmnón*, “beneath the cliff.” It may also be called Suppentonia because it overhangs and seems to hang suspended.

One night, when almighty God had decided to reward the labors of the same venerable man Anastasius, a voice came from the high cliff and cried out in a prolonged sound:

“Anastasius, come!”

After he had been called, seven other brothers were also called by name. After a short interval the voice that had been uttered fell silent and called an eighth brother. When the community clearly heard these voices, there was no doubt that the deaths of those who had been called were approaching.

Within a few days, therefore, the venerable Anastasius died first, and the others in the same order were taken from the flesh in which they had been called from the summit of the cliff. But the brother whom the voice had called after a brief silence lived only a few days after the others had died and then ended his life, making it clear that the interval of silence in the voice had signified a short span of life.

A remarkable event occurred, however. As the venerable Anastasius was departing from the body, there was a brother in the monastery who did not wish to live longer than he did. He threw himself at Anastasius’s feet and began to ask him with tears:

“By the one to whom you are going, I adjure you: do not allow me to remain in this world seven days longer than you.”

Before the seventh day had passed, that brother too died, although he had not been called with the others during that night. Thus it was made perfectly clear that his death could have been obtained only through the intercession of the venerable Anastasius.

Peter. Since that brother was neither called with the others and yet was taken from this life through the intercession of the holy man, what else can be understood except that those who are of great merit before the Lord can sometimes obtain even things that have not been predestined?

#### Apparatus to the Latin recension

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Suppentonia is now the fortress of Saint Elias.]

[Note: [Col. 0185D] Where the printed text says “in the place I mentioned,” the cited edition reads “which, as I said above, is called Suppentonia.”]

[Note: [Col. 0185D] The site’s precipice explains the Greek name *Ὑπόκρημνον*, “beneath the cliff.” The editor suggests that “Suppentonia” may likewise derive from its overhanging, suspended position.]

[Note: [Col. 0188D] At the brother’s plea, printed editions read *vivam*, “that I may live”; the editor follows the unanimous manuscripts and the Greek recension’s *ποιῆσαι*, “to make/cause,” supporting “do not allow/cause me to remain.”]

[Col. 0188B] **GREGORY.** [Note: Germanus and some others read *obtinere* (“to obtain”).] Those things that have not been predestined can in no way be obtained (Gratian, *Cause* 23, Question 4, canon 21, “Obtineri”); but the things which holy men accomplish by praying have already been predestined in such a way that they may be obtained through prayers. For even the predestination of the everlasting kingdom has been so ordained by almighty God that the elect reach it through labor, insofar as by asking they merit receiving what almighty God determined before the ages to give them.

**PETER.** I would like you to prove more clearly, if possible, that predestination can be assisted by prayers.

**GREGORY.** What I have asserted, Peter, can readily be proved. Surely you know that the Lord said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called” (Genesis 21:13). He had also said to him: “I have made you the father of many nations” (ibid. 17:4). Again he promised him, saying: “Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (ibid. 22:17). [Note: The printed editions read “like the sand of the sea”; we have supplied the remaining words from the manuscripts.] From this it is plainly evident that almighty God had predestined the offspring of Abraham to be multiplied through Isaac; and yet it is written: “Isaac entreated the Lord for his wife, because she was barren, and he heard him and granted conception to Rebekah” (Genesis 25:21). If, therefore, the multiplication of Abraham’s descendants through Isaac was predestined, why did he take a barren wife? Clearly, then, predestination is fulfilled through prayers, since the one through whom God had predestined Abraham’s descendants to be multiplied obtained by prayer the ability to have children. [Note: The German manuscript and several others read “so that he might have a son.”]

[Col. 0188D] **PETER.** Since reason has disclosed the mystery, no doubt remains for me.

**GREGORY.** Do you wish me to tell you something about the regions of Tuscany, so that you may learn what sort of men lived there and how near they were, in knowledge, to almighty God?

[Col. 0189A] **PETER.** I do, and I earnestly request this.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Anastasius, abbot of the monastery called Hypocremnum (“Below the Cliff”)”

[Col. 0186B]

**GREGORY.** At that same time, the venerable man Anastasius—whom I mentioned earlier—was a notary [Note: Both manuscripts read “notary”] of this holy Church of God of the Romans, which by God’s grace I now serve. Desiring to serve God alone in quiet, he abandoned the *scrinium* and chose the monastic life. Having renounced the world in the monastery mentioned above, which is called Subcryptum, he persevered there for many years and passed his life in holy conduct. He was also entrusted for a considerable number of years with the governance of that same monastery, keeping watch over it without sleep.

At that place a huge stone overhangs from above, while beneath it a very deep precipice may be seen. When almighty God finally decreed that the venerable Anastasius should receive relief from his labors, one night a voice came from the height of the stone with a resounding sound, saying: “Anastasius, come here.” After he had been called, seven other brothers were called by name. When the voice had been silent for a short while, it called the eighth brother as well. Thus the entire community, having plainly heard that voice, became certain that the death of those who had been called was near. [Note: The manuscripts read *synodia*, and indeed more correctly; nevertheless, we have not presumed to alter the text, since, just as *exodia* and *exodeia* can mean “departure,” so *synodia* and *synodeia* seem capable of meaning “assembly.”] Within a few days, the most devout man Anastasius died first, and the others, one after another, were released from the bonds of the body and departed to the Lord, just as they had been called from the summit of the stone. [Col. 0186D] [Note: Colbert reads “from the summit of the mountain.”]

But the brother whom the voice, after becoming silent, called a little later lived for a few days after the others had died, and then he too was perfected in the Lord. Thus it was shown that the interval of silence of the one calling [Col. 0187A] had signified for him a brief delay before death. [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “he indicated beforehand.”]

After this, something remarkable happened. When the venerable Anastasius had departed from this present life, there was a brother in the monastery who did not wish to live on after him. Falling at his feet, he entreated him with tears, saying: “May you have such standing with the one to whom you are going that you do not allow me to remain in this world seven days after you.” [Col. 0187] Before the seventh day, therefore, he too died, although on that night he had not been called together with the others. It is therefore clear [Note: The printed edition has erroneously introduced *ouk* (“not”) in place of *oun* (“therefore”).] that only the prayer of the most devout Anastasius, having been heard, was able to bring about this man’s departure.

**PETER.** Since this brother was not among the others who were called, yet departed from this world through the prayers of the holy man, what else are we to understand except that those who are perfect before the Lord can often rightly be heard even concerning things that have not been predestined? [Note: Colbert reads “were able.”]

**GREGORY.** They cannot in any way be heard concerning things that have not been predestined; but the things that holy men accomplish by praying have already been predestined so that they may obtain them through their prayers. For even the inheritance of the eternal kingdom has been predestined by almighty God for the elect, and he has willed that they receive it through much labor and supplication—the very things he predestined before the ages to give them. [Note: Both manuscripts read “having been predestined”; the same manuscripts read “he has willed.”]

**PETER.** I wanted this to be shown to me with complete clarity: whether predestination can cooperate with prayer.

**GREGORY.** What I have proposed, Peter, can be recognized briefly. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “can be understood.”] As you know, God said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your offspring be called.” Again: “I have made you the father of many nations.” And again he promised him, saying: “Blessing I will bless you, and multiplying I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand beside the shore of the sea.” Hence it has become clear that almighty God predestined the offspring of Abraham to be multiplied through Isaac. [Note: The manuscripts read “for it is written that”; Colbert adds “offspring” after “the Lord.”]

Yet it is written that Isaac entreated the Lord concerning his wife because she was barren, and he heard him and granted conception to Rebekah. If, then, he predestined Abraham’s offspring to be multiplied through Isaac, why did he take a barren wife? From this, therefore, it is evident that predestination is fulfilled through prayers: Isaac was heard through prayer and was enabled to beget children, and through him God had predestined that Abraham’s offspring should be multiplied. [Note: Instead of “it is evident,” the Royal manuscript reads “it is clear that.”] [Note: The same manuscript reads “his offspring he had predestined.”]

[Col. 0187D] **PETER.** Nothing remains to me of disbelief; the clear assurance has revealed the mystery.

**GREGORY.** Do you want me to tell you something from the regions of Tuscany, so that you may learn what sort of men arose there and how near they were, in knowledge, to almighty God? [Note: Perhaps read “that I may tell you,” so that the sentence becomes: “so that you may learn what sort of men arose there and how near they were in knowledge to almighty God.”]

[Col. 0190A] **PETER.** I do, and I request this in every way.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Boniface, bishop of the city of Ferentia

[Col. 0189D] [Note: German and other older manuscripts write “Boniface.”]

**GREGORY.** There was a venerable man named Boniface, who held the episcopal office in the city called Ferentis [Note: Thus more correctly the Royal Codex, nine hundred years old, the Saint-Germain manuscript, and nearly all the manuscripts; the printed editions have “he held the office of bishop and fulfilled it in character.”] and fulfilled it in his conduct (Martyrology, 14 May). Gaudentius the presbyter, who is still alive, recounts many miracles of this man. He had been raised in Boniface’s service and is therefore able to speak of him with all the greater truth, since he had witnessed these things personally. [Note: The Chartres manuscript, the German manuscript, and the first Theodorean read “insofar as he had been present with him.”]

This church suffered from very serious poverty, which is usually a guardian of humility in good minds; it possessed nothing for all its support except a single vineyard. One day, when hail descended upon it, the vineyard was so devastated that only a few small and scattered clusters remained on a few vines. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “perhaps one little cluster here and there on a few vines.”] When the aforesaid most reverend man, Bishop Boniface, entered it, he gave great thanks to almighty God, because he recognized that even in his poverty he was still being tested by hardship.

When the time came for the clusters that remained to ripen, he appointed a guardian for the vineyard as usual and ordered that it be watched with diligent vigilance. One day he instructed Constantius, his nephew and a presbyter, to prepare all the wine vessels in the episcopal residence and all the casks, coating them with pitch as had previously been customary. When the presbyter, his nephew, heard this, he was greatly astonished that a man who had no wine should order the wine vessels to be prepared, as though he were insane. Nevertheless, he did not dare ask why he gave such orders; instead, obeying the command, he prepared everything as usual. [Note: Pope Adrian I cites this testimony in his letter to Charlemagne concerning the Seventh Synod, chapter 16, in volume VII of the Councils.]

[Col. 0189C] Then the man of God entered the vineyard, gathered the clusters, and carried them to the winepress. He ordered everyone else to leave and remained there alone with a little boy, whom he placed in the winepress and made tread the few clusters. When a little wine began to flow from them, the man of God began to receive it with his own hands in a small vessel and distribute it, as a blessing, among all the casks and vessels that had been prepared, so that all the vessels appeared barely to have been moistened with that same wine. When he had put a little of the wine into all the vessels, he immediately summoned the presbyter and ordered the poor to come.

Then the wine began to increase in the winepress, until it filled all the vessels of the poor that had been brought. When he saw that he had adequately supplied them, he ordered the boy to descend from the winepress. [Note: Many manuscripts read “to climb up”; the editions of Gilot, the Vatican manuscript, and some others read “to depart,” which agrees better with the Greek version.] He closed the storeroom, left it secured with his own seal, and soon returned to the church. [Note: The Compendious manuscript lacks “and.”]

On the third day he summoned the aforementioned presbyter Constantius, said a prayer, and opened the storeroom. He found the vessels into which he had poured the very small quantity of wine flowing abundantly, so that the wine overflowing them would have covered the entire floor had the bishop delayed entering even a little longer.

Then he sternly ordered the presbyter not to tell anyone of this miracle for as long as he lived in the body. He feared, of course, that if human praise assailed him because of the power of the deed, he would become inwardly empty through the very thing that made him appear great to people outwardly. He was also following the example of the Master, who, to instruct us in the way of humility, commanded his disciples concerning himself that they tell no one what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead (Matthew 17:9). [Note: The second Theodorean reads “to introduce us.” The printed editions before Gussanville have “to lead us.”] [Note: The German and Compendious manuscripts read “that they should by no means tell.” A little later, however, the text reads: “he ordered them to tell no one.”]

[Col. 0192B] **PETER.** Since a suitable opportunity has presented itself, I would like to ask what our Redeemer intended when, after restoring sight to two blind men, he ordered them to tell no one, yet they went away and spread his fame throughout that whole land (Matthew 9:27). Did the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in this matter will something that he was unable to accomplish, so that the miracle he wished to remain concealed could not in fact be hidden?

**GREGORY.** Through his mortal body our Redeemer gave us an example of action in everything he did, so that, following his footsteps according to the measure of our strength, we might proceed with an un stumbling foot along the path of the works of this present life. When he performed a miracle, he ordered it to be kept silent, yet it could not be kept silent. Thus his elect, following the examples of his teaching, may indeed wish in their hearts that the great things they do remain hidden, but, so that they may benefit others, those deeds are revealed against their will. In this way it is both a sign of great humility that they desire their works to remain unspoken and a sign of great usefulness that their works cannot remain unspoken. [Note: The third Chartres manuscript and the first Theodorean add “and of great edification.”]

The Lord, therefore, did not will something to happen and then prove unable to accomplish it. Rather, by the authority of his teaching he gave an example of what his members ought to will and of what happens to them even against their will.

**PETER.** What you say is pleasing.

**GREGORY.** Since we have mentioned Bishop Boniface, let us continue with a few further things that remain concerning his works. At another time, the feast day of the blessed martyr Proculus was approaching. A noble man named Fortunatus lived in that place. With many prayers he asked the same venerable man that, when he celebrated the solemn Mass at the shrine of the blessed martyr, he would turn aside to his house to give a blessing. [Note: The manuscripts read “Proculus.”]

The man of God could not refuse what charity, proceeding from Fortunatus’s heart, requested of him. When the solemn Mass had been completed and he had come to the table of the aforementioned Fortunatus, before he had said the hymn to God, a man suddenly stood before the door with a monkey and struck cymbals, as certain people who seek their livelihood by the art of performing are accustomed to do.

When the holy man heard the sound, he was indignant and said: “Alas, alas, this wretched man is dead; this wretched man is dead. I have come to a table of refreshment and have not yet opened my mouth in praise of God, while he has come with a monkey and struck cymbals.” [Note: The German manuscript, followed by Gussanville, omits “hearing,” although all the other manuscripts retain it.] Yet he added: “Go and, out of charity, give him food and drink; nevertheless, know that he is dead.”

When the unfortunate man had received bread and wine from that house, he wished to go out through the door. But suddenly a huge stone fell from the roof and struck him on the head. He was knocked down and carried away in their hands, half alive; on the following day, in accordance with the holy man’s judgment, he completely died.

From this, Peter, we should consider how much fear is owed to holy men, for they are temples of God. When a holy man is moved to anger, who else is stirred to anger except the inhabitant of that same temple? The anger of the righteous is therefore to be feared all the more because he who is present in their hearts is not powerless to inflict whatever punishment he wishes.

At another time, Constantius the presbyter, his nephew, sold his horse for twelve gold pieces. He placed them in his own chest and went away to carry out some task. Suddenly poor people came to the episcopal residence and insistently begged that the holy Bishop Boniface give them something to relieve their poverty. But because the man of God had nothing to give, he began to be distressed in his thoughts, lest the poor should leave him empty-handed.

Then he remembered that Constantius the presbyter, his nephew, had sold the horse he usually rode and had that very price in his chest. While his nephew was absent, he went to the chest and, piously compelled, broke its fastenings, took the twelve gold pieces, and distributed them among the needy as he saw fit. Thus, when Constantius the presbyter returned from his task, he found the chest broken and did not find the price of his horse that he had placed in it.

He began to shout loudly and cry out in great fury: “Everyone here is alive; I alone cannot live in this house.” At his cries the bishop came, along with everyone who was present in the episcopal residence. When the man of God tried to calm him with gentle speech, he began to answer angrily, saying: “Everyone lives with you; I alone cannot live here before you. Give me back my solidi.” [Note: He means the gold pieces mentioned above. Concerning the gold solidus, Cassiodorus, *Various Letters* 1.10, says that the ancients regarded six thousand denarii as one solidus, so that the rounded form of the shining metal might fittingly contain the age of the world like a golden sun. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, and the notes on the letter, where there is frequent occasion to discuss the solidus.]

Moved by these words, the bishop entered the church of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin. He raised his hands, spread out his vestment, and, standing, began to pray that God would give him something with which he could appease the madness of the raging presbyter. When he suddenly turned his eyes toward his garment between his outstretched arms, he found twelve gold pieces in his bosom, shining so brightly that they seemed to have just then been drawn from a fire.

He immediately left the church, threw them into the bosom of the enraged presbyter, and said: “Here are the solidi you sought. But know this: after my death, you will not be bishop of this church because of your greed.” From the truth of this judgment it may be inferred that the presbyter had been preparing those same solidi in order to obtain the bishopric. But the man of God’s word prevailed, for Constantius ended his life while still holding the office of presbyter.

At another time, two Goths came to him for hospitality, declaring that they were hurrying to Ravenna. With his own hand he gave them a small wooden vessel filled with wine, which might perhaps have been enough for their meal on the journey. The Goths drank from it until they reached Ravenna. They remained in that city for several days and used the wine they had received from the holy man every day. Thus, when they returned to the same venerable Father at Ferentia, they never ceased drinking, yet the wine in that little vessel never failed them, as though the wine in the wooden vessel given by the bishop did not increase but was continually being born. [Note: The printed editions read “they drank.” The Goths, however, read with a change in the punctuation of the manuscripts: “they might drink.”] [Note: Six Norman manuscripts read “bringing it,” to which the Vallicellian manuscript may be added, where “carrying it” is found. Most printed editions agree with the Norman manuscripts. There are many Italian cities called Ferentum, Ferentia, Ferentanum, or Ferentinum, whether in Apulia, Latium, or Etruria. The Ferentia discussed here is in Etruria; formerly it was an episcopal city, and Viterbo, only five miles distant, later succeeded it as the episcopal see. It is clear from the words closing chapter eight—“Do you want me to tell you something from the regions of Tuscany?”—that Gregory is speaking of a city in Tuscany, or Etruria.]

Recently an elderly cleric came from that region and told things about him that ought not to be suppressed. He said that one day he entered the garden and found it covered with a great multitude of caterpillars. Seeing that all the vegetables were being destroyed, he turned toward the caterpillars and said: “I adjure you in the name of the Lord our God Jesus Christ: leave this place and do not eat these vegetables.” Immediately, at the word of the man of God, they all went away, so that not even one remained within the garden. [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have “locusts”; nevertheless, the manuscripts later again read “the same caterpillars.”]

But why should it surprise us that we recount these things from the time of his episcopate, when by then he had grown in both rank and character before almighty God? More marvelous are the things that this elderly cleric testified he had seen him do while still a boy. He said that when Boniface lived with his mother as a child, he would leave the house sometimes without an undershirt and often without a tunic, and would return wearing neither. For whenever he found someone naked, he would strip off what he himself was wearing and clothe that person, wishing this to be seen only by the eyes of almighty God, from whom he hoped for his reward. [Note: The *hypokamision* is an undershirt or shirt, in French *chemise*; it is also called an inner garment. Sometimes it means a sacred vestment, and Symeon of Thessalonica teaches that it is the same as the *penula* or *phelonion*. Here, however, it can only mean an ordinary secular garment. The same must be understood of *sticharion*, which, although it sometimes signifies an ecclesiastical or monastic garment, here denotes a short tunic also used by laypeople.]

His mother frequently rebuked him, saying that it was not right for him, though poor himself, to give clothing to the poor. One day she entered the granary and found that nearly all the grain she had prepared as provisions for her entire household for the whole year had been given by her son to the poor. When she began to beat herself with slaps and blows because she had seemingly lost the year’s provisions, the boy Boniface, God’s servant, arrived and began to console her with whatever words he could. When she would accept no consolation, he asked her to leave the granary, in which a little of all their grain was found to remain.

The boy, God’s servant, immediately devoted himself there to prayer. Shortly afterward he came out and led his mother back to the granary, which was found so full of grain that it contained more than it had before, when his mother had rejoiced that she had gathered enough provisions for the whole year. At this sight the repentant mother herself began urging him to give, since he could so quickly obtain whatever he asked for. [Note: The Gemetic and Pratellian manuscripts read “to ask”; the first Audomarian, Bigotian, and Lyr manuscript read “to compel.”]

She was accustomed to raise hens in the vestibule of her house, but a fox would come from the neighboring countryside and carry them away. One day, while the boy Boniface was standing in the same vestibule, the fox came as usual and seized a hen. He immediately entered the church, prostrated himself in prayer, and said aloud: “Does it please you, Lord, that I should be unable to eat from the provisions of my mother? For this fox has eaten the hens she raises.” Having risen from prayer, he left the church. At once the fox returned, released the hen it was holding in its mouth, and fell dead to the ground before his eyes. [Note: The first Audomarian and Lyr manuscripts read “dying at that very moment”; the second Audomarian and Gemetic manuscripts read “it itself dying.”]

[Col. 0200A] **PETER.** It is exceedingly marvelous that God deigns to hear the prayers of those who hope in him even in matters of little importance. [Note: The printed editions add “it seems” or “it seems to me,” against the manuscripts.]

**GREGORY.** This, Peter, happens through the great providence of our Creator: through the small things we experience, we are to learn to hope for greater ones. The holy and guileless boy was heard in matters of little importance so that through small things he might learn how much confidence he ought to place in God when making great requests.

**PETER.** What you say is pleasing.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Boniface, bishop of the city of Ferentia

[Col. 0190A]

**GREGORY.** There was a man named Boniface, of virtuous conduct, in a city called Ferentia. [Note: Colbert reads “named Boniface.”] He adorned its episcopate in every way with goodness. Gaudentius the presbyter recounts many wonders about him—Gaudentius, who is still alive and who was raised in his service. For he can truthfully tell as much about him as he personally saw while present. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “the bishop who.”]

This church was held by very severe poverty; yet it was accustomed always to possess good thoughts as guardians of humility. It had nothing for all its administration except one vineyard. One day, when hail came upon it, the vineyard itself was destroyed, so that not a single bunch of grapes remained except perhaps one cluster here and there on sparse vines. The aforementioned most devout man, Bishop Boniface, entered it, raised hymns of thanksgiving to almighty God, and did so even though he was living in such poverty and distress.

When the time came for the few remaining clusters to ripen, he appointed a guardian over the vineyard according to custom [Note: Colbert reads “when the time for their ripening had arrived.”] and ordered it to be kept under sleepless watch. One day he instructed Constantius the presbyter, his nephew, to have all the wine vessels in the episcopal residence prepared and pitched, as was customary. When his presbyter-nephew heard this, he was greatly astonished that, having no wine, he irrationally ordered the wine vessels to be prepared. Yet he did not dare inquire why he had given such an order; obeying his command, he prepared everything according to custom.

Then the man of God entered the vineyard, gathered the grapes he found, and carried them to the winepress. He ordered everyone to leave and remained inside alone with a respectable little boy. [Note: The manuscripts read “ordering them all to leave, and he remained alone with a respectable…”] He placed the boy in the winepress and made him tread those few clusters.

When a little wine began to flow from them, the man of God received it with his own hands in a very small vessel [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “in the smallest vessel”] and distributed it among all the vessels that had been prepared as a blessing, so that all the vessels could scarcely be moistened with that same wine. After this blessing had been placed in all the vessels, he called the presbyter and immediately ordered the poor to come.

Then the wine began to increase in the winepress, until all the vessels of the poor that had been brought were filled. When he saw and became convinced of this, he ordered the boy to climb out of the winepress. He closed the storeroom, affixed his own seal, left it securely guarded, and immediately returned to the church.

After the third day, he summoned the aforementioned Constantius the presbyter, said a prayer, and opened the storeroom. He found the vessels in which the small quantity of wine that had been pressed out had been poured, pouring forth wine abundantly. If the bishop had delayed entering even briefly, the entire floor of the storeroom would have been covered by the wine overflowing from them. [Note: Colbert reads “to be drenched.”]

Then he sternly ordered the presbyter not to disclose this miracle to anyone until the bishop had departed from the present life, fearing that, through human praise, he might suffer some harm because of the power manifested in the miracle. [Note: Zacharias added this sentence and thought, though there are no traces of it in the Latin text: “For human praise is accustomed to injure good works greatly.”] Following also the example of the Teacher, who led us along the humble road of humility, he commanded his disciples concerning the signs they had witnessed that they tell no one until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

[Col. 0191B] **PETER.** Since a suitable occasion has arisen, I wish to inquire what it means that our God and Redeemer, while granting light to two blind men, ordered them not to tell anyone, whereas they went away and spread his fame throughout that entire land. Did the only-begotten Son of the Father, coeternal with the Holy Spirit, in this matter have a will that he was unable to fulfill, so that the miracle which he wished to remain unspoken could in no way be concealed? [Note: The manuscripts read “was unable.”]

**GREGORY.** Our God and Redeemer, through his mortal body, provided us with an example of conduct in everything he did, so that we too, working miracles according to our abilities and following his footsteps in this manner, might walk with an un stumbling foot amid the works of the present life. In a marvelous enactment of law, he ordered the miracle to be kept quiet, yet it could not be kept quiet. Thus the elect who follow the example of his teaching may intend that the greatest miracles they perform remain hidden, but, so that others may benefit, those miracles are made known. This is both the greatest humility—that they wish their works to remain hidden—and the greater benefit—that those works cannot remain hidden.

The Lord did not wish something to happen which he was unable to accomplish. Whatever is said about his willing or not willing something, while he was bodily present among human beings, he gave us as an example for our instruction. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “he became an example”; Colbert reads “he gave examples.”]

**PETER.** I approve what you say.

**GREGORY.** Since we have mentioned Bishop Boniface, I think it right to recount a few further works of his that we left unfinished. At another time the feast day of the blessed martyr Proculus was approaching. [Note: The manuscripts read “Proculus.”] In that place lived a very noble man named Fortunatus. He made many entreaties to this venerable man, asking that, while celebrating the divine liturgy at the feast of the blessed martyr, he turn aside to his house and give a blessing.

The man of God did not refuse this, because Fortunatus had requested it with faith and sincere love. When the holy divine liturgy had been celebrated at the martyr’s feast and he came to Fortunatus’s table, before he could offer the appointed prayer to God at the table, a man suddenly appeared before the door with a rattle and struck cymbals, as certain beggars are accustomed to seek food through a performance. [Note: Colbert reads: “Fortunatus came to the table in memory of the aforementioned martyr before offering to God the visible food on the table, as is customary among certain people,” followed by a passage that is not acceptable.] [Note: Colbert reads “he is present with rattles and…” Perhaps *seistron* (“rattle”) should be read. In Latin the corresponding word is *simia*, “monkey”; we do not see what the rattle has in common with a monkey.]

The holy man, disgusted by the sound of the cymbals, said: “Woe, woe! This wretched man has died.
