I have come to the table of gladness, and I have not yet opened my mouth in praise of God, while he has come with rattles and struck cymbals.” He added: “Go, and out of charity give this man food and drink; but know that he has died.”

This wretched man, after receiving bread and wine from that house, wished to leave through the door. Suddenly a large stone fell from the roof and struck him on the head. He fell, and they carried him away half-dead in their hands. On another day, according to the judgment of the man of God, he met the end of his life.

From this event, Peter, one can understand how fearsome the holy men of God are, for they are temples of God. If they happen to be moved to anger, the one who dwells within them exercises his power through them. The anger of the righteous is therefore so fearsome because he who is always present in their hearts is able to bring about whatever vengeance they desire.

At another time, Constantius the presbyter mentioned above, his nephew, sold his horse for twelve coins. He placed these in his own chest and went out to work. [Note: The manuscripts read *arkla* (“chest”). Shortly afterward the Royal manuscript has “to work.”]

Suddenly poor people arrived at the episcopal residence. They shamelessly begged the holy man of God, Bishop Boniface, to give them something to relieve the want of their poverty. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “that he give them something—whatever it might be—to relieve the want of their poverty.”] The holy man, having nothing to give, began to be distressed in his thoughts, unwilling to send the poor away empty-handed.

Then he remembered that Constantius the presbyter, his nephew, had sold his horse and had the money he received in his chest. [Note: The manuscripts read *logarion*. *Logarion*, or *logarin*, does not properly mean “price,” but a sum of money or a definite quantity of coins, as the learned Du Cange proves by numerous collected testimonies. Hence *logarismos* means an account, reckoning, or calculation.] While Constantius was absent, Boniface entered the place where the chest stood and, with a pious purpose, broke its locks. He took the twelve coins and distributed them among the needy as he pleased. [Note: Colbert reads “as he preferred.”]

When Constantius the presbyter returned from his work and saw the lock of the chest broken, and did not find the money he had received as the price of his horse, he began angrily to shout and cry out in a loud voice: “Everyone here is able to live; I alone cannot live in this house.” At his cries the bishop and everyone who was in the episcopal residence came running.

The man of God wished to calm him and began to urge him with flattering words. But Constantius answered with abuse, saying: “Everyone lives with you; I alone cannot live before you. Give me back my money.” [Col. 0195A] [Col. 0195C] [Note: The *phelonion* properly means a sacred vestment, used especially by bishops and presbyters. See Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople, *Mystagogy*, and Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters* 1.24.8. Sometimes, however, *phelonion* is an ordinary garment, equivalent to the Latin *penula*. In writers contemporary with Gregory it often denotes even a humbler kind of clothing. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers* 1.4, writes: “He would receive the poor man’s cloak as though he were venerating a soldier’s *logon*.”]

Moved by his cries, the bishop entered the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary. Wearing his *phelonion* and extending his hands, he began to pray that God would provide him with something by which he could repay the presbyter what he demanded and quiet his anger. While he was praying and holding his raised hands beneath the *phelonion*, he turned his eyes toward himself and suddenly found twelve coins between his two hands, in the vestment. [Note: Colbert reads “in the garment.”] They shone so brightly that they seemed to have come out of the fire at that very moment. [Note: The same manuscript reads “on that very day.”]

He immediately left the church, threw them into the bosom of the angry presbyter, and said: “Here is the money you sought. But know this: after my death you will never become bishop of this church because of your greed.” This was true, for the presbyter had been preparing the money in order to obtain the bishopric. But the word of the man of God did not fail; Constantius remained in the order of presbyters and received the end of his present life. [Note: The manuscripts read: “for the same Constantius, remaining in the order of presbyters…”]

At another time, two Goths, saying that they were going to Ravenna, were received for lodging by this holy man. As he sent them on their way, he filled a small wooden vessel with wine and handed it to them with his own hand; it might perhaps have been enough for them while they ate on the road. Until they entered Ravenna they drank abundantly from it. After spending several days in that city, they still did not run out of the wine given them by the holy man in that very small vessel. When they returned to him, they brought wine from the same supply, drinking their fill of it every day and never pouring anything into the same vessel; rather, it continued as though it were bubbling forth continually. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “but it continued to flow forth endlessly.”]

An old cleric recently arrived here from that region. He recounts the following things about the same holy man Boniface, which I do not consider right to suppress. [Note: Colbert reads “he narrated.”] He said that one day, when Boniface entered the garden, he found it covered by a great multitude of caterpillars. Seeing every vegetable being destroyed, he turned toward the caterpillars and said: “I adjure you in the name of the Lord, our God and Savior Jesus Christ: depart from here, and do not dare eat these vegetables.” [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “depart.”] At the word of the man of God, that entire multitude immediately went away, so that not even one remained inside the garden.

Why is it surprising that we recount these things, which he performed during the time of his episcopate, when by the grace of almighty God he had increased both in the rank of priesthood and in miracles? The things that this old cleric testified he had seen him do while he was still a child are even more marvelous.

He said that while Boniface was still living with his mother and was a very young child, he would leave the house sometimes without an undershirt and sometimes without a tunic, and would return without them. [Note: *Hypokamision* is an undershirt or shirt; *sticharion* is a tunic. Here both terms refer to ordinary secular clothing.] Whenever he saw someone naked, he would strip off what he himself was wearing and clothe that person, wishing this to be seen only by the eyes of almighty God, from whom he hoped for his reward.

His own mother frequently rebuked him, saying that it was not right for him, though needy himself, to give garments to the poor. One day she entered the granary and found that almost all the grain she had prepared for the management of her entire household throughout the year had been handed over by her son to the poor. Seeing this, she began to lament and beat her face, as though she had lost all the food for the year.

[Col. 0198C] In the midst of this, Boniface, the child of God, arrived and began to calm her with words of exhortation. When she paid no attention to his admonition, he began to ask her to leave the granary, in which a little grain still remained. After she had left, the child of God prostrated himself in prayer in that very place. Shortly afterward he came out and led his mother into the granary, which was immediately found full of grain—more abundantly than before, when his mother had heaped it up and rejoiced over having stored provisions for the whole year.

When she saw this miracle, the moved mother began to tell him to distribute wherever he wished, since he could so quickly receive from God what he requested. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads “birds”; it also reads “he took them.”]

She was accustomed to raise chickens in the forecourt of her house. A fox would come from the neighboring field and carry them away. One day, while the boy Boniface was standing in the same forecourt, the fox came as usual and snatched a chicken. Boniface immediately entered the church, prostrated himself in prayer, and said: “Does it please you, Lord, that I should be unable to eat from the birds my mother raises? For this fox has eaten them all.” [Note: Colbert reads “this fox has eaten them.”]

He rose from prayer and left the church. Immediately the fox returned, released the chicken that it was holding in its mouth, and, falling to the ground before his eyes, died. [Note: The Royal manuscript reads: “When he had risen from prayer and left the church, immediately…”]

[Col. 0199A] **PETER.** It is exceedingly marvelous that God deigns to hear the prayers of those who hope in him even in the most insignificant matters.

**GREGORY.** This happens, Peter, through the greatest providence of our Creator, so that through the small things we receive we may believe and hope concerning the great things as well. This innocent and holy child was therefore heard in the most insignificant matters, so that through small things he might learn how much confidence he ought to dare to place in God when making the greatest requests. [Note: Colbert reads “through the providence of our Creator.”]

**PETER.** I approve what you say.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Fortunatus, bishop of the city of Tuder

[Col. 0199D] [Note: Tuder is now Todi, an episcopal city of Umbria.]

**GREGORY.** There was also, in those same regions, another venerable man named Fortunatus, bishop of the Church of Tuder (Martyrology, 14 October). He possessed immense power by the grace of driving out spirits, so that at times he expelled legions of demons from possessed bodies and, intent upon the discipline of continual prayer, overcame the multitudes that opposed him.

Julian, a defender of our Church, was very close to this man. He died in this city not long ago. I learned what I am about to relate from his account, for he had often been present at Fortunatus’s deeds through the boldness of familiarity and, after remembering them, retained their sweetness in his mouth like honeycomb, for our instruction. [Note: The German, Longipontine, Vallicellian, first Chartres, Bigotian, and second Theodorean manuscripts read “through the experience” rather than “through the boldness”; we retain “through the boldness” because of the support of the other manuscripts and the Greek version.]

A certain noble matron in the neighboring districts of Tuscia [Col. 0200C] had a daughter-in-law who, not long after she had taken the matron’s son in marriage, had been invited, together with her own mother-in-law, to the dedication of the oratory of the blessed martyr Sebastian. On the very night before the day on which she was to proceed to the dedication of the aforesaid oratory, overcome by carnal pleasure, she could not abstain from intercourse with her husband. When morning came, conscience alarmed her because of the pleasure of the flesh that had been indulged, but shame compelled her to proceed; fearing the faces of men more than she feared God’s judgment, she went with her mother-in-law to the dedication of the oratory.

[Note: “To proceed,” in Ambrose, Gregory, and other ecclesiastical writers, means to approach holy places, to go to them for religious purposes, or even to perform a sacred act. Gregory, Book formerly IV, Letter 39: “Never presume to proceed with him.” Likewise, formerly Book XI, Letter 59, now Book XIII, Letter 48, Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, is advised that whenever he feels any distress he should not proceed—that is, he should not celebrate the sacrifice—as is clear from the context of the letter. See Ambrose, Sermon 17, and consult Menardus in his notes on the Sacramentary, formerly p. 177, and on the Concordia of Reg., p. 746.]

[Note: Jerome, in his *Apology to Pammachius*, shows that the Romans regarded it as sacrilegious to enter churches after even lawful intercourse: “Why,” he says, “do they not dare to go to the martyrs? Why do they not enter churches?” This woman undoubtedly received the sacred Eucharist, which ecclesiastical laws forbid to spouses after carnal intercourse. See Canon 21, *Omnis homo*, *De consecratione*, distinction 2, and Mabillon’s notes on the letter of Abbot Vaselinus, vol. I of the *Annals*, p. 346.]

[Note: The Norman manuscripts, the first Chartres manuscript, and two Theodore manuscripts read: “to dedicate the oratory.”]

But as soon as the relics of the blessed martyr Sebastian entered the oratory, an evil spirit seized the matron’s aforesaid daughter-in-law and began to torment her before all the people. When the presbyter of the same oratory saw her being tormented most violently, he immediately took a linen cloth from the altar and covered her with it; but suddenly the devil seized him also. Since he had presumed to undertake something beyond his strength, he was compelled, through his own torment, to learn what it was. Those who were present lifted the girl in their arms, carried her out of the oratory, and took her to her own house.

When the ancient enemy continued to wear her down with relentless torment, her relatives, who loved her according to the flesh and pursued her remedy out of that carnal affection, handed her over to sorcerers in order to obtain a cure—so that, while attempting temporarily to help her body by magical arts, they might utterly extinguish her soul. Thus she was taken to a river and plunged into the water. There the sorcerers worked for a long time with incantations, trying to make the devil who had entered her come out. But by the wondrous judgment of almighty God, while one demon was driven away from her by their perverse art, a legion suddenly entered her.

From that moment she began to be shaken by as many movements, and to resound with as many voices and cries, as there were spirits possessing her. Then her parents, having taken counsel, confessed the fault of their unbelief and brought her to the venerable Fortunatus, bishop, leaving her in his care. After receiving her, he devoted himself for many days and nights to prayer, and applied himself to his petitions with as much perseverance as he found the legion’s host, present in a single body, standing against him.

[Note: The manuscripts compel this reading. The printed editions altered it to “into which.”]

After not many days he restored her to her parents sound and unharmed, as though the devil had never possessed any authority over her.

## 196

At another time the same man, the servant of almighty God, drove an unclean spirit from a certain possessed man. When evening was already falling and the evil spirit saw that the hour was private and free from human observation, it pretended to be a stranger, began to walk around the streets of the city, and cried out: “O holy bishop Fortunatus! See what he has done! He has driven a stranger from his lodging. I am looking for somewhere to rest, but I cannot find a place in his city.”

A certain man was sitting in his lodging beside the embers with his wife and little son. Hearing the spirit’s voice, and asking what the bishop had done to him, he invited the supposed stranger into his lodging and made him sit beside the embers with him. While they conversed with one another, the same evil spirit entered his little son, threw him into the embers, and immediately tore his soul from him there. The wretched father, now bereaved, understood whom he himself had received and whom the bishop had driven out.

**Peter:** What are we to make of this? How did the ancient enemy obtain the power to kill in the house of a man who, thinking him a stranger, had invited him in out of hospitality?

**Gregory:** Many things appear to be good, Peter, but are not, because they are not done with a good intention. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark” (Matthew 6:25). For when the intention that precedes an action is perverse, every deed that follows is evil, even though it appears to be upright.

I judge that this man, who was bereaved while apparently showing hospitality, was not delighted by an act of compassion but by disparaging the bishop. The punishment that followed made this clear, because that earlier reception was not without blame. There are indeed some who strive to do good in order to obscure the merit of another’s action. They are not nourished by the good they do, but by the praise with which they suppress others. For this reason I think that the man who received the evil spirit as a guest was intent more on display than on the deed itself, wishing to appear to have done something better than the bishop, so that he himself might receive the one whom Fortunatus, the man of God, had driven out.

[Col. 0204C]

**Peter:** It is as you say; the outcome of the deed proved that the intention in the reception was not pure.

[Note: The German, Val. Cl., Longip., the second Theod., Comp., and Prat. read: “the pure reception in the deed.”]

**Gregory:** At another time, when a certain man had lost his eyesight, he was brought to Fortunatus to seek his intercession and obtained it. For when the man of God had prayed and impressed the sign of the cross upon his eyes, the darkness of blindness immediately departed from them, and light was restored.

[Note: Christians of ancient times used the sign of the cross extremely frequently; see Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3. On its efficacy in performing miracles, see Petavius, volume II, on Epiphanius, p. 57. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 3 against Julian*, relates that the apostate, in the greatest fear and danger, resorted to the sign of the cross and by it drove away demons.]

Moreover, the horse of a certain soldier had become rabid, so that it could scarcely be restrained by many people; and whoever it could attack, it tore their limbs with its bites. It was therefore bound, as best it could be, by many men and brought to the man of God.

[Note: This word does not always mean an ordinary soldier, but sometimes denotes an official distinguished by the rank of some command. Some hold that *stratiotae* specifically designated certain men among the emperor’s guards; the learned Du Cange does not approve this.]

He immediately stretched out his hand over its head and made the sign of the cross; all its madness was changed into gentleness, so that afterward it was milder than it had been before that insanity.

### 197

Then the same soldier decided to offer his horse to the holy man, having seen it changed from its madness by the exceedingly swift command of the miracle. When Fortunatus refused to accept it, while the soldier persisted in his prayers that his offering not be despised, the holy man took a middle course: he granted the soldier’s request but refused to accept the gift as payment for the virtue displayed. First he supplied a fitting price, and afterward accepted the horse offered to him.

[Note: The Bigot manuscript reads: “As soon as he had given …”; this was formerly read in the first Audomar manuscript. In Val. Cl. it likewise reads *dedit* instead of *edidit*.]

For when he saw that the soldier would be saddened if he did not accept it, charity compelled him to purchase what he did not need.

[Col. 0205B]

Nor ought I to keep silent about this virtue of the man, which I learned about twelve days ago. A poor old man was brought to me. Since conversation with the elderly is always pleasing to me, I carefully asked him where he was from, and he replied that he was from the city of Tuder. I then said to him: “I ask you, Father, do you know Bishop Fortunatus?” He replied: “I know him—indeed, I know him very well.” I continued: “Tell me, I beg you, whether you know any of his miracles, and make known to me, who desire to hear it, what kind of man he was.”

He replied: “That man was far removed from the people of our own time whom we see around us. Whatever he asked of almighty God, he obtained as he asked it. I shall tell you one of his miracles, which now comes to mind.

“One day the Goths came near the city of Tuder. They were making their way toward the region of Ravenna, and had taken away two little boys from an estate belonging to the aforesaid city of Tuder. When this was reported to the most holy man Fortunatus, he immediately sent for them and had the Goths summoned to him. Addressing them with gentle words, he first sought to soften their harshness, and then said:

“‘What price do you wish? I will give it. Return the boys whom you have taken, and grant me this favor as a gift.’

“Then the one who appeared to be their leader replied: ‘Whatever else you order, we are ready to do; but these boys we will certainly not return.’

“The venerable man gently threatened him, saying: ‘You are grieving me, my son, and you do not listen to your father. Do not grieve me, lest it prove harmful to you.’

“But the Goth remained hardened in his heart and departed, refusing. The following day, as he was about to leave, he came again to the bishop. The bishop once more begged him, in the same words, to return the boys. When he absolutely refused to consent, the bishop, saddened, said: ‘I know that it will not be good for you to leave after grieving me.’

“The Goth disregarded these words and returned to his lodging. He sent ahead the same boys, placed upon horses, with his men. He himself mounted a horse and followed immediately afterward. When he had reached the same city and was before the church of the blessed apostle Peter, his horse’s foot slipped; the horse fell with him, and his thigh was immediately broken, so that the bone was divided into two parts.

[Note: The manuscripts read “his horse’s”; the editors, correcting them, changed it to “the horse.”]

“He was lifted in people’s arms and carried back to his lodging. He immediately sent for and recalled the boys whom he had sent ahead, and sent word to the venerable Fortunatus, saying: ‘I beg you, Father, send your deacon to me.’

“When the bishop’s deacon came to the man lying there, he brought forward the boys whom he had flatly refused to return to the bishop, and handed them over to the deacon, saying: ‘Go and say to my lord the bishop: “Because you cursed me, behold, I lie stricken. But take back the boys you asked for, and, I beg you, intercede for me.”’

“The deacon received the boys and brought them back to the bishop. Fortunatus immediately gave him blessed water, saying: ‘Go quickly and pour it over the body of the man lying there.’

“The deacon went, entered the Goth’s lodging, and sprinkled the blessed water over his limbs.

[Note: For the use of blessed water and miracles resulting from it, see Epiphanius, *Panarion*, heresy 30, on the Ebionites, no. 12; and Photius, codex 96, who reports that Chrysostom cured the son of a certain Euclia from a most desperate illness by sprinkling blessed water. See also *Historia Tripartita*, Book IX, reporting from Theodoret that Marcellus, bishop of Apamea, ordered blessed water to be sprinkled; when this was done, the demon fled, unable to endure the water’s power.]

“A wondrous and profoundly astonishing thing occurred: as soon as the blessed water touched the Goth’s thigh, the entire fracture was strengthened and his thigh was restored to its former health. At that very hour he rose from his bed, mounted his horse, and continued along the journey he had begun, as though he had never suffered any bodily injury.

“Thus it came about that the man who, though bound to obedience, had refused to return the boys to holy Fortunatus even for a price was compelled by punishment to give them without a price.”

[Note: Gussanville reads “was compelled to give them,” against the other manuscripts, both printed and handwritten.]

When these matters had been completed, the old man still wanted to tell me other things about him. But since some people were present whom I was occupied in exhorting, and since the later hour of the day had already arrived, I was not able to hear for long about the deeds of venerable Fortunatus—deeds which, if permitted, I always desire to hear.

[Col. 0208D]

On another day the same old man told an even more remarkable story about him, saying:

“In the same city of Tuder there lived a certain man named Marcellus, a man of good conduct, together with his two sisters. When illness befell his body, he died at the very evening of Holy Saturday, as the dawn of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was approaching. Since his body had to be carried some distance, it could not be buried that same day.

“While a delay therefore arose before the burial could be completed, his sisters, afflicted by his death, ran weeping to the venerable Fortunatus and began to cry out to him in loud voices: ‘We know, Father, that you possess the life of the apostles: you cleanse lepers and give sight to the blind. Come and raise our dead brother.’

“When the bishop learned that their brother had died, he too began to weep over his death and answered them: ‘Go away, and do not say such things, for it is the command of almighty God, which no human being can oppose.’

“When they departed sorrowfully, the bishop remained grieved over his death. On the following Sunday, before the first light of dawn, he summoned two of his deacons and went with them to the dead man’s house. Approaching the place where the body lay lifeless, he devoted himself there to prayer.

“When he had finished praying, he rose and sat beside the dead man’s body. In a quiet voice he called him by name, saying: ‘Brother Marcellus.’

“The dead man, as though awakened from a light sleep by the nearby voice, immediately opened his eyes, looked at the bishop, and said: ‘What have you done? What have you done?’

“The bishop answered: ‘What have I done?’

“He replied: ‘Yesterday two men came to me. They led me out of this body and brought me to a very good place. But today one was sent and said: “Bring him back, because Bishop Fortunatus has come to his house.”’

“When he had spoken these words, he immediately recovered from his illness and remained longer in this life. Yet we must not believe that he lost the place he had received. There is no doubt that, through the prayers of his intercessor, he was able to live better after death when he returned, since even before death he had striven to please almighty God.

“But why say much about his life, when even now, at his body’s resting place, we possess so many proofs of his virtues? He releases the possessed from demons and heals the sick whenever this is requested in faith, just as he habitually did without ceasing while alive; and these things continue at his dead bones.

“But gladly, Peter, let me bring the words of my narrative back again to the region of Valeria. I had the opportunity to hear of its very remarkable miracles from the mouth of the venerable Fortunatus, whom I mentioned much earlier [namely, at the beginning of chapter 4]. He frequently comes to me even now; and while he tells me the deeds of the men of old, he fills me with fresh delight.”

## CHAPTER X  
### On Fortunatus, Bishop of the City of Tuder

[Note: In the same manuscript the title reads simply “of the bishop.”]

[Col. 0199A]

**Gregory:** There was another man of exceedingly devout conduct in the same regions of Tuscia, named Fortunatus, who was appointed bishop of the church of Tuder. Having received grace from God, he was an extraordinary expeller of unclean spirits, so that at times he drove legions of demons from the bodies they inhabited and overcame, through persistent and steadfast prayer, the many attacks that came against him from them. Julian, the defender of our church, became this holy man’s closest friend. He died in this city not long ago. I learned the account I am about to give from him, for Julian enjoyed great frankness with Fortunatus and knew his deeds precisely; he always carried their sweetness in his mouth through memory, like a honeycomb, for our strengthening.

He used to say that a very noble matron in the neighboring parts of Tuscia had, not long before, taken a bride for her son. She had been invited, together with her mother-in-law, to the dedication of the oratory of the blessed martyr Sebastian.

[Note: The printed edition, together with the Regius manuscript, reads “in”; Colb. has “in the neighboring parts.”]

On that night, when the day of the dedication of the aforesaid oratory was about to dawn, overcome by the pleasure of the flesh, she was unable to abstain from her husband.

[Note: Colb. reads: “When the day of the dedication of the oratory was about to dawn, moved by pleasure …” The text is defective.]

When morning came, she did not fear the pleasure of the flesh that had taken place; she chose to proceed, blushing more before the face of human beings than fearing God’s judgment, and therefore went with her mother-in-law to the dedication of the oratory.

When the relics of the holy martyr Sebastian entered the oratory, an evil spirit seized the matron’s aforesaid daughter-in-law and made her become possessed before the whole people. The presbyter of the oratory, seeing her violently possessed, took the linen cloth from the altar and covered her. Immediately the devil entered him also, because he had dared to undertake something beyond his strength, so that, driven onward by his own affliction, he might learn what he was suffering.

Those who were there lifted the girl in their arms from the oratory and carried her to her own house. While the primeval evil enemy was crushing her by tormenting her with the utmost violence, her relatives, loving her according to the flesh and hastening to obtain healing for her through treatment, brought sorcerers to her, wishing by magical arts temporarily to care for the body but thereby to extinguish the soul utterly.

She was therefore taken to a river and thrown into the water. The sorcerers, using many incantations, wished the devil who had mounted her to come out. But a wondrous judgment of almighty God occurred: while they expected one demon to be driven from her by their perverted art, a legion suddenly entered her.

[Note: The manuscripts read “legion.”]

The girl then began to be shattered by such violent convulsions of the body and to howl with so many voices that it became evident to everyone that she was being tormented by a multitude of demons. Her parents then took good counsel, ascribing the cause to their own unbelief, and brought her to the exceedingly devout man Fortunatus, the bishop, begging him to help the afflicted woman. They left her with him and departed.

[Note: The Regius manuscript adds that they begged and entreated him to help her, and rejoiced when she was restored.]

The man of God received her, devoted himself for many days and nights to prayer before God, and persevered in prayer with such persistence as he found necessary when the multitude of the legion present in a single body stood against him. After not many days he restored her to her parents healthy and strong, as though the devil had never exercised authority over her.

### 195

At another time this venerable man, the true servant of almighty God, freed through his holy prayer a certain man held by an unclean spirit. The evil spirit that had departed, as evening was falling and night had come and everyone was quiet, pretended to be a stranger. It began to wander through the city’s streets, shouting:

“Alas for the holy man Fortunatus the bishop! What has he done? Behold, he has driven a stranger from his cell. I seek somewhere where I ought to rest, but I cannot find a place in his city.”

[Note: The manuscripts read “somewhere where I ought to rest.” The printed text has “I seek.” The editor suggests that *ἀναπαῆναι* should perhaps be read *ἀναπαυθῆναι*, “to rest.”]

A man heard this voice while sitting in his house beside the fire with his wife and his noble little child. He called the stranger, asked what the bishop had done to him, brought him into his house, and made him sit beside the fire. While they sat and conversed with one another, the same evil spirit entered his noble little child, threw him into the fire, and immediately caused him to give up his soul in the flames. The wretched man who endured this thereby learned whom the bishop had driven out and whom he himself had received.

**Peter:** What, then, are we to say about this? How did the primeval evil enemy obtain the power to kill in the house of the man who, believing him to be a stranger, had received him into his own dwelling for the sake of hospitality?

**Gregory:** Many things are regarded as good, Peter, but are not, because they are not done with a good disposition. Hence the Lord’s truthful voice says in the Gospel: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark.”

[Note: Both manuscripts read “is dark.”]

In every deed, if the beginning is made with deceit, the whole work that follows is found to be crooked, even if it is thought to be upright. I therefore do not think that this man, whom I have heard fell into blindness while wishing to show hospitality, did this out of compassion; rather, he did it while blaming the bishop. The judgment that followed made it clear that the reception he had offered was not without fault.

There are therefore many who undertake to perform a good deed in order to cast the virtue of another’s work into shadow. They do not choose to do good for the sake of reward, but because they wish to be praised and to overturn the good deeds of others. Hence I suppose that this man, who received the evil spirit for the sake of hospitality, did so more for display than out of compassion, so that he might appear superior to the bishop: what Fortunatus, the man of God, had driven out, he hastened to receive.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “he himself received it”; Colb. reads “he hastened to receive it.”]

[Col. 0203C]

**Peter:** It is as you have said; the outcome of the deed proved it, and there is no doubt about the matter.

[Note: Colb. reads: “Just as you have said.”]

**Gregory:** At another time, a certain man who had lost the light of his eyes was brought to this holy man, requesting through petitions that he might obtain his help—and he did obtain it.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “having lost”; Colb. has the same reading with a single lambda.]

[Note: Both manuscripts read “to obtain it.”]

For when the man of God had prayed and placed the sign of the cross upon the man’s eyes, he immediately recovered his sight, and the darkness of blindness was driven away.

Again, a soldier’s horse was held by the most violent madness, so that it could scarcely be restrained by many men. Whoever it could attack, it struck and tore their limbs with its bites. When it had therefore been restrained and tied by many people, it was brought to Fortunatus, the man of God.

[Note: This word does not always mean an ordinary soldier, but sometimes denotes an official distinguished by the rank of some command. Some hold that *stratiotae* specifically designated certain men among the emperor’s guards; the learned Du Cange does not approve this.]

He immediately stretched out his hand, made the sign of the cross over the horse’s head, and changed all its madness into gentleness. Thereafter it became gentler than it had been before it acquired that madness.

The soldier then decided to offer the horse to this holy man, having seen it swiftly healed of its madness by the wondrous command. When the bishop did not wish to accept the horse, the soldier persisted in begging that his offering not be rejected.

[Note: The text has been restored from the manuscripts. Previously it read: “although the bishop did not wish …”]

The holy man took a middle course: he fulfilled the soldier’s request but did not wish to accept the gift because of the miracle that had occurred. First, therefore, he gave the soldier a proper payment, and only then accepted the horse offered to him.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “He first gave the soldier a fitting honor, and then accepted the horse.”]

For if he had refused to accept it, the soldier would have been deeply distressed. Compelled by charity, he bought what he did not need.

[Col. 0206B]

Nor do I think it right to pass over this deed among the powers of this holy man, which I learned twelve days ago. A certain poor old man came to me. Since the company of old men is always pleasing to me, I began carefully to ask him where he was from; he said that he was from the city of Tuder.

I added: “I ask you, Father, do you know Bishop Fortunatus?”

He answered: “I know him, and I know him very well.”

I then said to him: “Tell me, I beg you, if you know any of his miracles, and, since I desire to hear it, tell me what kind of man he was.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “relate it,” with the accent on the antepenult; this is better, since it is the second-person imperative.]

The old man answered: “That man was far removed from the people of this generation whom we now see. Whatever he asked of almighty God, he immediately received.”

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “from the generation of people whom we now behold.”]

“I shall try to tell one of his miracles, which has now come into my mind.

“One day the Goths arrived near the city of Tuder. They were heading toward the region of Ravenna and took away two noble children from an estate subject to the same city of Tuder.

[Note: The manuscripts read “belonging to” or “subject to” the same city of Tuder.]

“When this was reported to the most holy man Fortunatus, he immediately sent for the Goths and summoned them to him. He began by addressing them with flattering words, wishing first to calm their harshness. Then he spoke to them about the children, saying:

“‘What honor do you desire? I will give it to you. Return to me the children whom you took. If you do this, you will confer a great favor on me, and I acknowledge my gratitude because you are giving them to me as a gift.’

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “I acknowledge my gratitude because you offer them to me as a gift.”]

“The first of them, hearing this, replied: ‘Whatever else you command us, we are ready to do; but we cannot in any way return these children.’

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Whatever else you order us to do,” which renders the Latin more faithfully.]

“The venerable man gently said to him: ‘You are grieving me, my son, because you do not listen to me, your father. Do not wish to grieve me, lest it somehow prove harmful to you.’

“But the Goth remained savage in his heart, was not persuaded, and departed.

“On another day, as he was leaving the city, he came again to the bishop. The bishop once more began to plead with him in the same words concerning the children already mentioned. Since he still refused to return them, the bishop said: ‘You are grieving me. Believe me: I know that it will not be good for you to depart, leaving me grieved.’

[Note: The manuscripts read: “to return them. The bishop, grieved, said: ‘Believe me, I know that it is not good for you.’”]

“The Goth despised his words, returned to his camp, and sent ahead the same children, whom the bishop had been asking for, mounted on horses with his men.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “Having mounted them, he sent them ahead with …”]

“He himself likewise mounted his horse and followed behind them. When he came into the same city, before the church of Saint Peter, his horse’s foot slipped; the horse fell with him and broke the Goth’s thigh, so that the bone was split in two.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “His thigh was broken.”]

“The people present lifted him in their arms and carried him back to his camp. Immediately, with great urgency, he sent and recalled the children whom he had sent ahead, concerning whom the bishop had pleaded. He also sent word to the same venerable man, Fortunatus the bishop, saying:

“‘I beg you, venerable Father, send your deacon to me.’

“When the deacon came to him, he brought forward the children whom he had utterly refused to return and handed them over to the deacon, saying:

“‘Go and say to my lord the bishop: “Behold, because you cursed me, I lie stricken. But take back the children you sought, and, I beg you, offer prayer for me, so that through your holy prayer I may obtain healing.”’

“The deacon received the children from him and returned to the bishop. Having reported these things to him, the devout man Fortunatus immediately gave him blessed water and sent him, saying:

“‘Go quickly and sprinkle this water over his body.’

“The deacon departed, entered the Goth’s lodging, and sprinkled the blessed water over his limbs. A wondrous and terrifying event occurred: when the water touched the Goth’s thigh, the entire fracture was immediately strengthened, and his thigh was restored to its former health. At that very hour he rose from his bed, mounted his horse, and continued on the road he had begun, as though he had suffered no injury whatsoever to his body.

“This happened so that the man who had not wished to return the children to the holy man Fortunatus the bishop with an honorable payment, being subjected to punishment, might return them as a gift.”

When this story had been completed, the old man still wished to tell me other things about him. But because many people were present who needed to be admonished by us, and I could no longer remain at leisure, and because the day was already declining toward evening, he did not have the opportunity to let me hear more about the deeds of the venerable Fortunatus. If it were permitted, I would wish to hear them continually.

[Col. 0207D]

On another day the same old man related something even more wondrous about him, saying:

“In the same city of Tuder there lived a man named Marcellus, conducting himself honorably and dwelling with his two sisters. He fell ill in body, and on the very evening of Holy Saturday, as the dawn of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ was breaking, he completed his life.

“Because the place where his body was to be buried lay far away, they were unable to bury it on the evening of Holy Saturday. Since a delay therefore arose before he could be buried, his sisters, grieving over his death, ran weeping to the venerable man Fortunatus the bishop. Falling at his feet with sighs and tears, they said:

“‘We know, venerable Father, that you follow in the footsteps of the apostles and receive everything you ask of God. You cleanse lepers and give sight to the blind. Come, then, and raise our brother who has just died.’

“When the bishop heard of his death, he was deeply saddened and began to weep. He answered them:

“‘Withdraw from me, and do not wish to say such things. His death has occurred at the command of almighty God, and what you ask exceeds my power.’

“When they withdrew sorrowfully, the bishop remained grieving that evening. Before the light of Holy Easter had dawned, at the hour before sunrise, he summoned two of his deacons and went with them to the dead man’s house.

“Approaching the place where the lifeless body lay, he devoted himself there to prayer. When he had completed his prayer, he rose and sat beside the dead man. In a quiet voice he called him by name, saying: ‘Brother Marcellus.’

“The dead man heard this voice and, as though awakened from a light sleep, opened his eyes, looked directly at the bishop, and said: ‘What have you done?’

“The bishop answered: ‘What have I done?’

“He replied: ‘Yesterday two men came to me. They led me out of this body and brought me to a very beautiful place. But today one was sent and said: “Bring him back, because Bishop Fortunatus has come to his house.”’

[Note: With these words the chapter ends in Colb.]

“When these words had been spoken, he immediately grew strong again after his illness and remained for many more years in this life. We believe that he did not lose the place he had received, and there is no doubt about this. Through the intercession of the one who prayed for him, he was able to live better after being raised from the dead, since before his death he had striven to please almighty God.

“But why say much about the conduct of this blessed Fortunatus? Even now, at the place where his precious body lies, a multitude of miracles is performed. He frees the possessed from the slavery of unclean spirits, heals the sick, and grants healing to all who ask in faith. Just as he habitually did these things without weariness during his present life, so after his departure from this world, by the grace of almighty God, the same things are performed through his precious body.

“And now, Peter, I gladly bring the account of my discourse back again to the regions of Valeria. I have had the opportunity to hear of very great miracles there from the mouth of Fortunatus, whom I mentioned above. Even to the present he is accustomed to come to me frequently, and, as he tells me the virtues of the men of old, he fills me with fresh joy.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “about the regions.”]

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “to come to me”; another reading is “to appear before me.”]

## CHAPTER XI  
### On Martyrius, a Monk of the Province of Valeria

[Col. 0212A]

There was a certain man in the same province named Martyrius (Martyrology, 23 January), a very devout servant of almighty God, who gave this sign as testimony to his virtue.

[Note: This Martyrius is distinct from the monk Martyrius of Lycaonia praised in Homily 39 on the Gospels. Guitmund, Book II of *On the Eucharist*, was mistaken in distinguishing them. The former’s name is entered in the Martyrology on 23 January.]

One day his brothers had made him a loaf baked beneath the ashes, but had forgotten to impress upon it the sign of the cross, as in that province loaves are customarily marked with a piece of wood, so that they appear divided into four quarters.

[Note: Thus Regius, Germanus, two other manuscripts of Saint-Germain, Norm., and others. In the printed editions loaves are usually said to be marked with a sign.]

[Note: Hence in Suidas, “a square loaf,” that is, bread to be divided into four parts. A *quadra* is therefore a piece of bread. Hence Juvenal, *Satire* 5: “So that you may think it a good thing to live on another’s quarter-loaf.” And Horace, Book I, Letter 17: “And a quarter-loaf will be split for me from the divided gift.” Likewise in the passage circulated under Virgil’s name in the *Moretum*: “He shapes the work with his palms and spreads it into a circle, and marks it with impressed squares at equal intervals.” Although this cross-shaped figure was impressed on the bread for the more convenient division of the loaf, some religious significance was nevertheless added by marking it with the sign of the cross. Thus bread divided into three parts was sometimes baked to symbolize the Trinity. Hence Saint Paulinus, Letter 3 to Alypius, at the end: “We have sent one loaf to Your Holiness as a sign of unity, in which the fullness of the Trinity is also contained.”]

The servant of God arrived while they were reporting the matter to one another, and learned that the bread had not been marked. When the loaf was already covered with embers and ashes, he said: “Why did you not mark it?” As he said this, he made the sign of the cross with his finger toward the embers. Immediately, when he made the sign, the bread gave off an immense crackling, as though a huge pot had burst in the fire.

When it had afterward been baked and removed from the fire, it was found marked with the cross—not because it had been touched, but because faith had made the mark.

## CHAPTER XI (Greek Text)  
### On Martyrius, Monk of the Land of Valeria

[Col. 0211A]

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Thus he used to tell me that …”; Colb. likewise, omitting “to me.”]

He therefore used to relate that in the same land of Valeria there was a man named Martyrius, who served almighty God with great zeal and made his manner of life manifest through his deeds. One day the brethren subject to him made bread baked under ashes, but neglected to make upon it the sign of the precious cross, as it is customary in that land to mark loaves, so that the bread appears marked into four portions.

[Note: Colb. reads: “his own brethren.”]

Martyrius, the same servant of God, arrived and, hearing them tell one another of this, learned that the bread had not been marked.

[Note: Colb. reads: “arriving and understanding this as they told it among themselves.”]

The same loaf was already covered among the coals beneath ashes. He said to them: “Why, brothers, did you not mark it?” Then, bringing his hand near the fire and making the sign of the cross, the loaf at once made such a sound in the fire that one might have thought a great pot had broken.

[Note: Regius reads “beneath the ash”; Colb., “beneath the cinders.”]

[Note: Colb. reads: “bringing his hand near the fire, [he made] the sign of the cross”; Regius, “bringing [his hand] near, [he made] the sign.”]

After the bread had been baked and taken out of the fire, it was found marked with the sign of the cross—a sign which no hand had touched, but faith had made.

## CHAPTER XII  
### On Severus, Presbyter of the Same Province

[Col. 0212B]

In that same region there was a valley called Interorina, which many, in rustic speech, call Interocrina. In it lived a man named Severus, whose manner of life was exceedingly admirable, a priest of the church of the blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin (Martyrology, 15 February).

[Note: Here “priest” means a simple presbyter, although in older writers and in authors of this period it can be understood of a bishop.]

One day, when a certain head of a household had come to the final day of his life, he sent messengers in haste and asked Severus to come to him as quickly as possible and to intercede for his sins by his prayers, so that, having repented of his evil deeds, he might leave his body freed from guilt.

It happened, however, that this priest was occupied in pruning a vineyard. When those who came to him spoke, he said: “Go ahead; behold, I am following you.” Since he saw that only a small amount of work remained, he delayed briefly in order to complete what little was left. When it was finished, he began to go to the sick man.

As he went, those who had come earlier met him and said: “Father, why did you delay? Do not trouble yourself, for he has already died.”

When he heard this, Severus trembled and began to proclaim in a loud voice that he was his murderer. Weeping, he reached the dead man’s body and threw himself on the ground before the bed with tears.

[Note: The first Theodore manuscript reads: “he gave himself to prayer on the ground.”]

As he wept bitterly, beat his head against the ground, and called himself responsible for the man’s death, the one who had died suddenly received his soul again. When the many people standing around saw this, they uttered cries of astonishment and began to weep even more from joy.

When they asked him where he had been and how he had returned, he said: “The men who were leading me were exceedingly grim. Fire came from their mouths and nostrils, and I could not endure it. As they led me through dark places, a youth of beautiful appearance suddenly met us, together with others who were traveling with us. He said to those who were dragging me: ‘Take him back, because the presbyter Severus is mourning; the Lord has given him to him because of his tears.’”

[Note: The Compendium reads: “a young man appeared.”]

Severus, therefore, immediately rose from the ground and offered the man, now repentant, the assistance of his intercession. For seven days the revived sick man did penance for the sins he had committed; on the eighth day he departed from the body rejoicing.

Consider, Peter, I beg you, how much the Lord regarded this Severus, of whom we are speaking, as his beloved, since he did not allow him to be saddened even for a little while.

### 205

**Peter:** These things are exceedingly wondrous, and I find that until now they had been hidden from me. But what are we to say about the fact that men of this kind cannot now be found?

**Gregory:** I believe, Peter, that many such men are not lacking even in this world. For if they do not perform such signs, it does not follow that they are not such men. The true measure of a life lies in the virtue of its deeds, not in the display of signs. There are many who, although they perform no signs, are nevertheless not unlike those who do.

**Peter:** How, I ask, can it be shown to me that there are some who perform no signs and yet are not unlike those who do?

**Gregory:** Surely you do not know that the apostle Paul is the brother of Peter, first among the apostles in apostolic leadership?

**Peter:** I know it clearly. There is no doubt that, although he was the least of all the apostles, he labored more than all of them.

**Gregory:** You rightly recall this. Peter walked on the sea with his feet (Matthew 14), while Paul suffered shipwreck at sea (2 Corinthians 11).

[Note: Most manuscripts read “on the sea,” or “into the sea,” on foot.]

And in the same element Paul could not travel by ship where Peter made his journey on foot.

[Note: In Germanus and all the Norm. manuscripts, the reading is “there in one.” In three Saint-Germain manuscripts and the Regius manuscript it reads “there Paul,” and so forth. In all the Norm. manuscripts: “where Paul could not travel with the ship, there …”]

It is therefore plainly evident that, although the virtue of the two differed in the miracle, their merit in heaven does not differ.

**Peter:** I entirely approve what you say. For I now clearly understand that it is life, not signs, that must be sought. But since the signs that are performed bear witness to a good life, I ask you to relate any further examples there may be, so that you may feed me, who hunger, with examples of the good.

GREGOR. I should like to relate to you, in praise of our Redeemer, something about the miracles of the venerable man Benedict, [Note: [Col. 0216B] Compendiensis reads *sed ad haec exempla*, “but for these examples,” instead of *sed ad haec explenda*, “but for completing these things.”] but I see that the present day cannot suffice for completing them. Let us therefore speak of these matters more freely if we take up another beginning.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Severus, priest of the same region

[Col. 0211B]

In the same territory of the city of Tuder, between two mountains in a valley locally called Interocrina, there is a church of our Lady, the holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin. A certain man named Severus [Note: [Col. 0211D] Royal manuscript: “very remarkable in his manner of life”; Colb.: “very remarkable and wondrous.”] was a priest in that church, possessing an exceedingly admirable manner of life.

On the final day of a certain householder’s life, the man came and sent an urgent message to the same priest, entreating him to come to him without delay and intercede for him, so that through confession and repentance the sins he had committed might receive absolution before he departed from this body.

It happened by chance that the priest was occupied with pruning the vine. [Note: [Col. 0211D] Royal manuscript: “the priest was engaged in pruning the vine, and to those …”; the remaining words are as printed.] He said to those who had come to him: “Go ahead, and behold, I too shall catch up with you.” But when he saw that only a little remained of his work, he decided to persevere briefly so that he might finish it. Having completed it, he began to go to the sick man.

As he was departing, those who had previously come to him met him on the road and said: “Why, Father, were you late? Do not trouble yourself any longer, for he has died.” When the priest heard this, he became utterly shaken and began to lament [Note: [Col. 0213D] Colb.: “to weep and lament.”], calling himself loudly that man’s murderer.

Weeping, he reached the place where the dead man’s body lay and threw himself upon the ground before his bed [Note: [Col. 0214D] Manuscripts: “with tears upon the ground.”]. As he wept bitterly, struck his head against the ground, and declared himself responsible for the man’s death, suddenly the dead man recovered his soul [Note: [Col. 0214D] Both witnesses: “received it back.”].

When those standing around saw this, they were overcome with profound astonishment at the miracle and began to weep still more from joy. They asked the man where he had been and how he had returned. He replied:

“Certain very severe-looking men had taken me away. Fire came forth from their mouths and nostrils, and I could not endure it. While they were leading me through dark places, suddenly a very handsome young man, together with others, met us [Note: [Col. 0214D] The same witnesses read “came to meet us” (*hypantēsei*)] and said to those dragging me: ‘Turn him back, because the priest Severus is weeping for him. For the Lord has granted him to the man’s tears.’”

The priest Severus, the man of God, then rose from the ground and gave thanks to God. After instructing the man in matters of repentance, he obtained for him through his prayer remission of his sins. The sick man, restored to this life, lived for seven days, practicing repentance for what he had done. On the eighth day, rejoicing, he departed to the Lord.

Consider, then, with what love the Lord held the priest Severus, since he did not permit him to be troubled even for an hour.

[Col. 0214B] PETRUS. Truly these things are exceedingly marvelous, and until the present [206] they had escaped my knowledge. But what are we to say of this—that men of such quality can no longer be found?

GREGOR. I do not doubt, Peter, that even now many such men exist in this world. Nor, if they do not now perform such miracles, should it on that account be disbelieved that they are such men. [Note: [Col. 0214D] Royal manuscript: “not on this account”; Colb.: “not for this reason.”] The discernment of a godly way of life lies in the power of works, not in the display of signs. For there are very many who do not perform signs and yet are not unlike those who do perform them.

PETRUS. I beg you, from what source can this be demonstrated to me—that there are some who do not perform signs and yet are not unlike those who perform signs?

GREGOR. Surely you do not fail to know that the apostle Paul is a brother to Peter, the foremost of the apostles, in the apostolic office? [Note: [Col. 0214D] Royal manuscript: “of the apostle and chief.”]

PETRUS. I certainly know it, and there is no doubt about this; yet although he is the least of all the apostles, he labored more than all of them. [Note: [Col. 0214D] Manuscripts: “and I am convinced, and there is no doubt”; Royal manuscript: “more than all.”]

GREGOR. As you know, Peter walked upon the sea with his feet, whereas Paul suffered shipwreck in the sea. Behold: in one and the same element, where Paul could not travel by ship, Peter made his journey on foot. It is therefore plainly evident [Col. 0215A] that although the power of the two was unequal in the miracle, the merit of both is equal in heaven.

PETRUS. I confess that I entirely approve what you say. For now I clearly understand that it is life, and not signs, that is sought; indeed, the signs themselves that are performed bear witness to a virtuous life. I therefore implore you: if any further examples remain, make them clear to me, so that you may nourish me, who hunger, on examples of good men. [Note: [Col. 0215B] Manuscripts: “what you say.”]

GREGOR. I wanted to relate to you, for the praise and glory of our Redeemer God, something about a devout man named Benedict. But I see that the time of day cannot suffice for relating these matters. Therefore, with God supplying the strength, I shall now undertake another beginning of the narrative and tell it at greater leisure. [Note: [Col. 0215B] Colb. adds: “proposing it, I relate it with praise, through the cooperation and grace of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power unto the ages of ages. Amen.” The Royal manuscript has the same, but ends with “I relate it.”]

## BOOK TWO. THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0215]

This second book, containing the Life of Saint Benedict, should be read before the works of the great restorer of Western monasticism, volume 76 of this Library.

## BOOK THREE. THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0215]

### CHAPTER I. Concerning Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola

[Note: [Col. 0215D] The Royal manuscript contains an index of the chapters.]

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Gussanville refutes this story of Saint Paulinus’s voluntary servitude at great length—indeed, in a dissertation—as have many others. We stated our view of the controversy in the preface. Nola is a well-known Roman colony in Campania and an episcopal city under the archbishopric of Naples.]

[Col. 0216C]

[277] While I am devoting myself especially to the neighboring Fathers [Note: [Col. 0216D] Thus Theodorian, German, Norman, and other manuscripts, with which the Greek translation agrees; the printed editions read “regions” (*partibus*).], I had left aside the deeds of earlier men, so that the miracle of Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola, who surpassed many whom I have mentioned in virtue and in time, might appear to have been omitted from memory. But now I return to what came before and touch upon it as briefly as I can.

For just as the deeds of good men commonly become known more quickly to those like them, so, as our elders proceeded by the examples of the righteous, the famous name of the venerable man mentioned above became known, and his admirable work extended itself toward instructing their zeal. It was necessary for me to trust their old age so confidently that it was as though I had seen with my own eyes the things they related. [Note: [Col. 0216D] Printed editions: “to the dignity of their old age.”]

When Italy had been devastated in the regions of Campania during the time of the raging Vandals, and many people had been carried away from this land into the African region, Paulinus, the man of God, gave to captives and needy persons everything that he could possess for the use of the episcopal household. [Note: [Col. 0217D] The printed editions read *episcopi*, “of the bishop,” instead of *episcopii*, “of the episcopal household,” against the English, Norman, German, Theodorian, and other manuscripts, and against the Greek translator.]

When absolutely nothing remained that he could give to those who asked, a widow came one day and reported that her son had been led into captivity by the son-in-law of the king of the Vandals. She asked the man of God for the price of the young man, if perhaps his master might deign to accept it and allow him to return to his own country.

The man of God carefully sought what he might give to the woman who was asking, but found nothing with himself except himself. He therefore replied to her:

“Woman, I have nothing that I can give you. But take me myself; declare me to be the servant subject to your authority, and, so that you may recover your son, hand me over into slavery in his place.”

When she heard this from the mouth of so great a man, she thought it was mockery rather than compassion. But he was an exceedingly eloquent man [Note: [Col. 0217D] Two Gemet. manuscripts and Prat.: “and distinctly and worthily educated from the flower of his earliest youth”;] and thoroughly trained even in secular studies. He quickly persuaded the doubtful woman to believe what she had heard and not to hesitate to hand over the bishop into slavery in exchange for the recovery of her son.

Thus both of them proceeded to Africa. When the son-in-law of the king, who held her son, came out, the widow approached him to make her request and first begged him to give her back her son. But when the barbarian man, swollen with the arrogance of pride and puffed up by the joy of temporary prosperity, disdained not only to do this but even to hear the request, the widow added:

“Behold, I offer this man as his substitute. Only show me compassion and return my only son to me.”

When the man saw that he had a handsome face, he asked what trade he knew. [Note: [Col. 0217D] He is called a “pagan” (*gentilis*) not because he was devoted to idolatry—for he was a Christian, though an Arian like the other Vandals—but in the sense in which the Romans called even allied barbarians *gentiles*. See Du Cange, *Glossary*.]

The man of God Paulinus answered:

“I know no particular trade, but I do know how to cultivate a garden well.”

When that pagan man heard this, he accepted it very gladly, since he learned that Paulinus was skilled in tending vegetables. He therefore took him as a slave and returned the son to the woman who was begging him. Having received him, the widow departed from the African region.

Paulinus, however, undertook the care of cultivating the garden. Whenever the king’s son-in-law entered the garden, asked about his gardener, and perceived that the man was very wise, he began to abandon his friends and household companions, converse more and more often with his gardener, and delight in his words.

Paulinus was accustomed each day to bring him fragrant and green herbs for his table, receive bread, and return to the care of the garden. [Note: [Col. 0217D] Thus the manuscripts: alternatively “fragrant” or “sweet-smelling.” Nowhere do we read “vegetables,” as in the printed editions; the Greek translator supports this reading.]

When this had continued for a long time, one day, while his master was speaking with him more privately, he said:

“Consider what you are doing, and take thought for how the kingdom of the Vandals should be governed, because the king is soon to die, with all speed.”

When the son-in-law heard this, he did not keep silent, since he was loved by that same king above all others. He reported what he had learned from his gardener, namely, that he was a wise man.

When the king heard this, he immediately replied:

“I should like to see this man of whom you speak.”

His son-in-law, Paulinus’s temporary master, answered:

“He is accustomed to bring me green herbs for my meal. I shall therefore have him bring them here to the table, so that you may recognize the man who has told me these things.”

And so it happened. When the king reclined for his meal, Paulinus came from his work carrying fragrant and green herbs. [Note: [Col. 0220D] Printed editions: “every green vegetable.”]

When the king suddenly saw him, he trembled. He summoned Paulinus’s master, his kinsman through his daughter, and disclosed to him the secret that he had previously concealed:

“What you heard is true. For last night in a dream I saw judges sitting in judgment against me; this man too was sitting among them, and, by their judgment, the whip that I had once received was taken away from me. [281] But ask who he is. I do not suspect that a man of such great merit, apparently a common person, is what he seems.”

The king’s son-in-law then took Paulinus aside and asked who he was. The man of God replied:

“I am your servant, whom you accepted as a substitute for the widow’s son.”

The other persistently demanded that he tell not merely what he was now, but what he had been in his own country. He pressed him with repeated questioning. [Note: [Col. 0220D] Becc. and Big.: “with frequent questioning.” The second Gemet.: “with frequent repetition and questioning.”] The man of God, constrained by solemn oaths and no longer able to deny his identity, confessed that he had been a bishop.

When his possessor heard this, he was exceedingly frightened and humbly offered:

“Ask whatever you wish, so that you may return to your own land from me with a great gift.”

The man of God Paulinus replied:

“There is one benefit that you can confer upon me: release all the captives from my city.”

All of them were immediately sought out throughout the African region. Together with ships laden with grain, they were released and sent in the company of the venerable Paulinus, to satisfy his request.

After not many days, the king of the Vandals died and lost the whip which, by God’s dispensation, he had received for his own destruction but for the discipline of the faithful. Thus it came about that Paulinus, the servant of almighty God, foretold the truth, and that he who had handed himself over alone into slavery returned from slavery to freedom with many others. He imitated Him who assumed the form of a servant so that we might not be slaves of sin. Following in His footsteps, Paulinus became voluntarily a slave alone for a time, so that afterward he might be free with many.

[Col. 0221A] PETRUS. When I happen to hear of what I cannot imitate, I would rather weep than say anything.

GREGOR. Concerning his death, too, it is written at his church that, when he was afflicted by pain in his side, he was brought to his final extremity. While his entire house remained firm, the room in which the sick man lay trembled when an earthquake occurred, and struck with immense terror all who were present there. Thus that holy soul was released from the flesh.

It came about that great fear seized those who were able to witness Paulinus’s death. But since the virtue of Paulinus, which I mentioned above, is of the highest and most inward kind, let us now, if you please, turn to his outward miracles. Many people already know these, and I learned of them from the reports of religious men in such a way that I cannot doubt them at all. [Note: [Col. 0221C] In the printed editions Gussanville has the following before “Concerning”: “The virtue of Paulinus is very inward.” These words occur in none of the manuscripts available to us.]

### CHAPTER I. Concerning Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola

[Note: [Col. 0215D] Gussanville refutes this story of Saint Paulinus’s voluntary servitude at great length—indeed, in a dissertation—as have many others. We stated our view of the controversy in the preface. Nola is a well-known Roman colony in Campania and an episcopal city under the archbishopric of Naples.]

[Col. 0215C]

[278] While I was attending to the neighboring Fathers and dwelling upon their miracles in my account, I left aside the deeds of the great. For who is not astonished by the miracle of Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola? He surpasses all others both in time and in the power of his miracle.

Since his memory was overlooked, I now bring it forward so that he may be thought present and visible, and I append this account to what has already been said, as briefly as I can. For it is customary for our elders to make the deeds of good men diligently known through the narratives of those who follow the examples of the righteous. Thus the radiant name of the exceedingly devout man mentioned above became known. His admirable work extended itself toward the edification of their efforts. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Manuscript: “I extended myself toward their edifying efforts.”]

I am therefore compelled to believe securely concerning his very great way of life that the things they relate are such as I myself saw with my own eyes.

During the time of the raging Vandals, many places in Italy became deserted, and the regions of Campania were made entirely uninhabitable. Many people were captured by them and carried away from this land into the region of Africa.

The man of God Paulinus distributed among the captives and needy everything he possessed for the use of the episcopal household. 

When nothing at all remained that he ought to give to those who asked, a certain widow came to him one day and said that her son had been carried into captivity by the son-in-law of the king of the Vandals. She asked the man of God for his price, if his master might perhaps be willing to accept it and permit him to return to his own country. [Note: [Col. 0217D–0218D] The term *rex* among medieval Greek writers means the same as *basileus* among the ancients, namely “king”; the term *basileus* was reserved by the Greeks of Constantinople for emperors. Some, however, also used it of Persian kings, while they called various other rulers *rēges*. Thus Anna Comnena in her *Alexiad* calls Henry IV emperor “the king of Germany.” It should also be noted that in the Royal manuscript *amēras* is read instead of *rēgas*, the name by which kings were called among the Arabs, and so forth. Gussanville conjectured from this Arabic word that the Royal manuscript had been copied by an Arab. Perhaps the word entered the Greek translation from an Arabic version, mentioned in the preface. It means “lord.” Consult Du Cange, both in his Greek Glossary and in his notes on Joinville and Cinnamus.]

The man of God carefully and eagerly sought whether he could find anything that he ought to provide for the woman who was asking, but found nothing with himself except himself. He replied to her:

“Woman, I have nothing to give you. I give you myself as a slave subject to your authority; and so that you may recover your son, hand me over into slavery in his place.”

[279] When she heard this from the mouth of such a man, she thought it was mockery rather than compassion. But he was an eloquent and intelligent man, diligently trained even in secular studies. He quickly persuaded the doubtful woman to believe that what he had said was true and not to hesitate to hand over the bishop into slavery for the recovery of her son.

They both proceeded to Africa. When the king’s son-in-law, who held her son, came forward, the widow approached him and begged him to give her son back. But that barbarian, exalted by the arrogance of pride and puffed up by the joy of temporary prosperity, disdained not only to do this but even to hear it.

The widow added:

“Behold, I offer this man as his substitute. Only show compassion to me and return my only son to me.”

When he saw the man’s pleasant face, he asked what trade he knew. The man of God Paulinus answered:

“I know no trade, but I know how to care properly for a garden.”

When that pagan man heard this, he accepted him with great pleasure, because Paulinus was experienced in tending a garden. He therefore accepted him as a slave and returned the son to the woman who was pleading with him. Having received him, she withdrew from the African region.

Paulinus undertook responsibility for caring for the garden. The king’s son-in-law began to enter the garden more frequently, converse with his gardener about various matters, and perceive that he was exceedingly wise. Abandoning all his household friends, he continually conversed with him and took delight in his words.

Each day Paulinus supplied his table with fresh and fragrant herbs. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Manuscript: alternatively, “freshly fragrant herbs.”] Having obtained bread, he returned to the care of the garden.

When this had continued for a long time, one day, while his master was conversing with him, Paulinus said to him privately:

“Consider what you are about to do, and take forethought for how the kingdom of the Vandals should be governed. For the king is dying by every means.”

When he heard this, the king’s son-in-law, who was loved by the king above all others, did not remain silent. He reported everything that he had heard from his gardener.

When the king heard this, he replied:

“I wish to see the man about whom you speak.”

His son-in-law, Paulinus’s temporary master, answered:

“He is accustomed to bring fresh herbs from the garden for my meal. I shall therefore have him bring them to your table, so that you may know who has told me these things.”

And so it happened. When the king reclined for his meal, Paulinus entered from his labor carrying fragrant herbs and fresh vegetables. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Manuscript: “When the *amēras* suddenly saw him, he trembled.”]

When the king suddenly saw him, he trembled. He summoned Paulinus’s master, who was related to him through his daughter, and disclosed to him the mystery that he had previously concealed:

“What you heard is true. For during this very night I saw in a vision rulers seated upon a tribunal against me; this man was seated among them, and the scourge that I had once received was removed from me by their judgment. [282] Ask him, then, who he is. For I do not suppose that this man, who possesses such rank, is a layman, as he appears to be.” [Note: [Col. 0219D] Manuscript: “being in this rank, a layman.”]

Then the king’s son-in-law took Paulinus aside and questioned him about who he was. The man of God replied:

“I am your slave, whom you accepted as a substitute for the widow’s son.”

The other continued to question him insistently, asking not what he was now but what he had been in his own country. After investigating this at length, the man of God, forced to yield and unable to break the oaths that had been imposed upon him, confessed that he was a bishop. [Note: [Col. 0219D] Manuscript: “after investigating.”]

When the man who held him heard this, he was exceedingly afraid and approached him with complete humility:

“Ask whatever you wish of me, so that you may return to your own land with the greatest gifts.” [Note: [Col. 0220D] Manuscript: “approached him.”]

The man of God Paulinus replied:

“There is one gift of kindness that I ask, and that you can grant me: release all the captives from my city.”

They were immediately sought throughout the whole region of Africa. All were brought aboard ships with provisions of grain and, traveling in his company, were released for the satisfaction of the exceedingly devout man Paulinus.

After not many days, the king of the Vandals also died, and he lost the scourge which, by God’s permission, he had held for his own destruction but for the discipline of the faithful. Thus it came about that Paulinus, the servant of almighty God, foretold what was to happen truthfully, and that he who had handed himself over alone into slavery returned from slavery to freedom with many others, imitating Him who assumed the form of a servant so that we might no longer be slaves of sin.

Following in His footsteps, Paulinus became voluntarily a slave alone for a time, so that afterward he might become free with many. [Note: [Col. 0222D] Perhaps “alone”; nevertheless, the manuscript supports the printed editions.]

[Col. 0222A] PETRUS. While I am permitted to hear what I cannot imitate, I prefer to weep rather than say anything.

GREGOR. Concerning the death of this holy man, an account is preserved in his church: when pain had touched his side and he was already at the point of death, while the entire house remained firm, the chamber in which he lay sick trembled when an earthquake occurred and struck everyone present there with the greatest fear. Thus that holy soul, released from the bonds of the body, departed to the Lord.

This happened so that the greatest fear might enter those who were able to witness Paulinus’s death. Since his virtue, which I mentioned above, was exceedingly great, let us now, if you please, turn to his external miracles, which are already known to many. I learned of them from so many serious men who related them that I cannot doubt them at all. [Note: [Col. 0222D] These words, omitted in the printed editions, have been restored from the Royal manuscript; see above, col. 279, line 35, and below, col. 219, line 8. The meaning is thereby made clearer, and the Greek translation corresponds perfectly to the Latin text.]
