### CHAPTER II. Concerning Saint John, pope

[Col. 0221B]

In the time of the Goths, when John, the most blessed man and pontiff of this Roman Church, was traveling to Justin the Elder, the emperor, [Note: [Col. 0221D] The printed editions read “Justinian,” a gross error perhaps occasioned by the Greek translator, which reads *Ioustinianon* in both editions and manuscripts. All the Latin manuscripts—English, Norman, Royal, three German, Compendiensis—read “Justin.” This Pope John governed under Justin, not Justinian; when Justinian began to reign, John had already died. Moreover Justinian could not then have been called “the Elder,” since no other emperor of that name yet existed. This Justin was called “the Elder” to distinguish him from the other Justin, who gained the empire about 565.] [284] he arrived in the region of Corinth. On the journey it was necessary for a horse to be sought for him to ride.

When a certain nobleman heard this, he offered him a horse which his wife was accustomed to ride because of its great gentleness. He stipulated that, once a suitable horse had been found for the pontiff at another place, the horse he had given should be sent back for his wife. [Note: [Col. 0222C] Gilot and Vatican manuscripts: “once another horse could be found”; Gussanville: “once a suitable horse could be found.” We reproduce the manuscripts with great fidelity.]

This was done. The venerable man mentioned above was carried by that horse as far as a fixed place. As soon as he found another horse, he sent back the one he had received.

When the wife of the nobleman wished, as usual, to ride the horse, she could no longer do so. After carrying so great a pontiff, it refused to carry a woman. It began, as though in contempt, to demonstrate by immense snorting and neighing, and by the unceasing movement of its whole body, that it could not carry a woman after carrying the pontiff.

When her husband wisely observed this, he immediately sent the horse back to the same venerable man, earnestly begging him to keep permanently the horse which he himself had sanctified by sitting upon it and had made his own by right of riding it.

Our elders also commonly relate another miracle about this holy man. When he came to Constantinople, to the gate called the Golden Gate, crowds of people came out to meet him. In the sight of everyone, he restored sight to a blind man who begged him for it, placing his hand upon him and driving the darkness from his eyes.

### CHAPTER II. Concerning John, pope of Rome

[Col. 0222B]

In the time of the Goths, the most blessed man John, patriarch of this church of the Romans, traveled to Justinian, the former emperor. [Note: [Col. 0222D] Manuscript: “to the former emperor.”]

[283] As he was traveling toward the region of Corinth, a horse was needed for the patriarch to ride on the road. A certain nobleman heard this and brought him a horse which his wife habitually rode because of its great gentleness, so that, when the patriarch departed for another place and a suitable horse had been found, this one might be sent back for his wife.

The most holy man mentioned above therefore mounted the horse and traveled as far as the appointed place. When they had found another horse, they sent the first one back. [Note: [Col. 0222D] Manuscript: “having found another horse, they sent that one back.”]

As was customary, the wife of the very noble man mentioned above wished to mount the horse, but from that time she was entirely unable to do so. After carrying the most holy patriarch, it refused to carry a woman. It began to become agitated with great neighing and snorting, moving its whole body incessantly and seeming, as it were, to say:

“After carrying the patriarch, I will not consent to carry a woman.” [Note: [Col. 0222D] Manuscript: “moving and striking” (perhaps “leaping”), and …]

Her husband clearly understood this [Note: [Col. 0222D] Manuscript: “plainly understood it.”] and immediately sent the horse to the patriarch, begging him to keep forever the horse which he himself had mounted and sanctified by his own use.

I have heard another miracle concerning this holy man from our elders. They said that, when he came in Constantinople to the gate called the Golden Gate, crowds of people came out to meet him. In the sight of everyone, he restored light to a blind man who begged him for it; for, placing his hand upon him, he banished the darkness from his eyes.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning Saint Agapitus, pope

[Col. 0224A]

After not much time had passed, when the affairs of the Goths demanded it, the most blessed man Agapitus, pontiff of this holy Roman Church in which, by God’s dispensation, I serve, also went to the emperor Justinian. [Note: [Col. 0224D] We discussed Agapitus’s journey to Justinian in the Life of Cassiodorus, book II, chapter 5, section 4 at the end and section 5.]

While he was still traveling, in the region of Greece, a mute and lame man was brought to him for healing. He could utter no words at all and was never able to rise from the ground.

When his relatives brought him weeping, the man of God carefully asked whether they had faith in his healing. They declared that they possessed a firm hope for his salvation through the power of God and by the authority of Peter.

Immediately the venerable man devoted himself to prayer. Having begun the solemnities of the Mass, he offered sacrifice in the presence of almighty God. When this had been completed, he came out from the altar, took the lame man by the hand, and, while the people stood by and watched, immediately raised him from the ground so that he stood upon his own feet.

When he placed the Lord’s body in the man’s mouth, the tongue that had long been mute was released for speech. Everyone marveled and began to weep for joy, and fear and reverence immediately seized their minds when they saw what Agapitus had been able to do through the power of the Lord and with Peter’s assistance.

### CHAPTER III. Concerning Agapitus, pope

[Col. 0223A]

After not much time had passed, when the affairs of the Goths were pressing, the most blessed man Agapitus, who had become patriarch of this holy church of God of the Romans, which, by God’s favor, I now serve, traveled to the emperor Justinian. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Manuscript: “went up.”]

While he was traveling through the regions of Greece, a lame and speechless man was brought to him one day to be healed. He could utter no word whatsoever and had never been able to rise from the ground.

When his neighbors brought him to the patriarch in tears, the man of God carefully asked whether they had faith in his healing. They declared that, through the power of God and from the authority of Peter, they possessed a steadfast hope for his salvation. Immediately this exceedingly devout man devoted himself to prayer. Having completed the liturgical service, he offered a sacrifice before almighty God.

When the service had been completed, he came out from the altar, took the lame man by the hand, and, while all the people stood by and watched, raised him immediately from the ground so that he stood upon his own feet.

When he placed the Lord’s body in his mouth, that entirely speechless tongue was instantly released and began to speak. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Manuscript: “that speechless tongue.”] All who were present marveled and were filled with tears mingled with joy. Fear seized their thoughts as they observed what Agapitus had been able to do through the power of the Lord with Peter’s assistance. [Note: [Col. 0223D] Manuscript: “what Agapitus was able to do.”]

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning Datius, bishop of Milan

[Note: [Col. 0224D] Datius too is discussed in the same *Life of Cassiodorus*, book II, chapter 5, section 5, and chapter 7, section 5.]

[Col. 0224C]

[285] During the reign of the same emperor, when Datius, bishop of the city of Milan, was traveling to Constantinople on account of the faith, he came to Corinth. He sought a spacious house in which to lodge, one capable of accommodating his entire retinue, and scarcely found one.

From a distance he saw a house of suitable size and ordered that it be prepared for his lodging. The inhabitants of the place said that no one could stay there, because the devil had inhabited it for many years and for that reason it had remained empty.

The venerable Datius replied:

“On the contrary, for that very reason we ought to lodge in this house: because the evil spirit has invaded it and driven human habitation from it.”

He therefore ordered that lodging be prepared for him there and entered confidently, intending to endure the contests of the ancient enemy. [Note: [Col. 0224D] Prat. and the second Gemet. manuscript: “ordered a bed to be prepared for himself.” The printed editions of Gilot and Vatican agree.]

In the silence of the dead of night, while the man of God was resting, the ancient enemy began, with immense voices and loud cries, to imitate the roars of lions, the bleating of sheep, the braying of asses, the hissing of serpents, the squealing of pigs, and the screeching of mice. [Note: [Col. 0225D] Printed editions: “the grunting of pigs and the squeaking of mice.”]

Datius was suddenly roused by the voices of so many animals. He rose in great anger and began to shout loudly against the ancient enemy:

“It has gone well for you, wretch! You are the one who said, ‘I shall set my throne at the north, and I shall be like the Most High’ (Isaiah 14:14). Behold: through your pride you have become like pigs and mice. You who unworthily wished to imitate God, behold, as you deserve, you imitate beasts.”

At these words, so to speak, the evil spirit became ashamed of its humiliation. Did it not become ashamed, when it no longer entered that same house to display the monstrous apparitions it had been accustomed to produce? Thus afterward the house became a dwelling place of the faithful, because when one truly faithful man entered it, the lying and unbelieving spirit immediately departed from it.

But we must now be silent about earlier events and proceed to those that have happened in our own days.

[286]

### CHAPTER IV. Concerning Datius, bishop of the city of Milan

[Col. 0223C]

In the time of the same emperor Justinian, Datius, bishop of the city of Milan, was traveling to Constantinople on a matter concerning the faith. When he arrived at Corinth, he sought a spacious house in which he could lodge, one capable of containing his entire retinue.

Since he could not find one, he saw a lofty house of appropriate size and ordered that it be prepared for him as lodging. The inhabitants of the place said that no one could live in it because the devil had inhabited it for many years, and for this reason it had remained vacant.

The exceedingly devout man Datius replied:

“On the contrary, for this reason we ought to lodge in this house: because the evil spirit entered it and drove human habitation from it.”

He therefore ordered that a lodging be prepared for him there, being eager to endure without anxiety the struggles of the ancient enemy. He entered and remained there. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Manuscript: “eagerly … the struggles of the primal enemy.”]

In the quiet of the night, while the man of God was resting, the ancient enemy began, with countless voices and immense cries, to imitate the roaring of lions, the cries of sheep, the braying of wild asses, the hissing of snakes, the grunting of pigs, and the screeching of mice. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Manuscript: “the grunting of pigs,” perhaps “the squeaking.”]

Datius was immediately awakened by the voices of so many beasts. He rose and, exceedingly angry with the ancient enemy, began to shout in the loudest voice:

“You have received what you deserve, wretched one! You are the one who said, ‘I shall set my throne above the clouds of heaven, and I shall be like the Most High.’ Behold: because of your pride you have become like pigs and mice. You who unworthily wished to imitate God, behold, as you deserve, you imitate beasts.”

The evil demon became ashamed of this man’s voice and, so to speak, of its own expulsion. From then on it did not enter that house to produce such manifestations. Thus the same house became a dwelling place of the faithful in the latter days. For when one truly faithful man entered it, the spirit of falsehood and unbelief immediately departed from it.

It is therefore now permissible to pass over the ancient events and come to those that have occurred in our own days.

### CHAPTER V. Concerning Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium

[Note: [Col. 0225D] On Sabinus and the city of Canusium, see book II, chapter 15; the Martyrology lists him on 9 February.]

[Col. 0225B]

Certain exceedingly devout and serious men from the region of Apulia, testifying concerning what has become widely known among many people about Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium, used to say that this same man had lost the light of his eyes through prolonged old age, so that he could see absolutely nothing.

When Totila, king of the Goths, heard that Sabinus possessed the spirit of prophecy, he did not believe it at all but sought to test what he had heard. When he arrived in those regions, the man of God invited him to dinner.

When they had come to the table, the king did not recline but sat at the right hand of the venerable Sabinus. While [288] a boy, as was customary, was offering the venerable man a cup of wine, the king secretly extended his hand, took the cup, and himself offered it to the bishop in place of the boy, wishing to discover whether, by the spirit of prophetic insight, he could recognize who was offering him the cup. [Note: [Col. 0225D] First Carnotinian manuscript: “by a spirit of foreknowledge”; another: “by foreknowledge”; Val. Cl. and first Theodorian manuscript: “by the spirit of prophecy.”]

The man of God took the cup, although he did not see the attendant, and said:

“May this hand live.”

At these words the king rejoiced but was also put to shame, because although he had been detected, he had nevertheless found in the man of God what he had been seeking.

As the life of this venerable man continued into extreme old age, his archdeacon, inflamed by ambition to obtain the episcopate, attempted to kill him with poison. After corrupting the wine-server’s mind with gifts so that he would offer the bishop a cup mixed with poison, the archdeacon’s bribed servant presented the venerable bishop with the poisoned cup at mealtime, when the man of God had reclined to eat. [Note: [Col. 0227D] Two Carnotinian manuscripts, Compendiensis, Val. Cl., Gemet. and several Norman manuscripts read “when he had corrupted the mind of one of his boys” or “of one boy.” We follow the German and other manuscripts, both written and printed, supported by the Greek translator.]

The bishop immediately said to him:

“You drink what you are offering me to drink.”

The boy, trembling and realizing that he had been discovered, preferred to drink and die rather than suffer punishment for the guilt of such a murder. When he brought the cup to his mouth, the man of God restrained him:

“Do not drink it. Give it to me; I shall drink it. But go and say to the one who gave it to you: ‘I indeed drink the poison, but you will not become bishop.’”

Having made the sign of the cross, the bishop drank the poison without fear. At that same hour, in another place where his archdeacon was, the archdeacon died, as though the poison had passed through the bishop’s mouth into the archdeacon’s inward parts.

Yet although corporeal poison was lacking for inflicting death upon the bishop, the poison of his own wickedness killed the archdeacon before the sight of the eternal Judge.

PETRUS. These things are marvelous and exceedingly astonishing in our own times. Yet the life of this same man is said to have been such that anyone who knew his conduct ought not to be surprised at his power.

### CHAPTER V. Concerning Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium

[Col. 0226B]

Certain exceedingly devout and serious men from the regions of Apulia, testifying concerning what has become widely known among many people, said of Sabinus, bishop of the city of Canusium, that this same man had lost the light of his eyes in prolonged old age, so that he could see nothing at all. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Manuscript: “what has become more widely known among many.”]

Totila, king of the Goths, heard that he possessed the spirit of prophecy. [Note: [Col. 0226D] The word “spirit” was omitted in the Vatican and Gussanville editions and has been restored from the manuscript.] He did not believe this at all but undertook to test what he had heard. When he arrived in those regions, the man of God invited him to dinner.

When they came to the table, the king did not wish to recline but sat at the right hand of Sabinus, the exceedingly devout man. While the boy was, [287] as usual, handing the wine cup to the same venerable man, the king secretly extended his hand, took the cup, and then himself handed it to the bishop in place of the boy, wishing to determine whether, by the spirit of foreknowledge, he could recognize who was handing him the cup. [Note: [Col. 0226D] Manuscript: “secretly.”]

The man of God received it, although he did not see the one serving him, and said:

“May this hand live.”

The king rejoiced at these words and at the same time was humiliated by what had been detected through him. Whatever he had sought in the man of God, he found.

When the life of this exceedingly devout man had been prolonged and he had reached advanced old age, his archdeacon, inflamed by desire for the episcopate, wished to kill him with a poisonous drink. Having corrupted the mind of his wine-server with gifts, he arranged that the servant should hand him a cup of wine mixed with poison at the hour of the meal. [Note: [Col. 0227D] Manuscript: “having corrupted the soul of his wine-server, he arranged that …”]

When the man of God had reclined to dine, the servant corrupted by gifts handed the holy man the cup of poison that he had received from the archdeacon.

The bishop said to him:

“You drink this which you have brought to me.”

The boy became terrified, knowing himself to be guilty. He preferred to drink it and die rather than endure tortures for the audacity of such a murder. [Note: [Col. 0227D] Manuscript: “he preferred to do this rather than suffer torment.”]

As he raised the cup to his mouth, the man of God stopped him:

“Do not drink it; rather, give it to me, and I shall drink it. Go and say to the one who gave it to you: ‘I drink the poison, but you will certainly not become bishop.’”

The bishop therefore made the sign of the life-giving cross and drank the poison without fear. While his archdeacon was elsewhere, he died at that very hour—as though the poison had entered the archdeacon’s inward parts through the bishop’s mouth.

Yet the poison did not physically touch the bishop so as to bring about his death; rather, the poison of his own wickedness killed the archdeacon before the eternal Judge.

PETRUS. These things are truly marvelous and exceedingly astonishing in our own times. Since the life of this man is attested to have been of such a kind, how could anyone who understood his conduct fail to marvel at his power?

### CHAPTER VI. Concerning Cassius, bishop of the city of Narnia

[Col. 0228B]

GREGORIUS. Nor shall I be silent about this, Peter, which many people now present here from the city of Narnia earnestly testify to me. In the same time of the Goths, when the aforesaid king Totila came to Narnia, Cassius, the venerable man and bishop of that city, went out to meet him. [Note: [Col. 0227D–0228D] The name is also found as *Narnius* or *Narnis* in many manuscripts. Narnia—Narna in Strabo—is an episcopal city of Umbria at the foot of a mountain, with the river Nar flowing beneath it. Saint Cassius is commemorated on June 26.]

Because Cassius’s face was habitually red by its natural complexion, the king Totila did not believe that this resulted from his constitution but rather from constant drinking, and he despised him utterly. [Note: [Col. 0228D] Most manuscripts read “by his complexion.” Gregory uses this word for what is commonly called “temperament,” as is clear from *The Book of Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 4, or chapter 3, and *Moralia* XXIX, section 45. The Greek words *krasis* and *physis* have the same meaning and correspond to “complexion.”]

But almighty God, wishing to show how great was the man who was being despised, caused an evil spirit, in the field of Narnia where the king had arrived, to enter one of his soldiers, a *spatharius*, in the presence of the whole army [Note: [Col. 0228D] On this term, see the note to Book II, chapter 14.], and began to torment him cruelly.

When the possessed man was brought before the king’s eyes to the venerable Cassius, [289] the man of God prayed and drove the spirit out of him by the sign of the cross. After that it did not dare to enter him again.

Thus it came about that, from that day onward, the barbarian king revered the servant of God sincerely, though he had previously judged him utterly contemptible because of his appearance. For when he saw that Cassius was a man of such great virtue, that savage mind subsided from its haughty arrogance.

### CHAPTER VI. Concerning Cassius, bishop of the city of Narnia

[Col. 0227B]

[The supplied source ends here.]

Gregory: “Nor will I keep silent about this either, Peter, which I have heard from the testimony of many people who come to us each day from the city of Narnia. They said [Col. 0227C] that, during those same Gothic times, the aforementioned king Totila arrived at the city of Narnia. Cassius, bishop of that city, a man exceedingly reverent in his way of life, went out to meet him. The man had such a complexion that his face appeared flushed [Note: [Col. 0227D] The manuscript reads *it appeared somewhat reddish*.]. When King Totila saw him, he thought that he was not naturally like that, but rather that it resulted from drinking a great deal of wine; and so he utterly despised him.

“But almighty God, wishing to show what kind of man he was whom Totila despised, caused an evil spirit, after the king had arrived on the plain of Narnia, to enter one of his sword-bearers before the whole army and to begin tormenting him most cruelly. When the man had been brought before the king’s eyes to the most reverent Cassius, the man of God, after offering a prayer and sealing him with the sign of the cross, drove the demon out of him; and thereafter it did not dare approach him again. Thus it came to pass that from that very day the barbarian king revered from his heart the servant of God whom previously he had greatly despised because of the appearance of his face. For when he saw a man of such power, that savage disposition toward him, which had been swollen with the pride of arrogance, was scattered.”

### Chapter VII. Concerning Andrew, Bishop of the City of Fundi

[Note: [Col. 0229D] Concerning this city, see above, book I, chapter 1.]

[Col. 0229A]

But behold, while I am recounting the deeds of strong men, there suddenly comes to mind what divine mercy did for Andrew, bishop of the city of Fundi. I wish this account to benefit its readers especially in this respect: that those who dedicate their bodies to continence should not presume to live with women, lest sudden ruin steal upon the mind all the more easily because the presence of the desired form also serves what is wrongly desired.

There is no uncertainty about the event I relate, since there are almost as many witnesses to it [Note: [Col. 0229D] The Beccensis and Bigotian manuscripts say, “They are witnesses to so great a matter.”] as there are inhabitants of that same place. This venerable man, while leading a life full of many virtues and guarding himself under priestly discipline in the stronghold of continence, did not wish to remove from the care of his episcopate a certain religious woman whom he had previously kept with him [Note: [Col. 0229D] The same manuscripts, together with Lyranus and the first Audomarensis, read: “He did not take care to remove her from the administration of his episcopate.”]. Confident of his own continence and hers, he allowed her to live with him.

As a result, the ancient enemy sought an entrance for temptation into his mind. He began to impress her appearance upon the eyes of his mind, so that, enticed, he might conceive wicked thoughts. One day a certain Jew, coming to Rome from Campania, was travelling along the Appian Way [Note: [Col. 0229D] The second Carnotensis, Valcluse, Compendium, and all the Norman manuscripts except Gemeticensis and Pratensis read: “He was travelling on the road to Capua.”]. When he reached the hill of Fundi and saw that evening was already approaching, and found nowhere to turn aside, he came to the temple of Apollo and settled there for the night. Fearing the sacrilege of that place, although he had no faith in the cross, he nevertheless took care to protect himself with the sign of the cross.

At midnight, disturbed by the dread of the solitude, he lay awake. Suddenly he looked and saw a crowd of evil spirits proceeding as though in attendance upon some authority; their leader, however, was seated in the midst of the place. He began to examine the causes and deeds of each of the spirits serving him, so that he might discover how much wickedness each had committed.

While the individual spirits were reporting what they had done against good people, one sprang forward and disclosed how great a temptation of the flesh he had stirred up in the mind of Bishop Andrew through the appearance of the religious woman who lived in his episcopal residence. When the evil spirit presiding over the others heard this eagerly, he considered the gain to himself all the greater because he had inclined the mind of a holier man toward the downfall of perdition. The spirit who had confessed this added that, up to the previous evening, he had dragged the bishop’s mind so far that, while flattering the woman, he had struck her on the back with a slap.

Then the evil spirit, the ancient enemy of the human race, gently encouraged him to complete what he had begun, so that, through the bishop’s ruin, he might hold a unique palm of victory among the others.

When the Jew who had arrived saw this while remaining awake, he trembled in great anxiety and fear. Then the evil spirit who presided over all those serving spirits ordered them to inquire who the man was who had dared to lie down in that very temple. The evil spirits went to him and examined him more closely; they saw that he was marked with the mystery of the cross and, wondering, said: “Woe, woe! An empty and sealed vessel.”

When they reported this, the entire crowd of evil spirits disappeared. The Jew who had seen these things rose at once and hurried to the bishop. Finding him in his church, he took him aside and asked what temptation was troubling him. The bishop, ashamed, did not wish to confess his temptation.

When the Jew said that he had fixed the eyes of an evil desire upon that particular servant-woman of God, and the bishop still denied it, he added: “Why do you deny what you are being asked about, when yesterday evening you were brought to the point of striking her buttocks with a slap?”

At these words, seeing that he had been exposed, the bishop humbly confessed what he had previously denied obstinately. Concerned for the man’s ruin and shame, the Jew told him how he had learned of the matter and what he had heard about it in the assembly of the evil spirits.

When the bishop recognized this, he immediately prostrated himself on the ground and gave himself to prayer. At once he expelled from his residence not only that servant of God but every woman who lived there in his service. In the same temple of Apollo he suddenly established an oratory of the blessed apostle Andrew, and was thereafter entirely freed from that temptation of the flesh. He also led the Jew, through whose vision and rebuke he had been saved, to eternal salvation. After instructing him in the mysteries of the faith and cleansing him with the water of baptism, he brought him into the bosom of the holy Church.

Thus it came to pass that the Hebrew, while attending to another’s salvation, reached his own; and almighty God, through the very means by which he had preserved one man in the good life, led another to that good life.

Peter: “This event, which I have heard, gives me both fear and hope.”

Gregory: “Indeed, we ought always to trust in God’s mercy and to fear because of our weakness. For behold, we have heard that the cedar of paradise was shaken, but not uprooted, so that for us, who are weak, its shaking may give rise to fear, and its stability to confidence.”

### Chapter VII. Concerning Andrew, Bishop of the City of Fundi

### [Col. 0230A]

While I am recounting the deeds of greater men, there suddenly comes to mind what divine mercy did for Andrew, bishop of the city of Fundi. I particularly urge readers to take heed of this: those who consecrate their bodies to continence should not dare to live with women, lest their minds be subjected to so great a fall; for an appearing form brings desire into the mind and inclines it toward evil. There can be no doubt about the matter I relate, since it has as many witnesses as there are inhabitants of that same city.

This most reverent man led a life filled with virtues and preserved the guardianship of his inner self in holiness through continence [Col. 0230B] [Note: [Col. 0230D] The manuscript reads “well.”]. He had with him a certain nun who had previously lived with him; but he did not wish to remove her from the episcopal residence or from his own care [Note: [Col. 0230D] The manuscript reads *from the episcopal residence*, and so below.], being fully confident of his own purity and hers. He therefore allowed her to live with him in the episcopal residence.

As a result, the ancient enemy sought an entrance for temptation into his soul. He began to place her beauty before the eyes of his mind [Note: [Col. 0230D] The Latin translator has *in lecto* (“in bed”), where *illectus* (“enticed”) should be read; or, as the written manuscripts have it, *inlectus*.], so that he would even entertain improper thoughts in bed.

One day a certain Jew, coming from the regions of Campania to Rome, travelled along the Appian Way. When he arrived at the upper road leading to Fundi, and saw that the day was already declining toward evening, he could find no place where he ought to lie down. Coming near the temple of Apollo that stood there, he entered it in order to remain for the night.

Fearing the pollutions occurring in that place, although he had no faith in the cross, he nevertheless took care to secure himself with the sign of the cross. Around midnight, when everything was quiet, terrified both by the desolation of the place and by his own isolation, he lay awake.

Suddenly he looked intently and saw a great crowd of evil spirits proceeding as though in the train of some authority [Note: [Col. 0230D] The same word is still used in this sense in book IV, chapter 17. It is also written *obsequium*. For other meanings see Cangius, *Glossary*.]. He saw their leader seated in the chair of authority in that place [Note: [Col. 0230D] The manuscript reads: “having seated him in his own chair.”]. He began to interrogate each of the spirits who served him about their deeds and practices, seeking to discover how much wickedness and evil each had committed [Note: [Col. 0230D] It appears that *καθ’ ἕκαστον* or *ἑκάστων* should be read.].

While all of them, in response to his inquiry, were describing what they had done against the good, one sprang into the middle and explained what temptation he had aroused in the soul of Andrew the bishop through the beauty of the nun who lived with him in the episcopal residence, and what disturbance of the flesh he had produced.

When the evil demon presiding over the other spirits heard this, he received it with great pleasure [Col. 0231A] and acknowledged that a great gain had been brought to him, since he had inclined the soul of a holy man toward a destructive fall. The evil demon who had reported these things added:

“Until this past day I did not cease troubling him, but I was unable to drag away his mind. Yesterday evening, however, I brought it about that he touched the buttocks of the holy virgin passionately with his own hand.”

Then the evil devil, the ancient enemy of the human race, summoned him flatteringly and said: “Hasten to complete what you have begun, so that, through his fall, you alone among the others may obtain the palm of victory [Note: [Col. 0231C] The learned Cangius discusses this word and its origin at length in his *Glossary*; consult him.].”

When the Jew, remaining awake, saw these things, he was overcome by great fear and distress [Note: [Col. 0231D] The manuscript reads: “He was thrown into distress.”]. The devil who held first place over all the spirits ordered them to inquire who the man was who had dared to lie down in their temple.

The evil spirits went to him and examined him carefully. Seeing that he was sealed with the sign of the cross, they wondered and said: “Ah! A vessel of ballast, empty and sealed” [Note: [Col. 0231D] This barbarous Greek word is derived from *saburra*, “ballast,” and signifies “empty,” since ships loaded with ballast or sand are regarded as empty. See Cangius. In the Regia manuscript it reads: “empty and rotten.”].

When they reported this, the whole disturbance of the evil spirits disappeared. The Jew who had seen these things rose immediately and hastened to the bishop. Finding him in his church, he took him aside and sought to learn from him what temptation held him captive. The bishop, ashamed, did not wish to confess his temptation.

Then the Jew said: “Did you not fix your eyes upon that servant of God with a shameful desire?” The bishop continued to deny it even then [Note: [Col. 0232C] The manuscript reads: “He denied it … Why do you deny what …”].

The Jew added: “Why do you deny what you are being asked about? Were you not brought so low that yesterday evening you approached her buttocks with your hand, passionately?”

Then, convicted by the Jew’s words, the bishop confessed with complete humility what he had previously denied so firmly. Wishing to console him in the shame of his fall, the Jew began to explain how he had learned this and what he had heard about him in the gathering of the evil spirits.

When the bishop heard and understood these things, he immediately lay down upon the ground and gave himself to prayer. At once he expelled from the episcopal residence not only that servant of God but every female who was there in her service. He made the temple of Apollo an oratory of the blessed apostle Andrew [Note: [Col. 0232C] The manuscript reads “Peter.”]. He was freed from the temptation of the flesh, since by God’s grace it was completely driven away from him.

He drew to eternal salvation the Jew who had rebuked him through that vision. After teaching him the mysteries of the faith and cleansing him with the water of baptism, he brought him into the bosom of the holy Church.

Thus it came to pass that the Hebrew, who had hastened to another’s salvation [Note: [Col. 0232C] The manuscript reads: “to the salvation of the other.”], reached his own. And almighty God, through this means, led one man to the good life, while preserving another in it.

Peter: “This event, which I have heard, gives me both fear and hope of salvation.”

Gregory: “So it is fitting for us always to trust in God’s compassion and to fear because of our weakness [Note: [Col. 0232C] The Vatican edition reads, “to have trusted.”]. For behold, we have heard that the cedar of paradise was shaken, but not uprooted, so that for us who are weak its shaking may produce fear, while its stability produces courage.”

### Chapter VIII. Concerning Constantius, Bishop of the City of Aquinum

[Note: [Col. 0233D] Concerning the city of Aquinum and Bishop Constantius, see book II, chapter 16. His feast is celebrated on September 1.]

A venerable man named Constantius was bishop of the city of Aquinum. He died recently, during the time of my predecessor, Pope John of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0233D] Namely, John III, who began to occupy the see in the year 561.]. Many who were able to know him intimately testify that he possessed the spirit of prophecy.

Among many things, religious and truthful men who were present relate this: on the day of his death, when the citizens standing around him wept most bitterly for the departure of so beloved a father, they asked him through their tears: “Whom shall we have after you, Father?”

The father himself answered them through the spirit of prophecy: “After Constantius, a mule-driver; after the mule-driver, a fuller. O Aquinum, you must endure this also.”

After uttering these prophetic words, he breathed out his final breath. When he had died, the pastoral care of his church was undertaken by his deacon Andrew, who had once tended horses in the stables along the roads. When he too had departed this life, a man named Jovinus was summoned to the episcopate; he had been a fuller in that same city [Note: [Col. 0233D] The manuscripts differ. In the Gemeticensis manuscripts we read, “Jobinus was appointed”; in the Compendium, “Jovinus was appointed”; in the second Theodulfian, “he was summoned.” The German manuscript reads, “Jubinus obtained the episcopal office.” Most Norman manuscripts have the same reading, omitting *to the episcopal office* and changing *Jubinus* to *Jovinus*.].

While he was still alive, all the inhabitants of that city were so devastated by the swords of the barbarians and the violence of the plague that after his death neither could a bishop be appointed nor could anyone be found for whom one might be appointed. Thus the saying of the man of God was fulfilled: after the death of the two who followed him, his church had no pastor.

### Chapter VIII. Concerning Constantius, Bishop of the City of Aquinum

[Col. 0234A]

A man named Constantius, exceedingly reverent in his life [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript reads: “very earnest and reverent in his life.”], was bishop of the city of Aquinum. He died not long ago, during the time of my predecessor, John, the patriarch who departed this life in blessed memory.

Many testify that he possessed the gift of prophecy—truthful and serious men who knew him very well and who were present in person and claimed to have witnessed what they related.

On the day of his death, all the citizens of his city stood around him and wept for him as for a most beloved father who was already about to die. As they wept, they asked him: “What shepherd shall we have after you, Father?”

He answered them through the spirit of prophecy: “After Constantius, a stableman; after the stableman, a fuller [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript reads “stable-boy.”]. Woe to you, city of Aquinum, that you must endure this also.”

After speaking these prophetic words, he received the end of life. When he had died, Andrew, his deacon, took up the pastoral care of the same church. Andrew had once guarded the horses’ stables belonging to the military officials. When he too withdrew from the present life, Jobinus [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript reads “is introduced.”], who had been a fuller in that city, attained the rank of bishop.

While he was still alive, all who inhabited that city were destroyed by barbarians, by the sword, and by the bitterest famine. Consequently, after his death, neither could the man who ought to become bishop be found, nor could anyone be found for whom a bishop might be appointed. Thus the prophecy of the man of God was fulfilled: after the departure of the two who came after him, that church could no longer have a pastor [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript reads: “did not have a pastor.”].

### Chapter IX. Concerning Frigdianus, Bishop of the City of Lucca

[Col. 0233C]

Nor will I keep silent about what I happened to learn two days ago from the account of the venerable Venantius, bishop of Luna [Note: [Col. 0233D] Several letters of Gregory exist to and concerning him: formerly book III, now book IV, letters 21 and 22; and formerly book IV, now book V, letter 7, elsewhere numbered 5.].

He related that a man of extraordinary virtue named Frigdianus was bishop of the Church of Lucca, which was near his own [Note: [Col. 0234D] Some manuscripts read “Frigdianus”; others “his neighbor,” referring to Saint Frigdianus.]. All the inhabitants there testify to the following celebrated miracle [Note: [Col. 0234D] Gemeticensis and many Norman manuscripts read “Frigidianus.” He is listed among the saints on March 18.].

The river Auser, which flowed beside the walls of that city, often overflowed its channel and spread across the fields, destroying whatever crops and plantings it encountered [Note: [Col. 0234D] The German, two Theodulfian, Longipontanus, and most Norman manuscripts read “Ausaris.”]. Since this happened frequently and placed the inhabitants of that region in great difficulty, they made strenuous efforts to divert it through other places. But although they labored for a long time, they could not turn it from its own channel.

Then the man of God, Frigdianus, made himself a small rake, approached the riverbed, and devoted himself to prayer alone. Commanding the river to follow him, he dragged the rake across the ground wherever it seemed good to him. The entire body of the river’s water followed him, abandoning its own channel, so that it completely deserted the place of its customary course and claimed for itself a channel where the man of God had marked the ground by dragging the rake. From then on it no longer harmed crops or plantings that would be useful for human sustenance.

### Chapter IX. Concerning Frigdianus, Bishop of the City of Lucca

[Note: [Col. 0234D] Thus the manuscript reads, along with the Latin text itself; hence the corrupt form *Luna* in the printed edition.]

Nor will I keep silent about what happened to me two days ago: I heard it from the account of the most reverent man Venantius, bishop of the city of Luna. As he was approaching the city of Lucca, he related that Frigdianus, bishop of that same church, was a man of wondrous power, and all who live there bear witness to him.

He said that the river Auser flows near the walls of that city. Frequently, when floods occurred, the river left its own bed, inundated the neighboring fields, and destroyed all the plants and cultivated land [Note: [Col. 0234] This note is missing from Migne’s printed edition.].

When this happened more and more often, great necessity pressed upon the inhabitants. They therefore expended much labor and effort, trying to make the river pass through other places, but they were entirely unable to move it from its own channel.

Then the man of God, Frigdianus, made himself a modest little hoe, stood beside the riverbank, and, bending himself to prayer alone, commanded the river to follow him through the places he himself indicated, as he dragged the hoe through the ground.

The entire body of the river’s water left its own bed and followed the holy man. Thus no moisture remained thereafter in its former place; wherever the man of God had drawn the ground with the hoe, there the river made its course, and from then on it inflicted no harm upon the plants or the cultivated land [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscript reads “did not cause.”].

### Chapter X. Concerning Sabinus, Bishop of Piacenza, Who Restrained the River Po by His Letter

[Col. 0236B]

From the account of this same venerable Bishop Venantius I learned another miracle, said to have occurred in the city of Piacenza [Note: [Col. 0235D] Piacenza is an episcopal city under the archbishop of Bologna. It is one mile distant from the Po.]. The most truthful man John, who now occupies the office of prefect in this Roman city [Note: [Col. 0235D] Pratensis and the first Gemeticensis read “the place of the prefecture”; Lyranus, Beccensis, and the first Audomarensis read “the prefectural office.” This John served as prefect in Rome, meaning that he acted as deputy or lieutenant. The Greeks say *topotērētēs*, “lieutenant.”], and who was born and raised in that same city of Piacenza, attests, as the bishop relates, that the event took place.

They say that in that city there was a bishop named Sabinus, a man of wondrous virtue [Note: [Col. 0236D] Sabinus is entered in the Martyrology on December 11. See Baronius in his notes on the Martyrology. He lived in the time of Saint Ambrose, who also celebrates him in his writings.].

One day his deacon announced to him that the Po, having left its channel, had occupied the fields of the Church, and that its water covered all the places there that would otherwise have produced nourishment for human beings [Note: [Col. 0236D] Other manuscripts read “for human beings,” “for vegetables,” or “for crops.” The German manuscript first reads “for human beings,” then “for vegetables.”].

The venerable Bishop Sabinus answered: “Go and say to it: ‘The bishop commands you to restrain yourself and return to your own channel.’”

When his deacon heard this, he despised and ridiculed him. Then the man of God summoned a notary and dictated:

“Sabinus, servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the river Po: I command you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that you no longer leave your channel in these places, and that you do not presume to damage the lands of the Church.”

Then he added to the notary: “Go, write this, and throw it into the water of that river.”

When this had been done, the water of the river received the command of the holy man and immediately restrained itself from the lands of the Church. Returning to its own channel, it did not thereafter presume to overflow into those same places.

In this event, Peter, what else is confounded except the hardness of disobedient human beings, when, through the power of Jesus, an irrational element obeyed the command of a holy man?

### Chapter X. Concerning Sabinus, Bishop of the City of Piacenza

[Col. 0235A]

[Col. 0235B] From the account of that most reverent man Venantius, the bishop, I learned another miracle which he testified had occurred in the city of Piacenza. John, who now holds the office of prefect in this city of the Romans, a thoroughly truthful man born and raised in that same city of Piacenza, also bears witness with the bishop to this miracle.

He said that a man named Sabinus, possessing wondrous power [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscript reads: “being wondrous,” followed by “in the same city, etc.”], became bishop in that city. One day his deacon announced to him that the river Po, having crossed beyond its own channel [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscript reads: “had spread over the field.”], had taken possession of the fields of the Church, and that its water had covered everything in those places that was intended to grow for the nourishment of human beings [Note: [Col. 0235D] The manuscript reads “in those places.”].

The bishop Sabinus, most reverent in his life, answered: “Go and say to it: ‘The bishop informs you that you must restrain yourself and return to your own place.’”

When his deacon heard this, he mocked and ridiculed him. The man of God summoned a notary and dictated to him:

“Sabinus, servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, a written command to the river Po: In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ I command you henceforth not to leave your place, and not to presume to damage the land of the Church.”

Then he added to the same notary: “Go, write this, and throw it into the river’s water.”

When this had been done, the river received the command of the holy man and immediately withdrew from the land of the Church [Note: [Col. 0235D] These words, *from the land*, omitted in the printed editions, have been restored from the Regia manuscript. They are necessary for the completeness of the sense.]. Returning to its own place, it did not thereafter dare to overflow into the lands of the Church.

In this event, Peter, the hardness of disobedient human beings is put to shame, because, through the power of the Lord Jesus, the non-rational element obeyed the command of the holy man [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript reads “of the command.”].

### Chapter XI. Concerning Cerbonius, Bishop of Populonia

[Col. 0237A]

The venerable Cerbonius, bishop of Populonia [Note: [Col. 0237D] See the Roman Martyrology, October 20. Populonia was once a very celebrated city of Etruria, concerning which Virgil writes in book X of the *Aeneid*:

“Populonia, the mother-city, had given him
Six hundred young men experienced in war.”

After its destruction, the episcopal see was transferred to Massa, a cultivated and substantial town of Etruria not far away. In our manuscripts, as among the geographers, Populonia receives various names: *Populonia*, *Populonium*, *Populona*, and *Populonum*.], gave in our days a great proof of his holiness.

Since he was deeply devoted to the practice of hospitality, one day he received passing soldiers as guests. When the Goths arrived, he hid them and, by concealing them, preserved their lives from the Goths’ wickedness.

When this was reported to Totila, the impious king of the Goths, he was inflamed with the madness of the most savage cruelty. He ordered Cerbonius to be brought to a place called Merulis, eight miles from that city, where Totila was then seated with his army [Col. 0237B], and ordered him to be thrown before the people to bears to be devoured.

The treacherous king himself sat in the spectacle to watch the bishop’s death, and a great crowd of people gathered. The bishop was brought into the middle, and a savage bear was sought out for his death, one accustomed to tear human limbs most brutally and so to satisfy the spirit of the wicked king.

The bear was released from its cage. Inflamed and rushing toward the bishop, it suddenly forgot its own ferocity; bending its neck and humbly lowering its head, it began to lick the bishop’s feet. Thus it was plainly shown to everyone that toward that man of God the hearts of beasts had become human, while the hearts of human beings had become like those of beasts.

The people who had come to watch the death were then transformed, amid a great outcry, into wonder and reverence. The king himself was moved to honor the bishop, since divine judgment had arranged that he who had previously refused to follow God in preserving the bishop’s life should at least follow the beast in gentleness.

Some of those who were present at the time still survive and, together with the entire people there, testify that they saw this.

From the account of Venantius, bishop of Luna, I also learned another miracle concerning this man. In the church of Populonia over which he presided, he prepared a tomb for himself. But when the Lombard people came into Italy and ravaged every place, he withdrew to the island of Ilva [Note: [Col. 0237D] Most manuscripts read *Elba* or *Helba*. It is an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea opposite Populonia, which Virgil celebrates in book X of the *Aeneid* because of the three hundred soldiers sent from there as reinforcements to Turnus when he fought against Aeneas:

“But Ilva, an island rich in inexhaustible
veins of steel, sends three hundred men.”].

When illness overtook him and he was approaching death, he commanded the clergy who served him:

“Place me in the tomb I prepared for myself at Populonia.”

They replied: “How can we bring your body there, since those places are held by the Lombards and we know that they range everywhere there?”

The holy man answered: “Bring me without anxiety; fear nothing. Hasten to bury me; and as soon as my body has been buried, withdraw from that place with all speed.”

When he had died, they placed his body in a boat. As they sailed toward Populonia, the air gathered clouds and an immense rainstorm broke out [Note: [Col. 0239D] The printed editions read “the clouds having gathered in the air.” The manuscripts—German, Longipontanus, Norman, and others—require the alternative reading.].

But to make it clear to everyone whose body that vessel carried, throughout the stretch of sea twelve miles from the island of Ilva to Populonia, a violent rainstorm descended on both sides of the boat, while not a single drop of rain fell into the boat itself.

The clergy reached the place and committed the body of their priest to burial. Keeping his command, they hurried back to the boat. As soon as they were able to enter it, the most savage Lombard commander, Gummarith, arrived at the very place where the man of God had been buried. From his arrival it became clear that the man of God had possessed the spirit of prophecy, since he had commanded his attendants to depart quickly from the place of his burial.

### Chapter XI. Concerning Cerbonius, Bishop of the City of Populonia

[Col. 0238A]

Cerbonius, a man most reverent in his conduct, bishop of Populonia, gave in our days the greatest proof of his holiness. For he devoted himself with every effort to hospitality. One day he received passing soldiers and lodged them as guests. When the Goths arrived, he concealed them and preserved their lives from the Goths’ wickedness by hiding them.

When the impious Totila, king of the Goths, heard this, inflamed by evil and unhealthy cruelty, he ordered Cerbonius to be taken to the place called Merulis, eight miles from that city, where he was then seated with his army [Col. 0238B]. He ordered him to be thrown before the entire people as food for bears.

When that most impious king had seated himself among the people to watch the bishop’s death [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript reads: “and a great commotion of the people gathered …”], a great tumult of the people arose. The bishop was brought into the middle, and a very savage bear was found and selected for his death. It was accustomed to tear human bodies most brutally, so that it might satisfy the soul of the wicked king.

When the bear was released from its cage, it ran eagerly toward the bishop with the greatest fury. Suddenly, however, it forgot its own beastliness; bending its neck and placing its head beneath the bishop’s feet [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript reads “having placed it beneath them.”], it began to lick them with complete humility.

Thus it was openly shown to all that, toward that man of God, the hearts of beasts had been changed into those of human beings, while the hearts of human beings had become like those of beasts. Then all the people who had gathered to see his death began with a great cry to marvel at his reverence [Col. 0238C].

The king himself likewise, seeing the judgment that had come from above, began greatly to revere him. He who had previously refused to follow God in preserving the bishop’s life at last followed the beasts in gentleness [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript reads “in the gentleness of sheep.”].

All who were present there at the time were eyewitnesses of this miracle. Many of them still survive and testify that they saw it together with the entire people of that place.

I heard from Venantius, bishop of Luna, as he related it, another miracle concerning this holy man. In the same church of Populonia over which he presided, he prepared a tomb for himself. When the Lombard people came into Italy and plundered every place, he withdrew to the island of Ilva.

When illness came upon him and he was about to die, he commanded the clergy who served him:

“Bury me in the tomb that I prepared at Populonia.”

They answered: “How can we carry your body there? Those places are held by the Lombards, and we know that they range everywhere.”

The holy man said to them: “Take me there without anxiety and fear nothing. Hasten with all diligence to bury me; and immediately, when my body has been committed to burial, withdraw swiftly from that place.”

When he had died, they placed his body in a small boat, as he had commanded, and sailed toward Populonia. As they departed, the air became clouded and a very violent rain began.

To make clear to everyone whose body that boat carried, throughout the entire sea crossing—twelve miles from the island of Ilva to Populonia—a most violent rainstorm descended on both sides of the boat, while not one drop of rain fell within it.

The clergy reached the place, committed the body of their priest to burial, and, keeping his commands, hurried back to the boat. When they had entered it, the most savage Lombard king, Gummarith, arrived at the place where the man of God had been buried. His arrival proved that the man of God possessed the spirit of prophecy, since he had commanded his attendants to depart quickly from the place.

### Chapter XII. Concerning Fulgentius, Bishop of the City of Otricoli

[Col. 0240B]

The miracle I have related concerning the division of the rain was also displayed in the honor of another bishop. An elderly cleric who is still alive testifies that he was present at the event, saying [Note: [Col. 0239D] Consult Bollandus, under May 21.]:

Bishop Fulgentius, who presided over the Church of Otricoli [Note: [Col. 0239D] Otricoli, also called Utriculum or Ocriculum, was a town of Umbria and formerly an episcopal city. Tacitus calls it *Ocriculi*.], was utterly hated by the most cruel king Totila. When Totila approached those regions with his army, the bishop arranged through his clergy to send him gifts [Note: [Col. 0240D] The German, Norman, Valcluse, Longipontanus, Theodulfian, and other manuscripts commonly read *exenia*, here and elsewhere. At the end of a handwritten copy of the *Pastoral Rule* in the Belvacensis Church, however, certain poems about Bishop Hugh contain the reading:

“Xenia is appointed; Christ, it is your work.”

In book VI of the Letters—formerly book V, letter 62, now letter 65—Saint Gregory also has *xenia*, both in the manuscripts and the printed editions. This should be read here as well, since *xenium* is a gift sent to a guest (*xenos*).], hoping perhaps to soften the savage fury of his anger by means of gifts.

When that impious man saw them, he immediately despised them. Filled with anger, he ordered his men to seize the bishop with every harshness and hold him for his judgment.

The fierce Goths, ministers of his cruelty, seized him, surrounded him, and ordered him to stand in one place. They marked a circle on the ground and commanded him under no circumstances to extend a foot beyond it.

While the man of God stood in the intense heat of the sun [Note: [Col. 0240D] Two Audomarensian manuscripts and Pratensis read “stood.”], surrounded by the same Goths and confined within the marked circle, suddenly lightning, thunder, and such a force of rain broke out that those who had been assigned to guard him could not endure the downpour [Col. 0241A].

Although a tremendous flood arose, not a single drop of rain fell within the same circle in which the man of God Fulgentius stood.

When this was reported to the most cruel king, that savage mind, which had previously thirsted for the bishop’s punishment with insatiable fury, was turned to great reverence for him.

Thus almighty God works the miracles of his power against the proud minds of the flesh through those whom they despise, so that truth may crush the necks of those who arrogantly exalt themselves against its commands through the agency of the humble.

### Chapter XII. Concerning Fulgentius, Bishop of the City of Otricoli

[Col. 0239B]

The miracle I have related concerning the division of the rain was also shown to have occurred in connection with another reverent bishop [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscript reads: “to have occurred in the reverence of another bishop.”]. An elderly cleric, who is still alive, testifies from his own presence that this event took place.

He said that Fulgentius, the bishop who presided over the Church of Otricoli, knew that the most savage king Totila was utterly enraged against him. When Totila approached those regions with his army, the bishop was compelled to send him gifts through his clergy, hoping perhaps that he might soften the cruelty of his anger by gifts [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscript reads “gifts.”].

When that impious man saw them, he utterly despised them. Filled with anger, he ordered his men to seize the bishop with every expression of wrath and hold him for his judgment.

The beastlike Goths, servants of his cruelty, seized him and stood around him. They ordered him to remain in one place and marked a circle in the ground [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscript reads “having carved a circle.”], so that he would not dare stretch his foot outside it.

While the man of God stood in the sun, surrounded by the same Goths and confined within the boundary marked by the circle, suddenly lightning and thunder arose, together with such a violent downpour that those who had taken responsibility for guarding him could not endure the force of the rain [Col. 0242A].

Within the outline of the circle, where the man of God stood under guard, not a single drop of rain fell.

When they reported this to the most savage king, that beastlike disposition, burning with insatiable fury to torture the bishop, was turned to the greatest reverence.

Thus almighty God works the wonders of his power against those who exalt themselves in their own minds, through those whom they despise, so that truth may bend the necks of those who proudly rise up against the commands of truth through the humble.

### Chapter XIII. Concerning Herculanus, Bishop of the City of Perugia

[Col. 0241A]

Floridus, a bishop venerable in life, recently related a very memorable miracle, saying:

“The most holy man Herculanus, my foster-father, was bishop of the city of Perugia [Note: [Col. 0241D] This is a very celebrated city of Etruria on the Tiber, distinguished by its bishopric and academy. The length of its siege, mentioned here, shows how well fortified it was. In this city Mark Antony, besieged by Augustus, was compelled by hunger to surrender; hence the proverb ‘Perugian famine.’]. He had been taken from monastic life and raised by God’s grace to the dignity of the priesthood.

“In the time of the treacherous king Totila, the army of the Goths besieged that city continuously for seven years [Note: [Col. 0241D] Some suspect that *months* should be read rather than *seven years*. None of our manuscripts supports their conjecture. The city may have been said to be besieged for as long as Totila or the Gothic army occupied the Perugian territory bordering the Roman lands.]. Many of the citizens fled because they could not endure the danger of famine.

“Before the seventh year had ended, the Gothic army entered the besieged city. Then the commander over that army sent messengers to King Totila, asking what he ordered to be done with the bishop and the people. Totila commanded him:

“‘First strip the bishop’s skin from the crown of his head to his heel in the form of a leather thong, and then cut off his head. Kill with the sword all the people found there.’

“Then the same commander led the venerable Bishop Herculanus onto the city wall and cut off his head. When he was already dead, he split his skin from the crown of his head to his heel, so that it might appear that a thong had been stripped from his body. Immediately afterward he threw his body outside the wall.

“Some men, moved by human compassion, placed the severed head upon the neck and, together with the body of a small child who had been found slain there beside the wall, committed the bishop’s body to burial [Note: [Col. 0242D] Most manuscripts read *abscissum*, from *abscido* or *abscindo*.].

“After that slaughter, when forty days had passed, King Totila ordered the citizens of that city, wherever they had been scattered, to return to it without any fear. Those who had previously fled from hunger returned after receiving permission to live.

“Remembering what kind of life their bishop had led, they sought where his body had been buried so that they might bury it with the honor due to it in the Church of the blessed apostle Peter.

“When they went to the tomb and dug up the earth, they found the body of the child buried with him, already decayed after forty days and full of worms; but the body of the bishop was as though it had been buried that very day.

“What is even more worthy of reverent wonder is that his head had been joined to his body as though it had never been cut off: no trace of the incision appeared. They turned the body over and examined it to see whether any sign of another cut could be found; they discovered the whole body sound and uninjured, as though no stroke of iron had touched it.”

Peter: “Who would not be astonished at such signs occurring among the dead for the awakening of the living?”

### Chapter XIII. Concerning Herculanus, Bishop of the City of Perugia

[Col. 0242A]

Floridus, the most reverent bishop, has just related to me this memorable miracle. He said:

“The most holy man Herculanus, who had brought me up, became bishop of the city of Perugia. By God’s grace he had been raised from monastic life to the rank of the priesthood.

“In the days of the impious king Totila, the army of the Goths vigorously besieged that city for seven years. Since many citizens could not endure the distress of famine [Note: [Col. 0242D] The manuscript reads “bear it.”], they fled from the city.

“Before the seventh year had been completed [Note: [Col. 0242D] The manuscript reads “the seven-year period”], the Goths captured the city they had been besieging. Then the commander of that army sent to King Totila and asked what he ordered to be done with the bishop and the people.

“He commanded him:

“‘First remove a leather thong from the bishop’s skin, from the crown of his head to his heel [Note: [Col. 0242D] The manuscript reads *lōron*; later it has *lōrin*.], and then cut off his head. Kill with the sword all the people found there.’

“Then the same commander brought the most reverent man, Bishop Herculanus, up onto the city walls and cut off his head. After he was dead, he split the skin from the crown of his head to his heel, so that it might appear that a thong had been stripped from his body. Immediately he threw his corpse outside the wall.

“Some men, overcome by human compassion, placed his severed head upon his neck and, together with the body of a noble little child who had been found slain there, committed the bishop’s body to burial beside the wall.

“After the capture, when forty days had passed, King Totila ordered all the citizens of that city, wherever they had been scattered, to return to it without any fear. All those who had previously fled because of the famine, having received permission to live, returned to it.

“Remembering what kind of life their bishop had led, they searched for the place where his body had been buried, so that they might bury it with the honor owed to it in the church of the blessed apostle Peter.

“When they went to the tomb and dug up the earth, they found the body of the child buried with him, entirely corrupted and full of worms, since forty days had already passed. But the bishop’s body remained sound, as though it had been buried that very day.

“The greatest and most venerable wonder was that his head had been joined to his body as though it had not been cut off, and no trace of the cut appeared upon it. They therefore turned the body over and examined it, seeking whether any sign whatever of the severing could be seen. They found the whole body sound and intact, as though not even a single wound of iron had touched it.”

Peter: “Who would not be astonished at such signs occurring among the dead for the awakening of the living?”

### Chapter XIV. Concerning Isaac, the Servant of God

[Col. 0244A]

[Col. 0244B] In the earlier period of the Goths there lived near the city of Spoleto a man named Isaac, venerable in his way of life. He survived almost to the end of the Gothic period. Many of our people knew him, especially the holy virgin Gregoria, who now lives in this city of Rome near the church of the blessed Mary, ever-virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] He was entered in the catalogue of the saints on April 13.]

When, in the time of her youth, she had fled to the church after her marriage had already been arranged and was seeking the manner of life of a religious woman, she was defended by this same man and, with the Lord’s protection, brought to the habit she desired. Because she fled an earthly bridegroom, she was deemed worthy to have a bridegroom in heaven.

I learned many things about this man from the venerable Father Eleutherius, who had known him intimately, and whose life gave credibility to his words. This venerable [Col. 0244C] Isaac was not originally from Italy; I am recounting those miracles of his that he performed while living in Italy.

When he first came from the regions of Syria to the city of Spoleto, he entered a church and asked the custodians to grant him as much freedom as he wished for prayer, and not to force him to leave during the more private hours. He immediately stood in prayer and spent the entire day praying, joining to his prayer the following night. On the second day also, he remained indefatigable in prayer through the following night and joined the third day to his prayer.

When one of the custodians saw this, inflated by the spirit of pride, he suffered the loss of failure precisely where he ought to have advanced. He began to call him a pretender and, in coarse language, an impostor—one who displayed himself praying for three days and nights before the eyes of men. He then ran up and struck the man of God with a slap, so that, as though he were a pretender to a religious life, he would leave the church in disgrace.

But suddenly an avenging spirit seized him, threw him down at the feet of the man of God, and began to cry out through his mouth: “Isaac is driving me out.” No one knew by what name the foreign man was called, but that spirit disclosed his name by crying out that he could be driven out by him. Immediately the man of God bent over the afflicted man’s body, and the evil spirit that had entered him departed.

At once the whole city learned what had happened in the church. [Col. 0245A] Noble and common men and women alike began to run together, each trying to carry him off to his own house. Some humbly wished to offer him estates for the construction of a monastery, others money, and others whatever support they could provide.

But the servant of the omnipotent Lord accepted none of these things. Leaving the city, he found a deserted place not far away and built himself there a humble dwelling. As many people went to him, they began, following his example, to be kindled with a desire for eternal life and, under his instruction, devoted themselves to the service of the omnipotent Lord.

When his disciples repeatedly pressed him humbly to accept the properties that were being offered for the needs of the monastery,

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Longip., “indicated humbly”; Val. Cl., “entreated humbly.”]

he, a diligent guardian of his poverty, held firmly to this judgment, saying: “A monk who seeks possession on earth is not a monk.”

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Both Theod. and all the Norm. manuscripts, together with Germ., read “not possessions,” as in the printed editions. Saint Thomas, *Opusc.* 17, chs. 6, 14–16, and Saint Bonaventure, *Opusc.* 19, ch. 6, use this example of Isaac to commend the religious state of the poor. Nevertheless, monks who have been assigned possessions for the necessities of life are not to be condemned. Otherwise Gregory himself would not be free from blame, since he took care to enrich the monasteries he founded with sufficient revenues. [Col. 0246D]]

Thus he feared losing the security of his poverty just as greedy rich men are accustomed to guard their perishable wealth.

There his life became renowned through the spirit of prophecy and through great miracles among all who lived near and far away. One evening he had iron tools thrown into the monastery garden, tools that we commonly call spades. He said to his disciples: “Throw this many spades into the garden, and return quickly.”

That same night, when he had risen as usual with the brothers to offer praises to the Lord, he ordered them, saying: “Go and cook a meal for our workers, so that it may be ready first thing in the morning.”

When morning came, he had the meal he had ordered prepared carried out. Entering the garden with the brothers, he found as many workers laboring there as he had ordered spades to be thrown into it. They had entered as thieves, but, their minds changed by the Spirit, they seized the spades they found and, from the hour when they entered until the man of God came to them, cultivated all the uncultivated spaces of that garden.

As soon as the man of God entered, he said to them: “Rejoice, brothers; you have worked hard. Now rest.” He immediately gave them the food he had brought and refreshed them after the fatigue of such labor. When they had been sufficiently restored, he said: “Do not do evil. Whenever you want something from the garden, come to the garden entrance, ask calmly, receive it with a blessing, and cease from the wickedness of theft.”

He immediately ordered vegetables to be gathered and had them loaded onto the men. Thus it happened that those who had come to harm the garden returned filled and unharmed, with the reward of their labor.

[Col. 0248A] At another time some travelers came to him asking for mercy. They were clothed in torn garments and covered with rags, so that they appeared almost naked. When they asked the man of God for clothing, he silently heard their words. He immediately called one of his disciples privately and ordered him, saying: “Go and look in that forest, in such-and-such a place, for a hollow tree; bring me the clothing you find in it.”

The disciple went away, searched for the tree as instructed, found the clothing, and secretly brought it to his master. The man of God received it, showed it to the naked travelers who had asked for clothing, and gave it to them, saying: “Come, since you are naked. Here—take these and clothe yourselves.”

When they looked at them, they recognized the clothing they themselves had put there and were struck with great shame. Those who had deceitfully sought another’s clothing received their own back in confusion.

At another time a certain man, commending himself to Isaac’s prayers, sent him through a boy two baskets full of food. The boy stole one of them and hid it along the road, but delivered the other to the man of God and related the request of the one who had commended himself to him by this gift.

The man of God received it kindly and admonished the same boy, saying: “We give thanks, but take care: do not rashly dare to touch the basket that you placed along the road, because a serpent has entered it. Be careful, lest, if you try to take it up thoughtlessly, you be struck by the serpent.”

At these words the boy was deeply ashamed. He rejoiced that he had escaped death, but for a little while he became sad,

[Note: [Col. 0248D] Longip. and many Norm. manuscripts, “became exceedingly sad.”]

because, although he had undergone a salutary punishment, he had nevertheless suffered the exposure of his shame. Returning to the basket, he watched carefully and anxiously, and found that, just as the man of God had foretold, a serpent held it.

This man, therefore, was endowed beyond comparison with the power of self-restraint, contempt for passing things, the spirit of prophecy, and steadfastness in prayer. Yet one thing appeared blameworthy in him: he sometimes possessed such great joy that, unless one knew him to be filled with so many virtues, one would not have believed it at all.

[Col. 0248D] PETER. What, I ask you, are we to say this was? Did he voluntarily loosen the reins of his joy, or, though strengthened by so many virtues, was his mind drawn—even against its will—toward present delight?

[Col. 0249A] GREGORY. Great, Peter, is the dispensation of the omnipotent God. It often happens that, while granting certain people greater goods, he permits some lesser faults to remain in them, so that their minds always have something by which they ought to reproach themselves. Thus, while they desire to be perfect but cannot be, and labor over what they have not received without prevailing through their labor, they do not exalt themselves over what they have received; rather, they learn that they do not possess the greater goods from themselves,

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Secundus Aud., “gifts.”]

since they cannot conquer even small and insignificant faults in themselves.

For this reason, when the Lord had brought the people into the promised land and destroyed all their powerful and mighty adversaries, he preserved the Philistines and Canaanites for a longer time, so that, as it is written, Israel might be tested by them (Judg. 3:4). For, as has been said, he sometimes leaves certain small reprehensible faults even in those to whom he grants great gifts, so that they always have something against which to wage war and, after conquering great enemies, do not lift up their minds when even the smallest adversaries still weary them.

Thus, in a wondrous way, one and the same mind flourishes in virtue and grows weary through weakness. It sees itself built up in one respect and again laid waste in another, so that, through the good it seeks but cannot attain, it may humbly preserve what it possesses.

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Bigot. and Becc., “partly constructed and partly see itself destroyed.”]

But why should it surprise us to say this about a human being, when that heavenly region itself suffered losses in part among its citizens and stood firm in part, so that the chosen angelic spirits, seeing others fall through pride, might stand all the more strongly because they stood more humbly? That region benefited from its own losses and was more solidly established for the condition of eternity through the destruction of part of it.

So it also happens in each soul: through a small loss it is sometimes preserved for great gains, as a safeguard of humility.

PETER. I approve what you say.

---

## Chapter XIV. On Isaac, a prophetic abbot near Spoleto, of Syrian origin

[Col. 0243A]

[Col. 0243B] In the ancient times of the Goths, near the city of Spoleto,

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Manuscript: “there was a certain very devout citizen.”]

there was a man named Isaac, exceedingly venerable in his way of life. He survived even to the last times of the Goths. Many of our people knew him, but above all the holy virgin Gregoria, who now lives in this city of the Romans near the venerable church of the holy Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God.

When, in the time of her youth, she had been betrothed to a man and the marriage had already been arranged, she took refuge in the church and, desiring the holy manner of life of a solitary, was defended by this man and, with the Lord’s favor, brought to the habit she desired. Leaving her earthly bridegroom, she was deemed worthy to be betrothed to the heavenly Bridegroom.

[Col. 0243C] I heard the venerable Father Eleutherius explain many things about this holy man. He possessed great openness toward him and knew him very well. His manner of life lent credibility to his words.

This exceedingly devout Isaac was not from Italy; rather, I am recounting those miracles of his which he performed while living in Italy.
