When he first came from the regions of Syria and arrived at the city of Spoleto, he entered the church and asked the resident custodians to grant him as much freedom as he wished for prayer and not to force him to leave during the secret hours.

[Col. 0243D] He stood in prayer and continued praying throughout the entire day, joining the following night to his prayer. Likewise, on the second day and the following night he remained in prayer without weariness, and in the same way joined the third day to his prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Manuscript: “in the …”; and shortly afterward, “when he saw him.”]

One of the resident custodians saw this. Inflated by the spirit of pride, he brought upon himself the penalty of failure precisely where he ought to have advanced. For he began, with contemptuous words, to call him a pretender and an impostor—

[Note: [Col. 0243D] Manuscript: “to call him.”]

one who had displayed himself praying for three days and nights for the sake of show before the eyes of men.

After saying this, he hurried away, struck the man of God with a slap, and intended that the pretender to a devout life should leave the church in disgrace.

[Col. 0246A] But suddenly an evil spirit entered him in vengeance for the servant of God, threw him down at Isaac’s feet, and began to cry out through his mouth: “Isaac is driving me out.”

No one knew by what name the foreign man had been called, but the evil spirit revealed his name and cried out that it could be driven out by him.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Manuscript: “it cried out.”]

Immediately the man of God bent over the body of the afflicted man and, by the power of the Lord Jesus, drove out from him the evil spirit that had come upon him.

When the miracle that had occurred in the church became known throughout the city, men and women, noble and common alike, began to hurry together, each trying to seize him first for his own house.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Manuscript: “to seize him in his own house.”]

Some promised to offer fields for establishing a monastery for him; others wished to provide money and expenses for his support.

But the servant of the omnipotent God would not accept anything whatsoever from them and left the city. Not far away he found a deserted place and built himself there a dignified cell.

Many people went to him. Following his example, they began to be inflamed with a desire for eternal life, and under his instruction devoted themselves to the service of the omnipotent God.

His disciples began humbly to entreat him to accept, for the needs of the monastery, the money that was being offered to him.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Manuscript: “possessions.”]

But he firmly guarded the rule of his poverty, saying: “A monk who seeks property on earth is not a monk.”

Thus he feared losing his concern for his own poverty just as avaricious rulers are accustomed to preserve perishable wealth by guarding it.

There he was adorned with the spirit of prophecy, and the splendor of his life became known to all who lived nearby and at a distance through his miracles.

One day toward evening, in the monastery garden, he had an iron tool called a *lisgarion* thrown down.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Manuscript: *lisgar*; and shortly afterward, “as many *lisgaria* … into the garden.”]

Then he said to his disciples: “Go, throw the *lisgaria* that you have into the garden, and return quickly.”

That night, when he had risen as usual to send up the morning hymns to the Lord with the brothers, he ordered them, saying: “Go and cook food for our workers, so that it will be ready in the morning.”

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Manuscript: “with the tools … so that in the morning …”]

When day had come, he had the food that he had ordered prepared carried out and entered the garden with the brothers. He found as many workers laboring in the garden as he had ordered *lisgaria* to be thrown there.

[Col. 0245] They had entered as thieves, but, their intention having been changed by the Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 0246D] The manuscript adds: “of the saint.”]

they seized the *lisgaria* they found and, from the very hour when they entered the garden until the servant of God came to them, did not cease working. They worked all the vegetables in the garden that had not been cultivated.

[Note: [Col. 0246D] “*Lasanion* properly signifies a vegetable, *lachanon*. Favorinus: “*Lasania* in Greek are vegetable beds.” In the Codex Regius one reads *lasania, prasiai* (perhaps *prasiai*), “the things that are not …” However the passage is read, Zacharias differs from Gregory and understands vegetables, referring to the uncultivated areas of the garden mentioned by the holy Doctor. The Greek words may be explained as follows: “By digging they worked the vegetables and cultivated what was needed.”]

The man of God entered among them and said: “Rejoice, brothers; now stop, for you have worked very hard.”

He brought food and, after such great labor, made them glad with it. When they had eaten their fill, he said to them: “Do not wish to do evil any longer. If you have need of anything from the garden, come freely through the entrance, ask for it, and receive it with a blessing; but desist from the sin of theft.”

Immediately he ordered vegetables to be gathered and had them loaded onto the men. Thus it happened that those who had come to the garden to steal returned filled and unharmed, together with the reward for their labor.

[Col. 0247A] At another time some strangers came to him seeking alms, clothed in ragged garments, so that they appeared naked. While they were asking him for clothing and speaking secretly among themselves, the man of God heard them. He called one of his disciples and privately ordered him, saying:

“Go into that forest, to such-and-such a place, and you will find a hollow tree. Search inside it and bring me whatever clothing you find there.”

The brother went away as instructed, searched, and found the tree and the clothing. He brought these and privately gave them to his master.

The man of God received them and gave them to the strangers who, pretending to be naked, had asked for clothing, saying to them: “Since you are naked, take these and clothe yourselves.”

When they saw them and recognized that they were the things they had hidden,

[Note: [Col. 0248D] Manuscript: “they are; and, realizing it, the greatest … seized them.”]

great shame overtook them. While they had deceitfully sought another’s clothing, they received their own back in disgrace.

At another time a certain man, commending himself to Isaac’s prayers, sent him two baskets full of loaves. The same boy hid one of them along the road, but brought the other to the man of God and announced the request of the sender, who was commending himself to Isaac’s prayer through these gifts.

The man of God received them cheerfully and admonished the same boy, saying: “I give thanks, but look to the basket that you placed along the road. Do not dare to approach it rashly; rather, do so carefully, because a serpent has entered it. If you wish to lift it thoughtlessly, you are going to be bitten by the serpent.”

At these words the boy was deeply ashamed, but rejoiced again that he had escaped death. Although he became gloomy for a little while because of his shame, nevertheless he accepted this salutary chastisement.

Returning to the basket, he found, just as the man of God had foretold, that a serpent held it.

This man, therefore, illumined by the power of self-restraint and the grace of the prophetic spirit, having abandoned all passing things, was exceedingly steadfast in prayer and excelled greatly in this.

Yet one thing was regarded as blameworthy in him. Such constant joy was present in him that, unless one knew him to be filled with so many powers, one would in no way have believed it of him.

[Col. 0247D] PETER. What are we to say this was, I ask you? Did he, by his own choice, raise the rein of joy too loosely, or, as he increased in so many powers and his soul was illumined by them, was he drawn toward present joy?

[Col. 0250A] GREGORY. Great, Peter, is the dispensation of the omnipotent God. It often happens that, while granting some people great goods, he also permits small defects to remain in them, so that their soul may always have something by which it ought to humble itself.

Thus, insofar as they suppose themselves perfect yet find themselves to be in a state of deficiency, they labor in those things which they have not received. For, despite laboring through the achievements they have received, they cannot conquer their defects, so that they may not become proud. From this they recognize that they do not possess even the greatest virtues from themselves, since they cannot conquer small and insignificant faults.

Something similar is written in divine Scripture. When the Lord had brought the people of Israel into the promised land, he destroyed all their adversaries who possessed power and strength. But he preserved the Philistines and Canaanites for a time, so that, as it is written, Israel might be disciplined by them. For they did not always walk as had been said to them.

Therefore, to those to whom he had given the greatest gifts he left certain small defects, so that they might always have something with which they could wage war, and, when the greatest enemies had been conquered by them, might not be lifted up in their reasoning when even small adversaries still resisted them and afflicted them.

This happens in a wondrous way: one and the same mind flourishes in power but grows weak through weakness, so that it sees itself built up in part and again falling in part. Through the good it seeks to attain but cannot, it humbly preserves what it has.

Why should it be surprising if we say this about human beings, when the heavenly region itself endured partial loss among its citizens, while the others stood more firmly?

[Note: [Col. 0250D] Manuscript: “the heavenly choir.” The reading of the printed editions, which we have retained, agrees better with the Latin text: “that heavenly region.”]

For, while the chosen ranks of angels saw others fall through pride, they themselves became stronger in proportion as they stood more humbly. The loss of that homeland advanced it toward eternal establishment, and through partial destruction it was solidly renewed.

So it also happens in certain souls, that through a small loss they may arrive at the greatest gains while guarding humility.

PETER. I approve what you say.

---

## Chapter XV. On Eutychius and Florentius, servants of God

[Col. 0249C]

GREGORY. I must not be silent about something else that I learned from the account of the venerable priest Sanctulus, from the same region. You do not doubt his words, since you know his life and faith very well.

At the same time, in the region of Nursia, two men lived a life and followed a habit of holy conduct. One was called Eutychius, the other Florentius.

Eutychius had grown greatly in spiritual zeal and the fervor of virtue

[Note: [Col. 0249D] The printed editions read “had exercised himself,” against the manuscripts.]

and strove, by exhortation, to lead many souls to God. Florentius, however, led a life devoted to simplicity and prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: διήνυειν, “he spent/passed [his life].”]

Not far away there was a monastery that had been left without a superior after the death of its rector. The monks wished Eutychius to preside over them. He yielded to their prayers, governed the monastery for many years, and trained the souls of his disciples in the pursuit of holy conduct.

So that the oratory in which he had previously lived would not remain alone, he left the venerable Florentius there.

While Florentius was living there alone, one day he prostrated himself in prayer

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: “and he was praying to … God that he might … deem it worthy to grant him such [help] as he commands.”]

and asked the omnipotent Lord to deem it worthy to grant him some assistance for living there. As soon as he had completed his prayer, he left the oratory

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: “monastery.”] and found a bear standing before the doors.

When it lowered its head toward the ground

[Note: [Col. 0252D] Longip., “bowed its head.”]

and displayed no ferocity in its movements, it plainly indicated that it had come to serve the man of God, as the man of God immediately recognized.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: “But the man of God, having recognized this …”]

Since four or five sheep had remained in the same cell and there was absolutely no one to feed and guard them,

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: “the one feeding these or … having entrusted them, he ordered …”]

he entrusted them to the bear and ordered it, saying: “Go, drive these sheep out to pasture, and return at the sixth hour.”

[Note: [Col. 0252D] The sixth hour is noon; the ninth, three in the afternoon.]

It began to do this continually. The care of shepherding the sheep was entrusted to the bear, and the beast, while fasting, fed those whom it had been accustomed to eat.

[Note: [Col. 0251D] Manuscript: ἐθισθεῖσα, “having been accustomed.”]

When the man of God wished to fast, he ordered the bear to return with the sheep

[Note: [Col. 0252D] Manuscript: “together with the sheep.”]

at the ninth hour; when he did not wish to fast, at the sixth. The bear obeyed the man of God’s command in everything: when ordered to return at the sixth, it did not return at the ninth, nor, when ordered to return at the ninth, did it return at the sixth.

As this continued for a long time, the fame of such great virtue began to spread far and wide in that place.

But since the ancient enemy snatches the wicked through envy to punishment precisely where he sees the good attaining glory,

[Note: [Col. 0252D] Bigot. and Becc., “arrive.”]

four of the venerable Eutychius’s disciples became intensely envious because their master did not perform signs while the man whom he had left there alone appeared so renowned for this great miracle. They ambushed and killed the bear.

When it did not return at the hour at which it had been ordered, the man of God Florentius became suspicious. Waiting for it until the evening hour, he began to be distressed that the bear, which in his great innocence he was accustomed to call “sister,” had not returned.

The next day he went into the field to look for both the bear and the sheep and found the bear killed. After investigating carefully, he soon discovered by whom it had been killed. He then gave himself over to mourning, grieving more over the brothers’ wickedness than over the bear’s death.

The venerable man Eutychius drew him to himself and tried to console him. But the same servant of God, stirred by great pain in his presence, began to pray, saying: “I hope in the omnipotent God that, in this life, before the eyes of all, those who killed my bear, which had harmed them in no way, will receive the recompense for their wickedness.”

[Note: [Col. 0252D] Germ., “from the omnipotent God”; Secundus Aud., “in the omnipotent God.”]

Divine vengeance immediately followed his words. The four monks who had killed the bear were struck by elephantiasis, so that their limbs rotted and they died.

When this happened,

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Manuscript: “having happened.”]

the man of God Florentius was exceedingly terrified and feared that he had cursed the brothers. Throughout the whole of his life he never ceased to weep because he had been heard.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Manuscript: εἰς τὸν ἐκεῖνον, “into that …” (an incomplete or corrupt reading).]

He called himself cruel and declared himself a murderer in their deaths.

We believe that the omnipotent Lord did this so that this man of extraordinary simplicity, no matter how great the pain that moved him, would not again dare to hurl the dart of a curse.

[Col. 0253B] 312 PETER. Do we really believe it is very serious if, perhaps, in a fit of anger, we curse someone?

GREGORY. Why do you ask me whether this sin is serious, when Paul says: “Nor will the abusive possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10)? Consider, then, how grave is the fault that separates one from the kingdom of life.

PETER. What if a man, not out of malice but through carelessness of tongue, hurls a word of cursing at his neighbor?

GREGORY. If, Peter, an idle word is condemned before the strict Judge, how much more a harmful one? Consider, therefore, how deserving of condemnation is the person who is not free from malice, if even speech devoid of the usefulness of goodness is punishable.

PETER. I understand.

GREGORY. The same man of God did another thing that ought not to be passed over in silence. When his reputation had spread far and wide, a certain deacon who lived at a distance decided to go to him and commend himself to his prayers.

When he came to his cell, he found the entire area around it full of countless serpents. Greatly frightened, he cried out: “Servant of God, pray.”

At that time there was remarkable calm weather. Florentius came out, raised his eyes and palms toward heaven, and asked that the Lord remove that plague as he knew best.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The printed editions read λίμον, “famine,” by a manifest error.]

At his prayer the sky suddenly thundered, and that same thunder killed all the serpents that had occupied the place.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] Manuscript: “those serpents that had occupied the place.”]

When the man of God Florentius saw them lying dead, he said: “Behold, Lord, you have killed them; who will carry them away from here?”

Immediately, at his words, as many birds came as there had been dead serpents. Carrying them away one by one and throwing them at a distance, they made the place of his dwelling completely clean of serpents.

PETER. What virtue, what merit, are we to say he possessed, since the omnipotent God came so near to his mouth?

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Manuscript: “the omnipotent God became so swift [in answering].”]

GREGORY. Before the singular purity and simplicity of the omnipotent God, Peter, the purity and simplicity of the human heart have great power. For the servants of God, separated from earthly activities, do not know how to speak idle words; nor do they permit their minds to be scattered or polluted through speech. Thus, more than others, they obtain a hearing from their Maker, since, insofar as possible, they strive to conform to him through the purity and simplicity of their thoughts.

But we, mixed into the crowds of the world, often speak idle words and sometimes even gravely harmful ones.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The printed editions add “also,” which is more serious.] Our mouth becomes as distant from the omnipotent God as it becomes close to this world. We are dragged far downward when, through continual speech, we mingle with worldly people.

Isaiah expressed this well after he had seen the King, the Lord of hosts. He reproached himself and repented,

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Manuscript: ἐταλάνιζε, “lamented himself” or “called himself wretched.”]

saying: “Woe is me, for I have been silenced, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. 6:5). He showed why he had unclean lips

[Note: [Col. 0255D] The printed editions read “showed”; Compend., “appeared.”]

when he added: “I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips” (ibid.).

He grieved that he possessed the uncleanness of lips, but he indicated where he had contracted it when he declared that he dwelt in the midst of a people having unclean lips. For it is exceedingly difficult for the tongue of worldly people not to pollute the mind that it touches. When we condescend to them in certain conversations, and, becoming accustomed to this little by little, continue to enjoy speech that is unworthy of us, we eventually no longer wish to return from it—the speech to which we came unwillingly, as though led there by condescension.

Thus it happens that we pass from idle words

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Manuscript: “and [to] harmful [words] … to serious [ones].”]

to harmful ones and from light words to more serious ones. Our mouth is heard less and less by the omnipotent Lord in prayer, the more it is polluted by foolish speech, because, as it is written: “He who turns his ear away from hearing the law,

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Manuscript: “from not hearing.”]

his prayer will be rejected” (Prov. 28:9).

Why then should it be surprising if we are heard slowly by the Lord when we ask him for something, since we hear the Lord who commands us

[Note: [Col. 0255D] Manuscript: “who commands.”]

either slowly or not at all? And why should it be surprising that Florentius was heard more quickly in his prayer, since he obeyed the Lord’s commands more quickly?

[Col. 0256D] PETER. There is nothing that can be offered in reply to such an evident argument.

GREGORY. Eutychius, who had been Florentius’s companion on the Lord’s way, became more renowned after death through the power of signs.

[Note: [Col. 0256D] The printed editions have “became more renowned after death.” Many churches in Italy are consecrated to God under the name of Saint Eutychius or Eutycius. See Bollandus, May 23. Saint Florentius is counted among the patrons of the episcopal church of Foligno in Umbria, where he lies.]

For although the citizens of that city are accustomed to recount many miracles about him, this is the chief: until the times of the Lombards, the omnipotent God deigned continually

[Note: [Col. 0258D] Manuscript: εὐδόκει, “was pleased” or “deigned.”]

to work through his garment.

Whenever rain was lacking and prolonged drought scorched the earth with excessive heat, the citizens of that city would assemble, lift up his tunic,

[Note: [Col. 0258D] Consult what we noted on this word above, book I, chapter 9, col. 190, note λ (for us, col. 198, note i).]

and offer it before the Lord with prayers. As they went through the fields praying with it, rain was suddenly granted, enough to saturate the earth fully.

From this it became clear how much power and merit

[Note: [Col. 0258D] Manuscript: “holiness.”]

his soul possessed within, since the garment displayed outwardly turned away the wrath of the Creator.

---

## Chapter XVI. On Martin, a monk of Mount Marsicus

[Col. 0257A] Recently, in a part of Campania, a man named Martin, greatly venerable, led a solitary life on Mount Marsicus. For many years he was enclosed in a very narrow cave.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] He was received among the saints and commemorated on October 24.]

Many of our people knew him and had witnessed his deeds. I learned much about him from the accounts of the late Pope Pelagius, my predecessor,

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Pelagius II, who assumed the papacy in the year 579.]

and from those of other deeply religious men.

His first miracle was this: as soon as he entered the opening of the mountain mentioned above, a drop of water burst forth from that same rock, which had hollowed itself out into a narrow cave. It was sufficient for Martin, the servant of God, for daily use—neither was there more than enough nor was there less than necessity required.

By this the omnipotent God showed how much care he took for his servant, providing him in solitude with drink from the hardness of a rock, after the ancient miracle (Num. 20).

[Col. 0257D] 316 But the ancient enemy of the human race, envious of his strength,

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The printed editions read “of his virtues,” contrary to all our manuscripts.]

tried by his customary art to drive him from that cave. For, entering in the form of a beast dear to him—namely, a serpent—

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Primus Carnot., “with the beast dear to him, namely, a serpent, having entered.”]

he attempted to expel him from that dwelling by causing terror.

The serpent began to come alone into the cave to be alone with the solitary man; when Martin was praying, it would lie down before him, and when he lay down, it would lie down beside him.

But the holy man, completely unafraid, would extend his hand or foot toward its mouth, saying: “If you have received permission to strike, I do not forbid you.”

When this continued for three years without interruption, one day the ancient enemy, overcome by such courage, roared, and the serpent threw itself down the steep side of the mountain into the abyss. As it departed, it burned all the bushes of the place with the flame that came forth from it.

By burning the entire side of the mountain, it was compelled by the omnipotent God to show how great had been the power of the one by whom it had been defeated and driven away.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Some manuscripts read “from whom, having been defeated, he departed”; others, “who, having been defeated, departed.” The Germanensis has the latter among others. The Greek interpreter has the same reading.]

Consider, I ask you, on what summit of the mind this man of God stood, who lay secure with a serpent for three years.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] The editors changed *mentis* (“of the mind”) to *montis* (“of the mountain”), contrary at least to the evidence of our manuscripts.]

[Col. 0260A] PETER. I tremble to hear it.

GREGORY. At the beginning of his time of enclosure, this venerable man resolved that he would no longer see a woman—not because he despised the sex, but because, having observed the appearance of temptation, he feared falling into vice.

When a certain woman heard this, she boldly climbed the mountain and shamelessly rushed to his cave. But when he saw her from a little distance and noticed the woman’s clothing as she approached him, he devoted himself to prayer, pressed his face to the ground, and lay prostrate until the shameless woman, exhausted from waiting at the window of his cell, withdrew.

On that same day, as soon as she descended from the mountain, she ended her life. From the sentence of her death it was made clear that she had gravely displeased the omnipotent God by distressing his servant through her brazen audacity.

Source preparation: Embedded Greek and Latin textual apparatus retained with English glosses; the incomplete repeated Greek boundary heading is explicitly preserved.

At another time, while many people were hastening to him with religious devotion, and the path leading those who hurried to his cell along the steep side of the mountain was narrow, a little boy, walking carelessly, fell from that same mountain and plunged all the way down to the valley which lies beneath it and appears, from above, as though in a depth. For in that place the mountain rises to such a height that the enormous trees growing up from the valley below seem, to those looking down from the mountain, to be mere shrubs. [Note: The Vallicellensis and Longipontanus manuscripts read “thickets” (*frutecta*).] All who were coming were therefore thrown into confusion, and the greatest care was taken to search everywhere for the body of the fallen boy. Who could have thought anything other than that he was dead? Who could even have imagined that his body had reached the ground intact, when, with cliffs everywhere intervening, it might have been torn to pieces? [Note: The first manuscript of Gembloux reads “while obstacles were placed.”] Yet, when the boy was sought, he was found in the valley not only alive but unharmed.

Then it became plainly evident to everyone that he could not have been injured because Martin’s prayer had borne him up in his fall. Above his cave, moreover, there projected a great rock, which, although it seemed attached to the mountain by only a small part, overhung Martin’s cell and threatened every day to fall, bringing about both its own collapse and his death. Mascator, the nephew of the illustrious Armentarius, came with a great multitude of peasants and begged the man of God [Note: Longipontanus reads “that they themselves” (namely, the peasants) “might be able,” and so forth. The following readings—“while the crowd which had come was attempting,” and “the mass itself which they were trying to tear away”—confirm the Longipontanus reading.] to be willing to leave that cave, so that he himself might be able to tear the rock that was about to fall away from the mountain, and God’s servant might then dwell safely in his cave. [Note: The printed editions read “Mascator, an illustrious man, the grandson of Armentarius,” and so forth.] Since the man of God would not agree to this at all, he nevertheless ordered him to do what he could, while he himself withdrew to a more remote part of his cell. If the enormous mass had fallen, there was no doubt that it would have destroyed the cave as well and killed Martin.

While the crowd that had come was attempting, if possible without endangering the man of God, to lift the huge stone that hung above them, an astonishing event suddenly occurred before everyone’s eyes. The mass they were trying to tear away was suddenly wrenched loose by those same laboring men; and, so that it would not touch the roof of Martin’s cave, it leapt aside and fell farther away, as though fleeing from harm to God’s servant. Anyone who faithfully believes that all things are ordered by divine providence understands that this happened at the command of almighty God through angelic service. [Note: The Compendium reads “here, when he first came.” Both Theodorus manuscripts read “here, when he first …”]

When he first withdrew to that same mountain, while he was not yet living in a closed cave, he fastened an iron chain to his foot and attached it at the other end to a rock, so that he would not be able to go farther than the length of that chain allowed. When the venerable Benedict, whose memory I mentioned earlier, heard of this, he arranged to send him a message through one of his disciples: “If you are a servant of God, let not a chain of iron hold you, but the chain of Christ.” [Note: [Col. 0261D] This refers, of course, to Benedict mentioned throughout Book II.] [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “he fastened an iron chain to his foot.”]

At these words Martin immediately released the fetter from his foot. Yet afterward he never extended his freed foot beyond the place to which he had been accustomed to extend it when it was chained; and without a chain he restrained himself within as small a space as that in which he had previously remained while bound. Afterward, when he had shut himself up in the cave of that place, he also began to have disciples. They lived apart from his cave and used to draw water from a well for their daily needs. But the rope from which the bucket hung for drawing water frequently broke. Therefore Martin’s disciples asked for the same chain that the man of God had released from his foot, attached it to the rope, and fastened the bucket to it. From that time onward, although the rope was soaked with water every day, it never broke in any way. For when that rope touched the chain of the man of God, it too drew into itself the strength of iron, so as to bear the water. [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “for drawing up the water.”]

**Peter:** These deeds please me because they are marvelous, and greatly because they are recent.

## Chapter XVI. Concerning Martin, the monk who lived on Mount Marsia

[Col. 0258A]

**Gregory:** In the regions of Campania, on the mountain called Marsia, there lived a man named Martin, exceedingly reverent, who led a solitary life and for many years shut himself away in a very narrow cave. Many people, including some of our own acquaintances, knew him and witnessed his deeds in person. I myself learned much about him from the accounts of Pelagius, my predecessor, whose memory is blessed, and from the narratives of other earnest men. [Note: The manuscript reads “my predecessor.”]

They first related this miracle about him, saying that when he shut himself in the cave of the aforesaid mountain, moisture issued from the rock in just such quantity as was sufficient for Martin, the servant of God, for his daily needs: no more was added, nor did it fail when he was in need. In this event almighty God showed how great a care he had for his servant. For, as in the ancient miracle in the wilderness, he supplied this man with drink from the dryness of a stone.

But the ancient enemy of the human race, jealous of Martin’s virtues, struggled by his customary art to drive him from the cave. [Note: [Col. 0258D] The manuscript reads ἀρχέκακος (*archekakos*, “the primeval evil one”) for “ancient enemy.”] Entering into a serpent, his familiar beast, he tried to terrify him, thinking that through fear he might expel him from his cave-dwelling. Thus the serpent began to be found in the cave, alone with the solitary man. While the saint was praying, the serpent stretched itself out before him. Whenever Martin bent over, it likewise bent over with him. [Note: The manuscript reads “like him.”] This holy man therefore remained utterly fearless and placed his hand, or even his foot, before the serpent’s mouth [Note: The manuscript reads “offered/presented” (*paretithei*).], saying: “If you have received permission to harm me, I do not prevent you.”

While this continued without interruption for three years, one day the ancient enemy, overcome by such patience and strength, roared, and the serpent flung itself sideways down the precipice beneath the overhanging part of the mountain. All the forests of that place, and the entire side of the mountain, were scorched and withered by the flame issuing from it. Thus almighty God compelled it to reveal how great its power was, though, defeated and disgraced, it withdrew. [Note: The manuscript reads “having compelled.”] [Note: The printed editions read “Consider, then, their …”]

Consider, I beg you, at what height of mind this man of God stood, who lived without anxiety for three years with a serpent. [Note: The manuscript reads “dwelt with” (*synōikēsen*).]

[Col. 0259A]

**Peter:** I tremble at the mere hearing of it.

**Gregory:** During the first period of his life, when this venerable man shut himself in his cave, he resolved that henceforth he would not look upon a woman—not because he despised the female sex, but because he feared falling into the vice that might arise from contemplating beauty. A certain woman, hearing this, boldly climbed the mountain [Note: The manuscript reads “confidently/boldly.”] and shamelessly came to his cave. When he saw her approaching from a little distance and recognized from her clothing that she was a woman, he gave himself to prayer, lowered his face to the ground, and remained prostrate in prayer until that shameless woman, exhausted, withdrew from the window of his cell.

When she descended from the mountain, she died that same day. From the verdict pronounced through her death it became clear to everyone that she had greatly displeased almighty God by grieving his servant through such audacity.

[Col. 0259B]

At another time, while many were hastening to him for the sake of prayer and the path by which they climbed to him was extremely narrow—for it lay along the slope of the mountain and was very difficult to traverse until the top of the ascent, where his cell was situated—a respectable little boy, walking without fear, fell from the height of the mountain and was carried down to the valley lying beneath it. That valley is seen from the mountain’s height as though it lay in an abyss. For that mountain rises to such a height that the trees in the valley, although enormous, are thought by those looking down from the mountain’s summit to be mere shrubs.

All those who were coming were therefore thrown into confusion, and they began searching with the utmost care and concern for where they might find the body of the fallen boy. Who could have expected him to be found other than dead? [Note: The manuscript reads: “Who expected him to be found, unless dead?”] Or who could have supposed that his body would reach the valley intact rather than scattered by the violence of so great a fall? When they searched for the boy in the valley, they found him not only alive but entirely unharmed. Then it became evident to all that the boy had been preserved from injury in such a fall through the prayer of the exceedingly reverent Martin.

Above that same cave there projected a cliff, from which a fragment of rock could be seen hanging over Martin’s cell, threatening him every day with death and the cell with collapse. Mascator, the nephew of the illustrious Armentarius, came to him with a multitude of peasants and begged the man of God to be willing to leave the cave, so that he might, if he could, lift away the stone that had broken loose from the cliff and that God’s servant might thereafter live in that same cave without anxiety. But the man of God did not agree with him at all in this matter; nevertheless, he ordered him to do whatever he was able to do. He himself withdrew to the more private part of the cell.

There could be no doubt that, if the mass of that stone had fallen, it would have crushed the cell together with Martin and killed him. While the crowd that had come was struggling to lift the enormous stone leaning down from above, if they could do so without endangering God’s servant, an exceedingly marvelous event occurred before everyone’s eyes. The fragment of rock they were striving to tear away was suddenly pulled loose by the very men who were laboring; and, so that it would not come near the roof tiles of Martin’s cell, it fell at a distance, as though fleeing from harm to God’s servant. [Note: The manuscript reads “the roof tiles.”] Everyone who faithfully hopes that all things are governed by divine providence believes that this was accomplished by the command of almighty God through angelic service.

At the beginning, when he had given himself over to the mountain, although he was living in the cave and had not yet closed it, he bound his foot with an iron chain. [Note: The manuscript reads “while living in the cave itself, he fastened himself with a chain.”] He fixed the other end of it to a rock, so that thereafter he could not go out except as far as the length of the chain allowed. When the exceedingly reverent Benedict, a man of venerable life, heard this—he whose memory I mentioned above—he took care to make this known to him through one of his own disciples: “If you are a servant of God, let not an iron chain hold you, but the chain of Christ.” [Note: The manuscript reads: “If you are a servant … let not an iron chain hold you.”]

At these words Martin immediately released the chain from his foot. Yet afterward he never extended his freed foot beyond the place where he had been accustomed to extend it when it was bound; rather, without a chain, he allowed himself to go only as far as he had gone previously while chained.

Later, after he had shut himself in the cave, he began to receive disciples. They lived apart from his cave and drew water from a well for their own needs. [Note: [Col. 0262D] The manuscript reads παραμέρως (*paramerōs*, “apart”).] The rope to which the bucket was attached, by which they drew the water, repeatedly broke. [Note: The manuscript reads “the bucket.”] Therefore his disciples asked for the chain that the man of God had released from his foot and fastened it to the rope and the bucket. From that time onward, although the rope was soaked in water every day, it never again broke. For when that rope was fastened to the chain of the man of God, it drew the strength of iron into itself.

[Col. 0262C]

**Peter:** These miracles are exceedingly pleasing to everyone, and even more so because they have happened recently.

## Chapter XVII. Concerning the monk who came from Mount Argentarius and raised a dead man

[Col. 0261A]

**Gregory:** In our own times there was a man named Quadragesimus, a subdeacon of the Church of Buxentum, who used to pasture his flock of sheep in the region of Aurelia. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “Baxentinae”; nevertheless, “Buxentinae” should be read. Pliny mentions the people of Buxentum. Buxentum was formerly an episcopal city; now it is a town in Lucania commonly called Pisciotta. Others identify it with Polycastrum. It is thought to have received its name from the abundance of boxwood growing there.] [Note: [Col. 0262D] The Greek manuscript reads Βουζεντίας … αὐτοῦ … μέρεσιν Ἀβρελίας (*Bouzentias … autou … meresin Abrelias*, “of Bouzentia … his … in the regions of Abrelia”), and likewise below.] [Note: [Col. 0262D] Mount Argentarius is a mountain in Tuscany extending into the sea between the Port of Hercules and Telamon. Hence Rutilius writes, “Mount Argentarius is poured into the midst of the waves.” From this the editors infer that Aurelia was in Tuscany.]

Through the account of this very truthful man, an extraordinary event that had taken place secretly became known. [Note: Longipontanus alone reads: “the son of the mother, a poor woman, died” (*mulieris matris filius def.*; the abbreviated reading is uncertain).] As I said, while he was caring for his flock in Aurelia, there was a venerable man from the mountain called Argentarius, who outwardly displayed the monastic habit and fulfilled it in his conduct. Every year he used to come from that same Mount Argentarius to the church of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; and, as Quadragesimus himself related, he stayed with this subdeacon for the sake of hospitality.

One day, when he had entered his host’s house, which was not far from the church [Note: Longipontanus and the second Theodorian manuscript read “which he had.”], the husband of a very poor woman died nearby. They washed him according to custom, clothed him, and wrapped him in a linen cloth, but, evening having arrived, they were unable to bury him. [Note: Gilot and most printed editions read *sabbato*; the manuscripts require *sabano*. *Sabanum* means the same as *linteum*, “linen cloth”; see Cange in both Glossaries, Hugo Menard’s notes on the Book of Sacraments (note 326) and *Concordia Regularum*, pp. 610 and 896, and Ruinart’s notes on Victor of Vita, p. 191.] [Note: [Col. 0263D] The Greek manuscript reads ἀμφιάσαντες καὶ τῷ Σαμβάνῳ περικλύσαντες (*amphiasantes kai tō Sambanō periklysantes*, “having clothed him and enclosed him in the burial cloth”); the last word may be περικλείσαντες (*perikleisantēs*, “having enclosed”).] The widowed woman therefore sat beside the dead man’s body, spending the night in great weeping and giving expression to her grief through continual cries of lamentation.

When this continued for a long time and the woman did not cease weeping, the man of God, who had been received as a guest, was moved with compassion and said to the subdeacon Quadragesimus: “My soul sympathizes with this woman’s grief. I beg you, rise, and let us pray.”

They both went to the nearby church and devoted themselves together to prayer. When they had prayed for a long time, the servant of God asked the subdeacon Quadragesimus to bring the prayer to an end. [Note: The first Theodorian manuscript reads “wished the prayer to be completed by the subdeacon.”] When this had been done, he gathered dust from the steps of the altar and, together with Quadragesimus, approached the dead man’s body. There he again gave himself to prayer. [Note: [Col. 0263D] At the second prayer the Greek manuscript reads ἐπιτεθῆναι (*epitethēnai*, “to be brought to completion”).]

After he had prayed for a long time, he no longer, as before, wished the prayer to be completed by the subdeacon. Instead, he himself gave the blessing and immediately rose. Since he was carrying in his right hand the dust he had gathered, he removed with his left the linen cloth covering the dead man’s face. When the woman saw this, she began vehemently to protest and to wonder what he intended to do.

After removing the cloth, he rubbed the dead man’s face for a long time with the dust he had gathered. As he continued rubbing, the dead man recovered his soul, yawned, opened his eyes, raised himself, and sat up. [Note: The reading may be corrupt; perhaps “he sat up” (*anekathisen*).] He was astonished at what had happened to him, as though he had been awakened from a very deep sleep.

When the woman, exhausted by lamentation, saw this, she began to weep still more from joy and to cry out even louder. The man of God restrained her gently, saying: “Be silent, be silent. But if anyone asks you how this happened, say only this: ‘The Lord Jesus Christ has performed his work.’” [Note: The manuscript adds “among you.”]

Having said this, he left the house, immediately departed from the subdeacon Quadragesimus, and was never seen again in that place. [Note: The manuscript’s preferable reading is: “Having said this to them, he went out.”] For, fleeing temporal honor, he arranged that he should never again be seen in this life by those among whom he had been witnessed performing so great a miracle. [Note: The manuscript adds “among them.”]

**Peter:** I do not know what others may think, but I consider this a greater miracle than all the others: that the dead return to life and that their souls are secretly summoned back to their bodies.

**Gregory:** If we attend only to visible things, we must indeed believe that way. But if we weigh invisible things, it is plainly evident that it is a greater miracle, through the preaching of the word and the consolation of prayer, to convert a sinner than to raise a dead man in the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0265D] The Greek manuscript reads ὑπὲρ τὸ ἐν σαρκί (*hyper to en sarki*, “beyond what is in the flesh”) in this comparison.] In the one case, the flesh is restored to life only to die again; in the other, the soul is raised to live forever.

Let me set before you two persons, so that you may understand in which of them the miracle was accomplished by greater power: Lazarus, whom we believe had already become faithful, whom the Lord raised bodily from the dead, and Saul, whom he raised inwardly from sin. [Note: The manuscript reads “raised Lazarus, or Saul.”] After Lazarus’s bodily resurrection, nothing is said about his virtues. But after the resurrection of Paul’s soul, our weakness cannot contain how many virtues he performed in sacred discourse. [Note: The manuscript reads “in sanctified discourse … which our weakness …”]

How were his most savage thoughts transformed into the tender entrails of piety? How did he desire to die for his brothers, whose death he had previously rejoiced in? How, filled with knowledge of all Scripture, did he judge that he knew nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified? How willingly was he scourged with rods for Christ, whom previously he had pursued with swords? [Note: The manuscript reads “whom formerly he pursued.”] Though exalted by the dignity of the apostolate, how did he voluntarily become a little child in the midst of the disciples? How was he raised to the mysteries of the third heaven? Yet through compassion he bent the eye of his mind toward arranging the marriage bed of married people, saying: “Let the husband render the debt owed to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:3). [Note: The manuscript reads “and he himself …”]

He was mingled in contemplation with the company of angels, yet did not disdain to consider and arrange the affairs of those who live according to the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0266D] The Greek manuscript reads πλὴν οὐ παραιτεῖται (*plēn ou paraiteitai*, “yet he does not refuse”).] He rejoiced in weaknesses and took pleasure in insults; for him to live was Christ, and to die was gain. And what he himself lived in the flesh was already outside the flesh.

See, then, how he lives who has returned from the hell of the mind to the life of compassion. [Note: The manuscript reads “from the inaccessible mind.”] It is therefore a very small miracle to raise someone in the flesh—unless, perhaps, through the quickening of the flesh he is also restored to the life of the mind, so that what is accomplished outwardly by a miracle may bring about his inward conversion and give him life. [Note: The manuscript reads “so that the same may happen to him.”]

**Peter:** I had believed this to be far inferior, but now I have recognized how incomparably greater it is than that. Yet, I beg you, continue the account you began, so that, while time is available, the hour may not pass without spiritual edification. [Note on the preceding list: Compendium, Chartres, the Theodorian manuscripts, Longipontanus, and Vallicellensis, together with the German manuscript, read “that those [thoughts] of his”; Gembloux and other Norman manuscripts, followed by the printed editions, read “that his, or even the most cruel, thoughts were transformed.” The manuscript note at the final comparison reads: “unless perhaps when through … [he] is restored.”]

## Chapter XVIII. Concerning Benedict the monk

[Col. 0265D]

**Gregory:** A certain brother lived with me in the monastery. He was exceedingly devoted to sacred Scripture, was older than I, and used to edify me concerning many things of which I was ignorant. From his account I learned that there was a man named Benedict in the region of Campania, within forty miles of the city of Rome. [Note: The Roman Martyrology mentions him on 23 March.] He was young in age but advanced in character, and firmly disciplined himself according to the rule of holy conduct. [Note: That is, “conversion” or “conduct”; the word is often used in this sense, especially in sacred books. See Galatians 1:13 and 1 Peter 2:12. In the manuscripts one word is also very often found in place of the other.]

In the time of King Totila, the Goths found him and sought to burn him together with his cell. They kindled a fire and set it around him; everything nearby burned, but the fire could not burn his cell. [Note: The Greek manuscript reads “they wished to burn him together with his cell.”] [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “but they could not burn his cell.”] When the Goths saw this and became even more savage, they dragged him from his dwelling. [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Greek manuscript reads ἐξεκαμφθέντες (*exekampthentes*, “having been bent aside”); the editors conjecture ἐξεκαυθέντες (*exekauthentes*, “having been inflamed”).] Not far away they saw a heated oven that had been prepared for baking bread. They threw him into it and closed the oven. But on the following day he was found so unharmed that not only had his flesh not been touched by the fire, but not even the edges of his clothing had been burned. [Note: The Greek manuscript reads “but not even the edges of his garments had been singed by flame.”]

**Peter:** I hear of the ancient miracle of the three young men who, thrown into the fire, were not harmed (Daniel 3).

**Gregory:** In my opinion, that miracle happened in one respect similarly, but in another respect differently. [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Greek manuscript reads τοῦτο (*touto*, “this”) in the comparison.] At that time the three young men were thrown into the fire with their hands and feet bound. On the following day the king searched for them and found them walking unharmed in the furnace, with their garments undamaged. From this it may be understood that the fire into which they had been thrown did not touch their clothing but consumed their bonds, so that at one and the same time the flame exercised its power in the service of the righteous for their comfort, but did not exercise it for their torment.

## Chapter XIX. Concerning the church of blessed Zeno the martyr at Verona, into which the waters flooding beyond the open door did not enter at all

[Col. 0268C]

A similar event, but in the opposite element, occurred in our own days in connection with this ancient miracle. John the tribune recently informed me about it in his own report. He said that Count Pronulphus, when he was there, testified that he had been with King Autharic at that time in the very place where the marvelous event occurred and had seen it himself. [Note: [Col. 0268D] The Beccensis and Bigotianus manuscripts read “when he had visited him” (*cum illum adiisset*).] [Note: The name of this king is written variously in the manuscripts: Autharius, Authoricus, Authalaricus, Autharic, and so forth. See Letter 17 of Book I. The manuscripts support the preceding wording; the printed editions read “and thence now [occupied] the greatest [districts].” Flaccus also testifies that the Tiber repeatedly rose in this fashion: “We saw yellow Tiber, with its waves violently turned back from the Tuscan shore, go forth, overthrowing the king’s monuments and the temples of Vesta” (*Odes* I.2).]

The aforesaid tribune related that about five years earlier, when the Tiber overflowed its bed at this city of Rome and rose so high that its waters poured over the city walls and then occupied the largest districts of the city, the river Athesis, swollen at Verona, reached the church of blessed Zeno, the martyr and bishop. [Note: [Col. 0267D] The Greek manuscript reads ὁ Τιβέρνις ποταμὸς τὸ ῥεῖθρον αὐτοῦ ὑπερβλύσας ἐξῆλθε· τοσοῦτον δὲ ὑπερηύξησεν, ὥστε ἐπάνωθεν (*ho Tibernis potamos to rheithron autou hyperblysas exēlthe; tosouton de hyperēuxēsen, hōste epanōthen*): “the river Tiber overflowed and left its channel; it rose so greatly that [the water came] over the walls.”] [Note: [Col. 0270D] It further reads ἐν αὐτῇ διεβάλλετο· τότε οὖν καὶ ἐν βηρόῃ τῇ πόλει ὁ σατέσις (*en autē dieballeto; tote oun kai en Bēroē tē polei ho Satēs*): “it spread through it; then also in the city of Beroē the Satēs [river rose].”] [Note: Zeno’s title of martyr is justly questioned; see above all Tillemont, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical History*, vol. III, under Saint Zeno.] Although the doors of that church were open, the water did not enter it at all. Rising little by little, it reached the church’s windows, which were close to the roof. [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Greek manuscript reads τῶν κεράμων (*tōn keramōn*, “the roof tiles”) for “the windows.”] There the water stood and closed off the church door, as though the liquid element had been transformed into the solidity of a wall.

Many people were inside, but the whole church was surrounded by the waters and they had no way to get out. [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Greek manuscript reads ὅθεν ἐξελθεῖν (*hothen exelthein*, “from where to go out”).] Fearing that they would perish there from thirst and hunger, they came to the church door and drew water to drink—the water which, as I said, had risen as high as the windows—yet it did not flow into the church in any way. [Note: Longipontanus, Vallicellensis, and the Compendium read “by the magnitude” of the waters.] Thus it could be drawn as water, but could not spread as water. Standing before the door, it displayed to everyone the merit of the martyr: it was water for their assistance, but was not water for invading the place. I have rightly said that this was not unlike the ancient miracle of the fire, which did not touch the garments of the three young men but consumed their bonds.

**Peter:** The deeds of the saints that you relate are exceedingly marvelous and deeply astonishing to the weakness of people today. But since I hear that so many men of wondrous virtue have recently lived in Italy, I should like to know whether they ever suffered the snares of the ancient enemy, or whether they grew through those very snares. [Note: The second manuscript of Chartres reads “and whether they advanced through the snares,” and so forth.]

**Gregory:** Without the labor of combat there is no prize of victory. [Note: The manuscript reads “the prize of victory” (*brabeion*) in place of “the palm.”] How, then, did they become victors unless they fought against the snares of the ancient enemy? For the evil spirit is always lying in wait for our thoughts, words, and deeds, seeking perhaps to find something by which he may appear as our accuser before the judgment of the eternal Judge. Do you wish to know how he is always present in order to deceive?

## Chapter XX. Concerning Stephen, a priest of the province of Valeria, from whose shins the devil pulled his boots

[Col. 0269C]

Some who are now with us bear witness to the event I am about to relate. [Note: Longipontanus and the two Theodorian manuscripts read “bear witness that a man venerable in life …”] A venerable man named Stephen was a priest of the province of Valeria and a close kinsman of our deacon Boniface, the administrator of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Greek manuscript reads τῷ βίῳ (*tō biō*, “in life”) in its description of Stephen.] [Note: There is information about him in the letters. We suspect that he is the man who is said to have been sent to Constantinople in Letter 40 of Book XIII, formerly Letter 47 of Book II; several letters addressed to him survive, as will be clear from the index.]

One day, after returning home from a journey, he carelessly addressed his servant and said: “Come, devil, take off my boots.” [Note: “Boots” may refer both to shoes and to leg-coverings; hence Acts 12:8: “Put on your boots,” where the Greek text has σανδάλια, “sandals.”] At his words, the straps of his boots immediately began to loosen with extraordinary speed, so that it became plainly evident that the devil himself, the one he had named, had obeyed him in taking off his boots.

As soon as the priest saw this, he was terrified and began to cry out in a loud voice: “Away, wretch, away! I was not speaking to you, but to my servant.” At his words the devil immediately departed, and the straps remained just as they had been found, already largely loosened. From this event it may be understood how greatly the ancient enemy, who is already present in bodily actions, lies in wait for our thoughts. [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Greek manuscript reads ἀρχαῖος (*archaios*, “ancient”) where its text has ἀρχέκακος (*archekakos*, “primeval evil one”).]

**Peter:** It is exceedingly difficult and frightening always to be vigilant against the enemy’s snares and to stand continually as though in battle formation. [Note: [Col. 0272D] Pratellensis reads “the snares of the faithless enemy.”]

**Gregory:** It will not be difficult if we attribute our protection not to ourselves but to heavenly grace, while nevertheless remaining watchful under its protection as far as we are able. [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Greek manuscript reads εἰς τὴν φυλακὴν καὶ σκέπην ἡμῶν γρηγ… (*eis tēn phylakēn kai skepēn hēmōn grēg…*, “under our protection and shelter let us keep watch”).] If the ancient enemy begins to be driven from the mind, divine generosity commonly brings it about that he should not only cease to be feared, but should himself be terrified by the virtue of those who live well. [Note: [Col. 0271D] The Greek manuscript reads ἀλλὰ καὶ μᾶλλον (*alla kai mallon*, “but also, rather”) in the final contrast.] [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “Labor is useful.”]

## Chapter XXI. Concerning the nun who drove out the demon

[Col. 0271B]

The most holy old man Eleutherius, whose memory I mentioned above in Chapter 14, was a witness to the event I am about to relate and took care to make it known to me. In the city of Spoleto there was a girl, already of marriageable age, the daughter of one of the city’s leading men. [Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads “a chaste noblewoman”; Beccensis reads *nobilis*, “noble,” in place of *nubilis*, “marriageable.” An older German reading has “who was already called nuptial,” the daughter of a nobleman.] She burned with desire for the heavenly life, but her father tried to resist her on the way of life. She disregarded her father and assumed the habit of holy conduct. [Note: The first manuscript of Chartres reads “she sought it.”]

For this reason her father disinherited her from his property and gave her nothing else except six ounces’ worth of a small estate. [Note: Vallicellensis reads “in six ounces.” Nearly all manuscripts read “with a gift” (*cum xenio*); see the note above at Chapter 12.] Many girls of noble birth, stirred by her example, began to convert under her influence and to serve the almighty Lord with a consecrated virginity.

One day the same Eleutherius, an abbot and venerable in life, came to her for exhortation and edification and sat conversing with her about the word of God. Suddenly a peasant came from the same small estate that she had received from her father as six ounces’ worth. As he stood before them, he was seized by an evil spirit, fell down, and began to exhaust himself with violent screeching and bleating.

Then the holy woman rose and, with an angry face, commanded him in a loud voice: “Come out of him, wretch; come out of him, wretch.” At her words the devil immediately answered through the mouth of the afflicted man: “Even if I come out of this man, into whom shall I enter?”

A little pig happened to be grazing nearby. Then the holy woman commanded: “Come out of him and enter this pig.” At once the devil came out of the man, entered the pig he had been ordered to enter, killed it, and departed.

**Peter:** I should like to know whether she ought at least to have granted the unclean spirit permission to enter the pig.

**Gregory:** The deeds of Truth provide rules for our conduct. For our Redeemer himself was addressed by the legion that held the man: “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of pigs” (Matthew 8:31). He expelled them from the man and permitted them to enter the pigs and drive them into the abyss.

From this it may also be understood that, without the permission of almighty God, the evil spirit has no power against a human being. He could not even enter the pigs unless permitted. We therefore must willingly submit ourselves to the one to whom all adversity is subjected against its will, so that we may be more powerful than our enemies to the extent that, through humility, we become one under the authority of the author of all things. [Note: [Col. 0273D] Pratellensis reads: “submit and entrust ourselves, subjecting all adversities, so that …” (*subdi et adversa omnia subjiciendo committere, ut tanta*, etc.).]

What is surprising, moreover, if the elect, while placed in the flesh, can perform many wondrous deeds, when even their dead bones often live on in many miracles?

[Boundary note: The supplied source ends after repeating the Greek heading for Chapter XXI: ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΚΑʹ. Περὶ τῆς μοναστρίας τῆς φυγαδευσάσης τὸν δαίμονα (“Chapter XXI. Concerning the nun who drove out the demon”).]

Concerning the matter which I am now relating, the most holy man Eleutherius the presbyter—of whom I made mention above—is a witness; indeed, he himself related it. For he said that in the city of Spoleto there was a certain girl, already of marriageable age but still a virgin, who was the daughter of one of the city’s leading men. [Note: The edition omits λοιπὸν τοῦ γάμου θυγάτηρ, “now a daughter of marriageable age,” along with other words that seem necessary for the sense.] Having been inflamed with longing for heavenly life, she hastened toward it with all eagerness. Her father, however, struggled to oppose her on the way of life. [Note: Manuscript: “against her most excellent resolve. But she …”] But she abandoned her father and adopted the habit of the monastic life. Consequently, her father, from his own estate, made her disinherited [Note: Manuscript: “without inheritance”], and left her nothing except six ounces of a small property.

Following her example, many girls of the noblest families began to renounce the world for her sake and to serve the almighty Lord in sanctified virginity. [Note: Manuscript: “in chastity.”] One day the same man, Eleutherius, most reverent in his manner of life, came to visit her for the sake of instruction and edification. While he was sitting with her and they were conversing about divine matters, a farmer came to her from the suburb where she had received the six ounces from her father, bringing a gift. While he was standing before them, he was suddenly struck by an evil spirit, fell down, and began to suffer terribly with loud cries.

Then that most holy woman rose [Note: Manuscript: “that virgin rose.”] and, with a stern face and a powerful voice, commanded the unclean spirit, saying: “Come out of him, wretched one; come out.” [Note: Thus the manuscript; the reading is sound.]

At her voice the devil answered through the mouth of the possessed man, saying: “And if I come out of him, into whom am I to enter?” [Note: Manuscript: “Now, by chance, a small pig was grazing nearby. And that most holy virgin …”]

As it happened, a noble pig was grazing nearby. That most holy woman then permitted him, saying: “Come out of him, and enter that pig.” Immediately he came out of the man, entered the pig into which he had been ordered to go, killed it, and departed.

[Col. 0274A] PETER. I should like to know precisely whether she ought to have granted the pig to the unclean spirit. [Note: Manuscript: “whether he ought.”]

GREGORY. The examples of the rule of life that we have proposed are deeds of Christ, the Truth. For when our Redeemer, God, expelled the legion from the afflicted man, the spirits begged him, saying: “If you cast us out, permit us to enter the herd of pigs.” Having cleansed the man, he allowed them to enter the pigs and drown them in the sea. From this it is shown that the evil spirit has no power against man without the permission of almighty God, since it had no power even over pigs without permission.

Therefore it is necessary for us to submit to him to whom all adversities, even against their will, are subjected. Thus we shall be as much stronger than our enemies as we become one with the ruler of all through humility. [Note: Manuscript: “with the almighty and ruler of all.”] What wonder, then, if the elect, while they still dwell in this flesh, can perform many miracles, when even the dead bones of some live with great miraculous power?

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the presbyter of the province of Valeria who invisibly held a thief at his tomb after death

[Col. 0273B]

In the province of Valeria the event I am relating took place, and I learned of it through the account of my abbot, Valention, of blessed memory. There was there a venerable priest who, together with his clerics, devoted to the praises of God and to good works, led a holy life. When the day of his calling came, he died and was buried in front of the church. Sheepfolds adjoined that church, and the place where he was buried was accessible to those going to the sheep. [Note: The earliest witnesses read: “was accessible for the same sheep to be entrusted to the keeping of the shepherds.”]

One night, while the clerics were chanting inside the church, a thief came to enter the folds and steal something. He took a ram and hurried out. But when he reached the place where the man of God was buried, he suddenly became stuck and could not move his feet. He laid the ram down from his neck and wanted to release it, but he could not loosen his hand. [Note: Gemet.: berbicem; hence the French word brebis.]

Thus the wretched man remained standing, guilty and bound, with his booty. He wanted to release the ram, but could not; he wanted to leave with the ram, but was unable. In a wondrous manner, the thief who had feared being seen by the living was held by the dead man. Since his steps and hands were thus fettered, he remained motionless. [Note: One manuscript reads “his steps and hands were bound.”]

When morning came and the praises of God had been completed, the clerics came out of the church and found an unknown man holding a ram in his hand. They wondered whether he was carrying off the ram or offering it, but the culprit quickly revealed the punishment brought upon him by his guilt. Everyone marveled that the thief, having entered the holy man’s domain, stood bound to his booty through the merit of the man of God.

They immediately devoted themselves to prayer for him and, through their prayers, scarcely managed to obtain that the man who had come to steal their property might at least be permitted to leave empty-handed. Thus the thief, who had stood captive for a long time with his booty, finally departed empty and free.

PETER. It is evident how great is the sweetness of almighty God toward us, since such delightful miracles are performed for our sake. [Note: Two manuscripts read: “how great are the sweetnesses of almighty God above us.”]

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the presbyter who invisibly held the thief after death in the region of Valeria

[Col. 0274B]

In the region of Valeria an event occurred which Valention, my superior, of blessed memory, explained to me and thereby made known. There was there a most reverent priest who, persevering with his clerics in the praise of God, in good works, and in holy conduct, completed his life. [Note: Manuscript: “he died.”] When the day of his calling came, he received the end of life and was buried in front of the church.

The sheepfolds approached the same church, and the place in which he was buried was a passage for those going to the sheep. One night, while the clerics were chanting inside the church, a thief came to the sheep. He entered the fold, seized a ram, and hurried out.

When he came to the place where the man of God was buried, suddenly his feet became stuck in the earth, and he could not move from the place. [Note: Manuscript: “his feet were stuck, and he could not leave the place.”] He lowered the ram from his shoulder, wishing to release it, but he could not loosen his hand. Thus he stood, wretched, bound by an invisible force and disgraced, with his stolen property.

He wished to release the ram but could not; he wished to leave with the ram but likewise could not. In a wondrous manner, the thief, who did not wish to be seen by the living, was invisibly held by the dead man. While his step remained fixed and his hand unmoving, morning came. When the hymns of God had been completed, the clerics came out of the church.

Finding an unknown man holding the ram in his hand, they were uncertain about him and wondered: “Did he take the ram, or is he bringing it as an offering?” But the guilty man quickly disclosed the truth. Everyone marveled that, through the holiness of the man of God, the one who had entered to steal stood bound to his stolen property.

They immediately gave themselves to prayer for him, asking that he be released. When their prayer was heard, the thief, who had stood for many hours with his booty like a captive, finally went out—empty, but nevertheless free. [Note: Manuscript: “empty.”]

PETER. It is plainly shown in what sweetness almighty God is disposed toward us, he who is pleased to bring about such pleasant miracles around us.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the abbot of Mount Praeneste and his presbyter

[Col. 0276A]

GREGORY. A mountain rises above the city of Praeneste, on which there is a monastery of the blessed Apostle Peter. [Note: Praeneste, now Palestrina, is an episcopal city of Latium, twenty-one Roman miles from Rome. Virgil mentions its former site on a mountain ridge, singing in Aeneid 7, “And the men of lofty Praeneste …”; it now lies at the foot of the mountain. Beccens. reads: “built in honor of Saint Peter.” Longip. and Val. Cl. read “is situated”; the two Gemet. witnesses likewise have “By the report of men of God, etc.”] It is inhabited by servants of God. Through the account of men of God, I happened to hear, while I was still at the monastery, the great miracle I am relating; [Note: Most manuscripts read positum rather than positus; despite grammatical considerations, no correction has been made, since Gregory often disregards grammatical rules.] the monks of that monastery testified that they knew it.

In that monastery there was a venerable father of holy life who nurtured a certain monk and brought him to reverent conduct. [Note: Theodorus reads: “advanced him in years.”] When he saw that the monk had grown in the fear of the Lord, he had him ordained presbyter in that same monastery. After his ordination, it was revealed to him that his departure from this life was not far away.

He asked the aforementioned father of the monastery to permit him to prepare a tomb for himself. The father answered him: “I shall certainly die before you, my son; nevertheless, go and prepare your tomb as you wish.” He therefore went away and prepared it.

Not many days later, the old father was seized by a fever and came to the point of death. With the presbyter standing beside him, he commanded him, saying: “Place me in your tomb.” When the presbyter replied, “You know that I am about to follow you, and that this tomb cannot contain us both,” the abbot immediately answered: “Do as I have said, because your tomb can contain us both.”

He died and was placed in the same tomb which the presbyter had prepared for himself. Soon afterward bodily illness also overtook the presbyter, and as the illness increased he quickly completed his life.

When the brothers had carried his body to the tomb he had prepared for himself, they opened the tomb, and all who were present saw that there was no place where he could be laid, because the body of the father of the monastery, which had been placed there earlier, occupied the entire tomb.

When the brothers who had brought the presbyter’s body saw the difficulty that had arisen concerning his burial, one of them cried out: “O Father, where is what you said—that this tomb would contain us both?”

At his words, suddenly, while everyone watched, the body of the abbot, which had previously been placed there and was lying on its back, turned onto its side and provided an empty place in the tomb for the burial of the presbyter’s body. Thus, because that place might contain them both, the dead man fulfilled what he had promised while alive.

But since this event I have mentioned took place near the city of Praeneste, in the monastery of the blessed Apostle Peter, do you wish to hear something also about the guardians of that apostle’s church in this city, where his most sacred body is laid?

PETER. I do, and I earnestly beg that you do so.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the abbot in the city of Praeneste and his presbyter

[Col. 0275A]

GREGORY. Above the city of Praeneste rises a mountain on which the monastery of the blessed Apostle Peter has been founded. [The Greek text is corrupt at this point.] Since servants of God lived there, and since I was present in my monastery, it happened that I heard from monks of the aforementioned monastery the great miracle I am relating; those same monks insisted that they knew it.

They said that their monastery had a superior, a man exceedingly reverent in his manner of life, who had brought up a certain monk and trained him in good character and great devotion. When he saw him growing greatly in the fear of the Lord, he had him ordained presbyter in his monastery.

After the man had been ordained, it was made known to him through a revelation that his departure from this life was near. He therefore asked the aforementioned father of the monastery to allow him to prepare a tomb for himself. The father replied: “I shall die before you, my child; nevertheless, go and prepare your tomb as you wish.”

He went away and made it ready. Not many days later, the father was seized by a fever and came to his final breath. While the presbyter stood beside him, he commanded him, saying: “Bury me in your tomb.”

The presbyter answered: “You know, Father, that I too shall follow you in these days, and the tomb cannot contain us both.” The superior said to him: “Do as I have told you, for your tomb has room for the two of us.” [Note: The edition reads: “the two of us.”]

He died, therefore, and was buried in the tomb which the presbyter had prepared for himself. Immediately bodily weakness also seized the presbyter, and in that illness he soon completed his life.

His body was carried by the brothers to the tomb which he had prepared for himself. When the tomb was opened, all who were present saw that there was no place in it capable of containing him also. For the body of the father of the monastery, which had been placed there, occupied the whole tomb.

The brothers who had brought the presbyter’s body, seeing the difficulty that had arisen concerning his burial, cried out. One of them said: “Ah, Father, where is what you said—that this tomb had room for the two of us?”

At his voice, while everyone watched, suddenly the body of the superior, which was lying there on its back, turned by itself onto its side [Note: Manuscript: “onto its flank”] and provided a place in the tomb where the presbyter’s body could be laid. [Note: Manuscript: “could be placed.”] What he had promised while alive, he fulfilled when dead: that place contained them both.

This miracle, then, which I have related, occurred in the city of Praeneste, in the monastery of the most blessed Apostle Peter. Would you like to hear another event that occurred in this city concerning the guardians of the church where his hallowed body lies?

[Col. 0278A] PETER. I very much wish this to happen, and I earnestly beg it.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Theodore, the church-warden of the church of the blessed Apostle Peter in the city of Rome

[Col. 0277B]

GREGORY. There are still some people who know Theodore, the guardian of that church. [Note: Theodore’s name appears in the Roman Martyrology on 26 December.] Through his account an event that happened to him became known, an event most worthy of remembrance. He said that one night, when he had risen early to trim the lamps near the door, he stood, as was customary, on the wooden steps placed beneath the lamp and tended its light.

Then suddenly the blessed Apostle Peter, dressed in a white robe, stood below him on the pavement and said to him: “My fellow freedman, why have you risen so early?” [Note: Or “fellow servant,” as many manuscripts read. The expression may mean “you who have obtained freedom together with me” or “you with whom I have been brought into freedom.” Zacharias renders it by σύντροφε, meaning “companion,” “fellow traveler,” or “table-companion.”]

After saying this, he vanished from the eyes of the one who was looking at him. Such fear then fell upon Theodore that all strength left his body, and for many days he was unable to rise from his bed.

What else did the blessed apostle intend by this event for those who serve him, except to show them the presence of his regard—that whatever they do out of reverence for him, he himself always sees without interruption as the reward of recompense?

PETER. I do not find it so remarkable that he was seen, but rather that the man who saw him, though healthy, became ill.

GREGORY. Why are you surprised at this, Peter? Has it slipped your mind that when the prophet Daniel saw that great and terrifying vision, and trembled because of it, he immediately added: “And I fainted and was ill for many days” (Daniel 8:27)? The flesh cannot receive the things that belong to the spirit. Therefore, whenever the human mind is led beyond itself to see something, this bodily vessel, which cannot bear the weight of a talent, must sometimes become weak. [Note: Some witnesses read “the spirit of God.”]

PETER. An open explanation has dissolved the difficulty in my thoughts.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Theodore, the church-warden of Saint Peter in Rome

[Col. 0278B]

GREGORY. Until the present there are still some who know Theodore, the guardian of the same church. Through his account an event that happened to him became known, a matter exceedingly worthy of remembrance.

He said that one night, when he had risen very early to clean the lamps near the door, and was standing, as was customary, on the wooden steps while tending the light of the lamps, he suddenly saw the blessed Apostle Peter standing beneath him in a white robe.
