He said to him: “Companion, why did you rise so early?”

After saying this, Peter became invisible to his eyes. Such fear fell upon him that all the strength in his body failed, and for many days he was unable to rise from his bed.

What else can be understood from this event except that the blessed apostle wished to show his servants the sight of his presence? Whatever they do out of reverence for him, he himself continually sees without delay and grants the reward of recompense.

PETER. It is truly remarkable that he was deemed worthy to see the apostle. But I am again amazed that the man who saw him, although he was healthy, became ill.

GREGORY. Why are you surprised at this event, Peter? Have you lost your reason? Did not the prophet Daniel tremble when he saw that great and terrifying vision? He himself says: “And I became ill for many days.” Flesh cannot contain the things of the spirit. Therefore, whenever the human mind is led outside itself in order to see something spiritual, it is absolutely necessary that this fleshly vessel become weak, since it cannot bear the weight of the talent.

PETER. The explanation laid open before me has set my difficulty in thought straight.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning Acontius, the church-warden of the same church of the blessed Peter

[Col. 0280A]

GREGORY. Not long ago, as our elders relate, there was another guardian of that church named Acontius, a man of great humility and gravity. [Note: A few witnesses read Abundius, followed by the printed editions; Abundius also occurs in the Greek version and is entered in the calendar of saints on 24 April.] He served almighty God so faithfully that the blessed Apostle Peter himself showed by signs what esteem he held for him.

A certain paralytic girl who lived in his church crawled on her hands, dragging her body across the ground because her lower back was paralyzed. [Note: Longip. reads: “with loosened knees.”] For a long time she asked the blessed Apostle Peter that she might be worthy to be healed.

One night Peter appeared to her in a vision and said: “Go to Acontius the church-warden, ask him, and he will restore you to health.” [Note: Most printed editions read: “he himself will restore your health.”]

Although she was certain of the vision, she did not know who Acontius was. She therefore began dragging herself here and there through the church in order to discover who Acontius might be.

Suddenly the man she was seeking came toward her. She said to him: “I beg you, Father, tell me who Acontius the guardian is.”

He replied: “I am.”

But she said: “Our shepherd and nourisher, the blessed Apostle Peter, has sent me to you, so that you may free me from this illness.”

He answered her: “If you have been sent by him, arise.” He took her by the hand and immediately raised her to her proper standing.

From that hour all the nerves and limbs of her body became firm, so that no trace of her paralysis remained. But if we attempt to recount all the things we have learned that took place in his church, we would certainly have to remain silent about all the others. Therefore our account must turn to the fathers whose lives have recently shone throughout the provinces of Italy. [Note: Some witnesses read: “to the reverent fathers.”]

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning Abundius, church-warden of the same church of Saint Peter

[Col. 0279A]

GREGORY. Not long ago, as our elders relate, there was another guardian of the same church named Abundius. He possessed the greatest humility and faithfully served almighty God.

Therefore the same blessed Apostle Peter showed by signs what expectation those who sincerely serve him ought to have concerning Abundius. [Note: Manuscript: “what they owe him.”]

A certain paralytic girl who lived in his church crawled on her hands, dragging her body over the ground because her kidneys were paralyzed. She often prayed to the blessed Apostle Peter that she might be granted health.

One night Peter appeared to her in a vision and said: “Go to Abundius the church-warden, ask him, and he will give you health.” She did not know who Abundius was.

Having received assurance from the vision, she began dragging herself here and there through the church, seeking Abundius so that she might learn who he was. Suddenly the man she was seeking met her. She said to him:

“I beg you, Father, show me who Abundius the guardian is.”

He answered her: “I am.”

She then said to him: “Our shepherd and nourisher, the blessed Apostle Peter, has sent me to you so that you may free me from this disease.”

He said to her: “If you have been sent by him, arise.” Taking her by the hand, he immediately raised her upright. [Note: The manuscript adds: “having taken her by the hand, he immediately raised her up according to her stature. From that hour …”]

From that hour all her limbs and nerves were so strengthened that no trace whatsoever of her paralysis remained.

If we wished to recount all the miracles that occurred in his church and that we have learned about, we would necessarily have to remain silent about all the remaining accounts. I consider it more necessary, however, that our account return to the fathers who have recently shone in Italy. [Note: Manuscript: “return to those whose life was made illustrious through virtues. In the region of Samnium, etc.”]

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Menas the solitary monk

[Col. 0280C]

Recently, in the province of Samnium, there was a venerable man named Menas who led a solitary life. [Note: Most manuscripts here and elsewhere read Samnia. His commemoration is observed on 11 November.] He was known to many of our people and died approximately ten years ago. Regarding the account of his deeds, I do not introduce a single witness, because almost as many people bear witness to his life as know the province of Samnium.

He possessed nothing for his own use except a few small containers for bees. [Note: Germ., Gemet., and other Norman witnesses read “bees.”] When a certain Lombard wished to steal from those bees [Note: Or: “among those same bees.”], the man first rebuked him verbally, and immediately afterward the man was afflicted by an evil spirit and thrown down before Menas’s feet.

As a result, his name became famous among all the inhabitants and also among that barbarian people, and thereafter no one dared enter his cell except humbly. [Note: Two manuscripts read “humbly.”]

Often bears came from the neighboring forest and tried to eat his bees. When he caught them, he beat them with the staff that he habitually carried in his hand. Before his blows those enormous beasts roared and fled; they who scarcely feared swords were frightened by blows from the staff in his hand.

His entire concern in this present life was to possess and seek nothing in this world, and to kindle in the desire for eternal life all who came to him out of charity. Whenever he recognized anyone’s faults, he never spared him correction; rather, kindled by the fire of love, he eagerly strove to attack them fiercely with his tongue.

The inhabitants living nearby, and those dwelling far away, had made it their custom that each day of the week each person would send him an offering, so that he might have something to place before those who came to him.

At one time a certain landowner named Carterius, overcome by an impure desire, abducted a consecrated woman and joined her to himself in an unlawful marriage. As soon as the man of God learned this, he sent word through whatever messengers he could find of the rebuke that Carterius deserved to hear.

Since Carterius was conscious of his crime and did not dare approach the man of God, fearing that Menas might rebuke him harshly, as he was accustomed to rebuke sinners, he prepared his offerings and mixed them among the offerings of the others, so that the holy man might receive his gifts without recognizing them.

But when all the offerings had been brought before him, the man of God sat silently and carefully examined them one by one. Choosing all the others and setting them aside separately, he recognized through the spirit the offerings sent by Carterius. He rejected and cast them away, saying:

“Go and say to him: ‘You have taken away your offering from almighty God, and you send me your offerings? I do not accept your offering, because you have taken away God’s offering.’”

As a result, great fear seized all those present, because the man of God judged so knowingly concerning someone who was absent.

PETER. I suspect that many of these men could have undergone martyrdom, if the time of persecution had overtaken them. [Note: Some witnesses read: “if the storm of persecution had found them at that time.”]

GREGORY. There are two kinds of martyrdom, Peter: one hidden and the other public. Even if persecution is absent outwardly, the merit of martyrdom may exist inwardly, when virtue burns in the soul, ready for suffering.

That martyrdom can exist even without open suffering is attested by the Lord in the Gospel. When the sons of Zebedee, while still weak in understanding, sought the greater places of honor, he said to them: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” (Matthew 20:22). When they answered, “We can,” he said to both: “You will indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right or left is not mine to give you” (ibid.).

What does the name “cup” signify except the drink of suffering? Since it is clear that James died in suffering, while John rested in the peace of the Church, we conclude without hesitation that martyrdom exists even without open suffering, since the one who did not die in persecution is nevertheless said to have drunk the Lord’s cup.

Why, then, should we not say of such and so great men, whom I mentioned above, that if the time of persecution had come, they could have become martyrs? They endured the ambushes of the invisible enemy, loved their adversaries in this world, resisted every worldly desire, and offered themselves as a sacrifice to almighty God in their hearts. Thus they were martyrs even in a time of peace.

In our own times, moreover, when an opportunity arose, it happened that even people of lowly status and ordinary worldly life—people from whom no heavenly glory seemed able to be expected—attained the crowns of martyrdom. 

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Menas the hermit

[Col. 0279C]

Recently in the region of Samnium there was a most reverent man named Menas who chose the solitary life. He was known to many of our people and completed his life approximately ten years ago.

Concerning his deeds I do not present one witness, for as many people testify to his manner of life as have known the region of Samnium.

He possessed nothing at all for his entire livelihood except a few vessels for bees. A certain Lombard wished to steal them. The man of God instructed him with an admonishing word. Immediately afterward the man was struck by an evil spirit, fell at Menas’s feet, and was convulsed.

As a result, his name came to be honored by the barbarian people themselves, just as by the neighboring inhabitants. Thereafter no one dared enter his cell except in humility.

Often bears came from the neighboring forest and tried to eat his beehives. When he caught them, he beat them with the ferula—the staff he was accustomed to carry in his hand. Under his blows those savage beasts retreated roaring and fled. They who did not yield to swords feared the blows from his hand delivered through the staff.

His entire concern in the present life was to awaken those who came to him out of love to desire eternal life. If he ever recognized someone’s fault, he in no way spared him correction. Rather, burning with the fire of love, he considered how he might attack them with his tongue.

The inhabitants near the place, and those who lived far away, had the custom of sending him each day of the week their own blessing or offering, so that he might have something with him which he ought to set before those who came to him. [Note: Manuscript: “which he ought.”]

At one time a certain landowner named Carterius, overcome by an impure desire, abducted a consecrated woman [Note: Manuscript: “a certain girl.”] and joined her to himself in an unsuitable union. When Menas, the man of God, heard of this, he made known to Carterius through messengers whom he was able to find what he deserved to hear. [Note: Manuscript: “he made this known to him.”]

Carterius, conscious of his guilt, did not dare approach the man of God, fearing that Menas might rebuke him as he did the other sinners. He therefore prepared his offerings, mixed them among the other offerings, and sent them, hoping that Menas might receive the gifts without recognizing them.

When the offerings of everyone had been brought before him, the man of God sat silently and examined them one by one. After selecting all the others and setting them aside, he recognized through the spirit the offerings that Carterius himself had sent. He rejected and cast them away with contempt, saying:

“Go and say to him: ‘You have taken away the offering of almighty God, and you send me these blessings? I do not accept your offering, because you have taken away God’s offering.’” [Read ἀπῇρας, “you have taken away,” here and below.]

As a result, great fear fell upon those present, because the man of God judged so wisely concerning matters unknown to them.

PETER. I suppose that many of these men could have endured martyrdom if the time of persecution had overtaken them.

GREGORY. There are two kinds of martyrdom, Peter: one hidden and another manifest. Even if persecution is not outwardly present, the dignity of martyrdom can exist secretly, when the soul vigorously resists sufferings with readiness.

That martyrdom can exist apart from visible punishments is shown by the Lord in the Gospel. To the sons of Zebedee, who in the weakness of their understanding were seeking the great places of sitting, he said: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” When they answered, “We can,” he said to both: “You shall indeed drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to give, but for those for whom it has been prepared.” [Note: The edition reads “to sit.”]

What does the name “cup” signify except suffering? It is shown here that James was brought to completion through suffering, while John rested in the peace of the Church. Thus it is shown in every respect that martyrdom exists even without visible suffering, since the one who did not die in persecution is nevertheless said to have drunk the Lord’s cup. [Note: Manuscript: “was granted rest.”]

How, then, can we fail to say of such and so great men, whom I have mentioned above, that if the time of persecution had overtaken them, they could have given themselves to martyrdom? They continually endured the ambushes of the hidden enemy, loved their adversaries in this world, resisted every worldly desire, and offered themselves as a sacrifice to almighty God.

I shall try to relate how, even in a time of peace, in our own recent days, certain worldly and unassuming people became martyrs and were adorned with the crown of martyrdom in the glory of heaven when a fitting occasion arose.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning forty peasants who were killed by the Lombards because they refused to eat sacrificial meat

[Col. 0284B]

About fifteen years ago, as those who were able to be present testify, forty peasants were captured by the Lombards [Note: The commemoration of these and the following martyrs is observed on 2 March.] and compelled to eat meat sacrificed to idols. When they resisted fiercely and refused to touch the sacrilegious food, the Lombards who held them began threatening them with death unless they ate what had been sacrificed.

But they preferred eternal life to the present, transitory life. They remained faithful and, all together, were killed in their steadfastness. What, then, were these men except martyrs of the truth? Rather than offend their Creator by eating what was forbidden, they chose to end their lives by the sword.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning forty farmers who refused to eat polluted food and were beheaded by the Lombards

[Col. 0283B]

Fifteen years ago, as those who say they were present among them at that time testify, forty farmers were captured by the Lombards and compelled to eat the meat of their sacrifice.

When they resisted very strongly and would not consent to touch the polluted food, the Lombards who had captured them began threatening them with death unless they ate the sacrificed meat.

But they loved eternal life more than this temporary and passing life. They stood faithfully in their confession, and all were slaughtered in that confession. [Note: Manuscript: “they stood, and in their confession …”]

Were they not all therefore made martyrs of the truth? Rather than eat what was forbidden and offend their Creator, they chose instead to escape this life by the sword. [Note: Manuscript: “and offend their Creator, they chose …”]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the multitude of captives who were killed because they refused to worship a goat’s head

[Col. 0284C]

At the same time, when the Lombards were holding nearly four hundred other captives, they sacrificed a goat’s head to the devil according to their custom. They ran around it in a circle and dedicated it to him with an impious song. After first worshiping it themselves with bowed necks, they compelled those whom they had captured to worship it as well.

But a very large number of those captives chose rather to advance through death toward immortal life than to preserve mortal life by worshiping. They refused to obey the sacrilegious commands and disdained to bow to a creature the neck they had always bent before the Creator.

Therefore the enemies who had captured them, inflamed with fierce anger, killed with swords all those whom they could not have as participants in their error. What wonder, then, if, when the time of persecution broke out, those men could have become martyrs? Even in the peace of the Church they had always afflicted themselves through self-restraint and held to the narrow path of martyrdom.

When the moment of persecution arrived, even those who seemed, during the peace of the Church, to follow the broad roads of this world were deemed worthy to receive the palms of martyrdom. [Note: The printed editions read “when persecution was pressing in.”]

Yet we do not treat as an established rule for everyone what we say about these chosen men. When the time of open persecution breaks in, many who appear contemptible during the peace of the Church can undergo martyrdom; likewise, those who were previously believed to stand firmly in the peace of the Church sometimes collapse through fear of weakness. [Note: Various witnesses read “through fear in adversity.”]

But we confidently acknowledge that the men of whom we spoke could have become martyrs, because we already infer this from their end. Those whom we know to have persevered in hidden strength of soul until the end of life could not have fallen even in open persecution.

[Col. 0285B] PETER. It is as you say. But I marvel at the dispensation of divine mercy toward us, which restrains the savagery of the Lombards and does not allow their sacrilegious priests—who seem to regard themselves as victors over the faithful—to persecute the faith of the orthodox.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the captives who refused to worship a goat’s head and were slaughtered

[Col. 0283C]

At that same time the Lombards seized as many as four hundred other captives. According to their custom they sacrificed a goat’s head to the devil, running around it in a circle and sending up a song in an impious chant, bowing their necks before it and praying. [Note: The printed editions incorrectly read “three hundred,” whereas the Latin text has “four hundred.” Manuscript: “with impious songs and hymns …”]

They compelled those whom they had captured to do the same unanimously. But the whole multitude of captives chose rather to draw immortal life to themselves through temporary death than to obey their impious commands and, praying along with them, live a deadened life.

They could not bow to a creature the neck they had always bowed to the Creator. [Note: The editions read “to the Creator himself.”] Therefore the enemies who had captured them, inflamed with the fiercest anger, killed with swords all those whom they could not make participants in their own error. [Note: Manuscript: “inflamed, killed them all with swords.”]

What wonder, then, if when a time of persecution came those men gave themselves to martyrdom? During the peace of the Church they had continually worn themselves down through self-restraint and held fast to the narrow road of martyrdom, while those who traveled the broad road of the world, when persecution came upon them during the Church’s peace, were deemed worthy to receive crowns of martyrdom. [Note: Manuscript: “when persecution came upon them, martyrs …”]

We firmly and openly maintain that these chosen men of whom we speak could have given themselves to martyrdom even in a time of open persecution, just as many who appeared pitiable and insignificant during the peace of the Church could do so. [Note: Manuscript: “in the time of the Church’s peace.”] It often happens, however, that in a time of persecution those whom we previously believed strong during the peace of the Church fall into cowardly weakness.

But this did not happen to those of whom we spoke as capable of becoming martyrs. Their end clearly shows that they could not have fallen even in open persecution, since they stood unmoved in the hidden strength of their souls until the end of their lives.

[Col. 0286B] PETER. I marvel at the mercies of divine providence: how it restrains the harshness of the Lombards and does not permit their sacrilegious priests—who think themselves faithful because they appear victorious—to persecute the orthodox faith. [Note: Manuscript: “of their sacrilegious priests.”]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the Arian bishop who was struck blind

[Col. 0285B]

GREGORY. They often attempted to do this, Peter, but heavenly miracles resisted their savagery. I shall therefore relate one miracle which I learned only three days ago through Boniface, a monk of my monastery who had been with the Lombards until four years ago.

When the bishop of the Lombards, an Arian, came to the city of Spoleto and had no place there in which to celebrate his solemn rites, he began asking the bishop of that city for a church which he could dedicate to his error.

When the bishop strongly refused, the Arian who had come declared that on the following day he would forcibly enter the church of the blessed Apostle Paul, which stood nearby. When the guardian of that church heard this, he hurried there, closed the church, secured it with bolts, extinguished all the lamps at evening, and hid himself in the innermost part of the church.

At the first twilight of the following day, the Arian bishop arrived with a crowd, prepared to break down the closed doors of the church. But suddenly all the doors were shaken simultaneously by divine power; the bolts were thrown far away, and all the barriers of the church opened with a great crash. Light poured down from above, and all the lamps that had been extinguished were relit. [Note: Some witnesses read “all the royal doors together” or “all the doors of the sanctuary.”]

The Arian bishop, who had come intending to use force, was suddenly struck with blindness and had to be led back to his dwelling by other people. When all the Lombards living in that region recognized what had happened, they no longer dared profane Catholic places.

The event occurred in a marvelous manner: because the lamps in the church of the blessed Paul had been extinguished on account of that Arian, at one and the same time he lost his light and light returned to the church.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the Arian bishop who was blinded

[Col. 0286B]

GREGORY. They struggled with all their strength to do this, Peter, but heavenly miracles resisted their cruelty. I shall therefore relate one event which I learned three days ago through Boniface, a monk of my monastery who had been with the Lombards until four years ago.

He relates that when the bishop of the Lombards came to the city of Spoleto—being an Arian—and had no place there in which to celebrate his festival, he began seeking from the bishop of that city a church which he might dedicate according to his own error.

The bishop emphatically refused to do this. Then that Arian declared that on another day he would enter the church of the blessed Apostle Paul there by force. [Note: Manuscript: “with his arm.”]

When the guardian of the same church heard this, he hurried there and secured the church. When evening came, he extinguished all the lamps and hid himself in the innermost part of the sanctuary.

When the light of day followed, at the very dawn the Arian bishop arrived at the church after gathering a crowd of people, ready to break down the closed doors. Suddenly all the doors, shaken together by divine power, opened with a great crash, their bolts having been thrown far away. [Note: Manuscript: “with a sound.”]

When light had been poured down from above, all the extinguished lamps were lit. But the Arian bishop, who had wished to use force, was suddenly struck with blindness and, led by other hands, returned to his own dwelling.

When the Lombards who were in that region learned of this, they no longer dared to set foot in Catholic churches. God arranged the matter wondrously, so that in a single moment the Arian lost his light, while light returned to the extinguished lamps in the church of the blessed Apostle Paul. [Note: Manuscript: “in the extinguished lamps.”]

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the church of the Arians which was dedicated in the city of Rome by Catholic consecration

[Col. 0288A]

But I will not keep silent about what divine mercy also recently showed in this city, two years ago, for the condemnation of that same Arian heresy. Of the events I relate, some were learned by the people, while others the priest and the church officials testify that they heard and saw themselves.

The church of the Arians in that district of this city called the Subura [Note: Concerning the church of Saint Agatha in the Subura, and the location of the Subura, see the *Italian Diary* of R. P. D. Bernard de Montfaucon, p. 131 and following; *De Consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter 22, “Arianorum”.] had remained closed until two years previously. It was decided that it should be dedicated as a Catholic church, after the relics of the blessed martyr Sebastian and Saint Agatha had been brought there [Note: In the Gilot and Vatican editions: “of blessed Stephen and Saint Martha.” In Paris 1640: “of blessed Stephen and Saint Matthew.” We follow the English, Norman, and other manuscripts. See Book IV of the Letters, indiction 12, letter 19.]. This was done.

For when we came with a great multitude of people, singing praises to the almighty Lord, we entered that same church. While the solemn celebration of Mass was already taking place there, and the crowd was pressing together because of the narrowness of the place, some of those standing outside the sanctuary [Note: Two Chartres manuscripts, Vallicellianus Cl., and four Norman manuscripts: “who were beside the sanctuary.” The following account is illuminated and corroborated by what Victor of Vita relates in Book II of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, no. 6, p. 28 of the new edition: “A certain priest saw the very basilica of Faustus filled with innumerable crowds of people, and shortly afterward emptied and filled with a multitude of swine; by this vision it was signified that, after the Catholics had been driven out, this basilica was to be handed over to the Arians, who would defile it after the manner of swine.”] suddenly sensed a pig running back and forth between their feet. Each one felt it and pointed it out to those standing beside him. The same pig then made for the doors of the church and filled all those through whom it passed with astonishment; yet no one could see it, although it could be felt. Divine mercy showed this so that it might be evident to all that an unclean inhabitant was leaving that place.

When the celebration of Mass had been completed, we departed. But that same night a great uproar arose in the roof of the church, as though someone were running about inside it. On the following night a heavier noise increased, suddenly sounding with such terror that it seemed as though the entire church had been overturned from its foundations. Immediately afterward it ceased, and no further disturbance by the ancient enemy appeared there. Through the terrifying noise he had made, however, it became known how, compelled by force, he had left the place that he had long occupied.

A few days later, while the weather was perfectly clear, a cloud descended from heaven upon the altar of that church and covered it with its own veil. It filled the entire church with such terror and such sweetness of fragrance that, although the doors stood open, no one dared to enter. The priest and the officials, as well as those who had come to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, saw the phenomenon but could not enter; instead, they drew toward themselves the sweetness of that wondrous fragrance.

On another day, when the lamps hung there without light [Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read “were found without light.”], they were kindled by a light sent from heaven.

A few days later again, after the solemn rites of Mass had been completed, the official left that church after extinguishing the lamps. After a short while he entered again and found the lamps he had extinguished burning [Note: The printed editions read: “which he had left extinguished”; and shortly afterward, “more anxiously,” instead of “more carefully.”]. Thinking that he had extinguished them carelessly and that for this reason they had been rekindled, he extinguished them with the greatest care, went out, and shut the church more carefully. But after an interval of three hours he returned and found all the lamps he had extinguished burning again. Thus, by that very light, it became plainly evident that the place had passed from darkness to light.

**Peter.** Although we are caught up in great tribulations, nevertheless the astonishing miracles of our Creator that I hear about testify that we are not altogether despised by him.

**Gregory.** Although I had resolved to relate only what happened in Italy, would you like us, to demonstrate the condemnation of that same Arian heresy, to pass in our account to Spain and then return from Africa to Italy?

**Peter.** Go wherever you wish; I shall gladly accompany you, and gladly return with you.

## Chapter XXX. Concerning the church of Saint Agatha in the Subura

[Col. 0287A]

**Gregory.** Nor will I pass over in silence what the mercy from above was pleased to show in this city two years ago for the condemnation of the same Arian heresy. Of the matters I relate, some are known by the people, while the priests and guardians of that church testify that they heard and saw the others.

Accordingly, as I said before, in this city of the Romans, in the district called the Subura, there was a church of the Arians, which had remained shut until two years before this. It was decided that the relics of the blessed Sebastian and of the holy martyr Agatha should be deposited in it [Note: The manuscript reads “should be deposited” (*katatethōsin*).], since it was to be dedicated; and so it was done.

As we went with a very great multitude of people, offering hymnic praises to the almighty Lord, we came to that church; and, entering it, we celebrated the rites of the divine liturgy. Because of the narrowness of the place, the crowd pressed itself together. Some of those standing outside the sanctuary suddenly noticed a pig running here and there among their feet. As each one noticed it [the text is corrupt here] and informed the person standing near him, the same pig went out through the doors of the church and stirred all through whom it passed to amazement. Yet it could not at all be seen, although, as has been said, they noticed only that it was running about.

God's mercy displayed this so that it might be made manifest to all that the unclean demon dwelling in that place had departed. When the sacred liturgy had been completed, we left the place. That same night a great noise arose among the tiles [Note: The manuscript reads “tiles” (*keramois*).] of that church, as though someone were wandering and running about among them. On the following night a heavier sound grew louder. For suddenly such a fearful crash occurred [Note: The manuscript reads: “a fearful crash occurred such that …”] that one might think that the whole church had been raised up from its foundations. Thereafter it departed, and no further disturbance of the ancient adversary appeared there. By the fearful sound which it made, it showed how, compelled by force, it was leaving the place which it had occupied for a long time.

A few days later, when the air was in the greatest calm [Note: The manuscript reads “most beautiful.”], a cloud descended from heaven above the altar of that church and covered it with its own shade [Note: The manuscript reads “covering.”]. It filled the whole church with such fear and sweetness of fragrance that, though the doors were open, no one dared enter. The priest and all the guardians, and all those who had gathered to perform the rites of the liturgy [Note: The manuscript reads “the guardians and all …”], saw this wonder but could not enter, though they drew the sweetness of that marvelous fragrance toward themselves.

On another day, when the lamps hung without light [Note: The manuscript reads “hanging,” as the Latin has it.], all were lit by a light sent from God. Again, a few days later, when the office of the divine liturgy had been completed, the guardian extinguished the lamps of that church and went out. Shortly afterward, entering again, he found burning all the lamps which he had extinguished. Thinking that he had extinguished them accidentally and that this was why they had been rekindled, he extinguished them very carefully, went out, and secured the church. But after an interval of three hours he returned and found again shining all the lamps which he had extinguished. From this light, therefore, it is shown that that place had returned from darkness to light.

**Peter.** Even if we are involved in great tribulations, nevertheless the astonishing miracles of our Creator which I hear testify that we are not utterly rejected by him.

**Gregory.** Since I had resolved to relate only what had been done in Italy, do you wish us, in order to display the condemnation of that same Arian heresy, to proceed in our account to Spain and then return from there through Africa to Italy?

**Peter.** Go wherever you wish [Note: The printed editions read “to go.”], for I too shall gladly go with you and gladly return again with you.

## Chapter XXXI. Concerning Herminigild, son of Liuvigild, king of the Visigoths, who was killed by his own father for the Catholic faith

**Gregory.** As we have learned from the reports of many people who come from the regions of Spain, Herminigild, son of Liuvigild, king of the Visigoths, was recently converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith through the preaching of the most reverend Leander, bishop of Hispalis, who had long been closely joined to me in friendship [Note: His feast is celebrated on 13 April. Concerning him, consult Mariana, *History*, Book V, chapter 12. The name of the king is given as Lauvieldus in Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter 38. Concerning Saint Leander, see the letter prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*, and the notes on it. In most manuscripts one reads “Spolitan bishop” instead of “Spalitan,” or “Hispalitan.” The conversion was encouraged by Ingundis, wife of Herminigild and daughter of Sigibert, king of the Franks.].

His Arian father tried both to persuade him with rewards and to frighten him with threats into returning to that same heresy. But when Herminigild answered with the greatest steadfastness that he could never abandon the true faith which he had once come to know, his angry father deprived him of his kingdom and stripped him of all his possessions. Since he was still unable to soften the strength of his mind, he shut him in a harsh prison and bound his neck and hands with iron.

The young King Herminigild therefore began to despise the earthly kingdom [Causa 24, question 1, chapter 42: “He began”] and, seeking the heavenly kingdom with ardent desire, lay bound in sackcloth, pouring out prayers to almighty God for his strengthening. The more he recognized, while fettered, that nothing existed which could be taken away from him, the more sublimely he despised the glory of the passing world.

When the day of the Paschal feast arrived [Causa 1, question 1, chapter 72: “When it arrived”], in the silence of the dead of night his treacherous father sent an Arian bishop to him, so that he might receive from that bishop’s hand communion in the sacrilegious consecration and thereby be deemed worthy to return to his father’s favor. But the man devoted to God reproached the visiting Arian bishop as he deserved, and drove his treachery away from himself with fitting rebukes. Although he lay bound outwardly, he stood inwardly secure upon the lofty summit of his mind.

When the bishop returned to him [Note: Many Norman manuscripts, together with the second Chartres manuscript, read: “When the Arian bishop had returned, the father …”], his Arian father raged and immediately sent his officers [Note: The interpreter renders this as “the more distinguished men among the nobles or magnates,” apparently understanding *apparitores* as equivalent to the Greek *epiphaneis*, “the prominent ones”] to kill the steadfast confessor of God where he lay. And this was done. As soon as they entered, they drove an axe into his skull and took away his bodily life. By this they were able to destroy in him what he himself, even before he was killed, had resolved to despise [Note: The printed editions read: “which he too had resolved to despise.”].

But, to reveal his true glory, heavenly miracles were not lacking. During the silence of the night, the singing of psalms began to be heard at the body of that king and martyr—and rightly of a king, because he was also a martyr. Some also report that lamps appeared burning there at night. Thus it came about that his body was rightly venerated by all the faithful as that of a martyr.

The treacherous and murderous father, moved by repentance, regretted what he had done, but did not go so far as to attain salvation. He recognized that the Catholic faith was true, but, terrified by fear of his people, he was not deemed worthy to embrace it. When illness overtook him and brought him to his final extremity, he took care to commend to Bishop Leander—whom he had previously afflicted most severely—his son King Rechared, whom he was leaving in his own heresy, so that Leander might do for him what he had done for his brother through his exhortations. After making this commendation, he died.

After his death [Note: On the conversion of Rechared and of the entire Visigothic people, consult Letter 122 of Book IX, indiction 11, formerly Letter 127 of Book VII, indiction 11], King Rechared followed not his treacherous father but his martyred brother. He was converted from the perversity of the Arian heresy and led the entire Visigothic nation to the true faith, permitting no one under his rule to serve in the army who, through heretical treachery, was not afraid of becoming an enemy of the kingdom of God [Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read: “heretical perversity.”].

It is no wonder that he became a preacher of the true faith, since he was the brother of a martyr, whose merits also assist him so that he may bring so many people back to the embrace of almighty God. In this matter we must consider that all this could in no way have happened if King Herminigild had not died for the truth. For, as it is written: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). We see this happening in the members, just as we know that it happened in the head. In the Visigothic nation one man died so that many might live; and when one faithful grain fell in order to obtain life for souls, a plentiful harvest arose.

**Peter.** A remarkable event, and one that fills our own times with astonishment.

## Chapter XXXI. Concerning King Herminigild, formerly an Arian, who was slain by his own father because he embraced the orthodox faith

**Gregory.** As I have learned from the reports of many people now coming from the regions of Spain, Herminigild, the king, son of Liuvigild, king of the nation of the Visigoths, returned from the Arian heresy to the orthodox faith, with Leander, bishop of the city of Hispalis, proclaiming it. Leander had formerly been genuinely attached to me in friendship [Note: The manuscript reads “has been attached.”].

The father of the aforementioned Herminigild, Liuvigild, being an Arian, hastened to make him return to that same heresy. He did not cease flattering him with promises of gifts and again terrifying him with threats. But Herminigild, standing firm, replied that he could never abandon the true faith which he had once learned.

His father became angry, deprived him of his kingdom, and stripped him of all his property. Since he could not soften the steadfastness of his reasoning even in this way [Note: Perhaps “in this way,” since the Latin text reads *sic*], he shut him in a very narrow prison and secured his hands and feet with iron.

The same King Herminigild, although still young, began to despise the earthly kingdom utterly and to seek the heavenly kingdom with complete desire. Bound in sackcloth, he lay there offering supplications to almighty God for his strengthening. Bound by his love of God, he despised the glory of the passing world from the height of his mind, recognizing that nothing existed which could separate him from that love.

When the feast of holy Easter arrived, in the stillness of the night his impious father secretly sent an Arian bishop to him, so that he might receive from the bishop’s hand a share in their unlawful liturgy and thereby be deemed worthy to return to his father’s favor.

But this man, given to God, utterly rejected the Arian bishop who came to him. He exposed his evil faith as it deserved and drove him away from himself. Although he lay bound outwardly, within himself he stood unconcerned in the light of his reason [Note: The manuscript reads: “he lay unconcerned.”].

When the Arian bishop returned to his impious father and reported what had been said to him [Note: The manuscript reads: “He reported to him what had been said to him by the other. The latter, gnashing his teeth against him, immediately sent the prominent men …”], the father gnashed his teeth against him. Immediately he sent the most prominent of his officials and ordered them to kill the steadfast confessor of God where he lay. And this was done. For when they entered to him, they drove an axe into his skull and took away his bodily life.

[The passage enclosed in brackets is absent from the manuscript and appears corrupt, or at least considerably confused, in this place.] Thus they were able to kill him; the remaining words of this corrupt passage are materially uncertain: “so that even before he was killed he himself, having stood within himself, might rebuke and appropriate him.”

But to display his true glory, heavenly miracles did not fail to occur there. During the silence of the night, songs of psalmody began to be heard at the body of the king and martyr, and burning lamps appeared there. [Sic.] For this reason his body came to be honored by all the faithful, clearly as that of a true martyr.

His impious and child-murdering father, repenting because of what he had done, disturbed himself with grief, but did not surrender himself so as to gain salvation. He recognized that the Catholic faith was true, but, fearing his own nation, was not deemed worthy to embrace it [Note: The manuscript reads: “to approach it.”].

When illness came upon him and carried him to his final extremity, he hastened to commend to Leander the bishop—whom he had previously afflicted severely—his son and king Rechared, whom he was leaving in his own heresy, so that Leander might work in him what he had done in his brother through his teaching. When this commendation had been completed, he died.

But King Rechared, following not his impious father but his martyred brother, returned from the ill-omened Arian heresy and led the entire Visigothic nation to the true faith. He did not permit anyone to serve under his rule who had become an enemy of the kingdom of God through the impious Arian heresy.

He therefore became a herald of the true faith. Because he was the brother of the martyr, the merits that came from that martyr assisted him, so that he might bring such a great multitude of people back into the garden [Note: The manuscript reads “bosom”] of almighty God.

In this matter we must understand that none of this could have been accomplished if King Herminigild had not died for the truth, as it is also written in the Gospel: “Unless the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” We see this taking place in the members, just as we know that it took place in our head, Christ. For in the nation of the Visigoths one man died so that many might live; and while one faithful grain fell in order to secure the faith of souls, a great harvest arose.

**Peter.** Truly a wondrous event, filled with astonishment in our own times.

## Chapter XXXII. Concerning the African bishops who, after their tongues had been cut out by the Arian Vandals in defense of the Catholic faith, suffered no loss of their customary speech

[Note: Concerning the African bishops who spoke after their tongues had been cut out, see Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, Book V, chapter 6, p. 76 of the edition of D. Théodore Ruinart; and Procopius, Book I, *On the Vandalic War*: “Many had their tongues cut out from their throats; yet even in my own time they walked about Byzantium, using complete speech and feeling nothing of their former punishment. Of these, two, after they had consorted with women of prostituted modesty, ceased to speak.” So Procopius. Yet do not suppose that these events occurred under Justinian’s rule, since Justinian had not yet been born. Huneric began to reign around 484, and Justinian in 527.]

**Gregory.** In the time of the Emperor Justinian, while the Arian persecution that had arisen among the Vandals against the Catholic faith was raging violently in Africa, certain bishops, standing bravely in defense of the truth, were brought before the court. Since the king of the Vandals [Note: This was Huneric, or Heneric, according to Victor of Vita and Procopius.] could not bend them to his treachery by words or gifts, he thought that he could break them by tortures. When he commanded them to be silent in that very defense of the truth [Note: Pratensis reads: “when he tried to impose silence on them”], and they nevertheless did not keep silent against the treachery—for fear that by keeping silent they might appear to have consented—he was carried away by fury and had their tongues cut out at the root.

It is a remarkable event, known to many elderly people, that afterward, even without tongues, they spoke in defense of the truth just as they had formerly been accustomed to speak with their tongues.

**Peter.** It is exceedingly wondrous and utterly astonishing.

**Gregory.** It is written, Peter, concerning the Only-Begotten of the Most High Father: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Concerning his power it adds: “All things were made through him” (ibid.). Why, then, should we wonder if the Word who made the tongue was able to utter words without a tongue?

**Peter.** I approve what you say.

**Gregory.** At that time these men, as refugees, came to Constantinople. When I myself had been sent to the emperor to deliver the responses of the Church [Note: See the beginning of the letter prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*], I found there an elderly bishop who testified that he had still seen their mouths speaking without tongues. With their mouths open, they would cry out: “Look and see: we have no tongues, and yet we speak.”

To those who looked, it appeared—as he related—that, since their tongues had been cut out at the root, a kind of chasm lay open in their throats; nevertheless, from their empty mouths they formed complete and perfectly articulated words. One of them there fell into sexual indulgence and immediately lost the gift of the miracle. This was evidently by the just judgment of almighty God: since he had neglected to preserve continence of the flesh, he was not to possess words of virtue without a bodily tongue [Note: The printed editions read “words of truth.”].

But let what we have said concerning the condemnation of the Arian heresy suffice. Let us now return to the signs that recently occurred in Italy.

## Chapter XXXII. Concerning the African bishops who, after their tongues had been cut out for the orthodox faith, spoke again

**Gregory.** In the time of Justinian Augustus, when the Arian persecution that had arisen among the nation of the Vandals against our Catholic and orthodox faith was raging fiercely in Africa, some of the bishops there, standing firm in defense of the truth, were brought before the public. Since the king of the Vandals, unable to incline them toward his own impiety by deceptive words and promises of gifts, could not persuade them, he tried to draw them over by many tortures [Note: The manuscript reads: “he tried by threats and tortures.”].

When he failed even in this, he ordered them to keep quiet and not to speak on behalf of the defense of the truth. But they absolutely refused to do so, lest by remaining silent they be thought to consent to him. The same king, boiling over with rage [Note: The manuscript reads: “in his rage”], ordered their tongues to be cut from their throats.

A miracle full of wonder occurred, known to many of the elders of our own time. After their tongues had been cut out, they spoke in defense of the truth just as they had formerly spoken with their tongues.

**Peter.** It is truly wondrous and exceedingly astonishing.

**Gregory.** It is written, Peter, concerning the Only-Begotten Son of the Father without beginning: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” The Evangelist, adding a statement about his power, says: “All things came into being through him.” Why, then, should we wonder if the Word who made the tongue was able to utter words without a tongue? [Note: The manuscript reads: “What wonder is it, then, if the Word …”]

**Peter.** I approve what you say.

**Gregory.** At that time these men came as refugees to Constantinople. During the period when I had been sent to the emperor to fulfill the Church’s responses, I found an elderly bishop who testified that he had seen their mouths speaking without tongues. Opening their mouths, they said to everyone: “See that, although we have no tongues, we speak.”

They were visible to everyone, and, as he said, this was indeed how they were [Note: The manuscript reads: “they existed.”]. Since their tongues had been cut out at the root, their throats appeared open like a kind of chasm [Note: The manuscript reads: “with the throat opening … empty …”]. Yet, although the mouth was empty, complete words came forth.

When one of them there fell into fornication, he was immediately deprived of this wondrous gift. By the just judgment of God [Note: The manuscript reads: “By the just judgment of God, so that he who …”], since he had scorned the preservation of bodily continence, he was not to possess the power to speak without a bodily tongue.

But I think that what has been said concerning the condemnation of the Arian heresy is sufficient. Let us return our account to the signs that have recently occurred in Italy.

## Chapter XXXIII. Concerning Eleutherius, the servant of God

**Gregory.** The Eleutherius whom I mentioned above (Book I, chapter 21) [Note: His name is recorded in the sacred calendars on 6 September], abbot of the monastery of the blessed Evangelist Mark, situated in the outskirts of the city of Spoleto [Note: The first Theodosian manuscript reads: “situated in the city of Spoleto”], lived with me for a long time in my monastery in this city, and there he died. His disciples reported that he had raised a dead man by praying [Note: The printed editions read “by weeping.”].

He was a man of such great simplicity and compunction that there could be no doubt that those tears, issuing from so humble and simple a mind, could obtain much from almighty God.

I shall therefore relate one of his miracles, which he himself simply acknowledged to me when I questioned him. One day, while he was traveling, evening came and he had no place in which to withdraw [Note: The Gemeticensis and the second Theodosian manuscript read “to receive him,” a usage well attested in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “What new guest has come to our dwelling?”]. He came to a monastery of virgins. There was a small boy there whom an evil spirit used to torment every night.

When the holy women received the man of God, they asked him, saying: “Father, let this boy stay with you tonight.” He kindly received him and allowed him to lie beside him that night.

When morning came, the nuns began to inquire anxiously of the same father whether the boy they had given him had done anything to him during the night. Astonished that they should ask this, he replied: “Nothing.” Then they explained the matter of the boy and told him that the evil spirit never left him on any night. They earnestly begged him to take the boy with him to the monastery, since they could no longer bear to see his torment.

The old man consented and led the boy to the monastery. After the boy had been there for a long time, and the ancient enemy had not dared to approach him at all, the old man’s heart was excessively elated with joy concerning the boy’s salvation. In the presence of the brothers he said: “Brothers, the devil was playing with those sisters there; but when the boy came to the servants of God, he did not dare approach him” [Note: Some manuscripts read “was playing with them”; both readings are found].

Immediately after he said this, at that very hour and moment, the boy was tormented in the presence of all the brothers, as the devil attacked him. When the old man saw this, he at once broke into lamentation. While the brothers tried for a long time to console him, he replied: “Believe me: none of you will have bread enter his mouth today unless this boy is freed from the demon.”

Then he prostrated himself in prayer with all the brothers, and they continued praying until the boy was healed of his torment. He was healed so completely that afterward the evil spirit no longer had the power to approach him.

**Peter.** I believe that a small measure of pride had crept into him, and for that reason almighty God wished to make his disciples helpers with him in that miracle.

**Gregory.** That is so. Since he could not bear the weight of the miracle alone, he shared it with the brothers and so bore it. I myself experienced how powerful this man’s prayer was.

Once, while I was staying in the monastery, I suffered a collapse of my vital powers and, frequently distressed, seemed at every moment to be approaching death. The physicians call this illness *syncopis* in Greek. Unless the brothers frequently restored me with food, my vital spirit seemed about to be completely cut off [Note: Longipontanus reads “interrupted,” a reading supported by the second Theodosian manuscript].

When the day of Easter approached, and on the holy Sabbath—on which everyone, even little children, fasts—I was unable to fast, I began to fail more from grief than from illness. But my sorrowful soul quickly found an excellent plan. I took the same man of God secretly into the oratory and asked him to obtain through his prayers from almighty God that strength to fast might be given to me that day. And this was done.

As soon as we entered the oratory, and I humbly asked him, he gave himself to prayer with tears. Shortly afterward, when his prayer was complete, he came out. At the sound of his blessing, however, my stomach received such strength that food and illness were completely removed from my memory. I began to wonder who I was and who I had been, for even when the illness returned to my mind, I recognized nothing in myself of what I had previously remembered.

When my mind was occupied with the administration of the monastery, I completely forgot my illness. But if, as I have said, the illness returned to my memory, then, feeling myself so strong, I wondered whether I had not eaten. When evening came, I found such strength in myself that, had I wished, I could have prolonged the fast until the following day.

Thus I came to prove in myself that the things said about him were also true, even those in which I had not personally taken part.

**Peter.** Since you said that this man possessed great compunction, I desire to learn more fully the power of his tears. Therefore, I ask you to explain to me how many kinds of compunction there are.

## Chapter XXXIII. Concerning Eleutherius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mark at Spoleto

**Gregory.** The aforementioned Eleutherius, of whom I have spoken above, was abbot of the monastery of the blessed Evangelist Mark, situated at Spoleto, in a mountainous place [Note: The manuscript reads “in an Arian place”; perhaps it should read *in the pomerium*]. Whenever he came to this city, he lived with me in my monastery in close fellowship; he died in his own monastery [Note: The manuscript reads: “he came … he died.”]. His disciples said of him that by prayer he raised a dead person. For the man possessed such innocence and compunction that there could be no doubt that those tears, proceeding from so humble and guileless a mind, could obtain much from almighty God.

I too shall relate a miracle of his which, when I asked him, he himself candidly acknowledged to me. He said that one day, as he was making a journey, evening overtook him. Since there was no place where he ought to lodge, he entered a monastery of virgins. There was there a little boy whom an evil spirit threw down every night. When those holy women received the man of God, they begged him, saying: “Honored father, let the boy rest with you tonight.” He received this gladly and let him rest with him that night.

When morning came, the nuns began carefully to ask the same father whether anything had happened to the boy in the night. Wondering why they asked him this, he replied that nothing had happened. Then they informed him about the boy: the evil spirit never left him on any night. All together they earnestly begged him to take the boy with him to his monastery, for they could no longer bear to see him thus thrown down by the demon [Note: The manuscript reads “thrown down; he yielded.”]. The old man yielded and took the boy with him to his monastery.

After the boy had spent a long time in the monastery and the ancient enemy had in no way dared to approach him, the old man's soul, in its joy over the boy's salvation, became improperly exultant, as though the boy had been healed through him. Before the brothers present he said: “Brothers, the devil was playing with those nuns; but when this boy came to the servants of God, he did not dare to approach him.” After these words, at that very hour, the devil fell upon the boy and threw him down before all the brothers. Seeing this, the old man immediately gave himself to lamentation.

While he lamented for a long time and the brothers urged him to relent a little [Note: The manuscript reads “to give way a little”], he answered them: “Believe me: today bread shall enter the mouth of none of you unless this boy is freed from the demon.” Then he prostrated himself in prayer with all the brothers, and they persisted in prayer [Note: The manuscript reads “in prayer”] until the boy was freed from the demon. The boy was so completely healed [Note: The manuscript reads “was healed, so that henceforth completely …”] that thereafter the evil spirit could not approach him.

**Peter.** I think that a little pride entered into him, and that for this reason almighty God wished to make his disciples his helpers in this miracle.

**Gregory.** So it was. Since he could not bear the weight of the miracle alone, he shared it with the brothers. I learned by experience in myself how great was the power of this man's prayer. For while I was in the monastery, I suffered at one time a collapse of the life-giving spirit, and, repeatedly distressed at every instant of an hour, I drew near to death. Physicians customarily call this illness in Greek *syncopē*. Unless the brothers frequently sustained me with food, my vital spirit was about to be torn away from its depths [Note: The manuscript reads “to be torn away”].

When the day of holy Easter came, on the holy Sabbath, when all fast, even reverent little children [Note: The manuscript reads “little children”], I could not fast. I began to fail more from grief than from illness [Note: The manuscript reads “more than from illness”]. But my sorrowful soul quickly found an excellent plan. Secretly I led that same man of God, Eleutherius, into the oratory and asked that by his prayer strength to fast might be given to me by almighty God. And this happened.

When we entered the oratory and I asked him with great humility, he gave himself to prayer with tears. Shortly afterward, when the prayer was completed, at the sound of his blessing my stomach received such strength that food and illness were wholly removed from my memory. I began to wonder who I was and who I had become. Even when the illness returned in me, I recognized nothing of what I had formerly suffered. When my mind was occupied in administering the monastery, I forgot my illness altogether. But if, as I said, the illness returned to remind me, I wondered, seeing myself in such strength although I had not eaten. By evening I found such power in myself that, had I wished, I could have prolonged the fast until the next day. From what happened to me, therefore, I believe true even those things said about him of which I was not an eyewitness.

**Peter.** Since you said that this man possessed the greatest compunction, I desire clearly to learn the very power of tears, and I ask you to say how many kinds of compunction there are.

## Chapter XXXIV. How many kinds of compunction there are

**Gregory.** Compunction is divided into many forms, according to the several sins mourned by penitents. Hence Jeremiah also says in the voice of penitents: “My eye brought forth divisions of waters” (Lamentations 3:48).

In chief, however, there are two kinds of compunction, because when the soul thirsts for God it is first pierced by fear and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears because, recalling its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by the prolonged anguish of grief, a certain security regarding the hope of pardon arises, and the soul is set aflame with love for heavenly joys.

The one who previously wept for fear of being led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. The mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are like, what the fellowship of the blessed spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is. It mourns more because it is deprived of everlasting goods than it formerly wept when it feared eternal evils.

Thus perfect compunction arising from fear draws the soul toward compunction arising from love [Note: Longipontanus reads “leads,” a reading followed by the printed editions].

This is well represented in the sacred and truthful history by the figurative account that says that Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon a donkey, sighed. Her father said to her: “What is the matter with you?” She replied: “Give me a blessing. You have given me a southern and dry land; add also a watered land.” Her father gave her the upper and lower watercourses (Joshua 15:18 and following) [Note: Two Theodosian manuscripts and one Chartres manuscript read “the upper watercourse and the lower watercourse.”].

Achsah sits upon a donkey when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. She sighs and asks her father for watered land because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning.

There are some who have already received the gift of speaking freely for justice, protecting the oppressed, giving their possessions to the needy, and possessing the fervor of faith; yet they do not have the grace of tears. They possess southern and dry land, but still lack water, because, although they are established in good works in which they are great and fervent, it is exceedingly necessary that they should weep over the evils they previously committed, whether through fear of punishment or through love of the heavenly kingdom.

But because, as I have said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her the upper and lower watercourses. The soul receives the upper watercourse when it afflicts itself with tears out of desire for the heavenly kingdom. It receives the lower watercourse when it dreads the punishments of hell with tears.

The lower watercourse is indeed given first, and afterward the upper. But because compunction arising from love surpasses it in dignity, the narrative had to mention the upper watercourse first and the lower afterward.

**Peter.** I approve what you say. But since you said that Eleutherius, a man of venerable life, possessed this degree of merit, I would like to ask whether we should believe that there are still such people in the world.

## Chapter XXXIV. Concerning the distinction between kinds of compunction

**Gregory.** Compunction is divided into many forms of beauty when all the faults of penitents are mourned. Hence Jeremiah says in the person of penitents: “My eye brought forth divisions of waters.”

There are therefore two principal kinds of compunction. When the soul thirsts for God, it is first pierced by fear and afterward by longing. At first it wastes itself away in tears, remembering its own evils and fearing that it may fall under eternal punishment because of them. But when it has remained in great anguish of grief, its dread comes to an end. A kind of freedom regarding forgiveness and confidence in it is born within the soul, and it is then kindled by longing for heavenly joy.

The soul that first wept from fear of being carried away to judgment later begins again to weep bitterly because it is far from the kingdom. The mind looks upon the choirs of the angels, their fellowship, the greatness of the blessed spirits, and the vision of God himself. It mourns more and more because it is deprived of abiding goods, whereas previously it mourned while fearing eternal evils.

Thus perfect compunction leads the soul from fear into love.

This is well written in the sacred and true history, in both historical and figurative narrative, concerning Achsah, the daughter of Caleb. She sat upon a donkey and sighed. Her father said to her: “What is the matter with you?” She answered him: “Give me a blessing. You have given me the dry land of the south; add to it the watered land.” Her father gave her the watered land above and the watered land below.

Achsah, sitting upon the donkey, signifies the soul that sits upon the passions of the irrational flesh. That she sighed and asked her father for watered land signifies that we must seek from our Creator, with great groaning, the gift of tears.

There are many who have been deemed worthy of a teaching gift, who can speak the cause of truth with confidence, comfort those in distress, assist those in need, and become zealous concerning the faith, yet have not yet received the gift of tears [Note: The manuscript reads: “that is, they have the southern land, the dry land.”]. These possess the dry southern land, but still lack the watered land. For although they are engaged in good works, they must still weep over the evils they have committed, either because of fear of judgment or because of longing for the kingdom of heaven, so that they may enter where the great and fervent enter.

As I said, there are two kinds of compunction. Therefore her father gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land. The soul receives the upper watered land when it mourns in tears through its care for the enjoyment of the heavenly kingdom [Note: The manuscript reads: “The soul receives the upper watered land when, mourning in tears, it desires to receive the enjoyment of the heavenly kingdom.”]. It receives the lower watered land when it mourns through fear of eternal punishment.

Yet the lower watered land is given first, and afterward the upper. Because compunction arising from longing surpasses the other in dignity, the narrative necessarily mentions the upper watered land first and the lower afterward.

**Peter.** I approve what you say. But since you said that this most reverent Eleutherius possessed such merit, I wish to ask whether we should believe that there are still people of this kind in the world.

## Chapter XXXV. Concerning Amantius, a priest of the province of Tuscia
GREGORY. Floridus, bishop of the Church of Tibur [Note: This should be read from all the manuscripts as *Tiburtinae* or *Tuburtinae*, not *Tudertinae*, as the editions have it. Tibur is an episcopal city in Latium on the Anio River, now called Tivoli; it differs considerably from Tudertum, commonly called Todi, an episcopal city in Umbria on the Tiber.]—whose truth and holiness are not unknown to your affection—told me that he had with him a certain presbyter named Amantius [Note: His name is entered in the Martyrology on September 26], a man of exceptional simplicity. He is said to possess this power: following the apostles’ example, he lays his hand upon the sick [Note: Another reading: “and restores health,” as found in the German manuscript and in some manuscripts derived from the Norman tradition], restores them to health, and however severe the illness may be, it departs at his touch.

He added that the man also possessed this miraculous power: wherever he found a serpent, however monstrous and fierce, as soon as he had marked it with the sign of the cross, he killed it, so that by the power of the cross which the man of God traced upon it with his finger, its entrails burst and it died. If at any time a serpent fled into a hole, he blessed the mouth of the hole with the sign of the cross, and immediately the serpent was dragged out dead.

I myself also took care to see this man of such great power. After he had been brought to me, I arranged for him to remain a few days in the house for the sick, where, if he possessed any gift of healing, it could be tested more quickly. There a certain man who had lost his mind lay among the other sick; physicians call this condition *phreneticus*, using the Greek term. One night, when he uttered loud cries like a madman and disturbed all the sick with immense shouting, so that no one there could sleep, the situation became exceedingly pitiful: because one man was suffering badly, all the others suffered even more.

But, as I learned carefully first from the most reverend Bishop Floridus, who at that time was staying there together with the aforementioned presbyter, and afterward from the boy who was serving the sick that night, the same venerable presbyter rose from his own bed, silently approached the bed of the delirious man, laid his hands upon him, and prayed. Immediately he took him, now in a better condition, and led him with him to the upper rooms of the house, to the oratory. There he devoted himself more freely to prayer on his behalf and at once brought him back to his own bed cured. From then on the man uttered no further cries and disturbed none of the sick by shouting; having completely recovered his reason, he no longer aggravated another’s illness. From this single deed of his we learned to believe all the other things we had heard about him.

PETER. It is a great edification for life to see men performing such wonders and to behold the heavenly Jerusalem on earth in its citizens.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Amantius, bishop of the province of Tuscia

[Col. 0302A]

GREGORY. Floridus, the bishop of Tibur, whose truth and righteousness are not unknown to your affection, told me that he had with him a certain presbyter named Amantius [Note: The manuscript reads *Amandzium*], a man of the greatest innocence. He bears witness that this man possesses such power that, laying his hand upon the sick according to the custom of the apostles, he immediately grants healing [Note: The printed editions read “they receive”; “for whatever…”]. For whatever severe illness may hold someone, the disease is driven away by the mere touch of his hands.

He also added this to the account of the miracle concerning him: wherever he finds a serpent, however savage and twisted its nature may be, if he marks it with the sign of the cross, it immediately dies. For by the power of the cross, through which the man of God imprints the sign upon it with his finger, the beast dies as its entrails are torn apart. If a serpent ever takes refuge in a hole, he likewise seals its opening with the sign of the cross, and at once the serpent emerges dead.

I earnestly desired to see this man, who possessed such power [Note: The manuscript reads, “I desired to see him.”]. After he had been brought to me, I arranged for him to remain a few days in the hospital. I can briefly relate what gift of healing took place there.

Among the sick in the hospital there was a man whose mind was impaired; medical science calls this illness *phrenitis* in the Greek language. At night he uttered loud and incessant cries, clearly being unsound in mind, and disturbed all the sick, so that none of those lying there could sleep. Thus a most pitiable situation arose: because one man was suffering badly, all the others were tormented still more on his account.

I first learned what had happened from Floridus the bishop, who at that time was staying there together with the aforementioned presbyter [Note: The manuscript reads, “who was then resting there”]. I later learned it also from the boy who served the sick that night. He said that the same most reverend presbyter rose from his bed, silently approached the bed of the delirious man [Note: The manuscript reads, “of the man suffering from *phrenitis*”—perhaps *phrenitiōntos*], laid his hands upon him, and prayed.

Immediately, when the man was in a better condition, he lifted him up and led him with him to the upper rooms of the house, into the oratory. There, bending himself to prayer on his behalf, he immediately brought him back healthy to his own bed, so that thereafter he neither uttered cries nor disturbed any of the sick at all. For, having completely recovered the soundness of his reason, he no longer added the disturbance of another’s illness. From this one miracle performed by him, of which we ourselves were witnesses, we believe all the things heard about him to be true.

PETER. The greatest edification comes to a community from seeing men performing miracles and seeing the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem present on earth.

357 **CHAPTER XXXVI. On Maximianus, bishop of the city of Syracuse**

[Col. 0304B]

GREGORY. I do not think that I should keep silent about the miracle which almighty God deigned to display concerning Maximianus, his servant—now bishop of Syracuse, but at that time father of my monastery [Note: The Roman Martyrology mentions him on June 9. The events related here are confirmed by the letter to Leander prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*. Several letters of Gregory to him are extant; read them. In Letter 17 of Book V, indiction 13, he mourns Amicus, who had already died.]

While, at the command of my bishop, I was serving in the palace of Constantinople as an ecclesiastical representative, that same venerable Maximianus came to me there with some brothers, compelled by affection. When he was returning to my monastery at Rome, he was caught in an exceedingly violent storm in the Adriatic Sea and, by an immeasurable and extraordinary miracle concerning himself and all who were with him, came to know both the anger and the grace of almighty God.

For when the winds rose with violence and the waves swelled and raged against their destruction, the nails of the ship were lost [Note: So read most of the better manuscripts. Valentinianus-Claromontanus reads “when the bolt was lost”; the editions have “when the bolts were lost”], the mast was cut down, the sails were thrown into the waves, and the whole vessel, shaken by the violence of the waves, was loosened from all its framework. With its seams thus gaping, the sea entered and filled the ship up to the upper planks, so that it seemed not so much that the ship was within the waves as that the waves were already within the ship.

Then all those sitting in the ship, no longer merely near death but terrified by death’s very presence and sight, were thrown into great confusion. They gave one another the kiss of peace [Note: Clearly the kiss of peace, which according to ancient custom preceded reception of the Eucharist. In the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 63: “Let the brothers approach the peace, then Communion.” See the learned Menard in his notes on the appendix to the *Sacramentary*, at the words “Meanwhile let him kiss the archdeacon,” formerly p. 378, now note 986. Observe here the ancient custom of reserving and carrying the Eucharist on journeys; and read what Ambrose writes about his brother Satyrus, *On the Death of Satyrus*, Book I, no. 43 of the new edition, together with the note on that passage], received the body and blood of the Redeemer, and each commended himself to God, asking him graciously to receive their souls, whose bodies he had allowed to be handed over to so fearful a death.

But almighty God, who had struck their minds with such terror, preserved their lives still more wondrously. For eight days the same ship, filled with water up to the upper planks, continued on its course and floated. On the ninth day it was brought into the harbor of the fortress of Cotron [Note: The manuscript reads “the fortress of Croton.” Gregory is plainly speaking of Croton in Bruttium on the Ionian coast, not the Etruscan Croton, which does not lie on the sea].

All who had been sailing with the aforementioned venerable Maximianus came out unharmed. After Maximianus himself had also come out last of all, the ship immediately sank in the depths of that same harbor, as though, when they had disembarked, it had lost the support provided by their weight.
