The vessel that had carried people and, filled with water, had floated on the open sea was unable to carry water without people in the harbor once Maximianus and his brothers had left it. Thus almighty God showed that he had held it up by his own hand: once emptied of people and abandoned, it could not remain upon the waters.

358 **CHAPTER XXXVI. On Maximianus, bishop of the city of Syracuse**

[Col. 0303B]

GREGORY. I consider it right not to pass over in silence the miracle which almighty God deigned to display concerning Maximianus, his servant—now bishop of the Syracusans, but at that time the head of my monastery. For while I was serving in Constantinople, at the command of my patriarch, as an ecclesiastical representative, that same most reverend Maximianus came to me with brothers out of affection [Note: The manuscript reads, “came there to me”].

When he was returning to Rome, he was overwhelmed by the most violent storm on the sea of Adria [Note: The manuscript reads, “the sea of Adria”]. Through an extraordinary and unfathomable miracle concerning him and those who were with him, he came to know both the anger and the compassion of almighty God.

For when violent winds arose and the waves increased, the fastenings of the ship were torn away, the mast was broken, the sails were thrown into the sea [Note: The manuscript reads, “the nails were torn out, the mast was broken, the sails…”], and the whole ship, shaken by the force of the waves, was loosened from all its joints. When its joints had thus been loosened, as has been said, the sea entered inside and filled the ship up to the upper planks, so that the ship seemed not so much to be in the waves as the waves to be inside the ship.

Therefore all those in the ship, no longer merely seeing death approaching but beholding it present before their eyes, fell into great terror. They exchanged the kiss of peace, received the body and blood of our God and Lord Jesus Christ the Redeemer, and entrusted their souls to him, asking that he graciously receive them, whose bodies he had permitted to be delivered to such a dreadful death.

But almighty God, who had struck their thoughts with terror, wondrously preserved their lives. For eight days their ship, filled with water up to the upper planks, as has been said, sailed on while pursuing its course. On the ninth day it was guided into the harbor of the fortress of Cotron [Note: The manuscript reads, “the fortress of Croton.”]

All those who had sailed with the aforementioned most reverend man Maximianus disembarked. Maximianus himself disembarked last of all; immediately afterward, in that same harbor, the ship sank, having remained afloat only until its burden had been lightened. The vessel, which had carried people and, full of water, had sailed on the open sea, could not carry water in the harbor without the people, once Maximianus and his brothers had left it. In this way almighty God showed that he himself had sustained it by his own hand: when left empty of people [Note: The manuscript reads, “empty of ballast”], it could not remain upon the waters.

360 **CHAPTER XXXVII. On Sanctulus, presbyter of the province of Nursia**

[Col. 0305B]

GREGORY. About forty days ago you also saw with me the venerable presbyter Sanctulus, whose memory I mentioned earlier (Chapter 15), a man of venerable life who was accustomed to come to me every year from the province of Nursia. But three days ago a monk came from that same province and struck me with the sorrow of grave news, reporting that this man had died.

Although I do not recall this man’s sweetness without a sigh, I now relate without fear the miracles that I learned from his neighboring priests, men endowed with remarkable truthfulness and simplicity [Note: The editions read “with marvelous power,” contrary to the manuscripts and the Greek translator]. Just as intimacy among those whose hearts love one another offers great boldness in charity, I was often led by affection to question him, and he was compelled to confess to me a few things concerning what he had done.

At one time, when the Lombards were pressing olives in a press [Note: The German manuscript and most others read “pressing olives”], so that they might be liquefied into oil [Note: This is a manner of expression especially familiar to our Gregory; it also occurs in contemporary or nearly contemporary writers. Gregory of Tours, *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 9: “He put into him the thought that he ought to leave the desert and return to the world,” that is, “that he should return.” Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 23: “They send Augustine … so that he might obtain from blessed Gregory that they should not have to undertake so dangerous a pilgrimage”], he brought an empty wineskin to the press. Cheerful in face and spirit [Note: So read the German, Royal, Norman, two Chartres manuscripts, a fragment of another, two Theodulf manuscripts, Longipontanus, and others. The editions read: “as he was cheerful in face and spirit.” Cheerfulness is also praised in saints and in monks themselves, even when devoted to penitence. Macarius the younger, archimandrite of Nitria, is praised for receiving visitors with a cheerful face and delighting them with witty speech, attracting younger men to monastic discipline by a certain graciousness. See Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret, and Palladius in the *Lausiac History*], he greeted the laboring Lombards with a joyful expression, presented the wineskin, and, more by commanding than asking, told them to fill it for him.

But those pagan men, who had already labored fruitlessly all day and could not extract oil from the olives by pressing them, took his words badly and assailed him with insults. The man of God replied to them with an even more cheerful face, saying [Note: So read the German manuscript together with Longipontanus, Valentinianus-Claromontanus, and many others. The Greek translator has the same reading. The Norman manuscripts, except for Gemetensis and the second Audoen manuscript, read “if you believe me.” The second Chartres manuscript agrees. The first reads “if you pray for me,” which the editors retained]:

“Pray for me in this way: fill this wineskin for Sanctulus, and thus it will return from you.”

When they did not see oil flowing from the olives, and saw the man of God persisting in asking them to fill the wineskin, they became exceedingly angry and began to dismiss him with still greater insults and abusive words. But the man of God, seeing that no oil at all was coming from the press, asked that water be given to him. With everyone watching, he blessed it and threw it with his own hands into the pressed olives.

Immediately after this blessing such an abundance of oil burst forth that the Lombards, who had previously labored for a long time in vain, filled not only all their own vessels but also the wineskin that the man of God had brought. They gave great thanks to him because, having come to ask for oil, he himself by blessing had given them what he requested.

[Col. 0308B] At another time a severe famine had settled everywhere, and the church of blessed Lawrence the martyr had been burned by the Lombards. Wishing to restore it, the man of God employed many craftsmen and supplied even more laborers. It was necessary to provide the workers’ daily expenses without delay. But because the famine pressed with such necessity, bread ran out. The laborers began urgently to seek food, for through want they had no strength for their work.

When the man of God heard this, he consoled them outside with words, promising what he did not possess. Yet inwardly he was grievously distressed, unable to provide the food he had promised. As he anxiously went here and there, he came to an oven in which the neighboring women had baked bread the day before. Bending down, he looked to see whether perhaps some bread had been left behind by those who had baked it.

Then suddenly he found a loaf of remarkable size and unusual whiteness. He picked it up, but did not wish to carry it to the craftsmen, lest it perhaps belong to someone else and he incur guilt under the pretext of compassion. He therefore carried it to the neighboring women, showed it to everyone, and asked whether it had been left there by any of them.

All the women who had baked bread there the previous day denied that it was theirs, insisting that they had taken all their own loaves from the oven in their full number. Then the man of God, rejoicing, went to the many craftsmen with the single loaf and urged them to give thanks to almighty God. He told them that God had supplied their food, invited them immediately to eat, and set the loaf before them.

When they had been sufficiently and fully satisfied, he collected from it more fragments than the loaf itself had contained. The following day he brought those fragments to them for food; but what remained from the fragments exceeded even the fragments that had been served. Thus for ten days all those craftsmen and laborers were satisfied from that one loaf. They ate from it every day, and every day enough remained to be eaten on the following day, as though the fragments of that loaf increased through being eaten and restored food to the mouths of those who consumed it.

[Col. 0309A]

PETER. A marvelous event, and one that ought greatly to astonish everyone as an example of the Lord’s work.

GREGORY. The same Lord, Peter, fed many from one loaf through his servant—he who by himself satisfied five thousand men with five loaves, who multiplies a few grains of seed into countless crops of grain, who also produced the seeds themselves from the earth and created all things together from nothing.

But so that you may not continue wondering at what the venerable man Sanctulus did outwardly by the Lord’s power, hear what he was inwardly by the Lord’s power. One day a certain deacon had been captured by the Lombards and was being held bound by them; those who had captured him intended to kill him. As evening approached, the man of God Sanctulus asked the same Lombards to release him and spare his life, but they absolutely refused to do so.

When he saw that they had decided upon the man’s death, he asked them to hand him over to his custody [Note: Valentinianus-Claromontanus, with the German manuscript, reads “for safekeeping.”]. They immediately replied:

“We give him to you for safekeeping, but on this condition: if he escapes, you yourself shall die in his place.”

The man of God willingly accepted this and took the aforementioned deacon under his protection. At midnight, when he saw that all the Lombards were overcome by deep sleep, he woke him and said:

“Rise and flee quickly. May almighty God set you free.”

But the deacon, not forgetting his promise, replied:

“I cannot flee, Father, because if I flee, you will certainly die in my place.”

The man of God Sanctulus urged him to flee, saying:

“Rise and go; may almighty God rescue you. I am in his hand, and they can do to me only as much as he permits.”

The deacon therefore fled, and the guarantor remained behind as though he had been deceived. When morning came, the Lombards who had handed over the deacon for safekeeping came and asked for the man they had entrusted to him. The venerable presbyter replied that the deacon had fled.

Then they said:

“You yourself know best what is fitting.”

The servant of the Lord answered firmly:

“I know.”

They said to him:

“You are a good man. We do not wish to kill you through various tortures. Choose whatever death you wish.”

The man of God replied:

“I am in God’s hand. Kill me by whatever death he permits me to suffer.”

Then all the Lombards who were present there agreed that they should cut off his head, so that they might end his life by a swift death without severe torture. When the Lombards who were found in that place learned that Sanctulus—who among them, because of the reverence due to his holiness, was held in great honor—was to be killed, they all gathered, rejoicing in their customary cruelty, to watch the spectacle of his death [Note: Lyranus and the first Audoen manuscript together with Gemetensis read: “and, as is their custom, surrounded him for the spectacle of death. Thus, amid the ranks…”]. They formed ranks around him.

The man of God was led into their midst, and from among all the strong men one was chosen who was beyond doubt capable of severing his head with a single blow. The venerable man, led among the armed men, immediately turned to his own weapon—that is, he asked that he be granted a little time to pray. When this had been granted, he stretched himself upon the ground and prayed.

After he had prayed for a somewhat longer time, the chosen executioner struck him with his foot to make him rise, saying:

“Rise, bend your knee, and stretch out your neck.”

The man of God rose, knelt, and stretched out his neck. Seeing the sword drawn and held against him, he is said to have publicly uttered only these words [Note: He undoubtedly invoked Saint John the Baptist, who was venerated with great devotion among the Lombards, as Paul the Deacon says, *History of the Lombards*, Book V, chapter 6. This led Queen Theodelinda to build, at great expense, a basilica dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, adorn it with gold and silver ornaments, and enrich it with estates near Modicia, or Monza, not far from Milan. See Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapters 22–23]:

“Saint John, receive it.”

Then the chosen executioner, holding his unsheathed sword, raised his arm high with great force to strike him, but he could not bring it down. For when he had raised the sword into the air, his arm suddenly became rigid and remained immovable, with the sword held upright toward heaven.

Then the entire crowd of Lombards who had come to watch that spectacle of death turned to praise of God. They began to marvel and to venerate the man of God with fear, for it had plainly become evident what holiness belonged to the man who had bound his executioner’s arm in the air.

He was therefore asked to rise, and he rose. They then begged him to heal the arm of his executioner. He refused, saying:

“I will not pray for him at all unless he first gives me an oath that he will not kill a Christian with this hand.”

The Lombard, who, so to speak, had lost his arm by stretching it against God, was compelled by the pressure of his punishment to swear that he would never kill a Christian.

Then the man of God ordered him:

“Lower your hand.”

He immediately lowered it. He added:

“Put the sword back into its sheath.”

And he immediately did so.

All the Lombards, recognizing that the man possessed such power, eagerly wished to offer him as gifts the oxen, beasts of burden, and other livestock they had plundered. But the man of God refused to accept such a gift. Instead he sought the gift of a good reward, saying:

“If you wish to grant me something, give me all the captives you hold, so that I may have the means to pray on your behalf.”

This was done. All the captives were released with him, and, by the ordering of heavenly grace, while one man offered himself to death for one man, he freed many from death.

[Col. 0313A]

PETER. It is a marvelous event. Although I myself learned it from others, I nevertheless truly confess that whenever it is told to me, it becomes new again.

GREGORY. Do not marvel at Sanctulus because of this deed; rather, if you can, consider what sort of spirit it was that possessed his mind in such integrity and raised him to such a height of virtue. Where was his soul when he so steadfastly resolved to die for his neighbor, despised his own life for the temporal life of one brother, and stretched his neck beneath the sword? What force of love held that heart, which did not fear its own death for the salvation of a single neighbor?

We certainly know that the same venerable man Sanctulus did not even know the elements of letters well. He did not know the commandments of the Law. But because love is the fulfillment of the Law (Romans 13:10), he kept the whole Law in love of God and neighbor. What he did not know outwardly through learning, he lived inwardly through love.

Although he had perhaps never read what the apostle John said about the Redeemer: “Since he laid down his life for us, so we also ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:13), he knew this lofty apostolic command by putting it into practice rather than by knowing it.

Let us compare, if you please, our unlearned knowledge with his learned ignorance. Where our knowledge lies low, his discipline rises above it. We speak, empty of virtues, as though standing among fruitful trees: we smell the fruit but cannot eat it. He knew how to seize the fruit of virtues, although he did not know how to smell them through words [Note: The German and several Norman manuscripts read “to smell them.”].

[Col. 0313C]

PETER. What do you think is the reason, I ask you, that good men are taken away so quickly—men who could have lived for the edification of many—and either cannot be found at all or, if they are found, are already exceedingly rare?

GREGORY. The wickedness of those who remain deserves that those who could have been useful should be taken away swiftly. As the end of the world approaches, the elect are removed so that they may not see worse things. Thus the prophet says:

“The righteous man perishes, and no one takes it to heart; and men of mercy are gathered away, because there is no one who understands” (Isaiah 57:1).

Again it is written:

“Open, that those who trample her may go out; remove the stones from the road” (Jeremiah 50:26).

Solomon likewise says:

“A time for throwing stones, and a time for gathering stones” (Ecclesiastes 3:5).

As the end of the world therefore presses upon us, it is necessary that living stones be gathered for the heavenly building, so that our Jerusalem may grow to the measure of its construction [Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads, “because the end of the world is rising”]. Yet we do not believe that all the elect are taken away, so that only the wicked remain in the world. For sinners would never return to the lament of repentance if there were no examples of the good to draw their minds toward repentance.

[Col. 0316A]

PETER. I complain in vain that the good are taken away, while I see the wicked also perishing in multitudes.

359 **CHAPTER XXXVII. On Sanctulus, presbyter of the province of Nursia**

[Col. 0306B]

GREGORY. About forty days ago you saw with me the most reverend presbyter Sanctulus, a man venerable in life. He was accustomed to come to me every year from the province of Nursia. Three days ago a monk came from that same province and said that this man had died; this report bent me down beneath heavy sorrow.

Although I cannot recall this man’s sweetness without a sigh, nevertheless I relate his miracles without restraint, which I learned from the priests living near him, men of great truthfulness and fidelity. The souls of those united to one another by love bring forth frankness toward one another. Thus, questioned by me—indeed, compelled more by affection—he used to relate a few of the things he had done.

At one time, when certain Lombards were pressing olives and squeezing them so that they might produce oil, he came upon them carrying a wineskin containing ballast [Note: The manuscript reads, “an empty wineskin.”]. As was his custom, being cheerful both in soul and [Note: The manuscript reads, “in body”] in face, he greeted the laboring Lombards with a gracious expression. Bringing forward the wineskin, he told them to fill it with oil, speaking more as one giving an order than as one making a request.

But those pagan men, because they had labored all day to no purpose and were unable to extract oil from the olives [Note: The manuscript reads: “because they were weary from laboring all day without result and were unable to bring forth oil from the olives,” they regarded his words as worthless and sent him away with insults.

The man of God answered them again with a gracious face, saying:

“Pray for me in this way, and fill this wineskin for Sanctulus, so that it may return from you in this condition” [Note: The manuscript reads, “so that it may return from us.”].

When they did not see oil coming forth from the olives and saw the man of God persisting in having the wineskin filled, they became exceedingly angry and sent him away with the greatest insults and threats.

But the man of God, seeing that no oil at all was coming forth as the olives were being pressed, asked that water be given to him. With everyone watching, he blessed it and threw it with his own hands into the pressed olives.

As soon as this had happened, such an abundance of oil emerged that the Lombards, who had previously labored for so long without result, filled not only all their own vessels but also the wineskin which the man of God had brought. They confessed that they owed him the greatest thanks, because he had come to ask for oil and by his blessing had himself given them what he had requested [Note: The manuscript reads, “what he asked for.”].

[Col. 0307B]

At another time a very great famine spread everywhere. The church of blessed Lawrence the martyr had been burned by the Lombards. Wishing to rebuild it, the man of God gathered many craftsmen and still more laborers. It was therefore necessary to provide the daily expense of food for the workers without any delay.

But as the necessity of the famine pressed upon them, bread failed. The laborers began to seek food, for they had no strength to work because of hunger. When the man of God heard this, he consoled them with words, promising them what he did not have. Yet he was greatly distressed inwardly because he had no means of providing the food he had promised. In his anxiety he ran about here and there [Note: The manuscript reads, “he moved about”].

Coming to an oven in which the neighboring women had baked bread the day before, he bent down and looked to see whether perhaps some bread had been left there. Suddenly he found a loaf of marvelous size and unusual whiteness [Note: The manuscript reads, “brightness.”]

He lifted it up, but did not wish to carry it to the craftsmen, lest it perhaps belong to someone else and he fall into wrongdoing under the pretext of compassion. He therefore carried it to the neighboring women, showed it to everyone, and asked whether it had been left there by any of them.

All the women who had baked bread there acknowledged that it was not theirs, insisting that they had taken all their own loaves from the oven intact.

Then the man of God, rejoicing, went to the many craftsmen with the single loaf. He urged them to give thanks to almighty God and announced that God had provided them with food. Immediately he invited them to eat and set before them the loaf that had been found.

When they had been filled to satiety, more fragments were found than the loaf itself had contained [Note: The manuscript reads *periesethēsan*; perhaps *eperisseuthēsan*, “were left over”]. The next day he set those fragments before them to eat. Once again they were satisfied, and the fragments of bread increased [Note: The manuscript reads, “he caused to be left over”].

Thus, when he continued to set the remaining fragments before them, it came about that for ten days all those craftsmen and laborers ate from that one loaf and were satisfied. Each day they ate from it as much as they could consume, and just as much again remained—enough to suffice and even remain over for the following day. That loaf restored the bodies of those who ate it to strength, while through the fragments it increased beyond measure from day to day.

[Col. 0310A]

PETER. A marvelous event, and exceedingly astonishing, for this deed looks toward the Lord’s example.

GREGORY. The Lord himself, Peter, even now satisfied many through his servant from one loaf—he who by himself filled five thousand men from five loaves [Note: The manuscript reads, “he satisfied”]; he who multiplies from a few grains of seed countless fruits of the harvest; he who also brought forth the seeds themselves from the earth and together created all things from nothing.

But so that you may not continue wondering at what the venerable man Sanctulus did outwardly by the Lord’s power, hear what he was inwardly by the Lord’s power. One day a certain deacon had been captured by the Lombards and was held bound among them; those who had captured him wished to kill him.

As evening approached, the man of God Sanctulus pleaded with the Lombards that they grant this man his life. They absolutely refused to do so. When he saw that they had securely decided upon his death, he asked them at least to entrust the man to him for safekeeping.

They replied:

“We give him to you for safekeeping, but on this condition: if he flees, you shall die in his place” [Note: The manuscript reads, “we give him to you.”].

The man of God willingly accepted this and received the aforementioned deacon into his protection. Around midnight, when he saw all the Lombards held fast by very deep sleep, he woke the deacon and said:

“Rise and flee quickly. Almighty God will set you free” [Note: The manuscript reads, “will rescue you.”].

The deacon, not forgetting his promise, replied:

“I cannot flee, Father. For if I flee, you will unquestionably die in my place.”

The man of God Sanctulus urged him to flee, saying:

“Rise and go. Almighty God will rescue you. I am in his hand, and they can do to me only as much as he permits.”

The deacon therefore fled, and the guarantor remained behind, as though deceived. When morning came, the Lombards who had handed the deacon over to the presbyter for safekeeping came to him, seeking the man whom they had entrusted to him.

The most reverend presbyter told them that the deacon had fled. They said to him:

“You yourself know well how the matter was arranged.”

The servant of the Lord answered boldly:

“I know.”

They said to him:

“You are a good man, and we do not wish to kill you after punishing you with various tortures. Choose whatever death you wish” [Note: The manuscript reads, “after punishing you through various trials.”].

The man of God replied:

“I am in the hand of God. Kill me by whatever death he permits me to suffer.”

Then all the Lombards who were present there agreed that they should cut off his head, so that they might rid him of life by a merciful death without the heaviest punishment [Note: The manuscript reads, “without the heaviest torture … release him from life.”].

When the Lombards who were found in that place realized that Sanctulus—who among them, because of reverence for his holiness, was held in the highest honor—was about to be killed, they all gathered, rejoicing in their customary cruelty and standing in ordered ranks [Note: The manuscript reads *enordinōs*. These adverbs occur in the Greco-barbarous language; *ordinon*, *ordinos*, and *ordinia* correspond to the Latin *ordo*, “order.” There is also *ordinarios*, “ordinary,” and *ordineuein*, “to arrange”], and awaited his death.

When the man of God had been brought into their midst, one man was chosen from among all the physically powerful men, one of whom there could be no doubt that he would sever his head with a single blow. This most reverend man, brought forward among the armed men, immediately ran toward his own weapon; for he asked that a little time be granted him to pray [Note: The manuscript reads, “a little freedom.”]

When this had been granted, he spread himself upon the ground and began to pray. After he had lingered in prayer for a short while, the man chosen to kill him prodded him with his foot and said:

“Rise, bend your knee, and stretch out your neck.”

The man of God rose and did as he had been ordered. When he had stretched out his neck and saw the sword unsheathed against him, he publicly uttered this one word, as they say:

“Saint John, receive it.”

Then that chosen, flesh-eating man, holding the naked sword, raised his arm high with all his strength to strike him, but could not bring it down. For when he had raised the sword into the air, his arm suddenly remained immovable.

Then the whole tumult of the Lombards who had come to witness his death was turned into praise of God. They began to marvel and to venerate the man of God with fear [Note: The manuscript reads, “they believed with fear; for it was plainly shown…”]. It had clearly been shown what holiness belonged to the man who had bound the arm of the flesh-eating executioner in the air.

He was therefore asked to rise, and he rose. They pleaded with him to heal the arm of that executioner. But the holy man refused, saying:

“I will not pray for him at all unless he first gives me an oath that he will not kill a Christian with this hand.”

That Lombard, who, so to speak, had lost his arm by stretching it against God, was compelled by the pressure of his punishment to swear that he would never kill a Christian.

Then the man of God ordered him:

“Lower your hand.”

He immediately lowered it, and at once put the sword back into its sheath.

All the Lombards, recognizing that the man possessed such power, strove to offer him as gifts the sheep, oxen, and other livestock they had plundered [Note: The manuscript reads, “which they were plundering.”] But the man of God did not wish to accept such gifts. Instead he sought a gift of good reward, saying:

“If you wish to give me some gift, grant me all the captives you have, so that I may have a reason to pray for you.”

This was done, and all the captives were released with him. Thus heavenly providence arranged matters so that, while he offered himself alone to death for one man, he might ransom many from death.

[Col. 0314A]

PETER. It is truly a marvelous event. I have also heard from others that it is true; nevertheless, I confess that whenever it is told to me, it is renewed within me [Note: Perhaps from *rēscere*, “to spread among the people”; consult Du Cange’s *Glossary* concerning the word. The manuscript reads *legetai*, “it is said.”].

GREGORY. Do not marvel at Sanctulus because of this deed. Rather, if you can, consider what sort of spirit it was that so completely governed his uncorrupted mind and raised him to such a height of power. Where was his soul when he so eagerly hastened to die for his neighbor, despised his own life for the temporal life of one brother, and stretched his neck beneath the sword?

What intensity of longing held his heart, so that he did not fear death for the salvation of his neighbor? Yet what is still more marvelous is that he did not even know letters. We know with certainty that the same most reverend man Sanctulus did not even know well the elements of written characters. He did not know the commandments of the Law.

But because love is the fulfillment of the Law, he kept the whole Law in love of God and neighbor. What he did not know outwardly through learning, he lived inwardly through longing. Although he had perhaps never read what the apostle John said about our Redeemer Jesus Christ—that just as he laid down his life for us, so we ought also to lay down our lives for our brothers—he fulfilled this lofty apostolic command in deed rather than knowing it through learning.

Let us compare, if you wish, our unlearned knowledge with his educated ignorance: where our condition lies, and where his rises above it. We, speaking emptily in the power of words, are like people standing among fruitful trees: we smell the fruit, but cannot eat it. He knew how to grasp the fruit in deed, although he did not know how to smell it through words.

[Col. 0314C]

PETER. What do you suppose is the reason, I ask, that good men are taken away so quickly—men who could have lived for the edification of many—and either cannot be found at all, or, if they are found, are found only rarely?

GREGORY. The wickedness of those who remain deserves this. Those who could have benefited others are therefore taken away swiftly, so that, as the end of the world approaches, they may not see more difficult things.

Concerning this the prophet says:

“The righteous man has perished, and there is no one who reflects in his heart; and the men of mercy are gathered away, because there is no one who understands.”

Again it is written:

“Open, so that those who trample upon her may go out. Remove the stones from the road.”

For this reason Solomon also says:

“A time to throw stones, and a time to gather stones.”

Since the end of the world is now hastening, it is therefore necessary that living stones be piled up for the heavenly building, so that our Jerusalem may grow beyond measure according to the proportion of its construction.

We do not, however, believe that all the elect are taken away, leaving only the wicked in the world. For sinners would never return to the lament of repentance if there were no examples of the good drawing their minds toward it.

[Col. 0315A]

PETER. I therefore seek in vain to know why the good are taken away, while I clearly see the wicked perishing.

**CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the vision of Redemptus, bishop of the city of Ferentinum**

[Col. 0316A]

GREGORY. In this matter, Peter, do not be surprised at all. For you knew Redemptus, bishop of the city of Ferentinum, a man venerable in life, who departed this world about seven years ago. [Note: He is commemorated on 8 April. Ferentinum is an episcopal city of Latium, in the territory of the Hernici.] When I was still living in the monastery, he was very closely attached to me; and, when I asked him, he himself told me what he had learned concerning the end of the world in the time of my predecessor, the younger John. [Note: That is, of Pope John III.] This had become widely known.

For he said that one day, while making his customary circuit of his parishes, [Note: Here “parishes” means villages and village churches; this usage is scarcely found in earlier or contemporary writers. Yet *parochia* is used in the same sense in the synodal letter to Egidius concerning the new bishopric of Dunum Castrum, in the appendix to the works of Gregory of Tours, column 1341.] he came to the church of the blessed martyr Eutychius. [Note: In Germanus and the second Theodorus, Juthicius; the first Carnotensis has Justicius, with the Greek translator agreeing. The second Carnotensis has Justinus; the *Compendium* has Zoticius; the first Theodorus has Judicius. The others read Eutychius or Eutycius. In the Roman Martyrology, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, one reads: “At Ferentinum among the Hernici, Saint Eutychius the martyr.”]

As evening came on, he ordered a bed to be prepared for him beside the martyr’s tomb, and there rested after his labor. In the middle of the night, as he said, he was neither asleep nor fully able to remain awake; rather, as often happens, his mind was weighed down by sleep while remaining conscious. The blessed martyr Eutychius then stood before him and said: “Redemptus, are you awake?” He replied: “I am awake.” The martyr said: “The end is coming for all flesh; the end is coming for all flesh; the end is coming for all flesh.”

After this threefold utterance, the martyr’s vision, which had appeared to the eyes of his mind, vanished. Then the man of God arose and gave himself over to mourning in prayer. Immediately those terrible signs followed in the heavens, so that fiery spears and battle-lines could be seen from the northern quarter.

Soon the savage nation of the Lombards, drawn out from the womb of its dwelling-place, [Note: In almost similar language, Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 4, calls Scandinavia, from which the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards emerged, “the workshop of nations, the womb of peoples.”] attacked our neck. The human race, which in this land had risen in excessive multitude, like a dense field of grain, was cut down and withered. [Note: The *Compendium* reads: “like ears of grain in a field.”] Cities were depopulated, camps overthrown, churches burned, monasteries of men and women destroyed, [Note: Beccensis and Bigot have “deserted,” which is also found in the second Carnotensis. The first Carnotensis and the third have “dissolved.”] estates abandoned by their inhabitants and deprived of every [Note: The first Carnotensis has “cultivation.” What the holy Doctor describes here he recounts elsewhere in almost the same words, especially in what was formerly Homily 18 on Ezekiel, now book II, near the end.] cultivator. The land lies empty in solitude; no owner inhabits it. Wild beasts have taken possession of the places formerly held by the multitude of human beings.

What is happening in other parts of the world, I do not know. But in this land in which we live, the world no longer announces its end; it displays it. Therefore, the more swiftly we recognize that temporal things have fled from us, the more urgently we must seek eternal things.

We ought to have despised this world even if it had flattered us and soothed our minds with prosperity. But now that it is pressed down by so many scourges, wearied by such adversity, and daily heaps so many sorrows upon us, what else does it cry out to us but that it must not be loved? There were many further deeds of the elect that ought still to have been recounted, but I suppress them in silence because I am hastening to other matters.

PETRUS. Since I observe many who dwell within the bosom of the holy Church doubting concerning the life of the soul after the death of the flesh, I ask you to say, for the edification of many, either what reasons are available or whatever examples of souls come to mind, so that those who suspect otherwise may learn that the soul does not perish together with the flesh. [Note: Thus the manuscripts, although the printed editions read: “or by what reasoning it can be recognized, or whether …”]

GREGORY. This is a very laborious work, especially for a mind occupied and directed toward other matters. But if it can benefit some, I shall undoubtedly subordinate my own inclination to the usefulness of my neighbors, and, insofar as God grants me strength, I shall demonstrate in the following fourth book that the soul lives after the flesh. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts have “may I be able.”]

## Greek version of Chapter 38. Concerning the vision of Redemptus, bishop of the city of Ferentinum

[Col. 0315A; p. 369]

GREGORY. Concerning this matter, Peter, do not be surprised. For you knew Redemptus, the most devout man in his life, bishop of Ferentinum, who departed from this world about seven years ago. When I was still in the monastery, he approached me with great openness. [Note: The manuscript reads: “when I was present.”] He knew this matter that I am relating, as did John, the last of those who preceded me, who had only recently departed from this world, and it had also been made widely known to everyone.

When Redemptus himself had been questioned by me, he told me, saying that one day, while going around his parishes according to custom, he came to the church of the blessed martyr Eutychius. [Note: The manuscript reads “Jutychus.” The same name is consistently found below.]

When evening came, he ordered that his bed be placed near the martyr’s coffin. There he rested from his weariness. Around midnight, as he said, he was neither completely asleep nor able to remain awake. Rather, as often happens, he lay weighed down, while his soul remained awake. [Note: The manuscript reads “weighed down.”]

The same blessed martyr Eutychius stood beside him and said: “Redemptus, are you awake?” He answered him: “I am awake.” The martyr said to him: “The end is coming for all flesh; the end is coming for all flesh; the end is coming for all flesh.”

After this threefold utterance, the martyr’s vision, which had appeared to his spiritual eyes, disappeared. Then the man of God rose and gave himself over to grief in prayer.

Immediately those fearful signs followed in the heavens. For fiery swords and formations were seen from the northern quarter. At that time the savage nation of the Lombards, coming out from its own dwelling-place, attacked our neck. They cut down and withered the multitude of human beings that had become extremely dense in this land, like a crop of grain.

The cities were left without inhabitants; the forts were overthrown; churches were burned; monasteries of men and women were destroyed. [Note: The manuscript reads “were burned.”] The suburbs, abandoned through the neglect of human beings, [Note: The manuscript reads “were left deserted.”] were left empty, and the land lies idle; no one who cultivates it dwells there. Wild beasts seized the places over which the multitude of human beings had formerly held power.

What is happening in other parts of the world, I do not know. But in this land in which we live, the world no longer merely announces its end; it plainly shows it. Therefore it is necessary for us to seek eternal things with such earnest labor as we recognize that temporal things have swiftly escaped from us.

We must regard this world as hateful, even when it flattered us, when it prospered in its affairs and nourished the soul. For now, burdened by so many scourges, oppressed by such perversion, and doubling our pains each day, it cries out nothing else except that it should not be loved. [Note: The manuscript reads “oppressing,” and shortly afterward “grieving” instead of “being grieved.”]

There are still many deeds of the elect that I ought to have related. [Note: The manuscript reads “which I ought to relate.”] But I cover them in silence because I am hastening toward other matters.

PETRUS. I observe many within the bosom of the holy Church of God doubting about the soul’s life after the death of the flesh. I therefore beg you to say, for the edification of many, whatever examples come into your mind, so that those who are in doubt may learn that the soul does not die together with the flesh.

GREGORY. This is an exceedingly laborious undertaking, especially when the mind is occupied and being drawn toward other matters. But if there are some whom it can benefit, I abandon my own wish and labor for the benefit of my neighbors; and, with God supplying the strength, I shall show, as I am able, in the following fourth book, that the soul remains immortal after the completion of the flesh. [Note: The manuscript reads “I labor for the neighbor.”]

# Book Four

## Chapter 1. Why eternal and spiritual things are believed less readily by carnal people, because they do not know by experience what they hear

### Latin version

[Col. 0317C; p. 372]

GREGORY. After the first parent of the human race had been expelled from the joys of paradise because of his fault, he came into the misery of this blindness and exile that we endure. For, having sinned and been poured out of himself, he could no longer see those joys of the heavenly homeland that he had previously contemplated.

In paradise the human being had been accustomed to delight in the words of God and, through purity of heart and elevation of vision, to participate in the spirits of the blessed angels. But after he fell here, he withdrew from that light of the mind with which he had been filled (Homily 32). [Note: Two Theodorus manuscripts read: “into this exile and blindness that we endure.”]

Born from his flesh in the blindness of this exile, we have heard that there is a heavenly homeland; we have heard that its citizens are the angels of God; we have heard that the spirits of the righteous and perfected are companions of those same angels. But carnal people, because they cannot know those invisible realities by experience, doubt whether what they do not see with bodily eyes exists.

This doubt could not exist in our first parent, because, although he had been excluded from the joys of paradise, he remembered what he had lost, since he had seen it. These people, however, cannot feel or remember what they have heard, because, unlike him, they possess no experience of it, not even from the past. [Note: Most Norman and Vallicellian manuscripts read: “because no one … possesses experience.”]

It is as if a pregnant woman were sent to prison and gave birth there, and the child born in prison were brought up and grew there. If the mother who gave birth to him were to name for him the sun, moon, stars, mountains and fields, flying birds and running horses, while he, born and raised in prison, knew nothing but the darkness of the prison, he would indeed hear that these things existed, but, because he had not known them by experience, he would rightly doubt that they were real.

So human beings, born in the blindness of their exile, hear that lofty and invisible things exist, but doubt whether they are truly real, because they know only the lowly visible things in which they were born. [Note: Two Theodorus manuscripts read: “these frail things.”]

Therefore the Creator of the invisible and visible, the Only-Begotten Son of the Father, came for the redemption of the human race and sent the Holy Spirit into our hearts, so that, made alive through him, we might believe what we still cannot know by experience.

All of us who have received this Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance (Ephesians 1:14) do not doubt the life of invisible things. But whoever is not yet firmly established in this faith ought without hesitation to submit himself to the words of mature men and believe those who already possess, through the Holy Spirit, experience of invisible things. For a child would be foolish if, because he knows nothing but the darkness of prison, he thought his mother was lying about the light.

PETRUS. I greatly approve what you say. But whoever does not believe that invisible things exist is certainly an unbeliever; and whoever is an unbeliever does not seek faith in the matter about which he doubts, but reason.

### Greek version: That spiritual things are more necessary than carnal things

[Col. 0318C; pp. 371–374]

**GREGORY.** After the joy in paradise, when the fault of disobedience had been committed, the ancestor of the human race was cast out from there and came into this exile of blindness and distress which we endure. For by sinning and being carried outside himself he could no longer behold the joy of that heavenly homeland which he had seen before.

[Note: [Col. 0317D–0318D] In the manuscript, after the table of chapters, the opening reads: *Μετὰ τὴν ἐν τῳ παραδείσῳ τρυφὴν ὁ προπάτωρ τοῦ ἀνθρωπίνου γένους, τὸ πταῖσμα τῆς παρακοῆς ἐργασάμενος, ἐξεβλήθη τοῦ παραδείσου καὶ ἐν ταῖς μερίμναις καὶ ἀνάγκαις τοῦ σώματος ἃς ὑπομένομεν ἦλθεν. Ἁμαρτήσας γὰρ καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐνεχθεὶς οὐκέτι λοιπὸν …*—“After the delight in paradise, the ancestor of the human race, having committed the fault of disobedience, was cast out of paradise and came into the bodily cares and necessities that we endure. For, having sinned and been carried outside himself, he no longer …” The variant breaks off where the printed note does.]

While in paradise, the human being was accustomed to hear the words of God and, through purity of heart and elevation of contemplation, to dwell among the blessed angels. But after falling here, he departed from that faculty of thought whose light had filled him.

[Note: [Col. 0318D] The manuscript reads *τοὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγους*, “the words of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0318D] For “blessed angels,” the manuscript reads *ἁγίων*, “holy.”]

Born from his flesh in this blindness of exile, we hear that there is a heavenly homeland and that its citizens are angels; we hear that the spirits of the righteous made perfect are companions of those blessed angels. But carnal people, unable to know those unseen realities, fall into fear through lack of experience and remain distrustful, supposing that things which bodily eyes cannot behold do not exist.

Our first ancestor did not have this fear. Though driven from the joy of paradise, he still remembered what he had seen and lost. But those born afterward cannot understand or remember what they hear, because they possess no sure experience of it from the past.

It is as though a pregnant woman were put in prison and gave birth there. The child, reared and grown within the prison, knows nothing but its darkness. If his mother names the sun, moon, stars, mountains and plains, flying birds and running horses, he hears that they exist; yet because he has not known them by experience, he disbelieves that they are real.

So people born in the blindness of this exile hear that lofty and unseen things exist, but distrust their reality, for they know only the wretched visible things among which they were born.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] The manuscript reads *ἐν τούτῳ τῷ κόσμῳ γεννηθέντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι*, “people born in this world.”]

Therefore the Creator of visible and invisible things, the Only-Begotten Son of the Father, came to redeem the human race and caused his Holy Spirit to dwell in our hearts, so that, made alive through him, we might believe those things which we still cannot know by experience. All who have received this Spirit as the pledge of our inheritance do not doubt the life of invisible beings. Whoever is not yet firmly established in this assurance ought unhesitatingly to give himself in faith to the words of mature men and believe those who through the Holy Spirit already possess experience of invisible things.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] For “experience,” the manuscript reads *τὴν γνῶσιν*, “knowledge.”]

The child is foolish if he thinks his mother lies about the light merely because he knows nothing but the darkness of prison.

**PETER.** What you say pleases me greatly. One who does not believe that invisible things exist is certainly an unbeliever; and an unbeliever, in the matter about which he doubts, seeks not faith but assurance.

## Chapter 2. That even an unbeliever does not live without faith

### Latin version

[Col. 0320C]

GREGORY. I say boldly that even an unbeliever does not live without faith. For if I wished to question that unbeliever about which father or which mother he had, he would immediately answer, “This man and that woman.” If I then asked whether he knew when he was conceived or had seen when he was born, he would admit that he neither knew nor had seen any of these things; and yet he believes what he did not see. For he unhesitatingly declares that he had that man as his father and that woman as his mother.

PETRUS. I confess that until now I did not know that an unbeliever possessed faith.

GREGORY. Unbelievers do indeed possess faith—but would that it were faith in God! If they possessed that, they would not be unbelievers. But from this very point they must be refuted in their unbelief and summoned to the grace of faith: if they believe concerning their own visible body what they have by no means seen, why do they not believe invisible things, which cannot be seen bodily? [Note: The same manuscripts read “evidently.” What the holy Gregory teaches here had already been largely said and developed by Arnobius in Book II *Against the Nations*.]

[Note: [Col. 0320D] Two Gemetensis manuscripts and Pratensis also have the reading “even unbelievers have faith”; the remainder of the printed abbreviated wording is corrupt and is not silently completed.]

### Greek version

[Col. 0319C–0322A]

**GREGORY.** I dare say that even an unbeliever does not live without faith. If I ask an unbeliever what father or mother he had, he immediately answers, “That man and that woman.” If I then ask whether he knows when he was conceived or saw when he was born, he admits that he neither knows nor saw any of these things; nevertheless he believes what he did not see, and testifies without hesitation that he had that man for father and that woman for mother.

**PETER.** I confess that until now I did not know that an unbeliever too has faith.

**GREGORY.** Unbelievers do have faith—but would that it were in God! If they securely possessed that faith, they would not be unbelievers. From this they should be summoned to the grace of faith, because their distrust is refuted by their own case: if they believe about their own body what they never saw, why do they not believe invisible things which cannot be bodily seen?

## Chapter 3. That God created three living spirits

### Latin version

[Col. 0321A; p. 376]

For the reason that the soul lives after the death of the flesh is evident, though faith must be added to the argument. Almighty God created three living spirits: one that is not covered by flesh; another that is covered by flesh but does not die together with flesh; and a third that is covered by flesh and dies together with flesh.

The spirit that is not covered by flesh belongs to the angels. The spirit that is covered by flesh but does not die with flesh belongs to human beings. The spirit that is covered by flesh and dies with flesh belongs to cattle and all irrational animals.

Thus the human being was created in the middle, lower than an angel and higher than an animal; accordingly, he has something in common [Note: We have followed the construction of the manuscript. The printed editions read: “therefore, being lower than an angel, he who was created in the middle, and higher …”] with the highest and something in common with the lowest: immortality of spirit with the angel, but mortality of flesh with the animal. This will continue until the glory of the resurrection absorbs even the mortality of the flesh, and the flesh, by clinging to the spirit, is preserved forever, because the spirit itself, by clinging to God, is preserved in God. [Note: In an earlier Gemetensis manuscript the reading was formerly “the spirit itself, by clinging, is preserved in God,” with *to the flesh* omitted. In another Gemetensis manuscript: “the spirit itself is preserved in God.” The Greek translator appears to have read: “because the spirit itself, clinging to God, is preserved in him” (*pneuma proskollōmenon tō Theō*). For the resurrection and the life after resurrection, see the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 15, and the commentators on this chapter, especially Estius, who praises the holy Fathers who wrote more learnedly on the resurrection, adducing many of their testimonies.]

Yet this flesh does not wholly cease even in the reprobate amid their punishments, because, while continually wasting away, it continues to exist. Thus those who sinned in spirit and flesh, while remaining alive essentially forever, die without end in both flesh and spirit.

PETRUS. Everything you say pleases the understanding of the faithful. But while you distinguish the spirit of human beings from that of animals with such precision, what is the meaning of Solomon’s words: “I said in my heart concerning the sons of men, that God would test them and show that they are like beasts; therefore there is one destruction for man and beasts, and the condition of both is equal” (Ecclesiastes 3:18)?

Pursuing the same judgment in detail, he adds: “As a man dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and man has nothing more than beasts” (ibid., 19). He then adds a general conclusion: “All things are subject to vanity, and all go to one place; all were made from the earth, and all alike return to the earth” (ibid.). [Note: The manuscript reads *apò ktḗnous* (“than an animal”). Here the printed editions have corrupt punctuation, which obscures the sense: they read continuously, “nothing, which still …”]

### Greek version

[Col. 0322A–0322D; p. 375]

That the soul will live after the death of the flesh I shall try to show by argument, with faith of course assisting. Almighty God created three living spirits: one not covered by flesh; another covered by flesh but not dying together with it; and a third covered by flesh and dying together with it.

The spirit not covered by flesh is that of angels. The spirit covered by flesh but not dying with it is that of human beings. The spirit covered by flesh and dying with it is that of cattle.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] At the second kind, the manuscript reads *καλύπτεται, οὐχ ἅμα*, “it is covered, [but] not together [with the flesh does it die].”]

The human being, created in the middle, lower than the angel and higher than the animal, has something in common with what is above and something with what is below: immortality of spirit with the angel, and death of the flesh with the animal. This remains so until the glory of the resurrection makes even the flesh’s mortality immortal. For the flesh, cleaving to the spirit, is preserved forever, because the spirit itself, cleaving to God, is preserved in him.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The translation follows the manuscript’s construction. The printed editions instead arrange the clause: *τοίνυν, κατώτερος ὢν τοῦ ἀγγέλου ὅστις ἐν μέσῳ ἐκτίσθη, καὶ ἀνώτ…*—“therefore, being lower than the angel, he who was created in the middle, and higher …”; the printed variant is truncated as shown.]

Thus even among the reprobate the flesh does not wholly disappear in punishment: continually wasting away, it abides, so that those who sinned in spirit and flesh, while continuing essentially alive, may die without end in flesh and spirit.

**PETER.** All that you say pleases the assurance of the faithful. But since you have distinguished the human spirit from that of cattle by so great a distance, what does Solomon mean when he says: “I said in my heart concerning the speech of the sons of man, that God will judge them and show that they are beasts; for the sons of man and the beast have one event, one event for them all”? Continuing the same judgment closely, he adds: “As this one dies, so that one dies, and there is one breath in all; and what advantage has man over the beast? None.” He then adds the universal judgment: “All is vanity; all goes to one place; all came from dust, and all returns to dust.”

[Note: [Col. 0322D] The manuscript reads *ἀπὸ κτήνους*, “than/from an animal.” The printed editions corrupt the punctuation and obscure the sense by running together *οὐδέν. Οἷς ἀκμήν*—“nothing. To these words still …”.]

## Chapter 4. Concerning Solomon’s question in which it is said: “There is one destruction of man and beasts”

### Latin version

[Col. 0321D; p. 380]

GREGORY. The book of Solomon in which these words are written is called Ecclesiastes. *Ecclesiastes* properly means “one who gathers the people.” [Note: The translator adheres more closely to the letter: “Ecclesiastes properly means one who gathers the people” (*ho laon athroizōn*).]

In an assembly a judgment is pronounced by which the disturbance of a noisy crowd is quieted. When many hold different opinions, they are led to one judgment through the reasoning of the speaker. This book is therefore called Ecclesiastes because Solomon in it took upon himself, as it were, the mind of a disturbed crowd, so that by inquiry he might express what an inexperienced mind might perhaps feel through temptation.

For as many judgments as he raises by way of inquiry, so many different persons he seems to receive into himself. [Note: The second Carnotensis reads: “so many voices of different people he receives into himself”; the third reads: “so many voices of persons.”] But the true Ecclesiastes, as if extending his hand, quiets everyone’s disturbance and recalls them to one judgment, when at the end of the same book he says: “Let us all hear the conclusion of the matter: Fear God and observe his commandments; for this is the whole of man” (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

For if he had not received into himself the persons of many through his speech in the same book, why, at the end of his discourse, would he urge everyone together to listen? He who says at the end of the book, “Let us all hear together,” bears witness concerning himself that, receiving the persons of many into himself, he did not speak as though he were alone.

Thus there are some statements in the same book that are raised by inquiry, and others that are resolved by reasoning. There are still others that he presents from the standpoint of a soul undergoing temptation and still devoted to the pleasures of this world; and others in which he explains the things belonging to reason, so as to restrain the mind from pleasure. [Note: The *Compendium*, the third Carnotensis, and two Theodorus manuscripts read: “others which he utters from the mind under temptation”; the second Carnotensis: “others which he utters carnally from a mind under temptation”; Vallicellianus: “which he utters from one tempted.”]

There he says: “This therefore seemed good to me: that a person should eat and drink and enjoy happiness from his labor” (Ecclesiastes 5:17). Farther below he adds: “It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting” (Ecclesiastes 7:3). If eating and drinking are good, it would seem better to go to a house of feasting than to a house of mourning. From this it is clear that he introduced the former from the standpoint of the weak, but added the latter as a definition of reason. For he immediately explains the reasons of reason itself and shows what benefit there is in a house of mourning, saying: “For in it the end of all human beings is admonished, and the living considers what will be” (ibid.). [Note: The first Gemetensis, the first Audomariensis, and Lyranus read “what is to come.”]

Again it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ecclesiastes 11:9). Shortly afterward it adds: “Youth and pleasure are vanity” (ibid., 10). By later condemning as vain what he had previously seemed to recommend, he plainly indicates that he introduced those words as if from carnal desire, but added these from the judgment of truth.

Just as, first expressing the pleasure of carnal people and setting aside concern, [Note: The first Carnotensis reads “love” and omits “setting aside concern.”] he declares that eating and drinking are good, but afterward condemns this by the judgment of reason when he says that it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting; and just as he proposes that a young man should rejoice in his youth as though speaking from the deliberation of carnal people, yet afterward declares by a definition of judgment that youth and pleasure are vain, so also our Ecclesiastes proposes, as if from the mind of the weak, the judgment of human suspicion when he says: “There is one destruction of man and beasts, and the condition of both is equal. As a man dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and man has nothing more than beasts” (Ecclesiastes 3:10).

Yet afterward, by a definition of reason, he gives his own judgment, saying: “What more does the wise man have than the fool, and what does the poor man have except that he may go there where there is life?” (ibid. 6:8). [Note: In most witnesses *a* (“than”) is omitted.] He who said, “Man has nothing more than beasts,” later defined that the wise man possesses something not only more than an animal but also more than a foolish human being: namely, that he may go there where there is life.

These words first indicate that human life is not here, since he testifies that it is elsewhere. Man therefore has this advantage over animals: animals do not live after death, whereas man begins to live at the very time when, through the death of the flesh, he completes this visible life.

Farther below he also says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do with all your strength, [Note: The manuscript reads “as much as your strength permits.”] because there is no work, reasoning, knowledge, or wisdom in the underworld, where you are going” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). How, then, is there one destruction of man and animal, and an equal condition for both? Or how does man have nothing more than animals, when animals do not live after the death of the flesh, while the spirits of human beings, carried down to the underworld after the death of the flesh because of their evil deeds, do not die even in that death?

Thus, despite the two statements being so different, it is plainly demonstrated that the true Ecclesiastes introduced the one from carnal temptation but later defined the other from spiritual truth.

PETRUS. I am glad not to have known what I asked, since in such subtlety I have happened to learn what I did not know. But I ask you to bear with me patiently if I too, following the example of our Ecclesiastes, take upon myself the role of the weak, so that by inquiring on their behalf I may more closely benefit those who are weak.

GREGORY. Why should I not patiently bear your accommodation to the weakness of your neighbors, when Paul says: “I have become all things to all people, so that I might save all” (1 Corinthians 9:22)? Since you too are acting now through a loving accommodation, you ought all the more to be honored in this matter, in which you imitate the practice of that excellent preacher. [Note: Here *venerari* is used passively, contrary to the rules of the grammarians, but in the manner customary with Gregory. See *Moralia* XVIII.13 and *Pastoral Rule* II.6. In the same way he uses *meditari*, *perscrutari*, *intueri*, and similar verbs in a passive sense, as becomes immediately clear to an attentive reader.]

## Chapter 4. Concerning the saying of Ecclesiastes

### Greek version

[Col. 0322D; pp. 378–379]

[Note: The Greek heading should be read “Concerning the saying of Ecclesiastes,” not “of the ecclesiastical [writer],” as the printed editions give it; below, the book is called *Ecclesiastes*.]

GREGORY. The book of Solomon in which these things are written was called Ecclesiastes. Ecclesiastes properly means “one who gathers the people.” In an assembly, therefore, a judgment is set forth by which the disturbance of the multitude is quieted. While many understand different things, all are led through the Ecclesiastes’ defense to one judgment.

For this reason the book was called Ecclesiastes. Solomon in it took upon himself, as it were, the mind of a troubled people, so that through inquiry he might say everything in such a way that even an inexperienced mind might finally understand through experience. For as many judgments as he raises through inquiry, so many different persons he has received into himself. [Note: The manuscript reads “through reproof”; the printed editions read “as many judgments.”]

But the true Ecclesiastes, as though extending his hand, quiets the disturbance of everyone and brings them back to one judgment, [Note: The manuscript reads “to one number.”] as he says at the end of the same book: “Hear the whole conclusion of the matter: Fear God and observe his commandments.” That is, “Every human being.”

For if he did not receive the persons of many through his defense in the same book, why, at the end of his speaking, did he exhort everyone together to listen? He himself says at the end of the book: “Let us all hear together.” Therefore he is his own witness that, having received the persons of many into himself, he did not speak as though he alone were speaking.

There are other things in the same book that are raised by inquiry, and others that are resolved through defense. There are still others that he utters from the standpoint of the soul undergoing temptation, while it is still surrendered to the desires of the world. And there are others in which he reports what belongs to defense, so that he may lead the soul away from delight in present things. [Note: The manuscript reads “may lead it away.”]

There he says: “I saw that it is good for someone to eat and drink and enjoy happiness from his labor.” Further on he adds: “It is good to go to a house of mourning rather than to a house of drinking.” If eating and drinking are good, he would have thought it better to go to a house of drinking than to a house of mourning. [Note: The manuscript reads “it was thought.”] From this it is evident that he brought forward the former from the standpoint of the sick, but presented the latter from the perfection of apologetic reasoning.

For he immediately interprets the very arguments of the defense and shows what benefit there is in the house of mourning, saying: “For in it the end of all human beings is admonished, and the living considers what is to be.”

Again it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth.” And shortly afterward: “Youth and folly are vanity.” By condemning as vain what had earlier been presented in the form of admonition, he clearly demonstrates that he uttered those words as if from carnal desire, but added these from the judgment of truth.

Just as earlier, speaking from the standpoint of carnal people, he declared pleasure and said that eating and drinking were good while neglecting concern, but afterward condemned this more fully through the judgment of his defense by saying that it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of drinking; and just as he proposed that the young man rejoice in his youth from the standpoint of carnal people, but afterward demonstrated through his declaration that youth and folly are vain, so [Note: The manuscript reads “thus.”] our Ecclesiastes sets forth, as though from the reasoning of the weak, the judgment of human suspicion when he says that there is one death for man and animal and that the subjection of both is alike: “As a man dies, so they die; there is one breath in all, and man has nothing more than an animal.”

He then gives his own judgment through the definition of the defense, saying: “What advantage does the wise man have over the fool? The poor man knows where he should go, toward life.”

The one who said that man has nothing more than animals later declared that the wise man has something more—not only more than animals but also more than a foolish human being—namely, that he may go there where life is. These words plainly indicate that human life is not here, but that he testifies elsewhere that it exists.

Man therefore has this advantage over animals: animals do not live after death, but man begins to live at the moment when, through the death of the flesh, he completes visible life.

The same writer says farther below: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do with all the strength you possess, [Note: The manuscript reads “as much as your strength permits.”] because there is no work, thought, knowledge, or wisdom in Hades, where you are going.”

How, then, is there one end for man and animal, and equal subjection for both? Or how does man have nothing more than an animal?

Since animals do not live after the death of the flesh, while the spirits of human beings, carried down to Hades after the death of the flesh because of their evil deeds, do not die even in death itself, it is plainly shown that the death of both is not equal. The true Ecclesiastes brought forward the former statement from the standpoint of carnal desire, but afterward declared the latter from spiritual truth.

PETRUS. I confess that I did not know what I asked, while I have happened, amid such subtle reasoning, to learn what I did not know. But I ask you to bear with me patiently, so that I may take upon myself the role of the weak according to the example of Ecclesiastes, and may be able, through their inquiry, to benefit those near us.

GREGORY. Why should I not patiently endure your accommodation to the weakness of your neighbors, since Paul says: “I have become all things to all, so that I might save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22)? [Note: The printed editions read *some one*, contrary to the manuscript and to the Greek text of Saint Paul’s letters, with which the Syriac and Arabic versions agree. The Vulgate reads: “that I might save all,” correctly following the preceding words, “I have become all things to all.” Properly: “that I might save some altogether.”] In doing this now through the accommodation of love, you imitate the practice of the preacher in this matter.

## Chapter 5. Concerning the soul’s invisible and sudden departure, and whether what cannot be seen exists

### Latin version

[Col. 0328A]

PETRUS. It happened that I was present when a certain brother was dying. Suddenly, while he was speaking, he gave up his vital breath; and the man whom I had previously seen speaking with me, I suddenly saw dead. But I did not see whether his soul had departed or not. [Note: Here three further words omitted in the printed editions have been restored.] It seems very difficult to believe that a thing exists which no one can see.

GREGORY. What is surprising, Peter, if you did not see the soul as it departed, when you do not see it even while it remains in the body? When you are speaking with me now, do you believe that I am lifeless merely because you cannot see my soul within me? The nature of the soul is invisible, and therefore it leaves the body invisibly, just as it remains invisibly within the body. [Note: Thus the manuscript; the printed editions read “invisible.”]

### Greek version: Concerning a soul suddenly departing from the body

[Col. 0327A–0327B]

**PETER.** It happened that I was present when a certain brother was dying. While he was speaking he suddenly cast off the vital breath, and the man whom I had previously seen speaking with me I suddenly beheld dead. But I could not see whether his soul had gone out or had not gone out. It seems very difficult to believe that something exists which no one can behold.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] The editors restore here the three words *εἴτε οὐκ ἐξῆλθεν*, “or had not gone out,” which the printed editions had omitted.]

**GREGORY.** What is surprising, Peter, if you did not behold the soul going out, when you cannot behold it even while it remains in the body? When you are now conversing with me, do you believe me lifeless because you cannot see my soul? The soul’s nature is unseen; therefore it goes out of the body invisibly, just as, while in the body, it remains unseen.

[Note: [Col. 0327D] The manuscript has *ἀοράτως*, “invisibly”; the printed editions have *ἀόρατος*, “invisible.”]

## Chapter 6. As the life of the soul remaining in the body is recognized from the movement of the limbs, so the life of the soul after the body must be considered from the power of miracles in the saints

### Latin version (continues in the next supplied section)

[Col. 0328B; p. 381]

PETRUS. But I can consider the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s own movements, because, unless the soul were present in the body, its limbs could not move. Through what movements or works, then, can I see the life of the soul after the flesh, so that from visible things I may infer what I cannot see?

[Note: In many manuscripts and printed editions, chapter 6 does not begin here but at the words: “In this matter, if I find your affection prepared.”]

GREGORY. I do not say that it is recognized in the same way, but in a different way. [Note: The printed editions, contrary to the English, Norman, and other manuscripts, read: “not indeed subtly, but diligently.”] For just as the power of the soul gives life to and moves the body, so divine power fills what it has created: it gives life to some by inspiring them, grants others that they may live, and gives still others only that they may exist.

Since you do not doubt that God is the Creator and Ruler, the One who fills and surrounds, transcends and sustains, unbounded and invisible, you ought likewise not to doubt that he has invisible servants. For those who minister ought to tend toward the likeness of the one whom they serve, so that those who serve the invisible may be understood to be invisible.

What else do we believe these to be except the holy angels and the spirits of the righteous? Therefore, just as, by considering the movement of the body, you discern from below in your mind the life of the soul remaining in the body, so you ought to discern from above the life of the soul departing from the body, because it can live invisibly and must remain in the service of the invisible Creator. [Note: The first Carnotensis and the third together with the first Gemetensis read “you weigh in your mind”; another Gemetensis reads “from the least.”]

PETRUS. Everything is rightly said, but my mind recoils from believing what it cannot see with bodily eyes. [Note: The printed editions read “what cannot be seen”; the reading “what it cannot see” is found in all the Norman manuscripts, three Carnotenses, two Theodorus manuscripts, Vallicellianus, and others. Only the German manuscript has “what cannot be seen.” It is not absurd to say that the soul or mind sees with bodily eyes—that is, through the eyes—since it is commonly believed to perform all bodily movements through bodily organs. The following makes clear that this is Gregory’s teaching.]

GREGORY. When Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1), this is truly said to be believed which cannot be seen. For what can be seen cannot be a matter of faith.

To bring you briefly back to yourself: no visible things are seen except through invisible things. Behold, the eye of your body looks upon all bodily things, yet that bodily eye would see nothing bodily unless an incorporeal thing sharpened it for seeing. Remove the mind, which is not seen, and the eye that used to see is open in vain.

Take the soul away from the body, and certainly the eyes remain open in the body. [Note: The second Gemetensis reads “closed.”] If they saw by themselves, why do they see nothing when the soul departs? From this, then, gather that even visible things are seen only through invisible things.

Let us also place before the eyes of the mind a house being built, enormous masses being lifted, and great columns hanging from machines. I ask you: what performs this work—the visible body that draws those masses with its hands, or the invisible soul that gives life to the body? Remove what is unseen in the body, and at once all the things that seemed to move remain motionless: visible bodies of metal.

From this it must be considered that, in this visible world also, nothing can be arranged except through an invisible creature. For just as almighty God, by inspiring or filling things that subsist through reason, gives life to and moves invisible beings, so those invisible beings themselves, by filling them, move and give life to the carnal bodies that are seen. [Note: The second Carnotensis and Lyranus, together with most Norman manuscripts, read “make meaningful”; the German and second Theodorus read “give life to the meaning”; Vallicellianus and the first Carnotensis read “gradually give life”; the third Carnotensis reads “give life through sense.”]

PETRUS. I confess that, conquered by these arguments, I am almost compelled to think that these visible things scarcely exist, though earlier, taking upon myself the role of the weak, I doubted invisible things. Everything you say therefore pleases me. Yet just as I recognize the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s movement, so I wish to recognize the life of the soul after the body from certain manifest things that bear witness to it. [Note: In ancient manuscripts this passage and similar ones read *alligationibus* and *alligatione*—“bindings” or “arguments.” Hence Zacharias rendered these words by *desmou* and *desmō*. Below: “No reason, I think, withstands this argument.” The corresponding Greek is: “No defense, I think, has been left against this bond, this argument.”]

GREGORY. If in this matter I find your heart prepared by your affection, I am confident that I shall labor little in my argument. Would the holy apostles and martyrs of Christ have despised the present life and surrendered their souls to death, unless they knew that a more blessed life of souls would follow?
