You yourself say that you recognize the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s movements; and behold, those who surrendered their souls to death and believed that life exists for souls after the death of the flesh shine forth in daily miracles. For the living sick come to their lifeless bodies and are healed; perjurers come and are struck down by a demon; the demon-possessed come and are delivered; lepers come and are cleansed; the dead are brought and raised. Consider, then, how their souls live there where they live, since their dead bodies here live through so many miracles. If, therefore, you discern the life of the soul remaining in the body from the movement of its members, why do you not perceive the life of the soul after the body through the power of miracles even in dead bones?

PETER. No objection, I think, withstands this argument, in which visible things compel us to believe what we do not see.

## Chapter VI. On the Soul and Body of the Saints

[Col. 0327B]

PETER. Yet I can infer the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s own movements. For if the soul were not present in the body, the members of that body could not move. But in what movements, or in what actions, do I perceive the life of the soul after its departure from the flesh, so that from things perceived I may understand that it exists, when I cannot perceive them?

GREGORY. The divine power not only fills all things that it created, just as the power of the soul gives life to and moves the body, but also gives them life by breathing into them. To some it grants that they may live; to others, merely that they exist. You do not hesitate, then, to believe that God is invisible and without limitation, creating and shepherding, filling and protecting, transcending and enduring. You ought not, therefore, hesitate to believe that he also has invisible ministers. For those who serve him ought to be extended into his likeness, since they serve him whose likeness they share. Thus, so that there may be no disbelief, the things that serve the Invisible must be invisible. What do we believe these to be, unless the holy angels and the spirits of the righteous? Therefore, just as by observing the movement of the body you infer that the soul’s life remains in the body, so you ought to infer the higher from the lesser: that the soul, even when it departs from the body, can live invisibly, since it must remain for the service of the invisible Creator.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “or it is necessary to [refer] to the …”]

PETER. Everything is rightly pleasing.

[Note: Thus the manuscript; the editions read: “are found.”]

But the mind recoils from what it cannot behold with bodily eyes.

[Col. 0330A]

GREGORY. When blessed Paul says that faith is “the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen,” it is right in this respect to believe even what cannot be perceived. For, moreover, not even what is seen can be believed. Nevertheless, as far as I can, I shall turn you back to yourself by a brief consideration: nothing visible is perceived without invisible things. Behold, the bodily eye perceives all bodily things. Yet that same bodily eye could not see anything bodily unless an incorporeal thing moved it toward seeing. Remove, then, the unseen faculty of reason, and the eye that sees has been opened in vain. Remove the soul from the body, and plainly the eyes remain open in the body, but see nothing. If, therefore, they saw by themselves, why do they see nothing when the soul withdraws?

Understand from this, then, that visible things themselves are not perceived except through invisible things. Let us suppose that a house is built before the eyes of the mind, raised to a great height with the greatest weight, and that enormous columns are suspended on cranes. Who, I ask you, performs this work: the visible body, which lifts those very weights with its hands, or the invisible soul that gives life to the body? Remove the unseen element from the body, and immediately all those masses of metal, which were seen moving, remain motionless. Understand from this, then, that without the invisible creature nothing in this visible world can be governed. For just as almighty God, breathing into and filling all things that subsist according to reason, gives life to and moves invisible things, so those invisible things themselves fill, move, and give intelligence to visible bodies.

PETER. I gladly confess, released from this bond, that these visible things are almost nothing; previously, having taken upon myself the role of the sick, I doubted concerning invisible things. Everything you say is therefore pleasing. Yet just as I recognize the soul’s life while it remains in the body from the body’s movements, so I desire to recognize its life after its departure from the body through manifest things that bear witness.

GREGORY. In this matter, if I find a heart prepared in the bond of your affection,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “if I find [it] in the bond.”]

I am confident that I shall labor little. If the holy apostles and martyrs of Christ had not known that the life awaiting souls is more blessed, how would they have despised the present life and surrendered their souls in the death of the flesh? You yourself say that you recognize the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s movements. And behold, those who placed their souls in death, believing that life exists for souls after the death of the flesh, shine forth in daily miracles. For living sick people come to their dead bodies and obtain healing.

[Col. 0331A]

Perjurers come and are thrown down by a demon.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “are struck.”]

The demon-possessed come and are delivered from the demon. Lepers come and are cleansed. The dead are carried in and raised. Consider, then, how their souls live there where they live, since their dead bodies here live through so many miracles. If, therefore, you grasp the life of the soul while it remains in the body from the movement of the members, why do you not perceive the life of the soul after its departure from the body through the power of miracles occurring in dead bones?

PETER. No defense, I think, remains against this bond, since we are compelled by visible events to believe what we contemplate.

## Chapter VII. On the Departures of Souls

[Col. 0332B]

GREGORY. A little earlier (Chapter V) you complained that you had not seen the soul of a dying person depart; but this itself was already a fault, that you sought to see an invisible matter with bodily eyes. For many among our people, cleansing the eye of the mind by pure faith and abundant prayer, have often seen souls departing from the flesh. Therefore it is now necessary for me to relate both how departing souls have been seen and how much they themselves saw while departing, so that examples may persuade the wavering mind concerning what reason cannot fully establish.

[Col. 0332C]

For in the second book of this work (Chapter 35) I already stated that the venerable man Benedict, as I learned from his faithful disciples, while situated far from the city of Capua, saw at midnight the soul of Germanus, bishop of that city, carried toward heaven by angels in a fiery sphere. As he gazed upon that same soul ascending, he relaxed the bosom of his mind and saw the whole world gathered before his eyes, as though beneath a single ray of the sun.

## Chapter VIII. On the Vision of the Departure of a Soul

[Col. 0331B]

GREGORY. A little earlier you said that, when someone was dying, you did not see his soul departing; and thus this too was a fault, that you sought to behold with bodily eyes something invisible. For many of our people, cleansing themselves with pure faith and sincere devotion through the eyes of the mind, have often seen souls departing from the body. Therefore it is now necessary for me to relate how departing souls have been seen and how much those souls saw as they departed. Thus, the examples will persuade the wavering soul, which argument was unable fully to convince.

## Chapter IX. On the Departure of the Soul of Germanus, Bishop of the City of Capua

[Col. 0331C]

In the second book of this work I spoke about the life of the most devout man Benedict, as I learned from his faithful disciples: while he was far from the city of Capua, he saw at midnight the soul of Germanus, bishop of that city, being carried by angels in a fiery sphere and ascending into heaven.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “in his life.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads, “of Capua.”]

When he saw that same soul ascending, he opened the bosom of his mind and, as though the whole world had been gathered beneath a single ray of the sun, saw it with the eyes of his mind.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “he saw with spiritual eyes.”]

## Chapter VIII. On the Departure of the Soul of the Monk Speciosus

[Note: He is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on the Ides of March.]

[Col. 0332C]

I also learned from the stories of those same disciples that two noble men, brothers by birth and educated in secular studies, one named Speciosus and the other Gregory, devoted themselves to his rule in holy conduct.

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript and both Theodulf manuscripts read, “in the practice of a holy life.”]

The same venerable Father made them live in the monastery that he had built near the city of Terracina. They had possessed much money in this world, but distributed everything to the poor for the redemption of their souls and remained in the same monastery. One of them, Speciosus, had been sent for the monastery’s business near the city of Capua. One day his brother Gregory was sitting and eating with the brothers at table. Raised up in spirit, he saw the soul of his brother Speciosus, who was so far away, depart from the body. He immediately reported this to the brothers and hurried there; he found his brother already buried, and yet learned that he had died at the very hour when he had seen him depart from the body.

## Chapter IX. On the Departure of the Soul of the Monk Speciosus

[Col. 0331C]

I learned from the accounts of those same disciples that two noble men, genuine brothers and trained in secular learning, one named Speciosus and the other Gregory, devoted themselves to that man’s rule in holy conduct.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “education.”]

[Col. 0331D]

The same most devout father made them live in the monastery that he had built near the city of Terracina. They had acquired great wealth in this world, but distributed all of it to the poor for the redemption of their souls and remained in that monastery. One of them, namely Speciosus, was sent for the needs of the monastery near the city of Capua.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “as they say, for a need … of Capua.”]

[Col. 0334A]

One day his brother Gregory, sitting at table and eating with the brothers, was lifted up in spirit and saw the soul of his brother Speciosus depart from the body, although he was so far away from him.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “at such a distance.”]

He immediately announced this to the brothers. He then hastened there and found his own brother already buried. He learned that he had died at the very hour when he had seen his soul departing from his body.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “his [soul] from the body.”]

## Chapter IX. On the Soul of a Certain Recluse

[Col. 0333A]

While I was still living in the monastery, a certain devout and most faithful man told me that some people traveling by ship from the regions of Sicily toward Rome, while they were in the middle of the sea, saw the soul of a servant of God who had been enclosed in a cell in Samnium being carried to heaven. When they came ashore and investigated whether the matter had truly happened, they discovered that the servant of God had died on the very day on which they learned that he had ascended to the heavenly kingdom.

## Chapter X. On the Soul of a Recluse Who Ascended to Heaven

[Col. 0334A]

A very earnest and most faithful man told me this while I was still in the monastery.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “while I was still in the monastery, he told me, saying.”]

Some people, he said, traveling by ship from the regions of Sicily toward Rome, while they were in the middle of the sea, saw the soul of a certain servant of God who had been enclosed in Samnium ascending into heaven.

[Note: The manuscript reads: “while they were [there], they saw the soul of a certain enclosed servant of God ascending in heaven,” and so forth.]

When they came ashore and investigated whether what they had seen was true, they found that the servant of God had died on the very day on which they had learned that his soul was going to the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: The editions read, “whether what they had seen was true.”]

## Chapter X. On the Departure of the Soul of Spes, Abbot

[Note: He is listed in the Roman Martyrology on the fifth day before the Kalends of April.]

[Col. 0334A]

While I was still in my monastery, I learned the following through the report of a very venerable man. He said that the venerable Father named Spes had built a monastery in a place called Cample, situated about six miles from the ancient city of Nursia. Almighty and merciful God protected him by chastising him with a continual scourge and reserved for him the greatest severity and grace of his providence. How much he loved him while chastising him, he later demonstrated by healing him completely.

[Note: The first Gembloux manuscript reads, “serenity”; the third Chartres manuscript reads, “security.”]

For forty years he afflicted his eyes with the darkness of continual blindness, leaving him no light or even the slightest glimpse of sight. But since no one can endure his scourging if grace abandons him, and unless the same merciful Father who inflicts the punishment grants patience, correction of sins soon increases our sin through impatience, it happens miserably that our fault takes its increase from the very place where it ought to have hoped for an end. Therefore, seeing our weakness, God mingles protection with his scourges, and in striking his chosen children he is now mercifully just, so that later he may justly have mercy on them.

[Col. 0333C]

Thus, although he pressed the venerable old man with outward darkness, he never deprived him of inward light. While he was wearied by the scourge of the body, he possessed consolation of heart through the protection of the Holy Spirit. When the forty years of blindness had been completed,

[Note: The second German manuscript, the second and third Chartres manuscripts, the earlier Gembloux manuscript, and most of the Norman manuscripts read, “the time having been removed.” The other Gembloux manuscript and the Vallicellian manuscript read, “the time having been completed.”]

the Lord restored his sight, announced that his death was near, and instructed him to preach the word of life in the monasteries that had been built all around, so that, having received the light of the body, he might open the light of the heart by visiting the brothers throughout the region. Immediately obeying the command, he traveled around the brothers’ monasteries and preached to them the precepts of life that he had learned through practice.

On the fifteenth day, after completing his preaching, he returned to his monastery. There, summoning the brothers and standing in their midst, he received the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and then began with them the mystical singing of the psalms. While they were singing psalms, he remained intent upon prayer and gave up his soul. All the brothers who were present saw a dove come out of his mouth. Immediately, when the roof of the oratory had been opened, it passed through heaven while the brothers watched. We should therefore believe that his soul appeared in the form of a dove so that almighty God might show by that very form how simply and purely of heart this man had served him.

## Chapter XI. On the Departure of the Soul of Elpidius, Archimandrite of the City of Nursia

[Note: Thus the manuscript. The printed editions read incorrectly, “bishop.”]

[Col. 0334B]

While I was still in the monastery, I learned from the account of a very devout man what I am also relating. He said that the most devout Father named Spes had built monasteries in the place called Cample, which lies about six miles, or somewhat less,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “farther inward.”]

from the city called ancient Nursia. Almighty and merciful God chastised him here and removed him from eternal punishments.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “delivered him.”]

For in his greatest providence he showed both the threat and the compassion. How much he had loved him while previously scourging him, he later demonstrated by healing him completely. He filled his eyes for a period of forty years with the abiding darkness of blindness,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “made him blind.”]

leaving him no light, not even a glimmer of the least sight. No one can endure the scourge if grace abandons him, unless the merciful Father himself, who imposes the punishment, grants patience. For through impatience the chastisement itself adds sin to us; and so, miserably, it happens that from the place where our fault ought to receive forgiveness, it receives an increase of suffering. Therefore, observing our weaknesses, God mingles patience with his scourges, so that in chastising his chosen children he may appear merciful and just toward those on whom he will afterward justly have compassion.

[Col. 0334D]

Thus, although he darkened this most devout old man with outward darkness, he never deprived him of inward light. While he was being storm-tossed by the scourge of the body, he possessed consolation of heart through the protection of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Formerly the text read ἐκείνης instead of σκέπης. Gussanville recognized the corruption in this passage but supplied no remedy, although he had access to the King’s manuscript, in which σκέπης is read. In the Roman edition, however, he carefully retained all the errors, as we demonstrated in the preface.]

When he had completed his fortieth year in blindness, the Lord restored his sight to him and announced that his death was approaching. He commanded him to proclaim the word of life in the monasteries founded by him throughout the region, so that, having recovered the light of the body and visited the brothers around him, he might open the light of their hearts.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “that he might distribute their light.”]

Immediately obeying the command of the one who had ordered him, he went around the brothers’ common monasteries and delivered to them the commandments of life that he had learned by practicing them.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “he went around.”]

After fifteen days, having completed his preaching, he returned to his monastery. In the oratory he summoned the brothers and, standing in their midst, partook of the Lord’s body and blood and, together with them, performed the mystical hymns of the psalms. While they were still singing psalms, he remained at prayer and gave up his soul. All the brothers present saw a dove come out of his mouth. When the roof of the oratory had been opened, it immediately ascended into heaven before the eyes of the brothers. We therefore believe that his soul appeared in the form of a dove so that almighty God might show them, through that form, with what purity of heart this man had served him.

## Chapter XI. On the Departure of the Soul of a Presbyter of Nursia

[Note: Thus the Pratelli manuscript and the first Audomar manuscript. The first Chartres manuscript reads, “of a certain presbyter from the province of Nursia.” The Greek interpreter supports this reading. In the German manuscript and most others, as in the printed editions, it reads “of Ursinus.”]

[Col. 0336B]

Nor will I keep silent about what the venerable abbot Stephen, who died in this city not long ago and whom you also know well, reported as having occurred in the same region of Nursia. He said that a certain presbyter there governed the church entrusted to him with great fear of the Lord.

[Note: The reference is Distinction 32, canon “Presbyter.”]

From the time of his ordination, he loved his presbytera as a sister but guarded against her as against an enemy. He never allowed her to come near him and, under no circumstances, permitted her to approach him; he completely cut off from himself all intimacy of association with her.

[Note: “Presbytera” here means his wife. Thus the wives of presbyters were called, borrowing the title from their husbands; they loved them chastely, having renounced marital relations. “Converted wives” are mentioned in the Second Council of Arles, canon 5. See Baronius, under the year 405, no. 60; the Fourth Council of Orléans, chapter 17; the Second Council of Tours, canon 20; and Auxerre, chapter 21. The term presbytera is also sometimes found among ecclesiastical writers for elderly widows, in Greek πρεσβύτιδες, as in the Council of Laodicea, its final chapter, and in Athanasius, To the Virgins. Gregory may perhaps be speaking of these women, since they were distinguished by a particular habit. — Gussanville.]

Holy men possess this characteristic along with all their other virtues: in order always to remain far from illicit things, they often cut themselves off even from what is permitted. Therefore this man, so that he might not incur any fault through her, even refused to have necessities ministered to him by her.

When this venerable presbyter had completed a long life, in the fortieth year of his ordination he was seized by a severe fever and brought to the point of death. His presbytera, seeing that his limbs had already become slack and that he lay stretched out as though in death, placed her ear near his nostrils to determine whether any breath of life still remained in him. Feeling this, and possessing only the faintest breath, he gathered his voice with whatever small effort he could manage in order to speak. As his spirit grew warm, he cried out:

“Move away from me, woman. The little spark is still alive; take away the straw.”

When she had withdrawn, and the strength of his body increased, he began to cry out with great joy:

“Let my lords come well; let my lords come well. Why have you deigned to come to such a tiny servant of yours? I am coming, I am coming; I give thanks, I give thanks.”

As he repeated these words again and again, his acquaintances, who stood around him, asked to whom he was saying them. He replied to them in amazement:

“Do you not see that the holy apostles have come here? Do you not see blessed Peter and Paul, the foremost of the apostles?”

Then, turning again toward them, he said:

“Behold, I am coming; behold, I am coming.”

With these words he gave up his soul. And because he had truly seen the holy apostles, he also bore witness by following them. This often happens to the righteous: at their death they see visions of the saints who have gone before them,

[Note: People of lighter minds readily admit such visions everywhere; the impious ridicule them, while the wiser weigh them carefully. Saint Cyprian approved them and used them more than once to establish faith. See his letters 10, 34, 40, 54, and 56. — Gussanville.]

so that they may not fear the painful sentence of their own death; rather, when the fellowship of the citizens within is shown to their minds, they are released from the bond of their flesh without the weariness of pain or fear.

## Chapter XII. On the Departure of the Soul of the Presbyter from Nursia

[Col. 0335B]

Nor do I think it right to pass over this either: the most devout man, Abbot Stephen, who died in this city not long ago and whom you yourself know well, related that this happened in the same region of Nursia. He said that a certain presbyter there shepherded the church entrusted to him with the greatest fear of the Lord.

From the time of his ordination, he loved his companion as a sister, but, fearing her as an enemy, never allowed her to approach him on any pretext.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “he never allowed.”]

He entirely cut off from her the intimacy that comes from companionship. For holy men possess this characteristic along with all their other virtues: they remain not only always far from what is unfitting, but often cut themselves off even from what is fitting. Therefore the same man, so that he might not fall into any fault through her, would not even consent to have his necessary needs attended to by her.

This most devout presbyter, after passing through many years of life and reaching advanced old age, was seized in the fortieth year of his ordination by the burning of a severe fever and brought to the point of death. His former companion, seeing that all his limbs had become lifeless and that he was now approaching death, placed her ear near his nostrils and hastened to determine whether any breath of life still remained in him.

[Note: Perhaps “having placed [it] upon [them].”]

He perceived this, although only the faintest breath remained in him; and as his spirit was warmed,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “his spirit being warmed more by the nod of God.”]

he gathered as much breath as he could to speak, opened his voice, and said:

“Go away from me, woman. The fire still lives; take away the straw.”

When she withdrew and the strength of his body increased, he began to shout with great joy:

“Let my lords come well. Why have you deigned to come to your unworthy servant? I am coming, I am coming; I give thanks, I give thanks.”

As he repeatedly uttered the same words, his acquaintances, who stood there, asked to whom he was saying this. Amazed, he answered them:

“Do you not see that the holy apostles have come together here? Do you not see blessed Peter and Paul, the foremost of the apostles?”

Then, turning toward them again, he said:

“Behold, I am coming; behold, I am coming.”

With these words he gave up his soul. Thus he truly saw the apostles, and he testified that he was following them. It consequently happens among the righteous that, at their death, when saints go before them, they behold visions, so that they may not fear the torment of the sentence of death. Rather, when it is shown to their inward understanding with whom they share fellowship, they are released from the bond of their flesh without pain or fear.

## Chapter XII. On the Soul of Probus, Bishop of the City of Reate

[Col. 0338B]

I think it fitting to make known this event also, which Probus, a servant of God who now presides over the monastery in this city called Renatus,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “presides over a monastery in this city called Reate.”]

related to me. He spoke about his uncle Probus, who had been bishop of the city of Reate, saying that, when the end of his life drew near, he was seized by a very serious illness. His father, named Maximus, sent boys throughout the surrounding places and tried to gather physicians, in case they might somehow be able to help his illness.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “he struggled.”]

When the physicians came from the neighboring places and examined his pulse, they announced that his departure would occur soon.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “when they had assembled and … examined him, they announced immediately.”]

As the hour advanced and the time for the meal had arrived, the venerable bishop was concerned more for their welfare than for his own. He therefore asked the physicians who had arrived to go up with his aged father to the upper rooms of the episcopal residence and take nourishment.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “to go up with his father to the upper room.”]

They all went up to the upper house. Only one little boy remained beside him.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “a small child.”]

The boy is still alive, as the aforementioned Probus says. While he was standing beside the bed of the man who lay there, he suddenly saw certain men approaching the man of God, dressed in white robes. The light of their faces surpassed the brightness of their garments.

[Note: Another reading is, “who surpassed the brightness of their radiance.”]

Struck by the brilliance of their splendor, the boy began to shout aloud, asking who they were. At the boy’s cry Bishop Probus was also disturbed; he saw the men entering and recognized them. He began to console the shouting boy, saying:

“Do not be afraid, my son, for the martyrs Saint Juvenal and Saint Eleutherius have come to me.”

Unable to endure the novelty of so great a vision, the boy ran rapidly outside the doors and told his father and the physicians what he had seen. They hurried down, but found the sick man whom they had left already dead, for those whose vision the boy could not endure had taken him away with them.

## Chapter XIII. On the Soul of Probus, Bishop of the City of Reate

[Col. 0338B]

It is reasonable, I think, to make this known as well: Probus, the servant of God who now presides over a monastery in this city called Renatus, told me about his father Probus, who had become bishop of the city of Reate. When the end of his life drew near, a very severe illness seized him. His father, Maximus by name, sent children through the surrounding places and labored to gather physicians, so that they might contribute whatever they could to his illness.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “when they had assembled and … examined him, they announced immediately.”]

When the physicians had come from the neighboring places and examined his pulse, they announced that his departure was soon to occur. As the hour advanced and the time for the meal had now arrived, the most devout bishop was concerned more for their welfare than for his own.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “more for their welfare than for his own salvation.”]

Therefore he asked the physicians who had arrived to go up with his aged father to the upper rooms of the episcopal residence and take nourishment.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “with his father in the upper room.”]

They all went up into the upper house. Only one little boy, standing beside him, was left behind; he is still alive, as the aforementioned Probus says.

While he stood beside the bed of the man who lay there, he suddenly saw certain men approaching him, clothed in white robes. By the light of their faces they surpassed the brightness of their garments. Struck by the flash of their radiance, the boy began to shout aloud, asking who they were.

Bishop Probus was disturbed by the boy’s cry. He saw the men entering and recognized them. He began to console the shouting boy, saying:

“Do not be afraid, for the holy martyrs Juvenal and Eleutherius have come to me.”

Unable to endure the novelty of such a vision,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “the vision.”]

the boy fled at the fastest pace outside the doors. He told his father and the physicians about what he had seen. They came down immediately and found the sick man whom they had left already dead. It was therefore clear that those men had taken him with them, since the boy who remained here had been unable to endure the sight of them.

## Chapter XIII. On the Passing of Galla, the Handmaid of God

[Note: Read her encomium in the Roman Martyrology under 5 October. She is believed to be the same woman to whom Saint Fulgentius wrote *On Widows*.]

[Col. 0340B]

Meanwhile, I do not think this should be left unsaid either, since I learned it from the report of serious and faithful persons.

[Note: The first Chartres manuscript reads, “which I learned from the report of grave and faithful citizens.”]

In the time of the Goths, Galla, a most noble young woman of this city, daughter of the consul and patrician Symmachus, was given in marriage while still in the years of adolescence and was widowed by her husband’s death within a single year. Although the abundance of the world, her youth, and her wealth called her to marry again, she chose instead to be joined to God in spiritual marriage, which begins in mourning but reaches eternal joys, rather than to submit to carnal marriage, which always begins in gladness and moves toward its end in mourning.

Because her bodily constitution was extremely hot, the physicians began to say that unless she returned to the embraces of a man, she would, through excessive natural heat, grow a beard contrary to nature. This indeed happened afterward. But the holy woman feared none of the outward deformity, because she loved the beauty of the inward Bridegroom. Nor did she fear that what would be disfigured in her was not loved in her by her heavenly Bridegroom.

As soon as her husband died, she cast off secular dress and devoted herself to the service of almighty God in the monastery near the church of blessed Peter the apostle. There, for many years, devoted to purity of heart and prayer, she generously gave alms to those in need.

[Note: The Becc manuscript reads, “she turned to service in the church of blessed Peter the apostle, and there for many years, devoted with a simple heart to prayer …”]

When almighty God had determined to repay her labors with an everlasting reward, she was struck by a cancerous ulcer in the breast. At night, two lampstands customarily shone before her bed, because, being a friend of the light, she hated not only spiritual but also bodily darkness.

One night, while she lay exhausted by this illness, she saw the blessed apostle Peter standing before her bed between the two lampstands. She was not terrified or afraid; rather, taking courage from love, she rejoiced and said to him:

“What is it, my lord? Have my sins been forgiven?”

He, with the gracious expression that belonged to him, inclined his head and nodded, saying:

“They have been forgiven. Come.”

But because Galla loved one of the nuns in that monastery more than the others, she immediately added:

“I ask that Sister Benedicta come with me.”

He answered her:

“No; let that particular woman come with you. The one whom you are asking for will follow on the thirtieth day.”

After these words, the vision of the apostle standing beside her and speaking with her disappeared. Immediately she summoned the mother of the entire community and told her what she had seen and heard.

On the third day she died together with the sister whom she had been ordered to accompany. The one whom she herself had requested followed on the thirtieth day. This event, which occurred in that same monastery, remains memorable there to this day. The younger nuns who now live there, holy virgins, relate it in detail as it was handed down by the elder Mothers, as though they themselves had been present at that time and had witnessed so great a miracle.

[Note: Gregory’s custom of calling nuns, especially those advanced in age, “mothers” is noteworthy. In these *Dialogues* we often read of monks designated by the title “Fathers,” particularly in Book II; we shall discuss this more fully in the notes to the letters.]

## Chapter XIV. On the Death of Galla, a Nun, Daughter of the Patrician Symmachus

[Col. 0339B]

Moreover, I think it right not to pass over this either, which a person of very high standing and fidelity made known to me by his account.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “I think.”]

He said that, in the time of the Goths, a certain Galla, a most noble maiden of this city, daughter of Symmachus the consul and patrician, was given to a husband while she was young; after living with him for one year only, she became a widow when he died. The prime of youth, desire for the world, and the deceit of wealth summoned her to enter upon a second marriage. But she chose rather to be united to God in spiritual marriage, which begins in mourning and ends in eternal joy, than to be subjected to carnal marriage, which begins in gladness but proceeds to an end in mourning.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “having been joined [in marriage].”]

As her bodily constitution was extremely hot, physicians began to say that, unless she returned to the embrace of a man, the exceedingly intense heat of her nature would cause her to grow a beard. This subsequently occurred. But that holy woman took no thought for outward ugliness, for she loved the beauty of the Bridegroom within. Nor was she ashamed of what was unbeautiful in her; rather, she was ashamed of what was not loved by the heavenly Bridegroom.

As soon as her husband died, she put off worldly dress and devoted herself to the service of almighty God in the monastery beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter. There she continued for many years in innocence of heart and persevering prayer, generously giving alms to those in need. But when almighty God determined to grant an eternal reward for her labors, she was struck in the breast by cancer.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “she was struck by the blow of cancer in her breast. And …”]

In the quiet of the night, two lamps began to shine before her bed. For, being a lover of light, she hated not only intelligible darkness but bodily darkness as well. One night, as she lay exhausted by the same illness, she saw the blessed apostle Peter standing before her bed between the two lamps.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “not at all.”]

Not in the least alarmed or afraid, but rather taking confidence from love, she rejoiced and said to him: “What is it, my lord? Have my sins been forgiven?” He, with his kindly countenance—as indeed is his manner—nodded, inclining his head, and said: “They have been forgiven; come.”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “with a gracious [countenance].”]

Galla, who loved a certain most devout woman in the same monastery above the others, added: “I ask that Sister Benedicta come with me.” He answered her: “No; rather, let that particular woman come with you immediately. But she whom you ask for will follow you after the thirtieth day.” After these words, the vision of the apostle standing by and conversing with her was taken away. She immediately summoned the mother of the community and told her everything that she had seen and heard. On the third day she departed to the Lord together with the sister who had been commanded.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “virgin.”]

But the one whom she herself had requested met the end of her life on the thirtieth day.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “day from life.”]

This event, performed in that same monastery, remains remembered to this day.

[Col. 0341B]

For, handed down there by the elder Mothers (sic), it is related there in such detail by the young women now living there, who are holy virgins, as though they had been present at that time and had seen so great a miracle.

## Chapter XIV. On the Passing of Servulus the Paralytic

[Col. 0341B]

In the midst of these matters, it should be known that, when the souls of the elect depart, the sweetness of heavenly praise often bursts forth, so that, while they gladly listen to it, they are scarcely permitted to feel the dissolution of the flesh from the soul.

[Note: Thus all the manuscripts, although the printed editions read, “sweet praises of heaven often burst forth, so that while they gladly hear them …”]

I remember having related this also in the *Homilies on the Gospel* (Homily 15). In the portico through which those going to the church of blessed Clement pass, there was a certain man named Servulus, whom I do not doubt that you also remember. He was poor in worldly possessions but rich in merits, and a long illness had weakened him. For as long as we were able to know him, he lay paralyzed until the end of his life. Why should I say that he could not stand, when he was never able even to rise from his bed to sit, never able to bring his hand to his mouth, and never able to turn himself onto his other side?

[Col. 0341C]

His mother and another of his brothers were present to serve him. Whatever he was able to receive through alms, he distributed to the poor through their hands. He knew no letters at all, but bought books of Holy Scripture for himself and, welcoming devout people as guests, made them read these books carefully before him. Thus, according to his capacity, he fully learned Holy Scripture, although, as I have said, he was completely ignorant of letters.

He always strove to give thanks in his suffering and devoted himself day and night to hymns and praises of God. But when the time had come for such great patience to receive its reward, the pain of his limbs returned to his vital organs. When he recognized that he was near death, he urged the strangers whom he had welcomed as guests to rise and sing psalms with him in expectation of his departure.

As he himself was dying and singing psalms with them, he suddenly silenced their singing with a great cry of terror, saying:

“Be silent! Do you not hear how many praises resound in heaven?”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “how they echo.”]

While he turned the ear of his heart toward those praises that he heard within, that holy soul was released from the flesh. As it departed, such a great fragrance of odor spread through the place that all who were present were filled with indescribable sweetness. By this they plainly understood that the praises of heaven had received it.

A monk of ours was present at this event; he is still alive. With great weeping he regularly bears witness that, until his body was handed over for burial, the fragrance of that odor did not leave their nostrils.

## Chapter XV. On the Passing of Servulus the Paralytic

[Col. 0342B]

It is necessary to make this known as well: often, when the souls of the elect are departing from the body,

[Note: The manuscript reads, “from the bodies.”]

praise is performed in heaven, so that, while the souls gladly listen to it, they may not feel how they endure the dissolution from the flesh.

I remember having related this in the homilies on the Gospel. In the portico leading along the road to the church of blessed Clement, there was a certain man lying there named Servulus, whom I do not suppose you fail to know. Although he was poor in the goods of this life, he was rich in righteousness. A long illness had paralyzed his body. From the time we were able to know him until the end of his life, he lay paralyzed.

What need is there to say more? He could not stand at all; he could never sit upright in his bed, never bring his hand to his mouth, and never turn himself onto his other side.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “to another side.”]

His mother and another of his brothers attended him in service. Whatever he received from almsgiving, he distributed again to the poor through his own hands.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “through their hands.”]

He knew no letters whatsoever, but bought books of Holy Scripture for himself. Welcoming certain devout men as guests, he made them read them carefully before him. Thus it happened that, as far as he was able, he learned Holy Scripture usefully, although, as I said, he knew no letters at all.

He always bore his suffering thankfully and devoted himself night and day to the praise of God. When the time had come for such great patience to receive its recompense, the pain of his limbs ceased. When he recognized that he was approaching death, he asked the men whom he had received as guests to rise and sing to God with him in expectation of his soul’s departure.

While he himself, dying, was singing with them, he suddenly stopped them from singing with fear and a great cry, saying:

“Be silent! Do you not hear how praises resound in heaven?”

[Note: The manuscript reads, “how they echo.”]

Focusing on those praises, which he heard within, in the ears of his heart, that holy soul was released from the bonds of the body. When it departed, such a fragrance of sweetness came upon that place that all who stood there were filled with it. Thus it became clear to everyone that the praises in heaven had received it.

A monk of ours was present at this event, and he remains alive to this day. With much weeping he testifies that, until they handed his body over for burial, the scent of that fragrance did not depart from their nostrils.

## Chapter XV. On the Passing of Romula, the Handmaid of God

[Col. 0344B]

## Chapter XVI. On the Passing of the Nun Romula

In the same Homilies (Homily 15) [Note: [Col. 0344D] Two Gemeticus manuscripts, as many Theodorus manuscripts, and a third Carnotensis manuscript read: “to which Speciosus … bore witness.”], I recall having related the following event, which my fellow presbyter Speciosus, who knew the matter, confirmed when I narrated it.

At the time when I entered the monastery, an old woman named Redempta [Note: [Col. 0344D] The Roman Martyrology gives the names of these three virgins on 23 July.] lived in this city, wearing the monastic habit, near the church of blessed Mary ever-virgin. She had been a disciple of that Herundina [Col. 0344C], who, endowed with great powers and wonders [Note: [Col. 0344D] We have already noted that the city of Praeneste is situated on a mountain.], was said to have led the eremitical life on the Praenestine mountains.

Two disciples also lived with this Redempta in the same habit: one named Romula, and the other, who is still alive, whom I know by face but not by name. These three therefore lived together in one dwelling, rich in good character but poor in worldly possessions.

The Romula whom I have mentioned surpassed her fellow disciple in the great merits of her way of life. She possessed remarkable patience and the highest obedience; she guarded her mouth in silence and was exceedingly devoted to continual prayer. But because those whom people already regard as perfect often still possess some imperfection in the sight of the supreme Creator—just as inexperienced people often see seals not yet fully carved and praise them as already perfect, while the craftsman still examines and smooths them, and, although he hears them praised, does not cease striking and improving them—so something of this kind also occurred in her case.

The Romula mentioned above was struck by the bodily illness which physicians, in the Greek language, call *paralysis* [Col. 0345A]. For many years she lay in bed, almost entirely deprived of the use of her limbs, yet the blows of this illness did not drive her mind to impatience. Rather, the loss of her limbs became an increase of virtues, for she grew all the more diligent in prayer precisely because she was wholly unable to do anything else.

One night she called the Redempta mentioned above, who raised both her disciples as daughters, saying: “Mother, come; mother, come.” She immediately rose with the other disciple, as both of them later related, and as many others also learned; I too came to know the matter at that same time.

When, therefore, at midnight they stood beside the bed of the woman lying there, suddenly light sent down from heaven filled the entire space of the cell, and a radiance of such brilliance flashed forth that it struck the hearts of those standing there with immeasurable fear. As they themselves later related, every part of their bodies became rigid, and they remained in sudden astonishment.

For a great sound began to be heard, as though a large multitude were entering, and the door of the cell began to shake, as though it were being pressed by a crowd of people entering. As they said, they sensed a multitude coming in, but because of the excess of fear and the brilliance of the light, they could not see anything: fear weighed down their eyes, and the brightness of so great a light dazzled them. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Germanus and Beccus add: “and a most pleasant fragrance followed that light.”]

The light was immediately followed by a fragrance of wondrous sweetness, so that the pleasantness of the scent refreshed their spirits, which the light sent forth had terrified. But since they could not endure the force of that radiance, Romula began in a gentle voice to comfort the Redempta who stood trembling beside her, the teacher of her character, saying: “Do not be afraid, mother; I am not dying just now.”

While she repeatedly said this, the light that had been sent forth gradually withdrew, but the fragrance that followed remained. Thus the second and third days passed, while the fragrance continued to permeate the place. On the fourth night she again called her teacher. When she came, Romula asked for the viaticum and received it. [Note: [Col. 0345D] Although *viaticum* is often understood in councils and ecclesiastical writers as absolution, here it signifies the Eucharist customarily received by the dying. See the preceding chapter on viaticum, and consult the learned Tillemont, vol. VI of the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical History*, on the Council of Nicaea, article 15, regarding the meaning of this word in the Nicene canon. It must be understood in the same sense in Paulinus, *Life of Saint Ambrose* 47: “Honoratus, a priest of the Church at Vercellae, heard for the third time the voice of one calling … and, descending, offered the Lord’s body to Saint Ambrose; when he had received and swallowed it, he gave up his spirit, carrying good viaticum with him.”]

Redempta and the other disciple had not yet withdrawn from the bedside when suddenly, in the street before the door of the cell, two choirs of singers appeared. As they themselves said, they distinguished two kinds of voices in the singing: men sang the psalmody, and women answered. While a heavenly funeral rite was being performed before the door of the cell, that holy soul was released from the flesh. As she was led up to heaven, the higher the singing choirs ascended, the more softly the psalmody began to be heard, until both the sound of the psalmody and the sweetness of the fragrance, receding into the distance, came to an end.

### Greek Recension

**395. Chapter XVI. On the Passing of the Nun Romula**

[Col. 0343B]

In the same Homilies on the Gospel I remember having related an event which my fellow presbyter Speciosus himself, when I narrated it to him [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscript reads: “Speciosus my presbyter himself, when I narrated it to him.”], confirmed that he knew.

At the time when I sought the monastery, an old woman named Redempta, living in the sacred monastic habit [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscript reads *monachikō*, “in the monastic habit,” and shortly afterward “of the holy ever-virgin.”], lived in this city of the Romans near the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God [Col. 0343C]. She had become a disciple of that Herundina who had greatly increased in powers and wonders [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscript reads “in powers and wonders”], and who was said to have led an eremitical life above the Praenestine mountains.

This Redempta had two disciples in the same sacred habit: one was named Romula; I do not know the name of the other, but I know her by face, and she is still alive. These three therefore remained in one dwelling, rich in good character but living in poverty during this present life [Note: [Col. 0343D] The manuscript reads “living in poverty.”]

The Romula whom I mentioned surpassed her fellow disciple in the greatest merits of the religious life. She was a daughter of supreme patience and obedience, a guardian of her mouth, steadfast in prayer, and devoted to silence. But since people suppose certain persons to be perfect, while in the eyes of the Creator of all they still possess some imperfection—for just as seals not yet perfectly carved are often praised by the ignorant as already finished, although the craftsman still files and strikes them, embellishing them without ceasing even while he hears them praised—something of this kind also occurred in her case. [Note: [Col. 0343D] In the Vatican and Gussanville manuscripts there is a lacuna, supplied here from the Royal manuscript; thus the Greek corresponds fully to the Latin [Col. 0344D].]

The Romula mentioned above happened to be afflicted with a bodily illness which physicians call *paralysis* in Greek [Col. 0346A]. [Note: [Col. 0346D] The manuscript reads *paresis*; shortly afterward, *parēseōs*.] Lying in bed for many years, she remained motionless through the loss of the service of her limbs. Yet the scourges of the illness did not drag her mind into impatience. Rather, these pains of her limbs became an increase of strength in her, for she became more earnest in prayer precisely because she could in no way do anything else.

One night she called the aforesaid Redempta, who raised both her disciples as daughters, saying: “Come, mother, come.” At once Redempta rose with the other disciple and went to her, as became clear from the account of both women and of many others. I too learned this at that very time.

When, therefore, at midnight they stood beside the bed of the woman lying there, suddenly, light being sent from heaven, it filled every part of that cell. Such a flash shone forth in the brilliance of that light that it terrified the hearts of those standing there; and, as they afterward related, every limb of their bodies became rigid. While they remained in astonishment, a great sound began to be heard, as though a large multitude were entering, and the doors of the cell shook, as though a crowd entering were pressing against them. They supposed, as they said, that a multitude of people was entering [Note: [Col. 0346D] The manuscript reads “of people entering.”] But because of the excess of fear and the flashing of the light [Col. 0346C], they could see nothing: their eyes were weighed down by fear and were blinded by the brilliance of so great a light.

A wondrous scent of fragrance followed that light, so that, although the light had terrified their souls, the fragrance nevertheless refreshed them even more. Since they could not bear the brilliance of that light, Romula began in a flattering voice to console the Redempta who stood beside her trembling, the teacher of her character, saying: “Do not be afraid, mother; I am not dying now.”

As she repeatedly said this, the light that had been sent there gradually withdrew [Note: [Col. 0346D] The manuscript reads “which was in her.”], but the fragrance that followed remained. When the second and third days had passed, the scent of the fragrance poured forth continued in this way [Col. 0346D]. On the fourth day she again called her own teacher [Note: [Col. 0346D] The manuscript reads “her own teacher.”] When she came, she asked that the Lord’s body be given to her as a companion for the journey, and she received it.

Redempta and the other disciple had not yet withdrawn from the bedside when suddenly, in the street before the doors of the cell [Col. 0347], two choirs of singers appeared. As they said, they distinguished two kinds of voices in the psalmody: men and women answering one another. While this heavenly glorification was being performed before the doors of the cell, that holy soul was released from the bonds of the body. As she ascended into heaven, the higher the choirs of singers rose, the more softly the psalmody began to be heard, until both the sound of the psalmody and the scent of the fragrance, receding into the distance, came to an end.

## Chapter XVI. On the Passing of Tharsilla, the Holy Virgin

[Note: [Col. 0347D; 0348D] Her commemoration is observed in the Roman Martyrology on 24 December.]

[Col. 0348A]

Sometimes, for the consolation of a departing soul, the author and giver of life himself is accustomed to appear. Therefore I shall repeat what I recall having said about my aunt Tharsilla in the Homilies on the Gospel (Homily 38). Among her two other sisters, she had risen to the summit of holiness through constant prayer, austere conduct, and singular abstinence.

In a vision my great-grandfather Felix, bishop of this Roman Church [Note: Saint Felix III, as we established in the *Life of Saint Gregory*], appeared to her and showed her a dwelling of perpetual radiance, saying: “Come, for in this dwelling of light I receive you.”

Soon afterward she was seized by a fever and reached the final day of her life. As is customary when noble women and men are dying, many people gathered to console their relatives, and at the hour of her departure many men and women stood around her bed. Suddenly, looking upward, she saw Jesus coming and began to cry out loudly and urgently to those standing around: “Go away, go away; Jesus is coming.” While she fixed her attention on the one whom she saw, that holy soul departed from the body.

At once so great a fragrance of wondrous sweetness filled the place that the sweetness itself showed everyone that the author of that sweetness had come there. When her body was stripped according to the custom for washing the dead, the skin on her elbows and knees was found to have become hardened and thickened like that of a camel as a result of her long practice of prayer [Note: Several manuscripts read “through the long use of prayer”; this was formerly read in Germanus, but now the reading is “through the long …,” as corrected]. Her dead flesh bore witness to what her spirit had continually done while she lived.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XVII. On the Passing of Tharsilla, the Holy Virgin**

[Col. 0347A]

Often, for the consolation of the departing soul, the very leader and recompensing giver of the deeds of our life appears. Therefore I shall now relate what I remember having said about my aunt Tharsilla in the Homilies on the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscript reads “to have been said.”]

She persevered with all her strength in uninterrupted prayer between her two sisters, living in seclusion. Through the elevation of her abstinence she greatly increased in humility. In a vision Felix, my great-grandfather, who had become patriarch of this Roman Church, appeared to her and showed her a dwelling of eternal brilliance, saying: “Come, for in this dwelling of eternal light [Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscript reads “of eternal light.”] I receive you.”

When a fever came upon her, she reached the final day of death. As it is customary, when noble men and women are dying, for many to come to console their relatives, many men and women stood around her bed at the very hour of her departure. Suddenly, as she looked upward, she saw Jesus coming and began with the greatest eagerness of spirit [Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscript reads “with great joy and eagerness.”] to cry out to those standing around her: “Go away, go away; Jesus is coming.”

As she fixed her attention upon the one whom she saw, that holy soul departed from the body. Such a fragrance of wondrous sweetness was poured out there that through it everyone could plainly know that the author of the fragrance had arrived. When they stripped her body according to the custom performed for the dead, they found the skin on her knees and elbows hardened like a camel’s through intense prayer and kneeling. Thus her dead flesh bore witness to what her spirit had done while she lived.

## Chapter XVII. On the Passing of the Girl Musa

[Col. 0348C]

Nor shall I remain silent about what the aforesaid servant of God Probus used to relate concerning his sister, a little girl named Musa [Note: See chapter 120 of this book]. He said that one night the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary, appeared to her in a vision and showed her girls of the same age, dressed in white. When Musa wished to join them but did not dare approach them, the blessed Virgin Mary asked her whether she wished to be with them and to live in her service. When the girl answered, “I do,” she immediately received from Mary the command to do nothing frivolous or childish thereafter, to abstain from laughter and play, and to know for certain that on the thirtieth day she would come to her service among the same virgins whom she had seen.

After seeing these things, the girl was changed in all her conduct and vigorously swept all childish frivolity away from herself. When her parents were astonished that she had changed, they questioned her. She told them what the blessed Virgin and Mother of God had commanded her and informed them on what day she would depart to her service.

On the twenty-fifth day she was seized by a fever. On the thirtieth day, when the hour of her departure was near, she saw that same blessed Virgin and Mother of God coming to her with the girls whom she had previously seen in the vision. When Mary called her, she began to answer her, lowering her eyes reverently and crying out in a clear voice: “Behold, Lady, I am coming; behold, Lady, I am coming.” With these words she gave up her spirit and, departing from her virginal body, went to dwell with the holy virgins. [Note: Val. Cl. reads: “as she was departing from her body.”]

[Col. 0349B] **Peter.** Since the human race is subject to many and countless vices, I think that the heavenly Jerusalem may be filled for the most part with little children and infants.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XVIII. On the Passing of the Girl Musa**

[Col. 0347C]

Nor shall I pass over in silence what the aforesaid Probus, the servant of God, related to me concerning his own sister, named Musa, who was a little girl. He said that one night the all-holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary appeared to her in a vision and showed her girls of her own age [Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscript reads “of the same age.”]

She tried to mingle with them but did not dare. The blessed ever-virgin and Mother of God Mary then asked her whether she wished to be with them and to live in her service. The girl answered: “I do.”

Immediately she received a command from Mary that henceforth she should do nothing childish or inappropriate, abstain from laughter and play [Note: [Col. 0347D] The manuscript reads “games”], and know that on the thirtieth day she would come into Mary’s service among the virgins whom she had seen.

After seeing these things, the girl changed in all her habits and, with strenuous determination, swept away every childish frivolity from herself. Her parents, seeing that she had changed in this way, questioned her in astonishment. She told them what the blessed Virgin and Mother of God Mary had commanded her and disclosed on what day she would depart to her service.

On the twenty-fifth day she was seized by a fever [Note: [Col. 0350D] The manuscript reads “On the twenty-fifth day she was seized by a fever.”] On the thirtieth day, when the hour of her departure drew near, she again saw that same blessed Virgin and Mother of God coming to her with the girls whom she had earlier seen with her in the vision. When Mary called her, she began to answer her, with a downcast, blushing gaze and in the gentlest voice: “Behold, Lady, I am coming; behold, Lady, I am coming.”

With these words she gave up her spirit, and, departing from her virgin body, she went to dwell with the holy virgins.

[Col. 0350B] **Peter.** Since the human race is subject to many and immeasurable passions, I think that the greatest part of the heavenly Jerusalem is destined to be filled with infants.

## Chapter XVIII. How the Entrance to the Heavenly Kingdom Is Closed to Certain Little Children by Their Parents When They Are Badly Raised, and Concerning a Blasphemous Boy

**Gregory.** Although we must believe that all baptized infants who die in infancy enter the kingdom of heaven, we must not believe that all little children who have begun to speak enter the heavenly kingdom, because for some little children the entrance to that kingdom is closed by their parents if they raise them badly.

There was a man, widely known throughout this city, who three years ago had a son, as I suppose, five years old. Loving him excessively in a worldly manner, he raised him indulgently. That child—something painful to say [Note: Some manuscripts of Normanus read: “which it is impious to say”]—as soon as anything displeased him, was accustomed to blaspheme the majesty of God. Struck by the plague that occurred in this city three years ago, he came to the point of death.

While his father held him in his arms, as those who were present testified, the boy saw evil spirits coming toward him. With trembling eyes he began to cry out: “Stop them, father, stop them, father.” As he cried this, he turned his face away in order to hide from them in his father’s arms.

When his father, seeing him trembling, asked what he saw, the boy added: “Black men have come; they want to take me.” After saying this, he immediately blasphemed the name of the Divine Majesty and gave up his spirit.

Thus almighty God showed for what guilt he had been handed over to such executioners. The offense which his father had failed to restrain while he was alive, God allowed him to repeat while dying, so that the one who had lived blasphemously for a long time through the patience of the Divinity might at last blaspheme and die through the judgment of the Divinity. In this way the father might recognize his guilt: through neglect of his little son’s soul, he had nourished not merely a little sinner but a great one for the fires of Gehenna.

But setting aside this sad matter for the moment, let us return to the joyful things that we had begun to relate [Note: Others read “let us return to the joyful things”].

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XIX. Question: Whether All Baptized Children Enter the Kingdom, and Concerning the Boy Who Blasphemed**

[Col. 0350B]

**Gregory.** We do not doubt that all baptized infants who die in infancy enter the kingdom of heaven. But we must not believe that all who have begun to speak enter it [Note: [Col. 0350D] The manuscript reads “we must believe”; shortly afterward, “the heavenly kingdom”]. For many little children the entrance to that same kingdom is closed by their parents if they raise them badly.

In this city there was a man known to everyone who, three years ago, had a son who, as I suppose, was about five years old [Note: [Col. 0350D] The manuscript reads “who, as I supposed, was five years old”]. Loving him excessively according to the flesh, he raised him without discipline. Thus the child acquired the habit—something dangerous even to say—of blaspheming the majesty of God whenever any thought whatsoever entered his mind.

This child, struck by the plague that occurred here three years ago, came to die. While his father held him in his arms, as those present testified, the boy saw the spirits of wickedness coming toward him. Trembling and closing his eyes, he began to cry out: “Avenge me, father, avenge me.” Crying these words, he lowered his face into his father’s bosom, wishing to hide himself.

When his father saw him trembling, he asked him what he was seeing. The boy answered: “Black men have come, wanting to seize me.” After saying this, he immediately blasphemed the name of the Divine Majesty and at once gave up his soul.

For almighty God wished to show on account of what sin he had been handed over to such servants: what his father had refused to prevent while he was alive, God allowed him to carry with him while dying. The one whom divine mercy had permitted to live blasphemously, divine justice allowed to blaspheme even while dying, so that his father might recognize his sin—the father who, neglecting the soul of his little son, had raised not a little sinner but a great one for the fire of Gehenna.

But since we have now completed this sorrowful and gloomy story, let us return to those more joyful matters which I began to relate [Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscript reads “let us return.”]

## Chapter XIX. On the Passing of Stephen, the Man of God

[Note: [Col. 0352D] His memory is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 13 February.]

[Col. 0352A]

From the aforesaid Probus and other devout men I learned what I took care to make known to my hearers concerning the venerable Father Stephen in the Homilies on the Gospel (Homily 35). For, as the same Probus and many others testify, he was a man who possessed nothing in this world and sought nothing; he loved only poverty according to God, always embraced patience amid adversity, avoided the gatherings of worldly people, and continually desired to devote himself to prayer.

Of him I shall relate one virtuous deed, so that from this one deed his many other virtues may be assessed. One day, after harvesting the crop that he had sown with his own hands, he brought it to the threshing floor. He had nothing else with his disciples to serve as provisions for the entire year [Note: [Col. 0352D] Val. Cl. reads “for the expenses of the year.”]

A man of perverse intention, goaded by the thorns of the ancient enemy, set fire to that same crop where it lay on the threshing floor. Another man who saw what had happened ran to the servant of God and reported it. After telling him, he added: “Woe, woe, Father Stephen! What has happened to you?”

With a calm face and tranquil mind Stephen immediately answered him: “Woe has happened to the one who did this; for what has happened to me?”

These words show the height of virtue at which his mind was established. He had possessed only one thing to sustain him throughout the whole year, yet he lost it with such unconcern. He felt greater sorrow for the man who had committed the sin than for himself, who endured the loss caused by that sin. He did not measure how much he had lost externally, but rather how much the guilty man had lost inwardly.

When the day of death came and pressed him to leave the body, many people gathered so that, as that holy soul departed from this world, they might commend their own souls to it. While all those who had gathered stood around his bed, some saw angels entering but were entirely unable to speak; others saw nothing at all. Yet such intense fear struck everyone present that no one could remain there as that holy soul departed.

Those who had seen something and those who had seen nothing alike fled, seized and terrified by one fear, so that it might be clearly understood what and how great a power had come to receive that departing soul—one whose departure no mortal could have endured.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XX. On the Life of the Holy Stephen**

[Col. 0351A]

From the aforesaid Probus and other men I learned what I took pains to announce to my hearers in the Homilies on the Gospel concerning the most devout Father Stephen. For, as the same Probus and many others testify, he was a man possessing nothing in this world and seeking nothing, except that he loved only poverty according to God [Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscript reads “loving only poverty.”] He always endured those who opposed him, drew them to himself [Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscript reads “drew them to himself.”], and avoided the assemblies of worldly people. He desired to devote himself continually to prayer.

Therefore I shall report one deed of his powers, so that from this one it may be possible to understand the rest. One day he harvested the crop which his own hand had sown [Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscript reads “which his hands had sown”] and brought it to the threshing floor. He had nothing else with his disciples for the sustenance of the whole year except this [Note: [Col. 0351D] Perhaps “for nourishment.”]

A man of perverse intention, pierced by the thorns of the ancient enemy, lit a fire and burned the same crop lying on the threshing floor. Another man, seeing what had happened, ran and reported it to the servant of God. After reporting it [Note: [Col. 0351D] The manuscript reads “he added.”], he said: “Woe, woe, Father Stephen! What has happened to you?”

He answered him with a cheerful face and undisturbed mind: “What has happened to the man who did this? For what has happened to me?”

From this understand at what height of power and rank his mind was established: he lost with such unconcern the one thing he had for sustenance throughout his whole life [Note: [Col. 0352D] The manuscript reads “he lost.”], and he grieved more for the man who had committed the sin than for the loss he himself suffered through that sin [Note: [Col. 0352D] The manuscript reads “than for the loss which he endured through it.”] He did not measure how much he himself had lost externally, but rather how much the one guilty of the offense had suffered inwardly [Note: [Col. 0352D] The manuscript reads “how much the guilty one had suffered.”]

When the day of death came and compelled him to leave the body, many gathered there so that, as that holy soul departed from this world, they might entrust their own souls to it. As all who had gathered stood beside his bed, some saw angels entering but could not speak at all. Others saw nothing whatsoever; yet an intense fear disturbed everyone present, so that no one could remain there as that holy soul departed.

Both those who had seen and those who had not seen were seized by one fear and fled. Thus it was plainly shown who and what sort of beings received that holy soul as it departed—one whose departure no mortal could have endured.

## Chapter XX. How the Merit of a Soul Is Sometimes Revealed More Truly after Death Rather Than at the Moment of Departure

[Col. 0352D]

But amid these matters we must recognize that the merit of a soul is sometimes not shown at the moment of its departure but is revealed more certainly after death. Thus the holy martyrs [Col. 0353A] endured much cruelty from unbelievers, yet, as we stated above (chapter 6), they shine daily through signs and miracles at their dead bones.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXI. Concerning Righteous Souls, That They Are Not Seen at Their Departure, and What Follows**

[Col. 0351D]

In addition to all this, it is also known that the dignity of a soul is not always displayed at its departure but is reliably revealed after death. Thus the holy martyrs endured much cruelty from unbelievers. Yet, as we said above, they shine daily through signs and miracles in their dead bones.

## Chapter XXI. On the Two Monks of the Abbot Valention

[Note: [Col. 0353D] The *Compendium* reads “Valentinus.” Several printed editions read “Valentius.” The Greek interpreter agrees with “Valention.” His commemoration is celebrated on 14 March.]

[Col. 0353A]

Concerning the life of the venerable Valention, who afterward presided over me and my monastery in this city of Rome, as you know, but had previously governed his monastery in the province of Valeria: while the Lombards were raging and had come there, I learned from his own account that they hanged two of his monks from the branches of a tree. The two men died on that same day.

When evening came, the spirits of both began to sing psalms there in clear and distinct voices, so that even those who had killed them were greatly astonished and terrified when they heard the voices of the singers. All the captives who were present there also heard those voices and afterward became witnesses to their psalmody.

Almighty God therefore wished the voices of those spirits to reach the ears of their bodies so that all who live in the flesh might learn that, if they strive to serve God, they live more truly after the death of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0353D] Two Theodorus manuscripts, both Gemeticus manuscripts, and the *Compendium* add “after the flesh.”]

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXII. On the Two Monks Hanged by the Lombards on a Tree**

[Col. 0354A]

The venerable Valentius, distinguished by a most devout life [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “Valentius, distinguished by a brilliant life …, as you know …”], who, as you know, afterward presided over me and my monastery in this city of Rome, had previously governed his own monastery in the region of Valeria [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “governed it.”]

He related that when the Lombards, raging with anger, came there, they hanged two of his monks from the branches of a tree. After being hanged, the two died that very day.

When evening came, the spirits of both began to sing there with bright and audible voices. When those who had killed them heard the voices of the singers, they were astonished and greatly afraid. All the captives who were there also heard these voices and became true witnesses of the psalmody [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “the psalmody and the voices.”]

For this reason almighty God permitted the voices of the spirits to be heard in the dwelling places of human beings [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “the voices of the spirits”], so that those living in the flesh might learn that, if they earnestly strive to serve God, they truly live even after the death of the flesh.

## Chapter XXII. On the Passing of Suranus, the Abbot

[Note: [Col. 0353D] His name is entered in the sacred calendars on 24 January.]

[Col. 0353A]

While I was still in the monastery, I learned from the testimony of certain devout men that, during this time of the Lombards, in the nearby province called Sura [Note: We have added *juxta* (“nearby”), read in all our manuscripts but neglected and omitted in the Gussanville edition.], [Note: [Col. 0353D] As is his custom, he calls a territory or district a “province.” Sura, or rather Sora, was once a city of Latium, twelve miles from Ferentinum and the same distance from Atina. In the *Book of Origins* of Marcus Porcius Cato, fragments of which were published by Onuphrius Panvinius, p. 47, one reads: “The Sorani, Ferentinates, Freginates,” and so forth. It must be distinguished from Surrentum, the city of the Picentines.], there was a venerable father of a monastery named Suranus.

When captives came to him, fleeing from the plundering of the Lombards, he gave them everything he seemed to possess in the monastery. After he had exhausted all his own clothing and that of the brothers in almsgiving, and everything in the storeroom, he spent whatever he could find in the garden [Note: [Col. 0354D] Lyranus and Beccus add “in the oratory.”]

When all his possessions had been expended, the Lombards suddenly came upon him, seized him, and began demanding gold. When he told them that he had absolutely nothing, they led him to a nearby mountain in which stood a forest of immense size. A captive who had fled was hiding there in a hollow tree. One of the Lombards drew his sword and killed the venerable man mentioned above.

When his body fell to the ground, the entire mountain and forest were immediately shaken, as though the earth, trembling, were saying that it could not bear the weight of his holiness.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXIII. On the Passing of Suranus, the Abbot**

[Col. 0354B]

While I was still in the monastery, I learned this account from certain very devout men. They said that in the region called Sura [Col. 0354C] there was a man, a most devout father of a monastery, named Suranus [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “a man most devout in his life, a father of a monastery, named Suranus, who …”]

He gave to the captives who came to him everything he possessed in the monastery, including his own clothing, the clothing of the brothers, and everything in the storeroom [Note: [Col. 0354D] *Exodus* in the Glossary of Du Cange means expenditure, expense, or outlay; hence *exodiazein* and *exodiai*, “to spend,” and *exodiastes*, “steward.” In the Royal Manuscript, however, *diedōken* is read instead of *exod…*. It also adds “and in the garden,” which appears in the Latin text.]

When all his possessions had been exhausted, the Lombards suddenly arrived, seized him, and began demanding gold. He answered that he had nothing at all. Then they led him to a neighboring mountain, where there was a huge and densely wooded forest. A captive who had fled there was hiding beneath a hollow tree [Note: [Col. 0354D] The manuscript reads “in hiding.”]
