At that very place one of the Lombards drew his sword and killed the most devout man mentioned above. When his body fell to the ground, the entire forest and mountain shook, as though the trembling earth had uttered a cry, unable to bear the weight of his holiness [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscript reads “having trembled.”]

## Chapter XXIII. On the Passing of the Deacon of the Church of the Marsi

[Note: [Col. 0355D] See the Roman Martyrology, 14 March.]

[Col. 0356A]

There was also in the province of the Marsi a deacon whose life was exceedingly venerable [Note: [Col. 0356D] This is the same as Valeria, in Latium, beside Lake Fucinus. The now-ruined episcopal seat of the city of the Marsi is now at the town of Piscina]. The Lombards found and seized him, and one of them drew his sword and cut off his head.

But when his body fell to the ground, the very man who had beheaded him was seized by an unclean spirit and collapsed at the dead man’s feet. Thus he showed that, because he had killed a friend of God, he had been handed over to the enemy of God.

**Peter.** What is this, I ask you? Why does almighty God permit those whom he does not allow to remain hidden after death—once their holiness is revealed—to die in this way?

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXIV. On the Passing of the Deacon from Marsa**

[Col. 0355A]

There was again in the region of Marsa a deacon exceedingly devout in his way of life [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscript reads “the Lombards found another exceedingly devout deacon.”] The Lombards found and seized him. One of them drew his sword and cut off his head.

When his body fell to the ground, the man who had cut off his head was seized by an unclean spirit and fell at the feet of the dead man [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscript reads “of the dead man.”] Thus it was shown that, because he had killed a friend of God, he had been handed over to the enemy of God.

**Peter.** What is this, I ask you, that almighty God permits those whom, after death, he does not allow to remain hidden as to the holiness they possessed, to die in this way?

## Chapter XXIV. On the Death of the Man of God Who Had Been Sent to Bethel

[Col. 0356B]

**Gregory.** Since it is written: “Whatever death overtakes the righteous, his righteousness shall not be taken away from him” (Wisdom 4:7; Ezekiel 33), what harm does it do the elect, who are undoubtedly advancing toward eternal life, if they die a painful death for a short time? Perhaps there is sometimes some fault in them, even if very small, which ought to be cut away in that same death.

Thus it happens that the wicked receive power against the living, but when those people die, the wicked are more severely punished for having received power to exercise their cruelty against the good. So it was with the same executioner who was permitted to strike the venerable deacon while he was alive but was not permitted to rejoice over him after his death.

The sacred Scriptures also testify to this. The man of God who was sent against Samaria ate on the way through disobedience, and a lion killed him on that same journey. But immediately Scripture says: “The lion stood beside the donkey and did not eat the corpse” (1 Kings 13:28).

This shows that the sin of disobedience was forgiven in the very death, because the same lion that had dared to kill him while alive did not dare to touch him once he was dead. It received the power to kill him, but it did not receive permission to eat from the corpse of the dead man. Since he had fallen into fault during life, he had become righteous through death after his disobedience had been punished.

Thus the lion that had first killed the sinner’s life afterward guarded the corpse of the righteous.

**Peter.** I accept what you say, but I wish to know whether the souls of the righteous can now be received into heaven before the restoration of their bodies [Note: [Col. 0356D] Two Theodorus manuscripts, Germanus, and most manuscripts of Normanus add “before the resurrection.”]

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXV. On the Death of the Man of God Who Was Sent to Samaria**

[Col. 0355B]

**Gregory.** It is written that, whatever death overtakes the righteous, his righteousness shall not be taken away from him. What, then, can harm the elect, whose destiny is eternal life, if they die for the present by a bitter death? Often a small fault is also left in them, which ought to be cut away in death itself. Thus it happens that, while they are still alive, their adversaries receive power against them, so that, when they are dying, vengeance may be wrought through the cruelty of those adversaries [Note: [Col. 0355D] The manuscript reads “through these very things.”]

So it was with this carnivorous beast, which was permitted to strike the most devout deacon while he was alive, but was not permitted to do so after he had died. The sacred sayings also testify to this. The man of God sent to Samaria was killed on the road because he disobeyed. Moreover, it is written that the lion stood beside the donkey but did not eat from the carcass.

Thus it is shown that the sin of disobedience was forgiven in death itself. The lion dared to kill him while alive, but once he was dead it did not dare touch him. It received authority to kill him, but did not receive permission to eat from the corpse. Since the man who had fallen into fault during life had become righteous through death, the lion that had first killed the sinner’s life afterward guarded the corpse of the righteous.

[Col. 0355D] **Peter.** I accept what you say, but I wish to know whether the souls of the righteous can now be received in heaven before the reception of their bodies.

## Chapter XXV. Whether the Souls of the Righteous Are Received into Heaven before the Restoration of the Body

[Note: This teaching of Gregory readily resolves the difficulty arising from certain intricate passages in Bernard and other holy Fathers concerning a delay of beatitude. The righteous in whom some stains still remain to be purged are delayed from glory; but perfect righteous persons are immediately received into heavenly dwellings. At the final judgment, however, the saints will receive a new increase of glory, since to the blessedness of the soul will be added the happiness and blessed incorruptibility of the restored body.]

[Col. 0356D]

**Gregory.** We can neither affirm this of all the righteous nor deny it of all. For there are souls of certain righteous people that are delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwellings. What else is indicated by this penalty of delay except that they possessed some deficiency in perfect righteousness?

Yet it is clearer than daylight that the souls of the perfect righteous, as soon as they leave the confines of this flesh, are received into heavenly dwellings. Truth itself bears witness to this, saying: “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke 17:37). That is, wherever our Redeemer himself is in the body that he assumed, there, without doubt, the souls of the righteous will be gathered.

Paul also desires to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). Therefore whoever does not doubt that Christ is in heaven cannot deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also speaks concerning the dissolution of his body and his dwelling in the heavenly homeland [Note: The Norman manuscripts read: “desiring the dissolution of his body and habitation.”]: “We know that if our earthly house of this tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5:1).

**Peter.** If the souls of the righteous are now in heaven, what will they receive on the day of judgment as the reward for their righteousness?

**Gregory.** At the judgment they will certainly receive an increase [Note: The second Carnotensis manuscript and most Norman manuscripts read: “for now souls rejoice only in the reward of their own glory; afterward, however …”]: now they enjoy only the blessedness of their souls, but afterward they will also enjoy the blessedness of their bodies, rejoicing in the very flesh in which they endured sufferings and torments for the Lord.

Regarding this growth of their glory, Scripture says: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isaiah 51:7). Likewise, before the day of resurrection, it is written concerning the souls of the saints: “They were each given a white robe, and they were told to rest for a little while longer, until the number of their fellow servants and their brothers should be complete” (Revelation 6:17).

Those who have now received one robe will therefore have two at the judgment, because now they rejoice only in the glory of their souls, but then they will rejoice in the glory of both their souls and their bodies.

**Peter.** I agree; but I should like to know how it happens that the dying often foretell many things.

### Greek Recension

**Chapter XXVI. Question Concerning the Souls of the Righteous**

[Col. 0355D]

ΓΡΗΓΟΡΙΟΣ. We can neither say this about all the righteous nor deny it altogether. For there are souls of certain righteous persons that are separated by certain intervals from the dwelling places of the heavenly Kingdom. What else does this indication of the penalty signify, unless that they had some deficiency in their complete righteousness? [Note: The manuscript reads, “What other indication does this show?”] [Note: The manuscript reads, “that they had some deficiency in righteousness.”] For it has been established more clearly than light that the souls of the perfected righteous are immediately received into heavenly seats when they emerge from the prison of the flesh. Truth itself bears witness through itself, saying: “Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” That is, where our Redeemer himself exists together with the flesh that he assumed, there without doubt the souls of the righteous will also be gathered. Paul too desired “to depart and to be with Christ.” Whoever, therefore, does not doubt that Christ exists in heaven will not deny that Paul’s soul exists in heaven. For he himself says concerning the dissolution of the body and dwelling in the heavenly homeland: “We know that if our earthly house of this tent is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.”

PETRUS. If the souls of the righteous are now in heaven, what is it that they will receive on the day of judgment in return for their righteousness?

GREGORIUS. This will wonderfully be added to them at the judgment: now they receive blessedness of souls alone, but then also of bodies. Thus they will rejoice in that very flesh in which they endured sufferings and torments for Christ. For this double glory of theirs it is written: “In their land they shall possess double.” Before the day of resurrection this too was written concerning the souls of the righteous: “They were each given a single white robe, and it was said to them that they should rest yet for a little while, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers should be fulfilled.” Those, therefore, who received a single robe will receive two robes at the judgment. For now they rejoice in glory only through their souls, but then through their souls together with their bodies.

PETRUS. I agree; but I want to know in what manner it happens that many people, when dying, foretell many things?

CAPUT XXVI. In what ways the dying foretell certain things; and concerning a certain advocate, the monks Gerontius and Mellitus, and the boy Armentarius.

GREGORIUS. Sometimes the very power of the soul, through its own subtlety, foresees something. Sometimes souls about to depart from the body learn what is to come through revelation. Sometimes, when they are already close to leaving the body, they cast the incorporeal eye of the mind, divinely inspired, upon heavenly mysteries.

That the soul sometimes, through its own subtlety, knows what is to come is clear from the following event. A certain advocate—understand here a patron of legal cases—who died in this city two days earlier from pain in his side, shortly before he died called his boy and ordered him to prepare his clothing for going out.

[Note: Thus the German version and most manuscripts, including the better ones. The first Aud., Lyr., and Gemet. read “when the advocate Cumquodeus.” The Greek translator has the same reading; Gussanville reads Godeus, supported by the Royal Manuscript of Zachary’s version, which has Κόδεος. The word “advocate” has many meanings; here understand a patron of legal cases.]

[Note: The first Aud., together with Bec. and Lyr., and the second Theod., read “two years earlier.”]

When the boy saw him behaving as though he were mad and did not obey his commands at all, the man rose, put on his clothing, and said that he was going by the Appian Way to the Church of blessed Xystus. Shortly afterward, when his illness grew worse, he died. It had been decided that his body should be buried at the shrine of the blessed martyr Januarius on the Praenestine Way. But because this seemed too far to those who had charge of his funeral, they suddenly decided to set out with his funeral procession along the Appian Way. Without knowing what he had said, they placed him in the very church he had foretold.

[Note: The manuscripts Compend. and Val. Cl. read “those who carried him.”]

Since we know that this man had been entangled in worldly cares and eager for earthly profits, from where could he have foretold this, unless the soul’s own power and subtlety foresaw what was going to happen to his body?

That it also often happens through revelations that the dying know what is to come we can gather from events that we know took place among us in monasteries. In my monastery there was a brother named Gerontius about ten years ago. When he had been brought low by severe bodily illness, he saw in a nocturnal vision men clothed in white, of exceedingly radiant appearance, descending from above and entering this very monastery. [Note: The manuscript reads, “men dressed in white and radiant.”] When they stood before the bed of the sick man, one of them said: “We have come for this purpose: to enlist some brothers from Gregory’s monastery into the army.” Then, commanding another, he added: “Write down Marcellus, Valentinian, Agnellus, and certain others whom I do not now remember.” When these had been entered, he added: “Write down this very man who is looking at us.” [Note: The word is omitted in many manuscripts of the shorter recension.]

Having been convinced by this vision that the words spoken were true, the brother mentioned above told the other brothers in the morning which men from that very monastery were shortly about to die. He also announced that he himself would follow them. On another day the brothers mentioned above began to die, and they followed one another in death in the same order in which their names had been written. Finally, he himself died—the man who had foreseen the death of those brothers.

During the epidemic which three years earlier had ravaged this city with the most violent disaster—namely, in the year 590—a monk named Mellitus lived in the monastery of the city of Portus. He was young in years but a man of extraordinary innocence and humility. Struck by that same epidemic, as the day of his calling approached he was brought to the point of death.

When Felix, the bishop of that city, a man exceedingly reverent in his life, heard this—for he also related the matter to me—he hastened to visit him. He wished to strengthen him with exhortatory words so that he would not fear death, and he began to promise him a longer span of life through divine mercy.

But Mellitus replied that the course of his life had been completed. He said that a young man had appeared to him carrying letters and had said: “Open them and read.” When the letters had been opened, he asserted that he had found himself and all those who had been baptized at that time by the aforementioned bishop listed in those same letters in golden letters. First, as he said, he found his own name, and then the names of all who had been baptized at that time.

From this he became certain that he and they would soon depart from this life. And so it happened: he died that very day, and after him all those who had been baptized followed, so that within a few days none of them remained alive.

It is therefore clear concerning them that the servant of God mentioned above had seen them written in gold for this reason: eternal brightness had their names fixed within itself.

[Note: In the older Gemetian Codex a new section, or another chapter, begins here. In the other Gemetian manuscript it begins at the words “For you know Ammonius,” and so forth.]

Just as these men were able to learn what was to come through revelations, so souls about to depart can sometimes also glimpse heavenly mysteries, not in dreams but while awake.

You know well Ammonius, a monk of my monastery. When he was still living in the worldly condition, he married the legitimate daughter of Valerian, the advocate who lived in this city. He devoted himself assiduously and without interruption to his service. Therefore he knew well everything that took place in his household.

After he had entered the monastery, he told me that during the epidemic which severely afflicted this city in the time of the patrician Narses, there was in the house of the aforementioned Valerian a boy named Armentarius, remarkable for his simplicity and humility.

[Note: Gregory wrote many letters to Narses. Yet this account seems to concern another Narses: the energetic commander who defeated the Goths in Italy in the reign of Justinian Augustus, but later betrayed it by summoning the Lombards. See what we wrote about him in the Life of Cassiodorus.]

[Note: He seems to have been called this because he tended cattle; in Greek, Βουκόλος, “herdsman.”]

When the house of that advocate was being devastated by the same disaster, the boy too was struck and brought to the point of death. Suddenly he was taken away from those present, but afterward returned to himself and had his master summoned. When the master came, he said to him:

“I was in heaven, and I learned which people from this household are going to die. That man, and that man, and that man will die; but you must not be afraid, for you will not die at this time. But so that you may be convinced that I truly say that I was in heaven, behold, I have received permission to speak in every language. As you know, I had no knowledge at all of the Greek language. Nevertheless, speak to me in Greek, so that you may know whether what I testify—that I have received all languages—is true, and I will answer you.”

His master then spoke to him in Greek, and the boy answered in the same language, so that everyone present was astonished.

In that same household there lived a Bulgar by birth, a spatharius of the aforementioned patrician Narses. He was brought quickly to the sick boy and spoke to him in the Bulgarian language. But the boy, who had been born and raised in Italy, answered in that same barbarian language as though he had been born among that people.

[Note: The manuscript reads “among that nation.”]

Everyone who heard him speak those two languages, which they knew he had previously not understood, believed that he was speaking truthfully about all the others, which they could not test.

His death was delayed for two days. On the third day, for a reason hidden in God’s judgment, he gnawed his hands, arms, and elbows with his teeth, and thus departed from the body.

[Note: The printed editions read putebant (“they thought”). We follow the version, the Greek text, three Carnotian manuscripts, the German manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and others.]

[Note: The manuscript reads “until death.”]

When he had died, all those whom he had foretold were immediately taken from this life. No one else in that household died in that same season of the epidemic except those who had been announced by his voice.

PETRUS. It is exceedingly frightening that one who was deemed worthy to receive such a gift was afterward punished with such a penalty.

GREGORIUS. Who can know the hidden judgments of God? Those things that occur in the divine tribunal, which we cannot comprehend, we ought to fear rather than investigate.

ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΚΖʹ. Inquiry concerning souls, through the revelations of the monks Gerontius and Mellitus, and concerning the death of the boy Armentarius.

GREGORIUS. Sometimes, by their own will and through their subtlety, souls foresee certain things. Sometimes, when souls are departing from their bodies, they learn what is to come through revelation. Moreover, when the soul is approaching the point of leaving the body, through divine inspiration it directs the incorporeal eye of its mind toward heavenly mysteries.

[Note: This manuscript reading is better than ἐπινοίᾳ, which appears in the printed edition.]

That the soul, by its own will and subtlety, recognizes the things that are going to happen is made clear by what occurred.

For the advocate Conchodeus—who died in this city two days earlier from pain in his side—shortly before his death called his boy and ordered him to prepare his clothing so that he might go out. [Note: The manuscript reads Κόδεος.] But the boy, supposing that his master had become deranged, did not obey his commands at all. The man himself rose, dressed himself in his clothes, and said that he would go by the Appian Way to the church of the blessed Xystus.

Shortly afterward, overcome by his illness, he died. [Note: The manuscript reads “overcome.”]

It had been arranged that his body should be buried at the church of the blessed martyr Januarius on the Praenestine Way. [Note: The manuscript adds “on the road, that his body be buried.”] But because the place was far away, those attending to his funeral suddenly decided to go out with the funeral procession along the Appian Way and bury him in the church in which he himself had said he would go, although they did not know what he had foretold. And this is what happened.

We know that this man had been entangled in worldly cares and was eagerly pursuing earthly profits. From where, then, could he have foretold what was going to happen to his body, unless he had plainly foreseen it by the soul’s will and through its subtlety?

That the dying often learn what is going to happen through revelation can be demonstrated from the following events, which we have discerned to have occurred among us in the monasteries. [Note: The manuscript reads γεγονῶσι, “having occurred.”]

In my monastery there was a brother named Gerontius. About ten years ago, when he had been brought low by severe bodily illness, he saw in a vision during sleep men of distinguished appearance and exceedingly radiant form descending from above and entering the monastery. When they stood before his bed, one of them said:

“We have come for this purpose: to enlist some brothers from Gregory’s monastery into the army.”

Then, commanding another, he added:

“Write down Marcellus, Valentinian, Agnellus, and certain others whom I do not presently remember.”

When these had been entered, he added:

“Write down this very man who is looking at us.”

Believing from this vision that the words spoken were true, the brother mentioned above told the other brothers in the morning which men were going to die from that same monastery. He also announced concerning himself that he would follow them.

On another day the brothers mentioned above began to die. They followed one another in death in the order in which they had been named in the register. Finally, he too died—the man who had foreseen the death of those brothers.

During the epidemic which three years earlier had ravaged this city with the most violent disaster, a monk named Mellitus lived in the monastery of the city of Portus. He was young in age but a man of extraordinary innocence and humility. Struck by the disaster of that same epidemic, as the day of his calling approached he was brought to the point of death.

[Note: The manuscript reads, “although young in age, yet a man of innocence and humility, being carried away by the disaster.”]

When the bishop of that city, Felix, heard this—the bishop who also related the matter to me—he hastened to visit him. [Note: The manuscript has φίληξ, perhaps φῆλιξ, “Felix.”] He wished to strengthen him with exhortatory words so that he would not fear death.

He began to speak to him about God’s compassion and patience and to promise him a longer span of life. [Note: The manuscript adds “and patience.”]

But Mellitus answered him, saying that the time of his life had been completed. He said that a young man had appeared to him carrying letters and saying:

“Open them and read.”

When they had been opened, he said that he had found himself and all those who had been baptized at that time by the aforementioned bishop written in those letters in letters of gold, during the feast of Easter. First, as he said, he found his own name, and then the names of all who had been baptized at that time.

From this he became certain that he and those others would soon depart from this life. And so it happened: he died that very day, and after him, within a few days, all those who had been baptized at that time followed, so that none of them remained in this life.

It is therefore true concerning this matter that the servant of God mentioned above saw them written in gold because eternal brightness had their names fixed within itself. [Note: The printed editions corruptly read πεποιημένα; the manuscript has πεπηγμένα, “fixed” or “fastened.”]

Just as these men were able to discern what was to come through revelations, so souls departing from the body can often behold heavenly mysteries, not through dreams but while awake.

This will also become clear from the following case. You know well Ammonius, the monk of my monastery. When he was still living in the worldly condition, he married the legitimate daughter of Valerian, the advocate who lived in this city, and he continually devoted himself to his service. Therefore he knew well everything that took place in his household.

Afterward, when he had come to the monastery, he told me that during the time of the patrician Narses the epidemic had severely ravaged this city. [Note: The manuscript reads Ἀρσῆ.]

In the house of the aforementioned Valerian there was a boy named Boukolos, living with great innocence and humility.

When that household too was being afflicted by the same disaster of the epidemic, the boy himself was struck and brought to the point of death. Suddenly he was snatched away from those present, but he returned to himself and had his master summoned.

When his master came, he said to him:

“I was in heaven, and I learned which people from this household are going to die: this man, and this man, and this man. But you must not fear, for you will not die at this time.

“But so that you may be convinced that I truly say that I was in heaven, behold, I have received permission to speak in every language. As you know, I had no knowledge at all of the Greek language. Nevertheless, speak to me in Greek, so that you may know that I speak truthfully, and I will answer you.”

His master then addressed him in Greek, and the boy answered him in the same language, so that everyone present was astonished.

In that same household there was also a spatharius of the aforementioned patrician Narses, a Bulgar by birth. He was brought to the boy and spoke to him in the language of the Bulgars.

But the boy, who had been born and raised in Italy, spoke in answer in that same barbarian language as though he had been born among that people.

All who heard him speak those two languages, which they knew he had previously not understood, believed that he was speaking truthfully about the other languages as well.

His death was made manifest after two days. On the third day, by God’s hidden decision—something unknown to us—he consumed his hands, arms, and elbows with his teeth. [Note: The manuscript reads “and when he had died, he departed from the body.”] And thus he departed from the body. When he had died, all those whom he had foretold immediately withdrew from this life. No one else from that household died in that same time of the epidemic except those who had been announced by his voice.

[Note: The manuscript reads “truly.”] [Note: The manuscript reads “I will speak as follows.”] [Note: The manuscript reads “among that people.”]

PETRUS. It is exceedingly frightening that one who had been deemed worthy to receive such a gift was afterward subjected to such a judgment.

GREGORIUS. Who can know the hidden judgments of God? Since we cannot comprehend those things that occur in the divine judgment, we ought to fear them rather than investigate them.

CAPUT XXVII. Concerning the death of Theophanius, count of Centumcellae.

To complete what we began concerning departing souls, which often know many things beforehand, we must not remain silent about what I learned from the testimony of many concerning Theophanius, count of the city of Centumcellae, while he was residing in that same city.

[Note: Gilot. and Vatic. corruptly read Centerelensis. All the English, Norman, German, Compendian, and other manuscripts, as well as the Greek interpretation, have Centumcellensis. A “count” here is one who was sent from the comitatus, or court, to govern important cities and administer justice to their inhabitants. On the various offices of counts, see Cassiodorus, book VI of the Variae. There will be a more suitable occasion to discuss counts elsewhere.]

He was a man devoted to works of mercy, intent upon good deeds, and especially diligent in hospitality. Although occupied with the responsibilities of his office and engaged in earthly and temporal affairs, as became clear at the end, he did these things more from duty than from personal intention.

When the time of his death was approaching, a very severe storm prevented his body from being carried out for burial. His wife, weeping most bitterly, asked him:

“What shall I do? How can I carry you out for burial, when because of the violence of the storm I cannot even leave the doorway of this house?”

He replied:

“Do not weep, woman, for as soon as I have died, the calm weather will return at that very hour.”

At once death followed his words, and calm weather followed his death.

This sign was accompanied by other signs. His hands and feet, swollen with the fluid of gout, had become transformed into wounds, and they stood open as pus flowed from them.

[Note: The printed editions read putebant (“they thought”). We follow the version, the Greek text, three Carnotian manuscripts, the German manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and others.]

But when his body had been stripped according to custom for washing, his hands and feet were found to be sound, as though they had never had any wound at all. [Note: Val. Cl. reads “as though they had no trace of a wound.”]

He was therefore carried out and buried. On the fourth day his wife decided that the marble placed over his tomb should be changed. When that marble had been removed from above his body, such a fragrant odor came forth from it as though, from his putrefying flesh, spices had boiled up in place of worms.

When I related this in my homilies, some of the weaker brethren found it difficult to believe. One day, as I was sitting in an assembly of nobles, the very craftsmen who had changed the marble in his tomb appeared, wishing to ask me something concerning their own affairs. Before the clergy, the nobles, and the people, I questioned them about the miracle. [Note: In the second Carnotian manuscript and some Norman manuscripts: “the same fragrance of odor, after the marble had been changed.”] They testified that they too had been filled in a wonderful manner with the same fragrant odor, and they added several other details that increased the wonder concerning that tomb, which I now consider too lengthy to relate.

PETRUS. I see that my inquiry has now been sufficiently answered, but there is still something that troubles my mind with a question. Since it was said above that the souls of the saints are already in heaven, it undoubtedly remains that the souls of the wicked too must be believed to be nowhere except in hell. But I do not know what truth holds concerning this matter, for human opinion does not accept that the souls of sinners can be tormented before the judgment.

ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΚΗʹ. Concerning the death of Theophanius, count of Centumcellae.

To complete what we began concerning departing souls, namely, that they know many things beforehand, we must not be silent about this matter which I learned from the testimony of many concerning Theophanius, the count who lived in the city of Centumcellae.

This man devoted himself to works of mercy and, above all, attended to hospitality. Although he was occupied with the cares of government and outwardly practiced earthly and temporal affairs, how he was glorified at his death became clear. [Note: The manuscript has the incomplete reading πῶς δὲ ἐλαμπρ… (“but how he was glorified …”); the remainder is uncertain.]

When the time of his death approached, an exceedingly severe storm made it impossible for him to be carried out even for burial. His wife, with the most violent weeping, said to him:

“What shall I do? How shall I be able to carry you out for burial, when I cannot even leave the door of the house because of the great violence of the storm?”

He answered her:

“Do not wish to weep, woman, for immediately when I die, fair weather will return.”

At these words he met his end, and calm weather followed his death.

Other signs also occurred at his death. His hands and feet, swollen by the fluid of gout, had become hardened and opened by the discharge of fluid. But when, according to custom, they had stripped his body in order to wash it, his hands and feet were found sound, so that no trace of hardness was found in them. [Note: The manuscript reads “of gout”; perhaps ποδάγρας or ποδαλγίας, “gout” or “pain in the feet.”]

He was therefore carried out and buried. On the fourth day after his burial, his wife decided to change the marble placed above his tomb. When it had been lifted from his body, a fragrant odor was emitted from his flesh, as though spices were bubbling up from his rotting flesh in place of worms. [Note: The manuscript has “an odor was sent forth from his flesh in place of …”]

When I related this in my Gospel homilies, some of the weaker brethren came to doubt it. One day, as I was sitting in an assembly with noblemen, the very craftsmen who had changed the marble of his tomb came and asked me about one of their affairs. [Note: The manuscript has “themselves, reverent men.”] I questioned them about this miracle before the clergy and all the people. [Note: The manuscript reads “I asked them, and they answered, saying, ‘In a wondrous manner …’”] They answered, saying that in a wondrous manner they themselves had been filled with that fragrance. They also related several other matters as an addition to the wonder concerning that tomb, but I consider it too lengthy to recount them.

PETRUS. I now see that the inquiry I made has been sufficiently answered. Yet this matter still pricks my mind with a question: since it was said above that the souls of the saints are already in heaven, we must also believe that the souls of the unjust are in Hades. But I do not know what the truth is concerning this matter. Human reasoning does not accept that the souls of sinners can be judged before the day of judgment.

CAPUT XXVIII. That just as the souls of the perfected are in heaven, so, after the dissolution of the body, the souls of the wicked are to be believed to be in hell.

GREGORIUS. If you have believed, on the authority of sacred Scripture, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, you must also believe in every respect that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For from the retribution of eternal justice, through which the righteous already rejoice, it necessarily follows that the unrighteous are also tormented in every respect. Just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that fire burns the rejected from the day of their departure.

PETRUS. For what reason should we believe that bodily fire can hold an incorporeal thing?

ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΚΘʹ. That just as the souls of the righteous are in heaven, so those of sinners depart into Hades.

GREGORIUS. If you have believed, through the assurance of sacred Scripture, that the souls of the saints are in heaven, you must certainly also believe that the souls of the unjust are in Hades. For from the retribution of the innermost justice by which the righteous are glorified, it necessarily follows that the unjust too are judged in every respect. [Note: The manuscript reads “that all the unjust are judged.”] Just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so we must believe that fire consumes the unjust from the day of their departure.

PETRUS. And in what manner must we believe that bodily fire can hold an incorporeal form?

CAPUT XXIX. On what grounds it should be believed that bodily fire can hold incorporeal spirits.

[Note: On this question consult Augustine, City of God, book XXI, chapter 10.]

GREGORIUS. If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held within the body, why should it not also, after death, since the spirit is incorporeal, be held by bodily fire?

PETRUS. In every living person the incorporeal spirit is held within the body because it gives life to the body.

GREGORIUS. If, Peter, the incorporeal spirit can be held in that which it gives life to, why should it not also be held there in punishment where it is put to death? We say that the spirit is held by fire in the sense that it is in the torment of fire, seeing and feeling it. For it suffers fire precisely by seeing it; and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned.

Thus a bodily thing burns an incorporeal one, when invisible burning and pain are drawn from visible fire, so that through bodily fire even an incorporeal mind is tormented by an incorporeal flame.

[Note: Both Theod. manuscripts, Val. Cl., and the second Aud. read etiam corporea flamma, “also by a bodily flame.” In the first Gemetian manuscript, a later hand deleted the first syllable of incorporea so that it subsequently read corporea flamma, “bodily flame.” The printed editions have “as though in the torment of fire, both seeing and feeling it … is punished.” In the second Aud. manuscript, vivendo, “while living,” appears instead of videndo, “while seeing.”]

We can also gather from Gospel statements that the soul suffers the burning not only by seeing but also by experience. For Truth’s own voice says that the rich man died and was buried in hell. That his soul was held in fire is indicated by the voice of that same rich man, who beseeches Abraham:

“Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.”

When, therefore, Truth declares that the sinful rich man is condemned in fire, what wise person will deny that the souls of the rejected are held in fires?

PETRUS. Behold, reason and testimony incline my mind toward belief, but once released it returns again to its former resistance. For I do not understand how an incorporeal thing can be held and afflicted by a bodily thing.

GREGORIUS. Tell me, I ask you: do you suppose that the apostate spirits cast down from heavenly glory are bodily or incorporeal?

PETRUS. Who possessed of sound judgment would say that spirits are bodily?

GREGORIUS. Do you acknowledge that the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal or bodily?

PETRUS. I have no doubt that the fire of Gehenna is bodily, in which bodies are certainly tormented.

GREGORIUS. Certainly Truth will say to the rejected at the end:

“Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

If, therefore, the devil and his angels, although incorporeal, are to be tormented by bodily fire, what is surprising if souls, even before they receive bodies, can experience bodily torments?

PETRUS. The reasoning is clear, and henceforth the mind ought not to doubt concerning this question.

ΚΕΦΑΛ. Λʹ. Inquiry into how we should believe that incorporeal spirits can be held by bodily fire.

GREGORIUS. If, while a human being is alive, the incorporeal spirit is held within the body, why should it not also, after death, since the spirit is incorporeal, be held in bodily fire?

PETRUS. For this reason the incorporeal spirit is held within the body in the living, because it gives life to the body.

GREGORIUS. If the incorporeal spirit, Peter, can be held in the body that it gives life to, why should it not also be held there in punishment where it is put to death? We say that the spirit is held by fire because it is in the torment of fire, seeing and feeling it. That fire which it endures consumes it as it sees it.

This occurs so that a bodily form may burn an incorporeal one, just as from this visible fire burning and invisible pain pass into the mind. For, as far as we can demonstrate from the Gospel sayings, through bodily fire the incorporeal mind, being inflamed, is melted.

The soul endures the burning not only by seeing but also by experience. Truth’s own voice said concerning the rich man that he died and was buried. That his soul was held in fire is shown when it says:

“Being in Hades, he entreated Abraham, saying: ‘Send Lazarus, so that, after dipping the tip of his finger in water, he may cool my tongue, because I am in anguish in this flame.’”

When, therefore, Truth says that the sinful rich man is condemned in fire, what wise person will deny that the souls of the rejected are held in fire? [Note: The manuscript reads “condemned and hidden in fire.”]

PETRUS. Behold, by this defense and testimony the mind is inclined toward belief, but after passing beyond them it turns back again to uncertainty. [Note: The manuscript reads “but after being released … it turned back.”] For I do not understand how an incorporeal thing can be held and struck by a bodily form.

GREGORIUS. Tell me, I ask you: do you consider the apostate spirits, cast out from heavenly glory, bodily or incorporeal?

PETRUS. Who, reasoning soundly, would say that spirits are bodily? [Note: The manuscript has ὑγιής, “sound-minded,” rather than ὑγιή, “sound.”]

GREGORIUS. Do you say that the fire of Gehenna is incorporeal or bodily?

PETRUS. I do not doubt that the fire of Gehenna is bodily, in which bodies will truly be judged.

GREGORIUS. Christ, our God, who is Truth itself, will say to the condemned at the consummation:

“Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”

If, then, the devil and his angels, although incorporeal, are to be judged by bodily fire, what is surprising if souls, before receiving bodies, can also experience bodily torments? [Note: The manuscript reads “torments.”]

PETRUS. Since the defense is clear, the mind ought no longer to doubt concerning this inquiry.

CAPUT XXX. Concerning the death of King Theodoric the Arian.

GREGORIUS. Since you have come laboriously to believe this, I think it worthwhile to strengthen your faith by relating what has been reported to me by faithful men.

Julianus, the second defensor of this Roman Church in which, by God’s will, I serve, died about seven years ago. While I was still in the monastery, he frequently came to me and was accustomed to converse with me about the benefit of the soul.

One day he told me the following:

[Note: This chapter begins here in the Gemetian manuscript.]

[Note: This was the king of the Goths in Italy, concerning whom we have written at length in the Life of Cassiodorus, especially book I, chapters 3–6. See also Paul the Deacon, Miscellaneous History, book XV, and Gregory of Tours, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 40. A place formerly known as “Theodoric’s Hell” is mentioned in the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, third century, part II, p. 379.]

In the time of King Theodoric, my father-in-law’s father had been carrying out the collection of the canon in Sicily and was already returning to Italy.

[Note: Those who performed this office were called canoniciarii, as can be seen in Cassiodorus, especially book VI of the Variae, formula 8, and book XII, chapter 13. They collected not only grain but also money; hence Cassiodorus’s expression canonici solidi, book II of the Variae, letter 25. See also Sidonius Apollinaris, book VI, letter 10, and the learned notes of Savaron.]

His ship put in at an island called Lipari. Since a solitary man of great virtue lived there, while the sailors were repairing the ship’s rigging my father-in-law’s father decided to visit that man of God and commend himself to his prayers.

When the man of God saw them, he conversed with them about various matters and said:

“Do you know that King Theodoric is dead?”

They immediately replied:

“May it not be so! We left him alive, and no such news about him has yet reached us.”

The servant of God added:

“He is indeed dead. Yesterday, at the ninth hour, he was brought between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, stripped of his belt, barefoot, and with his hands bound, and thrown into this neighboring cauldron of Vulcan.”

[Note: This was John I, who succeeded Hormisdas in the year 523.] [Note: In some Norman manuscripts the reading is “island,” confirmed by the Greek version.]

When they heard this, they carefully recorded the day. On their return to Italy, they found that King Theodoric had died on the very day on which the servant of God had been shown his departure and punishment.

Because Theodoric had killed Pope John by grievously afflicting him in prison and had also slaughtered the patrician Symmachus with the sword, he appeared to have been justly cast into the fire by those whom he had unjustly judged in this life.

ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΛΑʹ. Inquiry whether there is a purifying fire after death.

GREGORIUS. Since you have believed after the labor of this discussion, I add to your faith by relating those things that have been made known to me by faithful people.

Julianus, the second among the defensores of this holy Roman Church of God, which by Christ’s grace I serve—he died seven years ago, while I was still in the monastery—was accustomed to come to me frequently and converse about the benefit of the soul.

One day he told me that in the time of Theodoric the king, his father-in-law’s father was administering the collection of the canon in Sicily.

As he was returning to Italy, the ship put in at an island called Lipari. [Note: The manuscript reads “collection.” A little later it reads “when he had returned.”] A certain man practiced the solitary life there and possessed the power of great deeds. While the sailors were repairing the ship’s rigging, my aforementioned relative decided to visit that man of God and commend himself to his prayers.

When the man of God saw him, after speaking with them about matters beneficial to the soul, he added:

“Do you know that King Theodoric has died?”

They answered him:

“May it not be so! We left him alive, and until now we have heard nothing of the sort concerning him.”

The servant of God replied:

“He died yesterday. At about the ninth hour he was brought between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, stripped of his belt, barefoot, and with his hands bound, and was thrown into the burning fire there on the neighboring island of Vulcan.”

[Note: The manuscript reads “he truly died yesterday.”] [Note: The manuscript reads “of Vulcan.”]

When they heard this, they carefully marked the day. On their return to Italy, they discovered that King Theodoric had died on that very day on which the servant of God had learned through revelation of his departure and the torment of his judgment.

Because Theodoric had killed Pope John by gravely afflicting him and imprisoning him, and had slaughtered the patrician Symmachus with the sword, he appeared to have been justly cast into the fire by those whom he had unjustly judged in this life. [Note: The manuscript reads “he killed him in prison”; shortly afterward, “having been cast into the fire.”]

CAPUT XXXI. Concerning the death of Reparatus.

At the time when I first began to yearn intensely for the desires of a withdrawn life, there was an honorable old man named Deusdedit, a close friend of the nobles of this city and also assiduously joined to me in friendship. He told me the following:

In the time of the Goths, a certain distinguished man named Reparatus came to the point of death. [Note: *Spectabilis* was a title of honor; see Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VII, chapter 37, on the formula by which this rank was conferred. Those who held it were counted among the counts of the first rank; compare Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book II, letter 28.] After lying for a long time mute and rigid, he appeared to have completely lost his vital breath, and his body remained lifeless.

When many had gathered around him and his household was mourning him as already dead, he suddenly revived, and the tears of all the mourners turned into astonishment.

When he had returned, he said:

“Send a boy quickly to the Church of the blessed martyr Laurence, which is called by the name of its founder Damasus, and let him see what is happening to the presbyter Tiburtius and hasten to report it.”

At that time Tiburtius was said to be enslaved to bodily desires. Florentius, who is now presbyter of that church, remembers well his life and the character of his conduct.

While the boy was on his way, the same Reparatus, who had returned to himself, related what he had learned about Tiburtius in the place to which he had been taken. He said:

“A huge pile of wood had been prepared. Tiburtius the presbyter was brought and placed upon it, and when fire had been put beneath it, he was burned.

“Another pyre was being prepared, whose summit appeared to extend from earth to heaven. A voice was sent forth asking whose it was.”

Having said these things, Reparatus immediately died. The boy who had been sent to Tiburtius found him already dead.

Reparatus had been taken to the places of punishment; when he saw these things, he returned, related them, and died. This plainly shows that he saw them not for himself but for us, who are still permitted to live, so that while we have time we may correct ourselves from evil works.

Reparatus saw a pyre being built, not because wood burns in hell so that fire may be produced, but because, in order to explain these things to the living, he saw things concerning the burning of the wicked (*pravorum*), from which corporeal fire is customarily fed among the living. Through familiar things, those who heard might learn what they ought to fear concerning unfamiliar ones.

ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΛΒʹ. Concerning the death of Reparatus.

At the beginning of the time when I was yearning with great desire for a solitary life, an exceedingly honorable old man named Deusdedit, who was a friend of all the nobles of this city and attached himself to me in friendship, told me the following: [Note: The manuscript reads ἰδίαν ζωήν, “one’s own life,” rather than “solitary life”; it also has the fragmentary reading συντυχίαις … οὗτός μοι, “at conversations/meetings … this man [told] me.”]

In the time of the Goths, a man named Reparatus came to the hour of death. He lay for a long time in a state of collapse, so that everyone thought that his vital breath had been drawn out from its depths and that his body remained lifeless. [Note: The manuscript reads ἡμιθανής, “half-dead.”]

When many had gathered around him, together with his household, they mourned him as though he had already died. [Note: The printed editions corruptly read φαμιλίου. Although φαμίλιος sometimes occurs, it means “servant” and is masculine; the printed reading τῆς φαμιλίου corresponds here to the Latin *familia* (“household”) mourning.] Suddenly he revived, and the tears of all who were weeping were turned into astonishment.

The sick man said:

“Send a boy without delay to the church of the holy martyr Laurence, called Damasus, which is so named after the one who founded it, so that he may see what is happening to the presbyter Tiburtius and hasten to report it.”

At that time Tiburtius was said to be enslaved to bodily desires. Florentius, who is now presbyter of that same church, knows well his manner of life and the character of his conduct.

While the boy was on his way, the same Reparatus, who had returned to himself, related what he had seen in the place to which he had been taken. He said:

“A very large pile of wood had been prepared. When Tiburtius the presbyter had been brought, he was placed upon it, and when fire had been put beneath it, he was burned.

“Another pile of wood was being prepared, whose summit appeared to extend from earth all the way to heaven. A voice came and said whose it was.”

After these things had been said, the same Reparatus immediately died. The boy sent to Tiburtius found him already dead.

It is therefore plainly established concerning this matter that Reparatus was taken to the places of punishment so that he might see what he saw, return, relate it, and immediately die—not for his own sake but for us who still remain in this life, so that we might correct ourselves from evil works.

Reparatus saw wood being prepared, not because wood is burned in Hades, but so that these things might be explained to the living. He saw those things concerning the burning of worms, from which fire is customarily fed among bodily living beings, so that through familiar things those who heard might learn what they ought also to fear concerning things unknown. [Note: The manuscript adds “so that the fire may …”]

CAPUT XXXII. Concerning the death of the Curialis, whose burial was burned.
