A very terrible event also occurred in the province of Valeria, as a man of venerable life, Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse—who for a long time presided over my monastery in that city—was accustomed to relate, saying:

[Note: Concerning Saint Maximianus, see Book III, chapter 36, and Gregory’s several letters to him.]

A certain curial official there, on the most holy Sabbath of Easter, received a young daughter of someone at baptism.

[Note: In Cassiodorus, Book IX of the *Variae*, chapter 2, there is an edict of King Athalaric in favor of the curial officials, in which he calls them “the lesser senate.”]

After returning home following the fast and becoming drunk on a great quantity of wine, he asked that this same girl remain with him, and that night—something unspeakable even to say—he violated her. When he had risen at daybreak, the wretched man began to consider going to the bath, thinking that by bathing he might wash away the stain of his sin. He therefore went, washed, and began to be afraid to enter the church. If he did not go to church on so solemn a day, he was ashamed before people; but if he went, he feared God’s judgment. Human shame therefore prevailed, and he went to church. Trembling and afraid, he began to stand there, each moment suspecting at what hour he might be handed over to an unclean spirit and tormented before the entire people.

Yet, although he was exceedingly afraid, nothing adverse happened to him during that celebration of the liturgy. He went out rejoicing and entered the church the next day without fear. For six consecutive days he continued joyfully and confidently, thinking that the Lord had either not seen his crime or, having seen it, had mercifully forgiven it.

[Note: The Vulgate reads: “or, having seen it, had mercifully forgiven it.”]

[Note: Concerning this word, in the sense in which it properly means “to enter the church,” see what was already said in the notes to chapter 10 of Book I. From the time of Tertullian it seems already to have been established for this meaning: “If,” you say, “one must go out, may the household’s occupation never arise more than then,” *To His Wife*, Book II, chapter 4.]

On the seventh day he died suddenly. When his body had been committed to burial, for a long time, while everyone watched, a flame came out of his tomb and burned his bones so completely that it consumed the entire tomb, and the earth that had been heaped over the grave appeared to have been dug away. In doing this, almighty God showed what his soul had secretly suffered: the flame also consumed his body before human eyes. In this matter God likewise deigned to give us who hear it an example capable of causing fear, so that from this reflection we may understand what a living and conscious soul suffers for its guilt, if even insensible bones are consumed by so great a punishment of fire.

**PETER.** I should like to know whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment.


### Greek recension

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the death of a curial official and how his spirit was burned

[Col. 0371B]

Maximianus, a man most reverent in life—now bishop of Syracuse, formerly head of my monastery in this city—told me that a very terrible event had happened in the country of Valeria. [Note: The manuscript reads *τῷ βίῳ*, “in life,” for the base *τῇ ζωῇ*, likewise “in life.”]

He said that on the holy and sacred Sabbath of Easter a curial official there received at baptism the young daughter of someone. [Note: The manuscript has the damaged reading *ἁγίῳ βαπτ...*, “at holy bapt[ism],” for the base *βαπτίσματι*, “at baptism.”]

After the fast he went back to his house, got drunk on much wine, and asked that this same daughter remain with him. That very night—an act unlawful even to mention—he violated her. In the morning the wretched man rose and considered going to the bath, thinking to wash the pollution of his sin away with water. He went and bathed. Then, remembering what he had done, he was held by fear and dread at the thought of going to church. Yet he was ashamed before people if on so great a day he did not go to church; while if he went, he feared God’s judgment. Human shame prevailed, and he went into the church.

There he stood trembling and afraid, continually watching for the hour when he might be handed to an unclean spirit and burst apart before all the people. He completed the liturgy with great fear; when he saw that he had suffered nothing adverse, he left rejoicing. On the following day he went carelessly to church again. For six days he went on in joy and unconcern, believing that the Lord had either not seen his offense or, having seen it, had mercifully forgiven it. On the seventh day he died suddenly. [Note: The manuscript reads *ἑβδόμῃ ἡμέρᾳ*, “on the seventh day,” for the base *τῇ ζ΄ ἡμέρᾳ*, also “on the seventh day.”]

After his body had been given to burial, a flame came out of his tomb while all watched and burned his bones so thoroughly that it consumed the whole tomb and the earth lying above it. Almighty God allowed this to happen in order to show what his soul endured in secret, when flame consumed his body, and so that we who hear might fear the example and understand what a living, conscious soul will suffer for its sin when even insensible bones are burned by the punishment of so great a fire.

**PETER.** I should like to know whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and likewise whether the wicked recognize the wicked in punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the wicked the wicked in punishment

**GREGORY.** The answer to this question is demonstrated more clearly than light itself in the Lord’s words that we cited above. For when it had been said:

“There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day; and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any; but even the dogs came and licked his sores” (Luke 16:19),

it was added that Lazarus died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man died and was buried in hell. When he lifted up his eyes while in torment, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom; and he himself cried out, saying:

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am suffering in this flame.”

Abraham said to him:

“Son, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise his evil things.”

But the rich man, now having no hope of salvation for himself, turned to seeking the salvation of his own people, saying:

“I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment” (ibid.).

These words plainly declare that the good recognize the good and the wicked recognize the wicked. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus at all, he would never have spoken to the rich man in torment about Lazarus’s past suffering, saying that Lazarus had received evil things during his life. And if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man in torment would never have remembered his brothers, even though they were absent. For how could he fail to recognize those present who had even taken care to plead on behalf of the absent?

This also demonstrates what you did not ask: that the good recognize the wicked, and the wicked recognize the good. For the rich man is recognized by Abraham, who said to him, “You received your good things during your life”; and the chosen Lazarus is likewise recognized by the rejected rich man, who asks that he be sent and calls him by name, saying, “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (ibid.).

Through this mutual recognition, the fullness of retribution increases: the good rejoice more greatly when they see those rejoicing with them whom they loved; and the wicked, while suffering with those whom they loved in this world despite their contempt for God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by the punishment of those others.

Among the elect something still more marvelous occurs: they recognize not only those whom they knew in this world, but also recognize as though seen and familiar the good whom they never saw. For when they behold the ancient Fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they always knew through the practice of their works will not be strangers to them through sight. Since all there behold God in a shared radiance, what can they not know there, where they know the One who knows all things?

[Note: The German, Norman, and other manuscripts read *et induebatur*, “and he was clothed,” in the description of the rich man.]

[Note: The same manuscripts read *et ipse clamans dixit*, “and he himself, crying out, said,” for the base *et ipse clamavit, dicens*, “and he himself cried out, saying.”]

[Note: The Beccensis manuscript reads *conversatione*, “conduct,” for the base *contritione*, “affliction.”]

### Greek version

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Question whether the righteous recognize the righteous, and sinners sinners, in the age to come

**GREGORY.** The proof of this question is shown more brightly than light itself by the Lord’s words which we cited above. For it was said that there was a certain rich man who dressed himself in purple and fine linen and rejoiced splendidly every day. A certain poor man named Lazarus had been cast at his gate, covered with sores, desiring to be filled from the crumbs falling from the rich man’s table; but the dogs also came and licked his sores.

Moreover, it is written that Lazarus died, was carried by the angels, and was taken into Abraham’s bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. In Hades, lifting up his eyes while in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom; and he himself cried out and said:

“Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in anguish in this flame.”

But Abraham said:

“Child, remember that you received your good things during your life, and Lazarus likewise his evil things.”

The rich man, having no further hope of salvation, turned instead toward the salvation of his own family and said:

“I beg you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, so that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torment.”

[Note: The manuscript reads *αὐτῷ*, “to him,” for the base *οὕτω*, “thus.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *διαμαρτυρῇ*, “that he may testify/warn,” for the base *διαμαρτύρηται*, with the same sense.]

Through these words it is plainly shown that the good recognize the good and the wicked the wicked. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus at all, he would not have spoken to the rich man in torment about his former suffering, saying that he had received evil things during his life. And again, if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man in torment would not have remembered his absent brothers. How, then, could he fail to recognize those present who had remembered the absent and taken care to plead for them?

This matter also demonstrates what you did not ask: that the good recognize the wicked, and the wicked the good. For the rich man was recognized by Abraham, who said to him, “You received your good things during your life”; and the chosen Lazarus was likewise recognized by the rejected rich man, who begged that he be sent and called him by name, saying, “Send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.”

In this recognition of both parties, the greatness of retribution increases: the good rejoice more abundantly when they see those rejoicing with them whom they loved; and the wicked likewise suffer with those whom God detested in this world but whom they themselves loved. Thus not only their own punishment but also the sight of the others burns them more intensely.

[Note: The manuscript reads *οὕσπερ*, “those whom,” for the base *ὧνπερ*, “of those whom,” in the clause about those whom the good loved.]

Among the elect something still more marvelous occurs: they recognize not only those whom they knew in this world, but also recognize as familiar those whom they never saw. For when they behold the ancient Fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they always knew through imitation of their works will not be unknown to them through sight. Since all there behold God together in the same splendor, what is there that they do not know, where they know the One who knows all things?

[Note: The manuscript reads *τρυφῇ οὐκ*, “in that eternal delight they will not,” for the base *κληρονομίᾳ οὐκ*, “in that eternal inheritance they will not.”]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning a religious man who saw the prophets as he was dying

For one of our religious men, a man of a highly praiseworthy life, died four years ago. [Note: First Carnot: *valde venerabilis vel laudabilis*, “highly venerable or praiseworthy.”] As other religious men who were present testified, at the hour of his departure he began to see the prophet Jonah, Ezekiel also, and Daniel, and to call them his lords by name. While saying that they had come to him, and paying them reverent homage with eyes cast down, he was taken out of the flesh. This plainly shows what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life, if this man, while still in corruptible flesh, recognized holy prophets whom he had certainly never seen.
### Greek recension

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the man who saw the prophets at his departure

[Col. 0375B]

About four years ago one of our men, a man of highly praiseworthy conduct, was about to die. As devout people who were then present testified, at the hour of his departure he saw the prophet Jonah together with Ezekiel and Daniel, and began to call them his lords by name. [Note: The manuscript reads *ἐπαινετὸς τῇ πολιτείᾳ*, “praiseworthy in conduct,” for the base *ἐπαινετῆς πολιτείας*, “of praiseworthy conduct.”]

Paying them honor, he said to those standing beside him, “These men have come to me.” As he said this a light appeared, and he departed from the flesh. This clearly shows what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life: while this man was still in corruptible flesh, he recognized the holy prophets whom he had never seen.

[Note: The manuscript reads *ζωῇ ἐν ὅσῳ*, “in life, while,” for the base *ἐν ᾗ*, “in which,” at the start of the concluding clause.]

## CHAPTER XXXV. That sometimes even souls unknown to one another recognize one another at departure; concerning those who will receive punishments or corresponding rewards for faults or good deeds; and concerning the deaths of John and Ursus, Eumorphius, and Stephen

[Col. 0376C]

It often happens that, as the soul departs, it recognizes even those with whom it is destined to be assigned to one dwelling because of an equality of faults or likewise of rewards.

The venerable elder Eleutherius, concerning whom I related much in the preceding book (chapter 33), stated that in his monastery he had a biological brother named John, who fourteen days before his death foretold his departure to the brothers. As he counted the passing days, he was seized by fever three days before he was called from the body. When the hour of death came, he received the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. He summoned the brothers and ordered them to sing psalms before him. He himself assigned them the antiphon, saying:

“Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Psalm 117:19).

While the brothers stood before him and sang, he suddenly uttered a loud, prolonged cry and said:

“Ursus, come!”

As soon as he had said this, he was taken from the body and ended his mortal life. The brothers were astonished, since they did not know what the dying brother had been calling out.

After his death, great sorrow arose in the monastery. On the fourth day, however, the brothers had some necessary business that required them to send someone to another monastery situated a long distance away. When they arrived there, they found all the monks of that monastery in profound grief. They asked them:

“What has happened to you, that you are weighed down by such great sorrow?”

They replied:

“We lament the desolation of this place, because one brother, whose life held us together in this monastery, has been taken from this light. Today is the fourth day since he departed.”

The visiting brothers carefully asked what he had been called. They answered:

“Ursus.”

When the hour of his calling was investigated precisely, they found that he had left the body at the very moment when he had been summoned through John, who had died among the brothers at the other monastery. From this it may be inferred that the merit of both had been equal, and that they were granted the privilege of living together in one dwelling, since they also happened to leave the body together.

[Note: Most manuscripts read *vocatosque fratres ... psallere praecepit*, “and he ordered the brothers he had summoned to sing beforehand.”]

[Note: The first Carnot and Vallicellian manuscripts read *de semetipso*, “about himself,” for the base *per semetipsum*, “by himself.”]


[Col. 0377C]

Nor will I keep silent about what happened to me while I was still a layman and living in my house, which had come to me by paternal inheritance in this city. A certain widow who lived near me was named Galla. She had a young son named Eumorphius. Not far from her lived a certain Stephen, who was an *Optio* in a military unit.


The aforementioned Eumorphius, when he came to the end of his life, called his servant and ordered him:

“Go quickly and tell Stephen the *Optio* to come at once, because, behold, the ship is ready, so that we may be taken to Sicily.”

The boy thought that Eumorphius had lost his mind through illness and was therefore speaking deliriously, and he was entirely unwilling to obey him. But Eumorphius insisted more forcefully:

“Go and report to him what I say, for I am not delirious.”

The boy therefore went out to go to Stephen. When he had reached the middle of the road, someone met him and asked:

“Where are you going?”

The boy replied:

“I have been sent by my master to Stephen the *Optio*.”

The other immediately said to him:

“I am coming from him, but he died at this very hour, before me.”

The boy returned to his master Eumorphius, but found him already dead. Thus, while another man met the boy on the road and the boy returned from the middle of the journey, the distance between them made it possible to infer that both had been called and had died in the same instant.

[Note: Three German manuscripts, the Royal manuscript, two Carnot manuscripts, two Theodorian manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and others read *qui in numero Optio fuit*, “who was an Optio in a military unit.” The Vallicellian manuscript has the surname “Optio.” A third Carnot manuscript reads, “who was in the number of the Optio.” The reading followed here is genuine. An *optio* is one who acts in place of a military commander, as though chosen or adopted by him, or one assigned as an assistant to a centurion. Plautus writes in *Asinaria* 3: “Take Leonidas as your *optio*.” Consult the *Thesaurus Linguae Latinae* of Robert Stephanus and other lexica. Here *in numero* means “in the cohort.” It is used in this sense in Book 8, indiction 1, letter 5—formerly Book 71, indiction 1: “If any of those belonging to the military units hasten to enter monasteries,” and so forth. In the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Roman Empire, section 40, the heading is: “Which units from those mentioned above are maintained in the provinces listed below within Italy: the senior Jovians,” and so on. Optatus of Milevis, Book III, *On the Donatist Schism*, chapter 4, in the new edition: “The harassed soldiers returned to their units.” Ambrosiaster, or the author of the commentary on the letters of Saint Paul, on Ephesians 4: “Although each of these has its own units, and they are legions.” Those who have edited the *Dialogues* up to now, paying no attention to these matters, corrupted this passage. They read: “who was otherwise called Optio.” This is unknown to the manuscripts and changes the meaning. The Greek version, in which the words “being an Optio in a unit” occur, would by itself have sufficed to restore the Latin text.]

**PETER.** What is said is exceedingly terrible. But I ask you: why did a ship appear to the departing soul, or why did the dying man say beforehand that he was to be taken to Sicily?

**GREGORY.** The soul does not need a vehicle. But it is not surprising if, while the man was still in the body, there appeared to him something that he had been accustomed to see bodily, so that through this it might be indicated where his soul could be taken spiritually.

As for his saying that he was to be taken to Sicily, what else can be understood except that, more than in other places, the cauldrons of torment are visible in the islands of that land, where the fire boils up? As those who know them are accustomed to relate, the fire overflows from their openings and increases day by day. As the end of the world approaches, it is therefore clearly shown that, as the fire gathers to itself a greater multitude of those who are to be burned, so the places of torment are seen to open more widely.

[Note: Both Theodorian manuscripts and the Vallicellian manuscript read *apparere*, “to appear,” for the base *aperiri*, “to be opened.”]

Almighty God wished this to be shown for the correction of the living in this world, so that the minds of unbelievers—who do not believe that the torments of hell exist—might see the places of torment whose existence they refuse to believe when they hear of them.

But that the elect and the rejected, whose conduct has been similar, are led to common places, the words of Truth would satisfy us even without examples. For he himself says in the Gospel concerning the elect:

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

If in that eternal blessedness there were no difference in retribution, there would be one dwelling place rather than many. There are therefore many dwelling places, in which the distinct ranks of the good rejoice together because they share in merit, and yet all who labor receive one denarius (Matthew 20:9). They are distinguished by many dwelling places because the blessedness they receive there is one, while the quality of retribution is unequal, according to the different works by which they attain it.

The Truth, announcing the day of judgment, says:

“Then I will say to the reapers: Gather first the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn them” (Matthew 13:30).

The reapers, the angels, bind the weeds into bundles for burning when they join like people with like in similar torments: the proud with the proud, the sexually immoral with the sexually immoral, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the unbelieving with the unbelieving, so that they may burn together. When those who have sinned alike in their offenses are led to similar torments, the angels, assigning them to penal places, bind them as bundles of weeds for burning.

[Note: Two Theodorian manuscripts read *distincte*, “distinctly,” for the base *distincti*, “distinct/distinguished.”]

[Note: Two Audian manuscripts and the Lyrensis, together with both Gemetian manuscripts, read *et ligate ea fasciculos*, “and bind them as bundles,” for the base *et ligate ea in fasciculos*, “and bind them into bundles.” Pratensis reads *et ligate ea fasciculis*, “and bind them in bundles.”]



**PETER.** The explanation has made the reason clear in answer to my question. But I ask: what is the meaning of the fact that some people seem to be taken from the body as though by mistake, return lifeless, and each says that he heard that he was not the person who had been ordered to be taken away?

## Greek recension

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On souls unknown to one another, reciprocal recompense for good and evil, and the deaths of John, Ursus, Eumorphius, and Stephen

[Col. 0375D–0382D]

It often happens that, as the soul departs, it recognizes even those with whom it is destined to be assigned to one dwelling because of equality in faults, and likewise because of corresponding achievements.

The venerable elder Eleutherius, concerning whom I related much in the preceding book, stated that in his monastery he had a biological brother named John, who fourteen days before his death foretold his departure to the brothers. As he counted the passing days, he was seized by fever three days before he was called from the body. When the hour of death came, he received the divine mysteries, the Lord’s body and blood. He summoned the brothers and ordered them to sing psalms before him. Responding to them, he himself supplied the troparion concerning himself, saying:

“Open for me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it.”



While the brothers sang before him, he suddenly raised his voice and cried:

“Ursus, come!”

Having said this, he immediately left the body and completed his mortal life. The brothers were astonished, not knowing what the dying brother had cried out.

After his death, great sorrow arose in the monastery. On the fourth day, however, the brothers had necessary business requiring them to send someone to another monastery situated far away. When they arrived there, they found all the monks in that monastery deeply distressed. They questioned them about why they had buried themselves in such grief, and they replied:

“We lament the desolation of this place. For one brother, whose manner of life held us together here, has today been four days removed from this light.”

The visiting brothers carefully asked what he had been called. They answered:

“Ursus.”

When they investigated the hour of his calling precisely, they found that he had left the body at the very moment when, through John, who had died among them, he had been summoned. From this it is shown that the worth of both in righteousness had been equal. They were therefore granted life together in one dwelling, and it happened that they also left the body together.

Nor will I keep silent about what happened to me while I was still a layman and living in my house, which had come to me by paternal inheritance in this city. A certain widow who lived near me was named Galla. She had a young son named Eumorphius. Not far from her lived a certain Stephen, who was an *Optio* in a military unit.



The aforementioned Eumorphius, having come to his senses as he reached the end of his life, called his servant and ordered him:

“Go quickly and tell Stephen the *Optio* to come at once, because, behold, the ship is ready, so that we may be taken to Sicily.”

The boy thought that Eumorphius had lost his mind through illness and was therefore speaking deliriously, and he was entirely unwilling to obey him. But Eumorphius insisted more forcefully:

“Go and report to him what I say, for I am not delirious.”

The boy therefore went out to go to Stephen. When he had reached the middle of the road, someone met him and asked:

“Where are you going?”

The boy replied:

“I have been sent by my master to Stephen the *Optio*.”

The other immediately said to him:

“I am coming from him, but he died at this very hour, before me.”

The boy returned to his master Eumorphius, but found him already dead. Thus, while another man met the boy on the road and the boy returned from the middle of the journey, the distance between them made it possible to infer that both had been called and had died in the same instant.

**PETER.** What is said is exceedingly terrible. But I ask you: why did a ship appear to the departing soul, or why did the dying man say beforehand that he was to be taken to Sicily?

**GREGORY.** The soul does not need a ship when it leaves the body. But it is not surprising if, while a man is still in the flesh, something he was accustomed to see bodily is shown to him, so that he may understand that the soul can be carried away spiritually.

As for his saying that he was to be taken to Sicily, what else can be understood except that, more than in other places, the tormenting fire is seen bursting forth on the islands of that land? As those who know it relate, the fire overflows from its hollows and grows greater day by day. As the end of the world approaches, it is therefore clearly shown that, as the fire gathers to itself a greater multitude of those who are being burned, so the places of torment are seen to open more widely.

Almighty God wished to show this for the correction of those living in this world, so that he might convince the minds of unbelievers who do not believe that the tribunals of Hades exist. He therefore caused them to see the places of torment which they were unwilling to believe in when they heard of them.

Even if there were no examples, the words of Christ the Truth would assure us that the elect whose practice in goodness has been alike receive the places of rest in common, and that the rejected likewise receive the places of punishment in common. For concerning the elect he says in the Gospel:

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

If in that eternal blessedness there were no difference in retribution, there would be one dwelling place rather than many. There are therefore many dwelling places, in which the distinct ranks of the good rejoice together because they share in merit, and yet all who labor receive one denarius (Matthew 20:9). They are distinguished by many dwelling places because the blessedness they receive there is one, while the quality of retribution is unequal, according to the different works by which they attain it.

The Truth, announcing the day of judgment, says:

“Then I will say to the reapers: Gather first the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn them” (Matthew 13:30).

The reapers, the angels, bind the weeds into bundles for burning when they join like people with like in similar torments: the proud with the proud, the sexually immoral with the sexually immoral, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the unbelieving with the unbelieving, so that they may burn together. When those who have sinned alike in their offenses are led to similar torments, the angels, assigning them to penal places, bind them as bundles of weeds for burning.




**PETER.** The explanation has made the reason clear in answer to my question. But I ask: what is the meaning of the fact that some people seem to be taken from the body as though by mistake, return lifeless, and each says that he heard that he was not the person who had been ordered to be taken away?

[Note: The manuscript reads *ὁ τῷ βίῳ εὐλ...*, “the man reverent in life,” for the base *ὁ τῇ ζωῇ εὐλαβέστατος ἀνήρ*, “the man most reverent in life.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *καθ’ ἑκάστην ἡμ...*, “on each day,” for the base *καθ’ ἡμέραν*, “day by day.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *οἷς ἀντιφωνῶν*, “responding to them”; the printed editions read *ὃς ἀντιφωνῶν*, “who, responding.”]

[Note: The word *τροπάριον*, “troparion,” is common for songs used in the Greek Church and corresponds in some measure to Latin antiphons, as Goar observes on the *Euchologion*, p. 32. Zacharias uses it in that sense here, though it is also often applied to odes and hymns. *Troparia* is derived from *τρέπω*, “I turn” or “I convert”; see Du Cange’s Greek Glossary.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *τὴν πρόσκαιρον ζωὴν τελέσας*, “having completed his temporary life,” for the base *τὴν θνητὴν ζωὴν τελειώσας*, “having completed his mortal life.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *ἀδελφοὺς τεθλ...*, “the brothers grieved...,” for the base *μοναχοὺς τεθλιμμένους πάνυ*, “all the monks deeply distressed.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *κατεβάπτισαν*, “submerged/plunged themselves,” for the base *κατεχθόνισαν*, “buried themselves,” in grief.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *τελειωθέντος ἐκκλήθη*, “he was called through John, who had completed [his life],” for the base *τελευτήσαντος γέγονε κληθείς*, “he came to be called through John, who had died.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *ἐν εὐσεβείᾳ*, “in piety,” for the base *ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ*, “in righteousness.”]

[Note: The manuscript’s cited form is *γενικῷ*, “family/ancestral”; the base text also prints *γενικῷ* in the phrase “family house.”]

[Note: The Greek does not mean precisely the same thing as the Latin designation. In Greek writers *ὀπτίων ἐν νουμέρῳ* refers to an official connected with the distribution of military provisions; Procopius describes the office in the *Secret History* and in *The Vandalic War*, Book I, chapter 17, and Book II, chapter 20.]

[Note: The manuscript reads *ἐβούλετο* for the base *ἠβούλετο*; both mean “was willing,” here negated as “was wholly unwilling.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *ὑπήντησεν* for the base *ἠπήντησεν*; both mean “met.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *βασανιστήρια*, “places of torment,” for the base *κριτήρια*, “tribunals/places of judgment.”]

[Note: The printed editions insert *οἱ πονηροὶ μετὰ τῶν πονηρῶν*, “the wicked with the wicked,” after “the proud with the proud”; this is not to be approved, and the base proceeds with “the sexually immoral with the sexually immoral.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *ἐν τοῖς βασάνοις*, “in the torments,” for the base *τοῖς τῶν βασάνων τόποις*, “to the places of torments.”]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning those who seem to be taken from the body as though by mistake; and concerning the calling and recall of the monk Peter, the death and restoration to life of Stephen, and the vision of a certain soldier

**GREGORY.** When this happens, Peter, if it is properly considered, it is not a mistake but a warning. For heavenly mercy, out of the great abundance of its compassion, arranges that some people, even after departure, suddenly return to the body and fear—at least after seeing them—the torments of hell, which they had not believed when they heard of them.

A certain Illyrian monk who lived with me in the monastery in this city used to tell me that, while he was still living in the desert, he learned the following. A certain monk named Peter, a native of the region of Iberia, had attached himself to him in a place of desolate wilderness called Evasa. [Note: Here Iberia is perhaps Spain, as it was formerly called, and Evasa is the island of Ebusus, now commonly called Ibiza; see the notes to the letter formerly numbered Book IX, letter 61, now Book XI, letter 67.] As the Illyrian monk had learned from Peter’s own account, Peter had died from an illness before he sought the desert. But immediately restored to his body, he testified that he had seen the punishments of hell and innumerable places of flame. He also declared that he had seen certain powerful men of this world suspended in those same flames.

When he had already been led away so that he too might be cast into them, [Note: Most manuscripts read *illo*, “to that place”; some read *illuc*, “thither.”] he said that suddenly an angel of radiant appearance had appeared and prevented him from being plunged into the fire. The angel said to him:

“Go out, and from now on pay the greatest attention to how you must live.”

After this voice, his limbs gradually growing warm, he awoke from the sleep of eternal death and related everything that had happened around him. Thereafter he subjected himself to so many fasts and vigils that, even if his tongue had remained silent, his manner of life would have proclaimed that he had seen and feared the torments of hell. By the wondrous generosity of almighty God, his death had been arranged in such a way that he would not die eternally.

[Note: The Carnot manuscript reads: “But because hardness is exceedingly burdensome to the human heart.”]

Because the human heart is extremely hardened, even the display of punishments is not equally useful to everyone. The illustrious Stephen, whom you know well, used to tell me about himself. He said that, while he was staying in Constantinople on a certain matter, he died when illness overtook him. Since a physician and an embalmer had to be found to open and prepare his body, and they could not be found that day, his body lay unburied through the following night.

[Note: This was a title of honor, which no one was permitted either to confer upon or assume for himself unless the emperor had granted the authority. The formula for conferring the title *illustris vacans* is found in Cassiodorus, Book VI of the *Variae*, chapter 11.]

He said that he was taken to the places of hell and saw many things that he had previously heard of but had not believed. When he was presented before the judge who presided there, he was not received by him, saying:

“I ordered Stephen the smith to be brought, not this man.”

He was immediately returned to his body, while Stephen the smith, who lived nearby, died at that same hour. Thus the truth of the words he had heard was confirmed when what happened concerning the death of Stephen the smith was revealed.

Three years ago, during the plague that devastated this city with the most grievous calamity—and during which, as you know, arrows coming from heaven were visibly seen striking each person individually—the same Stephen died. A certain soldier in this same city of ours was struck by the same plague and reached the point of death.

He was taken out of his body and lay lifeless, but soon returned and related what had happened to him.

[Note: What Gregory records about a soul departing and returning is certainly marvelous. The matter may be illuminated from Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapters 10–12, where he explains his view and offers examples. For the philosophers’ opinions, see what Leonardus Coquaeus and Ludovicus Vives report about Er the Pamphylian and a certain eunuch in their commentary on Book XXII, chapter 28, of Augustine’s *City of God*. In presenting the empty opinions of Plato, Varro, and Porphyry on resurrection, he observes that, taken up and joined together, they resolve the whole question of the eternal resurrection of the flesh. —Gussanville.]

He said—for the event then also became known to many—that there was a bridge, beneath which flowed a black, dark river exhaling an unbearable stench and giving off a mist. Beyond the bridge there were pleasant, green meadows adorned with fragrant flowers and herbs, in which assemblies of men clothed in white seemed to be gathered. The fragrance in that place was so great that the very sweetness of the scent satisfied those walking and dwelling there.

There were individual dwellings, each filled with the greatness of light. A house was being built there for someone of remarkable power; it appeared to be constructed of golden bricks, but it was impossible to discover whose it was.

Along the bank of the aforesaid river there were some dwellings. The rising mist of foulness touched some of them, while the foulness rising from the river did not touch others.

The test on the aforesaid bridge was this: whoever among the unjust wished to cross it slipped into the dark and stinking river; but the righteous, whom guilt did not hinder, reached the pleasant places by a safe and unhindered step.

He also confessed that he had seen Peter, the chief of the ecclesiastical household, who had died four years earlier, placed below, bound and weighed down in the most terrible regions by a great weight of iron. When he asked why this was so, he said that he heard the explanation that we, who knew him in that ecclesiastical household, recall when we consider his deeds. It was said:

“He suffers this because, whenever he was ordered to inflict punishment, he served the infliction of blows more from a desire for cruelty than from obedience.”

No one who knew him is unaware that this was true.

He also said that he saw a certain foreign presbyter who, when he came to the aforesaid bridge, crossed it with as much authority as he had lived with integrity. On the same bridge he recognized the Stephen whom I mentioned earlier. When Stephen wished to cross, his foot slipped, and, already thrown over the bridge from the middle of his body, he began to be pulled downward by the thighs by certain most dreadful men rising from the river, while certain men clothed in white and exceedingly beautiful pulled him upward by the arms.

While this struggle continued, with good spirits pulling him upward and evil ones downward, the one who was seeing these things returned to his body and did not learn what ultimately happened to Stephen.

From this it may be understood concerning Stephen’s life that the evils of the flesh were contending in him with the practice of almsgiving. Since he was pulled downward by the thighs and upward by the arms, it is plainly evident that he had loved almsgiving but had not perfectly resisted the vices of the flesh, which were pulling him downward. Yet what prevailed in him under the examination of the hidden Judge remains unknown both to us and to the one who saw these things and was recalled.

It is nevertheless certain that, after Stephen had seen the places of hell and returned to the body, as I related above, he did not amend his life completely. Many years later he again departed from the body, still facing the contest between life and death.

From this it follows that even when the punishments of hell are displayed, this happens for some as assistance and for others as testimony: the former see the evils they must avoid, while the latter are punished all the more because, although they did not see the punishments of hell, they nevertheless knew of them through certain and indubitable demonstrations and neglected to avoid them.

[Note: Gussanville reads: “the punishments of hell, seen and known.” All the manuscripts and printed editions compelled the restoration of the negative particle *nec* (“not even”). The sense is that people are punished more severely because, although they had not seen the punishments of hell, they nevertheless knew of them through certain and indubitable demonstrations and neglected to avoid them.]

**PETER.** What, I ask you, is the meaning of the fact that in pleasant places a certain house appeared to be built of golden bricks? It would be very ridiculous if we believed that in that life we still needed such metals.

### Greek version

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning souls suddenly snatched away and returned again

**GREGORY.** When this happens, Peter, if it is properly understood, [Note: The manuscript reads *γενομένου*, “when this had happened,” for the base *γινομένου*, “when this happens.”] it is not error but admonition. For God’s compassion, by an extraordinary gift of mercy, arranges this so that many, after departure, return again in the body, in order that they may fear, having seen, the torments of Hades, which they did not believe when they heard of them.

[Note: The phrase means “a certain monk, Illyrian by name,” though Gregory is speaking of the monk’s homeland. Likewise, shortly afterward the Greek translator attributes the name of the solitary place Evasa to the elderly monk.]

A certain Illyrian monk who lived with me in the monastery in this city related to me that, during the period when he was still living in the desert, he learned what he was about to recount. He said that a certain monk named Peter, from the region of Iberia, had attached himself to an old monk named Evasa and lived with him in a remote desert place. From that old monk’s own account he learned that, before he sought the desert, Peter had died when illness overtook him. [Note: The manuscript reads *οἰκῆσαι*, “to dwell [in the desert],” for the base *αἰτήσηται*, “to seek/request [the desert].”] Immediately restored to the body, however, he said that he had seen the torments of Hades and immeasurable places of flame; he also declared that he had seen certain powerful men of this world hanging in the same fire.

When he was being led away to be thrown into that place himself, he said that an angel of flashing appearance suddenly appeared and prevented him from being cast into the fire. The angel said to him:

“Go, and watch carefully how you are to live from now on.”

After this voice, his limbs gradually growing warm, he awoke from the sleep of eternal death and related everything that had happened around him. Thereafter he devoted himself to so many fasts and vigils, because he had seen and feared the torments of Hades, that, even if his tongue had been silent, his manner of life spoke. Thus, by the wondrous providence of God, his death was arranged so that he would not die eternally.

Since the human heart is extremely hardened, perhaps even the display of punishments may turn some people back to repentance. The illustrious Stephen, whom you know well, also related to me what had happened to him: while he was staying in Constantinople on a certain matter, illness overtook him and he died. A physician and an embalmer were sought to open and embalm him, but they could not be found that day. When night came, his body lay unburied.

He said that he was taken to the places of Hades and saw many things which, although he had heard of them previously, he had not believed. When he was presented before the ruler presiding there, he was not received by him, saying: [Note: The manuscript reads *παρ’ αὐτῷ*, “with/before him,” for the base *παρ’ αὐτοῦ*, “by him.”]

“I ordered not this man but Stephen the smith to be brought.”

He was immediately restored to the body, while Stephen the smith, who lived nearby, died at that very hour. Thus the words he had heard were believed to be true when what happened concerning the death of Stephen the smith was shown.

[Note: The manuscript reads *σμυρνίσαι μου*, “to embalm me,” for the base *σμυρνίσαι αὐτόν*, “to embalm him.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads *γινόμενον*, “the event as it was happening,” for the base *γενόμενον*, “what happened,” concerning the death of Stephen the smith.]

[Source ends here, incomplete.]

Source/review notes: Independent Greek and Latin recensions are retained in source order. The printed Greek *ἀπέτυχε* (“failed to obtain”) conflicts with manuscript *ἐπέτυχε* (“obtained”) and the Latin; both readings are preserved explicitly.

Three years ago, then, during the plague that rendered this city uninhabited through the most grievous disaster caused by the pestilence, arrows coming from heaven and striking each person one by one were seen with bodily vision. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscript: “by which you also know of it.” The reading is uncertain.] During that time the aforementioned Stephen also died. [Note: [Col. 0383D] We have already discussed the meaning of this word in Book I, chapter 10, note 7, column 46. See also volume LXXV, *Life of Saint Gregory*, compiled from his writings.]

A certain soldier in this same city of ours, struck by the calamity of that pestilence, died. His lifeless body lay there. But shortly afterward his soul returned to his body; when he came to himself, he related what he had seen, so that this became evident to many. He said as follows:

“There was a bridge, beneath which darkness, blindness, unbearable stench, and mist rising around it were seen. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscript: *ἀνυπόστατος*, ‘unsubstantial’ or ‘insupportable’; the printed text has *ἀνύποιστος*, ‘unbearable.’] A river also flowed underneath it. Before the bridge there were exceedingly beautiful green meadows, adorned with the most fragrant plants and varied flowers. Companies of men clothed in white were seen in them. So great was the fragrance in that place that those who moved about and dwelt there were satisfied by breathing that same fragrance.

“There were various dwellings there, filled with the greatest light, and a house of wondrous beauty was being built there. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscript: ‘a house of wondrous fragrance and beauty’; the phrase is abbreviated in the printed text.] It appeared to be constructed with golden bricks. [Note: [Col. 0383D] Manuscript: *βησάλοις*; both forms are used.] He could not discover whose house it was.

“On the bank of the aforesaid river there were also very many dwellings. From some of them the stench and mist rose and approached; others they could not touch at all. The bridge mentioned above was a place of testing. For whenever one of the unjust wished to cross by it, he was thrown into the dark and exceedingly foul river. [Note: [Col. 0385D] Manuscript: ‘to cross’; the same reading occurs below.] But the righteous, in whom there was no fault, passed over it with an unconcerned and unhindered step and went away to the most fragrant places.

“There he said that he saw Peter, the chief of the ecclesiastical household, who had died four years earlier, hanging head downward in those dreadful places and bound with a great weight of iron. When he asked why Peter was enduring this, he said that he heard the same things that we also know, who knew him in this ecclesiastical house and remember his deeds. [Note: [Col. 0385D] Manuscript: *συμμορίας*, ‘association’ or ‘company,’ rather than the printed reading.] For he had been told that he was enduring this because, whenever he was ordered to inflict blows on someone for a fault, he served his own most savage desire rather than obedience. All who knew him know that this was so.

“There also, he said, he saw a certain foreign presbyter who, when he came to the bridge mentioned above, crossed it with as much confidence as the integrity with which he had lived here. He said that he also recognized Stephen, whom I mentioned earlier, at that same bridge. When Stephen wished to cross, his foot slipped, and from the middle of his body downward he hung outside the bridge. Certain dreadful men rose from the river and dragged him down from the thighs, while other well-clad [Note: [Col. 0386D] Manuscript: *λευχειμονοῦντες*, ‘clothed in white,’ a reading that agrees better with the Latin] and exceedingly handsome men dragged him upward by his arms.

“While this struggle was taking place—the good spirits pulling upward and the evil ones downward—the man who was watching it returned to his own body, and he never learned what finally happened to Stephen.

“From this event concerning Stephen’s life it is possible to understand that the evils of the flesh were contending with the works of mercy. For while he was being dragged downward by the thighs but upward by the arms, it became very clear that he loved almsgiving, but had not completely resisted the passions of the flesh, by which he was dragged downward. [Note: [Col. 0386D] The manuscript reads: ‘he did not resist completely through the things by which they dragged him downward.’]

“Thus, by God’s hidden judgment, it was made known what had prevailed in him. For both we and the man who saw these things and returned remain unaware of what happened to him. [Note: [Col. 0386D] The printed form *συνεκροτοῦσαν* may perhaps be *συνεκρότησαν*, ‘they contended together,’ or the third-person plural imperfect *συνεκρότουν*. Compare the Septuagint, Psalm 5:9, where *ἐδολιοῦσαν* occurs for *ἐδολίουν*, from *δολιόω*.]

“It is shown concerning this same Stephen, as I related above, that even after seeing the places of Hades and returning to his body, he did not completely reform his life. After a long time, he departed from the body amid the struggle between life and death. Hence this event makes clear that the punishments of Hades, when displayed, become for some a means of security, but for others a cause of greater condemnation: those who see the evils may become afraid, while others are condemned more severely because, even after seeing and learning of the punishments of Hades, they did not reform themselves. [Note: [Col. 0386D] Manuscript: ‘to greater condemnation.’]”

## 435 — PETER

What does this mean, I ask you, that in pleasant and most fragrant places a house was seen being built for someone with golden bricks? [Note: [Col. 0387D] Manuscript: *βήσαλα*, ‘bricks.’] It seems very foolish to me if we believe that in that other life we again need such mines.

### GREGORY

Who in his right mind would understand it in that way? From what was shown there, it is plainly possible to understand what kind of work is being performed here by the person whose dwelling was being built in that manner. Since the gift of eternal light is obtained through the distribution of alms, it is wonderfully shown that such a person builds his dwelling with gold. What I omitted above and failed to mention should not be passed over in silence. [Note: [Col. 0387D] The following two words, omitted in the printed editions, have been restored.] The soldier who had seen these things said that the same golden bricks [Note: [Col. 0387D] Manuscript: *βήσαλα*] were carried for the construction of the house by old men and young men, girls and boys. From this it is inferred that those who had received acts of mercy here were seen to be the workers there.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] The Vulgate Greek wrongly prints singular *ἀνιστάμενον*, “rising,” where the grammatical context requires the plural.]

## Latin version — Chapter XXXVII  
### What the construction of a house in pleasant places means; concerning Deusdedit, whose house was seen to be built on the Sabbath; and concerning the punishment of the Sodomites

A certain religious man named Deusdedit lived here near us. He used to make shoes. [Note: [Col. 0388D] He is listed in the *Roman Martyrology* on 10 August.] Another person saw by revelation that his house was being built, but its builders were seen to work only on the Sabbath. Investigating that man’s life carefully afterward, he discovered that from whatever he earned each day, anything left over after food and clothing he regularly brought on the Sabbath to the Church of blessed Peter and distributed to the needy. From this consider that it was not without reason that the construction of his house increased on the Sabbath.

### GREGORY

Who, if he has sound understanding, would interpret this literally? From what was shown there, it is plainly made known what the person is doing here for whom that dwelling is being built. For whoever obtains the reward of eternal light through generosity in almsgiving is plainly building his dwelling with gold. The same soldier who had seen these things related what I omitted above: that the same golden bricks for the building of the house were carried by old men and young men, girls and boys. From this it is gathered that those toward whom mercy had been shown here were themselves seen to be the workers there.

### PETER

I see that I have been properly informed concerning this matter. But I ask: what are we to say about the fact that the mist and stench touched some dwellings, while they could not touch others? And what are we to say about the river and the bridge that he saw? [Note: [Col. 0388D] This is the reading required by the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts, although the printed editions read: “What does it mean that someone saw the bridge and the river?”]

### GREGORY

From the images of events, Peter, we weigh the merits of the matters involved. He saw the righteous cross by the bridge and go away to pleasant places, because “narrow indeed is the way that leads to life” (Matthew 7:14). He saw the foul river flowing beneath it, because here the rottenness of vices drags the minds of carnal people downward every day. [Note: [Col. 0388D] Several Norman manuscripts read “this rottenness.”]

The fact that the stench and mist touched some dwellings but could not touch others means that many people perform good works, yet the desire for carnal passions still touches their minds. It is entirely just that the mist of stench should enter there, where the stench of the flesh still gives pleasure here.

Thus blessed Job, seeing that the pleasure of the flesh is stench, pronounced judgment upon the lustful and sexually slippery, saying: “Their sweetness is worms” (Job 24:20). [Note: [Col. 0389D] Two Theodorian manuscripts, the Vallicellian manuscript, two Gemetian manuscripts, and others read: “The sweetness of him is a worm.” The Greek text supports this reading.] Those who have completely cleansed their hearts from every carnal pleasure clearly show that the mist and stench do not touch their dwellings at all.

Allegorically, the mist and stench should be understood as carnal pleasure. When it takes hold of someone’s mind, it clouds and darkens it, so that the splendor of the true light cannot be seen. From the place where a person delights in sensual pleasure below, he suffers blindness concerning the things above.

### PETER

Can this be proved from the testimony of Scripture: that the faults of carnal people are likened to the punishment of stench?

[Note: [Col. 0388D] At the explanation of the house, Germanus reads *nam quoniam*, “for since.”]

[Note: [Col. 0388D] In the investigation of Deusdedit's life, Vallicellianus reads *inveni*, “I found.”]

[Note: [Col. 0389D] At the scriptural proof about stench, Germanus, two Gemetensis, and other Norman manuscripts read *putamus*, “we think”; the edition prefers the reading agreeing with the Greek.]

## Greek version — Chapter XXXVIII
### Concerning Deusdedit the shoemaker

[Col. 0387B–0390A; pp. 438–439]

A most devout man named Deusdedit lived near us. His trade was shoemaking. Someone saw by revelation that a house was being built for him, but its builders worked only on the Sabbath. The observer investigated his life carefully and found that, from each day's earnings, Deusdedit customarily carried whatever remained after food and clothing to the church of the blessed apostle Peter on the Sabbath and distributed it to the needy. Thus the building of his house increased on the Sabbath for good reason.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] Greek *τζαγγάριος* means a maker of shoes, more precisely high boots covering feet and legs, from *τζάγγαι*. Cangius discusses these in his Greek Glossary. The manuscript has the broken reading *τέχνη … σκυτοτομικὴ. περί*, “trade … leather-cutting/shoemaking. Concerning …”.]

**PETER.** I see that I have been properly instructed. But what does it mean that mist and stench touched some dwellings but could not touch others, and what do the river and bridge mean?

[Note: [Col. 0387D] The manuscript has the broken variant *λέγωμεν … τῶν οἰκοδομημάτων τῶν μὲν ἡ ὁμί…*, “what shall we say … of the buildings, of some the mist …”.]

**GREGORY.** From the images, Peter, we weigh the realities. He saw the righteous cross the bridge and reach pleasant places because the road to life is exceedingly narrow.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] For “cross,” the manuscript reads *περᾶσαι*, “to cross.”]

The foul river ran beneath it because the corruption of passions drags the mind of carnal people downward each day. Mist and stench touched some dwellings but not others because many do good works while desire for fleshly passions still touches their minds. The mist of stench justly enters there for those whom the stench of flesh still charms here.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] The manuscript reads *θέλγει*, “charms, delights.”]

Thus blessed Job, seeing fleshly pleasure as stench, says of the sexually immoral and unstable: “Their sweetness is a worm.” Those who wholly cleanse their hearts from fleshly pleasure have dwellings untouched by mist and stench. Allegorically these mean fleshly pleasure: when it possesses reason, it clouds and darkens it against the true light. From the quarter in which one delights below, one suffers dimness concerning things above.

**PETER.** Can Scripture prove that carnal faults are likened to punishment by stench?


## Greek version — Chapter XXXIX  
### Concerning the judgment of the Sodomites

### GREGORY

It can. For we have heard the Book of Genesis bearing witness that the Lord rained fire and brimstone upon the Sodomites (Genesis 19:24), so that the fire might burn them up and the stench of the brimstone might kill them. [Note: [Col. 0389D] The Gemetian manuscript reads “sulfur.”] Since they had been inflamed by an unlawful desire for corruptible flesh, they perished alike through burning and stench, so that in their punishment they might know that they had surrendered themselves to eternal death through the stench of their sensual pleasure.

### PETER

Concerning these matters about which I was fearful, I confess that no further inquiry remains in me.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] At the scriptural testimony, the manuscript reads *τῆς βίβλου τῆς γεννέσεως*, “of the Book of Genesis.”]

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Where fire and brimstone are rained upon the Sodomites, the manuscript reads *ἐπὶ τούς*, “upon the …”.]

## Latin version — Chapter XXXVIII  
### That souls still residing in the body sometimes see something punitive from the spiritual realm; concerning the boy Theodore; concerning the death of Chrysaorius and of a certain monk of Iconium

### GREGORY

It must also be known that sometimes souls still residing in their bodies see something punitive from the spiritual realm: some for their own edification, others for the edification of those who hear.

I remember having already related publicly in my Homilies [Note: [Col. 0389D] Two Carnotian manuscripts read “in the Homilies before the people.”] the story of a very restless boy named Theodore. He followed his brother into my monastery more from necessity than from willingness. [Note: [Col. 0390D] The first Carnotian and the second Theodorian manuscripts add “to whom it was very burdensome.”] It was exceedingly burdensome to him if anyone said anything to him for the sake of his salvation. He could neither do good things nor even hear them. He constantly declared by swearing, becoming angry, and mocking that he would never adopt the habit of holy conduct.

During the plague that recently consumed a large part of the people of this city, he was struck in the groin and brought to the point of death. When he was breathing his last, the brothers gathered so that by praying they might protect him as he departed. His body was already dead throughout its extremities; only in his chest did a little vital warmth remain.

The brothers all began to pray for him with greater earnestness, the more quickly they saw him approaching departure. Suddenly, in the presence of the brothers, he began to shout and interrupt their prayers with loud cries, saying:

“Go away, go away! Behold, I have been given to a dragon to be devoured, but because of your presence he cannot devour me. He has already swallowed my head in his mouth. Give way, so that he may not torment me any longer but may do what he is going to do. If I have been given to him to be devoured, why do I suffer delay because of you?” [Note: [Col. 0392D] The first Theodorian manuscript reads “because of the dragon.”]

Then the brothers began to say to him: “What are you saying, brother? Make the sign of the holy cross upon yourself.”

He replied with great cries: “I want to make the sign, but I cannot, because I am pressed down by the scales of this dragon.”

When the brothers heard this, they fell prostrate on the ground with tears and began to pray more fervently for his deliverance. Immediately the sick man began to shout loudly, saying:

“Thanks be to God! Behold, the dragon that had taken me to devour me has fled. Driven away by your prayers, it could not remain here. Now pray for my sins, for I am ready to turn back and abandon worldly life completely.” [Note: [Col. 0392D] The word “healed” is absent from the German, Norman, and Carnotian manuscripts.]

Thus the man who, as has been said, was already dead throughout the extremities of his body was preserved for life and turned to God with all his heart. After his mind had changed and he had long been disciplined by scourges, his soul was finally released from the flesh.

But Chrysaorius, as his relative Probus—whom I mentioned earlier (Book II, chapter 12)—was accustomed to relate, was a man of great standing in this world, but as full of vices as of possessions. [Note: [Col. 0392D] Both Theodorian manuscripts and the Vallicellian manuscript read “very rich.”] He was swollen with pride, subject to the pleasures of his flesh, and inflamed by the fires of greed in acquiring possessions.

When the Lord determined to put an end to so many of his evils, he allowed him to be struck by bodily illness. When he came to his final hour, at the very moment when he was about to depart from the body, he saw with open eyes dreadful and exceedingly black spirits standing before him and violently pressing upon him in order to drag him to the gates of Hades. [Note: [Col. 0392D] Gregory frequently uses this word for “press upon” or “urge,” especially in his letters. Virgil likewise uses *urgere* in *Georgics* I.443 in the sense of “threaten” or “press upon,” as noted in the index of Schrevelius’s 1666 edition.] 

He began to tremble, grow pale, and sweat, asking in a loud voice for a reprieve. He called for his son Maximus, whom I have since seen as a monk, crying out in extreme and confused agitation:

“Maximus, hurry! I have never done you any harm. Receive me on the security of your faith.”

Maximus, disturbed, immediately arrived in mourning and shouting, and the whole household gathered. But they could not see the evil spirits that were pressing heavily upon him; they perceived their presence through the confusion, pallor, and trembling of the man who was being dragged away. [Note: [Col. 0392D] The German and Norman manuscripts read “that I might drag him away.”]

Because of fear of their dreadful appearance, he turned this way and that on his bed. He was lying on his left side but could not endure seeing them; he turned toward the wall, and there they were also present. When, being held fast, he despaired of ever being released, he began to shout loudly:

“A reprieve, at least until morning! A reprieve, at least until morning!”

While he was saying this, he was torn from the dwelling of his flesh. It is therefore clear that he saw these things for our sake, not for his own, so that his vision might benefit us, whom divine patience still awaits with long-suffering. For what benefit did it bring him to see the dreadful spirits before his death and ask for a reprieve, when he did not receive the reprieve he requested?

There is also now among us a presbyter named Athanasius from Isauria, who relates that a terrifying event occurred in Iconium. [Note: [Col. 0393D] Several manuscripts, together with the Greek translation, read “of Lycaonia.” The Norman manuscripts mentioned above have “of Lyconia”; in the Prat manuscript neither “of Iconium” nor “of Lyconia” is found.] There, he says, is a monastery called “of the Galatians,” [Note: [Col. 0393D] That is, the monastery of the Galatians.] in which a certain monk was held in great esteem. He was seen to have good morals and to be well ordered in all his conduct; but, as the end revealed, he was very different from what he appeared.

For although he presented himself as fasting with the brothers, he was accustomed to eat secretly, and the brothers knew nothing at all of this vice. When bodily illness came upon him, he was brought to the end of his life. As he approached his final moment, he had all the brothers present in the monastery summoned to him.

They expected to hear something great and desirable from such a man, as they supposed, who was dying. But he, distressed and trembling, was compelled to reveal to them to what enemy he had been handed over and by whom he was being forced to depart. He said:

“When you believed that I was fasting with you, I was secretly eating. And now, behold, I have been handed over to a dragon to be devoured. It has bound my knees and feet with its tail; then, putting its head inside my mouth, it draws out my spirit by sucking it away.”

After these words he immediately died. He was not granted time to remain alive so that, by repenting, he might be delivered from the dragon he had seen. It is clear that he saw this solely for the benefit of those who heard, since he made known the enemy to whom he had been handed over but did not escape from him. [Note: [Col. 0393D–0394D] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read “so that he might free himself.” Whether that expression can properly be used here we do not investigate; Scripture clearly recognizes Christ alone as the liberator of humankind.]

### PETER

I should like to be taught whether we ought to believe that purifying fire exists after death.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] The specified Norman witnesses read “of Lyconia”; Pratensis has neither “of Iconium” nor “of Lyconia.” This witness detail remains separate from the preceding Lycaonia note.]

## Greek version — Chapter XL  
### Concerning souls that, while still in the body, see something of judgment; and concerning Theodore the boy, Chrysaorius’s death, and a certain Isaurian monk

### GREGORY

It is clear that souls still residing in their bodies often see some punishment from the spirits of wickedness: some for their own edification, others for the edification of those who hear.

There was a certain Theodore, a very disorderly boy, concerning whom I remember having spoken publicly in my homilies. In my monastery he followed his brother more from compulsion than from willingness. Since he was exceedingly disobedient, if anyone said anything good to him for the sake of his salvation, he was unwilling not only to do it but even to hear it. He never tolerated coming into the form of holy conduct; instead, by swearing, becoming angry, and mocking, he passed his life in this way.

During the plague that has recently carried off the greater part of the people of this city, he too was struck in the thigh and carried toward death. When he reached his final breath, all the brothers gathered so that by praying for him they might be able to entreat God for mercy at his departure. His body was already dead in every part, and only a little vital warmth remained in his chest.

All the brothers prayed for him with such persistence as they saw him hastening eagerly toward departure. Suddenly he began to cry out in a very loud voice and interrupt the prayers of the brothers standing around him, saying:

“Depart from me! Behold, I have been given to the dragon for food, but because of your presence it cannot eat me. It has already swallowed my head in its mouth. Give way, so that it may not judge me any longer. But what it has to do, it will do quickly. If I have been given to it for food, why do I endure delay?”

Then the brothers began to say to him: “What are you saying, brother? Make upon yourself the sign of the honorable and life-giving cross.”

He answered with the greatest cry: “I want to make the sign of the cross, but I cannot, for I am weighed down by the saliva of this dragon.”

When the brothers heard this, they lay upon the ground and began to pray with tears more fervently for his deliverance. Immediately the sick man began to cry out in a loud voice:

“Thanks be to God! Behold, the dragon that had taken me for food has fled. It was driven away by your prayers and could not remain here. Now pray for my sins, for I am ready to turn back and abandon worldly life completely.”

This man, who, as has been said, was dead throughout every part of his body but was being preserved for life, afterward turned to God with all his heart. His mind was changed by being sufficiently worn down by the scourge, and thus his soul was released from the flesh.

On the other hand, Probus, whom I mentioned earlier and who was closely acquainted with him, related that a certain man named Chrysaorius was extremely distinguished in this world, but was burdened with as many passions as he possessed wealth. He was puffed up with pride, subjected to the desires of his flesh, and eagerly striving to heap up wealth while variously contending with greed. When the Lord was pleased to bring an end to so many of his evils, he allowed him to fall into bodily illness.

When he had reached his final hour and the moment approached when his soul was to depart from the body, he saw, with his eyes open, dreadful and shadowy spirits standing before him and violently pressing him, so that they might carry him away to the locks of Hades.

He began to tremble, grow pale, and be drenched in sweat, shouting loudly and asking for a reprieve. Calling his son Maximus with an intense and confused cry, he said:

“Maximus, run! I have never done you any harm. Receive me in your faith.”

Maximus, greatly disturbed and weeping, came immediately. With him came the entire household. But they could not see the evil spirits that were violently pressing upon him. They inferred their presence from his confession, pallor, and trembling.

Because of fear of their dark appearance, he turned this way and that. Lying on the left side of his bed, he could not bear their sight; when he turned toward the wall, he saw them present there also. Finally, despairing of being released and being constricted by anguish, he began to cry out loudly:

“A reprieve even until morning! A reprieve even until morning!”

While saying this, he was released from the bonds of the body. It is plainly shown that he saw these things not for his own sake but for ours, so that we might make progress through the sight of him—us, whom divine patience patiently awaits. For what did it benefit him to see the dreadful spirits before his death and ask for a reprieve, when he did not receive the reprieve he requested?

There is also now among us a presbyter named Athanasius, from the region of Lycaonia and the city of Iconium, who related that a terrifying event had occurred there. He said that there was a monastery called “of the Galatians.” In it a certain monk was thought by everyone to possess the greatest discipline and reverence. But, as the event revealed at the end, he was far from what he appeared to be.

He displayed himself as fasting with the brothers, but secretly was accustomed to eat, a fact the brothers did not know at all. When bodily illness came upon him, he was carried to the final stage of life. Realizing that he was approaching the end, he had all the brothers in the monastery gathered.

They expected to hear something great and desirable from such a man, as they supposed, at the moment of his death. But he, mourning and trembling, and being pressed to depart from the body, was forced to disclose to what enemy he had been handed over. He said:

“When you believed that I was fasting with you, I was secretly eating apart from you. And now, behold, I have been handed over for food to the dragon. It has bound my feet and knees with its tail; then, putting its head inside my mouth, it draws out my spirit by sucking it away.”

After he had said these things, he died immediately. He was not permitted to remain so that he might be delivered through repentance from the dragon he had seen. This clearly shows that he saw it solely for the benefit of us who hear: he revealed the enemy to whom he had been handed over but was unable to escape from him.

### PETER

I ask to be taught whether one must believe that purifying fire exists after death.
