## Latin version — Chapter XXXIX  
### Whether there is purifying fire after death

### GREGORY

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Walk while you have the light” (John 12:35). Through the Prophet he also says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). The apostle Paul, explaining this, says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2). [Note: [Col. 0396D] One manuscript reads “acceptable.”]

Solomon also says: “Whatever your hand can do, do with all your strength, for there is neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in Hades, where you are going” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). David likewise says: “For his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 117).

From these statements it is plainly established that as each person departs from this life, so he is presented at the judgment. Nevertheless, it must be believed that before the judgment there is purifying fire for certain lighter faults, because the Truth says that if anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:31).

This statement makes it understood that certain faults can be forgiven in this age and certain others in the age to come. For what is denied concerning one fault, it follows that it may be understood as granted concerning others. Yet, as I said, this must be believed possible only concerning the smallest and lightest sins: such as habitual idle speech, immoderate laughter, or negligence in the management of one’s household affairs—faults from which even those who know how they ought to avoid sin scarcely remain free—or an error arising from ignorance in matters that are not serious. [Note: [Col. 0396D] The phrase “of the matter” is absent from Gratian, distinction 25.]

All these things, if they have not been forgiven in those who are still living in this life, weigh upon them even after death. For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation, he adds:

“If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest; for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he built upon it remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:12–15).

Although this may be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life, nevertheless, if anyone takes it to mean the fire of future purification, it must be carefully considered that Paul said that the person who builds wood, hay, and straw upon this foundation can be saved through fire—not the one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon it, that is, greater and harder sins which then cannot be dissolved, but wood, hay, and straw, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire can easily consume.

Yet this must be known: even there, no one will obtain purification from the smallest sins unless, while still living in this life, he has earned it through good deeds, so that he may obtain it there.

## Greek version — Chapter XLI  
### An inquiry whether purifying fire exists after death

### GREGORY

The Lord says in the Gospel: “Go while you have the light.” Through the Prophet he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The apostle Paul, interpreting this, says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.”

Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do with all your strength. For neither work, nor knowledge, nor wisdom exists in Hades, where you are going.” David also says: “For his mercy endures forever.”

From all these testimonies it is plainly shown that as each person departs from the things here below, so he will appear at the judgment. Nevertheless, one must believe that there is purifying fire before the judgment for certain lighter faults. For the Truth has said that if anyone blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, he will not be forgiven either in the present age or in the age to come.

From this judgment it is possible to understand that some faults can be forgiven in this world and others in the world to come. For what must be denied concerning one thing can accordingly be understood as granted concerning others. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads: “it is possible to understand; nevertheless, as I said.”]

Nevertheless, as I said, this must be believed possible only concerning the smallest sins: idle speech, disorderly laughter, or negligence in household care, together with the failure to recognize such faults and to understand how they ought to be distinguished. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads “how they ought.”] Because of the error of ignorance, all these may not seem serious, but after death they are found to be serious if someone has left them unforgiven while still living in this life.

Paul says that Christ is the foundation, and adds: “Whoever builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, and straw—the fire itself will test what sort of work each person’s is. If anyone’s work that he built remains, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire.” [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads: “what sort of work it is; the fire will test it.”]

This may be understood of the fire of tribulation proposed in this present life. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads “of the fire of tribulation.”] Nevertheless, if someone also takes it concerning the fire of future purification, [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads “of the judgment to come.”] it must be understood soberly that Paul said that the person who can be saved through fire is not the one who builds iron, bronze, or lead upon this foundation—that is, great, hard sins that then cannot be dissolved—but wood, hay, and straw, that is, light and very small sins, which the fire easily consumes.

Let this be known: even concerning light and very small sins, no one easily obtains purification there unless, while still living in this life, he cleanses himself through good works so that he may be deemed worthy to attain it there. [Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript reads “cleanses himself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0395D] In interpreting Paul’s fire, the manuscript reads *νοηθῆναι δύναται πλὴν ἐὰν τις*, “it can be understood; nevertheless, if someone …”.]

## Latin version — Chapter XL  
### Concerning the soul of Paschasius the deacon

When I was still young and living in the condition of a layman, I heard from certain distinguished and knowledgeable men that a deacon named Paschasius, belonging to this apostolic see, whose very orthodox and luminous books on the Holy Spirit are preserved among us, was a man of extraordinary holiness. He devoted himself especially to works of almsgiving, cared for the poor, and despised himself. [Note: [Col. 0396D] On Paschasius, see Bollandus, volume VII of the May *Acta Sanctorum*, page 438. His two books on the Holy Spirit against Macedonius are included in various libraries of the Fathers. Casimirus Oudin attributes them in the supplement to his *Bibliotheca* to Faustus of Rhegium; Guillelmus Cave disputes this in his *Historia litteraria*, sixth century.]

In the dispute that arose among the faithful, through zeal for the faith, concerning the election of Symmachus and Laurentius, [Note: [Col. 0397D] Symmachus was elected in the year 498, not by unanimous consent, since many favored Laurentius, the archdeacon, including Paschasius. On this schism, see Baronius under the relevant year.] he chose Laurentius as the one who should be advanced to the pontifical office. But when all the others agreed and Symmachus was ordained, he, having been defeated, persisted in his own judgment until the day of his death, loving and preferring the man whom the Church had rejected from being advanced as its bishop.

It happened that this same Paschasius died during the time of Symmachus, bishop of the apostolic see. At his funeral, his dalmatic having been placed upon the bier, a demon-possessed man touched it and was immediately healed. [Note: [Col. 0397D] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions add “and was immediately healed.”]

A long time afterward, the physicians ordered Germanus, bishop of Capua, whom I mentioned above (Book II, chapter 35, and Book IV, chapter 7), to bathe for the sake of his bodily health at the hot baths called Angulan baths. [Note: [Col. 0397D] *Angulan* or *Angulus* was a city of the Vestini, now called Città di Sant’Angelo in Abruzzo, between Adria and the Aternus, according to Pliny.] When he entered those baths, he found the aforementioned deacon Paschasius standing there and serving among the hot waters.

When Germanus saw him, he was greatly afraid and asked what so great a man was doing there. Paschasius replied:

“I have been assigned to this place of punishment for no other reason than that I agreed with Laurentius and took a position against Symmachus. But I ask you to entreat the Lord for me. You will know that you have been heard if, when you return here, you do not find me.”

The man of God, Germanus, devoted himself to prayer for him. After a few days he returned, but he did not find Paschasius in the same place. Since he had sinned not through malice but through an error of ignorance, he was able to be purified from his sin. It must nevertheless be believed that he obtained this through the abundance of his almsgiving, so that he was able to merit forgiveness at the time when he could no longer perform any work.

### PETER

What does this mean, I ask you, that in these last times so many things concerning souls are being revealed which were previously hidden, so that the future age seems to be bringing itself upon us and opening itself to us through open revelations and manifestations?

## Greek version — Chapter XLII
### Concerning the soul of Paschasius the deacon

[Col. 0395D–0398C; p. 446]

While I was still passing through youth and living as a layman, I heard eminent and knowledgeable men relate that Paschasius, a deacon of this apostolic see—whose orthodox and luminous books on the Holy Spirit remain among us—was wonderfully holy, devoted to almsgiving and care of the poor.

[Note: [Col. 0395D] The manuscript varies the opening with *ἔτι μου … ἄγοντος … ὑπάρχοντος*, “while I was still … passing [my youth] … and existing [in the lay condition].”]

In the dispute arising among the people through zeal for the faith over Symmachus and Laurentius, he chose Laurentius as the one who should rather be advanced as patriarch. When all agreed and Symmachus was ordained, Paschasius, though defeated, persisted in his judgment until death, loving and preferring the man whom the Church had rejected as her bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] The manuscript has the awkward expansion *Λαυρ. τίς ἆρα προβῆναι πατριάρχης Λαυρέντιον ἐπελέξατο*, “Laur… which man then should advance as patriarch, he chose Laurentius.”]

Paschasius died under Symmachus. At his funeral a possessed man touched the dalmatic placed on the bier and was immediately healed. Long afterward physicians ordered Germanus, bishop of Capua, to bathe for his health at the baths of Anglanum. He found Paschasius standing and serving in their heat. Germanus was afraid and asked what so great a man was doing there.

Paschasius answered: “I was assigned to this place of judgment only because I assented to Laurentius's party against Symmachus. Implore the Lord for me. You will know that you were heard if, on returning, you do not find me.”

[Note: [Col. 0398D] The manuscript has the broken reading *δι’ ὧν εἰς*, “because of the things through which, into …”.]

[Note: [Col. 0398D] Printed editions read *δυσώπιστον*; the contextual text is *δυσώπησον*, “implore, beseech.”]

Germanus applied himself to prayer. After a few days he returned and did not find Paschasius. Since Paschasius sinned through ignorant error rather than malice, he could be purified. One must believe that through his almsgiving he obtained this and was judged worthy of forgiveness when he could no longer work.

[Note: [Col. 0398D] The printed Greek reads *τούτου ἀπέτυχε*, “he failed to obtain this,” contradicting the sentence. The manuscript separately reads *τούτου ἐπέτυχε*, “he obtained this.” Both readings are retained; the manuscript supplies the coherent main sense.]

**PETER.** Why in these last times are so many formerly hidden things about souls revealed? Is it so that through manifest revelations we may behold the coming world displaying itself to us?


## Latin version — Chapter XLI  
### Why so many things concerning souls are revealed in the last times

### GREGORY

It is so. As the present age draws nearer to its end, the future age is already touched by its very nearness and is disclosed by more evident signs. Since in this present age we do not see one another’s thoughts at all, but in the future age we see all our thoughts in one another’s hearts, what should I call this age except night, and what should I call the age to come except day?

Just as, when night is ending and day begins to dawn, darkness is in some way mixed with light before the rising of the sun, until the remnants of the departing night are completely transformed into the light of the succeeding day, so the end of this world is now mingled with the beginning of the future age, and the darkness that remains from it already shines through a certain mingling with spiritual realities.

Thus we already perceive many things belonging to that world, but we do not yet know them perfectly, because we see them as if in a kind of twilight of the mind, like things seen before sunrise.

### PETER

I approve what you say. But concerning such a man as Paschasius, this question troubles me: after death he was led to a place of punishment, yet the garment from his bier was able to drive an evil spirit from a possessed man.

### GREGORY

In this event the great and manifold dispensation of almighty God must be recognized. By his judgment it happened that Paschasius himself received inwardly, for a certain time, what he had sinned, while before human eyes he nevertheless performed marvelous deeds after death through his body—the same man who, before death, had performed pious works known to those who saw them.

Thus neither were those who had seen his good deeds deceived concerning the value of his almsgiving, nor was the fault left unpunished which he had not believed to be a fault and therefore had not extinguished with tears.

### PETER

I understand what you say. Nevertheless, constrained by this explanation, I am now forced to fear not only the sins of which I am aware in myself but also those of which I am unaware. Since a little earlier the discussion concerned the punitive places of Hades, I ask you: where should we believe Hades to be—above this earth or beneath it?

[Note: [Col. 0398D] At the future age's approach, Pratensis and Beccensis read *ipso jam appropinquante*, “with it itself now approaching”; the first Gemetensis has *ipsa jam quasi propinquante*, “with it now, as it were, approaching.”]

[Note: [Col. 0400D] On Paschasius's garment, two Carnot manuscripts, Vallicellianus, and the first Theodorus support the printed construction; Carnot says it “drove away evil spirits.” Germanus, the second Theodorus, and Norman witnesses read that “the garment could be touched and the evil spirit driven away.”]

## Greek version — Chapter XLIII  
### An inquiry why so many things concerning souls are revealed in the last times

### GREGORY

It is as you have supposed. The nearer the end of the present world approaches, the more the presence of the world to come is recognized through manifest signs. In the present world we do not see one another’s thoughts at all, but in the world to come we see all our things in one another’s hearts. What shall I call this world except night? And what shall I call the world to come except day?

For just as night reaches its end and day begins to shine, while before sunrise darkness is in a certain way mingled with light until the remnant of night has passed and the light of the following day has returned completely, so the end of the present world, now mingled with the dawning of the world to come, causes certain things from its darkness to shine through their mingling with spiritual realities.

Consequently, we now understand many things belonging to that world, but we do not yet know everything perfectly. Rather, as if in a certain brightness of the mind, we see these things like things visible before the sun.

### PETER

I am pleased by what you say. But concerning this man Paschasius, my question is stirred by the fact that after death he was taken to a place of judgment, while his garment, lying upon the bier, immediately healed the man held by an evil spirit when he touched it.

### GREGORY

In this matter the nature of the almighty God’s dispensation is recognized with great clarity. By God’s judgment it happened that Paschasius himself received inwardly, for a short time, what he had sinned, while God nevertheless willed that miracles should be performed before human eyes through his body after death. Before his death, people had known him to perform works of piety.

Thus those who had seen his good deeds would not be scandalized concerning his almsgiving, nor would his fault be left without punishment—a fault that he did not believe to be a fault and therefore did not extinguish with tears.

### PETER

I consider what you say. Therefore, restrained by this defense, I am compelled to fear not only the sins I recognize within myself but also those of which I am ignorant. Since a little earlier there was discussion of the punitive places of Hades, I ask where we must believe Hades exists: above this earth or beneath it?

[Note: [Col. 0399D] The manuscript reads *μήποτε τὸ πταῖσμα*, “lest perhaps the fault …”.]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] For Peter's being forced to fear unknown sins, the manuscript reads *δειλιᾶσαι*, “to be afraid.”]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] For the discussion of punitive places, the manuscript reads *λόγος κεκίνηται*, “a discussion has been raised.”]

[Note: [Col. 0399D] In Peter's question, the manuscript reads *ὑπάρχειν ὑποληπτέον ἐπάνω*, “must it be supposed to exist above …”.]

## Latin version — Chapter XLII  
### Where Hades is to be believed to be
Source preparation: Parallel Latin and Greek recensions are both retained; textual variants preserve their supplied forms with English glosses.

## Latin recension — continuation of the preceding chapter

**GREGORY.** Concerning this question I dare not pronounce anything with certainty. For many have thought that Hades exists in some region of the earth; others, however, have supposed that it is beneath the earth. Yet this thought presses upon the mind: if we say that Hades lies below because it is situated beneath, then, since the earth is beneath heaven, Hades ought reasonably to be understood as beneath the earth. Hence the Psalmist also says: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest Hades” (Psalm 85:13). Thus the upper Hades may be understood as the earth, and the lowest Hades as what lies beneath the earth. John too, in all likelihood, agrees with this expression. He says that he saw a book sealed with seven seals, and that no one was found worthy, either in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth, to open the book and loose its seals; and he adds: “And I wept greatly” (Revelation 5:4).

[Latin apparatus, Col. 0400D: The German and Norman manuscripts read *superior terra*, “the upper Hades is the earth”; two Chartres manuscripts read *credatur* (“let it be believed”).]

Yet afterward he says that this book was opened by the Lion from the tribe of Judah. What else does the book signify except divine Scripture, which our Redeemer alone opened? For he became man, died, rose again, and was taken up, and opened all the mysteries hidden within it. No one in heaven—that is, no angel—was found worthy; no one on earth—that is, no human being living in the body; nor anyone beneath the earth—that is, no soul departed from the body—could open for us the mysteries of sacred Scripture apart from the Lord. Since, therefore, it is said that no one beneath the earth was found worthy to open the book, I see nothing that prevents us from believing that Hades exists beneath the earth.

[Latin apparatus, Col. 0401D: Gembloux and other Norman manuscripts read *in ea*, “in it,” referring to sacred Scripture.]

**PETER.** I ask you: must we believe that the fire of Gehenna is one, or should we judge that, as there are as many differences among sins, so also there are as many punishments of fire prepared?

## Greek recension — Chapter XLIV

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΜΔʹ. Question where Hades is to be believed to be.**

**GREGORY.** Concerning this question I dare not pronounce anything with certainty. For many have thought that Hades exists in some region of the earth; others, however, have supposed that it is beneath the earth. Yet this thought presses upon the mind: if we say that Hades lies below because it is situated beneath, then, since the earth is beneath heaven, Hades ought reasonably to be understood as beneath the earth. Hence the Psalmist also says: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest Hades” (Psalm 85:13). Thus the upper Hades may be understood as the earth, and the lowest Hades as what lies beneath the earth. John too, in all likelihood, agrees with this expression. He says that he saw a book sealed with seven seals, and that no one was found worthy, either in heaven, on earth, or beneath the earth, to open the book and loose its seals; and he adds: “And I wept greatly” (Revelation 5:4).

[Apparatus, Cols. 0399D–0400D: A manuscript reads λέγωμεν ὑποκάτω (*legōmen hypokatō*, “let us say that it lies beneath”). The German and Norman manuscripts read *superior terra*, “the upper Hades is the earth”; two Chartres manuscripts read *credatur* (“let it be believed”). The Greek manuscript expands the Psalm reference as τὸ ὑπὸ καὶ τοῦ ψαλμωδοῦ λέγεσθαι ὅτι τὸ ἔλεός σου μέγα ἐπ’ ἐμὲ καὶ ἐῤῥύσω τὴν ψυχήν (*to hypo kai tou psalmōdou legesthai …*, “and the Psalmist says, ‘Your mercy is great toward me, and you delivered my soul’”). It further reads ὥστε ἀνώτερος ἡ γῆ, ᾅδης δὲ κατώτατος ὁ ὑπὸ τὴν γῆν, καὶ Ἰωάννης… (*hōste anōteros hē gē, hadēs de katōtatos ho hypo tēn gēn, kai Iōannēs…*): “so that the earth is the upper Hades and the lowest Hades is beneath the earth; and John too agrees with this expression.”]

Yet afterward he says that this book was opened by the Lion from the tribe of Judah. What else does the book signify except divine Scripture, which our Redeemer alone opened? For he became man, died, rose again, and was taken up, and opened all the mysteries hidden within it. No one in heaven—that is, no angel—was found worthy; no one on earth—that is, no human being living in the body; nor anyone beneath the earth—that is, no soul departed from the body—could open for us the mysteries of sacred Scripture apart from the Lord. Since, therefore, it is said that no one beneath the earth was found worthy to open the book, I see nothing that prevents us from believing that Hades exists beneath the earth.

[Apparatus: Gembloux and other Norman manuscripts read *in ea*, “in it,” referring to sacred Scripture. The Greek manuscript reads μόνος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν (*monos ho Theos hēmōn*, “our God alone”). The printed Greek has the erroneous ὑπερκάτω (*hyperkatō*, “above-below”); the editors restore ὑποκάτω (*hypokatō*, “beneath”) from Revelation and the Regius manuscript.]

**PETER.** I ask you: must we believe that the fire of Gehenna is one, or should we judge that, as there are as many differences among sins, so also there are as many punishments of fire prepared?

## CHAPTER XLIII. Whether There Is One Fire of Gehenna or Several

**GREGORY.** There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in the same way. Each person feels there as much punishment as his guilt requires. For just as in this world many stand beneath one sun, yet do not all feel the heat of that same sun equally—one being more heated, another less—so there, in one fire, the mode of burning is not the same for all. For what the diversity of bodies does here, the diversity of sins does there: they have a fire that is not different, yet it burns each of them differently. [Note: The first Chartres manuscript has: “there he will feel as much punishment.” The other two Chartres manuscripts have: “there punishment will be felt as much.”] [Note: The earlier Chartres manuscript has: “because it heats some more,” and so forth.] [Note: A manuscript reads: “is burned.”]

**PETER.** I ask you: are we to say that those who have once been plunged into that fire will burn forever?

### Greek recension — Chapter XLV

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΜΕʹ. Question whether the fire of Gehenna is one or another (the source prints δώρημα, ‘gift,’ as an acknowledged error).**

**PETER.** I ask you: must we believe that the fire of Gehenna is one, or should we judge that, as there are as many differences among sins, so also there are as many punishments of fire prepared?

**GREGORY.** There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in the same way. Each person feels there as much punishment as his guilt requires. For just as in this world many stand beneath one sun, yet do not all feel the heat of that same sun equally—one being more heated, another less—so there, in one fire, the mode of burning is not the same for all. For what the diversity of bodies does here, the diversity of sins does there: they have a fire that is not different, yet it burns each of them differently.

**PETER.** I ask you: are we to say that those who have once been plunged into that fire will burn forever?

[Greek apparatus, Cols. 0401D–0402D: The manuscript reads λέγειν οὐδείς (*legein oudeis*, “no one [is able] to say”) at the transition into Gregory’s answer. At the description of punishment it reads καίεται (*kaietai*, “is burned”).]

## CHAPTER XLIV. Whether Those Assigned to the Fires of Gehenna Burn Forever

**PETER.** I ask to learn whether we must believe that those once thrown into that fire are burned continually.

**GREGORY.** This is firmly established and entirely true. For just as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there will be no end to the torment of the wicked. Truth itself has said: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). It is therefore evident that what God promised is true, and that what he threatened will in no way prove false. [Note: [Col. 0402D] The Norman manuscripts and some others read the genitives *gaudii … tormenti* (“of joy … of torment”), yielding “there is no end of the joy of the good, nor of the torment of the wicked.”] [Note: [Col. 0402D] Gembloux reads *ibunt ii in supplicium* (“those will go into punishment”) at Matthew 25:46.]

**PETER.** What if someone says that God threatened sinners with eternal punishment for this reason: to restrain them from committing sins?

**GREGORY.** If what he threatened was false, in order to correct those who sin from injustice, then what he promised would also be false, in order to summon them to righteousness. But who, even if insane, would dare say this? And if he threatened what he did not intend to fulfill, then, while wishing to call him merciful, we are forced to proclaim him deceitful—which it is impious to say. [Note: A manuscript has: “what he promised to the righteous, so that …”]

**PETER.** I wish to know how it is just that a fault committed within a finite period should be punished without end.

**GREGORY.** You would rightly say this if the strict Judge examined not the hearts of human beings but their deeds alone. The wicked sinned within a finite period because they lived within a finite period. For they would certainly have wished, if they could, to live forever, so that they might sin forever (On Penance, Distinction 1, chapter 60). They show that they desire always to live in sin, since, while they live, they never cease to sin. It therefore belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those should never lack punishment who in this life never wished to lack sin. [Note: A manuscript has: “they would have wished, if it had been possible.”]

**PETER.** Yet no just person feeds upon cruelty, and a delinquent servant is ordered to be beaten by a just master so that he may be corrected from wickedness; he is beaten so that he may be reformed. But if the wicked, handed over to the fires of Gehenna, do not attain correction, for what end will they burn forever? [Note: The first Audley and Laon manuscripts add: “by which they will burn forever.”]

**GREGORY.** Almighty God, because he is compassionate, does not feed upon the torment of the wretched; but because he is just, he is never sated by vengeance upon the wicked. All the wicked assigned to eternal punishment are punished for their own iniquity. Yet they will burn for a purpose: so that all the righteous may see in God the joys they receive, and in those others may behold the punishments they escaped. Thus they will recognize themselves as debtors to divine grace forever, all the more because they see forever the evils being punished which they overcame through God’s assistance.

**PETER.** Then where is their holiness, if they will not pray for their enemies whom they will then see burning, although it was said to them: “Pray for your enemies” (Matthew 5:44)?

**GREGORY.** They pray for their enemies during the time when they are able to turn their enemies’ hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for on behalf of enemies except what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance for the knowledge of the truth, and that they may recover from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Timothy 2:25)? How, then, will they pray for them at that time, when they can no longer in any way be turned from works of iniquity toward righteousness?

The same reason therefore explains why prayer is not then offered for people condemned to eternal fire as explains why prayer is not now offered for the devil and his angels, who have been assigned to eternal punishment. The reason why holy men do not now pray for unbelieving and ungodly people who have died is likewise that, knowing them to have been assigned to eternal punishment, they shrink from having the merit of their prayer nullified before the sight of the just Judge. [Note: The second and third Chartres manuscripts, with the Norman manuscripts, have: “for those whom they already know to have been assigned to eternal punishment.” The first Chartres manuscript has: “since they already know that those assigned to eternal punishment …,” followed by the continuation “they shrink from this.”]

If the righteous who are now living do not at all sympathize with the unjust who have died, although they themselves still know that they must endure some suffering in the flesh, how much more strictly will they regard the torments of the wicked then, when, freed from every fault of corruption, they will cling more closely and firmly to righteousness? For their minds will be so absorbed by their adherence to the most just Judge that they will have no desire whatsoever for anything that diverges from the exactness of his eternal rule. [Note: A manuscript has: “because of the reasoning.”] [Note: A manuscript has: “does not agree.”]

**PETER.** There is nothing more that I can answer, since the explanation has been made clear. But this question now troubles my mind: how can the soul be called immortal when, as is evident, it dies in perpetual fire? [Note: A manuscript has: “nothing remains that can be answered.”]

In the explanation of prayer it reads τῆς ἁμαρτίας (*tēs hamartias*, “of sin”), καὶ ἀσεβῶν τελευτησάντων (*kai asebōn teleutēsantōn*, “and of impious persons who have died”), and τοῦ δικαίου κριτοῦ (*tou dikaiou kritou*, “of the just Judge”). In the closing exchange it reads διὰ τὸν λογισμόν (*dia ton logismon*, “because of the reasoning”), συνᾴδῃ (*synadē*, “agrees”), and δύναται (*dynatai*, “can”).]

[Latin apparatus, Cols. 0402D–0405D: Gembloux reads “they will go into punishment.” Audley I and Laon add “by which they will burn forever.” Other witnesses read “be converted … be saved” and “captives” in the prayer-for-enemies argument. Beccensis reads “is tormented in fire.” The Chartres and Norman witnesses preserve the precise variants concerning those already known to be assigned to eternal punishment.]

## CHAPTER XLV. How the Soul Is Called Immortal, If It Is Established That It Is Punished by the Sentence of Death

**GREGORY.** Since life is spoken of in two ways, death must also be understood in two ways. One thing is the life we have in God; another is the life we have in that by which we have been formed and created—that is, one thing is living blessedly, and another is existing essentially. The soul, therefore, is understood to be both mortal and immortal. It is mortal because it loses blessed life; but it is immortal because it never ceases to exist spiritually, and cannot lose the life of its nature, not even when it has been condemned to perpetual death. For there it loses blessedness, but it does not lose existence. From this it follows that it must suffer death without death, decline without cessation, and an end without end, so that its death is immortal, its decline without cessation, and its end without limit. [Note: Most Norman manuscripts have: “likewise, it loses blessedness.”] [Note: Two Theodorean manuscripts, the second Gembloux manuscript, and other Norman manuscripts have: “it loses being blessed”; the Chartres manuscript has: “it loses blessedness.” The earlier manuscripts are supported by the Regius Greek version.] [Note: The Beccensis manuscript has: “it follows.”]

**PETER.** Who, when approaching the end of life, would not fear such an inexorable sentence of condemnation, whatever his deeds may have been, when, although he now knows what he has done, he still does not know how subtly his deeds will be judged?

### Greek recension — Chapter XLVII

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΜΖʹ. Question how the soul, called immortal, is subjected to the sentence of death.**

**GREGORY.** Since life is spoken of in two ways, death must also be understood in two ways. One thing is the life we have in God; another is the life we have in that by which we have been formed and created—that is, one thing is living blessedly, and another is existing essentially. The soul, therefore, is understood to be both mortal and immortal. It is mortal because it loses blessed life; but it is immortal because it never ceases to exist spiritually, and cannot lose the life of its nature, not even when it has been condemned to perpetual death. For there it loses blessedness, but it does not lose existence. From this it follows that it must suffer death without death, decline without cessation, and an end without end, so that its death is immortal, its decline without cessation, and its end without limit.

**PETER.** Who, when approaching the end of life, would not fear such an inexorable sentence of condemnation, whatever his deeds may have been, when, although he now knows what he has done, he still does not know how subtly his deeds will be judged?

[Greek apparatus, Col. 0406D: The manuscript reads μακαρίως εἶναι (*makariōs einai*, “to exist blessedly”) where the Latin witnesses distinguish blessed life or blessedness. It also reads ἐπιγνώσεται (*epignōsetai*, “will recognize”) in Peter’s closing question.]

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning a Certain Holy Man Who Was Afraid When He Came to Die

**GREGORY.** It is as you say, Peter. Yet often fear alone purifies the departing souls of the righteous from lesser faults, as you have frequently heard me relate concerning a certain holy man. When he came to die, he was greatly afraid; but after his death he appeared to his disciples in a white robe and revealed how splendidly he had been received.

### Greek recension — Chapter XLVIII

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΜΗʹ. Concerning a certain holy man who feared death.**

**GREGORY.** It is as you say, Peter. Yet often fear alone purifies the departing souls of the righteous from lesser faults, as you have frequently heard me relate concerning a certain holy man. When he came to die, he was greatly afraid; but after his death he appeared to his disciples in a white robe and revealed how splendidly he had been received.

[Greek apparatus, Col. 0406D: The manuscript reads τινος ἁγίου ἀνδρός (*tinos hagiou andros*, “of a certain holy man”).]

## CHAPTER XLVII. How Some Are Strengthened by Revelation So That They Do Not Fear Death; and Concerning the Monks Anthony, Merulus, and John

[Note: Very many have written about oneiromancy—fools, foolish things. J. Launoy, Parisian theologian, in his book entitled *On the Vision of Simon Stock*, chapter 7, where he demolishes a vision of this sort, reports eight judgments concerning dreams that are not to be despised. Read the ruling issued by the Faculty of Theology of Paris on 24 January 1534, which is one of those eight; you will read it with profit. Gussanville.]

Sometimes, however, almighty God strengthens the minds of those who are trembling by means of prior revelations, so that they are not at all afraid at death. For a certain brother named Anthony lived with me in the monastery. With many daily tears he longed for the joys of his heavenly homeland. When he meditated upon the sacred writings with the greatest diligence and fervor of desire, he sought in them not words of knowledge but tears of compunction, so that his mind, stirred by these things, might burn more ardently and, abandoning what is lowest, fly through contemplation to the realm of the heavenly homeland.

By a nocturnal vision he was told: “Be ready, and, because the Lord has commanded it, depart.” [Note: Thus the German, Theodorean, Vallicellian, Norman, and other manuscripts read; the printed editions omit *and* and read: “because the Lord commanded you to depart.”] When he said that he did not have the provisions necessary for departure, he immediately heard this reply: “If the matter concerns your sins, they have been forgiven.” After hearing this once, he still remained in great fear and trembling; and on another night he was again addressed in the same words. Then, after five days, he was seized by fever and departed while all the brothers were praying and weeping.

Another brother in the same monastery was named Merulus. He was devoted with great fervor to tears and prayers; psalmody almost never ceased from his mouth, except when he was taking nourishment for his body or giving his limbs over to sleep. [Note: The printed editions, contrary to the evidence of our manuscripts, read “and almsgiving.” A monk who possessed nothing would more appropriately be described as devoted to prayers than to almsgiving.] In a nocturnal vision he saw a crown of white flowers descending from heaven upon his head. Soon afterward he was seized by bodily illness and died with great peace of mind and cheerfulness. Fourteen years later, Peter, who now presides over the same monastery, wished to prepare a burial place [Note: Bigot reads: “who presides over this monastery,” namely the monastery of Saint Andrew.] for himself near the tomb in which Merulus had been buried. As he worked there, he says, such a fragrant sweetness rose from the tomb that it seemed as though the scent of every kind of flower had been gathered there. From this it was plainly evident how true was what Merulus had seen in the nocturnal vision. [Note: The manuscript has: “while he was laboring there.”]

In the same monastery there was another man named John, a young man of excellent character, [Note: The Roman Martyrology treats of him and of two other holy monks on 17 January.] who surpassed his years in understanding, humility, sweetness, and gravity. [Note: Thus the first German manuscript, supported by the Theodorean, Vallicellian, and Norman manuscripts. The second German manuscript reads “who went beyond his age”; the third, “who surpassed his age”; the Regius, “who exceeded his age.” John the Deacon, in Book I, chapter 20 of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, has the same reading, “who surpassed his age.” A similar expression occurs at the beginning of Book II of the *Dialogues*, in the Prologue, “surpassing his age in character,” and in Homily 14 on the Gospels, no. 5: “the boys who here surpassed their years in character.” The editors did not attend to these passages and, disregarding the manuscripts, used *transigebat* instead of *transibat*.] [Note: A manuscript has: “and the labor of asceticism.”]

When he fell ill and was brought to the point of death, an old man appeared to him in a nocturnal vision. Holding a staff, he touched him with it and said: “Rise. You will not die immediately from this illness; but be ready, because you will not remain here for a long time.” [Note: A manuscript has: “since you have no long time to spend here.”] When he had already been given up by the physicians, he was suddenly healed and recovered. He related what he had seen and, as I said, devoted himself to God’s service for two years beyond the measure of his age. [Note: A manuscript has: “so that he surpassed the contest of his age”; both readings are used, including for age, as Cangius demonstrates in his *Greek Glossary*.]

Three years before this, another brother had died and been buried by us in the cemetery of the same monastery. As we were all leaving the cemetery, John himself was found there, as he later related, pale and trembling. He was called from the tomb by the brother who had died. The end that followed immediately afterward made the meaning of this clear: ten days later, seized by fever, he was released from the bonds of the body.

**PETER.** I wish to be taught whether what is shown through nocturnal visions ought to be observed.

### Greek recension — Chapter XLIX

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΜΘʹ. How some are strengthened by revelation not to fear death, and concerning the monks Anthony and Merulus.**

[Greek apparatus, Cols. 0406D–0409D: Anthony is described as διάγων (*diagōn*, “dwelling/living”) in the monastery. His mind is said to be ἀποκειμένης (*apokeimenēs*, “laid up/stored away”); his tears are a κλαυθμὸν κατανύξεως (*klauthmon katanyxeōs*, “weeping of compunction”); and his ascent is τῇ ἐπουρανίου πατρίδος θεωρίᾳ (*tē epouraniou patridos theōria*, “in contemplation of the heavenly homeland”). The manuscript says he δειλίᾳ γέγονεν (*deilia gegonen*, “became afraid”). Of Merulus it reads ἐξέλειπε (*exeleipe*, “ceased”), ἀσθενείᾳ (*astheneia*, “illness”), and ποιῆσαι θελήσας κάμνοντος (*poiēsai thelēsas kamnontos*, “wishing to do [this] while he was ill”). Of John it reads καὶ πόνῳ ἀσκήσεως (*kai ponō askēseōs*, “and labor of asceticism”), τὴν κείραν (*tēn keiran*; the editors note that both expressions are used of age), and ἐπειδὴ χρόνον (*epeidē chronon*, “because [you have] time”). Peter’s question has ὀφείλῃ (*opheilē*, “ought”).]

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Whether Dreams Should Be Observed, and How Many Kinds of Dreams There Are

**GREGORY.** On this point, Peter, we must understand that dream-images affect the mind in six ways. Sometimes dreams are produced by the fullness or emptiness of the stomach; sometimes by deception; sometimes by thought together with deception; sometimes by revelation; and sometimes by thought together with revelation. We all know the first two that I mentioned through experience; the other four we find in the pages of Holy Scripture. [Note: The printed editions have “the first two things,” against the manuscripts.] [Note: The manuscript reads: “they arise”; it continues, “sometimes by revelation, and again sometimes by thoughts together with revelation, and the …”]

For if dreams were not often produced through deception by the hidden enemy, the wise man would never have indicated this when he said: “For dreams have caused many to err, and they have perished who hoped in them” (Ecclesiasticus 34:7). Or again: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Leviticus 19:26). These words plainly show the detestation in which such dreams are held, since they are joined with divinations. [Note: The Greek manuscript perhaps has διαμαρτυρίας (*diamartyrias*, “by testimony”) as one word in place of the transmitted reading.] [Note: The manuscript reads “a certain wise man”; by this title Gregory denotes the author of Ecclesiastes, as has already been observed in Book XXVII of the *Morals*, no. 53.]

Again, if dreams did not sometimes arise from thought together with deception, the wise man would not have said: “Many cares follow dreams” (Ecclesiastes 3:15). [Note: Taius, Book IV, chapter 7, attributes this saying to Solomon.]

And if dreams did not sometimes arise from the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen in a dream that he was to be preferred to his brothers (Genesis 37), nor would the angel have warned Mary’s betrothed in a dream to take the child and flee into Egypt. [Note: The manuscript has: “the angel addressed him, saying, ‘Take the child and flee into Egypt.’”]

Likewise, if dreams did not sometimes arise from thought together with revelation, the prophet Daniel, explaining Nebuchadnezzar’s vision, would not have begun from the root of thought, saying: “You, O king, began to think upon your bed what would happen after these things, and he who reveals mysteries showed you what was to come” (Daniel 2:20). A little later he says: “You saw, and behold, an image stood before you, and that image was great and lofty,” and the rest of the dream (Daniel 2:31ff.). By reverently presenting the dream and what was to be fulfilled, and by making clear from what thought it arose, Daniel plainly shows that it is often generated from thought together with revelation. [Note: Lyra and the first Audley manuscript have: “what is revealed.”]

Since dreams therefore vary among so many kinds of causes, they should be believed with proportionately greater difficulty, since it is not easily apparent from what impulse they come. Holy men, however, distinguish between deceptions and revelations, discerning the very voices or images of visions by a certain inward perception, so that they know what they receive from the good spirit and what they suffer from deception. For if the mind is not vigilant concerning such things, the deceiving spirit immerses it in many vanities; it often foretells very many true things so that at last it may ensnare the soul through some falsehood. [Note: The Beccensis manuscript has: “they perceive.”] [Note: The Pratel manuscript adds: “as we shall be able to relate.”]

### Greek recension — Chapter L

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. Νʹ. Whether dreams should be observed and from what causes they arise.**

Sometimes dreams are produced by the fullness or emptiness of the stomach; sometimes by deception; sometimes by thought together with deception; sometimes by revelation; and sometimes by thought together with revelation. We all know the first two that I mentioned through experience; the other four we find in the pages of Holy Scripture.

For if dreams were not often produced through deception by the hidden enemy, the wise man would never have indicated this when he said: “For dreams have caused many to err, and they have perished who hoped in them” (Ecclesiasticus 34:7). Or again: “You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams” (Leviticus 19:26). These words plainly show the detestation in which such dreams are held, since they are joined with divinations.

Again, if dreams did not sometimes arise from thought together with deception, the wise man would not have said: “Many cares follow dreams” (Ecclesiastes 3:15).

And if dreams did not sometimes arise from the mystery of revelation, Joseph would not have seen in a dream that he was to be preferred to his brothers (Genesis 37), nor would the angel have warned Mary’s betrothed in a dream to take the child and flee into Egypt.

By reverently presenting the dream and what was to be fulfilled, and by making clear from what thought it arose, Daniel plainly shows that it is often generated from thought together with revelation.

Since dreams therefore vary among so many kinds of causes, they should be believed with proportionately greater difficulty, since it is not easily apparent from what impulse they come. Holy men, however, distinguish between deceptions and revelations, discerning the very voices or images of visions by a certain inward perception, so that they know what they receive from the good spirit and what they suffer from deception. [Greek apparatus, Cols. 0409D–0411D: The manuscript’s list reads γένωντο· ποτὲ δὲ δι’ ἀποκαλύψεως, ποτὲ δὲ πάλιν διὰ τῶν λογισμῶν ὁμοῦ καὶ ἀποκαλ… καὶ τὰ μέν (*genōnto; pote de di’ apokalypseōs, pote de palin dia tōn logismōn homou kai apokal… kai ta men*): “they arise; sometimes by revelation, and again sometimes by thoughts together with revelation, and the …”. It reads εὑρίσκονται (*heuriskontai*, “are found”); οὐκ ἄν τις ἀνὴρ σοφός (*ouk an tis anēr sophos*, “a certain wise man would not …”); πεποιήκασι (*pepoiēkasi*, “have done”); and possibly διαμαρτυρίας (*diamartyrias*, “by testimony”) as one word. At the angelic warning it reads ἐχρημάτισε λέγων, παράλαβε τὸ παιδίον καὶ φεῦγε εἰς Αἴγυπτον (*echrēmatise legōn, paralabe to paidion kai pheuge eis Aigypton*, “he addressed him, saying, ‘Take the child and flee into Egypt’”). The closing cautions read οὐκ ὀφείλει (*ouk opheilei*, “ought not”), παναγάθου (*panagathou*, “all-good”), πλανῶντος (*planōntos*, “deceiving”), and ἐν πολλαῖς ἀπάταις αὐτὸν τὸ παραδ… (*en pollais apatais auton to parad…*, “to surrender him into many deceits …”).]

[Editorial note, Col. 0410D: By “a certain wise man” Gregory means the author of Ecclesiastes, as noted in *Morals* XXVII.53.]

## CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning a Certain Man to Whom Long Years of Life Were Promised in a Dream but Were Cut Short by Death in a Short Time

As recently happened to a certain one of our own: because he paid close attention to dreams, long years of this life were promised to him in a dream. After he had gathered much money as provision for a longer life, he died so suddenly that he left everything untouched and carried nothing of good work away with him.

### Greek recension — Chapter LI

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΝΑʹ. Concerning the man deceived by a dream.**

As recently happened to a certain one of our own: because he paid close attention to dreams, long years of this life were promised to him in a dream. After he had gathered much money as provision for a longer life, he died so suddenly that he left everything untouched and carried nothing of good work away with him.

[Greek apparatus, Col. 0411D: The manuscript reads συνάξας αἰφνίδιον τῷ θανάτῳ ὑπήχθη· σῶα καὶ ἄπτωτα τὰ πάντα καταλείψας μηδὲν ἐξ ἔργου ἀγαθοῦ μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ κομισάμενος (*synaxas aiphnidion tō thanatō hypēchthē …*): “after gathering [the money], he was suddenly subjected to death, leaving everything whole and untouched and carrying with him nothing from any good work.”]

## CHAPTER L. Whether It Benefits Souls If the Bodies of the Dead Are Buried in a Church

[Note: Saint Paulinus once proposed the same question, wishing to learn from Augustine whether it benefits anyone after death for his body to be buried near the memorial of a saint. The holy Doctor answered him in his work *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*. Saint Augustine explains the reason and purpose for which the bodies of the faithful are buried in Book I of *The City of God*, chapter 13, and in *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapters 2, 3, 7, 8, and 9. In chapter 12 of the same book of *The City of God*, and in *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapters 4, 5, and 6, he also explains how a Christian loses nothing when tyrants forbid burial, and how care for the dead benefits them. See Augustine teaching this in the *Enchiridion*, chapters 109 and 110; *On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*, chapter 1; and the second of the Eight Questions of Dulcitius. In our own times, anyone can be buried in churches if money is paid; without payment, not even the good may be buried. Let Saint Gregory be read, Book I of the Letters, letter 12. [Note: Gussanville erred in assigning that letter: it contains no discussion of burial. Rather, Books VIII—formerly VII—letter 3, and IX, letter 3, should be read.]]

**PETER.** I remember who that man was; but I ask you, let us complete what we began. Do we think that it benefits souls if the bodies of the dead are buried in churches?

**GREGORY.** If grave sins do not weigh them down, burial in a church benefits the dead in this respect: whenever their relatives come together in those sacred places, they remember their own whose tombs they see and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But when grave sins weigh them down, their bodies are placed in churches not so much for absolution as for a greater accumulation of condemnation. We can demonstrate this more clearly if we briefly relate what occurred in our own days.

### Greek recension — Chapter LII

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΝΒʹ. Whether the souls of those buried in churches receive benefit.**

]
