But when grave sins weigh them down, their bodies are placed in churches not so much for absolution as for a greater accumulation of condemnation. We can demonstrate this more clearly if we briefly relate what occurred in our own days.

[Greek apparatus, Col. 0411D: Peter’s request reads ἠρξάμεθα (*ērxametha*, “we began”), which the editor marks as the true reading, and ἐπιγίνεσθαι νομ… ἐὰν τῶν… (*epiginesthai nom… ean tōn…*, “we think benefit accrues … if the [bodies] …”). Gregory’s answer reads θεωροῦντες (*theōrountes*, “seeing”), τίθενται· τοῦτο δὲ τρανῶς ἀποδεῖξαι δυνάμεθα (*tithentai; touto de tranōs apodeixai dynametha*, “they are placed; and this we can demonstrate clearly”), and ἐν ὀλίγῳ διηγησώμεθα (*en oligō diēgēsōmetha*, “let us relate it briefly”).]

## CHAPTER LI. Concerning a Certain Nun Buried in the Church of Saint Lawrence, Who Appeared Half-Burned

A man of venerable life, Felix, bishop of Portus, was born and raised in the province of Sabina. [Note: On Felix and the city of Portus, see Letter 25 of Book IX and Letter 46 of Book XII.] [Note: The Sabine people are Italians, enclosed by the rivers Anio, Tiber, Nar, and Velinus. The ancient Sabines are celebrated by Virgil in Book VII of the *Aeneid*: “Behold Clausus, leading a great host from the ancient blood of the Sabines”; and in Book II of the *Georgics*: “The ancient Sabines once cultivated this way of life.”]

He testified that a certain nun had lived in the same place. She had practiced continence of the flesh, but she did not refrain from a forward tongue and foolish speech.

After she died, she was buried in the church. That same night, the guardian of the church saw in a revelation that she had been brought before the sacred altar and cut in two through the middle: one part of her was consumed by fire, while the other part remained untouched. When he arose in the morning and related this to those present, wishing to show them the place where she had been consumed by fire, they found before the altar the place where the burning of the flame had appeared upon the marble, as though that woman had actually been burned there by corporeal fire. From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot, after death, obtain help from sacred places to escape judgment. [Note: The manuscript has: “It is plainly shown that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot obtain help from sacred places after death to escape judgment.”]

### Greek recension — Chapter LIII

**ΚΕΦΑΛ. ΝΓʹ. Concerning the nun buried in Saint Lawrence’s church, half of whose body was found burned.**

A man of venerable life, Felix, bishop of Portus, was born and raised in the province of Sabina.

He testified that a certain nun had lived in the same place. She had practiced continence of the flesh, but she did not refrain from a forward tongue and foolish speech.

After she died, she was buried in the church. That same night, the guardian of the church saw in a revelation that she had been brought before the sacred altar and cut in two through the middle: one part of her was consumed by fire, while the other part remained untouched. When he arose in the morning and related this to those present, wishing to show them the place where she had been consumed by fire, they found before the altar the place where the burning of the flame had appeared upon the marble, as though that woman had actually been burned there by corporeal fire. From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot, after death, obtain help from sacred places to escape judgment.

[Greek apparatus, Cols. 0411D–0414D: The manuscript begins ὁ τῷ βίῳ … Φιλὴξ ὁ τῆς πόλεως ἐκ τῆς χώρας Σαβ… γέγονε· μοναστρίαν δέ τινα ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ χώρᾳ ὑπάρχειν ἔλεγεν ἥτις… (*ho tō biō … Philēx …*): “Felix, venerable in life, became bishop of the city from the Sabine region; he said that a certain nun lived in that same region who …”. It later reads τοῖς συνοῦσιν αὐτῷ διηγήσατο καὶ τὸν τόπον δὲ αὐτοῖς ὑπέδειξεν ἐν ᾧ ἡ αὐτὴ μονάστρια τῷ πυρὶ κατεκάη· ἐλθόντες γὰρ ἔμπροσθεν τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου, εὗρον… (*tois synousin …*): “he related it to those with him and showed them the place where the nun was burned; coming before the altar, they found …”. Its conclusion reads φανερῶς δείκνυται ὧν αἱ ἁμαρτίαι συγκεχωρημέναι οὐκ εἰσὶ πρὸς τὸ ἐκφυγεῖν τὴν κρίσιν (*phanerōs deiknytai …*): “it is plainly shown that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot obtain help from sacred places after death to escape judgment.”]

## CHAPTER LII. Concerning the Burial of the Patrician Valerian
Joannes too, a very distinguished man who held the office of prefects’ deputy in this city [Note: [Col. 0413D] That is, the deputy of the prefects. See Gregory, Book II, Letter 32. In the Panormitan section he preserves: “It is sufficient for me to have chosen you as guardian of your place.” And below: “Appoint guardians of your place,” etc. “Give orders to your guardians of the place,” that is, those fulfilling your functions. Thus in Suidas: τοποτηρητής, “guardian of a place,” a kind of dignity. See Henri Estienne’s Greek Thesaurus. Accordingly, the sense of this passage does not seem to have been rendered perfectly by these words of the recent French version: “Who exercises the office of prefect in this city,” when it ought rather to have said: “Who is the prefects’ deputy or lieutenant in this city.”], whose integrity and truthfulness we know, testified to me that the patrician Valerian had died in the city called Brixa [Note: [Col. 0414D] The German, Theodulfian, and Norman manuscripts have this reading. Brixia is a well-known episcopal city under the archbishop of Milan and subject to the Venetians. It is also read as Brixa in the Greek translator.]. The bishop of that same city, having accepted payment, provided a place in the church where he was to be buried.

This Valerian, however, remained frivolous and slippery right into extreme old age and refused to put an end to his depraved behavior. On the very night on which he was buried, the blessed martyr Faustinus, in whose church his body had been buried, appeared to the church’s custodian and said:

“Go and tell the bishop to throw out from here these stinking remains that he has placed here; if he does not do so, he himself will die on the thirtieth day.”

The custodian was afraid to report this vision to the bishop and, when warned again, evaded doing so. On the thirtieth day, however, the bishop of that city, having returned to bed in good health and sound condition at evening, died a sudden and unexpected death.

# CHAPTER LIV

## Concerning the burial of the patrician Valerian

[Col. 0414B]

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LIV. Concerning the burial of the patrician Valerian

John, the most distinguished man who had become prefect in this city, a man of what truthfulness he was, we all know. He therefore related to me that the patrician Valerian, having come to the city called Brixa, happened to die there. The bishop of that same city, having received money from his people, provided a place in the church in which he was to be buried [Note: [Col. 0414D] Manuscript: “in which his body was destined to be buried.”]

This same patrician Valerian lived very slipperily until extreme old age [Note: [Col. 0414D] Manuscript: “He lived in a very depraved manner.”], unwilling to impose a bridle upon his disorders. On the same night on which his body was buried in the church, the blessed martyr Faustinus, whose church it was, appeared to its custodian [Col. 0414C] and said:

“Go and tell the bishop to throw outside the stinking flesh which he placed here; for, if he does not do this, he will die on the thirtieth day.”

When the custodian saw this vision, he was afraid to report it to the bishop. After being similarly warned a second time, he declined to tell him. On the thirtieth day the same bishop, being in good health and, toward evening, having reclined upon his bed, died by a sudden and unknown death.

# CHAPTER LIII

## Concerning the body of Valentinus, which was cast out of the church after his death

The venerable brother Venantius, bishop of Luna, who is present here even now, and the most distinguished man Liberius, a nobleman of great integrity, testify that they themselves and their people witnessed the event they relate, which recently occurred in the city of Genoa [Note: [Col. 0416D] It is a very famous city, sufficiently well known from the republic over which it presides.].

There, as they say, a man named Valentinus, defender of the church of Milan, died. He was extremely dissolute and wholly occupied with every kind of frivolity. His body was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Syrus.

At midnight, voices arose in that same church, as though someone were being forcibly expelled and dragged out. At these voices the custodians ran up and saw two exceedingly dreadful spirits. They had bound the feet of Valentinus with a kind of fetter and were dragging him outside the church, while he cried out and shrieked violently. Terrified, the custodians returned to their beds.

When morning came, they opened the tomb in which Valentinus had been placed but did not find his body. Searching outside the church to discover where it had been thrown, they found it placed in another tomb, with his feet still bound, just as he had been dragged from the church.

From this event, Peter, understand that those weighed down by grave sins, if they arrange to be buried in holy places, remain subject to judgment for their presumption, so that the holy places do not free them but rather their guilt of rashness accuses them.

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LV. Concerning the body of Valentinus, a defensor, which was cast out of the tomb after death

[Col. 0414C]

The most devout brother Venantius, bishop of the city of Luna, who is present here even now, and Liberius, the most distinguished man, a devout and truthful man [Col. 0414D], say that they themselves, together with their own people, were present at the event about which they relate, which occurred in the city of Genoa [Col. 0415A].

For a certain Valentinus by name, who was defensor of the church of Milan [Note: [Col. 0415D] Manuscript: “of Milan”], died there: a man exceedingly polluted and occupied with every disorder [Note: [Col. 0415D] Manuscript: “exceedingly sullied and occupied with every disorder.”]. His body was buried in the church of the holy martyr Syrus.

At midnight voices arose in the same church, as though someone were being forcibly expelled from it. The custodians, running at these voices, saw two dreadful spirits [Note: [Col. 0415D] Manuscript: “a certain dreadful spirit”] who had tightly bound the feet of the same Valentinus with a fetter and were dragging him outside the church, crying and lamenting very bitterly. Terrified at this, they returned to their own beds.

When morning came, they opened the tomb in which Valentinus had been buried, but did not find his body there. Searching outside the church, they found it thrown into another tomb, with his feet still bound, just as he had been dragged from the church.

From this event, Peter, understand that those whose sins are grave, if they cause themselves to be buried in holy places, leave behind an exposure and condemnation of their pollution: they are not redeemed by the holy places but are rather accused by the fault of their presumption.

# CHAPTER LIV

## Concerning the body of a dyer buried in a church and afterward not found

Many of the dyers who live in this city testify to what happened here. When one of the leading men of their trade had died, his wife buried his body in the church of the blessed martyr Januarius, near the gate of Saint Lawrence.

On the following night, from his tomb, and with the custodian listening, his spirit began to cry out: “I am burning, I am burning.”

After he had uttered these cries for a long time, the custodian reported this to his wife. She then sent to the church men skilled in the same trade, wishing to discover the condition of his body in the tomb, since he was crying out such things.

They opened the tomb and found his clothing intact. It is preserved in that same church to this day as testimony to the event. His body, however, they did not find at all, as though it had never been placed in that tomb.

From this we must infer by what punishment his soul had been condemned, since even his flesh had been cast out of the church. What benefit, then, do holy places provide for those buried in them, when those who are unworthy are divinely expelled from those same holy places?

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LVI. Concerning the body of the dyer who was buried in a church and afterward was not found

[Col. 0415B]

What happened in this city is also attested by many of the dyers who live here. When the leading man of their trade had died, his body was buried by his wife in the church of the blessed martyr Januarius, which is near the gate of Saint Lawrence [Col. 0415C].

When night came, his spirit began to cry out from his tomb, with the custodian listening: “I am burning, I am burning.” While he cried these words for a long time, the custodian of the church reported it to his wife. When she heard this, she sent men of the same trade to the church to investigate carefully what had happened and in what condition his body was in the tomb, since he was crying out such things.

They came and opened the tomb. They found his clothing sound and untouched; it is preserved to this day in the same church as testimony to this event. His body, however, they did not find at all, as though it had not been buried in that tomb.

From this event it is possible to understand under what condemnation his soul exists, since his body was cast out of the church [Col. 0415D]. What benefit, then, do holy places provide for those buried there, when those who are unworthy are divinely thrown out of the holy places?

# CHAPTER LV

## What can aid souls after death toward absolution; concerning a priest of Centumcellae and the soul of Justus the monk

[Col. 0416D]

**Peter.** What, then, can benefit the souls of the dead?

**Gregory.** If sins are not incapable of being forgiven after death, the sacred offering of the saving sacrifice often greatly assists souls even after death, so that sometimes the souls of the departed themselves appear to seek it.

For the aforesaid Bishop Felix says that he learned from a venerable priest, who had lived until two years previously and resided in the territory of the city of Centumcellae [Note: [Col. 0417D] Centumcellae, now Civita Vecchia, is a town of Etruria on the Tyrrhenian Sea, forty miles from the city of Rome.], and who presided over the church of the blessed John situated in a place called Tauriana, that this priest used to bathe whenever bodily necessity required it in the same place where the hot waters produced great quantities of steam.

One day, when he had entered there, he found an unfamiliar man prepared to serve him. This man removed his shoes from his feet, received his clothing, and, when he came out from the hot baths, supplied him with *sabanum* [Note: [Col. 0417D] We have already observed at Book III, chapter 17, that *sabanum* means linen cloths.]. He performed every service with great devotion.

When this had happened repeatedly, the priest, on one day when he was going to the baths, said to himself:

“I ought not to appear ungrateful to the man who is accustomed to serve me so devotedly when I bathe; I must bring him something as a gift.”

So he carried with him two round offerings [Note: [Col. 0417D] These seem to have been round loaves, shaped like cakes, among the offerings presented in the sacrifice of the Mass. One part served for consecration and the other was distributed to the people. Hence the man says here, “This bread is holy.” See the eminent Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 23. Gussanville.]. As soon as he reached the place, he found the man and, as usual, made use of his service in every respect. He bathed, and when he was dressed and wished to leave, he offered what he had brought with him to the man who served him, as a blessing, asking him kindly to accept what he was offering out of love.

The man replied sadly and sorrowfully:

“Why are you giving these things to me, Father? This bread is holy; I cannot eat it. I—for you see me—was once the master of this place, but because of my sins I have been assigned here after death. If you wish to do something for me, offer this bread to almighty God on my behalf, and pray for my sins. Know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and no longer find me.” [Note: [Col. 0417D] The German, Theodulfian, Norman, and other manuscripts add: “For I whom you see.”]

With these words he disappeared. By vanishing, he made it known that the one who had appeared to be a man was a spirit.

The priest then afflicted himself with tears for him throughout an entire week, offering the saving sacrifice every day. When he later returned to the baths, he no longer found him.

Thus it is shown how greatly the offering of the sacred sacrifice benefits souls, since the spirits of the dead themselves ask the living for it, and signs indicate that through it they appear to be released.

I do not think I should keep silent about what I remember having occurred in my monastery three years ago. A monk named Justus had been trained in the medical art. While I was living in that monastery, he regularly served me and used to watch over me during my continual illnesses.

He was overcome by bodily sickness and brought to the point of death. His own brother, named Copiosus, attended him in his illness; he too now earns the means of temporal life in this city through the same medical art.

When the aforesaid Justus realized that he had reached the end, he disclosed to his brother Copiosus that he had three gold coins hidden away. This could not be concealed from the brothers. They carefully investigated all his medicines and found the three gold coins hidden in a medicinal preparation.

As soon as this was reported to me, I could not bear calmly such a grave evil in a brother who had lived communally with us. For it had always been the rule of our monastery that all the brothers should live in common, so that none of them was permitted to possess anything privately [Note: [Col. 0420D] Gussanville, together with the German manuscript: “that the brothers should live in common, so that…” We follow three Chartres manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and others, together with the earlier printed editions.].

Overcome, therefore, by great sorrow, I began to consider what I ought to do for the dying man’s purification and what provision I ought to make as an example for the living brothers.

I summoned Pretiosus, the superior of that monastery, and said to him [Note: [Col. 0420D] Beccensis, here and below, “Speciosus.”]:

“Go, and do not allow any of the brothers to approach him as he lies dying, nor let him hear words of consolation from any of them [Note: [Col. 0420D] The printed editions: “See that no one…”]. But when, at the point of death, he asks for the brothers, let his natural brother tell him that, because of the coins he secretly possessed [Note: [Col. 0420D] The same printed editions add: “because of the gold coins,” against the manuscripts.], he has become detestable to all the brothers. Thus, at least in death, may bitterness pierce his mind concerning his guilt and cleanse him from the sin he committed.

“When he has died, do not place his body with the bodies of the brothers. Instead, make a pit for him somewhere in a dung heap and bury his body there. Throw the three gold coins he left upon him, while all of you cry out together: ‘Your money be with you for your destruction’ (Acts 8:20). Then cover him with earth.”

In all this I wished one benefit for the dying man and another for the living brothers: that the bitterness of death might free him from his guilt, and that so great a condemnation might prevent them from sharing in such a sin. And this is what happened.

When the monk reached the point of death and, in great distress, sought to commend himself to the brothers, none of them consented to approach him or speak with him. His natural brother told him why he was detested by them. Immediately he groaned bitterly over his guilt and, amid that sorrow, departed from the body. He was buried as I had ordered.

All the brothers, however, were greatly disturbed by the judgment pronounced against him. Each began to bring forward things of little value, even the most insignificant objects, which the rule of the community had always permitted them to possess, and they became exceedingly afraid that something might be found among them for which they could be reproved [Note: [Col. 0421D] The printed editions: “among them.”].

When thirty days had passed after his death, my heart began to sympathize with the deceased brother. I considered his punishments with profound grief and sought some means of delivering him.

I summoned the same Pretiosus, the superior of our monastery, and said sorrowfully:

“It is a long time that our deceased brother has been tormented in the fire. We ought to show him charity and help him as far as we can, so that he may be delivered. Go, therefore, and from today offer the sacrifice for him continuously for thirty days, ensuring that not a single day passes on which the saving offering is not sacrificed for his release.”

He immediately departed and obeyed the command.

While we were occupied with other matters and did not count the days as they passed, the deceased brother appeared one night in a vision to his natural brother Copiosus. When Copiosus saw him, he asked:

“What is it, brother? How are you?”

He replied:

“Until now I was in a bad state, but now I am well, because today I received Communion.”

Copiosus immediately went to the monastery and reported this to the brothers. The brothers carefully counted the days and found that it was precisely the day on which the thirtieth offering for him had been completed.

Copiosus did not know what the brothers were doing for the deceased, and the brothers did not know what Copiosus had seen concerning him. At the same moment, when he learned what they had done and they learned what he had seen, the vision and the sacrifice agreed perfectly. It became evident that the deceased brother had escaped punishment through the saving offering.

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LVII. Question: What can aid souls after death, and concerning the priest from Centumcellae and the soul of Justus the monk

[Col. 0415D]

**Peter.** What, then, can benefit the souls of those who have died after death? [Note: [Col. 0416D] Manuscript: “What, then, can…”]

**Gregory.** If sins are not unforgivable after death, the sacred offering of the saving sacrifice can greatly assist souls. Hence the souls of the dead themselves have often been seen seeking it, as Bishop Felix mentioned above says he learned from a priest who was exceedingly devout in life [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “that a certain priest, two years ago… in the surrounding district…”].

This priest was still alive until two years before and lived in the territory of the city of Centumcellae. He formerly presided over the church of the blessed John in the place called Tauriana. It was the custom of this priest, whenever bodily need required it, to bathe in the same place where the hot waters produce great steam [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “The same priest, then, used to go to the hot waters in that same place whenever bodily need required it; and one day, having entered there to bathe…”].

Having entered that place one day, he found an unknown man ready to serve him. He removed his shoes from his feet and received his garments. When the priest came out from the hot waters, the man gave him linen cloths and performed every service with great honor.

When this had happened repeatedly, the priest, going to the hot waters one day, reflected within himself that he ought not to appear empty-handed to the man who habitually served him with such devotion when he bathed [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “He said: I ought not to be empty-handed toward that man who customarily serves me so genuinely when I bathe.”]. “I must carry him some gift” [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “to offer him something”].

So the priest took two offerings with him and went. When he arrived at the place, he again found the man. As usual, the man performed every service for him [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “He performed all the service; when he had bathed and dressed and was now about to leave…”]. The priest bathed, dressed, and, as he was about to leave, gave the offerings he had carried with him to the man who served him, as a blessing, asking him to accept them as an act of love.

The man replied in mourning and sorrow:

“Why do you give these things to me, Father? This bread is holy, and I cannot eat it. I whom you see was once the master of this place. But because of my sins I have been condemned here. If you wish to do something for me, offer this bread to almighty God on my behalf and pray for my sins. Know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and no longer find me.”

Having said this, he became invisible. Since the man had appeared to be human and then became invisible, it was understood that he was a spirit.

The priest persisted in tears for him throughout a week [Note: [Col. 0418D] Manuscript: “persistently”], offering the saving sacrifice to God every day. When he afterward returned to the hot waters, he no longer found him there.

From this it is shown how greatly the offering of the sacred sacrifice benefits souls, since even the spirits of the dead ask the living for it, and by signs they indicate that through it they are released from their sins.

I also think I ought not to pass over in silence what I remember happened in my monastery three years ago [Note: [Col. 0419D] Manuscript: “I judge it right.”]. A monk named Justus, who knew the medical art, used to serve me whenever I was in the monastery and to remain with me during my daily illnesses [Note: [Col. 0419D] Manuscript: “He was accustomed to serve every day and to attend my illnesses that continually befell me. Thus, having been overtaken by bodily sickness, he was brought to the end; and his own brother, named Copiosus, attended him in his illness,” etc.].

He therefore fell into bodily illness and was brought to the point of death. He had a brother named Copiosus, who attended him in that illness and who is still alive, earning the income of temporal life in this city from the same medical art.

When the aforesaid Justus recognized that he was approaching the end, he disclosed to his brother Copiosus that he had three gold coins hidden away. This could not be concealed from the brothers. They carefully examined all the medicines and found the three gold coins hidden there [Note: [Col. 0419D] Manuscript: “The monks of the monastery could not remain unaware of this. Having carefully examined all the medical preparations, they found the same three coins hidden there; and when…”].

When this evil concerning the brother who lived communally with us was reported to me, I could not bear it patiently [Note: [Col. 0419D] This manuscript differs slightly from the printed editions in wording, but not in sense]. For it had always been the rule of our monastery that all the brothers should live in common and possess nothing privately.

Overcome by sorrow, I began to consider what I ought to do for the purification of the dying man and for the instruction and correction of the living brothers. Calling the steward of the monastery to me, I said:

“Go, and do not allow any of the brothers to approach that dying man, nor let him hear a word of consolation from any of them. But if, as he draws near death, he summons the brothers, let his natural brother tell him that, because of the three coins he secretly possessed, he has become detestable to all the brothers. Perhaps, even in his death, by condemning his mind concerning this fault with the bitterest scourge, he may be cleansed from the sin he committed.

“When he dies, do not bury his body where the other brothers are buried. Instead, make some sort of tomb for him in the dung heap and bury his body there. Throw upon him the three coins he left, while all cry out together: ‘Your money be with you for your destruction’ [Note: [Col. 0420D] Manuscript: “Let your money be with you.”]. Then cover him with earth.

“In all these things I wished one benefit for the dying man and another for the living brothers: that the bitterness of death might free him from his fault, while fear of so great a condemnation might prevent them from becoming participants in such a fault.” And this is what happened.

When the same monk came to death and, being greatly distressed, sought to commend himself to the brothers, none of the monks consented to approach him. His natural brother told him why he had become detestable to them. Immediately, because of his sin, he groaned openly and, amid that groaning, departed from the body. He was buried as I had ordered.

All the brothers, greatly disturbed by the judgment pronounced against him, began to bring forward into the midst the worthless and smallest things that the rule of the community had always permitted them to possess. They were exceedingly afraid lest anything be found among them by which they might be condemned [Note: [Col. 0421D] Manuscript: “The rule permitted them to have these things; they were greatly afraid lest anything be found among them which was destined to condemn them.”].

When thirty days had passed after his death, my soul began to sympathize with the deceased brother, to consider his grievous punishments with profound pain, and to seek whether there might be some help for his release [Note: [Col. 0422D] Manuscript: “After his death, when thirty days had passed, my soul began to sympathize with the deceased brother and, with the greatest pain, to consider his sufferings.”].

Then I summoned the same steward of our monastery and said in sorrow:

“It is enough that the deceased brother is being tormented in the fire. We ought to help him through charity as far as we can, so that he may be released from his punishment. Go, therefore, and from today cause an unbloody sacrifice to be offered for him continuously for thirty days, allowing not a single day to pass on which the saving sacrifice is not offered for his release.” [Note: [Col. 0422D] Manuscript: “For thirty days.”]

He immediately agreed and made the necessary arrangements.

While we were occupied with other matters and did not count the days as they passed, the deceased brother appeared by a vision one night to his natural brother Copiosus. When Copiosus saw him, he asked:

“What is it, brother? How are you?”

He replied:

“Until now I was in a bad state, but now I am well, because today I received Communion.”

Copiosus immediately went to the monastery and reported this to the brothers. The brothers carefully counted the days and found that it was the day on which the thirtieth offering for him had been completed.

Copiosus did not know what the brothers were doing for him, and the brothers likewise did not know what Copiosus had seen concerning him. On the same day he learned what they had done, and they learned what he had seen. Since the vision and the sacrifice agreed together, it became clearly evident [Note: [Col. 0421] It seems that *δεικνύνονται* should be read, and below *τεθαυμένος* instead of *ἀπεθαμμένος*. Edition.] that through the saving sacrifice the deceased brother had been released from punishment.

# CHAPTER LVI

## Concerning the life and death of Cassius, bishop of Narnia

[Col. 0421C]

**Peter.** The things I hear are truly marvelous and bring no little joy.

**Gregory.** So that the words of the dead may not fall into doubt for us, the deeds of the living confirm them.

Cassius, bishop of Narnia, a man venerable in his life [Note: [Col. 0421D] He was entered in the sacred calendar on 29 June. What is related about him here is explained more fully in Homily 37 on the Gospels.], was accustomed to offer sacrifice to God every day and, amid the mysteries of the sacrifices, to sacrifice himself with tears. Through a vision granted to one of his priests, he received a command from God, saying:

“Do what you are doing; carry out what you are carrying out. Let neither your foot nor your hand cease. On the feast of the Apostles you will come to me, and I will repay you your reward.”

After seven years, on that same day of the feast of the Apostles, having completed the mysteries of the sacred liturgy and received the mystery of Holy Communion, he was released from the body.

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LVIII. Concerning the life and death of Cassius, bishop

[Col. 0422C]

**Peter.** The things I hear are truly very marvelous and bring no little joy.

**Gregory.** So that the words of the dead may not come into doubt for us, all the deeds of the living confirm them.

Cassius, bishop of Narnia, a man devout in life, was accustomed to offer an unbloody sacrifice to God every day [Col. 0422D]. While celebrating the mysteries of the sacred sacrifice with many tears [Note: [Col. 0422D] Manuscript: “performing the mysteries of the sacred sacrifice with tears…”], and while he was within the altar, he received a decree from God [Note: [Col. 0422D] Manuscript: “from the Lord”] through a vision of one of his own priests, who said:

“Work at what you are working; let neither your foot nor your hand cease. At the feast of the holy Apostles you will come to me, and I will repay you your reward.”

After seven years, on that same day of the feast of the Apostles, having completed the mysteries of the sacred liturgy and received the mystery of Holy Communion, he was released from the body.

# CHAPTER LVII

## Concerning a certain man captured by enemies, whose bonds were loosed at the hour of the offering; and concerning Baraca the sailor, saved from shipwreck by the saving offering

[Col. 0424A]

We also heard that a certain man was held captive among enemies and bound in fetters. His wife was accustomed to offer sacrifice for him on appointed days. After a long time he returned to his wife and made known on which days his bonds had been loosed. His wife recognized that these were the very days on which she had offered the sacrifice for him.

This is confirmed with complete certainty by another event that occurred seven years ago. Agatho, bishop of Palermo, as many faithful and devout men have testified and continue to testify to me, was ordered, during the time of my predecessor of blessed memory, to come to Rome [Note: [Col. 0424D] Sicilian bishops were required to come to Rome once every three years. Gregory granted that this should occur only once every five years. See Book VII, formerly Book VI, Letter 19, now Letter 22.]. He endured a storm of extraordinary violence, so that he despaired of escaping such a peril from the waves.

His sailor, named Baraca [Note: [Col. 0424D] The first Carnotensis manuscript reads *Varica*; the third, *Varaca*, which is the reading found in all the manuscripts.], who now serves in the clerical office of that same church, was steering a small vessel called a *carabus* behind the ship. When the rope broke, he suddenly disappeared amid the heaps of waves together with the *carabus* he was steering.

The ship on which the bishop was traveling, after many dangers and battered by the waves, finally reached the island of Ustica [Note: [Col. 0424D] Most manuscripts read *Ostica*. It is one of the Aeolian Islands of Sicily.].

When the third day had passed and the bishop saw no sign of the sailor who had been swept away in the *carabus* anywhere on the sea, he was deeply distressed and believed him dead. Nevertheless, out of charity, he performed for him the service owed to the dead: he ordered that a saving sacrifice be offered to almighty God for the release of his soul.

When this had been offered, the ship was repaired, and he proceeded to Italy. When he reached the Roman harbor, he found there the sailor whom he had thought dead.

Then he rejoiced with unexpected joy and asked him how he had been able to remain alive for so many days amid that great danger at sea.

The sailor explained that, whenever he had been tossed about in the waves of that storm with the *carabus* he was steering, he had swum with it when it was full of water and had repeatedly remained above its keel whenever it was turned upside down [Note: [Col. 0424D] The first Theodulfian manuscript has *ceraphum* throughout instead of *carabus*. A *carabus* is a small boat made of wicker and leather; see Isidore’s Glosses and Du Cange.].

He added that, after doing this continuously day and night, his strength had finally collapsed from hunger and exhaustion. He then explained how divine mercy had preserved him, as he still testifies:

“While struggling and weakening in the waves, I was suddenly weighed down in mind, so that I did not think I was awake, nor yet that I was overcome by sleep. And behold, while I was in the midst of the sea, someone appeared and brought me bread for food. As soon as I had eaten it, I recovered my strength. Not long afterward a ship passed by, took me from that danger among the waves, and brought me to land.”

When the bishop heard this, he asked for the day and discovered that it was the very day on which the priest had offered the sacrifice of the sacred offering to almighty God for him on the island of Ustica.

**Peter.** I myself, while staying in Sicily, learned that the things you relate had all occurred.

**Gregory.** I believe that this happened so openly among the living, even though they did not know of one another, so that it might be shown to all who do such things without knowing that, if sins are capable of being forgiven, the offering of the sacred sacrifice can benefit the dead toward their absolution.

But we must understand that the sacred sacrifice benefits those dead who, while living here, obtained that the good deeds performed on their behalf by others here should also help them after death.

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LIX. Concerning the one invisibly released from his irons, and concerning the sailor saved from shipwreck

[Col. 0423A]

We also heard this: that a certain man was held captive among enemies and bound in fetters, for whom his wife was accustomed to offer sacrifice on appointed days [Note: [Col. 0423D] The word “this,” which seems redundant and to impede the construction, or at least to suspend the sense for a long time, is absent from the Royal Manuscript. The manuscript reads *σύμβιος* here and below rather than *σύζυγος*.].

After a long time he returned to his wife and made known the days on which his chains had been loosed. She said that these were the very days on which she had offered the offering for him.

This is also shown to be certain by another event that occurred seven years earlier, as many faithful and devout men related to me and testify. When Agatho, bishop of Palermo, having been ordered by my predecessor of blessed memory to come to Rome [Note: [Col. 0423D] Since this word means “successor,” an error is evident here.], endured a storm of extraordinary violence, he was so despairing of escaping from the danger of such waves that he had no hope.

His sailor, named Baraca, who now serves in the clerical ministry of his church, was steering the *carabus* behind the ship. When the rope was cut, he was lifted up together with the *carabus* he was steering and disappeared amid the waves.

The ship on which the bishop was traveling came, shattered by the violence of the waves, with great difficulty to the island called Ustica. When three days had passed and they saw neither the sailor nor the *carabus* that had been torn away from him anywhere in the sea, the bishop, deeply distressed, believed him lost. He spent the gift he owed to the dead in liturgical service and almsgiving, ordering that a saving sacrifice be offered to almighty God for the release of his soul. While it was being offered, the ship was saved and proceeded to Italy.

When he came to the Roman harbor, he found there the sailor whom he had supposed dead. Then he rejoiced with unimaginable joy and asked the sailor how he had been able to live for so many days amid such danger at sea.

The sailor replied and explained how, in the storm of the waves, when the *carabus* he was steering had filled with water, he swam with it, and how, whenever it was turned upside down, he remained above its keel [Note: [Col. 0423D] Manuscript: “the keel,” instead of “the turning.”].

While he did this continually day and night, his strength finally collapsed through hunger and exhaustion [Note: [Col. 0426D] Manuscript: “When he did this without ceasing, his strength at last fell utterly through exhaustion and pain.”]. He explained how God’s loving-kindness had preserved him [Note: [Col. 0426D] Manuscript: “He showed how, amid the waves…”], as he still testifies:

“While laboring and struggling in the waves, I was suddenly weighed down in my mind, neither being overcome by sleep nor believing that I was awake. While I was in this state of ecstasy in the midst of the sea, someone appeared and gave me bread for food. As soon as I ate, I recovered my strength. After this, a ship passed nearby, took me from that danger and from the violence of the waves, and guided me to land.”

When the bishop heard this, he asked for the day and found that it was the day on which the priest had offered a sacrifice of the sacred offering to almighty God for him on the island of Ustica.

**Peter.** I heard, while I was in Sicily, that all the things you relate had occurred [Note: [Col. 0426D] Manuscript: “The things you have related, when I went to Sicily…”].

**Gregory.** I believe that this happened so openly among the living and those who did not know of it, so that it might be shown to all who do such things, whether they know or do not know, that, if sins are not unforgivable [Note: [Col. 0426D] The manuscript reads “sins”; the printed editions read “forgivable,” contrary to the saint’s meaning.], the offering of the sacred sacrifice can bring great benefit and relief to the dead.

Let this be known: the sacred sacrifice benefits those dead who, while living in the present life, restrained themselves from evil works. Therefore, after death, the good things performed here on their behalf by others also help them.

# CHAPTER LVIII

## Concerning the power and mystery of the saving sacrifice

In this connection we must consider that the safer course is for each person, while alive, to do personally the good that he hopes will be done for him by others after his death [Note: [Col. 0425D] Two Chartres manuscripts and both Theodulfian manuscripts read: “while he himself lives, let him do for himself.”]. It is happier to depart free than to seek freedom after being bound.

Therefore we ought to despise the present age with all our mind, since we already see it passing away; we ought to offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily sacrifices of his flesh and blood.

For this sacrifice alone saves the soul from eternal destruction. Through the mystery it renews for us the death of the Only-begotten, who, although he rose from the dead and no longer dies, and although death no longer rules over him (Romans 6:9), nevertheless, living in himself immortally and incorruptibly, is again sacrificed for us in the mystery of the sacred offering [Note: [Col. 0425D] Vallicellian manuscript: “again the true body.”].

There his body is received; his flesh is distributed for the salvation of the people; his blood is poured out not into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful.

Let us therefore consider what this sacrifice is for us, since for our absolution it continually represents the passion of the Only-begotten Son.

What believer could doubt that, at the very hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that things below are joined to things above; that earthly things are united with heavenly things; and that one reality is made from visible and invisible things?

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LX. Concerning the power of the holy mysteries of the divine liturgy

[Col. 0426C]

From these things it has become clear [Note: [Col. 0426D] Manuscript: “Among these things it is clear”] that the better way is for each person to do, while he lives, the good which he hopes will be done for him by others after his death [Note: [Col. 0426D] Manuscript: “the good which he hopes will be done for him by others, let him do for himself while he lives.”].

For it is more blessed to depart free than, after the chains, to seek freedom. Therefore we ought to despise the present age with all our mind, since we see it already flowing away, and to offer God daily sacrifices of tears and daily offerings of his flesh and blood.

For this sacrifice alone frees and saves the soul from eternal death, and through the mystery makes present for us that death of the Only-begotten Son of God. He, having risen from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer rules over him. Yet, remaining immortal and incorruptible, he is again sacrificed for us through the mystery of the sacred sacrifice.

His flesh is divided there for the salvation of the people. Likewise his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful.

Let us therefore understand that, for our forgiveness and release, it continually imitates the passion of the Only-begotten Son of God. For what believer could doubt that, at the hour of the sacrifice, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in the mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; that things below share in things above; that earth is mingled with heavenly things; and that one thing is made from visible and invisible realities?

# CHAPTER LIX

## Concerning afflicting the heart amid the sacred mysteries, and guarding the mind after compunction

When we do these things, it is necessary that we sacrifice ourselves to God in contrition of heart. For when we celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, we ought to imitate what we perform.

Then the sacrifice will truly be offered to God for us, when we have made ourselves a sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0428D] The Vallicellian and Beccensis manuscripts read: “acceptable to God.”].

But we must strive, even after the times of prayer, as far as God grants us strength, to preserve the soul in its own weight and vigor, lest afterward wandering thought dissolve it, lest empty joy steal upon the mind, and lest the soul lose the profit of compunction through the carelessness of flowing thoughts.

Thus Hannah deserved to obtain what she had asked from the Lord, because after her tears she remained in the same steadiness of mind. Of her it is written: “And her face was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Samuel 1:18). Since she did not forget what she had asked, she was not deprived of the gift for which she had prayed.

## Greek parallel

### Chapter LXI. Concerning humbling the heart amid the divine mysteries and guarding the mind

[Col. 0427B]

It is necessary, while we perform these things, that we offer ourselves to God as a sacrifice in contrition of heart. For while celebrating the mysteries of the Lord’s passion, we ought to imitate what we perform.

Then we truly offer sacrifice to God for ourselves, when we make ourselves a sacrifice.

But we must strive, both during and after the time of prayer, as God gives strength, to preserve our souls in his power and vigor [Col. 0427B], not allowing them to be weakened by wandering thought and so dissolved, lest empty joy of mind, dragging them away, and the restlessness of flowing concern cause the soul to lose the gain of compunction through the distraction of passing thoughts.

Thus Hannah was deemed worthy to obtain what she asked from the Lord, because after her tears she guarded herself in the same fear of thought. Concerning her it is written that her face was no longer changed [Note: [Col. 0427D] Manuscript: “Her face no longer fell; for, since she did not forget what she had vowed…”]. Since, therefore, she did not forget what she had asked, she was not deprived of the gift for which she had prayed.

# CHAPTER LX

## Concerning forgiving the sins of others, so that our own may be forgiven us
But amid all this it must be understood that the person rightly asks forgiveness for his own offense who first forgives what has been done against him. For the offering is not accepted unless discord has first been driven from the heart, as the Truth says: “If you bring your offering before the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your offering there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then come and offer your offering” (Matthew 5:23). [Notes: Two Gemet. manuscripts and other Norman manuscripts, except Becc., read with Val. Cl., “at the altar.” The same Gemet. manuscripts read, “leave your offering there,” etc.]

In this matter one must consider: if every fault is removed by an offering, how grave is the fault of discord, for which not even the offering is accepted? We must therefore go in our minds to our neighbor, even though he is far away and separated from us by distance; we must submit our spirit to him and appease him by humility and goodwill. Thus, when our Creator sees such a disposition and the pleasing intention of our mind, he may release us from sin, since he accepts the offering made for the offense (Matthew 18:27).

By the testimony of the Truth’s own voice we have learned that the servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he did penance, received from his lord remission of the debt. But because he did not forgive his fellow servant the debt owed to him—one hundred denarii—he was ordered to have exacted from him again what had already been forgiven him. From these statements it is plainly evident (On Penalties, Distinction 4, chapter “Constat”) that, if we do not forgive from the heart what has been done against us, what we were rejoicing had already been forgiven us through repentance will again be demanded from us.

Therefore, while the time of indulgence granted by the judge remains, while the judge endures, and while he who examines our offenses awaits our conversion, let us melt the hardness of our mind in tears and form within our dealings with our neighbors the grace of kindness. I say with confidence that after death we shall have no need of a saving sacrifice if, before death, we have ourselves become a sacrifice to God.

## Chapter LXII. On forgiving the offenses of others, so that our own may likewise be forgiven

[Column 0427B]

Let this be known: the person who rightly asks forgiveness for his own offenses is the one who first forgives the offenses committed against him. [Note: Ms. reads τῶν ἑαυτοῦ πταισ[μάτων], “his own offenses.”]

For the offering is not received unless enmity is first driven from the soul, as the Truth says: “If you bring your offering to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your offering there before the altar, and go; first be reconciled to your brother, and then come and bring your offering.” [Notes: Ms. reads: “No one receives the offering unless wickedness has first been driven from the soul; for Truth itself has said: ‘If …’” Ms. reads: “Leave your offering lying there before …”]

From this matter we must understand how serious the offense of enmity is, since every offense is loosed through the offering, yet because of enmity the offering is not received: God does not accept such an offering.

We must therefore unite ourselves mentally with our neighbors, even if they are distant from us, submit our souls to them with humility, and please them through goodwill. [Note: Ms. reads ὑποτάξαι, “to submit.”] For whenever our Creator sees in truth that such is our disposition and that our mind is well-pleasing, he releases us from sin, accepting this offering on behalf of our offenses.

The voice of the Truth bears witness, and we have learned that the servant who owed ten thousand talents, when he came to sincere repentance, received cancellation of the debt from his lord. But because he did not forgive his fellow servant the hundred denarii that he owed him, he was ordered to repay everything that had already been forgiven him.

From these plainly stated things it follows that, if we do not forgive from the heart the offenses committed against us, we shall again be required to pay what we had rejoiced had been forgiven through repentance.

Therefore, while we have received a time of respite from the judge who examines our offenses—for he awaits our return—let us dissolve the harshness of our mind in tears and establish grace and kindness toward our neighbors. And I say confidently that we shall have no need of a saving sacrifice after death if, before death, we ourselves become a sacrifice to God.

[Column 0429]

For today I received holy Communion.’ This same brother, immediately afterward, in the monastery, etc.”

“Few of the departed support the works of the living, so that we may not fall into cowardice. For Cassius, bishop of the city of Narni, a man exceedingly devout in his life, every day [offered himself] to God.”

“Come to me after the Apostles, and I will give you your reward.” After seven years, on that same day of the feast of the Apostles, while he was celebrating the mysteries of the holy liturgy and had received divine Communion, he was released from the bonds of the body.

“She supposed that he was dead and, in her distress, regarded him as a corpse. Yet, because of the service of charity that she owed to the dead, she ordered a sacrifice to be offered to almighty God for the repose of his soul. When this had happened, they repaired the ship and reached Italy.

When they arrived at the city and entered the harbor, they found there the sailor whom they had thought had died. The bishop, rejoicing at this unexpected miracle, began to ask him how he had survived so many days, etc.”

# Letters of Gregory the Great

## Preface to the Letters of Saint Gregory, Pope I

[Column 0431]

We are now about to offer you, pious and devoted reader, a new edition of the letters of Gregory in every respect; we are therefore compelled to preface it by submitting to your most equitable judgment the reasoning behind our undertaking.

### I. On the excellence and dignity of the work

There is no need for us to labor at explaining what is sufficiently well known concerning the excellence and dignity of this work. All learned people know that the letters of the holy Fathers should be preferred to their other writings, because in them the author’s intellect, personal qualities, and character shine forth more clearly.

This is especially evident in the letters of Saint Gregory, in which are outlined his exceptional prudence, pastoral solicitude, lavish generosity toward the poor, strength and humility of spirit, and his other virtues, so that a complete portrait of that most holy pope is presented. Peter Gussanvillaeus has said much in commendation of the Gregorian letters on this point; we have judged it appropriate to append below the relevant section of his preface.

### II.

In another brief preface by the same learned man, which he placed before the letters he published, he explains in these words what he accomplished in his edition:

> “When we saw that, among the other works of so great a man, this particular offspring was especially celebrated by the approval of theologians, well worn through the use of canonists, suitable for establishing the doctrines of the faith, highly useful for illuminating and preserving ecclesiastical discipline, and eminently valuable for regulating the conduct of prelates and private persons, we considered that we ought to labor with a special degree of diligence so that it might be published as accurately as possible, and in a form capable of pleasing the learned and assisting the less learned.
>
> “Accordingly, first, we restored the text, which in all earlier editions had, I do not know through what misfortune, been grievously corrupted. We compared at least thirty-five manuscript copies: some we ourselves examined with our own eyes and scrutinized with our own hands; others we investigated on the authority of learned men, in excerpts that they had courteously sent us.
>
> “With these aids we removed corruptions and either transferred to the margin the variant readings that seemed to possess some importance [Note: Those that had been in the margin we restored to the text within brackets. Editor.] or inserted them into the notes for the sake of fuller explanation.”

### III.

We readily concede that Gussanvillaeus removed some blemishes from the earlier editions, though—something we say reluctantly—only a few, as will immediately become clear to anyone reading our notes. We therefore undertook a new labor and effort: manuscripts had to be summoned from every quarter and carefully read, largely the same manuscripts that Gussanvillaeus mentions, though in them we often read something different from what he did.

One example has just come to our attention in Letter 6 of Book V, formerly Letter 4 of Book IV, where the printed editions read: “After the almost general collapse of the cell itself.” At this passage the learned man notes that in the Tellerian, Lyrensian, and Pratellian manuscripts the word *cellae* is absent. We say nothing here about the Tellerian manuscripts, which we once consulted but are now unable to examine again. Regarding the other two, however, which we currently have before our eyes and are carefully inspecting, we emphatically affirm that the word *cellae* is by no means absent from them.

Thus, not placing complete trust in other men’s eyes, we undertook below a new collation of Saint Gregory’s letters with various manuscript copies, so that the edition we had planned and long been preparing might appear with the greatest possible accuracy. The result of the labor we undertook will immediately be evident to anyone who consults our notes. For there is scarcely a letter in which we have not either restored a corrupt passage or at least supplied a new and by no means contemptible reading.

As a sample of passages corrected and restored by us, a few examples from the first book alone will suffice; to run through the rest would involve almost immeasurable labor.

### IV.

In Letter 6 of this book, the former reading was: “As though with the words of a deserted widow, I say with the prophet,” instead of: “As though with the words of destroyed Judea.”

A little later the printed editions read: “Therefore, you who had not yet slaughtered those same beasts, why did you now refuse to eat through obedience?” All the manuscripts showed that *you wished* must be read, and the integrity of the sense required this reading. Saint Gregory adduces the testimony of Scripture, “Slaughter and eat,” and explains that the beasts must first be slaughtered before they may be eaten. Hence he presses his friend in these words: “Therefore,” he says, “you who had not yet slaughtered those same beasts, why did you now wish to eat through obedience?” If *you did not wish* is written instead, the sense is utterly overturned.

In the same place the earlier printed editions read: “Or do you not know that the very beasts that you wrote about refused to be killed by the sword of your mouth?” But, without consulting the manuscripts, they printed this reading, which is found identically in them: “Or do you not know that the beast about which you wrote refused to be killed by the sword of your mouth?”

In Letter 20, formerly Letter 10, the previous reading was: “But if discord has so armed its factions among you that, through fear of scandal, your will has armed the factions.” The manuscripts give: “so that, through the swelling of scandal,” and it cannot be read otherwise without damage and grave difficulty to the sense. The passage concerns the swelling of pride, from which scandals and quarrels were generated in the Church of Salona.

In Letter 25, formerly Letter 24, Saint Gregory, according to the editions published above, writes: “And yet, suspended in the contemplation of invisible things, he [Paul] recalls the mind’s gaze to the bedchamber of carnal things.” But the old handwritten books consistently read: “And yet, with the contemplation of invisible things suspended, he [Paul] recalls the mind’s gaze to the bedchamber,” and so forth.

Elsewhere in the same letter the other editions present this reading: “In these things, as in a square stone, the structure of holy faith rises, and the rule of every life and action stands firm. Whoever among them,” and so forth. This plainly does not accord with the mind of the holy Doctor, who in this passage presents the four ecumenical councils as a sure rule of faith; he says nothing about life, morals, or actions. In the reading fabricated without warrant by the editors, however, those same councils are called “the rule of every life and action.”

But read as in the manuscripts: “Because in these things [lacuna] the structure of holy faith rises; and [that] of every life and action may exist, whoever does not possess their solidity, even though he is seen to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.”

In Letter 34, formerly Letter 33, the printed copies contain the following: “But if perhaps I am considered less believing in the cause of God.” If the editors had seriously and attentively consulted the manuscript books, they would have read: “But if perhaps I am considered excessive in the cause of God, and am suspected because of the ardor of my zeal.” These final words wonderfully confirm the manuscript reading.

We neglected to observe that, in the heading of the first letter, the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts requires the reading: “Gregory, servant of the servants of God,” although this is omitted in the printed editions.

These examples are sufficient for the diligent reader to understand that the labor we spent over many years in revising Saint Gregory’s letters anew was not fruitless.

Whenever respect for the received reading prevented us from departing from it because it rested on the authority of most of the manuscripts, we thought it sufficient to record the variant readings that occurred, even if they might have been regarded as the best and most genuine. Thus, in Letter 72, formerly Letter 70, the reading is obscure: “For here the yield was so small” (*parva nativitas*) “that, unless grain is gathered from Sicily with God’s help, famine will press heavily upon us.”

We would consider much better the reading supplied by the manuscript copy of the *Life of Saint Gregory* by John the Deacon, preserved in the Bigot Library at Rouen, Book II, chapter 59: “For here the sowing was so small” (*parva sativitas*); where the superscription reads *vel satio*, “or: sowing.” Nevertheless, we retained “the harvest was so small,” a reading in which both the printed and manuscript copies agree, and we inserted the distinctive reading of the Bigot copy into the notes.

### V.

After the text of the letters had been corrected and restored, it was necessary to consider the order both of the books and of the letters themselves.

As for the books, their order and number must be derived from the indictions, or years, of Saint Gregory’s pontificate. For the *Register* contains no letters except those written by Gregory after he had already been appointed to govern the Church. Since this most holy man held the office of pope for thirteen years and six months, with a few additional days, individual books of letters had to be assigned for each individual year.

John the Deacon also numbered them in this way, in Book IV of the *Life*, chapter 71. After saying in chapter 68 that Gregory had held and adorned the see of the Catholic and Apostolic Holy Roman Church for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, he adds in chapter 71 that he left in the archive as many books of letters as the years he lived—in the pontificate. Hence he left the fourteenth book of letters, corresponding to the seventh indiction, incomplete.

It must not be concealed, however, that the printed editions—and indeed most manuscript copies—read: “Hence he left the thirteenth book,” and so forth. But this is a serious error, easily corrected from the context of the narrative. If, according to John the Deacon, there are as many books of Gregory’s letters as there were years of his pontificate, and if it is established by the same writer and by other incontestable testimonies that Gregory lived in the pontificate for thirteen and a half years, the last incomplete book of letters cannot be the thirteenth but must be the fourteenth. Moreover, according to John, the incomplete book of letters corresponds to the seventh indiction; but Book XIII cannot correspond to that indiction, as is clear.

We have also at last discovered the true reading in the Ulticensian Codex, that is, the monastery of Saint Evroul, a manuscript of excellent quality and six hundred years old. But lest anyone suppose that this escaped John because he was thinking of something else and paying insufficient attention, let the same author’s testimony in his preface to Pope John be added. He says:

> “If, however, it should seem otherwise to anyone, as often happens, let him return to the fullness of your archive and read through as many parchment books of the letters of that same Father as he is proved to have lived years.”

Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk who flourished in the eleventh century, had certainly read this in John the Deacon. For in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he says: “Saint Gregory left to posterity as many books of letters as he lived years in the pontificate—that is, thirteen and a half.”

The testimony of Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, may be brought against this. In his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 1, speaking of Gregory’s letters, he says: “Gathering these into one volume, he divided them into twelve books, which he ordered to be called the *Register*.”

This perhaps gave the editors the opportunity to distribute the cited letters into twelve books, at least outwardly, although in reality all the printed copies present fourteen books. For the second book is counted twice, once under the tenth indiction and again under the eleventh. Likewise, the seventh book is counted twice, under the first and second indictions.

To the testimony of Saint Ildefonsus we reply that he was entirely unfamiliar with the reading of Saint Gregory’s works. After mentioning the letters, he adds: “He is also said to have published other excellent little works, but they have not yet come into our hands.” It seems almost certain to us that even the letters had not come to his knowledge.

Therefore greater credence should be given to John the Deacon, Sigebert, and almost all the manuscripts that comprise Gregory’s letters in fourteen books. For although there are some manuscript copies in which the letters are presented without any division into books, none has come to our attention that, when dividing them into books, distributes them among fewer than fourteen.

The following note of our J. Mabillon, attached to John the Deacon’s preface, appears to support the number twelve: “Pope Adrian I is said to have reduced the more select letters into twelve books of decretals, below, Book IV, chapter 71.” But this is a slip of the pen, an error departing from the learned writer’s intention, or else it must be attributed to the printers. For in the cited passage of Gregory’s *Life*, John the Deacon mentions not twelve but only two books of decretals collected by Pope Adrian.

Moreover, the issue here is not selected decretal letters of Gregory, but the complete collection and compilation of all his letters of whatever kind. Nor are we concerned with the number of books into which Pope Adrian divided the aforementioned letters; the controversy concerns only the division instituted by Gregory himself.

### VI.

Restoring the order of the letters required still greater labor. From repeatedly reading them, we easily discovered that many had been removed from their proper places and transferred elsewhere.

The antiquity of this fault is demonstrated by many ancient manuscripts, written about seven hundred years ago, at the end of which numerous letters are collected—especially in the Norman manuscripts—with this heading: “Letters omitted from the preceding indictions.” In most manuscripts there are thirty-one.

Paul the Deacon’s collection, sent to Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, contains more. We believe it to be a supplement to Gregory’s *Register*, for we observed that many of the fifty-four letters contained in it are absent from most manuscripts.

Nor can any reason be devised why so learned and wise a man would have taken care to copy those few letters before the others, since for the most part they teach us nothing worth knowing. Thus, when scribes found many letters wandering and scattered outside the order of the *Register*, and when the printers who followed them encountered the same situation, they began to force them into various books, but scarcely ever according to any prior method.

Hence arose the defect and disordered arrangement of the letters, which can easily be detected from the sequence of events mentioned in them and from even a moderate knowledge of the history of that period.

This defect did not escape Peter Gussanvillaeus, whose words in the preface to the letters are as follows:

> “Furthermore, let it be far from me to establish or defend the order of each letter. Indeed, I freely acknowledge that very many have been placed in the wrong locations. The notes will demonstrate this throughout. Yet I did not wish to disturb the received sequence, lest—as has been rashly done in certain other books—we cast darkness before readers, for whom citations of Saint Gregory’s letters, scattered through every kind of book, would become useless or at least burdensome.”

This was certainly a sound method by which a man otherwise most diligent sought to avoid so much labor. But once an evil has been recognized, is it never permissible to remedy it? Far be it from us to suppose that restoring the legitimate order of the letters would cast darkness upon readers. Rather, darkness should be feared where there is no order at all. From an orderly arrangement of matters, however, the greatest light shines forth.

To come to the matter itself: how greatly must a reader be tossed about by doubt when, after learning from the earlier books of letters that a certain well-known bishop has died and that another has been ordained in place of the deceased, he later reads in the sequence of the subsequent books a letter addressed to that same bishop, whom he knows already to have been removed from the living, as though it had been written to him after his return to life? It would not be difficult to bring forward many examples of similar confusion. We shall do so when we demonstrate the order of the letters restored by us through certain arguments.

As for the inconvenience Gussanvillaeus says is caused by citations of the letters according to the old order, citations scattered through so many books and writings, we shall provide a twofold index of the letters. The first will follow the restored order, compared with the previously received order; the second will follow the old order and usage, compared in reverse with the former, just as was done in the publication of Augustine’s letters, without objection from any learned man.

Thus the cited letters will be found without difficulty. By consulting the index according to the old sequence of the letters, the reader will immediately learn what number each letter now bears and where it is located.

To the two indexes just mentioned we shall add a third, in alphabetical order, compiled from the names of those to whom the holy Doctor writes, and a fourth, geographical index.

### VII.

From the list of the letters we have removed many items that had previously been inserted improperly. These include what is read at the beginning of Book II, under the tenth indiction, concerning the deposition of Laurence the archdeacon and the Greater Litany in the basilica of Saint Mary; in Book XI, under the sixth indiction, the history of Phocas’s coronation and the killing of Maurice and his sons, which is placed before all the letters of that indiction, together with the sermon of blessed Gregory during the time of the plague, beginning: “It is necessary, dearest brothers,” and so forth; the acts of certain synods held at Rome; and finally various privileges granted by Saint Gregory.

We judged that all these should be relegated to the end, together with the Creed mentioned by John the Deacon in Book II, chapter 2, which is found at the beginning of almost all manuscript copies of the letters.

Conversely, we thought that certain letters, whether written by Gregory or addressed to Gregory, should be restored to the *Register*. Some had been exiled into other works; others had only recently been brought out of darkness. We shall take care to record in their proper place to whose diligence these restorations are owed.

### VIII.

After, with the aid of manuscripts, removing corruptions from the text and wording and restoring the true reading in a thousand places, and after arranging both the books and the letters, it was necessary to consider their contents and summaries.

In these summaries everything contained in each letter must be outlined and represented concisely. Yet most of the arguments that have hitherto been prefixed to the letters—as will be clear to anyone who examines them carefully—touch only minimally upon the purpose and aim of Gregory as writer.

Thus before the first letter of the earlier book one reads only: “That once a year they [the bishops of Sicily] should meet together in a provincial council.” But who does not recognize this as a mutilated summary? It says nothing about Peter the subdeacon, whom Saint Gregory commends in that same letter as his representative in Sicily because of his proven virtue and experience; nor does it say anything about the manner in which synods are to be celebrated.

The summary of the following letter, the second, is even less acceptable, since it concerns entirely the grain that was not sent in full, although this is only a small part of the letter. The holy pope’s principal concern in it is to compel Justin, the praetorian prefect of Sicily, first softened by friendly and honorific words, to make peace with the ecclesiastical men with whom he was at odds and to perform the office of judge with the utmost equity.

The same should be understood of the remaining letters. To pursue the matter further would be tedious and unwelcome. Therefore it was necessary to undertake the composition of new summaries, which, prefixed to the letters, might carry before the reader’s understanding a kind of torch.

With no less diligence we undertook to explain and illuminate difficult passages, of which there are very many. To do this more reliably, we devoted our principal effort to establishing and extracting from the manuscripts the true reading, insofar as this was possible. For when the wording is uncertain, conjectures are indulged more freely, and learned men often fight one another and beat the air in a vain effort.

The most abundant harvest of notes and observations on Gregory’s letters was supplied to us especially by two highly learned men: Antonius Dadinus Alteserra, a professor of Toulouse, and Peter Gussanvillaeus.

For the benefit of students of canon law, Alteserra wrote annotations on most of Saint Gregory’s works, revealing the author’s profound knowledge of both branches of law, and dedicated them to Pope Clement IX. We have borrowed a few of these and, adding his name at the end, distinguished them from our own as a mark of honor and gratitude.

Concerning the notes that P. Gussanvillaeus inserted into his edition, it is worthwhile to hear his own preface:

### IX.

> “Concerning the notes added—or, if you prefer, interwoven—something must be said so that we may forestall the objections of the captious.
>
> “In this work one encounters many obscure and recondite words, expressions that are not readily understood, unusual phrases, names of cities and regions, and many other matters belonging to ancient custom; civil laws and legal enactments; canons of ecclesiastical government; and principles of faith and morals.
>
> “Yet not everyone can be a grammarian, philologist, antiquarian, geographer, historian, jurist, canonist, and theologian all at once—nor, as the Greek proverb says, ‘not even Heracles [can contend] against two.’
>
> “For this reason various assistants had to be summoned from different quarters, who might bring help to difficult passages, light to obscure ones, and ingenuity to tangled ones, thereby aiding and advancing the efforts of readers.
>
> “We drew much, of course, from the storehouses of ancient and recent authors; several learned men also shared material with us, wishing to serve the republic of letters and sound morals.”

These words make clear that the notes Gussanvillaeus attached to Gregory’s letters were merely adopted by him, while having other authors as their sources. Thus, in approving them, the scholars testify that they had read “the notes on the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory collected by M. P. Gussanvillaeus, priest.”

But whom did this prudent man summon as his assistants and collaborators? If public rumor is to be trusted, the principal role in composing and elaborating these notes belonged to the distinguished N. Julien, whose emblem—a lily bearing the motto “Here is the lily”—is said to appear after the dedicatory letter.

There are, however, those who attribute these notes and observations chiefly to the distinguished D. Auget, doctor and associate of the Sorbonne. We are compelled to adopt this view. Through the kindness of the distinguished D. Auget—the brother of that same doctor, a royal counselor and treasurer of France at Paris—we obtained a supplement to the notes on Saint Gregory’s letters, written by that doctor in his own hand. In it we plainly detected the same style as in the other notes, the same manner of expression and of explaining matters.

We are therefore persuaded—and the brother mentioned above, a man of proven integrity, had previously assured us of this—that the remaining notes, at least for the most part, must be attributed to this most learned doctor.

It is not for us to pass judgment on these notes. Certainly, whatever we were permitted to retain, we took care to reprint in this edition, adding the name of Gussanvillaeus. Those from which the stricter laws of criticism, or other certainly serious considerations, compelled us to abstain may be read in Gussanvillaeus’s edition by those who delight in varied and manifold learning.

For in that edition every branch of knowledge and every art is lightly sampled, with innumerable testimonies heaped together from sacred and profane writers, Greek and Latin alike. Whether these testimonies are relevant or beside the point, let others judge.
