The notes we took from the Augetian supplement, although very few, will be identified by adding his name at the end.

### X.

As for the notes that we ourselves have elaborated, we thought it necessary to pursue brevity above all, remembering the famous saying: “A flooded river quickly gathers mud.”

We took particular care to avoid traversing and exhausting all commonplaces, whether theological, ethical, or of another kind, although we omitted nothing that could contribute to unraveling difficult passages or illuminating obscure ones.

Whenever passages occur that seem to require more thorough explanation, the *Life of Saint Gregory* composed by us should be consulted with the aid of its indexes; and the diligent reader will acknowledge that his needs have been adequately met.

### XI.

Only one matter concerning the headings of the letters requires observation. Saint Gregory was the first of all to decree, with sufficient humility, that at the beginning of his letters he should be styled “servant of the servants of God.” John the Deacon says this in Book II of the *Life*, chapter 1, and adds that Gregory left this lesson of humility to all his successors, to be preserved in the Roman Church by hereditary right.

John’s testimony gives rise to several questions, which it now seems useful to resolve.

1. Why does this title, so dear to Gregory, appear in so few letters? For if we except three—those that occur first in three books, namely Books VIII, IX, and XII, following the old order—the others lack this title.

2. How can the most holy pope be praised for adopting this title of humility, unknown to the other pontiffs, when Pope Damasus used it in Letter 4 to Stephen and the other bishops of Africa? Peter Gussanvillaeus also adduces this letter for the present purpose, in his notes on Letter 1 of Book VIII.

3. How could John the Deacon have been unaware that Augustine and many others had furnished their letters with this same heading? Let Saint Augustine be read, Letter 217 to Vitalis: “Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ, and through him servant of his servants.” Fulgentius likewise heads Letter 5 in this manner: “To the holy brother and fellow presbyter Eugippius, Fulgentius, servant of the servants of Christ.”

I pass over several other testimonies produced by Gussanvillaeus, either because they are drawn from suspect authors, such as the excerpts taken from Eusebius of Emesa, or because they are irrelevant, since they contain examples of bishops from an age much later than Gregory’s.

To the first objection I reply that all the letters sent by Saint Gregory originally bore this title, “servant of the servants of God,” but that it was omitted for the sake of brevity both by antiquarians and by printers. Nevertheless, it ought at least to have been prefixed to the first letter—and indeed it is found there in the manuscripts and in this new edition—so that from that heading the form and manner of the others might be determined.

To the second objection, he replies that the letter praised under the name of Damasus is now regarded by learned men as doubtful, not to say spurious and fabricated, and is attributed, together with many other interpolated wares, to Isidore the Merchant. Apart from the other reasons advanced by learned men who have pronounced upon the matter with mature and sifted judgment, he adduces as evidence of its falsity the date at which it is said to have been written—namely, the year 405, as is clear from the consuls named—although Damasus had already been dead for twenty years.

To the third, he answers that Augustine, and following his example the holy Fulgentius, disciple of the most holy Doctor (I say nothing of others), did occasionally call themselves “servants of the servants of God” at the beginning and in the address of their letters, and that this does not overturn the testimony of John the Deacon. For when he asserted that Saint Gregory was the first of all to adorn himself at the beginning of his letters with this title of humility, “first of all” must be understood as “first of all the Roman pontiffs,” as is sufficiently clear from the sequence of his words, where he says that this hereditary right, this document of humility, was left to all Gregory’s successors. By this pious stratagem also the wisest Father wished to restrain and repress the Thrasonian arrogance of John of Constantinople, who vaunted himself as ecumenical. Most of the Roman pontiffs followed his example, though not all; for some assumed the titles of bishop, others of pope. Some were content with their bare name, as Zacharias, and occasionally refrained from mentioning their dignity. At present, in bulls the supreme pontiff always uses this title, “Servant of the servants of God”; in briefs, he uses the papal name. The most learned Congius observes in his Glossary that not only other bishops, but also kings and princes, have more than once used this same form of address, “Servant,” and so forth. They all agreed with Augustine, *City of God*, book XIX, chapter 15: “In that order of peace among human beings in which some are subject to others, just as humility benefits those who serve, so pride harms those who rule.”

Before leaving this argument, the Magdeburg Centuriators must be chastised. In centuria 6, chapter 7, in the section “On Association,” they have thus corrupted the testimony of John the Deacon: “John the Deacon, book II of the *Life*, chapter 1, says: ‘Gregory, rejecting the superstitious title of pontiff, was the first of all to write himself servant of servants in his letters.’” But where did it enter the mind of this writer of Saint Gregory’s *Life* to call the name of pontiff superstitious, when he uses it everywhere, as may be seen in his preface and in book I, chapters 1 and 25? Let the heterodox now be ashamed to reproach us with the corruption of ancient writers, when they are plainly convicted of the very crime with which they never cease to accuse us. But concerning this charge by which they attempt to defame us, elsewhere.

## XII

The ancient manuscript codices which we examined and compared in revising Gregory’s *Register* must now be recorded.

The Corbie manuscript, now belonging to the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, is a codex of venerable antiquity, as nearly all the celebrated manuscripts of that monastery are.

The Rheims manuscript, namely that of the archmonastery of Saint-Remi, is of approximately the same age.

We received for use five manuscripts from the very rich and splendid Colbert Library, through the kindness of the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Jacques-Nicolas Colbert, archbishop of Rouen and primate of Normandy; no one is unaware how much all literature and all lovers of letters owe him. Of these manuscripts only two are complete. One, the older, which we shall call the Old Manuscript, contains the letters divided into fourteen books and in many places gives the day on which they were written. The other does indeed contain all the letters, and in the same order as the former, but is not divided into books at all.

The distinguished Monsieur Clément supplied us with two handwritten codices from the Royal Library, with the consent of the most illustrious abbot of Louvois, its superintendent, who shows himself a patron and Maecenas to all students of the liberal arts and especially of sacred literature.

Two Tellerian codices have recently been added to the praised codices of the truly royal library. They were a gift of the most illustrious and most reverend Charles-Maurice Le Tellier, archbishop of Rheims, whose own most excellent archbishop had previously granted us access to them, in accordance with his supreme courtesy and benevolence toward all who labor in the field of letters, and especially in the study of sacred antiquity. In these ancient copies, which seemed to us entirely similar, it is often noted on what day, or at least in what month, and under which indiction Gregory’s letters were issued.

We obtained a codex of approximately seven hundred years’ antiquity from the library of the metropolitan church of Saint Gatianus at Tours. From it also we extracted many indications of the dates on which the letters were written. We shall designate it by the name Tours, Saint Gatianus, so as to distinguish it from another Tours manuscript, namely that of the greater monastery near Tours, which we likewise examined carefully.

The distinguished monastery of Saint-Albans near Angers furnished us with another notable codex, in which some letters bear an indication of the time when they were written; but far fewer than in the Colbert, Tellerian, and Tours codices mentioned above.

But no assistance was more immediately useful to us than that provided by the manuscript codices of our monasteries in Normandy, where this latest edition was prepared. Seven copies altogether were supplied to us from there, all of excellent quality and remarkable completeness. Some were seven hundred years old, others at least six hundred. Their names are as follows: the Gemetic manuscript, that is, of the monastery of Saint Peter at Jumièges; the Audoen manuscript, that is, of the royal monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen; the Michaeline, namely that of the monastery of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea; the Bec manuscript, that is, of the celebrated monastery of the Blessed Mary of Bec-Hellouin; the Séez manuscript, or that of the monastery of Saint Martin at Séez; the Lyre manuscript, that is, of the Blessed Mary of Lyre in the diocese of Évreux; and finally the Pratelli manuscript, namely that of the monastery of Pratelles in the diocese of Lisieux. Since there is almost always the greatest agreement among these codices, we customarily designate them collectively as the Norman manuscripts.

The following should be observed concerning the Audoen manuscript. On the first folio, left blank after the volume had been bound, I read, written in a more recent hand, Berengar’s confession. It is preceded by these words: “In the year from the incarnation of the eternal Principle, 1078, in the month of February, indiction 2, and in the sixth year of the pontificate of our lord Gregory, universal pontiff, the seventh, etc.” This is how it is read in the Roman council VI, volume X of Labbe’s Councils, under the year 1079, with a few words altered. For example, the manuscript reads *sempiterni principii* (“of the eternal Principle”), while Labbe’s edition has *sempiterni principis* (“of the eternal Prince”).

We do not doubt that this Berengarian confession was written on this folio immediately after it had been issued and published. Such was plainly the custom at that time: whatever had recently been composed was copied into any readily available codex, provided that enough clean parchment remained to receive it. From this we infer that the Audoen codex was written at least in the middle of the eleventh century.

If antiquity alone were considered, the Corbie codex, now in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, should have been placed first among all the codices listed. Paul the Deacon sent it to Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, as is evident from Paul’s own letter prefixed to the collection of Saint Gregory’s letters in this book, which our Dom J. Mabillon arranged to have included in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume I, page 397. This codex contains only fifty-four letters—which is why we have listed it last of all—of which thirty-four were corrected and emended by Paul’s own hand. But concerning this collection, see what was said above; concerning Paul, consult the brief preface to the *Life of Saint Gregory* which he wrote.

We inspected all these codices with our own eyes and carefully excerpted their various readings. We must now speak of the Vatican and English manuscripts, which we were unable to see.

The distinguished Stephen Baluze communicated to us the variant readings of four Vatican codices, to whom we owe many other things as well; for, to say nothing of the rest, he himself pointed out and supplied the Colbert manuscripts to us. The man who examined and compared Gregory’s letters with the aforementioned codices of the Vatican Library—a man certainly of acute judgment, extraordinary diligence, and tireless labor—gives the following notice at the beginning of his paper codex:

“On the same day I began comparing the letters of the first book with three manuscript copies in the Vatican, one of which is covered with tawny leather and marked with the number 2534 and the letter A. It lacks the first letter and half of the second. Another is covered with red leather and marked with number 2538 and the letter B. It contains the beginning of the letters with this heading: ‘Here begin the letters from the *Register* of blessed Pope Gregory, in the month of September, indiction 9, namely in the first year of his ordination.’ The third is covered with red leather, without a number; it once belonged to a Carthusian, is on page 1, and is marked with the letter C. The fourth manuscript copy of the letters of Saint Gregory the Great was given to me by the keepers on 18 February 1600. It is marked with number 190 and by me with the letter D. It contains seven hundred and fifteen letters, arranged in no order and with no division into books, but all mixed together. The variant readings from the printed text follow. At the end one reads: ‘I completed the corrections of this entire *Register* on 5 December 1600.’”

If other codices later examined and reviewed by the same learned man have been added to the four mentioned, we shall note this in its proper place.

The great fidelity with which the variant readings of those codices were collected and transcribed fully convinces us of their reliability, both because they almost everywhere agree with our own manuscripts and because our Dom Claude Estiennot observed the same readings in the manuscripts mentioned above. Indeed, before this collection of variant readings, made more than a hundred years ago, was known to us, that most religious and learned man, who was then living in Rome, examined those Vatican codices with the greatest care at our request and diligently noted where they differed from the printed editions, as assistance for the new edition. When what he sent us was compared with the various readings previously excerpted, we found it to agree with them entirely.

Thomas James’s *Gregorian Vindication* offered us the variant readings of six English codices. The heterodox thought very highly of this work; but, immortal God, what is it when compared with the Vatican collection! For James concealed a great many variant readings of the highest importance, readings by which even corrupt passages could have been healed.

Apart from the Gussanville edition, the editions we chiefly used are the Paris edition of 1518, printed by Master Berthold Rembolt; likewise the Paris edition of 1571, which appeared under the care of the most learned John Gilot; and the Vatican edition. When we occasionally mention the more recent editions, we mean this Vatican edition and especially the Gussanville edition.

We must now append that part of Gussanville’s preface which concerns the letters. Concerning that preface, and concerning the notes of the same author reprinted in our edition, we think this warning should first be given: although we do not reject them, since they were approved by three doctors of the Sorbonne and sanctioned by a royal diploma, we certainly do not venture to guarantee them ourselves.

## From the general preface of Peter Gussanville

“The letters follow the dialogues. They commonly call it the *Register* or *Regest*, that is, the records and memorials of the deeds of Saint Gregory. For learned men are accustomed to study the letters of the holy Fathers above all, so that from them they may draw forth the gifts of each author’s intellect, images of his character, the sinews of his prudence, the discipline of the Church, the history of the times, and solutions to difficult questions, together with the duties owed among those with whom they maintained relations. The letters of Saint Gregory provide all this in abundance.

Who would not recognize in these written records the force and skill of his intellect, his resourcefulness, strength of spirit, Christian humility, zeal, and the other virtues? How greatly he labors to preserve and uphold discipline, as though it were a crime to dispense from the canons or release anyone from them! He does not display authority, nor loosen the reins of the will so that whatever one wishes may be permitted. Nothing bent his unbroken spirit except the clear advantage of the Church, or compelled it except urgent necessity.

He knew on what occasion that rigor ought to be softened by paternal concession—not by trampling upon the rules, but by restoring them and bending them slightly, according to the judgment of prudent and watchful charity. Just as the strictest right can sometimes be the greatest injustice, so imprudent relaxations overturn, undermine, and destroy discipline.

Let us illustrate both points with a few examples. Against the expression ‘ecumenical bishop,’ understood in its own sense, he never ceases to set the canons and the practice of the Church. He assails newly ordained bishops with the same arguments and shows favor to none, bringing against them the very arguments which Saint Gregory Nazianzen had formulated in his *Monody*, as though he had taken them from it word for word. He firmly rejected the bigamist, even though Queen Brunhild was pleading his cause, and alleged no other reason than the canons . . . .”

“I omit the rest, since it is too long.”

---

# SAINT GREGORY THE GREAT

## Register of Letters (C, G, S)

### Book One

In the month of September, indiction 9, which was the first year of his ordination.

### First Letter: To All the Bishops of Sicily

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to all bishops established throughout Sicily.

He declares that his responsibilities in Sicily have been entrusted to the subdeacon Peter. He decrees that the bishops of that province are to assemble once a year. He instructs them concerning what must be provided for and done in council.

#### Note on the title

All printed editions and most manuscript codices read *Epistolae*. In two, namely the Royal and Angers manuscripts, one finds *Regesti* and *Regestum*, which we do not deny to be the purer forms, from the verb *regero*, that is, “I enter into a codex or register.” The word *Registrum* has been established by usage, and indeed by ancient usage. See the Glossary of Du Cange, with this caution, however: among writers older than Gregory the Great in whom *Registrum* is observed, do not include Gregory of Tours. He uses *Regestum* everywhere, as in book X of his *History*, chapter 19:

“This the bishop could not deny, for these writings were found together in one of the chests, entered in the *Regest* of King Chilperic.”

And in book IX, chapter 34:

“She entered the *Regest* and opened a chest filled with necklaces and precious ornaments.”

Here *Regestum* appears to mean a chamber.

#### Note on the indiction

Or rather, in the ninth year of the indiction. An indiction is a cycle or number of fifteen years; when the cycle has been completed, the count returns from fifteen to one. Some hold that it was instituted by Constantine the Great. There were various indictions: the Constantinopolitan, according to which the years of Saint Gregory’s pontificate are reckoned, began at the beginning of September.

Concerning this indiction, see Ambrose, in his letter to the bishops of Aemilia, which is letter 23 of the first class, number 16: “The indiction begins in September.” Consult also his book *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 17.

Before Ambrose, Saint Athanasius mentions the indiction in his book, or letter, *On the Councils*, number 15, where he testifies that the Council of Antioch was held under the consulship of Marcellinus and Probinus, in the fourteenth indiction. Petavius doubted whether this passage belonged to Athanasius, *On the Doctrine of the Times*, book II, chapter 4, page 363; but all scruples on this matter are removed by those of our own order who recently published Athanasius’s works. Consult Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, volume IV, under Constantine the Great, page 144.

Indictions are found attached to several constitutions of the Emperor Constantius in the Theodosian Code. The indication of the indiction does not seem to have been attached to councils before Chalcedon, in the year 451, nor is it recorded as having been used by the supreme pontiffs before Gregory the Great.

Mabillon agrees with Cointius that the use of the indiction in Frankish documents was almost nonexistent before the beginning of the ninth century and extremely rare in historical matters; nevertheless, Mabillon maintains that it did occasionally occur, even in the sixth century, in the acts of councils and other records.

The indiction seems to have received its name from the taxes and levies imposed each year. Hence the taxes themselves are sometimes called *indictions*. Victor of Utica, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, book II, chapter 1, says of King Hunneric: “He burdened the provinces of his kingdom with various accusations and indictions.”

Besides the Constantinopolitan indiction, which Gregory used in his letters, perhaps because he entered upon his pontificate at its beginning, namely on 3 September, there are two other very well-known indictions: the Caesarean, which begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, and the papal or Roman, which begins on the following Kalends of January.

For more on indictions, see Baronius under the year of Christ 312, number 100 and following; Petavius, *On the Doctrine of the Times*, book II, chapter 40; Du Cange, *Glossary*; and Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book II, chapter 24.

---

### Letter One: To All the Bishops Established in Sicily

“We have perceived that it is very necessary” (Gratian, Distinction 94, chapter 1)—“as was the judgment of our predecessors—to entrust everything to one and the same person,” so that where we cannot be present ourselves, our authority may be represented through the person whom we appoint. For this reason we have entrusted to Peter, the subdeacon of our see, with God’s help, our responsibilities throughout the province of Sicily.

For we cannot doubt his actions, since, with God’s help, we recognize that we have entrusted to him the whole patrimony of our Church.”

#### Note on the absence of a metropolitan in Sicily

The first book, letter 18, strongly suggests that there was then no metropolitan in Sicily; so does book II, letter 24, in which Gregory orders that bishops to be ordained for Sicily be sent to Rome.

Second, book II, letter 7, to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, in which Gregory, entrusting to him the responsibilities of the Apostolic See, grants him authority to judge even minor cases in Sicily.

Third, the heading of book VIII, letter 5.

Fourth, the fact that Sicilian bishops were compelled to assemble for the Roman council either every year, or every three years, or finally every five years.

Some are troubled by Constantine’s letter to Chrestus of Syracuse, in which he commands him to take with him as companions two men “of the second see, of the second throne.” But learned men almost universally agree that presbyters are meant here, namely priests of the second order. See Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius, letters 11 and 25, book IV.

Moreover, it was the ancient custom for the Roman pontiff, in distant provinces outside Italy, to appoint as his vicars the metropolitans themselves and sometimes bishops. But in Sicily, which had no metropolitan other than the Roman bishop, he entrusts his responsibilities even to a subdeacon.

Although Gregory later appointed Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, as his own vicar and the vicar of the Apostolic See in Sicily, as we shall see below.

On the vicars of the Apostolic See appointed throughout the various provinces of the Christian world, see the notes and observations of Antoine Dadin d’Auteserre on the letters of Saint Gregory.

In any case, before Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, whom Leo the Great is said to have entrusted with his responsibilities in the East, we should mention Acholius and Anysius, bishops of that same see, whom Damasus and Siricius appointed as their vicars throughout Eastern Illyricum—that is, Macedonia, Achaia, Thessaly, both Epirus provinces, Crete, both Dacias, and so forth. See the very learned Tillemont, under Damasus, volume VIII of the *Commentaries on Ecclesiastical History*.

Several letters of Gregory to Peter the subdeacon exist, as will be clear from the index.

#### Note on *patrimony*

In some editions one finds *patrocinium* (“protection”), against the Vatican, Gallican, and other manuscripts, as well as against the old printed editions. The reading should be *patrimonium* (“patrimony”), as is also proved by the two letters that follow.

The Roman Church had patrimonies in various provinces—in Africa, Dalmatia, Gaul, and elsewhere—as we understand from various letters of Gregory, book I, letter 75, book III, letters 22 and 33, and so forth. We say nothing here of the better-known patrimonies in Italy, Sicily, Sardinia, and Corsica.

“We have also perceived that this must be done: once a year your Fraternity must assemble at the city of Syracuse or of Catania, in a universal gathering held with the honor it deserves, as we have commanded you, so that whatever concerns the welfare of the churches of that province—whether the relief of poor and oppressed people, or the admonition and correction of all whose offenses may be brought to light—you may arrange together with Peter, the subdeacon of our see, with suitable moderation.

Let hatred be far removed from this council; let it not become nourishment for crimes; let inward envy waste away; and let that most execrable discord of souls be absent. Let the priests recognize their own concord, pleasing to God, and charity.

Carry out all these things with such maturity and tranquility that the gathering may most worthily be called an episcopal council.”

#### Note on councils

How necessary councils are—both for suppressing doctrinal novelty, correcting Christian morals, and judging disputes among bishops—is clearly evident from many other letters of Gregory, as well as from the letters of earlier pontiffs: Cornelius; Julius I to the Eastern bishops in the case of Athanasius; Liberius to the Emperor Constantius; Damasus; Innocent I; Leo; and others.

—Gussanville.

#### Note on Syracuse

Syracuse, commonly called Saragossa by the Spaniards and Siragosa by the Italians, is a very famous city of Sicily and an episcopal see under the archbishop of Monreale.

#### Note on Catania

Catania is called *Catana* by Pliny and Mela, and *Catina* in other usage. It is a celebrated city of Sicily. In many manuscripts one finds *Catinensium* (“of the people of Catania”).

---

### Letter Two: To Justin, Praetor of Sicily

He friendly but seriously urges Justin to cultivate peace with the priests and equity toward all, and to ensure that the full grain allowance is sent.

Gregory to Justin, praetor of Sicily.

#### Note on the heading

In the printed editions one finds *simulationem* (“simulation”), but the Vatican manuscripts and nearly all the others support our reading. Concerning this word, which has the same meaning as *simultatem* (“hostility” or “enmity”), see what was said above in book XIV of the *Moralia*, number 73.

#### Note on the reading *in tantum*

This is the reading of the manuscripts, not *in tantum vos*, as the common editions have. Below likewise, contrary to the printed editions, *inter vos* (“between you”) should not be read.

“Since what the tongue speaks is attested by the conscience, I confess that I have long loved and greatly honored you, when you were entangled in no preoccupation with any dignity. The very modesty of your bearing required certain efforts to ensure that you should be loved even against your will.

When I heard that you had come to administer the praetorship of Sicily, I rejoiced greatly. But when I learned that a certain hostility had begun to creep in between you and the clergy, I was exceedingly saddened.

Now, since you are occupied with the care of your administration and I with the responsibility of this governance, we can rightly love each other in a special way only insofar as we do no harm to the common good. Therefore I beg you by almighty God, before whose terrible judgment we shall have to render an account of our actions, always to keep His regard before your eyes and never to admit anything from which even a slight disagreement might arise between you.

Let no profit draw you into injustice; let neither threats nor friendship turn you aside from the path of uprightness. Consider how short life is. Think upon the Judge to whom you will one day go, you who exercise judicial authority.

Therefore we must carefully consider that we leave all profits behind in this world, while we carry with us to judgment only the causes of our costly gains. We ought therefore to seek those advantages which death cannot take away, but which the end of the present life reveals as lasting forever.”

#### Note on *Citonatus*

Earlier editions had *Ciridanus*, and in the margin cited three letters written to Ciridanus—namely letter 21 of book VII, indiction 2, and letters 38 and 39 of book X—in support of the error.

But the reading *Citonatus* is established by many manuscripts—the Vatican, Moissac, Cluny, Châlons, Val-Dieu, Bigot, English, and all the more authoritative codices. It is also supported by the editions of Venice 1504, Paris 1508 and 1571, and others. Sigonius likewise read *Citonatus* in *On the Kingdom of Italy*, where he cites this letter.

The name *Citonatus* is well attested among the ancients. A bishop Citonatus subscribed to the Second Roman Council under Sylvester in the year 324. Citonatus, bishop of Caralis, took part in the Third Council of Constantinople under Agatho in the year 680. The name *Citonatus* is also found in the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, written by Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.

On the other hand, the name *Sironatus* appears in Sidonius Apollinaris, book II, letter 1. The ancients called the man *Citonatus* whose mother had given birth to him quickly and easily, almost without pain; *Seronatus*, by contrast, was one whom his mother had borne late and with difficulty, only after many long labors.

—Gussanville.

“But concerning the grain which you write about, the magnificent Citonatus asserts something quite different: only so much was sent as would suffice to repay what was owed for the past indiction and to replenish the *sitonicum*.”

#### Note on *sitonicum*

*Sitonicum* comes from Greek ἀπὸ τοῦ σίτου, “from grain,” and means grain. Sometimes it denotes a fixed quantity of grain supplied each year; sometimes a public granary, as here.

The Romans cultivated Africa, Sardinia, and above all Sicily. Cicero says in the fifth speech against Verres: “None of you is unaware, gentlemen, that the whole utility and advantage of the province of Sicily consists in grain, especially . . . . . We are fed and sustained by it.” The grain levy, which contained all the grain paid by the provinces, was established in the time of Augustus.

“Take care of this matter, for if anything less is sent here, it is not one individual but the whole population together that is slaughtered.”

#### Note on the overflow of the Tiber

For the previous year the overflowing Tiber had overturned the Church’s granaries, and several thousand *modii* of wheat had perished. See Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 1.

“For the administration of the patrimony of Sicily I have sent, with God as author, a man of such character as I believe will suit you perfectly, if, as I have discovered, you love what is right.

As for your reminding me that I ought to remember you, I confess that, provided no injustice creeps in through the snares of the ancient enemy, I have learned such modesty from your glory that I am not ashamed to be yours.”

---

### Letter Three: To Paul the Scholastic

He reproves Paul because he congratulates him on the pontificate. He commends Maurentius and Peter the subdeacon to him.

#### Note on *scholasticus*

Anyone eloquent, articulate, and trained in oratory and the more refined branches of literature was called a *scholasticus*. Thus Eulogius is so called by Palladius, and Serapion, because of the elegance of his intellect, earned the surname *Scholasticus* in Saint Jerome’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*.

The name was also applied to a lawyer, judge, or assessor to a judge. See below, letter 44; book V, letter 36; and book IX, letter 58.

In the African Council, canon 64, the emperor is asked to grant authority for the appointment of scholarly advocates. The same is established in the Council of Milevis, chapter 16. See the Code, book XII, title 62, and Synesius, letters 105, 155, and 156, to Domitian the Scholastic.

#### Note on *eminentissimo*

We follow the Roman and Gallican manuscripts and others, not the common codices, which read *excellentissimo* (“most excellent”).

#### Note on *exconsul*

Had he held the consulship, so that he could be called an ex-consul? But the consulship had been abolished by Justinian in the year 541. His successor Justin attempted to restore that dignity, though unsuccessfully.

But just as consuls and former consuls were appointed by written commissions, as is clear from Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book VI, chapters 10 and 20, so, without doubt, ex-consuls were also created by written commission, just as among us certain counts of the sacred consistory are appointed by letters patent, in French *par brevet*. This is confirmed by book II, letter 53: “He requested the documents of his ex-consulship,” and so forth.

#### Note on *domno*

This is used instead of *domino* (“lord”); similarly *domna*, *caldus*, *frigdus*, *mna*, and many others. It is frequent in ancient codices. See Ausonius Popnia, *On the Use of the Ancient Reading*, book I, chapter 5; and Gregory of Tours, “Lady Brunhild,” book IX of the *History*, chapter 20.

The Greeks also use this word, δόμνα. See Oppian, *Cynegetica*, book I. Brissonius likewise uses the form in *Parerga*, from book XXXVIII, section “Lucius,” *On Legacies*, part 2. There are several examples in the Digest. See Menardus’s notes on the *Concordance of Rules*, chapter 70.

—Gussanville. See Mabillon’s fuller notes on letter 72 of Saint Bernard.

#### Note on *chartularius*

*Chartularii* are commonly those who serve documents or charters. There were various kinds: some in the Church, others in the palace, and others in the army. There will be another occasion to discuss ecclesiastical *chartularii*.

In particular, *chartularii* are those who handle, collect, or administer the registers or documents of fiscal debts. The author of the *Miscellaneous History*, book XXII, says: “Since he was a *chartularius*, he collected the public taxes after making the calculation.” The person in charge of these was called the great *chartularius*, according to Ducas, chapter 30.

A *chartularius* was also in charge of the imperial horses, as we learn from Zonaras, under Leo the Isaurian, page 83, and from Nicetas, under Isaac Angelus, book III, number 2. Codinus, *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*, chapter 3, number 6, writes that the great *chartularius* earned that title after the *protostrator* at court. His principal duty, he says, was to bring the emperor’s horse to the palace gate whenever the emperor was departing abroad or leaving the palace for any reason.

Hence the foremost nobles of the court were granted that dignity. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapters 1 and 3, calls Narses, prefect of Italy, an imperial *chartularius*; and in this letter Maurentius is called a magnificent *chartularius*.

Gregory to Paul the Scholastic.

“Whatever pleasures arise to me from the honor of the priestly office I do not greatly value; but I am not a little grieved that you take pleasure on my account in this matter, since you know my desire perfectly and yet believe that I have advanced. For my greatest advancement would have been if what I wanted could have been fulfilled—if I had been able to accomplish the will you have long known, by attaining the desired repose. But because I am now held in the city of Rome, bound by the chains of this honor, I have something for which even I may rejoice at your glory. And because, when the most eminent Lord Leo, ex-consul, comes, I do not suppose that you will remain in Sicily, and since you too will begin to be kept at Rome, bound by your own honor, you will learn what grief and bitterness I shall suffer.

“Therefore, when the magnificent Maurentius the *chartularius* arrives, I ask you to join him in the needs of the city of Rome, because outside we are being pierced without respite by hostile swords. But we are pressed even more gravely by the internal danger of a soldiers’ revolt.

We commend to your glory in every respect our subdeacon Peter, whom, with God as author, we have sent to administer the patrimony of the Church.”

#### Note on the date

In the Tours, Saint Gatianus manuscript, this letter is written as having been sent in the month of October, indiction 9.

---

### Letter Four: To John, Bishop of Constantinople

He complains that John had arranged for his election to be confirmed by the emperor. He commends himself to John’s prayers. He promises a synodal letter.

#### Note on John the Faster

This is John called the Faster, in Greek νηστευτής, so named διὰ τὸ καταφιλωσοφῆσαι λίαν τῶν ἡδονῶν, τυραννῆσαί τε τῶν παθῶν, αὐτοκράτορά τε τῆς κοιλίας γενέσθαι—that is, “because he had practiced philosophy against pleasures to an extraordinary degree, had tyrannized over the passions, and had become master of his belly,” as Theophylact Simocatta says, book VII of the *History of Maurice*, chapter 6.

He was appointed to the place of Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, although unwilling, as the present letter shows, under the Emperor Tiberius in the year 586, when he was a deacon of the Great Church, according to Theophanes in the *Chronographia* and Cedrenus in his *Compendium of Histories*.

He was a man of great virtues. Thus Sophronius, patriarch of Jerusalem, in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 231, calls him ἄνδρα ἀρετῆς οἰκητήριον, “a man who was a dwelling-place of virtue.”

The high esteem in which Gregory the Great held John’s holiness is also shown by several letters in which he calls him “most holy”; indeed, even after John’s death, when people may truly be praised, Gregory calls him “most holy” in book VI, letter 66, at the end of which he names him “holy John.”

Isidore of Seville, almost Gregory’s contemporary, speaks of him in the following terms in chapter 26 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “John, bishop of Constantinople, of holy memory, a Cappadocian by birth, a man of incomparable abstinence and most generous in almsgiving,” and so forth. He repeats the same account in his book *On Illustrious Men*.

John was distinguished not only by the glory of his virtues but also by his celebrated learning. Witness the book *On Baptism*, which, according to the account of Isidore above, he dedicated to Leander, bishop of Seville. There are other witnesses as well; on these, see Morinus at the end of his book *On Penance*, page 77.

—Gussanville.

Gregory later reproached John severely, however, for usurping the title “ecumenical,” or “universal.” This matter will be discussed below.

In the Colbert manuscript this letter is headed: “In the month of December, indiction 9.”

“Gregory to John, bishop of Constantinople.”

If the virtue of charity consists in love of one’s neighbor, and if we are commanded to love our neighbors as ourselves, why is it that Your Beatitude does not love me as you love yourself? For with what ardor, with what devotion, [Note: [Col. 0447D] How great is the weight of the episcopate, and how dangerous it is, the holy Fathers have demonstrated clearly enough. One witness will suffice for all: Chrysostom, Homily 3 on chapter 1 of the Acts of the Apostles, where he speaks in these few but forceful words: “I do not think that among priests there are many who are saved, but far more who perish.” GUSSANV. Yet concerning the burdens and dangers of the episcopate, no one wrote better than the holy Doctor himself: at the very beginning of the *Dialogues*, in numerous letters, and especially in the book of the *Pastoral Rule*.] I know that you wished to flee the burdens of the episcopate, and yet you did not resist having these same episcopal burdens imposed upon me. It is therefore clear that you do not love me as you love yourselves, since you wished me to undertake burdens that you did not wish to have imposed upon you.

But because I, unworthy and weak, have taken up an old and thoroughly shattered ship—for waves enter it from every side, and its rotten planks, battered by daily and violent storms, resound with the noise of shipwreck—I beg Almighty God that in this danger you extend to me the hand of your prayer, since you can plead all the more earnestly the farther you stand from the confusion of the tribulations that we endure in this land.

[Col. 0448A] [Note: [Col. 0448C] The custom had become established that each patriarch, immediately after his consecration, should send to the other patriarchs a summary of his faith, so that it might serve as a kind of token of the same faith and communion. Among Saint Cyprian’s writings there are several early instances of this practice, for example Letter 42, to Cornelius. Gelasius says in Letter 2, to Laurentius: “Because it is the custom of the holy Roman Church for a priest newly appointed to present the outline of his faith to the holy Churches,” and so forth. Gregory had already said in Letter 1, to Euphemius of Constantinople: “The Apostolic See ought to indicate by letter, in accordance with the practice of those who preceded it, the priest newly appointed to it; this was once an ancient ecclesiastical rule among our fathers,” and so forth. Before Gregory, Hilary had done the same in Letters 5 and 6. It is well known that Roman pontiffs also sent kings a confession of their faith. As an example I cite Pelagius I’s Letter 16 to King Childebert, a fragment of which Gratian cites in *Causa* 25, Question 1, chapter 10, “Satagendum.” GUSSANV.]

I am sending the synodical letter with consequent haste, since, at the very beginning of my ordination, oppressed by many serious responsibilities, I dismissed [Note: [Col. 0448D] On Bacauda, see below, Letter 8.] our brother and fellow bishop Bacauda, the bearer of this letter [Note: [Col. 0448D] That is, I dismissed him. See Book III, indiction 11, Letter 48; Book VII, Letter 15; Book IX, Letter 125; Book XIII, Letter 13.]. (Compare John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 46.)

## LETTER V. TO THEOCTISTA, THE EMPEROR’S SISTER

He laments that he has been snatched from the repose of contemplation into the tumult of affairs. He compares the contemplative life with Rachel and Mary, and the active life with Leah and Martha.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0448D] LETTER V.—Concerning Theoctista, see below Letters 26 of Book VII and 45 of Book XI.] to Theoctista, the emperor’s sister.

I cannot express in words with what devotion my mind submits itself to Your Reverence, nor do I labor to reveal myself, since, even while I am silent, you read in your heart what you think of my devotion. But I am astonished that you have withdrawn from me the affection you formerly bestowed upon me [Note: [Col. 0448D] *Continentia* has more than one meaning at the beginning of this letter. In the first place it means goodwill and affection; later it means the condition or position of a bishop. In Spelmann’s *Glossary*, *continentia*, or *contenementum*, French *contenance*, is the esteem and form of status by which someone maintains his position in the commonwealth. See the extensive note of Alteserra on this word.], because of this present state of pastoral office, in which, under the appearance of the episcopate, I have been brought back to the world, and in which I serve the cares of earthly affairs to an extent I remember never having served them in secular life.

For I have lost the profound joys of my tranquility, and, collapsing inwardly, I seem outwardly to have risen. Hence I lament that I have been driven far from the face of my Creator. Every day I was striving to become something beyond the world and beyond the flesh, to drive away from the eyes of my mind every bodily phantom, and to behold the heavenly joys incorporeally. And, longing for the face of God not merely with words but with the marrow of my heart, I used to say: “My heart has said to you: I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Psalm 26:8).

Desiring and fearing nothing in this world, I seemed to myself to stand upon a kind of summit of things, so that I almost believed fulfilled in me what I had learned from the prophet by the Lord’s promise: “I will raise you above the heights of the earth” (Isaiah 58:14). For the one who tramples, through contempt of the mind, even those things that appear lofty and glorious in the present world is raised above the heights of the earth.

But suddenly, driven from the summit of things by the whirlwind of this temptation, I fell into fears and terrors, because although I fear nothing for myself, I greatly fear for those entrusted to me. I am shaken by the waves of causes on every side and overwhelmed by storms, so that I may rightly say: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has submerged me” (Psalm 68:3).

I desire to return to my heart after attending to causes, but, shut out from it by the vain tumult of thoughts, I cannot return. Thus what is within me has become far removed from me, so that I cannot obey the prophetic voice which says: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isaiah 46:8). Oppressed by foolish thoughts, I am compelled only to cry out: “My heart has abandoned me” (Psalm 39:13).

I loved the beauty of the contemplative life as though it were Rachel: barren, but seeing and beautiful (Genesis 29). Although in her repose she gives birth to fewer children, she sees the light more subtly. But by what judgment I do not know, Leah has been joined to me in the night—that is, the active life: [Note: [Col. 0449D] He does not disparage hierarchical offices, as Gussanv. pretends in his notes, vainly setting Ambrose, Theodoret, and Jerome against Gregory; rather, Gregory declares himself unequal to them. He laments that he has become entangled in earthly cares and secular affairs, which he experienced as casting darkness over his mind and weakening the clear and penetrating vision of divine contemplation. “Under the appearance of the episcopate,” he says in this very letter, “I have been brought back to the world . . . I serve the cares of the earth . . . I am shaken on every side by the waves of causes and overwhelmed by storms . . . Oppressed in this office by the tumult of secular affairs,” and so forth. He writes in the same sense in Letter 25 of this book: “Whoever is called a pastor is heavily occupied with external cares, so that it often becomes uncertain whether he is carrying out the office of a pastor or that of an earthly magistrate.” For formerly the legal cases of Christians were heard not before secular judges but before the bishop himself. Moreover, Gregory was tormented by the greatest cares because of the evils Italy suffered from the Lombards, and Rome itself was in fear, as he states in Homily 7 on the Gospels.] fruitful, but bleary-eyed; seeing less, although bearing more.

I hastened, with Mary, to sit at the Lord’s feet and receive the words of his mouth; and behold, with Martha I am compelled to serve in external matters and to busy myself with many things (Luke 10:39 and following). Believing that the legion of demons had been driven away from me, I wished to forget those whom I knew and rest at the Savior’s feet; and behold, against my will and under compulsion, I am told: “Return to your house and declare how much the Lord has done for you” (Mark 5:19).

But who can proclaim God’s miracles amid so many earthly cares, when it is already difficult for me even to remember them? [Note: [Col. 0450D] In Vatican Manuscript 1031: “Oppressed . . . by the burden of this tumult.” These words are absent from three other Vatican manuscripts whose variant readings we possess. Our manuscripts likewise do not admit this reading.]

For in this office I am oppressed by the tumult of secular affairs, and I see myself to be among those of whom it is written: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Psalm 72:18). For he did not say, “You cast them down after they had been lifted up,” but “while they were being lifted up,” because the wicked, while they seem outwardly to rise, supported by temporal honor, fall inwardly.

Their very elevation is therefore a ruin: while they are upheld by false glory, they are emptied of true glory. Hence he says again: “They shall fail like smoke fails” (Psalm 36:20). Smoke indeed fails as it rises and vanishes as it spreads itself abroad. So it happens when present prosperity accompanies the life of a sinner: by the very means through which he is shown to be exalted, he is brought to nonexistence.

Again it is written: “My God, make them like a wheel” (Psalm 82:14). A wheel is raised at its rear and falls at its front. The rear, for us, represents the goods of the present world, which we leave behind; the front represents eternal and enduring things, to which we are called, as Paul testifies when he says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians 3:13).

Therefore, when a sinner prospers in the present life, he is made like a wheel: falling at the front, he is lifted up at the rear. For when he receives in this life the glory that he must leave behind, he falls away from the glory that comes after this life.

There are indeed many who know how to govern outward advancement in such a way that through it they do not fall inwardly. Hence it is written: “God does not reject the mighty, since he himself is mighty” (Job 36:5). And Solomon says: “The intelligent person shall possess the helm” (Proverbs 1:5).

But these things are difficult for me, and very burdensome; for what the mind has not willingly received, it cannot properly administer. Behold, the most serene lord emperor [Note: [Col. 0450D] He perhaps alludes to the proverb, “You have clothed me in the skin of a lion,” which is derived from Lucian: “For so long I did not notice that beneath the lion’s skin he concealed a ridiculous sort of ape.” GUSSANV.] ordered a lion to be made into an ape. And indeed, [Note: [Col. 0450D] In the same sense Saint Chrysostom says in Homily 52 on the Acts: “A ruler is not one who has been called to the office, but one who truly is so. For just as a king would not make someone a physician or an orator, so neither would he make him a ruler. Letters or a title do not make a ruler.” Some printed editions read *provisione* (“by provision”) rather than *jussione* (“by command”), but the manuscripts do not support that reading; Alteserra nevertheless follows it.] by his command I may be called a lion, but I cannot be made a lion.

Therefore he must attribute all my faults and negligence not to me but to his own mercy, since he entrusted the ministry of virtue to a weak man. (Compare John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 47.)

## LETTER VI. TO NARSÉS, THE PATRICIAN

He laments that he has been cast down from the delight of contemplation.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0450D] LETTER VI.—Baronius wrongly confuses this man, in the year 568, with the other Narses, who under the emperor Justinian was patrician, prefect of Italy, and supreme commander of the army. The Narses to whom Saint Gregory writes was initially the bodyguard—*hyperaspistēs*, “shield-bearer”—of the general Comentiolus under Maurice, approximately thirty years after the death of the earlier Narses. Yet he was not inferior to the other in military glory, as may be seen in contemporary authors. His virtue was especially conspicuous against the Persians, to whom he was such a terror that Persian infants trembled at the mere mention of Narses, according to Book XVII of the *Miscellaneous History*. Simocatta gives an extensive account of his distinguished deeds in his *History of Maurice*. Finally, softened by hope and promises and summoned to court by Phocas, he was burned alive. Constantine Manasses says of him in his epitome:

“Phocas made Narses, the general, the wonder of the Romans,  
Food for the fire . . . . .”

GUSSANV.] to Narses [Note: [Col. 0451C] *Patricius* was initially a name of nobility, and later of rank and authority. Justinian, in Book I, Title 12 of the *Institutes*, calls the patriciate the highest dignity, one dissolved only by death; Cassiodorus says the same in Book VI, Form 2. Constantine the Great established the patricians and called them so because he wished them to be the fathers, associates, and counselors of his own and future emperors, immediately subordinate to the consuls and holding their office permanently. In the same way, Romulus treated the hundred elders whom he selected as a public council; because of their authority and age they were called fathers and senators. This was the origin of the ancient patricians.

Saint Jerome, in Letter 10 to Furia, mentions the same father as both consular and patrician. Cassiodorus, in Book VIII, Letter 9, counts the purple cloak and Roman shoes among the insignia of the patriciate. I also find provincial governors often called patricians, presumably because they were usually chosen from the body of the patricians. Certainly Fasagnates of the Armenians is called a patrician in Book XIX of the *Miscellaneous History*, where he governed Armenia under Constans, the grandson of the emperor Heraclius; and Sabbatius, patrician of Armenia, governed that province under Justinian Rhinotmetus.

Our historians too—Fredegar and others—often called the governors of the Transjurane district and of the Scutingi in Burgundy, now dukes, patricians. Saint Audoen, in the *Life of Saint Eligius*, calls the patricians of Burgundy by that name. Those who governed the provinces of Arles and Marseille for a time under the Frankish kings are called by Gregory the Great “patricians of Gaul” or “of the Gauls.” Thus in Book II, Letter 33—now Letter 3—he writes to Dynamius, patrician of Gaul, who was governor of the province of Marseille. Among us this was the title used for the governors of the aforementioned provinces.

Gregory of Tours, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 24: “King Guntram, having removed the patrician Agricola, bestowed the honor of the patriciate upon Celsus, a man skilled in legal learning.” And chapter 42: “Ennius, surnamed Mummolus, earned the patriciate from King Guntram.” Patricians were also often called consuls.

GUSSANV. In some Vatican manuscripts the reading is “to Narses the patrician woman”; in others and in ours it simply reads “to Narses.”] the patrician.

While you describe the sweetness of contemplation in lofty terms, you have renewed my lament over my ruin, because I heard what I lost inwardly when, undeserving, I rose outwardly to the summit of government. Recognize that I have been struck by such grief that I can scarcely speak; for the darkness of sorrow occupies the eyes of my mind.

Everything that is seen is sad; whatever is thought delightful appears lamentable to my heart. I consider, falling from the lofty summit of my repose, to what a low condition I have ascended through outward advancement. [Note: [Col. 0452B] The printed editions read: “to how great a fall of outward advancement,” and so forth. We follow the Vatican and Royal manuscripts, as well as the Norman manuscripts.]

Sent into the exile of office, away from the face of my Lord because of my sins, I say with the prophet, as though I were the voice of devastated Judah: “He who used to comfort me has gone far from me” (Lamentations 1:16). [Note: [Col. 0452C] The printed editions, with serious error, read as though it meant “as though of a deserted widow.” All the manuscripts contradict them.]

But since, by creating a similarity of cause and name, you fashion your rhetorical conclusions and declamations in your writings, you certainly call an ape a lion, dearest brother. We see you doing what we often do when we call mangy puppies leopards or tigers.

For I, good man, have lost my children, as it were, because through earthly cares I have lost my good works. Do not therefore call me Naomi—that is, “beautiful”—but call me Mara, because I am full of bitterness (Ruth 1:20). [Note: [Col. 0452C] The editors preferred “I am beautiful . . . I am full,” because they thought “beautiful” unsuitable for Gregory. But the manuscripts contradict them, and another passage of Sacred Scripture is offered in which *pulchra* is read.]

As for your saying that I ought not to have written that you should plow with buffalo in the Lord’s field (Amos 6:13), because both buffalo and all the wild beasts were offered on the linen shown to blessed Peter, you yourself know that what follows is: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). [Note: [Col. 0452C] The printed editions read “when you plowed with buffalo,” contrary to the manuscripts, which have “when you should plow with buffalo.”]

You, then, who had not yet slaughtered those same beasts, why did you already wish to eat them in obedience? [Note: [Col. 0452C] The reason would not be obscure if we possessed this letter to Honoratus.] Concerning the matter of our brothers, I judge that what you wrote will happen, if God helps. ## LETTER VII. TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

He finds it grievous to be crushed by many responsibilities and to be praised by Anastasius.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0452D] Gussanv. appended an extensive observation to this passage concerning Anastasius, whom he thinks was Anastasius of Sinai, famous for his learning. But Leo Allatius demonstrates in his *Dissertation on the Writings of the Simeons* that Anastasius the monk of Mount Sinai was a different person from the patriarch of Antioch. The Bollandists affirm the same under April 21. Evagrius, Book IV, chapters 23 and following—especially chapter 39—and all the historians after him recount Anastasius’ exile and restoration. Nicephorus Callistus, *History*, Book XVII, confuses not only the Sinaitic Anastasius with the patriarch but also the younger Anastasius with the elder. The younger Anastasius was the successor of the elder; Gregory writes to him in Book IX, Letter 49. All agree that the Anastasius discussed here was expelled from his see by Justinian because he vigorously defended orthodox doctrine on the incorruptibility of Christ’s body against Justinian’s delirious views. Gregory was appointed in his place; see below.] to Anastasius, bishop [Note: [Col. 0453B] “Of Antioch” is absent from the Corbie, Norman, and most other manuscripts.] of Antioch.

I received the letters of Your Beatitude as a weary man receives rest, a sick man health, a thirsty man a spring, and one burning with heat shade. For those words did not seem to have been expressed through the tongue of flesh; rather, they revealed the spiritual love that you carried, as though the mind itself were speaking through itself.

But what followed was very harsh: your love ordered me to carry earthly burdens. And you who had previously loved me spiritually, afterward, as I suppose, loving me temporally, pressed me down to the earth by placing a burden upon me, so that, having completely lost the uprightness of my mind and having lost the keenness of contemplation, I may say not through the spirit of prophecy but through experience: “I have been bowed down and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 118:107). [Note: [Col. 0453C] In recent editions, after “exceedingly,” the following is added: “For such burdens of responsibilities oppress me that my mind cannot in any way be raised to heavenly things.” The Vatican, Royal, Corbie, and Norman manuscripts reject this addition. We have also excluded below two shorter fragments from the same letter that were inserted into the text.]

For I am shaken by many waves of causes and afflicted by the storms of a tumultuous life, so that I may rightly say: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has submerged me” (Psalm 68:3).

Therefore, stretch out to me, who am in danger, the hand of your prayer—you who stand upon the shore of virtues. As for your calling me the mouth of the Lord, a lamp, and one who benefits many, this too adds to the accumulation of my iniquities: when iniquity ought to have been punished in me, I receive praise instead of punishment.

I cannot express in words the tumult of earthly affairs under which I am burdened here; yet you can gather something of it from the brevity of this letter, in which I say less to the person whom I love more than all others.

Moreover, I inform you that I entreated the most serene lords with all the prayers I could muster [Note: [Col. 0453C] Not that he should restore Anastasius to his see, since Gregory wanted to retain him in Rome; rather, that he should restore his honor. See the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 12, where a distinction is made between legal right and honor; the Council of Nicaea, chapter 8; and the Council of Ephesus, in the synodical letter to the council of Pamphylia concerning Eustathius.

The letter of the Council of Nicaea concerning Meletius says: “The council decrees, with greater clemency toward Meletius, that he remain in his own city and no longer have authority either to lay hands upon anyone, to administer, to appoint anyone to an ecclesiastical office, or to appear in another region or city for that purpose, but that he retain only the title of his dignity. Those whom he has ordained to sacred orders, however, once they have been confirmed by a more legitimate ordination, are thereafter to be admitted to communion, and they are to be permitted to enjoy their honors and perform their sacred functions,” and so forth. These words are taken from Gelasius of Cyzicus, *History of the Council of Nicaea*, Book I, chapter 33, and from Theodoret, Book I of the *History*, chapter 9.

Observe, nevertheless, that Anastasius had the legal right, though he was prevented from exercising it, since he is considered to have been unjustly deposed. Gregory of Tours, Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 20, mentions Ursicinus, bishop of Cahors, whose right was preserved, though diminished and restricted. At the Council of Chalcedon, Act 11, deposed bishops are said to possess the dignity of the episcopate and the necessary allowances: “the dignity of the episcopate and the appropriate provision.”

GUSSANV. What Gregory requested on Anastasius’ behalf is clear from the following Letter 28. By “the most serene lords” he means the emperor Maurice and his son Theodosius, already crowned, as is evident from Theophanes and other Greek writers.]

that, with your honor restored, they would permit you to come to the threshold of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and, for as long as it should please God, to live here with me, so that, while I had the privilege of seeing you, we might relieve the weariness of our exile by speaking together of our eternal homeland. (Compare John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 25; Book IV, chapter 25.)

## LETTER VIII. TO BACAUDAS, BISHOP OF FORMIAE

He unites the deserted Church of Minturnae with the Church of Formiae.

[Note: [Col. 0454B] LETTER VIII.—Minturnae was formerly a city of Latium, an episcopal see on the border of Campania, slightly above the mouth of the Liris River; today its ruins are scarcely visible. The place is nevertheless called La Scaffa, or La Barca del Garigliano, because the Liris is crossed there by boat. It was united to the Church of Formiae by this letter, but both were later transferred to a nearby place, namely Gaeta, together with the body of Saint Erasmus. See Baronius in the *Martyrology*, under June 2, where he discusses Saint Erasmus. GUSS.]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0454C] He was already mentioned in Letter IV.] to Bacaudas, bishop [Note: [Col. 0454C] Formiae was an episcopal city in Latium, on the coast of the Gulf of Formiae, commonly called the Gulf of Gaeta; today there is an elegant and pleasant village there, commonly called Mola. Horace celebrates this city and its location in *Carmina*, Book III, Ode 17:

“From that founder you derive your origin,  
who is said to have held the walls of Formiae

He also praises the Formian hills for their excellent wine, of which they are especially fertile, in Book I of the *Carmina*, Ode 20. In the Royal and most Norman manuscripts, instead of *Formiensi*, the reading is *Firmiensi* or *Firmianae*.] of Formiae.

Both the necessity of the times presses us and the diminution of persons requires that we come to the aid of deserted Churches by a salutary and prudent arrangement. And therefore, since we have learned that the Church of Minturnae has been utterly deprived both of clergy and of people through desolation, and since we have judged your petition on its behalf—that it should be joined to the Church of Formiae, in which the body of the blessed martyr Erasmus rests and over which Your Fraternity presides [Note: [Col. 0454C] The reason for unions of this kind is the usefulness or necessity of the Church. For example: 1. when the population has declined considerably; 2. when Churches have been destroyed and cannot easily be restored to their former condition; 3. when two bishops cannot conveniently be supported from the revenues, so that one may suffice for the time being. See Saint Gregory, chapters “Et temporis,” “Postquam,” *Causa* 16, Question 1, concerning religious houses; chapter 2, concerning age and qualifications; and chapter “Ea de te.”

In the same way the emperor Justinian united several offices. *Novels* 8 and 24–29. Churches are united in three ways: 1. when they are merged and grow together into a single body, so that there is one Church and one benefice; Justinian calls this *henōsis* (“union”), and the benefice is called not only *synēmenon* (“joined”) but also *hēnōmenon* (“united”); 2. when they are joined so that one is inferior and the other superior, in which case a vicar is necessary, chapter “Exstirpandae,” section “Qui vero,” concerning benefices; 3. when the same minister is placed over both while each retains its own title and rank. See *Extra*, “Ne sede vacante,” chapter 1; *Causa* 16, Question 1; and the chapter “Et temporis.”

The union of bishoprics was eventually reserved solely to the Roman pontiff. See *Extra*, Book I, Title 7, concerning the transfer of a bishop, chapters 1, 2, and 4, and chapter “Quod translatione,” in the same book, Title 30. The union of other benefices is permitted to bishops, Book V, Title 3, chapter “Sicut unire.”

GUSSANV. We shall see many similar unions below. Depopulated cities compelled them to do this because of the continual wars of the Goths and Lombards, over which the holy Doctor laments, especially in Homily 17 on the Gospels, section 16.]

## LETTER IX. TO PETER, THE SUBDEACON

That a dispute concerning the boundaries of estates should be settled by forty years’ possession.

[Col. 0455B]

Gregory to Peter, the subdeacon.

Gregory, servant of God, priest, and abbot of the monastery of Saint Theodore, situated in the province of Sicily, in the territory of Palermo, informed us that the men of the estate of Fulloniacum [Note: [Col. 0455C] LETTER IX.—The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read “of Saloniacum.”], belonging to the holy Roman Church, wish to invade the boundaries of the estate of Gerdimia, which adjoins the aforesaid estate of the holy Roman Church—boundaries which they have possessed quietly and lawfully for innumerable years.

Therefore (Causa 16, Question 4, chapter 2), we wish you, upon going to the city of Palermo, to examine the matter according to this principle: the ownership of the property is to remain with the possessor, as it has been possessed until now. Thus, if you find that the aforementioned monastery of Saint Theodore has possessed for forty years, with undisturbed right, the boundaries concerning which the dispute has arisen [Note: [Col. 0455C] Another manuscript reads “contention.”] [Note: [Col. 0455C] Just as possession of thirty years still suffices in secular matters, so it formerly also applied in ecclesiastical matters; see *Causa* 16, Question 3, chapters 2, 4, 8, and 9, and the *Decretals*, Book II, Title 26, chapter 3 and elsewhere. It seems that Gregory was the first to extend this to forty years, since Gelasius speaks of thirty years in Letter 10.

The forty-year possession is discussed under the titles “On Exceptions” and “On Prescription.” Prescription is one of the exceptions derived from the lapse of time, whether the matter concerns movable or immovable property. It should be noted, however, that a hundred-year prescription is granted to Churches and all pious places, in the Code, “On Sacred Churches,” law “Ut inter.” Attached to this is the following *authentica*: “Those actions that are excluded in some cases by a ten-year, in others by a twenty-year, and in others by a thirty-year prescription are excluded, when they belong to a religious place, after forty years, while the prescriptions of three-year or four-year usucaption remain in force; only the Roman Church enjoys the period or privilege of one hundred years.” This *authentica*, as it stands, certainly reserves the hundred-year prescription to the Roman Church alone. But if one reads Novel 131, chapter 3, from which they insist that this *authentica* was taken, one will not find there the hundred-year prescription of the Roman Church—or else I am using mendacious manuscripts. For it says: “In place of the ten-, twenty-, and thirty-year prescriptions relating to temporal property, we order that only the forty-year prescription be brought against the holy Churches and all other venerable places, the same rule being observed in the execution of legacies and inheritances left for pious causes.” Perhaps for this reason Saint Gregory admits the forty-year prescription in this passage.

GUSSANV. Alteserra maintains that the Roman Church—and indeed the Roman Church alone—enjoys a hundred-year prescription under Novel 131, chapter 6. But Gregory, less indulgent toward his own interests, admits a forty-year prescription here. Gussanv. denies this. We do not dare settle the dispute between the dissenting parties. We may nevertheless observe that Gussanvillaeus here contradicts himself: he claims that Gregory was the first to extend prescription to forty years, yet afterward praises a novel older than Gregory in which this very rule is established. Perhaps he meant to suggest that Gregory was the first of the Roman pontiffs to decree anything concerning a forty-year prescription.

On prescription based on thirty years’ possession, see Apollinaris Sidonius, Book VIII, Letter 6: “At almost that same time, he says, the law concerning thirty-year prescription had been proposed; once its decisive headings had been abolished, the entire lawsuit was prolonged into a sixth five-year period and brought to an end.” Sirmondus comments on these words: “This is Valentinian’s novel on the thirty-year prescription, applicable to all cases.”]

do not thereafter permit any vexation—even if something could have belonged to the holy Roman Church—to be brought against them, but take every measure to secure their undisturbed peace.

But if the agents of the holy Church demonstrate that they did not possess the property for forty years with undisturbed right, but that some dispute concerning the same boundaries was at some time raised during that period, let it be settled peacefully and legally by appointed arbitrators. [Note: [Col. 0456D] In the Corbie manuscript, “the agents,” as it is also read in the old edition of Rembam and in Gilot’s edition; the other reading is corrupt, for here the holy Doctor speaks of the administrators of Church property.]

For we wish not only never to revive disputes that have once been raised, but also to hasten by every means to quiet whatever improper claims are brought from outside.

## LETTER X. TO BACAUDAS AND AGNELLUS, BISHOPS

Concerning the transfer of the Jews’ synagogue if it impedes the services of the Church.

[Col. 0457A]

Gregory to Bacaudas and Agnellus, bishops. [Note: [Col. 0457C] In one Vatican manuscript and in most manuscripts, especially the Norman ones, the words “concerning the Jews” are added.]

The Jews residing at Tarracina petitioned us that the place which they had hitherto possessed as a synagogue might, by our authority also, be granted to them permission to possess it. *Note: [Col. 0457C] In Vatican manuscript D, “under the name of a synagogue.”* *Note: [Col. 0457C] The same codex reads: “that we should grant them, by our authority also, permission to possess it.”* But since it has come to our attention that the place itself is so near the church that even the voice of those singing psalms reaches it, we wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Peter that, if it were indeed the case that a voice from that place resounded in the church, the place should be deprived of Jewish celebrations. *Note: [Col. 0457C] Thus the manuscripts, whereas the printed editions read, “the Jews should be deprived.” We restore many other readings in this letter below in accordance with the manuscript codices.* Therefore let your Fraternity, together with the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop of ours, carefully inspect the place itself; and if it is such that anything seemed to you to impede the church, provide another place within the same fortress where the aforesaid Hebrews may assemble, so that they can celebrate their ceremonies without hindrance. Let your Fraternity provide such a place, if they are deprived of this one, that no complaint may subsequently arise from it in the future. We prohibit the aforesaid Hebrews from being burdened or afflicted contrary to the rule of reason; but, since they are permitted to live according to Roman laws, let them, with justice consenting, arrange their affairs as they know how, without anyone hindering them—except that they may not possess Christian slaves.

## LETTER XI. TO THE PATRICIAN CLEMENTINA

He consoles her concerning the death of Eutherius.

*Note: Letter XI. It is prefaced in the Colbert manuscript with “In the month of November, in the ninth indiction.” The two Teller manuscripts agree. We conjecture that Clementina lived at Naples from Book III, Letter 1.*

Gregory to the patrician Clementina.

We have received the letter of Your Glory, which spoke of the death of Eutherius, once of glorious memory, and we declare

*Note: [Col. 0457C–D] They wrongly suspected that this Eutherius was a bishop. Gregory never confers this title of honor, “of magnificent memory,” on bishops. I do not know how it entered the summary of this letter, unless because its end speaks of administering an episcopal residence, perhaps vacant through Eutherius’s death. But the matter is not Eutherius’s episcopal residence, but the Roman one, for whose administration Gregory had retained that deacon. GUSSANV.* that our hearts are no less confounded by such grief than yours, since we see men of approved reputation gradually being taken from this world, whose ruin is already demonstrated by the very effects of its affairs. But we ought to withdraw from this by carefully turning our minds away, lest its ruin entangle us along with itself. Indeed, the loss of friends ought to grieve us all the more tolerably because the condition of mortality requires that we shall lose them. Yet He who permitted and granted that the support of bodily life should be taken away is powerful to console us, and Himself to approach the place that had been left desolate.

*Note: Perhaps this is the same man who afterward became apocrisiarius at Constantinople, mentioned in Book X, Letter 39, and Book XII, Letter 24.*

As for the deacon Anatolius, whom you requested to be sent to you, the reason prevents us from doing this more than any severity of rigor does.

*Note: The duties of the vicedominus were various, as is shown below in several letters of Saint Gregory. Here the reference is to the one whose responsibility is to administer the episcopium. He is sometimes called the church’s steward (*oeconomus ecclesiae*), as in Book V, Letter 55, and in Frodoard, Book II of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 13. Anastasius mentions vicedomini of the Roman Church more than once in his *Lives of the Pontiffs*. This was formerly the foremost dignity in the palace of the supreme pontiff. The vicedominus had charge of the entire household. In processions he rode first after the pontiff, according to the Roman Order. Today he is called the major-domo. Concerning vicedomini, see the *Decretum*, Distinction 89, chapters “Diaconum” and “Quia”; and the *Decretals*, Book V, Title 3, “On Simony,” chapter “Consulere.” For those who paid money for such offices were judged guilty of simony. See also the *Capitularies*, Book III, chapter 26, and Book V, chapter 120. Sometimes they were distinguished from stewards: the latter belonged to the clergy, the former to the bishop. GUSSANV. Consult Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Cassiodorus mentions vicedomini among the Goths, *Variae*, Book V, Letter 14.*

For we have appointed him vicedominus, and entrusted the administration of the episcopium to his discretion.

## LETTER XII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF THE OLD CITY

He admonishes him not to continue harassing the monastery.

Gregory to John, bishop of the Old City.

*Note: Letter XII. Orvieto, a strongly fortified city of Etruria, is still an episcopal city.*

Agapitus, abbot of the monastery of Saint George, has informed us that he suffers many afflictions from Your Holiness—not only in matters that might provide the monastery with some assistance in a time of need, but also because you prohibit Masses from being celebrated in that monastery and forbid the dead to be buried there. If this is so, we exhort you to desist from such inhumanity, and to permit the dead to be buried there and Masses to be celebrated, without any further opposition, lest the aforesaid venerable man Agapitus again be compelled to lodge a complaint concerning the matters mentioned.

*Note: The chief cause of exemptions was the oppression of subjects, which Saint Gregory often recalls in these letters. This is an ancient complaint of the Church, concerning which Saint Bernard says in Sermon 23 on the *Song of Songs*: “Prelates often wish to be objects of fear to those entrusted to them, rarely of benefit … Learn that you ought to be mothers to your subjects, not masters; strive rather to be loved than feared,” and so forth. Saint Gregory was almost the first to grant exemptions to monks—not indiscriminately to all, nor everywhere, but to a few and with restrictions. The careless Gratian, in Cause 25, Question 2, chapter 2, misuses a letter of Saint Leo in order to fabricate antiquity for privileges, contrary to the Council of Chalcedon and to Saint Leo’s own letter.
