GUSSANV. We did not wish to suppress this observation of Gussanville, although it goes rather far beyond the limits, lest he have occasion to complain that its omission worked against us. In any case, it is very easy to prove that exemptions of monasteries are much older than Gregory. Certainly the monastery presided over by a certain abbot Peter, around the year 525, was free from the authority of the bishop of the Byzacene province, in whose diocese it was situated, and depended only on the primate of Carthage, as is clear from a petition by that same Peter presented at the Carthaginian council under Boniface, bishop of that city. It survives in volume IV of Labbe’s *Councils*, pages 1628 and following. In another petition, on page 1646, many examples of similar exemptions in the African Church are brought forward. What Peter, together with his entire congregation, presented concerning their privileges appears to have been approved by Boniface, bishop of Carthage.*

## LETTER XIII. TO DOMINIC, BISHOP OF CENTUMCELLAE

He commends Luminosa, the widow of Zemarchus, so that her *comitiva* may be preserved for her.

Gregory to Dominic, bishop of Centumcellae.

*Note: Letter XIII. Commonly Civita Vecchia, formerly an episcopal city of Etruria, once destroyed by the Saracens and now a town in the diocese of Viterbo.*

It is indeed the duty of the priestly office that you should extend consolation to widows and to women deprived of the protection of a husband’s authority, so that, in the place where they are deprived of human support in this world, they may find remedies through priestly protection. Therefore, since Luminosa, the widow of the most illustrious tribune Zemarchus, has entrusted herself, after God, to our protection, we admonish you to comfort her in whatever she may need, and let no one trouble her in any matter.

*Note: Thus the Vatican, Corbie, Norman, and other manuscripts, whereas the printed editions read “an honorable woman.”*

*Note: There were various ranks of tribunes: tribunes of the cavalry, treasury tribunes, tribunes of the plebs, and military tribunes. Cassiodorus’s *Variae* also mention tribunes of pleasures; the *Code*, Book XII, titles 11 and 55, tribunes of the schools and of the watch. For their office, the relevant writers should be read. GUSSANV.*

But since the *comitiva* which her husband had undertaken to administer has now, with the permission of Theodore the palatine, been assigned to this woman herself, so that she may carry it out—or to whomever she herself prefers—until the completion of the present indiction is celebrated, do not permit anyone to trouble her until she has fulfilled it.

*Note: By “palatines” here we understand counts of the lower rank, who could be sent into the provinces by counts of the first rank. Both codes have a title concerning each class. Concerning the former, see the scholiast on Julian the Antecessor, chapter 82. Palatines are those who belong to the count of private affairs or to the count of sacred largesses. Gregory the Great also mentions these palatines in Book X, Letters 9, 26, and 52, and Book XI, Letter 25. Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 24.*

*Note: *Comitiva*, commonly the dignity of a count. Here it is taken for a certain profitable administration which could be entrusted to others by the palatine. I believe such offices included the *comitiva of commerce*, the *comitiva of mines*, the *comitiva of granaries*, the *comitiva of gold*, the *comitiva of aqueducts*, and the *comitiva of riverbanks and channels*, concerning which Cassiodorus writes in Book II of the *Variae*. There are many titles concerning this in the *Code*, Books I, VI, and XII. Some *comitivae* were of the first order, others of the second, and others of the third. In many places in the *Code* various kinds of counts are mentioned: the count of private affairs, mentioned by Theodoret in Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 11; the count of sacred largesses; of the sacred palace; of the sacred patrimony; of the sacred consistory; of the soldiers; of the houses; of the schools; of the patrimony of Italy; of commerce; of the *siliquatarii*; of the sacred vesture; of the sacred stable; of the household troops; of the chief physicians; of the *foederati*; of the treasury; of the guards; of mines; of gold; of aqueducts; of riverbanks; of administration; of matrons; of customs; of granaries; of treasures; and the palatine count. Spartianus traces the origin of counts to the emperor Hadrian, who, after transferring the senate to his palace and receiving the leading senators into the cohort of his friends, began to maintain a kind of domestic senate, which was called the emperor’s entourage, and the senators themselves were called counts. The emperors used their counsel and assistance in war and peace; hence that frequent number of counts mentioned above. Among them Spartianus, in his account of Hadrian, also numbers the count of the *spatharii*, whom the Greeks call *protospatharios* (πρωτοσπαθάριον), the prefect of the royal bodyguard. GUSSANV.*

Act in such a way that you make God your debtor for these services, and that our own mind may rejoice the more warmly in the consolations you have provided.

## LETTER XIV. TO DEMETRIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

That he should receive certain men formerly doubtful in the faith, but now seeking again the Catholic communion.

Gregory to Demetrius, bishop of Naples.

*Note: Letter XIV. This man was later deposed for serious crimes, as appears from Letter 6 of Book II.*

Stephen, the bearer of this letter, when his judgment was wavering concerning certain articles of faith, had suspended himself from communion with the Catholic Church on account of this doubt, until God, the judge of truth, recalled him to the path of rectitude. You should know that, after satisfaction had been received, he has been admitted to communion in the Catholic faith.

But since we have learned that he has certain companions in his doubt there in the city of Naples, the aforesaid Stephen is also known to have promised us this concerning them: that if we should heal their uncertainty at the peril of our own soul, by placing ourselves between them, they too could immediately be converted to Catholic communion, without resistance or excuse. *Note: The printed editions read “resistance.”*

Therefore, by these letters, we admonish you to receive them into the Catholic faith and communion, as they themselves appear to have requested on the pledge and at the risk of our own faith; and by whatever means you can, recall them from darkness to the light. Otherwise, once such a matter has been brought to our attention, if we pass it over in silence, we may incur the loss caused by negligence concerning their souls.

*Note: This example of Saint Gregory teaches with what gentleness one should deal with those who return to the unity of the Church. See the African Council, canons 33 and 35. GUSSANV.*

## LETTER XV. TO BALBINUS, BISHOP OF ROSELLA

He commands him to visit the Church of Populonia and ordain priests and deacons.

Gregory to Balbinus, bishop of Rosella.

*Note: Letter XV. Rosella or Rusella, formerly an episcopal city of Etruria, long since destroyed; its ruins are now commonly called Roselle, about two miles from the episcopal city of Rosetto, toward Siena. GUSSANV.*

It has come to our attention that the Church of Populonia is so deprived of the service of a priest that neither penance can be administered there to the dying nor baptism to infants.

*Note: Populonium and Populonia, formerly an episcopal city of Etruria, where Populonia now lies destroyed, on the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea opposite the island of Elba. GUSSANV. Concerning Populonia, see Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 11, note g.*

*Note: They wonder why, when a bishop is absent for a long time, neither penance can be given to those who are dying nor baptism administered to infants—namely, those who judge ancient customs by our own and regard whatever differs from them as more obscure. I infer how few priests there then were not so much from the deficiency which Saint Gregory censures—for many could have died within a few days—as I confirm it from the very ordination he prescribes amid such scarcity. He orders only four to be ordained, and thus provides for the holy Church with fitting caution, although it was almost entirely deprived of priestly service. From Justinian’s Novel 3 it is clear that in the entire Church of Constantinople, which had been formed from several churches and contained 525 clerics, there were no more than sixty priests. We shall say more about this below. I add one point: at that time, by canon 6 of the Council of Chalcedon, no one was ordained absolutely—no one who was not specially assigned and incardinated to a particular church, martyr shrine, or monastery (εἰδικῶς); no one who had not served for several years in that same church; no one who had not first been proclaimed (εἰ μὴ ἐπικηρύττοιτο), that is, publicly proposed and examined before clergy and people. It was not as happens today, when colonies of unemployed priests migrate from one diocese to another to offer substitute service or to live from the awesome Mystery. Is it surprising that, with so many precautions, the number of priests declined? Moreover, there were then no bishops without sees who could confer ordinations in another diocese; letters dismissory—“from whomever,” and so forth—were of no use. GUSSANV.*

Moved, therefore, by the burden of such a pious and necessary matter, we order Your Love, instructed by the authority of this command, to approach the aforesaid Church as visitor, so that you may ordain there one cardinal priest and two deacons.

*Note: After a bishop had died, fallen into crime, or become insane, another bishop assumed the burden of visitation, as can be seen in the case of Contumeliosus in the time of Pope John II, and in that of Agapetus, as well as in several letters of Saint Gregory. After elections had been restored, Hincmar mentions visitors in several letters whom he, as metropolitan, nominated and delegated with the king’s approval. See Sirmond, at the end of volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, where the formulas of designation are also preserved. Do not confuse these visitors with others whom the Council of Laodicea, canon 57, calls *periodētai* (περιοδευταί), who were not bishops. Saint Gregory, however, is speaking of bishops, as does Pope John II in Letters 3 and 4, in the case of Contumeliosus. GUSSANV.*

In the parishes of the aforesaid Church, likewise ordain three priests whom you judge suitable for such an office by the reverence of their life and the gravity of their conduct, and in whom the established rules of canonical discipline are in no way violated, so that provision may be made for the holy Church with fitting caution.

*Note: There is no reason for anyone here to dream of the cardinals of our own age, who arose only much later; otherwise one would have to say that every bishop had the right to appoint priests and deacons as cardinals, something encountered twice in the letters. Thus the name is old, but the dignity is new, and the purple more recent. By a cardinal priest I understand the proper, or titular, bishop; *cardo* and *titulus* mean the same thing. Thus a cardinal priest and a cardinal deacon were those who were at the hinge (*in cardine*), that is, those who stood first in their order and were attached to that title. In legal sources I find cardinal prefects, whom Alciatus says were prefects of the praetorium in Asia and Africa. GUSSANV. *Cardinalis* means the same as “principal.” Consult Du Cange concerning the meaning of the word, and Alteserra in his notes on this letter. In Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book VII, Letter 31, the expression *princeps cardinalis* occurs.*

## LETTER XVI. TO SEVERUS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA

He commands him to come to Rome with his followers to be judged in a synod.

Gregory to Severus, bishop of Aquileia.

*Note: Letter XVI. Concerning the schism of Severus on account of the condemnation of the Three Chapters, see Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 27; Baronius, under the year 590, no. 43; and Bollandus, under 5 February, pages 670 and following. We discuss those Three Chapters in the note to Letter 2 of Book III, formerly Book III and now Book IV, and at great length in the *Life of Saint Gregory*.*

*Note: Aquileia, formerly the most renowned city of the Carni, the metropolis of Venetia and Istria. Its bishops, especially during the schism over the Three Chapters, claimed for themselves the name of patriarchs. After the schism had ended and they had returned to favor with the Apostolic See, the title was left to them and granted in the interest of peace. The city suffered various calamities from the Goths and Lombards and now lies almost deserted because of the harshness of the climate; its patriarchal see was transferred to Udine, in the province of Friuli. This Severus, to whom Saint Gregory writes, is called bishop of Grado in Letter 40 of Book II, formerly, and now Letter 33 of Book XIII, because at that time the bishops of Aquileia had their seat on the island of Grado. GUSSANV.*

Just as the Lord embraces with complete eagerness one who is walking through trackless places and again taking up the straight path, so in the end He is saddened more deeply by one who abandons the known path of truth than He had once rejoiced over one who was converted. For it is a lesser fault not to know the truth than not to remain in the truth once known. And one thing is committed by someone who errs, another by someone who acts knowingly.

We indeed had rejoiced insofar as you had long ago been incorporated into the unity of the Church; now, however, we are more abundantly confounded that you have been separated from Catholic fellowship. Therefore, in accordance with the command of the most Christian and serene lord of the world, conveyed by the bearer of this letter, we wish you to come with your followers to the threshold of the blessed Apostle Peter, so that, with God as author, a synod having been assembled, the doubt that has arisen among you may be judged.

*Note: By “lord of the world” he designates the emperor, who presided over the Romans, concerning whom Maro sings: “The Romans, lords of the world,” *Aeneid*, Book I.*

*Note: The printed editions read “that which is just may be judged,” but this is a gloss found in none of the manuscripts. We examined four Vatican manuscripts, as well as those of Reims, Corbie, Tours, and the Norman manuscript.*

## LETTER XVII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF ITALY

That the sons of the Lombards baptized in the Arian heresy may be reconciled to the Catholic faith.

Gregory to all the bishops of Italy.

Since the most impious Authari prohibited the sons of the Lombards from being baptized in the Catholic faith during the Easter solemnity that has recently been completed, and since the Divine Majesty destroyed him for this fault, so that he would not see another Easter solemnity, it is fitting that Your Fraternity admonish all the Lombards throughout your districts that, since a grave mortality threatens everywhere, they should reconcile those same sons, baptized in the Arian heresy, to the Catholic faith, so that they may appease the anger of the almighty Lord against them.

*Note: Letter XVII. In other sources he is called Antharith; by Paul the Deacon, Flavius Authari; by Gregory of Tours, Book X of the *History*, chapter 3, Aptacharius. He was the Arian king of the Lombards. Concerning his death, Paul the Deacon writes, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 36: “King Authari … died, as they say, after receiving poison, after he had reigned for six years,” namely in the year 590. We discussed the name Flavius, which he assumed because it was especially pleasing to the Romans, in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book II, where we also treated the other matters concerning this ruler.*

Admonish those whom you can; with all the power you possess, seize them by persuasion and urge them toward the true faith; proclaim eternal life to them without ceasing, so that when you come into the presence of the strict Judge, you may be able to display before Him the profit gained through your pastoral concern.

## LETTER XVIII. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

That he should provide Marcellus with what is necessary for food and clothing, and arrange for shepherds to be substituted in place of those who have fallen.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

We have been informed that Marcellus, assigned to penance in the monastery of Saint Adrian, within the city of Panormus, belonging to the Church of Barunitana, suffers not only the deprivation of food but also the severe hardship of excessive nakedness.

*Note: This is how it is written in most manuscripts. In one Vatican manuscript it reads “of the Barrolitana Church,” and in another “of the Barulitiana.” The printed editions have “Barbicana” or “Barubicana.”*

Therefore, by the present command, we must order Your Diligence to provide for him food, clothing, and a bed for continence, and for his boy an allowance of grain, in whatever amount you judge sufficient, so that his poverty and nakedness may be relieved by such provision, and so that what you assign to that man may afterward be charged to your accounts.

*Note: That is, for sustaining him in life, so that, oppressed by want, he may not perish. The Gauls use the term in the sense of “for his subsistence, his maintenance.” Gregory uses the word in the same sense below, Letter 44; Book III, Letter 28; Book V, Letter 30; and the *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 20, admonition 21.*

Act, therefore, so that you both fulfill our command and, by managing this matter well, may share in the same reward.

Moreover, we have directed you to investigate the following matter, setting aside the old custom that has now become established: if any cities in the province of Sicily are known to be vacant of pastoral government because of the sins of priests who have fallen, examine whether any persons worthy of the priestly office can be found from the clergy of those churches or from the monasteries. Having first investigated the seriousness of their conduct, send their names to us, so that the flock of each place may not remain for a long time deprived because of the fall of its shepherd.

If, however, you find vacant places but no suitable person of that dignity from the same Church, likewise report the matter to us after diligent investigation, so that the one whom God judges worthy of such ordinations may be provided.

*Note: The common editions read, “so that God may provide,” contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. The sense is: “so that the one whom God judges worthy may be provided.” Gregory often arranges and connects words in an inverted order.*

For it is not right that, because of the transgression of one person, the Lord’s flock should be able to scatter through precipitous places without a shepherd.

*Note: In the Norman, Corbie, and Tours manuscripts, “through presumed [places].”*

Thus both the ordering of the places will be advanced, and the fallen will have no hope of returning to their former rank, so that they may repent more effectively.

*Note: This word does not have a single meaning in ecclesiastical writings. Some fell into idolatry, others into heresy, others into schism, and others through bodily sin. Because they had fallen, as it were, by a more serious—or certainly more shameful—fall, if they were clerics there was no hope of their returning to their former rank, according to the discipline of those times, which the holy man sets forth in several letters. The Council of Epaon, chapter 22, agrees with the Council of Agde, chapter 50: “If a bishop, priest, or deacon has committed a capital crime, falsified documents, or given false testimony, he shall be removed from the honor of his office, shut up in a monastery, and there, as long as he lives, receive only lay communion.” Innocent I, Letter 2 to Exuperius, is strict toward incontinent priests. The Council of Neocaesarea, chapters 9 and 10, speaks more obscurely and raises other difficulties. Hence it is unclear why, at times, more leniency was shown toward those who had obtained certificates of sacrifice or actually sacrificed, and toward heretics and schismatics. Perhaps outsiders had to be attracted by any means, while sons were punished more severely. Saint Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, Book II, chapter 16, teaches that pagans and heretics should be received differently. Thus he grants almost anything to the Donatists so that they may return to the unity of the Church. Concerning those who fell through bodily sin, the diligent reader should consult Saint Augustine, Letter 64 to Aurelius, where he explains Romans 13 and asks why this kind of vice is punished by the Church more severely than others. Theodoret, however, displays the Church’s indulgence in the case of the incestuous Corinthian, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, Book V, chapter 28, “On Penance”: “But concerning the man who committed fornication at Corinth, what will they say who not only considered him worthy of the divine sacraments but also granted him the grace of teaching? When those under him boasted as though they were true, learned, and wise, the divine Apostle rebuked them, saying: ‘And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this might be removed from your midst.’ Yet after he had handed over to Satan the man who was a teacher and had dared to commit the greatest disgrace, he again snatched him from Satan’s hands and restored him to the body of the Church,” and so forth. He then concludes: “Such compassion did the teachers of the Church have. For they were spiritual physicians: they preserved the health of the healthy, but expelled the diseases of those who were afflicted.” GUSSANV. Concerning the irrevocable deposition of fallen clerics, see below, at Letter 52 of Book IX.*

## LETTER XIX. TO NATALIS, BISHOP OF SALONA

That he should restore the archdeacon Honoratus to his rank; then, if the dispute continues, they should plead their case at Rome. See Book II, Letter 18.

Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona.

Having examined the proceedings that you sent us, drawn up in your council, in which the archdeacon Honoratus is condemned, we have found them full of the seeds of quarrels, since charity recognizes nothing among you.

*Note: In many Vatican manuscripts, “is accused.”*

*Note: Letter XIX. A word common among jurists for the place where judges hear cases. In councils and ecclesiastical writers it is used for the part of a church set apart from the others, into which the bishop, priests, and ministers withdrew before and after the sacred rites. Thus in Severus Sulpicius, *Dialogues*, Book II, concerning the *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 1. The Council of Laodicea, chapter 21, calls it the *secretarium* or *diaconicum*. Sidonius Apollinaris, Book V, Letter 17, calls it the *receptorium*. Saint Gregory, Letter 56 of Book V, calls it the *salutatorium*. There was a larger and a smaller *secretarium*. The larger was properly called the *salutatorium*, because there the bishops, before proceeding to the altar to celebrate the sacred rites, received the greetings of the faithful or commended themselves to their prayers. Members of the Church were admitted there, widows made professions there, and councils were sometimes held there. The third, fourth, sixth, and seventh Councils of Carthage, the Council of Milevis, and the plenary African Council were held in the *secretarium* of the basilica, as each inscription records. So too the Council of Zaragoza and the Second Council of Arles. Liberatus the Deacon, in his *Brief Account*, chapter 13, calls the place where the Council of Chalcedon was held the *secretarium*. See Book III, Letter 56. It was located in the lower part of the nave, toward the south. See Mabillon, *Commentary on the Roman Order*, § 3. These *salutatoria* sometimes contained lodgings, as appears in Gregory of Tours, Book II of the *History*, chapter 21, and Book VII, chapter 22. In the smaller *secretarium*, the priests who were about to celebrate the sacred rites put on their sacred vestments and performed the other things pertaining to the sacred liturgy. Severus Sulpicius appears to indicate this in the passage cited above. Partly from GUSSANV.*

Since at one and the same time one person is unwillingly promoted to the honor of the priesthood and removed from the office of the diaconate as though unworthy, it is just that no one should be compelled to advance against his will; likewise, I think it must be judged unjust that an innocent person be removed from the ministry of his own order.

Nevertheless, since discord hostile to God excuses your party, we admonish

*Note: The printed editions read “accuses,” whereas nearly all the Vatican, Reims, Corbie, Norman, and other manuscripts read “excuses.”*

 you to restore to the archdeacon Honoratus his place and administration, and to have him provide services appropriate to the divine ministries in harmony with you.

*Note: Understand “the archdeaconate,” which was not, as today, assigned to a priest but belonged only to deacons, as is clear from this letter. Anyone wishing to know many things about deacons that are commonly unknown should read Codinus, *On the Offices of the Court of Constantinople*, and John, bishop of Citrum, in his *Responses to Cabasilas*. GUSSANV. Why Natalis wished to remove Honoratus from the archdeaconate by promoting him to the priesthood will become clear below. Thus Anatolius, patriarch of Constantinople, once made Aetius, an archdeacon whom he disliked, a priest in order to remove him from the archdeaconate. “He,” Saint Leo says in Letter 84 to Marcian, “not finding anything in his faith to accuse or in his morals to condemn, accomplished the deposition of an innocent man under the appearance of honor.”*

If the matter of scandal is still being nourished among you, let the aforesaid archdeacon, having been admonished, appear before our hearing; and let Your Love send on its behalf an instructed representative, so that, with these persons present and the Lord assisting us, once personal favoritism has been set aside, we may determine what is appropriate in favor of justice.

## LETTER XX. TO HONORATUS, DEACON OF SALONA

Concerning his dispute with his bishop and the custody of the Church’s property.

*Note: Letter XX. The Colbert manuscript prefaces it with “In the month of November, in the ninth indiction.” The Tours and Saint Gall manuscripts agree. In the Albani or Angers manuscript, as in the printed editions, it reads “in the month of December,” and so forth.*

Gregory to Honoratus, deacon of Salona.

*Note: The printed editions read “to the archdeacon,” but this is not found in the manuscript codices.*

*Note: Salona was formerly the metropolis of Dalmatia, on the coast by the river Salon; it is now destroyed. The city of Spalato grew from its ruins, and the archbishopric was transferred there. It is commonly called Spalatro.*

Having learned of the contradictory letters that you and your bishop sent us against one another, we grieved because charity recognizes nothing among you.

Nevertheless, we command you to carry out the duties of your order. And if, through the abundance of grace, the cause of your scandal can be settled there, we believe that you will have gained much for your souls.

But if discord has so armed its parties among you that your will must remain in the swelling of scandal, come without partiality to our hearing, and let your bishop send on his behalf whichever instructed person he chooses, so that, after everything has been carefully weighed, we may establish whatever appears necessary for the parties.

*Note: The *cimelia* here are the vessels, ornaments, and possessions of the Church, whose care belonged to the archdeacon. In Letter 50 of Book III, Gregory mentions the Church’s *cimeliarchium*. If you have the opportunity, consult Gussanville’s extensive observation on this passage. How richly the churches were once endowed with ornaments may also be understood from Optatus, *On the Schism of the Donatists*, Book I, chapter 18, where he writes of the wealth of the Church of Carthage, even while persecution was raging: “For the churches possessed very many ornaments of gold and silver, which Mensurius, bishop of Carthage, could neither bury nor carry away with him, and which he entrusted to certain faithful elders, having made a memorandum.”*

We wish you to know, however, that we shall strictly require an account from you that all the *cimelia*, whether belonging to your own church or collected from various churches, are now kept with the utmost care and fidelity.

*Note: Thus the Vatican and other manuscripts. It signifies “without delay.”*

*Note: We preferred this reading, found in the Vatican, Reims, Norman, and other manuscripts, to the reading of the printed editions: “if those things which belong either to your own church, etc., are not preserved.”*

If any of these things should be lost either through negligence or through someone’s fraud, you will be held liable for this, since, by virtue of the archdeaconate, you are more closely bound to the custody of that church.

*Note: The common editions corruptly read “as though in fear,” whereas nearly all the Vatican, Reims, Corbie, Norman, and other manuscripts read “as in the swelling of scandal.”*

## LETTER XXI. TO NATALIS, BISHOP OF SALONA

He opens his heart to him, congratulating him on his episcopate, and asks for the assistance of his prayers.

Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona.

We have received the letters of Your Reverence, which—[Note: EPISTLE XXI (formerly 20).—That is, concerning advancement or promotion, as it is also read in two Vatican manuscripts.]—gave thanks for our advancement, when they were presented by the deacon Stephen whom you sent. And indeed, the favor and zeal of charity shown therein are most worthy of belief, since the order of your pontificate prompted you to rejoice with us. [Note: The editors changed *vestri* (“your”) to *nostri* (“our”) without consulting the manuscript codices; for *vestri* is read in all the Norman manuscripts, in four Vatican manuscripts, and so forth.] Therefore, made happier by your greeting, we disclose the state of our mind: I accepted the burdens of this honor with a troubled spirit. But because I could not resist the divine judgments—[Note: It means “to resist”; see Book VII of the Moralia. *Resultatio* is likewise read in the same sense in Book VIII of the Moralia, no. 59, and Book IX, no. 22. Thus the *Tripartite History*, Book V, chapter 11: “Concerning the resistance of the Jews … they tried to resist the Romans.”—] I necessarily recalled my mind to the more joyful side.

For this reason we ask Your Reverence, in the language of a letter, that both we and the Christian flock entrusted to our care may enjoy the support of your prayers, so that by the firmness of this assistance we may be able to overcome the storms of the times. [Note: In the Colbertine manuscript these words seem to belong to the following letter. They are read in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus.]

In the month of February, in the ninth indiction.

[Note: EPISTLE XXII (formerly 21).]

## EPISTLE XXII. TO NONNOSUS

He says that he will grant Maurentius the possession he requested.

Gregory to Nonnosus.

May Almighty God reveal to your heart with what devotion and affection I am joined to you. And if I cannot fulfill this affection through letters, nevertheless, whenever I find the opportunity, I shall try to show it by deeds. Moreover, having offered the customary greeting, I inform you that, when your humble servant, Lord Maurentius, comes concerning the possession which Your Glory requested, we shall comply in every respect.

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO GREGORY, GOVERNOR OF ITALY

He bears witness to their mutual affection.

Gregory to Gregory—[Note: EPISTLE XXIII (formerly 22).—It is extremely difficult to know this Gregory’s rank from the inscription of this letter. In two Vatican manuscripts it reads “to the bishop of Italy,” as it also appears in the old Colbertine manuscript. In one Vatican manuscript: “to the prefect of Italy.” In the Rheims manuscript: “to the governor of Italy,” with the agreement of another Colbertine manuscript, the Pratellian, the Michaelian, and others. Most of the Norman manuscripts, however, have simply “to the governor.” That Gregory was not a bishop is also clear from the title “Your Excellency.”—] governor of Italy.

I have always known the goodness of Your Excellency—[Note: A title of honor which Gregory uses toward kings, queens, exarchs, and other persons of the highest rank and authority, as we shall often see below.]—but now, with experience added, I have recognized it anew. Therefore I beseech Almighty God to guard you by his protection, and to grant you grace both with himself and with the most serene princes.

But if no perversities of the people who intervene divide us—[Note: The printed editions read “divide you,” contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts.]—be fully certain that I am entirely yours. [Note: The printed editions add “and joined to you in affection.” Since this is absent from four Vatican manuscripts, the Regius, Corbey, Norman, and others—and is found in no old codex—we have judged that it should be removed.]

I trust in Almighty God that I also show this to you through the testimony of my own declaration. Therefore, having offered the customary greeting, I ask that, whenever circumstances require, you take care to refresh me by your communications.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He orders him to distribute a fixed sum of solidi to certain women devoted to God, to the priest Paulinus, and to two monks.

Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

It has been reported to us that certain women devoted to God, citizens of Nola—[Note: Nola is still an episcopal city of Campania, under the archbishop of Naples, and is especially famous as the see of Saint Paulinus.]—who are living in the Aboritana house—[Note: This word is variously read in the manuscripts: *Horridana*, *Aboritana*, and *Aboridana* in several copies—] are enduring excessive lack of food and clothing. We ought to assist them in accordance with God’s command and, with the Lord’s help, relieve their poverty as far as we can.

Therefore, by this present order, we command Your Experience to give them forty gold solidi from this present ninth indiction, and thereafter, in the succeeding indictions, to provide twenty solidi annually, which may be charged to your accounts.

Furthermore, we order you to give two solidi each, at present only, to the priest Paulinus of the monastery of Saint Erasmus, situated on the flank of Mount Soracte—[Note: It is a mountain in Etruria, today Monte di San Oreste, named after the neighboring town. This mountain has already been mentioned in the *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 7.]—and to the two monks serving in the oratory of Saint Michael, which is known to be located in the fortress of Lucullanum beside the basilica of Saint Peter—[Note: It is a small island of Campania in front of Naples, joined to it by a bridge. It is now called Castel dell’Ovo, from the shape of that island.]—and these payments likewise shall be charged to your accounts.

Thus act, so that you too may share in the reward of the expenditure.

## EPISTLE XXV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, AND THE OTHER PATRIARCHS

He extensively discusses the burden, qualities, and duties of a shepherd, and finally professes the faith according to the standard of the councils.

[Note: EPISTLE XXV (formerly 24).—We have restored this title through the testimony of at least twenty manuscripts, with which the old editions agree—the Venetian edition of 1504, the Paris editions of 1508 and 1571, and others. It is read in the same way by John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 3, and by Ivo, Part IV, chapter 117. Concerning this John, called “the Faster,” see what we said above, Epistle 4. GUSSANVILLE. In the Vatican edition “Gregory of Antioch” had dropped out. In other printed editions it reads “Anastasius, the patriarch”; we have been compelled to write “the former patriarch” on the authority of four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, the English, and nearly all the others.]

Gregory to John of Constantinople—[Note: Concerning Eulogius, see below, Epistle 52.]—to Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch—[Note: He was a monk from Mount Sinai, appointed in place of Anastasius the Great, who had been expelled by the emperor Justin in the year 572. He was certainly a man of great virtues, except that he occupied the see of a living bishop and so eminent a man. Evagrius says remarkable things about him in Book V, chapter 6, and Nicephorus in Book XVII, chapter 36. After having governed the see of Antioch peacefully for twenty-three years, he left it to his predecessor when he died in the year 594. GUSSANVILLE.]—John of Jerusalem, and Anastasius, the former patriarch of Antioch—[Note: That is, “by the same example,” namely because several letters were sent to individual persons in identical copies. The same expression occurs in Epistle 80 of this book, and formerly in Epistles 39 and 111 of Book VII, second indiction, now 69, and in Book IX, Epistle 106. Some think it means the same as *litterae pariculae* or *pariclae*, and this is the conjecture of the distinguished Jerome Bignon in his notes on Marculf. Claudius Salmasius gives another opinion in his book *On the Manner of Usury*, where he says: “A *paricula* of a document, in Greek τὸ ἶσον, is a copy transcribed from an authentic exemplar; hence *exemplare*, to copy from an authentic document, so that it is equal to the original, τῷ πρωτοτύπῳ. Thus *pariculae* documents differ from authentic and original documents, just as in Greek τὸ ἶσον and τὸ ἰσότυπον differ from ἀρχέτυπον and πρωτότυπον.” GUSSANVILLE. Consult, if desired, Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, Book I, chapter 2, no. 7. The same expression occurs below, Epistle 80, and in Book IX, Epistles 60 and 106. See the *Theodosian Code*, title “On Judgments and Judgments Read from Copies.” In another way, what *a paribus* means is explained in the Pratellian manuscript, in a note to Epistle 28 of Book IX. Antonio, the subdeacon, says that the document customarily made in the transfer and purchase of property is properly called *a paribus*, because that copy is retained and preserved both by the buyer and by the seller. Accordingly, blessed Gregory sometimes used this practice, sending his letters to different persons while retaining a copy with himself, lest his letter should be cancelled or corrupted on the journey. This note is of the same antiquity as the codex itself, which purports to be [perhaps] eight hundred years old. On this conjecture all Gregory’s letters could have been called *a paribus*. Concerning the order of the patriarchs as it is preserved here, we spoke in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book II, chapter 1; and concerning the inscription *a paribus*, we have already treated the matter.]

When I consider that, unequal to the merits of the office yet resisting with all my heart, I have been compelled to bear the burdens of pastoral care, a darkness of sorrow confronts me, and my sad heart sees nothing except those shadows that allow nothing to be seen. For what purpose is a bishop chosen by the Lord except to be an intercessor for the sins of the people? With what confidence, then, do I come before him as an intercessor for the sins of others when I am not secure concerning my own?

Suppose someone were to ask me to become his intercessor before a powerful man who was angry both with himself and unknown to me. I would immediately reply: “I cannot come to intercede, because I do not know him through diligent familiarity.” If, then, I would rightly be ashamed to become an intercessor before a person of whom I had no confidence, how great is the audacity of my occupying before God the place of intercessor for the people when I do not recognize myself as familiar to him through the merit of my life?

In this matter I must fear something still more serious. As we all clearly know, when someone who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry party is provoked to worse things. I greatly fear that the flock of the faithful entrusted to me may perish through the addition of my guilt, although until now the Lord had patiently tolerated its offenses.

When, however, I somehow suppress this fear and apply my consoled mind to the duties of the episcopal office, I am frightened by the very immensity of the task. [Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 3.]

I consider that the ruler must watch with every care so that he may be pure in thought, outstanding in action, discerning in silence, useful in speech, near to each person through compassion, raised above all others through contemplation, a companion in humility to those who do good, and upright against the vices of those who sin through zeal for justice.

When I strive to examine all these qualities with careful inquiry, the very breadth of my reflection constricts me in each one. For, as I have said, the greatest care must be taken that the ruler be pure in thought, so that no impurity may defile him who has undertaken the office of wiping away the stains of pollution even from the hearts of others. It is necessary that the hand which undertakes to wash away filth strive to be clean, lest, if it itself holds on to the mud, it soil more severely whatever it touches.

For it is written: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11). Those carry the vessels of the Lord who, by the example of their conduct, undertake to lead the souls of their neighbors to the inner sanctuaries. Let him who carries living vessels to the temple of eternity in the embrace of his own conduct consider how greatly he must be cleansed in himself.

For this reason the divine voice commands that upon Aaron’s breast—[Note: Concerning this, see Exodus 28. In Hebrew *ḥoshen*, in Greek λόγιον, and in others λογεῖον. Concerning this word, see Budaeus, *Commentary on the Greek Language*. “Among the ancients,” he says, “a *λόγιος* was one who was able to interpret and express the institutions of each nation in its native language; later all eloquent men were so called, as well as prophets or diviners. A *λόγιον*, however, is an oracle or divine response in prose, like χρησμός, according to certain grammarians, in verse.” See Philo, *Life of Moses*, Book III, but especially Saint Jerome, *To Fabiola, On the Priestly Garment*, who reads … The same words concerning the breastplate are found in the second part of the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 2. GUSSANVILLE.]—the breastplate of judgment be fastened with bands, so that the priestly heart may not be possessed by wandering thoughts, but may be constrained by reason alone. He who has been appointed as an example of life for others must not think anything indiscriminate or useless; by his gravity he must always show how much reason he carries in his breast.

The names of the twelve patriarchs are also vigilantly attached to this breastplate. To carry the inscribed Fathers upon one’s breast means to think continually upon the life of the ancients. The priest then walks blamelessly when he constantly looks upon the examples of the Fathers who preceded him, continually considers the footsteps of the saints, and restrains unlawful thoughts lest the activity of his conduct extend beyond the boundary of his order.

Again, when I turn my attention to the duties proper to a shepherd, I consider how carefully it must be arranged that he be outstanding in action, so that by living he may announce the way of life to his subjects, and the flock, which follows the shepherd’s voice and conduct, may advance more effectively through examples than through words. Whoever is compelled by the necessity of his position to say great things is compelled by that same necessity to display great things.

That voice more readily penetrates the hearts of hearers which the life of the speaker commends; for what he commands by speaking, he helps to accomplish by showing. Hence the prophet says: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who announce good news to Zion” (Isaiah 40:9). The person who employs heavenly preaching must be seen to have already abandoned the lowest earthly works and to stand at the summit of things; and he draws his subjects more easily toward better things in proportion as, through the merit of his life, he cries out from above.

For this reason divine law commands that the priest receive, separately, the right shoulder of the sacrifice (Leviticus 7:33 and following), so that his activity may be not only useful but also distinguished. He must not merely do what is right among the wicked; he must also surpass his subjects who act well in moral virtue just as he surpasses them in the honor of his office.

The breast, too, is given to him with the shoulder as food, so that he may learn to offer to his Creator from himself what he is commanded to take from the sacrifice. He must not only think in his breast about what is right, but also invite those who look upon him to higher things through the shoulder of his actions.

He must desire none of the things of the present life and fear none of them. He must despise the world’s allurements by considering the inward terror, and he must disdain terrors by contemplating the sweetness within. Therefore, by the command of the heavenly voice, the priest is bound on both shoulders by the covering of the ephod, so that he may always be fortified against adversity and prosperity by the ornament of the virtues.

Thus, in Paul’s words (2 Corinthians 6:7), “walking with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left,” when he strives only toward the things that lie ahead, he must not bend toward any side of inferior pleasure. Prosperity must not raise him up, adversity must not disturb him, pleasant things must not flatter him into delight, and harsh things must not press him into despair. By humbling his attention under no passions, he shows how beautifully the ephod is spread over both shoulders.

The ephod is rightly commanded to be made of gold, violet-blue, purple, scarlet twice dyed, and twisted linen, in order to show with how great a variety of virtues the priest must shine. In the priest’s clothing, gold shines above all, so that the understanding of wisdom may principally gleam in him.

To it is added hyacinth, which gleams with an airy color, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding he may rise not toward private favor but toward love of heavenly things. He must not, by being caught unwarily in his own praises, be emptied even of his understanding of the truth.

Purple is mixed with gold and hyacinth, so that the priestly heart, when it proclaims the highest things, may also restrain within itself the impulses of vices and oppose them as if by royal authority. Thus it may always look upon the nobility of its inner regeneration and defend the character of the heavenly kingdom by its conduct.

Peter speaks of this nobility of spirit: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). John’s words also strengthen us concerning this power by which we subdue vices: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

Scarlet, twice dyed, is added to gold, hyacinth, and purple, so that before the eyes of the inner Judge all works of virtue may be adorned by charity, and so that everything which shines before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Arbiter by the flame of inward love.

This charity, because it loves God and neighbor at the same time, shines like scarlet from a double dyeing. Therefore, whoever so longs for the likeness of the Creator that he neglects the care of his neighbors, or so carries out the care of his neighbors that he grows cold in divine love, because he neglects either one of these, does not know how to possess twice-dyed scarlet in the ornament of the ephod. [Note: The printed editions read “grows cold,” whereas the manuscripts have “grows languid.”]

But when the mind is directed toward the commandments of charity, it undoubtedly remains that the flesh must be disciplined through abstinence. Hence twisted linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet, for linen grows from the earth with a shining appearance. What is signified by linen except bodily chastity, white with the splendor of purity? [Note: So read the manuscripts and the old edition. The Vatican manuscripts and Gussanville have “shining with whiteness.”]

This chastity is joined to the beauty of the ephod as twisted linen because chastity is brought to the perfect brightness of purity when the flesh is wearied through abstinence. When, among the other virtues, the merit of afflicted flesh also increases, twisted linen gleams as one of the various forms of the ephod.

Again, when I turn my attention to the shepherd’s proper use of speech and silence, I consider with anxious care that he must be discerning in silence and useful in speech, lest he either say what ought to be silent or remain silent about what ought to be said. For just as careless speech leads into error, so indiscreet silence abandons in error those who could have been instructed.

Often imprudent rulers, fearing to lose human favor, are afraid to speak what is right freely. In accordance with the voice of the Truth (John 10:12–13), they no longer serve the guardianship of the flock with the care of shepherds but in the manner of hired servants, because they flee when the wolf comes, hiding themselves under silence.

For this reason the Lord rebukes them through the prophet, saying: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isaiah 56:10). [Note: In three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and most others: “saying, ‘You have not gone up,’” with Isaiah’s testimony omitted. This is how it is read in the old Paris edition and in Gilot.]

Again he complains, saying: “You have not gone up in opposition, nor set a wall for the house of Israel, to stand in battle on the day of the Lord” (Ezekiel 13:5). To go up in opposition means to oppose the powers of this world with a free voice for the defense of the flock entrusted to one’s care. To stand in battle on the day of the Lord means to resist, out of love for justice, those who contend in wickedness.

For a shepherd to fear speaking what is right—what else is this than to offer his back through silence? When he exposes himself on behalf of the flock, he sets a wall against its enemies for the house of Israel.

Again it is said to the sinful people: “Your prophets saw false and foolish things for you, and they did not disclose your iniquity to you, to provoke you to repentance” (Lamentations 2:14). In sacred Scripture, prophets are sometimes called teachers, because by declaring that present things are passing away, they reveal what is to come.

The divine word rebukes them for seeing false things because, while they fear reproving faults, they flatter sinners uselessly with promises of security. They do not disclose the iniquity of sinners because they fall silent rather than reproach them.

The key of opening is the word of correction, because by reproving it exposes the fault which often is unknown even to the person who committed it. Hence Paul says: “So that he may be able to exhort with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9).

Through Malachi it is said: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and the law is sought from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7). Through Isaiah the Lord admonishes us, saying: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1).

Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, so that, before the coming of the Judge who follows in terror, he himself may advance by crying out. [Note: The printed editions read “who ascends to the priesthood.”] But if a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice of proclamation will a mute herald give?

For this reason the Holy Spirit descended upon the first shepherds in the form of tongues (Acts 2:4), because those whom he fills he immediately makes speak of him.

Moses is commanded that, when the priest enters the tabernacle, he be surrounded by bells, so that he may have the voices of preaching and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Watcher through silence. For it is written: “Let the sound be heard when he enters or leaves the sanctuary in the presence of the Lord, and he shall not die” (Exodus 28:35).

The priest entering or leaving dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge against himself if he walks without the sound of preaching.

Appropriately, then, are bells described as inserted into his garments. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than right actions, as the prophet testifies: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131:16)? Thus bells cling to his garments, so that the priest’s works themselves may proclaim the way of life together with the sound of his tongue.

It must also be considered that, when the ruler prepares to speak, he must pay attention to the care with which he speaks, lest, if he is carried away into speaking disorderly, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error, and, while he perhaps desires to seem wise, he foolishly sever the bond of unity.

Hence the Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). Salt signifies the wisdom of speech. Whoever strives to speak wisely must greatly fear that the unity of his hearers may be disturbed by his eloquence.

Paul says: “Do not think more highly than one ought to think, but think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3). Hence, according to the divine voice, pomegranates are joined to the bells on the priest’s garment (Exodus 28:33).

What else is signified by pomegranates except the unity of faith? For just as many seeds within a pomegranate are protected by a single outer rind, so the unity of faith covers the innumerable peoples of the holy Church, whom diversity of merits holds within.

We therefore join pomegranates to bells when, in everything we say, we preserve the unity of faith. [Note: We always read in the manuscripts the feminine noun *cortex*, “rind.” See Book XXIII of the *Moralia*, no. 31, and Book XXV, no. 20.]

Again, when I turn my attention to considering what kind of ruler one must be in compassion and what kind in contemplation, I consider that he must be near to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation. Thus, through the entrails of mercy, he may transfer into himself the weakness of others, and through the height of contemplation he may transcend even himself by seeking invisible things.

He must not, while seeking what is high, despise the lowly things of his neighbors; nor, while accommodating himself to the lowly things of his neighbors, cease to seek what is high. [Note: The Vatican and other manuscripts have “weaknesses,” and below “the weak.”]

For this reason Paul is carried into paradise and examines the secrets of the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2 and following); yet, suspended in that contemplation of invisible things, he recalls the attention of his mind to the bed of the carnal, and, although holy marriage is intended for the procreation of children, he grants something even to their pleasure, saying: “But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render the conjugal due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:2).

Behold, he is already admitted to heavenly secrets, yet through the bowels of condescension he examines the bed of the carnal. The eye of the mind which he has raised to invisible things he bends toward the intimate matters of married couples. He transcends heaven through contemplation, yet does not abandon the bed of the carnal through concern, because, joined by the bond of charity to both the highest and the lowest, he is powerfully carried upward in himself by the strength of the spirit and is gently recalled downward in others by compassion.

Because of this compassion of charity he says again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). Again he says: “To the Jews I became as a Jew” (1 Corinthians 9:20). He did this not by abandoning the faith but by extending compassion and transforming himself into the person of unbelievers, so that from himself he might learn how he ought to show mercy to others, and might grant them what he would rightly have wished to be granted to himself if he had been in their condition.

Again he says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5:13), because he knew both how to transcend himself in contemplation and how to accommodate himself to his hearers through condescension.

For this reason Jacob saw angels ascending and descending, with the Lord resting above and the stone anointed below—[Note: The printed editions read “with the Lord resting above the ladder,” and so forth. The word “ladder” is absent from all the better Vatican and other manuscripts. It is likewise absent in the *Pastoral Rule*, Part I, chapter 5.]—because upright preachers not only seek above, through contemplation, the holy Head of the Church, namely the Lord, but also descend below through compassion to his members.

For this reason Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle. He who is caught up within in contemplation is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers the mysteries of God; outside, he carries the burdens of the carnal.

Even when uncertain about matters, he always returns to the tabernacle and consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant, undoubtedly providing an example to rulers: when they are uncertain outside how they should act, they should always return to the mind as though to the tabernacle and consult the Lord as though before the ark of the covenant, by seeking inwardly within themselves the pages of sacred Scripture concerning the matters about which they are uncertain.

The Truth himself, revealed to us through the assumption of our humanity, remains devoted to prayer on the mountain and performs miracles in the cities, preparing a path of imitation for good rulers. Even if they seek the highest things through contemplation, they must nevertheless mingle with the needs of the weak through compassion.

Charity rises wonderfully toward what is high when it mercifully draws itself down toward the lowly things of its neighbors; and the more kindly it descends to the lowest, the more vigorously it returns to the highest.

In this compassion, the person who presides must show himself to be such that none of his subjects will be ashamed to reveal even their hidden matters to him. Thus, when the little ones endure the waves of their temptations, they may flee to the shepherd’s mind as to a mother’s breast; and what they foresee will defile them with the filth of the sin that assails them, they may wash away through the comfort of his exhortation and the tears of prayer.

For this reason twelve oxen carry before the doors of the temple the bronze sea, that is, the basin, for washing the hands of those who enter (3 Kings 7:24–25). Their faces project outward, but their hindquarters are hidden.

What is signified by the twelve oxen except the entire order of shepherds? Concerning them the law, as Paul explains it, says: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain” (1 Corinthians 9:9).

We see their public works, but we do not know what awaits them afterward before the strict Judge in hidden retribution. When, however, they prepare the patience of their condescension for washing away the confessions of their neighbors, they carry the basin before the doors of the temple, as it were. Thus whoever strives to enter the gate of eternity may reveal his temptations to the shepherd’s mind and wash the hands of his thought or action as though in the basin of the oxen.

It often happens that, while the ruler’s mind recognizes the temptations of others through condescension, he himself is also struck after hearing of their temptations, because the water of the basin, through which the multitude of the people is cleansed, is undoubtedly defiled. While it receives the filth of those whom it cleanses, it seems to lose the serenity of its own purity.

But the shepherd must not fear this, because, with God weighing all things subtly, he is freed from his own temptation all the more easily in proportion as he is wearied more mercifully by the temptation of another.

Again, when I turn my attention to considering what kind of ruler one ought to be in humility and what kind in strictness, I consider that he must be a companion in humility to those who act well and must stand upright against the vices of sinners through zeal for justice.

Thus he must not in any way prefer himself to the good; but when the fault of the wicked demands it, he must recognize the authority of his office. He must suppress his honor and count himself equal to subjects who live well, yet rise up against the faults of the perverse through zeal for justice. [Note: He explains this sentence at length as an extremely serious matter, lest pre-eminence become an argument for ambition and an encouragement to domination. Read Saint Bernard, *On the Song of Songs*, sermon 23: “Learn that you ought to be mothers of your subjects, not their lords; strive to be loved rather than feared; and if severity is sometimes necessary, let it be paternal, not tyrannical … Why do you make heavier the yoke of those whose burdens you ought rather to bear?” Saint Paul went before them when, in Romans 13, he discussed the rulers of the world, who are not a terror to good works but to evil. Those who do good deserve praise, and they have no reason to fear authority. GUSSANVILLE.]

For this reason Peter, by God’s authority holding the primacy of the holy Church, refused to be excessively venerated by Cornelius, who was acting well and humbly prostrating himself before him; he recognized himself as like Cornelius and said: “Rise; do not do this, for I am also a man” (Acts 10:26).

But when he discovered the fault of Ananias and Sapphira, he immediately showed with what power he had risen above the others (Acts 5:3 and following). With a word he struck their life, which he had detected through the scrutiny of the Spirit; and he remembered that he was supreme within the Church against sins, although he did not recognize this before brothers who were acting well and were honoring him excessively.

In the one case the holiness of their conduct earned the communion of equality; in the other the zeal for punishment revealed the authority of power. [Note: The printed editions have “revealed the force”; we follow the English, Norman, Corbey, and other manuscripts.]

For this reason Paul did not know himself to be superior to brothers who were acting well when he said: “Not that we lord it over your faith, but we are fellow workers for your joy” (2 Corinthians 1:23). He added: “For you stand by faith,” as though explaining what he had said: “We do not lord it over your faith because you stand by faith. We are equal to you in that we recognize you standing.”

He likewise did not know himself to be superior to his brothers when he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7), and again: “We are your servants through Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5).

But when he found a fault that ought to be corrected, he immediately remembered that he was a teacher, saying: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Corinthians 4:21).

The highest position is therefore rightly governed when the one who presides rules over vices rather than over brothers. He governs authority well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows how to rise above faults through it and knows how, through it, to become equal with the others.

514 Thus the virtue of humility must be maintained in such a way that the rights of governance are not dissolved, lest, while some superior casts himself down farther than is fitting, he be unable to restrain the life of his subjects under the bond of discipline; and likewise the severity of discipline must be maintained in such a way that, while zeal is kindled beyond necessity, gentleness is not utterly lost. For vices often pretend to be virtues, so that stubbornness wishes to appear frugality, extravagance generosity, cruelty zeal for justice, and laxity compassion (Gratian, Distinction 41, chapter 6). Discipline, therefore, or mercy, is greatly deprived if either is maintained without the other. But both mercy, which gives counsel justly, and discipline, which strikes piously, must be preserved with the great art of discernment. Hence, when the Truth teaches through the Samaritan’s action, the half-dead man is carried into an inn, and wine and oil are applied to his wounds (Luke 10:33 ff.), so that by the wine the wounds may be made to smart, and by the oil they may be soothed. For it is necessary that the person in charge of healing wounds apply the sting of pain in the wine and the gentleness of compassion in the oil, so that what is putrid may be cleansed by the wine, while what is to be healed may be comforted by the oil.

Therefore let there be love, but not love that makes one soft; let there be strength, but not strength that provokes. This is well signified by the ark of the tabernacle, in which, together with the tablets, there are both the rod and the manna: for when the knowledge of Holy Scripture is in the heart of a good ruler, there should be both the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness.

[Note: Thus four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and others, where the printed editions have “that the wounds may be made to smart by the wine.” Below, these same manuscripts read “strictness” instead of “strength.”]

Having undertaken the burden of pastoral care, when I consider all these things and many others of this kind, I seem to be what I cannot be—especially because in this position whoever is called a Pastor is heavily occupied with worldly concerns, so that it often becomes uncertain whether he is carrying out the office of a pastor or of an earthly official.

[Note: In Vatican manuscripts 1031 and 160, “of an earthly official” is read instead of “of a worldly administrator.”]

Indeed, whoever is placed over the governance of his brethren cannot be entirely free from worldly cares; nevertheless, great care must be taken lest he be excessively weighed down by them. Hence it is rightly said to Ezekiel: “The priests shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long; but they shall surely trim their heads” (Ezekiel 44:20). For what do hairs on the head signify except worldly thoughts in the mind? Since they arise insensibly above the brain, they express the cares of the present life; because they emerge inopportunely from a negligent and sluggish awareness, they advance, as it were, without our perceiving them.

Therefore, since all who preside ought indeed to have worldly responsibilities, but ought not to devote themselves excessively to them, the priests are rightly forbidden both to shave their heads and to let their hair grow long. Thus they neither cut away entirely from themselves the thoughts of the flesh concerning the life of their subjects, nor again allow them to grow excessively. Hence it is rightly said: “Let them surely trim their heads,” so that the concern of temporal responsibility may emerge to the extent necessary, yet be cut back promptly, lest it grow beyond measure.

While, therefore, the bodily life of their subjects is protected through the administration of external care, and again the mind’s inward attention is not obstructed by moderate care, the hair of the priest’s head is, as it were, preserved so that it may cover the skin, yet cut back lest it cover the eyes. But here I see that the moderating principles of this discernment cannot be maintained, because so many dangers threaten every day that they overwhelm the mind at the same time as they destroy bodily life.

[Note: The editors preferred “most holy brother,” although all the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts read in the singular, “holy brother,” and so forth. In the individual copies of this letter sent to the patriarchs, the name inscribed was not that of all the patriarchs but only of the one to whom the letter was sent. This especially confirms Baronius’s conjecture, discussed in the Life of Saint Gregory by John the Deacon, book 2, chapter 1.]

Therefore, most holy brother, I beg you by the Judge who is to come, by the multitude of many thousands of angels, and by the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven: help through the intercession of your prayer me, who am growing weary beneath this burden of pastoral care, lest the burdens I have undertaken press me beyond my strength. Yet remembering what is written, “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16), I also offer what I ask. But I shall receive what I offer. For while we join ourselves to you through the assistance of prayer, as we walk across a slippery path we hold one another’s hands in turn; and through the great provision of charity it comes about that charity is fixed more firmly in each of us, insofar as each relies upon the other.

[Note: This is the second, and indeed the principal, part of the letter, on account of which John the Deacon, book 2, chapter 3, calls it a synodical letter. This accords with the mind of the holy doctor, as is evident from the following letter: “Just as to the other patriarchs ... I have sent you a synodical letter.” After giving at the beginning of his pontificate the symbol of faith, which may be read at the end of the letters, Gregory sent each patriarch, according to the custom received from antiquity, a particular confession of faith concerning the ecumenical councils. The same custom is mentioned in Letter 52 of Book 9: “Hence it is that whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, they send synodical letters to one another, in which they confess that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other general councils.”]

Furthermore, since one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, I confess that I accept and venerate the four councils, just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel.

[Note: That is, the word of God is partly written and partly handed down; both are to be venerated by the faithful. Council of Trent, session 4. For this reason Christ had said concerning the Holy Spirit: “He will teach you all truth,” which he teaches takes place in the sacred councils. See Acts, chapter 15: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us,” and so forth.]

I mean the Council of Nicaea, in which the perverse doctrine of Arius was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was condemned; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with the fullest approval, because in them, as in a squared stone, the structure of holy faith rises. Whoever does not hold their solidity, whatever life and action he may possess, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.

[Note: We have restored this reading from two Colbertine manuscripts—the third is mutilated—and from the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, where the earlier reading was: “the rule of every life and action is established.” “Whoever ...”]

I likewise venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called the letter of Ibas, although full of error, was rejected.

[Note: This letter was read at the Council of Chalcedon, Act 10, and the legates of the supreme pontiff judged it as follows: “Having reread the documents, we recognized, in accordance with the judgment of the most reverend bishops, that the most reverend Ibas was rightly approved as innocent; for, having reread his letter, we recognized that he was orthodox, and therefore we decree,” and so forth.]

Theodore is proved to have fallen into the impiety of unbelief by separating the person of the Mediator of God and human beings into two subsistences.

[Note: The printed editions carelessly have “in two substances.”]

The writings of Theodoret, by which the faith of blessed Cyril is criticized, are also rejected as produced with the audacity of madness. Whatever persons the aforesaid venerable councils reject, I reject; those whom they venerate, I embrace. Since they were established by universal consent, whoever dares either to dissolve what they bind or to bind what they dissolve destroys himself, not them.

[Note: This passage is quoted, with a slight alteration, in Distinction 15, chapter “Sicut.” From it theologians conclude that the authority of synodal acts flows from communion with the saints and from Catholic consensus, which Saint Leo, Letter 61, calls unanimity.]

Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema. But whoever holds the faith of the aforesaid synods, peace be with him from God the Father through Jesus Christ, his Son, who with him lives and reigns, God consubstantial with him in the unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## LETTER XXVI. TO ANASTASIUS, PATRIARCH OF ANTIOCH

He complains about the burden of pastoral care.

Gregory to Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch.

[Note: Letter 26, formerly 25. The seventh letter of this book is composed in almost the same words; there we noted that it had not been sent to Anastasius. In this letter we have made many corrections, chiefly from the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts, among which there is almost everywhere remarkable agreement.]

I found the writings of Your Beatitude as a weary man finds rest, as a sick man finds health, as a thirsty man finds a spring, and as one burning with heat finds shade. For those words did not seem to have been expressed through the tongue of the flesh, since they disclosed the spiritual love that you bore, as though the mind itself were speaking through itself.

But what followed was very hard, because your love commanded me to carry earthly burdens. You who had previously loved me spiritually afterward, as I think, loving me temporally, pressed me down to the earth by placing a burden upon me, so that, having utterly lost all uprightness of mind and having lost the sharpness of contemplation, I say—not through the spirit of prophecy but through experience: “I am bowed down and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 118:107). For such burdens of business weigh me down that my mind is in no way raised toward higher things. I am shaken by many waves of affairs, and after those periods of quiet leisure I am afflicted by the storms of a tumultuous life, so that I rightly say: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Psalm 68:3).

To me, then, who am in danger, extend the hand of your prayer—you who stand upon the shore of virtues. But when you call me the mouth of the Lord and a lamp, and affirm that by speaking I benefit many and can shine upon many, you have, I confess, brought my own judgment of myself into the greatest uncertainty.

For I consider who I am and find nothing in myself corresponding to this sign of goodness. Yet I consider who you are, and I do not think that you can lie. When I want to believe what you say, my weakness contradicts me. When I want to argue against what is said in my praise, your holiness contradicts me. But I beg you, holy man, let us reach some agreement concerning this conflict of ours, so that, even if what you say is not so, it may be so because you say it.

Furthermore, just as I sent a synodical letter to the other patriarchs, your fathers, so I have sent one to you, because for me you have always been what you received by the gift of almighty God that you are, not what you are thought not to be by human will.

[Note: He subtly distinguishes between bishops who are from God and those who are from human beings, while nevertheless treating both as legitimate. Those who make decisions about every matter according to the highest technical points of law, and thereby prepare a path for schisms and disputes through rash and insufficiently cautious zeal, do not seem to have noticed this adequately.]

I have entrusted the bearer of this letter, Boniface, the defensor, with certain matters that he ought to disclose more privately to Your Holiness.

[Note: He is elsewhere called procurator, syndicus, or ἔκδικος (“defender”). This word did not always have the same meaning. Under Justinian, a defender of the Church was called ἐκκλησιέκδικος (“church-defender”) in Novel 56. Codinus, Suidas, and Balsamon read δεφένσωρ (“defensor”). Some defended criminal causes, others civil causes, and others the poor against the powerful. Some were judges. See the Council of Africa, canon 42, concerning defenders of churches to be requested from the emperors. This is how the ancient Code of the Roman Church reads. The office of the defenders of the Roman Church was chiefly to watch over the defense and interests of the poor and of the churches, and to administer the patrimonies of the Roman Church situated in various provinces. Gregory the Great instituted seven regional defenders; see Book 8, Letter 14. See also Cangianus, Glossary.]

I have sent you, as a lover of yours, the keys of blessed Peter the apostle, which, when placed upon the sick, commonly shine forth through many miracles.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 23; book 4, chapter 25.)

## LETTER XXVII. TO ANASTASIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CORINTH

He mournfully reports his ordination and commends Boniface the defensor.

Gregory to Anastasius, archbishop of Corinth.

[Note: Letter 27, formerly 26. Corinth is a city especially well known from the letters of the apostle Paul. Horace, Book 1, Ode 7, calls it “two-seaed,” and in Greek διθάλασσος, because it lies on an isthmus that separates two seas by narrow passages, one to the east and the other to the west; hence the Greek διθάλασσος, “between two seas.”]

The judgments of God are as much to be feared by human understanding as they are impossible to investigate. Since mortal reason cannot comprehend them, it must necessarily bow beneath them with the neck of a humble heart, so that, wherever the will of the Ruler leads it, it may follow with obedient steps of the mind.

But, considering my weakness and recognizing that I could not attain the summit of the apostolic see, I preferred to avoid this burden, lest I should succumb in pastoral government through the action of an administration beyond my strength. But because it is not possible to oppose the decree of the Lord who disposes all things, I obediently followed what the merciful hand of the Ruler wished to accomplish in me.

[Note: Although there are many apostolic churches, because they were founded by apostles, the Roman Church is called “the apostolic see” by antonomasia.
