Hence the Roman bishop is simply called “the apostolic,” even by the Greeks, as we have shown in the notes to the Life of Saint Gregory by Paul the Deacon.]

For it was necessary to inform your fraternity—even if the present occasion had not arisen—that, although I am unworthy, the Lord has deigned to place me over the apostolic see. Since both the matter itself demanded this and the occasion had arisen through the arrival of the bearer of this letter, Boniface the defensor, we took care not only to fulfill the desires of charity toward your fraternity in writing, but also to report my ordination, which we believe was something you desired.

[Note: Concerning him, see the preceding letter.]

Therefore, let your charity gladden us through a reciprocal letter concerning the unity of the Church and the desired news of your well-being, so that the bodily absence which the separation of places makes us endure may be made present to us through an exchange of writings.

We also exhort you: since we have sent the bearer of this letter, mentioned above, to the feet of our most gracious prince for certain necessary matters, and since the instability of the times commonly generates many obstacles to travel, let your priestly affection provide whatever he may need either for the arrangements of his journey by land or for securing passage by ship, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, he may complete the journey assigned to him more quickly.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 64.)

## LETTER XXVIII. TO SEBASTIAN, BISHOP OF RHISINUM

He seeks to discover the mind of Anastasius, the patriarch expelled from his see, whom he wished to live with him in his honor.

Gregory to Sebastian, bishop of Rhisinum.

[Note: Letter 28, formerly 27. Rhisinum, commonly Risine, was formerly an episcopal city in the province of Dalmatia, in Western Illyricum, on the Adriatic Sea, according to Holstenius in his notes on Sacred Geography. Some wish to place it at the innermost recess of the Rhisonian Gulf, now called the Gulf of Cattaro; others on the coast, not far from ancient Epidaurus, distinguishing it from Rezana by placing it between Epidaurus to the north and Arsecinium to the south. In time the episcopal see was transferred to Castrum Novum and became subject to the archbishop of Epidaurus, or Ragusa, under Turkish rule. Gussanville. The name of this city is difficult to establish, as is the title of the letter, from the manuscripts. In Vatican manuscript D it reads “to the bishop of Poresmium,” as also in the Rheims and Gemetic manuscripts. In Vatican C, “to the provost of Resmium.” In Vatican B, “to the bishop of Resmium,” which is read in most manuscripts, namely Colbertine, Corbie, and Norman; nowhere, however, is “Rhisinum” found. Yet “Risimiensis” occurs in one or another Vatican manuscript. In the Royal manuscripts it reads “Serminensis.”]

Although I have deserved to receive no writings from Your Beatitude, nevertheless I do not forget even one who forgets me; I rouse one who is negligent and disturb one who is sluggish with the goads of love, so that whoever does not wish to offer something of himself may at least, when urged, know how to return what he owes.

Furthermore, I inform you that I made a petition to my most pious lords, filled with the strongest prayers, asking that they should send the most blessed lord Anastasius, patriarch, after granting him the use of the pallium, with me to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass. Thus, if he were not permitted to return to his see, he might at least live with me in his honor.

[Note: Whether the use of the pallium should be distinguished from the pallium itself, and whether permission for both should be sought from the emperor, is left to the reader. The fortunes of the pallium have varied, and after so many classical authorities it is tiresome to repeat them. Whoever knows its form, origin, use, privilege, and necessity knows enough. The title in the Decretals concerning the authority and use of the pallium teaches a few things, leaves more to our investigation, and raises many difficulties, as does the letter of Paschal II to the bishop of Palermo concerning the election and authority of the elected, chapter 4.

Saint Gregory affirms at a synod that the pallium was given for money; Zacharias denies this. No one who has read the Eighth Council of Constantinople, canon 27 in Latin and canon 14 in Greek, and the Fourth Lateran Council under Innocent IV, canon 5, will deny that it was granted not only to metropolitans but also to bishops—rarely in the West and commonly in the East. In the age of Gregory I, the honor of the pallium did not yet belong to all metropolitans. In the time of Gregory VII, no archbishop was permitted to carry out his office without the pallium, although it could not be obtained without first giving an oath of fidelity. The use and manner of using it were disputed many times, as though for altar and hearth. Thus the fullness of the authority conferred by this insignia was not always and everywhere the same. Scholars disagree as to whether it originated with the emperors. Certainly, in Liberatus’s Breviary, chapter 21, it is returned to the emperor by a bishop. Vigilius grants it to Auxanius, and Saint Gregory to Syagrius, only with the emperor’s consent. The one who first uncovers the originator of the pallium will easily untie this knot.

Is its form the same among Latins and Greeks? In the Eighth Council of Constantinople, canon 14, it is called ὠμοφόριον, “shoulder-garment.” The Latins translate this as pallium. Concerning the omophorion, see Codinus, On the Office of the Court of Constantinople; Malaxos, Life of the Patriarchs; and Balsamon, Response 26 to the patriarch of Alexandria. It represented the figure of a lamb, εἰς τύπον τοῦ ἀγνοῦ, “as a type of the lamb.” Germanus, in his Ecclesiastical History, distinguishes between the patriarchal and episcopal omophorion. The latter had crosses woven into it: ἔχει δὲ καὶ σταυρούς, “and it also has crosses.” Hence it may have been called πολυσταύριον, “the many-crossed garment,” in which there were τριγώνια, “triangles,” or γαμμάδια, “gamma-shaped ornaments.” Other words for ornaments of a not dissimilar kind also occur, such as ῥάβδος, “rod,” and σάκκος, “sackcloth garment.” Let the reader consult Liutprand, Embassy to Nicephorus Phocas; Procopius, Book 14, chapter 12; and the Decree, Distinction 10. I would also add Saint Peter Damian, Book 7, Letter 4, to the empress Agnes, if he had weighed the truth more carefully and been free of prejudices. Gussanville. Here Gussanville raises many doubts and resolves few. This subject is discussed again in Letter 11 of Book 9. Meanwhile, consult Menard’s note 782 on the Book of Sacraments.]

But whatever the reason was for my retaining these writings, the bearer of this letter will make known to you. Nevertheless, learn the mind of that same lord Anastasius, and report to me in your letters whatever he thinks about this matter.

## LETTER XXIX. TO ARISTOBULUS, FORMER PREFECT AND ANTIGRAPHUS

He consoles him and asks that, when translating his letters from Latin into Greek, he render not the words but the meaning.

Gregory to Aristobulus, former prefect and antigraphus.

[Note: Letter 29, formerly 28. Perhaps this is the Aristobulus mentioned by Simocatta, Book 3 of the History of Maurice, chapter 3. Since he was superintendent of the imperial household—called prefect of the palace or curopalates, τῆς βασιλικῆς οἰκίας προεστῶτα, “one set over the imperial household”—he was sent by the emperor Maurice to the army to calm the revolt that had arisen among the soldiers, softening their harsh and implacable minds partly by words and partly by gifts. Gussanville.]

[Note: “Antigraphus” signifies a chancellor or notary. In Greek, ἀντιγραφεὺς, “one who writes copies or replies,” means a copyist, responder, or writer of replies. Budaeus, in his notes on the Pandects, under the title “On the Office of the Quaestor,” says that the Greek called counter-checkers, in French contrôleurs, ἀντιγραφεῖς, while their writings were called ἀντίγραφα, as though “counter-written.” Ἀντιγραφεῖς (“copyists or responders”) were also called masters of the archives. Ἀντιγράφειν (“to revise and write a reply”) means to revise and write a reply; someone who revised his own work with the intention of correcting it was said to rewrite it. By the skill of the antigraphi the emperor’s ordinances, letters, responses, and rescripts were drafted: they supplied only the meaning, not the handwriting. After dictating, they reviewed and corrected what had been dictated when the scribes and archivists read it back. See more in Hofmann’s Lexicon. That he also served as an interpreter is shown by these words: “If it should happen that I receive a lengthy letter to interpret,” and so forth.]

To fulfill my affection, language, I confess, is insufficient; but whatever I feel about you, your own affection expresses better to you. I have heard, however, that you are suffering certain adversities. Yet I am not greatly saddened by this, because often a ship that could have reached the open sea through favorable conditions is driven back at the very beginning of its voyage by an adverse wind, but, driven back, is recalled to port.

Furthermore, if it should happen that you receive my lengthy letter for translation, I ask you to transfer not word for word but meaning from meaning, because often, when the exactness of words is attended to, the force of the meaning is lost.

## LETTER XXX. TO ANDREW, THE ILLUSTRIOUS

He grieves over his elevation to the episcopate and sends him a key from the body of Saint Peter.

Gregory to Andrew, the illustrious.

[Note: Letter 30, formerly 29. This title was assigned to prefects of the praetorium, commanders of soldiers, and other persons of high dignity. Indeed, until the kings of the Franks were called “Most Christian” by the Roman pontiffs, they gloried in this title, “Illustrious Man,” as is evident from their charters. The formula by which the title “illustrious” or “illustrated” was conferred may be found in Cassiodorus, Book 6 of the Variæ, formula 11. The printed editions read “to Andrew the illustrious of Debiria,” but the last words are absent from all the manuscripts we have consulted. In the Andegavian manuscript “Illyrian” is read instead of “illustrious.”]

May almighty God show your most gentle heart that, although absent in body, I have not withdrawn in spirit from your charity. For even if I wished to, I could not forget your goodness. But if you love me, mourn that you know I have reached the rank of the episcopate, because the occupations of this world are so great in this office that I see myself almost separated from the love of God through the episcopal order. I mourn this incessantly and ask you to entreat the Lord for me.

Furthermore, I have sent you the most sacred key from the body of the holy apostle Peter, which, when placed upon the sick, commonly shines forth through many miracles; for it also contains within it something from his chains.

[Note: The same is said in the following letter; Book 3, Letter 33; Book 6, Letter 6; Book 11, Letter 14; and Book 12, Letter 7. With similar religious devotion, for protection and safekeeping, it was customary to wear the Gospels suspended around the neck. John Chrysostom, Homily 19 to the people of Antioch. Alteserra.]

Therefore, may those same chains that held that holy neck, when suspended, sanctify your neck.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 50.)

## LETTER XXXI. TO JOHN, FORMER CONSUL, PATRICIAN, AND QUAESTOR

He sends him the key of Saint Peter and something from his chains.

Gregory to John, former consul, patrician, and quaestor.

[Note: Letter 31, formerly 30. Concerning this title, see note c on Letter 3 of this book.]

[Note: Concerning the dignity of the patriciate, see Cassiodorus, Book 6 of the Variæ, formula 2. See also the Life of Cassiodorus written by us in French, Book 1, chapter 5, number 6.]

Having experienced the goodness of Your Excellence, I am bound to you by such love that your memory can in no way be erased from my heart. Yet I am not a little saddened by this love, because you learned that I was seeking quiet and have led me into disturbance. Since you did this with a good intention, may almighty God repay you with eternal blessings; but may he release me from the danger of this position as he wills, because, as my sins deserved, I have become not a bishop of the Romans but a bishop of the Lombards, whose agreements are swords and whose favor is punishment.

[Note: Synthiciae are agreements and contracts, from the Greek συνθήκη. Spatha means sword, hence spatharius. See concerning this word chapter 14 of Book 2 of the Dialogues. The meaning, therefore, is this: the agreements and contracts of the Lombards—that is, all the rights that among the Romans are established through agreements and contracts—are enforced by violence and the sword.]

Behold where your patronage has brought me. Every day I groan, pressed down by occupations, and cannot breathe. But you, who are still able to do so, flee the occupations of this world, because, as I see, the more a person advances in it, the farther he declines from the love of God.

[Note: Let clerics take note that this was said to a layman. Gussanville.]

Furthermore, I have sent you the most sacred key from the body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which, when placed upon the sick, commonly shines forth through many miracles; for it also contains within it something from his chains. Therefore, may those same chains that held that holy neck, when suspended, sanctify your neck.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 51.)

## LETTER XXXII. TO PHILIP, COUNT OF THE EXCUBITORES

He explains why he finally consented to the episcopate and commends the affairs of Italy.

Gregory to Philip, count of the excubitores.

[Note: He was prefect of the soldiers or guards who kept watch at night in the imperial palace. See Simocatta, Book 3, chapter 11. Gussanville.]

[Col. 0484B]

Insofar as a human being is unable to examine and investigate heavenly judgments, he must bend the neck of his heart beneath them, so that, because he does not know by what judgment what is assigned to him is arranged, he may be found neither brazen in seeking a position nor obstinate in rejecting it.

Therefore, although unworthy to undertake the burdens of the episcopate, I submitted myself to the command of almighty God and to your will. You wished me to preside over it more by the abundance of grace than by the judgment of my merits. For God, on whose account you love me though I am unworthy, is able to repay you this kindness forever, so that the grace you show toward his unworthy servants may earn for you a far greater reward from him.

I ask Your Excellence to keep the affairs of Italy commended to you, so that, while you freely assist those who make petitions, you may obtain as quickly as possible everything you ask from God.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book 1, chapter 54.)

## LETTER XXXIII. TO ROMANUS, PATRICIAN AND EXARCH OF ITALY

He asks that Blandus the bishop either be judged in a synod or be permitted to return to his church.

Gregory to Romanus, patrician and exarch of Italy.

[Note: Letter 33, formerly 32. He was the third exarch of Italy, appointed by the emperor Maurice in place of Smaragdus. He died at Ravenna in 598, where at that time the seat of the exarchs of Italy was located. He is mentioned by Paul the Deacon in his History of the Lombards and by Rubeus in his History of Ravenna. Gussanville.]

[Note: An exarch is exactly the same as a prefect, ἔξαρχος, apparently derived from ἐκ τοῦ ἄρχοντος, “from the ruler,” because he was sent by the emperor to govern Italy. He was the highest magistrate, namely one who represented the emperor and possessed supreme authority in the province. Thus we read of the exarch of Italy, the exarch of Africa, and so forth. He was called the exarch of Ravenna because the exarch, or prefect, of Italy had his seat in the city of Ravenna. The first to bear the name of exarch was Longinus, who was sent by the emperor Justin to protect Italy against the Lombards. See Paul the Deacon, History of the Lombards, and Jerome Rubeus, History of Ravenna. Gussanville.

Here Gussanville seems to make the prefect and exarch of Italy one and the same supreme magistrate; but this is incorrect, since Italy had exarchs and prefects at the same time, as is clear from Gregory’s letters. Above, Letter 23 is addressed to Gregory, “overseer,” or prefect, of Italy. Below, in Letters 37 and 38, George is called prefect of Italy, while Romanus is exarch. In Book 5, Letter 1, to John, bishop of Ravenna, we read: “But through the most excellent Romanus, the patrician, and through the most eminent prefect, and through the other noblemen of his city,” and so forth. In Book 5, Letter 40, we read that Gregory the prefect endured the labors of watchfulness and the guarding of the city during the Roman siege; that is, he was prefect of the city. Concerning the city prefect, see Cassiodorus, Variæ, Book 6, formula 4: “Not only Rome has been entrusted to your authority, but the ancient laws have also wished your power to extend within the hundred-mile jurisdiction ... You also hear appeals from the designated provinces.” The urban prefect demanded the accounts from the prefect of the grain supply. Below, Letter 37: “But so that the glorious man Maurilius, former prefect, may set out his accounts without suspicion of oppression, and so that the aforesaid excellent man Domnus Georgius, the prefect, may execute his accounts without injury to his reputation.” See Book 10, Letter 21. Gussanville adds much concerning ecclesiastical exarchs, but it does not belong to this place.]

Writing to Your Excellency: even if no reason at all [Col. 0485A] were available, we ought nevertheless, out of fatherly charity, to be concerned for the security of your welfare, so that we may learn through frequent messengers what we desire to hear about you.

Moreover, it has reached us that Blandus, bishop of the city of Hortanum [Note: [Col. 0485C] Hortanum, Orta in Paulus the Deacon, commonly Orta, was formerly a city of Etruria on the river Tiber, now a town in the Patrimony of Saint Peter, whose episcopal see was transferred to the city of Castellana, Città di Castello. GUSSANVILLE. In three Vatican manuscripts it is written Hortonensis.] has now for a long time been detained by Your Excellency in the city of Ravenna, [p. 522] with the result that the Church, lacking a rector, and the people, like a flock without a shepherd, are wasting away, and that infants there [Note: [Col. 0485C] Why did infants die without baptism when the bishop was absent? Because the ordinary minister of baptism is the bishop, and formerly there was a baptistery only in that church of the city where the bishop had his seat; even today at Florence, Pisa, Parma, Padua, Bologna, and elsewhere, infants are ordinarily immersed in the sacred waters only in the baptisteries of the cathedral churches. Both points are established by Josephus Vicecomes, *On the Ancient Rites and Ceremonies of Baptism*, book I, chapter 8; Mabillon also observed the same in his *Italian Journey*, no. 25. The bishop himself celebrated the baptism of infants, as may be seen in Gregory’s *Sacramentary*, in the chapter on Holy Saturday. “A trace of this custom,” says the aforementioned Vicecomes, book I, chapter 28, “still remains at Milan, where infants born during the week immediately preceding Easter or Pentecost are ordered to be brought to the principal church of the city, so that the archbishop of that church may administer baptism to them according to the solemn rite; and it is prescribed that every priest, both of the city and of the diocese, abstain from that solemnity” (*Fourth Provincial Council*). Yet it is known from Jerome’s *Dialogue against the Luciferians* that in earlier centuries priests baptized outside the cities; indeed, they sometimes baptized even in the episcopal city, though not without the bishop’s authorization, as Tertullian says, *On Baptism*, chapter 17. Certainly, in former times baptism was celebrated only by the bishop’s command, as Ignatius testifies in his *Letter to the Smyrnaeans*: “It is not permitted to baptize without the bishop.” Here Gussanville asks why infants are said to die without baptism, since, according to Tertullian’s own testimony, any traveler of either sex could baptize them. The question is clever in appearance but actually futile, since it is sufficiently and abundantly clear that people do not always do what they could do, as examples will make plain. Without a judge, anyone could assign each person his right; without a leader, brave soldiers equipped with weapons could rout the enemy; any Christian could learn what is necessary from any educated person, even if the shepherd were absent or asleep. Yet let us suppose that there were no judge: immediately the unjust would rage with impunity; no leader: the army would be routed; no shepherd: error, ignorance, and impiety would grow strong. In the same way, any believer without the care of a bishop can repent, live well, and baptize in an emergency. Yet few repent, few live well, and few baptize unless a shepherd is present. The canons ordered baptism to be delayed; during so long a delay there was danger, compounded by negligence concerning both one’s own and another’s salvation. I do not discuss Tertullian’s intention, which the reader may perhaps not grasp, in *On Baptism*, chapters 17 and 18. Nor do I introduce the canons of the Councils of Neocaesarea and Laodicea. I say only this: laypeople had the right to baptize in an emergency, but they did not exercise it, either deceived by hope of recovery or deterred by fear lest they seem, through rash presumption, to have violated the canons. See the Sixth Council of Paris, chapter 29, concerning the absence of a priest, persons dying without confession, and infants who often died without baptism. GUSSANVILLE. But above all, read Augustine’s Letter 228 to Honoratus, especially no. 8.] die for lack of baptism because of their sins.

And again, because we do not believe that Your Excellency has detained him except for some probable reason of misconduct, it is necessary that, after a synod has been held, it be made clear whether any charge is being brought against him. If a fault is found in him so serious that it leads to degradation from the priesthood, we must seek another ordination, [Col. 0486A] lest the Church of God remain neglected and deserted in those matters without which the Christian religion does not permit it to exist. But if Your Excellency finds the matter to be otherwise than what is being reported, let him return to his own church, so that he may fulfill his office among the souls entrusted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0486C] In the Colbert manuscript these words belong to the following letter, to Venantius, and so forth.]

In the month of March, in the ninth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO VENANTIUS, THE EX-MONK AND PATRICIAN OF SYRACUSE

He reproves Venantius for abandoning the monastic habit; urges him to come to his senses as quickly as possible; and teaches him whose counsel he ought to heed.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0486C] LETTER XXXIV (elsewhere XXXIII).—This is how the title of the letter is read in all the Vatican, Royal, Corbie, English, and Norman manuscripts, except that Syracusan is absent in one or two of the Vatican manuscripts. As for the dignity of chancellor, which the editors gratuitously confer upon him, all the manuscripts—both of the letters and of John the Deacon’s *Life of Saint Gregory*—are completely silent about it. We have therefore judged that Gussanville’s note under the word “Chancellor” should be removed. Gussanville likewise observes in an earlier note that in the Gemetic and Audoen manuscripts it reads “to Venantius and Exarch of Italy.” We certainly have these manuscripts before our eyes, and have noticed no trace of this title in them; rather, everywhere it reads as we have expressed it in the title. Nor do the Pratellian and Lyran manuscripts disagree with the Gemetic and Audoen, as the learned man imagines. Venantius, having cast off the monastic habit, had married an Italian woman, by whom, as we learn from Letter 123 of Book IX, he had two daughters, Barbara and Antonina, addressed in Letter 34 of Book XI. From Letter 42 below we understand that certain Sicilian monks had gone so far in their wickedness as to take wives publicly. Gregory urges John, bishop of Syracuse, in Letter 35 of Book XI, to ensure by exhortations, prayers, and threats that Venantius, who was near death, return to his habit, or at least do so at the point of death. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 16, excommunicates monks who have taken wives. Gregory below, in Letter 42, orders such men to be recalled to the monastery. Yet he was more indulgent toward this Venantius. Hence, in the time of Saint Bernard—when it was disputed whether a monk’s marriage was valid—some opponents produced Gregory the Great and Augustine’s book *On the Good of Widowhood* against Saint Bernard; because of his great reverence for the holy Fathers, he scarcely answers them except in *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 17. See Horstius’s note on Bernard’s Letter 76, and consult our commentaries on the life of Saint Gregory. Certainly, this letter makes it clear that Gregory despaired of Venantius’s salvation unless he withdrew from marriage and again put on the monastic habit.] to Venantius, the ex-monk and patrician of Syracuse.

Many foolish people thought that if I were raised to the order [Col. 0487A] of the episcopate, I would refuse to address you and to correspond with you frequently. But that is not so, because the very necessity of my office now compels me not to remain silent. For it is written: “Cry aloud, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58:1). And again it is written: “I have appointed you a watchman for the house of Israel; you shall hear a word from my mouth, and announce it to them from me” (Ezekiel 3:17). What follows for the watchman or hearer from this announcement, whether withheld or delivered, is immediately made clear:

“If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him, and do not speak to him so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked man, and he does not turn from his iniquity and from his wicked way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you shall have saved your soul.”

Hence Paul also says to the Ephesians: “Today my hands are clean from the blood of all of you. For I did not shrink from announcing to you the whole counsel of God” (Acts 20:26–27). He would not, therefore, have been clean from the blood of all if he had refused to announce God’s counsel to them, because when a pastor refuses to rebuke those who do wrong, he undoubtedly kills them by his silence.

Compelled by this consideration, whether you wish it or not, I shall speak, because with all my strength I desire either that you be saved or that I be freed from responsibility for your death. You remember what habit you once wore, and, setting aside the judgment of heavenly severity, you recognize into what state you have fallen. Weigh your guilt while there is time; while you are able, dread the severity of the future Judge, lest you then feel it bitterly when you can escape it no longer through any tears. Consider what is written: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matthew 24:20). In winter the cold’s torpor hinders walking, and according to the commandment of the Law it is not permitted to walk on the Sabbath. Thus he tries to flee in winter or on the Sabbath who seeks to flee from the anger of the strict Judge when it is no longer permitted him to walk.

While there is time, then, while it is permitted, flee the judgment of so great a terror. Consider what is written: “Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). You know from the Gospel that divine severity accuses us concerning idle speech and carefully demands an account of every useless word (Matthew 12:36). Consider, then, what it will do concerning a perverse deed, if in its judgment it rejects some people for their speech.

Ananias had vowed money to God (Acts 5:2 and following), but afterward, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, he took it back [Caus. 17, q. 1, canon 3]. You know with what death he was punished. If, then, he deserved the danger of death who took back from God the money he had given, consider how great a danger you will deserve at the divine judgment, since you have withdrawn not money but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had vowed yourself under the monastic habit.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] These words are absent from the manuscripts and should be regarded as a gloss that entered the text from the margin.]

(Consider the judgment of God deserved by one who vows himself to God and then, immediately ensnared by the desires of the world, lies about what he has vowed.)

Therefore, if you listen to the words of my correction [Note: [Col. 0488D] The printed editions read incorrectly, “if you hear securely.” Below they have “bound” instead of “devoted,” and “turns away” instead of “opposes”; we have restored the readings from the Vatican and other manuscripts, which remarkably agree with one another.] and follow them, you will learn at the end how gentle and sweet they are. Behold, I confess that I speak in grief, and, weighed down by sorrow over your deed, I can scarcely utter words; yet your mind, conscious of its own action, can scarcely endure what it hears: it blushes, is confused, and resists. If it cannot bear the words of dust, what will it do at the judgment of the Creator?

Yet I confess that I believe it a great mercy of heavenly grace that, although it sees you fleeing from life, it still preserves you for life; that, although it sees you growing proud, it bears with you; and that through its unworthy servants it supplies you with words of rebuke and admonition. Only this must you carefully consider: what Paul says, “We exhort you, brothers, not to receive the grace of God in vain”; for he says, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:1–2 and following).

But I know that when my letter is received, friends immediately gather, educated clients are summoned, and counsel concerning the cause of life is sought from the supporters of death. Since they love not you but your possessions, they say nothing to you except what pleases you for the moment. Such men were, as you yourself remember, those counselors who recently led you into so great a crime.

To say something from a secular author [Note: [Col. 0488D] These words are from Seneca, Letter 3: “Discuss everything with a friend, but first discuss the friend himself. After friendship has been established, trust is proper; before friendship, judgment.”], everything should be discussed with friends, but first concerning the friends themselves. If, however, you seek a human counselor in your case, accept me, I beg you, as your counselor. No one can be more faithful to you in counsel than one who loves not what is yours but you yourself.

May almighty God reveal to your heart how great is the love and charity with which my heart embraces you, insofar as divine grace is not offended. For I pursue your fault in such a way that I love your person; I love your person in such a way that I do not embrace the vice of your fault.

If, then, you believe that I love you, present yourself at the thresholds of the apostles and use me as your counselor. [Note: [Col. 0488D] All the editors corrupted this passage, reading: “But if perhaps in the cause of God I am believed to be too little trustworthy” [Col. 0489C]. All the Vatican, Colbert, Norman, and other manuscripts decidedly prefer our reading. What follows confirms it: “and I am suspected because of the ardor of my zeal.”]

But if I am perhaps thought to be excessive in the cause of God, and am suspected because of the ardor of my zeal, I bring the whole Church into the counsel of this deliberation. Whatever all judge to be beneficial, I oppose in no respect; rather, what is decided in common I gladly carry out and approve.

May divine grace preserve you as you fulfill what I have urged. (Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapters 44 and 48.)

## LETTER XXXV. TO PETER, BISHOP OF TERRACINA

He is to restore the place previously granted to the Jews. Those who disagree with the Christian religion are to be attracted with kindness.

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Terracina [Note: [Col. 0489C] Tarracina, also called Anxur, today Terracina, is still an episcopal city in Roman Campania, approximately midway between Rome and Capua.]

Joseph, the bearer of this letter (Ivo, part I, chapter 285), a Jew, informed us that, concerning a certain place where they used to gather to celebrate their festivals [Note: [Col. 0489C] Concerning the Jews, see below, Letter 45; Book III, Letter 26; Book IV, Letter 6. In the *Decretals*, book V, title 6, canon 9, Pope Clement III says: “Faith must be persuaded, not forced.” Saint Augustine, Book II *Against the Letters of Petilian*, chapter 83: “No one is to be compelled unwillingly to the faith”; he is speaking of the Donatists. The same author, Letter 84: “We do not persecute them out of hatred for harming them, but out of love for healing them.” In the same place: “Paul was compelled to the truth by the great violence of Christ compelling him.” At Saint Gregory’s command, Book III, Letter 26, pagans—who, according to Nicephorus, Book XIV of the *History*, chapter 12, are more easily converted—are burdened with a much heavier load if they refuse to convert. This is indirect force. In Book IV, Letter 6, the burden of the Jews’ payment is reduced so that they may wish to convert; and, recognizing their perfidy, by which they frequently return to their vomit, Gregory adds after the Council of Agde, canon 34: “And if they themselves come with less faithfulness, nevertheless those who are born from them are baptized with greater faithfulness.” In Book I, Letter 45, he considers this perfidy to arise because they are led to the baptismal font more by force than by preaching. I would add: also by hope of advantage. Indeed, if we consult the histories, very many repeated baptism several times for that reason. What does it matter whether they come through love of gain or fear of punishment, if they come with an evil will? Gregory Nazianzen speaks very aptly, Oration 8: “Nothing is more useful or safer than that willing people should rule willing people; for our law wishes no one to be led by force or governed under compulsion and against his will. In this way even other forms of government cannot be maintained and preserved, since nature has arranged that whatever is held by force, when an opportunity is seized, immediately asserts its freedom—still less can ours be called government rather than guidance, since nothing preserves it so much as freedom of will.” But the words that follow are still more emphatic: “For the mystery of piety belongs to the willing, not to those who are tyrannized.” GUSSANVILLE. In this observation Gussanville seems to oppose Gregory himself, as though Gregory had written contradictory things, but unjustly. It is one thing to attract Jews to the faith by gentleness, kindness, and rewards, and to impose heavy burdens—provided they are not unjust—on those who refuse; it is another thing to force unwilling people to baptism by physical coercion.]

the Jews residing in the fortress of Terracina [p. 525] had been accustomed to assemble, but that Your Fraternity had expelled them and that, with your knowledge and consent, they had moved to another place for the same purpose of celebrating their festivals, and that they now complain that they have again been expelled from that place.

But if this is so, we wish Your Fraternity to desist from conduct giving rise to such a complaint and to permit them to assemble, as was customary, in the place which, as we have said, they obtained for their gathering with your knowledge. Those who disagree with the Christian religion must be gathered into the unity of the faith by gentleness, kindness, admonition, and persuasion, lest those whom the sweetness of preaching and the foreseen terror of the future Judge could have invited to believe be driven away by threats and terrors. It is therefore necessary that they assemble kindly to hear the word of God from you, rather than fear an austerity extended beyond measure.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] LETTER XXXVI.—The most distinguished Stephen Baluzius recovered and published this letter from the Colbert manuscript in volume V of his *Miscellanies*, p. 469.]

## LETTER XXXVI. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

He should reread constantly the memorandum given to him. He adds certain admonitions breathing the highest equity and prudence.

[Col. 0490A]

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to Peter the subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0490D] Concerning this formula for addressing letters, which John the Deacon, book II, chapter 1, says Gregory was the first to use, we spoke in the preface.]

As you proceed to Sicily, you must reread constantly the memorandum I gave you, so that you may understand that the greatest care must be taken concerning bishops, lest they become involved in secular affairs except insofar as the necessity of defending the poor compels them. As for the matters concerning monks and clerics inserted in the same memorandum, I do not think they should be raised at present. But let your experience guard these instructions with the same care with which it can fulfill my desire in this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] What follows to the end of the letter will be better understood from Letter 44 of this book.]

Moreover, it has come to me that from the time of the defensor Antoninus until now, within this decade, many have suffered various acts of violence from the Roman Church, so that some publicly complain that their boundaries were forcibly invaded, their slaves taken away, and even their movable property removed by force and not by any judicial process. In all these matters I want your experience to be exceedingly vigilant, and whatever it finds to have been taken by force during this decade, or unjustly retained under the name of the Church, let it restore, by the authority of this present command of mine, to the person whose property it recognizes it to be. Otherwise the person who has suffered violence would be compelled to come to me and undertake the labor of so long a journey, while he could not prove to me whether what he says is true.

Therefore, considering the majesty of the coming Judge, restore everything taken through sin, knowing that you bring me great profit if you gather reward rather than riches. We have learned that very many complain about lost slaves, saying that if some slave, perhaps fleeing from his master, professed himself to belong to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, the rectors of the Church immediately treated him as a slave belonging to the Church, acting without any judicial process but defending the slave’s declaration with their own power. This displeases me as much as it departs from the judgment of truth.

Therefore, I want your experience to correct without delay whatever it discovers to have been done in this way, and, if any such slaves are now held as Church property, they ought to be restored before judgment, just as they were taken without judgment. Then, if the holy Church has any lawful claim to them, their possessors should be summoned through properly ordered legal action.

Correct all these matters irrevocably, because you will truly then be a soldier of the blessed apostle Peter if, in his affairs, you preserve custody of the truth even without showing partiality toward him. But if you see that anything can justly belong to the Church, take care never to attempt to defend it by force; especially since I have also established by decree, under threat of anathema, that titles must never be imposed upon urban or rural estates by our Church. Whatever is due to the poor by reason must also be defended by reason, lest, while a good cause is badly handled, we be accused before almighty God of injustice in something that is justly sought from us.

[Col. 0491B]

As for noble laymen or a distinguished man, I beg that they love you because of your humility, not fear you because of your pride. Yet whenever you discover them committing some injustice against the poor, immediately turn humility into firmness, so that you may always be submissive toward those who act well and opposed to those who act badly. Act in such a way that your humility is neither slack nor your authority rigid, so that uprightness may season your humility and humility make your uprightness gracious.

Moreover, as it was customary for them to assemble on the birthday of the bishop pontiff, forbid them to come on the day of my ordination, because foolish and vain excess does not please me. But if it is necessary for them to assemble, let them assemble on the feast of the blessed apostle Peter, chief of the apostles, [Note: [Col. 0491C] The bishops make the same profession when, in their letters and memoranda, they preface their statements by saying that they are bishops by the grace of the apostolic see. All learned people know that “apostolic see” is used for Saint Peter, and conversely. In this sense many preachers are said, at the beginning of the Christian commonwealth, to have been sent by Saint Peter into various provinces—that is, by the apostolic see. In the same sense Pope Nicholas I, Letter 24: “Let no one presume to contradict the most blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.” Consult Quesnellius, volume II, notes and observations on Saint Leo, p. 857.] so that they may give thanks to him through whose generosity they are shepherds.

Farewell. Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year of the emperor Maurice.

[p. 527]

## LETTER XXXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He should assist Maurilio, the former prefect.

[Col. 0492A]

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

If we consider the profession of our order and the office whose ministry we exercise, we ought to assist the afflicted as far as we can, with justice accompanying us. Since, therefore, we have learned that the distinguished man Maurilio, the former prefect [Note: [Col. 0491C] One who has left the prefecture; compare *ex-consul*, *ex-praetor*, and in Cicero *pro-quaestor*. In Greek, *apo hypaton*, *apo quaestoron*, “former consul,” “former quaestor.” Some write *exconsul*, *exquaestor*. [Col. 0491D] See Letter 69 below, “the distinguished man, former praetor,” and above, Letter 33. GUSSANVILLE.] is residing as an innocent man within the ecclesiastical enclosures [Note: [Col. 0491D] There were places of asylum from which no one could be removed except with the superior’s consent. See Book I of the Code, title 12, chapter 3, where the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian establish many regulations concerning ecclesiastical precincts. In Cause 17, question 4, many authorities are cited from Nicholas, Gelasius, the Council of Tribur, John VIII, and the Twelfth Council of Toledo, chapter 10. Add the Councils of Aurelian I, IV, and V, Mâcon II, and Saint Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 38, now Book X. These places are also called “the Lord’s enclosures” and include the church’s courts and porticoes, the bishop’s house, thirty or forty paces around it, and the houses located within them. Eventually this immunity ceased because of abuses. These precincts are wrongly confused with the *decanica*, mentioned in Novel 79, chapter 3; in Gaul, *le chapitre*. The *decanica* were appendages of the church in which clerics were sometimes detained as in free custody. Before Boniface VIII they were not tormented in workhouses and prisons; rather, the monastery served them as a prison. See below, Letter 59, now 61. GUSSANVILLE. The words “within the ecclesiastical enclosures” are absent from all the manuscripts we have been able to see. Nevertheless, to spare Gussanville’s notes, we have judged that they should be retained.] your Fraternity should hasten to assist him insofar as possible.

This is not because, God forbid, we doubt the justice of the most excellent lord Georgius, the prefect, or think that he departs in any way from the path of reason. We have found him an upright man in all good matters in the administration of so great a dignity [Note: [Col. 0492C] Recent printed editions add “as you know,” which is not found in the older manuscripts.]. Rather, it is so that the distinguished man Maurilio, the former prefect, may present his accounts without suspicion of oppression, and that the aforementioned most excellent lord Georgius, the prefect, may conduct the accounting without damage to his reputation.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO MALCHUS, BISHOP OF DALMATIA

He compels Bishop Stephen to submit to judgment and carries out whatever has been judged.

Gregory to Malchus, bishop of Dalmatia [Note: [Col. 0492D] Dalmatia was formerly part of Illyricum properly so called, where the Dalmatian people lived; after the First Dalmatian War it was reduced to a province. In time, with Liburnia added, it grew and extended from the Liburnian or Flanatic Gulf as far as the Drilon. Who this Malchus of Dalmatia was is unknown, unless he took his name from the province of Dalmatia itself, which is probable, since he was a bishop there, although I do not know of which see. GUSSANVILLE.]

John, a most eloquent man and counselor of the most excellent lord Georgius, prefect of Italy, informed us that he had disputes with Bishop Stephen [Note: [Col. 0492D] Now Scutari in Italian, a city formerly episcopal in Dalmatia and later the metropolis of the province of Praevalitana, until the emperor Justinian raised his native city Acrida, which he named Justiniana, to that dignity. Senecio, bishop of the city of Scodra, subscribed the Council of Ephesus. GUSSANVILLE. In one Vatican manuscript and all the Norman manuscripts it reads Scodensis.] of the city of Scodra concerning certain affairs, and requested that judgment be established between him and the bishop.

Therefore we have taken care to admonish Your Fraternity by this present command that you compel the aforementioned bishop to come and choose a court of judgment. Whatever may be established by the sentence of the chosen judges between the aforementioned John, the distinguished man, and the oft-mentioned bishop, do not fail to carry it into effect, [p. 528] so that the plaintiff may give thanks for the justice he has obtained, and the defendant, when brought to judicial inquiry, may have no complaint that injustice has been inflicted upon him.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO ANTHEMIUS THE SUBDEACON

He rebukes him for neglecting the poor. He orders generous and liberal assistance to be offered to the ladies Pateria, Palatina, and Viviana.

Gregory to Anthem(i)us the subdeacon.

When you were departing, I gave you instructions, and afterward, I remember, I imposed through repeated commands the duty of caring for the poor. If you learned that any there were in need, you were to report it by returning letters, yet you have scarcely taken care to do this for a few.

I want you, as soon as you receive this present order, to offer forty solidi for the footwear of the children of my lady Pateria [Note: [Col. 0493C] The earlier reading, “of my Paterichia,” was corrupt. We have restored the text from the better manuscripts—Sorb., Victor., Royal, Cistercian, Vatican manuscripts nos. 618, 2534, and 2538, another unnumbered Vatican manuscript, 620, Rheims, Catalan, and Seguierian. The last is the manuscript of the illustrious chancellor of France, eight hundred years old and of excellent quality; above the word *thiae* a later hand reads *amitae*, as though someone wished to add an interpretation of the word *thiae*, Greek *theias*, which in Latin means “aunt.” I also add that the Chartres manuscript of Saint Peter reads “of my aunt Pateria.” GUSSANVILLE. The learned man had not consulted this evidence when, in John the Deacon’s *Life of Saint Gregory*, he himself retained the corrupt reading “of my Paterichia.” Yet if he had consulted John the Deacon’s manuscripts, he would have read “of my aunt Pateria.”], and four hundred modii of wheat.

To my lady Palatina, widow of Urbicus, twenty solidi and three hundred modii of wheat. To my lady Viviana, widow of Felix, twenty solidi and three hundred modii of wheat. Let all eighty solidi be charged together to your accounts.

Bring the total amount of the payment with all haste, and, with the Lord’s help, arrive by Easter Day. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 55.)

## LETTER XL. TO FELIX, BISHOP OF MESSANA

So that Paulinus, a bishop and pilgrim, may govern the monastery of Saint Theodore.

[Col. 0493C]

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Messana.

We are also confident that it will please you if the burdens of the peregrination of your brother, the venerable Bishop Paulinus, are relieved, so that, under his governance and to a common reward, the monastery of blessed Theodore, founded in your city, may serve almighty God with greater devotion.

We have already learned from his report that you also wished this to be done. Therefore we have instructed the rector of our patrimony to gather together, after seeking them out, the monks of the aforementioned bishop’s monastery, and not delay in placing them in that same monastery with those who are now there, so that under that rector they may devote themselves more worthily to the care of their souls.

We have taken care to make this known to Your Reverence, [Note: [Col. 0493D] LETTER XL (elsewhere XXXVIII).—The following letter asserts the same principle: each person’s right is upheld, and no one invades another’s possessions. At the Council of Gangra, canons 6, 7, and 8: “According to the mind of the bishop,” “contrary to the mind,” “apart from the bishop.” At Antioch, canon 9: “To have authority over his own parish.” At the First Council of Constantinople, canon 2: “Nor to confuse the churches.” It speaks of metropolitans who love to enlarge their boundaries. At Ephesus, canon 8, it is decreed that the canons of the holy Fathers should not be disregarded, nor secular power’s arrogance gradually intrude under the pretext of administering sacred affairs, so that we may imperceptibly lose the freedom acquired for us by our own blood, and so forth. Let the reader take note. Moreover, the African Fathers allude to and explain this canon in their synodal letters to Boniface and Celestine. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 4, is also relevant; Saint Gregory seems to have had it in mind in this letter, since his reverence for the sacred canons and his careful preservation of ancient discipline were extraordinary. GUSSANVILLE.] lest, because you have been passed over, you should be distressed that anything has been arranged in your diocese.

## LETTER XLI. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

He should gather the monks dispersed throughout Sicily into the Messana monastery of Saint Theodore.

[Col. 0494B]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0494C] LETTER XLI (elsewhere XXXIX).—The printed edition had incorrectly inserted “Peter the Deacon.”] to Peter the subdeacon.

[Note: The old copies do not agree here. In Vatican D, Corbie, Tours, Michaelino, Jumièges, and the other Norman copies, it reads, “the illustrious Paulinus, bishop.” In Rheims this letter is absent.]

The venerable Paulinus, bishop of the city of Tauri [Note: The name of this city is also written variously in the manuscripts. In the Vatican it reads Tarrinae; elsewhere Tauranae or Taurinae. It was formerly an episcopal city of the Bruttians, destroyed by the Saracens between Rhegium and Hipponium.], in the province of the Bruttians [Note: In some Vatican copies and in the Norman manuscripts, “of the Brittians.” A little later, one Vatican copy reads *occisione* (“slaughter”) instead of *occasione* (“occasion”).], assured us that his monks had been scattered by a barbarian incursion and were now wandering throughout Sicily, and that, being without a superior, they neither cared for souls nor observed the discipline of their state of life [Note: Saint Gregory discusses monastic discipline in various letters. Here he condemns and restrains the wandering, acephalous, and irregular. I understand “wandering” to mean those who do not remain stable in cloisters but, having abandoned their station, mingle among the peoples, learn their practices, and serve their idols. I call those “acephalous” who, loving license, do not endure the yoke of a superior. By “irregular” I understand those who scarcely value at a farthing the observances of the order, status, and rule of their own monastery—things which they call “rules”—and who think themselves bound to them by no religious obligation. For I do not see what else Saint Gregory could designate by “the discipline of their state.” GUSSANVILLE.].

For this reason we order you, with every care and diligence, to seek out all these monks, bring them together, and place them with the aforesaid bishop, their superior, in the monastery of Saint Theodore situated in the city of Messina, so that both those who are now there—for we have learned that they too are without a superior—and those whom you find belonging to his congregation and bring back may together serve almighty God under his direction. Know that we have communicated this matter [Note: In those codices in which Paulinus is called “the illustrious man,” the text here reads: “And this matter to the illustrious man.”] to the venerable Felix, bishop of that same city [Col. 0495A], so that he may not be distressed if anything is arranged in the diocese entrusted to him without his knowledge [Note: The published editions incorrectly read, “in the diocese granted to himself.”]. (Above, Letter 40.)

### 530. LETTER XLII. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

[Note: LETTER XLII (formerly 40).—In the Colbert manuscript, the month of April is prefixed to this letter. In most manuscripts it occurs in a confused and misplaced order, but in Vatican D in excellent order.]

He is to restrain wandering monks, those devoted to private property, and married monks; and he is not to allow those converted from the clergy to monasticism to return to the Church in which they served.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon.

[Note: He was the fifth bishop of Sorrento, elected in the year 580. He subscribed to the Roman synod held by Saint Gregory in 595 and died in 598; Amandus succeeded him, concerning whom see Book X, Letters 18 and 19. GUSSANVILLE.]

Our brother and fellow bishop John has informed us, through Justus his cleric, in a written memorandum [Note: It is written in distinct sections: *κεφάλαιον γράφιον* (“a written capitulary”). GUSSANVILLE.], among other matters, that certain monks of monasteries situated in the diocese of Sorrento [Note: Sorrento, commonly called Sorrento, was formerly an episcopal city in Campania and is now an archiepiscopal city. GUSSANVILLE.] move from monastery to monastery as they please and, out of a desire for worldly things, withdraw from the rule of their own abbot; moreover—and it is known that this is not permitted—each of them is devoted to private property [Col. 0495B] [Note: On monks’ private property, see Book XII, Letter 24, to John the subdeacon, and chapter 33 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, where the holy Father vividly depicts this most wicked vice. In chapter 55 of the same Rule he says that the monks’ beds should frequently be searched, because of private possessions, lest any be found. The punishment with which Saint Gregory fined a monk who possessed private property, as we would say today, may be found in John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 15.].

Therefore, by this present command, we instruct your Experience that no monk may henceforth move from one monastery to another, and that you permit none of them to possess anything privately. But if anyone should presume to do so, let him be returned, with appropriate punishment, to the monastery in which he first entered the religious life and to the rule of his own abbot from which he had fled, lest, if we leave so great an evil unchecked and uncorrected, the souls of those who perish be required of the soul of their superiors [Col. 0496A].

[Note: Saint Benedict permitted clerics and priests to enter his monasteries; see the Rule, chapter 60. From this Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, proves in Letter 29 that not only criminals should be received into monasteries for penance and conversion.]

If any should happen—[Note: These two words are found in almost no manuscripts. Thomas James strongly rages against their addition in his *Vindiciae Gregorianae*: “These words, *on whatever occasion*, serve to enlarge the monastic order,” he says; “they were added and sewn into the text by some benighted person; they do not appear in the parchment manuscripts.” Who would not laugh at the outpouring of bile by this heterodox man over such a trifling matter? In the same place he notes that the English manuscripts read *conversationem* (“way of life”) instead of *conversionem* (“conversion”). Certainly in the Norman manuscripts, the Vatican, and most copies, we read *conversionem*.] on whatever occasion—from the clergy into the monastic life, they are not to be permitted, of their own will, to return to that same or another Church in which they had formerly served, unless the monk’s life has been such that the bishop under whom he formerly served judges him worthy of the priesthood, so that he may be chosen by that bishop and ordained in the place which he determines.

And since we have learned that some monks have advanced to such a great abomination as to take wives publicly, seek them out with the utmost vigilance; and once found, return them, with fitting punishment, to the monasteries of which they had been monks (Gratian, 16, question 1, canon 32; and 27, question 1, canon 39). Nor should you fail to deal likewise with those who come from the clergy to the monastic life, as we said above [Col. 0496B]. In this way you will appease the eyes of God and be found a sharer in the reward that has been fulfilled.

[Note: LETTER XLIII (formerly 41).—Saint Isidore of Seville mentions this letter in his *Book of Ecclesiastical Writers*. “He also wrote,” he says, “certain letters to the aforesaid Leander, one of which he adds in those same books of Job under the title of a preface. Another speaks of baptism by immersion, and so forth.” The Fourth Council of Toledo also speaks of it, canon 4, under the presidency of Saint Isidore. Thus it is clear that Alcuin doubted this letter without sufficient reason when he says in Letter 10: “As for the letter which they say was written by blessed Gregory concerning single immersion, we have not found it in his book of letters which was brought to us from Rome…. Therefore we are uncertain whether it is his or whether it was written under his name by some author of that sect.” Saint Licinianus, bishop, also praises this letter in writing to Saint Gregory. See Book X, final letter.]

### LETTER XLIII. TO LEANDER, BISHOP OF SEVILLE

He groans beneath the burden of the episcopate. He rejoices in King Reccared’s conversion. He approves the rite, introduced by the Spaniards because of the Arians, of a single immersion in baptism. He sends several books.

Gregory to Leander, bishop of Seville [Note: For Saint Leander, see the preceding letter to the books of the *Moralia*, together with our brief notes illustrating it.].

[Note: Seville, today Sevilla, is a very large city of Spain and a celebrated emporium on the river Baetis, commonly called the Guadalquivir. Formerly it was the metropolis of Baetica and is now the metropolis of Vandalia or Andalusia, bearing the rank of an archbishopric. GUSSANVILLE. “Of Seville” is not read in the Vatican, Reggio, Corbie, Norman, and most manuscripts. In some it merely says, “to the bishop of Spain”; in Colbert, “to the bishop of the Spains.” In the manuscript of the Reverend Capuchin Fathers at Rouen: “To Leander, bishop of Seville.”]

I would have wished to answer your letters with my whole attention [Col. 0497A], unless the burden of pastoral care so exhausted me that I would rather weep than say anything. Your Reverence also understands this attentively in the very text of my letters, when I speak carelessly to one whom I love intensely.

For I am shaken in this place by so many waves of the world that I cannot in any way steer to harbor the old and decaying ship which, by the hidden dispensation of God, I have undertaken to govern. Now waves rush against it from the front; now, from the side, foaming masses of sea swell up; now the storm pursues it from behind. Amid all this confusion I am compelled at one moment to turn the helm directly toward the adversity itself; at another, by inclining the side of the ship, to evade the threats of the waves obliquely.

I groan because I feel that, through my negligence, the bilge of vices is increasing, and that, with the storm violently opposing us, the rotten planks already resound with the noise of shipwreck [Col. 0497B]. Weeping, I recall that I have lost the peaceful shore of my rest; and, sighing, I look toward the land, which nevertheless I cannot hold because the winds of circumstances oppose me.

Therefore, dearest brother, if you love me, extend to me the hand of your prayer amid these waves, so that, by helping me in my distress, you may yourself become stronger in your own labors through the exchange of that reward.

I am wholly unable to express in words the joy I feel because I have learned that our common son, the most glorious King Reccared [Note: For his conversion and that of the Visigoths, see Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 31, and, more fully, the historians of Spain, especially Rodrigo of Toledo, Book II, chapter 15. GUSSANVILLE.], has been converted to the Catholic faith with complete devotion. When you describe his character to me in your letters, you have made me love even one whom I do not know.

But because you know the snares of the ancient enemy, since he prepares a harsher war against victors, may your Holiness now keep more vigilant watch over him [Col. 0497C], so that he may bring his good beginnings to completion, may not exalt himself over his perfected good works, may hold the faith he has learned also through the merits of his life, and may show by his deeds that he is a citizen of the eternal kingdom, so that after the passage of many years he may pass from one kingdom to another.

[Note: It is now only the supreme pontiffs who are adorned with this title. Formerly it was common not only to bishops but also to priests and deacons. Read Ennodius, Book V, Letter 13, where, addressing the deacon Hormisdas, he says, “and since your holiness knows very well.” Indeed, in Sermon 9 of the appendix to Saint Ambrose’s works, Ambrose himself—or Maximus—addresses the Christian people in this manner, imitating the Apostle, who calls the Romans and others adhering to Christ through faith “holy.” Gregory, however, customarily uses “your holiness” only of bishops.]

Concerning triple immersion in baptism (Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, canon 89), nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have perceived, because, in one faith, a diversity of custom does no harm to the holy Church.

We, however, by immersing three times, signify the sacrament of the three-day burial, so that, when the child is brought out of the water three times, the resurrection after three days may be represented. If someone should perhaps think that this is also done in honor of the supreme Trinity, it is nevertheless no obstacle to immersing the person to be baptized once in the water; for since there is one substance in three subsistences, it cannot in any way be blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, since in the three immersions the Trinity of persons may be signified, and in the single immersion the unity of the Godhead.

But because until now the infant was immersed three times in baptism by heretics, I do not think this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the Godhead, and while they do what they used to do, they boast that they have overcome our custom [Col. 0498A].

[Note: The same is confirmed by the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 5, which also uses Gregory’s authority and adds that both forms of immersion are to be considered irreproachable: “But to avoid the scandal of schism or the practice of heretical doctrine, let us retain single immersion, lest those among us who immerse three times seem to approve the assertion of heretics by following their practice.” The Arians used triple immersion to signify that there were three natures in the three persons. It should nevertheless be noted that, before Saint Gregory, councils and Fathers spoke of triple immersion as necessary and instituted by God; Saint Thomas explains this in Part III, question 66, article 8. Triple immersion is discussed in *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapters 78 and following; Dionysius, *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 2; Apostolic Canon 50; Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, chapter 27, and *On Baptism* and *On the Crown*, chapter 3; Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27; Augustine, Sermon 201, *On Time*; Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, Book II, chapter 7; Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*. As for single immersion, Saint Thomas does not appear to cite any testimony earlier than the Fourth Council of Toledo, which was later than Gregory the Great. GUSSANVILLE.]

To your most beloved fraternity I have sent books, a list of which I have inserted below. As for the things that, you write, were said in the exposition of blessed Job and ought to be sent to you, since I had delivered them in homilies with words and meanings still tepid [i.e. insufficiently developed] [Note: Some editions read “with meanings as well as words requesting them.” The Vatican, Gallican, and other manuscripts support our reading.], I have tried as best I could to transfer them into the form of books, which are still being copied by the scribes.

And if the haste of the bearer of this letter had not constrained me, I would have wished to send you everything without any diminution, especially because I wrote this very work for your Reverence, so that I might seem to have labored in my work for the one whom I love above all others.

Moreover, if you know that time has been granted you away from ecclesiastical duties, you already know what this means. Although absent in body, I always see you present to me, because I carry the image of your face impressed within my heart.

Given in the month of May. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 32.)

### 533. LETTER XLIV. TO PETER, SUBDEACON OF SICILY

He orders the correction of many abuses contrary to law. He decrees concerning the celibacy of subdeacons.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily.

Because we dismissed your *responsalis* late [Note: LETTER XLIV (formerly 42).—This does not mean an agent who managed ecclesiastical affairs at the imperial court, but a messenger or courier who, after delivering the letters he carried and receiving a reply, was to return as quickly as possible. Or perhaps it refers to someone managing ecclesiastical business by order of Peter the subdeacon. Understood in this way, the term *responsalis* is sufficiently explained in the notes to Book I of the *Moralia*, column 1.], being occupied with the duties of the Paschal feast, we were unable to release him sooner [Col. 0499A]. But, having carefully investigated all the matters about which you took care to inform us, you will learn below how we have arranged them.

We have learned that the farmers of the Church are being severely burdened in the prices of grain, so that the fixed rate is not maintained for them in a season of abundance [Note: These were farmers on the Sicilian estates of the Roman Church. Each year they were required, under a tax lease, to return a fixed number of *modii* of grain, although they sometimes paid money instead of grain. After Sicily was brought under the authority of the Roman people, Sicilian farmers paid the Romans a tenth of the grain they harvested…. But, says Cicero, *Against Verres*, speech 5, when a farmer had sold his grain, or wished to preserve it, or did not wish to transport it to the place where it was required, he asked as a favor and concession that he be permitted to pay for the grain whatever the grain was worth. From this beginning and from accommodations made by magistrates the practice of valuation was introduced…. The offense therefore did not lie in valuation itself, but in joining the grain levy to valuation. The tenant farmers were burdened when, in a plentiful grain supply and while grain was selling at a lower price, they were compelled to pay much money above the public price. Verres had done this as praetor of Sicily for three years. Cicero therefore accused him because, when a *modius* of wheat in Sicily cost two, or at most three, sesterces, he exacted from the farmers three denarii—or twelve sesterces—for each *modius* of wheat. The most holy pontiff takes precautions that nothing similar be done to the farmers on the Sicilian estates of the Church; indeed, because it had happened, he censures it.].

We wish the measure used in their purchases to follow the public prices at all times, whether less or more grain is produced. As for grain lost in shipwreck, we wish it to be fully accounted for, provided that your negligence does not cause any failure to transport it, so that, when the proper time for shipment is neglected, the loss may not arise from your fault [Note: Those responsible for supplying the grain were likewise responsible for transporting it. See *L. Mediterraneae*, Code, “On Grain Supply and Taxes”; Cicero, *Against Verres*, Book 5. The Sicilian tenants of the Roman Church were bound by the same law as all Sicilians had formerly been. Thus the risk of the grain belonged to the tenant or landholder if it perished in a shipwreck, unless it happened by accident or through the fault and negligence of the agent, because the grain had been shipped at an unsuitable time, or unless the force of the storm was proved by reliable witnesses. See the Theodosian Code, vol. V, p. 57.].

We have seen that it is very inequitable and unjust for anything to be taken from the farmers of the Church as a *sextariaticum* and for them to be compelled to deliver a larger *modius* than is placed in the Church’s granaries [Note: There are sixteen *sextarii* in a *modius*. Fannius writes:

> An amphora holds three *modii*; the *sextarius*  
> draws from the *modius* sixteen times.

A plebiscite proposed by two tribunes of the plebs, Publius and Marcus Silius, in the year 510 from the founding of the City, provided: “There shall be sixteen *sextarii* in a *modius*…. The *sextarius* shall equal one pound less a twelfth.” Thus the *modius* contained twenty-four Roman pounds of twelve ounces each. A *sextariaticum* was taken when, beyond the lawful measure of the *modius*, tenants were compelled by an unjust custom to add one or more *sextarii*; hence the burden is later called the “burden of addition.” The same abuse is deplored and condemned by Gregory in Book XIII, Letter 34, where he says that Pantaleo the notary found in the Sicilian territory of Syracuse that the *modius* with which the Church’s tenants were compelled to deliver grain contained twenty-five *sextarii*.].

Accordingly, by this present admonition we order that the farmers of the Church never be required to give *modii* containing more than eighteen *sextarii*—unless perhaps there is something which sailors, according to custom, take in addition and which they themselves attest is lost or diminished on the ships.

We have also learned that a most unjust exaction is made on certain Church estates [Note: What Gregory, Cassiodorus, and many others often call a *massa* is more commonly called a *mansus* or *mansum*. It is a field of a definite extent and measure, corresponding well to what others call a cultivated holding, an equipped farm, in French *une ferme*, *une métairie*, or *une cense*, where slaves, animals, and necessary equipment formed part of such a *massa* or *mansus*. This term should not appear to be confused with a *casa* or *casula*, which was a very small holding, for there was a distinction between those living in *casae* and those holding *mansi*. See Gregory, Book XII, Letter 9: “A *massa* with all its estates,” and so forth. GUSSANVILLE. A *massa* is clear from Gregory himself. In Book V, Letter 31—formerly Book XII, Letter 12—entitled “To the tenants of estates,” two Teller manuscripts read “to the tenants of estates or farms,” in French. The same appears in three Colbert manuscripts and in Paul the Deacon’s collection. The term *massa* is used in the same sense by Senator, Book VIII, Letter 23: “the *massa* annexed below,” and so forth.], such that the tenants are required to pay seventy-three and a half [units], which is an intolerable statement [Note: The printed editions read “from seventy-three and a half.” Two Colbert manuscripts have “from seventy-three, or three and a half”; another, “from seventy-three and a half.” But in the Vatican, Corbie, Norman, and most of the better manuscripts it reads: “seventy-three and a half are exacted”—namely, one *modius* out of twenty. Below it reads, “let them pay seventy-two,” namely one out of thirty-five. See John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 69. From Cicero, *Against Verres*, speech 5, we learn that from Sicilian farmers, besides the tithe, three fiftieths and three solidi out of fifty were exacted. This passage, however, is read variously in the manuscripts. Vatican D has “let them pay seventy-one”; so also the Norman, Angers, and two Teller manuscripts. Other Vatican copies read “let them pay seventy-one.” Corbie agrees, changing the word *ad* to *et*. Other Vatican copies read “seventy-one,” or “seventy measures of wine.” Perhaps *vina* is the same as *bina*, with *v* used for *b*, as frequently occurs. Although it is not easy to determine precisely what these expressions, poorly suited to modern usage, once meant, it is nevertheless clear that they concern certain methods of paying a tax. See Cassiodorus, Book I of the *Variae*, Letters 14; Book II, Letter 17; Book VII, Letters 20 and 21; but especially consult Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Tertia*, where he quotes from Cassiodorus a passage concerning the exaction of pairs and threes.].

Nor is even this enough: they are said to demand something additional according to a custom already established for many years. We utterly detest this practice and wish it to be removed completely from the estates. But let your Experience calculate both this charge—whatever is taken beyond the proper pound—and the other minor burdens, and whatever is taken from the farmers beyond equitable proportion. Let him reduce everything to one total rent, and, according to what the strength of the farmers can bear, let them pay the full and balanced rent at seventy-two [units] [Col. 0500B]. They must not be required to pay siliquae beyond the pound, a larger pound, or burdens greater than the pound [Note: Concerning the *siliquaticum*, see King Theodoric in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book II, Letter 30; Book III, Letter 25; Book IV, Letter 19. It was a burden imposed on farmers: from everything sold in the markets—grain, wine, and oil—they had to provide a fixed portion in order to receive permission to sell. Gregory takes care that no *siliqua* beyond the just weight of the pound be exacted from the farmers.]. Rather, by your valuation, as their capacity permits, it should be included in the total rent, so that no disgraceful exaction may occur.

To prevent, after my death, these very burdens—which we have removed from the additional charges and incorporated into the principal rent—from being added again in some form, so that the total rent is found to have increased and the farmers are further compelled to pay additional burdens, we wish you to prepare certificates of security concerning the rents in such a way that you write in them that each person must pay a specified rent, with siliquae [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “vegetables.”], burdens, or grain charges excluded.

Whatever came to the administrator’s use from these small items, we wish, by this present command of ours, to come to your use from the total rent.

Above all, we want you to take careful heed that unjust measures are not used in collecting the rents [Col. 0501B]. But if you find any such measures, break them and establish new and correct ones, because my son, the servant of God, the deacon, has already found such measures, though he did not have permission to alter them. Therefore, apart from the fair measures, the customary exceptions, and the poor food [Note: In the Norman, two Teller, Corbie, Tours, and most manuscripts of the Life of Saint Gregory written by John the Deacon, it reads “and poor food.” The Angers manuscript reads “and poor food,” with a different spelling.], we wish nothing else to be exacted from the Church’s tenants.

Furthermore, we have learned that the first payment of the *burdatio* [Note: *Burdatio*, says Alteserra in his note on this passage, is a rent paid by farmers on account of the estate called a *burda*, our “bord.” Below: “We have also learned that the farmers have again paid the *burdatio*.” Gussanville, however, thinks that *burdatio* means a burden, tax, or rent, so called from *burdae* or *burdones*, that is, mules used to carry such burdens.] greatly oppresses our farmers, so that, before they can sell the products of their labor, they are compelled to pay the taxes. Since they have nothing of their own from which to pay, they borrow from public auctioneers [Note: Vatican A and C, together with two other manuscripts, read *auctionariis*, as do Tours of Saint Gatien, Corbie, the Norman manuscript, and several copies of John the Deacon. Vatican D and two Teller manuscripts have *auctionariis* or *autionariis*. “Auctioneers” perhaps means those who conduct auctions, that is, publicly sell goods under the auctioneer’s staff.], and pay heavy interest for the same benefit; as a result they are oppressed by severe losses.

Accordingly, by this present admonition we order that whatever they might have been able to borrow from outsiders for this purpose be provided by your Experience from public funds, and be collected from the Church’s farmers gradually, as they have the means, lest, when they are pressed by immediate need, they be compelled to sell cheaply what might later have been sufficient to make the payment, and thus find it entirely insufficient [Col. 0501C].

It has also come to our attention that excessive charges are being collected from the marriages of the farmers.
