We therefore order that all marriage charges together never exceed the sum of one solidus [Note: This was a gift which tenant farmers, to some extent servants of their lords, paid in order to be permitted to marry.]. If any are poor, they ought to pay even less; but if any are wealthy, they must in no way exceed the aforesaid sum. We do not wish this marriage payment to be entered into our account at all, but it is to benefit the tenants.

We have also learned that, when certain tenants die, their parents are not permitted to succeed them, but their property is taken for the use of the Church. We therefore establish that the parents of deceased tenants who live on Church property must succeed them as heirs, and that nothing is to be taken from the substance of the deceased. But if someone leaves young children, careful persons are to be chosen to whom their parents’ property may be entrusted for safekeeping until the children reach an age at which they can manage their own property.

We have also learned (Gratian, 16, question 6, canon 5) that, when someone from the household commits an offense, punishment is inflicted not upon the offender but upon his property. We therefore order that whoever commits an offense be punished in his own person, as is fitting [Col. 0502B]. His property, however, is to be entirely spared, except perhaps for a small amount that may serve the needs of the officer sent to him [Note: The reading “from communion,” found in the Froben edition and in Gratian, is erroneous and contrary to the sequence of the text. GUSSANVILLE.].

We have also learned (Gratian, 16, question 10) that whenever a tenant takes something unjustly from one of his farmers, the amount is indeed exacted from the tenant, but is not returned to the person from whom it was taken. We therefore order that whatever has been violently taken from anyone belonging to the household be restored to the person from whom it was taken, and not benefit our own interests, lest we ourselves appear to be the authors of violence [Col. 0502C].

Furthermore, we wish that whenever you send those who are in your service to deal with any cases arising outside the estates, they may receive small payments from them, but only in such a way that the payments benefit those persons themselves, because we do not wish the Church’s purse to be polluted by dishonest profits [Note: *Saccus* is a word common to all languages. Hence *sacculus*, *saccellus*, *sacellarius*, *saccellarius*, *saccularius*, *sacco*, and *saccarius* are commonly used by jurists for purses, a treasury, a treasure-house, or a repository of money. In Greek: *σακέλη*, *σακέλιον*, or *σακκέλλη*, *σακκέλλιον*. Binius is therefore wrong to distinguish *sacellarius* from *saccellarius* in meaning in his note on Book IV, Letter 34. We read *sacculum* and *sacellum*, *sacellarius* and *saccellarius*, used interchangeably for the same thing. Unless perhaps *sacellum* is derived from *sacrum*, as in Augustine, *City of God*, Book VI, chapter 3, following Varro under the word *Capellae*, some of which were roofed and others, among pagans, unroofed. Moreover, some *saccula* served as holding places or prisons, as in Balsamon, concerning the *chartophylax* and *protecdicus*: “the patriarchal *sacella* that guards criminals”; others served for alms, whether of the Church, the emperor, or monks. Some *sacellarii* were greater and others lesser. See Balsamon, Codinus, and John, bishop of Citre, in his responses. GUSSANVILLE.].

We also order your Experience to guard most carefully that tenants are never established on Church estates for the sake of profit. For while profit is sought, the tenants are frequently changed; and what else results from such changes except that the Church’s estates are never cultivated? [Col. 0503A]

The *libellatica* themselves [Note: *Libellatica*, so called from the *libelli* in which leases of fields were written, properly means the leases themselves, in French *les baux à ferme*. See Book II, Letter 1. In Cassiodorus, Book V of the *Variae*, Letter 7: “We have learned from your report that our estates in Apulia have been entrusted to Thomar under the title of a *libellum*”—that is, by a contract or written lease, a *bail*. Sometimes such leases were made fraudulently, and under the appearance of a leasehold or emphyteutic right the Church was stripped of its property. Hence in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 47, chapter 10: “Let no one presume to seize ecclesiastical property, movable or immovable, and let those things which appear to have been lost by the Church’s administrators, through fear or favor, to someone under a leasehold or emphyteutic right, fraudulently and to the Church’s detriment, return to their former right.”] are to be regulated according to the amount of the rent.

We wish you to receive from the Church’s estates no more for storehouses and storerooms [Note: Sometimes *cellaria* means dwellings; here it means a storeroom, *ἀποθήκη*, under the charge of a cellarer. *Cellaria* can mean the things stored in storerooms. Thus Severus Sulpicius, speaking of the Council of Ariminum, says: “The emperor ordered provisions and stores to be given to the bishops.” Sometimes, however, *cellaria* means cells. Note in Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, the phrase *cellas promas*, “store-chambers,” meaning tombs. Among monks it means a monk’s dwelling. See the *Code*, “Privilege,” under the title “On the Meaning of Words,” in the sixth book. Gregory of Tours, Book IX of his *History*, chapter 6, calls his chamber or bedroom a *cellula*. In chapter 15 he mentions the *cellula* of Bishop Athalocus, that is, his room. See below, Book IV, Letter 4. GUSSANVILLE. Whether this explanation is relevant to the passage, let the prudent reader judge. Meanwhile we shall offer another. Cicero, *Against Verres*, speech 5, mentions grain given freely by Sicilian farmers, beyond the tithe, to the praetor or his officials “for the household’s expenses.” “Let as much be given,” he says, “for the household expenses as has always been given.” Saint Gregory takes care that the administrators of the Sicilian estates do not take more from the farms for their own storerooms and those of the Church’s defenders and agents than custom allows.], than custom permits; but let those which we have ordered to be purchased for you be purchased from outsiders.

Three pounds of gold unjustly taken from Peter, the tenant of Subpatriana, have come to our attention. Carefully investigate the matter through Fantinus, the defensor; and if they were manifestly taken unjustly and improperly, restore them without any delay.

We have also learned that the peasants paid again the *burdatio* which Theodosius had by no means paid on their behalf, so that they were charged twice over. This happened because his property was insufficient to meet the Church’s debt. But since we have been informed through our son, the servant of God Diaconus, that this same loss can be adequately compensated from Theodosius’s property, we wish five hundred and seven solidi to be restored to those same peasants without any diminution, lest they appear to have been charged twice. If, however, beyond the peasants’ loss, forty solidi also remain from Theodosius’s property, which you are said to have in your possession, we wish them to be returned to his daughter, so that she may recover the property which he had given in pledge. We also wish his father’s *batiola* to be restored to her.

[Note: A small vessel, from *batus* or *bata*. The old glossaries have *batiola*, Greek ποτήριον (*potērion*, “cup”). Plautus, in the *Colax*: “He had a golden *batiola* weighing eight pounds.” Nonius Marcellus, who also cites Varro’s *On Agriculture*, book I. Among the Greeks one finds βατιακή and βατιάκιον for a kind of *proculum*. GUSSANV. In the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus one finds *baciola*. But in three Colbert manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and many others, *baciolam* is read. It is written variously as *baciola*, *batiola*, and *batiolica*. See Spelman, *Glossarium archaeologicum*, p. 77. In Plautus, *Stichus*, verse 4:

> Those who have wealth at home drink from bowls and *canthari*,  
> and from *batiolae*.

Arnobius, book II, *Against the Gentiles*: “*polubrum, siliquastrum . . . batiolae, scopae, scyphus*,” and so forth.]

Campanianus, the illustrious master of the soldiers, had left twelve solidi annually to his notary John from the Varronian estate. We strictly command you to pay these every year to the niece of Euplus, the tenant, although she received all of Euplus’s movable property, except only the solidi. We also wish you to give her twenty-five solidi from his solidi.

[Note: The Greek-Latin glossaries have ὑπόθεμα (*hypóthema*), “support,” “stand”; elsewhere ὑποπόδιον (*hypopódion*), “footstool,” “bench,” “support.” It seems to be what Latins commonly call a *repositorium*. There were two kinds: larger ones, placed beneath tables, τραπεζοφόρα (*trapezophóra*). Cicero, book VII of the *Letters to Friends*: “If you want the *trapezophorum* which you had intended for yourself, you will have it.” Others were smaller, for supporting plates and dishes, which the Gauls call *chapelets* (“little rings”), *colliers* (“collars”), or *porte-assiettes* (“plate-stands”). Athenaeus, book IV, mentions the θύβη (*thýbē*), in which a dish with its food is placed. See Lazarus Bayus, *On Vessels*. GUSSANV. In all the Vatican, English, Teller, Colbert, and other manuscripts, *suppostorium* is read, not *suppositorium* as in the printed editions, although the meaning of both words is the same. Here it may mean a vessel, in French *soucoupe*; this seems to be suggested by the mention of the accompanying cup—for so the manuscript codices read—that is, the cup given in pledge. Consult Cangius’s *Glossary*.]

A certain silver *suppostorium* is said to have been pledged for one solidus, and a cup for six solidi. Question Dominicus the secretary, or others who may know; recover the debt, and restore the aforesaid vessels.

We give thanks for your diligence, because, although I commanded you concerning my brother’s affairs to send his silver back, you forgot it as though someone had mentioned it to you on behalf of the least of your slaves. Now, at least, let your Experience strive to accomplish this, rather than your negligence; or send back with all speed whatever of his property you discover to have been in Antoninus’s possession.

[Col. 0504B] Concerning the case of the Jew Salpingus, a letter has been found which we have had sent to you. Read it again, investigate carefully his case and that of a certain widow who is said to be involved in the same affair, and concerning the fifty-one solidi which are known to be owed, give an answer as seems just to you, so that another person’s property may in no way be unjustly defrauded from the creditors.

[Note: In Vatican A and D, *qui reddi deberi* (“which are owed to be returned”) is read. In C and two other manuscripts, *qui redhiberi noscuntur* (“which are known to be restored”). Concerning this verb, which Apollinaris Sidonius frequently uses, especially in book IX, letters 11 and 14, as does Ennodius, book III, letter 10, Sirmond observes that it usually means *redhibere*, “to return what one owes.”]

[Note: In two Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, Corbie, and others, this is read instead of *creditoribus* as in the printed edition: “so that you will not unjustly withhold another person’s property from anyone.” In Vatican A and B it reads: “so that you will unjustly become debtor to no one concerning another person’s property.”]

Half of Antoninus’s legacy has been given to him; the other half will be redeemed. We wish this half to be made up to him from the common property, and not only to him but also to the defensores and pilgrims to whom he left something by way of legacy, and we wish the legacy to the household to be paid, insofar as it concerns us. Therefore, having calculated the account for our share—that is, for nine twelfths—pay it.

[Note: The French have *pour les trois quarts* (“for the three quarters”). So below, *haeres in sex uncias* means “an heir in six twelfths,” that is, “for half.” GUSSANV.]

From the solidi of the Church of Canusium, we wish you to distribute something to the clergy of that Church, so that those who are now suffering poverty may have some means of support; and if God wills that a bishop be ordained there, he may have something from which to live.

[Note: Gratian and Ivo cite this decree, as well as the following one: “If any persons from the ecclesiastical household,” and so forth. Canonists labor to defend both as genuine works of Saint Gregory; I would rather think that one or the other is superfluous and interpolated, since their meaning is nearly the same, with only slight changes in wording. Let the learned reader examine and judge. I acknowledge, however, that a distinction could be made between clergy who had been slaves of the Church before being promoted and freeborn men who possessed property of their own. The property of the former seems to have belonged entirely to the Church; the property of the latter passed to their own parents, after the necessities required for the support and clothing of those who had fallen had first been taken out. As for monks, since they could possess nothing of their own, the same law was observed as for slaves. Consult the canonists on the canon “Concerning the Fallen,” cause 16, question 6, and what Saint Gregory adds below in this letter concerning a fallen servant of God. We have already said much about the fallen in letter 18. GUSSANV. Earlier editions read *de lapsis sacerdotibus vel levitis* (“concerning fallen priests or Levites”); we rejected the last words because they are found in none of the better manuscripts.]

Concerning fallen priests or anyone from the clergy, we wish you to observe this rule: do not involve yourself in any way with their property. Instead, seek out the poorest regular monasteries, which know how to live according to God, and consign the fallen to those monasteries for penance. Let the property of the fallen benefit the place to which they are entrusted to perform penance, so that those who take responsibility for correcting them may themselves receive support from their property. If, however, they have parents, let their property be given to their lawful parents, provided that adequate provision is made for the support of those who have been assigned to penance.

But if priests, Levites, monks, clerics, or any others from the ecclesiastical household should fall, we wish them to be given over to penance, but their property is not to be withdrawn from ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Nevertheless, they may receive enough for their own use to sustain themselves in doing penance, lest, if stripped of everything, they become burdensome to the places to which they have been assigned. If they have parents in possession of property, their possessions are to be given to those parents, so that through them the Church’s rights may be preserved.

[Col. 0505C] Three years previously, the subdeacons of all the Churches of Sicily had been forbidden, following the custom of the Roman Church, to have intercourse with their wives in any manner.

[Note: Thus the law of celibacy was gradually imposed on subdeacons. As a result, they eventually came closer to the sacred orders, so that at length they were permitted to enter the sanctuary and touch the sacred vessels, with the older canons of the Council of Laodicea, chapter 11, and of Agde, canon 66, having been set aside. GUSSANV. See various constitutions concerning the celibacy of subdeacons in Thomassin, part I, book II, chapters 61–63. We discussed this subject at length in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II.]

[Note: Here “particular” is used, as in the following letter. GUSSANV.]

But it seems harsh and unreasonable to me that a man who has not embraced the practice of this continence and has not previously promised chastity should be compelled to separate from his wife and thereby—God forbid—fall into something worse. Therefore, it seems to me that all bishops should henceforth be told not to presume to make anyone a subdeacon unless he has promised to live chastely. In this way, the things of the past which were not sought through a deliberate purpose of the mind will not be forcibly demanded, while future conduct will be carefully guarded.

[Note: In the printed editions, *praeterita mala* (“past evils”) is read. Since we searched for it in vain in the Vatican and other manuscripts, where we find only *praeterita* (“past things”), we rejected the added word *mala*.]

Those who, after the same prohibition issued three years earlier, have lived continently with their wives are to be praised and rewarded, and encouraged to remain in their good conduct. But those who, after the prohibition was issued, refused to abstain from their wives are not to be admitted to sacred orders, because no one ought to approach the ministry of the altar unless his chastity has been tested and approved before undertaking that ministry.

To Liberatus, the merchant who has entrusted himself to the Church and lives on the Cincian estate, you are to provide an annual allowance.

[Note: That is, an annual pension for the support of life. See above, letter 18, note b, and Homily 20 on the Gospel, col. 1521. In the following letter, 45, *continere* is read in the same sense.]

Determine for yourself what the amount of this allowance ought to be, so that, once reported to us, it may be charged in your accounts. As for the present indiction, I have already received it from our son, the servant of God Diaconus.

Fantinus the defensor: a certain monk named John, dying, left him heir to six twelfths of his estate. Give him what was left to him, but warn him that he must not presume to do this again. Set an amount for what he is to receive for his labor, so that his labor may not be fruitless; and let him remember that one who lives on the Church’s stipends must not pant after private gain.

[Note: In former times monks were able to make wills concerning their property. See the Theodosian Code, book V, title 3, and the notes of Gothofredus. Later they were deprived of the power to make wills: Justinian, Novels 5 and 123, chapter 38. It is not easy to reconcile this act of John the Monk with another concerning the abbess Sirica, whose will is annulled in book IX, letter 7, especially since Sirica had assigned part of the legacy to a hospital, whereas here the legacy was given by John to Fantinus the defensor. Mabillon conjectures that Gregory perhaps allowed this dispensation because Fantinus the defensor had earned such a privilege by the assistance he had rendered to the monastery. See book I of *On Diplomatics*, chapter 2, no. 10. From the permission granted to Probus the abbot to make a will, as a special privilege and for serious reasons, it is clear that monks were then forbidden to make wills. See Gregory’s rescript to Probus the abbot in the appendix; formerly letter 22 of book IX, in the fourth edition, and what we have said on this subject in the *Life of Saint Gregory*. Certainly nothing was farther from the holy Doctor’s mind than to leave anything private to monks, as is especially clear in the preceding letter 42.]

But if anything comes to the Church without sin or covetous desire through those who conduct the Church’s affairs, it is fitting that they should not be left without reward for their labor; nevertheless, it is to remain for our judgment to determine how they ought to be rewarded.

Investigate carefully the case concerning Rusticianus’s silver, and carry out whatever seems just to you. Admonish the illustrious Alexander that he must settle his case with the holy Church. If he should perhaps neglect to do so, pursue the same case as best you can, with fear of God and maintaining due propriety. In this matter we also wish you to show some generosity; and, if it can be done, let what is to be given to others be remitted to him, provided that he brings to an end the case which he has with us.

[Note: Earlier editions read *exerceat* (“conducts”).]

Restore without any delay the donation of the servant of God who fell and was assigned to a monastery, so that, as I said above, the place itself—which bears the burden of her care—may have the income from her property for her support. Also recover whatever of her property is being held by others, and hand it over to the aforesaid monastery.

Send us the revenues of the Hospital on the New Road, in the amounts you reported to me, since you have them in your possession. As for the *actionarius* whom you appointed over that estate, give him something, as seems appropriate to you.

Concerning the servant of God who lived with Theodosius, named Extranea, it seems to me that you should provide her with an annual allowance, if you see that this is useful, or else return the donation which she made.

Restore without any delay the monastery house which Antoninus had taken from the monastery for thirty solidi, once the solidi have been recovered.

[Note: *Amula*, says Papias, is a wine vessel. The Roman *Ordo* uses the word for the little pitchers in which wine and water are contained for the sacrifice at the altar. Some authors call it *ama*. GUSSANV. See the notes of Alteserra on this passage.]

After carefully investigating the truth, restore the onyx vessels, which I have sent back through the bearer of this letter.

Send Saturninus to us, if he is available and is not occupied with you.

Felix, the tenant of Domna Campana, whom she had left free and ordered to remain exempt from investigation, said that the subdeacon Maximus had taken seventy-two solidi from him. He asserted that, in order to pay them, he had either sold or pledged all the property he possessed in Sicily. But the legal experts said that he could not remain exempt from investigation concerning fraud.

While returning to us from Campania, he died in a storm. We wish you to investigate his wife and children and, concerning everything he had pledged or sold, release the pledged property, restore the price of what was sold, and in addition provide them with some means of support, because Maximus had sent him to Sicily and had taken from him there the things he claimed. Therefore, ascertain what was taken and restore it to his wife and children without any delay.

Read all these matters over carefully, and set aside all that familiar negligence of yours. Have my letters, which I sent to the peasants, read again throughout all the estates, so that they may know, by our authority, how they ought to defend themselves against violence; and let either authenticated originals or copies of them be given to them.

Take care to preserve everything without diminution, because concerning the things about which I write to you in order that justice may be safeguarded, I am acquitted of responsibility, while you, if you are negligent, become liable. Consider the terrible Judge who is coming, and let your conscience tremble now at his arrival, so that then it may not fear without cause, when heaven and earth tremble before him. You have heard what I want; see what you do. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, chapter 59.)

## LETTER XLV. TO ALL THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT ILLYRICUM

That they should receive bishops expelled by the enemy and supply them with necessities.

Gregory to all the bishops throughout Illyricum.

[Col. 0508B] Jobinus, a most distinguished man and our son, superintendent throughout Illyricum, has informed us in writing that, in letters addressed to him by imperial authority, he was ordered to have the bishops whom the fury of hostile forces had expelled from their own places joined to those bishops who still reside in their own places, for the sake of support and the expenses of the present life.

Although an imperial command urges your Fraternity to do this, we nevertheless have a greater command from the eternal Prince, by which we are compelled even more fearfully to carry it out: when necessity demands, we must love in the distribution of material assistance not only our brothers and fellow bishops, but even those whom we suffer to be opposed to us.

It is therefore necessary for you, first obedient in this matter to the heavenly Prince and also consenting to the imperial commands, willingly to receive our brothers and fellow bishops, whom the constraints of captivity and various necessities oppress, so that they may be comforted and live together with you through ecclesiastical support.

Not indeed so that the dignity of the episcopal throne may be divided through their sharing in communion, but so that they may receive from the Church, according to the capacity of its resources, sufficient provisions.

[Note: Letter XLV (formerly 43). In the printed editions: *juxta possibilitatem sufficientiae* (“according to the possibility of sufficiency”).]

For in this way we are shown both to love our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority whatever in your Churches, but we earnestly exhort you to sustain them through your assistance.

In the month of June, in the ninth indiction.

(Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapter 16.)

## 541. LETTER XLVI. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

He commands that he provide the necessities of life to Godiscalchus’s poor and blind son.

[Col. 0508D]

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

The divine commandments admonish us to love our neighbors as ourselves. Since we are commanded to love them with this charity, how much more ought we to assist them in the necessities of the body, so that, if not in every respect, at least through some supports, we may relieve their distress?

Since, therefore, we have observed that the son of the most worthy man Godiscalchus suffers not only from loss of sight but also from poverty and want of food, we have deemed it necessary to provide for him insofar as our means permit.

[Note: Letter XLVI (formerly 44). Thus three Vatican manuscripts, with the other manuscripts of better quality agreeing. In the Vatican manuscript designated B, however, it reads “the son of Fliimuth.” In A and C, “the son of Ovadiscalchus.” This may perhaps have occasioned the form *Odiscalchus*, which we find in Corbie and all the Norman manuscripts.]

Therefore, by this present command we order your Experience to provide each year, for his support, twenty-four modii of wheat, twelve modii of beans, and twenty wine-decimals, so that the amount may later be charged to your accounts.

[Note: These seem to be wine casks or measures, as below in book X, letter 30, now book XII, letter 27. Anastasius, in his account of Hadrian: “Two wine-decimals, each weighing sixty pounds.” GUSSANV. In Vatican B: “and wine-decimals, three times twenty.” In the other C: “and twenty wine-decimals.” In the royal manuscripts: “and wine-decimals, three times twenty, are to be supplied.”]

Act, therefore, so that the bearer of this letter suffers no delay in receiving the Lord’s gifts, and so that you may be found to share in the reward of a well-administered trust.

(Compare John the Deacon, book II, chapter 55.)

## LETTER XLVII. TO VIRGILIUS OF ARLES AND THEODORUS, BISHOP OF MARSEILLES

Jews are not to be compelled to baptism, but gently encouraged to embrace the faith.

[Col. 0509B]

Gregory to Virgilius of Arles and Theodorus, bishop of Marseilles in Gaul.

[Note: Letter XLVII (formerly 45). The manuscripts differ in the inscription of this letter. In Vatican B and C it reads, “To Virgilius and Theodorus, bishops of Gaul.” In D, “To Virgilius and Theodorus, bishop of Marseilles.” So also in Corbie, Rheims, Normandy, and Angers. Saxius places Paschasius between Virgilius and Licerius, who died in 588, in his *Pontiffs of Arles*. Because Paschasius occupied the see for only a short time, Saxius believes that Gregory of Tours omitted him; indeed, in the ancient diptychs of the Church of Arles edited by Mabillon in volume III of the *Analecta*, Paschasius is listed in the same order. Mabillon thinks that Saint Virgilius died around the year 616. Certainly Theodosius of Arles conducted the funeral of the blessed Rusticula, whose death in 632 is established by Charles le Cointe in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*, under the years 556, no. 17, and 632, no. 15. See Mabillon’s notes on the *Life of Blessed Rusticula*, no. 31, and on the *Life of Saint Virgilius*, no. 7.

Moreover, Gussanvillaeus unjustly charges the Lérins chronicler with error for saying that Virgilius was abbot of Lérins after Saint Honoratus. In the *Life of Virgilius*, which Vincentius Barralis published from a very ancient parchment manuscript, Honoratus is called Virgilius’s predecessor, but not his immediate predecessor, according to the manuscript itself. For the chronologist writes, in part I, p. 81, that Hilary succeeded Honoratus in the episcopate around the year 430. Then, on p. 94, he observes from Arnold Wion and from Virgilius’s own *Life*, written at the beginning of the eighth century, that Virgilius was made bishop of Arles in 591. He does not investigate whether, when he was raised to the episcopate, he had been abbot of Lérins, as his *Life* states, or of Autun, as Gregory of Tours records in book IX of his *History*, chapter 23. You would search in vain for more about Virgilius in the father of Frankish history. The Bollandists discuss him under 5 March.]

To Virgilius of Arles,

[Note: Arles, in French *Arles*, is a city of Provence on the Rhône River and an archiepiscopal see. That the Church of Arles was never subject to the Church of Vienne, as Gussanvillaeus argues, is proved by Quesnellius in his fifth apologetic dissertation for Saint Hilary of Arles, chapters 4 and following.]

and to Theodorus, bishop of Marseilles in Gaul.

[Note: This man was distinguished for holiness. From about 580 to 590, amid various storms, he governed the Church of Marseilles and suffered much from the rulers of Marseilles because he supported King Childebert, whereas those rulers favored King Guntram, Childebert’s uncle. Gregory of Tours, an eyewitness, gives the whole account at length in book VI, chapter 11; book VIII, chapter 12; and book IX, chapter 22. GUSSANV.]

Although there was no suitable occasion of time or circumstance for writing to your Fraternity and returning the greeting due to you, it has nevertheless come about that at one and the same time I should discharge what was appropriate concerning the affection of fraternal love and should not be silent about a complaint brought to us concerning how the souls of those in error are to be saved.

[Note: Newly ordained bishops were accustomed to receive letters of communion shortly after their ordination, and even Roman prelates did not omit this practice. “There was once this ancient ecclesiastical rule among our fathers,” says Gelasius I in letter 1 to Euphemius, “that the apostolic see should announce by letters the appointment of a newly ordained priest.” See his second letter to Laurentius and letter 12 to Aeonius of Arles. Pope Hilary had earlier done this in letters 5 and 6 to Leontius of Arles, and through him to all the bishops of Gaul. Gregory himself did the same, not only to patriarchs but also to the bishops of the principal sees. See above, letters 25 and 27.

Pelagius I, recently elected pope, wrote as follows in letter 8 to Sapaudus of Arles: “We believe that what the grace of almighty God has accomplished with us has been brought to your Charity’s attention. For this reason it would have been fitting for you to be sent to us, so that by a common visitation we might enjoy great joy with one another. Nevertheless, mindful of fraternal charity and having found an opportunity through the bearers of this letter, we offer the service of fraternal greeting.”

Obeying this injunction of Pelagius, Virgilius and Theodorus wrote to Gregory after hearing of his consecration. He now replies to them, both because an appropriate occasion has arisen and in order to return the greeting due to them.]

Indeed, many men of the Jewish religion living in this province, and from time to time traveling to the region of Marseilles for various affairs, have brought to our attention that many Jews settled in those parts have been brought to the baptismal font more by force than by preaching.

I consider an intention of this sort worthy of praise and acknowledge that it proceeds from love of our Lord. But I fear that, unless a suitable result in accordance with sacred Scripture accompanies that same intention, it will either produce no work deserving of reward or, in some respect, will be followed—God forbid—by the loss of the souls whom we wish to rescue.

For when someone comes to the baptismal font not through the gentleness of preaching but through compulsion,

[Note: Gregory of Tours writes that King Chilperic of Neustria forced many Jews to baptism in the year of Christ 582, book VI of his *History*, chapter 17. The same practice under Childebert’s rule may be inferred from this letter to the bishops of Arles and Marseilles, in which Gregory the Great disapproves of it.

In Spain also, around the year 613, King Sisebut compelled Jews to receive baptism, issuing a law that a Jew who refused baptism was to receive a hundred lashes after being shaved and be punished with the penalty of exile. The Fourth Council of Toledo, held about twenty years later, prescribed in canon 57 concerning the Jews that thereafter no one should use force to make anyone believe.

If we believe Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 65: “The emperor Heraclius . . . , sending to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asked him to order all the Jews in his kingdom to be baptized into the Catholic faith; Dagobert immediately carried this out. Heraclius himself resolved to do the same throughout all the provinces of the empire.” Baudemund, a contemporary writer, likewise attests that Dagobert did this in the *Life of Saint Amandus*, bishop of Tongeren. But Adrian Valesius, *Frankish History*, book XIX, refutes Fredegar and others who, following him, make the same claim about Heraclius. On the ancient practice of baptizing Jews and unbelievers, see further discussions on both sides by Launoy and Nicolai.]

and returns to his former superstition, he dies in a worse state from the very place from which he seemed to have been reborn.

Your Fraternity should therefore call such people forward through frequent preaching, so that they may desire to change their former life more because of the teacher’s gentleness. In this way our intention is rightly accomplished, and the convert’s mind is not turned back again to its former vomit.

Speech must therefore be addressed to them which will burn away the thorns of error within them and illuminate by preaching what is darkened in them, so that your Fraternity may receive a reward through frequent admonition and, insofar as God grants it, lead them to the renewal of a new life.

(Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 43.)

## LETTER XLVIII. TO THEODORUS, DUKE OF SARDINIA

He orders him to have his official undergo judgment with the abbess Juliana, but to protect Pompeiana in her pious case, without prejudice to the law.

[Col. 0511B]

Gregory to Theodorus, duke of Sardinia.

[Note: Letter XLVIII (formerly 46). *Praefecto* (“to the prefect”). In later Greek, δουκατον (*doukáton*) means a prefecture. Ὁ δοῦξ (*ho doûx*), “duke,” occurs in Constantine’s *On the Administration of the Empire*; in Codinus, δοῦκας (*doúkas*), and so forth. GUSSANV. The character of Theodorus is described in the following letter.]

[Note: Sardinia, commonly *Sardegna*, is a large Italian island between the Balearic and Tyrrhenian Seas, under Spanish rule, whose chief city is Caralis, concerning which the following letter speaks. Sardinia then belonged to the African diocese and was its seventh and last province.]

The justice which you carry in your mind ought to be demonstrated before men by the light of your actions. Juliana, abbess of the monastery of Saint Vitus, which Vitula, of blessed memory, had built,

[Note: In Vatican C, “of Saint Justus.”]

has informed us that your official Donatus is holding a possession belonging by right to the aforesaid monastery. Since he sees himself surrounded by the patronage of Your Excellency,

[Note: The printed editions have *erigi* (“to be supported”).]

he scorns to come to have the case examined. But now let Your Glory order that same official to undergo an arbitration with the aforesaid servant of God, so that whatever the arbitrators determine concerning such a dispute may be put into effect, and so that whatever he sees himself either losing or retaining may be attributed not to an act of power but to the justice of the law.

[Note: An honorific form of address, also used by Saint Leo in letter 54 to the empress Pulcheria: “This is owed especially to Your Glory.”]

Furthermore, the religious woman Pompeiana, who is known to have built a monastery in her own house, has complained that the mother of her deceased son-in-law wishes to annul his will, so that her son’s final decision may be rendered void. For this reason we have deemed it necessary to exhort Your Glory with paternal charity to accommodate yourself willingly to pious causes, without prejudice to justice, and benignly to order that whatever legal right belongs to these women be preserved.

We ask the Lord graciously to direct the path of your life and to order the dignity of your office with prosperous administration.

## LETTER XLIX. TO HONORATUS THE DEACON

What should be suggested to the emperors on behalf of the inhabitants of Sardinia.

Gregory to Honoratus the deacon.

[Note: Letter XLIX (formerly 47). He seems to be the Honoratus who, in the earlier printed editions at the beginning of book II, is said to have been made archdeacon of the Roman Church in place of Laurentius. We have relegated this letter to the appendix. Our conjecture is supported by one Vatican manuscript, which reads “to Honoratus the archdeacon.” At that time he was serving at court, perhaps performing the office of *apocrisiarius*. It should not be concealed, however, that in the Vatican manuscript designated D one reads “to Honoratus, deacon of Salona,” but this is corrupt. See book II, letter 53.]

Since, although unworthy, we have undertaken the office of government, we ought to attend to the needs of our brothers insofar as our ability permits.

[Note: He is sufficiently well known from the many letters written to him or concerning him.]

Therefore Januarius, metropolitan of Caralis,

[Note: Caralis, called *Calaris* by later writers and commonly Cagliari, is still the principal city of the island of Sardinia. It was formerly both its civil and ecclesiastical metropolis, as is clear from this very letter. It lies on the sea on the southern coast of the island. Holstenius conjectures from Saint Gregory’s letter 8 of book VII, now book IX, indiction 2, that six bishops of Sardinia were subject to the metropolitan of Caralis. See the additional material he provides on this subject in his notes to *Sacred Geography*, p. 3. GUSSANV.]

our brother and fellow bishop, having come here to the city of Rome, has informed us that Theodorus, the illustrious master of the soldiers, who is known to have undertaken the command of the island of Sardinia, is carrying out many measures there contrary to the commands of our most pious lords—commands by which they have removed, with appropriate clemency and gentleness, many burdens from the possessors and citizens of their empire.

For this reason, at a suitable time, we wish you to make representations to our most pious lords in accordance with what the provincials of the aforesaid island justly and properly request. Earlier also, imperial decrees were sent to Edantius, the illustrious master of the soldiers, then duke of Sardinia for the seventh indiction,

[Note: Imperial *sacra*, or simply *sacra*, are rescripts or commands of the emperors. Saint Augustine, *Against the Donatists after the Conference*, chapter 31: “They carry the *sacra* of many emperors; we carry only the Gospels.” Above, letter 45, *sacri apices* (“sacred letters”). In the acts of the Council of Chalcedon we read of “divine letters,” “divine sanction,” and “letters of divinity.”]

by which they ordered all the present burdensome regulations to be removed, so that their commands, proceeding from their generous mercy, might remain unshaken under whatever dukes might happen to preside at any given time, and so that their reward might not be squandered by those administering their office.

Thus they may pass their lives peacefully under the rule of the merciful lords, and may receive, when the eternal Judge comes, multiplied recompense for the prudent counsel which they now grant to their subjects with tranquil minds.

## LETTER L. TO ANTHEMIUS THE SUBDEACON

That women should not live with monks; and that boys should not be received into the monasteries of certain islands before their eighteenth year.

[Col. 0513A]

Gregory to Anthemius the subdeacon.

Just as we have assumed the office of governance, with God ordering it as pleased him, so we ought to be concerned about the souls entrusted to us. We have learned, however, [Note: [Col. 0513C] EPISTLE L (also 48).—Thus it is read in all the Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others. In the old edition, the name formed from *Eumorphiana* was altered into *Orphiana*. In the more recent editions it is finally read as *Orphiaria*, which Gussanville says is a small island of the Tyrrhenian Sea, not far from Palmaria and Pontia. From the location of Eumorphiana we conjecture that it is the same island now called the Island of Saint Mary. The letter is written to Anthemius, governor of Campania, concerning the monks inhabiting it, since, like Palmaria, it lay opposite the coast of Campania.] that on the island of Eumorphiana, where the oratory of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, is known to be situated, many men with their wives, from various estates, have taken refuge there because of the necessity created by barbarian ferocity. [Note: [Col. 0513D] That is, “we judged it inappropriate”; hence in two Vatican manuscripts it reads: “which we judged inappropriate.”] We have judged it inappropriate that, while other places of refuge are nearby, women should live there with monks. Therefore, by this present order we command your Experience that from this time forward you permit no woman to live or remain there, whether she belongs to ecclesiastical jurisdiction or to anyone else. Instead, since, as has been said, so many nearby places exist, let them provide a refuge for themselves wherever they prefer, so that all association with women may be removed from there. Otherwise, if we cease to exercise the care incumbent upon us and to ward off the snares of the enemy, then, should anything different occur there—God forbid—we may be found blameworthy.

Accordingly, do not delay giving the bearer of this letter, Felix the abbot, fifteen hundred pounds of lead, of which he is known to be in need on that same island; afterward this is to be charged to your accounts when the reckoning of the entire amount is known (Gratian, 20, question 1, canon 5). Act, then, so that you yourself may determine whether it can usefully be expended on the construction of that island. [Note: [Col. 0513D] This law, which forbids children to be received into monasteries before eighteen years of age, is understood to concern only the monasteries of those islands, as will immediately be clear to the reader. Hence it is useless to oppose this prohibition to the rule of Saint Benedict, which permits the admission of children under that age.] Since the gathering of monks on the islands is difficult, we also prohibit children from being received into those same monasteries before the age of eighteen. If any are there now, let your Experience remove them and send them to the city of Rome. We wish you to observe this same rule in every respect in Palmaria and the other islands. [Note: [Col. 0513D] An island, also a small one, in the Tyrrhenian Sea opposite Terracina, about thirty-seven miles distant from it. That these islands were cultivated by monks so that they might live in greater seclusion is also shown by Saint Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book V, chapter 5.]

## EPISTLE LI. TO ALL THE MONKS ESTABLISHED ON THE ISLAND OF CHRIST’S MOUNT

He orders those irregular monks to obey Abbot Horosius.

Gregory to all the monks [Note: [Col. 0514D] EPISTLE LI (also 49).—It retains its name to this day, commonly Monte Cristo. It is a high mountain, or rock, in the Tyrrhenian Sea, encompassing almost the whole of the island that bears the same name. It should nevertheless be observed that the manuscript codices differ in the heading of this letter. In Vatican 4 it reads, “to all … established on the island of Gorgona.” Codex B has, “to all the monks established on Christ’s Mount.” The word “island” is also omitted in the Colbert manuscript.] established on the island of Christ’s Mount.

[Col. 0514A] It has come to our attention that you observe none of the precepts of the monastic rule. For this reason we have been compelled to send to you the bearer of this present order, Abbot Horosius, so that, carefully investigating all your activities, he may arrange whatever seems right to him and report to us what he has ordered. Accordingly, we admonish you to render him complete obedience and to observe whatever he arranges with due reverence, as though it had been arranged by me.

## EPISTLE LII. TO SYMMACHUS, THE DEFENDER

Concerning the construction of a monastery in Corsica; the correction of the monks in Gorgona; and the association of priests with women.

Gregory to Symmachus, the defender.

My son Boniface the deacon told me that your Experience had written that a monastery formerly built by Labina [Note: [Col. 0514D] Thus three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and the Corbie manuscript read *Labinia*, or *Labina*. In the printed editions, *Albinae*.] a devout woman was standing ready, so that monks ought to be established in it. I certainly praised your diligence, but I want another site to be provided, apart from the place already granted for the same purpose. It should nevertheless be a site on the sea, because of the uncertainty of the time, and should either be fortified by the configuration of the place or be capable of being fortified without great labor, so that we may send monks there. In this way the island itself, which until now has had no monastery, may also be improved through this way of life.

To carry out and arrange this matter, we have sent Abbot Horosius, bearer of this present order. Your Experience is to travel with him around the shores of Corsica. If a place belonging to any private person can be found suitable for this purpose, we are prepared to pay a worthy price so that we may establish something secure. We have instructed the aforesaid Horosius to proceed to the island of Gorgona [Note: [Col. 0514D] It is commonly called La Gorgona. It is an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, situated approximately midway between the coast of Tuscany and the island of Corsica. GUSSANV.] [Note: [Col. 0514D] In Vatican manuscripts C and D, the Norman and Corbie manuscripts, it reads *perexeat*. We retain *pergat* (“proceed”), which is the reading of the other Vatican manuscripts and the printed editions.], and your Experience is to go there with him. Punish all the evils which we have learned were committed there in such a way that, through your punishment, the aforesaid island may remain corrected even in the future. The said Abbot Horosius is to establish the monasteries of this island and then hasten to return to us.

Your Experience must therefore act so that, in both matters—whether by providing a monastery in Corsica or by correcting the monks in Gorgona—you hasten to obey not our will but the will of almighty God.

[Col. 0515A] Furthermore, we wish the priests who live in Corsica to be forbidden to associate with women, except only with a mother, a sister, [Note: [Col. 0515B] I doubt that this word has not intruded, since such association is fraught with danger and highly suspect. See the Council of Nicaea, canon 3; Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 20, concerning the presbyter Ursinus. Hence, when he says in book VII, letter 39, that they should not abandon their wives, I interpret him to mean that they should not abandon responsibility for them but should provide them with sustenance. At Agde, canon 16: “Married men are not to be ordained unless the room in which they live has been separated.” The Second Council of Tours, canon 12, concerning a bishop who has a wife, says: “For the sake of the jealous God, let them be separated by such a distance from the proximity of their dwelling that …” Canon 20 of the same council provides that priests should not remain with their wives but should lie apart, alone in a cell, praying and sleeping. “Since, according to the judgment of the canons, no cleric is permitted to remain with his wife,” and so forth. The Council of Carthage III, canon 17, nevertheless creates a difficulty which more exacting critics may consider. Meanwhile, I refer the reader to Gregory of Tours, *History*, book I, chapter 38, and his *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 76 and 78. GUSSANV. The councils of Gaul assembled during this very sixth century do indeed forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons ordained after marriage to associate with their wives. Agde, canon 16; Tours II, canons 12 and 19; Orléans IV, canon 17; Lyons III, chapter 1. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, book I, chapter 39, and *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 78. Yet Saint Gregory implies that this had not at that time been forbidden in Italy, provided that shameful suspicion was absent, both here and in book IX, letter 59, and *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 2. This custom was supported by Apostolic Canon 5: “A bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall not dismiss his wife under the pretext of religion.”] or wife, who must be governed chastely.

As for the three men concerning whom your Experience wrote to my aforesaid son, the deacon Boniface, since they are in great need, provide whatever you judge sufficient for them; we shall later charge it to your accounts. [Note: [Col. 0515D] We find this in no other codex except the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus.] Given in the month of July.

## EPISTLE LIII. TO FELIX, BISHOP OF SIPONTUM

He orders him to visit the church of Canusium and ordain two parochial presbyters there.

Gregory to Felix, bishop [Note: [Col. 0515D] Sipontum, commonly Siponto, was formerly a city and episcopal see of Apulia, on the coast at the foot of Mount Garganus, but it was destroyed. It was succeeded by Manfredonia, which may be called the new Sipontum. GUSSANV.] of Sipontum.

It has come to our attention that the church of Canusium [Note: [Col. 0516B] Canusium, commonly Canosa, a city of Apulia. Formerly an episcopal see; around the year 844 or 845 its see was united with the archbishopric of Bari. GUSSANV.] has been so deprived of the ministry of the priesthood that neither penance can be provided there for those who die nor baptism for infants. Moved, therefore, by the great burden of so pious and necessary a matter, we order your Fraternity, instructed by the authority of this command, to go as visitor to the aforesaid church and to ordain two parochial presbyters. You must, however, ensure that they are worthy of such an office by the reverence of their life and the gravity of their conduct, and that no canonical regulations stand in their way, so that proper and holy protection may be provided for the church.

## EPISTLE LIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SORRENTO

That he solemnly place the relics of Saint Agatha in the monastery of Saint Stephen.

Gregory to John, bishop of Sorrento.

[Col. 0516A] It is easy to grant assent to devout requests, so that faithful devotion may quickly attain its fulfillment. Since Savinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Stephen on the island of Capri [Note: [Col. 0516C] Capreae, or Caprea, commonly Capri, an island adjoining Campania. GUSS. In one Vatican manuscript, the Norman manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, and many others, it reads *Cabris*. In the Tours manuscript, *Calabris*.], has informed us that he was long ago permitted to possess there the relics of Saint Agatha the Martyr [Note: [Col. 0516C] The antiquity of the cult of Saint Agatha is proved both by the fact that her name occurs in the canon of the Mass and by the fact that it is inscribed in the ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage, edited by our Th. Ruinart at the end of the *Acts of the Martyrs*.], and wishes the sacred remains themselves to be placed in his monastery, we therefore order you to go to the aforesaid monastery and, [Note: [Col. 0516C] “There,” that is, in the very place where the relics are to be placed; it is not required that no human corpses have been buried anywhere in this monastery. How could there have been no bodies lying there, when the monks had no other place in which to bury their brothers? Indeed, nothing prevented the burial of the bodies of deceased faithful in the churches or oratories themselves, which were not consecrated without the sacred relics, as is clear from *Dialogues*, book IV, chapters 50–53. Why the most holy pontiff added this precaution is considered by Gussanville. There are two possible reasons. First, the laws did not allow buried bodies to be moved: “Audacity proceeds to the tombs of the dead and to consecrated mounds,” says Julian, *Augustus*, book V of the Theodosian Code; and Justinian, *On the Violation of Tombs*. Since earlier generations always regarded the removal of a stone, the disturbance of earth, and the tearing up of turf as close to sacrilege, see Sponde, *On Sacred Cemeteries*, book I, part I, chapter 9. Second, the relics of martyrs were not to be mixed with profane bones or the remains of impious persons, since without the relics buried beneath the altar neither a church nor an oratory was consecrated.] if it is established that no body has been buried there, solemnly place the aforesaid sacred remains there, so that he may obtain the fulfillment of his devotion. [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Sacred remains” means relics, as is understood both from this passage and from many other letters. See book II, letter 12, and elsewhere throughout.]

## EPISTLE LV. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

That he permit neither the poor to be oppressed nor the son of a free woman to be compelled into slavery.

Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

I remember that I have often admonished you, not only through frequent commands but also when you were present, that you should act there in our place not merely for the interests of the Church but especially to relieve the needs of the poor, and that you should defend them more vigorously from anyone’s oppression.

The bearer of this letter, Gaudiosus, has informed us that the agents of the holy Roman Church—which, by God’s authority, we govern—are inflicting violence upon him. He asserts that the men of the aforesaid Church wish to claim his children. After he produced documents, we learned that Sirica, the wife of the bearer of this letter, had once been granted by Ecia of glorious memory to a certain woman named Morena by a deed of gift, [Col. 0517A] and that Morena had freed her by letter. [Note: [Col. 0517D] EPISTLE LV (also 53).—Concerning the manumission of slaves, see the very learned observation of Altaserra on this passage.] We therefore believe it improper that sons born of a free woman should be reduced to slavery.

Accordingly, by this present authority we command your Experience to examine these very documents carefully, as we have done, with your mind freed from other concerns, so that, if there are no documents on the part of the Church that ought to prevail against this man’s documents, you withdraw from troubling him without any further reconsideration. It is harsh if, when others grant freedom in return for payment, the Church—which ought to protect such freedoms—revokes them.

Again and again, therefore, we necessarily admonish your Experience that, if any disputes arise there between the poor and the holy Roman Church, you examine them with complete integrity of mind [Col. 0517B] and conduct the affairs of the patrimony in such a way [Note: [Col. 0517D] We restore this reading from the Vatican manuscripts and our own. In the printed editions it reads: “so that he does not depart from justice through kindness.”] that you do not depart from justice through kindness.

## EPISTLE LVI. TO PETER, THE SUBDEACON

What he should provide for distribution to the poor at the celebration of a dedication.

Gregory to Peter, the subdeacon.

Since we devote ourselves eagerly to the festivals of the saints, we have judged it necessary to send the page of this present command to your Experience. We inform you that we have arranged, with the Lord’s help, for the oratory of blessed Mary, recently built in the cell of the brothers where Abbot Marinianus is known to preside, to be solemnly dedicated in the month of August, so that what we have begun may, by the Lord’s work, be brought to completion.

[Col. 0517C] But because of the poverty of that community, we ought to contribute on that festival day; therefore we wish you to provide for distribution to the poor at the celebration of the dedication: ten solidi in gold, thirty amphorae of wine, [Note: [Col. 0517D] EPISTLE LVI (also 54).—The manuscripts disagree here. We follow Vatican D, all the Norman manuscripts, the English manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, and the Rheims manuscript. Vatican B reads: “three hundred sextarii of grain … three hundred hens.” In the printed editions: “two hundred modii of grain, oil, etc. … rams.”] two hundred lambs, two orcae of oil, [Note: [Col. 0517D] The word is Spanish, derived from Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 13, and Isidore, book XX, chapter 6; it is a type of amphora. Gregory of Tours, *History*, book IV, chapter 44: “They stole seventy vessels, commonly called *orcae*, containing oil and fish sauce.” There were sixty *orcae* of oil in Senator, book III, letter 7. We also learn from Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1204, that ashes were stored in *orcae* among the Romans. On banquets at the dedication of churches, see Altaserra on this letter.] twelve wethers, and one hundred hens, which may afterward be charged to your accounts.

Arrange immediately, therefore, that these things be done without any delay, so that, with God as author, our wishes may quickly attain their fulfillment.

## EPISTLE LVII. TO SEVERUS, THE BISHOP

Concerning the choice of the bishop of Ariminum.

Gregory to Severus, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0518D] EPISTLE LVII (also 55).—The care and visitation of the church of Ariminum are entrusted to Ficolinus, a man of exceptional integrity and ability who lived near that church. Four years after the death of John, bishop of Ravenna, we read that the visitation of the church of Ravenna was likewise entrusted to Severus, book IV, letter 25. While Castorius, bishop of Ariminum, was confined at Rome by illness, responsibility for the church of Ariminum had been entrusted to Leontius of Urbino, indiction 11, letter 24; afterward to Sebastianus, as we learn from letter 21 of indiction 15.]

[Col. 0518A] We have learned from a letter of your Fraternity that certain persons agreed, in the case of Ocleatinus, on an episcopal election. Since we do not approve him, they ought not to persist in his candidacy. Announce to the inhabitants of that city that, if they find in that church someone worthy of this office, they should all turn to his election. Otherwise, the bearer of this letter will indicate to you the person about whom we have spoken, and in whose election the decree should be made.

You must be diligent and careful in the visitation of that church, so that its property may be preserved unimpaired and its interests administered in the customary manner under your direction.

## EPISTLE LVIII. TO ARSICINUS, THE DUX, THE CLERGY, THE ORDER, AND THE PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF ARIMINUM

That they should not elect Ocleatinus as bishop.

[Col. 0518B]

Gregory to Arsicinus [Note: [Col. 0518D] In the printed editions, *Ursicinus*; below, *Odeatinus*, instead of *Ocleatinus*.], the dux, the clergy, the order, and the people [Note: [Col. 0518D] Ariminum, commonly Rimini, a city that remains episcopal today in the province formerly called Aemilia, now commonly Romagna. It lies between Ravenna and Ancona, on the Adriatic Sea. It is now subject to the archbishop of Ravenna as its metropolitan and to the supreme pontiff as its lord and prince. GUSSANV.] of the city of Ariminum.

The text of the report sent to us indicates how ready is your devoted expectation of a bishop. But since the one who ordains must be especially diligent in such matters, our care is certainly vigilant in deliberating about this. We therefore admonish your Charity by this letter that no one should trouble himself by approaching us on behalf of Ocleatinus. If someone useful for this purpose is found in the same city, provided that he cannot be reproved by us, let your election unite around him. If no worthy person is found for this purpose, we have indicated to the bearer of this letter the person to whom you should likewise give your consent.

Be unanimous in praying faithfully that whoever is to be ordained may both prove useful to you and offer a priestly service worthy of our God.

## EPISTLE LIX. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

Let him provide thirty solidi annually for the support of Palatina.

Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

If we respond with a compassionate mind to the needs of our neighbors, we undoubtedly find the merciful Lord responsive to our own needs. Palatina, an illustrious woman, has informed us that she is subject to many continuing hardships. Therefore, by this present authority we command your Experience not to delay giving her thirty solidi annually for her support, which may afterward be charged to your accounts. [Note: [Col. 0519C] In one manuscript of Teller, the subscription reads: “Given in the month of August, indiction 9.”]

Act, then, so that by serving well you may receive the benefit of your reward and bring our commands to completion.

## EPISTLE LX. TO THE CLERGY, THE ORDER, AND THE PEOPLE RESIDING AT PERUSIA

That they should not delay the election of a bishop any longer.

Gregory to the clergy, the order, and the people residing at Perusia [Note: [Col. 0519C] EPISTLE LX (also 58).—Commonly Perugia, a large city of Italy on the border of Etruria and Umbria, still an episcopal city today. GUSSANV.].

We are astonished, beloved brothers in Christ, that you see the Church of God without a rector for so long a time and give no thought to the governance of yourselves and of the whole people. For it is well known that, if a flock lacks the care of a shepherd, it goes along byways and therefore more easily falls into the snares of its lurking enemy. [Note: [Col. 0519D] In the printed editions and in some manuscripts: “and therefore more familiarly.” Our reading was supplied especially by the Vatican manuscripts.] It is therefore necessary to seek out from among those who serve the Church one who, in the fear of the Lord, can worthily undertake the ministry of shepherd, and who, under the Lord’s protection, may serve there as the dispenser of the divine sacraments, so that he may daily offer a pure sacrifice of the heart for the children of your Church and show the flock how it should proceed toward the heavenly homeland.

## EPISTLE LXI. TO GENNADIUS, THE PATRICIAN AND EXARCH OF AFRICA

That he order Theodorus, the *magister militum*, to cease harassing the poor and the Church.

[Col. 0519C]

Gregory to Gennadius, the patrician and [Note: [Col. 0519D] EPISTLE LXI (also 59).—That is, the prefect of the praetorium, whom Justinian wished to reside at Carthage and placed over the prefects of the other provinces. Since Sardinia was one of the seven provinces of Africa, for this reason complaints concerning Theodorus, the prefect or dux of Sardinia mentioned above in letters 48 and 49, were brought to this exarch.] exarch of Africa.

The submission of the necks of your enemies testifies that you constantly keep the fear of God before your eyes and pursue justice. But so that the grace of Christ may preserve your glory in the same prosperity, promptly suppress whatever you recognize to be wrongly committed, as you are accustomed to do. Thus fortified with the weapons of justice, may you overcome hostile attacks through the power of faith, which is the safer summit of virtue. [Note: [Col. 0519D] We restore this from the manuscripts, especially the Vatican and Norman manuscripts; previously it read: “which is the summit of the whole …”]

Marinianus [Note: [Col. 0519D] This is a city in Sardinia, called the Tower of Libysson by Pliny, book III, chapter 7; and the Tower of Bysson by Ptolemy, book III, chapter 3. Finally, it is called *Turribus* in the Peutinger Tables and by the anonymous geographer of Ravenna.] our brother and fellow bishop of the city of Turris has sorrowfully reported to us that the poor of his city are being entirely harassed and afflicted by losses of their property. [Note: [Col. 0519D] That is, by losses of benefits or temporal goods.] Moreover, the religious persons of his church [Note: [Col. 0520C] The word *religiosus* has been so far removed from its original meaning that it was necessary to add this note, lest anyone suppose that monks are meant here rather than clerics and other faithful persons. See Lyons II, canon 2, where wills are discussed. Sidonius Apollinaris, book IV, letter 28, describing Vettius, an illustrious man, says that he was secretly and delicately religious, “not under a little cloak, but under a military cloak.” See book III, letter 22. GUSSANV.] are suffering serious harassment from the men of Theodorus [Note: [Col. 0520D] In Vatican B, “of the magnificent man,”] the *magister militum*, and enduring bodily injuries. Matters have even progressed to the point that, which is an unspeakable thing, they are thrust into prison. He also says that, even in matters belonging to his Church, he is seriously obstructed by the aforesaid illustrious man. [Note: [Col. 0520D] Previously it read: “whatever they may be, if nevertheless …”]

You know how contrary all this is—if indeed it is true—to the discipline of the commonwealth. Since it is appropriate that your Excellence correct all these things, I salute your Eminence and ask you not to permit them to happen any further. Rather, by your action, order that man to cease harming the Church and that none of them be burdened by requisitions or services beyond what reason permits. If there are any disputes, let them be settled not through fear of official power but according to legal procedure. [Note: [Col. 0520D] Thus three Vatican manuscripts read it. In another manuscript marked D, and in the Corbie, Norman, and many others, only this is read: “order that …” In the printed editions: “by your action order him diligently to …”]

Therefore, I ask you, with the Lord assisting you, to correct all these matters through the threat of your command, so that, if the illustrious Theodorus or his men do not abstain from such actions out of regard for justice, they may at least do so out of fear of your command. In this way justice may flourish freely in the provinces entrusted to you, to your praise and reward. [Note: [Col. 0520D] The printed editions introduced *nostrae* (“our”) instead of *vestrae* (“your”); we have corrected it from the Vatican, Gallican, and English manuscripts. Sense and the purpose of the letter likewise require this reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0520D] EPISTLE LXII (also 60).—This and letter 64 seem to be one letter, with a few words altered at the beginning.]

## EPISTLE LXII. TO JANUARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CARALIS IN SARDINIA

That he protect Catella from the harassment of certain persons, while preserving justice.

Gregory to Januarius [Note: [Col. 0520D] Thus it is read in the Vatican and other manuscripts. In the printed editions: “to the archbishop of Caralis.”], archbishop of Caralis in Sardinia.

[Col. 0520C] If our Lord himself, as the testimony of sacred Scripture declares, professes to be the husband of widows and the father of orphans, then we too, as members of his body, ought with the deepest affection of mind to imitate our head and, while preserving justice, be present to orphans and widows whenever necessary.

Since we have been informed that Catella, a devout woman whose son is serving here in the holy Roman Church—which, by God’s authority, we govern—is being harassed by the provocations or disturbances of certain persons, we have found it necessary to exhort your Fraternity by this present letter not to decline to offer protection to the aforesaid woman, while preserving justice. Know that by such actions you both make the Lord your debtor and bind our charity toward you more closely.

We wish the causes of the aforesaid woman, whether they exist now or may arise in the future, to be settled by your judgment, so that legal harassment may be removed from her, while she is in no way excused from the justice of judgment. [Note: [Col. 0521D] This must be read from the Vatican manuscripts and all the others. In the printed editions: “by our judgment.”]

I pray the Lord to direct your way toward him in a prosperous course and, in his mercy, to lead you to the kingdom of the glory that is to come.

## EPISTLE LXIII. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS IN SARDINIA

He commends Pompeiana, so that she may not be burdened contrary to equity.

[Col. 0521B]

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis in Sardinia.

Although your Fraternity appropriately devotes itself, out of zeal for justice, to protecting various persons, we nevertheless believe that you are especially ready to offer comfort to those whom our letter commends to you. Pompeiana, a devout woman, has informed us through her agent that she continually suffers many unreasonable hardships from certain persons, and she is known to have begged us to commend her to you by our letter.

Therefore, saluting your Fraternity with the proper affection of charity, we have necessarily commended this woman to you, so that, with justice accompanying you, [Note: [Col. 0521D] EPISTLE LXIII (also 61).—Vatican B reads: “let your Fraternity permit her to be burdened by no one …” The printed editions: “let her be burdened in no case …” We follow two Vatican manuscripts and others of higher authority.] your Fraternity may not permit her to be burdened in any matter contrary to equity, nor suffer any losses without due consideration.

If she happens to have any causes, let the dispute be aired in argument before chosen judges, [Col. 0521C] [Note: [Col. 0521D] We are compelled to accept this reading by the agreement of the old manuscripts and editions. In the recent editions it reads: “before those who are disputing.”] and let whatever is decided be peacefully brought to completion with you offering assistance, so that a reward for such a work may remain with you and she, commended by our letter, may rejoice that she has found justice.

## EPISTLE LXIV. TO JANUARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CARALIS

He commends Catella, a devout woman.

Gregory to Januarius, archbishop of Caralis in Sardinia.

The necessity of pastoral governance compels us to devote ourselves more diligently to the causes of orphans and widows than to other concerns. [Note: [Col. 0521D] EPISTLE LXIV (also 62).—In the printed editions: “And since it has been reported to us …”]

It has been reported to us that Catella, a devout woman whose son is serving here in the holy Roman Church—which, by God’s authority, we govern—is being harassed by the provocations or disturbances of certain persons. We have therefore found it necessary to exhort your Fraternity by this present letter not to decline to offer protection to the aforesaid woman, while preserving justice. Know that by such actions you both make the Lord your debtor and bind our charity toward you more closely.

We wish the causes of the aforesaid woman, whether they exist now or may arise in the future, to be settled by your judgment, so that legal harassment may be removed from her, while she is in no way excused from the justice of judgment.

I pray the Lord to direct your way toward him in a prosperous course and, in his mercy, to lead you to the kingdom of the glory that is to come.

## EPISTLE LXV. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

That the house of Petronius, improperly marked as titled property, be restored to Theodora, that widow.

Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

Just as we ought not to lose property belonging by right to the Church, so we likewise judge it uncivilized to desire what belongs to others. Since we have learned that the house of Petronius, the notary of the holy Roman Church—which, by God’s authority, we govern—was unreasonably marked with a title by Constantius, then the defender, [Note: [Col. 0521D] EPISTLE LXV (also 63).—The scribes were so called from their insignia. They wrote either in the Palace, in the army, or in the Church, and accordingly their orders and duties differed; it is not our intention to pursue these distinctions. GUSSANV.] we entrust to your Experience, by the page of this present command, that, with every excuse and delay set aside, you remove the title and restore the same house without delay to Theodora, the widow of the aforesaid Petronius, the bearer of this letter. [Note: [Col. 0521D] Valentinian, book III of the Code, *On Vacant Property*: “The titles by whose addition estates are preserved for our property are not posted except by public attestation.” It is said that these were wooden tablets, Greek *σανίδας*, according to Novel 30, *On the Protectors of Cappadocia*, chapter 8; in French, written placards, notices, or posters. Saint Augustine alludes to this practice, *Exposition on the First Epistle of Saint John*, tract 7: “Withdraw, plunderers; withdraw, invaders of Christ’s possession. In your possessions, where you wish to rule, you have dared to break the titles of the Almighty. He knows his titles; he claims his possession for himself. He does not erase the titles, but enters and possesses. Thus, when someone comes to the Catholic Church, baptism is not erased, lest the emperor’s title be erased,” and so forth. The aforementioned Novel establishes penalties against those who break titles. GUSSANV. See book V, letter 41, and the Acts of the synod at the end of the letters, formerly book IV, letter 44: “A new and highly reprehensible custom has arisen in the Church: when its rectors suspect that urban or rural estates may belong by right to its patrimony, they mark them with titles after the manner of the treasury,” and so forth. Concerning titles customarily placed as a sign of possession, see Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book IV, letter 14: “With titles affixed to his houses, you will claim them for the rights of our treasury.” See also book V, letter 7.] Otherwise, God forbid, widows might suffer harm precisely where they ought to find consolation and relief.

## EPISTLE LXVI. TO FELIX, BISHOP OF MESSANA

Which customs should be preserved and which abolished. He advises him amicably not to send gifts to him or come to Rome.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Messana.

[Note: [Col. 0522D] EPISTLE LXVI (Alternative numbering: 64).—Whether it is a due introduced by law or by unlawful lapse of time. Thus many things have been brought into the Church which ought long ago to have been removed by the example of Saint Gregory, and which justice now forbids to be exacted, as does prudence, and as do the canons. See the Second Council of Chalon, canons 16 and 17. GUSSANV.]

It is fitting that we, by our careful consideration, remit customs which are known to impose a burden upon the Churches, lest they be compelled to provide anything to those from whom they ought rather to expect such things to be provided for themselves. You must, however, preserve inviolate the customary allowance of the clergy and of the others, and send them each year what is customary. But as for us, we forbid you henceforth to send anything.

And since we do not take pleasure in gifts, we received with thanks the *Palmatian* garments which your Fraternity sent us [Note: [Col. 0523C] I understand *vestes palmatae* to mean garments decorated with palms, as though interwoven with palm motifs, made in what is called Phrygian or embroidered work. It is well known that the *palmata* garment was formerly held in high esteem among the Romans. It was worn by emperors and distinguished men. GUSSANV. Our Mabillon held nearly the same opinion concerning the *Palmatiana* in the Life of Saint Gregory, which he included in volume I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*. We readily subscribe to the opinions of learned men, and do not approve Cardinal Baronius’s conjecture that *Palmatiana* grapes, or Palmatian wine, are intended. The principal gifts with which the kings and the Roman senate honored their friends were embroidered togas and *tunicae palmatae*, as Livy testifies in Books X and XXX. Concerning the *tunica palmata*, see further Ferrarius, *De re vestiaria*, Book II, chapter 8. A Mass published by Illyricus mentions a sacred garment called *Palmatica*, as Hugo Menard observes in his notes on the *Sacramentary*, note 940.]; but, lest you should thereby suffer any loss, we had them sold for a fair price and sent that price to your Fraternity item by item.

But since we have learned that your Charity wishes to come to us, we admonish you by this present letter that you should not undertake the labor of coming. Rather, pray for us, so that, although distances on the road separate us, our spirits may nevertheless, with Christ’s help, be joined to one another in charity; and thus, aiding one another by mutual prayer, we may hand over the office entrusted to us intact to the Judge who is to come.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 24.)

## EPISTLE LXVII. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

[Note: [Col. 0523C–D] EPISTLE LXVII (Alternative numbering: 61).—In the Norman, Colbert, Corbeiensis, Germanic, and several other manuscripts, the reading is simply “to Peter.” In four Vatican manuscripts “the subdeacon” is added. The Andegavensis agrees. The printed editions formerly read “to Anthemius the subdeacon.”]

That he provide an annual allowance for Pastor, who is suffering from weakness of the eyes.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

If, with compassionate goodwill, we respond to the needs of our neighbors, we undoubtedly find the merciful Lord responsive to our own petitions. We have learned that a certain Pastor, who suffers from excessive weakness of sight, has a wife and two slaves, and who had once been illustrious together with Jonathan, is subject to very many necessities [Note: [Col. 0523D] A man’s proper name, as in Ausonius. GUSSANV.].

Therefore, by the page of this present command, we admonish your Experience not to delay in giving, for his support, three hundred measures of wheat each year, and an equal number of measures of beans [Note: [Col. 0523D] Thus restored from one Vatican manuscript, the Corbeiensis, and the Norman. In the others it reads “one hundred measures.”], which may thereafter be charged to your accounts.
