Act, then, so that, both ministering well and receiving the benefit of your reward, you may carry out our command effectively.

[Note: [Col. 0523D] This is found only in the Turonian manuscript of Saint Gatianus and in the Colbert manuscript, although in the latter it appears to belong to the following epistle.]

In the month of August.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 55.)

## EPISTLE LXVIII. TO ANTHEMIUS THE SUBDEACON

He is to ensure that the sacred furnishings of the Church of Venafrum, which the clergy had sold to a Jew, are restored, and that he compel the guilty parties to do penance.

Gregory to the subdeacon Anthemius.

Fuscus, the chief physician, moved by the ardor of faith, brought forward a petition, saying that Opilio, a deacon and servant of God, and Crescentius, clerics [Note: [Col. 0523D] EPISTLE LXVIII (Alternative numbering: 66).—Thus we restore the reading from the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, whereas it formerly read “the deacon”; but also “the servant of God Crescentius.”], of the Church of Venafrum [Note: [Col. 0523D] Venafrum, commonly Venafri, a city of Campania not far from the river Volturnus; it is still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Capua. The manuscripts spell the name variously. Vatican B has *Venafanae*; C, *Benafanae*; D, *Benafranae*. The Norman, Corbeiensis, and old edition follow Vatican C.], having forgotten the fear of the future judgment, had sold the sacred vessels of the aforesaid Church to a certain Hebrew—which it is shameful even to say [Note: [Col. 0523D] Here “vessels” means sacred vessels, ornaments, and furnishings. GUSSANV. Against the crime of those clerics, it is pleasing to direct the words of Optatus: “Yet this monstrous crime has been doubled by you, when you broke the chalices that carry Christ’s blood . . . . . avaricious men, when you sell them; sacrilegious men, when you sold them thoughtlessly . . . . . Perhaps filthy women bought them for their own use; pagans bought them, intending to make vessels in which they might burn offerings to their idols.” Optatus, Book VI, *On the Donatist Schism*, chapter 2. See also chapter 5.]: namely, two silver chalices, two crowns with dolphins [Note: [Col. 0524C] A *corona* is a chandelier in the form of a crown or circle fitted with various lamps. Dolphins are not merely ornaments of such chandeliers but also their supports. Anastasius, in his Life of Sylvester: “Constantine gave four crowns with twenty dolphins of the purest gold”; and below: “A golden crown before the body of blessed Peter with five dolphins.” The same author, in his Life of Sergius: “He ordered that the *canthari* and crowns which from ancient times hung before the sacred altar and the confession of blessed Peter the Apostle be taken down.”], and, from other crowns, lilies [Note: [Col. 0524C] Anastasius, in his Life of Leo III: “This holy bishop had lilies placed upon the columns.” Vatican C reads *lilia*, “lilies.”], six large pallia and seven small ones [Note: [Col. 0524D] The manuscripts vary here, including the Vatican manuscripts. A has “one larger pallium and six smaller ones”; B, “seven larger and smaller pallia”; C, “six larger and smaller pallia”; D, “six larger and smaller pallia.” The Norman and Corbeiensis agree. Pallia are frequently mentioned among sacred furnishings. Gregory of Tours, Book VII of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 22: “And when the altar, together with the offerings, had already been covered with a silken pallium.” And Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 13: “Either from the veil of the doorway, or from the little pallia which hang upon the walls.” *Pallia* may also mean priestly and sacred vestments, which were likewise precious in monasteries. Theodore the Studite, in his Testament, article 19: “You shall not use an elaborate and costly garment, except a priestly one.”].

Therefore, as soon as your Experience receives this present order, have the aforesaid ecclesiastics appear before you without distinction. When the truth has been investigated, if the matter is found to be as reported, have the aforesaid Hebrew, who, forgetting the force of the laws, presumed to purchase sacred treasures [Note: [Col. 0524D] The printed editions corruptly read “civilly sacred.” Concerning sacred treasures, see what was said in Epistle 20.], summoned before the provincial judge, and compel him without delay to restore the aforesaid furnishings, so that nothing belonging to the said Church may thereby be diminished.

As for the aforementioned deacon or clerics who committed so great a crime, do not delay in binding them to penance [Note: [Col. 0524D] This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts, where the printed editions have “send into exile.”], so that by their tears they may wash away so grave and serious an offense.

## EPISTLE LXIX. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON OF SICILY

All the disputes and business of the monastery are to be entrusted to an experienced layman.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon of Sicily.

Just as it is fitting that it should be our concern to remove monks from legal disputes, so that they may devote themselves piously and diligently to divine ministries, so it is necessary for our provision to establish how their affairs are to be arranged, lest a mind distracted by various legal concerns dissipate its attention and, weakened, grow sluggish in celebrating its customary work.

Accordingly, the abbot John, bearer of this letter, asserts that he has many matters of business belonging to his monastery [Note: [Col. 0525D] Namely, the monastery of Saint Lucy in Syracuse, as is clear from Epistle 39 of Book VII.]. Therefore, by the page of this present letter, we admonish your Experience that you should speak with Faustus, who had been chancellor to an illustrious Roman man, formerly praetor [Note: [Col. 0525D] In Vatican A: “who had been chancellor to the Roman illustrious man”; B: “who had been chancellor to the illustrious man of the city of Rome, formerly praetor”; in the Corbeiensis: “from the praetor’s chancery,” with the Lyrensis and Audomarensis agreeing. The reading in the Turonian is corrupt. In the Beccensis: “who was from the praetor’s chancery.”], a chancellor [Note: [Col. 0526D] This was the same as a scribe or notary. He was so called because he stood within the barriers, so that his archives might be more secure. Cassiodorus calls the chancellor’s office “the service of the barriers,” Book XI of the *Variae*, letter 6. See Agathias, Book I, concerning the officials of Narses.]. If you find him willing to undertake this matter, you should generally entrust the monastery’s business to him at a fixed salary.

For it is advantageous, at the cost of a small inconvenience, that the servants of God should remain free from the uproar of lawsuits, so that the interests of the monastery do not perish through negligence and the minds of God’s servants remain freer for the Lord’s work.

## EPISTLE LXX. TO ALL THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT SICILY

How they are to guard against the exactions of fictitious defenders.

Gregory to all the bishops throughout Sicily.

The devotion of your Fraternity, long since tested, compels us to exercise such careful concern on your behalf, since you are known to hasten eagerly to our assistance when you hear of harm done to our Church. We have learned that certain persons in the island of Sicily, pretending to be defenders of the Apostolic See, burden you with forced services for grain and other things [Note: [Col. 0526D] EPISTLE LXX (Alternative numbering: 68).—In many copies, “for grain” is absent.], and we have therefore judged it necessary to oppose their deceit by this present letter.

Accordingly, greeting your Fraternity with the charity that is due, we strongly admonish you not to leave such persons any opportunity henceforth to insinuate themselves among you. Whoever he may be, if he is truly a notary or defender of our See, unless he brings you a specific letter from us or from the rector of our patrimony, let him obtain no forced services in the name of our Church. Do not permit him to impose any burdens upon you; rather, let him arrange his journey for his own purposes, at his own expense, in whatever way he knows best. Do not allow anyone to be harassed by him in those places.

For preserve with steadfastness these orders which we have issued in our letters for the peace of you and your people, so that, freed from this burden, you may be found devoted and more ready for divine service.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] EPISTLE LXXI. Alternative numbering: 69.]

## EPISTLE LXXI. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

That he protect Cyriacus and Joanna, his wife, who converted from Judaism to Christianity.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

We ought, insofar as reason permits, to offer benevolent assistance to those in need of the help of our recommendation. Therefore, by our command, we have decided to commend to your Experience Cyriacus and Joanna, his wife, bearers of this letter, so that you do not permit anyone to oppress or burden them contrary to justice. Rather, whenever necessary, let them enjoy your assistance with justice consenting, so that, equity being preserved, they may rejoice that our recommendation has benefited them in all things through your intervention.

But because the aforesaid woman is said to be suffering harassment because, after receiving a betrothal pledge, she converted from Judaism to the Christian religion, and because she has asserted that the matter in question has already been judged and concluded, your Experience is to investigate it carefully. If you learn that the case has been adjudicated, do not permit any further complaint against the aforesaid woman to arise in any way. Rather, let what has been judged be preserved in every respect, lest she who is known to have chosen the better part be shaken by the disputes of wicked men.

## EPISTLE LXXII. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

That all the Sicilian bishops should not come to Rome before winter. Peter is to procure an abundant supply of grain beyond the usual amount and send it to the city at the proper time.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

You have learned from our preceding letter that we wished our brothers and fellow bishops residing on the island of Sicily to assemble for the feast day of blessed Peter the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0526D] EPISTLE LXXII (Alternative numbering: 70).—See above, Epistle 36, which Baluzius was the first to publish.]. But because the affair which, as is said, temporarily hindered their journey in connection with the illustrious Justin, formerly praetor [Note: [Col. 0526D] Concerning the dispute between Justin and the bishops of Sicily, see above, Epistle 2.], and because the time now permits neither coming nor returning, we do not wish them to undergo the fatigue before winter.

We do, however, wish Gregory of Agrigentum [Note: [Col. 0526D] Agrigentum, commonly Girgenti, a coastal city of Sicily, still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Palermo. GUSSANV.], Leo of Catania, and Victor of Palermo [Note: [Col. 0527C] Panormus, commonly Palermo, a coastal city, now an archiepiscopal see and the capital of Sicily. GUSSANV.] to travel to us in every respect before winter [Note: [Col. 0527C] The Vulgate editions and many manuscripts read “to you,” but “to us” must be read, as Epistles 33 of Book II and 12 of Book XI prove; from them it is clear that those bishops, at least Gregory and Victor, were ordered to come to Rome to clear themselves.].

With fifty pounds of gold, purchase new grain from outsiders, and store it in Sicily in places where it will not spoil, so that in February we may send as many ships there as possible and have that grain brought to us. But even if we cease sending ships, provide ships yourself and, with the Lord’s help, send this same grain to us in February, except only the grain which we await, according to custom, to be sent now in September or October.

Your Experience must therefore arrange matters so that the ecclesiastical tenants gather the grain without suffering any harassment, since the harvest here has been so small that, unless grain is gathered from Sicily with God’s help, severe famine threatens [Note: [Col. 0527C] Others would say, “there has been a poor harvest”; Gallic, *petite récolte*, “small harvest.” GUSSANV. It should be observed that in the Bigot manuscript of the Life of Saint Gregory by John the Deacon, *sativitas* or *satio* is read instead of *nativitas*, Book II, chapter 60, where this epistle is quoted.].

As for the ships which have always been entrusted to the holy Church, protect them in every respect; the letters of the illustrious Leo, the former consul, which have also been sent to you, support this instruction [Note: [Col. 0527D] Namely, through official documents and letters, as we have already noted above.].

Many people come here asking that certain lands or islands belonging to our Church be granted to them on emphyteusis. We deny the request to some, but have already granted it to others. Let your Experience, however, look to the advantage of the holy Church, remembering that it received the administration of that patrimony before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the Apostle. And although letters may be sent from here, do not permit anything that harms the patrimony to be done, since we do not remember having granted, or intending to grant, anything without reason.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 60.)

## EPISTLE LXXIII. TO PETER THE SUBDEACON

Concerning the restoration of the possessions and money of the Church of Taurominium.

Gregory to Peter the subdeacon.

The greater the reverence that the Churches show to the Apostolic See above others, the more carefully it ought to protect them. And because the houses, lands, and possessions belonging by right to the Church of Taurominium [Note: [Col. 0527D] Taurominium, commonly Taormina, formerly a coastal episcopal city of Sicily on the eastern shore of the valley of Demona, between Messina to the north and Catania to the south. GUSSANV.] are said to have been occupied by agents of our Church contrary to the order of justice, we assign your Experience, by the page of this present command, the task that, once the truth has been learned, you restore to the aforesaid Church all that you discover to have been occupied.

Since it has also come to our attention that, while Bishop Victorinus was still alive, the money belonging to that Church was lost, we wish you to offer assistance to our brother and fellow bishop Secundinus in recovering it [Note: [Col. 0527D] That is, help or support. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 31, says of the cellarer, “let assistance be given him.” Above, Epistle 63, *vobis solatiantibus*, that is, “you assisting.” The word is frequently used below in the same sense.], and to cooperate, preserving equity, in the interests of that Church wherever necessary.

Hasten, therefore, to put into effect everything contained in this present command, so that you may be praised in the aforesaid bishop’s reports for having preserved equity.

## EPISTLE LXXIV. TO GENNADIUS, PATRICIAN AND EXARCH OF AFRICA

He incites him to suppress the efforts of the heretics against the Church. The primate is not to be chosen according to order of place. He is not to reside outside the city. Numidian bishops who wish to come to Rome are not to be hindered.

Gregory to Gennadius, patrician [Note: [Col. 0527D] EPISTLE LXXIV (Alternative numbering: 72).—The exarchs have already been discussed above, in connection with Epistle 33. Some bishops were formerly made exarchs; they presided over several provinces as primates, as Gussanville observed in his note on Epistle 33. Monks also had their exarchs, as Theodoret teaches in his letter to Saint Leo, among his letters in the Quesnell edition, p. 531, chapter 7: “And Alypius, the exarch of the monks who are among us.”], and exarch of Africa.

Just as the Lord has caused your Excellency to shine forth in this life with the light of victory in wars against hostile forces, so ought you to confront the enemies of His Church with every vigor of mind and body, so that your reputation may shine more and more through both kinds of triumph: in secular wars, by vigorously resisting the adversaries of the Catholic Church on behalf of the Christian people, and in ecclesiastical battles, by fighting bravely as the Lord’s soldiers.

For it is known that men of heretical religion, if—God forbid—they obtain the opportunity to do harm, rise up violently against the Catholic faith, so that, if they can, they may pour the poisons of their heresy into the members of the Christian body and corrupt them. We have learned that, with the Lord opposing them, they are raising their necks against the Catholic Church and wish to bend the faith of the Christian name. But let your Eminence suppress their efforts and press their proud necks beneath the yoke of rectitude.

Command the council of Catholic bishops to be admonished, so that it does not make a primate according to the order of place, setting aside the merits of his life [Note: [Col. 0528C] The dignity and rights of primates or metropolitans in all the provinces of Africa were attached not to the civil metropolis—except Carthage, which was the head of Africa in both ecclesiastical and civil affairs—but to the antiquity of the episcopate. See Du Pin, *Historical Dissertation* 1, § 9, or the *Sacred Geography of Africa*, pp. 53–54, prefixed to the latest edition of Optatus’s works. See also Tillemont, *Life of Saint Augustine*, articles 70, 136, and 146. Hence the dignity of metropolitan sometimes fell to men less suited to it. For this reason the wisest pontiff attempted to abolish this otherwise unusual custom; but the larger part of the African bishops, whom Gregory’s policy excluded from the primacy, resisted. They opposed the ancient custom, which he later allows to remain unchanged in Epistle 77: “Concerning the appointment of primates . . . except those who come from the Donatists to the episcopate, whom we absolutely forbid to be advanced to the dignity of the primacy, even when the order of the clergy carries them to that same position.” Whether in Africa, besides metropolitans or primates, some bishop was called *senex* is denied by Cardinal Noris, *On the Pelagian Heresy*, Book II, chapter 8. Tillemont asserts the contrary in the *Life of Saint Augustine*, article 136; see his discussion. The question, and the matter of the Donatists, are treated at length in the Life of Saint Gregory.], since before God it is not the more distinguished rank but the conduct of the better life that is approved.

Let the primate himself not reside indiscriminately throughout the villages, as is customary, but in a single city chosen by them, so that provision may be made for a stronger means of resisting the Donatists through the better spirit of the dignity he has acquired.

From the council of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0529D] Numidia was formerly one of the provinces of Africa, lying between Africa proper to the east, Mauretania Sitifensis to the west, and the Mediterranean Sea to the north. GUSSANV.], permit any who desire to come to the Apostolic See; and if anyone wishes to impugn the life of any one of them, oppose him.

[Note: [Col. 0529D] Thus Vatican D, Corbeiensis, Norman, and Remensis read, where the printed editions have: “The glory of your Excellency indeed greatly advances. . . .”]

Your Excellency’s glory greatly advances before the Creator if, through you, the fellowship of the scattered Churches can be restored. For when He sees gifts bestowed for the glory of His name recalled, He grants still greater gifts, insofar as He sees the dignity of His religion enlarged through them.

Moreover, offering you the affection of a father’s charity, we ask the Lord to make your arm strong for suppressing your enemies and to sharpen your mind, through zeal for the faith, like the point of a flashing sword [Note: [Col. 0529D] The printed editions read “so that He may make your arm”; the manuscripts have “who may make your arm.”].

## EPISTLE LXXV. TO GENNADIUS, PATRICIAN AND EXARCH THROUGHOUT AFRICA

Gregory praises Gennadius highly because he conquers peoples not for earthly reasons but so that the Christian religion may spread. He gives thanks for the inhabitants settled on the patrimony of the Roman Church. He commends Hilary, rector of that patrimony.

Gregory to Gennadius, patrician and exarch throughout Africa.

If so great prosperity in your Excellency’s military actions did not arise from the merit of faith and for the sake of the Christian religion [Note: [Col. 0529D] EPISTLE LXXV (Alternative numbering: 73).—The printed editions read *miranda fuerat*, “the prosperity would have been wonderful.” But all the Vatican and Gallic manuscripts read *fuerant*, which must be connected with what follows: “these things had been granted to ancient military commanders.”], these things would not be greatly remarkable, since we know that they too had been granted to the ancient commanders of armies.

But since, with God granting future victories, you anticipate them not by carnal foresight but rather by prayers, it becomes astonishing that your glory descends not from earthly counsel but from God’s gift from above. For where does the articulate report of your merits not run? It says that you frequently seek wars not from a desire to shed blood but for the purpose of enlarging the state in which we see God worshiped, so that the name of Christ may spread everywhere through the subject peoples by the preaching of the faith.

Just as your external works of virtue make you eminent in this life, so the inward adornments of your character, proceeding from a pure heart [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Vulgate editions read “in the future life, through participation in heavenly joys.” We follow the Vatican, Regius, Norman, and other manuscripts.], glorify you in the future participation in heavenly joys.

For we have learned that your Excellency has provided very much for the interests of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in feeding his sheep, so that you restored considerable districts of his patrimony which had been stripped of their cultivators by granting them to the inhabitants of Datitia [Note: [Col. 0530D] The Beccensis has “to inhabitants granted”; in Gratian, at the cited place, “of the Dacians.” Perhaps *Daratitii* should be read, meaning peoples of the neighboring region of Dara, which, as Cluverius observes, is inhabited by poor and needy people.].

Whatever, therefore, you bestow upon him with a Christian mind, you await its repayment through hope at the future judgment. For this reason, we have also judged the bearer of this letter, Hilary, worthy of being commended to your Eminence, so that in whatever he represents as necessary for himself, provided that justice leads the way, you may show him your customary kindness.

Offering you, moreover, the greeting of a father’s charity, we ask the Lord and our Savior mercifully to protect your Eminence for the consolation of the holy commonwealth and to strengthen you more and more by the firmness of His arm, so that His name may be spread among the neighboring peoples.

## EPISTLE LXXVI. TO GAUDIOSUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS OF AFRICA

After words of courtesy, he commends Hilary.

Gregory to Gaudiosus, master of the soldiers of Africa [Note: [Col. 0530D] In two Vatican manuscripts: “to Gaudiosus, resident in Africa.” In the others and in our editions: “to Gaudiosus, master of the soldiers of Africa.”].

Just as the light of a lamp is diffused through all the neighboring places which it illuminates, so the probity of anyone’s good actions becomes known not only where he lives but throughout various provinces, as report spreads, so that, when there can be no knowledge of his presence, the circulation of reputation accomplishes what the truth of the matter could have shown through personal presence.

For we have learned that the various judges who are sent to administer the province of Africa love your glory with the greatest familiarity. This would not happen unless they perceived the sincerity of your mind, so that they might conduct the administration they had received with the participation of your counsel. Indeed, we give the greatest thanks to God when we recognize that provinces have such native inhabitants of their own who possess inborn nobility, associate with powerful men, and, when the opportunity of the times permits, stand by their provincials as a remedy.

Therefore, offering you the affection of a father’s charity, we commend to your glory the bearer of this letter, whom we have sent there to arrange the affairs of the poor, so that you may grant him whatever is necessary, with justice preserved [Note: [Col. 0530D] Namely, Hilary, or Hilarius, mentioned in the preceding epistle. From John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book II, chapter 35: “He appointed industrious men as rectors of the patrimonies . . . . . Hilary, notary of Germanicianum.” Augustine, bishop of Hippo, shows that Germanicianum was situated not far from Hippo: “The Germaniciani,” he says in Epistle 251, “belong to the care of our Humility.”].

I ask the Lord, who preserves your life in every good thing, to direct your actions by the gift of His mercy.

## EPISTLE LXXVII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF NUMIDIA

What he previously refused, he now grants out of respect for ancient custom: that the senior bishop may be elected primate by that very fact. He excludes a Donatist. He urges the Numidian bishops to peace, to the defense of the Church, and to concern for the souls of their neighbors.

Gregory to all the bishops of Numidia.

If at any time, dearest brothers in Christ, among flourishing crops some unwelcome mixture of weeds intrudes, the cultivator’s hand must remove it by the roots, lest it interrupt the future fruit of the fertile harvest. Let us, therefore, who, although unworthy, have undertaken the cultivation of the Lord’s field, hasten to make the crop free from every scandal of weeds, so that the Lord’s field may bear more abundant fruit.

For through our chartularius Hilary [Note: [Col. 0531C] EPISTLE LXXVII (Alternative numbering: 75).—Saint Gregory calls Hilary a chartularius here and in seven other letters, but in ten others, alternately as it were, calls him a notary. He held both the office of chartularius and that of notary in the Roman Church.], you asked our predecessor of blessed memory that all the customs observed for you in former times should be preserved, customs which long antiquity has maintained from the beginnings of the ordinances of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, down to the present [Note: [Col. 0531C] The Roman pontiffs profess to preserve inviolate the privileges of all Churches. Thus Leo the Great, Epistle 54, to Marcian: “The privileges of the Churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Synod, cannot be shaken by any wickedness . . . . In carrying out this work faithfully, with Christ’s help, I must persevere in service.”].

And indeed, in accordance with the substance of your report, we grant that the custom—which, as is evident, usurps nothing contrary to the Catholic faith—shall remain unchanged, whether concerning the appointment of primates or concerning the other provisions. But we absolutely forbid those who have come from the Donatists to the episcopate to be advanced to the dignity of the primacy, even when the order of the clergy carries them to that same position [Note: [Col. 0531D] The words “of the clergy” are absent from the Norman, Corbeiensis, and most Vatican manuscripts. Regarding this word, the Roman correctors of Gratian’s Decree say: “The author of the Gloss seems not to have had the word *clericorum*, just as neither Ivo nor most manuscript copies of Gratian had it.”].

Let it suffice for them merely to care for the people entrusted to them, and not also to take precedence, in attaining the summit of the primacy, over those bishops whom the Catholic faith has both instructed and brought forth within the bosom of the Church.

You, therefore, dearest brothers, anticipate our admonitions through the zeal of the Lord’s charity, knowing that the strict Judge will bring everything we do to examination and will approve each of us not on the privilege of a higher rank but on the merits of our works.

I ask you to love one another in Christ with mutual peace and to confront heretics and the enemies of the Church with one united purpose of heart. Be concerned for the souls of your neighbors. Persuade those whom you can bring to the faith by preaching charity and by setting before them also the fear of the future judgment, since you have been appointed shepherds, and the Lord of the flocks expects from those shepherds to whom He has entrusted them the fruit of a multiplied flock.

If each of you carefully promotes the increase of his own flock, He will certainly adorn you with the manifold gifts of the heavenly kingdom.

Moreover, offering you the greeting of brotherly affection, I ask the Lord to make you, the shepherds of the souls whom He has chosen, worthy before Him, and to direct our actions here so that He may receive them worthily in the life to come.

## EPISTLE LXXVIII. TO LEO, BISHOP IN CORSICA

He commissions him to visit the Church of Saona.

Gregory to Leo, bishop in Corsica [Note: [Col. 0531D] EPISTLE LXXVIII (Alternative numbering: 76).—A very well-known island of the Tyrrhenian Sea, called *Cyrnus* in Greek, lying between Liguria to the north and Sardinia to the south, from which it is separated by a strait of [reading uncertain] paces. It is now subject to the dominion of the Republic of Genoa. GUSSANV.].

Pastoral concern binds us to attend with anxious consideration to a Church deprived of a priest’s governance.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] The Roman bishop had been accustomed to this in the provinces subject to him as metropolitan, among which was Corsica. But he also sometimes appointed a visitor for the churches of foreign nations. John II ordered that a visitor be assigned to the Church of Reggio in Gaul, Epistles 4, 5, 6. That the neighboring bishop should care for the church after its bishop’s death is decreed by the Council of Riez, A.D. 439, and the Second Council of Orléans, A.D. 553, canon 6. In the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 52, chapter 8: “If any bishop should meanwhile die, the archbishop shall appoint a visitor to that see according to the sacred canons, who, together with the count, shall protect that church from being plundered until the death of that bishop reaches your knowledge” (the Fathers of Quierzy are addressing the prince). Earlier they had said: “If an archbishop should die, the neighboring bishop shall provide for that see until,” and so forth. After elections were restored under Charles the Great, it is evident from the letters of Hincmar of Reims that visitors were appointed by the king to attend the elections. See above, the note to Epistle 15.]

and since we have learned that the Church of Saona, many years ago, upon the death of its bishop, was left wholly without a leader, we have decided to impose upon your Fraternity the task of visiting it, so that under your administration its welfare may be properly carried forward.

[Note: [Col. 0532D] Thus read the English, Norman, royal, Colbertine, Corbie, Anjou, and two Vatican manuscripts. In Vatican manuscripts A, B, C, and D, however, “Harnensem” is read. In the Tours manuscript, “Sajonensem.” In the old printed edition, “Sagonensem.” Saona, or Sagona, was a known city of Corsica in the Middle Ages, between Calvi to the north and Ajaccio to the south; today it is destroyed.]

[Note: [Col. 0532D] The consensus of all the Vatican, royal, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts compels acceptance of this reading. The editors altered *profligari* to *propagari*, which is equivalent to *disponi* (“to be arranged”), as the following words show: “that by your administration ecclesiastical interests … may … be arranged.” The Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 6, and the Sixth Council of Toledo, canon 16, use the same term in nearly the same sense.]

In that church and in its parishes we also grant you permission to ordain deacons and priests. Nevertheless, it must be your diligent concern to examine them carefully, so that their persons may in no way be rejected by the sacred canons. Those whom your Fraternity has found worthy of so great a ministry, and whose morals and conduct you have recognized as harmonious with this ordination, you may, by permission of our authority, freely promote to the aforesaid office.

Thus we wish you to exercise authority over all the affairs of the aforesaid church as its own bishop, until our second letter. [Col. 0532C] Therefore, be diligent and attentive in all these matters, so that under your administration the ecclesiastical interests may in every way be beneficially arranged, with God as their guide.

## LETTER LXXIX. TO MARTIN, BISHOP IN CORSICA

He grants permission to transfer from the Church of Tainate to the Church of Saona.

Gregory to Martin, bishop in Corsica.

It is right that we should lend a kindly ear to those who make just requests, so that the petitioners may find the remedies they hope for and the Church may not lack the solicitude of a pastor. And since the Church of Tanate, in which your Fraternity was formerly honored with priestly dignity, has been so occupied and destroyed by the hostile violence of the perpetrators of crimes that no hope of returning there remains, we hereby constitute you, according to the terms of your petition, without doubt a cardinal priest of the Church of Saona, which has long been deprived of the assistance of a bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0533C] Epistle LXXIX (formerly 77). Thus read the Corbie, Norman, and several other manuscripts. In the Vatican manuscripts it is written either “Taitanis,” “Tainates,” or “Tainatissam”; “Tamitana” is found nowhere.]

[Note: [Col. 0533C] This cardinal title was discussed above, in the note to Epistle 15. Alteserra believes that this class of cardinal priests was not permanent but temporary. They were bishops driven from their sees by barbarian violence and assigned by the Roman pontiff to vacant churches for support and sustenance. If their city was subsequently recovered from the enemy, they returned to it. This is approximately Alteserra’s view; but we do not at all approve the opinion of that learned predecessor. A cardinal priest, therefore, is an incardinated priest attached to a title; nor were such priests then assigned to vacant churches from among bishops expelled from their sees, except when all hope of recovering their former sees had disappeared. If, contrary to expectation, some churches were rescued from the hands of the barbarians and restored to better condition, either the bishops of those churches, who had been incardinated elsewhere, returned to their former spouses, or new pastors were ordained for the restored churches.]

Accordingly, with watchful zeal and in accordance with the precepts of the canons, arrange and order everything with the love of God, so that your Fraternity may rejoice that your wishes have been fulfilled and that God’s Church may be filled with reciprocal joy at having received you as its cardinal priest. (Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapter 15.)

[Note: [Col. 0533D] That some priests belonged to the first order and rank, and others to the second order, is too well known to require a note. Saint Gregory, Homily 22 on Ezekiel, calls them priests of the greater or lesser order; Gregory of Tours does likewise, book V of the History, chapter 49. Origen, Homily 6 on Leviticus, treats of the distinction between lesser and greater priestly offices. Optatus of Milevis, book I: “Why are deacons constituted in the third priesthood and priests in the second?” This is less well known. Sidonius Apollinaris supplies an example, book IV, letter 25, where he calls John the archdeacon, who had not yet been elevated to priestly dignity, a priest of the second order. Indeed, in book IV, letter 11, I read of a bishop of the second order. In book VII, letter 6, he places bishops after the chief priests of cities; by these I understand priests or chorepiscopi, through whom the ministries of the lesser orders were supplied. See book XII, Letter 30. Gussanvillaeus is mistaken regarding John the archdeacon: when Sidonius calls him a priest of the second order, Gussanvillaeus assumes that he was a priest.]

## LETTER LXXX. TO THE CLERGY AND NOBLES OF CORSICA

Because they had excessively delayed the election of a bishop, he himself appoints Martin. Meanwhile, until Martin arrives, he entrusts the visitation to Leo.

Gregory to the clergy and nobles of Corsica, from their peers.

[Note: [Col. 0534C] On the inscription “from their peers,” we have already discussed the matter above, in the note to Epistle 25.]

Although you have now for a long time failed to grieve that God’s Church is without a bishop, we are nevertheless compelled to consider its governance both by the care of the office we have undertaken and, to a very great degree, by the bond of affection we have for you, knowing that the welfare of your souls is likewise involved in its governance. For if the care of a pastor is lacking to a flock, it easily falls into the snares of the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0534C] Sidonius, book VII, letter 6, expresses this no less truthfully than elegantly: “If the widowed Church does not receive an heir to her dignity through an unbroken succession, priesthood dies in her, not the priest; and so what hope, you may ask, remains where the end of a man brings religion to an end?” Elsewhere he calls the condition of such a church a rule that is wavering, tottering, and fluctuating. At the Second Council of Chalon, A.D. 813, canon 51: “Governance must be provided, lest people, deprived of the assistance of prelates in the daily circumstances of life, grow exhausted.” Whether these words should be emended from Burchard, the reader may judge. On the necessity of a bishop, see above, Epistle 32. Let them also read the controversy over the residence of pastors explained at Trent by Brother Bartholomew Carranza of Miranda, A.D. 1547. Gussanv.]

Since, therefore, the Church of Saona has long been deprived of the assistance of a priest, we have deemed it necessary to constitute our brother and fellow bishop Martin a cardinal priest there, and to entrust to our brother and fellow bishop Leo the task of visiting it. To him also we have granted permission to ordain priests and deacons in that church and its parishes, and we have permitted him to exercise authority over its affairs as its own bishop for as long as he remains there.

[Note: [Col. 0534C] Since Martin, a cardinal bishop, is appointed to the Church of Aleria, while Leo is simultaneously entrusted with the visitation of this church and is also granted permission to ordain priests and deacons as though he were its own bishop, some conclude either that an error has entered the text or that another church was entrusted to Leo. Gussanv. Gussanvillaeus’s anxiety is needless here. Leo is granted the right to ordain, and so forth, only until Martin’s arrival, and is ordered to repair and arrange the church’s interests—especially its temporal interests—which had been greatly neglected and diminished during its long vacancy. It was not fitting that the arriving bishop should be burdened with that unpleasant business and be forced to begin his episcopate amid lawsuits. Hence ancient canons decreed that the property of a deceased bishop should be preserved for his successor rather than plundered: Chalcedon, canon 21; Second Council of Orléans, canon 6; Second Council of Worms. How much Saint Gregory’s mind recoiled from dividing episcopal authority between two persons is sufficiently shown by Epistle 45 above.]

Therefore, by this present letter we admonish you to receive the aforesaid visitor with every devotion and to show him obedience in matters consistent with reason, as is proper for sons of the Church, so that, supported by your devotion, he may be able to accomplish everything recognized as pertaining to the welfare of the aforesaid church.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO THE CLERGY, ORDER, AND PEOPLE OF MEVANIA

He urges them at last to agree upon the election of a bishop. Meanwhile, he entrusts care of the church to the priest Honoratus.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at the Church of Mevania.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] In the printed editions, erroneously, “of the Church of Vivania” or “of Viania.” But we find the name of this city in the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts. Gussanvillaeus, who retained the old error, admits that no mention of a city of Vivania is found among geographers. Mevania, now commonly Bevagna, was formerly an episcopal city of Umbria, on the river Clitumnus. The Colbertine manuscript has “the Church of Eutina.”]

Whenever some matter is entrusted to several people to carry out, while each person disagrees with another, access is opened more to losses than to advantages.

[Note: [Col. 0535] [The note appears at the foot of columns 535 and 534, but the callout letter (b) was not printed in the text.] Antonius Augustinus, seeing Haloander and Portius playing with the words *decies* and *deciens*, *centies* and *centiens*, as though they differed in meaning, wished not merely to refute their opinion but also to investigate the cause of such writing. Being, as he was, a man of keen perception, he detected that the letter *n* inserted in these words belonged solely to pronunciation, and indeed to a softer pronunciation. Lipsius added that the letter had been wrongly inserted by copyists, since, as he himself says, the ancients customarily represented long vowels in one way and contracted vowels in another. They wrote the latter singly, as is done today, and doubled the former. A later age, seeking brevity, used an apex for doubling: by “apex” I mean the transverse line that they customarily placed over long vowels, â, ê, ô, û. In support of this view he cites Quintilian, Isidore, and others. He then adds that in ancient books this apex also gave occasion for the erroneous spellings *quotiens*, *totiens*, *vicensimus*, *aquonsus*, and *formonsus*, when they had in fact encountered *quoties*, *vicesimus*, *formosus*, and so forth. See Antonius Augustinus, *De emendatione*, book II, chapter 6, and Lipsius, *On the Correct Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, chapter 5. Gussanv.]

Foreseeing this, and lest such a thing should happen to your church, we have chosen for the present to entrust its care and interests to the priest Honoratus, so that through him the affairs and interests of the church may both be managed and in every way safeguarded. Therefore, by this present letter we exhort your affection to agree among yourselves in a worthy election with one united will, so that a priest may be appointed for you, and no longer allow God’s Church to remain without the service of a bishop.

[Col. 0535D] Until a priest has been ordained for that church,

[Note: [Col. 0535D] This is the model of the great vicars, as they are called, who, when a see was vacant or a bishop was occupied elsewhere, sustained the burdens of the episcopate. In the preceding letter we said that these men were called priests and bishops of the second order, according to Sidonius Apollinaris. Claudianus was approximately such a man, concerning whom Sidonius writes in poem 11, as was Justus of Auvergne, concerning whom he writes in the same place. Savaro. Gussanv.]

we have entrusted all the care of its administration to the aforesaid priest, as we have said. Therefore, let your affection hasten to show itself in all these matters, so that your ready devotion of mind may demonstrate that you love the Church. (See book III, Epistle 64.)

## LETTER LXXXII. TO LAURENCE, BISHOP OF MILAN

He appoints someone to settle the dispute that had arisen over the money claimed.

Gregory to Laurence, bishop of Milan.

[Note: [Col. 0536C] Letter LXXXII (formerly 80). A letter of King Childebert to him survives in the appendix to the works of Saint Gregory of Tours, column 13, 47, where he is called patriarch.]

On receiving the letter of your Fraternity, I gave thanks to almighty God, who relieved me through the welcome report of your recovery. But since you state that a definite sum of money is to be restored from the exaction of the patrimony of the province of Sicily, belonging to the holy Church over which, by God’s authority, you preside, because at that time the patrimony of your church was being collected there by agents of the holy Roman Church, it was necessary, in accordance with the tenor of the letters sent by you, to examine the total of the sums received and paid out and to investigate carefully the substance of the entire accounting. After these matters had been examined, nothing was alleged to be due back from the holy Roman Church to your church.

[Note: [Col. 0536C] This word and its meaning were discussed above in note x to Epistle 44. Although properly *redhibere* means “to return what one owes,” as we observed from the learned Sirmondus, it is sometimes used absolutely for “to return,” as Sirmondus also noted in his commentary on book III, letter 10 of Ennodius.]

But since, when your deacon Constantius offered a different account of the matters alleged by our agents, the examination of the case became uncertain—although it could have been investigated more precisely if there were some person with whom the matter could be definitively settled—it is necessary that your Holiness appoint someone for this purpose, with whom the Roman Church may firmly determine the matter. Thus, whether it owes nothing, this may be made clear by judgment; or, if it owed something and has restored it, the person whom you appoint may solemnly provide security.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO JANUARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CAGLIARI

The ambition of the deacon Liberatus is to be restrained, and he is in no way to be incardinated without the formal release of his own bishop.

[Col. 0536B]

Gregory to Januarius, archbishop of Cagliari in Sardinia.

You have evidently gladdened our heart by your letter, in which you testified that you had remembered our commands. Since we retain in memory what you say we instructed your Fraternity, we briefly reply by this present letter concerning how matters should be arranged when our authority is awaited.

As for Liberatus, concerning whom your Fraternity informed us, and who is said to be performing the office of deacon: if he was not made a cardinal by your predecessor, he must in no way be placed before the deacons ordained by you, lest you seem, as it were, to reject those whom you recognize as having been approved by you through ordination.

[Note: [Col. 0536C] Letter LXXXIII (formerly 81). Concerning this matter, John the Deacon writes, book III, chapter 21: “Gregory retained with such devoted care the most ancient order of ecclesiastical custom, handed down from the apostles and solemnly preserved down to his own time, that he would not place anyone, however distinguished by holiness, wisdom, or nobility, before earlier clerics in assembly, seating, standing, or signing.” To the same effect is the Council of Agde, canon 3: “A bishop shall place no later cleric before an earlier one.” The same is said of bishops in the African Council, canon 53. See Pope Leo, letter 5, to Doro, bishop of Beneventum. Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 5 of Saint Felix:

> That earlier man would have deserved the rank of his companion’s honor,  
> the priest; this highest dignity was separated by seven days.

Among the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, see the plaintive petition of Ibas: “Nor should he prefer lesser men to greater … but should preserve justice for all in honors, customs, and dignities.” Gelasius, letter 9: “For the sake of no advantage should he prefer either a priest or a deacon to those who had been ordained before them.” Gussanv.]

Therefore, restrain the aforesaid Liberatus with every effort from the perversity of his purpose, since the spirit of ambition inflates him, and establish him as the last among the deacons. Otherwise, while he strives unlawfully to be preferred, he may be judged unworthy of the position in which he now stands.

If, however, you are persuaded by his obedience and afterward wish to make him a cardinal, remember that you must abstain from all incardination unless he has obtained, in solemn form, the release of his own bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0537B] Earlier editions read *concessionem*. By *cessionem* he means letters of dismissal, in Greek ἀπολυτικὰς γραφάς (*apolytikas graphas*), “letters of release.” Balsamon describes what these are in his commentary on canon 11 of the Fourth Council and canon 17 of the Sixth Council. There he also notes the privilege of the bishops of Constantinople and Carthage, who admitted any clerics subject to another jurisdiction without letters of dismissal—παρὰ γνώμην τῶν κειροτονησάντων αὐτούς, “against the knowledge of those who ordained them.” It is worth observing that current practice requires letters of dismissal from the bishop of one’s birthplace alone; but according to the apparent prescription of the ancient canons, anyone among the laity could be enrolled in the clergy, while only clerics were forbidden to change allegiance through a change of prelate, and a bishop was forbidden to adopt clerics belonging to another jurisdiction. See the Council of Sardica, canons 18 and 19; the African Council, canon 21; Pope Innocent’s decree, title 14, in Pope Leo’s *Decretals*, no. 39; Gelasius, *Decretals*, chapter 23; and canon 15 after the Council of Nicaea. A notable example is Saint Paulinus, baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and consecrated by Lampius at Barcelona, as his letter to Augustine, 35, teaches. Countless examples exist of people tonsured without letters of dismissal from the bishop of their birthplace, by bishops who were not their own—or even by persons who were not bishops. See book VI, *On the Time of Ordinations*, chapters 1, 3, and 4, and the Council of Trent, session 23, canons 9 and 10, *On Reform*. In these passages the reader will observe that the bishop of one’s birthplace, the bishop of one’s domicile, the bishop of one’s benefice, or certain others could at times confer either major or minor orders, not merely the tonsure. Gussanv.]

For you cannot doubt that justice requires you not to delay giving others what you desire to have preserved for yourself.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO HILARY, A MONK OF AFRICA

He orders that a council be convened as soon as possible to investigate Argent(i)us, bishop of Lamiga.

[Note: [Col. 0537C] This title is highly suspect to me, although it appears in all the manuscript copies and printed editions. “Chartularius” should perhaps be read instead of “monk,” since this is the same Hilary of whom Saint Gregory speaks in the preceding Epistles 73 and 75 and in book III, Epistle 33. Gussanv. What prevents him from having been both a monk and a chartularius? Certainly the title varies in none of the manuscripts. But Gussanvillaeus, as Alteserra judges, begrudged the monks the honor of an apostolic mission entrusted to the monk Hilary. Let us hear the learned man himself, commenting on this letter: “He entrusts his authority to Hilary the monk, so that a council may be held through his diligence … Many centuries later Brother Peter of Castro Novo and Radulphus, monks of the Cistercian order, undertook a mission against the Albigensian heretics,” and so forth. How many similar examples could be brought forward if time permitted!]

To Hilary, monk of Africa.

The deacons Felicissimus and Vincentius of the Church of Lamiga, submitting a petition contained below, have informed us that they suffered grave injustice at the hands of Argentius, bishop of that same city, and that, after receiving payment, he installed Donatists in the churches. They also report that, among other offenses, he committed another serious crime—one that it is impious even to name.

[Note: [Col. 0537D] I do not know what city in Africa this was, unless it was the city of Lamigia in Numidia, according to Holstenius, *On the Roman Patriarchate*, p. 68. Gussanv. In the account of Numidia published by Sirmondus, volume I, no. 436 of the new edition, two bishoprics of nearly this name are listed: Lammiggizensis and Lamiggigensis. Consult note 101 of our Theodorus Ruinart in *History of the Vandal Persecution*.]

For this reason we have decided to impose upon your experience, by the text of this present command, that you not fail to commit the aforesaid bishop to a suitable process of satisfaction, and that, through your diligence, a council be held in those regions according to custom. All the matters contained in the text of the submitted petition are to be investigated canonically and with careful inquiry in the presence of the parties.

[Col. 0538A] Whatever is determined by their judgment must, with you carrying it out, be completed in every respect. Therefore, we wish you to apply yourself to this case with complete vigor, so that no delay may be attached to the examination of what we have commanded. You should know that you will incur no slight offense if, by attempting any excuse, you make our command slow to take effect.

[Note: [Col. 0538B] Bishops are to be judged in a synod. See the Council of Sardica, canon 3; the Council of Carthage, canon 12; the Council of Antioch, canons 12, 14, 15, and the final canon. This was also the practice of Saint Gregory, as will become clear below, book II, indiction 11, Epistle 8. I am therefore astonished at the supine ignorance, or astonishing itch for flattery, of certain theologians who either do not see this truth, so evident, or attempt to obscure it. See the practice of the Gallican Church in Gregory of Tours, *History*, book V, chapters 18, 20, 27, and 49; book VII, chapter 16; book VIII, chapter 20; book X, chapter 18, and elsewhere. As for Roman practice, Gelasius himself must be heard, letter 4, or the memorandum to Faustus, and letter 13, to the Dardani.]

## LETTER LXXXV. TO GENNADIUS, PATRICIAN OF AFRICA

He commends Droculfus, who has returned from the enemy.

Gregory to Gennadius, patrician of Africa.

Droculfus, bearer of this letter, coming over from the enemy to the Roman side, inflamed by the good reputation of your Excellency, which has spread far and wide, has hastened with the greatest eagerness to present himself in your service.

[Note: [Col. 0538C] Letter LXXXV (formerly 44 of book X). Alteserra and Gussanvillaeus inquire what is to be understood here by “the enemy.” Alteserra says that *hostis* means the army. He does not think that Droculfus served in the Roman army and, having returned from the army, approached the patrician Gennadius. Gussanvillaeus does not agree, dwelling especially on the words “you come from the enemy to the Roman state” and “still stationed among the enemy.” Certainly *hostis* often means “army,” as is clear from the testimonies cited by both men; but that *hostes* has the same meaning is not so evident to us. As far as this passage is concerned, we readily adopt Gussanvillaeus’s view. Droculfus, or Droctulfus, as Vatican manuscript A has it, was a Lombard, not a Roman, as his name sufficiently indicates. But having defected from the Lombards to the Roman side, he had asked Saint Gregory for a letter of recommendation to Gennadius. For Gregory, “to come to the Roman state” means to embrace the cause of the Roman state, as in book V, Epistle 40, to the emperor Maurice: “Because he was ready with all his heart to come over to the Roman state.” If Droculfus had served in the Roman army, what great matter would it have been for him to have heard many good things about Gennadius? But for Gennadius’s reputation to have spread even among the enemy was a very great thing. Saint Gregory signifies this when he says that Droculfus heard good things about him “while still stationed among the enemy and foreigners.” This letter is absent from the English, Norman, and most other manuscripts. It is found in Vatican A and in the Reims manuscript.]

Since he asks that our letter commend him to you, we greet you with fatherly affection and ask that your Excellency deign to employ him as God may put it into your heart and as may be useful, so that he may be able to experience in himself the good things he heard about you while still among the enemy, and so that, before the eyes of almighty God, he too may increase the rewards of your Excellency among your other merits.

# BOOK TWO

In September, in the tenth indiction.

[Col. 0539]

[Note: [Col. 0539C] LETTER I.—Before this letter, the editions and many manuscripts—namely the Vatican, Colbertine, royal, and others—preface the words “in the time of Pope Gregory,” and so forth. They then include the record of the deposition of Laurence, Roman archdeacon, and the substitution of Honoratus in his place. A document concerning the Greater Litanies follows. Since these matters do not belong to the letters, we have sent them to the end; they are also absent from the English, Norman, and Corbie manuscripts.]

## LETTER I. TO PETER, THE NOTARY

The monks of Tropea are to be assisted in every way if they live religiously.

[Col. 0539A]

Gregory to Peter, the notary.

We have learned from the bearer of this letter that the monastery of the holy Archangel, which is established at Tropea, is in need of food.

[Note: [Col. 0539C] Tropea, commonly called Tropea, was a maritime city of the Bruttii at the Vatican promontory, where the Gulf of Hipponium ends; it is now still an episcopal city of Further Calabria under the archbishop of Reggio, twelve miles west of Hipponium, commonly called Monteleone. At the acts of the Sixth Council of Constantinople, session 4, Theodorus signed as bishop of the holy Church of Κροπεία (*Kropeia*). The name is also read in the Seventh Synod, session 1. Gussanv.]

Therefore, let your Experience watch over it carefully; and if you learn that the monks of that place are conducting themselves well, you shall hasten in every way, supported by this authority, to assist them wherever it is manifestly clear that they are in need. You should know that whatever you provide by our command will be charged to your accounts.

They also assert that a small parcel of land belonging to our church, lying near their own, weighs one solidus and two tremisses. If this is so,

[Note: [Col. 0539D] What a solidus is, learn from Cange’s *Glossary*. We formerly discussed the gold solidus, which we think is meant here, in the *Life of Cassiodorus*, book II, chapter 4, no. 6. Its character and value should not, however, be reconstructed from the Salic, Alemannic, and other laws cited below by Gussanvillaeus. We shall discuss these matters more fully elsewhere, especially book III, indiction 11, Epistle 33, to Dynam(i)us.]

grant them, by way of a lease, the use of it for the sum of one tremissis.

[Note: [Col. 0540C] A tremissis is one-third of a solidus. A pound is composed of 72 solidi. That a solidus contained 40 denarii is inferred from the Salic, Alemannic, Bavarian, and Ripuarian laws. Gussanv.]

Therefore, let it be your concern to carry out all these arrangements, if, as we have said, the monks of that place persist diligently in God’s service as is fitting. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, chapter 55.)

## LETTER II. TO PRAEJECTUS, BISHOP OF NARNI

On the occasion of the deadly plague, the citizens are to be exhorted to repentance and faith.

Gregory to Praejectus, bishop of Narni.

[Note: [Col. 0540C] In *Italia sacra*, volume III, he is called Projectitius, bishop of Narni and of the destroyed city of Interamna, appointed in A.D. 565. He died in 595. Interamna is said to have been desolated because Totila ordered it destroyed around A.D. 547, after killing its bishop Proculus. Hence the bishops of Narni administered it until A.D. 606, when Interamna was restored and Anastasius was acclaimed its bishop. Gussanv. In the manuscripts the name of this bishop is written variously as Praejectio and Projectio, but most often as Praejectus, as in many Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Corbie, royal, and Anjou manuscripts. In the printed editions, with the agreement of the Colbertine manuscript, it is Praejectitius.]

To Praejectus, bishop of Narni.

[Note: [Col. 0540C] Narni, commonly Narni, is a still episcopal city of Umbria, situated on the river Nera between Otricoli and Interamna.]

It has come to our attention that, because of impending sins, a deadly plague is raging altogether in your city of Narni, a matter that has afflicted us exceedingly.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] The printed editions read *afflixit*, “afflicted,” against four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others. On the meaning of the verb *addico*, see book II of the *Moralia*, no. 15. See also book IX, no. 32, and book XXII, no. 22: “For if he is captivated by prosperity and rejoices in the calamity of the one who hates him.” A little earlier: “When we are not captivated by advancement.”]

Therefore, greeting your Fraternity, we urge you by every means not to cease admonishing and exhorting the Lombards or Romans who live in that place, and especially the pagans and heretics, so that they may be converted to the true, upright Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0540D] On the bishop’s zeal, see above, book I, Epistle 17, and below, book V, Epistle 41.]

For in this way either divine mercy will perhaps, on account of their conversion, come to their aid even in this life, or, if it should happen that they depart from it, they will be freed from their sins—which is still more to be desired. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, chapter 50.)

## LETTER III. TO VELOCES, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He orders him to pursue the Lombard duke Ariulf from behind if he makes a raid toward the Roman or Ravenna territories.

Gregory to Veloces, master of the soldiers.

We previously made clear to your Glory that soldiers were ready to come there; but since your letter had indicated that the enemy had gathered and was making raids in this direction, this circumstance held them here. Now, however, it has seemed useful to send some soldiers there, and your Glory should take care to admonish and encourage them to be ready for labor.

When an opportunity arises, speak with our glorious sons Maurilius and Vitalianus, and do whatever, with God’s help, they decide for the welfare of the Roman state. If you learn that Ariulf—I need hardly say this—has made a raid here or toward the Ravenna territories, work to pursue him from behind as befits brave men, so that, with God’s help, your reputation may advance further in the Roman state in proportion to the quality of your labor.

Above all, however, we admonish you to release without any delay or excuse the household of Maloin, Adobin, Vigild, and Grussing, who are known to be with the glorious Maurilius, master of the soldiers, so that the men of the aforesaid persons, coming there with them, may travel without any impediment.

[Note: [Col. 0541C] Letter III (formerly 21 of book XII, indiction 7). In the Colbertine manuscript and in the collection of Paul the Deacon it reads: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of October, indiction 10.”]

## LETTER IV. TO SABINUS, THE SUBDEACON

The garden of Felicianus is to be transferred to the monastery of the handmaids of God.

[Col. 0540C]

Gregory to Sabinus, the subdeacon.

The duty of piety urges us to provide for monasteries with prudent consideration, lest those known to have been assigned to God’s service should suffer any want—which God forbid. Therefore, by this authority we command your Experience to hasten, without offering any excuse, to transfer for ownership to the monastery of Euprepia the garden formerly belonging to the priest Felicianus, situated in the First Region before the steps of Saint Sabina. In this monastery a congregation of the handmaids of God is known to be assembled. Thus, through the benefit of our generosity, and with God himself giving aid, they may continue in God’s service with secure minds.

[Note: [Col. 0541C] Letter IV (formerly 19 of book XII, indiction 7). See below, Epistle 12. In the Colbertine manuscript the letter ends as follows: “On the third day before the Nones of October, indiction 10.”]

## LETTER V. TO FELIX, BISHOP OF MESSANA

A basilica is to be consecrated after a lawful and secure endowment has first been received.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Messana.

[Col. 0541B] Januarius, a subdeacon of the Church of Messana, submitted to us in a petition—whose contents are given below—that he had founded, out of devotion, a basilica in the city of Messana, which he desires to be consecrated in honor of Saints Stephen, Pancratius, and Euplius. Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid building lies within the legal jurisdiction of your city, and [Note: [Col. 0541C] EPISTLE V (alternative numbering: 10, book XII, indiction 7). This condition has already been discussed above, book I, epistle 54. The danger was, namely, that it might be thought that the worship due to the holy martyrs buried in this place long ago was being rendered to their bodies.] if it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after first receiving a lawful endowment—namely, ten fiscal solidi free from the taxes of the present year—and after he retains for himself only the usufruct of the remainder of his property, investigate all these matters carefully. If the amount of the revenues offered, or of what they will leave at the time of their death, can suffice for the repair of the roof, the lights, and also the annual provisions of those who serve there, then in reality let the gift be bound by the municipal records. But if what we have specified is not fulfilled through your diligence, you should have no doubt that you or your heirs will make good from your own property whatever amount the Church’s interest requires. When these matters have therefore been arranged, let the desired blessing be granted. [Col. 0542A] Do not confer the rite of dedication before the order of the gift set out above has been fulfilled; and declare, according to custom, that nothing further is owed there to the founder’s legal right, except for the procession, which is owed in common to all Christians. As for the sacred relics, you shall place them there after receiving them with due reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0541C] In Paul the Deacon’s collection is added: “Given on the Nones of October, indiction 10.”]

## EPISTLE VI. TO THE NEAPOLITANS

They are to elect, without delay or disagreement, a bishop in place of Demetrius, who was deposed for unspeakable crimes.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0541D] EPISTLE VI (alternative numbering: 3). Many of Saint Gregory’s epistles are addressed in this manner: “To the clergy, the order, and the people.” Thus nearly, in Leo I’s epistles 45 and 46, alternatively 22 and 23: “To the clergy, the honored men, and the people residing at Constantinople.” Here, by “the order,” distinguished from the nobles, understand the more distinguished citizens or magistrates; for in conferring magistracies the Romans observed an order, proceeding from the lower to the higher. “Order” is used in the same sense by Augustine, in the *Breviculus*, conference 3, chapters 13, 15, and 17. It should nevertheless be observed that in Norman, Corb., and many manuscripts, *ordini* is omitted.] to the clergy, nobles, order, and people residing at Naples.

Although the sincere devotion of your spiritual children toward their mother Church needs no exhortation, nevertheless, lest she think herself neglected, she ought to be encouraged by an epistolary address. For this reason I approach your affection with an admonition of paternal charity, so that with abundant tears we may unanimously give thanks to our Redeemer, who did not permit you to wander along byways under so perverse a teacher, but exposed the crimes of an unworthy pastor.

For Demetrius, who had not even previously deserved to be called a bishop, was found entangled in crimes so numerous and so grave that, if he had received judgment without mercy according to the character of his crimes, he would unquestionably have been punished with the most severe death under both divine and human laws. But because he was spared for repentance, he was deprived of the honor of the priesthood. We cannot allow the Church of God to remain long without a teacher, since the canonical rules have also established that, when a pastor has died or been removed, the Church ought not to be deprived of a priesthood for long. Therefore I have considered it necessary to admonish your charity by this letter, so that no delay or disagreement—which ordinarily generates scandals—may arise in the election of a pontiff.

Seek with every care a person such that you may rejoice in the concord of all united, and that he may in no way be rejected by the canons; so that whoever, with Christ’s grace, has been ordained may, with Christ himself assisting him, worthily complete the administration of the office which the most infamous of men had polluted by badly exercising it.

[Note: [Col. 0541D] It is also called the “mother,” “senior,” or “cathedral” church; its daughters are the baptismal churches, so to speak, in a direct line, while the other basilicas and oratories are in a collateral line. For that reason public Masses and processions were not permitted in the latter. In the chapters of Hincmar I read *matrices ecclesias*—“mother churches”—for baptismal or parish churches. Elsewhere they are called auxiliary churches, in French *des secours*, “subsidiary churches.” GUSSANVILLE. We spare this note of Gussanville’s out of consideration for parish churches. Nor do we entirely approve his claim that these were baptismal churches. Since the solemn minister of baptism was the bishop alone, as our learned Edmond Martène proves excellently in *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book I, chapter 1, article 3, baptisteries existed only in cathedral churches or neighboring places, as has already been shown above. Moreover, it is wrongly said that no public Masses or processions were formerly held in basilicas, as we have clearly proved by incontrovertible examples in the preface to the homilies on the Gospels.]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] Printed editions read *referatis*, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] We have restored this reading on the unanimous agreement of the Vatican, Royal, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts. Previously it read: “He led you, while walking along byways, to the right path, and he exposed the crimes of so unworthy a pastor.”]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] Thus read the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, Tours, and old editions. More recent editions preferred *nequitiis* (“wickednesses”) instead of *negotiis* (“crimes” or “affairs”).]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] This is the reading that must be retained, rather than *ductore* (“guide”), which later editors preferred; it is supported by the Vatican, Norman, Tours, Rheims, and other manuscripts, and agrees with the earlier editions.]

[Note: [Col. 0542D] The canons repeatedly declare that a pastor must not be imposed upon unwilling people, and reason itself supports this. Celestine, writing to the bishops of Gaul: “No bishop is to be given to unwilling people; the consent of the clergy, people, and order is to be sought according to their desire.” Leo I, epistle 84, no. 5: “No one is to be ordained when the people are unwilling and have not asked for him, lest a city either despise or hate a bishop whom it did not want, and become less religious than it ought because it was not allowed to have the one it chose,” and so forth. One may add what Saint Cyprian writes in epistle 68: “Priestly ordinations ought to be carried out only with the awareness of the assembled people, so that, in the presence of the people, the crimes of the wicked may be exposed or the merits of the good proclaimed; and so that the ordination may be legitimate and just when it has been examined by the vote and judgment of all.” He confirms this from the Acts of the Apostles. See epistle 29 of the book formerly II, now III, indiction 11, around the middle, where he describes with truthful and Christian zeal what must be carefully considered in the election of pastors. GUSSANVILLE.]

[Note: [Col. 0543C] In Norman, Corbie, and some others: “be rejected.” The following are listed by Gussanville among those who are to be rejected according to the canons: laymen before a year has passed since their conversion; those who have not yet reached thirty years; curials and those who have exercised secular authority; criminals, neophytes, unwilling men, bigamists, the physically mutilated, the unskilled, and those ignorant of the canons, psalms, and Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, according to the Third Council of Tours and the Second Council of Chalon; illegitimate persons, schismatics, and others. See the prohibition in the Pontifical concerning the order in which holy orders are to be conferred.]

[Note: [Col. 0543C] In Tours, Saint Gatien’s manuscript, the note reads: “In the month of October, indiction 10.”]

(See below, epistles 9 and 10, and book X, epistle 62.)

## EPISTLE VII. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to exercise Gregory’s authority in Sicily, while major cases are reserved.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0543C] EPISTLE VII (alternative numbering: 4). John the Deacon, *Life of Saint Gregory*, book II, chapters 11 and 12: “Gregory the Great, having been elected pope, chose the holiest of the monks as his close associates; among them was Maximian, abbot of his monastery, whom he later made bishop of Syracuse”—in the year 591, as the Bollandists prove under 9 June—“and entrusted him with his authority throughout Sicily.” Saint Gregory speaks of him in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36, and in homily 34 on the Gospels. That he died in 594 is clear from book V, epistles 17 and 22.] to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

We discharge our heavenly commands more effectively when we share our burdens with our brothers. Accordingly, over all the Churches of Sicily we have decided that you, Maximian, a most reverend man, our brother and fellow bishop, shall minister in place of the Apostolic See, so that everyone there who is counted among the religious may be subject to your fraternity by our authority, and so that from now on they will not need to cross such great stretches of sea to come to us over minor matters.

But if any difficult matters should arise that cannot at all be settled by your judgment, let these alone demand our decision, so that, relieved of small matters, we may attend more effectively to major cases.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] Here and elsewhere the manuscripts always read *reverentissimus*; so too the earlier editions. It has nevertheless now become customary to write *reverendissimus*, though this is less correct according to the rules of the grammarians: *reverens* means one who gives honor, whereas *reverendus* means one to whom honor is owed. GUSSANVILLE. The learned man’s reasoning proves, contrary to his own intention, that *reverendissimus*, not *reverentissimus*, should be read. But since *reverentissimus* occurs frequently in the manuscripts, it is not derived from *reverens, reverentior*, as though it meant one who gives more honor than others; rather, it has the same meaning as *reverendissimus*, namely, one to whom greater honor is owed, with *t* used for *d*—a substitution that grammarians know often occurs among ancient writers.]

[Note: [Col. 0544B] Not everyone agrees about these cases. They are commonly called “major” cases when they concern the condition of the universal Church, such as questions of faith, the canonization of saints, and so on. Innocent III, *Decretals*, book I, *On the Translation of a Bishop*, chapter 1, places that translation among the major cases that, according to canonical statutes, must be referred to the supreme pontiff. Here Saint Gregory understands by “major cases” matters which, although private, are nevertheless of some importance and not sufficiently accessible to Maximian. The reader may consult the history of the Sixth Council of Carthage and the synodal letters to Boniface and Celestine. Concerning major cases among the Jews, Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book IV, chapter 8, writes: “But if the judges do not know how to give judgment concerning the matters brought before them, as often happens to human beings, let them send the case in its entirety to the holy city; then the high priest, the prophet, and the council, having assembled, shall decide what seems best.” GUSSANVILLE.]

We assign this authority not to a place but to a person, because from the life you have already led we have learned what we may also expect from your future conduct.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] Thus in Colbert and Tours, Saint Gatien. In the Vatican: “In the month of October.”]

In the month of December, indiction 10.

(Compare John the Deacon, volume III, chapter 25.)

## EPISTLE VIII. TO CANDIDUS, BISHOP

The customary allowances must not be denied to a sick cleric.

Gregory to Candidus, bishop of the Old City.

When bodily punishment occurs—whether for purification or for vengeance is, in this matter, known only to God’s judgment—we ought not add affliction to those who have been scourged, lest, God forbid, the offense of guilt fall upon us.

And because Calumniosus, the bearer of this letter, asserts that, on account of the punishment he is suffering, your Church is denying him the benefits customarily granted to him, we therefore exhort your fraternity by this letter not to allow this illness to prevent him from receiving what is customary, since, as you know, illness often occurs among the various persons serving in the Church.

If they should be deterred by this example, no one who serves the Church could afterward be found. Therefore, according to the order of his position, let your fraternity not cease, in contemplation of the divine judgment, to provide the sick man from the modest resources that may accrue to the Church whatever could have been supplied to him if he were well, so that in administering this matter you may rather appear to convert the customary payments into almsgiving.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] Later editions added *imminet* (“threatens”), and shortly afterward *et ideo* (“and therefore”).]

[Note: [Col. 0544D] This text is quoted in the *Decretals*, book III, *On a Sick Cleric*, chapter 1, with several words changed. In the Digest, *On the Status of Freedmen*, book XL: “Those whom we care for when they are sick are understood to serve us also, although they desire to serve and are prevented by ill health.” The reader should note the words “desiring to serve” there, and in our letter “those serving in the Church.” The Church’s benefits are owed only to those who serve, or at least to those who desire to do so, so that the obstacle does not lie with them. Hence Justinian, book I of the Code, title 3, section 10: “We decree that all clerics established in the several Churches shall themselves sing the nocturnal, morning, and evening offices, lest, merely from the consumption of ecclesiastical goods, clerics appear to have only the name of clerics,” and so forth. GUSSANVILLE. What Saint Gregory’s view was concerning infirm priests is made clearer below, especially book IV, epistle 13, to Clementius, where the illness of Adeodatus is discussed.]
