(See above, book I, epistle 12; compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 33.)

## EPISTLE IX. TO THE NEAPOLITANS

They are to test Paul for a longer period and join themselves to him in humble charity; in the end, if he produces fruit among souls and God so inspires, they will obtain him as bishop.

Gregory to the order and people residing at Naples.

What judgment your affection has formed concerning Paul, our brother and fellow bishop, has been made clear by the report sent by you. Since you have tested him in so few days that you desire to have him as your cardinal bishop, we rejoice. But because one ought not to be hasty in matters of the highest importance, we too shall decide what must be done by mature deliberation, with Christ’s help; and, as time passes, it will become clearer to you what sort of man he proves himself to be.

Therefore, dearly beloved children, if you truly love the aforesaid man, obey him, and with devoted minds come to meet him in peaceful assembly, so that mutual love may bind you to one another so firmly that the enemy, flying about in rage, may find no way in any of you by which he can enter to break the unanimity under which he might creep in.

When we perceive that the aforesaid bishop has produced for our God the fruit among souls that we desire—with Christ himself assisting him—then whatever divine inspiration afterward supplies to our heart concerning his person and your desire, we shall do.

[Note: [Col. 0545C] Paul here seems to have been bishop of Nepi, according to epistle 26 of this book. In epistle 15: “He is hastening to return to his Church.” In indiction 11, epistle 1, he suffered a serious injury at Naples. In epistle 2, Saint Gregory consoles him. In epistle 35, he is permitted to return to his own Church, namely after the deposition of Demetrius, discussed in epistle 6 of this book. Paul had been sent there to act as visitor or administrator. The Neapolitans wanted to have him as their cardinal bishop; Saint Gregory refused, and rightly according to the canons, cause 7, question 1, chapter “Constitutum,” from Carthage, in these words: “No intercessor or administrator may retain the see to which he was appointed as intercessor, whatever the zeal or seditions of the people; rather, he must see to it that a bishop is provided for them within a year. If he neglects this,” and so forth. The Gloss adds: “He is forbidden to be elected, lest he be able to appropriate it. Thus a guardian is forbidden to marry his ward.” GUSSANVILLE. Gussanville does not sufficiently notice that Gregory does not refuse outright, but merely requests delay, so that through longer and more mature experience he may determine whether it is in the interest of the Neapolitans for Paul to be ordained their bishop.]

## EPISTLE X. TO PAUL, BISHOP OF NAPLES

Meanwhile he is to discharge episcopal duties in such a way that the testimony and votes of the Neapolitans may be confirmed.

Gregory to Paul, bishop [Note: [Col. 0545D] This is how it is read in all copies, both manuscripts and printed editions. Yet this Paul was only visitor of the Church of Naples, as may be read below, epistles 15 and 26. This example easily refutes Alteserra’s opinion concerning cardinal bishops, whom he considers appointed only temporarily and solely for the purpose of visitation. For Saint Gregory both grants this same Paul, bishop of Nepi, as visitor of the Church of Naples and nevertheless refuses to make him immediately its cardinal bishop.] of Naples.

If we safely administer the priestly office that we have undertaken, both divine assistance and the affection of spiritual children will undoubtedly be with us. Therefore let your fraternity strive to conduct itself in all things so that the testimony concerning you held by the clergy, nobility, and people of the city of Naples may be strengthened by the increase of your goodness.

Thus you must devote yourself with constant diligence to exhorting the aforesaid people, so that the divine farmer may store in his granaries the fruit of your word that you have produced among them.

[Note: [Col. 0545D] Strong words for certain pastors who, detesting their dioceses and parishes as though they were Scythian deserts, regard constant residence as a kind of exile and deportation—imitators of Sittius, who, ordered to remain in his homeland, considered himself an exile, as Espensaeus reports from Appian. The Council of Sardica, canon 14: “If any layman, in the city where he resides, does not assemble for three Sundays”—that is, for three weeks—“let him be deprived of communion.” If such regulations were made concerning laymen, much more is it neither permitted nor fitting for a pastor, and so forth. Saint Gregory adds the people’s exhortation, that is, the ministry of the word, which must be distributed constantly, as Paul says: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel,” for necessity is laid upon me. GUSSANVILLE.]

Until, with the Lord revealing it, we are able to deliberate concerning what the aforesaid children of ours request that we do, we grant you permission to ordain clerics from among the laity, and also to celebrate manumissions solemnly in the same Church.

[Note: [Col. 0546C] Gussanville discusses clerical tonsure at great length, but since he himself admits that the material he has assembled and collected is ancillary, we have judged that it should be cut, and in its place the note of our Hugh Menard, no. 660, on the *Book of Sacraments* should be read. Clerical tonsure must be distinguished from the rite of solemnly cutting the hair, discussed in the *Book of Sacraments*, column 234, where there is a prayer for the cutting of the hair; consult note 901 and following. Our Mabillon, in the preface to the third century of the Benedictine order, section 19, does not agree with Morinus, who, in *On Sacred Ordinations*, exercise 15, chapter 3, holds that clerical tonsure was ordinarily conferred only with the order of lector or doorkeeper, and that it did not begin to be given separately before the seventh century—a view Gussanville seems to adopt.]

[Note: [Col. 0546D] Constantine the Great permitted manumissions to take place in the Church. Code, book I, title 13: “It was long ago decreed that in the Catholic Church masters may grant freedom to their servants, if they do so in the sight of the people and with Christian bishops present, so that, for the memory of the act, some document may be drawn up in the form of a record, in which they themselves sign in place of witnesses.” Saint Augustine, sermon 21: “You lead your slave whom you are to free by the hand into the Church. Silence is made, a document is read aloud, or your request is presented. You say that you are freeing your slave because he has preserved his faith toward you in all things.” Among the works of Ennodius there is a petition by which the slave Gerontius is absolved from his master before the bishop.]

We wish you to pay without delay the customary allowances of the clerics and priests of the aforesaid Church. In supervising this matter, watch so diligently that, abstaining from everything unsuitable or unlawful, they may remain in the service of our God in a worthy ministry of obedience, with you also exhorting them.

[Note: [Col. 0547B] Thus in the old Colbert manuscript and in Tours, Saint Gatien.]

In the month of January, indiction 10.

(See below, epistle 15.)

## EPISTLE XI. TO THE PEOPLE OF NEPI

Concerning Leontius, sent there so that they may obey him.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at [Note: [Col. 0547B] EPISTLE XI (alternative numbering: 8). Nepi, more correctly Nepet, commonly Nepi, was formerly an episcopal city of Etruria, situated between Rome and Viterbo. Its episcopal see was joined to Sutri.] Nepi.

We have entrusted the care and administration of the city to Leontius, a most illustrious man and bearer of this letter, so that, keeping watch over all matters that he recognizes as pertaining to your welfare or that of the state, he may arrange them himself.

Therefore we admonish your affection by this letter that you must show him obedience in all things, and that none of you should consider him contemptible when he acts for your benefit. For whoever resists his proper administration will be recognized as resisting our own disposition.

Whoever listens to him in the matters we have mentioned will listen to us. But if anyone—which we do not believe—should, after this admonition of ours, think that he may despise him, let him know without doubt that the danger will be his own.

[Note: [Col. 0547B] Printed editions read: “whoever resists his fitting arrangement.” On the word *resultare*, which follows, see note d to epistle 21 of book I.]

## EPISTLE XII. TO CASTORIUS, BISHOP OF ARIMINUM

Concerning the consecration of the oratory of the Holy Cross.

Gregory to Castorius, bishop of Ariminum.

Timothea, an illustrious woman, submitted to us in a petition—whose contents are given below—that she had founded, out of devotion, an oratory within the city of Ariminum, on property belonging to her, which she desires to be consecrated in honor of the Holy Cross.

Therefore, dearest brother, if the building mentioned lies within the legal jurisdiction of your city, and if it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after first receiving a lawful endowment—namely, two-thirds of all her property, excluding her household, whether movable, immovable, or self-moving goods—and after she retains the usufruct for the days of her life, with the gift bound by the municipal records, you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public Masses, provided that no baptistery is constructed there at any time in the future and that you appoint no cardinal priest there.

[Note: [Col. 0547B] When Saint Gregory the Great discusses the dedication of oratories, he ordinarily requires five conditions: that no body be buried there; that a sufficient endowment be assigned; that no baptistery be established there; that no cardinal priest be appointed there; and consequently that no public Masses be celebrated there, since only cardinal priests—that is, priests permanently attached to a title—were permitted to celebrate them.]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] See above, concerning treasure, book I, epistle 20. GUSSANVILLE.]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] “Two-thirds”—in French, *les deux tiers*. Nearly the whole of this epistle is found in chapter 15 of epistle 7 of Pope Zachary to Pippin and the bishops of Gaul. GUSSANVILLE.]

[Note: [Col. 0547C] “A formal judicial record,” *un acte en bonne forme*. Some distinguish between *gesta* and *facta*, as Accursius does; Alciatus denies the distinction in his commentary on *On the Meaning of Words*, law 19. Bartolus agrees, holding that in common usage they differ in nothing. In former times each municipality or town had its own record-keeper or public notary, who wrote down or received the donations and wills of private persons and the other dispositions of townspeople, and entered them in the public records; for this reason they were called municipal acts. GUSSANVILLE. Gregory used the same precaution below, book IX, epistles 70 and 83, and book XII, epistle 11. In one Vatican manuscript and in the Norman, Corbie, Royal, and other manuscripts, *mancipalibus* is read instead of *municipalibus*.]

[Note: [Col. 0547D] Concerning oratories and their consecration, see the first distinction *On Consecration*. Anyone may have an oratory at home; Masses may not be celebrated there, lest the rights of others be impeded, chapter “Patentibus,” *Decretals*, *On Privileges*. With the bishop’s permission Masses may sometimes be celebrated in oratories, but not on the principal festivals: Council of Agde, canon 21; Council of Arvernus, canon 15. Here Saint Gregory forbids a priest to be appointed cardinal in an oratory. I understand this to mean a parish priest who has a parish—or, as the Fourth Council of Orléans, canon 33, puts it, a diocese—to govern. Hence the prohibition against constructing a baptistery also follows. GUSSANVILLE. See book IX, epistles 70 and 84.]

[Note: [Col. 0548B] He does not exclude private Masses, which heretics oppose with such great effort. I shall briefly explain why he forbids public Masses to be celebrated in an oratory. There is one Catholic Church, composed of individual particular Churches, living by the same Spirit and sharing the same sacraments under the same pastor. Each particular Church is one and, in its own way, represents the universal communion of the holy faithful; it has its own pastor, by whom its individual members ought to be governed, sustained, and nourished. Christ commanded this, the apostles taught and established it, the councils decreed it, reason supports it, and custom has grown up around it. Hence the frequent and solemn assemblies of the whole Christian people at the same place on appointed days, common prayers, the same liturgy, the same sermon, and the sacraments distributed according to the same rite and by the same hand. Saint Gregory therefore feared that, through other Masses celebrated outside the mother Church, the people might be dispersed and so sacred a unity dissolved. The Council of Sardica had the same intention in canon 15, which provides that, if a bishop must at times remain in the countryside, he should go to the nearest place where there is a priest, so that he may not appear to spend Sunday without the Church. Theodulf agrees in the chapters, chapters 45 and 46: “Let the people not be drawn away from the public solemnities of Mass … but let priests … and people assemble together at the holy mother Church for the public celebration of Mass.” See the distinction between *conventus* and *conventicula* among the better authors; also what the Council of Nantes, chapter 1, established concerning not admitting another parish’s parishioner to Mass; and what the Council of Agde, canon 21, understands by a lawful and customary assembly. The word “processions,” concerning which see distinction 24, chapter “Presbyteri,” and *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “Certum,” as well as the other regulations, had almost slipped from memory. From these it is clear that the gathering of the people must not be freely permitted at every place. That gathering of the people is expressed by procession and by the attendance or assembly of the people—something that those who discuss the antiquity of processions would have done well to notice. In any case, understand “public Masses” as those to which the people were required to assemble with their pastor. GUSSANVILLE. Saint Gregory gives entirely different reasons when he forbids public Masses in monasteries. See book IV, epistle 43.]

Consequently, if she should perhaps prefer that Masses be celebrated there, she must know that she is to request a priest from your affection, so that no other priest may presume to do anything there at all.

[Note: [Col. 0548D] In the common editions: “to have them celebrated for herself”; and below, “nothing else” instead of “nothing otherwise.” We follow the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

As for the sacred relics, you shall place them there after receiving them with due reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0549B] Here I understand relics and sacred remains, without which at that time scarcely any altar was consecrated, as may be seen in *On Consecration*, distinction 1. The same is the closing clause of epistle 5 above.]

## EPISTLE XIII. TO IMPORTUNUS, BISHOP OF ATELLA

He admonishes a suffragan bishop concerning the priest whom he has appointed to preside in a church of that bishop’s diocese.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0549B] EPISTLE XIII (alternative numbering: 10). This seems to be Importunus, bishop of the city of Atella, mentioned in epistle 77 of book IX, indiction 2.] to Importunus, bishop of Atella.

We believe that your fraternity will gladly embrace measures that have been prudently arranged. Since we have learned that the church of Saint Mary of Campisonis [Note: [Col. 0549C] The words “formerly before Campiso” had once entered the printed editions; we have removed them because the manuscripts require it.] situated in your parish [Note: [Col. 0549C] Thus all manuscripts and printed editions read. Nevertheless, everyone who has read the monuments of antiquity knows that *parish* is often used for *diocese*, and conversely *diocese* for *parish*. John Filesacus proves this with many testimonies at the beginning of his book *On the Origin of Parishes*, where he mentions canon 21 of the Third Council of Toledo: “The complaint of many demanded this constitution, because we have learned that bishops rage through their parishes not as priests but cruelly.” Gregory of Tours, *History*, book V, chapter 5, says that one bishop had fifteen dioceses under him. And Aldhelm, *On the Praises of Virginity*, calls the Catholic Church “the parish of the Churches.” Therefore there is no need to dispute over the name. GUSSANVILLE. Cangius discusses in his *Glossary* how the diocese of a bishop or the district of a priest came to be called a parish.] is vacant of a priest, we have certainly appointed the bearer of this letter, the priest Dominicus, to preside in that same church,

[Note: [Col. 0549C] The earlier reading was “know that we appointed.” From this passage Binius concludes, in the margin of the epistle, that the pope confers benefices in another diocese; but he does not explain what these benefices were, by what document or right they were conferred, whether this occurred against the bishop’s will, or in what places. It is in fact established by ancient canon law that the clerics of each diocese were ordained by their own bishop with the consent of the clergy and people, and accordingly that those benefices which were then decreed for them, or the right to ecclesiastical stipends, were granted by him. I cite the Councils of Antioch, canons 9 and 22, and the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 22. We read that ordinations were sometimes attempted and carried out by metropolitans in the dioceses of subordinate bishops; but we must assess such attempts or actions according to the canons, so that they may be for building up, not for destruction. I would believe that the holy pontiff, as the most zealous defender of the common law, was moved by some just and particular reason to send and appoint a priest to that church, perhaps because it had remained vacant and neglected longer than was proper—and, as he says, prudently—being sure that the bishop would not resist, the people would not object, and the clerics would not take offense. GUSSANVILLE. See Thomassin, part II, book I, chapter 41, and Alteserra on this passage, where he holds that at that time minor benefices were conferred extraordinarily by the pontiff; he uses the testimony of John of Salisbury, epistle 230, although John lived many centuries after our Gregory. He adds: “The Roman pontiff began to intervene in the conferral of benefices from the time when he was declared the ordinary of ordinaries in the general Council of Lateran, chapter 5.”]

Therefore your fraternity must arrange without delay for the revenues of that church to be provided to him, and you must likewise have the revenues of the tenth indiction, which have already been collected, restored without delay to the aforesaid man,

[Note: [Col. 0550C] This is equivalent to saying: “the revenues of the current year, already collected.” ALTESERRA.]

so that, with God’s help, he may diligently provide for the needs of that same church, whose revenues he receives.

## EPISTLE XIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF VELITRAE

The bishop’s see is transferred to a safer place.

Gregory to John, bishop [Note: [Col. 0550C] EPISTLE XIV (alternative numbering: 11). Velitrae, commonly Velletri, was a city of Campania on the Appian Way, twenty miles from Rome. It is still an episcopal city, although its see has been joined to Ostia.] of Velitrae.

Temporis qualitas (Gratian, Part II, Cause 7, Question 1, chapter 44) admonishes us to transfer the episcopal sees formerly established in certain cities to other places of the same diocese that we consider safer, so that the inhabitants may now dwell there and more easily avoid barbarian danger.

[Note: The transfer of episcopal sees cannot take place without the authority of the supreme pontiff, since it concerns major cases. Thus the Church of Ceneta, because it was situated in an unsafe place exposed to incursions by the Trevisans, was transferred to a safer location by the authority of Innocent III. Innocent himself is the witness, Book II, Letter 8. The transfer of episcopal sees likewise does not take place without the consent of the ruler . . . . . Thus the Church of Maguelone was transferred from the island of Maguelone to Montpellier in the year 1536, with the consent of the supreme pontiff and King Francis I. Alteserra.]

For this reason, we command you, John, our brother and fellow bishop of the city of Velitrae, and your see, henceforth to migrate to the place called Harenata, at Saint Andrew the Apostle, so that you may be freer from the attack of hostile forces and may there arrange the customary solemn feasts.

[Note: Thus it is read in the Tours and Saint Gall manuscript.]

[Note: Thus it is read in all the manuscripts and printed editions of Saint Gregory’s letters. In Ivo: “arrange the custom of solemn festivals.” Likewise in Burchard. John the Deacon has: “arrange the festivals according to the custom of solemn occasions.” In Gratian’s Decree: “arrange the custom of solemn festivals.” However it may be written, the meaning is the same, which I express as follows: At the principal and more solemn festivals, clergy and laity from the entire diocese gathered at the mother church, as was established by several conciliar canons. I cite the canons of Agde, 21; Clermont, 15; Orléans I, 23; Orléans IV, 3, and others. Therefore, when the location of the see was changed, the festivals were no longer arranged in the former city, but at Saint Andrew in Hatenata a public assembly of all the faithful had to be called, so that they might celebrate the principal feasts with their bishop. Gussanville.]

In the month of February, indiction 10. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 17.)

### Letter XV. To Paul, Bishop

He urges Paul, to whom he had entrusted the Neapolitan Church, though he was already thinking of returning, to remain there. He replies concerning the deacon Peter that Peter has nothing to fear and that no opportunity for underhanded action will be found in Gregory’s presence.

[Col. 0550B]

Gregory to Paul, bishop.

I appointed you for the present to preside over the Neapolitan Church so that you might convert as many people as possible to God by persuasive preaching. And although you ought to carry this out with your whole purpose, before you have produced this fruit for the Lord you are hastening to return and asking me to arrange that same Church quickly, although it is not my intention to be idle in this matter. But because I desire to fortify its interests with the greatest stability, I must consider and deliberate on this for a long time, so that, with Christ revealing the way, I may arrange it with a worthy appointment.

Meanwhile, therefore, let your Fraternity devote itself so attentively to the winning of souls that the judgment I have formed concerning you may be strengthened by the effectiveness of your work. As for what you wrote about the person of the deacon Peter, the distinguished Theodorus has now reported everything to me. And so, since I have learned from your testimony that Peter is attached to you and is striving for the interests of the Church, he ought to fear neither anyone’s hostility nor anyone’s enmity. Rather, the more he perceives that others envy him, the more watchfully he should persevere in the interests of the Church and in God’s service, so that they may be unable to harm him.

Your Fraternity, moreover, need not henceforth be apprehensive about him, because no underhanded action will find a place with me.

[Note: Letter XV (alternative number 12).—Concerning this matter, Saint Bernard writes in Book II of *On Consideration*, chapter 14: “It is a fault which, if you believe yourself free from it, will make you, in my judgment, sit alone among all whom I have known who have ascended episcopal chairs . . . . . Such is the ease of believing, from whose most cunning little foxes I have found no great man sufficiently protected against their craft. Hence their frequent anger counts for nothing; hence the frequent condemnation of the innocent; hence prejudgments against the absent.” Thus Saint Bernard. Let the powerful pay attention, let prelates take heed, let each person beware.

As for “underhanded action” and “concealed misrepresentation,” let the reader consult the jurists and canonists: it means extorting or, as it were, stealing something through a false account. Rescripts obtained from them in this way are entirely invalid. See Book II, Letter 6, indiction 9: “Not believing petitions that have not been examined.” See the same Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 4, where he declares that even he himself and pontiffs can be deceived, because we are human beings and not prophets; and what is surprising if we are sometimes led by the mouths of liars toward something else? Gussanville.]

### Letter XVI. To Maximian, Bishop of Syracuse

He places Paulinus of Tauriana over the Church of Lipara.

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

A Church established in fortified places ought not to be without the office of a pastor.

[Note: Letter XVI (alternative number 26).—The printed editions have *locis inimicis*, “in hostile places.” But it should be read, as in the manuscripts, *locis munitis*, “in fortified places.” In other places, namely those open to enemy incursions, the shepherds themselves were forced to flee, while the sheep were scattered. See Letters 17 and 50 of this book. In some manuscripts, especially the Vatican manuscript, one nevertheless finds *locis minutis*, “in small places.”]

Since, therefore, the Church of Lipara is known to be deprived of a priest, let your Fraternity without delay appoint Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Tauriana, to preside over the aforesaid Church of Lipara, so that he may diligently discharge the administration of his office in that Church and may not cease arranging whatever he has learned to be suitable for its interests. You shall also admonish the entire clergy that they must obey him canonically in all things, so that, with the aforesaid Church being governed by the said brother and our fellow bishop, its interests in every respect may, with Christ’s help, be advanced.

[Note: In the Turin and Saint Gall manuscripts: “Given on the day before the Kalends of March, indiction 10.”]

### Letter XVII. To Paulinus, Bishop

He is to reside in the Church of Lipara but visit Tauriana at a suitable time.

[Col. 0552A]

Gregory to Paulinus, bishop.

[Note: Letter XVII (alternative number 13).—Paulinus is called bishop of Tauriana in Book I, Letter 41, where we read that the monks of Tauriana were scattered on account of the barbarians. In Letter 40, Paulinus himself is described as a bishop living abroad in Sicily, perhaps because he could not reside in Tauriana, whose Church Gregory assumes to have been scattered. Paulinus is therefore ordered to gather and support the Church of Tauriana through the diligence of visitation, while he is to govern the Church of Lipara, where he could reside more securely.

Lipara, still so called today, is the principal island of the Aeolian Islands, with an episcopal city of the same name under the archbishop of Messina, thirty thousand paces north of the coast of Sicily. Gussanville.]

We wish you to know that we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Maximian that, by our authority, he should appoint your Fraternity to preside over the Church of Lipara. You must obey him in every respect, and we command you to devote yourself appropriately to the interests of that Church. Whatever you recognize to be necessary for its welfare, we wish you to carry out without hesitation.

[Note: He had read this in Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 24: “Let the abbot”—which is also to be understood of other prelates—“know that it is his duty to be useful rather than to preside.”]

You shall visit the Church of Tauriana whenever you consider the time suitable. Let your Fraternity therefore hasten to fulfill all these instructions, so that by your presence you may beneficially govern the Church of Lipara and, through the diligence of visitation, may not cease gathering together and supporting the Church of Tauriana.

[Note: It is the shepherd’s task to gather the sheep; it is the wolf’s task to scatter them.]

[Note: Thus in two manuscripts of Teller and in the Colbert manuscript.]

Given in the month of March, indiction 10.

### Letter XVIII. To Natalis, Bishop of Salona

After rebuking Natalis for his constant banquets, he orders him to restore the archdeacon Honoratus to his position.

Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona.

From the many people coming from your city, dearest brother, I have learned that, having abandoned pastoral care, you are occupied solely with banquets (Gratian, Distinction 44, chapter 5).

[Note: Letter XVIII (alternative number 14).—See Espensaeus, Book II of the *Digressions on the First Epistle to Timothy*, chapter 14, where he discusses a wine-drinking bishop; also the Council of Trent, session 25, *On Reform*, chapter 1; and the First Council of Milan, concerning the bishop’s table. Gussanville. Concerning Natalis, see Letters 19 and 20 of Book I, and the two that follow this one. Natalis excused himself concerning the banquets; Saint Gregory replied to him in Letter 52, formerly 37. Saint Martin, according to Sulpicius, *Dialogues* I.17, never agreed to receive Vincentius, a prefect outstanding in every virtue, at a banquet. Saint Ambrose, by contrast, was accustomed to feed consuls and prefects, as is clear from the same testimony of Sulpicius.]

I would not have believed what I heard had I not confirmed it through the evidence of your actions. For since you do not apply yourself to reading at all, do not devote yourself to exhortation at all, and even remain ignorant of the practice of ecclesiastical office, this demonstrates that you do not know how to show reverence to those under whom you have been placed.

Although my predecessor of holy memory had forbidden you in his letters to retain in your heart, against your archdeacon Honoratus, the pain of such prolonged resentment,

[Note: Thus it is read in the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, although the printed editions have: “and although you have often been rebuked by me, and these matters have been strictly forbidden you,” and so forth.]

and although I too had strictly forbidden and commanded you concerning this, you, neglecting God’s commandments and disregarding our letters, tried by a cunning stratagem to degrade the aforesaid Honoratus, your archdeacon, under the pretext of promoting him to a more distinguished rank.

[Note: At that time a presbyter was not permitted to fulfill the duties of an archdeacon. Thus, once Honoratus had been promoted to the presbyterate, he would have lost the rank of archdeacon and been stripped of his extensive authority. For this reason Sidonius writes of John, bishop of Chalon-sur-Saône, in Book IV, Letter 25: “Later, as time and labor passed, the archdeacon—who, whether in rank or ministry, had long been retained because of his industry—could not be advanced in dignity, lest he be released from his authority as archdeacon.”]

Consequently, after removing him from the position of archdeacon, you summoned another man who could obey your ways, although, as I think, the aforesaid man displeased you for no other reason than that he prevented you from giving the sacred vessels and coverings to your relatives.

[Note: We have stated above that the custody of sacred things and the administration of ecclesiastical property had been entrusted particularly to the care of deacons and especially of the archdeacon. That this practice did not prevail in the Eastern Churches during the time of Saint John Chrysostom is demonstrated by homily 14 of that holy Doctor on the Acts of the Apostles, where he clearly teaches that this duty belonged to presbyters.]

We wished both then, through my predecessor of holy memory, and now, through me, to examine this matter by careful investigation. But you, conscious of your own actions, delayed sending a representative prepared for judgment.

Therefore, after so many admonitions, let your Fraternity repent of the error of its guilt and, as soon as it receives my letters, receive the aforesaid Honoratus back into his position. If you should delay doing so, know that the use of the pallium granted to you by this see has been withdrawn. If, even after losing the pallium, you persist in the same obstinacy, know that you are to be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

After this, it will be necessary for us to investigate your causes more closely and to determine, with the greatest care and scrutiny, whether you ought to remain in the episcopate itself.

As for the man who, against the rule of justice, agreed to be promoted to another’s position (Gratian, Part II, Cause 7, Question 1, chapter 40), we depose him from the honor of that archdeaconate.

[Note: In the printed editions: “to the archdeaconate of another.”]

If he thereafter presumes to minister in the same position, let him know that he is deprived of participation in sacred communion.

[Note: Here, as also in Saint Cyprian, communion was denied not only in abstention from all things but specifically the mouth, prayer, greeting, communion, and table. Hence some conclude that parish priests or rectors possess a certain power of excommunication. Filesacus treats this question at greater length in *On the Sacred Authority of Bishops*, chapter 3. Saint Gregory reports that Saint Benedict exercised some power of excommunication in *Dialogues* II.23. Certainly, if presbyters have the right to exclude penitents from communion, there is dispute over the wording. Let the response of Theophilus of Alexandria to Menas be read. Gussanville.]

You, therefore, dearest brother, must not provoke us any further, lest you find very harsh those whom, though placed over you in charity, you despise. Once Honoratus the archdeacon has been restored to his position, send me promptly a representative prepared for the case who can demonstrate through his arguments that this ought rightly to have been done. For we have decided that the same archdeacon should come to us, so that, after hearing the assertions of both parties, we may decide whatever is just and whatever is pleasing to almighty God.

We defend no one out of personal affection; rather, with God as our guide, setting aside regard for any person, we preserve the rule of justice. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 34.)

### Letter XIX. To All the Bishops of Dalmatia

He explains what was done in the case of Natalis and Honoratus.

Gregory to all the bishops established throughout Dalmatia.

Although we desire frequently to visit your Fraternity through letters sent back and forth, nevertheless, whenever circumstances require, we wish to settle two matters on the occasion of one, so that we may relieve your fraternal spirits of the burden of a visit and explain more carefully matters that arise, lest what is unknown be able to trouble your minds.

[Note: Letter XIX (alternative number 15).—Thus the manuscripts read, whereas the printed editions have “one matter.”]

Our brother Natalis, bishop of the city of Salona,

[Note: In many manuscripts “Natalis” is absent.]

when he wished to promote Honoratus, the archdeacon of his see, to the order of the presbyterate, and Honoratus thereafter declined to rise to a higher rank,

[Note: According to the discipline of those times, the archdeacon was inferior to any presbyter in order, rank, and dignity, although in the privileges and revenues of his ministry he surpassed the presbyter in the administration of external affairs. This perhaps explains his avoidance of the presbyterate: once he had accepted it, he would have had to withdraw from that administration.]

had requested my predecessor of holy memory, by a petition he sent, not to compel him to enter that order against his will. For he declared that this was being done not for the sake of promoting him but because of resentment.

[Note: That is, because he would not be grateful.]

For this reason, my predecessor of holy memory had already sent letters to Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, forbidding him to promote the aforesaid Honoratus the archdeacon against his will or to retain in his heart the pain of the resentment he had conceived. Although I too had strictly forbidden these things,

[Note: The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, have: “and although he had often been rebuked by us, and these matters had been strictly forbidden him,” and so forth.]

he, neglecting not only God’s commandments but also disregarding our letters, tried, as it is said, to degrade the aforesaid archdeacon cunningly, under the pretext of promoting him to a more distinguished honor.

Consequently, after removing him from the position of archdeacon, he summoned another man to minister in the place of the deposed archdeacon.

[Note: In the common editions: “he summoned.”]

We think that Honoratus could have displeased his bishop for no other reason than that he prevented him from giving the sacred vessels to his relatives.

[Note: He explains why Honoratus was least welcome and why the bishop wished to degrade him cunningly: namely, by making him a presbyter, to strip him of the authority of the archdeaconate, which surpassed presbyteral authority. Here “relatives” is understood broadly as kinsmen, not simply those who gave birth to him. Writers of this age often use the word in this broad sense, as Gregory of Tours does in *History* II.4 and IX.19 and 33. Moreover, the Antiochene synod of the year 341 had foreseen this squandering of ecclesiastical goods for the benefit of relatives and guarded against it in canon 25, by which a bishop guilty of so great a crime is ordered to pay the penalty to the provincial synod.]

Both my predecessor of holy memory at that time and I now wished to examine this matter by careful investigation. But he, conscious of his own guilt, put off sending a representative to the judgment, lest the truth of his actions, once examined, become evident.

We therefore arranged to admonish him again by letters delivered through the bearer of this present communication, after he had already been warned by so many letters and had remained obstinately stubborn up to now, so that, as soon as the bearer of these letters arrived, he would receive Honoratus the archdeacon back into his former position.

[Note: That is, “upon his arrival.” In Acts 8:29: “Approach and join yourself to the chariot.”]

If, with his heart already hardened, he should still contumaciously postpone restoring him to the same rank, we order that he be deprived, for his repeated contumacy, of the use of the pallium granted by this see. If, even after losing the pallium, he should persist in the same obstinacy, he is likewise to be excluded from participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

For it is just that those who despise people placed over them in charity should experience harshness from justice.

We therefore do not now deviate from the path of the justice that the aforesaid bishop has scorned. Rather, after restoring to his position the man whose guilt has in no way become clear to us, we order Bishop Natalis to send to us a representative prepared for the case, who can demonstrate through his arguments that his intention was and is righteous.

We have also summoned the same archdeacon to come to us, so that, after hearing the assertions of both parties, we may decide whatever is just and whatever is pleasing to almighty God. For we defend no one out of personal affection; rather, with God as our guide, setting aside regard for any person, we preserve the rule of justice.

### Letter XX. To Antoninus, Subdeacon

After setting out the same case again, he orders Antoninus to urge Natalis to restore Honoratus to his position and, if Natalis does not comply, to deprive him first of the use of the pallium and then of communion. Once Honoratus has finally been restored, the bishop is to send a representative, while the archdeacon himself is to come to Rome, so that both may state their case. A guarantor is also summoned for the bishop Malchus.

[Col. 0555C]

Gregory to Antoninus, subdeacon.

Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona, had requested my predecessor of holy memory, by a petition he sent, that his bishop not compel him against his will, contrary to custom, to be promoted to the order of a more distinguished rank. For he declared that this was being done not for the sake of promoting him but because of resentment.

[Col. 0555D]

For this reason my predecessor of holy memory had already forbidden Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, in his letters, to promote the aforesaid Honoratus the archdeacon against his will or to retain any longer in his heart the pain of the resentment he had conceived.

Although I too had strictly forbidden these things, Natalis, neglecting not only God’s commandments but also disregarding our letters, tried by a cunning stratagem to degrade the aforesaid archdeacon under the pretext of promoting him to a more distinguished honor. Consequently, after removing him from the position of archdeacon, he summoned another man who could obey his ways.

We think that Honoratus the archdeacon could have displeased his bishop for no other reason than that he prevented him from giving the sacred vessels to his relatives. Both my predecessor of holy memory then and I now wished to examine this matter by careful investigation, but Natalis, conscious of his own actions, delayed sending a representative to judgment.

We have therefore decided to support your experience with the authority of this present command, so that, upon reaching Salona, you may at least urge Natalis, our brother and fellow bishop, who has been admonished by so many letters, to receive the above-mentioned archdeacon immediately back into his position.

If he should contumaciously delay doing this, as is his custom, forbid him, by the authority of the apostolic see, the use of the pallium granted by this see. If you observe that, even after losing the pallium, he still persists in the same obstinacy, deprive that bishop also of participation in the Lord’s body and blood.

We command that the man who, against the rule of justice, agreed to be promoted to another’s position be deposed from the honor of that archdeaconate. If he thereafter presumes to minister in the same position, we deprive him of participation in sacred communion.

For it is just that those who despise people placed over them in charity should experience harshness from justice.

Once Honoratus the archdeacon has been restored to his position, let the aforesaid bishop, compelled by you, send a representative prepared for the case who can demonstrate to me through his arguments that his intention was or has been righteous. We also command the same archdeacon to come to us, so that, after hearing the assertions of both parties, we may decide whatever is just and whatever is pleasing to almighty God.

For we defend no one out of personal affection; rather, with God as our guide, setting aside regard for any person, we preserve the rule of justice.

[Note: Letter XX (alternative number 16).—He had administered some property of the Roman Church, as appears from Letter 46 of this indiction and Letter 22 of indiction 11. Letter 47 of Book IV, indiction 13, reports that he suddenly died at Rome on the very day on which he had stated his case and been condemned.]

As for our brother and fellow bishop Malchus, see to it that you entrust him to a guarantor, so that he may come to us as quickly as possible. Then, with every delay and postponement set aside, once he has explained the accounts of his actions, may he return safely to his own affairs.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 9.)

### Letter XXI. To Jobinus, Prefect of Illyricum

He rejoices that the province, devastated by the barbarians, is being restored under Jobinus’s government. He commends the administrator of the patrimony and urges Jobinus not to assist Bishop Natalis against justice.

[Col. 0557A]

Gregory to Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum.

[Note: Letter XXI (alternative number 17).—In nearly all editions and in certain manuscript codices, the reading was “to Jobinus, bishop of Illyricum.” With the help of certain manuscripts we have corrected this reading, which the context of the letter shows to be erroneous, since the context clearly indicates a particular secular dignity. See also Letter 43, now 45, of Book I, which begins: “Jobinus, our most distinguished son, prefect throughout Illyricum.” Gussanville. In the Vatican manuscript: “to the prefect, former prefect of Illyricum.” In two manuscripts of Teller and in the Rheims manuscript: “bishop of Illyricum.” In the Norman, English, Corbie, and other manuscripts, which we follow: “prefect of Illyricum.”]

Although the scarcity of couriers, because hostility has occupied the roads, prevents us from fulfilling the duties of paternal affection by returning visits, nevertheless, whenever an opportunity arises, we do not cease to visit your Excellency through letters sent back and forth. Thus, though we cannot see face to face those whose presence we cannot behold, we may at least in some measure behold them through letters exchanged in turn.

We rejoice, therefore, that the Lord has willed to care for the province afflicted under your eminent administration: the province which, on one side, He wounds with the scourge of barbarian devastation, He now heals on the other through your Excellency, as though through a remedy applied over the wound.

Attend, therefore, to the dignity granted to you as the gift of the one who bestows it, and through the administration of the government entrusted to you make your Creator more favorably disposed toward you. Then, when He sees what He has granted being recalled to His glory through the merits of good works, may He make you more illustrious in this life and grant you the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.

We commend to your Excellency the bearer of this letter, whom we have sent there to administer that small patrimony. Bound to you by the bond of charity, we ask the Lord on your behalf that He direct your actions in this life in such a way that, because of their merit, He may lead you to the eternal kingdom.

As for our brother and fellow bishop Natalis, let Your Glory give him no assistance whatsoever against justice,

[Note: Thus, according to Gregory, this ignorance increases the sin rather than removing it; it accuses rather than excuses.]

because it is necessary that he feel the vengeance of canonical punishment all the more severely insofar as he is ignorant even of the canonical rule itself.

[Note: This note appears at the foot of column 557, but its callout number has not been printed in the text. Letter XXII, alternative number 7, indiction 13.]

### Letter XXII. To All the Bishops of Illyricum

He confirms the ordination of Bishop John.

Gregory to all the bishops established throughout Illyricum.

Your pastoral concern also brings us joy, and it makes your Fraternity secure concerning his ordination, provided that the order of ancient custom is preserved.

Since, therefore, from the letters that you sent to us through the presbyter Maximian and the deacon Andrew, we have learned that all of you agreed concerning the person of John, our brother and fellow bishop, and that the will of the most serene prince concurred with yours, we received great exultation that such a man had, with God’s authority, been advanced to the office of the priesthood, having been proved worthy by the judgment of everyone’s election.

Therefore, according to the desire expressed in your petition, we confirm by the authority of our assent the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop in the priestly order in which he has been established. We declare that we regard his consecration as valid by sending him the pallium.

Since, according to custom, we have entrusted him with the exercise of our functions, we have consequently judged it necessary to exhort your Fraternity not to delay obeying him in those matters that concern ecclesiastical order and the rectitude of discipline, or in other matters that are not opposed by the decrees of the canons. In this way, the obedience you display will demonstrate that you elected him with sincere judgment.

(See above, Book I, Letter 45, indiction 9; and below, Letter 23.)

### Letter XXIII. To John, Bishop

He congratulates John on having been elected by the unanimous consent of all. In accordance with custom, he grants him the pallium and the vicariate of the apostolic see. He urges him to fulfill the pastoral office with the utmost prudence and charity.

Gregory to John, bishop of Justiniana Prima in Illyricum.

[Note: Letter XXIII (alternative number 8, indiction 13).—Justiniana Prima, also called Achridus and now Locrida in Albania, was formerly a city of Macedonia near Lake Lychnidus. It is still a substantial city, situated on a high hill, where the emperor Justinian was born. He not only restored it but also adorned it with many privileges, especially metropolitan jurisdiction over the province of Praevalitana, indeed even primatial dignity and the vicariate of the Roman see, which he obtained from Pope Vigilius, as recorded in Novel 131. It was called “Prima” to distinguish it from Ulpian of Upper Moesia, which was called Justiniana Secunda, and from other cities of the same name restored by that emperor. It lies between Dyrrachium and Thessalonica, under Turkish rule. Gussanville.]

It is plainly a sign of goodness when, in the election of one person, the consent of all agrees.

[Col. 0558C]

Since, therefore, the report received from our brothers and fellow bishops declares that you have been summoned to the priestly office by the united consent of the entire council and by the will of the most serene prince, we have offered great thanks, with profound exultation, to almighty God our Creator. He has made your life and actions so worthy of approval in the past that, what is highly praiseworthy, He has caused you to please the judgment of all.

We too agree completely with them concerning your Fraternity. And we beseech almighty God that, just as His grace has chosen your Fraternity, so He may guard you in all things by His protection.

[Note: From this letter and Letter 57 of Book V it appears that Saint Gregory granted the pallium to certain Greek bishops, though not to all, and not to the patriarchs themselves, as Letter 15 of Book V teaches. Therefore, the patriarchs did not seek the pallium from another source; indeed, they seem to have granted it to their own subjects without opposition from Rome. This agrees with the fragments of the Eighth Council of Constantinople, chapters 17 and 27, and with John VIII, Letters 190 and 199. Whether the material of the pallium was the same, and whether the Eastern form was identical with the Western form, is another dispute of the sort called “a quarrel over goat’s wool.” If there had been a major or serious difference, each side would have reproached the other for it. Nor would the Latins in the ninth century, as someone fancied, have readily put aside linen and adopted the Greeks’ wool, which Isidore of Pelusium had mentioned many centuries earlier. Aug.]

We have sent you the pallium in accordance with custom (Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 10), and, by a renewed grant, we decree that you exercise the functions of the apostolic see. We admonish you to conduct yourselves toward those subject to you in such a conciliatory manner that they may be moved to love your rectitude rather than fear it.

[Note: Below, Book III, indiction 11, Letter 53. Saint Jerome, Letter 62, to Theophilus: “So that we may venerate Christ’s pontiffs . . . not through fear of masters but with the honor due to fathers . . . . Let them be content with their honor; let them know that they are fathers, not masters.” Gussanville. Gregory, his disciple, had read this in the Rule of Saint Benedict. Specifically, in chapter 64 the holy Father commands the abbot to strive to be loved rather than feared.]

If their fault should at some point demand it, take care to correct their excesses in such a way that you never abandon paternal affection in your heart. Be vigilant and solicitous in guarding the flock entrusted to you, and strict in your zeal for discipline, so that the lurking wolf may not, by any deceptive means, succeed either in disturbing the Lord’s fold or in harming the sheep.

Hasten to win souls for our God with the full intention of your mind. Recognize that you have assumed the name of pastor not for repose but for labor.

[Note: Those who eagerly seek the burden that ought to be feared even by angelic shoulders, while handing off the burden of the day and the heat to vicars, retain for themselves the honor, power, and revenues. Concerning such men, Jodocus Clicthovaeus, a doctor of the Sorbonne, once said in a public sermon, as reported by Espensaeus, Book III of the *Digressions*, chapter 22: “Such men will go to paradise through their vicars and to hell in their own person; thus some, while they were in the lower ranks, were distinguished in preaching, but when they became most illustrious, they fell silent.” One might say that, for some, the pastoral staff is an unworked weapon with which veterans, once discharged from military service, departed, whereas the episcopate imposes a greater obligation to renew the battle. More may be found in Saint Chrysostom, Homily 3 on the Acts of the Apostles. See Letter 11 of Book V, formerly Letter 12 of Book IV. Gussanville.]

Let us therefore exhibit in our work what is signified by our name. If we weigh the prerogative of the priesthood with sound judgment, it will be an honor to those who are diligent and govern well, but certainly a burden to the negligent. Just as this name leads those who labor and are solicitous for the salvation of souls to eternal glory before God, so it leads the idle and sluggish toward punishment.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts read; the editors changed the word to *urget*, “presses” or “drives.”]

Let the people entrusted to you recognize in your speech that there is another life. Let your Fraternity’s teaching be for them a welcome stimulus to correction, and your life an example for imitation. Let your sermon of preaching disclose what they ought to love and what they ought to fear; let the effectiveness of your conduct obtain for itself the fruit of such eternal recompense.

Meanwhile, let this chiefly constrain you in your deliberative care: never attempt to make unlawful ordinations. But if it should happen that some are promoted to the clerical order [Col. 0559C], or perhaps to a higher rank, let them be ordained not because of rewards or petitions, but because of their merits. In no ordination should your Fraternity in any way secretly appropriate advantages for itself, lest—God forbid—it become entangled in the snares of the simoniacal [Note: [Col. 0559D] Ecclesiastical authors commonly call the simoniacal practice a heresy, so as to show more clearly how execrable it is. The same was done several centuries later concerning the law of investitures. GUSSANV.] heresy. For what does it profit a man, as the Truth teaches, if he acquires the whole world and brings detriment upon his own soul (Matthew VIII, 36)? Therefore it is necessary that we attend to God in everything we undertake, despise perishable and temporal things, and direct our heart’s desire toward the goods of eternity. [Note: [Col. 0560C] In most manuscripts, *xenia*. He gives the reason why he does not accept them, lest he seem to condemn altogether this acceptance of gifts. In the *Digest*, Book I, title 16, “On the Office of a Proconsul,” §3: “A proconsul ought not wholly to abstain from gifts of hospitality, but should set a limit. He should neither abstain from them fussily nor exceed the proper measure of such gifts greedily.” And shortly afterward: “Hear what we think: there is an old proverb, οὔτε πάντα, οὔτε πάντῃ, οὔτε παρὰ πάντων—“neither everything, nor at every time, nor from everyone.” For it is very inhumane to accept from no one; to accept indiscriminately is most contemptible; and to accept everything is most avaricious.” Finally he concludes: “Nor are gifts of hospitality to be extended to the status of presents”; that is, presents are more than gifts of hospitality. Alciatus, on Law 194, “On the Meaning of Words,” explains almost every kind of present, and says that a *xenium* is properly a gift given to guests; but in law it is understood as a small present customarily sent to judges to curry their favor. GUSSANV.]

I had absolutely not wished to accept your Holiness’s *xenia*—gifts of hospitality—because it would have been highly inappropriate for us to appear to have received gifts from brothers who had been despoiled and afflicted. But your representatives overcame me by another argument, [Note: [Col. 0560D] Without doubt, they brought them to Saint Peter.] carrying them to the one from whom the offerings of your Fraternity could not be rejected. For you must strive above all to ensure that, as we said earlier, you procure imperishable gifts for the Judge of souls who is to come, so that he may regard both you for the work of your reward and us likewise for our exhortation. (See above, Letter 22.)

## LETTER XXIV. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to examine carefully a presbyter commended by Felix and send him to Rome if he finds him worthy of the episcopate.

[Col. 0560B]

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

Felix, a man of consular rank and bearer of this letter, has informed us that there is in those regions a certain presbyter who appears worthy, by the merit of his life, to be advanced to the episcopal order. Therefore let your Fraternity have him brought before you and, as I am confident you will, examine him carefully because of the danger to his soul. If you find that he is worthy of being advanced to this rank, let him be sent diligently to us, so that, with God’s direction, we may ordain him pastor in the place we shall have appointed. [Note: [Col. 0560D] LETTER XXIV (formerly 18).—At that time the bishops of Italy, Sicily, and the other neighboring provinces were consecrated only by the Roman pontiff, as patriarch of the West, or with his permission, etc. ALTESERRA.]

We commend to you Felix, the bearer of this letter, a man of consular rank and a *chartularius*, [Note: [Col. 0560C] In Vatican B and C: “Felix to your Charity.” In A: “Felix by vicarious charity.” We follow the readings of the Norman, Corbie, Vatican D, etc. On the dignity of the *chartularius*, see Alteserra here.] subject to the preservation of your Fraternity’s justice, so that in whatever he justly requests he may find fraternal affection. (Compare John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 13.)

## LETTER XXV. TO BENENATUS, BISHOP

He delegates the visitation of the Church of Cumae, so that Benenatus may both protect that Church and arrange for a suitable priest to be elected from its clergy.

[Col. 0561A]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0561C] LETTER XXV (formerly 19).—This bishop was of Misenum, as is clear from Letter 45, where he adds to his own Church of Misenum the Church of Cumae, whose visitor he had appointed in this letter. He is also mentioned in Book V, Letter 34, and Book IX, Letters 4 and 50. Formerly the text read, “to the bishop who was visitor of the Church of Cumae”; these words are absent from the Corbie, Norman, Rheims, and three Vatican manuscripts.] to Benenatus, bishop.

Since Liberius, formerly bishop of the Church of Cumae, is known to have departed this life, we solemnly delegate to your Fraternity the responsibility for visiting that deprived Church. You must undertake it in such a way that no one presumes to make any encroachment upon the Church with respect to promotions of clergy, revenue, furnishings, services, or anything else. [Note: [Col. 0561D] “Promotions” means appointments in which the visitor was forbidden to intervene unless specially delegated to do so; thus, above, in Letter 10, we read that this was delegated to Paul while he administered the Church of Naples. See Book I, Letters 18 and 81, and below, Letter 45. Alteserra understands the “advancements of the clergy” to mean their stipends, which the most holy pontiff forbids him to diminish.]

Therefore your Charity will hasten to go to the aforesaid Church, and we wish you to admonish its clergy and people by continual exhortations that, setting aside [Note: [Col. 0561D] In the printed editions: “through the zeal of opposing parties.” The Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts have prompted the omission of these two words.] partisan zeal, they should unanimously seek to have placed over them a priest who is both found capable of so great a ministry and in no way rejected by the venerable canons. When he has been requested, he is to come to us for consecration with the formality of a decree confirmed by everyone’s subscriptions and accompanied by a letter of testimony from your Love.

We also admonish your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be elected from another Church, unless—something we do not believe will occur—no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of the city in which you are carrying out the visitation. [Note: [Col. 0561D] Would that this rule, sanctioned, repeated, and impressed upon us by councils and holy Fathers, did not lie idle in our own times! In the decrees of Pope Celestine, chapter 18, we read: “Then let one be chosen from another Church, if no worthy person can be found among the clergy of the city in which the bishop is to be ordained. For first those men must be rejected, so that persons from elsewhere may deservedly be preferred.” Each man had the fruit of his service in the Church in which he had passed his entire life through all its offices; let no one intrude into another’s stipend, nor dare to claim for himself the reward owed to another. Let clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being burdened, and let them not fear to reject those whom they recognize as being forced upon them from outside, etc. The reader may consult Pope Nicholas’s letter to Charles the Bald, about the year 865, where he calls the contrary practice, which was spreading more freely in Gaul, a reckless violation of the canons. To eliminate it, he says, special diligence must be applied and it must be uprooted from its foundations with the pruning hook of the decree, as he himself puts it. What they say concerning bishops, a prudent person will apply in the same way to other dignities, offices, and priesthoods. See the Code, Book I, title 6, “Concerning Bishops and Clergy,” law 11: “In Churches which, as commonly happens, are established in the estates of different persons, whether in villages or in whatever places, clergy are to be ordained not from another estate or village, but from the place where the Church is known to exist,” etc. GUSSANV.]

Before all else, take care that no layperson presume to aspire to this position on the basis of any manner of life or merit. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Vatican A and B read: “lest a person of whatever manner of life or merit aspire to the episcopate.” The printed editions read: “lest anyone aspire to the merit of any manner of life.” We follow Vatican D, Rheims, Norman, the Royal manuscripts, etc.] Otherwise you would incur the peril of your own order—God forbid. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Many canons provide safeguards against promoting laymen immediately to holy orders; see them in Thomassin, Book I, Part II, chapter 85.]

## LETTER XXVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He entrusts him with the visitation of the Church of Nepi.

[Col. 0562A]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0562D] LETTER XXVI (formerly 20).—The printed editions read, “to the bishop who is visitor of the Church of Nepi.” The Vatican manuscripts read, “to John, bishop of Nepi.” We follow the Norman, Corbie, Rheims, etc.] to John, bishop.

Since we have entrusted our brother and fellow bishop Paul with the visitation of the Church of Naples, your Fraternity must not cease undertaking the visitation of the Church of Nepi, so that, as the Paschal feast requires, everything demanded by the sacred solemnity may in every respect be fulfilled through your ministry.

Until we are able to deliberate what ought to be done concerning the person of the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop of ours, let your Fraternity strive to show yourself so diligent and watchful in every respect that the absence of the aforesaid man is in no way felt. [Note: [Col. 0562D] Thus the old Colbertine and Tours manuscripts, and Saint Gall.]

In the month of April, in the tenth indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO RUSTICIANA, PATRICIAN

The good conceived in the heart through the Creator’s gift must be completed with prompt and steadfast devotion. If anyone schemes accusations against them, their entire hope must be turned toward God.

[Col. 0562B]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0562D] She had moved from Rome to Constantinople, as can be inferred from Letters 22 of indiction 1 and 22 of indiction 6.] to Rusticiana, patrician.

On receiving the letter of Your Excellency, I was refreshed by the welcome news of your good health, and I pray that the Lord in his mercy may protect and guide your life and actions. But I was greatly surprised that you had turned aside from your resolve and vow to travel to the holy places and undertake this good work. Whenever some good thing is conceived in the heart through the gift of the Creator, it must necessarily be completed with prompt devotion, lest, while the cunning adversary strives to ensnare the mind, he continually suggest obstacles by which the mind, weakened through its preoccupations, may not bring its desires to fulfillment.

Therefore it is necessary for Your Excellency to anticipate every obstacle that opposes pious purposes and to long with all the efforts of your heart for the fruit of the good work, so that you may be able to live peacefully in the present age and possess the heavenly kingdom in the future.

As for what you wrote—that Passivus had contrived certain accusations against you, while the most pious emperors not only refused to hear them willingly but also received them harshly—consider whose gift this was. Turn the whole hope of your mind toward him who powerfully opposes men in this world, so that they may not be able to harm you as much as they desire; let him repel wicked human intentions by the opposition of his arm and, as he is accustomed to do, mercifully break their efforts himself.

Through you I ask that greetings be conveyed in my name to the glorious lord Appio and lady Eusebia, lord Eudoxius and lady Gregoria.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO STEPHANUS, CHARTULARIUS

He orders two monks who deserted their state to be forced back; he forbids new customs to be imposed upon the monastery.

Gregory to Stephanus [Note: [Col. 0563D] LETTER XXXVIII (formerly 20, indiction 7).—In the collection of Paul the Deacon, Letter 45, with the agreement of two Teller manuscripts and the Norman manuscripts, as well as Vatican D, the reading is “to Stephanus, *chartularius*, or *chartarius* of Sicily.” Vatican and Teller manuscripts add: “concerning the restoration of monks.” Read Letter 3 of indiction 11, to John, abbot of Saint Lucia at Syracuse, concerning this Stephanus.] the *chartularius*.

Knowing that Your Greatness loves the Lord with your whole heart, we have thought it necessary to bring to your attention that we have learned of acts committed on the estates belonging by right to Julius, the late patrician of blessed memory, [Note: [Col. 0563D] We restore this reading from the manuscripts, whereas the printed editions have: “concerning the law of the late patrician man of blessed memory.” In two Teller manuscripts, instead of *in massis*, we read *in marsis*.] contrary to the Lord’s commands and to the rule of the canons. This is so that what has been perpetrated may be corrected and others may thereafter not presume to attempt such things.

It has therefore been reported to us that at the estate called Marato [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Norman has *Marathodis*; two Teller manuscripts have *Mirathodis* or *Marathodis*; two Corbie manuscripts and the old Colbertine have *Maratodis*. The printed editions read: “that the abbot … had fled.”], where the monastery of Saint George is situated, two monks have fled. One of them has already taken a wife, while the other, having become a layman, lives a secular life. Yet it is asserted that these men are not even free members of the estate’s household; and even if they ought to have acted according to their status, it was contrary to God’s will that, after attaining the service of a divine office, they should return to secular life and dress.

Therefore I urge you, with consideration of the eternal Judge, to have these monks forced back without delay, lest, through their example and—God forbid—your sin, the discipline of the other monasteries be dissolved. Rather, through the support of Your Greatness, let the hope of other monks attempting such things be removed.

The aforesaid abbot also asserts that the presbyter of the aforesaid estate wishes to impose new customs upon the monastery—customs that had not existed during the three years since the monastery was founded—namely, that if anything is offered there by faithful men out of generosity to God, he claims that he ought to receive a portion of it. Let Your Greatness take care to ascertain this diligently. If it was not so from the beginning, do not permit anything else to be newly imposed as time passes, especially since we have learned that the monastery possesses only scant resources and is poor, and that the abbot himself is entirely hospitable, as many attest. [Note: [Col. 0564D] Paul the Deacon’s collection adds: “given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.”]

## LETTER XXIX. TO MAURILIUS AND VITALIANUS

If Ariulphus proceeds toward Rome, they are to follow him from behind.

Gregory to Maurilius and Vitalianus [Note: [Col. 0564D] LETTER XXXIX (formerly 22, indiction 7).—The text formerly read *Mauricius*.] commanders of the army.

On receiving the letters of Your Glories, we gave thanks to God because we learned of your safety and rejoiced greatly in your concern; and at once the things you wrote about were prepared. But the magnificent man Aldio [Note: [Col. 0564D] The printed editions add: “a man worthy of remembrance.”] wrote to us after the arrival of your men that Ariulphus was already nearby, and we feared that the soldiers being sent to you might fall into his hands.

Nevertheless, here too, insofar as God helps, our son, the glorious commander of the army, has prepared himself against him. And if that enemy himself should come here, let Your Glories, as you are accustomed to do, accomplish with God’s help whatever you can against him from the rear. [Note: [Col. 0564D] Thus the manuscripts read instead of *perexerit*, found in the printed editions. Above, Book I, Letter 52, *perexeat* occurs in the same sense.]

For we hope in the power of almighty God and in that of the blessed Peter himself, prince of the apostles, on whose feast-day Ariulphus desires to shed blood, because he will soon find Peter himself opposed to him.

## LETTER XXX. TO MAURILIUS AND VITALIANUS

He warns them about the doubtful loyalty of the people of Suana and about Ariulphus’s army, which is ready for action.

[Col. 0564C]

Gregory to Maurilius and Vitalianus, commanders of the army.

Through our son Vitalianus, with whom we instructed you to confer both orally and in writing, we have humbly addressed Your Glories. On the eleventh day of the month [Note: [Col. 0564D] LETTER XXX (formerly 23, indiction 7).—In the collection of Paul the Deacon, “of January.” This letter is absent from most manuscripts.] of January, Ariulphus sent on this letter, which we have forwarded to you. Therefore, read it again and see whether the people of Suana [Note: [Col. 0564D] Suana, commonly Soana, a city of Etruria, still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Siena.] have remained in the loyalty that they promised to the state.

Receive from them hostages worthy of your confidence, bind them again with oaths, return to them what you took as a pledge, and heal them through your words. But if you learn with complete certainty that they have spoken with Ariulphus concerning their submission, or at least have given him hostages—as the letter of Ariulphus that we sent you has made us doubtful—then, after carefully considering sound counsel lest your soul or ours be burdened in any way by oaths, do whatever you judge useful for the state.

But let Your Glories act in such a way that there is nothing for which we may be reproached by our adversaries, and that, wherever the interests of the state require it, nothing is neglected—may the Lord avert such a thing.

Moreover, glorious sons, be diligent, because, as I have learned, he has an army assembled [Note: [Col. 0565C] That is, he has gathered an army. *Hostis*, both here and frequently among writers of the Middle and later Ages, means precisely “army.” See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, where this Gregorian passage is illustrated by many testimonies collected elsewhere.] and is said to be staying at Narina [Note: [Col. 0565C] Paul the Deacon has *Nardias*.]. If he wishes, with God angered against him, to make his way here, plunder his territories as far as the Lord helps you, [Note: [Col. 0565D] Paul the Deacon has *depraedate*, “plunder.”] or at least carefully inspect the scouts whom you send. [Note: [Col. 0565D] Thus the Valley and Corbie manuscripts read: “the scouts whom you send.” Similarly, in Theophylact Simocatta, Book VI, chapter 9, after the victory the Romans turned to pleasure and drinking and forgot the guard, “which the Romans are accustomed in their native language to call *skoulkai* [σκοῦλκαι].” The same word, *skoulkai* [σκοῦλκαι], occurs in Leo’s Constitution 17, *skoulkatores* [σκουλκάτωρες], *skoulkeuein* [σκουλκεύειν], and in Constantine, *On the Administration of the Empire*, *exskoulkatores* [ἐξκουλκάτωρες], “scouts,” and *exskoulkeuein* [ἐξκουλκεύειν], “to reconnoiter.” See the glossaries of Meursius, Rigaltius, and Lindeburgius on the ancient laws. GUSSANV. In the Lombard Law, Book I, title 14, §6: “If anyone refuses to march in the army or to go on the *sculea*.” There *exercitus* and *sculca* mean the military service to which vassals were bound. Some read *scultas*, but Du Cange refutes them in both glossaries.] Otherwise, news of a disastrous action may run to us. [Note: [Col. 0565D] The old Colbertine manuscript adds: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the tenth indiction.”]

## LETTER XXXI. TO ALL THE NEAPOLITAN SOLDIERS

Concerning the obedience to be shown to the tribune Constantius.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] LETTER XXXI (formerly 24, indiction 7).—This letter is omitted from most manuscripts, especially the Norman and English ones, as Thomas Jamezius observes. It is found in the collection of Paul the Deacon and is cited in Cause 23, question 1, canon 7.]

[Col. 0565B]

Gregory to all the Neapolitan soldiers.

Among the other good merits of military service, its highest praise is to show obedience to the interests of the holy state [Note: [Col. 0566C] He uses this expression again below and very frequently elsewhere, in the same sense in which it is also often used in the Rule of Saint Benedict, for example, chapter 35: “if some are occupied with greater duties”; chapter 65: “let him be appointed, as we have previously arranged, so that the entire welfare of the monastery…”] and to obey whatever has been usefully commanded. We have learned that your devotion has done this now as well: you obeyed our letters by which we appointed the magnificent man Constantius tribune to take charge of guarding the city, and you demonstrated the obedience appropriate to military devotion.

Therefore, by this present letter, we have taken care to admonish you that, as you have done, you must show the aforesaid magnificent tribune every obedience for the benefit of our most serene lords and for the preservation of the city, so that whatever we recognize as having been well conducted by you up to now, you may increase through the vigilance and care of the present time.

## LETTER XXXII. TO PETER, SUBDEACON OF SICILY

He gives many instructions concerning the administration of the patrimony, in which justice, religion, prudence, and a generous disposition toward the needy shine forth; his personal affection for Peter is also readily apparent.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily.

Our defensor Romanus has informed me that [Col. 0566A] [Note: [Col. 0566] [ [Col. 0566] This note appears at the foot of column 566, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text.] the monastery of the handmaids of God situated on the estate of Monotheus [Note: [Col. 0566D] Paul the Deacon has *Monostheo*. Vatican D has *Monastheo*; Vatican A, *Monasterio* or *Monotheo*.] suffered violence from our Church of Villanova, concerning the estate said to have been released to that same monastery. If this is so, let your Experience restore both the estate to them and the rents from that estate that you exacted for the two indictions. [Note: [Col. 0566D] The same manuscript has “which you collected.” Vatican D and the Royal manuscripts agree.]

Since many Jews remain among the Church’s tenants, I want you, if any of them wish to become Christians, to remit some part of their rent, so that, encouraged by this benefit, others too may rise to such a desire. [Note: [Col. 0566D] On Jews to whom something is to be remitted if they become Christians, see below, Book V, Letter 8.] [Note: [Col. 0566D] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “may be urged.”]

The cows that are now sterile with age, and the male oxen that appear entirely useless, ought to be sold, so that at least their price may be converted to some useful purpose. I also want all the herds of mares, which we maintain at great cost and little use, to be sold, retaining only four hundred younger ones for breeding. From these four hundred, one is to be given to each tenant, so that each year they may return something from them, since it is exceedingly harsh for us to spend sixty solidi on the shepherds and receive not even sixty denarii from these same herds. Therefore let your Experience arrange that some be distributed among all the tenants, as we have said, while others you sell and convert into money. Assign the shepherds themselves among the estates, so that they may produce some benefit from cultivating the land. All the bronze objects that may belong to the Church’s property, whether at Syracuse or at Palermo, are to be sold before they completely perish through age.

[Col. 0566C] 593
