When our brother Cyriacus, servant of God, came to Rome, I carefully questioned him whether he had spoken with your knowledge about accepting a reward in the case of a certain woman. The same brother says that, according to your report, he learned that he had been sent by you so that the person who had sent him to offer the reward might be tested. I believed him, and immediately received him back into familiar favor. I brought him before the people and clergy and increased his *presbyterium*, placing him in a higher position among the defenders, while praising his fidelity before everyone, because he had acted so faithfully in your service. For that reason I quickly sent him back to you. [Note: [Col. 0567D] That is, I conferred a new clerical office upon him and entrusted him with a new administration of Church affairs. *Presbyterium* is often used for the body of clergy, called the senate of the Church, or *hierateion* [ἱερατεῖον], in Antioch, canon 3; sometimes it means the dignity of a presbyter. Both meanings are found in the Council of Ancyra, canon 18. Saint Ignatius at one time calls it a sacred system, *systēma hieron* [σύστημα ἱερὸν], and at another a holy presbyterate, *hagion presbyterion* [ἅγιον Πρεσβυτέριον]. Cornelius, in Cyprian, Letter 46, says that the presbyterate is convened when a synod is called. Saint Gregory gives a third, related meaning, understanding *presbyterium* not as a body or strictly as a presbyterate, but as a certain part of governance—as honor, office, course, or administration of the Church, in the words of Saint Paul, 1 Corinthians 12:28. The Council of Chalcedon, canon 2, grants defenders “ordination and rank,” *cheirotonian kai axian* [χειροτονίαν καὶ ἀξίαν], and therefore dignity in the presbyterate. Read Sidonius Apollinaris, final letter of Book IV, concerning a second-order deacon who was a priest and whom they increased in dignity. The nature of this administration is somewhat less clear in our own times because of the introduction of new law. It would be clearer if we had retained canon 8 of Ephesus and if each province had preserved the old law intact, without any force being done to it according to ancient custom, etc. See Book I, Letter 77. GUSSANV. Below, Book V, Letter 33, *presbyterium* designates the customary stipend of the clergy under the name of the presbyterate. See Volume II of the *Musei Italici*, Roman Order 12, whose second part is almost entirely about the presbyteria customarily distributed throughout the year. The term *presbyterium* also signified a gift: the newly consecrated pontiff distributed money to each member of the senate and clergy, already in the age of Gregory the Great. See Anastasius, under Deusdedit, Boniface V, and Severinus. That distribution of money, which was also made on certain solemn occasions during the year, was commonly called a *presbyterium*. See the work cited above, Roman Order 11, §§22, 23, 56. It should be noted that the Royal manuscripts and Paul the Deacon read: “I brought him before the people and clergy, I brought out the *polypticum*, the *presbyterium*, etc.” A *polypticum* is a record in which proceedings are entered. See Book II of the *Lives*, chapter 24, and Book IX, Letter 40.]

Since you are in great haste, and although I am ill I desire to see you—you have proved him yourself in every respect—leave him in your place in the Syracusan region [Note: [Col. 0567D] There were two stations of the Roman Church’s patrimony in Sicily, one at Palermo and the other at Syracuse. See Book X, Letter 49. ALTESERRA.] and hasten to come to me, so that, if it pleases almighty God, we may deliberate together whether he himself should return there or another should be appointed in your place. I have likewise sent Benenatus the notary, so that he may preserve your place in the patrimony in the region of Palermo until almighty God ordains what he wills.

I sharply rebuked Romanus for his fickleness, because, as I have now discovered, while he held the hospice he was more occupied with his own interests than with his rewards. Therefore, if it should seem right to you, leave him in your place. See how you may fortify him by frightening and admonishing him, so that he may know that he must act piously and diligently toward the peasants, and show himself wholly changed and energetic toward outsiders and townspeople. In saying this, however, I am choosing no person; I leave the matter to your judgment.

In the region of Palermo, it is enough for me to have chosen someone to safeguard your place. [Note: [Col. 0567D] These were formerly called vicars or lieutenants, in French *lieutenants*. We have already discussed this word in the *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 52. Among the Greeks the corresponding term is *topotērētēs* [τοποτηρητής]. There is a letter of Theodore the Studite to Nicetas, “the lieutenant,” *Nikētā topotērētē* [Νικήᾳ τοποτηρητῆ], and it is Book II, Letter 120.] I wish to see what you will provide in the Syracusan region. When you come, bring with you the money and ornaments from Antoninus’s share or property. Bring also the rents of the ninth and tenth indictions that you collected, together with all the accounts.

If it pleases God, make every effort to cross into this city shortly before the feast-day [Note: [Col. 0568C] At that time the feast of Saint Cyprian was celebrated with solemn observance. Historians call it the “Cyprianic” storm; sailors used the same term for a violent storm that usually occurred around this season, which modern seafarers call a hurricane, perhaps stirred up by the east wind. Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 16, quotes the following from Procopius: “All the Carthaginians honor Cyprian, a holy man, and they built for him a worthy temple outside the city near the seashore, about which many things are related. Completing the other religious observances, they celebrate his annual feast, which they call the Cyprianic feast.” Sailors too, as I mentioned earlier, commonly call and announce the winter by the name of that feast, since it tends to threaten around the time when the Libyans decreed that this feast should be celebrated perpetually. Thus Musculus translates it. The Greek differs somewhat, as the curious will observe. By “winter” understand a fierce sea-storm, *keimōna* [κειμῶνα]. GUSSANV.] before the birthday of blessed Cyprian, lest some danger—God forbid—arise from the weather-sign that always threatens at sea during those days.

Furthermore, you should know that, because I opposed the servant of God Pretiosus severely for a fault that was not serious, and sent him away from me sad and embittered, [Note: [Col. 0568C] The supreme pontiff had opposed the servant of God severely for a fault that was not serious and had sent him away from him in sadness; hence the grave sting of conscience that had to be recorded in this letter. This is certainly a grave lesson for prelates, if there are any who command with harshness and power and treat their subjects as though they were balls. Saint Ambrose perhaps speaks to such men in his *Apology of David*, chapter 9: “Let them therefore hear and feel the wound of sin, for it is an incurable illness not to feel the bitterness of the wound.” That Saint Gregory, a man greatly distinguished for prudence, knowledge, and truth, was superstitious in this matter—or, as people commonly say, scrupulous, or, in Latin terms, anxious, timid, and hesitant because of excessive religious concern—hardly any sensible person would admit. Certainly it is more credible that those who refuse to follow his example will be less religious. GUSSANV.] I am not lightly gnawed at in my thoughts.

I wrote to the lord bishop that he ought to send him if he wished, but he absolutely refused. I neither ought nor can grieve him, because, being occupied in the causes of God, he must be strengthened by consolation, not depressed by bitterness. Yet this same Pretiosus, as I hear, is greatly saddened that he is not returning to me. But I cannot, as I said, grieve the lord bishop, who does not wish to release him, and I remain uncertain between the two.

Therefore, if indeed you possess greater wisdom in your small body, arrange this matter so that both my will may be done and the lord bishop not be saddened. Yet if you see him become even slightly saddened, say nothing further about it. I was nevertheless deeply distressed that he excommunicated the lord Eusebius, a man of such advanced age and such serious illness. Therefore you must say privately to that same lord bishop that he should not be rash in pronouncing judgments, because cases to be decided by judgment must first be measured by careful and repeated consideration. (See Letter 34.)

When the recruiting officers arrive—who, as I hear, are already gathering recruits there—assign the matter to the guardian of your place, so that he may offer a small *xenium* and thereby make them favorably disposed toward him. Also give something to the praetor’s office, according to ancient custom, before you come, but do so through the hands of the man whom you leave behind, so that you may win their favor for him.

And lest we appear wholly inhuman to them, instruct the guardians of your places to carry out in every respect the things that, by command, I have charged your Experience to give to each individual and monastery. [Note: [Col. 0569C] In the Vatican manuscripts and Paul the Deacon, the order of the periods is reversed, and the text reads: “Let them fulfill the three hundred … to be entrusted. Therefore those things … let them fulfill; but these matters, with the Lord’s help … we shall deliberate. Before this time, however …”] When you come, with the Lord’s help, we shall deliberate how these matters are to be arranged. I do not think that the three hundred solidi which I have sent through you to the poor should be entrusted to their discretion. Let them therefore fulfill the obligations for each place and person.

Before this time, I remember having already written that the bequests which, according to the record of the defensor Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0569C] Or according to the register, in which he had recorded individually whatever he was obliged to distribute to monasteries and the poor by Gregory’s command. Alteserra understands the term here as referring to a tenure or possession subject to certain obligations; Gussanvius understands it as a testament. Choose whichever interpretation you prefer. Vatican D reads, “from the death of Antoninus.” The sequence of the letter certainly proves that he had died.] are owed by us should be paid to monasteries and others, as had been established. I do not know why your Experience has delayed fulfilling this.

Therefore we wish you to fulfill these same bequests, from our share of the Church’s money, so that when you come to me you do not leave there behind you the groaning of the poor against you. Bring with you also the bonds [Note: [Col. 0569C] Namely, written acknowledgments of debt, *chirographa*, or instruments of indebtedness. See Luke 16:6: “Take your bond.” See Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 18.] found among the property of that same Antoninus.

Now, from the report of Romanus, I learned that when Redemptus’s wife was dying, she said orally that a silver bowl should be sold and the proceeds given to her freedmen; she also left a silver dish to a certain monastery. In both matters we wish her wishes to be fulfilled in every respect, lest from trifling possessions we incur greater sins.

[Note: Vaticanus A reads “to a certain monastery,” and below “to fulfill” instead of “be fulfilled.”]

From the report of Abbot Mariniana, I learned that the construction at the Praetorian monastery has not yet even been brought halfway to completion.

[Note: Vaticanus D reads “at the Praetorian palace”; Reg. supports this reading.]

What else, then, can we do but praise the zeal of your Experience?

[Note: This seems to be the reading, in accordance with the supreme pontiff’s intention: while ironically praising his zeal, he censures Peter’s sluggishness. Vaticanus A and Paulus, however, read “favor.”]

But now, having been admonished, rouse yourself and show yourself, as far as you can, in the construction of that monastery. I said that nothing was to be given to them for expenses; I did not prohibit you from building the monastery with those resources. But act in such a way that you absolutely require the man whom you have left in your place at Palermo to build this same monastery at the expense of the Church and from its grain supply, and that the private complaint of the abbot does not come back to me.

Furthermore, I have learned that you recognize certain properties, or perhaps several estates, as belonging to another’s legal ownership, but that, because of the entreaties or fear of certain persons, you are afraid to restore them to their owners. If you were truly a Christian, you would fear God’s judgment more than the voices of men.

[Col. 0570B]

Consider that I, too, continually admonish you about this matter. If you neglect to fulfill it, you will also have my words as testimony against you.

But if you find certain God-fearing laymen who ought to be tonsured and made actionarii under a rector, I accept this entirely willingly. It is necessary also that letters be sent to them.

[Note: The meaning of Saint Gregory’s words here about tonsure is obscure. The matter concerns laymen who fear God and who ought to be tonsured so that they may become actionarii under a rector. Among jurists, rector means one who governs a province, whether under the title of praetorian prefect, count, proconsul, legate, or corrector. By actionarius or actor they understand a syndic who conducts the affairs of others before a judge. Perhaps those who conducted the Church’s cases had to be tonsured so that they might appear like clerics—not properly so, but as associates, such as the Fossarii, Psalmists, Deaconesses, Ascetics, and others of that kind. Even today there are such persons among the Fathers of the Oratory, Christian Doctrine, and the Missions: for the most part pure lay servants, yet tonsured and wearing a habit suggestive of clerical status.

I offer another interpretation. It is clear that certain persons were administrators of the patrimony of the Roman Church. Under them were actors, or actionarii, as principal assistants, upon whom the burden of business rested; this is well known from classical authors and jurists. They were generally slaves, although they were placed over other slaves. Thus, in this letter Saint Gregory seems to order such actionarii, taken from among the laymen, to cut their hair, as though to claim their freedom and to transfer them, in some fashion, into the clerical order, so that they might possess greater authority over the others. The conjecture is confirmed by the necessity mentioned below of sending letters—namely, letters that would guarantee their freedom. It is for you, reader, to judge.

Gussanville, in this note, before discussing the tonsured men, according to his custom digresses about barbers and male and female hair-cutters; we have judged those portions ought to be removed, while retaining the rest, in which he does not depart so far from the point. We think, however, that the laymen ordered to be tonsured here were truly made clerics. For, as John the Deacon teaches, *Life*, book II, chapter 15: “No laymen administered any office of the palace or ecclesiastical patrimony; rather, men of the clergy undertook all duties belonging to ecclesiastical jurisdiction,” laymen being assigned solely to military service with weapons [lacuna].]

Regarding the case of Commissus’s son, the scholar, you consulted the legal experts, and what he claims is not justified by the laws. We do not wish to burden the interests of the poor, but, for the labor he undertook here, we wish you to give him fifty solidi, which are certainly to be charged to your accounts.

[Note: Vaticanus A reads, “Regarding the case of the aforementioned son, unless you consulted the scholars”; Vaticanus D, “unless you consulted the scholars.” Reg. reads, “Regarding the case of the son of the aforementioned [person]”; this may signify “of the aforementioned.”]

Regarding Prochisi’s case, for whatever expenses you incurred from the Church’s property, either satisfy him there from the proceeds of your revenues, or, if those revenues are plainly insufficient for reimbursement, it is necessary that the payment be received here from the deacon.

[Note: Reg. reads “Prochiti.”]

Do not presume to say anything about the subdeacon Gelasius, because his crime requires the gravest penance until the end of his life.

[Note: Reg. and two Vatican manuscripts read “requires the gravest penance until the end of his life.”]

Furthermore, you sent us one wretched horse and five good asses. I cannot ride that horse, because it is wretched; and I cannot ride those good animals, because they are asses. But we ask that, if you intend to satisfy us, you send us something worthy of the occasion.

[Note: That is, “to make us content.”]

[Note: Vaticanus A reads, “send something worthy with you”; Vaticanus D, “send something worthy with you.”]

We wish you to give Abbot Eusebius one hundred gold solidi, which are certainly to be charged to your accounts.

We have learned that Sisinnius, who was judge of Samnium, is suffering severe poverty in Sicily. We wish you to provide him annually with twenty *decimates* of wine and four solidi.

[Note: Reg. reads “twenty decimated measures of wine”; Vaticanus D reads “fourteen *batai* of wine.”]

Anastasius the religious is said to live near the city of Palermo, in the oratory of Saint Agnes; we wish six gold solidi to be given to him.

Six solidi are also to be given to the mother of the administrator Urbicius; they will be charged to your accounts.

Regarding the case of the handmaid of God Honorata, it seems to me that you should bring with you all the property that is known to have belonged to the Laurinensian [Note: The manuscripts Vaticanus, Reg., Tellerianus, and Thuanus read “Laurinensian.” The printed editions have “Larinensian.” Holstenius, *Annotations on Sacred Geography*, p. 21, thinks “Carinensian” should be read. Gussanville objects that the Carinensian Church had been united with the Rhegian Church, as is clear from book V, letter 9—now book VI, letter 10—and therefore did not have a bishop at that time. But that union took place only in the sixth year of Saint Gregory’s pontificate, after the death of the Carinensian bishop.]

Church before the time of Bishop John’s episcopate. Let that same handmaid of God come with her son, so that we may speak with her and do what is pleasing to God.

We wish the copy of the Heptateuch from Antoninus’s property to be given to the Praetorian monastery; let the remaining books be brought with you.

[Note: “Heptateuch” means the book containing the first seven books of Sacred Scripture.]

## LETTER XXXIII. TO JUSTINUS, THE PRAETOR

That, after laying aside all suspicion, he should show every charity and fitting reverence to Bishop Leo, who had been completely cleared of false accusations.

[Col. 0571C]

Gregory to Justinus, the praetor.

[Note: Letter XXXIII [formerly 23]. It was formerly read “to the presbyter,” but the context of the letter, as well as Letter 2 of Book I, shows that it should be “to the praetor”; I have restored that reading on the authority of at least sixteen manuscripts. This Justinus is the same man to whom Gregory had already written in Book I, Letter 2, and about whom, in Letter 37—now 38—of Indiction 11, he complains to his successor Libertinus that, out of avarice, he had refrained from correcting a certain Jew. In the English, Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts, “to the praetor” is read. In Vaticanus D, however, there is only “to Justinian, concerning receiving Leo.” “Justinian” is also read in two Tellerian manuscripts, the Colbertine manuscript, and Paulus’s collection.]

It is characteristic of the ancient enemy’s envy that those whom, because God resists him, he cannot deceive into committing wicked actions, he tears apart for the moment by falsely fabricating opinions about them.

Since, therefore, a sinister rumor had spread certain accusations against our brother and fellow bishop Leo concerning his priestly conduct, we ordered a strict investigation to determine whether they were true, and we found in him no fault in the matters that had been reported. But lest anything seem to have been omitted, or any doubt remain in our heart, we made him give solemn oaths before the most sacred body of blessed Peter.

[Note: Although, according to the rules of law, certain knowledge cannot exist in every doubtful case, and the defendant ought to be acquitted when the plaintiff fails to prove his case, canon law had nevertheless introduced the taking of an oath over the Gospels, relics, or something similar. This was done so that, as Hincmar says, “the hearts of the weak may not be struck by the evil reputation of a presbyter, nor our ministry be brought into disrepute.” Indeed, a popular form of purification had entered the Church: by touching red-hot iron, by boiling or cold water, and even by single combat, in which they contended in the field or by the cross; see Ansegisus, book III, chapter 46. Other vain and evil observances of the same kind also existed, which at last had to be cut away by the sickle of the canons. Saint Gregory wished oaths to be given before Saint Peter’s body. In the time of Ambrose, people swore at Milan before the bodies of the saints. Augustine likewise sent people to Saint Felix of Nola. Gregory VII used the Eucharist in such purgation. The Council of Meaux, canon 38, forbids a bishop to swear over the sacred objects. Let the reader consult the *Extravagantes*, book V, titles 34 and 35, and *Causa* II, question 5. Moreover, the beginning of this letter seems to have been taken from Letter 78 of Saint Augustine, concerning the presbyter Boniface. Gussanville. On the various judgments or ordeals used to uncover hidden or doubtful crimes, see our Edme Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book III, chapter 7, where the subject is treated at great length.]

After he had given these oaths, we rejoiced with great exultation, because his innocence clearly shone forth through this examination. Therefore let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with every expression of charity, and show him the reverence appropriate to a priest. Let no doubt remain in your hearts concerning matters that have now been cleared up.

But you ought to adhere to the bishop named above with such devotedness in all things that you may fittingly and honorably be seen to honor God in the person of him whose minister he is.

[Note: In Paulus’s collection: “Given on the third day before the Nones of June, in the tenth indiction.”]

## LETTER XXXIV. TO MAXIMIANUS, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He consoles Abbot Eusebius, whom Maximianus had imprudently afflicted.

Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

I remember frequently admonishing you that you ought never to be hasty in delivering a judgment. Now I have learned that, moved by anger, your Fraternity excommunicated the most reverend Abbot Eusebius.

[Note: Letter XXXIV [formerly 26, indiction 7]. Eusebius was already mentioned in Letter 32 above. From this brief letter, which Gregory writes to a bishop of exceptional holiness and also a very close friend, we learn that friends should not be flattered and blinded by praise, but freely admonished and sometimes even rebuked. We should also learn that anger must be guarded against even by holier men, and that nothing should be decided rashly.]

I was greatly surprised that neither his long-standing manner of life, nor his advanced age, nor his prolonged illness moved your angry spirit. Whatever excess he may have committed, the affliction of his illness itself ought to have been sufficient punishment for him. When divine discipline crushes a man, it was superfluous to add human scourges.

Perhaps you were permitted to go too far in the case of such a person so that you might become more cautious in lesser matters and weigh your decision carefully for a long time whenever you intend to strike someone with a sentence.

Yet, just as you aggravated that same man with great anger, so now console him with equally great gentleness. For it is most unjust that those who have loved you more should find you, without cause, more severe toward them.

## LETTER XXXV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He congratulates him on the charitable services he performed for the sick Bishop Castorius. He asks that Castorius be sent to him through Sicily. He entrusts to the bishop of Ravenna the care of the suffragan bishops whom hostile forces prevented from traveling from Rome.

[Col. 0573B]

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

We are commanded by the Lord’s precepts to love our neighbors as ourselves and to feel compassion for their illnesses as though they were our own infirmities. Mindful of this, your Fraternity, in the manner appropriate to you, first took care to visit our brother and fellow bishop Castorius with compassion, and afterward received him in the city of Ravenna because of the increasing affliction of his body.

Thus you have undoubtedly made not only us, through your abundant charity, but also God your debtor, since you are shown to have sympathized with your brother’s illness and not merely visited the sick man in the affliction of his bodily member but also received him.

I had entirely refused, because of his simplicity, to ordain him there; but the persistence of those who requested it made it impossible for me to resist.

[Note: Rhem. reads, “but the power of the influential.”]

If it can be done, you will greatly benefit both me and him if you send him to me, even through Sicily, provided you judge that the journey will not be burdensome for him.

[Note: Perhaps because, on account of the Lombard armies occupying all the roads, it would not have been safe to travel to Rome by land, whereas passage by sea was freer and safer.]

As for the bishops belonging to us who cannot come here because of the hostile forces stationed between us, let your Fraternity care for them. Do so, however, in such a way that they are not recalled to the city of Ravenna for their own affairs, lest we seem at this time to harass or weary them in any way.

But if there are matters in which they seem justly open to criticism, they must always be admonished through letters from your Fraternity. If, however—which God forbid—anything more serious should occur, we wish you to report it carefully to us, so that, strengthened by the testimony of your investigation, we may arrange what accords with the laws and canons by a sound plan, with the Lord’s help.

[Note: Vaticanus C reads, “by a salutary plan, with the Lord’s help.”]

In the month of July, in the tenth indiction.

[Note: This is the reading of the Tours, Saint Gatien, and Colbertine manuscripts.]

## LETTER XXXVI. TO EUSEBIUS, THE ABBOT

He rebukes him for pride, because he rejected the favor and communion restored to him by Bishop Maximianus. He gives him one hundred solidi.

Gregory to Abbot Eusebius.

Believe me, your Charity: I have been deeply saddened by your sadness, as though I myself had suffered an injury in your person. But afterward, when I learned that, even though our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Maximianus had restored his favor and communion, your Affection did not wish to receive communion from him, I understood that what had previously been done was also just.

The humility of God’s servants ought to appear in a time of affliction. Those who rise up against their superiors plainly show that they disdain being servants of God. What was done by him ought certainly not to have been done; yet it ought to have been received by you with complete humility. And again, when he restored his favor, you ought to have gone to him with thanksgiving.

Since you did not act in this way, I understand that we have a great need of tears.

[Note: The Vulgate editions read “still.”]

For it is not a great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored, since any secular person does this as well. Rather, we ought to be especially humble toward those from whom we suffer anything. For the Psalmist says: “See my humility before my enemies” (Psalm 9:14).

[Note: Saint Bernard, in his *Apology to Abbot William*, says: “Woe once, and woe again, to the proud poor.” And in Letter 42 to Henry of Sens: “I am amazed that certain abbots of monasteries in our order break this rule of humility through hateful contention, and, under a humble habit and tonsure—which is worse—are so proudly minded that, while they do not allow their subjects to go beyond a single little word of their commands, they themselves disdain to obey their own bishops. They strip churches so that they may be emancipated; they redeem themselves so that they may not obey. Christ did not act so,” and so forth. It is not my place to dwell longer on this hateful subject. Gussanville.]

What sort of life do we lead, that we are unwilling to be humble even toward our fathers?

Therefore, dearest son, I ask that all bitterness depart from your heart, lest perhaps the end be near and the ancient enemy, through the wickedness of discord, block the way to the kingdom of heaven.

Furthermore, we have caused one hundred solidi to be given to your Affection through the subdeacon Peter. I ask that you receive them without considering them an injury to yourself.

[Note: “I have turned every way in order to discover Saint Gregory’s intention, but it has not yet occurred to me. For who would believe that anyone would ask for, and consider an injury, the gift of one hundred gold coins?” Gussanville. Saint Gregory used a similar manner of speaking when he gave alms to persons holding some position of honor. See Indiction 3, Letter 31, and Indiction 6, Letter 19. The very humble pontiff was evidently afraid that, because of their sense of empty honor, they might be ashamed to be supported by alms or might disdain them as injurious to their dignity.]

## LETTER XXXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SQUILLACE

He appoints John bishop of Squillace on the condition that he return to the Church of Lissus if it should be liberated from the enemies; that he abstain from unlawful ordinations; and that he carry out the pastoral office entrusted to him worthily.

[Col. 0575A]

Gregory to John, bishop of Squillace.

[Note: Letter XXXVII [formerly 25]. Scyllaceum, which Gregory called Squillacium and which is commonly called Squillace, was formerly a city of the Bruttians and remains an episcopal city under the archbishop of Rhegium. It lies on the shore of the Ionian Sea, in further Calabria and the kingdom of Naples, between Locri and Consentia, and enjoys the title of a principality. We read in Gratian, *Causa* 25, question 2, chapter *Ita nos*, that it was once deprived of its episcopal see because of the repeated murder of bishops. Gussanville. Cassiodorus, Book XII, Letter 15, should be consulted concerning this city; it calls it the chief city of the Bruttians and describes its origin and location.]

The care of the pastoral office admonishes us to appoint proper priests over Churches that have been deprived of their pastors, priests who must govern the Lord’s flock with pastoral solicitude. Therefore, since the city of Lissus had been captured by enemies, we judged it necessary to appoint you, John, its bishop, as a cardinal priest in the Church of Squillace, so that you might fulfill, with a view to the future reward, the care of souls once undertaken.

Although you have been driven from your Church by the approaching enemy, you ought to govern another Church that is vacant of a shepherd. Do so, however, on the condition that, if that city should be liberated from the enemies and, with the Lord’s protection, restored to its former condition, you return to the Church in which you were previously ordained.

[Note: The better manuscripts read this, not “of Lissus,” as in earlier editions. Lissus, in Hierocles and Ptolemy, was a city on the coast of the province of Praevalitana in Illyricum, on the Adriatic Sea, now Alessio. Some, following Dionysius, *Roman Antiquities*, book I, think that the city of Lista rather than Lissus is intended. Holstenius maintains, however, that Lista never had a bishop. See his annotations on *Sacred Geography*, pp. 3, 16, and 124, and on Ortelius, p. 106.]

But if the aforesaid city remains oppressed by the continuous calamity of captivity, you are to remain in this Church, in which we have incardinated you.

We command you never to perform unlawful ordinations. Do not permit to enter the sacred orders a bigamist, a man who has not taken a virgin as his wife, one ignorant of letters, one maimed in any part of his body, a penitent, or anyone subject to any other disqualifying condition.

[Note: The printed editions add “or of the curia, or of anyone else.” The first two words are absent from the Vatican, Norman, Rhegian, and other manuscripts.]

If you find any such persons, do not dare to promote them.

Nor should you accept Africans indiscriminately, or unknown foreigners seeking ecclesiastical orders, on any account, because some Africans are Manichaeans and some have been rebaptized; while many foreigners, even though already established in the minor orders, have often been proved to claim a higher honor for themselves.

[Note: From this I infer that some persons were then admitted and promoted without letters of dismissal from their own bishop, since through such letters their faith and conduct would have been sufficiently established. Gussanville.]

We also admonish your Fraternity to watch carefully over the souls entrusted to you, and to attend more to the profit of souls than to the advantages of the present life. Let him be diligent in preserving and administering the Church’s possessions, so that, in every respect, when the Judge who is to come comes to judge, he may approve that you have worthily discharged the pastoral office entrusted to you.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He entrusts to him the visitation and care of the Church of Croton after the death of its bishop.

Gregory to John, bishop of Squillace.

The direct report of the death of that bishop has made the matter clear.

[Note: Letter XXXVIII [formerly 17]. The printed edition incorrectly reads, “The death of Paulinus of the Church of Turris,” and then, “of the bishop of that Church of Turris.” In three Vatican manuscripts, where this letter is more concise, the reading is “of the bishop of Croton,” and in several others, “of that bishop” alone. The same reading occurs in Vaticanus D, the Tours, Saint Gatien, Norman, Corbey, and other manuscripts, as well as in John the Deacon’s manuscripts, *Life of Saint Gregory*, book III, chapter 22. It is a formula by which a visitor was appointed for vacant Churches. The following letter nevertheless shows that the Church of Croton is intended here.]

Therefore we solemnly entrust to your Fraternity the task of visiting that deprived Church. You ought to carry it out in such a way that no one presumes to appropriate anything from the promotions of its clergy, its revenues, its furnishings, its ministries, or anything else belonging to the patrimony of that Church.

Your Fraternity will therefore hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and, through frequent exhortations, hasten to admonish its clergy and people, so that, setting aside factional zeal, they may with one and the same agreement seek to have placed over them a priest who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and who is in no way rejected by the venerable canons.

When he has been requested, let him come to us for consecration with the solemnity of a decree strengthened by the subscriptions of all and with a letter bearing the testimony of your Affection.

[Note: Some editions read “let him come to be consecrated.”]

We admonish your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be chosen from another Church, unless perhaps no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of that city in which you are performing the office of visitation—a situation we do not believe will occur.

Above all, take care that no layperson of any manner of life or merit presume to aspire to this office, lest you incur the danger of your own order, which God forbid.

[Note: In the edition of Baluze the letter ends here. In Vaticanus D and the manuscripts of John the Deacon, what follows concerning the monasteries is added. The printed editions agree with them. In the three other Vatican manuscripts—A, B, and C—the letter ends at the words “or ministries,” with “etc.” added.]

As for any monasteries established in that parish, we permit them to remain under your care and administration until a proper bishop has been ordained there, so that the vigilance of your solicitude may, with God’s help, respond through suitable action to their way of life.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO THE CLERGY, ORDER, AND PEOPLE OF CROTON

That they should obey John, the visiting bishop, and request a suitable priest for themselves.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at Croton.

[Note: Letter XXXIX [formerly 27]. “To John, the clergy, etc.” entered the editions by mistake. John is not mentioned in the Colbertine, Tellerian, Norman, Vatican, Rhegian, or other manuscripts, nor can the letter be thought to have been written to John, since Saint Gregory speaks of him in the third person.]

[Note: Croto or Croton, called Crotona by more recent writers and commonly Crotone, was formerly a city of the Bruttians in Magna Graecia, on the Ionian Sea. It was the city of the famous athlete Milo of Croton and is now in further Calabria, in the kingdom of Naples. It remains an episcopal city under the archbishop of Rhegium. Gussanville. Several manuscripts read “of Cotrona”; Reg. 3800 reads “of Ortoria.”]

Having learned of the death of your bishop, we took care solemnly to entrust the visitation of the deprived Church to our brother and fellow bishop John.

[Note: That is, John, bishop of Squillace, to whom the preceding letter was addressed.]

We commanded him not to permit anyone to usurp anything from the promotions of the clergy, the revenues, the furnishings, or the ministries. It is fitting that you obey his frequent exhortations, so that a priest may be sought for ecclesiastical office who in no respect deviates from the venerable canons.

[Note: The printed editions read: “It is fitting; and, setting aside disturbance, seek with one and the same agreement a priest to be set over you.” We follow Vaticanus D, Norman, and Rheims. In the three Vatican manuscripts A, B, and C, in the Royal manuscripts, in the Audegavense manuscript, and in most manuscripts, the words “permit anyone to usurp anything,” followed by “etc.,” conclude the letter. Thus those witnesses cannot establish the true reading. The printed editions also insert, “and who can be found worthy of so great a ministry,” which is absent from our manuscripts.]

When he has been requested, let him come to us to be ordained with the solemnity of a decree strengthened by the subscriptions of all and with a letter from the visitor accompanying him. Above all, take care that you do not presume to choose a layperson of any kind of life or merit.

[Note: On the distinction between request and election, see the *Extravagantes*, book I, titles 5 and 6. Honorius III explains the terms in the final chapter, *De postulatione praelatorum*: “Although,” he says, “the votes unanimously agreed to elect the bishop of Sutri as archbishop of your Church, since he was bound to his own Church and could not freely transfer himself without our permission, we judged, with the advice of our brothers, that the election made of him should be annulled as an attempt contrary to the canons, since he could not lawfully be elected but rather could be requested.” The question is one of terminology, unknown to the ancient Fathers. Gussanville.]

You should know that not only is such a person in no way to be promoted to the summit of the episcopate, but also that you cannot obtain pardon through any intercessions.

[Note: Through these words Saint Gregory shows how strongly he wished to resist the promotion of a layman to the episcopal summit without prior training in the clerical service and without several years of experience. He even declares that he would grant no indulgence to anyone who ambitiously aspired to that dignity, but would instead proceed against him with the full rigor of the law and the canons. Gussanville.]

Know without doubt that all among you who are found to have aspired from the lay state are to be excluded from office and communion.

## LETTER XL. TO JOHN, BISHOP

That he should judge the case of Viulandus against Gravinianus without delay.

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

To settle the disputes of litigants by a speedy judgment is plainly both consistent with equity and characteristic of strength. Since, therefore, Viulandus, the bearer of this letter, appeals to your judgment concerning the deacon Gravinianus, against whom he says he has a case, let your Fraternity summon the deacon before your tribunal. Removing all delay, investigate the truth of the case carefully, and compel both parties in every way to observe and fulfill whatever the order of justice dictates and whatever has been determined by your sentence.

## LETTER XLI. TO CASTORIUS, THE BISHOP

That neither Bishop Castorius nor his successors, after the death of the abbot of Ariminum, should inventory or administer the monastery’s property; that they should not appoint another abbot instead of the one requested by the community; and that they should not celebrate public Masses in the monastery.

[Col. 0578B]

Gregory to Castorius, bishop of Ariminum.

The text of the petition submitted to us reports what tearful prayers Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Thomas, established in the city of Ariminum, poured out before us.

[Note: Letter XLI [formerly 28]. This is the reading of the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts. The printed editions instead read “and in the practices of monastic discipline.”]

For this reason we exhort your Fraternity that, when the abbot of that monastery dies, your Church should in no way interfere in inventorying or administering the property of that monastery, whether already acquired or yet to be acquired.

As abbot of that monastery, we wish you to appoint not someone else but the man whom the entire community, by common agreement, requests as worthy in character and suitable for monastic discipline.

We absolutely forbid public Masses to be celebrated there by the bishop, lest in the retreats of God’s servants any opportunity be given for popular gatherings, and lest, through this, simpler souls—God forbid—often be drawn into scandal by the more frequent entrance of women.

[Note: The printed editions read “draws”; and they add that more frequent entry by women, or of women, should be prevented.]

We establish that this page of our writing is to be kept firm and inviolate by you and by the bishops appointed after you for all future time, so that your Church may, with the Lord’s help, be content with its own rights alone, and that this monastery, serving no one thereafter except the general or canonical jurisdiction, may, with all vexations and burdens removed, complete the divine work with the fullest devotion of spirit.

[Note: Paulus the Deacon’s collection reads: “Given on the sixth day of June, in the fourteenth indiction.” The old Colbertine manuscript has: “Given on the day …, in the thirteenth indiction.” The printed editions read: “In the month of July, in the thirteenth indiction.” We suspect these chronological notices are false, although the reason has been explained elsewhere. Since this letter is transmitted in a substantially different form in the Tours, Saint Gatien, and Royal manuscripts from that found in the printed editions, and since a charter concerning the privileges of monasteries is attached to it, we have arranged for both ancient documents to be published. It appears in Baronius under the title of a constitution concerning the exemption or exception of monks.]

See Letter 12 above.

Gregory to Castorius, bishop of Ariminum.

The text of the petition submitted to us reports what tearful prayers Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Thomas, established in the city of Ariminum, poured out before us.

For, according to his report, we have learned that in many monasteries monks have suffered numerous acts of prejudice and many burdens at the hands of bishops. It is therefore necessary that your Fraternity’s provision arrange their future peace through a salutary ordinance, so that those living in these monasteries in the service of God may, with His grace assisting them, persevere with a free mind.

But lest anyone presume to inflict any trouble upon the monks because of that custom which rather ought to be corrected, it is necessary that the provisions which we have taken care to enumerate below be guarded by the zealous attention of the bishops in such a way that they cannot thereafter become an occasion for disturbance.

[Note: This is presented as a title in larger type.]

## On the Privileges of Monasteries
Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose place we preside over this Roman Church, we forbid and prohibit that any bishop or secular person henceforth presume, in any manner, to raise pretexts, devise frauds, or make any incursions concerning the revenues, possessions, or charters of monasteries, or concerning the cells or estates belonging to them. But if some dispute should happen to arise between land coming into the possession of their churches and monasteries, and it cannot be settled peacefully, let it be brought to an end without deliberate delay before chosen abbots and other God-fearing Fathers, with the holy Gospels placed between the parties.

When the abbot of any community dies, no outsider shall be appointed, but only someone from that same community whom the united society of the brothers has freely chosen for itself; and whoever is elected shall be appointed without fraud or any form of bribery. If they cannot find a suitable person among themselves, let them carefully choose someone from another monastery in the same way to be appointed. Nor, once an abbot has been established, shall any person be placed over him on any pretext, unless—God forbid—there are evident crimes of the sort which the sacred canons prescribe should be punished.

It must likewise be carefully observed that, against the abbot’s will, monks may not be taken from there to govern other monasteries, to receive sacred orders, or to undertake clerical office. We altogether forbid bishops to make ecclesiastical inventories of the possessions or of the monastery. But if circumstances require it, let the abbot of the place, together with other abbots, draw up an account of the property found, and let the matter be settled by their counsel or judgment. At the death of an abbot, moreover, let the bishop in no way interfere in listing, safeguarding, or administering the monastery’s possessions, whether acquired, donated, or still to be acquired.

[Note: The same author forbids this in Book VIII, Letter 4, and Book X, Letter 3. He confirms the prohibition on the basis of custom in Book VI, Letter 46; here, however, he discloses the genuine reason: that no opportunity for a popular gathering should be provided in the retreats and refuges of the servants of God, and so forth. He readily permits Masses to be celebrated in the monastery by priests with the bishop’s permission; but he takes the greatest care that the bishop himself should not celebrate public Masses there, for the two reasons clearly expressed in the body of the letter. See Book III, Letter 63; Book V, Letter 38; Book VI, Letter 46.]

We also altogether prohibit him from celebrating public Masses in the monastery, lest any opportunity for a popular assembly be provided in the retreats and refuges of the servants of God, or a new entry be made by women, which is entirely harmful to their souls. Nor may he dare to place a cathedra there, or exercise any authority to command, or issue any order, however slight, unless he has been asked to do so by the abbot of the place, so that the monks may always remain under the authority of their own abbots. Nor shall anyone retain a monk in any church, or advance him to any office, without a testimonial or permission from those abbots.

We therefore decree that this page of our writings shall be preserved by all bishops, firm and inviolate for all time to come, so that they may be content, with the Lord’s help, solely with the rights belonging to their own Church, and that monasteries in no way be subjected to ecclesiastical exactions, forced services, or any secular obligations; nor serve any canonical rights, [Note: The following text is corrupt.] but, freed from harassment and every burden, may carry out the divine work with the fullest devotion of spirit. (See Letter 15, Book VIII.)

## LETTER XLII. TO LUMINOSUS, THE ABBOT

He writes that all burdens have been removed from his monastery, so that the divine work may be carried out there with complete tranquility and devotion.

[Col. 0580C]

Gregory to Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saint [Note: Letter XLII.—In Teller’s manuscript, “of Saint Andrew.”] Thomas at Ariminum.

We have willingly received your petition and that of your community, adapting our response to your requests in accordance with the statutes of the Fathers and the form of law. Indeed, through the letter sent by our command to our brother and fellow bishop Castorius, and to his successors, we have entirely removed from him and from your monastery every possibility of inflicting injury, so that henceforth you may neither be subject to his harassment, nor have the monastery’s possessions inventoried, nor be required to receive a public procession there. We have left him only this jurisdiction: that, in place of a deceased abbot, he should appoint another whom the common consent of the community has chosen as worthy.

Now that these matters have been settled, [Col. 0580D] devote yourselves to the work of God, 605 and apply yourselves constantly to prayer, lest it appear that you have sought security of mind in prayer while, God forbid, you have improperly evaded episcopal discipline.

## LETTER XLIII. TO FELIX, THE BISHOP

He entrusts him with the visitation of three vacant churches.

[Col. 0581A]

Gregory to Felix, bishop [Note: Letter XLIII [elsewhere 29].—In Vatican manuscripts A and B: “To Felix, bishop of Acropolis, visitor of the province of Lucania.” In Corbie: “To Felix, priest and visitor,” and so forth.] of Acropolis [Note: Formerly an episcopal city in Lucania, now a town of obscure name, commonly called Agropoli, situated in the Gulf of Salerno. See H. H. Hosten’s notes on *Ancient Italy*, p. 286. GUSSANV.] .

Since the Churches of Velia [Note: Velia, formerly an episcopal city of Lucania on the coast of the Tyrrhenian Sea, between Paestum and Buxentum, where Castel’ a Mare della Bruca now stands. GUSSANV.] (Gratian 12, q. 1, c. 14), Buxentum [Note: Buxentum or Buxentium, now Policastro, a city of Italy that remains episcopal, under the archbishop of Salerno in Lucania, now called the Citerior Principality in the Kingdom of Naples. GUSSANV.], and Blandana [Note: Blanda, formerly a city of Lucania. Cluverius proves this in *Ancient Italy*, Book IV, p. 1263; Holstenius supports him, p. 22, and says that it is now called Porto di Sapri. GUSSANV.], which are situated near you, are known to be without the governance of a priest, we therefore solemnly entrust their visitation to your Fraternity. Above all, we admonish you that wherever clergy, deacons, or religious persons belonging to the aforesaid Churches or to their dioceses are found, you must make every effort to ensure strictly and canonically that they live [Note: In recent Vulgate editions: “you shall strive to admonish them in every way.” “To admonish” has been added, contrary to the Vatican manuscripts and others.] in every respect as they should. They must have no unrestricted license to exceed the bounds in any matter; rather, through your guidance and oversight, let them remain blameless in the manner of life and habit in which they now live [Col. 0581B] —you should know that, if anything otherwise occurs, it will in every way be charged to your negligence.

If you foresee that priests or deacons are to be ordained in any of the Churches, and if they are persons whom the canonical rules do not in any way reject on account of their morals or quality of life, you shall have full authority to ordain them [Note: Some manuscripts read “you shall provide,” as do the Norman manuscripts and others.]. Carefully investigate where the liturgical vessels and other furnishings of those Churches are stored. When you have found them, hasten to report them to us, so that, once we know what should be done, we may arrange it with the Lord’s help.

## LETTER XLIV. TO LUCILLUS, THE BISHOP

He orders him to compel his clergy to pay without delay the rent owed for the African Church lands they held.

Gregory to Lucillus, bishop [Note: Letter XLIV [elsewhere 30].—He was later deposed for crimes, according to Book IX, Letter 63, indiction 2, and Trajan was appointed in his place, according to Book X, Letter 1. Rocchus Pirrus, in his *Melitense Notice*, p. 592, thinks that he is the man called Lucidus in the title of Book XIII, Letter 18; but I do not see how this can agree with the statements above, since he had already long been deposed. Moreover, all manuscripts, both written and printed, read *Lucido*, and none reads *Lucillo*. Finally, the same title lists Trajan himself, who had succeeded him. GUSSANV.] of Melita [Note: In Italian, Malta, an island in the Mediterranean Sea between Africa and Sicily, sixty miles from Cape Pachynus; [Col. 0582C] under the dominion of the Knights of Saint John of Jerusalem, where an episcopal see still exists under the archbishop of Palermo. GUSSANV.].

It is very much in keeping with the purpose of our office to urge those subject to us to keep faith in agreements, so that, while they are seized by an inconsiderate desire for gain, they do not turn a peaceful settlement into a quarrel. Thus the report has reached us from your Fraternity that your clergy, who hold lands belonging to the African Church, disdain to pay the rent on those possessions [Note: At the Council of Chalcedon, canon 3, it was forbidden for clergy to be tenants of other people’s property. See Carthage, canon 16; Arles II, canon 14; and Vernum, canon 16. Saint Jerome says most aptly in Letter 2 to Nepotian: “How can clergy be stewards and administrators of public houses and estates, when they are commanded to despise their own?” Here, it seems, a dispensation was granted to them for legitimate reasons. Not, as some maintain, did Innocent III, in chapter *Vestra* on leases, approve of Church tithes being leased only to clergy; rather, he allowed them to be leased to anyone, contrary to what the bishops had decreed. Saint Paulinus, in the fifth poem on the birth of Saint Felix, relates that this martyr leased three lean *iugera* of farmland, but did not hold them as his own property, cultivating them with his own hands and without a servant. He seems to have violated the wording, not the meaning, of the canons. GUSSANV.]. If this is true, and these facts have been brought to your attention, your negligence has nourished their fault. For this reason we admonish you by this present letter not to allow those same clerics any delay or excuse in paying the rent. But if they put off keeping faith out of regard for honesty, compel them through your discipline to fulfill what reason requires. For if a complaint about this matter reaches us again, we shall begin to form a different opinion of you, and we shall punish them as they deserve.

## LETTER XLV. TO BENENATUS, THE BISHOP

He unites the Churches of Cumae and Misenum and appoints Benenatus bishop of both.

Gregory to Benenatus, the bishop.

Both the character of the times (Gratian 16, q. [.....], c. 48) and the proximity of the places invite us to unite the Churches of Cumae and Misenum, since they are separated from one another by no great distance, and, because of sins, there is not such a large population that each should have its own priest, as was formerly the case. Since, therefore, the priest of the fortress of Cumae has completed the course of this life, know that by this document of our authority we have united both Churches and entrusted them to you, and know that you are the proper bishop of both Churches.

Whatever you judge should be arranged and administered concerning their patrimony, or the ordination or promotion of the clergy, in accordance with the statutes of the canons, you shall have, as their actual priest, free authority to do by the consent and permission of our authority. Live wherever you perceive it to be more convenient and beneficial, provided that you administer with vigilant and prudent care the other Church, from which you are at present physically absent [Note: Recent editions changed the text to: “the Church at which you are not physically present.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.], so that the divine mysteries may there be solemnly celebrated with the Lord’s help [Note: Vatican A, the Norman manuscripts, and some others read “the ministries.”].

607 [Note: It is generally in the interest of ecclesiastical administration that parishes should, through a new arrangement, be enlarged, reduced, divided among several, or several brought together into one. The synods first assumed this authority, then the supreme pontiffs, and finally individual bishops, each in his own diocese. I identify one reason for these changes: the salvation of the people. Something similar occurs with bishops who abandon their former see and move to another; concerning them, see the Council of Sardica, canons 1 and 2; Antioch, canons 3 and 21; Chalcedon, canon 5; and many canons cited in Gratian 7, q. 1. GUSSANV. Moreover, Ughellus repeatedly observes in *Sacred Italy* that the union of the Churches of Misenum and Cumae did not last long. On the union of benefices, see above, Book I, Letter 8.]

Your Fraternity should therefore always watch over exhortation and the salvation of souls with a care proportionately greater, recognizing that you have taken upon yourself the burdens of governing united Churches.

## LETTER XLVI. TO JOHN, THE BISHOP

He explains that he did not answer his letters because of illness. He urges him to incline the Roman official toward peace with Ariulph. He says that he will write to the emperors about compelling the schismatic bishops of Istria to return to unity. One who has already been ordained must not be ordained again. He instructs him to warn the Exarch about the danger facing the city of Naples. Mercy should first be shown to the faithful and then to the enemies of the Church. He says that he has been consoled by the correction of Bishop Natalis. He demands an accounting from Bishop Malchus, formerly administrator of the patrimony.

[Col. 0583B]

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

Do not attribute the fact that I did not answer the many letters of Your Blessedness to my sluggishness, but to my illness, because, through my sins, at the time when Ariulph, coming to the city of Rome, killed some and mutilated others [Note: Letter XLVI [elsewhere 32].—A Beneventan duke after Faroaldus. See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 17. Many copies incorrectly read “Arnulphus.” GUSSANV. In the Norman manuscript, “Arinulfus”; in Vatican A, “Agilulfus.”], I was so afflicted with grief [Col. 0584A] that I fell into a colic attack [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “into the distress of colic.”]. I was greatly surprised that the very familiar concern of Your Holiness was of no help to this city or to my necessities. But as your letters circulated, I realized that you were indeed acting diligently, yet had no one before whom you could act [Note: The manuscripts differ here, but the phrase “yet not having anyone before whom you could act” is absent from the Norman manuscript. Vatican manuscripts read “with whom you might act,” “with whom he might act,” or “with whom you might act”; Vatican D reads, “you have carefully undertaken to act and are without blame.” “Therefore through my sins,” and so forth. The Norman manuscript agrees.]. I therefore attribute this to my sins, because the man who is now in office both pretends not to fight against our enemies [Note: Printed editions read “to resist,” contrary to the Vatican manuscripts and others.] and prevents us from making peace. Even if he now wished to make peace, however, we could not do so at all, because Ariulph, having the army of Authari and Nordulf, demands that their *precaria* be given to him [Note: The word is used in different ways by different authors. According to its etymology, it means something granted for use to one who asks for it, for as long as the grantor permits. Thus one speaks of *precarium* power, a *precaria* soul, *precarium* aid, a *precarium* right, and a *precarius* profit. See the Digest, Book LXIII, title 26, where many provisions are made concerning *precarium*. In canon law, however, a *precaria* is considered a contract in which, for property donated to a Church, the Church returns to the donor double or triple its value for use; this is found in Gratian, cause 10, question 2, chapter 4, from the Council of Meaux of 845, canon 22. It is therefore not revoked at the grantor’s pleasure but ends with the recipient’s death, unless the *precaria* was made unreasonably. See also the *Decretals*, Book III, title 14, concerning *precariae* renewed every five years. At Agde and Epaon, we find *precatoriae* in place of *precariae*. The Council of Leptines, canon 2, mentions a *precaria*, but obscures the matter. GUSSANV. Learnedly stated, but here *precarium* seems to mean the same as a military *roga*, mentioned shortly afterward and also in Book V, Letter 30; Book IX, Letter 124; and Book XII, Letter 5, unless by it you understand money promised by Ariulph to those armies.], so that he may deign to discuss some matter of peace with us.

Concerning the case of the bishops of Istria [Note: The schismatics on account of the Three Chapters, a matter sufficiently discussed in the *Life of Saint Gregory*.], I had already found everything to be as Your Fraternity wrote to me, in the orders that came to me from the most devout rulers [Col. 0584B], in such a way that for the time being I should suspend coercion against them. I greatly rejoice in your zeal and ardor on account of what you have written, and I acknowledge that I have become your debtor in many ways. Nevertheless, know that I shall not cease to write back to the most serene lords about this same matter, with the greatest zeal and freedom. But the anger of the aforementioned most excellent man Romanus the Patrician ought not to trouble you, because, inasmuch as we precede him in rank and office, so much more ought we patiently and seriously to tolerate whatever faults he may have.

If there is ever any opportunity of obtaining something from him, let Your Fraternity act upon him so that we may make peace with Ariulph, even if we can achieve only a little by it, because the Roman military force has been taken away [Note: In Audoinus and some other manuscripts, “has been taken away,” followed by the printed editions. The Vatican manuscripts to which we adhere read this word; it has already been discussed in Book III of the *Moralia*, section 22. See also Book XXV, section 3.] , as he himself knows. The Theodosian soldiers [Note: Almost all manuscripts read this; the Vulgate editions read “the Theodosiani.” They were soldiers of the legion that had received its name from Theodosius, the son of the emperor Maurice.], however, who remained here, since they do not receive their *roga* [Note: *Roga* (ῥόγα): a gift, honorarium, or stipend. *Rogatores* (ῥογάτορες): salaried men; *rogeuein* (ῥογεύειν): to serve for pay. Hence *erogare*, *erogatores*, and *erogatorii*. *Rogalia* are days on which *rogae* were distributed. Thus Landulf the Wise, concerning Tiberius II: “He took Anastasia as his wife … and distributed a great *roga*,” that is, he scattered a great deal of money. The word frequently occurs among Latin and Greek writers of the Middle Ages. Xylander, in his notes on Cedrenus, interprets ῥόγαν as soldiers’ pay, or gifts of the emperors presented on the Kalends of January, on the birthdays of rulers, and on the anniversaries of royal cities. GUSSANV. Among sacred writers, *roga* is also used for a gift distributed to those serving in the Church. Anastasius the Librarian, concerning Agatho: “He distributed a *roga* to all the clergy and for the lamps,” and so forth. In the glossary of Isidore, revised by Jan Georg Graevius, *roga* is an alms.], scarcely attend even to guarding the walls; and if the city, abandoned by everyone, has no peace, how will it survive?

Furthermore, concerning the girl about whom you wrote to us, who was redeemed from captivity, Your Holiness should know that an unknown person cannot easily be investigated, although you say that we ought to have sought to learn from what origin she came. But as for your statement that someone who has already been ordained should be ordained again [Note: It is truly ridiculous to think that someone should be ordained again solely because he came to the priesthood with a minor fault, as is explained below. Yet neither in the age of Gregory the Great nor for six hundred years afterward was it ridiculous to question ordinations conferred or received from heretics and schismatics, or even from Catholics contrary to the canons. At the First Council of Constantinople, canon 4, the ordination of Maximus as bishop of Constantinople was declared null, and the ordinations he had performed were considered invalid, because he had bribed bishops to ordain him. The only fault in the ordination of Pope Constantine was that, having been elected from the laity, he had not observed the canonical intervals between orders; nevertheless, he was deposed in a Roman council attended by twelve bishops selected from Gaul. Concerning the bishops, priests, and deacons whom Constantine himself had consecrated, the same council promulgated that, if any of those bishops had previously been a priest or deacon, he should return to his former rank; and if they were acceptable to the people of their city, then, after a new decree of election, they should come in the customary manner, with clergy and people, to the apostolic see and receive consecration by the blessing of Pope Stephen, Constantine’s successor. Lucius III received schismatics through repeated ordination. Famous controversies were seriously and extensively debated concerning those ordained by Ebbo, bishop of Reims, and by Pope Formosus. See Morinus, *On Sacred Orders*, Part III, Exercise 5; Peter Damian, his entire sixth opuscle, entitled *Gratissimus*; Peter Lombard, distinction 25; and Gratian, 1 q. 1.], this is extremely ridiculous and foreign to the judgment of your intelligence—unless the example brought forward concerns a case about which the man alleged to have done such a thing must also be judged. Let such thinking be far from Your Fraternity (Gratian, distinction 68, chapter 1). For just as one who has been baptized once must not be baptized again, so one who has once been consecrated cannot be consecrated again in the same order. But if someone has perhaps come to the priesthood with a minor fault, penance should be imposed for the fault, while the order itself must nevertheless be preserved.

Concerning the city of Naples, with the most excellent Exarch pressing the matter urgently, we inform you that Arigis [Note: He is called Arigis by Paul the Deacon; in the *Chronicle of the Dukes of Benevento and Princes of Salerno*, Archis; in the chronicle of an anonymous monk, Arichis. He was the second duke of Benevento, successor of Zotto, and held office for fifty years. As for *se fecit*, it means “he went” or “departed.” *Facio* and *facesso* are equivalent; hence *facessere*, “to depart.” Donatus, commenting on Terence’s *Phormio* at the phrase “hinc haec facessat,” explains it as “let her make herself depart,” that is, “let her go away”; similarly, “hinc se faciat” means “let him go from here,” “huc accedat” means “let him come here,” while “haec hinc facessat” means “let her proceed” or “let her go elsewhere.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book V: “Psyche, invited by the charm of such places, approached nearer and, somewhat more confidently, made herself inside the threshold.” This is taken from Salmasius on Tertullian’s *Pallium*, chapter 3, concerning the passage “where wealthy Ammon from Libya makes for him,” which Rigaltius emended as: “where wealthy Ammon from Libya pastures sheep beside the Nile.” He says that this conjecture will be demonstrated in a new edition of Tertullian which he is preparing shortly. GUSSANV.] has joined Ariulph, as we have learned, has acted against the interests of the state, and is lying in wait for that city. Unless a commander is sent there quickly, it must already be regarded as utterly lost.

As for what you say, that alms should be sent to the city of the schismatic Severus after it has been burned, Your Fraternity thinks this because you do not know what rewards she sends to the palace against us. Even if she sent nothing, however, we ought to consider that mercy must first be shown to the faithful and afterward to the enemies of the Church. [Col. 0586A] The city of Fanum is nearby [Note: There are so many Italian cities of this name that it is difficult to determine which one is meant here. The principal one is Fanum Fortunae. Fanum, without qualification, was in Umbria and was episcopal.], and many captives have been taken there. Last year I wished to send assistance to it, but I did not dare to do so through the midst of the enemy.

It therefore seems to me that you should send Abbot Claudius there with a certain amount of money, so that he may redeem any free persons whom he finds held there in servitude for a price, or any who are still captives. As for the amount of money to be sent, let it be certain to you that whatever you decide is agreeable to me. But if you are dealing with the excellent man Romanus the Patrician so that we ought to make peace with Ariulph, I am prepared to send another person to you, with whom arrangements concerning the price may be made more effectively [Note: More safely and advantageously may the matter be settled concerning the price to be paid, the amount of money, and the conditions under which it is to be paid. GUSSANV.].

I was greatly saddened concerning our brother and fellow bishop Natalis, because I had learned that he had displayed a certain arrogance. But because he corrected his conduct himself, he consoled my grief by overcoming himself. For this reason admonish our brother and fellow bishop Malchus on my behalf, so that, before he comes to us, he may render his accounts [Note: In French, “that he render his accounts.” Gregory uses this expression also in Letter 22, indiction 11. GUSSANV.] and only then depart elsewhere, if necessary. And if we discover that his actions have been good, it may perhaps be necessary for us to restore to him the patrimony that he held.

## LETTER XLVII. TO DOMINICUS, THE BISHOP

A congratulatory letter on his ordination, in which the delay is compensated by extraordinary charity. He praises charity as the mother of virtues and urges that it be held with unwavering stability. Just as he defends the privileges of the Roman Church, so he preserves the rights of every individual Church.

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop [Note: Letter XLVII [elsewhere 39].—Carthage, a once exceedingly famous city of Africa [Col. 0587D], was the chief city of the proconsular province, and its bishops were the primates of all Africa, since the primacy of the other provinces was attached to no other city but was granted to the senior or most ancient bishop of the province.] of Carthage.

We received, with the greatest joy, the letters of Your Fraternity, delivered to us rather late by Donatus and Quodvultdeus, our most reverend brothers and fellow bishops, and also by Victor the deacon and Agisegius the notary. Although we thought that we had suffered a loss through the delay, we nevertheless found in it a gain of more abundant charity, since the delay of time appears not to have interrupted but to have nourished the affection which, through the Lord’s mercy, we recognize to have been firmly established in you through regard for the priesthood, the practice of reading, and the maturity of your age. It would not flow so abundantly from you if your minds did not contain many rich and overflowing veins.

Let us therefore, most holy brother, hold this mother and guardian of the virtues with unwavering stability. Let no deceitful tongues diminish it in us; let none of the ancient enemy’s snares corrupt it. For it joins what is divided and preserves what is joined. It raises the humble without swelling them with pride. It brings down the elevated without casting them into despair. Through it, the unity of the universal Church, which is the bond of Christ’s body, rejoices in the equality of minds among its individual members, even though there is diversity among the members. Through it, those same members leap for joy in another’s happiness even when afflicted in themselves, and waste away in another’s sorrow even when joyful in themselves.

For, as the teacher of the nations bears witness, when one member suffers, the other members suffer with it, and when one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. I have no doubt that you groan over our distress, just as we are entirely certain that you rejoice in your peace [Note: Vatican C reads “over our persecution.”].

The joy your Fraternity expresses at our ordination displays toward me the affection of a completely sincere charity. Yet, when I consider this office, I confess that the force of grief pierces my heart. The burden of the priesthood is heavy. A priest must first live as an example to others, and then ensure that his mind is not exalted by the examples he displays. He must always think of the ministry of preaching, considering with the greatest fear that the Lord, when he was about to depart to receive the kingdom and was entrusting talents to his servants, said: “Conduct business until I come” (Luke 19:13).

We truly conduct that business if, by living and speaking, we gain the souls of our neighbors; if, by preaching the joys of the heavenly kingdom, we strengthen the weak in divine love; if, by proclaiming the punishments of Gehenna with dreadful force, we bend the obstinate and proud; if we spare no one against the truth; and if, devoted to heavenly friendships, we do not fear human enmities. The Psalmist understood that in doing this he had offered himself to God as a kind of sacrifice when he said: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God, and do I not waste away over your enemies? With perfect hatred I hate them; they have become enemies to me” (Psalm 138:21).

But I dread the burden of my weakness in this matter, and I see that the master of the household, having received the kingdom, will return to demand an account from us. With what state of mind can I endure him, when from the business of winning souls entrusted to me I bring back either no profit or almost none? Therefore, dearest brother, help me by your prayer, and the things you see me fearing, weigh daily in yourself with the fear of prudent vigilance. Through the bond of charity, what I say about myself is also yours, and what I desire you to do is also mine.

As for ecclesiastical privileges [Note: Saint Gregory neither rejects privileges universally nor grants them indiscriminately; he proceeds along the safer middle path. Those things are unjust which disturb natural law, divine law, canon law, or the public welfare. Those things are just which do not so much dissolve the law as supplement and assist it, while justice is preserved and equity advises and compels. Thus privileges are provided not so much for the privileged persons themselves as for the Church and the salvation of the faithful, with equal concern for the common good. If privileges are supported by such considerations, I shall uphold them, and the canons of Chalcedon 4 and 8 will not stand in their way. GUSSANV.], about which Your Fraternity writes, let it hold this without hesitation: just as we defend our own rights, so we preserve the rights of each and every Church. I grant no one more than he deserves, even when favor is present, nor, when ambition urges it, do I take away from anyone what belongs to him by right. I desire to honor my brothers in every respect, and I strive to support each one with honor, provided that there is nothing which one can lawfully oppose to another.

I rejoice greatly in the conduct of your representatives. Through them it has been shown to me how much you love me, since you have sent me chosen brothers and sons. [Note: In the Tours manuscript and Saint-Gatien: “Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, indiction 10.” Some copies incorrectly read “the day before the Kalends of March.”] Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the tenth indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 1.)

## LETTER XLVIII. TO COLUMBUS, THE BISHOP

Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Pudentiana, is to be deposed by a council if, corrupted by money, he allowed a Donatist bishop to be made in his city. Certain other private matters are to be settled privately. He laments the spread of the Donatist heresy and kindles pastoral zeal so that Catholics may not be allowed to defect to it.

[Col. 0588C]

Gregory to Columbus, the bishop [Note: Letter XLVIII [elsewhere 33].—The Vulgate editions add “of Numidia,” which is absent from the four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, and others.].

It is known, dearest brother in Christ, that the ancient enemy, who by crafty persuasion first cast the human race from the delights of paradise into this wretched life [Note: Vatican B: “from the paradise of delights.”], and already then inflicted upon the human race the punishment of mortality, now attempts by the same craft to infect the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep with transferred poisons, so that he may more easily seize the flock and rightfully claim it for his own power. But we who, although unworthy, have undertaken to govern the apostolic see in the place of Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 0588D], are compelled by the very office of the pontificate to oppose the common enemy with whatever efforts we can.

Accordingly, Constantius and Mustellus, the bearers of the present petition, made their representations to us and assert [Col. 0589A] [Note: Pudentiana was a city of Numidia, about which nothing is found among the ancient geographers.
