In the Carthaginian Conference, chapter 201, Cresconius, bishop of Pudentiana, is mentioned on Donatus’s side, together with Memmianus, the Catholic. In the Carthaginian Calendar, extracted from ancient parchment manuscripts of the monastery of Cluny, one reads: “3 Kalends of May, martyr Pudentius.” Gregory seems to have remembered a church built in honor of this martyr.]—they are deacons of the Church of Pudentiana, situated in the province of Numidia—that Maximian, bishop of that same Church, permitted a Donatist bishop to be made in the place where he resides, having been corrupted by a bribe from the Donatists [Note: Vatican A: “without lawful permission,”] although, even if earlier custom had permitted this, the Catholic faith forbade it to remain and continue.

For this reason, therefore, we have necessarily decided by the present letter to exhort your Fraternity [612], so that, when Hilary our chartularius comes to you [Note: See Book I, Letter 84. In the printed editions it reads “Hilary.”], after a universal council of the bishops has been assembled [Note: He means the provincial council, namely, of the whole of Numidia. GUSSANV.], with the terror of the coming judgment kept before their eyes, this case may be investigated with careful and diligent inquiry. And if this charge is proved against the aforesaid bishop by suitable documents from the present petitioners, let him by every means be degraded from the dignity and office that he holds [Note: He indicates deposition, not, I think, ceremonial degradation, whose form is prescribed by the Roman Pontifical. On degradation, see the canonists under “Penalties,” and Gerson, *On the Removability of the Pope*, consideration 15.], so that he may return to the gains of repentance through acknowledgment of his offense [Col. 0589B], and so that the others may not presume to attempt such things.

For it is just that the man who, as is reported, sold our Lord Jesus Christ to a heretic, having accepted money [Note: [Col. 0589D] One is said to sell Christ for money when, corrupted by a bribe, he permits someone to become a bishop. Let the inventions of recent writers concerning simony cease—by which they seem to cleanse it for themselves through the intervening words “price,” “reward,” “motive,” and “equivalence.” See Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 3 on the Acts of the Apostles*, chapter 1. The Greek reads: *Ποίῳ γὰρ συνειδότι ἂν γένῃ, σπουδάσας ἢ διὰ σαυτοῦ, ἢ [Col. 0590C] δι` ἑτέρου, ποίοις ὀφθαλμοῖς ἀντιβλέψῃς ἐκείνῳ τῷ συνεργήσαντι; τί ἕξεις ἀπολογήσασθαι*—“What sort of conscience will you have, after contriving it either by yourself or through another? With what eyes will you face the one who assisted you? What defense will you have to offer?” That is: “Whom will you approach as one privy to it, if you have arranged it either through yourself or through another? With what eyes will you look upon the one who helped you? What will you have to say in your defense?” Nicholas Clemangius also treats this question of simony at length in his work *On Simoniacal Prelates*, as does Saint Peter Damian in the book he calls *Gratissimus*, which nevertheless must be read cautiously. GUSSANV.], be removed from handling the mysteries of his most holy body and blood.

But if, apart from this crime, some dispute concerning losses or private affairs is being pursued between them, as the petition of the deacons themselves contains, let your Fraternity, together with our aforesaid chartularius, investigate it after a proper examination [Note: The printed editions have “by private judgment,” a reading not found in manuscripts of the best quality], and let it be decided between both parties as justice proceeds [Note: An old edition reads “with justice preceding.” The manuscripts do not support this.].

Moreover, from the representation of the present petitioners we have learned that the Donatist heresy is daily spreading because of our sins, and that very many, once permission has been granted for a price, are being baptized again by the Donatists after Catholic baptism [Col. 0589C]. How serious this is, brother, we must weigh with the full attention of our minds. Behold, the wolf now tears the Lord’s flock apart not secretly at night, but in broad daylight; we see him raging amid the slaughter of the sheep, and we oppose him with no concern and no arrows of words. What fruits, then, shall we display to the Lord from the flock that has been multiplied, if we idly watch the very flock that we undertook to feed being devoured by the beast?

Let us therefore strive to set our hearts aflame in imitation of earthly shepherds [Col. 0590A], who, bound by rain and frost, often spend winter nights wholly awake lest even one sheep—and perhaps a valuable one—perish. If a predator has bitten it with its ravenous mouth, with what effort they labor, with what burning anguish of heart they breathe, into what cries they leap, driven by distress, to rescue the captured animal, lest the Lord of the flock demand from them whatever they have lost through negligence!

Let us therefore keep watch lest anything perish; and if something should perhaps be captured, let us bring it back to the Lord’s flock by the words of divine utterance, so that he who is the Shepherd of shepherds may mercifully deem us, by his judgment, to have kept watch over his fold.

You must also attend carefully to this: if the same bishop has brought any lawful complaint against the bearers of the present letter, it must be investigated with meticulous inquiry [Col. 0590B]; and if they too perhaps deserve to be punished justly for their fault, we by no means judge that they should be spared because they have wearied themselves by coming to us [613] [Note: So read in four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Tours, Corbie, Reims, and others, followed by the old editions. In the recent editions the words “because they have wearied themselves by coming to us” are omitted.].

[Note: So Tours and Saint Gatien. In the manuscripts used by the Roman editors, this date belongs to the following letter, to Januarius.]

In the month of August, in the tenth indiction.

## LETTER XLIX. TO JANUARIUS, ARCHBISHOP

After hearing complaints about Bishop Januarius, he sends John the notary to compel the parties to appear for judgment and to execute whatever has been judged. He chiefly rebukes Januarius because he excommunicated Isidore for no reason except his own injury.

Gregory to Januarius [Note: LETTER XLIX [formerly 34].—Thus in the English manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and some Vatican manuscripts. In others: “to John, bishop.” This is especially so in Vatican A and B, where the following is added as the letter’s summary: “Here he commands that a bishop must never dare to excommunicate a cleric for injuries done to himself.”], archbishop of Cagliari.

If we consider with integrity of mind the priestly office that we administer, an indivisible harmony of charity ought to unite us with our sons, so that, as we are fathers in name, we may also be proved fathers in affection and action [Col. 0590C]. Since, then, we ought to be such as we have said, we are astonished that so great a mass of complaints has arisen against your Fraternity. Indeed, we still hesitate to believe it.

But so that we may be able to recognize the truth, we have sent John, the notary of our see, supported there by our command, so that he may compel the parties to be present at the judgment of the chosen judges and, by his own execution, bring to effect whatever shall have been judged.

Accordingly, by the present letter we exhort your Fraternity to examine beforehand the merits of the cases brought before you [Col. 0591A]. And if you recognize that you have acted or retained anything unjustly, restore it before judgment, out of regard for the priesthood.

Among the many complaints, Isidore, a man of illustrious rank, has complained that he was unjustly excommunicated and anathematized by your Fraternity [Note: Vatican B: “Isidore, coming from your Fraternity,” omitting “the illustrious man.”]. When we wished to learn from your cleric who was present why this had been done, it became clear that there was no other reason except that he had insulted you [Note: The Church’s censures may not be used to avenge personal injuries. Read Saint Augustine, Letter 7 to Auxilius: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God”; nor should you suppose that unjust agitation cannot creep upon us because we are bishops, and so forth. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book VIII, chapters 39 and 40. The difference between excommunication and anathema is taught by the canons, causa 11, question 3, chapters *Debent* and *Cum aliquis*. See also the Council of Meaux, canon 56, where not only a certain and manifest cause is required for excommunication, but also the consent of the archbishop or fellow bishops is necessary for anathema—something few people notice. See below, Book XII, Letter 26. GUSSANV. See causa 24, question 3, canons 6 and 9, and elsewhere.].

This greatly afflicts us, because, if it is so, you show that you think of nothing heavenly, but signify that your conduct is earthly, since, in revenge for a personal injury—which the sacred rules forbid—you have brought upon him the curse of anathema. Therefore, from now on be altogether cautious and watchful, and do not again presume to inflict such things upon anyone in defense of your own injury. For if you do anything of the kind, know that afterward it will be avenged upon you.

## 614 LETTER L. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He unites the Church of the Three Taverns, which had been desolated by enemies, to that of Velitrae.

Gregory to John [Note: LETTER L [formerly 35].—In the Norman, Corbie, Colbert, and Vatican B and C manuscripts, only “to the bishop” is read. In Vatican A: “to the bishop of Squillace.” In the Reims manuscript: “to the bishop of Velitrae.”], bishop of Velitrae.

After hostile impiety, through the agency of sins, has so desolated the Churches of various cities [Gratian 16, question 1, canon 49] that, with the people diminished, no hope of restoring them has remained, we are compelled by much greater care to ensure that, when their priests have died [Note: “Priests” almost always means bishops. Gregory sometimes calls an ordinary presbyter a priest, as in *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 12, where the presbyter Severus is twice called a priest.], the remnants of the people, governed by no pastoral direction, may not—God forbid—be seized by the snares of the cunning enemy of the faith along deserted paths.

Therefore, often reminded by concern for this matter [Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts: “moved,”], this plan settled in our heart: to entrust them for governance to neighboring bishops [Col. 0591C]. Accordingly, we have decided to commit to your Fraternity the care and governance of the Church of the Three Taverns [Note: The Three Taverns was once a city and episcopal see of Latium, whose remains are visible on the Appian Way, not far from Cisterna, according to Luca Holstenius, *Annotations*, pp. 10 and 219. It was about twenty-one Roman miles from the city of Rome. GUSSANV. Almost all manuscripts read “of the Three-Tavern people.” The city is famous from Paul’s journeys. See Acts, final chapter, verse 15.], which must be attached and united to your Church, so that, with Christ’s help, you may rightly become priest of both Churches. Whatever you judge should be arranged concerning its patrimony, the ordination of its clergy, or their advancement, arrange with vigilant and canonical care, since, as its proper bishop, you have free authority by our present permission.

Therefore, dearest brother, remembering profitably the Lord’s commands, watch over the government of the people entrusted to you and the gaining of souls, so that, when you stand before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, you may present to our Redeemer—so that he may rejoice in it—the fruit of good works that will belong to your reward.

## LETTER LI. TO ALL THE BISHOPS

It is futile for schismatics to boast of persecution. After the condemnation of the Three Chapters, nothing in the faith was changed. It is wrong to infer from Italy’s scourges that Italy itself had erred. He sends the book of Pelagius and trusts that, if they read it with a pure heart, they will return to the Church, which invites her sons back to herself.

Gregory [Note: LETTER LI [formerly 36].—The title of this letter is not uniform in the manuscripts and printed editions. In Vatican C: “Gregory the universal, concerning the case of the Three Chapters.” But “universal” was written in error for “to all,” which is read in Vatican A, B, and D, where “concerning the Three Chapters” is also added. The Norman manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, the Colbert manuscript, and nearly all others have the same. In Tours the letter is entitled “to all the defenders of the Three Chapters.” Hence the editors’ error is serious where the title reads “to all the bishops throughout Hibernia.” Learned men conjectured that “Istria” or “Iberia” should be read instead of “Hibernia”; yet no manuscripts support this conjecture. It might nevertheless be admitted if Iberia, that is, Spain, had been divided by schism on account of the Three Chapters; but we find no trace of this either in Gregory the Great or in the historians. Mabillon observes in the preface to the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, volume I, section 6, that Saint Donatus, an abbot and disciple of Facundus, bishop of Hermiane—who wrote to Justinian concerning the Three Chapters—went to Spain. But nowhere do we read that the bishops of Spain were led by him to the side of the schismatics and for this reason suffered the serious persecution mentioned here. What Gregory’s letter does say, however, fits the bishops of Istria perfectly: the exarch, as well as Gulfar, master of the soldiers, and other leading men, strongly pressed them, as they persisted in schism, to return to the unity of the Church. Gregory congratulates these men in Book V, Letters 46 and 47, and Book IX, Letter 93.], to all the bishops concerning the Three Chapters.

I received your letter with the greatest joy; but my joy will be far greater if I am granted the opportunity to rejoice in your return [615]. The opening of your letter made known that you were suffering serious persecution. Yet, when such persecution is endured without reason, it contributes nothing to salvation. For no one may expect a reward for guilt.

You ought to know, as blessed Cyprian says, that punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause [Note: This saying is found in Cyprian, not in these exact words but in substance, namely in *On the Unity of the Church*, approximately midway through: “He cannot be a martyr who is not in unity; he can be killed, but he cannot be crowned.” Likewise in Letter 52 to Antonianus, toward the middle. It is also found in several places in Saint Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, Book III, chapter 47: “It is not punishment but the cause that makes Christ’s martyr.” Likewise in the commentaries on Psalms 34 and 68. The truth of this statement is demonstrated by Theodoret, *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, discourse 8, *On Martyrs*. GUSSANV.]. Since this is so, it is utterly inappropriate for you to boast of the persecution you mention, by which it is clear that you are not at all advancing toward eternal rewards [Col. 0593A].

Let the integrity of the faith therefore at last lead your Charity back to the mother Church that gave you birth. Let no inclination of mind separate you from the unity of concord; let no persuasion wear you out by drawing you back from the right path [Note: Thus in four Vatican manuscripts, the Reims, Corbie, Tours, and most Norman manuscripts. In others, as in the printed editions: “by repaying.”].

For in the synod in which the Three Chapters were discussed, it is plainly evident that nothing concerning the faith was shaken or changed in any respect; rather, as you know, only certain persons were dealt with there [Note: Whatever some may dream, what those Three Chapters were is evident from these words of the Fifth General Council, session 8: “We anathematize the aforesaid Three Chapters, that is, Theodore of Mopsuestia together with his impious writings, what Theodoret wrote impiously, and the impious letter called the letter of Ibas, and their defenders,” and so forth. The Council of Chalcedon, which had received Theodoret and Ibas favorably and had not sufficiently condemned Theodore’s impious writings, had given rise to this famous controversy. The Eutychians, the supporters of Dioscorus, the Nestorians, the Acephali, the Corrupticolae, the Incorruptibles, and other monsters of that kind attacked the council, each with his own inventions and constructions and, as happens, with varying fortunes. Justinian, anxious to repair unity, seized every opportunity that presented itself. Some suggested that the whole disagreement could easily be silenced and that everyone would swear to the words and faith of the Council of Chalcedon if the Three Chapters were condemned. Justinian listened, pressed, and persisted. Vigilius seemed uncertain, sometimes agreeing and sometimes refusing. Catholic bishops withdrew into opposing parties: some feared that Chalcedon was being deceived, while others thought that by this strategy they could establish it more firmly. Meanwhile the schismatics encouraged disorder. At last they came to the council, at which, if the historians are to be trusted, the condemnation of the Three Chapters seems to have widened the division, broken the net, and introduced a new schism, so that Catholics were set against one another. See the letters of Pelagius I and Pelagius II, and elsewhere. GUSSANV.].

One of these persons, whose writings clearly deviated from the rectitude of the Catholic faith, was not unjustly condemned [Note: Theodore of Mopsuestia is indicated. For the writings of Theodoret and Ibas were dealt with rather than the persons whom the Council of Chalcedon had approved. See above, Letter 25 to the patriarchs, near the end. Liberatus explains by what devices bishops who had been dead for a hundred years were examined and condemned in his *Breviary*, chapters 23 and 24, and finally concludes: “I believe it is clear to all that through Pelagius the deacon and Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, this scandal entered the Church.” Theodore himself also cried out that he and Pelagius ought to be burned alive, since through them this scandal had entered the world.].

As for your writing that, since that time, Italy has been scourged more than the other provinces, you ought not to turn this into her reproach, since it is written: “Whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6) [Col. 0593B]. If, then, matters are as you say, she has been more greatly loved by God and approved in every respect from the time when she deserved to endure the scourges of her Lord.

But because the matter is not as you attempt to assert in order to insult her, consider the reason.

After Pope Vigilius, of blessed memory, had been established in the imperial city, he pronounced a sentence of condemnation against Theodora, then empress, or against the Acephali [Note: [Col. 0594C] Facundus of Hermiane, Book I, chapter 5, says that those who, although departing in some respects from the teaching of Eutyches, their author and head, nevertheless disdain to follow the teaching of the Catholic Church, whose head is Christ, remain as though headless and are called *Acephali* by the Greeks; more significantly, we may call them Semi-Eutychians [Col. 0594D]. Others give other reasons for the name: Leontius, *On the Sects*, chapter 5; Ado of Vienne, *Chronicle*; and Nicephorus, Book XVIII, chapter 45. Eventually all Monophysites who attacked the Council of Chalcedon with one accord were called Acephali, although they split into diverse sects.] [Note: We read that Vigilius condemned Theodore, bishop of Caesarea, in his fifteenth letter; a fragment of that condemnation also appears after Vigilius’s sixteenth letter in volume V of the Councils, p. 334. But no mention is found of a sentence against the empress Theodora. She is doubtless said to have been condemned through the condemnation of the Acephali, whose party she supported.], and then the city of Rome was entered and captured by enemies [Col. 0594A] [Note: Vatican B: “was handed over.”].

Did the Acephali therefore have a good cause, and were they unjustly condemned, because such things happened after their condemnation? Far from it. Neither should any of you, nor anyone else instructed in the mysteries of the Catholic faith, say or in any way admit this.

Having understood these things, therefore, withdraw at last from this course of thought. So that satisfaction concerning the Three Chapters may be abundantly poured into your minds after every doubt has been removed [616], I have judged it useful to send you the book that my predecessor, Pope Pelagius, of holy memory, wrote concerning this matter [Note: By this book we must understand Pelagius’s seventh letter, his third to Helias and the bishops of Istria, which begins: “Charity is the mother of virtues.” Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 20, testifies that Saint Gregory wrote it in the name of Pope Pelagius.].

If, setting aside the zeal of voluntary defense, you are willing to read it repeatedly with a pure and watchful heart, I trust that you will follow it in every respect and nevertheless return to our unity. But if, after reading this book, you wish to persist in the opinion that you now hold, you plainly show that you are devoting yourselves not to reason but to obstinacy.

Therefore, once again, with compassion I admonish your Charity: since, with God’s help, the integrity of our faith has remained inviolate in the matter of the Three Chapters, return to your mother, the Church, which awaits and invites her sons, laying aside the swelling of your minds—all the sooner because you know that she daily awaits you for your sake [Note: Thus in the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and Reims manuscripts, without the phrase “having no compassion,” which appears in the printed editions.].

## LETTER LII. TO NATALIS, BISHOP

The profane banquets to which he gave himself and his neglect of sacred reading cannot properly be excused by him. He rejoices in his zeal for exhortation. He is distressed at being praised. Not only heretics but also those within the Church must be recalled to upright living. He complains that his own decision and that of his predecessor were despised; nevertheless, he spares the man who has returned to his office and promises the greatest equity in judging his case.

Gregory to Natalis, bishop of Salona.

As though I had forgotten the sequence of my preceding writings, I had resolved to speak to your Blessedness only of matters that would bring sweetness; but when your letter, by its reasoning, recalls me to my earlier writings, I am perhaps compelled once again to relate certain things that are less pleasing. (See Book III, Letter 22.)

In defense of banquets, your Fraternity recalls Abraham’s banquet, at which, as sacred Scripture testifies, he is said to have received three angels (Genesis 18). Yet by this example we do not rebuke your Blessedness for a banquet if we understand that receiving angels is an act of hospitality. Again, you relate that Isaac, after being satisfied, gave his son a blessing (Genesis 27:27).

Both these events of the Old Testament were accomplished historically, yet they also signified something allegorically. Would that, as we read through the events that happened, we might also be able to perceive by foresight the things that ought to happen! For by welcoming one in the three angels, by greeting one in the three angels, he declared that the three subsistences of the Trinity are of one substance. The other, having been satisfied, blessed his son, because the mind of one who is filled with divine banquets is directed toward the power of prophecy.

The divine banquets are the words of sacred Scripture. If, then, you read constantly, and, taking an example from outward things, penetrate to inward realities, you fill the belly of your mind as though satisfied from the hunt in the field, so that, placing before you the son—that is, the people who have been received—you may announce what is to come.

But in this world the person who prophesies anything about God is now dimmed, because it is surely fitting that here the one who sees less through desire should have a mind that flashes inwardly through understanding [Note: LETTER LII [formerly 27].—The printed editions: “through allegory.”]. Draw these matters, then, toward yourselves; and if you recognize yourselves to be such, there is no reason for you to doubt our estimation [Note: In the Vulgate editions: “your estimation.”].

I also find that your Blessedness rejoices if you bear the name of “glutton” together with the author of the deed. I shall explain this briefly. If something false is said about you, then you bear this name truthfully together with the author of the deed. But if it is true about you, who would doubt that it was false about him? A similar name cannot absolve you, since your circumstances are different. For a thief also received the cross together with him and was destined to perish; but because his own guilt held him, the identical crucifixion did not absolve him.

I, however, beg with as many prayers as I can, that your most holy Fraternity may be joined to our Creator not only in name [Note: Thus the Norman, Reims, and other manuscripts; disregarding them, the printed editions read: “that your most holy Fraternity may be joined to our Creator not only in name but also in cause.” The sense is lacking in the latter reading.] but also in cause. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 33.)

As for banquets [Note: [Col. 0595D] Recent editions read *convivia autem communia*, “common banquets,” but we find the final word in no manuscript.] that are held with the deliberate purpose of extending charity, your Holiness rightly praises them in your letters. Yet it must be understood that they truly arise from charity when no one’s life is attacked in them in his absence, no one is criticized in mockery, and empty stories about secular affairs are not heard, but words of sacred reading are heard; when the body is served no more than is necessary, and only its weakness is refreshed, so that it may be available for the practice of virtue.

If you do these things at your banquets, I confess that you are teachers of abstinence.

As for the testimony of the Apostle Paul that you set before me, where he says, “Let him who does not eat not judge him who eats” (Romans 14:3), I consider it wholly inappropriate. For I neither fail to eat, nor did Paul say this so that the members of Christ, who are joined to one another in his body—that is, in the Church—by the bond of charity, should in no way care for one another.

But if neither I had any relation to you nor you to me [Note: A grave principle, not sufficiently noticed by the common people. Right reason dictates that one whom we cannot correct should not be rebuked. But if his care has been entrusted to us, we must nevertheless rebuke him, because the duty of charity and also of justice compels us to do so. Read Letter 8 of John Climacus to the Shepherd, numbers 23 and 24.], I would rightly be compelled to remain silent, so as not to rebuke one who could not be corrected. This saying, therefore, was spoken only concerning those who make a practice of judging people whose care has not been entrusted to them.

But since, by God’s authorship, we are one, if we remain silent about the things that ought to be corrected in us, we commit a serious offense. Behold, your Fraternity was distressed that I had rebuked you concerning banquets, although I, who, even if not in life, nevertheless exceed you in position, am prepared to be corrected and amended by everyone [618]. I consider only that man my friend through whose tongue, before the appearance of the strict Judge, I cleanse the stains of my mind.

As for your assertion, dearest brother, that you cannot read while oppressed by tribulations, I consider it an inadequate excuse, since Paul says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Romans 15:4).

If sacred Scripture was prepared for our consolation, then we ought to read all the more when we see ourselves wearied beneath the burden of tribulations. But if we must rely only upon the saying that you placed in your letter, in which the Lord says, “When they hand you over, do not think about how or what you will speak, for it will be given to you in that hour what you should say. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19), then the sacred utterances have been commanded to us in vain, since those filled with the Spirit have no need of outward words.

But it is one thing, dearest brother, to trust without doubt during a time narrowed by persecution, and another thing to act in the tranquility of the Church. We ought now, through this Spirit, to acquire by reading what we may be able, if such a circumstance should arise for us, to demonstrate even by suffering.

I greatly rejoiced at your letter because you confess that you devote yourselves to the work of exhortation. For by this I know that you diligently attend to the care of your order, if you take care to draw others to your Creator.

But when, in the same place, you say that you are not like me, you immediately saddened me after giving me joy, because I think my praises are being spoken in mockery, since I do not recognize them as true. Yet I give thanks to almighty God that through you heretics are indeed recalled to the holy Church.

But you must also take care that those who are contained within the bosom of the holy Church [Note: In Vatican D and the Norman manuscripts: “so that they too may be kept within the bosom of the holy Church and live accordingly.” The Reims and Corbie manuscripts agree.] live in such a way that they do not become its adversaries through wicked conduct [Col. 0597B]. For if they serve not divine desire but earthly ambitions and pleasures, alien children are being nourished within her bosom.

As for your admission that you cannot be ignorant of ecclesiastical orders, I too know this about you in every respect. For that reason I am greatly saddened, because, although you know the order of things, you have sinned knowingly against me—which is worse.

After writings from my predecessor and me had been sent to your Blessedness concerning the case of Honoratus the archdeacon, then, with the decision of both of us despised, the aforesaid Honoratus was deprived of his own rank. If any one of the four patriarchs had done this, such great contumacy could not in any way have passed without the gravest scandal [Note: Because the Roman pontiff, the successor of Saint Peter, must be heard and honored by those four patriarchs, since by divine right he has authority over them and, by a special privilege, bears concern for all the Churches.].

Nevertheless, after your Fraternity returned to its own order, I remember neither the injury done to me nor that done to my predecessor. (See Book I, Letters 19 and 20, and Book XII of this work, Letters 17, 19, and 20.)

As for your saying [Note: Others read “in your times,” as in three Vatican manuscripts and most of the Norman manuscripts.] that in our times those practices should be preserved which were handed down and maintained by my predecessors [Col. 0598A], far be it from me to violate in any Church the statutes handed down by my elders to my fellow priests, because [Note: The same view is held by Leo the Great, Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne; Gregory VII, Book I, Letter 24; and Honorius II, in a letter to Burchard, bishop of Meaux: “By the office entrusted to us, we ought to love our brother bishops and preserve for the Churches committed to them by God their own rights.” Innocent II, in a letter to Manasses, bishop of Meaux: “The care of the government we have undertaken warns us, by the Lord’s arrangement, to apply attentive concern and vigilance to each person, so that no confusion may be introduced into ecclesiastical arrangements, but rather that each person’s own right and proper dignity may be preserved.” Innocent III says the same in Book I of his letter to the bishop of Troyes and in Letter 39. GUSSANV. Above all, our Gregory should be heard, Book XI, Letter 37, formerly Book IX, Letter 32: “For if each bishop’s jurisdiction is not preserved for him, what else is being done except that the ecclesiastical order, which ought to have been guarded by us through whom it should be preserved, is being thrown into confusion?”].

I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers. But when your representatives arrive, I shall learn what is just between you and the aforesaid Honoratus the archdeacon [Note: Thus, more correctly, the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, rather than the recent printed editions, which read “what has happened between you and the aforesaid Honoratus the archdeacon.”]. From my own examination you will understand that, if your party is supported by justice, you will suffer nothing adverse from me, just as you have not suffered it before.

But if justice often comes to the aid of the aforesaid Honoratus the archdeacon in his claim, by his acquittal I shall show that, even when I know the persons involved, I do not recognize persons in judgment.

Concerning the matter of excommunication [Gratian 24, question 3, chapter 15] [Note: In recent Vulgate editions, though with the intervening condition “a second time”; the word “time” is superfluous and is not read in the Reims, Corbie, Norman, or most manuscripts, nor in the old printed editions. The Roman editors have already noted that it is absent from the three oldest copies used in preparing Gratian.], which, after the condition had been inserted, had already been imposed a second or third time, as I may say, out of necessity, your Blessedness complains without justification, since the Apostle Paul says: “Being ready to avenge every disobedience” (2 Corinthians 10:6).

But let these matters now pass; let us return to our own concerns. For if he acts rightly, I cannot fail to be united with Lord Natalis, to whose affection I know myself to be greatly indebted.

[Note: LETTER LIII [formerly 10; Book XII, indiction 7].—This letter is absent from many manuscripts. It is found in Vatican D, the Colbert manuscript, and the collection of Paul the Deacon, where it is the forty-ninth.]

## LETTER LIII. TO HONORATUS, THE DEACON

That he should favor Venantius, who, after offering thirty pounds of gold, petitioned the emperors for the documents of the ex-consulship.

Gregory [Note: This is the same man to whom Letter 49 of Book I is addressed; see the notes there. At that time he was staying in Constantinople, carrying out the office of *apocrisiarius* for the province.] to Honoratus the deacon.

My son, Lord Venantius, grandson of the late patrician Opilio, came to the blessed apostle Peter to ask me most earnestly that I commend his case to Your Excellency. For he holds no honors, and he requested letters of ex-consulship, for which he sent thirty pounds of gold, so that they might be obtained for him.

[Note: Vatican D reads *exconsultus*, and Colbertinus *exconsultus*, doubtless by abbreviation for *exconsulatus*. We have already observed that, long before the pontificate of Gregory the Great, the consulship had been abolished by the Emperor Justinian Augustus, namely in the year 541. Justin, his successor, did indeed consider restoring consuls in some fashion, thinking that he would thereby do something pleasing to the Roman people; but once that supreme dignity had been extinguished, it could never be restored to its former condition, since this would have created resentment against the emperors. Thus, in Gregory’s time, ex-consulship was merely an empty name of honor. Just as certain men are now made counts of the sacred consistory by letters-patent, in French *par brevet*, so at that time letters of ex-consulship were granted—or rather sold—as a mark of honor. For the condition of the state had then deteriorated to such a point that the emperors were compelled even to sell smoke, in order to assist the distressed republic and replenish the exhausted treasury.]

In this matter I want Your Excellency to devote yourself most earnestly, because he is a man to whom even honor ought to be granted without payment. And since, as I have said, he is prepared to buy those letters, it is not especially necessary that anything should be said about him by me to the most serene sovereigns; rather, let Your Excellency act on his behalf, so that, having offered the customary payments into the treasury,

[Note: That is, at the customary price. *Sacellum*, from *saccus* and *sacculus*, here signifies the treasury or public fisc. Hence *sacellarius*, one who carries purses for almsgiving, commonly called an almoner.]

he may deserve to receive the honors. Nevertheless, if you can deal with him somewhat more favorably, you will receive the greatest reward. But act in such a way that his labor in coming here to us is not in vain. If you should find anything difficult in this matter, you must also indicate that he is making this request through me, and inform the most serene Lords of his goodness, modesty, and wisdom.

[Note: EPISTLE LIV.—Our Dom Lucas d’Achery first brought this to light from two manuscripts of the Library of Fleury and included it in the second volume of the *Spicilegium*.]

## EPISTLE LIV

### Here begins the letter of Saint Licinianus, bishop, concerning the *Book of Pastoral Rule*, addressed to Saint Gregory, pope of the city of Rome

He praises the *Book of Pastoral Rule*, but objects that there will be no one to celebrate the sacred mysteries unless men who are sometimes less qualified are ordained. He requests Gregory’s books on Job and other moral subjects.

[Col. 0599B]

To the most blessed Lord Pope Gregory, Licinianus, bishop.

[Note: Isidore says of him in Book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 29: “Licinianus, bishop of Carthage Spartaria—commonly called Cartagena in Spain—was learned in the Scriptures, and we have read some of his letters. We have also read one concerning the sacrament of baptism, and several to Eutropius, later bishop of Valencia; but the rest of his industry and labor have not come to our knowledge. He flourished in the time of the Emperor Maurice; he died at Constantinople, reportedly killed by poison at the hands of rivals. But, as it is written, ‘Though the righteous be taken before his time by whatever death, his soul shall be in refreshment.’”]

We have read the *Book of Pastoral Rule* published by Your Holiness and, by the assistance of divine grace, delivered to us, with all the greater pleasure because we recognize that it contains spiritual rules. Who would not read more willingly a book in which, through constant meditation, he may find medicine for his soul; in which, after despising the fleeting affairs of this age, changing amid their own mutability, he may open the eyes of his mind toward the dwelling-place of eternal life?

This book of yours is the court of every virtue. In it prudence establishes a boundary of discernment between good and evil; justice gives each person his due, while subjecting the soul to God and the body to the soul. In it fortitude is always found equally strong in adversity and prosperity: it is neither broken by reverses nor exalted by success. In it temperance breaks the fury of lust and imposes a measured restraint upon pleasures. In it you comprehend everything that pertains to sharing in eternal life; and you describe not only a rule of life for pastors, but also grant a rule of living to those who hold no office of governance.

For in your fourfold arrangement pastors find what sort of men should come to this office; what sort of life they should lead once they have come; how and what they should teach; and what they should do lest they become exalted upon so lofty a priestly summit. Your outstanding teaching is confirmed by the holy Fathers of old, teachers and defenders of the Church—Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory of Nazianzus. All these bear witness to you, just as the prophets bore witness to the apostles.

Saint Hilary says, explaining the words of the Apostle, the teacher of the nations:

[Note: A different and sounder reading is found in the recent edition of Saint Hilary’s works: “For he signifies that those things which properly concern discipline and morals are useful for the dignity of the priesthood if those things also which are necessary for teaching and defending the knowledge of the faith are not lacking among the rest; because it is not immediately the mark of a good and useful priest either to act merely innocently or merely to preach with knowledge, since one who is innocent benefits only himself unless he is learned, and one who is learned is without the authority of teaching unless he is innocent.”]

“Thus he signifies that those things which belong properly to discipline and morals are useful for the dignity of the priesthood if those things also which are necessary for teaching and defending the knowledge of the faith are not lacking among the rest. For it is not immediately the mark of a good and useful priest either merely to act knowingly or merely to preach knowingly, since even the innocent person suffices only for himself if he is learned, and the learned person—unless by teaching through his manner of life [the printed text is defective].”

Saint Ambrose confirms this book of yours in the books he composed *On Duties*. Saint Augustine confirms it, saying:

[Note: In Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XIX, chapter 19, it reads: “In action, honor in this life, or power, is not to be loved …” He wished to explain what the episcopate is, since it is the name of a work, not of an honor. “For it is Greek, and the word is derived from the fact that the one who is set over others watches over those over whom he is set, caring for them; for *ἐπί* means ‘over,’ while *σκοπός* means ‘attention.’ Therefore *ἐπισκοπεῖν*, if we wish, may be rendered in Latin as ‘to watch over,’ so that one may understand that he is not a bishop who loves to preside rather than to be useful. Thus no one is forbidden the pursuit of knowing the truth, which belongs to praiseworthy leisure; but a superior position, without which a people cannot be governed, although it is held and administered as is proper, is nevertheless sought in an improper manner. Therefore the love of truth seeks holy leisure, while the necessity of charity undertakes a just duty. If no one imposes this burden, one should devote oneself to receiving and contemplating the truth; but if it is imposed, it must be accepted because of the necessity of charity. Even then, however, the delight of truth must not be wholly abandoned, lest that sweetness be taken away and this necessity become oppressive.”]

“In action, honor in this life—*sine* [read: *sive*, ‘or’] power—is not to be loved, since all things are vanity under the sun; but the work itself which is carried out through that honor or power, if it is done rightly and usefully, that is, so that it may contribute to the salvation of subjects according to God … For this reason the Apostle says: ‘Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work.’ He wished to explain what a bishop is [perhaps: ‘the episcopate’], since it is the name of a work, not of an honor. For it is a Greek word, derived from the fact that the one set over those over whom he is set watches over them, caring for them; for *episcopus* [perhaps: *episcopatus*] means ‘attention.’ Therefore, if we wish, we may say in Latin *superintendere* (‘to oversee’) for *episcopum*. Let him understand that he is not a bishop who has said that he presides [read: ‘has loved to preside’], rather than to be useful. Thus no one is forbidden the pursuit of knowing the truth, which belongs to praiseworthy leisure; but a higher position, without which a people cannot be governed, although it is held and administered as is proper, is nevertheless sought improperly. Therefore charity seeks holy leisure; one ought to devote oneself to apprehending and safeguarding truth. But if it is imposed, it must be undertaken because of the necessity of charity. Yet even so the delight of truth must not be relinquished for convenience, lest that sweetness be taken away and this necessity become oppressive.” (*On the Trinity*, Book VIII, no. 1.)

Saint Gregory confirms this, Gregory whose style you follow and whose example you wished to imitate by concealing yourself, so as to avoid the burden of the priesthood; what that burden is, your whole book clearly declares. Yet you bear what you feared. Your burden is carried upward, not downward—not something that presses you toward the depths, but something that raises you to the stars. Through God’s grace, the merit of obedience, and the effectiveness of good works, what seemed burdensome because of human weakness becomes easy.

You say things that agree with the apostles and apostolic men. You have spoken beautiful things beautifully, and in these things you have shown yourself beautiful. I do not want you to resemble an unseemly painter who paints beautiful things, because spiritual doctrine proceeds from a spiritual mind. A human painter is valued more highly by most people than an inanimate painting. But do not attribute this to flattery or adulation; attribute it to truth, since it is not fitting for me to lie, nor for you to praise what is false.

Therefore, plainly and faithfully, I have seen you and all that is yours as beautiful, and I have found myself quite unseemly in comparison with you. For this reason I beg you, by the grace of God which abounds in you, not to reject one who pleads with you, but willingly to teach me what I confess that I do not know. Necessity compels us to do what you teach.

For when no qualified man is found who can enter the priestly office, what is to be done except that an unqualified man, such as I am, should be ordained? You command that an unqualified man not be ordained. But let your prudence consider whether perhaps it is enough for a man’s qualification that he know Jesus Christ, and him crucified. If this is not enough, no one in this book will be called qualified; indeed, no one will be a priest if he must be qualified.

We openly resist bigamists, lest the sacrament be corrupted. But what if a man who has had one wife touched another woman before his marriage? What if he has never had a wife, yet has not remained untouched by a woman? Console us by your writing, so that we may not be punished either for our own sin or for another’s. We greatly fear that necessity may compel us to do what we ought not.

Look: we must obey your commands, so that one may become such as apostolic authority requires; yet the person sought is not found. Faith, then, which rests upon hearing, will cease; baptism will cease if there is no one to baptize; those most holy mysteries which are performed and administered through priests and ministers will cease. Danger remains on both sides: either a man who ought not to be ordained is ordained, or there is no one to celebrate or administer the sacred mysteries.

A few years ago, Bishop Leander of Spalis, returning from the imperial city, passed by and saw us. He told us that Your Beatitude had published homilies on the Book of Holy Job. Since he was hurrying on, he did not show them to us when we asked for them. Later, however, you wrote to him concerning the triple immersion, and in that letter you mentioned that you were displeased with that work (*Book I, Epistle 43*), but that, following a more beneficial plan, you had decided to transfer them into the sequence of the books.

[Note: Some of our scholars who recently edited the works of Saint Hilary think that Licinianus was deceived by a false title. They argue that Jerome nowhere mentions Hilary’s little books on Job, but rather, in his *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, a treatise on Job; in the *Apology against Rufinus*, and in Epistle 101 to Pammachius, as well as elsewhere, homilies on Job. Perhaps, however, “little books on Job,” “treatise,” and “homilies” all refer to precisely the same work of Hilary. Our scholars discuss this matter at considerable length in their preface to the recent edition of Saint Hilary’s works, nos. 25 and 29.]

We certainly possess six little books of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, which he translated from the Greek of Origen into Latin; but he did not explain everything according to the order of the Book of Holy Job. I am quite astonished that so learned and holy a man should have translated Origen’s nonsense about the stars. I cannot be persuaded in any way, most holy Father, to believe that the stars of heaven are rational spirits, since Holy Scripture declares that they were made neither with the angels nor with human beings.

May Your Beatitude therefore deign to send me the work on the Book of Holy Job, as well as the other moral books which you mention having composed in this *Book of Pastoral Rule*, to my humble self [perhaps *meae* is lacking].

[Note: Supreme pontiffs and bishops were formerly addressed by this distinguished title of honor, as occurs frequently in Augustine, Jerome, and others. I offer one example from Ennodius, *Book IV, Epistle 22*, to Pope Symmachus: “May the mercy of your crown, when entreated, raise up the little ones.”]

For we belong to you, and we take pleasure in reading your works. For it is my desire—and it is a noble desire, as your Gregory says—to learn until the very end of old age [perhaps “and” is lacking]. May God, the Holy Trinity, preserve your crown unharmed for the instruction of His Church, as we desire, most blessed Father.

## BOOK THREE

In the month of September, in the eleventh indiction.

[Col. 0603]

## EPISTLE I

### To Peter, subdeacon

He sends the subdeacon Epiphanius to investigate the sedition raised against Bishop Paul. He orders Peter to assist him in prosecuting the guilty, without any delay or respect of persons. Slaves are to be recalled to the churches of the city.

[Col. 0603A]

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

[Note: BOOK III. Some manuscripts read BOOK II, indiction XI. EPISTLE. The castle of Lucullanum has already been discussed under Book I, Epistle 24.]

What a crime has been committed in the castle of Lucullanum against our brother and fellow bishop Paul was made clear to us by a report sent here. Since Scholasticus, the magnificent judge of Campania, happened to be present here in these days, we specifically instructed him that he ought to correct the madness of so great a perversity through strict punishment.

But because the bearer of the aforesaid report has now urged us to send someone,

[Note: The Normannian manuscript reads “urged us …”; the Corbeiensis, “suggested to us …”]

we have therefore sent the subdeacon Epiphanius there, so that, together with the aforesaid judge, he may investigate and determine by whom the sedition was instigated or committed, and may punish it with a fitting penalty.

[Note: It is not a recent practice for ecclesiastical and secular judges to investigate the same matter together and inflict punishment deserving of vengeance. See the Council of Orléans IV, in the time of Vigilius, in the year 545, canon 20; Mâcon I, canon 7; and Gregory of Tours, bishop, *History*, Book V, chapters 5 and 48. Gussanville.]

Let Your Experience therefore hasten to assist with all your strength in this matter, so that the truth may be discovered and punishment may proceed against the offenders.

Since, then, the slaves of the illustrious Clementina are said to have participated in the same crime and to have loudly uttered words that stirred up the sedition, if this is so, subject them strictly to the punishment that awaits them,

[Note: The edition of Gussanville corruptly reads “subject her to the impending punishment,” as though Clementina herself were to be subjected to vengeance and punishment, rather than her slaves. The following words remove all doubt: “they must be struck all the more,” namely the slaves.]

and let your severity not be more lenient on account of her rank, because they deserve to be struck all the more severely inasmuch as, being the dependents of a noble woman, they sinned out of sheer pride.

You must also investigate carefully whether the aforesaid woman had any knowledge of so monstrous a crime, or whether it was committed with her knowledge, so that everyone may learn from our defense how dangerous it is to transgress not only by hand but also in words against a priest.

For if anything in this matter is attempted or neglected, know that it belongs to your fault and, rather, to your danger; you will find no ground for an excuse before us. For just as this matter, if it is investigated and corrected with the utmost strictness, commends you to us, so, if it is treated lightly, know that our indignation against you will be sharpened.

[Note: The manuscripts—Vatican, Normannian, Corbeiensis, and others—require this reading, “if it is treated lightly,” rather than the reading of the printed editions, “if it is attempted.”]

If any slaves henceforth flee from the city to the monastery of Saint Severinus,

[Note: Saint Severinus, apostle of the Noricans, whose body was transferred to the castle of Lucullanum, where a famous monastery was built in his honor. See Bollandus, under 8 January.]

or to another church of that castle, as soon as this becomes known to you, do not permit them to remain there in any way; they must be recalled within the city to a church. If they have a just complaint against their masters, they must leave the churches through an appropriate arrangement.

[Note: Slaves may therefore justly complain against their masters and flee to a church for that reason. See the Councils of Orléans I, canon 3; Epaon, canons 34 and 30; and Orléans IV, canon 24. In the *Code*, under *On Judgments*, the laws *Servus* and *Cum debitori*. For many reasons slaves proclaimed their desire for freedom against the will of their masters, as the jurists report; or at least they sought to be sold to others, once the power of a harsher master had been removed. See the lucid text in the *Code*, from which Christians who drive sick servants from their homes and provide none of their necessities should learn shame, as though those servants had no connection with them. It is found in Book VII, title 6, single law, paragraph “But we know.” Such abandoned slaves enjoyed freedom against the will of their masters.]

But if they have committed a pardonable offense, let them be returned without delay to their masters after receiving from them an oath concerning the granting of pardon. (See above, Book II, Epistles 9, 10, and 15, and below, Epistle 15.)

## EPISTLE II

### To Paul, bishop

He consoles him concerning the injury he has suffered.

[Col. 0604B]

Gregory to Paul, bishop.

[Note: EPISTLE II.—He was bishop of Nepi, to whom Gregory had entrusted the visitation of the vacant Church of Naples. See what is said of him in Epistle 9, indiction X. Gussanville.]

Although the injury you suffered has grieved us deeply, we nevertheless have some grounds for consolation, because we have learned that your praise is contained in this matter: according to what the report sent to us has revealed, you endured it for the sake of upright equity.

Therefore, so that this matter may contribute to the greater glory of Your Fraternity, it must neither break your steadfastness nor turn you from the way of truth. For among priests the greater reward is to remain on the path of truth even after suffering injuries.

And lest the madness of so great an impiety remain unpunished, and the pernicious disorder break out into something worse, we instructed Scholasticus, the magnificent judge of Campania, who happened to be present here, that he ought to punish this with a fitting correction.

[Note: The printed editions read “a memorable man.”]

But because your men asked us to send someone,

[Note: The common editions read “that we should send someone.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.]

know that for this reason we have sent the subdeacon Epiphanius there. Together with the judge named above, he will be able to investigate and establish the truth, so that through his diligence a fitting punishment may be imposed upon those by whom it is established that so great a crime was instigated or committed. (See above, Epistle 1.)

## EPISTLE III

### To John, abbot

He approves Boniface’s appointment as provost. He requests the tunic of Saint John. In the dispute with Florianus he wishes something to be conceded so that the matter may be brought to a settlement. He rebukes the abbot because both he and the brothers neglect sacred reading and prayer. He urges him to take more diligent care of the souls of the brothers, of guests, and of the poor.

[Col. 0605A]

Gregory to John, abbot.

[Note: EPISTLE III.—That is, of Saint Lucy of Syracuse. See Book VII, Epistle 39.]

Your Excellency requested that Brother Boniface be ordained by you as provost in your monastery. I was greatly surprised that this had not been done earlier. For from the time I arranged for him to be given to you, you ought already to have ordained him.

[Note: From chapter 65 of Saint Benedict’s Rule, concerning the provost of a monastery, you will learn more accurately what office he held than from the note of Gussanville, who asserts that his duty was to keep the money and manage affairs.]

As for the tunic of Saint John, I received the news with complete gratitude,

[Note: John the Deacon relates in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, Book III, chapter 59, that it belonged to Saint John the Evangelist, had been placed at Rome in the Constantinian basilica, and had shone forth through many miracles.]

because you took care to inform me. But let Your Excellency endeavor to send me the tunic itself—or, better, the same bishop who possesses it, together with his clergy and with the tunic—so that we may enjoy the blessing of the tunic and may receive some reward from that bishop and clergy.

[Note: *Merces* is sometimes contrasted with loss. Cicero, *To Lentulus*, Book I, Epistle 9: “Not with so great a reward as with the greatest grief of mine.” Below, in Epistle 31, *merces* means a benefit, in French *un bon office*. Gussanville.]

As for the case being disputed with Florianus, I wished to cut it short, and I have already lent him eighty solidi. I believe he intends that these be repaid to him on account of the monastery’s debt, and I absolutely want the same case to be settled, because the chartulary Stephanus

[Note: See concerning him Book II, Epistle 28, and Book V, Epistle 41.]

is said to be pressing for the aforesaid Florianus to transfer it into the public court, and it is burdensome for us to litigate with the public authorities. Therefore it is necessary for us to concede something, so that we may bring the same case to a settlement. Once this has been done, we shall, with God’s help, notify Your Excellency.

Be wholly solicitous for the souls of the brothers. It is enough that the reputation of the monastery has already been stained through your negligence. Do not go out frequently. Appoint an agent in these cases, and devote yourself to reading and prayer.

Be diligent concerning hospitality; give as much as you can to the poor, but in such a way that you preserve what must be restored to Florianus.

Among the very brothers of your monastery whom I see, I do not find them devoting themselves to reading. Therefore you must consider how great a sin it is that God has sent you sustenance from another person’s offering, while you neglect to learn God’s commandments.

As for the six ounces of the estate, if we do not see an authentic document or copies, we can do nothing. But I sent an instruction to Florentinus, the servant of God,

[Note: Vatican B reads “to Florentinus the defender”; Vatican A and C simply read “to Florentinus.”]

that, if the truth is established for him, he should restore those same six ounces to you. Once they have been restored, we shall either grant the remaining six ounces in emphyteusis,

[Note: This is the reading of four Vatican manuscripts, the Normannian, and the Andegavensis. The printed editions read: “or convert them into revenue.”]

or convert them into revenue.

## EPISTLE IV

### To Boniface, bishop

The desire for human praise in good works must be avoided.

Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Rhegium.

[Note: EPISTLE IV.—The Normannian, Corbeiensis, and Vatican D read *Regitano*. Vatican B and the Colbertinus read *Regio* or *Rhegio*. Vatican A reads *Rhegino*; B, “to the priest of Rhegium.” Rhegium was formerly a city of the Bruttians and is now the chief city of Further Calabria, possessing an archiepiscopal title; it lies on the shore of the Sicilian Strait opposite Messina. Cassiodorus gives the etymology of the name in *Variarum*, Book XII, Epistle 14: “The citizens of Rhegium, the last of the Bruttians, were separated from the body of Sicily by the violent force of the sea, whence their city received its name.” For “separation” is called *ῥήγιον* in Greek.]

From certain people who came here I learned that Your Fraternity is devoting yourself intensely to works of mercy. I gave thanks to almighty God because, in accordance with the voice of the excellent preacher, “now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3:8).

But I confess that this somewhat troubled my mind: you yourselves announce these same works to many people. From this I concluded that your mind is striving not to please the eyes of God, but human judgment.

Therefore, dearest brother, when you perform good works outwardly, you must guard them inwardly with great caution, lest the desire to please people creep in and all the labor of the good work be rendered useless. For who are we, that we seek to be pleasing to human beings? What else are we than dust and ashes?

But let Your Fraternity desire to please Him who is not far from appearing and whose every recompense will have no end.

[Note: This is how the Colbertinus and the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus read.]

In the month of October, in the eleventh indiction.

## EPISTLE V

### To Peter, subdeacon

He orders him to protect a widow in all her cases from the violence of wicked men.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

Just as we do not wish to disturb the privileges in the judgments of laymen,

[Note: This epistle is cited in *Extra*, under *On Privileges*, chapter 2, with the addition “lest the jurisdictions of laymen and clergy, since they are distinct, prejudice one another; each must be confined within its own limits.” Our bishops were granted by emperors and kings the right to defend the cases of the poor and oppressed widows. Thus in the *Code*, under *On Bishops Hearing Cases*, laws 1, 10, and 12; and under *On Bishops and Clergy*, laws 28, 46, and 49. More clearly, in the Council of Mâcon II, by order of King Guntram, chapters 12 and 14; Tours II, chapter 26; Saint Gregory, Book I, Epistles 13 and 59; and the Council of Chalcedon, canon 5. Auget.]

so we want you, with measured authority, to resist those who prejudice them. To restrain violent laymen is not to act against the laws, but to lend assistance to the law.

Since Deusdedit, the son-in-law of Felix of Orticello, is said to have inflicted violence upon the bearer of this letter and to be unlawfully detaining the property in question, so that the humiliation of her widowhood appears not to arouse compassion but to strengthen his wickedness, we order Your Experience to offer her the support of your protection both against the aforesaid man and in all the other cases in which the aforesaid woman asserts that she has suffered prejudice. Do not permit anyone to oppress her, lest you be found in any respect to neglect either what is entrusted to you—while preserving equity—or the poor and widows, who, finding no help there, might suffer loss through the remoteness of this journey.

## EPISTLE VI

### To John, bishop

He deprives him of holy communion because of Bishop Adrian, whom he unjustly condemned, and orders Adrian to be restored to his place and rank.

[Col. 0607B]

Gregory to John, bishop of First Justiniana.

[Note: EPISTLE VI.—First Justiniana, now Locrida, an archiepiscopal city in Macedonia, Justinian’s native place, from whom it received its name. See Gussanville’s note on Book II, Epistle 23.]

After the long tribulations which Adrian, bishop of the city of Thebes,

[Note: Thebes of Phthiotis, commonly Ziton, an episcopal city of Thessaly in Greece, formerly in the region of Phthiotis on the Pelasgian Gulf, commonly the Golfo dell’Armiro, opposite Demetrias. It was subject to the metropolitan of Larissa, but later became archiepiscopal. Gussanville.]

suffered at the hands of his fellow priests as though from enemies, he fled to the Roman city. Although his first complaint had been against John, bishop of Larissa,

[Note: Larissa, still commonly Larizza, an inland city and formerly metropolis of Thessaly, on the river Peneus in the district of Pelasgiotis, between Mount Pierius to the north and the Pelasgian Gulf to the south; it is still a large city under Turkish rule. Gregory must be understood to mean this city, not the other Larissa of Thessaly, a maritime town in Phthiotis between the Maliac and Pelasgian gulfs, which was not episcopal.]

namely that he had not been judged by him in pecuniary matters reserved by law; afterwards he complained still more gravely against Your Fraternity, by whom, he maintained, he had been unjustly deposed from the rank of priesthood. But we, not believing petitions that had not been examined, reread both the proceedings before our brother and fellow bishop John and those before Your Fraternity.

Indeed, concerning the judgment of the aforesaid John, bishop of Larissa, which had been suspended by appeal, the most pious Lords of the realm, by orders sent to the bishop of Corinth,

[Note: See the note on Book I, Epistle 26.]

made a sufficient decision. We too, by letters sent through the bearers of this letter to the aforesaid John of Larissa, have, with Christ’s help, decided the matter.

[Note: We restore the text from the Norman, Rheims, and Vatican manuscripts. The reading of the common editions is senseless: “We decided, when we examined the dispute of the differing judgment, the examination of which the imperial commands had entrusted to you; and, having inspected the series of proceedings … held, we found,” etc.]

But when we examined the dispute in the differing judgment, the examination of which imperial commands had entrusted to you, and considered the sequence of proceedings held before Bishop John concerning criminal matters, we found that you had investigated almost nothing concerning the charges named and brought before you. Instead, by certain machinations, you produced witnesses against the deacon Demetrius for the condemnation of that bishop, witnesses who asserted that they had heard him give testimony against him concerning something which it is not even lawful to hear. When Demetrius, who was present, denied having said it, you acted contrary to priestly custom and canonical discipline and delivered the deacon, stripped of his rank, to the provincial proconsul.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “you delivered” or “you delivered [plural].” See also the *Digest*, title *On Examinations*. In the *Code*, Book IX, title 41, the distinguished, soldiers, teachers, clerics—unless infamous—elders, minors, and others are excepted by written law from torture. In France few are excepted if the indications are serious, even in the ecclesiastical forum, provided the crime is atrocious. Auget.]

Though he was torn by many lashes and might perhaps, under the compulsion of torture, have lied against his bishop, we found that to the end of the case he confessed absolutely nothing concerning the matters about which he was questioned. Nor did we find anything else in the proceedings themselves, either in the depositions of witnesses or in Adrian’s statement, which could harm him. Rather, Your Fraternity alone, from some impulse of mind unknown to me, disregarding divine and human law, pronounced a precipitate sentence condemning him. Even if this had not been suspended by appeal, being pronounced against laws and canons it could not itself stand in law.

After it became clear beyond doubt that an appeal had been made to you, we wondered why you had not sent, in accordance with the undertaking set forth to our deacon Honoratus by the representatives of your Church, even your own men, who could have accounted for your judgment.

[Note: An undertaking given either in writing or orally.]

This conduct convicts you either of obstinacy or of a trembling conscience. If, therefore, the matters laid before us are supported by truth,

[Note: The common editions read “plain.” In the Norman manuscript we read: “If, therefore, these matters … are supported by truth.”]

because we see that, on the occasion of our vicariates, you presume unjust things,

[Note: The Norman manuscript reads “that we presume unjust things.” The reading “that we do not presume unjust things,” found corruptly and without better sense in three Vatican manuscripts, is defective.]

we shall later, with Christ’s help, decide concerning them according to what we have resolved.

As to the present matter, however, after first annulling and reducing to nothing the decrees of your aforesaid sentence, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we decree that for thirty days you be deprived of holy communion and seek from our almighty God forgiveness for so great an offense with the utmost penitence and tears. If we learn that you have carried out this sentence of ours too laxly, know that, with the Lord’s help, not only the injustice but also the contumacy of Your Fraternity will be punished more severely.

We determine, with Christ accompanying us, that the aforesaid Adrian, our brother and fellow bishop, whom your sentence, as we have said, condemned in no way according to canons or laws, shall return to his place and rank. Thus neither may the sentence of Your Fraternity, pronounced contrary to the path of justice, harm him, nor may your charity remain uncorrected, for the appeasing of the indignation of the future Judge. (See below, Epistles 7 and 38; compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 26.)

## EPISTLE VII

### To John, bishop

He shows from the order of the trial that Adrian’s unjust condemnation was procured by the machinations of John the metropolitan. He consequently decrees that John must abstain from all jurisdiction over Adrian, and threatens deprivation of holy communion unless he obeys.

Gregory to John, bishop of Larissa.

Frater noster Adrian, bishop of the city of Thebes, coming to the city of Rome, tearfully complained that he had been condemned on certain charges by Your Fraternity and by John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, neither lawfully nor canonically. Since for a long time we saw no representative of the opposing party arrive here who ought to have answered his objections, we necessarily entrusted to a rereading, for the sake of discovering the truth, the acts conducted among you. From these we learned that the deacons John and Cosmas—one removed from office for sexual misconduct, the other for frauds involving ecclesiastical property—had brought before our most devout emperors accusations against him involving both financial and criminal charges.

By their commands they wished you to investigate the matter, with due observance, naturally, of the rigor of the law and the canons: you were to issue a firm legal judgment concerning the financial charges, but concerning the criminal charges, after a more careful examination had been made by their Clemency, you were to submit your recommendations. If Your Fraternity had received such upright commands with an equally upright mind, you would never have readily admitted into an accusation against their bishop men who had been removed from their offices for their offenses and who were already acting with a hostile spirit—especially since their deceit was exposed by the report submitted to the most devout lords, when they admitted, with the consent of all the clergy, that they had brought these charges against their own bishop.

[Note: For this expression, which is read in all the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, the printed editions have “of an unchanging disposition.”]

After this, however, let me briefly and cursorily review some of what was done before you. First, a charge was brought before Your Fraternity concerning Stephen, a Theban deacon, whose life Bishop Adrian, as though knowing it to be utterly disgraceful, had not deprived him of the honor of his order. None of the witnesses brought forward says that this charge ever came to Bishop Adrian’s knowledge, except that Stephen alone is said to have confessed—Stephen who, by his shameful life and by his own profession, was deserving of condemnation.

A second charge appears to have been brought against him: that infants were prohibited by his order from receiving holy baptism and thus died in the darkness of sin, unwashed by baptism. Yet none of the witnesses brought forward against him claimed to know that any such matter had come to Bishop Adrian’s knowledge. They said that they had learned it from the infants’ mothers, whose husbands, as was alleged, had been removed from the Church for their offenses. Nor did they claim that the children died unbaptized, as the malicious report of the accusers asserted, since it was established that they had been baptized in the city of Demetrias.

[Note: The four Vatican manuscripts read “unwashed” (inablutos).]

[Note: Demetrias, commonly called Dimitriada, was a city of Thessaly in the Pagasaean Gulf and in the region of Magnesia. Formerly an episcopal city under the metropolitan of Larissa, it is now so regarded.]

These, then, concern the criminal charges.

As for the financial charges, the inquiry conducted by the men appointed by the emperor testifies to the most serene emperors how you rendered judgment. For when the aforesaid Adrian had repeatedly suspended your judgment by appeal, as we learned from the depositions of four witnesses produced before John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, he was thrust into a most rigorous imprisonment and was compelled by Your Fraternity to submit a petition in which he would confess the charges brought against him.

[Note: *Letter VII.* See Novel 83, concerning financial and criminal cases involving clergy.]

In the petition which he submitted, he is found to have agreed with your judgment concerning the financial charges. But he passes over the criminal charges by a certain doubtful and ambiguous path of words, so that he might both frustrate your intention, which was concealed beneath certain veils, and himself withdraw from confession behind the obscurity of a perplexed expression.

[Note: We have judged that this is how the passage should be emended, with Vatican A providing guidance. The reading of the printed editions, *imperplexae*, does not fit what precedes.]

When the appeal submitted by his representatives, together with the other matters conducted before you, had been conveyed to the most devout emperors, they appointed our deacon Honoratus and Sebastian, the illustrious *antigrapheus*, as commissioners. After everything had been carefully examined, the most serene lords released him from all the commands.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts A and C read *antigrapheo*. The Norman manuscripts support this reading. Concerning this office, see Book I, Letter 29. Consult Cangius’s glossaries, both Latin and Greek.]

But by certain carefully devised machinations another imperial command was again extracted, ordering John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, to conduct a careful investigation and judgment concerning all the charges mentioned above. In his tribunal all of Bishop Adrian’s clergy, and the deacon Demetrius under torture, declared that this entire accusation against Bishop Adrian had been fabricated through Your Fraternity’s machinations.

Nor was any of the criminal charges that had been brought against Bishop Adrian in your court proved against him. Rather, a cruel and deceitful examination was conducted against the deacon Demetrius and certain other persons, contrary to the canons and the laws. In that examination almost nothing was found by which the often-mentioned Adrian ought lawfully to have been condemned, but rather grounds on which he could have been acquitted.

[Note: The Norman and Regius manuscripts perhaps read: “nothing at all.”]

But concerning John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, and his most wicked judgment, which deserves condemnation, we shall treat elsewhere, with the Lord’s help. We have found, however, that Bishop Adrian suffered both from your hatred, contrary to priestly conduct, and that Your Fraternity condemned him in financial cases without any legal basis.

Therefore, since he had been deposed by the aforesaid John, bishop of Prima Justiniana, contrary to the law and the canons, he could not be deprived of the rank of his honor. We have decreed that he be restored to his own Church and recalled to the order of his proper dignity.

Although you ought to have been deprived of communion in the Lord’s body because, having disregarded the admonition of my predecessor of holy memory—which removed him and his Church from the jurisdiction of your authority—you had again presumed to retain some jurisdiction over them, nevertheless, acting more humanely and meanwhile preserving for you the sacrament of communion, we decree that Your Fraternity abstain entirely from the jurisdictional authority which you previously exercised over him and his Church.

Instead, in accordance with the letters of our predecessor, if any case concerning faith, crime, or money should arise against the aforesaid Adrian, our fellow priest, it is to be heard either by those who are or shall be our representatives in the royal city, if the matter is of moderate importance, or, if it is serious, it is to be brought here to the apostolic see, so that it may be settled by the judgment of our court.

But if at any time, on any occasion or by any seizure of opportunity, you attempt to act against what we have established, know that you are deprived of holy communion; and we decree that you may not receive it, except at the final hour of your life, unless permission has been granted by order of the Roman pontiff.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts A and C read “unless it has been granted”; the Norman manuscripts read “unless it has been granted,” and so forth.]

For we establish this in harmony with the definition of the holy Fathers: whoever does not know how to obey the sacred canons is worthy neither to minister at the sacred altars nor to receive communion.
