[Note: Gussanville thinks the text should read: “nor is he worthy to receive communion or to minister at the sacred altars.” Our reading is clear, and we have derived it from the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

As for the sacred or other movable and immovable property of that Church, which Your Fraternity is said to have retained until now, you shall restore it to him without any delay. We attach to this letter a record of the property that has been reported to us.

[Note: The printed editions read *diceris*, “you are said.” The manuscripts correctly read *dicitur*, “it is said”—namely, “Your Fraternity is said to retain.”]

If any dispute arises between you concerning these matters, we wish it to be aired before our representative in the royal city.

(See above, Letter 6. Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 26.)

## LETTER VIII. TO NATALIS, ARCHBISHOP

He orders that Florentius, a bishop deposed without a council’s judgment, be recalled from exile and that his case be reconsidered after the bishops have been summoned.

Gregory to Natalis, archbishop of Salona.

Since all matters require careful investigation of the truth, those that concern the removal of priests from their ranks must be weighed with particular strictness. In such matters it is not merely a question of the humble positions that have been established, but, in a certain sense, of resistance to divine blessing.

[Note: *Letter VIII.* The printed editions read “of human matters.” We follow the Corbie, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

This consideration also moved us to address Your Fraternity concerning the person of Florentius, bishop of the city of Epidaurus, for your encouragement.

[Note: Epidaurus, commonly Ragusa, is a maritime city of Dalmatia, now self-governing and the capital of the republic, though tributary to the Turks. It has a famous commercial harbor and the strong fortress of Saint Lawrence. Formerly it was only an episcopal city under the metropolitan of Sirmium in western Illyricum; today it is an archbishopric. It was greatly devastated by a terrible earthquake in 1567. Several cities, together with certain neighboring islands, are subject to this republic.]

We have been informed by certain persons that he was accused in criminal cases and that, without any canonical proofs being sought and without the judgment of a priestly council being rendered, he was unlawfully deposed from the office of his dignity by authority.

[Note: The printed editions read “with judgment having preceded.”]

[Note: Since a harmonious judgment of the priests in synod had removed him from the episcopal rank without just causes, a synodal inquiry, episcopal deliberation, and canonical proof were necessary. The following letter repeats the same point in the clearest terms.]

Since no one can be removed from the rank of the episcopate except by the judgment of a united body of priests and for just causes, we urge Your Fraternity to have the aforesaid man brought out of the exile into which he has been thrust and to have his case investigated by episcopal deliberation.

If he is convicted by canonical proof in the matters of which he has been accused, he must without doubt be punished with canonical retribution. But if a synodal inquiry establishes that the matter is otherwise than it has been judged to be, then the accusers too must fear the proper rigor of the law, while the accused must retain unimpaired the support of his innocence.

[Note: It is established by the canons that bishops are judged by synods; we have discussed this above, Book I, Letter 82, now 84, or certainly by twelve bishops, as Leo IV acknowledges in his letter to the bishops of Britain. This follows canon 12 of the Council of Carthage.]

[Note: Grammarians show that not only Junius but also Apuleius and Cicero used the verb *criminor* in the passive sense.]

We have entrusted the execution of the aforesaid matter to our subdeacon Antoninus, according to our instruction, so that through his diligence both what is approved by the laws and canons may be decreed and, with the Lord’s help, what has been decreed may be carried into effect.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 28.)

## LETTER IX. TO ANTONINUS, SUBDEACON

He is to see that all Florentius’s property is restored to him if he is acquitted by the bishops who have been summoned.

Gregory to Antoninus, subdeacon.

It has come to our attention that Florentius, bishop of the city of Epidaurus, after his property had first been seized, was condemned for certain crimes that had not been proved, without a priestly council.

Since no one ought to suffer canonical punishment when a canonical judgment has not been pronounced in his condemnation, we instruct Your Experience to press our brother and fellow bishop Natalis, so that he may have the aforesaid man brought out of the exile into which he is now said to have been thrust.

[Note: *Letter IX.* Florentius had not yet been restored in February, indiction 1. See Book VIII, Letter 10.]

After a council of bishops has been summoned, if the matters of which he has been accused are canonically proved, we wish the judgment of our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Natalis to have its proper force against him. But if he is acquitted by a general judgment, do not thereafter permit him to be subjected to anyone’s prejudice, and have his property restored through the strict diligence of your care.

The more heavily you weigh the importance of such matters, the more promptly and vigilantly you must strive to complete their execution.

## LETTER X. TO SAVINUS, SUBDEACON

Gregory accepts and venerates the four books of the Gospel in the same way as the four councils. He declares that the faith of Chalcedon was not violated at the Fifth Synod. Savinus must therefore return to the unity of the Church.

Gregory to Savinus, subdeacon.

Wicked men who have departed have disturbed your minds, understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions. They claim that something was diminished concerning the holy Council of Chalcedon in the time of Justinian of pious memory, although we venerate that council with complete faith and devotion.

And just as we receive the four books of the holy Gospel, so we receive the four councils of the holy universal Church.

[Note: We have explained what was done concerning them in Book II, Letter 51.]

[Note: Observe how ingenious charity is here, how great its desire for unity and its hatred of schism: it covers the truth, as it were, with an added salve, so as to soften the mind of this subdeacon and reconcile him to the Church. Read Book IV, Letter 39, to Constantius, where he says that the matter concerned persons about whom nothing is contained in the Council of Chalcedon.]

[Note: What Gregory teaches here is expressed in nearly the same words in Book IV, Letter 39. The holy Doctor’s meaning is that whatever was established outside or beyond the definition of faith concerning persons or other matters does not pertain to the Council of Chalcedon. This is also the teaching of Pelagius II, especially in Letter 3 to Etius and the other bishops of Istria, which we said above was written by Gregory. The principal reason for refusing to accept certain things enacted in the final sessions as belonging to the Council of Chalcedon was that they had been established either in the absence of, or against the opposition of, the apostolic legates and without the approval of Saint Leo.]

As for the persons concerning whom something had been done after the council’s conclusion, the matter was discussed during the time of Justinian of pious memory. It was handled in such a way, however, that the faith was not violated in any respect and that nothing was done concerning those persons beyond what had been established at the same holy Council of Chalcedon.

But we anathematize anyone who presumes to diminish anything from the definition of faith delivered at that council, or to alter its meaning under the pretext of correcting it. We preserve it in every respect exactly as it was delivered there.

You, therefore, dearest son, ought to return to the unity of the holy Church, so that you may bring your life to its end in peace. Otherwise the evil spirit, who cannot prevail against you through other works, may find in this matter a means of opposing you, at the hour of your departure, at the entrance to the heavenly kingdom.

## LETTER XI. TO THE ALBAN ORDER AND PEOPLE

He has appointed a bishop for them.

Gregory to the order and people residing in Albano.

[Note: *Letter XI.* Albanum, commonly Albano, is a city of Latium that grew from the ruins of Alba Longa. It lies fourteen miles from the city of Rome and is one of the six older cardinal bishoprics traditionally assigned to the cardinal order.]

We have brought no delay to your worthy desires. For we have appointed our brother and fellow bishop Hominobonus as your priest.

[Note: That is, “approved,” “good,” or “laudable.” Vincentius of Lérins, *Commonitory* 1, chapter 4, and *Commonitory* 2, chapter 1, says that in questions a Catholic Christian should consult the opinions of those who have proved themselves worthy teachers.]

In the month of November, indiction 11.

## LETTER XII. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP

He is to send to Rome the accusers of Gregory, bishop of Agrigentum, and the documents pertaining to his case.

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

Some time ago I wrote to Your Fraternity that you should send to the city of Rome those who had made certain accusations against Gregory, bishop of the city of Agrigentum.

[Note: Gregory the Great ordered Gregory of Agrigentum and Leo of Catania to come to Rome, indiction 9, Book I, Letter 72. Leo returned to Catania completely acquitted, indiction 10, Book II, Letter 33. Gregory of Agrigentum awaited his accusers in Rome.]

We now urge you through this present letter to ensure that this is done with still greater urgency. Therefore send the men themselves, together with the other documents—that is, the records and petitions that were submitted—with all speed.

We absolutely do not permit any delay or excuse to be sought. Once they have been sent promptly to the city of Rome, as we have said, we shall know, with the Lord’s help, what more beneficial disposition we ought to make concerning his person.

## LETTER XIII. TO AGNELLUS, BISHOP

He appoints Agnellus over the Church of Terracina in such a way that he does not remove from him the rights or authority of the Church of Fundi.

Gregory to Agnellus, bishop of Fundi,

who is now incardinated in the city of Terracina.

[Note: *Letter XIII.* Fundi, commonly Fondi, is still an episcopal city in Latium.]

The report of the clergy and people residing at Terracina has greatly gladdened us, because it bears good testimony concerning Your Fraternity.

[Note: The matters that follow belong to the inscription and are absent from the Norman manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and two Teller manuscripts. They occur in three Vatican manuscripts.]

Since, after the death of their bishop Peter, they ask that you be appointed their cardinal priest, we have judged that their wishes must necessarily be fulfilled, so that they may rejoice that they have obtained what they request and we may appear to have granted what is expedient.

[Note: *Postulatio*, “petition,” “request,” “desire,” and “election,” and likewise *postulari*, “to be requested,” “desired,” or “elected,” are used here for the same thing, whether clergy or people are in view. “We have greatly praised your election,” he says in the following letter. Yet *postulare* is stronger than *petere*, “to ask.” Thus in Curtius, concerning Darius, who was defeated yet wished arrogantly to dictate terms of peace, we read: “He demanded rather than asked that…” Gussanville’s distinction notwithstanding, petition and election differ to some extent. See the notes to Book II, Letter 39.]

Since, because of the devastation caused by the enemy, no one is permitted to live either in your city or in your Church, we therefore appoint you, by our authority, cardinal priest of the Church of Terracina. We admonish you to be concerned, with God’s protection, for the souls of the people residing there, so that the snares of the crafty and perverse enemy may not harm the flock entrusted to you by any device. Let your flock, enclosed by the protection of your care, rejoice that it has obtained the guardianship of a worthy shepherd.

Let your conduct provide the people with examples of good living; let avarice have no strength in you. By your preaching, let those who do not know letters learn what God commands. Let your way of life teach the people whom you govern how they may live in the fear of God. Practice in your deeds what you teach and preach to your subjects. Let your actions contribute to the correction of others, and let them take the imitation of your life as an aid to themselves.

Hasten to display yourself in all your works in such a way that whoever either neglects instruction through reading or is unable to be formed by reading may nevertheless find in you a living text and structure.

[Note: Vatican A reads “and inscription.” Another reading, found in the Norman, Tours, and other manuscripts, is “construction.”]

With the full attention of your mind, therefore, hasten to win souls for our Lord in such a way that a reward worthy of you may be found before him on the day of recompense.

Whatever you carefully and canonically arrange or provide for concerning the property of the aforesaid Church, its patrimony, the appointment or advancement of its clergy, and everything generally pertaining to it, you shall have complete authority to carry out in every respect, as its proper priest.

It is also necessary for Your Fraternity to know that, although we have appointed you cardinal priest of the aforesaid Church of Terracina,

[Note: In earlier centuries, if one considers the word itself, bishops and presbyters were called by the same name among Greek and Latin authors, even in the sacred books. See Jerome, Letter 85, to Evagrius; Theodoret, at the beginning of his Letter to the Philippians and in his commentary on 1 Timothy 3; and Acts 20:17. In Saint Gregory, a bishop is scarcely ever designated by the name “presbyter”; more often he is called “priest.” A cardinal priest is a proper priest, as though permanently attached to a title. In Saint Gregory and others, *incardinare* means to establish a bishop, abbot, presbyter, or deacon in a particular Church. See Book I, Letter 15; Book IX, Letters 9, 10, and 86; Book X, Letter 3; and Book XII, Letter 11.]

you must nevertheless not cease to be bishop of the Church of Fundi or neglect its care and governance. For we command Your Fraternity to preside over the aforementioned Church of Terracina in the manner we have stated, without in any way removing from you the rights or authority of the aforesaid Church of Fundi.

(See below, Letter 24. Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 15.)

## LETTER XIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF TERRACINA

He urges them to obey their bishop Agnellus in everything.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at Terracina.

The petition which you presented and conveyed to us has disclosed the desires of your affection, and we have greatly praised your election, because you earnestly request that our brother and fellow bishop Agnellus, already approved by his merits, be appointed your cardinal priest.

[Note: This is how the passage is read in the Tours and Saint Gatien manuscripts.]

Since a favorable and praiseworthy petition ought neither to be denied its fulfillment nor burdened with delay, we have therefore, in accordance with your wishes and request, established the aforesaid Agnellus, by a formal command, as cardinal priest of your Church.

For this reason I admonish Your Affection with paternal exhortation that you must render him obedience in all things, so that, strengthened by the support of your charity, he may, with the Lord’s help, successfully fulfill the care and governance of the Church which he is known to have undertaken at your request.

In the month of December, indiction 11.

## LETTER XV. TO SCHOLASTICUS, THE JUDGE

When Florentius the subdeacon declined the episcopate by fleeing after being elected by the Neapolitans, another must be considered for election.

Gregory to Scholasticus, judge of Campania.

[Note: In some editions, “to the duke of Campania.”]

While we were deeply distressed that the city of Naples had been deprived of the assistance of a bishop, the bearers of the present letter arrived with a decree drawn up for our subdeacon Florentius, and amid so great a burden of thought we found in it some relief.

[Note: Vatican C reads “they had indicated.” The printed editions agree with this.]

But when our aforesaid subdeacon, fleeing that city, tearfully avoided his ordination, know that our sadness increased, as though because of an even greater dispensation.

[Note: The printed editions have “from a certain despair,” a reading supported by some manuscripts.]

Therefore, sending you greetings, we urge Your Greatness to summon the leading men or the people of the city and consider the election of another man who may worthily be advanced to the priesthood with Christ’s help. Once a formal decree has been made and sent to this city, let the ordination there finally proceed, with Christ’s assistance.

But if you do not find a suitable person to whom you can give your assent, at least choose three upright and wise men to send to this city in the name of the whole community, so that the entire people may consent to their judgment.

Perhaps, when they come here, by the mercy of God they will find someone who may be irreproachably ordained bishop for you. Thus your deserted city may lack neither an inspector of its conduct within nor, through the care provided by a bishop, an opening through which hostile snares may enter from without.

(See above, Letter 1. Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 8.)

## LETTER XVI. TO PETER, BISHOP

He commends the presbyter Valerian, who has arrived to ransom captives.

Gregory to Peter, bishop.

[Note: The heading of this letter differs in the manuscripts and editions. The Norman, Rheims, and other ancient manuscripts read only “To Peter, bishop.” Vatican A reads “Letter to the bishop of Barcis”; B and C read “Letter to the bishop of Bancis,” as do the Colbert manuscripts. The Angers manuscript has “bishop of Bancis.” The Roman edition reads “bishop of Vibicis.” See the following note by Gussanville concerning Barcis.

We read *de Baricis* from the manuscripts of Moissac, Cluny, Cîteaux, the Sorbonne, Saint Victor, and others; some of these read *de Barcis*. The ancient editions agree: Venice 1504; Paris 1508, 1518, and 1586; Lyons 1539; and others. Later editions read *de Vibicis*, whose origin I cannot see.

*Baricis* is a corrupt form of *Barce*. From that city came the Barcaean people, whom Africans, speaking corruptly, call Baricians, says Saint Jerome in Letter 129 to Dardanus, although the common editions of Jerome read *Barcianos*. Erasmus’s emendation correctly gives *Baricianos*, as do the Roman edition of 1470, the Venetian edition of 1488, and the Lyons editions of 1508 and 1513. The same reading is found in the manuscripts of Saint Victor in Paris, Saint Theodoric of Rheims, and two manuscripts belonging to the distinguished Parisian cantor Claude Joly.

Barce was formerly a city of Africa and the metropolis of Libya; Scipio Africanus, after conquering Africa, made it tributary to the Roman people. Sidonius Apollinaris writes in poem 7:

> Which once, as captive, gave tribute to Barce.

It is now called Barca and is the chief city of the region of the same name, which lies between Egypt and the Great Syrtis along the Mediterranean Sea.

Gussanville adds that, according to Alteserra, captives were transported to Africa for commercial purposes, to be sold as slaves, and were especially put up for sale in the city of Barce. For this reason Gregory sent the presbyter Valerian to Africa to ransom captives and commended him to the bishop of Barce.]

Although we do not doubt that Your Fraternity willingly devotes itself to pious causes, nevertheless, because we think that our letter will make you more inclined to do so, we inform you by this present communication that the bearer of this letter, the presbyter Valerian, has come to those regions for the redemption of captives.

You ought to give him assistance in all things with the greater eagerness, the more you recognize that he has undertaken the labor of a long journey out of mercy (*merces*).

[Note: Gussanville proposed reading “without expectation of payment” or “with the expectation of an eternal reward.” But here *merces*, “reward,” is used for mercy, as in the French *merci*. It has the same sense in Book IV, Letter 31, and frequently in other authors. Hincmar, bishop of Laon, writes to King Charles: “I beseech your mercy, that your heart may be favorably disposed toward me.” Religious persons who devote themselves to ransoming captives are said to act “for the sake of the reward,” or, in French, *de la Merci*.]

In this way, with your assistance, he will accomplish what he intends, and Your Fraternity will find with God the great recompense for the aid you have provided, as you desire.

[Note: This is how the passage is read in the ancient Colbert manuscript and the Tours and Saint Gatien manuscripts.]

In the month of January, indiction 11.

## LETTER XVII. TO GRATIOSUS, SUBDEACON

He is to hand over the house of the abbess Flora, with its gardens and guest quarters, for the construction of a monastery.

Gregory to Gratiosus, subdeacon.

We ought to provide, with appropriate consideration, for those who choose the religious life, lest some occasion of necessity make them sluggish or, God forbid, weaken the strength of their way of life.

Therefore, by this present authority, we command you to hand over to the abbess Flora the house situated in this city, in the fourth region, near the place called “White Hens,” together with the garden belonging to the right of the holy Roman Church, over which, by God’s authority, we preside. Campana Patricia is known to have once lived in this house.

[Note: Vatican B and D, the Rheims manuscript, and the old editions have this reading. The Roman correctors noted that it should be read thus from an old Vatican codex.]

You are likewise to hand over the garden and the guest quarters enclosed by the door within the same house.

[Note: *Letter XVII.* The more recent editions added *ad*, so that the phrase would read, according to the rules of grammar, “near the White Hens.” The manuscripts—Vatican, Norman, and others—do not contain this preposition, nor do the old printed editions.]

She is to possess these properties unquestionably by right of ownership. In that house, with Christ’s help, she may construct a monastery in which she can live with her community. Thus both she and whoever succeeds her in her place and dignity may possess the aforesaid house and garden, with everything belonging to them, by the peaceful and undisturbed right granted by us out of pious consideration, as we have said.

## LETTER XVIII. TO THE COUNSELOR THEODORUS

He confirms in writing the gift of the boy Acosimus, already made to Theodorus.

Gregory to Theodorus, counselor.

Those who labor for ecclesiastical interests deserve to rejoice in ecclesiastical recompense, so that those who voluntarily subject themselves to the burdens of service may properly be consoled by our provisions.

[Note: *Consolari* is used passively in this sense by Gellius and Priscian.]

Since we have learned that you, Theodorus, our most eloquent counselor, have been deprived of the service of slaves, we therefore command that a boy named Acosimus, of Sicilian nationality, be given and handed over to your right and ownership.

[Note: To give is to transfer ownership, which can be transferred only to one who consents; therefore the transfer is completed by the recipient’s acceptance. The person accepting the delivery acquires no right merely through acceptance. According to Cujacius, delivery is the giving of possession. Thus ownership is acquired here by the giving, while possession alone is acquired by delivery.]

Since you already possess him, having received him by our will, it was necessary for you to be supported by the authority of this document as testimony and confirmation of the gift for the future, so that, under the Lord’s protection, you may always possess him securely and without fear of anyone’s attempting to revoke the grant, as his owner.

For we do not think that anyone will wish or attempt in any way to revoke so small a gift granted to you because of your devotion, since at one and the same time it is shameful to undo what has been well done by predecessors and shameful to teach others that one may someday issue a decision revoking one’s own generosity.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “and it is to be feared.”]

## LETTER XIX. TO PETER, SUBDEACON

He is to send relics of Saint Severinus for the consecration of a church.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

Our heart is pierced by the pious inspiration of the Godhead when we dedicate places once assigned to detestable errors to the reverence of the Catholic religion.

[Note: *Letter XIX.* Concerning consecration, see Distinction 1, chapters 20–22, on the dedication and purification of churches. I would scarcely dare to assert that churches of Catholics seized by Arians or other heretics and later restored to Catholics were always dedicated anew by a new rite. Gussanville. Whatever may be true of earlier centuries, Gregory, certainly well versed in the rites of the Church, reconsecrated basilicas polluted by heretics. See Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 30.]

Since we desire to consecrate, in honor of Saint Severinus, the church situated near the Merulana house in the third region, which Arian superstition held for a long time,

[Note: He may be the man called the apostle of the Noricans, whose remains were later transferred to Naples. See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book I, chapter 19, and Eugippius, abbot, in the *Life of Saint Severinus*. Concerning his relics, see below, Book IX, Letter 83, and Book XI, Letter 31.]

let Your Experience send the relics of the blessed Severinus with the greatest care and due reverence, so that, with the grace of the Almighty assisting us, we may fulfill what we have resolved in our hearts must be accomplished.

## LETTER XX. TO GRATIOSUS, BISHOP

He unites the Church of Saint Anthemius with that of Nomentum.

Gregory to Gratiosus, bishop of Nomentum.

[Note: *Letter XX.* Nomentum, or Numentum, was formerly an episcopal city of Valeria. It was succeeded by the fortress commonly called Lamentana, in the Sabine territory.]

After hostile impiety, through the agency of sins, had so devastated the Churches of various cities that, with the population declining, no hope of repairing them remained, we are constrained to exercise much greater care lest, when their priests have died, the remnants of the people—without any shepherd’s guidance—should, God forbid, be snatched away by the devious snares of the crafty enemy of the faith. Therefore, often admonished by concern for this matter [Note: Recent editors read “moved”], this plan settled in our heart: that we should entrust them to neighboring bishops to govern. And so we have determined to commit to your fraternity the care and governance of the Church of Saint Anthemius, situated in the territory of Cures among the Sabines [Note: They think this is the same as the bishopric of Cures among the Sabines. Cures was the principal city of the Sabines, now a village called Torre or Turre, on the river Himella, according to Leander. Others identify it with the village of Curese in the same region, near the monastery of Farfa. The Sabine region formerly extended farther than present-day Sabina. Moreover, Dulcitius, bishop of Saint Anthemius, subscribed to the third Roman synod under Symmachus, in the year 499, and to the sixth Roman synod under the same Symmachus, in 504. Yet he is expressly called bishop of the Sabines at the first Roman synod under the same Symmachus, in 504. GUSSANVILLE. It is worth noting the learned man’s conjecture that in the Normannian manuscripts one reads *sancti Anthemi*, not *sancti Anthemni*.], which must necessarily be joined and united to your Church, so that, with Christ’s help, you may rightly serve as priest of both Churches and carefully arrange whatever seems necessary to you concerning its property or the appointment and advancement of its clergy, in a vigilant and canonical manner; for, as its own bishop, you will have unrestricted authority by this present permission of ours.

Therefore, dearest brother, mindful of the Lord’s commandments, watch beneficially over the governance of the people entrusted to you and over the winning of souls, so that, when you stand before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, you may present to our Redeemer—so that you may rejoice in him—the fruit of good works that belongs to your reward. [Note: Thus the Turonian manuscript of Saint Gatianus and the old Colbert manuscript. I do not understand on what grounds Gussanville observes that this letter was written in February, in the eleventh indiction, when Letter 9 belongs to November. These chronological indications agree very well: since the indiction began in September, a letter given in November necessarily preceded one given in February.] In the month of February, in the eleventh indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapter 15.)

## LETTER XXI. TO PASCHAL, DEMETIANUS, AND CASTORIUS

He returns to orphans the property pledged to the Church by their father and entirely remits the money he owed.

[Col. 0620A]

Gregory to Paschal, Demetianus, and Castorius, sons of Urbicus, a defensor [Note: The words *from Tibur* are absent from most manuscripts. Tibur, commonly called Tivoli, was a city of Roman Campania and is still a bishopric.] from Tibur.

It is part of our office to provide such assistance to those deprived of their parents that, by releasing something of what is justly owed to the Church, we may be able to relieve their hardships. Therefore, after a careful examination of the matter, since it is established that your father Urbicus, formerly a defensor, died a debtor of a considerable sum from the Sabine patrimony and from Carsiolanum [Note: I have corrected the text in accordance with sixteen manuscript copies, since it formerly read *Cardolanum*. Holstenius reads *Cartiolanum* in the Vatican manuscripts. He argues that the reading should be *Carseolanum*. Carseoli stood at the junction of the territories of Tibur, Reate, and the Marsi. They are now in the land of the Marsi, on the opposite side of the mountain, and are commonly called *le celle Carsoli*. GUSSANVILLE. Vatican A reads *Cardiolano*. The Andegavian manuscript has *Harciolano*.], which had been entrusted to his administration, and although all his property is pledged to the Church for this reason, yet cannot suffice to repay what he had consumed, nevertheless, out of consideration for piety, we permit and grant you possession and ownership of the property of that same father of yours, which will doubtless benefit your interests. You may be confident that no one will again disturb you in any way concerning what we have released and granted to you. [Note: Thus it is read in the Turonian manuscript of Saint Gatianus and in the old Colbert manuscript.] In the month of March, in the eleventh indiction.

## LETTER XXII. TO ANTONINUS, SUBDEACON

He is to arrange for a bishop to be elected for Salona and ordained at Rome. He warns that only excellence of life and conduct should be considered in the election. He is to entrust the Church’s inventoried property to selected men for safekeeping. Bishop Malchus is to abstain from it and hasten to come to Rome to complete at last the accounts of the patrimony he administered.

Gregory to Antoninus, subdeacon and rector of the patrimony [Col. 0620C] in Dalmatia.

Rumor spreading throughout these parts has announced to us that Natalis, the brother and fellow bishop of our Church at Salona, has died. If this is true, let your Experience hasten with every diligence and concern to admonish the clergy and people of that city, so that by common consent they may choose for themselves a priest to be ordained. After a decree has been made concerning the person elected, you shall endeavor to transmit it to us, so that he may be ordained with our consent, as was done in former times.

Above all, take care of this: that in this election no payment of rewards, in any form, intervene, nor should the influence of any persons prevail. For if someone is elected through the patronage of certain individuals, once ordained he is compelled by the demands of respect to obey their wishes; and thus it comes about both that his Church’s property is diminished and that ecclesiastical order is not maintained. They must therefore choose for themselves, under your supervision [Note: Thus the Vatican and Normannian manuscripts, and others. Saint Gregory often uses this word to mean “to be pressing” or “to urge”; among the various meanings of the verb, this is the best here. Recent editions read “while you admonish.”], a person who will not serve any improper desire, but who may be found worthy of so great an office, distinguished by life and conduct.

As for the property and ornaments of that Church, have a faithful inventory of its goods written up in your presence. And to prevent anything from being lost from the property itself, admonish the deacon Respectus and Stephanus, the chief notary [Note: This term has such a broad range that it can scarcely be defined. I would say that it means the first person of any order, recorded in wax—that is, on a waxed tablet—or entered in a register. In all the Normannian manuscripts and in Vatican D one reads *chief notary*. Vatican A has *chief notary in the presence of notaries*. Notaries are listed among the lesser ecclesiastical orders, together with the defenders, says Alteserra in his commentary on this letter.], to take complete custody of the property, warning them that they will have to make restitution from their own resources if anything is diminished through their negligence.

As for Malchus, our brother and fellow bishop, we want you to charge him expressly not to involve himself in this matter at all. For if we learn that anything has been done or attempted through him against our will, he should understand that serious guilt and danger will attach to him. Also take care to admonish him that he must be diligent in rendering and completing the accounts of our patrimony that he administered; for this purpose, he must hasten to come to us from Sicily, setting aside every excuse.

Therefore, let him not presume in any way to interfere in the affairs of the Church of Salona, lest he become still more liable or culpable. For he is said to possess much of the property of the aforesaid Church, and common opinion almost asserts that he took part in selling its property or in other unlawful acts. If this proves to be true, as is said, by manifest evidence, let him be certain that this will by no means remain unpunished. [Note: The most equitable pontiff orders that the bishop’s election be conducted at the Church’s expense, because it is especially in the Church’s interest that a shepherd be ordained for it as soon as possible.]

[Note: Ancient practice considered the office of steward so necessary, and protected it with so many canons, that one may wonder not merely that it has been suppressed, but that its memory has almost been abolished and condemned. I say “condemned”; for who would dare revive it? Now clerics’ goods are no longer those of the Church, the poor, or the dispensers of the faithful, but become the private property of their masters. Once this door has been opened, evils and scandals of every kind rush into the Church, while every good man laments. Nor do I believe that the discipline of the clergy—so much desired and vainly attempted by so many expedients—can be restored by any better means than by freeing pastors from the administration of temporal goods. Thus greed, pride, and litigation would be restrained; the canons concerning the life and conduct of clerics would be put into execution; residence would be established; the study of letters would be encouraged; and men would devote themselves to God alone. Let the reader consider the Sixth Council of Paris, canon 29, and Saint Gregory there cited from the *Pastoral Rule*, book II, chapter 7. GUSSANVILLE.] Let the necessary expenditure be distributed through the steward who was found there at the time of the aforesaid bishop’s death, so that he himself may explain his accounts to the future bishop as he knows how. Indeed, you must conduct everything that we have commanded you to do with the advice of our son Marcellus, the most illustrious and eloquent [Note: Proconsul of Dalmatia. See book IX, letter 5.] man. In this way you will be able to fulfill carefully and energetically everything contained in this document of instruction, so that no fault of neglect may affect you.

## LETTER XXIII. TO PETER, SUBDEACON

Secundinus the abbot is to be deposed for his crimes, and Theodosius, requested by the community, is to be ordained in his place.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon in Campania.

Although dreadful and utterly detestable reports have reached our ears that Secundinus committed crimes, this alone can suffice for his condemnation: he is said to have confessed it himself. We have learned that he stated that, while he was third in succession to the position of abbot, he fell from the state of his religious habit into bodily transgression [Note: That is, he loosened the restraints of continence contrary to the purpose of a chaste life. Such an offense was formerly called, among higher clerics, a “fall,” in Greek *πτῶμα* (*ptōma*): partly because, as punishment for it, they fell from their ranks, and partly because they slipped from the purpose of their order, to which a vow of continence is attached. Below, in book XII, letters 30 and 31, we shall read of a bishop of Dioclea who was removed for this reason, and of another ordained in his place.].

Although, stained by so great a crime, he ought by no means to have advanced to the rank of abbot, nevertheless, since after this reckless act and such pollution he seized that office, though unworthy, we command your Experience, by the force of this authority, that after the aforesaid Secundinus has been removed from the office of abbot, you have Theodosius—whom the community itself requested to be ordained [Note: The Normannian manuscripts, with which Vatican D here and almost always agrees, omit *to be ordained*. Below, where we read “whose appointment is concerned,” they read only “whose concern it is.” The Corbian manuscript does likewise.]—solemnly ordained abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin by the person responsible for the appointment, so that, with God’s help, he may watch over the care of the community entrusted to him with prudent diligence. As for the estates and gardens of that monastery, defend them with ecclesiastical protection insofar as reason permits.

## LETTER XXIV. TO LEONTIUS, BISHOP

He is to govern the Church of Ariminum while Bishop Castorius is ill and absent.

Gregory to Leontius, bishop [Note: In all the Normannian and Colbert manuscripts, and in three Vatican manuscripts, the word *of Urbino* is absent. Urbino, commonly called Urbino, was formerly a bishop’s city in Umbria and is now an archbishopric.] of Urbino.

We are keeping Castorius, our brother and fellow bishop, here because of his bodily illness. Since he is now unable to return to his Church, we have therefore arranged to delegate to your fraternity, during his absence, the duty of visiting his Church. We admonish your Charity to administer all its interests so effectively that, through your presence, it will not feel that its own priest is absent.

Whatever you think should be arranged for the interests of that Church, you will in every respect have permission to do so from us. As for its revenues, ornaments, and furnishings, let your attentive concern and care preserve them securely. [Note: Vatican A and C read, “take care to secure them through your concern.” Vatican D, agreeing with the Normannian manuscripts, reads, “take care of them with the attention of your concern.” The Regius manuscript reads, “let your care preserve them securely.”] [Note: See above, letter 43, indiction 10.] Apart from the ordination of clergy, we want you to act in that Church in every other matter as its cardinal and proper priest. [Note: See above, book II, indiction 10, letter 45, and elsewhere.] (Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 52. See above, letter 9; below, letter 25; book V, letter 34.)

## LETTER XXV. TO THE CITIZENS OF ARIMINUM

He reproves them for their treatment of their bishop’s illness and orders them to obey Leontius in everything.

Gregory to all the inhabitants of Ariminum.

If you wish to consider your fault more attentively, dearest sons, you ought to purge yourselves before God by constant prayer, because you did not receive your bishop with a devoted mind or as sons should receive him. The unrest and affliction you inflicted upon him brought him to the point that he suffered bodily illness. Yet we have learned nothing of the matters reported to us concerning him; we have observed only that he is weak, and for that reason we have arranged to keep him here.

Since he is presently unable to return there, we have necessarily appointed our brother and fellow bishop Leontius as visitor of your Church [Note: For how provision should be made for a Church whose bishop falls ill, see below, book XIII, letters 5 and 6; also the Council of Meaux, canon 47, and the First Council of Orange, canon 30.]. We have also instructed him in our letters to arrange everything relating to the care and welfare of the Church as though he were its own bishop.

Therefore obey him in everything, so that, aided by your beneficial devotion, he may complete the visitation entrusted to him [Note: All the Vatican, Normannian, Corbian, and Rhegian manuscripts forced this restoration, whereas the text formerly read “by your virtue, beneficial in all things.” The word *jutus* troubles the editors, although it was familiar to our Gregory and not unusual among other writers, whether contemporary or earlier. Ennodius, book IV, letter 14, has *jutus magnitudine vestra* (“aided by your greatness”). And in the epithalamium addressed to Maximus: “Now aided by Pierian favor.” Here *jutus* and *jutum* mean *adjutus* and *adjutum*, “aided,” from the verb *juvo*, “I help.”]. (Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 52.)

## LETTER XXVI. TO MAGNUS, A PRIEST

He absolves Magnus, whom Bishop Laurentius had unjustly excommunicated. He urges him to serve his Church purely and diligently and to admonish the clergy and people to elect a suitable bishop without dissension.

Gregory to Magnus, priest of the Church of Milan.

Just as guilt properly requires someone to be excluded from sacramental communion [Note: The printed editions read “suspended.” We follow four Vatican manuscripts, the Normannian manuscripts, and others.], so such punishment must in no way be inflicted upon the innocent. We have learned that Laurentius, formerly our brother and fellow bishop, deprived you of communion although no guilt appeared in you [Note: The manuscripts unanimously read this. The more recent editions preferred to change *exstantibus* to *exigentibus*.]. Therefore, protected by the authority of this instruction of ours, carry out your office without fear and receive communion without any apprehension.

We have also considered it necessary to exhort you to present yourself in all the interests of your Church purely and diligently, so that no offense arising from neglect may affect you, and so that, if any fault in you is found—or has been hidden—for which you were deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood, you may wipe it away by the purity of your faith.

Admonish, therefore, the clergy and people not to disagree in any way when choosing a priest, but by common consent to choose for consecration as bishop a person whose actions are praiseworthy and whose character may be pleasing to God and to human beings. Otherwise, if the matter is handled differently, damage may befall ecclesiastical property through conflicting factions, God forbid. [Note: This chronological indication is confirmed by two Teller manuscripts, the Colbert manuscript, and the Turonian manuscript of Saint Gatianus.] In the month of April, in the eleventh indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 33. See below, letter 29.)

## LETTER XXVII. TO MARINIANUS AND BENENATUS

They are to investigate Bonifacius; if he is found guilty, he is to be deprived of holy communion and confined in a monastery.

Gregory to Marinianus, abbot of Palermo, and Benenatus, notary and rector of the patrimony of Palermo.

If we delay pursuing or punishing those things by which God is gravely offended, we provoke the patience of the Divinity to anger. For many reports of wrongdoing by certain people living in the city of Palermo have reached us. Since these matters require more serious correction, they must neither be believed rashly nor investigated negligently.

For this reason we instructed Victor, our brother and fellow bishop, that, if the reports were true, he should pursue and punish them. Now Bonifacius, a most illustrious man and bearer of this letter [Note: In the Normannian and Corbian manuscripts, *Victor Bonifacius* appears, with *most illustrious man* omitted.], has come here and complains that he was unjustly deprived of communion and forced to suffer other serious hardships at the hands of the aforesaid bishop.

Since no one should be condemned without an inquiry, we have written to that brother and fellow bishop of ours that, if a person who can testify concerning him is found, he should send that person to you for examination. We have therefore considered it necessary to exhort you by this document of instruction, so that, without regard to anyone’s status and keeping the fear of God before your eyes, you may investigate with complete impartiality whatever is said to you about him, mindful of the coming judgment.

If, in your inquiry, it becomes clear that he is guilty of some criminal offense, then by our authority he is to be not only deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood but also confined in a monastery, where he must perform penance [Note: Since public penance could scarcely be imposed upon men of high standing, the bishops of the Churches judged that they should be treated according to the manner used for clerics, namely, relegated to monasteries. A trace of this compromise appears in the Council of Narbonne, in the year 589, canon 6: “According to the councils of the ancient orthodox fathers, the fraternity decreed that, whenever a cleric or a distinguished citizen is found guilty and assigned to a monastery, the abbot in charge shall deal with the person sent to him as the bishop has expressly ordered. If the abbot chooses to act otherwise, he shall be suspended for a time as punishment, because the person is sent for the purpose of correction, not to be stuffed indiscriminately with various dishes.” See Baronius, under the year 598, numbers 31 and 32.], so that he may be able to cleanse the stains of his crime before the eternal Judge by fitting lamentation.

But if nothing is said against him in your inquiry, or if something is alleged but proves not to be true, and you cannot discover by any evidence that he committed what is reported, you must report everything to us. We do not want the aforesaid Bonifacius to suffer any harassment from anyone. For just as it is right that worthy punishment should proceed against offenders, so it is unjust that anyone should be subjected irrationally to various afflictions.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO ROMANUS, PATRICIAN

He recommends the needy and noble orphan Armenius to him and asks him to provide a position or employment from which he may be supported by daily income.

Gregory to Romanus, patrician throughout Italy [Note: This is how certain reliable manuscript copies read, and four English manuscripts agree with them. In others it reads: “To Romanus, patrician, and to the people throughout Italy.” Earlier editions read: “To all the bishops throughout Italy.” But three considerations lead me to reject this heading: first, “I love your Eminence”—he would not ordinarily address bishops in this way; second, “as you know, he has been deprived of both parents”—who would believe this known to all the bishops? Third, “your Piety should provide him with a position or employment”—not all the bishops could provide this. It is therefore clear that this letter was sent to some distinguished layman who could provide the magnificent Armenius with a position or employment—“a charge, an office,” in French. GUSSANVILLE. The Normannian, Michaelian, Gemetian, and Bec manuscripts, together with the English manuscripts, agree on the heading “To Romanus, patrician throughout Italy.” Others—namely, the Audoen, Lyr, and Pratel manuscripts—give “To the people throughout Italy.” Vatican A and D, the Rhegian, Corbian, and Andegavian manuscripts agree with this. Vatican B reads “to all throughout Italy.” The Colbert manuscript has “to the bishops throughout Italy.”].

Whatever is generously given out of compassion and consideration for piety both assists its giver here and brings him the desired reward on the day of recompense. Since this is so, and because I greatly love your Eminence, I am making known to you an opportunity for reward.

Armenius, a magnificent man, son of Antonius, formerly a most illustrious man, compelled me by his poverty to write to you on his behalf. Since, as you know, he has been deprived of both parents, he awaits the protection and support of your Eminence. [Note: Here this word means assistance—“subsistence,” in French. Pelagius I uses it in this sense in his letter 15 to Sapaudus, bishop of Arles. See above, book I, letter 5.] Therefore, may your Christian Charity, as is its custom, out of pious consideration and insofar as it recognizes what is useful, provide him with a position or employment [Note: Here *actio* means an action or administration; hence *actionarius*, one placed in charge of an action or administration. See above, book I, letter 44; below, book V, letter 44.], from which he may be supported by daily income. For this is the greatest praise and reward: to spend on orphans what, in return for their services, could have been provided to their parents.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE PRIESTS AND CLERGY OF MILAN

He does not press for the election of Constantius, although Constantius is well known and dear to him. He gives an excellent portrayal of what a pastor ought to be and of the electors’ proper attitude. From the disasters of the world he urges that its end and judgment are near.

Gregory to the priests, deacons, and clergy of the Church of Milan.

We received a letter from your Charity, but no signature had been included in it; nevertheless, the persons of the bearers, Magnus the priest and Hippolytus the cleric, gave it credibility. After rereading it, we learned that all of you agree concerning our son Constantius, a deacon of your Church, whom I had long known well. When I was giving the responses of the apostolic see in the royal city, he stayed with me for a long time, and I never found anything in him that could ordinarily be criticized [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts generally omit this word; it is present in the Normannian manuscript and in many others.].

Nevertheless, because it has always been the purpose of my earlier decision not to involve myself on behalf of any individual in matters concerning the assumption of the burdens of pastoral care, I support your election with prayers, asking that almighty God, who always foreknows our future actions, provide you with such a pastor that in his speech and conduct you may find the pastures of divine exhortation; in whose mind humility may shine together with uprightness, and severity together with compassion; who may show you the way of life not only by speaking but also by living [Note: In the Vulgate editions: “not only by reading or speaking.”], so that your Charity may learn from his example to sigh for the desire of the eternal homeland.

Therefore, dearest sons, warned by the authority of our office [Gratian, part VIII, question 2, chapter 2], we urge you, in this matter of receiving a bishop, not one of you to disregard the common good in pursuit of his own advantage. If anyone seeks his personal interests, let him not be deceived by a frivolous judgment, because a mind bound by desire cannot examine freely the person whom it ought to prefer.

Weighing, therefore, what benefits everyone, always offer complete obedience in all things to the one whom divine grace has placed over you. Once someone has been placed over you, he must no longer be judged by you; rather, he must be judged with such careful scrutiny now that afterward he will not be subject to your judgment. Once, by God’s authority, a pastor has been consecrated for you, entrust yourselves to him with your whole mind, and serve in him the almighty Lord who has placed him over you.

[Note: See book XXV of the *Moralia*, number 40 and following.]

But since pastors’ persons are commonly provided according to the merit of their peoples, seek spiritual things, love heavenly things, and despise temporal and passing things. Hold firmly to this certainty: you will have a pastor pleasing to God if you yourselves please God in your actions.

Behold, we now see all the things of this world ruined, the things we used to hear in the sacred Scriptures would perish. Cities overturned, fortresses torn down, churches destroyed; no cultivator inhabits our land. Among the very few of us who have been left behind for a little while, the human sword rages without cease amid the disasters of heavenly blows.

The evils of the world that we formerly heard would come, we now see; the wounds of the lands themselves have become, as it were, pages of books for us. In the destruction of all things, therefore, we must consider that nothing we loved had any lasting substance. Look with anxious mind toward the approaching day of the eternal Judge, and anticipate his terror through repentance. Wash away the stains of all your sins with tears. Restrain the anger that threatens eternally by temporal lamentation. For our merciful Creator, when he comes to judgment, will console us with greater grace insofar as he now sees that our sins are being punished by us.

We have sent the bearer of this letter, our subdeacon John, so that, with God’s favor, by his diligence [Note: That is, by pressing forward, insisting, and exerting himself. We have already shown that *imminere* can sometimes mean the same as “to urge” or “to press.”], he may cause your elected candidate to be consecrated bishop according to the custom established by his predecessor, with the support of almighty God.

For just as we demand that others respect their rights, so we preserve the rights of each individual. (See above, letters 26; below, letter 30.)

## LETTER XXX. TO JOHN, SUBDEACON

He is to investigate the wishes of the Milanese at Genoa; if they agree on Constantius, he is to have Constantius consecrated by his own bishops.

Gregory to John, subdeacon.

The higher the apostolic see is established, by God’s authority, above all Churches, the more this matter concerns us amid our many cares: namely, where our judgment is awaited for the consecration of a bishop [Note: This letter and the preceding one make it clear that the ordination and consecration of the bishop of Milan were formerly carried out by decision and with the consent of the Roman pontiff. After Constantius died, Saint Gregory sent Pantaleon the notary to arrange for Deusdedit, his successor, to be consecrated according to custom.].

Since Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan, has died, the clergy have informed us in their report that they unanimously agreed on our son Constantius, their deacon. But since that report was not signed, and we must omit nothing relating to precaution, you must therefore proceed to Genoa [Note: Genoa and Janua, commonly Genoa, a famous city of Liguria, now an archbishopric and the principal city of the republic of the same name, are sufficiently well known. GUSSANVILLE.].

Since many Milanese are staying there, driven together by barbarian violence, you must summon them and investigate their wishes collectively. If no disagreement separates them from the unity of the election, and you discover that everyone’s wishes and consent continue to rest on the aforesaid son of ours, Constantius, then have him consecrated by his own bishops, as ancient custom requires, with the assent of our authority, the Lord providing support.

By preserving this custom, the apostolic see will retain its proper authority, and will not diminish the rights it has granted to others. (Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 24. See above, letter 29.)

## LETTER XXXI. TO ROMANUS, PATRICIAN

He recommends Constantius, who is especially dear to him.

Gregory to Romanus, patrician and exarch of Italy.

We believe that your Eminence has already learned of the death of Laurentius, bishop of the Church of Milan. Since, as we have learned from the clergy’s report, the election of all rests upon our son Constantius, the deacon of that Church, it was necessary, in order to preserve the custom, to send a member of our Church [Note: Namely, John the subdeacon, who served among the clergy of the Roman Church.] who, after discovering that everyone’s wishes and consent harmoniously converged upon him, might have him consecrated by his own bishops, as ancient custom requires, though still with our assent. [Note: This letter and the preceding one establish that the bishop of Milan was a metropolitan and had suffragan bishops.]

Accordingly, fulfilling our obligation of greeting with fatherly affection, we ask that, whether the aforesaid Constantius has been consecrated bishop or not, your Eminence may, wherever necessary, deign to extend to him, with justice favoring it, your assistance [Note: Gussanville argues that *solatium* here means “reward.” But it more properly means “aid,” as we have already shown; it is often used in this sense in the Rule of Saint Benedict.], so that this reward may both exalt you here among your enemies and commend you in advance to God in the life to come.

He is particularly my own; he was once joined to me by great intimacy. And those whom you recognize as ours, you ought to receive as your own and love in a special way. (See above, letters 29 and 30.)

## LETTER XXXII. TO HONORATUS, ARCHDEACON

He confirms his absolution and entrusts to Antoninus the examination of the matters about which he had complained.

[Col. 0628D]

Gregory to Honoratus, archdeacon of Salona.

Long ago, an instruction from our predecessor and from us had been sent to your Belovedness, in which you had been absolved from the charges brought against you—charges made calumniously—and we had ordered you restored to the rank of your order without any dispute. But because, not long afterward, when you came to the city of Rome, you complained—improperly, as regards certain matters done there—about the alienation of sacred vessels, and while, on this account, we were detaining in this city persons who could have answered your objections, your bishop Natalis departed this life, we judged it necessary to confirm by the present letter both the instructions of our predecessor and our own, which, as stated, we had formerly sent for your absolution.

Therefore, absolving you more fully from all the charges brought against you, we wish you to remain in the rank of your order without any dispute, so that the inquiry raised against you by the aforesaid man may in no way prejudice you for any reason. But concerning the charges about which you complained, we have urgently instructed Antoninus, subdeacon and rector there of the patrimony of the holy Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside, that, if indeed he finds ecclesiastical persons implicated in these matters, he should determine the cases themselves with the utmost strictness and authority.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXII.—In several of our manuscripts the reading is *definiat* (“let him determine”); Antonius Augustinus agrees with this in Book III of his *Emendationes*, chapter 9. This concerns the word. As for the matter itself, in this subdeacon and in others I seem to see everywhere an image of ecclesiastical judges, whether ordinary judges—whom they call officials—or delegates; it may be worthwhile to have observed this. For our laws, at the assembly of Blois and in several judgments, provide that this office should be entrusted to no one but priests, even though under canon law and by the example of the supreme pontiffs it may appear capable of being entrusted to others. Certainly, if we judge the matter according to equity and justice, it is scarcely fitting that priests and bishops should be judged, interdicted, suspended, excommunicated, or absolved with supreme authority by a simple cleric or subdeacon. Indeed, we read that the Gallican clergy held the same view at a public assembly in 1625, when deliberation was given to the judgment of Étienne Louytre against the bishop of Lyon. They complained that episcopal dignity had been violated above all because a priest, a doctor of the Sorbonne and dean of Nantes, delegated by the Apostolic See, had judged a bishop. I point out this stone; I do not move it. Let others roll it. GUSSANV.]

But if the matter concerns persons over whom the force of ecclesiastical jurisdiction cannot extend, let him send us without any delay the proofs concerning each individual charge, deposited among the public records, so that, being thoroughly informed, we may know what we ought, with Christ’s help, to arrange concerning them. (See Book I, letters 19 and 20; Book II, letters 17 and 52. Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 9.)

## EPISTLE XXXIII. TO DYNAMIUS, PATRICIAN

He states that he has received four hundred solidi from the revenues of the Roman Church. He sends a cross filled with sacred relics.

Gregory to Dynamius, patrician of Gaul, etc.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXIII.—There is scarcely room to doubt that this was the Dynamius mentioned by Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book VI, chapters 7 and 11. He also wrote the Lives of several saints. Fortunatus celebrates his praises in Book VI of his poems, 11 and 12. At that time he did not disdain to administer the Gallic patrimony of the Roman Church. Yet two years later he ceased to administer it. See Book VI, letter 6: “But since Dynamius now cannot,” etc. We must nevertheless not conceal that Vatican A reads “to Damianus, patrician of Gaul”; Vatican B, “Dinomius”; Colbert, “Damio.” But in Vatican D, the Norman manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, and others, “Dynamius, patrician of Gaul” is read quite clearly.]

[Note: The title “patrician of Gaul” belonged at that time to those high officials whom either the kings of Burgundy entrusted with the government of the province of Arles, or the Austrasian kings of the Franks entrusted with the government of Marseille; and perhaps also to others who were governors of some province and supreme commanders in war. See Adrian Valesius, Book VI of *Frankish History*, and Bignon on the *Formulas of Marculf*, no. 35. Since, therefore, the Dynamius mentioned by Gregory of Tours was governor of the province of Marseille, and no other person of that name appears among the governors of Marseille or Arles during this period, an almost decisive argument follows that our Dynamius is not to be distinguished from the man mentioned by Gregory of Tours and Fortunatus. Moreover, Dynamius did not intrude a bishop into Marseille, as Gussanville supposes, but two into Uzès. See Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 7. Gussanville, following Adrian Valesius, *Frankish History*, Book XI, p. 137, wrongly attempts to prove from Gregory the Great, Book VII, letter 12, that this Dynamius lived religiously with his brother Aurelian after losing his wife. Consult the cited letter 12 and compare it with Book VII, letter 36, and Book XI, letter 74.]

He demonstrates how well a man manages his own possessions when he faithfully administers those of another. Your glory has shown this to us: devoted to an enduring offering, it has brought to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, the fruits of your revenues.

[Col. 0630B] By faithfully expending what belongs to him, you have made these offerings of yours with him. For it is fitting that the distinguished men of this earth, who think upon eternal glory, should act in such a way that, in what they possess temporarily, they prepare for themselves a reward that is not temporary. Therefore, offering you the due salutation of affection, we beseech almighty God both to fill your life with present blessings and to extend it to the exalted joys of eternity.

For through our son Hilary [variant: Hilarius] we have received four hundred Gallic solidi from the aforesaid revenues of our Church.

[Note: Since the distinction between Gallic and Roman solidi is not known to everyone, and since Gregory the Great frequently mentions solidi and their subdivisions, it will be worthwhile to explain it somewhat more fully. The gold coin received the name *solidus* under the emperor Constantine the Great. From then on, the words *solidus* and *aureus* designated the same coin in the Roman Empire. See Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 9. Around the same time the weight of the solidus was reduced. In Pliny’s time, forty-two gold coins were struck from a pound. Many maintain, from Book XII of the Theodosian Code, law 119, that under Constantine the Great there were eighty-four gold coins or solidi to the pound; Gronovius refutes them in Book IV, chapter 13, and proves that even then a pound of gold was divided into seventy-two solidi. The weight of the solidi was the same under Valentinian, as is clearly gathered from a law enacted in the year 367, *Theodosian Code*, Book XII, title 6, law 13, concerning receivers, superintendents, and treasurers: “Let a pound be reckoned as seventy-two solidi.” Thus there were six solidi in an ounce, four scruples in a solidus, and twenty-four siliquae. That the weight of the solidi remained the same in Gregory the Great’s time is shown by letter 38 of the second indiction, where Maurus, receiving merchandise worth four hundred solidi from Felix and promising six siliquae per solidus as profit, becomes debtor for five hundred solidi.

The ratio of gold to silver also varied at different times. From Pliny, Book XIX, chapter 1, it is gathered that in his time the ratio of gold to silver was twelve to one. Under Constantine the Great and his successors the same ratio was maintained until the year 396. In that year Arcadius and Honorius ordered that one gold solidus should be paid by the possessor for twenty pounds of bronze. *Code*, Book X, title 70, concerning the assessment of bronze. At that time six gold solidi equaled a pound of silver. In the year 397 the emperors ordered five solidi to be paid for each pound of silver; the ratio of gold to silver was now 1 to 14⅖, and one solidus equaled twenty-five pounds of bronze, or six thousand denarii. Cassiodorus attests this in *Variae*, Book I, letter 10: “They decreed six thousand denarii to be one solidus.” At that time among the Romans a solidus equaled fifty silver denarii.

Among the Franks, however, the twelvefold ratio of gold to silver persisted into the sixth century. This is clearly gathered from a notable passage in Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, in the *Life of Saint Remigius*: “In the testament drawn up by blessed Remigius, the reader should note that the quantity of solidi is reckoned as forty denarii, as solidi were then valued. The same is contained in the Salic Law of the Franks and continued generally until the time of Charlemagne, as is contained in his capitularies.” Forty denarii made two ounces of silver; six solidi made one ounce of gold. The chief distinction between the Gallic solidus and the Roman solidus, however, was that Gallic gold was far inferior to Roman gold. This will be clearer in Book VI, letter 7.]

We have sent the blessing of blessed Peter the apostle—a small cross into which gifts from his chains have been inserted.

[Note: Among the Greeks, *eulogia* (εὐλογία) means “a little gift.” See below, Book V, letter 48; Book VIII, letter 47; Book IX, letter 35; and Gregory’s *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 8; Gregory of Tours, Book VIII, chapter 7. In Holy Scripture itself, “blessing” is used for “gift,” Genesis 33:11.]

These gifts once bound his limbs for a time; may they free your necks from sins forever. Around its four sides are contained gifts from blessed Lawrence’s gridiron on which he was burned, so that this object, where his body was burned for the truth, may kindle your mind to love the Lord.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO PETER, SUBDEACON

He is to reconcile Bishop Festus with his fellow citizens.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

Brother and fellow bishop Festus complains that he is despised and scorned by his own clergy and citizens.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXIV.—Some read “Sixtus,” incorrectly. That he was bishop of Capua is clear from Book V, letter 12.]

[Note: The cause of the contempt about which Festus complained can be inferred from Book V, letter 33: it was his own avarice.]

For this reason we command your Experience to approach them with calm exhortation, so that, once any causes of hatred that may exist have been quieted, you may reconcile them in mutual and God-pleasing charity, so that he may provide what is fitting for sons, and they may offer what is proper to a father. If there are any other causes, we command you to provide the aforesaid bishop with assistance, subject nevertheless to justice and equity.

[Note: This reading occurs in the Norman manuscript, the Vatican manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, and the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus.]

In the month of May, eleventh indiction.

## EPISTLE XXXV. TO PETER, SUBDEACON

He is to send two or three men from the Neapolitan clergy to Rome, so that they may elect a bishop on behalf of all. The future bishop is to be supplied with necessities. One hundred solidi and one slave are to be given to Paul, who is withdrawing, as payment for his labor.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

Our brother and fellow bishop Paul has repeatedly asked us to allow him to return to his own Church.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXV.—We spoke of this bishop in Book II, letter 9. From letters 1 and 2 of this book it is known how unworthily he was treated at the Lucullanum estate near Naples. This perhaps explains his desire to revisit his own Church.]

Since we saw that this was reasonable, we necessarily judged that his request should be fulfilled. Therefore let your Experience approach the clergy of the Church of Naples, so that they do not fail to choose two or three of their number and send them here to elect a bishop. Let them also inform us by their report that those whom they send are to act on behalf of all in this election, so that, by God’s authority, a bishop may be ordained for that Church. For we can no longer tolerate its being without its own ruler.

If they should in any way attempt to delay your admonition, exercise ecclesiastical authority against them. Whoever does not willingly consent in this matter will thereby give evidence of his perversity.

But arrange for one hundred solidi and one orphan boy, whom he himself may choose, to be given from the same Church to our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Paul as payment for his labor. Warn those who come here on behalf of all to elect a bishop—

[Note: Vatican B and some others read: “so that they may bring the entire wardrobe of the bishopric.” Hence it appears that the bishop’s wardrobe was not the property of an individual but of the Church, and that it was customarily handed from hand to hand, as money was. Nowadays, however, designated bishops pay their annates from their own resources, purchase clothing, and incur expenses; by this arrangement every avenue to the episcopate is closed to the poor.

The word *vestiarium* is used either for a wardrobe or storage place for clothing, or for the wardrobe itself, necessary to each person according to his condition, as in the Digest, Book XXXIV, title 2, law 21. In Greek they write *vestiarium* (βεστιάριον) for a wardrobe or clothing establishment; *vestiarium, to entos* (βεστιάριον, τὸ ἐντός) for a storeroom; and *vestiarius* (βεστιάριος) for one who has charge of the wardrobe. Hence *paidopoulos tou vestiariou* (παιδόπουλλος τοῦ βεστιαρίου), the second official under the wardrobe superintendent, and *protovestiarios* (πρωτοβεστιάριος), the chief superintendent. See Codinus. Nicetas calls him *archizoupanos* (ἀρχιζούπανος), or simply *zoupanos* (ζούπανος), the chief superintendent of the imperial wardrobe. Partly from GUSSANV.]

—that they must understand that the entire wardrobe of their bishop is to be brought, and that they should bring with them as much silver as they foresee that the man who has been ordained bishop will be able to use for his needs.

Hasten to carry out all this vigorously and strictly, and send the chosen men here from the clergy with all speed, as we have said, so that, since various nobles of the city of Naples are presently here, we may together with them both discuss and, with the Lord’s help, deliberate about the episcopal ordination. (See Book II, letter 15.)

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO SABINUS, DEFENDER

He is to bring Bishop Januarius and the presbyter Epiphanius, accused of crimes, to Rome. He is also to assist Pompeiana, Theodosia, and Isidore if they wish to come to Rome.

Gregory to Sabinus, defender of Sardinia.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXVI.—The common editions add “and to Anthimius, subdeacon,” contrary to the authority of the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and Colbert manuscripts, and indeed contrary to the whole sequence of the letter, where the singular is used: “your Experience,” and below, “you shall investigate.”]

Some serious matters have reached our ears. Since they require canonical correction, we command your Experience, together with John the notary and setting aside every excuse, not to fail to bring here with the utmost urgency our brother and fellow bishop Januarius, so that, once he is present, what has been reported to us may be investigated by careful inquiry.

As for the religious women Pompeiana and Theodosia, if they wish to come here in accordance with their request, provide them with every assistance, so that, aided by you, they may fulfill their wishes.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and several others read “with the assistance of those who are accompanying them.”]

Above all, make it your concern in every way to bring with you, as he requested, the most eloquent Isidore, so that the nature of his case—which he is known to have against the Church of Caralis—may be weighed more closely and brought to a lawful conclusion.

Moreover, since certain crimes have been reported to us concerning the person of the presbyter Epiphanius, you must investigate everything more carefully. Whether it is the women with whom he is said to have committed sexual sin, or others whom you judge to know something about the same matter, hasten to bring them here together, so that the truth may be clearly disclosed to ecclesiastical strictness.

[Note: This is cited in the *Extravagantes*, “Concerning witnesses and testimony,” chapter 3. The Gloss notes: first, that women may be produced as witnesses against clerics; second, that accomplices in crimes may be admitted as witnesses; third, that in criminal matters the testimony of women is not accepted. Although women have always been excluded from petitions, testimony, accusations, and judgments for various reasons, it is nevertheless clear from the laws and customs of many peoples that they have often been admitted. See the Digest, “Concerning witnesses,” law 18; “Who may make a will,” law 20, section “A woman.” In canon law, see the *Extravagantes*, “Concerning witnesses,” chapters 3 and 33. Gratian, Cause 15, question 3, cites several passages from civil law. Current French practice shows that women are admitted both under French law and in ecclesiastical courts. As for accomplices in crimes, Alexander III says that they cannot testify, since they suffer from the same disease: *Extravagantes*, “Concerning witnesses,” chapters 10 and 20; and Clement III, “Concerning confession,” chapter 1. According to the provisions of both bodies of law, those who have confessed concerning themselves should not be questioned about the consciences of others. AUGET.]

You both shall take care to fulfill all these matters so effectively that no guilt for negligence may fall upon you, knowing that it entirely belongs to your danger if this instruction of ours should in any way be treated sluggishly.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO BONA, ABBESS

He orders a monastery to be built and confirms everything bequeathed to her by the presbyter John.

Gregory to Bona, abbess.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXVII [variant: 44, fourteenth indiction, and 49, second indiction].—The old edition reads “to Bonos, abbot.” This reading is confirmed by the ending of the letter, according to the Norman manuscripts, three Roman manuscripts, and several others: “not only by you but also by your successors”; hence the reference is to men, not women.]

Ecclesiastical welfare suffers no loss if, after the truth has been established, it restores property belonging to others. We have learned that John, formerly a presbyter of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, built an oratory in a house belonging to him in this city of Rome, near the Baths of Agrippa, and in that place left certain revenues as a bequest through the provisions of his will. In the same oratory he established a congregation of servants of God, and, so that all these things might be fulfilled as they ought, he is known to have assigned them by the page of his will to our predecessor of holy memory, Pelagius.

But because death prevented him from carrying this out, and because the house itself with its garden is being held by the agents of our Church, and because the will of the deceased has therefore not yet been fulfilled, justice strongly urges us to complete, through your diligence, this pious disposition and what was entrusted to our predecessor.

[Note: In the Norman manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts: “Our concern has completed the intention of this pious disposition; and what was entrusted to our predecessor we have foreseen must be completed. Therefore we judged it necessary that the oratory should be dedicated with the Lord’s protection. And because—”]
