Since, however, because of the difficulties of the time, a new congregation of servants of God could not be established there, we decree that a congregation of women should at least be founded, and for this reason that the place itself should be solemnly dedicated.

And because the monastery where you formerly lived had been placed in danger of ruin, we have determined, with God’s approval, that you should reside there in every respect with your congregation—

[Note: Beccarius and Pratellus read: “should reside there, so that a congregation could exist in the monastery of the aforesaid house and the impending danger to the property could be avoided. Hence—”]

—so that, in the monastery of the aforesaid house, a congregation might serve our Lord and Redeemer according to the will of the deceased, and you might avoid the impending danger.

Therefore it is necessary that both now and in future times the praises of God be celebrated there in every way by the congregation that exists now or that will succeed it.

Considering, therefore, the will of the aforesaid presbyter, we establish that a monastery is to exist there perpetually and that the same house, entire with its garden and the property listed below, which was left by the testator, is to belong to it by right of ownership: namely, the estate of Magulianum with its appurtenances, on the Nomentan Way at approximately the eleventh milestone; a shop in this city, situated near the Palacenes;

[Note: This is a place in the city of Rome where the monastery of Saint Lawrence the Martyr stood, mentioned by Anastasius the Librarian in his account of Gregory IV. GUSSANV.]

—and a *salgamum* situated before the house of the aforesaid monastery.

[Note: The word *salgamum*, perhaps derived from *sal* (“salt”), refers to whatever was preserved for food in vessels with salt or substances possessing the power of salt, such as apples, figs, grapes, cucumbers, and so forth. See Martini’s Lexicon. In Justinian’s Code, Book XII, title 42, there is a law “concerning *salgamum* not to be provided to guests,” which states: “Let no count, tribune, superintendent, or soldier extort from his hosts mattresses, wood, or oil in the name of *salgamum*.” Here, however, *salgamum* means a *cella salgamaria*, a storehouse or shop in which *salgamum* was kept and sold by *salgamarii*. The Council of Chalcedon complains, in its eleventh act, that *salgamarii* had been ordained bishops; hence the gravest damage to the Church.]

Your Belovedness must therefore watch over these matters diligently, so that the praises of God may be celebrated there, as we have said, with devoted and salutary zeal according to custom, and so that the aforesaid property belonging to it may not, through any negligence on your part, be lost for any reason.

We have established that not only you but also those who succeed you in the aforesaid monastery are likewise to provide this care concerning the monastery and the property described above.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Norman manuscript read: “not only by you but also by your successors in the aforesaid oratory.”]

[Note: The old Colbert manuscript adds at the end of the letter: “In the month of May, eleventh indiction.”]

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO LIBERTINUS, PREFECT

He is to punish Nasas the Jewish deceiver and free the Christian slaves purchased by him.

Gregory to Libertinus, prefect of Sicily.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXVIII [variant: 37].—The Corbie, Pratell, and Michaelino manuscripts read “to Libertinus, praetor.” The Rheims manuscript and Vatican D read “former praetor.” If one of these readings had to be chosen, we would prefer the first. Saint Gregory complains below about Justinus, who had been praetor of Sicily, as is shown by Book I, letter 2, addressed to him; and here he admonishes Libertinus, who may have been appointed his successor, to correct what Justinus had neglected to remedy. Nevertheless, we retain “prefect,” because it is read in three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, five others, and most of the rest. It was no less the prefect’s responsibility than the praetor’s to remove the abuses about which the holy pontiff complains.]

From the very beginning of your administration, God wished you to proceed as the avenger of his cause, and in his mercy he has preserved this reward for you with praise. For it is reported that a certain most wicked Jew named Nasas, under the name of blessed Elijah, built an altar with punishable audacity and deceived many Christians there by sacrilegious seduction into worshipping it. It is also said that he purchased Christian slaves and assigned them to his service and advantage.

Although the distinguished Justinus ought to have punished him most severely for such crimes, he was, as we have been informed, softened by the medicine of avarice and delayed avenging the insult to God.

[Note: See the Code, Book I, title 9, “Concerning Jews and worshippers of the heavenly bodies,” the law beginning “Certain Jews,” where Jews are forbidden to counterfeit Christian rites, incorporate the cross into their practices, and so forth. GUSSANV. The holy Doctor does not disapprove of the worship and honor shown to Elijah, but of the wicked arts of the most wicked Jew. We nevertheless read that a temple of the holy prophet Elijah was built at Petrion by the emperor Zeno after his return from the Persian expedition. In the church of Elijah, which they called the Lord’s church, there is an epigram by Gregory of Nazianzus in Leunclavius’s edition. It remains true, however, that in the Latin Church, at least until the time of Saint Bernard, no feast day of Saint Elijah had been established; Bernard, in letter 98 of the new edition, answers the question why the Church assigned a feast day among the just of the Old Law only to the Maccabees.]

Let your Glory investigate all these matters with strict examination. If you find that the report is true, hasten to punish that wicked Jew most strictly and bodily, so that by this act you may both win the favor of our God and offer yourself to later generations as an example worthy of imitation in return for your reward.

As for the Christian slaves—

[Note: In the Code, Book I, title 10: “A Jew shall neither purchase a Christian slave nor acquire one by gift or any other title. If any Jew should . . . he shall be punished not only by loss of the slave but also by capital sentence,” etc. The following law states: “A Greek, or pagan, or Jew, or Samaritan, or any other heretic—that is, one who is not orthodox—may not possess a Christian slave,” etc. See distinction 54 and the *Extravagantes*, Book V, title 6, “Concerning Jews,” chapter 2. Below, there are frequent references to Jews, as well as in the councils of Gaul, where more matters appeared to have been permitted to Jews; pursuing these is not our purpose. GUSSANV. See below, Book IV, letter 21, and Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book IV, chapter 27, where he reports that the pious emperor enacted a law forbidding any Christian to serve Jews; and that if a slave of the Christian religion were found in a Jew’s possession, the slave was to be granted freedom and the Jew fined.]

—bring every one whom he is shown to have purchased unequivocally to freedom, in accordance with the commands of the laws, lest, God forbid, the Christian religion be polluted by subjection to Jews.

Correct everything, therefore, with the utmost strictness and all possible speed, so that we may not only thank you for this discipline but also, when necessary, offer testimony to your goodness. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 43.)

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO THE BISHOPS OF CORINTH

He sends a deacon to investigate the reported reconciliation between Adrianus and the bishops who accused him.

Gregory to all the bishops of Corinth.

It is our desire that those who are at odds should return to harmony, and that those whom a difference of will makes divided in affection should be united in grace.

Reading, therefore, the letter of your Fraternity again, we learned that those who had said certain things against our brother and fellow bishop Adrianus had now made peace with that bishop, and we have at present felt great joy at their unity.

[Note: Perhaps this is the man whom Gregory absolved after he had been unjustly condemned by certain bishops, in letters 6 and 7 of this indiction. GUSSANV.]

But because we do not tolerate what was said remaining unexamined, we are sending a deacon of our See to investigate these matters. The nature of the crime reported to us strongly impels us not to disregard what we have heard, especially since you have indicated that the accusers and the accused have made peace with one another. We must examine this more carefully, lest their agreement prove to have been contrived. If, God forbid, it should be established that it was made not from charity but in return for a reward, it must be punished by a more serious correction.

For we, who hasten, with God revealing them, to remove evils that are indeed true by canonical means, cannot in any way leave a fault subsequently committed without punishment.

[Note: The Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus, agreeing with the Paris edition of 1518, adds: “In the month of June, eleventh indiction.”]

## EPISTLE XL. TO PETER, SUBDEACON

He is to send the deacon Numerius to Rome for consecration if he judges him worthy of the episcopate. If the servant-girl Catella sincerely seeks the monastic habit, he is to redeem her from Felix.

Gregory to Peter, subdeacon of Campania.

A few days ago we wrote to you that you ought to question Numerius, deacon of the Church of Nuceria, with care—

[Note: EPISTLE XL [variant: 39].—Nuceria was formerly a city of Campania in Picenum, now in the Principality of Citerior in the Kingdom of Naples; it remains an episcopal see under the archbishop of Salerno.]

[Note: That is, inquisitively and diligently; Gregory frequently uses the word in this sense. In the following letter: “You shall take care to learn the truth with all care,” that is, with the utmost zeal and concern. Likewise in letter 42: “Let him carefully describe each one.”]

—and, if there were nothing that could prevent him from attaining the priestly rank, send him here to be consecrated, with God’s authority. Therefore, if, after carrying out the inquiry we mentioned, you are going to send the aforesaid deacon to us, take care to admonish the clergy and people of that city not to delay coming with him, as many as are able, so that, in their presence, if it pleases God and he is to be ordained, he may be consecrated.

Moreover, since the defender Felix is said to possess a girl named Catella, who, with many tears and intense longing, desires the monastic habit, but whose aforesaid master does not permit her to be converted—

[Note: “To be converted,” that is, to be clothed in the habit of conversion, to become a nun or servant of God, means the same thing. The law of nature commands, the Gospel confirms, the canons acknowledge, and emperors and kings establish that slaves are not to be admitted to the habit of conversion without their master’s consent. It is a principle of natural law that each person’s right be preserved. Paul says, 1 Timothy 6: “Let all who are under the yoke as slaves,” etc.; and adds, “If anyone teaches otherwise,” etc. The Fathers—Ambrose, Primasius, Jerome, Chrysostom, and other ancient writers—explain this passage, and modern commentators agree with them. On the canons, see Apostolic Canon 81; Canon 4 of the Council of Chalcedon; Canon 3 of the Council of Gangra; and chapter 23 of the Aachen capitulary. Pope Gelasius decrees deposition and excommunication against those who act otherwise. This is cited in distinction 54, together with several other authorities. See also the *Extravagantes*, Book I, title 18.

Concerning the monastic profession of slaves without their master’s knowledge or against his will, the reader may consult the constitutions of the emperor Leo, 9, 10, and 11, which it will not be unpleasant to read. The emperors nevertheless enacted more severe measures against unbelieving masters, especially Jews, as we observed above in letter 38. See the *Authenticum*, Novella 5, chapter 2, and Novella 123, chapter 4.

Hence later canons enacted many provisions in favor of slaves, as in the *Extravagantes*, “Concerning Jews,” chapters 1 and 2, Book V: “Slaves are not taken away from faithful masters, but are freed upon payment of a price.” Hesselius treats this subject more fully in his commentary on Paul, 1 Timothy 6; consult him. The same matter is frequently mentioned in the following letters. GUSSANV.]

—we therefore wish your Experience to visit the aforesaid Felix and carefully inquire into the girl’s disposition.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read: “Let him see Felix.”]

If you find that it is as reported, offer the girl’s price to her master and send her here, with God’s help, accompanied by respectable persons, so that she may be given to a monastery.

Act in such a way that, through any delay in your action, the soul of the aforesaid girl may suffer no harm in fulfilling her desire.

## EPISTLE XLI. TO PANTALEON, NOTARY

The violator of a virgin must either marry her or, after corporal punishment, be forced into a monastery. A deacon held captive is to be redeemed at the Church’s expense.

Gregory to Pantaleon, notary.

Evangelus, deacon of the Church of Sipontum, has complained to us that his daughter was violated by Felix, which is a shameful thing to say.

[Note: EPISTLE XLI [variant: 40].—That he was a nephew of Felix, bishop of Sipontum, is shown by letter 43.]

Therefore, supported by the authority of this instruction, you must go to the city of Sipontum. After taking wise men there as your assistants, you shall learn the truth with the utmost care. If you find the matter to be as reported, hasten either to have the man who violated her take the woman he violated as his wife by executing the proper marriage documents, or, after corporal punishment, to hand him over, deprived of communion, to a monastery where he may perform penance—

[Note: Many laws on this subject may be found in the Digest, “Concerning the Julian Law on public violence.” Several canons also occur in the *Extravagantes*, “Concerning adultery and fornication.” Clerics discovered in this crime were deposed and confined in a monastery to perform penance, distinction 81, chapter “If any cleric.” The learned writer assumes that the violator was a cleric, which can easily be inferred from the punishment inflicted upon him. AUGET.]

—so that he may have no permission to leave thereafter in any manner unless our instruction should perhaps permit it.

Moreover, since the aforesaid deacon states that he was redeemed from enemies and therefore has incurred a debt, if you discover that his property is not sufficient to repay that debt, we command you to press our brother and fellow bishop Felix to pay his price from the Church’s resources without delay, so that the aforesaid Evangelus the deacon may without delay be freed from the burden of the debt to which he is subject.

## EPISTLE XLII. TO FELIX, BISHOP

The ecclesiastical furnishings, money, and other property of the Church of Sipontum are to be inventoried, and the inventory sent to Rome.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sipontum.

The concern of our office binds us very firmly to ensure, with God’s help, that we provide such careful oversight of ecclesiastical affairs that no loss may arise in them through neglect. Therefore, your Fraternity, together with Boniface and Pantaleon, the bearer of this letter and notaries of our see, should take care diligently to record, one by one, the property of the churches known to belong to the Church of Sipontum, so that the same inventory may accurately contain, after a truthful inspection of the property, both the churches’ furnishings and their ordinary silver, as well as anything else.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] EPISTLE XLII [Al. 41].—A *brevis* is called an inventory, a roll—French *rôle*—that is, a document containing a summary of any things whatever. In Greek, πιττάκιον (*pittacium*). Saint Jerome uses the word in this sense in Letter 6, to Florentius; Saint Benedict, chapters 32 and 41 of the Rule; Lupus of Ferrières, Letter 80; and others. Hence *imbreviare*, “to reduce to an inventory,” occurs in Hincmar, Hoveden, and others. GUSSANVILLE. See above, Book II, Letter 5. Gussanville is mistaken, however, when here he cites chapter 41 of Saint Benedict’s Rule.]

which has been set down by you. Let your Fraternity not attempt to offer any delay or excuse in this matter; rather, with every excuse set aside, hasten by every means to fulfill what has been imposed upon you by us, and send us the same inventory, signed by your own hand, through the aforesaid Pantaleon, so that, with divine grace assisting us, we may decide what ought beneficially to be done about it.

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO FELIX, BISHOP

He reproves the bishop concerning the fornication committed by his nephew and imposes upon him the execution of the sentence pronounced against the offender.

[Col. 0639A]

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sipontum.

We expected your Fraternity, through your preaching, to convert some people to God and to recall those acting wickedly to uprightness. For this reason we are greatly saddened, because, on the contrary, your own fault has been clearly exposed in the wickedness of your nephew Felix, whom you raised.

[Note: [Col. 0639C] EPISTLE XLIII [Al. 42].—It is cited in the *Extraordinary Collection*, On Adultery, chapter 2. See also the Council of Meaux, A.D. 845, chapters 64–66.]

It has therefore come to us that the aforesaid Felix deceived the daughter of Evangelus, your deacon, by fornication—a crime dreadful even to mention. If this is true, although he ought to be punished by the law with a severe penalty,

[Note: [Col. 0639D] I inquire what penalty he means: deportation, the prohibition of water and fire, deposition, bodily punishment? He appears to mean death. See Cause 36, question 2, and in the *Code*, Book IX, titles 12 and 13, and Novel 143. GUSSANVILLE.]

yet, softening the rigor of the law to some degree, we command that the matter be arranged as follows: either he shall have as his wife the woman whom he violated, or, if he should judge this unacceptable, then, after being more strictly and physically punished and excommunicated, he shall be confined in a monastery, where he is to perform penance, with no permission to leave it without our command. Your Fraternity should therefore see to it that these things are carried out, so that nothing in them may in any way be omitted. For if anything should be attempted otherwise—which we do not believe will happen—grave danger will afterward threaten him, and no slight guilt will begin to attach to you.

## EPISTLE XLIV. TO BONIFACE, BISHOP

He is to restore to Stephania the property seized by the agents of his predecessor.

Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio.

[Col. 0639C] Just as the Church ought not to lose her own property (Gratian, Cause 12, question 2, chapter 49), so she ought not to invade what belongs to another in the heat of rapacity. Stephania, the bearer of this letter, complains that certain property of hers was forcibly seized, during the time of your predecessor, the late Bishop Lucius, by his agents. Since she has requested that it be restored to her with justice in her favor, your Fraternity should therefore carefully investigate, in the fear of God, what she alleges. And if you find that the matter is as the woman has stated, see that everything wrongfully taken is restored without any loss or delay.

[Col. 0640A] For it is exceedingly harsh for the Church to retain another’s property contrary to reason. Therefore hasten to bring the complaint of the aforesaid woman to a beneficial conclusion, so that neither we may again suffer trouble on this account nor this matter demonstrate you to be avaricious or negligent.

## EPISTLE XLV. TO ANDREW, BISHOP

He urges him to resign the priesthood if he is conscious of sin with a concubine. Because he ordered a woman to be beaten with rods, he commands him to abstain from celebrating Mass for two months.

Gregory to Andrew,

[Note: [Col. 0639D] EPISTLE XLV [Al. 43].—Tarentum, commonly Taranto, was formerly a city of the Sallentines in Magna Graecia, on the gulf of the same name; today it belongs to the Kingdom of Naples, in the province of Otranto, where there is a strong Spanish garrison. It bears the title of a principality. Formerly an episcopal see, it has now been made an archiepiscopal see. GUSSANVILLE.]

bishop of Tarentum.

Whoever, conscious of his guilt, strives to appease the tribunal of the eternal Judge by worthy repentance will behold it without fear (Gratian, distinction 33, chapter 7). We have discovered with manifest certainty that you had a concubine,

[Note: [Col. 0639D] He immediately adds: “And in matters that are uncertain . . . we have chosen to commit this to your conscience.” I would understand both passages together. Andrew had had a concubine before his ordination; this is clear to Saint Gregory. Some suspicion had arisen that he had continued relations with the same concubine after ordination. Saint Gregory confronted him regarding his conscience. This is evident from the following words: “And that you share in that crime, concerning which an opposing suspicion has also arisen in some quarters.” GUSSANVILLE. Gussanville labored in vain to explain Saint Gregory’s meaning, since the following letter makes it clear.]

and that some people have also formed the contrary suspicion concerning this. But because judgment ought not to be absolute in uncertain matters, we have chosen to commit this to your conscience. Therefore, if you recall that, after being constituted in the sacred order, you were defiled by intercourse with her, then, having laid down the honor of the priesthood, do not presume in any way to undertake its administration. Know that, if you remain in the order in which you are while conscious of this crime and concealing the truth, you will minister at the peril of your soul and will unquestionably have to render an account to our God.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] In more recent editions, the words “and that you share in that crime” are appended here; we have found them in no manuscripts. Gussanville admits that they are absent from eleven manuscript codices, yet judged that they should be retained. Certainly they are absent from seven Norman manuscripts, four Roman ones, the Corbie, Rheims, Tours, Angers, and others. They appear to have been added by correctors because of Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 33; earlier editions do not know them.]

We therefore exhort you again: if you recognize that you have been deceived by the cunning of the ancient enemy, hasten, while it is permitted, to overcome him by suitable repentance, lest you be counted as his partner on the day of judgment—which we do not wish. But if you are not conscious of this guilt, you must remain in the order in which you are.

Moreover, because you assigned a woman from the Church’s register to be cruelly beaten with rods, contrary to the order of the priesthood,

[Note: [Col. 0640D] A *matricula* was a list or book in which were recorded those who were supported at the Church’s expense. Hence they were called *matricularii*. They were poor people, orphans, and widows, who were called *matriculariae*. GUSSANVILLE. That the woman beaten with rods was one of the Church’s registered dependents is indicated by the fact that this was done at the bishop’s command, since responsibility and authority over the Church’s register belonged to him. ALTESERRA.]

[Note: [Col. 0640D] Concerning a bishop who strikes, see Espensaeus at length, *Digression on Timothy*, Book II, chapter 3, and also below, Letter 53. GUSSANVILLE.]

although we do not at all believe that she died afterward, eight months later, nevertheless, because you were unwilling to respect your own order, we decree that you abstain from the administration of Masses for two months. During that time, suspended from your office, it is fitting that you mourn what you have done. For it is exceedingly appropriate that, since the examples of praiseworthy priests do not move you toward the tranquil uprightness of this life, at least the medicine of correction should compel you.

[Note: [Col. 0641C] The bishop is being suspended from the sacred altars and commanded to mourn, so that by this means at least the swelling of domination in him may be restrained and his spirit subdued. I therefore understand “the medicine of correction” as the use of canonical discipline, necessary to curb the license of sinners; impunity would nourish that license, and excessive leniency would foster it. Away with the austerity of Tertullian, Novatian, and others. Let the rigor of Saint Cyprian and the other Fathers, and of the Council of Elvira and other councils against the lapsed, be softened, though we must still reject the weakness of the priest Eli. Through so many dispensations and so many favors, the laws, whether relaxed or distorted, become worthless, lose their force, and collapse. But what government can stand without laws? What good are laws if it is either permitted to transgress them with impunity or if pardon is readily granted everywhere? Let the reader compare our customs with those of ancient times, so that from this he may learn how necessary is the medicine of correction and how harmful is the ready granting of pardon. A prudent physician applies remedies by which wounds are healed, not merely those by which they are covered and crusted over. In ancient times the use of relaxations was uncommon, but observance of the laws was vigorous; now sin floods in through abundant remissions. GUSSANVILLE.]

(Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 43.)

## EPISTLE XLVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP

Andrew, bishop, is to be forbidden the ministry if, while constituted in the sacred order, he has had intercourse with a concubine. He is to be suspended from celebrating Mass because he had a woman beaten with rods. The complaints of the clergy against him are also to be investigated.

Gregory to John,

[Note: [Col. 0641D] EPISTLE XLVI [Al. 45].—In the Vatican D, Colbert, Pratell, and some others, *Gallipolitan* is read. Callipolis, commonly Gallipoli, is an episcopal city of Calabria under the archbishop of Otranto.]

bishop of Callipolis.

From the proceedings that your Fraternity sent to us, it has been discovered that Andrew, our brother and fellow bishop, undoubtedly had a concubine. But because it is uncertain whether he had intercourse with her after being constituted in the sacred order, you must admonish him with serious exhortation: if, while placed in the sacred order, he knows that he became involved with her, let him desist from the office he holds and presume in no way to administer it. If, suppressing his sin while conscious of it, he should nevertheless presume to administer, let him know that the peril of his soul threatens him at the divine judgment.

[Col. 0642C] As for the registered dependent whom he had beaten with rods, although we do not believe that she died from it even eight months afterward, nevertheless, because he caused her to be afflicted in this way contrary to the order of his office, suspend him from the solemn celebration of Mass for two months, so that at least this humiliation may teach him what kind of person he should henceforth show himself to be.

[Note: [Col. 0642C] That is, a *matricularia*, or a woman who was enrolled among the Church’s registered dependents and supported at the Church’s expense.]

Moreover, in a petition submitted to us, which is held among the records concerning subordinates, the clergy of the aforesaid bishop state that they have endured many evils from him. For this reason your Fraternity should carefully investigate everything and correct and arrange the matter in a reasonable way, so that they may not hereafter be forced by this affair to return to us.

[Note: [Col. 0642D] Thus the Tours, Saint-Gatien, old Colbert, and Corbie manuscripts read.]

In the month of July, in the eleventh indiction. (See above, Letter 44. Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 27.)

## EPISTLE XLVII. TO THE CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF SALONA

He approves the election of Honoratus as bishop.

[Col. 0642A]

Gregory to the clergy of the Church of Salona.

Having reread the letter of your affection, we have learned that you elected Honoratus, your archdeacon,

[Note: [Col. 0642D] EPISTLE XLVII [Al. 46].—Honoratus and his disputes with Natalis, bishop of Salona, were discussed above in Book I, Letter 20. His election as bishop of Salona was invalid, and Maximus, favored by the emperor Maurice, was imposed upon the see of Salona by the provincial bishops. Concerning this matter and the varying fortunes of Honoratus, see our commentaries on the Life of Saint Gregory, Book II.]

and you should know that it was altogether pleasing to us that you chose for the episcopal order a man long tested and serious in character. Since we have also known his person well for a long time, we approve him and have wished that, in accordance with your desire, he should be ordained your priest. For this reason we exhort you to persist in his election without any hesitation. Nothing should turn you away from his person; for just as this election is now proved praiseworthy, so, if—God forbid—someone should seduce your affection into turning away from him, it will both burden your souls and place the stain of infidelity upon your reputation.

As for those who dissent from the unity of your desired election,

[Note: [Col. 0642D] The printed editions read, “who thoughtlessly dissent.” The Rheims manuscript reads, “who dissent from the desired unity.” We follow the Norman, Tours, Angers, Vatican, and other manuscripts. None of our manuscripts supports the reading of the common editions.]

we had them admonished by our subdeacon Antoninus so that they might be able to agree with you.

[Note: [Col. 0642D] The Regius manuscript reads, “by Anthimus.”]

We also instructed him some time ago concerning what ought to be done regarding Malchus, our brother and fellow bishop. But since we have written to Malchus as well, we believe that he will cease without delay from disturbing you. If, however, he should in any way neglect to obey, his obstinacy will by every means be punished with the severity of canonical vengeance.

## EPISTLE XLVIII. TO COLUMBUS, BISHOP

After first expressing singular benevolence toward him, he urges him not to allow boys to be ordained, nor orders to be conferred through favor or venality, and asks him to report the condition of the council. He sends him something enclosed among the keys of blessed Peter.

[Col. 0642C]

Gregory to Columbus,

[Note: [Col. 0642D] EPISTLE XLVIII [Al. 47].—The printed editions add “bishop of Numidia.” This is not erroneous, although “of Numidia” is absent from the Norman, Vatican, Corbie, and all the manuscripts we have been able to consult.]

bishop.

Even before I received your Fraternity’s letter, I learned, through truthful report, that you were a good servant of God. After receiving it, I understood more fully that what rumor had long spread abroad was certain; and I rejoice greatly in your merits, because you show by your character and actions that your life is worthy of praise. Since I perceive that these qualities have been bestowed upon you by heavenly majesty, I congratulate you and bless our God and Creator, who does not deny the gifts of his mercy to humble servants.

For this reason I confess the truth: your Fraternity has kindled me toward love of you with so great a flame of charity, and my spirit is so united to you, that I both desire to see you and, though you are absent, always attend to you in my heart. You understand well that these things are so. For certainly the unity of souls in charity can unite us more fully than bodily presence can be revered.

[Note: [Col. 0643D] We have emended this from five English manuscripts, with which the Beccensis, Michaelinus, and Sagiensis agree. The common reading of the manuscripts is nevertheless: “the unity of minds in charity can unite us more than bodily presence can be revered.” The printed editions have the same reading, changing only *animos* to *animorum*.]

Moreover, I now know—and knew clearly even before your letter bore witness to it—that you cling with your whole mind, heart, and soul to the Apostolic See and are devoted to it. Having therefore first offered the greeting due in charity, I exhort you not to cease remembering what you promised to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Be solicitous, then, for the primate of your synod, so that boys may in no way be admitted to sacred orders,

[Note: [Col. 0643D] He is not speaking here of the titles of bishoprics and abbeys, which the Church once lamented were granted to five-year-old boys; he is speaking of the orders themselves, which must not be conferred upon anyone who has not reached the lawful age. Theologians debate in the schools whether boys before the use of reason can validly be consecrated deacons, priests, or bishops. Canonists, in distinctions 77 and 78, assign to each order a fixed age for admission, fixed intervals at which it may be administered, and a fixed period to be spent at each grade, lest advancement be precipitous and too much haste incline one toward a fall. The holy Fathers excluded neophytes for many reasons, rejecting the ignorance, inexperience, pride, favor, and venality that most often occur in their promotions. The following letter, cited in Cause 1, question 1, bears upon the same matter. I have often read the entire cause and letter in seminaries, and it would be useful to explain them canon by canon. GUSSANVILLE.]

lest they fall all the more dangerously because they hasten all the sooner to climb to higher things. Let there be no venality in ordination; neither the power nor the supplication of persons should prevail against these prohibitions. For without doubt God is offended if anyone is advanced to sacred orders not on merit but through favor—God forbid—or through venality.

[Note: [Col. 0644D] Let those who confer priestly offices and the patrons attend to this. Let them look solely to the glory of God, the building up of the Church, and the salvation of souls; let favor, power, supplication, and venality be silent.]

If you learn that these things are happening, do not remain silent; oppose them vigorously. For if you should perhaps neglect to investigate such matters or conceal them once discovered, not only will the bond of sin bind those who commit these acts, but no slight guilt in this matter will also attach to you before God. Therefore, if anything of this kind is committed, it must be restrained by canonical vengeance, lest so great a crime gain strength through concealment when the sin of others is spared.

[Note: [Col. 0644D] Thus it is read in three Vatican manuscripts, the Corbie, Audun, and others. The printed editions, however, read: “lest so great a crime, when the sin of others is spared, gain strength through dissimulation.”]

I received with affection Victorinus, the bearer of this letter, your Fraternity’s deacon, whom I think to be your imitator, and I have released him to return quickly. Through him I have also sent you, as a blessing, the keys of blessed Peter, in which something taken from his chains is enclosed.

Moreover, concerning the unity and peace of the council which, with God as its guide, you intend to convene, let your charity gladden our hearts by carefully reporting everything.

## EPISTLE XLIX. TO ADEODATUS, BISHOP

After a friendly greeting, he urges him to fulfill his office, especially not to ordain anyone except those advanced in age and pure in conduct, and not to permit venality in ordination. He is to make use of the advice of Bishop Columbus. Finally, after the synod has been completed, he is to inform Gregory about its harmony.

[Col. 0644A]

[Note: [Col. 0644D] We have already explained what the primates were like in the African Church; this is shown more fully in the commentaries on the Life of Saint Gregory.]

Gregory to Adeodatus, bishop and primate of the province of Numidia.

The sequence of your writings has clearly made known how strongly the affection of your love has bound your Fraternity to us. It has provided us with a great source of joy that we have learned that your letters were composed with kindly devotion and burn with a love pleasing to God. As we briefly said, the letter you sent so expressed your mind that its author seemed by no means absent. For those whose spirit does not differ from one another in mutual affection ought not to be judged absent.

Although, as you write, neither your strength nor your age permits you to come to us, so that we might rejoice in the bodily presence of your Fraternity, nevertheless, because our spirit is united to you and yours to us, we are present to one another in every respect, as we behold one another with minds united by love.

Moreover, greeting your Fraternity with the fitting affection of charity, we exhort you to take care diligently and wisely to exercise the office of primate, which you hold by God’s authority, so that your having attained this rank may benefit your soul and provide others in the future with an example worthy of imitation.

Be especially attentive, then, in ordinations,

[Note: [Col. 0644D] Gratian reads this passage in this form and cited it at the indicated place. It is also read thus in the Norman manuscripts, Vatican C, and others, as well as in the old printed editions: “make experienced and serious men participants in your counsels.” Two Vatican manuscripts, without differing in sense, read: “make them participants in your council.” The more recent common editions read: “your synod.”]

and do not admit anyone aspiring to sacred orders unless they are advanced in age and pure in conduct, lest those who hasten to be immature should cease ever to be what they are. First examine the life and character of those who are to be placed in the sacred order; and, so that you may be able to appoint worthy persons to this office, do not allow the power or supplication of any persons to snatch them away from you. Above all, you must be careful that no venality arise in ordination, lest—God forbid—greater danger threaten both those ordained and those who ordain.

Whenever, therefore, it is necessary to deliberate on these matters, admit serious and experienced men to share in your counsels and weigh the matter with them in common deliberation. Above all, it is fitting for you to make use in everything of Columbus, our brother and fellow bishop. For we believe that, if you do what must be done with his advice, no one will be able to find anything in you to criticize in any way. Know that it will be as pleasing to us as though it were done with our own advice, because his life and character have been approved by us in every respect, so that it is evident to all that nothing done with his agreement is stained by any mark of guilt.

The bearer of this letter, Victorinus, the deacon of the aforesaid fellow bishop of ours, has been such a herald of your merits

[Note: [Col. 0645C] Vatican B reads, “as our friends” (*ut amicos nostros*).]

that he greatly renewed our spirits concerning your conduct. We pray Almighty God to make the good things he reported about you shine forth more fully through works pleasing to him.

Therefore, when the council you intend to convene has been completed with God’s help, gladden us concerning its unity and harmony, and make us fully informed about it.

## EPISTLE L. TO THEODORUS, BISHOP

He praises him for carefully examining and reporting on the lives of priests. He commands Bishop Paul to remain in the monastery in penance. He orders Paul’s property to be inventoried and preserved. An investigation is to be made into Boniface, who has been seriously accused.

Gregory to Theodorus,

[Note: [Col. 0645C] EPISTLE L [Al. 49].—The name is written in various ways. In the Norman manuscripts, with three Vatican manuscripts agreeing, it is *Lilibitanus* or *Lilibetanus*. Vatican B has *Libuitanus*. Colbert has *Liuvitanus*. Angers has *Tillibitanus*. Lilybaeum was formerly a celebrated city of Sicily; it was succeeded by the place now commonly called Marsala, in the valley of the Mazara, commonly Val di Mazara. Lilybaeum is especially known in the councils through Paschasinus, bishop of that city, who was the legate of Saint Leo the pope at the Council of Chalcedon.]

bishop of Lilybaeum.

Your Fraternity’s solicitude is altogether pleasing to us, because you both investigate what you learn about the lives of priests and report what you have investigated.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Vatican C reads: “so that, therefore, this solicitude . . . may continue without diminution.”]

In order that you may persist without weakening in this solicitude, which we praise in you, be diligent and watchful. If you learn that any excesses have been committed there by anyone—God forbid—then, if the persons involved can be corrected there, let them be corrected reasonably; otherwise hasten to report the matter in writing to our brother Bishop Maximianus, so that, informed by you, he may know what should be done. Let nothing therefore call you back from investigating wicked actions or reporting them. For the more we praise your vigilance now, the more culpable you will be found if you conceal such acts through any dissimulation.

[Col. 0646A] We wish the former bishop Paul to remain in penance in the monastery where he is. You must by every means take care that the property found with him is kept in the *cimiliarchium* of your church.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] The *cimiliarchium* was discussed above in Book I, Letter 20, concerning Honoratus.]

You are also to make a received copy of it according to the inventory of the property found,

[Note: [Col. 0645D] That is, a written description, copy, or transcript.]

and send it to the archive of your church.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] *Scrinia* are chests, boxes, or cabinets in which records are kept; to the French, *le trésor*, “the treasury.” Hence *scriniarius*, an archivist or keeper of records, or, better, as Suidas has it, *chartularius*. The Greek forms σκρίνιον and σκρινιάριος are also found. See the *Code*, Book XII, title 19. There were various archives: of petitions, memoranda, dispositions, letters, and also of sacred largesses, records, financial officers, and so forth. In Budaeus, some archives were stationary and others traveling. GUSSANVILLE. See Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book XI, chapters 20–22 and 24.]

As for his clergy, if any of them are still present there, it is fitting that you make another corresponding copy,

[Note: [Col. 0646C] Or, “from the counterparts.” See what we said about this word in Book I, Letter 25.]

in which your Fraternity acknowledges that it has sent from those same things a corresponding copy into our archive, so that, whenever necessary, all the property may be restored without loss to the appropriate person.

As for Boniface, a serious accusation has reached us concerning him. Your Fraternity must investigate whether his crimes are true, examining the matter together with the *loci servator* of the praetor.

[Note: [Col. 0646C] The reading of the printed editions must not be accepted: “with the guardian of the place.” The *loci praetoris servator* was his deputy. [Col. 0646D] See above, Book II, Letter 32.]

## EPISTLE LI. TO MAXIMIANUS, BISHOP

Intending to write briefly about miracles performed by the Fathers in Italy, he asks Maximianus to report those he remembers.

Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

My brothers who live with me familiarly urge me in every way to write briefly about some of the miracles of the Fathers that we have heard occurred in Italy. For this task I greatly need the support of your charity, so that you may briefly indicate to me those things that come back to your memory and that you have had the opportunity to learn.

[Note: [Col. 0646D] EPISTLE LI [Al. 50].—Vatican A and B read, “of your truth.”]

I remember that you told me certain things about Abbot Nonnosus,

[Note: [Col. 0646D] He was superior of the monastery located on Mount Soracte, under a very strict abbot, as Gregory says in the *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 7. Later he himself became abbot of that monastery, perhaps. Saint Gregory calls him “Lord Nonnosus,” in accordance with the provision of Saint Benedict’s Rule, chapter 63: “Let the abbot, who is believed to take the place of Christ, be called Lord and abbot.”]

who was next to Lord Anastasius of Pentoma, but I have consigned some of them to forgetfulness. I therefore ask you to have this, and anything else there may be, written into your letters and sent to me quickly—unless you yourself are hastening to come to me.

## EPISTLE LII. TO PRISCUS, PATRICIAN

From the alternation of prosperity and adversity he teaches humility. He rejoices at the recovery of the emperors’ favor. He commends Sabinianus and Castus.

Gregory to Priscus, patrician of the East.

If we attend truthfully to the course of this life, we find nothing in it firm, nothing stable. Just as a traveler proceeds now over level ground, now over rough, so, while remaining in this life, we encounter now prosperity and now adversity; finally, they succeed one another in turn and are mingled in reciprocal alternation.

Although the order of mutability corrupts everything in this world,

[Note: [Col. 0647D] The common editions read, “the order of mutability confounds.” The agreement of the Vatican, Norman, Tours, Corbie, and other manuscripts requires the alteration.]

we ought neither to be elated by prosperity nor broken by adversity. With our whole mind, therefore, we must yearn for the place where everything remains firm, where prosperity is not changed by adversity. In this life, then, by the wonderful governance of Almighty God, things are arranged so that prosperity follows adversity or adversity follows prosperity, in order that, when humbled, we may learn to mourn whatever we have done wrong and, when exalted again, may hold the memory of adversity in our minds as an anchor of humility.

[Note: [Col. 0647D] Most manuscripts omit *flere*, “to mourn,” without damage to the sense.]

This should not therefore be attributed to the anger of our Creator but to his grace, through which we learn to preserve his gifts all the more faithfully the more humbly we hold them.

Since, therefore, we have learned that, with Almighty God as author, you have recovered the emperor’s complete favor, we rejoice with great exultation on your behalf, wishing that the governor of all things may both support your life always with present blessings and extend it to everlasting joys. I say these things to you because I love you greatly and know that I am loved by you.

But demonstrate the fact that you love me by showing favor to Sabinianus, the bearer of this letter, so that, whenever need requires, he may obtain your patronage. The illustrious Castus, meanwhile, is a herald of your praises in the Roman regions; I commend him to your Excellency with paternal affection.

## EPISTLE LIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He attributes the feigned and inept response concerning the case of the priests John and Athanasius—which in no way accords with the holiness of Bishop John—to a wicked young man, whose counsels the bishop was excessively inclined to follow. He presses most forcefully for the case to be concluded according to the canons. He commends his *apocrisiarius* Sabinianus.

Gregory to John,

[Note: [Col. 0647D] EPISTLE LIII [Al. 52].—Concerning John of Constantinople, read what we said in Book I, Letter 4. We shall say more in Book II of the Life of Saint Gregory concerning the case of the priest John and the monks of Isauria.]

bishop of Constantinople.

Although consideration of the case moves me, charity nevertheless urges me to write, because I have written once and twice to my most holy brother, Lord John, but did not receive his letters. For someone rather worldly was speaking to me in his name; and if those letters were his, then I was not watchful, since I believed of him something quite different from what I found. For I had written concerning the most reverend man, John the presbyter, and concerning the complaints of the monks of Isauria, one of whom, though also a priest, was beaten with rods in your church; and your most holy Fraternity wrote back to me—as I recognize from the name on the letter—that you did not know what matter I was writing about. At this reply I was exceedingly astonished, silently turning this over in my mind: if he speaks the truth, what could be worse than for such things to be done against God’s servants while the one who is present does not know?

For what excuse can a shepherd have if a wolf devours the sheep and the shepherd does not know? But if your Holiness knew both the matter about which I wrote and what had been done either against John the presbyter or against Athanasius, the Isaurian monk and priest, and yet wrote to me—I do not know what answer I should give to this, when Truth says through Scripture: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

I ask you, most holy brother: has that great abstinence of yours reached the point that you wish, by denying it, to conceal from your brother what you know has happened? Would it not have been better for flesh to enter that mouth for eating than for false speech to come out of it to mock your neighbor? Especially since Truth says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the heart—those are the things that defile a person” (Matthew 15:11).

But far be this from us, lest I believe such a thing of your most holy heart. Those letters were headed with your name, but I do not think they were yours. I had written to the most blessed man, Lord John; but I believe that your familiar young man wrote back to me—the one who has not yet learned anything about God, who does not know the depths of charity, who is accused by everyone in criminal matters, who daily plots the deaths of various people through secret wills, fearing neither the Lord nor showing shame before human beings.

Believe me, most holy brother: if you possess a perfect zeal for truth, correct him first, so that through the example of those who are near you even those who are not near you may be better corrected. Do not accept his counsel; he ought to be directed according to the counsel of your Holiness, not your Holiness bent according to his words. For if he listens to him, I know that he will not be able to have peace with his brothers.

As for me, with my conscience bearing witness, I confess that I wish to have no quarrel with anyone, and I avoid it with all the strength I possess. And although I earnestly desire to have peace with all people, especially with you, whom I love exceedingly—if indeed you are the person whom I have known—for if you do not observe the canons and wish to overturn the statutes of the Fathers, I do not recognize who you are.

Act, therefore, most holy and dearest brother, so that we may recognize one another, lest, if the ancient enemy moves two people through scandal, he kill many through a most wicked victory. To speak openly, because I seek nothing through pride, if that young man of whom I have spoken did not hold the summit of wicked action in your Fraternity, I could for the time being have kept silent even about what I know concerning the canons, and from the very beginning I could have confidently sent back to him the persons who came to me, knowing that your Holiness would receive them with charity.

But even now I say: either receive those same persons in their orders and grant them peace; or, if you are perhaps unwilling to do this, setting aside all dispute with me, observe, concerning their case, the statutes of the Fathers and the limits of the canons. If you do neither, we do not wish to provoke a quarrel, but we do not avoid one coming from you.

As for what the canons say concerning bishops who wish to be feared through beatings, your Fraternity knows very well (Gratian, Distinction 45, chapter 1). For we have been made shepherds, not persecutors. And the excellent preacher says: “Reprove, exhort, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2). This, however, is a new and unheard-of preaching, which demands faith through beatings.

But I ought not to discuss these matters at length in letters, because I have sent my beloved son, the deacon Sabinianus, to the feet of the Lords to give ecclesiastical responses; he will discuss everything with you more precisely. If you do not wish to quarrel with us, you will find him ready for everything that is just. I commend him to your Blessedness, so that at least he may find that Lord John whom I knew in the royal city. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapters 44 and 9.)

## LETTER LIV. TO THE PHYSICIAN THEOTIMUS

After a most friendly greeting, he commends Sabinianus.

Gregory to Theotimus the physician.

There were certain ancient philosophers who said that there was one soul in two bodies—not joining two people by affection, but dividing one substance of the soul between two. We, on the contrary, say that among many there is one soul, not by dividing the substance but by joining hearts. For it is written concerning those first believers: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). I read this in the Acts of the Apostles in such a way that I recognize it in myself and Lord Theotimus, because he is so united in spirit with me that, though present to me in body, he has never been absent; and though absent in body, he is always present through the spirit.

I give thanks to almighty God, who pours the grace of his charity into the depths of your mind; and I pray that he may increase his gifts in you more and more, granting us here present blessings and, in the age to come, eternal joys. I commend to your charity my son, the deacon Sabinianus, who is coming, asking that you love our people with the same love with which you love me.

## LETTER LV. TO THE BISHOP MAXIMIANUS

He provides for the support of Bishop Agatho, against whom strict punishment had been imposed.

Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

After canonical severity has been exercised against Agatho, formerly a bishop, according to the nature of his offenses, it is necessary, out of consideration for humanity, to arrange how he may be supported. Therefore let your Fraternity hasten to send to the Liparitan Church, in which the aforesaid Agatho exercised the office of priest, and let it send from there, for the present, fifty solidi sufficient for his sustenance. For it would be exceedingly impious if, after punishment, he were left subject to the necessity of food.

## LETTER LVI. TO THE BISHOP JOHN

He is no longer to wear the pallium in the streets unless he shows that it was granted to him by the Roman pontiffs. Henceforth he is not to sit in the secretarium itself wearing the pallium. He is to investigate certain of his clergy and forbid the contumacious to exercise the sacred ministry. He grants the use of the mappulae only to the first deacons of the Church of Ravenna.

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

Not much time has passed since certain matters were reported to us concerning your Fraternity (Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 7), about which, when Castorius, notary of the holy Church over which, by God’s authority, we preside, came there, we remember having informed you in detail. For certain things had reached us as being done in your Church against custom and against the path of humility, which alone, as you know well, is the elevation proper to priestly office. If your Wisdom had received these matters meekly and with episcopal diligence, you ought not to have been angered by them; rather, you ought to have corrected them with thanksgiving. For it is contrary to ecclesiastical custom (Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 8) if what is corrected—even, God forbid, unjustly—is not endured with the greatest patience.

Your Fraternity, however, was excessively agitated and, as though satisfying yourself with a swelling of heart, wrote to us that you had used the pallium only after the sons of the Church had been dismissed from the secretarium, and during Mass, and that in the solemn litanies you had appropriated certain words, openly confessing that you had acted against the custom of the universal Church.

For how can it be lawful for you to do in the streets, amid the uproar of the people, during the time of ashes and sackcloth, what you excused as unlawful for you to do in the assembly of the poor and nobles and in the secretarium of the Church? Yet this, dearest brother (Gratian, same distinction), we do not think unknown to you: scarcely any metropolitan anywhere in the world has been heard to claim the use of the pallium for himself outside the time of Mass. And that you know this custom of the universal Church well, you have made abundantly clear to us in your letters, in which you transmitted to us the attached decree of our predecessor, Pope John, of blessed memory, stating that all customs granted to you and your Church by the privilege of our predecessors ought to be preserved.

You therefore acknowledge that the custom of the universal Church is one thing, since you claim by privilege the practices that you carry out. Accordingly, as we think, no uncertainty can remain for us in this matter. Either the custom of all metropolitans must also be observed by your Fraternity, or, if you say that something has been specially granted to your Church, you must produce the decree by which these things were granted to the Church of Ravenna by the earlier pontiffs of the city of Rome. If this cannot be produced, it remains that, since you claim to do such things neither by general custom nor by privilege, you are proved to have usurped what you did.

And what shall we say to the future Judge, dearest brother, if we defend that heavy yoke and burden on our necks—not for ecclesiastical dignity, but for a certain worldly dignity—judging ourselves oppressed if we lack such a weight even for a short time? We wish to be adorned with the pallium, perhaps unadorned in character, while nothing shines more splendidly upon an episcopal neck than humility.

Therefore, if your Fraternity has firmly resolved to defend its honors by whatever arguments it can, you ought either to follow the general custom as an unwritten practice, or defend yourself by written privileges. But if, finally, none of these exists, we do not wish you to offer other metropolitans an example of such presumption.

But lest you perhaps think that, in writing these things to you, we have neglected what fraternal charity requires, know that we have carefully searched in our archive for the privilege of your Church. Certain things were found that could entirely oppose your Fraternity’s claims, but nothing by which your Church’s side could be strengthened in matters of this kind. Concerning the very custom of your Church that you bring forward, which, as you say, existed formerly among you, know that we have already taken sufficient care, inquiring of our sons Peter the deacon, Gaudosus the primicerius, and Michael the defensor of our see, as well as others who had been sent by our predecessors from here to Ravenna on various missions. They most emphatically denied that you had done these things in their presence.

It is therefore apparent that nothing could have been done secretly unless it was unlawfully usurped. Hence what was introduced secretly ought not to persist with any stability. Correct, therefore, with the consideration due to charity and with fraternal kindness whatever you or your predecessors have presumptuously done. Do not attempt, whether by yourself or by the precedent of your predecessors, to depart in any way from the rule of humility.

To summarize briefly what I said above, I admonish you that, unless you prove that these things were granted to you as a privilege by the generosity of my predecessors, you should no longer presume to wear the pallium in the streets, lest you begin not to have it at Mass while boldly usurping it in the streets.

Concerning the secretarium, since your Fraternity both sat wearing the pallium and received the sons of the Church, and excused the action, we make no complaint for the present, because, following the judgment of the synods, we refuse to punish lesser offenses that are denied. We have learned, however, that this was done once and again, and we now forbid it to be done any further. Let your Fraternity be entirely vigilant, lest what is still being tolerated as an incipient presumption be punished more severely when it advances.

You have also complained that certain members of the priestly order of the city of Ravenna, with sins hanging over them, are entangled in serious crimes. We wish you either to investigate their case there, or, if the difficulty of proof due to the distance of the places does not prevent it, to send them here for the very purpose of investigation. But if they disdain to come either to your judgment or to us—supported, as we do not believe, by the patronage of the great—and if they are unable to answer contumaciously the charges brought against them, after your second and third admonition, we wish you to forbid them the ministry of sacred office. Report to us in writing their contumacy, so that we may deliberate how you ought carefully to examine their conduct and correct it according to the canonical definitions.

Let your Fraternity know that we consider ourselves entirely absolved concerning this matter, since we have entrusted these cases to you for careful investigation. If all their sins go unpunished, the whole burden of this investigation will rebound as a danger upon your soul. You should know that your charity will have no excuse before the future Judge if you do not correct the offenses of your clergy with the utmost severity of canonical rigor and permit those against whom these matters have been established to profane the sacred orders any longer.

As for what you wrote concerning the use of mappulae by your clergy (Gratian, Distinction 93, chapter 22), our clergy have strongly opposed it, saying that this had never been granted to any other Church, and that the clerics of Ravenna had never presumed to do anything of the sort, either there or in the city of Rome, with a clear conscience; nor, if it had been attempted, would such an act create a precedent for them through a furtive usurpation. Even if this had been presumed in any Church, they assert that it should be corrected, since it is presumed not by concession of the Roman pontiff but by mere surreptitious appropriation.

But, preserving the honor of your Fraternity, although contrary to the will of the aforesaid clergy of ours, we permit your first deacons—of whom certain people have testified to us that they had used them even earlier—to use mappulae solely in your service. We most emphatically forbid anyone else, or the same persons at another time, to do this. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 2.)

## LETTER LVII. OF JOHN, BISHOP OF RAVENNA, TO POPE GREGORY

He humbly answers each charge and defends the privileges of his Church by custom; he requests that they not be diminished.

My most reverend fellow servant Castorius, notary of your apostolic see, delivered to me the letter of my lord, a companion of honey and wound. Yet it fixed its spurs so deeply that it did not remove the place for medicine. For one who reproves pride while following divine judgment rightly declares himself, in a certain sense, gentle and peaceful.

You therefore recalled that I, through ambition for novelty, had usurped the use of the pallium beyond what had been granted to my predecessors. May the conscience of my own lord, governed by the divine right hand, by no means permit this to be believed, nor allow his most sacred ears to be opened to uncertain report. First, although I am a sinner, I know how serious it is to cross the boundaries fixed for us by the Fathers, and that every exaltation has nothing but ruin in it. For if our ancestors did not tolerate pride in kings, how much more must it not be endured in priests?

Next, I recall that I was nourished in the bosom and embrace of your holy Roman Church and, with God’s help, advanced within it. With what audacity could I have presumed to oppose that most holy see which transmits its rights to the universal Church, for the preservation of whose authority, as God is my witness, I have gravely stirred up the envy of many enemies against myself?

But let my most blessed lord not think that I have attempted anything against ancient custom. This is attested by many and nearly all the citizens of this city; even if the most reverend notary had consented, he could have attested it among the official records. For when the sons of the Church descend from the secretarium and the deacons enter so that they may proceed at once, it has been customary for the first deacon to vest the bishop of the Church of Ravenna with the pallium, which he has likewise customarily used in the solemn litanies.

Let no one, therefore, attempt to creep in against me before my lord, because, if God is my guardian, he cannot prove that any novelty was introduced by me. May almighty God make clear to your purest heart how I have obeyed your commands and interests whenever the case required it. I attribute this to my sins: after all the labors and hardships that I endure within and without, I should deserve to encounter such a recompense.

Yet this also consoles me among other things: sometimes the holiest Fathers chastise their sons for this sole reason, that they may make them better; and after this devotion and satisfaction toward the holy Church of Ravenna, which belongs peculiarly to you, may you not only preserve its ancient privileges but also grant it greater ones in your time.

As for what your Apostleship writes about the mappulae presumed by my priests and deacons, I frankly confess that I am reluctant to mention anything further, since the truth itself, which alone prevails before my lord, ought to suffice. For since this is permitted to the lesser Churches established around the city, your Apostleship could also discover, if it deigned to inquire of the venerable clergy of its first apostolic see, that whenever priests or levites of the Church of Ravenna came to Rome for episcopal ordination or for a response, they all proceeded before the eyes of your most holy predecessors with mappulae, without any rebuke.

Thus, at the time when I was ordained there by your predecessor, a sinner, all my priests and deacons who proceeded with me in the service of the lord pope also used them. And because our God, who foresees everything, has placed all things in your hand and in your purest conscience, I adjure you by that very apostolic see which you formerly govern by your character and now also by the honor due to it: do not, on account of my merits, diminish in anything the privileges that the Church of Ravenna, which is intimately yours, has hitherto enjoyed. Rather, in accordance with the prophetic saying, let it be transferred, according to its desert, upon me and my father’s house.

Since, therefore, I have placed in the venerable archives, for greater satisfaction, all the privileges granted to the holy Church of Ravenna by your predecessors, arranged according to the times of my predecessors’ consecrations—and since they have also been found to be authentic—it is now in God’s and your power to order whatever, once the truth is known, you judge should be done. For, desiring to obey the commands of my lord’s Apostleship, although ancient custom has prevailed, I have taken care to abstain until a second command.

## LETTER LVIII. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN

If Cosmas has no means by which to pay, he is to reach an agreement with his creditors; and by paying the agreed sum, he is to free Cosmas’s sons.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

Cosmas says that, through various necessities arising from dangerous circumstances, he has become bound by many debts, so that he says his sons are being detained by his creditors on account of them. If this is so, the matter has greatly moved us. Therefore we exhort your Charity, since this concerns the distribution of the property of the poor, to investigate his case with the greatest care; and if you find that he is truly burdened by the aforesaid debts and has no property from which he can repay them, approach his creditors and, in order to recover his sons, settle with them for whatever amount you determine.

And since, as has been said, he has no means of repayment, pay it from the property of the poor by our present authority; knowing that whatever is given there through your provision is to be reckoned among the revenues of our patrimony. In the month of August, indiction 11. (See Letter 45, indiction 12. Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 55.)

## LETTER LIX. TO SECUNDINUS, BISHOP

The baptistery is to be removed from the monastery, so that the monks may celebrate the work of God more securely.

Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina.

[Editorial and textual notes]

- [Col. 0648D.] “We have repaired this corrupt passage, especially with the help of the Norman manuscripts. The printed editions have more than one reading. In the Roman edition I read: ‘and he wrote nothing to me against this; I do not know what I should answer.’ In Gussanville: ‘and he wrote to me; against this I do not know what I should answer, when by Scripture …’”

- [Col. 0648D.] “This is why he was surnamed ‘the Faster’ (Jejunator).”

- [Col. 0648D.] “The printed editions read, ‘Far be it that I …’; we follow the Vatican, Norman, and Corbie manuscripts, which agree with one another.”

- [Col. 0648D.] “Editions before Gussanville read, ‘in wicked deeds’; the manuscripts resist this reading.”

- [Col. 0648D.] “The more recent editions read, ‘if you have zeal for charity’; the manuscripts disagree.”

- [Cols. 0648D–0649D.] “Saint Gregory is everywhere solicitous for the observance of the canons; below: ‘Observe the statutes of the elders and the limits of the canons.’”

- [Col. 0649D.] “The more recent editions preferred ‘through the swelling of pride,’ which none even of our ancient manuscripts has.”

- [Cols. 0649D–0650D.] “This is understood in the same sense as Apostolic Canon 28, Canon 26 in Greek, concerning a cleric who strikes. Above, Letter 45, Espensaeus was indicated. See Gregory of Tours, *Histories*, Book VIII, chapter 39, on Baudegisel, bishop of Le Mans. It is worth noting here that striking for correction was once permitted, at least for more serious and mortal faults, from Braga III, canon 6, and Agde, canon 41. A bishop, however, ought not to beat with his own hands, nor through a layman, but through a cleric. *Extra*, *De sent. excomm.*, chapter *Universitatis*. Gussanville: the author of the *Life of St Thomas of Canterbury* reports that, in the twelfth century, a bishop subjected a canonical cleric to public beating with rods.”

- [Col. 0650D.] “Thus the Norman, Corbie, Vatican B, C, D, Reginensis, and other manuscripts; the printed editions have ‘not strikers.’”

- [Col. 0650D.] “LETTER LIV [otherwise 66]. Four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others have this reading, whereas the printed editions have ‘not affection.’ Consult Augustine, *Confessions*, Book IV, where he explains this opinion of the ancient philosophers in vigorous style.”

- [Col. 0650D.] “The printed editions read, ‘who pours the grace of his charity into the depths of your mind.’”

- [Col. 0650D.] “The vulgate editions add: ‘Given in indiction 11.’”

- [Col. 0650D.] “LETTER LV [otherwise 55]. Agatho or Agathus, bishop of Lipari, was deposed for crimes, according to this letter. From Letters 16 and 20, indiction 10, Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Tauromenium, was appointed in his place. Saint Gregory mentions the new bishop of Lipari in Book VII, Letter 22, to Cyprian the deacon. Gussanville.”

- [Col. 0651C.] “LETTER LVI [otherwise 54]. See Book I, Letter 19.”

- [Cols. 0651C–0651D.] “That bishops did not wear the pallium throughout the whole time of Mass, but only until the reading of the Gospel, is clear from Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 136. They were then accustomed to rise and lay aside the pallium, as though Christ, the true shepherd, had arrived. See the Eighth Synod against Photius, session 10, canon 27 (14 in the Greek numbering). Symeon of Thessalonica likewise reports in his book *On the Temple and the Mass*: ‘While the Gospel is read, the pontiff lays aside the pallium, showing his servitude and subjection to the Lord. For since he is known to speak through the Gospel and is, as it were, present, the pontiff then does not dare to wear the symbol of his incarnation; instead, having lifted it from his shoulders, he hands it to the deacon, who stands beside the pontiff holding it folded in his right hand and precedes the sacred gifts.’ Gussanville.”

- [Cols. 0651D–0652C.] “Who these ‘poor’ and ‘nobles’ are, I ask. Gussanville. Accept our conjecture: after the bishop, the Church consisted of clergy and laity. In Book III, Letter 31, and elsewhere, he calls clerics ‘soldiers of the Church.’ Here he calls laypeople ‘sons of the Church’; among them he commonly calls the more honourable ‘the order’ and the rest ‘the people’—Book I, Letter 60; Book II, Letter 8; Book V, Letter 14. In addressing an election of a bishop, he writes to clergy, order, and people; he distinguishes those commonly called the order here by the title ‘nobles,’ and perhaps those of the people by the name ‘poor.’”

- [Col. 0652C.] “The printed editions, except the older ones, read, ‘therefore no [doubt] can remain for you’; the manuscripts disagree.”

- [Cols. 0652C–0652D.] “This is read in the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts; accordingly the vulgate reading must be corrected: ‘Or, if … a decree or command granted by earlier pontiffs of the city of Rome, which …,’ from which a different sense results.”

- [Col. 0652D.] “I would add: a special custom of that place, although unwritten, ought to be proved by witnesses. For this seems sufficient. Gussanville.”

- [Col. 0652D.] “Thus the older editions, with the manuscripts agreeing. Yet in the Norman manuscript and in two Vatican manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and the Tours manuscript, instead of ‘defend yourself’ is read ‘make use of it.’”

- [Col. 0652D.] “On this passage Alteserra says: ‘A privilege is suspect if it is not found in the chamber of blessed Peter, that is, in the archive of the Apostolic See,’ chapter *Ad audientiam*, *Extra de praescriptionibus*. Gussanville.”

- [Col. 0652D.] “The more recent editions read ‘from the Fathers’; the old copies disagree.”

- [Col. 0652D.] “Thus the Norman and Tours manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, and others. Vatican A and the Reginensis read: ‘that you should no longer presume [to wear] the pallium in the streets.’ The printed editions added *ferre*, ‘to wear’: ‘that you should no longer presume to wear the pallium in the streets.’ On the pallium, moreover, see often elsewhere, especially in the commentaries on the life of Saint Gregory, which may be consulted by means of the index.”

- [Col. 0653D.] “With this weapon the African Fathers defended themselves against Zosimus’s admonitory letter. Gussanville.”

- [Col. 0653D.] “Thus Vatican C and D, Audoenensis, Jumièges, Pratellensis, Lyranus, with which the old printed editions agree. Vatican A reads: ‘if they have either been unwilling or unable to answer.’ Four English manuscripts, the Michaelian, and the Sagiensis read: ‘if they have presumed to answer.’ The more recent printed editions read: ‘if they have been unwilling to answer.’”

- [Col. 0653D.] “By common law every bishop judges the cases of his own clerics. Therefore these words do not delegate to the bishop of Ravenna, from the supreme pontiff, jurisdiction over his clerics in another’s stead; rather, they merely give him courage to undertake confidently the case about which he despaired, certain that the Roman pontiff would labour to ensure that decisions made according to the canons were carried into execution. Auget.”

- [Cols. 0653D–0654D.] “The use of the mappula or linen cloth continued until the maniple, no longer for wiping dirt but for ornament, was substituted for it around the tenth century. Alcuin and Amalarius mention mappulae in the ninth century. See Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 24, section 1, and note 736 of our Menard on the *Book of Sacraments*.”

- [Col. 0654D.] “LETTER LVII [otherwise 55]. This letter is lacking in the Vatican, English, Norman, Corbie, Tours, and other manuscripts. It survives in the Rheims manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Teller manuscripts.”

- [Col. 0654D.] “In the Rheims manuscript, ‘my lord’ is absent.”

- [Col. 0654D.] “Rheims: ‘crushed pride.’”

- [Col. 0654D.] “Rheims: ‘With what excesses [could I oppose] that see which [has] rights in the universal Church?’ To these words Gussanville appended this note: ‘He acknowledges the primacy. Nor is it surprising that it is acknowledged by an Italian bishop, when those far away confess it of their own accord. From innumerable testimonies I produce one or two. Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, called the Roman Church the head of all Churches, as Victor of Vita reports, *Vandalic Persecution*, Book II, chapter 15. Cyprian, Letter 59 in the new Oxford edition, near the end: “They dare to sail and to carry letters from schismatics and profane persons to Peter’s chair and to the principal Church, whence the unity of the priesthood arose.”’”

- [Col. 0655C.] “The Rheims manuscript and the old Colbert manuscript read: ‘the citizens of this city, even in the official records, could have testified, if the most holy and reverend notary had consented.’”

- [Cols. 0655C–0655D.] “*Procedere* properly means to come together for sacred rites, and is used especially of sacred persons, just as *incedere* is used of grandees and kings walking with dignity and majesty—indeed, even of gods, as Juno in Virgil, *Aeneid* I: ‘But I, who walk as queen of the gods’; likewise: ‘And in her gait the true goddess was revealed.’ On this word see often elsewhere, especially note 471 to the *Sacramentary*.”

- [Col. 0655D.] “For this matter read the many examples reported by Saint John Climacus in the fourth step of the *Ladder*, sections 26, 29, 31, 33, 34, and so forth. You will recognize the remarkable prudence of prelates in punishing and the astonishing obedience of subjects in suffering: punishments rightly decreed by the former, even against those who did not deserve them, were borne by the latter with equanimity as though deserved. Gussanville.”

- [Cols. 0655D–0656C.] “After this letter, the privilege granted by Pope John to the Church of Ravenna is appended in two Teller manuscripts and in the older Colbert manuscript in these words: ‘Copy of the decree: John to his most beloved brother Peter. We know that it accords with reason that we should adorn with the vestment of the pallium those whom, in cities where the honour of the priesthood shines upon them by the inspiration of divine mercy, it is established that this was also granted from the Apostolic See to pontiffs who lived in previous times.
