Therefore, by the present authority, we grant to your charity the use of the pallium, as your predecessors are known to have had it; and we wish all things concerning the privilege of your honour to remain which are established to have been observed for your Church in earlier times, so that you may grieve that none of its privileges has been diminished. And, the pope’s subscription: May God keep you safe. Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the reign of the lord Emperor Justin.’ The most learned Baluze, who published this decree from the Colbert manuscript in *Miscellanies*, Book V, rightly judges that, as in that Colbert manuscript, ‘Justinian’ should be written instead of ‘Justin.’”

- [Cols. 0656D–0657D.] “LETTER LVIII [otherwise 56]. Note the history of the widow in 4 Kings 4 and the parable in Matthew 18. The most ancient Roman law of the Twelve Tables allowed the body of a living debtor to be cut up, torn apart, and divided among creditors; Aulus Gellius, Book XX, chapter 1. Later, debtors and those who gave themselves into bondage for them were consigned to prison and subjected to beatings at the creditor’s discretion; Livy, *Annals*, Book VIII, mentions this and notes the reason for abolishing the custom. The emperor Constantine freed debtors to the fisc from the penalty of imprisonment, *Code*, Book X, title 19, law 2. The most cruel emperors Diocletian and Maximian did not permit the children of debtors to serve creditors for debt, *Code*, Book IV, title 10, law 12. Justinian, in Novel 134, chapter 7, provides that a debtor’s son shall not be retained for his father either as a pledge, in servile service, or for hire; and he subjects a creditor who violates this law to corporal penalties. Prison, moreover, is a kind of slavery. See Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 27. In Gaul creditors seize a dead debtor’s body, and, preventing its burial, commit the living [relative] to prison. Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 62 on Matthew 18, fiercely attacks merciless creditors, especially those who harshly oppress peasant farmers indebted to them. Saint Augustine, explaining Christ’s teaching on forgiving debts in *Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, indeed wishes debtors to be admonished concerning their duty, but denies that they should be compelled harshly; he teaches that debts should rather be remitted. Auget.”

- [Col. 0657D.] “This alone we read in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatien, the old Colbert manuscript, and Vatican A.”

- [Col. 0657D.] “LETTER LIX [otherwise 57]. This is omitted in all the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, Corbie, and other manuscripts. That Secundinus was bishop of Tauromenium is established from many letters written to him.”

Long ago we ordered (Gratian, 18, q. 2, c. 7) that the baptistery should have been removed from the monastery of Saint Andrew, which is above Mascala, on account of the monks’ disturbances, and that an altar should be erected in the same place where the fonts are located. The completion of this work has been delayed until now. We therefore admonish your Fraternity that, once you have received this present letter, you must no longer introduce any delay; but, after the place of the fonts has been filled in, an altar for celebrating the sacred mysteries must be erected there without any postponement, so that the monks mentioned above may be able to celebrate the work of God more securely, and so that our mind may not be stirred against your Fraternity because of your negligence.

[Note: This was evidently troublesome and unusual for the monks. The baptistery is forbidden in monasteries for the same reason that public Masses are forbidden there: lest a popular gathering be occasioned in the retreats of God’s servants. See above, Book II, Letter 41. Gratian, citing this passage, has “inconveniences” (molestias) in place of “disturbances” (insolentias).]

[Note: The fonts of the baptistery were dug into the ground; they did not project above the pavement, as ours do. This is presupposed by Chrysostom, Homily 40 on chapter 15 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians; Ambrose, Homily 16 on Psalm 118; Gregory himself in the Book of the Sacramentary, on Pentecost Saturday; and Isidore of Seville, Book II, On Divine Offices, chapter 24, where he clearly indicates that one descended into the baptismal font by three steps. Traces of that arrangement remain in many places. On the Lateran baptistery Onuphrius writes: “In the middle it has a font hollowed out in the ground to a depth of five cubits . . . there is a descent into it by three steps.” Here understand “cubit” with Suetonius as an ell, not with Servius as the distance to which both hands are extended.]

EPISTLE LX. TO THE PATRICIAN ITALICA. In the very cases concerning the poor, he chooses silence so as not to become involved in litigation. He grants Cyprian authority to settle the case with Italica, if she herself wishes it, while preserving the rights of the poor.

[Col. 0657C]

Gregory to Italica, patrician.

[Note: We conjecture that this Italica was the wife of Venantius, mentioned in Book I, Letter 34, on the basis of Book IX, Letter 123, written to both of them, where Barbara and Antonina are mentioned; they are known to have been Venantius’s daughters.]

We received your letters, full of sweetness, and the news of your excellent health made us rejoice. With regard to them, the sincerity of our mind is such that our paternal affection permits us to suspect nothing hostile concealed beneath their tranquility. But may almighty God grant that, just as we think well of you, so your mind may answer us with goodwill, and that you may display in your deeds the sweetness you offer in words. For glorious health and beauty on the surface of the body are of no benefit if a wound lies hidden within. That discord is especially to be feared which has external peace as its retinue.

[Note: Vatican manuscript D reads “internal” (interior).]

As for what your Excellence has earnestly attempted in the aforesaid letters to recall to our memory, know that we wrote to you that we wished to settle nothing with you concerning the cases of the poor amid scandal or forensic tumult. We remember having written this, and, with the Lord’s help, we know that we restrain ourselves from contentious lawsuits by ecclesiastical moderation, and in accordance with that apostolic principle, “with joy to endure the seizure of our goods.” But we believe that you know that our silence and patience will not prejudice the poor in these matters before the bishops who come after me.

Accordingly, fulfilling our above-mentioned promise, we have now determined to remain silent concerning these cases themselves; nor, in matters where we perceive that kindness is being practiced inadequately, do we wish to involve ourselves personally in the business. But lest you should perhaps infer from this, glorious daughter, that we still altogether reject whatever pertains to concord, we have instructed our son Cyprian the deacon, who is coming to the regions of Sicily, that, if you intend to arrange anything concerning these matters in a salutary manner and without sin to your soul, he should settle it with you by our authority, so that we may no longer be troubled by those affairs whose outcome has been arranged with gentleness.

[Note: In the printed editions it reads “whose effect must be dispensed”; but the manuscripts of the Vatican, Normandy, Rheims, and others compel us to adopt another reading.]

May almighty God, who knows how to bend even things that are altogether impossible toward possibility, assist you: may he dispose your cases with an intention of peace, and, for the reward of your soul, provide for the poor out of the goods belonging to this Church.

EPISTLE LXI. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP. How he ought to conduct himself in his own Church.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

We have received the letter of your Charity, in which you informed us that, by God’s favor, you had been well received by your Neapolitan citizens, your sons. For this we gave thanks to almighty God. You ought therefore to repay their affection by your conduct: restrain the wicked, release the good with discretion and the greatest kindness, and frequently exhort them to follow the better courses, so that they may rejoice to have found in you a father’s character, and so that you may, with the Lord’s cooperation, execute more diligently the charge of governance entrusted to you.

EPISTLE LXII. TO EUTYCHIUS, BISHOP. He urges him to persevere in converting the worshipers of idols. He requests the praetor’s protection for him.

Gregory to Eutychius, bishop of Tyndaris.

[Note: EPISTLE LXII [elsewhere 60]. Tyndaris, still commonly called Santa Maria di Tindaro, was formerly an episcopal city of Sicily between Mylae and Pactae; it is now ruined, on the coast facing the Lipari Islands. Gussanville. In four Vatican manuscripts, the Normandy manuscript, Rheims, Regius, and most others, the reading is “Tindarinus” or “Tundarinus.” In two Teller manuscripts, “Londarinus.”]

I received the letter of your Fraternity, delivered by Benenatus, a cleric of your Church, and I gave thanks to almighty God because we learned that you were occupied with matters concerning the soul and with those that pertain to God. For you wrote to us that certain worshipers of idols and of the doctrine of the Angellians were to be found in the districts over which you preside; you stated that many of them had been converted, while some defended themselves by appealing to the name of influential persons and to the character of the places.

[Note: So read four Vatican manuscripts, five English manuscripts, seven Norman manuscripts, Rheims, and others. These may perhaps be the Angellians about whom Nicephorus writes in Book XVIII of his History, chapter 49: “There are, moreover, others called Severites . . . They say that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Paraclete, namely the Holy Spirit, another; but that none of these separately possesses a nature of its own, rather that they have one God or Godhead common to them and existing in them; and that, by sharing indivisibly in that Godhead, each is God. They consider there to be one subsistence—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—but the one God, substance, and nature to be common.” These Angellians, however, were so called by their opponents from a place in Alexandria called Angelium, where those who held first rank among them used to assemble. Their opponents likewise called them Sabellians. In place of “of the Angellians,” the printed editions read “of the angels.” There were indeed formerly people who went mad in the worship of angels. Augustine writes of them under the thirty-ninth heresy: “The Angelics, inclined toward the worship of angels,” whom Epiphanius declares to have entirely died out in Heresy 60. Whether Gregory here means errors disseminated by those heretics, or others, is uncertain.

Saint Paul writes in Colossians 2:18: “Let no one deceive you, delighting in humility and the worship of angels.” Theodoret explains the Apostle’s words as follows: “Those who defended the Law also induced people to worship angels, saying that the Law had been given through them. This vice remained for a long time in Phrygia and Pisidia. Therefore the synod that met at Laodicea in Phrygia prohibited people by law from praying to angels, canon 35 . . . They were evidently led to this by humility, saying that the God of all could neither be seen, touched, nor comprehended, and that they ought to win divine favor for themselves through angels.”

But do not suppose that all worship of angels was condemned by the Apostle or by the ancient Fathers. Hear a few witnesses. Eusebius says in Demonstration of the Gospel, Book III, page 107: “We have been taught to venerate angels according to the reason and degree of their dignity, so that we may offer the honor of adoration only to God, who is King of the universe.” Ambrose, in his Book On Widows, asserts that angels should be entreated. “Our weakness,” says Hilary on Psalm 129, “needs their intercession.”]

In order to assist the good works of your Charity, we have sent our letter to the glorious praetor of Sicily, so that, with the Lord’s help, he may support you with whatever strength he can, and so that what has laudably begun may be salutarily completed. Your Fraternity ought therefore to exercise the greatest concern in this matter. For you truly follow an episcopal life if, through your zeal and your tongue, you bring back into the unity of the Church those who dissent from the truth of the faith.

EPISTLE LXIII. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP. Concerning the consecration of the monastery of the abbess Gratiosa.

[Col. 0660A]

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

[Note: EPISTLE LXIII [elsewhere 59]. After the deposition of Demetrius, bishop of Naples, when Paul, bishop of Nepi, and afterward Florentius, his subdeacon, refused the election made in their favor, Fortunatus was elected with the consent of Saint Gregory in the year 593. He subscribed to the Roman council in the year 595. Concerning Florentius, see above, Letter 15. Gussanville.]

Religious desires ought to be carried into effect without difficulty. And so the abbess Gratiosa, together with her congregation, having submitted a petition, requested what is contained in the document attached below this letter: namely, that Rustica, of patrician memory, by the final disposition of her will, had wished a monastery for the handmaids of God to be constructed in the city of Naples, in her own house, in the Herculian quarter, in the district called Lampadius, where she had arranged for the aforesaid Gratiosa to preside as abbess.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts A and C read: “in the district formerly called Lampadi.” The more recent printed editions read: “in the district in which Lampadius established a monastery of handmaids of God, [and] was buried, in which.” We do not know whence these words were derived, and it is no less obscure what sense is to be assigned to them.] She is also known to have built an oratory and, according to her wish, to have left it four ounces of her entire estate.

[Note: That is, a third part of her property.]

She desired it to be consecrated in honor of blessed Mary, ever virgin, and Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, dearest brother, by this present command we have decided to exhort your Charity that, having first inspected the will to determine whether it is legally valid, and having discovered that the same four ounces were truly transferred to that monastery, you should, whenever they request it, proceed without reluctance to the aforesaid place and perform the solemnities of the venerable dedication.

[Note: The fact that monasteries formerly went for several days without liturgy is demonstrated by the rules of the ancient monks, as Cardinal Bona shows in Book I, chapter 18, number 3, of On Liturgical Matters. In the preface to the second century of Benedictine history, section 4, Mabillon observes that in the seventh century the daily celebration of Mass had not yet become so customary among priests that each one approached the altar every day to celebrate the sacred rites. From Book IV of the Dialogues, chapter 56, it is known that Cassius, bishop of Narni, was accustomed to offer sacrifice to God daily. Mabillon praises several others in the same place who throughout the seventh century attended the sacred rite daily; this, he says, appears to have been less common in earlier centuries.]

Thus, whenever necessary, venerable Masses may be celebrated by the priests serving in the place described above; and your Fraternity and the priests are not to inflict upon it any trouble beyond the careful observance of discipline. Nor is your Fraternity to consider as something to be claimed for itself anything that may come as an offering through the devotion of different people. Whether gold, silver, land, or clothing, the aforesaid foundation is in every way to possess it, and whatever may happen to be offered there is to benefit the handmaids of God serving in that place.

[Note: This passage is obscure in the more recent editions, chiefly because of punctuation: “let them claim, or if anything . . . . . be claimed.” It is to be explained as follows: “nor should your Fraternity consider that it may claim for itself anything that . . . .” In the Norman manuscript, three Vatican manuscripts, and most others, the reading is: “or if anything should come as an offering through the devotion of various people, whether a white garment, with the handmaids of God . . . should advance,” and so forth. In the old printed editions, supported by many manuscripts, the words “should consider it claimable for itself” are omitted.]

EPISTLE LXIV. TO CHRYSANTHUS, BISHOP. He is to seek a bishop for the Church of Mevania, ordain priests, and there confirm infants.

Gregory to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto.

Two years ago we assigned to your Fraternity the responsibility of visiting the Church of Mevania, in which, following the practice customary among the scribes of our chancery, we did not wish you to undertake anything concerning the promotion of clerics.

[Note: EPISTLE LXIV [elsewhere, in the second indiction, 76; in Vatican manuscript 77]. See Book I, Letter 81.]

Now, however, the clerics of the aforesaid Church who have come here as bearers of this letter said that they have no priest either in that Church or in its parishes.

[Note: Gussanville anxiously asks to whom the care of this Church was then entrusted: perhaps to some deacon, as once happened according to canon 77 of Elvira; perhaps to a doorkeeper, as in a certain council of Toledo. Had the learned man attended to Book I, Letter 81, formerly 78, he would have understood that Saint Gregory had entrusted the care of the Church of Mevania to Honoratus the priest. For the confirmation of infants and the performance of other episcopal duties, the assistance of neighboring bishops, such as Chrysanthus here, was doubtless employed.]

We therefore exhort your Fraternity that, if you are able to find a person of such character as can worthily be promoted to the rank of the episcopal office, you should send him here as quickly as possible with the solemn decree and the testimony of your letters. But if such a person cannot now be found, seek out with every effort and diligence persons who can be ordained there to the priestly order. First investigate their life and conduct carefully, so that neither the sacred canons nor ecclesiastical regulations may in any respect stand in their way. In this way the people living there—who sadly complain that they have been deprived of communion because of the lack of priests—may rejoice that they have recovered it, and so that the solemn celebrations of Mass may not be absent from those churches. Your Fraternity should also make a point of going there to confirm the infants, so that nothing may reproach you for neglecting pastoral care.

EPISTLE LXV. TO MAURICIUS AUGUSTUS. He asks him to moderate or alter the law by which he had forbidden both those involved in public administration and soldiers to be received into monasteries.

Gregory to Mauricius Augustus.

[Note: EPISTLE LXV [elsewhere 62]. In Vatican manuscript B and some others: “to Mauricius Tiberius Augustus.” Mauricius was a Cappadocian by birth, an energetic man distinguished for military glory. Because of his exceptional abilities and outstanding achievements in war, the emperor Tiberius Constantine made him his colleague in the empire and his son-in-law, giving him his daughter Constantina in marriage. He administered the empire with the highest distinction for twenty years, and was finally deprived of both life and empire by Phocas, together with his wife and nine children. They say that this happened to him by the just judgment of God because twelve thousand prisoners were slaughtered by Chagan, leader of the Avars, although Mauricius could easily have ransomed them at little expense and refused to do so. The story is well known and is found especially among the Greek historians: Evagrius, Simocatta, Zonaras, Glycas, Cedrenus, Theophanes, Constantine Manasses, and Nicephorus Callistus, all of whom praise his virtues remarkably. The Latins treated him more harshly, especially John the Deacon, who called him an extremely avaricious and rapacious ruler, hostile to God and a tyrant. Gussanville. We pass over here the fuller discussion of this emperor, since we shall often have a more convenient opportunity to discuss his virtues and vices in the Life of Saint Gregory; consult that work.]

Omnipotent God holds him guilty who is not pure in everything he does and says to the most serene lords. I, however, an unworthy servant of your Piety, speak in this petition neither as bishop nor as a servant by right of the commonwealth, but by private right; for, most serene lord, you were already my lord from the time when you were not yet lord of all.

When Longinus, the most illustrious man, the strator, came, I received the law of the lords; but at that time, exhausted by bodily illness, I was unable to make any reply to it.

[Note: He was called a strator, one who mounted the emperor on his horse and saddled the horse for him. There is a title “On Stratores” in Book XII of the Code. Their duty was to inspect the horses supplied by provincials. They were commanded by the πρωτοστράτωρ (protostrator), whom Codinus calls “the grand equerry.” In the absence of the grand domestic, he bore the emperor’s sword, and so forth. Each patrician also had his own strator; for in Theophanes I find the strator of the patrician Priscus and of others. Gussanville.] In that law the piety of the lords decreed that whoever had been involved in public administrations should not be permitted to enter ecclesiastical office.

[Note: Not everyone was permitted to become a cleric. Monasteries were open to all; that is, the offenses that led people to monasteries excluded them from the clerical state, as the Council of Nicaea teaches in canon 2 and the letter of Siricius to Himerius. Indeed, having administered public affairs was an impediment. Innocent I writes to Victricius, bishop of Rouen: “If anyone, after the remission of sins, has held the military belt of the world, he must absolutely not be admitted to the clerical state.” And afterward: “Some of our brothers attempt to make clerics of curiales or of any persons occupied with public functions,” and so forth. See the whole of Letters 2 and 24, and the other canons cited in Distinction 51; also Saint Gregory, according to the former order of the editions, Book VII, first indiction, Letter 11, to the bishops of Sicily. Who these curiales and others excluded from the clerical state were is explained by Innocent himself in Letter 24: advocates, soldiers, officials, and actors. See the gloss on chapter 1 of Distinction 51, chapter 2, and the Decretals, Book I, concerning those bound to render accounts. Gussanville. By a constitution of Constantine the Great, those liable to public accounts and attached to public offices were barred from sacred orders unless the emperor consented. See the law “Officiales,” in the Code of Theodosius, Book III, title “Concerning Bishops and Clerics.” Innocent I approved this law, lest the Church should grieve over those recalled from such offices to the clerical order, canon “Aliquantos” and the following, Distinction 51. Gregory praised the same law when renewed by Mauricius, knowing that often a man who seeks the ecclesiastical order while still worldly wishes to change the world, not leave it. He repeats this below, first indiction, Letter 5, elsewhere 11. Alteserra.]

He praised this very highly, knowing most clearly that someone who hastens to enter ecclesiastical office after abandoning worldly dress wishes to change the world, not leave it. But I was altogether astonished that the same law says that he may not convert in a monastery, since his accounts can be settled through the monastery, and arrangements can be made for the place where he is received also to assume his debts.

[Note: This is how it is read in four Vatican manuscripts, the Normandy manuscripts, and others, whereas the printed editions have “his debts should be paid.” Since, according to Novel 5, chapter 4, whatever property a monk had already became the property of the monastery, it was entirely just that his debts should be paid by the monastery.]

For even if someone wished to convert with a devout mind, he would first restore things unjustly taken and would think about his soul all the more truly because he was freer of burdens. The law further states that no one who has been branded on the hand may be permitted to convert.

[Note: Everyone knows that slaves were formerly branded and marked with letters, with punctures made in the skin that would remain permanently; hence the proverb, “No one is more lettered than the Samians.” Similar marks were burned into soldiers; brands were inscribed on them, sometimes as a disgrace and sometimes for identification. Vegetius, Book II, chapter 5, writes: “Soldiers marked and inscribed with punctures destined to remain in the skin customarily swear.” In the Code, Book XI, title 9, concerning the Fabricenses: “Brands, that is, public marks, are imposed on the arms of the Fabricenses in imitation of recruits.” Hence Tertullian, On the Crown: “A branded soldier who has received his discharge.” And Saint Cyprian, To Donatus: “You whom the spiritual camp has already marked as a soldier.” Gussanville. See Procopius on Isaiah 44, at the words “Another shall write upon his hand, ‘I belong to God.’” He writes in Greek: Τὸ δὴ, τῇ χειρὶ, διὰ τὸ στίζειν ἴσως πολλοὺς, ἐπὶ καρπῶν, ἢ βραχιόνων, ἢ τοῦ σταυροῦ τὸ σημεῖον, ἢ τὴν Χριστοῦ προσηγορίαν. That is: “The reason he said ‘upon the hand’ is perhaps that many used to have the name of Christ or the sign of the cross branded upon their palms or arms.” Jerome writes on that passage: “He will write upon his hand, ‘I belong to God,’ so that, as a new recruit in the service of Christ, he may boast that he is a soldier.” Victor of Utica also reports that heretics practiced this, at the beginning of Book II of On the Vandal Persecution, where he speaks of a certain Clementianus who had the words “Manichaean, disciple of Jesus Christ” written on his thigh. Six things were necessary for a soldier: first, that he not be a merchant; second, that he be examined; third, that he give the military oath; fourth, that a sword be girded upon him; fifth, that a public mark be inscribed on his arms; sixth, that he be entered and written in the register. Gussanville.]

I confess to my lords that I was exceedingly alarmed by this constitution, because through it the way of heaven is closed to many, and what had hitherto been permitted is prohibited. For many are able to lead a religious life even while wearing secular dress. And there are many who, unless they leave everything, cannot possibly be saved before God.

What am I, speaking these things to my lords, except dust and a worm? Yet because I perceive that this constitution is directed against God, the author of all things, I cannot remain silent before my lords. For power over all human beings was given from heaven to the piety of my lords for this purpose: that those who desire good things may be assisted, that the way to heaven may be opened more widely, and that the earthly kingdom may serve the heavenly kingdom.

And behold, it is openly declared that a man who has once been branded in the earthly military service may not serve the Lord Jesus Christ unless he has either completed his military service or been discharged because of bodily weakness.

[Col. 0663C]

[Note: The emperors are addressed in the plural because Theodosius, still a child, had already been admitted into partnership in the empire by his father Mauricius in the year 591, as we have already observed.]

[Note: Promotion to the honor of the clerical state was not permitted; indeed, according to the Digest, Book 50, title 4, those liable for public obligations could not be promoted to any honors whatever, nor could they convert in a monastery, as Saint Gregory testifies. Nevertheless, slaves could not adopt the monastic discipline against the will of their masters. It is clear from Book VII, first indiction, Letter 11, that Saint Gregory later corrected this rule concerning those liable to public accounts: “They are not to be received unless they have first been released from public accounts.” Gussanville.]

In response to this, behold, Christ will answer through me, his lowest servant and yours, saying: “I made you a count of the excubitors from a notary, Caesar from a count of the excubitors, and emperor from Caesar; and not only this, I also made you the father of emperors. I entrusted my priests to your hand, and you withdraw your soldiers from my service?” Answer, I beg you, most pious lord, your servant: what will you reply in judgment to your Lord when he comes and says these things?

But perhaps it is believed that none of them converts with a pure heart. I, your unworthy servant, know how many soldiers converted in the monastery during my days and performed miracles, signs, and mighty works. Yet by this law it is now forbidden that any such person should convert.

Let my lord, I beg, inquire which earlier emperor issued such a law, and consider more carefully whether it ought to have been issued. It must indeed be considered very seriously that people are now prohibited from leaving the world at the very time when the end of the ages has drawn near. For behold, there will be no delay: with heaven and earth burning, the elements flashing, and the terrible Judge appearing with angels and archangels, with thrones and dominions, with principalities and powers, if he forgives all sins but declares this one law to have been enacted against him, what excuse, I ask, will there be?

Therefore, through that same terrible Judge, I beseech him not to allow the many tears, the many prayers, the many fasts, and the many alms of my lord to be darkened for any reason in the sight of almighty God; but let your Piety either soften its force by interpretation or alter the law itself, because the army of the lords grows stronger against its enemies when the army of God grows stronger in prayer.

[Note: The printed editions read “by moderating”; the reading “by interpreting” is found in the manuscript of Gembloux, at Bec, and in some others. Four Vatican manuscripts, the Audomarus manuscript, Lyré, Pratelles, Regius, and most others have “by interpreting,” to which our reading almost always agrees.]

I, indeed, as one subject to the command, caused the same law to be sent through the various regions of the earth. But because the law itself is in no way in agreement with almighty God, behold, through the written page of my petition I have announced it to the most serene lords. Thus I have fulfilled what I owed on both sides: I have rendered obedience to the emperor, and I have not kept silent about what I perceived on God’s behalf.

EPISTLE LXVI. TO THEODORUS, THE PHYSICIAN. Having demonstrated the injustice of the law that was enacted, he urges Theodorus, when presenting his letter to the emperor, to persuade him to revoke the law.

Gregory to Theodorus, the physician.

[Note: EPISTLE LXVI [elsewhere 65]. This man was Mauricius the emperor’s chief physician, a man shrewd and eloquent by nature, as Simocatta says in Book VI, chapter 11, and Nicephorus after him in Book XVIII, chapter 29. Priscus the Patrician, commander of Mauricius’s army and prefect of the East, sent him as ambassador to the king of the Avars with a successful outcome. On this matter see the authors cited and the Miscellaneous History, Book XVII, under the thirteenth year of Mauricius. Gussanville.]

[Note: After “physician,” the printed editions add “and so forth”; we have found this only in the Colbert manuscript.]

My tongue is not sufficient to express how many good things I have received from almighty God and from my most serene lord, the emperor.

[Note: That is, “to explain,” as it is also read in Vatican manuscript B.]

For these blessings, what is there for me to repay except to love their traces purely? But because of my sins—though I do not know whose suggestion or counsel was responsible—last year he issued such a law in his state that anyone who truly loves him ought to weep bitterly. At that time I could not answer the law because I was ill. Now, however, I have made some suggestions to the same lord.

For he commands that no one who has held a public office, no one who is an optio or has been branded on the hand, or who has served among the soldiers, may convert in a monastery unless perhaps his military service has been completed.

[Note: This is how it must be read from the Norman, Corbie, Tours, Regius, and all the manuscripts that I have been able to consult. I have no doubt that it is likewise read in the English, Vatican, and other manuscripts of the highest quality. But those who collated the letters of Saint Gregory with those codices, not understanding what “optio” or “obtio,” as it is read in the Regius manuscript, signified, considered it an error and preferred to read “no one who has been marked by office or by hand.” We explained the meaning of this word in the notes on chapter 35 of Book IV of the Dialogues. Observe here the grammatically unusual construction, which conflicts with the rules: “no one who is an optio . . . may be permitted to convert in a monastery.” The same construction occurs in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 58: “When someone newly comes for conversion, he is not to be granted an easy entrance.”]

This law was first issued, according to those who know the ancient laws, by Julian, of whom we all know how hostile he was to God. If our most serene lord did this because perhaps many soldiers were converting and the army was diminishing, did almighty God subject the Persian empire to him through the valor of soldiers?

[Note: He refers to the notable victory won over the Persians, when the strongly fortified city of Martyropolis was captured. The military events may be read in Theophanes. Moreover, Mauricius restored Chosroes, king of the Persians, after he had been driven from his kingdom; hence it may be said, to some extent, that the king and kingdom were subjected to him.]

Were not his tears alone heard, and did God not, in an order unknown to him, subject the Persian empire to his rule? It seems very harsh to me that he should prohibit his soldiers from the service of the one who both gave him everything and granted him dominion not only over soldiers but also over priests.

If the purpose is to preserve property, could not those very monasteries that received soldiers have returned other people’s property and retained only the men for conversion? Because these things grieve me deeply, I made my petition to the same lord.

But let your Glory present my petition to him privately at an appropriate time. I do not want it to be delivered publicly by my representative, because you, who serve him more intimately, can speak to him more freely and openly about what concerns his soul. He is occupied with many matters, and his mind scarcely finds itself free from the greater cares.

You, glorious son, speak on Christ’s behalf. If you are heard, it is gain for the soul of the aforesaid lord and for your own. If you are not heard, you have gained profit for your own soul alone.

[Note: The printed editions read, “you have gained a profit.” We follow all the Vatican manuscripts, which almost always agree with our reading, as do Corbie and others.]

EPISTLE LXVII. TO DOMITIAN, THE METROPOLITAN. He defends the exposition, in the spiritual sense, of the account of the rape of Dinah in Genesis 34, which he had formerly given. He congratulates Domitian both because, although occupied with secular affairs, he meditates on the Scriptures, and because he proclaimed the faith to the Persian emperor.

Gregory to Domitian, metropolitan.

[Note: EPISTLE LXVII [elsewhere 63]. This man was bishop of Melitene and metropolitan of Armenia, a relative of the emperor Mauricius, a prudent and industrious man, most powerful in word and deed, and most effective in undertaking great affairs, as Evagrius says in Book VI, chapters 16–18. Concerning him, see Theophylact Simocatta, Book IV of the History of Mauricius, chapter 14; and Book VIII, chapter 11: “Domitian, prelate of Melitene, related by birth to Mauricius, a holy priest honored for his rank and still holier in the manner of his life, gracious in speech, skillful in action, and most prudent in counsel, proceeded with imperial authority to Chosroes,” and so forth.

How highly Mauricius regarded him is indicated by Simocatta in Book VIII, chapter 11. At the beginning of Heraclius’s reign, tablets were found wrapped and sealed, containing everything Mauricius wished to be done after his departure from this life. When, in the fifteenth year of his reign, he had fallen into a dangerous illness, he made arrangements concerning the empire and designated as guardian for his sons, who were still underage, his kinsman Domitian, the noble bishop of the Church of Melitene, a man dexterous in practical affairs and still more dexterous in counsel. Therefore the emperor entrusted matters of greater importance to him for resolution because of his outstanding prudence. Simocatta mentions him in many places.

Concerning his death, Theophanes writes in his Chronography: “In the fifth indiction, in the month of January, Domitian, bishop of Melitene and kinsman of the emperor, died, and was buried by Cyriacus, the patriarch, at the Church of the Holy Apostles, while the entire senate honored his memory with funeral ceremonies.”

Melitene, or Melitina, now Malatia, was formerly, according to Niger, the chief city of the region of Melitene; afterward it was the metropolis of the province of Lesser, or Second, Armenia, situated on the Euphrates between Caesarea and Samosata. Gussanville.]

Receiving the writings of your sweetest and most gracious Blessedness, I rejoiced greatly, because they spoke to me at length about Holy Scripture. And because I found in them beloved banquets, I eagerly consumed them. Mixed among them are also certain matters concerning external and necessary affairs. You acted as though preparing a banquet for the mind, so that the dishes served might please more through their variety. And although external matters, like inferior and meaner foods, may have less flavor, they were nevertheless expressed by you so wisely that they are gladly received, since even contemptible foods often become sweet through the seasoning of a good cook.

While preserving the truth of the history, what I had said earlier about its divine significance ought in no way to have been rejected. For although, since you wish it so, its significance does not fit me, nevertheless, from the surrounding passages themselves, what has been said from it can unquestionably be maintained. For its corrupter is also called “the prince of the earth” (Genesis 34), by whom the devil is plainly signified, since our Redeemer says: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). He also seeks the woman in marriage, because the evil spirit, having first corrupted the soul by hidden seduction, hastens to possess it openly.

Therefore Jacob’s sons, fiercely angered, take up swords against all of Shechem’s household and against his homeland (Genesis 34), because all who have zeal must themselves also pursue those who become helpers of the evil spirit. They first command these men to undergo circumcision, and afterward kill them while they are in pain. For often stricter teachers, if they do not know how to moderate their zeal, although through preaching they cut away the vices of corruption, nevertheless, when the offenders are already lamenting what they have done, continue to rage against them through the harshness of discipline and prove more severe.

Those who had already cut away their foreskins ought not to have been put to death, because those who lament the fault of lust and turn carnal pleasure into grief ought not to experience the harshness of discipline from their teachers. Otherwise the Redeemer of the human race himself is loved less, if the soul is worn down on his behalf more than it should be. Hence Jacob’s sons are told: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the Canaanites” (ibid., 30). For when teachers cruelly pursue what sinners are already lamenting, the love of their Redeemer grows cold in the weakened mind, because it sees itself afflicted precisely where it does not spare itself.

I have said this, then, to demonstrate from the surrounding passages that the interpretation I offered is not improbable. But what your Holiness said to me for my consolation in connection with that same passage, I gladly accept, because, in the interpretation of Holy Scripture, [Note: Neither are the Fathers to be violated, nor are they to be introduced indiscriminately as though they had deprived those who came after them of every possible meaning. Nevertheless, we must strive not to assert anything against their will, when they almost unanimously cry out against it. GUSSANV.] nothing that does not resist sound faith ought to be rejected.

For just as, from a single piece of gold, some make necklaces, [Note: Omitting the two words “others make rings,” we have restored them from all the manuscripts—Vatican, Norman, Tours, Corbie, and others.] others rings, and others bracelets for adornment, so from the single meaning of Holy Scripture expositors compose, through innumerable interpretations, ornaments of various kinds; yet all of them contribute to the beauty of the heavenly Bride. [Note: A recent edition reads “the meaning of Scripture,” which we would gladly follow if the manuscript codices permitted it. But all of them have “understanding” or “knowledge.”] I rejoice greatly that your sweetest Blessedness, though occupied even with secular affairs, vigilantly brings your intelligence back to the understanding of sacred eloquence. For it is necessary that, if those affairs cannot be avoided altogether, these should not altogether be neglected.

But I ask you, through the almighty Lord, to extend the hand of prayer to me, laboring amid such great waves of tribulation, so that through your intercession I may be lifted to the heights, while the weight of my sins presses me down into the depths. Although I grieve that the emperor of the Persians was not converted, I nevertheless rejoice wholeheartedly that you preached the Christian faith to him. For although he did not deserve to come to the light, your Holiness will nevertheless receive the reward of your preaching. For the Ethiopian enters the bath black and leaves it black, but the bath attendant still receives his coins.

Regarding Maurice, you rightly say that from his action I should recognize the statue from its shadow—that is, discern greater things from the smallest. Yet in this we believe him, because sacraments and pledges bind his soul to us.

## BOOK FOUR. In the month of September, in the twelfth indiction.

[Col. 0667]

### 681. LETTER ONE, TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He congratulates him on having been elected by the unanimous consent of all. He urges him to respond to the affection of his people, to assist their needs, and to correct their faults promptly. He prays for his progress in good things. He sends him the pallium.

Gregory [Note: BOOK IV. Elsewhere BOOK III, LETTER 1. Concerning this matter, see above, letters 20 and 31. I observe that deacons were generally advanced to the episcopal office, rather than priests or archpriests. Priests, that is, devoted themselves only to prayer, reading, teaching, and the administration of the sacraments. The administration of external affairs was entrusted to deacons; hence, through practice, they acquired great facility, skill, and prudence in conducting business, assumed authority within the clergy, and formed closer relationships with prominent laymen. Historians report that very many deacons possessed such influence among clergy and laity that they not only became arrogant toward priests, but even openly resisted their own bishops as though they were censors. GUSSANV. Gussanvillaeus made these observations about deacons because Constantius was a deacon of the Church of Milan when he was unanimously elevated to its episcopal see.] to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

Receiving the letter of your Fraternity, I gave great thanks to almighty God, because I was deemed worthy to be uplifted by the celebration of your ordination. Since, by a heavenly gift, the assent of all united harmoniously in your election, your Fraternity ought to weigh this with the greatest consideration: after God, you are deeply indebted to those who, with such submissive devotion, wished you to be preferred to themselves.

It is therefore fitting that you respond to their conduct in all things with priestly kindness [Note: The printed editions preferred “to assist,” which is not found in the manuscript codices.] and hasten to meet their needs with compassionate piety. If some of them perhaps have faults, rebuke these with timely corrections [Note: Thus the Norman manuscripts and most others. In four Vatican manuscripts, the Royal manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, and the Paris edition of 1518, one reads “to rebuke,” referring back to “it is fitting,” which precedes it.], so that priestly indignation itself may be joined with the sweetness of virtue, and so that you may be loved by your subjects even when you are greatly feared. This brings your person to great reverence in their judgment, because just as rash anger and habitual anger are despised, so measured indignation against faults generally becomes more feared the longer it is delayed.

Our subdeacon John, on his return, reported to us many good things about your Fraternity. Concerning these we ask almighty God that he himself may bring to completion what he has begun, so that he may show that you have progressed inwardly and outwardly, now among human beings and afterward among the angels.

Moreover, we have sent you the pallium, to be used according to custom for the solemn celebrations of Mass. But I ask that, when you receive it, you uphold its honor and character through humility.

### LETTER TWO, TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He hopes that Queen Theodelinda and the three bishops who separated from Constantius over the Three Chapters, after receiving their letters, will return to his communion. Desiring peace with the Lombards, he asks Constantius to inform him about what has taken place between the Franks and the king of the Lombards.

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

My very dear son Boniface, the deacon, secretly reported to me something from a written communication of your Fraternity [Note: LETTER II. In the Becc manuscript, “written separately.”]—namely, that three bishops, having sought rather than found an opportunity, had separated themselves from the communion of your pious Fraternity, saying that you [Note: In the year of Our Lord 553, the Three Chapters were condemned at the Fifth Council. The condemnation was followed by a very serious schism, since many bishops were persuaded that the condemnation undermined the faith and damaged the authority of the Council of Chalcedon. It was no light task to eradicate this opinion from their minds. Vigilius, who then presided over the Apostolic See, had refused to assent to the definition of the Fifth Council, perhaps from pious but unfortunate motives, and had thereby given occasion to the schism—or at least added strength to it. His successor, Pelagius I, because he assented to the Fifth Council, was so hated by the Western bishops that they refused to recognize him as pope, and it was necessary, by Pelagius’ command, for a priest of Ostia to carry out that office in place of the bishop, as Binius reports after Anastasius. Pelagius II, the Roman pontiff in 578, left no stone unturned in his effort to reconcile the minds of the faithful, offended by the condemnation of the Chapters, but he did not succeed. Hence the use of the written declarations discussed in this and the following letter, so that, once such clouds had been dispersed, provision might be made for the unity of the universal Church and for the restoration of the Fifth Council. See the following letters 3 and 4. GUSSANV. Add also 35. For a fuller account of the Three Chapters, see the Life of Saint Gregory.] had consented to the condemnation of the Three Chapters and had given a written declaration to that effect. [Note: Among legal scholars there are many kinds of written declarations. Here I understand a sworn declaration, written and signed, by which they promised that they would henceforth consent to the condemnation of the Three Chapters and would never resist it. Our own age has revived similar declarations. GUSSANV.]

Indeed, if anything concerning the Three Chapters has been mentioned in any word or writing whatsoever, your Fraternity remembers it well, although your predecessor Laurence issued to the Apostolic See a very strict declaration, to which men of the highest rank and the lawful number of signatories subscribed. Among them I too subscribed, since at that time I was serving as urban praetor [Note: Vatican B has “urban prefecture.”]. Because such a division had arisen over nothing, it was right that the Apostolic See should take care that the unity of the universal Church be preserved in every way in the minds of priests.

As for the report that our daughter Queen Theodelinda [Note: She was the daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians; first she was the wife of Authari, king of the Lombards, and then, after he was killed by poison six years later, she married Agilulf, duke of Turin, who was made king of the Lombards. The writers praise this woman’s outstanding piety, especially Saint Gregory, who wrote several letters to her and sent her the books of the Dialogues. He knew that she was devoted to the faith of Christ and preeminent in good works, as Paul the Deacon says in Book IV, chapter 5, On the Deeds of the Lombards. He calls her Theudelinda and greatly extols her piety and generosity toward the Church in chapter 6. GUSSANV.] has suspended herself from your communion after hearing this report, it is entirely clear that, although she was briefly led astray by the words of wicked men, nevertheless, when the notary Hippolytus and the abbot John arrive, she will seek your Fraternity’s communion in every way. I have also sent her my letters, which your Fraternity should transmit without delay. Concerning the bishops who appeared to suspend themselves [Note: Vatican A has “who did not suspend themselves.”], I have written another letter. When you have had it shown to them, I have no doubt that they will repent before your Fraternity of the superstition of their pride.

You have also informed me subtly and briefly about what has happened concerning King Agilulf [Note: The same man as Agilulf, mentioned shortly before.] and the Frankish kings. I ask that your Fraternity inform me in every way of whatever else you learn. But if you see that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, is accomplishing nothing with the patrician, promise him support from us, for I am prepared to assist him in his cause, if he is willing to arrange something useful with the republic.

### LETTER THREE, TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

Constantius has given no written declaration concerning the Three Chapters. The faith of the Council of Chalcedon is preserved intact in the Roman Church. The bishops who have separated must therefore return to unity.

[Col. 0670C]

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

It has come to us that certain bishops of your diocese, seeking an opportunity rather than finding one, have attempted to divide themselves from the unity of your Fraternity, saying that you had given a written declaration at Rome concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters. They say this because they do not know how readily I would ordinarily believe your Fraternity even without such a declaration. For if this had been necessary, you could have been believed on your bare word. I, however, do not recall that the Three Chapters were mentioned among us either verbally or in writing.

But if they return quickly, they must be spared on account of their error, because, in the words of the Apostle Paul, “They understand neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions” (1 Timothy 1:7). For we confess, with truth as our authority and conscience as our witness, that we preserve in every respect undefiled the faith of the holy Council of Chalcedon, and that we dare neither add anything to its definition nor subtract anything from it.

But if anyone attempts to think or assert anything against the faith of that council, whether more or less, we anathematize him without delay and declare him alien from the bosom of Mother Church. Whoever, then, is not healed by this confession of mine no longer loves the Council of Chalcedon, but hates the bosom of Mother Church. If, therefore, they presumed to speak from zeal for their souls about the very matters they appeared to have dared, it remains for them, once this satisfaction has been accepted, to return to the unity of your Fraternity and not divide themselves from the body of Christ, which is the holy universal Church.

### LETTER FOUR, TO QUEEN THEODELINDA

He grieves that she has suspended herself from Constantius’ communion. He asserts that nothing was done against the faith of the Council of Chalcedon in the time of Justinian. He urges her to accept Constantius’ ordination and join herself to him in communion.

[Col. 0671C]

Gregory to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards.

We have learned from the report of certain persons that your Glory has been led to such a scandal against the holy Church that she has suspended herself from communion with the Catholic unity. Just as deeply as we love you sincerely, so deeply do we grieve over you, because you trust inexperienced and foolish men who not only do not know what they are saying, but can scarcely understand what they have heard. [Note: LETTER IV. This is the form of address used by Gregory as a mark of honor toward kings, emperors, their wives, and other distinguished persons. The title “majesty,” by which kings are now honored, had not yet been adopted. Horace, however, addresses Augustus in this way in Book II, Letter 1:

“If I could, I would also—but your majesty does not admit  
a small poem.”

And in Cassiodorus, Book III of the Variae, letter 27, one finds “royal majesty.”]

For they say that, in the time of Justinian of pious memory, certain measures were enacted against the Council of Chalcedon. Since they neither read nor believe those who read, they remain in the very error they have themselves fabricated about us. [Col. 0671D] We confess, with conscience as our witness, that nothing was changed or violated concerning the faith of the same holy Council of Chalcedon. [Note: Because the condemnation of the Three Chapters is mentioned here, albeit only lightly, Constantius wisely refrained from offering this letter to Theodelinda, as is clear from letter 39. The wise pontiff praised him for this and wrote that another letter should be given to the queen without causing scandal—one that mentioned neither the Fifth Council nor the acts concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters. It is numbered 38.]

Whatever was done in the time of the aforesaid Justinian was done in such a way that the faith of the Council of Chalcedon was in no respect disturbed. But if anyone dares to speak or think anything against the faith of that council, we condemn his opinion under threat of anathema. Since, then, you know our integrity from the testimony of our conscience, it remains that you never separate yourself from communion with the Catholic Church, lest all your tears and so many good works perish if they are found to be alien from the true faith.

It is therefore fitting that your Glory hasten to send to the most reverend brother and my fellow bishop Constantius, whose faith and life were long ago approved by me, and that you inform him by letters sent to him that you have graciously accepted his ordination and that you are in no way separated from communion with his Church. I think it unnecessary to say more about this, since, even if there was some doubt in your heart, I believe that, when my son the abbot John and the notary Hippolytus arrived, it was removed from your heart.

### LETTER FIVE, TO BONIFACE, BISHOP

He should attend to the conduct and reputation of his clergy. Concerning his subdeacons he decrees what he had previously decreed concerning the Sicilians in Book I, Letter 44.

Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio [Note: LETTER V. Elsewhere “of Regium,” as it is read in all the Norman manuscripts, in Vatican D, and elsewhere. Below also: “the clergy of the city of Regium.”].

It is certainly an insult to priests to have to be admonished about divine worship. What they themselves ought to demand is shamefully demanded of them. Nevertheless, lest—which we do not think possible—your Fraternity neglect in any respect matters pertaining to the work of God, we have decided to exhort you especially about this matter.

We therefore admonish you that under no circumstances should the clergy of the city of Regium be relaxed through your Fraternity’s leniency in matters demanded by their office. Rather, in matters pertaining to God, they must be compelled with the utmost urgency and diligence. We also wish you to take care of the reputation of the aforesaid clergy, so that nothing evil or contrary to ecclesiastical discipline may be heard about them; for their office ought to contribute to their adornment, not to the disgrace of their conduct. [Note: See Book I, Letter 44.]

As for your subdeacons (Gratian, Distinction 32, chapter 9), we decree that what we established concerning the Sicilians must be observed. Do not allow that decree of ours to be corrupted by anyone’s obstinacy or presumption, so that, while all the foregoing is preserved with the greatest strictness through you, you may neither prove to be a transgressor of our admonition—as we believe you will not—nor allow the pastoral order of governance entrusted to you to accuse you of negligence in any matter.

### LETTER SIX, TO CYPRIAN, DEACON

He is to investigate and punish the crime committed against the convert Petronilla by Agnellus, her corrupter, and ensure that what was taken from the monastery is restored.

[Col. 0672D]

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon and rector of Sicily.

It has been reported to us (Gratian, 19, question 3, chapter 8) that a woman named Petronilla, born in the province of Lucania [Note: A province of Italy. It was formerly part of Greater Greece; today it is the province of Basilicata in the Kingdom of Naples, together with part of the southern section of the Principality. GUSSANV.], was converted through the exhortation of Bishop Agnellus, and that all her possessions, insofar as she was able to possess any, [Note: To bring out the true meaning, the construction should be understood as follows: Petronilla gave to the monastery which she entered all that she possessed—although the monastery was entitled to it by law—and gave it specifically to that monastery by title of donation. We have often observed that Gregory’s style abounds in hyperbaton and inversions and transpositions of words. Gregory’s purpose, therefore, is that everything taken from the monastery, together with all its fruits and accessions, should return there. To achieve this, he observes that all the possessions Petronilla was able to have belonged to the monastery she entered, first by common right—namely, under imperial law, by which a person’s goods pass to the monastery upon monastic profession, Novel of Justinian 5, Novel 123, chapter 38—and especially by the specific title of donation. There can be no doubt about Saint Gregory’s judgment and intended purpose if one reads Book IX, Letter 7: “Because,” he says, “it has been decreed by the clear definition of the law that those who enter a monastery for the sake of conversion have no further permission to make a will, but that their possessions become the property of that monastery.”] although they could have belonged to her by right, she nevertheless transferred to that same monastery, which she had entered, also specifically by title of donation.

When the aforesaid bishop was dying, he left half of his property to a certain Agnellus, his son, who is said to be a notary of our Church, and half to the same monastery. But when they had fled to Sicily because of the calamity that had struck Italy, the aforementioned Agnellus is said to have violated her after corrupting her morals, and, realizing that she was pregnant, to have led her secretly out of the monastery [Note: That is, he led her out secretly. “To lead away” properly means to lead aside.], and to have taken away all her possessions, both her own and those which she could have received from her father’s share [Note: This refers to the possessions that had been taken away, not to Petronilla herself, as the printed editions have it against the manuscripts.], and, after committing so great and so serious a crime, to have defended them as his own property.

We therefore urge your Dilection to have the aforesaid man or the aforesaid woman brought before you for strict examination, and to investigate the case itself with the utmost precision according to its deserts. If you find it to be as it has been reported to us, determine this affair, stained by so many iniquities, with the utmost severity required for purification, so that strict punishment may come upon the aforesaid man, who had regard neither for his own status nor for hers and who was the cause of so many crimes. [Note: Marriages with consecrated virgins are forbidden; see the Council of Tours I, chapter 6: “Those who unite themselves to consecrated virgins through an unlawful relationship, or who abandon the religious profession they have undertaken, are both to be excluded from communion, because if anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him.” Consult also the Council of Paris III, chapter 5, and Tours II, chapter 20. “He who takes a consecrated virgin as his wife is to be struck with capital punishment,” according to the constitution of Chlothar II, which is included among the councils of Gaul after the Council of Paris V.]

After that vengeance has first been carried out and she has been placed under penance in a monastery, all the possessions taken from the aforementioned place must be returned, together with all their fruits and accessions.

### LETTER SEVEN, TO GENNADIUS, PATRICIAN

He should support Bishop Columba, who is investigating the council in Numidia and correcting abuses. He should restrain the internal wars of the Churches.

[Col. 0673C]

Gregory to Gennadius [Note: LETTER VII. The patricians have already been mentioned frequently. We read that Constantine the Great established their dignity. See Tillemont, History of the Emperors, under Constantine.] patrician and exarch of Africa.

We are confident that your religious Excellence’s mind is especially inflamed, through emulation of divine love, against whatever is improper in the Churches. We therefore willingly entrust to you the correction of ecclesiastical affairs in proportion to our confidence in the pious intention of your mind.

Let your Excellence know that certain persons arriving from parts of Africa reported to us that many things were being done in the council of Numidia contrary to the tradition of the Fathers and the decrees of the canons. Since we could no longer tolerate the frequent complaints concerning these matters, we entrusted their investigation to our brother and fellow bishop Columba, whose seriousness—confirmed by the reputation that has spread about him—no longer permits us to doubt him.

Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we urge your Excellence to lend him the strength of your assistance in all matters pertaining to ecclesiastical correction, lest, if something badly done is neither investigated nor punished, it grow into future abuses through the license granted by long passage of time. [Note: All the Vatican manuscripts except D have “may grow into future excesses.”]

But know, most excellent son, that if you seek victories, if you are concerned for the security of the province entrusted to you, nothing else will contribute more to this than being zealous for the lives of priests and restraining, as far as possible, the internal wars of the Churches.

### 687. LETTER EIGHT, TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

He should ensure that the will of the deceased Stephen concerning the construction of a monastery is fulfilled.

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

We think that your own office ought sufficiently to compel you to bring pious undertakings to completion. But lest anyone’s intervention soften your zeal by inducing leniency, we have judged it necessary to exhort you specifically about these matters.

It has indeed come to us that, when your Stephen was departing from this life, he ordered a monastery to be founded in a testamentary provision [Note: LETTER VIII [elsewhere numbered 10]. In the old editions and the Vatican manuscripts: “in the wording of his last will.”]. His desire is said to have been delayed until now by Theodosia, his honorable female heir [Note: This is how the Norman, Royal, Vatican, and other manuscripts read. The printed editions instead have: “whose desire is said to have been delayed by Theodosia ...” The sentence is certainly more cumbersome, but it is no less characteristic of Gregory’s style.]. Therefore we urge your Fraternity to devote the greatest diligence to this matter and to admonish the aforementioned woman [Note: Elsewhere, “move her,” as it is read in Vatican C.], so that within a year she may arrange for the monastery to be established as ordered and may construct everything according to the deceased man’s will, without dispute.

But if, through negligence or cunning, she delays completing anything within the aforesaid period—whether because it cannot be established in the place where it was intended, or because it is agreed that it should be established elsewhere, and it is neglected through continued delay—we then wish the monastery to be built through the efforts of your Fraternity. Once everything has been arranged, the property and revenues that were left are to be assigned to that venerable place through you, without any diminution.

Thus you will both escape a sentence of negligence before your dread Judge and, in accordance with the most pious laws, make good through episcopal diligence the delayed pious wishes of the dead.

### LETTER NINE, TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

A proven man is to be appointed to each monastery of the servants of God, and through him their affairs are to be managed so that the nuns may not wander about. Penalties are decreed for their lapses. Councils are to be held twice each year. Jewish slaves who flee to the Church for the sake of the faith are to be claimed for freedom. Chrismation is not to be repeated on the foreheads of the baptized; priests are to anoint only the breast, and afterward bishops the forehead. A monastery is to be built according to the will of the deceased Peter, if a sufficient amount of revenue is available.

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

Your own pastoral zeal ought certainly to have urged you to guard wisely and beneficially, even without the support of our exhortation, the flock you had received, and to preserve it with diligent vigilance from the crafty seizures of its enemies. But because we have found that your charity also needs the authority of our letter to increase its strength, it was necessary for us, through fraternal affection, to strengthen your wavering spirit toward the pursuit of religious vigor.

For it has come to us that you are giving insufficient protection to the monasteries of the servants of God situated in Sardinia. Although your predecessors had prudently arranged that certain proven men from the clergy should care for them and attend to their needs, the arrangement is now said to have been entirely neglected, so that the women consecrated principally to God are themselves compelled, through public officials, to go about for taxes and other public duties, and are forced to travel through villages and estates to meet fiscal demands, and improperly to involve themselves in affairs suited to men. [Note: Fiscal matters are taxes. This is evident from Book I of the Code, title 3, law 3, concerning bishops and clergy: “Concerning those clergy who possess estates, your exalted authority shall not only refuse to excuse them from bearing the burdens of others, but shall also compel them, on account of the estates they possess, to pay the fiscal assessments. For all clergy, etc.” I would interpret “to undergo [these matters] through public officials” as meaning that they must go from house to house among public officials, submit themselves to them, solicit them, and conduct their business through them. By “public officials” we mean magistrates, officials, messengers, and perhaps even tax collectors, since fiscal matters are involved. GUSSANV.]

Let your Fraternity remove this evil through an easy correction, by carefully appointing one man proven in life and conduct, whose age and position provide no grounds for evil suspicion, who can assist those monasteries with fear of God, so that thereafter the women may not wander outside their venerable places for any private or public matter contrary to the rule. [Note: Concerning wandering nuns, see Isidore of Pelusium, Book I, Letter 367.] Whatever must be done for them is to be done reasonably through the man whom you appoint.

Let the women themselves, offering praises to God and restraining themselves, give no further occasion in their monasteries for evil suspicion in the minds of the faithful. But if any one of them, whether through a previous permission or through the corrupt habit of impunity, has been led into an adulterous fall or is hereafter led into an abyss, [Note: This should be read according to Vatican A, all the Norman manuscripts, and the Corbie manuscript. The manuscripts do not agree among themselves. In the Rheims manuscript it reads: “has been led into the lapse of adultery, or into theft.” Tours has “or into theft”; the Royal manuscript has “has fallen into her own [lapse].” One Vatican manuscript supports the Rheims reading. None of the old copies contains the printed reading “or into fornication.” Our Gregory calls the fall of a nun adultery because, as Saint Augustine teaches in Psalm 83, if a consecrated woman marries, she is regarded as an adulteress of Christ.], after the appropriate severity of punishment, we wish her to be sent to another, stricter monastery of virgins for penance, so that there she may devote herself to prayers and fasts, make progress through repentance, and provide the others with a fearful example of stricter discipline.

But anyone who is found to have committed any iniquity with such women is to be deprived of communion if he is a layman. If he is a cleric, he is also to be removed from his office and immediately thrust into a monastery to mourn his offenses.

We also wish you to celebrate councils of the bishops twice each year, as this is said to have been the custom of your province and as the authority of the sacred canons commands. [Note: Thus the Council of Nicaea, canon 5: the first before Lent, the second around the autumn season. The matter concerns a provincial synod. The same is found in Antioch, canon 20, and Chalcedon, canon 19. The holy Council of Trent, session 24, On Reform, chapter 2, established that these should be renewed at least every three years. GUSSANV.] In this way, if any one of them diverges from the form of his professed purpose in conduct or character, he may be rebuked through the fraternal correction of the others; and, for the security of the flock entrusted to them and the condition of souls, the matter may be handled with paternal vigilance.

It has also come to us that Jewish male and female slaves, fleeing to the Church for the sake of the faith, are either restored to their unbelieving masters or that a price is paid so that they will not be restored. [Note: Concerning these matters, see above. By virtue of imperial constitutions, slaves who fled for the sake of the faith were claimed for freedom against the will of their masters, without any price being paid. Hesselius, cited above, teaches in Book II, Letter 39, indiction 11—now Book III, Letter 40—that this could have happened. It is nevertheless certain that this privilege did not apply everywhere, both from many letters of Saint Gregory and from our Gallican councils, as from the Council of Orléans III, chapter 13. For the Jews seem not to have been deprived of their slaves, whether household-born or purchased, unless they wished to lead them from the faith into their own error, or imposed something upon them that the Christian religion forbids, or afflicted them with tortures out of hatred for the faith. In these and similar cases, the Jews were punished by losing their slaves, or else the slaves were redeemed at a fixed price—namely, twelve solidi, as the Council of Mâcon I, chapter 16, states. GUSSANV.]

We therefore urge you not to permit such a wicked custom to continue. If any Jewish slave (Gratian, Distinction 54, chapter 16) takes refuge in a venerable place for the sake of the faith, do not allow him in any way to suffer prejudice. Whether he was formerly a Christian or has now been baptized, he must in every way be defended in freedom, without any loss to the poor, through the religious protection of ecclesiastical piety.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] All the Norman, Vatican, English, Tours, Corbie, Reims, Cistercian, Vindobonensis, and other manuscripts unanimously read this way, and indeed with excellent sense. Evidently, since the priests of Sardinia—perhaps as a result of commerce with the Greeks—were anointing the forehead with chrism, the bishops of that island, relying on their own right confirmed by the ancient tradition of the Fathers, were themselves also marking the foreheads of those baptized at confirmation. Gregory disapproves this repetition of the forehead-anointing. But in order to preserve for bishops their proper right of marking foreheads, he keeps priests farther away from that marking, allowing them, as in the Roman Church, not even the anointing of the crown of the head, but only that of the breast. In certain manuscripts, with the word *bis* removed and the sense corrupted, one reads: “Let bishops not presume to mark baptized infants on their foreheads with chrism” [Col. 0678D]. Moved, unless we are mistaken, by the absurdity of this reading, all the editors—and before them some copyists—substituted *presbyteri* for the word *episcopi*, although the former is scarcely found in one or another manuscript.]

“Let bishops not presume to mark baptized infants twice on their foreheads with chrism; but let priests (Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 4, canon 119) anoint those who are to be baptized on the breast, so that bishops may afterward anoint them on the forehead.”

[Col. 0677B] With regard also to founding monasteries that various persons have been ordered to build, if you see that some of those to whom the task was assigned are delaying it by excuses, we wish you to be diligently vigilant, in accordance with what the laws prescribe, lest—God forbid—the pious wishes of the dead be nullified by your leniency. As for the monastery that Peter is said formerly to have ordered to be built in his own house, we have arranged that your Fraternity carefully investigate the amount of the revenues left there (Gratian 16, question 1, canon 14).

[Note: [Col. 0678D] Thus we read in all the Norman, Corbie, and Reims manuscripts. In Vatican manuscripts C and D there is also *modum habet substantiae*. In the printed editions one finds *modus habetur substantiae*, to which Augentius adds: “These are customary expressions among jurists, meaning a certain quantity of property sufficient for the monastery’s needs.” *Modus* is also opposed to a burdensome estate, to which no one is compelled to have recourse. Code, book XVI, title “On the law of the free…”]

And if the estate does indeed possess sufficient means, after everything that is said to have been diminished or dispersed from those properties has been gathered together, let this be founded with every diligence and without any delay. But if the resources are either inadequate or burdensome, after everything has been carefully investigated, as prescribed, we wish you to report to us, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may know what decision we can make concerning its construction.

[Col. 0677C] Let your Fraternity therefore apply itself diligently to all the matters mentioned above, so that it may be found neither to have transgressed the sequence of our instructions nor, guilty before the divine judgment, to have displayed too little zeal in its pastoral office. (Cf. John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 45.)

## LETTER X. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF DALMATIA

They are not to ordain any bishop at Salona without his consent and permission. If, however, they all agree on someone other than Maximus, he is to be consecrated.

Gregory to all the bishops throughout Dalmatia.

[Col. 0678A] Your Fraternity ought indeed, out of regard for the divine judgment, to close your carnal eyes, omit nothing that pertains to God [Note: [Col. 0678D] LETTER X [15].—Here the manuscripts diverge. Vatican B reads, “with the mind’s intention raised up.” Corbie, together with Vatican A and C, reads, “with the mind’s intention directed aright,” omitting *a*; Vatican D, followed by Tours, Reims, and the Norman manuscripts, reads, “and the mind’s intention directed aright,” which we think should be followed. The printed editions have, “from the mind’s intention directed aright.”] and place no human face before the uprightness of justice. But since your conduct has become so entangled in secular affairs that, forgetting every path of priestly dignity within you and every awareness of heavenly fear, you strive to accomplish not what pleases God but what pleases yourselves, we have found it necessary to send you these more severe and specific written instructions. By the authority of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, we order you absolutely not to presume, in the city of Salona, to lay hands on anyone, so far as the ordination of a bishop is concerned, without our consent and permission, nor to ordain anyone in that city otherwise than we have stated.

[Col. 0678B] But if, whether of your own accord or compelled by anyone, you presume or attempt to do anything contrary to this, we shall decree that you be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0679B] Thus four Vatican manuscripts and Reims. In the Norman and Corbie manuscripts it reads, “so that you may be alienated from the heavenly mysteries, and that he whom you ordain…”], so that, because of this very act of yours or because of your willingness to transgress our command, you may be excluded from the heavenly mysteries, and that the man whom you ordain may not be regarded as a bishop.
