For we do not wish anyone whose life can be censured to be rashly ordained. But if the deacon Honoratus is shown to be unworthy, we wish you to report to us concerning the life and character of the person who is to be elected, so that whatever must be done in this matter may, with our consent, be salutarily carried out.

We trust in the almighty Lord that, so far as our intention is concerned, we shall never permit anything that could burden our soul, nor anything that could burden your Church. But if, regarding any person, the unanimous consent of all should be given in such a way that, with God as its author, the person is worthy and no one dissents from his ordination, we wish him to be consecrated by you in that same Church of Salona, by the permission granted in this present letter—except only in the case of Maximus, concerning whom many serious evils have been reported to us. If he does not cease striving for a higher rank, it remains, in my judgment, that, after careful investigation, he should also be deprived of the office he now holds.

[Note: [Col. 0679B] In Vatican the date “in the month of November, indiction 12” is prefixed to this letter. In Tours Saint Gatianus, at the end, one reads: “In the month of September, indiction 12.”]

## LETTER XI. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP

The fourth parts of newly acquired revenues are also to be distributed according to canonical apportionment. A priest or other cleric is not to become abbot unless he relinquishes the care of the Church in which he ministered. When a bishop dies, the Church’s property is to be inventoried carefully but without charge. Visitors and their clerics are to be provided with a stipend. A virgin who is not yet sixty is not to become abbess.

[Col. 0679A]

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

Formerly, by our authority, we had entrusted your Fraternity with the task of correcting in our place anything in Sicily [Note: [Col. 0679B] LETTER XI.—Among the manuscripts and printed editions that differ at this point, we have preferred five Norman manuscripts, Reims, Corbie, Vatican B and D, and Tours. In the last two, however, *excideretur* is read instead of *excederetur*, through a scribal error. Vatican A and C have *exciderunt*. Michael agrees. The Royal manuscript has *exciderat*. The manuscripts differ only in this word; but the printed editions contain many departures from the true reading, with phrases that appear in none of the manuscripts. Thus they read: “If anything should fall away from the Church in Sicily, and in the other…”] that exceeded its due limits, or anything that was being conducted improperly, as well as anything in the other venerable places. But since a complaint has reached us concerning certain matters that have until now been neglected, we have again determined to stir your Fraternity specifically to their correction.

We have learned (Gratian 12, question 2, canon 19) that, concerning newly acquired ecclesiastical revenues, the canonical distribution of the fourth parts is not being made, but that the bishops of the places distribute only a fourth of the ancient revenues, while retaining for their own uses what is now acquired.

[Col. 0680A] [Note: [Col. 0679C] The printed editions have *quam rem pravam*, “which evil thing.” *Quamobrem*, “wherefore,” is plainly better, as in all the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Reims, and other manuscripts.]

Wherefore let your Fraternity hasten vigorously to correct this evil and surreptitiously introduced custom, so that, whether from former revenues or from those that have now accrued or shall accrue, the fourth parts may be distributed according to canonical apportionment. For it is improper that one and the same property of the Church should in some way be regarded under a twofold right—that of usurpation and that of the canons.

Do not permit priests, deacons, or clerics of any order who serve the Churches (Gratian 16, question 1, canon 38) to be abbots in monasteries [Note: [Col. 0679C] By these and similar words nothing else is prescribed than that the title of abbot and the care of a monastery are not to be assigned to an extraneous cleric who holds a title in a secular Church and is not a monk. If such a cleric, after leaving the Church he served, has already become abbot, he must choose either to relinquish the abbacy, if he does not wish to renounce his title in his Church, or to abandon the care of his Church, if he decides to remain in the office of abbot. These matters are treated more fully in our edition of the Life of Saint Gregory.] but either, after relinquishing clerical service, let them advance to the monastic orders; or, if they decide to remain in the position of abbot, let them in no way be permitted to retain clerical service.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] All the manuscripts agree in this reading: seven Norman manuscripts, four Vatican manuscripts, Tours, Corbie, Reims, and others. The old printed editions agree. In the more recent editions one finds: “or, once clerical service has been admitted, let them not be promoted to the monastic orders,” a reading that we have found in none of the manuscripts. Moreover, do not suppose, with the learned Ludovicus Dupin, volume VI, page 277, that Gregory’s intention was that clerics should not pass over to the monks. Gregory nowhere said this. Indeed, writing to Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, concerning a deacon embracing the monastic life, he says in book XII, letter 35: “We exhort you not to impede his devotion, by which he strives to maintain so ready a commitment to the holy purpose; rather, kindle him with whatever encouragements you can, by pastoral admonition,” and so forth. The Council of Toledo IV, canon 49 (in Loaisa, canon 50), says: “Clerics who desire the monastic way of life, because they wish to follow the better life, ought to be granted free entrance into monasteries by the bishop; nor should the purpose of those who strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation be obstructed.” From Gregory’s words, “Let them in no way be permitted to retain clerical service,” an otherwise most learned man concludes that Gregory the Great forbade the same person to be both abbot and priest. It is remarkable that this should be asserted by someone not wholly ignorant of the ancient discipline of East and West. The archimandrites—eighteen of them, all priests—wrote to the Emperor Marcian against Eutyches; see volume VI of the Councils, Labbé’s edition, column 131. Twenty-three archimandrites, eighteen of them priests and one a deacon, subscribed to the condemnation of that heresiarch; ibid., column 231. In the same place Saint Leo, in letter 75, writes to the emperor, to Pulcheria Augusta, and to sixteen abbots of Constantinople, all of them priests except one who was a deacon. Finally, volume V of the Councils, column 171, in the fifth session of the Council of Constantinople under Menas, reports a supplicatory petition signed by fifty-three priest-archimandrites and one deacon-archimandrite. Cointius proves that many abbots in the West were also ordained priests, under the year 674, number 55 and following. This is also certain from Gregory himself, whose letters to abbots who were priests, or which mention such abbots, are found in book I, letter 9; book V, letters 3 and 4; book VIII, letter 26; book XIII, letters 8, 10, and others. Gussanvillaeus gives further examples here in note 3.]

For it is very inappropriate that, when someone cannot diligently fulfill one of these functions according to its importance, he should be judged capable of both, so that each in turn—the ecclesiastical order obstructs the monastic life, and the monastic rule obstructs ecclesiastical usefulness.

We have also taken care to admonish your Charity about this (Gratian 12, question 2, canon 45): if any bishop should depart from this life, or—God forbid—be removed for his offenses, when the hierarchs and all the leading clergy have assembled and are making an inventory of the Church’s property in his presence, everything discovered is to be carefully recorded, and not, as was formerly said to happen, [Col. 0681A] as though certain valuable objects or anything else belonging to the Church were being taken as payment for making the inventory.

[Note: [Col. 0680D] Perhaps *hierarchis*, although this is how it is read in all the manuscripts and printed editions. Some editions vary. The Lyon edition of 1539 has in the margin: “Alternatively, *oeconomis*.” The correctors of Gratian’s decree, 12, question 2, canon 45, read *oeconomis*. I understand the reference to be to visiting bishops, who are mentioned immediately afterward. Gussanvillaeus. Vatican A and B, as well as the Pratellian manuscript, read *Ierathicis*.]

[Note: [Col. 0681C] It sets “valuable objects” in opposition to money counted out: *species* can mean grain, provisions, and quantities of supplies. Gussanvillaeus. We are certainly not unaware that *species*, among jurists and other writers, often means grain, oil, wine, and vegetables. Thus Gregory of Tours, replying to Felix, bishop of Nantes, in book V of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 5, says: “If you had had him as a priest at Marseille, ships would never have brought oil or other provisions.” Yet *species* often denotes any more valuable household equipment, and that meaning seems more appropriate here in Gregory’s letter to Maximian. Gregory of Tours, book VI, chapter 38: “Great treasures of gold and silver, and many valuable objects, were found there.” The very learned Du Cange provides many other examples for this word.]

For in this way we wish the things belonging to the support of the poor to be preserved, so that no opportunity for commercial exploitation may at all remain in their property for ambitious men.

Let the visitors of the Churches, and their clerics who are worn out with them while traveling through parishes not belonging to their own city, receive, by your arrangement, some assistance for their labor. For it is just that they should receive a stipend in the place where they are found to lend their service for a time.

[Col. 0681B] [Note: [Col. 0681C] We are not criticizing current dispensations, but representing the institutions of earlier times. The Code, book I, title 3, law 47, decrees that, when an abbess dies, the oldest woman is not to be chosen, since not all are equally good; rather, with the holy Gospels set before them, a suitable woman, useful and worthy to preside, is to be appointed, since it is fitting that every principate and every human office be assigned not on the basis of age, lot, or accidental circumstances, but on the basis of superior merit. Saint Gregory here requires sixty years for a virgin to become abbess. The Council of Trent, session 25, *On Regulars and Nuns*, chapter 7: “An abbess and prioress … is to be elected who is not under forty years of age and who has lived commendably for eight years after her solemn profession,” and so forth. Gussanvillaeus.]

We most earnestly prohibit young women from becoming abbesses (Gratian 20, question 1, canon 12).

[Note: [Col. 0681D] In Vatican A: “Therefore let no bishop, or your Fraternity, permit any woman except one who is sixty years old … to receive the veil.” The common text reads: “Therefore let your Fraternity permit no woman … to receive the veil.” We follow three Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, Corbie, Tours, and others.]

Therefore let your Fraternity permit no bishop to veil a virgin unless she is sixty years old and her age and character require it [Note: [Col. 0682C] “To receive the veil,” that is, to become abbess; for the blessing of an abbess with the veil was more solemn than that of other consecrated women. Nor was it the intention of the holy pontiff that no virgin should receive the veil unless she were sixty. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that in ancient times consecrated virgins did not receive the veil immediately after making their vow of virginity. Hence the Council of Agde, canon 19: “Consecrated women, however approved their life and conduct may be, are not to receive the veil before the fortieth year of their age.” And the Council of Zaragoza under Damasus, canon 8: “It has likewise been read that virgins who have vowed themselves to God are not to receive the veil until they have been proved at forty years of age.” This distinction between receiving the veil and making the vow or profession of virginity is also clear from Innocent I’s letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapters 12 and 13. Although we do not doubt that many virgins formerly received the sacred veil before the age of forty. See Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Virgin*, chapter 5; *On Psalm 118*, number 20; and book I, *On Virgins*, chapter 11. These passages establish that in earlier times the veil was solemnly given to virgins at the altar, while its blessing belonged to the bishops. Consult note 615 on the *Book of Sacraments*.]

so that, after correcting with the Lord’s help both the matters mentioned earlier and the present matter through the force of your discipline, you may hasten to bind again with canonical bonds the long-disordered state of venerable things [Note: [Col. 0682D] To restore the collapsed discipline of monasteries according to the canons, and to ensure that they live according to the prescription of their rule. Gussanvillaeus.], and so that divine affairs may be administered not through inappropriate human preferences but with suitable rigor.

[Note: [Col. 0682D] This is found only in the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of October, indiction 12. (Cf. John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 34; book II, chapter 54; book III, chapter 23.)

## LETTER XII. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP

The crime by which a certain man’s wife was taken away and sold to another is to be punished.

[Col. 0681C]

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

[Col. 0682A] So many evils continually being committed in that province are reported to us that, because of the sins producing them, we believe it will quickly perish, unless almighty God avert this. The bearer of this letter, on arriving, complained tearfully that many years ago some man or other had received him from the baptismal font on an estate belonging to the Church of Messina, and that, through various forms of persuasion, he had been violently [Note: [Col. 0682D] *Violenter*, that is, with difficulty and against one’s will; Terence uses the word in this sense in the *Phormio*. Force and right are opposed, although they are composed of the same letters. What is not done by right is said to be done by force. Yet often we extort by persuasion things that are not done by right. In marriage, however, the will must be completely free. Cicero says in his speech *For Caecina*: “When we speak of the law and of the legitimate disputes of men, and in these matters we use the word force, a very slight degree of force must be understood.” Gussanvillaeus.] joined to that girl, by whom he says he already has young sons, and whom that man is now said to have forcibly separated from him, taken away, and sold to another man. If this is true, your Affection sees what an unheard-of and cruel evil it is.

Therefore we admonish you to investigate and examine this great crime with that vigor which we know you certainly possess in pious causes. And if you discover that it is as the bearer mentioned above has reported, you will not only take care to restore what was wrongly done to its former condition, but you will also hasten by every means to impose a punishment capable of appeasing God.

[Col. 0682B] Attack with particular severity the bishop who neglects to correct and reform his own people when they commit such acts, declaring that if a complaint about any one of those belonging to him should again reach us [Note: [Col. 0683C] The word *eorum* is to be supplied, namely, “about any one of those belonging to him.” The editors preferred *pertinet*, “belongs,” but against the manuscripts. We would have followed them when, in place of *procedere*, they printed *procedit*, but we are compelled to follow the unanimous agreement of the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Tours, Reims, and other manuscripts.], canonical punishment will be inflicted not on the offender but on the bishop himself.

[Note: [Col. 0683C] Vatican adds: “In the month of October, indiction 12.” The same is found in Tours Saint Gatianus.]

(Cf. John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 54.)

## LETTER XIII. TO CLEMENTIUS, BISHOP

If Adeodatus the priest was absent from his Church solely because of illness, he is to be restored to his position.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0683C] We have restored the heading of this letter from Vatican, Norman, Colbert, Reims, Corbie, Tours, English, and other manuscripts, as well as from the manuscripts of Gussanvillaeus, which he does not identify except for six English manuscripts. The printed editions have “to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse”; how they came to read this in the manuscript, together with the Roman correctors of Gratian, is entirely unknown to us.] to Clementius, primate-bishop of Byzacena.

Although the petition of Adeodatus, the bearer of this letter (Gratian 7, question 1, canon 3), who says that he was improperly expelled from his place in the priesthood, is explained to you in the text of the petition submitted to you, we have nevertheless judged that it should be rewritten somewhat more clearly.

[Note: [Col. 0683D] Released by his bishop for certain business, he had been absent from his Church for two months because of illness; another man was substituted in his place, and Adeodatus requests restoration. I am astonished at customs so unlike our own. See the Council of Trent, session 23, *On Reform*, chapter 1. I would believe that the absence of pastors today has arisen, increased, and been excused because, contrary to canon 6 of Chalcedon, priests are plentiful, and can in some way supply the places of the absent, whereas in Saint Gregory’s time they were ordained only when necessary; consequently, unless they were constantly present, the people complained that they had been abandoned. Their scarcity was useful; we perish through abundance. The question also arises whether pastors may lawfully feed their people, whether personally or through substitutes, by word, example, and prayer, and fulfill their duties through delegated labor. Sound reason denies this, if the diligence of such a person was the reason for his election. Digest, law 31, title *De solutionibus*, confirms it: “Among craftsmen there is a great difference in skill, natural ability, learning, and training. Therefore, if someone has promised to build a ship himself … and it was specifically agreed that he would complete it by his own work, a surety who builds it himself will not release the principal debtor.” And in the Code, title 10, *On Decurions*, law 60: “No one who is bound by the tie of his family to the council may discharge the municipal functions through any substitute, but must personally perform the duty owed to his homeland,” and so forth. Bartholomew Carranza, cited above, book I, letter 79, demonstrates this with compelling authorities and arguments in his book *On Residence*, read at Trent and printed at Venice in 1547. Gussanvillaeus.]

He asserts that our brother and fellow bishop Quintianus released him from his position in order to attend to certain personal matters, and that he was absent from his Church for two months because of illness; taking advantage of this circumstance, our aforesaid brother ordained another priest in his place.

We therefore exhort your Fraternity to investigate his case carefully and rigorously. If you find that he was absent from his Church, as stated, because of evident illness, do not allow the ordination of another priest to create any prejudice against him, but see that he is restored to his position without any hesitation. But if the matter is said to be otherwise than his submitted petition indicates, investigate his case canonically and lawfully, and, with the Lord’s help, decide whatever seems right to you according to God, so that no further question concerning this matter may return to us.

We especially admonish your Charity (Gratian, same place): if his petition proves true and he is restored to his proper rank, you must exercise careful and strict supervision over the priest who was ordained in his place. If he reached that rank without any payment, so that he could not have fallen into the simoniacal heresy, we wish him to be ordained in whatever other vacant Church there may be [Note: [Col. 0684D] A recent edition has *volumus cardinari*. The manuscripts cited above, as well as Gratian, read *ordinari*, which we follow.]. But if anything of the kind that God forbid is found in him, he is also to be deprived of the priestly order, which he is shown to have accepted not to meet the necessary needs of the Church but solely out of ambition.

## LETTER XIV. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP

He is to receive the deacon Felix into his Church.

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

The bearer of this letter, the deacon Felix, although he did not fall into the doctrine of the heretics and did not depart from the Catholic faith, had withdrawn into the separation of the Istrians, deceived by wicked suspicions against the synod of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0684D] Namely, the fifth general council, held at Constantinople concerning the notorious Three Chapters. On its account many withdrew from communion with the Catholic Church, especially in Africa and Istria, because they claimed that certain decrees had been issued in that fifth synod in contempt of the Council of Chalcedon. These matters are treated more fully in the Life of Saint Gregory and above, book II, indiction 10, letter 51.]. When he came to Rome, however, after we had, with the Lord’s help, explained the matter to him, he corrected his error by receiving communion in the Lord’s body [Note: [Col. 0684D] The printed editions add “and blood.” The manuscripts do not contain the final word.]

Since, therefore, as has been said, he did not fall into heresy but erred concerning the sacred mysteries of the universal Church as though from an intention directed toward what was right, we have, out of concern for his weakness and needs, and especially with a view to supporting him in his poverty, arranged that he be incardinated in your Church of Syracuse, either so that he may perform the office of deacon or, at least, so that he may receive the benefits of that office solely for the support of his poverty. We wish this to depend on the judgment of your Fraternity.

We urge your Fraternity to hasten to carry this out. We also commend his person to you, so that you do not allow him to be subjected to any hardship or want; otherwise you would be found either to have neglected the course of our recommendation or to have shown less generosity toward the poor than your office requires. For we have also arranged that an annual allowance be given to him from our Church, so that we might share in the same work that we urge you to undertake.

(Cf. John the Deacon, book III, chapter 20.)

## LETTER XV. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

Theodosia, intending to build a monastery in her house, is to receive his assistance.

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

[Col. 0684C] The religious woman Theodosia, desiring to fulfill the wishes of her late husband Stephen by building a monastery, asked us to send our letters to your Fraternity, so that through our recommendation she might more readily obtain your assistance. She states that her husband had arranged for a monastery to be built on the estate called Piscenas, which had come under the rights of the Xenodochium of the former bishop Thomas.

Since the owner rightly appears unwilling to permit its establishment on another’s property, even if the possessor permits it [Note: [Col. 0685C] Namely, so that the owner may not later be deprived of the revenues of a rent-paying estate—French *des lots et ventes*, and similar charges—because of the mortmain, as the French call it; in Latin, perpetual possession, because the property never passes to another owner and never returns to its original owner. Gussanvillaeus. Concerning that monastery, see above, letter 8, and below, book V, letter 2. An emphyteutic lessee cannot alienate an estate without the owner’s consent, Code, final title, *On the right of emphyteusis*. For the same reason a monastery cannot be founded on another’s estate against the owner’s will, even with the consent of the possessor—that is, the emphyteutic lessee—lest the owner’s condition be worsened by the act of the emphyteutic lessee. Emphyteutic lessees do not have ownership of the estate, but a right in the property, law *Si domus*, final paragraph, *On legacies*. They are therefore not called owners but possessors. Augustine, *On the Unity of the Church against the Donatists*, formerly chapter 17, now 20: “A slave in relation to his master, and a tenant in relation to his possessor.” An emphyteutic estate is called an emphyteutic possession. The same author, book I against the letters of Petilianus, chapter 82: “When he had purchased the possession, and it was emphyteutic.” Gregory distinguished these three—owner, possessor, and tenant or lessee—in the *Moralia*, book XIV, chapter 21, according to the old edition: “Because he was not heard as owner, he was regarded not as possessor of the field but as a tenant.” Alteserra.]

we have determined to grant her request: namely, that in the house under her own legal title, which she says she possesses at Cagliari, she should, with the Lord’s help, build a monastery of servants of God.

But since she says that this house is burdened with guests and visitors, we exhort your Fraternity to strive to assist her in every way and to provide your protection for her devotion, so that your cooperation and solicitude may make you a participant in the reward of the deceased man and in her own undertaking. As for the relics that she requests to be placed there, we wish your Fraternity to deposit them with due reverence.

## LETTER XVI. TO CYPRIAN, DEACON

The scattered ecclesiastical vessels that Italian priests brought to Sicily are to be collected and kept with the utmost care.

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon and administrator of Sicily.

We have been informed that various priests of Italy, fleeing to Sicily, brought with them many sacred vessels belonging to their Churches [Note: [Col. 0685D] The ancients called sacred furnishings by one general term, *the ministry of the Church*. Gregory of Tours, book III of his *History*, chapter 10: “Among the other treasures, Childebert, returning from Spain, brought back the most precious ecclesiastical furnishings—namely, sixty chalices, fifteen patens, and twenty Gospel cases, all decorated with pure gold and precious gems.” See the same author, book II *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 7; and Alcimus Avitus, letter 6 to Bishop Victorius, where he replies that God is not pleased when the vessels of heretics are taken away and offered to the Church unless they are purified by being melted in furnaces and beaten out into sheets. He holds the same opinion about their temples, believing that an insensible object which was first polluted cannot be cleansed by any sanctification. Gregory the Great held a different view, as did before him Honoratus, bishop of Novara, who converted an idol temple into a church; for its dedication Ennodius, the deacon of Pavia, submitted to Honoratus a discourse, which is the second in Ennodius.] and that, whether because those priests died or because they dispersed the goods improperly, nearly all of them have perished.

Moved by this matter, we exhort your Affection to send agents throughout every part of Sicily. If anywhere you find sacred vessels or ecclesiastical property lying about carelessly, have them collected with the greatest strictness and, after assembling them, deposit them with the bishops of the individual Churches under a record and receipt [Note: [Col. 0686D] We have restored this from the Vatican, Norman, Reims, Corbie, and other manuscripts. Here *notitia* and *desusceptum* signify a register, catalogue, or inventory. Previously it was read: “receive them under the record of witnesses, and deposit them with the bishops of the Churches.”], where, until the time of peace demands their return, they are to be kept with the utmost security, with the Lord’s help.

[Col. 0685C] We wish the persons who deliver these objects to receive not only a receipt for all the property itself, but also for you to retain a detailed record of it, so that, whenever necessary, the items may, with the Lord’s help, be restored without diminution to those to whom they were entrusted.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Tours Saint Gatianus has this reading. The old Colbert manuscript reads “in the month of September,” and the printed editions agree with it. We have preferred the reading of the Tours manuscript because several letters of this indiction have already preceded it and are dated in the month of October.]

In the month of November, indiction 12.

## LETTER XVII. TO FELIX, BISHOP

He is to restore from the Church’s funds to the redeemer the twelve solidi for which the cleric Tribunus was redeemed.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Siponto.

## How Provision Is to Be Made for the Ransom of Captives; and How the Enactment of the Holy Canons and of Secular Laws Clearly Teaches This

Since this is known to everyone, we have been astonished that your Fraternity, moved by no compassion, has offered no assistance toward the ransom of your cleric Tribunus, the bearer of this letter. Therefore, what you have delayed doing voluntarily, hasten at least to do when admonished by our exhortation, lest—if, which we do not believe, you should think it ought to be neglected—necessity begin to impose upon you what your will avoids.

Since the aforesaid Tribunus reports that he was captured by enemies and purchased for one hundred and twelve solidi, and complains that he is being pressed to repay them, you ought to investigate the matter carefully. And if you discover that this is so, and that he has no means by which he can repay the price paid for him, restore the aforesaid solidi from the Church to his redeemer. For it is exceedingly harsh if he finds no remedy from the Church in whose service he ministers.

Therefore, setting aside excuses, restore without any delay the price that is shown by manifest truth to have been paid for him, as we have said, so that neither his creditor may regret having helped a man afflicted by necessity, nor he himself, freed from the burden of sorrow and with an untroubled mind, fail to discharge the ministry of his office diligently and properly.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] LETTER XVII.—As regards secular laws, the law *Sancimus*, Code, “On Holy Churches,” ch. 21, will stand for all. Add Novella 120, chs. 9 and 10. See First Council of Orléans, canon 5; Rheims, canon 22.]

[Note: [Col. 0686D] The editions read “one hundred and twelve solidi.” “One hundred” has intruded contrary to the authority of the manuscripts. Certainly the price of a slave did not usually exceed twelve solidi.]

In the month of January, in the twelfth indiction.

## LETTER XVIII. TO MAURUS, ABBOT

He grants the church of Saint Pancratius to the monks in perpetuity, both so that the celebration of Masses may not thereafter be neglected and so that the work of God may be performed daily at the martyr’s body.

Gregory to Maurus, abbot.

The care of the churches, which is plainly attached to priestly duties, compels us to be so vigilant that no fault of neglect may appear in them. Since, however, we have learned that the church of Saint Pancratius, which had been entrusted to priests, had frequently been neglected, so that on the Lord’s Day the people came to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass but, finding no priest, returned murmuring, our judgment, after mature deliberation, decided that, once those priests had been removed, we ought by God’s grace to establish a community of monks in the monastery adjoining that church. Thus the abbot who presided there would necessarily have the care and responsibility of the aforementioned church.

[Note: [Col. 0687C] Previously it read: “the church … having frequently been neglected.” We follow the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts. Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Honorius, testifies that he was the founder of this church at Rome on the Via Aurelia. There, however, Saint Gregory preached a homily to the people, which is Homily 27 on the Gospels. Partly from Gussanville. This monastery of Saint Pancratius is now the seminary of the Discalced Carmelites. See Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 75.]

[Note: [Col. 0687C] Even then the practice had become established that several priests might be assigned to one title. Thus, in the Roman synod held under Symmachus in the year 499, and also under Gregory himself in 594, sometimes one, sometimes two, three, or four priests of one and the same title are found subscribed.

Panciroli observes, however, that the basilica of Saint Pancratius was not originally granted the honor of a title because it lay outside the city: titles were not assigned to extramural basilicas. Nor were stations assigned to them unless they were patriarchal churches. Hence the phrase “entrusted to priests” may perhaps be used because it did not have a cardinal priest, nor other priests assigned and entirely devoted to it.

Public Masses were sometimes celebrated even in basilicas that were not distinguished by the name of titles, when the gathering of the people, because of relics or the cult of martyrs, required it. Gussanville therefore gratuitously regards these words as suspect, since they are absent from none of the manuscripts, whether written or printed.

Moreover, Gussanville, together with other recent editors, reads *missarum solemnia audituri*—“about to hear the solemn rites of Mass”—as though it were dangerous to say that the people celebrated sacred rites. Yet the reading given here is found in all the Vatican, Norman, Regius, Corbie, and other manuscripts. Elsewhere nothing prevents the people from being admitted as participants in the offered sacrifice, as assistants and fellow participants. Indeed, in the Canon of the Mass we read: “for whom we offer to you,” or “who offer this sacrifice to you.” See Note 36 to the Sacred Book.]

We have foreseen that you, Maurus, should be appointed over this monastery, establishing that the lands of the aforesaid church, and whatever should enter it or accrue from its revenues, must be assigned to your aforementioned monastery and belong there without diminution, provided, of course, that whatever must be made or repaired in that church is unquestionably repaired by you.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] Vatican B reads: “on the mountain adjoining the same church.”]

But lest, once the priests to whom the church itself had previously been entrusted have been removed, it appear to be without its ministries,

[Note: [Col. 0688C] Another reading is *mysteriis*, “sacred mysteries,” as found in Vatican A and other manuscripts.]

we therefore command you by the force of this authority not to cease appointing there a foreign priest who can celebrate the solemn rites of Mass.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] Do not suppose that a priest from another diocese is meant here, opposed to a cardinal or titular priest, and perhaps a resident priest, by an outsider. Taking the opportunity provided by this passage, Gussanville observes that in ancient times monasteries had either no priest or only one, and that he was an attached outsider. But this is mistaken. The passage concerns a monastery scarcely begun. Maurus is indeed designated as abbot, but if no monks, or only a few, were attached to him, what is surprising if not even one of them was a priest? A foreign priest therefore had to be sought, perhaps from some neighboring monastery. For if this priest had not professed the monastic life, how could he have consented to live in the monastery and lead the stricter life of monks? The earlier reading was: “there you should employ.”]

Nevertheless, it is necessary that he both live in your monastery and receive the means of subsistence from it.

But above all, let this be the chief concern of your care: that the work of God should unquestionably be performed there every day at the most sacred body of blessed Pancratius.

[Note: [Col. 0688C] Following Saint Benedict, Rule, chapters 43 and 47, he calls the divine office the “work of God.” See also Book X, Letter 61. Already at the beginning of the sixth century it was customary that, in places where the relics of saints were preserved, the divine offices should be performed by their own clergy or by neighboring clergy. Council of Epaon, canon 25: “The relics of saints are not to be placed in rural oratories unless, perhaps, clergy of some parish happen to live nearby who may serve the sacred ashes by frequent psalmody.”]

These matters, therefore, which we assign to you to be carried out in accordance with the sequence of this command, we wish not only you to complete but also to have perpetually observed and fulfilled in this manner by those who succeed you in your office and place, so that no neglect may thereafter be found in the aforesaid church.

[Note: [Col. 0688D] The old Colbert manuscript adds: “in the month of January, in the twelfth indiction,” which is noted in the old Paris edition and in the Vatican manuscript.]

## 19. LETTER XIX. TO LEO, ACOLYTE

He commends to him the church of Saint Agatha in the Subura.

Gregory to Leo, acolyte.

The care of venerable places admonishes us to consider their usefulness in every respect. Since, therefore, the church of Saint Agatha situated in the Subura, which was once a cave of heretical depravity,

[Note: [Col. 0689C] Namely, Arian depravity, as is explained in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 30.]

has by God’s favor been restored to the worship of the Catholic faith,

[Note: [Col. 0688D] Concerning the church of Irac, see Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 30. The Subura is a well-known district of the city of Rome, mentioned by Martial, Book VII, epigram 30:

“Everything is born for me in the Subura.”

And by Horace, *Epodes* 5:

“The old adulterer, whom everyone laughs at,

the Suburan dogs bark at.”

Our Dom Bernard de Montfaucon, who carefully examined the sacred sites of Rome, denies that the present church of Saint Agatha was situated in the ancient Subura, and explains the origin of the name “in the Subura” in chapter 9 of his Italian Diary.]

you are therefore admonished by the tenor of this authority not to cease collecting each year the rents of all the houses located in this city that can be shown to have belonged to the aforesaid church in the time of the Goths.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] Since, under the Gothic kings, who were Arians, this church had passed to the Arians so that they might hold their assemblies there, they enlarged and enriched it with many gifts and revenues.]

You shall make every effort to expend these revenues on whatever is necessary for the roofs, the lights, and other repairs of the same church. Whatever may remain, we command you faithfully to enter into the ecclesiastical accounts.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] Thus the Norman, Tours, Saint Gatian, Colbert, and other manuscripts.]

In the month of April, in the twelfth indiction.

## 20. LETTER XX. TO MAXIMUS, THE USURPER

He removes Maximus, who had been violently intruded, and the bishops who ordained him, from every priestly office until the truth of the imperial command has been established.

[Col. 0689B]

Gregory to Maximus, the usurper, at Salona.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] See Letter 10 above.]

Although someone’s other merits of life may be such that nothing in them could obstruct his ordination to the priesthood, the crime of ambition alone is condemned with the severest rigor of the canons. We have therefore learned that, by either a stolen or fabricated order of the most devout rulers, although you were not worthy in life, you rashly thrust yourself into the priestly order, venerable to all.

[Note: [Col. 0689C] Recent editions, less faithfully than the manuscripts, read: “you seized the rank of the priesthood.”]

We believed this without any hesitation because your life and age are not unknown to us, and also because we know the mind of our most serene lord the emperor: he is not accustomed to involve himself in priestly affairs, lest he be burdened in any way by our sins.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] The same accords with what is found in Theodoret, Book IV of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18, and in Gregory II, Letter 1 to Leo the Isaurian, concerning sacred images at the Seventh Council. Saint Louis did not wish to involve himself in priestly affairs. See his *Pragmatic Sanction*, published in 1668, in its genuine and complete form, not the mutilated version once issued among certain synodal statutes of the diocese of Paris. Auger.]

An unheard-of outrage is added: even after our prohibition—which was issued under excommunication against you and those who ordained you—you are said, after priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy had been beaten, to have been brought forward by military force.

[Col. 0690A]

We cannot in any way call this a consecration, because it was performed by excommunicated men.

Therefore, since you have violated so great and so distinguished a dignity of the priesthood without any precedent, we command that, until I learn from letters of the Lord or of our representative that you were ordained not by a stolen but by a genuine command,

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Maximus seemed liable to exclusion from the bishopric of Salona for many reasons: ambition, simony, violence, disregard of the election, contempt for the authority of the supreme pontiff, and diplomas or commands stolen from the emperor or fabricated. Above all, Saint Gregory insists that the emperor’s commands appeared to be of doubtful authenticity; he insists that the matter had been arranged without the knowledge of the Roman representative and without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, whose jurisdiction included Salona.

Maximus had added stubborn defiance by violating the censures. But why, some ask, such commands from the emperor? In those times, I answer, it was necessary to serve the necessities of the age, with the canons temporarily set aside. Thus the Roman pontiff himself was confirmed by the emperor; thus the investitures of later centuries were foreshadowed, investitures which we subsequently see revived, in some fashion, under the covering of nominations.

Let others dispute the law. Saint Gregory testifies to the fact, and historians do likewise. Nor is the memory or origin of our annates and bulls, by which provision is made for richer bishoprics and benefices, so ancient. Saint Gregory nevertheless seems to deny that it was customary to promote bishops by such commands—namely, those subject to the Roman pontiff—although the reason he adduces applies equally to all.

In any case, the canons ask that no pastor be appointed against the will of the people, and reason supports them; hence rulers acquire considerable legal influence in the promotion of bishops. Gussanville.]

you and those who ordained you shall presume to touch nothing pertaining to priestly office, nor shall you approach the worship of the sacred altar until our rescript has arrived.

If you presume to act against these commands, may you be anathema before God and before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, so that, in contemplation of your judgment, your punishment may provide an example of retribution to the other Catholic Churches.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Thus it is read in the Vatican, Norman, Tours, Saint Gatian, Colbert, and other manuscripts.]

In the month of May, in the twelfth indiction.

## 21. LETTER XXI. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP

Jews may not retain a Christian slave; but the Christians who have long cultivated Jewish lands are to continue cultivating them under the law of the colonate.

[Col. 0690B]

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Luna was a very ancient city of Etruria, formerly an episcopal city on the border of Liguria at the mouth of the river Macra, commonly called the Magra. It was destroyed around the year 856. Sarzana, a city under Genoese rule, succeeded it in episcopal dignity and lies three thousand paces from it. Gussanville.]

We have learned from the reports of many people that Christian slaves are being held in servitude by Jews living in the city of Luna. This matter seemed to us all the more grievous because your Fraternity’s patience has been so conspicuous.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Thus the old edition, together with nearly all the manuscripts—the Norman, Corbie, Rheims, Tours, Regius, and Vatican manuscripts. Vatican A, however, reads: “the more this was brought about by the patience of your Fraternity.” The reading found in recent editions, namely, “the more this matter was brought about by the patience of your Fraternity,” occurs nowhere else.]

It was your duty, in view of your position and out of regard for the Christian religion, to leave no opportunity for simple souls to serve Jewish superstition—not merely through persuasion, but, in a sense, by the force of authority.

Therefore we exhort your Fraternity that, in accordance with the course prescribed by the most devout laws,

[Note: [Col. 0690D] In the Code, Book I, title 10: “Let no heretic, Jew, or pagan have, possess, or circumcise a Christian slave.”]

no Jew be permitted to retain a Christian slave under his control.

[Col. 0690C]

But if any such slaves are found in their possession, their freedom must be preserved, with the protection of the law, by the assistance of the legal enactments.

Those, however, who are on their estates, although they too are free by the strict force of the laws, should nevertheless, because they have long remained attached to the cultivation of those lands—as owing the condition of the estate—

[Note: [Col. 0691C] That is, a burden, debt, legal obligation, and so forth. In Vatican A it reads: “owing the condition of the place.” Regius agrees.]

continue cultivating the fields to which they are accustomed, pay the aforesaid men their rents, and fulfill all that the laws prescribe concerning coloni or *originarii*, without anything further being imposed upon them as a burden.

[Note: [Col. 0691C] Some coloni cultivate for wages; others cultivate under a status requiring them to pay a fixed rent from the land and never depart. See Book II of the Code, title “Concerning Agricultural Tenants, Tax-Payers, and Coloni,” where there is also much concerning *originarii* and *ascriptitii*, matters beyond our present purpose.

Here *jus colonarium* is used for the condition of a colonus, or for the right to demand from a colonus such an annual rent. *Originarii* are those born from *ascriptitii* on the very soil; they could not be sold without the land. *Ascriptitii* are those who had remained on the soil for thirty years, which constitutes a title by prescription, or who had promised in a double written instrument that they would never depart from it. Gussanville.]

If anyone should wish either to move one of these people to another place or to retain him in his own service, let him reckon that he has condemned himself by the rigor of the law: by his own rashness he has forfeited the colonate right and the right of ownership.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Thus the Norman, Regius, Corbie, and Vatican A and C manuscripts, as well as the old edition. Vatican B reads: “he will condemn himself by the severity of the law.” In D: “he condemned the right of ownership by the severity of the law.” Recent printed editions have: “he condemned the right of his own ownership by the severity of the law.”]

In all these matters, therefore, we wish you to apply yourself so diligently that you may neither be found guilty as the shepherd of a ravaged flock nor, through a lesser zeal among us, allow your Fraternity to become blameworthy.

## 22. LETTER XXII. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He urges him to assist Venantius, bishop of Luna, in correcting his clergy and the other religious persons.

[Col. 0691B]

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

We have learned from a report concerning certain people coming from the region of the Laudenses that the religious life of those places has so strayed from the path of ecclesiastical discipline that in no way do they observe the statutes of canonical order in their conduct and actions.

[Note: [Col. 0691D] Recent editions read “of the people of Luna,” as in the Regius manuscript; but all the Norman, Tours, Rheims, Teller, and Vatican D manuscripts read “of the Laudenses.” Laus Pompeia, now Lauda, commonly Lodi, is a city of Insubria and an episcopal see on the bank of the river Adda or Addua. [Col. 0692C] The old city was destroyed by the Milanese in 1119; another, not far from its ruins, was built in its place and is now very large. Since the clergy of Lodi were subject to the archbishop of Milan as their metropolitan, Saint Gregory rightly wrote to Constantius concerning the correction of their morals.]

Because these matters had to be examined more carefully and punished more severely, I instructed Venantius, the bearer of this letter, our brother and fellow bishop, to correct them without delay. But because of the magnitude of the disorder among the offending persons, he judged himself alone insufficient for such an investigation. He therefore asked us to add your Fraternity’s assistance and authority to him in examining the matter.

Although brotherly affection ought to demand this of you even without our letters, nevertheless by this special letter we exhort you also to summon to your presence, together with our aforesaid brother, all the clerics and other religious persons of the aforementioned city and its territory concerning whose excesses there is any suspicion,

[Note: [Col. 0692D] The Norman manuscript reads: “concerning whose suspected excesses there is something.”]

and, carefully investigating everything before God out of fear of the future judgment, correct with canonical punishment anyone whom you find to have departed from the statutes of the canons.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Even laymen are sometimes included under the designation “clerics.” See Book I, formerly Letter 59, now 61, and John Filesacus, commentary on Vincent of Lérins’ *Commonitorium*, no. 12. Profane authors, sacred Scripture, and the ancient Fathers contemporary with Saint Gregory confirm this interpretation. Partly from Gussanville.]

Do not allow those who do not exhibit in their conduct what they display in their habit to wander any longer through precipitous paths in your places. You ought to restore them to the standard of rectitude by your pastoral vigilance.

Therefore, once you have investigated all things diligently, correct and regulate what has been reported to us in these matters and hasten to quiet it for the future. In this way it will benefit your soul if you scrutinize the concerns of your office watchfully and vigorously, and you will not allow the judgment we have always held of your maturity and strictness to be frustrated.

## 23. LETTER XXIII. TO HOSPITO, DUKE OF THE BARBARICINI

He favors Felix and Cyriacus as they labor to convert the Barbaricini from idolatry.

[Col. 0692B]

Gregory to Hospito, duke of the Barbaricini.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] In the Regius, Colbert, Teller, Corbie, Norman, and three Vatican manuscripts the reading is “duke of the barbarians.” Holstenius proves that the Barbaricini were inhabitants of Sardinia in his notes on Ortelius, page 28, from this ancient Praenestine inscription: “Sextus Julius Rufus, son of Sextus, of the Pollian tribe, evocatus of the deified Augustus, prefect of the First Cohort of Corsicans and of the cities of the Barbaricini in Sardinia.” Concerning them, see the following letter and Book XI, Letter 22.]

Since there is no Christian among your people, I know that you are better than your whole people because you alone are found to be a Christian among them. For while all the Barbaricini live like irrational animals, do not know the true God, and worship wood and stones, you show how far you surpass them all by worshiping the true God.

But carry out the faith you have received also in good deeds and words. Offer to Christ, in whom you believe, what you are able to offer: bring to him as many as you can, have them baptized, and admonish them to love eternal life.

If perhaps you cannot do this yourself because you are occupied with another task, I ask you, by sending greetings, to assist in every way our men whom we have sent there—namely, my brother and fellow bishop Felix and my son Cyriacus, servant of God. While you help their labors, show your devotion to the almighty Lord; and may he himself be your helper in good works, since you assist his servants in their good work.

We have sent you through them the blessing of the holy apostle Peter, which I ask you to receive graciously.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] Thus the Tours, Saint Gatian, two Teller, Vatican, and Norman manuscripts.]

In the month of June, in the twelfth indiction.

## 24. LETTER XXIV. TO ZABARDA, DUKE OF SARDINIA

He gives thanks that Zabarda intends to make peace with the Barbaricini on the condition that they serve Christ.

[Col. 0693A]

Gregory to Zabarda, duke of Sardinia.

From the letters of my brother and fellow bishop Felix and Cyriacus, servant of God, we have learned of your excellent qualities. We give great thanks to almighty God that Sardinia has received such a duke, one who knows how to discharge earthly duties to the state and also understands how to offer the service of his homeland to almighty God.

For they wrote to me that you intend to make peace with the Barbaricini on the condition that you bring those same Barbaricini into the service of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Procopius records that barbarians were expelled from Africa by the Vandals. Holstenius thinks that these were the peoples of Sardinia, on the basis of the Praenestine inscription that he cites in his notes on Cluverius, page 28. Gussanville. Concerning them, see Letter 22 above and Letter 27 below.]

I was greatly delighted by this, and, if it pleases almighty God, I will soon make your gifts known to the most serene rulers.

Complete, then, what you have begun. Show almighty God the devotion of your hearts, and assist as much as you can those whom we have sent there to convert the Barbaricini. Know that such works will greatly help you both before earthly rulers and in the presence of the heavenly King.

## 25. LETTER XXV. TO THE NOBLES AND LANDOWNERS IN SARDINIA

He reproves them for not turning their peasants away from the worship of idols; if they cannot accomplish this, they are at least to aid Felix and Cyriacus, who were sent for this work.

Gregory to the nobles and landowners residing on the island of Sardinia.

From the report of my brother and fellow bishop Felix and of my son Cyriacus, servant of God, I have learned that nearly all of you have peasants devoted to idolatry on your estates.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Thus the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, where the particle *vel* has a connective force.]

I have been greatly saddened by this, because I know that the fault of subjects weighs down the life of their superiors, and when sin is not corrected in a subject, the judgment is turned back upon those who rule.

Therefore, distinguished sons, I exhort you to show zeal for your souls with every care and concern, and to consider the account you will render to almighty God concerning your subjects. They have indeed been entrusted to you so that they may serve your earthly interests, while you, through your providence, may provide for their souls the things that are eternal.

If they render to you what they owe, why do you not render to them what you owe? Namely, that your greatness should continually admonish them and restrain them from the error of idolatry, so that, once led to the faith, they may make the almighty Lord favorable toward them.

For you see how closely the end presses upon this world; you see how at one time the human sword and at another the divine sword rages against us. Yet you, worshipers of the true God, see the people entrusted to you worshiping stones and remain silent?

What, I ask, will you say at the fearful judgment, when you have received enemies of God under your authority and yet disdain to subject them to God and bring them back to him?

Therefore, after offering the greeting due to you, I ask that your greatness keep especially vigilant over zeal for God, and hasten to inform me in your letters which and how many people each of you has led to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Thus all editions. The Regius manuscript reads: “that you should diligently arouse your greatness.” The Colbert manuscript reads: “that your greatness should be aroused … that you should watch.”]

What you perhaps cannot accomplish for some reason, entrust to our aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Felix or to my son Cyriacus, and provide them assistance for the work of God. Thus you may share in the reward of life in proportion to the assistance you now provide to the good work.

## 26. LETTER XXVI. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

Clerics who despise him are to be compelled to discipline. A peasant obstinate in unbelief is to be burdened with the payment of rent. Clerics who have fallen through sexual misconduct are to be deposed irrevocably. Candidates are to be examined carefully before ordination. He grants the priests of Sardinia what he had forbidden: namely, that those whom they baptize may, when bishops are absent, be touched on the forehead with chrism.

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

From the report of our brother and fellow bishop Felix and Cyriacus, abbot, we have learned that in the island of Sardinia priests are oppressed by lay judges, and that your Fraternity’s ministers despise you, while, as it appears, concern is shown among you only for simplicity and discipline is neglected.

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Printed editions read: “compel the clerics to maintain discipline.”]

Therefore I exhort you, setting aside every excuse, to govern the Church you have received with God as its author, to compel the clerics to maintain discipline, and to strive not to fear anyone’s words.

As I hear, you prohibited your archdeacon from living with women, and to this day you are despised in that prohibition. Unless he obeys your command, we wish him to be deprived of his sacred order.

Another very grievous matter has occurred: the peasants whom your Church possesses have until now been permitted, through your Fraternity’s negligence, to remain in unbelief. Why do I admonish you to bring outsiders to God when you neglect to correct your own people from unbelief?

Therefore it is necessary for you to watch in every way over their conversion. For if I should find a pagan peasant belonging to any bishop in the island of Sardinia, I will take severe action against that bishop. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 47.)

But if a peasant is found to be of such faithlessness and obstinacy that he absolutely refuses to come to the Lord God,

[Note: [Col. 0693D] Concerning pagans and Jews, whether they are to be compelled or attracted to the faith, see Book I, Letters 35 and 47; Book V, Letter 7; and Book IX, Letter 6.

Thus, in Luke 14, they are compelled to enter—not merely by persuasion, but by indirect force. Saint Augustine, Book II *Against the Second Letter of Gaudentius*, chapter 17: “But as for what seems to you—that the unwilling should not be compelled to the truth—you are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God, who makes them willing while they are compelled unwillingly,” and so forth. Let the reader continue to the end of the chapter.

And in the letter to Vincent, which is now Letter 93, formerly 48: “You see that one must not consider what someone is compelled to do, but what it is that compels him. Is it good or evil? Not that anyone can become good against his will, but that, through fear of suffering what he does not wish to suffer, he abandons the resistance that obstructs his mind, or is compelled to recognize a truth previously unknown, so that, fearing, he either rejects the falsehood about which he was not contending or seeks the truth he did not know, and willingly holds what he had previously been unwilling to hold,” and so forth.

Concerning this coercion, see above, Book I, Letter 34. See also Augustine, Letter 50 to Boniface, where much is said in this connection; Saint Gregory, Book VII, second indiction, Letter 5; and Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book V, chapter 11. Gussanville.]

he must be burdened with so great a burden of rent that the punishment of the exaction itself may compel him to hasten toward rectitude.

Pervenit etiam ad nos (Gratian, Distinction 50, canon 9) [Col. 0695B] [Note: Gregory holds this opinion: that those who have fallen in this way ought never to be restored to the clerical order. Read the whole of Distinction 50, in which this question is debated on both sides, with many authorities cited on either side. The passage of Augustine cited from Letter 50, now 185, to Boniface, is especially pertinent. He acknowledges that the Church established that no one, after penance for a crime, should receive clerical office, return to the clergy, or remain in the clergy. He says that this was done not from despair of pardon but from the strictness of discipline—a discipline devised against feigned penances. Such penances were feigned through affected desires for honors and power. Despair of attaining temporal eminence would be a greater and more varied remedy. Nevertheless, he says, something may be withdrawn from this severity on account of unforeseen circumstances. GUSSANV. What we ought to understand by the sacred orders is explained in note 684 and the three following notes to the book of the Sacraments.] certain men who had fallen from the sacred orders, whether after penance or before it, were being restored to the duties of their ministry—something which we have absolutely forbidden—and in this matter the most sacred [Note: The Council of Nicaea, canon 10; the Council of Ancyra, canon 1; the apostolic canon 29; in the decrees of Pope Siricius, chapter 7; in the decree of Innocent, chapters 21 and 33, etc. GUSSANV.] canons also contradict this practice. Therefore, whoever, after receiving sacred orders, has fallen into the sin of the flesh must be deprived of the sacred order in such a way that he may no longer approach the ministry of the altar.

But lest those who have been ordained should ever perish, care must be taken regarding whom we ordain, so that it may first be examined [Col. 0696A] whether their life has been continent for many years, [Note: Norm., Corb., Vatican A and C read this way, and the old editions agree. The more recent editions preferred: “whether they have devoted themselves to prayer.” Vatican B reads: “whether they have devoted themselves to prayer and reading.”] whether they have been devoted to reading, and whether they have had a love of almsgiving. It must also be investigated whether any of them may have been married to two wives. It must likewise be seen that no one who is uneducated, or who is subject to public office, is compelled after sacred ordination [Note: The earlier reading was: “to public exaction,” which is rejected [Col. 0696C] by the manuscripts.] to return to public administration.

[Note: Those being advanced to orders, who aspire to the priesthood, are examined in this age by various investigations before being placed over the tribunal of penance. I omit the quantity and quality of their clothing, hair, linen collars, and other matters of this kind. I pass over the external discipline, distinguished with admirable variety according to the judgment of each superior, which seems to be observed much more rigidly than the sacred canons. There are, however, men who, scarcely investigating anything concerning prudence and common sense, inquire, as it seems to me, into knowledge itself in whatever way they can. “How many daughters of pride are there?” they ask. “How many potential parts of temperance?” and so forth. As though any theologian possessed so ready a memory that he could answer five hundred such questions on the spot! What if the examiners in turn were permitted to ask how many excommunications and irregularities there are, how many articles of faith, how many heresies, how many doctrines of morals in the Sacred Scriptures, how many canons of the Church, and how many Christian virtues? Perhaps their tongues would cleave to their palates. I would therefore judge that the first inquiry should concern morals, then prudence and common sense: whether they have a method of learning, whether they devote themselves to reading the Sacred Scriptures, what their zeal for the canons is, and whether they are capable both of being taught and of teaching. On these foundations we may safely build. Meanwhile, let the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 24; the Third Council of Tours, canons 2 and 3; the Second Council of Chalon, canons 1 and 2; and the Second Council of Aachen, held in 836, chapter 2 in its several articles, be read. Moreover, it is worth observing that among the many clerical qualifications Saint Gregory lists continence and love of almsgiving as almost especially important—that is, complete chastity and contempt for money together with its legitimate use. GUSSANV.]

Let your Fraternity therefore investigate all these matters carefully, so that, while each man is ordained only after careful examination, [705] he may not be quickly deposed after ordination. Make known to all the bishops under you what we have written to your Fraternity, because I did not wish to write to them myself, lest I should seem to diminish your honor.

It has also come to our attention that some people were scandalized because we had forbidden presbyters to touch with chrism those who [Note: Here we reproduce the reading of six English manuscripts, as many Norman manuscripts, Corbie, two Teller manuscripts, and the Sorbonne manuscript; the old Venetian editions of 1505 and the Paris editions of 1518, 1571, and 1586, as well as Basel 1564, agree with them. I have no doubt that this is how it was read in the ancient manuscripts of Rheims and Tours, although those who examined those codices and collected their variant readings say nothing about the matter, since they collated them at this point with the old editions, to which they are entirely conformed. Of the Vatican manuscripts, only two agree with the other manuscripts. The old Colbert manuscript also differs. In another, more recent Colbert manuscript, both in Letter 9 and in Letter 26, the reading is “presbyters should chrism those to be baptized,” not “those who have been baptized.” Since the true reading is now established, the position adopted by certain theologians from these corrupt passages seems to collapse: namely, that Saint Gregory, after previously opposing the Sardinian presbyters because they were usurping the episcopal right of signing infants on the forehead with chrism, later allowed them to do so where bishops were absent. For since the holy Doctor speaks only of infants who are to be baptized, and not of those already baptized, although he permits presbyters to perform a chrismation or anointing even on the foreheads of those not yet baptized, this must be referred solely to the rite of baptism, not to the signing customarily performed by bishops and regarded as the sacrament of confirmation. At first sight this argument seemed to conflict with the common opinion of theologians concerning the privilege granted or confirmed by the most holy pontiff to the Sardinian presbyters: that they might sign and confirm infants in place of absent bishops. Yet the following considerations have finally compelled us to agree with them as well. It is certain that Saint Gregory, in the later letter, namely Letter 26, granted what he had forbidden in the earlier one, Letter 9; and that the permitted anointing and signing—whatever its precise nature—was, according to the ancient usage of the Roman Church, indeed of nearly all the Western churches, never performed by presbyters but only by bishops. The Sardinian presbyters were granted the right to administer it under no other condition than that bishops were absent. But what other rite can be imagined besides sacramental chrismation? Anointing the baptized with chrism, whether on the breast or on the crown of the head, belonged to presbyters in every church, and therefore in the Roman Church as well, provided that they had received permission from the bishop to baptize. “But,” you will say, “Saint Gregory is speaking of infants who are to be baptized; since they were not yet baptized, they were not yet suitable recipients of confirmation.” The holy Doctor is speaking of infants who were being baptized and, according to the custom of that time, were being signed at nearly the same time. Certainly, where Letter 9 reads, “But let presbyters anoint those to be baptized on the breast, so that afterward bishops may anoint them on the forehead”—that is, the infants whom he had just said were to be baptized—one could argue in the same way: “Therefore bishops were signing and confirming those not yet baptized, but only about to be baptized.” Accordingly, no one should understand Gregory to mean catechumens who were to be touched with chrism on the forehead before immersion. We read that those to be baptized were anointed before immersion with ordinary oil, but never with chrism. On this matter see Bede, On the Song of Songs, chapter 1, verse 15. Furthermore, as we have already observed, Gregory is speaking of the forehead-chrismation reserved to bishops and performed only upon the baptized. This is proved by the restriction in his concession: “where bishops are absent.” For, as Innocent I explains in Letter 1 to Decentius of Gubbio, chapter 3: “Presbyters, whether outside the presence of the bishop or with the bishop present, may, when they baptize, anoint the baptized with chrism, but with chrism consecrated by the bishop; they may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs exclusively to bishops when they confer the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete.” Moreover, by the words “according to the ancient usage of our Church,” he sufficiently indicates that a different custom prevailed in other churches. The practice of the Eastern churches is well known. We say nothing here about the Spanish, or even the Gallican, churches; for it is not our purpose to examine either the canons of Elvira and Toledo or the Council of Orange, famous for the sharp controversy between Sirmond and Aurelius. We note only one fact about Africa, to whose exarchate Sardinia had been attached: African presbyters had been forbidden by many canons to prepare chrism; nevertheless, John the Deacon, in his Letter to Senarius, which Mabillon published in volume 1 of the Italian Museums, assumes that they prepared chrism around the ninth century. “Nor should it trouble you,” he says in section 8, “that necessity occasionally assumes a certain force, as is now said to happen in Africa, so that presbyters prepare the holy chrism; this would rightly be disturbing if pontifical authority had not granted permission for it.” Hence it is clear that what the higher order established could be done by presbyters in such extreme necessity was in some manner made possible by the pontiffs.]

are to be baptized. We did this according to the ancient usage of our Church; but if some are altogether distressed about this matter, where bishops are absent we grant that presbyters should also touch those to be baptized on the forehead with chrism (Gratian, Distinction 95, canon 1; Book IV of the Sentences, Distinction 7, chapter 1. See above, Letter 9).

## LETTER XXVII. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

He is to demand accounts from the xenodochia; the clerics appointed there must be known for probity and diligence. If the man who accused the presbyter Epiphanius in written letters fails to prove his charge, he is to be deprived of communion. The cleric Paul, caught in criminal acts, is to be assigned to penance. Clerics are to be ordained, and clerical marriages contracted, without payment; virgins are to receive the veil without payment. Clerics are not to seek the patronage of laymen.

[Col. 0697A]

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis.

Your Fraternity ought indeed to be so solicitous about pious affairs that you would need no admonition from us at all to bring them to completion. Nevertheless, since certain matters have come to our attention that require correction, there is nothing inappropriate in our authoritative letter also reaching you. [706]

[Col. 0697B] For this reason we inform you that it has come to our attention that it was customary for [Note: [Col. 0698B] LETTER XXVII [Formerly 24].—Entrusting the administration of pious institutions to the care of bishops is not a recent practice. See the Code, “Concerning Bishops and Clerics,” laws *Omnes* and *Omnia privilegia*, and law 46, *Sancimus*. Also, “Concerning Sacred Churches,” law *Illud*. See also the Extravagants, “Concerning Religious Houses,” chapters 3 and 4, and in the Clementines, *Quia contigit*, under the same title; and the Council of Trent, session 22, chapter 9. At Chalcedon, canon 8, the laws of Gaul agree, and usage confirms them. Saint Augustine says in Tractate 97 on the Gospel of John: “Xenodochia and monasteries were called by new names, but the institutions themselves existed even before they received those names, and are established in the truth of religion,” and so forth. The apostate emperor, writing to Arsacius, chief priest of Galatia, says in Sozomen, Book V, chapter 16: “Establish numerous xenodochia in every city, so that strangers may enjoy our benevolence . . . . It has been provided from what resources you are to obtain the funds for these things,” and so forth. He did this, indeed, from hatred of Christians, but nevertheless in imitation of them. His words show that at that time xenodochia were under the control of our bishops. Hence they were called the xenodochia of the churches. See the Ecclesiastical History in Three Parts, Book IX, chapter 31, where the wife of Theodosius is described as visiting the xenodochia of the churches. See also Letter 8 of this book. GUSSANV.] the xenodochia established in the territory of Caralis to submit detailed accounts at regular intervals to the bishop of the city, under whose protection and supervision they were to be administered.

Since your Charity is said to have neglected this until now, we urge you, as has been stated, to require the xenodochium officials who are or have been appointed in those institutions to submit their accounts to you in detail at regular intervals. And [Note: Nowadays they often grant hospitals, xenodochia, and other institutions of this kind even to laymen who are married, as though they were lay benefices; nor is there any investigation of their life, morals, or diligence, since they are intent only on the revenues and, being absent, are not even concerned in a dream about the care and administration of the institutions. In the *Notice of the Gallican Clergy*, printed in 1646, volume 2 of the *Mémoires du clergé*, there is much useful material concerning the administration of hospitals and other pious institutions, in which this letter of Saint Gregory ought to have been included. In the large collection of royal sanctions and edicts commonly called *La grande conférence des ordonnances*, under the title “Concerning Hospitals, Hostels, and Other Pious Institutions,” there are almost innumerable records on this subject, both in the text and in the annotations. A diligent student will not regret reading them; yet he will read with indignation the words of Louis Bochell: “Since our kings have recognized that excessive avarice has crept among ecclesiastics, and that they apply the goods of the poor to their own private profit rather than to their sustenance, etc., they have taken the administration away from them, etc.” With his leave, I would say: not everywhere, nor from all of them. GUSSANV.] men of such character must be appointed over them as are found to be outstanding in life, morals, and diligence—religious men, in particular, whom judges have no power to harass. Otherwise, if such persons were appointed as could be summoned before their court, an opportunity would be provided for the property of the needy who lie there to be squandered. We wish you to exercise the greatest care over these matters, so that no one may be appointed without your knowledge and your Fraternity’s negligence may not go so far as to permit their property to be plundered.

[Col. 0698B] Furthermore, you know that the bearer of this letter, the presbyter Epiphanius, was criminally accused by letters from certain [Note: [Col. 0698D] The earlier text corruptly read “priests.” We have restored this reading from very many manuscript codices and editions, including the Venetian edition of 1504. The Roman correctors also noticed this, adding in the margin, at the passage cited by Gratian: “or, of the Sardinians.” GUSSANV. Most of our manuscripts agree.] Sardinians [Col. 0699A] (Gratian, Cause 5, Question 6, canon 4). After examining his case as we wished, and finding nothing in him to support the accusations, we absolved him and ordered him to return to his place. Therefore, we wish you to investigate the authors of his alleged crime. Unless the person who sent those [707] letters is prepared to establish, by the strictest proofs, what he alleged, let him in no way approach the communion of the holy mysteries.

[Note: You see how important it is that calumniators of the Church be punished. In the Code, Book IV, title “Concerning Evidence,” the final law says: “All accusers know that they ought to bring before the public judgment a matter supported by suitable witnesses, or established by the clearest documents, or demonstrated by indications more certain and clearer than daylight.” And in Book IX of the Code, title 2, final law: “Let no one think that the license to lie will go unpunished, since the similarity of the punishment demands that calumniators be brought to justice.” Let the reader note that this is cited in Cause 2, Question 8, canon 3, as though from a letter of Eutychianus. Read the whole of Question 6 of Cause 5, where Saint Gregory is cited in three canons concerning calumny, though not with great exactness. The author of the *Incomplete Work*, Homily 42 on Matthew 22, explains how one ought to deal with calumniators. GUSSANV.]

As for the cleric Paul, who is frequently said to have been caught in criminal acts and who, abandoning his clerical habit and returning to lay life, had fled to Africa, if this is so, we have decided that he should first undergo corporal punishment and then be assigned to penance [Note: Concerning this matter, see above, Letter 43 of Book III, indiction 11.], so that, in accordance with the apostolic judgment, his spirit may be saved through the affliction of the flesh and so that he may be able, through continual tears, to wash away the earthly stains of sin that he is said to have contracted by his wicked deeds.
