No religious person is to associate, in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons, with those who have been suspended from ecclesiastical communion [Note: That excommunicated persons are to be avoided everywhere in the world by other bishops is an ancient institution. The Council of Nicaea mentions it in canon 5, using the words κατὰ τὸν κανόνα, “according to the canon,” which the Council of Antioch likewise treats as an ancient rule in chapters 2 and 6, and elsewhere. GUSSANV.].

Concerning the ordinations and marriages of clerics, and concerning those who receive the veil as virgins, let no one presume to accept any payment, as is said to be done nowadays, unless they themselves should prefer voluntarily to offer something.

Concerning women who have left monasteries for lay life and taken husbands, we have discussed more fully with the aforementioned presbyter of your Fraternity what ought to be done. Your Holiness can be more fully informed by his report.

Let religious clerics beware of the assemblies and patronage of laymen, and let them in every respect be subject to your jurisdiction according to the canons, lest, through your Fraternity’s leniency, the discipline of the Church over which you preside be dissolved. [Col. 0699C]

But those who committed fornication with the women mentioned above, who had left the monasteries, and who are now said to have been suspended from communion—if your Fraternity finds that they have suitably repented of such a crime—we wish you to restore to sacred communion (Gratian, Cause 27, Question 1, canon 29).

## LETTER XXVIII. TO CANDIDUS, THE DEFENDER

He is to provide two tremisses each year to Albinus, who has been deprived of his sight.

[Col. 0700A]

Gregory to Candidus, the defender.

It is fitting that pontifical assistance should be present to those suffering need. For this reason, by the authority of the present letter, we command your Experience not to fail to provide each year, without any delay, two tremisses to Albinus, the son of the former colonus Martinus, who has been deprived of his sight [Note: [Col. 0700C] LETTER XXVIII.—The Pratell manuscript reads “two tremisses”; perhaps “twelve” should be read instead. The suspicion arises because two tremisses would have been a small alms. A tremissis is only one-third of a gold coin or solidus; a solidus, however, was one-quarter less than our own louis d’or, since the latter weighs 126 grains and the former 96, while six solidi made an ounce of 576 grains. Medieval and later writers and laws frequently mention this tremissis; it was approximately equivalent to our silver écu.], without doubting that this will certainly be charged to your accounts.

[708]

## LETTER XXIX. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP

Phausiana, which formerly had a bishop, is to have one now as well.

[Col. 0700B]

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis.

It has come to our attention that in a place within the province of Sardinia called Phausiana [Note: [Col. 0700D] LETTER XXIX.—Nearly all the manuscripts read this way. Among geographers it is called Phausania, and today it is commonly called Terranova. It is a coastal town of Sardinia, whose episcopal see was under the archbishop of Torres; it was first joined to Emporiensis, which in the sixteenth century was transferred to Castel Aragonese. Partly from GUSSANV.] there was formerly a custom of ordaining a bishop, but that this custom was abolished for a long time because of circumstances.

Since we now know that, through a shortage of priests, some pagans remain there and live in a bestial manner, entirely ignorant of the worship of God, we urge your Fraternity to hasten to appoint there, according to the former custom, a bishop who is suitable for this work in morals and speech, and who will strive with pastoral zeal to lead the straying back to the Lord’s flock. Thus, while he is there for the benefit of souls, you will neither be found to have asked for something unnecessary nor will we have cause to regret that we restored what had long been destroyed without purpose.

## LETTER XXX. TO CONSTANTINA, THE AUGUSTA

He deters Constantina, who is requesting the head of Saint Paul, by recounting various miracles. He adds that it is the Roman custom to grant only *brandea* to those who request relics. He responds to the objection based on the custom of the Greeks. Finally, he promises that fragments of Saint Paul’s chains will be struck off with a file.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0700D] LETTER XXX.—She was the daughter of the emperor Tiberius Constantine, whom her father gave in marriage to Maurice and to whom he handed over the empire in place of a dowry. After the murder of the emperor Maurice by the wicked Phocas, she was first thrust into a monastery and then, a year later, was killed with her three daughters on the order of the same tyrant. See the Byzantine historians for more about her. GUSSANV.] to Constantina, the Augusta.

[Col. 0701A] Your Serenity, distinguished by devotion to religion and love of holiness [Note: In the Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and several Vatican manuscripts the reading is *perspicua*, “conspicuous” or “illustrious.”], has commanded me by your orders that, for the church being built in the palace in honor of the holy apostle Paul, the head of that same Saint Paul, or something else from his body, ought to be sent to you.

Although I would have desired you to command me things in which, by rendering the easiest obedience, I could more fully have called forth your favor toward me, I was seized by greater sadness because you command what I neither can nor dare do. For the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul shine forth in their churches with such great miracles and terrors that no one can approach them even to pray without great fear.

Indeed, when my predecessor of blessed memory wished to move the silver that was above the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter, although it was still nearly fifteen feet away from that body, a sign of no small terror appeared to him [709] [Note: Pope Adrian likewise writes in approximately 772, in a fragment of a letter to Charlemagne: “He asked us to give him the holy body. But, as we sent you long ago, having been terrified by a revelation, we in no way dare to disturb anything further from the bodies of the saints.” GUSSANV.].

I too wished to improve something near the most sacred body of the holy apostle Paul. Since it was necessary to dig deeper beside his tomb, the custodian of that place found some bones not actually joined to the tomb. Because he dared to lift them and transfer them to another place, certain frightening signs appeared, and he died a sudden death.

Moreover, when my predecessor of holy memory likewise wished to improve something near the body of the holy martyr Lawrence, and it was not known where the venerable body had been placed, the area was excavated in search of it. Suddenly his tomb was unknowingly opened, and all those who were present and laboring there—the monks and the *mansionarii* [Note: Who the *mansionarii* were is explained in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapters 24 and 25, and especially in chapter 5 of Book I, where see the notes to Zacharias’ Greek translation. Other meanings of this word, unrelated to the holy Doctor’s purpose, may be found, if desired, in the notes of Gussanville.] who saw the body of that martyr, though they did not dare to touch it at all, died within ten days, so that no one who had seen that holy and righteous body of his could remain alive [Note: The Norman, Corbie, and several others read “who saw his holy and righteous body.” Vatican B and D read “who saw his holy body.” The more probable reading appears in the Regius manuscript: “who saw his holy, righteous body.” We nevertheless do not dare to adopt it, since no other copy supports it.].

But let the most tranquil Lady know that [Note: Baron likewise speaks in exactly this way in his notes to the Roman Martyrology, 17 July. Yet examples exist of relics granted by Gregory the Great himself. From Ripamonti, *Ecclesiastical History of Milan*, Book VIII, pp. 522–523: “Gregory . . . granted to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, most august relics . . . among which are seen relics of the Baptist himself, liquid blood in a flask, ashes from a burned body, and, together with a tooth, a small portion of a skull . . . finally, there are cloths that absorbed the blood of martyrs and fragments of bones . . . . So that all these things might be valued more highly by posterity, and so that no one might suspect the customary adulteration of relics, an inventory of these relics, written by Gregory’s own hand, was added; in it everything is transcribed and marked in Lombard letters.” Likewise from Mario Vipera, in Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, volume VIII, column 19: “Linianus, bishop of Benevento, took part in the solemn translation of the body of the most blessed deacon and martyr Modestus from the city of Benevento on 3 July 591, by the permission of Gregory the Great and at the request of Arichis, the most pious duke of Benevento, from the monks of Saint Mary at Olivola, situated outside the city of Benevento. The body was honorably received by the bishop with his clergy, by the duke, and by the entire people; it was placed in that church and buried there until the basilica dedicated in his honor had been completed.” Nor do the *brandea* alone, as concessions, appear to be implied in Indiction 11, Letter 19, and Indiction 2, Letter 15. Mabillon perhaps remembered these examples when, in the preface to the second century of the Benedictines, Observation 8, he moderated the wording of Baronius or his own: “Such translations were carried out more sparingly during the pontificate of Saint Gregory.” We have treated these matters cursorily in the Life of Saint Gregory.]

it is not the custom of the Romans, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body; instead, only a *brandeum* is sent in a small box [Note: [Col. 0702C] Vatican A and B, as well as the Regius manuscript, read *buxide*, from *buxus*, boxwood, from which the object called in French a *boîte* was made.] and placed against the most sacred bodies of the saints [Note: These were pieces of cloth and coverings that, after being applied to the revered remains of martyrs, were distributed to the faithful from the contact itself as though they were relics of the saints themselves. Several manuscripts read *prandeum*, corresponding to the Greek word. Consult the lexicographers concerning this term.]. Once it has been taken away, it is deposited with due veneration in the church that is to be dedicated, and through it so many miracles occur there as if their bodies had been brought there in person.

Thus [710] it happened that in the time of Pope Leo of blessed memory, as tradition handed down by our forebears relates, when certain Greeks doubted such relics, the aforementioned pontiff cut this very *brandeum* with scissors brought to him, and blood flowed from the incision.

For in Rome and throughout the entire West it is wholly intolerable and sacrilegious if anyone should attempt to touch the bodies of the saints. If anyone presumes to do so, it is certain that such audacity will in no way remain unpunished.

For this reason we are exceedingly astonished at the custom of the Greeks, who claim that they raise the bones of the saints, and we scarcely believe it. For two years ago certain Greek monks came here and, under cover of the night, near the church of Saint Paul, [Note: Such frauds, pious in name but sacrilegious in reality, are condemned by all who are truly pious. Irreligious men practice them: seeking what is their own and mocking solid piety under the appearance of empty devotion, they strip themselves of genuine piety. Optatus the African, in a passage not yet adequately corrected, mentions in Book I Lucilla, who before receiving the spiritual food kissed the bone of a certain dead man; Balsamon considers this a custom among the Donatists, in his commentary on the Council of Carthage, canon 61. Augustine says in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 28: “Others sell the limbs of martyrs—if indeed they are the limbs of martyrs.” Gregory of Tours, Book IX, chapter 6, mentions a notorious rogue who carried false relics throughout Gaul and was finally exposed at Paris. Would that our own age had not witnessed similar things, and that bishops, at last—late indeed, but earnestly—would consider abolishing such abominable abuses of relics, distinguishing true relics from false ones by certain and indisputable evidence, as we read that the Council of Zaragoza did around the year 590 by applying fire. Whoever wishes to know more should read the letter of Boniface to Zacharias concerning Adalbert; Adrian’s letter to Charlemagne concerning the body of Saint Candidus; the capitulary of Aachen, chapter 42, so that false names of martyrs and uncertain memories of saints may not be venerated, from the African Council, chapter 50; the Council of Mainz, canon 51; and so forth. GUSSANV.] they dug up the bodies of the dead lying in a field [Col. 0703A] and hid their bones [Note: Another reading is “collected them,” as in Vatican A], keeping them for themselves until they departed.

When they had been seized and carefully interrogated about what they were doing, they confessed that they intended to carry those bones to Greece as relics of saints. From their example, as stated above, an even greater doubt has arisen in us as to whether it is true that they are genuinely said to raise the bones of the saints.

What, then, am I to say about the bodies of the blessed apostles, when it is established that, at the time when they suffered, faithful men came from the East to reclaim their bodies as those of their own citizens? These bodies were carried as far as the second milestone from the city, to the place called the Catacombs.[^c0064-1] 711 But while all their assembled multitude was striving to remove them from there, the force of thunder and lightning terrified and scattered them with such overwhelming fear that they did not dare attempt anything of the kind again. Then the Romans came out and, by the Lord’s mercy, lifted the bodies—an action they had deserved to perform—and placed them in the places where they are now buried.

Who, therefore, most serene lady, could be so rash as, knowing these things, to dare not merely touch their bodies but even to look upon them in any way? Since such orders had been given to me by you—orders which I could in no way have obeyed, as far as I can see—they were not yours; rather, certain people wished to stir up your piety against me, so that—God forbid—they might deprive me of the favor of your will. For that reason they sought a passage on which you might find me, as it were, disobedient. But I trust in almighty God that nothing can be stolen from your most kindly will, and that you will always possess the power of the holy apostles, whom you love with all your heart and mind, not through their bodily presence but through their protection.

As for the sudarium, which you likewise ordered to be sent, it is with his body, which cannot be touched, just as no one can approach that body. But since so religious a desire on the part of the most serene lady ought not to remain unfulfilled, I shall hasten to send you a portion of the chains that the holy apostle Paul himself wore around his neck and on his hands, from which many miracles are displayed among the people—provided that I can succeed in removing it by filing. For when many people frequently come to seek a blessing from those same chains, so that they may receive a small particle of the filings, a priest stands by with a file; for some petitioners, something is quickly shaken off from the chains themselves, so that no delay is needed. For others who ask, however, the file is drawn along the chains for a long time, and yet nothing can be obtained from them.[^c0064-2]

In the month of June, in the twelfth indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, book III, no. 56.)

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE PHYSICIAN THEODORUS

He gives thanks for money sent for the poor. He urges him to read Holy Scripture. He commends Narsetes. He sends gifts, paintings.

Gregory to Theodorus, physician of the emperor.[^c0064-3]

I give thanks to almighty God, because places do not divide the hearts of those who truly love one another. For behold, dearest and most glorious son, although we are far separated from one another in body, we are nevertheless present to one another in charity. Your actions testify to this, as do your letters; I have experienced it concerning the present, and I recognize it concerning your glory while you are absent. May this make you beloved among human beings and worthy before almighty God forever.

Since charity is the mother of virtues, you produce the fruits of good works because you hold the root of those fruits in your heart. I received with joy, I confess, and with sadness what you sent, by God’s prompting, for the redemption of captives. I rejoiced for you, because I learned that you were thinking about preparing a dwelling in the heavenly homeland; but I was deeply saddened for myself, because in addition to my responsibility for the possessions of the holy apostle Peter, I must now also give an account of the possessions of my dearest son, my lord Theodorus. I am going to be examined as to whether I spent them carefully or negligently.

May almighty God, who has poured the inward compassion of his mercy into your mind and granted you the grace to think carefully, reveal you rich in virtues at the coming of our Savior, concerning whom the distinguished preacher says: “Although he was rich, he became poor for us” (2 Corinthians 8:9). May he make you stand free from every fault and grant you heavenly things in place of earthly things, and enduring joys in place of transitory ones.

As for what you write about the prayers being offered for you at the most sacred body of the holy apostle Peter, hold this certain: although your tongue speaks, your charity commands it to be done. Would that we might be worthy to pray for you! I do not doubt, however, that I myself am unworthy. But many worthy people are here, those who are redeemed from the enemies by your offering and faithfully serve our Creator. With regard to them you have fulfilled what is written: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will intercede for you” (Sirach 29:15).

But because the one who presumes more loves more, I have some complaint concerning the mind of my most beloved son, my lord Theodorus. He has received from the Holy Trinity the gift of intelligence, the gift of possessions, and the gift of mercy and charity; yet he is continually entangled in worldly affairs, occupied with constant journeys, and neglects daily to read the words of his Redeemer.

What, indeed, is Holy Scripture except a kind of letter from almighty God to his creature? Certainly, if your glory were established somewhere else and you received writings from an earthly emperor, you would not cease or rest, nor give sleep to your eyes, until you had first learned what the earthly emperor had written to you. The Emperor of heaven, the Lord of human beings and angels, has sent you his letters for your life; yet, glorious son, you neglect to read those same letters eagerly. Therefore, I beg you, take pains and meditate daily on the words of your Creator. Learn the heart of God in the words of God, so that you may long more ardently for eternal things and so that your mind may be kindled with greater desires for heavenly joys. For its rest will then be greater in proportion to the absence now of any rest in its love for its Creator. In order that you may do these things, may almighty God pour into you the Spirit who comforts. May he fill your mind with his presence and, by filling it, lift it up.

Know concerning me that I suffer here many and countless bitter things. Yet I give thanks to almighty God, because I am afflicted far less than I deserve.

I commend to your glory my most dear son, your dependent, my lord Narsetes.[^c0064-4] I know that you already keep him commended in every respect, but I ask you to continue doing what you do, so that, when I ask for what I see being done, I may submit myself by my request to your reward.[^c0064-5] Moreover, I received your Excellency’s blessing with the charity with which it was sent.

I have presumed to send you one duck with two little ducklings, as a token of your love,[^c0064-6] so that whenever your eye is drawn to look upon it, the memory of me may also be recalled to your mind amid the occupations and tumult of lawsuits.

## LETTER XXXII. TO NARSETES, PATRICIAN

He declares that he will pursue the case of the presbyters against John the patriarch strictly according to the norm of the canons. He commends Narsetes, whom he has recommended, to Theodorus. He excuses the brevity of the letter because he is weighed down by tribulations.

Gregory to Narsetes the patrician.

Your most gentle charity has said much to me in its letters in praise of good works. To all this I reply briefly: “Do not call me Naomi, that is, Beautiful; call me Mara, that is, Bitter, because I am full of bitterness” (Ruth 1:20).[^c0064-7]

As for the case of the presbyters that is being conducted with my brother and fellow bishop, the most reverend John the patriarch, I think we are suffering the very opponent whom you say wishes to observe the canons. I briefly confess to your charity that, with the help of almighty God, I am prepared to pursue this case with every strength and with all weight.[^c0064-8] If in it I should see that the canons are not being observed by the apostolic see, almighty God will show me what I should do against those who despise them.[^c0064-9]

As for what your charity wrote to me, namely that I should thank my son, my lord Theodorus, the chief physician and former prefect, on your behalf, I have done so, and I have not ceased to commend you as far as I could. But please forgive me for replying to your letters so briefly, because I am weighed down by such great tribulations that I can scarcely read or say much in letters. I tell you only this briefly: “For I have forgotten to eat my bread, from the sound of my groaning” (Psalm 101:5).

I ask that all who are with you be greeted in my place. Give my greetings to our lady Dominica, to whom I gave no reply because, although she is Latin, she wrote to me in Greek.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO THE SUBDEACON ANTHEMIUS

He orders that solidi be given every year to three converted Jews.

Gregory to the subdeacon Anthemius.

Since our Redeemer graciously deigns to convert to himself those whom he rescues from Jewish destruction, we ought to assist them with reasonable moderation, lest—God forbid—they suffer want of food. Therefore, by the authority of this command, we order you not to delay giving, beginning with the thirteenth succeeding indiction and every year thereafter, solidi to Justa’s children from among the Hebrews—that is, to Julianus, Redemptus, and Fortuna—and you are to know that these sums must in every respect be charged to your accounts.[^c0064-10]

## LETTER XXXIV. TO PANTALEON, PREFECT

He urges him to suppress the audacity of the Donatists and to send Bishop Paul to Rome as quickly as possible.

Gregory to Pantaleon, prefect of Africa.[^c0064-11]

It is not unknown to your Excellency how vigorously the law prosecutes the most abominable depravity of heretics.[^c0064-12] These people, therefore, whom both the integrity of our faith and the strictness of secular laws condemn: it is no small sin if they find an opportunity to rage during your administration.

In those regions, as we have learned, the audacity of the Donatists has grown so greatly that, by their destructive authority, they not only expel priests of the Catholic faith from their churches, but do not fear to rebaptize those whom the water of regeneration had cleansed through a true confession. We are greatly astonished—if the report is indeed true—that, while you are stationed there, such wicked men have been permitted to go beyond all bounds.

First, consider what judgment you leave people to form about you if those who were restrained by sound reason under the administrations of others find under yours a path for their excesses. Next, know that God will require the souls of these lost people from your hand if you neglect to correct so great a sacrilege to the extent that your ability demands. Let your Excellency not receive these words with displeasure. Since we love you as our own sons, we point out what we do not doubt will benefit you.

Send our brother and fellow bishop Paul to us with all haste, so that no one may be given any opportunity or excuse for hindering him.[^c0064-13] Then, having learned the truth more fully, we shall be able, with God’s help, to determine by rational deliberation how vengeance for so great a crime should be carried out.

## LETTER XXXV. TO BISHOPS VICTOR AND COLUMBUS

After calling a council, they are to resist the Donatists promptly and courageously. They are to send Bishop Paul to him, so that, once the Donatists’ crimes have been more clearly explained by him, Gregory may decide more safely how they should be punished and suppressed.

Gregory to Victor and Columbus, bishops of Africa.

We have all learned from the circumstances of our own lives how an illness neglected at its beginning gains strength.[^c0064-14] If, then, the care of learned physicians were to oppose this illness while it is arising, we know that it would cease before, if treated late, it caused extensive harm. The reasoning behind this consideration must therefore strongly impel us to resist with all our ability when diseases of souls begin, lest, while we neglect to apply salutary remedies, they steal away the lives of many whom we are striving to win for our God.

It is therefore our duty to fortify with watchful care the sheepfolds over which we seem to have been appointed guardians, so that the lurking wolf may everywhere find pastors opposing it and have no way of entering them.

We have learned that the attacks of the Donatists have so disturbed the Lord’s flock in those regions as though it were governed by no shepherd’s direction. We have also been informed of something that we cannot mention without profound grief: many of them have already been torn by poisonous teeth.[^c0064-15] Finally, they are said, with most wicked audacity, to have expelled Catholic priests from their churches and, after rebaptizing many to whom the water of regeneration had given salvation, to have killed them in their most abominable depravity.

This greatly saddens our hearts: how could such a crime, committed in condemned presumption, have been permitted while you were stationed there?

Therefore, in letters sent one after another, we exhort your Fraternity that, after deliberation and the summoning of a united council, you must resist this disease while it is still arising, eagerly and with all your strength,[^c0064-16] so that it may neither gain strength through neglect nor shake the flock entrusted to you with the losses of pestilence. For if, in any way—which we do not believe—you neglect to resist the iniquity at its beginning, they will wound many with the sword of their error. It is certainly most grievous to permit those whom we can first rescue from bondage to become entangled in the devil’s deceitful snare. It is better to prevent anyone from being wounded than to inquire, after the wound has been inflicted, how the wounded person might be healed.

Considering this, hasten to overwhelm the sacrilegious depravity with diligent prayer and with the strength you possess, so that the next messenger, with the grace of Christ assisting, may bring us greater joy at their punishment than sorrow at their transgression.

Moreover, send our brother and fellow bishop Paul to us with all the diligence and haste you can command, so that, having learned from him more precisely the circumstances of so great a crime, we may, with the support of our Creator, apply to this most abominable depravity the medicine of a correction worthy of it.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO LEO, BISHOP

Subdeacons are not to associate sexually with their wives. The wife of the subdeacon Speciosus, who had been forced into a monastery because of a second marriage, is to be released.

Gregory to Leo, bishop of Catania.

We have learned from the reports of many people that this custom formerly prevailed among you: that subdeacons might lawfully have sexual relations with their wives.[^c0064-17] To prevent anyone from presuming to do this again, a deacon of our see, a servant of God, prohibited it in the following manner by the authority of our predecessor: at that time, those who were already married were to choose one of two alternatives—either to abstain from their wives or, certainly, not to presume to serve in any way.

It is said that at that time the subdeacon Speciosus suspended himself from office on this account. Until the time of his death he held the office of notary, but he ceased from the ministry that a subdeacon ought to perform. After his death, because his widow Honorata married another man, we have learned that your Fraternity assigned her to a monastery.[^c0064-18]

Therefore, if the facts are as we have been informed, namely that her husband withdrew from office, the fact that the woman entered a second marriage ought in no way to count against her, especially if she had not been joined to the subdeacon under an agreement to abstain from sexual relations.

If, then, you recognize that the truth is as we have learned, it is entirely appropriate that you release the woman named above from the monastery, so that she may return to her husband without any fear.

For the future, let your Fraternity be wholly vigilant in this matter, so that when men are promoted to this office you examine it with the greatest care. If they have wives, they must not be granted permission to have intercourse with them; rather, following the example of the apostolic see, establish by your own strictness that they observe all these requirements.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO MAXIMIAN, BISHOP

He orders that Euplus’s paternal and maternal property be restored.

Gregory to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse.

Euplus, the bearer of this letter, states that Eusanius, bishop of the city of Agrigentum, was his father, and indicates that many possessions belonging to his mother remained with him. Since he asserts that the bishop died intestate, he therefore asks that his mother’s property be restored to him and that he be permitted to obtain the substance of the aforementioned bishop, his father.

Regarding this matter, by the terms of this command we entrust the matter to your Fraternity, so that you may carefully investigate it. If anything belonging to his mother can be found with the aforementioned church, and if there is nothing that could reasonably prevent the aforementioned Euplus from receiving it, have it restored to him according to his rightful share.[^c0064-19]

Likewise, concerning the paternal possessions that he is known to have possessed before becoming a bishop, if he did not transfer them in any way into the legal ownership of his church, make sure that he receives whatever you know legally belongs to his portion. For it is wholly contrary both to reason and to our purpose if we refuse to restore and satisfy anyone with what justly belongs to him.

Let your Fraternity therefore hasten to carry this out, so that the bearer named above is not again compelled to return to us concerning this matter. Our predecessor of blessed memory had sent an order that, after Euplus’s fall, all his possessions should remain with the church. We believe that he ordered this so that the possessions might not suffer further loss through him. Now, however, we judge it equitable that the son should not be burdened by his father’s fault, but that, through your administration, he should receive whatever can legally belong to him.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO QUEEN THEODELINDA

He grieves that she has been led astray by ignorant people. He professes that the faith of the four holy synods, especially that of Chalcedon, is preserved intact in the Roman Church. He urges her not to remain outside Bishop Constantius’s communion.

Gregory to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards.

Reports from certain bishops have reached us that your glory has been led so far into opposition to the holy Church that she has withdrawn herself from communion with Catholic unanimity. The more purely we love you, the more deeply we grieve over you, because you trust ignorant and foolish people who not only do not know what they say but can scarcely understand what they have heard. Since they neither read nor believe those who read, they remain in the very error that they themselves have fabricated about us.

We venerate the four holy synods: Nicaea, in which Arius; Constantinople, in which Macedonius; the First Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius; and Chalcedon, in which Eutyches and Dioscorus were condemned.[^c0064-20] We profess that whoever thinks differently from these four synods is alien to the faith of truth.

We condemn all whom they condemn, and we absolve all whom they absolve. Under pain of anathema, we strike the person who presumes to add anything to or subtract anything from the faith of those four synods, especially the Council of Chalcedon, concerning which certain ignorant people have formed suspicions and an occasion for superstition.[^c0064-21]

---

[^c0064-1]: Baronius reads *Catatumbas* in the *Martyrologium*, on 20 January; some manuscripts and printed editions agree with him. Many ancient and better manuscripts, however, read *catacumbas*. When the eminent Cardinal Bona was consulted about this, he wrote to me on 9 September 1670: “The reading must certainly be *catacumbas*, for this is how most of the older Vatican manuscripts read. As for the origin of the word, I have found nothing beyond what Baronius notes in the *Martyrology* on 3 and 10 January. Everywhere it is understood as referring to subterranean places in which the bodies of martyrs used to be buried. In the latest edition of his ecclesiastical dictionary, published in 1669, under *Coemeterium*, Dominicus Magri cites Latinus Latinius as asserting that the word is derived from the Greek *catacumbe*, meaning a hollow and deep place. In another letter, dated 15 November of the same year, he writes: ‘I see from your letters that you still have doubts about the word *catacumbae*. I discussed the matter with Dominicus Magri, who possesses all the learned works of Latinus Latinius and hopes soon to publish them. Among them are certain manuscript notes on the Roman Martyrology in which Latinius writes about the catacombs what Magri transferred into his own dictionary.’ At the end of the letter he adds: ‘After I had written, Dominicus Magri sent me this page, which I append here, written in his own hand.’ The page contains the following: ‘In my account I follow the opinion of the most learned Latinus Latinius concerning the word *catacumba*, as he himself observes in his marginal notes on the Roman Martyrology, rejecting Cardinal Baronius’s correction. For the Greek word κατακύμβη (*katakymbē*) means “beside a hollow and deep place,” from the noun κύμβος (*kymbos*), since among the Latins the letter *y* is very often changed into *u*, as is frequently found. The noun *tumba*, moreover, is not Latin; nor were those places near tombs, but rather in the caverns of the earth, where Christians gathered and celebrated assemblies, and where later they buried the bodies of holy martyrs.’” Nearly the same account appears in *Roma subterranea*, book I, chapter 1, where *catacumbas* is said to derive from the Greek κατά (*kata*) and κύμβος (*kymbos*), that is, as Hesychius explains, κοῖλος μυχός, βυθός (*koilos mychos, bythos*), “a hollow recess, or a place situated at the bottom and deep.” Likewise, in book III, chapter 12, the term *catacumbas* is used and the places are described, and this letter of Saint Gregory is reported. I add that *cymba* is also derived from κύμβος; among the Savoyards, valleys are commonly called *combes*. — GUSSANV. The claim made here by Saint Gregory—that the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul remained in the same place where they had previously been buried—may be opposed by the First Letter of Pope and Martyr Cornelius, which speaks of their translation in his own time. That letter, however, is spurious and was fabricated long after Gregory, for it contains passages sewn together from Gregory’s letters, especially Letter 109 of Book IX, indiction 2, where the following words are falsely attributed to Cornelius: “Whoever inserts himself into the root of charity and does not fall away from the truth,” and so forth. One more difficult problem remains. In the ancient Roman calendar published by Aegidius Bucherius, a most learned Jesuit priest, we read: “On the third day before the Kalends of July: Peter at the Catacombs, and Paul at Ostia, in the consulship of Fuscus and Bassus.” This means, as our Dom Theoderic Ruinart explains in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 692, that in the year 258, when the translation of the holy apostles took place, it occurred on the very day on which their feast was celebrated. The translation is strongly supported by Antonius Pagi, a highly skilled historian of the Church, in his discussion of the year 258, and he confirms it with the agreement and testimony of Pearson himself. We therefore cannot deny that Gregory, when writing to Constantina, may at some point have suffered a lapse of memory. — GUSSANV.

[^c0064-2]: This date for the writing of the letter is given by the Vatican, Norman, Tours, Saint Gatianus, Colbert, Old Corbie, and other manuscripts.

[^c0064-3]: “LETTER XXXI [elsewhere numbered 40, indiction 13]. We add ‘of the emperor,’ on the authority of all the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts. On this subject reread Letter 66 of Book III, indiction 11.” 

[^c0064-4]: Alteserra says that physicians call their patients *suscepti*, that is, clients or persons entrusted to their care. Augustine writes on Psalm 45: “Someone is ill; a physician is called; the physician calls the sick person his *susceptus*.” Lawyers likewise call their clients *suscepti*.

[^c0064-5]: Vatican manuscript A reads: “that by asking I may make myself subject to your reward.”

[^c0064-6]: In the common editions: “with two little Attic [objects].” The Norman and Corbie manuscripts read “with two little *actaca*.” Our reading is supplied by the Vatican manuscripts; Vatican D has “with two little aquatic ducklings,” while A, B, and C have “with two little ducklings.” Alteserra and Gussanvillaeus considered the passage corrupt. Alteserra proposed *Anaitem*, from Anaea, a city of Caria in Asia Minor: “He gives three slaves as a gift, that Anaitic woman and two little Attic [objects].” Gussanvillaeus continues: “so that whenever your eye is drawn to look upon her, the memory of me may also be recalled.” But would it be fitting for so serious and chaste a pontiff to place a girl rather than little Attic objects before Theodorus’s eyes so that the sight might revive the memory of a friend and rekindle affection? With some plausibility Alteserra read *unum anacem*, a type of vessel, concerning which Gregory of Tours writes in his book on the miracles of Saint Julian: “Four of these, having escaped by flight, carried back to their homeland a paten and a vessel called an *anax*.” He interpreted *Attica* as earthenware vessels, so called from the region of Attica where they were made and which, he says, Italians commonly call porcelain. Cangius does not reject this conjecture. If the Corbie and Norman manuscripts are to be followed, perhaps Gregory is sending Theodorus three painted panels: he calls the first an *anax* because it displayed a bird elegantly painted for that age, and calls the other two *actaca*, namely colored depictions of pleasant shores. For if the Attic region took its name from ἀκτή (*aktē*), “shore,” a word used by Cicero, Virgil, and Ausonius, because most of it lies by the sea, then beautiful or pleasant shores could have been called *actaca* or *actacae*. We leave this conjecture of highly learned men to the judgment of other scholars. But what prevents us from accepting the obvious sense, supplied especially by the Vatican manuscripts? Gregory sends his physician, familiar and friend, one duck with two little ducklings—that is, a mother and two young. A duck is, of course, a familiar and common bird; yet some are seen painted in exquisite colors, distinguished by a crown on the head and fragrant, and such birds are even kept among the rarer birds in royal courts. Why should we not say that Gregory took care to send such a duck—perhaps not yet seen in Constantinople—to his physician friend, whom he certainly knew to be interested in natural things and curious about raising rarer animals? This interpretation requires no remote explanation; it is offered by the restored reading of the best Vatican manuscripts: “one duck with two little ducklings,” that is, little ducks. From *anaticis*, scribes and those who labored to publish Gregory’s works, paying too little attention to the force of the word, produced *aticis*, and later *Atticis*.

[^c0064-7]: The printed editions read: “Do not call me Naomi, that is, beautiful … bitter, I am full.” The Vatican, Norman, Royal, Corbie, and other manuscripts support the reading translated above.

[^c0064-8]: The Vatican manuscripts disagree among themselves. Codex D has *eximere* (“to remove”); Codex C has *exire* (“to go out”); they agree with the Norman manuscript, while Vatican B has *exercere* (“to pursue”) and, as a variant, *exire*. The translation follows the sense of pursuing or conducting the case.

[^c0064-9]: This reading is found in three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others, and agrees with the older printed editions. More recent editions read “of the apostolic see.”

[^c0064-10]: Recent editions read “to the daughters … Juliana, Redempta, and Fortunata.” The Norman, Tours, English, and Vatican manuscripts support the reading translated above. In two Vatican manuscripts, *Fortunae* appears instead of *Fortunato*.

[^c0064-11]: LETTER XXXIV [elsewhere numbered 32]. Three Vatican manuscripts, three Norman manuscripts, and the Rheims manuscript read “to the bishop of Africa.” This inscription is certainly erroneous, as anyone will see who considers the title of Excellency with which Gregory addresses Pantaleon, for he never addresses bishops in that way. Moreover, the sequence of the letter plainly indicates that it was written not to a bishop but to an exarch or prefect.

[^c0064-12]: The reference is to the imperial laws, some of which against the Donatists are frequently cited by Augustine, while others were issued by later emperors. See the Theodosian Code and the Justinian Code, book I, title 6, “That Holy Baptism Is Not to Be Repeated.”

[^c0064-13]: The manuscripts generally read as translated above, especially the Norman and Vatican manuscripts. Some editions read: “so that no opportunity or excuse for hindering him may be given.”

[^c0064-14]: Recent printed editions read: “from the needs that we suffer, established in this city, we have proved.” All the Vatican, Corbie, English, Tours, and other manuscripts resist that reading.

[^c0064-15]: The common editions read: “Finally, they are said to have expelled canonical priests … and to have killed many …” We would not have altered that reading if the common agreement of the English, Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Tours, and Royal manuscripts had not compelled us. Let the note appended by Gussanvillaeus concerning canonical priests stand. We were compelled to remove another note by the same author concerning the words “from the needs that we suffer in this city,” which he interpreted as referring to the disasters of Italy. But “in this city” is a corrupt reading, as we have already noted.

[^c0064-16]: Shortly after Saint Cyprian, the faction of the Donatists broke into schism. At alternating times it seemed to subside, then flare up again, for more than three hundred years, until the age of Saint Gregory. — GUSSANV.

[^c0064-17]: Concerning the continence of subdeacons, see above, Letter 5, and Book I, Letter 44. The matter is also cited in Gratian, Distinction 32, canon 2, and Cause 27, Question 2, canon 20.

[^c0064-18]: Many canons teach that clerics’ widows were not permitted to marry again. Some are cited in Distinction 28, canons 10–12, from Saint Gregory, Book XI, Letter 62, now Book XIII, Letter 51; from the Council of Orléans, canon 13; and from the collection of Martin of Braga, canon 29. Add the Council of Auxerre, canon 22: “A presbyter’s widow, a deacon’s widow, or a subdeacon’s widow may not take another husband after his death.” The same prohibition appears in the decrees of Gregory II, chapters 1 and 2. In the First Roman Council, held in the same year, A.D. 721, and in the First Council of Toledo, I find the same words as in canon 29 of Martin of Braga’s collection. I attribute the reason for this prohibition to the consent or vow of the women; for husbands were not promoted to the higher orders unless the women had either themselves vowed conversion or had given a pledge that they would not remarry but would remain unmarried after their husbands’ deaths. — GUSSANV. The earlier reading was: “Honorata was joined to her husband,” which has been changed because of the unanimous agreement of the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Tours, and other manuscripts.

[^c0064-19]: LETTER XXXVII [elsewhere numbered 36]. A bishop may make a testament concerning hereditary property acquired before or after his episcopate. But property acquired after his episcopate from church possessions may not be alienated either by testament or during his lifetime. Gregory, Book XII, Letter 38: “No one doubts that just as priests have no power to alienate possessions acquired during their episcopate, so, concerning those which they possessed earlier, they are not forbidden to decide whatever they wish.” If a bishop has children, however, he cannot make a testament in favor of the Church from property acquired before his episcopate except with the legitimate share of the children preserved. This is established by the present letter.

[^c0064-20]: In four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Corbie, and Royal manuscripts, the reading is: “Nicaea, at which Arius; Constantinople, at which Macedonius; Ephesus, at which Nestorius and Dioscorus; Chalcedon, at which Eutyches was condemned.” That reading conflicts with the history of the councils.

[^c0064-21]: In the Norman and Corbie manuscripts, with better sense, the reading is: “from which an occasion for suspicion arose,” followed by “to add.” In Vatican A and B: “a doubt has arisen; to the faith [incomplete reading].” In C and D: “an occasion for superstition has arisen to add to the faith.” In the Royal manuscript, “superstition” is absent.

Since you have learned our orthodoxy from my explicit tradition [Note: The word “tradition” is absent from Vatican C, Norman, Regius, and Corbie manuscripts.] or profession, it is fitting that you should no longer entertain any scruple of doubt concerning the Church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Rather, persist in the true faith and establish your life upon the rock of the Church—that is, upon the confession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles—lest all your tears and so many good works perish [Note: Not because they were disputing about the faith, but because obstinacy in schism is akin to heresy and scarcely fails to involve it, since it leads one away from the Church, which is the pillar and foundation of the truth.] if they are found to be alien to the true faith. For just as branches wither without the strength of the root, so works, however good they may appear, are nothing if they are separated from the stability of faith.

It is therefore fitting that Your Glory should, with all speed, send word to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Constantius, whose faith and life I formerly approved, and inform him by letters that you receive his ordination kindly. Since you are in no respect separated from communion with his Church, we may truly rejoice together, as over a good and faithful daughter. Know, moreover, that you and your works please God in this respect: if, before his examination takes place, they are approved by the judgment of his priests. (See above, Letter 4.)

## LETTER XXXIX. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He should not swear to the citizens of Brescia that he has by no means condemned the Three Chapters; instead, in a letter he should profess the complete faith of the Council of Chalcedon. He should not name John of Ravenna during the solemn celebration of the Mass unless ancient custom requires it, or unless John himself is accustomed to name him. In writing again to Theodelinda, he no longer mentions the Fifth Synod, which nevertheless established nothing contrary to the preceding four. He should restrain Fortunatus. He should not remove Ursicinus from the condition of his status.

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

Having read through the letters of Your Holiness, we learned that you are in deep sorrow, especially on account of the bishops [Note: LETTER XXXIX [formerly 37].—This is how we read it in the Norman, Vatican, Regius, and other manuscripts. The printed editions have “on account of the bishop.”] and citizens [Note: Commonly Brescia; in Gaul, Bresse. It remains a city with a bishop, under the archbishop of Gussano.] of Brescia, who are ordering you to send them a letter in which you must swear that you have by no means condemned the Three Chapters. If your predecessor Laurence did not do this, it ought not to be demanded of you. But if he did, he was not in communion with the universal Church and transgressed the oaths of his pledge. Since, however, we believe that the same man kept his sworn commitments and remained in the unity of the Catholic Church, there is no doubt that he swore to none of his bishops that he had by no means condemned the Three Chapters.

From this Your Holiness may conclude that you ought not to be compelled to do something that your predecessor did in no way do. Yet, so that those who wrote these things to you may not seem to be scandalized, send them a letter in which you declare, under threat of anathema, that you neither diminish anything from the faith of the Council of Chalcedon nor accept those who diminish it; that you condemn everyone whom it condemned and absolve everyone whom it absolved. I believe that they can be satisfied very quickly in this way.

As for what you wrote—that many of them are scandalized because you name our brother and fellow bishop John of the Church of Ravenna during the solemn celebration of the Mass—you must inquire whether this was an ancient custom; and, if it was customary, it should not now be criticized by foolish men. But if it was not customary, you should not do something that might cause scandal to some.

Nevertheless, I diligently tried to ascertain whether that same John, our brother and fellow bishop, names you at the altar; they emphatically say that this does not happen. If he does not mention your name, I do not know what necessity compels you to mention his. Yet, if this can be done without scandal to anyone, it is highly praiseworthy for you to do so, because you show the charity that you have toward your brothers.

[Note: This recitation of names during the solemn celebration of the Mass frequently occurs in ancient documents. The names were written on tablets, or diptychs, about which disputes were sometimes raised. One tablet was for the living, the other for the dead, and by this practice they testified to their mutual communion. The Greek word δίπτυχο̋, “folded in two,” derives from πτύχη, “a fold”; hence, double tablets. Balsamon, in canon 1 of the First and Second Councils of Constantinople, calls this recitation ἀναφορὰ τοῦ ὀνόματο̋ τοῦ ἐπισκόπου, “the offering or recitation of the bishop’s name.” It was not, however, only the bishop’s name that was customarily recited at the altar; the letters of Leo to Anatolius, Letter 40, chapter 3, and Letter 46, chapter 2, show that the names of outsiders were also recited. Saint Gregory suggests the same in these words: “If that same John, our brother and fellow bishop, names you at the altar.” Gussanus. Menardus discusses the diptychs at greater length both in his notes on the Concordia Regularum, chapter 4, section 4, and in notes 69 and 70 on the Sacramentary; see also Cardinal Bona, On Liturgical Matters, book II, chapter 12.]

As for what you wrote—that you were unwilling to send my letter to Queen Theodelinda because the Fifth Synod was mentioned in it—if you thought that she might thereby be scandalized, you acted rightly by not sending it. Therefore, we now act as you wished, so that we may praise only the four synods. Nevertheless, I want you to know concerning that synod which was subsequently held at Constantinople and which many call the Fifth, that it established or held nothing contrary to the four most holy synods. For in it matters were dealt with concerning persons alone, not concerning the faith, [Note: At the Council of Chalcedon, Theodore of Cyrus and Ibas were judged expressly in acts 8, 9, and 10. Thus Saint Gregory appears either not to have paid sufficient attention or to have intended something else. That he was speaking only of Theodore of Mopsuestia is indicated by Letter 36, now 51, book II, indiction 10. As for his statement about the canons, it either proves that the holy man suffered some human lapse, that the canons are not being referred to in their proper place—act 15—or that by “canons” the decree of faith itself is to be understood. The Greeks called definitions concerning the faith διατυπώσεις, “formulations,” but those concerning discipline ὅροι, “rules.” See Gelasius of Cyzicus, On the Council of Nicaea, part II. Gussanus.] and those persons were not mentioned at the Council of Chalcedon. Rather, after the canons had been explicitly stated, a dispute arose and a final proceeding was conducted concerning persons. Nevertheless, we acted as you wished and made no mention at all of that synod.

We have also written to the aforesaid daughter of ours, the queen, concerning the bishops, as you requested. You should restrain Ursicinus, who wrote certain things to you against our brother and fellow bishop John, from his purpose by your letters, through both kindness and reason. We want Your Fraternity to be concerned about Fortunatus, lest evil men in some way steal him away from you. For I hear that he ate at the Church’s table with your predecessor Laurence for many years, even until now; that he sat among nobles; and that he served in the ranks [Note: I judge this to be the reading on the basis of the Venetian edition of 1504, although the manuscripts and printed books contradict it, reading “served for countless years.” The error apparently arose from the ignorance of copyists who perhaps did not recognize that numerus could mean a military unit, that is, a cohort, and so forth. In French: bande, troupe, compagnie. We have discussed this word further in chapter 35 of book IV of the Dialogues. Gussanus. Yet Gussanus himself followed those supposedly ignorant copyists: here he reads “served for countless years,” and in book IV, chapter 35, of the Dialogues, where all the manuscripts read “who was an optio in the numerus,” he corrupted the reading into “who was otherwise called an optio.” How carelessly, then, does he say that the manuscripts contradict this reading, “served in the ranks”? It is certainly read this way in seven Norman manuscripts, two Regius manuscripts, and most others; the alternative reading, “served for countless years,” is utterly absurd.] with the knowledge of our brother.

After so many years, it now seems to Your Fraternity that he should be removed from the condition of his status. This seems to me wholly inappropriate. I therefore conveyed this instruction to you through him, but privately. Nevertheless, if there is anything reasonable that can be brought against him, it ought to be examined in our judgment. As for our son, Lord Dynamius, if it pleases almighty God, we shall send him a letter through your agent.

## LETTER XL. TO MARCELLUS THE SCHOLASTICUS

Concerning Maximus, who seeks pardon, he indicates amicably that the uprightness of discipline does not permit it.

Gregory to Marcellus [Note: LETTER XL [formerly 38].—Scholasticus sometimes means a learned, wise, or eloquent man; sometimes an advocate or legal patron. We think it should be interpreted in the latter sense when it follows a name, as in the headings of letters of this kind, and when it is appended as a title of rank. From this one may infer the esteem in which advocates were then held: the supreme pontiff, when writing to them, gives them the designation and title “Your Glory,” just as he does to prefects, patricians, exarchs, and even kings.] the scholasticus.

The charity of Your Glory is always so vigilant in our heart that no bodily absence can keep it away. For although you are far from our bodily eyes, you are never absent from the sight of our mind. Indeed, our desire frequently urges us eagerly to write to you, but our occupation does not permit it. Since, therefore, the knowledge of Your Nobility does not fail to recognize how many occupations entangle our position, let it consider that whenever we cease from the duty of writing, this is due not to our will but to necessity.

Yet we do not see what excuse Your Glory can offer for seeking us in your letter later than usual. In this matter I ought to have defended myself by silence alone, but the fervor of charity did not allow my tongue to remain silent. Therefore, greeting you with every affection and tenderness, we inform you that we are deeply saddened because you have wished to ask from us things which, while we seem to be fulfilling your will, we cannot do because reason stands in the way; and thus, against our desire, we appear to distress you. Ecclesiastical discipline in no way permits us to leave this matter without correction; nor is it fitting for you to make such requests, lest you seem—God forbid—to consent not to uprightness but to indiscipline.

As for the case of that same Maximus, about whom you write to us, whom we have already deprived of communion in the sacred body if he should presume to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass: when the proper time comes, it will be judged and settled after mature deliberation, as may please our God. We pray almighty God both to preserve you here through his favor [Note: The printed editions read “through his protection.”] and to lead you to the rewards of eternal life. [Note: These words are absent from the Norman manuscripts and many others. They are found in the Colbert and Vatican manuscripts.]

In the month of August, indiction 12. (See above, Letter 10.)

## LETTER XLI. TO THE CLERGY, ORDER, AND PEOPLE OF ORTONA

He appoints Barbarus as visitor. Above all, he warns them not to elect a layman as bishop.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at Ortona [Note: LETTER XLI [formerly 39].—Commonly Ortona, formerly a city of Samnium on the Adriatic coast, twelve miles east of Teate. It is now in Further Abruzzo, in the kingdom of Naples, and remains an episcopal city under the archbishop of Teate. Gussanus. In the Rheims manuscript and one Vatican manuscript it reads “Cotrona.”].

Having learned of the death of your bishop [Note: He was called Blandus, according to Letter 33 of book I, if the three Vatican manuscripts are to be trusted; for instead of Hortensis they read Hortonensis, as we observed at the end of note c on that same letter.], we took care to appoint our brother and fellow bishop Barbarus [Note: He was bishop of Beneventum, an industrious man and highly approved by Saint Gregory, to whom Gregory entrusted the visitation of the Church of Palermo even after Victor’s death, according to Letter 16 of book XI, now Letter 13 of book XIII. The same book mentions him in Letter 19, now 14. Ughellus nevertheless thinks, in volume VI of Sacred Italy, that this Barbarus—whom he also says was called Barbatus—was the third bishop of Teate, to whom Gregory entrusted the visitation of Ortona because his Church was nearer. Gussanus. In the Rheims manuscript “John” is read instead of “Barbarus.” The same is found in Vatican D. In another Vatican manuscript, the Tours manuscript, and the Regius manuscript, the bishop’s name is omitted. This letter is absent from our other manuscripts. It exists in the Colbert manuscript.] formally to visit the Church that has been left without a bishop.

We instructed him not to allow anyone to usurp anything concerning revenue, adornment, or ecclesiastical ministries [Note: The Rheims manuscript reads: “that he allow nothing concerning the advancement of clergy, revenue, and so forth.”], and you ought to obey him in his continual exhortations. Know this, however: we have given him permission, if necessary, to ordain priests and deacons—whomever he may find worthy of this office—so that a priest may be sought for ecclesiastical service who in no respect departs from the venerable canons and may be found worthy of so great a ministry [Note: All the Vatican and Regius manuscripts, as well as the Tours manuscript, read this way. The Rheims manuscript also agrees, except that it omits “and may be found worthy of so great a ministry.” The printed editions read: “so that . . . a priest who in no respect disagrees with the venerable canons, and so great a ministry . . . may be commonly chosen.”].

When he has been requested, let him come to us for ordination with the formality of a decree strengthened by the subscriptions of all, accompanied by the visitor’s letter. Above all, take care that you do not presume to elect a layman of any kind of life or merit. Know that not only will such a man in no way be advanced to the height of the episcopate [Note: The printed editions read “advanced.”], but you yourselves will be unable to obtain pardon through any intercession. You should know without doubt that all those among you who are found to have sought advancement from the lay state are to be excluded from office and communion.

## LETTER XLII. TO VALENTINUS, ABBOT

Monks must not bring women into the monastery or make them their spiritual co-mothers.

[Col. 0717B]

Gregory to Valentinus, abbot [Note: In the Colbert manuscript this letter is addressed to Venantius.].

It has come to our attention (Gratian, 18, question 21, canon 20) that women freely enter your monastery and, what is even more serious, that your monks make women their commatres, or spiritual co-mothers, and thereby maintain imprudent intercourse with them. Therefore, so that on this pretext the enemy of the human race may not deceive them by his cunning—God forbid—we admonish you by the terms of this command that henceforth you permit no women to enter your monastery on any pretext, and that you do not allow your monks to make them their commatres.

For if this should come to our ears again in any way, know that you will be subjected to such severe punishment that the others will undoubtedly be corrected by the nature of your amendment. [Col. 0717C] (See book II, Letter 25.)

## LETTER XLIII. TO BONIFACE, A MAGNIFICENT MAN

He should come to Rome to answer for his faith, no longer by letters but in person. Those who share his doubts may come safely, since Gregory will use reason, not power, toward them.

Gregory to Boniface, a magnificent man of Africa [Note: LETTER XLIII [formerly 41].—The printed editions omit “man”; the manuscripts do not.].

If Your Greatness were concerned about the life of your soul as earnestly as I had heard, you would by no means seek to answer me concerning your faith by letters, but in person. For although you bring forward bodily illness as an excuse, once the time of health had been awaited you could have undertaken the effort for the sake of the advantage of eternal salvation, so that you might rejoice in our reasoning and we in your belief [Note: The printed editions read “health” instead of “life,” and “was able” instead of “could ask.” All our Vatican, Norman, Regius, Corbie, Tours, Rheims, and Colbert manuscripts confirm the reading we present.].

There is no need now to repeat what I wrote in my letters, nor to demonstrate it by another line of reasoning, because, in a mind unwilling to accept it, even an evident argument commonly becomes an obstacle [Note: All the manuscripts read this more appropriately than the printed editions, which have “nor to demonstrate it by any reasoning.” This agrees with the holy Doctor’s intention, since he judged that Boniface should be convinced by reason. Yet he writes that another argument should not be added to the arguments he had already employed.]. But come in person, present yourself at the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and depart with whatever dispute you wish unless I demonstrate everything I have written from the text itself. Nevertheless, I exhort you: while time for life remains, let your soul not be found divided from the Church of that same blessed Peter, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted and the power of binding and loosing has been granted. Otherwise, if his benefit is despised here, he may close the entrance to life there.

[Col. 0718B]

Those who share your doubts, if they wish to come to me, should fear no violence from me as though proceeding from authority. For although we act in this way in every case, in matters especially that belong to God we hasten to constrain people by reason rather than by power.

## LETTER XLIV. TO MAXIMIANUS, BISHOP

He should send back to Bacauda the men from Bacauda’s clergy who have been promoted to sacred orders in Sicily and whom Bacauda is reclaiming.

Gregory to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse.

Our brother and fellow bishop Bacauda has informed us that certain men from his clergy have attained sacred orders in the regions of Sicily. Since he states that he has neither a priest nor deacons [Note: LETTER XLIV [formerly 42].—He says that his clerics were ordained in the regions of Sicily, probably, as I think, after being driven from his own diocese by war. I suspect that they were promoted without letters of dismissal, as though they were natives or belonged to him by reason of domicile; the law of the canons recalls them in the Council of Nicaea, canons 15 and 16. Gussanus.], he has requested that they be sent back to him.

Therefore, wherever your Fraternity finds them, as the bearer of this letter indicates, send them here without delay, so that they may be recalled to the Church in which they formerly served and so that the aforesaid bishop may obtain from them the assistance he desires.

## LETTER XLV. TO FANTINUS, DEFENSOR

He sends sixty solidi to be paid on Cosmas’s behalf.

Gregory to Fantinus, defensor.

The bearer of this letter, Cosmas the Syrian, stated that he had contracted a debt in the business he was conducting, and we believed it to be true, as many others and his own tears attest. Since he owed 150 solidi, I wanted his creditors to reach some agreement with him, since the law provides that a free man may in no way be held for a debt if there are no assets that can be applied to that debt. [Note: Novel 134, chapter 7, where the son of a debtor is concerned. Because we have learned that such injustice is committed in various places in our commonwealth—that creditors presume to retain debtors’ sons, whether as a pledge, for servile service, or for hire—we prohibit it in every way and order that anyone committing anything of the kind shall not only forfeit the debt but also add an equal additional amount, to be given to the person detained by him or to that person’s parents. After this, the local judge shall also subject him to corporal penalties, because he presumed to retain, hire out, or pawn a free person for debt. I have copied out the entire law because it contains many noteworthy matters. Gussanus.]

Accordingly, as he asserts, it may be possible for his creditors to agree to eighty solidi. But since it is excessive to demand eighty solidi from a man who possesses nothing, we have sent you sixty solidi through your notary, so that you may speak carefully with those same creditors and explain that, according to the laws, they cannot hold his son, whom they are said to be detaining. If it can be done, persuade them to accept something less than the amount we have given.

Whatever remains of those sixty solidi, hand over to him, so that he may be able to live from it with his son. But if nothing remains, or if his debt can be reduced to that same sum, strive to arrange it, so that he may afterward work freely for himself.

Act diligently, however, so that once they have received the solidi, they provide him in writing with a full release [Note: In French, “a complete discharge.” Jurists often call the instrument establishing release a muniment, because it makes and keeps a person secure against the attack of any litigant.]. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, no. 55.)

## LETTER XLVI. TO RUSTICIANA, A PATRICIAN

He reproves her for returning too quickly from Mount Sinai.

Gregory to Rusticiana, a patrician.

Receiving the letters of Your Excellence, I gladly learned how you had traveled to Mount Sinai. But believe me: I too would have wished to go with you, but not to return with you. Although it is very difficult for me to believe that you visited holy places and saw many Fathers [Note: That is, the monks of the monastery of Mount Sinai. Saint Gregory’s second letter of book XI is addressed to Palladius of this monastery, either its abbot or a monk, to whom Gregory sends a hood and tunic. Notice here that monks are honored with the title and designation “Fathers,” a usage accepted among both Greek and Latin writers. The Greeks called their accounts of them the Lives of the Fathers and their sayings the Apophthegmata of the Fathers; in collections made by Cotelerius one often reads: “One of the Fathers related.” The title “abbot” likewise came to be applied to all, or at least the more distinguished, monks in the Eastern Church. Among the Latins, Venantius Fortunatus provides the following testimony in his Life of Saint Martin:

> There he founded a monastery beneath a lofty cliff,  
> a monk distinguished by the honor of the episcopate.  
> Many holy companies of Fathers gather there.

The designation “Fathers” should not be denied to religious men; Theophilus Raynaudus of the Society of Jesus wrote a special dissertation on this subject. Jerome proves the antiquity of the custom, although he condemns it: “I do not know,” he says in chapter 4 of his commentary on Galatians, “by what license in monasteries we either call others by this name of father or consent to be called so ourselves.”].

For, I suppose, if you had seen them, you would not have been able to return so quickly to the city of Constantinople. But since love for such a city has in no way departed from your heart, I suspect that Your Excellence has paid no attention in your heart to the holy things you saw bodily.

May almighty God enlighten your mind by the grace of his mercy, grant you wisdom, and make you consider how fleeting all temporal things are. For while we are saying these things, time is running on, the Judge is coming, and the world—which we unwillingly refuse to leave—behold, is already near the point at which we shall leave it unwillingly.

Give my greetings to Lord Apion and Lady Eusebia, and to their daughters. As for that lady whom you commend to me in your letters as my nurse, I love her exceedingly and do not wish her to be burdened in anything. But we are pressed by such great difficulties that at this time we cannot even excuse ourselves from the angariae [Note: This word frequently occurs in these letters for exactions, public services, compulsory duties, and forced labor. Jurists use it for the provision of horses or transport for the public service, in French les postes, or for the conveyance of certain goods, such as arms. They also use the form parangariae. These are compulsory services, burdens, and forms of taxation. Budaeus notes the word as Persian; Suidas does likewise. When we are compelled to provide, pay, or do more than is lawful or than we owe, it is an angaria. In French, the labor that lords forcibly exact from their colonists, tenants, or peasants is called corvées. Why should we not derive angaria from angere, “to constrain”? Gregory also discusses angariae in Letter 68 of book I, now Letter 70. Gussanus.] and burdens.

## LETTER XLVII. TO SABINIANUS, DEACON

The pride of Maximus, who had caused Gregory’s writings to be publicly torn up, must be restrained. What should be answered to his accusation concerning the murdered Bishop Malchus. Romanus is to be reminded about two matters.

[Col. 0720B]

Gregory to Sabinianus, deacon [Note: LETTER XLVII [formerly 1, indiction 1].—In the Vatican manuscript: “To Sabinianus, deacon at Constantinople.” There he served as apocrisiarius, or representative, for Gregory’s province. This letter is found outside the order of the Register, at the end among the omitted letters, in many manuscripts, especially the Norman. It exists in the first collection of Paul the Deacon, where the index gives the heading: “To Sabinianus, deacon of Constantinople.”].

You have learned what was done in the case of Maximus the transgressor [Note: Concerning him, consult Letter 20 above, addressed to Maximus himself.]. But after the most serene lord emperor sent orders that he should by no means be ordained, he then broke out into even greater pride. For the retainers of the glorious man Romanus, the patrician, accepted gifts from him and had him ordained in such a way that they would have killed Antonius, the subdeacon and administrator of the patrimony, unless he had fled [Note: In Audoenus and several other manuscripts: “Thus they had Antonius ordained . . . and would have killed him unless he had fled.”].

After I learned that he had been ordained contrary to reason and custom, I sent letters instructing him not to presume to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass unless I first learned from the most serene lords what they had ordered concerning his person [Note: In Paul’s first collection, the first hand reads domnis, “lords”; the second reads dominis, “to the lords.” Hence it should be observed that those collected letters were first written by a rather unlearned cleric and afterward corrected and emended by Paul’s hand, at least through number 34.]. He had my letter publicly read out, or posted in the city, and publicly caused it to be torn up; then he rose openly in contempt of the apostolic see [Note: In the same collection, “he rose openly.”]. You know how I endure this, for I am sooner prepared to die than to allow the Church of the blessed apostle Peter to degenerate in my days. You know my character well, since I have tolerated him for a long time; but if I once decide not to tolerate him, I will go gladly against every danger. Therefore, with God’s help, it is necessary to meet the danger, lest he be driven by excess to sin. Consider what I say and weigh from what great sorrow it proceeds [Note: In Vatican A: “Therefore weigh what I say, and from how great a sorrow.”].

It has come to me, moreover, that he sent some cleric who said that Bishop Malchus had been killed in custody for the sake of money. On this matter, briefly suggest one thing to our most serene lords: if I, their servant, had wished to involve myself in the death of the Lombards, the Lombard nation would today have neither a king, nor dukes, nor counts, but would be divided in utter confusion. But because I fear God, I shrink from involving myself in the death of any man.

Bishop Malchus, however, was neither in custody nor under any form of affliction. On the day when he pleaded his case, he was, without my knowledge, taken by the notary Boniface to Boniface’s house, where a meal was prepared for him; he ate there and was honored by Boniface, and suddenly died during the night. I think your affection has already learned this [Note: The manuscripts disagree here. Audoenus and Norman read: “But Malchus was not even in custody.” Vatican A and D support this. Paul’s collection reads: “But now he was not even in custody.”]. I wished to send our man Exhilaratus because of this matter, but since I thought that the case had already been dealt with, I restrained myself.

Your Affection should tell Lord Romanus that, concerning Felix, as he wrote to the most excellent man [Note: His dignity was the highest among the patricians. See Theodoret, book V of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 27; Cedrenus, Codinus, Zonaras, and Evagrius. In later centuries there were several such officials, up to twenty-four. Their chief, as I infer, was the master of offices. The Sixth Council of Constantinople, act 2, calls him μαγίστρη̋ τῶν βασιλικῶν ὀφφικίων, “master of the imperial offices,” or master of the palace offices. Chalcedon, act 1, calls him μαγίστρη̋ τῶν θείων ὀφφικίων, “master of the divine,” that is, court, offices. The word is also found in Saint Athanasius, in the Apology to the Emperor Constantius, and in Saint Basil, Letter 84, and elsewhere. The forms μαγίστηρ and μαγιστριανό̋ also occur. The dignity of master was called μαγιστερία, “mastership.” In Simocatta, book III, chapter 15: “Theodore, honored with the office of mastership.” King Childebert of the Franks, in a letter to the same Theodore, writes: “of your distinguished mastership.” Gussanus. The formula “of the dignity of master” is found in Cassiodorus, book VI of the Variae, section 6.] the master, I will, God willing, prepare letters and send them through my agent. For now, since I am writing to no one else, it was difficult for me to write to the master alone. He must also be told that the palace official Catellus is, according to what Virigantinus says, recklessly wasting his property. I could scarcely persuade Catellus that he ought to give that same Virigantinus a small portion of his mother’s property for expenses at the monastery where Virigantinus devotes himself to reading and is unable to work.

# BOOK FIVE

In the thirteenth indiction, the fifth year of his ordination.

## LETTER I. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

Clergy serving churches must not be placed over monasteries.

[Col. 0721C]

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna, and others.

It has come to me (Gratian, 18, question 1, canon 26) that in some places belonging to Your Fraternity, once consecrated to monasteries, there are now dwellings of clerics or even laymen. While those who are in the churches pretend to live religiously, they seek to be placed over monasteries, and through their way of life the monasteries are destroyed.

No one [Note: It is certainly not entirely appropriate to combine monastic quiet with pastoral care of laypeople. Hence Gregory, who had become pope from a monastic life, lamented the beauty of the contemplative life in book I, Letter 5. Nevertheless, Siricius desired and intended that monks be attached to clerical offices.
