Gelasius established that they should be promoted through shorter intervals between orders, as being more suited to the clergy by reason of their monastic life: “For,” he says in Letter 9, chapters 2 and 3, “it is fitting that there be a distinction between a person devoted to divine worship and one coming from the way of life of the laity.” Gregory holds that, in order to be suited to the episcopate, a devout man should first become a subdeacon or a monk, as below in book XII, Letter 12: “He should be encouraged,” and so forth. From this it is clear, says Thomassinus, part I, book III, chapter 14, that monastic life was regarded as taking the place of the minor orders and even of the subdiaconate, or at least that the labors of monastic life were regarded as the intervals between orders. See the decree of Boniface IV in Gratian, 16, question 2, canon 25; Innocent III, On the Status of Monks, title 35, chapter 5; and Holstenius, Roman Collection, p. 253.] can both serve ecclesiastical duties [Note: Gratian reads “ecclesiastical offices.”] and remain orderly under the monastic rule, so that the one who is compelled to remain daily in an ecclesiastical monastery may himself maintain discipline in that monastery [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read “in ecclesiastical service.”].

Therefore, wherever this has been done, let Your Fraternity hasten to correct it, for I will in no way tolerate sacred places being destroyed through the ambition of clerics. Act accordingly, so that you may quickly report to me that this matter has been corrected. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, no. 54.)

## LETTER II. TO FELIX, BISHOP, AND CYRIACUS, ABBOT

The servants of God founded by Theodosia are to be introduced into the monastery.

[Col. 0723A]

Gregory to Felix, bishop, and Cyriacus, abbot.

The complaint of Theodosia, a religious woman subject to you, is sufficiently explained in the sequence of the report. In it we have reread several charges, many of which do not pertain to priestly gentleness, brought against Januarius, our brother and fellow bishop, so that, after she had founded a monastery of servants of God, [Note: [Col. 0723C] Concerning this monastery of Theodosia, see above, Book IV, Letter 15.] [Note: [Col. 0723C] It is cited at 18, question 2, chapter 26, where Gratian proves that certain monasteries were exempted because of bishops’ avarice: neglecting the salvation of souls, they stripped monasteries of their possessions. See Book VI, Letters 29 and 43, and Book VIII, Letter 15. Here we have altered the received reading, “to the disturbance of avarice,” at the urging—indeed, the compulsion—of the manuscripts.] everything relating to avarice, disturbance, and injury [Note: [Col. 0723D] Three Vatican manuscripts read: “what was presented at the time of the dedication of the oratory itself.”] was said to have been presented at the time of the dedication of the oratory itself. Therefore, if matters are as we learned from her report before her death, and if you recognize that anything improper was committed in this matter, we urge you, after first removing every prejudice, to take care that Musicus, abbot of the Agilitan monastery, hasten to devote himself entirely to the monks whom he had begun to ordain there, so that, with that venerable place arranged by you, with the Lord’s help, in a proper and orderly manner, [Note: [Col. 0723D] The Rheims manuscript reads, “in a decent and venerable manner.”] neither the frequent complaint of the aforementioned religious woman concerning her unfulfilled good wishes may disturb us, nor may it be to the detriment of your soul if so pious a purpose should languish through some delay caused by your negligence—which we do not believe possible.

## LETTER III. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP

Presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons who have stained themselves with the crime of sexual immorality are to remain permanently deposed from their rank. After completing penance, they are to receive communion among the laity. He permits Saturninus, a former presbyter, to assume responsibility for certain monasteries. He sends a garment for a woman to be baptized, and a copy of the *Pastoral Rule* to the presbyter Columbus.

[Col. 0723C]

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

The rereading of the text of the letter sent by your Fraternity made your concern clearly known to us, but learning of your bodily illness saddened us. Nevertheless, the Lord’s scourges must be patiently endured, [Col. 0724A] for illness is frequently granted for correction. Before God, he considers a person purified when what presently causes him sorrow in this life does so. Therefore, even while placed in illness, we must give thanks to our Creator and pray that this chastisement may profit us in the life to come.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] LETTER III [elsewhere 16].—Gratian combined one chapter from Letters 5 and 16, now 6 and 15, in Distinction 50, chapter 10. There the reader will observe that Saint Gregory is always consistent when dealing with ministers of the Church who have fallen. Nevertheless, after penance he permits an abbot to retain the first place among the monks. The same occurs in Letter 17, now 4. GUSSANVILLE.]

Moreover, replying to the questions of your Fraternity, we decree that the deacon and abbot of Portovenere, [Note: [Col. 0723D] Portovenere, commonly called Porto Venere, was formerly an episcopal city in Liguria, on the Gulf of Luni, opposite the city of Luna; it is now a small town with a fortress. GUSSANVILLE.] whom you report to have fallen, should neither be permitted nor able in any way to return to the sacred order. You should assign him, deprived of the sacred order, to penance. If afterward his conduct and manner of life should merit it, let him hold the first place among the other monks, wherever you shall determine. [Col. 0724B] Likewise, subdeacons whom a similar fault binds are irrevocably deposed from their office and are to receive communion among the laity. In place of the fallen deacon at Portovenere, you shall ordain another who is to fulfill this office.

As for Saturninus, the former presbyter, [Note: [Col. 0723D] Some manuscripts read, not improperly, “the former presbyter,” as in the Norman manuscript and the old edition. In most manuscripts the name is written Saturus, or Saturnus.] we have decreed that he must provide a written guarantee that he will never presume to approach the ministry of the sacred order. But we permit him to exercise responsibility for the monasteries on the islands of Gorgona and Capraria, [Note: [Col. 0723D] Commonly called Capraia, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea between Tuscany [Col. 0724D] and Corsica. GUSSANVILLE. Concerning Gorgona, see Book I, Letter 52.] and to remain in the condition in which he now is, without anyone’s opposition. [Note: [Col. 0724C] See below, Letter 6. We noted above that a presbyter who has fallen, although he cannot be recalled to the sacred ministry, may nevertheless exercise oversight of monasteries, GUSSANVILLE, if he had held the office of abbot before his fall.]

Let your Fraternity therefore guard those entrusted to you with vigilant care and, as far as you are able, rebuke them for evil deeds by your preaching, so that you may be found to fulfill the purpose of your office as is fitting, and may make God the rewarder of your action. We earnestly desire to see you and to rejoice in God at your presence and salvation. [Note: [Col. 0724C] In Book III, Letter 21, he discusses with the bishop of Luna the baptism of Jews; here he sends a garment for a woman to be baptized. [Col. 0724D] In Letter 6 of Pope Paul to King Pepin: “The distinguished envoy of your fellowship brought us the most precious gift of heavenly grace, namely a *sabanum*, in which our sweetest and most beloved spiritual daughter, washed in the most sacred laver and received. We received it with great joy amid an assembled crowd inside the hall of the sacred body of your helper, blessed Petronilla … while celebrating the solemnities of the Mass with great rejoicing, and through the same *sabanum* brought to us, etc.” The memory of these baptismal garments and *sabana*, whose use was to receive those baptized from the sacred font and dry them, survives in the books, though scarcely anything remains in the rites. Innumerable authors testify concerning the garments, among them Saint Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 7. Concerning *sabana*, Victor of Utica, *On the Persecution of the Vandals*, Book III, where he discusses Muritta and Elpidophorus. See our notes on Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 17, and Book IV, chapter 55.]

We have sent a garment for the woman who is to be baptized, and we always desire that you write such things to us. We have sent the copy of the *Pastoral Rule* to the presbyter Columbus through the bearer of this letter; do not detain him. We shall quickly send another copy for your use.

## LETTER IV. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He decrees concerning the fallen what he decreed in the preceding letter. He writes to Constantius that, while punishing John, he must beware of anger. He takes measures to protect Constantius’s reputation. The case of Fortunatus is to be concluded at Rome.

[Col. 0725A]

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

If permission is granted to the fallen to return to their own order, the force of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since no one would fear entertaining desires for wrongful action when he hopes to return. (Gratian, Distinction 50, chapter 1.) Your Fraternity has consulted us whether Amandinus, a former presbyter and abbot, who was deposed by his predecessor because of his fault, should be restored to the order in which he had been placed. We decree that this is neither permitted nor possible by any means. [Col. 0725B] Nevertheless, if his conduct should perhaps merit it, although deprived in every respect of the sacred office, arrange him in the monastery before the other monks, as you shall judge appropriate. Above all, therefore, take care that no supplication persuade you in any way to restore the fallen to the sacred order, lest their punishment be thought not imposed but merely postponed for a time.

As for Vitalianus, the former presbyter, [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Norman manuscript and most others read “former presbyter”; likewise below, where Saint Gregory treats of Saturninus, Saturnus, or Saturus—for these are the forms read in most manuscripts. The Regius manuscript reads “former presbyter and abbot.”] concerning whom you write that he must be held under strict custody, we shall send him to Sicily so that, deprived of hope of departure, he may at least then bind himself to the lamentations of penance. We have also decreed that Jobinus, formerly deacon and abbot of Portovenere, be deprived of his office, and we have written that another should be ordained in his place. Likewise, we decree that the three subdeacons whom your Fraternity has reported to have fallen are permanently to be deprived of their office, [Col. 0725C] and that they are to receive nothing except sacred communion among the laity. We have required Saturninus, the former presbyter, to provide a guarantee that he will never presume to approach the ministry of the sacred order. [Note: [Col. 0725D] The recent edition reads incorrectly, “to make him more cautious.”] We wish him to remain on the same island on which he had been, deprived of the sacred order, while permitting him to have and exercise responsibility and oversight of monasteries. We believe that, made more cautious by his fall, he will now guard those entrusted to him more carefully.

Concerning John, the notary of your Church, the charity with which we love you and have long loved you moved us to write that, while his fault provokes you, you should not command anything to be done that pertains to sin. Taking care of this, therefore, investigate the affairs of your Church carefully, [Col. 0725D] by whatever means you can, so that you may neither offend God nor allow him to find anything by which he can accuse you before men. For we wrote not to defend John or commend his person contrary to reason, but lest your soul, more seriously burdened by the stimulus of anger, should be implicated in anything. Therefore, as we have said, you must not neglect to investigate the affairs of your Church with careful inquiry and fear of God.

Your letter also caused us great astonishment concerning the person of Fortunatus and your most beloved Fraternity. But either the letter itself was not written by you, [Note: [Col. 0725D] Three Vatican manuscripts and three Norman manuscripts read, “these things were said.”] or, if it is indeed yours, we do not at all recognize in it our brother, Lord Constantius. You ought, and still ought, to bear in mind that we write for the sake of your reputation. For when the aforementioned Fortunatus states that he suffered violence there and was unable to find the assistance [Note: [Col. 0725D] This is to be read from the manuscripts Regius, Norman, and Vatican, where the printed editions have “to be fortified by help.”] of a defender, what does this affect except your reputation? Therefore, lest this matter obscure your reputation in the eyes of some people, or cause any harm to your Church if his case is just, you ought to send here a representative instructed in the matter, so that, after the merits of the case have been weighed, it may be concluded without prejudice to you. For especially after his complaint, if judgment should be pronounced there in favor of your side, he will be thought to have been overcome not by reason but by power alone.

For the charity by which we are bound to you, we do not cease to admonish you concerning what you ought to do for the sake of your reputation. We know that, although this exhortation may sadden you for a time, afterward, when the intensity of contention has been set aside, it will make you rejoice. [Note: [Col. 0725D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “in December, indiction 13.” We have judged the readings of Colbert and Tours Saint-Gatien preferable.]

In the month of September, indiction 13.

## LETTER V. TO DOMINICUS, BISHOP

He congratulates him for having endeavored, with pastoral zeal, to restrain the Donatists; nevertheless, he does not approve the harsher judgment of the African council against bishops who neglected this duty.

[Col. 0726C]

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage. [Note: [Col. 0726D] LETTER V [elsewhere 3].—“Of Carthage” is absent from the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

Prosper, the bearer of this letter and your representative, came to us. After other expressions of your affection, [Possibly *affatus*, “addresses”; nevertheless, *affectus* is read in all our manuscripts.] he presented to us a second letter from you, together with the record of the synod held among you, accompanied by the presentation of the imperial commands. [Note: [Col. 0726D] Sacred imperial letters, sacred documents, divine commands. See Book I, Letter 47, now 49. GUSSANVILLE.] Having reread these, we rejoiced both in the zeal with which you exercise your pastoral office and in the fact that, on the occasion of religion, you removed the calumnies brought against the most pious rulers by persons seeking profit. We rejoiced especially because your Fraternity took such care to preserve the African province that you did not neglect, with priestly fervor, to restrain the deviant sects of heretics. [Col. 0726D] Concerning the suppression of all these matters, even before we were consulted by the documents of your charity, we remember having defined the matter with such precision that [Col. 0727A] we do not think it necessary to reply to you again about it.

Although these things are so, and although we desire all heretics always to be restrained by Catholic priests with vigor and reason, nevertheless, looking carefully at the matter, we were greatly concerned lest what was done among you should produce scandal, God forbid, among the leaders of other councils. [Note: [Col. 0727C] The canons of the African Council had long urged bishops to take care concerning heretics, but with lighter penalties. Council of Milevis II, chapters 24 and 25.] For a sentence was issued by you at the conclusion of the official proceedings. While exhorting the investigation of those heretics, you added that those who neglected this duty were to be punished by deprivation of property and rank.

It is therefore best, dearest brother, that in matters requiring correction outside, internal charity should first be preserved, [Note: [Col. 0727C] This expresses the meaning of Saint Paul in Philippians 2:2–3: “Having the same charity, united in mind, thinking the same thing, doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but in humility considering one another superior.” Saint Augustine explains this passage in his customary manner in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 71; the reader should consult that passage and add another from the same Augustine, Letter 59 to Paulinus, in the solution of question 7, concerning humble Thelo. Saint Gregory pursues the same point at greater length in *Homily 10 on Ezekiel*, near the middle, and also in *Homily 7 on the Gospel*: “On the way of God, regard as your superiors—especially those not entrusted to you—your neighbors; for you do not know what good lies hidden in those whom you see doing some wrong,” etc. GUSSANVILLE.] and that we should be humble in spirit—which we judge especially characteristic of your dignity—[Col. 0727B] even toward persons inferior in rank. Then you will oppose the errors of heretics with united strength more effectively, when, in accordance with the custom of your priestly office, you take care inwardly to preserve ecclesiastical harmony.

## LETTER VI. TO VICTOR, BISHOP

He is to restore Gregory the abbot, afflicted by lengthy penance because of negligence. He is to recall Martia, a nun. Victoria is to be handed over to Fantinus for careful examination. Anastasius the physician is henceforth not to enter the monastery of virgins.

Gregory to Victor, bishop of Palermo. [Note: [Col. 0727D] LETTER VI [elsewhere 4].—“Of Palermo” is absent from the Norman manuscript and many others.]

The bearer of this letter, Gregory, abbot and presbyter of the monastery of Saint Theodore, could in no way have been permitted, after his fall, to preside any longer over that monastery’s almost universal administration. [Note: [Col. 0727D] At this point Gussanville observes that the word “cell” is lacking in the Lyre, Pratelles, and Teller manuscripts. Certainly, as regards the Lyre and Pratelles manuscripts, they agree with the Audoenus and other Norman manuscripts, in which “cell” is read; indeed it occurs in six English manuscripts and in most others. It is nevertheless absent from Vatican D. That “cell” is here used for “monastery” is evident. So too it is frequently used in the Dialogues, especially in Books I and II.] [Col. 0727C] For one who through his negligence led so many disciples to hell ought never to have been placed over the rest. But because he has here among us been afflicted by lengthy penance, your Fraternity must receive him into the aforementioned monastery and restore him to his place, yet in such a way that Urbicus, the superior of my monastery, must appoint one of the servants of God to become his superior, so that what is neglected through this man’s carelessness may be preserved through the other’s vigilance. [Note: [Col. 0728C] This was formerly the name among monks for the man who stood second to the abbot. See especially chapter 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2.]

I also hear that Martia, a nun from the monastery of the handmaids of God which is [Note: [Col. 0728C] In Saint Gregory’s time there were several monasteries of nuns in Sicily. Among them was the one that, according to an old tradition, had been founded by Saint Gregory and later given to the Cassinese monks. It is now called San Martino delle Scale. GUSSANVILLE.] Saint Martin’s, was unjustly transferred to another monastery; [Note: [Col. 0728D] That is, transferred; for *migrare* is sometimes used to mean “transfer.” Thus Gellius, Book II, chapter 29: “The cassita moved its nest.” GUSSANVILLE.] and that Victoria, who was next in line for her position, dispersed the monastery’s property, as I hear, so that she herself might attain the post of prioress and meanwhile be found next after the abbess. Your Fraternity must strive to correct this with all possible speed. [Note: [Col. 0728D] We restore this reading from the Corbie, Norman, and most of the better manuscripts. The printed editions read, “whose fault it may be.”] You understand whose fault it is that, although I am so far away, I recognize what is happening in your city and, occupied with so many concerns, arrange what ought to be done.

Therefore, we wish the aforementioned Martia to be recalled to her own monastery and her own place. Victoria is to be handed over to our defensor Fantinus, so that, after examining her, he may discover to whom she gave any of the monastery’s property. [Col. 0728B] After she has been examined, we wish her to be sent to another monastery, and that Fantinus the defensor report carefully to us, so that we may know what more definite sentence ought to be determined concerning her.

I hear that many evils have occurred in that same monastery through Anastasius the physician. [Note: [Col. 0728D] The printed editions have a corrupt and barbarous reading: “if either he himself or another should at any time enter the monastery of virgins.” This reading is rejected, and ours confirmed, by six English manuscripts, seven Norman manuscripts, the Vatican manuscripts, the Corbie manuscript, and others.] If he ever enters that monastery of virgins or another such monastery, let the fault fall upon your Fraternity, which holds the flock entrusted to it but neglects to guard it. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, no. 42.)

## LETTER VII. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP

If Saturninus, the former presbyter, has ministered after his fall, he is to be deprived of communion until the day of his death.

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

When your Fraternity reaches the island of Gorgona, investigate what has been reported to us concerning Saturninus, the former presbyter. (Gratian, Distinction 50, chapter 10.) For it has come to us that, after he had been deposed from the priestly order because of his fall through crime, [Note: [Col. 0728D] That a person who has fallen must never return to honor has been stated a hundred times. GUSSANVILLE.] he presumed to approach the ministry of the presbyterate [Note: [Col. 0728D] We restore “of the presbyterate” from the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, in place of “of the priesthood,” formerly read in the editions.] and to offer sacrifices to almighty God. If your Fraternity finds that this was done, deprive him of participation in the sacred body and blood of the Lord and reduce him to penance, [Col. 0729A] so that he may remain under the same excommunication until the day of his death, [Note: [Col. 0729B] Namely, in deprivation of participation in the sacred body and blood of the Lord; I do not think that communion in civil matters, or even in sacred prayers, was taken away. GUSSANVILLE.] and let him receive only the viaticum [Note: [Col. 0729B] Here this signifies Eucharistic communion. For a long time it has been customary to understand by the term “viaticum” only the Eucharist administered to those on the point of death. Among the ancients, however, “viaticum” meant everything that helped one depart safely from this life. Thus, for penitents, absolution; for catechumens, baptism; and for those departing from the body, viaticum was necessary. The Council of Nicaea, canon 12, forbids that they be deprived of it according to the rule of the ancient law. Thus communion, although now used almost exclusively for receiving the Eucharist, was formerly also the name for the absolution granted to penitents: reconciliation, peace, or communion, in Cyprian, Letter 52; the Council of Arles I, final canon; and Innocent I, Letter 3 to Exsuperius, bishop of Toulouse, chapter 2. Do not, with Gussanville, imagine that those who interpret “communion denied” as referring not to the sacred viaticum but to the reconciliation of penitents are making this a Novatian position; observe the very broad distinction. The error of the Novatians was that the Church could not forgive mortal sin, indeed that it perished by receiving sinners. Therefore they denied reconciliation even to the fallen who had completed full penance. But Innocent’s response to Exsuperius concerns only those who, after baptism, had devoted themselves continually to sexual incontinence and pleasures and, at the end of life, demanded both penance and reconciliation to communion. “Concerning these,” he says, “the earlier custom held that penance should be granted to them, but communion denied … lest the ease of granting communion should leave people secure concerning reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling.”] at the time of his departure. [Note: [Col. 0729D] The recent edition reads, “on the day of his departure,” contrary to the manuscripts, which agree with Gratian.]

But if your Fraternity learns that he is performing such penance that he may justly be shown mercy and admitted to receive communion among the laity before his departure, we leave this to the judgment of your Fraternity. [Note: [Col. 0729D] This is the reading of the Tours Saint-Gatien, Colbert, old, and Vatican manuscripts, while at least most of the other manuscripts are silent.]

In the month of October, indiction 13.

## LETTER VIII. TO CYPRIAN, DEACON

He is to persecute the Manichaeans. The burdens of taxes are to be reduced for Jews who have converted to Christ. He is to lend solidi to the peasants.

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon, [Note: [Col. 0730B] This phrase is absent from many manuscripts: “and administrator, etc.”] and administrator of the patrimony of Sicily.

[Col. 0729B] Concerning the Manichaeans who are on our estates, I have frequently admonished your Affection [Note: [Col. 0730C] Concerning these madmen, see Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, heresy 46, where he discusses the five elements—smoke, darkness, fire, water, and wind—and the two ships, the sun and moon, in which there are holy powers that transform themselves into males in order to seduce women of the opposing faction, etc. GUSSANVILLE.] that you must persecute them with the utmost diligence [Note: [Col. 0730C] Vatican A and some manuscripts read, “must strive with the greatest diligence.”] and bring them back to the Catholic faith. If circumstances require it, investigate the matter carefully yourself; but if other business prevents you, do so through others.

It has come to my attention that there are Jews on our estates who are entirely unwilling to convert to God. It seems to me, therefore, that you should send letters throughout all the estates where Jews are known to be present, promising them expressly on my behalf that whoever among them converts to the true Lord our God, Jesus Christ, [Col. 0730A] will have the burden of his estate reduced to some extent. [Note: [Col. 0730C] The recent edition reads “the burden of the tax,” contrary to all the Vatican, Tours, Norman, and other manuscripts. Concerning this method of attracting Jews or pagans to the faith, we have already spoken above, Book III, Letter 26, now Book IV. Some might call this persuasion “Thessalian persuasive compulsion” (*κειθανάγκην*), as Cicero says in his letter to Atticus. See Book II, Letter 32. Partly from GUSSANVILLE.]

I also wish this to be done in such a way that, if one of them converts, and owes a tax of one solidus, a tremissis (one-third of a solidus) should be remitted to him; if he owes three or four, one solidus should be remitted. If he owes more, the remission should be made according to the same proportion, or certainly according to what your Affection judges appropriate, so that the burden of the convert may be lightened without placing the Church’s interests under an excessive loss. [Col. 0730B] Nor do we do this uselessly if, by relieving their tax burdens, we lead them to the grace of Christ, because, although they themselves come with less sincerity, those who are born from them are baptized with greater faithfulness. [Note: [Col. 0730C] Take care not to understand this as admitting Jews to baptism when the ministers know that they are coming with insufficient sincerity. This was never the Church’s position, although some examples to the contrary are produced, such as Synesius, whom his letter to Enopius, preserved in Nicephorus, Book XIV, chapter 55, seems to show to have doubted the resurrection of the flesh. See Saint Augustine’s entire book *On Faith and Works*, especially chapter 6: “People are not to be admitted to receive baptism in such a way that no diligence is exercised there to prevent what is holy from being given to dogs.” He then mentions abstinence, fasting, and exorcisms: “They are exorcised,” he says, “they are scrutinized: with what vigilance they come, with what zeal they burn, with what care they are attentive,” etc. Saint Leo, Letter 4 to the bishops of Sicily, chapter 6: “In baptizing the chosen, who according to apostolic rule are to be examined by exorcisms,” etc. Concerning these preliminary examinations before baptism, repeated seven times, see Rupert, *On the Divine Offices*; Alcuin, *On the Divine Office*; the Roman Order; Amalarius; Fortunatus; and others. Concerning the caution with which Jews should be received, see the Seventh Council, canon 8. GUSSANVILLE.] Thus we gain either them or their children. Therefore, whatever we remit from the tax for Christ’s sake is not burdensome.

Furthermore, before this time, when the deacon John came, your Affection wrote something to me. I reread everything at once, then allowed many days to pass, and after the delay of many days, retaining in my memory what I had read, I replied to each point. But now, as I think, one item escaped me, and I suspect that I gave no answer concerning it. For you had written that solidi should be given as loans to the peasants through the hands of certain tenants, so that, by taking them from others or by means of forced exactions or the prices of goods, they would not be burdened. [Note: [Col. 0731D] Most Norman manuscripts and others omit *debiti*, “of debt.” Gussanville suspects an error here and confesses that he does not understand what the phrase means. The matter is nevertheless clear. To prevent the peasants who possessed the estates of the Roman Church from being forced to borrow money from usurers at serious loss—namely, to repay it with heavy interest—Saint Gregory approves giving interest-free loans through the hands of the tenants. Concerning forced exactions, see the note on Book IV, Letter 46. “Angariae” sometimes means any kind of vexation or injury, as the learned Cange observes in his *Glossary*.]

This point was very pleasing to me. If I have already written about it, preserve what has been written. But if, as I suspect, I have not replied to anything on this subject, you must not delay, in response to this definite admonition, to provide solidi for the benefit of the peasants, since the Church’s property is not lost and the peasants’ welfare is thereby relieved. [Note: [Col. 0731D] Four English manuscripts read, “having received the admonition, to give,” etc.] You must also, without any hesitation, provide whatever else you consider useful. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, no. 43.)

## LETTER IX. TO PETER, NOTARY

The church furnishings of the Church of Miriensis are to be returned when a bishop has been ordained there.

[Col. 0731B]

Gregory to Peter, [Note: [Col. 0731D] The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read “to the notary in Sardinia.”] notary at Reggio.

The bearers of this letter were requesting the return of the church furnishings of the Church of Miriensis, which Severinus, formerly bishop of Squillace, had carried away with him. Since ecclesiastical property must be secured by careful vigilance, we have decided that a bishop should be ordained in that same city, to whom these furnishings may be entrusted. [Note: [Col. 0731D] The printed editions read, “in the same Church or city.”] But since they report that Leo the archdeacon and other [Col. 0731C] clergy of that same Church are there, we order your Experience to remind them to proceed to their own Church and elect a bishop to be ordained for them, so that, once he has been consecrated there with God’s favor, he himself may receive the property of his Church without any uncertainty.

## LETTER X. TO FELIX, BISHOP

He threatens strict correction unless the bishop of Sardica obeys his primate, the bishop of Justiniana Prima.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sardica. [Note: [Col. 0731D] Sardica is commonly called Sofia by the Greeks and Turks. [Col. 0732D] It was formerly the metropolis of New Dacia, situated between Naissus and Philippopolis, famous for the council held there in 347; it is now the capital of Bulgaria, toward the river Ciabrus and Mount Haemus. GUSSANVILLE. “Of Sardica” is absent from all the Norman manuscripts. In four Vatican manuscripts, the Colbert manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s collection, the reading is “to the bishop in Sardica.”]

You yourself do not doubt, from your own subordinates, how obedience and reverence should be shown to [Col. 0732A] superiors. In this matter it is especially useful when humility, without compulsion, observes what the rigor of discipline imposes. It has therefore come to us that your Fraternity disdains to obey our brother John, bishop of Justiniana Prima, according to custom, and that you have been unwilling to subscribe, as customary, either to his decree or to the report he sent to us. If this is so, we are saddened, because you provide clear evidence of pride. How blameworthy this is, especially in a priest, is proclaimed by the words of divine admonition.

Therefore we exhort you, laying aside the swelling of your mind, not to cease showing yourself humble and obedient to the aforementioned brother and our fellow bishop, your ordainer, so that God may rejoice in the harmony of your Fraternity [Col. 0732B] and others may take from you an example of goodness. For if, which we do not believe, you should persist in pride, know that we shall impose upon your defiance a strict and canonical correction of discipline. [Note: [Col. 0732D] See the Council of Antioch, chapters 5 and 9; Nicaea, canon 6; the Apostolic Canons, canon 35; Carthage, canon 19; in the decrees of Pope Leo, canon 32, Distinction 21; and in the collection of Martin of Braga, chapters 2, 3, and 4. See also Cause 9, Question 3, canons 1, 2, etc. The penalty for a disobedient bishop is abdication and excommunication, according to Antioch, chapter 10. GUSSANVILLE.] You therefore do well to present yourself voluntarily, with healthy reflection, as one who is compelled to be such by canonical coercion. [Note: [Col. 0732D] Paul’s collection reads, with a second hand, “therefore you will act well.”] For after our admonition you will no longer be permitted, according to your own will, to remain disobedient to your superiors contrary to custom; nor should you suppose that we will disregard or delay the ecclesiastical punishment of such great indiscipline.

## LETTER XI. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He permits the pallium to be used in solemn litanies on only four days of the year.

[Col. 0732C] Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

I find your Fraternity greatly distressed because the propriety of wearing the pallium during the litanies is forbidden. Yet through the most excellent patrician, the most eminent prefect, and other distinguished men of your city, you press your request importunately that this should be granted.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] In the printed editions, “the most excellent Roman patrician.” This name is absent from our manuscripts.]

We, however, carefully inquiring of Adeodatus, formerly a deacon of your Fraternity, learned that it had never been the custom for your predecessors to wear the pallium at the litanies except on the solemnities of blessed John the Baptist, blessed Peter the Apostle, and blessed Apollinaris the martyr.

[Note: [Col. 0732D] Solemn processions of clergy and people to a place appointed for a station are not rarely called “litanies” by ancient authors, because in those processions litanies, that is, prayers and supplications, were sung. In Book XXX of the Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, Arcadius Augustus forbids all such people to assemble within the city, by night or by day, for the performance of a litany, in profane gatherings. [Col. 0733D] To say nothing of others, Gregory himself calls a procession a litany in his sermon *On Mortality*: “Let the litany of the clergy,” he says—that is, the assembly of clergy proceeding to the station—“go out,” etc. See Book VI, Letters 34 and 61.]

Yet we ought by no means to have believed him, since many representatives in your city have repeatedly declared that they had never seen anything of the kind. On this matter, however, greater weight ought to be given to many witnesses than to one person testifying on behalf of his own Church.

But because we do not wish your Fraternity to be distressed, nor the petition of our sons to be frustrated by us, we grant the use of the pallium, until we learn something more precisely, at solemn litanies—that is, on the feast day of blessed John the Baptist, of blessed Peter the Apostle, and of blessed Apollinaris the martyr—and also at the celebration of your ordination.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] The anniversary of a bishop’s ordination was customarily celebrated with solemn rites. Augustine, Homily 24: “When the anniversary day of our ordination arrives, then especially the honor of this office is considered, as though it were being conferred for the first time.”]

In the *secretarium*, according to the former custom, after receiving and dismissing the sons of the Church, your Fraternity should put on the pallium and proceed in it to the solemn celebration of Mass. You should arrogate nothing further to yourself through the rash presumption of audacity, lest, while something is irregularly seized in outward dress, even those things that could properly have been permitted should likewise be lost.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] We do not read “Given” in any manuscripts. In the Tours and Saint-Gatien manuscripts it reads: “Given in the month of November, indiction 13.”]

Given in the month of October, indiction 13.

(See John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 3. See above, Book I, Letter 19; below, Letter 56, otherwise 54.)

## LETTER XII. TO PETER, BISHOP

He assigns a quarter of the revenues of the Church of Agrigentum as an allowance for visitation.

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Tricala.

[Note: [Col. 0733D] Thus it is read in four Vatican manuscripts and in the Corbie manuscript, instead of “Tricalitan,” which the more recent printed editions have. In the Gembloux manuscript it appears as “Trecasinus.” In Corbie, agreeing with the old editions, it is “Troecalitanus.” Tricala, or Triocala, was formerly an episcopal city of Sicily on the southern coast, between Agrigentum and Mazara. It now lies in ruins, and its site is called Santa Maria di Montevergine. Partly from GUSSANV.]

Since the Church of Agrigentum has been entrusted by us to the care of your Fraternity’s visitation, we have judged it useful to provide something from it for your labors. Therefore we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Maximianus that the quarter which the bishop of that same Church ought to receive should be assigned to you from the day of your visitation, or for as long as you exercise that responsibility there.

[Note: [Col. 0734C] Ecclesiastical revenues and offerings were divided into four parts. The first went to the bishop and his household, for hospitality or the reception of guests, as Saint Gregory teaches below, Letter 44, and Book VIII, Letter 7, as well as in the letter to Augustine formerly numbered 31 in Book XII and now 64 in Book XI. [Col. 0734D] Saint Gregory grants this quarter to the bishop visiting the Church of Agrigentum, who performs all episcopal functions in that Church. In this letter we have altered many things in accordance with the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts, without noting them, since the sense remains the same.]

Therefore it is necessary for your Fraternity to consider carefully that, since you receive the fruit of the Church, you should diligently devote your labors to it: gather souls to God there, restrain the wicked from iniquity, and nourish those beginning good works by words of exhortation, remembering what is written about the universal Church: “She does not eat the bread of idleness” (Prov. 31:27).

## LETTER XIII. TO GAUDENTIUS, BISHOP

He entrusts the visitation of the Church of Capua to him.

Gregory to Gaudentius, bishop of Nola.

[Col. 0734A]

Since Fuscus, bishop of the Church of Capua, who was residing in the city of Rome, has departed from this life, we have taken care to direct this present letter to your Fraternity in the manner in which we provide for all the Churches, so that you may undertake the visitation of the aforesaid Church.

[Note: [Col. 0734D] The printed editions read “Festus” or “Sixtus,” but incorrectly.]

You must do so in such a way that you allow no one to presume upon anything belonging to the promotions of the clergy, the revenues, the ornaments, the furnishings, or anything else that evidently belongs to the aforesaid place.

[Note: [Col. 0734D] The same vigilance is enjoined upon a visitor in Book II, Letter 25; below, Book VI, Letter 21, and elsewhere. Around the eleventh century, the property of deceased bishops was seized by laymen; nor did heirs prevent this, since nothing belonged to them. This abuse had to be restrained by many canons, as Peter Damian testifies in Book V, Letter 6, and frequently elsewhere; see Cause 12, Question 2. Read chapters 45, 46, 47, and 48. At Chalcedon, chapter 22, it is clear that this complaint was not new, since the practice had already been prohibited by earlier canons. In the Sixth Synod, chapter 35, the metropolitan is forbidden to seize the property of the Church or of a deceased bishop. AUGET.]

Rather, it is fitting that you show every vigilance and precaution toward the clergy and people of that Church, so that they may serve diligently and devoutly in vigils and ecclesiastical service, and so that, through your Fraternity’s earnestness and exhortation, they may conduct themselves in divine service in such a way that their service can be found irreproachable.

(Gratian, Decree, Distinction 61, chapter 19.)

## LETTER XIV. TO THE CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF CAPUA

Concerning the visitation of the Church of Capua entrusted to Gaudentius.

Gregory to the clergy of the Church of Capua residing at Naples.

Since Fuscus, bishop of the Church of Capua, who was residing here, has departed from this life, we have taken care to solemnly entrust the visitation of the abandoned Church to our brother and fellow bishop Gaudentius, bishop of the city of Nola. We instructed him not to allow anyone to appropriate anything belonging to the promotions of the clergy, the revenues, the ornaments, or the furnishings.

You ought to obey him in his constant exhortations, so that you may persevere with vigilant care in ecclesiastical service and in the praises of God, and order your conduct according to the worthy discipline of ecclesiastical governance. Let none of you dare to oppose his commands; rather, show obedience to his arrangements both in every ecclesiastical observance and in the protection of your Church, so that, while your obedience is given to his administration, the welfare of your Church may in no respect be neglected and his care for it may be all the more attentive.

## LETTER XV. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He reproves five things in him. He wishes to honor the Church of Ravenna, but does not permit that honor to be seized through pride.

Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.

First, I am distressed because your Fraternity writes to me with a double heart: you offer one kind of flattery in your letters, while displaying another manner, worldly in character, upon your tongue. Secondly, it is grievous to me that my brother John still retains on his tongue those mockeries that notaries who are still boys are accustomed to use. He speaks biting words and seems to take pleasure in such cunning. In the presence of friends he flatters; in their absence he speaks against them.

Thirdly, it is grievous and utterly detestable to me that, whatever the hour may be, he brings shameful accusations against his servants, calling them effeminate and even using still harsher names.

[Note: [Col. 0735C] Vatican manuscript D reads: “because he brings shameful accusations against his servants or others, whoever they may be, or whatever the hour may be.” All the editions and the Royal manuscript read: “at whatever hour he rages.”]

After this comes the fact that there is no discipline for preserving the life of the clergy; he merely presents himself as lord over his clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0735C] The Norman manuscript reads “dominion.”]

The last matter, though first in the weight of its arrogance, is that, concerning the use of the pallium outside the church—which he had never presumed to do in the time of my predecessors, and which had never been presumed by any of his predecessors, as our representatives testify— Except when relics were being deposited—which nevertheless only one person could be found to have said—he not only did this with the greatest audacity in contempt of me during my days, but also did it repeatedly.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] The printed editions read “no one ever presumed,” altering the sense against the testimony of the manuscripts. Gregory says that John had never presumed to do this under earlier supreme pontiffs, or that his Fraternity had never used the pallium at the litanies. In the printed editions the sense is that none of John’s predecessors, indeed no one during Gregory’s lifetime, had ever assumed this for himself.]

[Note: [Col. 0735D] In the more recent editions: “who would say, in my days, in contempt of me,” with a word omitted; hence the sense has been weakened.]

From all these things I conclude that the honor of the episcopate exists wholly in outward display, not in the mind. And indeed I give thanks to almighty God that, at the time when the matter reached me—a matter that had never reached the ears of my predecessors—the Lombards stood between me and the city of Ravenna. For perhaps I would have had to show people how severe I know how to be.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] So the old editions, together with all the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts; the more recent editions have “discreet.” Here “severe” has the sense of strict or stern.]

But lest you think that I wish in any way to burden or diminish your Church, remember where the deacon of Ravenna stood at the solemn celebrations of the Roman Masses, and inquire where he stands today; you will recognize that I desire to honor the Church of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] The printed editions read “at the solemn celebrations of the Roman Masses.” We follow three Vatican manuscripts, most of the Norman manuscripts, and several others.]

But I cannot tolerate anyone seizing anything whatsoever through pride. Nevertheless, concerning this matter I have already written to our deacon in Constantinople, instructing him to inquire through all those who have under them even thirty or forty bishops. And if anywhere it is the custom for bishops to walk with pallia at the litanies, far be it from me to appear to diminish in any respect the honor of the Church of Ravenna.

Reconsider, therefore, my dearest brother, everything I have said above. Consider the day of your calling; consider what account you will have to render for the burden of the episcopate. Correct those habits of a notary. See what is fitting for a bishop in speech and in conduct. Be wholly sincere toward your brothers. Do not say one thing while holding another in your heart. Do not seek to appear more than you are, so that you may be able to become more than you appear.

Believe me: when I came to this place, I was so full of deliberation and so full of charity toward your Fraternity that, if you had wished to preserve that same charity of mine, you would never have found even now such a brother, loving you with such purity and striving toward you with such complete devotion. But after learning your words and conduct, I confess that I recoiled.

Therefore I ask you, by almighty God, to correct all those faults I have listed, especially the vices of duplicity. Allow me to love you; and, both for the present life and for the life to come, it may be useful to you to be loved by your brothers. Answer me in these matters not with words but with your conduct.

(See John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 6.)

## LETTER XVI. TO DATIANUS, BISHOP

He kindly asks him to sympathize with him in his affliction.

Gregory to Datianus, metropolitan bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] LETTER XVI [otherwise 14, indiction 7]. In the index of Paul the Deacon’s Collection it reads “Domitianus.” Two letters exist to Domitianus, bishop of Melitene and a relative of the emperor Maurice; in the superscription of both letters—Book III, Letter 67, and Book X, Letter 50—he is called a metropolitan bishop, as Datianus or Domitianus is here. This bishop sometimes lived in Constantinople, where Sabinianus was to confer with him; this suits Domitianus, whom the emperor kept at court and used as an adviser. That both Datianus and Domitianus were among Gregory’s intimates is clear from the letters written to them. Thus Book III, Letter 67 begins: “The writings of your most sweet and most blessed Beatitude”; and Book X, Letter 50: “How great the sincerity of charity is in your mind.” These expressions closely correspond to the opening of this letter: “The writings of your most sweet Beatitude, which must be embraced in every way in the arms of the heart.” From all this it is almost established that this Datianus is the same person as Domitianus. We have nevertheless not altered the name, since only the index of Paul’s Collection has “Domitianus.” This letter is absent from the English and Norman manuscripts and from most others; we have collated it with Vatican manuscripts A and D, the Colbert manuscript, and Paul’s Collection.]

I received with sorrow the writings of your most sweet Beatitude, which must be embraced in every way in the arms of the heart; I read them again with joy. For who in this land would not mourn—a land given over to the swords of barbarians, which now scarcely has anyone left living in it, yet has someone dying in it every day? And yet, amid however great a sorrow, whose heart would not your letter shake into joyful exultation? In it, with the power of speech and the intelligence of surpassing wisdom, you spoke to me from the depths—not with the tongue of the flesh, but with the tongue of charity.

Since I have been somewhat gladdened by drawing from the fountain of your security, I ask you also to touch the grief of our sorrow and, through the teaching of charity, draw our affliction into yourselves. For you will not cleanse the filth of our grief unless you too soil the hand of your heart through compassion. Just as dirty vessels are customarily cleansed with earth so that they may be freed from the contamination of the soil, so you, if you turn your attention for a little while to our care in order to help us, are, as it were, cleansing mud with mud.

But because you do this both by working and by praying, if earthly activity soils anything in you on our behalf, the water of prayer immediately washes it away.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] The Colbert manuscript reads: “the water of prayer washes it.”]

Since, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, show by sharing in our labors that we are one. I am prevented by the brevity proper to a letter from recounting the evils I suffer both outwardly and inwardly. But our common son, the deacon Sabinianus, will disclose to your most sweet holiness the wounds that need healing. Through the recovery that follows from the work of heavenly grace, recognize that the physician is the one who sees the wound.

I am not sending boys resembling a bishop unless I, the bishop, have first been freed from earthly entanglements with the help of almighty God and your Beatitude. For when I find myself within myself, then I seek outside myself those who resemble me—that is, the deformed.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] Vatican manuscript A reads: “I do not send boys resembling bishops.” The Colbert manuscript likewise reads: “boys resembling bishops.”]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] Vatican manuscript D: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, indiction 3.” The Colbert manuscript reads: “Given on the day of the Kalends of January.” The Collection of Paul has the same, but adds “indiction 3.”]

## LETTER XVII. TO CYPRIAN, DEACON

He grieves over the death of Bishop Maximianus and indicates John, archdeacon of Catania, as his successor.

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon.

I received your most bitter letters concerning the death of our lord Maximianus in the month of November.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] LETTER XVII [otherwise 38]. Four Vatican manuscripts and others read “in the month of November.” We have discussed Maximianus at length in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, where the indices will provide information.]

He indeed has reached the rewards he desired, but the unhappy people of the city of Syracuse must be mourned, since they did not deserve to have such a shepherd for long. Therefore let your Love take care that someone be chosen for ordination in that same Church who will not seem unworthy to inherit the place of its governance after our lord Maximianus.

I believe that the majority will choose the presbyter Traianus, who, as they say, is of good character; but, as I suspect, he is not suitable to govern that place. Nevertheless, if no better man can be found, and if he is not entangled in any crimes, one may yield to him under the pressure of extreme necessity.

But if my preference is sought in this election, I tell you confidentially what I wish: no one in that Church after our lord Maximianus seems to me so worthy as John, archdeacon of the Church of Catania. If it is possible for him to be chosen, I believe that a very suitable person will be found. But you must first inquire of him privately about any crimes that could impede him. If he is found free of them, he may rightly be elected.

If this is done, our brother and fellow bishop Leo will also have to grant him a release, so that he may be found free to be ordained.

[Note: [Col. 0737D] The clergy were so bound to their own Church that it was not lawful even to elect them as bishops of another Church without permission being obtained, or, as it is called, release. See the formula of release in volume II of the Councils of Gaul, concerning the cleric Anno: “Therefore receive him, commended to your care, and, released from our jurisdiction, keep him among the number of your sheep,” etc. The same applies to Wilfrid the deacon, Berno the acolyte, Arnegisus the presbyter, and others. Concerning Leo, bishop of Catania, see Book III, Letter 34, now Book IV, Letter 36.]

I have therefore taken care to disclose these matters to your Love. It will now be your responsibility to examine everything carefully and arrange whatever is pleasing to God.

## LETTER XVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP

What Gregory himself and his predecessor Pelagius did concerning John’s usurpation of the title “universal bishop.” He asks him to abstain from it and presses him with many arguments. He warns him to beware of flatterers.

Gregory to John, bishop of Constantinople.

Your Fraternity remembers how much peace and harmony among the Churches it found at the time when it was raised to priestly honor. Yet, I do not know with what audacity or under what swelling of pride, it attempted to seize for itself a new name, from which the hearts of all the brothers could have been brought to scandal.

In this matter I am greatly astonished, since I remember that, before you could come to the episcopate, you wanted to flee from it. Yet now that you have obtained it, you desire to exercise it as though you had run toward it with ambitious longing. You who admitted that you were unworthy to be called a bishop have at last been brought to the point where, despising your brothers, you desire to be called the only bishop.

In this matter, letters of great gravity were sent to your Holiness by my predecessor of holy memory, Pelagius. In them he dissolved the acts of the synod that had assembled among you concerning the case of our former brother and fellow bishop Gregory, because of that wicked title of arrogance. He also prohibited the archdeacon whom he had sent, according to custom, to the feet of the lords, from celebrating the solemnities of Mass with you.

After his death, when I, unworthy as I am, was brought to the governance of the Church, I took care to address your Fraternity—first through other representatives of mine, and now through our common son, the deacon Sabinianus—that you restrain yourself from such presumption. I did so not in writing but in plain speech. And, if you were unwilling to correct yourself, I prohibited him from celebrating the solemnities of Mass with your Fraternity, so that I might first appeal to your Holiness under a kind of reverent shame, in order that, if this wicked and profane swelling could not be corrected through shame, we might then proceed to what is strict and canonical.

Since wounds that must be cut away should first be touched with a gentle hand, I ask, I implore, and with all the sweetness I can muster I entreat your Fraternity to oppose all who flatter you and confer upon you the name of error. Do not consent to be called by a foolish and proud title.

[Note: [Col. 0739D] LETTER XVIII [otherwise 38]. Vatican manuscript D and the Rheims manuscript read: “For indeed, while weeping, I say.”]

Indeed, I say this weeping, and in the deepest anguish of my heart I count it among my sins: that my brother, who has been established in the rank of bishop for the purpose of bringing the souls of others to humility, has not even now been able to be brought back to humility; that he who teaches others the truth has not consented to teach himself, even when I entreated him.

Consider, I ask, that through this rash presumption the peace of the whole Church is disturbed and the grace poured out upon all in common is opposed. You can grow only as much as you have determined within yourself. You become greater in proportion as you restrain yourself from usurping the proud and foolish title. You advance precisely to the degree that you do not seek to arrogate to yourself something by derogating from your brothers.

Love humility, therefore, dearest brother, with all your heart; through it the harmony of all the brothers and the unity of the holy universal Church can be preserved. Certainly, when the Apostle Paul heard some say, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” and “I to Cephas” (1 Cor. 1:13), he was horrified at this tearing apart of the Lord’s body, by which its members in some way attached themselves to different heads. He cried out most vehemently, saying: “Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (ibid., 13).

If he avoided subjecting the members of the Lord’s body to particular heads outside Christ—even when those heads were apostles—what will you say at the examination of the final judgment to Christ, the head of the universal Church, when you attempt to place all its members beneath yourself through the title “universal”?

[Note: [Col. 0739D] Vatican manuscripts A and B read: “to other heads outside Christ.”]

Who, I ask, is proposed for imitation in this perverse title except the one who, despising the legions of angels established in fellowship with him, attempted to rise to the summit of singularity, so that he might appear subject to no one and alone preside over all? He also said: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne. I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13).

For what are all your brother bishops of the universal Church except the stars of heaven? Their life and speech shine among the sins and errors of human beings as among the darkness of night. When you desire to place yourself above them under an exalted title and to trample upon their name in comparison with your own, what else do you say but: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne”?

Or are not all the bishops clouds, who rain through the words of their preaching and flash with the light of good works? When your Fraternity despises them and attempts to press them beneath yourself, what else does it say but what the ancient enemy said: “I will ascend above the heights of the clouds”?

As I contemplate all this in tears and fear the hidden judgments of God, my tears increase and sighs cannot be contained in my heart: that the most holy man, our lord John, of such abstinence and humility, has through the seductive tongues of his intimates burst into such pride that, in his desire for a perverse name, he seeks to resemble the one who, wishing proudly to be like God, lost even the grace of the likeness that had been given him, and therefore lost true blessedness because he sought false glory.

[Note: [Col. 0739D] Thus the Vatican, English, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “The Apostle Peter is the first member ... of the Church ... and yet under one head they are members of the Church.” In three Vatican and Norman manuscripts, “of the singular” is replaced by “of the individual.”]

Certainly Peter, first of the apostles, a member of the holy and universal Church, and Paul, Andrew, and John—what are they except heads of individual communities? Yet under one head they are all members. And, to gather everything into a brief compass of speech, the holy ones before the Law, the holy ones under the Law, and the holy ones under grace—all these, completing the body of the Lord, have been established among the members of the Church, and no one who was truly holy ever wished to be called “universal.”

[Note: [Col. 0739D] The printed editions read “to call,” supported by some Vatican manuscripts; we have preferred “to be called,” which is found in Vatican manuscript D and in the English, Norman, and Rheims manuscripts.]

Let your Holiness recognize how greatly that person swells within himself who desires to be called by a name that no one who was truly holy ever presumed to bear.

Did not, as your Fraternity knows, the venerable Council of Chalcedon call the bishops of this apostolic see, which by God’s arrangement I serve, “universal,” offering them this honor?

[Note: [Col. 0740D] In the third session of this council, certain supplications presented to the Roman pontiff are reported, in which he is called ecumenical or universal. Although these were read at the council, the council did not reject the title. The same must be said of Paschasinus’s speech reported in this session, in which he likewise gives the pope this title.]

Yet no one ever wished to be called by such a title; no one seized this rash name for himself, lest, if he appropriated for himself the glory of singularity in the rank of pontiff, he should appear to deny it to all his brothers.

But I know that these things arise for your Holiness from those who serve you with a deceptive familiarity. I ask your Fraternity to keep vigilant against them and not to offer yourself to be deceived by their words. They should be regarded as greater enemies in proportion as they flatter more through praise.

Leave such men. And if they are determined to deceive someone, let them at least deceive the hearts of worldly people, not of priests. “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke 9:60).

[Note: [Col. 0740D] The printed editions read: “without burying the dead,” etc.]

But say with the Prophet: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be immediately turned back in shame” (Ps. 69:4). And again: “May the oil of the sinner not fatten my head” (Ps. 140:5).

Therefore a certain Wise Man rightly warns: “Let many be your peacemakers, but let one out of a thousand be your counselor” (Sir. 6:6). “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33).

For when the ancient enemy cannot break into a strong heart, he seeks out weak persons to attach to it; and, as though ladders had been placed against a fortified wall, he climbs up. Thus he deceived Adam through the woman placed beside him. Thus, when he killed blessed Job’s children, he left the weak woman alive (Job 2:10), so that, since he could not penetrate Job’s heart by himself, he might at least enter it, if possible, through the woman’s words.

Therefore let all who are weak and worldly-minded around you be broken by their own persuasion and flattery, for it is through this that they bring upon themselves the eternal hostility of God, even though they appear to be perverse lovers of you.

Certainly the Apostle John was once crying out: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18), according to what the Truth foretold. Pestilence and the sword rage throughout the world; nations rise against nations; the earth is shaken, and the world, with its inhabitants, is dissolved as the earth gapes open.

[Note: [Col. 0741D] We have changed much here, following the manuscripts, the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other witnesses. Vatican manuscript D, which differs from the other three, reads: “The earth is shaken; cities with their inhabitants are swallowed up as the earth gapes open.” The printed editions read: “The earth is shaken; the world with its inhabitants is swallowed up as the earth gapes open.” This reading has been assembled from another corrupt text. Below, where it reads “an army of priests is prepared for him,” it formerly read “the departure of priests has been prepared”; GUSSANV corrected that reading. The corrected reading is supported by the four Vatican manuscripts and all the Norman manuscripts.]

For everything that was foretold is happening. The king of pride is near, and—what it is sacrilegious to say—an army of priests is prepared for him, because those who had been placed to provide leadership in humility are serving the neck of arrogance.

But in this matter, even if our tongue does not openly oppose it, the power of the one who personally resists the vice of pride is raised up in vengeance against arrogance. Hence it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Again it is said: “The one who exalts his heart is impure before God” (Prov. 16:5). Against the proud person it is written: “Why does earth and ashes grow proud?” (Sir. 10:9). The Truth itself says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

To lead us back to the way of life through humility, the Truth deigned to demonstrate in himself what he admonishes us to do, saying: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

For this reason the only-begotten Son of God assumed the form of our weakness: for this reason the invisible one appeared not only visible but also despised; for this reason he endured the mockery of insults, the disgrace of derision, and the torments of suffering, so that humble God might teach human beings not to be proud.

How great, therefore, is the power of humility, for the sake of teaching which alone the one who is immeasurably great became small even unto the passion of death? Because the pride of the devil offered itself as the origin of our destruction, the humility of God was found to be the instrument of our redemption. Our enemy, created among all things, wished in his pride to appear above all things. But our Redeemer, remaining great above all things, deigned to become small among all things.

What, then, do we bishops say, who have received the position of honor from the humility of our Redeemer and yet imitate the pride of that enemy? Behold, we know that our Creator descended from the summit of his exalted height in order to give glory to the human race, while we, created from the lowest things, glory in diminishing our brothers.

God humbled himself down to our dust, while human dust sets its mouth in heaven and ranges over the earth with its tongue; and the human being—rottenness and a son of man, a worm—does not blush or fear to be exalted (Job 25).

Let us recall, dearest brother, what the wisest Solomon says: “Before the thunder, lightning goes before it; and before a fall, the heart is exalted” (Sir. 32:14). In contrast, it is added: “Before glory, one will be humbled.” Let us therefore be humbled in mind if we strive to attain a firm height. Let not the eyes of the heart be darkened by the smoke of arrogance, which, the more it swells, the more quickly vanishes.

Let us consider what the commands of our Redeemer admonish us, when he says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). Through the Prophet he also says: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Certainly, when the Lord was bringing the still-weak hearts of his disciples back to the way of humility, he said: “If anyone wishes to be first among you, he will be the least of all” (Matt. 20:27). From this it is clearly understood that the one who is truly exalted is the one who is humbled in his thoughts.

Let us therefore fear being counted among those who seek the first seats in the synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi. Against this the Lord says to his disciples: “Do not allow yourselves to be called Rabbi. For one is your teacher, and you are all brothers. And do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father” (Matt. 23:7–8).

What, then, dearest brother, will you say at the terrible examination of the coming judgment, when you desire to be called not only father but also universal father in the world?

Let the wicked suggestion therefore be guarded against, and every incitement to scandal be fled. Scandals must indeed come, but woe to the person through whom the scandal comes (Matt. 18:7).

Behold, through this wicked title of arrogance the Church is divided and the hearts of all the brothers are provoked to scandal. Has it escaped your mind that the Truth says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths of the sea” (ibid.)?

It is written: “Charity does not seek what belongs to itself” (1 Cor. 13:4). Behold, your Fraternity arrogates to itself even what belongs to another. Again it is written: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Rom. XIII, 10). Yet you attempt to take honor away from everyone, which you unlawfully desire to usurp for yourself alone.

Where, dearest brother, is what is written: “Keep peace with all and holiness, without which no one will see God” (ibid.)? Where is what is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9)?

It is fitting for you to consider lest some root of bitterness, springing up above, should obstruct the way, and through it many be defiled. Yet if we neglect to consider this, heavenly judgments will keep watch against so great a swelling of pride. And we, against whom such a grave fault is committed through so wicked an act, observe what the Truth commanded, saying:

“If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. And if he does not listen to them, tell the Church. But if he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a publican” (Matthew XVII, 3).

746 Thus I have tried, once and twice, through my representatives, to reprove in humble words what is being sinned against throughout the whole Church; now I write in my own person. I have omitted nothing that I ought humbly to do. But if I am despised in my reproof, it remains that I must bring the matter before the Church.

In saying this, may almighty God show your Fraternity how great is the love by which I am bound toward you, and how greatly in this matter I grieve, not against you but for you. Yet in this matter I cannot place a person—even one whom I love greatly—before the evangelical commands, the decrees of the canons, and the interests of the brethren.

I have received the most sweet and gracious letter of Your Holiness [Note: In Vatican manuscript B, “most sweet and most gracious.”] concerning the priests John and Athanasius. With the Lord’s help I shall answer you about it below, for I am hemmed in by so many tribulations and pressed by the swords of the barbarians that I can scarcely breathe, let alone attend to many matters. [Note: The Colbert manuscript and others, especially the Norman manuscripts, read “surrounded.”] [Note: We find this in none of the manuscripts except the Colbert manuscript, where “the fourth indiction” is written.] Given on the Kalends of January, in the thirteenth indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, no. 54.)

## LETTER XIX. TO THE DEACON SABINIANUS

He is to deliver the preceding letter, softened out of reverence for the emperor, to Bishop John. The latter had craftily persuaded the prince to urge Gregory to maintain peace with him. Gregory arouses Sabinianus’s courage against John’s arrogance.

**Gregory to the deacon Sabinianus.** [Note: LETTER XIX [Elsewhere 29].—Sabinianus, deacon of St. Gregory, was then his apocrisiarius, or representative, at the imperial court, and later succeeded him in the pontificate. In the Norman and most manuscripts, the name is read as Savinianus.]

I did not wish to compose two letters concerning our most reverend brother John, bishop of Constantinople. But one brief letter has been written, which seemed to contain both elements together—that is, firmness and conciliatory language. Therefore, let your affection take care to deliver the letter I have now sent, out of regard for the emperor’s wishes. For another letter of a similar kind will subsequently be sent, one in which his pride will not rejoice.

For he has gone so far as to send here, under the pretext of the priest John, records in which he almost continually calls himself the “ecumenical patriarch” (οἰκουμενικὸς πατριάρχης). But I hope in almighty God that heaven’s majesty will dissolve his hypocrisy.

I wonder how he was able to deceive your affection, so that you allowed our lord the emperor to be persuaded to send me his letters on this matter, in which he admonished me that I ought to maintain peace with John. If he wishes to uphold justice, he ought to have admonished that man to restrain himself from the proud title, and peace would immediately have been established between us.

Yet you did not sufficiently consider with what craft the aforesaid brother John brought this about. He did this so that our lord the emperor would be heard and he himself would appear to have been confirmed in his vanity—or so that he would not be heard by me and his mind would be stirred up against me.

But we shall hold to the right path, fearing nothing else in this matter except almighty God. Therefore, let your affection be troubled by nothing. Whatever you see in this world to be powerful against the truth, despise for the sake of the truth, trusting in the grace of almighty God and in the help of the blessed apostle Peter.

Recall the voice of the Truth, which says: “Greater is he who is in you than he who is in the world” (1 John IV, 4). In this matter, therefore, whatever must be done, do it with the highest authority.

Since we can in no way defend ourselves against the swords of our enemies, and since, out of love for the commonwealth, we have lost silver, gold, slaves, and clothing [Note: The printed editions have “for the benefit of the commonwealth.”], it is exceedingly shameful that through them we should also lose our faith. For to consent to that wicked title is nothing other than to lose the faith.

Therefore, as I have already written to you in earlier letters, do not presume ever to proceed with him. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, no. 55. See above, Letter 10; below, Letters 20, 21, and 43.)

## LETTER XX. TO MAURICE AUGUSTUS

He praises the emperor’s zeal for the peace of the Church. He depicts the hypocrisy of Bishop John. He shows that by the ambitious title John was usurping, the whole Church, the venerable synods, the pious laws, and the commands of Christ himself were being disturbed; consequently, John’s pride must be restrained by imperial authority. Gregory declares that, unless John listens to him when admonished humbly and gently, he will resist him steadfastly together with God.

**Gregory to Maurice Augustus.**

Our most pious lord, appointed by God, watches with upright spiritual zeal, amid the other burdensome concerns of emperors, also over the preservation of priestly charity. He piously and truthfully understands that no one can rightly govern earthly affairs unless he knows how to administer divine affairs, and that the peace of the commonwealth depends upon the peace of the universal Church.

For what human virtue, most serene lord, or what strength of fleshly arm would dare raise irreligious hands against the height of your most Christian empire, if the united mind of the priests were striving to implore its Redeemer on your behalf with their voice and, as was fitting, by their merits? Or what sword of the fiercest nation would rage with such cruelty toward the death of the faithful, unless our life—we who are called priests but are not such—were burdened by the most wicked deeds?

But while we abandon what is fitting for us and contemplate what is unfitting for us, we join our sins to the barbarian forces, and our guilt sharpens the swords of the enemy, weighing heavily upon the strength of the commonwealth.

What, moreover, shall we say, who press down the people of God, over whom we preside unworthily, with the burdens of our sins; who destroy by our example what we preach with our tongue; who teach wickedness by our deeds and pretend by our voice alone to uphold what is just?

Our bones are worn down by fasts, yet our minds swell with pride. Our bodies are covered with despised garments, yet in the arrogance of our hearts we surpass purple. We lie in ashes, yet we despise exalted things. [Note: Recent editions read “we do not despise exalted things,” against the Vatican, English, Norman, and other manuscripts.] Teachers of humility, leaders of pride, we conceal wolfish teeth beneath a sheep’s appearance.

But what is the end of all this except that we persuade human beings while being manifest to God?
