Therefore, most providently, our most pious lord seeks the peace of the Church in order to restrain military disturbances, and deigns to restore the hearts of the priests to this bond of unity. This I desire, and, insofar as it concerns me, I offer obedience to your most serene commands.

But because this is not my cause but God’s, and because it is not I alone but the whole Church that is being disturbed; because the pious laws, the venerable synods, and even the commands of our Lord Jesus Christ are being disturbed by the invention of a proud and pompous expression, let our most pious lord cut into the place of the wound and bind the resisting sick man with the bonds of august authority. [Note: The manuscripts do not agree here. Gemet, Audoen, Pratell, Lyr, and three Vatican manuscripts read: “let him bind the sick man with the bonds of authority, for by binding this matter you thoroughly raise up the commonwealth.” The Regius manuscript differs slightly: “let him bind him with the bonds of authority. For while you repress this, you raise up the commonwealth.” The Colbert manuscript agrees with this. We follow Vatican A and others.]

For by binding these things, you raise up the commonwealth; and while you cut away such matters, you take thought for the continuance of your reign.

It is clear to all who know the Gospel that, by the voice of the Lord, the care of the whole Church was entrusted to the holy apostle Peter, prince of all the apostles. For it is said to him: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John XXI, 17). It is said to him: “Behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII, 31). It is said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew XVI, 8).

Behold: he received the keys of the heavenly kingdom; the power of binding and loosing was granted to him; the care and primacy of the whole Church were entrusted to him. Yet he is not called the universal apostle, while my most holy fellow priest John attempts to be called the universal bishop. I am compelled to cry out and say: “O times, O customs!”

Behold, everything in the regions of Europe has been handed over to the power of the barbarians: cities have been destroyed, fortresses overturned, provinces laid waste, and no cultivator inhabits the land. Idol-worshipping peoples rage and rule daily toward the death of the faithful. Yet priests, who ought to lie weeping on pavement and ashes, seek names of vanity for themselves and glory in new and profane titles.

Am I defending my own cause in this matter, most pious lord? Am I avenging a personal injury? [Note: Vatican D, followed by most printed editions, reads “am I avenging it, and not rather the cause of almighty God and the cause…” We follow three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Colbert, Regius, and others.] Is it not the cause of almighty God, the cause of the universal Church?

Who is this man who presumes, against the evangelical statutes and the decrees of the canons, to usurp a new name for himself? Would that he alone who desires to be called universal could be so without diminishing others.

And certainly we know that many priests of the Constantinopolitan Church have fallen into the abyss of heresy, and have become not merely heretics but even founders of heresies.

From there came Nestorius, who, believing that Jesus Christ, the Mediator between God and humanity, was two persons, and not believing that God could become human, broke out even into Jewish unbelief. From there came Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, is God.

If, therefore, someone in that Church seizes that title for himself—something which, in the judgment of all good people, he has thereby effected [reading uncertain]—then, God forbid, the whole Church falls from its condition when he who is called universal falls. [Note: This passage is obscure, though it is read this way in the Norman, Regius, three Vatican manuscripts, and most others. The printed reading is no clearer when *fecit* is changed to *fuit*. Vatican D alone has: “which made him the head of all good things,” with excellent sense. Jamesius reads in the English manuscripts: “by which he makes himself the head of all good people, and therefore…” The Sagiensis manuscript has: “which is the head…” Let the reader prefer whichever reading he wishes.]

[Note: He assails this new designation with many arguments: (1) when the universal bishop falls, the whole Church falls; (2) none of the Roman pontiffs assumed this name; (3) if even a Roman pontiff were called by it, all priests would be deprived of their due honor; (4) the designation opposes canonical precepts; and (5) all suffer scandal on this account. At the Seventh Synod, act 2, Pope Adrian contends with Tarasius concerning the name “ecumenical patriarch” and concedes it. See Adrian’s letter and the opinions of Basil of Ancyra, Stauratius of Chalcedon, Nicephorus of Dyrrachium, Epiphanius of Catania, Gregory of Sinope, the monk Saba, and the monk Gregory. The same title occurs in act 3, in the heading of the Easterners’ letter and in the votes of Bishops Agapius, John of Constantinople, Basil, and others. Leo IX, writing to Michael, patriarch of Constantinople, says of St. Leo I: “He utterly rejected the proud designation by which it seemed that equal dignity was taken away from all bishops throughout the world, while it was arrogated wholly to one.” See the entire letter. What if the Greeks gave their patriarch the name “ecumenical” only because he presided over a certain whole part of the world, as Anastasius the Librarian seems to have understood in the preface to the Seventh Synod in the Roman edition? Read St. Jerome, Book V on Isaiah, at the words of chapter XIII, “the sound of a multitude,” and “I will visit the evils of the world,” where he explains what is meant by “the whole earth,” “the world,” and *oikoumenē*.—Gussanville.]

But may that blasphemous name be far from Christian hearts: in it the honor of all priests is taken away, while one man madly arrogates it to himself.

Certainly, for the honor of the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, the title was offered through the venerable Council of Chalcedon to the Roman pontiff. [Note: It would more accurately be said: “in the universal Council of Chalcedon,” namely in action 3, in several booklets and in the vote of Paschasinus, legate of the holy Leo, and in action 6, in the vote of the same Paschasinus. They interpret the word *per* as “during,” and so forth. See above, Letter 18, near the middle.] Yet none of them ever agreed to use this title of singularity, lest, while something private was granted to one person, all priests should be deprived of their proper honor. [Note: Thus the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, and Regius manuscripts; in some, *vocabulo* appears instead of *nomine*. The printed editions read: “he assumed this title of singularity,” and do not agree with this reading.]

What, then, is the meaning of our not seeking the glory of this title even when it was offered, while another presumes to seize it for himself even though it was not offered to him?

He, therefore, is the one who must be bent by the commands of the most pious lords, because he scorns to offer obedience to the canonical precepts. He must be restrained because he injures the holy universal Church, swells in his heart, desires to rejoice in the title of singularity, and by a private title places himself even above the honor of your empire.

Behold, we all suffer scandal on this account. Let the author of the scandal, therefore, return to a right life, and all quarrels among priests will cease.

For I am the servant of all priests insofar as they live priestly lives. But whoever raises his neck against almighty God through the swelling of empty glory and against the statutes of the Fathers—I trust in almighty God that he cannot bend me to himself, even with swords.

What has recently occurred in this city upon hearing this title, I have explained in greater detail to the deacon Sabinianus, my representative. Let the piety of my lords, therefore, consider me as their own special possession, me whom they have always favored and specially protected. [Note: Here the verb *continere* should be interpreted in the same way as in Letter 5 of Book I, where the noun *continentia* occurs. See the notes.] I desire to offer obedience to you, yet I fear being found guilty of negligence in the heavenly and terrible judgment.

Therefore, at the request of the aforesaid deacon Sabinianus, either let our most pious lord himself deign to judge the matter, or bend the often-mentioned man so that he finally ceases from this intention. [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read: “or would not bend the often-mentioned man away from this intention at last” (perhaps *non cesset*, “does not cease”).]

If, then, he yields to the most just judgment of your piety or to your merciful commands, we give thanks to almighty God and rejoice in the peace granted by you to the whole Church.

But if he persists longer in the same contention, we already hold firmly the sentence of the Truth concerning this matter, which says: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11; XVIII, 14). And again it is written: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Proverbs XVI, 18).

For my part, while offering obedience to the commands of my lords, I have written both gently to my aforesaid fellow priest and humbly admonished him to amend himself and abandon this pursuit of empty glory. If he wishes to listen to me, he has a devoted brother. But if he persists in pride, I already see what will follow, since he has found in me an adversary of whom it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6).

## LETTER XXI. TO CONSTANTINA AUGUSTA

He urges her to continue opposing John’s ambition. He criticizes his hypocrisy, perversity, and pride. He complains that the emperor and Maximus are protecting him. Out of reverence for the prince, he excuses the fact that Maximus was ordained without his knowledge, but reserves judgment and examination of his other offenses.

**Gregory to Constantina Augusta.**

Almighty God, who holds the heart of Your Piety by the right hand of his majesty, protects us through you and prepares for you, in return for your temporal deeds, the rewards of eternal recompense.

For when my deacon and representative Sabinianus wrote, I learned how much justice your serenity is extending in the causes of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, against certain people who are proudly humble and deceptively gracious. [Note: The printed editions read “certain proud people, outwardly humble and gracious.” We follow the Norman, Colbert, Collection of Paul the Deacon, and others.]

And I trust in the generosity of our Redeemer that you will receive this good deed, in the heavenly homeland as well, as a recompense from the most serene Lord and your most pious sons. [Note: The printed editions read “also in the recompense of the heavenly homeland.”]

There is no doubt that you will receive eternal goods, freed from the bonds of sins, since in the causes of his Church you have made him to whom the power of binding and loosing was given your debtor. Therefore, I ask again that you permit no one’s hypocrisy to prevail against the truth.

For there are some who, in accordance with the words of the distinguished preacher, deceive the hearts of the innocent by sweet speeches and blessings. They are despised in clothing [Note: Vatican D and the Collection of Paul read “but not in heart.”], yet they swell in heart. They seem to despise everything in this world, yet they seek to acquire all that belongs to the world at once. They confess themselves unworthy of all human beings, yet they cannot be content with private titles, because they seek a title by which they may appear more worthy than everyone else.

Therefore, let Your Piety, whom almighty God has appointed, together with the most serene lord, to preside over the whole world, render its service through the favor of justice to the one from whom it received the right to exercise such great power. For the more truly it serves the author of all things in carrying out the truth, the more securely it will rule the world entrusted to it.

Moreover, I report that I received the letter of my most pious lords, commanding me to be at peace with my brother and fellow priest John. It was indeed fitting for a religious ruler to give such an order to priests.

But since that same brother of mine, through a new presumption and pride, calls himself the universal bishop, and even arranged to have himself recorded under this proud title in a synod during the time of my predecessor of holy memory—although all the acts of that synod were annulled while the apostolic see objected—the most serene lord has given me a sad indication: he did not rebuke the man who is proud, but rather sought to divert me from my position, although in this matter I defend the truth of the humility and uprightness of the Gospels and the canons. [Note: Thus the Collection of Paul, three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Colbert, and others. Recent printed editions read “the virtue of humility and uprightness of the statutes of the Gospels and the canons”; Vatican D also has this reading.]

In this matter, my aforesaid brother and fellow priest is acting against the evangelical sentence, against the blessed apostle Peter, against all the Churches, and against the statutes of the canons.

But almighty God exists, in whose hand are all things, of whom it is written: “There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord” (Proverbs XXI, 30).

Indeed, the most holy brother mentioned above often tries to persuade the most serene lord of many things. But I know well that his many prayers and tears will not allow anything contrary to reason or to his own soul to be taken from him by anyone.

Yet it is exceedingly sad that it should be patiently tolerated for the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop of mine, despising everyone, to attempt to be called the sole bishop. But what else is signified by this pride of his except that the times of Antichrist are already near?

For he imitates the one who, scorning the legions of angels in their fellowship and joy, attempted to burst forth to the summit of singularity, saying: “I will exalt my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah XIV, 13).

Therefore, through almighty God I ask that you not allow the times of Your Piety to be stained by the exaltation of one man, nor give your assent in any way to so perverse a title. And in this matter may Your Piety in no way despise me, for even if Gregory’s sins are so great that he deserves to suffer such things, the apostle Peter has no sins that would make him deserve to suffer them during your reign.

Therefore, again and again I ask through almighty God that, just as your earlier imperial parents sought the grace of the holy apostle Peter, so you too may take care to seek and preserve it for yourselves. Because of the sins of us who serve him unworthily, let his honor with you in no way be diminished. He is able now to be your helper in all things and afterward to forgive your sins.

For twenty-seven years now we have lived in this city amid the swords of the Lombards. It need not be explained how much the Church distributes to them each day so that we may be able to live among them.

But I shall briefly state that, just as in the region of Ravenna Your Piety has, with the first army of Italy, a treasurer who provides the daily expenses when circumstances arise [Note: Here *saccellarius* means a quaestor placed in charge of the treasury. The word is derived from *sacculi*, “small bags.” See Letter 44 of Book I.], so in this city I am their treasurer in such matters.

And yet this Church, which at one and the same time spends so much continually on clergy, monasteries, the poor, the people, and even the Lombards, behold, is still burdened by the affliction of all the Churches. They groan greatly over the pride of this one man, although they presume to say nothing.

The bishop of the city of Salona, Maximus [Note: Concerning Maximus, see above, Book IV, Letters 10 and 20.], was ordained without my knowledge or that of my representative, and something has occurred that never happened under any earlier princes.

When I heard this, I immediately sent to that same transgressor, who had been irregularly ordained, instructing him not to presume in any way to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass unless I first learned from the most serene lords whether they had ordered what he had done. I issued this command under threat of excommunication.

But he despised and disregarded me and, relying on the audacity of certain laymen—of whom he is said to offer many rewards after stripping his Church—he has continued to presume to celebrate Mass. He also refused to come to me in accordance with the command of the lords.

Yet, obeying their pious command, I released from my heart the offense of Maximus, who had been ordained without my knowledge, namely that he had presumed to omit me and my representative from his ordination, as though he had been ordained with my authorization.

But I cannot, for God’s sake, pass over without investigation his other perverse acts—that is, the temporal wrongs of which I have learned, whether because he was elected with money or because, though excommunicated, he presumed to celebrate Mass.

I hope and pray to the Lord that none of these charges may be found true in him and that his case may be concluded without danger to my soul.

Before these matters were investigated, however, the most serene lord issued a command that, when he came, I should receive him with honor. It is exceedingly serious that a man about whom so many grave reports are made should be honored before he is examined and investigated.

And if the cases of the bishops entrusted to me are settled by the most pious lords through the advocacy of others, what am I, unhappy man, doing in this Church?

Yet I give thanks to almighty God and attribute it to my sins that my bishops should despise me and seek refuge against me with secular judges.

I mention this briefly because I am waiting for a little while. If he delays coming to me for long, I shall in no way cease to exercise canonical severity against him.

But I trust in almighty God that he will grant long life to the most pious lords and that under your hand he will dispose of us not according to our sins but according to the gifts of his grace.

I report these things, therefore, to my most tranquil lady, because I know how greatly her unblemished conscience is moved by zeal for uprightness and justice.

## LETTER XXII. TO THE NOBLES OF SYRACUSE

Since they had entrusted the election of their bishop to Gregory’s judgment, he seeks to appoint someone who will imitate his predecessor Maximianus.

**Gregory to the nobles of Syracuse.**

The letter you sent bears witness to your praise, since it signifies that you wisely declined the burdens of election. [Note: The printed editions read: “the letter of election which you sent signifies that you have declined its burdens.” We follow the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts.] And because you entrusted this matter to our judgment, and, while recounting many good qualities of the bishop Maximianus of venerable memory, requested that someone like him be ordained for you, you are acting as faithful sons ought to act.

For you bear witness to these things about a worthy and diligent father, and, although others speak against him, you do not remain silent about his virtues even after his death. Therefore, we pray almighty God both to reward you according to the sincerity of your will and mercifully to forgive those who speak against him.

Your greatness should nevertheless know that we have no one whom we can give to that city as a man equal to the most reverend Maximianus. But since Agatho has been chosen by the clergy and people of the Church of Syracuse, while another has been chosen by some others, the one elected by the clergy and people must come to us again, so that, when both are present face to face, the one who pleases God and appears more useful may be ordained.

For it is our desire that, with the grace of Christ, such a bishop be ordained there as, with God’s help, will prove in all things an imitator of the virtues of the aforesaid bishop, whose conduct you commend.

## LETTER XXIII. TO THE NOTARY CASTORIUS

He urges the people of Ravenna to elect a bishop as soon as possible. They are to elect one worthy in merit, not one generous with rewards.

**Gregory to the notary Castorius.** [Note: In the index of letters in the Collection of Paul the Deacon, the addressee is called the deacon Castrianus; the heading of the letter itself reads “the notary Castorius.”]

The death of our brother and fellow bishop John has greatly saddened us, especially because that city has at this time lost the comfort of pastoral care.

Since many considerations demand that a priest should be ordained for that Church without delay, with Christ as guide, we therefore command your Experience to take every possible measure to exhort the clergy and people not to delay in choosing a priest to be consecrated for them.

But we wish you especially to admonish them not to consider their private interests in a matter of general concern. Therefore, let there be no buying and selling in this election, lest, while they seek rewards, they lose the discernment required for election and judge one worthy of this office who has pleased them not by merit but by payment. [Note: Recent printed editions read “the virtue of discernment”; the older editions and manuscripts agree with the reading here.]

Let them recognize clearly and absolutely that whoever presumes to purchase the gift of God through the sale of money is not only unworthy of the priesthood but will certainly be liable to other offenses as well.

Let the one elected, therefore, be chosen not for generosity in rewards but for worthiness in merit. For punishment will fall upon both the one elected and those who elect him [Note: Thus four Vatican manuscripts, the Collection of Paul, and the Regius manuscript in the Norman and Colbert collections.] if they attempt with sacrilegious intent to violate the integrity of the priesthood.

Whether one or two candidates are elected, make sure that five of the senior priests and five of those previously mentioned [Note: The printed editions read “five of the preceding deacons.” The word “deacons” is absent from the Regius, Colbert, three Vatican manuscripts, most Norman manuscripts, and the Collection of Paul.] come together to us in every respect.

As for the clergy, apart from those who intend to come, if you judge that any others who are present are necessary, send them to us without delay, so that no excuse or any postponement may arise in ordaining the Church. [Note: The Collection of Paul concludes the letter as follows: “Given on the thirteenth day [that is, of February], in the thirteenth indiction.”]

## LETTER XXIV. TO THE EXARCH ROMANUS

He is not to protect the priest Speciosus, who is resisting his bishop, nor to act as patron for nuns who have returned to secular life.

**Gregory to Romanus, exarch of Italy.** [Note: On Romanus, see Letter 33 of Book I. The printed editions add to the heading, “residing at Ravenna”; since this is found in none of the manuscripts, it has been removed.]

In Your Excellence, the audacity of wicked people ought to find the goads of correction rather than the comfort of defense. For it is exceedingly serious if a wrongful action should happen to find refuge there from which the censure of discipline ought to proceed.

It has therefore come to us that a certain priest named Speciosus, who, when circumstances required it, had been assigned to a monastery by our brother and fellow bishop John, subsequently left it against the will of his pastor and, disregarding the force of ecclesiastical constitution, resisted the aforesaid bishop, relying upon your protection. [Note: Vatican D reads “and the force of ecclesiastical custom.”]

Since this undoubtedly brings reproach upon Your Excellence, it is necessary that, after exercising discernment, you suspend your protection of him. Otherwise, if on account of your name he should for a time be disobedient or obstinate toward his pastor, and should defend your judges against you, he would be forced to offend Your Excellence on this account, while we too would be saddened by your discord.

Furthermore, we have learned—something which it is shameful even to say—that certain women who until now have remained in religious and monastic dress have laid aside their clothing and their veil and joined themselves to husbands, a matter which we cannot report without profound grief. [Note: The printed editions read “their sacred garment.” The ancient custom of veiling virgins should be recalled from Tertullian’s book *On the Veiling of Virgins*, although he does not speak there only of consecrated virgins. Concerning the solemn imposition and blessing of the veil for consecrated virgins, Jerome writes to Demetrias on preserving virginity: “I know that, at the bishop’s invocation, the holy bridal veil covered the virgin’s head.” Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virgins*, says: “The day of Easter has come; throughout the world the mysteries of baptism are celebrated; consecrated virgins are veiled.”]

They are said to be supported in daring to speak or attempt such things by the protection of your favor, although the bitterness of the wrongdoing itself does not permit us to believe this. [Note: The printed editions read, with excellent sense, “to do or even attempt this.”]

We therefore ask that you in no way involve yourselves in so great a sin. For the sake of God, we cannot permit such wickedness to remain unpunished.

Therefore, we ask again that Your Excellence not involve itself in defending such cases, lest God defend his own injury and the guilt of others produce discord between us.

[Note: Thus the Vatican and Turin manuscripts, Saint Gall. This is absent from our other manuscripts.] In the month of February, in the thirteenth indiction. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, no. 40.)

## LETTER XXV. TO BISHOP SEVERUS

He entrusts the visitation of the Church of Ravenna to him.

**Gregory to Severus, bishop of Ficulina.** [Note: Ficulum, called Ficocle by modern geographers and commonly Cervia, according to Ferrarius, was once a city of Aemilia on the Adriatic coast, between the mouths of the Savio and Rubicon rivers, now in Romandiola and still an episcopal see.—Gussanville.]

A direct report has made known the death of John, the bishop. Therefore, we solemnly entrust the visitation of the abandoned Church to your Fraternity. You must conduct it in such a way that no one presumes to usurp anything from the advancement of the clergy, its revenue, furnishings, ministries, or anything whatsoever belonging to the patrimony of that same Church. [Note: The printed editions add: “according to the previously established manner.”]

According to custom.

[Note: LETTER XXVI [Elsewhere 21]. This letter, like the preceding one, is absent from the Norman manuscripts and many others.]

## LETTER XXVI. TO THE PEOPLE OF RAVENNA

He reports that the visitation of the Church of Ravenna has been entrusted to Severus.

**Gregory to the clergy, the order, and the people residing at Ravenna.**
Your bishop’s death having become known to us, we took care to entrust solemnly the visitation of the Church left without a shepherd to our brother and fellow bishop Severus of Ficulina. We instructed him not to allow anything belonging to the Church—whether the advancement of clerics, income, furnishings, or ministries—to be usurped by anyone. You ought to obey his repeated exhortations, etc. According to custom. (See above, Letter 25.)

## LETTER XXVII. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN. He is to investigate whether the deceased bishop diminished the Church’s property. He is to urge the clergy and people to elect his successor.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

We now believe that your affection has learned of the death of Bishop Theodore. But since he is said to have made a will, you must investigate carefully whether he had consumed or diminished any part of his Church’s property. And if you learn that he improperly diminished anything from it, act so that the property itself may by every means be restored by the person whose responsibility it is.

You should also admonish the clergy and people of that place that, setting aside every delay, they should elect the man who, with God’s revelation, ought to be ordained their bishop.

> **Note:** Letter XXVII [Al. 22].—The bishop of Lilybaeum, as is clear from Letter 13 of Book VI, where the ordination of a bishop for the same Church is discussed. Letter 50 of Book III also exists, addressed to the same Theodore. AUGET.

> **Note:** Not through prophecy or an extraordinary and unusual vision, but through the movement of God’s Spirit, by which a mind free from every prejudice seeks what belongs to God with a single heart.

*(Gratian, Cause 12, Question 5, chapter 2.)*

## LETTER XXVIII. TO THE DEACON CASTORIUS. He is to investigate the life of the bishop of Pisaurum and of other priests; if he discovers anything improper, he is to report it. He is to protect the guardian, so that he may carry out what was entrusted to him for the poor.

Gregory to the deacon Castorius.

> **Note:** Letter XXVIII [Al. 24].—Vatican manuscript D: “To Castorius, notary.”

Certain matters concerning the bishop of Pisaurum have reached us which must in no way be left unexamined. Therefore we command your Experience to investigate carefully his life and conduct. And if you should discover anything that might, God forbid, stain the integrity of his priesthood, send him to us with your written account of what you have learned to be true, using every appropriate precaution, so that, once informed, we may, with God’s revelation, consider more precisely what ought to be done according to the truth.

You should be concerned not only with him but also with the life of the other priests. And if you are able to perceive anything improper in any one of them, hasten to report it to us, so that, with God’s help, the perversity of their conduct may be salutarily corrected.

> **Note:** Pisaurum, commonly Pesaro, formerly a famous city of Umbria at the mouth of the river Pisaurus, commonly called the Foglia; it is still an episcopal see, under the archbishop of Urbino in the duchy of Urbino.

A certain Adeodatus, a citizen of Pisaurum, is also reported to have appointed Thomas guardian, naming his son and his household servant as heirs, and adding this condition: if his heirs should happen to die while still minors, all his property was to be distributed to the poor through the hands of the aforesaid guardian.

> **Note:** Thus five English manuscripts and the Becc manuscript, supported by several printed editions, including Paris 1586, where *sed defunctis* is read. In this passage *obitis* means “the dead.” Certainly, unless it is read in this way, the sense is defective: the aforesaid guardian is said to be hindered by certain persons—namely, by those who had been appointed heirs—from fulfilling the deceased man’s wishes. In the printed editions *ab iis* is omitted, although it appears in all the manuscripts. Moreover, the testator’s will could not be carried out so long as the heirs appointed by him were alive; therefore they had already died.

But after the death of those who had been appointed heirs, certain persons are said to be obstructing the aforesaid guardian, so that the deceased man’s will cannot be fulfilled. Therefore, if you find that the matter is truly as we have been informed, make it your care and concern reasonably to protect and defend the aforesaid guardian, so that he may carry out whatever was entrusted to him.

But since it is said that this same guardian wishes to purchase something in the *diaconia* established there, hasten to assist him to the utmost, so that, with your cooperation, what was left for pious causes with a view to reward may be completed without anyone’s hindrance.

> **Note:** When the city was divided into regions and a deacon was placed over each region, the places in which the poor, widows, orphans, and elderly of each region were maintained by the regional deacons were called *diaconiae*. They were, in a sense, public hospitals for the poor. When their principal use gradually declined and the buildings themselves were destroyed, the name *diaconia* remained attached to their chapels and oratories; their supervising deacons were later called the cardinal deacons of the city of Rome. Anastasius, in his life of Hadrian I, writes: “That distinguished pontiff established *diaconiae*, in which he also did many good works, granting them fields, vineyards, olive groves, male and female slaves, various possessions, and movable property, so that from their revenues, as the *diaconiae* prospered through frequent collections, the poor of Christ might be refreshed.” This letter also shows that *diaconiae* existed outside Rome. See below, Book X, Letter 21. Cangius discusses the *diaconiae* at greater length in his *Glossary*, as do Mabillon in volumes I and II of the *Museum Italicum*.

As for the monk Valerian, whom you delivered, after his correction, to the monastery of blessed John situated at Classe, we certainly wish him to remain in that same monastery. Moreover, so that your Experience may suffer no hardship in meeting expenses, we wish you to meet all your expenses from the revenues of the holy Roman Church that have been gathered there under your supervision. If anything remains, bring it to us when you come.

## LETTER XXIX. TO THE DEFENDER VINCOMALUS. He appoints him defender of the Church.

Gregory to the defender Vincomalus.

> **Note:** Letter XXIX [Al. 25].—This letter contains the formula of the diploma by which a defender was appointed.

For the sake of the Church’s usefulness, we have determined that, if you are bound to no status or bodily condition, nor were you a cleric of another city, and if no canonical statutes stand in your way, you should accept the office of defender of the Church, so that you may carry out incorruptibly and energetically whatever we entrust to you for the benefit of the poor.

> **Note:** Here “condition” means the service that patrons sometimes reserved for freedmen or manumitted persons. By contrast, those manumitted by direct and complete emancipation were freed from every service arising from a burdensome condition. Cangius discusses these conditions at greater length. A “man bound to a body,” or a “man of the body,” is one who is attached to the soil, owes a poll tax, or is in another servile condition. See Cangius’s *Glossary*.

You shall use this privilege, which after deliberation we have conferred upon you, so that you faithfully devote your services to completing everything we assign to you, and render an account of your actions under the judgment of our God.

We dictated this letter to be written by Paterius, a notary of our Church.

> **Note:** He appears to be the man called the *secundicerius* in Letter 22 of Book IX, now at the end of the letters, and who published the *Book of Testimonies* from the works of Saint Gregory. GUSSANV.

> **Note:** Thus reads the Tours, Saint-Gatien manuscript.

In the month of March, in the thirteenth indiction.

## LETTER XXX. TO MAURICIUS AUGUSTUS. He gives thanks to the emperors for sending thirty pounds of gold as alms. He praises Scribo, both for his faithful distribution of that sum and for the military pay generously provided.

> **Note:** Letter XXX [Al. 2 of Book VIII, indiction 3].—This letter is absent from Vatican manuscripts B, C, and D. In the Norman manuscript it appears among the omitted letters. It is found in Paul’s Collection.

Gregory to Mauricius Augustus.

The piety of our lords, which has been accustomed mercifully to sustain its servants,

> **Note:** That is, to cherish and support them. See Book I, Letters 44 and 45, and Homily 20 on the Gospels.

has here shone forth with such benevolent assistance that the poverty of all the afflicted has been relieved by its generosity. For this reason, with tearful prayer we all beseech the almighty God who has moved the hearts of your Clemency to this purpose to preserve the empire of our lords safe in constancy of his love, and, by the aid of his majesty, to extend their victories among all nations.

Accordingly, the thirty pounds of gold that my fellow servant Busa delivered were faithfully distributed by Scribo to priests, the needy, and others.

> **Note:** The Greek expression is ὃν σκρίβωνα Ῥωμαῖοι κατονομάζουσιν, “whom the Romans call a *scribo*,” in Theophylact Simocatta, *History of Mauricius*, Book I, chapter 4, and Book VII, chapter 3. In Suidas, it means the prefect of the emperor’s protectors, or the commander of the emperor’s household cavalry and infantry: *skribōn*, in Latin, “superior to the bodyguards.” In Agathias, Book III of his *History*, it means a palace guard. The word is found in Anastasius in the lives of Vigilius and Theodore. GUSSANV.

And since certain religious women have come to this city from various provinces, fleeing captivity—some of whom, insofar as the capacity of the places permits, have been assigned to monasteries, while those who could not be accommodated in them live separately and lead lives of poverty—it was decided that whatever remained after provision for the blind, the maimed, and other disabled persons should be distributed to them, provided that not only needy natives but also visiting foreigners received the mercy of our lords.

Thus it came about that all together they prayed harmoniously for the life of our lords, so that almighty God might grant you long and peaceful times and permit the most fortunate offspring of your piety to flourish for a long time in the Roman state.

> **Note:** Recall the meaning of this word from Book II, Letter 46. In the old edition and in Vatican manuscript, it is incorrectly read as *togae*.

The soldiers’ pay was likewise distributed by the aforesaid fellow servant of mine, Scribo, in the presence also of the illustrious Castus, master of the soldiers,

> **Note:** Castus was a brave man and commander of the army of the emperor Mauricius. He fought brilliantly against Chagan, king of the Avars, but was captured by treachery and later ransomed for a great sum. See Simocatta, Book II, chapters 10 and 17; and the *Miscella*, Book XVII, under the fourth year of Mauricius. GUSSANV.

so that all might receive the gifts of our lords with due discipline and thanksgiving, and might turn away every complaint that had formerly been accustomed to dominate them.

> **Note:** The printed editions read, “which had formerly been given to them.” We have corrected this from the English and Norman manuscripts and Paul’s Collection.

> **Note:** In Paul’s Collection and the Norman manuscript: “Given on the twelfth day of the month of March, indiction 13.”

## LETTER XXXI. TO THE MANAGERS OF THE ESTATES. Until the administrator of the Gallic patrimony arrives, they are to obey the patrician Arigius.

Gregory to the managers of the estates throughout Gaul.

> **Note:** Letter XXXI [Al. 12, indiction 7].—In Paul’s Collection and Vatican manuscript D, addressed to the managers of estates or farms established throughout Gaul. The heading indicates that Saint Peter’s patrimony in Gaul consisted not so much of alms or money as of landed possessions.

Although you are situated amid the turmoil of nations, reason itself nevertheless compels us to suspect that you are far removed from others in good conduct. For just as the name of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, shows the household of the Church to be more illustrious than so great a multitude, so you ought to surpass the others in moral distinction. You must constantly admonish those over whom you preside to act well, to recognize whom they serve, and to abstain from the plunder and wickedness of the nations, so that the household of the Church may be honored not only in name but also in merits.

Know that we are thinking about you with the greatest care. We have decided to send one of our men, who can protect and govern you, with letters of recommendation to the most excellent king, with Christ’s help. But the season of winter prevented the journey. In the meantime, therefore, we have decided to commend you to the illustrious patrician Arigius. Strive to obey him with complete kindness and obedience, as befits servants of blessed Peter, and fulfill whatever is commanded you for the benefit of the Church.

We have also determined that, after deducting what is customarily due for his benefit, you should deliver the remainder. Let the rents, collected faithfully and with every diligence, remain in the custody of one among you whom you select by common agreement. When the man whom we send from our side arrives, he will be able to receive them from him.

> **Note:** That is, from his retinue and household. This is a very ancient expression. Pope Liberius writes in a letter preserved by Saint Hilary, fragment 4 of the new edition, column 1327: “Following the tradition of our ancestors, I sent from my side to Alexandria, to the aforementioned Athanasius, the presbyters of the city of Rome, Lucius, Paul, and Helianus.” Saint Leo writes in Letter 28: “When, on account of the faith … I was sending someone from my side”; and in Letter 31: “Bishop Julius, the presbyter Renatus, and also my son, the deacon Hilary, whom I sent from my side in my place.” See Quesnell’s notes, p. 850. Read the chapters of Charles the Bald, title 3, chapter 2. Hence the legates of the supreme pontiff were called *a latere*. Emperors also had their own legates *a latere*: William of Tyre, Book XVIII, chapter 24. “Moreover, from the imperial side an illustrious *apocrisiarius* is sent.”

For we are not doubtful that the revenues can be faithfully preserved by the man whom you choose. Therefore, be irreproachable and obedient in everything, so that the man who comes to administer this patrimony may know how he ought to reward each of you according to your diligence.

> **Note:** Vatican manuscript D adds: “In the month of March, on the twelfth day, indiction 13.” Paul’s Collection incorrectly assigns indiction 3, and the Colbert manuscript no more correctly assigns indiction 4.

(See Book VI, Letter 57; Book IX, Letter 118.)

## LETTER XXXII. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN. After the death of Bishop Maximian, he is to punish severely certain clerics whom the bishop had imprisoned for sorcery.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

The most holy man Maximian, our fellow bishop, desiring to cleanse the Church of God of wicked men, was commendably vigilant, as you know, concerning the life of ecclesiastics. While he carefully watched over their conduct with pastoral concern, he learned that certain men had been stained by the sorcery commonly called *canterma*.

> **Note:** Letter XXXII [Al. 13, indiction 7].—See many canons in Cause 26, Question 5; Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 19; the Council of Narbonne, chapter 14, A.D. 589; the Council of Leptines, chapter 5, A.D. 743; the Third Council of Tours, chapter 42, A.D. 813; and others. Among more recent authors, see Costanus of Toulouse, *Memorable Legal Questions*, Book I, chapter 16. GUSSANV.

> **Note:** A barbarous word, corresponding in Latin to *carmen* and *incantatio*, and in French to *charme*. Among Italians it is *stregaria* or *malia*, according to Dominico Magri’s vocabulary. It is a form of sorcery performed by enchanters through certain songs. The writers do not record what particular kind of sorcery it was. The distinguished Cangius thinks that *Canterma* may perhaps be read as *Canterina*, so that the Italian word has been rendered. In Italian, *canterini* are people who sing frequently and readily. It is well known that enchantment takes its name from magical songs. GUSSANV. See Book IX, Letter 65, formerly Book VII, Letter 67.

He therefore ordered them to be held in custody.

> **Note:** See the statute in canon 20 of the Fifth Council of Orléans, a practice unknown to our customs, even though new statutes multiply daily and clerical discipline is reformed with such care. The final law of the Code, title “On the Custody of Prisoners,” agrees with this, as noted above in Book II, Letter 52, now Book XIII, Letter 45. In former times the *catechumena*, *decanicum*, or *skeuophylacium* served for holding accused persons. This is illustrated by Letter 12, formerly Letter 2, of Gregory II to the emperor Leo the Isaurian, at the beginning of the Second Council of Nicaea, where the distinction between palace and churches in punishing criminals is described: “The pontiffs do not act in this way. When someone has sinned and confessed, instead of hanging or beheading him, they place the Gospel and the cross around his neck and cast him, as into a prison, into the sacristy and treasury of the sacred vessels; they send him away to the Church’s *diaconia* and *catechumena*, imposing fasting upon his entrails, vigils upon his eyes, and praise upon his mouth. When they have sufficiently chastised and afflicted him with hunger, they give him the precious body of the Lord and make him drink the holy blood; and when they have restored him as a chosen vessel and made him free from sin, they send him pure and innocent to the Lord.” GUSSANV.

But because, through our sins, death overtook him and he was unable to avenge the crime, your Affection must hasten to investigate the whole matter with the greatest care and must strive to punish them according to the enormity of their offense, in a manner consistent with the laws, as you know that the aforementioned bishop, moved by zeal for correction and justice, would have wished to act in this punishment for God’s sake if he had lived.

Therefore, let your Affection show every zeal toward almighty God in this matter with all strength and persistence, and inflict due retribution upon his enemies, so that you may fulfill what is written: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and do I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Psalm 138:21).

If, then, your Affection is kindled by this zeal, let it be shown in the punishment of those who have abandoned God and have done something against him through sorcery.

> **Note:** The printed editions read *in eos*, where the sense is impossible. It should therefore be read *in eorum*, namely, “in their punishment”; all the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts confirm this. Below, too, we have restored many readings from the same manuscripts.

But if it cannot properly be carried out there, they should be sent to us—provided it can be demonstrated here how they may be convicted there without difficulty.

> **Note:** This is how it is read in the manuscripts. The editors changed *non valet* to *non vales* to conform to grammatical rules. They should have observed, however, that Gregory frequently uses deponent verbs with passive meaning, as here *exsequi* is used.

But since I consider that impossible, strict and vigorous correction must be administered there through you.

I trust that the illustrious lord Libertinus, the praetor, will be your helper in such a matter, with consideration for almighty God.

> **Note:** Concerning Libertinus, see Book III, Letter 38.

In this matter, however, you ought not to have become lenient at all, even if some secular judge might have been able to oppose you.

Your Affection should also reasonably protect the possessions of the physician Archelaus and must not allow him to be unjustly oppressed by anyone.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO BISHOP GAUDENTIUS. He is to distribute a quarter-share to the Capuan clerics serving at Naples. He is to restore ten solidi to the impoverished archdeacon.

Gregory to Gaudentius, bishop of Nola.

> **Note:** Letter XXXIII [Al. 26].—He was recently mentioned in Letters 13 and 14 of this book. The word “Nolan” is omitted in the Norman manuscript and several others.

Those who serve in ecclesiastical duties ought to receive ecclesiastical support insofar as circumstances require. Therefore, by this letter we exhort your Fraternity to distribute to the clerics of the Church of Capua who reside in the city of Naples a quarter-share for their presbyterium from whatever has accrued annually to the aforementioned Church, according to ancient custom, allotting it in proportion to the status of the persons, so that, having some assistance toward their stipends, they may be encouraged to devote themselves with more devoted minds to their ministry and service toward that same Church.

> **Note:** According to each person’s merits. For at that time worldly distinctions of rank were not yet so frequently observed, as they came to be in later centuries. The Apostle said: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.” Cyprian agrees in Letter 34, where he speaks of the readers Celerinus and Aurelius: “Let them be honored with the same distributions as the presbyters, and let the monthly allocations be divided in equal amounts,” and so forth. Read the little book of the deacon Theodore to Pope Leo, and the Council of Chalcedon, concerning the many years of military service by which a man might merit the clerical state. See Act 3 of that same council. GUSSANV.

Moreover, your Fraternity must restore without any hesitation the ten solidi that the former bishop Fuscus of the aforesaid Church took from his archdeacon Rusticus, because he is said to have fallen into such poverty that it would have been more appropriate to give something to him than to take anything from him.

For it is harsh, far removed from the duty of a priest, both to neglect a person placed in necessity and shamefully to desire money with the eagerness of accumulation.

> **Note:** Vatican manuscript reads: “In the month of March, indiction 13.”

(See Book II, Letter 32.)

## LETTER XXXIV. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN. He is to restore the fallen monk Cicero to the Church of Misenum, whose servant he had been.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

> **Note:** Letter XXXIV [Al. 27].—Misenus, the bishop mentioned in Book II, indiction 10, formerly Letter 19, now Letter 25, and in several other places.

Our brother and fellow bishop Benenatus reports that a certain monk named Cicero, who for his offenses was assigned to penance by our beloved son the deacon Peter—then a subdeacon and administrator of our patrimony—was a servant belonging to his Church, and asks that he be restored to him together with his property.

> **Note:** In Book I, Letter 41, Gregory orders that wandering monks throughout Sicily be collected and restored to their bishop. In Book II, Letter 28, he urges the chartularius Stephen of Sicily to ensure without delay that monks who had returned to secular life and dress be sent back. See Book I, Letter 42. Cicero was one of these apostate monks.

You must therefore investigate the matter carefully. And if it is established that this is true, restore the aforesaid Cicero without delay, together with the property said to have been deposited with the defender Fantinus, to the ownership of the Church of Misenum,

> **Note:** The Norman, Vatican, Corbie, and Misenum manuscripts read this way.

so that, after he tore himself away from monastic life through a lapse caused by guilt, he may recognize the yoke of ownership which, had he remained in that way of life, he might have escaped.

> **Note:** Vatican manuscript A reads: “from which a lapse of guilt carried him away from monastic conduct.” Manuscripts B and C read: “which a lapse of guilt carried away,” followed by “the yoke of ownership,” and so forth. All our manuscripts read *dominii*, where the editors have *domini sui*.

> **Note:** This suggests that, as a servant of the Church, he had shaken off his master’s yoke by his monastic profession. GUSSANV. See the Roman synod, formerly Letter 44 of this book, now placed after the letters.

> **Note:** This passage is absent from the Norman, Corbie, and several other manuscripts, but is found in the Vatican, old Colbert, Turin, Saint Gall, and Reginensis manuscripts.

In the month of May, indiction 13.

## LETTER XXXV. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN. He is to compel three monks to return to the monastery of Saint Martin; he is to favor the administrators of that monastery and restore its slaves.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

The abbot Theodosius of the monastery of Saint Martin has informed us that you have retained there three monks whom he had sent to Sicily for the benefit of his monastery, and he has asked us to have them recalled to his monastery with your assistance.

> **Note:** Letter XXXV [Al. 28].—Recent printed editions read: “three of them remained there …” We return to the older editions, since all the manuscripts agree with the reading given here.

Your Affection, knowing how passionately and fervently we are accustomed to pursue such matters, must have them sought out with careful investigation and, once found, sent under suitable precaution and strictness to the aforesaid abbot, against whom they have been disobedient.

Be vigilant, therefore, lest regular discipline be harmed either by delay or by the remission of the appointed penalties.

We wish you to provide every prompt assistance to the bearers of this letter, whom the aforesaid abbot Theodosius is known to have sent to attend to the interests of that monastery, so that, with your cooperation, they may reasonably complete what has been entrusted to them.

You must also investigate by every means the slaves of that monastery whom the aforesaid abbot claims are being wrongfully detained by men of our Church. If you find that this is so, have them restored without any delay.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO SEVERUS, THE EXARCH’S COUNSELOR. He is to persuade the exarch to make peace with Agilulf, king of the Lombards.

Gregory to Severus, counselor of the exarch.

Those who assist judges and are bound to them by sincere affection ought to advise and suggest to them what both saves the soul and does not diminish their reputation. Since, therefore, we know with what faithful sincerity you love the most excellent exarch, we have taken care to inform your Greatness of what has happened, so that, once you know these things, you may reasonably urge him to agree.

Know that Agilulf, king of the Lombards, does not refuse to make a general peace, provided that Lord Patricius is willing to grant him a judicial hearing.

> **Note:** That is, if he is willing to negotiate with him on equitable terms and the damages unjustly inflicted on both sides are repaired according to the judges’ decision. GUSSANV.

For he complains that many wrongs have been committed against him in his territories within the bounds of the peace. And since he asks that satisfaction be given him if judgment should determine that he is in the right,

> **Note:** The printed editions, corruptly and contrary to the manuscripts, read: “if the reasoning of the judges …”

he likewise promises in every way to make satisfaction if it is established that anything has been committed in peacetime by his side.

Since there is no doubt that what he requests accords with justice, there ought to be a judgment, so that, if wrongs have been committed by either side, they may be settled, provided that a general peace can be established and strengthened under God’s protection.

> **Note:** The same printed editions, without consulting the manuscripts, read: “that peace may be made and firmly secured under God’s protection.”

You know well how necessary this is to all of us. Act wisely, as you have been accustomed to do, so that the most excellent exarch may consent to this without delay, lest it appear that peace is being rejected through him, which would be disadvantageous.

For if he is unwilling to consent, he promises to make a special peace with us; but we know that various islands and other places will certainly be destroyed. Let him consider this and hasten to have peace, so that, during this postponement at least, we may have a little rest and the strength of the state may, with the Lord’s help, be restored more effectively.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO BISHOP FORTUNATUS. He is to dedicate a monastery in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Michael, where the priests serving there are to celebrate Masses; whatever the faithful happen to offer is nevertheless to benefit the monks.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

The abbot Theodosius of the monastery of Saint Martin has informed us by a petition, reproduced below, that in the house formerly belonging to Martin, his predecessor Andrew the abbot constructed, according to Martin’s wishes, a monastery in which monks were to live.

> **Note:** Letter XXXVII [Al. 15, indiction 2].—The Vatican and old Colbert manuscripts read: “according to his wishes, he constructed an oratory for his predecessor Andrew beside the Baths of Eria.” In Paul’s Collection: “according to his wishes, an oratory, in accordance with the wording of the document.”

Since he asks that it be dedicated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Michael the archangel, we have thought it appropriate to exhort your Affection by this letter to go without delay to the aforesaid place whenever he requests it, and to perform the solemn rites of the venerable dedication.

Whenever necessary, let the priests of your Church who serve at the holy place celebrate the venerable sacrifices of the Mass. Yet neither your Fraternity nor the priests are to inflict any burden there beyond the careful maintenance of discipline.

> **Note:** Vatican manuscript D reads: “for the careful maintenance of discipline.”

If anything useful should accrue there through the devotion of various people, they must not claim it for themselves. Whatever the faithful happen to offer should benefit the monks serving in that place.

> **Note:** The old Colbert manuscript adds: “On the sixth day of the month of June, indiction 13.” Paul’s Collection reads: “Given on the day mentioned above,” namely, June 6, indiction 14.

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO ELIAS, PRIEST AND ABBOT. He accepts his explanation; he sends the Gospels; he binds Epiphanius to the Roman Church through the diaconate; he surpasses his modest request for assistance by generosity.

Gregory to Elias, priest and abbot of Isauria.

I have received the most delightful letters of your Holiness, in which you have satisfied me, so that I should not be saddened that you did not come, as I desired, to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

I very much wished to see you; but if bodily illness or the weakness of age prevented you, this is enough for me: wherever your Holiness may be, pray earnestly for me. For although we are separated in body by distance, we are always inseparable in charity.

As you instructed us, we have sent the Gospels.

You instructed us to advance your son Epiphanius to the sacred order and send him back to you. *(Gratian, Cause 1, Question 1, chapter 122.)*

> **Note:** Letter XXXVIII [Al. 30].—The printed editions add: “either bodily illness or weakness of age stood in the way or was an impediment.” This is a gloss absent from the manuscripts.

But in one matter we listened to you; in the other we could not listen. He has indeed been made a deacon, but whoever has once received a sacred order in this Church no longer has permission to leave it.

> **Note:** I recognize the practice, but I do not find its origin. Indeed, I do not think it always prevailed uniformly, since I see that some who were promoted at Rome were sent elsewhere. Clearly, they are not bound by so strict a bond that it cannot be dissolved. Saint Paulinus, in Letter 6 to Severus, if I remember correctly, says that he was dedicated to the priesthood of the Lord, not to a particular place. The same may have happened in other cases. GUSSANV.

If I could not see you, I nevertheless have consolation in this matter, because I rest in your son.

You wished fifty solidi to be sent to you for the needs of your cell. Thinking that this was a great deal, you gave us ten of them so that we would send forty. But lest even this should perhaps be burdensome, you were kind enough to give us still more of that amount.

Since we have found you exceedingly generous toward us, we return a similar favor to that generosity. We have sent fifty, and, lest they perhaps be too little, we have added another ten. And lest even that should still be insufficient, we have arranged for another twelve to be added.

> **Note:** In the recently cited little book of the deacon Theodore, in connection with Letter 33, *continentia* is used for “assistance”: “I enjoyed the assistance of Cyril.” The same sense appears in Pelagius, Letter 15, and in Gregory himself, Book I, Letters 18 and 44; Book III, Letter 28; and Book V, Letter 30. Here, however, *continentia* means affection, benevolence, or favor. See the notes on Book I, Letter 5. Vatican manuscript D reads: “in your benevolence.”

In this we recognize your charity, because you rely upon us as you ought to rely upon us.

But by almighty God I ask you to offer constant prayers for me, so that I may be freed more quickly from the sins by which I am bound and the tribulations under which I suffer, and may enjoy the joys of the heavenly homeland.

You indicated in your letters how you pray for me; know that this greatly relieved me. But now, after my request, do even more than you did when I did not ask.

You should not be saddened that I have bound the aforementioned beloved son of mine, the deacon Epiphanius, to this Church through the diaconate. Since you yourself cannot serve blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, bodily, serve him through your son, and enjoy the profit of heavenly recompense.

May the Holy Trinity guard you under its protection and shield you, in the wilderness of the present life, from the enemies who pursue and confront you. May it forgive whatever past sins you have, and by the hand of its mercy remove from you whatever still lies ahead. May it guide you, lead you to the end, and receive you into eternal joy.

May it grant you to reach the lot of the elect, and pray for me, a sinner, so that I may deserve to be absolved.

> **Note:** Recent printed editions read: “and, for my sins, so that …” This differs from the reading found in Teller, Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.

> **Note:** Thus the old Colbert and Vatican manuscripts read.

In the month of June, indiction 13.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO BISHOP ANASTASIUS. He congratulates him on his restoration to the see of Antioch and gives a more concise account of his own and Italy’s calamities.

Gregory to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0763D] EPISTLE XXXIX [Al. 37].—Formerly this evangelical and angelic hymn was used as an act of thanksgiving. Gregory of Tours, in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, relates that, upon seeing a certain miracle, the entire people sang the hymn “Glory to God in the highest.” Consult Menard’s note 1083 on the book *The Sacred Hymns*.]

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14); for that great river, which once had left Antioch’s parched banks dry, has at last returned to its proper channel and waters the valleys lying beneath it, so that one may bear a thirtyfold, another a sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold fruit. There is now no doubt that many flowers of souls are springing up in its valleys and reaching maturity through the streams of your speech. Therefore we render due praise to almighty God with the voices of our heart and mouth, from our inmost being, and in your blessedness we rejoice not only with you but with all who are subject to you.

I received the letters of your holiness, sweetest and most pleasing to me, sweating, so to speak, the very labor itself. [Note: In Paul’s Collection: “exhorting.”] And indeed I know that, after those heights of repose in which you touched the heavenly secrets with the hand of your heart, it is exceedingly burdensome to endure external matters. [Note: Bishops of every sort were called “apostolic,” and their sees “apostolic,” as learned students know. Therefore, lest I repeat what has already been done, see Filesacus, *On the Sacred Authority of Bishops*, chapter 9, §15, where he confirms this with various testimonies. There is, however, a special reason in the case of the see of Antioch: Saint Peter first sat there. Thus below the see of Alexandria is also called apostolic because Saint Mark, Peter’s disciple, first administered it. GUSSANVILLE.]

But remember that you govern an apostolic see, and you temper sorrow more quickly, since you have become all things to all people. [Note: In the Bec manuscript it reads, “in the Book of Judges.” And indeed, at chapter 3:15, Ehud is praised, who used both hands as though each were his right. If Saint Gregory is alluding to the First Book of Chronicles, it should read, “some are described.”]

In the Books of Kings, as your perfect holiness knows, someone is described who used both hands as though each were his right (1 Chronicles 21). In this matter I have no doubt concerning my most beloved and holy former patron, my lord Anastasius: while he draws earthly works toward heavenly usefulness, he turns the left hand into the service of the right, so that the heavenly intention may carry out its work—that is, the right hand—and the care of temporal matters, when directed toward the usefulness of justice, may exchange the left for the strength of the right.

Indeed, these things cannot exist without great labor and weariness. But let us remember the labors of those who came before us, and what we endure will not be hard. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). “We were burdened beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we were weary even of living. Indeed, we ourselves had within us the sentence of death, so that we would not place our trust in ourselves” (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). Yet “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the glory that is to come, which will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). [Note: Paul’s Collection and Vatican D read, “the glory that is to come”; three other Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, and others, “the future glory.”] How, then, can we, weak sheep, pass through the heat of this age without labor, when we know that the rams have sweated grievously in it? [Note: “Leaders of the flock” means the apostles. Saint Augustine uses the same expression in many places to designate bishops, for example in Letter 89, now 157, to Hilary; on Psalm 103, exposition 3; and on Psalms 28, 65, and 72. “The sons of rams” are Christians subject to their prelates. GUSSANVILLE.]

I am unable to set forth either with pen or tongue how many tribulations I suffer in this land: from the swords of the Lombards, from the injustices of judges, from the insolence and importunity of lawsuits, from the care of those subject to me, and even from bodily distress. [Note: The printed editions wrongly read, “which I suffer”; this addition weakens the sense.]

Even if I can speak briefly about these matters and others, I hesitate lest, while your most holy charity is afflicted by its own tribulations, I should increase your burden with mine. But may almighty God, by the abundance of his merciful generosity, fill the mind of your most holy blessedness with every consolation, and through your intercession grant that I, unworthy as I am, may one day rest from the evils I suffer. [Note: These words do not occur in the genuine letters of Saint Ignatius, but only in the spurious ones; their antiquity can nevertheless be established from this.]

Amen. Grace. I place these words, which I have taken from your writings, in my letters for this reason: that your blessedness may recognize, concerning Saint Ignatius, that he is not only yours but also ours. For just as we have his teacher, the chief of the apostles, in common, so none of us should claim as private the disciple of that same chief.

We received your blessing with the disposition of mind that we ought, finding it richly fragrant and full of good taste. We give thanks to almighty God because fragrant and flavorful are the things you do, say, and give. Let us therefore speak together about your life; let us all say together: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

## EPISTLE XL. TO MAURICIUS AUGUSTUS

He complains that he has been called a fool, that concerning Ariulf’s disposition toward peace greater credence is given to others than to him, and that Italy is meanwhile being led away captive. He earnestly exhorts the emperor to show the priests the reverence due to them. He enumerates the wounds he himself has received. He excuses Gregory the prefect and Castorius the master of soldiers. He declares that divine judgment will be different from imperial judgment.

[Col. 0765B]

Gregory to Mauricius Augustus.

In the most serene commands of the lords, while their piety sought to rebuke me concerning certain matters, it spared me not at all by its indulgence. For in them it courteously calls me a fool under the name of simplicity. In sacred Scripture, when simplicity is understood in a good sense, it is often carefully joined to prudence and uprightness. Thus it is written of blessed Job: “There was a man simple and upright” (Job 1:1). And blessed Paul the apostle exhorts us, saying: “Be simple in evil and prudent in good” (Romans 16:19). Truth itself also exhorts us, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matthew 10:16). It indicates how very useless it is if either prudence is absent from simplicity or simplicity from prudence. Therefore, wishing to make his servants instructed in all things, he wanted them to be both simple like doves and prudent like serpents, so that in them the cunning of the serpent might sharpen the simplicity of the dove, and the simplicity of the dove temper the cunning of the serpent.

I, then, who in the most serene commands of the lords am declared simple without the prudence that should accompany it, deceived by Ariulf’s cunning, am plainly called a fool; and I myself confess that this is so. For if your piety were silent about it, the facts themselves cry out. If I had not been a fool, I would certainly not have come here to endure what I suffer amid the swords of the Lombards.

But concerning what I reported about Ariulf—that he was ready with his whole heart to come over to the commonwealth—because I am not believed, I am also reproached as having lied. [Note: EPISTLE XL [Al. 31].—That is, he was ready to come to terms with the commonwealth and conclude a treaty.] Even though I am not a priest, I know that this is a grave insult to a priest: that one who serves the truth should be believed false. [Note: Thus the Vatican, English manuscripts, Norman manuscripts, and Corbie manuscript. In the printed editions, supported by the Codex Regius, it reads, “because of Ariulf.” In the Regius, however, “because of Arnulf” is found. Ariulf was duke of Spoleto, according to Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 17.]

And long ago I learned that Nordulf was believed more than I, Leo more than I, and now those who seem to be in the middle of affairs are trusted more than my assertions.

Indeed, if the captivity of my land did not increase from moment to moment, I would gladly remain silent about my contempt and mockery. But this also afflicts me greatly: the very matter for which I endure the charge of falsehood is the means by which Italy is daily being led captive beneath the Lombards’ yoke. While none of my recommendations is believed, the strength of the enemies grows monstrously.

Yet I submit this to my most merciful lord: let him think whatever evil he wishes about me, but concerning the welfare of the commonwealth and the cause of Italy’s deliverance, let him not readily lend his pious ears to just anyone; let him believe facts rather than words.

Let our lord not grow angry with priests too quickly on the basis of earthly power, but, with excellent consideration, let him rule them on account of him whose servants they are, so that he may also show them the reverence due to them. For in the divine utterances priests are sometimes called gods and sometimes angels. Thus through Moses, concerning one who is to be brought for an oath, it is said: “Bring him to the gods” (Exodus 22:8), that is, to the priests. [Note: In Hebrew, the term also sometimes means “judges.”] And again it is written: “You shall not revile the gods” (ibid. 22:28), that is, the priests. And the prophet says: “The lips of the priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7).

What is surprising, then, if your piety deigns to honor those whom God himself, granting them honor in his utterance, calls either angels or gods?

Ecclesiastical history also testifies that when written accusations against bishops had been presented to the emperor Constantine of blessed memory, he accepted the accusation documents, but summoned the bishops who had been accused and, in their presence, burned the documents he had received, saying: “You are gods, appointed by the true God. Go and settle your cases among yourselves, for it is not fitting that we should judge gods.” [Note: The printed editions read, “discuss them.” Concerning this celebrated deed of Constantine the Great, see Baronius under the year 325, no. 42 and following; among more recent writers, see Tillemont, *History of the Emperors*, under Constantine the Great. See Sozomen, Book I, chapter 16.]

In this judgment, however, my pious lord, he benefited himself more through humility than he benefited them through the reverence he showed. Before him there had been pagan princes in the commonwealth who, not knowing the true God, worshiped wooden and stone gods, yet still paid the greatest honor to their priests. [Note: The Norman manuscript reads “and indeed”; three Vatican manuscripts, “also.”] What is surprising, then, if a Christian emperor deigns to honor the priests of the true God, when pagan princes, as we have said, knew how to show honor to priests who served wooden and stone gods?

I submit these things, therefore, to the piety of the lords not on my own behalf but on behalf of all priests. I am a sinful man. And because I sin daily and without ceasing against almighty God, I suspect that it may be some remedy for me at his dread judgment if I am struck by unceasing blows every day. I believe that you appease the same almighty Lord all the more the more strictly you afflict me, who serve him badly.

I have already received many blows, and through the commands of the lords that followed I found consolations I had not expected. If I can, I shall quickly enumerate these blows.

First, my peace was taken away—the peace I had made with the Lombards situated in Tuscany, without any loss to the commonwealth. Then, when peace had been corrupted, soldiers were taken away from the city of Rome. Some were killed by the enemy, while others were stationed at Narni and Perugia; [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “at Perusia,” and below, “Perusia.” In the Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, “at Perusium” is found.] and in order that Perugia might be held, Rome was abandoned.

After this came the more grievous blow of Agilulf’s arrival. I saw with my own eyes Romans tied with ropes around their necks like dogs and led away to Gaul to be sold. And because we who were inside the city escaped his hands under God’s protection, an attempt was made to find grounds on which we might appear culpable—namely, why grain was lacking, although it cannot possibly be stored in great quantity in this city for a long time, as I explained more fully in another report. [Note: This is recounted at greater length in the final homily on Ezekiel. See Paul the Deacon, Book IV of his *History*, chapter 8.]

As for myself, I was not disturbed at all, because, with my conscience as witness, I confess that I am prepared to endure any adversity, provided only that I escape all these things with the salvation of my soul. But I have been considerably afflicted on behalf of the distinguished men Gregory the prefect and Castorius the master of soldiers. They did not neglect in any way to do everything that could be done, endured the most severe labors of watchfulness and guarding the city during that same siege, and after all this were struck by the grave indignation of the lords. From this I clearly understand that it is not their deeds but my person that burdens them. Since they had labored together with me in tribulation, they are now being troubled together with me after their labor.

As for the fact that the piety of the lords threatens me with that fearful and terrible judgment of almighty God, I beg the same almighty Lord that he not do this any further. For we still do not know who is what there. The outstanding preacher Paul says: “Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the things hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4:5).

I say this briefly: although I am unworthy and sinful, I place greater confidence in the mercy of Jesus who is to come than in the justice of your piety. There are many things concerning his judgment that human beings do not know, because perhaps what you praise he will condemn, and what you condemn he will praise.

Amid all these uncertainties, therefore, I return to tears alone, asking that the same almighty God both govern our most merciful lord here with his own hand and find him free from every sin at that terrible judgment. And if it is necessary that I please people, may he make me please them in such a way that I do not offend his eternal grace.

## EPISTLE XLI. TO CONSTANTINA AUGUSTA

He informs the empress that the Corsicans and Sicilians are being unjustly and excessively burdened. Even if less money were available for Italy’s expenses, the groans of the oppressed should nevertheless be restrained.

[Col. 0768B]

Gregory to Constantina Augusta.

Although I know that the most serene Lady thinks about the heavenly homeland and the life of her soul, I consider myself gravely at fault if I keep silent about matters which ought to be brought forward out of fear of the almighty Lord. (Gratian, 12, question 1, canon 8.) [Note: Gratian reads, “when the most devout …” (the supplied variant is incomplete).]
