When I learned that there were many pagans on the island of Sardinia, that they still served the sacrifices of idols according to the depraved custom of paganism, and that the priests of that island were sluggish in preaching our Redeemer, I sent there one of the bishops of Italy, who, with the Lord’s cooperation, led many pagans to the faith. [Note: The printed editions read “but some,” against the manuscripts. The better reading is: “But he reported to me a sacrilegious matter,” namely, the bishop sent to preach in Sardinia.]

But he reported to me a sacrilegious matter: those who sacrifice to idols there pay a fee to the judge so that they may be permitted to do this. When some of them had been baptized and had ceased sacrificing to idols, that same fee—which they had previously been accustomed to pay for the sacrifice of idols—was still demanded from them by the judge of the island even after baptism. [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts, the Regius, and the Norman read, “they had abandoned.”]

When the aforesaid bishop rebuked him, he replied that he had promised so large a payment of influence that it could not be fulfilled unless even such matters were included. [Note: Here *suffragium* is used for money given or promised to courtly patrons for the purpose of obtaining office. The term also designated the action itself, and therefore there was no occasion to apply the Julian law concerning canvassing; indeed, the emperors themselves accepted payments under the title of *suffragium*, or despotic influence. Thus Cujacius in his exposition of Novel 8, *On Governors*, in which Justinian abolished every kind of influence-buying. See the preface to that novel and chapters 1 and 7, where much is found against the sale of offices. See also Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapters 13 and 23. GUSSANVILLE.]

The island of Corsica, however, is oppressed by such excessive demands and the burden of exactions that those who live there can scarcely meet what is demanded even by selling their children. Hence it happens that, abandoning the pious commonwealth, the landowners of that island are forced to flee to the most wicked nation of the Lombards. What could they suffer from barbarians more grievous or cruel than being so constrained and oppressed that they are compelled to sell their own children?

On the island of Sicily, a certain Stephen, chartularius of the maritime districts, is said to perpetrate such injustices and such oppressions—invading the places belonging to individuals and, without stating the causes, placing titles upon their estates and houses—that, if I wished to recount one by one the records concerning him that have reached me, I could not complete the account in a large volume. [Note: Concerning the titles, see above, Book I, Letter formerly 63, now 65.] [Note: He is undoubtedly the same man mentioned in Book III, Letter 3, indiction 11. A *chartularius* of the maritime districts was one who handled and administered the public revenues of those districts; in French, *receveurs des droits, de contributions, d’impositions*. See Cujacius on the third law of the Code, title *On the Regular Contributions of the Imperial Treasury*, and Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book VII, chapter 2, where much is said about chartularii. Partly from GUSSANVILLE.]

May the most serene Lady carefully examine all these matters and restrain the groans of the oppressed. I do not suppose that these things have reached your most pious ears. For if they could have reached them, they would certainly not have continued until now. They must be brought to the most pious lord at an appropriate time, so that he may remove from his soul, his empire, and his children such a great and grievous burden of sin. [Note: The printed editions read: “that he may remove such a great and grievous deed and burden of sin.” The reading here is the one I know.]

I know that he will say that whatever is gathered from the aforesaid islands is sent to us for Italy’s expenses. But I submit this so that, even if less is allocated to expenses in Italy, he may nevertheless restrain the tears of the oppressed from his own empire. For perhaps this is also why such great expenditures yield less benefit in this land: because they are collected with some admixture of sin.

Therefore let the most serene lords order that nothing be collected with sin. And I know that, even if little is assigned to the needs of the commonwealth, the commonwealth is greatly aided by it. [Note: The common editions read, “is helped.” The phrase “even if,” and so forth, follows. All the Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, Paul’s Collection, and others have *quam*, referring back to *respublica*.]

Even if it should happen that the commonwealth is less aided through smaller expenditures, it is nevertheless better for us not to live temporally than for you to encounter some obstacle to eternal life. Consider what the minds and what the hearts of parents can be when they sell their children so that they themselves may not be tortured. Those who have children of their own know well how the children of others ought to be pitied.

Therefore it is enough for me to have briefly brought these matters forward, lest, if your piety did not know what is happening in these regions, the strict Judge should punish me for the guilt of my silence.

## EPISTLE XLII. TO SEBASTIAN, BISHOP

He is driven by the pains of this life toward love of heavenly things. He recounts what he suffers. He praises Sebastian because he refused to assume the governance of the Church offered by Anastasius. If he should ever decide to consent to it, Gregory asks him not to place anyone above him in his affection.

Gregory to Sebastian, bishop of Sirmium. [Note: EPISTLE XLII [Al. 35].—The printed editions read “to the bishop of Rhisinium.” Paul’s Collection and Vatican D read “to the bishop of Riminum.” The title we present is supplied by three other Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, all the others, the Regius, Colbertinus, Corbie, and so forth. It is also read thus in John the Deacon, Book III, chapters 43 and 49, both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions.]

I received the sweetest and most pleasing letter of your brotherhood. Although your holiness is never absent from my heart, these letters made you present to me, as though bodily. But I ask almighty God to protect you with his right hand and grant you both a peaceful life here and, when it pleases him, eternal rewards. [Note: The printed editions read, “and to us”; this is not found in the manuscripts.]

But if you love me with the love with which you have always loved me when present, I ask you to pray for me more earnestly, so that almighty God may quickly release me from the bonds of my sins and, stripping me of the burden of this corruption, make me free in his sight.

Although the sweetness of the heavenly homeland is immeasurable and draws us toward itself, there are nevertheless many pains in this life that daily impel us toward love of heavenly things. They please me in this one respect: they do not permit anything in this world to please me.

For what we suffer in this land because of the person of your friend, my lord Romanus, we are wholly unable to express. I say briefly, however, that his malice has surpassed the swords of the Lombards, so that the enemies who kill us seem more merciful than the judges of the commonwealth, who consume us through their malice, [Note: Vatican D adds, “robberies, deceptions, and crimes.”] robberies, and deceptions in thought.

To care at one and the same time for bishops and clergy, for monasteries and the people; to keep watch anxiously against the plots of the enemy; to remain perpetually suspicious of the deceptions and malice of the commanders—your brotherhood can judge more accurately what labor and sorrow this involves, the more purely you love me, who suffer these things. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, no. 49.)

Furthermore, while fulfilling the duty of greeting, I report what has reached me through the testimony of Boniface the defensor: our most holy brother, my lord Anastasius the patriarch, wished to entrust you with the governance of a Church in one of his cities, but you refused to consent. [Note: That the bishop of Rhisinium had a close relationship with Anastasius is clear from Book I, Letter 27, now 28, when Anastasius had been driven from his see. GUSSANVILLE.] I gladly embraced and greatly praised this judgment and wisdom of yours, and I considered you happy and myself unhappy, since I consented to assume the governance of a Church at such a time.

If, however, your mind should ever decide to consent to this out of condescension toward the brethren and devotion to works of mercy, I ask you not to place anyone above me in your affection. There are vacant Churches in Sicily, without bishops; and if, with God as author, you wish to govern a Church, you can do so better near the threshold of blessed Peter the apostle, with his help. But if you do not wish it, remain happily as you are, so that this intention may endure in you, and pray for us unhappy people.

May almighty God, wherever he wishes you to be, guard you with his protection and lead you to heavenly gifts. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, no. 13.)

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO EULOGIUS AND ANASTASIUS, BISHOPS

He sends them both the letters of his predecessor Pelagius and his own letters to John, who arrogates to himself the title of universal bishop. He earnestly exhorts them to attack John’s pride with common counsel and one spirit.

Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, and Anastasius, bishop of Antioch. [Note: EPISTLE XLIII [Al. 36].—He was the forty-seventh bishop of Alexandria, a man distinguished for piety and learning. Concerning him, see John Moschus, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 146 and 147; Evagrius, Book V, chapter 16. Photius mentions his writings in the *Bibliotheca*, codices 208, 225, 226, 227, 230, and 280. GUSSANVILLE.]

Since the outstanding preacher says, “Inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I honor my ministry” (Romans 11:13), and elsewhere again says, “We became as little children in the midst of you” (1 Thessalonians 2:7), he unquestionably sets before us who follow him an example: we must hold humility in our hearts and preserve the dignity of our order in honor, so that humility in us may be neither timid nor our elevation proud.

Eight years ago, in the time of my predecessor Pelagius of holy memory, our brother and fellow bishop John, seeking an occasion from another matter in the city of Constantinople, held a synod in which he attempted to call himself universal. [Note: Pelagius II’s letter, of which the holy doctor speaks shortly below, is dated March, indiction 5; from that date to indiction 13 eight years are counted.] As soon as my predecessor learned of this, he sent letters by the authority of Saint Peter the apostle and annulled the acts of that synod. I have taken care to send copies of these letters to your holiness.

He also prohibited the deacon who, according to custom, attended the feet of the most pious lords in order to deliver the responses of the Church from celebrating the solemn Mass with our aforesaid fellow priest. Following his judgment, I too sent similar writings to our aforesaid fellow priest, copies of which I considered it appropriate to send to your blessedness. My principal purpose is that, concerning this matter, by which the whole body of the universal Church is disturbed by a new pride, we may first approach the mind of our aforementioned brother with a modest intention. If he is unwilling to bend from the rigidity of his arrogance, then, with the help of almighty God, we shall consider more carefully what ought to be done.

[Note: Gussanville contends that this title was not new. He says that in the Constantinopolitan Council under Menas, in the year 536, the same title occurs a hundred times, which Binius wishes to regard as an intrusion: “Unless,” he says, “we say that Constantinople was called universal with reference to the bishops and priests subject to it in the East.” See the title of Novel 42, which Binius cites, and the note of the same compiler on Act 3 of the Council of Chalcedon, where he argues that, contrary to Saint Gregory in many places, this universal title was used more than once by the supreme pontiffs, for example by Saint Leo in Letter 54, now 78—which is false. Saint Gregory does indeed call himself Roman bishop and bishop of the universal Church, just as here he calls Eulogius and Anastasius patriarchs of the universal Church. GUSSANVILLE.]

As your venerable holiness knows, through the holy Council of Chalcedon this title of universality was offered to the pontiff of the apostolic see, which, by God’s arrangement, I serve. But none of my predecessors ever consented to use this excessively profane title, because, if one patriarch is called universal, the name of patriarch is taken away from the others.

Far be this from us; far be it from a Christian mind that anyone should wish to seize for himself something by which he might appear, even in the slightest degree, to diminish the honor of his brethren. Since, therefore, we do not wish to accept the honor that was offered to us, consider how disgraceful it is that anyone should have wished to usurp it violently for himself.

Therefore let your holiness never call anyone “universal” in your letters, lest, by offering an undue honor to another, you take away what is due to yourself. Nor should a sinister suspicion trouble your mind concerning the most serene lords in this matter, for they fear almighty God and in no way consent to do anything contrary to the evangelical statutes or the most sacred canons.

Although I am separated from you by long distances of land and sea, I am nevertheless entirely joined to you in heart. In every respect I trust this concerning your blessedness toward me: since you love me in return, you are not far from me.

Therefore we give even greater thanks to that mustard seed (Matthew 13:31–32), which, from the appearance of a small and contemptible seed, has spread so widely through branches rising from the same root and extending in every direction that all the birds of heaven nest in them. [Note: Thus the manuscripts unanimously; the printed editions read, “and more.”]

And thanks be to that leaven which mixed the whole mass of the human race into unity through three measures of flour (Matthew 13:33). [Note: The same printed editions read, “whereby [it leavened] three [measures],” etc.]

And thanks be to the small stone that was cut from the mountain without hands and filled the whole face of the earth (Daniel 2:35). [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts read, “so that, from the whole human race brought back into unity, the entire body of the Church might be perfected.”]

It spread itself everywhere to this end: that, from the human race restored to unity, the body of the whole Church might be perfected, and that this partial distinction of members might contribute to the usefulness of the entire structure. [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and the Corbie manuscript read, “of the entire framework.”]

Therefore we too are not far from you, because in him who is everywhere we are one. Let us therefore give thanks to him who, having abolished hostilities, made one flock and one sheepfold throughout the whole world in his flesh, under one shepherd. Let us always remember what the preacher of truth exhorts us, saying: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 6:3). And: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:14). He also says to other disciples: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12:18). For he saw that the good cannot live at peace with the wicked, and therefore, as you know, he prefaced his words with “if it is possible.”

But since peace cannot be firmly established unless both sides participate—when the wicked flee it, the good must hold to it with all their heart—it is admirably said, “so far as it depends on you,” so that peace may remain in us even when it is rejected by the minds of wicked people.

We truly hold this peace when, with charity and justice together, we prosecute the faults of the proud; when we love them but hate their vices. A human being is the work of God, but vice is the work of the human being. Let us therefore distinguish what God has made from what the human being has made; let us neither hate the human being because of his error nor love the error because of the human being.

With united mind, therefore, let us attack the evil of pride in the human being, so that the human being himself may first be freed from his enemy, namely, error. Our almighty Redeemer will grant strength to charity and justice; he will grant unity of his spirit to us, who are far separated from one another. He is the one by whose craftsmanship the Church, constructed like an ark with the four sides of the world, joined by a framework of incorruptible wood and bound together with the bitumen of charity, is shaken neither by any hostile spirit nor by any swelling wave that comes from outside.

But just as we must ask that, by his grace guiding us, no wave approaching from outside may disturb us, so, dearest brothers, we must pray with all the depths of our hearts that, by the right hand of his providence, he may drain away the accumulation of the inner bilge-water within us.

For the adversary, the devil, raging against the humble and, “like a roaring lion, going about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8), no longer merely circles the sheepfolds, as we see, but fixes his teeth so forcefully in certain vital members of the Church that no one can doubt that, unless the prudent company of all the shepherds hastens together unanimously with the Lord’s favor, the entire flock—God forbid—will soon be torn apart.

Consider, dearest brothers, who is close at hand to follow, whose beginnings are erupting in such perversity even among priests. For he of whom it is written, “He is king over all the sons of pride” (Job 41:25), is near. I am compelled to say this with profound sorrow: our brother and fellow bishop John, despising the Lord’s commands, the apostolic precepts, and the rules of the Fathers, is trying to rush ahead in the name through pride. [Note: The printed editions read, “what is nearby.”]

May almighty God show your blessedness with what grievous groaning of reflection I am tormented: he who was once so very modest, he who was beloved by everyone, he who seemed occupied with almsgiving, prayers, and fasts, has taken boastfulness from the ashes in which he sat and from the humility he preached, so that he attempts to ascribe everything to himself and, through the pomp of his speech, endeavors to subject to himself the members that belong solely to the one Head, namely Christ. [Note: He understands “head” in an essential sense, as the source from which all grace flows into the individual members of the body. Nevertheless, the supreme pontiff is also, in another sense, the head of the whole Church: as its chief minister and visible center of ecclesial unity, to whom all must be joined and adhere as to a head. Concerning Christ as head of the Church, see Letter 38, now 18. GUSSANVILLE.]

It is no surprise that the tempter, who knows that pride is the beginning of every sin, [Note: Vatican D reads: “And then he first dared to suggest it to the first human being above all else, and now he directs it against certain people at the end of their virtues. And he who…”] used it above all in the first human being and now places it before certain people at the end of their virtues, so that, for those who seemed, to some extent, to have escaped his most cruel hands through their good practices in life, he may set a snare at the very goal of their good work and, as it were, at the very completion of their perfection.

Therefore one must pray most earnestly, and implore Almighty God with constant prayers to turn this error away from his mind and remove from the unity and humility of the Church this evil of pride and confusion. With the Lord’s favor, we must join together and take every precaution lest, through the poison of a single utterance, living members of Christ’s body perish. For if this may be said with impunity, the honor of all the patriarchs is denied. And if perhaps the one who is called universal perishes in error, no bishop at all will be found to have remained in the state of truth.

> **Note [Col. 0773D]:** Thus in the Vatican manuscript D, five English manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, Corbie, Paul’s Collection, and the old editions. In the recent editions, supported by the Regius manuscript and certain Vatican manuscripts: “therefore I entreat.”

Therefore you must steadfastly and without prejudice preserve the Churches as you received them, and not allow this temptation of diabolical usurpation to claim anything for itself through you. Stand firm; stand secure. Do not dare ever either to issue or to accept writings bearing the falsity of the universal title. Prevent all the bishops subject to your care from being polluted by this exaltation, so that the whole Church may recognize you as patriarchs not only in good works but also in the authority of truth. If any adversity should follow, we must persevere with one accord and show, even by dying, that in suffering the loss of universality we do not cherish anything especially our own.

> **Note [Col. 0774D]:** Here we return once more to the reading of the old editions, confirmed by the authority of all the Vatican, English, Norman, Regius, and Paul’s Collection manuscripts, etc. The recent editions have: “because, in condemning the title of universality, [we do not love] our own [interest] especially.” In this letter of Gregory we recognize many excerpts from Letter 8 of Pelagius II.

Let us say with Paul: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21). Let us hear what the first of all shepherds says: “If you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed” (1 Pet. 3:14). Believe me: the honor we have assumed for preaching the truth, if necessity demands it, we shall relinquish more securely for that same truth than we hold it. For my part, pray—as is fitting for your most beloved Blessedness—that I may show by my deeds what I dare to say to you.

## LETTER XLIV. TO BISHOP LEONTIUS

**On better administration of the visitation of Rimini.**

> **Gregory [Note [Col. 0774D]:** Letter 44 [Al. 42].—That is, to Urbinus the bishop, from Book III, Letter 24, indiction 11. In the Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, only “to Bishop Leontius” is read.]

Gregory to Leontius, bishop and visitor of the Church of Rimini.

We have learned from the complaint of the clergy of the Church of Rimini (Gratian, 18, q. 2, c. 6), of which you are visitor, that after removing them all, your Fraternity entrusted the administration of its patrimony and its other affairs to your own men.

> **Note [Col. 0774D]:** The printed editions read: “after removing all the clerics.”

If this is so, we do not believe that the complaint of that clergy is unreasonable. On this matter we exhort you in these words: arrange for everything belonging to the aforesaid Church to be administered and conducted by its own men, whom you yourself shall select, or by the deacon who bears this letter, so that no just occasion for murmuring against you may be left to them. If, however, there is perhaps some suspicion of their unfaithfulness, appoint your own men to serve alongside them in the administration, so that they may be obliged to watch over one another with reciprocal care and render accounts to you in every respect.

Whatever may accrue from the revenues of that Church must, according to custom, be divided into four portions: one, namely, to be supplied to the clergy, and another to the poor. Of the remaining two portions, we wish three shares to be made: one for the repair and maintenance of the buildings, another to be sent for the support of Castorius, the proper bishop, and the remainder to be retained by you. If anyone in the clergy of the aforesaid Church should prove worthy to be ordained priest, deacon, or to another rank, you will have free authority from us to promote him.

Therefore be vigilant in winning souls, and be concerned for the uprightness of the clergy. Do not permit the assets of the Church whose visitation you administer to perish or deteriorate through any unjust concealment, lest—God forbid—you incur both the stain of perpetual danger before God and the guilt of wrongdoing before us.

Furthermore, we have learned that you obtain several grain allowances from the public treasury and that, as a result, you are constrained by embarrassment and are not as effective as you ought to be in the affairs of the Church or in defending the poor.

> **Note [Col. 0775D]:** In the common editions: “that you receive some grain allowance from the public treasury,” that is, from the fiscus. He censures Leontius because, not content with his proper stipends, he accepted grain from the treasury. Sulpicius Severus praises the Aquitanian, Gallic, and British bishops who attended the Council of Rimini because they refused to use the grain allowances and storehouses—that is, lodgings—offered them by Augustus, preferring to be supported at their own expense, with only three exceptions (Book II of the *Sacred History*).

Therefore you must abstain from what causes embarrassment and be content with the stipends you receive from the Church. For if, after our exhortation, you wish to act otherwise, we shall form a different judgment of you. You are teaching those entrusted to you to serve avarice, instructing them not to be content with sufficient stipends.

> **Note [Col. 0775D]:** Letter 45 [Al. 15, indiction 2].—This letter is absent from the English manuscripts and from most others. It is read in the San-Victor manuscript, in the Remigius manuscript of seven hundred years’ antiquity—different from the Rheims manuscript often mentioned—and in one of the Vatican manuscripts.

## LETTER XLV. TO ANDREW THE SCHOLASTIC

**He commends Castorius the chartularius.**

Gregory to Andrew the scholastic.

The quality of your known devotion, which you once showed to blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles, demonstrates how confidently we ought to presume upon the sincerity of your glory. Although we are fully confident that you are ready in mind to assist in his affairs, it is nevertheless not out of place if, in a letter of ours written out of abundance, we request those things which you have done of your own accord.

Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask that, since we have sent the bearer of this letter, Castorius our chartularius, there for necessary affairs, you assist him in all things by your support and, wherever necessary, come to his aid with the counsel of your goodness, so that, supported by the consolation of your Christian charity, he may prove diligent and capable of completing what has been entrusted to him. In this way you do what belongs to you, and you compel us to pray for you more earnestly.

May Almighty God fortify you beforehand with the protection of his grace and, as you desire, mercifully order your actions in his fear, so that here he may strip you of every evil and lead you to eternal joys.

## LETTER XLVI. TO BASILIUS

**He praises his zeal for the unity of the Church and encourages him not to be deterred from working for the return of the schismatics.**

> **Gregory [Note [Col. 0776D]:** Letter 46 [Al. 94, indiction 2].—In Vatican manuscript A, “to Basil, bishop,” but incorrectly, as is shown by the title “Basil,” which indicates his rank. Moreover, at the end of the letter Saint Gregory mentions his sons, which would rarely be appropriate for a bishop.]

Gregory to Basil.

Our heart greatly rejoices with your greatness because we find you so diligent in your actions that you acquire glory among human beings and the rewards of recompense from Almighty God.

> **Note [Col. 0776D]:** Or “obtain,” namely, the actions, as is read in three Vatican manuscripts.

Among the other praiseworthy things that you do, we have learned both through the testimony of many and now fully through our own report how the fervor of love once inflamed you against the schism of the Istrians for the unity of the Church. Therefore we implore the mercy of our Redeemer that his grace may assist you in all things and grant you to fulfill with devotion what he has permitted you to desire.

Since the benefits of recompense increase in proportion as zeal for labor increases, we greet you with paternal affection and exhort you that, when an opportunity presents itself, you must exercise your effectiveness with greater earnestness and strive by every possible means to accomplish this, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may fulfill your praiseworthy desire for the return of those who have gone astray.

> **Note [Col. 0776D]:** In the same manuscripts: “we greet you with paternal sweetness.” Letter 47 [Al. 95, indiction 2].

Your Greatness should also take care in every way to assist the bearer of this letter, Castorius our chartularius, whom we have sent there for certain affairs, so that he may increase his own good works.

May Almighty God protect and guard you, your sons, and your entire household from every adversity by his protection, and grant you both prosperity in the present life and joy in the life to come.

## LETTER XLVII. TO MASTALON

**He praises his zeal for the unity of the Church and urges him not to be deterred from working for the return of the schismatics.**

Gregory to Mastalon.

From the report of our representatives we have learned that such a fervor of divine zeal has inflamed you for love of the unity of the Church that you do not cease to recall to the bosom of Mother Church all whom you are able, and, as a good and faithful servant, do not cease daily, with the utmost attention of mind, to make profit for the Lord and our Redeemer from the gift entrusted to you.

When you came to us, we learned as best we could from the evidence of our physical sight what you were like. But now, through the testimony of your deeds, we recognize more desirably the good that, inspired by God, lay hidden in the charity of your heart.

Therefore, rendering thanks to divine mercy with ineffable praise, we exhort your Affection and encourage you with such admonitions as we can, so that, to the extent that the punishment of those who hide their received talent disturbs you, the Lord’s invitation to desire the profit of those who make gain—and thereby rejoice in receiving the heavenly kingdom—may strengthen you in equal measure.

For you should know, dearest son, that the fruit of this zeal which you have undertaken will not lack its own reward. Therefore no opposition from those who hinder you—or, if there is any, none—ought to disturb you, because the more, with the Lord cooperating, the good is accomplished through the difficulty of the matter, the more glorious the hope of reward will be for you. For whatever victory is won through the sweat of arduous labor arises all the more splendidly from apparent hopelessness.

We have also learned that Theodosius, our son, your follower and a good fellow-worker in this zeal, is diligently vigilant with you in the care of winning souls. We trust that, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, Almighty God will soon be his rewarder.

## LETTER XLVIII. TO ANDREW THE SCHOLASTIC

**After excluding Donatus because of his faults and John because of his ignorance, he explains that Marinianus, whom he knew well, was ordained unwillingly, and commends him to Andrew.**

[Col. 0777C]

Gregory to Andrew the scholastic.

We wished to fulfill the will of the most excellent lord Patricius in the person of Donatus the archdeacon. But because it is exceedingly dangerous to lay hands rashly on anyone, we took care to examine his life and conduct through careful investigation. Since many things were found—as we wrote to that same lord Patricius—which removed him far from the episcopate, we feared God’s judgment and did not venture to consent to his ordination.

> **Note [Col. 0777C]:** Letter 48 [Al. 45].—The recent edition reads: “which would remove him from the episcopate because of his fault,” a reading found nowhere in the manuscripts except Vatican manuscript B.

Nor did we venture to ordain the priest John, who did not know the Psalms, because this fact showed that he possessed too little diligence in his own calling.

> **Note [Col. 0777D–0778D]:** At the Second Council of Nicaea, canon 2: “We decree that anyone who is to be advanced to the episcopal rank must know the Psalter completely,” and so forth. Let the diligent reader consult and weigh the entire canon and judge from it what the council’s general view was concerning the knowledge and learning of bishops. Nicephorus reports from Gennadius, in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XV, chapter 23, that he consecrated no priest who had not previously kept the Psalter diligently in his mouth. See Book XII, Letter 6, now Book XIV, Letter 7, concerning Rusticus the deacon, who was rejected from the bishopric of Ancona because of ignorance of the Psalms. The Eighth Council of Toledo, canon 8: “It is decreed that no one of whatever ecclesiastical dignity shall receive a rank who does not perfectly know the entire Psalter, or the customary canticles and hymns, or the proper rite of baptism.” In the constitutions of Riculfus, bishop of Soissons, in the year 889, chapter 5: “We admonish each of you to strive to retain the Psalms” and so forth “by heart, truly, and correctly.” Saint Jerome likewise says in Letter 4 to Rusticus: “Let him learn the Psalter word for word,” and in Letter 7 to Laeta, on the education of her daughter: “Let her first learn the Psalter,” and so forth. Moreover, the custom long prevailed of singing the Psalms by heart and without a book, and traces of this custom still remain in certain places, such as the Church of Lyon and that of Rouen. I say nothing of the Carthusians and other ancient ascetics, among whom novices are required to learn the Psalter by heart during their first year after conversion, because they were accustomed to sing it by heart in church. Gussanville. For encomia of the Psalms, see Basil, Ambrose, Augustine, and others.]

After these men had been excluded, when we were pressed, together with them, to choose someone from among their own number, and they admitted that they had no one suitable for this office, while an even greater affliction held us all, they finally and repeatedly requested the venerable brother Marinianus the priest, whom they had long known to have lived with me in the monastery, doing so with a common and unanimous voice and consent.

Though he resisted, he could scarcely, after various efforts, be persuaded to consent to their request. Since his life is well known to us and we know him to be diligent in winning souls, we offered no delay in his ordination.

> **Note [Col. 0777D]:** Thus in the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and other manuscripts, where the editions read: “we did not presume.”

Therefore let your Glory receive him as is fitting and extend to his novelty the assistance of consolation. For, as you know, the novelty of any office is extremely burdensome to everyone.

I have great confidence that Almighty God, who has deigned to place him over his flock, will sharpen him for caring for its inward needs and, by the mercy of his grace, strengthen him for conducting its outward affairs. But since, after the long repose of his former life, his novelty is undoubtedly troubled, as we have said, I ask that, whenever he comes fleeing the storms of worldly tempests, he may always find in your mind a harbor of quiet and rejoice in the goodness of your charity.

How much he may suit you in association, you will soon discover, because he has come to the episcopate unwillingly.

> **Note [Col. 0778D]:** Saint Gregory explains most fully, in the book *On Pastoral Rule*, especially Part I, for what reason even those who are called to the episcopate ought not readily to approach it.

## LETTER XLIX. TO LEANDER THE BISHOP

**He sends books for the exposition of blessed Job and the book of the *Pastoral Rule*.**

[Col. 0778C]

Gregory to Leander, bishop of Hispalis.

> **Note [Col. 0778D]:** Letter 49 [Al. 46].—In Corbie and the Norman manuscript only “to the bishop” is read. In three Vatican manuscripts: “to the bishop of Spain.” We have already spoken of him in the notes to the letter prefixed to the books of the *Moralia*, and elsewhere.

How ardently I long to see you, since you love me greatly, you may read in the tablets of your heart. But because I cannot see you, separated as you are by a great distance of land, I have done the one thing that charity toward you dictated: I have sent to your Holiness, through the arrival of our common son, the priest Probinus, the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, which I wrote at the beginning of my episcopate, and the books that you have long known me to have composed as an exposition of blessed Job.

I did not send your Charity the codices of the third and fourth parts of that work, because I have already given monasteries the codices from those same parts.

> **Note [Col. 0779D]:** Thus we restore the reading according to the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and other manuscripts, whereas the editions read: “because I find only those codices which I excerpted from the same parts, which I have already given to monasteries.” What could be more tangled and obscure?

Let your Holiness read these attentively, and bewail my sins still more attentively, lest it be counted as a graver fault for me that I seem to know what I neglect to do. How greatly I am oppressed in this Church by the tumults of affairs, the brevity of my letter itself makes known to your Charity, since I say little to one whom I love more than all others.

## LETTER L. TO JOHN THE ABBOT

**He is to proceed to the monastery of Saint Andrew to restrain and punish the vicious.**

[Col. 0779B]

Gregory to John, abbot of Regio.

> **Note [Col. 0779D]:** In many and better manuscripts “of Regio” is omitted.

It is neither right nor fitting for us to pass over matters that concern the correction of religious persons. Therefore it has come to our attention that many crimes are being committed in the monastery of Saint Andrew, which is situated near Vulcanus.

> **Note [Col. 0779D]:** He perhaps means the island of Vulcano, adjacent to Sicily and near Lipara, now commonly called Vulcano. Concerning it, Virgil writes in *Aeneid* VIII:

> “The house of Vulcan and the land called Vulcanian.”

Therefore, supported by the command of our authority, you must proceed to that monastery and examine all the reported matters through careful investigation. If you find that things are indeed as reported—God forbid—then punish them according to the Rule, so that an appropriate correction may teach them thereafter to abstain from wicked and unlawful acts.

## LETTER LI. TO BISHOPS PETER AND PROVIDENTIUS

**He writes that he will satisfy them concerning the faith and promises that he will cause no trouble for them when they come to Rome.**

[Col. 0779C]

Gregory to Peter and Providentius, bishops of Istria.

> **Note [Col. 0779D]:** This bishop is called so in all the Vatican, English, Norman, Teller, and other manuscripts, not “Prudentius,” as in the printed editions.

God, who rejoices in the unity of the faithful and reveals the truth to those who seek it, may open to your hearts, dearest brothers, with what desire I wish you to be held within the bosom of the holy universal Church and to remain united in its fellowship.

I do not doubt that this will happen if, having cast aside the spur of contention, you attend sincerely to receiving satisfaction concerning the matters about which you are uncertain. From the report of my returning notary Castorius I have learned that your Fraternity desires to come to me, provided it is promised that you will suffer no trouble.

Knowing this, I both desire it and, kindled by the ardor of charity, invite you to undertake the labor of coming to me, so that, conferring together, we may speak collectively about what is true and pleasing to our Redeemer and hold to it in every way.

With the grace of divine protection assisting me, I am ready to satisfy you concerning the matters about which you doubt. I trust in the clemency of Almighty God that my satisfaction will take such inward hold upon you that nothing doubtful will thereafter remain for your Charity.

For what the four most holy councils taught and defined, we too, like our predecessor the most holy Pope Leo, teach, follow, and hold; nor do we dissent in any way from their faith. But because a person who is present gives greater satisfaction than a letter, I exhort you, dearest brothers, to come to me, as I have said, provided that, once you have received an explanation, no disagreement separates you from the harmony of the holy universal Church.

Let your Charity be certain of this: I shall receive you with the affection that is fitting and release you with favor. Nor do I permit or consent that you, or any others who may wish to come to me for this reason, should suffer any affliction or trouble.

> **Note [Col. 0780D]:** The Norman, Rheims, and certain other manuscripts read “I permit”; the old editions agree.

Whether divine mercy should move your hearts to agree with me, or—God forbid—you should happen to remain in that disagreement, we shall arrange, according to my promise, to release you to return to your own homes whenever you wish, without injury or trouble.

> **Note [Col. 0780D]:** Thus it is read in two Vatican manuscripts, but not in our old manuscripts.

In the month of August, indiction 13.

> **Note:** Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 37.

## LETTER LII. TO JOHN THE ARCHBISHOP

**He praises Bishop Secundinus because he properly investigated and concluded the case of Anastasius. He pardons the clerics Paul and Clematius, who had withdrawn from the accusation of Anastasius, but permanently excludes Euphemius and Thomas from the sacred orders that they had received as the reward of their crime. He orders that the customary stipends be distributed to each and that whatever Paul had spent for the benefit of the Church be restored to him.**

[Col. 0780C]

Gregory to John, archbishop of Corinth.

> **Note [Col. 0780D]:** Letter 52 [Al. 51].—The common editions read “to the bishop.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.

The equity and diligence of our brother and co-bishop Secundinus, which we had long known to be good, have also been demonstrated by the indicated sequence of the judgment.

> **Note [Col. 0780D]:** In Corbie, Regius, and the Norman manuscript: “the sequence of the judgment showed.” The old editions agree. In the recent editions: “the indicated sequence of your writings showed.” This reading is found in three Vatican manuscripts, except for the words “of your writings,” which we have found in no manuscript.

In this matter he greatly pleased us and made us glad, because in the case of Anastasius, formerly a bishop, which we had entrusted to him for examination, he diligently exercised his vigilance and judged the crimes he had discovered as justice required and as was fitting.

> **Note [Col. 0780D]:** The printed editions read “he punished,” contrary to the manuscripts.

In all these things, however, we give thanks to Almighty God, who, when certain accusers withdrew, revealed the truth to his examination, lest the cause of such great crimes be able to remain hidden.

Since, in the same sentence by which the aforesaid Anastasius is known to have been justly condemned and deposed, the aforesaid brother and co-bishop punished certain persons in such a way as to reserve the matter for our judgment, we have therefore thought it appropriate to indicate by this letter what must be held and observed concerning them.

As for Paul the deacon, the bearer of this letter (Gratian, 2, q. 4, c. 6), although his own fault severely disgraces and rebukes him because, deceived by a promise, he recently withdrew from the accusation of his former bishop, who had been deposed, and, out of a desire for gain, consented to remain silent against his own soul rather than disclose the truth, nevertheless, since it is more fitting for us to be merciful than strict, we pardon him this fault and judge that he should be restored to his rank and place.

> **Note [Col. 0781C–0781D]:** The jurists discuss the penalty of one who withdraws from an accusation when they explain the Turpillian decree of the Senate. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book V, chapter 21, concerning the suspension of a bishop from communion because he had withdrawn from an accusation. We indicate here the antinomy that exists among the canons concerning accusations against bishops. Neither laymen nor lower clerics are permitted to accuse their bishops; yet the same persons are permitted to accuse them. See Cause 2, Question 7. The Council of Chalcedon resolves the difficulty in canon 21: “Clerics or laymen who accuse their bishops or clerics indiscriminately and without proof are not to be admitted to the accusation unless their own reputation is first examined.” The Council of Constantinople I treats the same matter still more clearly in canon 6, which the reader should consult. I add one point: if it is permissible to accuse, then it is also permissible to admonish and correct the offender when charity, not malicious zeal, demands it. For it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act maliciously against my prophets” (Ps. 104:15). Gussanville.

We believe that the affliction he endured from the time the sentence was pronounced can suffice as punishment for this fault.

But Euphemius and Thomas, who received sacred orders in exchange for abandoning the accusation, we wish to remain deprived of those same sacred orders, just as they were deposed, and we decree that they may never be restored to the sacred orders under any pretext of excuse. For it is exceedingly unworthy and contrary to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline that they should exercise an honor which they obtained not through merit but as the reward of a crime.

Nevertheless, since it is more fitting for us to devote ourselves to mercy than to strict justice, we wish Euphemius and Thomas to be restored only to the rank and place from which they had been promoted to sacred orders, and to receive throughout all the days of their lives the customary maintenance of those places, as they had previously done.

> **Note [Col. 0781D]:** This means the clerical stipend, the *sportula* or allotted subsistence allowance, which it was customary to give to clerics serving in that place. The same matter is immediately repeated concerning the deacon Paul and Clematius in different words. Gussanville.

As for Clematius the lector, I likewise decree, out of consideration for kindness, that he be restored to his rank and place.

To all of them—that is, to the deacon Paul, Euphemius, Thomas, and Clematius—your Fraternity must diligently provide their customary benefits, according to the place and rank each one holds, without any reduction, beginning with the present thirteenth indiction.

Since the aforesaid deacon Paul recalls having spent much for the benefit of your Church and desires to be assisted by the support of your Fraternity in recovering it, we exhort you, if this is so, to help him in every possible way to recover what he gave and to assist him with your support. For no principle permits him to suffer unjust loss in what he expended for the benefit of the community.

Moreover, it is established that, at the prompting of the aforesaid brother and co-bishop Secundinus, the deacon Paul gave three pounds of gold for the benefit of your Church. Your Fraternity must restore this sum without delay, lest—God forbid—it appear that you are burdening him not reasonably but merely by your own arbitrary will.

> **Note [Col. 0781D–0782C]:** In the Turin, Saint Gall, and old Paris edition of 1518, the following is added: “in the month of August, indiction 13.” And indeed the thirteenth indiction is noted in the sequence of the letter.

> **Note [Col. 0782C–0782D]:** Letter 53 [Al. 50].—In Gussanville, supported by two Teller manuscripts, it is dated June 6, indiction 13. It should therefore be placed before the former Letters 43 and 44 of the same indiction, dated in July. But in the manuscript Collection of Deacon Paul it is dated August 12, indiction 13. It survives complete among the letters of John VIII and is Letter 94 to Rostagnus of Arles. In two Vatican manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, and the Rheims manuscript, it is addressed to “Virgil,” and so forth, and sent into Gaul through John the priest and Sabinianus the deacon. Two other Vatican manuscripts differ only slightly.

## LETTER LIII. TO BISHOP VIRGIL

**He grants him his vicariate in the kingdom of Childebert. He warns him to prevent the stain of simony and not to allow laymen suddenly to become bishops. Concerning the use of the pallium and the extent to which he must exercise the apostolic vicariate.**

[Col. 0782B]

Gregory to Virgil, bishop of Arles.

O how good is charity, which makes absent persons present to one another through the image of love; which unites what is divided, orders what is confused, joins together those who are unequal, and completes what is imperfect. How rightly the distinguished preacher calls it “the bond of perfection,” because the other virtues indeed produce perfection, but charity also binds them together so that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

I find you full of this virtue, dearest brother, as both those who come to me from the regions of Gaul and the words of your letters sent to me testify.

As for your request, according to ancient custom, for the use of the pallium and the exercise of the apostolic see’s vicariate, let me not suspect that you have sought either the height of a transient power or the adornment of external dress in our vicariate and pallium.

> **Note [Col. 0782D–0783C]:** Below, Book II, Letter 64: “From the ancient times of my predecessors, the bishop of Arles received the pallium.” Virgil was already archbishop in indiction 9 and had exercised his office for several years without the pallium, as is clear both from his life and from Book I, Letter 47. The necessity of the pallium had therefore not yet been introduced, nor did ecclesiastical authority yet depend upon that instrument of external dress.

> **Note [Col. 0782D–0783C]:** For the beginning of this legation in Gaul, see Pope Zosimus’s Letters 5 and 11 to Patroclus of Arles, as well as Pope Hilary’s Letters 8, 9, and 10. After Zosimus, the other Roman pontiffs did not favor the bishops of Arles so greatly—Boniface II, Celestine I, and Leo I—until Symmachus, in the year 514, granted Caesarius of Arles the use of the pallium together with the vicariate of the apostolic see. Then, around the year 545, Vigilius granted the same privilege first to Auxanius and afterward to Aurelianus, in Letters 7 and 10; later Pelagius I granted it to Sapaudus in Letter 12; and finally Gregory the Great granted it to Virgil. After Virgil, we read of no bishop of Arles being endowed with those privileges until, toward the end of the ninth century, John VIII entrusted his own vicariate in Gaul to Rostagnus of Arles, who appropriated this letter and the following one with only a few omissions.

But since it is clear to everyone from where the holy faith emerged in the regions of Gaul, when your Fraternity revives the ancient custom of the apostolic see, what else is happening but that a good offspring returns to the bosom of its mother? We therefore gladly grant what you have requested, lest we seem either to withhold from you any of the honor due to you or to disregard the petition of our most excellent son, King Childebert.

But from this point onward the matter requires greater diligence, so that as your honor grows, your responsibility may also advance; so that your vigilance in guarding others may increase; so that the merits of your life may become an example to those subject to you; and so that your Fraternity may never seek its own interests through the grace of the honor it has received, but only the gains of the heavenly homeland.

For you know what the blessed apostle says with a sigh: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21).

According to the report of certain persons, I have learned that in the regions of Gaul or Germany no one attains sacred orders without the payment of money.

> **Note [Col. 0783C–0784C]:** Much is inserted here that is found word for word in other letters. See below, Letters 57 and 58. Here he means either the regions of Germany, or all Gaul, because the Franks came from Germany; or Lugdunensian Gaul, which Sidonius Apollinaris, Book V, Letter 7, calls “Lugdunensian Germany”; or, finally, the German provinces subject to the king of the Austrasians, namely, beyond the Rhine: Thuringia, which, after being conquered by Theodoric, the son of Clovis the Great, also received Christian laws, as Gregory of Tours testifies in Book III of his *History*, chapters 4, 7, and 9; and, on this side of the Rhine, Mainz, called Germania Prima, and Cologne, called Germania Secunda. Below, Book VIII, Letter 30, Augustine is made bishop by the bishops of the Germanies—that is, he was ordained by Virgil himself, the bishop of Arles. As for simony spreading in Gaul, beginning in the time of Brunhild, it is discussed in the *Life of Saint Eligius* by Saint Audoenus, bishop of Rouen, mentioned shortly below.

If this is so, I say with tears and denounce with groans that, when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it will not be able to stand long outwardly either.

We know from the Gospel what our Redeemer did through himself: he entered the Temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:12).

> **Note [Col. 0783D–0784C]:** Saint Hilary explains the matter in the same sense in his commentary on Matthew 21. In the dove, according to the examples of prophecy, we understand the Holy Spirit. In the seat is the seat of the priesthood. Therefore he overturned the seats of those who sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, those whose ministry entrusted by God has become a commercial transaction. Gregory worked through many letters with prelates of eminent authority and with the kings themselves to remove the stain of simony from Gaul. See below, Letter 55, and Book IX, Letters 11, 106, 109, and 110; Book XI, Letters 55, 56, 57, 59, 60, and 61. In the time of King Dagobert, at the urging of Saints Audoenus and Eligius, a council was held against simoniacal corruption. All agreed, by one counsel in the Holy Spirit and together with the king’s command, that no one should be admitted to priestly office after paying a price. Thus Saint Audoenus, Book II of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, chapter 1. Nevertheless, this stain had not yet been wiped away in the ninth century, as John VIII shows in Letter 94. Indeed, in the twelfth century Ivo of Chartres lamented that simony in Gaul was being defended by the custom of the Roman Church, in Letter 153. What Gregory the Great writes here against the Simoniacs he repeats in exactly the same words in Book V, Letter 58, and at greater length in Book IX, Letter 107.

For to sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom Almighty God, consubstantial with himself, gives to human beings through the laying on of hands. From this evil, as I have said, what follows is already indicated. For those who presumed to sell doves in God’s Temple have had their seats overturned by God’s judgment.

That error, moreover, spreads among those subject to them with continual increase. For the very man who is advanced to the sacred order in exchange for payment, already corrupted at the very root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. And where is what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:8)?

And since the first simoniacal heresy arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that the man whom someone ordains and advances for a price, by advancing him causes him to become a heretic?

[Note: He uses “heresy” in a broader sense for simoniacal depravity. See Launoius, *Book on Simony*, Observations 3, 4, 5, and 11.]

Another matter, likewise, has been reported to us as utterly detestable: that certain men from the lay state, out of a desire for temporal glory, are tonsured after bishops have died and suddenly become priests.

[Note: See Book II, Letter 25. Gregory forbids laymen to be tonsured and, when churches are vacant, immediately ordained bishops, as was customary in Gaul, in this letter and in Letter 55, as well as in Book IX, Letters 11, 106, 109, and 110. The same practice had been forbidden to the Gauls by Zosimus, Letter 9, to Patroclus of Arles; Celestine I, Letter 2, to the bishops of the Province of Vienne and Narbonne; Symmachus, Letter 5, to Caesarius of Arles; Felix IV, Letter 8, to the same; the Council of Arles II, canon 1; and Arles IV.]

In this matter it is already clear what sort of man comes to the priesthood when he suddenly passes from lay status to sacred leadership. And the man who has never been a soldier does not fear to become a leader of the religious.

[Note: In the same sense below, Letter 55, concerning laymen who, once tonsured, climb precipitously to the episcopate: “Priests seize leadership for themselves who have not seen the beginning of religious warfare.” Gregory the Great also uses the word “religious” to mean a cleric: Book IV, Letter 22, “all the clerics and the other religious”; and Book IX, Letter 107, one who is suddenly “planted in the religious state” is said of one who has suddenly become a cleric so that he may be elected bishop.]

What preaching will such a man have, who perhaps has never heard another’s? Or when will he correct the sins of others, who has not yet mourned his own? And since the Apostle Paul forbids a neophyte to come to the sacred orders, we must understand that just as a neophyte was then called one who had only recently been planted in the faith, so now we count among neophytes one who is still new in holy conduct.

(Gratian, Distinction 48, chapter “Sicut.”)

We know, moreover, that walls under construction do not first receive the weight of beams until they have been dried by the moisture of their newness, lest, if they receive the burdens before they have been strengthened, they bring the whole structure down to the ground at once. And when we cut down saplings for a building, we wait for the moisture of their greenness to dry first, lest, if the weight of the structure is placed upon them while they are still fresh, they bend because of their very newness and, once broken, quickly collapse—though they had seemed to be raised prematurely to a height. Why, then, is this not carefully observed in human beings, when it is considered with such care even in wood and stone?

For this reason, your Fraternity must make every effort to admonish our most excellent son, King Childebert, so that he may utterly drive the stain of this sin from his kingdom, in order that almighty God may grant him greater rewards in proportion as He sees him both loving what He Himself loves and avoiding what He hates.

Accordingly, with God’s authority, we entrust to your Fraternity our functions in the churches that lie under the rule of our most excellent son Childebert, in accordance with ancient custom, while the proper honor of each metropolitan is preserved according to the old usage. We have also sent the pallium (Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 6), which your Fraternity is to use within the church only for the solemn celebrations of Mass. If, however, any bishop should perhaps wish to travel farther away, he may not go to other places without the authority of Your Holiness.

[Note: Some call the greater causes of faith “major cases” and maintain that they must be reserved for the supreme pontiff. Saint Gregory did not judge so, unless perhaps they could not be decided in the provinces because of their extreme difficulty. Certainly they are referred to the apostolic see only after an inquiry has first been made and the truth has been examined and debated locally. See Letter 55 below: “When its uncertainty is perhaps considerable … after the truth has been examined more carefully,” and so forth. See Cyprian, Letter 55; Pope Hilary, Letter 8. For what would happen in a similar case among the Jews, see Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, Book IV, chapter 8, whose testimony we cited in Letter 4, Indiction 10, concerning these same major cases. GUSSANV.]

If any inquiry concerning the faith, or perhaps any other matter among the bishops, should arise that is more difficult to determine, let it be debated and decided after twelve bishops have been assembled. If it cannot be decided, let it be referred to our judgment after the truth has been examined. May almighty God guard you with His protection and grant that you preserve in your conduct the honor you have received.

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscripts, with the Collection of Paul agreeing. But in two Tellerian manuscripts and in the printed editions the letter is read as dated June 6, Indiction 13.]

Given on August 12, Indiction 13.

## LETTER LIV. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF CHILDEBERT’S KINGDOM

They are to obey Virgilius of Arles, to whom Gregory has entrusted his functions; they are to come to synod when summoned by him; and they are not to travel to distant places without his authority.

[Note: LETTER LIV [Elsewhere 52].—The bishops under Childebert’s kingdom were nearly all the bishops of Gaul. For Childebert possessed the kingdom of the Austrasians and the kingdom of Burgundy, which he had acquired through the death and testament of his uncle Guntram. His cousin-brother Chlothar possessed a few cities in Neustria along the Loire, Seine, and Isère rivers and by the Ocean; except for these and Gothia, which belonged to the Goths, all the rest of Gaul then obeyed Childebert. On the boundaries of the kingdom of Austrasia and the kingdom of Burgundy, consult Adrian Valesius, Books VII and IX of *Frankish History*. GUSSANV. In the Register and in two Vatican manuscripts, B and C, the title of this letter reads: “To all the bishops of Gaul who are under the kingdom of our most excellent son Childebert.”]

Gregory to all the bishops of Gaul who are under Childebert’s kingdom.

Divine providence has established different degrees and distinct orders, so that, while those of lesser rank show reverence to their superiors and superiors extend affection to their inferiors, a single concord is woven from diversity and the administration of each office is rightly carried out. For the whole community could not otherwise subsist unless an arrangement of such great difference preserved it.

Because creation cannot be governed or live in one identical equality, the pattern of the heavenly armies instructs us: since there are angels and archangels, it is clear that they are not equal, but that one differs from another in power and rank, as you know.

[Note: The printed editions, supported by a few manuscripts, read “in one and the same quality.” Our reading is found in all the English and Norman manuscripts, in Corbie, and in two Vatican manuscripts. The following words prove it to be correct: “that they are not equal.”]

If, then, among those who are without sin there is this distinction, who among human beings would refuse willingly to submit to an arrangement which he knows even the angels obey? From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn, and the integrity of concord remains firm in an alternating and God-pleasing love.

Since, therefore, each office is completed beneficially when there is one superior to whom recourse may be had, we have judged it appropriate, according to ancient custom, to grant our functions in the churches under the kingdom of our most excellent son, King Childebert, to our brother Virgilius, bishop of the city of Arles. Thus, with God’s protection, the integrity of the catholic faith—that is, of the four holy synods—may be preserved with vigilant devotion; and if some dispute should arise among our brothers and fellow priests, he may restrain it with the strength of his authority and with prudent moderation, exercising in turn the functions of the apostolic see.

We have also instructed him that, if a dispute should arise in which the presence of others is necessary, he should assemble our brothers and fellow bishops in suitable number, examine the matter beneficially while preserving equity, and decide it with canonical integrity.

[Note: He is not to decide alone except in minor matters, even though he exercises the functions of the Roman pontiff.]

But if, which may almighty God keep far away, any dispute concerning the faith should occur, or a matter should arise whose uncertainty is perhaps considerable and which, because of its importance, requires the judgment of the apostolic see, let him examine the truth with the greatest care and endeavor to bring it to our notice by his report, so that it may without doubt be concluded by us with an appropriate judgment.

And since it is necessary that, whenever he sees it to be appropriate, bishops should assemble at suitable times with him to confer, we exhort you that none of you presume to disobey his commands or put off attending the common assembly, unless bodily illness should perhaps prevent someone, or a just excuse connected with some matter should not permit him to come.

Those who, because of some necessity, cannot assemble in synod should send in their place a priest or deacon, so that whatever, with God’s help, has been decided by our representative may reach the absent bishop by a faithful report through the person he has sent.

[Note: The same manuscripts read “with unshaken firmness.” We would not depart from them unless the common agreement of the manuscripts compelled us.]

Thus the decisions may be preserved with unshaken firmness,

[Note: In the printed editions: “And let no excuse of anyone violate what he has established.” Vatican D supports this reading.]

and no excuse of any kind may dare to violate them.

We have also foreseen that you must be admonished of this: none of you should attempt in any way to travel to more distant places without the authority of the aforementioned brother and our fellow bishop Virgilius, knowing that the commands of our predecessors, who granted their functions to his predecessors, unquestionably prescribe the same.

Furthermore, we exhort each of you to be solicitous about his office, so that he who desires to receive the promised reward of feeding may guard the flock entrusted to him with vigilance and prayer, lest the lurking wolf invade and tear apart the sheep entrusted to him, and punishment take the place of reward.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we desire and with all our prayers entreat almighty God to make your love grow ever more fervent in the constancy of His love, and to grant that you may be held firmly in the peace of the Church and in one great concord.

It has also been reported to us that certain persons are being brought to the sacred orders through simoniacal heresy, and we have commanded the aforementioned brother and our fellow bishop Virgilius to prohibit this in every respect. In order that your Fraternity may know this and carefully observe it, this letter itself is to be read aloud before you.

[Note: Thus the old Colbert manuscript and the Collection of Paul. In two Tellerian manuscripts the month and indiction agree, but August 11 is assigned instead of the 12th.]

Given on August 12, Indiction 13.

## LETTER LV. TO KING CHILDEBERT

He says that he has granted Virgilius his functions and the use of the pallium at the king’s request; he urges the king in turn to support Virgilius in prohibiting simony and in preventing laymen from suddenly becoming bishops.

[Note: LETTER LV [Elsewhere 53].—This Childebert was the younger Childebert, king of the Austrasians, son of King Sigibert and Brunhild.]

Gregory to Childebert, king of the Franks.

Your Excellency’s letter made us exceedingly glad, for it testifies that you are concerned with pious affection for the honor and reverence due to the priesthood. In this way you show all that you are faithful worshipers of God, since you love His priests with grateful and fitting veneration and hasten, with Christian devotion, to do whatever contributes to their advancement.

Therefore we gladly received what you wrote and willingly granted what you desired. Accordingly, with God’s favor, we entrusted our functions, according to ancient custom, to our brother Virgilius, bishop of the city of Arles, and we also granted him the use of the pallium, as ancient custom has established.

But because certain matters have been reported to us which greatly offend almighty God and profoundly compromise the honor and reverence of the priesthood, we ask that they be corrected in every way through the vigorous exercise of your authority,

[Note: The printed editions read “with your authority consenting.”]

lest, while reckless and perverse actions oppose your praiseworthy devotion, the fault of others—God forbid—burden either your kingdom or your soul.

It has come to us that, when bishops die, certain laymen are tonsured and climb to the episcopate by a precipitous leap. And one who has not been a disciple becomes a teacher through inconsiderate ambition.

And since he has not learned what he might teach, he bears the priesthood in name only; for in speech and conduct he remains a layman as before. How, then, will he intercede for the sins of others who has not first mourned his own? Such a pastor does not protect the flock but deceives it. For, since shame prevents him from persuading others to do what he himself does not do, what else follows except that the Lord’s people remain to be ravaged by plunderers and perish at the very place from which they ought to have received the great support of saving protection?

[Note: The holy man repeats this same point once and again elsewhere; it is certainly worthy of being impressed upon us and strengthened by frequent repetition, lest those who reject knowledge or confine it within narrow limits be rejected by God. The burden of pre-eminence is great because of the countless difficulties surrounding it; but the necessity of preaching is especially grave, and one who has not absorbed all sacred Scripture cannot easily discharge it. John Gerson should be read, sermon delivered at the Council of Rheims, consideration 2, where, after many points relevant to this matter, he says: “Knowledge of the sacred Scriptures is required, together with all the other things that concern morals.” Hence, when a pastor is consecrated, he is asked: “Do you know both Testaments?” Let those who answer “I know” consider with what conscience they do so. That is what he says. GUSSANV.]

Your Excellency’s dignity may judge how corrupt and perverse this is from your own ordering of affairs. It is certain that you do not place a commander over an army before the value of his service and his loyalty have become known to you, and before the virtue and diligence of his past life have shown him to be suitable. If an army to be governed is entrusted only to men of this kind, one may rightly infer from this comparison what sort of commander souls ought to have.

Yet it is shameful for us, and we are embarrassed even to say it, that priests seize leadership for themselves who have not seen the beginning of religious warfare.

At the same time, another matter has been reported to us which is exceedingly abhorrent: that the sacred orders are conferred through simoniacal heresy—that is, after a reward has been received.

Since it is exceedingly pestilential and contrary to the universal holy Church for someone to be placed in a sacred order not for his merits but for a price, we exhort Your Excellency to order that so detestable a crime be prohibited throughout your kingdom. For the man who does not fear to purchase the gift of God with money and presumes to seek advantages which he does not deserve to possess by grace has shown himself wholly unworthy of this office.

I therefore admonish you of these things, most excellent son, because I desire your soul to be saved. I would also have written these things long ago,

[Note: Thus the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, instead of “I wished to write.” The printed editions read “I wished to write.”]

if countless occupations had not greatly hindered my intention. But when a suitable opportunity for replying presented itself, I did not omit what I ought to do.

Therefore, as we salute Your Excellency with paternal affection, we ask that everything we have commanded the aforementioned brother and our fellow bishop to do and to preserve be completed with the support of your favor, and that you not permit any of it to be overturned in any way by anyone’s arrogance or pride.

[Note: The printed editions add: “But just as it was preserved by each of his predecessors under the reign of your glorious father, so also … with wholly careful devotion preserved.” We do not find these words in any manuscript.]

Rather, just as it was preserved by his predecessor under the reign of your glorious father, so also, with your assistance, let it be preserved with careful and fitting devotion.

It is therefore right that this be repaid to us in turn; and just as we did not delay fulfilling your will, so you, for the sake of God and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, should ensure that our statutes are observed in every respect, so that the praiseworthy and God-pleasing reputation of Your Excellency may spread everywhere.

[Note: Thus the old Colbert manuscript. In the Collection of Paul it is dated May 16. In two Tellerian manuscripts, August 10, Indiction 14.]

Given on August 12, Indiction 13.

## LETTER LVI. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP

He grants the use of the pallium and confirms the privileges of the Church of Ravenna.

[Col. 0789C]

[Note: LETTER LVI [Elsewhere 54].—After John, bishop of Ravenna, died in 595, the people of Ravenna unanimously elected as bishop Marinianus, a presbyter and citizen of their city, whom they had known to have lived for a long time with Saint Gregory in the monastery. Though he resisted for a long time, Gregory could scarcely persuade him to consent to the election made on his behalf. Although he had been a monk, he nevertheless appeared somewhat hostile to monks, as may be seen in Book V, Letter 24, now Book VI. Paul the Deacon also speaks of him in Book IV, chapter 11. GUSSANV.]

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Moved by the benevolence of the apostolic see and by the order of ancient custom, we have determined to grant the use of the pallium to your Fraternity, which has evidently undertaken the office of governing the Church of Ravenna.

You must remember to use it only after the sons of the Church in your own city have been dismissed, when you proceed from the salutatory to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass; when the Masses have been completed, you must again arrange to remove it in the salutatory.

[Note: He commonly calls the laity the “sons of the Church,” but the clergy the “soldiers of the Church.” See Book VI, Letter 3: “lest, therefore, the sons of the Church,” and so forth. Before the celebration of Mass, the bishop sat in the secretarium, now commonly called the sacristy, to receive the greetings of the faithful; after they had been dismissed, he put on the sacred vestments and proceeded to the altar. Hence that place was called the salutatory. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book II, chapter 21; Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 24, no. 2.]

[Note: Above, “the secretarium,” and so forth, Book I, Letter 19. GUSSANV.]

Outside the church, however, we permit you to use it no more than four times a year, at the litanies which we prescribed for your predecessor John. We nevertheless admonish you that, just as, by the Lord’s generosity, you have received this distinction for the honor of the priestly office, so you should strive to adorn the office you have undertaken by the integrity of your conduct and actions, to the glory of Christ.

For you will be conspicuous in both forms of honor in turn if the goodness of your mind also corresponds to this bodily vesture. We also confirm by our authority all the privileges which are known to have been previously granted to your Church, and decree that they remain unimpaired.

## LETTER LVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP

After the most wicked predecessor Anastasius, he is to govern the Corinthians in such a way as to wipe away all stains of the preceding contagion. He grants him the use of the pallium and urges him to suppress simony in the places subject to him.

[Col. 0790B]

[Note: LETTER LVII [Elsewhere 55].—Vatican D, Norman, and Corbie read: “you must strive with great effort.” Vatican A, B, and C read: “you must strive very greatly.”]

Gregory to John, bishop of the Corinthians.

After our God, to whom nothing is hidden, cast away from the government of His Church the disgraceful plague of pollution and wished to bring you to its rule, you must take the greatest care that, after the wounds and various evils of the former wicked pastor, the Lord’s flock may find in your Fraternity consolation and a salutary remedy.

[Note: The printed editions read: “and the various contagions of the former evil pastor.”]

Let the hands of your actions therefore wipe away the stain of the preceding contagion in such a way that no trace of that detestable depravity remains, or that it permits any memory of it to remain.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “nor let it allow any memory to remain.” The Norman reads: “or let it allow any memory to remain.”]

Let your care for those subject to you be praiseworthy. Let discipline be exercised with gentleness. Let correction be accompanied by discretion. Let kindness temper anger, and zeal sharpen kindness; let one be seasoned by the other, so that excessive punishment neither afflicts more than is fitting nor, on the other hand, leniency breaks the uprightness of discipline.

Let the instruction of the people entrusted to you be your Fraternity’s work. Let them see in you what they may love and perceive what they may hasten to imitate. Let them be taught to live by your example. Under your leadership, let them not stray from the right path; following you, let them reach God, so that you may receive as many rewards from the Savior of the human race as you have worked for Him as gains of souls.

Work, therefore, dearest brother, and devote the whole power of your mind and heart to this task, so that in the future you may deserve to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Luke 19:17).

We have sent the pallium, as you requested in your letter, which we received through our brother and fellow bishop Andrew. You must use it in the manner approved for your predecessors, who used it with the permission of our predecessors.
