Furthermore, it has come to us that in those regions no one reaches the sacred order without giving a payment. If this is so, I say with tears and announce with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen within, it will not be able to stand long without.

We know from the Gospel what our Redeemer Himself did: He entered the temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:12). To sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with Himself, gives to human beings through the laying on of hands.

From this evil, as I have said, it is already indicated what follows: because those who presumed to sell doves in God’s temple had their seats overturned, with God as judge.

That error, moreover, spreads among those subject to them with continual increase. For the very man who is advanced to the sacred honor, already corrupted at the very root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. And where is what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:8)?

And since the first simoniacal heresy arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that the man whom someone ordains and advances for a price, by advancing him causes him to become a heretic?

[Note: The common editions read “to the sacred order.” Below they read “and since the first,” instead of “and since the first simoniacal heresy.”]

Since, therefore, the holy universal Church utterly condemns this most wicked depravity, we exhort your Fraternity to suppress so detestable and so monstrous a sin by every means and with all diligence in all the places subject to your care.

For if we thereafter perceive anything of this kind being done, we shall correct it no longer with words but with canonical punishment, and we shall begin to form another judgment of you, which we ought not to form.

Your Fraternity knows that formerly the pallium was not given unless a payment had been made. Since this was improper, we prohibited by strict interdict, at a council held before the body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that anything be received either for this or for ordinations.

[Note: We shall present the acts of this council after all the letters.]

Therefore you must consent to have no one brought to the sacred orders either through payment, favor, or the supplication of certain persons. For the sin is grave, as we have said, and we shall not tolerate its remaining without correction.

We received the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Andrew late because, when our brother and fellow bishop Secundinus reported it, we learned that Andrew had forged our letters for himself in the execution of the orders of John, bishop of Larissa.

[Note: A recent edition, without the support of the better manuscripts, reads: “we learned that he had fabricated your letters …” In John … he had invented an excuse. On the case of John of Larissa against Adrian, bishop of Thebes, see Books III, Letters 6 and 7. Here *in exsecutione* means “in carrying out the commands of John of Larissa.”]

And unless the good things we heard about you had persuaded us otherwise, we would have had no reason to receive him.

[Note: Thus the old Colbert manuscript, although other manuscripts do not agree. In Vatican D, Rheims, and two Tellerian manuscripts, the indiction is given as 14. Why it is retained as Indiction 13 may be learned from the final note to the following letter.]

Given on August 15, Indiction 13.

## LETTER LVIII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT HELLAS

He congratulates them on the correction of Anastasius, whose downfall should serve them as a warning. They are to obey John, his successor. They are not to allow clerics to be ordained or promoted either for payment or through anyone’s favor or supplication.

Gregory to all the bishops established throughout the province of Hellas.

[Note: LETTER LVIII [Elsewhere 56].—This title is read in various ways in the manuscripts. Vatican D has “through Archelaida.” The English manuscripts read “to the bishops established in Adrellada,” or “Arellada”; the Norman and Corbie have the same, with “to the bishops established in the province of Arellada.” The Register reads “to the bishops established in the province of Arellada.” In the three Vatican manuscripts which we have preferred, it is “through Heltadia.” Hellas properly means Achaia, which is near Corinth, from which it received the word of God. Hence Paul says, 2 Corinthians 1:1: “the Church of God which is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in all Achaia.” Perhaps, therefore, Saint Gregory says “the bishops of Hellas,” following the ancient custom by which they were subject to the bishop of Corinth.]

I give thanks with you to almighty God, dearest brothers, who caused the hidden wound inflicted by the ancient enemy to become known to everyone and suppressed it by a salutary incision from the body of His Church.

Because of this we must both rejoice and grieve: rejoice over the correction of the crime, but grieve over the brother’s downfall. Since, however, one person’s downfall is often another person’s warning, let anyone who fears falling pay attention to this, give no opening to the enemy, and not suppose that what is being done can remain hidden.

For the Truth cries out: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26). This saying is already a herald of our actions and, with Him as witness, brings into public view by every means what is done in secret. Or who would try to hide his actions from the One who is both their witness and their judge?

Because sometimes, while one thing is attended to, another is not guarded against, each person must be vigilant against all the enemy’s snares, lest, while he conquers in one place, he be overcome in another.

Even an earthly enemy who desires to invade fortified places uses the following tactic in battle: he secretly lays ambushes and presents himself wholly for the capture of one place, so that, while defenders gather at the place where danger is pressing, other places about which there is no suspicion may be seized.

[Col. 0792C]

Thus it happens that the enemy who was recognized and driven back by the courage of those resisting him secretly obtains what he could not gain by open combat.

But since in all these matters we need the help of divine protection, let each of us cry aloud to the Lord from the heart, saying: “Lord, do not keep Your help far from me; look to my defense” (Psalm 21:20). For it is clear that unless He Himself helps and defends those who cry to Him, our enemy cannot be defeated.

Moreover, as we received the letter of your affection through our brother and fellow bishop Andrew, know that we have not sent the pallium to our brother John, bishop of the Corinthians. It is especially fitting that you obey him, since both the order of ancient custom supports his authority and his good qualities, to which you yourselves bear witness, invite you to do so.

For I have learned from the reports of certain persons (Gratian, I, question 1, chapter 117) that in those regions no one reaches the sacred order without giving a payment. If this is so, I say with tears and announce with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen within, it will not be able to stand long without.

We know from the Gospel what our Redeemer Himself did: He entered the temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. 21:12). To sell doves is to receive temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with Himself, gives to human beings through the laying on of hands.

From this evil, as I have said, it is indicated what follows: because those who presumed to sell doves in God’s temple had their seats overturned, with God as judge.

That error, moreover, spreads among those subject to them with continual increase. For the very man who is advanced to the sacred order, already corrupted at the very root of his advancement, is more ready to sell to others what he bought. And where is what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment” (Matt. 10:8)?

And since the first simoniacal heresy arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that the man whom someone ordains and advances for a price, by advancing him causes him to become a heretic?

Therefore we exhort you that none of you permit this to happen again, and that no one dare promote anyone to the sacred orders either because of another’s favor or because of supplication,

[Note: Unless here it means “but only,” as in John 17:12, where “unless the son of perdition” means “but only the son of perdition.” Consult the commentators, who note many passages of this kind in sacred Scripture.]

unless his quality of life and conduct has shown him worthy of it. For if we again learn that it has been done otherwise, know that it will be restrained by strict and canonical punishment.

[Note: In two Tellerian manuscripts and in Vatican D the indiction is marked as 14. But since in all the manuscripts, including the Vatican manuscripts that arrange the letters according to the order of the indictions, this letter is found in the sequence written under Indiction 13, we ought not to move it from its place. The same reasoning applies to the preceding letter, which was written at the same time.]

Given on August 15, Indiction 13.

# BOOK SIX

Under the fourteenth indiction, in the sixth year of his ordination.

[Col. 0793]

## LETTER I. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP

What should be held valid in the testament of his predecessor John.

[Col. 0793C]

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Just as no effect should be granted to those making unjust demands, so the petition of those desiring what is legitimate should not be delayed. Therefore the priests, deacons, and clergy of your Fraternity, having presented a petition to us, complained that John, your former predecessor,

[Note: BOOK VI. Elsewhere BOOK V.]

## EPISTLE I

In the Council of Agde, canon 51, A.D. 506: “If a bishop, having drawn up a will, should bequeath anything belonging to ecclesiastical property, it shall otherwise have no validity unless he supplies an equal amount from his own property.” The same is stated in the Council of Épaone, canon 17, A.D. 517. The ancients distinguished the personal possessions of clerics from the property of the Church, which belonged to them in their capacity as clerics. They could give and bequeath the former; as for the latter, they could neither give nor bequeath it. Whatever they acquired during their clerical office from the goods of the Church passed neither to themselves nor to their heirs, but to the Church whose ministers they were. This was certainly an excellent arrangement, preventing them from growing rich on ecclesiastical property or enriching their heirs while neglecting the poor. Let the diligent student consult Gratian, Causa 12, Question 3, canons 4 and 5, and the Decretals, Book III, titles 25, *On the Property of Clerics*, and 26, *On Wills*, etc. There he will note that even in the time of Alexander III, at the end of the twelfth century, clerics were not permitted to make wills concerning movable goods acquired through the Church, but only to distribute moderate alms from them during their lifetime. In the Council of Antioch, canons 24 and 25, regulations are made concerning the property of the Church and of bishops; in the Council of Carthage, canon 32, concerning the private property and purchases of clerics. — GUSSANVILLE.

Having drawn up his will, he is said to have written various provisions burdensome to his Church. And they requested that these provisions, since the law prohibited them, should on no account be paid to the detriment of his Church.

[Note: In two Vatican manuscripts, the Regius, the Corbie manuscript, one Rheims manuscript, and almost all the Norman manuscripts, *after his posthumous inheritance*. In the Bec manuscript, *after his posthumous heir*. The same reading occurs in six English manuscripts.]

And although, after his inheritance and succession had been repudiated, no obligation compels you to satisfy these provisions, nevertheless, as an additional precaution, we earnestly exhort you to ensure that whatever he arranged to be done contrary to the statutes of the laws, whether from the property of his Church or from things acquired during his episcopate,

[Note: The printed editions read, *from his Church*.]

your fraternity neither grant authority for it nor consent to it in any way.

[Note: In Vatican A and C, with the agreement of the Norman, Regius, and Corbie manuscripts: *your fraternity should neither advance nor in any way*. In Vatican B: *your fraternity should neither approve*. In Vatican D: *your fraternity should prohibit, and should not in any way*.]

But if he wished or decreed that something should be done concerning his own property, which he possessed before his episcopate and which he had not previously transferred to his Church, it must in every respect retain firm validity; and let no member of the clergy attempt, under any pretext, to overturn it contrary to reason.

For while he was alive, he repeatedly requested us to confirm by our authority the things he had bestowed upon that monastery which he himself had built beside the church of Saint Apollinaris; and we promised that we would do so. Therefore we have judged it necessary to exhort your fraternity

[Col. 0795A]

not to allow anything that he bestowed or established there to be diminished in any way, but to take care that everything be preserved with firm stability. Since he is known to have mentioned this monastery and the things bestowed there in the will he drew up,

[Note: In the more recent editions, incorrectly: *and of the collections*.]

you should know that we did not confirm these things because we were following his final will, but because, as we have said, we had promised this to him while he was alive. Let your fraternity therefore hasten to carry out all these matters with such care that both what he established in the aforesaid monastery and what was confirmed by us may be preserved, while those things which he decreed by his will to be given or done to the detriment of his Church may acquire no validity, since the law expressly prohibits them.

## EPISTLE II. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF RAVENNA

He testifies that Bishop Marinian’s faith is entirely orthodox.

[Col. 0795B]

Gregory to the clergy and people of the Church of Ravenna.

It has come to our attention that certain men, overcome by the instigation of an evil spirit, have wished to corrupt your minds concerning our brother and fellow bishop Marinian by false speech, saying that this same brother of ours venerates the holy Council of Chalcedon less than is proper. On this matter, he himself, being present, gives all of you complete satisfaction concerning the integrity of his faith; and we testify in every respect that, nourished from infancy in the bosom of the holy universal Church, he has held the right proclamation of the faith, attested by his life.

For he venerates the holy Council of Nicaea, at which Arius was condemned; the Council of Constantinople, at which Macedonius was condemned; the First Council of Ephesus, at which Nestorius was condemned; and the holy Council of Chalcedon,

[Note: The Norman, Regius, and three Vatican manuscripts read: *at which Nestorius, Dioscorus, and Eutyches were condemned*. The old printed editions have the same reading.]

at which Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned.

[Col. 0795C]

But if anyone should ever presume to speak anything against the faith of these four councils, and against the *Tome* and definition of Pope Leo of holy memory,

[Note: The reference is to Letter 10, now Letter 24, of Saint Leo, written to Flavian. In reality it was an encyclical sent to all the bishops of the Christian world and solemnly ratified at the Council of Chalcedon, sessions 2, 5, and 6. *Tome* designates a volume or codex, as may be seen in Jerome’s letter to Pammachius and Oceanus; it could denote not only a large book but also a moderate-sized treatise or letter. Hence Ephrem, patriarch of Antioch, rebuked the Eutychians when they mocked Pope Leo because he called his doctrinal letter to Flavian, patriarch of Constantinople, and to the entire Council of Chalcedon a *tome*. According to Salmasius, in his commentary on Solinus, p. 1317, a *tome* properly means the same as a trunk or codex, and a stalk or branch cut from a tree. By these names the ancients called sheets joined together and rolled into one volume, because they resembled a staff; unwritten sheets were fastened together in this manner, as we learn from Cassiodorus. From this usage the words *codex* and *tome* were extended to designate any volume.]

let him be anathema. Therefore, receiving your fullest assurance, love your pastor with undivided charity and a pure heart, so that his intercession, poured out more purely before God, may benefit you.

## EPISTLE III. TO MAXIMUS OF SALONA

Maximus, accused of simony and many other offenses, is summoned to Rome.

[Note: This letter is found partly in Gratian, Causa 2, Question 4, chapter *Accusatum*, and partly in the Decretals, title *On Simony*, chapters 4 and 5. — GUSSANVILLE.]

Gregory to Maximus,

[Note: That is, to the man who invaded and usurped the see of Salona.]

the usurper of the Church of Salona.

Whenever something is said to have been done contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, we dare not leave it unexamined, lest guilt through dissimulation accuse us before God. It has therefore come to us that you were ordained through the simoniacal heresy. But many other things have also been reported here concerning you, one of which in particular made it necessary for us to prohibit you most urgently by our letters from celebrating the solemn rites of Mass until we could learn more accurately what the matter was.

Therefore, lest the children of the Church appear for a long time to be without a pastor,

[Note: The printed editions read: *lest through these things which…*]

and lest what is being reported, if left unexamined, spread this kind of vice among very many people, we exhort you to hasten to come to us, setting aside every excuse, so that, justice being preserved, we may, with Christ revealing the truth, investigate and conclude these matters according to the canonical statutes. Act in such a way that you now cause no further delay in coming, lest your very absence make you more liable to the charges being brought against you; and lest this matter compel us to pass a harsher judgment upon you—not only because of the alleged crimes which you evade purging, but also because of the guilt of disobedience—namely, a judgment imposed by the council upon one who is contumacious.

## EPISTLE IV. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN

He orders two thousand measures of wheat to be given to Bishop Zeno for distribution among the needy.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

Our brother and fellow bishop Zeno has informed us that certain people in his city are suffering from a need of food. Since we desire, insofar as possible, to provide them with some assistance, we therefore assign and order you, by this present letter, to give our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop one thousand measures of wheat—or, if he is able to transport more, as many as two thousand. We exhort you, therefore, to cause no delay or excuse in supplying these provisions, so that, while the opportunity permits, he may, with God’s help, return safely to his own place and be able more quickly to assist those suffering want. (See John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 15.)

## EPISTLE V. TO QUEEN BRUNICHILD

He praises her for the proper education of her son. He commends the priest Candidus, appointed administrator of the patrimony that was in Gaul.

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

[Note: Brunichild, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths who ruled in Spain and Septimania, or Gothic Gaul, by his wife Golswintha, married Sigebert, king of the Franks, and by him had Childebert, the father of Theodebert and Theodoric. Mariana says that Brunichild was praised by Gregory, bishop of Rome, in two letters—or rather in ten—and therefore supposes that the crimes of Fredegund were attributed to Brunichild by our historians. This claim does not deserve refutation. Gregory died on 12 March, in the ninth year of the reign of the brothers Theodebert and Theodoric, nine years before Brunichild’s death. At that time she had not yet ordered the murder of more than one or two nobles; she had not yet ordered the execution of Desiderius, bishop of Vienne; nor had she yet cruelly killed her grandsons. Moreover, Gregory learned from her own letters how many and what kinds of basilicas Brunichild had built, but he could not easily know how many and how atrocious were the crimes she committed. Finally, Gregory sometimes praises her because she was inclined to show consideration for the Church of Gaul and to take care of Candidus, Augustine, and others whom he commends to her. On these matters Adrian Valesius has written fully and accurately in Book XVII of his *History of the Franks*, which should be consulted. — GUSSANVILLE. Many others besides Mariana have tried to remove from Brunichild the suspicion of so many crimes, among them Cordemoy, in his *History of the Franks*, written in French not long ago. We have discussed these matters in the life of Saint Gregory, which should be consulted.]

The goodness of your Excellence, worthy of praise and pleasing to God, is attested both by the governance of the kingdom and by the education of your son. With provident concern you have not only preserved his worldly prosperity unharmed, but have also provided for the rewards of eternal life, planting his mind, as was fitting and commendable, through maternal instruction in the root of the true faith. Hence it rightly came about

[Note: The celebrated deeds of Childebert, including those in Italy, are widely related by Gregory of Tours, Paul the Deacon, and others, although Paul shows himself somewhat less favorable toward the Franks.]

that he surpassed all the kingdoms of the nations, since he both purely worships and truly confesses the Creator of those nations. But so that faith may shine more gloriously in him together with works, let the words of your exhortation kindle him, so that, just as royal power displays him as exalted among human beings, the goodness of his conduct may make him great before God.

Since the experience of many matters urges us to trust in your Christian devotion, we therefore greet you with paternal affection and ask that, for love of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whom we know you love with all your heart, you support our beloved son, the priest Candidus, bearer of this letter, together with the small patrimony whose administration we have entrusted to him, through the help of your protection. Thus, strengthened by the favor of your authority,

[Note: Concerning him, see above, Book III, Letter 33; Book V, Letter 31; below, Letters 6 and 7; and Pelagius I, A.D. 557, in his letter to Sapaudus of Arles.]

he may properly administer and beneficially govern that patrimony, which is known to serve the expenses of the poor,

[Note: The printed editions read: *and, if anything has been taken away from it, supported by your help, may carefully investigate it and, God willing, restore it to its former condition. For the administration of the patrimony…* The Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts compelled us to depart from the received reading. In Vatican A and B, however, we read only: *for not without…*, continuing through *the Church’s own property*.]

and restore to the right of that patrimony anything that may have been taken from it. For it is an increase of your praise that, after so many years, a man belonging properly to the Church has been sent to administer that same patrimony.

May your Excellence therefore graciously devote herself to the matters we request, so that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom the Lord Jesus Christ gave the power of binding and loosing, may grant your Excellence joy here in your offspring and, after the course of many years, cause you to be found, freed from every evil, before the sight of the eternal Judge.

## EPISTLE VI. TO KING CHILDEBERT

He praises his devotion to the Catholic faith and commends Candidus as administrator of the patrimony, appointed in place of the patrician Dynamius.

Gregory to Childebert, king of the Franks.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript and four Vatican manuscripts read *Hildebert*.]

As far as royal dignity surpasses other human beings, so far the kingdom of your realm certainly excels the kingdoms of all other nations. That you are a king is not remarkable, since there are other kings also; but that you are Catholic—which others are not worthy to be—is truly remarkable.

For just as the splendor of a great lamp shines in the darkness of earthly night through the brightness of its light, so the brightness of your faith glows and flashes amid the dark unbelief of other nations. Whatever the other kings boast of possessing, you possess. Yet they are surpassed by you in this respect even more greatly, because they do not possess the chief good that you possess. Therefore, so that they may be overcome by you in conduct as well as in faith, may your Excellence always show kindness to your subjects. And if there are matters capable of offending your mind, do not punish them without investigation.

[Note: The printed editions, corruptly and contrary to the faith of the English, Norman, and other manuscripts, read *do not leave them unexamined*.]

Then you will truly please the King of kings, that is, the almighty Lord, more fully, if, restraining your power, you believe yourself less permitted to do what you are able to do.

Since you preserve the sincerity of the faith both in mind and in conduct, the love of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, which is evident in you, clearly shows whose possessions have thus far been well governed and preserved under the authority of your eminence for the sake of the Christian religion. But since the patrician Dynamius, who at our recommendation devoted himself personally to their administration, cannot now, as we have learned, govern them, we have sent our beloved son Candidus, the priest who bears this letter, to administer them, lest the patrimony established there should perish through negligence. After greeting your Excellence with paternal affection, we commend him to you in every respect and ask that, if some prejudice has perhaps been inflicted there, or if the property of that patrimony is being detained by anyone, it may be corrected by the justice of your authority and whatever has been taken away restored to its former right. Thus, just as your faith does, your equity too may shine among all the nations—something greatly glorious and praiseworthy.

Moreover, we have sent your Excellence the keys of Saint Peter, containing a portion of his chains within them,

[Col. 0799A]

so that, hung around your neck, they may protect you from every evil.

## EPISTLE VII. TO THE PRIEST CANDIDUS

He orders him to purchase, from the revenues of the patrimony, boys from England and clothing for the use of the poor.

Gregory to the priest Candidus,

[Note: EPISTLE VII [formerly 10]. These words are entirely absent from the Norman manuscript and most of the other manuscripts; they are nevertheless found in Vatican B and C, with *Gaul* changed to *the Gauls*.]

as he goes to the patrimony of Gaul.

As you proceed, with the help of our Lord God Jesus Christ, to administer the patrimony that is in Gaul, we wish your affection to purchase, from the solidi you receive, clothing for the poor or English boys who are seventeen or eighteen years old, so that they may be dedicated to God and make progress in monasteries. In this way the Gallic solidi,

[Note: Without loss, since Gallic gold was worth considerably less than Roman gold. The Novel of Majorian states: “No collector shall refuse a solidus of full weight under the pretext of a fraudulent assessment, except the Gallic one, whose gold is valued at a lower rate.” Gussanville attacks here those who transport grain grown in one parish to another place for consumption. But he has not understood Saint Gregory’s meaning. Above, in indiction 11, Letter 33, Gregory wrote to Dynamius: “We have received from the aforesaid revenues of our Church four hundred Gallic solidi.” Below, in Letter 53, to Virgilius of Arles: “Since your predecessor held this small patrimony for many years and kept the revenues collected there, let your fraternity restore them to us through the priest Candidus so that they may be sent to us.” And in Letter 55: “Let your fraternity take care to send us the revenues from our small patrimony.”]

which cannot be spent in our land, may be usefully spent at their proper destination.

If you are able to recover any of the revenue money said to have been taken away, we also wish you to purchase clothing for the poor from it, or, as we have said, boys who are advancing in the service of almighty God. But since those who may be found there are pagans, I wish a priest to be sent with them, lest any illness befall them on the journey, and so that he may baptize those whom he sees to be dying. Let your affection therefore act in such a way that it hastens diligently to fulfill these instructions. (See John the Deacon, Book II, no. 6.)

## EPISTLE VIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF EPIRUS

He approves Andrew’s election as metropolitan. He urges them to imitate him, obey him, and be united with him, and to watch individually over their flocks. Clerics promoted among them are to be commended neither by money nor by favor toward any person, but by their character.

[Col. 0799C]

[Note: The Norman, Vatican, Colbertine, and most manuscripts read: *Theodoric*, or *Theodoric . . . Alcissonus*.]

Gregory to Theodore, Demetrius, Philip, Zeno, and Alcissonus, bishops

[Note: There were two provinces called Epirus in Illyricum, Old and New, as is clear from the official description of the empire. New Epirus, now upper Albania, or Albania properly so called, had Dyrrachium as its metropolis. Old Epirus, which some call lower Albania and which is now Chimera and Arta, had Nicopolis as its metropolis, on the Ambracian Gulf, commonly Preveza on the Gulf of Arta. This title is to be understood of the latter. — GUSSANVILLE.]

of Epirus.

The message of your letters

[Note: Through the ignorance of copyists, a very serious error had entered all the manuscript codices and subsequently the printed books, where the reading was *of the Nicomedian or Nicomeditan city*. That *of Nicopolis* is the correct reading is clear for many reasons. First, Nicopolis was the metropolis of Old Epirus, as everyone knows; Saint Gregory sent the pallium to its bishop, which he certainly would not have sent to the bishop of Nicomedia, who at that time was subject to the patriarch of Constantinople. Moreover, what common concern could the bishops of Epirus have had with the bishop of Nicomedia? Had they ever taken charge of his ordination, as the letter nevertheless reports? Finally, the same Andrew who in this letter is called bishop of the Nicomedian city is designated Nicopolitan in the title of the letter formerly numbered 70 in Book VII, now 68 in Book IX, indiction 2. Saint Gregory writes to him as he does to many other metropolitans. In the letters formerly numbered 2 and 3 in Book XII, now 3 and 4 in Book XIV, the same Andrew is explicitly called Metropolitan of Nicopolis, and is mentioned as already dead. Nevertheless, in this letter *Nicomeditan* is read in all the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts, although we do not hesitate to correct it.]

has informed us, dearest brothers, that our brother Andrew has been solemnly ordained, by God’s favor, bishop of the city of Nicopolis. Since you indicate that his consecration took place with the consent of the clergy and the provincials, we rejoice; and we pray that the good qualities you testify concerning him may remain in him and, with the cooperation of God’s grace, increase, because the goodness of those set over others is certainly the salvation of those subject to them.

Therefore, you ought to hasten to imitate more diligently those qualities which, by praising them in his person, you show to be pleasing to you. For among human beings it is blameworthy, and before God it is punishable, to refuse to imitate in anyone a good quality that one approves.

Let your testimony therefore be matched by obedience. Let no one contradict him in those matters which, while preserving integrity, he has enjoined upon the Church for the common good. Let each of you willingly display his devotion, so that, while a priestly concord that is pleasing to God and faithful

[Note: The printed editions read: *and not feigned*.]

exists among you, no envy may be able to loosen or disturb the bond of mutual charity. For the crafty enemy will have no access to your hearts, since he knows that he can neither capture nor enter where sincere charity has fully found a place.

Moreover, dearest brothers, be vigilant and diligently provide the pastoral care that you have undertaken and owe to the flock entrusted to you. Meet the enemy’s deceits with vigilance

[Note: The printed editions read: *resist with prayer, and obey with undefiled faith*. We follow Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

and prayer. In undefiled faith, entrust to our God the people over whom you preside, so that your priestly office may profit you before the sight of the eternal Judge not unto punishment but unto a crown.

Know, therefore, that we have sent the pallium to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Andrew, and that we have granted him all the privileges which our predecessors conferred upon his predecessors.

Moreover, it has come to us that in those regions sacred orders are conferred in exchange for payment. If this is so, I say with tears and denounce with groaning that, when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it will not be able to stand long outwardly either. We know from the Gospel what our Redeemer did himself: he entered the Temple and overturned the seats of those selling doves. For to sell doves is to receive temporal payment for the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, bestows upon human beings through the laying on of hands.

From this evil, as I have said, what follows is already indicated: those who presumed to sell doves in the Temple of God have had their seats cast down by the judgment of God. This error is propagated among those subject to them with increasing force. For as soon as someone is advanced to sacred orders, having already been corrupted at the very root of his advancement, he is prepared to sell to others what he bought.

And where is what is written: “You received without payment; give without payment”? And since the simoniacal heresy first arose against the holy Church, why is it not considered, why is it not seen, that whoever ordains a man for a price thereby acts to advance a heretic?

For this reason I admonish and solemnly charge you to be entirely vigilant, so that no payment, no favor, and no entreaty from any person may claim anything for itself in sacred orders. Rather, let the man be advanced to this office whom the seriousness of his character and his conduct commend. For if—which we do not believe— we should discover that anything of this kind is being done, we shall correct it with canonical severity, as is fitting.

May almighty God, who by the power of his wisdom orders all things wondrously and mercifully preserves what he has ordered, grant you both the will and the ability to do what he commands.

## EPISTLE IX. TO BISHOP DONUS

He tells him to add moral adornment to the pallium with which he honors him. He confirms the ancient privileges of the Church of Messina.

[Note: EPISTLE IX [formerly 8]. This letter is absent from the English, Corbie, Rheims, and Norman manuscripts. It is found in the Colbertine, Regius, and all the Vatican manuscripts except Vatican D.]

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messina.

Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See and by the order of ancient custom, we have determined to grant the use of the pallium to your fraternity, which is known to have undertaken the office of governance in the Church of Messina, at those times and in that order in which we have no doubt that your predecessor also used it. At the same time we admonish you that, just as you rejoice to have received from us the use of this kind of adornment for the honor of the priestly office, so you should strive to adorn the office, received by our authority, through the excellence of your character and actions, for the glory of Christ.

[Note: The remaining words found in the printed editions are absent from all the aforementioned Vatican, Regius, and Colbertine manuscripts. They occur in the old printed editions, where this letter is addressed to Marinian, and in other copies. In some printed editions, *Maximian* is read instead of *Donus*.]

For in this way you will be conspicuous through a corresponding mutual adornment, if all the good qualities of your mind also accord with this bodily garment. We confirm by our authority all the privileges that are known to have been previously granted to your Church, and decree that they remain inviolate.

[Note: Or: *which you are known to have undertaken in the governance of the Church of Messina*, as the printed editions read.]

## EPISTLE X. TO BISHOP BONIFACE

He unites the Church of Carina to that of Reggio.

Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio.

[Note: EPISTLE X [formerly 9]. So read the manuscripts, or *of Regium*. Nowhere, however, do we find *of Reggio*, as in the earlier editions.]

After the death of the bishop of the Church of Carina, since the desolation of the place and the diminution of its population do not permit another to be ordained,

[Note: The more recent printed editions read: *nor does the habitation of the deserted place permit it*; contrary to the English, Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

[Note: Carina was formerly an episcopal city of the Bruttians in Italy; it is now destroyed and was not far from the city of Reggio on the Sicilian Strait. John, bishop of Carina, signed the Lateran Council under Martin I in A.D. 649. The Greek form τῶν Καρινῶν, “of the Carinans,” appears in the subscriptions.]

we are bound by even greater concern to ensure that those remaining there, if deprived of the guidance of a pastor, are not seized through the pathless snares of the crafty enemy of the faith.

[Note: The printed editions read: *lest, when their priests have died, those remaining there, if [deprived] of a pastor . . .* We follow the manuscripts.]

This plan therefore took shape in our mind: that the Church should be entrusted to your care. We have made this clear through the present letter.

We decree that it be added and united to your Church, so that, with Christ’s help, you may rightly serve as priest of both Churches and, with vigilant and canonical care, arrange whatever seems necessary to you concerning its patrimony or the ordination of its clergy, since, as its proper priest, you will have free authority to do so by this present permission of ours.

Therefore, dearest brother, remembering profitably the Lord’s commands, watch over the government of the people entrusted to you and the winning of souls in such a way that, when you stand before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, you may present to our Redeemer the fruit of good works belonging to your reward, in which he may rejoice.

## EPISTLE XI. TO BISHOP FORTUNATUS

He permits Gratian, a deacon of the Church of Venefrana, to be incardinated into the Neapolitan Church. He forbids clerics to be summoned before laymen for judgment and forbids him himself to delay the hearing of cases. He urges pastoral vigilance.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

We remember that your fraternity asked us to allow Gratian, a deacon of the Church of Venefrana,

[Note: Or, as the manuscripts read, *of Benefrana*.]

to be transferred to your Church for incardination. Since he has neither a bishop whom he can obey nor a Church of his own in which, because the enemy prevents it, he ought to exercise his ministry, we have judged that your request should not be delayed. Therefore, by this present letter, we have deemed it necessary to grant him to you, so that, with our authority intervening, you may, by God’s favor, establish that deacon as a member of your Church.

Since it has come to us that clerics and other religious persons of your city and parish are being summoned by others,

[Note: That is, brought before secular judges through the transfer of jurisdiction. In A.D. 452 Valentinian subjected clerics to lay judges by an edict, except in cases concerning faith and religion. Justinian and many others granted bishops, clerics, and monks the privilege of the forum. See Novels 79, 83, and 123. Canon 9 of the Council of Chalcedon forbids a cleric who has a dispute with another cleric to proceed to secular courts, ἐπὶ κοσμικὰ δικαστήρια, “to secular tribunals.” Now the defendant follows the plaintiff’s forum. See the Decretals, *On the Competent Forum*, and Gratian, Causa 11, Question 1. — GUSSANVILLE.]

we prohibit this from happening in the future. We do not wish your cleric, monk, or any other religious person of your city or parish to be summoned by anyone or brought before another’s tribunal.

But if anyone wishes to raise a legal question concerning such persons, let him know that he must approach your fraternity. Or, if some suspicion should happen to arise against them in any manner, as commonly occurs, and they should desire the judgment of chosen judges, let them have the right, under your authority, to choose judges. In this way, neither will you appear to have lost jurisdiction, nor will the plaintiff, by litigating before a suspected judge, appear to have suffered prejudice. Know that we also instructed the subdeacon Anthemius to observe this.

Your fraternity ought therefore to watch diligently, with pastoral care, over the monasteries of your city and parish and over all those subject to you, and to be wholly concerned with their life and conduct. Just as we are known to preserve these privileges for you, so you must diligently display your vigilance in all things, as is fitting, so that you cannot be found blameworthy in any matter through neglect.

But if you—which we do not suppose—should think that these matters may be disregarded, know that the administrator of the patrimony of our Church who is, or shall be, established there has permission to compel you by every means to do what you voluntarily put off.

You should also strive to ensure that those who have a case against anyone subject to your jurisdiction are not harassed before your fraternity by vexatious delays, lest we appear to have preserved these privileges for you only so that the other party might be wearied and harmed. (See John the Deacon, Book III, no. 20.)

## EPISTLE XII. TO MONTANA AND THOMAS

He frees Montana and Thomas, servants of the Roman Church, and permits them, having been instituted heirs by the priest Gaudiosus, to enjoy the legacies.

Gregory to Montana and Thomas.

Since our Redeemer, the creator of the whole creation, was moved by compassion to assume human flesh for this purpose: that, by the grace of his divinity, the bond of servitude by which we were held captive having been broken, he might restore us to our former freedom—it is salutary that human beings whom nature originally brought forth free, but whom the law of nations subjected to the yoke of servitude, should by the beneficent act of manumission be restored to the freedom in which they were born.

[Note: EPISTLE XII.—Thus we restore the reading from the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and other manuscripts, according to the foregoing. In the printed editions one reads: “that they may be restored to the freedom in that nature in which they had been born.”]

[Note: Concerning manumission, see above, Book II, Letter 10. Formerly it was exceedingly difficult to grant slaves their freedom and make them Roman citizens, as the learned Tillemont notes in his article on Constantine, §40, pp. 168–169. But Constantine, by a law he enacted, granted not only bishops but also all clerics permission to assert their servants into freedom. To make slaves free was likewise to make them Roman citizens, as is also clear from this letter of Gregory.]

And therefore, moved by consideration of piety and of this matter, we hereby make you, Montana and Thomas, servants of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s help we serve, free and Roman citizens from this day forward; and we release to you all your peculium.

[Note: In recent editions: “the peculium of servitude.” *Peculium* derives from *pecunia*, “money,” as though “little money.” It is defined as that which, with the permission of a father, the law, or a master, is granted to a son under paternal authority or to a slave, separately from the father’s or master’s accounts. What is called the “peculium of servitude” by some is called the “master’s peculium” by others, because it belongs to the master, who may retain it by his own right. GUSSANV.]

And because you, Montana, acknowledge that you have turned your mind toward the monastic way of conversion, for this reason we hereby give and grant you the two *unciae* which the priest Gaudiosus is known to have left you by the disposition of his final will, in the manner of an institution—namely, everything which may in every way benefit the monastery of Saint Lawrence, over which the abbess Constantina presides, and in which, by God’s mercy, you are hastening to convert.

[Note: Among jurists, *institutio* is the appointment of an heir; among canonists it is the verbal conferral of some benefice. See the title “On Institutions” in the Decretals and in the Sixth Book. Here it is understood as the appointment of an heir; in French, *faire un tel son héritier*, “to make someone one’s heir.” GUSSANV.]

But if it should be established that you have concealed from us in any way anything belonging to the aforesaid Gaudiosus, all of it shall without doubt be subjected to the right of our Church.

To you, the aforesaid Thomas, whom, in addition to the fullness of your freedom, we wish to serve among the notaries, we likewise give and grant by this deed of manumission the five *unciae* which the aforementioned priest Gaudiosus left to you by hereditary title in his last will, together with the betrothal gift which he had written out for your mother.

[Note: By *sponsalia* he means the dowry, for which a dotal instrument had been drawn up. Plautus, in the *Poenulus*:

“Do you therefore promise  
Your daughter as my wife?”  
Hanno: “I promise, with a thousand gold  
Philippi as dowry,” etc. GUSSANV.]

This is granted subject to the following law and condition: if you should happen to die without legitimate sons—that is, sons born from a legitimate marriage—everything that we have granted you shall return undiminished to the right of the holy Roman Church. But if you should lawfully have sons from a wife, as we have said, and leave them surviving, we establish you as lord of those same possessions without any such condition, and grant you free power to make a testament concerning them.

[Note: He does not mean adopted sons, but those who according to the laws are considered born from a legitimate marriage. GUSSANV.]

Know, therefore, that we and our successors shall preserve without any opposition whatever we have established and granted by this deed of manumission. For the order of justice and reason demands that whoever wishes his own commands to be preserved by his successors should unquestionably observe the will and statutes of his predecessor (Gratian, Causa 25, Question 1, chapter 15).

We dictated this deed of manumission to the notary Paterius for writing, and subscribed it with our own hand, together with the three senior priests and three deacons, for the fullest confirmation; and we delivered it to you. Done in the city of Rome (Gratian, Causa 2, Question 2, chapter 68).

[Note: The printed editions read: “from marriage.”]

## EPISTLE XIII. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN

He is to assist Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum, in restoring the condition of his Church.

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon and rector of Sicily.

Know that we have given permission to the clergy of the Church of Lilybaeum, who came here to have a priest ordained for themselves, to seek a bishop for themselves.

[Note: EPISTLE XIII.—Recent printed editions read *qui rapientes*, “who seizing,” against the unanimous testimony of our manuscripts.]

When they found Decius, a foreign presbyter, they earnestly requested that he be consecrated for them, and we considered it necessary to fulfill their petition. Therefore let your Affection not neglect to assist him in every way, so that, since the former bishop of that Church, Theodore, left many matters requiring correction, he may, aided by your help in everything, and with equity duly preserved, be able to exist more freely from the disturbances of lawsuits and in the praises of God.

[Note: See Letter 50 of Book III, indiction 11, to the same Theodore, in which many things that he must do are indicated. It should nevertheless be observed that this is lacking in several manuscripts—namely, the Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and Vatican D—where one finds: “let him not neglect, so that, aided in everything by your help …”]

## EPISTLE XIV. TO NARSE, THE COUNT

He declares that the presbyter Athanasius fell into the doctrine of Manichaeus, while John was free from heresy; that whoever denies that Adam’s soul died when he sinned is a Pelagian; and he suspects that later copies of the Council of Ephesus have been falsified, advising that ancient copies be sought.

Gregory to Narses, the count.

[Note: Concerning him, see Book I, Letter 6, and indiction 12, Letter 32.]

Your Charity, concerned about our judgment, took pains to write what it thought about the book that had been sent against the presbyter Athanasius.

[Note: Recent editions read *sensi*, “I judged,” against the manuscripts.]

After examining part of it carefully, we found that he had fallen into the doctrine of Manichaeus. But the man who, by placing a sign against certain passages, showed that they were heretical also falls into the Pelagian heresy, because he marked as heretical certain passages that are expressed in a Catholic and entirely orthodox manner.

For where it is written that, when Adam sinned, his soul died, the author later explains in what sense he called it dead: it lost the blessedness of its condition. Whoever denies this is not a Catholic. For God had said: “At whatever hour you eat, you shall die the death” (Genesis 2:17).

[Note: The Vatican, Norman, and most others read “on the day,” or “on whatever day.”]

When Adam therefore ate from the forbidden tree, we know that he did not die in body, since afterward he fathered children and lived many years. If, then, he did not die in soul—which it is impious to say—God himself lied when he foretold that he would die on the day on which he sinned.

But it must be understood that death occurs in two ways: either through the absence of life, or through separation from the quality of life. Thus, when Adam’s soul is said to have died by eating what was forbidden, this means not the absence of life but separation from the quality of life: he who had been created to live happily in joy would thereafter live in punishment.

Whoever marked this passage as heretical in the book sent to me by my brother John, bishop, is a Pelagian, because this proposition is plainly Pelagius’s. The apostle Paul openly refutes it in his letters. I omit citing each of the passages from his letters, because I am speaking to one who knows them.

[Note: This appears from the letter of the synod to Pope Celestine, which is reported by Binius in volume IV of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 17; in the Cologne edition of 1606, in the editions of 1618 and 1672, Part II, act 5, at the end of this letter, which begins: “Your Holiness’s zeal concerning piety,” etc. GUSSANV.]

Pelagius, however, who was condemned at the Council of Ephesus, said this with the intention of showing that we had been redeemed by Christ in vain. For if we did not die in soul through Adam—which it is impious to say—we were redeemed in vain.

As we investigate the Council of Ephesus, however,

[Note: Theodoret, in Book IV of his *Heretical Fables*, under the heading “On the Messalians or Euchites, and on the Enthusiasts,” and in Book IV, chapter 11, of his *Ecclesiastical History*, speaks of Adelphius as an old man at death’s door, whose heresy Flavian of Antioch detected by remarkable ingenuity. The leaders of that heresy were Sabbas (in two Vatican manuscripts, *Saba*), not Sava, Adelphius, Daodes, Simeon, Hermas, and certain others. Against them Latoius, bishop of Melitene, and Amphilochius of Iconium wrote. Among other things, they said that baptism was of no benefit to those who received it: like a razor, it removes former sins but does not cut out the root of sin; whereas continual prayer uproots the root of sin entirely and expels from the soul the evil demon assigned to it by lot from the beginning. Photius, in the *Bibliotheca*, codex 52, reports that toward the end of the fourth century a synod was held at Side against the Messalian heresy—that is, of the Euchites or Adelphians—over which Amphilochius presided with twenty-five bishops. From it a synodal letter was sent to Flavian of Antioch, who also held a synod for the same reason. He testifies that Adelphius, although he professed to detest the heresy, was not admitted because his repentance was not heartfelt, etc. Saint Maximus, in his commentaries on the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 6, mentions Adelphian monks who, after living perfectly (*akros*, ἄκρως) for three years from their profession, thereafter allowed themselves everything. Nilus speaks of the monk Adelphius in his still-unpublished book *On Voluntary Poverty*; a fragment of it is cited by Henri Valois in his notes on chapter 2 of Book IV of Theodoret’s *History*. GUSSANV.]

we find absolutely nothing about Adelphius, Sava, and the other persons who are said to have been condemned there; and we suppose that, just as the Council of Chalcedon was falsified in one place by the Church of Constantinople, so something was done in the Council of Ephesus.

[Note: Namely, in canon 28, which could not be approved by the Roman pontiffs. Thus Saint Gregory rejects below the canon of the First Council of Constantinople, since the Roman clergy could not tolerate the expansion of the borders of the bishop of Constantinople. GUSSANV.]

Therefore let your Charity seek out ancient copies of that same council and see there whether anything of this kind is found; then send me the copy you discover, and as soon as I have read it I shall send it back. For he must not place indiscriminate trust in recent copies; this is what has made me uncertain, and I have not yet wished to write anything concerning this matter to my aforesaid brother John, bishop.

Roman copies, however, are far truer than Greek ones, because we have neither your subtleties nor your falsifications.

[Note: Thus read four Vatican manuscripts, six English manuscripts, as many Norman manuscripts, and the Corbie and Royal manuscripts. We do not know how the reading of the printed editions arose: “because our copies, just as they have no acuteness, so also have no impostures.”]

As for the presbyter John, know that his case was decided by a synod, in which I plainly learned that his adversaries wished, and for a long time attempted, to make him a heretic, but were entirely unable to do so.

[Note: One cannot help wondering that Christian people should have burned with such uncontrollable zeal—or rather struggled under such monstrous envy and blind hatred—that they attempted to tear away those who were within the Church from their mother’s breasts and expose them to be torn apart by savage teeth. Saint Gregory develops the same argument at the beginning of the following letter, and wonders that the truth was so neglected by such zealots that they did not even know the heresy which they were alleging. GUSSANV.]

Greet on my behalf your people, who are ours, and through me our people, who are yours, greet you warmly. May almighty God protect you with his hand amid so many thorns, so that unharmed you may pluck the flowers whom the Lord has chosen. (See indiction 15, Letter 31; cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 36.)

## EPISTLE XV. TO JOHN, THE BISHOP

He absolves the presbyter John, who had been unjustly condemned, and declares him free from every stain of heresy. He commends him to John, bishop of Constantinople.

Gregory to John, bishop of Constantinople.

Just as the perversity of heretics must be restrained by zeal for the true faith, so the integrity of a true confession must be embraced. For if one who confesses faithfully is despised, the faith of all is brought into doubt, and deadly errors arise from ill-considered severity. Thus not only are wandering sheep not recalled to the Lord’s folds, but even those already within are cruelly exposed to be torn apart by savage teeth.

Let us therefore, dearest brother, weigh this carefully, and let us not permit anyone who truthfully professes the Catholic faith to be afflicted under the pretext of heresy, lest—God forbid—we allow heresy to be created under the appearance of correction.

We were greatly astonished that those who had been appointed by you as judges in the matter of faith against John, a presbyter of the Church of Chalcedon, should, neglecting the truth, have trusted an opinion and refused to trust one who professed his faith firmly—especially since, when the accusers of the man were asked what the heresy of the Marcianists was which they mentioned and by which they sought to make him guilty, they openly declared that they did not know.

[Note: EPISTLE XV.—I have found no author who identifies what that heresy was. GUSSANV. Perhaps one should read “of the Marcionites.”]

From this it is clearly understood that, without regard for God, they wished only by their own will to burden his person—not justly, but against their own souls.

[Note: John is heard; he presents a statement of his faith; the judges investigate; and after a council has been held he is absolved, as appears from the words of the following letter: “the decision of the holy council with me,” etc. The same letter treats the matter more fully, teaching that it is unbelief not to have faith in the faithful, and that not to believe one who confesses truthfully is not to purge heresy but to create it. The same question is treated in Letters 16 and 17. GUSSANV. See Book II, Letter 44, or Book IX, Letter 39.]

Accordingly, after a council had been held, as the record of the proceedings conducted before us shows, we carefully examined and discussed everything necessary. Since we could find no guilt at all in the aforementioned presbyter, especially because the statement of faith which he presented to the judges delegated by you agrees in every respect with the sincerity of the true faith, we rejected the judgment of those same judges and, by our own decision, declared him Catholic and free from every heretical crime, by the revealing grace of Christ our God and Redeemer.

Since we have sent him back to your Holiness, you ought to receive him kindly, as he shows himself to all, extend priestly charity to him, and protect him from every disturbance. You should not permit anyone to occupy himself with harassing him; but just as you defend others from oppression, so you should not withhold your assistance from him. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 36.)

## EPISTLE XVI. TO MAURICE AUGUSTUS

He is not to permit the entirely innocent presbyter John to be afflicted again as though liable to heresy.

Gregory to Maurice Augustus.

Since the uprightness of your faith, most Christian of princes, shines in you like a ray sent down from heaven, and since it is known to all that Your Serenity warmly embraces and loves with your whole heart the complete profession by which, through God’s favor, you possess strength, we have clearly perceived that it is greatly necessary to plead on behalf of those whom one and the same faith illumines, so that your lordly piety may protect them by its favor and guard them from every harassment.

[Note: Printed editions read *relatis*, “after the matters had been reported,” which is not found in the manuscripts.]

For when people despise their confession, they appear to contradict the true faith. Since the Apostle proclaims that confession with the mouth leads to salvation, whoever refuses to believe a right confession accuses himself in condemning another (Romans 10:10).

When, therefore, we reread in council what had been done against John, presbyter of the Church of Chalcedon, and likewise the sequence of the judgment, we recognized that he had suffered even greater injustice: although he cried out and demonstrated that he was Catholic, he was crushed not by the guilt of an offense but by a long and uncertain accusation, especially since his accusers openly declared in reply that they did not know the heresy of the Marcianists which they had mentioned.

[Note: If an accusation requires a formal indictment, it must contain the name of the accused and the accuser, the crime, and the place, day, hour, and so forth of the crime. The accuser must also have proofs ready; otherwise he must suffer the penalties of a false accuser. AUGET.]

Those who ought immediately to have been rejected at the very threshold of the trial were nevertheless allowed to persist in their uncertain accusation against him. But lest even their statements should be able to tear him apart, he produced a statement of faith in which he openly sought to show himself a professor and adherent of the true faith.

The judges appointed by the most holy John, our brother and fellow bishop, unjustly and irrationally neglected this statement while attempting to occupy themselves with his condemnation, and thereby showed themselves blameworthy.

[Note: Judges who are led by favor become infamous and are liable to the injured party for the valuation of the lawsuit. See the Code, “On the Punishment of Judges Who Judge Badly,” final law; and in the Sixth Book, “On Judgments and Res Judicata,” chapter 1, concerning canonical penalties imposed by the Council of Lyons.]

No one doubts that it is unbelief not to have faith in the faithful. Since, therefore, after everything had been carefully investigated and discussed, the definition of the holy council with me declared the aforementioned presbyter John Catholic, by the grace of divine power revealing the truth, and no mark of heretical perversity was found in him, I beg that your pious protection order him to be kept unharmed from every harassment and permit no disturbance to be imposed upon a confessor of the Catholic faith.

For not to believe one who truthfully confesses is not to purge heresy but to create it. If this is permitted, an occasion for unbelief will arise, and those very persons will fall into the faults which they rashly wish to correct.

Let the Most Serene Lord therefore consider these matters with pious foresight. As I have asked, I again entreat with abundant prayers that he not permit the innocent to be afflicted anew as though guilty, so that almighty God—who sees that Your Clemency loves and defends the integrity of Catholic uprightness pleasing to him—may cause you, once your enemies have been conquered, to rule a peaceful commonwealth here, and to reign with his saints in eternal life. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 36.)

## EPISTLE XVII. TO THEOTISTUS

He is to protect the presbyter John, who was absolved by a council from the charge of heresy imposed upon him, from every harassment.

Gregory to Theotistus, kinsman of the emperor.

We know that Your Excellence’s Christianity has always been devoted to good works; and therefore we provide you with opportunities for reward—things which you are certainly known to love—so that, by providing for your merits, we may join ourselves to them.

We therefore inform you that John the presbyter, bearer of this letter, has been found free from the charges of which he had been accused. After holding a council and examining his faith with careful scrutiny, as he requested, we found no fault in him concerning an erroneous confession.

[Note: EPISTLE XVII.—In the recent edition one reads *ut potuimus*, “as we were able,” for no reason and against the testimony of the manuscripts.]

But since, by God’s mercy, he appeared to be a professor and devotee of the true faith, we absolved him by our decision, especially since his accusers confessed that they did not know what the heresy of the Marcianists was which they had mentioned.

Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask that you deign to protect him by the favor of your support. And lest anyone afterward wish to afflict him uselessly or inflict any harassment upon him in any way on this account, may Your Excellence’s defense protect and defend him against such things all the more earnestly for your reward, so that unjust tribulation may not consume him again, and that the creator and Redeemer of the human race, whom you worship with sincere confession, may reward you in return for this among the many good works that you perform.

[Note: This is absent from almost all manuscripts; it is found in the old Colbert manuscript and in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus.]

In the month of October, indiction 14.

[Note: EPISTLE XVIII.—This letter is not found in the English, Norman, Corbie, and most other manuscripts; it is nevertheless found in the Vatican, Rheims, and Royal manuscripts.]

## EPISTLE XVIII. TO JOHN, THE BISHOP

He grants the use of the pallium and confirms ancient privileges.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

[Note: He was made bishop of Syracuse after serving as archdeacon of Catania, and was consecrated by Gregory the Great in the year 596. He imitated the virtues of his predecessor; for in Book VI, Letter 9—now Book VII—Gregory praises him for sending alms to be distributed to the poor. He died most holily in 609. The Church of Syracuse celebrates his feast on 28 October. GUSSANV.]

Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See and by the order of ancient custom, we have determined to grant the use of the pallium to your Fraternity, which is known to have undertaken the office of governance in the Church of Syracuse, namely at those times and according to that order in which you do not doubt that your predecessor also used it.

[Note: In the Rheims manuscript: “And according to that order by which you do not doubt that the other priests of the island of Sicily, or your predecessors, also used it. We nevertheless admonish you that the reverence due to the Apostolic See not be disturbed by anyone’s presumption. For the condition of the members remains whole only if no injury assails the head of the faith. Let the authority of the canons always remain sound and inviolate. So that, just as you have received from us the use of this …”]

We further admonish you that, just as you rejoice to have received from us the use of this dignity for the honor of the priestly office, so you should strive to adorn the office you have received by the excellence of your conduct and actions, to our glory in Christ.

Thus you will be conspicuous in reciprocal honor if the goodness of your mind also agrees with the outward habit of this body.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “and your mind also agrees.”]

For by our authority we confirm all the privileges which are known to have formerly been granted to your Church, and we decree that they remain unimpaired. (See above, Book V, Letter 17.)

## EPISTLE XIX. TO DOMINICUS, THE BISHOP

He urges them to assist one another with mutual prayers, so that their mutual affection may obtain heavenly joy.

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop in Africa.

[Note: A bishop of Carthage, to whom several letters survive. GUSSANV.]

The expression of your letters, full of priestly charity, makes Your Holiness cling so memorably to our minds that you seem not to be absent in body, since through affection you are always present in our hearts.

Therefore, so that the affection which we have for one another may obtain for us the benefit of heavenly joys, let us be mutually helpful and offer one another the assistance of mutual prayer, so that divine mercy may grant us, by the gift of its clemency, both to preach what it loves and to follow what it has granted to be preached through us.

May it so order the ministry of our office by its protection that we may bring back fruit from what has been entrusted to us when the Lord comes, and, with the help of his grace, may be brought with the gain of others to the future rewards of justice.

[Note: The Gembloux manuscript and some others read *perducamus*, “may we bring.”]

Since it is written, “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16), in order that we may deserve to reach these things, it is fitting that I devote myself to prayer for you at the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and that you pray for me at the shrine of Saint Cyprian the martyr.

For our prayers are lifted into the ear of the Lord’s mercy all the more swiftly when the ardor of charity intensifies them as they are poured out in turn for one another.

But because Your Holiness refused to address me only in bare words and also added gifts to your letters—

[Note: Most manuscripts read *exenia*. Concerning this word, see Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 12.]

—we received them with thanksgiving; nevertheless, we take greater delight in the affection of your mind than in the abundance of your possessions.

## EPISTLE XX. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN

He is to persuade Leo, bishop of Catania, to surrender a certain presbyter to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

Just as your Affection zealously labored on behalf of our brother and fellow bishop John, so that, with God as author, he might be ordained in the Church of Syracuse, so now it is necessary that, through your affectionate efforts, the supports of governance also be supplied to him.

[Note: EPISTLE XX.—In Letter 19 of Book IV, now Book V, Letter 17, Saint Gregory had instructed that efforts be made to obtain John’s release from Leo. After the release, John, once ordained, asks back his own presbyter who had been ordained in the Church of Catania; Saint Gregory instructs that Leo be persuaded of this gently and mildly. You see here the practice of that age concerning one’s own clergy. GUSSANV.]

He claims to have had a certain presbyter of his own, who is nevertheless said to have been ordained in the Church of Catania by our brother and fellow bishop Leo. Since he is going to a new Church and needs to have his own people there, so that when he is oppressed by the turmoil of lawsuits he may find a place of rest in his private quarters, you must gently and sweetly persuade the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Leo to surrender the aforesaid presbyter to him, lest he appear, after having so kindly released someone for ordination, perhaps to abandon him once ordained.

But just as our same brother and fellow bishop John, as far as I have learned from his mind, does not forget that he is Leo’s archdeacon even though he has undertaken the episcopate, so the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Leo ought to regard him as his own and offer him his assistance not only concerning the person of one presbyter but in whatever matter he may need his help.

[Note: Thus it is read in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus, the Colbert manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript. In most manuscripts, however, this is absent.]

In the month of November, indiction 14. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book III, no. 20.)

## EPISTLE XXI. TO PETER, THE BISHOP

He commends three Churches deprived of their own bishops.

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Hydruntum.

[Note: EPISTLE XXI.—Hydruntum or Hydrus, commonly Otranto, formerly an episcopal city of Calabria and now an archiepiscopal city in the kingdom of Naples. GUSSANV.]

Pastoral care compels us to look with vigilant concern after Churches deprived of the governance of a priest, lest, when their own ruler has died, something contrary—God forbid—should arise against the regulations of the Fathers.

Since, therefore, we have learned that the Churches of Brundisium, Lippias, and Gallipoli have been left entirely without bishops after the death of their pontiffs, we have consequently decided to entrust their visitation to your Fraternity.

[Note: Brundisium, commonly Brindisi, French Brindes, formerly an episcopal city and later made archiepiscopal, was once the chief city of the Calabrians in the kingdom of Naples; it is now in the province of Otranto, on the Adriatic coast opposite Tarentum. GUSSANV.]

[Note: Lippias: Ptolemy has *Luppiae*, Antoninus *Lipia*; Mela calls it *Lupias* and says that it was a town of Calabria not far from Brundisium. Pliny, Book III, chapter 10, calls the military station *Lupia*. It is now the village called La Rocca between Brindisi and Otranto, according to the native Galateo.]

[Note: Above, Letter 45 of Book II, indiction 11, now Book III, Letter 46. GUSSANV.]

You should conduct this visitation in such a way that you allow no one to diminish anything belonging to the advancement of the clergy, the income, adornment, services, or whatever else belongs to the patrimony of those Churches.

Therefore your Fraternity shall hasten to go to the aforesaid Churches and, by frequent exhortations, hasten to admonish their clergy and people to seek, without factional preference and with one common agreement, priests to be placed over them who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and who will in no way be rejected by the venerable canons.

When candidates have been requested—

[Note: According to Gregory, a person is said to be “requested” when he is chosen for the episcopate by a common decree of the clergy and people: Book I, Letter 60; Book II, Letter 39; Book VII, Letters 20 and 21; Book IX, Letter 88. Among canonists, however, *postulatio* is a unanimous petition by which someone who according to the canons cannot be admitted to the clergy or to an ecclesiastical dignity, including a regular one, is nevertheless admitted by dispensation and grace, after the matter has been examined by a superior. Since a request conflicts with the common law, it must therefore be made by the unanimous judgment of all, to such an extent that if a request and an election occur together, the number of those requesting must be twice as great as the number of electors; see chapters 3 and 4, “On the Requesting of Prelates,” in the Extravagantes.]

—let them come to us for consecration with a formal decree confirmed by the signatures of all and with a letter of testimony from Your Affection. Above all, you must ensure that no layperson of whatever character or merit presumes to aspire to this office, lest you incur, God forbid, the peril of your own order.

As for any monasteries established in their dioceses, we grant that they shall remain under your care and governance until their own bishop has been ordained, so that, with the vigilance of your concern suited to their purpose, they may, with God’s help, respond in action.

[Note: This is absent from the manuscripts except the Royal, the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus, the old Colbert manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript.]

In the month of January, indiction 14.

## EPISTLE XXII. TO PETER, THE BISHOP

He is to consecrate a Church and a baptistery.

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Aleria in Corsica.

[Note: EPISTLE XXII.—Only Vatican B reads “to the bishop of Aleria in Corsica.” In the Royal manuscript: “to the bishop of Alexandria and the clergy of Corsica.” In the others: “to the bishop of Corsica.”]

Since on the island of Corsica, in a place called Nigeunum, on an estate called Cellas Cupias, belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s command we serve, we have ordered a basilica with a baptistery to be founded in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and the martyr Lawrence, for the winning of souls, for this reason we exhort your Fraternity in these words: you must go without delay to the aforesaid place, and, after performing the solemn rites of the venerable dedication, we wish you solemnly to consecrate the aforesaid church and baptistery.

[Note: These were not baptisteries built in the corners of basilicas, as they are now, but separate buildings. See Paulinus, Letter 12, to Severus: “You built a baptistery between two basilicas.” That the baptistery had the form of a tower is shown by the verses concerning the basilica:

“He established a fountain beneath a towered covering,” etc.

Above the fonts there was suspended a vessel in the form of a dove, in which the sacred body of Christ was kept for the use of those recently baptized:

“From the sacred font the priest, their parent, leads forth  
Infants with snowy body, heart, and habit,  
And, surrounding the tender lambs with festive altars,  
Fills their mouths with life-giving food.”

In the supplication of the clergy and monks of Antioch, reported in act 5 of the Council of Constantinople under Menas, against Severus: “For golden and silver doves, in the form of the Holy Spirit, are hung above the divine baths and altars,” etc. GUSSANV.]

You shall place the relics received with reverence.

[Note: Thus read the Norman, Corbie, and most manuscripts. The printed editions have: “with the utmost reverence.”]

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He is to compel the bishop of Amalfi to reside in his Church.

Gregory to the subdeacon Anthemius.

It has come to our attention (Gratian, Decree, Part II, Cause 7, Question 1, canon 20) that Pimenium, [Note: [Column 0813D] EPISTLE XXIII.—Amalfi and Amalphis, commonly Amalfi, formerly an episcopal city in Campania, now an archiepiscopal city of the Kingdom of Naples, in the Principato Citeriore, on the coast, not far from Salerno. It is believed that the use of the nautical compass was first discovered there. GUSSANVILLE.] bishop of the city of Amalfi, is not content to reside in his own church, but wanders outside through various places. When others see this, they too do not remain in the fortress, but, following his example, prefer to live elsewhere. And because by doing this they themselves rather invite enemies to plunder them, we therefore command you by this authority never to cease warning the aforesaid bishop that he must not presume to do this hereafter, but must reside in his own church according to priestly custom. If, after your warning, you should discover that he has not corrected himself, you shall assign him to a monastery and take every care to inform us, so that you may learn again from our order what you ought to do.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO MARIANIAN, BISHOP

He shows that some complain without cause that the case between the Church of Ravenna and Abbot Claudius is being examined at Rome; he promises an equitable judgment.

Gregory to Marinian, bishop of Ravenna.
