We received the letter of your Fraternity, delivered by the deacon Virgilius, in which you reported that certain members of the clergy and people [Note: [Column 0814C] EPISTLE XXIV.—Cases should of course be determined where they first arose, unless the judges are suspected, or, in more important cases, a higher authority is approached by way of appeal—as happened in both respects in the case of John of Chalcedon. See the Council of Sardica, canon 3, which favors the Roman pontiff, and the Councils of Carthage, canons 19, 20, 23, and 28; in the African Council, canon 91, and so forth. Certainly the case between the Church of Ravenna and Abbot Claudius could have been settled by a provincial council according to the laws and canons: at Nicaea, canons 5 and 6; at Antioch, canons 9, 14, 15, and 20; at Chalcedon, canon 19, and so forth. GUSSANVILLE. Leaving aside the other arguments that might be brought against Gussanville’s judgment, this is sufficient: it is the first reason given by the most holy and equitable pontiff for repelling the complaints of Marinian and his supporters. Namely, the judges before whom they wanted to compel Claudius to plead his case were suspect. Marinian, from whom Claudius complained that his monastery was suffering harassment, was to preside over the provincial synod. Even if the archbishop had abstained from deciding this dispute, there was good reason to fear that the provincial bishops would favor their metropolitan rather than the abbot.] have loudly asserted that it was contrary to the laws and canons for the case between your Church and Abbot Claudius to be examined and judged here. If they understood the ecclesiastical order, or recognized the parties between whom the dispute arises, they would in every way refrain from this needless complaint—especially since the case could not be pleaded there, where the aforesaid abbot complained to your predecessor that he had suffered injustice and was still suffering from it. This objection might perhaps be made if he did not have recourse to a higher authority and seek to have the merits of his case settled before him. Do you not yourself know [Note: [Column 0814D] This matter was dealt with in Epistles 14, 15, and 16 of this book. GUSSANVILLE. The printed editions read “in the case.”] that the case which arose between the presbyter John and our brother and fellow bishop John of Constantinople was, according to the canons, brought to the apostolic see, and was decided by our judgment? If, then, a case from that city where the emperor resides was brought to our consideration, how much more must a matter arising among you be settled here, once the truth has been ascertained? Do not let the words of fools there move you, nor imagine that through us any loss is being inflicted on your Church. For if you inquire of God’s servant Secundinus, your deacon, and of Castorius, our notary, you will learn from them how your predecessor wished this case to be arranged. Your Fraternity acted wisely in sending persons for the matter itself and refusing to listen to empty words. We trust in almighty God that, after the truth has been examined with greater precision, an ending pleasing to God will be given to this case—so that no further complaint remains and neither party is unjustly oppressed. [Note: [Column 0815D] Thus it is read in all our manuscripts and in most printed editions. Gussanville notes that some manuscript codices have *sparta*, but he does not say which. Certainly not the Vatican, English, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, or Royal manuscripts. The difficulty is that Saint Gregory is so concerned about this *spatha*, as is clear from this letter and the following one, Epistle 61. If *spatha* means a sword—for the word has no other meaning—it was not so important that the supreme pontiff should be so anxious to have it sent to him. Yet it may have been some distinguished sword, like the sword of the Virgin of Orléans, commonly called “the Maid’s sword,” which is preserved in our own day in the treasury of Saint-Denis. Why should we not suppose that the matter concerns a sword kept among the sacred relics, one consecrated by the blood of some martyr?] As for the sword which our beloved son Peter the deacon, then serving there as defender, left for us with your predecessor, send it to us through God’s servant Secundinus and Castorius the notary, the bearers of this letter.

## EPISTLE XXV. TO MAXIMUS OF SALONA

He must at last obey and, after thirty days, set aside every excuse and come to Rome, where his case will be concluded according to the canons. Meanwhile, because of his pride, he is to remain deprived of holy communion and must not trouble Bishop Paulinus or the archdeacon Honoratus.

[Column 0815B]

Gregory to Maximus, usurper of the Church of Salona. [Note: [Column 0815D] EPISTLE XXV.—The printed editions have: “To Maximus in Salona,” or rather, “To Maximus who seized the bishopric in Salona,” as it is read in Vatican B. The other manuscripts have the title that we have printed.]

While, in response to our letters, you delay presenting obedience by seeking various excuses, while, despite being so often admonished by us to come in satisfaction of the truth [Note: [Column 0816D] In the Norman, Corbie, and most manuscripts: “factione.”], you continue to postpone your arrival, you give greater credence by this very conduct to the charges made against you. Even if there seemed to be anything else lacking that could weigh against you or harm you, you are acting so that delay alone may make you guilty and accuse you. Humble yourself at last, submit yourself to obedience, and hasten to come to us without any excuse, so that, once the truth has been sought and known, whatever is equitable and canonical may be decreed according to the fear of God. Be assured that we shall preserve justice for you and the statutes of the canons, and, with the Lord revealing the truth, its author, we shall bring your case to a conclusion favorable to justice. For your request (Gratian, Decree, Part II, Cause 6, Question 5, canon 1)—that we should send someone there in whose presence proof could be given concerning the matters alleged—would be to some extent excusable if reason ever imposed the burden of proof on the accused. But since this burden rests not on you but on your accusers, do not cease to come to us, as we have said, once the delay has ended. Either the accuser will promptly appear and support by suitable proof the allegations made concerning simony or other matters; or, at least, in whatever concerns the welfare of the case itself, through the intervention of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, a just dispensation will be granted, so that before God no guilt arising from our failure to act in a matter that has reached our conscience may confound us. As for your statement that the most serene lords [Note: [Column 0816D] In accordance with the canons cited in the preceding epistle. Indeed, Saint Gregory was eventually forced to take this course, as will be clear from the following passages: Book VII, Epistles 80–82, now Book IX, Epistles 79–81. GUSSANVILLE.] ordered that the hearing should take place there, we have received no other command from them concerning this matter except that you should come to us. But if, perhaps, while they were occupied with many thoughts for the welfare of their state, which has been granted to them by divine generosity, and distracted by various concerns, someone made a representation to them and their order was obtained by concealment, then—since it is known both to us and to everyone that the most pious lords [Note: [Column 0816D] Thus with the Norman, English, Vatican, and other manuscripts; the older printed editions have this reading, while the more recent editions, differing from them, read “to direct.”] love discipline, preserve order, honor the canons, and do not involve themselves in priestly cases—we are diligently carrying out what benefits both their soul and their state, and what the regard of the terrible and awesome Judge compels us to do.

Therefore cease from all excuses and do not delay coming here, so that, strengthened by our investigation of the truth, we may at last bring your case to an end. We have learned that you greatly fear and are wholly alarmed lest we perhaps take vengeance on you because you are known to have advanced irregularly into the priestly order without our consent. This is indeed an intolerable offense; but, in accordance with the commands of the most serene lord emperor, if you do not continue any longer in the error of your defiance, we release you from it and will not in the least proceed against you on that account. But we do not permit the other matters reported to us to pass without investigation.

Since we formerly sent you letters ordering you not to dare celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in any way until we learned the will of that same most serene lord, you acted arrogantly and craftily so as not to receive those letters, although you learned their decision by whatever means, and refused to observe it. Therefore we confirm what we previously sent you in writing: you must not dare celebrate the solemn rites of Mass until everything reported against you has been carefully investigated and examined. If, however, in perverse presumption you dare to celebrate, know that you are not free from the threat of the communion from which you were previously forbidden. For even if there were no other offenses, [Note: [Column 0816D] The Africans decreed at Carthage III, canon 7, that contumacy alone suffices for someone to be deprived of communion. It is cited in Part II, Cause 4, Question 5, where various forms of exclusion from communion are to be observed, whether in one’s own church or in a parish. GUSSANVILLE.] for this one offense of pride alone we deprive you of communion in the Lord’s body and blood. Therefore, offering the obedience that is due, hasten to come to us with the utmost urgency, as we have said, and you shall have a period of thirty days in which to prepare your journey; then, setting aside every excuse, do not delay coming here.

If any occasion should arise through judges, military force, or the populace to obstruct your journey, we recognize the craftiness with which this is being done. You must therefore now consider how you will render an account—here to human beings, and in the future judgment to almighty God—of the obligation you have incurred, since by your contempt you have provoked a strict judgment against yourself.

Furthermore, it has come to me that my brother and fellow bishop Paulinus and [Note: [Column 0817D] From this it is clear that Honoratus had been restored to his order, from which Natalis had removed him by deceitfully promoting him to the presbyterate. See Epistle 19 of Book I, and elsewhere. GUSSANVILLE.] Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona, because they refused to consent to your presumption, are suffering serious harassment at your hands, so much so that, after giving sureties, they have been confined and forbidden altogether to leave the city or their homes. If this is so, then, even if belatedly returning to a sound mind, suspend your harassment of both of them upon receiving this letter, so that they may have free permission either to come to me, if they wish, or to depart elsewhere for whatever purposes they require.

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO THE SALONITANS

He asserts that he is not moved against Maximus by private hatred; but he wonders that scarcely any of them have abstained from communion with Maximus.

Gregory to his most beloved sons, the clergy and nobles residing at Salona. [Note: [Column 0817D] EPISTLE XXVI.—This is how the letter is inscribed in five English manuscripts, all the Norman, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts, and Vatican D: “Gregory to the presbyters, deacons, clergy, nobles, and people residing at Jadera.” The Royal manuscript reads: “to the presbyters, deacons and clergy, nobles and people residing there, and the soldiers.” Nevertheless, we have followed the reading of the other editors, both because it appears in three Vatican manuscripts and because another letter was written to the people of Jadera with nearly the same subject. Who could persuade himself that two letters with nearly the same meaning were sent to the clergy and people of Jadera, or Jadera, and that none was sent to the Salonitans, whose Church Maximus had invaded? Moreover, the body of the letter reads: “I have been greatly astonished, because among the numerous clergy and people of the Church of Salona…” Therefore he is writing to the Salonitans. And what is more, he immediately mentions Honoratus, archdeacon of the Church of Salona.]

It has come to me that certain men of perverse mind have tried to suggest to you, in order to wound the feelings of your affection, that I am moved against Maximus by some kind of hatred and that I desire to carry out not what is canonical but what belongs to rage. But far be this from me—far be it from a priestly mind that it should be moved by private zeal in any matter. I, however, both concerned for your welfare (Gratian, Decree, Part II, Cause 1, Question 6, canon 2) and fearing the judgment of almighty God upon my soul, desire that the case of Maximus be carefully investigated: whether he is not burdened by crimes that contradict the sacred order, and whether he is not attempting to attain priestly office through simony—that is, by offering rewards to those who elected him. He will then be a free intercessor for you before the Lord, if he comes to the place of intercession without being bound by his own offenses.

Yet his guilt of pride is already plainly revealed by the fact that, when summoned to come to us, he resists, retreats, and is afraid, using various excuses. Why, then, is he trembling, if his conscience does not accuse him of the matters with which he has been charged? Behold, your affection has long been without a shepherd; and, as almighty God makes known to you, I deeply and wholeheartedly sympathize with your abandonment. For I hear of the lacerations taking place in the Lord’s flock. But when the shepherd is absent, who will keep watch against the wolves? Therefore urge the aforesaid Maximus to come here to us, so that, if we can find him innocent, we may confirm him. But if the things reported about him prove true, your affection will no longer remain so long deprived through the interposition of his person. [Note: [Column 0818D] Recent editions read “I urge,” but this is not found in the manuscripts.]

Be assured concerning me that I am moved against him neither by hatred nor by the zeal of private interest; rather, with God as author, I decree whatever is canonical and just.

But I have been greatly astonished (Gratian, Decree, Part II, Distinction 93, canon 2) that among the numerous clergy or people of the Church of Salona scarcely two men from the sacred orders have been found—namely, my brother and fellow bishop Paulinus and my most beloved son Honoratus, archdeacon of that Church—who would not consent to communicate with Maximus, the man who seized the priesthood, and who recognized themselves to be Christians. You, dearest sons, ought to have considered your orders and recognized as rejected the man whom the apostolic see had rejected, so that he might first, if possible, be cleansed of the charges brought against him; only then should your affection have communicated with him, lest it become a participant in his guilt. Nevertheless, we are bound to your charity by the innermost bonds of compassion. Since we have learned that some of you were forcibly pressured to consent to him and to communicate with him, we pray almighty God to absolve you from all guilt for your sins and from every bond of another’s obligation, to grant you in this present life the grace of his protection, and to allow us to rejoice over you in the eternal homeland. [Note: [Column 0818D] Thus it is read in the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of March, indiction 14.

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF JADERA

He asserts that he is moved against Maximus solely by zeal for justice. He urges them to suspend themselves from communion with Maximus and to receive holy communion from those whom they know do not communicate with Maximus.

Gregory to the presbyters, deacons and clergy, nobles [Note: [Column 0819D] Jadera, commonly Zara, formerly an episcopal city of Western Illyricum and the chief city of Liburnia, now the center of the district of Jadera, commonly the *Comtado di Zara*. It is now an archiepiscopal and strongly fortified city on the coast of Dalmatia, under Venetian rule. I nevertheless think that the Jadera mentioned here was the city now called Zara Vecchia, situated midway between modern Jadera and Scardona. This letter resembles Epistle 26 and treats the same subject. GUSSANVILLE.] and people residing at Jadera, and to those who had communicated with Maximus the transgressor. [Note: [Column 0818D] EPISTLE XXVII [formerly 48].—This epistle has various inscriptions. The Norman manuscripts, together with Vatican D, the Colbert and Corbie manuscripts, and most others, have: “to the clergy, nobles, soldiers, and people residing at Jadera.” In Vatican B and C it is inscribed: “to the presbyters, deacons and clergy, nobles and people residing at Jadera, and to the soldiers.” Vatican A likewise has this, omitting “and to the soldiers.” In the Royal manuscript: “and to the soldiers residing at Jadera.”]

It has come to me that some of you, deceived by ignorance or necessity, have communicated with those who, as you know, have been deprived of communion by the apostolic see because their guilt required it; while others, with salutary discernment and under the Lord’s protection, have suspended themselves from them. As much as I rejoice over those who have remained steadfast, so much do I grieve over those who have strayed, because they have received the mysteries of holy communion—which divine mercy has granted us for absolution—for the ruin of their own souls. And because, as almighty God makes known to you, I deeply and wholeheartedly sympathize with your charity, I entreat and advise you with paternal affection: let everyone suspend himself from illicit communion and entirely shun those whom the apostolic see does not admit into its fellowship of communion, lest he stand guilty before the sight of the eternal Judge precisely where he might have been saved.

I have also learned that certain men of perverse mind have tried to suggest there that I am moved against Maximus by some kind of hatred, and that I desire to carry out not what is canonical but rather what belongs to rage. But far be this from me—far be it from a priestly mind that it should be moved by private zeal in any matter. I desire to have the case of Maximus investigated, concerned both for the people residing in those regions and for my own soul, and fearing the judgment of almighty God; and, with the Lord revealing it, to determine with complete sincerity what is canonical. Since we have often written to him that he must not celebrate the sacred rites of Mass before we could ascertain his case, otherwise he would be deprived of communion, his guilt of pride is now plainly revealed by the fact that, although repeatedly admonished, as I have said, to come to us, he resists, retreats, and is afraid, using various excuses. Why, then, is he trembling, if his conscience does not accuse him of the things alleged?

Knowing these things, and since you can no longer claim any excuse based on ignorance, I order, exhort, and admonish you to suspend yourselves in every way from fellowship with the forbidden communion, and let none of you presume to communicate, against his own soul, with anyone who communicates with the priest Maximus mentioned above.

Yet because, as I have said, I hear that some of you have fallen through ignorance and that others have been forcibly compelled to communicate, I beseech almighty God both to preserve continually by his grace those who in no way consented to this wickedness and to repay them with the generosity they desire, and to absolve from all guilt for their sins and from every bond of another’s obligation those whom zeal, ignorance, or any other cause has drawn into guilt; and to grant all of you in this present life the grace of his protection, allowing us to rejoice over you in the eternal homeland. Therefore, so that this intercession may benefit you before God our Savior, show obedience to our exhortations for the salvation of your souls, and receive holy communion from those whom you know have abstained, or are abstaining, from communion with the aforesaid Maximus.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO CANDIDUS, BISHOP

He is to select monks suitable for the presbyteral office, with the consent of their abbot, and ordain them presbyters.

Gregory to Candidus, bishop of the greater Old City. [Note: [Column 0820D] Most manuscripts have simply “to the bishop.”]

Your Fraternity has informed us that you have no presbyters and that for this reason you are suffering no small hardship. Since you report that certain monasteries located in your parish contain monks who may be suitable for this office, and request authority to promote them to this order, we therefore grant you permission by this letter to take monks from the monasteries situated in your parish, with the consent of their abbot, and ordain them presbyters. Above all, however, take care to investigate carefully the life and conduct of those who are to be placed in this office, and then ordain them if they are worthy. But if any fault should become evident in them that, by canonical prohibition, prevents them from being advanced to this order, let no petition or personal favor [Column 0820C] insinuate itself upon you, so that you should lay hands on such men. Otherwise—God forbid—this honor will become a punishment for them and begin to be a sin for you. [Note: [Column 0820D] In Vatican, “in the month of March, indiction 14.”]

## EPISTLE XXIX. TO MARIANIAN, BISHOP

He must not burden the monastery contrary to the arrangement of his predecessor, confirmed above in Epistle 1. He must not listen to those who offer harmful advice. He must value money less than the salvation of souls. He must not allow monasteries to suffer harassment from clerics.

Gregory to Marinian, bishop of Ravenna.

We are astonished that your Fraternity’s judgment has been so quickly altered, so that you do not perceive what you are asking. We are grieved by this, because you give clear evidence that the words of those who offer harmful advice have had more influence with you [Column 0820D] than devotion to divine reading has achieved. Although you ought to defend monasteries and diligently gather religious men there, so that you may gain profit from the gathering of souls, you instead desire to exercise burdens upon them, as your letter testifies; and, what is worse, you seek to make us participants in your guilt, since, with our consent, you wish to burden the monastery founded by your predecessor [Column 0821A] under the pretext of managing certain affairs and cases. [Note: [Column 0821D] Thus nearly all the manuscripts read it. The older editions altered it to “under the care of certain matters,” while the more recent editions, with the Royal manuscript, have “under the management of certain matters.”]

You ought to remember that, in your presence, and also in the presence of various presbyters, deacons, and your clergy, we granted what they requested contrary to the instruction of his testament. Yet the arrangement your predecessor had made concerning that monastery was confirmed. Now, disguising this fact, you ask us to issue contrary orders. We know that these requests are not truly yours; but, since you do not refuse to listen to those who speak inappropriately, you burden not only your own reputation but also souls. Therefore, because I love you greatly, I earnestly admonish you—and consider this strictly—that you [Note: [Column 0821D] The printed editions have, correctly, “so that you may consider this carefully.”] should not care more for money than for souls. [Note: [Column 0821D] This was said above in Epistle 42 of Book IV, now Book V, Epistle 44. Read Saint Bernard’s *Apology to William*, where he explains Persius, Satire 2: “What place has gold in a holy person?” It will be worth reading what precedes and follows. See also *To the Knights of the Temple*, at the beginning, chapter 5, and *Sermons on the Song of Songs*, sermon 23. See Saint Polycarp’s Letter to the Philippians. GUSSANVILLE.] Money should be regarded only peripherally, but for this you must labor with the whole intention of your mind [Column 0821B] and strive with greater force. [Note: [Column 0821D] Recent editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read “and look upon it more intensely.”] Devote vigilant care and attention to this matter, because our Redeemer does not seek gold from a priest’s office but souls.

Furthermore, it has come to us that the monasteries under your authority are being burdened by the importunity of clerics and by their various harassments. To prevent this from happening hereafter, restrain it by a strict warning, so that the monks living there may freely rejoice in the praises of our God.

As for the clerics Romanus and Dominicus, who rashly presumed to leave this city without our blessing, although they deserved to be punished by a greater penalty, they should nevertheless be released as an act of benevolence, so that they may be urged to return to their office. [Note: [Column 0821D] This sentence alone is found in the Turin, Saint Gall, and old Colbert manuscripts.]

In the month of April, indiction 14.

## EPISTLE XXX. TO SECUNDUS

He must hasten to secure peace with King Agilulf. He must stir Bishop Marinian to mercy toward the poor.

Gregory to Secundus, servant of God, at Ravenna. [Note: [Column 0822D] The commonly printed editions have “to Secundinus, servant of God,” not “to Secundus.” The English, Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts read “to Secundus.” Vatican B alone has “not from equals.”]

After Castorius returned and reported to us everything that had taken place between you and King Agilulf, we foresaw that no one should be able to find an excuse against us on account of delay, and therefore decided to send him back there with all possible speed. Learn from him what must be done; be diligent, and press forward in every way so that this peace may be arranged, because, as is reported, some are trying to obstruct it. Therefore hasten to act vigorously, so that your labor may not remain without effect. For these regions and various islands have already been placed in the gravest danger.

Stir up our brother Bishop Marinian with whatever words you can (Gratian, Decree, Part II, Distinction 86, canon 6), because I suspect that he has fallen asleep. Some people came to me, among them certain elderly beggars. I questioned them carefully about whom they had received what from, and they reported in detail how much had been given to them on their journey and by whom. When I diligently asked them what the aforesaid brother had given them, they replied that they had asked him but had received absolutely nothing from him, not even bread for the journey, although giving to everyone had always been customary for that Church. They said: “He replied to us, saying, ‘I have nothing that I can give you.’” And I wonder whether a man who has clothing, silver, and storerooms has nothing to give to the poor.

Tell him, therefore, to change his mind along with his position (ibid.). Let him not suppose that reading and prayer alone are sufficient, so that he may sit apart in devotion but bear no fruit through his hand. Let him have an open hand, come to the aid of those suffering need, and regard another’s poverty as his own; for if he does not have these qualities, he holds the title of bishop in vain. I admonished him about his soul in one of my letters, but he gave me no answer at all, and so I believe he did not even deign to read it. It was therefore no longer necessary for me to admonish him about anything concerning his soul by letter; I wrote only what a counselor might dictate concerning earthly matters. For I ought not to weary myself in dictating to a man who does not read. Your Fraternity should therefore speak to him privately about everything and admonish him how he ought to conduct himself, lest through his present negligence he lose, God forbid, his former life.

## EPISTLE XXXI. TO THE RAVENNATES

Whoever posted written accusations against Castorius by night is to be deprived of holy communion unless he publicly proves the truth of his accusation or confesses his error.

Gregory to Marinian, bishop of Ravenna, together with the other brothers and fellow bishops, presbyters, levites, clergy, nobles, people residing in the city of Ravenna or living outside it, and soldiers.

Someone, filled with the counsel of an evil spirit, secretly posted at night in a public place of the city an accusation against Castorius, our notary and representative, speaking of his alleged crime and craftily opposing me concerning the making of peace. [Note: [Column 0822D] I would call it a libelous notice: a public posting by which someone either imputes false crimes to another or publicly reveals true but hidden ones. GUSSANVILLE.] Since whoever speaks truthfully ought not fear making himself known, he must come forward publicly and demonstrate whatever he has presumed to say in his accusation. If he does not come forward and publicly confess, whoever he may be who presumed to do this, or who gave his consent to the counsel of so great an iniquity, we determine, by the spirit of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, that he is to be deprived of participation in His holy body and blood. If, because he remains concealed and is unknown, he cannot be held by disciplinary measures, [Note: [Column 0823D] Recent printed editions read: “if, although conscious of so great an evil, he nevertheless presumes, despite the prohibition, to receive…”] and if, conscious of so great an evil and already forbidden, he presumes to receive the Lord’s body and blood, let him be struck by the punishment of anathema and be cut off from the body of the holy Church as a deceitful and pestilential person.

But if there is perhaps someone to whom we send letters, wishing him well, without knowing that he is the author or accomplice of this deed, let the very prayer we make for him before almighty God be void. If, however, after coming forward publicly in that same city, he is able to demonstrate what he said—or, recognizing that he cannot prove what he wrote, openly confesses his error—he is not to be deprived of participation in the Lord’s body and blood, nor is he to remain separated from the body of the holy Church. For before almighty God we daily recognize our own faults: although we preserve the discipline of restraint, we nevertheless forgive and show indulgence toward the errors of others. [Note: [Column 0823D] The printed editions have: “so that, while discipline is preserved, we may nevertheless…”] [Note: [Column 0823D] Thus it is read in the Turin, Saint Gall, and Vatican manuscripts.]

In the month of April, indiction 14.

## EPISTLE XXXII. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP

If a Jewish or pagan slave desires to convert to the Christian faith, he is to be vindicated into freedom.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

We previously wrote to your Fraternity that, concerning those who, with God’s help, desire to come from Jewish superstition to the Christian faith, their masters should have no license to sell them; rather, from the moment they revealed their desire and intention, they ought in every respect to be defended into freedom. But because, as we have learned, they neither weigh our intention nor the provisions of the laws with sufficiently careful discernment, and do not consider themselves bound by this condition in the case of pagan slaves, your Fraternity ought to be solicitous about them (Gratian, distinction 54, canon 15) [Note: [Col. 0823D] Recent editions add *and if they are of the Jews*, perhaps for greater clarity; this is not found in the manuscripts. For more on the slaves of Jews, see Epistle 9 of Book IV. See Valentinian’s Third Novel, of the year 425, which Sirmond placed in the first volume of the Councils of Gaul; also the Code, *On the Jews*, Book XVII, and the following title, *Lest a Christian slave*]. If, moreover, not only a Jew but also any pagan should wish to become a Christian from their service, after his desire has been made known, no one should have the power to sell him to any Jew under any device or pretext [Note: [Col. 0823D] *Ingenium* means any device or contrivance. Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 22: “When the bishop protested and said that this man had repeatedly sought devices by which he might depose him from the episcopate.” Our Gregory, Book XII, Epistle 25: “He should not presume, by any device or excuse, to marry off his sons somewhere outside”], but the person who desires to convert to the Christian faith must, through your protection, be vindicated into freedom by every means.

Those, however, who must lose slaves of this kind should be dealt with by you through careful consideration, lest they perhaps irrationally judge their interests to be obstructed. Thus, if they have bought pagans from foreign regions for purposes of commerce, and within three months—while a buyer to whom they are to be sold is being found—a slave should happen to flee to the Church and say that he wishes to become a Christian, or should reveal this desire even outside the Church, they are of course to receive the price from the Christian buyer [Note: [Col. 0824D] Recent editions, against the English, Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts, read: “for whom they ought to be sold, no one is found”]. But if, after the prescribed three months, one of these slaves declares his desire and wishes to become a Christian, no one may thereafter buy him, nor may his master dare to sell him under any pretext whatsoever; rather, he must unquestionably be led to the rewards of freedom, since he is understood to have kept him not for sale but for service to himself [Note: [Col. 0824D] The same recent editions read *comparasse*]. Let your Fraternity therefore observe all these matters so vigilantly that neither the supplication of certain persons nor anyone’s rank may enable them to evade it. (See John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 46.)

## Letter XXXIII. To Bishop Leo

If the Samaraeans circumcise pagan slaves, he is to vindicate them into freedom without returning their price to the Samaraeans.

[Col. 0824C]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0824D] **Epistle XXXIII [Al. 32].**—Vatican A reads “to Leontius, bishop of Catania”] to Leo, bishop of Catania.

A detestable matter, wholly contrary to the laws, has come to our attention. If it is true, it seriously accuses your Fraternity, since it proves you culpable through insufficient vigilance.

We have learned that Samaraeans living at Catania bought pagan slaves and rashly presumed to circumcise them [Note: [Col. 0824B] Whether those whom the holy Doctor here calls Samaraeans were Jews is unclear. Certainly, in Book I of the *Moralia*, no. 22, he calls Samaritans *Samarians*, or *Samaraeans* according to many manuscripts. But *Samarites*—as they are called by Hilary in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 21—are not known to have existed or to have lived in Italy at that time. In Cassiodorus, Book III, Epistle 45, Jews seem to be intended by these words: “But now a people hardened in Samaraean superstition exists with shameless brow.” Jews are thus called contemptuously. See Book VIII, Epistle 21]. [Note: [Col. 0824D] Apply here what we said on Epistle 9, Book IV.] Therefore it is necessary that, exercising priestly zeal in this matter in every way, you diligently investigate it with the utmost alertness and care. If you find that it is so, vindicate the slaves themselves into freedom without delay and by every means, and extend ecclesiastical protection to them. Do not allow their masters to receive anything whatsoever by way of price [Col. 0825A]; they ought not only to be punished by this loss but also struck with another penalty under the laws. (See John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 48.)

## Letter XXXIV. To Castorius, Notary

He is to inquire how many solemn litanies there have been since earliest antiquity in which the bishop of Ravenna used the pallium.

[Col. 0825D]

Gregory to Castorius, our notary at Ravenna [Note: [Col. 0825D] **Epistle XXXIV [Al. 77].**—We have added this from the manuscripts. Castorius was not a notary of the Church of Ravenna but of the Roman Church, and was then residing at Ravenna].

When Florentinus, a deacon of the Church of Ravenna, was dealing with us on behalf of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus concerning the use of the pallium, we asked him what the ancient custom was. He replied that in all litanies the bishop of the Church of Ravenna used the pallium. We learned from others that this was not so, and it became evident from the letters of John, formerly bishop, which we had shown to him. But he asserted what he had been ordered to say [Col. 0825B]. For when you had forbidden that same John, formerly bishop, to presume to use the pallium disorderly and rashly, he wrote to us that this had been the ancient custom: that the bishop of that city used the pallium in solemn litanies. We have sent copies of those letters for your information [Note: [Col. 0825D] Vatican B reads “from the time when” instead of “when”].

Adeodatus, moreover, a deacon of the aforesaid Church, when he was here and likewise earnestly sought to discuss the use of the same pallium, we wished to learn the truth and therefore had him questioned in the same way about the custom. To persuade us that he should be believed and to obtain from us what he was asking, he testified under oath that it had been the ancient custom for the bishop of his city to use the pallium in four or five solemn litanies.

Therefore let your Experience diligently attend to this and inquire how many solemn litanies there have been from antiquity [Note: [Col. 0825D] See above, Book V, Epistle 11, and below, Epistle 61]. He should not seek information by calling them “solemn,” but by calling them “greater,” so that, once it has been established how many solemn litanies there were, from what the aforesaid deacon Adeodatus testified and the letter of the aforesaid Bishop John admits, we may learn how often he was accustomed to put on the pallium at the litanies and most willingly grant the request. But he should not inquire of those who are presented by the ecclesiastical party; rather, he should ask others whom he knows to be free from partiality, and should carefully report to us whatever he discovers through diligent investigation, so that, once the truth has been ascertained, as we have said, we may relieve the spirits of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus.

## Letter XXXV. To Anthemius, Subdeacon

He sends money for the redemption of captives and orders him to devote himself diligently to this work.

[Col. 0825D]

Gregory to Anthemius, our subdeacon at Naples.

We cannot say how great the grief and distress in our heart are over what has happened in the regions of Campania; you can yourself infer it from the magnitude of the calamity. For this reason, as a remedy for the captives who have been seized, we have sent, through the bearer of this letter, the magnificent Stephen, solidi to your Experience, admonishing you that you must be entirely solicitous and act energetically. You should hasten to redeem free persons whom you know cannot afford their own ransom. If they are slaves and you discover that their masters are so poor that they cannot rise to redeem them, do not cease to purchase these persons also. Likewise, take care to redeem the Church’s slaves who have been lost through your negligence.

For all whom you redeem, you must in every way prepare a detailed record [Note: [Col. 0825D] For the meaning of *notitia*, see above, Book III, Epistle 16, and here, Book IV], containing their names, who is staying where, what he does, or where he is from [Note: [Col. 0826D] Five English manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and many others read: “you will strive immediately to make …”], which you can bring with you when you come. Hasten to show yourself diligent in this matter, so that those who are to be redeemed may not, through your negligence, incur any danger, and so that you may not afterward become gravely culpable in our eyes. Above all, work to see whether you can purchase the captives themselves at a lower price [Note: [Col. 0826D] French: “the summary statement, the sum, the amount, the total.” Gussanville].

Describe the total amount with complete accuracy and care, and send us the description with all speed [Note: [Col. 0826D] Thus the old Colbert manuscript and the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus]. In May, in the fourteenth indiction.

## Letter XXXVI. To Bishop Secundinus

If Sincerus abstained from his father-in-law’s succession, he is not to allow the latter’s creditors to harass him. He is to arrange for him, however, to have free permission to go wherever he may find the means of supporting life.

[Col. 0826C]

Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium [Note: [Col. 0826D] Three Vatican manuscripts and others read “bishop of Tauromenium”].

Both the principle of law and natural equity admonish us that anyone who either refuses an inheritance or abstains from the succession of his parents ought not to bear hereditary burdens [Note: [Col. 0827C] An inheritance is “lying” when it has not yet been accepted. It is accepted when the heir declares by word or deed that he receives it. It is omitted when the heir allows himself to be excluded by the passage of time. It is repudiated when the person to whom it has devolved refuses to accept it. Gussanville].

Since, therefore, Sincerus, the bearer of this letter, has reported that his father-in-law Hilarus died completely destitute, and that his wife, Hilarus’s daughter, had involved herself in no way with Hilarus’s property [Note: [Col. 0827C] The printed editions incorrectly read “and his daughter,” since the addition of *-que* leaves it uncertain whose daughter is meant—the wife’s or Hilarus’s], and since he complains that he is being pressed by Hilarus’s creditors to pay the paternal debt, your Fraternity should investigate the matter carefully. If what he says is true, strive to extend priestly protection to them, and do not permit them to be harassed contrary to reason or to suffer any loss [Col. 0826D]. For it is exceedingly harsh that he should unjustly suffer expense from that which brought him no benefit.

If the aforesaid bearer wishes to come here with his wife, since he says that he cannot remain there, let them enjoy your support for God’s sake. Do not allow anyone’s adversity there to retain them merely according to his own will or to trouble them irrationally. Let them have free permission to go wherever they wish [Col. 0827A], so that, with God’s generosity, they may at least find elsewhere the means of living [Note: [Col. 0827C] This is how it is read in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus, the old Colbert manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript]. In June, in the fourteenth indiction.

## Letter XXXVII. To Bishop Columbus

He had given letters to the rector of the Sicilian patrimony for his deacon Rogatianus, so that a certain case might be settled more quickly. He sends to Columbus Peter, formerly bishop of Numidia, whom, after learning the case more fully there, he is to judge canonically together with those implicated. He is not to tolerate the infection of the children or slaves of Catholics by the baptism of the Donatists.

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia [Note: [Col. 0827D] **Epistle XXXVII [Al. 36].**—Many letters to Columbus survive, as the indexes will show].

We have received the letter of your Fraternity, full of priestly sweetness, delivered by the bearer of this letter, the deacon Rogatianus. Its gracious language greatly rejoiced us, especially because through it we learned of your good health, which is what we desire [Col. 0827B]. We have long known your Holiness’s devotion, and now possess it just as you describe it. For we do not require assurance of the sincerity your Fraternity shows toward us [Note: [Col. 0827D] According to the jurists, *satisfactio* is the provision of a pledge or surety. In French: “I believe him on his word, without security.” The same word occurs at the end of the letter of Marcianus of Alexandria: “So that, once assurance has been received in every respect.” Gussanville], since we know it from the love of our mind that is directed toward you.

For the bearer mentioned above, whom you commended to us by letter, we have given a letter to the rector of the Sicilian patrimony, so that he may compel the opposing party to do what is just, in order that, once its evasive excuse has been set aside, the dispute over the entire case may be brought to an end more quickly.

We therefore inform your Holiness that a certain man named Peter came to us, asserting that he had been a bishop and asking us for a remedy in his case. At first he reported matters that might have deserved pity; but upon investigation we afterward found the facts to be very different from his account, and his conduct greatly saddened us. Since, however, being separated by so great a distance, we could not learn the inner details of his case with sufficient precision, we were unable, in our uncertainty, to decide it.

Now, since the aforesaid deacon, on his return, asked that Peter be released with him, and Peter himself requested that he be sent to you, we knew that your Holiness possesses, as is fitting, zeal for the faith and love of justice. We were therefore pleased, and granted what they requested. Since you can learn the case more precisely in person, we exhort you to preserve for Peter whatever is just and canonical, so that the vigor of uprightness may be fulfilled by you in every respect and his case may be judged according to the fear of God and the rules of the Church. If anyone is said to have been an accomplice or participant with the aforesaid Peter in the matters of which he is accused, he must be carefully investigated and, once the truth is known, judged canonically in the same way.

Furthermore, an altogether grievous matter, hostile to right faith, has come to our attention: Catholic people—and, what is worse, religious people—consent to have their children and slaves, or others under their authority, baptized into the heresy of the Donatists [Col. 0828B] [Note: [Col. 0827D] In Gregory’s age this term is shown by John Filesacus, commentary on the *Commonitorium* of Vincent of Lérins, no. 12, to denote not only monks and clerics but indeed any Catholic Christian].

If this is true, your Fraternity must strive with the utmost effort to correct it, so that the integrity of the faith may remain undefiled through your care and innocent souls—which could have been saved by Catholic baptism—may not perish through the infection of heretics [Note: [Col. 0827D] This does not mean that the baptism of heretics was considered invalid by Stephen I’s successor, a devoted disciple of Augustine, but that those who through such baptism entered the fellowship of heretics would grow accustomed to their practices and become infected by their errors. Although Athanasius, Basil, Optatus, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Ambrose, even after the Council of Nicaea, seem to have rejected entirely the baptism of heretics, one should not therefore say with Gussanville: “The ancients teach almost with one voice … that baptism conferred by heretics has no power of cleansing.” For now no one except a heretic denies that baptism is valid regardless of who confers it, provided it is consecrated by the evangelical words. Yet it is clear that nothing belongs to the faith except what has come down continuously from the apostles; our faith does not rest upon new revelations. Certainly, in the famous controversy between Stephen and Cyprian, when Cyprian rejected baptism given by a heretic because of the minister’s perversity and infidelity, and consequently judged that those coming from heresy should be baptized again, while Stephen argued that baptism received even from heretics was valid because of the force and efficacy of the evangelical words with which it was conferred and should not be repeated, he pressed this point above all: “If anyone comes to us from any heresy, let nothing be innovated except what has been handed down, so that hands may be imposed for penance.” Indeed, as Augustine says in Book II *On Baptism*, chapter 9, the whole world was held by the strength of custom. In Book IV, chapter 6, Cyprian was acting against the custom of the whole world, which he derives from the apostles in Book V, chapter 23. Jerome, in his dialogue *Against the Luciferians*, likewise presents the custom of not rebaptizing heretics as perpetual throughout the universal Church from the time of the apostles. Eusebius also attests the same in Book IV of his *History*, chapter 4].

Therefore, whoever among the persons mentioned above has allowed one of his own to be baptized by the Donatists must strive with every strength and all diligence to recall that person to the Catholic faith. If, in future, anyone permits this to be done to one of his own under any excuse whatsoever, he must be entirely excluded from the clergy.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] **Epistle XXXVIII, formerly XXXVII.**]

## Letter XXXVIII. To Anthemius, Subdeacon

He commends to him Alexandria, widow of Vincomalus.

[Col. 0828C]

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon.

To the extent that widows who live uprightly are deprived of the comfort of husbands, ecclesiastical protection must be extended to them with equal urgency. Therefore we assign you this duty in writing, so that you hasten to provide Alexandria, a magnificent woman and formerly the wife of Vincomalus, with protection wherever necessary, with every effort and care, while of course preserving equity, and so that you diligently advance her interests. Do not permit anyone to harass her or force her to suffer distress. Rather, as we have said, whenever the case requires it, let her enjoy the assistance of your care, so that no one may attempt to take advantage of her affliction and oppression while you are present there.

## Letter XXXIX. To Cyprian, Deacon

He commends John, who has returned from schism, and orders that eight solidi be given him annually.

Gregory to Cyprian, deacon [Note: [Col. 0829D] Two Teller manuscripts read “to Cyprian, subdeacon”].

You must, with equity preserved, regard in every respect as commended to your affection John, the devout bearer of this letter, who has returned from the schism of the Istrians to the bosom of the holy Church, having received understanding through God’s revelation [Col. 0829B]. You must extend ecclesiastical protection to him whenever his case requires it. We also wish you, beginning with this fourteenth indiction, to give him each year that many solidi [eight, as specified in the heading] for his support [Note: [Col. 0829D] Recent editions, against the Vatican, English, Norman, and other manuscripts, read “for the support of his expenses”], and you should know that you are to charge them in every respect to your accounts [Note: [Col. 0829D] Those same editions read “of the present year’s indiction … eight solidi.” We follow the Vatican, Norman, Regius, and Rheims manuscripts].

## Letter XL. To Bishop Donus

If Georgius lives more uprightly, he is to assist his support.

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messana.

Georgius, the bearer of this letter, wishing, as he says, to live in your city, asked that he be commended to your Fraternity by our letter [Col. 0829C]. Since he promised to restrain himself from wrongful conduct, we judged that what he requested should not be denied. Therefore, for God’s sake, let your Holiness be solicitous for his soul and recall him by your exhortations to the path pleasing to God. If, with the Lord’s help, he suspends himself from every wrongdoing as he promised and wishes to live honorably, let your Fraternity, as you deem appropriate, assist his support for your reward, lest he perhaps seem to take necessity as an excuse for doing evil [Note: [Col. 0829D] There is a twofold mercy in this case: provision is made both for the soul and for bodily necessity. Gussanville].

Let your Fraternity also consider what you may have to endure from his importunity: he has come to you with our letters, although we ourselves endured his great persistence in pleading without granting him any authority.

[Note: [Col. 0830] [This note appears at the foot of column 830, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text.] **Epistle XLII, formerly XLI.**—They think that the Monastery of Saint Hermes, situated in the city of Palermo, was one of the six founded in Sicily by Saint Gregory, because in Epistle 4 of Book IV, now Book V, Epistle 6, speaking of the abbot Urbicus, he says that he was superior of his monastery. Gussanville.]

## Letter XLI. To Bishop Rufinus

In the Church of Massa Nicoterana he is to ordain a priest who, in place of the bishop assigned to penance, may baptize and celebrate Masses.

[Col. 0830A]

Gregory to Rufinus, bishop of Vibo [Note: [Col. 0829D] Thus in all the manuscripts, instead of “of Vibo.” Vibo Valentia was also called Hipponium by some, Bivona by others, and Bibona by still others; it was once an episcopal city of the Bruttians on the shore of the Gulf of Hipponium, commonly the Gulf of Saint Euphemia, now a town in the province of Further Calabria in the Kingdom of Naples, not far from Mount Leonis, whose successor city it became. Gussanville. The Norman, Vatican D, Colbert, and many others read only “to Rufinus, bishop.” Four other Vatican manuscripts have “bishop of Vivenna”].

From a report by the inhabitants of Massa Nicoterana [Note: [Col. 0830D] Nicotera still retains this name; it lies between Tropea and Vibo and remains an episcopal city in Further Calabria under the archbishop of Reggio. It is mentioned in the Seventh Synod, act 1, in the subscription of Sergius, bishop of Νικοτερῶν (*Nikoterōn*, Nicotera). Gussanville], whose bishop has been assigned to penance for certain offenses, we have learned that there is no priest there who can celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass, to such an extent that they even assert that their children have remained without baptism.

Since for this reason they earnestly requested that a priest ought to be ordained in the same Church, to which your Fraternity is providing visitation, we therefore exhort you by this letter to inquire among the clergy of that Church whose life and conduct might be suitable for this office, and hasten, with the Lord’s help, to consecrate him there as priest. For it is exceedingly harsh that, while the case of their bishop is being carefully investigated, that Church should have no priest capable of celebrating the sacred work there [Note: [Col. 0830D] This date is confirmed by the testimony of the Vatican, Colbert, and Tours manuscripts]. In July, in the fourteenth indiction.

## Letter XLII. To Bishop Victor

That he is to ordain a priest in the monastery.

Gregory to Victor, bishop of Palermo.

Urbicus, abbot of the Monastery of Saint Hermes, situated at Palermo, together with his congregation, earnestly requested from us that a priest be ordained in the same monastery to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass. Since a request of this kind should not be postponed, we have necessarily decided to exhort your Fraternity by this letter to consecrate without delay, with the Lord’s help, whichever person from that congregation is chosen for this ministry and whose life, conduct, and actions can be suitable for so great an office. Thus neither will he have to leave his monastery for this reason, nor will he be forced to bring in an outsider to perform the sacred work.

## Letter XLIII. To Venantius, Patrician

He expresses his sorrow over the disagreement between Venantius and Bishop John; Venantius is to show the bishop reverence and pursue their cases while preserving charity.

Gregory to Venantius, patrician and former monk [Note: [Col. 0830D] **Epistle XLIII [Al. 42].**—See Epistle 34 of Book I and Epistle 59 of Book IX. We have discussed Venantius at great length in the Life of Saint Gregory].

The letter you sent has found us greatly saddened, because we have learned that a scandal has arisen between you and our brother and fellow bishop John, whose harmony we had hoped to enjoy. Whatever the cause may have been, anger ought not to have erupted to such a degree that, as we have heard, your armed men broke into the bishop’s residence and committed various outrages in a hostile manner, and that this matter temporarily separated you from paternal charity.

Could not any dispute, whatever it was, have been settled calmly, so that neither the interests of the parties would suffer loss nor goodwill suffer injury? We are not unaware of the gravity, holiness, and gentleness of the aforesaid brother of ours. From this we infer that, unless excessive anguish had compelled him, his Fraternity would never have reached the point concerning which you say that you were distressed.

Nevertheless, as soon as we learned this from his letter, we wrote to him, advising him to receive your offerings as before and to permit the solemnities of Mass to be celebrated in your house—or, if you wished, to celebrate them himself—and to pursue his case while preserving charity [Col. 0831B]. Since we neither wish anyone to be in disagreement nor wish disagreement to continue, we decided that the same exhortation should be repeated.

Therefore, dearest son, it is necessary that you show him priestly reverence, as sons ought, and not provoke his spirit to anger. For with whom will you have secure favor if, God forbid, you are at odds with a priest? Accordingly, laying aside the swelling of your hearts, strive to conduct the cases you have against one another in such a way that charity may remain undefiled between you and that each may gently secure the other’s advantage [Note: [Col. 0831D] These offerings had nearly fallen into disuse, although in the primitive Church they were frequent and were later established and prescribed by canons. See the Council of Gangra, canons 5–8; the Council of Cologne, 1549, canon 20; the Fourth Council of Milan, title “On Parochial Rights,” the final title of Part II of the constitutions; and so forth. Gussanville. Consult the preface of our John Mabillon to Part I of the third Benedictine century]. (See John the Deacon, Book III, no. 48.)

## Letter XLIV. To Bishop John

He exhorts him to show Venantius his former goodwill.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Although there was a cause that not unjustly provoked your Fraternity’s spirit to anger, so that you did not wish to receive the offerings of Lord Venantius or allow the sacred solemnities of Mass to be celebrated in his house, nevertheless earthly affairs must be conducted in such a way that no quarrel can separate us from the bond of charity. Therefore, as we wrote previously, we exhort your Holiness to receive the offerings of the aforesaid man in every respect with sweetness and God-pleasing sincerity, and to permit the mysteries of Mass to be celebrated in his house.

Thus, as we wrote, if he should wish it, you ought to go to him and, celebrating Masses in his presence, restore your former favor. You ought to extend priestly affection to sons and, insofar as reason supports it, not neglect the jurisdiction of your Church in these matters. Considering this, your Fraternity must strive to conduct yourself toward them with such prudent moderation that you may both beneficially accomplish what the quality of the matter requires and not depart from the grace of paternal charity.

## Letter XLV. To Bishop Leontius

He grants permission to dedicate a church and confirms the donations of its founders.

Gregory to Leontius, bishop of Rimini.

We grant permission to dedicate the Basilica of the blessed martyr Stephen, which your Fraternity reports was burned by fire [Col. 0832B] and which, as you also recently stated, has been restored [Note: [Col. 0831D] Four Vatican manuscripts and others read “restored”]. We also wish the shrines containing the relics of that same blessed martyr Stephen to be placed there.

Therefore, dearest brother, you must go to the aforesaid Church and solemnly perform the dedication both of the Church and of the newly constructed altar, so that, with the Lord’s help, the devotion of those awaiting that consecration may be fulfilled. Whatever was formerly granted to that place by its founders, we wish to remain in the same intention and with the same force in which it was given.

## Letter XLVI. To Bishop Felix

He is to have his episcopal chair removed from the monastery and is not to celebrate public Masses there again.

[Col. 0832C]

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Pesaro [Note: [Col. 0831D] On Pesaro, see above, Book V, Epistle 28].

We are astonished that your Fraternity, disregarding the wording of the instruction given to you by my predecessor of holy memory, consecrated the monastery constructed by John, the bearer of this letter, in a manner contrary to the practice required by ancient custom.

That instruction also commanded, among other things, that you dedicate the place itself without public Masses. Yet, as has come to us, after a chair was installed there, the sacred solemnities of Mass are being celebrated publicly [Note: [Col. 0832D] Public Masses are those to which all the faithful are accustomed to be summoned and to assemble. Pelagius, the immediate predecessor of Saint Gregory, had forbidden the bishop to celebrate public Masses in the monastery under discussion, so that the tranquility of the monks might be safeguarded and a large gathering of people might not take place there. The holy pontiff rebukes the bishop for acting otherwise].

If this is true, we exhort you in these words to cease every excuse and have your chair removed from there by every means, and not to celebrate public Masses there again. But, as both custom and the wording of the instruction declare, if they should wish Masses to be celebrated there for themselves, a priest is to be sent by you [Note: [Col. 0832D] A bishop is not permitted to place his chair in a monastery, lest the freedom and exemption of the monastery be violated by the chair, which is a sign and indication of episcopal jurisdiction, says Alteserra in his commentary on this letter].

In that same monastery we wish the congregation of God’s servants to remain as the aforesaid John requested, as it now exists, and, with God’s grace, always to remain. As for the chalice which, it has been reported, was taken from him by your Fraternity, hasten to restore it to him, if that is so [Col. 0833A] [Note: [Col. 0833C] The Norman, Regius, and some other manuscripts read: “But hasten to restore the chalice which … was offered to him”]. Let your Holiness therefore strive to fulfill these instructions so carefully that the aforesaid bearer will not again need to return to us because of this matter.

## Letter XLVII. To Bishop Leo

He is to protect John, who has returned from the schism of the Istrians, and support him with an annual allowance.

Gregory to Leo, bishop of Fano [Note: [Col. 0833C] Fano, or Fanum Fortunae, commonly called Fano, was formerly a city of Umbria and is now in the Duchy of Urbino, on the Adriatic coast between Rimini and Senigallia. It remains an episcopal city, immediately subject to the Roman pontiff and within his dominion. Gussanville].

Just as schismatics who persist in their perverse zeal must be rebuked and detested, so those who return to the bosom of Mother Church must be consoled and nevertheless supported. Since, therefore, John, the devout bearer of this letter, having recovered his understanding, has been converted from the error of the Istrians to the unity of the holy Church through God’s mercy [Col. 0833B], we have decided to exhort your Fraternity to regard him as commended to you in every respect, with due regard for reason, and to protect him through your favor.

We have also arranged that something from the Church should be provided for him each year, so that after his conversion he may not succumb to any necessity. Since, therefore, he earnestly asked to be commended to your Holiness, it is your duty, for your reward, to ensure that, as we have said, he is supported by your assistance in every respect.

## Letter XLVIII. To Urbicus, Abbot

He is to receive Agatho into the monastery if his wife also wishes to convert in the same way.

Gregory to Urbicus, abbot of the Monastery of Saint Hermes, situated at Palermo [Note: [Col. 0833C] The Norman manuscript and most manuscripts do not contain what follows. Vatican A alone has the words “which is established at Palermo”].

Whoever, pierced by divine inspiration, hastens to turn to God after abandoning the activities of this world must be received with charity and refreshed in every respect by gentle consolations, so that, with God’s help, he may delight in persevering in the manner of life he has chosen.

Since Agatho [Note: [Col. 0833C] Alteserra thinks that this Agatho was the Roman pontiff, because Anastasius says: “Agatho, a Sicilian by birth, from among the monks, sat [as pope],” etc. But since Agatho was not elected pontiff before the year 679, we judge him to be different from this man.], the bearer of this letter, desires to convert in the monastery of your charity, we exhort you to receive him with all sweetness and love, kindle his desire for eternal life through continual exhortation, and diligently take care for the salvation of his soul. Thus, while he remains with devoted mind in the service of our God under your admonition, both his abandonment of the world may benefit him and his conversion may contribute to your reward.

You should understand, however, that he is to be received only if his wife also wishes to convert in the same way. Since the two have become one body through the bond of marriage, it is incongruous for one part to convert while the other remains in the world (see Gratian, 27, question 2, chapter 25).

828 ## Letter XLIX. To Bishop Palladius

He sends relics for the dedication of four altars in the basilica that Palladius had built.

[Col. 0834B]

Gregory to Palladius, bishop of Saintes in Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0833D] LETTER XLIX [otherwise 50].—He was the tenth bishop of Saintes, of noble lineage. King Guntram hated and harassed him because he had openly received in his city Gundobald, who was aspiring to the kingship, and secretly sheltered under his roof messengers of Fredegund. On this matter see Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book VII, chapter 31, and Book VIII, chapters 2, 7, and 43. He is also discussed in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 57 and 60, and Book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 8. Fortunatus, Book I, poem 3, praises him for building the church of Saint Stephen. He attended the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. His name is read in the calendars of the Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0833D] The Santones, or Mediolanum Santonum—commonly Saintes—were an episcopal city of Gaul, under the archbishop of Bordeaux, metropolitan of Aquitania Secunda, and capital of the province of Saintonge [Col. 0834C]. We restore the title from the Colbert, Vatican, and Norman manuscripts; the printed editions read “bishop of the Santones.”]

The bearer of this letter, Leuparicus, your presbyter, on arriving informed us that your Fraternity had built a church in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and also of the martyrs Laurence and Pancratius, and had placed thirteen altars there.

[Note: [Col. 0834C] Vatican B and some other manuscripts read “twelve altars.” The Greeks have one altar within each individual church, as Cardinal Bona observes in *On Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 14, no. 3. This letter of Gregory the Great shows a different Latin custom; so too does Ambrose, Letter 20 to his sister Marcellina, no. 26, writing of the peace granted to Catholics by Valentinian: “Without delay, it was announced,” he says, “that the emperor had ordered the soldiers to withdraw from the basilica . . . . . . The soldiers rushed forward in rivalry to announce this at the altars, signaling the token of peace by kisses.” Baronius explains why several altars were sometimes built: “The tombs of martyrs,” he says, “were altars, and where martyrs were buried, an altar customarily was erected.” This is clear from Prudentius, *On the Crowns* (*περὶ Στεφάνων*), hymns 3, 4, and 5; Saint Augustine, Sermon 5 on Saint Stephen, and *The City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 27; Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book V, chapter 49, and *The Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapters 33 and 91; and Paulinus, Poem 4. Indeed, from Letter 32 of the same Paulinus, in the new edition, it is certain that already in his age altars had been erected over the tombs and relics of confessors. In the first capitulary of Charlemagne, of 805, no. 6, provision is made that altars should not be excessive in churches.]

We learn that four of these still remain unconsecrated, because, God willing, you intend to place there the relics of the saints mentioned above. Since we have reverently provided relics of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of the martyrs Laurence and Pancratius, we urge you to receive and place them with due reverence, with the Lord’s help. Above all, you must ensure that those serving there do not lack the assistance necessary for their sustenance.

[Note: In the Agathenian collection, canon 36 reads: “All clerics who faithfully and diligently serve the Church are to receive from the priests—namely, from the bishop—the stipends due for their holy labors, according to the merit of their service and the ordering of the canons.” Truly golden words. — Gussanville.]

[Note: Galf. translates *assistance*. *Suffragor*, by transference, means “I favor” or “I assist.” *Suffragium* means support for food and maintenance; see the Third Council of Toledo, canon 3.]

## Letter 50. To Brunichild, Queen

He sends the relics she had requested and urges her to provide for the peace and welfare of those who serve them.

[Col. 0835A]

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

The tenor of your letters, which expressed a religious disposition and the zeal of a pious mind, not only caused us to praise the purpose of your will but also gladly invited us to grant your requests. We ought not to refuse what Christian devotion and the desire of an upright heart demanded, especially since we recognized that you were asking for and wholeheartedly embracing things that could greatly protect the faith of believers, bring about the salvation of souls, and preserve it as well. Therefore, saluting Your Excellency with the honor due to you, we inform you that we have given to the bearer of this letter, Leuparicus, whom you wrote was a presbyter and through whom we received your written message, relics of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, according to your request and with the reverence appropriate to them.

[Note: During Gregory’s pontificate, Latins scarcely dared to touch the bodies of saints or raise them from their tombs. Gregory of Tours frequently calls “relics of the saints” the veil of a saint’s tomb, or the pallium placed upon that tomb, wax or oil from the lamps and candles customarily burning there, dust collected from the site, herbs or flowers placed there, and similar objects. *Dialogues* II.38: “Even in the shrines of the martyrs, we perceive that they display not so much benefits through their bodies as benefits through their relics.”]

But, so that your praiseworthy and religious devotion may shine forth ever more brightly in you, you must take care that the benefits of the saints be deposited with reverence and due honor, and that those serving there be afflicted by no burdens or vexations. Otherwise, if external necessity presses upon them, they may perhaps be rendered useless and sluggish in God’s service, and—God forbid—they may suffer injury and neglect because the benefits bestowed by the saints have been disregarded.

[Note: Constant service gave rise to clerical immunities; it is regrettable that sluggish creatures rejoice in them. — Gussanville.]

Let Your Excellency therefore provide for their peace, so that, while they are kept free from every disturbance through your beneficence, they may offer praises to our God with a tranquil mind, and your reward may increase in eternal life.

[Note: In the *Regestum*, followed by the more recent editions, *collocata* (“placed”). In Vatican B, *collecta* (“collected”). We follow Corbie, Normandy, three Vatican manuscripts, and others.]

[Note: [Col. 0835D] LETTER LI [otherwise 57, indiction 13].—That this letter and the following seven were sent at nearly the same time is evident because Augustine is named in each as bearer or carrier of the present letter. The time at which they were delivered is known from the sequence of the journey. Cointius sets it out in the *Ecclesiastical Annals* for 596 and 597, but he is not to be followed where, on p. 443, he denies that Augustine visited the diocese of Tours. Augustine’s route was Rome, Lérins; from Lérins to Marseille, Aix, Arles, Vienne, Lyons, and Autun; thence to King Theodoric of Burgundy and King Theudebert of Austrasia. Theudebert held court at Metz, Theodoric at Chalon. Although we have no letter on Augustine from Gregory to Chlothar, king of Neustria, it is nevertheless clear from Book XI, Letter 61, that Augustine was most kindly received and aided by King Chlothar himself. Having greeted the kings, as he went on to the sea to cross into England, he could certainly have visited Pelagius of Tours; he then crossed the Loire in the province of Anjou at Ponts-de-Cé (otherwise Caesar’s Bridge, commonly *le pont de Cé*), as Gotselin writes in his *Life* of Augustine. Moreover, although this letter to Augustine is nowhere found in the register of Saint Gregory’s letters, it is preserved by Bede, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, chapter 23, and by John the Deacon, Book II of the *Life*, chapter 34.]

## Letter 51. To the Brothers Going to England

He urges Augustine’s companions to complete the journey they have begun to England and to obey Augustine, whom he has appointed their abbot.

[Col. 0836A]

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to the servants of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Since it would have been better not to begin a good work than to turn back in thought from what has been begun, you must, dearest sons, apply the greatest zeal to completing the good work that, with the Lord’s help, you have undertaken. Therefore let neither the hardship of the journey nor the tongue of malicious men deter you; but with every exertion and every fervor carry out what you have begun, with God as your guide, knowing that great labor is followed by the glory of eternal reward.

When Augustine, your superior—whom we have also appointed your abbot—returns, obey him humbly in all things. Know that whatever is completed among you at his admonition will profit your souls in every respect. May Almighty God protect you by his grace and grant me to see the fruit of your labor in my eternal homeland. Thus, although I cannot labor together with you, may I nevertheless be found with you in the joy of reward, since I desire to labor with you.

May God keep you safe, dearest sons.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, was reigning, in the fourteenth year, and in the thirteenth year after the consulship of that same lord of ours, in the fourteenth indiction.

## Letter 52. To Pelagius and Serenus, Bishops

He commends Augustine, going to England with his companions, and Candidus, the administrator of the patrimony.

[Col. 0836C]

Gregory to Pelagius of Tours and Serenus of Marseille, his fellow bishops in Gaul.

[Note: The manuscripts do not agree on the superscription of this letter. In two Teller manuscripts, Rheims, Vatican D, and Bede, it is erroneously addressed “to Aetherius, archbishop of Arles,” although Aetherius was bishop of Lyons. In three Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and the *Regestum*, it is addressed only to Pelagius and Serenus. In Colbert, instead of *Turnis* (“Tours”), one finds *Turonis*. The meaning of *a paribus* (“from a common source”) was explained above, at Letter 25 of Book I.]

[Note: Serenus had succeeded Theodore in the church of Marseille. A letter was also sent on this same occasion to Aetherius of Lyons; Bede preserves it in Book I, chapter 24: “To his most reverend brother Aetherius, fellow bishop: Gregory, servant of the servants of God. Although among priests…” It ends: “May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.” Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, was reigning, in the fourteenth year, and in the thirteenth year after the consulship of that same lord, in the fourteenth indiction. Bede is mistaken, however, in thinking that Aetherius was bishop of Arles; Aimoinus later made the same error. Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 8, and Fredegar in his *Chronicle*, chapter 22, more correctly recognize Aetherius as bishop of Lyons.]

Although among priests possessing a charity pleasing to God religious men need no recommendation, nevertheless, since a suitable occasion for writing has presented itself, we have taken care to send our letter to your Fraternity. We inform you that we have sent there, for the benefit of souls and with the Lord’s help, the bearer of this letter, Augustine, a servant of God whose zeal we know with certainty, together with other servants of God. Your Holiness must hasten to assist him with priestly zeal and provide him with your support. So that you may be more ready to offer assistance, we have taken care to explain the matter to you in detail, knowing that once you understand it, you will devote yourselves wholly, for God’s sake, to providing aid, since the situation requires it.

We also commend to your charity in every respect our common son, the presbyter Candidus, whom we have sent to administer the small patrimony of our Church.

[Note: Thus, besides Bede, two Teller manuscripts and Vatican D.]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

## Letter 53. To Virgilius, Bishop

He commends Augustine and Candidus the presbyter, and urges Virgilius to restore the patrimonial revenues collected by his predecessor.

Gregory to Virgilius, bishop and metropolitan of Arles.

Although we trust that your Fraternity is devoted to good works and willingly offers itself in matters pleasing to God, nevertheless we think it useful to address you with fraternal charity, so that you may increase, prompted also by our letters, the support that it is proper for you to provide spontaneously.
