Therefore we inform Your Holiness that we have sent there, for the benefit of souls, the bearer of this letter, Augustine, a servant of God whose zeal and devotion are well known to us, together with other servants of God, as he himself will be able to explain when he appears before you. You must assist him in this matter with prayer and aid, and, whenever the need requires, offer him the support of your assistance and refresh him, as is fitting, with fatherly and priestly consolation. Thus, when he has received the support of Your Holiness, if—as we hope—he succeeds in winning something for our God, you too may acquire a reward, since you have devotedly supplied an abundance of assistance for good works.

Your Fraternity, as one who is united with us in purpose, should also regard with every care our common son, the presbyter Candidus, and the small patrimony of our Church, so that, with the help of Your Holiness, something from it may benefit the sustenance of the poor. Since your predecessor held this patrimony for many years and kept the revenues collected there in his possession, let Your Fraternity consider to whom the property belongs and for whom it is to be expended, and, with regard for his soul, restore these revenues to our aforesaid son Candidus the presbyter, to be sent on to us. For it is utterly detestable that what was preserved by kings of the nations should be said to have been taken away by bishops.

[Note: By “kings of the nations” he undoubtedly means the Gothic kings who long occupied Narbonese Gaul and Aquitaine.]

## Letter 54. To Desiderius and Syagrius, Bishops

He commends Augustine and Candidus.

Gregory to Desiderius of Vienne and Syagrius of Autun, his fellow bishops in Gaul.

[Note: Desiderius was the twenty-eighth bishop of Vienne. Because, with episcopal zeal, he reproved Brunichild’s corrupt conduct, she first drove him into exile; then, at the Council of Chalon, presided over by Arigius, bishop of Lyons and a participant in the queen’s counsels, he was deprived of his episcopal rank in 603 and, some years later, buried beneath stones. Ado of Vienne gives a detailed account in his letter to the church of Vienne. Fredegar the Scholastic, the Chronicle of Bèze, and the Life of Saint Columbanus should also be consulted.]

[Note: Vienne was a celebrated city of Gaul. Thus Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.1: “In this Gaul, two cities above all are renowned as distinguished and excellent mothers of cities, Lyons and Vienne, both of which the Rhône flows through.” He then adds accounts of the deeds of martyrs who suffered in those cities, from which their churches derive their special dignity. For some time Vienne rivaled the Church of Arles in ecclesiastical authority; now it presides over only six episcopal sees.]

[Note: Syagrius was made bishop after having been a citizen of Autun, and was a man of outstanding virtue. Fortunatus writes to him in Book V, number 5: “To the holy lord Syagrius, most worthy pope of the apostolic see.” Ado of Vienne calls him a man of supreme holiness, and he is called “holy” in canon 5 of the Council of Metz. He subscribed to the Second Council of Lyons in 567, the Fourth Council of Paris in 573, the First Council of Mâcon in 580, the Third Council of Lyons in 583, and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. According to Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 28, he attended the baptism of the younger Chlothar, king of the Franks, in 591. He died in 600. For in the following year Saint Gregory sent letters to several bishops of Gaul to eradicate the simoniacal heresy, but none to Syagrius; and in his letters to Senator Lupus and Thalassia he indicates that Syagrius had already died, calling him “of revered memory.” Some have incorrectly called him Brunichild’s brother, without any foundation. — Gussanville.]

[Note: Autun—also called Augustodunum, Augustudunum, or Augustidunum, and commonly Autun—is a well-known city of Gaul in the duchy of Burgundy, still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Lyons. Its people were formerly called the Aedui, whose chief city it was. At the request of Queen Brunichild, Saint Gregory granted Syagrius the pallium, as is clear from Letter 5 of Book VII, now Book IX, Letter 11. — Gussanville.]

We have good confidence in the sincere charity of your Fraternity, because, out of love for the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, you devoutly offer support to our people, especially since the nature of the matter demands that you come forward and labor even of your own accord. We therefore inform Your Holiness that we have sent there, for the sake of souls and at the Lord’s direction, the bearer of this letter, Augustine, a servant of God whose zeal and devotion are well known to us, together with other servants of God. When your Fraternity has learned in detail from his report what has been entrusted to him, you must provide him with every kind of support that the matter requires, so that you may prove to be, as is proper and fitting, helpers in a good work. Let your Fraternity therefore show itself devoted in this matter, so that by your deeds we may prove true the good things about you that we have learned through report. We commend to you in every respect our beloved common son, the presbyter Candidus, to whom we have entrusted the small patrimony of our Church established in those regions.

[Note: By the name of Saint Peter the Roman Church, the see of Saint Peter, is sometimes meant. This has given careless readers occasion to misunderstand ancient ecclesiastical records. When they read that preachers were sent by Saint Peter into Gaul, Spain, and other provinces, they immediately asserted that the Gospel had been proclaimed in those places by Saint Peter’s disciples during the apostolic age, whereas they should have understood “Saint Peter” to mean his successors and the Roman see, from which the faith was propagated throughout the western provinces. On this subject see Quesnellius’s notes on Saint Leo, volume II, p. 887.]

## Letter 55. To Protasius, Bishop

He urges him to press Virgilius of Arles concerning the revenues to be sent to Rome and asks him to keep Candidus in his care.

[Col. 0839B]

Gregory to Protasius, bishop of Aix in Gaul.

[Note: He became the tenth bishop of Aix after serving as *vicedominus* of the Church of Arles. — Gussanville. Corbie, the English manuscripts, and the Norman manuscripts read *Protagius*.]

[Note: Aix, *Aquae Sextiae*, commonly Aix-en-Provence, is a famous and very ancient city of the Gallic province, formerly the metropolis of Narbonese Gaul II and still an archiepiscopal see. In the Norman manuscripts and several others, the words “bishop of Aix” are absent; they are present in Colbert, Vatican, and other manuscripts.]

The excellence of your love for the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, has been revealed not only by the prerogative of your office but also by the devotion that you display toward the interests of his Church. Since we have learned this from Augustine, the servant of God and bearer of this letter, we greatly rejoice in the affection and love of truth that are in you, and we give thanks because, although absent in body, you show that in mind and spirit you are with us, displaying toward us the fraternal charity that is fitting.

Therefore, so that the good reputation that has been proclaimed about you may be confirmed by the truth of events, tell our brother and fellow bishop Virgilius to take care to send to us the revenues that his predecessor received for many years from our small patrimony and kept in his possession, since they belong to the poor. If he should perhaps attempt in some way—which we do not believe—to excuse himself, explain the case as it truly stands, since you know the truth of it more precisely and at that time were administering the office of *vicedominus* in that Church.

[Note: Under Sapaudus of Arles. The concern of an ecclesiastical *vicedominus* consisted chiefly in administering and protecting the temporal property of the Church or of the bishop. See Book II, Letter 71.]

You must also make clear that he should not retain in his possession the property of Saint Peter and of his poor. If our people should perhaps need it, do not refuse your testimony in this matter, so that the blessed apostle Peter, for whose love you do these things, may repay you by his intercession both in this life and in the life to come, both for the truth and for your devoted good will. We earnestly commend to Your Holiness our common son, the presbyter Candidus, to whom we have entrusted this patrimony. (See above, Letter 33.)

## Letter 56. To Stephen, Abbot

He praises the order of his community, urges him carefully to preserve it, and thanks him for the spoons and rings.

Gregory to Stephen, abbot.

[Note: In Colbert, “to the abbot of the monastery at Lérins.” In two Vatican manuscripts and others one reads “of the monastery” or “of Mount Quirinal,” perhaps through a transposition for *qui* or *quod Lirino*. In Corbie, Normandy, and most manuscripts, only “to Stephen, abbot” is given. Gussanville is undoubtedly mistaken when he denies that the monastery of Lérins is intended here, arguing that no abbot Stephen is listed in the chronology of the saints of Lérins by Barralis Salernitanus or elsewhere. One would search elsewhere in vain for a complete catalogue of the abbots of Lérins. Vincentius Barralis’s chronology does not include all the abbots of Lérins; as he himself says on p. 186, neither Gussanville nor the leading authorities after him has supplied a complete list. His list contains a gap from 490 to 579, when Marinus flourished. After him he places Chonon, to whom Gregory writes below, in Book XI, Letter 12. Is Stephen omitted because there was nothing exceptional about him? Certainly Gregory reproves the negligent relaxation of the abbot Stephen whom he here urges to vigilance and diligence in the letter to Conon, abbot of Lérins and Stephen’s successor. Barralis lists no more than twelve abbots from about 400 to the end of the tenth century, whom the Church enrolled among the saints. Of many others he says nothing at all, except for two who were otherwise famous: Faustus, bishop of Riez, and Leotmund, son of Charlemagne. Stephen himself is counted among the abbots of Lérins in the fuller index of *Gallia Christiana*. See Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, p. 241.]

The report of Augustine, the servant of God and bearer of this letter, has made us glad, because he told us that your Belovedness is vigilant, as is proper; moreover, he affirmed that the presbyters, deacons, and the whole community live as one in unity and harmony.

[Note: Thus there were already several presbyters and deacons in the monastery, and not only at Lérins. See Jerome, Letters 60 and 61, chapter 16.]

Since the goodness of superiors is a salutary rule for their subjects, we pray Almighty God to kindle you always in good works by the grace of his mercy, to protect those entrusted to you from every temptation of diabolical deceit, and to grant that you and they may live in charity and in a manner pleasing to him.

Since the enemy of the human race does not cease to lie in wait for our actions, but by continual cunning strives to deceive those who serve God in some respect, we therefore urge you, dearest son, to exercise your vigilance attentively. Guard those entrusted to you through prayer and careful oversight in such a way that the prowling wolf may find no opportunity to tear anyone apart. Then, when you have returned safely to our God those whose care you have undertaken, may his grace repay your labor with rewards and multiply in you the desire for eternal life.

We have received the spoons and rings that you sent, and we give thanks to your charity, because, by sending objects necessary for the poor’s use, you have shown how much you love them.

[Note: He calls the small dishes in which porridge is served “rings,” because of their round shape. Gussanville renders the word in French as *des porte-assiettes, des colliers de Maures* (“plate-holders, Moorish necklaces”). But the rings Gregory mentions here were intended for the use of the poor.]

## Letter 57. To Arigius, Patrician

He commends Augustine, his companions, and Candidus.

Gregory to Arigius, patrician of Gaul.

We have learned from Augustine, the servant of God and bearer of this letter, how greatly goodness and gentleness, together with charity pleasing to Christ, shine in you. We give thanks to Almighty God, who has granted you these gifts of his mercy, through which you may become highly praiseworthy among men and, what is truly useful, glorious in his sight.

[Note: In Corbie and Normandy, *respondeat* (“may he repay”).]

We therefore pray Almighty God to multiply in you the gifts he has granted, to preserve you and all yours by his protection, and to order the activity of Your Glory in this world in such a way that it may benefit you both here and, what is more to be desired, in the life to come. Saluting Your Glory with fatherly affection, we ask that the bearer of this letter and the servants of God who are with him may receive from you whatever assistance they require, so that, having found your favor, they may, with the Lord’s help, better fulfill what has been entrusted to them.

We also commend to you in every respect our son Candidus the presbyter, whom we have sent to administer the patrimony of our Church located there, trusting that you will receive from our God a corresponding reward if, with devoted intent, Your Glory provides assistance to the property of the poor.

[Note: In all these letters, whenever he speaks of the small patrimony, he commends it as the property of the poor. The same is commonly said of the Church’s goods, which many—alas!—very often divert to other uses. When they are to be reclaimed and defended, they are called the property of the poor; when they are to be consumed, they become the property of clerics. Thus the poor are mocked, but God is not mocked. See Book VIII, Letter 28. — Gussanville.]

## Letter 58. To Theodoric and Theudebert

He commends Augustine, whom he has instructed to take with him to England some nearby presbyters, and Candidus, the ecclesiastical administrator of the patrimony.

Gregory to Theodoric and Theudebert, brothers and kings of the Franks, his peers.

[Note: In this and elsewhere, the compiler of Gregory’s letters placed Theodoric before his elder brother Theudebert, preserving the chronological order in which the letters were to be delivered. For those coming from Rome had to visit Theodoric, king of Burgundy, before Theudebert, king of the Austrasians; the royal residence of Theodoric at Chalon came before Theudebert’s seat at Metz, as Adrien de Valois observed in Book XVI of his *Frankish History*. — Gussanville.]

After Almighty God has adorned your kingdom with the righteousness of faith and made it conspicuous among other peoples for the integrity of Christian religion, we have conceived great hope concerning you: namely, that you desire your subjects to be converted in every respect to the faith in which you are their kings and lords.

We have therefore learned that, by God’s mercy, the people of the English eagerly desire to become Christian, but that the priests who are nearby neglect them and fail to kindle their desires by their exhortations.

[Note: Thus the following letter does not display pastoral concern. Saint Paul’s zeal did not sleep in this way; he became all things to all people so that he might win all. Likewise the African Fathers censured the carelessness of bishops who, though they lived near the Donatists, did not labor to attract their neighbors everywhere to the Catholic faith. Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 34 on Acts* 1: “If even one person should depart uninitiated, has he not overturned that person’s entire salvation?” That is: if even one person dies uninitiated, has he not destroyed his whole salvation? What would he have said about pastors who, while so many thousands of heretics perish in their parishes, sleep soundly on both ears? — Gussanville. Formerly the text read *sacerdotes vestros* (“your priests”). The final word is absent in the Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts.]

For this reason we have decided to send there Augustine, the servant of God and bearer of this letter, whose zeal and devotion are well known to us, together with other servants of God. We have also instructed them to take with them from the surrounding region some presbyters, with whom they may learn the minds of the people and, as God grants, assist their wishes by their exhortation.

Therefore, saluting Your Excellency with the paternal charity with which we salute you, we ask that those whom we have sent may deserve to find your favor. Since this concerns the salvation of souls, may your power protect and assist them, so that Almighty God, who recognizes that you support his cause with devoted mind and complete zeal, may order your affairs by his mercy and, after your earthly power, lead you to the heavenly kingdoms.

We also ask that Your Excellency keep in every respect in your care our most beloved son Candidus the presbyter and the small patrimony of our Church established in those regions, so that the blessed apostle Peter, prince of the apostles, may repay you by his intercession because, in view of your reward, you provide protection for the property of his poor.

## Letter 59. To Brunichild, Queen of the Franks

He asks her to provide protection and aid to Augustine going to England and to Candidus, administrator of the patrimony.

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

Your Christianity became known to us in former times in such a genuine manner that we have no doubt at all about its goodness. Rather, we hold it certain in every respect that, in the cause of faith, it joins itself devoutly and diligently to the work and supplies abundant assistance from its religious sincerity.

Therefore, confidently relying on this, we salute you with paternal charity and inform you that news has reached us that the English people, by God’s will, desire to become Christian, but that the priests who are nearby do not exercise pastoral concern for them. To prevent their souls from perishing in eternal damnation, we have taken care to send there the bearer of this letter, Augustine, a servant of God whose zeal and devotion are well known to us, together with other servants of God, so that through them we may learn their wishes and, with your cooperation also, consider their conversion as far as possible. We have likewise instructed them to take with them from the surrounding region some presbyters for carrying out this work.

Your Excellency, accustomed to readiness for good works, should, both out of consideration for our request and from reverence for divine fear, deign to keep him in your care in every respect, offer him the grace of your protection with earnestness, and bring the support of your patronage to his labor. So that you may receive the fullest reward, ensure that he can go safely under your protection to the aforesaid people of the English, so that our God, who has adorned you in this world with good things pleasing to him, may grant you to rejoice here and in eternal rest with his saints.

We also commend to Your Christianity our beloved son Candidus the presbyter and the patrimony of our Church established there, and ask that he receive in every respect the grace of your protection.

## Letter 60. To Eulogius, Bishop

He observes that the two of them are bound by a special bond of charity; therefore he joins in his grief. So as not to increase his sorrow, he refrains from recounting the evils he suffers from the Lombards. He wonders why Eulogius did not answer the letter directed against John of Constantinople’s pride. He sends gifts in return.

Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria.

Charity, the mother and guardian of all good things, which binds many hearts together in unity, does not consider a person absent whom it holds present to the eyes of the mind. Since, dearest brother, we are held together in the root of this charity, bodily absence can claim nothing against us, nor can the distance between our regions claim anything; for we who are one are surely not far from one another. We always desire this to be common to us with our other brothers as well.

There is, however, something that binds us to the Church of Alexandria by a certain special bond and compels us, in a particular way, to be more ready in our love for it. For, as is clear to all, the blessed evangelist Mark was sent from the holy apostle Peter, his teacher, to Alexandria.

[Note: Hence it is called an apostolic see, as noted above in Letter 37 of Book IV, now Book V, Letter 39. — Gussanville.]

Thus we are bound by the unity of this teacher and disciple, so that I seem to preside over the see of the disciple because of the teacher, while you preside over the see of the teacher because of the disciple.

We are also bound to this unity of hearts by the merits of Your Holiness, whom we recognize as beneficially following the institutions of its founder, and whom we always perceive to turn with complete devotion toward the bosom of its teacher, from which the preaching of salvation arose there.

[Note: Recent editions read *unde illi praedicatione* (“from which preaching came to it”).]

Therefore, when we received the pages of Your Holiness, our heart rejoiced over the fraternal visit as much as it was oppressed by sorrow over the burdens you reported. In fraternal compassion we groan with you because you are suffering. But since upheaval is spreading everywhere in different forms, in a common necessity one must be less troubled by one’s own distress and strive rather to conquer by patient endurance what cannot altogether be avoided.

[Note: The editions read *in diversa* (“in different directions”). We have removed *in*, following the manuscripts.]

Yet how much we suffer from the swords of the Lombards, amid the daily plundering, mutilation, and slaughter of our fellow citizens, we refuse to relate, lest, while speaking of our sorrows, we increase yours through the compassion that you show us.

[Col. 0844B] 837 Moreover, some time ago we sent our letter to our common son, the deacon Sabinianus, who was carrying out the responses of the Church in the royal city; [Note: [Col. 0843D] He refers to Letter 43 of Book V, in which he complains about the pride of John of Constantinople. Eulogius did not answer this letter, either because he interpreted the word “ecumenical” more favorably, or because he thought it safer to abstain from those controversies.] he ought to have forwarded it to your Fraternity. If you received it, we are surprised that you did not reply to us at all concerning it. And therefore, since care must be taken lest anyone’s pride introduce scandal into the Churches, it is necessary that, rereading that letter attentively, you preserve with every effort and complete attention whatever pertains to your honor and to the peace of the Church.

May Almighty God, who by the grace of his mercy has bestowed upon you a priestly spirit and charity, protect you in his service, guard you inwardly and outwardly from every adversity, and graciously grant that the souls of those who have gone astray may be converted to him through your preaching.

We received the bearer of this letter, Isidore, a deacon and our common son, with the charity that was appropriate; [Note: [Col. 0844D] From the bishop of the Church of Saint Mark. GUSSANV.] he was bringing us a blessing from Saint Mark the Evangelist. You, indeed, shining with the merit of a good life, have sent us sweet-smelling woods that are near paradise. But we, because we are sinners, have sent you from the West wood which, being suitable for the construction of ships and signifying the tumult of our mind, is always tossed upon the waves of the sea. We certainly wished to send larger pieces, [Note: [Col. 0844D] Thus in all the Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and others. The older editions read *navis angustia* (“the narrowness of the ship”), whereas the more recent editions have *navis angusta* (“the narrow ship”).] but this narrow ship could not receive them. In the month of August, in the fourteenth indiction.

## LETTER LXI. TO CASTORIUS, THE NOTARY

What serious and trustworthy men at Ravenna swore had formerly been observed concerning the use of the pallium must be observed at Ravenna.

[Col. 0844D]

Gregory to Castorius, the notary.

The illustrious lord Andreas repeatedly presses me to restore the use of the pallium according to the ancient custom in the Church of Ravenna. And you know that Bishop John wrote to me that it had been the custom of that Church for its bishops to use the pallium during solemn litanies. Adeodatus, the deacon of this Church, when he strongly petitioned me for the same matter, confirmed under oath that the bishops of that place had been accustomed to use the pallium during the litanies four times a year. But the aforesaid lord Andreas says in his letters that, apart from Lent, the bishop of Ravenna used the pallium during the litanies at all times. He even claims that these were solemn litanies, although he does not blush to call them daily litanies. Hence I was utterly astonished.

But let your experience consider neither any person nor anyone’s words; let it keep only the fear of God and uprightness before its eyes. Let it summon the older men, as well as the archdeacon of that Church, whom I do not suspect of committing perjury for another’s honor, and others who had been in sacred orders before the time of Bishop John—or, if there are any more mature men outside the sacred orders. Let them come before the body of Saint Apollinaris, touch his tomb, and swear what the custom had been before the time of Bishop John; for, as you know, that man was exceedingly presumptuous and tried arrogantly to claim many things for himself. 838 Whatever is sworn by trustworthy and serious men, we wish this to be observed in that Church according to the memorandum appended below.

But see that you do not act negligently, lest anyone corrupt your faith or devotion in this matter—for I know your zeal. Act carefully, yet in such a way that the aforesaid Church is not burdened contrary to justice, but that the usage which existed before the time of Bishop John is preserved for it. Do not summon only two or three persons to satisfy you, but as many of the oldest and most serious men as you can find, so that we neither deny that Church what its earlier custom was, nor grant what was sought through a novel presumption. Do everything gently and kindly, so that your action may be firm but your speech mild. Recall with you the sword that was left there, as we wrote some time ago, and carefully heed what our son Boniface, the deacon, and the illustrious Maurentius, the chartularius, have written to you.

I swear by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity of divine power, and by this body of blessed Apollinaris the martyr, that I testify without favor toward any person and without any intervening advantage. But this I know, and have learned through my own experience: before the time of John, formerly bishop, the bishop of Ravenna had the custom of using the pallium in the presence of this or that apocrisiarius of the apostolic see, on this or that day, and I have not learned that he usurped it secretly or in the absence of the apocrisiarius. (Compare John the Deacon, book IV, no. 6.)

## LETTER LXII. TO PETER, THE BISHOP

He should grant the abbot Opportunus of Saint Leontius the relics he requests.

[Col. 0846A]

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Hydruntum.

Opportunus, abbot of the monastery of Saint [Note: [Col. 0845D] LETTER LXII [Al. 73, indiction 4].—In the Norman manuscript, the Colbert manuscript, and three Vatican manuscripts, A, D, and E, it reads “Saint Leucius.” In Vatican B, “Saint Laurence.”] Leontius, which is situated at the fifth milestone from the city of Rome, [Note: [Col. 0845D] By the *sanctuaria* he perhaps means some veil or *brandeum*—that is, relic-contact cloth—stolen and then granted anew. See Book IV, Letter 30, and Mabillon’s preface to the second century of the Benedictine history, observation 8.] requests that the relics of that martyr, which, as he asserts, were stolen from the Church dedicated to his name, be granted to him again, so that they may be placed in the same location. Therefore, dearest brother, since the body of that most blessed martyr is known to be in the Church of Brundisium, whose visitation you oversee, it is fitting that, by our command, you comply with the wishes of the aforesaid man, so that he may obtain the fulfillment of the devotion he requests. [Note: [Col. 0845D] At the end, according to other editions, it reads: “Given in the month of August, in the fourth indiction.” Only one Vatican manuscript contains this, while four others are silent; indeed, among all those we used, only the Colbert manuscript includes it. Even there, however, it is uncertain whether this chronological note belongs to the following letter—namely Letter 74, in the fourth indiction, according to the other editions—or rather to the present letter written to Peter, which had previously been assigned to the fourth indiction.]

## LETTER LXIII. TO GENNADIUS, THE PATRICIAN

He complains that Bishop Paul was prevented from coming to Rome. He says that, as soon as he recovers from his illness, he will undertake the examination of Paul’s case.

[Col. 0846B]

Gregory to Gennadius, patrician of Africa.

We do not doubt that Your Excellency remembers that two years ago we wrote on behalf of our brother and fellow bishop Paul, asking you to provide him, since he desired to come to us, with the support of your rank, because he was said to be suffering harassment from the Donatists. Thus, once it had been reported that he could not obtain assistance there against them, we might, after learning the truth, have offered him fraternal assistance and considered, with a salutary decision, what ought to be done against the madness of such pernicious presumption. [Col. 0846C] And, so far as the aforesaid brother made known to us, he not only failed to deserve anyone’s support, [Note: [Col. 0846D] Recent editions read *sed minime* (“but by no means”). Two Vatican manuscripts read *sed ut minime*, which is also found in the old edition. We follow the Rheims, Corbie, and Norman manuscripts.] but was prevented by various obstacles from approaching the city of Rome without hindrance. Yet when we had reread to him a letter from you, he replied that he was suffering not from the hatred of certain people because he restrained the Donatists, but rather, as he maintained, that he was enduring the ingratitude of many in defense of the Catholic faith. He reported many other matters which, since the appropriate time for speaking had not arisen, we decided to retain in silence. [Note: [Col. 0847D] Another reading is *silentio reticere* (“to suppress in silence”), as found in the old editions and the Vatican manuscripts.]

Since, then, the matter concerns not earthly affairs but the salvation of souls, and since your assertion and his are different, we could not give a careful response without investigating the truth, because when we received Your Excellency’s letter we were confined by bodily illness. But when Almighty God, if it pleases him, restores us to our former health, we will investigate the truth as diligently as we can. And according to what we are able to learn, we will, by God’s mercy, arrange the case in such a way that the salvation of the souls over which you, for your reward, are pleased to labor will not only be restored where it has already been lost by those in error, but that the salvation existing among the worshipers of the true faith will also be preserved by the grace of our Redeemer. [Note: [Col. 0847D] The editions read “by the grace that disposes,” *gratia disponente*.]

Concerning the bishop mentioned above, whom you assert has been deprived of communion, we were greatly surprised that this was reported to us not by his primate but by a letter from Your Excellency.

## LETTER LXIV. TO DOMINICUS, THE BISHOP

The pastoral office must be exercised through charity. He congratulates Dominicus for exercising it in this way and thanks him for the gifts.

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage.

[Col. 0847B] Truly marvelous is the power of charity, beloved brother. After the arrival of heavenly grace had bent spiritual things down toward what is lowly, and after it had reconciled the human being—himself divided against himself by carnal enticements—it so expanded in human minds that it bent the lofty, exalted the humble, reconciled those at variance, softened the fierce, joined together the separated, repaired what was broken, and bound together in one the nations of humanity divided by so many distances of waters, lands, and climates, joining their minds together by the bond of its sweetness. What human weakness of tongue could adequately set forth the praises of such greatness? Its praise is perfect in heaven, but on earth its form should be displayed rather than spoken, so that, since its nature and greatness cannot be fully expressed by our mouths, they may be shown more clearly through our compassion. Although we praise it to some extent with our lips, we must at the same time confess it with our hands, lest anyone who is merely its praiser and not its doer sharpen the judgment against himself, because in the sight of the Judge such a person aggravates by his favorable words what he has omitted in action. [Note: [Col. 0847D] The recent edition’s *faciamus* (“let us do”) is preferable; it occurs in none of the manuscripts available to us.]

Although separated from you by distances of place and situated far away from you in body, with God’s power assisting us we preserve this charity most diligently toward you. You, too, ought to display it not only toward us but toward your brothers and sons with paternal and fraternal affection. For how could it not be practiced with the greatest care, when its perfection consists not so much in the love of brothers and sons as also in the love of enemies?

Therefore, dearest brother, let us who are bound by the office of pastoral care love our brothers (1 John 3:14). Let us join even our adversaries to ourselves in affection, for the sake of the Lord’s commandment (Matthew 5:44). Let us pursue peace with all people and holiness, without which no one will see God (Hebrews 12:14). Let us be engaged in pious works and abound in virtues. Let the rational of judgment [the breastpiece] shine in our breast, joined with the action of the shoulder-piece (Exodus 28:28 ff.). Let us proceed in the sight of God and of all Israel. Let us offer examples to the flock entrusted to us, so that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:16). Let speech be on our tongue and the fervor of zeal in our spirit, so that we may truly be counted among those of whom it is written: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one rested upon each of them” (Acts 2:3). For tongues of fire truly dwell within us if, in exhorting our brothers and sons, we are kindled by the fervor of the divine Spirit.

Let us cultivate the Lord’s field entrusted to us while we may; let us sow in fear while there is time; let us not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we shall reap without growing weary (Galatians 6:8–9). Let us be among those of whom the Psalmist says: “Going, they went and wept, scattering their seeds” (Psalm 125:6). To invite us to the fruit of this labor, he added: “But coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.” Let us therefore keep watch, and, leaving earthly concerns behind, let us long for heavenly things. Forgetting what lies behind, let us stretch ourselves with greater effort toward what lies ahead (Philippians 3:13). Let our mind not dissipate amid worldly variety, but let it run and converge wholly toward the one end which David regarded with wondrous sweetness when he said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26:4). May the hearts of good rulers be melted by this love. May the whole mind be suspended upon these things. While we are still placed on earth, may a frequent rain of tears bear fruit in heaven from the cloud of compunction. For then, beloved brother, we truly and rightly descend to the love of our neighbors, if we persevere in the love of God with our whole heart, our whole soul and mind, and all our strength.

841 As for the temporal gifts sent by you, although we have no need of such things, we nevertheless received them with due charity. What we do need is your proper charity and the concern you show for the governance entrusted to you, and we rejoice in these. For they become much sweeter to us when they have been seasoned with the sweetness of a priestly mind and a devout manner of life. [Note: [Col. 0847D] Thus the Norman, Corbie, Regius, and Rheims manuscripts and Vatican D, together with many others. In three Vatican manuscripts it reads: “when they have been seasoned with a priestly mind and the sweetness of a devout manner of life.” We found no manuscript support for the reading in the editions: “when the minds of priests have been seasoned with a devout manner of life.”]

## LETTER LXV. TO MAURICIUS, THE EMPEROR

He sends certain African bishops from Rome to Constantinople, so that they may testify to the emperor Mauricius himself that the laws against the Donatists are being neglected. He arouses Mauricius against those who disregard his laws.

[Col. 0848D]

Gregory to Mauricius [Note: [Col. 0848D] LETTER LXV [Al. 63].—The Cistercian manuscript adds “and Tiberius.” Tiberius was one of the sons of the emperor Mauricius Augustus, but had not yet been admitted to a share in the empire. Why, then, would Saint Gregory have written this letter jointly to him and to his father Mauricius, while overlooking his elder brother Theodosius, who had already been invested with the purple? In three Vatican manuscripts and the Regius manuscript it reads: “To Mauricius Tiberius Augustus.” This was undoubtedly the inscription in the manuscript from which the Cistercian was copied. But since Mauricius Tiberius was the surname of Mauricius, the copyist wrote “to Mauricius and Tiberius.”] Augustus.

Amid the cares of war and the countless anxieties that you sustain with tireless devotion in governing the Christian commonwealth, it is a cause of great joy to me, together with the whole world, that Your Piety always watches over the guardianship of the faith with singular concern—the faith by which the empire of the lords shines. Hence I am entirely confident that, just as you defend God’s causes out of love for a religious spirit, so God protects and assists Your Majesty by the grace of his own majesty.

How Your Piety’s serenity has been moved against the most shameful depravity of the Donatists by consideration of justice and zeal for the most sincere religion is made perfectly clear by the tenor of the commands that have been sent. But the most reverend bishops coming from the province of Africa assert that these commands have been set aside through such careless dissimulation that neither the judgment of God is feared there, nor have the imperial commands thus far obtained their effect. They add that in the aforesaid province, with the rewards offered by the Donatists prevailing, the Catholic faith is being publicly sold. On the other hand, the glorious Gennadius complained to me in similar terms about one of those who were making such complaints. Two others likewise gave testimony concerning the same matter. [Note: [Col. 0849D] Thus it reads in the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and other manuscripts, where the editions have “two other reliable men.” Shortly afterward we restore *in* before *causa* from all the manuscripts. In the Beccensis manuscript, instead of *saecularis judicis intererat* (“a secular judge was involved”), it reads *saeculares judices intererant* (“secular judges were involved”). We have made many other changes in agreement with the manuscripts but do not mention them because they are minor.]

But since the involvement of a secular judge was required in the case itself, I thought that these bishops should be directed to the presence of Your Piety, so that they might personally report to your most serene ears what they confess they have suffered for the Catholic faith. Therefore I beg that, for the salvation of their souls and the life of your most pious offspring, Your Christian Majesty command by a strict decree that those whom you recognize as such be punished, extend the hand of rescue to halt the ruin of those who are perishing, apply the medicine of correction to their deranged minds, and drive from them the bites of error. [Note: [Col. 0849D] The editions read “the diseases of error from them,” *ab eis morbos*, against the manuscripts: the Anglic, Norman, Vatican, Regius, Rheims, and Corbie.] Thus, when the darkness of pernicious depravity has been driven away by the remedy of your pious provision and true faith has spread the rays of its serenity there, a heavenly triumph before the eyes of our Redeemer will await you, because those whom you defend outwardly from the enemy you also free inwardly from the poison of diabolical deceit—which is the more glorious achievement.

## LETTER LXVI. TO ATHANASIUS, THE PRIEST

He declares him free from every stain of heresy and promises to write this to the bishop of Constantinople.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0849D] LETTER LXVI [Al. 74].—Previously it was read “to Anastasius,” contrary to the testimony of very many manuscripts and old editions. This is also established by the context of the letter, in which all manuscripts and printed editions read “to Athanasius,” as does Letter 5 of Book VI, now Book VII, where all copies have *Athanasius*. Those who corrupted the title ought to have noticed this. The same error occurs in the printed editions of John the Deacon, although the manuscripts protest against it. GUSSANV. See the Chronological Index of the History of Eastern Monasticism, p. 65.] to Athanasius, priest of Isauria.

Just as we are afflicted and grieve over those whom the error of heretical depravity has cut off from the unity of the Church, so we rejoice with those whom the profession of the Catholic faith holds within its bosom. And just as pastoral concern requires us to oppose their impieties, so it is appropriate for us to extend favor to the pious professions of these men and to declare that what they believe is sincere. [Note: [Col. 0850D] As in the case of John of Chalcedon above, Letter 15. GUSSANV.]

Therefore, when a contrary suspicion arose concerning you, Athanasius, priest of the monastery of Saint Mile, called Tamnaco, situated in the province of Lycaonia, [Note: [Col. 0850D] This is a region of Asia Minor, part of Cappadocia, lying southward toward Cilicia and separated from it by Mount Taurus, between Isauria to the west and Lesser Armenia to the east. Its metropolis is Iconium, now commonly called Cogni. GUSSANV.] you chose to have recourse to the apostolic see over which we preside, so that the integrity of your profession might become apparent. You also asserted that, after being physically beaten, you had done certain things unjustly and violently.

Although acts done under compulsion are not at all accepted by the discipline of the canons and are rightly considered invalid, because the one who compels another to confess and do what is unjust himself dissolves those acts, nevertheless the confession that is shown to proceed from spontaneous will must rather be accepted and embraced—as you are recognized to have done before us. Yet, so that nothing ambiguous might remain for us, we decided to write concerning you to our most holy brother and fellow bishop John, bishop of the city of Constantinople, so that he might inform us by letter of what had taken place. [Note: [Col. 0850D] Lycaonia was subject to him as patriarch of Constantinople, according to the Council of Chalcedon, canons 9, 17, and 28.]

After being admonished by us several times, he replied and informed us that a book had been found in your possession containing many heretical statements, and that for this reason he had been moved against you. Since he took pains to send it to us for your justification, we carefully read through its earlier sections. And because we found in it manifest poisons of heretical depravity, we forbade that it be read again. [Note: [Col. 0850D] Recognize here the ancient power and practice of the Roman pontiffs to prohibit certain books, a power to which even members of the Eastern Churches, subject to the patriarch of Constantinople or otherwise, were obliged to submit.]

But because you testified that you had read it in simplicity, and, to remove the basis for ambiguous suspicion, presented us with a written statement in your own hand, in which, setting forth your faith, you openly condemned all heresies in general and everything contrary to the integrity of the Catholic faith or profession; professed that you had always accepted and continued to accept everything received by the four holy universal synods, and had condemned and continued to condemn everything they condemned; promised both to accept and to preserve the synod held in the time of the emperor Justinian concerning the Three Chapters; willingly consented when we forbade you to read the book in which the poison of pernicious deceit was woven; also rejected and condemned everything stated or secretly inserted in it against the integrity of the Catholic faith; and promised that you would not read it again—moved by these considerations, and since, from the page of the statement approved by you, your Catholic faith became perfectly clear to us, God preserving it, we declare according to your profession that you are free from every stain of heretical perversity and are Catholic, and that in all things you have shone forth as a professor and follower of sincere faith, by the grace of Christ Jesus the Savior. We also grant you free permission to return to your monastery and resume your place and rank there without hindrance.

Concerning this, we also wish to send our letter to our beloved brother, the bishop of the city of Constantinople, who was ordained in place of the aforesaid holy John. But since it is not customary for us to write before his synodical letter has been brought to us, we have delayed. Once it has been delivered to us, we will communicate this to him when the proper time arrives. [Note: [Col. 0851A] It was not only newly promoted patriarchs who were accustomed to send a synodical letter to the Roman pontiff; the Roman pontiff himself also immediately sent letters to them after their promotion, as witnesses and attestations of his faith. Saint Gregory did this in Letter 24, now Letter 25, of Book I. The words of Pope Gelasius I in Letter 2 to Laurentius are so clear that they cannot be obscured by any darkness: “It is the custom of the priest of the Roman Church, when newly appointed, to send the form of his faith to the holy Churches,” and so forth.] (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, nos. 36 and 23. See the index: indiction 11, Letter 52; indiction 13, Letter 18.)

## BOOK SEVEN

In the fifteenth indiction and the seventh year of his ordination.

[Col. 0851]

845 [Note: [Col. 0851D] BOOK VII. Alternatively, BOOK VI. LETTER I.—In the Colbert manuscript, this letter is preceded, in the same red ink as the title of the book, by: “In the month of October, in the fifteenth indiction.” The same is observed in the Vatican manuscript.]

## LETTER I. TO FORTUNATUS, THE BISHOP

He should restore to her husband the wife who has been proved free; nor should the husband consider dismissing her again.

[Col. 0851B]

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Your Fraternity knows more carefully for what reason the bearer of this letter came here last year, compelled to do so with her mother. [Note: [Col. 0851D] Vatican B reads “knows more sharply.”] Her husband, your cleric, is known to have removed her from his marital companionship because she had been accused of servile status. They assert that, while you were here, you promised that if, with the Lord’s help, she could prove herself free, you would restore her to her husband.

Your Fraternity should know that, God revealing it—the author of freedom—she has been proved free, [Note: [Col. 0851D] Vatican A and B add: “and no mark of servitude was found in her.”] and no servile stain has been found in her. Once this is known, we wish her to be restored by you to her husband without any delay, nor should that man thereafter seek grounds for an excuse by which he could dismiss her. [Note: [Col. 0851D] Thus four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, and others, where the printed editions read: “let him seek some pretext on any occasion.”] For if, contrary to our belief, this is not fulfilled by you, and he should perhaps delay receiving her, know that we will correct him with strict punishment. [Note: [Col. 0852D] The Vatican edition, against the manuscripts, reads “we will correct him”—namely, the cleric.]

## LETTER II. TO COLUMBUS, THE BISHOP

Bishop Paul has now been released to go to the royal city. He says that Columbus wrote to him too late and refutes his excuse.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0852D] LETTER II.—Many letters of Saint Gregory to this bishop survive, from which it is possible to investigate what sort of man he was.] to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

We received your Fraternity’s letter, brought by the bearer, your deacon, in which you reported to us what had been done among you concerning Bishop Paul. This was done so late that the man himself could no longer be found here. For our most illustrious son Gennadius, the patrician, had also sent his chancellor to us concerning the same case. But when we had inquired whether he wished to engage in a confrontation with us in Paul’s presence, he replied that he had not been sent for that purpose, but only to bring here three men from Paul’s Church who were supposed to say many things against him.

Since, then, we found neither the chancellor ready to bring charges nor the standing of those men such as could be deemed competent for the accusation of a bishop, [Note: [Col. 0852D] See Cause II, Question 1, canons 4, 5, and 7, taken from Letter 52—Letter 50 in Gratian—of Saint Gregory’s Book XI; also *Extra*, title “On Accusations,” Book V, chapter 1: “If he is not a legitimate accuser, let the accused not be wearied”; Cause 3, Question 8, canon 1: “Accusations of bishops,” and so forth; likewise Question 5 in many chapters. GUSSANV.] we could not delay the often-mentioned Bishop Paul by opposition when he hoped through his petitions to be released to the royal city. Instead, we immediately allowed him to depart according to his request, together with the other two bishops whom he had brought with him.

If there were any matters that could reasonably be said against him, your Fraternity ought, as it has now done, to have reported everything carefully as soon as he came here. As for your indication that you suffer the hostility of many because we visit you more frequently by our letters, there is no doubt, most reverend brother, that the good endure the hatred of the wicked and that those intent upon divine works are harassed by the adversities of the perverse. But the more the things that are wrong surround you, the more urgently you ought to devote yourselves to the care of the governance entrusted to you, [Note: [Col. 0853D] Three Vatican manuscripts add: “and keep watch over the flock of Christ.”] and to watch over the protection of Christ’s flock. And the more the opposition of the wicked presses upon you, the more eagerly—and the more confidently assured of the promised reward—the care of pastoral concern ought to kindle you. [Note: [Col. 0853D] The Norman and Corbie manuscripts read: “to advance toward pastoral concern.”] Thus you may be able to offer the supreme Shepherd gain from the work entrusted to you.

## LETTER III. TO GENNADIUS, THE PATRICIAN

He asks him not to pass judgment with a troubled mind on Count Ruferius and the fellow citizens summoned before him. He requests that Anastasius the tribune be restored to his position.

Gregory to Gennadius, patrician of Africa.

For those who wish to be commended to Your Excellency by our letters, confident in your kindness, we do what is requested. Count Ruferius, together with his fellow citizens, was summoned by you, as we have learned, to the province of Africa, and they asked that the support of our letters might benefit them with you. [Note: [Col. 0853D] At that time, Alteserra observes in this passage, counts were governors of individual cities, while dukes were appointed over entire provinces; he proves this from many passages in Gregory the Great and Gregory of Tours.]

Therefore, greeting Your Excellency with paternal affection, we ask that you permit no one unjustly to prejudice them in your judgment. Rather, just as we know that you watch over those entrusted to you with pious and prudent care, so, with the Lord inspiring you, make calm provision concerning them [the reading at *de beatis* is uncertain], and deal more carefully and cautiously with the affairs of that island. [Note: [Col. 0854D] He means the island of Corsica, as is clear from the end of the letter. When the Vandals occupied Africa, Sardinia, Corsica, and other islands were subject to them. After defeating the Vandals, Justinian wished Sardinia to be counted as part of Africa. Hence, in the description of Africa, Sardinia is the seventh province. Corsica, being a neighboring island, may likewise have been attached to it. Thus Gregory writes to Gennadius, the exarch or prefect of Africa, asking him to care for Corsica.] Take care that, if an army is sent there through careless planning without a suitable person able to govern it, [Note: [Col. 0854D] The Norman and Corbie manuscripts add: “and prudent planning.”] assistance may be provided to the enemy.

Since they assert that Anastasius the tribune, whom Your Excellency had appointed there, conducted himself well and did not involve himself in any injury to the province, and since they now deeply regret that he has been removed, let Your Excellency command that he be sent there again and strengthened by your exhortations, so that the man who has already pleased by good conduct may not be incited by anyone’s persuasion to act badly. Let him not lose, by doing the opposite—which we do not wish—so great a reputation, which he deserved through good administration.

Therefore we ask that Your Excellency act so that Africa, which testifies to your goodness, may also recognize it in Corsica.

[Note: [Col. 0854D] LETTER IV.—In the Norman, Colbert, and many other manuscripts, this letter is the fifth of this book, while what is here the fifth is placed fourth. Cyriacus had succeeded the recently deceased John. Learn what sort of man Cyriacus was from the following Letter 6.]

## LETTER IV. TO CYRIACUS, THE BISHOP

Tranquillity should be desired but sometimes postponed for the benefit of many. A bishop must take care that the disturbance of thoughts, which cannot be wholly expelled, does not overwhelm the mind. The unity of the Church is strengthened by a reciprocal confession of faith and by mutual charity. One must abstain from the title “universal bishop.” Eudoxius should not have been counted among the heretics.

[Col. 0853D]

Gregory to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople.

[Note: In the Cistercian Codex, with the agreement of the Norman manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts, “our common son George.”]

We received your common sons, George the priest and Theodore [Col. 0854A] your deacon, with the charity that was fitting; and we rejoice that you have come from the administration of ecclesiastical affairs to the governance of souls, because, according to the voice of Truth: “The one who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). And to the servant who ministers well it is said: “Because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:23). To this is immediately added concerning eternal recompense: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

In your writings (Gratian, Part II, Question 1, Canon 9), however, you state that you greatly sought rest. But by this you show that you have appropriately come to pastoral solicitude, because just as a position of governance must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee from it. And as it is written: “No one takes this honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Hebrews [Col. 0854B] 5:4).

Again, that same outstanding preacher says: “If one died for all, then all have died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). And it is said to the shepherd of the holy Church: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). From these words it is gathered that if one who is capable refuses to feed the sheep of almighty God, he shows that he does not love the supreme Shepherd at all.

For if the Father’s only-begotten Son went forth from the Father’s hidden place into our public realm in order to accomplish the welfare of all, what shall we say if we prefer our own hidden retreat to the welfare of our neighbors? Rest, therefore, must be desired with all our heart, yet it must sometimes be postponed for the gain of many. For just as we ought to flee occupation with our whole desire, so, if there is no one to preach, we must willingly take the burden of occupation upon our shoulders. We are taught this by the work of two prophets, one of whom tried to avoid the office of preaching, while the other desired it.

When the Lord sent him, Jeremiah answered, saying: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jeremiah 1:6). And when almighty God was seeking someone to preach, saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” [Note: In the printed editions, contrary to the English manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others, and even contrary to the sacred text, “Who among you will go?”] Isaiah voluntarily offered himself, saying: “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6:8). Thus from both there proceeded an outwardly different voice, but it did not flow from a different source of love.

There are, indeed, two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Isaiah, therefore, desiring to benefit his neighbors through the active life, sought the office of preaching; whereas Jeremiah, desiring through the contemplative life to cling diligently to the love of his Creator, objected lest he be sent to preach. What one laudably desired, the other laudably feared: the one, lest by speaking he lose the gains of silent contemplation; the other, lest by remaining silent he suffer the losses of diligent work.

But this must be carefully observed in both: the one who refused did not resist completely, and the one who wished to be sent first saw himself cleansed by the altar’s coal, lest either anyone, being unpurified, dare approach the sacred ministries, or one whom heavenly grace chooses should proudly resist under the appearance of humility.

I find in your letters that with great desire you seek serenity of mind and, once disturbance has been driven away, yearn for tranquility of thought. But by what means your Fraternity can attain this, I do not know. For one who has undertaken to steer a ship must keep watch all the more carefully the farther he leaves the shore, so that at times he may foresee coming storms from their signs; at times, when they approach, overcome them with a straight helm if they are small, or, if they swell violently, turn the side of the ship obliquely and evade their assault; and often keep watch alone while all those to whom no care of the ship has been entrusted are resting.

How can you have serenity of thought after assuming the pastoral burden, when it is written: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters” (Job 26:5)? According to John’s wording, “the waters are peoples” (Revelation 17:15). The giants groaning beneath the waters means that whoever in this world has grown great, as though by a certain bodily mass, through the rank of power, feels the weight of greater tribulation in proportion as he has taken upon himself the care of governing peoples.

But if the power of the Holy Spirit breathes upon an afflicted mind, what happened bodily to the Israelite people immediately happens to us spiritually. For it is written: “The children of Israel walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea” (Exodus 15:19). And through the prophet the Lord promises, saying: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and the rivers will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2). The rivers overwhelm those whom the affairs of this age confuse through disturbance of mind. But one whose mind is held by the grace of the Holy Spirit crosses the waters and is not overwhelmed by the rivers, because even amid the crowds of peoples he directs the steps of his journey in such a way that he does not lower the head of his mind before the affairs of the world.

I too, who came unworthy to a position of governance, once resolved, conscious of my weakness, to seek more secluded places. But when I saw that the heavenly judgments opposed me, I submitted the neck of my heart to the yoke of my Creator, considering especially this (Gratian, Distinction 40): that no secluded place can save the soul without God’s grace. We sometimes see this even in the very wanderings of the elect. Lot was righteous in the perverse city itself, but sinned on the mountain (Genesis 19).

But why do we say these things, when we know greater examples? What is more delightful than paradise? What is more secure than heaven? Yet a human being fell from paradise through sin, and an angel fell from heaven. We must therefore seek the strength and ask for the grace of him without whom nowhere [Note: Thus we restore the reading from the Vatican, Norman, English, and other manuscripts. The printed editions read: “without whom nowhere can we exist without danger and guilt, and with whom nowhere without righteousness,” which cannot possibly be the correct sense.] can we be without guilt, and with whom nowhere can we be without righteousness.

Care must therefore be taken that disturbance of thought does not overwhelm the mind, for it cannot be driven away completely. Whoever is in a position of governance must sometimes necessarily think also about earthly matters and care for external things, so that the flock entrusted to him may be able to endure what it must accomplish. But it must always be guarded with the greatest care that this concern does not exceed its proper measure, so that, when it is freely admitted into the heart, it is not permitted to grow excessively.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet Ezekiel: “The priests shall not shave their heads, nor let their hair grow long; they shall carefully trim their heads” (Ezekiel 44:20). For what do the hairs on the head signify, by way of allegory, except thoughts [850] in the mind? While they arise imperceptibly above the brain, they signify the cares of the present life; because they sometimes emerge from an inattentive sense at an inopportune time, they advance as though without our noticing.

Since, therefore, all who govern ought indeed to have anxieties and external concerns, yet ought not to be heavily burdened by them, the priests are rightly forbidden both to shave their heads and to let their hair grow long: they must neither cut off completely their carnal thoughts concerning the lives of those subject to them, nor again allow them excessive freedom to grow. It is also rightly said: “Let them carefully trim their heads,” so that temporal concerns and anxieties may emerge as far as necessary, yet be cut back quickly lest they grow beyond measure.

Thus, while the life of the body is protected through the external administration of care, and again the intention of the heart is hindered by immoderate concern [Note: The printed editions read “the intention is not hindered.” We have removed the negation on the authority of the Norman, Rheims, and other manuscripts], the hairs on the priest’s head are both preserved to cover the skin and cut back lest they cover the eyes.

Moreover, we received your letters, sent in full faith, and we give thanks to almighty God, who guards his seamless tunic woven from above—that is, his Church— [Note: Cyriac, having been promoted to the see of Constantinople, sent, according to custom, a letter attesting the sincerity of his faith and his devotion to preserving communion. Saint Gregory calls this a “vicarious confession,” because, as he immediately adds, they sent it to one another in turn at the beginning of their episcopates, as noted above. This letter is cited in Distinction 40, canon 10, and is cited in support of the fifth canon. Gussanville explains why it is cited for the fifth canon in the first note to this letter.] from every division caused by error through the reciprocal confession of the faithful, united in grace. Against the deluge, so to speak, of so many sins in the perishing world, he constructs an ark from many timbers, in which the elect of almighty God may be preserved for life.

For when we send one another the confession of our faith in turn [Col. 0857A] and show our charity toward one another, what else are we doing in the holy Church except coating the ark with pitch, lest the flood of error enter and kill either spiritual people as though they were human beings, or carnal people as though they were animals?

But since you have wisely proclaimed the orthodox faith, it remains undoubtedly necessary that you guard the peace of hearts with greater prudence, because Truth says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:49). The apostle Paul also exhorts us, saying: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). Again he says: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:14).

You will truly have this peace with us [Note: The printed editions read “with you.”] if you avoid the pride of a profane title, in accordance with what the same teacher of the nations says: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words” (1 Timothy 6:20). For it is exceedingly wrong if those who have become preachers of humility glory in the exaltation of an empty title, when the true preacher says: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14).

He, therefore, is truly glorious who glories not in temporal power but, for Christ’s name, in his own suffering. In this respect we embrace you from the depths of our heart; in this respect we recognize you as priests, if, rejecting verbal vanity, you hold the place of holiness with holy humility.

For behold, we have been scandalized by the use of a wicked title [Note: That is, “universal” or “ecumenical,” a designation that Cyriac may have appended in his writings. Gussanville.] and retain no small grievances in our mind, which we express in our speech. Your Fraternity knows, however, that Truth says: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:23–24).

In this matter it must be considered that although every fault is erased by an offered sacrifice, so great is the evil of scandal generated in another’s heart that the Lord does not accept from the one who has sinned even the sacrifice itself, which ordinarily removes sin. Take care, therefore, to wipe away quickly the scandal from your heart, so that almighty God may regard the sacrifice of your offering as acceptable.

Moreover, although you have proclaimed the orthodox faith truly and carefully, among those whom you judged should be condemned by the most holy general councils, we find that you condemned a certain Eudoxius [Note: On the same subject, see below, Letter 31, now 34, and Book VII, Letter 30, in the first indiction. Saint Gregory eventually rejoiced that he had received ample satisfaction from the testimonies concerning Eudoxius produced by Eulogius from Basil, Gregory, and Epiphanius. Theodoret may also be added, in Book IV of the *Heretical Fables* and in Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, in several chapters. This Eudoxius was bishop of Germanicia; afterward, like a boar, he leapt upon the see of Antioch and then, through many frauds, climbed to the throne of Constantinople. His teaching was a stream of Arian treachery, with which he agreed with Aetius and Eunomius. From him came the Eudoxians, and then the Eunomians, whom we read were condemned in Canon 1 of the First Council of Constantinople. According to Theodoret, Book IV of the *History*, chapter 12, this Eudoxius bound the emperor Valens by oath, after Valens had been initiated by the sacred mystery of baptism itself, to persevere in the Arian doctrine, and so forth. In chapter 32 of the same book, he reports that Eudoxius persuaded Valens to draw the Goths into his communion. Gussanville.]

We find the name neither in the Latin language, in the synods, nor in the books of the bishops of blessed memory—Epiphanius [Note: Gussanville wrongly maintains that Epiphanius’s name inadvertently entered the text because, he says, Epiphanius had not yet been read at Rome. Certainly the name is found in all the manuscripts, and from Book VIII, Letter 30, we learn that Eulogius, writing to our Gregory to remove his scruples about this matter, brought forward certain testimonies of Epiphanius concerning Eudoxius.], Augustine, and Philaster—whom we know to have disputed especially against heretics.

If someone truly condemns him on the authority of the Catholic Fathers, we undoubtedly follow that person’s judgment. But if, in your synodical letter, you wished to condemn by name also those who are condemned outside the holy synods by the writings of the Fathers, your Fraternity omitted many of them from your letter; whereas if you wished to condemn those rejected by the general synods, you added this one unnecessarily.

Amid all this, however, it must be understood that, in order for us to be permitted freely to profess the orthodox faith and to arrange peacefully and harmoniously everything that must be done, we must continually pray for the life and offspring of our most serene lords, so that almighty God may subject barbarian nations to their feet and grant them long and happy times, in order that through the Christian empire the faith that is in Christ may reign.

## Letter V. To Cyriac, Bishop

He praises him for thinking humbly and modestly about himself, and from this infers that he is strong. He urges him most amicably, once the occasion of scandal has been removed, to preserve what belongs to peace and love. He commends the faith of John and Athanasius.

Gregory to Cyriac, Bishop of Constantinople.

When I was formerly in the royal city carrying out the responses of the apostolic see, I recognized the goodness of your Holiness. And because the care of souls has now been entrusted to you, I rejoice greatly. Although unworthy, I appeal to almighty God with whatever prayers I can offer, that he may always increase his grace in you and make you gather the gains of souls for the eternal homeland.

But since you say that you are weak for the work to which you have been brought, we know that the first virtue is knowledge of one’s weakness. From this we conclude that you can fulfill the ministry you have undertaken well, because we see you recognizing your own weakness [Note: Letter V. A great lesson for pastors: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight.” Humility should be placed beneath charity like a foundation, or added to it like seasoning: “We are weak, but you are strong; you are noble, but we are despised,” says Paul. Where vanity, swelling, and pride are found, priestly charity is absent. Even Cicero, a pagan, says: “A puffed-up and swollen mind is vicious; the mind of the wise never swells and never becomes bloated.” The author of the letter to Demetrias, quoted by Ambrose in Book IV, Letter 33, speaking of humility and charity, says: “These virtues are divided from one another in nothing, and their connection is so inseparable that whoever is established in one possesses both together. For just as humility is part of charity, so charity is part of humility,” and so forth. Let priests beware lest, while they flatter themselves concerning charity in other works—almsgiving, zeal, prayers, obedience—they disdain to follow the footsteps of humble Christ in clothing, furnishings, table, and retinue. See John Gerson’s sermon for the day of the Lord’s Circumcision, consideration 4, where he presents truths that are hard and almost iron. Gussanville.] out of humility.

For we are all weak, but the weaker person is the one who cannot consider his own weakness. You, most blessed brothers, are strong for this reason: because, distrusting your own strength, you place your confidence in the power of almighty God.

I cannot express in the words of a letter how closely my mind is bound to your charity. But I pray that almighty God, by the gift of his grace, may multiply the same charity that exists between us and remove every occasion of scandal, lest the holy Church, united by the confession of the true faith and held together by the joined hearts of the faithful, suffer any harm—which God forbid—from priests disputing among themselves [Note: Later editions, in place of this word, which is found in all our manuscripts and in the old edition, inserted a variant reading.]

Although in everything I say, and in everything in which I oppose the proud actions of certain people, I never abandon the inward keeping of charity through the generosity of almighty God, I carry out externally the things that belong to justice in such a way that I do not set aside the things within that belong to love and affection. You, for your part, always return the service of my love to me, and preserve what belongs to peace and charity, so that, remaining one in mind, and not permitting any disagreement to enter between us, we may thereby be able to obtain more effectively from the Lord what we ask, through the very unity of our hearts.

Moreover, I commend to your Holiness John, presbyter of Chalcedon, and Athanasius of Lycaonia, so that no one may insinuate himself against them through deceitful speech. I examined their faith carefully and found them sound in their confessions, which were also submitted in writing.

May the holy Trinity protect you with its hand and always make you vigilant and solicitous in guarding souls, so that in the eternal recompense you may be crowned not only for your own work but also for the improvement of those subject to you. (See above, Book VI, Letters 14, 15, 16, 17.)

## Letter VI. To Maurice Augustus

He rejoices at Cyriac’s election.

Gregory to Maurice Augustus.

Almighty God, who has made your Piety the guardian of ecclesiastical peace, preserve you in that faith which you preserve in priestly unity; and, while you humbly subject your heart to the yoke of heavenly mercy, by heavenly grace it comes about that you tread down your enemies with the foot of strength [Note: Letter VI. Vatican manuscript B reads, above: “of authority.”]. For it could not have been a small reward that, after John of holy memory had been taken from this light, your Piety long hesitated in ordaining a priest, deferred the time somewhat longer, and, in fear of almighty God, sought counsel, so that God’s cause might be arranged with great fear.

Therefore I judge my brother and fellow-priest Cyriac very suitable for pastoral government, since the long deliberations of your Piety produced him for that same rank. All know how diligent and how well trained [Note: In three Vatican manuscripts, in all the Norman manuscripts, and in Corbie: “experienced.”] he formerly was in administering ecclesiastical affairs. Hence I do not doubt that by heavenly dispensation [Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read “disposition.”] it was brought about that he who had managed small matters well should fittingly undertake greater ones and pass from the care of affairs to the governance of souls.

For this we pray with all our prayers that almighty God may repay this good deed to the serenity of our lords and to their pious offspring both in the present age and in eternal recompense; and that he may grant to the aforesaid brother and fellow-priest of mine, who has been set over the Lord’s flock, to exercise the care of souls with full solicitude, so that he may irreproachably both correct what is wrong in those subject to him and foster what is right for growth, in order that your Piety’s judgment concerning him may be confirmed not only before human beings but also before the eyes of heavenly Majesty.

I did not permit the venerable men George the priest and Theodore the deacon to remain in this city, because of the command of our lords and the approach of the winter season.

## Letter VII. To Peter, Domitian, and Elpidius

He reproves them because at Cyriac’s ordination they had cried, “This is the day which the Lord has made.” The faults of shepherds harm subjects, and those of subjects harm shepherds.

Gregory [Note: Letter VII. Thus it is read in all the Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and Vatican D manuscripts and in other older witnesses. In the Regius manuscript and in some Vatican manuscripts: “to Maurice the patrician, Peter, etc.” Vatican C adds “of Greece” after “bishops.”] to Peter, Domitian, and Elpidius, bishops.

I greatly rejoice that you received the ordination of the most holy man Cyriac, my brother and fellow-priest, with great joy. Since we have learned from the preaching of the apostle Paul, “If one member rejoices, all the other members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26), you must consider how greatly I rejoice with you in this matter, in which not one member but many members of Christ have rejoiced.

Yet, insofar as I could gather from a cursory reading of your Fraternity’s letter, great joy carried you away into immoderate praise of this same brother of mine. For you say that he appeared in the Church like the sun, so that you all cried: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24). Certainly the promise belongs to the life to come, where it is said: “The righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43; Wisdom 3:7).
