For how can anyone still placed in this life, however great his strength of virtue, shine like the sun in a life in which the corruptible body weighs down the soul and the earthly dwelling depresses the mind that thinks many things (Wisdom 9:15); in which we see another law in our members resisting the law of our mind and leading us captive under the law of sin which is in our members (Romans 7:23); in which we have within ourselves the answer of death, that we may not trust in ourselves (2 Corinthians 1:9); in which the Prophet also cries: “Fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me” (Psalm 54:6)?

For it is also written: “The wise man remains as the sun; the fool changes as the moon” (Sirach 27:12). The comparison with the sun is drawn not for brilliance of radiance but for perseverance in good work. The good beginning of his ordination could not yet be praised by you for perseverance [Note: The printed editions read, “the beginning could appear,” but you could not yet praise him for perseverance.]. But when you say that you cried, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” you ought to have considered of whom this was said. For first it is said: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Psalm 117:22–23). Then immediately concerning this same stone follows: “This is the day which the Lord has made.” For he who is called a stone because of the strength of his building is called day because of the grace of illumination; and he was also made day because he was incarnate. We are commanded to rejoice and be glad in him because he overcame the darkness of our error within us by the light of his power. [Note: Every day passages of Scripture are bent by a certain accommodation and, through unfamiliar usage, diverted to other persons or meanings—now called ingenious, now blasphemous, or at least rash, according to the disposition of the judges. Thus in 1648, in proposition 14, Cellotius was reproved by the sacred Faculty of Paris because he had applied to monks the words “holy, innocent, undefiled,” etc. He defended himself by this exception: “We frequently read certain applications in the holy Fathers; nor is it proud to compare religious with Christ, since we hear him himself saying: ‘Be holy, for I am holy’; and Christ: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect’; likewise: ‘I said, you are gods,’ etc. And what belongs to Christ alone the Church applies to all confessors who are bishops: ‘You are a priest forever,’ etc.” So he says. I add that in the Roman Sacerdotale printed at Venice in 1597 these words occur when the rite is prescribed for receiving a prelate or legate in procession: “Priest and bishop,” etc.; “Behold the great priest,” etc.; “He gave him the blessing of all nations,” etc.; “You are fellow citizens of the saints,” etc.; “Hear the prayers of suppliants,” etc.; “Look upon the face of your Christ.” Gussanville. In these matters the most wise decree of the Council of Trent, session 4, must be observed.] Therefore that expression ought not to have been given in praise of a creature when it belongs to the Creator alone.

But why do I reprove these things, when I know how much joys carry the mind away? For your charity produced in you great gladness, and the tongue followed that gladness of mind in praise. Since this is so, this praise can no longer be called a fault, since charity discovered it. But of my most holy brother only this should briefly have been said to me, which I could sufficiently receive: that I should know who he was who had formerly given me especially this proof of his greatness—that, while occupied with so many matters of ecclesiastical administration, he kept his heart tranquil amid turbulent crowds and always restrained himself in gentleness. This is no small praise of a great and unshaken mind: not to have been disturbed amid crowds of cases.

Moreover, your Fraternity must persist in constant prayers that almighty God may preserve in the aforesaid brother and fellow-priest of ours what has been well begun and always lead it to better things. This must always be prayed by you most holy men and by the people subject to him. For the merits of rulers and peoples are so connected that often the life of subjects becomes worse through the fault of those set over them, and often the life of shepherds sins through the merit of the people [Note: In the Norman manuscripts and many others, “of those preceding”; and shortly afterward, “of subjects.”].

That the evil action of one set over others greatly harms subjects is attested by the Pharisees, concerning whom it is written: “You shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you neither enter yourselves nor allow those entering to enter” (Matthew 23:13). That the fault of peoples greatly harms the life of shepherds we learn from the deed of David (2 Kings 24). For he, praised by God’s own testimony and conscious of heavenly mysteries, puffed up by the swelling of sudden self-exaltation, sinned by numbering the people; yet, while David sinned, the people received the punishment. Why was this? Because the hearts of rulers are disposed according to the merit of their peoples. But the just Judge corrected the vice of the sinner by the punishment of those through whose fault he sinned. Yet because he himself, namely by choosing pride, was not free from fault, he too received the punishment of his sin. For raging wrath, which struck the people bodily, also cast down the ruler of the people by inward grief of heart.

Consider these things, therefore, in relation to one another; and just as he who has been set over you and your peoples must intercede for all, so all of you ought to pray for his conduct and character, that before almighty God you may profit by imitating him and that he may be helped by your merits. Let us all also pray together constantly, with as many tears as we can, for our most serene lords and their pious offspring, that heavenly grace may preserve and guard their life and subject the necks of nations to Christian rule.

## Letter VIII. To Stephen, Bishop

In return for the praise given him against his will, he praises Stephen’s constant preaching, through which the patrician Maria and many others were brought back to the Church. Constantine the prefect should be urged always to keep God’s judgment before his eyes.

Gregory to Stephen, bishop.

The writings of your Holiness spoke to me words of deep-rooted charity, so that the mind passed through the pen into the letters as though the mind itself were speaking to me in person. For this I give great thanks to almighty God, because, though our bodies are separated and you are far removed from us, charity between us remains undivided [Note: Letter VIII. Vatican D reads, “because also with our bodies divided.” Later editions: “because also with bodies separated.”]. You indeed show me in your letters much favor, more than I, unworthy as I am, ought to hear. And it is written: “Do not praise a man while he lives” (Sirach 11:30). Yet, though I was not worthy to hear such things, I ask in your prayers that I may become worthy, so that if you did not say good things of me because they are so, they may be so because you said them.

I was greatly delighted concerning the illustrious patrician Maria, because she has been added to the holy fold of God. I do not doubt that this was brought about by your constant preaching, because by the fruit itself you show how greatly you labor for the Catholic faith. I also suppose that many come to the Church through her; all this redounds to your praise, because it is written: “Where there are very many crops, there is manifest strength of oxen” (Proverbs 14:4) [Note: The editions read, “there is the greatest strength.” We follow the Norman, English, Colbert, Vatican 2, and other manuscripts. So it is also read in the indicated passage of Proverbs.]. For the power of preachers is made manifest where a harvest of souls rises.

The more you love our common son, the most excellent lord Constantine the prefect, the more constantly you ought to exhort him that, in the cases in which he is involved, he may always keep the judgment of almighty God before the eyes of his heart and strive to please him alone who is able both to protect in the present life and to recompense with the rewards of the heavenly homeland. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 62.)

## Letter IX. To John, Bishop

He gives thanks for the alms sent to Rome. In judging cases, John should consider God alone. He should no longer have Gregory’s writings read at table.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

The blessing which your Fraternity sent for the poor was distributed with his own hands, under our administration, by Candidus, your man and bearer of the present letter; perhaps it seemed little to you according to your intention. But we judge it to be exceedingly great and beyond measure according to the extent of your resources, since, though you have innumerable poor persons there among you for the exercise of merciful generosity, you also seek other places far away [Note: Letter IX. The editors corrupted this passage and overturned its sense by adding one syllable and changing the punctuation. It was formerly read: “But concerning the other cases, I remember that I have already replied to you in previous letters,” etc. Shortly afterward they inserted “you ought first to inquire,” which is found in no manuscript.].

As to the other cases, I remember that I have already replied to you in previous letters; you ought to do nothing else except perform all things with the consideration of almighty God alone, and let no person soften you away from the vigor of discipline, nor let violent indignation harden you, which God forbid, into some rigidity of immoderate severity [Note: Incorrectly, in the earlier printed editions, “violent disdain.”].

Moreover, I hear that your Fraternity has some of the things which I remember writing read aloud at your table before strangers. This does not seem to me to be something that should be done, because what you do out of charity may be ascribed by some, so far as I am concerned, to vainglory. Therefore have the sayings of the ancients read before strangers, so that those who hear may be instructed by their authority [Note: He wishes the sayings of the ancients to be read. In the first Milanese council, under the title “On the bishop’s table”: “At his table there should be a reading of the sacred books, so that the guests may be refreshed not only by food for the body but also by feasts for the soul.” In the Third Council of Tours, canon 5: “A bishop ought not to devote himself to excessively lavish banquets, but should be content with spare and moderate food. So long as he dines, sacred reading should rather be recited before his table than idle words resound from whisperers.” Gussanville.]. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 76.)

## Letter X. To Agnellus, Abbot

He should choose a provost on the basis of merit of life. He should watch diligently over the brothers.

Gregory [Note: Letter X. It was wrongly read formerly, “to the bishop.” For Castorius was still alive. Gussanville. This observation of Gussanville is confirmed by all the Norman, Tours, English, Vatican, and other manuscripts.] to Agnellus, abbot of Rimini.

[Col. 0864B] Having learned from our son Secundus, servant of God, who reported it, that your Charity, lacking a superior, is wholly struggling in governing the brothers, [Note: [Col. 0864D] In the printed editions, *Secundino* (“Secundinus”); otherwise in all the Norman, Corbie, and three Vatican manuscripts.] ...

857 If, therefore, the man who follows you in rank is such that he can be found diligent in arranging the cell, guarding the brothers, and winning souls, he ought to come to this place without hesitation. But if he is not such as the place requires, then even from the lowest rank, if such a man is found among the brothers—under the Lord’s protection—who by the merits of his life offers a worthy example of his manner of living, and in whom the vigor of divine fear is active, [Note: [Col. 0864D] That is, it is not benefits that should be assigned to men, but men to benefits, because the common good must always be considered, not private advantage.] then surely not the place but the usefulness of this man must be considered; [Note: [Col. 0864D] The printed editions have *ut tali exemplo* (“so that by such an example”); we follow the Norman, Vatican, Rheims, Corbie, and other manuscripts.] so that, following such an example as a standard of good imitation, all the brothers may extend themselves toward it, and their lower position may no longer make them sluggish in doing good, while in the one who has advanced they see before them what they should imitate. Therefore, let there be no doubt in your Charity concerning this appointment: it is not a position but suitable conduct that is being sought. For before God that man holds the higher place who has pleased His eyes by the instrument of good conduct, even if here he is considered insignificant.

[Note: [Col. 0864D] He shows how easily monks may stray from the straight path of conduct if vigilance does not keep watch, and how great the effort must be so that they may rise to the summit of the perfection they have begun. GUSSANV.]

For this reason, as we trust, it is fitting that you keep careful watch over the brothers, lest by wandering through unlawful thoughts they stray from the straight path of conduct and, through negligent guardianship, offer the enemy an opening for attack. Rather, they should cling more earnestly to prayer, so that the Lord may perfect their devout beginnings by the gift of His mercy, [Note: [Col. 0864D] Thus we restore the text from the English, Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts; previously it read: “may perfect by the gift of His mercy, and make the imperfect rise to the summit of perfection.”] and bring their imperfect efforts to the fullness of perfection. [Col. 0865A]

## LETTER XI. TO RUFINUS, BISHOP OF EPHESUS

He commends a certain cleric who does not know letters.

Gregory to Rufinus, [Note: [Col. 0865B] Letter XI.—Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia Minor, on the coast of Ionia, was formerly famous among the pagans for the temple of Diana, and among Christians for the Third General Council held there in 431. It was especially renowned because of the letter Paul wrote to the Ephesians and because of his preaching there for three years. [Col. 0865C]] bishop of Ephesus.

The longstanding love of your friendship has moved us to visit your Fraternity by this present letter. For we have been greatly refreshed by joy because we have learned all good things from the report of your health. Yet in these matters we beseech the almighty Lord that, just as in this present life—which is in a certain sense the shadow of the future—He has granted you joy in the passing soundness of your body, so in that heavenly homeland, where true life exists, He may grant you joy in the perfect salvation of your soul and make you rejoice in a common exultation.

The bearer of this letter, therefore, desiring to be commended to you by our letters, was questioned by us as to whether, as befits a cleric, he had learned letters; he replied that he did not know them. [Note: [Col. 0865C] I understand the reading to be “learned,” as the following makes clear: “Let your tongue be a book for him who does not know how to read.” Pope Gelasius, Letter 9 to the bishops of Lucania on restoring the ruins of the clergy, among the many conditions he requires for a monk to be admitted to the clergy, states: “If he has acquired learning, without which he could scarcely perhaps fulfill even the ministry of doorkeeper.” He repeats the same requirement for laymen being admitted to ecclesiastical offices: “Or without learning,” he says. The Council of Trent, Session 23, *On Reform*, chapter 4, requires that those who receive the tonsure know how to read and write. By force of that decree, as I believe, the Church of Meaux, assembled in general chapter on 29 December 1563, prohibited anyone from thereafter being enrolled among the canons unless he knew how to read and also to speak and understand Latin; since they were principal members of the senate of the Church, they ought at least in this respect to surpass the other ordinary clerics. GUSSANV.]

What further commendation of him we should offer to your Fraternity, I do not know, except that you ought to be concerned for his soul and watch over him with pastoral diligence, [Note: [Col. 0865D] Recent editions read: “watch with pastoral guardianship.”] so that, since he does not know how to read, your tongue may be a book for him, and in the goodness of your preaching or conduct he may see what he should imitate. A living voice commonly draws the heart more powerfully than reading words that pass before it. But while this inner instruction of spiritual teaching is breathed into him by you, let outward care also not be lacking, so that through its assistance he may reach the desire for spiritual things; [Note: [Col. 0865D] Recent editions have “may arrive.” They then add, “and may also obtain temporal things,” followed by “lest, if this ...”; these words are rightly absent from all the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, Royal, and other manuscripts.] lest, if this is despised, there be no one for whom preaching may be provided.

## LETTER XII. TO RESPECTA, ABBESS

He grants privileges to the monastery of Saint Cassian.

Gregory to Respecta, [Note: [Col. 0865D] Letter XII.—Thus in the Norman, Corbie, and Vatican D manuscripts. In Vatican A: “To the abbess of Gaul at Massilia.” Other editions differ little, reading: “To the abbess of the Gauls at Massilia.” In the Colbertine manuscript: “of the Massilian Gauls.”] abbess.

A devout petition ought to be completed by the accompanying fulfillment of its desire, so that both the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may unquestionably acquire strength. Therefore, for the monastery consecrated in honor of Saint Cassian, over which you are recognized as presiding, in accordance with the petition of our sons Dynamus and Aureliana, who are shown to have joined to their own house, by their religious devotion, the buildings belonging to them, we have determined to grant the following privileges:

We decree that when the abbess of the aforesaid monastery dies, an outsider shall not be appointed, but one whom the community has chosen from among its own members. Nevertheless, if she is judged worthy of this ministry, she shall be ordained by the bishop of that place. In the property or administration of this monastery, however, we decree that neither the bishop nor any member of the clergy shall have any authority; rather, we establish that all these matters belong to the care of your solicitude, or of whichever abbess succeeds you in that place.

[Note: [Col. 0866C] We have already spoken of Dynamus in Book III, Letter 33, indiction 11. Recent editions read *Aureliano* instead of *Aurelianae*, against all the Vatican, Norman, Royal, Corbie, and other manuscripts, as well as the old editions. It may be conjectured from this letter that Aureliana was Dynamus’s sister, since the monastery at Massilia is said to have been given through the joint wishes of both of them. We should not say that she was Dynamus’s wife, since we read that this patrician’s wife was Eucheria, with whom he was buried in the basilica of the blessed martyr Hippolytus. Nor is it recorded that Dynamus married another wife after Eucheria. Consult Adrian Valesius, *History of France*, Book XI, p. 137.]

[Note: [Col. 0866B] In the sixth century, John Baptist Cuesnayus asserts that there were four monasteries at Massilia or in the city itself: those of Saint Victor, Blessed Mary of Yvelino (de Veaune), Saint Savior, and Saint Cassian, in *Cassianus Illustrated*, chapters 17 and 25, and in *Religious Massilia*, or *Annals of Massilia*, Part III, Corollary 5, §§ 1–2. The first was for men, the others for women. Cassian himself founded the monasteries of Saint Victor and Blessed Mary of Yvelino outside the walls of Massilia. Another monastery, dedicated to Saint Savior, was later built within the city walls and remains famous today. Gregory the Great now grants privileges to the monastery established or restored under the name of Saint Cassian by Dynamus and Aureliana. [Col. 0866B]]

On the day of the anniversary or dedication of the aforesaid monastery, [Note: [Col. 0866D] Gussanvillaeus understands this to mean the day of the dedication. But the following fifth line distinguishes the two days; therefore, the anniversary of Saint Cassian should be understood. In Book XI, Letter 76, when speaking of the churches of the English, Saint Gregory allows the faithful to celebrate solemnity with religious banquets on the day of the dedication or on the anniversary of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there.] the bishop shall come there to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass; [Note: [Col. 0866D] The editors have altered this passage to read: “The bishop shall come there to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass.” All the English, Norman, and Rheims manuscripts, and most of the more important manuscripts, precede us.] yet he must discharge this office in such a way that his cathedra shall not be placed there except on the aforesaid days, while he is celebrating the solemn rites of Mass. When he departs, his cathedra shall likewise be removed from that same oratory. On the other days, the offices of Mass shall be performed by the presbyter appointed by that bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0866D] If you wish, consult the Council of Carthage under Reparatus, in 535; the letter of Pontius, bishop of Arles, in volume VI of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, p. 430; and Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 13, § 5.]

Furthermore, concerning the life and conduct of the handmaids of God, that is, of the abbess who is appointed in the monastery described above, we establish that the bishop is to exercise care according to the fear of God. Thus, if the fault of any inhabitant there requires that she be subjected to punishment, he must by every means punish her in accordance with the force of the sacred canons.

With these things established and granted by us, strive to show yourself in every respect more solicitous and earnest in the administration of your community, so that the malice of the wicked enemy may find there nothing that can be defiled. Therefore, we decree that all these provisions embraced by this page of instruction be observed in every respect and by everyone in your monastery forever, with Christ’s protection, so that the benefits of the privileges granted may always remain inviolably secure.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Thus in the old Colbertine manuscript and in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus, where this letter is addressed “to Respecta, abbess.”]

In the month of November, indiction 15.

## LETTER XIII. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP

He is to sell from the sacred vessels, in the presence of the defensor John, only as much as is needed to ransom captives.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Fano.

Just as it is reprehensible and deserving of punishment for anyone [Note: [Col. 0867D] Recent editions read “certain vessels”; the Norman and other manuscripts read “anyone.”] to sell consecrated vessels except in the cases prescribed by law and the sacred canons, so no reproach or penalty should be imposed if they are sold for the sake of ransoming captives. Since, therefore, we have learned from the report of your Fraternity that you incurred a loan of money for the redemption of captives and have no means by which to repay it, and that for this reason you wish, with our authority, to sell sacred vessels, we have taken care to give our consent in this matter, since the decrees both of the laws and of the canons agree, and we grant you permission to sell the sacred vessels.

[Note: [Col. 0867D] Recent editions have “so that you may be able to repay.”]

But, lest their sale bring reproach upon you, they must be sold in the presence of our defensor John up to the amount of the debt, and their price must be paid to the creditors. Thus, when this matter has been completed with such observance, neither shall the creditors suffer the loss of the money lent, [Note: [Col. 0867D] “Of the money borrowed,” in the same recent editions.] nor shall your Fraternity incur reproach now or at any time.

## LETTER XIV. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP

He should not be shaken by accusations. In place of the bishop deposed by him, he is to ordain another within three months.

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

[Col. 0868A] [Note: [Col. 0867D] Letter XIV.—From this letter we read excerpts in the *Extra*, under accusations, especially in the chapters *Qualiter* and *Quando*, from a letter of Innocent III and from the Lateran Council. GUSSANV.]

You should know that I learned long ago, from the report of many people, how the ancient enemy of the human race thought to attack you with the arrows of tongues and the snares of evil hearts. [Note: [Col. 0867D] On the same subject, read several texts in cause 11, question 3, chapters 49–59. From this one may see how great an evil credulity is in prelates: slanderers rejoice by it, while good men are worn down. Gregory knew this and remedies it in this letter. Lucian published a book on the matter; consult it. AUGET.] But in all the adversities that arise in this life, as you know, only the judgment of the almighty God is to be weighed, and one must always return to one’s own heart, lest the tongue of anyone entangle us where conscience does not accuse us. For the conscience that defends a person leaves him free even amid accusation; yet no one can be free, even without accusation, if conscience alone accuses him inwardly and condemns him.

Therefore, concerning your Holiness, far be it from Christian judgment to admit as even a slight suspicion those things that we believe have been fabricated by the rumors of slanderous men. [Note: [Col. 0868D] Thus we restore the text with the help of the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and Royal manuscripts. Some Vatican and Royal manuscripts, however, read *adducere* (“to bring forward”) instead of *adduci* (“to be brought forward”). The printed editions formerly read: “so that we might believe those things which ... have been fabricated to be brought forward in some degree of suspicion.” Gratian supports our reading in citing this passage.] For we also hold the testimony of sacred Scripture: when greater evils are alleged, they should not be believed unless proved, but, once proved, they should be punished swiftly.

For God Himself, who created all things and observes everything He made, moved by the punishment of grave evils, says: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has risen to me; [Note: [Col. 0869C] The printed editions read “I shall descend.”] I will descend and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that I have heard, and I will punish; or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Genesis 18:20ff.). Why would God descend in order to learn what had been done? Or what would He not know who is everywhere? But, in order to give an example of discernment for our ignorance, and to show that we should not believe grave evils merely because we have heard them, He says that He will descend to learn—although it is clear to everyone that, without descending, He would know everything.

I have said this to show how excessive a form of levity it is if anyone strives to believe grave evils that cannot be proved. Therefore, your Holiness ought to separate your mind from the rumors and slander of malicious men and think only of the things that belong to eternal life [Note: [Col. 0869C] The Norman, Corbie, and most Vatican manuscripts read *interna* (“inner things”).] and contribute to the benefit of your subjects. Perhaps the ancient enemy wished to entangle you in such a concern so that, while your mind is continually occupied with matters that belong to him, you might think less about what belongs to others, offer no word of consolation to your subjects, and oppose those acting perversely with no severity.

For in bodily battle it commonly happens that the enemy attacks with particular force the one carrying the standard, so that, if the one watched by the others receives a wound, the entire multitude may quickly be scattered and captured. Therefore, your Fraternity must not feel the wound of this opinion brought against you, [Note: [Col. 0869D] This is indeed very difficult, for slander disturbs even the wise. Ecclesiasticus 7. Theodoret rightly says concerning Psalm 118: “Let not the proud slander me. Slander is a sorrowful thing, slander is hard, though it brings a great reward,” and so forth. GUSSANV.] but must care for the life and improvement of those entrusted to you, so that before the coming Judge you may be able to render an account both of your innocence and of the improvement of your subjects.

As for the other matters appropriate to the needs of the present time, we have instructed our defensor Marinianus to communicate them to you orally.

As for the bishop whom we have found to have been deposed by your Fraternity, [Note: [Col. 0869D] With colleagues joined to you. For just as bishops ought not to be promoted by one person, so neither ought they be deposed by one. If you seek the reason, you will find it in the Council of Aachen of 816, canon 9: “That a bishop is ordained not by one but by all the bishops of the province was established lest the tyrannical authority of one person attempt anything against the faith of the Church,” and so forth. AUGET.] after the sacred canons—as you know—command that a Church not remain vacant for more than three months when an obvious crime has appeared in him, [Note: [Col. 0869D] This was stated above and will be stated below in Letter 39, now 42: “within three months,” from the Council of Chalcedon, canon 25. GUSSANV.] you must by every means take care to ordain another bishop in his place, because the Church ought not to remain long without its own ruler.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] The printed editions have “in the month of May.” The month of March is noted in the Vatican, old Colbertine, and Tours manuscripts.]

In the month of March, indiction 15.

## LETTER XV. TO GEORGE, THE PRESBYTER

When Jesus Christ descended into hell, He freed only those who had believed that He would come and had kept His commandments by living accordingly.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0869D] In the Vatican manuscript: “Gregorio.”] to George, the presbyter, and Theodore, deacon of the Church of Constantinople.

[Col. 0869B] Mindful of your goodness and charity, I strongly reproach myself for having released you to return so quickly. But since I saw that, once and again, you insistently pressed me to release you, I considered that it would be burdensome if your Charity remained with us. Yet when I learned that, because of the winter season, you had remained on the road for so long, I confess that I regretted dismissing you so quickly. For if your Charity was unable to complete the journey you had undertaken, it would have been better for you to remain with me than away from me. [Note: [Col. 0870C] The Tours, Norman, and several other manuscripts read “was unable.”]

Furthermore, after your departure, when my most beloved sons, the deacons, told me, I learned that your Charity had said that our almighty Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, descending into hell, saved all who there confessed Him to be God and freed them from their due punishments. In this matter I want your Charity to think very differently. For when He descended into hell, He freed by His grace only those who, while they were living in the flesh, believed that He would come and kept His commandments by their way of life.

It is clear, however, that after the Lord’s incarnation no one can be saved—even among those who hold His faith—if they do not have a life corresponding to that faith, since it is written: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny Him” (Titus 1:16). John also says: “Whoever says that he knows Him but does not keep His commandments is a liar” (1 John 2:4). James, the brother of the Lord, likewise writes: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:20).

If, therefore, believers are not now saved without good works, while unbelievers and reprobates were saved without good conduct when the Lord descended into hell, then the lot of those who did not see the Lord’s incarnation was better than that of those born after the mystery of His incarnation. The Lord Himself testifies how foolish it is to say or think this, when He says to His disciples: “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matthew 13:17; Luke 10:24).

But lest I delay your Charity in my discussion, let it learn what Philaster said about this heresy in the book he wrote concerning heresies. His words are these:

> “There are heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and there, after death, made Himself known to all, so that those who confessed Him there might be saved; whereas this is contrary to the prophet David, who says: ‘In hell, who will confess you?’ (Psalm 6:6), and to the Apostle: ‘As many as sinned without the law will also perish without the law’ (Romans 2:12).” [Note: [Col. 0870C] The words quoted are found almost identically in Philaster’s *Book of Heresies*, in the chapter entitled “The Heresy Concerning Christ’s Descent into Hell.” Many things follow there that Saint Gregory omits. Saint Augustine testifies that Philaster was careless in the book he wrote to Quodvultdeus concerning heresies, in the letter prefixed to that treatise; Augustine reports this heresy only from Philaster. GUSSANV.]

The blessed Augustine also agrees with these words in the book he wrote concerning heresies.

As we consider all these matters, hold to nothing other than what the true faith teaches through the Catholic Church: that when the Lord descended into hell, He rescued from the prison of hell only those whom, while they were living in the flesh, He had preserved by His grace in faith and good works. For when the Gospel says, “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32), [Note: [Col. 0870D] This agrees with Augustine in many passages. GUSSANV.] it means all the elect. For no one could be drawn to God after death who had separated himself from God by living badly.

May almighty God guard you by His protection, so that wherever you are, you may feel the help of His grace in soul and body. [Note: [Col. 0870D] The Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus adds: “In the month of April, indiction 15.”]

## LETTER XVI. TO ANGNELLUS, BISHOP

He delegates the visitation of the Church of Formiae.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Letter XVI.—This letter is omitted in the Norman, English, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts, perhaps because it contains the formula for imposing a visitation, already found in many letters. It survives in the Royal, Colbertine, and Vatican manuscripts, except for one Vatican manuscript marked D, which generally agrees with the Norman and English manuscripts.]

Gregory to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina.

The direct report has made known the death of Bacauda, the bishop. Therefore, we solemnly entrust to your Fraternity the task of visiting the Church that has been deprived of its bishop. [Note: [Col. 0870D] Namely, the Church of Formiae, as is clear from Book I, Letter 8, where we spoke of Formiae.] You must carry this out in such a way that no one presume to seize anything belonging to its revenues, clerical advancements, furnishings, ministries, or any other part of its patrimony.

Therefore, your Fraternity will hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and will urgently admonish its clergy and people, through repeated exhortations, so that, setting aside factional interests, they may with one and the same agreement seek to have placed over them a priest who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and who is in no way rejected by the venerable canons.

When he has been requested, he should come to us for consecration with the formal decree confirmed by the signatures of all and with letters bearing the testimony of your Charity. [Note: [Col. 0871C] The same manuscript adds: “We also admonish.”] We also admonish your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be chosen from another Church, unless perhaps no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of the city itself in which you are carrying out the visitation—a situation we do not believe will occur.

Above all, take care that no layperson presume to aspire to this office, whatever his manner of life or merit, [Note: [Col. 0871C] Thus in the Tours manuscript. In Vatican: “lest he aspire to the merit of any manner of life.” In the printed editions: “lest any layperson presume to aspire to the merit of this manner of life.”] and that you do not, God forbid, incur the danger of your order.

[Note: [Col. 0871C] The Tours manuscript reads: “whatever is there.”]

## LETTER XVII. TO SABINIANUS, BISHOP

Having set forth Maximus’s disobedience, he summons Sabinianus, who has already separated himself from Maximus, and the others adhering to Maximus, to Rome; he promises them complete security and, if justice permits, absolution.

Gregory to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] In Vatican B: “to Savinus, bishop of Tibur.” In the Royal manuscript: “to Sabinus, bishop of Todi.” In the Colbertine: “to Sabinus, bishop of Tablina”; perhaps this should be read as an abbreviated *Tiburtino*, “of Tibur.”]

If you had carefully considered the rule of ecclesiastical discipline and the order of ancient custom, neither would any fault of unlawful presumption have stolen upon you, nor would others have incurred danger through your sin. Thus there is no doubt that you know that, when certain reports concerning Maximus reached us—reports that would seriously impede his advancement to the priesthood—we did not consent to him, nor did we wish him to proceed to what he was striving for until a worthy satisfaction had been offered concerning the matters reported.

Although you ought to have preserved this judgment, the result was rather that the aforesaid Maximus, seizing the episcopate in the avidity of a blind mind, rashly bent you to his will against our prohibition. But, lest the matters reported to us then remain unexamined, he was summoned by our letters to come here. When he delayed through perverse determination, we took care to admonish him in repeated letters, under threat of exclusion from communion, that he should come to us for his purification without postponing his excuse. But he chose to submit to excommunication rather than to offer obedience.

Thus it happened that the perversity of his mind dragged others with him into its own perdition—a thing wicked to say. But now, because we have learned that you dissent from his wickedness, we exhort you by this present letter both not to communicate with him and not to mention his name during the solemn rites of Mass, so that your eventual separation from him may at least benefit your soul.

Do not delay to come to us, therefore, but hasten also to bring with you whatever other bishops and religious persons you can. Thus, after the case has been examined more subtly, your absolution, if the matter requires it, ought to be granted suitably and properly, [Note: [Col. 0871D] The printed editions read “and ours,” against the English, Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts.] and those who have fallen into the sin of the same rashness may, with the help of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, be recalled to the way of salvation in a manner pleasing to Christ.

Let every bishop or religious person who comes to us know that he will suffer no prejudice or injustice, [Note: [Col. 0871D] Recent editions read: “but, once the truth has meanwhile been learned.”] but that, after the truth has been learned, those things pleasing to our Redeemer will be established. Thus, with the Lord’s assistance, it may become clear to everyone from this exercise of our authority that we are moved not by personal hatred against anyone, but by zeal for God and by concern for the order of the Church.

## LETTER XVIII. TO MARTIN, THE DEACON

He restores him, canonically cleared of the charges brought against him, to his place and order.

[Col. 0872C]

Gregory to Martin, deacon and abbot.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Letter XVIII.—Two considerations make me doubt the title. First, the sequence of the letter suits a cleric better than a monk, since it speaks of a Church, not a monastery. Second, he wishes the man to remain in the place and order in which he had been, which I understand as fulfilling the divine office, not as bearing the role of abbot. We would scarcely attribute to an abbot the place, order, and ministry of a deacon in his monastery. Perhaps the copyist was misled by the word *religiosos*, which he thought was said only of monks. GUSSANV. This conjecture of Gussanvillaeus is supported by no manuscript evidence; in all the manuscripts this Martin, or Martianus, is consistently called an abbot. The same scholar proposes another, still weaker, conjecture concerning the corruption of this letter.]

Just as crimes truly spoken against religious persons deserve to be punished, so those against whom they have been brought must nevertheless be acquitted when no guilt binds them. Since, therefore, certain reports concerning you had reached us which seriously stained the purpose of your office, we took care to investigate them for a long time and with careful inquiry.

And since we found nothing that could harm you, so that no suspicion might remain concerning the things that had been reported, we ordered you to offer strict oaths at the most sacred body of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as a complete satisfaction demonstrating that you were innocent of them. [Note: [Col. 0872D] Formerly, a presbyter accused of an infamous crime had to clear himself by taking an oath and touching the holy Gospels or the relics of the saints, as here; likewise in Book II, indiction 10, Letter 23, now 33; Book VII, indiction 2, Letter 80, now 79; Book IX; Book XI, Letter 8, now Book XIII, Letter 6; and elsewhere. In the capitularies of Charlemagne, year 779, chapter 10: “Let them stand at the cross, and if the one who swore prevails, let the accuser amend his legal claim.” In later centuries these purgatory oaths were required from clerics under accusation, together with three, five, or seven colleagues of their order, as Ivo of Chartres says in Letters 54 and 206. For this reason they were called sacramental witnesses, fellow-swearers, or compurgators, as may be seen in the ancient laws of the Alemanni and Bavarians. This is what is meant by clearing oneself “with a third hand,” “with a fifth hand,” or “with a seventh hand.” The hand has always been understood as a symbol of faith, and is still used in legal proceedings. The Council of Agde, canon 3, says that an accused presbyter is to clear himself with seven companions of his order. The Council of Lérida, canon 10, says that he must clear himself with seven colleagues; see also cause 2, question 4, chapters 12–13. Likewise Hildebert of Le Mans, Letter 69, says that a suspected dean must be cleared and declare his innocence by oath with seven members of his order. The same is read in Letter 30 of Hincmar, where an accused presbyter must clear himself through seven witnesses. According to the decree of Lucius III, chapter *Ex tuarum*, concerning canonical purification, an accused presbyter must demonstrate his innocence through canonical purification with seven or five members of his order. In title 6 of the Alemannic law it is written that one must swear with six companions; in the Law of the Frisians, with twelve. On canonical purification, see what we said concerning Book II, indiction 10, Letter 23. GUSSANV.]

Therefore, after we had received the satisfaction that was required, we determined that your Charity should in every respect be absolved and that you should return to your Church, in precisely the place and order in which you had previously served. We further determined that you should suffer no contradiction or disturbance from anyone concerning the matters reported to us.

We admonish you henceforth to show yourself so cautious and attentive that in conduct and action you may correspond to your office, so that every opportunity for anyone to speak adversely against you may be entirely removed.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] In the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus: “with the first hand, in the month of March, [Col. 0874D] indiction 15.” But in the second hand: “in the month of May,” as is also read in the old Colbertine manuscript and in three Vatican manuscripts.]

In the month of May, indiction 15.

865 ## LETTER XIX. TO MARINIANUS, ARCHBISHOP

Because Castorius pleads the burden of the episcopate on account of illness, another bishop is to be ordained for the people of Ariminum. He orders that this man be chosen by the clergy and people, examined by the bishop of Ravenna, and sent to Rome for consecration.

[Col. 0873B]

Gregory to Marinianus, archbishop of Ravenna.

How the priest ordained by us, [Note: [Col. 0874D] EPISTLE XIX [Al. 50].—Recent editions read *capitis*, as is evident. Our reading is found in the Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts, as well as in Gratian. Shortly afterward the same manuscripts add *qui*; since, in the wording previously supplied, the sense was awkward, we have removed it.] because of the bodily ailment with which it is known that he is afflicted, has until now left the Church of Ariminum deprived of pastoral governance, your Fraternity learned long ago. When, moved by the petitions of the inhabitants of that place, we repeatedly urged him that, if he felt himself improved from the same ailment by which he was detained, he should, with the Lord’s help, return to his own Church, he was awaited for four years, extensions having been granted. When, at the urging of the clergy and citizens who came from there, and at our own more insistent exhortations and the petitions pressing us, we urged him that, if he were able, he should return with them by the Lord’s help, he sent us a written petition asking that, since he could in no way rise to the governance of that Church or undertake the office he had received because of the ailment by which he was detained, we should ordain a bishop for that Church.

Therefore, because the care of concern imposed upon us for all the Churches binds us, lest the flock of the faithful be without pastoral guardianship any longer, and because we were compelled by their petitions and by his renunciation on the ground of his inability, it seemed to us that a bishop ought to be ordained for the Church of Ariminum. Accordingly, after issuing the customary commands, we did not fail to admonish the clergy and people of that Church to come together in harmonious deliberation to choose an overseer for themselves. We therefore urge your Fraternity to have summoned to you the man whom all have chosen with one accord, as they are known to have requested from us; examine him carefully in every respect. And if, with the Lord’s help, none of those things in him that are condemned to death in the text of the Heptateuch [Note: [Col. 0874D] This is Epistle 30 of Book XII, now 32 of Book II. It is also called this by Hincmar; others call it the *Heptateuch*. The term is used by Saint Jerome in Letter 7 to Laeta and Letter 28 to Lucinus, and by Sidonius Apollinaris, Book V, Letter 15. By this word are signified the five books of Moses and the two others, Joshua and Judges. GUSSANV.] is found in him, and if his life has pleased you according to the report of faithful persons, send him to us with the page of the decree and also a letter bearing your testimony, so that, with the Lord arranging it, he may be consecrated by us as bishop of that Church. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 39.)

## EPISTLE XX. TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF ARIMINUM

Because of the illness of their bishop, they are to choose another who is worthy.

Gregory to the clergy and people residing at Ariminum.

[Col. 0874B] Pastoral care compels us to attend with vigilant consideration to Churches deprived of the governance of a priest. And therefore, because your Church has long been deprived of the pastoral governance of its own priest by the bodily ailment with which you know that he is afflicted, moved by your petitions, we did not fail to admonish the same bishop that, if he felt himself improved from that ailment, he ought to return to the ministry of the priesthood he had undertaken. Once or repeatedly admonished by us, he is now known to have informed us, having presented a written petition, that because the same ailment pressed upon him he could in no way rise to the governance of that Church or undertake the office he had received. Compelled by this despair concerning the man, we judged it necessary to consider the ordination of a bishop for your Church. We therefore urge you all, with one and the same accord and without tumult, to choose for yourselves, with the Lord’s help, such a priest to be placed over you as will neither be rejected by the venerable canons nor fail to be found worthy of so great a ministry. When he has been requested, let him come to us for ordination with the solemn decree, confirmed by the subscriptions of all, and accompanied by the document of the visitor, so that your Church may, with the Lord arranging it, have its own priest. We wish, moreover, that the man whom your unanimity has chosen be brought without any delay to our brother and fellow bishop Marinianus at Ravenna, so that, after he has been carefully examined and investigated by him, he may also be confirmed by his testimony when he comes to us.

## EPISTLE XXI. TO BISHOP SEBASTIAN

He is to urge the clergy and people of Ariminum to choose a suitable bishop.

[Col. 0875A]

Gregory to Bishop Sebastian.

Pastoral care compels us to attend with vigilant consideration to Churches deprived of the governance of a priest. And therefore, because the Church of Ariminum, in which your Fraternity performs the office of visitation, has long been deprived of the pastoral governance of its own priest by the bodily ailment with which you know that he is afflicted, moved by the petitions of the clergy and citizens, we did not fail to admonish the same bishop that, if he felt himself improved from that ailment, he ought to return to the ministry of the priesthood he had undertaken. Once or repeatedly admonished by us, he is now known to have informed us, having presented a written petition, that because the same ailment pressed upon him he could in no way rise to the governance of that Church or undertake the office he had received. Compelled by this despair concerning the man, we judged it necessary to consider the ordination of a bishop for that Church. We therefore urge you to compel the clergy and people of that Church by vigilant admonition to choose for themselves, with the Lord’s help, such a priest to be placed over them as may be found fit for so great a ministry and in no way be rejected by the venerable canons. When he has been requested, let him come here for consecration with the solemn decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all and also with the testimony of your letters, so that that Church may, with the Lord’s help, have its own priest. [Note: [Col. 0875D] EPISTLE XXI [Al. 52, indiction 2].—We read these words in none of the manuscripts.] In the month of May.

## EPISTLE XXII. TO THE DEACON CYPRIAN

He is to arrange that the bishops of Sicily, who formerly used to travel to Rome every third year and now every fifth year, should assemble for the feast of Saint Peter in such a way that no suspicion may arise in the praetor. He is also to admonish the bishops of Lipara and Rhegium, and to console Libertinus.

Gregory to the deacon Cyprian.

Your Affection knows that it was formerly customary for our brothers and fellow bishops from Sicily to assemble at Rome once every three years; but, taking account of their labor, we established that they should present themselves here once every five years. Since, however, it has now been a long time since they assembled here, we wish you to urge them to celebrate here with us, if God brings it about, the feast of Saint Peter. But lest some suspicion perhaps arise in the praetor if he learns that they have been instructed to come here, take care to handle this through your own agency, making our will understood, so that they may indeed come here on the appointed day, as we have said, and that no suspicion may arise in the praetor concerning them. You will likewise admonish the bishops of Lipara and Rhegium to come here.

As for the magnificent man Libertinus, be solicitous that no deceit ensnare him, because some letters concerning the city of Ravenna have been sent to us; we have sent that very letter on to you, so that from it you may learn how you ought to conduct yourself toward him. Console him, moreover, so that he may not distress himself, because we believe that our most excellent son the exarch will not trouble him. For we did not delay writing concerning him. But because that exarch is occupied in the Po, we have not received his letter. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book III, no. 24.)

[Note: [Col. 0875D] EPISTLE XXII [Al. 29].—From Letter 16 of Saint Leo to the bishops of Sicily, the date and reason for this custom may be gathered: namely, that they should attend the council under the Roman pontiff, their metropolitan, by virtue of the ancient canons, which had decreed that synods be held each year so that, through common deliberation, all the institutions and decrees of the canons might remain inviolable among all the priests of the Lord. Saint Leo, however, wanted three to assemble each year. Therefore, if they went to Rome individually once every three years, it is clear that there were then nine bishops in Sicily. This custom had fallen into disuse; he restores it, with the year postponed and the day changed. See Book I, Letter 1.]

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO FORTUNATUS AND ANTHEMIUS

They are to urge Stephen to restore the property he took from the woman betrothed to him after she entered a monastery. If he refuses, they are to report him so that he may be compelled to return it.

Gregory to Bishop Fortunatus and to the subdeacon Anthemius [Note: [Col. 0875D] EPISTLE XXIII [Al. 20].—In two Vatican manuscripts, *through Campania* is added.] the defensor.

Catellus, the bearer of this letter, informed us that his sister, who had been betrothed to a certain Stephen, had, through the prompting of divine mercy, entered religious life in a monastery at Naples, and that the same Stephen was unlawfully retaining her house and some of her property. But since the legal decrees [Note: [Col. 0876D] Vatican A reads: “customarily punish with a fine.” We approve this reading.] have determined that a betrothed woman who wishes to convert is not to be punished by any penalty at all, your Fraternity, together with the subdeacon Anthemius, should diligently and carefully investigate the truth.

But if, as we have been informed, you discover that the aforesaid Stephen is unjustly retaining the house or anything else, let your exhortation urgently admonish him to restore without any delay or dispute whatever he unlawfully holds, lest he postpone restitution of another’s property under any pretext of excuse. If you perhaps discover that he disregards your exhortation, report to us both this matter and precisely how the truth of the case stands, so that, once the merits of the affair are known, he may be compelled by another means, as equity demands, to restore what he scorns to return voluntarily out of consideration for decency. Commending the bearer of this letter to your Fraternity, we urge you not to permit him to suffer prolonged delay there on this account.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] In the *Code concerning Bishops and Clerics*, law 36, we learn that if a betrothed man or woman, after dowry-gifts had been given and received, wished to dedicate himself or herself to divine service, withdraw from secular life, live as a nun, and remain in the fear of God, the man was compelled …, while the betrothed woman had to return double what she had received. This seemed contrary to the religion of our mildness. Therefore, by the present law … the betrothed woman is to restore to her fiancé not double, as previously, but only what she had received as dowry-gifts, and she is not to be compelled to return anything more unless she is proved to have received it, etc. GUSSANV.]

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO THE PRIEST CANDIDUS

He is to ransom four Christians who were being held at Narbonne in Jewish service.

Gregory to our priest Candidus [Note: [Col. 0877D] EPISTLE XXIV [Al. 21].—In almost all the manuscripts, *through Gaul* is omitted; it is nevertheless read in Vatican A.] in Gaul.

Dominicus, the bearer of this letter, informed us tearfully that four of his brothers had been ransomed from captivity by Jews and were now being held at Narbonne [Note: [Col. 0877D] Narbonne, or more properly Narbo, in antiquity Narbo Martius, formerly the chief city of Gallia Narbonensis or Gallia Braccata. It is still a large city in the province of Occitania, distinguished by an archiepiscopal title. GUSSANV.] in the service of those same Jews [Note: [Col. 0877D] Concerning Christians held in Jewish service, see above, Book III, Letter 38, and Book IV, Letter 21.]. And because it is altogether grievous and execrable that Christians should be in the service of Jews, we urge your Affection by this letter to investigate the matter with complete care and diligence. And if it is truly so, and it has become clear to you by manifest proof that neither they themselves have the means by which to ransom themselves nor the aforesaid bearer possesses them, it should be your concern to ransom them, knowing that whatever you give for them will without doubt be charged to your accounts. [Note: [Col. 0877D] This is found only in the Tours manuscript of Saint Gatianus and the old Colbert manuscript.] In the month of June, indiction 15. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book VI, no. 44.)

## EPISTLE XXV. TO GREGORIA

He consoles her, although she has confessed her sins, because she is anxious about their remission, by citing the example of the sinful woman whom he supposes to have been Martha’s sister. He shows that asking in vain for a divine revelation of forgiveness is fruitless.

Gregory to Gregoria [Note: [Col. 0877D] EPISTLE XXV [Al. 22].—A *cubicularius*, in French *camérier*, is one who attends the bedchamber or its entrance; it sometimes seems to be used for the secretary of secrets, *Novels* 8, 24, 26, 27, or for an archivist. GUSSANV. Vatican B reads “Gregory to Theoctista the patrician.” The Regius manuscript reads “to Gregoria Bubalaria Augusta.”] chamber-attendant to the Augusta.

I received the letter of your desired sweetness, in which you earnestly accused yourself of the multitude of your sins. But I know that you love the omnipotent Lord fervently, and I trust in his mercy that the sentence which proceeded from the mouth of Truth concerning a certain holy woman also proceeds concerning you: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47). How they were forgiven was also shown by what followed, for she sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word (Luke 10:39). Suspended in the contemplative life, she had already passed beyond the active life, which her sister Martha still maintained (ibid., 40).

She also diligently sought the buried Lord; bending over the tomb, she did not find his body. Even after the disciples had departed, she remained weeping before the entrance of the tomb, and she was worthy to see alive the one whom she had sought as dead; she announced to the disciples that he had risen (Matthew 28:1; Luke 24:1 ff.). This too was done by a wondrous dispensation of God’s mercy: life was announced by the mouth of a woman, because death had been offered in paradise by the mouth of a woman.

At another time, when she saw the Lord after his resurrection together with the other Mary, she approached and held his feet. Bring before your eyes, I beg you, whose hands held whose feet. The woman who had been sinful in the city, the hands that had been polluted by iniquity, touched the feet of the one who sits at the right hand of the Father above the heads of the angels. Let us consider, if we can, what depths of heavenly mercy these are: that a woman who had been plunged by guilt into the depths of the abyss should, on the wing of love, be lifted so high by grace.

It has been fulfilled, dear daughter, it has been fulfilled—what the prophetic voice promised us concerning this time of the holy Church: [Note: [Col. 0878D] Here, as often elsewhere, he uses the sense rather than the exact words. Hence the text of Zechariah does not agree with the Vulgate or with the other versions. The Vulgate and Saint Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew read: “On that day there shall be a fountain opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman.” The Hebrew interlinear reads: “On that day there shall be an open vein for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for menstruation.” The Septuagint reads: “On that day every place shall be opened for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for transformation and separation.” The Chaldaic, Syriac, and other versions differ somewhat as well, but this has no bearing on our subject. GUSSANV.] “On that day the house of David shall be an open fountain for the washing of the sinner and of the menstruous woman” (Zechariah 13:1). The house of David is for us sinners an open fountain for washing, because through the mercy already opened by David’s Son, our Savior, we are cleansed from the filth of our iniquities.

But when your Sweetness added in your letters that you would continue to trouble me until I wrote to you that it had been revealed to me that your sins were forgiven, you asked for something both difficult and useless: difficult, because I am unworthy to receive such a revelation; useless, because you must not become secure concerning your sins until the final day of your life, when you will no longer be able to mourn those same sins. Until that day comes, you must always fear your faults with suspicion and trembling, and wash them away with daily tears.

Certainly the apostle Paul had already ascended to the third heaven, had been led into paradise, and had heard secret words that it was not lawful for a human being to utter (2 Corinthians 12:2–4); nevertheless, still trembling, he said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Corinthians 9:27). He still fears who is already being led to heaven; and will one who still lives on earth now recklessly refuse to fear?

Consider, dearest daughter, that security is usually the mother of negligence. Therefore, you must not have in this life a security that makes you negligent. For it is written: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14). And again it is written: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). During the brief period of this life, therefore, it is necessary that trembling hold your mind, so that afterward it may rejoice without end through the joy of security.

May the omnipotent God fill your mind with the grace of his Holy Spirit and, after the tears that you pour out daily in prayer, lead you to eternal joys. [Note: [Col. 0879D] Vatican B and C state that this letter was written in June, indiction 15. Vatican A says July.] (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, no. 60.)

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO THE PATRICIAN THEOCTISTA

He congratulates her because, amid human turmoil, she devotes herself to reading and longs for eternal things. He asks whether the Augusta pursues the same studies. He discusses at greater length the two kinds of compunction. He urges Theoctista to watch diligently over the education of the royal children and to inspire in them mutual charity and gentleness toward their subjects. With half the money Theoctista had sent, he ransoms captives; with the remainder he supports nuns, whose holiness he believes has preserved Rome. He sends a key from the body of Saint Peter and recounts a miracle concerning it.

[Col. 0879B] Gregory [Note: [Col. 0879D] EPISTLE XXVI [Al. 23].—The printed editions read “to Theoctista and Andrea together.” The Regius manuscript reads “to Theoctista the patrician and Andrea”; the Vatican manuscripts A, B, and C agree. We have preferred the heading found in the other manuscripts, namely the English, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and Colbert manuscripts.] to Theoctista the patrician.

Because your Excellence, placed amid such great turmoil of affairs, is full of the abundance of the sacred word and continually longs for eternal joys, I give great thanks to the omnipotent God, because I see fulfilled in you what is written concerning the elect fathers: “The children of Israel walked on dry ground through the midst of the sea” (Exodus 15:19). But, on the contrary: “I have come into the depths of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Psalm 68:3). You, however, as I see, walk with dry steps through the waves of secular affairs toward the promised homeland.

Let us therefore give thanks to that Spirit who, when he fills hearts, lifts them up; who amid human turmoil creates solitude within the mind. In whose presence no part of a compunctive soul is hidden. [Note: [Col. 0879D] The printed editions, against Saint Gregory’s intention and against the manuscripts, read “no place … is secret,” with the negation removed. Vatican D reads “is not secure.”]

You draw in the fragrance of eternal sweetness, and therefore you ardently love the bridegroom of the soul, so that with the heavenly bride you can say to him: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song of Songs 1:3). But in your Excellence’s letters I found this lacking, [Note: [Col. 0880D] Gussanville, incorrectly, reads “because he did not wish to say anything about …”] that you did not tell me how diligently the most serene lady reads, or how she is moved to compunction in reading. Your presence ought to benefit her greatly, so that amid the waves of affairs which she continually endures and from which, willingly or unwillingly, she is drawn outward, she may always be recalled inwardly to love of the heavenly homeland. You ought also to investigate how often tears are granted to her for the sake of her soul, and whether she is still moved to compunction by fear or already by love.

There are two kinds of compunction, as you know. One fears eternal punishments; the other longs for heavenly rewards, because the soul thirsting for God is first moved to compunction by fear and afterward by love.

Beforehand it afflicts itself with tears, because, when it recalls its evils, it fears suffering eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by prolonged anxiety and sorrow, a certain security born of hope for pardon arises, [Note: [Col. 0880D] Lest anyone quibble over the wording and suppose this letter contrary to the preceding one: just as Gregory contrasts presumption with certainty, so he contrasts a certain security with that complete and fearless security which he condemned in the earlier letter.] and the spirit is inflamed with love of heavenly joys. The one who previously wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

For the mind contemplates what those choirs of angels are, what that fellowship of blessed spirits is, and what the vision of God’s inner brightness is; and it mourns more because it is absent from everlasting blessings than it mourned earlier when it feared eternal evils. Thus perfect compunction born of fear draws the soul toward compunction born of love.

This is well described in a sacred and truthful history by a figurative narrative, which says: “Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, sitting upon a donkey, sighed. Her father said to her: ‘What is the matter with you?’ She answered: ‘Give me a blessing. You have given me a southern and dry land; add also a watered land.’ And her father gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land” (Joshua 15:18–19). Achsah sits upon a donkey when the soul presides over the irrational impulses of its flesh. Sighing, she asks her father for watered land, because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great desire.

There are some who have already received as a gift the freedom to speak on behalf of justice, protect the oppressed, give their own possessions to the needy, and possess the ardor of faith, but who do not yet have the grace of tears. Such people certainly possess southern and dry land, but still need watered land; for, although they are engaged in good works in which they are great and fervent, they must continually weep for the sins without which they cannot live, whether out of fear of punishment or out of love of the heavenly kingdom. [Note: [Col. 0880D] The printed editions read “they greatly desire.” We have corrected many other passages in this letter on the authority of the English, Norman, Vatican, Corbie, and other manuscripts; we have not announced these corrections because they are of lesser importance.]

But since, as I said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her the upper watered land and the lower watered land. The soul receives the upper watered land when it afflicts itself with tears through desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower watered land when it fears the punishments of hell with tears. In fact, the lower is given first, and afterward the upper watered land. But because compunction born of love is far superior in dignity, it was necessary to name the upper watered land first and the lower afterward.

You, therefore, who by the working of the omnipotent Lord know both kinds of compunction by experience, must diligently investigate how much you benefit your most serene lady daily through your words.

I ask you especially to take care to instruct in character the young lords whom you nurture, and to admonish the illustrious eunuchs assigned to them that they should say to them things that move their minds toward charity among themselves and toward gentleness toward their subjects, lest, if they conceive some hatred among themselves now, it later break out openly. For the words of those who nurture them will be milk if they are good, or poison if they are bad. Let them therefore now suggest such things to them as will later show how good were the things they drank from the mouths of their nurses.

Furthermore, my beloved son the deacon Sabinianus brought the thirty pounds of gold sent by your Excellence, to be given for the ransoming of captives and distributed to the poor. I rejoice over this, but I am afraid for myself, because before the terrifying Judge I shall have to render an account not only for the property of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, but also for your possessions. May the omnipotent God repay you heavenly things for earthly things and eternal things for temporal ones.

I inform you that from the city of Croton, which lies on the Adriatic Sea in the land of Italy and was captured by the Lombards in the past year, many noble men and women were led away as booty; sons were separated from parents, parents from sons, and spouses from spouses. Some of them have already been ransomed. But because they demand high prices for them, many have remained until now among the wickedest Lombards. I immediately sent half the money you transmitted for their ransom.

With the remaining half I have decided to buy bedding for the servants of God whom you call in Greek *monastriai* [Note: [Col. 0881D] A Greek word familiar to everyone, meaning “nun” in Latin. They are also called *ascetriae* (“female ascetics”). GUSSANV.], because they suffer severe nakedness in their beds during the most bitter cold of this winter. There are many of them in this city. According to the register by which they are administered, their number is three thousand. Indeed, they receive eighty pounds annually from the property of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. But what is that for such a great multitude, especially in this city, where everything is purchased at a high price?

Their life, moreover, is of such a kind, and so severely disciplined by tears and abstinence, that we believe that, if they did not exist, none of us could by now have remained for so many years in this place amid the swords of the Lombards. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, no. 27.)

[Col. 0881D] Furthermore, I have sent the blessing of the apostle Saint Peter—a key from his most sacred body. Concerning this key, the following miracle occurred, which I shall recount.

When a certain Lombard who had entered the city found it in the Transpadane regions, he despised it because it was Saint Peter’s key. But because he saw that it was made of gold and wanted to make something else for himself from it, he drew out a knife to cut it. Immediately, possessed by a spirit, he drove the knife with which he intended to cut it into pieces into his own throat, and at that very hour he fell dead.

Since the Lombard king Authari and many of his men were present there, and the man who had struck himself lay dead apart while the key lay separately on the ground, an exceedingly great fear came upon everyone, so that no one dared lift the key from the ground. Then a certain Catholic Lombard named Minulfus, who was known to be devoted to prayer and almsgiving, was summoned, and he himself lifted it from the ground.

On account of this miracle Authari had another golden key made and sent it together with this one to my predecessor of blessed memory, reporting what miracle had occurred through it. I have therefore taken care to send that very key to your Excellence, through which the omnipotent God slew a proud and faithless man, so that through it you, who fear and love him, may obtain both present and eternal salvation.

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO BISHOP ANASTASIUS

Anastasius, in agreement with the emperor, thought it not very important that the bishop of Constantinople should use the title “universal.” Gregory argues that by this title the faith of the whole Church is corrupted.

Gregory to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch.

I received the long-desired letter of your most sweet Holiness, delivered by our common son the deacon Sabinianus, in which words flowed not from the tongue but from the soul. And it is no wonder that one speaks well who lives perfectly. Since, through the Spirit as teacher, you learned the precepts of life in the school of the heart [Note: [Col. 0882D] The printed editions read “through precepts.”], to despise all earthly things and hasten toward the heavenly homeland, to the extent that you have advanced in goodness, to that extent you also think good things about others.

When I heard many things worthy of praise about me in the writings of Your Blessedness, I understood the intention: you wished to recall not what I am, but what I ought to be. But when you say that I ought to remember my own character and give no place without reason to the malignant spirit that seeks to sift souls, I indeed remember that I have always possessed evil habits, and I hasten with the greatest effort, if I can, to overcome and erase those same habits in myself. If, however, as you believe, I have possessed something good, I trust in the help of the omnipotent God that I have not forgotten it.

But, as I see, Your Holiness wished your letter, in the preceding words of sweetness and in this following word, to resemble a bee, which carries both honey and a sting, so that it might satisfy me with honey and pierce me with its sting. [Col. 0882D] But amid these things I return to meditate on Solomon’s saying: “The wounds of one who loves are better than the kisses of an enemy who flatters” (Proverbs 27:6).

As for your statement that we ought to give no place to scandal without reason, this has already been written to me repeatedly by your most devout Lord, your son, for whose life we must pray without ceasing. I know that what he said from authority you say from love. Nor did I wonder that you placed imperial words in your letters, because love and power have the greatest kinship with one another. [Col. 0883A] For both have held primary authority, and both always speak through authority. [Note: [Col. 0883D] The Tours, Norman, Corbie, Vatican, and other manuscripts have this reading, as does the old edition. Recent editions read *praesunt principaliter*, “exercise primary authority.”]

When receiving the synodical letter of our brother and fellow priest Cyriacus, it was not right for me to delay on account of the profane title, lest I disturb the unity of the holy Church. Nevertheless, I took care to admonish him concerning that same superstitious and proud title, saying that he could not have peace with us unless he corrected the arrogance of the aforesaid word, which the first apostate invented.

You, however, ought not to say that this matter is nothing, because if we bear it calmly, we corrupt the faith of the whole Church. For you know how many not only heretics but also founders of heresies have gone forth from the Church of Constantinople. And, to say nothing of the insult to your honor, if one bishop is called “universal,” the universal Church collapses if the one universal falls. But away with this folly; away with this frivolity from my ears. I trust in the omnipotent Lord that he will soon fulfill what he promised: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11).

Occupied with many matters, I have replied briefly to the statements of your letters; for what I ought not now to say in writing remains marked in my mind. I ask that Your Blessedness always recall me in your holy prayers, so that your intercessions may rescue me from temporal and eternal evils. Pray earnestly and fervently for our most serene lord the emperor, because his life is greatly necessary to the world. I shall say no more, since I do not doubt that you also know this.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO THE PHYSICIAN THEODORUS

He praises the alms sent for captives and the poor. He sends in return a key from the body of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0883C]

Gregory to Theodorus, physician at Constantinople.

My most beloved son, the deacon Sabinianus, returned to me without bringing any letter from Your Glory; instead, he carried away what had been sent to the captives and the poor, and from this I understood the reason. For you did not wish to speak to me by letter because you had addressed a word to Almighty God through a good work. This same work of yours has its own voice, which cries out to the secret ears of God, as it is written: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will plead for you” (Sirach 29:15).

Indeed, I confess that it is painful for me to spend another’s property and, in addition to what I possess from the resources of the Church, to impose accounts concerning the goods of my most cherished son, the lord Theodore.
