Nevertheless, I rejoice with your kindness, because you carefully attend to and preserve what Truth says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). And also what is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “Let your abundance supply their need, so that their abundance may also be a supply for your need” (2 Corinthians 8:14). Tobias admonishes his son, saying: “If you have much, give generously; but if you have little, gladly share even from your small amount” (Tobit 4:9).

You therefore observe all these commandments; but we ask you to pray for us, lest we distribute the fruits of your labors indiscriminately and not as necessity requires, and lest, where you lessen sins, we should instead increase them. May Almighty God guard you with his protection, and grant you such human favor in the earthly palace that, after a long time, he may lead you to the eternal joys of the heavenly palace.

[Note: The printed editions read “it will pray,” which is less strong than “it will plead for you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Epistle XXVIII [otherwise 2].—The printed editions read “to the secret ears of God.”]

As a blessing from Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, whom you greatly love, we have sent you a key from his most sacred body. Iron from his chains is enclosed in it, so that what bound his neck for martyrdom may release yours from every sin.

## 875. Epistle XXIX. To Andreas

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Epistle XXIX [otherwise 26].—The common editions add “the Scholastic,” which is not found in the Vatican, English, Corbie, Colbert, and other manuscripts.]

*On despising the dignities of the world, so that one may be free for heavenly pursuits.*

Gregory to Andreas.

Having received the letter of Your Greatness and learned of your well-being, I rejoiced; and I was greatly delighted by the kindness of the most devout lady, who deigned to show you her favor. I also rejoice exceedingly that the lady Constantina, a most distinguished young woman, was taken away from the allurements of this world before she married.

But when you said that you had entered the military service of her husband and wished to be commended to the most serene lord emperor, so that he might assign you some duty wherever he judged you useful, this touched my mind with no small sorrow, because I had always thought that the goodness of your character was directed toward something else.

[Note: This letter recalls Andreas from the waves of worldly affairs to the shore of Christian rest. Nearly the same thought is found in Saint Augustine, *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 16: “In this life people seek rest and security through great labors, but they do not find them through perverse desires. For they wish to rest in things that are restless and impermanent,” and so forth. The reader should continue to the end of the chapter. — Gussanville.]

I know many who, placed in public service, suffer greatly because they are not permitted to be at leisure and mourn their sins; and why you desire to entangle yourself, I do not know. Why, illustrious son, do you not consider that the world is at its end? Everything is driven forward daily, and we are led to render an account before the eternal and fearful Judge. What else, then, ought we to do but think about his coming?

Our life is like that of a person sailing:

[Note: This reading is better supported by the Vatican, Norman, English, Royal, Corbie, and other manuscripts than the printed editions, which read: “For the person who sails stands, sits, lies down, and goes.” The meaning is that the sailor, whether he stands, sits, or lies down, is always moving and hastening toward the harbor, carried along by the winds in the vessel. The words that follow—“So also are we”—make this meaning of the holy teacher sufficiently clear.]

the one who sails may stand, sit, or lie down; he goes, because he is carried forward by the movement of the ship. So also are we: whether awake or asleep, silent or speaking, walking, willing or unwilling, with every passing moment we move daily toward the end.

When the day of our end arrives, where will be all that is now sought with such care and gathered with such anxiety? Therefore we must not seek honors or riches, which are left behind. But if we seek good things, let us love those which we shall possess without end. If, however, we fear evils, let us fear those which the rejected endure without end.

What mental occupation is involved in serving a most devout ruler, with its desire for earthly favor and its fear that this same favor may be lost if it is attained? Consider, then, what punishment it is either to be worn out by the desire for prosperity or to tremble from fear of adversity.

I therefore advise Your Greatness rather to remain in the purpose you once held, living for a short time in a pleasant refuge of pilgrimage, and to lead a quiet and tranquil life; to devote yourself to sacred readings, meditate on heavenly words, kindle yourself with love of eternity, perform good works concerning earthly matters according to your strength, and hope for the everlasting kingdom as their reward. To live in this way is already to possess a share in eternal life.

[Note: The Norman, Royal, Corbie, and three Vatican manuscripts read “in an acceptable refuge.”]

I say these things, illustrious son, because I love you greatly. And because you are heading into storms and waves, I draw you back to shore with the ropes of my words; and if you are willing to follow the one who pulls you, once placed upon the shore of your rest you will recognize what dangers you have escaped and what joys you have found.

Moreover, I give thanks because you took care to reassure me concerning the two persons who came with the illustrious Callicinus, although we already have no small evidence of the evils of the person whom Your Greatness previously mentioned.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Royal manuscript read “Gallinicus”; the printed editions read “Gallitio.” Perhaps the name is Callinicus, whom we learn from Book IX, Letter 9, and many other records to have been exarch of Italy. Manuscript forms of the name vary greatly; the same person could have been written Callinicus or Callicinus through a slight transposition.]

But because these are evil times, we bear everything with groaning. May Almighty God guard you with his protection, grant you to act well here, and allow you to rejoice with him forever in eternal glory.

[Note: The printed editions read “in the eternity of life.”]

## Epistle XXX. To Narsa the Religious

*He consoles one who is afflicted. He shows that a Christian must not refuse adversity. Why he does not write to the inhabitants of monasteries or to others living in Constantinople. He rejoices at the death of Esychia. What Lady Dominica should do. He sends small gifts. He commends Anatolius.*

Gregory to Narsa the Religious.

When I was sending the Roman defender to the royal city, he sought your writings for a long time, but they could not be found. Later, however, they were discovered among many letters from others.

[Note: [Col. 0886D] Epistle XXX [otherwise 27].—This is the reading of the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts; the printed editions read “I sought.”] In it your sweetness informed me of your afflictions and spiritual tribulations and disclosed the adversities inflicted by evil people.

But, I ask you, recall in all these matters what I believe you will never forget: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12). In this regard I say confidently that you live less piously if you have suffered less persecution.

Let us also hear what the same teacher of the nations says to his disciples: “You yourselves know, brothers, our entrance among you, that it was not empty, but that we first suffered and were treated with insults” (1 Thessalonians 2:1). Behold, dearest son, the holy preacher declared that his entrance would have been empty if he had not endured insults; and your Charity wishes to speak good things but refuses to suffer evil. Therefore it is necessary that, amid adversities, you gird yourself more tightly, so that adversity itself may increase your desire for the love of God and your pursuit of good works.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “to speak good things,” as in the Norman, Corbie, and Vatican D manuscripts.]

[Note: The Vatican A manuscript reads “among the adversaries, let him gird himself more tightly.”]

[Note: The Turon, Royal, and three Vatican manuscripts read “the desire for good admonition.”]

Thus seeds of crops covered by frost sprout more fruitfully, and thus fire is pressed by the blast so that it grows. I know, indeed, that you suffer a violent storm from the perverse speech of so many evil tongues and endure waves of contradiction in your mind. But let what the Lord says through the Psalmist return to your heart: “I heard you in the hidden place of the storm; I tested you at the waters of contradiction” (Psalm 80:8). For if, amid those who contradict you, you do what belongs to God, then you are proved to be a true worker.

Your sweetest Charity wrote to me that I should write some admonition to the monasteries established through your prayers and instruction by our son, the lord Paul. But if they are vessels of God, I know that through the grace of compunction they possess within themselves a fountain of wisdom, and they ought not to receive the small drops of my dryness.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “but if they are from the way.” Vatican B reads: “but if they are from the way of God.”]

Your perfect wisdom recalls that in paradise there was no rain, but a fountain rose from the middle of paradise to water the face of the earth. Those souls, therefore, which through the grace of compunction possess a fountain within themselves do not need the necessary rain of another’s tongue.

You also announced to me by letter the death of Lady Esychia, and I rejoiced with great exultation, because that good soul happily reached her own homeland, having labored in a foreign homeland.

Greet on my behalf my illustrious daughters, Lady Dominica and Lady Eudocia. But since I have long heard that the aforementioned Lady Dominica has been made a superior, let your Charity watch carefully over her in this matter. Since she is no longer compelled to serve in the labor of the earthly palace, let her flee completely from all the commotions of this world, give herself wholly to God, and leave nothing of herself outside herself. Let her also gather as many souls as she can into the service of their Creator, so that their minds may receive the grace of compunction through his word, and so that she herself may be freed from all her sins more quickly, in proportion as the souls of others also break free from the bonds of their sins through her life and speech.

Because no human being in this world is without sin—and what else is sinning but fleeing from God?—I say confidently that this same daughter of mine has some sins. Therefore, in order to satisfy perfectly her Lady, that is, eternal Wisdom, she must return with many others to the one from whom she alone has fled. The guilt of her turning away will not be charged against her if, on returning, she brings back a gain.

I ask you to greet on my behalf the lord Alexander and the lord Theodore. As for your writing that I should write to my most excellent daughter, Lady Gurdia, and to her most holy daughter, Lady Theoctista, and to their distinguished men, the lord Marinus and the lord Christodorus, and admonish them concerning their souls, your sweetest Greatness knows well that today in the city of Constantinople there are no people who can translate a dictated text well from Latin into Greek.

[Note: The emperor Maurice had a sister named Gurdia or Gordia, who, according to Simocatta, Book VIII, chapter 13, was married to Philip, commander of the East. After Maurice’s death, when Phocas was banished to Chrysopolis, she was also banished there. Others may investigate whether this Gurdia is the same woman who married first Marinus and then Philip.]

[Note: This Theoctista is different from Theoctista, the sister of the emperor Maurice. The woman mentioned here was Gurdia’s daughter; Maurice’s sister Theoctista, to whom Letter 26 of this book and Letter 5 of Book I were addressed, had Joanna as her mother. See Moschus, chapter 128.]

[Note: Recent manuscripts read “those who translate from Greek into Latin and from Latin into Greek.”]

[Note: Concerning translators and translation, see Lipsius, *Century 1*, Letter 72: “I wish you would allow yourself somewhat more freedom and not everywhere press so firmly upon the footprints of Latin speech. Translation bound by this care is cramped, constricted, thin, and often obscure. Each language plainly has its own genius, which you should neither tear away nor rashly command to migrate into a foreign body. How many…” The diligent reader should read the whole letter, so that he may understand that in translations one must depart from the original in order to keep to the proper path, and that keeping to the path of translation means not always adhering to the path of the original. — Gussanville.]

For while they guard the words and pay no attention to the meaning, they neither make the words intelligible nor preserve the sense. For this reason I wrote briefly to the aforementioned daughter of mine, Lady Gurdia, and remained silent toward the others.

I have sent you two *camisias* and four *oraria*, which I humbly ask you to offer to the aforementioned men as a blessing from Saint Peter.

[Note: Later Greek writers use *camisia* for a garment: ὁ ἐπὶ καμάτων χιτών, “the tunic used for labor.” Condinus, speaking of lectors, writes: Μετὰ τῶν ἱματίων καὶ ἐπιρριπταρίων αὐτῶν φοροῦντες καὶ καμίσια ἐπάνω τῶν ἱματίων, “wearing, together with their garments and outer coverings, camisias over their garments.” Elsewhere, speaking of psaltes, he writes: Εἰσέρχονται καὶ οἱ ψάλται μετὰ τῶν ἐπιρριπταρίων καὶ καμισίων αὐτῶν, “the psaltes also enter with their outer coverings and camisias.” In the dialogues of Saint Gregory we read *hypocamisium* (ὑποκαμίσιον), meaning an under-tunic. Victor of Vita mentions *camisias* in his account of the Vandal persecution. — Gussanville.]

[Note: Here *orarium* means a sweat-cloth or linen cloth with which the face is wiped. It was longer than it was broad, like a bandage. Cardinal Bona suspects that, from this oblong shape, the word was transferred into the Church and applied to the sacred stole. See Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 24, section 6, where he discusses the *orarium* at greater length. For its meaning as a stole, see note 755 on the *Sacred Book*.]

Furthermore, a certain dying man left me a little boy. Thinking about his soul, I sent him to your Sweetness, so that he might live in service to you on earth through the person by whose means he may attain the freedom of heaven.

I ask your sweetest Charity frequently to visit my most beloved son, the deacon Anatolius, whom I sent to the royal city to conduct the Church’s business. After the labors he endures in secular affairs, may he find rest with you in the word of God and, as though with a white linen cloth, wipe away the sweat of that earthly labor.

Commend him to all the persons known to you, although I know that, if he is fully known, he needs no commendation. Show through him how much you love the holy apostle Peter and how much you love me.

May Almighty God guard your sweetest Charity, which is so dear to me, from inward and outward enemies; and, when it pleases him, may he lead you to the heavenly kingdoms.

(See Book I, Letter 6.)

## Epistle XXXI. To Cyriacus, Bishop

[Note: [Col. 0888D] Epistle XXXI [otherwise 28].—The same letter appears as Letter 24, now 25, of Book I. — Gussanville.]

*On removing a profane title, so that the peace of the Church may be preserved and the scandals of many removed.*

Gregory to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople.

We received the letter of Your Blessedness, which spoke to us not with the words of the tongue but with those of the soul. For it opened a mind that nevertheless was not closed to me, since I had personally experienced its sweetness.

Therefore I continually give thanks to Almighty God, because if love—the mother of virtues—remains in your heart toward us, you will never lose the branches of good works, since you possess the root of goodness itself.

It is therefore necessary that you first show me and all your brothers the beauty of this same love in this work: that you hasten to remove the word of pride through which grave scandal is generated in the Churches, fulfilling in every way what is written: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3). And again: “Give no occasion to the adversary for the sake of reproach” (1 Timothy 5:14).

True love is shown only if there is no schism among us through the swelling conceit (*typhus*) of pride.

[Note: The Norman and other manuscripts read “through *typhus*.” Concerning this term, see Book XXIII of the *Moralia*, number 25.]

I call Jesus as witness in my soul that, from the greatest to the least, I wish to give no human being an occasion for scandal. I want all to be great and honorable, provided that their honor does not detract from the honor of Almighty God. For whoever desires to be honored against God is not honorable to me.

But so that you may know my disposition toward Your Blessedness, I have sent my beloved son, the deacon Anatolius, to the feet of the most devout lords, so that he may satisfy their piety and your fraternity. I seek to harm no one in this matter, but to preserve humility pleasing to God and harmony in the holy Church.

And because the enemy of Almighty God, the Antichrist, is near, I earnestly desire that he find nothing distinctive—not only in the conduct but even in the title—of priests. Therefore let those things that have been introduced in a new manner be removed in the same order in which they were introduced, and peace will remain among us undisturbed in the Lord.

For what sweetness or love will there be among us if we comfort one another with our words but wound one another by our actions? Let Your Holiness therefore act so that we may feel in the marrow of our hearts the good things you say, so that, while the hearts of priests are united and we pray for the lives of the most devout lords, we may deserve to be heard all the more quickly, since peace illuminates your prayers before the eyes of God and the stain of discord does not obscure them.

## Epistle XXXII. To Anastasius, Presbyter

*On removing the dispute that had arisen between the father of the monastery called Neas and the bishop of Jerusalem.*

Gregory to Anastasius, presbyter.

[Note: In Gussanville’s edition, “Atharasius,” contrary to the manuscripts and other printed editions. Gussanville was misled by the reading in the common editions, “to the presbyter of Isauria.” He naturally assumed that this was Athanasius, the presbyter of Isauria, to whom Letter 67 of Book VI is addressed. But in the manuscripts the present man is consistently called Anastasius; and he seems rather to have been a presbyter of the Church of Jerusalem than of Isauria.]

Because “a good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12:35; Luke 6:45), your Charity showed this both by your habitual conduct and now by speaking to me in your letter. In it I found two men contending over virtues: you arguing for love, and another arguing for fear and humility.

Although occupied with many matters, and although ignorant of the Greek language, I nevertheless sat as judge in your dispute. Having sought the truth, I found that you yourself defeated your opponent in my judgment through the apostolic sentence that I brought forward while you were contending: “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear; for fear has punishment, and whoever fears is not perfect in love.”

I know how greatly your Fraternity possesses perfect love. And because you love Almighty God greatly, you ought to have great confidence concerning your neighbor. Places and ranks do not make us close to our Creator; either good merits unite us to him or evil ones separate us.

Since it remains uncertain what each person is inwardly like, why did you not dare to write, when you did not know which of us was superior, you or I? I know that you live well, but I know that I am burdened with many sins. Yet even if you yourself are a sinner, you are still much better than I, because you carry only your own sins, whereas I carry both my own and those of the people entrusted to me.

In this I see you as exalted, in this I see you as great: you have made no progress in the eyes of human beings toward a great and lofty position. In such a position, when honor is bestowed outwardly by people, the mind is often plunged downward because it is weighed down by burdensome cares.

But Almighty God has appointed you, according to what is written, “ascents in the heart, in the valley of tears” (Psalm 84:6).

You could have appeared much higher and more sublime than I if you had not accepted the leadership of the monastery called Neas. For, as I hear, the appearance of monks is indeed maintained in that monastery, but many worldly things are carried on under the guise of holiness.

Even so, I shall consider that you have reached this position by heavenly grace if, under your leadership, those things that displease Almighty God in that place are corrected.

But because quarrels have always tended to exist between the father of that monastery and the shepherd of the Church of Jerusalem, I believe that Almighty God wished your Charity and my most holy brother and fellow priest Amos to be in Jerusalem at the same time so that the quarrels I have mentioned might be endured.

Now, therefore, show how much you formerly loved one another. I know that both of you are abstinent, both learned, and both humble. Therefore it is necessary that the glory of our Savior be praised, according to the voice of the Psalm, “with tambourine and choir” (Psalm 150:4).

[Note: Saint Augustine anticipated this interpretation in his commentary on Psalm 68: “Tambourines are made from leather dried and stretched.” And on Psalm 149: “In the tambourine the leather is stretched; in the psaltery the strings are stretched; in both instruments the flesh is crucified.” He continues: “Let it be stretched upon the wood and let the desire of the flesh be dried; the more tightly the cords are stretched, the more sharply they sound,” and so forth. — Gussanville.]

In the tambourine there is a sound from dry skin, whereas in the choir there is harmony of voices. What, then, is signified by the tambourine if not abstinence, and by the choir if not unanimity? Since you praise the Lord through abstinence in the tambourine, I ask you to praise him through unanimity in the choir.

Truth itself also says: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:50). What is signified by salt if not wisdom, as Paul testifies when he says: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6)? Since we know that through instruction in the heavenly word you possess salt, it remains for you also to maintain peace between yourselves with your whole heart through the grace of love.

I say these things, dearest brother, because I love you both greatly, and because I am entirely afraid that the sacrifices of your prayers may be stained by some disagreement between you.

I received with thanksgiving the blessing that you first sent through Exhilaratus, the *secundicerius*, and later through the deacon Sabinianus. It was fitting that you should send holy things from a holy place and demonstrate by your own gift the one whom you serve continually.

[Note: Above we discussed the *primicerius*, namely in Book III, Letter 22. Others call him *secundocerius*. The word occurs several times in Codinus and in the *Notitia Imperii. — Gussanville.]

May Almighty God protect you with his right hand and keep you unharmed from every evil.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, number 61.)

## Epistle XXXIII. To Maurice Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Epistle XXXIII [otherwise 19].—Vatican B reads “what [he owed] to the unity of the faith.” This letter and the following one are omitted in Vatican C, but occur in all our other manuscripts.]

*He argues that he was rashly called indiscreet because he reproved Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople, who calls himself universal.*

Gregory to Maurice Augustus.

Your providence as devout lords, lest some scandal perhaps be generated in the unity of the holy Church through disagreement among priests, deigned once and twice to admonish me to receive kindly the representatives of my brother and fellow priest Cyriacus and to release them quickly so that they might return.

Although, most devout lord, you issue all your commands suitably and prudently, I nevertheless find that, according to their judgment, I am accused of indiscretion because of this admonition.

If my spirit was wounded, and not slightly, by a proud and profane title, could I have been so indiscreet as not to know what I owed to the unity of the faith and to ecclesiastical harmony, and therefore refuse to receive my brother’s representatives and synodical letter because of bitterness arising from any cause?

Far be this from me. It would have been excessive folly for me to think so.

For one matter concerns preserving the unity of the faith, and another concerns restraining arrogance. The times therefore had to be distinguished, lest the novelty of my aforementioned brother be disturbed by some issue. Accordingly, I received his representatives with great affection. I showed them every charity I owed; I honored them more than ancient custom had done; and I had them celebrate the sacred solemnities of the Mass with me.

For just as my deacon ought not to serve in presenting the sacred mysteries to one who has either committed the fault of arrogance or does not correct it when committed by others, so his ministers ought to be present with me in the celebration of the Mass, since, by God’s protection, I have not fallen into the error of pride.

[Note: The old editions and nearly all manuscripts read “novelty.” Here “novelty” refers to Cyriacus’s recent elevation to the episcopate. Recent editions read “charity” instead.]

I took care to admonish that same brother and fellow bishop of mine that, if he desired to have peace and harmony with everyone, he should restrain himself from the title of this foolish name.

Concerning this matter, Your Devoutness instructed me in its commands, saying that scandal ought not to arise among us because of the title of a frivolous name. But I ask the imperial piety to consider that some things are frivolous and entirely harmless, while others are exceedingly harmful.

When the Antichrist comes and calls himself God, will that not be a very frivolous thing? Yet it will be exceedingly destructive. If we attend to the quantity of speech, what are the syllables? But if we consider the weight of iniquity, it is universal destruction.

I say confidently that whoever calls himself, or desires to be called, the universal priest anticipates the Antichrist in his pride, because by being arrogant he places himself above the others.

He is led into error by no different pride, because just as that perverse one wishes to appear God above all human beings, so whoever desires to be called the sole priest raises himself above the other priests.

But since Truth says, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11; 18:14), I know that every arrogance is broken all the more quickly the more it is inflated.

Let Your Devoutness therefore command those who have fallen into the outward form of pride not to generate scandal through the title of this frivolous name.

[Note: Vatican A and all the Vatican manuscripts read “through the arrogance of the frivolous title.”]

For I am a sinner, but by God’s authorship I hold to humility; I do not need to be admonished toward humility.

May Almighty God preserve the life of our most serene lord for a long time, for the peace of the holy Church and the benefit of the Roman commonwealth. For we are certain that, if you live—you who fear the Lord of heaven—you will permit no proud force against the truth to prevail.

## Epistle XXXIV. To Eulogius, Bishop

*The representatives of Cyriacus were received at Rome and admitted to communion; but Gregory’s deacon ought not to have communicated with Cyriacus, who was guilty of intolerable pride. His synodical letter was orthodox, except that it condemned a certain Eudoxius whom Gregory believes had hitherto not been condemned. He shows that the monks of Isauria were unjustly condemned for heresy under John, Cyriacus’s predecessor.*

Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, and Anastasius, bishop of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0892D] Epistle XXXIV [otherwise 31].—The Norman, Corbie, Royal, and other manuscripts add “as equals.”]

The love by which I am greatly bound to you does not permit me to remain silent, so that Your Holiness may know whatever is taking place among us and, not deceived by false rumors, may follow the path of justice and uprightness, as you have begun to do, with still greater perfection.

The representatives of our brother and fellow priest Cyriacus arrived and brought me his synodical letter. As Your Blessedness knows, there is serious discord between him and us because of the title of the profane name. Nevertheless, I thought that his representatives, sent concerning the matter of the faith, ought to be received, lest the fault of arrogance that has arisen in the Church of Constantinople almost against all priests should make dissension in the faith and a quarrel in ecclesiastical unity.

Since these same representatives humbly requested this, I had them celebrate the solemnities of the Mass with me.

[Note: “With me” is absent from the Corbie and Vatican D manuscripts and from nearly all the Norman manuscripts.]

As I also took care to inform the most serene lord emperor, the representatives of our brother and fellow priest Cyriacus ought to communicate with me, since, by God’s authorship, I have not fallen into the error of pride.

But my deacon ought not to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass with the aforementioned brother Cyriacus, because through the profane title he has either committed the fault of pride or is following it. If, God forbid, my deacon were to proceed while Cyriacus remained in such arrogance, we might appear to confirm the vanity of the foolish name.

[Note: The sense of this verb has already been discussed elsewhere. See note 471 on the *Sacred Book*.]

I also took care to admonish that same brother to correct himself from such arrogance, because if he does not correct it, he will in no way have peace with us.

Moreover, our same brother spoke of everything in his synodical letter in a Catholic manner, by God’s authority. But he condemned a certain Eudoxius, whom we have found condemned neither in the synods nor reproved by his predecessors in their synodical letters.

[Note: Concerning him, see above, Letter 4 to Cyriacus.]

The canons of the Council of Constantinople do condemn the Eudoxians, but they do not say who their author Eudoxius was. The Roman Church has hitherto neither possessed nor accepted those canons or the acts of that synod; nevertheless, it accepted from that synod what was defined against Macedonius. It rejects the other heresies mentioned there because they had already been condemned by other Fathers.

[Note: This is certainly strange, since, apart from Sozomen, Socrates and Theodoret—who wrote Greek history after Eusebius—mention Eudoxius and the Eudoxians more than once. Indeed, without mentioning Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Epiphanius, Athanasius does so in his first oration against the Arians and in his book *On the Synods*. From whom else shall we obtain Greek history if not from Greek writers? Cassiodorus had done precisely this: many years before Saint Gregory, he published a tripartite history in Latin, compiled from Socrates, Sozomen, and Theodoret, with the assistance of the translation of Epiphanius Scholasticus. The Romans could have read it.]

Concerning the Eudoxians, however, the Roman Church has so far recognized nothing. In the history of Sozomen, some things are related about a certain Eudoxius who is said to have seized the episcopate of the Church of Constantinople.

But the apostolic see also refuses to accept that history, because it contains many falsehoods, praises Theodore of Mopsuestia excessively, and declares him to have been a great teacher of the Church until the day of his death.

It follows, then, that if anyone accepts that history, he contradicts the synod held in the time of Justinian of blessed memory concerning the Three Chapters. Whoever cannot contradict that synod must necessarily reject that history.

In the Latin language, up to the present, we have found nothing about this Eudoxius either in Philaster or in blessed Augustine, who wrote much about heresies, or in the other Fathers.

If, therefore, Your Charity knows of any approved Greek Father who has spoken about him, let me know in your letters.

[Note: Eulogius did this: he showed that Eudoxius had been condemned by Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Epiphanius, as can be seen in Book VIII, Letter 30.]

Moreover, three years ago, when necessity arose concerning the monks of Isauria, who were accused of heresy, my former brother and fellow priest, the lord John, sent me a letter in which he endeavored to show that they had contradicted the definitions of the Council of Ephesus; and, as though taken from that same council, he sent us certain chapters against which they were said to have opposed themselves. [Note: These chapters were taken from the pseudo-Council of Ephesus, celebrated by John of Antioch and others who at that time supported both Nestorius and Pelagius and Coelestius, as Letter 49 of Book IX shows. See Book VI, indiction 14, Letter 11.]

Among other things, it contained a statement about Adam’s soul: that it had not died in sin, because the devil does not enter into the human heart; and that whoever said this should be anathema. When this had been read back to me, I was deeply saddened. [Col. 0893D] For if the soul of Adam, who was the first to sin, did not die in sin, how was it said to him concerning the forbidden tree, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die the death” (Genesis 2:17)? Certainly Adam and Eve ate from the forbidden tree, and yet afterward lived in the flesh for more than nine hundred years. It is therefore clear that he did not die in the flesh. If, then, he did not die in his soul—which it is impious to say—God pronounced a false sentence about him when he said that on the day he ate he would die. But away with this error; away with it from the true faith.

For we say that on the day the first man sinned, he died in his soul, and that through him the whole human race was condemned to this punishment of death and corruption. Through the second man, however, we trust that we can be freed both now from the death of the soul and afterward, in the eternal resurrection, from every corruption of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0894D] The printed editions less appropriately read *sic autem*, “but thus,” instead of *sicut autem*, “but just as.”]

As we also said to the aforementioned responsales, we say that Adam’s soul died through sin—not with respect to the substance of life, but with respect to the quality of life. For since substance is one thing and quality another, his soul did not die in such a way that it ceased to exist, but it died in such a way that it was no longer blessed. Nevertheless, Adam afterward returned to life through repentance.

884. That the devil enters the human heart is not denied, if the Gospel is believed. For it is written there: “And after the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). And again it says there: “When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas that Judas should betray him” (ibid., 2). Whoever denies this falls into the Pelagian heresy.

Therefore, since, when examining the Council of Ephesus, we found that it contained nothing of this kind, we also had a very ancient codex of that same council brought to us from the Church of Ravenna; and we found that it agreed with the council we possess, so that it differed in no respect and contained nothing else in its definition of anathema and condemnation except what the twelve chapters of Cyril of blessed memory condemn. While here, we explained this whole matter much more fully and precisely to his aforementioned representatives, and gave them complete satisfaction.

Therefore, lest either this or anything similar creep in there and scandalize the holy Church, it was necessary for us to bring these matters to your holiness’s attention. And although we know our brother and fellow bishop Cyriacus to be orthodox, nevertheless, on account of others we must be cautious, so that before they come forth publicly, the seeds of error may be trampled down.

[Col. 0894D] I received the writings of your holiness when the common son Sabinianus the deacon arrived. But since the bearer of these letters was already prepared to depart and could not be detained, I shall reply to these matters when my responsalis, the deacon, arrives. (See above, Letter 31.)

## LETTER XXXV. TO DOMINICUS, BISHOP

He should correct monks who evade regular discipline and wander about with impunity. He should deter bishops from defending them.

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage.

Although we believe that your Fraternity is solicitous, with pastoral vigilance, for the care of monasteries, nevertheless we have considered it necessary to inform you of what we have learned concerning a monastery situated in the province of Africa.

The bearer of these letters, the abbot Cumquodeus, complains that whenever he wishes to restrain under regular discipline the monks whom he is known to govern, they rashly abandon the monastery and wander freely wherever they wish. [Note: Letter XXXV [Al. 52].—Similar names derived from God were familiar among the Africans, as is evident from Augustine and from the catalogue of Africa, in which many bishops named Quodvultdeus are listed. Consult our Theodorus Ruinart, in *Vandalic History*.]

Because this is altogether harmful to them and displays to others an example of destruction, we exhort your Fraternity that, if the matter is so, you exercise ecclesiastical correction upon them and without doubt suspend them from such presumption by an appropriate punishment; [Col. 0895B] and that, by a salutary provision, you subject their proud spirits to the yoke of discipline in such a way that those whom their example could have incited to the excess of this wickedness may be recalled from their fault by their correction, and that the monks may learn, as is right, to obey their superiors. [Note: The printed editions read *coerceat* (“restrain”); we follow all the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts.]

Since he reports that certain bishops defend monks who transgress, your Fraternity should be especially vigilant in this matter and restrain them by every means, through your own threats, from such a defense. [Note: This is read only in the Tours manuscript, Saint Gatianus, and Vatican A and B.]

In the month of July, indiction 15.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO DYNAMIUS AND AURELIA

Always intent upon prayer, reading, and good works, they should advance toward better things. He promises a book.

Gregory to Dynamius and Aurelia, throughout Gaul.

The page of your writings, struck by the act of reading, brought us great joy by declaring your devotion, because it showed that, by seeking the nourishment of sacred reading and desiring the joys of the heavenly homeland, you not only love a religious way of life in name but also practice it. [Note: Letter XXXVI [Al. 33].—This is how it is read in almost all the manuscripts. In Vatican D and two Teller manuscripts, however, *Dynamiae* is read instead of *Dynamio*. Dynamius is already known from Letter 33 of Book III and Letter 12 of this Book VII, where Dynamius is joined with Aurelianus, or Aureliana, as almost all the manuscripts read. Is this Aurelia the same person as that Aureliana? Or should *Aureliae* be read as *Aurelio*? Certainly, in Book XI, Letter 75, the heading reads *Aurelio*, whom Saint Gregory, as Gussanvillaeus conjectures, consoles over the death of his brother Dynamius. Gussanvillaeus’s conjecture is supported by Adrien Valesius, *Frankish Affairs*, Book XI, p. 137. Yet in the cited Letter 75 Dynamius’s name is concealed; and perhaps *Aureliae*, not *Aurelio*, should be read. But the scarcity of manuscript codices prevents us from resolving this difficulty, since this letter appears almost exclusively in Vatican A.]

And since we trust that you will obtain what you desire, our heart rejoices with yours in vehement exultation. For divine grace does not abandon such a desire, as Truth itself informs us by the testimony of its voice, saying: “Everyone who seeks finds, the one who asks receives, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:8; Luke 11:12). Strengthened, therefore, by this certainty, we ought not to doubt anything concerning the mercy of the same Redeemer, but confidently to hope with unwavering hope. For he who granted the will will not frustrate us through the generosity of his gift; rather, he entirely grants the strength to obtain it. Indeed, already to desire this earnestly is itself a gift.

Nevertheless, we ought to presume upon heavenly grace in such a way that we are not negligent in prayer or in work. The voice of the same Truth expresses this when it says: “It is necessary always to pray and not grow weary” (Luke 18:1). Let us therefore ask by praying, seek by reading, and knock by working. Let the mind be watchful, suspicious on every side, and everywhere attentive, so that it may always be able to avoid the snares of the one who lies in wait.

But because the more our enemy recognizes each person as cautious against him, the more subtly he schemes by his skill to overthrow the hearts of those who resist him, let us ask the almighty Lord with continual tears and supplication that he not allow us to be corrupted by the infection of his poison; but that, against the battles and hidden suggestions which he introduces, he may surround us with the shield of his power. Against that shield his darts may be shattered when they strike, and the blow of his attack may not wound our heart; rather, by his grace, may God grant us both to understand his snares and to overcome them.

As for the book which we would send, we did not have one prepared of the kind that would instruct you, as you requested; but we shall send one later.

886. ## LETTER XXXVII. TO DOMINICA

He rejoices that she has returned to the unity of the Church. He urges her to come to Rome to her husband.

Gregory to Dominica, the wife of John.

Your letters made us exceedingly joyful, because, with God’s protection, we learned that you had been joined to the unity of the Church. Indeed, as you yourselves write, you ought to have done this earlier, since the wife of such a man ought not to have been separated, even briefly, from the unity of communion.

You ought to have considered, glorious daughter, how great a multitude of the faithful abides in the bosom of Mother Church, and with how many virtues the priests who died in this faith shone forth, or how many miracles they still perform at their bodies; [Note: [Col. 0896D] Letter XXXVII [Al. 34].—Recent editions read *vel quanta adhuc*, “or how much still.”] and you ought not to have judged them, but to have trusted such men and priests more than yourself.

Nevertheless, amid these things we give thanks to almighty God, because he poured the light of his truth into your heart, so that, after the darkness of your error had been driven away, he might show you the right path which you ought to follow and hold.

We do not wish to release your glorious husband from us for as long as we live, and therefore do not at all expect that he will return to you. Indeed, he desires to come to you, but once he is in the city of Rome he cannot—he is not permitted to do so—because he is entirely bound by the bonds of our affection. It is therefore better that you hasten by every means to come to him, because the members ought rather to follow their head and accompany him wherever he goes. [Note: The printed editions read *quocunque iverit* (“wherever he may go”).]

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO DONUS, BISHOP

He should give Faustinus fifteen pounds of silver, either from the Church’s money or from sacred vessels, for the redemption of his daughters.

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messana. [Note: Letter XXXVIII [Al. 35].—Rochus Pirrhus argues in his account of Sicily that this Donus was not bishop of Messana but of Misenum or Mesena, and that he succeeded Benenatus, mentioned in Letter 31 of Book II, indiction 10, and in Book XI, Letters 32 and 33. He supports this with many arguments, especially from the fact that this letter mentions the Church of Meria, which is not in Sicily. Yet Rochus Pirrhus does not take account of Book XI, Letter 22, which was written to the bishops of Sicily, among whom this Donus appears; nor could Donus have succeeded Benenatus, who is mentioned much later, twice, namely in Letters 32 and 33 of Book XI. Moreover, all manuscripts and printed codices read *Messanensi* or *Messano* in all four letters, which is the same thing. GUSSANV.]

Both the sacred canons (Gratian, 12, question 2, chapter 14) and legal statutes permit the property of the Church to be sold for the redemption of captives. Therefore, since the bearer of these letters, Faustinus, is shown to have incurred a debt of three hundred and thirty solidi so that he might free his daughters from the yoke of captivity, and since, after repaying thirty, he is clearly unable to repay the remaining amount, we exhort your Fraternity in these words: from the silver of the Church of Meria, whose dependent he is known to be, which is with you, you must by every means give him fifteen pounds, receiving from him a written acknowledgment (*desusceptum*) [Note: [Col. 0898D] Above, Book IV, Letter 40, now Book IV, Letter 31.], so that, after selling the silver and repaying the debt, he may be able to be freed from the necessity of his obligation. [Note: In Gregory, *miles* ordinarily denotes a cleric; here perhaps a proprietor. See Du Cange, *Glossary*; especially see Letter 3 of the following book, where mention is made of a certain Church in the possession of Faustinus in the diocese of Consentia. This, apparently, was the Church of Meria. Although it was not in Sicily but in Bruttium, Pirrhus wrongly inferred that it belonged to the diocese of Misenum rather than that of Messana. It belonged to neither, but lay farther from Misenum than from Messana. Gussanvillaeus unjustly accuses Pirrhus of failing to attend to certain letters of Saint Gregory, for Pirrhus himself cites them, on p. 289.]

Your Fraternity must also be careful that, if the aforementioned Church possesses ordinary silver, he receive the amount written above; [Note: What we French call *argent monnayé*, coined silver.] otherwise, in this matter you must provide from sacred vessels the amount we have specified. For, just as it is altogether grievous to sell ecclesiastical property needlessly, so, when such necessity is pressing, it is also a fault to prefer the property of a Church in extreme distress to its captives and to cease from their redemption.

## LETTER XXXIX. TO JOHN, BISHOP

A dispute that has arisen between two abbots concerning the boundaries of their lands should be settled in his presence by employing a surveyor.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Lest the hearts of religious men be separated from mutual charity—which God forbid—by the contention of secular matters, great care must be taken that a matter which has been brought into dispute may receive the easiest possible conclusion. [Note: Letter XXXIX [Al. 36].—Recent editions, neglecting the manuscripts and older printed editions, read *contentio* (“contention”).]

Therefore, since, as the abbot Caesarius of the monastery of Saint Peter, situated in a place called Baiae, informed us, we have learned that a serious dispute concerning certain boundaries has arisen between him and John, the abbot of the monastery of Saint Lucy, situated in the city of Syracuse, we have arranged that their quarrels be brought to an end by the determination of a surveyor, so that the dispute between them may not be prolonged. [Note: In Vatican D, Pratellianus, Audoenus, and some others, *agrimessoris* occurs here and below, but corruptly. Alteserra observes that this letter settles the boundary dispute by a surveyor and does not require a hearing before the governor, a point he proves by citing many laws.]

For this reason we have written to Fantinus, the defensor, that he should send to your Fraternity John the surveyor, who has traveled from the city of Rome to Palermo. We therefore exhort you to go with him to the places concerning which the dispute exists, and, with both parties standing face to face, have the places under litigation delimited in your presence, [Note: Concerning this matter, see above, Book I, Letter 9.] while preserving for both parties the forty-year limitation period.

Whatever shall have been determined, let your Fraternity carefully and diligently ensure that it is observed, so that no quarrel may arise from it again and no complaint may reach us.

We believe that it is not unknown to your Fraternity that the venerable abbot Caesarius was formerly ours, and therefore, without prejudice to justice, we commend him to you in all things. And because he is altogether inexperienced in secular cases, it is necessary that he be assisted by your care; nevertheless, you must preserve reason and justice in everything, as is fitting.

## LETTER XL. TO EULOGIUS, BISHOP

The see of Saint Peter at Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch is one and the same; hence the singular union of the bishops who sit there. He praises him for opposing heretics. He offers wood and sends gifts in return.

Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria.

Your most gracious holiness spoke at length in your letters about the chair of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, saying that he himself still sits in it through his successors. Indeed, I acknowledge that I am unworthy not only to be among those who preside in honor, but even to be counted among those who stand. Yet I gladly accepted everything that was said because he spoke to me of Peter’s chair—he who holds Peter’s chair. [Note: Letter XL [Al. 37].—This is because the Church of Alexandria was founded through blessed Mark, the disciple of Saint Peter. GUSSANV. In Rheims and Vatican D this sentence is read as follows: “I acknowledge that I am unworthy not only [of this], but I gladly accepted everything that was said, because he who sits upon Peter’s chair spoke to me of Peter’s chair in honor of those who preside, but also among the number of those who stand”; Vatican [D] reads, “holds.”]

And although no special honor pleases me in any way, I nevertheless rejoiced greatly, because, most holy men, what you bestowed upon me you bestowed upon yourselves. For who does not know that the holy Church is founded upon the firmness of the chief of the apostles, who drew firmness of mind from his name, so that he was called Peter from *petra*, “rock”? To him Truth’s voice says: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19). To him it says again: “And you, when once you have turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). And again: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

Thus, although there are many apostles, nevertheless, because of the primacy itself, the single see of the chief of the apostles has prevailed in authority; and it is one in three places. He himself exalted the see in which he also deigned to rest and end his present life. He himself adorned the see to which he sent his disciple the evangelist. He himself established the see in which, although he was going to depart, he sat for seven years.

Since, therefore, the see is one and the same, and three bishops now preside over it by divine authority, whatever good I hear about you I attribute to myself. If you believe anything good about me, attribute it to your merits, because we are one in him who said: “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, so that they too may be one in us” (John 17:21).

As I fulfill the duty of a greeting, I declare that I rejoice with great joy because I have learned that you labor continually against the barking of heretics. I beseech almighty God to assist your blessedness with his protection, so that through your tongue he may uproot from the bosom of the holy Church every root of bitterness, lest it sprout again, hinder many, and many be defiled through it.

For, having received the talent, you consider what was commanded: “Trade until I come” (Luke 19:13). I, therefore, although I am able to conduct no trade, nevertheless rejoice in the profits of your commerce, knowing this: although my activity does not make me a partner in it, charity makes me a partner in your labor. For, as I judge, the good of one’s neighbor becomes common even to the inactive person who knows how to rejoice jointly in another’s deeds.

Furthermore, I wished to send wood; but your blessedness did not indicate that it was necessary. We could send much larger pieces, but no ship of such a kind comes here that could carry them. I consider it embarrassing to send smaller ones. Nevertheless, let your blessedness inform me by letter what I ought to do.

I have also sent, as a small blessing from the Church of your beloved Saint Peter, six small Aquitanian cloaks and two *oraria*, because I love you greatly and therefore presume even upon small things. Love itself possesses its own authority, and it is entirely certain that whatever one presumes through love will not be an offense. [Note: The word *Aquitanica* may refer to *bigerrigae*, garments so called from the Bigerriones, peoples of Aquitaine. Yet those garments were extremely cheap, as is clear from Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* 2, *On the Virtues of Blessed Martin*, chapter 1, and were more suitable for the poor than for the patriarch of Alexandria. A cleric or archdeacon whom Martin had ordered to clothe a poor man seized from nearby shops a Bigerrian garment [lacuna], purchased for five silver pieces and angrily laid it at Martin’s feet. Perhaps, however, these cloaks sent to Eulogius were intended for clothing the poor. Vatican A reads *Equitanica*. Among the Aquitanians are also the Santones, among whom certain garments called *bardocuculli* were once very well known. Hence Martial, Book IV, Epigram 128:

“Gaul clothes you in a Santonian hooded cloak (*bardocucullus*).”]

I received the blessing of Saint Mark the Evangelist, inserted in your letters according to the brief. [Note: The printed editions read *juxta breve* (“according to the brief”), against the manuscripts. Our reading is supported by Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 9: “Then, as a kind of omen, he placed a brief written document upon the altar.” Below, he orders that brief to be received. Here *schedula*, a small written document, is meant.]

But because I do not willingly drink *colatum* and *viritheum*, I ask for *cognidium* instead, having presumed upon it because last year your holiness caused it to become known in this city after a long interval. [Note: Many copies read *collatum*, but *colatum* is better; this is interpreted as juice expressed through a strainer or colander, filtered and clarified, as physicians say. Concerning it, see Raderus on Martial. *Juritheum* may perhaps derive from *julus*, an Arabic word signifying syrup, or *Syrum opum*, that is, “Syrian juice,” with the Greek addition θεῖον (*theion*), meaning “divine”; or it may mean a small vessel of precious, divine juice. *Cognidium* may mean a spiced wine or aromatized wine. The learned Herbelot, highly skilled in the Oriental languages, conjectured that it was a peppered drink (*piperatum*), from *jacuth* and *lara*, in his *Onomasticon of Obscure Words*. I owe this interpretation to that most learned man. Whoever wants more should read the *Various Readings* of Hieronymus Mercurialis, Book VI, chapter 29, in the Venetian edition of 1644, where these three kinds of drink are treated fully, carefully, and expressly, taking the occasion from this letter of Saint Gregory. GUSSANV. That *viritheum* should be read is proved by three Vatican manuscripts, four Norman manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and three Colbertine manuscripts. In two Norman manuscripts, namely Audoenus and Lyranus, and also in the Royal manuscript, *juritheum* is read. In the oldest Colbertine manuscript, however, the reading is *viritheum* or *vitreum*. What we should understand by *colatum*, *collatum*, or *collactum*—for it is written variously—together with *viritheum* and *cognidium*, we cannot easily determine. Papias, cited by Du Cange, shows that it was a kind of refined beverage among the Egyptians or Alexandrians. Perhaps they were wines that received different names from the various places where they abounded, as among the Italians *Falernum*, *Calenum*, and so forth, celebrated by poets, and among us many others praised in the songs of our poets. In Epiphanius, Κόλλαθον (*Kollathon*) is a certain measure of liquids known among the Syrians.]

For here we buy from merchants the name of *cognidium*, not the substance itself. I ask, however, that your holiness’s prayer support me against all the bitterness I suffer in this life and defend me from it through your intercessions before almighty God.

## LETTER XLI. TO CYPRIANUS, THE RECTOR

He should arrange for a suitable bishop to be ordained for the Church of Locri.

Gregory to our rector Cyprianus in Sicily. [Note: Letter XLI [Al. 38].—In Vatican B: “to Cyriacus, our notary throughout Sicily.” In Rheims: “to Cyprianus.” In the Royal manuscript: “to the deacon governing throughout Sicily.”]

The inhabitants of the city of Locri brought to us a certain presbyter whom they wished to have ordained as their bishop. [Note: Locri, called Epizephyrian from the promontory of Zephyrion, was once a large episcopal city of Bruttium in Magna Graecia, on the Ionian Sea. Hieracium, an episcopal city of Further Calabria, commonly called Girace, in the Kingdom of Naples, grew from its ruins. GUSSANV. Vatican A, B, and D read “of the city of Lutrensis.”]

But since he was found altogether unworthy, so that they should not remain long without their own bishop, they promised in the office, at our admonition, to seek another diligently and, with God’s help, bring him to us for consecration. [Note: [Col. 0901D] Vatican A reads *in secreto*, “in private,” instead of *in scrinio*, “in the office.”] Therefore, when the bearer of these letters arrives, have Marcianus, a presbyter of the diocese of the Church of Tauriana, who now resides in the Church situated at Massalargia, in the diocese of the Church of Catania, summoned to you by every means. [Note: Vatican A and D read “in Massa Largia”; Vatican B reads “in Massalaria.”]

Let it be the task of your diligence to investigate with the utmost care whether he is free from the crimes that prevent someone from approaching the episcopate. If he answers that he is free from them, hasten to send him with the bearer of these letters, so that, after a decree has been made concerning him, he may come to us, with God’s protection, to be ordained. But if there is anything that could stand in his way, dismiss the man who has come to your Fraternity with every care and speed, so that, when he returns to his own region, another may be sought according to what has been set forth above. [Note: Thus read in Vatican, Tours, Saint Gatianus, and the old Colbertine manuscript.]

Given in the month of August, indiction 15.

## LETTER XLII. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP

Since the canons permit neither a fallen bishop to be restored to his place nor a church to remain vacant for more than three months, he should ordain a bishop for Cornelii.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

From a letter of your Fraternity we have learned that the sons of the Church of Cornelii are asking you, with continual supplication, to consecrate for them a priest in place of their former bishop who fell, and that you are uncertain what ought to be done in this matter and are awaiting an explicit command from us. [Note: Letter XLII [Al. 39].—Cornelii, or the Forum of Cornelius, commonly Imola, was a city of Italy, formerly belonging to the Senones in Aemilia, now called Romagna, on the river Vatrenus, commonly Santerno, between Bologna and Ravenna. It is subject to the dominion of the supreme pontiff and remains an episcopal city under the archbishop of Ravenna. GUSSANV.]

Since no principle permits someone who has withdrawn criminally to be restored to the place from which he fell (Gratian, distinction 50, chapter 11), and since the statutes of the sacred canons do not permit a church to remain without a bishop for more than three months, lest, when the shepherd has fallen, the ancient enemy should—God forbid—tear apart the Lord’s flock by lying in wait, your Fraternity ought to consent to their petition and ordain a bishop in place of the fallen one. For although, when they were not asking, you ought previously to have admonished them toward this through your exhortations, now that they are asking you should not delay through any excuse, because the Church of God ought not to remain long deprived of its own bishop. [Note: Concerning the fallen, see above, Book IV, Letter 26; Book V, Letters 3 and 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Letter XLIII [Al. 40].]

## LETTER XLIII. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP

On removing clerical domination from monasteries.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Some time ago it had reached us through the report of many that the monasteries situated in the region of Ravenna were being excessively burdened by the domination of your clerics, so that, under the pretext of administration, they possessed them, which is grievous to say, as though they were their own property. We felt no little sorrow for them and sent letters to your predecessor, instructing him to correct this in every respect. But since he was quickly overtaken by the end of his life, so that this burden might not remain upon the monasteries, we recall that we wrote these same things to your Fraternity. And because, as we have learned, correction in this matter has until now been neglected, we have now decided to send these written instructions to you again.

We therefore exhort you, after removing every delay and every excuse, to strive so to free those monasteries from such a burden that henceforth no cleric, or anyone constituted in a sacred order, may have permission to enter them for any other reason than prayer alone, or, if they should happen to be invited to perform the sacred mysteries of the Mass.

But lest the monasteries perhaps sustain some burden through the promotion of any monk or abbot, you must take care that if any abbot or monk from any monastery should enter the office of the clergy or sacred order, he may no longer have any authority there, as we have said, lest the monasteries be compelled to bear, under the cover of this occasion, the burdens we prohibit.

Let your holiness, already admonished for the second time, not delay correcting all these matters with vigilant care, lest, if afterward we should find—which we do not believe—that you are negligent, we be compelled to provide for the peace of the monasteries in another way. For let it be known to you that we will no longer permit the congregation of God’s servants to remain subject to such a necessity.

But lest any excuse concerning the monks arise for you, let your Fraternity send here a person whom you have judged useful in the work, and we shall assign to him monks who may come with him to you. When you have examined them, you should appoint them in the monasteries, provided that the places are such that they can find there the means to subsist.

## LETTER XLIV. TO CYPRIANUS, THE DEACON

He should ensure that Theodorus the sorcerer, or any of the clerics of Messana, does not oppose Paula.

Gregory to Cyprianus, the deacon.

Paula, the bearer of these letters, has complained to us that a certain Theodorus, formerly a Jew, is exceedingly hostile to her without justification, to the point that—impious as it is to say—he is attempting to harm her through wicked magical practices, and that this same Theodorus is vigorously defended by men of the Church of Messana in connection with this crime. [Note: Letter XLIV [Al. 41].—The Beccensis Codex has *exjudaeum*, written as one word, instead of *ex Judaeo*; both describe him as formerly a Jew. Vatican B and the Norman manuscripts read *maleficorum* (“of evildoers” or “of sorcerers”), instead of *maleficiorum* (“of evil deeds” or “of magical practices”). The manuscripts and old editions read this way; recent editions have *fortius instigari* (“to be more strongly incited”).]

Therefore, let your Dilection take care that none of the ecclesiastics attempt to oppose the aforementioned woman in this matter. But be diligent yourself, insofar as you can, in investigating it. And if the aforementioned Theodorus proves to be guilty of such great wickedness, have him punished through those whose responsibility it is, with such strict retribution that God may be appeased and it may serve as an example of correction to others. [Note: [Col. 0903B; 0904B] Vatican D and the Norman manuscripts read *in hoc [lacuna] faciat vindicari*: “in this matter [lacuna] let [your Dilection] have punishment inflicted.”]

## LETTER XLV. TO CLAUDIUS, THE ABBOT

He should come to Rome as soon as possible.

Gregory to Claudius, the abbot.

When the most reverend bishop Severus arrived, I believed that your Dilection would also come at the same time to the threshold of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, because this had been reported to me, and I rejoiced greatly at the report. [Note: [Col. 0904B] Letter XLV [Al. 41, ind. 4].—Vatican A reads *viro clarissimo*, “a most illustrious man,” instead of *viro reverendissimo*, “a most reverend man.” This letter is absent from the other Vatican manuscripts, the Norman and English manuscripts, and most manuscripts.]

But I believe that you were hindered by the business of the monastery and therefore did not come to me. When I received the letters which your Dilection had sent earlier, I reread them privately, as you wished. But concerning the three persons about whom you had written, I saw nothing that seemed possible, especially concerning the person who had been here with me. I do not suspect that anything useful can be done with him, since he appeared to me to be sluggish either through the simplicity of his nature or through negligence. [Note: [Col. 0904B] The same Vatican codex reads *operationibus*, “activities,” instead of *occupationibus*, “occupations.”]

Therefore, if your Dilection can accomplish anything there, let it investigate and arrange matters carefully, and then come to me. But if you cannot come, you should at least come after some time, to stay with me for five or six months, if life permits, and then return to your own home. May the grace of almighty God guard you from every adversity.

# BOOK EIGHT

Indiction 1, in the month of September.

## LETTER I. TO PETER, BISHOP

He urges him to continue turning the inhabitants away from the worship of idols. He sends fifty solidi for clothing those who are to be baptized.

Gregory to Peter, bishop of Corsica. [Note: Book VIII; in other editions, Book VII. Indiction 1, Letter 1 [Al. 2].—In certain manuscripts and old editions the heading reads: “To Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto.” GUSSANV. This Peter was bishop of Aleria in Corsica, as appears from Letter 22 of Book VI, where the same Mount Negeugni is mentioned. Vatican F incorrectly addresses the letter to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch. From this point onward, Gregory’s letters have been collated with six Vatican manuscripts, A, B, C, D, E, and F.]

893 Having received the letters of your Fraternity, we returned great thanks to almighty God, because he has deigned to relieve us of the burden of so many souls gathered together. Therefore let your Fraternity diligently strive, with the Lord’s assistance, to bring the work you have begun to completion. Whether you hasten to bring back to the faith those who were once faithful but, through negligence or necessity, have returned to the worship of idols, after imposing a penance of several days [Note: Here Saint Gregory imposes penance for a number of days; Saint Leo, Letter 92, Response 19 to Rusticus of Narbonne, is somewhat stricter, imposing public penance. The Council of Orange II, canon 20, bars such persons from ecclesiastical assemblies. The Council of Rheims of 630, canon 14, decrees that those who associate with idolaters must perform an appropriate period of penance. If the ancient authorities are pleasing, read Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, throughout. Gussanville. What prevents us from saying that the penance imposed by Saint Gregory was public? This is what Gussanville rashly asserted when he said that the holy Doctor had departed from Saint Leo’s severity.]—so that they may repent of their guilt and hold all the more firmly to that to which, with God’s help, they return, the more perfectly they have lamented that from which they depart—or whether you hasten to gather to almighty God those who have not yet been baptized, by admonishing them, entreating them, terrifying them with the coming judgment, and also giving them a reason why they ought not to worship wood and stones—so that, when he comes and the dread day of judgment arrives, your holiness may be found among the number of the saints. For what more useful and sublime work will you undertake than to think about the bringing to life and gathering of souls, and to bring an immortal profit to your Lord, who has given you a place from which to preach?

We have also sent your Fraternity fifty solidi for purchasing clothing for those who are to be baptized [Note: It is more widely known than needs proof that in former times those being baptized were entirely stripped of their own clothing and, after emerging from the water and being anointed, were accustomed to be clothed in a white garment covering the whole body. Below, Letter 23, the most holy pontiff orders that this garment be purchased at the Church’s expense for poor candidates for baptism, while others bought it at their own expense. See Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 30, *On the Holy Lights*, and Ambrose, *On Those Initiated into the Mysteries*, book I, chapter 7. Consult also note 327 on the *Book of Sacraments*.]; and we have arranged that the estate your Fraternity requested, belonging to the Church situated on Mount Negeugnus, should also be given to the presbyter of that Church, so that, whatever it yields, he may receive that much less from the solidi which he had been accustomed to receive. [Col. 0904B]

Your Fraternity also requested that you should establish for yourself an episcopium [Col. 0905A] in the Church which is not far from that same mountain [Note: All the manuscripts that we have been able to consult read *episcopum*; nevertheless, I conjecture that *episcopium* should be read, and the context supports it. For Peter will be more useful in proportion as he is nearer in residence to those peoples. Observe that a bishop could scarcely have been permitted to change his lodging, leaving the episcopium that ordinarily belonged to the cathedral Church—the place which in modern usage bishops call the palace. On this change of residence, see Saint Gregory, book V, now book VI, Letter 23, to Anthemius; the Council of Carthage III, canon 5, “It has pleased us,” etc.; Carthage IV, chapter 14; and the Council of Meaux, chapters 25, 26, 28, and 36. Gussanville. His conjecture that *episcopium* should be read rather than *episcopum* is supported by most manuscripts, where *episcopum* is read; these letters can signify *episcopium* as well as *episcopum*.], which I accepted with complete willingness, because the nearer it is, the more abundantly he will be able to benefit the souls settled there.

As for the bearer of this letter, on account of your holiness’s intercession we have made him an acolyte [Gratian, Part I, Question 1, chapter 121]. We have sent him back to serve you, so that, if he serves more fully in winning souls, he may advance further. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, no. 49.)

### LETTER II. TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH. He strengthens him against the heresies. After praising the bond of mutual charity and recalling his friend’s gifts, he prays for his long life.

Gregory to Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch.

I received the letters of your most gracious Blessedness, [Col. 0905B] which poured forth tears instead of words [Note: LETTER II [Elsewhere 3].—The printed editions have *excusi*, “I poured out”; they had *pluebant*, “they were raining.”]. For in them I saw a cloud flying upward in its accustomed manner, but bearing with it a certain darkness of sadness. At the very beginning I could not easily discern whence or whither it was going, because, owing to the darkness I have mentioned, I did not fully understand the causes.

Yet it is fitting that your holiness should always bring to mind, as you do, what the Apostle to the Gentiles says: “In the last times perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, proud” (1 Timothy IV, 1), and the rest, which it is painful for me to say and unnecessary for you to hear. Behold, in your holy old age your Blessedness is troubled by many tribulations; but consider whose seat you occupy [Note: The editors disliked this reading and, against the manuscripts, preferred “may he hold the seat.” See note 1 on Book I of the *Moralia*, no. 23, from which you will learn that this manner of speaking was not unusual for Gregory and the other Fathers. Consult also Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4.]. Is it not the seat of the one to whom the Voice of Truth said: “When you have grown old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John XXI, 18)? Yet in saying this I recall that your holiness has labored under many adversities from your youth onward. Therefore, with the good king, let it say: “I will reflect upon all my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isaiah XXXVIII, 15).

There are many who, as you write, make their pleasure out of our wounds; but we know who said: “You will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful” (John XVI, 20). And immediately he added: “But your sorrow will be turned into joy.” Since we already endure the things foretold, it remains that we should also hope for the things promised. Those of whom you say that they add burdens who ought to have lifted them—I know that they are the ones who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew VII). Yet they must be endured all the more because they persecute us not only with an evil mind but also under a religious appearance.

As for the fact that they alone, above others, desire to possess what it was not right for them to have even together with their brothers, we are not at all disturbed, because we trust in almighty God that those who covet what belongs to others will quickly be deprived even of what belongs to them. For we know who said: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XIV, 11). And again it is written: “The heart is exalted before ruin” (Proverbs XVI, 18).

In these days, as I learn, new battles with heretics have arisen, about which I previously wrote to your Blessedness, as they strive to empty out the prophets, the Gospels, and all the sayings of the Fathers. But while your holiness remains alive, we hope in the grace of our protector that their mouths, which have opened themselves against the solidity of truth, will quickly fall silent; for however sharp the swords that are thrust forward, when they strike a rock they rebound shattered.

This too is a great grace of almighty God: that there is no unity among those who have separated themselves from the teaching of the holy Church [Note: Namely, one faith and one charity. Outside the Church there is neither true faith nor charity. Thus they easily proceed to further divisions. Gussanville.]. For “every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Luke XI). And the holy Church is always instructed more subtly in her own teaching when she is attacked by the questions of heretics, so that what was said by the Psalmist about God against heretics may plainly be fulfilled: “They were divided by the anger of his countenance, and his heart drew near” (Psalm LIV, 22). For while they are divided in their perverse error, God brings his heart near to us, because, instructed through adversity, we discover his meaning more subtly.

I refrain from recounting to your Blessedness what evils we suffer from the swords of barbarians and what from the perversity of judges, lest I increase the groaning of one whom I ought to lessen by consoling. But amid all these things I am comforted by the instructions of our Author, who says: “I have told you these things so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have tribulation” (John XVI, 33). For I consider to whom it was said: “This is your hour, and the power of darkness” (Luke XXII, 53).

If, then, the power of light will afterward exist, since it was said to the elect, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V, 14), and as it is written, “The righteous will obtain them in the morning” (Psalm XLVIII, 15), [Note: The Roman Psalter reads *obtinebunt*, “they will possess.” The Vulgate version reads: “And the righteous will rule over them in the morning.” The Old Psalter has: “And the upright will rule over them in the morning.” So too do the Greek, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic versions. The Hebrew reads: “And the righteous will subject them in the morning.” Jerome has “upright” instead of “righteous.” Estius interprets the passage as follows: “They will rule,” that is, it will happen early and soon that the righteous will rule them. For the Hebrew phrase “in the morning” means “early” or “quickly.” Gussanville. The learned editor notes this in order to correct the earlier reading *obtinebant*, “they were obtaining”; nearly all the manuscripts contradict it.] then everything that we suffer in the hour and under the power of darkness is not to be mourned.

896 Your most gracious holiness indicates to me that, if it could have been done, you would have wished to speak with me without paper and pen, and that you grieve that almost the whole breadth of East and West lies between us. But I speak the truth about what I feel: your mind speaks to me on paper without paper, because in the words of your holiness only charity sounds; and although we are separated by place, we are not divided, since we are joined by the bond of love bestowed by almighty God.
