Why, then, do you seek to receive the wings of the silvered dove (Psalm LXVII, 14), when you already possess them? Its wings are the love of God and of neighbor. Through them the holy Church takes flight; through them she rises above all earthly things. If your holiness did not possess them, you would not have come to me through your letters with such great charity.

I ask you to pray more earnestly for the weakness of my heart, so that almighty God, through your intercession, may protect my mind from every evil, rescue me more quickly from so many storms of this tempest, and lead me to the shores of eternal rest.

I have received all the exceedingly rich blessings that you sent—the blessings that you, a man of God poor in spirit, transmitted to me, concerning which you say: “For what should a poor man give except poor things?” [Note: Thus read five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, the Colbert manuscript, and others; they are supported by the old edition. The more recent editions have: “For what indeed should he give?”] But unless you were poor through the spirit of humility, your blessings would not have been rich.

May almighty God protect you from every evil by his own protection; and since your life is exceedingly necessary for every good, may he lead you, after many more years, to the joys of the heavenly homeland. [Note: Two Teller manuscripts add: “In the month of November, indiction I.”] (Compare John the Deacon, book III, no. 49; book IV, no. 67.)

### LETTER III. TO DONUS, BISHOP OF MESSANA. The place for burying a body must never be sold. Certain slaves are to be restored.

[Col. 0907C]

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messana.

Our son Faustinus, a most eloquent man, came to us and complained that his father, the late Peltrasius, had left certain property belonging to another under the jurisdiction of your Church for the sake of his burial. He himself knows what the laws of the world provide in this matter, and we have heard it as well: an heir is compelled to make restitution if his predecessor has bequeathed what belongs to another (see the law *Cum Alienam*, *On Legacies*). But because we know that your Fraternity lives according to the law of God, not according to the law of the world, it seems to me exceedingly unjust that an electrum cup and a boy who is said to belong to the Church of Consentina, in whose diocese the property of a certain Church is situated, should be held by your Fraternity. Since the most reverend man Palumbus, now bishop but then archdeacon, testified that this was so, you ought entirely to have trusted his testimony and restored what belonged to another.

As for the golden brooch that the aforesaid man also left at his death [Note: Many printed editions incorrectly have “a tablet.” It was a valuable golden brooch, a gift that emperors used to bestow, as Gussanville observes.], you ought, in my opinion, to have considered how large his estate was, if there was anything from which those whom he had left behind could be supported, and then to have accepted it in payment for his burial. [Col. 0908A]

Although you know that our institution has entirely forbidden our ancient custom in our Church, and that we do not consent to anyone’s obtaining places for burying the body at a price [Note: The same practice is prohibited below in Letter 56, now Letter 3, indiction II, to Januarius of Cagliari; it is cited in Cause 13, canon 12, where see the three following canons, and in *On Burials*, chapter “Abolendae,” from Innocent III, *On Simony*, chapter 2. See also Thomas of Thomassin, part III, book I, chapters 65–68.], if the gentile men of Shechem, as we believe, freely offered Abraham a burial place for his deceased wife Sarah, to be buried in a place of his own, and were scarcely compelled by his great insistence to accept a price for the burial place (Genesis XXIII, 6), what ought we, who are called bishops, to consider when burying the bodies of the faithful? We therefore entrust this matter to your Fraternity’s judgment.

The aforementioned most eloquent man also complained to us that Sisinnius, the defender of your Church, is irrationally retaining slaves belonging by right to him. He asserts that it was also determined by the judgment of Maximianus, bishop of holy memory, that the detainer should return them [Note: The printed editions, together with the old Colbert and Regius manuscripts, read “the detaining party.” Our reading occurs in all the other manuscripts.], but that he has voluntarily delayed restoring them until now.

We therefore exhort your Fraternity, if the case has already plainly been judged, to ensure that what was established is carried out. Otherwise, appointing an executor [Note: The editors, rejecting “executor,” preferred “defender.” Gussanville nevertheless admits that “executor” is read in nearly all the manuscript codices. On this word see Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4, and Letter 57 of Book V.] let the case be brought before our brother and fellow bishop Secundinus, so that, when it has been declared whose jurisdiction the slaves in question belong to, the one may not seem to suffer prejudice here, nor the other hostility. [Note: We restore *invidiam*, “hostility,” supported by all the manuscripts; without consulting them, the editors preferred *injuriam*, “injury.”]

### LETTER IV. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP. He grants permission to consecrate a monastery.

[Note: LETTER IV [Elsewhere 6].—This letter is missing from the English, Norman, Corbie, and several other manuscripts. It is found in the Rheims, Regius, old Colbert, and five Vatican manuscripts.]

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

We have learned from your Fraternity’s report that, as stated below, you have founded within the city of Luna, out of your devotion, a monastery of maidservants of God in your own house, which you desire to be consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs John and Paul, as well as Hermes and Sebastian.

Therefore, dearest brother, if it is established that no body has been buried there, after your Fraternity has first made a lawful donation—namely, one silver chalice weighing six ounces [Note: See what the proportion of the chalice to the paten was. They cite a passage from Columella, Book XII, chapter 43, where by *patenae* he understands broad vessels with large rims. Certainly, in the early centuries the paten had to be large enough to contain several circles of offerings, not as thin as those used now, but much thicker and more nearly approaching the form of ordinary bread. Gussanville. The breaking of the offerings also took place upon those patens. See Mabillon, commentary on the *Roman Order*, p. 55.], one silver paten weighing two pounds, two linen cloths, one covering for the altar, ten made-up beds, twenty heads of bronze vessels [Note: The Tours manuscript has “twenty capitals”; another reading has “thirty capitals.”], thirty heads of iron tools, the Faborian estate and Lumbricata in their entirety, situated in the territory of Luna approximately two miles from that city, beside the river Macra [Note: In Vatican manuscript F this river is called the Macha; in three other manuscripts, the Marra.], together with two slaves, namely Maurus and John, and only two pairs of oxen [Note: The printed editions have only eleven pairs of oxen. Perhaps the numeral II was mistaken for XI, although it signified only two. The editors adopted “eleven.” We follow the Vatican, Colbert, and Rheims manuscripts.]—and after these gifts have been recorded in the municipal registers, you shall solemnly consecrate the oratory of the aforesaid monastery without public Masses, and do the rest according to custom. In the month of November, indiction I.

### LETTER V. TO SEVERAL METROPOLITANS AND BISHOPS. Those bound by public accounts are not to be received either into the clergy or into a monastery; soldiers are first to be tested for three years before assuming the monastic habit.

[Col. 0909B]

Gregory to Eusebius of Thessalonica [Note: LETTER V [Elsewhere 11].—Thessalonica, commonly Salonica, is still a very famous city on the Thermaic Gulf of the Aegean Sea, called by the Italians the Gulf of Salonica. It was formerly the metropolis of Macedonia, not only civil but ecclesiastical, and the seat of the apostolic vicariate for Eastern Illyricum from the time of Damasus until the time of Vigilius, who partially granted this privilege to the bishop of Justiniana Prima at the request of the emperor Justinian. Gussanville.], Urbitio of Dyrrachium [Note: Dyrrachium and Epidamnus, commonly Durazzo and in French Duras, were a very famous maritime city of Macedonia in the province of Albania, at the mouth of the river Argentaro, which flows into the Adriatic Sea. It was formerly the metropolis of Epirus Nova and is now subject to Turkish rule. From Dyrrachium come *Dyrrachinus* and *Dyrrachitanus*, not *Dyrracitanus*.], Constantius of Milan, Andrew of Nicopolis, John of Corinth, John of Justiniana Prima, John of Crete, John of Scorita [Note: Might it rather be written “of Scodra,” from the city of Scodra, formerly an episcopal city of Dalmatia and now the capital of Albania, commonly Scutari? But no manuscripts support this.], John of Larissa, Mariniani of Ravenna, Januarius of Cagliari in Sardinia, [Note: If the bishops of Sicily had had a metropolitan, Gregory would have addressed this letter to him individually, as he did to the other metropolitans mentioned above, rather than to all the bishops. Hence it is inferred—and this is proved by many other arguments—that Sicily then lacked a metropolitan.] and to all the bishops of Sicily.

I have taken care to send your Fraternity the law given by the most devout emperor (Gratian, Distinction 52, chapter 1), lest those who are bound either to military service or to public accounts should come to the ecclesiastical habit or enter monasteries while fleeing the danger arising from their affairs [Col. 0909C]. I especially exhort you on this point: those who are entangled in the activities of the world are not to be hastily received into the clergy of the Church, because, when they live in the ecclesiastical habit no differently than they had lived before, they do not strive to flee the world but merely to change it.

If such people also seek a monastery, they must in no way be received unless they have first been released from their public obligations. If anyone from the military ranks [Note: The military units are cohorts, squadrons, and troops of soldiers. See *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 35, note a.] hastens to enter a monastery, he is not to be received rashly unless his life has been carefully investigated. According to the regular norm, they must be tested in their own habit for three years, and then, with God’s approval, receive the monastic habit.

If, after being tested and received in this way, they strive to do penance for their sins for the sake of their souls, then, for the sake of their life and heavenly gain, their conversion is not to be rejected. On this matter also, believe me, the most serene and Christian emperor is entirely pleased, and he willingly accepts the conversion of those whom he knows are not entangled in public accounts. [Note: This sentence is found in the Vatican, old Colbert, and Corbie manuscripts, but not in the others.] In the month of December, indiction I.

### LETTER VI. TO AMOS, PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM. He orders that Peter, a fugitive acolyte of the Roman Church, be apprehended and sent to Rome deprived of communion.

[Col. 0910C]

Gregory to Amos, bishop of Jerusalem.

Since we trust that your Fraternity loves the statutes of the canons and the force of discipline, we have thought it appropriate to disclose to your holiness the fault of one of our clerics, lest deceit enable him to steal away from you in order to evade the strictness of the ecclesiastical order. Thus, through your vigilance, he may be subjected to the discipline from which he has fled.

We have learned that Peter the acolyte, whom we had arranged to serve in the royal city under our beloved son Sabinianus the deacon, who was carrying out ecclesiastical responses [Note: Among ecclesiastical authors around the time of Saint Gregory, *observare* means to perform one’s duty, exercise one’s office, or carry out one’s ministry. Thus the Council of Angers of 453, canon 8: “Concerning monks who abandon the path of observance they had begun”; canon 10: “Concerning laymen or clerics who refuse to observe the service to which they have been ordained.” The Council of Epaon, canon 5: “Let no presbyter presume to observe … unless,” etc. The Council of Orléans III of 538, chapter 5: “Let it be assigned for the restoration of the basilica or for the substance of those observing there.” Orléans IV, canon 4: “Concerning foreign clerics, who are forbidden to minister unless the strictness of the pontiff has ordered them to observe [or remain under supervision] after they have been tested.” Canon 26 of the same council: “Concerning clerics who, while observing in the houses of powerful men, neglect to fulfill what they owe the Church.” Gussanville. Here *observare* means to remain continually with someone for the sake of office and honor, and to serve him. *Acolyte* has the same meaning as attendant or officer. Nevertheless, it is clear from Letter I of this book that acolytes sometimes performed more spiritual duties: “We have sent him back to serve you, so that, if he serves more fully in winning souls …”], has fled and come to your Church.

If this is true, your Fraternity should take care to keep him safe and, when an opportunity is found, send him back here. Or, if he has perhaps left your Church out of fear of this and is hiding in various places so that he cannot be apprehended, order that he be diligently sought throughout all your parishes, and, once found, send him to us as we have said. We also wish you to recognize that he is to be deprived of communion through your action: he must not dare to receive the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood until he returns to us, unless he is perhaps confronted by imminent danger of death.

### LETTER VII. TO LEO, BISHOP. He is to distribute among the clergy, according to the merit of their labor, the quarter portion set aside from his church’s revenues.

[Col. 0911B]

Gregory to Leo, bishop of the people of Catania.

The order of reason has distinguished ranks of authority and established judgments for this purpose (Gratian, Part II, Question 1, chapter 63): so that superiors may not be able to occupy themselves uselessly in oppressing their subjects, nor subjects in turn have unrestrained license to rebel against their superiors.

Therefore, because during the fifteenth indiction recently elapsed certain acolytes of your Church brought complaints against you under a formal charge [Col. 0911A], and because we did not want either those complaints to remain to the discredit of your Fraternity or ourselves to appear not to hear their petitions, we entrusted their careful investigation to our beloved son Cyprian the deacon. After examining what had been referred to him, he disclosed more precisely to our inquiry what he had decided concerning each charge.

Among other matters, the clergy established that, regarding the quarter portion [Note: LETTER VII [Elsewhere 8].—In Vatican manuscript B: “This is to be observed by the clergy.” On the partition and division of the Church’s goods, see Book V, Letter 44.], one portion should go to those assigned to the sacred place and the other two portions to the clergy. The bearers of this letter, the presbyter Donatus and the deacons Theodosianus and Viator, together with a report from others who hold sacred orders, complained to us that this had been prejudicially established to their disadvantage, contrary to ancient custom. For they asserted that from this same quarter portion they had always received two parts, while the clergy received the third, and they asked that this decision not remain to their prejudice. We judged that this matter ought to be entrusted to your Fraternity’s arrangement.

We therefore wish that whatever may come to your Church from revenue or under any other title, you should set aside from it a quarter portion without any diminution, and distribute it discreetly, according to the fear of God, among the presbyters, deacons, and clergy, as seems best to you. Let your freedom to give be such that each receives according as the merit of his labor requires, so that those who deserve it may feel themselves comforted by this temporal benefit, while the others, with the Lord’s help, strive to improve by imitating them.

### LETTER VIII. TO VITALIANUS, BISHOP. He is to bring back the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, to the religious habit; confine her in a monastery; and suspend from holy communion those who resist.

[Col. 0912B]

Gregory to Vitalianus, bishop of Sipontum.

If you had known how to be a guardian of the religious habit, or if you had been a bishop [Gratian, Part II, Question 1, chapter 18], you would not have allowed the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers and of glorious memory, while you were stationed there, either to return to secular clothing after discarding her religious garments or to send us her perverse letter.

But because you are oppressed by excessive indolence and sluggishness, an unlawful matter has at present been committed there with impunity, to your disgrace. For, as we have said, if you had been vigilant, the punishment of the most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her fault did [Note: This seems to be taken from Law 3, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Praetorian Guard of the East and Illyricum*, where the emperors speak of useless judges who should be removed from administration and others substituted in their place: “To the judgment of our clemency,” they say, “let not crimes but punishment be reported.”].

Since, then, you are so dull and so negligent that, unless you have experienced canonical correction in your own case, you do not know how to preserve strictness and discipline in others, we shall show you, at an appropriate time, if it pleases the Lord, how vigilant you ought to be.

Therefore, receiving this present letter, awake, and, at last aroused, carry out what your indolence has delayed until now. Let it be your task, together with our defender Sergius, to apprehend the woman mentioned above and immediately not only to restore her, without any excuse, to the religious habit she has wickedly despised, but also to confine her in a monastery where she can be kept under strict custody. Show such vigilance concerning her that, through your strictness, she may recognize how wicked was the act she committed.

If in this matter any layman should attempt to resist you by any means—which we do not believe—suspend him from participation in the most sacred communion [Note: The more recent edition adds “of clerics or laymen.”] and hasten to report to us, so that, since he did not perceive by his own judgment how detestable was the presumption he made, he may learn it from the quality of the correction.

In all these matters, strive to show yourself so cautious and vigilant that neglect does not multiply your fault, but that diligence may at least lessen it somewhat. [Note: Two Teller manuscripts add at the end of the letter: “In the month of February, indiction I,” a reading not found in any other manuscript known to us.] (Compare John the Deacon, book III, no. 39.)

### LETTER IX. TO SERGIUS, DEFENDER. Concerning compelling the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, to resume the religious habit.

[Col. 0913A]

Gregory to Sergius, defender.

If you were a man [Gratian, Part II, Question 1, chapter 19], or if you possessed any strictness [Note: The printed editions have “or discretion,” against all the Vatican, Norman, Tours, Corbie, and other manuscripts], you ought to have been such a guardian of regular discipline that unlawful acts committed there would have been corrected by punishment before a report of them reached us.

But because excessive stupidity makes you negligent, we are offended not only by those matters but are also provoked to punish your sluggishness. Therefore, setting aside every delay and every excuse, hasten, together with our brother and fellow bishop Vitalianus, to apprehend the daughter of Tullianus, of glorious memory, master of the soldiers [Note: Vatican manuscript B has “master of the soldiers”], who, after casting off the religious garments she had voluntarily assumed, has disfigured herself with secular clothing. Bring her back again to the religious habit and send her to a monastery where she can be kept under the strictest custody.

Do not permit her custody to be relaxed in any way until you receive our further letter. For if you are negligent or slow in this matter in any way, know that you will be punished with such utmost strictness that, through the penalty’s cutting correction, you may learn what you do not know of yourself [Note: Another reading is “while revealing it.” Our reading is found in five Vatican manuscripts and most of the Norman manuscripts]. For, as we said, if you possessed human understanding, we ought to have learned from you, even through punishment, that the orders you are now commanded to carry out had already been carried out. (Compare John the Deacon, book III, no. 40.)

### LETTER X. TO SABINIANUS, BISHOP OF JADERA. He was as offended by his communion with Maximus as he was later appeased by his penance. He commends his case in the royal city to his representative. He urges him to pastoral care. He commissions him to investigate the case of Bishop Florentius.

[Col. 0913C]

Gregory to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera.

Just as punishment is rightly owed to persistent guilt, so pardon must be granted to those who repent. For just as that matter rightly arouses anger against itself, so this one customarily promotes concord wholly in its love.

Therefore, because, after neglect had first driven your Fraternity away from the association and communion of Maximus [Note: LETTER X [Elsewhere 12].—The same matter is treated in Letter 17 of Book VII and Letter 28 at the end, as well as in Book VI, Letter 27, where the bishop’s name is suppressed. Gussanville.], the seriousness of the priesthood later recalled you to your senses so fully that you were not at all content merely to be separated from him, but, receiving yourself within the monastery’s enclosure, mourned the fault committed some time ago, do not doubt that you have been restored to our favor and communion [Note: The more recent edition reads: “having been received into our favor for communion.”]. For as much as your fault had previously offended our charity, so much has your penance appeased us.

We therefore exhort you, dearest brother, to devote yourself earnestly to pastoral care of the Lord’s flock and to watch diligently that you may gain profit from the sheep entrusted to you. Thus the reward of abundant recompense may overflow for you in proportion to the many fruits of labor you have offered at the coming of the eternal Judge.

Strive, therefore, to rescue those who have fallen into sin; strive to show the erring the way to return; strive to recall those deprived of communion to the healing grace of communion. Let your return be for others an act of charitable rescue and an example of salvation, so that, while your vigilant care directs the wandering steps of the sheep toward the fold of the supreme Shepherd, they may not be left exposed to the teeth of wolves, and a worthy recompense—which above all must be sought—may welcome you into eternal life.

As for the case about which you wrote to us, asking that we should be concerned lest some action be secretly taken against you in the royal city, do not let this matter trouble your minds. We have instructed our representative with complete diligence that he must show himself vigilant and cautious. And we trust in the power of our God that matters will be so conducted that no adversity will be able, contrary to reason, either to disturb or in any way oppress you.

Moreover, the inhabitants of the city of Epidaurus [Note: [Col. 0914D] On Florentius’s case, see Letters 8 and 9 of book III, indiction 11.] most earnestly requested that Florentius, whom they call their bishop, be restored to them by us, asserting that he had been unjustly driven into exile merely to satisfy the will of Bishop Natalis. Therefore, if your Fraternity has learned anything concerning his case, let it inform us carefully by letter. But if you have not yet learned of it, make inquiry and report to us, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may be able to deliberate with certainty whatever ought to be [Col. 0914C] decided concerning him. [Note: [Col. 0914D] Thus we read in Vatican manuscripts A, B, and C, and in the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of February, in the first indiction. (Cf. John the Deacon, book IV, no. 11.)

## LETTER XI. TO CANDIDUS, ABBOT OF SAINT ANDREW’S

He confirms the agreement and settlement between the monastery of Saint Andrew and Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

Gregory to Candidus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri.

[Note: [Col. 0914D] LETTER XI [formerly 13].—This is the monastery which Saint Gregory had built in the city from his own house, and in which he was first a monk and then abbot. John the Deacon, in his Life of Gregory, book I, chapter 6. GUSSANV.]

Just as consideration for our position reminds us to take care that the affairs of monasteries be brought to a salutary conclusion through an intention of peace, so again reason constrains us to strengthen, by the authority of our consent, those matters that have been usefully settled. Otherwise, perhaps, if some excuse is brought forward—a course very contrary to religious purpose and equity—renewed contention may throw something into doubt and produce litigation out of peace. Therefore, since a suitable and carefully considered settlement has been made, with our consent, between you, Candidus, abbot of the monastery of the apostle Saint Andrew, situated in this Roman city on the Clivus Scauri, [903] who administer the interests of that monastery, and Maurentius the glorious master of the soldiers, [Note: [Col. 0915D] Vatican manuscript B: “master of the soldiers.”] concerning the succession and inheritance of John, the kinsman of the aforesaid man, who entered the said monastery and died there; [Note: [Col. 0915D] Here we have deleted *quia*, following nearly all the manuscripts and restoring the sense. For what meaning was contained in this sequence of words: “Finally, because with the faith …”? We have followed the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.] and finally, since the sincerity of the aforesaid most glorious master of the soldiers has long been known and thoroughly established by us, so that it ought altogether to suffice for satisfaction—even if he were to confirm by a bodily oath that he had engaged in no fraud or concealed anything, but had disclosed everything completely—we therefore, by the tenor of this decree and command of ours, approve and fully confirm the settlement and decision made between you and the aforesaid glorious Maurentius. We decree that it may not be overturned in whole or in part by any means, but that it shall possess perpetual validity.

If anyone—which we do not believe—should in any way attempt to bring forward an intention contrary to this, let him know that he is guilty before God, since he strives to rescind what has been usefully settled; for he should recognize that nothing is thereby derogated from that decision and settlement. Therefore, so that the security of the oft-mentioned glorious Maurentius might remain unimpaired, and so that you might be unable to doubt anything that has been settled, we have granted him a similar command for the protection of both parties.

## LETTER XII. TO ADEODATUS AND MAURENTIUS, BISHOPS

He praises their care for ecclesiastical order and uprightness and urges them to persevere. He commends Bishop Paul.

[Col. 0915C]

Gregory to Adeodatus and Maurentius, bishops of Africa, his peers.

[Note: [Col. 0915D] LETTER XII [formerly 14].—In Vatican manuscript D and several other manuscripts: “dearest brothers . . . with which you are endowed.”]

I rejoice greatly, dearest brother, in the good of your sincerity, because the testimony of Paul, our brother and fellow bishop, who has brought this letter, has confirmed the gravity with which I had previously heard that you were endowed. He indicated how much greater your concern for ecclesiastical order and your care for uprightness are, insofar as he both observed this personally and learned more fully of it in his own defense. Since, as you know, it is a great thing before our God for anyone to persevere continually in good works, let the concern of your Fraternity appropriately sharpen itself in fostering the cause of justice, [Col. 0915D] and, insofar as possible, let it permit nothing to be done contrary to the safeguards of ecclesiastical vigor. [Note: [Col. 0916D] The printed editions read: “so far as it may be possible for the support of your provision to be made,” and so forth.]

Let no matter divert you from such an intention. But if there are things that offend the sincerity of your affection and exceed the rules of canonical discernment, [904] strive to apply vigilant care; and correct them by exhorting, persuading, and warning, [Col. 0916A] while preserving the unity of charity. [Note: [Col. 0916D] Thus in the old manuscripts. The printed editions, although the more recent manuscripts read otherwise, have: “to preserve the unity of charity.”] To the extent that your strength permits, strive with God’s help; restrain the author of the excesses with the priestly bridle of correction, and lead him back from the pathless road by word and deed. [Note: [Col. 0916D] In the same recent manuscripts, although they are contradicted by the manuscripts: “lead him by the tongue and bring him back by action.”] Thus display your effectiveness in everything, so that almighty God, who is the author of good will and the examiner of intention, may both assist your willingness here and reward it in the life to come.

We commend to your Fraternity the aforementioned Paul, our brother and fellow bishop, and urge you to let him experience appropriately the charity that you proclaim.

## LETTER XIII. TO COLUMBUS

He commends Bishop Paul.

[Col. 0916B]

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

We infer how confidently we ought to rely upon the charity of your Fraternity from the quality of the disposition that we hold toward you. Nor do we suppose that you love the Apostolic See otherwise than it loves you. Therefore, since we know that those whom we recognize as appropriately devoted in the Church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, are especially dear to you, whose life and conduct are adorned by priestly dignity, we commend them particularly to you. Of his sincerity, indeed, we already possess firm evidence from the past.

Our brother and fellow bishop Paul, the bearer of this letter, reminds your Holiness that you are not unaware of the great storms and adversities by which he is shaken there. Since he asserts that the complaints which, as you have indicated, reached you concerning him are not true, but have been stirred up against him by the instigation of his adversaries, and since he trusts that, with truth as his patron and with you aware of the facts, he can overcome everything with the Lord’s help, we urge you, dearest brother, to extend to him fitting assistance wherever the justice of his case is clear, and to help him with priestly compassion.

Therefore let no matter, and let no power of persons, hold you back from the pursuit of equity. Relying instead upon the Lord’s commands, despise everything contrary to uprightness. Stand steadfastly in defense of the cause of justice. Do not refuse to endure hatred, if any arises, for the sake of truth, so that you may find a greater reward when our Redeemer comes, insofar as, not neglecting his commands, you have devoted yourself to the favor and defense of justice.

[Note: [Col. 0916D] LETTER XIII [formerly 16].—In Vatican manuscripts A, B, D, and F, and in the old Colbert manuscript, it is read thus.]

In the month of March, in the first indiction. (See above, book VI, letter 61; book VII, letter 2; and letter 12 of this book.)

## LETTER XIV. TO BONIFACE, FIRST DEFENDER

He decrees that seven defenders are to be honored with the rank of regional officials.

[Col. 0917A]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0917C] LETTER XIV [formerly 17].—This title varies both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions. Some read: “To Boniface, concerning the privileges of the defenders.” Others: “To Boniface the defender, concerning the privileges of the first defender.” In others it appears as: “To Boniface, first defender, concerning the privilege of the first defender.” On the regional defenders, see above, at letter 26 of book I. GUSSANV. Anyone who reads the old codices cannot doubt what is said here about the disagreement among the manuscripts concerning the heading of this letter. Nevertheless, all the Norman manuscripts, as well as the English and Corbie manuscripts, agree on the title that we have placed before the others for that reason. The various readings cited by Gussanville are found in the Vatican and Colbert manuscripts.]

To Boniface, concerning the privileges of the defenders.

Those who faithfully labor for ecclesiastical interests ought to be favored with the benefit of an appropriate reward, so that we may appear properly to have answered their services, and so that they may become more useful through the grace of the consolation granted to them. Since, therefore, the office of the defenders is known to labor in the causes of the Church and in the service of bishops, we have seen fit to grant them the following prerogative of recompense: we establish that, just as regional officials have long been constituted in the corps of notaries and subdeacons through the generosity granted by earlier pontiffs, [Col. 0917B] so also seven defenders who have pleased by the demonstrated usefulness of their experience shall be honored with regional rank.

We decree that, during the absence of the bishop, each of them may sit in the assembly of the clergy and retain in every respect the privileges of his rank. Moreover, if someone who had previously held the first place comes to another province and perhaps resides there for his own advantage, it is necessary to preserve the first place in every respect for the man who can be first among all the defenders—namely, the one who, even before attaining the first place, did not cease to remain continually present in ecclesiastical interests and in the service of the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0917C] This means a college, order, or body. We have already noted that there were eleven principal schools of imperial officials or servants, besides ten others, and so forth. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, book X, chapter 25, concerning the bishop who dismissed the entire school of his predecessor. GUSSANV.]

Accordingly, we establish that these decrees of our constitution, which have been arranged for the privileges and ordering of the defenders, are to be observed with perpetual stability and without any opposition—whether what we have decreed in writing or what appears to have been arranged in their presence before us—and we decree that they may not be overturned or altered, in whole or in part, by any bishop for any reason. For it is exceedingly harsh, and especially contrary to the good character of priests, for anyone to strive, under any excuse whatsoever, to rescind what has been properly ordered and, by his example, teach others at some later time to dissolve what he himself has established.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] These words are found in three Vatican manuscripts and in the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of April, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XV. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He grants many privileges to the monastery of Saints John and Stephen.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

[Note: [Col. 0917D] LETTER XV [formerly 18].—This privilege, which Saint Gregory had drawn up for the monastery at Classis, he later extended to all monasteries at the council held at Rome at the Lateran, in the fourth indiction. That decree is found in the volumes of the councils after the letters of Saint Gregory. GUSSANV. In two Teller manuscripts it begins: “How valuable and how necessary it is …”]

Your previous office, which you exercised in the administration of a monastery, informs you how necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to arrange for their perpetual security. Therefore, since we have learned that the monastery of the blessed John and Stephen, which is situated in the city of Classis, [Note: [Col. 0917D] Classis was a town, or new harbor, commonly called Classe, three miles from the city of Ravenna toward Ariminum. [Col. 0918C] Augustus Caesar built this new harbor to station a fleet there, from which it received its name. Others maintain that it was built by Pompey. It is discussed by Procopius, Agathias, Evagrius, Paul the Deacon, and others. GUSSANV.] and over which our common son Claudius is known to preside as abbot, [Col. 0918B] has suffered many prejudicial acts and burdens from your predecessors, [Note: [Col. 0918C] This was the distinguished man who presided over the monastery of Saints John and Stephen in the city of Classis and was greatly loved by Saint Gregory. He remained in Rome with him for a long time, because the holy pontiff was especially refreshed by his consolation in the word of God, as he himself testifies in the following letter. He died in the year 602. GUSSANV. See the preface to the commentaries on the Books of Kings and the Song of Songs, which we owe especially to this Claudius.] it is fitting that the provision of your Fraternity should arrange their future peace by a salutary ordinance, so that those who live there in the service of God may persevere with a free mind, with his grace also supporting them.

But lest, on the basis of that custom which more urgently needs correction, anyone at any time presume to inflict any trouble upon them there, it is necessary that the matters which we have taken care to enumerate below be guarded by the diligence of your Fraternity in such a way that no further opportunity for causing disturbance may arise from them.

[Note: [Col. 0918C] Here we reject the reading of the more recent editions, which, against the unanimous testimony of the sincere manuscripts—the Norman, both Vatican, both Rheims, Corbie, English, and others—read: “Therefore we forbid that any bishop or layman should further dare …” Below, they have *occasionem minuere* (“to diminish on the occasion”) instead of *exquisitione minuere* (“to diminish by an exaction”).]

Therefore, let no one further dare to diminish, by any kind of exaction, [Col. 0918C] anything from the revenues or charters of the aforesaid monastery, or from any place belonging to it in any manner whatsoever, [Note: [Col. 0918D] A legal term that I would here express by “an encroachment upon another’s property.” French: *une entreprise sur les biens d’autrui*. GUSSANV.] nor commit any acts of intrusion or fraud.

But if some dispute should arise between the Church of Ravenna and the aforesaid monastery, and it cannot be settled peacefully, let it be concluded before chosen men from both parties who fear God, without deliberate delay, [Note: [Col. 0918D] He gives the same command in book IX, letter 47. See in the *Code*, title “On judgments,” law 14: this is not a new practice. In the Decretals, Cause 3, question 9, chapter “We exhort”; in the title “On canonical purgation,” chapter 5; and in Clement 1, “On heretics,” section “Moreover.” The author of the *Imperfect Work on Matthew*, homilies 12 and 44, and Saint Chrysostom, homily 9 on the Acts, mention this practice; from this it is concluded that the two did not live in the same century. AUGET.] with the sacred Gospels placed between them.

When the abbot dies, [Note: [Col. 0919D] The more recent editions inserted “of any congregation,” against the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.] no outsider is to be appointed unless the community itself chooses someone from the same congregation by its own free will; and whoever is chosen is to be ordained without fraud or any form of bribery. If they are unable to find a suitable person among themselves, let them diligently choose someone from another monastery in the same way to be appointed.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] The consensus of the principal manuscripts—the Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and Colbert manuscripts, joined by two Vatican manuscripts and the old editions—compelled us to prefer this reading, although the reading of the recent printed editions may seem more suitable, since it does not apply to an abbot who is still living.]

Nor is any person to be placed over the monastery of an incoming abbot on any pretext, unless, God forbid, there are crimes present of the sort that the sacred canons show to be punishable.

Likewise, care must be taken that, against the will of the abbot of that monastery, monks are not taken from it to organize other monasteries, or for sacred orders or the clerical office. But if they are numerous and sufficient for celebrating praises to God or completing the needs of the monasteries, let the abbot devoutly offer from those who remain any whom he is able to find worthy before God.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] The Norman and Corbie manuscripts read: “whom he considers before God.” Vatican manuscript B: “whom he sees before God.” Vatican manuscripts A, E, and F: “whom he is able before God.”]

If, while having enough, he refuses to give them, then the bishop of Ravenna may take those who remain to organize other monasteries. But no one is to be brought from there into ecclesiastical office unless the abbot of the place, having been asked, offers him of his own will. (Gratian, Distinction 58, chapter 1.)

Whoever, however, has proceeded from the aforesaid monastery into the ecclesiastical order is thereafter to possess neither any authority nor any permission to reside there.

[Note: [Col. 0919D] Formerly monks were ordained priests for two reasons: either for monasteries or for secular churches and parishes, as is found in many chapters of Question 1 of Cause 16. Gregory is therefore not speaking here about monks who are ordained for their own monasteries, but only about those who were taken from the monastery by the bishop, with the abbot’s permission, to administer ecclesiastical office, as is clear from the preceding words of this same letter. Saint Augustine’s letter 48, formerly 81, should be read; there he urges monks to undertake the duties of the Church. GUSSANV.]

It must also be observed that, whenever circumstances require it, an inventory of the property or charters of that monastery is not to be made by ecclesiastics, but by the abbot of the place together with other abbots. [Note: [Col. 0920D] The printed editions read: “He shall make a certification of the things found.”]

[907]

Whenever the abbot should wish to come or send someone to the Roman pontiff for the benefit of his monastery, he is to be permitted to do so in every way.

Moreover, although monasteries ought eagerly to await the arrival of bishops, since we have been informed that the aforesaid monastery was burdened in the time of your predecessor on the pretext of providing lodging, it is fitting that your Holiness should moderate this appropriately, so that the bishop of that city may approach the monastery whenever he wishes, for the sake of visiting and exhorting it. (Gratian, Cause 18, question 2, chapter 28.) But let the bishop fulfill the duty of charity there in such a way that the monastery incurs no burden.

As for your Fraternity, the aforesaid abbot not only does not fear your frequent visits to the monastery, [Note: [Col. 0920D] The printed editions read “does not fear.” Below they read “desire.” We follow the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts.] but even eagerly desires them, knowing that through you the monastery’s resources cannot be burdened in any way.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] We read this only in the Vatican and Colbert manuscripts.]

Given in the month of April, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XVI. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He warmly commends Abbot Claudius on his return from Rome.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

The reason that Claudius, our common son and abbot, the bearer of this letter, has remained with us for so long until now is that he was, as you know, a great consolation to us in the word of God. We would even have wished to retain him here longer, [Note: [Col. 0920D] The recent printed editions read: “unless we knew that he himself was hastening to his monastery and that his presence was altogether necessary …”] if he himself had not hastened to his monastery and if we did not know that his presence was altogether necessary to the community of his brothers.

Therefore, since we judged that he should be released, as he requested and as the needs of the situation required, we commend him to you and urge your Holiness to receive him with priestly affection; to extend to him and his monasteries paternal charity, as is fitting; to refresh him with the consolation of your kindness; to devote yourself earnestly to his protection; and, by the benefit of your support, to make him free from every disturbance, permitting him to devote himself to the peace and interests of the brothers. Love him especially, just as you know that he is loved by us, so that he may recognize in himself, in even greater measure, the affection of your charity that he formerly experienced, and may rejoice that he has found us in you.

## LETTER XVII. TO MAURENTIUS

He rejoices in his devotion to sacred reading. He laments the scarcity of those who study and promises to be his companion.

[908]

[Note: [Col. 0920D] LETTER XVII [formerly 25, book XII, indiction 7].—This letter is absent from the English, Norman, and most manuscripts. In the old editions it was read as “To Luvinus, bishop of Catania.” But that reading, although supported by Vatican manuscript A, is corrupt; for Saint Gregory would not have written to a bishop, “your Glory.”]

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

I would have been very pleased if my beloved son, the deacon Cyprian, had returned to me entirely when he came back. But after your Glory kept him in Sicily, I know with complete certainty that my aforesaid son returned to me in body, but remained in Sicily in mind.

In saying this, however, I rejoice in your peace as much as I grieve over my own occupations. And I urge you above all: if sweetness has touched the palate of your heart with inward delight, let your soul be so carried inward that everything sounding outside may be sad, and everything that delights outside may be sad.

I commend you for avoiding human gatherings, because often the mind that desires to be renewed in God through the grace of compunction grows old again through corrupt conversations and words. I sought to discover who might accompany you in the fellowship of sacred reading, but I found no one, and I grieved deeply over the poverty of goodness.

Although I, a sinner, am extremely occupied, nevertheless, if you wish to come to the threshold of the blessed apostle Peter, you will be able to have me as a close companion in sacred discourse.

May almighty God guard you with heavenly protection and grant that you remain fortified against the snares of the ancient enemy.

## LETTER XVIII. TO AGNELLUS, BISHOP OF TERRACINA

He orders that the practitioners of idolatry who are discovered be punished; he does not permit anyone to be excused from guarding the walls.

Gregory to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina.

It has come to our attention that certain people there—something that it is impious even to say—worship trees and perpetrate many other unlawful acts against the Christian faith. [Note: [Col. 0921C] At Arles, in the year 452, canon 23: “If, in the territory of any bishop, unbelievers light torches or venerate trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to eradicate this, let him know that he is guilty of sacrilege,” and so forth. See also Auxerre, in the year 578, canons 1 and 3; and Saint Augustine, *Sermon on Various Matters* 241. GUSSANVIL. In the penitential of Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, from the time of Louis the Pious, which our very learned Menard presents in his notes to the *Book of Sacraments*, column 467, six penitential canons are assigned for those who follow omens, auspices, divinations, or engage in certain idolatrous superstitions, such as making and fulfilling vows at trees, springs, or a barrier. Menard notes that these were chiefly taken from the Council of Auxerre, canon 1; he should also be consulted on the *Concordance of the Rule*, pages 746 and following. From this it is proved by very certain evidence that remnants of idolatry survived in Gaul long after the time of Gregory the Great. Indeed, since Halitgar represents the Roman Penitential, it is clear that in Italy and other places where the Roman Order was observed, idolatry had still not been eradicated at that time.]

We are astonished that your Fraternity has delayed correcting this by strict punishment. Therefore, by this letter we exhort you to have these people sought out by diligent investigation and, once the truth is known, to inflict such vengeance upon them that God may be appeased and their punishment may serve as an example of correction to others.

[909]

We have also written to Mauro, the viscount, [Note: [Col. 0921D] A viscount is one who exercises jurisdiction in a city in place of a count. For, as was noted above, dukes were appointed over provinces and counts over cities. Some judges in Normandy still retain the name; see Du Cange, *Glossary*.] so that he may provide assistance to your Fraternity in this matter, provided that you cannot find some excuse for failing to apprehend these people.

Since we have learned that many excuse themselves from guarding the walls, let your Fraternity take care that no one be permitted to be excused from such watches by invoking our name, the name of his Church, or any other pretext, [Note: [Col. 0922C] This part of the letter is cited in the title “On ecclesiastical immunity,” chapter 2 of the Extravagants; they attribute it to Gregory IX, but incorrectly. It reads as follows: “Your Fraternity shall not permit anyone, by invoking our name, the name of his Church, or in any other way, to be excused from guarding the walls, but shall compel all generally to this duty, so that, with everyone keeping watch, the protection of the city may be more effectively secured by the Lord’s help.” I add that not even clerics are immune from legitimate guardianship, the care of orphans, or the protection of widows: Distinction 86, final chapter. GUSSANV.] but let everyone be compelled generally, so that, while all keep watch, the city’s protection may be secured more effectively with the Lord’s help.

## LETTER XIX. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He restores his former favor to Comitiolus, who has deserved well of the Roman Church.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] LETTER XIX [formerly 20, book X, indiction 5].—This letter is absent from almost all manuscripts; it exists in Vatican manuscript A.]

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

When my beloved son, the deacon Cyprian, came, he reported the praiseworthy diligence of Comitiolus and the benefit that he had provided for us at the fortress of Urminatum. [Note: [Col. 0922D] Vatican manuscript A reads “at the fortress of Minatum.”] We had also previously learned many good things about him through various testimonies.

Since we have heard that he is not now with you as he once was, we ask your Glory that, if there is anything by which he has perhaps justly offended your minds, you forgive it, whatever it may be, for our sake, restore your full favor to him, and receive him again into the intimacy that he formerly enjoyed with you. You should extend your favor to him as to one truly your own, in whatever manner circumstances may require, without prejudice to justice.

Act, therefore, so that we may learn that your favor has been fully restored to him, either from his own report or from the reports of others.

## LETTER XX. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He commends the wife of John, whose legal status had been called into question.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

John, the bearer of this letter, complains that his wife, who had fled the harassment of a certain Georgius, has remained for a long time within the venerable precincts and has so far found no assistance. [Note: [Col. 0922D] LETTER XX [formerly 21].—Concerning these matters, see above, letter 37, formerly 35, of book I. This kind of immunity was not always observed in the same way; we gather some information about the ancient practice from the *Code*, title “Concerning those who flee to the Church.” You will scarcely find anything older. The Gallican canons and the Capitularies of our kings show what was done in Gaul.]

Since he asserts that there is a dispute concerning her status, and has asked that she be commended to your Fraternity, we exhort you by this letter to extend protection to that woman while preserving equity, and to permit no one to burden her in any way contrary to the order of reason.

[Note: [Col. 0922D] A question of status—that is, of freedom, whether someone is free or a slave—requires higher judges, *Codex*, final law, title “Where the question is one of status.” Therefore it cannot be submitted to arbitrators, *Non distinguemus*, section “On liberal causes,” title “On arbitrators.” ALTESERRA.]

But if the question of her status persists, let it be the concern of your diligence that the matter come to judgment by legal means, without any oppression, so that, once the truth is known and the law has determined what it requires, neither party may grieve that it has suffered any prejudice.

[Note: [Col. 0923D] Thus we read in the old Colbert manuscript alone and in four Vatican manuscripts.]

In the month of May, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XXI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to free Felix, born of Christian parents, from the service of Samaraeus.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Felix, the bearer of this letter, has complained to us that, although he was born of Christian parents, he was given by a certain Christian to Samaraeus—something it is a crime to say. [Note: [Col. 0923D] By “Samaraeus” we understand this Jew. See book VI, letter 33, indiction 14. From letter 32 of the same book it is clear that what is read below means that the laws prohibit Christians from serving Jews.]

Although neither the force of law nor reverence for religion permits people of such a superstition to possess Christian slaves in any manner, he nevertheless asserts that he remained in Samaraeus’s service for eighteen years. But when your predecessor of holy memory, Maximian, learned of this, Felix says that he, moved by the priestly zeal that was appropriate, freed him from Samaraeus’s wicked service.

But since it is said that the son of that same Samaraeus became a Christian after five years, and certain people are attempting, as Felix himself says, to reduce the aforesaid Felix to his service, let your Holiness diligently investigate what we have been told. If you find that the matter is so, strive to protect him and permit no one to burden him under any pretext. Since the laws plainly prohibit the slaves of a superstitious sect from being returned to the service of their masters after they have preceded them into the faith, how much more must this man, born of Christian parents and made a Christian from infancy, be spared such a question in every way—especially since he could not have been his father’s slave, and since it is clear that his father, through a wicked presumption, is instead liable to suffer the penalty imposed by the laws.

Therefore, as we have said, let the protection of your Holiness reasonably defend him in such a way that no one may have any opportunity whatsoever to afflict him under any pretext. (Cf. John the Deacon, book IV, no. 47. See book VI, letter 33, indiction 14.)

## LETTER XXII. TO RUSTICIANA, PATRICIAN

He urges her to come to Rome. He gives thanks for the ten pounds of gold sent to be spent on the redemption of captives.

[911]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0923D] LETTER XXII [formerly 23].—Concerning her, see already letter 21 of book II, indiction 10. GUSSANV.] to Rusticiana, patrician.

I remember that I wrote to Your Excellence long ago, and repeatedly pressed you [Note: [Col. 0923D] The printed editions read “admonished.” We follow the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, Colbert, and other manuscripts. Gregory not infrequently uses *imminere* in the sense of “to urge.”] to hasten to revisit the threshold of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. I do not know what pleasure the city of Constantinople possesses, or what forgetfulness of the city of Rome, that I have so far obtained nothing from you in this matter.

We have carefully considered how much it could benefit your soul for the gathering of the rewards of eternal life; and how much it would also suit your glorious daughter, Lady Eusebia, in every respect. You can consider these matters even more carefully.

If you seek out my son Peter, your man, whom I have learned to be wiser than his age and devoted to maturity, you will discover how great the love is here among all who live around Your Excellence, and how great their desire is that they may deserve to see you again.

And if, by the Lord’s command, we are admonished in the sacred writings that we must love even our enemies, we must consider how great a fault it is not to love those who love us. But if someone should perhaps say that we are loved, we know with complete certainty that no one can love those whom he does not wish to see.

But if you fear the swords and wars of Italy, you ought carefully to observe how great is the protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in this city, where, without a multitude of people and without military assistance, we have been preserved unharmed for so many years amid swords, by God’s authority. [Note: [Col. 0924D] Vatican manuscripts B and D: “with God as our helper.”]

We say these things because we love you. But may almighty God grant whatever he sees to be beneficial forever for your soul and whatever he sees to be beneficial at present for the reputation of your household.

I received the ten pounds of gold that Your Excellence sent for the redemption of captives, delivered by my aforesaid son. But I ask that the heavenly grace which granted you the ability to give them as a reward for your soul may also grant me the ability to distribute them without any taint of sin, [912] lest by the means through which you cleanse yourselves from sins, we ourselves become stained.

May almighty God, who sees your bodily weakness and your absence from home, always console you by his grace and through the life and health of my sweetest son, Lord Strategius, so that he may nourish him both for you over many years and for himself unto eternity. May he fill you and your entire household with present blessings and grant you possession of heavenly grace.

We ask that you greet the glorious Lord Eudoxius on our behalf.

## LETTER XXIII. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER

He is to assist Jews approaching the Christian faith and proceed to Agrigentum.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0924D] LETTER XXIII [formerly 24].—Thus read the manuscript codices, or “Fandinus.” The printed editions have “Faustinus.”] to Fantinus, defender.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] In the manuscripts it is read sometimes as *Domina*, sometimes as *Dominica*; nevertheless, in the greater number and the better manuscripts, *domna*.]

**Domna**, abbess of the monastery of Saint Stephen, which is situated in the territory of Agrigentum, having reported it, we learned that many Jews, moved by divine grace, wished to convert to the Christian faith [Col. 0924D]; but that it was necessary for someone to proceed there on our mandate. Therefore, by the tenor of this authority, we command you that, with every excuse set aside, you hasten to proceed to the aforesaid place [Col. 0925A] and, God being propitious, assist their desire by your exhortations.

[Note: [Col. 0924D] This monastery was situated one thousand paces from the city of Agrigentum, and some remains of it still exist. An ancient church of Saint Mary is visible there. Thus Rocchus Pirrus in his account of Agrigentum. GUSSANV.]

If, however, it seems burdensome or distressing to them to endure the Paschal solemnity, and you recognize that they are now hastening toward baptism, lest—God forbid—a lengthy delay should be able to turn their minds back, speak with our brother, the bishop of that place, so that [Note: [Col. 0925C] Gregory Nazianzen, Orations 39 and 40, and Chrysostom, in his oration *On the Baptism of Christ*, etc., testify that among the Greeks baptism was customarily administered on the solemnities of Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost. Among the Latins, although not a few adopted this practice—and for that reason Pope Siricius rebukes them in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 2, for administering baptism at the feasts of Christ’s Nativity, Epiphany, and the Apostles—and although, as regards Epiphany, the bishops of Sicily likewise did this, for which reason Saint Leo severely reproved them in Letter 16; and although others, going still further—for which reason the Second Council of Mâcon, in 583, chapter 3, censures them—baptized their children on nearly every martyr’s feast; and although, finally, even very eminent men formerly practiced this on Christ’s Nativity, on which day Avitus of Vienne reports in a letter to King Clovis that Clovis was baptized, and on which day we also read below, in Letter 30, that the English were baptized; nevertheless, it was the custom of the Roman Church that baptism be administered at Easter and Pentecost, and indeed only at those times. These two seasons alone are noted by Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 19; by the Siricius just mentioned; by Leo I, Letters 16 and 136; by Gelasius, Letter 3 to the bishops of Lucania; by Gregory II, Letter 3 to all the clergy and people of Thuringia; and by Nicholas I, *Responses to the Bulgarians*, chapter 69. Numerous councils likewise enacted the same: Gerunda in 517; the Second Council of Mâcon, cited above; Mainz I in 813; Paris VI in 829; Worms in 868; and Tribur in 895. Finally, ninth-century authors who wrote about the divine offices testify that this custom was observed in their own times. Between that period and the age of Rupert, who died in 1135, this custom gradually ceased.]

he have them baptized, with the mercy of almighty God protecting them, after penance and abstinence have been imposed for forty days, either on Sunday or, should some especially solemn feast happen to occur, because the season itself, on account of the calamity threatening it, urges that their desires not be deferred by any delay.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] It is unlawful to impose penance on one who has been baptized. It was prescribed for the person being baptized, so that he might thereby cease from sin and become accustomed to Christian conduct. See Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 20: “Those who are about to enter baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils,” etc. He immediately adds the reason: “For at the same time we make satisfaction for our former sins through the discipline of flesh and spirit, and we prepare defenses against the temptations that will follow.” The same author, *On Penance*, chapter 6, notes that punishment is contemplated while pardon is still pending. “The sinner,” he says, “must weep before pardon, because the time of penance is likewise a time of danger and fear; nor do I reject the divine benefit—that is, the abolition of sins—for those who are about to enter the water to be saved in every way, but one must strive to reach it,” etc. I ask that priests who are too ready to grant absolution consult this passage. As for the Lent preceding baptism, see the Council of Laodicea, canon 45, which provides that no one be admitted to baptism if two weeks of Lent have already elapsed. GUSSANV. Cyril of Jerusalem, Preface to the *Mystagogical Catecheses*, Catechesis 1: “The appointed period prescribed for you is a long one, containing forty days of penance.” In Catechesis 3 he calls it the course of the fast. Saint Augustine, Sermon 13 to the Neophytes: “Throughout the whole of Lent they”—the *competentes*, or catechumens already placed in the third stage—“devoted themselves to prayers and fasts,” etc. So also Siricius, Letter 1 to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 2. See more in the notes on the *Sacramentary*, cols. 379–381.]

Whichever among them you discover to be poor and unable to afford clothing for himself, we wish you to purchase and provide him with the garment he is to wear at baptism; you should know that whatever price you pay is to be charged to your accounts [Col. 0925B].

[Note: [Col. 0926D] See the notes on Letter 1 of this book.]

But if they choose to wait for holy Easter, speak again with the bishop, so that for the present they may become catechumens, that he may visit them frequently, take care for them, and kindle their minds by the admonition of his exhortation; so that, the feast for which they wait being delayed for as long as it is, they may prepare themselves all the more and endure the wait for it with fervent desire.

Moreover, it should be your earnest and diligent concern to investigate whether the aforesaid monastery, over which the aforementioned *domna* presides, is self-sufficient or suffers some necessity. And whatever you learn to be true, as well as what has been done concerning those who desire to be baptized, hasten to report to us in detail.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] This is read in Vatican A, B, D, and F, and in the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of June, in the first indiction. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, no. 49.)

## LETTER XXIV. TO SABINIAN, BISHOP OF JADERA

He congratulates him because, where obedience is required, he obeys, and where resistance is required, he resists. He strengthens his spirit against hatred of Maximus. He declares that a presbyter cannot, for any reason, remain in the sacred order or be restored to it after his fall.

[Col. 0926A]

**Gregory to Sabinian, bishop of Jadera.**

[Note: [Col. 0926D] On Sabinian, see above, Letter 10.]

I rejoice sufficiently, dearest brother, in your sincerity, because I recognize, with the careful discernment of judgment and with priestly zeal, that you both obey where obedience is required and resist where resistance is required. With how great an eagerness of devotion you submitted to what we imposed on account of the fault of your past transgression, the page of your letter, which you sent by the bearer of this present letter, has disclosed. For it could not have been received otherwise by a beloved brother than as a command by one who is dutiful. Therefore I trust in the mercy of almighty God that his grace so protects you that, having thereby also been absolved from other things, you may rejoice that you have obeyed beneficially.

As for the fact that your charity has shown itself distressed by the hostility of Maximus, the traitor and excommunicate, you ought not to be troubled. Rather, it is fitting that you patiently endure for a little while the waves swelling vainly, and that by the strength of perseverance you place beneath your feet the foam of the waves. Patience knows how to make light what is heavy, and steadfastness how to overcome what rages. Therefore, let adversity not cast down your spirits but kindle them. Let priestly vigor show you more courageous in all things. For the true proofs of truth are to show oneself more ready in difficulties and stronger than anyone in adversity.

Therefore, so that the strength of uprightness may not be shaken by any impulse from the goodness of its own deliberation, direct the steps of your mind, as you have begun, upon the solidity of that rock on which you know that our Redeemer founded the Church throughout the whole world [Col. 0926C–0927A], so that the straight footprints of a sincere heart may not stumble on a pathless way.

As for the matters about which you wrote to us, or which the bearer of this letter explained while present before us, do not think that we have carelessly omitted them; rather, we are thinking about them with complete concern.

We have already explained everything in detail, both previously and now once again, to our most beloved son Anatolius the deacon, exhorting him to hasten to do strictly and diligently, with the help and support of our Creator, whatever pertains to the welfare and tranquility of your charity and of your sons [Note: [Col. 0927D] In recent editions *augere*—“to increase”—has entered erroneously in place of *agere*—“to do.”]. Therefore, let neither sorrow affect your fraternity nor the hostility of anyone distress you. For, with the grace of the divinity assisting us, we trust that we shall soon be present, so that both the presumption of the aforesaid traitor and excommunicate may be more strictly restrained, and your tranquility may come, as you desire. We have by no means failed to write also to our most excellent son the Exarch, who is endeavoring to commend him to us, concerning his depravity.

As for the presbyter about whom your fraternity consulted us through the report of the bearer of this letter, know that after his fall he cannot, for any reason, either remain in the sacred order or be restored to it.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] On those who have fallen and are never to be admitted to the functions of the orders, see Letter 18 of Book I and Letter 26 of Book III, now Book IV, etc.]

Nevertheless, one must act more gently toward him because he is said to have readily confessed the crime he committed.

Furthermore, this same bearer has reported certain privileges of your Church granted by our predecessors. Concerning these matters we wish to be informed more fully by your charity; or, if any writings concerning them lie in the archive of your Church, it is necessary that copies be sent here, so that we may willingly restore whatever pertains to the honor of your Church or to the *genius*—that is, the character, distinction, or privilege—of the aforesaid Church.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] Understand *ornament* as splendor, distinction, or a privilege already granted from ancient times and therefore legitimately sought. See Henri Estienne, *Schediasmata*, chapter 18; John Brodaeus, *Miscellanies*, Book IX, chapter 20. Syagrius, bishop of Autun, asks below for a pallium “for the genius and honor of his Church,” Book IX, Letter 108.]

Urge our glorious common son Marcellus more insistently to come here if he wishes, because I greatly desire to see him. But if he chooses to remain there, conduct yourselves toward him in the charity that is fitting, so that you may be able, as is proper, to respond to the affection he has for you. May almighty God, by the gift of his grace, guard and protect you [Note: [Col. 0928D] The Vulgate reads: “may he protect you and guard you”], and always kindle your heart toward what pleases him.

## LETTER XXV. TO VICTOR, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

The Jews are not to be troubled in those matters that have been granted to them.

[Col. 0927D]

**Gregory to Victor, bishop of Panormus.**

Just as the Jews must not have license to presume anything in their synagogues beyond what has been permitted by law, so in those matters that have been granted to them they must suffer no prejudice. The petition that the Hebrews living here in the city of Rome have submitted on behalf of those dwelling in Panormus informs you about what they have complained of; it is contained below. If, therefore, their complaint is supported by truth, your fraternity ought, after carefully examining the sequence of the law, to observe and preserve whatever has been decreed concerning this matter, so that neither you may appear to do anything unjust nor they to suffer prejudice. But if there is something that can reasonably obstruct the restoration of what has been requested, let judges be chosen by both parties who can determine what accords with equity. If the dispute should perhaps be unable to reach an end there, the case must come to us, so that matters that appear friendly to justice may be decided without your incurring anyone’s hatred [Col. 0928A–B].

[Note: [Col. 0928D] In the Rheims manuscript and Vatican D: “without the scruple of your envy.” In Vatican F: “without the pest of envy.” The sense of the reading we retain is: “Let the matter be settled in such a way that you incur no one’s hatred.” This is especially useful for pastors, for they scarcely benefit unless they win the goodwill of those placed under their care.]

Until the case itself receives its conclusion, therefore, let your fraternity refrain from consecrating the places said to have been taken away.

## LETTER XXVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

Pantaleo the notary is to investigate which clerics sold sacred vessels.

**Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.**

Because it has come to us that certain clerics from a Church in Italy have sold sacred vessels in Sicily, we have therefore sent our notary Pantaleo to investigate those same vessels with careful inquiry. But after he became occupied in the service of your holiness, we have learned that he neglected this matter. Therefore your fraternity ought to provide with suitable care that, at the time you judge useful, you release him to carry out these very tasks, so that you may be able to receive assistance from him and he may beneficially accomplish, with God’s help, what has been entrusted to him; for it is necessary that he come here in the following indiction and, standing before us, inform us in detail about everything.

[Note: [Col. 0928D] The printed editions read: “from the Churches of Italy”; the manuscript codices forbid us to follow that reading.]

## LETTER XXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

The deacons of Catania are not to presume to appear wearing *campagi*.

**Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.**

The order of ecclesiastical vigor is thrown into confusion if either unlawful things are rashly presumed or things not permitted are attempted with impunity. It has therefore come to us [Col. 0928D] that the deacons of the Church of Catania have presumed to go about wearing *campagi*—that is, footwear [Note: [Col. 0928D] The printed editions read erroneously *compagis*. A *campagus* is footwear worn by prelates at Mass, from the Greek word καμπή, “a bending,” or “a curve.” See Saussay, *Panoplia of Bishops*, Book VII, chapter 1, section 4. Salmasius, in his work on Trebellius, argues that *campagi* were the same as the ancient patrician shoes. Isidore says that these patrician shoes were customarily fastened crosswise; Hesychius calls them hollow and deep footwear because they rose as high as the middle of the shins. Rubenius, *On the Clothing of the Romans*, Book II, chapter 15, thinks that *campagi* were like sandals. Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book II, chapter 18: “Because Bede reaches as far as the feet, when discussing linen garments, so that we ourselves may explain the matter of the sandals, or, by another name, the *campagi*, which remain on the feet.” This should be read *campagis*, not *campobis* as printed. Honorius of Autun, *Gemma animae*, Book I, chapter 210, concerning the *campagi*, or sandals, of bishops: “It is,” he says, “a kind of cut footwear by which the foot is partly covered and partly seen bare.”]—although, as you well remember, no one throughout Sicily has hitherto been permitted to do this except only the deacons of the Church of Messana, to whom it is undoubtedly known to have been granted formerly by our predecessors.

Since, therefore, an attempt of such boldness is not to be treated lightly, let your fraternity investigate the whole matter with the greatest exactness; and if you find that it is as it has reached us, let us know in detail whether they presumed to do this on their own authority or by someone else’s authority, so that, having learned the truth, we may determine what ought to be done. For if we negligently overlook things that are wrongly usurped, we open a path of excess for others.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Thus in the old Colbert manuscript and in three Vatican manuscripts, namely A, D, and E. In Vatican B, followed by the printed editions, “in the month of June.”]

In the month of June, in the first indiction. (John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 8.)

## LETTER XXVIII. TO VICTOR AND COLUMBUS, BISHOPS

They are to compel Valention, the bishop, to restore to Crisconius the churches occupied from his parish and the property taken from the parish of the deceased bishop of that parish.

[Col. 0929B]

**Gregory to Victor and Columbus, bishops of Africa, his peers.**

As much as the ecclesiastical order, when blamelessly preserved, pours joy into our heart, so much does it impose the weariness of grief when it is torn apart, because the rashness of wickedness attempts to overturn discipline, dissolve what was once laudably established, and presume what ought to be punished with greater severity.

The complaint of our brother and fellow bishop Crisconius, brought by the bearer of this present letter, has reached us, namely that, though no fault required it and no judgment of a council determined it, the churches anciently assigned to his parish [Col. 0929D] were irrationally occupied by our brother and fellow bishop Valention nearly fifteen years ago, and that he furthermore took away the property of his predecessor for his own—something grievous to say—arbitrary disposal.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] In three Vatican manuscripts and all the Norman manuscripts: “by Avalention.” In Vatican B: “by Valentio.”]

If the truth is indeed as stated, we cannot say how perverse and execrable this is, especially for one devoted to the religious life.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] The Vatican edition reads: “for a religious superior.”]

Therefore, since neither leniency nor any delay should be permitted in this matter, we admonish your fraternity by this present letter to investigate it most carefully. And if his complaint is shown to be evident, let your charity provide without delay for the restoration of the property taken and the parishes occupied, and let him recover everything, with your assistance, every excuse having ceased and justice favoring him, in such a way that neither the labor of preserving it afflicts him nor the invader gains any profit from his loss. Let zeal for equity kindle you; let the uprightness of justice kindle you.

[Note: [Col. 0929D–0930C] He judges that one must return to the sources of canonical discipline. In nearly this way all councils, gathered in the Holy Spirit, teach; for one is not permitted to live without rules or to establish private rules at will in each diocese.
