Would that those who so insistently cry out that uniformity in minor ceremonies is necessary would agree among themselves on the principal matters of discipline and not busy themselves with newly enacted rules that collide with one another. GUSSANV.]

Strive earnestly to preserve in all things the ancient arrangement of ecclesiastical order. Show yourselves strict and vigilant amid guilt and innocence, so that those who possess justice may have great confidence in the zeal for your uprightness, while every opportunity for the restless to transgress in the future may be cut off.

[Note: [Col. 0930C] In two Teller manuscripts the letter ends: “in the month of July, indiction 1.”]

## LETTER XXIX. TO EULOGIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

He does not know the book of Eusebius on the acts of the martyrs that Eulogius had requested. Why he sent short pieces of wood. He promises longer ones and refuses payment.

[Col. 0930B]

**Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria.**

The address of a learned man is always useful, because the hearer either learns what he knew he did not know or, what is more, recognizes what he did not know that he did not know. In this matter I have now become one of the hearers, since your most holy Beatitude took pains to write that I should send the acts of all the martyrs collected by Eusebius of Caesarea in the time of Constantine of blessed memory. But before your Beatitude’s letter I knew neither whether these had been collected nor whether they existed [Col. 0930C].

[Note: [Col. 0930C] In three Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and the Corbie, Colbert, and Rheims manuscripts, it reads: “neither whether they were collected nor whether they were”; but this makes no sense. We have followed Vatican B and F, in which it reads: “neither whether they had not been collected.” In the printed editions: “neither whether they had not been collected.”]

I therefore give thanks, because, instructed by the writings of your most holy teaching, I have begun to know what I did not know.

[Note: [Col. 0930C–0931D] Besides what Eusebius reports about the holy martyrs in his *Ecclesiastical History*, he published two separate books concerning their acts. The first, which he calls *Συναγωγὴ ἀρχαίων μαρτύρων*—“Collection of the Ancient Martyrs”—contained authentic acts of ancient martyrs, insofar as it is lawful to gather from what he says about this book in *History* IV.15, near the end of Book V, and elsewhere. In the second, entitled *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, he recounts what he himself had seen and heard in person concerning the martyrs of his own province. We possess this book of Eusebius after Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*. But the first, if it has not utterly disappeared, lies so deeply hidden that no one has yet been able to find it at all. During the persecution under Diocletian, the sacred Christian books were attacked with such ferocity that scarcely even the names of nearly countless books reached posterity. Perhaps Eusebius’s book on the Acts of the Martyrs suffered this fate. Consult the index to the Life of Saint Gregory written by us, under the word “Martyrology.”]

For, besides what is contained in the books of that same Eusebius concerning the acts of the holy martyrs, I have learned that there is nothing in the archive of our Church or in the libraries of the city of Rome, except for a few items gathered in the volume of a single codex.

[Note: [Col. 0931D–0932D] Some think that this passage should be understood as referring to the Roman Martyrology called “the ancient” one. But the distinguished and highly learned Henri Valesius clearly refuted this in his dissertation appended to Eusebius, where he argues that before Usuard there was no Roman Martyrology at all; that the one Gregory refers to here was shared with the other Western churches, namely the Martyrology published under the name of Jerome; and yet it is not sufficiently established either that Jerome himself compiled it or that it was translated from Eusebius. See more in Valesius and in the Bollandists, General Preface to the *Acta Sanctorum*, chapter 4, section 4. Partly from GUSSANV. This is inconvenient for the newer editors who repeatedly introduce Vatican manuscripts.]

We possess, however, in a single codex the names of nearly all the martyrs, collected with their commemorations distinguished for each individual day, and on each day we celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in their honor. Yet in that same volume it is not indicated how each one suffered; only the name, place, and day of martyrdom are given. Thus it happens that many are known to have been crowned with martyrdom on the individual days I mentioned, from different lands and provinces. But we believe that you, most blessed one, possess these things. The items you wished to have sent, however, we sought and did not find; nevertheless, we continue to seek them without finding them, and if they can be found, we shall send them.

As for your writing that the pieces of wood were short, this was caused by the kind of ship by which they were sent. If a larger ship had arrived, we could have sent larger pieces of wood as well. As for your saying that, if we send larger pieces, you will pay the price, we give thanks for your generosity but are forbidden by the Gospel to accept payment. We did not purchase the wood that we are sending, and how can we accept a price when it is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8)? Therefore, in accordance with the capacity of the ship, we have now sent small pieces of wood by the shipmaster, a description of which is appended below. In the following year, if it pleases almighty God, we shall prepare larger ones. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 26.)

[Col. 0931C]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Here and elsewhere in these letters, *benedictio*—“blessing”—means a gift. It is also frequently understood in this sense in Sacred Scripture, as when Jacob says to his brother in Genesis 33: “Accept this little gift … be gracious to me and accept the blessing that I have brought,” verses 10–11. Among the Greeks this is likewise understood under the name *eulogia*, and even among the Latins. The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 54: “Let it in no way be permitted … to accept a *eulogia* or any sort of little gift.”]

We received the blessing of Saint Mark the Evangelist—or rather, what is more correct, of Saint Peter the Apostle—in the sweetness in which it was sent. Having returned the greeting addressed to us, we ask that your Beatitude deign to pray for us, so that we may soon deserve to be rescued from present evils and not be excluded from future joys.

## LETTER XXX. TO EULOGIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

He rejoices over the conversion of the heretics of Alexandria and over the concord of the faithful. He in turn writes about the conversion of the English. Concerning Eudoxius the heretic and others, he acknowledges that Eulogius has fully satisfied him. He rejects the title “universal pope,” which the Council of Chalcedon had offered to his predecessors.

**Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria.**

[Note: [Col. 0932D] In the Norman, Corbie, and English manuscripts: “of the patriarch.”]

Our common son, the bearer of this letter, bringing your holiness’s writings, found me ill [Col. 0931D–0932A] and left me ill; consequently, it happened that, at the abundant fountain of your Beatitude, the small amount of water in my brief letter could scarcely trickle forth. Yet it was a gift from above that, while I was suffering bodily, I received the writings of your most sweet holiness, which made me rejoice greatly over the doctrine of the heretics in the city of Alexandria and the concord of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0933D] Thus the English, Norman, and Corbie manuscripts; in other printed editions: “over the teaching of the Alexandrian Church, the conversion of the heretics, the concord,” etc.], so that this very joy of mind might temper the severity of my distress.

Indeed, we always rejoice with fresh exultation in your good works, but we by no means consider it something new that you act so perfectly. For that the people of the holy Church are increasing, that spiritual crops are multiplying for the heavenly granary—this we have never doubted to proceed from the grace of almighty God, which flows abundantly into you, most blessed men. We therefore give thanks to almighty God, because we see fulfilled in you what is written: “Where there are very abundant crops, there is the evident strength of oxen” (Proverbs 14:8). For if the strong ox had not drawn the plow of the tongue across the soil of the hearts of those who heard, such a harvest of the faithful would certainly not have arisen.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] In recent editions: “But since what increases in the good works you perform also benefits others,” etc.]

Since I know that you rejoice with others in the good works you accomplish, I return your grace to you and announce something similar, because, while the English people, situated in a remote corner of the world, still remained faithless in the worship of wood and stone [Note: [Col. 0933D] In the same recent editions, against the manuscripts: “in their unbelief” (*perfidia*)], it pleased God, with the assistance of your prayer, that I should send there, under God’s authority, a monk of my monastery to preach.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] He means Augustine, superior of the monastery of Saint Andrew.]

After I had given him permission, he was made a bishop by the bishops of the German lands [Col. 0932C].

[Note: [Col. 0933D] He refers to the bishops of Gaul. Since the Franks originated from the Germans, they too were called Germans. Apollinaris Sidonius, Book V, Letter 7, calls the province of Lyon “Lyonese Germany,” because of the Burgundians, who were German by origin.]

He was led, with their assistance also, to the aforesaid people at the end of the world, and by now reports have reached us concerning its salvation and his work, because such great miracles shine forth among that people, performed either by him himself or by those who were sent with him, that they seem to imitate the power of the apostles in the signs they display. At the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, which has passed during this first indiction, more than ten thousand English were reported by that brother and fellow bishop to have been baptized. I have recounted this so that you may know what you accomplish among the Alexandrian people by speaking and what you accomplish at the ends of the world by praying. For your prayers are in the place where you are not, while your holy works are displayed in the place where you are. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 39.)

[Col. 0933A]

Furthermore, concerning the person of Eudoxius the heretic, whose error I found nowhere in the Latin language, I rejoice that your Beatitude has satisfied me most fully.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] On Eudoxius the heretic, see what we said in the notes to Letter 4 of Book VI, now Book VII. GUSSANV.]

For you brought forward the testimonies of the most courageous men Basil, Gregory, and Epiphanius, and we recognize that the man against whom our heroes hurled so many darts has been manifestly overthrown.

As for the errors now said to have arisen in the Church of Constantinople, you replied with great learning and in a manner befitting the judgment of so great a see. Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, because the tablets of the covenant are still within the ark of God. For what is the priestly heart except the ark of the covenant? Since spiritual teaching is vigorous within it, without doubt the tablets of the law lie there.

Your Beatitude also took pains to indicate that you no longer write to certain people the proud titles that have sprung from the root of vanity, and you addressed me, saying: “As you commanded.” I ask you to remove the word “command” from my hearing, because I know who I am and who you are. In position you are my brothers; in character, my fathers. Therefore I did not command, but merely took care to point out what seemed useful.

Yet I do not find that your Beatitude wished to retain perfectly what I brought to your attention. For I said that you ought not to write such a thing either to me or to anyone else; and behold [Note: [Col. 0934D] Vatican B reads “the word of superstition.”], in the preface of the letter you sent to me—the very person who had prohibited it—you took care to insert the word of proud address, calling me “universal pope” [Col. 0933B–C].

I ask that your most sweet holiness do this no more, because what is withheld from you is being offered to another beyond what reason requires. I do not seek to prosper through words but through conduct. Nor do I regard as honor that in which I recognize that my brothers lose their honor. For my honor is the honor of the universal Church. My honor is the solid strength of my brothers. I am truly honored when the honor due to each individual is denied to no one. For if your holiness calls me “universal pope,” you deny that you are what you acknowledge me to be—the universal one. But may this be far from us! Let words that inflate vanity and wound charity depart.

Indeed, your holiness knows that this title was offered to my predecessors at the holy Council of Chalcedon and afterward by succeeding Fathers. Yet none of them ever wished to use this title, so that, while they loved the honor of all priests in this world, they might preserve their own before almighty God [Col. 0933D–0934A].

Therefore, having paid the greeting due to you, I ask that you deign to remember me in your holy prayers, so that the Lord may release me from the bonds of my sins through your intercessions, since I cannot do so by my own merits. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 69.)

## LETTER XXXI. TO SECUNDINUS

He is not to allow the monastery to come under the power of a layperson.

**Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina.**

The petition submitted by the monks of the Castellian monastery, which is contained below, has disclosed their complaint.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] The Castellian monastery, built by Cassiodorus and ennobled by the retirement of so great a man, was near Squillace. Consult the Life of Cassiodorus prefixed to his works in the latest edition, Part II, section 6 and following. See also Cassiodorus, *On the Institution of Divine Literature*, chapter 20.]

Therefore let your fraternity investigate with careful diligence the matters they assert. And if you find that they are supported by truth, provide them with protection and arrange, according to custom, for the monastery united to their monastery to be governed there by monks appointed from their congregation. For the order of reason does not permit a layperson to withdraw that monastery from their administration at his own discretion, especially against the will of its founders, nor does it permit anyone to claim a right over it for himself.

## LETTER XXXII. TO SCHOLASTICUS, DEFENDER

He is to pay the Church’s tenant a wage proportionate to his labor.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] This letter is absent from most manuscripts. Of all the Vatican manuscripts, only Codex A contains it. It is also read in the Saint-Victor manuscript.]

**Gregory to Scholasticus, defender.**

Alexander Frix, the bearer of this letter and a tenant of our Church, has complained to us that he worked for a period of three years in the house—that is, the church—built at Catania by our beloved son the deacon Cyprian, and that he did not receive a wage appropriate to his labor. Although it is said that during that period he worked for many people, so that you also learned of the matter while you were here, nevertheless we command you by this authority to investigate it carefully. And if he worked more in that house than the payment he received warrants, we wish you to add to it, according to the measure of his labor, whatever you judge he has earned beyond the four solidi and two tremisses that he is said to have received from the aforesaid deacon, knowing that it is to be charged to your accounts.

## LETTER XXXIII. TO DOMINICUS

He praises his modesty, charity, and reverence for the Apostolic See.

[Col. 0934D]

**Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage.**
The writings of Your Holiness, which we received from the bearer of this letter, spoke with such priestly modesty that they seemed somehow to charm us with the bodily presence of their author. For a rare exchange of words does no harm where a continuous affection of love remains in the hearts.

921 Great indeed is the power of charity, beloved brother, which by the bond of its sincerity binds hearts together in mutual affection and does not allow them to be dissolved from the bond of grace: it joins those who are separated, preserves those who are united, and makes those unknown to one another known through love. Whoever, therefore, fixes his mind upon the hinge of this love cannot be torn from the dwelling of the heavenly homeland by any assault of adversity; for wherever he turns, he does not depart from the threshold of the commandments.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXIII [Al. 32].—Recent printed editions, against all the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, and other manuscripts, read *from the boundary* instead of *from the threshold*. And certainly *threshold* belongs with *hinge*, not *boundary*. Thus, in order that Gregory’s comparison may remain consistent, after saying “whoever fixes his mind upon the hinge of this,” he ought to have added: “does not go beyond the threshold of the commandments.”]

Hence, in praise of this same charity, it is said by the distinguished preacher: “Which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14).

[Note: Vatican manuscript B reads: “which is the bond of perfection.”]

We therefore see how great is the praise of charity, which not only generates perfection in the mind but also binds it. Since the language of your letter reveals you to be inflamed by the fire of this virtue, I rejoice with abundant exultation in the Lord, and I desire that it shine forth in you more and more, because it is the light of the flock and the pastor’s flame.

[Note: Recent editions read: “for it is fitting for a pastor, fitting for the Lord’s pastor.”]

It is fitting—indeed, it is fitting—for the Lord’s priest to shine in character and life, so that in him, as in the mirror of his life, the people entrusted to him may both choose what to follow and see what they ought to correct.

Moreover, knowing whence priestly ordination in the African regions took its beginning, you act commendably in returning, through love of the Apostolic See, with prudent remembrance to the origin of your office, and in remaining steadfast in a worthy devotion toward it. For it is certain that, by offering to its honor whatever reverence and devotion you show to it as priests, you invite it to be bound to you by a corresponding affection.

[Note: In the recent edition, against the testimony of the manuscripts: “whatever reverence and devotion you show to the priestly order.”]

For the rest, dearest brother, let us ask the almighty Lord in continual prayer to direct the steps of our hearts into the path of his truth; and, so that he may lead us to the heavenly kingdom, let him grant that by the grace of his protection we may show in our works that we bear the office of his name.

[Note: The Vatican, Colbert, and Teller manuscripts agree on this date.]

In the month of August, in the first indiction.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SCILLITUM

Let him preserve unimpaired the privileges of the monastery of Castellium. Let him restore what was taken under the appearance of a gift. Let him watch over the conduct of the monks. Let him defend the monastery’s rights. Let him restore the land granted to him by the abbot. (See above, Epistle 31.)

[Col. 0935D]

Gregory to John, Bishop of Scillitum.

It is exceedingly grave and plainly contrary to the priestly calling to wish to disrupt the privileges formerly granted to any monastery and to attempt to invalidate arrangements established for its tranquility. The monks of the monastery of Castellium, which is situated in your city, have therefore complained to us that you are hastening to introduce into that monastery certain practices contrary to what your predecessors permitted and long custom has preserved, and that you are disturbing its ancient order by a novel act of prejudice. Accordingly, we exhort Your Fraternity by these words: if this is so, refrain from troubling it without any excuse, and do not attempt by any pretext to tear away what has long been preserved for it; rather, strive to maintain everything intact and without resistance of any kind. Know that you are not permitted more in this monastery than was permitted to your predecessors.

They have likewise complained that Your Fraternity has taken certain things from the monastery under the appearance of a gift.

[Note: EPISTLE XXXIV [Al. 33].—The manuscripts commonly read *under the appearance of a gift*. In Vatican manuscript D these words are inserted: “under the appearance, as though of a grant.”]

If you recall having accepted anything improperly from it, you must restore it without delay, lest the guilt of avarice severely condemn you, whom priestly generosity ought rather to show as liberal toward monasteries. Having therefore preserved all that, as we have said, was permitted and maintained by your predecessors, make it your concern to remain vigilant regarding the conduct and life of the monks residing there; and if you find anyone behaving improperly there or, God forbid, involved in any offense of impurity, correct him with strict and regular discipline. For just as we wish Your Fraternity to abstain from things improperly usurped, so in every way we admonish you to be diligent in matters relating to the rectitude of discipline and the protection of souls.

The monks of the aforesaid monastery have also reported that the fortress called Scillitum was founded on land belonging to their monastery, and that for this reason its inhabitants, by written agreements, promised to pay an annual rent, but later despised this obligation and needlessly suspended payment of it.

[Note: Elsewhere, *solatium*. This word occurs very frequently, but does not always mean the same thing. Here it is used for a payment or revenue rendered to the lord or owner on account of the estate or land. It also often occurs for wages. Gussanville. Moreover, this letter makes clear that monasteries once possessed very extensive lordships, so that entire fortresses and villages depended upon them. Since this is said of the monastery of Castellium, enriched by the generosity of Cassiodorus, who would easily refuse to believe the same of other monasteries whose founders were kings and emperors?]

Your Fraternity must therefore carefully ascertain the truth; and if you find the matter to be so, earnestly see to it that they do not delay in providing what they promised, since justice also requires it, so that they may possess in peace what they hold and the monastery’s rights may not suffer prejudice.

Furthermore, the monks of the aforesaid monastery have complained to us that their abbot granted to Your Fraternity, under the pretext of building a church, land within the fortress of Scillitum extending over six hundred feet, by way of a donation; and therefore we wish as much of it as the walls of the church can enclose to be claimed for the church’s rights. Whatever may lie outside the walls of that church must return without difficulty to the rights of the monastery, since neither the provisions of secular laws nor those of the sacred canons permit monastery property to be separated from its legal ownership under any title. Therefore restore without delay the donation of that land, which was made contrary to justice.

923

## EPISTLE XXXV. TO LEONTIUS, FORMER CONSUL

The citizens of Jerusalem sometimes serve Babylon, and conversely. He praises Leontius’s gentleness, humility, and justice. He thanks him for his gifts and sends him dust enclosed in a key from the chains of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0937B]

Gregory to Leontius, former consul.

Since in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also wooden and earthen vessels, and some indeed for honor while others are for dishonor (2 Timothy 2:20), who does not know that within the bosom of the universal Church some are assigned, as vessels of dishonor, to lowly affairs, while others, as vessels of honor, are fitted for pure and noble tasks? Yet it often happens that citizens of Babylon serve Jerusalem under compulsion, and that citizens of Jerusalem—that is, of the heavenly homeland—are assigned to the forced service of Babylon.

[Note: *Service*, *ministry*, or *the obligation of service*. Gussanville.]

For when God’s elect, endowed with great character, adorned with modesty, and not seeking their own profits, are assigned to earthly affairs, what else are they doing but serving as citizens of holy Jerusalem in Babylon’s work? And when certain men, unrestrained in wicked conduct, occupy a place of holy honor and seek their own praise even in the things they appear to do well, what else are they doing but paying Babylon’s forced service to the heavenly Jerusalem? Thus Judas, associated for a long time with the apostles, preached the Redeemer of the human race and performed signs with the others; but because he had been a citizen of Babylon, he rendered his work as forced service to the heavenly Jerusalem. Joseph, on the other hand, having been taken into Egypt, served in an earthly palace, carried out administrative duties in temporal affairs, and rendered whatever was justly owed to a transitory kingdom.

[Note: Recent editions have altered *justly*, which is found in all the manuscripts, to *unjustly* at will.]

But because he was a citizen of holy Jerusalem, he performed Babylon’s service only as the forced service described above. I believe, therefore, good man, that you are his follower: although involved in earthly affairs, I recognize that you conduct yourself with a gentle spirit, preserve the fortress of humility in every respect, and render to each person what is just. For many report so much good about your excellence that I do not wish merely to hear it but to see it; yet the good opinion I have of one whom I am not permitted to see nourishes me.

The woman who poured out the alabaster and filled the house with perfume (Luke 7), representing holy Church—that is, all the elect—also serves as a type. Whenever we hear something good, we draw in, as though through the nostril, the fragrance of its sweetness. And when the Apostle Paul said, “We are the good odor of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:15), it is plainly understood that he presented himself as a taste to those present, but as an odor to those absent. We, therefore, who cannot receive nourishment through the taste of your presence, are nourished through the fragrance of your absence.

We also rejoice greatly that the gifts you sent were not unlike your character.

[Note: Binius recorded a little about the oil from Baronius; Gretser discusses much more in Book I, *On the Holy Cross*, chapter 79, and explains Saint Gregory’s passage as referring to oil that flowed from the wood of the Lord’s cross. Gussanville. Bede, *On the Holy Places*, chapter 20: “For from the knots of the holy wood a fragrant liquid, similar to oil, flows; and if even a small particle of it touches someone, it heals every illness.”]

For we received oil of the holy cross and aloe wood: one to bless whatever it touches, the other to give off a pleasant fragrance when burned. It was therefore fitting that a good man should send things capable of appeasing the Lord’s anger toward us. You also sent many other things for the storerooms,

[Note: Concerning storerooms, see above, Book I, Epistle 42, now 44. Gussanville.]

because, since we subsist in mind and body, it was necessary that we should be sustained by you in both. Yet your exceedingly sweet spirit declares itself very much ashamed of the things sent and sets against that very shame the shield of charity. But I rejoice completely in these words, because from such a testimony of the mind I recognize that one who is ashamed even to give what is his own can never take what belongs to another.

You call your gifts small, although they are great; but, I believe, you do so so that they may profit still more from the very humility of your excellence. And you ask me to receive these good things with a willing mind. But amid these matters, recall to mind the two small coins of a certain widow (Luke 21).

If she pleased God by offering little with a good intention, why should one who has given much with a humble mind not please human beings? Moreover, we sent you a blessing of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles: the key of his most sacred tomb, in which a blessing from his chains has been inserted, so that what bound his neck for martyrdom may free yours from every sin.

[Note: In the Norman, Colbert, and most manuscripts, two other letters follow the preceding letters under the first indiction: one to the distinguished Adeodata, which is now Book X, 49, and another to Januarius, bishop of Caralis, which is third in the following order of Book IX.]

## BOOK NINE

In the month of September, in the second indiction.

[Col. 0939]

925

[Note: BOOK IX. Also BOOK VII. Indiction II. EPISTLE I.—In the Colbert and Royal manuscripts the following precedes: “Maximus was raised,” etc., as it is read in other printed editions at the beginning of Book VII, indiction 1, or Book VIII. We have judged that this material should be sent to the end. In Vatican manuscript A, Epistle 1 of Book IX, *On the Penance and Satisfaction of Maximus the Transgressor*, is also placed first. In Vatican manuscript D only this is read: *On Maximus the Presumptuous: He was raised*, etc. In Vatican manuscript E: *On the Presumption and Penance of Maximus*. In Vatican manuscript F: *On the Penance of Maximus, bishop*.]

## EPISTLE I. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

He rebukes him because, on the Lord’s Day, before the solemn celebration of Mass, he had plowed up someone’s crop in furrows and, after the sacred rite, had himself uprooted the boundary stones.

[Col. 0939A]

Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Caralis.

The Apostle Paul, preacher of the almighty Lord, says: “Do not rebuke an older man” (1 Timothy 5:1). But this rule of his is to be observed in a case where the fault of an older man does not draw the hearts of the younger into ruin by his example. Where, however, an elder gives the young an example leading to destruction, he must be struck with strict rebuke. For it is written: “You are all a snare to the young” (Isaiah 42:22). And again the prophet says:

[Note: Thus it is found in many manuscripts and older printed editions, and in John the Deacon, although in a few manuscripts one reads: “and a boy of a hundred years,” etc. The context of the letter itself, as well as the various versions, favors our reading. The Vulgate: “And the sinner who is a hundred years old shall be accursed.” Hebrew: “And the sinner, the son of a hundred years, shall be accursed.” The Septuagint translators: “And the sinner who is a hundred years old shall also be accursed.” Syriac: “Whoever sins when a hundred years old shall be accursed.” The Chaldean and Arabic versions read likewise. Gussanville. In Vatican manuscript D, where the reading is, as in the other manuscripts, “a sinner of a hundred years,” this variant is added: “and a boy of a hundred years.” Gratian likewise reads this in Cause 2, Question 7, Canon 28. Paul.]

“And the sinner who is a hundred years old is accursed” (Isaiah 65:20).

Such wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still measured it with human consideration, we would already strike it with a fixed sentence of condemnation. For I have been told that on the Lord’s Day, before you celebrated the solemn Mass, you went to plow up the crop of the bearer of this letter, and that after plowing it you celebrated the solemn Mass. After the solemn Mass, you did not even fear to uproot the boundaries of that man’s property.

Everyone who hears of this knows what punishment ought to follow such an act. We had been uncertain about so great a perversity; but when our son Cyriacus, the abbot, was questioned by us while he was at Caralis, he testified that he had learned it to be so. And because we are still sparing your gray hairs, we exhort you: come to your senses at last, old man, and restrain yourself from such levity of character and perversity of conduct. The nearer you become to death, the more vigilant and fearful you ought to be.

Indeed, a sentence of punishment ought to have been hurled against you; but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, for the present we remain silent. We decree, however, that those whose counsel led you to do this shall be excommunicated for two months, yet in such a way that if anything human should happen to them during those two months, they are not to be deprived of the blessing of viaticum. Henceforth be cautious about their counsels; and guard yourself carefully, lest, if you are their disciple in evil when you ought to have been their teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.

[Note: In four Vatican manuscripts, “in the month of October, indiction 11” is added. But in the Colbert manuscript, “in the month of September, indiction 11” precedes this letter.]

(Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapters 32 and 44.)

## EPISTLE II. TO VITALIS, DEFENDER OF SARDINIA

Let him carry out the excommunication decreed against Januarius’s counselors. Let him restore the full price of the gift.

Gregory to Vitalis, defender at Caralis.

What we have learned about our brother Januarius, bishop, can be explained to you by the bearer of this letter and by copies of our writings. Therefore let Your Experience carefully carry out the excommunication which we have decreed against his wicked counselors, so that those who fall may learn that they must not walk carelessly.

Moreover, we have sent through the bearer of this letter the price of the wheat that had been transmitted to us as a gift, to Redemptus the defender.

[Note: EPISTLE II [Al. 53, Book IX, indiction 6].—Other editions read *Redeemer*. *Redemptus* is preferable, as the following letter suggests, where the same defender is mentioned.]

Let Your Experience see to it that neither you nor the man who carried it takes any share of profit from its price, but that he restore the whole amount, either to each person individually or to all together, without diminution, and send me their written acknowledgments concerning that price. For if I learn that anything has been done otherwise than I command, I shall exact no small vengeance on account of it.

## EPISTLE III. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

Nothing is to be demanded for a granted place of burial. If something is voluntarily offered for lights, however, it may be accepted.

Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Caralis.

Nereida, a distinguished woman, has complained to us that Your Fraternity is not ashamed to demand from her one hundred solidi for the burial of her daughter and is striving to inflict upon her, in addition to the groaning of grief, the further distress of financial loss. If the truth is as she states, then, since it is exceedingly grave and far removed from the priestly office to seek a price for earth granted to corruption and to wish to make profit from another’s mourning, let Your Fraternity refrain from this demand and do not trouble her hereafter—especially since she also recalls that Hortulanus, from whom she asserts that she herself was born, was exceedingly generous toward your Church.

After we, by God’s authority, attained the honor of the episcopate, we likewise completely prohibited this vice in our Church and did not permit the wicked custom to be taken up again, remembering that when Abraham sought from the sons of Emor—that is, from Ephron son of Seor—a burial place for burying his wife’s body at a price, he refused to accept the price, lest he appear to have gained an advantage from a corpse (Genesis 23). If therefore that pagan man showed such consideration, how much more ought we, who are called priests, not to do this?

I therefore admonish you lest this vice of avarice should again be presumed upon, even among others. But whenever you permit someone to be buried in your Church, if his parents, relatives, or heirs should voluntarily wish to offer something for lights, we do not forbid you to accept it.

[Note: EPISTLE III [Al. 56].—Burial in churches has already been discussed in the note to chapter 50 of Book IV of the *Dialogues*. Saint Ambrose sufficiently shows this to be an ancient custom, Book I, *On Abraham*, chapter 9, no. 80: “There were not yet temples of God of this kind in which the remains of the faithful might be buried to the Lord.” New edition, column 308.]

[Note: Here the reference is to lights at the funerals of the dead. Gregory frequently discusses lights in churches, especially in the *Dialogues*. Consult the notes to the *Book of Sacraments*, 577 and 1060.]

But we altogether forbid anything to be requested or demanded. This is highly irreligious, lest the Church should perhaps, God forbid, be called venal, or lest you appear to rejoice in human deaths if you strive by any means to seek profit from their corpses. (See Book VIII, Epistle 3.)

As for the other matters included in the aforesaid Nereida’s petition, we exhort you either to settle them by a peaceful arrangement, if this can be done, or at least not to fail to send an instructed representative to the judgment assigned by us. For this reason we have sent our defender Redemptus, the bearer of this letter, there: both to compel the parties to attend the proceedings and to bring to completion, through the urgency of his execution, whatever has been judged.

[Note: That is, to be present for the case. The word is found in Pliny’s letter to Rufus, Book V: “The judges were sitting, the centumviral court had assembled, they were being observed”—that is, cases were being pleaded before them. “A long silence for the advocates,” namely, while the silence-officers provided the hearing and suppressed the murmuring. Auget.]

[Note: Two Teller manuscripts read: “in the month of March, indiction 11.”]

## EPISTLE IV. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

Until the peace arranged with Agilulf is confirmed, he must beware of a renewed invasion of Sardinia. He again rebukes Januarius, out of brotherly affection, for plowing up the crop.

[Col. 0941C]

Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Sardinia.

[Note: EPISTLE IV [Al. 2].—The printed editions read “to the bishop of Caralis.” Januarius was indeed bishop of Caralis. Nevertheless, since all the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, Royal, and other manuscripts read “to the bishop of Sardis” or “of Sardinia,” we have judged that they should be followed.]

We learned what our enemies did in Sardinia before the letter of Your Fraternity reached us. And because we feared this would happen long ago, we now grieve with you that what we foresaw has occurred. If vigilance had been exercised in accordance with what we wrote when announcing to both you and our excellent son Gennadius that this would happen, the enemy would either not have come there or, on coming, would have suffered the danger they caused. Let what has happened sharpen your vigilance for the future. Nor do we, with the Lord’s help, fail to do whatever we can that may be useful.

You should also know that the abbot whom we sent to Agilulf a long time ago has arranged peace with him, as our excellent exarch has written to us, God being propitious. Therefore, until the agreements confirming that peace have been written down, lest our enemies wish during this delay to come again into those regions, have watchmen and guards deployed at all places. We trust in the power of our Redeemer that no renewed attack or ambush of the enemy will harm you.

[Col. 0942B]

What you have written—that many people are bringing complaints against you to us—is true. But among these various matters nothing has saddened us as much as what our most beloved son Cyriacus, the abbot, reported: that on the Lord’s Day, before Mass, you had the crop in the field possessed by Donatus plowed up. As if that were not enough, after the sacrifice was completed, you went there yourself and uprooted the boundaries.

For this reason I exhort you to consider carefully, with an attentive mind, the office you hold; to avoid entirely whatever can burden either your reputation or your soul; and not to consent to commit such an act at anyone’s persuasion. Recognize that you have undertaken the leadership not of earthly affairs but of souls. There you must fix your heart, there your concern, there you must apply all your effort; and you must think diligently about their profit, so that when the Lord comes you may return the talents he entrusted to you multiplied, and may deserve to receive from him the fruit of your reward and to be exalted among faithful servants in eternal glory.

Know that what I censure or rebuke does not proceed from harshness but from brotherly affection, because I desire to find you before almighty God a priest not merely in name—which leads only to punishment—but also in merits, which looks toward reward. For since we are one member in the body of our Redeemer, I am wounded when you sin, and I likewise rejoice in good action. (See above, Epistle 1.)

You also wish us to appoint a representative from our side, to whom you should carefully communicate your cases so that they may be reported back to us.

[Note: Hence legates *a latere* are chosen from among those who are continually engaged in the service of the supreme pontiff; concerning them, see chapter *Ad eminentiam*, under *On Excommunication*, in the *Extra*. Others are simply legates, concerning whom there is the title *On the Office of a Legate*, in Book I of the *Extra*, where some chapters concerning a legate *a latere* are also inserted. Finally, there are legates born by reason of their churches, such as the archbishop of Rheims and similar figures; concerning them, see Canon 1, *On a Legate*, in the Sixth Book. Conrad Braun comprehensively treated the entire doctrine of legates in five books in 1548. Gregory of Tours, Book V of the *History*, chapter 29: “The king sends men from his side.” Gussanville. See the notes to Epistle 31 of Book V. Council of Carthage under Boniface, A.D. 419, Canon 3: “If the one who asks that his case be heard again should move the Roman bishop by his entreaty, so that he sends a presbyter from his side.” This passage confirms the antiquity of legates *a latere*, already asserted elsewhere.]

Write whatever you wish to our most beloved sons Peter and Theodore the counselor, so that, once it has been reported to us through them, whatever reason may advise in these matters may be arranged with the Lord’s revelation. Concerning our brother and fellow bishop Marinianos, there will be an inquiry once peace with the aforesaid Agilulf has been fully confirmed, and whatever the order of reason dictates will be done.

## EPISTLE V. TO MARCELLUS, PROCONSUL OF DALMATIA

He rebukes him for having favored Maximus. He explains how he may return to favor with him.

Gregory to Marcellus, proconsul of Dalmatia.

[Note: EPISTLE V [Al. 3].—This letter is not contained in the Royal, Norman, English, Corbie, Rheims, or Colbert manuscripts. Of the Vatican manuscripts, only Codex A contains it. See above, Book III, Epistle 22. It was formerly read as *Marcellinus*. This is indeed how it appears in the Vatican manuscript, in which alone the letter is generally found; but from the other letters in which the same man is mentioned—all of which are contained in the manuscripts—we should read *Marcellus*.]

We received a letter from Your Excellency in which you declared that you had incurred our displeasure and, for this reason, wished by a direct satisfaction to regain our favor.

[Note: French, *disgrâce*. Ptolemy Flavius, in his *Conjectures*, says that this word is somewhat harsh and rare among the ancients. Certainly in this meaning it seems exceedingly rare, if it occurs at all. Commonly they use it for the fault of an ungrateful spirit, which Cicero called *ἀχαριστία* (*acharistia*, ingratitude). Tertullian, *On Repentance*, chapter 1, calls it *ingratia*. Gussanville.]

Indeed, reports concerning Your Excellency have reached us of such a kind as ought never to have been committed by a faithful man. For everyone asserts that you were responsible for the whole affair of Maximus, through which the plundering of that Church, the destruction of so many souls, and the audacity of unheard-of presumption first began.

Since you ask to regain our favor, it is appropriate that with the whole intention of your mind, as is fitting, you should satisfy our Redeemer concerning such matters, with tears; for if satisfaction has not been made to him, what can our release or favor certainly contribute?

[Note: Thus the holy Fathers speak: Christ brings Lazarus back to life, while the apostles loose his bonds. Consider this statement as directed against rash absolutions and indulgences, if any are granted. Gussanville.]

Yet while we still see you involved in the ruin of presumptuous men or in the defenses of those who have gone astray, we do not see what kind of satisfaction you are making either to God or to human beings. Your Excellency will then plainly and unmistakably know that you are satisfying God and human beings, if you bring what has gone astray back to rectitude and what has been presumptuous back to the rule of humility.

[Note: The Rheims manuscript, which contains letters omitted from nearly all the other manuscripts, reads: “strive to recall.”]

If this is done, know that through it you will obtain both God’s favor and that of human beings.

## EPISTLE VI. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

The synagogue occupied by Peter, recently baptized, is to be restored to the Jews; they are not to be compelled to the faith. The citizens’ minds are to be reconciled to one another through fear of the enemy, and the city is to be more strongly fortified.

[Col. 0944A]

Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Caralis.

The Jews who came here from your city complained to us that their synagogue, situated at Caralis, was occupied without your consent, with grave scandal, by Peter—who, by God’s will, had been led from their superstition to the worship of the Christian faith—together with certain undisciplined men whom he had enlisted, on the day after his baptism, that is, on the Sunday of the very feast of Easter; and that there he had placed an image of the Mother of God and of our Lord, a venerable cross, and a white *birrus* in which he had been clothed when he rose from the font.

[Note: EPISTLE VI [Al. 5].—Cicero uses *exleges* for those unwilling to obey the laws. Gussanville.]

[Note: In Greek, βῆριον, βίρρος, βίρριον, hence *birrophoroi*. Some read, but incorrectly, “a white *pyrrus*,” as Jonas does in *On the Institution of Images*, Book I. The word is sometimes used for a servile garment, as in Suidas. I would suppose that it is used here for any kind of garment. Consult Salmasius on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*. Some used *byrrus* or *burrus* for a cheap garment, French *bure* or *bureau*. Here it is used for an expensive one; thus Isidore, *Rule*, chapter 14: “A *birrus* is an expensive garment and is consequently forbidden to monks.” Some consider the *birrus* to have been a kind of shorter cloak, customary among clerics even in the time of the Council of Gangra—namely, a short mantle covering only the shoulders and arms. Gussanville. Concerning the *birrus*, see the note to this Epistle 42 of Book I, where an important passage mentioning *byrri* is quoted from Sulpicius Severus. Explaining this passage, Salmasius considers the *byrrus*, *lacerna*, and *chlamys* to be the same garment, differing only in name. He says that the *byrrus* was generally the color of *byrrus*, that is, reddish, from which it took its name; for, he says, the Latins called what the Greeks called πυρρόν (*pyrron*) *burrus* or *byrrus*. But cloaks of any color were also called *byrri* metaphorically. When the Romans had abandoned the toga, they used *byrri* or *lacernas*. For the rest, see the edition carefully prepared by Hornius.]

The same matter was attested to us in written reports by our sons Eupaterius, the distinguished master of soldiers, and the magnificent and devout governor in the Lord, together with other nobles of your city. They also added that you had intended this, and that the aforesaid Peter had been forbidden to dare it.

[Note: Perhaps this was the man to whom Book XI, Epistle 22, is addressed, where he is called Spesindeus.]

When we learned this, we praised you entirely, because, as truly became a good priest, you wished nothing to be done from which just blame could arise. But since, by not involving yourself at all in the things wrongly done, you showed that you disapproved of what had been done, we have considered the intention and, rather, the judgment of your will in this matter. We therefore exhort you by these words: after removing from there, with the veneration they deserve, the image and the cross, you must restore what was taken away by force. For just as legal definition does not allow the Jews to erect new synagogues, so it permits them to possess their old ones without disturbance.

Therefore, the aforesaid Peter and the others who gave him assistance or consent in this undisciplined wickedness must not reply that they did this out of zeal for the faith, so that necessity might thereby be imposed upon the Jews to convert. They must be admonished and must know that toward them this moderation is to be used: they are to be drawn to willingness not to resist, not compelled against their will. For it is written: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Psalm 58:8); and: “I will confess to him of my own will” (Psalm 27:7).

Your Holiness should therefore strive, with the assistance of your sons who, together with you, disapprove of these things, to bring about concord among the inhabitants of your city through priestly exhortation, as befits you. For especially at this time, when there is fear of the enemy, you must not have the people divided.

Since we are no less concerned for you than for ourselves, we have also taken care to indicate this: once this peace has ended, Agilulf, king of the Lombards, will not make peace.

[Note: That is, during this truce. It is nevertheless clear from Epistles 42 and 43 of this book that peace with the Lombards was later more firmly established.]

It is therefore necessary that Your Fraternity, while the opportunity remains, provide for your city and other places to be more strongly fortified, and ensure that provisions are stored abundantly in them, so that when the enemy comes there, God being angry with him, he will find nothing to damage and will depart in confusion. We too are thinking about you as much as we can, and we are urging those whom it concerns to prepare themselves, with God’s help, to resist; for just as you regard our tribulations as your own, so we likewise regard your afflictions as ours.

## EPISTLE VII. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

Although the abbess did not wear the monastic habit, her testament is nevertheless invalid under imperial law; therefore what Sirica unlawfully gave to others is to be returned to the monastery.

Gregory to Januarius, Bishop of Caralis.

Since those entering a monastery for the sake of conversion (Gratian, 19, question 3, chapter 7) henceforth have no permission to make a will [Note: [Col. 0945C] EPISTLE VII.—Those professing the monastic life never possessed the power of making wills, as Saint Gregory teaches here most clearly, if divine law and the sacred laws are taken into account. For one may make a will only concerning one’s own property. But monks possess nothing of their own, as is demonstrated by all the monastic rules—namely, those of Pachomius, Basil, Augustine, Benedict, and others. Consult the Harmony of the Rules, at chapter 42; the Rule of Saint Benedict, pp. 612 ff.; and the observations of our Hugh Menard. Yet according to human laws monks were sometimes able to make wills; and if they died intestate, they had as heirs their children, parents, or agnates; when these were lacking, their property passed to the monastery, according to the single law of the Theodosian Code, On the Property of Clerics and Monks. Augustine, Letter 239: “So fully, however, does that property under discussion belong by the same law to the presbyter Honoratus that, although he had been ordained elsewhere, while he was still living in the monastery at Thagaste, if he had died without selling his property or transferring it to anyone by an explicit gift, no one but his heirs would have succeeded to it, just as the brother Aemilianus succeeded to those thirty solidi in place of his brother Privatus.” Later the power of making wills was taken away from monks, so that upon entering a monastery their property passed to the monastery: Justinian, Novel V and Novel 123, chapter 38. Gregory, Letter formerly 22, indiction 4, now in the appendix, grants Abbot Probus permission to make a will. Likewise to the monk Adeodatus, Book XIII, Letter 3. Under pontifical law monks may make wills by dispensation of the supreme pontiff: chapter *Cum ad Monasterium*, On the Status of Monks. See Mabillon, On the Wills of Abbots, Book I of *De re diplomatica*, chapter 2, no. 10.], it has been decreed by the clear provision of the law that their property becomes the property of that same monastery. Since this is known to almost everyone, we were brought to great astonishment by the report concerning Gavinia, abbess of the monastery of the saints Gavinus and Luxorius [Note: [Col. 0946C] Thus it is read in three Vatican manuscripts and in most others, not *Gravini*, as the printed editions have it. We read that Saint Gavinus, or Gabinus, suffered martyrdom at Torres in Sardinia on the third day before the Kalends of June. Saint Luxorius also suffered in Sardinia, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. We believe that this monastery in Sardinia was dedicated to the memory of both martyrs.], namely, that Sirica, abbess of her monastery, after assuming the office of governance, was said to have left certain bequests by will to various persons.

And when we were investigating, with concern for your holiness, why she had allowed property belonging to the monastery to be held by others, your common son Epiphanius, your archpresbyter, who happened to be present, replied that the aforementioned abbess had refused, until the day of her death, to put on the monastic habit, but had remained in the garments worn by the *presbyterae* of that place [Note: [Col. 0946C] It is not clear to me what garments the *presbyterae* wore. The term *presbyterae* was applied to women whose husbands had converted and been ordained presbyters, after they had promised to maintain continence thereafter. Converted wives are mentioned in the Council of Arles II, canon 5. See Baronius, at the year 405, no. 60; the Council of Orléans IV, canon 17; Tours II, canon 20; Auxerre, canon 21. The name *presbyterae* is also sometimes found among ecclesiastical writers for elderly widows, called in Greek *presbytides* (πρεσβύτιδες), as in the Council of Laodicea, final canon, and in Athanasius, *To the Virgins*. Perhaps Saint Gregory is speaking of these women, since they were distinguished by a particular kind of dress. Just as the wives of presbyters were called *presbyterae*, so the wives of bishops were called *episcopae*, in Tours II, canon 13. See also the same council, canon 19; Auxerre, canons 21 and 22, and elsewhere. GUSSANVILLE. Mabillon notes, *De re diplomatica*, chapter 2, no. 10, that in an old parchment containing a fragment of this letter, which Antonius Vion Herouvallius communicated to him, the reading is *plebeiae* rather than *presbyterae*. He judges that reading preferable, so that the sense would be that Sirica was dressed in common clothing, such as the laywomen of that place wore. We have encountered no manuscript in which *presbyterae* is not read. Indeed, the dress of a *presbytera* suited this abbess better than the clothing of a common woman.]. To this the aforesaid Gavinia replied that this had been permitted almost by custom, going so far as to claim that the abbess who had preceded the aforementioned Sirica had likewise worn such garments.

When, therefore, we had begun to have considerable doubts concerning the nature of the clothing, it seemed necessary to discuss with our counsellors and with the other learned men of this city what ought to be done according to the law. After deliberation, they replied that, once the abbess had been solemnly appointed by the bishop and had presided over the governance of the monastery for many years, until her passing from this life, the matter of the clothing might perhaps concern the fault of the bishop who had allowed her to remain so dressed; nevertheless, it could not prejudice the monastery, but by manifest right her property belonged to that place from the time when she entered it and was established as abbess.

And therefore, since the xenodochium claims to be improperly retaining possession of property left unlawfully, we exhort you in these words: since both the monastery and that xenodochium are situated in your city, you must provide with every care and diligence that, if this possession derives not from any prior transaction but from the legacy of the aforesaid Sirica, it be restored to the said monastery, with all contention and excuse set aside. But if it is said to have come from some other transaction, then either, after your fraternity has learned the truth between the parties, let it determine what the legal order requires, or let the parties mutually choose arbitrators who can distinguish their allegations [Note: [Col. 0947C] In Vatican D, *dirimere*; in the Norman manuscript, *discingere*; in the printed editions, *discindere*. We follow four Vatican manuscripts.]. Whatever they decide must be preserved by your provision in such a way that no quarrel remain between these venerable places, whose mutual peace must be fostered with the greatest care.

All the other property being held on the basis of the testament of the aforementioned Sirica—for that testament is not permitted by legal sanction to have any validity—must therefore, through the priestly diligence of your fraternity, be restored in every respect to the rights of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0947C] Vatican A and B read *studio separentur*, that is, “be separated through diligence” from the property of the xenodochium, so that they may be restored to the monastery.], because imperial legislation expressly decreed [Note: [Col. 0947C] See the Code, Book I, titles 19, 21, 22, and 23, and the *Decretum*, distinction 10.] that things done contrary to the laws are to be regarded not only as useless but also as nonexistent (Gratian, 25, question 2, chapter 13).

[Note: [Col. 0947C] EPISTLE VIII.—We have restored this title from many manuscript codices and from the ancient and more reliable editions. GUSSANVILLE.]

## EPISTLE VIII. TO THE BISHOPS OF SARDINIA

They are to receive the Paschal announcement, according to custom, from the metropolitan; nor are they to leave the island without his permission.

Gregory to Vincent, Innocent, [Note: [Col. 0947C] Bishop of Torres, a city of Sardinia; concerning it, see what we said at Letter 59, now 61, of Book I.], Marinianus, Libertinus, Agatho, [Note: [Col. 0947C] Bishop of Phausania. On Phausania see what was said at Letter 29 of Book III, now Book IV. I have found nothing concerning the other four bishops of Sardinia. It should be noted in passing that these six bishops were suffragans of the bishop of Cagliari, who in this letter is also called metropolitan. GUSSANVILLE.] and Victor, bishops of Sardinia.

[Note: [Col. 0947C] The question of on what day and at what time the Paschal feast ought to be celebrated was often debated in the Church, perhaps with more heated zeal than was proper. Ancient authors report that Saint John the Evangelist favored the Quartodecimans. Pope Victor of Rome decreed, with censures added, that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, many bishops agreeing with Saint Irenaeus. Finally, at Arles I in 314, canon 1, it was decreed that Easter should be observed throughout the whole world on one day and at one time, and that, according to custom, letters should be sent to all by the Roman pontiff. The matter was again discussed and settled eleven years later at the Synod of Nicaea; responsibility for preparing the Paschal cycles was entrusted to the bishop of the Church of Alexandria, who was to send those prepared to Rome, so that by this means the bishops of the whole world might agree in celebrating Easter. Few are unaware that these announcements of the coming Easter were customarily made by a deacon at the feast of Epiphany, since that practice has continued almost to our own times, as the official books, or *Rituales* as they are called, testify. In the Roman *Sacerdotale* printed at Venice in 1597, this announcement is found and sung. See Orléans IV, canon 1; Auxerre, canon 2. Observe, however, from Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book V, chapter 17, that there was doubt about the day of Easter and that it was sometimes not celebrated everywhere at the same time. GUSSANVILLE. See also Cointius, at the year 539, no. 15.]

We have learned that it is the custom of your island, after the Paschal feast, for you yourselves to go—or to send your representatives—to your metropolitan [Note: [Col. 0947C] The rights of the metropolitan are to be preserved inviolate according to the provisions of the canons: Nicaea, canon 4; Antioch, canons 9, 11, 12, 19, and 20; Carthage, canon 23. GUSSANVILLE. Vatican D and E read “to the metropolitan city”; the Rhemes manuscript agrees.], whether you know this or not, so that he should send you a written announcement concerning the coming Easter. And, as is reported, some of you, postponing this according to custom, also turn the hearts of others toward disobedience.

It is further reported that certain of you, seeking to cross the sea on account of matters arising in your churches, dare to travel without the knowledge or letters of the aforesaid metropolitan, as the canonical order prescribes. We therefore exhort your fraternity, as you follow the ancient custom of your churches, both with regard to receiving the Paschal announcement and whenever necessity compels any of you to travel anywhere for your own affairs, to seek permission from that same metropolitan according to the rule prescribed for you [Note: [Col. 0948C] Recent printed editions read “to ask permission, thereby correcting this fault.” The older editions, following Vatican D and the Rhemes manuscript, read “to ask a concession.” Vatican B reads “to ask for letters.”]. Do not presume to disregard him in anything—unless, which we do not wish, you happen to have some cause against that same metropolitan, so that on this account those who hasten to seek it may have permission to request the judgment of the Apostolic See, a privilege that you know is permitted by the canons and also by the institution of the ancient Fathers (Gratian, 26, question 7, chapter 45) [Note: [Col. 0948C] We have restored this wording from three Vatican manuscripts, three Colbertine manuscripts, and the Rhemes manuscript. The Norman manuscripts come close, omitting only “through the canons.” The printed editions read: “so that on this account you may seek the judgment of the Apostolic See. For those who hasten to request permission, as you know, are permitted by the canons, and also by the institution of the ancient Fathers.” Gregory is alluding to the Sardican canons, though theologians dispute their meaning.].

[Note: [Col. 0948D] EPISTLE IX.—See below, Letter 95, to the same exarch. He had succeeded Romanus in the exarchate.]

## EPISTLE IX. TO CALLINICUS, EXARCH OF ITALY

He rejoices that the schismatics are returning to the Church. The emperors should be informed of this. The only thing forbidden by them is that the schismatics be compelled to unity. He complains about Callinicus’s chief official. He asks him henceforth not to call the schismatic Justinus into his council.

Gregory to Callinicus, exarch of Italy.

Amid these matters, when you announced to me victories over the Slavs [Note: [Col. 0948D] The Latins call them *Sclavi* and *Sclavini*, later writers *Slavi*, and the Greeks σθλάβοι and σθλαβῖνοι (*Sthlábōi* and *Sthlabînoi*). The form σκλάβοι (*Sklábōi*) is also found in Simocatta and other later writers. Helmold writes of them as follows, Book I, chapter 1: “The name of the Slavs spread so widely that it almost escaped all reckoning. For, spreading toward the north and east, they brought provinces and broad regions under their rule. At length, gradually conquered by princes at various times, they were compelled to serve, and their name began to be turned into contempt and reproach, so that it came to designate people of servile and dependent condition.” In Greek, *Sthlabogeneis* (σθλαβογενεῖς); in French, *esclaves*. GUSSANVILLE. Concerning the Slavs, see also below, Book X, indiction 3, Letter 36. Meanwhile consult Theophanes, *Chronicle*, and Simocatta, Book I, chapter 7.], know that I was relieved by great joy, because the bearers of this letter, sent by your Excellency from the island of Capritana [Note: [Col. 0949D] This is a small island in the innermost recess of the Adriatic Gulf, near the coast of the province of Forum Julii. The city on it, still an episcopal see, which is under discussion here, is Caprulae, commonly called Cahorle or Caorla.], hastening to be joined to the unity of the holy Church, have been sent to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

For you prevail more greatly over your enemies if you bring back under the yoke of the true Lord those whom you recognize as enemies of God. And you conduct your own affairs among men with greater strength in proportion as you have pursued God’s affairs among men with a sincere and devoted mind.

As for the copy of the order that was sent to you in defense of the schismatics, which you wished to have shown to me, your most beloved Excellency ought to have considered it carefully. Although the order itself was obtained surreptitiously, you were not commanded in it to repel those coming to the unity of the Church, but merely not to compel, at this troubled time, those unwilling to come. Therefore you must hasten to bring this very matter to the attention of our most pious emperors, so that they may know that in their time the schismatics, with the help of almighty God and through your efforts, are hastening of their own accord to return.

Your Excellency will learn through our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus what I have decreed concerning the organization of the island of Capritana. But know that I was deeply saddened by the fact that your chief official, who had accepted the petition of a bishop wishing to return, claimed that he had lost it, and that afterward it was held by the adversaries of the Church. I believe that this happened not through his negligence but through his venality. I therefore wonder why your Excellency did not at all punish him for this fault [Note: [Col. 0949D] The Rhemes manuscript reads, “because your Excellency did not punish him for this fault”; three Vatican manuscripts read, “because your Excellency did not punish them for this fault.”]. Yet because I wondered at this, I quickly reproached myself. For where the lord Justinus gives counsel, he who is not at peace with the Catholic Church, heretics cannot be condemned [Note: [Col. 0949D] The printed editions read *haeretici adduci*, “heretics may be brought forward.” The reading *addici*, found in five English manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, the Regius manuscript, and nearly all the others, means “to be condemned,” as we have shown elsewhere. This reading also confirms the preceding reading of the three Vatican manuscripts, “against them”—that is, against the heretics—“he did not at all punish this fault.”].

Furthermore, you report that you wish to celebrate in the city of Rome the feast day of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. We pray almighty God to protect you by his mercy and grant the fulfillment of your wishes. But I ask that the aforesaid most eloquent man come with you; if he does not come, let him withdraw from your service. Or certainly, if your Excellency should perhaps be unable to come because of urgent affairs, let him either enter into communion with the unity of the holy Church, or, I ask, let him not participate in your counsels. I hear that he is a good man, if only he were not involved in the worst error.

As for the case of Maximus, since we can no longer endure the importunity of your sweetness, you will learn what we have decided from the report of the notary Castorius (cf. John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 44).

## EPISTLE X. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He is to ordain a bishop for the island of Capritana unless John, having been admonished by him, returns to the unity of the Church and to his own people. He is to investigate and settle the case of Maximus, calling upon Constantius of Milan if necessary.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

The bearers of this letter, the distinguished men Vicedominus and Defensor, have come to us, asserting that in the fortress called Nova [Note: [Col. 0950D] EPISTLE X.—Nova, once an episcopal see in Venetia, is now a place in the March of Treviso, between Concordia and Treviso. It is commonly called Cittanova distrutta and is subject to Venetian rule. GUSSANVILLE.] a certain bishop named John, coming from Pannonia, had been installed; the island belonging to that fortress, called Capritana, was attached to it as though by diocesan jurisdiction.

They add that, after that bishop had been violently removed and expelled, another was ordained there [Note: [Col. 0950D] Thus the Colbertine, Vatican D and E, Rhemes, Norman, and other manuscripts read it. The editors rearranged the passage as follows: “after that bishop had been violently expelled by the Istrian bishop.”]. Concerning this second bishop, however, they report that it had been agreed that he should live not in the aforesaid fortress but on his own island. While he was living there with them, he did not wish to remain in the error of schism; and together with all his people he submitted a petition to our most excellent son Callinicus, the exarch, asking that he and all those who were with him should be united to the Catholic Church, as we have said.

But, as they say, after being persuaded by the schismatics, he returned to them, and now all the people who live on the aforesaid island are deprived of the protection of a priest. For although they desire to be united to the holy Church, they can no longer receive the man who has returned to the error of the schismatics, and they request that another be ordained for them.

But because it is necessary for us to examine everything strictly and carefully, we have determined that your fraternity should send to that bishop and admonish him to return to the unity of the Catholic Church and to his own people. If, after being admonished, he refuses to return, the flock of God must not be deceived by the error of its shepherd. Therefore let your holiness ordain a bishop there and have that same island within his diocese until the Istrian bishops return to the Catholic faith. Thus the rights of each church within its diocese will be preserved, and protection and the care of governance will not be lacking to a people abandoned by its shepherd.

In all this, however, your fraternity must watch carefully, so that the same people who have come to the Church may be admonished with even greater diligence to remain steadfastly fixed in their return and not fall back through wavering thoughts into the pit of error.

Let your fraternity also endeavor to ask the most excellent exarch to make these matters known through his own representations to the ears of the most pious emperors. Although the order delivered to him appears to have been obtained surreptitiously, he was not commanded in that order to prevent those wishing to return to the Church from doing so, but merely not to compel the unwilling during this present period.

Let the aforesaid son of ours therefore take the administration of this matter into his care, so that through his replies he may act in such a way that there be no doubt about whatever he decides. We have also written concerning this to our common son Anatolius, so that the matter may be carefully made known to the most pious rulers.

I have continually and importunately received letters from my most excellent son, the lord Callinicus the exarch, on behalf of Maximus [Note: [Col. 0951D] The case of Maximus and Honoratus has already been dealt with frequently; see below, Letters 79, 80, and 81.]. Overcome by his persistence, I had nothing further to do except entrust the case of that same Maximus to your fraternity.

If, therefore, the same Maximus comes to your fraternity, let Honoratus, the archdeacon of his church, also be brought forward, so that your holiness may determine whether he was rightly ordained, whether he has fallen into the Simoniac heresy, whether any bodily crimes have been charged against him, and whether he knew himself to be excommunicated when he presumed to celebrate Mass. Whatever seems right to you under the fear of God, decree it, so that, God being the author, we may give our assent to your decision.

But if the aforesaid son of ours should regard your fraternity with suspicion, let our most reverend brother Constantius, bishop of Milan, also come to Ravenna, sit with you, and decide together with you concerning the same case. Be assured that whatever pleases both of you will please me.

For just as we must not be obstinate toward the humble, so we must be firm toward the proud. Therefore, as your fraternity has learned in the pages of sacred Scripture, let it decree whatever it judges just in this matter.

## EPISTLE XI. TO BRUNICHILD, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

He grants the pallium to Bishop Syagrius. He admonishes her not to confer sacred orders as a reward or favor, and not to make laymen bishops suddenly. He praises her affection toward Augustine and urges her to strive to restore the schismatics to concord and to suppress the remnants of idolatry and other vices in her kingdom. He discusses the book sent to her.

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

How firmly your Excellency’s mind is established in the fear of almighty God, you show, among the other good works you perform, by your praiseworthy love for his priests. We rejoice greatly in your Christianity, because you honor those whom you venerate as servants of Christ and whom you truly love, and you strive to increase their honors.

It is fitting for you, most excellent daughter [Note: [Col. 0951D] All the Norman manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, the Colbertine manuscript, and others read in the plural, “most excellent daughters.”], it is fitting for you to be such that you can remain subject to the ruler. For you confirm the kingdom of your power and the peoples subject to you precisely by submitting the neck of your mind to the fear of almighty God; and by subjecting yourselves to the service of the Creator, you bind your subjects more devotedly to your service.

Accordingly, having received your letters, we indicate that your Excellency’s zeal has greatly pleased us. We wished to send the pallium to our brother and fellow bishop Syagrius [Note: [Col. 0951D] Two matters concerning the pallium are noteworthy here. First, it is given to a bishop. Second, the emperor’s approval is added. The earliest record we have of a pallium granted by the Roman pontiff is in Symmachus, Letter 11, to Theodore, metropolitan of Laureacum in Pannonia. The same pontiff specially honored Caesarius of Arles with the privilege of the pallium, as we read in his *Life*, Book I, no. 22. Thereafter the use of the pallium was granted chiefly to those entrusted with apostolic vicariate authority, and also to others, whether metropolitans or mere bishops, from whom great assistance was expected for the benefit of the Church—those who flourished through virtues, nobility, or great favor with kings. For this reason Syagrius received the pallium from Gregory the Great. This was broadly the practice of granting the pallium until Pope Zachary. At his command, in 742, a synod was convened by Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, in which it was decreed that metropolitans should thereafter seek the pallium from the Roman See and obey all Saint Peter’s commands, as Boniface himself writes in Letter 105 to Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury. This rule spread first throughout Gaul, then gradually through Spain and other regions, and began to be observed by all.].

For this reason, and because our most serene lord the emperor has a willing disposition toward it and altogether desires that it be granted, as our deacon who was conducting the affairs of the Church before him has informed us, we wished to send it according to your request [Note: [Col. 0952D] This letter establishes that the pallium was not granted without the emperor’s consent. The same is clear from the first and second letters of Pope Vigilius, who granted the pallium to Auxanius of Arles only with the approval of the emperor Justinian. Was this because it was a kind of imperial ornament? Learned men have fought over the question and have adopted various opinions. See the illustrious de Marca, *De concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, Book I; Cointius, at the year 599. But above all see Cantelius, *History of Metropolitan Cities*, volume I, part I, dissertation 3, chapter 2.]. Much favorable testimony concerning our aforesaid brother has also reached us, both from you and from others, especially concerning his life, as we learned when John, the regionary deacon, returned to us [Note: [Col. 0953C] The seven regionary deacons were considered the principal deacons of Rome. Unlike the titular presbyters, they were subject to the archdeacon, who was first among those seven. Each of them had charge of the deaconries located in the region assigned to him. See Mabillon, preliminary commentary on the *Ordo Romanus*, chapter 3. Saint Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 14, established that just as regionary officials had long been constituted in the school of notaries and subdeacons through the generosity of former pontiffs, so also among the defenders seven men who had pleased by the usefulness of their experience should be honored with the regionary dignity.].

And when we heard what he had done for our brother Augustine, we blessed our Redeemer, because we perceived that he fulfilled the name of priest even by his works. But many matters intervened that prevented us from doing this for the time being.
