First, the man who had come to receive the pallium was entangled in the error of the schismatics [Note: [Col. 0953C] Namely, those who had stubbornly defended the Three Chapters against the Fifth Council, chiefly alleging that, if those three chapters were condemned, the authority of the Council of Chalcedon would be injured, since Ibas, together with his letter and the commendation of Theodore of Mopsuestia, had been approved there, and Theodoret had been restored to his see. That controversy was therefore troubling Gaul. The same schismatics are discussed somewhat below.].

Second, you wished it to be understood that this had been sent not at your request but on our own initiative. Moreover, the man who desired to use it had not asked us by a formal petition to grant it to him, and we ought by no means to provide so great a benefit without his request—especially since ancient custom has established that the honor of the pallium should not be given unless the merits of the case require it and the recipient makes a vigorous request [Note: [Col. 0953D] Perhaps so that the emperor would have no reason to suspect that Rome, disdaining Greek rule, was seeking the assistance of neighboring nations through the pallium; for that reason the pontiff offered it to no one, indeed granted it to no one except one who requested it forcefully. See the Cantelius cited above.] (Gratian, distinction 100, chapter 2).

Nevertheless, lest we appear to wish to delay your Excellency’s desire under the pretext of some excuse, we have arranged for the pallium to be sent to our beloved son Candidus, the presbyter, instructing him that he should confer it in our place with the proper observance. Therefore the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Syagrius must, by making a request together with several of his bishops, hope to obtain it through his own action and present that request to the aforesaid presbyter, so that by God’s grace he may worthily receive the use of the same pallium.

Therefore, so that this concern may bear fruit for you before the eyes of our Creator, let the solicitude of your Christianity watch over it carefully. Do not allow anyone under your rule to approach a sacred order through the payment of money, the patronage of any persons, or the right of family connection. Instead, let the one whose life and character have shown him worthy be chosen for the office of bishop or of any other sacred order.

For if, which we do not wish, the honor of the priesthood becomes purchasable, the Simoniac heresy—which first arose in the Church and was condemned by the judgment of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0953D] Recent editions read “by the judgment of Peter,” but nearly all the manuscript codices, as well as the older editions of 1504, 1508, 1539, and others, disagree. By “the Fathers” he means the apostles. See below, Letter 106, where, intending to attack simony solely by the authority of Christ and the apostles, he begins: “We address your fraternity by apostolic titles, relying upon the rules of the Fathers and the commands of the Lord,” and so forth. In Book XI, Letter 61, he says: “Simony has been condemned by the authority of the Apostles.”]—may arise and weaken the strength of your kingdom, God forbid. For it is an altogether grave crime, beyond what can be expressed, to sell the Holy Spirit, who redeemed all things.

Let it also be a concern of yours that, as you know, the distinguished preacher entirely forbids a neophyte to approach the governance of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0954C] Saint Gregory explained clearly what a neophyte is in Letter 50 of Book IV and again below, Letter 112, indiction 2, where he forbids men to be taken quickly from lay clothing into the clergy and made bishops. This had already been decreed in the Council of Orléans V, canon 9, and later in the Council of Auvergne II, canon 9: “No one from among the laity is to be ordained bishop without a year of conversion having first been completed,” so that during that year he might be more fully instructed by learned and approved men in spiritual disciplines and rules. There is also a canon of Pope Paschal on this matter in Ivo, *Decretum*, part II, chapter 84. It is recorded in the *Chronicle of Saint Albinus* that Geoffrey, bishop of Angers, resigned the episcopate after seven years, when many accused him and complained before Pope Urban II that, at Urban’s command, a neophyte and almost illiterate man had been ordained. Following Urban’s advice, he abandoned his see and became a monk at Cluny. GUSSANVILLE.], so do not permit any layman to be consecrated bishop.

For what kind of teacher will one be who was not a disciple? Or how can one provide leadership to the Lord’s flock who was not previously subject to the discipline of a shepherd? If, therefore, someone’s life is such that he is worthy to be promoted to this order, he ought first to serve in the ministry of the Church, so that through the experience of long training he may see what he ought to imitate and learn what he ought to teach. Otherwise the burden of governance may not be borne by one whose conversion is too recent, and the immaturity of advancement may become an occasion of ruin.

We have learned through the reports of various faithful people how your Excellency has conducted yourself toward our brother and fellow bishop Augustine, and how great an affection, with God’s help, you have shown him. For this we give thanks and beseech the mercy of divine power, that he may preserve you here by his protection and, just as he has caused you to reign among human beings, so also after many years may cause you to reign in eternal life.

Furthermore, for the sake of your reward, strive to bring back to the unity of concord those whom the error of the schismatics separates from the unity of the Church. They remain until now in the blindness of their ignorance for no other reason than that they flee ecclesiastical discipline and perversely wish to possess the freedom to live as they please, since they understand neither what they defend nor what they follow.

But we venerate and follow in every respect the Council of Chalcedon, from which they derive their deadly clouds of excuse [Note: [Col. 0954B] That is, the schismatics who defended the Three Chapters against the Fifth Council, especially because they claimed that condemnation of the Three Chapters would injure the authority of Chalcedon.]. If anyone presumes to diminish or add anything to its faith, we anathematize him.

Yet the stain of error has so permeated them that, trusting their ignorance, they shun the universal Church and all four patriarchs, not rationally but solely with a malicious mind. Thus the man sent to us by your Excellency, when we asked him why he remained separated from the universal Church, professed that he did not know. Nor was he able to understand what he was saying or what else he was hearing.

We likewise exhort you to restrain your other subjects under the discipline of moderation, so that they may not sacrifice to idols, nor be worshipers of trees [Note: [Col. 0954D] Pliny, book 16, final chapter: “The Druids—for thus the Gauls call their magicians—hold nothing more sacred than mistletoe and the tree on which it grows, provided it is oak,” etc. Concerning the Alemanni, whom Theodebert, king of Austrasia and grandson of Brunhild, ruled beyond the Rhine, Agathias, book I, writes: “They worship certain trees, the courses of rivers, hills, and groves, and, as though performing lawful rites for them, sacrifice horses and many other animals, cutting off their heads.” That Christians should not fulfill vows at springs and trees called sacred is prohibited by canon 22 of the Second Council of Tours, and likewise by canon 3 of the Council of Auxerre: “Cut down the springs or trees which they call sacred,” says Eligius according to Audoenus. From Vossius, book III, *On the Vices of Speech*: *sacrivus* means the same as “consecrated” or “dedicated to the gods.”] or present sacrilegious sacrifices from the heads of animals [Col. 0954C], because it has come to our attention that many Christians both hasten to the churches and—what must not be said—do not withdraw from the worship of demons [Col. 0955A]. Since these practices are wholly displeasing to our God, who does not possess divided minds, see to it that they are beneficially restrained from these unlawful acts, lest—God forbid—the sacrament of holy baptism be made for them not for deliverance but for punishment.

If, therefore, you know of violent men (Gratian, 23, question 4, chapter 47), adulterers, thieves, or those devoted to other wicked acts, hasten to appease God by correcting them, so that the scourge of faithless peoples—which, as far as we see, has been aroused for the vengeance of many nations—may not be brought upon you; lest, if—which we do not believe—the wrath of divine vengeance is stirred up by the deeds of criminals, the plague of war destroy those whom God’s commandments do not recall from wrongdoing to the path of righteousness. It is therefore necessary that with every effort and continual prayer we hasten to turn to the mercy of our Redeemer, where there is a safe place and great security for all. For there, when anyone stands firm, neither danger crushes him nor fear harasses him.

As you requested, we are sending the book to be offered to you by our most beloved son, the priest Candidus, because we are eager to share in your good zeal. May almighty God keep you under his protection, defend your kingdom from faithless peoples by the extension of his arm, and lead you after long cycles of years to eternal joys. [Note: [Col. 0955C] This is how it is read in four Vatican manuscripts and in the Colbert manuscript; elsewhere we shall demonstrate that they are mistaken.] Given in the month of October, in the first indiction.

## LETTER XII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

That he had not—as some complained—imitated certain customs of the Church of Constantinople in arranging the rites of the Mass.

[Col. 0955C]

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

A certain man arriving from Sicily told me that some of his friends, whether Greeks or Latins I do not know, were murmuring—almost as though out of zeal for the holy Roman Church—about my arrangements, saying: [Note: [Col. 0955C] LETTER XII [Elsewhere 64].—Thus read the four Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, the Rheims and Regius manuscripts, and others, with the agreement of the early printed editions. More recent editions, by changing *quomodo* (“how”) to *quoniam* (“because”), gave learned men an opportunity to err. Among these was our Menard, note 6 on the *Book of the Sacraments*, whose opinion we certainly did not accept, as is clear from the observation we made on his note; yet it could have been refuted with little difficulty by establishing the genuine reading from the manuscripts and the old printed editions.] “How does he propose to suppress the Church of Constantinople when he follows its custom in everything?” When I asked him, “Which of its customs do we follow?” he replied: “Because you have caused the *Alleluia* to be said at Mass outside the season of Pentecost; because you cause the subdeacons to proceed stripped; because [Note: [Col. 0955D] Concerning the *Alleluia*, Saint Augustine, letter 119, chapter 17, now letter 55, writes: “But that the *Alleluia* should be sung in the Church only during those fifty days is not observed everywhere. For on other days also it is sung in various places in different ways. During those days, however, it is sung everywhere.” In the *Tripartite History*, chapter 39, from Sozomen, it is stated that among the Romans the *Alleluia* was sung once each year, on Easter Day. For more about this word, see the book published by the eminent Cardinal Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 16, section 7. GUSSANV.] the *Kyrie eleison* is said; because you have ordered the Lord’s Prayer to be said immediately after the canon.”

I replied that in none of these matters had we followed another Church.

For the *Alleluia* to be said here is reported to have been taken from the Church of Jerusalem, through the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory; and therefore, in this matter, we have rather cut away the custom that had here been handed down by the Greeks. [Col. 0956B] [Note: [Col. 0956C] The printed editions read *ideo magis* (“therefore more”), against the manuscripts, at least most and the better ones, in this place. It is otherwise difficult to determine what this Greek custom, first accepted at Rome and later discontinued, was. Perhaps it was the practice of singing the *Alleluia* at funerals and during Lent. Certainly that the *Alleluia* was once sung by the Romans at the funerals of the dead is testified by Jerome in the *Epitaph of Fabiola*. Menard also gathers this from the Codex of Ratold; add to these the Mozarabic Missal. Indeed, certain Spanish churches sang the *Alleluia* during Lent even before the Fourth Council of Toledo, whose canon 10 abolished this practice.]

As for making the subdeacons proceed stripped, that was an ancient custom of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Recent editions read *sed quia* (“but because”). We have removed *quia*, both because it is absent from the manuscripts and because it obstructs the sense.] But it pleased one of our pontiffs—I do not know which one—to order them to proceed clothed. For did your churches receive their tradition from the Greeks? From where, then, do they now have the practice that the subdeacons proceed in linen tunics [Note: [Col. 0956D] Four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and most other manuscripts read: “The subdeacons in these tunics,” or “in these, in tunics.”], unless they received it from their mother, the Roman Church?

As for the *Kyrie eleison*, we neither said it nor do we say it as it is said by the Greeks. Among the Greeks everyone says it together; among us it is said by the clergy, and the people respond. The same number of times *Christe eleison* is also said, which among the Greeks is not said at all. [Col. 0956C] [Note: This is clear from the ancient Greek liturgies, in which *Christe eleison* is not found. GUSSANV.] At daily Masses, however, we omit certain things that are usually said and say only *Kyrie eleison* and *Christe eleison*, so that we may remain somewhat longer in these words of supplication. [Note: [Col. 0956D] All the liturgies establish that before Gregory’s time it had been the custom of the universal Church for the Lord’s Prayer to be said at Mass. This is also attested by Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* V; Jerome, book III *Against the Pelagians*; and Augustine, sermon 42 among the fifty, sermon 227: “After the sanctification of the sacrifice,” he says, “we say the Lord’s Prayer.” The same is gathered concerning the Gallican churches from Gregory of Tours, book II *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 30, and *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 16. Thus Gregory the Great instituted nothing other than that the Lord’s Prayer should be said at a more fitting point within the Mass. This is suggested both by the complaint of the murmurers—“immediately after the canon,” etc.—and by Gregory’s own response: “We therefore say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the canon”; and by John the Deacon, book II, chapter 20: “Gregory judged that the Lord’s Prayer should be recited over the offering immediately after the canon.” Consult Hugh Menard’s notes 83 and 84 on the *Book of the Sacraments*.]

“We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer for this reason: it was the custom of the apostles that at that very [Note: [Col. 0957B] These words exclude other prayers, but not the Gospel words always used for consecration. Indeed, that long prayers were recited in the celebration of the liturgy from almost apostolic times is testified by Justin Martyr, *Apology* 2, at the end: “He carries out the Eucharist at length . . . and when he has finished the prayers and thanksgiving, all the people present acclaim with joyful approval, saying, Amen . . . . The president, after completing the thanksgiving, distributes the Eucharist . . . through those among us who are called deacons and ministers.” More extensively concerning this, see the *Life of Saint Gregory*. Amalarius had inferred from these words of Gregory that the Lord’s Prayer alone sufficed for consecrating Christ’s body and blood, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book IV, chapter 26; Mabillon observes in his retraction of that work that Amalarius later corrected this in his *Commentary on the Roman Order*, chapter 12. That is, he removed the entire passage in which he had attributed the consecration to the Lord’s Prayer, so that he might be consistent with himself and attribute the whole power of consecrating the wine to the mixing in of a consecrated particle.] with that prayer alone they consecrated the victim of the offering. And it seemed very inappropriate to me that we should say over the offering the prayer which a scholar [Note: [Col. 0957C] That is, a learned and educated man. For the author of the canon, see Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 11, no. 2. There he praises the letter of Pope Vigilius to Eucherius—called *Eutherius* in some printed editions—which the distinguished Baluze shows to have been written to Profuturus, both in his notes on Gratian and in his new collection of Councils.] had composed, and should not say over Christ’s body and blood the very tradition which our Redeemer composed.

Moreover, among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer is said by the entire people, whereas among us it is said by the priest alone. In what respect, then, have we followed the customs of the Greeks? Rather, we have restored our ancient customs or established new and useful ones, in which, nevertheless, we are not found to imitate others. [Note: [Col. 0957D] Thus read the Norman, Vatican, Regius, Corbie, and other manuscripts, in agreement with Amalarius, book IV *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 26. I therefore wonder that the edition reads *comprobamur* (“we are approved”).]

Therefore, when your charity has occasion to go to the city of Catania or to the Church of Syracuse, let your charity instruct those whom it believes or understands may have murmured about this matter, having conferred with them, and let him not cease to teach them as though on another occasion. But as to what they say concerning the Church of Constantinople (Gratian, Distinction 22, chapter “Concerning Constantinople”), who doubts that it is subject to the apostolic see? [Gratian, Distinction 22, chapter “Concerning Constantinople.”] [Note: [Col. 0957D] In some copies of Gratian this clause is absent—namely, in the Paris edition of 1542, the Venetian edition of 1588, and a few others—but most manuscript and printed copies of Gratian contain it. Rightly so, since Gratian could not have read otherwise than he had read in Saint Gregory. For this clause is contained in all the manuscripts and printed editions of Gregory’s *Register*; and all who, when occasion arose, cited this letter read it in this form, as we shall mention below. Even Jamesius himself, who misses no opportunity to attack Gratian and the Roman correctors, included the same clause, since it is found in six English manuscripts. The Roman correctors therefore appropriately, though prudently according to their custom, restored this clause, which was absent from certain corrupt copies, from uncorrupted manuscripts of Gratian and from the purest sources of Saint Gregory. They did not think it necessary to warn readers about this matter, perhaps because they had not seen those corrupt copies, or, if they had seen them, considered them unworthy of notes. GUSSANV.] This is what the most devout lord emperor [Note: [Col. 0958B] In nearly all printed copies and in some manuscripts one reads: “and our brother Eusebius, bishop of that same city.” The word *Eusebius* was added through the carelessness of scribes, since at that time there was no bishop named Eusebius in Constantinople; only John the Faster and Cyriacus held that see during Saint Gregory’s time. Nor is the word *Eusebius* found in the better manuscripts—namely, the Tellerian, Corbie, Moissiac, Rheims, Thuane, Regius, Lyré, Prat, Carnot, Cluniac, the six English manuscripts, and Vatican manuscripts 621 and 622, according to the testimony of the eminent Cardinal Bona, 9 September 1670. The same error entered the editions of John the Deacon, book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, chapter 21, where this letter is cited and *Eusebius* appears at its end, although it is absent from John the Deacon’s manuscript copies: from the ancient manuscript of the monastery of Saint Peter at the Catalaunian Mountains, another very ancient manuscript of Saint Theodoric of Rheims, another of Saint Mary of Rheims, another of the monastery of Charles’s Place, commonly called Chailly, another of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and another of the library of the Oratorian congregation at Troyes. Nor is this word found in Amalarius Fortunatus, who cites the entire letter in book IV *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 26, or in Flacius Illyricus’s refutation of Bruno’s invective, page 64, where he cites the same letter. GUSSANV.] and our brother, the bishop of that same city, constantly profess.”

Nevertheless, if either that Church or another has anything good, I am prepared to imitate it in goodness, both I and my subordinates whom I prohibit from unlawful practices. [Note: [Col. 0958D] This letter teaches that not all the customs of the Churches should be sought from the Roman Church. Add book XII, formerly letter 31, now book XI, letter 64, the response to Augustine’s third question, through which even the blind can see that one custom of the Mass is observed in the Roman Church and another in the Churches of Gaul; nor should the English be rashly compelled to imitate the Romans, etc. GUSSANV.] For he is foolish who thinks himself superior because he refuses to learn the good things he has seen. (Compare John the Deacon, book II, chapter 21.)

## LETTER XIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

That the agents of his Church, together with Felix, should choose judges without delay.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Felix, a man to be remembered, [Note: [Col. 0958D] LETTER XLI [Elsewhere 102].—Vatican manuscript B reads “the illustrious man.” The Norman manuscripts and others agree.] has complained to us in his letters that the agents of your fraternity have unlawfully and contrary to legal order seized properties which he had held, asking that what was taken from him be restored and declaring that, if they wished to plead their case, he was ready to stand before a court with them without any delay. If this is so—and you are not ignorant of what legal reason requires—you ought, setting aside all delay, to appoint agents of your Church so that they may choose with him judges [Col. 0959A] capable of investigating and bringing to an end the dispute concerning a matter both urgent and of primary importance. [Note: [Col. 0959D] The printed editions read “who are able to investigate and conclude the case both as to the immediate and the principal matter,” against many manuscripts, which have the reading involving both the importance and the principal character of the matter.] Otherwise, if the matter is delayed for any reason, he may appear to suffer prejudice and the Church’s party to fail to obtain justice. Act, then, so that a judgment may be chosen with all speed. For we wish the cases of your Church to be conducted in such a way that it suffers neither loss contrary to equity nor any reproach on your account. [Note: [Col. 0959D] We have restored *sustinere* (“to suffer”) in place of *pertinere* (“to pertain”), which is found in the printed editions.]

## LETTER XIV. TO FELIX IN SICILY

That he has written to John the bishop to appoint agents of his Church who, with Felix himself, should undergo judgment without delay.

Gregory to Felix in Sicily.

Having received the letters of your eminence, we were saddened that you reported the unreasonable seizure by the agents of the Church of Syracuse of certain properties which you say you had held. But we believe that this has not come to the knowledge of our brother and fellow bishop John. For once the truth had been learned, anything done unlawfully could readily have been corrected.

And because legal prudence has decreed that the case of a matter both urgent and of primary importance should be heard in one and the same judgment, and because we cannot decide anything against an unheard party, we have written to our aforesaid brother that he should appoint agents of his Church who may, without delay, submit to judgment with you through judges chosen for the purpose. [Note: [Col. 0959D] LETTER XIV [Elsewhere 101].—The printed editions, contrary to the testimony of many manuscripts, read a phrase concerning the importance and ownership of the case.] Thus you will not lose your property without an inquiry, as you complain, nor will the other party appear to suffer prejudice.

Therefore let your eminence introduce no difficulties into the choice of judges [Col. 0959C] [Note: [Col. 0959D] The printed editions read “let him interpose delays or difficulties.” In correcting this, we relied especially on the Vatican, English, and Norman manuscripts.] or postpone approaching the case. For we are entirely certain of the character of the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop: he will not refuse to do whatever the order of reason requires. [Note: [Col. 0959D] In the old Colbert manuscript this letter is dated “given in the month of October, in the second indiction.”]

## LETTER XV. TO CHRYSANTHUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO

That he should place the martyrs’ relics in the basilica at Reate.

Gregory to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto. [Note: [Col. 0959D] LETTER XV [Elsewhere 12].—Spoleto, commonly called Spoleto, is still an episcopal city of Umbria and the capital of the duchy of Spoleto. GUSSANV.]

Paul, deacon of the Church of Reate [Note: [Col. 0959D] Reate, commonly called Rieti, is an episcopal city of Umbria, situated in the duchy of Spoleto. GUSSANV.], has requested us by a petition that the relics of the blessed martyrs Hermes, Hyacinth, and Maximus should be placed near the springs in the basilica of blessed Mary ever-virgin, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, which stands within the city of Reate. Therefore, dearest brother, if it is established that no body has been buried in that place, you shall reverently and without hesitation receive the shrines of the aforesaid martyrs and carefully consecrate them.

## LETTER XVI. TO SERENUS, BISHOP OF ANCONA

That he should admonish his deacon Severus to restore silver to the Church of Firmum.

Gregory to Serenus, bishop of Ancona. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Ancona, still commonly called Ancona, was formerly a city of suburban Picenum; it remains an episcopal city and the capital of the March of Ancona, immediately subject to the Roman pontiff. GUSSANV.] [Note: [Col. 0960D] LETTER XVI [Elsewhere 13].—It was formerly read *Severo* (“to Severus”); we corrected it from all the Norman, Vatican, Colbert, and other manuscripts.]

The most reverend Passivus, our brother and fellow bishop, arriving here, reported that the silver belonging to his Church, deposited by his predecessor Fabius with your deacon Serenus according to the circumstances of the time, had been entrusted to him. Although part of it has been restored, he asserts that part remains with him and that he delays restoring it under some pretext. Therefore we exhort your fraternity in these words: you should endeavor to admonish him so that he may restore without dispute what he received. Or, if he believes that he can excuse himself from restoring it for some reason, you must hear the matter between him and the agents of the Church of Firmum, together with our brother and fellow bishop Armenius, and, after carefully examining the truth, bring the case to such an end that neither the aforesaid deacon appears to suffer prejudice nor the aforementioned Church appears to endure unjust loss.

## LETTER XVII. TO DEMETRIAN AND VALERIAN

That he decrees that the money spent by the Church on their ransom may never later be reclaimed from them.

Gregory to Demetrian and Valerian, clerics of Firmum. [Note: [Col. 0960D] LETTER XVII [Elsewhere 14].—Firmum, commonly called Fermo, was formerly a city of suburban Picenum, now called the March of Ancona. GUSSANV.]

Both the decrees of the sacred canons (Gratian, 12, question 2, chapter 15) and legal authority permit ecclesiastical property lawfully to be spent for the ransom of captives. [Note: [Col. 0960D] Concerning the redemption of captives on many occasions, see question 12, part 2, in several canons. GUSSANV.] Therefore, since we have learned from you that approximately eighteen years ago the most reverend bishop Fabius of the Church of Firmum, now deceased, spent eleven pounds of silver from that Church on the ransom of you and of your father Passivus—our brother and fellow bishop, but at that time a cleric—and also of your mother, and since you fear that what was given may at some time be demanded back from you, by the authority of this decree we have anticipated removing your suspicion.

We establish that neither you nor your heirs shall at any time suffer the burden of a demand for repayment on this account, nor shall anyone raise any claim against you, because equity requires that what was spent from a motive of piety should not become the burden or affliction of those who were ransomed. (See above, letter 16.)

[Note: [Col. 0961D] LETTER XVIII [Elsewhere 17].—This letter is not found in the English manuscripts or in most others. Of the Vatican manuscripts, only Codex A contains it. It also exists in the Remigian manuscript, as do the other letters absent from certain manuscripts.]

## LETTER XVIII. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He commends the Church’s patrimony in Sicily.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

The care of our office admonishes us to entrust ecclesiastical interests to vigorous persons. Therefore, since we have found you, Romanus, to be a faithful and attentive defender, we have decided to commit to your administration, from the present second indiction, the patrimony of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s mercy we serve, situated in the territories of Syracuse, Catania, Agrigentum, and Milazzo. It is therefore necessary that you go there without delay [Note: [Col. 0961D] That is, without postponement or delay. See book I, letter 68.], so that, mindful of the divine judgment, you may strive to show yourself effective and faithful in remembering our admonition, lest you be found to incur—God forbid—the danger of any neglect or fraud. Rather, act so that you may be commended to divine grace for your faithfulness and diligence. We have sent instructions to the household of that same patrimony according to custom, so that nothing may in any way prevent you from carrying out what has been entrusted to you.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] LETTER XIX [Elsewhere 18].—This letter too is absent from many manuscripts. It exists in the Remigian and Vatican A manuscripts.]

## LETTER XIX. TO THE COLONI OF THE SYRACUSAN PATRIMONY

That they should obey Romanus, the defender.

Gregory to the colonists of the Syracusan patrimony.

I want you to know that our decision has placed you under the care of our defender. Therefore we order you to obey without any difficulty whatever he foresees and commands you to do for the benefit of ecclesiastical interests. [Note: [Col. 0961D] In the Remigian manuscript: “whatever he foresees and enjoins upon you, you must obey without any difficulty.”]

We have given him authority to punish with strict vengeance those who are disobedient or attempt to remain defiant. We have likewise charged him not to delay, through the diligence of his care, in reclaiming according to ecclesiastical law slaves who are hiding outside or lands that have been invaded by anyone. For you should know that he has been warned, at his own peril, never to presume under any pretext to commit violence or seizure against the property of others.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] LETTER XX [Elsewhere 19].—This letter, together with the three immediately following it, is also omitted from most manuscripts. Otherwise Gregory’s style sufficiently proves that they are his; perhaps they were omitted by scribes because they were written on nearly the same subject. They are preserved in the cited Vatican A manuscript, the Saint-Victorin manuscript, and the Remigian manuscript.]

## LETTER XX. TO PETER IN SICILY

That he should assist Romanus as he assumes the administration of the Syracusan patrimony.

[Col. 0961D]

Gregory to Peter of Sicily.

Knowing that devotion is increased by paternal commendations, we must hasten through our letters to add the favor of our support to the things which we confidently believe you will undertake voluntarily, to the glory of your eminence.

We therefore inform you that we have entrusted to Romanus, the defender and bearer of this letter, the patrimony of our Church situated in the territories of Syracuse, Catania, and the neighboring regions, under God’s protecting grace. Therefore, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask that you support him with your prudence and furnish him in all things with your assistance, as we trust you will. Thus, while he has the support and consolation of your favor, you will show more clearly the charity which you bear toward us, and we shall hasten to respond in every way, when necessary, to your goodwill.

## LETTER XXI. TO LIBERTINUS, FORMER PREFECT

That he should assist the new Roman defender with his counsel.

[Col. 0962B]

Gregory to Libertinus, former prefect. [Note: [Col. 0962D] LETTER XXI [Elsewhere 20].—Libertinus was praetor of Sicily in the year 594, according to book V, letter 32, in the thirteenth indiction.]

Your eminence’s devotion, tested and known to us, moves us to address you by letter and ask that you show yourself an assistant in ecclesiastical affairs. Therefore, since by God’s authority we have entrusted to Romanus, the bearer of this letter, the care of the patrimony of our Church situated in the territory of Syracuse and Catania, we greet your eminence and ask that you join him and offer him assistance in all things.

And lest, because of his inexperience, he fail to understand some useful matters, instruct him carefully with your counsel and, as you are accustomed to do, lend him your assistance in carrying out these duties, so that, while with your help he successfully performs what has been entrusted to him, you may receive a reward for your goodness, and we may be more earnestly moved to implore almighty God’s mercy for the life of your eminence.

As for the matter about which the bearer of this letter spoke to me, or about which our most reverend brother John, bishop, wrote, nothing could meanwhile be attempted or done, because the person before whom the matter could be pursued has not yet been established in any authority.

## LETTER XXII. TO CIRIDANUS

That he should favor Romanus, the defender.

Gregory to Ciridanus. [Note: [Col. 0962D] The printed editions formerly read “to Libertinus Ciridanus,” incorrectly. We have removed the first name on the authority of Vatican manuscript A.]

The goodness of your eminence, spread abroad by a truthful messenger, gives us such certainty about you that we ought not to distrust it in any matter, but rather, as one truly a wise son of our Church, should specially commend a matter to you.

Therefore we have sent Romanus, our defender and the bearer of this letter, under God’s protection, to administer our Church’s patrimony situated in the territories of Catania and Syracuse. Greeting your eminence with paternal affection, we ask that he find everywhere the affection of your charity and enjoy the support of your favor wherever necessary, so that, in your presence, he may not feel our absence. Thus, when he has safely completed with your assistance what has been entrusted to him, we may become your debtors in thanksgiving, and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose causes you expend yourself, may repay you here and in the future.

## LETTER XXIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

The cases entrusted to Romanus, the defender, concerning Leontius against Leo, the bishop, and Archelaus, the physician.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Our son, the illustrious Leontius, former consul, has made a serious complaint against our brother and fellow bishop Leo, and his complaint has greatly disturbed us, because a bishop ought not to act so rashly and lightly. We have entrusted this matter for careful investigation to Romanus, who is coming.

The person sent by him complains of your fraternity that the interests of our brother and fellow bishop Domitian, metropolitan, [Note: [Col. 0963D] Concerning him, see book III, letter 67, and book X, letter 50.] are burdened by your defense of Archelaus, a most distinguished physician. [Note: [Col. 0963D] LETTER XXIII [Elsewhere 22].—The reading formerly was *Marchilai*, which Vatican A also has. But in book V, letter 32, thirteenth indiction, where Saint Gregory mentions the same physician, the name is written *Archelaus* in the Norman manuscripts, in the Vatican manuscripts, and in Paul the Deacon’s collection, to say nothing of other ancient copies; nor do the printed books disagree.]

Certainly your fraternity ought justly to defend its sons—or, as may perhaps be the case, the affairs of the holy Church—and should give the adversaries no occasion for slander. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that you observe this in every respect, even while speaking in this way. We have nevertheless charged the same Romanus, who is coming, to arrange with you whatever is right in this matter.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] LETTER XXIV [Elsewhere 16].—It is absent from the English manuscripts and most others; it is found in Vatican manuscripts A, B, and D.]

## LETTER XXIV. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

That he should at last ensure the fulfillment of the will of Rustica, the testatrix, which had been neglected for many years.

[Col. 0963C]

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

Our son Theodosius, abbot of the monastery built in Campania by the former patrician Liberius, has informed us that, approximately twenty-one years ago, Rustica, a former woman of illustrious rank [Note: [Col. 0963D] The text formerly read *ante nos* (“before us”), which we corrected from the cited manuscripts.], first making a will, appointed her husband Felix her heir and assigned him the task of building a monastery there in Sicily under this condition: if he did not within a year pay all the legacies left to the freedmen, or did not organize the aforesaid monastery as she had wished, then the holy Roman Church should unquestionably claim for itself the portion which she appeared to possess in the estate of Cumae [Col. 0964A], and should lend its assistance either for paying the same legacies or for constructing the monastery itself.

Therefore, since, as is said, the property left has not yet been completely transferred to that monastery and part of the estate is still held by his heirs, let your experience investigate and examine the case with the greatest care. First, if the heir has fallen under the condition of the will by which our Church has a claim, we want you to investigate and learn this clearly, and to carry out what benefits the poor require according to the order of the matter. Then be earnestly concerned with the organization of that cell or the restoration of the property left, so that the pious will of the testatrix may be fulfilled in both respects and the unjust holders may recognize, through the just loss of what they have retained, the guilt of their wrongful retention.

We therefore want you, with complete vigor, both to investigate this case and, with the Lord’s help, to bring it to completion, so that the pious devotion of the woman who made the arrangement may at last attain its effect. We also want you to assist that monastery in every matter, while preserving justice, so that lay persons who, as if on the founder’s behalf, ought to have provided the support of assistance may not have the power to harm it. [Note: [Col. 0963D] In Vatican A and B, the Regius manuscript, two Colbert manuscripts, and two Tellerian manuscripts, this letter is dated: “Given in the month of June, in the second indiction.”]

## LETTER XXV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SORRENTO, ETC.

That they should grant relics to Gregory, the former prefect, who wishes to build a basilica.

Gregory to John, bishop of Sorrento; Agnellus, bishop of Terracina; Felix, bishop of Portus; [Note: [Col. 0964D] LETTER XXV [Elsewhere 11].—Roman Portus, or Portus Augustus, commonly called Porto. It was formerly a city of Etruria and remains an episcopal city in the patrimony of Saint Peter; its bishopric is one of the six conferred upon the senior cardinals. GUSSANV.] Fortunatus, bishop of Naples; Primærius, bishop of Nuceria; Gloriosus, bishop of Ostia; [Note: [Col. 0964D] Ostia, also commonly called Ostia Tiberina, because it lies opposite the mouth of the Tiber River, twelve miles from the city of Rome. GUSSANV.] and Albinus, bishop of Formiae. [Note: [Col. 0964D] Some printed editions and manuscript copies incorrectly have *Formae*, and others, worse still, *Fermiae*. Concerning this city, see what was said in book I, letter 8. GUSSANV. Vatican A and B read “Albinus of Formiae,” or “of Firmum.”]

Our glorious son Gregory, former prefect, requests that the shrines of the blessed martyrs resting in places within your dioceses be granted to him, for he desires to build a basilica in their honor at his own expense. Therefore, dearest brothers, in accordance with our command you ought to comply with the wishes of the aforesaid man, so that he may obtain the desired result of his devotion in the consecration. [Note: [Col. 0964D] This wording is found in Vatican manuscripts A, B, and F, as well as in two Tellerian manuscripts and the old Colbert manuscript.]

In the month of November, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXVI. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

That he should return to Calixenus, Ammonia’s nephew and Stephania’s son, the house which she donated to the Roman Church.

Gregory to Romanus.
to the defender.

[Column 0964D] Although the law’s principle does not permit those things which pertain to the rights of the Church to be alienated, [Column 0965A] nevertheless the severity of strictness must sometimes be tempered where regard for mercy especially invites it—particularly when the amount is such that it neither burdens the giver nor, to some extent, relieves the poverty of the recipient. And therefore, because Stephania, bearer of this present letter, came here with her young son Calixenus, whom she asserts she had borne by Peter, her former husband, and who was suffering under extreme poverty, and because by continual entreaty and tears she asked us to have restored to the same Calixenus a house of property in the city of Catania, which Ammonia, formerly her mother-in-law and Calixenus’s grandmother, had offered to our Church by deed of gift, asserting that the aforesaid Ammonia had no authority to alienate it, but that it belonged in every respect by right to her son Calixenus; our most beloved son, the deacon Cyprian, who investigated the case, opposed this, saying that the complaint of the aforesaid woman had no legal basis and that she could not reasonably claim or recover the house itself in her son’s name. But lest we seem to leave the tears of the aforesaid woman fruitless and to follow the path of severity more than to embrace the causes of compassion, by this present instruction we command you to restore to the aforesaid Calixenus both the house mentioned above and the gift made by Ammonia concerning that house, which is known to be there in Sicily. For, as we have said, in doubtful matters it is better not to enforce strictness but rather to incline toward kindness, especially when, through the relinquishment of a small possession, neither the Church is burdened nor mercy is denied to an orphan and a poor man.

[Note: [Column 0965D] LETTER XXVI [Al. 23].—This is established by the fortieth letter of this book, whose beginning is: “In the month of November of the present second indiction. By our instruction we commanded Your Experience,” etc.]

Given in the month of November, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

Ecclesiastical protection must not be indiscriminately extended to everyone.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

It has come to our attention that certain men, possessing altogether too little discretion, desire to involve us in their dangers, and thus wish to be defended by ecclesiastical persons in such a way that the ecclesiastical persons themselves may also be held liable for their guilt. Therefore, by this present instruction, I admonish you—and through you our brother and fellow bishop, the lord John, as well as the others who may be involved—that you should extend ecclesiastical protection, whether you receive letters from me or whether none have been sent, with such moderation [Column 0966A] that those who are involved in public thefts may not appear to be unjustly defended by us, lest we in any way transfer upon ourselves the reputation of evil-doers through the audacity of indiscriminate defense. Rather, insofar as is fitting for the Church, assist them by admonishing them and by offering the word of intercession, so that you may both bring them aid and not stain the reputation of the holy Church.

[Note: [Column 0966D] In four Vatican manuscripts and the old Colbert manuscript: “In the month of December, in the second indiction.” In one Tellerian manuscript the same date is prefixed to the letter.]

(Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 56.)

[Note: [Column 0965D] LETTER XXVII [Al. 24].—See Letter 152 among the letters of Saint Augustine: “You say that it is the duty of your priesthood to intervene on behalf of defendants, and that, unless you obtain your request, you are offended, as though you did not receive what was your duty.” Augustine answers this question in Letter 153, which the reader should consult, as also Cause 23, questions 3, 4, and 5. Certainly Saint Gregory himself seems here to have expressed the opinion of Saint Augustine, which reads: “I would say this most confidently: whoever intervenes for a man so that he need not restore goods taken away, and whoever does not compel, as far as he can honorably do so, one who flees to him to make restitution, is an accomplice in fraud and crime,” etc. And near the end of the letter: “Yet even here we do not intervene so that, according to earthly customs and laws, what belongs to others should not be restored,” etc. GUSSANV.]

## LETTER XXVIII. TO ANTONIUS, THE SUBDEACON, AND DOMETIUS, THE ABBOT

By his authority he confirms the reconciliation of harmony between the hospice and the monastery.

Gregory to Antonius, the subdeacon, and to Dometius, the abbot and presbyter, from among his peers.

[Column 0966B] Just as it is grievous and full of reproach for a controversy arising from secular affairs to persist for a long time between persons serving almighty God, so it is praiseworthy and in keeping with religious zeal to prefer, through earthly means, a peace pleasing to God, and from transitory things to acquire the lasting gains of charity. And therefore, because a long-standing dispute had arisen concerning the estates of Faianum, Nasonianum, and Libinianum, situated in the province of Sicily, in the territory of Palermo, between the administrators of the monastery of Saints Maximus and Agatha—which is called Lucuscanum—and, on the other side, the administrators of the hospice established in this city of Rome, which is called that of Valerius, a salutary settlement has now, by God’s authority, been reached between you, our subdeacon Antonius, the head of the aforesaid hospice, and, on the other side, our most beloved son Dometius, the abbot and presbyter of the aforesaid monastery, with agreements having been made. It is therefore necessary that every occasion of discord be forestalled and that what has been done be confirmed by authoritative action.

Accordingly, by the tenor of this present instruction we have judged that the following must be decreed: all documents, and whatever else might in any way provide assistance under the law or through any privilege, whether by lapse of time or otherwise, to the parties—God forbid that they should wish to act against one another—shall, as you yourselves request, be void and annulled in every respect; only the written agreement now made between you shall be valid and shall possess perpetual force. If anything has perhaps been inserted into it through negligence or ignorance with less than complete firmness, let it receive from this our authority the strength of the fullest protection and solidity. Let nothing remain by which, at any time, what has been prudently and peacefully settled through religious zeal, as was fitting, might incur any doubt. Rather, let everything written down in the same agreements remain firm, inviolate, and without any opposition, so that, once all material for dispute has been entirely removed, no occasion for contentious litigation may henceforth arise between those among whom harmony ought immutably to remain because of charity. [Column 0967A]

For the protection of the monastery mentioned above, we have likewise issued a similar instruction to the aforesaid Dometius, the abbot and presbyter.

[Note: [Column 0967D] Four Vatican manuscripts and the old Colbert manuscript agree.]

In the month of January, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXIX. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP OF LUNA

He should either strongly urge Fidentia to satisfy Adeodata, her recently converted daughter, or assist the latter before the judges.

[Column 0967B]

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

Your Fraternity will learn from the written petition submitted and kept among the records what complaint Adeodata, the bearer of this present letter and handmaid of God, has brought against her mother Fidentia. And since the judgment of equity admonishes us that, with due regard to reason, the greatest episcopal assistance ought to be available to converts, we therefore exhort your Fraternity by these letters to have her aforesaid mother summoned before you, and to persuade her with calm exhortation not to cease voluntarily from doing what she can be compelled by legal reason to do, [Column 0967C] so that neither the mother may appear to be afflicted nor the daughter to suffer prejudice.

But if—which we do not believe—she should wish to postpone following your admonition, extend protection to the aforesaid religious Adeodata against her, and assist her with your support before the judge, or wherever necessity may require, with greater insistence. Apply yourself to carrying out this case in such a way that, once compelled by legal authority, she may be forced, against her will, to do what she has voluntarily postponed.

As for the aforesaid bearer, let your Fraternity keep her commended in all things, with equity preserved, so that, while you provide her protection, she may remain, with God’s protection, without any disturbance in the habit she has assumed.

[Note: [Column 0967D] LETTER XXIX [Al. 28].—This passage had been corrupted in earlier editions, but it has been corrected with the help of numerous manuscripts and older editions.]

[Note: [Column 0967] [ [Column 0937] This note appears at the foot of column 937, but the callout number was not printed in the text.] LETTER XXX. Al. 29.]

## LETTER XXX. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He should see that the estate of Venus is restored to the monastery of Saint Mark.

[Column 0967D]

Gregory to Anthemius, the Neapolitan subdeacon.

The right of equity requires that what was restored by our predecessors after the truth had been established should not now be held again by our Church without cause, lest what plainly stands contrary to a religious purpose appear to have been restored not truly but fictitiously and rather deceitfully. And therefore, because Stephen, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mark, which is known to have been established beside the walls of the city of Spoleto, complained to us that the estate of Venus, situated in the province of Campania, in the territory of Minturnae, which we know was restored to him by an instruction of our predecessor of blessed memory, Benedict, is now being unjustly retained by our Church, we therefore command you by this authority that, if it is being held by men of our Church, you restore it to the legal possession of the aforesaid monastery without any delay or dispute.

But if it is being held not by our people but perhaps by certain outsiders, we wish you to act with energetic diligence so that in every way it may be restored to the legal possession [Column 0968B] of the monastery mentioned above, so that he himself, with your assistance, may receive what belongs to him without any hardship, and another may not unjustly profit from the loss of the monastery.

## LETTER XXXI. TO FAUSTUS

He should without hesitation deposit with Anthemius the property belonging to the Church of Vulturnum.

Gregory to Faustus.

Just as ecclesiastical property must be restored to the appropriate persons without any delay, so the caution of the one making the restoration must be attended to, so that no subsequent trouble may arise for him from that restoration. And therefore, because, at the time when Constantius, formerly the defender and your father in glory, administered the Campanian patrimony entrusted to him, he is known to have retained with him, on account of the responsibility assigned to him, the furnishings of the Church of Vulturnum—which, because of its sins, was without clergy and a bishop—and because we have learned that you now hesitate to restore them without our consent, we exhort you by these letters to restore them without difficulty to the subdeacon Anthemius, under a written receipt for the items received, [Column 0968C] so that the Church’s property may be held in full by those to whom it belongs and your Glory may be free of every doubt.

[Note: [Column 0967D] LETTER XXXI [Al. 30].—The printed editions resist the manuscripts. Consent has been restored.]

[Note: [Column 0967D] Vulturnum, commonly Castel del Vulturno, was formerly a city of Italian Campania and an episcopal see, at the mouth of the river Vulturnus; now it is a small fortress. GUSSANV.]

[Note: [Column 0968D] Thus we restore the reading from five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, the Regius manuscript, and others, where the printed editions read “sub depositi.” Desusceptum, here and elsewhere in these letters, is a written record containing a list and account of the things received. See Book III, Letter 50. Below, the printed editions read “in safety” instead of “in full,” which is found in five Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, all the Colbert manuscripts, the Regius manuscript, and others.]

## LETTER XXXII. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He should receive the furnishings of the Church of Vulturnum from Faustus, keep them secure, and record them.

[Column 0968D] Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

We have learned that the furnishings of the Church of Vulturnum, which the defender Constantius had retained on account of the responsibility assigned to him, when that Church was without clergy or a bishop, remained with his heir. And because we have learned that his son, the glorious Faustus, hesitated to restore them [Column 0969A] without our consent, we urged him by our letters to restore the furnishings of that Church to Your Experience without any hesitation. Therefore let Your Experience receive those furnishings under a written receipt for the items received, [Column 0969B] and take care to hold them in full, and let the quantity and quality of the same be reported to us and made known with every exactness.

[Note: [Column 0968D] LETTER XXXII [Al. 31].—We have already often explained what is to be understood by “furnishings.” See note 553 to the Sacred Book.]

[Note: [Column 0969D] The printed editions read “in safety.” But the manuscripts of Remigius and Saint Victor, which almost alone together with Vatican A transmit this letter, read otherwise. Furthermore, in Letter 31, written for the same reason, the great majority of manuscripts read “in full.”]

## LETTER XXXIII. TO ANDREAS

He consoles him concerning his illness, showing that it is a pledge of divine love and the pruning of a fruitful branch.

Gregory to Andreas.

Hearing that grief and illness had afflicted Your Glory very severely, I was deeply grieved. But immediately, recognizing that the illness had completely left you, I quickly turned my sorrow into joy and gave great thanks to almighty God, because he struck in order to heal and afflicted in order to lead you to true joys. For it is written: “The Lord chastises the one whom he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6). Hence Truth itself says: “My Father is the cultivator, and every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will remove; but every one that bears fruit, he will prune, so that it may bear more fruit” (John 1:1–2).

An unfruitful branch is removed because the sinner is uprooted completely. A fruitful branch, however, is said to be pruned because it is cut back through discipline so that it may be brought to more abundant grace. Thus the grains of ears of wheat, threshed on the threshing floor, are stripped of awns and chaff. Thus olives, pressed in the press, flow into the richness of oil. Thus bunches of grapes, beaten underfoot, dissolve into wine. Rejoice therefore, good man, because in this scourging of yours you perceive both your advancement and the fact that you are loved by the eternal Judge.

Moreover, on my behalf I ask you to greet my daughter Gloriosa, your wife. May almighty God guard you with heavenly protection, and may he now console you through the abundance of his gifts and afterward through the repayment of rewards.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO VENANTIUS, THE BISHOP

He should ordain presbyters or deacons in the city of Aldio and exhort them to convert the unbelievers.

Gregory to Venantius, bishop.

[Column 0969D] Whenever we are asked for what it is fitting that we should urge, we must not delay granting it, lest we appear to postpone good desires which ought rather to be encouraged. And therefore, because the glorious Aldio, master of the soldiers, earnestly desires, as he has informed us in his letters, that presbyters or deacons be ordained in his city, [Column 0970A] let Your Fraternity carefully investigate those who are chosen for ordination. And if there is nothing that canonically prevents their ordination, let it strive to ordain them with God’s favor.

It is also fitting that you speak with them, so that through the diligence of their exhortation they may recall the people living there from unbelief, strive to turn them away from the worship of the pagans, [Note: [Column 0970D] That is, “to turn away”; similarly Pliny uses suspendere of the flow of the eyes, meaning “to turn away” or “to stop.” GUSSANV.] teach them to persist in the fear of almighty God, and love the rewards of eternal life, so that this consecration may bring glory before God to them and salvation to the people living there.

[Note: [Column 0970D] LETTER XXXIV [Al. 33].—The printed editions add “of Luna,” which is absent from the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Colbert, Regius, and other manuscripts. Nevertheless, we do not deny that this Venantius was bishop of Luna.]

## LETTER XXXV. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN

He commends John, who is to act in place of the prefect, but on the condition that the Church not be burdened by him, as had happened in the case of Vigilius.

[Column 0970B] Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

Although Your Fraternity is so discreet and endowed with suitable gravity that, without being admonished, you understand from yourselves what ought to be offered to each person, nevertheless, because John, the magnificent man who has arrived to act there in place of the prefect, asked that he be commended by our letter, let Your Holiness, whenever necessary, extend to him the protection of your favor, with due regard to reason, and endeavor to assist him in a priestly manner with your support, so that, while he is in your presence, he may neither suffer unjustly from the oppression of others nor himself become unreasonably burdensome to others.

But because it has come to our attention that Vigilius, who previously acted there in place of the prefect, exacted from you, so to speak, loans through the occasion of our letters, by which we commended him because we had been compelled by his request to do so, we find it difficult to bear—if it is true—that he obtained this not on his own authority but as though through our letter. Therefore Your Fraternity must know that we commend to you those who make such demands in such a way that you ought to assist them insofar as is possible and just, but not in such a way that any burden is imposed upon your Church on this account.

[Note: [Column 0970D] LETTER XXXV [Al. 34].—The printed editions give “Given in the month of September,” which is found in no manuscript. We therefore judged that the old Colbert manuscript should be followed, in which one finds “In the month of February,” and the Remigius manuscript agrees.]

Given in the month of February, in the second indiction.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

When Jewish merchants return from Gaul, the Christian slaves they have brought back must either be handed over to those who commissioned the purchase or sold to Christians within forty days. He must beware of Basil, the Jew, who gives slaves to his Christian sons.

[Column 0970D] Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

When we learned how greatly Your Fraternity’s zeal had been kindled on behalf of the Christian slaves whom the Jews purchase in the regions of Gaul, we indicate that your concern pleased us so much that our own deliberation judged that they ought to be prohibited from such commerce. But when Basil the Hebrew came with other Jews, we learned that their purchase was imposed upon them by various public judges, and that it happened that slaves were purchased indiscriminately from pagans and Christians alike. Therefore it was necessary to arrange the matter by a careful regulation, so that neither those giving the orders would be frustrated nor those who claim that they obey against their will suffer any unjust loss.

Accordingly, let Your Fraternity see to it with vigilant concern and preserve the following arrangement: when they return from the province mentioned above, the Christian slaves whom they happen to bring back [Column 0971A] must either be handed over to those who commissioned the purchase or, at any rate, sold to Christian buyers within forty days.

Once that number of days has passed, none of them may remain with them in any manner. But if some of these slaves should perhaps contract such an illness that they cannot be sold within the prescribed days, care must be taken that, once they have been restored to their former health, they likewise be sold in every way. For it is not fitting that a thing free from fault be made liable to loss.

Since, however, whenever something new is established, it is accustomed to impose a rule upon the future so that it does not condemn what has already passed at great expense, if any slaves purchased in the preceding year have remained with them, or have recently been taken away from you, let them, while they are placed with you, have the right to alienate them, lest, through ignorance, they incur a loss before the prohibition—something which it would be right for them to bear after being forbidden.

[Note: [Column 0971D] LETTER XXXVI [Al. 35].—The word has various meanings in law; here it is readily explained of the judges who had imposed the purchase.]

[Note: [Column 0971D] This passage is read in various ways in the manuscripts. Vatican A has: “so that the many expenses of the past may not be of advantage”; the printed editions agree in part, reading: “so that they may not favor the past through many expenses.” Vatican B, E, and F read: “so that they may not commend the past through many expenses.” Vatican D reads: “so that it may commend many past expenses,” with the Rheims manuscript agreeing. We have followed all the Norman manuscripts.]

[Column 0971C] Furthermore, it has been reported to us that the aforesaid Basil wishes to give certain slaves by deed of gift to his sons, who are Christians by God’s favor, so that, under cover of this pretext, with only the title of master removed, they may serve him; and afterward, if they should perhaps think that they must flee to the Church in order to become Christians, they may be claimed not for freedom but under the ownership of those to whom they had previously been given. Your Fraternity must watch over this matter in a becoming manner. If he wishes to give slaves to his sons, then, so that every opportunity for fraud may be removed, let them in every way become Christians and not remain in his house. But when circumstances require him to use their services, let them be commanded to provide him with what it is fitting and proper for them, for God’s sake, to offer even to their own father.

## LETTER XXXVII. TO CHRYSANTHUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO

He must not allow monks fleeing to his diocese to be indiscriminately restored to communion. A slave freed on the condition that he become a monk must not leave the monastery.

[Column 0971D]

Gregory to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto.

Since it is characteristic of discipline to prohibit what is unlawful and salutarily cut away transgressions, its judgment must be carefully preserved. For if it is neglected, everything falls into confusion, when one person destroys whatever another builds by guarding it.

The presbyter Valentinus therefore complained to us that, if a monk of his monastery is deprived of communion because of a fault, he goes to your territories and receives communion without any reservation. If this is so, then, since not only the order of the rule is dissolved [Column 0972A] but also material for destruction is thereby supplied, you must strictly and most diligently forbid the presbyters under you to presume to do this in the future.

But if someone should complain that he has been excommunicated unjustly, let Your Fraternity investigate the matter with careful inquiry, and, once the truth has been learned, arrange the case in such a way that neither injustice may long prevail to the affliction of the innocent nor the force of discipline be broken or dissolved through indiscriminate presumption.

[Note: [Column 0972D] LETTER XXXVII [Al. 36].—Concerning the excommunication of monks for faults, see the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, chapter 23 and the four following chapters. Consult also the Harmony of Rules, chapter 30, where the agreement of almost all who promulgated monastic rules on this communion is demonstrated.]

[Column 0972B] Moreover, the aforesaid presbyter complained to us that a certain deacon had manumitted two slaves belonging to him under this condition: that they should become monks and remain in the same monastery where he himself had been; he had added that, if anyone presumed to act otherwise, he would be subjected again in every respect to the yoke of slavery. One of them, however, had entirely disregarded this condition, abandoned the monastery with reckless audacity, and joined himself to the clergy.

Your Fraternity must investigate this also with careful inquiry, and, if you find it to be so, conduct yourself in this matter with fitting priestly zeal, so that he may have no opportunity to leave the monastery and the will of the manumitter may nevertheless not be passed over under any excuse.

[Note: [Column 0973C] The printed editions read “and because.” We have made many other minor corrections, where the sense nevertheless appeared more obscure.]

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He should deal with Felix so that, once he has received the principal sum of the price, he may be content with it.

Gregory to Anthemius, the subdeacon.

Maurus, the bearer of this present letter, asserts that he received certain merchandise from Felix, the magnificent man, for four hundred solidi, and promised to pay six siliquae per solidus as profit on the price. [Column 0972D] When this amount of profit had been added together, he had purchased two written securities: one for four hundred and fifty solidi and the other for fifty solidi, promising that he would repay them at a fixed time.

[Note: [Column 0973C] A solidus contained twenty-four siliquae. Felix therefore had promised one hundred solidi as profit on merchandise worth four hundred solidi, issuing or giving a written double security: one for four hundred and fifty solidi and another for fifty solidi.]

[Note: [Column 0973C] The printed editions corruptly read: “having gathered together in one [place] the amount of profit, two…”]

[Note: [Column 0973C] Vatican D, and the manuscripts of Audoen and Lyran, read “to have purchased,” but incorrectly.]

But because, as he reports, he suffered no small loss in this merchandise, and after repaying four hundred and ten solidi is compelled to fulfill the remaining profit, he laments that as a result he is subject to an even greater necessity, or rather to despair, and therefore asks that he be aided in some way. If this is so, Your Experience should work with the aforesaid magnificent son of ours, together with our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus and our glorious son Maurentius, master of the soldiers—for we are also writing to them—so that in this matter, as befits a Christian and a nobleman, he may be more kind than severe, more merciful than strict, and may not expect profit from another’s loss, but may be content with the principal sum of the price received, so that whatever he remits to the poor man, almighty God may compensate him by a multiplied repayment, as he has promised.

[Note: [Column 0973C] No one fails to acknowledge that usury is prohibited by divine, canonical, and civil law, although the relevant laws and the persons to whom they apply are not everywhere the same. At the Council of Orléans in 538, canon 27: “Let a cleric from the diaconate upward not lend money at interest; nor let him hope to receive more from benefits granted than is given; nor, in conducting business, let him engage in shameful profit-seeking like public officials who supervise merchants in response to the people, nor dare to conduct prohibited business under another’s name. If anyone presumes to act against these decrees, after communion has been granted, let him be degraded from his order.” Nearly the same is read in Apostolic Canon 44, nor is the Council of Nicaea, canon 17, dissimilar. I observe two points: “from the diaconate upward,” and “after communion has been granted.” Sidonius Apollinaris, Letter 24 of Book IV, to his Turnus, says much about usury, which will cause difficulty for an attentive reader. Let the chapter “Per vestras,” in the Extravagantes, concerning gifts between husband and wife, be read, as well as Gregory of Tours, Book III, chapter 32, concerning the bishop of Verdun: “If you wish to lend your money, we shall return it with lawful interest.” I shall not linger longer, lest I remain stuck in the deep mud. GUSSANV.]

Therefore let Your Experience act diligently, so that in every way you may impose this upon him as a favor and free this man from the burden of the obligation.

[Note: [Column 0973] [ [Column 0973] This note appears at the foot of column 974, but the callout number was not printed in the text.] LETTER XXXIX [Al. 38].]

## LETTER XXXIX. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER IN SICILY

He should grant six solidi each year to Gaudiosus, a poor man.

[Column 0973B]

Gregory to Romanus, the defender of Sicily.

The words of the divine commandments admonish us to provide ecclesiastical assistance to those suffering necessity. Therefore, because our most beloved son, the deacon Cyprian, asserts that Gaudiosus, the defender of our see, who is known to reside at Syracuse, is constrained by the need of poverty, we command Your Experience by this present authority not to delay giving him six solidi each year from the present second indiction, so that he may enjoy the comfort of this remedy and you may undoubtedly know that what you have given is to be charged to your accounts.

(Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 55.)

## LETTER XL. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He should, setting aside every delay and excuse, carry out what had been commanded above in Letter 26.

[Column 0973C]

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

In the month of November of the present second indiction, [Column 0974A] by our instruction we commanded Your Experience that you should finally restore to Calixenus, the son of Stephania, the house at Catania which Ammonia, the grandmother of that same Calixenus, had bestowed upon our Church in holy devotion, together with the same donation. You delayed doing this, as is said, on the excuse that [Column 0974B] the record of that donation had not been erased from the polyptychs.

[Note: [Column 0974C] LETTER XL.—“Instruction” and “instructional order” occur frequently below in our Gregory and in Gregory of Tours—as well as in other writers—and in him these terms especially signify commands of kings and distinguished persons delivered in writing. See Gregory of Tours, Book VI of the Histories, chapter 46.]

[Note: [Column 0974C] Concerning the record, see above, Letter 16 of Book III, now Book IV. This is an example of a deed of gift inserted into polyptychs, that is, the Church’s books, which present estates and annual revenues in summary form. See John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 24, and consult the learned Cangius. If one considers the etymology, a polyptych is a tablet having several folds. Concerning these and diptychs, see at length chapter 4 of Book I of the Harmony of Rules, section 4. In the manuscript of Saint Victor and the old edition, the reading is “in the promises.”]

[Note: [Column 0974D] Charaxare sometimes has the same meaning as “to engrave.” Augustine, On the Debate between the Church and the Synagogue: “For when he had first received on Mount Sinai the two tablets engraved with the Decalogue.” Gregory of Tours, Book VIII, chapter 19: “He ordered two knives to be engraved more deeply into Fredegundis and infected with poison.” Elsewhere it means “to paint”; Gregory of Tours, Book VII, chapter 36: “Are you that painter who, in the time of King Chlothar, engraved images upon the walls and ceilings of oratories?” Here, however, charaxata means erased, or crossed out with transverse lines, as is customary. In the testament of Saint Remigius preserved by Hincmar: “If any erasure or engraving is found in it, it was made in my presence while it was being reread and corrected by me.”]

957 You should recognize that this was an inappropriate statement, since the text of our instruction ought to have been entirely sufficient for your protection. Therefore, having received this present authority, restore without delay the aforesaid house and the donation to the aforementioned orphan Calixenus. For we know that you yourself recognize what is just, and nevertheless we grant the aforesaid house to that same orphan out of our kindness.

## LETTER XLI. TO JULIANUS, THE SCRIBE

He is not diverted from zeal for justice by human considerations; he will therefore investigate Maximus and deliver judgment according to the canons.

[Column 0974B]

Gregory to Julianus, the scribe.

If the proper order of secular offices and the discipline handed down by our ancestors are preserved, who would tolerate ecclesiastical orders being confused through rash presumption, matters heard being neglected, and things requiring correction being postponed through an inadequate dismissal? Certainly you do well to love charity and to urge concord. But because consideration of our position compels us not, for God’s sake, to leave unexamined the matters that have come to our attention, we shall therefore, when Maximus arrives, carefully investigate from him the things that have been said about him.

[Column 0974C] And we trust in the protection of our Creator that, once the truth has been learned, we shall be diverted neither by anyone’s favor nor by anyone’s fault from the state of the canons and the uprightness of equity, [Column 0975A] but shall gladly preserve what agrees with reason. For if, God forbid, we neglect ecclesiastical care and vigor, negligence destroys discipline, and surely harm will come to the souls of the faithful, since they receive such examples from their pastors.

But as for what you write—that the will of the palace and the people’s affection for him are not at odds—this does not turn us away from zeal for justice, nor does it cause our purpose to fail in seeking the truth through sin. Therefore, magnificent son, everyone must strive to win God’s love for himself. For without divine grace, what shall I say that human affection is worth in the future, when even now it does us greater harm?

[Note: [Column 0974D] LETTER XLI [Al. 11, indiction 7].—Concerning the usurper of the see of Salona, about whom much has been said in the preceding letters.]

[Note: [Column 0975D] Vatican D incorrectly states that this letter was given in the month of March, on the tenth day, in the fourteenth indiction. The same indiction is recorded in the Colbert manuscript; but in Paul’s Collection it is said to have been given on the second day of the month of March, in the second indiction. In the Pratellian manuscript and other Norman manuscripts: “on the tenth day of the month of March, in the second indiction.”]

## LETTER XLII. TO AGILULPH, KING OF THE LOMBARDS

He gives thanks for the peace that has been arranged. He asks him to command his dukes not to disturb the peace.

[Column 0975B]

Gregory to Agilulph, king of the Lombards.

We give thanks to Your Excellency, because, hearing our petition, you arranged a peace that would benefit both parties, just as we had confidence in you. For this reason we have greatly praised the prudence and goodness of Your Excellency, because by loving peace you have shown that you love God, who is its author. For if—God forbid—it had not been made, what else could have been done except that, amid the sin and danger of both parties, the blood of the wretched peasants, whose labor benefits both sides, should be shed?

But in order that we may experience this peace benefiting us, just as it was made by you, we ask, greeting you with paternal affection, that whenever an opportunity arises you instruct by your letters your commanders stationed in various places, and especially in these regions, to guard this peace faithfully, as was promised, and not to seek any opportunities from which either some dispute or some ingratitude might arise, so that we may be able to give thanks more fully for your will.

We received the bearers of this letter, as they truly are your men, with the affection that was proper, since it was just that wise men who announced that peace had been made, with God’s favor, should be received and dismissed with charity.
