[Note: [Col. 0975D] EPIST. XLII [Al. 41].—Recent editions read *quod abesse gaudemus* (“which we are glad is absent”); shortly afterward, *agi debuit* (“ought to have been done”).]

## LETTER XLIII. TO THEODELINDA, QUEEN OF THE LANGOBARDS

He gives thanks because she has worked diligently to bring about peace.

[Col. 0975D]

Gregory to Theodelinda, queen of the Langobards.

We have learned from the report of our son Probus, the abbot, that Your Excellency has worked diligently and kindly, as is your custom, to bring about peace. Nor could we have had any other confidence in your Christianity unless you had shown in every way your labor and goodness in the cause of peace.

Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, who so governs your heart by his mercy that, just as he has granted you the true faith, so also he permits you always to do what pleases him. For, most excellent daughter, you should not think that you have gained a small reward from the blood that would have been shed on both sides. Therefore, giving thanks for your will, we beseech the mercy of our God to repay you here and in the future, in body and soul, with an equivalent measure of good things.

[Note: [Col. 0976D] After *vicem* (“equivalent”) the printed editions add *et retributionem* (“and recompense”), which is absent from the manuscripts.]

Moreover, greeting you with paternal affection, we urge you to act toward your most excellent husband in such a way that he does not reject fellowship with the Christian commonwealth.

[Note: [Col. 0976D] Namely, Agilulf or Agiulf.]

For, as we believe you also know, it is useful in many ways if he wishes to enter into friendship with it. Therefore, as is your custom, always strive for what pertains to the favor and reconciliation of the parties; and whenever an opportunity for earning a reward presents itself, labor so that your good works may commend you more fully before the eyes of almighty God.

## LETTER XLIV. TO FELIX IN SICILY

He complains that Felix unjustly accuses John, the bishop, as though he were avoiding judgment, although Felix himself had delayed it. He urges him to bring the dispute quickly to an end by the authority of judgment.

959

Gregory to Felix in Sicily.

Since the gravity of our most reverend brother John, the bishop, is well known to us, Your Glory’s letter greatly surprised us, because it indicated that he had been unwilling to do anything according to our admonition. Indeed, it seemed difficult either for us not to believe you or for us to suspect such things about him, since his character and conduct, which we knew, did not allow us to form such an opinion.

While our mind therefore hung in doubt between the two possibilities, we discovered that he had wished judgment to take place between you and his Church, but that he had delayed Your Glory’s action instead. Your own man, the bearer of this letter, could not deny this. We were saddened that Your Glory, which avoids judgment, should have wished to complain against him after it was established that he had obeyed what reason required, indeed voluntarily, as we wrote.

Nor was it necessary to write to him again, lest he appear previously to have delayed the matter intentionally. But so that we might not perhaps seem to cause you distress, we nevertheless thought it advisable to write again, out of an abundance of caution. Since we are certain that he will not refuse to do whatever equity determines, it is necessary for Your Glory not to inflame your feelings against him through resentment, but to strive to enter into judgment, in which, by one and the same investigation, both the question of possession and that of ownership may be distinguished.

[Note: [Col. 0977D] In French, *le possessoire et le pétitoire*: the possessory and proprietary actions. Hence *momentaria possessio*, *momenti beneficium*—that is, the immediate restoration and return of possession taken away by force or in some other manner. The person dispossessed is restored at once, while the question of ownership is deferred. In Symmachus’s Letter 27, Book I: “In cases,” he says, “in which immediate restoration is sought, appeals ought not to be accepted.” On these matters see the legal commentators. Concerning ownership, in the same letter Symmachus says: “When I said that this pertained to the question of ownership, the constitution was read by the advocates; it grants judges the power, but does not impose the obligation, that whenever they judge concerning possession of an inheritance, they should also, if the circumstances require, immediately investigate the right of ownership,” and so forth. Saint Gregory wishes the same to be done in Felix’s case. GUSSANV.]

For we cannot prejudicially write anything to one who wishes to come to judgment, because we ought to lend our hearing to one party in such a way that, nevertheless, we unquestionably reserve the matter intact for the other party, especially one whose allegation has not been heard. Therefore act, as we have said, so that, once the truth is known, the authority of judgment may define the merits of your affairs. For while we wish to suffer no prejudice,

[Note: [Col. 0977D] That is, harm or loss. The word has the same sense below, Book X, Letter 49.]

we much more wish what is just to be preserved for you, as for our true sons.

## LETTER XLV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

Having exposed Felix’s bad faith, he urges John to order without delay that the dispute he initiated be brought to an end.

[Col. 0977B]

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Some time ago our son Felix, a man of glory, complained to us in his letters that the boundaries of certain possessions of his had been violently overrun by men of your Church, and that he could find no justice with you. But it seemed incredible to us either that this had been perpetrated while you were present or, if it had reached your ears, that it had not been corrected.

Nevertheless, lest we should appear to have neglected his complaint, we wrote to Your Fraternity that either, if the allegations were true, you should restrain them, or at least make the agents of his Church undergo judgment with him. Afterward, sending the man to us with a letter, he reported that you had been unwilling to do anything.

Because we know the discretion of Your Holiness, while our mind remained in doubt, we discovered that he had delayed the matter more, whereas you had been prepared for judgment to take place.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] In the Vatican manuscripts D and in the manuscript of Saint-Victor: “so that you ought to have conducted the judgment.”]

And although there had been no need to write to you again on this matter, since it is clear that you had wished to do before you what reason required, nevertheless, lest we perhaps seem to have disregarded his complaint, we have for this reason sent you this letter, urging you even now, without further delay, to send your men with him to judgment. There the question both of immediate possession and of ownership may be brought to an end,

[Note: [Col. 0978D] Here and in the preceding letter, Alteserra understands *causa momenti* as the possessory action, because, he says, in a possessory case *possessio momentanea*, or provisional possession, is restored immediately and quickly.]

so that afterward neither he may have anything about which to complain nor your Church appear prejudicially to retain anything.

Since the man whom he sent to us produced a document of compromise and judgment,

[Note: [Col. 0978D] The decision of an arbitrator, to whose arbitration the parties voluntarily submitted their dispute. GUSSANV.]

in which it was read that the possession called Asinaria, which he recently asserted had been invaded by your men, had been restored by judgment in the time of your predecessor, Maximian of blessed memory, we thought it necessary to send you a copy of it.

Therefore, if you clearly discover that the matter was handled in this way—that is, if the possession itself was restored with the consent of your predecessor and was possessed by the aforesaid man—have it restored without any dispute, while, of course, leaving open the question of ownership, as was established in the same judgment. But if the matter is otherwise, this too must likewise be distinguished by the decision of a court.

Let Your Fraternity therefore arrange diligently and without any delay for all these matters to be carried out in this way, with the calmness proper to you, so that neither a murmur of resentment may be raised against us nor the aforesaid man be forced to become troublesome to us again.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] In the editions: “nor against you.” We have changed this reading, following two Vatican manuscripts, A and D. The Saint-Victor manuscript, however, supports the printed editions. A few manuscripts contain this letter.]

(See above, Letters 13 and 44.)

[Note: [Col. 0978D] EPIST. XLVI [Al. 45].—In the first Teller manuscript this letter is addressed to Savinus, the subdeacon.]

## LETTER XLVI. TO SERGIUS, THE DEFENSOR

He is to record the inheritance accruing from John to Pantaleon’s mother-in-law while Pantaleon is occupied with the affairs of the Church. He is also to investigate most carefully the sacred furnishings left with John.

[Col. 0978B]

Gregory to Sergius, the defensor.

You are certainly aware from your experience that Pantaleon, the notary, is occupied with ecclesiastical business. And because John, the uncle of his mother-in-law Megalis, is reported to have died intestate and without children, with no closer relative surviving, we enjoin you by this order to ensure that she does not suffer loss through the absence of her son-in-law. For if this is so, the law plainly summons the aforesaid woman to the succession of her intestate uncle.

You must therefore take our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Vitalian, together with Boniface the notary, as assistants to you, and diligently record in a written inventory every object that the deceased is established to have left, until the aforesaid Pantaleon returns.

[Note: [Col. 0978D] Thus in three Vatican manuscripts, the Colbertine, the Regius, the Remigius, and several Norman manuscripts, followed by the old printed editions. The same reading occurs below in those manuscripts. More recent editions prefer *in tutum* (“in safety”).]

To enable you to fulfill this better, also endeavor to take as your assistant our son John, the eminent tribune. We have complete confidence that, if you disclose our will to him, he will not refuse to place himself devotedly at your service.

It should likewise be a concern of your diligence, since the aforesaid John is said to have had certain sacred vessels in his possession, both to investigate them carefully and to secure them with every precaution, and to report to us precisely whatever is found.

Let your experience therefore hasten anxiously to carry out and attend to these instructions, so that you cannot be found blameworthy. For if you should prove negligent, know that you will incur our displeasure in such a way that afterward you will be unable to defend yourself by any excuse.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] These words are found in both Teller manuscripts and in the Colbertine. But in four Vatican manuscripts they are preceded by: “In the month of March, indiction 2.” In the Remigius: “In the month of May, indiction 2.”]

Given in the month of April, indiction 2.

(See Book VIII, Letter 26.)

## LETTER XLVII. TO SABINUS, THE SUBDEACON

Together with five bishops, he is to investigate the complaints of the clergy of Regium against their bishop, so that, informed by their report, he may decide the matter himself at Rome.

Gregory to Sabinus, the subdeacon.

The clergy of the Church of Regium, having submitted a petition to us, have complained of many things against our most reverend brother Boniface, their bishop, asking that they should be granted permission to come to us, so that the cases themselves might be examined carefully here.

But since we have not meanwhile foreseen that the aforesaid brother should be brought here, it seemed good to us to appoint the same case there for investigation.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] All the Norman manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, the Regius, Colbertine, Rheims, and others compel this reading, whereas the editions read “to appoint a person there to investigate the same case.”]

Therefore, with the holy Gospels present, let your experience, together with our most reverend brothers and fellow bishops Paulinus, Proculus, Palumbus, Venerius, and Marcianus, without regard to any person, investigate with complete equity and diligence both the complaint of the clergy against their bishop, as we have said, and any complaint he may perhaps have against them.

Whatever you ascertain to be true, report to us carefully and diligently together with the aforesaid brothers, so that, made more certain by your report, we may decide what ought to be done.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] In Vatican manuscripts B and F: “In the month of April, indiction 2.”]

[Note: [Col. 0979D] EPIST. XLVIII [Al. 47].—This letter is absent from several manuscripts and printed books. GUSSANV. It is found in four Vatican manuscripts, the Colbertine, Rheims, Regius, and Remigius.]

## LETTER XLVIII. TO PAULINUS, BISHOP OF TAURENTUM, AND OTHERS

They are to go to Regium together with Sabinus to investigate the complaints of the clergy against their bishop.

[Col. 0979C]

Gregory to Paulinus, bishop of Taurentum; Proculus, bishop of Nicotera; Palumbus, bishop of Consentia;

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Consentia, commonly Cosenza, a city formerly famous among the Bruttians, situated on the river Crathis, commonly the Crate; now the principal city and archiepiscopal see of Citerior Calabria, in the Kingdom of Naples. GUSSANV.]

Venerius, bishop of Vibo; and Marcianus, bishop of Locri.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Concerning Locri, see Letter 41 of Book VII. GUSSANV.]

The clergy of the Church of Regium, having submitted a petition to us, have complained of many things against our most reverend brother Boniface, their bishop, asking that they should be granted permission to come to us, so that the cases themselves might be examined carefully here.

But since we have not meanwhile foreseen that the aforesaid brother should be brought here, it seemed good to us to appoint the same case there for investigation. Therefore, with the holy Gospels present, let Your Fraternity sit together with the deacon Sabinus; and, as is fitting for priestly office, without regard to any person, and so forth, as above.

## LETTER XLIX. TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

He rejoices over his orthodox profession of faith. Thanks are to be given to God because only the orthodox are promoted to orders. Prayer is to be offered for the emperor, who suppresses heretics. Anastasius is to seek an authentic copy of the Council of Ephesus. Simoniacs are to be excluded from sacred orders.

Gregory to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] He is called Anastasius the younger of Sinai. He succeeded Anastasius the Great in the year 599 and occupied the see for nine years, that is, until the seventh year of the reign of Phocas. At that time, when civil war broke out at Antioch, the Jews dragged Anastasius from the throne with a rope tied to his feet and subjected him to an utterly disgraceful death. On this, see the *Miscellaneous History*, Book XVII, and Cedrenus, under the final year of Phocas. The Alexandrian Chronicle gives the same account, Olympiad 347. Nicephorus likewise relates it, Book XVIII, chapter 43. But he is certainly mistaken, since he reports that this happened to Anastasius the Great, who had died nine years earlier. The same error appears in the *Miscellaneous History* and in Anastasius the Librarian. GUSSANV.]

I have received the writings of Your Fraternity, which rightly preserve the profession of faith; and I have offered great thanks to almighty God, who, even when the pastors of his flock are changed, preserves unchanged after them the faith that he once delivered to the holy Fathers.

The distinguished preacher says: “No one can lay another foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11). Whoever therefore holds firmly, with love of God and neighbor, to the faith that is in Christ has laid within himself that same Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man, as a foundation.

[Note: [Col. 0980D] Gratian, *Decretum*, Part I, Question 1, chapter 26.]

It is therefore to be hoped that where Christ is the foundation, the building of good works will also follow.

Truth itself also says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber; but whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10:8). Shortly afterward he adds: “I am the door.” He therefore enters the sheepfold through the door who enters through Christ.

But he enters through Christ who thinks and preaches truly concerning the same Creator and Redeemer of the human race, and who guards what he has preached; who undertakes the summit of governance for the duty of bearing a burden, not from desire for the passing honor of glory. He also watches carefully over the care of the flock entrusted to him, lest either wicked people tear God’s sheep apart by speaking perverse things, or evil spirits destroy them by persuading them to delight in vices.

Certainly we remember blessed Jacob, who had served for a long time for his wives, saying: “For twenty years I was with you; your sheep and goats were not barren. I did not eat the rams of your flock, nor did I show you anything captured by a beast. I bore every loss; whatever was lost through theft, you demanded from me. By day and by night I was scorched by heat and frost, and sleep fled from my eyes” (Genesis 31:38).

If, then, the man who tended Laban’s sheep labored and kept watch in this way, with how much labor and with how many vigils must he attend who tends the sheep of God?

[Note: [Col. 0981D] In Scripture bishops are called shepherds rather than rulers. The books of both covenants are full of this expression, and it would be tedious to cite their texts. Christ the Lord himself, the chief shepherd, called himself by this name: “I am the good shepherd.” I take the reasoning from Theophylact, commentary on John 21, where he establishes a distinction between *boskein* and *poimainein*, between providing pasture and governing a flock: “For *poimainein* already signifies a harsher form of oversight, whereas *boskein* signifies the gentler.” See Augustine, Tractate 123 on John, where he treats the manner of feeding at length and abundantly, and Theodoret on Ezekiel 34. GUSSANV.]

But in all these matters may he himself instruct us, who became human for our sake and deigned to become what he had made. May he pour into both my weakness and Your Charity the spirit of his love, and in every anxiety and vigilant guardianship open the eye of our heart.

As men of right faith are brought forward for sacred orders, unceasing thanks must be offered to the same almighty God. We must always pray for the life of our most pious and most Christian lord the emperor, for his most tranquil wife, and for his most gentle offspring. In their time the mouths of heretics are silenced: although their hearts boil with the madness of perverse understanding, in the time of a Catholic emperor they do not dare to express the evil opinions they hold.

Moreover, while Your Fraternity was speaking about the preservation of the holy councils, you professed that you preserve the first holy Council of Ephesus. But because, from an annotation in a heretical codex sent to me from the imperial city, I learned that certain Catholic chapters had been condemned together with heretics, since some people think that the “first Council of Ephesus” was the one held in that same city and formerly reported to have been composed by heretics, it is entirely necessary for Your Charity to seek that same council from the holy Churches of Alexandria and Antioch and to discover how it is truly preserved.

Alternatively, if you wish, we can send from here what we have preserved from antiquity in our archives. For the council that was held under the appearance of the first Council of Ephesus asserts that certain chapters submitted to it were approved, although they are the teachings of Celestius and Pelagius. Yet since Celestius and Pelagius were condemned in that council, how could it have accepted chapters whose authors it condemned?

[Note: [Col. 0981D] Above, in Book V, and now in Book VI, Letter 14, he mentioned the corruption of that council in favor of the Pelagians. So that the reader may understand, I add that John of Antioch, together with more than forty bishops, held a separate pseudo-council, nevertheless at Ephesus, in which they condemned Cyril while favoring Nestorius and excommunicated other bishops who were then sitting in the true council, restoring, as appears from this passage, the Pelagian heresy. It is plausible that part of the acts of this pseudo-council slipped into the codex of the true Council of Ephesus through the carelessness of copyists, who, deceived by the city’s name and the date, failed to distinguish between the bishops of opposing parties and their judgments. GUSSANV.]

Since it has come to our attention that in the Churches of the East no one reaches sacred orders except through the gift of rewards, if Your Fraternity recognizes that this is so, let this be your first offering to almighty God: restrain the error of the simoniacal heresy from the Churches subject to you. For, to say nothing else, what sort of men can those be in sacred orders who are elevated to them not by merit but by rewards?

May almighty God preserve Your Charity by heavenly grace and grant you to bring back to eternal joys a manifold harvest and an overflowing measure from those entrusted to you.

[Note: [Col. 0982] The note appears at the foot of column 982, but its callout number was not printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0982] EPIST. L. Al. 32, Book XI, indiction 6.]

## LETTER L. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He is to send Benenatus, who denies his crime, to Rome together with the accuser and other persons.

[Col. 0982A]

Gregory to Anthimius, the subdeacon.

We have learned that Benenatus of Misenum denies the crime that he previously confessed in writing in his own hand. Therefore, because denial of such a crime requires not only a more thorough investigation but also a more severe punishment, by the authority of this letter we command your experience to send the same Benenatus, his accuser, the persons concerning whom he has been accused, and everyone whose name appears in the written accusation, here with every precaution and speed, so that the truth of this case may be examined and ascertained by a strict investigation, as is fitting.

[Note: [Col. 0982] The note appears at the foot of column 982, but its callout number was not printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0982] EPIST. LI. Al. 33, Book XI, indiction 6.]

## LETTER LI. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

He is to investigate the remainder of the money given for the construction of the fort at Benenatus’s house and ensure that it is all spent on that very project.

Gregory to Anthimius, the subdeacon.

It has come to us that Benenatus, formerly bishop of Misenum, received solidi there for the construction of a fort. Since part of those solidi is said to have remained with him, your experience must investigate the matter carefully. If you clearly discover that any of those solidi remain, let the count of the aforesaid city, under a written record of what has been received, take possession of them, and insist that, with God’s help, they be applied to the construction of that place, just as they were given.

For reason in no way permits what is known to have been given for the common benefit to be applied to anyone’s private uses.

[Note: [Col. 0982D] EPIST. LII [Al. 54].—This letter would more easily be erased than corrected. Manuscript codices demonstrate that it was enlarged by various additions, and learned men whose palate has any taste agree. Whoever he was, an exceedingly audacious person inserted material concerning the lapsed that directly contradicts Saint Gregory’s decisions. Anyone can readily detect the *anakolouthia* (ἀνακολουθία) of the discourse, which Quintilian calls “inconsequence” and others, by an invented term, “incoherence.” The text itself teems with countless errors, and the manuscripts are almost continually at variance. Out of thirty manuscripts, scarcely one or two contain the enormous fragment concerning the lapsed, which begins: “And because Your Holiness …” There are few that contain the other fragment concerning images near the end of the letter. The very ancient Rheims manuscript, in which all the letters of the Roman pontiffs from Gelasius to John VII are copied, does not contain the addition concerning the lapsed. Nevertheless, Saint Anselm, Book I, Letter 56, accepts and defends it through the human thoughtlessness that is common in such matters, before the sun of criticism had risen. At what time so absurd a corruption occurred is not entirely clear. Many reject it as the work of Isidore Mercator—I mean that famous fabricator or falsifier who, during the eighth century, wrote a book of canons in Spain and was the first to publish the forged Decretals. It is nevertheless established from a letter of Paul the Deacon, said to have died in the year 801, addressed to Adalard, abbot of Corbie, that the letter in question was one of the fifty-four letters of Saint Gregory that Paul had been able to collect. Since this addition is found in it, it is clear that the letter was already corrupted at that time. I wish to warn the reader that I have found more than two hundred variant readings in this letter—not to call them corruptions—with which it is entirely overgrown. I shall set down here only the principal ones, lest I weary the reader. GUSSANV.

Although we do not approve this criticism by Gussanville in every respect, we have decided to append it because it contains much worthy of knowing. We particularly reject two claims made by Gussanville. First, this complete letter, which is found in all the Vatican, English, Tours, Norman, Rheims, Colbertine, Corbie, Saint-Victor, Regius, Remigius, and other manuscripts, should not appear rejectable merely because of one or another addition. Second, Paul the Deacon could have collected only the fifty-four letters that he sent to Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie. This seems to imply that the other Gregorian letters were entirely unknown in Paul’s age; Gussanville certainly dreamed this up, for Paul the Deacon contains no word at all about such a small number of Saint Gregory’s letters. What we think of his collection has already been stated in the preface. Moreover, we have discussed Secundinus at great length in the *Life of Saint Gregory*.

[Col. 0983B–C]

## LETTER LII. TO SECUNDINUS

He praises his writings as breathing truth, charity, and humility. He says that solitaries, like single combatants, are particularly attacked by the ancient enemy. The Eastern Churches follow, with one understanding, the complete faith of Saint Leo and of the Council of Chalcedon. He attacks the defenders of the Three Chapters. He proves that the letter of Ibas conflicts with the definition of the holy council. He teaches that the origin of the soul is uncertain, but that it is certainly bound by original sin until baptism. He sends images and explains their legitimate use.

Gregory to Secundinus, servant of God, enclosed.

[Note: [Col. 0984C] In some manuscripts the title reads: “To his most beloved son Secundinus, servant of God, enclosed; Gregory, servant of the servants of God.” In others: “Gregory to Secundinus, servant of God, confined”; in still others, “enclosed.” GUSSANV.]

[Note: [Col. 0984C] The Greeks call such persons *enkleistoi* (ἐγκλείστοις), namely those who, out of a desire for a higher life, withdrew from human society and lived a solitary life in caves and underground hollows. Anastasius the Librarian calls them *inclusi* and *cionitae*; Theodore the Studite calls them *clusii* in Catechesis 38. They were also called Hesychasts, Greek *hesychastai* (ἡσυχασταὶ), a term taken from Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, article 133; Justinian later used the term in *Novella* 5: “Unless some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, maintain a secluded life in a dwelling, as though they had been withdrawn from communion to better things.” See *Novella* 133. GUSSANV.]

I have received the writings of Your Charity, and they tasted to me as though seasoned with the honey of love. Oh, how full of the inspiration of life are the things spoken through the grace of the Spirit! They displayed no ornament of eloquence, no affectation of words,

[Note: [Col. 0984C] Or “conceit.” For this word see Book XXIII of the *Moralia*, no. 25, note a (Patrologia Latina, vol. 76, col. 265, note g).]

but, possessing only the root of truth and charity, they breathed the love of the heavenly homeland through everything they said.

[Note: [Col. 0984D] Thus almost all manuscripts: *fragrabant*, “they breathed forth” or “were fragrant with.” The printed editions read *efflabant*, “they breathed out.”]

In them your affection earnestly asked me to write for you a small work of exhortation. But you must know, dearest son, that I am weighed down by such pains of gout and such turmoil of cares that, although I never remember having been anything, I nevertheless clearly see that I am no longer what I was.

Your Charity also declares that even beyond the age of fifty you remain subject to youthful desires. In this too you fulfill the precept of the divine oracle, which says: “The righteous man is first an accuser of himself” (Proverbs 18:17).

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that you suffer greater ambushes from the crafty enemy, since you have prepared greater battles against him. For the more fervently he knows you to long for the heavenly homeland, the more ardently he seeks the machinations of deception against you.

We who lead our lives among many people, although fearful and timid, nevertheless stand as though in battle formation, because we have undertaken war against the ancient enemy. But you who lead a solitary life—what else should I call you than single combatants,

[Note: [Col. 0984D] Eight manuscript codices read *monomachos* (“single combatants”), and, in my opinion, not incorrectly, since the context seems to require it: “you who, through the ardor of virtue, hasten to go out even before the battle line.” GUSSANV. Most manuscripts, however, read *monachos* (“monks”), namely the Vatican manuscripts, most Norman manuscripts, the Colbertine, Regius, Corbie, Saint-Victor, Rheims, and Remigius. We found *monomachos* only in the Bec manuscript and in the Tours manuscript of the Greater Monastery. The reasoning given by Gussanville persuades us that this is the correct reading. Jamezius reports that it is also found in the English manuscripts.]

you who in the ardor of virtue hasten to go out even before the battle line? Why, then, should the enemy not attack singularly one whom he sees to be attacking him singularly?

We who live among human beings are often tempted by the crafty enemy through human beings. But you who travel the road of the present life outside the crowds of humanity must endure greater contests, in proportion as the master of temptations himself approaches you.

For you cannot be free from prayers and praises of God without some interruption of time. Even if the intention remains continually ready, human weakness itself nevertheless falls back upon itself, so that at times it lies exhausted and grows sluggish in the exercise of its devotion.

But as soon as the ancient enemy finds the mind idle, he approaches it to speak under various pretexts. He recalls to it certain deeds of the past; words once heard resound indecently in its thought; and if anything shameful was formerly done, he places its image before the eyes of the heart, so that he may defile one whom he cannot stain through present things by means of past evils.

[Note: [Col. 0984D] Vatican manuscripts A and F, and one Corbie manuscript: “And the deceived mind often renews pleasure from it.” Another Corbie manuscript: “turns it into pleasures.” The printed editions: “And the deceived mind is often snatched from it into pleasure.” We follow the Norman, Colbertine, Rheims, Regius, Remigius, Tours, and Greater Monastery manuscripts, together with one Vatican manuscript.]

And he often restores pleasure to the deceived mind from the very thing over which it has long afflicted itself through repentance, so that it truly says with the Psalmist: “My scars have become putrid and festering, because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6).

A scar is indeed the mark of a wound, but of one that has been healed. A scar therefore returns to putrefaction when the wound of sin, already healed through repentance, stirs the mind into delight in itself.

Often, through the snares of the crafty enemy, we see with the eyes of the heart what we have never done. When pleasure imperceptibly steals into this experience, although a person may already grieve over what he has done, the unhappy mind nevertheless becomes distressed that it has not done certain things over which it grieves.

These are the darknesses of our heart, which in this life we endure both willingly and unwillingly. Who, then, should be sought against these things except the helper in times of need and tribulation?

I received with great pleasure the fact that your Charity inquired of me about its uncertainty: whether the Churches of the East follow the faith and teaching of Pope Leo of holy memory, lest perhaps their convictions be divided among themselves in defense of the Three Chapters. Therefore I wish your loving concern to be certain that the aforementioned most holy Churches of the East, with one conviction and one teaching, hold the faith of Leo of holy memory, and preserve and venerate the holy Council of Chalcedon together with us in such a way that no one is regarded as a bishop who has not been a defender and follower of that council.

For this reason, whenever bishops are ordained in the four principal sees, they send one another synodal letters in which they acknowledge that they preserve the holy Council of Chalcedon together with the other four general councils; [Note: What follows up to “for the council” is absent from Paul’s Collection. There are many other gaps of this kind in this codex.] just as we too reject and judge worthy of anathema anyone who presumes either to diminish anything concerning the faith of that council or to add anything to it. For the council that was held generally after it is accepted by us for this reason: because, following that council in all things, it preserves its honor and authority.

Therefore your most beloved affection should consider all the more earnestly this point—your affection which chiefly lives in good morals, afflicts itself through abstinence, and applies itself with particular zeal to God’s teaching—lest, by following the error of schismatics, it be found separated from the holy universal Church. And what benefit will all those labors bring if they are not found within the unity of the faith, [Note: In recent editions, corruptly: “if it is not found.” All the English, Norman, Rheims, Colbert, and other witnesses support the reading given here.] which above all guards the soul in good deeds before the eyes of almighty God?

Hence it is said: “My dove is one, my perfect one” (Song of Songs 6:8). Hence the Lord says to Moses: “There is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock” (Exodus 33:21). What place is there that is not in God, since all things are contained by him through whom they were created? Yet there is a place with him—namely, the unity of the holy Church—in which one stands upon the rock while humbly holding fast to the firmness of its confession. Concerning this place it is added: “Then you shall see my back parts.” Standing upon the rock, that is, in the holy Church, we shall see God’s back parts when we contemplate the joys of the heavenly homeland that have been promised for the end.

But perverse men, who, having found an occasion in the Three Chapters, flee ecclesiastical discipline, fear to be reproved for their carnal actions, refuse to submit to the commands of the apostolic see, and reproach us as though we were concerned with a faith that they themselves do not understand—while they are neither upright in faith nor attentive to good works—strive to appear to be fighting for the faith. Thus they become worse every day, while the fault within them grows coarse, [Note: The more recent witnesses, contrary to the manuscripts, read “which also seeks to appear laudable, as though arising from zeal.”] which even seeks to appear praiseworthy, as though from the ardor of zeal.

But in accordance with what is written, “You will know them by their works” (Matthew 7:16), let your Charity observe their life and examine the merit of their intention. To speak briefly to your affection about this same matter: the holy Council of Chalcedon spoke about general matters up to the definition of the faith and the promulgation of the canons. For after the promulgation of the canons it undertook to quiet particular disputes among bishops.

But you recognize the letter that the most reverend Ibas denies to be his, because it lies at the end of the council. That letter asserts that Nestorius was condemned unheard and without an investigation, while it suspects Cyril of having fallen into the doctrine of Apollinaris. And if the entire preceding text of the council is read, it is found how greatly this letter opposes that council: for the holy council declares Nestorius to be a heretic, as he truly was, and venerates blessed Cyril as a Catholic father.

Therefore a letter that defends one who was condemned by the council and accuses one who was venerated by the council is plainly shown to be opposed to the definition of the holy council. But since its defenders are accustomed to say that Ibas wrote this letter at a time when Cyril was still regarded with suspicion because of the Twelve Chapters, which he had not yet explained, consider carefully what is read in this very letter: that peace had been established between the Eastern bishops and blessed Cyril. If, then, this same letter was written after the peace of reconciliation and after the removal of doubt through satisfaction, it is clear that it is not Catholic, since it calls a Catholic father, praised throughout the entire volume of the council, a heretic.

I have said these things briefly because in the letters I have not found the principal reasons from which your Charity derives its uncertainty in this matter. [Note: What is read here up to the section beginning “But concerning ordinations” is absent from most manuscripts. It is found in the Collection of Paul the Deacon; in a manuscript of the Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs in the library of the Capuchin Fathers at Rouen; in one Colbert manuscript of approximately the ninth century; in another Colbert manuscript of the ninth or tenth century; and in the Gemeticensis marked 20, which contains the letters of Saint Augustine and, at the end, this letter of Saint Gregory to Secundinus, although it contains nothing about images. It is likewise found in two Teller manuscripts and in Vatican manuscripts A and D II; for this letter was collated with two Vatican D manuscripts. The copies used by Gratian, Ivo of Chartres, Saint Anselm, and Hincmar contained the same material. See Hincmar, in the Capitula addressed to priests, and Saint Anselm, book I, letter 56. Hence Gussanville, in the preceding note, carelessly asserted that scarcely one or two codices contain the enormous fragment concerning the lapsed. We nevertheless think that assertion should be rejected, both because of the reasons supplied by that learned man and because of others to be briefly set out below. This argument was treated most learnedly by Cardinal d’Aguirre, volume II of the Councils of Spain, dissertation 10, “On the ancient discipline of the Church … concerning those who have fallen into the sin of the flesh.”]

And since your Holiness (Gratian, distinction 50, chapter 16) [Note: Learned men long ago observed that this addition concerning lapsed clerics being restored to their order after worthy satisfaction is spurious. For, they ask, who would reconcile that statement of the false Gregory—“After worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return to honor”—with Gregory the Great’s letters: book IV, letter 26, indiction 12; indiction 13, letters 3 and 4; indiction 15, letter 42; and indiction 1, letter 25? We add one or two arguments to those of others. Under this title, “your Holiness,” Gregory addresses bishops and sometimes abbots adorned with the priesthood, but never monks, nor abbots who were not priests. See indiction 10, letter 36; indiction 11, letter 3; indiction 14, letter 48; indiction 15, letters 10, 18, and 45; indiction 4, letters 12 and 76. Moreover, so many passages of Scripture have been heaped together to prove that sinners can obtain mercy that they diverge greatly from the proposed purpose. How foreign to Gregory’s supreme prudence it was to collect them uselessly, especially at a time when both illness and affairs kept him from lengthy writing and study!] has asked us to write authorities for you concerning rising again to priestly office after a fall, saying that you have read various canons on this subject and found differing opinions—some allowing restoration, others denying that it is possible. Accordingly, we venerate the holy general councils, beginning with Nicaea and including the other four held afterward, [Note: We have restored the text chiefly from Vatican D, since this passage was previously extremely corrupt. In Colbert and the Capuchin codex: “because, following him in all judgments, they agree unanimously, for we also follow the Fathers who preceded us.” The cited codices differ so greatly both from the printed editions and from one another that, if we wished to transcribe all the variant readings, this passage would have to be printed anew in its entirety.] because, following that council, the others agree unanimously in all canonical judgments. For we too ought to follow the Fathers who preceded us, since, with God as author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

Beginning, therefore, at the head and continuing to the fourth altar [Note: Printed editions: “minister.”] ministry, we recognize that this rule must be observed: just as the lesser is preceded by the greater in honor, so also in guilt; and the one whom a greater fault follows must be punished with a greater penalty, and thus afterward repentance is believed to be fruitful. [Note: We believe that one may return to honor not only in order to obtain forgiveness but also in order to be restored to one’s former ministerial rank, as the following makes clear. All students of sacred antiquity know that this conflicts with the ancient councils and with all the Fathers. Certainly the Council of Nicaea, praised here, orders a cleric guilty of some crime who was ordained through ignorance or concealment to be deposed. See canon 61 of the Apostles; Pope Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch, in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 35; Cyprian’s letters 64 and 68; Saint Basil’s first letter to Amphilochius, canon 3; and John II’s letter to Caesarius of Arles concerning the case of Contumeliosus, bishop of Riez, together with Caesarius’s judgment on that matter, in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, under the year 534. Anyone who has read the letters praised above will understand how opposed this doctrine of restoring lapsed clerics is to Saint Gregory’s mind. And lest anyone imagine that the holy Doctor departed from his earlier opinion and former rigor, let him read book XII, letter 8, concerning a deposed deacon: Gregory orders him restored if guilt or crime did not remove him from his rank, but not if he was deposed for bodily sin. Anselm of Canterbury attempted another way of reconciling Saint Gregory’s conflicting opinions, book I, letter 56, to Abbot William: “But since the same blessed Gregory forbids the restoration of lapsed clerics in other letters, so that he may not contradict himself, he is understood to have forbidden it in the case of public sins, but to have permitted it in the case of hidden sins through hidden repentance.” Yet the ancient canons, which Gregory defended, did not proceed in this way; indeed, they explicitly rejected this distinction, and we infer that it had not yet become wholly established even in Anselm’s age from these words of Urban II to the bishop of Constance: “Concerning priests, deacons, and subdeacons who, after receiving orders, have fallen into some crime, whether openly or secretly, it is indeed clear that the judgment of the canons excludes them from ecclesiastical offices. Nevertheless, let it be your responsibility …” I add that no trace of such a distinction exists in this doubtful fragment.]

For what benefit is there in sowing wheat and not gathering its fruit? Or in building a house and not dwelling in it? Therefore, after worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return to honor, as the Prophet says: “Will not the one who falls rise again?” (Psalm 40:9). And again: “The one who has turned away—will he not return?” (Jeremiah 8:4). And he says to the sinner: “On whatever day you turn and groan, you shall be saved” (Isaiah 30:15, according to the Septuagint).

Hence the Psalmist also says: “Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Psalm 50:12). When he asked not to be cast away by the Lord [Note: Thus two Vatican manuscripts. Paul’s Collection has “for the fault of the lapsed.” Printed editions have “for his fault.”] because of the fault of his fall, the king and prophet, shaken with fear, dreaded that he had likewise taken another man’s wife. And when the prophet exposed his crime, he repented and added: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (ibid., 14).

For if he had not offered God worthy repentance, he would never have preached to others. For he says: “I will teach the unjust your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you” (ibid., 15). When the Prophet saw that his sins had been cleansed through repentance, he did not hesitate to heal the sins of others by preaching, and he strove to offer himself to God as a sacrifice, saying: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (ibid., 19).

These things would suffice for this purpose, [Note: They are not sufficient at all, as we have already indicated; the same must be understood of the testimonies that follow. What do all those passages of Scripture prove that the author of this addition has heaped together? Hear the collector himself: “Let these things, dearest son, suffice for you, so that you may not doubt that the one whom you see wiping away his sins with tears obtains mercy in the sight of God, because he who came to redeem sinners by his blood does not despise the sinner who returns.” He plainly wanders from the point and does not address the issue he himself proposed. The matter concerns only restoration to rank, office, and ministry—or, as he barbarously puts it, rising again to priestly office after a fall once repentance has been completed. The rule established in the Church that no one, after repenting of any crime, should receive clerical status, return to it, or remain in it was established not from despair of pardon but from the rigor of discipline. Augustine, letter 185.] but every judgment is more readily believed the more it is confirmed by testimonies from sacred Scripture.

Concerning this the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel 18:32). Concerning sinners it is said: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, he shall be saved; all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion” (ibid., 22). If our Redeemer, who came not to destroy sinners but to justify them, has left the offenses of sinners in oblivion, who among human beings reserves them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is he that condemns?” (Romans 8:33)?

Returning to the fountain of mercy, let us bring forth the saying of the Gospel: “I will rejoice,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7). And the Lord himself bears witness that the lost sheep, leaving the ninety-nine that had not strayed, is carried back to the fold upon the shoulders of the compassionate shepherd.

If the lost sheep, having strayed, is carried back to the fold upon the shepherd’s shoulders after it has been found, why should this man, having fallen after repentance, not be restored to the Church’s ministry? As it is said in the Apocalypse concerning the Church’s ministry: “Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do the first works” (Revelation 2:5).

For what is more serious: to commit a carnal offense, without which few are found to be, or to deny the Son of God under oath? In this matter we know that this very blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, at whose sacred body we unworthy men sit, fell. But after the denial came repentance, and after repentance mercy was given, because afterward Christ did not expel him from the apostolate, although he had previously foretold that Peter would deny him.

Let these things, dearest Son, suffice for you, so that you may not doubt that the one whom you see wiping away his sins with tears obtains mercy in the sight of God, because he who came to redeem sinners by his blood does not despise the sinner who returns.

Concerning the ordinations of the pontiffs of the apostolic see, your Charity asks whether anything was added after the most blessed Hormisdas. But know that the ordinations of bishops were set forth up to the time of Pope Vigilius. [Note: What follows is found in almost all the manuscripts, up to the next section, “Images,” and so forth.]

We have sent, through the bearer of this letter, aloe, frankincense, storax, and balsam, to be offered to the bodies of the holy martyrs. [Note: This is read in the Norman, Corbie, Vatican, Teller, and other manuscripts; recent printed editions have “aloes.”]

Finally, in your letter you asked what should be answered to those who inquire of your affection concerning the souls of infants who die without the grace of baptism. You say: “If the body is held under original guilt, how will the soul, which is given by God, be guilty, since it has not yet consented to actual sin in the body?”

But concerning this matter, let your most beloved Charity know that there has been no small dispute among the holy Fathers concerning the origin of the soul. Whether it descended from Adam or is given individually to each person has remained uncertain, and they have acknowledged that the question is insoluble in this life.

For the question is serious and cannot be comprehended by human beings. If the soul is born from Adam’s substance together with the flesh, why does it not also die with the flesh? But if it is not born together with the flesh, why is it held bound by sins in that flesh which was brought forth from Adam?

Yet although this is uncertain, the following is not: unless a person is reborn through the grace of holy baptism, every soul is bound by the chains of original sin. Hence it is written: “No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day upon the earth” (Job 14:4–5, according to the Septuagint). Hence David says: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm 50:7). Hence Truth itself says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). Hence the Apostle Paul says: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

Why, then, can an infant who has done nothing not be clean in the sight of almighty God? Why was the Psalmist, born from a lawful marriage, conceived in iniquity? Why is one who has not been cleansed by baptismal water not clean? Why does every human being die in Adam if he is not held by the chains of original sin?

But because the human race rotted in its first parent as in a root, it drew dryness into its branches; and thus every human being is born with sin, from the same source from which the first human being refused to remain without sin.

I ought to have spoken about these matters more subtly and more boldly. But while the turmoil of cares presses upon me, and the bearer of this letter proved importunate when he ought to have allowed me time, I have said little about matters on which I owed much.

I ask almighty God to protect you with his grace and, through the intercession of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to preserve you unharmed from every evil, so that the ardor of heavenly desire may grow daily more fervently in your mind and, always renewed and always stronger than itself, may bring you ever more abundantly to the reception of heavenly rewards.

I have sent two codices of homilies which, as I said, I delivered in the Church while I still had the strength to speak, so that, since I cannot see you personally or converse with you diligently, I may nevertheless not be absent from your affection through what I have been able to write.

I have also tried to send a small garment, by which your Charity—since your spirit burns with southern warmth—may ward off the cold of Arcturus from the body outside.

But I ask that you pray for me with earnestness, so that through the help of your intercession I may deserve both to be rescued from present evils and to be brought into eternal joys.

## Images

The images that you asked to have sent to you through the deacon Dulcidius we have sent. [Note: Here almost all the manuscripts leave us. Nevertheless, the passage concerning images is cited both by Gregory II at the Roman council, volume VI of the Councils, page 1462, and by Hadrian I in his letter to Charlemagne concerning the Council of Nicaea, volume VII of the Councils, page 961. It is found in Paul’s Collection and in the same Vatican codices that contain the fragment concerning the restoration of lapsed clerics. Gussanville notes that it is found in Cistercian manuscripts, and Thomas Jamezius in one of the English manuscripts, where at the end of the Letters it reads: “The judgment of blessed Pope Gregory concerning images, excerpted from the decrees of the canons.”]

Your request therefore pleased us greatly, because with your whole heart and whole intention you seek the one whose image you desire to have before your eyes, so that the daily physical sight may train you, and, while you look upon his picture, you may burn inwardly toward the one whose image you desire to see.

We do nothing inappropriate if, through visible things, we demonstrate invisible things. Thus, when someone ardently desires to see another—or when a man in love desires to see his bride—and it happens that she goes to the baths or to church, he immediately prepares himself along the road she is taking, so that he may depart joyful from seeing her.

I know, of course, that you do not ask for an image of our Savior in order to worship it as God, but so that, in remembering the Son of God, you may grow warm with love for the one whose image you desire to see.

Nor do we prostrate ourselves before it as though before the divine nature; rather, we worship the one whom, through the image, we remember either as born, or as having suffered, or also as seated upon the throne. And when the picture itself, like writing, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either rejoices our mind by reminding us of the resurrection or soothes it by reminding us of the Passion.

Therefore we have sent you, through our aforementioned son the deacon, two *surtaria* [Note: Regino, under the year 753, reads *surcariis*. In Pope Stephen III’s letter to Abbot Hilduin it reads *surtariis*. Alteserra thinks that it was a type of garment on which images were painted. Baronius, under the year 754, §4, believes *surtaria* to mean the same as a shield on which images are painted; Cangius inclines to this view and says that one should read *scutarias* rather than *surtarias*.] containing an image of God our Savior, and of holy Mary, the Mother of God, and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, as well as one cross and also a key, as a blessing, from the most holy body of Peter, prince of the apostles, [Note: The Teller and Vallis manuscripts read: “So that through him you may be defended from the evil one, through whose holy wood you believe yourself to be fortified.” Gussanville.] so that through it you may remain defended from the evil one, by whose sign you believe yourself to be fortified, [Note: Some manuscripts read: “So that he may protect you from the one who prompts youthful passions in you. Remember that, persevering in your good works, you should kindle others with love for him, for whose love you have made yourself dwell in solitude; so that, by the evil of his life—or perhaps, ‘the evils’—which he suggests to you in your heart, you may afterward burn in other minds like torches.” Gussanville.] and so that he may protect you from the one who always prompts remembrance of youthful things; so that you may persevere in your good works, remain in his love to the end, and, for whose love you desire to dwell in solitude, kindle others with love for him, because of whom you have caused yourself to be held in solitude; so that, concerning all the evils of this life that the enemy suggests, you may burn with the fruits of your mind, once those evils have been left behind, like torches, for love of him, for whose sake you may even wish to end your life.

May he himself also protect you to the end—Jesus Christ our Lord, who deigned to redeem the whole world, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## LETTER LIII. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN

He is prepared to grant the clergy of Como the disputed property if they return to the unity of the Church.

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

Through the bearer of this letter, our common son the deacon Eventius, who brought us the written communication of your Fraternity, we have learned that the clergy of the Church of Como, whom you urged in priestly zeal to return to the unity of the Church, replied that such affection had not been shown toward them by us as would enable them, persuaded by love, to return to it. [Note: In the printed editions and some manuscripts, corruptly, “by you.” The clerics were complaining of the Church of Rome, not of the Milanese Church.] They asserted that various properties belonging to them were being unjustly held by others, among them by our Church, including the possession called the Maurian estate.

[Note: “The Church of Como,” commonly Como, is an ancient city formerly in Insubria, beside Lake Larius, commonly called Lake Como, north of Milan. Today it is in the Duchy of Milan under the rule of the Catholic king. It is suffragan to the archbishop of Aquileia, resident at Udine. Gussanville. Most manuscripts read *Comensis* rather than *Conomensis*.]

We have greatly praised the concern of your Holiness, because you did not neglect what it was proper for you to do. But neither do we permit the aforementioned possession to be detained contrary to the order of justice if it rightfully belongs to them, even if they have perhaps delayed returning to communion; rather, we wish it to be restored once the truth has been established.

If, however, inspired by God, they return to the unity of the Church, as we desire, we are prepared to grant it to them even if they have no legal claim to it. For we do not wish those whom we desirably await to return to the bosom of Mother Church to be excused on any pretext. [Note: That is, we do not wish to give them any occasion for excusing themselves or to cast any shadow by which they could be held in schism.]

Concerning the gardens which, in the memorandum you sent, you indicated belonged to your Church from the property of the Church of Italy, the aforementioned bearer informed us; [Note: Recent editions read “from the property of such a Church.” The Vatican, Norman, Rheims, and other manuscripts resist this. Below, the printed editions have “the bearer indicated to you.” It should instead read “indicated to us”: the manuscripts support this, and reason requires it.] we shall subsequently send a person there and, among other instructions, will clearly charge him to ascertain the truth through suitable investigation and to do whatever is just.

For if we do not permit others to be distressed contrary to equity, much less can we leave you, whom we love greatly, in distress. You will learn from the report of our aforementioned common son what our response is to each of the other matters.

We have also written, as you wished, to our most beloved son Anatolius the deacon in recommendation of your people.

## LETTER LIV. TO ANATOLIUS, DEACON OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He commends the people of Bishop Constantius.

Gregory to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.

Our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Constantius, intending to send his people there for the needs of his Church, wished them to be commended to your affection. Therefore, insofar as, with God’s command, you are able, [Note: Remigius reads: “with God’s help, you will have been able.”] assist them wherever necessary, while preserving justice, and offer them support, so that, strengthened by your assistance as is fitting, [Note: The same codex reads: “while they have been supported by your help, as Constantius deserves.”] they themselves may have less difficulty there and our aforementioned brother may recognize that the needs of his Church have been better advanced through your assistance.

## LETTER LV. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER OF PALERMO

Because the synagogues of the Jews were unjustly seized and consecrated, Bishop Victor is to pay their value.

Gregory to Fantinus, defender of Palermo.

Some time ago we wrote to Victor, our brother and fellow bishop, that, since certain Jews had submitted a petition to us complaining that the synagogues situated in the city of Palermo, together with their guesthouses, had been irrationally seized by him, he should refrain from their assembly until it could be determined whether the act had been justly carried out, lest it appear that an injury was being inflicted solely according to their will. [Note: Here and below, toward the end of the letter, *praeiudicium* means detriment, loss, or disadvantage.]

Respect for his priesthood readily prevented us from believing that our aforementioned brother had acted improperly. But because, according to the report of our notary Salerius, who was later found present there, we learned (Gratian, part II, question 14, cause 6, chapter 2) that there had been no cause for which they could reasonably have been seized, and that they had been consecrated inconsiderately and rashly, we therefore command your Experience that, since what has once been consecrated can no longer be restored to the Jews, you should see to it that the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop pay the price at which the synagogues themselves, together with the guesthouses beneath them or adjoining their walls, and the gardens connected with them, have been valued by the sons of the glorious Patricius Venantius and the abbot Urbicus. [Note: This is how it should be read, not *culta*, as in later editions. *Tulta* is an ancient barbarous word derived from *tollo*, meaning “removed” or “taken away.” Thus in book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 15, elsewhere numbered 16, where it reads: “But he has been removed from the earth.” Pope Zacharias also used this word in letter 15 to the bishops of the Franks, concerning Saint Benedict: “Himself returning to his own tomb, from which he was secretly removed.” I also find it twice in Anastasius, in the life of Hadrian, in the form *abstultas civitates*, “cities taken away.” See book III of the *Moralia*, no. 22, note f (Patrologia Latina, volume LXXV, column 131, note e).]

Thus what he caused to be seized may come into the right of that Church, and they may in no way appear to be oppressed or to suffer any injustice. The books and ornaments likewise taken away are also to be sought. If they have plainly been taken away, we wish these too to be restored without any ambiguity. For just as, as we previously wrote to them, they ought not to have the freedom to do anything in their synagogues beyond what the law has decreed, so neither should any detriment or loss be inflicted upon them contrary to justice and equity. (See book XI, letters 48 and 49.)

## LETTER LVI. TO FANTINUS

He compels the defender Candidus to return the acknowledgment of debt after the debt owed by the Jew Jamnus has been paid from the price of the ship.

Gregory to Fantinus, defender.

The Jew Jamnus, bearer of this letter, informed us that our defender Candidus, together with other creditors, had seized his ship and his property and had sold them for the money that had been lent, [Note: Vatican A reads “which he owed.” In the same place below, “and after all the debts had been paid,” instead of the earlier reading “from all the debts.” This is the only Vatican codex that contains this letter; it is also found in the manuscript of Saint Victor, but scarcely anywhere else.] and that, after all the written acknowledgments of debt had been returned, the aforesaid defender alone retained with him the written obligation, and had repeatedly refused to return it despite Jamnus’s entreaties, because, as he says, the principal of the debt had been paid.

We therefore command your Experience to investigate the matter with the greatest care; and if you find that it is so, compel him strictly, so that, without any further delay, he may return the acknowledgment belonging to the aforementioned bearer. [Note: Here and above, this refers to the written security for the obligation. Gregory of Tours uses it in the same sense, *History*, book IX, chapter 18: “And after giving sureties and signing written obligations, they promised that they would pay the individual thousands of solidi as compensation.” Cicero, *For His House*, and Seneca, *On Benefits*, book III, chapter 7, use it in nearly the same sense.]

Let your diligence therefore see to it that he does not come back to us again with a complaint about this matter.

## LETTER LVII. TO PRAEJECTA, ILLUSTRIOUS LADY

He approves the arrangements made between her and the defender Fantinus.

Gregory to Praejecta, illustrious lady.

Whenever our assent is awaited in certain agreements, the arrangement made for the security of the parties ought to be confirmed, so that what is being done does not come into doubt. [Note: Vatican D and E, Reginensis, and Colbertinus read “the matters that are being sought.”] Accordingly, having learned what has been agreed between your affection and Fantinus, our defender and rector of the patrimony in the territory of Palermo, concerning the portions belonging to you in Massalenas and Samanteria, in the province of Sicily, in the territory of Palermo, and concerning the house situated in the city of Palermo, which you had formerly offered to our Church by way of donation, we give our assent to these matters and confirm everything, just as it was arranged between you, by this document of protection.

Nor do we declare that any of these provisions is to be invalidated by us or by our successors, since it is entirely consistent with ecclesiastical moderation that what has been arranged [Note: Gratian, at the cited place, reads “or reasonably decided.”] or decided should not afterward be disturbed by any opposition (Gratian, part II, cause 25, question 2, chapter 12).

## LETTER LVIII. TO MARTIN THE SCHOLASTIC

He cannot pronounce a judgment after receiving too slight an account from him concerning the cases of the bishops. Let him confer with John, bishop of Syracuse.

**Gregory to Martin the Scholastic.**

Since a dispute arising from civil affairs requires, as your Magnitude knows, a more extensive investigation, let your Wisdom consider with how much care and vigilance the cases of bishops ought to be examined.

In the letter that you sent through the bearer of this present communication, you indicated only superficially the cases for which you had been sent to us by our brother and fellow bishop Crementius, while you entirely kept silent about their root. If their origin or character had been made more fully clear to us, we would certainly have strengthened the mind of our aforesaid brother with an open and appropriate reply concerning what should be determined in these matters.

Yet one thing displeased us greatly: you indicate that some bishops had gone to the imperial court without letters from their primate, or that they were holding illicit assemblies there. But because, as we have said, the origin or character of the cases is entirely unknown to us, we cannot pronounce anything definitively, lest—which is exceedingly blameworthy—we should seem to deliver judgment concerning matters insufficiently known.

Therefore it would have been very necessary for your Magnitude, in order to give us the fullest instruction, to have come here to answer our questions when you were delayed in Sicily. Nevertheless, after you saw our brother and fellow bishop John, we believe that you also saw us in him. And since he himself took pains to write to us concerning these same cases, we sent him our reply concerning what seemed right to us.

Since he is a priest of mature and prudent counsel, if you wish to discuss with him the cases for which you were sent, we are certain that in him you will find both what is useful and what accords with reason. (See Book XII, Letter 32.)

**[Note: Letter LVIII [elsewhere 62]. In Remigius, the Anglic manuscript, Regius, Colbertinus, Corbeiensis, and many other manuscripts: “concerning low matters.”]**

**[Note: Here it is used passively; Plautus used *perscruto* actively in the *Aulularia*: “I have already investigated him.” GUSSANV.]**

**[Note: Understand “the court,” “the imperial household,” or “the place where the prince habitually resides.” Thus jurists and historians commonly use the term.]**

**[Note: Printed editions have “we may neither and cannot.”]**

**[Note: Lucas Holstenius, in *Gregor. sac.*, title “On the Roman Patriarchate,” p. 2, did not grasp the meaning of this letter, gathering from it that the primate in Sicily was the Syracusan; yet Saint Gregory is speaking of the Africans, not the Sicilians, as is clear from the following letter.]**

---

## LETTER LIX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He indicates what the Byzacene primate did so that he would not be judged by the Roman bishop. Concerning his case, let him discuss with Martin the Scholastic whatever course has seemed appropriate.

**[Col. 0995D]**

**Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.**

I have received the letter of your Fraternity, in which you indicated that Martin, a most eloquent man, had come from the province of Africa to Syracuse and had spoken privately to you about something.

Your Fraternity indeed never ceases, whenever opportunity arises, to display your love for the blessed apostle Peter. Therefore we give thanks to almighty God, because wherever she is, there we do not find ourselves absent.

Yet your Holiness has not yet examined the case in question with sufficient subtlety. For a Byzacene primate had been accused of a certain crime, and our most pious emperor wished him to be judged through us according to the canonical statutes. But after receiving ten pounds of gold, Theodore, master of the soldiers, obstructed the matter so that it would not be done.

Nevertheless, our most pious emperor instructed us to send for him and to do whatever was canonical. But when we saw the opposition of the men, we did not wish to bring the same case to an end.

Now this same primate is saying certain things concerning his own counsel. It is very doubtful whether he speaks to us sincerely or merely because he is being attacked by his fellow bishops. For as to his saying that he submits to the apostolic see, if any fault is found in bishops, I do not know what bishop would not be subject to it. But when fault does not require it, all are equal according to the rule of humility.

Nevertheless, discuss with the aforesaid most eloquent Martin what seems good to your Fraternity. You should consider what he ought to do; we have written to him briefly concerning the case, because we ought not to trust unknown men indiscriminately.

If, however, you who see him in person judge that something more definite should be said to him, we entrust this to your Charity, whose love, by the grace of almighty God, we are certain of. You should not doubt that whatever you do, we have done also.

**[Note: Letter LIX [elsewhere 65].—The Scholastics were advocates in legal cases who devoted themselves especially to eloquence.]**

**[Note: Thus in the latest editions, to which many manuscript codices agree. Some, however, have “Vysacenus,” as often happens through the interchange of the letter B with V. Byzacium is a province of Africa, in which the kingdom of Tunis is now situated.]**

**[Note: “Of the soldiers” is absent from four Vatican manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and many others.]**

**[Note: Printed editions have: “we did not wish to undertake the same case.” Four Vatican manuscripts and many others disagree.]**

**[Note: Or: “through the grace of almighty God.” What is read in the printed editions—“in the cause of almighty God”—we have found in none of the older manuscripts.]**

---

## LETTER LX. TO ROMANUS AND THE OTHER DEFENDERS OF THE CHURCH’S PATRIMONY

Women are not to live with bishops or clergy established in holy orders; yet they are not to abandon their wives, but are to govern them chastely.

**Gregory to Romanus the defender, Fantinus the defender, Sabinus the subdeacon, Adrian the notary, Eugenius the notary, Felix the subdeacon, Sergius the defender, Boniface the defender, and six other patrons.**

Just as careful foresight knows how to block the paths of wrongdoing and to avoid what is harmful, so negligence lies open to excesses and tends to encounter what ought to be avoided. We must therefore devote great care to our concern and look equally to the reputation and prudence of our brothers and priests.

It has come to us that certain bishops are living in the same house with women under the pretext, as it were, of companionship. Therefore, lest this either provide just occasion for mockers to defame them or the ancient enemy of the human race easily seize an opportunity for deception, by the tenor of this order we instruct you to show yourselves energetic and vigilant.

If any bishops within the boundaries of the patrimony entrusted to you are living with women, restrain this entirely; and henceforth do not permit those women to live there in any way, except those whom the judgment of the sacred canons permits—namely, a mother, aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no evil suspicion can arise.

They do better, however, if they also abstain from living with such women. For it is read that blessed Augustine did not consent even to live with his sister, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.”

The caution of an educated man ought therefore to be a great instruction for us. For it is an incautious presumption not to fear what is weaker when one stronger fears it. He wisely overcomes what is illicit who has learned not to use even what is permitted.

We do not, of course, bind anyone unwillingly in this matter. Rather, as physicians customarily do, although the treatment may be bitter for a time, we prescribe it for the sake of health. Therefore we impose no necessity, but if they choose to imitate an educated and holy man, we leave the matter to their own will.

Let your Experience therefore take care and show diligence that what we have commanded to be prohibited may be observed. For if they are later found to have acted otherwise, let your Experience know that it will incur no slight danger in our judgment.

Moreover, let it be your concern to exhort these same brothers of ours, the bishops, to admonish those subject to them who are established in holy orders to observe in every way, in imitation of themselves, what the bishops themselves observe. Let this one addition be made: that, as canonical authority has decreed, these men must not abandon the wives whom they ought to govern chastely.

Given in the month of March, indiction 2.

**[Note: In two Teller manuscripts: “In the month of June, indiction 2.”]**

**[Note: Letter LX [elsewhere 39].—In the Norman manuscript and many others one reads *ex patronis*. In the Regius manuscript “Sabinus, etc.” is absent.]**

**[Note: This material is taken from Possidius, *Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 26—not in the same words, but with the same meaning. GUSSANV.]**

**[Note: After this letter, in the very old manuscript codex of the senator Claudius Puteanus of Paris, now preserved in the Royal Library, and in Colbert manuscript 1052, which we have often cited and which contains Gregory’s letters from indiction 1 to the end, the following is written: “Gregory to Wulfo” (or “Wulfo”), duke; and afterward, in smaller letters: “There he writes to him concerning the preservation of peace and that, with the Lord’s help, an arrangement should result concerning whatever excess has been committed by all against the state and by their people. In the month of March, indiction 2.” Nothing, however, of that letter remains to us.]**

---

## LETTER LXI

**[Note: Letter LXI.—The distinguished scholar Étienne Baluze brought this letter to light from ancient parchment manuscripts in Book V of his *Miscellanea*. We have left its barbarous style untouched, together with the learned man. Saint Gregory mentions it in his letter to Reccared, which is Letter 122 of this book.]**

### HERE BEGINS THE LETTER OF RECCARED, KING OF THE GOTHS, ADDRESSED TO BLESSED GREGORY, BISHOP OF ROME

He excuses himself for not having informed Gregory of his conversion four years earlier. He sends a golden chalice. He testifies to supreme reverence and goodwill. He commends Leander of Seville.

**[Col. 0997D]**

**To the holy and most blessed lord Pope Gregory, bishop, Reccared.**

At the time when the Lord, in his mercy, caused us to be separated from the infamous Arian heresy, the holy Catholic Church gathered us, improved by the course of faith, within her bosom. It was then our desire to seek with every intention and delight of mind such a most reverend man, who excels all other bishops, and in every way to praise for us human beings so worthy and acceptable a deed before God.

Therefore, while we were occupied by various circumstances and were carrying out the many concerns of the kingdom, three years passed without our being able to satisfy the desire of our heart. After this, we chose abbots from the monasteries and sent them to come to your presence, offer to Saint Peter gifts sent by us, and report more clearly to us the greeting of your holy Reverence.
