As they hastened onward and were already almost seeing the shores of Italy, they encountered a violent storm at sea and became lodged on certain rocks near Massilia; scarcely were they able to save their lives.

Now we have asked the priest whom your Glory had sent as far as the city of Malaca to come into our presence. But he, detained by bodily illness, was entirely unable to come to the throne of our kingdom.

Since we learned with complete certainty that he had been sent by your Holiness, we have sent a golden chalice adorned above with gems. Trusting in your holiness, we ask that you deign to offer it to the apostle who first shines in honor.

I also ask your Eminence, when opportunity permits, to seek us out in your sacred letters written in gold. For I do not think that, with the Lord inspiring you, the fullness of my heart can be hidden from you—how truly I love you.

Sometimes the grace of Christ is accustomed to join together, as though visibly, those whom stretches of land or seas divide. For those who do not see you bodily have your goodness revealed to them by report.

With every reverence I commend to your holiness in Christ Leander, priest of the Church of Seville, because through him your goodwill has shone upon us. And when we speak with that bishop about your life, we judge ourselves inferior to you in good works.

I rejoice to hear your greeting, most reverend and holy man, and I ask the prudence of your Christian character to commend us and our peoples—who, after God, are governed under our rule and have been acquired for Christ in your times—to the common Lord frequently in your prayers, so that through the same means the true love of God may happily grow strong among those whom the breadth of the world separates.

**[Note: Thus in the manuscript.]**

**[Note: Thus in the manuscript.]**

---

## LETTER LXII. TO ROMANUS THE DEFENDER

He is to restrain those who usurp the name of defenders. He is to remove Fortunatus from the affairs of the Church. He is to compel Martianus, who is disobedient to John, bishop responsible for the patrimony of the Roman Church, to go into exile.

**[Col. 0999A]**

**Gregory to Romanus the defender.**

It has come to us that the *tonsuratores* in Sicily, through a wicked presumption, are taking for themselves the name of defenders, and that they are not only useless to ecclesiastical interests but also, on this pretext, committing many acts of indiscipline.

Therefore, by our present authority, we command your Experience to investigate this carefully. If you find anyone assuming this name again apart from those who possess letters concerning this office, restrain him by strict correction.

But if you determine that certain men are energetic and faithful in ecclesiastical affairs, it is necessary for you to report them to us carefully, so that we may judge whether they are worthy of letters of appointment.

Moreover, we wish you to investigate carefully Fortunatus’s accounts concerning what he has done. Once everything that he is found to owe has been satisfied, do not permit him to pass any further through the patrimony or any action of our Church, because, as far as it has come to us, he has conducted himself in such a way that he ought not thereafter to have anything in common with our people.

Furthermore, it has been reported to us that a certain Martianus, who assumed for himself the name of defender, delayed showing obedience to our brother and fellow bishop John, to whom we had entrusted the care of our patrimony.

Investigate, therefore; and if it is true, let him be sent into exile, so that it may not go unpunished that he failed to obey the administrator of the interests of the Church from which he seized for himself the false title of honor. If there are any others who are disobedient to the administration of our aforesaid brother, you must in every way exact retribution from them by strict punishment.

**[Note: Letter LXII. Elsewhere 47; Book X, indiction 5. The *tonsuratores* may have been those placed over the tenants or owners of estates belonging to the Roman Church, who were tonsured as a sign of subjection, according to Roman custom. ALTESERRA.]**

**[Note: That is, documents by which the office of defender was conferred. Below: “so that we may judge by letter whether they are worthy.”]**

---

## LETTER LXIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to employ four bishops to depose Bishop Lucillus. He is to remove from office priests or deacons who are accomplices in the crime, deprive laymen of holy communion, and exhort the people of Malta to elect a bishop.

**Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.**

What complaint has been raised against Lucillus, bishop of the city of Malta, has been made clear by the page of your letters and of the records that you sent to us.

Therefore, because punishment for so great a crime ought not to be delayed at all, let your Fraternity bring three or four of our brothers and fellow priests to assist you, so that, with them also present and the truth of the matter established and satisfied, you may proceed without hesitation to depose the aforesaid Lucillus from the episcopal order, which he has stained by contamination with such a crime.

Since certain priests or deacons are said to have been aware of and participants in the revealed wickedness, let your Holiness investigate the matter by careful inquiry. If you find it to be so, remove them likewise from their rank of honor and assign them to monasteries where they may worthily perform penance.

But since many are said to have fallen into the stain of this sin through these men, it is fitting that you deprive all whose guilt has become clear of participation in the body and blood of the Lord. You should also admonish them more strictly by your letters to devote themselves to litanies and prayers and to cleanse by weeping the stain of sin that they have incurred.

We leave it to your judgment to determine when communion should be restored to them according to the measure of their penance. Yet you must carefully ensure that the viaticum is not denied to those who are pressed by the danger of death.

Moreover, let it be your concern to exhort the clergy and people of the city of Malta that, since they cannot be without their own pastor, they should, with God’s favor, choose a priest to be ordained for themselves.

As for the case of the priests and deacons accused of having fallen, investigate it with the utmost care. If it becomes clear that they are guilty of the crime, impose upon them strict and canonical punishment, so that, to the extent that their wickedness may have provoked God to anger, you may be able to appease him by correspondingly severe correction.

**[Note: Letter LXIII.—Concerning Bishop Lucillus and the island of Malta, see what was said in Letter 44, Book II, indiction 10.]**

**[Note: He means an investigation into Lucillus’s crime conducted according to legal forms and committed to writing; in common speech, “the depositions” or “the inquiry records.”]**

---

## LETTER LXIV. TO VITALIS, DEFENDER OF SARDINIA

He is to protect the clergy in such a way that neither the reverence due to bishops nor their discipline is weakened. He is not to allow the Church’s rural estates to be abandoned by their cultivators, or monasteries subject only to their bishops to be disturbed by others.

**Gregory to Vitalis, defender of Sardinia.**

It has been reported to us that certain clerics of the Church of Caralis, fleeing the discipline of their own bishop, seek the protection of your defense against him and thereby become—what is grievous to say—contumacious toward him.

If this is so, we have taken the matter extremely seriously. It is also said that, abandoning the activities of their own Church and occupying themselves with the services and labors of other Churches, they are found to be strangers wherever they have enlisted in military service.

Your Experience must therefore not presume to do anything of this kind henceforth. If, as commonly happens, some cleric falls into guilt and ought to seek you as his helper, approach the same bishop reverently. Once you have understood the merit of the case, appear before him not as a defender of guilt but rather as an intercessor, so that by this arrangement you may both bring assistance to the petitioner and prevent the rights of the superior from being disturbed.

If, however, there are any who have made just requests, assistance from the apostolic see must not be denied them through you. Nevertheless, the reverence due to every bishop must be preserved in such a way that the discipline of the clergy is not at all loosened through your protection.

It has also been reported to us that the peasants of the same estate of the Church of Caralis, abandoning the Church’s own rural lands, are performing agricultural labor on private estates. As a result, since their own cultivator is occupied elsewhere, the Church’s estates are declining and are not able to pay their taxes.

In this matter we want your Experience to be entirely vigilant, so that after receiving this order from us you do not permit anything of this kind to occur. You should know that, if you neglect it, you will arouse our displeasure against yourself because of your insufficient vigilance.

We have also learned that monasteries of servants of God, and likewise of women, are being disturbed according to each person’s inclination and in the prosecution of various cases. We have taken this very seriously, and therefore admonish your Experience: after receiving our authority, do not again permit anyone to usurp such a right. Rather, let the bishops of the place, under whose governance these monasteries live, arrange their affairs and interests.

For it is entirely inappropriate that, once their own bishop has been set aside, anyone else should involve himself in their affairs. The one who is compelled to render an account for the souls entrusted to him ought to regulate their life with suitable and orderly discipline.

**[Note: Alternatively, *omnino non grate*: “not at all gratefully.”]**

**[Note: Letter LXIV [elsewhere 66].—Recent editions, against the Norman, Vatican, both Rheims, Colbertine, Regius, Corbeiensis, and other manuscripts, read: “Therefore we notify your Experience that you are to do nothing.”]**

**[Note: The printed editions have “their own rights,” an evident error. The text is corrected from six Vatican manuscripts and others.]**

**[Note: Thus the cited manuscripts read; where the printed editions, following the Saint-Victor manuscript, have: “It must be so preserved that the reverence of one … and of the clergy …”]**

---

## LETTER LXV. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

Contumacious clerics are to be kept to their duties. A cleric is to restore property left to a monastery by a widow. Idol worshipers, diviners, and sorcerers are to be restrained both by exhortations and bodily punishments. The Church’s property is to be entrusted not to laymen but to approved clerics.

**Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Sardinia.**

It has come to us that certain of your clerics, puffed up with a spirit of pride, are postponing obedience to the commands of your Fraternity—which is grievous to say—and, occupying themselves more with the services and labors of others, are abandoning the activities of their own Church, where they are needed.

For this reason we are greatly surprised that you do not maintain ecclesiastical discipline among them, nor restrain them, as they wander carelessly along deviant paths, by the bridle of strict governance and bring them back to the rule of the office they have undertaken.

It is also said that some of these contumacious clerics flee to the protection of our defender Vitalis so that they may be defended against you. Therefore we have sent him our letters, so that he will not again dare irrationally to defend any of your clerics against you. If a case of guilt should arise and it is not grave but deserving of pardon, he should rather approach you as an intercessor than as a defender.

Take care, therefore, that nothing further reaches us concerning contempt for those subject to you.

We have also learned that a certain widow left her property to the monastery of Saint Julian, and that this property was seized by one of your clerics, who had administered the affairs of the deceased woman while she was still alive; he now appears to be craftily avoiding its restitution.

We therefore exhort you, if it proves true—as is said—that this is what happened, to compel him by strict enforcement to hasten to restore without diminution the things left to the monastery, and to force him, even at the cost of his shame, to return what he ought not to have dared to take while preserving the purity of his faith.

I believe that your Fraternity itself silently considers how shameful it is that we should appear to have to admonish you to restrain your cleric with the rigor of discipline.

Against worshipers of idols, diviners, and sorcerers we urge your Fraternity to keep watch with especially vigilant pastoral care. Speak publicly among the people against such men, and by persuasive exhortation recall them from so great a stain of sacrilege by warning them of the threat of divine judgment and the danger of the present life.

If, however, you find that they refuse to reform and correct themselves from such practices, we want you to seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, chastise them with blows and tortures by which they may be brought to correction.

If they are free, they must be sent into suitable confinement and strict penance, so that those who disdain to hear salutary words that recall them from the danger of death may at least be brought back to the desired health of mind by bodily tortures.

It has also been reported to us that, after entrusting the care of your patrimony to certain laymen, you later found them engaged in plundering and thereby driving away your peasants; they put off returning the things they improperly retain as though they belonged to their own authority, since they are not subject to your administration, and they disdain to render an account of their actions to you.

If this is so, you ought to investigate it strictly, and the case between them and the peasants of your Church should be examined with the greatest care. Whatever fraud is found among them, they must be compelled to restore it together with the penalty established by law.

Henceforth your Fraternity must beware of entrusting ecclesiastical property to secular men who do not live under your rule, and must instead entrust it to approved clerics from your own office. If any wrongdoing can be found among them, you will be able to correct, as in persons subject to you, what has been unlawfully done—persons whom the duty of their office before you more properly constrains than excuses. (Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 89.)

**[Note: Letter LXV [elsewhere 67].—Printed editions have “bishop of Caralis.”]**

**[Note: Printed editions read “leaving behind,” followed by “by a cleric,” etc., where the construction of the words is defective. We have corrected it from the manuscripts, especially the Norman.]**

**[Note: More recent copies read “that he should approach,” against the older exemplars.]**

**[Note: In many codices, both printed and manuscript, *intentione* is read. Thus Gratian had read it in the cited passage.]**

**[Note: The Norman, Rheims, Vatican B, and others read this way; several codices instead have *exfugationibus*. This reading is also found in Gratian.]**

**[Note: Gratian has: “so that among you they may more suitably administer the office of their station than accuse.” Here the reading found in the manuscripts, “not commend,” means “summon to court” or “accuse,” unlike the printed editions.]**

---

## LETTER LXVI. TO ANATOLIUS THE DEACON

He is to favor those who have returned from the schism of Istria to the unity of the Church.

**Gregory to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.**

The bearers of this letter, who, by God’s mercy, have returned from the schism of the Istrians to the unity of the Church, complain greatly about the wickedness of the bishops who are in those regions.

Since, for this reason, as they hasten to Constantinople, they ask that your support should be available to them, we exhort your Charity in these words: you should assist and cooperate with them without compromising justice, so that, with your help, they may both suffer less hardship there and more easily obtain what is just.

**[Note: Letter LXVI [elsewhere 68].—He was mentioned above in Letter 2, Book IV. GUSSANV.]**

---

## LETTER LXVII. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN

He is to judge together with Marinianus of Ravenna concerning the case of Maximus of Salona.

**Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.**

Maximus, the prevaricator of the Church of Salona, after he was unable to obtain anything through the greater secular powers, turned to the lesser and tried to prevail over us both by the excessive number of his pleas and by his attestation of good works.

I would have considered it inhuman if one who says that he greatly fears me could find me not at all more moderate in some respect. Therefore I have decided that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus should examine his case in the city of Ravenna.

If, however, his person is perhaps considered suspect, we want your Fraternity also, if it is not burdensome, to undertake the journey to the same city and sit together with the aforesaid brother in the same judgment.

Whatever seems right to the holiness of both of you, know that it will entirely seem right to me. I regard your judgment as my own, and whatever you both judge ought to be remitted, consider it certain that I remit.

Yet carefully weigh this: let us not appear either lenient through sin or harsh through injury to the holy Church.

We have entrusted the execution of this case to Castorius the chartularius, so that he himself may carefully report to us everything that has been done. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 12.)

**[Note: Letter LXVII [elsewhere 69].—By the “greater powers” he means the emperor himself and the leading officials, especially Marcellinus, proconsul of Dalmatia, to whom Letter 5 of this book is addressed. By the “lesser” he perhaps means Julian the Scribo, to whom Letter 41 above is addressed; from that letter it is clear that Julian acted as an intercessor for Maximus before the most holy pontiff.]**

---

## LETTER LXVIII. TO EUSEBIUS OF THESSALONICA AND OTHERS

They are not in any way to consent to the bishop of Constantinople arrogating to himself the title “ecumenical”; nor, if a synod is concerned with other matters, are they to allow the ancient statutes to be overturned.

**[Col. 0999D]**

**Gregory to Eusebius of Thessalonica, Urbicus of Dyrrachium, Andrew of Nicopolis, John of Corinth, John of Justiniana Prima, John of Crete, John of Larissa and Scodra, and several other bishops.**

**[Note: Letter LXVIII [elsewhere 70].—These words are not found at all in the Vatican, Regius, and several other manuscript codices.]**

The care of the government we have undertaken binds us to extend the vigilance of our office attentively and to instruct the minds of our brothers by admonitory speech, so that neither wicked presumption may deceive the ignorant nor a certain dissimulation excuse those who know.

Let your Fraternity know that John, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, has exceeded the limits of his modesty and measure against God, against the peace of the Church, and in contempt and injury to all priests. In the synod he unlawfully usurped for himself the proud and pernicious title “ecumenical,” that is, “universal.”

Our predecessor, Pelagius of blessed memory, recognizing this, annulled all the acts of that synod with entirely strict authority, except those things that had been dealt with there concerning the case of Gregory, bishop of Antioch, of venerable memory. He rebuked John with the strictest reprimand so that he would restrain himself from this new and presumptuous title of superstition, to such an extent that he prohibited his own deacon from proceeding unless he corrected so great an outrage.

Following everywhere the zeal for righteousness that he displayed, we preserve his statutes without opposition, God protecting us. It is fitting that the man whom the tribunal of the eternal Judge awaits in that same place to render an account should walk with unhindered steps in the straight path of his predecessor.

In this matter, lest we seem to omit anything that pertains to the peace of the Church, we have repeatedly admonished that most holy John in our letters to remove the title of pride and incline the arrogance of his heart toward the humility taught by our Master and Lord.

Since we have found that he disregarded this, we have not ceased, out of zeal for concord, to admonish also our most blessed brother and fellow priest Cyriacus, his successor.

But because, as we see, the enemy of the human race has now appeared in his advance as the end of this world approaches, so that he may have as his forerunner-priests those who ought to oppose him by living well and humbly, through this title of pride, I exhort and urge you: let none of you ever accept this name; let none consent to it; let none write it; let none admit it where it has been written or add his subscription to it.

Rather, as befits ministers of almighty God, let each of you keep himself intact from such a poisonous infection and give no place within himself to the crafty attacker, because this is done to the injury and division of the whole Church and, as we have said, to the contempt of all of you.

For if one man is, as he supposes, universal, it remains that you are not bishops.

**[Note: He refers especially to Letter 18, Book V, indiction 13.]**

**[Note: See Letters 4 and 31 of Book VII, indiction 15.]**

**[Note: This means being present at the sacred rites. We have already discussed the meaning of this verb several times. Consult Note 471 on the *Book of the Sacramentary*.]**
Furthermore, it has come to our attention that your Fraternity has been summoned to the city of Constantinople. And although our most devout emperor does not permit unlawful things to be done there, nevertheless, lest wicked men, having found an opportunity in your assembly, either seek a chance to intrude under the pretext of this title’s superstition, or plan to hold a synod for some other matter, so that by their crafty machinations they may introduce this into it—although whatever may be enacted without the authority and consent of the Apostolic See has no force—nevertheless, before almighty God I adjure and admonish you that none of you allow himself to be held there by any persuasions, blandishments, rewards, or terrors [Col. 1005B]; but, out of consideration for the judgment of eternity, show yourselves soundly and unanimously opposed to perverse desires. Supported by pastoral constancy and apostolic authority, shut out the robber and the invading wolf, and do not yield to him who rages for the division of the Church; lest you permit a synod to be held in this matter by any sort of subterfuge—a synod which is not legitimate at all, and indeed ought not to be called a synod.

[Note: In the recent Vulgate editions, “when an opportunity had been found”; we would not alter this, unless the unanimous agreement of the manuscripts—Norm., Vatic., etc.—compelled us.]

[Note: The printed editions read, “so that none of you.”]

[Note: In the English edition and several others, “which is not even legitimate”; hence it is not a synod at all. In Rhem., Vatic. D, and others: “because it is neither legitimate indeed nor …” In Vatic. B and F: “since it cannot even be called a synod, to be celebrated.” In Vatic. A: “although indeed it cannot be called a synod, to be celebrated.”]

We likewise admonish you that, if by chance nothing is done concerning the mention of this perverse title, but a synod is perhaps convened concerning another matter, you must be altogether cautious, circumspect, watchful, and concerned, lest anything there be decreed prejudicially or unlawfully against any place or person, or contrary to the canons. But if something must be discussed for the sake of an emerging need, let the matter under consideration receive such a form that it overturns none of the ancient statutes. Therefore, again before God and his saints, we admonish you to observe all these things with the utmost diligence and complete attention of mind. For if anyone—which we do not believe—should disregard this letter in any respect, let him know that he is separated from the peace of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Thus let your Fraternity act so that, when the Shepherd of shepherds comes in judgment, he cannot be found guilty concerning the office of governance that he received.

[Note: In Colbert., “In the month of June, indiction 2.”]

## LETTER LXIX. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He reproves him for not restraining the bishop of Naples, who was usurping things belonging to the city’s patron. He urges him not to allow an alms granted for several years to be exacted thereafter as though it were a debt. He commends the privileges of Naples and the affairs of the island of Prochyta.

[Col. 1005D]

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

[Col. 1006A] We were greatly surprised that, while you were stationed in the city of Naples, Theodorus, a man worthy of remembrance and bearer of this letter, was compelled to come to us concerning certain matters—especially since he complains that in this affair he suffered prejudice from our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus, contrary to ancient custom, although, as your Glory can testify, he asserts without doubt that the matter belongs to the care and administration of the patron of that city.

[Note: LETTER LXIX [formerly 71]. In Rhem. and Vatic. D and E: “Theodorus, your man, bearer of this letter,” etc. In Vatic. B: “the magnificent man.”]

[Note: I inquire whether he was the patron of the treasury or the lord of a fief. Tullius, *On Duties* I: “Those who had received conquered cities or nations into their allegiance by the custom of their ancestors were their patrons.” GUSSANV.]

If the matter is so, we are altogether distressed that the truth did not move you to defend him, so that you might freely state what the proper arrangement was and ensure that what longstanding custom rightly claims for itself be preserved. Since it is exceedingly serious for priests to seize anything for themselves contrary to ancient usage, thereby appearing to intrude upon laymen’s functions, we have taken care to write to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop what seemed right to us, and have sent your Glory a copy of those letters, so that from them you may quickly learn what ought to be preserved.

[Note: Thus Vatic. B, Rhem., Norm., etc., where the common reading is, “what ought to be investigated as soon as possible.”]

Furthermore, the aforesaid bearer informed us that he had given Vectanus, who had been count at the fortress of Missinata, twenty urns of wine for two years from the island of Prochyta, which was nearby, out of compassion, because he knew him to be noble and suffering from extreme poverty; and that now his successor is violently demanding these from the same island as though they were debts.

[Note: Vectanus has many successors, who demand as a debt, and with such importunity that some regret ever having been generous, what was granted under the title of alms. GUSSANV.]

Since he asks that this be prohibited, so that no such attempt may be made in the future, your Glory should take care to investigate the matter. And if the complaint is supported by the truth, and there was previously no custom of this kind, let justice persuade you to restrain such an oppressive burden, and take care that the administration of charity on the aforesaid island not impose the burden of prejudice.

[Col. 1006C] Since he has also asked that we commend to your Glory the privileges of his city and the affairs of that island, we exhort you, while preserving equity, to extend your protection to him wherever necessary. And if, in any matter, the welfare of the people over whom he presides is, as he says, burdened contrary to the order of reason, let the imposed burdens be lightened with your assistance to the measure of justice, and let their privileges not be trampled upon in any way; rather, let everything established by ancient usage remain inviolate in every respect. Let your Glory conduct yourself properly in these matters, so that you may be shown both to support the cause of justice and so that those who have been commended to you may report to us the good things concerning you that we always wish to hear.

[Note: In Vatic. D, Rhem., and others: “may report to us good things concerning you, as we always wish to hear.”]

## LETTER LXX. TO PASSIVUS, BISHOP OF FIRMA

He is to consecrate the oratory of Saint Sabinus.

[Col. 1007A]

Gregory to Passivus, bishop of Firma.

Valerianus, notary of your Church, informed us in a petition that, as stated below, he had founded, out of devotion, an oratory on his own property in the estate of Visianus, beside the walls of the city of Firma, and desired it to be consecrated in honor of blessed Sabinus the martyr. Therefore, dearest brother, if the construction mentioned lies lawfully within your parish, and it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after first receiving the lawful donation—namely, three solidi in annual revenue, free from fiscal taxes and bound by the municipal records—you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public Masses [Col. 1007B]. The arrangement must be such that neither a baptistery may ever afterward be constructed in that place nor may you appoint a cardinal presbyter there. If he should prefer to have Masses celebrated there—

[Note: In five Vatican manuscripts: “to have Masses celebrated for himself.”]

—he must know that he is to request a presbyter from your Dilection, so that no other priest may presume to undertake anything of this kind. You shall, however, reverently place there the sacred relics received.

[Note: That is, relics. See above, Letter 15.]

[Note: LETTER LXXI, formerly 73.]

## LETTER LXXI. TO CHRYSANTHUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO

He is to grant the relics of Saint Sabinus to Valerianus, the notary of Firma.

Gregory to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto.

Valerianus, notary of the church of Firma, asks in a petition that the relics of blessed Sabinus the martyr be granted to him, so that an oratory constructed at his own expense in the saint’s name may be solemnly consecrated [Col. 1007C]. Therefore, dearest brother, it is proper that you obey, by our command, the desires of the aforesaid man, so that he may obtain the fulfillment of his devotion in the consecration he requests.

## LETTER LXXII. TO CONSTANTINUS, BISHOP OF NARNIA

He entrusts the full administration of the church of Interamna to the Visitor.

Gregory to Constantinus, bishop of Narnia.

[Note: LETTER LXXII [formerly 74]. Thus in Anglic., Norm., and Corb. In the Vatican manuscripts, Constantium or Constantinum. It formerly read “to the bishop of Palermo,” which Gussanvillaeus corrected on the authority of sixteen manuscripts. Rochus Pirrus had already detected the same error in his *Description of Sicily*, vol. I, and Binius in his edition of the letters of Saint Gregory among the councils. Narnia is mentioned in Letter 2 of Book II, indiction 10.]

We remember that we once entrusted to your Fraternity the task of visiting the church of Teramnana.

[Note: Vatic. A reads “of Terracina,” followed by most editors. In the other Vatican manuscripts, and in Norm., etc., “of Teramnana,” the reading defended by Holstenius, *Annotations on Ancient Italy*, p. 95. *Teramnana* is used for *Interamnana*. Interamna is the city now commonly called Terni, or Terani, an episcopal city of Umbria on the river Nera between Spoleto and Narnia. Hence Cicero and Pliny speak of the people as *Interamnates*.]

But because it has come to our attention that, through the agency of sins, neither clergy nor people sufficient for the ordination of an interim bishop remain there—

[Note: Vatic. D: “for whom an interim bishop ought again to be ordained.”]

—we have judged it useful to entrust that same Church, and everything belonging to it, to your administration under God’s authority until we arrange its affairs as the Lord wills. Therefore you must take care that whatever may accrue in any matter from the possessions of that Church benefits you either in repairing the Church itself or in supporting its clergy—

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “in every way, either for the repair … or for the support of its clergy.”]

—so that you may receive some reward for your labor, and they may have some assistance for their sustenance.

We wish a detailed inventory of the movable property of the aforesaid Church to be drawn up and sent to us, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may determine from it what should be done.

[Note: *Cimelia* above, Letter 10, now 20, of Book I. In French, “les meubles, les biens meubles.” GUSSANV. Vatic. D and Rhem. read *mobilia*. We have retained *mobile*, which is found in the other Vatican manuscripts, Corb., and elsewhere.]

[Col. 1008B] As for the conduct and discipline of the clergy and of the sons of that Church, it is necessary for you to exercise great care and to keep watch with such pastoral zeal that you may not be blameworthy concerning their souls, but may rather be able to gain a reward before almighty God.

## LETTER LXXIII. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He commends Abbot Theodosius, asking that he not be oppressed excessively by the watches on the walls.

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

Our son Theodosius, abbot of the monastery known to have been founded in Campania by the former patrician Liberius—

[Note: LETTER LXXIII [formerly 75]. Perhaps the same monastery over which Servandus, a companion of the holy Father Benedict, once presided; see Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 35. Baronius considers that Liberius was prefect of the praetorium of Gaul under the Gothic kings Theodoric and Athalaric. Cassiodorus extensively praises him in Book XI, Letter 1, of the *Variae*.]

—has obtained from us by his prayers that we should commend him and his congregation to your Glory [Col. 1008C]. For he asserts that he is being grievously burdened, beyond his strength, with the watches on the walls.

[Note: The guarding of the walls falls not only upon clerics but also upon monks. See *Convenior*, Cause 23, Question 8, and digest his opinion. GUSSANV.]

We therefore ask your Glory that, if possible, he be relieved by you of this burden. But if it is altogether difficult for this not to occur, at least lighten and moderate the burden of anxiety for him through our recommendation, so that, when he wishes to devote himself more freely to the praises of God, he may pray to the Lord more securely on your behalf, since it is through your action that he has obtained some relief; and may also perceive that our letter has benefited him in your eyes.

## LETTER LXXIV. TO DOMNELLUS, THE DISTRIBUTOR

He declares his special goodwill and excuses himself for not having written when Castorius came to him.

[Col. 1009A]

Gregory to Domnellus, the distributor.

[Note: The person to whom distribution is entrusted. See the *Code*, Book XII, Title 38, especially Law 16: “Let the distributor with his own hand, without any deceit or fraud, count out the public allowance to the soldiers,” etc. Among us, something like “the treasurer of extraordinary war expenses,” *Erogator militaris annonae*. GUSSANV.]

You judge, I suspect, from your own mind how great a sweetness your greatness possesses in ours, because, as it is written, “the soul loves one who loves it.” Therefore, in that you love me, you know that you too are loved by me. And do not suppose that I failed to write to you when our chartularius Castorius came there through sluggishness, but because of illness and business. For we wish both to see you when you are present and, when you are absent, at least to converse with you by letter. Hence we also desire that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily lead you to his thresholds, so that we may deserve to enjoy your presence in the grace of almighty God.

[Note: We have supplied this from the authority of Vatican A, B, and E, and two Colbert manuscripts.]

In the month of July, indiction 2.

## LETTER LXXV. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He entrusts him with the visitation of the church of Misenum.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Knowing that the church of Misenum was deprived of the governance of a priest, we solemnly entrust the visitation of that Church to your Fraternity.

[Note: LETTER LXXV [formerly 25]. Misenum was formerly an episcopal city of Campania, whose metropolitan was Rome. In many manuscripts and printed editions it reads *Messenat.*, and in the following letter *Messonae*, instead of *Miseni*. Yet this passage does not concern the church of Messina; the church mentioned here was vacant because its bishop had died, whereas Donus, bishop of Messina, did not die before indiction 4. See Letter 46, indiction 4.]

You must perform it in such a way that no one presumes to seize anything from the advancement of the clergy, the revenue, the ornamentation, the ministries, or anything else belonging to the patrimony of that Church.

[Note: In four Vatican manuscripts: “whatever that may be.”]

Therefore your Charity shall hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and shall quickly admonish its clergy and people with continual exhortations to seek, without the spirit of contention and with one accord, the appointment of such a priest as can be found worthy of so great a ministry and in no way rejected by the venerable canons. Once he has been requested, and the decree has been solemnly confirmed by everyone’s signatures and by a letter bearing the testimony of your Dilection, let him come to us to be consecrated.

We also admonish your Fraternity not to allow anyone from another Church to be elected, unless perhaps no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of that city in which you are carrying out the visitation—something we do not believe will happen. Above all, you must ensure that no lay person of any way of life or merit presume to aspire to this office, lest you incur, God forbid, the peril of your own order.

[Note: Vatic. F: “lest a lay person aspire to the merit of any manner of life.”]

## LETTER LXXVI. TO THE PEOPLE OF MISENUM

They are to obey Fortunatus, the Visitor, and choose a suitable bishop for themselves.

[Col. 1010A]

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people residing at Misenum.

Knowing that your Church has been deprived of the governance of a priest, we have solemnly entrusted the visitation of that Church to our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus. We instructed him not to allow anyone to usurp anything from the advancement of the clergy, the revenue, the ornamentation, or the ministries.

You must obey his continual exhortations and, once tumult has been removed, seek with one accord the appointment of such a priest as in no respect departs from the venerable canons and can be found worthy of so great a ministry.

[Note: LETTER LXXVI [formerly 26]. Five Vatican manuscripts read, “seek a priest.”]

Once he has been requested, let him come to us for ordination with the solemn decree confirmed by everyone’s signatures and accompanied by a letter from the Visitor. Above all, you must ensure that you do not presume to elect a lay person of any kind of life or merit. Know that not only will such a person in no way be advanced to the height of the episcopate, but you will also be unable to earn pardon through any intercession. Rather, know with certainty that all among you who are found to have aspired to the office from the lay state are to be excluded from office and communion.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is to investigate the will of Importunus, bishop of the city of Atella. He is to arrange as soon as possible for a suitable bishop to be elected both for Atella and for Cumae.

[Col. 1010C]

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

[Note: LETTER LXXVII [formerly 53]. “Of Campania” is absent from Norm. It is present in old Colb. and many others.]

We have learned from the report of certain people that Importunus, bishop of the city of Atella, when he was departing this life, instituted his daughter-in-law heir to eight twelfths of all his property in a will, and his Church to the remaining four twelfths.

[Note: Those called to the whole inheritance were called heirs *ex asse*; those who received two of the three parts were heirs to eight *unciae*; those who received only one of the three parts were heirs to four *unciae*. The *as* was divided into twelve *unciae*. *Semis* signifies half an *as*.]

We therefore exhort your Experience to investigate this carefully, and not to allow anything that proves to belong to that Church to be held by any person, except only what is established to have been his own before his episcopal office. Whatever you discover either to have belonged to his Church before his episcopate or to have been acquired by the aforesaid bishop during his episcopal office must be preserved in the ownership of that Church, lest anyone presume to usurp any part of it thereafter under any pretext.

We wish you also to admonish the clergy and people of that Church with every possible insistence, so that without any delay they may choose for themselves a priest to be appointed who can govern the clergy, people, and property of that Church with careful and regular observance. Likewise admonish the clergy and people of that Church and of the others united to it even more insistently, so that they too, setting aside all delay and postponement, may choose a suitable priest for themselves, lest they remain for a long time—and especially at such a time—deprived of the governance of their own shepherd.

[Note: The printed editions read “deprived.” Five Vatican manuscripts, Norm., all the Colbert manuscripts, Teller., etc., contradict this. In both Teller manuscripts it is followed by: “In the month of July, indiction 2.”]

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He quickly concludes the affairs of a man commended by Eulogius. He complains that Eulogius writes nothing concerning the arrogance of the bishop of Constantinople. He explains why he did not send longer pieces of wood.

[Col. 1011B]

Gregory to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria.

I received the letters of your most sweet Holiness, delivered by the bearer of this letter, which spoke to me about the need to conclude his case quickly. But as soon as he came, he learned how the property he was seeking was held by our Church—

[Note: LETTER LXXVIII [formerly 69]. Vatic. D, E, F: “was held by your Church”; Rhem. supports this reading.]

—and he quickly gave an account to himself. As for what he held with others, he settled it without disturbance.

But concerning the matter about which your Holiness ought certainly to have written to me, you wrote nothing, and in this you judged me slow. Since I did not wish it perhaps to burst forth into the scandal of division, I refused to become the author of that division. For I chose that what was going to follow should emerge through others.

[Note: In some Vatican manuscripts and Rhem.: “which are obscure.” In Colbert.: “which are secure,” perhaps an abbreviation for “which are going to follow.”]

But later, with God as witness, you will prove that in a matter in which I wish to please God, I do not fear human beings.

[Note: In Vatic. B, E, F: “in which I see that I please God, human beings.” See Letter 43, formerly 36, indiction 13, and above Letter 70, now 68, which I believe was also sent to Eulogius. It is not clear what was done in that Constantinopolitan synod. GUSSANV.]

I have already taken care to write to you concerning this matter as you were coming to the city of Constantinople.

As for the pieces of wood, I had prepared larger ones, as your Beatitude had written; but the ship sent here was so small that it could not carry them unless they were cut apart. I did not wish them to be cut apart, but have left the decision about what should be done with them to your judgment.

[Note: The printed editions wrongly read “preserved.”]

If they are not necessary for you, we shall adapt them here to other uses. I ask, however, that your Holiness pray for me with greater earnestness, because I am continually oppressed by the pains of gout, the swords of the barbarians, and the afflictions of cares. But if you extend to me the aid of your prayer, I believe that you will strongly assist me against all adversities.

[Note: From the preceding Letter 42 it seems that peace had been concluded. But shortly afterward the war flared up again, as we stated in the Life of Saint Gregory.]

(Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 67.)

## LETTER LXXIX. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He commends Maximus to him and Castorius for judgment, prescribing the manner of proceeding.

[Col. 1012A]

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

You learned from the letters we previously sent to you what must be done concerning the case of Maximus.

[Note: LETTER LXXIX [formerly 89]. See above, Letter 10.]

But because we learned from Castorius, our chartularius and bearer of this letter, what your Fraternity’s disposition—and especially its request—was in this matter, we therefore entrust his case to your judgment if the same Maximus, having taken an oath, clears himself before you and our aforesaid chartularius of the heresy of simony, and, when questioned only about the other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, answers that he is free of guilt. You are to determine by what penance the offense of his having presumed to celebrate the solemnities of Mass while excommunicated should be cleansed.

[Note: In Homily 32 on the Gospels, no. 6, the holy Doctor recalls that custom: “The living sick come to the extinguished bodies of these martyrs, and are healed; the perjured come, and are tormented by a demon.”]

Therefore, whatever seems right to you according to God, arrange it confidently, and have no uncertainty concerning us. For whatever you decree in this matter, we both gratefully receive and willingly accept. We nevertheless exhort you to be careful and to moderate what you foresee must be done in such a way that, if it seems appropriate, you may treat him kindly while preserving, as is proper, the spirit of ecclesiastical rigor through suitable dispensation. We have instructed the bearer mentioned above about what he should do with you at present. Learn all the details from him, and conduct yourselves in every respect so that we may feel that our presence has been with you in your diligence.

(Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 13.)

## LETTER LXXX. TO CASTORIUS, NOTARY

He is to give Maximus his letter as a testimony of restored communion and favor, provided that Maximus, purified and penitent, receives Sabinianus and the others in charity.

Gregory to Castorius, notary.

The more you see that we trust you and entrust necessary matters to you, the more energetic and diligent you must show yourself. Therefore, if Maximus of Salona, having taken an oath, confirms that he is not involved in the heresy of simony, and, when questioned only about the other matters before the body of Saint Apollinaris, answers that he is innocent, and performs penance for his disobedience as we have assigned, we wish your Experience to give him the letter we wrote to him, in which we signified that we had restored to him both our favor and communion [Col. 1013A]. For just as it is proper for us to be severe toward those who persist in contumacy, so we must not deny a place of pardon to those who have humbled themselves and repented.

Furthermore, concerning our brother Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, and Honoratus, archdeacon of Salona, or the others who have gone to the Apostolic See, you must act with the utmost diligence together with Maximus, so that he may receive them with the charity that is appropriate, retain no resentment against them in his heart, and live with them in pure favor and sincere love.

## LETTER LXXXI. TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF SALONA

He restores favor and communion to the obedient, penitent, and purified man, and grants him the use of the pallium.

Gregory to Maximus, bishop of Salona.

Although, at the beginning of your culpable ordination, you added a serious evil through the fault of disobedience—

[Note: LETTER LXXXI [formerly 82]. Rhem. and three Vatican manuscripts add “another serious fault through disobedience.”]

—we nevertheless moderated the authority of the Apostolic See with the restraint that was proper and never burned against you to the extent that the case demanded.

[Note: The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read “until now.”]

But lest our displeasure, which you had aroused for yourself through ingratitude, be prolonged, the concern entrusted to us greatly troubled us, lest we seem negligently to overlook certain unlawful things we had heard about you.

[Note: Concerning this expression, see above, Letter 3, now 5. Here it signifies, in French, “the disgrace that you had incurred in our eyes.” He uses the expression variously and at will. GUSSANV.]

If you consider these matters carefully, you yourself confirmed your guilt by delaying to make satisfaction, and thereby stirred our zeal against you more sharply. But when at last, following sound counsel, you humbly submitted yourself to the yoke of obedience, and your Dilection, by doing penance, purified itself through the worthy satisfaction we had assigned, understand that the favor of fraternal charity has been restored to you and rejoice that you have been received into our fellowship, because just as it is proper for us to be strict toward those who persist in guilt, so toward those who repent we must be kind in granting pardon.

Once your Fraternity knows that you have recovered communion with the Apostolic See—

[Note: These words clearly prove that the letter of the Roman cardinals to the empress Agnes, found as the fourth letter in Book VII of the letters of Saint Peter Damian, rests on a badly constructed and ruinous foundation. GUSSANV.]

—send a person to us who may receive, according to custom, the pallium to be brought to you. For just as we do not permit unlawful acts to be committed, so we do not deny what belongs to custom.

[Note: The administration of the pontificate, the office of the Apostolic See. GUSSANV.]

Although the dispensation of our position has summoned us to grant these things, nevertheless the request of our sweetest and most excellent son, Domnus Callinicus the exarch, strongly urged us to deal with you more moderately. We neither endured nor could grieve his most beloved desire.

(Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 15.)

## LETTER LXXXII. TO ANATOLIUS, DEACON OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He is to favor Marcellinus, who has served the Roman Church well, and excuse him before the emperor.

Gregory to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.

[Col. 1014A] We ought to respond to good and devoted sons with conduct worthy of our office, so that, because we return what is owed, we may double what we freely ought to provide. Since, therefore, the bearer of this letter, our magnificent son Marcellinus—

[Note: LETTER LXXXII [formerly 83]. He was proconsul of Dalmatia. See Letter 5 above.]

—has conducted himself in the case of our brother and fellow bishop Maximus and of the Istrians, and hastens to devote himself to the interests of our Church, so that he can demonstrate the affection of his sincerity increasingly not only in words but also in deeds, we therefore exhort your Dilection in these words: when he comes to the royal city, meet him with every effort and complete attention, and strive to assist him with all your support in every matter, so that, strengthened by the help of almighty God and by yours, he may have less to endure there.

Treat him as one who truly belongs to us and strive in every respect to show him the effect of your charity—

[Note: Vatic. A, in which alone this letter is found almost entirely (for it is absent from Norm., the other Vatican manuscripts, Anglic., Rhem., and Colb.), reads “the effect of my charity.” Remig. and San Victor. read “the affection of my charity.”]

—so that he may recognize that a return has been made to him for past services and may be able to take from the future a great hope of reward for the devotion he promises to display toward ecclesiastical interests.

Since, as we have learned, the most serene lord emperor had ordered our aforesaid magnificent son to hasten to his presence, you should take the opportunity to explain that it was not guilt of disobedience but the case of our brother and fellow bishop Maximus that detained him. Although it was delayed, the matter nevertheless reached its conclusion through his efforts.

[Note: Remig. reads, “the most serene son of the emperor.”]

We also wished your Dilection to pay careful attention to this: he must not consent to involve himself in any matter where the poor are burdened, lest, perhaps, being pressed to some extent by the power of influential persons, he be compelled to do what cannot benefit his soul.

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “lest perhaps, if they can in any way prevail through the power of influential persons, he be compelled.”]

Therefore, handling everything with fear of God, consider above all the eternal reward.

## LETTER LXXXIII. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER OF PALERMO

He is to protect Januaria from the harassment of Anastasius and Bonifacius.

Gregory to Fantinus, defender of Palermo.

Januaria, bearer of this letter, states that she is suffering the greatest harassment, contrary to justice, from the freeborn Anastasius and Bonifacius, to the extent that they are attempting, as she says, to drive her from the possession which she is said to have held for many years.

[Note: LETTER LXXXIII [formerly 84]. Remig. adds, “even as she herself says, they strive.”]

Since she has asked to be defended against them by ecclesiastical protection, your Experience shall summon the aforesaid men before you and admonish them not to presume to do her harm. But if they believe that they have a just claim against the aforesaid woman, let them choose judges with her, and let whatever is determined between them be carried out, for the peace of the parties, with your assistance.

If you discover that they are delaying—

[Note: The printed editions read, “if he should discover … let him provide … let him permit.”]

—provide the aforementioned woman protection, while preserving equity, and do not in any way allow her to be burdened contrary to the order of reason.

## LETTER LXXXIV. TO BENENATUS, BISHOP OF TYNDARIS

He is to consecrate an oratory in honor of Saints Severinus and Juliana.

Gregory to Benenatus, bishop of Tyndaris.

[Note: LETTER LXXXIV [formerly 85]. The printed editions wrongly read “of Fundari”; it should nevertheless be read “of Tyndaris.” Tyndaris, or Tyndarium, was formerly a city of Sicily, now destroyed. In the old Colbert and Regius manuscripts it reads “Venatus, bishop of Tundari.”]

Januaria, a religious woman, informed us in a petition that, as stated below, she had founded, out of devotion, an oratory on her own property in the estate of Furianus and desired it to be consecrated in honor of Saints Severinus the Confessor and Juliana the Martyr.

Therefore, dearest brother, if the construction mentioned lies lawfully within your parish, and no body is established to have been buried there, then, after first receiving the lawful donation—namely, ten solidi in annual revenue, free from fiscal taxes—

[Note: Norm. reads “with free payments,” etc.; Corb. agrees.]

—and bound by the municipal records—

[Note: Corb., Norm., and two Vatican manuscripts read “attached to the municipal records.” Corb., however, reads *mancipalibus* instead of *municipalibus*.]

—you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public Masses. The arrangement must be such that neither a baptistery may be constructed in that place in future times nor may you appoint a cardinal presbyter there. But if the aforesaid foundress should wish to have Masses celebrated there—

[Note: Norm., Colbert., Corb., etc.: “Masses for herself.”]

—she must know that she is to request a presbyter from your Dilection, so that no other priest may presume to undertake anything of this kind. You shall, however, reverently place there the sacred relics received.

## LETTER LXXXV. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He orders him to give Januaria the relics of Saints Severinus and Juliana.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Januaria, a religious woman, asks in a petition that the relics of the blessed Severinus the Confessor and Juliana the Martyr be granted to her, so that an oratory constructed at her own expense in their name may be solemnly consecrated.

[Note: LETTER LXXXV [formerly 86]. Vatic. F reads “Julianus the Martyr.” Otherwise this letter scarcely differs from Letter 71 above and Letter 31, indiction 4.]

Therefore, dearest brother, it is proper that you obey the desires of the aforesaid woman by our command, so that she may obtain the fulfillment of her devotion in the consecration she requests.

## LETTER LXXXVI. TO CONSTANTINE, BISHOP OF MILAN  
He grants relics on condition that provision first be made for the support of those serving there before the place is dedicated.

Gregory to Constantine, bishop of Milan.

The bearer of this letter, Eventius, a deacon of your fraternity, has informed us, among other things, that you instructed him to ask us to send to you the relics of the blessed apostle Paul, as well as those of the blessed John and Pancratius. We have taken care to carry out your request.

Therefore let your Fraternity not delay investigating, with its customary diligence, so that in the places where these relics are to be deposited, lamps and the means of support for those serving there may be provided before the place itself is dedicated; and then let the relics sent to you be reverently placed in those same locations. Otherwise, if the provision mentioned above is now neglected, may the places dedicated to God not later—God forbid—be found deprived of the services of those who serve there.

[Note: **Letter LXXXVI [Al. 87].** The printed editions read *nobis talia intimavit* (“he informed us of such matters”). We have preferred the reading of Vatican manuscripts B, D, and E, as well as Norm., Corb., Rhem., Colbert., and others. In Corb., instead of *intimavit*, one finds *nuntiavit* (“he announced”).]

[Note: The reading is found in five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, Corb., Colbert., Rhem., and the old edition. In more recent editions: “that provisions for support . . . ought to be supplied.” See the note on Letter 78 of Book I.]

## LETTER LXXXVII. TO GAUDIOSUS, BISHOP OF EUGUBIUM  
He entrusts him with the visitation of the Church of Tadinum.

Gregory to Gaudiosus, bishop of Eugubium.

Knowing that the Church of Tadinum has long been deprived of the governance of its own priest, we solemnly entrust to your Fraternity the visitation of that Church. You must carry it out in such a way that no one presumes to appropriate anything belonging to that Church—whether the advancement of clerics, its income, its adornment and ministerial furnishings, or anything else included in its patrimony.

Therefore your Fraternity shall hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and, by constant exhortations, quickly admonish its clergy and people that, once discord has been removed, they should unanimously seek to have a priest appointed who may be found worthy of so great a ministry and who is in no way rejected by the venerable canons.

When he has been requested, he should come to us for consecration with the solemn decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all and accompanied by a letter of testimony from Your Charity.

We also admonish your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be chosen from another Church, unless perhaps no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of that city in which you are carrying out the visitation—something we do not believe will happen. Above all, you must ensure that no layperson, whatever his manner of life or merit, presumes to aspire to this office, lest—God forbid—you incur the danger of an ordination for which you are responsible.

[Note: **Letter LXXXVII [Al. 88].** Eugubium, commonly Eugubio, was formerly a city of Umbria at the foot of the Apennines. It is still an episcopal city, belonging to the duchy of Urbino and immediately subject to the Roman pontiff.]

[Note: Tadinum was a city of Umbria, whose episcopal see was joined to that of Nuceria. Its remains can be seen on the Via Flaminia near Gualdo, commonly Gualdo. Holstenius, in his notes on Cluverius’s *Ancient Italy*, says that Cluverius and Procopius incorrectly have *Taginates*, as does Pliny, Book III, chapter 14, instead of *Tadinates*. — Gussanville.]

[Note: Vatican A omits *strepitu* (“discord” or “turmoil”).]

[Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and Colbert. read: “lest any layperson presume to aspire to this on account of the merit of any manner of life,” etc.]

## LETTER LXXXVIII. TO THE PEOPLE OF TADINUM  
They are to obey Gaudiosus, the visiting bishop, and choose a suitable priest for themselves.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people of Tadinum.

Knowing that your Church has long been deprived of priestly governance, we have taken care solemnly to entrust the visitation of that Church to our brother and fellow bishop Gaudiosus, bishop of the Church of Eugubium.

We have instructed him not to permit anyone to usurp anything belonging to the advancement of clerics, the income, adornment, or ministerial furnishings of the Church. You must obey his constant exhortations and, once discord has been removed, unanimously seek to have appointed for you a priest who in no respect deviates from the venerable canons and who may be found worthy of so great a ministry.

When he has been requested, he should come to us for ordination with the solemn decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all and accompanied by the letter of the visitor.

Above all, take care not to choose any layperson, regardless of his way of life or merit. Know that not only will such a person in no way be advanced to the dignity of the episcopate, but you yourselves will be unable to obtain pardon through any intercession. Rather, you should know for certain that all among you who are found to have promoted a layperson shall be excluded from office and communion.

[Note: **Letter LXXXVIII [Al. 89].** Colbert. and two Vatican manuscripts read: “lest you presume to choose anyone on account of the merit of his life.”]

## LETTER LXXXIX. TO SEVERUS, BISHOP OF ANCONA  
He entrusts him with the visitation of the city of Aesis.

Gregory to Severus, bishop of Ancona.

After the city of Ausina has, with God’s help, been recovered and is known to be held by the state, the Church there must be the object of great concern, especially since our glorious son Bahan, master of the soldiers, is known to have expected our assistance in this matter.

Therefore we have taken care to send this letter to your Fraternity, so that you may visit that Church in the customary manner. You must carry out the visitation in such a way that no one presumes to appropriate anything belonging to the advancement of clerics, its income, adornment, ministerial furnishings, or anything else, as above in Letter 87.

[Note: **Letter LXXXIX [Al. 90].** The reading appears to be *Aesina*, or *Auxima Aesis*, now Jesi, and *Auximum*, now Osimo, situated in Picenum, today the March of Ancona. They are at approximately equal distances from Ancona: Auximum twelve miles to the west, Aesis fifteen miles to the south. Both are still episcopal cities and immediately subject to the Roman pontiff.]

## LETTER XC. TO THE PEOPLE OF AESIS  
They are to obey Severus, the visiting bishop, and establish a worthy bishop for themselves.

Gregory to the clergy, order, and people of the city of Aesis.

Knowing that your Church has long been deprived of pastoral care, and having learned that your city has been recovered and, with the Lord’s help, restored to the jurisdiction of the state, we took care solemnly to entrust the visitation of your Church to our brother and fellow bishop Severus, bishop of the city of Ancona. We also instructed him, as above in Letter 88, and so forth.

[Note: **Letter XCI [Al. 92].**]

## LETTER XCI. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES  
If Barbatianus is cautious in governance and humble in his own judgment, he is to appoint him abbot.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Because the father of the servants of God whom I had sent to the city of Naples has died, as God in his providence willed, it seemed good to me to send the bearer of this letter, the monk Barbatianus, to govern those same monks.

For the present we decree that he be their superior, so that, if his life should please your Fraternity, after some time you may appoint him their father. There are good qualities in him that please us. Yet he has one serious fault: he seems very wise in his own eyes. It is clearly evident from this root how many branches of sin may grow.

Therefore let Your Holiness watch over him carefully. If you discover that he has become cautious in governance and humble in his own judgment, then, with God’s authorization, advance him to the dignity of abbot. But if he makes insufficient progress in humility, defer his ordination and report the matter to me. (See Book X, Letter 24.)

## LETTER XCII. TO VICTOR, BISHOP OF PANORMUS  
He is to ordain as priest of the monastery of Praecoritum one of the monks themselves.

Gregory to Victor, bishop of Panormus.

A desire that is shown to concern the religious purpose and the salvation of souls must, with God’s authorization, be fulfilled without any delay. Since the community of monks residing in the monastery of Praecoritum is evidently in need of a priest to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass, and since they ask that one of their own community be consecrated to this office, we exhort your Fraternity by this letter to ordain without delay or excuse as priest in the aforesaid monastery the man whom, in unanimous agreement, they have chosen from among their own community.

You must also establish, on our authority, that he not be assigned either to the Church or to any other place, but remain there continually. Thus, while he is not occupied elsewhere, he may be found constant and useful in his office; and the community that requests his ordination may, whenever necessary, be refreshed by celebrating the solemnity of the sacrifice with due reverence.

[Note: **Letter XCII [Al. 93].** I maintain a profound silence concerning the hearing of confessions. Presumably they did not sin with a sin unto death; they expiated lesser sins by other remedies. I do not, God forbid, in any way condemn our entirely different custom. It is in the interest of truth to investigate what the practice of the ancients was. Piety changes its rites: formerly it rejoiced in the small number of priests and Masses; now it glories in their multitude. Formerly penance was rare but genuine, and the use of the keys more public; now the fruit of penance is secret and frequent—to say nothing of its often precipitous character, which outruns the ripeness of repentance; and when mature discretion is absent, it is abortive.

In a word, it does not appear that Pachomius, Paul, Anthony, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Augustine, or other men of holier life were constant visitors at a confessor’s feet. In our age, the better a person is, the more frequently he presents himself as guilty before the tribunal of penance. I condemn neither practice; for we do not all journey toward heaven by a single road. — Gussanville.

From Gregory’s silence, Gussanville incorrectly infers that monks at that time abstained from confession because they did not sin with a sin unto death. In the French treatise *On Confession* against Dallaeus, Part I, chapter 13, at the end, and chapter 17, we have certainly established the use of confession for expiating venial faults. See also chapter 20 of the Paris edition, pages 240 and following. Thus, when Gregory assigns the priest’s office, he mentions only the celebration of Mass as the chief and superior action, not as his sole duty, since priests also anointed the sick, presided over the burial of the dead, heard the confessions of penitents, and so forth.]

[Note: In the printed editions: “whenever necessary, while he celebrates the solemnity of the sacrifice, it may be refreshed,” a reading rejected by the English manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, Corb., and most Vatican manuscripts. Some Vatican manuscripts differ for a while both from the printed editions and from the other manuscripts, as do Remigius and Saint-Victor.]

## LETTER XCIII. TO GULFAR, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS  
After praising his zeal in bringing schismatics back to the Church, he urges perseverance and protection for those who return.

Gregory to Gulfar, master of the soldiers.

The bearers of this letter, who came to us from the region of Istria, reported such good things about your glory that they inflamed us greatly to give you thanks. We have learned that, amid the responsibilities of the government of those regions entrusted to you, you show particular concern for winning souls, and that you hasten to call the hearts of those who have gone astray back to the unity of the Church, so that, insofar as your desire extends, you do not wish anyone there to remain separated from the apostolic Church.

The love of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, has so inflamed you that you ardently desire with the greatest longing to restore to full unity his sheepfold, to which the Lord, Creator of all things, has entrusted the keys.

Glorious son, possess from so great and excellent a work a fixed confidence in divine recompense. In this, not only our exhortation but also the apostolic word confirms you: “He who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5).

However great temporal abundance or prosperity may be, it has its end, the limit of death. But the zeal that you have undertaken for winning souls possesses the firm certainty of its hope—namely, the recompense of eternal life.

Therefore, after expressing our paternal affection in greeting, we exhort Your Glory to pursue with still greater diligence the zeal for the unity of the holy faith that the author of unity himself has granted you. Call back as many as you can from the error of their schism into the bosom of Mother Church, and nurture them by continual exhortation.

In this also act so that those whom the Lord permits, through you, to be restored to his fold may be protected by the support of your defense, so that those who still remain in error may have nothing on which, when returning to sound counsel, they can bring an accusation.

For while you conduct God’s causes on earth, he himself also directs these actions of yours successfully by his protection, and in eternal life he will be your recompense for this great good, which you desire.

[Note: **Letter XCIII [Al. 96].** We have restored the text with the aid of Vatican A. What is found in Saint-Victor and the printed editions appears corrupt: “to whom all creatures have been handed over by the Lord.”]

[Note: Vatican A reads *et quousque potueritis* (“and as many as you are able”).]

[Note: The same manuscript reads *retributor existit* (“he proves to be a recompensor”).]

[Note: The reading is found there: *valeant amplius haesitare* (“may be able to hesitate further”). Here *applicare* seems to mean the same as bringing an accusation before a ruler or judges. Exodus 22:8, according to the Vulgate, says “he shall be brought before the gods”; according to the Hebrew source, “he shall be brought before the gods,” that is, before the judges; and in verse 9, “before the gods,” meaning before the judges, the case of either party shall come.]

## LETTER XCIV. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER  
He is to assist certain Istrians in reaching their bishop quickly in Sicily. He is to urge the bishop to come to Rome and provide his travel expenses.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

The bearers of this letter, who came here from the regions of Istria, asked to travel with our assistance to their bishop, who is now living in the region of Sicily. We have arranged for them to set out from here.

Therefore let your Experience arrange how they may reach their aforesaid bishop as quickly as possible, lest, as they assert, other schismatics from those regions arrive before them to persuade him. From what they indicate, the bishop himself desires to come to us for the unity of the faith. We must therefore cooperate with them so that, with the Lord’s help, they may accomplish the good things they desire.

Your Experience should therefore urge that same bishop, either personally, if he is nearby, or by letter, to hasten, with the Lord’s favor, to the threshold of the apostles, knowing that we shall receive him with every affection. We wish you to provide his travel expenses so that he may reach us.

But if it is burdensome for him to come here, and he intends to remain in Sicily, consenting to remain cautiously within the unity of the Church among those who pervert the Scriptures, do not delay informing us of this through your report, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may arrange how he can have suitable provision there.

It should also be the concern and support of your cooperation that the bearers of this letter reach that same bishop, so that when they arrive they may feel that they have received nothing less from us.

## LETTER XCV. TO CALLINICUS, EXARCH OF ITALY  
He commends certain people who have been restored to the unity of the Church and are returning from Rome to Istria.

Gregory to Callinicus, exarch of Italy.

From Your Excellence we have so much to hope for in the matters we request, and we already regard them as though they had been obtained, because what is requested is consistent with our office and because, amid the cares and uncertainties of worldly affairs, an accumulation of eternal recompense also awaits you on this account.

The bearers of this letter, who came to us from the region of Istria, wisely desired to avoid the error of the schismatics among whom they had been placed and to submit themselves to the unity of the Church. We discerned the good intention of their action and received them into the bosom of Mother Church with appropriate exhortation. Since they desired to serve in our Church, we gladly granted their request.

Therefore, after expressing our paternal affection in greeting to Your Excellence, we ask you to keep them commended to you because of the good desire that led them to hasten to the solid rock of the prince of the apostles, lest, mixed with the errors of those still wavering, they suffer shipwreck of the salvation they had despaired of attaining.

When they return to their own country, let them not be disturbed by the harassment of evil men on account of this good that they are known to have desired; rather, let them find the support of your protection in all things. Through their peaceful condition, may the hearts of others still living in schism be moved, and, provoked by the good example of your patronage, may they become their followers.

It contributes to the increase of your reward if, amid the cares of war, you protect the soul from the assault of the internal ambusher just as you protect the body from the external enemy.

[Note: **Letter XCV [Al. 98].** Other editions read *quae petimus velut*, and so forth. We have restored this passage from the Vatican, Rhem., Reg., and other manuscripts. In four Vatican manuscripts, however, *quae petimus* is omitted.]

## LETTER XCVI. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA  
He commends the same people mentioned above.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

The bearers of this letter came to us from the region of Istria and desired, with the Lord’s help, to submit themselves to the unity of the Church. We received them with affection because of the excellence of their desire, and, after exhorting them concerning the conduct proper to the unity they had attained, we also permitted them, as they desired, to serve in our Church.

Let your Fraternity receive them gladly and willingly provide them with whatever assistance they require, so that, when they return to their own country, they may not be wearied by any harassment from evil men in the good work they have undertaken.

Rather, act with still greater diligence before our most excellent son the exarch, so that by his commands he may make them secure in every respect among those whose responsibility it is there. Thus, through their peaceful condition, the minds of others still living in schism may also be moved toward the grace of conversion.

[Note: **Letter XCVI [Al. 99].** Vatican A, B, and E read *de conservatione* (“concerning preservation”), with Reg. agreeing.]

[Note: Manuscripts present this passage in various forms. In the Turin manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts one reads *noscimur militasse*, certainly in place of *noscimus*, as in Corb. In Rhem.: “we know that we have permitted them to serve in the Church.” In Vatican D: “the Church is known to permit them to serve,” but this is corrupt.]

[Note: Older editions read: “so that they may not be troubled by the evil men, lest they regret their good work,” a reading supported by Vatican A. More recent editions read: “so that they may be able to carry out the good work of their undertaking, without being troubled by evil men.” Our reading is found in Turin, Corb., three Vatican manuscripts, and others. In some manuscripts, however, *in bono* is replaced by *in bonum*.]

## LETTER XCVII. TO THE INHABITANTS OF THE ISLAND OF CAPRAE  
He congratulates them on their undisturbed love of ecclesiastical unity and instructs Marinianus to establish for them a bishop opposed to schism.

Gregory to the inhabitants of the island of Caprae in the province of Istria.

Our Redeemer, the Mediator of God and humanity, mindful of the human condition, so joins the lowest things to the highest that, while remaining in eternity, he orders temporal affairs by a hidden impulse and with pious governance. Thus the ancient enemy can in no way snatch from his hand those whom he foresaw, before the ages, as destined to be gathered into the bosom of Mother Church.

Even if any one of those among whom he dwells bodily is moved by the winds and for a time wavers like a branch, the root of right faith, which comes forth from concealment, nevertheless remains verdant by divine judgment and, when the appointed time has come, can display the fruit that had been hidden within it.

We recognize, by the illumination of heavenly attention, that this has now taken place in you through your desire. Rejecting the obstinacy of the schismatics among whom you live, you show, by the very execution of your purpose, that you wish with the greatest readiness of mind to be gathered into the Lord’s fold.
