Those who dislike division testify that they desire to be sound; by rejecting error, you show that you love what is right and avoid what is crooked.

For this reason both your earlier petition sent to us and the arrival of the present bearers, your representatives who requested salutary measures, have made us rejoice. Through them you signified that you reject the wandering steps of those who have gone astray and seek the straight path of salvation, by which, restoring yourselves to the unity of the holy Church, you might advance toward the recompense due to those who do good and who have been established within her bosom.

We have therefore gladly embraced your praiseworthy will, which will profit your souls forever, with complete joy. With the Lord’s help, we are arranging matters as follows.

If the bishop whom you had asked to be restored to your Church wishes to separate himself from the fall of the schismatics and join the unity of the Church, we have clearly written to our brother and fellow bishop Marinianus how, on our authority, he is to confirm your request.

But if—which we do not desire—he refuses to separate himself from their schism, we have written to that same brother and fellow bishop how your Church may obtain its own priest. Thus, in either case, your pious devotion of mind may attain its fulfillment and the Lord’s flock may be secure against the arrows of its plotting enemy.

[Note: **Letter XCVII [Al. 100].** Only the printed editions have *Capreae insulae* (“the island of Caprae”). We have supplied the remainder from the English, Norman, Rhemish, Corbie, and other manuscripts. In Reg. the marginal reading is *Caprianae insulae*.]

[Note: The opening presents the teaching of Saint Paul in Romans 8:30, which Saint Augustine explained in many books against the Pelagians. — Gussanville.]

[Note: Remigius and Reg. read: “which has been established within her bosom.”]

## LETTER XCVIII. TO THEODORUS, CURATOR OF RAVENNA  
He praises his zeal for peace. He warns him about the peace fraudulently sworn by Ariulfus. He refuses to subscribe the treaty with his own hand. He wishes the case of Augustus to be settled according to the laws of justice. He consoles the grieving Theodorus and prepares to send him a representative.

Gregory to Theodorus, curator of Ravenna.

Although many things that have gladdened our hearts previously reached us concerning you through our representatives, our son Probus, the abbot, now returning, has reported still greater things about your glory—things truly worthy to be proclaimed of a good and most Christian son.

Since he has related that you showed us such affection and such zeal in arranging the peace, greater than that shown even by our citizens who were previously found there, we ask the mercy of heavenly protection to repay you for this, in body and soul, both in this life and in the future. You did not cease to act vigilantly for the salvation of many, doing what was useful.

We therefore inform you that Ariulfus swore to preserve the peace, not—as his king swore—without qualification, but on condition that no offense be committed against him in any matter, or that no one march against the army of Arogis.

Because this is altogether unjust and deceitful, we treat him as though he had not sworn at all. He will easily find some small occasion for transgressing, and, if we are not suspicious of him, he will deceive us all the more.

Warnilfrida, moreover, without whose counsel Ariulfus does nothing, utterly refused to swear. The result is that, from the peace we greatly desired, we can scarcely obtain any remedy in those regions, because we remain suspicious—and shall continue to remain suspicious—of the very enemies of whom we have hitherto been suspicious.

Let Your Glory also know that the king’s men who were sent here are pressing us to subscribe the treaty. But, remembering the insults that Agilulfus is said to have spoken to Basil, a man of illustrious rank, through us, to the injury of blessed Peter—although Agilulfus himself has entirely denied this—we decided to refrain from subscribing.

We feared that, since we are petitioners and mediators between him and our most excellent son, the lord exarch, we might appear to be deceived in some respect if anything were secretly removed, and that our promise to him might be called into doubt. If some future necessity should arise, God forbid, he might then find an excuse for refusing to agree to our petition.

Therefore we ask you, as we have also asked our aforesaid most excellent son, to act according to the affection with which Your Glory is united to us. Before those men return from Arogis, let the king send them a letter in haste—which must nevertheless be brought to us—instructing them not to ask us to subscribe.

But if the matter requires it, we shall have our glorious brother, or one of the bishops, or at least the archdeacon, subscribe.

[Note: **Letter XCVIII [Al. 103].** He may perhaps have been a municipal magistrate responsible for the city’s grain supply; in Paris, the *prévôt des marchands*; elsewhere, the mayor of the city. This word has many meanings irrelevant here. In Greek, *λογιστής* (“accountant” or “administrator”). In the *Code*, Book III, concerning the method of fines, and elsewhere, the same office was held by the board of ten at Athens. — Gussanville.

It is impossible not to understand the office of the city curator from Cassiodorus, *Variarum*, Book 7, chapter 12, where the formula for this dignity is given. He governed the orders of the curia, regulated the prices of things sold, and watched over the welfare of all the citizens. Cassiodorus’s testimony shows that this was an ancient dignity. Vatican A reads *procuratori Ravennae* (“to the procurator of Ravenna”).]

As for Augustus, we give thanks for him and are striving that he settle his case with his adversary according to equity. We did not wish him to be compelled to appear there, yet we do not deny justice to his adversary.

[Note: To “produce” someone means to present him or another person in court. See the Digest, *On the Meaning of Words*, laws 22 and 246.]

[Note: Corb. reads *voluimus* (“we wished”); Vatican A reads *volumus* (“we wish”).]

As for the other matters, we have not yet found an opportunity to give you worthy thanks. We are sending a representative in a subsequent letter, through whom, by the charity with which we are bound to one another, we may, with the Lord’s mercy, be joined more closely.

Moreover, the grief of Your Glory deeply affects us. But because a wise man knows all that ought to be said for consolation, we refrain from consoling you with words and instead accompany you with prayer, asking that almighty God guard your life and health and those of all your people by the protection of his mercy, and comfort your heart, which has been placed in affliction.

[Note: **Letter XCIX [Al. 104].** Vatican A, D, and E read *commendemus* (“let us commend”); Norm., Rhem., and others differ.]

[Note: In the printed editions, *Gloriosum* is written as though it were a proper name. We suppose that Saint Gregory is speaking of his brother. See the material collected to illuminate this subject in Book I of the commentary on his life.]

## LETTER XCIX. TO OCCILIANUS, TRIBUNE OF HYDRUNTUM  
He urges him to relieve the city of Hydruntum, which has been burdened by Viator, a former tribune.

Gregory to Occilianus, tribune of Hydruntum.

We gladly received the news that Your Greatness had returned safely from the region of Ravenna to the city of Hydruntum under the orders of our most excellent son, the lord exarch. We pray the Lord to direct your actions by the assistance of his favor.

Our brother and fellow bishop Sabinus, who came to us, informed us of the serious complaints of his fellow citizens. He asserted that they had hitherto suffered many unlawful actions there at the hands of Viator, the former tribune of the city of Hydruntum.

Therefore, greeting Your Greatness with paternal affection, we exhort you to correct by judicial remedy whatever you recognize to have been wrongly done in the past. You know that this place belongs specifically to our Church. If the few country people who have remained there are afflicted by improper burdens or oppressions, they abandon the place itself; and, something we do not desire, an opportunity is thereby given to the enemy to invade it.

We therefore specially commend to you the aforesaid bishop and all the inhabitants of that place, so that they may not only not be burdened by any unlawful exactions, but may rather feel, because of our recommendation, that your support is present to them in all things.

Thus may the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whose property the place is, prove your recompensor, and may we more readily be of assistance in your interests.

## LETTER C. TO SABINIANUS, BISHOP OF CALLIPOLIS  
He is not to permit the people of Callipolis to be burdened by forced services.

Gregory to Sabinianus, bishop of Callipolis.

We have been informed that the people of the fortress of Callipolis, in which, with the Lord’s favor, we have appointed you priest, are being afflicted by severe troubles of various kinds and worn down by distant forced services and many expenses.

Therefore we exhort your Fraternity—since, as everyone knows, that place is recognized as belonging to our Church—to kindle in yourself the zeal of proper defense. Do not permit them to be burdened by unlawful exactions. For this reason we have had copies of the Church’s privileges given to you from our archive, so that, instructed in all things, you may not be ignorant of how you can defend the inhabitants of that place.

We also wish you to have responsibility for the people of the Callipolitan estate from the beginning of the coming third indiction, and to be extremely careful to relieve them of their troubles. With attentive care, ascertain what each person’s strength permits him to contribute from his payment for the benefit of the Church, and arrange for each to pay according to his means.

After carefully making a report concerning this arrangement, let your Fraternity not delay informing us what the people of the whole Callipolitan estate are able to provide, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may know how to make arrangements accordingly.

We have sent instructions to Sergius, the defender, so that in this matter he may not only dare not oppose you, but may rather provide you with assistance wherever he can.

[Note: **Letter C [Al. 105].** This letter and the preceding one incidentally show that even at that time many entire cities were subject to the authority of the Roman Church. See above, Book II, Letter 31. Hence it is clear that Saint Gregory appointed the tribune of Naples to its protection and commanded the soldiers stationed in the city’s defense—something he would not have presumed had he not been the city’s lord. The temporal power of the supreme pontiffs is treated more fully in the *Life of Saint Gregory*.]

## LETTER CI. TO SERGIUS, THE DEFENDER  
If Fruniscendus does not voluntarily pay what he owes the Church of Hydruntum, he is to compel him to submit to judgment.

Gregory to Sergius, the defender.

Our most reverend brother Peter, bishop of the city of Hydruntum, has complained to us through his deacon Vincent that Fruniscendus, formerly a son of his Church, is indebted in many respects. Not only does he refuse to make satisfaction for what he is bound to pay, but he also scorns submitting to judgment.

Therefore, by this present authority, we order Your Experience to admonish him diligently, so that, if he recognizes that he owes anything to the Church, he does not cease to make satisfaction without postponing the matter.

Otherwise, when the delay has ended, let him come under your compulsion to the judgment of the appointed judges. Whatever, after the truth has been ascertained through the holy Gospels, is determined must be brought to the result of enforcement by your diligence, so that the complaint in this matter does not return to us again.

[Note: **Letter CI [Al. 106].** In French, *redevoir*, as though from *redebēre*; Saint-Victor has the same form. Jurists use this word in another sense. See note x on Letter 44 of Book I and note v on Letter 82 of the same book.]

## LETTER CII. TO SERGIUS, THE DEFENDER  
He is to arrange for a slave fleeing from Gregory’s brother at Hydruntum to be captured and brought to Rome by ship.

Gregory to Sergius, the defender.

Our son, the magnificent man Occilianus, tribune of the city of Hydruntum, came to us and is known to have brought with him a boy named Peter, a baker by trade, who belonged by right to our brother.

We have now learned that this boy has escaped and is returning to that region. Therefore, before he can reach the city of Hydruntum, let Your Experience, with whatever speed you can, send letters either to the bishop of the city of Hydruntum, or to the aforesaid tribune, or to another person whom you know to be in your place there.

They must keep the wife or children of the aforesaid slave under the strictest guard and take care concerning him, so that when he arrives he may be detained. Then, with all his belongings—everything belonging to him—placed on a ship, he must by every means be sent here through a trustworthy person.

Therefore let Your Experience strive to accomplish all this with the utmost effectiveness and skill, lest, through neglect or delay, you offend our feelings, which we do not desire.

## Letter 103. To Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples  
### That soldiers should not lodge in a monastery of virgins

Gregory to Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples.

The abbess Agnella, bearer of this letter, has informed us that soldiers are lodging inside the monastery itself. We have been altogether astonished at why your Fraternity has tolerated this so patiently and has not seen to it with all speed that the matter be corrected. Therefore we urge you that, even now, it be the object of your energetic attention to press those responsible insistently, so that the soldiers may be removed from there without any excuse, and that thereafter no one may receive lodging or quarters there,

> [Note: In four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, the Regius, the Corbie manuscript, and most others, *hospitium* (“lodging”) is omitted. In Vatican A, *metatum* (“quarters”) is read, with *hospitium* omitted.]

lest the crafty enemy, finding an opportunity, should—God forbid—be able to exult in the deception of the religious life.

## Letter 104. To Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples  
### That he should hasten to send to Rome a thoroughly instructed man, so that the citizens of Naples may return to concord

Gregory to Fortunatus, Bishop of Naples.

We have received a report, brought by Stephen, from certain persons residing in the city of Naples concerning several matters. The magnificent man Theodore, *major populi*,

> [Note: Concerning this man, see also Book XI, Letter 25, where *Theodorico* was formerly read incorrectly instead of *Theodoro*. From both letters it may be inferred that responsibility for the care and guarding of the gates belonged to the *majores urbium*.]

came to us and had previously complained that prejudicial measures had been imposed upon them by your Fraternity. We have also received another report from certain persons living in the aforesaid city who support the party of the aforesaid *major populi*. From these reports we have clearly learned that the people have divided themselves into two factions.

And because it is grievous to us, and burdensome to you, that discord has arisen among the inhabitants of that city, whose unity and concord you ought to have promoted, for this reason we exhort your Fraternity in these words: without allowing any excuse, send here with all haste a properly instructed person who may, either before judges chosen by us or at least before delegates appointed by us, answer fully the intentions and objections of your adversaries, insofar as anything must be done on your behalf. Thus, once the truth has been ascertained, the case may here receive a salutary conclusion, so that, when all the matters that had entered into dispute have been reasonably settled, no further force may be given to this contention through any aggravation, but that peace and charity, as is fitting, may endure between you and your sons.

Since, therefore, the disputes that have arisen cannot be resolved there by any reasonable means—especially since such dissension has arisen among the inhabitants that there is no one who can answer in court or remain in order to defend either party—your Fraternity must act so that, in sending the person as we have said, you do not append any delay under any pretext.

> [Note: In Vatican A, *ut transmittenda* is read, with *in* omitted; this produces the sense.]

## Letter 105. To Serenus, Bishop of Marseilles  
### He commends Abbot Cyriacus, who is going to Syagrius, and admonishes him that images are to be preserved in churches

Gregory to Serenus, Bishop of Marseilles.

Do not attribute the fact that we are sending this letter to your Fraternity so late to sluggishness, but to the pressure of our occupations. We commend to you in every respect the beloved son who bears this letter, Cyriacus, abbot of our monastery, so that nothing may delay him in the city of Marseilles, but that, with the assistance of your holiness and under God’s protection, he may proceed to our brother and fellow bishop Syagrius.

Moreover, I report that it reached us some time ago that your Fraternity, seeing certain worshipers of images, broke up and threw out those very images in the churches.

> [Note: Above, Letter 52, concerning Secundinus. On images, Gregory teaches the same doctrine below, Book XI, Letter 12: images are neither to be broken nor worshiped. Thus the most holy Roman pontiff thought at the end of the sixth century. At the beginning of the eighth century the Iconoclasts emerged, around the time of Gregory II and Gregory III. After many councils had been held concerning either abolishing or retaining images, a decree in favor of images was finally made and promulgated at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787. The Gauls resisted for some time and, at the Council of Frankfurt in 794, condemned the Council of Nicaea, apparently because they had misunderstood it. Nor did they immediately yield. For, according to Sirmond, around 824 our bishops, assembled at Paris by order of Louis the Pious, seemed to recoil from the worship of images, supporting their doctrine with statements of the holy Fathers, and with such confidence that they believed they could persuade the supreme pontiff of it through their legates Jeremiah and Jonah. On relative and absolute worship, religious and civil, see the theologians; none, so far as I know, condemns Saint Gregory’s letter to Serenus. — Gussanville.]

We praised you for having zeal lest anything made by human hands should be worshiped, but we declare that you ought not to have broken those images.

> [Note: Some editions read *judicamus* (“we judge”), or *judicavimus* (“we judged”).]

For this reason pictures are used in churches: so that those who do not know letters may at least read by seeing them on the walls what they are unable to read in books. Therefore your Fraternity ought both to have preserved them and to have prohibited the people from worshiping them, so that those who do not know letters might have a means of acquiring knowledge of the history, while the people would not sin by worshiping the picture.

> [Note: The Vulgate manuscripts read *easdem Ecclesiae* (“the same [images] of the Church”); the Norman manuscript reads *easdem de Ecclesiis* (“the same [images] from the churches”).]

## Letter 106. To Syagrius, Aetherius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, Bishops  
### He sharpens his pen against simoniacs and neophytes, against forbidden cohabitation with women, and against neglect of the councils that ought to be held every year; he orders that councils be held annually, and that all these matters be treated at the council and reported to him through Abbot Cyriacus

Gregory to Syagrius of Autun, Aetherius of Lyon, Virgilius of Arles, and Desiderius of Vienne, bishops of Gaul, from their fellow bishops.

> [Note: In the Norman manuscript only, the heading reads “to Etherius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, bishops of Gaul, from their fellow bishops.” In the Rheims manuscript, Syagrius is added and placed before the others, but no mention is made of the episcopal sees.]

Our Head, who is Christ, willed us to be his members so that, through the bond of charity and faith, he might make us one body in himself. We ought to cling to him with such devotion of heart that, since without him we can be nothing, through him we may be what we are said to be. Let no thing divide us from the fortress of our Head, lest, if we shrink from being his members, we be abandoned by him and, like branches cast out from the vine, wither.

Therefore, if we desire to be worthy to become the dwelling place of our Redeemer, let us remain in his love with the whole devotion of our mind. For he himself says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

But since we cannot cling to the author of good in any other way unless we cut away from ourselves desire, which is the root of all evils,

> [Note: Gratian, Distinction 47, chapter 7.]

through this present letter—which joins us to one another in the language of the visitation we desire to make—we address your Fraternity according to the apostolic institutions, so that, relying upon the rules of the Fathers and the Lord’s commandments, we may exclude avarice from the temple of faith, since avarice is the service of idols, and may allow nothing harmful or disorderly to remain in the house of the Lord.

For some time now a report has been circulating among us that in the regions of Gaul the sacred orders are conferred through the Simoniac heresy. We are afflicted with intense sorrow if money has any place in ecclesiastical offices and what is sacred is made secular. Whoever therefore strives to purchase this by paying a price, attending not to the office but to the name, vainly desires not to be a priest but merely to be called one.

> [Note: Gratian, Part I, Question 1, chapter 2.]

What, indeed, is accomplished by this except that there is no examination of conduct, no concern for morals, and no investigation of life, but only he is judged worthy who has been able to pay the price? If this is weighed by the balance of sound judgment, the man who wickedly hastens to seize a position of usefulness for empty glory is, by the very fact that he seeks the honor, more unworthy of it.

Just as the man who, when invited, refuses, and when sought, flees, is to be brought to the sacred altars,

> [Note: Gratian, Part I, Question 66, chapter 3.]

so without doubt the man who seeks office voluntarily or thrusts himself forward importunately is to be rejected. For what does one who struggles to climb to higher things in this way accomplish, except that, while increasing outwardly, he diminishes inwardly, and while ascending externally, descends within to the depths?

Therefore, dearest brothers, let sincerity prevail in the ordination of priests; let consent be simple and free from venality; let election be pure, so that the man promoted to the summit of the priesthood may be believed to have been advanced not by the votes of those who sell their support but by the judgment of God.

For since it is an exceedingly grave crime to wish to buy or sell the gift of God for a price, the authority of the Gospel bears witness to this (Matthew 21). When our Lord and Redeemer entered the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves. What else is it to sell doves than to receive a price for the laying on of hands and to sell the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God grants to human beings? That their priesthood fell before God’s eyes was plainly signified by the overturning of the seats.

Yet the perversity of wickedness still exerts its strength. It compels to sell those whom it has deceived into buying. And while no attention is paid to what is commanded by the divine voice—“You received without payment; give without payment” (Matthew 10:8)—the contagion of the offense increases and is doubled in the same matter,

> [Note: In the Anglican, Regius, and four Vatican manuscripts, *delicti conditio* (“the condition of the offense”) is read. The Norman manuscript, Rheims manuscript, and others read differently. A little later, in the Rheims manuscript and Vatican D, where we read *ante omnes radice pestifera* (“before all others by a pestilential root”), the reading is *ante omnes radices pestiferas* (“before all others by pestilential roots”).]

namely, that of the buyer and the seller. And since it is clear that this heresy first crept into the Church with its pestilential root,

> [Note: Gratian, Part I, Question 1, chapter 13.]

and was condemned at its very origin by apostolic detestation, why is it not guarded against? Why is it not considered that the blessing of the man who is promoted so as to become a heretic is turned into a curse?

> [Note: Gratian, Part I, Question 1, chapter 4.]

Very often, therefore, the enemy of souls, when he cannot secretly introduce openly corrupt things, craftily attempts to overthrow people by casting over them the appearance of piety. He may persuade them that something ought to be accepted from those who possess it, so that it may be distributed to those who do not possess it, provided that in this way he may pour out his deadly poisons under the concealed shadow of almsgiving.

For neither would a hunter deceive a wild animal, nor a fowler a bird, nor a fisherman catch a fish, if the hunter placed the snare openly, or if the fisherman did not have the hook hidden beneath bait. The enemy’s cunning must therefore be feared and guarded against in every way, lest those whom he cannot overthrow through open temptation he may slaughter more savagely with a concealed weapon.

For it is not to be regarded as almsgiving if what is acquired from illicit things is distributed to the poor, because the man who receives wrongly with the intention of distributing as though rightly is burdened rather than helped.

> [Note: Gratian, Part I, Question 1, chapter 27.]

The almsgiving that pleases the eyes of our Redeemer is that which is not amassed from illicit things and wickedness, but which is given from permitted and honestly acquired possessions.

> [Note: Gratian, Part XIV, Question 5, chapter 7.]

Hence it is also certain that even if monasteries, hospices, or anything else are built from money given for sacred orders,

> [Note: In the Norman, Regius, and Vatican manuscripts, the words *de pecunia quae pro sacris ordinibus datur* (“from money that is given for sacred orders”) are omitted. They must nevertheless be understood.]

this does not contribute to their reward. For when the perverse buyer of honor is sent into a holy place and appoints others in his own likeness through the granting of advantage, by arranging many things wickedly he destroys more than the man who received the ordination money from him can build.

> [Note: The printed editions read *perversus emptor* (“the perverse buyer”). We have corrected many other matters of lesser importance in this letter from the manuscripts without noting them.]

Therefore, lest we strive to receive anything sinful under the pretext of almsgiving, the order of Sacred Scripture openly forbids us, saying: “The sacrifices of the wicked are abominable, those offered from crime” (Proverbs 21:27). Whatever is offered to God in sacrifice from crime does not appease the anger of almighty God but provokes it.

Again it is written: “Honor the Lord from your just labors” (Proverbs 3:9).

> [Note: Vatican A reads “from your offerings and your just labors”; Vatican B reads “from your substance, or from your just labors.”]

Therefore, whoever takes wrongly in order to give as though rightly plainly does not honor the Lord. Hence Solomon also says: “Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is as though he were sacrificing a son in the presence of his father” (Ecclesiasticus 34:24).

> [Note: The printed editions read “as though he were sacrificing a son.”]

Let us consider how great a father’s grief would be if his son were sacrificed in his presence. From this we can easily understand how great the grief stirred up before God is when a sacrifice is offered to him from plunder.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must turn away most carefully from committing the sins of the Simoniac heresy under the pretext of almsgiving. For it is one thing to give alms on account of sins, and another to commit sins on account of alms.

We embrace as worthy of no less detestation this matter, reported in Gratian (Distinction 59, chapter 3), that has also reached us: certain men, inflated by a desire for honor, are tonsured when bishops have died, suddenly become priests from laymen, and shamelessly seize the leadership of a religious profession, although they have not yet learned even to be soldiers.

> [Note: The Norman manuscript, Vatican A and D, and most manuscripts, together with the old edition, read *religiosi propositi* (“of a religious undertaking”), in agreement with Gratian. More recent editions read *praepositi* (“of the superior”).]

What do we suppose such men will provide for their subjects, when they do not fear to occupy the position of teachers before they have reached the threshold of discipleship? Therefore, even if someone’s character is blameless, it is necessary that he first be exercised in ecclesiastical offices through the distinct orders.

> [Note: The Norman manuscript reads: “so that, although someone may be of blameless merit…” This is how Gratian formerly read it.]

Let him see what he is to imitate; let him learn what he is to teach; let him be instructed in what he is to hold, so that afterward he may not go astray when he has been chosen to show the way to those who wander.

Let him therefore be polished for a long time through religious meditation, so that he may be pleasing, and then, placed like a lamp upon a lampstand, let him shine.

> [Note: Vatican A reads “so that the force of hostile winds…”]

Thus, when the adverse force of the winds rushes upon him, it will not extinguish the flame of learning that has been kindled but will increase it. For since it is written, “Let a person first be tested, and then let him serve” (1 Timothy 3:10), the man who is taken up as an intercessor for the people must be tested all the more beforehand, lest bad priests become the cause of the people’s ruin.

There can therefore be no excuse or defense against this, because it is plainly known to all what care the holy and distinguished teacher took in this matter: he forbids a neophyte to approach the sacred orders (1 Timothy 3). Just as a neophyte was then understood to be one newly planted in the way of holy faith,

> [Note: Gratian, Distinction 48, chapter 2.]

so now a neophyte must be regarded as one who, suddenly planted in the religious habit, has crept in to seek sacred honors.

Orders must therefore be approached in an orderly manner.

> [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the Norman manuscript read: “It is necessary to approach the orders.”]

For the man seeks a fall who, setting aside the steps, seeks to climb by a precipice to the highest summits of office. And since the same Apostle teaches, among the institutions of the sacred order, that hands are not to be laid hastily upon anyone (1 Timothy 5), what could be more hasty or precipitate than to begin at the summit and begin as a bishop before becoming a minister?

> [Note: The Norman manuscript adds: “and to be a teacher before he begins to be a disciple.”]

Whoever therefore desires to attain the priesthood not for the pomp of exaltation but for usefulness should first measure his strength against the burden he is about to undertake,

> [Note: The printed editions read: “and, if he is unequal to it, let him abstain, and let him approach that for which he thinks himself sufficient.”]

so that the man who is unequal may abstain, while even he who believes himself sufficient approaches it with fear.

Nor do we depart from the matter if, for the sake of a reasonable argument, we gather examples from irrational things. Timber suitable for construction is cut from the forests, yet the weight of a building is not laid upon freshly green wood until the lapse of many days has dried out its greenness and made it suitable for necessary use. If this precaution is neglected, the wood is quickly broken by the weight placed upon it, and the thing provided for assistance produces collapse.

For this reason physicians, who care for the body, do not offer to the sick certain remedies that have only recently been prepared. Instead, they leave them to mature with time. If someone administers them prematurely, there is no doubt that what was intended for health becomes the cause of danger.

Let priests therefore learn—let them learn in their office, since the care of souls has been entrusted to them—to preserve what men in various arts maintain through the teaching of reason. Let them restrain themselves from rash ambition, if not through fear, at least through shame.

But lest anyone should still wish to defend himself by appealing to a wicked custom,

> [Note: The printed editions read *ne forsan ab hoc* (“lest perhaps from this”). Vatican F reads *ne forsan ad hoc* (“lest perhaps for this”).]

let the discretion of your Fraternity restrain such men with the bridle of reason and not permit them to fall into unlawful practices,

> [Note: Vatican D and E read: “let your Fraternity restrain them with the bridle of discretion.”]

because whatever deserves punishment ought to be brought forward not for imitation but rather as an example of correction.

Nor can we negligently omit this matter, which likewise requires correction. For what does it profit to fortify everything if, through one opening,

> [Note: Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts read “a pernicious enemy”; the editions read “a pernicious enemy” in the same sense.]

a harmful enemy is given access?

Therefore women are to be forbidden to live with those who have been placed in the sacred order. To prevent the ancient enemy of the human race from exulting, it must be determined by common agreement that, apart from those whom the sacred canons include, they may not have other women living with them.

Although this prohibition may perhaps be bitter to some for a time, it is certain that afterward it becomes sweet through the very benefit to the soul, if the enemy is overcome in the place from which he was able to overcome.

Nor do we leave aside this matter in our concern: the holding of councils throughout the parishes, which the foresight of the Fathers established for the sake of usefulness. Therefore, lest there be any dissension among the brothers or any fuel for discord between superiors and subjects, the priests must come together as one, so that there may be discussion of impending matters and a salutary conference concerning ecclesiastical observance.

> [Note: The printed editions read *incidentibus* (“arising matters”).]

Thus, while past matters are corrected through this process,

> [Note: Other editions read “and they receive a rule for the future,” as found in Vatican A and F.]

and future rules are accepted, almighty Lord may everywhere be praised in the concord of the brothers.

Know that if you observe these things, his presence will be with you, for it is written: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matthew 18:20). If he deigns to be present where two or three are gathered, how much more will he not be absent where more priests have assembled?

It is indeed well known that the rules of the Fathers established that a council should be held twice a year. But lest some necessity perhaps prevent this from being fulfilled, we decree nevertheless that it be assembled once a year without any excuse, so that, in expectation of the council, nothing wicked and nothing unlawful may be presumed.

For very often, even if not out of love for justice, people refrain through fear of judgment from doing what everyone knows may displease the judgment.

Let us, dearest brothers, preserve this observance for our successors, and meditate upon everything written in the sacred books for our instruction, and urge all whom we can toward these things. For it is certain that if we devote ourselves with our whole heart to the salutary commandments, we escape every stain of vice, because, while we rely upon the things by which we are built up, we undoubtedly exclude the place of deception.

Therefore, concerning the matters stated above, we wish your Fraternity, with God as author, to convene a synod. In it, with the assistance of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Aregius and our beloved son Cyriacus the abbot, let everything contrary to the sacred canons, as we have said, be strictly condemned with the imposition of anathema.

> [Note: Recent editions read “Syagrius,” against the manuscripts.]

That is, no one may presume to give anything as a payment for obtaining ecclesiastical orders, or to accept anything for what has been given; nor may anyone suddenly dare to pass from the lay state to the office of sacred governance.

> [Note: This is the reading of the Norman manuscript and other manuscripts throughout. The printed editions read “may suddenly be able to reach.”]

Nor may other women live with priests, except those whom, as stated above, the sacred canons permit.

Our most reverend brother Bishop Syagrius, together with the whole synod, while our beloved son Abbot Cyriacus returns, should diligently report to us what has been done. Thus, when we carefully learn what has been decreed, with what caution, and in what manner, we may unceasingly give thanks to almighty God for your life and conduct.

(See the following letter.)

## Letter 107. To Aregius, Bishop of Gap  
### He consoles him concerning the death of his own people, exhorts him to perform his office diligently, permits the use of dalmatics for him and his archdeacon, and orders him to attend the synod to be convened through Syagrius

Gregory to Aregius, Bishop in Gaul.

> [Note: Aregius, or Arigius, also called Aridius by some, was a distinguished man and the seventh bishop of Gap, born of a noble Frankish family. He attended the Second Council of Valence in 584 and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. His Life survives, edited from manuscript codices by Father Peter Labbe of the Society of Jesus, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*. Gap, also called Vapincum or Vapingum, is a city and episcopal see of Gaul in the Dauphiné, under the archbishop of Aix, between Embrun and Die. — Gussanville.]

> [Note: The Norman manuscript and one Colbert manuscript read “to the bishop in Gaul.” Vatican B, D, E, and F read “to the bishop in Gauls,” as does the Rheims manuscript. Other Colbert manuscripts, together with the Regius, read “to the bishop of Gaul.”]

The affliction of your Fraternity, which we have learned you suffered because of the loss of your people, caused us such sorrow that, since charity has made one person out of two, we felt our heart suffer especially in your tribulations.

> [Note: The printed editions, supported by a few manuscripts, read “to burn especially in your tribulations.”]

Yet amid this grief I was greatly consoled when I recalled to mind the discernment of your holiness. It is fitting both that you bear sorrow patiently and that, because of the hope of another life, you should not prolong your mourning over death.

Nevertheless, lest any further tribulation remain in your mind, I urge you: cease grieving; stop being sad. For it is unfitting to be overwhelmed by the weariness of affliction on account of those whom we must believe to have reached true life by dying.

Those who do not know of another life, who do not trust that there is a passage from this world to something better, perhaps have a just excuse for prolonged grief. But we who know this, who believe it and teach it, ought not to grieve excessively over those who die, lest what appears to others to be an expression of piety become guilt in us. For it is in a certain sense a kind of distrust to be tortured by sadness contrary to what one preaches, since the Apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:12).

Having considered this reasoning, dearest brother, we must strive, as we have said, not to be afflicted over the dead, but to devote our affection to the living, toward whom both piety may be useful and love may bear fruit.

Therefore let us hasten to benefit those whom we can by rebuking, exhorting, advising, encouraging, and consoling. Let our tongue be nourishment for the good and a goad for the wicked; let it blunt the proud, soothe the angry, sharpen the sluggish, kindle the negligent through exhortation, persuade those who shrink back, speak gently to the harsh, and console the despairing.

Thus, because we are called guides,

> [Note: Vatican A reads “because we are called teachers.”]

let us show the way of salvation to those who walk in it. Let us be watchful in guarding; let us carefully fortify the entrances against the enemy’s ambushes. And whenever error has led a sheep astray from the flocks entrusted to us along crooked paths, let us strive with all our strength to call it back to the Lord’s folds, so that from the name of shepherd that we bear we may receive not punishment but reward.

Because all these things require the assistance of divine grace, let us implore the mercy of almighty God with constant prayers, so that he may grant us both the will and the ability to carry them out, and may direct us, with the fruit of good works, along that way of which he testified that he is the Shepherd of shepherds. Thus, since without him we can do nothing, through him we may be able to fulfill all things.

> [Note: The words *facere* (“to do”) are absent from five Vatican manuscripts, the Regius, and several Norman manuscripts.]

Moreover (Gratian, Distinction 23, chapter 10), our common son, the deacon Peter, informed us that when your Fraternity was here you requested that we grant you and your archdeacon permission to use dalmatics.

> [Note: Anastasius says that Pope Sylvester established the use of the dalmatic by deacons in the Church—that is, the Roman Church. When Symmachus specially honored Caesarius of Arles with the privilege of the pallium, he also distinguished Caesarius’ deacons by the use of dalmatics after the model of the Roman Church, as stated in the Life of Saint Caesarius, written in the sixth century, Book I, section 22.

> Dalmatics had broad sleeves, whereas tunics had narrow ones, as John the Deacon testifies in Book III, chapter 59, of the *Life of Saint Gregory*. Dalmatics were ankle-length, made of silk, white, decorated with gold, and marked by *clavi* or bands sewn on in purple. Since all Roman citizens wore tunics, tunics distinguished the orders. Senators wore a tunic distinguished by a broad purple *clavus*; equestrians wore one distinguished by a double but narrow *clavus*; the common people wore a plain tunic without *clavi*.

> Some think that the *clavi* of tunics and dalmatics were certain purple bosses, like the heads of nails woven into the garments; Gussanville agrees with this. But it seems more probable that those *clavi* were purple lines or bands crossing the garments down the middle. Alcuin and Remigius call them *virgulae* (“little stripes”); Amalarius and Honorius call them *lineae* (“lines”); John the Deacon calls them *zonae* (“bands”); and Rabanus calls them *tramites* (“paths”), just as Tibullus calls the golden *clavi* on women’s garments “paths.” They were also called *tabulae* (“panels”), because they resembled long panels.

> The ancient practice of narrow *clavi* remained in dalmatics, though without regard to the purple color. “Deacons,” says Amalarius in his extracts on the office of the Mass, “wear dalmatics … which military usage formerly wore.” The broad *clavus*, once peculiar to senators, also remained in the chasubles of priests. Baronius discusses the dalmatic in his notes on the Martyrology, on the last day of May; Ferrarius noted his error in describing it in Book III of *On the Matter of Clothing*, chapter 9.]

But because he was compelled by the weakness of his people to depart so hastily that neither the grief pressing upon him allowed him to remain longer, as the occasion and the desired matter required, nor our consideration of ecclesiastical procedure—since we were entangled in many affairs—allowed us rashly and suddenly to grant this new request, the fulfillment of what had been asked was delayed.

Now, recalling the good will of your charity, we grant what you requested in the form of this authority of ours, and we have granted that you and your archdeacon are to be honored by the use of dalmatics. We have sent the dalmatics themselves through our beloved son Abbot Cyriacus.

Moreover (Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 5), we wish your holiness to attend the synod that we have decreed should be convened by our brother and fellow bishop Syagrius against the Simoniac heresy. We also wish the pallium that we have sent to be bestowed upon that same brother, provided that he first promises to remove from the holy Church, by the synod’s decision, the unlawful practices that we have forbidden.

Concerning this synod, we wish your Fraternity to report the entire order of proceedings to us in a detailed written account, so that you—whose holiness we have thoroughly tested—may make us fully informed about everything.

## Letter 108. To Bishop Syagrius  
### He praises him for the service rendered to Augustine, grants him the use of the pallium, establishes that the Church of Autun is to hold the first place in that province after the Church of Lyon, and speaks again about the synod

Gregory to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun.

> [Note: In the Rheims manuscript, all the Norman manuscripts, and four Colbert manuscripts, *Augustiduno* is read.]

Charity, the teacher of all good things, which knows nothing alien, harsh, or disordered, exercises and strengthens hearts in such a way that nothing is burdensome, nothing difficult, but everything undertaken becomes sweet.

Since it is characteristic of charity to nourish concord, preserve what has been joined together, unite what has been separated, direct what is crooked, and strengthen the other virtues by the protection of its perfection, whoever inserts himself into its roots neither fails in freshness nor is barren of fruit, because effective work does not lose the moisture of fertility.

> [Note: This is the reading of many Norman manuscripts, the Vatican manuscripts, and most other manuscripts. The printed editions read “to nourish concord and preserve what has been joined together.”]

Therefore, dearest brother, I greatly rejoice and share your joy in the Lord, because I learn from the testimony of many that you are endowed with this same charity in such a way that you yourself properly display what belongs to a priest and commend yourself to others as an example worthy of imitation.

Since, therefore, we have learned that in the work of preaching—which I have long considered and endeavored to undertake among the English people through Augustine, then superior of my monastery and now our brother and fellow bishop—you have been, as was fitting, so careful, devoted, and helpful in every respect that your Fraternity has made me deeply indebted to it in this matter,

> [Note: Some editions read “so that your Fraternity made me very much its debtor,” as found in Vatican D and all the Norman manuscripts.]

and since consideration of so great a matter has reminded me of this,

> [Note: Vatican B reads “moved by this.”]

lest I appear unproductive toward you, I have not postponed your Fraternity’s request for any reason.

Therefore, in accordance with the desire expressed in your petition, we have determined, with God as author, to honor you with the use of the pallium, which you are to wear within your church only for the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass.

We have nevertheless decreed that it is to be given to you only if you first promise, through the decision of the synod, to correct the matters that we have ordered to be corrected. For we have considered it entirely fitting that, together with the gravity of mind which, by God’s favor, we have learned you possess, the splendor of an outward garment should also increase in you, especially since we believe that you requested this not for the pomp of excessive pride but for the character and honor of your Church.

And lest we seem in some way to have bestowed the munificence of this garment upon you without anything further, we have also taken care to grant the following: while preserving in every respect the place and honor of its metropolitan,

> [Note: The Norman manuscript reads “to its metropolitan”; this passage concerns the order and dignity of the Churches, not the preeminence of persons or a right of precedence.]

the Church of the city of Autun, over which almighty God has willed you to preside, is to stand after the Church of Lyon and is to claim for itself this place and order by the indulgence of our authority.

As for the other bishops, we decree (Gratian, Distinction 17, chapter 7) that, according to the time of their ordination, they are to observe their places, whether for sitting in council, subscribing, or in any other matter,

> [Note: From this Autun became the *protothronos*, or first see. In other respects, nothing is more confused than the seating and subscriptions not only of bishops but also of metropolitans in synods, if we consult their published acts; sometimes bishops even subscribed before archbishops. Therefore nothing concerning the dignity of sees can be established from such seating arrangements and subscriptions.]

and are to claim for themselves the prerogative of their respective orders, because the order of reason entirely instructs us

> [Note: Gratian, Distinction 100, chapter 9.]

that, when we must grant privileges together with the use of the pallium, we should do so in the manner we have described.

Since an increase of honor ought also to bring an increase of responsibility, so that the adornments of one’s conduct may correspond to the dignity of one’s clothing, your Fraternity must devote itself with the greatest zeal to every concern. [Note: [Col. 1036D] Norm., Vatican A, and F: “your Fraternity should exercise its zeal in all things.”] Let there be vigilant care concerning the conduct of those subject to you; [Note: [Col. 1036D] Recent witnesses: “let there be vigilant care, so that your…”] let your example be their instruction and your life their teacher. By the exhortation of your tongue, let them learn what they should fear and be taught what they should love, so that, when you have returned the talents entrusted to you with their profit multiplied, you may deserve to hear on the day of recompense: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:23; Luke 19).

Moreover, you should know that responsibility for convening the synod which we wrote that you and our other brothers should hold for the prohibition of illicit practices [Col. 1036D] rests especially upon your vigilance. Since we know that our most excellent sons, the kings of the Franks, show you great affection, you must act with every zeal and exert every effort so that, through the vigilance of your Fraternity, what we commanded concerning the convening of the synod may be fulfilled, and that everything which we have written there for the salvation of souls may be enacted. Thus you will show both your own zeal and how displeasing illicit practices are to you, while we shall appear to have made wise provision in choosing your person above all others for this task. (See above, Letters 106 and 107.)

## LETTER CIX. TO BRUNICHILD, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

Concerning those who suddenly become bishops from the laity, or are ordained through simony. That she should order a synod to be convened for eradicating these abuses and should establish by edict that Jews may not possess Christian slaves.

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

[Col. 1037B] Since the royal solicitude of Your Excellency is everywhere praiseworthy in its government, it ought to show itself still more vigilant and prudent for the increase of its glory, so that those whom you govern outwardly by counsel you may not permit to perish inwardly. Thus, through the fruit of pious solicitude, after the summit of the temporal kingdom which you now hold, you may, with God’s help, attain eternal joys and kingdoms.

We trust that this may indeed come about for you if, among your other good works, you take care concerning the appointment of priests. Their office, as we have learned, has there been brought to such a degree of ambition that priests are suddenly ordained from among the laity, which is exceedingly serious (Gratian, Dist. 61, c. 1). But what are such men going to do, and what benefit are they going to provide for the people, when they desire to become bishops not for usefulness but for honor? [Col. 1037C] These men, who have not yet learned what they ought to teach, do nothing else than make the unlawful advancement of a few the destruction of many, and ecclesiastical discipline is brought into confusion, since no regular order is observed. For one who approaches its governance rashly and precipitously, by what admonition can he edify those subject to him, when his example has taught not reason but error? It is truly shameful—shameful indeed—to command others to observe what one does not know how to keep oneself.

Nor do we pass over another matter which must likewise be corrected, indeed one which is utterly execrable and which we detest as most grievous: that sacred orders are there conferred through the simoniacal heresy, which first arose against the Church and was condemned by a solemn curse. [Col. 1037D] Thus it comes about that the dignity of the priesthood is despised and holy honor becomes a crime. Reverence perishes and discipline is removed, because the man who ought to correct faults commits them, and through wicked ambition the dignity of the priesthood is dragged into corrupt judgment. [Col. 1038A] For who would again venerate what is sold, or not consider cheap what is bought?

Therefore I am deeply grieved, and I sympathize with that land, because, while they disdain to receive as a divine gift the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God deigns to bestow upon human beings through the laying on of hands, they seek to obtain Him through rewards. I do not think that the priesthood can long endure there. For where the gifts of heavenly grace [Note: [Col. 1037D] LETTER CIX [Al. 114].—The printed editions read: “are judged to be for sale.”] are sold, service to God is not sought in a life of holiness; rather, money is honored in opposition to God.

Since, therefore, so great a crime is not only dangerous to those involved but also very harmful to your kingdom, we greet Your Excellency with fatherly affection and ask you to make God favorable to you by correcting this depravity. To ensure that it cannot thereafter be committed under any pretext, let your command establish that a synod be held, [Col. 1038B] where, in the presence of our beloved son Cyriacus the abbot, it shall be prohibited under the strict penalty of anathema that anyone should dare to pass suddenly from the lay state to the rank of bishop, or that anyone should give or dare to accept anything for ecclesiastical orders. May our Lord and Redeemer thus deal with what belongs to you as He sees Your Excellency piously and devotedly concerned with what belongs to Him.

We have taken care to assign special responsibility for the care and supervision of this synod, which we have decreed must be held, to our brother and fellow bishop Syagrius, [Note: [Col. 1037D] This may perhaps have given rise to the claim that Syagrius was related to Queen Brunichild. He is called her brother in the Aeduensian Breviary, according to the Sammarthani brothers in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*. They nevertheless depart from this opinion, since nothing concerning this pontiff’s royal descent is found in ancient books or writers. Certainly the words of Saint Gregory do not imply it in the least.] whom we know to be especially your own. We ask that you deign both willingly to hear him when he petitions and to assist him with your support, so that, once the contagion of this evil has been removed, the ordering of priests may proceed in every territory subject to your jurisdiction in a pious manner pleasing to God and advantageous to your reward.

To this brother of ours, because he showed himself extraordinarily devoted in the preaching which, by the Lord’s authority, was carried out among the English people, we have sent the pallium for use at the solemn celebration of Mass, so that, since he devoted himself to advancing spiritual matters, he might also be found to have advanced in the spiritual order through the support of the prince of the apostles.

We have also been utterly astonished that, in your kingdom, you permit Jews to possess Christian slaves. [Note: [Col. 1037D] The Council of Rheims later enacted the same thing, in 630, canon 11, and the Council of Leptines in 743, canon 3. But in Charlemagne’s Capitulary of 779, chapter 20: “Concerning slaves who are sold: let the sale take place in the presence of a bishop or count, or in the presence of an archdeacon, centenarius, vicedominus, or the count’s judge, or before well-known witnesses. And no one may sell a slave outside the market”—*foras marcham*, in French *hors le marché*, and so forth. This was evidently to ensure certainty concerning their religious status. GUSSANV.] For what are all Christians except members of Christ? We all know that you faithfully honor the head of these members. But let Your Excellency consider how contradictory it is to honor the head while permitting its members to be trampled by enemies. [Col. 1038D] [Note: [Col. 1038D] The printed editions read “to subject them.”] Therefore we ask that Your Excellency’s decree remove this evil of depravity from your kingdom, so that in this respect you may show yourself even more worthy a worshiper of almighty God, by freeing His faithful from His enemies. [Col. 1039A] (Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapter 2.)

## LETTER CX. TO THEODERIC AND THEODEBERT, KINGS OF THE FRANKS

That many are ordained through simony, that taxes are exacted from ecclesiastical estates, and that men suddenly become bishops from the laity. That they should ensure that a synod be held to correct these abuses and should establish that Jews may not possess Christian slaves.

Gregory to Theoderic and Theodebert, kings of the Franks.

[Note: [Col. 1039C] LETTER CX [Al. 115].—Or, “to Theuderic.” In the printed editions, “Theodoric” occurs in the headings. The latter words are absent from the Norman, Rheims, four Vatican, and Corbie manuscripts, but are found in two Vatican manuscripts.]

[Col. 1039C] Since the name of your kingdom once shone among the other nations through the grace of the Christian religion, you must strive earnestly to please more perfectly the almighty Lord, who grants salvation to kings, precisely in that by which you surpass the other nations in glory, and to have the faith which you honor as your helper in all things. Indeed, most excellent sons, we had wished to direct a message to you solely as a customary visitation, so that we might show our fatherly affection through the duties of charity. [Note: [Col. 1039D] More recent witnesses: “to direct our customary message.”] But because an unlawful matter grieves us exceedingly, it is fitting that we should address one matter while by silence leaving nothing unmentioned which requires correction. If you attend carefully, you will recognize that we are speaking entirely for the preservation of your salvation.

It is reported (Gratian, 1, q. 1, c. 28) that the simoniacal heresy, which first crept in against the Church of God through a planting by the devil [Note: [Col. 1039D] Recent witnesses: “through a diabolical undermining.”] and was struck and condemned at its very origin by the weapon of apostolic vengeance, dominates throughout your kingdom, even though in priests faith ought to be chosen together with life. If life is lacking, faith has no merit, as blessed James testifies when he says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2:18). For what works can belong to a priest who is demonstrably obtaining the honor of so great a sacrament through payment?

As a result, even those who seek sacred orders do not strive to correct their lives or reform their morals, but labor to accumulate the wealth with which sacred honor is purchased. [Note: [Col. 1039D] May God one day grant Saint Gregory’s voice a voice of power. The Council of Trent heard it in session XXIII, chapter 18, where it inquires about seminaries. The Lateran Council under Alexander III had heard it earlier, part I, chapter 18: “Since the Church of God, both in matters relating to bodily support and in matters contributing to the advancement of souls, is bound as a devoted mother to provide for those in need, so that the poor, who cannot be assisted by their parents’ resources, may not be deprived of the opportunity to study and make progress,” and so forth. GUSSANV.] Hence it also happens that the innocent and the poor, barred from sacred orders and despised, withdraw. While the poor man’s innocence is displeasing, there is no doubt that payment commends offenses there, because where gold is pleasing, vice is pleasing as well.

Thus not only is a deadly wound inflicted upon the soul of the ordainer and the ordained, but your Excellency’s kingdom is also burdened by the fault of your bishops, whose intercessions ought rather to have helped it. [Note: [Col. 1039D] Recent witnesses, against the manuscripts and old printed editions: “a wound is inflicted,” and shortly afterward, “the kingdom of your bishops.” The phrase “of your bishops” is certainly not found in the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, Regensburg, and other witnesses; the old printed editions agree with them.] For if the man is considered worthy of the priesthood whose merit lies not in his conduct but in the abundance of his payments, it follows that seriousness and diligence defend nothing in ecclesiastical honors, but that profane love of gold obtains everything. [Col. 1040C] [Note: [Col. 1040C] Vatican D and Rheims: “and while vice is rewarded.” Vatican F: “and while honor is rewarded for vice.”]

And while vices are rewarded with honor, the man who perhaps ought to have been punished is brought into the place of the avenger; hence [Note: [Col. 1040C] Rheims and Vatican D: “Priests are thereby driven not to advance but to destroy, not to go forward to heaven for good but rather to perish in hell for evil.” Regensburg, Remigius, and Vatican E also have *irritantur* (“are driven” or “are provoked”).] priests are shown to advance not but rather to perish. For when the shepherd has been wounded, who will apply medicine to heal the sheep? [Col. 1040B] Or when will he protect the people with the shield of prayer who exposes himself to be struck by the enemy’s darts? Or what kind of fruit will he produce whose root is infected with a grievous disease? Greater calamity, therefore, must be feared in those places where such intercessors are brought into positions of governance—men who provoke God’s anger against themselves rather than appeasing Him on behalf of the people, as they ought to have done.

We have also heard that the estates of the churches now provide taxes. [Note: [Col. 1040D] Under the Mosaic law the land of the priests was exempt from taxes. Under the new law, both ecclesiastical and civil laws provide nearly the same protection, as in the Third Lateran Council under Alexander III, canon 19, cited in *Extra*, “On Immunities,” and elsewhere, canon 4. In the *Sext*, under the same title, chapters 1 and 3, and in Cause 23, question 8, certain civil and ecclesiastical laws are cited. In the *Code*, under the title “On Sacred Churches,” the law beginning *Placet*, and so forth. Whether this immunity belongs to divine or human law is not for our institution to determine. GUSSANV.] [Note: [Col. 1040D] Vatican A, D, E, F, Remigius, and Colbert have “that they should not pay taxes.” Although this reading is found in only a few manuscripts, it does not seem contemptible. Saint Gregory is attacking simony here, which no one would deny to be unlawful. He advises the kings to abstain from it, especially since their generosity has freed the Church’s estates from otherwise lawful taxes.] We are greatly astonished at this, if unlawful payments are sought from those to whom even lawful ones are remitted.

Nor does our solicitude permit us to negligently omit this other evil: that certain men, enticed by the prompting of empty glory, suddenly seize the honor of the priesthood from the lay state and, what it is shameful to say and grievous to keep silent about, are not ashamed or afraid to appear as rulers who must be ruled and teachers who must be taught. [Note: [Col. 1040D] The printed editions read: “nor are they ashamed to become.”] They impudently assume the command of souls, although every path by which a guide should lead is unknown to them, and they are ignorant even of where they themselves should walk.

How wicked and rash this is is shown even by secular custom and discipline. For since an army commander is chosen only after becoming experienced through labor and diligence, those who desire to climb the summit of the episcopate with premature haste should consider what leaders of souls ought to be, at least by comparison with this matter, and should refrain from suddenly undertaking labors for which they are inexperienced. Otherwise blind ambition for honor will both become a punishment for them and sow destructive seeds of error for others, since they have not learned what they themselves are to teach.

Therefore, greeting you with fatherly affection, we ask, most excellent sons, that you strive to prohibit so detestable an evil from the boundaries of your kingdom, and that no excuse or suggestion against your soul find a place among you. For without doubt the person who neglects to correct what he can amend shares the guilt of the one who commits it. To enable you to offer a great gift to almighty God, order a synod to be convened. There, as we have commanded our brother bishops, and in the presence of our beloved son Cyriacus the abbot, it shall be established under the obligation of anathema that no one may ever give anything for an ecclesiastical order, no one may accept anything, and no one may suddenly pass from the laity to the priesthood. In this way our Redeemer, whose priests you do not permit to perish inwardly through the enemy, may repay you for this service both in the present life and in the life to come.

We have also been utterly astonished that in your kingdom [Note: [Col. 1041C] Our predecessors were more indulgent toward the Jews, as may be gathered from the Gallican councils. The Council of Mâcon, in 581, canon 16, shows that the practice of that time differed from what the laws of Valentinian III in 425 and numerous canons had commanded. The Third Council of Orléans, in 538, canon 13, permits Jews to have Christian slaves subject to them, provided they impose nothing upon them which the Christian religion forbids their masters to impose. The Council of Rheims, in 630, canon 2, seems not to dissent from the Third Council of Orléans. See the Council of Meaux, canon 73, in 845.] you permit Jews to possess Christian slaves. For what are all Christians except members of Christ? We all know that you faithfully honor the head of these members; but let Your Excellency consider how contradictory it is to honor the head while permitting its members to be trampled by enemies. Therefore we ask that Your Excellency’s decree remove this evil of depravity from your kingdom, so that in this respect you may show yourselves even more worthy worshipers of almighty God, by freeing His faithful from His enemies. [Col. 1041C] (Compare John the Deacon, book III, chapter 2.)

## LETTER CXI. TO VIRGILIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

He confirms the privileges granted by Pope Vigilius to the monastery of Arles.

Gregory to Virgilius, bishop of Arles.

Since the desire of a pious will (Gratian, 25, q. 2, c. 9) and the purpose of praiseworthy devotion should always be supported by priestly efforts, care must be taken that what has been arranged for the tranquility of monks and for a religious way of life may be disturbed neither by negligence nor by some presumption. But just as what reason demanded ought properly to have been defined, so what has been defined [Note: [Col. 1041D] LETTER CXI [Al. 116].—Most of the printed editions add: “unless perhaps where the authority is greater.” These words are not found in five Vatican manuscripts, Remigius, Regensburg, Saint-Victor, and others, nor in Anselm, book IV, chapter 7; neither are they found in the older editions, such as Venice 1504; Paris 1508, 1518, 1521, 1523; Lyon 1539; and others. The Roman correctors had already made some observation concerning this matter in Cause 25, question 2, canon 9. James notes that these words, which are absent from six English manuscripts, entered the text from the margin. Partly from GUSSANV.] must not be violated.

Therefore Childebert, king of the Franks, of glorious memory, inflamed by love of the Catholic religion, established within the walls of the city of Arles, as we find recorded in writing, a monastery for men, and for his reward granted certain possessions there for the support of its inhabitants. [Note: [Col. 1041D] The old Colbert, Corbie, and Norman manuscripts read “Cellibertus.”] So that his will might never be rendered void, and that what had been arranged for the peace of the monks might not be disturbed, he requested by letters that what he had conferred upon the rights of that monastery be confirmed by apostolic authority. He added to his petition that certain privileges should likewise be granted to the same monastery, both in the administration of its property and in the appointment of its abbot.

He knew that the faithful show such reverence toward the apostolic see that what has been arranged by its decree cannot thereafter be troubled by any unlawful usurpation. Since, therefore, both the royal will and the matter greatly desired called for action, our predecessor Vigilius, bishop of the Roman see, sent written instructions to your predecessor Aurelius, [Note: [Col. 1041D] This monastery is thought by the author of the *Pontificium Arelatense*, under Aurelianus, to be the one adjoining Montmajour outside the walls. “Aurelianus,” he says, “before his death in 555, saw completed and perfected the monastery which Childebert had ordered to be built at Arles during Caesarius’s lifetime, commonly called the monastery of Montmajour.” Vigilius endowed it with outstanding privileges, whose record is found in this letter of Gregory.] [Note: [Col. 1042D] He succeeded Auxanius. See the letters of Pope Vigilius to Aurelianus and to the bishops of Gaul in 546. In 549 he subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans. Vigilius wrote again to Aurelianus in 550, after receiving letters from him through Anastasius. Anastasius is mentioned two years later in the letter of the clergy of Italy to the Frankish legates who were traveling to Constantinople. The monastery mentioned here had begun to be founded at Childebert’s command in 548. See the Rule of the Monks composed by Aurelianus at the king’s command and included in the *Codex Regularum*, published by Holstenius. We have retained “Aurelius,” since it is read in all the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts.] in which all that the zeal of his praiseworthy purpose required was willingly confirmed through apostolic authority, since such a request could not properly meet with difficulty.

But so that your Fraternity may know what was decreed at that time, we have taken care to append the writings of our aforesaid predecessor to this letter. Having read through them, we exhort you to preserve everything inviolate with the priestly zeal appropriate to you. [Col. 1042C] [Note: [Col. 1042D] Rheims and four Vatican manuscripts read: “and that you should neither owe anything there nor permit anything of…” The printed editions have *illi* (“to it”) instead of *illic* (“there”), incorrectly.] Permit nothing improper and nothing unlawful to be imposed there, nor allow those provisions to be overthrown by any kind of usurpation.

For although what has once been sanctioned by the authority of the apostolic see requires no further confirmation, nevertheless, by an abundance of caution, we again strengthen by our authority in every respect all that our predecessor established for the peace of this matter. [Col. 1043A] Therefore let your Fraternity conduct itself in guarding these provisions in such a way that it excludes every opportunity for disturbance and urges others to carry them out, showing itself, as is fitting, vigilant and devoted in preserving the most pious will of the deceased.

## LETTER CXII. TO DESIDERIUS, BISHOP OF GAUL

Nothing concerning the pallium granted to his predecessors is found in the archive of the Roman Church. He should therefore send whatever he finds in the documents of his own church.

Gregory to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] LETTER CXII [Al. 117].—Vatican A and F: “to the bishop in Gaul.” Vatican B: “to the bishop of the Gallic city.”]

We have learned of the desire of Your Fraternity through the report of John the *regionarius*. We are quite willing to fulfill it, provided that we are carefully informed about what he has reported. He says that Your Affection has related to him that certain privileges were formerly granted to your church by the apostolic see, and that its priests anciently possessed the use of the pallium. Since you earnestly request that this be restored to you, we had it sought in the archive of our church, but nothing could be found.

Since, however, the more earnestly you desire to obtain this, the more concerned we suppose you to be, devote more vigilant care to searching the documents of your church. If any writings can be found there which may inform us, take care to send them here. For while we gladly grant new privileges, we most willingly restore old ones.

## LETTER CXIII. TO SYAGRIUS, BISHOP OF AUTUN

That he should compel Bishops Menas and Theodore to return to Italy.

[Col. 1043C] Gregory to Syagrius, bishop of Autun.

Since priestly dignity appears to surpass other dignities, whoever is adorned with it ought to show himself worthy of imitation by all, so that by his example he may harm no one but rather be able to shape the lives of those subject to him. For if conduct disagrees with one’s title, the more the episcopate itself elevates a person, the more it condemns him.

We have learned that a certain bishop named Menas, who went there from the diocese of the Roman Church at our direction, [Note: [Col. 1043D] Here “diocese” means the ecclesiastical province whose metropolis was Rome. The word has the same sense somewhat below: “from the diocese of our most reverend brother Constantius, bishop of the Church of Milan.” Here the right of metropolitan bishops is asserted—a right which bishops avoided out of dislike for discipline. In Regensburg, Rheims, and several manuscripts, especially Vatican ones: “from the jurisdictional arrangement of our diocese.”] has shown himself so frivolous that we are more ashamed of him, while the name of bishop is not an honor to him but a burden. Since it causes us shame to learn such things about him—things which we entirely condemn in the priests of other provinces—your Fraternity must not permit him to remain there any longer, but must compel him to return to us as quickly as possible. [Col. 1044A] Once you have found a suitable opportunity, send him to us, so that, restrained with the observance appropriate to him, he may strive to convert secular habits into priestly seriousness.

For it is sufficiently harmful and destructive that those who ought to have been built up should be destroyed through his example. [Note: [Col. 1043D] The printed editions read: “who should have been built up.”] In this matter not only is he found blameworthy, but so is anyone who does not resist. [Note: [Col. 1043D] Rheims and Vatican D: “who has not resisted us.”] For he appears to consent to the one who is in error who does not join in correcting and cutting off what ought to be removed. [Note: [Col. 1043D] The Vulgate editions read: “who does not correct.”] (Gratian, Dist. 83, c. 5.)

Since, moreover, a certain bishop named Theodore is said to have come there while avoiding the discipline of our most reverend brother Constantius, bishop of the Church of Milan, your Fraternity should diligently seek him out and send him back to his own bishop. Since it is written, “Whoever rejects discipline is unhappy” (Prov. 15:32), do not permit him to remain there under any excuse, so that those who might be deceived by their frivolity may be freed, and so that you may gain a reward from God on their behalf by preventing them from perishing in this folly.

## LETTER CXIV. TO BISHOPS VIRGILIUS AND SYAGRIUS

Concerning the case of Syagria, who, after professing religion, was said to have been forcibly joined to a husband.

Gregory to Virgilius, bishop of Arles, and Syagrius, bishop of Autun.

[Note: [Col. 1043D] We have restored the heading thus, following the Rheims, Norman, English, and other witnesses.]

The nature of the office entrusted to me, dearest brothers, compels me to break out into words of grief and to trouble your affection with the anxiety of charity, because you are said to have been excessively negligent and remiss there, where the earnestness of your devotion ought to have been sharply kindled by the uprightness of justice and zeal for chastity.

We have learned that a certain woman named Syagria, having attained a religious life and even changed her clothing, was afterward forcibly joined to a husband—which it is wicked to say—and that you were moved by no sorrow to defend her. If this is true, I groan all the more deeply, lest, God forbid, before almighty God you should possess the status of hirelings rather than the merit of shepherds, since you left a sheep to be torn apart in the wolf’s mouth without a struggle.

What will you say, and what account will you render to the future Judge, [Note: [Col. 1044D] The printed editions read *stupri scortatio*, “the prostitution of sexual violation.” Contemporaries of Gregory the Great did not expressly promise chastity and poverty, nor does the Benedictine order in our own age expressly profess them; neither did the regular canons, Carthusians, Carmelites, or Preachers do so at their original institution. Saint Francis was the first to require explicit mention of both.
