Nevertheless, both have always been part of the monastic condition, and monasticism in Gregory the Great’s age was governed by the same rules by which it is governed now. There is no doubt concerning conversion of life and obedience. For the rest, consult Gregory himself: on poverty, book IX, letter 7, and book X, letter 1; on perpetual chastity, book V, letter 24; on stability, book I, letter 34, and book XI, letter 28; on poverty, chastity, and stability, book I, letter 42.] when the violation of her chastity did not move you, when favor toward a religious habit did not rouse you to defend her, and when priestly consideration did not raise you to protect the integrity of her modesty?

Let the neglect of the past now return to your memory; let remembrance of this fault [Col. 1045A] [Note: [Col. 1045C] The printed editions read “urgently disturb you.”] disturb you urgently, and let consideration of your office impel you to encourage the woman mentioned above. Lest necessity have passed with time into consent, let your speech be healing for her. At your admonition, let her devote herself to prayer; let the laments of repentance not depart from her memory; let her offer our Redeemer a contrite heart, and let her repair through tears the losses of chastity which she was unable to preserve in her body.

Since, therefore, the aforesaid woman desires even now to devote her possessions to pious causes, as is reported, we exhort you to let her find your Fraternity’s favor in this matter and receive your support. Once the proper share of her children has been preserved, let it be lawful for her to decide concerning her property as she wishes. [Note: [Col. 1045C] Gussanville is troubled by the fact that this nun possessed property of her own. She had either gathered these goods after leaving the monastery, or, having possessed them before taking the religious habit, had recovered them when she was joined to her husband. Justinian, *Novella* 5, title 5, “On Monks,” book IV, established the following: “Let the monk know that whatever possessions he had when he entered the monastery belong to the monastery, and let him remove absolutely nothing.” But Syagria was not bound by this law; for although the Franks were governed by Roman laws enacted before the middle of the fifth century, they were not governed by Justinian’s Novels. Cassian writes, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 4, that some people, having been received too simply into certain monasteries, demanded the return of what they had brought in. To prevent this, Saint Benedict says in Rule, chapter 58: “If the one to be received has possessions, let him first distribute them to the poor, or, after making a formal donation, confer them upon the monastery.” Compare the observation in book IV, letter 6. The Rule of the Master employs a similar precaution, chapter 87: “Together with his soul, let him offer everything to God and to the monastery’s oratory, with religious witnesses, the bishop, priest, and deacon, or the clergy of the territory, subscribing; and let the written agreement itself stipulate that if he should ever wish to leave the monastery, he shall depart without his possessions.” See the observation on the former letter 22, indiction 4, concerning the wills of abbots and monks. It is now in the appendix.] For you undoubtedly do what is good if you help those who wish to dispose of their goods.

Therefore, dearest brothers, consider from how great a love these words proceed, and receive everything with the charity with which they are spoken. Since we are one body in the body of our Redeemer, I burn together with you in those matters which I perceive to harm you. Let the author of truth reveal to your heart with what intention and affection I have sent you this letter. Therefore, do not let this fraternal admonition grieve you, since even a bitter cup is willingly received when it is offered with the intention of bringing salvation.

Finally, dearest brothers, let us together beseech the mercy of our God in prayer, that in His kindness He may order our lives in His fear, so that we may serve Him here in a priestly manner and, in His presence hereafter, be able to stand secure and without fear.

## LETTER CXV. TO SYAGRIUS, BISHOP OF AUTUN

Concerning the parishes taken away from the bishop of Turin and another bishop established over them; that he should arrange for their restoration to him.

[Col. 1045C]

Gregory to Syagrius, bishop of Autun.

If in secular matters each person’s right and proper order must be preserved, how much more must no confusion be introduced into ecclesiastical arrangements, lest discord find a place where the blessings of peace ought to proceed? [Col. 1046A] This will be preserved if nothing is assigned to power, but everything to equity. [Note: [Col. 1045D] LETTER CXV [Al. 120].—Vatican B, D, E, F, and Rheims: “with this reverence.”]

It has indeed been reported to us that our most beloved brother Ursicinus, bishop of the city of Turin, after the captivity and plundering which he endured, has suffered grave injury in his parishes, which are said to lie within Frankish territory; and, finally, that another bishop was appointed there contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, although no crime of his demanded it. And lest the injurious wrong committed in this matter perhaps seem slight, an additional cause of grief was added: the property which his Church might have possessed was taken from him.

If these things are indeed true, it is exceedingly cruel and plainly contrary to the sacred canons that ambition should remove from his own altar an innocent priest who does not deserve a successor on account of any crime, and that everyone should attend to the cause of the one who has suffered this injustice, taking care that what they themselves do not wish to endure is not imposed upon others. For if access to a wrongful practice is not closed before it has stood open for long, it grows wider through use; and what reason shows to be forbidden will come to seem lawful by custom. But above all, let the solicitude of your Fraternity, out of regard for our recommendation and consideration of God, devote itself more earnestly to his defense, and not permit him to remain any longer, contrary to reason, removed from his own parishes. Let it accomplish this both on its own and by entreating the most excellent kings—whom we believe you will in no way distress—so that what has been wrongly done may be corrected and what has been violently taken away may, with truth as its advocate, be restored. For since it is written, “A brother helping a brother will be exalted” (Prov. XVIII, 19), your Charity should know that you will be received by almighty God in proportion as you willingly and steadfastly carry out his commands in helping your brother.

**LETTER CXVI. TO THEODERIC AND THEODEBERT, KINGS OF THE FRANKS.** That the parishes belonging to the bishop of Turin, situated in the Frankish kingdom and in which a new bishop had been ordained, should be restored to him.

Gregory to Theoderic and Theodebert, kings of the Franks.

The highest virtue in kings is to cultivate justice, to preserve each person’s rights, and not to permit what belongs to power to be done to their subjects, but to ensure that what is equitable is maintained. Since we trust that you both love and earnestly strive for this, we are prompted to point out to your Excellencies matters requiring correction, so that through our letters we may both come to the aid of the oppressed and acquire a reward for you.

They say, then, that our brother and fellow bishop Ursicinus, bishop of the city of Turin, is suffering a very serious injustice in his parishes situated within the boundaries of your kingdom, so much so that, contrary to ecclesiastical observance, sacerdotal dignity, and the determinations of the sacred canons, another man did not fear to be ordained bishop there, although no crime of his required it. And because it seemed insufficient that unlawful acts should not be joined to unlawful acts, the property of his Church, as is reported, was also taken away. If the truth is indeed so, since it is altogether intolerable that one whom guilt has not harmed should be oppressed by force, after offering a greeting in the language of paternal charity, we ask that your Excellency graciously endeavor, through our intercession, to grant voluntarily what you can provide out of love for ecclesiastical reverence and regard for equity; and, as we trust in your goodness toward justice, cause it to be preserved for him in every respect. When the truth has been disclosed, order both that what was unlawfully done there be corrected and that the property violently taken from him be restored with equity.

Nor should the fact that his Church is for a time held by his enemies cause him any harm. Rather, this should move your Christian hearts ever more strongly to come to his aid, so that, consoled by the gift of your generosity, he may not have to experience the losses of the captivity he has endured. For the sake, therefore, of your souls’ salvation, may this exhortation of ours find a place with you, so that, for the increase of your reward, you may raise him from his abasement by extending the hand of justice; and thus, because you preserve equity for priests, may you always flourish before the eyes of God through their prayers.

**LETTER CXVII. TO BRUNICHILDE, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS.** He recommends Hilary, asking her to protect him by her support.

Gregory to Brunichilde, queen of the Franks.

[Editorial note: **LETTER CXVII [Former numbering 122].**—Two sayings from Plutarch correspond to this. The first concerns Antigonus I: “When someone said that everything was honorable and just for kings, ‘Yes, by Zeus,’ he said, ‘for barbarian kings; but for us only honorable things are to be regarded as honorable, and only just things as just.’” The second concerns Antigonus III: “Antigonus III wrote to the cities that if he should order anything contrary to the laws by letter, they should not obey, but should consider him to have made the mistake through ignorance. Some of the supreme pontiffs imitated him. —Gussanville.]

Since the administration of a kingdom requires virtue, justice, and power together with equity, and since none of these can suffice without the others, how greatly concern for them shines forth in you is plainly shown by the praiseworthy way in which you govern the multitudes of peoples. Who, then, seeing this, could distrust the goodness of your Excellencies or be uncertain of obtaining a request, when she has judged it right to ask from you what she knows you willingly can grant to your subjects?

The bearer of this letter, Hilary, a servant of your Excellencies, believing that he would be aided by our intervention before your power, asked that the letters of our recommendation lend support to his request. He was confident that, just as you grant favors to others, he would obtain them more abundantly if our intercession spoke on his behalf. Therefore, after offering you greetings with the affection of paternal charity, we ask that, since he declares himself to be suffering from the adversities caused by the wickedness of certain people, your Excellencies’ protection should fortify him; and, so that he may not be unfairly burdened, command by your authority that he be kept safe. Thus, while, at your command and through your favor, no one’s hostility is allowed to prevail unjustly and solely according to personal will, we may give thanks for what we have obtained—requests which we make chiefly for the sake of increasing your reward—and blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, whom you venerate in us with Christian devotion by granting what we ask, may repay your Excellencies.

**LETTER CXVIII. TO VANTILO AND ARIGIUS.** He recommends Hilary, asking them to extend their protection to him.

Gregory to Vantilo and Arigius.

It adds greatly to the praise of your glory that Hilary, the bearer of this letter, trusts that he will be relieved by powerful protection if he should deserve to obtain the favor of your guardianship. He considers this so great a thing that, in order to obtain it, he has also taken care to enlist our recommendation as an aid. Since, then, we see that he eagerly wishes to flee for refuge to your patronage, we judged that we should not delay writing on his behalf. We are confident that you will extend your defense all the more willingly to those who ask for it, the more you recognize that those placed in grief and straits await it humbly.

For this reason, greeting your Glories with paternal tenderness, we ask that, since the aforesaid bearer declares himself to be subjected, contrary to reason, to the hostility of certain persons, he may find the protection he greatly desires; and that you permit him to suffer no trouble or harassment contrary to equity. Rather, let the favor of your patronage protect him from every affliction inflicted not by reason but by the will of his adversaries. Thus he may rejoice that he has found in you, as he hopes, the refuge he desires, and this may contribute something to your reward, while others likewise learn to seek from you, through us, consolation in tribulation.

**LETTER CXIX. TO ASCLEPIADOTUS, PATRICIAN.** He recommends Hilary, asking him to undertake his protection.

Gregory to Asclepiadotus, patrician in Gaul.

Those who cling to earthly kings should, to the extent that an opportunity to benefit others is granted them, be all the more ready in matters that earn a reward, so that by the fruit of good works they may both enjoy here the favor of those whom they serve and later deserve to enter the court of the heavenly kingdom. Although we trust that you love and are intent upon this, nevertheless, since a paternal address always adds something to good minds, we exhort you: whenever a suitable opportunity to help presents itself, do not at all delay what you ought to do. For whoever raises up a brother from grief, lifts up the oppressed, or consoles the sorrowful should not doubt that he will receive recompense from the One for whom he gives everything—he who says, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40).

Since, therefore, Hilary, the bearer of this letter, has asked that our letter recommend him to your protection because he declares that the hostility of certain people has unjustly flared up against him, confident that, with you as his patrons, no one’s hostility can harm him contrary to reason, we therefore greet your Glory with paternal affection and ask that he be fortified by the favor of your support. Grant him, on our intercession, more generously what you grant to others who ask justly; do not permit him to be oppressed contrary to equity, but extend to him the hand of assistance wherever the order of reason calls for it. Thus, to the increase of your glorious reward, he too may find in you what he has sought with all his heart, and you may be seen—something greatly glorious—to have come to the aid of one afflicted and humbly supplicating.

**LETTER CXX. TO CLAUDIUS IN SPAIN.** He praises him, declaring that the reputation of his virtue has made him dear. He exhorts him to advance in the light of truth and in love of the heavenly homeland. He recommends Cyriacus, his abbot and legate.

Gregory to Claudius in Spain.

Because the reputation of good people spreads like perfume, the fragrance of your glory has reached us here from the western regions. Sprinkled, so to speak, by the sweetness of this breeze, I confess that I have greatly loved one whom I did not know; with the hand of love I have drawn him into my heart. I was no longer loving someone unknown to me, since I had learned of his goodness. Although he is known to me through close attention but remains unknown to me in bodily sight, I can truthfully say of him: I know his person, but I do not know his home.

A great testimony to your praise is given by the report that your glory diligently clings to the excellent king of the Goths. Since the good are always displeasing to the wicked, it is certain that you are good, because you have pleased a good man.

Therefore, offering you the greeting that is your due, I desire that you continue in the practices you have begun, so that Solomon’s true saying may be fulfilled in you: “The path of the just proceeds like a shining light, and grows until the perfect day” (Prov. IV, 18). Now, when the light of truth shines upon us and the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom reveals itself to our minds, it is already day, but it is not yet perfect day. Perfect day will come when nothing of the night of sin remains in our minds. Grow, therefore, toward perfect day, so that, as far as the eternal homeland is seen, the increase of good works here may expand. Then the fruit of the reward will be greater in proportion as the zeal of labor has now increased.

For this reason we commend to your Glory our most beloved son Cyriacus, father of our monastery, so that, when he has completed what has been entrusted to him, no delay in returning may impede him. May almighty God protect you with the shelter of his heavenly arm, and grant that you may be glorious now among human beings and, after the passage of many years, among the angels.

**LETTER CXXI. TO LEANDER, BISHOP OF SEVILLE.** His letter, written with the pen of charity, reveals the elevation of his heart through the humility of his speech. He declares himself unworthy of praise: burdensome honor depresses his character, conquered by its weight he joins sins to sins, and, torn from the tranquility of the monastery, he has suffered shipwreck of mind. He offers pious consolation concerning the pains of gout. He sends the pallium.

Gregory to Leander, bishop of Spain.

I have received a letter from Your Holiness, written with the pen of charity alone. Your tongue had been dipped in your heart when it poured onto the page what it wrote. When it was read, good and wise men were present, and at once their hearts were moved to compunction. Each began, with the hand of love, to draw you into his own heart, because in that letter it was not possible merely to hear the sweetness of your mind but to see it. Each was kindled and amazed, and the very fire of the listeners showed what the ardor of the speaker had been. For unless flames first burn within themselves, they do not set another alight. Thus we saw with what charity your mind had burned, since it kindled others in this way.

They knew very little of your life, which I have always recalled with great veneration; yet the elevation of your heart became clear to them through the humility of your speech. Your letter says that my life is worthy of imitation by all; but since it is not as it is described, let it become so because it has been described, lest one who is not accustomed to lie should lie. Here I shall briefly repeat the words of a certain good woman: “Do not call me Naomi, that is, beautiful; call me Mara, because I am full of bitterness” (Ruth I, 20).

For today, good man, I am not the person you knew. I confess that, while progressing greatly outwardly, I have fallen inwardly, and I fear that I am among those of whom it is written: “You cast them down when they were being exalted” (Ps. LXXII, 18). For the one who advances in honors but falls in character is cast down precisely while being exalted.

Following the paths of my own heart, I had determined with all my strength to be “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people,” and to walk in the lot of him of whom the Psalmist again says: “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. LXXXIII, 7). In other words, I wished to ascend inwardly all the more truly the more humbly I lay outwardly in the valley of tears.

But now burdensome honor weighs me down greatly; countless cares resound around me, and whenever the mind gathers itself toward God, they tear it apart by their assaults, as though by swords. There is no rest of heart. It lies prostrate in the lowest places, crushed beneath the weight of its own thoughts. The wing of contemplation lifts it to higher things only very rarely, or not at all. The sluggish mind grows numb and, while temporal cares bark around it, is now almost reduced to stupor; it is forced at one moment to conduct earthly affairs, at another even to administer matters that are carnal. Sometimes, compelled by disgust, it is forced to arrange matters that involve guilt. Why say more? Defeated by its own weight, it sweats blood. If guilt were not reckoned under the name of blood, the Psalmist would not say: “Deliver me from bloodguilt” (Ps. L, 16). But when we join sins to sins, we also fulfill what was said through another prophet: “Blood has touched blood” (Hos. IV, 2). Blood is said to touch blood when one sin is added to another, so that the heap of iniquity is multiplied.

Amid all this, I beseech almighty God that you hold me up with the hand of your prayer, fallen as I am amid the waves of disturbance. I was sailing, as it were, with a favorable wind when I led a tranquil life in the monastery; but suddenly a storm arose in violent movements, carried me away into its confusion, and I lost the prosperity of my journey, because, having lost peace, I suffered shipwreck of mind. See, now I am tossed among the waves and seek the plank of your intercession, so that I who did not deserve to reach shore safely in an intact ship may at least, after my losses, be brought back to land on a plank.

Your Holiness writes that you are afflicted by the trouble of gout, whose continual pain has also worn me down severely. But consolation will be easy if, amid the scourges we suffer, we recall to mind the sins that we have committed; and we shall perceive that these are no longer scourges but gifts if we cleanse through pain of the flesh what we have sinned through the pleasure of the flesh.

Moreover, with the blessing of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have sent you the pallium, to be used only for the solemn celebration of Mass. Having sent it, I ought certainly to have admonished you how you should live; but I suppress my words, because your conduct surpasses your words.

May almighty God guard you by his protection and lead you, with abundant fruit of souls, to the reward of the heavenly homeland. How greatly I am weighed down by occupation and weakness is briefly attested by this letter, in which I say little to one whom I love greatly.

**LETTER CXXII. TO RECHARED, KING OF THE VISIGOTHS.** He praises the king for the Gothic people’s conversion to the faith, for the gifts offered to blessed Peter, and for rejecting the money of the Jews, by which they sought to have the law enacted against them rescinded. He reminds him that these things must be attributed to the praise of God and that the snares of the ancient enemy must be guarded against through humility of heart, purity of body, and gentleness of spirit. He sends relics.

Gregory to Rechared, king of the Visigoths.

I cannot express in words, most excellent son, how greatly I delight in your work and your life. In our own days we have heard of the power of a new miracle: through your excellence the entire Gothic people has been transferred from the error of the Arian heresy to the solidity of the true faith. I wish to cry out with the prophet: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI, 11).

For whose breast, even if made of stone, would not immediately soften, upon learning of so great a work, into praises of almighty God and love for your Excellency? I confess that I often enjoy telling my assembled sons of what has been accomplished through you, and often admiring it together with them. These things frequently stir me even against myself, because I, sluggish and useless, lie inert in idle leisure at the very time when kings labor for the gain of the heavenly homeland in gathering souls.

What, then, shall I say to the coming judge at that fearful examination, if I come there empty-handed, where your Excellency will lead behind you the flocks of the faithful whom you have now drawn to the grace of the true faith through diligent and continual preaching?

Yet, good man, I find great consolation in this gift of God: I love in you the holy work that I do not possess in myself. And when I rejoice with great exultation in your deeds, what is yours through labor becomes mine through charity. Therefore, concerning the conversion of the Goths, in your work and in our rejoicing, I wish to cry out with the angels: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

For, as I believe, we are all the more indebted to almighty Lord in thanksgiving because, although we have done nothing together with you, by rejoicing with your work we nevertheless share in it. Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, has himself plainly shown to all how willingly he received the gifts of your Excellency. For it is written (Gratian, 14, question 5, canon 11): “The vows of the righteous are pleasing” (Prov. XV, 8). In the judgment of almighty God, it is not what is given that is considered, but by whom it is given.

Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look” (Gen. IV, 4–5). In saying that the Lord looked upon the offerings, Scripture first carefully stated that he looked upon Abel. From this it is plainly shown that it was not the offerer who pleased God because of the gifts, but the gifts because of the offerer.

You have therefore shown how pleasing your offering is by giving, before the gold you intended to offer, the gifts of souls through the conversion of the subjected nation.

You say that the abbots sent to carry your offering to the blessed apostle Peter, exhausted by the violence of the sea, returned to Spain from the very journey. It was not that your gifts had been rejected—those gifts later arrived—but the steadfastness of those who had been sent was tested, to see whether they knew how to overcome dangers placed before their holy desire and not grow weary in mind amid bodily fatigue. For adversity placed in the way of good vows is a test of virtue, not a judgment of rejection (Gratian, 7, question 1, canon 48).

Who does not know how favorable it was that the blessed apostle Paul was coming to Italy to preach, and yet, while coming, suffered shipwreck (Acts XXVII)? Nevertheless, the ship of his heart remained intact amid the waves of the sea.

Moreover, I declare that what I learned from my most beloved son, the presbyter Probinus, has increased through your work in the praises of God. When your Excellency issued a certain decree against the perfidy of the Jews, those against whom it had been issued attempted to bend the rectitude of your mind by offering a sum of money. Your Excellency rejected it, and, seeking to please the judgment of almighty God, preferred innocence to gold.

This brings to mind the deed of King David. When water desired by him from the cistern of Bethlehem, which lay among hostile troops, had been brought by his obedient soldiers, he immediately said: “Far be it from me to drink the blood of these men” (1 Chron. XI, 19). Since he poured it out and refused to drink it, Scripture says: “He poured it out as a libation to the Lord.”

If, therefore, water rejected by an armed king was transformed into a sacrifice to God, let us consider what sort of sacrifice the king offered to almighty God who, for love of him, refused to accept not water but gold. Therefore, most excellent son, I shall say confidently: You poured out gold as a libation to the Lord, since you did not wish to possess it against him. These are great deeds and must be attributed to the praise of almighty God.

But amid these things the snares of the ancient enemy must be guarded against with vigilant care. The greater the gifts he sees in people, the more subtly he seeks to take them away. Highway robbers do not seek to seize travelers who are empty-handed, but those carrying vessels of gold or silver. The present life is a road, and each person must beware of ambushing spirits in proportion to the greatness of the gifts he carries.

Your Excellency must therefore guard with the utmost care the great gift received through the conversion of the subjected people, first by preserving humility of heart and then purity of body. Since it is written, “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11; XVIII, 14), it is plainly evident that the one who truly loves high things is the one who does not sever his mind from the root of humility.

Often the evil spirit, unable at first to oppose the good things that people have accomplished, comes afterward to the mind of the one who performed the work in order to destroy them. Through silent thoughts he shakes it with certain praises of its own, so that the deceived mind marvels at how great are the things it has done. When, through hidden swelling, it exalts itself before itself, it is deprived of the grace of the one who gave the gift.

Hence it is said through the prophet against the proud soul: “Trusting in your beauty, you fornicated in your own name” (Ezek. XVI, 15). For a soul to trust in its beauty is to presume upon a righteous action in itself. It fornicates in its own name when, in what it has done rightly, it does not seek the praise of its Creator to be magnified but seeks the glory of its own reputation.

Again, it is written through the prophet: “Because you are beautiful, descend” (Ezek. XXXII, 19). The soul descends precisely from the place where it is more beautiful, when, because of the beauty of virtue by which it ought to have been exalted before God, it falls from his grace through its own pride.

What, then, should be done in these matters except that, whenever the evil spirit brings back to our minds the good things we have done in order to lift us up, we should always recall our evils? Thus we may recognize that what we have done by sinning is ours, while we attribute only the gifts to almighty God when we avoid sins.

The purity of the body must also be guarded in the practice of good action, because, in the words of the preaching Apostle, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. III, 17). He says again: “This is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thess. IV, 3). Showing what sanctification he meant, he immediately adds: “That you abstain from fornication; that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the passion of desire.”

The reins of government must likewise be tempered toward subjects with great moderation, lest power steal upon the mind. A kingdom is governed well when the glory of ruling does not rule the mind. Care must also be taken that anger does not creep in, lest everything permitted be done too quickly.

For anger, even when it prosecutes the offenses of those who have sinned, must not go before the mind like a mistress; rather, it should follow behind reason’s back like a servant, coming to the forefront only when commanded. If it once begins to possess the mind, it considers even what it does cruelly to be just. Hence it is written: “The anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (James I, 20). Again it is said: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (ibid., 19).

With God as your author, I do not doubt that you observe all these things. But since an opportunity for admonition has arisen, I furtively attach myself to your good actions, so that what you do without being admonished, when an admonisher is added to you, you may no longer do alone. May almighty God protect you in all your actions by the extension of his heavenly arm, and grant you both the prosperity of the present life and, after the passage of many years, eternal joys.

We have also sent you, as a blessing, a small key from the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle. It contains iron enclosed from his chains, so that what bound his neck for martyrdom may free yours from every sin. I have likewise given the bearer of this letter a cross to present to you, containing a piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross and hairs of blessed John the Baptist, so that through the intercession of his forerunner you may always have the consolation of our Savior.

To our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Leander we have sent the pallium from the see of blessed Peter the apostle; we owe this both to ancient custom, to your practices, and to his goodness and dignity.

Editorial notes and textual apparatus (in source order):

- [Col. 1045D] Here, in volume IV of *Italia sacra*, he is placed as the sixth bishop of Turin, in 580. This letter, however, was written about 598. I therefore wonder that Philibert Pingon of Savoy, in his *Augusta Taurinorum*, names Agnellus as bishop in 589 and records no one until 800. Perhaps Agnellus is the man whom Gregory says in this letter was appointed bishop while Ursicinus was held captive. —Gussanville.

- [Col. 1046C] Turin, formerly Augusta Taurinorum, commonly Turino, is a very well-known Italian city, the seat of the Duke of Savoy in Piedmont; it now enjoys an archiepiscopal see. —Gussanville.

- [Cols. 1046C–D] Presumably this injury arose when a new bishopric of Maurienne was created out of Ursicinus’s parishes; see the First Council of Lyons, canons 2, 4, and 5, and the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 12. Maurienne originally belonged to the diocese of Turin, as Gregory of Tours writes in book I, chapter 14, of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*. Later, when it was occupied by the Franks under King Guntram, it had its own bishop. King Guntram also refused thereafter to leave to the bishop of Turin the parishes of Susa in the Turin diocese after annexing them to his dominions, because Turin was still under Lombard power. Ursicinus complained of this to the Roman pontiff. Gregory the Great wrote this letter and the following one to Bishop Syagrius and to Kings Theoderic and Theodebert, but in vain; the bishopric of Maurienne has remained to the present day.

- [Cols. 1046D–1047D] This is especially forbidden by the First Council of Lyons, canon 5: “What has been decreed by an observance most ancient and most celebrated we nevertheless repeat: no one may dare, while its incumbent lives, to aspire to a priestly rank in another’s place through ambition. If anyone has presumed to do so by any impious or rash intention, both the person ordained and those brethren proved to have been present at his ordination shall be struck by a perpetual sentence of excommunication.” —Gussanville.

- [Col. 1047D] The adopted reading, from the Corbie and Norman manuscripts, is *suam in hujus praejudicio cuncti causam attendant* (“let all attend to their own cause in this wrong done to him”). Four Vatican manuscripts, and the Saint-Victor, Tours, and Rheims manuscripts, read *praejudicium pro praejudicio* (“injury for injury”). The old editions likewise have this; more recent editions read *in hujus praejudicii cuncti causam*, etc., from which a sense is sought in vain.

- [Col. 1047D] The Norman, Rheims, Tours, Corbie, Saint-Victor, and most Vatican manuscripts very well read: “and let them strive that what they do not wish to suffer be not imposed on others.” The old editions read: “and that what they do not wish to suffer should not be imposed on others.” More recent editions read: “let those who do not wish to suffer it not impose it on others.”

- [Col. 1047D] Letter CXVI [formerly 121]: the Rheims manuscript and Vatican manuscript D read *custodire* (“to preserve”).

- [Col. 1047D] Printed editions read “the institutions of the canons” instead of “the determinations of the sacred canons.”

- [Col. 1047D] The Colbert manuscript, five Vatican manuscripts, and the Rheims manuscript read *ut virtute opprimeretur*, that is, “that he should be oppressed by force.”

- [Col. 1048D] Letter CXVIII [formerly 123]: another letter to this same Arigius survives as letter 57 of book VI.

- [Col. 1049D] Is this Hilary, mentioned here and in the preceding letter, the senator of Dijon of whom Gregory of Tours writes in chapter 42 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*? But that man is said to have lived and died in the fifth century. Certainly, if these letters were written in indiction 2, the Hilary in question is another; for Gregory of Tours, who speaks of Senator Hilary’s death and burial, himself died long before indiction 2.

- [Cols. 1049D–1050D] Vatican manuscript A reads: “and indeed let others similarly learn to seek in us”; scarcely any manuscript except the Remigius and Saint-Victor manuscripts contains this letter. The same must be said of the next two letters.

- [Col. 1050D] Letter CXIX [formerly 124]: Vatican manuscript A omits “patrician,” and so forth. Vatican manuscript A and the Remigius manuscript read *terrenis rebus* (“earthly things”) rather than “earthly kings.”

- [Col. 1050D] Letter CXX [formerly 125]: compare Aristotle, *Ethics* VIII, “like is friend to like” (ὅμοιον ὁμοίῳ φίλον), and Martial: “Worst wife, worst husband; I am surprised that you do not get on well together.”

- [Col. 1051D] Letter CXXI [formerly 126]: the manuscripts generally read “Leander, bishop of Spain.” Two Colbert manuscripts read “bishop of the Spaniards”; a third, “of the Spanish”; a fourth, “of Spain.” In the Regius manuscript, the Augustinian monastery manuscript, and indiction 2, it is “Leander, bishop of the Spaniards”; printed editions have “bishop of Seville.”

- [Col. 1051D] More recent editions read “from weakness” in place of “and weakness.” Four Vatican manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, and the Regius manuscript prefix: “In the month of August, indiction 2.”

- [Col. 1052D] Letter CXXII [formerly 127]: Hincmar sufficiently demonstrated this letter’s excellence when he sent it as a gift worthy of so great an emperor and king of the Franks, Charles the Bald, together with a very ample and lucid commentary on it; the reader may see that commentary in volume II of Hincmar’s works. —Gussanville.

- [Col. 1052D] On this conversion of the Visigoths, read book III, chapter 31, of the *Dialogues*, and consult the Life of Saint Gregory.

- [Col. 1053D] Saint Gregory customarily uses the words of this angelic hymn to express joy, as many letters below will show. For the ancients’ similar custom, see note 1803 on the *Book of Sacraments*.

- [Col. 1054D] The letter of King Reccared in which these matters are related was printed above; it is letter 61 of this book.

- [Col. 1054D] The Norman manuscript and most others read *fiduciam quippe anima* (“for a soul’s confidence”). The Corbie and Norman manuscripts read “seeks favor” rather than “seeks glory.”

- [Col. 1055C] Printed editions read *mentem surripiat* (“lest it steal away the mind”) rather than “lest power steal upon the mind.”

- [Col. 1055C] The Vatican, Corbie, Norman, and other manuscripts read “and to your character” rather than “and to our customs.”

[Note: [Col. 1055C] These words are absent from the English, Norman, Remigius, Corbie, and Saint-Victor manuscripts. They are found in the Regius, Colbertine, Rheims, and five Vatican manuscripts. Ennodius uses *anagnosticum* more than once for any written text, as in Letter 4 of Book I, to Faustus, “following the authority of the *anagnosticus*,” etc.; Sirmundus explains this in his notes on your letter. Also in Letter 5 of Book VIII, he speaks of the tediousness caused by the prolixity of the *anagnosticus*. On this passage Sirmundus writes: “*Anagnosticum* (ἀναγνωστικόν) is everything that is read or recited, just as *acroama* (ἀκρόαμα) and *akousma* (ἄκουσμα) designate what is heard. Therefore, just as Latin writers also use *acroama* for a saying or anything received by the ears, so they use *anagnosticum* for any letter or written document; one might also say *anagnosma* (ἀνάγνωσμα).” Partly from Gussanville.]

Also in the written document:

Some time ago your most gracious Excellency had instructed me, through the arrival of a certain young man from Naples, to write to the most devout emperor so that he might seek out in the archives the agreements that had formerly been issued between the emperor Justinian, of pious memory, and the laws of your kingdom, and from them determine what he ought to preserve for you. But two things strongly prevented me from doing this. First, because in the time of the aforesaid emperor Justinian, of pious memory, the archives were so suddenly consumed by a fire that scarcely any document from his period remained at all. Second—and this is something that should be said to no one—you ought to seek out for yourself the documents that are against you and bring them forward on my behalf. For this reason I urge your Excellency to arrange matters consistent with your character and diligently to pursue everything that pertains to peace, so that the years of your kingdom may be remembered with great praise through long courses of time.

Moreover, we have sent another key from the most sacred body of the blessed Apostle Peter. When it has been placed in a worthy position of honor, may it multiply by blessing everything that it finds among you.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] One Colbertine manuscript, itself an eighth-century codex, no. 408, omitting what follows here, concludes this letter—which it calls the second letter to Reccared and whose opening, likewise omitting “in the written document,” it assigns to the words “Some time ago”—as follows: “Moreover, we have received three hundred cowls as gifts sent to the poor of the blessed Apostle Peter by your Excellency; and, insofar as we can, we earnestly beseech you that the one whose poor you have protected by your generosity in clothing, you may have as your protector on the fearful day of judgment. The reason we have not now sent our man to your Excellency is the necessity of a ship, because no one can be found who is able to depart from these regions for the shores of Spain.”]

## LETTER CXXIII. TO VENANTIUS AND ITALICA

He consoles them, afflicted by their own troubles and by the general affliction of the whole world, which indicates that the end of the world is near.

[Col. 1056C]

[Note: [Col. 1056D] LETTER CXXIII [elsewhere 128].—The manuscripts and handwritten copies disagree about the inscription of this letter. In the Norman and English manuscripts it reads, “To Venantius, former monk and patrician, and to Italica, his wife.” In the Vatican, Colbertine, and Rheims manuscripts it reads, “To Italica, the patrician woman, and to Lord Venantius”; the old printed editions agree with these. The recent editions add “Chancellor of Italy,” which all the manuscripts reject. This Venantius, already well known from other letters written to him, had married Italica, by whom he had two daughters, Barbara and Antonina, mentioned below. After their father’s death, Saint Gregory wrote letters of consolation to them.]

Gregory to Lord Venantius, the patrician, and to Italica, his wife.

I took care to ask some people coming from Sicily, with the affection I owed you, about the health of your Excellency. But they gave me a sorrowful reply concerning the unremitting succession of your illnesses. [Note: [Col. 1056D] Three Vatican manuscripts, the Rheims and Colbertine manuscripts, and most of the Norman manuscripts read, “they replied with sadness to me.”]

In saying this, I myself also find nothing else about myself that I ought to report to you, except that, because of my sins, eleven months have now passed during which it is very unusual if I am ever able to rise from bed. For I am oppressed by such severe gout and by such great pains from my other sufferings that my life itself is a very heavy punishment to me. Every day I fail under pain and sigh while awaiting the remedy of death.

Among the clergy and people of this city, such great fevers and illnesses have broken out that scarcely any free person or slave remains who is fit for any duty or service. From the neighboring cities, reports of daily slaughter by mortality reach us. As for how Africa is being devastated by death and sickness, I believe that, the closer you are to it, the more accurately you have learned of it. Those arriving from the East report still greater desolations.

Since, therefore, you recognize in all these things a general affliction approaching with the end of the world, you ought not to be excessively distressed by your own troubles. Rather, as befits wise and noble people, turn your whole heart toward the care of souls, and fear the strict judgment all the more as it draws nearer. Devote yourselves to works of piety, of which it is written that they have the promise of the present life and of the future life (1 Timothy 4:8).

The Almighty God is able both to preserve the life of your Excellency here for a long time and, after many years have run their course, to lead you to eternal joys. On my behalf, I ask you to greet my most beloved daughters, Lady Barbara and Lady Antonina. I pray that heavenly grace may protect them and grant them prosperity in all things.

## LETTER CXXIV. TO DONELLUS, THE *EROGATOR*

He consoles him in illness. He rejoices that the military *roga* has again been imposed upon him. He advises that the money which the exarch had borrowed be repaid. He urges that special care be given to assist the city of Rome.

[Col. 1057C]

Gregory to Donellus, the *erogator*.

[Note: [Col. 1057D] The origin of this name for the office is explained in the letter by the words, “For concerning the military *roga*,” etc.]

We received a letter from Your Glory, full of the affection of a good son; from it our spirit was indeed saddened by the distress of your body. Nevertheless, we trust in divine mercy: the one who caused you to love Italy, miserable and cast down as it is, will himself restore bodily health to you and repay you with an eternal recompense.

We have received with complete approval your statement that you had again undertaken, against your will but by imperial command, the military *roga*. [Note: [Col. 1057D] Learn what *roga* means from note k on Letter 46 of Book II.] For we know that your greatness will meet the needs of the army with a more careful and salutary provision.

As for the six *centenaria* that had been entrusted to the treasury of the Church of Ravenna, your letter states that they were borrowed by the most excellent exarch for the daily payment of the soldiers. [Note: [Col. 1057D] Some interpret *centenaria* as a hundred pounds of gold. Isidore says—and this is correct—that a *centenarium* consisted of one hundred pounds and received its name from that fact. The Greeks call it *kentenarion* (κεντηνάριον). Gussanville.]

You know why they have not yet been restored. [Note: [Col. 1058D] In the Saint-Victor, Remigius, and Vatican A manuscripts, the words “have not at all been restored” are absent. This reading is found only in this one of the Vatican codices; it is omitted in the English, Norman, Rheims, and nearly all the others.]

You have written that it seemed to our aforesaid son, the exarch, that since peace had been brought to its conclusion, Your Glory should carefully consider whether it ought in any way to be presumed or undertaken that, from the funds belonging to those regions, you should first make the *roga* for those regions. Otherwise, if the prefecture of those regions neglects to recover the money it has received, those regions may consequently suffer the danger of being deprived of soldiers.

But those to whom the money is said to have been lent ought to be compelled by the lender to repay it, so that, as they know they must, they themselves may restore the money expended in *centenaria*. And the money that cannot be touched without danger to the person disbursing it must not, once it has been withheld from those to whom it is owed, be improperly scattered among others in view of the danger that threatens us.

We are saying this neither to a man newly involved in the matter nor to one ignorant of the circumstances of the Roman regions. For it is clear to him that, if peace is not restored, then in wartime human assistance cannot prevail in these places except through the power of the divine Majesty alone.

Your greatness therefore knows the will of the imperial lords and the great care with which they provide especially for the relief of the city of Rome, as is clearly demonstrated by their gifts. But the imminent danger facing these regions and the city is entirely your concern; you must come here with the money. [Note: [Col. 1058D] The printed editions read: “The imminent danger, which is entirely your concern and that of the city, together with the money.” We have corrected the defective inversion of the words, also found in the Saint-Victor manuscript, on the basis of the cited Vatican manuscript.]

If this is neglected and something adverse happens—which we do not wish—and, in consequence, you are unable to excuse yourself in any way before God or before the lords of earthly affairs by appealing to any person, then you will have no defense. For the city of Rome, because of our sins, has been worn down by various sicknesses, so that not even those assigned to guard the walls remain fit for service.

## LETTER CXXV. TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF SALONA

He congratulates him on having made full satisfaction. He sends him the pallium and instructs him to express by his conduct what it signifies. He tells him to deal with Bishop Sabinianus, Archdeacon Honoratus, and the cleric Massianus no longer out of hatred but out of charity.

[Col. 1058C]

Gregory to Maximus, Bishop of Salona.

Having received the letters of our brother and fellow bishop Marinianus, and also learning from the return of our chartularius Castorius, we have come to know that Your Fraternity has given full satisfaction concerning the matters about which there had been uncertainty. We have offered great thanks to Almighty God, because every trace of bitter resentment arising from an evil suspicion has been torn from the depths of my heart.

For this reason I wished to release Stephen, your deacon and our common son, with the greatest speed. But frequent attacks of my illnesses compelled him to remain with me for a few days. After I began to improve even slightly, however, I immediately arranged to send him back with joy.

Accordingly, we have sent the pallium for use, according to custom, at the sacred solemnities of Mass, and we wish you to vindicate its meaning in every respect. The dignity of this garment consists in humility and justice. Therefore, let Your Fraternity hasten with your whole mind to show yourself humble in prosperity and, in adversity, whenever it occurs, upright with justice; friendly toward the good and opposed to the wicked.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] LETTER CXXV [elsewhere 130].—In all the Norman manuscripts: “Never repressing the face of anyone who speaks for the truth, and never looking upon the face of anyone against the truth.”]

Never repressing anyone who speaks for the truth; devoting yourself to works of mercy according to the strength of your means, and yet desiring to persevere even beyond the strength of your means; sympathizing with the weak; rejoicing with those who show goodwill; counting the losses of others as your own; exulting in the joys of others as though they were your own; fierce in correcting vices; soothing the minds of your listeners when encouraging virtues; maintaining judgment without anger when angry, and, in tranquility, not abandoning the severity of your censure.

This, dearest brother, is the meaning of the pallium you have received. If you carefully preserve it, you possess inwardly what you have shown yourself to have received outwardly.

[Col. 1059B] Moreover, I commend our brother and fellow bishop Sabinianus to Your Fraternity in all things, and, for the time being, let any causes between you be postponed. Let charity remain firmly established between you, so that, even if contention should arise over external matters, judgment may proceed while charity does not abandon the heart.

We also commend our common son Honoratus, the archdeacon. Concerning him, if matters are as we learned from our chartularius Castorius—that through him three archdeacons previously were compelled, after completing five years, to leave in accordance with ecclesiastical custom—we wish him to find in you the charity proper to holiness. For judgment should not be demanded in a case that he himself judged. But if this is not so, then, with every swelling of the mind suppressed and all hatred laid aside, he must be received in charity and in no way removed from the position in which he was found.

We have also entrusted to our common son Stephen, the deacon, the cleric Massianus, who had fled to us, confidently certain that, since we are sending him to Your Fraternity, you ought to show in him not hatred but the grace of your authority.

May Almighty God guard you by his protection and grant that we may act in such a way that, after the waves of this temporal life, we may arrive together with joy at eternal things. [Note: [Col. 1059D] The printed editions read, “that we may arrive together at joys”; nearly all the manuscripts compel us to depart from this reading.]

## LETTER CXXVI. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN

He instructs him not to allow Philagrius to be unjustly oppressed either by members of his own Church, by the collectors of the levy, or by the bishop of Tortona.

Gregory to Constantius, Bishop of Milan.

[Col. 1059D] Although the scourge of blindness inflicted upon Philagrius, the bearer of this letter, strongly invites Your Fraternity to preserve justice for him, nevertheless, because he wished through us to make you more ready to restore what he asserts is being wrongfully withheld from him, we have judged it appropriate to send this letter to you.

He has complained that a field together with its vineyard was irrationally seized by members of your Church. [Note: [Col. 1060D] The Colbertine and Rheims manuscripts read, “that what was taken irrationally was not restored.”]

If this is so, possession taken from him by violence ought to be restored even before judgment. Yet, because your deacon, our common son Eventius, with the consent of the aforesaid bearer, determined that he could satisfy the claim of your Church through five witnesses, Your Fraternity must not cause the aforesaid Philagrius to labor against justice. Rather, by whatever means you can, diligently investigate the truth. If it can clearly be proved, as he established here, that the matter belongs to your jurisdiction, then, for God’s sake, satisfaction must be given to him quickly, so that he may withdraw from his claim without difficulty.

Otherwise, before any contention arises, let his property be restored with your provision, [Note: [Col. 1060D] We have restored this wording from the more reliable manuscripts. Some read “what was taken,” which has the same meaning. See what we have already said about this word at Letter 55 of this indiction. Gussanville.] so that thereafter each party may retain an unimpaired understanding of its own property.

Because he believes that he has offended your feelings by departing from there without your knowledge, Your Fraternity should show him the sweetness of your charity, so that he may realize that he has thought of a priest far differently from what he ought to have done. But since, as he says, he also often desires to present himself at the thresholds of the holy Apostles, whenever he wishes to come, let him encounter no impediment and instead have your greater support in this matter. [Note: [Col. 1060D] The printed editions read, “let him be turned away by no one’s impediment, but…”]

Moreover, the bearer named above has indicated that, among the other inhabitants of the city of Genoa, a levy has been imposed and that he too is being compelled to pay it. We are astonished that one who is more deserving of mercy should be burdened in your presence. If this is so, let Your Holiness once again permit no one to demand anything from him, because it is exceedingly inhumane to afflict by an assessment one whom his blindness already burdens. If he were in great need, he ought instead to receive mercy through the assessment.

Because he also complains that his boy is being unjustly detained by the Church of Tortona, [Note: [Col. 1060D] Ptolemy writes *Dertona* as δερτῶνα, and Strabo as δερθὼν, where θ entered through the scribal error of τ; for in Stephanus, his epitomator, we read δερτὼν πόλις Λιγυρῶν, “Derton, a city of the Ligurians.” This city, now Tortona, lies between Ticinum and Genoa and is an episcopal see under the archbishop of Milan. Gussanville.] let Your Fraternity take care to write to the bishop of that city, so that, if the matter is as alleged, he may restore the boy without any dispute.

If he should perhaps reply that the matter is otherwise, then the case must be examined either before you or before arbitrators, without any excuse being offered. For the same Philagrius has reported that his daughter, together with her sons and grandsons, concerning whom, as he says, there is no dispute, followed her husband, his boy named Maurus. Consequently, it has happened that through the person whose case is disputed, others concerning whom there is no dispute are also being held.

If this is established as true, the daughter must be returned to him together with her sons and grandsons without any quarrel. Then, once the case concerning the aforesaid Maurus has been examined, it must be settled as reason dictates. If, perhaps, there is also said to be some dispute concerning his wife, let this too be brought to an end through judicial intervention, so that, while you are present there, the aforesaid bearer will not again be forced to return to us concerning the matters mentioned.

[Note: [Col. 1061C] LETTER CXXVII.—Saint Columbanus mentions letters that he had written to Saint Gregory in Letters 1 and 2. The ancient author of the Life of Saint Salaberga writes that the holy pontiff replied to them. Yet Columbanus complains in Letter 1 that Satan had once and twice prevented his letters from reaching the most holy pope. Perhaps, however, after Saint Gregory had not received the first two, he read the third, which arrived more successfully, and later sent a reply to it, even though no letter to Columbanus survives among Gregory’s letters. We judge that this letter should at least be assigned to the year 599, since Columbanus mentions it in his letter to the Gallican bishops, who assembled on his account in the following year. The marginal notes belong to R. P. Fleming, O.F.M., who first printed this letter; we have added our own notes at the foot of the columns.]

## LETTER CXXVII

(From the acts and minor works of Saint Columbanus and of other saints of ancient Scotland and Ireland, first published by Father Fleming, a Franciscan, in 1667.)

On the celebration of Easter: the cycle of Victorius is rejected and the custom of the Scots is to be followed, a custom supported by Anatolius, whom Jerome praised. He consults Saint Gregory concerning bishops ordained through simony or after having fallen during the diaconate, and concerning monks who abandon their monasteries. He greatly desires to see Saint Gregory. He praises his book *Pastoral Rule* and requests expositions of Ezekiel and the *Song of Songs*.

[Col. 1061B]

To the holy Lord, and in Christ the Father [perhaps the scribal omission of “pope”], the most beautiful ornament of the Church, the most august flower, as it were, of all Europe that is withering, the outstanding watchman, possessing, as it were, the divine theory of chastity [so the manuscript reads], I, Bargoma [so the manuscript reads], a worthless dove in Christ, send greetings.

Grace [the manuscript reads “thanks”] and peace from God our Father and Jesus Christ. [The manuscript’s wording is seriously corrupt.] Holy Father, I should like not to have to ask you, in exaggerated language, about Easter, in accordance with the passage in the Song: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deuteronomy 32:7).

For although, as a petty speaker, I may apply to you, in writing, the celebrated saying of a certain distinguished Wise Man, which he is said to have uttered when he saw some woman finely painted [the manuscript reads “some man” and *contupictam*; perhaps *comptem pictam*, “beautifully painted”]: “I do not admire the art, but I admire the face,” nevertheless, relying on the confidence inspired by your evangelical humility, I presume to write to you and to entrust to you the matter of my distress. For there is no vanity in writing when necessity compels one to write, even to great men.

What, then, do you say about Easter on the twenty-first or twenty-second day of the moon, which—as I say, with your permission—is not Easter? Surely this is regarded as a darkness by many calculators. [Note: [Col. 1062C] The word may perhaps be *calculatoribus* or *calcenteris*. Jerome gives Origen the latter surname in one of his letters to Marcella; Didymus of Alexandria was also called this earlier. Both received the name because of the multitude of books they produced.]

For I believe that your effectiveness is not unaware of how Anatolius, a man of remarkable learning, as Saint Jerome says—whose material Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, inserted in extracts in his *Ecclesiastical History*, and whom Saint Jerome highly praised in his catalogue for this very work on Easter—argues against this age of the moon.

Against the Gallican “Investigators,” perhaps so called because they explored obscure and difficult matters, he pronounced, as he says, a dreadful judgment concerning those who err about Easter, saying:

“Certainly, if the rising of the moon is delayed until the end of the two watches, which indicates the middle of the night, then it is not light that overcomes darkness but darkness that overcomes light. This is certainly not to be accepted as Easter: that any part of darkness should dominate the light, since the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection is light, and light has no communion with darkness. And if the moon rises in the third watch, there is no doubt that it has risen on the twenty-first or twenty-second day, on which it is impossible for the true Pascha to be sacrificed.”

For those who define Easter as capable of being celebrated at this age of the moon can affirm it neither on the authority of divine Scripture nor without incurring the charge of sacrilege and stubbornness and endangering souls, since they affirm that the true light can be sacrificed while some domination of darkness remains—darkness that dominates all darkness.

Moreover, we read in a book of holy doctrine: “Easter, that is, the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection, cannot be celebrated before the beginning of the sixteenth day after the vernal equinox has passed, so that the equinox does not precede it.” [Note: [Col. 1062D] Victorius, at the urging of Hilary—then archdeacon of the Roman Church and later supreme pontiff—composed his cycle, or Paschal canon, in the middle of the fifth century. The Gallican Churches first adopted it, as is evident from the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, and afterward all the Western Churches did so. Aegidius Bucherius published it and supplied it with notes. Anatolius, whom Columbanus sets against Victorius, was an Alexandrian and flourished around the year 270. Eusebius testifies that he held first place among learned men. He also wrote canons on Easter, which Bucherius likewise published.]

Victorius has transgressed this in his cycle and has thereby long introduced an error into Gaul—or, to speak more humbly, confirmed an established one. For how can both of these things stand: that the Lord’s Resurrection should be celebrated before his Passion, which is plainly absurd even to imagine; or that the seven days sanctioned by the Lord’s command in the Law, during which alone it is ordered that the Lord’s Passover be lawfully eaten—days that must be counted from the fourteenth through the twentieth—should be exceeded against right and justice?

The twenty-first or twenty-second day of the moon is outside the right order of light, since the moon then rises after midnight; and when darkness surpasses light, it is said to be unlawful to celebrate a solemnity of light.

Why, then, do you, so wise a man, whose brilliant lights of sacred intellect have been spread throughout the world from ancient times, observe a dark Easter? I confess that I am astonished that this error of Gaul has not long ago been scraped away by you, as though it were a Schyntenian growth—unless, indeed, I suppose what I can scarcely believe: that, since you have not corrected it, you approve it.

Yet your expertise can be excused in another and more honorable way, if perhaps you fear the reproach of Hermagorean innovation and are content with the authority of your predecessors, especially Pope Leo. Do not, I beg you, rely in such a question only on humility or dignity, which are often mistaken. In this problem, perhaps “a living dog is better than a dead lion” (Ecclesiastes 9:4). For a living saint can correct what was not corrected by another who was greater [perhaps: “what was corrected”].

You should know that Victorius was not accepted by our teachers and by the ancient Irish philosophers and most learned computists, who were skilled in constructing calculations; rather, he deserved laughter or pardon than authority. Therefore, direct the support of your judgment to me, a timid pilgrim more than a pedant, and do not disdain to send, at the proper time [the manuscript has *matura*], the point of your conciliatory judgment to restrain this storm surrounding us. For I am not satisfied, after reading so many authorities, with the single opinion of those bishops who say only: “We must not celebrate Easter with the Jews.” [The words “celebrate Easter” are absent from the manuscript.]

Victor, the bishop, once said this too, but none of the Easterners accepted his interpretation. Rather, while this saying lulls the thorn of Dagon, it has absorbed the owl of error.

What, I ask, is this frivolous and so unpolished opinion, supported by no testimonies of divine Scripture: “We must not celebrate Easter with the Jews”? What does it have to do with the matter? Are the rejected Jews now to be believed to celebrate Easter, seeing that they are without a temple, outside Jerusalem, and that Christ—then prefigured—was crucified by them? Or should it rightly be believed that the Passover of the fourteenth day belongs to them [perhaps *lunae Pascha*, or *luna et Pascha*], and not rather be confessed to belong to God himself, who instituted the Passover and who alone knew perfectly why the fourteenth day of the moon was chosen for the passing-over? This may perhaps shed some light for the wise and for those like you.

Those who [the manuscript reads *quo*] raise this objection, although without authority, reproach God by asking why, in his foreknowledge, he did not earlier guard against the Jews’ obstinacy, so that, if he did not want us to celebrate Easter with them, he would have commanded nine days of unleavened bread in the Law. In that way, at least, the beginning of our solemnity would not exceed the end of theirs.

For if Easter is to be celebrated on the twenty-first or twenty-second day, nine days will be counted from the fourteenth to the twenty-second: seven commanded by God and two added by human beings. But if human beings may add something on their own to a divine decree, I ask whether this might not seem contrary to the saying in Deuteronomy: “This is the word that I give you: you shall neither add to it nor take away from it” (Deuteronomy 4:2).

But in writing these things more boldly than humbly, I know that I have tied myself to a most difficult channel of presumption, which I must navigate, though I do not know how. For it is neither appropriate in place nor in order that anything should be brought against your great authority as though for discussion, or that Western letters should ridiculously trouble you—who lawfully occupy the chair of the Apostle Peter, the holder of the keys—with questions about Easter.

Yet in this matter you should consider not so much my lowliness as the many teachers, both dead and living, who have affirmed the same things I have noted; believe that you are, as it were, engaging in conversation with them. Know that, piously speaking, I am opening my mouth full of chaff, even if in a disjointed and exaggerated manner.

Therefore either excuse Victorius or condemn him. Know that, if you praise him, there will be a matter of faith between you and the aforementioned Jerome, who praised Anatolius and held the opposite view. Whoever follows one will be unable to accept the other.

Your vigilance must therefore ensure that, in testing the faith of these two aforementioned authorities, who contradict one another, there be no disagreement between you and Jerome when the judgment is proclaimed. Otherwise we shall be pressed on every side and forced to agree either with you or with him. Spare the weak in this matter, lest you display the scandal of disagreement.

I openly confess to you that anyone who comes against the authority of Saint Jerome will be regarded in the Churches of the West as a heretic or as one to be rejected; for they grant him unquestioned faith in all matters of the divine Scriptures.

But enough concerning Easter.

As for those bishops who are ordained contrary to the canons, I ask what you judge concerning them—that is, those whom you have described as Simoniacs and whom the author Gildas has described as plagues. [Note: [Col. 1063D] We have judged this wording in need of correction, since the former text read *quaestu Simoniacis*—with the margin noting that the manuscript had *Simoniacos*—and *Giltos auctor*, etc. “Gildas” seems to be the wise man who wrote concerning the destruction of Britain and the correction of the ecclesiastical order. He is also indicated below: “The author questioned Gildas about these matters.” Saint Gregory complains about sacred orders being conferred simoniacally in Gaul in nearly all the letters he wrote either to the Gallican bishops or to the Frankish kings; see Letters 106, 109, and 110 of this book.]

Should one communicate with such men? For what is more serious, many in this province are known to be of this kind. What should be done concerning others who, after being violated in the diaconate, are afterward elected to the rank of bishop? [The manuscript reads *gradare* instead of *gradum*, “rank.”]

There are people whose consciences in these matters we know. Consulting us in our lowliness, they wanted to know for certain whether after this [a phrase completing the sense is missing, perhaps “they might minister”] they could do so without danger—that is, either after purchasing a rank with solidi, or after adultery in the diaconate, though I speak of concealed adultery with dependents. [Note: [Col. 1064D] He may mean concubines, or even wives taken before attaining sacred orders, whom it was thereafter considered adulterous to continue to keep in the place of wives.] Among our teachers this is considered no less a crime.

In the third place of my questions, answer me also, I beg you, if it is not burdensome: what should be done concerning those monks who, inflamed by regard for God and by a desire for a more perfect life, act against their vows, leave the places of their first conversion, and, against the wishes of their abbots, compelled by the fervor of monks, are either released or flee into the deserts?

The author Vennianus questioned Gildas about these matters, and Gildas wrote him a most elegant reply. Nevertheless, for one eager to learn, fear continually grows greater.

All these things, and many more [the manuscript reads “beautiful things”], which the brevity of a letter does not permit, ought to have been asked in person, more humbly and more purely, unless bodily weakness and care for my fellow pilgrims had kept me confined at home [something is missing here, perhaps “had held me, desirous”] to go to you, so that I might be able to draw from that spiritual vein of the living fountain and from the living wave of knowledge flowing from heaven and leaping up into eternal life.

And if my body followed my spirit, Rome would once again endure the experience of my contempt. Just as, according to the learned narrator Hieronymus, we read that some people once came to Rome from the furthest shores of the Heulian Sea and, astonishingly, sought something beyond Rome, so I too would now seek you—not desiring Rome, with due reverence for the ashes of the saints. Although I confess that I am not a wise man but one who thirsts, I would do the same if I were free to do so.

[Note: [Col. 1065C] In Letter 103, to Paulinus, where the holy Doctor mentions how famous Titus Livius was among peoples in the most remote regions. Moreover, from the Hieronymian context it is clear that *Huelini* or *Hualini*, rather than *Heulini*, should be read. The word is Greek, from the root ὕαλος or ὕελος, “glass” or “crystal.” Thus in Revelation 4:6 the sea is called θάλασσα ὑαλίνη, “a glassy sea,” that is, a crystalline or blue sea. In Jerome we read here: “From the furthest boundaries of Spain and Gaul.”]

1040 I have read your book containing *Pastoral Rule*: brief in style, extensive in teaching, rich in mysteries, and—as I confess—a work sweeter than honey to one in need. Therefore, I beg you, give to me, who thirst, the little works that you have composed on Ezekiel with marvelous skill, as I have heard. [Col. 1066A] I have read Jerome’s six books on him, but he did not expound even the middle portion. Yet, if you deign, send us some of what you have left in the city—namely, send the exposition of the book’s final parts. [Note: [Col. 1066C] We have presented this commentary of Gregory as genuine and have ascribed it to the holy Doctor, contrary to the most recent critics, who are sufficiently refuted both by this testimony of Columbanus and by many others.] And send a brief treatment, either by another author or in your own words, of the *Song of Songs* from the passage (Song 4:6) where it says, “[lacuna] I shall go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense” [Not present in the manuscript], through the end. Or, to expose the whole obscurity of Zechariah, bring to light what is hidden, so that the blindness of the West may thank you for these things.

I ask importunately and inquire about great matters—who does not know it? But you too, possessing great things [Possibly: “you possess,” since], know that little gains less, and much more, is wisely to be lent at interest. May charity persuade you to reply; may the roughness of paper not prevent you from explaining, since the bronze was for error, while the honor due to the heart is for me to give to you. It was mine to provoke, question, and beg; yours, if you do not refuse what has been freely received, is to lend out the talent and, at Christ’s command, give the petitioner the bread of instruction.

Peace be with you and yours. I beg you, blessed pope, to pardon the boldness with which I have written; and I ask you to pray, even once, for me, the most worthless sinner, in your holy prayers to the common Lord. I consider it entirely unnecessary to commend to you my people, whom the Savior decrees must be received as walking in his name. And if you wish to reply, as I heard from your holy Candidus, that what has been strengthened by the antiquity of time cannot be changed, this is plainly an ancient error; but truth, which reproves it, is always more ancient. [Note: [Col. 1066C] This is the Candidus whom Saint Gregory sent to Gaul to administer the patrimony of the Church, and whom he commended to Brunhild and King Childebert in letters 5 and 6 of Book VI. In the following letter, 7, he is called a presbyter.]

# BOOK TEN. In the Third Indiction

[Col. 1065]

## 1041 LETTER ONE. TO ROMANUS, DEFENSOR IN SICILY

He orders that the property of the Church of Malta, taken both by Lucillus, formerly its bishop, and by Peter, his son, be restored. To Bishop Trajan he grants monks for his consolation, but reserves the matter entirely to the discretion of the diocesan bishop. He declares that what Trajan acquired while he was abbot belongs not to him but to the monastery. He permits certain other matters to be removed.

[Col. 1065D]

Gregory to Romanus, defensor of Sicily. [Note: [Col. 1065D] LETTER ONE.—In the recent edition, “servant of the servants of God,” which we did not observe in our manuscripts. In one of the Colbert manuscripts the reading is “to Chromatius, defensor.” In the old Colbert manuscript and in the Vatican manuscripts there is prefixed: “In the month of October, indiction 3.” [Col. 1066D]]

It does no good to punish the offenses of priests and to avenge crimes by deposition, if those who are deposed after their crime has been proved begin to find in the loss of honor a consolation and in their downfall an advantage.

[Col. 1066C] Our brother and fellow bishop Trajan [Note: [Col. 1066D] Concerning him, see Book IX, letter 63.] has therefore complained to us that Lucillus, formerly bishop of the island of Malta, terrified by the wickedness of his disgrace, not only took away the property of the Church—which he had not governed but rather opposed—but also retained much of what belonged to that same Church from earlier times. Although he contributed nothing toward the construction or repair of the Church, with sacrilegious intent he sought to attach everything to his own profits. Since it is extremely serious and contrary to God that his deposition should be not a punishment but an advantage, let Your Experience strictly admonish him to restore without delay whatever he took or retains from earlier times.

If, perhaps relying on the wickedness implanted in him, he wishes to deny this, since it can easily be proved, sit together with our most reverend brother and fellow bishop John of Syracuse and investigate the truth of the matter by careful inquiry. Once proof has been obtained, whatever he is shown to have taken or concealed, let him publicly restore, confounded by shame, what he secretly took without shame. You should likewise admonish Peter, the son of the aforesaid Lucillus, since he too is said to have taken much from the aforementioned Church, to restore it honorably. Otherwise he too must be brought before your judgment, so that, after a careful inquiry, the case of both men may be concluded with one result.

Moreover, our aforesaid brother Trajan asked us that four or five monks should be given to him from his monastery, which is situated in the city of Syracuse. We judged that this should by no means be denied for his consolation. For when someone goes to an unfamiliar place, if he does not have his own people whose consolation he may enjoy, his mind, afflicted by sadness, rises less readily to matters of usefulness and begins to succumb before it begins to labor.

In this matter, however, lest we seem to diminish the prerogative of the privileges of our aforesaid most reverend brother and fellow bishop John, know that this has been granted to him with the reservation that everything remains subject to the judgment of our brother and fellow bishop John.
