Since, therefore, our aforesaid brother added to his request [Note: [Col. 1067D] See the notes on letters 7 and 14 of Book IX.] that he should have permission to take away the boys whom he purchased with his own money, as well as his own books and those of his father, or other property that he has in the same monastery, reason did not allow us to deny him. But lest we appear to grant his requests indiscriminately, know that the following observance must be maintained: whatever he purchased or acquired under any title after he was removed from the office of abbot, he is to have free power to take away.

Likewise, what his father is clearly shown to have built from his own property in the monastery in which he was converted, situated in the province of Valeria, [Note: [Col. 1067D] A province of Italy so called from the Via Valeria, which led through the Asinarian Gate to the Marsi; it lay between Umbria, Campania, Picenum, the Suburbicarian district, and Latium. This province contained various peoples—the Sabines, Marsi, Aequi, and others—and had about eleven bishoprics. GUSSANVILLE.] and what he took away when he departed under pressure from the enemy and carried with him, must without any doubt be returned to him. For the right of another acquisition is lost once something has been joined to the ownership of a monastery. But whatever he acquired while he was still serving there as abbot, he must recognize as belonging not to him but to the monastery itself. Therefore, we do not permit that property of the same monastery to be taken away any further by any means. [Note: [Col. 1067D] Here we have restored an entire sentence omitted in recent editions, from the Vatican, Norman, Rheims, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

Accordingly, let Your Experience, by offering assistance and administering justice, ensure without any delay that our aforesaid brother receives the legacy which Capitulana, the foundress of the aforesaid monastery, established by her last will that he should receive each year from that monastery.

## LETTER TWO. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He is to consecrate a church for monks, without public Masses, a baptistery, or a cardinal priest.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] LETTER II [Otherwise 3].—It is found in the Victorinus manuscript, but is absent from the English, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, Colbert, and Vatican manuscripts, except for one alone, namely Codex A, in which the following letter is also found, though the highly praised manuscripts just mentioned do not contain it.]

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

We do not think that it is unknown to Your Fraternity that Roman, a man of most distinguished memory, by the disposition of his last will, assigned for construction in a house belonging to him a church situated in your city. Since, by God’s mercy, the will of the deceased is known to have been fulfilled, let Your Holiness go there with earnest haste. If it is established that no body has been buried there, let him solemnly consecrate the place, with due reverence, in honor of the saints Hermes, Sebastian, and Cyriacus, and also Pancratius, without public Masses. [Note: [Col. 1068D] “Sebastian” is not read in the aforementioned Codex A.]

No baptistery is ever to be constructed in that place, nor are you to appoint a cardinal priest. But whenever the monks residing there wish Masses to be celebrated there, let them know that a priest must be requested from Your Affection, so that no other priest may presume to do anything of this kind.

## LETTER THREE. TO FANTINUS, DEFENSOR

He is to gather Romanus’s slaves and send the fruits of their labor to the monastery established by Romanus himself.

[Col. 1068C]

Gregory to Fantinus, defensor.

Slaves belonging to Roman, a man of distinguished memory, who arranged for a monastery to be established in his house situated at Naples, are said to be living in Sicily. [Note: [Col. 1068D] LETTER III [Otherwise 4].—The title *spectabilis* was not a wandering honor that could once be bestowed on anyone at will. “Antiquity rightly assigned the honor of *spectabilis* to those worn down by the sweat of military service,” says Cassiodorus, *Variae* II.28. He discusses below in the same letter the privileges attached to this dignity, and in VII.37 gives the formula of *spectabilitas*, or the wording by which this honor was conferred.]

Since, by God’s authority, the monastery itself is known to have been established according to his will, let Your Experience hasten to assist in every way the bearers of this letter, who have been sent there to gather those slaves again, [Note: [Col. 1068D] That is, to seek out fugitive slaves and compel and gather them together again.] and, once they have been collected, with your assistance arrange for estates to be leased to them where they are to work. Whatever is produced by their labor, after reserving enough for their subsistence, let the remainder be sent each year, with the Lord’s help, under the care of Your Experience to the aforesaid monastery.

## LETTER FOUR. TO SAVINUS, REGIONAL SUBDEACON

He is to investigate with the utmost diligence the priest Sisinnius, accused of idolatry and sodomy. If there are indications of guilt, he is to place him in prison. He is also to compel him to return the deposit entrusted to him for the children of the priest Victorianus.

[Col. 1069A]

Gregory to Savinus, regional subdeacon.

Since he who burns with zeal for rectitude does not fail to know that what is often a fault in laypeople is a sacrilegious crime in those constituted in sacred orders, and with what strictness such an offense must be punished, [Note: [Col. 1069D] LETTER IV [Otherwise 5].—In the printed editions, *gravissimo errore culpa non est* (“by a very serious error it is not a fault”) appears, contrary to the Norman, Reggio, Corbie, Tours, Rheims, and other manuscripts. Saint Gregory means that a fault which is lighter in laypeople is more serious in clerics, especially when they are constituted in sacred orders. Saint Chrysostom teaches the same in *Homily 77 to the People of Antioch*: “A priest who commits the same sins as his subjects will suffer not the same punishments but much more serious ones.” Partly from Gussanville.] [Note: [Col. 1069D] In Vatican D, in addition to this reading, there is added: “a distinctive offense.”] it has been reported by the account of certain persons that Sisinnius, a priest of the city of Reggio, is—something utterly intolerable even to hear—a worshiper and cultivator of idols, to the point of daring to keep a certain idol placed in his house.

It is also reported that he is stained by the crime of sodomy, a no less abominable offense. Therefore, since the wickedness of so great a crime must be investigated and punished by strict and careful inquiry, we command you by this authority to investigate it with watchful zeal and the utmost diligence. If you can apprehend any indications of the matter, reduce him to strict custody until you report to us, so that we may deliberate how such a monstrous crime ought to be examined and punished.

Know, however, that this case will undoubtedly show what zeal and diligence you possess against the most abominable crimes. Through it you must understand that you will either be highly commended by us for your vigilance or dangerously accused of negligence. It is therefore necessary that you show yourself so watchful in this investigation that you may both gladden us by your diligence and make God favorable toward you.

We have also been informed concerning the aforesaid priest that a certain priest, Victorianus, had entrusted him with money, together with various goods or ornaments, under an authority belonging to him. [Note: [Col. 1069D] That is, with his right to reclaim his property reserved and every form of usucaption excluded. Thus Alciatus explains the authority at law 115, *On the Meaning of Words*. Gussanville. This passage varies in the manuscripts. In the Norman: “Victor, the priest, entrusted various goods or ornaments to his authority, and money.” The Rheims and Vatican D read similarly, with “ornaments of his action” substituted. The Vatican B and E read: “Victor, his fellow priest, entrusted him with various goods or ornaments of his authority.”]

When he denied the deposit, he was convicted after judgment and sentenced to return it. Since he delayed restoring what he had been condemned to restore, the man said to have made the deposit died, and his children are said to be suffering from his necessity. Your Experience must carefully investigate this matter and bring it to its conclusion, while preserving due legal procedure—provided that, if the matter is as reported, he does not retain another’s property with treacherous intent and the orphans receive what belongs to them, even though they have lost their father.

## LETTER FIVE. TO SAVINUS, SUBDEACON

He is to admonish Maria finally to fulfill her father’s will and, even against her will, pay the two ounces of the estate left both to freedmen and to the Church of Saint George.

Gregory to Savinus, subdeacon.

The bearers of this letter, Stopaulus and Marcellus, formerly freedmen of Comitiolus’s guards, [Note: [Col. 1070D] LETTER V [Otherwise 6].—In Gaul, “bodyguard”: *somatophylax*, attendant, bodyguard, household protector, *spatharius*. Gussanville.] have complained to us, asserting that the two ounces of their estate which their former master had bequeathed to his freedmen by the written page of his will have not yet been paid to them by his heir, his daughter Maria, wife of the cleric Pardus. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Thus the manuscripts and old edition read; recent editions corrupted the passage into *ab aere legaverat*, “had bequeathed from money,” followed by “his daughter Maria, wife,” and so forth. The Vatican A reads *ab haereditate*, “from the inheritance.”]

They report that, in order to delay the legacy, the same heir has used threats to make them fear for their status. Since your diligence is requested to fulfill what has been left to them, we command you by this authority to admonish the aforesaid Maria not to delay fulfilling the will of her father and testator. Let it also be your concern that they not be subjected to any expenses contrary to law.

If she tries to defend herself against payment by some excuse, you must investigate the case carefully with the holy Gospels, and then define what the order of law and justice requires and put your decision into effect, so that this complaint does not return to us again. [Note: [Col. 1070D] This was customary in many councils. Our ecclesiastical judges use another formula, invoking the name of Christ; some have considered it so necessary that without it the entire authority of the instrument collapses. I add that some have doubted whether the oath of witnesses is valid when they bring their hand back to their breast without touching the Gospels. Gussanville.]

Since we have learned that the aforesaid testator bequeathed two ounces of his estate to the Church of Saint George, where he wished to be buried, let it be your care to claim those same two ounces in every possible way for the aforesaid place, if they have not yet been paid, so that the intention of his pious will may be carried out in every respect, even against the heir’s will. Do not permit what has been reported to be delayed any further in this matter.

For it is sacrilege and contrary to the laws if anyone attempts, through the efforts of an evil will, to retain for his own advantage what has been left to venerable places. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Another reading: “for it is sacrilegious,” as in the Norman manuscript.] (Gratian, 17, question 4, chapter 4.)

## LETTER SIX. TO THE CURATOR THEODORUS

He commends the wife of the prefect John.

Gregory to Theodorus, curator. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Namely, of Ravenna; concerning him and the office of curator, see the preceding book, letter 98, note a. LETTER VI [Otherwise 7].]

Although Your Glory’s goodness does not know how to consign those once commended to you to oblivion, nevertheless, knowing that our dearest son does not find repeated requests burdensome, we do not hesitate to write what we wrote long ago.

Since our most glorious son John, prefect of the city, is known to have sent the bearer of this letter, John the most distinguished man, to bring his wife here, we greet you with paternal affection and ask that, since our most glorious son cannot remain here while separated from her, Your Glory’s sincerity provide the woman who is coming with the protection of your support. And so that, under God’s protection, she may make her journey more securely to the city of Perugia, arrange for her to be supported by military assistance, so that the aforesaid glorious man may become still more devoted to your patronage and we may return thanks to Your Sweetest Glory.

## LETTER SEVEN. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He commends the wife of the prefect John.

[Col. 1071B]

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Our most glorious son John, prefect of the city, sent there the bearer of this letter, John the most distinguished man, for the purpose of bringing his glorious wife here under God’s protection. [Note: [Col. 1071D] LETTER VII [Otherwise 8].—This title often occurs in Gregory’s letters. Today it is freely offered to anyone; formerly it was granted only to those upon whom the prince had conferred this honor. The formal wording by which it was conferred is found in *Variae* VII.38.]

We too wish her to arrive here in every respect, so that we may have our aforesaid most glorious son with us not divided but whole. Let Your Fraternity therefore take care that she encounter no obstacle in coming, and diligently assist her so that she may arrive here more quickly. Conduct yourself toward her in whatever way necessity demands, so that she may not feel the absence of her husband, and may recognize that through you we are present to her in every respect.

## LETTER EIGHT. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He is greatly distressed that Marinianus neglected to recall a nun who had again been taken away from the monastery. He urges him to do so now with the utmost diligence.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna. [Note: [Col. 1071D] LETTER VIII [Otherwise 9].—In the old Colbert manuscript and also in the Vatican D and E manuscripts, this letter is addressed to Stephen. In the Reggio manuscript, it is addressed to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, by a recent hand.]

If the complaint of the bearer of this letter, Stephen the most distinguished man, is supported by the truth, let Your Fraternity understand that we are altogether distressed that you have been so sluggish and negligent that the wickedness of the deed reached us before its correction.

He has complained that a certain utterly wicked man named Peter, prompted by the devil, had once persuaded his female relative to leave the monastery and that she had been brought back by our notary Gratiosus, after her clothing had been changed. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Vatican F: “a certain Peter,” whom we do not know.] The utterly wicked man then expelled her again from the monastery through wicked persuasion and now shamelessly keeps her with him.

As we have said, this matter has greatly distressed us because of your negligence: why has she not yet been recalled and confined in the monastery? Let consideration of your purpose and zeal for chastity now kindle you to make every effort, by whatever means you can, so that you may quickly soften by her correction the severity that we have conceived from the perpetration of so great an iniquity. We have also commanded Vitalis, the defensor, not to delay assisting you in this matter.

But since the aforesaid Peter is said to be protected by a man belonging to our son, the magnificent Philoxenus, you must act insistently with that man, with every effort and affection, so that he may have her restored without any delay. We believe he will do this at once, since he is said to be an altogether good man.

If, however, contrary to our belief, the matter should be delayed by some excuse, then he must also be publicly challenged. [Note: [Col. 1071D] Gaul: “to summon him by a public act.” Gussanville.] Let Your Fraternity report this to us, so that we may write from there to the royal city, in order that what is honorably neglected may be punished with the vengeance it deserves. [Note: [Col. 1071D] He does not immediately order him to be bound by censures. Gussanville.]

## LETTER NINE. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to pay ten pounds of gold through Maximus to Basil, bishop of Capua, on behalf of Cethegus and Flora.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Our glorious children Cethegus and Flora, husband and wife, are sending Maximus, the most distinguished man, a *palatinus* of the private treasury, to Sicily on certain business of theirs. [Note: [Col. 1071D] LETTER IX [Otherwise 10].—Some distinguish the *palatini* into those of the largitions and those of the private treasury; others seem to conflate all the *palatini* of the sacred largitions, who belonged to the count of the sacred largitions. Their duty was to urge and press matters, and so forth. Symmachus also calls them *palatini of the sacred distributions*, *Book I*, chapter 29, where they are said to extract public revenues. Gussanville. The *palatinus* of the private treasury seems to us the same as the count of the private treasury, whose dignity and duties are explained by Cassiodorus, *Book VI*, formula 8.]

They wished ten pounds of gold from the revenues of the Church’s patrimony to be given to our most reverend brother Basil, bishop of the city of Capua, who is known already to be there, for his own uses. To prevent any delay or difficulty in returning the money, they handed the amount to our beloved son Boniface, the deacon.

Therefore, since it is not fitting for us to distress our children, especially where the Church suffers no loss, we command Your Fraternity by this letter that, according to the wishes of our aforesaid children, the glorious persons Cethegus and Flora, you are to give ten pounds of gold without delay to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Basil and to Maximus, the most distinguished man, after the return of the written acknowledgment. [Note: [Col. 1072D] We have judged this to be the restoration required by two manuscripts alone, the Rheims and Vossian, although all the other manuscripts and all printed editions had previously read “to our son.” The conjecture is preferable. Who does not know that Gregory the Great never addressed bishops in this way?]

Thus, since they encounter no delay in receiving it and may usefully carry out what was entrusted to them, and the Church’s share may be reasonably secured.

## LETTER TEN. TO ROMANUS, DEFENSOR

He is not to allow Basil, a bishop occupied with secular lawsuits, to remain in Sicily for more than four days.

[Col. 1073A]

Gregory to our Romanus, defensor of Sicily.

It has been reported to us that our most reverend brother Basil, a bishop, is occupied as though he were one of the lowest persons in lawsuits and is uselessly engaged in praetorian proceedings. [Note: [Col. 1073C] LETTER X [Otherwise 11].—I do not know by what reasoning the more recent editors, rejecting this reading, which is found in the Vatican, Tours, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts and in the old printed editions, propose instead: “as though he were one of the laity, to be occupied in secular lawsuits and to serve in praetorian proceedings.” Concerning the verb *observare*, which the manuscripts have in place of *deservire*, see what was said above at Book VIII, letter 6, indiction 1. See also Book IX, letter 92.] [Note: [Col. 1073C] See Espensaeus, Book II, *Digressions on Timothy*, chapters 8 and 10, where he either says or reports much on this matter. I cite one passage from Nicephorus, Book X, chapter 13, concerning the apostate emperor, who by malicious fraud ordered clerics to perform the office and service of senators, so that in this way the religion of true piety might be abolished, in contempt of Saint Paul’s command: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs.” Saint Gregory rightly observes, moreover, that such occupations make a cleric contemptible and destroy priestly reverence. The gloss on chapter 4, distinction 88, says that this Basil served the courts by pleading before judges. A learned man adds that Bishop Basil conducted cases in the secular forum, having become from a bishop a pleader or advocate. I do not dispute it; I wonder rather from what history he drew this. If I consult the words of the letter, Basil was occupied with secular cases and served the praetoria: this applies to judges, advocates, pleaders, notaries, scribes, court messengers, lictors, and other attendants and officials of the judicial forum. Why should they not rather class Basil among advocates, legal advisers, or judges? I know that ancient historians record one bishop tending sheep in the fields, another practicing weaving, another being concerned with shipbuilding. Perhaps the glossator had encountered a bishop who was a pleader or advocate before lay judges in a court. To me Basil does not seem to have sat as judge, but rather to have been a lover of secular business, contrary to Saint Paul’s teaching and the canons. I refer to distinction 88 and cause 21, question 3, in many canons. Nor should the phrases “cases” and “to serve the praetoria” cause alarm. Let those skilled in law judge, if they know the diverse meanings of these terms. Alciatus, on Law 198, *On the Meaning of Words*: “A praetorium is an imperial residence, because the ancients called any commander of soldiers a praetor. Thus Vegetius also uses *principia* for the commander’s tent. The name *praetorium* then began to be used for the more ornate house in which the head of a household resides in the country,” and so forth. This is his statement. Certainly this sense of *praetorium* occurs everywhere in the Digest, as also in Suetonius, Tertullian, and other ancient writers. Thus Basil’s courtly habits are disapproved, and he is recalled to pastoral duties. GUSSANVILLE. That Basil exercised not the office of judge but rather that of a legal procurator may be inferred from Saint Gregory’s saying that he had thereby become contemptible and had been regarded as one of the lowest persons—something that could not at all have been said if he had performed the office of judge. Moreover, the sense of *observatio* may be gathered from following letter 28, where we read: “that the case may reach its conclusion and no delay in procedure before you may weary the parties.” Here *observatio* means a legal proceeding, French *la procédure*.]

Since this conduct makes him contemptible and destroys priestly reverence, as soon as Your Experience has received this command, compel him to return by strict enforcement, so that, while you are pressing him, he may not be allowed to remain there for five days under any pretext. If you permit him to delay there in any way, know that you will begin to be gravely culpable before us together with him. [Note: [Col. 1074D] This is not found in our manuscripts, except that in the Reggio manuscript we find written: “in the month of December, indiction 3; in the month of November, indiction 3; in the month of January, indiction 3; in the month of February, indiction 3.” Such multiple chronological notes frequently coincide in the same letters in this codex; therefore none of them seems to deserve consideration.]

Given in the month of December, indiction 3. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 36; see letter 9.)

## LETTER ELEVEN. TO GODISCALCUS, DUKE

He rebukes him for having ordered the monastery doors broken and its goods plundered in anger. The flight of the monks to the enemy is not to be imputed to the abbot. He urges him to cease opposing the monastery and the abbot and instead to offer them protection.

Gregory to Godiscalcus, duke of Campania.

The useful concern of superiors is that in which reason governs everything and fury claims nothing for itself. Power must therefore be restrained beneath reason, and nothing should be done before the agitated mind returns to tranquility. For in a time of agitation anger considers just whatever it has done.

It has therefore reached us that Your Greatness was driven by such an impulse of fury that you not only had the doors of the monastery of the holy Archangel broken but also had whatever was found there plundered. Moreover, you are said to have burned so fiercely against the abbot of that monastery that, unless he had hidden himself while your anger lasted, he would have faced no slight danger. Finally, terrified by your fearsome conduct, he has so far not dared to leave the house into which he once withdrew.

Lest you perhaps seem to have done this without cause, you charge the monk of that monastery who fled to the enemy with the offense, insofar as the matter has reached us, asserting that he fled with the abbot’s consent. If this is so, we are distressed and greatly astonished at your wisdom. For if you think it permissible that the fault of some should harm others, many people can be subjected to this accusation.

The slaves of various nobles, the clerics of many churches, the monks of different monasteries, and the dependents of many judges have often surrendered themselves to the enemy. Therefore, if this is accepted as true, the masters of slaves, the bishops of clerics, the abbots of monks, and the judges of various fugitives would all stand under guilt and accusation.

Did not, even in the days of Your Greatness, many people from the city in which you reside flee to the Lombard soldiers? Who could be found so indiscreet and foolish as to think that their wickedness should be attributed to you? Weigh these matters carefully and judge the cases of others from your own, so that you may not be led by false suspicions into opposing certain people. [Note: [Col. 1074D] LETTER XI [Otherwise 12].—This means “to oppose certain people.” The same is the sense of the expression below, “keep yourself from opposing the abbot of the aforesaid monastery and the monastery itself.” This expression often occurs in Saint Gregory in this sense, namely in *Moralia* II.51, III.52, XI.39, XVI.45, and *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 16.]

If there is someone who can say something about the abbot of the aforesaid monastery that pertains to his fault and guilt, we do not wish to neglect this but rather, together with those concerned, to investigate the case with complete strictness and diligence, so that punishment may strike the guilty or truth absolve the innocent.

But if no one can be found who will assert against him what you alone allege, we urge you, magnificent son, to refrain from opposing the abbot of the aforesaid monastery and the monastery itself. Rather, offer them protection and, for God’s sake, charity. If there is anything by which your minds have perhaps been offended, forgive it at our intercession, and, as befits Christians and prudent men, lend your assistance to them instead, so that we may return thanks to you and you may acquire before almighty God a reward for the benefits and support you have bestowed upon his servants. [Note: [Col. 1075D] The Vatican B and D and the more recent editions add: “Given in the month of February, indiction 3.” The old Colbert manuscript reads “in the month of March”; Vatican A, “in the month of December.” It is therefore clear that the month in which this letter was written is uncertain.]

## LETTER TWELVE. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He commends Abbot Fuscus and his monastery.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Although both reason and the character of your position remind Your Fraternity that protection should be given to monasteries, and especially to those placed under your authority, nevertheless, because the bearer of this letter, Abbot Fuscus, wished his monastery to be commended by us as an additional safeguard, we exhort you in these words to protect it by your holy defense, since he asserts that the monastery itself is suffering from the disturbance caused by those arriving there. [Note: [Col. 1075D] LETTER XII [Otherwise 13].—The words “of those arriving” were absent from the Victorinus manuscript and the printed editions; we have restored them from the English, Rheims, and other manuscripts.]

Do not permit anyone to burden it contrary to the order of reason, so that, while no weight of injustice oppresses it, you may be seen to have beneficially performed what belongs to a priest, and the community residing there, occupied in the praises of God, may not be subjected to any unreasonable troubles.

## LETTER THIRTEEN. TO ROMANUS, DEFENSOR

He is to assist Abbot Fuscus so that he may receive without delay what belongs to his monastery.

Gregory to Romanus, defensor.

Fuscus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Erasmus, Maximus, [Col. 1075D] and Juliana, [Note: [Col. 1075D] EPISTLE XIII [Al. 14].—In Vatican A, which almost alone contains this letter and the following one, it reads: “which is situated at Naples and was founded by Alexandra.” San Victor favors our reading.] which, as you know, was founded at Naples by Alexandra, a woman of illustrious memory, asserts that the Papyrienian estate, situated there in Sicily, together with the hospice of Saint Theodore, is held in common with the aforesaid monastery. But, so that he should not have to endure delay in dividing it with those concerned, he asks that the assistance of your Experience be present to him. Therefore, by the tenor of this instruction, we charge you to hasten to support and assist him in every way, so that the estate itself may be divided without any delay according to the appropriate shares.

But if it should perhaps be said that the possessions which are held in common here are being retained by the aforesaid monastery, this ought not to serve as an excuse, since he is also prepared to divide those possessions without difficulty. Since, moreover, the legacy said to have been left by the aforesaid Alexandra to Pompeius is, according to the report, inherited by the same hospice—which is said to have succeeded to it by hereditary right in an eight-ounce share—[Note: [Col. 1076D] In the same Saint-Victor manuscript and in the more recent editions, “let the aforesaid abbot cause it to be restored to his monastery” is read, corruptly and with loss of sense. We have therefore rightly emended the text from Vatican A and the old printed editions.] the aforesaid abbot says that it should be restored to his monastery; and let your Experience also ascertain this. If it is so, let him take care that what was left be paid out in every respect. Let your diligence therefore show itself in this matter in such a way that, with justice supporting it, the labor of the aforesaid abbot, which he undertook by coming to us, should not prove fruitless.

## EPISTLE XIV. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER

He is to arrange that the books and veils of the monastery be restored to Abbot Fuscus.

Gregory to Fantinus, defender at Naples.

Fuscus, abbot [Note: [Col. 1076D] EPISTLE XIV [Al. 15].—In San Victor and Vatican A: “of the monasteries,” namely, one which bore the title of the Holy Archangels and another which was dedicated to Saints Maximus, Erasmus, and Juliana.] of the monastery of Saint Michael the Archangel, which is called Macharis, and of Saints Maximus, Erasmus, and Juliana, asserted that Constantius, the presbyter of his cell, had, because of the circumstances of the time, migrated to Sicily and had taken with him the books and veils of his monastery. Since he declares that Constantius has died and asks that what he identifies as belonging to his cell be restored to him, let your Experience ascertain the truth; and, if this is so, arrange for everything belonging to that monastery to be restored without any delay. For it is contrary to reason that what was removed from the monastery because of the circumstances of the time, as has been said, should rightfully be separated from it. Let your Experience therefore act so that, having learned the truth, you do not at all permit the aforesaid abbot, or whoever he sends in his place, to endure useless delay there.

## EPISTLE XV. TO CLEMENTINA, PATRICIAN

He declares that he harbors no scruple of hatred or anger toward her, but wholly paternal affection. He exhorts her nobly to forgive offenses.

[Col. 1076D]

Gregory to Clementia, the patrician.

A certain abbot reported to us that it had reached the ears of Your Glory that some slanderers had announced [Col. 1077A] that we had, God forbid, some hostile [Note: [Col. 1077D] EPISTLE XV [Al. 16].—The Gauls say une pique, that is, a hostile and ill-disposed mind, as he explains below. GUSSANV.] impulse against you. If this is so, those who deceitfully fabricated this story have proved themselves double under the appearance of purity: they wished to present themselves as faithful while wickedly causing you to doubt us.

But I, glorious daughter, having long known your goodness, and especially the chastity that has accompanied you from your youth, have always held you in great veneration and affection. But lest Your Glory now suspect that my heart is otherwise disposed, I declare that I have no scruple of hatred or anger toward you; rather, know that I show you paternal affection. Yet I must not conceal one matter that has been reported to me, lest charity begin to grow weaker if what ought to be said for correction is suppressed.

[Note: [Col. 1077D] Saint Augustine says very well in Letter 236, to Maximus the Donatist: “You know that silence is harmful to me; for I do not intend to pass my time amid the windy honors of the Church, but I consider that I shall have to render an account to the chief of all shepherds for the sheep entrusted to me. If perhaps you did not wish me to write these things to you, brother, you must forgive my fear. For I greatly fear that, if I were silent and concealed the matter,” and so forth. GUSSANV.]

[Col. 1077B] It has indeed been reported to me that, whenever anyone has offended you, you retain the grievance without granting pardon. If this is true, then, because I love you as much as I grieve over this, I ask you nobly to remove this fault from yourself and not allow the enemy’s seed to grow beside the harvest of good works. Let the words of the Lord’s Prayer be recalled, and let guilt not have greater force with you than forgiveness. Let the goodness of Your Glory surpass the offense, and, by forgiving in a salutary manner, make devoted the person whom persistent harshness could make disaffected.

Leave him something of which he may be ashamed, but do not preserve something over which he may grieve. For generally a measured leniency in correction has greater power than severity in carrying out punishment; [Note: [Col. 1077D] Six English manuscripts and several others read: “because this sometimes happens.”] indeed, the former sometimes makes a person more faithful and submissive, while the latter makes him obstinate [Col. 1077C] and antagonistic.

We do not say these things, to be sure, in order to withdraw you from zeal for uprightness, but so that you may not be in small matters what you ought to be in great ones. For whenever the nature of an offense demands severity, one must act so that punishment corrects the fault, while grace is not afterward denied to those who have been corrected.

Since, then, with paternal affection advising us, we admonish you for the sake of your soul, receive these words with the charity with which they are spoken, and accept them for the benefit of Your Glory, so that your good qualities may be both more conspicuous among human beings and purer before the almighty Lord. As for us, dearest daughter, confidently rely on us in everything, as you truly may; and since we always desire to hear of your prosperity, refresh us by sending letters frequently through those who travel here.

## EPISTLE XVI. TO THE TURRIANS AND TAURIANANS

They are to obey Venerius, the visiting bishop, and choose for themselves a suitable priest.

[Col. 1078A]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1077D] EPISTLE XVI [Al. 17, indiction 6].—We have recovered this heading from two old Colbert manuscripts and from Vatican A, B, and E. In one of the Colbert manuscripts, where this heading has been erased, its place is occupied by: “to the clergy, order, and people residing at Palermo.”] to the clergy, order, and people residing at Tauriana, Turris, and Consentia.

Having learned of the death of your bishop, and so forth, as in Book XI, Letter 39, with the name changed from John to Venerius.

## EPISTLE XVII. TO THE BISHOPS VENERIUS AND STEPHANUS

He entrusts the duty of visitation in the customary form.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1078D] EPISTLE XVII [Al. 18, indiction 6].—This letter was originally addressed only to Bishop Venerius; the two Teller manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, and others add Stephanus.] to Bishops Venerius and Stephanus.

A direct report has revealed the death of Paulinus, bishop of the Church of Tauriana, and also of the bishops of the illustrious Church of Turris. Therefore we solemnly entrust to your Fraternity the care of the Church deprived of its bishop. You must discharge it in such a way that no one may presume in any manner to seize anything belonging to the advancement of the clergy, its income, adornment, services, or anything else whatsoever in the property of those Churches.

Therefore let Your Affection hasten to go to the aforesaid Churches and, by frequent exhortations, hurry to admonish their clergy and people to seek, without factional interest and in unanimous agreement, the appointment of priests who can be found worthy of so great a ministry and who will in no way be rejected by the venerable canons. Once they have been requested, let them come to us for consecration with the solemn decree confirmed by the subscriptions of all and with a letter bearing the testimony of Your Affection.

We also admonish your Fraternity not to permit anyone to be chosen from another Church, unless perhaps no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clergy of the very city in which you are carrying out the visitation—something we do not believe will happen. Above all, take care that lay persons, whatever the merit of their manner of life, do not presume to aspire to this office, and that you do not, God forbid, incur the peril of your order [Note: [Col. 1078D] At the end of the Teller manuscripts it reads: “in the month of February, indiction 3.”].

## EPISTLE XVIII. TO CLEMENTINA, PATRICIAN

She is not to detain Amandus, elected bishop by the people of Surrentum.

Gregory to Clementina, the patrician.

[Note: [Col. 1078D] EPISTLE XVIII [Al. 17].—He succeeded John, to whom Saint Gregory wrote Letter 54 of indiction 9 and also Letter 25 of indiction 11. Amandus was ordained on 22 March in the year 600, as his epitaph, which is read at Surrentum in the church of Saints Felix and Baculus, proves: “Here rests the priest of God, Amandus, bishop of the holy Church of Surrentum, who sat for seventeen years and twenty-one days. He was buried on the thirteenth day, in the month of April, indiction 5, during the reign of Our Lord Heraclius, Roman Emperor Augustus, in his seventh year. Pray for me, holy Father.” The people of Surrentum venerate Amandus as a saint.] Know that the presbyter Amandus [Note: [Col. 1078D] Or “by the people of Sorentum,” as it is read in the Regius manuscript and in most manuscripts, and below, Letter 19, “of Sorentum.”] has been elected bishop by the people of Surrentum, glorious daughter. Since we have written that he must be sent here, you should not be saddened by his absence, because one who is with you in mind is not believed to be departing.

And since the man who formerly pleased you is welcome to those seeking a shepherd, rejoice more in Christian devotion, blessing almighty God [Note: [Col. 1079D] In recent editions: “rejoice more in this devotion through Christ’s mercy.”]; and gladly take care that he come to us more quickly, so that he may benefit others. For it belongs to sincere charity to rejoice when the person one loves is called to advance [Note: [Col. 1079D] Two Colbert manuscripts and four Vatican manuscripts add: “in the month of March, indiction 3.”].

## EPISTLE XIX. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is to investigate the life of Amandus, elected bishop, and send him to Rome as soon as possible.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

After the man who had been elected to the episcopate of the city of Surrentum did not appear suitable to us, they elected Amandus, presbyter of the oratory of Saint Severinus, which is situated in the fortress of Lucullanum. Therefore we order Your Experience to make every effort to send this presbyter to us with all possible haste, setting aside every excuse, so that, with Christ’s help, the desire of those who requested him may be fulfilled, if there is nothing that prevents him.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] This is certainly correct; therefore the canons decreed that legal matters should be conducted and settled where they originated. Saint Cyprian emphasizes this in Letter 55 to Cornelius, as noted above. GUSSANV.]

Since his life and conduct can better be ascertained there, where he has lived for a long time, let it be your concern, together with our brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 1079D] Namely, Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, to whom many letters in this Register are extant.], to investigate him carefully. If there is nothing capable of obstructing his admission to the sacred order, he must be sent to us without any further delay.

But lest our glorious daughter Clementina receive this with displeasure, let Your Experience go to her and do this with her consent. If, however, she should perhaps wish to resist, Your Experience must send him here without delay, as we have said, because the dispositions of our sons must be reconciled by us in such a way that the welfare of souls must nevertheless not be impeded.

[Note: [Col. 1079D] EPISTLE XX. Al. 19.]

## EPISTLE XX. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

The monks of Surrentum are not to spend for other purposes the money received for purchasing property.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

It has reached us that the monks whom, as you know, we sent to the city of Surrentum to fulfill the wishes of the former defender Antoninus are spending the money they had received for purchasing property. Since this indicates that serious need will soon threaten them, Your Experience, instructed by this authority, must take care and arrange that they do not recklessly and improperly spend those solidi.

To make your diligence praiseworthy in this matter, search with every effort and vigilance for properties to purchase for them. By receiving sustenance from their produce, the servants of God will neither spend the solidi they received to no purpose nor be forced to suffer want of food. Hasten, therefore, to show yourself in this matter with every vigilance and complete dedication, so that your effectiveness may remove from them the danger and from us every cause for anxious concern.

## EPISTLE XXI. TO JOHN, PREFECT OF ITALY

He complains about the grain withheld from the Neapolitan charitable institution.

[Col. 1080B] Gregory [Note: [Col. 1079D] EPISTLE XXI [Al. 20].—In the Corbie, Colbert, Tours, English, and Norman manuscripts: “to John, pope.” In Vatican E and F and in the Regius manuscript: “to John PP.,” which may perhaps mean that the copyists interpreted it as “pope.” In Rheims and Vatican D it reads “to John the prefect.” In Vatican A: “to John, bishop of Naples.” In one Colbert manuscript: “to John, pope of Italy.” In the old Colbert manuscript, the first hand has noted in the margin: “He writes to John the proconsul.” Perhaps PP. signifies Pater patriae, “Father of the Country.” [Col. 1080D] It is clear that Gregory is addressing some administrator of the commonwealth, not a bishop, as is evident from the title of eminence with which he honors him.] to John, prefect of Italy.

Whatever is given to the poor, if it is weighed with careful consideration, is not a gift but a loan, because what is given is undoubtedly received back with multiplied return.

You wrote to us that we should tell Dulcitius, who acts in your place, not to dare to spend anything beyond the diatyposis [Note: [Col. 1080D] The manuscripts of England, Normandy, Corbie, Rheims, Tours, and Vatican D read: “not to dare anything beyond the diatyposis in pride or ostentation.” Vatican A: “not to dare anything concerning the ecclesiastical matter.” Vatican B: “not to dare anything concerning the increased payment.” Diatyposis is a Greek word, from διατυπῶ, “I establish”; it signifies an instruction or regulation.] And although it is praiseworthy to anticipate the future, nevertheless the caution that is not fortified by the aid of piety is altogether weak. In this concern of yours, therefore, we find something for which to grieve on your behalf.

It is reported that Your Eminence has withheld the grain allowances and customary dues of the charitable institution that are supplied at Naples [Note: [Col. 1080D] We discussed charitable institutions at Book V, Letter 28. Some manuscripts and printed editions read “that are provided.”]. This might perhaps have been less astonishing if they had not been supplied during the time of your predecessor John. If that man—whose serious conduct is known to all—did not deny these things, let Your Wisdom consider what it would mean if an evil man surpassed you in any good work.

There was no reason for you to withhold this. Even if no one had wished to charge it to your accounts, it ought not to have burdened you to spend it from your own resources as a loan, so that such piety might be a patron through your assistance, having been a minister in the work [Note: [Col. 1080D] We believe that *precatio* (“a plea” or “petition”) entered corruptly into some manuscripts and printed editions, as it is read in manuscripts B, D, F, and the Vatican manuscripts.].

Your Eminence must therefore inspect this matter with the power you possess and should show your generosity more clearly by ensuring that what was not taken away by his predecessors [Note: [Col. 1080D] Recent editions, with no better sense: “what was not taken away by his successors.”] may continue to be supplied as usual [Note: [Col. 1080D] Others read *sollicite*, “carefully,” as do two Vatican manuscripts and several others.], so that you may encounter no adversity in those things which you do according to the Lord’s command; and so that the administration of this office may secure praise for you before human beings and provide a reward before almighty God.

[Note: [Col. 1081D] We have not read this in any manuscripts.]

Given in the month of April, indiction 3.

## EPISTLE XXII. TO LEO, BISHOP OF CATANIA

He is to protect the monastery of Saint Vitus from certain people’s harassment; he is to correct the monks joined to women with suitable discipline.

Gregory to Leo, bishop of Catania.

Martianus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Vitus, which is situated on Mount Etna [Note: [Col. 1081D] Mount Etna, commonly called Monte Gibello, the largest and best-known mountain in Sicily because of the fires it emits, is situated about fifteen Roman miles from the city of Catania. GUSSANV.], came to us, he says, with the consent of the congregation of that monastery and complained that the monastery itself was suffering many harassments and injuries from certain people.

Among these, something also moved us with the greatest indignation: [Col. 1081B] it has become so evident that the monastery itself is trampled upon and despised that even the monks living there are permitted, without fear, to join themselves to women. If this is so, you yourself can judge how serious a sin this is before God and how great a fault before human beings for your Fraternity, since you cannot defend yourself with any excuse.

Either you did not know that these things were happening, in which case you are severely accused of negligence; or you recognized that it had happened, in which case you appear to deserve even greater indignation for not having punished so great a crime with the strictest vengeance.

Therefore, by this letter, we admonish your Fraternity to hasten to investigate the matter with complete vigilance. If it finds that such iniquity has been perpetrated by certain people, let it diligently correct the crime of this perversity with suitable discipline [Col. 1081C], so that it may both appease God and show others the discipline of custody, lest anything similar be committed thereafter.

As for the harassments suffered by the aforesaid monastery, and the things said to have been seized from it, let Your Holiness ascertain the facts and show yourself in its protection to the extent that justice requires, so that it may in no respect be unduly burdened contrary to equity.

We wish the precept of our predecessor Pelagius, of blessed memory, addressed to Elpidius, your predecessor—under whose name we have caused copies to be written—to be observed without any opposition [Note: [Col. 1081D] In all copies of Saint Gregory’s letters, *Lapidium* is read mistakenly; but in the letter of Pelagius II, which is discussed here, the name is *Elpidius*. Thus also in Anselm of Lucca, *Collection of Canons*, Book VI, chapter 49, and in Gratian, *Decretum*, causa 8, question 3, chapter *Talia*. Rocchus Pirrus, who wrote specifically about all the bishops of Sicily, likewise says this about Leo when discussing the bishops of Catania: “Leo of Catania succeeded Elpidius, concerning whom Gregory wrote Letter 21 of Book VIII, now Letter 22 of Book X.” GUSSANV. The Regius manuscript, which Gussanville evidently did not consult, supports our reading and has [Col. 1082D] “to Elpidius.” In one Regius manuscript this letter is preceded by “in the month of February, indiction 7,” which must be regarded as an error. This letter is preserved in very few manuscripts; we have found it only in Vatican A and one Regius manuscript.].

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO ADRIAN, NOTARY OF SICILY

He is also to act both so that the crime of the aforesaid monks is punished and so that no one seizes their property.

[Col. 1081D] Gregory to Adrian, notary of Sicily.

[Col. 1082A] A wholly detestable and abominable matter has reached us, and we wonder why, if it is true, you have not learned of it. Martianus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Vitus, which is situated on Mount Etna, came to us and, presenting a petition, complained among other things that the monks of that monastery were living so perversely and wickedly that they dared to associate with women—which it is sacrilegious even to say.

Since we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Leo about this, instructing him, after investigating the truth, to correct it with the strictest severity if he finds the report true [Note: [Col. 1082D] EPISTLE XXIII [Al. 22].—Vatican A reads: “let him do this.” Apart from this codex, we have found this letter in no other manuscript except one Regius manuscript.], it is also necessary that Your Experience show itself in this matter wholly diligent in investigating the truth and punishing so great a crime, so that nothing may appear to be done either leniently or negligently.

In the other interests of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1082B], provide your assistance to the extent that equity requires, so that, if anything has been seized from it, as is said, it may be restored according to justice, and so that no injury may thereafter in any way arise there against the fear of God and the order of the laws.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He rebukes his negligence toward the monasteries. He laments the flight of Mauricius and other monks. He forbids monks to be tonsured in the future unless they have been tested for two years. Soldiers are not to be received into monasteries without his own consent.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Since your Fraternity shows too little diligence toward the monasteries subject to you, it both incurs the blame of criticism itself and causes us to grieve over your leniency [Note: [Col. 1082D] Recent editions read: “over your indolence and fickleness.” These words might certainly seem to have been spoken more harshly against the bishop. But they are entirely absent from the better manuscripts, namely, the Norman, Colbert, Regius, Corbie, and Rheims manuscripts. One of the Vatican manuscripts reads: “grieves over your indolence.”].

It has reached us that a certain Mauricius, who recently entered religious life in the monastery of Barbacianus, has fled from that monastery, taking other monks with him. In this matter the aforesaid Barbacianus is severely accused by his own precipitous action, since he rashly tonsured a secular man who had not previously been tested.

Did we not write to you that you should first test him and then, if he were suitable, make him abbot? [Note: [Col. 1082D] This refers to Letter 91 of the preceding book, addressed to the same Fortunatus.] Therefore, be diligent now regarding the man whom you have chosen. For when he sins, you sin, if he begins to conduct himself in such a way as to show himself unworthy of governing the brothers.

Moreover, let your Fraternity strictly forbid all monasteries [Col. 1082D] to tonsure in any way those whom they have received for conversion [Col. 1083A] before they complete two years in the religious life [Note: [Col. 1083D] From this passage someone might perhaps infer that the monastery governed by Barbacianus was not subject to the Rule of Saint Benedict, since that Rule allows novices to be admitted to profession after a year of probation. Although we do not now insist that the Benedictine Rule was observed in this monastery, the extension of the probationary period to two years in no way proves the contrary position. See what we have said on this subject in Book I of *The Life of Saint Gregory*, chapter 3, at the end.]. During this period, let their life and character be carefully tested, lest any of them either be dissatisfied with what he chose or fail to regard as binding what he selected.

For if it is a serious matter to associate untested people with the service of human beings, who could say how much more serious it is to attach those who have not been approved to the service of God? [Note: [Col. 1083D] See Book VIII, Letter 5, formerly Letter 11 of Book VII, indiction 1.]

But if a soldier wishes to convert, no one is to presume to receive him by any means without our consent before the matter has been reported to us. If this is not carefully observed, know that all the fault of your subjects will inexcusably rebound upon you, since you show by your actions that you are insufficiently diligent toward them [Note: [Col. 1083D] Vatican A, B, and E and the old Colbert manuscript read: “in the month of April, indiction 3.” Another Colbert manuscript reads: “in the month of May, indiction 3.”].

## EPISTLE XXV. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He is to restore the gates to Theodorus and the aqueduct to Rusticus at last. He may afterward bring a case against them if he wishes.

[Col. 1083B]

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

If you had wished to pay careful attention to the sequence of our letters [Note: [Col. 1083D] He refers to Letter 104 of the preceding book, formerly Letter 109.], you ought either to have restored voluntarily what you took or at least to have sent a properly authorized representative [Note: [Col. 1083D] San Victor and Vatican A, which almost alone contain this letter, read *personam instructam*, “an authorized representative,” as also below [Col. 1084D].] in the matter, according to our admonition.

While you try in some way to excuse yourself, asserting that, in what the opposing party carried out against your Fraternity, you became involved not voluntarily but because you were constrained by great conspiracies, you delayed to understand what we wrote. You indicated that the magnificent men Faustus and Dominicus had been sent not by you but by certain other associates of yours [Note: [Col. 1084D] “Your sons,” in the same manuscripts.], and thereby arranged that, while others litigated, you yourself could retain what you had taken.

But when the other party learned the text of your letter, it began to press us with repeated representations that what you had taken should be returned, saying that, if the aforesaid magnificent men wished to bring any action against it in their own name or that of others, it was ready to respond.

Since this did not appear to us to depart from the order of reason, especially after you had neglected, despite our admonition, to send an authorized representative to present the case, we therefore exhort your Fraternity, as soon as you receive this letter, to restore without any dispute the gates to Theodorus, a magnificent man and *maior* of the people, and the aqueduct to Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank and *senior* [Col. 1084A]. Do not insert any delay or excuse in this matter, lest you incur the blame of indiscretion by thinking that what you ought to have done voluntarily should, after being admonished, be deferred for any reason.

Once these matters have been restored to the aforesaid men, you shall be free, if you later wish to bring any case against them here before us. But if it is not you yourself, but your sons, as you assert, who complain that they have a case for which they ought to summon them before a public court, they shall be free to bring the matter of their case against them to a legal conclusion in whatever place they choose.

## EPISTLE XXVI. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He is to exhort John the *palatinus* neither to harass the soap-makers nor to favor those among them who withdraw from a pact confirmed by oath. If John does not heed the exhortation, the authority of the prefect is to be brought to bear.

[Col. 1084B]

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Augustinus, the bearer of this letter, who said that he had been sent as representative of the remaining soap-makers of your city, complained to us that John, a man of illustrious rank and *palatinus*, is needlessly afflicting many of them with hardships [Note: [Col. 1084D] Letter XXVI [Al. 27].—In the Rheims manuscript, with the agreement of Vatican D, the text continues: “and wished many new persons to be joined to their trade, so that whatever benefit might arise from his admission.” This shows that artisans had already at that time formed guilds in large cities. Lampridius attributes the establishment of those guilds to Alexander Severus: “He established,” he says in his *Life of Alexander*, “corporations of all the wine-dealers, bean-dealers, shoemakers, and indeed of all trades; he gave them defenders from among themselves and ordered what matters belonged to which judges.” From this letter one may infer that John the *palatinus* was the defender of the soap-makers.], and is trying to impose many new measures prejudicial to their guild.

Finally, as he says, John is compelling them to promise him that, if anyone wishes to join their trade, whatever profit comes from his admission should benefit him. He also adds that, according to the ancient custom, a pact concerning certain reasonable regulations of their trade was drawn up by common consent with a penalty attached, and was confirmed by the intervention of an oath. Now some of his associates, relying on his protection, wish to withdraw from it [Col. 1084C], and he wishes to extend protection to those who want to act in this way, so that—which is a serious thing to say—they may have greater confidence in his protection than fear of the penalty [Note: [Col. 1084D] Vatican A reads: “or fear of a false oath.”] or of the oath they swore.

If the matter is as reported, then, since his own conduct is also opposed to him—for by defending another’s sin he has made himself a participant in it—your Fraternity should address him with paternal exhortation, so that he may restrain himself from such conduct, impose nothing prejudicial upon them, and not afflict them with any losses contrary to reason.

It must likewise be ensured that the pact, where oaths have been sworn, is preserved, and that he does not seek temporal gains by violating it at the cost of his soul [Note: [Col. 1085D] Vatican A reads: “let them not seek”; and below: “let them incur”; shortly afterward: “let them not obtain.”], lest he incur the crime of perjury and fail to obtain the advantages he wickedly desired.

If—and we do not believe this will happen—you see that the aforesaid John, a man of illustrious rank, is delaying to heed your admonition, speak firmly with our most eminent son, the prefect, so that he himself may reasonably arrange for this to be corrected in whatever manner he foresees, as we have caused to be said at present. Thus, those who have sought the support of our protection will not be unjustly oppressed by someone’s will, and he will recognize that he has been restrained from an unbecoming action for the greater benefit of his soul.

[Note: [Col. 1085D] This is how it is read in the Vatican manuscript, except in Codices A and D; it is omitted in the other manuscripts and in the old edition.]

Given in the month of May, indiction 3.

## EPISTLE XXVII. TO ZITTANUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERY

He acknowledges that taxes must also be paid by religious persons.

[Col. 1085B]

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1085D] EPISTLE XXVII [Al. 28].—The old printed editions have “to Zizasimas the soldier.” Vatican A: “to Zizasimas, master of the soldiery.” Recent editions: “to Zittanus Zizazima, master of the soldiery.” In all our manuscripts except Vatican A, “to Zittanus” or “to Zitanus, master of the soldiery,” or “of the army” is read.] to Zittanus, master of the soldiery.

I acknowledge that I have received your letters written in Greek, in which you say that certain religious establishments [Note: [Col. 1085D] That is, “to pay”; the debtor “answers” when he pays. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book XVI, Letter 2: “It often happens that those who owe do not answer at the proper time.” In Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*: “to answer to another master.” Jerome is more relevant in Letter 11: “Let them answer; let them pay the taxes.” And in the preceding letter: “Who will answer for the taxes on the estates?” GUSSANV.] disdain to answer to the public law concerning the things that pertain to them.

This has caused me great sorrow, because it is characteristic of our state not only to inflict no injuries but also to bear injuries with equanimity—unless perhaps we are reasonably compelled to defend the property of the poor, lest we be found guilty before almighty God.

Therefore I have sent Your Glory what I wrote to Fantinus, the defender, so that he may compel all religious persons in the region of Palermo to appear before the appointed judges and give an account of their actions [Col. 1085C]. May almighty God grant you an abundance of heavenly mercy, so that in everything you do you may serve his grace.

[Note: [Col. 1085D] Three Vatican manuscripts, A, B, and E, and the Colbert manuscripts assign this date to the written letter.]

In the month of May, indiction 3.

## EPISTLE XXVIII. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER

He is to decide by his own judgment the cases between Sabinianus and Bishop Theodorus, both concerning expenses for guests and concerning other matters.

Gregory to Fantinus, the defender.

Sabinianus, a most distinguished man and bearer of this letter, informed us that a custom had formerly prevailed there: whenever travelers arrived from different places, the citizens of that same city [Note: [Col. 1086D] EPISTLE XXVIII [Al. 29].—That the care of guests rests upon the faithful, and especially upon bishops, is more evident than to require proof. Nevertheless, as piety grew cold, this charitable duty ceased—although the Church tried to revive it through various decrees of councils—and she did not succeed. Indeed, goods faithfully bequeathed by the faithful for this purpose were diverted elsewhere, for just causes, as they say. See Espensaeus, *Book II of the Digressions on Timothy*, chapter 1, where he collects much material concerning the hospitality of bishops and clergy. GUSSANV.] would meet the expenses from their own resources. Since they complained that this burden afflicted them, they had agreed on the matter with Theodore, formerly bishop of Lilybaeum [Col. 1086A], that fixed portions of their property should be entered in his church by way of donation, and that he would undertake this responsibility; once they had been relieved of anxiety, he himself would distribute from the Church whatever was necessary. He further stated that during the thirteenth and first indictions, while he held the office of defender of the aforesaid city, and while the bishop was absent, he had paid from his own resources what could have been supplied by the Church.

Since he requests that what he spent be restored to him, we therefore instruct Your Experience to make every effort to bring our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Decius to the point that either he settle the matter peacefully with him, if the facts are as alleged, or, if he believes that he can defend himself by some argument against restoring the expenses, [Note: [Col. 1086D] Victorinus, Remigius, and Vaticanus A, in which this letter is found almost exclusively, read *in judicio tuo partes assistant* (“let the parties appear before your court”).] appear before your tribunal. After investigating the truth with the greatest diligence, decide without delay whatever the order of equity recommends, so that the case may reach a reasonable conclusion and neither party be wearied before you by delay in the proceedings [Note: [Col. 1086D] This refers to forensic procedure, in French *la procédure*, which, when prolonged by the quibbles and evil practices of litigants or even judges, wears down the parties and reduces them to poverty.].

But if he considers the donations mentioned above burdensome to his church and perhaps wishes to return them to the donors, then, if any of those who receive them are clergy, they too should be warned by you either to pay according to their respective portions what they had been accustomed to contribute, or, if they wish to raise objections, the disputes between the parties must necessarily be resolved by your investigation, so that neither party may complain that it has suffered prejudice without having been heard. As for the other cases which the aforesaid bearer declares that he presently has with the aforementioned most reverend man, our brother, we likewise wish them to be decided by your judgment, with the holy Gospels placed between you.

## EPISTLE XXIX. TO CONSTANTIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN

That the still-doubtful case of Bishop Pompeius cannot yet be brought to a definitive conclusion.

[Col. 1086C]

Gregory to Constantius, bishop of Milan.

Having reread your letters, which you sent to us through Marianus, the bearer of this letter [Note: [Col. 1086D] EPISTLE XXIX [Al. 30].—Norman and two Vatican manuscripts read *Marinianum*.], we wrote back that your concern had been pleasing to us, since you had not tolerated concealing what had reached you concerning our brother and fellow bishop Pompeius, who must still be so named by us. But if your precision in examining the matter had matched your diligence in seeking information, nothing concerning what was said about him would have remained ambiguous [Col. 1087A]. It would have become clear whether it was true or fabricated [Note: [Col. 1087D] We restore the text chiefly on the authority of the Norman manuscripts. The old edition reads *an esse compositum potuisset, jam contra*, etc. The recent editions read *an esse compositum sciri potuisset; jam*, etc.; in either reading the sense is sought in vain. Here *compositum* means “fabricated” or “invented.”], since, as we have learned, a similar inquiry had earlier been raised against him in Sicily before our brother of revered memory, Bishop Maximianus. But because his case was investigated with exceptionally careful scrutiny, the man who had been accused of the crime was found innocent.

Now, therefore, since the allegations made against him were not investigated with the strictness that was required, and since the proceedings conducted on that account before Your Fraternity are shown to be sufficient neither for condemning nor for acquitting him, this is no trivial matter to be decided carelessly or in passing. For [Gratian, Part II, Question 3, chapter 74] it is exceedingly serious and improper that a definite judgment should be pronounced in a doubtful matter. These proceedings could indeed have been adequate for a decision [Col. 1087B] if the accused’s confession had followed them—provided, however, that the rigor of the examination had drawn that confession from hidden truth, rather than violent affliction having extorted it; for such treatment often compels even the innocent to confess themselves guilty.

Since the aforesaid bishop, as is reported, says that he was tortured in custody and burned with hunger, you must determine, if this is so, whether it is harmful if a confession was extorted in such a manner. When such cases receive judgment and an appeal is made to the Apostolic See, is not the person being judged also present, and is not the truth sought with the utmost strictness and from every side, so that it may then be decided whether the judgment ought to stand? Moreover, if the aforesaid bishop wishes to appeal to the Apostolic See, his case must be examined inwardly and with every care.

Therefore, since the man himself is absent and the proceedings that you sent to us, as we have said, do not appear adequately to satisfy us, we neither can nor ought rashly to decide anything concerning the bishop, lest, God forbid, we be found blameworthy in matters in which we have the lawful authority to reconsider the judgments of others.

As for what has been reported to you concerning the Alamanni, we are situated even farther away than you are. We have no doubt that it is untrue. Nevertheless, Your Fraternity did well to write for our information what you had heard [Note: [Col. 1087D] In recent editions the letter ends: “Given in the month of June, indiction 3,” but this does not occur in any of the manuscripts known to us.]. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 28.)

[Note: [Col. 1087] [[Col. 1087] This note appears at the foot of column 0188, but the callout number was not printed in the text.] EPISTLE XXX. Al. 9, indiction 5.]

## EPISTLE XXX. TO CASTORIUS, THE NOTARY

Again he instructs him to do what is just concerning the property said to have been granted to the monastery.

[Col. 1087D]

Gregory to Castorius, the notary.

You remember that we recently instructed Your Experience that, concerning the property said to have been granted by way of a gift to the monastery of Saints Mark, Marcellinus, and Felicula, situated at Ravenna, you ought to do what is just, since you know the case well [Col. 1088A]. For this reason we have once again thought it necessary to admonish you by our command, so that you may remain watchful and attentive in the matter itself.

If you ascertain that it was manifestly donated and that our Church has nothing which the parties can bring against it, do not create any obstacle preventing the monastery from retaining the property. But if, because—as we have said—you know the case well, you have something that can justly be alleged on behalf of the Church, you and the other party must submit to the judgment of chosen judges, so that both the truth may be discovered and whatever the order of equity recommends may be decided.

## EPISTLE XXXI. TO LIBERTINUS, FORMER PRAETOR

He encourages him to endure adversity patiently and willingly to accept clothing for the use of his household.

[Col. 1088B]

Gregory to Libertinus, former praetor [Note: [Col. 1088D] EPISTLE XXXI.—Thus the Norman, English, Colbertine, Rheims, Regius, and Vatican manuscripts read. Vatican D, however, has *praetori* (“to the praetor”). Nowhere do we find *expraefecto* (“former prefect”), as in the printed editions.].

We are not unaware of how greatly the distress of this world weighs upon you. But since, for those placed in the midst of profound tribulation, the only consolation is the mercy of the Creator, place your hope in him and turn your whole mind toward him. He both justly permits whomever he wishes to be afflicted and mercifully frees the one who trusts in him.

Give thanks to him, then, and patiently endure whatever has been inflicted upon you. For it belongs to a sound mind to bless God not only in prosperity but also to praise him in adversity. Let no murmuring against God creep into your heart amid the things you suffer, since it is unknown for what purpose our Creator is doing this.

Perhaps, noble son, while placed in prosperity you offended him in some way, and therefore he wishes to cleanse you by a merciful bitterness [Col. 1088C]. For this reason, let neither temporal affliction break you nor the loss of possessions torment you. If, by giving thanks in adversity, you make God favorably disposed toward you through your patience, then what has been lost will be restored in abundance, and, beyond this, eternal joys will be granted.

I ask you not to regard as an insult [Note: [Col. 1088D] The printed editions read “twenty annual garments,” against the English, Norman, Vatican, and other manuscripts.] the fact that we have written that twenty garments should be provided for your children through the Roman defender. For although what is offered from the possessions of the blessed apostle Peter may be small, it must always be received as a great blessing, since it will enable him to provide you with greater things here and to grant you eternal benefits before almighty God.

[Note: [Col. 1088D] Thus it is read in two Colbertine manuscripts and in Vatican A, B, D, and E.]

Given in the month of June, indiction 3. (See below, Epistle 51. Compare John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 55.)

## EPISTLE XXXII. TO SECUNDINUS, BISHOP OF TAUROMENIUM

He urges more lenient treatment of Leo’s wife, who, after leaving her husband because of suspicion of adultery and putting on religious clothing, had returned to him without consulting Secundinus.

[Col. 1088D]

Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium.

The bearer of this letter, Leo the *Chartarius*, came to us and stated that he himself had in no way been guilty toward his wife, who had left him because of the charge of fornication—which, he said, had stirred her all the more deeply [Note: [Col. 1089C] EPISTLE XXXII.—Vatican D and the Rheims manuscript read *quo eum vehementius stimulatum*, “by which he said that he had been more vehemently stirred,” etc.]—and for that reason had put on religious clothing. He said that, when Your Fraternity—whom we had entrusted with the investigation of this matter nearly three years earlier—made inquiries, it had not at all become clear that he had fallen into the guilt of fornication after entering into marriage.

He further stated that he had given his wife the strictest oaths that he was innocent in the matter about which suspicion had continued to trouble her, and that for this reason she had returned to him of her own accord.

But since he claims that Your Fraternity deprived her and her household of communion for this one reason alone: that she had secretly returned to him, putting you aside [Col. 1089B], we wish his household to receive holy communion, and we do not want the woman’s fault to keep her household under the punishment of this affliction for a long time.

As for the woman herself—that is, the wife of the aforesaid bearer—you must observe the following. If it has been clearly established that she could bring no charge against her husband, and, moreover, that her suspicion was removed by the oath which, as we have been informed, he gave, and that she thereafter returned to him of her own accord, then the severity of the judgment must also be moderated in her case, so that she may not remain deprived of communion for much longer.

But if the truth is perhaps otherwise than it has been represented to us, let the careful report of Your Fraternity instruct us, so that through our letters sent again and forth we may learn what ought to be done.

[Note: [Col. 1089D] Concerning separation on account of fornication, many theologians have debated the matter both under the old and the new law, especially in connection with Matthew 5, “except for the cause of fornication,” and Matthew 19, “unless on account of fornication.” Separation is permitted by one’s own authority with respect to the marriage bed, but not with respect to cohabitation. See *Cause* 23, Question 2, chapters 3 and 4; *Cause* 10, from the First Council of Toledo; and chapters 3, 4, and 5, *On Divorces*. Thus the woman in question had separated improperly, had improperly put on religious clothing, and had improperly returned to her husband without consulting the bishop to whom the investigation of the case had been entrusted. Nevertheless, I do not deny that the bishop rashly inflicted so severe a penalty. GUSSANV.]

## EPISTLE XXXIII. TO SECUNDINUS, BISHOP

If Bishop Dulcinus really left six ounces of his property to the Church of Locri and six to the monastery of Saint Christopher, he must not permit the said monastery to be troubled any further.

[Col. 1089C]

Gregory to Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium.

We have received the letter of Your Fraternity, in which you stated that our most reverend brother Marcianus, bishop of the city of Locri, had informed us differently concerning the case of the Church against the monastery of Saint Christopher, which is situated in your diocese—not with any intention of deceiving us, but because his clergy had not carefully instructed him concerning the truth of the matter [Col. 1090A].

Since you write that Dulcinus, his predecessor, had testified to nothing concerning the property of his Church, but had composed a document concerning his own possessions, especially those which had been bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery through the offerings of the faithful [Note: [Col. 1089D] EPISTLE XXXIII.—See above, Book IV, Epistle 8.], and had left six ounces to the Church and six to the same monastery by hereditary right, it is necessary that, if you remember that this is so not merely as an opinion but as an absolute fact, you permit no trouble to be inflicted upon the aforesaid monastery.

This is especially so since you testify that, in the time of Bishop Maximianus of revered memory, you and our brother and fellow bishop Ruffinus heard and decided the same case by his delegation and authorization, so that whatever could be found was divided between the parties, and whatever belonged to the Church [Col. 1090B] was returned internally [Note: [Col. 1089D] Thus Saint Victor’s manuscript and the edition read. Vatican A, apart from which and the Victorine manuscript cited shortly afterward only a few codices contain this letter, reads *intrinsecus redderetur* (“was to be returned internally”).].
