We therefore wish both parties to remain silent, and the decisions established by Your Fraternity together with the aforementioned former bishop Ruffinus to remain undisturbed, so that neither the Church’s party may again unjustly raise a claim nor the monastery, especially after your decision, appear irrationally to endure a dispute.

## EPISTLE XXXIV. TO ECCLESIUS, BISHOP OF CHIUSI

He is to investigate carefully John the Deacon, elected bishop by the people of Bagnoregio.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1089D] EPISTLE XXXIV.—The printed editions read *Eulogio*, despite all the manuscripts we consulted—five Vatican, four Colbertine, seven Norman, Turon, Rheims, and Regius—which read *Ecclesio*.] to Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi [Note: [Col. 1090C] Chiusi, commonly called Chiusi, is a city of Etruria on a hill beside the Clanis River, commonly called the Chiana. It is still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Siena. GUSSANV.].

Our glorious son Aufridus sent us a letter stating that, in the fortress of Bagnoregio [Note: [Col. 1090D] Otherwise *Balneoregium*, commonly Bagnarea, a city of Etruria and of the territory of Orvieto, commonly Orvietan, under the dominion of the pope; it is still an episcopal see immediately subject to the Roman pontiff. GUSSANV.], he and the inhabitants of that place had chosen John [Col. 1090C], a deacon, for themselves to be ordained bishop; Aufridus testified that his life was wholly good.

But since they do not know what is canonical, and we do not dare rashly to lay hands upon those whose qualifications are untested or unknown, Your Fraternity must diligently and vigilantly investigate his life and conduct by every means available. If there is nothing that can canonically stand in his way, it must also be determined whether he has shown zeal in the work of God or knows the psalms. [Note: [Col. 1090D] This matter was also discussed above, Book V, Epistle 48.]

If he proves to be such a man, send him to us with a letter testifying to his character. If he proves otherwise, inform us likewise by your letters, and exhort the inhabitants of that place [Col. 1091A], as we also wrote to our son Aufridus mentioned above, to choose another man who, by God’s grace, may be found suitable for this office [Note: [Col. 1091D] Recent editions add: “Given in the month of July, indiction 3.” In the manuscripts this chronological notice belongs to the following epistle.].

[Note: [Col. 1090D] We frequently read of deacons being promoted to the episcopate. See above, Book III, Epistles 29, 30, 31, 40, and 47. In the *Life of Saint Basil*, written by the very learned D. Hermant, Book II, chapter 20, it is observed that in that age neither was it prescribed by any canon nor established by custom that one should reach the episcopate through each successive rank. Men served for several years among the readers. From there they were promoted either to the administration of the diaconate or to the dignity of the presbyterate, and from either order they were then made high priests. Morinus agrees, *On Sacred Ordinations*, part III, exercise 3, chapter 2. Thomassinus disagrees, part I, Book II, chapter 36, numbers 11 and following.]

## EPISTLE XXXV. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He explains why he did not reply sooner, blaming his two-year illness on gout. The Palestinian monks who asked about the error of the Agnoites went not to Rome but to Constantinople. He had written to Anatolius concerning the Agnoites from the Latin Fathers the same things that Eulogius had written to him from the Greek Fathers.

Gregory to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria.

A year having passed, I received the most gracious letter of Your Holiness, to which, because of the severity of my illness, I have until now been unable to reply. For, behold [Note: [Col. 1091D] EPISTLE XXXV.—See Epistle 123 of Book IX, indiction 2. Vatican B reads *plene* (“fully”) instead of *pene* (“almost”).], nearly two years have now passed during which I have been confined to my bed and afflicted by such severe pains of gout that scarcely even on feast days can I rise for as much as three hours to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass [Note: [Col. 1091D] Thus the Regius, Norman, and other manuscripts read, and we have followed them, although this manner of expression seems unusual to us: *surgere missas celebrare*, “to rise and celebrate Mass,” instead of *surgere ad missas celebrandas*, “to rise to celebrate Mass.” Below we have restored *depellor* (“I am driven back”) in place of *compellor* (“I am compelled”), following the same manuscripts.].

Immediately afterward I am driven back to bed by severe pain, so that I can endure my torment while interrupting it with groans. At times this pain is moderate, at times excessive. Yet it is neither so moderate that it departs nor so excessive that it kills. Thus I, who am daily in death, am daily driven back from death. Nor is this surprising, since, as a grievous sinner, I am held for a long time enclosed in the prison of such corruption.

Therefore I am compelled to cry out: “Lead my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Psalm 141:8). But since I have not yet deserved to obtain this through my own prayers, I ask that the prayer of Your Holiness offer me the assistance of your intercession and set me free from the burden of sin and corruption [Col. 1091C], restoring me to that freedom of the glory of the children of God which you know so well.

Your most gentle and ever-honored Blessedness wrote to me that our common son, the deacon Anatolius, had written to you from the imperial city of Constantinople that certain monks from the region of Jerusalem had come to me to ask something concerning the error of the Agnoites [Note: [Col. 1091D] That is, they said that Christ, as a human being, did not know certain things. This error arose around the middle of the sixth century. Saint Gregory discusses it more fully in Epistle 42, now numbered 39. Saint John of Damascus, in his *Book on Heresies*, writes: “The Agnoites, who are called followers of Themistius, impiously and wickedly openly teach that Christ did not know the day of judgment, and they accuse him of sloth and cowardice. They are a sect of the Theodosians; for Themistius, who was the founder and teacher of their sect, taught that there was one united nature in Christ.” Gregory of Tours, in the prologue to his history, explains Christ’s words, “Neither the Son, but the Father alone,” differently, arguing that “the Son” should be understood as the Christian people, since he placed angels before the Son. I report this; I do not endorse it. GUSSANV.], and you say that he asked Your Holiness to write to me what he ought to think about this inquiry.

But no monks from the region of Jerusalem came to me to ask anything, nor do I suppose that our common son could have written to you anything other than what was the case; rather, I suspect that an interpreter made an error in his letters. For the same deacon wrote to me two years ago that monks had come from the aforesaid region to Constantinople [Col. 1092A] asking such questions, and that he had taken pains to ask me what I thought. Long before I received the letter of Your Holiness, I replied to him concerning this heresy with precisely what I later found in the letter of Your Holiness.

I gave great thanks to almighty God because, concerning all the questions raised by Romans and Greeks, the Fathers whose followers we are had spoken with one spirit. In many respects I found your letter to be exactly as though I were reading writings of the Latin Fathers composed against the aforesaid heresy. And, as far as I could, I considered how much I should love and praise the good in my most holy brother [Note: [Col. 1092D] Recent editions changed *perpendite*, which is read in all the Norman, Vatican, Rheims, Corbie, and other manuscripts, to *perpendi*, because the sense appeared clearer.], in whose mouth I recognized the venerable Fathers whom I love so greatly.

Let praise, then, be given to him; let glory be given on high to the one by whose gift the voice of Mark still cries from the chair of Peter. From the outpouring of his spirit, when the priest enters to investigate the mysteries—that is, into the Holy of Holies—spiritual bells resound in the holy Church, as though in a tabernacle, from the words of preaching [Col. 1092B].

Your preaching, therefore, is upright and greatly worthy of praise. But we beseech almighty God to preserve you for a long time in this life, so that, through the organ of God which you are, the voice of truth may sound more widely throughout the world.

As for me, I ask you to intercede for me, so that the road of this pilgrimage, which has become harsh for me, may quickly come to an end. Thus, although I cannot reach the promises of the eternal homeland through my own merits, I may reach them through yours and rejoice with the citizens of heaven. (See below, Epistle 39. Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 67.)

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF SALONA

He says that he is distressed by the invasion of the Slavs. He urges him to defend the poor and oppressed energetically but moderately against unjust judges. He is to continue striving to recall the Photinianists to the bosom of the Church.

[Col. 1092C]

Gregory to Maximus, bishop of Salona.

When our common son, the presbyter Veteranus, came to Rome, he found me so weakened by the pains of gout that I was completely unable to reply personally to the letters of Your Fraternity. Indeed, I am both deeply distressed and troubled by the people of the Slavs, who are pressing heavily upon you [Col. 1092]. I am distressed by what I already suffer on your behalf; I am troubled because they have begun to enter Italy through the route of Istria.

What shall I say about Julianus Scribo, when everywhere I see that our sins are answering us, so that we are troubled both externally by foreign peoples [Col. 1092D] [Note: [Col. 1092D] Recent editions read “and internally by perverse judges.” All our manuscripts and the old edition led us to remove *perversis* (“perverse”).] and internally by judges? But do not be distressed at all by such things, for those who live after us will see worse times, so that, in comparison with their own age, they will consider us fortunate to have had the days we did.

To the extent that Your Fraternity is able, you must stand up for the poor and the oppressed. Even if this proves entirely unable to help them, the devotion of mind that God has given is itself sufficient for almighty God. For it is written: “Rescue those who are being led away to death, and do not cease to free those who are being dragged to destruction” (Proverbs 24:11). If you say, “I do not have the strength,” he who examines the heart himself understands. In everything you do, therefore, seek to have the examiner of hearts favorably disposed toward you. Whatever may please him, do not fail to do it.

For human terrors and favors are like smoke, which is carried away and vanishes in a light breeze [Note: [Col. 1093C] Yet by this smoke and this breeze, as though by matters of the greatest weight—alas!—our conduct is very often weighed and made to incline.]. Know this with complete certainty: no one can please both God and wicked people. Your Fraternity should therefore consider that you have pleased almighty God to the extent that you know you have displeased wicked people.

Nevertheless, your defense of the poor should be moderate and dignified, lest, if anything is done too harshly, people conclude that you are acting arrogantly out of youthful impetuosity. Our defense must therefore be such on behalf of the oppressed [Note: [Col. 1093D] The printed editions read *vestra defensio* (“your defense”), against four Vatican manuscripts and all the Norman, Corbie, Regius, and other manuscripts.], so that the humble may feel protected and the oppressors may not easily find anything to criticize out of malice.

Consider, then, what is said to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezekiel 2:6). And blessed Job says: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion of ostriches” (Job 30:29). Paul says to the disciples: “In the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15). We must therefore walk with all the greater caution because we know that we live among the enemies of God.

As for the Photinianists, Your Fraternity must be wholly attentive to them and, as you have begun, strive to bring them back to the bosom of the holy Church. If any of them wish to come to me and receive instruction, let them first give an oath that they will not permit their people to persist in their error even after instruction has been received. Thereafter Your Holiness should promise them that they will suffer no violence from me, but that I will give them an explanation.

If they recognize the truth, let them accept it; if they do not recognize it, I will send them away unharmed. But if any of them wish to come to us in opposition to you, Your Fraternity must not hold them back, because those who come will either receive instruction, or—and know this for certain—they will never again see that land. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 55.)

[Note: [Col. 1093D] The Photinianists are the same as the Photinians, so called from Photinus, whose impious doctrines in a certain way revived in Theodore of Mopsuestia. See the seventh letter of Pope Pelagius II, which is the third to Helias, and which they maintain was dictated by Saint Gregory: “Truly descending from Paul of Samosata, although in the book *On the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ* he is found throughout his entire argument to have used the very words of Photinus and the other heresiarchs.” Those who insist that *Frontinianistis* should be read think that these were members of the schism of the Istrians.]

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO INNOCENTIUS, PREFECT OF AFRICA

He rejoices in Innocentius’s prefecture out of affection but grieves because of the burden of the office, which he greatly desires to become for him an occasion of eternal reward. He reports that a truce has been made with the king of the Lombards. He praises the books of Augustine when Innocentius asks for writings on Job. He gives thanks for the protection of the property of the Roman Church.

Gregory to Innocentius [Note: [Col. 1093D] EPISTLE XXXVII.—The Regius and two Colbertine manuscripts read “to the bishop of Africa.” In the margin of an older manuscript the same hand has written: “He is saddened because the bishop had accepted the prefecture.” Anyone familiar with Gregory’s letters will see that this letter was not written to a bishop, provided that he is not a stranger to the Gregorian letters.] prefect of Africa.

The lucid eloquence of Your Eminence, seasoned with the honey of the heart, has so deeply infused its flavor into us and carried us away in its love that what you write sounds sweet to us and what you do tastes pleasant. Nor is this undeserved, since the man adorned with good pursuits is great by judgment, not by favor.

When we learned that you had assumed the insignia of the prefecture [Note: [Col. 1094D] The *cingula* are the insignia of military and palace service, namely the belt and sword. Hence the expressions “honor of the belt” and “oaths of the belt” in the *Digest* and the *Code*. When an office or dignity ceased, one was said to lay down the belt, to be deprived of the belt, or to be unbelted. GUSSANV.], joy was mingled with our sadness. On the one hand we rejoiced in the advancement of our beloved son; on the other we were saddened, because from our own suffering we know how difficult it is, in troubled times, to be placed over important regions.

Therefore you must strive in every way to turn hardship into an occasion of reward. For, as you know, grain comes forth from land full of thistles, and a rose grows from thorns. Since the season suitable for sowing has now come for you, do not cease to sow the seeds of good works, so that you may bring back larger sheaves on the day of the harvest of joy and reach eternal glory through the merit of a passing honor.

Since we have learned what care you have shown in preparing the dromons [Note: [Col. 1094D] *Dromones* are very swift ships, so called from their speed, not from oak, from Greek δρόμος (*dromos*, “course” or “running”). Thus in Pliny we find *dromones* used of fish, Book XXXII, chapter 11. Hence *dromonarii*, those who operate these ships. The word occurs so frequently in this sense in Cassiodorus and many other authors that it is surprising that some still hesitate over it. I will give one example from the second letter of Pope Paul to King Pepin: “The emperor decreed that the fleet of dromons of Sicily be directed to the city of Otranto,” etc. *Stolus* means in French “a fleet”; Greek ναυτικὸς στόλος, “naval forces.” GUSSANV.], we relieve your anxiety with the desired news, informing you that, with the Lord’s favor, an agreement concerning peace has been reached with the king of the Lombards until the month of March of the coming fourth indiction. Whether this agreement will hold, we do not know, since afterward the same king was reported to have died, although this is still uncertain.

As for what you wrote concerning Anamundarus, we have done what you asked. Would that the outcome follow our intention, for, insofar as it depends on us, we do not deny the afflicted the consolation of our intercession.

As for your wish that a book on the exposition of blessed Job be sent to you, we are entirely pleased by your devotion, since we see you applying Your Eminence to a work that neither permits you to go wholly outside yourself nor prevents you from gathering back to the heart the parts of you scattered among worldly concerns. But if you desire to be fattened on a delicious pasture, read the works of blessed Augustine, your fellow countryman, and do not seek our bran in comparison with his fine flour [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Norman, Corbie, and Turon manuscripts read *similaginis* (“fine flour”); the two expressions have nearly the same meaning.].

Moreover, we have learned from the testimony of our *chartularius* Hilarius what protection and what affection Your Glory has shown toward the interests of the poor, as a lover of the blessed apostle Peter, chief of the apostles [Col. 1095B]. For this we offer abundant thanks and implore the mercy of almighty God to fortify you with the protection of his grace, and not to permit wicked men externally or evil spirits internally to prevail against you. Rather, may he graciously order your actions in his fear so that, just as he has made you glorious among human beings, he may likewise, after the passage of a long life, make you glorious among the number of his saints. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 78.)

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CAGLIARI

He is to ensure that neither those who have fled to the church suffer violence nor those who have previously been oppressed suffer losses.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1095D] EPISTLE XXXVIII.—In four Vatican manuscripts, Gemeticus, Lyranus, Audoen, Pratell, two Teller manuscripts, three Colbertine manuscripts, and the Regius, *Joanni episcopo Caral.* (“to John, bishop of Cagliari”) is read instead of *Januario*. This is erroneous, since Januarius was still alive and governed the Church of Cagliari for several years afterward, as is clear from the letters written to him below, especially Book XIII, Epistle 6, indiction 6.] to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari.

The letters of our most reverend brother Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, and of our most eminent son Innocentius, prefect, have shown how the lesser and poorer people in Sardinia are oppressed by those who are more powerful there [Col. 1095C] [Note: [Col. 1095D] The printed editions read *qui illis* (“who oppress them”), against the manuscripts—five Vatican, the Norman, and others—which read *qui illic* (“who are there”).]. Therefore, so that you may know what has been written to us, we have taken care to send you copies of those letters. Since the requests that ought to be made are being presented, it is necessary to act diligently so that what is promised may be fulfilled in practice.

If any of those concerning whom the dispute exists should perhaps take refuge in a church, Your Diligence must arrange the case in such a way [Note: [Col. 1095D] In four Vatican manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and most others, *diligentia vestra* (“Your Diligence”) is omitted.] that neither they themselves suffer violence nor those said to have been oppressed sustain losses.

It must therefore be your concern that those whose interests are involved give them an oath promising that the law and justice will be preserved; that they be urged in every way to come out; and that they give an account of their actions. You should also appoint a defender of your Church for them. Through his vigilance, whatever has been promised to them must be preserved, so that it may not become harmful to others [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Norman manuscript reads *noxa sit* (“be harmful”).] and so that the ecclesiastical right of refuge may benefit them while the legal order remains safeguarded.

Let Your Fraternity act accordingly, so that these matters, which ought to be corrected through your diligence, do not fail because of delay or any obstacle on your part.

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He refutes one by one the arguments that the Agnoites derived from Scripture and discusses them at greater length. He complains that he lacks interpreters skilled in the Greek language.

Gregory to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria.

As cold water to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a distant land (Prov. 25:25).

But what can be good news to me regarding the assistance of the holy Church, except the life and preservation of your most beloved Holiness, who, having received the light of truth, both illumines that same Church by the word of preaching and instructs it toward a better way by the examples of your conduct? Whenever I recall your unanimity in my heart and recognize that I remain fixed in your heart, I give thanks to almighty God, because charity cannot be divided by distance. For although we are far separated in body, in mind we are indivisible.

Our common son, the deacon Anatolius, informed me by his letters that in the royal city [Note: [Col. 1096D] EPISTLE XXXIX [also 42].—So the manuscripts read. Although the sense is obscure, the agreement of the witnesses compels us to accept this reading. In the printed editions one finds: “some ecclesiastical matters, once nevertheless concerning earthly matters, had been moved.” Our reading would become clearer by changing *quondam* to *quaedam*, as in the old Colbert manuscript, and reading: “he informed me . . . that no ecclesiastical matters [supply: had been moved], but certain matters concerning earthly causes, had been moved.”] no ecclesiastical matter had formerly been stirred up by earthly causes. But I believe that he had informed me of this before Your Beatitude spoke about the Church’s case. And I rejoice, because wherever you have been present, I do not consider myself to have been absent. For as a minister of truth, a follower of Peter, and a preacher of the holy Church, I know that you were able to speak those things which ought to have sounded forth from the see of the apostle Peter through the mouth of a teacher. [Note: [Col. 1096D] This passage was shown to require restoration by the manuscripts Colbert, Norman, and others; previously it had read: “the preacher knows that you were able to speak those things,” which scarcely accords with Saint Gregory’s meaning. We have corrected many other similar passages with the help of the clearer manuscripts, but they are minor matters about which it did not seem worthwhile to give notice.]

Some days ago, when Abramius of Alexandria arrived, I had written again to Your Holiness, explaining both what I thought about your writings against the heretics called Agnoites and why I had answered late. But the same Abrammius, compelled by the necessities of navigation, is said to have remained for a long time in the city of Naples. Accordingly, I write again in the sense of what I wrote earlier: regarding your teaching against the heretics called Agnoites, there was very much for us to admire; there was nothing to displease us. In the same sense I had already written at length to our common son, the deacon Anatolius. Your teaching agreed in every respect with the Latin Fathers, so that it would not surprise me that the Spirit should not be different in different languages.

[Col. 1097A] For what you said concerning the fig tree is precisely the sense in which blessed Augustine speaks. When the evangelist added, “For it was not yet the season for figs” (Mark 11:13), it is plainly understood that, through the fig tree, the Lord had sought fruit in the synagogue, which had the leaves of the Law but did not possess the fruit of works. The Creator of all could not have been ignorant that the fig tree had no fruit; everyone could know that when the season for figs had not yet come.

But concerning what is written, “As for that day and hour, neither the Son nor the angels know” (Mark 13:32), Your Holiness rightly understood that this must certainly be referred not to that same Son according to the fact that he is the head, but according to his body, which is us. Blessed Augustine uses this same interpretation in many places (Questions on the Eighty-Three Questions, question 60; Book I of *On the Trinity*, chapter 12; at the beginning of Psalm 6; and in Sermon 2 on Psalm 34).

He also gives another interpretation that may be understood of the same Son: almighty God sometimes speaks in human fashion, as when he says to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12). This does not mean that God then came to know that he was feared, but that he then caused Abraham himself to show that he feared God. Just as we call a day joyful, not because the day itself is joyful but because it makes us joyful, so the almighty Son says that he does not know the day which he causes not to be known—not because he himself does not know it, but because he does not at all permit it to be known. Hence the Father alone is said to know it, because the Son, consubstantial with him, possesses from the Father’s nature—which is above the angels—the knowledge of what the angels do not know.

This may also be understood more subtly: the incarnate Only-Begotten, having become for us a complete human being, [Note: [Col. 1097D] In the English, Norman, Colbert, Corbie, and three Vatican manuscripts, “in the nature indeed of divinity” is read. Yet the sequence of the argument proves that “humanity” must be read.] [Col. 1097D] in the nature of his humanity indeed knows the day and hour of judgment, but nevertheless does not know it from the nature of his humanity. What he knows in that nature, he does not know from that nature, because God, having become man, knows the day and hour of judgment through the power of his divinity. Thus, at the wedding, when the Virgin Mother said that the wine was lacking, he replied, “Woman, what have I to do with you? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4).

For the Lord of the angels was not subject to an hour—he who had made the hours and times among all the things he created. But because the Virgin Mother wished a miracle to be performed by him when the wine failed, he immediately answered her: “Woman, what have I to do with you?” As if he were plainly saying: “The power by which I can perform a miracle comes to me from the Father, not from my mother.” From his mother he could die, while from the nature of the Father he performed miracles.

Therefore, while hanging on the cross, he recognized that same mother as he was dying and entrusted her to the disciple, saying, “Behold, your mother” (John 19:27). He therefore said, “Woman, what have I to do with you? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). [Col. 1098A] That is: “In the miracle which I do not possess from your nature, I do not recognize you. When the hour of death comes, I recognize you as my mother, because I possess from you that by which I can die.”

Thus he denied that he possessed with the angels—which are creatures—the knowledge that he did not have from the nature of his humanity, in which he was a creature together with the angels. God and man therefore know the day and hour of judgment; but for this reason: because he is God and man. [Note: [Col. 1097D] The printed editions read: “He knows the hour of judgment, because God is man.” We have restored many passages here and throughout the letter from the Vatican, English, Norman, Rheims, and other manuscripts.]

The matter is entirely clear: whoever is not a Nestorian cannot in any way be an Agnoite. For if he confesses that the very Wisdom of God was incarnate, how can he possibly say that there is something of which God’s Wisdom is ignorant? It is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things were made through him” (John 1:1). If all things, unquestionably the day and hour of judgment as well. Who, then, would be so foolish as to presume to say that the Word of the Father made something of which he is ignorant?

It is also written: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands” (John 13:3). If all things, certainly the day and hour of judgment as well. Who, then, is so foolish as to say that the Son received into his hands something of which he is ignorant?

Concerning the passage in which he says to the women about Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?” (John 11:34), we felt exactly as you did. For if they deny that the Lord knew where Lazarus had been buried and therefore asked, they will certainly be forced to admit that the Lord did not know where Adam and Eve had hidden themselves after their transgression, when in paradise he said, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9), or when he rebuked Cain, saying, “Where is Abel your brother?” (Gen. 4:9). If he did not know, why did he immediately add, “The blood of your brother cries out to me from the ground”?

Although in this passage Severianus of Gabala says something else, maintaining that the Lord asked the women where they had laid the dead Lazarus as a kind of rebuke—as if, recalling Eve’s guilt, he plainly said to the women: “I placed a man in paradise; you have placed him in a tomb.” [Note: [Col. 1097D] Three Vatican manuscripts, the Norman, Corbie, and Colbert manuscripts read “Severianus of Gabala.” In Vatican B, “Gabelli” is found. Severianus, bishop of Gabala in Syria and a close associate, later the bitter enemy, of Saint John Chrysostom, wrote much that has either been published among the works of Saint John Chrysostom or collected in the Greek Fathers’ *Catena*. William Cave compiled a catalogue of many of his writings that are no longer extant in his *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*. We do not know from which of these works the material cited by Saint Gregory was taken. From this passage, and for several other reasons, Gussanvillaeus suspects that this letter is spurious, though he certainly does not establish the point. All the manuscripts in which the letter occurs contradict him.]

To this our same common son, the deacon Anatolius, replied with another question, saying: “What if someone objects to me that, just as the immortal One deigned to die in order to free us from death, and the eternal One before the ages willed to become temporal, so the Wisdom of God deigned to assume our ignorance in order to free us from ignorance?”

I have not yet answered him on this point, because until now I have been held by a severe illness. But now I have begun to recover through Your Holiness’s prayers, and, if I recover sufficiently to dictate, I shall answer him with the Lord’s help. I have nothing to say to you about these matters, lest I seem to teach you what you already know, because even medicines lose their power to heal when they are applied to healthy and strong limbs. [Col. 1099A]

Moreover, we report that here we suffer serious difficulty with interpreters. Since there are no interpreters who express meaning from meaning, but they always wish to transfer the exact properties of the words, they confuse the entire sense of what has been said. Consequently, what has been translated can in no way be understood without great labor.

I have received the blessing of Saint Mark the Evangelist and of Your Beatitude. I wished to send timber, but because the ship that came was small, it could not carry it. Although these very pieces that the Alexandrians who came saw are small. [Note: [Col. 1099D] The printed editions read: “These very things which those arriving from Alexandria saw and reported,” because they are small.] I had prepared other pieces, altogether larger for you, but they have not yet been transported to the city of Rome, because I expected that they would be hauled when the Alexandrian ship arrived; they remained where they had been cut. [Col. 1099B]

May almighty God preserve your life for the building up of the holy Church through many years, and inspire you to pray more earnestly for me, so that your prayers before almighty God may lift up the one whom his own sins weigh down. [Note: [Col. 1099D] Only in the recent editions does the letter end in this way: “In the month of February, in the third indiction.” Other manuscripts, both written and printed, disagree.] (See Letter 35.)

## EPISTLE XL. TO FORTUNATUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

He is to investigate the truth more carefully concerning the boys who accuse Peter of attempting a crime, at Peter’s own request.

Gregory to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples.

Your Fraternity has caused us great astonishment, either because you did not wish to decide the case of your cleric or because you did not rise to the task of deciding it. Peter, therefore, the bearer of this letter, came to us and complained that the boys by whom he says he was falsely accused of attempting a crime had not been examined as they ought, but only questioned verbally, and that for this sole reason he had been forbidden to proceed with you. [Col. 1099C]

Either what was said was true, and he should have been subjected to canonical punishment according to the nature of the case, or it was false, and he ought not to have remained under accusation for so long. Since both reason demands it and he, concerned for his own vindication, has approached the apostolic see so that what has been said against him may be investigated and the case concluded according to the examination, you must, together with our subdeacon Anthemius, carefully and rigorously require the truth from those boys. [Note: [Col. 1099D] EPISTLE XL [also 25].—The word “therefore” is omitted in the Norman and Vatican A manuscripts.]

If the aforesaid bearer of the letter proves guilty of the attempted crime, let him be punished in every respect with canonical vengeance. But if he is declared innocent, let him breathe again through speedy absolution, [Note: [Col. 1100D] Saint Augustine treats nearly the same case in Letters 136 and 137, now numbered 77 and 78. The reader may consult them to learn how one should proceed in a similar case.] and let him have permission to proceed with you. For just as suitable punishment must be exercised against the guilty, so absolution must not be delayed for the innocent.

Therefore let Your Fraternity diligently strive to bring this case to an end, so that you may not incur any reproach for negligence. [Col. 1100A]

## EPISTLE XLI. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

Together with Bishop Fortunatus, he is to investigate most carefully the truth of the charge brought against Peter.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

Peter, the cleric and bearer of this letter, has complained to us that certain boys falsely accused him, that his case was not examined with the strict investigation it required, and that he was not condemned by anyone, but merely forbidden by his bishop to proceed with him. We were extremely displeased to hear this, because, once the truth had been carefully investigated, he ought either to have been condemned as the nature of the case demanded or certainly acquitted as innocent. [Col. 1100B]

Since, therefore, both the case requires it and the aforesaid bearer urgently requests that a careful investigation be made in this matter, by this present authority we command you, together with our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Fortunatus and, if it seems appropriate to you, our glorious son Maurentius, to strive to learn the truth of the alleged crime through an exceptionally careful inquiry and examination. Then hasten either to punish the guilt or to vindicate the innocence, [Note: [Col. 1100D] EPISTLE XLI [also 26].—The recent editions read “to reveal the innocence.”] so that you may not appear to have been negligent in any respect and so that this case may no longer remain without a decision.

## EPISTLE XLII. TO EUSEBIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF THESSALONICA

Commending the pursuit of peace, he urges him not to allow the minds of the orthodox to be offended by certain persons who reject the Council of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1100C]

Gregory to Eusebius, archbishop of Thessalonica.

If we consider how great is the virtue of peace, we recognize with what zeal it must be cultivated. Our Lord and Redeemer deigned to leave and give it to his disciples as a great gift, so that through it he might make those who adhered to him with steadfast faith his companions by a pious participation. For it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). Whoever, therefore, desires to be an heir of the Father should not refuse to become his son by preserving peace. For whoever provides an opportunity for discord plainly makes himself deprived of so great a gift.

Since the sincerity of your faith has, as was fitting, been declared to us as Catholic and, by God’s favor, upright, we are suspended in great astonishment that you allow those whom you know to believe well and think rightly to be needlessly scandalized by the fault of certain persons, so that the reputation of Your Fraternity may be darkened by another’s guilt. For how can one be free from suspicion of error who shows patience toward one who errs? Or what estimation of himself does he offer if he does not foresee that the matters demanded by the fervor of faith must be openly cleared by a satisfactory explanation? [Col. 1101A]

It is reported that your presbyter Lucas and Peter do not wish to accept the Council of Chalcedon, and that for this reason the hearts of your orthodox sons are disturbed by no slight scandal. Since their zeal must not only be praised but altogether encouraged, we exhort you not to cease examining this matter with every vigor and with the careful concern proper to your Fraternity. [Note: [Col. 1101D] EPISTLE XLII [also 6, indiction 2].—The recent printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read: “and if he should find them guilty in this matter.”]

If it finds them innocent of this perversity, let Your Fraternity, after receiving their satisfaction, remove the scandal from the minds of your sons, and anathematize Severus and Nestorius in particular among all heresies. Thus, where suspicion of them has produced division, let the love of faith produce charity. [Note: [Col. 1101D] We have restored this passage from the Norman, English, Vatican, and other manuscripts, with which the old editions agree. The recent editions read: “Where suspicion of them has produced division, let the love of faith remove it and purification produce charity.”]

Let one salutary affection of concord bind together those whom the sincere and one confession of Catholic truth holds together. Nor should satisfaction be considered unworthy by those who doubt, since the Lord’s voice commands: “Do not despise one of these little ones” (Matt. 18:10). Whoever does not wish to despise the one who gives the command should not reject the words of the one who commands, because he whom our Redeemer testified to be the chosen vessel also admonished us to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3). Therefore, whoever does not refuse to be held by this bond of salvation should pursue the things that make for peace and give no place to the enemy, so that the one who might have raged more violently through the cruel division of brothers may be trampled down once unity has been established. [Col. 1101B]

But if, contrary to our hope, they are found to have been wounded by the arrow of this error, the healing of ecclesiastical exhortation must be applied to them, so that, if they are cured, they may remain among the Lord’s sheep, or else be cut off from the unity of the ecclesiastical body. In this way a great gain may arise from a small loss, and the part removed may make the whole free. For it is also the concern of a prudent shepherd not to delay casting out from the company of the healthy a sick sheep that does not accept treatment, lest it infect the others with the stain of its sickness, knowing that he can preserve the health of the rest only by expelling it. [Note: [Col. 1102D] The printed editions read: “The shepherd does not delay casting out the sick sheep.”]

Therefore, I again admonish you in fraternal charity to scrutinize this matter with the utmost vigilance and to preserve with the greatest care what we have written, lest you make the sound faith you hold doubtful through association with others. For whoever does not correct what must be cut away commits it. You must therefore weigh this with great concern and altogether great foresight, so that their person may not be a scandal to others nor their reputation harmful to you, and so that the shepherd’s gain from the sheep entrusted to your care may be as great as the sincere love and entrusted responsibility that make you solicitous for their protection. [Col. 1101D]

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP OF LUNA

At his request, he sends a servant of God whom he is to place over a monastery and for whom he himself is to show the greatest care.

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

We write that Your Fraternity’s concern has pleased us so greatly that it was our desire to complete in action what you requested. Since you wrote that we should send a person who could exercise the office of abbess in the monastery situated in your city, and since, with the support of divine mercy, we believe her capable of being energetic in the administration of that monastery, we have arranged for her to be sent there, so that, with God’s protection, she may be appointed abbess by you. For she came here only for the sake of prayer.

Since, therefore, we have sent the aforesaid servant of God to you in accordance with your wishes and letters, we exhort Your Fraternity to show concern for her and for her monastery, and to strengthen the community living there in the service of Jesus Christ our God and Redeemer by the voice of your exhortation and by the exhibition of good works. In all external matters concerning it, wherever necessary, present yourself on its behalf in such a way that those living there may find in you, as is fitting, great assistance and may not be burdened by want of anything. Thus, while every need has been removed from them through your provision, they may be able to persevere continually with a secure mind in prayer and the praises of God. In this way her chosen way of life will benefit them for salvation and you for reward. For greater grace is certainly acquired when the shepherd’s concern offers the Lord gain from the sheep entrusted to him. [Col. 1102B]

## EPISTLE XLIV. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP OF LUNA

He is to give twenty solidi, or even more, to the people of Fiesole for the repair of their churches.

[Col. 1102C] Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luna.

The attached letter discloses what the petition of the presbyter Agrippinus and the deacon Servandus contains concerning the Church of Fiesole, [Note: [Col. 1102D] EPISTLE XLIV.—Fiesole, commonly Fiesoli, now ruined. It was formerly a celebrated city of Tuscany; it is now a small town, though still an episcopal see under the archbishop of Florence, two miles north of Florence. GUSSANV.] which is subject to you. Therefore, if the matters contained there are supported by truth and persons have come to you who ought to be trusted in something, it is proper for you to give up to twenty solidi, or more if it seems right to you, for the repair of the churches said to be in ruins, under the form of a testament, [Note: [Col. 1103C] The document indicates that it was not issued because of death, but was confirmed with witnesses. Adrevaldus, *On the Translation of Saint Benedict*, Book I, chapter 2: “That testament of mutual exchange is preserved to this day in the public archives of your monastery.”] so that there may be a remedy there and your own security may be preserved.

As for the other things that are with you, send a record (*desusceptum*) concerning those same things, for future reference, so that when God grants peace those properties may be restored without delay or dispute to the right of the Church to which they belong.

## EPISTLE XLV. TO ECCLESIUS, BISHOP OF CHIUSI

He expresses sympathy for his illness, congratulates him on the prudent choice of a bishop, sends him a horse, and orders him to visit the churches so that those who have been baptized may receive the signing.

[Col. 1102D]

Gregory to Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi. [Note: [Col. 1103D] EPISTLE XLV [also 46].—So the English, Norman, Tours, Rheims, four Vatican, three Colbert, Corbie, and other manuscripts read. Vatican A has Eudosius. One of the Colbert manuscripts calls him bishop of the Church of Sion. The old editions retained the name Ecclesius, while more recent editions have Eulogius.]

On receiving the letters of Your Fraternity, we were saddened to learn from them that you had been seriously ill and were still weak. Although we desired to see Your Holiness, you nevertheless did well to remain there during this period, lest, by coming here, you should cause us renewed sadness through a relapse of your illness. [Col. 1103A]

As for the episcopate, we praised you because you did not choose a person rashly but acted cautiously, as was fitting. When you come, if it pleases God, we shall consider the matter together and, with God’s help, arrange whatever seems useful.

We have sent you one horse, of the kind we were able to find, as a blessing from Saint Peter, so that after your illness you may have something on which to ride.

As for the matters on account of which the bearers of this letter came here, you will learn everything that was done from their own report. Moreover, let Your Fraternity bestow the service of visitation upon those churches to which you can go without difficulty, so that those who are baptized there, by God’s favor, may not remain without receiving the signing. [Col. 1103B]

## EPISTLE XLVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to ensure that Crescentius, the vicar, does not suffer any injustice at the hands of Leontius, the former consul.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

When Crescentius, the bearer of this letter and our vicar, was ordered by our glorious son Lord Leontius, the former consul, to appear before him, he hesitated to leave the venerable precincts, lest some excuse should perhaps arise through him for others or it should be said that the public interest was being obstructed. We therefore allowed him to leave, provided equity was observed. [Col. 1103D]

Because this matter caused him to appear there, as he had been ordered, let Your Fraternity support him with due regard for justice and strive to act with your customary charity before the aforesaid most glorious Lord, so that he may not in any way be burdened contrary to the laws or to reason. Rather, see that justice is maintained for him in every respect, as befits his Christianity, so that Leontius may appear to have salutarily preserved for his own reward what the order of equity demands, and so that Crescentius may not feel himself burdened here contrary to what we promised would be done. (See Letter 50.) [Col. 1103C]

[Note: [Col. 1103D] EPISTLE XLVI [also 47].—When Italy was divided by Constantine the Great into its dioceses and seven provinces were assigned to the vicar of northern Italy, which thereafter claimed for themselves the name of Italy, ten provinces remained under the vicar of the city of Rome. These were called urban and suburban provinces: Campania; Tuscia and Umbria; Picenum; Sicily; Apulia and Calabria; Bruttium and Lucania; Samnium; Sardinia—which Justinian later assigned to the African diocese; Corsica; and Valeria. The urban prefect was distinct from the vicar of the city: the former was an urban magistrate, while the latter held authority over the rights of the provinces, as Symmachus says, Book IX, Letter 119. We do not think that the vicar whom Gregory mentions here possessed such extensive power. In Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 52, John, a magnificent man, is praised as holding in this city the office of prefects. Perhaps Crescentius, the vicar, was acting as the deputy of the urban prefect. Alteserra thinks that he was the vicar of the praetorian prefect. Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book VI, in the formula of the vicar of the city of Rome: “You have,” he says, “some share with the prefects . . . within the fortieth milestone you guard the rights of the most holy city . . . Senators who precede you in rank appear to request certain necessary things from you. You have what you may provide to those above you.”]

## EPISTLE XLVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He commends Apollonius, the master of soldiers.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Although we know that you show paternal kindness to the glorious Apollonius, master of soldiers and our common son, because he believed that the same measure of affection which you show him as a priest should be increased by our letters, we therefore commend him to Your Fraternity in this letter. We exhort you so that he may find in you the paternal consolation that is fitting, and may enjoy your assistance, as circumstances require, accompanied by justice. Thus, when he has experienced your greater affection toward him, he may both recognize what he trusts in you and perceive that our letter has been of benefit.

## EPISTLE XLVIII. TO LEONTIUS, THE FORMER CONSUL

He commends Apollonius.

[Col. 1104B] Gregory to Leontius, the former consul.

Knowing that you receive letters with paternal goodwill, it is beyond doubt that, if we strive to accomplish this matter, we shall willingly serve Your Glory, since we do not allow the desires of our sons to be saddened. Because our glorious son Apollonius, master of soldiers and bearer of this letter, wished to be commended to you by our letters, we greet Your Glory with paternal affection and ask that, with due regard for justice, he may find your favor and obtain the help of your protection wherever necessary. Thus, when Your Glory has granted to our recommendation what you customarily grant spontaneously, he may rejoice to find in you the assistance he desires, and we may offer abundant thanks to your most sincere goodness. [Col. 1104C]

## EPISTLE XLIX. TO ADEODATA, THE ILLUSTRIOUS

He strengthens her mind in contempt for temporal things and love of eternal things. He informs her that the case of Bishop Decius has been entrusted to John and Leontius.

Gregory to Adeodata, the illustrious.

Your letter brought us great joy, because it showed that you desire eternal life. But since the world’s fleeting glory usually obstructs this kind of devotion, we exhort you not to let any transient matter call back the most salutary deliberation of your mind or turn it aside from the path on which it has begun. Rather, let love of the heavenly homeland kindle you; let lasting rewards concern you; let your hope always aspire confidently to the promise of the coming Judge; and let temporal things purchase eternal ones for you, so that through this you may both be in true glory and be enrolled among the heavenly matrons.

Recall to your minds the prosperity of the times, the multitude of people, the splendor of offices, the glory of matrons, and the abundance of riches. Consider what all these things have become and where they are now, and from this judge how nothing they are, since the person who loves such things sees a waking dream. This recollection ought therefore to be a great instruction for you, because nothing that is enclosed by an end should be loved as something great.

Those things, then, are to be desired and loved above all: things that neither pass away once found nor fail once attained. But no one can breathe toward their desire without the grace of divine mercy. We therefore pray almighty God to grant you both the will to choose these things and the ability to obtain them, so that he may allow you to live here in his fear and afterward receive you into the company of the holy [Note: [Col. 1105D] EPISTLE XLIX [also 55, Book IX].—So the four Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, and others read. Since this did not please the editors, they changed “martyrs” to “matrons.”] martyrs.

Greeting Your Glory with paternal affection, we inform you that, concerning the case of our brother and fellow bishop Decius, it seemed to us that we ought to entrust its hearing to our brother and fellow bishop John and to the glorious Leontius, since he is said to be a good and just man. [Note: [Col. 1105D] Evidently concerning Domitian and the property of Theodore, as the following letter shows.] We are especially confident that, where the charity of the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop is present in judgment, neither party will be deprived of its rights nor will the Church be able to suffer prejudice.

## EPISTLE L. TO DOMITIAN, THE METROPOLITAN

Leontius has not yet come to Rome. He has supported him in carrying out the emperors’ orders. The case of Bishop Theodore has been entrusted to him and to Bishop John.

[Col. 1105C] Gregory to Domitian, the metropolitan bishop.

The matter itself testifies to how great is the sincerity of charity in your mind: you do not cease to preserve toward the absent the affection you show toward those present. Your letters therefore greatly urged us to love the glorious Leontius, our common son, because by telling us that he is joined to Your Holiness in friendship, you have shown what sort of man he is—namely, that no one but a good man could please a good man. He is therefore rightly to be loved, since he is found to be closely joined to you.

The same glorious man has remained in Sicily and has not yet come to the city of Rome. Nevertheless, in the matters entrusted to him by order of our most serene lords for the public welfare, we did not delay giving him whatever support reason allowed. [Col. 1106A]

We took care to urge the glorious Gregory, the former prefect, and the others who were residing in the ecclesiastical precincts [Note: [Col. 1105D] EPISTLE L.—That is, the ecclesiastical precincts served as an asylum.] to leave and present an account of themselves. After giving their word, they left with Marcus, a magnificent man and *scribo*, who had come to escort them. [Note: [Col. 1105D] It was customary that those who had fled to the Church’s asylum should not leave before a pledge had been given that they would suffer no violence. I offer one among many examples, from canon 1 of the Council of Orléans: “We decree that what the ecclesiastical canons have established and Roman law has ordained shall be observed: that it is entirely forbidden to remove accused persons from the atria of a church or from the bishop’s house, and that they may not otherwise be handed over unless, after oaths have been given according to the Gospel, they are assured against death, bodily harm, and every kind of punishment, so that an agreement concerning satisfaction may be reached with the one against whom the accused person is guilty. If anyone is convicted of violating these sworn assurances, he shall be guilty of perjury and be separated not only from communion with the Church and all clerics but also from the table of Catholics.” Note that the canon concerns murderers, adulterers, and thieves. GUSSANV.] They were prepared to go to Sicily.

Moreover, concerning the property of Bishop Theodore, which you wrote had been placed under the legal control of your Church, nothing more or better could have been done than to entrust the hearing of this matter to the aforementioned most glorious Leontius, about whom you give such testimony and to whom you say the case itself has been commended, and to our brother and fellow bishop John, whose holiness and concern we know. We urge them to investigate the truth with every possible subtlety and to bring the disputes of the parties swiftly to an end according to justice, so that neither the people of Your Holy Fraternity may be held there by a long delay nor the other party complain that it has suffered prejudice without being heard. Whatever decision is made for either party in this matter, be assured that it will be carried out without delay. For just as we do not wish anyone to be condemned without judgment, so we allow no decision that has been made to be postponed under any pretext.

May almighty God surround you with his protection and favor, preserve your steps in the path of his fear, and stir you to pray for me, so that through your intercessions my efforts may be directed into the way of life.

## EPISTLE LI. TO LEONTIUS, THE FORMER CONSUL

He has never asked anyone for protection except with justice favoring it. Although Libertinus may have committed fraud in public affairs, his property ought to have been punished, not his liberty. Anger should follow the mind’s rational judgment in punishing evil, not precede it.

[Col. 1106C]

Gregory to Leontius, the former consul.

[Note: [Col. 1106D] EPIST. LI.—In the printed editions the conjunction *et* has been omitted, although it is found in all manuscripts. In several manuscripts *cautiones* is read. We have retained *cautionis*, as do the Norman and Colbert manuscripts, because of what follows concerning this matter of security.]

Your Glory took care to send me a copy of Libertinus’s security-bond, so that it might show me with what obligation or intention that same Libertinus had approached the dignity of prefecture. 1079 After it had been reread by my glorious brother, the Patrician Palatinus, and by my counsellor, the magnificent Theodore, it was carefully reported to me, and appeared detestable both to me and to all who were able to learn of it.

[Note: [Col. 1106D] In four Vatican manuscripts, *ad praeturae* (“to the praetorship”) is read. Thus, in Book V, Letter 32, Libertinus is called a praetor; and in many letters where the printed editions call him prefect, some manuscripts call him praetor, while others call him prefect.]

But Your Glory should remember that you have never received letters from me recommending anyone except so that, with justice in your favor, you might extend your protection.

[Col. 1107A] And because the entire province together was returning thanks for this same Libertinus, I made the indication. For neither have I ever claimed to know who he was or what sort of cases he had, nor do I yet know these matters precisely. If, then, he is found guilty in this matter of the security-bond, and I do not know what defense he may offer concerning the other matters, I nevertheless know this one thing well and firmly: even if he committed some fraud in public affairs, his property ought to have been confiscated, not his freedom.

For in the fact that free men are beaten—to say nothing of the offense against Almighty God, to say nothing of the fact that Your Reputation is gravely burdened—the age of our most devout emperor is nevertheless completely darkened. For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the Roman emperors:

[Note: [Col. 1107D] The same point is repeated in Book XI, Letter 38, now Book XIII, Letter 31. Themistius, in Oration 11, asserts the same: “To rule over free men is one thing, to rule over slaves another; the former is superiority of virtue, the latter an excess of fortune.” You see, reader, that Saint Gregory is speaking here of barbarian kings, who treat their subjects as slaves, rejecting the title of father. The same Themistius says admirably in Oration 5, near the end: “Justice makes a father, anger a master, greed for money a merchant; but only the title of father is divine.” GUSSANV.]

kings of the nations are masters of slaves, whereas the Roman emperor is the master of free men.

[Col. 1107B] Therefore, whatever you do, you ought to do it only after justice has first been preserved and freedom has then been guarded in every respect. It is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, take care not to do to another” (Tob. 4:16). And Truth itself says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12).

You ought therefore to regard the freedom of those entrusted to you for examination as especially your own; and if you do not wish your own superiors to violate your freedom, preserve the freedom of your subjects by honoring it.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The printed editions read *custodire* (“preserve”), against the Tours manuscript, four Vatican manuscripts, the Remigius, Norman, Royal, and other manuscripts.]

For we know who said: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). Since his words do not pass away but are fulfilled in every respect, let us fear what he says again: “In the measure with which you have measured, it will be measured to you” (Matt. 7:2).

[Note: [Col. 1108D] Some manuscripts read *remetietur* (“it will be measured back”), as the Vulgate has it.]

[Col. 1107C] What, then, does Your Glory suppose? If we act arrogantly and cruelly, disregarding God, do we appease a human being for ourselves? By no means. For the very one who is despised stirs up against us the person whom, while despising God, we wish to appease. Let us therefore take every care to please God, who is able even to bring angry people back to gentleness.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The printed edition reads *placare Deum* (“to please God”).]

For, as I have said, even gentle people are provoked to anger when God is displeased.

If it is said that public frauds cannot be discovered without beatings and terror, I could have accepted this if Lord Leontius had not come in the matter of the accounts. For it is true that those who are deficient in understanding and speech are accustomed to go too far with their hands; and Your Glory cannot excuse yourself to me on this point.

[Col. 1107D] For, carefully investigating both what you hear and what you say, I discovered that 1080 you beat people without cause, although, with God’s help, you are able to conduct everything by words.

As for the cases of those whom you examine, I confess that, hearing many things I had never previously known, I am exceedingly ashamed. Therefore I keep silent about them both to you and to our most devout lord the emperor. For if it had been clear to me that they had just grounds in their accounts, I ought first to have addressed you by letter; and if I had not been heard, I would have brought the matter before the most serene lord emperor.

[Col. 1108A] But since nothing concerning their accounts is clear to me, for that reason, as I said, I have so far said nothing either to you or to the most devout prince. For it would be shameful for me to defend something whose justice had not first been established for me, since I love people on account of justice; I do not set justice aside on account of people.

Act, therefore, glorious son, so that in the undertaking entrusted to you you first have him appeased who contains all things, and then fulfill the interests of the most serene prince with every care. For I consider that you would not be free from sin if you were negligent in the undertaking entrusted to you by him.

[Col. 1108B] But since, by the bounty of Almighty God, Your Wisdom is capable both of investigating accounts vigilantly and carefully and of appeasing the judgment of the Creator toward you through gentleness, whenever anger invades your spirit, discipline your mind and conquer yourself. Delay the time of fury, and when your mind is calm, judge what is pleasing.

[Note: [Col. 1108D] The Vulgate reads *vindica* (“avenge”); we follow the Tours, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts.]

For anger ought to follow the mind’s reason in the punishment of evils, not precede it, so that, like a handmaid of justice, it may come behind rather than burst forward wantonly before its face. Sometimes it ought to be shown but not exercised; sometimes it ought to be exercised, but never followed. For when, in carrying out justice, we grow angry with a calm mind, we neither follow our anger nor conceal it: we exercise it.

The anger that disturbs the mind is shown to be something that must be avoided with the greatest care. Concerning it, Scripture says: “Let every person be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. For the anger of man does not accomplish the justice of God” (Jas. 1:19).

[Col. 1108C] Again it is written: “Who can dwell with a man whose spirit is quick to anger?” (Prov. 18:14). Again it is said: “Do not be with an angry man, nor walk with a furious man, lest perhaps you learn his ways and take a stumbling-block for your soul” (Prov. 22:24).

Against this, in praise of patience, it is written: “Better is the man who conquers anger than one who captures a great city.” Hence David, taking upon himself the role of the weak, says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Prov. 16:32). And he added what follows from that disturbance: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. 6:8).

For when the eye of the heart has been troubled by anger, we are brought to old age among our enemies, because among wicked spirits we are recalled to the likeness of the old man. Since, then, the sacred writings condemn the anger that moves the heart with so many testimonies, let us consider 1081 with what determination we ought to flee this vice, which, with God as judge, is so often rejected in his testimony.

[Col. 1109A] Another allegation has also come to light: that some are burdened more heavily than others, and that certain expenses made by order of the principal authority are not reckoned at all. Whether this is true, I do not know. Yet if it is so, you ought by no means to do this, both out of fear of eternal judgment and for the sake of ordinary human consideration.

Behold, glorious son, prompted by love for God and for you, I have briefly indicated everything I have felt and everything I have heard. It is the mark of a wise man both to weigh at greater length what he has heard briefly and to correct quickly whatever displeases God.

May Almighty God surround you with the protection of heavenly grace, so that here he may guard you from evil actions and wicked people, and afterward make you rejoice before him with a gracious reward in the eternal homeland. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 47.)

## Letter LII. To Amandinus, the *Domesticus*

He says that, in accordance with Amandinus’s request, he both received the things sent and wrote to the exarch concerning the prefect John. What he wrote to Amandinus about Libertinus ought not to have been received with displeasure, but as something written frankly by a friend.

[Col. 1109B]

Gregory to Amandinus, the *domesticus*.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] EPIST. LII.—There were many kinds of *domestici*, whose enumeration would require a longer discussion. At times they were like constant bodyguards for protecting the sacred person; at times they constituted a rank belonging equally to ecclesiastical and political dignity. On the ecclesiastical *domestici*, see Balsamon, in the *Quaestiones*, and John, bishop of Citrium, in the *Responsiones*; Codinus, *On Offices*, discusses both kinds, and so forth. GUSSANV. The word *domestico* is absent from the Norman, Rheims, and most manuscripts.]

The things that Your Glory sent through Paul, the bearer of this letter, and Timarchus, the *excubitor*, have been received in the manner you wished. We have also written to our most excellent son the exarch through the aforementioned *excubitor*, who has departed for him, directing him to send here the security-bonds of the agents acting in place of the prefect John and of Palatinus together; informing him that unless he sends them, the things transmitted by Your Glory are not to be touched until your arrival, but are to be preserved for you when you return.

Concerning the person of the glorious Libertinus, certain matters had previously reached us; and it was necessary that we not keep them silent from you, since you are truly sons whom we love. From what we found in Your Glory’s letters, you received those matters with displeasure, which was not fitting, although we do not remember having written anything harsh. Rather, we encouraged you to show him affection and favor.

But when you wrote back harshly in response to these matters, you wrote that in a dream you had been forbidden to send that very letter to us.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] The Norman, Remigius, and Vatican D manuscripts read “in response to these matters yesterday evening.”]

We give thanks to Almighty God, who watches over you while you are awake in such a way that he also admonishes you while you sleep. But since you write that in the same dream you were rebuked by me concerning the same matter, gather from this also what sort of person I am.

[Col. 1109D] And when I admonish you with paternal exhortation, you ought not to receive it with displeasure, because I who am sincere with you when you sleep do not permit myself to be two-faced with you when you are awake.

[Note: [Col. 1109D] The Norman, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Rheims manuscript read *convenio* (“I admonish” or “I address”), rather than the printed reading.]

1082

[Note: [Col. 1109D] EPIST. LIII.—This letter, together with the four following it, is omitted in most manuscripts.]

## Letter LIII. To Romanus, the Defender

He warns Leontius not to give his assent to the words of wicked men against the rights of the citizens of Naples.

[Col. 1110A]

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

It has come to our attention that certain men, moved by a purpose of evil will, are attempting to take away from Leontius, our glorious son, the islands belonging by right to the elders and citizens of the city of Naples, so that they may unjustly inflict and impose losses upon them.

[Note: [Col. 1110D] It is not entirely clear to me which islands he mentions. Some islands are washed on every side by the waves; others are houses in cities, as may be read in reputable authors, so called because they are not joined to other houses by common walls. There were more such houses, or islands, in Rome than other kinds, as Publius Victor teaches. Perhaps these islands belonged to the elders and citizens of the city of Naples; and, as Gregory says, their rights included Ischia, or *Icla*, and certain other maritime islands opposite Naples, which the Neapolitans enjoyed, relying on the commands and letters of earlier emperors. GUSSANV.]

For this reason we instruct you by this order to be vigilant. Although there may be no opportunity for fraudulent misrepresentation in this matter before him, if anything should perhaps be said, or if you should happen to discover that he has done something prejudicial—which we do not believe—then we wish you to tell him, by our command, that he must not give assent to the words of wicked men or involve himself in this offense.

For although they are entirely protected concerning those same islands by the commands of former emperors, nevertheless, while we were in the royal city, with our support their rights were so strictly secured by an order obtained from the most serene lord Prince Maurice that they have no just reason for fear.

Therefore, so that you may be more fully informed and may, if the case arises, give a clear account to the aforementioned glorious son of ours, we have arranged for copies of those orders to be sent to you. If necessary, we shall have the originals themselves sent as authenticated documents.

The only thing required is that, as we have said, you take care that no opportunity be opened there for anyone to carry out a fraudulent seizure.

## Letter LIV. To Donus, Bishop of Messana

He commends Gregory, the former prefect.

[Col. 1110C]

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messana.

Although our glorious son Gregory, the former prefect, has great confidence in your fraternity and does not doubt that priestly affection will be shown him by you, nevertheless, because he trusts that the measure of your charity will be increased at the urging of our recommendation, we have decided to exhort you by this letter to join in advancing his interests and to devote to his assistance whatever reason may advise.

And because he wishes, as he says, to undertake certain matters among your fraternity for his own protection, let him find a place with you, as is truly fitting for priests, and let him recognize that you sympathize with him with paternal affection. Thus, when the care of his affairs has been relieved through the zeal of your charity, he himself may be able to experience by your actions the confidence he has in you, and your fraternity may appear to have beneficially devoted itself to the wishes of one who asks.

1083

## Letter LV. To Leontius, the Former Consul

He commends Gregory, the former prefect.

Gregory to Leontius, the former consul.

Since the vigor of justice in your examination, and the truth, are sufficient to assist those whom you protect, there would have been no need for anyone’s recommendation before you, since you yourselves provide what ought to be requested on grounds of equity.

But so that we may not appear to disregard the wishes of those who ask, trusting that the devotion of good sons grows through paternal exhortation, we are therefore urged in every way to undertake before Your Glory what you voluntarily extend to everyone.

Accordingly, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask that you grant more abundantly to our glorious son Gregory, the former prefect, the grace of charity with which you are endowed;

[Note: [Col. 1111D] The Remigius and Victorinus manuscripts read: “grant, and cause justice to be preserved for him in every respect according to your custom, so that …”]

so that he may experience through genuine results whatever equity he trusts in your kindness, and so that we, learning the good things repeatedly said about you, may continually be able to pray to Almighty God for the safety of Your Glory.

## Letter LVI. To Amandinus, the *Domesticus*

He commends Gregory, the former prefect.

Gregory to Amandinus, the *domesticus*.

Trusting that Your Glory always presents yourself as devoted to the support of your friends, we make a point of commending to you the cases of those whom you love. Therefore, greeting you, we ask that our glorious son Gregory find you there such as he found you here;

[Note: [Col. 1111D] The printed editions have the faulty reading *quales nos hic habuit* (“such as he had us here”). It should read *quales vos hic habuit* (“such as he found you here”), as it is also read in the aforementioned Remigius, Saint Victor, and other manuscripts.]

and that both before our glorious son Leontius and elsewhere, wherever necessary, he may obtain the support of Your Glory and find great consolation in you. As far as possible, let the vigilant care of Your Glory provide that he not be subjected to anyone’s unjust affliction or burden, and let it strive to avert this through calm and mature counsel.

Thus, while he has you as helpers, as is fitting, both he and we may come to know more fully that, as we presume concerning Your Glory, you show us friendship not outwardly but—what is highly praiseworthy—with sincere hearts.

## Letter LVII. To Secundinus and John, Bishops

He commends Gregory, the former prefect.

[Col. 1111D]

Gregory to Secundinus and John, bishops of Sicina.

The love of good sons urges us to join diligently in advancing their interests and to assist them insofar as reason permits. Therefore, because 1084 our glorious son Gregory, the former prefect, presented himself kindly to everyone, he ought to enjoy everyone’s support.

[Col. 1112A] We exhort your fraternity in these words to hasten, upon his arrival there, to offer him assistance and support both before Leontius, the glorious former consul, in arranging his affairs, and before others wherever the case requires, so that, with justice favoring you, he may not incur any trouble or loss contrary to the order of equity, while you assist him in a priestly manner.

If, contrary to our belief, you should perceive that he is being needlessly burdened in any matter, you must act before the aforesaid glorious man, while preserving episcopal modesty, so that he may guard and maintain the word which he gave him through Azimarchus, the magnificent *scribo*, and may not permit him to be irrationally afflicted or to suffer loss.

Let your fraternity therefore take care to show yourselves attentive toward him and strive to conduct yourselves in his affairs according to God, so that he may find in you both priestly assistance and paternal affection.

## Letter LVIII. To Boniface, Bishop of Reggio

He orders that Gregory’s case with his church be settled without delay, and commends Gregory’s people to him.

Gregory to Boniface, bishop of Reggio.

It undoubtedly befits priestly seriousness that, if a bishop has any cases involving his church, he should settle them either by peaceful arrangement, if this can be done, or certainly by the intervention of judgment and without delay, so that, once the source of contention has been removed, only the harmony of peace may remain between him and his sons.

Our glorious son Gregory, the former prefect, has therefore informed us that some dispute has arisen between himself and your church concerning certain properties to which he lays claim.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] The Norman, Rheims, and Vatican D manuscripts read *Greg. expraefectus* (“Gregory, the former prefect”).]

[Col. 1112C] For this reason we exhort you either to end the matter once the quarrel has ceased, or, certainly, removing all delay, to cause the agents of your church to submit to the judgment of chosen judges, so that, after their decision has been given, neither may he appear to be burdened contrary to justice nor may your church appear to suffer prejudice.

Since he wished his people and the possessions he has there to be commended to you, your charity ought not to omit, in his cases, whatever reason prompts you to offer. Hasten to help him in every matter in which you are able, so that, with you assisting him, he may not find himself absent from the interests of his own affairs.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] EPIST. LIX.—This letter, together with the two following it, is absent from many manuscripts.]

## Letter LIX. To John and Fortunatus, Bishops, and Anthemius, the Subdeacon

He commends Gregory’s people and possessions.

[Col. 1112D]

Gregory to John and Fortunatus, bishops, and Anthemius, the subdeacon.
