[Note: [Col. 1112D] John was perhaps the bishop of Surrentum, to whom Letter 25 of Book IX was addressed. Fortunatus was a Neapolitan.]

We ought not to deny to our sons, when they ask, what it is fitting for us voluntarily to provide for them. Therefore, since 1085 our glorious son Gregory, the former prefect, has asked us to commend to your fraternity the possessions he has there and his people, we exhort you by this present letter to join in advancing his interests, with due regard for justice, and to protect his possessions and people as he desires.

Do not permit them to be harassed or burdened contrary to justice by anyone. Rather, act so that through your protection you may supply the presence of our aforementioned son, for he has conducted himself so well toward everyone, as you know, that he deserves every kind of support.

## Letter LX. To Azimarchus, the *Scribo*

Gregory’s late arrival in Sicily was not deliberate, but was caused by bodily illness.

Gregory to Azimarchus, the *scribo*.

Our glorious son Gregory, the bearer of this letter, delayed coming to Sicily not by choice, but was so weakened by bodily illness that he could scarcely recover over many days. You will still recognize the signs of this weakness in him.

As soon as he recovered somewhat, he did not neglect to come there, as he had promised Your Greatness. We have therefore decided to write this brief letter, lest, believing that he had delayed voluntarily, you should perhaps think that his delay had been caused by deliberate intention.

## Letter LXI. To Adeodatus, Abbot of Naples

He unites the Gazarian monastery with Adeodatus’s monastery until a bishop is appointed at Naples, but unites the Puteolan monastery permanently.

Gregory to Adeodatus, abbot of Naples.

A report from certain monks of the same monastery has reached us: the monks of the Gratterian monastery, situated at Plaia, had earnestly requested that they and their monastery be united with the monastery of Saint Sebastian, which was built at Naples in the former house of Romanus, where, as has been said, by God’s mercy you exercise the office of abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] EPIST. LXI [al. 39].—The printed edition reads “the Gazarian [monastery] … in Plagia … and the monks of the monastery of Saint Sebastian which …” We adhere to the English, Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and Vatican manuscripts.]

They had even, it is said, handed over all the documents of that monastery to your monastery. But because that monastery is situated in the Neapolitan diocese, and so that we may not appear, God forbid, to establish anything prejudicial, we wish that, until a bishop is appointed at Naples, the aforementioned Gratterian monastery, with everything belonging to it, remain meanwhile united to your monastery.

When a bishop has been ordained at Naples, we shall consider more carefully and firmly, with God’s grace, whether this union ought to extend permanently or be temporary.

Since, however, the monastery situated at Puteoli, called Falcidian, 1086 is reported to be so deprived of monks that not only is God’s work not celebrated there at all, but it is also almost regarded as abandoned—which is grievous to say—we have therefore decided, by this present authority, to unite it permanently with your monastery, together with everything belonging to it.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] Puteoli, commonly Pozzuolo, was formerly a well-cultivated city of Campania; it is still a bishopric under the archbishop of Naples. GUSSANV.]

We admonish you to appoint monks to both of the aforementioned monasteries, who will diligently care for them there and strive to perform the work of God according to regular discipline. Conduct yourself in these matters as is fitting, so that no fault may bring shame on them for neglect or on you for insufficient care.

Whatever you recognize as belonging to these monasteries, if it is being irrationally withheld by anyone, you shall have, by virtue of this authority of ours, full permission, with God’s help, to reclaim it, exact it, and vindicate it for your monastery, since it is fitting that you not be defrauded in any way of the property of those whose care you undertake.

But know that the monks whom you appoint to the monastery situated at Puteoli are to be under your discipline, yet are subject to the bishop of Puteoli, whose diocese it is, and not to the bishop of Naples.

## Letter LXII. To the Neapolitans

Neither John ought to have been elected bishop, since he is not chaste; nor Peter, if he is careless and a usurer. They should therefore provide for themselves another suitable man from the clergy of their church.

Gregory to the clergy and noble citizens of Naples.

It is neither new nor reprehensible in the election of a bishop for the votes of the people to be divided into two parts (Gratian, Dist. 8, question 1, chapter 17). But it is a serious matter when, in such cases, the election proceeds not from judgment but from mere favor.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] EPIST. LXII [al. 40].—That formerly the people’s votes were required for the canonical election of bishops, Saint Gregory teaches frequently in his letters. But I observe another custom introduced by a recent author, who, while treating another matter, noted the first letter of the bishops of Tarragon to Pope Hilary. There they speak of Silvanus, who, setting aside the rules of the Fathers and disregarding the institutions of the Apostolic See, had ordained a bishop when no people had requested one—that is, without awaiting the votes of the people or the consent of the inhabitants of the place. For this reason the Fathers of the Roman council acclaimed before the Pope, in defense of the ecclesiastical canons violated by that bishop: “We ask that discipline be preserved; we ask that the canons be guarded.” GUSSANV.]

Before your letters had circulated to us, we learned from the report of certain people that John the deacon, who was elected by one of the two parties, had a little daughter.

[Col. 1114C] Therefore, if they had wished to consider the matter properly, they ought neither to have elected him nor he to have consented. For with what presumption does he dare approach the episcopate who is shown, by the testimony of his little daughter, still not to possess the long-standing continence of his own body?

Peter, likewise a deacon, whom you assert was elected by you, is, as reported, altogether simple-minded. And you know that at this time such a man ought to be placed at the helm of governance who knows how to be concerned not only for the salvation of souls but also for the external welfare and protection of his subjects.

For you should also know that a report has reached us concerning him that he lent solidi at interest; you must investigate this with every care.

[Col. 1114D] If it proves to be so, elect another and without delay remove yourselves from association with such a person. For we impose hands on lovers of usury under no circumstances.

But if, after careful investigation, this is shown to be false—for his character is unknown to us, 1087 and we do not know whether what has been reported to us concerning his simplicity is true—then, with the decree made by you, he must come to us. We shall investigate his life and conduct more carefully and at the same time learn his understanding, so that, if he proves suitable for this judgment, we may, with the Lord’s help, fulfill your wishes in him.

Moreover, it should also be the object of your zeal to provide another suitable man, so that, if this man should not appear fit for the order, there may be someone toward whom your election can perhaps turn.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] It is a disgrace to the clergy when no one is chosen from the bosom of its own church. GUSSANV.]

For it will be a grave disgrace for that clergy if, should this man perhaps not be approved, they say that they have no other man who ought to be elected.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Recent editions add “in the month of August, indiction 3,” which none of our manuscripts has. In those manuscripts, however, this chronological note belongs to the following letter, as we shall presently show.]

## Letter LXIII. To Dominicus, Bishop of Carthage

He teaches with what disposition the scourge of plague should be received; what fruit should be gathered from it; and how those who are struck should be consoled.

[Col. 1115B]

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage.

We learned long ago how great a plague has invaded the regions of Africa; and because Italy also is not free from such a blow, our groans of sorrow are doubled.

But amid these evils and countless other calamities, our heart, dear brother, would fail in despairing distress unless the Lord’s voice had fortified our weakness in advance.

[Note: [Col. 1115D] Vatican A and F read *praemonuisset* (“had forewarned”).]

Long ago, indeed, the trumpet of evangelical teaching sounded for the faithful that, as the end of the world approached, plague, wars, and many other things—which, as you know, are still feared—would come (Matt. 24; Luke 21).

Therefore, since we suffer things that we knew beforehand, we ought not to be excessively afflicted by them as though they were unknown. For often one kind of death is a relief when compared with another kind of death.

How many mutilations and how many acts of cruelty have we seen, for which death alone was a remedy and life itself a torment? When David was offered a choice of death, did he not reject famine and the sword and choose to fall into the hand of God with his people (2 Sam. 24:14)?

From this, consider how great is the grace in those who die by divine striking, when they depart by that calling which is known to have been offered to the holy prophet as a gift.

Let us therefore give thanks to our Creator in all adversities, and, trusting in his mercy, endure everything patiently, because we suffer far less than we deserve.

Nevertheless, since we are scourged temporally in such a way that we are not left without the consolation of eternal life, it is necessary that, the more we know from these signs announcing it that the Judge is soon to come, the more we fortify the accounts we shall place before his tribunal through zeal for good action and tears of repentance.

[Col. 1115D] Thus, with his grace favoring us, these great blows may prove for us not the beginning of condemnation but the benefit of purification.

But because the nature of our weakness is such that we cannot help grieving for those who die, let the teaching of your fraternity be a solace to the afflicted. Let it make known to them the enduring good things that are promised, so that, strengthened by the most certain hope, they may learn 1088, in comparison with the future reward, not to grieve over the loss of temporal things.

[Col. 1116A] Let your tongue, as we also believe it does, restrain them more and more from committing evil deeds; let it explain the rewards of good things and the punishments of evil things, so that those who love good less may at least fear evil and refrain from those acts that deserve punishment.

For to commit deeds deserving of scourges while placed among scourges is especially to act arrogantly against the one who strikes and to provoke more sharply the anger of the one who is raging.

It is the first kind of madness to refuse to let anyone justly desist from his evils, and to wish God unjustly to cease from his vengeance.

But since these matters require divine assistance, let us, dear brother, join our prayers and beseech the mercy of Almighty God, so that he may grant us both to perform these duties worthily and mercifully move the hearts of the peoples to carry them out.

Thus, ordering our actions beneficially in his fear, may we deserve, under the guidance of his grace, without which we can do nothing, both to be rescued from the evils that are pressing upon us and to reach the joys above.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] This is how it is read in two Colbert manuscripts and in Vatican A, B, D, and E.]

In the month of August, indiction 3.

## Letter LXIV. To Romanus, the Defender

Although the *scribo* is a good man, he is not to lease the church’s property; rather, each year he is to offer Gentio what he would have earned from the lease.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

[Col. 1116C] Since our son Gentio, the magnificent man and *scribo*, is, by God’s favor, of such great goodness that he ought to be greatly loved, we should have conferred something upon him if we had been able.

For he had wished to hold property belonging to the church under the form of *libelli*.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] On this term, see what we said in Book I, Letter 44, concerning the word *libellaria*. GUSSANV.]

But because of the wicked *scribones*, we judged that in this matter we ought not to entrust even a good man with it. Therefore, setting aside from the property whatever could be turned to his advantage, we wish the same to be offered to His Greatness each year: namely, twenty pigs, twenty wethers, and sixty hens, in whatever manner you yourself may arrange.

[Note: [Col. 1116D] The Remigius manuscript does not have “twenty wethers.”]

We wish all these things to be reckoned among the items set aside.

## Letter LXV. To Adeodata

He excuses the delay in giving the relics, which he finally sends.

[Col. 1116D]

Gregory to Adeodata, the illustrious woman.

We did not delay by choice in giving the relics that Your Glory requested; rather, the outcome of the preceding matter caused us to hesitate. But Almighty God, observing the devotion of your heart and admonishing us through signs of miracles, did not permit you to be deprived of your purpose.

He therefore wished your desire to be delayed for a short time, so that, as miracles bore witness, your love for the veneration of the saints might grow and the exultation of your joy might become greater.

Since, therefore, the wishes of Your Glory have been fulfilled in the outcome of the matter requested,

[Note: [Col. 1117C] EPIST. LXV [al. 62].—The printed editions read *in affectu* (“in affection”), against the testimony of the manuscripts. The correct reading is *in effectu* (“in the outcome” or “in reality”).]

we exhort you to serve 1089 diligently the commands of the one whose heralds you venerate.

And just as, with religious devotion, you build earthly places in honor of the saints, so also hasten to secure for yourself a dwelling with them in heaven, so that you may deserve to have them as helpers in all things here and as companions in the life to come.

## Letter LXVI. To Decius, Bishop of Lilybaeum

After the customary security measures have been taken, he is to consecrate the monastery built by Adeodata.

[Col. 1117B] Gregory to Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum.

[Note: [Col. 1117C] EPIST. LXVI [al. 63].—In Vatican A, *Lilavitanus* is read; below, *Lilavitanam*.]

Adeodata, a distinguished woman, represented to us in a petition that the following is the case: namely, that within a house belonging to her by right, in the city of Lilybaeum, she had founded from the ground, out of her devotion, a monastery of handmaids of God, which she desired to have consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs of Christ Lawrence, Hermes, Pancratius, Sebastian, and Agnes. And therefore, dearest brother, since the building in question lawfully lies within your city, if it is established that no body has been buried there, after first receiving a lawful endowment—namely, ten solidi in revenue, exempt from fiscal taxes; three boys; three pairs of oxen; five other servants to serve in the monastery itself; ten mares; ten cows; four vine-props; forty sheep; and so forth—according to custom.

[Note: **Letter 67 [Al. 64].**]

## LETTER 67. TO HILARY, THE NOTARY

He orders that the ship sent for the support of the monastery be protected in every respect.

Gregory to Hilary, the notary.

You should know that the ship on which Vitalis, the bearer of this letter, is sailing was sent to our dearest daughter Adeodata, the abbess, for the support of her monastery. When it arrives there, by this authority of ours we order you to protect it in every respect and hasten to exempt and excuse it from every requisition or burden, as though it were specially ours. For, by God’s favor, such a great community is known to dwell in that monastery for our sake that we hasten to comfort and assist it more than our own Church in every matter. Therefore, once your experience has learned that our will regarding the aforesaid monastery is such, let it devote itself to the protection of the said ship, as we have instructed, so that, while you are there, it may suffer no delay or hindrance from anyone. For if—which we do not believe—you should attempt to be negligent in any respect, know that you will incur our severe displeasure.

## LETTER 68. TO OPPORTUNUS OF APRUTIUM

He comforts him, saddened by harsh correction, and exhorts him to complete conversion.

[Col. 1118B]

Gregory to Opportunus of Aprutium.

[Note: **Letter 68 [Al. 14, indiction 5].** In Vatican manuscripts A and E: “to Opportunus of Abrutium”; in Vatican B and one Colbert manuscript: “to Opportunus, bishop of Abrutium”; in Vatican D and two Teller manuscripts: “to Opportunus, abbot.” Aprutium in Samnium is called Interamna, commonly Teramo, because it lies between the rivers Turdinus and Viciola.]

It has come to my attention that, from the time when I saddened your affection with harsh words on account of certain matters that rightly displeased me, great sadness and continual sorrow of heart have arisen in you. Therefore, dearest son, I wish you to know that I spoke those words not from harshness of heart but from love for your soul.

Turn, then, with your whole mind to almighty God. Consider how insignificant this fleeting present life is. Hasten to win eternal rewards. As far as strength permits, chastise the flesh, which, as long as it lived in pleasures, chastised the soul. Show your kindness to your neighbors. Devote the hours of your life more frequently to psalmody and tears. Endure with equanimity the evils inflicted by your neighbors. If you suffer injury for the truth’s sake, regard it as gain, so that by doing these things, through the temporal hardships you endure by despising them, you may reach the heavenly kingdom.

May almighty God pour the salvation of heavenly grace over your heart and body, so that, through his Spirit, you may be able both to think rightly within and to act rightly outwardly.

# BOOK ELEVEN

In the month of September, indiction 4.

[Col. 1117]

## LETTER 1. TO JOHN, ABBOT

He commends himself to his prayers and prays eternal blessings for him. He sends beds and bedding for the use of pilgrims.

[Col. 1117D]

Gregory to John, abbot of Mount Sinai.

[Note: **Book XI. Al. Book IX. Letter 1 [Al. Book XII, indiction 7].** This appears to be John, abbot of Mount Sinai, surnamed Climacus, a man most famous throughout the East for holiness and writings. This letter makes no mention of his Ladder, from which he received the name *ἀπὸ τοῦ κλίμακος* (“from the ladder”), since he wrote it only after the death of Saint Gregory, who died in the year 604. The reader may consult his Life, written in French and prefixed to his works, in which he will learn many things most worthy of knowledge. — Gussanville.]

The holiness of your life is attested by your letter of humility. Therefore we give great thanks to almighty God, because we know that there are still those who are able to intercede for our sins. We, under the appearance of ecclesiastical government, are tossed upon the waves of this world, which frequently overwhelm us. But, as the hand of heavenly grace protects us, we are lifted from the depths.

You, therefore, who lead a tranquil life in such serene repose and stand secure, as it were, upon the shore, extend to us who are sailing—or rather, who are shipwrecked—the hand of your prayer. Help us, as we strive to journey toward the land of the living, with as many prayers as you can, so that you may be able to receive an eternal reward not only for your own life but also for our deliverance.

May the Holy Trinity protect your affection with the right hand of its protection, and may it grant you, by praying, admonishing, and displaying examples of good works, to feed rightly in the sight of your Redeemer the flock entrusted to you, so that you may be able to reach the pastures of eternal life with the flock you feed.

[Note: The printed editions read: “by showing zeal for good work, to feed [the flock] rightly in the sight of its Redeemer.”]

For it is written: “My sheep will come, and they will find pasture” (John 10:27). We find those pastures when, freed from the winter of this life, we are satisfied by the verdure of eternal life as by a new spring.

From our son Simplicius we have learned that beds or bedding are lacking in the hospice, which was built there by a certain Isaurian. Therefore we have sent fifteen *laenae*, thirty *rachanae*, and fifteen beds.

[Note: *Lectisternia* here means the same as covered or prepared beds. In chapter 22 of the Rule of Saint Benedict: “Let each one sleep in his own bed. Let each receive bedding according to his manner of life, in accordance with the provision of his abbot.” Thus, what purpose is served here, with Gussanville, by discussing the *lectisternia* once used by pagans in temples for supplication?]

[Note: Pilgrimage to Mount Sinai was frequent. The pope congratulates the patrician Rusticiana on her return from Mount Sinai and says that he would prefer to be her companion on the journey rather than on the return, Book IV, Letter 46. Among the places he reports having visited for religious reasons, Posthumianus, in Sulpicius Severus’ *Dialogue on the Virtues of the Monks of the East*, includes Mount Sinai. Sophronius records various pilgrimages of the Fathers to Mount Sinai in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 160, 170, and 180. On this occasion it is credible that Isaurian built the hospice on Mount Sinai, for which Gregory sends money and particular clothing for the use of the pilgrims who gathered there. — Alteserra. In Vatican manuscripts A and D, as well as in Lyranus, Audoenus, and Gemetensis, *Jericomio* is read. *Gerontocomia* are hospices for old men, and *Jericomia* may be called hospices for priests and clerics. On *gerontocomia*, that is, dwellings for old men, see Du Cange, *Constantinopolis Christiana*. Moreover, Hegesippus reports that the first *gerontocomium* was established by Hyrcanus, prince of the Jews. Emperor Maurice, imitating him among Christians, is said by Cedrenus to have built at great expense a house called an elaborate *vivarium* in which sick old men might be cared for, and so forth.]

[Note: From the Greek *κλαῖνα*, a thick garment, from *χλιαίνειν*, “to warm,” according to Hesychius and Suidas. The form *λαῖνα*, “a shaggy cloak,” is also found. Ennodius likewise uses the word, Book IX, Letter 17. — Gussanville. Here *laena* concerns bedding rather than clothing, as is clear even from these words: “We learned that bedding was lacking … Therefore we sent fifteen *laenae*.” See the learned Hugh Menard in his notes on the *Concordia regularum*, chapter 62, p. 893.]

[Note: Below, in Letter 75, Saint Gregory uses the same word, whose meaning scholars do not agree upon. To Sirmond, in Ennodius’ Letter 17, Book IX, it is a kind of footwear; to Hofmann, bundles of rushes that served especially monks and ascetics in place of pillows. Filesacus, in his commentary on Vincent of Lérins’ *Commonitorium*, interprets it as “breeches.” “From *ῥάκη*, *laena*, the Latin writers of the later age formed *racanos*,” says Du Cange in his notes on Cinnamus, p. 457. Consult his *Glossary*, as well as Le Moine, *Varia Sacra*, p. 287. The word occurs in Anastasius Bibliothecarius’ *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver*, chapter 9, no. 52. *Rachinae* are mentioned in the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 81, and by Saint Audoenus, Book II of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, chapter 37. See the learned Hugh Menard in his notes on chapter 62 of the *Concordia regularum*, p. 922.]

We have also provided funds for buying mattresses or for freight, which we ask you, out of affection, not to receive with disdain, but to distribute where it has been sent.

[Note: Alternatively, *culcitis*. *Culcitrae*, from *calcando*, “to tread down”; in French, *lit de plume*, *couche*; in Greek, *κοῦλκα*. Leo, in Constitution 6, has *κοῦλκα* and *βίγλα*. From this comes *ἐξκουλκεύειν*, “to unstuff” or “to keep watch.” — Gussanville.]

Given on the Kalends of September, indiction 4.

[Note: **Letter 2 [Al. 45, indiction 3].** In one Colbert manuscript this letter is the first of indiction 4.]

## LETTER 2. TO PALLADIUS, THE PRESBYTER

He consoles him, saddened by the words of his detractors. He teaches what should be done toward those who slander. He asks for prayers and sends clothing.

Gregory to Palladius, presbyter of Mount Sinai.

[Note: Sinai is a high mountain of Arabia Petraea, frequently mentioned in the sacred writings. — Gussanville.]

After receiving letters from your affection, I took care to inquire after my son Simplicius, and I discovered by what temptation your affection was being harassed. Yet it does not need the consolation of my words, since it itself says: “If they have called the master of the household Beelzebub, how much more his household servants?” (Matthew 10:25). It also says: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of this world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19). By “the world,” of course, it signifies carnal hearts that love the world.

Since, then, I hear that you know these things perfectly, I am astonished that your affection has been saddened by human words. Among words of praise or blame, one must always return to the mind; and if the good that is said of us is not found there, great sadness ought to arise. Conversely, if the evil that people say about us is not found there, we ought to leap for joy. What does it matter if people praise us while conscience accuses us? Or what sadness should there be if everyone accuses us and conscience alone shows us to be innocent?

We have Paul saying: “Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Job likewise says: “Behold, my witness is in heaven” (Job 16:20). If, then, our witness is in heaven and our witness is in our heart, let fools speak outside whatever they wish. What else do slanderers do but blow upon dust and raise earth into their own eyes, so that the more they blow the dust of slander, the less they see any truth?

Nevertheless, they themselves should be summoned, gently admonished, and satisfied in every way, remembering what the Truth says about them: “Lest perhaps we offend them” (Matthew 17:26). But if they do not wish to be satisfied by the truth, you have the consolation that you may observe in the holy Gospel. When it had been said to the Lord, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” (Matthew 15:12), he replied: “Leave them; they are blind, and leaders of the blind” (15:14).

The apostle Paul likewise admonishes us, saying: “If it is possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Romans 12:18). Since he was about to say that we should live at peace with everyone, and foresaw that this was difficult, he prefaced it with “If it is possible.” Yet he added what can be done when he said, “So far as it depends on you.” For if we wish to preserve love in our minds toward those who hate us, even if they do not have peace with us, we nevertheless unquestionably have peace with them.

Therefore, dearest son, guard your heart in every respect, as it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the sources of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

I have written this brief reply in remembrance of charity. But I ask that you pray for me, so that almighty God may deign to guard me both from evil spirits and from wicked people. For in this pilgrimage of my life many evils surround me at once, so that I may rightly say with the Psalmist: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They surrounded me like water all day long; they surrounded me all together” (Psalm 87:17–18).

May heavenly grace protect both us in the cities and you in the wilderness, for the ancient enemy is not excluded from temptation by earthly places. If he cast down man in paradise, what place outside paradise can there be into which he cannot penetrate the minds of human beings? Therefore we must trust solely in the protection of our Creator, to whom we cry from the depths of our heart: “Be for me a protecting God and a fortified place, that you may save me” (Psalm 70:3).

We have sent you, from the blessing of Saint Peter the apostle, a hooded garment and a tunic, which we ask you to receive with the same affection with which they were sent by us.

[Note: *Cuculla* was the garment both of monks and of others; the part covering the head and shoulders was called the *cucullus*. Gregory of Tours, Book VI, chapter 39: “When Bishop Sagittarius was attempting to flee with his head covered, someone drew his sword and cut off his head together with the hood.” The same occurs in the *Life of the Fathers*, chapters 8 and 17. Cassian, *On the Habit of a Monk*, chapter 11: “the covering of the hood,” and so forth.]

[Note: In one Colbert manuscript and in Vatican E is added: “In the month of September, indiction 4.” In the collection of Paul the Deacon: “Given on the Kalends of September, indiction 4.”]

## LETTER 3. TO PANTALEON, THE NOTARY

He orders that the deacon Deusdedit be ordained bishop of Milan and that he diligently arrange the interests of the Roman Church there.

Gregory to Pantaleon, the notary.

Your experience, supported by the authority of this present letter, is proceeding, with the Lord’s help, to the city of Genoa. There you are solemnly to have Deusdedit, a deacon of the Church of Milan, ordained bishop, provided that he has been elected by all and that nothing in his past life can lawfully stand in his way according to the sacred canons.

Moreover, since many interests of our Church there must, by God’s favor, be carried forward, you must be diligent and investigate and arrange everything usefully according to the chapter appended below, so that no fault of neglect may confront you, but rather that your vigilance may commend you to God and to men.

## LETTER 4. TO THE PEOPLE OF MILAN

After praising Constantius following his death, he rejoices that they have elected Deusdedit bishop. He rejects another man elected by the Lombards.

Gregory to the people, presbyters, deacons, and clergy of Milan.

We cannot adequately express in written words how greatly we are afflicted by the death of our brother and fellow bishop Constantius. But, would that the neighboring regions may not discover through a sudden calamity how many good things they have lost in one man.

For we were not unaware how solicitous he was in the discipline of ecclesiastical rule, nor how vigilant in protecting your city.

[Note: **Letter 4 [Al. 65, indiction 3].** Vatican D and Rheims: “Would that they may not feel it through a scarcely sudden calamity.” Vatican E and F: “Would that the neighboring regions may not feel a sudden calamity.” The Norman manuscript: “They lost, and would feel it through a sudden calamity.”]

But since, with the shepherd dead, it is not fitting for you to be without your own bishop, we gladly accepted the fact that, with God as your guide, you unanimously chose and signified your election of your deacon Deusdedit to the office of bishop. Therefore, since delay ought not to impede the desires of good endeavors, we hasten, with God’s grace, to fulfill your wishes in him.

And because the aforesaid man is known to us not by his character but only outwardly, you must be all the more diligent, since you understand that in this election not only your own advantage but also God’s cause is at stake. If, after careful inquiry, nothing in his past life can lawfully stand in the way of his candidacy under the sacred canons; if he is found suitable for maintaining discipline and exercising governance; and if, as you write, the consent of all agrees in his election, then, with the help of divine grace, we solemnly decree that he be ordained with the authority of these present writings.

But let what you report to us concerning Agilulf not disturb your affection. For we in no way give our consent to a man who is not elected by Catholics, and especially not to one elected by the Lombards. Nor, if he has been appointed through the usurpation of presumptuous authority, do we receive him into the place or order of a priest, since he is plainly shown to be an unworthy vicar of Saint Ambrose if he is ordained after being elected by such men.

[Note: “Vicar,” that is, successor. Below, Book formerly X, Letter 31, now in the promise of a certain bishop at the end of the letters: “To Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and to his vicar, blessed Gregory, or to his successors.” Anastasius, in his Life of Hadrian: “After taking an oath in faith and service to blessed Peter and to his vicar … Pope Hadrian.” Likewise in Leo III: “And just as he received the vicar of blessed …” Likewise in Vigilius: “To this Vigilius replied: Although unworthy, the vicar of blessed Peter the apostle …”]

[Note: Rheims reads: “if he has been made.”]

Nor should this matter frighten you or impose any necessity upon you, because the resources from which sustenance can be provided for the clerics serving Saint Ambrose are located not in enemy territory but, with God’s protection, in Sicily and in other parts of the republic.

Therefore, so that no delay may occur in ordaining the man whom you have elected, we have sent our notary Pantaleon, who is to have him consecrated, as is customary, with the authority of our consent.

[Note: The printed editions read “with our consent,” while the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts have “while he gives his consent.”]

We have also instructed him at present concerning the small estates that the presbyter Magnus once held in trust, and concerning the other interests of our Church, so that he may care for them or do whatever else he ought to do. Your affection should strive to show itself devoted to him in every matter, as is fitting.

## LETTER 5. TO INNOCENT, PREFECT OF AFRICA

He refers to him the complaints of Victor, bishop of Phausiana, so that he may restrain the harassment inflicted by the African judges.

Gregory to Innocent, prefect of Africa.

You may judge what one who desires Your Eminence to be the avenger of wicked deeds thinks of the benefit of its justice. Therefore we bring before you the full complaint, filled with grief, of our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Victor, bishop of Fausiana, so that you may correct the wicked in their wrongful conduct by practical measures and rescue those oppressed by the injustice they suffer.

[Note: See Book IV, Letter 29, concerning Fausiana.]

Our aforesaid brother complains that the African judges are practicing many acts of violence in their territories and many other things contrary to the manner prescribed by the edict; finally, that double taxes are being exacted there, a thing intolerable even to hear.

[Note: The printed editions read “from wrongful action.” We follow the Norman, English, four Vatican, and other manuscripts, which read “from the wicked action.” Vatican B reads “from wrongful action.”]

[Note: We have restored this chiefly from the English, Norman, Vatican, Tours, Corbie, and other manuscripts, with which the Paris edition of 1571 agrees. In the recent editions one finds “many or fines … violent.” In place of “in their territories,” many manuscripts have “in sacred or holy places.”]

[Note: The Vulgate reads “contrary to the fear of God.” Almost all the manuscripts, namely the English, Norman, two Vatican, and others, disagree.]

And since the correction of this evil especially awaits the authority of your dignity, we ask that you investigate it with careful inquiry and correct it as God commands you, so that you may come to the aid of the afflicted for the reward of your soul through the protection of justice, and by the example of this correction restrain others from wicked actions in the future.

[Note: We have taken this date from two Colbert manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, and Vatican B and E.]

In the month of October, indiction 4.

## LETTER 6. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He commends his deacon Florentius to Anatolius, his own deacon at Constantinople. He approves the proposed ordination. He reproaches him for negligence in a certain entrusted matter.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

We have received the letter of your fraternity, in which you stated that you wished to send your deacon Florentius to the royal city for the interests of your Church. Since you wished him to be commended to our dearest son Anatolius the deacon by a letter, we arranged to write to him that he should not delay assisting Florentius wherever necessary and possible. We have sent the letter itself to you, so that the person you appoint may carry it with him.

[Note: *Apices* here means letters or a letter, a part standing for the whole. Letters consist of written characters, or *apices*, and are therefore also called *litterae*. Hence “sacred characters” means imperial letters. Jurists use the word differently, speaking of *apices juris*, “the strict letter of the law,” which does not always agree sufficiently with equity. There were also other priestly *apices*, concerning which see Rubenius, *Electa*, Book II, chapter 33. — Gussanville.]

Regarding the person whom you say you wish to promote to the sacred order, it seems to us that, if there is nothing opposed to his life and no one raises against him the matter you reported, you should do what seems right to you. We intended to write to you that you should take care over other matters as well. But after we entrusted one matter to you and it was lost through your negligence, we chose to remain silent about the others, lest you likewise lose them.

## LETTER 7. TO ANATOLIUS, THE DEACON

He commends the deacon of Bishop Marinianus.

Gregory to Anatolius, deacon at Constantinople.

Our brother and fellow bishop Marinianus has written that he wishes to send his deacon to the royal city for the interests of his Church. Since he greatly wished the man to be commended to your affection, by this letter we exhort you to assist him wherever necessary, without compromising justice, and to hasten to help him in every respect, so that he may recognize in action the affection in which our aforesaid brother has great confidence.

## LETTER 8. TO ALEXANDER, PRAETOR OF SICILY

He commends John, deacon and rector of the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna in Sicily.

Gregory to Alexander, praetor of Sicily.

[Note: In the old edition: “to Alexander, prefect”; in recent editions: “to Alexander, presbyter of Sicily.” Vatican A and Rheims support the latter. Five English manuscripts, the Royal manuscript, and three Colbert manuscripts give the correct heading. Another Colbert manuscript reads “prefect of Sicily.”]

One who has no doubt about a son’s affection does not refuse to commend to him those whom he loves. Therefore, since the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna established in Sicily is said to have been so diminished that it seems as though no one were present there to administer its interests, it was necessary for our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus to consider how that patrimony might be administered so that it should not decline further.

[Note: Vatican D and E read “should fall away.” Rheims agrees.]

[Note: This is the reading of the Colbert, Norman, and other manuscripts, as well as of the old printed editions. Recent editions read: “Since he sent John for its administration.” We note this only so that Gregory’s phrasing may be recognized despite the more difficult and tangled wording.]

Since he has sent his deacon John to administer it, we greet you with fatherly affection and ask that you show him, as one sent by us, every kindness, as we trust you will.

## LETTER 9. TO LEO, BISHOP OF CATANIA

He commends Severus.

Gregory to Leo, bishop of Catania.

Our son Severus, a distinguished man and bearer of this letter, desires to come to Sicily and has asked to be commended to your fraternity by our letters. Therefore receive him when he comes with the priestly affection that is fitting, and provide him with your assistance wherever circumstances require it, so that, with you present, he may feel that he is nowhere laboring against justice, but rather, supported by your help, may securely enjoy the peace that he diligently loves. Thus we may rejoice in the tranquility that you have procured for him there.

[Note: **Letter 9 [Al. 5].** Another reading is “more securely,” as found in Vatican A and Victorinus, which alone among the manuscripts generally preserve this letter.]

## LETTER 10. TO TALITANUS

He exhorts Talitanus, administrator of the public patrimony, to defend the patrimony of the Roman Church from the harassment of the tax collectors.

Gregory to Talitanus.

Since we ought to have such confidence in your affection that, if the interests of our Church were being conducted among others, we would employ your distinction as an aid there, we ought to rejoice greatly that this cause is in your hands. For you ought not to neglect what, out of love for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, you could provide for him among others.

Since, therefore, we have learned that the administration of the public patrimony has been entrusted to your direction, we greet you with fatherly tenderness and commend to you, according to justice, the patrimony that belongs to our Church. If, as often happens, the public officials should seek, upon finding an opportunity, to inflict some harassment upon it, may the goodness of your greatness not permit this to occur, but protect it from all disturbance by those men.

[Note: We call *publicani* those who, by authority of the prince, collect taxes: fiscal agents, tax collectors, customs officials. In legal usage the term “men” often includes agents, procurators, clients, tenants, and so forth. It may be noted in passing that at the Council of Mâcon a certain bishop argued that women neither are nor can be called human beings. See Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book VIII, chapter 20. — Gussanville.]

In this way, while justice is preserved, let it attend to the interests of the poor, so that it may fulfill the role of almsgiving while justice is preserved, and so that a greater reward may thereby accrue to you before God’s eyes.

We therefore exhort you, dearest son, to show yourselves kind both toward the interests of our Church, which you love, and toward all the concerns of the Churches, so that you may duly fulfill what has been entrusted to you and make almighty God favorable to you—a matter to which you ought to devote the greatest effort.

## LETTER 11. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He is to act with Alexander so that Alexander’s case with Abbess Thecla may be settled without delay or contention.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

Since Thecla, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary, which is established at Naples in the former house of Felix the scholasticus, is known to have a case against Alexander, a distinguished man and her son-in-law, concerning certain matters, and has sent the bearer of this letter

[Note: This is undoubtedly Alexander, praetor of Sicily, to whom Letter 8 above is addressed.]

for the purpose of settling the case peacefully with him there, if possible, by the authority of your experience we order you not to fail to assist and cooperate with her wherever circumstances require, while preserving justice.

He should also strive to exhort the aforesaid distinguished man, so that, with all contention set aside, he too may proceed toward the settlement of her case with the intention of peace. If he should think it ought to be neglected, he will later be compelled, amid clamor and expense, to accomplish what he postpones fulfilling of his own good will. For, as we have been informed, he has frequently promised the aforesaid abbess by his letters that he would settle it, yet to this day he has delayed doing so.

Let your experience therefore act in such a way that either the case itself is settled, as we have said, or, if he certainly wishes to delay and you see that he does not intend to do what belongs to peace, report the matter to us carefully, so that we may know what ought to be done for the advantage of the monastery in question.

## LETTER 12. TO CONON, ABBOT OF LÉRINS

With what care and diligence he should govern the monastery entrusted to him. He commends Columbus, a presbyter.

Gregory to Conon, abbot of the monastery of Lérins.

[Note: **Letter 12 [Al. 8].** This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts and of the Paris edition of 1675. In most manuscript copies one reads “abbot of Syrinus.” That Conon was abbot of Lérins, as is read especially in the old Colbert manuscript, is clear from the fact that Saint Gregory learned of his diligence and vigilance through Bishop Menna, as is stated in this very letter. For from Book VI, Letter 52, we know that Menna was bishop of Toulon, and could easily have known the abbot of the neighboring island of Lérins. Conon, abbot of Lérins, is mentioned in the monastic martyrologies of Wion, Dorgain, Menard, and Bucelinus. From the first part of the *Chronology of Lérins*, p. 186: in a very ancient parchment codex of that monastery there is a catalogue of the saints and eminent men who flourished on the island of Lérins, among whom this man is numbered in the following words: “Saint Chononus, or Chononius, or Chonon, 29 May.” He flourished in the year 600. Moreover, not only on the island of Lérins but also on Lerone and the Stoechades there were very ancient monasteries, as Adolphe Valesius proves in his *Notitia Galliae*. Vatican D and E, Rheims, and the collection of Paul the Deacon read “to the abbot of Mount Lérins.” The island *Lerinus*, or *Lerina*, later called *Lirinus*, is Strabo’s Planasia; on the coast of Provence it lies scarcely two leagues from Antibes and five from Fréjus. Honoratus founded the monastery of Lérins before the year 410. He had been a monk and hermit under Saint Caprasius in the islands near Marseilles and later became bishop of Arles. See Book VI, Letter 56. Lérins was formerly a nourisher of saints and a nursery of bishops. Hence Sidonius Apollinaris, *Poem* 16, to Faustus:

> How many mountains that level island  
> Has sent to heaven; what was the holy life of aged Caprasius  
> And young Lupus; what grace remained with Father  
> Honoratus; who was that Maximus, whose city you govern,  
> Both monk and bishop and abbot, twice his successor,  
> Also celebrating in those praises  
> The journey of Eucherius coming and of Hilary returning.

Lupus was bishop of Troyes, Maximus of Riez, Eucherius of Lyons, and Hilary of Arles. Nor should Caesarius of Arles and Vincent the presbyter be omitted among the pupils of this island, men who may rightly be numbered among the earliest Fathers. Today this island is called Saint-Honorat de Lérins. Partly from Gussanville.]

The vigilance of superiors is the safeguard of those subject to them, because the person who watches over what has been entrusted to him avoids the enemy’s ambushes. We have learned from our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Menna how diligent you are in governing the brethren and with what zeal you remain vigilant in guarding them.

Just as the careless negligence of your predecessor often saddened us, so the diligence of your provision rejoices us. There is no doubt that the vigilance of your zeal will benefit you as a reward and others as an example of usefulness.

But since our adversary knows how to guard himself on every side, he seeks to break in through hidden means and uses crafty skill to overthrow anyone who resists him. Therefore let the vigilance of your affection continually kindle itself with ever more ardent care, and, with God’s help, fortify everything in advance, so that the raging wolf, running here and there, may find no opportunity to enter among the Lord’s sheep.

It should therefore be your concern, with the supporting grace of our Redeemer, to restrain and guard in every way those entrusted to you from gluttony, pride, avarice, idle talk, and every impurity, so that the greater reward may accrue to you from the government committed to you, the more your subjects, while you remain vigilant, may become victorious against the wickedness of the adversary.

Therefore, let the good find you gentle, and the wicked a corrector. In this correction, you should know that the following order must be observed: love the persons and pursue their vices, lest, if you should wish to act otherwise, correction pass over into cruelty and you lose those whom you desire to amend. For you must cut away the wound in such a way that you do not ulcerate what is sound; lest, if you press the iron more deeply than the matter requires, you harm the one whom you hasten to benefit. Let gentleness in you be cautious, not lax; and let correction be conscientious, not harsh. But let one be tempered by the other, so that the good may have, in what they love, something they must beware of, and the wicked, in what they fear, something they may love.

[Note: [Col. 1127D] This seems to have been drawn from the Rule of Saint Benedict, [Col. 1128D] chapter 64: “Let the abbot hate vices and love the brothers.”]

Attend carefully to these matters, dearest son, and guard them diligently, so that, when by such moderation you have returned unharmed to our God those whom you have undertaken to govern, on the day of eternal recompense you may deserve to hear him say: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Luke 19:17).

Moreover, we desire that our son, the priest Columbanus, who has been commended to your charity by his own merits, may prosper in your affection, and through our recommendation.

[Note: [Col. 1128D] In the Collection of Paul the Deacon there is added: “Given on the day of the Kalends of November, indiction 4.” This agrees with the Remigius Codex.]

## LETTER XIII. TO SERENUS, BISHOP OF MARSEILLES

The images of the saints ought not to have been broken; they should indeed not be worshiped, but should be permitted for instruction. By this reasoning, the minds of the faithful, whom the broken images had alienated, are to be won over. Wicked men are to be removed from intimacy and association.

[Col. 1128A]

Gregory to Serenus, bishop of Marseilles.

The beginning of your letter showed such priestly benevolence in you that our joy in your brotherhood became greater. But its conclusion differed so greatly from its beginnings that such a letter seemed to have come not from one mind but from different minds. From the fact that you doubted what we had written and sent to you, it became clear how incautious you are. For if you had carefully attended to what we admonished you with brotherly love, you would not merely have had no doubt, but would rather have understood what it was fitting for you to do with priestly dignity. For Cyriacus, once abbot, who carried our writings, was not possessed of such discipline or learning that he himself would dare to do something else, as you suppose, nor should you have adopted such a false suspicion concerning him. But because you postponed weighing salutary admonitions, it happened that you were now culpable not only in deed but also in your questioning.

For it had been reported to us (On Consecration, distinction 3, chapter 27) that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you had broken the images of the saints under the pretext, as it were, that they ought not to be worshiped.

[Note: [Col. 1128D] LETTER XIII [alternative numbering: 9].—On images, see above, Book IX, letter 105, indiction 2. The words of Saint Gregory forbidding the worship of images of the saints seem rather severe to Gussanville, who should be corrected by Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 94, article 2, reply to objection 1: “Images of the saints cannot and ought not to be worshiped with absolute worship, even of a lower kind, but only with relative worship; yet they are not properly said to be worshiped, nor was this the customary expression in ancient usage.”]

And indeed, because you had forbidden them to be worshiped, we praised you without reservation; but we censured you for having broken them. Tell me, brother: from what priest have you ever heard of such an act as the one you committed? If nothing else, at least this should have restrained you: that, scorning the other brothers, you should not think yourself alone to be holy and wise.

[Note: [Col. 1128D] Thus the Regius and other manuscripts, with the old editions agreeing. The recent editions preferred: “lest, despising the others.” On the honor due to sacred images, see above, Book IX, letter 52, at the end, and letter 105.]

For it is one thing to worship a painting, and another, through the story represented in a painting, to learn what ought to be worshiped. For what Scripture provides to readers, a painting provides to the uneducated who look at it: in it even those who do not know letters see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know how to read nevertheless read. Hence, especially for the Gentiles, a painting takes the place of reading. This you, who live among the Gentiles, ought especially to have considered, lest, while you were incautiously inflamed by righteous zeal, you should create a scandal among fierce-minded people.

Therefore what had been placed in the churches not for worship but solely for instructing the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken. And since antiquity, not without reason, permitted the stories of the saints to be painted in holy places, if you had tempered zeal with discretion, you could undoubtedly have obtained beneficially what you intended and gathered your flock rather than dispersing it; indeed, you could have gathered together those who had been dispersed, so that the title and merit of a shepherd might stand out in you, rather than the guilt of one who scatters the flock weigh upon you.

And now, while you carry out this incautious impulse of your mind, you are said to have scandalized your sons so greatly that the greater part of them suspended themselves from communion with you.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] “What,” says Gussanville, “will they think of this suspension, from the standpoint of the advocate of blind obedience?” The necessity of obedience should indeed not be extended beyond the established limits; but neither should it be so restrained that we favor rebels and seditious persons, or, indeed, the error of heretics concerning mutual excommunication.]

When, then, will you bring wandering sheep to the Lord’s fold, when you are unable to retain even those whom you have? Therefore we exhort you now at least to strive to be solicitous, to restrain yourself from this presumption, and to hasten with paternal gentleness, with every effort and every diligence, to recall to yourself the minds of those whom you know to have been separated from your unity.

[Col. 1129B]

For the dispersed children of the Church must be summoned, and it must be shown to them by testimonies of Sacred Scripture that it is not permissible to worship anything made by human hands, since it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Luke 4:8). Then it must be added that, because you saw that the painted images which had been made for the edification of the uneducated people—so that those who did not know letters might learn what had happened by contemplating the story itself—had passed into worship, you were moved to order those images to be broken.

And you must say to them: “If you wish to have them in the church for the instruction for which images were made in ancient times, I permit them in every way both to be made and to be kept.” And make clear that it was not the sight of the story itself, displayed with the painting as its witness, that displeased you, but the worship that had been improperly offered to the paintings. By speaking these words and soothing their minds, recall them to your concord. And if anyone wishes to make images, do not prohibit him at all; but forbid in every way that images be worshiped. Let your fraternity carefully admonish them in this respect, so that from seeing the event represented they may receive the ardor of compunction, and humbly prostrate themselves in worship of the holy Trinity alone, the Almighty.

We speak all these things both out of love for the holy Church and out of love for your fraternity.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] In the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts: “we speak to your fraternity out of love for your holy Church,” whereas the printed editions read: “we speak out of love for your holy Church to your fraternity.”]

Therefore, let my correction not break your zeal for righteousness, but rather strengthen you in the work of pious administration.

Furthermore, it has come to us that your affection willingly receives wicked men into its association, to such an extent that you keep as a close companion a certain priest who, after falling, is said still to be living in the pollution of his own iniquity. We do not altogether believe this, for whoever receives such a man does not correct crimes but rather seems to give others permission to commit similar acts.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The printed editions read: “lest perhaps someone should …”]

But lest some deception or concealment should have persuaded you to receive him and continue to regard him favorably, it is fitting not only that you drive this man far from you, but also that, with priestly zeal, you cut off his excesses in every way. As for the others who are remembered to be wicked, strive by paternal exhortation to restrain them from their wickedness and recall them to the way of righteousness. But if, God forbid, you see that they make no progress at all through salutary admonition, you should also cast them far from you, lest, because they are received, their wickedness seem not at all displeasing. Thus not only would they remain uncorrected, but others would also be corrupted by receiving them. Consider how detestable this is to human beings and how dangerous before God’s eyes: that vices should appear to be nourished by the very person by whom crimes ought to be punished.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The more recent editions, supported by scarcely one of our manuscripts, read: “Attend carefully with the ear of your heart.”]

Attend carefully to these matters, therefore, dearest brother, and strive to act in such a way that you both correct the wicked beneficially and do not introduce into the minds of your sons a scandal arising from association with evil men.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The Remigius Codex adds: “Given in the month of September, indiction 4.”]

(Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapters 30 and 45.)

[Note: [Col. 1130D] LETTER XIV. Alternative numbering: 17, indiction 7.]

## LETTER XIV. TO ASCLEPIODOTUS

He commends the Gallican patrimony of the Roman Church and sends a key containing relics.

Gregory to the patrician Asclepiodotus.

For prudent men such as you to adhere to kings is a source of comfort to many. For when they understand that a more distinguished position has been given them for the benefit of their souls, it is certain that they do not neglect opportunities for reward when they find them. Accordingly, we have learned from our dearest son, the priest Candidus, how eagerly and with what devotion your Excellency has applied yourself to the affairs of the poor with pious care.

But since nobility in some way imposes this law upon itself—that it should consider itself obligated by what it gives freely, and that, unless it increases its benefactions, it should regard itself as having given nothing—we greet your Excellency with paternal affection and confidently commend to you the aforesaid priest and the patrimony of our Church, so that, strengthened by the help of your grace, he may suffer no troubles or burdens.

Let care for this good work therefore advance in you, so that, with your support, the interests of the poor may prosper, and we may find true what we presume concerning your charity. Increase the protections of your favor, because among noble minds a good left without addition seems only half-complete.

And since we have asked the most excellent kings, our sons the Franks, to take this small patrimony under their protection, let it be accomplished with your assistance, so that what we request may become your responsibility. Thus, while we return thanks, we may pray more earnestly for the safety of your Excellency, and Almighty God may repay you both here and in the future for your good deeds.

We have also sent a key from the most sacred body of blessed Peter, containing a blessing from his chains, so that, suspended from your neck, it may protect you against every adversity.

## LETTER XV. TO ARIGIUS, BISHOP OF VAPINCUM

After a most friendly greeting, he commends the priest Candidus.

Gregory to Arigius, bishop of Gaul.

Search the secret places of your heart to discover how greatly the love of your fraternity is remembered among us, and you will gather it from the love that he has for us. And because sincere love is neither weakened by absence nor subject to forgetfulness, our mind is so often refreshed by imagining the presence of your fraternity that it is as though we saw you standing before us with bodily eyes; for one who remains joined to minds by the bond of love cannot be thought absent.

Since, therefore, we have observed in you so many ornaments of priestly gravity that we rejoice completely in your way of life and conduct, we make many promises to our minds concerning your solicitude. Because you conduct the affairs of God in such a way and watch over the flock entrusted to you so attentively, while nevertheless administering matters of secondary importance with prudent moderation, we commend to you the priest Candidus, the bearer of this letter and our common son, so that you may provide him assistance wherever necessary for the benefit of the poor.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Candidus, defender of the Gallican patrimony, had visited Gregory, as may be read in letter 54 of this book. This letter commends him to Arigius as he returns from Rome to Gaul, and the preceding letter commends him to Asclepiodotus.]

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The printed editions read: “supported by assistance, may he perceive that we have found you in his consolation.” The phrase “supported by assistance” is absent from the manuscripts; it disrupts the sense and should be omitted.]

Thus, while he belongs to your fraternity, as we trust he will, and is supported by your assistance, he may feel that we have found you in his consolation.

## LETTER XVI. TO THE PEOPLE OF MILAN

They are to show affection to Arethusa on her return to Milan and act so that her case may soon be concluded once a bishop has been appointed.

[Col. 1131C]

Gregory to the people, priests, deacons, and clergy of the Church of Milan.

The bearer of this letter, Arethusa, a most distinguished woman, has remained with us for a long time, as you remember, because of the legacy which our brother, the bishop of venerable memory Laurentius, had left to her, her husband, and her sons. For this reason we had sent our letter to our brother and fellow bishop Constantius, so that, with priestly diligence and without the tumult of disputes, he might settle the case with her. As you know, we believe, he had replied that he had wished to do this both formerly and still wished to do it at that time. But because the bearer of this letter has remained for a long time in this city and postponed her return there, the matter has not yet been decided.

Therefore, by this letter, we exhort your affection to show the aforesaid woman, when she comes there, the affection which the children of the Church ought to show. When, with God as author, the Church has been organized, act so that the case, which has been delayed for a long time, may be brought to an end without delay and with justice preserved. Thus neither will the aforesaid woman be seen to be wearied any further, nor will you appear, contrary to ecclesiastical purpose, to have denied those seeking it what is just.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] Understand this as: “show her the affection which the children of the Church ought to show.” Formerly the reading was: “show the affection which ought to be shown to the children of the Church.” The manuscripts reject that reading.]

[Note: [Col. 1132D] LETTER XVII. Alternative numbering: 11.]

## LETTER XVII. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He commends the widow Theodora, so that, because of her son’s ingratitude, she may not suffer poverty after having given him all her possessions when he married.

Gregory to Anthem­ius, subdeacon of Campania.

Theodora, widow of Sabinus the defender, having sent her man here, complained to us that she had been deceived by her son and by a certain Aligernus, whose daughter that son had married, so that at the time of the marriage she transferred all her possessions to the same son by way of a gift; and that she is now greatly despised and scorned by them, to such an extent that, after her property had been taken away, nothing remained to her from which she could support herself. Moreover, she asserts that she suffers such adversity from them that they do not permit even a slave belonging to her to serve her or provide her any assistance.

And because, if the matter is as she says, this is exceedingly serious and contrary to God, by the authority of this letter we command you to ascertain the truth. If you find the matter to be so, hasten to provide ecclesiastical protection and to assist her in every way while preserving justice, so that, while you are there, she may not again suffer any burden or oppression from the aforesaid men in any manner. Let it be your concern to ensure that she can lawfully receive assistance concerning the matter in which she complains that she was deceived, for it is altogether cruel that a woman who ought to hope for support from her son should through him instead be forced to endure need or poverty.

But if, perhaps, even the arrangement of her peace or her sole relief cannot be secured through your efforts, hasten to report to us, so that you may again learn from our instruction what you ought to do thereafter.

## LETTER XVIII. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is not to allow the men of Helena to be unjustly detained by the agents of the Roman Church.

Gregory to Anthem­ius, subdeacon.

Our glorious daughter Helena informed us through her men that certain persons belonging to her were being irrationally detained by the agents of our Church. Since she asks that they be restored to her, we therefore command you by this authority to investigate the truth with every diligence. If this is so, and there is nothing in them that can be claimed in the name of our Church, then, setting aside all delay, either restore the men themselves, or, if perhaps they are bound to our Church as dependents, provide substitutes for them in exchange.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] LETTER XVIII [alternative numbering: 12].—Someone who succeeds in another’s place is called a substitute (*vicarius*). Sometimes a slave-substitute was one who served a more important slave or took his place when he was absent or occupied. Thus Martial, Book II, epigram 18:

“Being a slave is enough; now I do not wish to be a substitute.”

Those were also called substitutes who were devoted in place of others, or who were given in compensation for other slaves. GUSSANVILLE.]

But if anything is said to belong to our Church, let the matter be brought to a conclusion without any delay; and let your experience carry into effect whatever has been judged, without any difficulty, so that there may not again be a necessity for our aforesaid daughter to send someone here.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] LETTER XIX. Alternative numbering: 13.]

## LETTER XIX. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He commends Donatus.

Gregory to Anthem­ius, subdeacon.

Donatus, the bearer of this letter, states that he is being burdened there by various forms of oppression and has asked to be supported by ecclesiastical protection. Therefore, by the authority entrusted to your experience, we instruct you to defend Donatus himself while preserving justice, and not to permit him to be subjected to any burdens or losses contrary to justice, so that, with your assistance, he may have no necessity to return here.

## LETTER XX. TO SCHOLASTICUS, DEFENDER

He is to lease to the impoverished bishop, in addition to the allotted *conduma*, a small vineyard. He is to restore the episcopal residence to him, without taking away what his father, the former bishop, acquired there. Finally, he is to hand over to him part of the legacy.

[Col. 1133B]

Gregory to Scholasticus, defender.

We remember having previously instructed your experience that, since our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Calumniosus declared that he was suffering a need of support,

[Note: [Col. 1133D] LETTER XX [alternative numbering: 14].—The Rheims manuscript reads: “he asserted that he was suffering the necessity of being destitute.” The Vatican D manuscript agrees.]

you ought to have assigned him one *conduma* belonging to the right of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] A *conduma* is a mass or estate belonging to the Church. A *conduma* was placed among the endowments of an oratory, church, or monastery. See below, Book XII, letter 11. Hincmar mentions a *conduma* of the Church of Rheims, called Tudiniacus, in the *Life of Blessed Remigius*.]

But because the same *conduma* is said to contain a small vineyard belonging to the right of our Church, and he likewise asks that this small vineyard be leased to him, we command you by this authority to lease that vineyard to him at three gold *siliquae*, with written contracts being drawn up, so that he may obtain some relief from it and the right of the Church may be preserved without any diminution.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] A gold *siliqua* was one twenty-fourth of a solidus. The solidus, as we observed in the note to Book III, letter 33, was one-sixth of an ounce. Thus the *siliqua* contained four grains and was equivalent to eight *asses*, according to the valuation of our coinage. *Libelli* have already been discussed in note r to Book I, letter 44.]

Furthermore, our aforesaid most reverend brother has complained to us that you have until now detained the episcopal residence of his Church and have used the occasion to pretend that you may appropriate to yourself the garments of your father the bishop, or other things found in the episcopal residence.

[Note: [Col. 1133D] The Rheims and Vatican D manuscripts read: “on the occasion of Bishop Blandinus.” The expression “from his own property” does not appear below in the cited manuscripts.]

Therefore, if this is so, we command you to leave the episcopal residence without delay, and not to take anything that can be shown to have been acquired for the Church from his own property by your aforesaid father during the time of his episcopate, since it is known to have been established by the sacred canonical laws that, among the things an overseer acquires during his episcopate, no one succeeds except the Church alone.

He also asserts that a certain Ferocinatus, having made a will, appointed our Church his heir, and left two estates from the *fundus* Campos, by way of a legacy, to the Church of Saint John situated before the gates of the city of Hortonepsis; and that these estates are now being detained by our Church. Since he asks that they be handed over to him according to the will of the deceased, let your experience, after reading the text of the will, and if you find the matter to be so, provided that nothing can reasonably be opposed by our Church, not delay handing the aforesaid estates over to our brother mentioned above. For while it is fitting that we also share our own property with such men, we in no way tolerate that what belongs to them should be irrationally detained by our people.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] Estates were so called from the houses or huts built upon them. Anastasius, in his account of Adeodatus, says: “He enlarged many new buildings and also acquired small estates.” The same author, in his account of Hadrian, says: “And many other estates, or small estates and masses.” In his account of Paschal: “With estates, small estates, and masses.” According to Gussanville, a *casale* consisted of several houses—a hamlet or village in French. William of Tyre, *History of the Holy War*, Book XXII, chapter 20: “They destroyed many suburban places, commonly called *casalia*, by setting fires and using other devices by which they could inflict harm.”]

## LETTER XXI. TO ROMANUS, DEFENDER

He is to grant Argent­ius, a hospitable man, the use and usufruct of a small plot of ten *modii*, so that he may practice hospitality more generously.

[Col. 1134B]

Gregory to Romanus, defender.

Since we know that Argent­ius, the bearer of this letter and a tenant of our Church, takes care of hospitality, it is necessary that we assist his efforts in some measure. Therefore, by the authority of this command, we instruct you to hasten, without any delay or excuse, to return to him the small plot of the Disterian estate which he held, measuring, as he asserts, approximately ten *modii*, so that he may possess it for the days of his life and contribute nothing from it toward the Church’s accounts, but may prosper in the hospitality that he provides. For it is right that in every way we should contribute to and support a good and praiseworthy work.

## LETTER XXII. TO SPESINDEUS, GOVERNOR OF SARDINIA

He is to assist Bishop Victor in converting and baptizing the Sardinians.

[Col. 1134C]

Gregory to Spesindeus, governor of Sardinia.

Without doubt, one shares in the reward of anyone who shows himself an assistant in good works. Since, therefore, many of the barbarians and provincials of Sardinia are said, by God’s favor, to be hastening most devoutly to the Christian faith, let your greatness appropriately apply its efforts to this cause and diligently assist our brother and fellow bishop Victor in converting and baptizing them.

Thus, while the souls of many are freed from destruction through the grace of baptism with your support, you may acquire both praise among human beings and, what ought to be earnestly sought, a great reward from the Almighty Lord. And we, returning thanks to you, may in every way show ourselves indebted to your greatness.

[Note: [Col. 1134D] LETTER XXII [alternative numbering: 17].—In the old Colbert manuscript he is called “Hope in the Lord.” In Vatican D the reading is “Gregory to Hope in the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 1134D] The printed editions omit *et* (“and”); we have added it on the authority of the Vatican manuscripts, five Colbert manuscripts, and others.]

## LETTER XXIII. TO VITALIS, DEFENDER OF SARDINIA

He is to assist Boniface in purchasing slaves among the Barbaricini.

Gregory to Vitalis, defender of Sardinia.

Let your experience know that we have sent the bearer of this letter, Boniface, our notary, there for the purpose of purchasing slaves among the Barbaricini for the benefit of the parish.

[Note: [Col. 1135D] LETTER XXIII [alternative numbering: 18].—In some manuscripts and old editions the corrupt reading *prothochii* occurs instead of *ptocho­dochii*; in other manuscripts *pto­chii* is more correctly found. The Greek *ptōcheia* means a house intended for feeding the poor, otherwise *ptōchodocheion*. GUSSANVILLE. Vatican A reads *protochii*, for *parochiae* (“parish”), which Victor has here. Below, however, it reads *in ministerio ptochii* (“in the service of the poorhouse”); because of the scarcity of manuscript witnesses, it is not easy to establish the true reading with certainty. We have found this letter only in Vatican A, the Victorine manuscript, and the Rheims manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 1135D] On the Barbaricini, see Book IV, letter 23. Procopius, *History of the Vandal War*, Book II, relates that they were driven from Numidia, a province of Africa, by the Vandals. “The Vandals,” he says, “who had long exercised their anger against these barbarians, sent not very many of them, together with their wives, to Sardinia, and ruled here (near Mount Aspis). As time passed, they occupied the mountains near Caralis; at first secretly carrying out raids against their neighbors, but later increasing to no fewer than three thousand, they openly made raids and took no care to remain hidden, ravaging the entire surrounding coast. For this reason they were called Barbaricini by their neighbors.”]

Therefore, let your experience assist him eagerly and carefully in every way, so that he may purchase at a good price such slaves as can be found useful in the service of the parish, and, after purchasing them, may return here more quickly, with God’s protection. Hast­en, then, to conduct yourself in this matter in such a way that you show yourself a lover of those for whose uses the slaves are being purchased, and that they may commend you to us for your concern.

## LETTER XXIV. TO JOHN, TRIBUNE OF SIPONTUM

He urges him to decide, together with Bishop Vitalianus, concerning the liberty of the bearer of this letter.

Gregory to John, tribune of Sipontum.

The bearer of this letter has repeatedly complained to us that Boniface, our notary, is inflicting violence upon him concerning his civil status. We arranged for the investigation of this matter to be brought to the attention of our brother and fellow bishop Vitalianus, who declared that he had examined the merits of the case. But because he says that he is in no way prepared to rise to deliver judgment, we exhort your greatness to sit with the aforesaid bishop for the sake of eternal reward; investigate the merits of the matter more clearly, and decide in writing whatever justice persuades you is right.

[Note: [Col. 1136D] LETTER XXIV [alternative numbering: 19].—Vatican A reads: “to be brought to completion.” None of our other codices contains this letter.]

If it becomes more certainly established to you that the man is free, let no one thereafter appeal to the merits of the matter already decided by any disturbance whatsoever; rather, once his freedom has been declared in the manner you judge appropriate, let him remain secure in it.

## LETTER XXV. TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF CARALIS

He praises him for refusing to build a monastery for men in a house adjoining the monastery of the servants of God. Nevertheless, he orders monks to be established either in the place from which the nuns have departed or in an abandoned monastery, and commends the matter to Januarius.

[Col. 1135D]

Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis.

Know that the concern of your fraternity was pleasing to us, since it displayed itself, as was fitting, with pastoral vigilance for the protection of souls.
