For it was reported to us that, according to the will of Epiphanius, once a lector of your Church, you forbade a monastery to be built in his house, lest, because the house adjoined a monastery of the servants of God, a deception of souls should result from it.

[Note: [Col. 1137C] This matter was already noted above, Book IV, letter 42; it is forbidden by the canons.]

We greatly praised you for having, as was fitting, guarded against the snares of the ancient enemy by appropriate foresight. But because it has come to us that Pompeiana, a religious woman, wishes to remove the servants of God from that monastery, recall them to the monasteries from which they had been taken, and establish there a community of monks, it is necessary that, if this has been carried out, the disposition of the deceased be preserved in every way (Gratian, 13, question 2, chapter 4).

[Note: [Col. 1137C] That is, “those who had been removed,” as the Norman manuscript also reads. Our reading, however, is found in five Vatican manuscripts, the Colbert manuscripts, and many editors.]

But if this has not been done, lest the testator’s will appear to have been entirely frustrated, we wish that, since the monastery of Urbanus, once abbot, located outside the city of Caralis, is said to have been so abandoned that not even one monk remained there, John—whom the aforementioned Epiphanius appointed abbot of the monastery which, as has been said, he had decided should be built in his house—should be ordained abbot, provided that nothing prevents him from being appointed.

[Note: [Col. 1137C] Recent editions read: “appoint John … as abbot, provided that nothing prevents him from being ordained abbot.”]

The relics which were to have been deposited in the house of the aforesaid Epiphanius should be placed there, and everything that Epiphanius had contributed toward the monastery he had designated for construction should be assigned to it in every way. Thus, even if his will concerning the place is not carried out because of the precaution mentioned above, his reward may nevertheless remain unimpaired.

[Col. 1136C]

Let your fraternity arrange all these matters together with Vitalis the defender, and strive to order them usefully, so that, just as you may receive a reward for your praiseworthy prohibition, you may likewise receive one for a good construction. Although it is unnecessary to commend this monastery to your fraternity, we nevertheless exhort you, for greater assurance, to keep it commended to you, with justice preserved, as is fitting for you.

## LETTER XXVI. TO JOHN, SUBDEACON

He is to intercede with the prefect on behalf of John the banker.

Gregory to John, subdeacon of Ravenna.

Your experience knows well how John the banker was often a source of relief to those in need through suretyship. It happened, therefore, that, now standing as surety for a certain Importunus, formerly a court official, he is suffering no small hardship, to such an extent that, having already remained for a long time in the Church, he is being afflicted most severely.

[Note: [Col. 1137C] One who gives surety without any thought of profit is simply a surety; one who does so for profit or gain is a surety in a qualified sense, since he wishes to pursue his own advantage and is therefore conducting his own business. Such a person is commonly called a co-surety. GUSSANVILLE.]

But because some suspected that he had become surety for the aforesaid Importunus not simply but for the sake of gain, he provided, as we have been informed, solemn oaths at the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, swearing not only that he had received no advantage from him at all, but also that he had had nothing promised to him, and that he had become surety for him simply as for the others.

Since the simplicity of an innocent man ought not to be afflicted for so long a time, act before our most excellent son the prefect in whatever ways you can, so that that banking establishment which has remained in the city of Rome may not be closed during his tenure, but may provide him assistance in this affliction as the reward of his service; and so that he may deign to release him by a direct order and not permit him to remain in this necessity any longer.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] I understand this to mean a shop or business establishment. Thus Ulpian, in the *Digest*, Book XLVII, title “On Insults,” law 15, section 7: “If someone should come to your house,” and likewise: “If someone should come to a station or shop.” The word *statio* can also refer to the establishments of notaries; its meaning must be determined from the subject matter, since it has many senses. Here the subject is a banker, whom we otherwise call a money-changer or *mensarius*, that is, a dealer in money—the French *banquier*, who lends circulating capital. Their shops stood in the forum, where they conducted banking and invested their own or other people’s money. See Alciatus, Book IV of the *Disputations*, chapter 22. The shops of bankers or money-changers were called *stationes* as a more respectable term, as above in Gregory.]

For it is not unknown even to him how simple and kind the man is, or how often he has been a remedy for others in their tribulations. Therefore strive to act before him, as we have said, with every gentleness, so that by releasing this man he may benefit many, and so that this path of relief may not, as we have said, be closed during his tenure.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] This is how it is read in three Vatican manuscripts. The old Colbert manuscript reads: “in the month of December.”]

Given in the month of November, indiction 4.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] LETTER XXVII [alternative numbering: 24].—In the Anglic, Norman, and Corbie manuscripts: “To John, subdeacon of Ravenna.” The reading “to John the religious” is found in the Vatican manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, the Colbert manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and others. This reading may be confirmed by what follows: “Since, therefore, you, John the religious …” For this is how it should be read in all the Norman, Corbie, Rheims, and four Vatican manuscripts, rather than “Since, therefore, you, John, being religious …,” as it appears in the printed editions.]

## LETTER XXVII. TO JOHN THE RELIGIOUS

He declares John, appointed over the tables of the poor and the distribution of charitable assistance, exempt from rendering accounts to human beings; but he exhorts him to remember that he will render an account to God, so that he may fulfill his work more diligently.

Gregory to John the religious.

Although the devotion of those who, with pious intent, devote the care of their solicitude to the weak and needy is able to defend them before everyone, nevertheless it is better if, for their own peace of mind, they are provided with protection concerning what they have done, lest from that by which they ought rather to be praised there arise an occasion of disturbance.

Since, therefore, prompted by your devotion to your purpose, we have chosen you, John the religious, to be placed in charge of the poor-house and the provision of charitable assistance [Col. 1138A]—whether *mensae pauperum* (“tables of the poor”) refers to the place where alms are distributed to the poor, as in Book VIII, Letter 20, now Book X, Letter 21; or to alms themselves and everything supplied to the poor, as here; or to a collection made for the poor, as in Cassian, *Conferences* 18.7—so that no uncertainty might arise for you from this administration, we have seen fit to support you with this written protection [Col. 1138C]. [Note: Here *munitio* means a charter, diploma, or written instrument, so called because the person to whom it is granted is thereby protected and made secure. See Book XIV, Letter 3.] By it we establish that, concerning what you have received, or may subsequently receive, for distribution to the tables of the poor or for the provision of charitable assistance, you shall never be compelled to render an account to anyone in any manner or by any device, nor shall you be required to endure any harassment.

But although we wish you to be released from every human accounting [Note: “We have changed much here only in the wording, most manuscripts persuading us to do so.”], you must know that you will render an account to our God concerning what we have entrusted to you. Therefore we urge you to maintain sincerity of faith; let your mind be more attentive to these matters, your care more earnest, your will more ready, your diligence more watchful, your devotion more conspicuous, and your service more effective. Thus, while completing this work diligently with divine help [Col. 1138D—the printed editions here read *intus* (“within”) instead of *jutus* (“helped”), against the manuscripts, including the Regius and Vatican manuscripts], those for whom you care may be profitably comforted by the support of your diligence, and you may receive the reward of your merit in eternal life, when the grace of our Redeemer compensates you.

*Given in the month of December, in the fourth indiction.*  
*(Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 51.)*  
[In recent editions: “in the month of January.” We follow the Vatican manuscripts.]

## LETTER XXVIII. TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE ENGLISH

Gregory rejoices with all the Romans over the conversion of the English. Augustine too ought to rejoice in God’s gift, but must beware of the pride of heart that may arise from the working of miracles. Miracles were performed both by Moses, who had not yet been released from guilt, and by the reprobate themselves. In these things Augustine should seek not his own glory but God’s glory and the salvation of souls. We should rejoice in one sign within us, namely, love.

Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English.

[Col. 1138D] The angelic hymn, formerly customary in thanksgiving, has already been discussed in Book V, Letter 39, note a.

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14; John 12), because the grain of wheat fell into the earth and died, lest he reign alone in heaven. [Note: Thus the Corbie and Norman manuscripts. Some read: “Having died and fallen into the earth, it brought forth much fruit, lest it should be alone.”] By his death we live; by his weakness we are strengthened; by his passion we are rescued from passion; and through his love we seek in Britain brothers whom we did not know. By his gift we have found those whom, without knowing them, we were seeking. [Note: The Christian faith had already spread through Britain almost from its very beginnings, as Alteserra rightly observes here, citing Tertullian, Arnobius, Clement of Alexandria, and Jerome; add Origen, *Homilies on Luke* 6. Yet by Saint Gregory’s time it had either nearly failed—which is why some called him the apostle of the English—or the Angles and Saxons, who occupied the greater part of the island, were idolaters in the manner of their pagan German forebears. Pope Gregory devoted himself wholly, through his agents, to their conversion. Partly from Gussanville.]

Who could adequately describe how great a joy arose here in the hearts of all the faithful, because the nation of the English, through the working of almighty God’s grace and the labor of your Fraternity, has been freed from the darkness of error and suffused with the light of holy faith [Col. 1139A]? Their utterly pure minds now trample the idols [Note: The printed editions read, “because with a mind and devotion entirely sound”;] to which they had previously been subject through mad fear; they bow with pure hearts before almighty God; they are bound by the rules of holy preaching so that they do not fall into wicked works; they submit in spirit to the divine commandments and are lifted up by understanding; and they humble themselves in prayer even to the ground, lest in mind they lie prostrate upon the earth.

Whose work is this, if not his who says, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17)? To show that he converts the world not by human wisdom but by his own power, he chose uneducated preachers whom he sent into the world. He has done the same here, since among the English people he has deigned to work great things through the weak.

But in this heavenly gift, dearest brother, there is something that must be feared with the greatest joy. I know that almighty God has displayed great miracles through your love among the people whom he wished to choose. Therefore it is necessary that you rejoice in this same heavenly gift with fear, and fear it even while rejoicing.

Rejoice, certainly, because the souls of the English are drawn through outward miracles to inward grace (Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People* 1.31). But fear lest, amid the signs that are performed, a weak mind raise itself in presumption, and lest, from the place where it is outwardly lifted up in honor, it inwardly fall through empty glory.

We must remember that when the disciples returned joyfully from preaching and said to their heavenly Master, “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name” (Luke 10:17), they immediately heard: “Do not rejoice in this, but rather rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (ibid., 20). Those who rejoiced in miracles had placed their minds in a private and temporal joy. But they are recalled from private to common joy, and from temporal to eternal joy, when they are told: “Rejoice in this, that your names are written in heaven.” Not all the elect perform miracles; nevertheless, the names of all of them are kept written in heaven. The disciples of Truth ought to find joy only in that good which they possess in common with everyone, and in which their joy has no end.

It remains, therefore, dearest brother, that amid the things you perform outwardly with God’s help, you should always judge yourself inwardly with careful discernment and understand with equal care both who you are and how great is the grace among that people for whose conversion you have received even the gift of performing signs.

Whenever you remember that you have sinned against our Creator, whether by word or by deed, always recall these things, so that the memory of your guilt may suppress the glory rising in your heart. Whatever you have received, or have already received, for the performance of signs, attribute it not to yourself but to those for whose salvation it was granted to you.

As I consider these matters, the case of a certain servant of God comes to mind, a man who had been chosen with distinction. Certainly, while Moses was leading God’s people out of Egypt, he performed remarkable signs in Egypt, as your Fraternity knows. Fasting for forty days and nights on Mount Sinai, he received the tablets of the Law amid flashes of lightning and peals of thunder, while the whole people trembled; he alone was joined to the service of almighty God even in familiar conversation (Exodus 19; 31). He opened the Red Sea; on the journey he had a pillar of cloud as his guide; he brought down manna from heaven for the hungry people [Note: This is a form of expression familiar to Gregory; see *Dialogues* II.33: so that lifting his head and causing rain to fall were one and the same moment.]; and, by a miracle, he supplied meat in the wilderness to those who desired it, until they were excessively satisfied (Exodus 13; 14; 16).

But when, at a time of thirst, they had come to the rock, he distrusted and doubted that he could draw water from it—the water which, at the Lord’s command, he opened into abundant streams [Col. 1140D; Note: This is the better reading of the Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, rather than that of the printed editions: “which, at the Lord’s command, he struck and opened the waters as they flowed out.”]. How many miracles he performed during the thirty-eight years that followed in the wilderness, who could count or investigate (Exodus 17; Numbers 20)? [Note: Saint Gregory seems not to have noticed that Exodus 17 and Numbers 20 recount different events, and that Moses doubted in the latter. Augustine discusses this in Psalm 105 and *Against Faustus the Manichaean* XVI.16–17; Theodoret, *Questions on Numbers* 38, and *Questions on Exodus* 27–28. Procopius confuses the two; all others distinguish them.]

Whenever some doubtful matter struck his mind, he returned to the tabernacle and sought the Lord in secret; and when God spoke, he was immediately instructed concerning it (Exodus 33 and following). He appeased the Lord when he was angry with the people through the intervention of his prayer. Those who rose up in pride and dissented in discord he caused to be swallowed by the openings of the split earth; he crushed enemies with victories and displayed signs to his own people (Numbers 26).

But when they had already reached the promised land, he was called up the mountain. There he heard that the offense he had committed thirty-eight years earlier, as I have said—when he had doubted that he could draw water from the rock—had been remembered. And because of it he learned that he would not be able to enter the promised land (Numbers 27).

In this we must consider how greatly the judgment of almighty God is to be feared: through that servant of his he performed so many signs, yet for so long he continued to retain that servant’s guilt in his mind.

[Col. 1140D] Therefore, dearest brother, if we know that even Moses died after his signs because of his guilt, although we know that he had been especially chosen by almighty God, how greatly ought we to tremble with fear, since we do not yet know whether we have been chosen? [Note: These words are directed against the vain confidence of the Calvinists. See *Morals* XX, no. 8 and following.]

As for the miracles of the reprobate, what should I say, when your Fraternity knows well what Truth says in the Gospel: “Many will come on that day and say to me: Lord, in your name we prophesied, and in your name we drove out demons, and in your name we performed many mighty works. But I will say to them: I do not know who you are. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity” (Matthew 7:22; Luke 13:27).

The mind must therefore be kept under strict control amid signs and miracles, lest perhaps it seek its own glory in them and exult in the private joy of its own exaltation. Through signs we must seek the gain of souls and the glory of him by whose power those very signs are performed.

But the Lord has given us one sign in which we may both rejoice greatly and recognize in ourselves the glory of election, saying: “By this it will be known that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). This is the sign the prophet sought when he said: “Give me, Lord, a sign for good, so that those who hate me may see and be put to shame” (Psalm 85:17).

I say these things because I wish to lay my hearer’s mind low in humility. Yet let your very humility have its confidence. For although I am a sinner, I hold the most certain hope that, through the grace of almighty God, our Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, your sins have already been forgiven, and that you have been chosen so that through you the sins of others may be forgiven.

You will not hereafter have sorrow over any guilt, since you are striving to make the conversion of many a cause of joy in heaven. Our same Creator and Redeemer, speaking of a person’s repentance, says: “So I tell you, there will be greater joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of repentance” (Luke 15:7).

And if there is great joy in heaven over one repentant person, what joy do we believe arose over so great a people converted from its error—a people that, coming to the faith, condemned by repentance the evil it had committed?

In this joy of heaven and the angels, then, let us repeat the words of the angels mentioned above. Let us all say, let us say: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

[Col. 1141D] In the collection of Paul the Deacon and in the Remigius manuscript there is added: “Given on the Kalends of January,” with the indiction omitted.

*(Cf. John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 40.)*

## LETTER XXIX. TO BERTHA, QUEEN OF THE ENGLISH

Gregory congratulates her on the conversion of the English. He earnestly urges her not to neglect any longer inflaming the king’s heart with a perfect love of the Christian faith.

[Col. 1141D]

Gregory to Bertha, queen of the English.

[Col. 1141D] The manuscripts of the English, Normandy, Corbie, Regius, and four Vatican manuscripts read *Berthae*. Three Colbert manuscripts do likewise. One Colbert manuscript reads *Adilbergae*, as do the printed editions. We have shown in the Life of Saint Gregory how this name arose. The reading should be *Berthae*, following Bede, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, chapter 25, and other historians. Bertha was the wife of Ethelberht, king of the Cantiaci in Britain; she was the daughter of Charibert, king of the Franks, granddaughter of Clotarius I, and great-granddaughter of Clovis the Great. Being a Christian, she labored greatly for the conversion of her husband. See the distinguished Adrian Valesius, Book IX of his *Frankish History*. Partly from Gussanville.

Whoever desires to acquire the glory of the heavenly kingdom after earthly royal power must labor with the greatest zeal to make gain for his Creator, so that he may ascend by the steps of his works to what he desires, as we rejoice that you have done.

Accordingly, when our dearest sons, the priest Laurence and the monk Peter, returned, they reported what glory your Excellency displayed toward our reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, how much comfort you gave him, and what affection you showed him. We blessed almighty God, who in his mercy has deigned to reserve the conversion of the English people as a reward for you.

For just as, through the ever-memorable Helena, mother of the most devout Emperor Constantine, he kindled the hearts of the Romans toward the Christian faith, so we trust that through the zeal of your Excellency he is working his mercy among the English people.

Indeed, long ago you ought to have inclined the mind of our illustrious son, your husband, through the benefit of your wisdom, as befits a Christian woman, so that for the salvation of his kingdom and his soul he might follow the faith that you profess. Thus, through him and through the conversion of the entire people, a worthy recompense might arise for you in the joys of heaven.

After your Excellency, as we have said, had been fortified by the true faith and instructed through letters [Col. 1142D—the Regius manuscript reads “having been admonished”], this ought neither to have been late nor difficult for you. And since, by God’s will, the time is now favorable, act so that, with divine grace cooperating, you may repair with increase what has been neglected.

Therefore strengthen the mind of your illustrious husband in love of the Christian faith through continual exhortation. Let your solicitude pour into him an increase of love for God, and so inflame his heart—even for the complete conversion of the people subject to him—that he may offer to almighty God a great sacrifice from the devotion inspired by your zeal [Col. 1142D—the printed editions, against the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, read “from the devotion of his own,” that is, of the king of the English].

Then what has been reported about you may both increase and in every respect be proved true, since your good deeds have now reached not only the Romans, who have prayed more earnestly for your life, but also various places, and even the most serene emperor at Constantinople. Therefore, just as joy has come to us from the consolations of your Christianity, so may joy come to the angels in heaven from the perfection of your works.

In the assistance of our aforementioned reverend brother and fellow bishop, and of the servants of God whom we have sent there, devote yourselves wholly and with all your strength to the conversion of your people, so that you may reign here happily with our illustrious son, your husband, and, after many years, may also attain the joys of the life to come, which know no end.

We pray almighty God to kindle the heart of your Excellency with the fire of his grace, so that you may perform the things we have said, and to grant you the fruit of eternal reward for works pleasing to him.

## LETTER XXX. TO VENANTIUS, FORMER MONK AND PATRICIAN OF SYRACUSE

On the occasion of both his own gout and that of Venantius, Gregory teaches that the sufferings of this life are God’s scourges, by which he mercifully corrects sinners. We should therefore recall our sins, give thanks to God, and forestall God’s judgment through repentance.

[Col. 1143A]

Gregory to Venantius, former monk and patrician of Syracuse.

[Col. 1143D] In this heading we follow the Norman, English, and Corbie manuscripts and most of those listed by Gussanville. The Regius manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts alone have “to Venantius of Syracuse.” The old Colbert manuscript agrees. In the printed editions there is a corrupt reading, “to the bishop of Syracuse,” except in Gussanville’s latest edition. Venantius is sufficiently known from the preceding letters, especially Book I, Letter 34.

In fulfilling the duty of a greeting, I wished to speak of the things I suffer. But I think it inappropriate to describe what you already know. For I am tormented by the pains of gout, which have been no less harmful to you than to me [Note: Gussanville’s edition incorrectly reads “not dissimilarly known”]; while they grow violently in us, they have made us diminish from life.

Amid these things, what else should we do except constantly recall our sins [Note: “our sins” is omitted in the Norman and Corbie manuscripts] and give thanks to almighty God? For we who sinned greatly through the indulgence of the flesh are cleansed through the affliction of the flesh.

We must also know that present punishment, if it turns the afflicted mind, is the end of the preceding guilt; but if it does not turn the mind toward the fear of the Lord, it is the beginning of the punishment that follows. We must therefore take care, and watch with our whole mind, turning ourselves entirely toward God in tears, lest we pass from torment to torments.

We must also consider with what great dispensation of mercy our Creator deals with us: he continually strikes those worthy of death, yet does not yet kill them. He threatens what he is going to do, but does not do it, so that the pains that go before may frighten us and, once converted to fear of the strict Judge, may hide us from his punishment at the end of life [Col. 1143D—the printed editions read “forever”; four Vatican manuscripts read “at the end”].

Who could say, who could count how many people, given over to their lust, rushing into blasphemies and pride, persisting in robbery and wickedness until the day of their death, lived in this world without ever suffering even a headache, yet were suddenly struck down and handed over to the fires of hell?

We therefore have evidence that we have not been abandoned, since we are continually scourged. Scripture bears witness, saying: “The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12:6).

In these very scourges of God, let us recall both his gifts and the losses caused by our guilt. Let us weigh how many good things the Lord has done despite our wickedness, and how many evils we have committed beneath his goodness.

Let us fulfill what the Lord says through the prophet: “Remind me, so that we may be judged together” (Isaiah 43:26). Let us now be judged in our own thought together with God, lest afterward we be judged strictly by God.

For what does Paul say? “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31).

Whoever, therefore, hastens to escape the severity of the sentence of the judgment to come must, through the bitterness of repentance, destroy for himself every sweetness of the present life. [Note: Recent printed editions read “put aside sweetness”; we follow four Vatican and four Colbert manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, Corbie, Regius, and others.] Whatever such good things exist [Note: The printed editions read “of this world”]—whose gifts are they, if not the Creator’s?

But God’s gift ought not to be freely possessed by us when, through the pleasure it gives, it separates us from the love of God, lest we prefer what has been given to the giver, and, while receiving good things, though we are evil, be separated from his fear by that from which we ought to have grown in it. [Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts. Recent editions freely changed *libere* to *haberi* (“to be possessed”), and below read *mala* (“evils”) for *mali* (“evil [men]”), and *idem* for *id est* (“that is”).]

May the Creator of all things, almighty God, pour these words that we speak to you in this letter into your mind through the inspiration of his Spirit; may he cleanse you from every defilement of guilt, and grant you here the joy of his consolation and, with himself, the eternal rewards that await.

I ask you to greet in my place my sweetest daughters, the ladies Barbara and Antonina.

[Col. 1144D] Four Vatican manuscripts and two Colbert manuscripts read: “in the month of January, in the fourth indiction.”

## LETTER XXXI. TO PASCHASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

Gregory grants Venantius relics of Saint Severinus for the consecration of an oratory.

Gregory to Paschasius, bishop of Naples.

John, servant and agent of the lord Venantius [Note: The Colbert, Regius, and two Vatican manuscripts read “at his lord’s request”], has petitioned that the relics of the blessed confessor Severinus be granted to his aforesaid master, so that an oratory built at his own expense in the saint’s name may be solemnly consecrated.

Therefore, dearest brother, it is fitting that you obey the desire of the aforesaid man at our command, so that he may obtain the fulfillment of his devotion in the consecration he requests.

[Col. 1144D] This final sentence is found in none of the manuscripts except the Regius.

*Given in the month of February, in the fourth indiction.*

## LETTER XXXII. TO MARINIANUS OF RAVENNA

Relics granted to Abbot Candidus. Gregory is afflicted by so many and such severe illnesses that living is a punishment. He asks for prayers that God may moderate his scourges and grant him patience.

Gregory to Marinianus of Ravenna. [Note: Vatican manuscripts B and E read “to Marinianus, bishop of Arabia”; the printed editions, “to Maximianus, bishop of Arabia.” These corrupt headings have been corrected from all the English and Norman manuscripts, four Colbert, two Teller, Corbie, Rheims, Regius, and Vatican manuscript D.]

When Abbot Candidus, the bearer of this letter, came to request relics—which have also been granted—I rejoiced at the nourishment provided by your Fraternity, because your devotion was evident in him. But I was equally saddened that I could not, as I wished, enjoy his presence, since he found me ill and, when he departed, left me still lying in sickness.

It has now been a long time since I have been able to rise from my bed. Sometimes the pain of gout torments me; sometimes I do not know what sort of fire spreads through my entire body with pain. Often it happens that, at one and the same time, burning struggles with pain within me, and both body and spirit fail me.

I cannot enumerate the many other afflictions beyond those illnesses I have mentioned. But I shall say briefly that the infection of harmful fluid soaks into me that living is a punishment for me, and I eagerly await death, which I believe can be the only remedy for my groans.

Therefore, most holy brother, implore for me the mercy of divine compassion, so that in his kindness he may moderate the scourges of his blows against me and grant me endurance in bearing them. May my heart not, God forbid, burst into impatience through excessive weariness, lest guilt that could have been well healed by the wound grow through murmuring.

[Col. 1145D] This final clause is absent from most manuscripts; it is found in Vatican manuscripts A, B, and E and in two Colbert manuscripts.

*Given in the month of February, in the fourth indiction.*  
*(Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 67.)*

## LETTER XXXIII. TO MARINIANUS OF RAVENNA

Gregory urges him to arrange the affairs of his church and come to Rome, where, under Gregory’s personal care, he may be cured of vomiting blood in peace. Meanwhile he is to abstain from fasts, vigils, and preaching.

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts A and F read: “When certain men of Ravenna came, they found me struck with most grievous sorrow.” Compare this letter with Letter XL.]

When a certain man from Ravenna came, I was struck by the deepest sorrow because he reported that your Fraternity was ill with vomiting blood. For this reason I carefully and individually had those whom we know here to be learned in medicine consulted, and I sent your Holiness in writing what each of them thought and prescribed.

Nevertheless, they all prescribe rest and silence above everything else. I am very doubtful whether your Fraternity can have these in your own church. Therefore it seems to me that, once the church there has been arranged—so that there are people capable of celebrating the solemn Masses, of carrying out the bishop’s responsibilities [Col. 1145D; Note: The Norman, Colbert, Regius, and Corbie manuscripts read “to exercise the bishop’s care,” that is, the episcopal office. This duty especially devolves upon bishops. Jerome, commenting on Titus 1, “but hospitable,” says that hospitality is required of a future bishop before all else: if all desire to hear, “I was a stranger and you received me,” how much more must a bishop, whose house ought to be a common lodging for all? A layperson receives one, two, or a few and fulfils hospitality; unless a bishop receives all, he is inhuman. Gussanville.], of providing hospitality and receiving guests, and of supervising the monasteries [Note: Later editors read “know how to preside,” adding the final word on their own authority and not from the manuscripts]—your Fraternity should come to me before the summer.

Then I can personally care for your illness as far as I am able, and safeguard your rest, because physicians strongly say that the summer season is dangerous for this illness. I am very much afraid that, if you undertake any duties amid the adversity of the season, you may be endangered still further by the same affliction.

I myself am also very weak, and it is altogether desirable that, with God’s grace, you return healthy to your church. Or certainly, if you are to be summoned, may you be summoned among your own people; and if almighty God should wish to summon me, who see myself close to death, before you, then I ought to pass away in your hands.

But if the season prevents you from coming, a small gift being given [Note: All the Vatican, English, Norman, Regius, and Corbie manuscripts, and two Colbert manuscripts, read *parvo exenio* (“a small gift”), where the printed editions read “by a small remedy”; the Remigius manuscript reads “by a small present”], arrangements can be made at the court for him himself to send one of his men with you as far as Rome. If, therefore, you feel that the same illness is weighing heavily upon you and you intend to come, you should come with only a few people, since, while staying with me in the episcopal residence, you will receive daily service from this church.

Moreover, I neither urge nor advise you, but strictly command you not to presume to fast at all, because physicians say that it is very harmful to this illness. I permit it only on five occasions in the year, if perhaps a great solemnity requires it.

You must also abstain from vigils. Let the prayers customarily recited over the paschal candle in the city of Ravenna, or the explanations of the Gospel given by priests around the Paschal solemnity, be delivered by someone else. Let your affection not impose work upon you contrary to your strength.

I have said these things so that, if you feel better and postpone your coming, you may know what you must observe by my command. [Note: Vatican manuscript D and the cited Rheims manuscript read, “if you judge better.”]

[Col. 1146D] The note explains that Gregory appears to indicate that these prayers for blessing the Paschal candle were particular to the church of Ravenna. Nevertheless, Menardus proves from the Fourth Council of Toledo and from Ennodius of Ticinum that the candle was already blessed with prescribed prayers in several other churches. See note 300 in the Book of the Sacraments, column 343 and following. Vatican manuscript D and the cited Rheims manuscript read: “the prayers which are customarily said in Ravenna over the candle by chant.”

*(Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 53.)*

## LETTER XXXIV. TO PASCHASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

The portion of the clergy and the poor that his predecessor had withheld from the church’s funds is to be distributed by Paschasius according to the arrangement prescribed in this letter.

[Col. 1146C]

Gregory to Paschasius, bishop of Naples.

When, by God’s authority, your Fraternity was advanced to the office of bishop, you remember that we established that, from the funds of your church, the portion of the clergy and the poor that your predecessor had not supplied—namely, four hundred solidi—should be set aside so that it might benefit the distribution to that clergy and those poor.

Since this must no longer be delayed, we wish your Fraternity to distribute it without any difficulty, according to the arrangement inserted in this letter, in the presence of our subdeacon Anthemius.

You are to give your clergy, individually as you deem appropriate, a total of one hundred solidi. To the *praejacentes*, whom we have learned number one hundred twenty-six, you are to give sixty-three solidi—that is, half a solidus to each.

To the priests, deacons, and foreign clergy, fifty solidi. To respectable needy people whom shame does not permit to ask publicly, one hundred fifty solidi, so that some may receive a third of a solidus each, others one solidus each, or more if it seems appropriate. [Note: The printed editions add: “some to two [tremisses], some,” and so forth.]

To the remaining poor, who are accustomed to ask publicly for alms, thirty-six solidi.

[Col. 1146D] The note identifies the *praejacentes* as those who had served in the church during the time of Paschasius’s predecessor and whose stipends had not yet been paid. This is clear from the expenditure of the four hundred solidi, which Gregory orders to be made and which is divided into five portions: one hundred solidi for the clergy currently serving in the church; sixty-three for those who had served before Paschasius’s ordination, namely the *praejacentes*; fifty for foreign clergy; one hundred fifty for respectable poor people; and thirty-six for beggars.

These facts are too clear to require proof. It is worth noting that Gregory wishes larger portions to be distributed to respectable and modest poor people than to beggars—four times as much, in fact—a point that few observe. The same distinction may be observed in relation to foreign clergy. The clergy whom Saint Gregory calls *praejacentes* Gregory of Tours calls “the predecessor’s school” (*History* 10.26). Note also the distinction between the church’s own clergy and foreign clergy.

There you have distributed both how much and to whom it must be given. But since, as we have foreseen, it must not be supplied equally to everyone, you must, together with the aforesaid subdeacon, give each person what you have judged appropriate. Take every possible care that, by devoutly and promptly distributing what another unjustly withheld, you may turn it to your own reward.

## LETTER XXXV. TO BARBARA AND ANTONINA

Gregory consoles them, deeply afflicted by their father’s approaching death.

Gregory to Barbara and Antonina. [Note: Some Colbert manuscripts read “Antonia,” others “Antonina,” as do the Vatican, Norman, and English manuscripts. Barbara and Antonina were daughters of the patrician Venantius; see above, Letter XXX.]

Having received the letters of your Excellency, which spoke through tears rather than words [Note: The printed editions read “spoke tears”], I am no less afflicted, dearest daughters, by sorrow over your father’s illness than you are. [Note: The printed editions read, corruptly, “we, concerning the beloved ones of my son,” in place of this reading; all the Vatican and Norman manuscripts and other manuscripts reject it.]

Nor can we regard your sadness as foreign to us, since by the law of charity it becomes our own. But because we must never despair of the mercy of our Redeemer, raise your spirits toward the consolation of your father and place your hope in the hand of almighty God.

We trust that, under his protection, he will guard you from every adversity, bring joy to your tribulation, and mercifully permit you to be established according to your father’s wishes.

If he fulfills the debt owed to human mortality, even then let no despair crush you, nor let the words of certain people strike terror into you. For, after God, who is the governor and protector of orphans, we shall be solicitous for your noble persons and hasten, with the Lord’s help, to provide for your welfare as far as we can.

Thus no violence from unjust people may disturb you, and we may repay you in every respect the debt we incurred through the goodness of your parents.

May heavenly grace therefore nourish you by its favor and defend you from every evil by its protection, so that the preservation of your lives may become our joy.

## LETTER XXXVI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

Gregory testifies to his sorrow over Venantius’s hopeless illness. Above all, action should be taken so that Venantius may return to the monastic habit, even at the end of his life. Gregory explains that he is greatly hindered because Venantius is now commending his daughters even to the emperor himself. John is to protect them as far as he can. Gregory permits John, as a friend, to come to Rome at a suitable time.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

I have received your letter, [Note: [Col. 1148C] EPISTLE XXXVI [Al. 31].—Vatican D has *quae mihi* [Col. 1148D] *dulcissimi . . . aegritudinem loquebantur*. Below, the Norman manuscripts have *desperare* instead of *desperate*.] which spoke to me of the illness of my most beloved son, the lord Venantius, [Col. 1148B] and recounted in detail everything that had happened concerning him. But when, at the same time, I heard both that he was desperately and seriously ill, and that wicked men were pressing their claims against the property of the orphans, I could scarcely contain the grief in my heart. Yet it was some consolation that tears burst forth from me through my groaning.

Therefore your Holiness must not neglect the first care that is required of you [Note: [Col. 1148D] The printed editions read “which is fitting” (*quam decet*).]: you must think about his soul, exhorting him, entreating him, placing before him God’s terrible judgment, and promising him God’s ineffable mercy, [Note: [Col. 1148D] Namely, to the monastic state, which he had renounced when he took a wife.] so that he may return to his religious habit, even at the point of death, lest the guilt of so great a sin stand in his way at the eternal judgment. Then it is your responsibility to consider how his daughters, the ladies Barbara and Antonina, ought to be settled, so that no opportunity may be given to wicked men.

For after he had bound me by oath to take responsibility for them, adding that I should provide for their settlement, he then followed this with something else in his letter which, I have no doubt, may obstruct my effort in this matter. He says that I should repeatedly petition the most pious lord emperor, so that the emperor himself may arrange for them to be settled as he sees fit. You can see how different this is from his former wish. [Note: [Col. 1148D] Another version has, “how contrary it is.” It is not worthwhile to call attention to other minor differences, whether already altered or to be altered below.]

For this reason I fear that a suitable opportunity may be given to the people located in Sicily who are seeking an opportunity to interfere in his affairs. For when they learn this, what will those men do who, although there was no cause, [Note: [Col. 1148D] Note the ancient practice of claiming the goods of debtors for the treasury by affixing the imperial seal, so that they might be held in custody for the emperor; Alteserra believes that Ambrose refers to this in Letter 33. He cites many laws of the Code on the same matter. He apparently assumes that Venantius, who had held some public office, was liable to render accounts to the treasury. Venantius himself had supplied another reason why his goods should be secured with the imperial seal, by commending them to the emperor.] were already attempting, as is said, to place the seal upon his property? Will not the circumstances seem to favor them and provide them with something like a legitimate pretext?

They may say: “They have been commended to the lord emperor. We cannot neglect them; the danger is ours. We are placing the property in safety until the lord emperor orders that they be brought to Constantinople.” Tell me, I ask, what am I to do in such circumstances, when a commendation to one who possesses authority appears to agree with their purpose?

He binds me by oath to arrange matters in such a way that either they remain in the city of Rome or are not removed from Sicily, while he is acting so that they will have no means either of bringing them here or of retaining them there. You, however, oppose the wicked men as far as you can. For the sake of almighty God, defend their property as though it were your own; and, if it is still possible, make provision in the aforesaid lord Venantius’s will so that every opportunity for violence may be removed.

But if it is decided that they should be commended to the palace, he ought not to lay upon me the burden of making me responsible for arranging their settlement, when only almighty God should know how I am considering that settlement. Therefore I have immediately written to my most beloved son, the deacon Anatolius, asking him to speak with the glorious patrician Rusticiana, to inquire and report how he ought to proceed concerning the persons whose names have been sent to me, so that he may quickly inform us of everything and, with God directing matters, whatever must be done may be arranged.

Furthermore, in the letters which you sent us, we found your Fraternity distressed [Col. 1149C] because we had apparently been unwilling to have you come here out of some ingratitude, whereas we did this for no other reason than your advantage, knowing that, because of the persons residing there, your presence was extremely necessary. But lest you should perhaps believe that this means that we have any ungrateful feeling toward you—which God forbid—if you wish to come, present yourself at the thresholds of the apostles at a suitable time. For, so far as we are concerned, we love your Charity so greatly that we wish to see you often. (See above, Letters 30 and 35, and Book I, Letter 34. Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 48.)

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He orders that clerics’ cases be referred to the bishops, lest episcopal jurisdiction be violated.

[Col. 1149D]

Gregory to Romanus, defender of Sicily.

It has come to our attention (Gratian 11, question 1, canon 39) that, whenever anyone has a case against any clerics, you disregard their bishops and cause those clerics to be brought before your tribunal. If this is true, since it is clearly very improper, we order you by this authority not to presume to do this again. If anyone has a case against any cleric, let him approach that cleric’s bishop, so that either the bishop himself may hear the case or judges may certainly be appointed by him. Or, if the matter must perhaps go before arbitrators, let the official authority delegated by the bishop compel the parties to choose a judge.

If, however, a cleric or layman has a case against a bishop, then you ought to intervene, so that either you yourself may hear the case between them or, at your admonition, they may choose judges for themselves. For if each bishop’s jurisdiction is not preserved for him, what else is being done except that through us—through whom the ecclesiastical order ought to be preserved—it is thrown into confusion? [Note: [Col. 1149D] EPISTLE XXXVII [Al. 32].—Vatican D and E read: “unless, apart from the ecclesiastical order that ought to be preserved there, everything is thrown into confusion.” The other Vatican manuscripts differ from one another in several details.]

It has also been reported to us that you expelled, by your own authority and without the knowledge of our most reverend brother John, bishop, certain clerics whom he had sent to do penance because of their guilt. If this is true, know that you have done something altogether dishonorable and deserving of no light reprimand. Therefore restore these clerics to their bishop without delay. And take care not to commit such an offense hereafter, for if you neglect this, know that you will incur our considerable displeasure. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 30.)

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO VITUS, THE DEFENDER

He appoints him defender of the Church.

Gregory to Vitus, defender.

[Note: [Col. 1149D] EPISTLE XXXVIII [Al. 33].—Here certain conditions necessary for obtaining and exercising the office of defender are listed; yet they are entirely absent from Vatican manuscript A, for there this letter begins with the words “with a view to the advantage of the Church.” This letter is contained almost solely in this codex [Col. 1150D].]

If you are bound by no obligation to any condition or corporation, have not been a cleric of another city, and no canonical statutes stand in your way, it has seemed good to our judgment, with a view to the advantage of the Church, that you accept the office of defender of the Church [Col. 1150C] and faithfully and energetically carry out whatever we entrust to you for the benefit of the poor. You are to use this privilege, which we have conferred upon you after careful deliberation, so that you may offer your faithful service in fulfilling everything entrusted to you by us, and render an account of your actions under the judgment of our God.

We have dictated this letter to be written by Paterius, the secondary secretary and notary of our Church, and have subscribed it ourselves. [Note: [Col. 1150D] In Vatican A, we dictated this letter to be assigned to Paterius, our secondary secretary.]

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He commends Vitus, who has been appointed defender.

Gregory to Romanus, defender.

Let your Experience know that Vitus, the bearer of this letter, [Note: [Col. 1150D] EPISTLE XXXIX [Al. 32].—They assign the origin of this word to the fourth century, but incorrectly; Arnobius used it, as did others. See Book I, Letter 42, now 44. Gussanville.] was formerly our servant. Since we know his fidelity and diligence well, we have decided that he should serve in the school of defenders, a formal letter having been solemnly given to him. [Note: [Col. 1150D] A “school” is any order of officials, singers, notaries, and so forth. See the *Sacramentary*, book, column 64, and note 253.]

Therefore, if you should wish to entrust him with anything for the advantage of the Church, have no doubt concerning him. Be entirely certain of his integrity, and do not suppose that he will act deceitfully or with duplicity in anything. There is only one thing: extend to him the affection that is owed to the faithful.

## EPISTLE XL. TO MARIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

Because of his hemorrhage, he is to abstain from fasting and avoid every form of aggravation.

Gregory to Marianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Many things are imposed upon us by illness which, if we were healthy, would rightly seem blameworthy. But since, placed in this fragile body, we cannot continue in any other way than by attending to its weaknesses, we ought not to be ashamed of what necessity imposes upon us.

And therefore, since physicians say that fasting is altogether harmful to those suffering from a hemorrhage, we exhort your Fraternity with earnest words [Note: [Col. 1151D] Vatican E has “we entreat.”] that, recalling to mind what you are accustomed to endure from illness, you not impose upon yourself the burden of fasting. [Col. 1151B] If, however, with God’s mercy, you recognize that you have improved sufficiently and that your strength can bear it, we permit you to fast once or twice a week.

But above all you must strive to ensure that you experience no aggravation, lest the illness, which is now thought to be milder and almost suspended, should later be felt more severely through an exacerbation. [Note: [Col. 1151D] EPISTLE XL [Al. 34, indiction 6]. Vatican D and E have “corruption of the blood.” Others have “rupture” or “ruptures of the blood.” See above, Letter 33.]

## EPISTLE XLI. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

Concerning the unjust seizure of the boundaries of Faustus’s properties.

Gregory to Romanus, defender.

Our most glorious son Faustus sent us a letter [Col. 1151C] requesting that he be heard, asserting that the agents of the Church of Syracuse had recently and violently taken away the boundaries of his property situated there in Sicily. Since we believe that this is altogether foreign to the knowledge and character of our brother and fellow bishop John, we wish you to see him.

If indeed, as is alleged, the property was recently taken from its possessor, and this has become clear to you through an open satisfaction, let it be restored to the dominion of the one from whom it was taken. [Note: [Col. 1151D] EPISTLE XLI [Al. 35].—That is, let it be restored. Cassiodorus uses *reformari* in the same sense in Book VIII of the *Variæ*, Letter 93: “we order the estates to be restored.” Bernard likewise says in his sermon on Saint Martin, “peace having been restored, he rested in peace.”]

Then, if the agents of the aforesaid Church reasonably believe that they have some claim in law within their boundaries, let them submit without delay to the judgment of chosen judges, so that the judgment of the judges may determine to whom the property belongs. In this way the bishop may be freed from the odium arising from the alleged unlawful seizure, and the case may be brought to an end according to legal procedure.

## EPISTLE XLII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

Concerning the unjust seizure of the boundaries of Faustus’s properties.

[Col. 1151D]

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

[Col. 1152A] Our most glorious son Faustus approached us with a formal petition, asserting that the boundaries of his property situated there in Sicily had recently been occupied by men of your Church. He therefore requested that, by the tenor of our order, the property violently taken from him should be restored.

Since, if the matter happened as he asserts, we believe it to be altogether foreign to the knowledge of your Fraternity, investigate it carefully. If, as he asserts, his boundaries were taken from the possessor contrary to the order of law, [Note: [Col. 1151D] EPISTLE XLII [Al. 36].—Clearly, the person dispossessed must first of all be restored, according to the principles of law.] let the property that has been seized return to the dominion of its possessor.

Then, if your Church has any useful claim to oppose by right of ownership, a judgment of chosen judges ought to be issued and the matter concluded by their decision, provided that the possessor’s right is in no way improperly disturbed by this. But once the case has been settled by judicial process, let the manifest facts recognize the ownership and justice of the matter without sacerdotal odium.

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

Let him at last conclude Rusticiana’s long-delayed case concerning the seized boundaries of her property.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Peter, a most distinguished man and steward of our glorious daughter, the patrician Rusticiana, has complained to us in his letters, asserting that after your Fraternity returned from the city of Rome, the boundaries of a certain property belonging to the aforesaid patrician were forcibly seized by men of your Church.

He stated that he had repeatedly lodged a complaint with you concerning this matter, and that at one point he appointed Martianus, a notary, to present the case to you. [Note: [Col. 1151D] EPISTLE XLIII [Al. 37].—Thus Vatican A and Remigius; the printed editions, together with Victor, have “to state the case to you.”] He asserts that Martianus postponed it through various delays, so that even now the parties have been unable to come forward to plead the case. [Note: [Col. 1152D] There were various kinds of notaries, as Cujacius reports. Some presided over the archives and public documents; others wrote or subscribed for those who were unskilled in letters; others undertook stipulations for those unable to do so, and so forth. Slaves once performed this office, but it was eventually forbidden by a constitution of Arcadius and Honorius. The two notaries appointed in each province were different from all these: one administered the accounts of the treasury, the other the records of the imperial largesses, as in the *Theodosian Code*, Book I, title 8. Partly from Gussanville.]

And because we love you with as much fraternal affection as we are saddened to hear anything that might bring you into disrepute, we therefore exhort you by this present letter: let every delay and excuse cease, and compel your men to submit to judgment together with the other party concerning the boundaries said to have been seized, so that both the question of the seizure and any dispute over ownership may be brought to an end. [Note: [Col. 1153C] Thus Victor. In Vatican A, and in no other of our manuscripts except Victor and Remigius, the reading is “so that, if there is any question of seizure, it may be settled by a dispute over ownership.”]

Let your Fraternity therefore ensure that this is done without delay, so that neither reproach may touch you nor complaint about the matter trouble us again.

## EPISTLE XLIV. TO RUSTICIANA, THE PATRICIAN

He asks her not to call herself his servant in her letters any longer. The veils she offered to blessed Peter have already been hung. He both grieves and rejoices over her gout. He demonstrates through various miracles that the monastery of Saint Andrew, to which she too had sent an alms, is most diligently protected by that apostle.

[Col. 1152D]

Gregory to Rusticiana, the patrician.

[Col. 1153A] I have received the letters of Your Excellence, which, while I was laid low by a most severe illness, entirely refreshed me by the news of your health, devotion, and sweetness. Yet I received one thing with difficulty: in those same letters to me, something that could have been said once was repeated again and again—“Your servant, your servant.”

For I, who through the burdens of the episcopate have become the servant of all, [Note: [Col. 1153C–D] Origen, Homily 6 on Isaiah: “For one who wishes to be saved does not come to the presidency of the Church, even if he presides, but to the service of the Church.” And below: “He who is called to the episcopate is called not to rulership, but to the service of the whole Church, if you wish to believe the Scriptures, because in the Church whoever presides is the servant of all,” etc. Gussanville.] how can she call herself my servant, when before I assumed the episcopate I was her own dependent? [Note: [Col. 1153C] As though he had been her vassal and devoted to her by a special title, that is, her client. “One is called another’s dependent or client,” says Alteserra on this passage, “just as a wife was called one’s own when marriage had been contracted by *coemptio* or by *conventio in manum*, because she came under her husband’s power,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “I shall join her to myself in lasting marriage and call her my own.” The manuscripts do not agree here. Vatican A and E read: “whose subject I was before I assumed the episcopate.” The Colbertine manuscript has: “whose dependent I was before the episcopate.”] Therefore I ask you, by almighty God, never to let this word appear in your letters to me again.

The gifts which you sent from a most pure and sincere heart to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, were received in the presence of all the clergy and hung there. [Note: [Col. 1153D] These veils were hung in churches. Gregory of Tours, in Book II, chapter 29 of his *History*, orders a church to be decorated with veils and curtains; and in chapter 31 says, “The church’s spaces are shaded with painted veils.” Audoenus, in the *Life of Eligius*, calls veils the ornaments of the basilica of the holy virgin Columba. Anastasius, in his account of Gregory III, says that in the Church of the Apostles he made veils of silk cloth hang between the columns. The same is found frequently elsewhere. Partly from Alteserra and Gussanville.]

But my son, the magnificent lord Symmachus, because he found me ill from the pain of gout and almost despairing of recovery, delayed giving me your letters and gave them to me only a long time after the veils had been received. Later, however, we found in the letters of Your Excellence that they ought to have been carried with a litany to the church of blessed Peter. This was not done because, as I said, we received the veils before the letters.

Nevertheless, the aforesaid man, together with your entire household, did what you wanted us to do with the clergy. [Note: [Col. 1154D] Vatican A, D, and E, and the Rheims manuscript, read “he performed this,” namely, the litany and procession, “which you wanted us to perform.”] Even if human voices were lacking, your offering itself has a voice before almighty God. For I trust in his mercy: since you covered his body on earth, his intercession will protect you from every sin in heaven, and he will govern your entire household by his provision and guard it by his vigilance.

[Col. 1153C] Concerning the trouble of gout which, as you indicated, has come upon you, I have been both greatly saddened and greatly rejoiced. I rejoiced because the harmful humor, descending toward the lower parts, has completely abandoned the upper parts; but I was saddened because I fear that in so frail a body you are suffering excessive pains. For where there is so little flesh, what strength can resist pain?

Indeed, you know what I have been like: bitterness of spirit and continual aggravation, together with the pain of gout, afflict me so greatly that my body has become dried up like a corpse in a tomb. Consequently, I can now rarely rise from my bed. If, therefore, the weight of my body has been reduced by the pain of gout to such dryness, what must I think of your body, which was already excessively thin before the pains began?

As for the alms you gave to the monastery of the blessed apostle Andrew, what need is there for me to say anything, since it is written: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will intercede for you” (Sirach 29:15). If that good deed itself has a voice before the secret ears of God, whether we cry out or remain silent, the very thing you have done well cries out.

I declare that there are such great miracles, such great care, and such great protection of the monks in that monastery of the same apostle that he seems to be its abbot in a special sense. For, to mention briefly a few of the many things that I learned from the abbot and prior of the monastery as they related them, [Note: [Col. 1154D] The printed editions read, “I learned from those relating them, I shall declare.” The manuscripts omit “I shall declare.”] one day two brothers were sent from there to purchase something for the benefit of the monastery. One was a younger man who seemed more prudent; the other was an older man, assigned to be the younger man’s guardian.

They both set out. From the money they had received, the one who had been sent as the younger man’s guardian secretly stole part of it without the other’s knowledge. As soon as they returned to the monastery and came before the threshold of the oratory, [Note: [Col. 1154D] Monks customarily went out in pairs, so that they might serve as witnesses to one another’s conduct. The Synod of Aachen, A.D. 817, canon 15, says: “Brothers are not to be sent on a journey alone, without another.” Alteserra.] [Note: Monks returning from outside went to the oratory beside the monastery gate to pray, so that by prayer they might expiate sins committed outside. Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 67. Alteserra.] the thief was seized by a demon, fell down, and began to be tormented.

When the demon left him, the monks gathered around and asked whether he had perhaps stolen something from what he had received. He denied it, and was again tormented. When released and questioned again, he denied it, and was tormented again. Thus eight times he denied it, and eight times he was tormented. After the eighth denial, he confessed how many coins he had stolen. He did penance, threw himself prostrate, acknowledged his sin, and, after receiving penance, was never again approached by the demon.

At another time, while the brothers were resting at midday on the feast day of the same apostle, [Note: [Col. 1154D] The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48, grants a midday sleep. See Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 3.] one of the brothers suddenly began to tremble with his eyes open but blind, and to utter loud cries. By these cries he testified that he could not bear what he was suffering.

The brothers ran together and saw him trembling with open eyes, crying out, and alienated from those present, perceiving nothing that could be happening outside. They lifted him in their arms and threw him before the altar of the holy apostle Andrew, and prostrated themselves in prayer for him. He immediately returned to himself and confessed what he had suffered.

He said that an old man had appeared to him and sent a black dog to tear him apart, saying, “Why did you wish to flee from this monastery?” Since he had been completely unable to escape the dog’s bites, certain monks came and begged the same old man on his behalf. The old man immediately ordered the dog to depart, and he himself returned to consciousness. He later often confessed, saying: “On the day when I suffered these things, I had resolved to flee from that monastery.”

Another monk also secretly wished to leave the same monastery. When he had considered this in his mind, he wished to enter the oratory, but was immediately handed over to a demon and violently tormented. The demon would leave him, and if he stood outside the oratory he suffered no harm; but if he attempted to enter, he was immediately handed over to the evil spirit and tormented.

When this had happened repeatedly, he confessed his fault: he had been planning to leave the monastery. The brothers then gathered and bound themselves to prayer for him for three days. He was so completely cured that afterward the evil spirit never again approached him. He said that, while he was being tormented, he saw the same blessed apostle and was rebuked by him for wishing to leave the monastery.

Two other brothers also fled from the same monastery. Beforehand, while speaking with the brothers, they gave signs that they intended to descend by the Appian Way toward Jerusalem. After leaving, however, they turned aside from the road. To prevent those following them from finding them, they discovered closed crypts near the Flaminian Gate [Note: [Col. 1155D] Vatican D and E, and the Colbertine manuscript, read “the Flammean Gate.” “Flaminian” seems to be the correct reading, since it was a well-known ancient gate of Rome. Shortly afterward these same manuscripts read “through the Meretronian Gate,” where Vatican A has “Meretronii” and all the Norman manuscripts have “Metrovi.”] and hid themselves inside.

When, in the evening, they were sought but could not be found in the community, certain brothers mounted horses and followed them. They left through the Metronian Gate in order to pursue them along the Latin or Appian Way. Suddenly, however, it occurred to them that they should seek them on the Salarian Way. They therefore went outside the city and turned their route toward the Salarian Way.

When they failed to find them there, they decided to return through the Flaminian Gate. As they returned, as soon as their horses came before the crypts in which the fugitives had hidden, the horses stopped, and, struck and compelled, refused to move forward. [Note: [Col. 1155D] The editors read “they could not,” considering it incongruous to attribute will to horses; the manuscript codices, including Regius, Rheims, Vatican, and others, read otherwise.]

The monks realized that such a thing could not be without a mystery. They looked toward the crypts and saw that their entrances had been blocked with masonry. Since their horses would go nowhere, they dismounted. They removed the stones that had been placed at the mouths of the crypts, entered, and found the fugitives lying on the ground in those same dark hiding places.

They brought them back to the monastery. As a result of this miracle they were so reformed that it greatly benefited them to have fled from the monastery for so short a time.

I have related these things so that Your Excellence might learn to whose oratory you gave your alms. May almighty God guard you in soul, body, and your entire household with heavenly protection, and grant you to live long for our consolation.

I ask you, in my place, to greet my most beloved son, the lord Strategius, together with his glorious parents, your children. (Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapters 58 and 67.)

## EPISTLE XLV. TO THE PATRICIAN THEOCTISTA

He shows in many ways that her mind ought not to be disturbed by slander, while the murmuring of slanderers must nevertheless be calmed by a peaceful and humble response. He also demonstrates, first, that marriages ought not to be dissolved for religious reasons; second, that all sins are completely forgiven in baptism; third, that after three years of penance there is no license to sin; and fourth, that even one who, compelled by necessity, anathematizes the thing for which he is reproached remains bound by the anathema. Many people have been falsely accused through ignorant zeal on those four points, but the accusers must nevertheless be pacified by reason and gentleness, and Theoctista herself must act in this way toward her own people.

[Col. 1156B]

Gregory to Theoctista, the patrician. [Note: [Col. 1156D] EPISTLE XLV [Al. 39].—She was the sister of the emperor Maurice; see above, Book I, Letter 5. In the manuscript Codex of the Capuchin Fathers at Rouen, this letter is entitled: “Concerning the calming of discord, Gregory to Theortista.”]

We ought to give great thanks to almighty God that our most pious and benevolent emperors have such close relatives from their own family near them, from whose conduct there is great joy for us all. Therefore we must continually pray for these same lords, that their lives, together with all that belongs to them, may be preserved for long and peaceful periods under the protection of heavenly grace.

I report what I learned when certain people informed me that, through the fickleness of the populace, an uproar of slander had arisen against you. As a result, I hear that Your Excellence has been distressed with no little weariness. If this is so, I am greatly surprised that you, who have fixed your heart in heaven, should be disturbed by words spoken by people on earth.

For blessed Job, when his friends who had come to console him broke out into reproach, said: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscience is on high” (Job 16:20). Whoever has the witness of his life in heaven ought not to fear the judgments of men on earth.

Paul, the leader of the good, also says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Again he says: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Galatians 6:4). For if we rejoice in praise and are broken by slander, we have placed our glory not in ourselves but in the mouths of others.

The foolish virgins did not take oil in their vessels, but the wise took oil in their vessels together with their lamps (Matthew 25). Our lamps are good works. Of these it is written: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

We take oil in vessels together with our lamps when we do not seek the splendor of glory from flattering neighbors because of our good deeds, but preserve it in the testimony of our conscience. In everything that is said about us from outside, we must return to the hidden places of the mind. Even if everyone condemns him, a person whose conscience does not accuse him is free; for even if everyone praises him, he cannot be free if his conscience accuses him.

Therefore Truth says concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” (Matthew 11:7). This is said by way of negation, not affirmation, as is shown by what follows: “But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments? Behold, those who are dressed in soft garments are in the houses of kings” (ibid., 8).

Although, according to the truth of the Gospel, John wore a rough garment, by way of symbolism those dressed in soft garments are people who delight in flattery and praise. It is denied that John was a reed shaken by the wind, because no breath from the human mouth could bend the strength of his mind.

But if we are lifted up by praise or humbled by reproach, we are reeds shaken by the wind. May this never be so—may it never be so in the heart of Your Excellence. I know that you diligently read the teacher of the nations, who says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

Nevertheless, if even a small sadness has arisen in your mind from this matter, I believe that almighty God kindly permitted it to happen. For he did not promise his chosen ones the joys of delight in this life, but the bitterness of tribulation, so that, as by a medicinal treatment, they might return through a bitter drink to the sweetness of eternal salvation.

What does he say? “The world will rejoice, but you will mourn” (John 16:20). On what basis? Under what promise? A little later it is added: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (ibid., 22). Again he says to the disciples: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

Consider, I ask you, where patience will be if there is nothing to endure. I do not suppose that Abel existed without Cain as a brother. For if the good were without the wicked, they could not be perfectly good, because they would not be purified. The companionship of the wicked is itself a purification for the good.

There were three sons of Noah in the ark; one became his father’s mocker. Although he himself had been blessed, he nevertheless received the sentence of the curse in his son. Abraham had two sons before he took Keturah as his wife, yet his carnal son persecuted the son of promise (Genesis 9). The great Teacher explains this, saying: “Just as the one who was according to the flesh persecuted the one who was according to the spirit, so it is now” (Galatians 4:29).

Isaac had two sons, but one, who was spiritual, fled before the threats of his carnal brother. Jacob had twelve sons, but the ten sold the one who lived more uprightly into Egypt. Since there was something in the prophet David that needed purification, it happened that the blessed father suffered persecution from his son.

Job says of the company of the reprobate: “I was a brother to dragons and a companion to ostriches” (Job 30:29). The Lord says to Ezekiel: “Son of man, unbelievers and subverters are with you, and you dwell among scorpions” (Ezekiel 2:6). One reprobate was mixed among the twelve apostles, so that the eleven might be tested by his persecution.

The prince of the apostles speaks to the disciples, saying: “He rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the abuse and conduct of the wicked. For by sight and hearing he was righteous, dwelling among those who day after day tormented the soul of the righteous with wicked deeds” (2 Peter 2:7–8).

The apostle Paul also writes to the disciples, saying: “Among a crooked and perverse nation, among whom you shine like lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Philippians 2:15).

Since, therefore, we know by the testimony of Scripture that in this life the good cannot exist without the wicked, Your Excellence ought in no way to be disturbed by the words of fools, especially [Note: [Col. 1157D] Recent manuscripts have: “because then there is certainly trust in the mercy of almighty God.” Our reading, which is that of the old printed edition, is supported by the Norman, Vatican, Colbertine, Rheims, Regius, and Remigius manuscripts.] because there is then certain confidence in almighty God, when something of adversity is received in this world for a good work, so that the full reward may be preserved for eternal recompense.

Therefore Truth says in the holy Gospel: “You will be blessed when men say every evil thing against you, lying because of my name” (Matthew 5:11). He also deigned to set his own reproaches before us as an example for our consolation, saying: “If they called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more those of his household?” (ibid., 10:25).

There are, however, very many who perhaps praise the life of good people more than they ought (Gratian, 6, q. 1, c. 11).

[Note: [Col. 1157D] We have added *fortasse* (“perhaps”) in deference to the manuscripts; otherwise, however, this reading is more acceptable to us.] And so that no pride may steal in through praise, almighty God permits the wicked to break out into disparagement and reproach, so that if some fault is born in the heart from the mouth of those who praise, it may be strangled by the mouth of those who condemn. Hence the teacher of the nations testifies that in his preaching he runs “through dishonor and good repute” (II Cor. VI, 8). He also says: “As deceivers and yet truthful.” If there were people who imposed a bad reputation on Paul, calling him a deceiver, what Christian, then, ought now to consider it unworthy to hear insults for Christ?

[Col. 1158D] We know what great virtue the forerunner of our Redeemer possessed: through the sacred writings he is called not only “more than a prophet,” but also an angel. Yet, as the account of his death testifies, after his death his body was burned by his persecutors.
