[Note: Theodoret recounts this briefly in *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 6: “At Ascalon and Gaza they cut open the bellies of men endowed with priestly dignity, and likewise of women who had professed perpetual virginity; they filled them with barley and threw them as food to pigs. At Sebaste, which is reckoned among that same people, they opened the tomb of John the Baptist and, after burning the bones, scattered the ashes.” GUSSANV.]

But why do we say these things about holy men? Let us speak of the Holy of holies himself, that is, of God who became human for us. Before his death he heard, as an insult, that he had a demon; after his death he was called a deceiver by his persecutors, when they said: “We know that that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again’” (Matt. XXVII, 63). How much, then, must we sinners endure from the tongues or hands of wicked people, who are to be judged at the coming of the eternal Judge, if even he, who comes as Judge, endured so much both before and after his death?

[Col. 1159A]

I have said these things briefly, dearest and most excellent daughter, so that whenever you learn that foolish people are disparaging you, you may not be touched by any, even the smallest, sadness of mind. But because the murmuring of foolish people can itself be quieted by calm reasoning, I believe it would be sinful if a good deed that can be done were neglected so that it might be done.

[Note: That is, as he immediately adds, there are scandals that must altogether be disregarded; but there are others which, when they can be avoided without sin, must not be disregarded, lest they be preserved together with sin. Thus Saint Paul taught that scandal should be avoided when speaking of eating meat, so that a weaker neighbor might not be offended (I Cor. VII; Rom. XIV). The Lord Christ had anticipated the same teaching in Matt. XVII–XVIII. See Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, II–II, question 43, especially articles 7 and 8. Saint Gregory uses nearly the same opinion in *Homily 7 on Ezekiel*: “In our good work, sometimes the scandal of our neighbor must be avoided, but sometimes it must be disregarded as nothing.” And below: “As far as we can without sin, we must avoid the scandal of our neighbors.” Read Innocent III, *On the denunciation of a new work*, chapter 2, where, without naming him, he reports this teaching of Saint Gregory, *Extravagantes*, book V, title 32. GUSSANV.]

For when we can appease mad minds and bring them back to salvation, we ought by no means to scandalize them. There are, indeed, some scandals that must altogether be disregarded; but there are others which, when they can be avoided without sin, must not be disregarded, lest they be preserved together with sin.

We learn this from the preaching of the sacred Gospel. When the Truth said, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth defiles a person” (Matt. XV, 11), and the disciples replied, saying, “Do you know that the Pharisees were scandalized when they heard this saying?” (ibid., 12), he immediately answered: “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted. Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind” (ibid., 13).

Yet when tribute was demanded, he first explained why he ought not to pay tribute, and immediately added: “But, so that we may not scandalize them, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for you” (Matt. XVII, 26).

What does it mean that, concerning some who were scandalized, he says, “Leave them; they are blind and guides of the blind,” while for others, so that they would not be scandalized, the Lord paid tribute—even though it was not owed? Why did he permit one scandal and forbid another from arising for others, except to teach us both to disregard those scandals that entangle us in sins and, by every possible means, to mitigate those that we can appease without sin?

[Col. 1159C]

Your Excellency can therefore, with the Lord’s protection, avoid the scandals of wicked people with great tranquility. Their leaders should first be summoned privately by you of their own accord, and an explanation should be given to them; certain erroneous propositions which they believe you hold should be anathematized in their presence.

[Note: *Recentiores*: “which they think you hold.”]

But if, as is said, they suspect that the anathema is being given falsely, it must also be confirmed by oath that you have never held, and do not now hold, those same propositions. Nor should it seem beneath you to satisfy them in such a manner, nor, because you are of imperial lineage, should there be any disdain toward them in your mind. For we are all brothers, created by the power of one emperor and redeemed by his blood. Therefore we must despise none of our brothers, however poor and contemptible they may be.

[Col. 1160A]

Certainly Peter had received the power of the heavenly kingdom, so that whatever he bound or loosed on earth would be bound or loosed in heaven. He walked upon the sea; he healed the sick with his shadow; he struck sinners dead by his word; he raised the dead by prayer.

And because, following the prompting of the Spirit, he had entered the home of the gentile Cornelius, the believers questioned him about why he had entered the gentiles’ house and eaten with them, and why he had received them in baptism. Yet this same first of the apostles, filled with such abundant grace of gifts and supported by such power of miracles, answered the complaint of the believers not by authority but by reason. He explained the matter in order: how he had seen a certain vessel, like a linen sheet, being lowered from heaven, containing four-footed animals of the earth, beasts, reptiles, and birds (Acts XI, 5 ff.); how he had heard a voice: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (ibid., 7); how three men had come, calling him to Cornelius; how the Holy Spirit had commanded him to go with them; and how the same Holy Spirit, who had been accustomed to come upon those baptized in Judea after baptism, came upon the gentiles before baptism.

For if, when he was being blamed by the believers, he had considered the authority he had received in the holy Church, he could have replied that the sheep entrusted to him did not dare to rebuke their shepherd. But if he had said something about his authority in response to the complaint of the believers, he would certainly not have been a teacher of gentleness. Therefore he appeased them with humble reasoning, and in the case of his own rebuke he even produced witnesses, saying: “These six brothers also accompanied me” (Acts XI, 12).

If, then, the shepherd of the Church, the chief of the apostles, who performed signs and miracles in an exceptional manner, did not disdain humbly to give an explanation when he was rebuked, how much more ought we sinners, when we are reproved for something, to appease those who reprove us by humble reasoning?

[Col. 1160D]

For, as you know, when I was staying at the feet of my lords in the imperial city, many of those who were accused of the aforementioned propositions used to come to me. But, with my conscience as witness, I confess that I never found in them any error, any depravity, or anything of what was alleged against them. Therefore, disregarding public opinion, I used to receive them familiarly and, even more, to defend them against their persecutors.

It was said against them that, under the pretext of religion, they dissolved marriages; that they said baptism did not completely remove sins; that if someone did penance for his iniquities for three years, it was afterward permissible for him to live wickedly; and that if, under compulsion, they anathematized something of what they were criticized for, they claimed that they were in no way held by the bond of the anathema.

If there are people who most certainly think or hold such things, there is no doubt that they are not Christians. I, together with all Catholic bishops and the whole Church, anathematize them, because they think and speak things contrary to the truth.

For if they say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be understood that, although human law has permitted this, divine law has nevertheless forbidden it.

[Note: The *Novella* of Julian—more properly, of Justinian—is cited, *Novella* 22, “On marriages,” concerning the grounds for divorce. Also book V of the *Code*, title 17, and the *Digest*, title “On divorces.” I add *Novella* 123, “On the Most Holy Bishops,” etc., especially chapter 40, “Let the marriage be dissolved.” GUSSANV.]

The Truth himself says: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX, 6). He also says: “It is not lawful to dismiss one’s wife, except on account of fornication” (ibid., 9).

Who, then, would contradict this heavenly Lawgiver? We know that it is written: “The two shall become one flesh” (Luke XVI; I Cor. VI; Gen. II, 24). If husband and wife are one flesh, and for the sake of religion the husband dismisses his wife, or the wife her husband who remains in this world—or perhaps even turns to illicit relations—what kind of conversion is this, in which one and the same flesh partly passes over to continence while partly remains in impurity?

But if both agree to lead a life of continence, who would dare accuse them, since it is certain that almighty God, who permitted lesser things, did not forbid greater ones? Indeed, we know that many holy people first led lives of continence with their spouses and afterward entered the governance of the holy Church.

Holy men customarily abstain even from what is lawful in two ways: sometimes so as to increase their merits before almighty God, and sometimes so as to cleanse the sins of their former life.

The three youths who were taken into the service of the king of Babylon requested vegetables for food and refused to use the royal provisions—not because it would have been sinful for them to eat what God had created. They therefore refused what was permitted so that their virtue might grow through continence.

David, however, who had taken another man’s wife and had been severely chastised for his fault, later desired to drink water from the cistern of Bethlehem. When the bravest soldiers had brought it to him, he refused to drink it and, pouring it out, offered it to the Lord. He was permitted to drink if he wished; but because he remembered having done what was unlawful, he laudably abstained even from what was lawful.

He who earlier had not feared to cause the blood of dying soldiers to be shed for his fault later judged that, if he drank the water, he would also have shed the blood of living soldiers, saying: “Shall I drink the blood of these men who went at the risk of their lives?” (I Chron. XI, 19).

Therefore, when good spouses desire either to increase their merit or to erase the sins of their former life, they may bind themselves to continence and pursue a better life. But if the wife does not follow the continence desired by the husband, or the husband refuses the continence desired by the wife, the marriage may not be divided, because it is written: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (I Cor. VII, 4).

[Note: If the marriage has been consummated, if the spouses have become “one flesh”; otherwise, according to our custom, it is dissolved through entry into religious life. GUSSANV.]

If there are people who say that sins are forgiven only superficially in baptism, what could be more faithless than this teaching, by which they hasten to undo the very sacrament of faith? In baptism the soul is principally bound to the mystery of heavenly cleansing, so that, radically freed from all sins, it may cling solely to him of whom the Prophet says: “But for me it is good to adhere to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Certainly the crossing of the Red Sea was a figure of holy baptism. In it, the enemies behind them were killed, but others were found before them in the wilderness. Thus all who are immersed in holy baptism have all their past sins loosed, because their sins die behind them like the Egyptian enemies.

But in the wilderness we find other enemies, because while we live in this life, before we reach the land of promise, many temptations weary us and hasten to block the path of those journeying toward the land of the living. Let him who says that sins are not wholly forgiven in baptism say that the Egyptians did not truly die in the Red Sea. But if he admits that the Egyptians truly died, he must necessarily admit that sins wholly die in baptism, since in our absolution the truth is plainly stronger than the shadow of truth.

In the Gospel the Lord says: “The one who has been washed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is entirely clean” (John XIII, 10).

[Note: Thus the manuscripts of Norm., Vatic., Corb., and others, although John reports it differently, namely, “except to wash his feet”; this is also the reading of the printed editions.]

If, then, sins are by no means completely forgiven in baptism, how is the one who has been washed entirely clean? For no one can be called entirely clean if something of sin remains in him. But no one resists the voice of the Truth: “The one who is entirely clean is clean altogether.” Nothing, therefore, of the contagion of his sin remains in the one whom the Redeemer himself declares to be entirely clean.

If there are people who say that penance must be performed for any sin for three years, and that after three years one may live in pleasures, they still know neither the principles of true faith nor the precepts of sacred Scripture.

Against them the outstanding preacher Paul says: “The one who sows in his flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. VI, 8). Again he says against them: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII, 8). To the disciples he adds: “But you are not in the flesh; you are in the spirit.” Those are in the flesh who live in carnal pleasures.

Against them it is said: “Corruption will not inherit incorruption” (I Cor. XV, 50). If they say that a brief period of penance ought to suffice for sin, so that afterward one may return to sin, the sentence of the first shepherd rightly strikes them: “What happened to them is an illustration of the true proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed pig to wallowing in the mud’” (II Pet. II, 21).

Penance has great power against sin, but only if a person perseveres in that same penance. For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22; XXIV, 13).

Again it is written: “The one who is baptized by a dead person and then touches him again—what benefit is there in his washing?” (Eccl. XXXIV, 30).

Every wicked deed that draws one toward death and does not live by the life of righteousness is dead. Therefore, the one who is baptized by a dead person and then touches him again is the person who laments the evil deeds he remembers having committed but becomes entangled in the same deeds again after his tears.

Thus the soul gains no benefit from the washing of that dead person if, by doing again what it lamented, it does not rise through the lamentation of penance to the uprightness of justice. For truly to do penance is to lament the sins committed and to avoid again the things that must be lamented.

[Col. 1163C]

If there are people who say that when someone, compelled by necessity, pronounces an anathema, he is not bound by the anathema, they themselves testify that they are not Christians. They think that they can dissolve the bonds of the holy Church by empty efforts and therefore do not consider the absolution of the holy Church, which it grants to the faithful, to be genuine, since they do not believe that its bonds have force.

[Note: The printed editions read, “if they do not consider its bonds to be true and effective.” In the printed editions, “if he has been anathematized” appears contrary to the manuscripts Reg., Remig., Norm., and others, and with a meaning far from that intended by the holy Doctor. Here *anathematizare* means “to swear,” as in Mark XIV, 71, not “to strike with an anathema.”]

There is no need to argue at greater length against such people, because they must be utterly disregarded and anathematized, so that in the very matter by which they believe they are deceiving the truth, they may truly be bound in their sins.

If, then, there are people who, under the Christian name, dare either to preach these aforementioned propositions of error or silently to hold them within themselves, we have undoubtedly anathematized them and do anathematize them.

[Col. 1163D]

Nevertheless, among all the propositions, as I said, I recognized absolutely no error concerning any of the aforementioned propositions in those who used to come to me in the imperial city, nor do I think that there was any. For if there had been, I would have recognized it.

Because, however, there are many believers who are inflamed by uninstructed zeal and often, while persecuting certain people as though they were heretics, create heresies, care must be taken for their weakness; and, as I said, they must be appeased by reason and gentleness. They are like those of whom it is written: “I testify about them that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. X, 2).

[Col. 1164A]

Your Excellency, who lives unceasingly in reading, tears, and almsgiving, ought, as I requested, to appease their lack of understanding through gentle exhortations and replies, so that you may find the glory of eternal reward not only for yourself but also for them.

Excessive love persuaded me to say these things to you, because I consider myself to grow in your joy and to diminish in your sorrow. May almighty God guard you with heavenly grace and, while preserving the piety of our lord and the tranquility of our most pious lady, extend your life further for the nourishment of the little lords.

## LETTER XLVI. TO ISAAC, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM

In reply to his synodical letter, he compares the Church to the ark, outside which there is no salvation. He praises Isaac’s faith, which he declares to be his own. He rejoices that the mouths of heretics have been silenced under a most Christian emperor. He urges Isaac to suppress simony in his churches and, by suppressing some quarrels and tolerating others, to mitigate disputes.

Gregory to Isaac, bishop of Jerusalem.

[Col. 1164C]

If we preserve the truth of the historical account, what else does it mean that, at the time of the Flood, the human race died outside the ark while life was preserved in the ark, except what we now clearly see: that all unbelievers outside the Church are destroyed by the flood of their sin, while the unity of the holy Church, like the structure of the ark, preserves its faithful in faith and charity?

That ark, clearly, is built of incorruptible wood,

[Note: *Epist.* XLVI [formerly XL]. The Vulgate has *laevigatis*; the Hebrew has *gopher*. Some rabbis translate it as “cedar wood.” Cedar abounds in Syria and is incorruptible. Saint Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 6, speaks of square timbers, and in chapter 7 distinguishes this ark of Noah from the ark of Moses, because the ark of Moses was made of incorruptible wood. Thus Cornelius a Lapide is mistaken here, or else is himself misled, in his commentary on Genesis. Saint Augustine, *Tractate 6 on John*, thinks that the wood was incorruptible. Saint Jerome, in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, reads “square,” which he interprets mystically of teachers. In Theodoret, *Dialogue* 1, “The Immutable,” the orthodox writer cites Saint Hippolytus, who says that the ark was made of incorruptible wood. Alcimus Avitus of Vienne, in his poem *On the Beginning of the World*, brings forests, oaks, and sturdy timber to the construction of the ark. GUSSANV. *Gopher* is a species of cedar. Pliny, says Buxtorf, mentions a certain cedar that does not suffer decay in book XIII, chapter 5.]

because it is built from strong souls who persevere in their goodness.

[Note: Nevertheless, there are also members of the Church who are weak in soul and do not persevere in their goodness, a fact which the Calvinists impiously deny. He therefore seems here to have in view only leaders powerful in work and speech, who, while feeding, governing, and guarding the faithful, build the mystical ark—that is, the Church—prepared to contain and preserve the peoples. GUSSANV.]

When each person turns away from secular life, it is as though wood is still being cut from the mountains. But when someone is brought into the order of the holy Church for the guardianship of others, it is as though an ark is built from wood that has been cut and prepared to preserve human life.

That ark, when the Flood had ceased, came to rest on a mountain, because, when the corruption of this life has ceased and the waves of evil deeds have passed, the holy Church will rest in the heavenly homeland as upon a lofty mountain.

Having read your letter, we rejoice that you are hastening toward the construction of this ark through the framework of right faith, and we give great thanks to almighty God, who, although the pastors of his flock have changed, preserves unchanged even after them the faith once handed down to the holy Fathers.

The outstanding preacher says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (I Cor. III, 11). Whoever, therefore, with love of God and neighbor, holds firm the faith that is in Christ has established within himself the same Jesus Christ, Son of God and of humanity, as a foundation.

We must therefore hope that where Christ is the foundation, the building of good works will also follow.

The Truth himself says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber. But whoever enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep” (John X, 1). A little later he adds: “I am the gate.”

Therefore, the one who enters the sheepfold through Christ enters through the gate. But the person enters through Christ who thinks and preaches truthfully about the same Creator and Redeemer of the human race, guards what has been preached, and accepts the summit of governance as an office of bearing a burden, not as a desire for the passing honor of glory.

He also watches diligently over the care of the flock entrusted to him, lest either wicked people, speaking evil things, tear apart the sheep of God, or evil spirits devastate them by persuading them to take pleasure in vices.

But in all these matters may he instruct us, the one who became human for us. May he who deigned to become what he himself made pour the spirit of his love both into my weakness and into your charity, and open the eye of our heart in every care and watchfulness of vigilance.

[Col. 1165C]

Since men of right faith are brought to the sacred orders, unceasing thanks must be offered to that same almighty God, and prayers must always be made for the life of our most pious and most Christian lord the emperor, for his most tranquil wife, and for his most gentle offspring. In their time the mouths of heretics fall silent, because, although their hearts boil with the madness of a perverse opinion, under an orthodox emperor they nevertheless do not dare to express openly the wrong things they think.

Thus we plainly see fulfilled what is written:

[Col. 1165D]

[Note: Augustine had anticipated this interpretation in his commentary on Psalm XXXII: “Now it is enclosed within mortal breasts and is bitter … He gathered the waters of the sea as into a wineskin, so that mortal skin might cover bitter thought.”]

“Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin” (Ps. XXXII, 7).

For the water of the sea has been gathered as into a wineskin because the bitter knowledge of heretics compresses within the breast whatever it thinks wrongly today and does not dare to express openly.

Your fraternity, spiritually instructed, has set forth the right faith in every respect and has explained with subtlety the things that needed to be investigated. Your faith, therefore, is our faith. We hold what you say, and we say what you hold.

Because it has come to our attention that in the churches of the East no one reaches sacred orders except through the giving of rewards, if your fraternity recognizes that this is so, let it offer this first offering to almighty God: suppress the error of the simoniacal heresy in the churches subject to you.

To say nothing of other matters, what sort of people can there be in the sacred orders who are advanced to them not by merit but by payment? We know with what severity the chief of the apostles pursued this matter. He pronounced the first sentence of condemnation against Simon, saying: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money” (Acts VIII, 20).

The Lord our God, the Creator and Redeemer of the human race, also made a whip from cords and overturned from the temple the seats of those selling doves (Matt. XXI). For what else is it to sell doves in the temple than to confer in the holy Church, for a price, the laying on of hands through which the Holy Spirit is given?

But the seats of those selling doves were overturned,

[Note: These words should be interpreted favorably. Simony does not prevent someone from truly and in reality being invested with sacred orders. An outward administration is not prevented by a hidden crime. Nevertheless, the person so promoted does not acquire a prescriptive right by possession, even after three years, because he was not truly—that is, not lawfully—promoted. We believe that this rule arose from abhorrence of so great a crime, since in other unlawful promotions the Church’s censure is more lenient. See the note on book II, letter 46.]

because the priesthood of such people is not counted as priesthood.

Moreover, it has come to me that in the church called Neas, within your Church in the city of Jerusalem, quarrels frequently arise. Therefore your Holiness ought carefully to weigh everything and to correct some matters gently, while tolerating with equanimity others that cannot be corrected.

For we clearly see that the holy Church says through the voice of the Psalmist: “The sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. CXXVIII, 1–2). Burdens are carried upon the back. Sinners therefore build upon our back when we carry with patience those whom we cannot correct.

A ship’s pilot, when he observes a wind opposing him, overcomes some waves by holding the rudder straight, but those which he foresees cannot be overcome he prudently avoids by changing course. Thus your Holiness should mitigate some matters by suppressing them and others by tolerating them, so that you may preserve in every respect the peace of those dwelling together in the holy Church of Jerusalem.

For it is written: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Heb. XII, 14). In a quarrel, the light of good intention itself is shut out from the mind. Hence the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. VI, 8).

And what good work remains in us if we lose peace from our heart, without which we cannot see the Lord? Act, therefore, in such a way that from those who might have perished through quarrelling you may also gather the profits of your reward.

May almighty God guard your charity with heavenly grace and grant you to carry back to eternal joys abundant fruit and an overflowing measure from those entrusted to you.

(See book VII, letter 32.)

## LETTER XLVII. TO ANATOLIUS, DEACON OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Neither John nor any other bishop should be deposed on account of bodily illness.

Gregory to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.

[Col. 1167A]

Your Charity wrote to me that our most pious lord had ordered my most reverend brother John, bishop of First Justiniana, to be replaced because of the head illness from which he suffers, lest, while that city lacks the rights of a bishop, it should—God forbid—perish at the hands of enemies.

Nowhere, however, do the canons prescribe that a bishop should be replaced because of illness. It is wholly unjust that, if bodily sickness attacks, a sick man should be deprived of his honor. Therefore this cannot in any way be done by us, lest sin come upon my soul through his deposition.

But it should be suggested that, if the man who is in charge is ill, an administrator be appointed who can take complete care of him and preserve his place in the governance of the Church without deposing him, and who can fulfill his duties in the guardianship of the city,

[Col. 1167B]

[Note: *Epist.* XLVII [formerly XLI]. An unwilling sick man is not replaced; another may be appointed to govern in his place. Should it be a presbyter from his own clergy? Or an outside bishop consecrated under the title *in partibus infidelium*, whom they call a coadjutor, with future succession? Or, without future succession, a suffragan while the see remains occupied? GUSSANV.]

so that neither almighty God may be offended nor the city be found neglected.

But if the same most reverend John should perhaps request, on account of his illness, to be released from the honor of the episcopate, his request should be granted once he has submitted it in writing. Otherwise, out of fear of almighty God, we are entirely unable to do this.

[Note: The printed editions read, “we do not dare.” We follow Reg., Remig., Vat., and many manuscript witnesses.]

If he does not wish to make this request, however, then, since it pleases the most pious emperor, whatever he commands is within his authority. Let him provide for the matter as he knows best. Let him only not involve us in the deposition of such a man. Whatever he does, if it is canonical, we follow it. If it is not canonical, we bear it as far as we can without our own sin.

(Compare John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 39.)

## LETTER XLVIII. TO URBICUS, ABBOT

He reproves his inconstancy and rashness. He himself orders who should be abbot and who should be provost in the Lucusian monastery.

Gregory to Urbicus, abbot.

Let your Love know that I am greatly saddened because such great confusion has arisen in our monastery’s congregation that, while you were arranging something concerning the appointment of an abbot at the Lucusian monastery, you made not one but nearly two abbots: Domitius the priest in the morning, as I hear, but in the evening Bon, the bearer of this letter, a servant of God. From this I see how lax the monastery’s rule has become, since neither the monks of that monastery have been ready to obey you, nor have you been able to make any decision consistently. I therefore groan exceedingly, because I find our monastery to be other than I had thought. This could have happened for no other reason than that your Love is disordered in its administration and cannot arrange anything with gravity; at one moment you strive weakly to flatter those who sin, at another you become excessively angry, disorderly, and beyond measure. For if you had been able to restrain yourself by the judgment of your mind, your maturity could have been held in respect, and the order of discipline could have been preserved in the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] EPIST. XLVIII [Al. 42].—It is read as *Lucuscano* in most manuscripts. Urbicus was formerly a provost, according to Book V, Letter 6; later he was abbot of Saint Hermes, otherwise of Saint John the Baptist, now Saint John of the Hermits, near Palermo, according to Book VI, Letter 48. By order of Saint Gregory, he appears also to have had charge of other monasteries of Sicily, among them the Lucusian monastery, which Gregory calls his own monastery because it had been built and founded through his munificence, together with five others in Sicily, as John the Deacon testifies, Book I, chapter 5. Rochus Pirrus states that Urbicus was the general provost of the Benedictine, or Gregorian, monasteries in Sicily, Book IV, part 2.]

I consider this deed all the worse because you presumed, without my order, to remove the aforementioned Bon, a monk, from the monastery that he had built—especially since I suspect that it is not suitable to his age for him to preside in an administration. Therefore we decree that Domitius the priest is to be abbot of the Lucusian monastery, and that the monk Lucifer is to become his provost, so that he may be able to rest upon his assistance. By our authority, then, we command you, with God’s help, to arrange these matters. If anyone should presume to oppose this arrangement, let him without doubt be sent to us.

Having received our letters, therefore, let your Love invite our brother and fellow bishop Victor to the Lucusian monastery, so that he himself may celebrate the solemnities of the Mass there and, with God as author, ordain the aforesaid Domitius abbot, lest, while we follow your counsel, we be led into error like the blind.

For your Love had wished the monk Catellus to become provost in the Lucusian monastery. After we ordered this to be done, we discovered that he is not a monk. For, having received a small *eulogia*, he did not hesitate, while on the journey, to cause a dispute by asking for a share. Your Love will be able to understand from how great a bitterness of heart this proceeded, if you had wished to know the Rule of the Monks.

[Note: [Col. 1168D] That is, the Rule written by Saint Benedict, where chapter 54 forbids monks to receive *eulogiae* without the abbot’s order. Saint Gregory, Book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36, says of Saint Benedict: “He wrote a rule for monks.”]

From your disciple, however, we have learned that you, who are called an abbot, do not yet know how to be a monk. And I believe that the cellarer Lucifer, whom we ordered to become provost, is of no different mind in this division.

[Note: [Col. 1168D] The printed editions have *cellarius*, “cellarer.” *Cellerarius* is preferable, as found in the English manuscripts, Vatican D, Victor, and many others. This reading is confirmed by Book XII, Letter 24, and by the Rule of Saint Benedict, where the monastery’s cellarer is frequently mentioned, but never a *cellarius*. In monastic rules, however, both *cellerarius* and *cellarius* are found, as may be seen in the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 581 and following.]

But it is more tolerable to endure an older brother than a new and inexperienced one.

## LETTER XLIX. TO URBICUS, THE ABBOT

He is to give forty solidi from the money of the Lucusian monastery to Peter, bishop of Tricala.

[Col. 1169A]

Gregory to Urbicus, the abbot.

When your Love receives this letter, let him take care, without delay or any excuse, to give forty solidi from the Lucusian monastery—of which our notary Salerius reported that they were in his possession—to our brother Peter, bishop of Tricala. Moreover, let it be your strict concern, as abbot of the aforementioned Lucusian monastery, to provide every year, in every possible way, food and clothing from it to the monks whom our aforesaid brother removed from that same monastery and took into his care for their salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] EPIST. XLIX [Al. 43].—In Vatican A, which almost alone, together with Remigius and Victor, contains this letter, the reading is *vestiarium*, “clothing treasury.”]

## LETTER L. TO ADRIAN, THE NOTARY

He orders Agathosa’s husband, who was tonsured and made a monk against her will, to be restored to her.

[Col. 1169B]

Gregory to Adrian, notary of Palermo.

Agathosa (Gratian, 27, question 2, canon 21), the bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband was converted to monastic life in the monastery of Abbot Urbicus against her will. Since this unquestionably pertains to the fault and discredit of that abbot, we command Your Experience to investigate the matter carefully, lest perhaps he was converted with her consent, or lest she herself promised to change her way of life. If you discover that this was the case, arrange both for him to remain in the monastery and compel her, as she promised, to change her way of life.

But if neither of these things is true, and you discover that the aforesaid woman did not commit some crime of fornication for which a man is permitted to leave his wife, we wish you, without any excuse, to restore her husband to her—or, if he has already been tonsured, to restore him nonetheless—lest his conversion become an occasion of perdition for the wife who has been left in the world.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] EPIST. L [Al. 44].—In Gratian, at the cited passage, the word “once” is absent.]

For although worldly law decrees that, for the sake of conversion, a marriage may be dissolved even against the will of either party, divine law nevertheless does not permit this to be done. For, except in the case of fornication, a man is in no way permitted to dismiss his wife, because once the man and woman have become one body through marital union, one cannot be converted in part while the other remains in the world.

[Note: [Col. 1169D] Gregory’s view seems to have been that, when one of the spouses had committed fornication, the other was permitted to enter a monastery and profess the monastic life with stability.]

[Note: [Col. 1169D] On this matter above. See Justinian’s Novella 123, chapter 40, which seems capable of being interpreted as referring to a ratified marriage—a matter that apparently did not occur to Saint Gregory at that time. Now, however, a ratified marriage is dissolved by entry into religious life, provided it has not been consummated. But if intercourse preceded the wedding, could the husband enter religious life against his wife’s will? GUSSANV. This novella is cited for this canon in the latest edition of the *Corpus Juris Canonici*; but instead of chapter 40, chapter 58 is assigned, as the novella is divided in Julianus.]

(See John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 41.)

## LETTER LI. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF SICILY

He prescribes litanies twice each week against the impending invasion of the enemy and exhorts the faithful to turn away from worldly corruption.

[Col. 1169D]

Gregory to all the bishops of Sicily.

[Col. 1170A]

In addition to the afflictions and groans that we have endured here from our enemies through a long succession of years, a greater fear torments us: we know that our enemies are hastening with every effort to invade Sicily. But lest the multitude of our sins provide prosperity for those who are plotting these things against us, let us turn with our whole heart to the remedies of our Redeemer, and meet with tears those whom we cannot resist by force.

For from the desolation of this province you ought to gather what must be guarded against and what must be feared most intensely. Therefore I exhort you, dearest brothers, to prescribe a litany every week, on Wednesday and Friday, without excuse, and to implore the assistance of heavenly protection against the attacks of barbarian cruelty.

[Note: [Col. 1170D] EPIST. LI [Al. 45].—*Litania*, from the Greek word λίσσομαι, “I beseech,” here signifies a public supplication. It took its name from the words “Kyrie eleison,” which are said first. Hence Saint Benedict, Rule, chapter 9: “after this … the supplication of the litany,” that is, “Kyrie eleison.” These matters are treated at length in the notes to the *Sacramentary* and below, in the appendix to the letters.]

But in order for you to make a way for your prayers to reach God’s ears, you must strive more vigilantly to support your words with deeds; for prayer is empty where conduct is wicked. Since, therefore, you see how enormous the danger threatening us is, you must all at once occupy yourselves with weeping and groaning. By priestly exhortation, restrain your children as quickly as possible from worldly corruption. Let them learn to despise what is unjust and love what pleases God, so that you may have them as helpers in obtaining the grace of divine mercy. Otherwise, if you neglect them, their conduct may outweigh the prayers of your prayers, and the sword of the raging enemy—God forbid—may cut down those whom the words of their admonisher do not correct.

Our God, however, is just and merciful: just toward those who persist in wickedness, and merciful toward those who are converted. Let us therefore run to him with the cries of a contrite heart and our whole mind, and ask from him the consolations of our deliverance. Since he is kind and gentle, if he sees us corrected from our evils and loving his commandments, he is powerful both to defend us here from the enemy and to prepare eternal joys for us in the future.

(See John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 53.)

## LETTER LII. TO DONUS, BISHOP OF MESSANA

What was adjudged between Placidus and the representatives of the Church of Messana is to be fulfilled.

Gregory to Donus, bishop of Messana.

No end is ever put to disputes if the fulfillment of what has been adjudged is delayed. Our son Placidus, a magnificent man, has therefore complained to us that Your Fraternity is unwilling to fulfill what was defined by God’s judgment between him and the representatives of your Church. If this is so, we are astonished that, although you ought to strive for your own peace, you should preserve for yourselves a cause of contention.

Accordingly, by this letter we exhort you to investigate the matter carefully. If anything remains unfulfilled—provided that nothing justly capable of obstructing it exists—let it be completed without discord, so that neither the aforesaid magnificent man may complain that he is being irrationally wearied, nor may you appear to have despised what is just, contrary to the purpose of your own order.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] The printed editions read: “and let there not be those to whom the aforesaid …” Below they have *of our order* instead of *of your order*, as is read in all the Vatican and Norman manuscripts, and elsewhere.]

[Note: [Col. 1171D] These words are absent from most manuscripts. They are found in Vatican B and E and in the Colbert manuscript, where, however, the indiction is given as 3.]

Given in the month of June, indiction 4.

## LETTER LIII. TO ADRIAN, THE NOTARY

He is to continue pursuing enchanters and diviners.

Gregory to Adrian, the notary.

It has come to our attention (Gratian, 26, question 5, canon 8) that you have pursued certain enchanters and diviners.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] EPIST. LIII [Al. 47].—That there was a great number of diviners around this time is shown by many conciliar canons, such as those of Venice, Agde, Orléans I, Auxerre, Narbonne, and Leptines. GUSSANV.]

Know that your diligence and zeal have been entirely pleasing to us. But we were displeased to learn that you doubted whether they might have insinuated something to us against your reputation, since you ought to be certain and know that this will serve more to commend you to us than to be charged against you as a fault.

Therefore let it be your concern to investigate diligently, and whatever enemies of Christ of this kind you find, correct them with such strict punishment that we may form an even better judgment of your experience, and that you may be able to commend yourself to our God—which is what you must strive for above all.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] In two Colbert manuscripts, this letter is preceded by: “In the month of June, indiction 4.”]

## LETTER LIV. TO DESIDERIUS, BISHOP OF GAUL

A bishop ought not to teach grammar. He commends the monks whom he is sending with Laurence and Mellitus to Britain.

[Col. 1171C]

Gregory to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] The bishop of Vienne, concerning whom see Book VI, Letter 54.]

Since many good things had been reported to us about your pursuits (Gratian, Distinction 86, canon 5), joy arose in our heart, so that we could not refuse to grant what Your Fraternity had requested should be granted to you. But afterward it came to us—something we cannot mention without shame—that Your Fraternity was explaining grammar to certain persons. We received this matter with such displeasure and rejected it so vehemently that we turned what had previously been said into groaning and sadness, because the praises of Christ and the praises of Jupiter cannot be contained in the same mouth.

Consider for yourself how serious and abominable it is for bishops to sing what is not fitting even for a religious layman.

[Note: [Col. 1171D] “Religious” here means a pious man, whom Gregory appears to wish to restrain from teaching grammar in schools and from reading pagan authors in the classroom. Nevertheless, many did this both in monasteries and in episcopal establishments and neighboring ecclesiastical places, as well as in general schools; and what was blamed as a fault in Saint Gregory of Nyssa is counted as praise in others. Indeed, Gregory himself, in Book V of his commentary on 1 Kings, chapter 3, no. 30, warmly praises the study of grammar and proficiency in the other so-called liberal arts, because they greatly assist us in understanding Sacred Scripture. Thus we judge that it is not the subject itself that is being condemned, but its improper use.]

Although our most beloved son Candidus the priest later came and, after being carefully questioned about this matter, denied it and tried to excuse you, it has nevertheless not yet departed from our minds that, just as it is detestable for this to be reported of a priest, so it must be ascertained through strict and truthful satisfaction whether it is so or not.

Therefore, if it is subsequently made clear that what was reported to us is manifestly false, and it is established that you do not devote yourself to trifles and worldly literature, we give thanks to our God, who did not permit your heart to be stained by the blasphemous praises of the impious. We shall then confidently and without any doubt consider granting what you request.

As for the monks whom we have sent, together with our most beloved son Laurence the priest and Mellitus the abbot, to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, we commend them to you in every respect, so that, with Your Fraternity providing them assistance, no delay may be able to prevent them from setting out.

(See John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 53.)

## LETTER LV. TO VIRGILIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

He urges that a synod be convened to eradicate simony. He is to restrain Bishop Serenus from the company of wicked men. He is to regard as commended the monks going to Augustine.

Gregory to Virgilius, bishop of Arles.

[Note: [Col. 1172D] EPIST. LV [Al. 49].—In Vatican A, D, and E, the name is *Vergilius*.]

Since the service of idols is called avarice in the testimony of divine Scripture, it is clear with what zeal it must be driven from the temple of God; yet some priests do not guard against it, as we say with grief. Fierce greed holds the heart captive, persuades it that what it commands is lawful evil, and acts in such a way that with one and the same sword it destroys both the giver and the receiver.

Who, then, could afterward find any place secure from avarice if God’s Church is opened to it by wicked priests? When does the one who invites the wolf inside preserve the sheepfolds inviolate? Shame upon the evil! He pollutes his hands with an illicit gift and believes that he raises others by his blessing, although he himself has already been cast down by his own iniquity and is nevertheless held captive by his ambition.

Since you testify that the rapacity of this evil has never entered the citadel of your mind and that your hands are innocent in ordinations, give thanks to Almighty God, and recognize that you are all the more indebted to him because, under his protection, you have remained unharmed by the contagion of this disease.

But these good qualities profit you less than they might if you have not carefully forbidden this in others as well.

[Note: [Col. 1172D] Vatican A, B, D, and E read *non vitastis*, “you have not avoided.” The Norman manuscript and most others agree.]

Just as this evil displeased you in yourself, so you ought to have shown zeal against it in your brother also.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] The printed editions read: “you ought with grief to have shown zeal against it in your brother.”]

For since divine commandments warn us that we must love our neighbors as ourselves, it is no small fault to despise something and not fear for others what each person fears for himself.

Therefore, dearest brother, now take care to repair by acting what you lost in others through your silence in correction, and restrain from this depravity as many as you can. Insist also that a synod be convened to eradicate this very heresy, so that, with the reward of your love, all may more carefully avoid what, by God’s authority, has been condemned by the decree of all.

Moreover, it has come to us (Gratian, 2, question 7, canon 59) that our brother and fellow bishop Serenus of Marseilles receives altogether wicked men into his company, so much so that he keeps as a familiar associate a certain priest who is said still to be entangled in his own iniquities after his fall.

This must be investigated carefully by you. If it is established, let it be your concern to correct the matter in our stead in such a way that the one who receives such a man may learn not to encourage him by familiarity but rather to restrain him by punishment, while the one who has been received may learn to wash away his sins with tears rather than heap iniquity upon impurity.

As for the monks whom we have sent to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine, let Your Fraternity regard them as commended in every respect. Strive to assist and support them in setting out, both personally and through others whom you can employ, so that, with your help, they may quickly reach, under God’s protection, the place to which they have been sent.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] The printed editions read *valeant pervenire*, “may they be able to arrive.” In two Teller manuscripts, *valeant exire*, “may they be able to depart,” is found. The following is added: “Given on the Kalends of January, indiction 4.” The same is read in Remigius, but “of January” is omitted.]

## LETTER LVI. TO AETHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYONS

He is to urge that a synod be convened. He is to send copies of his Church’s privileges. The writings of Irenaeus cannot be found. He commends the monks sent to Augustine in England.

[Col. 1173C]

Gregory to Aetherius, bishop of Gaul.

The language of your letters, full of venerable gravity, has so fixed your affection in our heart that we always desire to mingle our conversation with yours, so that, even if we cannot enjoy your bodily presence, absence may not be able to claim anything against us while this exchange continues.

For you show, by the humble and wholly willing way in which you receive our exhortation and proclaim that it must be kept inviolate, how brightly love for ecclesiastical order shines in you, how great is your love of discipline, and how great your zeal for observing salutary decrees.

Since, therefore, you possess a heart ready for the correction of others and condemn the evil of antiquity with the free voice that is fitting, and since our other brothers and fellow bishops share this same will, you ought, with one mind, to rise up against the enemies of the Lord and cast avarice from the house of God by synodal decree.

Let no fierce hunger for gold find a place in the conferral of ecclesiastical orders; let no flattery steal in; let no favor bestow anything. Let life be the reward of honor, advancement the increase of modesty, so that, when such observance prevails, one who seeks to rise by rewards may be judged unworthy, while the one whose conduct gives a good testimony may be honored worthily.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] In recent manuscripts *saeva*, “fierce,” is omitted. We do not know why, for it is read in almost all manuscripts and in the old edition, and the epithet is especially appropriate to the hunger and madness for gold.]

[Note: [Col. 1173D] This passage had to be corrected with the help of manuscripts. It had previously read: “let the reward of honor be advancement in life, increase in wisdom, improvement in character.” Our reading is taken from the Norman manuscript, three Vatican manuscripts, the Corbie manuscript, Saint-Victor, and Remigius. In Rheims and Vatican D, *sapientia*, “wisdom,” is added after *provectus*, “advancement.”]

Let this be your concern, dearest brother; let this vigilance always watch over your minds, so that you may show by your deeds that the zeal you display in your letters is a witness to your heart. Therefore, attend constantly and earnestly to convening a synod, and present yourself with such determination that you may fulfill the dignity of your name through the administration of your office.

As for what you request should be granted to your Church on the basis of ancient custom, we ordered a search to be made in the archives, but nothing was found. Therefore send us the letters that you say you possess, so that from them we may determine what ought to be granted.

We have also diligently sought for a long time the records or writings of the blessed Irenaeus, but thus far it has not been possible to find anything among them.

[Note: [Col. 1174D] Saint Gregory complains that he was unable to find either the writings or the records of Saint Irenaeus. We possess most of the writings—or rather, the Latin translation of his writings—but no one has yet produced authentic records. Saint Jerome gives Irenaeus the title of martyr only once, namely in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 64, although he frequently speaks honorably of his writings. Some indeed doubt his martyrdom. Perhaps for this reason Saint Gregory, when speaking of him, refrains from calling him a martyr. If you read William Cave, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, who attacks the martyrdom of Irenaeus, consult Tillemont afterward, volume III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, under Irenaeus.]

Furthermore, let Your Fraternity regard as commended in every respect the monks whom we have sent to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine. Show them your charity for God’s sake, and assist them earnestly with priestly zeal and hasten to help them set out on their journey through your support, so that, since nothing there may give them reason to remain, they may proceed more quickly and you may obtain a reward for what you have provided.

[Note: [Col. 1174D] In two Teller manuscripts: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.” In three Vatican manuscripts: “In the month of July, indiction 4.” In Remigius: “Given in the month of September, indiction 4.”]

Given on the tenth day of July, indiction 4.

(See the preceding Letter 49.)

## LETTER LVII. TO ARIGIUS, BISHOP OF GAP

He is to work for the condemnation of simony in a council. He is to favor the monks going to Augustine.

Gregory to Arigius, bishop of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 1174D] EPIST. LVII [Al. 51].—Concerning Arigius, bishop of Gap, see Letter 107, indiction 2.]

[Col. 1175A]

Since in fraternal love there is one heart and one spirit, just as the mind rejoices in another’s prosperity, so it is afflicted by adversity, because the law of love binds us to share in both.

[Note: [Col. 1175B] The printed editions read: “we are bound by the law of love to be participants.”]

Therefore a greater sorrow over your sadness had seized us, lest perhaps the affliction of prolonged grief should strike your heart with continual pain and burden your life with groans. But after receiving your letters of charity, we were consoled by the joy we had desired, and we gave thanks to Almighty God because we learned both that your unity remained unharmed and that your spirit had returned to consolation.

For there was no other way to judge concerning you except that, whatever adversity existed, you would undoubtedly overcome it through priestly patience.

We well remember how your zeal formerly burned in cutting off the simoniacal heresy. Therefore we exhort you to devote yourself more earnestly, so that, among the strict measures about which we have written, it may be condemned by the decree of a council. Thus, when the purpose of our will has been fulfilled through the assistance of your vigilance, you may offer to Almighty God a most acceptable offering consisting in the correction of vices, and display for the edification of others how brightly the care of pastoral office shines in you.

[Note: [Col. 1175B] Another reading has: “and for the edification of others,” as in the printed editions, but it is found in only a few manuscripts.]

The experience of your life urges us on, since we know that you surpass many by a great degree, and therefore we confidently anticipate great consolation from you in this matter.

[Note: [Col. 1175B] The printed editions read: “your fervor,” although almost all the manuscripts oppose this reading.]

Therefore carry through the support which, with God’s help, you have begun to provide, so that the good works begun in you with right intention may, with the help of God the Creator of all, be more rightly brought to completion.

Furthermore, let Your Fraternity show, as you are accustomed, your charity toward the monks whom we have sent to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine. Strive to assist them in setting out, both personally and through others whom you can employ, so that, since under your care they will encounter no difficulties or delays there, we may experience what we trust concerning you, and Almighty God may repay you with his grace for the conversion of the souls for whose sake they have been sent.

## LETTER LVIII. TO VARIOUS BISHOPS OF GAUL

He commends the monks going to Augustine in England.

Gregory

**[Note: [Col. 1175B] EPISTLE LVIII [otherwise 52].—Thus it is found throughout the older and more accurate manuscripts. In the third Colbert manuscript, instead of *Telonae*, *Tolosano* is read (as is also found in most printed editions), and instead of *Licinio*, *Leontio*. In the old Colbert manuscript, instead of *Cabilloni*, *Caralon* occurs. In two old Colbert manuscripts, *Rotomo* or *Rotumo* is found; in the others, *Rotomagensi*. We shall cite other variant readings from the manuscripts, examining separately each name in the title, whether of bishops or of cities. Cointius writes that this heading was corrupted, and that the names of other bishops besides Menna were added carelessly, in *Annales Ecclesiastici Francorum*, under the years 598, no. 5, and 601, no. 1. He relies on two arguments. He derives the first from the fact that, in a very ancient register of Gregory, the heading is worded as follows: “To Menna of Toulouse and several other bishops of Gaul.” The editions of Erasmus, both the Paris editions of 1518 and 1523 and the Nivelle edition of 1591, he says, followed this form for the most part. Yet nearly all manuscript codices exhibit the complete heading, in which Menna of Toulon or Telonna is read, followed by the names of other bishops. Moreover, *Tolosano* is found not in ancient parchment manuscripts but only in one or another of the more recent manuscript codices. He derives his second argument from the fact that both Aigulf of Metz and Melantius of Rouen had died in 598, and that Lupus could not then have been bishop of Chalon, since his predecessor Gratus had subscribed the Synod of Chalon during the reign of Chlothar II. Concerning Lupus, one should rather say, with the Sammarthani in *Gallia Christiana* and the Bollandists under 27 January, that Claudius Robert and Jean Chenu are mistaken, and that in the commonly printed catalogues Gratus is improperly placed before Lupus. As for Aigulf, Mabillon, in his observation on the life of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz, in *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. II, shows that Arnulf did not take possession of the see of Metz before 614. “Indeed,” says Cointius himself under the year 611, no. 1, “the chronology concerning the bishops of Metz depends upon the date of Arnulf’s ordination.” Yet, according to Cointius himself under the year 610, no. 14, Pappolus, Arnulf’s predecessor, died . . . after having held the see for three years and thirty days. Under the year 607, no. 19, Pappolus’s predecessor Arnoaldus died after having held it for eight years and one month. Therefore nothing proves that Aigulf, Arnoaldus’s predecessor, died before 603, since Arnulf did not enter upon the see of Metz before 614. There is greater difficulty concerning Melantius of Rouen if the third year of Clodoveus, in which Saint Audoenus is known to have been ordained, is assigned not to the year 646 but to 640, as Valesius, Cointius, Mabillon, and finally Henschenius have held after Adrian Valesius. For Romanus, Audoenus’s predecessor, is said to have held the see for thirteen years, and Hidulfus, before Romanus, for twenty-eight; consequently Melantius had died before the year 600. Yet perhaps Ordericus Vitalis was deceived or corrupted in the years assigned to Melantius and Hidulfus, just as the learned Francis de la Pommeraie demonstrates in his history of the archbishops of Rouen that he either erred or was corrupted concerning Peter, Victricius, Silvester, Gildardus, Flavius, and Evodius. Furthermore, that chronology which counts the sixteen years of Dagobert from the beginning of his reign in Austrasia, rather than from the death of his father Chlothar, although it has Fredegar as its author (a matter so obvious that no one before Adrian Valesius had noticed it), does not appear certain so long as so many arguments standing against it remain unresolved in Chifflet’s dissertation on the years of Dagobert. Certainly Valesius, Cointius, and Henschenius attempted in vain to weaken the force of the argument derived from the ordination of Saints Audoenus and Eligius, as Mabillon admits in the preface to the fourth century of the Benedictines, no. 201. Mabillon himself tried in vain: after approving Cointius’s reply in the preface to the second century of the Benedictines and rejecting the same reply in the preface to the fourth century, he finally returned to it, since no better solution occurred to him, in his separate dissertation on the year of the death of Dagobert I and the younger Clodoveus, in the third volume of the *Analecta*. Yet Henschenius decisively refutes that reply of Cointius in the preliminary exposition to the third volume of April, chapter 1, no. 3. Here is the unmistakable testimony of Saint Audoenus, *Life of Saint Eligius*, book II, chapter 2: “Accordingly, having assembled together in the city of Rouen on the fourteenth day of the third month (which was May, as the learned agree), in the third year of the still youthful King Clodoveus, on the Sunday before the Litanies, amid crowds of people and choirs of singers, we were consecrated bishops by the bishops without payment: I at Rouen, and he at Noyon.” From this the following decisive argument is established: the ordination of Eligius and Audoenus took place in the third year of Clodoveus, the youthful king, in which the Sunday letter was A, Easter fell on 9 April, the Ascension on 18 May, and the Sunday before the Litanies, or Rogations, on 14 May. Yet all these facts cannot coincide except in the year 646. Therefore that was Clodoveus’s third year. Indeed, the day of that ordination is recorded as 14 May in both accounts of Saint Audoenus; in both, we also read: “Blessed Bishop Audoenus governed the Church of Rouen for forty-three years, three months, and ten days; he migrated to Christ in his ninetieth year on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.” That is 24 August, which is three months and ten days after 14 May. Thus it is entirely certain that Audoenus and Eligius were ordained on 14 May, and that this date cannot be erased or separated from the day of consecration, as Charles le Cointe attempted when he asserted that they were consecrated on 21 May. Why not also claim that Saint Audoenus died on 31 August, contrary even to the testimony of all the *Acts* and Martyrologies? Another argument, whose solution no one has yet attempted, is supplied by the famous comet. It is mentioned by a contemporary author in the *Life of Saint Leodegarius*, by Bede, book IV of the *History*, chapter 12, by Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book V, chapter 35, and by Anastasius, in his book on the Roman pontiffs, under Donus. I omit the writers of a later age. Yet that comet which appeared when the death of Childeric had been announced, says the contemporary author, following Bede and Anastasius, was first seen in August of the year 678. Therefore Childeric did not die before that year. But Childeric held the monarchy for three years; before him Chlothar III held it for fourteen years, and Chlothar’s predecessor Chlodoveus II for seventeen. Therefore the reign of Chlodoveus II did not begin before 644, and in his third year, 646, Audoenus and Eligius were ordained. Audoenus was consecrated one or two years after the death of Romanus. Romanus held the see for thirteen years, and Hidulfus, Romanus’s predecessor, held the see of Rouen for twenty-eight years; he had entered it after Melantius in 602. To strengthen Valesius’s view concerning the year of the death of Dagobert I and the younger Clodoveus, Mabillon added a new argument in the dissertation mentioned above. Yet, with all respect to so great a man, that argument seems of lesser weight, although he considers it irresistible and especially suited to bringing the famous controversy to an end. For the inscription which he found in an old codex of the monastery of Fosses plainly proves that the inscription prefixed to the first book of the *Life of Blessed John, Abbot of Réomé*, by Abbot Jonas, is not genuine: on the one hand, there is the polished style of the *Life itself of Blessed John*, written by Jonas; on the other, the extreme barbarism of the Fosses inscription. Therefore the Fosses codex presents the inscription of the *Life of Blessed John* as interpolated and corrupted by someone entirely ignorant of grammar and perhaps of the art of computation as well.]**

of Menna

**[Note: [Col. 1177D] Toulon is a famous and ancient episcopal city of the Gallic province, under the archbishop of Arles. The author of *Gallia Christiana* was the first to count Menna among the bishops of Toulouse. Yet it clearly appears from the catalogue of the bishops of Toulouse compiled by Bernard Gui, preserved in a manuscript at Toulouse in the Library of the Dominican Fathers, that at that time there was no bishop of Toulouse named Menna. Moreover, Gregory had no reason to write to the bishop of Toulouse and commend his monks to him, since they were not going to pass through that city. The holy pontiff sent letters to the bishops of Toulon and Marseille because the monks were going to arrive at or pass through those cities; and to the bishops of Chalon, Metz, and Paris because those cities were the seats of the kings of Burgundy, Austrasia, and Neustria, whose assistance the monks departing for the conversion of the English especially needed. Hence they received letters of recommendation for each of these men, to be published below. Since the praised bishops possessed great favor and authority at the courts of those kings, it did not seem unreasonable to seek their assistance. Gregory’s reason for writing to the bishop of Rouen was that his monks might perhaps board a ship in that city in order to cross to England. The reason for addressing Licinius, bishop of Angers, was that this bishop, because of his exceptional holiness, was especially esteemed by the kings of Gaul, to whom he was related. Moreover, the route to the sea and to England ran through Angers; Augustine and his companions had also passed that way when they were making for Britain. Concerning Menna, the bishop, see book XIII, epistle 6.]**

of Toulon, Serenus of Marseille,

Lupus

**[Note: [Col. 1178B] Valesius proves in his *Description of Gaul* that *Cabilloni* should be read. Cabillonum is now commonly called Chalon-sur-Saône, a well-known city of the duchy of Burgundy, on the river Saône, an episcopal see under the archbishop of Lyon.]**

of Chalon,

Aigulf

**[Note: [Col. 1178B] Aigulfus, also Agilfus or Agilius, as it is read in two Vatican manuscripts, was bishop of Metz. Paul the Deacon, in his *On the Bishops of Metz*, writes that he was descended through a daughter from Chlodoveus, king of the Franks; Charles le Comte refutes him. See also the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Metz* in volume VI of the *Spicilegium* of Achery.]**

of Metz,

**[Note: [Col. 1178C] *Mettis* should be read, as Valesius proves in his *Description of Gaul*. Metz is a city within the borders of Lorraine, an episcopal see familiar to all, under the archbishop of Trier, the metropolitan of the First Belgic province. Partly from Gussanville.]**

Simplicius of Paris,

Melantius of Rouen,

**[Note: [Col. 1178C] Melantius, the eighteenth bishop of Rouen, was substituted by Queen Fredegund for Praetextatus after the latter had been driven into exile, as Gregory of Tours teaches in book VIII of his *History of the Franks*, chapters 31 and 41. But after the death of King Chilperic, when Praetextatus had been restored to his dignity and see with the support of King Guntram, Melantius was expelled and removed from Rouen, as Gregory records in book VII, chapter 19. Finally, after the murder of Praetextatus (for which he was openly accused both by the assassin and by the envoys of King Guntram), Melantius again governed the Church of Rouen with the support of Fredegund and was once more appointed its bishop by her. See Gregory, book VIII, chapters 31 and 41. Gussanville.]**

and Licinius.

**[Note: [Col. 1178D] Licinius was born of a noble family and, having been count of Angers, became the fifteenth bishop of Angers, around the year 600. His life, distinguished by its virtues, was written by Marbod, bishop of Rennes. He is mentioned in the Martyrology of Ado under 8 June. Angers—Ptolemy’s *Juliomagus*, in French Angers—was an episcopal city of Celtic Gaul, situated on the Maine between Tours and Nantes, famous for its university, and under the archbishop of Tours. Gussanville. In one Colbert manuscript, *Leontio* is read instead of *Licinio*.]**

to his fellow bishops among the Franks.

Although the care of the office you have undertaken reminds your Fraternity that you ought to come to the aid of religious men, especially those laboring for the sake of souls, with every effort, it is nevertheless not without purpose if the language of our letters has stirred your solicitude, because, just as fire grows greater when stirred by the wind, so the endeavors of a good mind advance through encouragement.

**[Note: [Col. 1178D] The Rheims manuscript lacks this passage down to “advance.”]**

For, since, with the grace of our Redeemer cooperating, so great a multitude of the English people is being converted to the grace of the Christian faith that our most reverend common brother and fellow bishop Augustine declares that those who are with him cannot by themselves suffice to carry out this work in the various places, we have resolved to send to him a number of monks, together with our most beloved and common sons, the priest Laurence and the abbot Mellitus. Therefore let your Fraternity show them the charity that is fitting, and hasten to assist them wherever necessary, so that, while your aid ensures that they encounter no reasons for delay there, they may rejoice that they have been relieved by your consolation, and you may be found to share, through the assistance you provide, in the cause for which they have been sent.

**EPISTLE LIX. TO THEODERIC, KING OF THE FRANKS. He urges the convocation of a synod and commends the same monks.**

Gregory

**[Note: [Col. 1179D] EPISTLE LIX [otherwise 53].—See what we said concerning him in Epistle 58, indiction 14.]**

to Theodoric, king of the Franks.

Your letter, a clear indication of your heart, has shown with such abundant eloquence how greatly prudence shines in you together with royal power that there can be no doubt about anything laudable that fame has reported concerning you. And since you have signaled that our exhortation has pleased your royal mind so greatly through the commendations of praise that you are resolved both diligently to establish and in every way to preserve whatever you recognize as belonging to the worship of our God, to the reverence of the Churches, and to the honor of priests, we urge you again, for the sake of your greater reward, to order a synod to be assembled and, as we wrote previously, to have bodily vices among priests and the depravity of simoniacal heresy condemned by the decision of all the bishops and cut away from the borders of your kingdom,

nor permit money there to obtain greater power than the Lord’s commandments allow. For, since all greed is the service of idols, whoever does not vigilantly guard against it, especially in the granting of ecclesiastical honors, is subjected to the ruin of unbelief, even if he seems to hold the faith that he neglects.

Therefore, just as you are concerned against external enemies, so also strive to be vigilant against the internal adversaries of souls, so that, by faithfully resisting the enemies of our God, you may both reign here happily under his protection and afterward, with his grace as guide, come to eternal joys.

Moreover, certain monks returning from him have reported how much good your Excellence did for our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine as he was setting out for the English people. Therefore, while offering abundant thanks, we ask that you deign to provide still more generously the support of your favor to these monks who have been sent to him, and assist them in their journey, so that, the more abundantly you bestow your benefits upon them, the greater recompense you may expect from almighty God, whom they serve.

**[Note: [Col. 1179D] In the Collection of Paul the Deacon there is added: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.” All those letters to the kings and bishops of Gaul, as well as to Augustine and to Ethelberht, king of Kent, which were carried by Mellitus and his companions, were written at approximately the same time. Moreover, in Epistles 64 and 66 below, in Bede, book I of the *History*, chapters 29 and 32, the same words are also appended at the end: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4,” which confirms Paul’s testimony.]**

**EPISTLE LX. TO THEODEBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS. He urges the assembly of a synod and commends the same monks.**

Gregory

**[Note: [Col. 1179D] EPISTLE LX [otherwise 54].—Concerning him also see Epistle 58, indiction 14.]**

to Theodebert, king of the Franks.

Whoever receives the words of paternal exhortation with a willing spirit and embraces them in the bosom of his heart undoubtedly professes that he will be a corrector of vices. This matter makes us sufficiently confident in your Excellence, for we retain as a pledge the words of one whom we know to be capable of fulfilling what he undertakes.

Therefore may your Excellence, adhering to the commands of our God, deign to apply yourself to assembling a synod for the sake of your reward, so that every bodily vice among priests, and simoniacal heresy—which first arose in the Churches through wicked ambition—may, under the imminent judgment of your authority, be removed by the decision of a council and cut away from the root. Otherwise, if gold is loved there more than God, he who is now calmly despised in his commandments may afterward be felt as angry in punishment.

And since we speak these things for your sake, we therefore do not cease to press them upon you repeatedly, so that we may perhaps be of service to our most excellent and beloved sons even by our persistence. For your kingdom is wholly benefited if what is done against God in those regions is corrected through the amendment brought about by your Excellence.

Moreover, from certain monks who have returned from him, we have learned how much good your Excellence did for our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine as he was setting out for the English people. In return, offering you the greatest thanks, we ask that you extend your benefits more abundantly also to the monks carrying this letter, whom we have sent to that same brother of ours, so that, while your patronage ensures that they encounter no difficulties there but complete their journey easily with Christ’s help, you may produce before the eyes of our God a richer fruit of your reward.

**EPISTLE LXI. TO CHLOTHAR, KING OF THE FRANKS. He commends the monks going to Augustine and urges the convocation of a synod against the simoniacs.**

Gregory

**[Note: [Col. 1179D] EPISTLE LXI [otherwise 55].—This Chlothar, whom some call the younger, was the son of Chilperic, grandson of the elder Chlothar, and great-grandson of Chlodoveus. After his father was murdered, he was proclaimed king when he was four months old. His uncle was Guntram. For Charibert and Sigibert, his uncles, had perished long before he was born. He had as a cousin Childebert, the son and successor of Sigibert; Childebert and his sons Theodebert and Theodoric attacked him, defeated him, and stripped him of a large part of his kingdom, so that for some time he ruled only in the farthest part of Neustria, along the Seine, Isère, and Somme rivers, and near the Ocean. But after the deaths of Theodebert and Theodoric, when Theodoric’s sons had been routed, driven away, and removed, and their great-grandmother, Queen Brunichild, had herself been killed, he alone obtained the entire monarchy and occupied the three Frankish kingdoms, namely Austrasia, Neustria, and Burgundy. Gussanville.]**

to Chlothar, king of the Franks.

[Col. 1181A]

Amid all the cares and anxieties that you endure in governing the peoples subject to you, to show yourselves helpers to those laboring in God’s cause is a source of exceptional praise and great reward. And because your previous good works have shown you to be such that we may hope for better things from you, we are most willingly moved to ask what contributes to your reward.

Accordingly, certain men who had gone with our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine to the English people, on their return reported how greatly your Excellence refreshed that same brother of ours by your affection when he was present with you, and with how many forms of support you assisted him as he was setting out.

**[Note: [Col. 1181D] The printed editions add: “But because those works are always pleasing to our God which do not depart from good beginnings.”]**

But because those whose works are pleasing to our God are always those who do not depart from the good things they have begun, we greet you with paternal affection and ask that you hold especially commended the monks carrying this letter, whom we have sent to the aforementioned brother of ours together with our most beloved sons, the priest Laurence and the abbot Mellitus.
