Whatever you have previously provided to him, bestow upon these men also, more abundantly, for the increase of your praise, so that, while your foresight enables them to complete their journey without delay, almighty God may prove the recompense of your good works and be for you a guardian in prosperity and a helper in adversity.

Moreover, it has come to us that sacred orders are being conferred there in exchange for money. We are deeply distressed if access to the gifts of God is obtained not through merits but by payment. And because this simoniacal heresy, arising first in the Church, was condemned by the authority of the apostles, we ask that, for the sake of your reward, you cause a synod to be assembled, so that, suppressed by the decision of all the priests and cut away from the root, it may find no further strength there to endanger souls and may not be permitted to arise again under any pretext. Thus may our almighty God exalt you against your adversaries in proportion as he sees that you possess zeal for his commandments and think carefully about the salvation of the souls that would otherwise have perished by the sword of this crime.

**EPISTLE LXII. TO BRUNICHILD, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS. He commends the monks going to Britain.**

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

We give thanks to almighty God, who, among the other gifts of his mercy that he has bestowed upon your Excellence, has filled you with such love of the Christian religion that you do not cease to work with devoted mind and pious zeal at whatever you recognize as pertaining to the gain of souls and the propagation of the faith.

How much favor and assistance your Excellence gave to our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Augustine as he set out for the English people was already made known by the report of fame, and afterward certain monks returning from him carefully related it to us. Others may indeed marvel at these things concerning your Christianity, since your benefits are still less known to them; but to us, who already know them by experience, they are not matters for wonder but for joy, because through what you bestow upon others you help yourselves.

You already know what great and wondrous things our Redeemer has worked in the conversion of the people mentioned above. For this reason you ought to possess great joy, since the consolations you have provided claim for you a greater share in this matter, through whose assistance after God the word of preaching became known there. For whoever helps another’s good makes it his own.

Therefore, so that the fruit of your reward may be increasingly abundant, we ask that you show the monks carrying this letter

**[Note: [Col. 1181D] EPISTLE LXII [otherwise 56].—Recent manuscripts read *praesentium apicum*, “of the present letters.”]**

whom we have sent, together with our most beloved sons, the priest Laurence and the abbot Mellitus, to the aforementioned most reverend brother and fellow bishop, because he says that those who are with him cannot suffice for him, the support of your patronage more generously, and deign to be present to them in every way. Thus, while better things follow upon the good beginnings made by your Excellence and they encounter no delays or difficulties there, may you call forth the mercy of our God toward yourselves and toward your nephews, whom we love so dearly, in proportion as you mercifully display yourselves in such causes for love of him.

**[Note: [Col. 1182D] In the Collection of Paul the Deacon: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.”]**

**EPISTLE LXIII. TO BRUNICHILD, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS. That she should order a synod to be assembled for uprooting simony.**

[Col. 1182C]

Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.

How many good qualities have been bestowed upon you by divine generosity, and how greatly the mercy of heavenly grace has filled you, is made clear, among the other testimonies to your merits, by the fact that you govern the fierce hearts of the gentiles with prudent skill and adorn royal power with wisdom—which is an even greater source of praise.

And since, just as you surpass many peoples in both respects, so also you surpass them in the sincerity of faith, we place great confidence in you for correcting what is unlawful. For the page of your writings, sent some time ago, bears witness to how your Excellence embraced our exhortation and with what devotion you desire to fulfill it.

But because the one who is the giver of good minds is also accustomed to be their helper, we trust that he will arrange your affairs with greater favor through his mercy, insofar as he sees that you yourselves are concerned for his cause. Do what belongs to God, and God will do what belongs to you.

Therefore order a synod to be assembled, and, as we wrote before, prohibit with the utmost diligence, by the decision of a council, the sin of simoniacal heresy from your kingdom, among other things.

**[Note: [Col. 1182D] EPISTLE LXIII [otherwise 57].—See book IX, Epistle 11.]**

Offer sacrifice to God after conquering the internal enemy, so that, with his help, you may conquer external adversaries; and in proportion to the zeal you have shown against his enemies, may you experience him as such in your aid.

Believe me, for, as we have already learned through the experience of many, whatever is gathered with sin is counted as loss. If, therefore, you wish to lose nothing unjustly, strive with the utmost care to possess nothing through injustice. For in earthly affairs the origin of sin is always the cause of loss.

If, then, you wish to rise above hostile peoples, if you hasten to be victorious over them with God as author, receive the commandments of the same almighty God with fear, so that he may deign to fight for you against your adversaries, who through the sacred word promised, saying: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent” (Exodus 14:14).

**[Note: [Col. 1183C] In the Collection of Paul the Deacon: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends, indiction 4.” In the Remigian manuscript: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.”]**

**[Note: [Col. 1183D] EPISTLE LXIV [otherwise 31, indiction 7].—This epistle is not found in many manuscript codices of the Register of Saint Gregory. Indeed, it is clear that it did not originally exist in the Vatican manuscripts, as is evident from Epistle 15 of Boniface, bishop of Mainz, to Nothelm, bishop of Canterbury, written in 745, in these words: “I ask that you arrange to send me a copy of that epistle which, as they say, contains the questions of Augustine, the pontiff and first preacher of the English, and the answers of Saint Gregory the pope: namely, that it is permitted to contract marriages within the third degree of relationship. And I ask that you carefully investigate whether the aforementioned writing can be proved to be by our Father Gregory or not, since, as the keepers of the archives affirm, it was sought in the archives of the Roman Church together with the other copies of the aforementioned pontiff but was not found.” Whether Nothelm sent that epistle to Boniface is not apparent; yet it is certain that it existed in England, since Bede inserted it in his writings. Bede flourished at the same time, and he did so in book I of his *History of the English*, chapter 27, as it is read in all manuscript and printed copies of that History, and even in the Saxon translation published by order of King Alfred of the English around the year 890. Pope Zacharias likewise cites testimony from the sixth question in the First Roman Council of 743, chapter 15. So also does Ecgbert, bishop of York, who was living in 747, in chapter 130 of his *Extracts*. Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, who flourished in 826, cites one of the questions contained in this epistle in book V, chapter 17. I omit Isidore, Regino, Anselm, Ivo, Gratian, and the other collectors of canons who inserted it in their writings. Yet it is also found in several manuscript codices, such as two Tellier manuscripts, the Chartres manuscript, Vatican D, the Bigot manuscript, the English manuscript, and the manuscript of Saint Remigius of Reims; it is also found in another codex of Saint Remigius containing several letters of pontiffs. (Gussanville perhaps means the very ancient copy mentioned by Jamezius, which he says is falsely entitled *The Penitential of Blessed Gregory*; for in that codex the disputed epistle appears in full.) It is likewise found in the ancient collection of an anonymous author preserved in manuscript at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. Add to these the Gemeticensis codex, no. 44, in which the Response of Saint Gregory to the eleventh question is found, and the manuscript of the Great Monastery at Tours, where it is contained in full. Although Gussanville does not deny this epistle to Gregory, he nevertheless considers many of its responses doubtful or even spurious. He attempts to prove this by conjectures so slight and weak that we would waste our time in refuting them. Bede indicates the time at which this epistle was sent in the passage cited: “Meanwhile the man of God Augustine came to Arles, and by Etherius, the archbishop of that city (Virgil should be read), according to the commands they had received from Saint Father Gregory, was ordained archbishop for the English people. On returning to Britain, he immediately sent the priest Laurence and the monk Peter to Rome, so that they might report to the blessed pontiff Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he himself had been made bishop; at the same time he received answers to questions that seemed necessary, which we have also thought it useful to insert in this History of ours: ‘Question of Augustine, bishop of the Church of the Cantuarians: Concerning bishops, how they should conduct themselves with their clergy, and so forth.’ Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, answered: [Col. 1185A] ‘Sacred Scripture bears witness, and there is no doubt that you know it well,’ and so forth, as in the printed editions. It is uncertain who first arranged this epistle in its present form, since Bede, from whose History, as I have said above, it was taken, reported it as one continuous text without any headings, calling it not an epistle but a little book. We have spoken somewhat more fully about this epistle for the benefit of those who have raised doubts about it, because it contains certain things that seem somewhat foreign to the character of Saint Gregory; but we shall discuss these matters in their order in the following notes. Partly from Gussanville.]**

**EPISTLE LXIV. TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE ENGLISH. He responds to various questions on which Augustine had consulted him.—1. Concerning the fourfold division of ecclesiastical goods.—2. Concerning clerics who marry after entering the clergy.—3. Concerning different customs of different Churches, which should not be condemned.—4. Concerning the penance of thieves and the restoration of ecclesiastical property.—5. Two brothers may marry two sisters.—6. Which degrees of consanguinity and affinity are prohibited in marriage.—7. Neophytes joined in a prohibited degree are neither to be separated nor deprived of holy communion, but are to be admonished to abstain.—8. How many bishops are necessary for the consecration of a bishop.—9. How a metropolitan should conduct himself in another province.—10. That a pregnant woman and a newborn child may be baptized. A woman undergoing menstruation is not prohibited from entering the church, but after intercourse married couples ought to abstain from entering the church.—11. When nocturnal pollution prevents celebration and communion.**

[Col. 1183B]

[Col. 1183C]

**[Note: [Col. 1185B] This title, like many others belonging to the letters, is not by Saint Gregory, as is clear. Gussanville.]**

Here begins the epistle concerning the explanation of various matters by Blessed Gregory, pope of the city of Rome,

[Col. 1184A]

which he sent across the sea to Saxony, to Augustine, whom he himself sent there to preach on his behalf.

**[Note: [Col. 1185B] This part of Britain has been called “transmarine Saxony” from the time when the Saxons crossed over from Germany to that island and occupied most of it. Gussanville. The word *transmarinam* is omitted in Vatican D and in the Remigian manuscript. In Bede, book I, chapter 27, where this epistle is reported, the prefixed title is not found.]**

**The First Question of Augustine.**

**[Note: [Col. 1185B] These words are not found in Bede, Vatican Codex D, or the Remigian manuscript. Instead, after the words “Question of Blessed Augustine, bishop of the Church of the Cantuarians,” the text immediately continues: “Concerning bishops,” and so forth.]**

I ask, most blessed father, concerning bishops: how they should conduct themselves with their clergy. I also ask about what comes to the altars from the offerings of the faithful, what portions ought to be made, and how a bishop ought to act in the Church.

**[Note: [Col. 1185B] The printed editions read: “concerning the ecclesiastical revenues to be divided.” Response.]**

**The Response of Saint Gregory, pope of the city of Rome.**
[Note: [Col. 1185C] In the printed editions there is prefixed: “how the bishop ought to act in the Church”; we have removed all this, at the urging of the manuscripts and Chifflet’s edition in the concordance of Bede and Fredegar the Scholastic, where you find this same letter—or rather, the first five books of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People written by the venerable Bede.] Sacred Scripture bears witness to this, as there is no doubt that you know it well, and especially the letters of blessed Paul to Timothy, in which he took care to instruct him how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God. It is, moreover, the custom of the Apostolic See (Gratian, Distinction 12, Question 2, Chapter 30) to give this instruction to bishops once ordained: that of every income which comes in [Col. 1184B], four portions ought to be made.

[Note: [Col. 1185C] The fourfold distribution of the Church’s goods has already been discussed above, Book III, Letter 11—now Book IV. GUSSANV. See the notes, and consult Book V, Letters 12 and 44, as well as Book VIII, Letter 7.]

One portion, namely, is for the bishop and his household, on account of hospitality and the reception of guests;

[Note: [Col. 1185C] Hospitality was discussed in Letter 29 of Book VIII, now Letter 28 of Book X. “Reception” likewise means the reception of guests and pilgrims.]

another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for the repair of churches.

But since your Fraternity, instructed in the rules of monastic life,

[Note: [Col. 1185C] In Vatican D and in Chifflet’s edition: “ought not to be made separately.” This was the practice of many bishops, such as Augustine, and so forth. Whether it was prescribed for individual bishops by any law, let others examine. It was established by several canons that canons should live in common, and also that bishops should have at least some clerics living and dining with them in the episcopal residence. See the Council of Tours II, chapters 12 and 13, A.D. 557; the Council of Paris VI, A.D. 829, chapters 20 and 21, in which Canon 14 of the Council of Sardica is cited—I do not know for what reason, unless perhaps at that time bishops residing in their own cities used a common table with their clerics. At Tours III, A.D. 813, chapter 5: “Let the bishop be content with frugal and moderate food”; chapter 6: “Let pilgrims and the poor be guests of bishops,” which also seems to have been established at Aachen II, A.D. 816, chapter 3. At Tours III, chapter 23: “Concerning the canons and clerics of cities who live in episcopal residences, that, dwelling in cloisters, they should all sleep together in one dormitory and eat together in one refectory . . . and receive food and clothing according to the means of the bishop,” and so forth. At Mainz, A.D. 813, chapter 9: “Let the canons eat and sleep together . . . Let them remain in their cloister,” and so forth. At Aachen, A.D. 816, chapter 112, a text of Saint Augustine concerning the common life of the bishop and clerics is cited, as well as chapter 113, where there are many arguments for bishops concerning their meditations [Col. 1186A]. At the Council of Meaux, A.D. 845, chapter 53, concerning canons: “Let them sleep in the dormitory and eat in the refectory,” and so forth. From this arose the still solemn accounts of the refectory in certain churches—*comptes du réfectoire* in French—an illustrious memorial of the common life and ancient assiduity, or, as they call it, residence [Col. 1186B]. At the Council of Pontyon, A.D. 876, chapter 8: “Let bishops establish in their cities, near their churches, a cloister in which they themselves, together with the clergy, may serve God according to the canonical rule.” GUSSANV. Trithemius reports, under the year 975, that some canons abandoned the institution of the common life in the tenth century. Ivo of Chartres, Letter 60, and Stephen of Tournai, Letter 160, testify to and lament the same abandonment by most people in the eleventh and twelfth centuries—for I say nothing of other writers of that age—namely, Ivo of Chartres, Letter 60, and Stephen of Tournai, Letter 160.]

ought not to live separately from his clergy in the Church of the English, which, by God’s providence, has recently been brought to the faith, he ought to establish among them the manner of life that existed at the beginning of the infant Church among our Fathers: none of them claimed that anything of what they possessed was his own, but everything was held in common among them (Acts 4).

[Note: [Col. 1186B] Vatican D and Rheims: “to establish this constitution.” Saint John Chrysostom explains this practice at length in Homilies 11 and 12 on the Acts of the Apostles, where the reader will find much that cannot be contained in a brief note. Gratian, in Cause 12, Question 1, cites, among others, Saint Clement and Urban I, Roman pontiffs. Learned men know how much weight ought to be granted to these authorities. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 39: “Among us everything is undivided, except our wives.” But this proposition must be restricted. In Tertullian’s time there was no community among Christians of movable and immovable property; they had not sold their possessions, nor placed all their money at the feet of the bishops. This is sufficiently indicated a few lines earlier, where he speaks of the chest and of the contribution that each person places in it if he wishes and if he is able. He therefore indicates only the working of love and the fraternal sharing of possessions with the needy. I note two things concerning the custom of the nascent Church: first, that money, goods, and the value of goods were not given into the hands of the apostles, but placed at their feet—search out the mystery; second, that this common life either belonged to only a few or lasted only a few days, while the blood of Jesus Christ was still warm and faith was freshly burning in believers, as Saint Jerome says in his letter to Demetrias, daughter of Juliana. Thus, according to Saint Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33, certain communities lived in common—a praiseworthy kind of Christians, certainly, but very remote from ordinary life and less suited to the interests of the commonwealth [Col. 1186D]. GUSSANV.]

## The Second Question of Augustine

[Col. 1184C] [Note: [Col. 1186D] Question II. In Chifflet’s edition and in Vatican D these words are omitted, and after the final words of the first response, “everything was held in common among them,” there immediately follows: “But if there are clerics,” and so forth. The same is found in the Capuchin manuscript at Rouen containing the decretal letters.]

For I desire to be instructed whether clerics who are unable to remain continent may marry; and, if they marry, whether they ought to return to secular life.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

If there are clerics outside the sacred orders who cannot remain continent (Gratian, Distinction 32, Chapter 3), they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally, because concerning these same Fathers of whom we have spoken, we read that what was distributed to each was given according to each person’s need.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Vatican D: “because also concerning those about whom.”]

Their support must therefore be considered and provided for, and they must be kept under ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may live uprightly, devote themselves to the chanting of psalms, and, with God’s help, preserve their hearts, tongues, and bodies from every unlawful thing.

[Note: [Col. 1186D] The printed editions read: “but living communally.” We follow the manuscripts Vatican D, Tours, Rheims, and Bede as edited by Chifflet. Gussanvilleus thinks this sentence should be removed, since it agrees neither with the sense nor with Gregory’s style. He adds that the four portions have already been discussed, so that it seems superfluous to discuss them again. Nevertheless, this sentence is found in the manuscripts of Tours, Rheims, Vatican, and Bede.]

But for those living a common life, what need is there for us to speak further about making portions, offering hospitality, and fulfilling mercy, since everything that is surplus to necessities must be expended on pious and religious causes, with the Lord and teacher of all saying: “What remains, give as alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41)?

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Tours: “with the teacher of all instructing.” The same reading is found in Bede.]

## The Third Question of Augustine

Although the faith is one,

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Question III. I have already said something about this matter in Book I, Letter 64. It is worthwhile to hear Saint Ambrose, *On the Saints*, Book III, chapter 1: “In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church; nevertheless, we too are human beings and possess understanding. Therefore, what is more rightly observed elsewhere, we also rightly preserve.” The eminent Cardinal Bona proves that various rites do not injure the unity of the faith, *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 6, numbers 2 and 3. If only the rubricists would read that passage. GUSSANV.]

why are the customs of the Churches [Col. 1187A] so different? One custom of the Mass is observed in the Roman Church, while another is maintained in the Churches of Gaul?

[Note: [Col. 1187C] Concerning the old Gallican Mass, or the rite of celebrating Mass once customary in Gaul, I inform the reader that one version was published by Matthias Flacius Illyricus in 1557 and another by Hugh Menard in 1642. Both are reported and compared by the most learned student of ecclesiastical antiquity, Charles le Cointe, *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, volume II, for the year 601, numbers 19 and 20. From the version published by Illyricus, many things are collected and observed against recent heretics, including that in its creed the Holy Spirit is read as proceeding from the Father and the Son. This is done both by Charles le Cointe, in the cited passage, numbers 21–30, and by William Peyratius in the French work *The Antiquities of the King’s Chapel*, Book II, chapters 18–23. Peyratius likewise affirms that Illyricus published the old Gallican Mass, explaining some of its rubrics in chapter 10 and following. The eminent Cardinal Bona denies this, *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 12. GUSSANV. See Mabillon’s preface to his book *On the Gallican Liturgy*, and the preface that Menard placed before his book *Sacramentary*. [Col. 1187D] Since the Mass has so often occurred in these letters, it may perhaps not be out of place to observe that it was so called from the dismissal. In Alcimus Avitus, Letter 1: “From this proper meaning of the word, it is announced in churches and palaces or courts that the dismissal is being made, when the people are dismissed from the observance.” See Sirmond’s notes on this passage.]

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

Your Fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which you remember having been nourished (Gratian, Distinction 12, Chapter 10). But I approve that, whether in the Roman Church, or in the Churches of Gaul, or in any other Church, you find something that may please almighty God more, you should carefully choose it and pour it into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith,

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Tours: “new in the faith.”]

as a distinctive institution gathered from many Churches. For things are not to be loved on account of places, but places on account of things. Therefore choose from each Church whatever is pious, religious, and upright, and, gathered together as though into a bundle, place these things among the minds of the English as a custom.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The same manuscript reads: “establish them as a custom.”]

## The Fourth Question of Augustine

I ask you to explain what ought to be done if someone steals something from a church.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

Your Fraternity can judge from the person of the thief how he may be corrected (Gratian, Cause 12, Question 2, Chapter 11). Some commit theft despite having means of support; others offend in this matter because of poverty. Therefore some must be corrected by losses, some by blows, some more severely, and others more lightly. And when the correction is somewhat severe, it must be administered out of charity, not fury, because this is done for the benefit of the one being corrected, lest he be handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

For we ought to impose discipline upon the faithful as good fathers customarily do upon their fleshly children: they strike them with blows for their faults, yet they seek to have as heirs those whom they afflict with pain, and preserve for those whom they seem to pursue in anger the possessions that they own. This charity, therefore, must be held in the mind,

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The printed editions read: “must be preserved.” The method of correction itself dictates this. We follow the manuscripts mentioned above and Bede.]

and it itself dictates the measure of correction, so that the mind does nothing at all outside the rule of reason.

You also ask how those things which they have taken by theft from churches ought to be restored. But

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Another and more difficult problem, which a recent author addressed quite suitably in a well-written French book on usury, p. 259: whether a creditor may receive money imposed upon a debtor as a penalty for delayed payment without incurring the taint of usury. “The holy Fathers and the supreme pontiffs,” he says, “seem to disapprove of this.” I do not dispute the law; I merely offer several considerations relevant to the matter [Col. 1188C]. At the beginning of the sixth century, if Gratian is trustworthy, Pope John I said: “In the ancient statutes of the Church it was decreed that whoever invades another’s property should not go unpunished, but should restore everything with increase. Hence it is also written in the Gospel: ‘If I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold.’” The secular laws likewise say: “Whoever steals another’s property,” and so forth. This is indicated in chapter 10 of the same work, from Eusebius. The text is reported in Cause 12, Question 2, Chapter 7. Saint Gregory, in the same place, chapters 8 and 9, falsely cited from Book IV, Letter 33, gives the common secular law: “Let the one who began pay 900 solidi; his accomplices, each 80 solidi. If they have caused a fire, let them pay nine times as much; if they have carried off plunder, let them restore it fourfold.” I am surprised that the Roman correctors left this citation intact. I also point to a law concerning sacrilegious persons added by Pope John VIII to the Gothic laws at the Council of Troyes, A.D. 878, from Sirmond; concerning Justinian and Charles, it is reported in Cause 17, Question 4, Chapter 21, together with several other texts on the same subject. At the Council of Trosly, A.D. 909, chapter 4, concerning the punishment of sacrilegious persons: “Let all their property, movable as well as immovable, be joined to the king’s treasury or to the Church whose property it is,” and so forth. The Gloss on Canon 10, Cause 12, Question 2, says that a tenfold penalty was established against thieves in Lombard, Gothic, and Salic law, but not in Roman law. 2 Kings 12:6: “He shall restore the sheep fourfold,” in accordance with Exodus 22:1. On this passage see Theodoret and Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* I–II, Question 105, Article 2, Reply to Objection 9, and II–II, Question 62, Articles 3 and 4. Zacchaeus, Luke 19, promises fourfold restitution. I do not see that those who receive such payments are accused of usury, nor that judges are reproved as patrons of usury when they punish an offense by imposing a monetary penalty. GUSSANV.]

let it be far from the Church to receive with increase what it appears to have lost from earthly goods,

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Tours and Vatican D: “and profits,” or “and profit from vain things.”]

and to seek profits from losses.

## The Fifth Question of Augustine

I ask whether two full brothers may marry two sisters who are descended from them through a long line of ancestry.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

This is permitted in every way. For nowhere in the sacred writings is anything found that seems to contradict this matter.

## The Sixth Question of Augustine

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Question VI. There was not one uniform practice in all ages concerning the prohibition of marriage between relatives, as appears in Cause 35, Questions 2 and 3. Formerly the prohibition was limited to the seventh degree, but at the Lateran Council under Innocent III it was reduced to the fourth. Here Saint Gregory grants an indulgence to the English, recently converted to the faith, allowing them to marry in the third generation. Many manuscripts read “in the fourth or fifth,” as the correctors of Gratian noted in Cause 35, Question 3, Chapter 20; the reader should consult that passage. Let him also see Gregory II, Letter 9 to Boniface. In all Bede’s copies, however, the reading is “in the third or fourth generation.” GUSSANV.]

Up to what generation may the faithful marry relatives, and may they marry stepmothers and relations?

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

[Note: [Col. 1189B] This text is commonly cited by every sort of author as Saint Gregory’s. It is suggested, however, by a law in Justinian’s Code, Book V, Title 4, *On Marriage*, Law 19, which reads as follows: “Permission to celebrate marriages between cousins has been granted by the salutary provision of this law, so that, with the authority of the ancient law recalled and the sources of accusation extinguished, marriage between cousins may be considered legitimate, whether they were born of two brothers, of two sisters, or of a brother and sister. Those born from such a marriage are to be regarded as legitimate and as successors to their fathers.” Given, and so forth. Arcadius and Honorius, the authors of this law, began to reign at the end of the fourth century. Their father Theodosius had known the contrary rule, as legal experts note and Saint Ambrose testifies in Letter 48. But the ancient law favored such unions. In Justinian’s *Institutes*, Book I, Title 10, *On Marriage*, section 5, Cujas reads: “The children of two brothers or sisters, or of a brother and sister, may be joined in marriage.” Justinian lived around the middle of the sixth century. Whether the Church held the same view as the emperors is a question. In Saint Ambrose, in the letter cited, it is said to be forbidden by divine law for cousins to enter into conjugal union, since they are joined to one another in the fourth degree. This is a difficulty that it is not the place of this note to resolve. Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book XV, chapter 16: “In ancient times men took their sisters as wives under the compulsion of necessity, an act made all the more blameworthy because religion prohibited it. As for marriage between cousins, because their degree of relationship is close to the brotherly degree, it was very rarely practiced according to custom, though permitted by law, since divine law had not prohibited it and human law had not yet done so.” This is another difficulty which Ludovicus Vives presses in his commentary on this passage, just as Peter Nannius explains the passage of Ambrose in his notes on volume V. At any rate, these two most holy Fathers do not explain any canonical law enacted on this matter. Hence some conclude that in earlier centuries it was kings, not pontiffs, who established impediments to marriage. Saint Augustine adds, in the cited passage, that certain marriages were prohibited by the limits of custom. GUSSANV.]

A certain earthly law (Gratian, Cause 33, Question 2, Chapter 20) in the Roman commonwealth permits the son or daughter of either a brother or a sister, or of two full brothers or two full sisters, to unite in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 1190B] Vatican C: “whether a brother and sister, or.” Bede agrees.]

But experience has taught us that offspring cannot increase from such a marriage. And the sacred law forbids the uncovering of the shame of kinship. Therefore it is necessary

[Note: [Col. 1190B] I appeal to the canonists to teach us the history of the impediments to marriage, whether those they call impediments that prevent marriage or those that dissolve it: by which pontiff they were devised, developed, tightened, relaxed, and spread throughout the world. I acknowledge and accept current practice; I do not dispute the law. I inquire into the facts and examine the successive ages, intending to scrutinize the canons. I seem to see some in Cause 30, many more in Cause 35, and others in the *Extravagantes* concerning spiritual kinship, consanguinity, affinity, and so forth. I select only those relevant to the matter under discussion [Col. 1190C]. First, nature itself introduced certain impediments; then, observing what was fitting, human beings, guided by reason, introduced others, either through voluntary custom, through an enacted law that corrected or confirmed custom, or through both. The custom did not prevail everywhere in the world: marriages that were invalid in Gaul were valid elsewhere. Thus, after a long period of uncertainty, they eventually reached as far as the seventh degree; indeed, they also devised various degrees of affinity—first, second, and third—which later had to be restrained. Innocent III accomplished this in the celebrated chapter *Non debet*, in the *Extravagantes* concerning consanguinity and affinity: he drew back the relationship, which had been extended too far, to the fourth degree. GUSSANV. What the practice was in Saint Gregory’s time is shown by Gregory himself in writing to Felix, bishop of Messina, Book XIV, Letter 12, in these words, which are found in John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 38: “Nor did I give them these instructions with the intention that, after they had been firmly rooted in the faith . . . they should unite within the line of affinity, that is, up to the seventh generation.”]

that now the third or fourth generation of the faithful should be permitted to marry one another. For the second generation, as we have said, must abstain from one another in every way.

[Note: [Col. 1190D] According to certain editions, there was doubt concerning the first and second, or, as we commonly say, concerning the first and second degrees. GUSSANV.]

But intercourse with a stepmother is a grave crime, because it is also written in the law: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father” (Leviticus 18:7). For a son cannot uncover his father’s nakedness; but because it is written in the law, “The two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24), whoever presumes to uncover the nakedness of his stepmother, who was one flesh with his father, has certainly uncovered his father’s nakedness.

[Note: [Col. 1190D] He explains “relation” as the wife of a brother—French *bellesœur*, though this is not the common usage. See Cause 35, Question 5, or, if there is time, consult the jurists and grammarians. The Greeks understand by *relations* συγγενεῖς (*syngeneis*), “blood relatives.” GUSSANV.]

Intercourse with a relation is likewise prohibited, since through the former union she became the flesh of one’s brother. For this reason John the Baptist was also beheaded and crowned with holy martyrdom. He was not told to deny Christ,

[Note: [Col. 1190D] Tours: “nor was he killed for confessing Christ.”]

and yet he was killed for confessing Christ; but because our Lord Jesus Christ had said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), since John was killed for the truth, he shed his blood for Christ.

## The Seventh Question of Augustine

I ask that it be explained whether those who have entered such shameful unions should be commanded to separate and be denied the offering of holy Communion.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

[Note: [Col. 1190D] Question VII. In some manuscripts this response is the eighth. In certain manuscripts and in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, Book I, it is joined to the following response, with the question omitted.]

Since there are many among the English who, while they were still in unbelief, are said to have entered this abominable marriage, they must be admonished, when they come to the faith, to abstain and to recognize that this is a grave sin. They must fear the dreadful judgment of God, lest for the sake of carnal pleasure they incur the torments of eternal punishment.

Nevertheless, they are not to be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord on this account, lest we seem to punish in them what they bound themselves to through ignorance before the washing of baptism. For at the present time the holy Church corrects some things with fervor, tolerates others with gentleness, and overlooks and bears with certain things through consideration,

[Note: [Col. 1191C] Vatican D and Rheims: “some things it considers through discretion and thus bears and overlooks, so that often . . .” Bede: “through consideration, overlooks, and thus bears and overlooks.” The printed editions: “things through ignorance.” This differs from Bede and our manuscripts.]

so that often, by bearing and overlooking the evil that opposes it, it may restrain it. All who come to the faith, however, must be admonished not to dare to commit anything of this kind. But if any do commit it, they must be deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord, because just as the guilt of those who acted through ignorance must to some extent be tolerated, so it must be vigorously pursued in those who are not afraid to sin knowingly.

## The Eighth Question of Augustine

I ask whether, when a great distance intervenes between places so that bishops cannot easily meet, a bishop may be ordained without the presence of other bishops.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

Indeed, in the Church of the English, where as yet you alone are found to be a bishop, you can ordain a bishop without other bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1191C] Question VIII. Thus the ancient editions of the *Register*, Venice 1504, Paris 1508 and 1518, as well as the more recent editions. The better manuscripts agree: the manuscripts of Chartres, Bigot, Saint-Remi, and Rheims; another manuscript of Saint-Remi containing the letters of the pontiffs from Gelasius to John VIII; Vatican manuscript no. 619; Isidore’s manuscript collection of canons at Saint-Victor in Paris; and another very ancient collection of canons by an anonymous author at Oxford, in the College of Corpus Christi. It is also so read in Bede, from whom we first received this letter, as noted above. I add Amalarius Fortunatus, *On Divine Offices*, Book II, chapter 1. Finally, Saint Gregory’s own statement requires this reading: “where you alone are,” since he adds that if bishops come from Gaul, they can assist; it does not mean that their presence is absolutely necessary, except when bishops have been ordained in nearby places. Hence it is evident that the reading of certain copies is corrupt: “You can ordain a bishop only together with bishops.” [Col. 1192C] Beveregius likewise notes this in his commentary on the first Apostolic Canon. Partly from GUSSANV.]

For when bishops come from Gaul, they will stand beside you as witnesses at the bishop’s ordination.

[Note: [Col. 1192C] Tours: “unless some bishops come from Gaul, who, in the order . . .” In Bede: “for when bishops come from Gaul, who . . . assist as witnesses.” Vatican D supports this.]

But we wish your Fraternity to ordain bishops in England in such a way that the bishops themselves are not widely separated from one another, so that there may be no need for them to be unable to assemble for the ordination of a bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] In Bede: “so that at the ordination of a bishop other shepherds, whose presence is very useful, may also be able easily to assemble.” The Tours manuscript agrees.]

The presence of some other shepherds is also very useful, so that they may assemble with the greatest ease. Therefore, when, by God’s authority, bishops have been ordained in places near one another, the ordination of a bishop ought in every respect not to take place without three or four bishops assembled.

For even in spiritual matters, so that they may be arranged wisely and maturely, we can draw an example from bodily things. Certainly, when marriages are celebrated in the world, married people are summoned, so that those who have already preceded others on the path of marriage may share also in the joy of the subsequent union.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] In the same manuscript and in Tours, with Bede agreeing: “in the joy also of the subsequent union.”]

Why, then, should not those who rejoice in the progress of the bishop being ordained, or who may together pour out prayers to almighty God for his protection, likewise assemble for this spiritual ordination, by which, through a sacred mystery, a human being is joined to God?

## The Ninth Question of Blessed Augustine

I also ask how we ought to deal with the bishops of Gaul and Britain.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

We grant you no authority over the bishops of Gaul (Gratian, Cause 25, Question 2, Chapter 3), because from the ancient times of my predecessors the bishop of Arles has received the pallium,

[Note: [Col. 1192D] Question IX. On the primacy of Arles, see above, Book I, Letter 47. See also Book V, Letter 53, and consult the commentaries on the Life of Saint Gregory.]

and we certainly ought not to deprive him of the authority he has received. If, therefore, it happens that your Fraternity travels to the provinces of Gaul, you must act together with the bishop of Arles, so that whatever faults there may be among the bishops may be corrected. If he should happen to be lukewarm in the vigor of discipline, he must be inflamed by the zeal of your Fraternity. We have also written to him (Indiction 4, Letter 68), so that, when your Holiness is present in Gaul, he may assist you with his whole heart, and so that you may restrain from the conduct of the bishops whatever is contrary to the command of our Creator.

You cannot, however, judge the bishops of Gaul by your own authority. Rather, by advising, encouraging, and showing them your good works as an example to imitate, you should reform the minds of the wicked toward the pursuit of holiness, because it is written in the law (Gratian, Cause 6, Question 3, Chapter 1):

[Note: [Col. 1192D] These words are praised by Hincmar of Rheims in his little work 33 against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 4: “The blessed Gregory says: You cannot put the sickle of judgment into a field that appears to have been entrusted to another.” The same ninth question is again cited in chapter 17 of that work.]

“While passing through another’s harvest, one must not put in the sickle, but crush the ears with the hand and eat them” (Deuteronomy 23:25).

Therefore you cannot put the sickle of judgment into the harvest that appears to have been entrusted to another. But through the affection of good works, strip the Lord’s grain of the chaff of their vices, and, by admonishing and persuading,

[Note: [Col. 1192D] The printed editions corruptly read: “as though cleansing it.”]

as though chewing it, convert it into the body of the Church. Whatever must be done by authority, however, must be undertaken together with the aforesaid bishop of Arles, lest what the ancient institution of the Fathers established be neglected.

[Note: [Col. 1192D] Tours: “but the care of all the bishops of Britain.”]

As for all the bishops of Britain, we entrust them to the care of your Fraternity, so that the unlearned may be taught, the weak strengthened by persuasion,

[Note: [Col. 1192D] The same manuscript: “those who have been persuaded strengthened by authority.” Vatican D: “those who have been strengthened corrected by authority.”]

and the perverse corrected by authority.

## Augustine’s Entreaty

[Note: [Col. 1193D] Entreaty. This entreaty and response are not found in the manuscripts of Tellier, Chartres, or the Capuchin manuscript at Rouen, nor in the editions of 1504, 1508, and 1518. They are likewise absent from all the copies of Bede from which we have this letter. Partly from GUSSANV. Nevertheless, they are found in Vatican D and in other manuscripts.]

I ask that the relics of Saint Sixtus the martyr be sent to us.

## Gregory’s Grant

We have done what you asked, so that the people who said that they venerated in that place the body of Saint Sixtus the martyr—although your Fraternity considers it neither genuine nor truly holy—may, while receiving the certain benefits of a most holy and proven martyr, not worship what is uncertain.

It seems to me, however, that if the body believed by the people to belong to a certain martyr shines forth there with no miracles, and if there are no people of greater age who claim to have heard from their parents the account of his passion, the relics you requested should be deposited separately, while the place where the aforesaid body lies [Col. 1193B] should be closed off in every way. The people must not be permitted to abandon what is certain and venerate what is uncertain.

## The Tenth Question of Augustine

If a pregnant woman ought to be baptized, or, after she has given birth, after how much time she may enter the church; or, so that what she has given birth to may not be overtaken by death, after how many days it is permissible for it to receive the sacrament of holy baptism; or after how much time her husband may join himself to her in carnal union; or, if she is subject to her monthly period, whether she may enter the church or receive the sacrament of holy Communion; or whether a husband who has had intercourse with his wife may enter the church before he has been washed in water or even approach the ministry of holy Communion—all these matters ought to be made known to the unformed people of the English.

## The Response of Blessed Pope Gregory

I do not doubt that your Fraternity has been asked about this, and I think that I have also supplied an answer. But I believe that, since you yourself were able to say and understand these things, you wished my response to confirm them for you.

Why should a pregnant woman not be baptized, since fertility of the flesh is not a fault in the eyes of almighty God? When our first parents sinned in paradise, they lost, by God’s just judgment, the immortality they had received. Since almighty God did not wish utterly to destroy the human race on account of its fault, he took immortality away from humanity because of its sin, yet in the kindness of his mercy preserved for it the fertility that produces offspring. Therefore, how can what has been preserved for human nature through the gift of almighty God be prohibited from the grace of holy baptism? It would be exceedingly foolish if the gift of grace seemed able to oppose the mystery through which every fault is utterly extinguished.

When a woman has given birth, after how many days she ought to enter the church,

[Note: [Col. 1193D] Question X. In Bede: “It is clear from the commandment of the Old Testament, which says: ‘If a woman has conceived seed,’ and so forth, up to ‘but if she has borne a female child, she shall remain in the blood of her purification for sixty-six days’” [Leviticus 12].]

you have learned from the precept of the Old Testament (Gratian, Distinction 3, Chapter 1): she must abstain for thirty-three days in the case of a male child, but sixty-six in the case of a female child (Leviticus 12).

This, however, must be understood mystically. For if, in the very hour in which she has given birth, she enters the church to give thanks, she is not burdened by any weight of sin. The pleasure of the flesh, not the pain, is sinful. In the union of the flesh there is pleasure, whereas in the birth of offspring there are pain and groaning.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Tours, with Bede agreeing: “for in the bringing forth of offspring there are groans.”]

Hence it is said even to the first mother of all: “In pains you shall give birth” (Genesis 3:6). If, therefore, we prohibit a woman who has given birth from entering the church, we turn her own punishment into guilt for her.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Rheims and Vatican D: “we double her punishment into guilt.”]

But there is no prohibition against baptizing either the woman who has given birth or what she has borne without delay if death threatens; whether at the very hour when she gives birth, or whether the child is baptized at the same hour in which it is born. For just as the grace of the holy mystery must be provided with great discretion to those who are alive and capable of understanding, so it must be offered without any delay to those over whom death hangs, lest, while time is still being sought for providing the mystery of redemption, death intervene and no one be found who can be redeemed.

She must not return to intercourse with her husband until the child who is born has been weaned. A bad custom, however, has arisen in the conduct of married people: women disdain to nurse the children they bear and hand them over to other women to be nursed. This seems plainly to have been devised solely on account of incontinence, because, unwilling to abstain, they shrink from nursing those whom they bear [Col. 1194C]. Accordingly, those women who, through this wicked custom, hand their children over to others to be nursed ought not to have intercourse with their husbands until the time of purification has passed; for even apart from childbirth, when they are held by their customary menstrual periods, they are forbidden to have intercourse with their husbands,

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Vatic. D, Bede, and Turon.: “while she undergoes her customary menstrual period.”]
 so that the sacred law strikes with death anyone who approaches a menstruating woman (Leviticus X). Yet a woman who, according to the ordinary course of nature, is suffering menstruation ought not to be forbidden to enter the church, because the natural discharge cannot rightly be imputed to her as guilt, and since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not just that she should be deprived of entry into the church [Col. 1194D]. For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her infirmity departed from her (Luke VIII). If, then, a woman in a flow of blood could laudably touch the Lord’s garment, why should a woman suffering her menstrual flow not be permitted to enter the Lord’s church?

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Bede and Rhemes: “when they are undergoing their customary menstrual periods.”]

“But,” you will say, “that woman was compelled by illness, whereas the women of whom we are speaking are constrained by customary practice.” Consider, therefore, dearest brother, that everything we suffer in this mortal flesh has been ordered, by God’s just judgment, as a result of the weakness of nature after sin. To hunger and thirst, to be hot or cold, to grow weary—all this arises from the weakness of nature. And what else is it to seek food against hunger, drink against thirst, breezes against heat, clothing against cold, and rest against weariness, than to seek certain remedies against infirmities?

[Note: [Col. 1195C] Turon.: “to set forth against illnesses,” perhaps for “to set against.”]

For women, their monthly flow of blood is an infirmity. If, therefore, the woman who, placed in sickness, touched the Lord’s garment rightly presumed to do so, why should it not be permitted to all women who are made infirm by the defect of their nature?

They ought not to be forbidden to receive the mystery of holy Communion during those same days [Col. 1195B]. If, out of great reverence, a woman does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she does receive it, she is not to be judged. It is characteristic of good minds to recognize their sins in some way even where there is no sin, because often something arising from sin is done without sin. Thus, when we are hungry, we eat without sin, although it was because of the sin of the first man that we came to hunger.

Menstruation is not itself any fault in women, since it occurs naturally. Yet the fact that nature itself has been so corrupted that it appears to be polluted even without any intention of the will [Note: [Col. 1195D] So Bede, Vatic. D, and Rhemes. But the printed editions read: “the defect comes from sin’s fault.”] is a defect arising from sin. Through this, human nature may recognize what it has become by judgment: the human being who willingly committed sin bears the guilt of sin unwillingly. [Note: [Col. 1195D] So Bede, Vatic. D, and Rhemes. But the printed editions read: “the defect comes from sin’s fault.”]

[Note: [Col. 1195D] The printed editions read “women who, when.” We have deleted *who*, not only because it is superfluous, but also because it has been added contrary to the authority of the manuscripts and to the detriment of the sense.]

Therefore, when women consider themselves during their menstrual period and do not presume to approach the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, they are to be praised for their sound judgment [Col. 1195C]. But when, carried away by the love of receiving the same mystery through the custom of a religious life, they long to receive it, they are not, as we have said, to be restrained.

For just as in the Old Testament external works were observed, so in the New Testament careful attention is paid not so much to what is done outwardly as to what is thought inwardly, so that it may be punished by a subtle judgment. Although the Law commands many things to be eaten as though unclean, the Lord nevertheless says in the Gospel: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the heart—those are the things that defile a person” (Matthew XV, 11). Shortly afterward, explaining this, he added: “For evil thoughts come out of the heart” (ibid., 19).

It has therefore been abundantly shown that what is shown in action to be defiled before almighty God is generated from the root of polluted thought. The apostle Paul likewise says: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure” (Titus I, 15). Immediately announcing the cause of this defilement, he adds: “For their mind and conscience are defiled.” If, then, food is not unclean to the one whose mind is not unclean, why should what a woman of pure mind suffers naturally be counted as uncleanness against her [Col. 1196B]?

[Note: [Col. 1195D] In the printed editions, “the women who, when.” We have deleted *who*, not only because it is superfluous, but also because it was added contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts and to the detriment of the sense.]

[Note: Among the Jews this was prescribed in Leviticus XVI, verse 15. The same practice was followed among the Gentiles: many were immersed in a flowing stream, others washed in tubs, others in basins, while attendants poured water over them. Saint Augustine mentions the Jews in *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 20. Clement of Alexandria mentions others at the beginning of the *Protrepticus*, with Hervetus’s commentary appended, and likewise in book III, chapter 9, of the *Paedagogus*, and in book VII of the *Stromata*. Tertullian hints at it in *On Baptism*, chapters 5 and 9. Saint Justin, near the end of the *Second Apology for the Christians*, addressed to Antoninus, says that demons persuaded the pagans to wash before approaching sacrifices, and that they had learned this from a prophet. Modern Jews do not wash, because they no longer have a sanctuary, as though the Lord had prescribed this washing solely for the sake of sacrifice. I leave this to your investigation, reader. GUSSANV.]

A man [Gratian, *On Penance*, distinction 7, question 4, chapter 7] who sleeps with his own wife ought not to enter the church unless he has washed with water; but even after washing he ought not to enter immediately. The ancient law commanded the Jewish people that a man who had intercourse with a woman should wash with water and not enter the church before sunset.

This may be understood spiritually, because a man is joined to a woman when the mind, through delight, is joined in thought to unlawful desire. Unless the fire of desire has first cooled in his mind, he ought not to consider himself worthy of the assembly of the brethren when he sees that he is burdened by the wickedness of an evil will.

Although different nations of people hold different opinions about this matter, and some appear to observe one practice and others another [Col. 1196C], nevertheless it has always been the custom of the Romans from ancient times, after intercourse with one’s own wife, to seek purification by washing and to refrain reverently for a short time from entering the church.

[Note: I should like this practice to be confirmed by more certain evidence, lest someone think that the statement was improperly inserted by another. [Col. 1196D] Saint Paulinus, in his letter to Alethius, mentions a *cantharus* at Rome in the basilica of Saint Peter; elsewhere he likewise suggests that fountains were placed at the entrances of temples. Eusebius, *History*, book X, chapter 4, agrees to some extent. Tertullian acknowledges and disapproves of the custom of washing in Africa in *On Prayer*, chapter 11; nor did he mean anything else in the *Apology*, chapter 39, as someone has supposed. Saint John Chrysostom reports the custom of washing in some churches in the East, *Homily 52 on Matthew*, though he does not greatly approve it. He speaks of the same matter in *Homily 74 on Matthew*, *Homily 72 on John*, and *Homily 6 on chapter II of the Second Epistle to Timothy*. See what the authors thought about the Hemerobaptists in their comments on chapter VII of Mark. I mentioned Saint Justin in the preceding note. I have searched the canons and found no decrees in favor of these washings. Accordingly, I take refuge in the rule of Saint Augustine, *Letter 119 to Januarius*, chapter 19. Perhaps in our own times some historian will arise who will trace the Roman practice in question, in an unbroken succession, from the apostles down to the age of Saint Gregory. GUSSANV.]

In saying this, we do not consider marriage itself to be a sin. But because even lawful intercourse between spouses cannot take place without the pleasure of the flesh, one must refrain from entering a sacred place, since that pleasure itself can in no way be without fault.

For the man who said, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me” (Psalm L, 7), had not been born of adultery or fornication but of lawful marriage. He who knew that he had been conceived in iniquities lamented that he had been born in sin, because a tree bears in its branch the diseased sap that it drew from its root. Yet in these words he does not call the intercourse of spouses itself iniquity, but specifically the pleasure of intercourse.

There are many things that are lawful and legitimate, and yet in performing them we are in some measure defiled—for example, we often pursue faults by becoming angry, and disturb the tranquility of our spirit. Although what is done is right, the disturbance of the mind at that moment is not approved.

He had become angry against the vices of sinners who said: “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Psalm VI, 8). Since the mind cannot raise itself into the light of contemplation unless it is tranquil, he grieved that his eye had been troubled by anger, because while he pursued evil deeds below, he was nevertheless forced to be confused and disturbed in contemplating things above. Anger against vice is therefore praiseworthy, yet troublesome, because he considered himself to have incurred some guilt by being disturbed [Col. 1197B].

[Note: In the Carnot manuscript the reading is as follows: “Thus marriage is good, and yet it has within itself some guilt arising from the pleasure of the flesh, because the lawful union of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure, and the intercourse of the flesh ought to be for the creation of children,” and so forth. This may perhaps be more correct and more consonant with the teaching of Saint Augustine, book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 12, and book V against Julian, chapter 7, and elsewhere; it is not, however, the reading found in Bede. GUSSANV. The variant reading noted here by Gussanville is supported by none of our manuscript codices. In the Rhemes manuscript it reads, “it should be for the sake of offspring, not the satisfaction of vices.” In Vatic. D, “and the intercourse of the flesh for the creation of children” is omitted. GUSSANV.]

Therefore the lawful union of the flesh ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and intercourse of the flesh ought to be for the purpose of creating children, not the satisfaction of vices.

If, then, a man uses his wife not seized by the desire for pleasure but solely for the purpose of creating children, he should certainly be left to his own judgment concerning entering the church or receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 1197C]. We ought not to forbid him to receive it if, placed in the fire, he does not know himself to be burning [Col. 1197D].

[Note: He seems to equate entering the church with receiving the Lord’s body, as though someone unworthy to communicate in Christ’s sacred body were also unworthy to enter the church. Saint Chrysostom is cited as holding nearly the same view. Let the reader consult chapter 32 of book IV of Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, where the story is told of a certain Curialis who had violated his own goddaughter and therefore did not dare enter the church. GUSSANV.]

But when, in the act of intercourse, it is not love of begetting offspring but pleasure that dominates, married people have something in their intercourse for which they should grieve. Holy preaching permits this to them, yet the mind is shaken by fear because of the permission itself. When the apostle Paul said, “If he cannot contain himself, let him have his wife,” he immediately took care to add: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (1 Corinthians VII, 9). For what is lawful and just is not granted by way of concession. By saying that it is granted by concession, he showed that it involves fault.

It must be weighed with vigilant attention that, when the Lord was about to speak to the people on Mount Sinai, he first commanded that same people to abstain from women. If, in that place where the Lord spoke through a creature subject to human beings, bodily purity was required with such care that those who were to receive the words of God were not to have intercourse with women [Col. 1198A], how much more ought those who receive the body of the almighty Lord to preserve purity of flesh within themselves, lest they be weighed down by the greatness of this immeasurable mystery?

Hence, through the priest, David is also told concerning his young men that, if they were pure from women, they should receive the bread of the Presence; they would not receive it at all unless David first acknowledged that they were pure from women.

A man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may receive the mystery of holy Communion when, in accordance with the judgment stated above, he is also permitted to enter the church.

## Augustine’s Eleventh Question

I also ask whether, after the illusion that customarily occurs in sleep, anyone may receive the Lord’s body, or whether, if he is a priest, he may celebrate the sacred mysteries.

## The Blessed Pope Gregory’s Response

The Testament of the old law [Gratian, distinction 6, chapter 1], as we have already said in the preceding chapter, calls such a person unclean and does not permit him to enter the church until evening unless he has washed with water [Col. 1198D].

[Note: Eleventh Question. The printed editions read “polluted to the Lord” and “and unless.” We follow Bede and the manuscript codices.]

[Note: In Bede: “although the spiritual people, understanding it differently, will receive it under the same interpretation as that stated above.” The Capuchin-Rouen codex differs slightly.]

This was then addressed specifically to that people; but when understood spiritually, it is received under the same interpretation as we have stated above, because the person who is defiled in thought by true images while being tempted by uncleanness is, as it were, deceived through a dream [Col. 1198D]. He must be washed with water so that he may cleanse the sins of his thought with tears. And unless the fire of temptation has first departed, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

Yet in this illusion a very necessary distinction must be made, because it must be considered very carefully from what cause it arises in the mind of the sleeper. Sometimes it results from overeating, sometimes from a natural bodily discharge or infirmity, and sometimes from thought.

When it has arisen from a natural discharge or infirmity, this illusion is in no way to be feared, because the mind that has suffered it unknowingly is to be pitied more than blamed for having caused it.

But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in the consumption of nourishment, and the receptacles of the humors are thereby burdened, the mind incurs some guilt on that account—but not such as to prohibit receiving the sacred mystery or celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, when perhaps a feast day requires the ministry to be performed [Col. 1198D] or necessity compels the mystery to be offered because no other priest is present [Col. 1198D].

[Note: Turon. and Vatic. D: “or requires the mystery to be offered.” The Vatican manuscript gives both readings.]

For if there are others who can perform the ministry [Note: Turon.: “the ministry”; this is also the reading in Bede.], an illusion caused by overeating ought not to prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, in my judgment, the priest should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery—provided that no shameful image has shaken the mind of the sleeper [Col. 1199C].

[Note: Vatic. D, removing the negation, reads: “if a shameful image has shaken the mind”; although this reading may seem to fit Saint Gregory’s purpose, we do not dare adopt it, since it is found neither in Bede nor in the other manuscripts. Otherwise, the received reading has excellent sense. The holy Doctor permits those who have suffered pollution from excessive food to approach to receive the sacred Eucharist, provided that no shameful thought has shaken the mind of those sleeping. For if the mind has been defiled by shameful images, he judges that one must abstain both from receiving and from celebrating the sacred mystery.]

For there are some in whom this illusion commonly arises in such a way that their mind, even while their body is asleep, is not defiled by shameful images. In this matter one point is shown: the mind itself is guilty, and is not then free in its own judgment, when it remembers that it saw nothing even while the body slept, yet remembers, while the body is awake, that it fell into gluttony [text uncertain; Col. 1199D].

[Note: Thus we restore the text from the manuscripts and Bede, although the sense is somewhat more obscure. In the printed editions I read: “It is shown that the mind itself is not then guilty but is entirely free in its own judgment, since, although it remembers nothing that it saw while sleeping, it nevertheless remembers, when the body is awake, that it fell into gluttony.”]

But if the illusion in the sleeping mind arises from shameful thought in the waking person, the mind’s guilt is evident. For the person sees from what root that pollution proceeded: knowingly he thought the thing, and unknowingly he suffered it [Col. 1199B].

But one must consider whether that thought arose from suggestion, from delight, or—and this is more serious—from consent to sin [Col. 1199D].

[Note: The holy Doctor discusses this more fully in *Moralia*, book IV, nos. 49 and following, and also in *Homily 16 on the Gospels*.]

Every sin is completed in three ways: by suggestion, by delight, and by consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, delight through the flesh, and consent through the spirit, because the serpent suggested the first fault, Eve, as flesh, took delight in it, and Adam, as spirit, consented. Great discernment is necessary, so that the mind may sit in judgment between suggestion and delight, and between delight and consent.

When the evil spirit suggests sin in the mind, if no delight in sin follows, sin has not been committed at all. But when the flesh begins to take delight, sin begins to be born. If the person also proceeds deliberately to consent [Col. 1199C], then sin is recognized as complete.

[Note: Vatic. D: “but if he consents to consent and deliberation.” Turon.: “but if he already consents with deliberation.”]

In suggestion, therefore, there is the seed of sin; in delight, its nourishment; in consent, its perfection [Col. 1199D].

[Note: Bede and Vatic. D: “the beginning of sin.”]

It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought the flesh draws into delight, and yet the mind does not consent to that delight [Col. 1200A]. Since the flesh cannot take delight without the soul, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is nevertheless in some way bound unwillingly in carnal delight, so that it contradicts and does not consent to it by reason, and yet remains bound by delight, lamenting bitterly that it is bound.

Hence that chief soldier of the heavenly army also groaned, saying: “I see another law in my members fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Romans VII, 23).

But if he was captive, he did not fight at all. Yet he did fight, and therefore he was not captive. He fought, therefore, according to the law of the mind, against which the law in his members fought. If this law fought, he was not captive. Thus the human being is, so to speak, both captive and free: free through the righteousness he loves, captive through the delight he bears unwillingly.

[Note: This passage is read variously in both the printed editions and the manuscripts. In Bede, Cologne edition of 1612: “it did not fight at all.” But if it did fight, why was he captive? In the Chifflet edition: “it did not fight at all, but it did fight; therefore he was both captive and fighting.” In the printed editions of Saint Gregory’s letters: “it did not fight at all. Therefore he was captive, and he was not captive. But it fought.” Thus the law of the mind was opposed by the law in the members; it fought, and therefore he was not captive. We have constructed our reading from the manuscripts Vatic. D, Gemet., Turon., and Capuc., which agree, except that Turon. reads, “if this fought, he was captive,” omitting the negation most erroneously.]

## LETTER LXV. TO AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF THE ENGLISH

He grants the use of the pallium. He likewise promises it to the bishop of London, whom he orders to be ordained by his own synod. He wishes the bishop of York to enjoy the full metropolitan dignity. He appoints Augustine primate of all Britain.

[Note: Letter LXV (also numbered 15, indiction 7). In Bede, book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 29, it reads: “To the most reverend brother Augustine, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.” GUSSANV. Other letters written by Saint Gregory to bishops and preserved by Bede bear a similar inscription, and there is no doubt that in at least most of his letters this most holy man called himself “servant of the servants of God.” But for the sake of brevity the longer titles have been omitted, both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions.]

Gregory to Augustine, bishop of the English.

Since it is certain that ineffable rewards of the eternal kingdom are reserved for those who labor for almighty God, it is nevertheless necessary for us to grant them the benefits of honors, so that, through the reward, they may be able to labor more abundantly in the pursuit of spiritual work.

[Note: Vatic. A and D: “the benefits of good things.”]

And because the new Church of the English has been brought, by the generosity of the same Lord and through your labor, to the grace of almighty God, we grant you the use of the pallium there solely for celebrating the solemn rites of Mass, so that in each place you may ordain twelve bishops who will be subject to your authority. Thus the bishop of the city of London must always thereafter be consecrated by his own synod and receive the pallium of honor from this holy and apostolic see, which, by God’s authority, I serve [Col. 1200C].

[Note: Vatic. D: “the bishop of London.” Londonium, Londinum, or Londinium—commonly London—is the chief and most celebrated city of England, situated on the River Thames and the capital of Middlesex County. Partly from GUSSANV. Among the English recently converted to the faith through the preaching of Augustine and his companions, Gregory established two metropolitan sees in Britain, one at London and the other at York, so that twelve bishops would be ordained under each metropolitan, as Bede relates in book I, chapter 29. A province certainly has twelve bishops, according to Gregory’s constitution, or at least ten or eleven and one metropolitan, according to the institution of Pelagius II, canon “Know that,” question 3, canon 6. But after Canterbury, which was the capital of the kingdom of Kent and the royal seat, was granted by King Ethelbert to Augustine, who established his own see and that of his successors there, and there died and was buried . . . the metropolitan dignity that Gregory had established at London was transferred to Canterbury, as is evident from the letter of King Coenwulf of Mercia to Pope Leo III, found in William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the English Kings*, book I, chapter 4 . . . . There was a long dispute over the primacy of Britain between the bishops of Canterbury and York. The bishop of Canterbury was declared, by the judgment of the Roman pontiffs, primate of all Britain and, as it were, pope of another world. Urban II ordered Anselm of Canterbury to sit at the Council of Bari beside the Roman archdeacon, who customarily sat before the pope. “Let us enclose this man,” he said, “within our world as the pope of another world.” On this matter see William of Malmesbury, *Deeds of the Pontiffs of the English*, book I, and Eadmer, book II, p. 52. ALTESERRA.]

As for the city of York, we wish you to send there a bishop whom you yourself judge should be ordained, so that, if that city and the neighboring regions receive the word of God, he too may ordain twelve bishops [Col. 1201A], so that he may enjoy metropolitan honor.

[Note: To constitute a province, Pelagius II requires ten or eleven cities and one king, letter 8. In the same place he teaches that a metropolitan bishop should have ten or eleven suffragan bishops. Provinces, however, have always been larger or smaller according to discretion: for example, the province of Lyon has always consisted, and still consists, of five cities; the province of Belgica Prima of four; the province of Germania Prima, or Mainz, likewise of four; and the province of the Graian and Pennine Alps of only three. Partly from GUSSANV.]

For, if his life continues, we also intend, with the Lord’s favor, to grant him the pallium, though we wish him to remain subject to the direction of your fraternity.

After your death, however, let him preside over the bishops whom he has ordained in such a way that he is in no respect subject to the authority of the bishop of London. Henceforth let this distinction of honor exist between the bishops of London and York: the one who was ordained first is to be regarded as senior.

By common counsel and harmonious action, let them determine whatever must be done for the sake of Christ, think rightly with one accord, and carry out what they have decided without disagreement among themselves [Col. 1201B].

Your fraternity, moreover, is to have subject to you, by the authority of the Lord our God, not only the bishops whom you ordain, nor only those who have been ordained by the bishop of York, but also all the priests of Britain, so that from the speech and life of your holiness they may receive a pattern of right belief and good living. Then, faithfully carrying out their ministry in faith and conduct, they may reach the heavenly kingdom when the Lord wills [Col. 1202C].

[Note: We supplied this conclusion from the passage cited in Bede, since it is absent from the manuscripts and printed copies of the *Register*. GUSSANV.]

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year, after the consulship of the same lord in the eighteenth year, indiction 4 [Col. 1201C].

[Note: Thus in Bede and in Paul’s Collection. Vatic. D reads: “Given on the Kalends of July, indiction 4.”]

## LETTER LXVI. TO EDILBERT, KING OF THE ENGLISH

He urges him to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to him, to listen willingly to Augustine, and to assist him. He explains why God sends signs before the imminent end of this world. He sends gifts and pours forth prayers to God.

Gregory to Edilbert, king of the English.

[Note: Letter LXVI (also numbered 60). The name of this king is read variously in both the manuscripts and printed editions. Vatic. D writes *Adalbertho*, supported by two Teller manuscripts, the Norman manuscript, and several English manuscripts. In the Colbert manuscripts, *Adelberto* or *Adilberto*, as also in Vatic. F. In Vatic. A, *Ildeberto*. In Vatic. B, *Alliberto*. In Victor., *Adilperchto*. In some English manuscripts, *Ethelberto*. We follow Bede chiefly, since the king’s name could not have been unknown to him.
