Moreover, by reading *Edilberthum* we obtain the etymology of the name: in the Saxon language *edit* signifies “honored” or “illustrious.” In Bede this title reads, in book I, chapter 32: “To the most glorious and excellent son Edilbert, king of the English, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.” In all the letters of Saint Gregory reported by the Venerable Bede, he prefaces them by calling himself “servant of the servants of God,” which confirms our opinion concerning this title, proposed in the preface to the *Register of Letters*, section 11, p. 481.]

For this reason almighty God brings good men to the government of peoples: so that through them he may bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all those over whom they have been placed. We recognize that this has been done among the English, over whom Your Glory has therefore been placed, so that through the good things granted to you, heavenly benefits might also be bestowed upon the people subject to you [Col. 1202A].

[Note: Vatic. D: “the benefits of his power”; and it adds, “or of his mercy.”]

Therefore, glorious son, guard with an attentive mind the grace you have received from God. Hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you; multiply the zeal of your righteousness in their conversion; attack the worship of idols; overthrow the buildings of their shrines; build up the character of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, threatening, encouraging, correcting, and displaying examples of good works, so that you may find in heaven as your rewarder the one whose name and knowledge you have spread on earth [Col. 1202B].

[Note: Saint Gregory adopted another opinion on this matter not long afterward, below, letter 76: “Tell him . . . that the shrines of idols should by no means be destroyed among that people,” and so forth. On this passage let the reader consider what we shall say from Augustine. In the Theodosian Code, title “On Pagans, Sacrifices, and Temples,” law 25: “We command that all their shrines, temples, and sanctuaries, if any still remain intact, be destroyed by order of the magistrates, and that they be purified by the placement of the venerable sign of the Christian religion.” GUSSANV.]

For he will also make the name of Your Glory more glorious to posterity, since you seek and preserve his honor among the nations. Thus Constantine, once a most pious emperor, recalled the Roman state from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it with himself to our almighty Lord God Jesus Christ, and turned himself and the subject peoples wholly toward him. As a result, that man surpassed the name of the ancient rulers by his praises, and surpassed his predecessors in reputation by as much as he exceeded them in good works.

Now, therefore, let Your Glory hasten to pour the knowledge of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, into the kings and peoples subject to you, so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit. And by as much as you have wiped away the sins of others among your subjects, by so much may you become more secure concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment of almighty God [Col. 1202C].

Our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop, trained in the rule of the monastery, filled with knowledge of sacred Scripture, and endowed with good works, by God’s authority, is urging you to listen willingly to whatever he tells you, carry it out devoutly, and preserve it carefully in your memory [Col. 1203A].

[Note: Vatic. F: “devoted to good works.”]

For if you listen to him when he speaks on behalf of almighty God, almighty God will more quickly hear him interceding for you. If, God forbid, you disregard his words, when will almighty God be able to hear him on your behalf, when you neglect to hear him on behalf of God?

Therefore bind yourself to him with your whole mind in the fervor of faith, and assist his efforts with the strength that God has divinely granted you, so that he may make you participants in his kingdom, whose faith you cause to be received and preserved in your kingdom [Col. 1203A].

[Note: In Bede: “cause to be received and preserved.” In the printed editions: “you receive and cause to be preserved.”]

Moreover, we want Your Glory to know that, as we recognize from the words of the Lord almighty in sacred Scripture, the end of the present world is now near, and the kingdom of the saints is coming—a kingdom that will never be able to end.

As that end of the world approaches, many things are imminent that have not occurred before: changes in the atmosphere, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places [Col. 1203B]. Yet not all these things will come in our own days; everything will follow after our days.

Therefore, if you recognize that any of these things are occurring in your land, do not let your mind be disturbed in any way, because these signs of the end of the age are sent beforehand for this reason: so that we should be concerned for our souls, fearful of the hour of death, and prepared in good works to meet the judge who is to come.

I have now spoken these few words, glorious son, so that when the Christian faith has grown in your kingdom, my speech also may grow broader among you; and the more fully the joys of the complete conversion of your people multiply in our mind, the more gladly may I speak [Col. 1204A].

[Note: The printed editions read “in your mind.” The sequence of the discourse, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts, shows that this reading should not be adopted.]

I have sent you small gifts, which will not be small to you when you have received them from the blessing of the blessed apostle Peter. May almighty God preserve and perfect in you the grace he has begun, extend your life here through the course of many years, and after a long time receive you into the assembly of the heavenly homeland [Col. 1203D].

[Note: This conclusion is taken from the passage cited in Bede, who reports the whole letter as it appears in our copies, except for the title and conclusion, as I said. GUSSANV.]

May heavenly grace preserve Your Excellency unharmed, my lord son.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, during the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year, after the consulship of the same lord in the eighteenth year, indiction 4.

[Note: In one of the Colbert manuscripts it reads: “Given on the Kalends of January, indiction 4.” The same is found in the Victorine manuscript and in the second Rhemes, or Remigius, manuscript.]

## LETTER LXVII. TO QUIRICUS, BISHOP, ETC.

Those who were baptized in heresy with invocation of the Trinity are not to be baptized again if they return to the Church; rather, they are to be reconciled either by the laying on of hands, by anointing with chrism, or by a profession of faith. Returning Nestorians are to be instructed in the true faith concerning the incarnate Word, which Gregory here confirms from Scripture; and if they anathematize Nestorius and venerate the synods accepted by the Church, they are to be received in their own orders.

[Col. 1204B]

Gregory

[Note: [Col. 1203D] EPISTLE LXVII [Alternative numbering: 61].—We have restored this title on the judgment of the most illustrious and learned Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, who speaks as follows concerning it in his appendix to the Council of Clermont under Urban II: “I have thought that the inscription of Gregory’s letter to the bishops of Ireland should be corrected by substituting Iberia, both because the inquiry made concerning the Nestorians sufficiently shows that the matter concerns the regions of the East, where alone that heresy flourished, and because at the beginning of the letter Gregory notes that the bishops’ legate, journeying to Rome, had lost the letters along with other belongings in the city of Jerusalem. This could be said of the Irish, situated in the far West, only in the most absurd fashion, whereas it perfectly suits the Iberians, situated on the borders of Pontus and having embraced the Christian faith from the time of Constantine himself. Gregory therefore, in responding to the consultation, says that Nestorians are to be received by the profession of faith alone, neither through repeated baptism, nor through the laying on of hands, nor through the conferral of chrism. He indeed commends the tradition of the Fathers, which taught that no other rite should be employed toward Nestorians. Nevertheless, there are manuscript codices that support this reading. The Cluniac and Thuanus manuscripts, in their indexes of letters, read *Iberia*, although the letter itself has *Hibernia*. The Vatican Codex 622, also, according to the recension of the most eminent Cardinal Bona, as he informed me in a letter dated 9 September 1670, has the same reading. So too Anselm of Lucca, in his *Canonical Collection*, book VIII, chapter 24: ‘To Quiricus, bishop, and the other bishops of Iberia.’ Nor should Christian Lupus be passed over; in volume I of the *Councils*, in his notes on the Fifth Council, page 738, he reads *Iberiae*, and on page 743 *Hiberiae*. GUSSANV.” We willingly agree with the conjecture of these learned men. It is confirmed by the Royal Codex and by the Collection of Paul the Deacon, whose index reads *in Iberia*. Nor should the observation of the Roman correctors concerning canon 44, distinction 4, *On Consecration*, from the letter to Quiricus, be disregarded. They say: “Thus *Iberia* was corrected from the original Vatican manuscript. Previously it was *Hibernia*.” As for the bishop’s name, in the ancient codices it is sometimes read *Quirinus*, sometimes *Quiricus.]

To Quiricus, bishop, and the other bishops in [Note: [Col. 1204D] Other copies have *Iberia*, a region of Asia now called by its inhabitants Gurgistan and by the French *la Géorgie*; it lies between Colchis to the west and Albania to the east and borders Greater Armenia. It is now subject to the rule of its own prince, though under the protection of the king of Persia. GUSSANV. Why should Iberia not be understood as Spain, which was once so called? See book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 36, in the notes. Among Saint Irenaeus’s writings, book I, chapter 3, the Iberians are Spaniards: “Neither do the Churches founded in Germany believe otherwise . . . nor those among the Iberians, nor those among the Celts.” Spain retained the name Iberia for a long time after Saint Gregory’s death, as is plainly established by the letter of Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, to Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, in volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, page 69. Taio flourished around the middle of the seventh century. Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, had already proposed several questions about baptism to the most holy pontiff, who replied in Letter 43 of Book I. Since the Arian heresy had shortly before been raging in Spain, why should the bishops of Spain not have consulted this supreme teacher and doctor of the Church concerning the rite for reconciling Arians? But, you may ask, why are so many other heretics mentioned after the Arians, and why is an inquiry and ruling made concerning their baptism? Perhaps the Arian heresy, which had raged so long in Spain, had brought in this mixture of heretics, most of whom were at least related to the Arians. Certainly, long experience has taught us that in provinces where either the Calvinist or Lutheran heresy dominates, other heresies are freely admitted and spread. Indeed, even if Spain had at that time been entirely free of these heresies, nothing prevented the bishops from inquiring into the baptism of those heretics, since even now its validity is widely debated in the schools.] Hiberia, to the Catholics.

Since distance is nothing to charity, let the letter unite those whom places divide. The bearer of this letter, therefore, having come to the Church of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, declared that he had received letters from your fraternity for us, and that he had lost them, together with other belongings, in the city of Jerusalem. In them, as he himself says, you sought to inquire whether priests and peoples confused by the error of the Nestorian heresy, when they return to the catholic Church, the mother of all the elect, ought to be baptized, or whether they should instead be joined to the bosom of that same mother Church solely by confessing the true faith.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] See Letter 37 of Book X, indiction 3, and the notes on it.]

We have indeed learned from the ancient institution of the Fathers (Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter 44) that those who have been baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the holy Church, are recalled to the bosom of the mother Church either by anointing with chrism, by the laying on of hands, or by the mere profession of faith.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Those who had been baptized among heretics were received into the Church in different ways upon their return, according to the various errors from which they suffered. First, some were ordered to be rebaptized, such as the Paulianists and others among whom the form of baptism was defective. Second, others were not baptized but were ordered to be anointed with chrism. These are always listed as five: in canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople, in canon 95 of the Council in Trullo, in the *Euchologion* taken from the Royal Library and published by de Marca, in Theodore the Studite’s Letter 4, cited by Balsamon, page 1099 (see also Theodore’s Letter 53 of Book I), and in the writing of the presbyter Timothy, in the same work, page 1050. There, I repeat, five are listed: the Novatians, the Tetradites or Quartodecimans, [Col. 1205D] the Arians, the Apollinarists, and the Macedonians. Third, others were neither baptized again nor anointed, but were received after renouncing their own heresy and the heresies of others. Among these are counted the Nestorians and Eutychians in all the authorities just mentioned, except canon 7 of Constantinople. These are the very groups whom the Council in Trullo, canon 95, designated by the names Manichaeans, Valentinians, and Marcionites—not because they actually professed those sects, but so that the council, condemning their impiety, might declare them related to its impiety. As for the genuine Manichaeans, Marcionites, and Valentinians, they were baptized again, as is clear from Timothy’s writing. As for Gregory’s statement that Arians were received in the West by the laying on of hands, do not understand this of the whole of the West. For in Gaul and Spain, the councils of Arles II, canon 17; Orange I, canon 2; Epaon, chapter 16; and Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 31; book IV, chapters 27 and 28; book V, chapter 39; and book IX, chapter 15, plainly testify that Arians, when they returned to the Church, were signed with chrism. [Col. 1206B] Moreover, we infer from Letters 1, chapter 1, and 4, chapter 8, of Siricius; Letters 2, chapter 8, and 22, chapter 4, of Innocent I; and Letters 129, chapter 7, and 135, chapter 2, of Leo I, that the discipline concerning the West asserted here by Gregory the Great was received in practice in the Roman Church itself and in certain other churches of Italy and neighboring provinces. Whether that anointing by which repentant heretics were signed both in the East and in Gaul and Spain was the sacrament of confirmation itself is debated by theologians.]

The West reforms Arians for entry into the holy Catholic Church by the laying on of hands, while the East does so by anointing with holy chrism.

[Note: [Col. 1206B] That is, heretics who maintain that there is only one nature in Christ, such as the Eutychians.]

But it receives Monophysites and others by the true confession alone, because the holy baptism that they received among heretics then receives in them the power of cleansing when either the former have received the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands or the latter, because of their profession of the true faith, have been united to the bosom of the holy and universal Church.

Those heretics, however, who are not baptized in the name of the Trinity (Gratian, ibid., chapter 84), such as the Bonosiaci [Note: [Col. 1206B] The printed editions have *Bonosiani*, contrary to most manuscripts, namely the Royal, Corbie, Norman, three Vatican manuscripts, Paul’s Collection, and others. The Bonosiaci were so called from a certain Bonosus, a bishop in Macedonia, who denied that Mary, the Mother of God, remained inviolate after giving birth. The Council of Capua, around the year 389, referred his judgment to the bishops of Illyricum. In discussing the Bonosiaci or Bonosians, Innocent I, Letters 20, 21, and 22, does not attribute to them what Baronius supposes: that they did not believe in Christ the Lord and therefore were not baptized in the name of the Trinity. The Council of Arles II, chapter 17, accepts their baptism as valid: “As for the Bonosiaci who come from the same error—and it is clear that they are baptized in the Trinity, like the Arians—when questioned, they have confessed our faith with all their heart; it is sufficient that they be received into the Church with chrism and the laying on of hands.” Perhaps they later added Photinianism to their errors; for Gelasius I, in the Roman synod’s decree on prohibited books, joins Bonosus with Ebion, Paul of Samosata, and Photinus. Even earlier, Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 14, had said that Audentius wrote books against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, and especially, with particular intent, against the Photinians, who are now called Bonosiaci. Concerning the Cataphrygians, see the treatise *On the Prescription against Heretics*, in Tertullian, chapter 52: “Other heretics also arose who are called ‘according to the Phrygians’; but they do not have one doctrine. For some are called ‘according to Proclus,’ and others are designated ‘according to Aeschines.’ They have one blasphemy in common and another blasphemy that is not common but peculiar to themselves. Their common blasphemy is that they say the Holy Spirit was indeed in the apostles but that the Paraclete was not; and that the Paraclete spoke more things through Montanus than Christ uttered in the Gospel.” Those heretics were called Cataphrygians by a single designation because the founders and leaders of that heresy—Montanus, Appelles, and the false prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla—came from Phrygia and the heresy chiefly spread in that province during the second century.] and the Cataphrygians, because the former do not believe in Christ the Lord, while the latter, with a perverse understanding, believe that the Holy Spirit is some wicked man, Montanus [Note: [Col. 1206D] The Rheims manuscript and Vatican D, following a distorted interpretation, have “the wicked Montanus.”], and many others like them—when they come to the holy Church are baptized, because what they received while in error in the name of the Holy Trinity was not baptism.

[Col. 1207A]

Nor can this be called a repetition of baptism, since, as has been said, it was not given in the name of the Trinity.

The Nestorians, however, because they are baptized in the name of the holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 1207D] That Collection, Vatican D, and the Rheims manuscript have: “but because the error of their heresy obscures them, since they are like the Jewish unbelief and do not believe in the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, and therefore to the holy . . .”], but because the error of their heresy obscures them, since they are like the Jewish unbelief and do not believe in the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten, when they come to the holy Catholic Church must be instructed in the firmness and confession of the true faith, so that they may believe in one and the same Son of God and man, our Lord Jesus Christ: the same one existing in divinity before the ages and the same one made man at the end of the ages, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

We say that the Word became flesh, not by losing what he was, but by assuming what he was not [Note: [Col. 1207D] Thus the Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts; the printed editions have “without changing,” a reading we would have followed had the manuscript codices not led us elsewhere.]. For through the mystery of his Incarnation the Only-Begotten of the Father increased what was ours; he did not diminish what was his.

Thus the Word and the flesh are one person, as he himself says: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). The Son of God who was in heaven was the Son of Man who spoke on earth.

Hence John says: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding” (1 John 5:20). He immediately added what understanding he gave us: “That we may know the true God.” Whom does he indicate here as the true God except the almighty Father? But he also added what he thought concerning the almighty Son: “And that we may be in his true Son Jesus Christ.”

Behold, he calls the Father the true God and Jesus Christ his true Son. He shows more clearly what he understands this true Son to be when he says: “This is the true God and eternal life.” If, therefore, according to Nestorius’s error, the Word were one person and the man Jesus Christ another, then the one who is truly man would certainly not be the true God and eternal life. But the Only-Begotten Son, the Word existing before the ages, became man. He is therefore the true God and eternal life.

Certainly, when the holy Virgin was about to conceive him and heard the angel speaking to her, she said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1:38). When she had conceived him and went to her kinswoman Elizabeth, she immediately heard from that same Elizabeth: “Why am I worthy that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

Behold, the same Virgin is called both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother. She is the handmaid of the Lord because the Only-Begotten, the Word existing before the ages, is equal to the Father; but she is his mother because in her womb, from the Holy Spirit and from her own flesh, he was made man.

She is not the handmaid of one person and the mother of another, because, while the Only-Begotten of God, existing before the ages, was born as man from her womb, by an investigable miracle she became both the handmaid of man through his divinity and the mother of the Word through his flesh [Note: [Col. 1207D] Paul’s Collection: “by an unfathomable miracle.”].

Nor was flesh first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and divinity afterward brought into the flesh. Rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb, the Word—while preserving the proper power of his nature—became flesh. And the Only-Begotten Son of God was born through the Virgin’s womb as a perfect man, that is, in the truth of flesh and of a rational soul.

Hence he is also called anointed above his companions, as the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8). He was anointed with oil, namely with the gift of the Holy Spirit. But he was anointed above his companions because all of us first exist as sinful human beings and are afterward sanctified through the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

But he who, existing as God before the ages, was conceived as man by the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb at the end of the ages was anointed by that same Spirit in the place where he was conceived. He was not conceived first and anointed afterward; rather, the very fact that he was conceived from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin’s flesh was his anointing by the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, all who return from the perverse error of Nestorius must confess this truth of his birth before the assembly of your holy fraternity, anathematizing Nestorius himself with all his followers and the remaining heresies. They must also promise that they receive and venerate the venerable synods received by the universal Church. Without any hesitation, therefore, let your Holiness receive them into your community while preserving their own orders [Note: [Col. 1208D] This was established by the eighth canon of Nicaea. The founders of heresies were excluded. Concerning such leniency toward heretical clergy, see Augustine, *Against Cresconius*, book II, chapter 12.], so that, while you investigate the hidden thoughts of their minds with diligent care and teach them through true knowledge the correct doctrines that they ought to hold, and while you create no opposition or difficulty for them concerning their own orders through gentleness, you may snatch them from the mouth of the ancient enemy. And the reward of eternal glory may increase for you before almighty God in proportion as you gather many who will rejoice without end with you in the Lord.

May the holy Trinity, as you pray for us, guard you with its protection and grant you still more abundant gifts in its love.

[Note: [Col. 1208D] In the Colbert manuscript and in Paul’s Collection: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.”]

## EPISTLE LXVIII. TO VIRGILIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

He commends Bishop Augustine, should he come to him.

[Note: [Col. 1208D] EPISTLE LXVIII [Alternative numbering: 63].—Bede’s copy reads: “To the most reverend and most holy brother Virgilius, fellow bishop, servant of the servants of God.” *History*, Book I, chapter 29.]

Gregory to Virgilius, bishop of Arles.

The affection that ought to be shown to brothers who come voluntarily is understood from the fact that they are often accustomed to be invited for the sake of charity. Therefore, if it should happen that our common brother Augustine, the bishop, comes to you, let your affection receive him warmly and sweetly, as is fitting, so that it may refresh him with the benefit of its consolation and teach others how fraternal charity ought to be cultivated.

Since it often happens that those who live far away learn first from others what needs to be corrected, [Note: [Col. 1209D] Vatican D has: “if perhaps any fault should have been brought against him.” The same codex above, where it reads “ought to be cultivated,” has “ought to be consoled”; Vatican E and the Rheims manuscript agree.] if he should bring to your fraternity any faults of priests or others, investigate everything carefully and minutely while sitting with him.

Show yourselves strict and vigilant concerning those things that offend God and provoke him to anger, so that, for the correction of others, punishment may strike the guilty while false suspicion does not afflict the innocent.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] This conclusion is taken from Bede at the passage cited above.]

May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] These words are absent from all our manuscripts except two Teller manuscripts.]

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord, the most devout Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, after the consulship of that same lord of ours in his eighteenth year, indiction 4.

## EPISTLE LXIX. TO BRUNICHILDA, QUEEN OF THE FRANKS

Concerning the correction of priests who lead corrupt lives.

Gregory to Brunichilda, queen of the Franks.

[Col. 1209B]

Since it is written, “Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable” (Proverbs 14:34), a kingdom is considered stable when the fault that is recognized is corrected quickly.

We have therefore learned from the reports of many people something that we cannot mention without excessive anguish of heart: certain priests in those regions behave so shamelessly and wickedly that it is disgraceful for us to hear of it and lamentable to report it.

Therefore, since the reputation of this wickedness has now spread so far, lest the corruption of others strike either our soul or your kingdom with the dart of its sin [Note: [Col. 1209D] EPISTLE LXIX [Alternative numbering: 64].—Vatican A has: “or your soul.”], we must rise up ardently to avenge these things, lest the crime of a few become the destruction of many.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Chrysostom, Homily 45 on Matthew 23: “Without light the people grope blindly; without salt they become corrupt; without leaven they become insipid; without a guide they fall into a pit; without a helmsman they are shipwrecked; through evil examples they collapse.”]

For wicked priests are the cause of the people’s ruin. Who would interpose himself as an advocate for the sins of the people if the priest, who ought to plead for them, commits more serious offenses?

But since those whose office it is to pursue these matters are stirred neither by concern to investigate nor by zeal to punish, let your written instructions be sent to us, [Note: [Col. 1209D] Gregory was considering summoning Augustine, bishop of the English, to Gaul so that, together with the Gallic bishops, he might investigate and correct priests who behaved shamelessly and wickedly, as the preceding letter also suggests.] and, if you command it, we shall send a person with your authority who, together with the other priests, must investigate these matters carefully and correct them according to God’s will.

For the things we have mentioned must not be ignored, because whoever can correct a matter and neglects to do so undoubtedly makes himself a participant in the offense.

Therefore, take care for your soul; take care for your grandsons, whom you desire to reign happily; take care for the provinces. Before our Creator shakes out his hand to strike, give the correction of this crime your most diligent attention, lest he strike afterward with greater severity precisely because he now waits longer and more mercifully.

Know, moreover, that you offer our God a great sacrifice of appeasement if you quickly cut away from your territories the stain of so great a crime.

[Note: [Col. 1209D] The old Colbert manuscript reads: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.” Certainly, if this letter was brought by Mellitus and his companions, it was written at the same time as the other preceding letters to which the same date is attached. Yet it can scarcely be believed that Saint Gregory wrote three letters to the same queen on the same day—namely Letters 62, 63, and 69 of this book.]

## EPISTLE LXX. TO CANDIDUS, PRESBYTER AND ADMINISTRATOR OF THE PATRIMONY

He commends the presbyter Aurelius, so that Candidus may entrust to him an oratory or some other place.

Gregory to Candidus [Note: [Col. 1210D] That is, in Gaul; for he was an Italian administering the patrimony of Saint Peter in Gaul. GUSSANV.], presbyter of Gaul.

The bearer of this letter, our son Aurelius the presbyter, coming from the regions of Gaul, has requested that, if somewhere among the possessions of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, an oratory or a place requiring a presbyter or abbot can be found, it be entrusted to him, so that he may find support for his present life and we may be seen to have granted his request.

Accordingly, we commend him to your affection in every way, so that, wherever necessity requires, your affection may cooperate with him and he may find there the assistance of our written authority.

## EPISTLE LXXI. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He rebukes him and the others who served as judges in the case of John the Deacon because they inflicted no punishment on Hilarus the subdeacon, who was a slanderer. He orders Hilarus, deprived of his office and publicly flogged, to be exiled. Paschasius, the bishop, is to choose a deputy administrator and a chief steward.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

Since crimes committed against the innocent, especially against those in sacred orders, ought to be punished more severely, [Col. 1210C] consider how culpable all of you are who sat in judgment in the case of John the Deacon, since Hilarus [Note: [Col. 1210D] EPISTLE LXXI [Alternative numbering: 66].—The punishment of a slanderer, which ought always to be kept before the eyes of those in authority and written in capital letters. Nowadays innocent people are commonly oppressed with impunity—not only deacons, but also presbyters and pastors—and informers are indulged, those who gnaw at the reputation of others with a malicious tooth under the appearance of devotion. GUSSANV.], his slanderer, was not punished by any decision of yours.

Nor should you think that this provides a sufficient excuse for you: that, when you wished to judge, our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius is said to have delayed you. For if zeal for righteousness had flourished in you, it would have been easier for many to persuade one person reasonably than for one person to delay many without cause.

Since, therefore, so great an evil must not pass without deserved vengeance, we wish our aforesaid brother Paschasius to be admonished to deprive that same Hilarus first of the office of subdeacon, which he is unworthy to hold, and then, after having him publicly flogged [Note: [Col. 1211C] Even in Augustine’s time, bishops often employed flogging with rods in judicial proceedings. See Letter 133. Public flogging has now withdrawn from the ecclesiastical forum. In a judgment of the Parliament of Paris in the year 1562, an official was declared to have judged wrongly and abusively when he condemned a cleric to public flogging, and ecclesiastical judges were prohibited from imposing such a punishment.], to have him deported into exile [Note: [Col. 1211C] This is reported in the chapter *Since More Severely*, *Extraordinary Decretals*, concerning slanderers. See below, Book XIII, Letter 45. The same punishment is established in canon 9, Cause 3, question 4, chapter 9; likewise in chapter 3, Cause 3, question 5; and canon 23, distinction 63. Ivo of Chartres, Letter 186, to the bishop of Orléans: “You ought to condemn the deposed man to perpetual imprisonment or drive him into eternal exile.” It is now not lawful for an ecclesiastical judge to send clerics into exile; that belongs to the royal authority. Choppin, *On Sacred Polity*, Book II, title 3, number 12, attests that this has been judged more than once. Fevretius says the same was confirmed by several judgments, *On Abuse*, Book VIII, chapter 4, number 11.], so that the punishment of one may serve as the correction of many.

If perhaps the injured reputation of his deacon should still not move his leniency, and if—in a matter we do not believe—he should remain sluggish in this, let your experience carry out what we have said and report to us his neglect [Note: [Col. 1211D] Vatican A has: “if the reputation of his leniency . . .”].

Moreover, the same brother is to be exhorted by our command to show himself vigilant in all things and not neglect to provide his Church with greater discipline, lest he incur sin on account of those entrusted to him and provoke us severely against him if, contrary to our wishes, he should prove careless or sluggish in the care of his office.

We also wish [Gratian, distinction 89, chapter 2] our aforesaid brother Paschasius to appoint for himself a deputy administrator and a chief steward [Note: [Col. 1211D] Concerning deputy administrators and hospitality, see Book I, Letter 11.], so that he may be capable and prepared both for visiting guests and for the matters that arise.

But if you see that he is negligent and delays fulfilling what we have said, his entire clergy must be called in, so that by common counsel they may themselves choose persons capable of being appointed to the duties mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 1211D] The old Colbert manuscript: “Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction 4.” Paul’s Collection and another Rheims manuscript: “Given on the sixth day before the Ides of July, indiction 4.”]

(Compare John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 31; Book II, chapter 54.)

## EPISTLE LXXII. TO AGAPITUS, ABBOT

He unites with Agapitus’s monastery another monastery that had been completely deserted by its monks because of enemy attacks.

Gregory to Agapitus, abbot.

[Note: [Col. 1212C] EPISTLE LXXII [Alternative numbering: 67].—Thus the English, Norman, Royal, Rheims, and most other manuscripts. The old edition: “Concerning venerable property, or when it is lawful,” and so also the recent Rheims manuscript. Recent editors preferred to change the beginning of this letter to: “lest care be lacking for venerable property or any form of worship.” In Vatican F, instead of “when it is lawful,” it reads “when it is pleasing.”]

Our care must diligently ensure that reverent service is not lacking to venerable places or, when permitted, to worship.

Since, therefore, the monastery situated on the estate of Marcianus [Note: [Col. 1212C] Another Rheims manuscript has “Martinianus.”] in the province of Campania is said to have been so utterly deserted by the community because of enemy attacks that not even one monk remained there who could provide any supervision or care, we have judged it useful to unite it to your monastery, together with all its property and with whatever rights of action belong to it [Note: [Col. 1212C] Concerning such unions, see above, Book I, Letter 8.], so that you may possess free and undisputed authority to hold its property or recover it from those who retain it.

It must also be part of your duty to assign monks there who, during the interval when the enemy is absent, should celebrate the Work of God there and serve appropriately.

Do not presume to neglect it under any excuse, since it has been entrusted to your care precisely so that you may provide supervision there.

Know, however, that we have entrusted the monastery itself to your administration in such a way that jurisdiction there belongs not to the bishop of Sorrento, in whose city your monastery is located, but to the bishop of Nocera, since the monastery lies within his diocese. We arrange the administration of this place in such a way that we nevertheless preserve each bishop’s rights inviolate.

## EPISTLE LXXIII. TO MARINIANUS, ABBOT

He entrusts the Church of Saint George to Marinianus and his successors.

[Col. 1212B]

Gregory to Marinianus, abbot.

Since we have learned that the Church of Saint George, situated in a place called [Note: [Col. 1212C] EPISTLE LXXIII [Alternative numbering: 68].—Finicchiarus observes, in another passage—namely Book III, indiction 2, Letter 27—that this man is called “abbot of Palermo,” in Bollandus, under 23 April. “And just as,” he says, “there was never any place in Rome known to have been called *Ad Sedem*, so it seems that the holy pope would not have written to an abbot likewise living in Rome concerning a church situated in Rome. Nevertheless, since that church already at that time—that is, in the year 601—needed so much repair that the Roman pontiff himself considered its care not to be neglected, it may be inferred from this alone that, wherever it was situated, it was extremely ancient and quite probably had been built in the very century in which Saint George suffered martyrdom, namely at the beginning of the fourth century. A feast of Saint George appears in the Sacramentary with its own preface. Tillemont discusses this holy martyr in volume V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, page 185. See Bollandus.] *Ad Sedem*, is receiving less care than it ought, and since your monastery is known to be attached to that church, we have judged it useful to entrust its care to you. We exhort you to provide appropriate supervision there and to ensure that the office of psalmody is solemnly performed.

Since it is certain that the church itself needs repair, we wish you to receive whatever may come to it and to spend it, as you deem appropriate, on its repair.

We wish both you and your successors, who by God’s authority shall assume the administration of the monastery, to provide the care commanded to you by this written decree and to observe in every respect what we have established.

## EPISTLE LXXIV. TO EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

His letter was falsified by the most wicked monk Andrew. Certain sermons were falsely attributed to Gregory himself by the same man. A confession of faith is to be demanded from Luke, a presbyter of suspect faith.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1213D] EPISTLE LXXIV [Alternative numbering: 69].—Concerning Eusebius and Andrew, see Photius, *Bibliotheca*, Codex 162.] to Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Col. 1213A]

The bearer of this letter, Theodore, a lector of your Church, came to the threshold of the holy apostles. Since, being a newcomer, he knew no one there, he innocently entrusted to the monk Andrew—who had been confined at Saint Paul’s—the objects and documents he had brought, as he would have done to someone long known to him, believing that Andrew’s mind corresponded to his habit, just as we too had previously believed.

But Andrew proved to be so depraved that, if his folly had been allowed to continue much longer under the appearance of confinement, he would have deceived many souls through the falsity of his wickedness and would have caused no small scandals wherever he could.

Among the other things that Andrew wickedly contrived and did, he also falsified the letter that you sent to us, which the aforementioned bearer had deposited with him, in such a way that anyone who read it would clearly judge that you neither thought soundly nor held Catholic views.

As a result, while we were diligently seeking the truth, the iniquity that had lain concealed was made public, and such enormities were discovered in him as would scarcely be believed even of some criminal layman.

Since, among his various evils, he also wrote certain sermons and labeled them with our name, and since we fear that he may have sent them somewhere, let your fraternity take care. If you find anything of this sort, have it both cut out and completely destroyed, so that what an uneducated man, ignorant of letters and of Sacred Scripture, labeled with our name, as we have said, may not infect the minds of anyone.

For we neither know Greek nor have ever written any work in Greek.

You will learn about his other evils and about what was decided concerning him by us in the council from the report of the aforementioned bearer, whom we commend to your fraternity in every respect, since he was present.

[Note: [Col. 1213D] Read Letter 42 of Book X, indiction 3, alternatively Letter 6 of Book VII, indiction 2.]

Moreover, we exhort and admonish you to warn our common son Luke the presbyter—concerning whom the people, as is said, are troubled by no small suspicion—to give a public account of himself and to confess his faith. He must openly declare in every way that he receives and follows the holy synods venerated by the Apostolic Church. Among other things, he must specifically anathematize and reject Nestorius, Severus, and their followers, so that, by this satisfaction, no scandal may remain in the hearts of your children against you on his account.

If, however, contrary to what we believe, he should delay doing this under some pretext, let there be nothing in common between you and him; he must be entirely separated from your familiarity and communion.

For, as we have already written, it is better to cast a diseased sheep out of the Lord’s fold than to lose the healthy ones because of the fault of one.

Therefore, dearest brother, pay careful attention to this; and strive so that you may have your children united and devoted, as is fitting, and so that no further complaint on this account may return to us. As for the bearer of this letter, as we have said, we commend him to you in every respect. Since he was previously innocently deceived by an evil monk, and afterward stood firm in his conviction of him, may he find here among your fraternity the reward for his labor, although I am confident that it will be repaid to him in his eternal homeland.

[Note: Another Rheims manuscript: “in his conviction of him.”]

[Note: Corbie manuscript: “But if he wishes to return.”]

But if he should again wish to come here to pray at the shrine of the holy apostles, let your fraternity send him without any delay. (Cf. John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 81.)

## LETTER LXXV. TO AURELIUS

He consoles him over the death of his brother and the tribulations he was suffering.

[Note: LETTER LXXV [Elsewhere 70]. It may perhaps be necessary to read *Aureliae*, as in the title of Letter 36 of Book VII, indiction 15. Yet establishing the true name is difficult because of the scarcity of manuscript copies. This letter is found in only a few witnesses: among the Vatican manuscripts, only manuscript A contains it. We have also found it in another Rheims manuscript and in the Victor manuscript.]

Gregory to Aurelius, a Frank.

When I heard of the death of your most beloved brother, no epistolary expression can convey the grief with which I was struck.

[Note: He perhaps means the patrician Dynamian, who is known to have been a friend of Saint Gregory from Letter 33 of Book III, indiction 2, and Letter 36 of Book VII, indiction 15.]

But I pray almighty God to console you by the breath of his grace and to guard you by heavenly protection both from evil spirits and from wicked men. For if, after his death, you are enduring disturbances from certain adversaries, do not be surprised. If you seek to enjoy good things in your own land—that is, in the land of the living—you must bear the evils inflicted by men in a foreign land.

[Note: Augustine, on Psalm 103, sermon 4, §4: “In the land of the dying is my hope; in the land of the living is my portion.” In Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 34, the Church is called “the land of the blessed” and “the land of the living,” because it will reign with Christ forever. Gussanvillaeus fruitlessly seeks a distinction between “the land of life” and “the land of the living,” nor does he distinguish the book of life from the book of the living. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, Part I, question 24, article 1.]

[Col. 1214C]

For the present life is a pilgrimage; and for one who longs for the homeland, the place of pilgrimage is a torment, even if it appears pleasant. But to you, who seek your homeland, amid the sighs that you utter I also hear the groans of human oppression rising up.

This happens by the wondrous dispensation of almighty God: while truth calls through love, the present world drives your spirit away from itself through the tribulations it inflicts. The mind leaves the love of this age all the more easily because it is both summoned and impelled.

Therefore, continue what you have begun: devote yourselves to hospitality, and labor most earnestly in prayer and tears. Give yourselves now more generously and abundantly to the almsgiving that you have always loved, so that the fruit of your work may afterward increase in your reward in proportion to the growth here of your zeal for labor.

[Note: In the Rheims and Saint-Victor manuscripts: “the fruit of the gift.”]

## LETTER LXXVI. TO MELLITUS, ABBOT

He gives him instructions to deliver to Augustine, to whom he was going, for facilitating the conversion of the English.

[Col. 1215A]

[Note: LETTER LXXVI [Elsewhere 71]. In Bede, Book I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 30, the title reads: “To his most beloved son Mellitus, abbot: Gregory, servant of the servants of God.” Gussanv.]

Gregory to Mellitus, abbot, in Francia.

After the departure of our congregation, which is with you, we have been left very anxious, because we have had no opportunity to hear anything about the success of your journey. But when almighty God has brought you to our most reverend brother Augustine, the bishop, tell him what I discussed with myself for a long time while considering the matter of the English—namely, that the temples of idols in that people should by no means be destroyed, but that the idols themselves which are in them should be destroyed.

[Note: Saint Augustine held the same view in Letter 47 to Publicola: “When temples, idols, and sacred groves are converted to the honor of the true God, what happens to them is like what happens to human beings when they are changed from sacrilegious and impious people into the true religion.” Theodoret, *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, sermon 8, on the martyrs, says that the temples and altars of the gods were indeed destroyed, but that all their materials were dedicated to the shrines of the martyrs. Somewhat differently, the Council of Epaon in 517, canon 33, stated: “We disdain to apply to holy uses the basilicas of heretics, which we hate with such abhorrence that we do not consider their pollution capable of being cleansed.” After the English were converted to the faith, Gregory had judged that the temples of idols should be destroyed, and on this matter he had written to King Æthelberht in Letter 66 of this same indiction. But he changed his view and more suitably judged that the temples should be purified and changed from the worship of demons into the service of the true God.]

Holy water should be made and sprinkled in those same temples; altars should be constructed and relics placed there. For if those temples have been well constructed, it is necessary that they be changed from the worship of demons into the service of the true God, so that, when the people see that the temples themselves are not destroyed, they may lay aside error from their hearts and, recognizing and worshiping the true God, may gather more familiarly in the places to which they are accustomed.

And because they are accustomed to kill many cattle in sacrifice to demons, this practice too should be transformed into some solemn observance: on the day of the dedication or on the feast days of the holy martyrs whose relics are placed there, let them make themselves shelters of branches around those same churches converted from temples,

[Note: No one is unaware that religious banquets were celebrated from the very beginnings of the Christian religion. Hence, after the Lord’s Supper, those banquets were called *agapae* (ἀγάπαι), because they were symbols of Christian charity. Such banquets later became customary at the feast of a church’s dedication. Sidonius Apollinaris, Letter 15 of Book IV: “Prepare a plentiful banquet and spacious couches, by many paths and for many crowds. Thus he sat amid the fellowship of good men. For people come to you once the appointed time of the future dedication has become known to all.” The same practice also occurred at the feasts of martyrs and other festivals, as many sacred writers testify: Gregory of Nazianzus, poem 2, *On His Own Life*; Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Gregory Thaumaturgus*; Jerome, Letter 19 to Eustochium; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 12, and Book III, chapter 27; Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 6, and Book II of *The Miracles*, chapter 16. Frodoard, Book I of the *History of Rheims*, quotes these words from the testament of Saint Remigius: “I leave you, Agricola, my nephew, the vineyard on this condition: that on feast days and every Sunday an offering from it be presented at the holy altars, and that annual banquets be provided, God permitting, for the priests and deacons of Rheims.” And below: “I give to my nephew Agathemerus the vineyard that I planted at Vindonissa and established by my labor, on this condition: that from its produce, on all feast days and Sundays, an offering be presented at the holy altars in my memory, and that, God permitting, annual banquets be provided for the priests and deacons of Laon.” The following passage of Theodoret, *On the Cure of Greek Affections*, sermon 8, at the end, should also be noted. Speaking of the more illustrious pagans, he says that they were accustomed neither to be buried in notable tombs nor to be honored with public annual feasts: “For they possess neither notable tombs, nor are they honored with public annual feasts” (Οὔτε γὰρ τάφους ἔχουσιν ἐπισήμους, οὔτε δημοθοινίαις ἐτεσίοις γεραίρονται). Later, however, when people feasted too freely, such banquets were condemned by the holy Fathers: Ambrose, homily on Elijah and fasting, chapter 17; Augustine, Letter 64 to Aurelius, bishop. Such drinking parties and banquets were also restrained by public laws: the *Capitularies*, Book IV, chapter 46; the Council of Nantes, canon 10; the Council of Auxerre, canon 2. Gussanv.]

and celebrate the solemnity with religious banquets. Let them no longer sacrifice animals to the devil, but kill animals for food in praise of God and give thanks to the giver of all things for their nourishment. Thus, while some outward joys are preserved for them, they may more easily consent to inward joys.

[Note: The prudent moderation of this counsel is not tolerated by the excessive zeal of certain people who delight in crying, “Destroy everything down to the foundations; uproot even the smallest fibers,” and so forth. Through such utterly misguided conduct many have been driven into schism or heresy whom moderation would have kept within the bosom of Mother Church. Others might perhaps return to the embrace of unity if certain stubborn people did not block the way with thorns—either by defending particular corruptions, by demanding rites that are indeed praiseworthy but perhaps less necessary, or by harassing other, less praiseworthy practices with undue insistence—practices which the holiest Fathers tolerated for the sake of unity. Our approach must be that of a fisherman, not of Aristotle, as stated in the letter of the bishops of Pontus to the emperor Leo after the Council of Chalcedon. Gussanv.]

For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut away everything from hard minds at once, since one who strives to climb to a lofty place must be raised by steps or gradual advances, not by leaps. Thus the Lord made himself known to the Israelite people in Egypt; nevertheless, he retained for them in his own worship certain sacrificial practices that they had been accustomed to offer to the devil, commanding them to sacrifice animals in his worship.

[Note: This is demonstrated by Leviticus 17: “They shall no longer sacrifice their offerings to demons, with whom they have committed fornication.” Gussanv.]

In this way, by changing their hearts, they would lose one aspect of sacrifice while retaining another: although the animals were the same ones they had been accustomed to offer, when they sacrificed them to God rather than to idols, the sacrifices themselves were no longer the same.

You must therefore tell these things to the aforementioned brother, so that, being present there, he may judge how he ought to administer everything. May God keep you safe, dearest son.

[Col. 1217A]

[Note: In two Teller manuscripts, with which the Vatican edition agrees, the date reads “12 Kalends of July,” but this is erroneous. Nor is the reading “15 Kalends of July” better in Bede, from whom this closing clause of the letter was taken. For, according to Bede himself, Book I, chapter 30, at the beginning, this letter was not written until after Mellitus’s departure. Yet according to the same Bede, chapter 29, when Mellitus was departing from Rome, Gregory gave him letters for Augustine on the 10th day before the Kalends of July, that is, June 22. At that time the nine letters to the leaders and princes of Gaul mentioned above, Letters 54–62, were also given to him, and some of them bear the date “10 Kalends of July,” even in Paul the Deacon’s collection. Therefore this letter to Mellitus was written not on the 15th, but after the 10th day before the Kalends of July.]

Given on the 15th day before the Kalends of July, during the reign of our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, in the nineteenth year, after the consulship of the same lord of ours in the eighteenth year, indiction 4.

## LETTER LXXVII. TO BONIFACE, DEFENDER IN CORSICA

He is to see that bishops are elected as soon as possible for Aleria and Ajaccio. He is not to allow the poor to be oppressed or clergy to be held before lay judges.

Gregory to Boniface, defender of Corsica.

It is not without fault on your part that, although you knew that the cities of Aleria and Ajaccio in Corsica had long been without bishops, you delayed urging their clergy and people to elect a priest for themselves.

[Note: LETTER LXXVII [Elsewhere 74]. Commonly called Ajazzo, it is still an episcopal city on the western coast of the island of Corsica, under the authority of the Genoese. In ecclesiastical matters, however, it is subject to the archbishop of Pisa; formerly it was called Ursinium. Gussanv. In the Tours and Normandy manuscripts it is called *Ajacium*.]

Since they must no longer remain without their own ruler, hasten, having received this authority from us, to exhort the clergy and people of each city not to disagree among themselves, but, with one accord, let each city elect for consecration the priest whom it desires. Once the decree has been made, let the one elected come to us.

[Note: On election by the clergy and people, see above, Letter 6 of Book II, indiction 10.]

But if they refuse to agree on one person and divide their choice between two, let them likewise come to us after making the customary decrees, so that, after we have investigated their life, conduct, and character, the one who appears more suitable may be ordained.

[Note: The printed editions read: “the one who appears more useful.”]

Because it is reported that many poor people there are being oppressed and subjected to injustice, let your experience take care of this matter and not permit them to be burdened contrary to justice. Rather, strive that neither those bringing claims be obstructed contrary to reason nor those against whom claims are brought suffer unjust loss.

Furthermore, it has come to our attention that certain clerics, while you are present there, are being held by laymen.

[Note: It was formerly considered unlawful for clerics to be judged by laymen. The Theodosian Code, final law, “Concerning Bishops,” states: “We reserve to episcopal judgment even those clerics whom an ill-fated presumer had decreed should indiscriminately be brought before secular judges. For it is not right that ministers of the divine office should be subjected to the judgment of temporal powers.” The same may be seen in Avitus, bishop of Vienne, Letter 61. The practices of our own times are different. Gussanv.]

If this is so, know that it will be reckoned to your fault, because, had you been a man, this could not have happened.

[Note: Thus the older editions, together with the Normandy manuscripts and most of the Vatican manuscripts, as well as both Rheims manuscripts. More recent editions read: “it ought not to have happened.”]

Therefore, from now on you must take care not to permit this. If anyone has a case against a cleric, let him approach that cleric’s bishop. If the bishop should happen to be suspected, an executor must be appointed either by him or—if the plaintiff refuses even this—by your experience. The executor must compel the parties, by mutual agreement, to choose judges. Whatever those judges determine must be brought fully into effect, with the law preserved, through the diligence either of yourself or of the bishop, so that no grounds remain on which they can afterward weary themselves with lawsuits.

[Note: One Colbert manuscript and Vatican manuscript B state that this letter was written in August, indiction 4. In Vatican manuscript D, instead of “in August,” we find “in March.”]

## LETTER LXXVIII. TO BARBARA AND ANTONINA

He prays for divine protection for them. He rejoices that they wish to come to Rome. He commends their affairs to Bishop John and the defender Romanus. He gladly accepts their gifts.

[Note: LETTER LXXVIII [Elsewhere 75]. See above, Letters 35 and 30.]

Gregory to Barbara and Antonina.

Having received your letters and learned fully of your well-being, I rejoiced greatly. I beseech almighty God to guard you by his protection both from evil spirits in your thoughts and from wicked people and every adversity; and may he so order you, by the grace of his fear, into worthy marriages that he may gladden us all by this ordering of you.

But you, my most beloved daughters, place your hope in his help, and always, by praying and doing good, avoid the snares of wicked people beneath the shadow of his protection. For whatever human consolations or adversities there may be are nothing unless his grace protects or his displeasure troubles us. Therefore place your hope in no human being, but bind your whole mind in trust in almighty God. While we sleep, he will protect you—he of whom it is written: “Behold, he will neither slumber nor sleep, who guards Israel” (Psalm 120:4).

As for your saying that you are hastening to the threshold of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, I desire this greatly and await it with ardent longing, so that I may see you, joined by worthy merits, in his Church. Thus you may gain some consolation from me, and I may gain no small joy from your presence. I have taken care to commend your affairs to my most reverend brother John, the bishop, and to Romanus, the defender, so that, with God’s help, they may complete what they have begun.

I have gladly received your two *rakanas*, which you said were the product of your labor.

[Note: *Racha*, *bracha*, *rhacos*, and *rachion* denote a kind of garment made of hair, a cloak worn by both monks and nuns. Hence the terms *raco-dytae* and *racendytai*, meaning monks wearing such cloaks, as in Nicephorus Xanthopulus, Nicetas Choniates, and Balsamon. We also find *rasa* and *rasophoroi*. Some call them *rachinae*. Others think that *racanae* and *rachinae* mean blankets or bed coverings. See John Filesac, commentary on Vincent of Lérins’ *Commonitorium*, §9. Fortunatus mentions a *rachaena* of Germanus, bishop of Paris, in his *Life*, chapter 45, where, when a man was feverish, a deacon carefully arranged him in his bed, wrapped all around in the servant of God’s *rachaena*. Gussanv. Seek other meanings of this word in the notes to Letter 1 of this book. Consult also Rosweyde’s *Onomasticon*, under the *Lives of the Fathers*, and Du Cange’s Greek Glossary, under the word Ῥάκος.]

Nevertheless, understand that I did not think it had been sent to me. For you seek praise from another person’s labor, since perhaps you have never yet set your hands to the spindle.

Yet this does not distress me, because I desire you to love reading Holy Scripture, so that, for as long as almighty God joins you to husbands, you may know how you ought to live and how you ought to order your household.

## BOOK TWELVE

Indiction 5, in the twelfth year of his ordination.

[Col. 1219]

## LETTER I. TO DOMINICUS, BISHOP OF CARTHAGE

He congratulates him on recovering from a serious illness. He urges that the reprieves granted to us in life be used so that we may come more prepared for judgment.

[Col. 1219A]

Gregory to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage.

You demonstrate, through the interpreter of your tongue, how abundant the charity of your heart is, seasoning the words of your letters with such sweetness that everything you write is pleasant and delightful. Thus, although we cannot embrace your fraternity bodily, we embrace it in the arms of love.

For what the length of the journey denies to kindred spirits, the service of charity provides. And since, just as we are refreshed by the health of beloved brothers, so we are saddened by their illness, we give thanks to almighty God, who has consoled our sorrow by the news of your recovery.

When we heard that you had contracted a very serious illness, before we received your letter, we were held in even greater sadness. But since, when we are rescued from the danger of death, it is uncertain for what purpose we are spared, dearest brother, let us turn this period of reprieve to the benefit of the soul. Since we shall render an account to the Judge who is to come, let us fortify our case before him with tears and good works, so that we may deserve to receive confidence concerning what we have done.

For even in secular cases a kindly judge frequently grants a reprieve for this purpose: that one who was not previously prepared may afterward come prepared to judgment.

[Note: BOOK XII. Elsewhere BOOK X. LETTER I. We restore here the sense that has been corrupted in recent editions by faulty punctuation and by the addition of the adverb “therefore” after “of reprieve.”]

And what kind of conduct is it if we neglect for the salvation of the soul what we carefully preserve in earthly affairs?

[Note: The printed editions read: “in earthly judgments.”]

Therefore, since, according to the apostle John, no one is without sin (1 John 1), let us recall the allurements of our thoughts, the lack of restraint in our speech, and the deeds of our sins. While it is permitted, let us erase the stains of our iniquities by knocking insistently,

[Note: “And to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7; Luke 11). On the difference between asking, seeking, and knocking, see Saint Augustine, *Retractations*, Book I, chapter 19, at the end, where he corrects what he had explained laboriously but less accurately in Book II of *The Sermon on the Mount*. Gussanv. In the Normandy manuscript it reads: “with great lamentation.”]

so that our just and merciful Redeemer may not exact vengeance from us according to our merits, but may be moved to pardon according to his mercy.

And since it is not enough for our office merely to weep over our own sins unless it also takes care concerning those of others, let us devote ourselves more diligently to the care of the flock entrusted to us. By persuading, exhorting, warning, and preaching, insofar as heavenly mercy grants us strength, let us hasten to fulfill our office in deed, so that, by the generosity of our Creator, we may await the reward we desire.

But since we cannot do anything good without divine help, let us, dearest brother, implore almighty God with joined prayers to guide us by his grace, together with the flock entrusted to us, along the way of his commandments, and to grant us to understand and do what pleases him—the one who, by the gift of his mercy, wished us to bear the name of shepherds.

Furthermore, through the transmission by your holiness of the blessing of the blessed martyr Agileus,

[Note: Or *Agileius*, as it is read in nearly all our manuscripts. For this martyr, who suffered at Carthage, consult the Roman Martyrology under October 15.]

we received it with the same charity with which it was sent to us by you.

[Note: We found these words in no manuscripts, except that at the beginning of Book XII, as is customary, “in September” is prefixed—for the indiction began in that month—and then follows “Gregory to Dominicus,” and so forth.]

In the month of September, indiction 5.

## LETTER II. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He orders twelve solidi to be given to Matthew, a man of illustrious rank, for his support.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon.

Whenever something is granted to those in distress after due consideration, for the sake of their support, it both pleases God and undoubtedly enriches the one who gives it. Therefore, by this authority, we command your Experience to ensure that you do not delay giving twelve solidi to Matthew, a man of illustrious rank and a legal scholar. Know that these are certainly to be charged to your accounts.

Therefore hasten to fulfill our order with thanksgiving, so that no delay may weary the recipient.

## LETTER III. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

Concerning a certain boy brought from Sicily to Misenum, where he had assumed the monastic habit.

Gregory to Anthemus, subdeacon of Campania.

Gallus, the bearer of this letter, a shipmaster, is known to have informed us, through a petition submitted to us, that he had brought a certain boy from the regions of Sicily to Campania for the sake of prayer.

[Note: LETTER III. In Pratel and certain manuscripts, *Messinati*; the printed editions read *Messenati*. But *Misenati* must be read, as is clear both because the boy was brought to Campania and there remained in a monastery, and because Anthemus, governor of Campania, orders the boy, while staying in the monastery, to be handed over to the shipmaster to be taken back to the region of Palermo.]

When he arrived at the port of Misenum, he remained there in a monastery for the sake of conversion. When the shipmaster carefully inquired into his status, out of concern for his own safety, the boy, as he asserts, publicly declared under the binding force of an oath that he was free and subject to no condition.

On his return, he complains that he was detained by the public officials, who demanded to know why he had presumed secretly to remove from those regions a slave belonging to the public authorities. After damages had been inflicted upon him, he also showed himself bound by a security to return the same boy, with all the strength at his disposal, to that region.

Moved therefore by concern for justice, let your Experience know that we have decided as follows: the slave himself, even though he has now assumed the monastic habit, must be returned to the region of Palermo, where the matter arose, and handed over to our defender Fantinus, so that he may prudently carry out what is to be done concerning him according to the tenor of our command, whose text can also instruct you.

We therefore wish you to receive a security from the bearer of this letter—

[Note: In both Rheims manuscripts and Vatican manuscript D: “a guarantor.”]

—who, receiving the slave himself from your hand, must clearly guarantee to you in writing there in the city of Naples that he will hand him over to our defender Fantinus without any excuse. With this precaution in place, the petitioner may be released from the bond of his security, and the matter of the slave may, with the Lord’s help, be settled as we have decreed.

## LETTER IV. TO FANTINUS, DEFENDER

He instructs Bishop Victor to bring Maurentius’s case against the Church of Palermo to an end.

Gregory to Fantinus, defender.

Our most glorious son Maurentius, master of soldiers, complains that he has a case concerning the estate of Gentina against the Church of Palermo, and he has sent the bearer of this letter with a formal mandate so that the matter may be settled without any excuse.

Therefore let your Experience, while preserving due respect, admonish our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Victor either to strive to settle the matter peacefully and without delay, or, if he should judge it more advantageous for himself to have it decided judicially, to appoint without any further delay, in his place, a properly authorized representative who must submit the matter concerning that estate to the judgment of our most glorious son, the patrician Venantius, and to your Experience,

[Note: LETTER IV. Gussanvillaeus considers this letter to have been transposed, since Venantius is known to have died during the preceding indiction. We think, however, that this Venantius should be distinguished from another ex-monk whose daughters were Barbara and Antonina. Both were certainly patricians, but this one was from Palermo and the other from Syracuse. Letter 55 of Book IX, indiction 2, should be understood as referring to the man from Palermo. Letters 40 of this book and 15 of Book XIII also survive addressed to the same man.]

so that the matter may be determined after the truth has been ascertained. Alternatively, if the parties wish, let them choose other judges while you oversee the process.

Whatever they determine with the holy Gospels set before them, we wish to be carried into effect by you, with the law preserved, so that afterward nothing may remain between the parties by which they could be wearied with renewed litigation.

[Note: Recent editions read “with recurring litigation.” The older printed editions are supported by Vatican manuscript A and the Victor manuscript. This letter is found in only a very few manuscripts.]

## LETTER V. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He commends Maurentius’s men.

[Note: We found this letter only in the Remigian manuscript, the Victor manuscript, and Vatican manuscript A.]

Gregory to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.

Since it ought to be enough for our most glorious son Maurentius with you that you know he is truly our own, we ought not to write how you should assist him. Yet, so that we may not appear to neglect your fraternity in his case when the opportunity has arisen, we commend the bearers of this letter and urge you to support them in every way, since he is known to have sent them there to receive his *precarium*.

[Note: The manuscripts mentioned read “may be supported.”]

So that you may provide this assistance more effectively—for it is undoubtedly true that you are occupied with many matters—appoint the notary Menna, since he is known to be diligent. Let him, in your name, strive to assist them in everything wherever necessary, because, as they report, they have been instructed concerning what they must do by a written set of orders.

[Note: Concerning the *precarium*, see note f to Letter 46 of Book I. Here and in the preceding letter, *precarium* appears to mean military pay, which Maurentius, master of soldiers, was requesting for himself and his men from the prefects or quaestors of the treasury stationed at Ravenna. Gregory calls them *saccellarii* in Book V, Letter 21, to the empress Constantina: “As in the regions of Ravenna the piety of our lords has a *saccellarius* for the first army of Italy,” and so forth. Saint Gregory asks that Marinianus and Theodorus—this city’s curator, as appears from Book IX, Letter 98, and the other its bishop—favor Maurentius so that he may obtain this pay as quickly as possible.]

Since I have now informed your holiness of his case through his own report, devote yourselves to his affairs in such a way that, just as we are confident in your fraternity and he has complete trust, his interests may, with God’s help, be successfully advanced through your support.

## LETTER VI. TO THEODORUS, CURATOR

He commends Maurentius’s men.

[Col. 1222C]

Gregory to Theodorus, curator.

Since we place as much confidence in your glory as in a truly beloved son, and are entirely assured of you, we commend to you those who belong to us. For this reason, greeting you with paternal affection, we ask that you deign to extend your protection to the bearers of this letter, whom our most glorious Maurentius, master of soldiers, has sent to receive his *precarium*.

[Note: LETTER VI. Concerning the *precarium*, see the note to Letter 46 of Book I. Here and in the preceding letter, *precarium* appears to mean military pay, which Maurentius, master of soldiers, was requesting for himself and his men from the prefects or quaestors of the treasury stationed at Ravenna. Gregory calls them *saccellarii* in Book V, Letter 21, to the empress Constantina: “As in the regions of Ravenna the piety of our lords has a *saccellarius* for the first army of Italy,” and so forth. Saint Gregory asks that Marinianus and Theodorus—this city’s curator, as appears from Book IX, Letter 98, and the other its bishop—favor Maurentius so that he may obtain this pay as quickly as possible.]

Thus, with your patronage, they may not be forced to endure there either unreasonable delay or hardship, but may receive without difficulty, through the assistance of your glory, whatever is due to the aforementioned most glorious man. In this way he may become even more devoted to our service, and we may be able to give thanks for him as is fitting.

## LETTER VII. TO SAVINELLA, COLUMBA, AND AGNELLA

Writing the same thing to each of them, he urges them to acquire heavenly treasures through more generous almsgiving.

[Col. 1223A]

[Note: LETTER VII. The heading of this letter varies in the Colbert manuscripts. In one it is the same as that of the many old manuscripts, which we have followed. In another it reads only, “To Savinella concerning almsgiving.” In others: “To Savinella, Columba, and Galla.” In the Tours manuscript, instead of “and Galla,” I read “and Galla, their mother,” as though Savinella and Columba were daughters and Galla their mother.]

Gregory to Savinella, Columba, and Agnella, of equal rank.

The good things I have heard about your work greatly gladden me, glorious daughter: you are said to do those things by which, while mercifully helping the needy, you obtain mercy for yourself, and, nourishing others temporally, satisfy them with eternal goods.

Therefore, because the one in whom you trust is faithful, confidently entrust what you give, so that on the day of tribulation you may receive what you expend.

[Note: More recent printed editions read “confidently commend” and shortly afterward “of reward,” instead of “of tribulation.”]

For the outstanding preacher says: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit for that day” (2 Timothy 1:12).

Behold, glorious daughter, consider how great is the certainty of good works. Let your hand always be generous in action, so that what is written may be fulfilled for you: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will intercede for you” (Ecclesiasticus 29:15).

Whoever desires to have abundant fruit in heaven must not fail to sow while there is time, so that on the day of harvest he may gather his sheaves with joy. For “those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm 125:5).

But what kind of harvest will come from such seed, let the Apostle say: “He who sows in his flesh will reap corruption from the flesh, but he who sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (Galatians 6:8).

So that poverty may not find us destitute, let us prepare this harvest for ourselves through manifold sowing. The more abundantly we desire to be satisfied, the more generously let us give to the one from whom we have received everything.

For the Lord himself says: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matthew 25:35), and so forth. At the conclusion it is added: “Amen, I say to you, insofar as you did it for one of these, the least of my brothers, you did it for me.”

Therefore practice these things with the greatest diligence, and, while doing them, seek no repayment for yourselves on earth, since temporal things are nothing to those who desire heavenly things. Fix your desires there, where whatever is repaid never comes to an end.

Therefore, while doing good, do not grow weary, so that you may store up treasures for yourselves there, where neither rust nor moth destroys and where thieves neither break in nor steal (Matthew 6).

[Col. 1223D]

Furthermore, greeting your glory with paternal affection, we inform you through the bearer of this letter, Hilary, our *chartularius*, that we have sent a key from the most sacred body of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. The key also contains a blessing from his chains. When it is hung around your neck, may it, through his intercession, become for you a grace of absolution corresponding to what those chains were for him—the cause of martyrdom.

May almighty God guard you in his fear and so kindle your heart always toward good works that he may grant you his grace here and afterward lead you to eternal joys.

## LETTER VIII. TO COLUMBUS, BISHOP OF NUMIDIA
