He is to investigate carefully the serious complaint of Donadeus against his bishop Victor, so that the guilty party may receive an appropriate punishment.

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

The seriousness and, merely by hearing it, the intolerable nature of the complaint of Donadeus, the bearer of this letter, who asserts that he was a deacon, will be made clear by the petition submitted by him, which is enclosed below for your Fraternity. But because word has reached us that he was deposed on account of a carnal sin, let Your Dilection investigate the matter with careful scrutiny; [Col. 1224B] and, if this is so, let him be confined to penance, so that by his tears he may be able to loose the bond of the crime he committed. But if he is shown to be innocent of such an act, then, together with the primate of the council or with our other brethren and fellow bishops, you must diligently examine everything contained in his petition. And if his complaint is supported by the truth, then, against his bishop Victor—who did not fear committing so great a crime against God and the priestly vocation—let this strictness of canonical force be maintained, so that from your judgment he may understand how unjust was what he did, and that he may here be restored to his order. For it is sufficiently perverse and is shown to be contrary to ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 1224D] EPISTLE VIII.—In the more recent editions, corruptly: “it is shown to be a censure against the Church.”] that, merely to satisfy someone’s wishes, a person should be deprived of the rank of the office he holds when neither his own fault nor any crime has cast him down from it [Col. 1224C] (Gratian, Distinction 55, chapter 7).

[Note: [Col. 1224D] In the same more recent editions there is added: “Given in the month of October, indiction 5.” All our manuscripts are wholly silent concerning this or any other chronological note.]

## EPISTLE IX. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is to remit one of the two annual solidi to the elderly Adeodatus, if he is truly poor.

Gregory to Anthem(i)us, subdeacon.

Adeodatus, the bearer of this letter, has informed us that many years ago he constructed a building on land belonging solely to our Church, on the condition that he would pay two solidi each year to the ecclesiastical treasury; and that after his death the land itself, together with the building erected upon it, would without any doubt remain the property of the Church. But because he asserts that he has fallen into such poverty that he cannot pay those same two solidi each year, as he had promised, and for this reason has asked that one be remitted to him, let Your Experience take care to ascertain the facts. And if he is manifestly as poor as he claims, we wish half of our charge to be remitted, so that each year he pays no more than one solidus, since both his advanced age and his poverty indicate that the burden he requests ought to be relaxed for him [Note: [Col. 1225C] EPISTLE IX [Alternative numbering 10].—Remigius: “with half of our due remitted.” Victor: “we wish to remit half of our presumed claim.”]. Let it therefore be your concern to ensure that, after his death, you preserve the ownership of the land and of the building erected upon it through the Church’s attentive and vigilant care [Col. 1225A] [Note: [Col. 1225C] In Vatican A: “let everything be preserved through the Church’s vigilant concern.” In Victor: “let everything be conserved with the Church’s utmost vigilance.” We have found this letter in only these three manuscripts. Nor do the two following letters occur in many copies.].

## EPISTLE X. TO FANTINUS, DEFENSOR

He is to press Isidore’s heirs to construct a hospice, or, if one has already been built, to assign the bequest to it.

Gregory to Fantinus, defensor.

Whatever the intention of pious goodwill commands to be done ought, so that it may reach completion, to be the concern of a priest. Therefore we instruct Your Experience that you must persistently and forcefully press the heirs of Isidore, a man of illustrious memory, so that they hasten, without any difficulty, to carry out what has been arranged concerning the hospice which their testator ordered to be built in the city of Palermo according to his last will [Note: [Col. 1225C] EPISTLE X [Alternative numbering 11].—“From him to whom the right over them passed, by whose property or inheritance they were enriched.” Gussanvilleus.]. Otherwise, if they continue to think that this matter may be neglected, they will incur both our anger and the anger of God, which proceeds from the laws and which they deserve for delaying the fulfillment of such an arrangement.

But if the amount assigned for the hospice that ought to be built there seems perhaps unable to suffice, let the site where that hospice was to have been established, or whatever was left there, be transferred to the hospice of Saint Theodore, which was once founded in the aforesaid city by Peter. Thus the heirs may be relieved of the concern and labor of establishing a hospice, and the deceased’s will may beneficially be fulfilled, since whatever the testator assigned to that purpose will nevertheless be expended for the same cause, even if in another place. Let Your Experience therefore take care that one of these two alternatives be carried out without any delay [Col. 1225C].

## EPISTLE XI. TO PASSIVUS, BISHOP OF FIRMIUM

He orders an oratory to be consecrated, after a proper donation has first been received, and a cardinal priest to be appointed there.

Gregory to Passivus, bishop of Firmium.

Anio, count of the fortress of Aprutium, in the territory of Firmium, has informed us by a petition, which is set out below, that he founded at his own expense, out of devotion, an oratory in the aforesaid fortress, which he desires to be consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Therefore, dearest brother, if the construction in question legitimately belongs to your diocese—in which you exercise the office of visitation—and if it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after the proper donation has first been received, namely: small plots of land with one tenant-farm, one pair of broken-in oxen, two cows, four pounds of silver, one furnished bed, fifteen head of livestock [Note: [Col. 1226C] In the Gallican copy: “fifteen head of white cattle.” Gussanvilleus.], two pieces of bronze, five iron tools [Note: [Col. 1226C] Thus we read in the manuscripts, except that Vatican A has aeramenta, “bronze objects,” instead of aeramenti, “bronze.” After the bronze objects, iron tools are mentioned, in the appropriate order.], six solidi in ready money, with the free men exempt from fiscal taxes and bound by municipal records [Note: [Col. 1226C] Above, Book II, indiction 10, letter 12. Gussanvilleus.], you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory [Col. 1226B].

We also wish you to appoint there a cardinal priest, so that whenever the aforesaid founder should perhaps wish Masses to be celebrated for him, or the gathering of the faithful should require it, there may be nothing to impede the performance of the solemn rites of Mass. The sacred vessels, once received, you shall place there with due reverence.

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Gussanvilleus recommended deleting the words “if the construction in question legitimately belongs to your diocese,” since they seemed to conflict with the words “in which you exercise the office of visitation.” I believe, however, that the words have been added to explain the sense in which Aprutium was Passivus’s diocese. It belonged to him, not because he was its cardinal bishop, but because he was its visitor and bishop, as it were, in commendam.]

[Note: [Col. 1225D] Elsewhere fundicampi. On conduma, see above, Book XI, letter 20. Gussanvilleus.]

[Note: [Col. 1226C] EPISTLE XI [Alternative numbering 12].—Passivus was the cardinal bishop of the Church of Firmium and had long been the visitor of Aprutium, which had been deprived of a shepherd, as the following letter indicates. The diocese of Aprutium therefore belonged to this bishop—not as to its proper priest, but as to a substitute to whom the care and oversight of that Church had been entrusted. This letter and the following one leave no room for doubt that this Church had been entrusted to Passivus; consequently, nothing here is superfluous, as Gussanvilleus suggests.]

## EPISTLE XII. TO PASSIVUS, BISHOP OF FIRMIUM

He urges Opportunus to advance in good pursuits; then to become a monk or subdeacon, and finally shepherd of Aprutium.

Gregory to Passivus, bishop of Firmium.

[Note: [Col. 1226C] EPISTLE XII [Alternative numbering 13].—“Of Firmium” is absent from three Colbert manuscripts, four Vatican manuscripts, and all the Normandy and Corbie manuscripts; in the latter Passibo is also read for Passivo.]

Your Fraternity knows well (Gratian, Distinction 61, chapter 18) how long Aprutium has been deprived of pastoral care [Note: [Col. 1226D] Or Abrutium, as in the Tours and Vatican A manuscripts. For what Aprutium is, see Book X, indiction 3, letter 68, and note d to Book III, chapter 11, of the Life of Saint Gregory (Patrologia Latina, vol. 75, col. 137, note a).]. We searched for a long time for someone who ought to be ordained there, but we were entirely unable to find one. Yet because Opportunus is greatly praised to me for his character, his devotion to psalmody, and his love of prayer, and is said to lead a thoroughly religious life, we wish Your Fraternity to summon him to you and admonish him concerning his soul, so that he may advance in good pursuits [Col. 1226C].

And if no crimes that, according to the rule of sacred law, are punishable by death stand in his way, he should then be urged either to become a monk or to become your subdeacon [Col. 1227A]. After a little time, if it pleases God, he should himself be promoted to pastoral care. But if serious offenses stand in his way, he should be admonished all the more to leave the world and lament these matters more perfectly. I ask that you pray for me, because, while I am worn down by the tribulations of my heart, I am also afflicted by severe bodily pains [Col. 1227D].

[Note: [Col. 1226D] Many manuscripts read Importunus. We think he is the same person to whom Saint Gregory wrote in Book X, letter 68. What is said here about devotion to psalmody—necessary even for bishops—is illustrated by the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2: “Henceforth no one of whatever ecclesiastical dignity shall receive a rank who does not perfectly know the whole Psalter or the complete set of the customary canticles and hymns.”]

[Note: [Col. 1226D] Gussanvilleus notes that neither all things nor only those things punished by death under the Old Law exclude a man from promotion; for example, theft and fornication were not punished by death, yet they did exclude a man from ordination.]

[Note: [Col. 1227D] See the notes on Book V, indiction 13, letter 1.]

[Note: [Col. 1227D] In two Colbert manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts, this letter is prefaced by: “In the month of October, indiction 5.”]

## EPISTLE XIII. TO FANTINUS, DEFENSOR

He is to secure the property of the deceased notary Primogenitus without delay, lest it be lost to the Roman Church or to the other heirs.

Gregory to Fantinus, defensor.

Let Your Experience know that our notary Primogenitus has passed from this sinful light. And because he is known to have left as heirs the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and his wife, who afterward placed herself under ecclesiastical protection, and to have appointed the son of his brother heir to one twelfth share [Note: [Col. 1227D] He had appointed his brother’s son heir to one uncia, leaving eleven other unciae to the Roman Church and to his wife. On an heir to an uncia, see the Digest, Book XXX, title 1, law 34, paragraph “Hence it is said,” and the Institutes, Book II, title 14, paragraph 6. Gussanvilleus.], as soon as you have received this instruction, before anyone learns of his death and commits fraud against his estate, you shall immediately take care to go to the place where his property is stored. With every concern and diligence, and in the presence of the boy Consent(i)us, who is said to be guardian of the property, and with witnesses summoned, let it be your diligent endeavor to inventory everything formally and carefully, and place it in the safest location you can foresee, so that at the proper time it may, with God’s help, be sent here with the same boy.

But whatever else you learn to belong to his estate, whether movable things or livestock [Col. 1227C], hasten to gather and secure it all with complete energy, so that no part of his property may be lost for any reason. Carry out all these matters with such careful and exact attention that, while you are there, no loss may occur among the property and no opportunity for any fraud or investigation may be left open under any pretext [Note: [Col. 1228D] The printed editions read corruptly: “without investigation.”]. Also hasten to inform us by your letters what the total amount of his revenues is.

[Note: [Col. 1227D] EPISTLE XIII [Alternative numbering 15].—Vatican A reads Primigentium.]

[Note: [Col. 1227D] The earlier reading was “whether corporeal things”; Gussanvilleus rightly disliked this reading. Our reading is supplied by Victor and Remigius, or the other Rheims manuscript; apart from Vatican A, this letter occurs only in those copies. By “bodies” are meant not only herds and flocks but also slaves.]

## EPISTLE XIV. TO AZIMARCHUS, SCRIBO

He urges the man rescued from danger at sea never to forget divine mercy.

Gregory to Azimarchus, scribo.

As much as news of your shipwreck grieved us, so much did the subsequent letter relieve us, when we learned that Your Greatness had reached Sicily safely [Col. 1228A]. We give thanks to our Creator, who protected you with his customary compassion and rescued you from the danger of the sea. Therefore you must always keep before your eyes the mercy of God, which you see has often been bestowed upon you, so that his grace may increase in you and may rescue you from inward dangers just as it has rescued you from outward ones. Greeting you, therefore, with paternal affection, we ask that, whenever occasion presents itself, you may relieve us by informing us of your safety.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] EPISTLE XIV, alternative numbering 17.]

## EPISTLE XV. TO ROMANUS, DEFENSOR

He is to assist Laurentius in settling the accounts of Bonifatius, the financial officer.

Gregory to Romanus, defensor.

Your Experience is not unaware that our interests are involved to some extent in the accounts of Bonifatius, our financial officer, because he left a portion of his estate to the hospice established at blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and entrusted his wife to us [Col. 1228B] [Note: [Col. 1228D] EPISTLE XV [Alternative numbering 16].—A numerarius, or tabularius, is one who calculates accounts and keeps the books of receipts and expenditures. Jurists discuss these officials extensively. Sidonius Apollinaris also mentions them, Book I, letter 11, and Book II, letter 1. Gussanvilleus. We have restored this reading, which was previously extremely corrupt in the common editions, with the help of Vatican A, which alone, together with Remigius and Victor, contains this letter. In the Victor manuscript and in the more recent printed editions one reads: “It has come to our attention that, in the accounts of our financial officer Bonifatius, you have some interest in his property.” The reading of the older editors is still more corrupt.].

And since Laurentius, a man of illustrious rank and the bearer of this letter, has been sent to prepare those accounts—that is, those of the ninth and tenth indictions—we instruct you by this letter to hasten to provide him with whatever assistance may be necessary in this matter and to help him while preserving equity. Thus, while you are attentive, the accounts may be satisfactorily concluded, the poor may benefit, and the widow who has been entrusted to us may be provided with peace and security.

But because you know how legal cases, and especially cases of this kind, are conducted, if you should perhaps see that the accounts cannot be settled without loss, you must go with our reverend brother and fellow bishop John to the most glorious Leontius, consult with him, and promise him, as far as you are able to explain the matter, whatever must be given either to him or to various advocates, provided that it does not proceed in parts, but is brought more swiftly to an end.

Above all, however, you must consider whether you ought to speak with that most glorious man before the accounts are begun, or at least for this reason: lest, if the case is submitted for examination, it should afterward create difficulty for us when it has to be decided. But since you will be better able at the present moment to judge what ought to be done, act according to what seems more useful.

Nevertheless, in making this promise you must be careful that, for the complete settlement of the case, no greater sum of solidi be promised in any way [Col. 1228D–1229A]. You should indicate to him, if the case requires it, that the deceased was altogether poor. To establish this, we have arranged to send you a copy of the inventory of the property found among his assets. But if he should refuse to agree to the amount of solidi mentioned above, we would rather return what reached the hospice than endure pointless hostility. If he agrees, you must act diligently so that a release may be obtained from him, so that, after the release has been given and the case settled, no subsequent dispute may in any way be raised concerning it. Whatever you give, know that it must be charged to your accounts [Note: [Col. 1229D] Thus the manuscripts of Remigius, Victor, and Vatican A; the common editions read: “we charge to your accounts.”].

## EPISTLE XVI. TO AZIMARCHUS, SCRIBO

He is to favor Laurentius, who is presenting to Leontius the accounts of Bonifatius, formerly a financial officer.

Gregory to Azimarchus, scribo.

We recall that, when he was here in the city of Rome, Your Greatness knew Bonifatius, formerly a financial officer, who, after making a will, left a portion of his inheritance to the hospice situated at Saint Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 1229B]. And since we said that we would take care that someone be sent to our glorious son Leontius to present his accounts, we have attended to having this carried out.

Therefore, because Laurentius, a man of illustrious rank and the bearer of this letter, is known to have been sent for this purpose, we greet Your Greatness with paternal affection and ask that you assist him in this matter and, as we trust you will, offer him your protection while preserving justice. Thus, supported by the aid of your most sincere goodness, you may gain a reward from almighty God concerning both the widow of the late Bonifatius and the poor to whom, as we have said, Bonifatius left a portion of his inheritance [Col. 1229C].

## EPISTLE XVII. TO MAURILIO, FORMER PREFECT

He amicably urges him to write more often.

Gregory to Maurilio, former prefect.

We are greatly surprised that Your Glory has postponed relieving us with news of your safety, although various people have come from Sicily. We do not know whether this should be attributed to forgetfulness of affection or to occupation [Col. 1229D]. Therefore, greeting you with the affection of paternal charity, we ask that, whenever an opportunity for writing presents itself, you refresh us with news of your health and of how matters are going with you. Thus, when we have been made joyful, according to our desire, by your prosperity, we may be able to give thanks to our Redeemer for you. May almighty God protect you by the grace of his mercy and preserve and guard you unharmed from every adversity.

[Note: [Col. 1229D] EPISTLE XVII, alternative numbering 19.]

## EPISTLE XVIII. TO EUPATOR, DUKE OF SARDINIA

He commends Valdarichus.

Gregory to Eupator, duke of Sardinia.

Because Valdarichus, the bearer of this letter, asks us to write to you in commendation of him, concerning a matter which we do not doubt Your Greatness would accomplish, out of regard for justice, even without anyone’s intercession, we have judged that his petition should not be disregarded. Since, therefore, he asks to be assisted by your protection so that he may return, as he desires, with his wife, whom he says is from the city of Rome [Col. 1230B], we greet Your Greatness with paternal affection and ask that he may enjoy your protection in this matter. Do not permit anyone there to impede them contrary to the order of justice, but be willing to support and assist their wishes for your own reward. Thus they may rejoice that they have been helped by your aid, and Your Greatness may be seen to have bestowed what is just and compassionate upon those who ask.

[Note: [Col. 1229D] EPISTLE XVIII [Alternative numbering 21].—In Remigius, Waldrichilla; in Vatican A, Baldarith; in Saint-Victor, Wandaricilla. No other manuscript contains this letter.]

## EPISTLE XIX. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He requests twenty-four wicker chairs.

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

Let Your Glory know that we instructed Anthem(i)us, the subdeacon, to take care to send us a number of wicker chairs [Col. 1230C]. If he cannot find any already made, let him bring the craftsman to himself, so that the man may work in his house and make at least twenty-four completely sound chairs. Since we are in great need of them, let Your Glory provide that this be done. And if you have perhaps already procured some chairs, send them to us. Also let Your Excellence arrange for the most illustrious Julian, the major domus [Note: [Col. 1230D] That is, the senior official of his household.], or anyone else who possesses any, to send them to us. Let Your Glory therefore act so that everything we have written may by every means be secured through your energetic attention.

[Note: [Col. 1229D] EPISTLE XIX [Alternative numbering 23].—Remigius and Victor read: “we have written.” Apart from these manuscripts and Vatican A, none of our copies contains this letter.]

## EPISTLE XX. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

He is to send his letter to Arogus concerning assistance for Subdeacon Savinus in hauling beams to the sea.

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

Because beams are needed for the churches of blessed Peter and Paul, we have instructed the subdeacon Savinus to cut a number of them in the regions of Bruttium and haul them to a place from which they can be transported here by sea [Col. 1230D–1231A]. But because he cannot undertake this alone, we have written to Arogus that he assign to Sabinus’s assistance the men under his authority, together with their oxen, promising that, when the work has been completed, we will send him a worthy gift. Therefore let Your Glory hasten to send our letter to him through a person from the city, conveying to him what we have written, so that the aforesaid subdeacon may learn of his willingness. But if he has departed after finding favorable sailing conditions, let Your Glory inform him of everything by your letters, so that he may know what he ought to do; and inform us likewise of what has been done.

[Note: [Col. 1230D] EPISTLE XX [Alternative numbering 24].—Baronius, volume VIII of the Annals, under the year 602, maintains that the reading should be Brutiorum, although almost all manuscript and printed copies object, unless perhaps the two manuscripts of Vossius and Rheims are excepted, which read Britiorum. Baronius’s reading nevertheless seems sounder, and conjecture supports it. For what common concern could the regional subdeacon Sabinus, the Italian master of the soldiers Maurentius, and Arogus, duke of Beneventum, mentioned in the following letter, have had with the Britons? The Bruttii were formerly a people of Italy opposite Sicily, between Lucania and the Sicilian Strait; the region is now called lower Calabria and belongs to the kingdom of Naples. Gussanvilleus. We have preferred the reading restored by Baronius, which Gussanvilleus wrongly claims is contradicted by the manuscript copies. He should have warned readers that this letter occurs in very few manuscripts. In fact, among all the copies we have examined, it occurs nowhere except in the Saint-Victor manuscript, which has Britannorum; in Vatican A and the Remigius manuscript it reads Britiorum, that is, Brutiorum. Anastasius the Librarian writes, in his account of Gregory II, that this pontiff restored the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul—others read Peter—using beams brought from Calabria; this proves that Calabria, that is, Bruttium, had a great abundance of building timber. The Sabinus whom Saint Gregory mentions here seems to be the same subdeacon to whom the holy pontiff, in Book X, letter 4, after delegating jurisdiction, ordered an investigation into certain crimes of which Sisinnius, a priest of the city of Regium, was accused. Regium was in Bruttium, according to Cassiodorus, Book XII of the Variae, letter 14.]

## EPISTLE XXI. TO AROGUS, DUKE

He orders him to assist Savinus, who is hauling beams cut for the churches of Saints Peter and Paul to the sea; he promises a gift.

Gregory to Arogus, duke.

Because we place such confidence in Your Glory—as we truly do in a son of ours—we are emboldened to ask you for something, judging that you will not allow us to be distressed, especially in a matter by which your soul may be greatly assisted. We inform you that a number of beams are needed for the churches of blessed Peter and Paul. Therefore we have instructed our subdeacon Savinus to cut a number of them in the regions of Bruttium and haul them to a suitable place by the sea [Col. 1231B–C].

Because he needs assistance in this work, we greet Your Glory with paternal charity and ask that you assign to your officials stationed in that place the task of sending to his assistance the men under their authority, together with their oxen. With your support, he will thus be better able to complete what we have instructed him to do. For we promise that, when the work has been completed, we will send you a suitable gift, one that will not be insulting. We know how to show consideration and to respond to our sons who display good will. Therefore we ask you again, most glorious son, to act in such a way that we may become your debtors for the benefit you have bestowed and that you may receive a reward for the churches of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 1232D] EPISTLE XXI [Alternative numbering 25].—To the duke of Beneventum; see note m on Book XI, letter 46, indiction 10. Observe here Gussanvilleus’s very serious error. In the notes to the cited letter he establishes two dukes of Beneventum at the same time, namely Ariulfus, as is clear from note i, and Arogus, from note s; but Ariulfus was duke of Spoleto, according to Paul the Deacon, Book IV of the History of the Lombards, chapter 17.]

## EPISTLE XXII. TO GREGORY, FORMER PREFECT

He is to lend Savinus twenty of his men and their oxen for hauling the beams.

Gregory to Gregory, former prefect.

Knowing how great is the affection for the churches of blessed Peter and Paul that remains in Your Glory’s mind [Col. 1231D], we necessarily seek to obtain your assistance, after God, through our letters, trusting that you will readily and devoutly provide whatever you know to be useful for them, since we do not doubt that Your Glory would willingly offer it even without our request [Col. 1232A].

Because beams are entirely necessary for the aforesaid churches, and because we have instructed the subdeacon Savinus to hasten to cut as many as twenty and haul them to the sea, we greet you with paternal affection and ask that Your Glory arrange for men with their oxen to provide assistance in this matter from the estates you hold there on emphyteusis. Thus, supported by your help, he may be able to carry out what has been assigned to him, and you may acquire a reward [Col. 1232A–B].

Act, therefore, as we have said and as we trust you will, glorious son, so that we may return thanks to you and that you may have the blessed princes of the apostles as helpers in all things, because of the love and devotion you show toward their churches.

[Note: [Col. 1232D] EPISTLE XXII [Alternative numbering 26].—Vatican A: “how great is the affection toward the churches of the blessed.” Remigius and Victor read “we are emboldened.” We have used only these three copies, since the letter is absent from the others. The same should be understood of the preceding Letter XXI and the following Letter XXIII.]

## EPISTLE XXIII. TO STEPHANUS, BISHOP

He is to send men with oxen to assist Savinus.

Gregory to Stephanus, bishop.

Although the very nature of Your Fraternity’s office reminds you spontaneously to assist the needs of the churches, it is nevertheless not out of place for our letter, in abundance of goodwill, to urge you to do what you ought to do willingly. Therefore we have thought it necessary to inform Your Fraternity that beams are greatly needed for the churches of blessed Peter and Paul [Col. 1232C].

Since we have instructed the subdeacon Savinus to cut a number of them and haul them to the sea, from which they can be brought here, and since it is clear that he needs assistance in this work, let Your Holiness endeavor to help him, as is fitting, with complete zeal and attention, and send oxen and men to his aid, so that he may find no excuse but may be able, with your assistance, to fulfill what we have commanded him.

Let Your Fraternity therefore act so as to devote to him whatever assistance lies within your power. For to the extent that the aforesaid subdeacon’s failure would be culpable if he became negligent while you were helping him, so much more culpable and serious would it be if Your Fraternity attempted, on any pretext, either to excuse itself or—something we do not believe—to show itself unwilling to help. You should know that this responsibility rests heavily upon Your Fraternity, whose Church you once customarily supplied with beams at your own expense.

## EPISTLE XXIV. TO JOHN, SUBDEACON OF RAVENNA

He orders that, after Constantius has been rejected, Maurus be ordained abbot if found worthy; that the monastery be cleansed of the plague of private property; and that the writings of Abbot Claudius, taken down from Gregory’s own speech but in many respects foreign to his meaning, be sent to him.

Gregory to John, subdeacon of Ravenna.

The monks of the monastery formerly ruled by Abbot Claudius came and asked that the monk Constantius be appointed abbot. I vehemently rejected their petition, because they appeared to me to be entirely worldly-minded, having sought to have as abbot a man who was excessively worldly [Col. 1233A–B]. For I learned that Constantius was devoted to private property. This fact especially proves that he does not possess a monk’s heart. I also learned that he had dared to travel alone, without any of his brothers, to the monastery situated in the province of Picenum [Note: [Col. 1233D] Picenum, commonly called the March of Ancona, a province of Italy belonging to the papal territory.]. From this action of his we learned that a man who walks without a witness does not live rightly, or how can he keep a rule for others when he does not know how to keep it for himself?

Therefore, withdrawing from this request, they asked for a certain cellarer named Maurus, whose life and ability are attested by many things; even Abbot Claudius once praised him to certain people. Let Your Experience therefore investigate carefully; and, if his life is worthy of the office of governance, have him ordained abbot by our reverend brother and fellow bishop Marinianus [Col. 1233C]. But if there is something that altogether disqualifies him and they are unable to find anyone suitable within their own congregation, let them choose someone elsewhere, and let the person they choose become abbot.

Be particularly diligent to tell our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop to restrain with the utmost care the practice of private property among four or five monks of the monastery in whom it has so far been impossible to correct it, and to hasten to cleanse this monastery of such a plague. For if private property is maintained there by the monks, neither harmony nor charity will be able to remain in that congregation. What, then, is the monastic habit except contempt for the world? How, therefore, do those who seek gold while placed in a monastery despise the world?

Let Your Experience act in such a way that neither the appointment of the abbot is delayed nor any further complaint about this matter reaches us [Col. 1234A].

[Note: [Col. 1233C] Gregory frequently indicates how greatly he detested private property among monks. How fiercely this most holy man, while he was abbot, attacked a monk laboring under this most wicked vice is shown by John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 15.]

[Note: [Col. 1233D–1234C] Jerome, Letter 22, to Eustochium, on the guardianship of virginity, tells of a monk who, being more thrifty than avaricious, left at his death one hundred solidi that he had acquired by weaving linen: “A council was held among the monks as to what ought to be done. Some said they should be distributed to the poor; others, that they should be given to the church; some proposed sending them back to his parents. But Macarius, Pambo, Isidore, and the others whom they call the Fathers, with the Holy Spirit speaking through them, decided that the money ought to be buried with him, saying: ‘Let your money be with you for destruction.’ Let no one think that this was done cruelly. Such terror seized everyone throughout Egypt that leaving behind one solidus was considered a crime.” John the Deacon reports that Gregory did the same, with a similar result, in Book I, chapter 15 and following.]

Moreover, because my most dear former son Claudius had heard me speak about certain matters from Proverbs, the Song of Songs, the Prophets, the books of Kings, and also the Heptateuch, which through weakness I was unable to commit to writing [Note: [Col. 1234D] The manuscripts of Normandy, Tours, and Reggio, and others, read Heptateuch; it is also found in the older printed editions.], he himself dictated them according to his own understanding, so that they would not perish through forgetfulness and so that he could bring them to me at a suitable time for them to be dictated more accurately [Note: [Col. 1234D] Recent editions read: “he himself rendered them according to his own understanding and style.” We follow Reggio, Colbert, Normandy, both Rheims manuscripts, Vatican, Corbie, Colbert, and others.]. When he had read them to me, I found that the meaning of what I had said had been altered in a highly unsatisfactory way.

Therefore let Your Experience, without any excuse or delay, go to his monastery, summon the brothers, and have them bring forward, in complete truth, however many sheets they have taken down from various Scriptures. Receive them and send them to me with the greatest speed [Col. 1234B].

As for your return, since we have learned that you have suffered considerable trouble, we are thinking, God willing, about it on a subsequent occasion.

[Note: [Col. 1234C] We have illuminated this passage, from which it is clear that Saint Gregory interpreted those sacred books in his homilies, in the prefaces or preliminary notices to the commentaries on the Books of Kings, the Song of Songs, and others.]

The fact that has been reported to me by certain persons—that the most reverend brother and my fellow bishop Marinian has public readings of the commentaries on blessed Job held at the vigils [Note: [Col. 1234D] That is, the books of the *Moralia on Job* contained in volume I of Gregory’s works.]—I did not receive favorably, 1196 because this work is not popular and produces more impediment than advancement for inexperienced hearers. But tell him to have the commentaries on the Psalms read at the vigils, which especially form the minds of secular people toward good morals. [Note: [Col. 1234D] These should by no means be understood as the commentaries on the penitential psalms elaborated by Gregory, as is commonly believed, since he later indicates that he was displeased that his writings became known to people while he was alive. He therefore refers either to commentaries published by Augustine or Ambrose, and so forth.] For while I am still in this flesh, I do not wish people easily to learn anything that I may happen to have said. For when the deacon Anatolius, of most beloved memory, gave the book of the *Pastoral Rule* to the lord emperor at his request and command, I received this with displeasure; the most holy brother and my fellow bishop Anastasius of Antioch translated it into Greek. And, as has been written to me, the emperor was greatly pleased with it; but I was greatly displeased that those who possess better things should occupy themselves with trifles.

In the third part of blessed Job, at the verse where it is written, “I know that my Redeemer lives,” I suspect that the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Marinian has a faulty copy. For in our archive that passage is found differently from the way I have learned it to stand in the copies of others; and therefore I had the passage corrected, so that my aforesaid brother might have it as it is in our archive. There are four words which, if absent from that passage, can cause the reader no small difficulty. Carry all this out carefully and quickly. And if you can do nothing with the excellent exarch, at least make it clear that you have not neglected these matters which you can accomplish.

What shall I say about Albinus’s case, concerning which we are openly answered contrary to justice? Nevertheless, you must consider it with greater strictness.

Moreover, some time ago we instructed Your Experience to act with our eminent son, the prefect, so that responsibility for the aqueducts should be entrusted [Note: [Col. 1235D] *Formae* are chambers by which an aqueduct is divided; in French, *les bassins, les réservoirs d'eau, les regards* (“basins, water reservoirs, inspection chambers”). They are masonry-built and arched channels, called δοχεῖα (“receptacles”) by the Greeks, according to Vitruvius, Book VIII, chapter 7. Sidonius Apollinaris, in Letter 5 of Book I to his Heroinus: “Meanwhile Rome too opened to view, and I seemed likely to drink in not only her *formae* but even her naval spectacles.” The official responsible for the *formae* was called the *comes formarum*, as may be read in the *Notitia Imperii* and in Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book VII, §6. GUSSANV.] to the vice-count Augustus, since he is an entirely conscientious and energetic man. Yet you have delayed so long that you have not even informed us what you have done. Therefore hasten now to act with every determination before that same eminent son of ours, so that the aqueducts may in every respect be entrusted to the aforementioned illustrious man, enabling him through his diligence to restore them to some degree. For the aqueducts are so despised and neglected that, unless greater care is given, they will perish completely within a short time. Thus, since you know how necessary and beneficial this matter is for the community, you must make every effort so that, as we have said, they are entrusted in every way to the aforementioned man on account of his diligence. [Note: [Col. 1235D] The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, read: “through your diligence … be entrusted.”] [Note: [Col. 1235D] These words occur in two Colbertine manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript, but at the beginning of the letter. In the vulgate editions one reads: “Given in the month of February.”]

Given in the month of January, in the fifth indiction.

## LETTER XXV. TO THE DEFENSOR ROMANUS

That the sons of the defensor Peter are not to marry outside the estate in which they were born.

[Col. 1235C]

Gregory to Romanus, defensor.

It is well known to Your Experience that Peter, whom we made defensor, originated from the estate belonging to the legal property of our Church called Vitelas. Since we ought therefore to show him such kindness that the interests of the Church are nevertheless not harmed, we command you by this instruction to admonish him strictly: he must not presume, by any device or excuse, to join his sons in marriage elsewhere, but they must be joined in that estate to which they are bound by law and status. [Note: [Col. 1235D] EPIST. XXV [Al. 28].—I do not believe that those in question were truly slaves, but either adopted dependants or people bound to the soil, a form of servitude considered more honorable. It is said that formerly there were no properly so-called slaves in Gaul; nevertheless, I remember reading in the custom or municipal law of Meaux, approved and published in the year 1509, article 78, the following law: “Persons of servile condition neither can nor ought, without the permission and pardon of their lords, to take free women as wives, or women of any condition other than that in which they themselves are and were born. If they attempt anything to the contrary, they shall be condemned to the fine commonly called *de for de mariage*, which shall accrue to the property of the lords whose slaves they are.” The example is as similar as milk is to milk, except that here a fine is imposed, whereas there the matter is enforced through fear. GUSSANV.] In this matter also it is entirely necessary that Your Experience be vigilant and frighten them, so that under no circumstance should they leave the estate to which they are subject by origin. For if any one of them should presume to leave it—which we do not believe—let him know for certain that our consent will never be given for him to live or be joined in marriage outside the estate in which he was born; rather, their land shall be marked with an additional charge. [Note: [Col. 1236D] I interpret this as meaning that I wish an increase in the annual assessment to be imposed upon them. In nearly the same sense jurists say *superindictum*. “The creditor dictates, the debtor writes”; land is “written” when it is leased at so high a rent; it is “written over” when the price is increased. GUSSANV. In Remigius and Victor, the only witnesses from which we have this letter, together with Vatican A, the reading is “and their land shall be entered as an additional charge.” Here “to write over their land” seems to mean to claim it for the property of the Roman Church by adding legal titles, what we commonly call “to reunite it.” See note b to Letter 65 of Book I.] You should know that you are then exposed to no slight danger if, through your negligence, any one of them attempts in any way to do anything that we prohibit.

## LETTER XXVI. TO MAURENTIUS, MASTER OF THE SOLDIERS

That, after the others have been released, he should not retain Domitius’s son.

Gregory to Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

The magnificent Domitius requested that we write to Your Glory so that, while the others are sailing, his son might likewise be allowed to sail. Although we are certain of Your Glory that you do nothing indiscreet but consider everything wisely, we nevertheless urge you that, if the others are released, he too should not be detained, lest he appear to be retained not for a rational reason but solely because of hostility toward his brothers. [Note: [Col. 1236D] Vatican A reads: “but solely because of enmity.”] You who are present, however, can better discern what is expedient, taking equity into consideration and also attending to the general good.

## LETTER XXVII. TO QUERTINUS, FORMER PREFECT

Why he does not wish to act on behalf of Bonitus, who is seeking administration of the prefecture.

Gregory to Quertinus, former prefect.

[Note: [Col. 1236D] EPIST. XXVII [Al. 30].—Previously the reading was “Your Grace,” which we changed after consulting the Remigian manuscript, the only one among the Gallic manuscripts examined by us in which this letter is found. Moreover, Saint Gregory never addresses those to whom he writes by the title “Your Grace.” Below, “Your Glory” occurs.]

We have received a letter from Your Glory in which you wrote that we ought to act on behalf of our glorious son Bonitus, so that the administration of the prefecture might be entrusted to him. We have known this same son of ours for many years—not merely for a short time—and therefore we are eager to support him in every respect, but not in a matter that could bring him bitterness and troubles. For the administration itself was offered to his first subordinate and to another, his junior, and they absolutely refused to involve themselves, knowing how burdensome it is, especially at this time, to undertake the administration. If it was burdensome for them, how much more difficult must it be for this man, who is engaged in public business on our behalf? [Note: [Col. 1237D] This passage, cited by Gratian, proves that in his time this letter was accepted among the Gregorian letters, although it survives in very few manuscripts, since we encountered it only in Remigius, Victor, and Vatican A.] Furthermore, it is both unprofitable and exceedingly laborious for a literate man to undertake the causes of financial accounts and bind himself to them in a way that is not expedient. [Note: [Col. 1237D] Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 88, chapter 8.] Above all, this consideration restrains us: we remember no one who emerged from this undertaking successfully except Your Glory, concerning whom we ask almighty God to preserve you by continual protection to the end. Therefore, considering this, we do not wish to involve ourselves in his injury. For what now appears useful will certainly later be full of labor and expense. But if he judges that this is necessary for his interests and wishes to act so that the administration may be entrusted to him, we do not oppose him; indeed, we already feel compassion for his future troubles, since from the example of those who preceded him we know what he will have to endure.

## LETTER XXVIII. TO COLUMBUS, BISHOP OF NUMIDIA

That Paulinus, who had savagely mistreated his clergy and sold sacred orders through sacrilegious commerce, must be restrained.

[Col. 1237C]

Gregory to Columbus, bishop of Numidia.

Since we have long known that Your Fraternity is distinguished by priestly seriousness and ecclesiastical zeal, we have judged it appropriate that you should take part in learning about matters requiring correction, lest, if they are put off through dissimulation, everyone should believe that whatever he can do is permitted. You do not need to be told how our brother Paulinus, bishop of the city of Tegessis, has acted: his clergy, or those constituted in holy orders, are said to have suffered bodily violence at his hands. [Note: [Col. 1238D] That is, to rage against one’s subjects.] [Note: [Col. 1237D] EPIST. XXVIII [Al. 32].—Most manuscripts read this way, although some, as do the older printed editions, have *Tagesis*. In the catalogue of Africa, both in Sirmond, vol. I, col. 435, and in Ruinart, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, p. 128, one reads “Domnicolus of Tigis.” Holstenius, in his notes on *Sacred Geography*, p. 69, wishes to read “Tuggensis” or “Tuccensis,” from Tucca, a formerly episcopal inland African city under the archbishop of Carthage. The Vatican edition reads “Regensis.” Indeed, in Ruinart’s *Catalogue of Africa*, Victor of Regia is listed among the bishops of Mauretania, p. 135, and Fortunius of Regiana among the bishops of Numidia, p. 128. But since no manuscript has *Regensis*, while they consistently have *Tegessis* or *Tegesis*, what purpose is served by further conjecturing about the see of this bishop? The old printed editions agree with the manuscripts.]

Since, as we have learned from their testimony, the matter had already become known to you before this complaint reached us, And because it must not be lawful for superiors to rage against their subjects as punishment, we have taken care to write to our brother and fellow bishop Victor, who holds the place of primate among you, [Note: [Col. 1238D] He succeeded Adeodatus in the primacy of Numidia; in Book III, indiction 2, Letter 49, we read of him as primate of that province.] so that together with Your Fraternity, or with whatever other brothers and fellow bishops you deem appropriate to summon, he may investigate with careful inquiry the case between our aforementioned brother and fellow priest and his clergy. [Note: [Col. 1238D] Recent manuscripts read: “the case concerning him should be investigated with careful inquiry.”] Therefore let Your Affection be attentive and take care that the matters reported to us do not pass unheard, 1199 lest discord be nourished in the Church, from which it must be removed with the utmost care. If the complaint of his clergy against him is true, let him recognize his fault—which he has deliberately refused to correct—through a judgment of ecclesiastical rigor, so that he may feel how serious his action is in the present and learn that in the future he can do nothing beyond what is permitted. [Note: [Col. 1238D] All the Norman manuscripts read: “which he has scorned to acknowledge.” Vatican B: “which he has scorned to denounce.” Vatican F: “which he has scorned to consider.”] Above all, therefore, we urge you to exercise more ardently the zeal that we know you possess for God.

And since our aforementioned brother Paulinus is said to confer ecclesiastical orders through the simoniacal heresy—a thing dreadful to hear—you must investigate this more carefully, together with the aforesaid primate or other bishops, and with every diligence. If it is found to be so, God forbid, you must act and strive so that both the one who is not afraid to accept the payment and the one who is not afraid to offer it may be struck by the sentence of canonical punishment, so that their correction may serve as a warning to many. Before this deadly root takes hold [Note: [Col. 1238D] The printed editions read “grows strong”; Remigius, “grows hot.” We follow Tours, the Norman manuscripts, and others.] and destroys more people, it must be condemned by the judgment of the entire council, so that no one ever dares to accept anything for any order, and no one to give anything; rather, let no one be promoted through favor, but through merit, lest the ecclesiastical order be thrown into confusion and uprightness of life be despised if one unworthy receives the reward of merit. [Note: [Col. 1238D] The Norman manuscripts read: “and if a proven life is held in contempt.”]

We have instructed our chartulary Hilary that, if the case requires it, he should not refuse to attend your investigation. If it is necessary, inform him by your letters that he must come there, so that, deliberating together with him, you may better decide what ought to be established. [Note: [Col. 1238D] In two old Colbertine manuscripts and in two Vatican manuscripts—namely, codices B and E—the letter is said at its beginning to have been written in the month of March, in the fifth indiction.]

## LETTER XXIX. TO VICTOR, BISHOP

That he should convene a council so that Paulinus’s violence against his clergy and his simony may be punished and suppressed, summoning Hilary if necessary.

[Col. 1239A]

Gregory to Victor, bishop. [Note: [Col. 1239D] EPIST. XXIX [Al. 33].—In recent editions *Panormitanus* has been rashly added, although it is absent from the manuscripts and the old edition. The gross error arose both because many of Saint Gregory’s letters are addressed to Victor of Palermo and because the editors thought that this letter, as well as the preceding one, should read “Regensis” rather than “bishop of the city of Tegessis.” Hence they supposed that Saint Gregory could have summoned a bishop from a neighboring island to correct the bishop of Regia.]

Just as it brings us great joy to know that our brothers are appropriately solicitous toward their sons with paternal affection, so we count it a great sorrow when neither regard for other brothers nor consideration of the priesthood can restrain them from unlawful actions. Your Fraternity cannot fail to know how grave and harsh is the complaint against our brother Paulinus, bishop of the city of Tegessis, brought by his clergy or by those constituted in holy orders, since what reached us in a distant place could not have remained hidden from you nearby. Because it must be guarded against with the utmost care that what they complain he has wrongfully inflicted upon them through bodily violence should either be presumed lawful or become worse through dissimulation, manifest excesses must always be suppressed with canonical moderation, so that one and the same measure may serve both as correction of the past and as a rule for the future. Therefore, together with our beloved common brother Columbus, bishop, or with whatever other priests you foresee, you ought to investigate carefully the case between our aforesaid brother and his clergy. If the complaint of those who appeal to you is supported by truth, correct the matter through regular discipline, so that he may recognize how evil his action was and learn henceforth not to exceed the limits of his office. Nor should you allow him, as is said, to disregard the order of your position, lest his contempt become danger to him and guilt to you. [Note: [Col. 1239D] Anyone who has read chapter 36 of Saint Benedict’s Rule will not doubt that this sentence was taken from it, since whatever is done wrong by the disciples concerns the person placed above them, namely the abbot.] For whatever a subordinate commits concerns the person placed in the higher position, unless it is carefully corrected.

But what is reported concerning this same brother Paulinus—that he gives ecclesiastical orders in exchange for payment—must be investigated by you with even greater care and complete strictness. If it becomes clear that this is so, which we do not wish, let your zeal for God be kindled to punish it, so that the avarice of the ordaining bishop may be turned into punishment for him and the unlawful ordination, deprived of effect, may not allow him to enjoy the desire of his ambition. In this matter we exhort you and above all admonish you to be so vigilant that, before the wickedness of the simoniacal heresy grows strong there through the fault of one man, it may be cut out at the root by the axe of your judgment through the action of a council. For whoever does not burn vehemently to correct this crime out of regard for his office should know that he shares in the guilt of the one from whom this particular disgrace first took its origin. [Note: [Col. 1240D] Vatican D and Rheims read: “has not risen to the occasion.”] [Note: [Col. 1240D] A recent edition reads “this special crime.” Saint Gregory calls the offense arising from money given and accepted simoniacally “a particular crime.”] Therefore, as we have said, you must act here with vigilance and diligence, so that the poison of this crime may neither defile nor destroy your council, which until now, by God’s protection, has been preserved free from such a wicked reputation. 1201

Moreover, we have instructed our chartulary Hilary not to delay joining you if the matter requires it. Therefore, if necessary, inform him by your letters that he must come to you, so that with God’s help you may settle all these matters beneficially together with him.

## LETTER XXX. TO CONSTANTINE, BISHOP OF SCODRA

He himself is to carry out what is established in the following letter to John against Paul’s crime, if he can; otherwise, he is to insist that John carry it out.

[Col. 1240B]

Gregory to Constantine, bishop of Scodra. [Note: [Col. 1240D] EPIST. XXX [Al. 35].—The printed editions and some manuscripts read *Constantius*. In most codices *bishop* is absent. Vatican A and one Colbertine manuscript read “bishop of Scodra.”]

The matters that the beloved Nemesion, bearer of this letter, who says that he is bishop of the city of Doclea, has reported to Your Fraternity concerning the crime of Paul of Doclea—formerly a bishop, as he himself states—would have to be explained more carefully, had his testimony not shown that you know everything, since he says that you sympathized with him and wished to help him but were entirely unable to do so. Because a crime of such magnitude must not be neglected or left unpunished, lest others, God forbid, take criminal boldness from its example, Your Fraternity should carefully reread the copies of the writings enclosed here, which we sent to our most reverend brother John, bishop of the First Justiniana, who is acting in our place. If you recognize that you can carry out everything according to their contents, then, by our authority, carry out and accomplish everything that we have commanded him. But if you see that this is difficult for you because of obstacles perhaps placed in your way by certain persons, you must ensure that our writings reach the aforementioned brother without excuse. You should also urge him to carry out more strictly what we have commanded him, and not to delay it on any pretext; rather, what has been wickedly done must be corrected by suitable amendment, so that one and the same measure may be both an appropriate punishment for the offender and a warning to others constituted in the same order.

## LETTER XXXI. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF THE FIRST JUSTINIANA

Having set out the crimes of Paul, bishop of Doclea, he prescribes remedies.

[Col. 1241A]

Gregory to John, bishop of the First Justiniana.

When evils that ought to be cleansed by penitential weeping are increased by further excesses, greater correction must be applied to offenders, so that they themselves may at least recognize their crime when punishment exacts vengeance and so that fear of ecclesiastical retribution may restrain others from unlawful acts. [Note: [Col. 1241D] EPIST. XXXI [Al. 34].—The Norman manuscripts and three Vatican manuscripts read: “of ecclesiastical protection.”]

Accordingly, the beloved Nemesion, bearer of this letter, came to us and reported—as did the copies of the proceedings that he brought here—that Paul, bishop of the city of Doclea, had, among other evils, fallen into a bodily offense and had been accused by his own clergy; and that, after an investigation had been held, the matter had become clear, as we cannot say without sorrow. Moreover, after he had been convicted, he had presented a document in which he confessed that the matters of which he had been accused were true. Consequently, sentence was passed, he was deposed from the episcopate, and in his place Nemesion was ordained bishop with the consent of Your Fraternity. [Note: [Col. 1241D] Doclea—called Antivari by some in common usage, and Catazo by Samson—is an episcopal city of Illyricum on Lake Scodra, commonly called Lago di Scutari. It was subject to the bishop of Scodra until Justinian made his native city Acrida, which he named Justiniana, a metropolitan see. See what we said concerning the First Justiniana in Letter 6 of Book III.]

But now, Paul himself, coming with the assistance of secular judges, entered the episcopal residence like a brigand, violently removed the Church’s property, and expelled Nemesion, bringing him to the utmost injury and almost to death. [Note: [Col. 1241D] A recent edition reads: “from the greatest injustice almost to death,” contrary to the English manuscripts, the Norman manuscripts, and others.] Since the wickedness of so great a crime must neither be concealed nor treated lightly, Your Fraternity must carefully investigate all these matters. If the truth is as we have been informed, have the aforesaid Paul compelled by strict enforcement to restore, without delay or excuse, whatever he took. If he says that he took nothing belonging to the Church but only his own property, although it was serious and unjust that he should not have sought this from you or from his metropolitan but should have undertaken it with rash audacity, nevertheless, if he took anything of his own, it must be established under Your Fraternity’s examination whether his claim is true. You must also carefully investigate whether he wasted anything belonging to the Church, so that he may be compelled in every way to make restoration and satisfaction from what he has now taken. If he delays restoring to the Church everything he wasted or removed from its resources, he is to be sent to a monastery, so that at least under compulsion he may return what he did not fear to take wrongfully.

If, however, after his deposition, he should presume—something we do not believe—to speak shamelessly and perversely about the episcopate or again aspire to it by any presumptuous means, let Your Fraternity’s vigor be wholly aroused against his insolence, and have him deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood and confined to a monastery until the day of his death to perform penance. Thus he may learn to cleanse by worthy tears the stains of the crime he committed, which he perversely desires rather to increase to the destruction of his soul.

Our aforementioned beloved brother Nemesion must unquestionably be restored to his place and to the office of the episcopate. You must therefore be solicitous that he not again suffer disturbance and trouble on this account, since this will contribute not only to his protection but also to the correction of others. [Note: [Col. 1241D] This is the excellent reading of the manuscripts and old edition. Other copies read “for the correction of this admonition.” Here *munitio* means defense and security—namely, of the legitimate bishop of Doclea.] Thus the presumption of wicked men will henceforth dare in no way to attempt anything against the statutes of the sacred canons or ecclesiastical discipline.

## LETTER XXXII. TO ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE COUNCIL OF BYZACENA

That they should investigate energetically and carefully the grave accusations against Crementius, their primate.

Gregory to all the bishops of the council of Byzacena. [Note: [Col. 1241D] EPIST. XXXII [Al. 36].—All the Norman manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, two Colbertine manuscripts, and the Corbie manuscript read *Visachi*. Other Colbertine manuscripts read *Vitachi*, while the more correct form is *Bisaceni*. The province of Byzacena was one of the seven provinces constituting the African diocese. See Letter 59 of Book IX. It is frequently discussed in the *History of the Vandal Persecution* by Victor of Vita, edited and annotated by our Theodosius Ruinart.]

Just as it is praiseworthy and prudent to show those in authority the reverence and honor due to them, so it is an expression of uprightness and fear of God not to postpone, through dissimulation, any correction that they require, lest, God forbid, disease begin to invade the entire body if the sickness is not cured in the head. Some time ago, certain reports concerning our brother Crementius, your primate, were brought to us—reports that would have pierced our heart with no slight sorrow. But because we were pressed by various tribulations, and especially by enemies raging on every side, we had no opportunity to investigate them. Since they are so serious that they must in no way be passed over without examination, we exhort Your Fraternity in these words: with every diligence and alertness, you must investigate their substance in many ways, so that, if the matters are true, they may be cut away by canonical punishment; or, if they are false, the innocence of our brother may not lie for long under the tearing apart of a wicked accusation. [Note: [Col. 1242D] Later manuscripts add “as they have been heard,” unnecessarily and contrary to the Corbie, Norman, Tours, Vatican, and other manuscripts.]

We therefore admonish you lest the sluggishness of indolence occur in your investigation: let neither regard for any person, nor favor, nor flattery, nor anything else soften any of you in examining what has been reported to us or drive you from the path of truth. Rather, gird yourselves as priests to investigate the truth for God’s sake. For if anyone presumes to show himself sluggish or negligent in this matter, let him know that he shares before almighty God in the crimes alleged, since he is not moved by zeal for God to scrutinize carefully the causes of so wicked a deed. [Note: [Col. 1243D] Recent manuscripts read: “or presumes to show himself sluggish or negligent.”] [Note: [Col. 1242D] Here I shall note four points. First, the text says “canonical punishment,” not arbitrary punishment: fixed and certain laws ought to establish penalties against crimes, and the measure of censure ought not to be left to the discretion of every judge. For, as Lactantius says, the judge is the minister of the law, not of his own mind or power; accordingly, he must use not his own sentence but that of the laws, *On the Anger of God*, chapters 17–18. Second, according to the same Lactantius, chapter 17, those are greatly mistaken who condemn either divine or human censure under the name of harshness: “He who punishes the wicked guards the safety of the good … He is the guilty one who either harms the innocent or spares the guilty … It belongs to reason to be angry; for offenses are removed and license restrained, and this is rightly and wisely done … It is necessary for the just person to be displeased by what is wrong … Therefore one must rise to punishment, not because we have been injured, but so that discipline may be preserved, morals corrected, and license suppressed. This is righteous anger.” He develops the same point at greater length in chapter 18; it would be useful to read it. Third, not only bishops but also primates are subject to canonical censure. Pope Adrian indicates this clearly in the capitularies addressed to Pippin, sections 5, 6, 14, 20, 27, and others. Fourth, sinful prelates may rightly be judged and condemned by their inferiors in a synod. See Letter 8 of this book concerning Victor, the primate. GUSSANV.] (See Letters 58 and 59, second indiction.)

## LETTER XXXIII. TO FIRMINUS, BISHOP OF ISTRIA

He congratulates him on his return to the unity of the Church. He urges him to oppose Satan’s arrows with the shield of steadfastness and to bring others back with him. He promises assistance and sends a garment.

[Col. 1243B]

Gregory to Firminus, bishop of Istria.

Our Redeemer does not allow one of his servants to perish. Through the inspiration of his mercy he so enlightens the person’s heart that, abandoning the darkness of error, he returns to knowledge of the light and the way of truth. Therefore, having received the letter of Your Beloved Fraternity, we rejoice with great exultation in the Lord that divine grace has recalled you to the unity of the Church, from which you had been separated through the instigation of stubborn and ignorant men. [Note: [Col. 1243D] EPIST. XXXIII [Al. 37].—The manuscripts read this, and better than the printed editions, which have: “that the grace of the Divinity recalled [him] to the unity of the Church …,” omitting *you*. See at the end, in the appendix, the promise of a certain bishop whom we think was Firminus.] [Note: [Col. 1243D] Speaking under the inspiration of the divine Spirit, he foretells the trials that shortly afterward tested Firminus’s steadfastness. See below, Book XIII, Letter 33. At the end of the letters you will find the formula for renouncing this schism, which was formerly Letter 31 of this book.]

But because the more the ancient enemy sees that he has been defeated, the more fiercely he does not cease to lie in wait, it is altogether fitting that you be watchful and vigilant and prepare the shield of steadfastness against his arrows, so that they may be shattered when they strike and have no power to penetrate within. Therefore, dearest brother, let no desire for possessions, no terrors, no blandishments, and no seductions—which strike souls with poisoned arrows of words—soften you from the fervor of your return or force you to turn back, lest you, who had overcome the strong one, be gravely overcome and, God forbid, be held captive after your victory. [Note: [Col. 1244D] The printed editions read: “lest you be more gravely overcome by the strong one,” which is certainly excellent, were it not contradicted by the manuscripts.] Rather, so that Mother Church, spread throughout the whole world by God’s favor, may recognize that you have returned to her bosom not idly, you must watch and labor with the utmost diligence so that you may bring others back with you. In this way you may not only repair through the good of your return the losses you caused by the example of your turning away, but also provide a gain, so that you may appear to have brought back to your Lord more people than you led away, both to obtain pardon for the past and to receive rewards in the future.

We shall therefore take every care, as is fitting, to consider the peace of Your Fraternity, because, now that by God’s protection you are one with us, we regard your interests no differently from our own. John the subdeacon has written to us about some of your needs. But we trust in the power of our God that Saint Peter, to whom you have returned, will not abandon you. [Note: [Col. 1244D] The Norman, Corbie, Vatican A, and some other manuscripts read: “ought not to abandon you.”] Now, from the blessing of that same Saint Peter, we have sent Your Fraternity a garment, which you must receive with the same affection with which it has been sent by us. [Note: [Col. 1244D] It is a garment or ornament. Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter 3: “so great, therefore, a preparation of materials”; and *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 12: “they carry about their entire womanhood in manifest adornment.” Arnobius, on Psalm 56: “If, therefore, you have a prepared heart against the preparations of demons,” and so forth. Hesychius has *paratōrion*. Warnefrid, *Life of Charlemagne*: “ornament or garment.” GUSSANV. *Paratura* is a woven border or *epiblēma*—an addition placed on a garment as an ornament. Matthew Paris, *Life of Richard, fifteenth abbot of Saint Albans*: “the abbot [gave] two embroidered garments with their ornaments.” Papias: “a prepared adornment.” ALTES.] [Note: [Col. 1244D] An old Colbertine manuscript reads “in the month of May”; another, “in the month of August.”]

In the month of May, in the fifth indiction.

## LETTER XXXIV. TO CIRIDANUS

Since what he himself ordered has been provided for the *sitonicus*, the Church must no longer be made to bear that loss.

Gregory to Ciridanus.

The letter you sent us some time ago from Your Glory has reached us. In it you indicated that, by order of the most serene princes, responsibility for the *sitonicon* had been entrusted to your care, and that all the quantity of wheat which had been received into the granaries of our Church ought in every respect to be handed over to you; and you wrote that we should arrange for this very amount to be prepared in kind.

We know, however, that this was not your doing, since such great benefits have indeed been brought to us by you; and you know how harsh and altogether difficult it would be to demand that goods which could neither be stored nor found for purchase at that time should be restored in kind. Nevertheless, so that we might be relieved of concern about this matter, it was our endeavor—even at considerable expense—to have the grain itself prepared in kind, exactly as you wished.

Afterward, through the bearer of this letter, the magnificent Eutychius, who declares that he is an illustrious prefect, you sent us another letter, requesting that the total amount of the same *sitonicon* received from the Church’s granary officials should be officially recorded in the public acts. Therefore, lest an opportunity—or an excuse—seem to arise for anyone at the Church’s expense, the Church’s defenders have recorded the quantity, as you instructed, and have requested what they thought useful.

Your Glory should examine this carefully and attentively, and should not disregard their words. For whatever loss may hereafter occur in connection with the aforesaid *sitonicon* in kind, you should know that it will in no way be chargeable further to the Church’s account, since the inhabitants of this city—men truly afflicted—assert that they cannot receive the aforesaid *sitonicon* without suffering loss themselves. Knowing all this, then, may Your Glory take care of the matters entrusted to you in such a way that you both advance the public interest and ensure that the burden of this undertaking does not again fall upon our Church, to the distress of the poor.

**Note:** Concerning the *sitonicon*, see Book I, Letter 2.

**Note:** Thus Victorinus, Vatican A, and Remigius, in which alone we find this letter. In the printed editions the reading is *parare in species*, “to prepare in kind,” in French *en espèces*.

**Note:** Those who are responsible for the granaries; the word is customary among legal writers. A *horreum* is a repository for grain, wine, produce, and so forth. Varro derives the word from *hordeum*, “barley”; Galen from Greek *ὠραῖα*. Gussanville.

---

## LETTER XXXV. TO DESIDERIUS, BISHOP OF VIENNE

He should not recall his deacon Pancratius from the monastic life.

Gregory to Desiderius, bishop in Gaul.

Pancratius, the bearer of this letter, who, as he says, is a deacon, presenting himself at the thresholds of the apostles, is known to have asked us to commend him especially to Your Fraternity. He also informed us that he had been attached to your Church in the clerical office.

Moved, therefore, by divine inspiration, he desired the grace of monastic conduct, and, wishing to remain there in the habit which he had assumed, he also states that he has been made a deacon of that same monastery. He allows himself to be torn away from the service of that place on no grounds whatsoever.

Now, as he asserts, Your Fraternity wishes to recall him to the service of your Church—not, indeed, with the intention of hindering him, but out of benevolent affection. We therefore urge Your Fraternity not to obstruct his eager devotion, which he is striving to maintain in his holy purpose. Rather, by whatever exhortations you can offer, kindle him through pastoral admonition, so that the fervor of this desire may not grow cold in him. He withdrew from the turbulent tumult of worldly cares and sought the monastery as a harbor of quiet; he ought not again to be entangled in the disturbances of ecclesiastical responsibilities, but should be permitted to remain securely, as he desires, in the praises of God.

**Note:** *EPIST. XXXV* [alternative numbering 39].—Prudentius, in the hymn to Saint Lawrence: “They kiss the thresholds of the apostles and martyrs.” Saint Paulinus, in the third poem on the feast of Saint Felix: “Their breasts are stretched upon the thresholds.” Fortunatus, Book IV, *On the Life of Saint Martin*: “Apollinaris licks the thresholds of the precious one.” Council of Chalon II, canon 45: “to visit the thresholds of the apostles or of any saints.” Basilicas of the saints were called their “thresholds,” because pilgrims were accustomed to visit them just as they visited the thresholds of the apostles existing at Rome.

**Note:** Remigius has *is known to have hoped that we would commend him*.

**Note:** Vatican D has “had served in your Church.” Rhemigius, Vatican A, and Remigius agree in reading “has served in your Church.”

---

## LETTER XXXVI. TO BONITUS, THE DEFENDER

He should assist the monks who are collecting their monastery’s fugitive slaves.

Gregory to Bonitus, the defender.

Our son Fortunatus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Severinus, which is situated in this city of Rome, is sending the monks who bear this letter there to recover the slaves belonging to his monastery, who are said to be hiding in that region. He has asked that the support of Your Experience be made available to them.

Therefore, by this present authority, we order you to hasten to cooperate with and assist them in every respect, while preserving justice, so that, with you present there and offering support in this matter, they may speedily and successfully bring to completion, with God’s help, what has been entrusted to them.

**Note:** *EPIST. XXXVI* [alternative numbering 40].—This appears to be the man whom John the Deacon, Book II, chapter 53, calls Benedictus, defender of the Carseolan patrimony in Latium. For nowhere else is a Benedictus who was a defender mentioned.

**Note:** In Vatican A, Remigius, and Victorinus—the only three of all the manuscripts we consulted that contain this letter—the reading is “of Saint Semetrius.”

**Note:** Remigius and San-Victor add “with God’s help.”

---

## LETTER XXXVII. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER, AND TO THE SUBDEACONS ANTHEMIUS AND SABINUS

He commends the men and possessions of Romanus, the former praetor.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender, to Anthemius, the subdeacon, and to Sabinus, the subdeacon.

We cannot refuse requests which it is proper for us willingly to grant. Therefore, since our glorious son Romanus, former praetor, has wished his possessions and the men who are in those regions to be commended to Your Experience, we instruct you by this command not to cease protecting his possessions and men while preserving equity. Strive in every matter and interest of his to cooperate and provide assistance, so that he may recognize that he has been helped by this commendation, and you may be proved to have faithfully carried out what was entrusted to you.

**Note:** *EPIST. XXXVII* [alternative numbering 41].—In Vatican A, “and to Sabinus” is omitted. Of all the manuscripts we have examined, only this codex, together with Victorinus and Remigius, contains this letter.

**Note:** Remigius and Victorinus read: “you may be proved in every respect to have rendered what was entrusted to you.”

---

## LETTER XXXVIII. TO DEUSDEDIT, BISHOP OF MILAN

A bishop may make a will concerning goods acquired before his episcopate; therefore Luminosа, a servant of God, is not to be troubled on account of a legacy from the will of his predecessor.

Gregory to Deusdedit, bishop of Milan.

No one doubts—for Gratian, *Decretum* 12, question 5, canon 1 and canon 12—that, just as priests have no permission to alienate property acquired during their episcopate, so they are not forbidden to dispose as they wish of property they possessed beforehand.

Accordingly, we recall that Your Fraternity formerly complained to us that Constantius, your predecessor, while already a bishop, had acquired certain immovable property which he had left by testamentary legacy to Luminosа, a servant of God, the daughter of his brother; and we decreed that, if this were established, your Church should suffer no prejudice on that account.

You ought to remember this and not cause any trouble to the aforesaid servant of God, nor take anything from what she possesses without investigation. But if the agents of your Church believe that this can be proved, report it to us by your letters, so that we may determine how the matter ought to be established—provided that, once the truth has been ascertained, neither your Church suffers prejudice nor she appears to be unjustly afflicted. For, according to the testimony of some, your aforesaid predecessor acquired this property not while he was a bishop, but while he was still a deacon.
