It is therefore necessary that, as we have said, the truth be established by proof. We commend this same servant of God to Your Fraternity, so that you may not allow anyone to burden or oppress her. If she is harassed, it might be thought that, under the pretext of this case, she is suffering what ought not to be suffered.

Therefore, if there is anything that ought to be corrected, let it be corrected through the moderate and plain guidance of your exhortation; or at least let it be reported to us carefully, so that you may remain free from reproach and we may in no way fail to do what is appropriate.

In the month of May, in the fifth indiction.

**Note:** *EPIST. XXXVIII* [alternative numbering 42].—It was formerly read as “to Deodatus.” We follow all the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, and other manuscripts.

**Note:** In the Rheims manuscript and in Vatican D and E: “to the daughter of his brother and to his brothers.”

**Note:** From this it is evident that deacons could alienate property acquired during their diaconate. I should believe the same of priests. The rule was not the same for bishops, as stated above. Gussanville.

**Note:** “Plainly,” that is, without judicial procedure. Hence *cognitio planaria* in law, meaning “without the noise of a trial.” Gussanville. In the Norman manuscript, agreeing with the old printed editions, the reading is “or let it be corrected by the moderate guidance of your plain exhortation,” with *a* omitted.

**Note:** Thus in three Vatican manuscripts and in the old Colbert manuscript. In another Colbert manuscript: “in August,” which is also the reading of the printed editions.

---

## LETTER XXXIX. TO FANTINUS, THE DEFENDER

From the inheritance of the deacon Servusdei, he is to give ten mares to the hospice and four to Luminosа, a servant of God.

Gregory to Fantinus, the defender.

We believe that Your Experience has already learned that our most beloved son, the deacon Servusdei, left the holy Roman Church, which we serve by God’s authority, as his heir. Since he established that four mares were to be given by way of legacy to Luminosа, a servant of God and his kinswoman, and since, at the request of our most beloved son Florentinus, the deacon, we have arranged that ten mares, together with their stallion, be given to the hospice of the Anicii, over which he is known to preside, we therefore command you by this order to hand over without excuse or delay to the bearer of this letter, who has been sent there for this purpose, both the four mares that were bequeathed and the ten mares granted to the hospice, along with the aforesaid deacon’s stallion.

**Note:** *EPIST. XXXIX* [alternative numbering 43].—He appears to be the same man as the one mentioned in Book I, Letter 44.

**Note:** This expression frequently occurs in Sacred Scripture for a breeding stallion, as in Sirach 33:6 and Jeremiah 5:8.

---

## LETTER XL. TO VENANTIUS, THE PATRICIAN

He promises that, once recovered, he will interpret certain deeds of Samson allegorically.

Gregory to Venantius, the patrician of Palermo.

I have received the letters of Your Most Desirable Excellency, in which I rejoiced at the conversation of one who was absent as much as I always desire the speaker himself to be present with me.

You wish, therefore, that certain deeds of Samson be explained allegorically. But such weakness has overtaken my body that, even if I have been able to undertake anything, my mind does not rise to carry it out. I rejoice, however, in your good desire, because, while you seek an exposition of the sacred words, you show how earnestly you seek the author himself of those words.

If, therefore, I recover my health and strength, I shall comply with your wishes, with the almighty Lord as author and helper. I ask that heavenly grace may guard you in all your actions, so that in good works it may fill you with aspiration and strengthen you by its assistance.

**Note:** *EPIST. XL* [alternative numbering 45].—We have shown above, in the notes to Letter 4 of this book, that this Venantius is different from the patrician who, while he was a monk, took a wife. Compare Gussanville’s notes on these letters, and you will be astonished at the learned man’s carelessness. In his note on Letter 4 he insists that this letter has been displaced, because Venantius, to whom he thinks it was written, had already died in the previous year. But in the note on this Letter 40—which for Gussanville is Letter 45—he observes: “Venantius recovered contrary to expectation, as we noted above.” Thus he recovered and was alive in the fifth indiction, although he had died in the fourth.

**Note:** Remigius has “if they have been able.”

---

## LETTER XLI. TO PANTALEON, THE NOTARY

Concerning the surviving money, clergy, and other goods of certain Churches.

Gregory to Pantaleon, the notary.

We expected Your Experience to make us fully and carefully informed about the silver of the Churches and about whatever other things you found, so that, from your report, we might deliberate more precisely about what ought to be done. But your report did not instruct us as it should have.

Let it therefore be your concern to deposit the silver of the Churches—which the clergy and people possess—with those whom you deem appropriate, in the Church treasury, with every care and precaution; and obtain from them an acknowledgement of receipt for that deposit. The silver of the Churches which, on account of the sins of the clergy and people, has been abandoned, bring here with you.

If you discover that three or four clerics remain in those Churches, report to us, after making a record, who each one is, what his condition is, and where he lives, so that, if we deem it necessary, we may determine what each ought to receive annually. Bring with you likewise objects which may perish through age, so that whatever seems useful may be arranged concerning them.

You, however, return under the Lord’s protection, once you have found a favorable voyage.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLI* [alternative numbering 46].—Formerly, incorrectly, *cimiliarcho*. I explained what a *cimiliarchium* is in the note to Letter 10, now Letter 20, of Book I.

---

## LETTER XLII. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He should warn Salustius not to trouble Luminosus, a servant of the Church, any longer.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

Luminosus, the bearer of this letter, asserts that he and his wife have suffered violence from Salustius, a man of illustrious rank, and has been compelled to come here by the necessity created by this situation.

Since he claims to be a servant of Saint Mary, which is in the parish of Grumentum, it is necessary that he be protected by ecclesiastical defense. Let Your Experience therefore not cease to provide ecclesiastical assistance to the petitioner mentioned above, and warn the person against whom he complains to restrain himself from troubling them.

If, however, he believes that he has some reasonable claim against them, let the matter be settled by the judgment of chosen arbiters, and let whatever is determined be fulfilled in every respect through your execution.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLII* [alternative numbering 48].—Grumentum is an inland city of Lucania, now commonly called Agrimente, says Gussanville, following Holstenius. Holstenius, in his notes on Ortelius, writes: “After more careful consideration, he thinks it was Agromentum, on the right bank of the river Aciris.” But what connection has Romanus, the defender of the Syracusan region in Sicily, with Agromentum in Lucania? Savinus was defender there in the third indiction, Letters 5 and 6; in this fifth indiction, Letters 21, 22, 23, and 24; and in the sixth indiction, Letter 24. Yet there may have been some reason why this business, Savinus being passed over, was entrusted to Romanus, the defender in the neighboring province. Perhaps Savinus was absent or ill. In any case, this letter occurs for us in only three manuscripts: Vatican A, Victorinus, and Remigius. We observed some variant readings in them, but none of great importance. Here, for example, instead of “of the parish of Grumentum,” the reading is “of the parish of the Church of Grumentum.” The three following letters are likewise absent from all our manuscripts except those three.

---

## LETTER XLIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He says that revenues should be collected in such a way that neither the debtors are distressed nor the Roman Church suffers loss.

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

Our sons Paschasius, a magnificent man, and Plancho, a man of illustrious rank, have complained to us that Your Holiness wishes to receive the revenues owed to the holy Roman Church nowhere except either in the suburb of the city or in the estate called Gelas.

I do not understand that this was done in the way those who murmur suppose. For I know the wisdom of Your Fraternity, and therefore I think that you proposed these arrangements so that, through the proposal itself, you might be able to receive useful revenues at whatever place was possible.

I praise, dearest brother, and warmly embrace the intention of such charity, because you care for our Church—which is certainly yours, just as yours is ours—as you care for your own. Nevertheless, the revenues which my most excellent sons Italicus and the household of Venantius promised are not to be demanded either in the suburb or from the estate of Gelas.

But whether they wish to pay in the Syracusan or the Panormitan district, let Your Holiness devote yourself solely to receiving beneficial revenues, according to the promise of the agreement or security which we sent.

Thus let Your Holiness make provision so that neither my aforesaid beloved sons are distressed by the loss of what they need from their suburban properties, nor our Roman Church suffers any loss or diminished benefit in receiving their revenues.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLIII* [alternative numbering 49].—Remigius reads “Paschasinus … and Blanca.” Vatican A and Victorinus read “and Blanco.”

**Note:** We have already observed that there were two stations of the Roman Church’s patrimony in Sicily at which rents and payments were made: Syracuse and Palermo.

---

## LETTER XLIV. TO ANTHEMIUS, THE SUBDEACON

The price is to be repaid to Accellus, who had redeemed Stephen from the enemy for eight solidi.

Gregory to Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania.

Stephen, the bearer of this letter, who declares that his wife is a handmaid of our Church, has made it known that he was purchased from the enemy by Accellus the elder for eight solidi. Since he states that he is unable to restore the money, let Your Experience investigate the matter carefully. If you discover that this is so and that he has no means by which he can repay his price, come to an arrangement with the aforesaid elder as far as you can, and confidently restore to him the price which he determines for you. When you come to render your accounts, we shall have whatever you have paid for the redemption of captives restored to you.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLIV* [alternative numbering 50].—Vatican, Remigius, and Victorinus read “his price.” Remigius, together with Victorinus, has *steterit* instead of *statuerit*.

---

## LETTER XLV. TO EUGENIUS, THE DEACON

He grants two plots of land for thirty-six years to needy servants of God.

Gregory to Eugenius, the deacon.

The servants of God of the monastery established in the city of Blera have reported that they are suffering very serious hardship concerning their lands. Since it is our duty to provide help to such persons, we order Your Experience by this authority to hand over to them the tract called Agellus, from the estate of Gratilliana, with its boundaries. We have granted them possession of it for thirty-six years, without prejudice to the rights of our Church.

We likewise grant them, for the same period of years, a small plot of thirty *modii* from the aforesaid estate, which they are known to possess as having previously been given to them by us. Thus, through this provision, the community established there may obtain assistance from this arrangement.

Supported by the authority of this order, let Your Experience not delay handing over the aforesaid lands to them, so that they may remain with a freer spirit in the praises of God.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLV* [alternative numbering 51].—Blera, commonly Bieda, was formerly a city and episcopal see of Tuscia; it is now a town belonging to the patrimony of Saint Peter, near the cities of Sutri and Viterbo and about ten miles distant. Gussanville.

**Note:** Vatican A reads “and the aforesaid estate which…”

---

## LETTER XLVI. TO FELIX, BISHOP OF PORTO

He gives John, a servant of the Church.

Gregory to Felix, bishop of Porto.

Moved by the grace of Your Charity, and wishing not to appear unproductive toward you—especially since we know that you possess too few servants—we therefore give and grant to Your Fraternity, by direct legal donation, John, a servant belonging to the Church, by nationality a Sabine, from the estate of Flaviana, approximately eighteen years old, whom you have already possessed for some time with our permission.

You are to have and possess him, and to claim and defend him as belonging to your right and property; and, as his master, you are to enjoy free discretion under the right created by this donation, whatever you may wish to do with him. You should know that neither we nor our successors will ever act against this deed of our munificence.

We have read and subscribed this donation, written out by our notary, granting you also permission to bind him whenever you wish, without awaiting your formal declaration, with lawful stipulation and surety interposed. Done at Rome.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLVI* [alternative numbering 52].—A direct donation is one made between living persons, because it transfers ownership to the recipient directly—that is, straightforwardly and immediately. Papias: “Direct, because it proceeds in a straight line.” Alteserra.

**Note:** Vatican A and D, the Pratellian manuscript, and both Rheims manuscripts read: “so that, as a master made fully secure in law by this donation, you may enjoy free discretion.”

**Note:** Grammarians and jurists dispute the origin of *stipulatio*: whether from *stips*, “a contribution,” or from *stipes*, “a trunk,” because it should be firm like a trunk.

---

## LETTER XLVII. TO VENANTIUS, BISHOP OF PERUGIA

He should send winter clothing without delay to Bishop Ecclesius, who is suffering from the cold.

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Perugia.

We have learned that our brother and fellow bishop Ecclesius is suffering greatly from the cold because he does not have a winter garment. Since he asked that something be sent to him by us, we have sent through the bearer of this letter an *amphimalum*, a tunic, or a breast-piece, to be sent by you to him without delay.

Therefore, make every effort to send it to our aforesaid brother with all possible speed, and do not fail to report to us in your letters that you have sent it. Since the cold is severe, ensure that there is absolutely no delay in sending it.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLVII* [alternative numbering 53].—In Greek it is written *ἀμφίμαλλον*. It was a garment covered with fleece on both sides, worn over a tunic. Hence Saint Martin, according to Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 2, chapter 1, secretly drew a tunic out from inside his *amphibalum*. *Amphimalum* and *amphibalum* are the same word, although the Latins more commonly use the latter. See Paulinus, Book IV, *On the Life of Saint Martin*; Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 59; Fortunatus, Book III, verse 19. Saint Remigius also uses the word in his testament, preserved by Flodoard, Book I, chapter 18: “I leave to my future bishop, my successor, a white Paschal *amphibalum*.” Cangius proves that it had an attached hood; consult him.

**Note:** Vatican A reads “or a breast garment, as previously for him.”

---

## LETTER XLVIII. TO LUCIDUS, BISHOP OF LEONTINI

He should ordain as priest for the monastery the man whom Abbot John selects from his community.

Gregory to Lucidus, bishop of Leontini.

Our son John, the abbot, has requested that a priest be ordained for him in his monastery from that same community. We have therefore decided to exhort Your Fraternity by this present authority: when he presents to you for ordination as priest a man from his community, carefully investigate everything concerning him that, according to custom, ought to be examined. If nothing is found in him that could stand in the way, ordain him canonically, as is customary.

Grant him no other privilege except that, in his own community, whenever the occasion requires, he may celebrate only the sacred mysteries of the Mass.

In the month of August, in the fifth indiction.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLVIII* [alternative numbering 54].—Thus the reading in the Tours, Norman, Anglican, and one Colbert manuscript. Vatican A has “Lucillus.” The Tellerian and certain other manuscripts have “Leontinus.”

**Note:** The manuscripts—Norman, Tours, and Vatican—have this reading, not “of the priests,” which had previously been printed in Gussanville and others.

**Note:** In two Tellerian manuscripts: “in the month of May, in the fifth indiction.” Certain Vatican manuscripts agree. The better reading is found in Vatican B: “in the month of August.” For in almost all the manuscripts this letter occurs at the end of Book XII. Thus it stands second to last in the Norman manuscript. Nothing proves more effectively that it was written at the end of the fifth indiction, which must have been completed at the beginning of September.

---

## LETTER XLIX. TO ROMANUS, THE DEFENDER

He should support the servants of the palace of the city of Rome when they request from Leontius the grain allowance granted by the emperor.

Gregory to Romanus, the defender.

We believe that Your Experience is not unaware of the hardship suffered by the various offices of the palace of the city of Rome concerning their grain allowances. Since the bearers of this letter have all chosen to send representatives there on their behalf, so that they may deal with our glorious son Leontius concerning the manner in which the grain allowances granted to them by the most serene princes are to be assigned and distributed, and since in this matter they have also asked that Your Experience cooperate with them, we therefore command you—because their poverty and need demand that this be granted even without their asking—that, whenever you see it to be suitable and timely, you provide them with whatever assistance you can.

In this way, what the most merciful princes have granted them through their innate clemency may be obtained by them, and you may not appear to have failed in your duty.

**Note:** *EPIST. XLIX* [alternative numbering 22, seventh indiction].—Vatican A reads “concerning the sons of Antoninus.” The sequence of the letter proves this to be a very bad reading. By “the offices concerned about their grain allowances” we are to understand those who held office.

---

## LETTER L. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He commends those converted from the error of the Monophysites.

Gregory to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria.

The bearers of this letter, who are coming to Sicily, have been converted from the error of the Monophysites and have united themselves to the holy universal Church. As they were proceeding to the church of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, they asked me to commend them to Your Beatitude by my letters, so that they might no longer be permitted to suffer any violence from the heretics who live near them.

One of them says that the monastery in which he lived was built by his parents. He therefore desires to receive authority from Your Holiness that the heretics who are in it either return to the bosom of the holy Church or be expelled from that monastery.

Let what we have reported to you suffice. For we know that Your Beatitude hastens to do with all fervor whatever pertains to zeal for almighty God.

For my part, I ask you to pray for me, because, amid the swords of the Lombards which I endure, I am being severely afflicted by the pains of gout.

**Note:** *EPIST. L* [alternative numbering 55].—On the Monophysites, see above, Book IX, Letter 61, now Book XI, Letter 67. They were an offshoot of the Nestorians and Severians. Gussanville.

---

# BOOK THIRTEEN

In the sixth indiction, the thirteenth year from his ordination.

---

## LETTER I. TO THE CITIZENS OF ROME

The Sabbath is not to be observed according to the letter. On the Lord’s Day the body may be washed when necessity requires.

Gregory, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons, the citizens of Rome.

It has come to my attention that certain men of a perverse spirit have sown among you doctrines that are wicked and contrary to the holy faith, so that they forbade people to perform any work on the Sabbath. What else should I call such men except preachers of Antichrist? When he comes, he will cause both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day to be observed by abstaining from every work.

Because he pretends that he will die and rise again, he wants the Lord’s Day to be held in veneration; and because he compels the people to Judaize, restoring the external observance of the law and subjecting Jewish unbelief to himself, he wants the Sabbath to be honored.

The saying spoken through the prophet, “Do not bring burdens through your gates on the Sabbath day” (Jeremiah 17:24), could be observed for as long as it was permitted to keep the law according to the letter. But after the grace of our almighty Lord God, Jesus Christ, appeared, the commandments of the law, which were expressed figuratively, cannot be observed according to the letter.

For if anyone says that this command concerning the Sabbath must be kept, he must necessarily say that the carnal sacrifices must also be offered and that the command concerning bodily circumcision must still be retained. But let him hear the apostle Paul speaking against him: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5:2).

We therefore understand and observe spiritually what is written concerning the Sabbath. For “Sabbath” means rest. But the true Sabbath is our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever recognizes the light of his faith, yet draws the sins of desire into his mind through his eyes, brings burdens through the gates on the Sabbath.

We therefore do not bring burdens through the gates on the Sabbath if, established in the grace of our Redeemer, we do not draw the burdens of sin into the soul through the bodily senses.

For the same Lord and Redeemer of ours is read to have performed many deeds on the Sabbath, so that he reproved the Jews, saying: “Which of you does not untie his ox or his donkey on the Sabbath and lead it to water?” (Luke 14:5). If the Truth itself did not command that the Sabbath be observed according to the letter, then whoever observes the Sabbath rest according to the letter of the law contradicts none other than the Truth itself.

Another matter has also been reported to me: that perverse men have preached to you that no one ought to wash on the Lord’s Day. Certainly, if someone wishes to wash for the sake of bodily luxury and pleasure, we do not permit this on any other day either. But if it is for the body’s necessity, we do not forbid it even on the Lord’s Day.

For it is written: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29). And again it is written: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14). Whoever forbids care of the flesh in its desires plainly permits it in cases of necessity.

For if it is a sin to wash the body on the Lord’s Day, then on that same day one ought not even to wash one’s face. But if this is permitted for one part of the body, why is it denied to the whole body when necessity demands it?

On the Lord’s Day, however, one must cease from earthly labor and devote oneself entirely to prayer, so that whatever negligence is committed during the six days may be expiated by prayers on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.

**Note:** *LIBER XIII. Alternative: Book XI. Letter I* [alternative numbering 3].—In recent manuscripts the reading is: “Gregory, bishop by the grace of God, to his most beloved…” Hence Gussanville seizes an opportunity to reject this letter almost entirely as spurious. “The entire letter,” he says, “seems altogether to belong to someone other than Gregory.” Yet he offers no reason why it should appear so. We judge otherwise, for it bears the mark of Gregory’s style and is found in almost all the manuscripts. As for the heading, “Gregory, bishop by the grace of God,” it is absent from all the Norman and Colbert manuscripts and from most others, as well as from the old edition. This title is unusual in Gregory’s letters, and therefore we had no hesitation in rejecting it.

**Note:** If we believe Gussanville, it follows from this letter that at that time it was not customary among the Romans to wash on the Lord’s Day. He then adds that some people were troubled by Saint Gregory’s response to Augustine’s tenth question, formerly Book XII, Letter 31, now Book XI, Letter 64. This scruple is certainly vain and should be banished far from the mind of a prudent man. Rather, this letter shows that it was customary at that time among the Romans to wash even on the Lord’s Day. Gregory tells us that perverse men preached against this custom, but he immediately refutes their ignorance and error.

**Note:** The Lord’s Day was to be devoted to prayer and reading, and to gathering publicly in the church, where divine and sacred rites were performed. This accords with natural law and was expressed with respect to the Sabbaths in the law of Moses. In the new law, however, the command was not immediately established, as some think, by an ecclesiastical canon rather than by the will of the emperors. From Justin, Tertullian, and Athanasius it is clear that Christians were accustomed to assemble, or hold synaxes, on the day of the sun, which we call the Lord’s Day; Athanasius implies that sacred rites were scarcely performed on any other day, in *Apology* 2, where he speaks of a broken cup.

The first to issue an ordinance requiring abstention from work on that day was Constantine, around the middle of the fourth century. The law is recorded in the Code, under the title *On Holidays*: “Let all judges, the urban populations, and the offices of every trade rest on the venerable day of the sun. Those living in the countryside, however, may freely and lawfully devote themselves to the cultivation of the fields, since it often happens that grain cannot more suitably be committed to the furrows on another day, nor vines to trenches, lest, through the loss of an opportune moment, the benefit granted by the foresight of heaven be lost.”

Other emperors legislated not so much about work as about legal proceedings. Thus Theodosius permitted emancipation and manumission on the Lord’s Day, while other cases and lawsuits were to cease. Public spectacles and obscene pleasures were nevertheless prohibited.

In Gaul, during the sixth century, several canons were promulgated on this matter and were submitted by our kings for judicial enforcement: the Council of Orléans III, canon 28, in the year 538; the Council of Verneuil, canon 14, in 755; Auxerre, canon 16, in 578; Mâcon II, canon 1, in 585; Narbonne, canon 4, in 589; in the seventh century, Chalon, canon 18, in 650; in the capitulary of Aachen, canon 81, in 789; Arles VI, canon 16, in 813; Rheims, canon 35, in 813; and Paris VI, canon 1, at length, in 829. Gussanville.

These things, dearest sons, guard with steadfast certainty and sound faith; despise the words of foolish men, and do not readily believe everything that you recognize as being said by them. Weigh it instead in the balance of reason, so that, while you resist the wind of error with firm stability, you may be able to attain the solid joys of the heavenly kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Of the Colbertine manuscripts, one, and Vatican F, have “in the month of September, indiction 6.” In Vatican A, however, “in the month of February” is read.]

*(John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 52)*

## Epistle II. To Adeodatus the Abbot

*He unites the monastery of Crateras with his monastery.*

**Gregory to Adeodatus, abbot at Naples.**

As greatly as our spirit rejoices, from the intent of its inward desire, in a congregation of brothers that is well ordered, so greatly is it shaken by vehement sorrow on account of the brothers of the monastery of Saint Marcellinus, who have been abandoned and brought almost to desolation, so that the care of pastoral solicitude may come to their aid more quickly. [Col. 1255B]

[Note: [Col. 1256D] **Epistle II [Al. 4].**—The Norman manuscripts read, “so greatly . . . is shaken by vehement sorrow for those placed in desolation,” omitting the rest. The old editions preferred this reading. The Vatican manuscripts have another reading, at least four of them.]

For the monks of the monastery called Crateras, founded near the city of Naples, are known to have informed us by a petition that the place itself has been almost entirely deprived of the service of God’s servants, so that scarcely any have remained there who are able merely to guard it. For this reason they are known to have tearfully begged and requested us to unite that monastery to your monastery, so that through your care, and thereafter through that of your successors, the place itself might, with God as its author, be ordered according to regular discipline.

But while our brother and fellow bishop Basilius of the Church of Capua was found to be present in this matter, he proved strongly opposed, asserting that the place had once been joined to another monastery of his diocese, and therefore ought by no means to be transferred to the jurisdiction of another Church.

[Note: [Col. 1256D] Recent editions have *monasterio alio*, “to another monastery”; that reading is rejected both by the agreement of the manuscripts and by the rules of grammar.]

Against this objection, the clergy of the Neapolitan Church again replied, with arguments presented in opposition, that the matter was quite otherwise than had been alleged. Since the parties held different views, and we did not wish to appear to establish anything uncertain, we appointed investigators and ordered a judgment to be held between them. When they had reported back, we learned by clear reasoning that our brother and fellow bishop Basilius had no right whatsoever in the aforesaid monastery of Crateras.

[Col. 1256A]

When this became known, we necessarily judged that we ought to grant our consent to the monks’ pious request. By the authority, therefore, of this present decree, we establish that the same monastery of Crateras is to be united to your dependent house.

We particularly admonish you that the place itself must thereafter be ordered by you with divine assistance in such a way that, for as long as the enemy permits, monks appointed by you should continually remain there in the praises of God, but in a time of disturbance they should be recalled within the city to their own cell.

We wish all the property belonging to the same monastery to be carefully sought out and gathered together, and to be suitably arranged as you see fit. Do not permit anyone to withhold anything belonging to that monastery; rather, do not neglect to restore everything to the jurisdiction of the dependent house, which is now yours, so that, when all things have been arranged in a wholesome order, those measures of ours which are pleasing to God, being supported by our authority, may remain unshaken forever.

[Col. 1256B]

## Epistle III. To Adeodatus the Monk

*He permits a donation made verbally before the donor entered the monastic life to be committed to writing and held valid.*

**Gregory to Adeodatus, servant of God.**

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that we grant what those who make just requests seek, especially when piety supports the will of the petitioners and truth does not abandon it.

Since, therefore, before you entered the monastery of Saint Hadrian, where you have taken up the monastic life, and made there a donation of your property, you verbally gave, as you have informed us, houses and gardens within the city, whether cultivated lands or vineyards on the estate called Carsinianus, as well as your shares in the estate of Fulloniacus, and some of your slaves to whom you had granted freedom; and although that donation may stand in law—especially since it is made by those who, abandoning the world with its pomp, choose to devote themselves to the service of God—nevertheless, so that no future time may be able to detract anything from this generosity through the cloud of forgetfulness, you desire to commit it to the memorial record of writing. You therefore ask us to grant you permission for it to be made firm.

[Note: [Col. 1256D] **Epistle III [Al. 5].**—This was one of the six monasteries which Gregory built in Sicily while still urban praetor. Consult the *Benedictine Annals* of Mabillon, Book VI, p. 164. The estate of Fulloniacus is mentioned in Book I, Epistle 9.]

For this reason, by this page of our decree, we freely grant you permission to do so, so that, when everything has been carefully set out by you, and they have learned through your designation what belongs to each of them, they may possess without dispute what has now been given to them in common, and your will concerning what you wished to belong to each person may not remain ambiguous.

Whatever you do with the intervention of such a document, do not doubt that it will be firm and stable, both by the truth of the matter itself and by this authority of ours. For you are not doing something new which the law forbids; rather, you appear to be setting forth something already done, and depositing it in the record of written memory for the wholesome purpose of cutting off litigation.

[Note: [Col. 1257C] He is referring, unless I am mistaken, to Justinian’s Novella 5, a brief extract of which is inserted in the *Code*, Book I, title 2, after Law 13. Law 13 mentions a person left without a written will; and by the force of that law, if Alciatus is to be believed, anyone—even a person dedicated to God—had freedom to make a will and could leave his property to whomever he wished. The following Novella corrected this. Therefore, I say, at the beginning of the sixth century monks were free to make wills and bequeath their property to anyone they wished. See the Authentic *Si qua mulier*, cited in Cause 19, question 3. GUSSANV.]

## Epistle IV. To Januarius, Bishop of Caralis

*He is to settle the dispute between the abbess Desideria and the abbot John, with the assistance of two bishops.*

[Col. 1257B]

**Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Caralis.**

When a dispute over worldly goods arises between religious persons, it must be ended with such priestly care that the controversy cannot grow through delay.

The abbess Desideria, bearer of this letter, has come here and complained that the property of her parents, and likewise of her full brother, which reasonably belongs to her, is being wrongfully detained by the abbot John.

[Note: [Col. 1257C] **Epistle IV [Al. 6].**—The abbess appears to be claiming the inheritance of her parents and of her full brother. This is so in many places. Under Roman law it makes no difference whether they are secular or religious persons: *Code*, “On Bishops and Clerics,” Law 56, *Deo nobis*, § 1. A monastery, however, succeeds to an inheritance in the place of a son. Under pontifical law, those who have professed the rule of Saint Francis are excepted, as may be seen in the Clementine *Exivi*, § *Cum enim*, title “On the Meaning of Words.” Under French law neither monks nor nuns succeed to inheritances; and legal scholars establish this custom by six arguments, which it would take too long to enumerate. GUSSANV. This conflicts with the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 59, and elsewhere; consult its interpreters and commentators. See the *Concordance of the Rules*, p. 995.]

And since she asks for the same case to be brought to an end by judicial proceedings, let Your Fraternity, taking with you our brothers and fellow bishops Innocentius and Libertinus, examine carefully with them the character of this matter. By equal counsel and common deliberation, hasten to show yourselves diligent in deciding it from every side, so that your decision may be free from every suspicion of partiality or negligence, and so that no litigation may remain between them after your judgment.

[Note: [Col. 1257D] Civil laws are used in ecclesiastical judgments. GUSSANV.]

If any uncertainty arising from the law should occur to you in delivering judgment, seek out a wise man whom you know to keep the fear of God before his eyes. Thus, once informed by him what is lawful, your decision will be unable to sustain any reproach.

[Note: [Col. 1257D] We have found this in none of the manuscripts.]

In the month of November, indiction 6.

## Epistle V. To Etherius, Bishop of Lyons

*How provision should be made when a bishop falls ill and cannot perform his office.*

**Gregory to Etherius, bishop.**

Although what we are saying is very sorrowful for us, and fraternal compassion rather urges us to weep than permits us to decide anything concerning what we have heard, nevertheless the responsibility of the government we have undertaken strikes our heart with an insistent goad, compelling us to take great care of the Churches and, before their welfare can perish, to arrange, with God as author, what ought to be done.

[Note: [Col. 1257D] **Epistle V [Al. 7].**—Recent editions read: “fraternal compassion urges us to weep.”]

[Note: [Col. 1258C] In the same editions: “and lest any of their welfare . . .”]

It has therefore come to us through the report of certain persons that a certain bishop has suffered such an affliction of the head that he is accustomed to act with his mind alienated, so that it is necessary to hear groans and weeping. Therefore, lest, while the shepherd is sick, the flock—God forbid—be exposed to be torn by the teeth of the attacker, or the interests of the Church itself perish, we must deal with the matter by prudent provision.

And because, while the bishop is alive, necessity caused by illness, not crime, removes him from his office, reason allows no one else to be ordained in his place unless he himself refuses; if he is accustomed to have intervals of illness, he must, by submitting a petition, acknowledge that he can no longer rise to this ministry, since illness has impaired his intellectual faculties, and he must request that another be ordained in his place.

[Note: [Col. 1258C] Thus five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, all the Rheims manuscripts, and the old printed editions; the sense is excellent. For “unless he refuses” means “unless he renounces the episcopal office.” Recent editors have altered the passage to *alium loco ejus, recusante eo* (“another in his place, he refusing”), thereby giving it an entirely contrary meaning.]

[Note: [Col. 1258C] A bishop is deposed against his will on account of crime; on account of illness he is not deposed unless he himself wishes it. See Book XI, Epistle 47.]

When this has been done, another who is worthy shall be solemnly elected by all and consecrated as bishop. This provision must be made, however: as long as the bishop remains alive in this world, the expenses owed to him are to be supplied from the same Church.

[Note: [Col. 1258C] On pensions, see Thomassinus, Part III, Book II, chapters 29–31. We know that these pensions were twice approved at the Council of Chalcedon for the benefit of Domnus, Bassianus, and Stephanus; yet great caution is needed if they are to be demanded with a clear conscience, and custom does not excuse the practice. I would say more about their legitimate use, had not the author of a French dissertation on pensions anticipated me; he published it in 1671 with approval and privilege. On p. 158 he certainly seems somewhat severe toward veterans who, after thirty, forty, or fifty years of service, obtain their discharge while retaining a pension as support and provision for old age; yet on p. 197 he plainly approves the granting, at assemblies of the French clergy, of pensions for the use of certain persons. But under what title—justice or almsgiving? This generosity comes from the goods of the poor. Still, what is said is said, and I would not withdraw it. For, as Saint Augustine reports more than once, for many people whatever they want is holy. Partly from GUSSANV.]

But if at no time he returns to the exercise of a sound mind, a faithful person of reputable life must be chosen, one who can prove suitable for governing the Church, care for the welfare of souls, restrain the restless under the bond of discipline, manage ecclesiastical property, and show himself mature and effective in all things. Even if he outlives the bishop who is now ill, he must be consecrated in his place.

As for the ordination of priests, deacons, or persons of any other order, if circumstances require it to take place in the same Church, Your Fraternity must understand that the matter is reserved to you,

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Three Vatican manuscripts read, “must know that it is to be reserved.”]

so that, if the Church is in your diocese, you may inquire into the life, character, and conduct of the person chosen for this purpose. If he is found acceptable, and there is nothing in him that canonical strictness can censure, he shall attain the designated order only through your ordination.

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Vatican F reads most correctly: “so that, if it belongs to your diocese.”]

Thus let Your Fraternity act and arrange these matters with vigilant foresight, so that God’s Church may no longer suffer neglect, and so that he may commendably remind his fellow priests to care for venerable places not only by word but also by example.

## Epistle VI. To Brunichild, Queen of the Franks

*Privileges granted to a monastery and hospice, after hearing her envoys, with Bishop Menna absolved. Concerning a bishop who suffered from an illness of the head. Concerning the ordination of a man who had married twice. He will send someone to Gaul to attend a synod. The privileges he sends are to be inserted in the public records.*

**Gregory to Brunichild, queen of the Franks.**

[Note: [Col. 1259D] **Epistle VI [Al. 8].**—The manuscripts disagree here. Vatican A reads, “among the various good things reported of you, this”; Vatican B, more briefly, “among all things, this”; Vatican D and the Rheims manuscript, “among the other things, this”; Vatican E and F and the Remigian manuscript, “among the things found among you, this”; the Norman manuscripts, “among the remaining things, this.”]

Among the other good qualities found in you, this holds first place above all: amid the waves of this world, which commonly trouble the minds of rulers with turbulent agitation, you so turn your heart toward the love of divine worship and the establishment of tranquility in venerable places,

[Col. 1259C]

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Vatican B reads: “you establish tranquility at the very roots.”]

as though no other concern troubled you. Since the conduct of such rulers is generally a great protection for their subjects, we declare the nation of the Franks happier than other peoples, because it has deserved to possess a queen so endowed with every virtue.

Recognizing from your letters that you have built the church of Saint Martin in the suburb of Augustodunum,

[Note: [Col. 1259D] This monastery has continued under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur. On it, consult Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, Book VII, p. 195, and frequently elsewhere, as the indexes will show.]

as well as the monastery of the handmaids of God,

[Note: [Col. 1259D] This is the monastery of Saint Mary, now commonly called Saint John Major; its abbess was Thalassia. See below, Epistle 9, and the *Benedictine Annals*, Book VII, p. 204.]

and also a hospice in the same city,

[Note: [Col. 1260D] Monks under Abbot Senator were responsible for it. It is now a monastery of virgins, under the patronage of Saint Andochius for eight hundred years.]

we rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to almighty God, who moves the sincerity of your heart to undertake these works.

For this reason, so that we too might in some measure share in your good works, we granted privileges to those places, for the tranquility and protection of those dwelling there, just as you wished; nor did we endure delaying even briefly the desires of Your Excellence, which deserved to be embraced.

Moreover, after first addressing you with a salutation of paternal charity, we inform you that, in accordance with your letters, we granted a private audience to our illustrious sons, your servants and envoys Burgoald and Varmaricarius,

[Note: [Col. 1260D] The Tours, Corbie, and Norman manuscripts read *Varmarius*.] They are known to have disclosed to us, with subtle explanation, everything they said had been entrusted to them.

[Note: [Col. 1260D] The printed editions read, “everything you had said.”]

In due course we shall take care to inform Your Excellence what has been done. For, with God as author, we desire with the utmost devotion to complete whatever is possible, whatever is useful, and whatever pertains to establishing peace between you and the commonwealth.

As for Menna (Gratian, II, question 5, chapter 7),

[Note: [Col. 1260D] This is Menna of Telesina in Campania, the bishop who was accused before Gregory and, by his order, returned to Rome; after his case had been examined more carefully, he was finally cleared and sent back to Gaul. For Menna of Toulon was not accused before the Roman pontiff as a bishop in Gaul, but before Virgilius of Arles, his metropolitan and indeed the vicar of the Apostolic See. See Book V, Epistle 54. On the manner of his clearing, see above, Book II, Epistle 33; Book VII, Epistles 18 and elsewhere.]

our most reverend brother and fellow bishop, after investigating what had been said about him and finding him guilty of nothing, and after he had also satisfied the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter under oath, demonstrating that he was free from the charges brought against his reputation, we permitted him to return there cleared and absolved.

For just as it was right that, if he had been guilty in any matter, we should canonically punish his fault, so it was not right that, with innocence assisting him, we should retain him longer or afflict him in any way.

Concerning a certain bishop whom, as the aforementioned distinguished men told us, an illness of the head prevents from administering his office, we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Etherius that, if he has intervals of this illness, he should, by submitting a petition, declare that he is unable to fulfill his office and request that another be ordained for his Church. For while a bishop is alive, and illness rather than guilt removes him from the administration of his office, the canons in no way permit another to be ordained in his place.

But if he never returns to the exercise of a sound mind, a person distinguished in life and character must be sought who can both care for souls and arrange the affairs and interests of that Church in a wholesome manner.

[Note: [Col. 1260D] The printed editions read, “and such a person, if he survives.”]

He must also be such that, if he survives, he may succeed to the bishop’s place.

As for those who are to be promoted to sacred orders or to the clerical ministry, we have decreed that they are to be referred and entrusted to our aforesaid most reverend brother Etherius—provided they belong to his diocese—so that, after an inquiry has been made there, if they are subject to none of the faults condemned by the sacred canons, he himself may ordain them.

Let Your Excellence therefore join your care to our arrangement, so that the interests of the Churches, which you love greatly, may not perish, and so that the rewards owed to your good works may increase.

Likewise, when asked whether a certain man who had married twice could enter sacred orders, we absolutely forbade it according to canonical rule. Far be it from us that, in your time, when you undertake so many pious and religious works, you should permit anything to be done contrary to ecclesiastical institution.

The aforementioned distinguished men, our sons, after presenting their memorandum, requested among other things what they declared had been entrusted to them by your command: that we should send to Gaul a person capable, after a synod had been convened, of correcting, with almighty God as author, everything committed against the most sacred canons.

In this matter we have recognized your concern for the life of the soul and for the stability of your kingdom. For, fearing our Redeemer and observing his commands in all things, you act here so that the government of your kingdom may endure for a long time, and so that after the passage of many years you too may pass from an earthly kingdom to a heavenly one.

At a suitable time, if God so wills,

[Note: [Col. 1261D] Civil wars that then broke out in the kingdom prevented Gregory’s legate from arriving. The synod which the most holy pontiff ardently desired to convene in Gaul against simony, the ordination of neophytes, and other abuses was not held until approximately thirty years later, as is shown by the many letters he wrote on this matter to princes and leading prelates: Book IX, Epistles 106–110; Book XI, Epistles 55, 57, 59–61, 68, and 69.]

we shall take care to fulfill the venerable desires of Your Excellence.

We have therefore endeavored to establish everything that Your Excellence requested for the protection of the places about which you wrote. But, lest the superiors of those places perhaps suppress these decrees of ours at some time because they recognize that certain things are forbidden to them, this same constitution is to be inserted in the public records, so that it may be preserved in the royal archives just as it is in ours.

May almighty God always preserve Your Excellence in his fear,

[Note: [Col. 1261D] The printed editions read: “may he thus fulfill your wishes, in the well-being of [your] sons . . . to whom you commend them.”]

and, through the intercession of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom you commend them, may he fulfill your wishes and those of your most illustrious sons, the kings, your grandsons, in such a way that, as you desire, he may grant you enduring joy in their continued safety.

[Col. 1261D]

[Note: [Col. 1261D] We have observed this date notation only in the Colbertine manuscripts.]

Given in the month of November, indiction 6.

## Epistle VII. To Theoderic, King of the Franks

*He praises the king’s piety and prudence. He discusses the same privileges, his envoys, and the establishment of peace with the commonwealth.*

[Col. 1262A]

**Gregory to Theoderic, king of the Franks.**

We gladly received the words of your letters, which indicated your safety. From them we recognized that your prudence has surpassed your age, so that it is clearly evident that, for the happiness of the Frankish people, the royal reins of Your Excellence’s power have been entrusted to you by the favor of heavenly grace.

Among your other qualities, this too is most worthy of praise and wonder: when you recognize what our most excellent daughter, your grandmother, desires for the love of almighty God, you hasten so diligently to help her

[Col. 1262B]

that by this means you may hold a kingdom with the angels both here in happiness and in the life to come.

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Recent editions read: “and may you live happily here and possess a kingdom in the future.”]

Since this proceeds, by God’s gift, from great discernment of judgment, we have promptly and willingly fulfilled everything that Your Excellence desired, so that the speed of our actions might show how greatly your good works have pleased us.

Moreover, saluting you with paternal affection, we inform you that everything which you entrusted to your illustrious servants, our sons Burgoald and Varmaricarius, to be done with us, has been made clear to us through a private conversation. We have praised you greatly, because you wisely attend to the present, as is fitting, and hasten to secure the future through the intervention of perpetual peace between you and the commonwealth,

[Note: [Col. 1262D] That is, “being united in peace.”]

so that, having become one, you may beneficially extend the stability of your kingdom forever.

[Col. 1262C]

In due course we shall inform you of what has been pleasing to God. For we desire whatever is useful and whatever is shown to be peaceful, and we strive to ensure that it can be accomplished. The only condition is that, in matters which are expedient, the will of God—without whom we can do nothing—must be present together with ours.

May the Holy Trinity always cause you to advance in its fear, and may it order your heart according to a moderation pleasing to itself, so that now your subjects may receive unending joy from you, and afterward you may receive unending joy from it.

## Epistle VIII. To Senator the Abbot

*The privilege of the hospice.*

**Gregory to Senator, presbyter and abbot of the hospice.**

[Note: [Col. 1262D] **Epistle VIII [Al. 10].**—Four Vatican manuscripts, two Tellerian manuscripts, and the Rheims manuscript read “to the abbot of the hospice,” or “of the Frankish hospice.” Corbie reads “to the bishop or abbot of the hospice.”]

[Col. 1262D]

[Note: [Col. 1262D] Some suspect that this privilege and the other two contained in the following two letters are spurious or interpolated. Their conjecture is opposed, first, by the agreement of all the manuscripts, including the Roman ones. For, as the eminent Cardinal Bona testified in a letter sent to Gussanville on October 14, 1670, three privileges for the hospice, for the monastery of Saint Mary, and for the church of Saint Martin of Augustodunum are found in the Vatican manuscripts, indiction 6; they begin: “When the hearts of Catholic kings are stirred by pontifical exhortations.” This testimony is found in column 1147 of the Paris edition of 1675. Certainly, the first privilege is read in at least five Vatican manuscripts, the second in four, and the third in three, as we learn from excerpts of the various readings transcribed from them.

Second, this privilege is praised in the *Life of Saint Hugh*, a monk of Autun, written in the tenth century. At that time Frodoard, in his *History of Rheims*, Book III, chapter 27, mentions another privilege which Pardulus, bishop of Laon, composed at the request of Charles the Bald for the benefit of the convent of Origny—not in his own words, but as the blessed Gregory had dictated it at the request of a certain queen concerning a monastery built by her; Pardulus himself likewise dictated it, repeating the curse which that same Lord Gregory had hurled against the usurper of the monastery. From this it is understood that this privilege, with its imprecations, existed in manuscript codices during the reign of Charles the Bald.

Certainly, in the copy of the monastery of Remigius at Rheims, which is more than eight hundred years old, it is found complete, as it is also in another Rheims manuscript, the Tours manuscript, and those of Colbert, Corbie, England, Normandy, and others.

Finally, to say nothing of the rest, another indisputable letter of Gregory the Great, belonging to this sixth indiction, establishes that privileges for the monasteries of Autun were granted by him at Brunichild’s request: “We granted privileges to those places, for the tranquility and protection of those dwelling there, just as you wished.”

Among these privileges are certain prohibitions imposed upon the superiors of those places, which are found in the commonly printed privileges: namely, that no one who has been ordained abbot or presbyter of the hospice or monastery may dare, by any deception, to rise to the office of bishop.

Certainly, if Gregory the Great had been left to his own character and innate gentleness, no one doubts that he would have refrained from the grave threat found in the closing clause of this privilege. But something had to be conceded to the authority of the queen, who demanded more severe ecclesiastical penalties against violators of her donation.

Thus the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Orléans, in 541, at the request of King Childebert, provided for the property of the hospice of Lyons on the condition that anyone who at any time, whatever his power or order, attempted otherwise should be struck with irrevocable anathema as a murderer of the poor, canon 15.

In similar cases the Fathers of the Council of Paris in 557, canon 1, and the Council of Tours in 567, canon 24, and the Council of Valence in 584, utter the same threats. Thus, in accordance with Brunichild’s wishes and the style and custom of the Gallican Church in the sixth century, Gregory arranged the closing clause of the privileges of Augustodunum. GUSSANV.]

When the hearts of Catholic kings are stirred by pontifical exhortations toward those things for which they ought to be stirred, and are kindled by such ardent desire, with divine grace going before them, that they themselves voluntarily ask for them, they ought to be granted with a spirit as cheerful and joyful as the things they desire would have had to be requested if they had been unwilling to do them.

Therefore, in accordance with the letters of our most excellent sons, the kings Brunichild and her grandson Theoderic, to the hospice in the city of Augustodunum, built by Siagrius, bishop of revered memory, and by our aforesaid most excellent daughter the queen, over which you are recognized to preside, we grant, concede, and confirm by decree of our present authority privileges of the following kind.

We establish that no king, no bishop, no person possessing any dignity, nor anyone else, may, under any pretext or occasion whatsoever, diminish, take away, or apply to his own uses anything that has already been donated to the hospice by our aforementioned most excellent sons the kings, or that may in the future be transferred to it by anyone else from his own lawful property; nor may anyone grant such things to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his own greed.

Rather, we wish everything that has been offered there, or that may be offered there, to be possessed forever, without any disturbance, both by you and by those who succeed you in your office and place, while all such things must in every way serve the purposes for which they were granted: the support and administration of those for whom they were intended.

We further establish that, when the abbot and presbyter of the aforesaid hospice and monastery dies, no one else is to be installed there through any stratagem of deception except the person whom the king of that province, with the consent of the monks, has chosen and judged worthy to be appointed according to the fear of God.

To exclude every occasion of greed, we add this provision to the present chapter: no king, no priest, nor anyone else, either personally or through an intermediary, may dare to receive gold or any other kind of benefit in connection with the appointment of the same abbot or with any matters belonging to the hospice; nor may the abbot himself presume to give anything on account of his appointment, lest on this pretext the offerings made by faithful people to holy places, or already made, be consumed.

And since many opportunities for deceiving religious persons are sought out by those wicked men, as they are called, we judge that the abbot and presbyter of the aforesaid hospice must in no way be deprived of office or deposed except when the specific cause of a crime requires it.

Therefore, if any such complaint should arise against him, the bishop of the city of Augustodunum must not examine the case alone,

[Note: [Col. 1264D] The printed editions read: “but with six other bishops of his,” a reading which we think must be rejected, both because it conflicts with the Vatican, Norman, Corbie, and other manuscripts, and because someone might falsely infer from it that the bishop of Augustodunum had his own bishops, as suffragans are now commonly called.]

but, taking six other fellow bishops with him, must investigate it with careful scrutiny, so that, when all have judged in agreement, the rigor of canonical discipline may either strike the guilty or absolve the innocent.

By a similar definition,

[Note: [Col. 1264D] Namely, in accordance with the desire of Siagrius and Brunichild.]

and according to the desire of the founders, we decree that none of those who in the future has been ordained abbot or presbyter of the same hospice and monastery may, by any deception, dare to advance to the office of bishop

[Note: [Col. 1264D] The printed editions read: “may dare to advance, lest in any way,” omitting the other words supplied by the Tours manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, five English manuscripts, and all the Norman manuscripts. Our reading seems more correct and more consistent with the mind of Saint Gregory, who often promoted abbots to the episcopate, as Gussanville says very well.]

unless he has first been deprived of the office of abbot and another has been substituted in his place. Otherwise, by consuming the property of the hospice or monastery through unjust expenditure, he might bring about the gravest necessity of destitution for the poor, travelers, and the other people who live from it.

We prohibit the bishop from having the right to take a monk from that place for promotion to an ecclesiastical order, or for any other reason whatsoever, without the consent of the abbot and presbyter, lest this usurpation be carried so far that places which must be built up through the recruitment of people are destroyed through their removal.

[Col. 1265A]

We therefore decree that all these provisions contained in the page of this decree and command of ours must be observed forever, both by you and by all who succeed you in the order and place which you now occupy, and by those whom the matter may concern.

If any king, priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, attempts to act against it, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor, and let him know that he has made himself guilty before the divine judgment through the iniquity he has committed.

Unless he restores what he has wickedly taken away, or mourns what he has unlawfully done through worthy repentance, let him be excluded from the most sacred body and blood of God and our Lord and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the eternal judgment.

But for all who keep what is just toward the same place, let there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace.

## Epistle IX. To Thalassia the Abbess

*The privilege of the monastery of Saint Mary in the city of Augustodunum.*

**Gregory to Thalassia, abbess.**

[Note: [Col. 1265D] **Epistle IX [Al. 11].**—This is how the name of the abbess is read in the Colbertine, Vatican, Norman, English, and other manuscripts of better quality. In some printed editions it appears as *Thessalia*.]

When, concerning matters to which the hearts of Catholic kings ought to be urged by episcopal admonitions, they are so inflamed by ardent desire through the prevenient grace of God that they themselves spontaneously ask for them, such things ought to be granted with an eagerness and cheerfulness proportionate to the fact that, even if they had been unwilling to do what they desire, they should nevertheless have been asked to do it. Therefore, in accordance with the written requests of our most excellent sons, the kings Brunhild and her grandson Theuderic, we grant, concede, and confirm by decree of our present authority the following privileges to the monastery of Saint Mary, where a congregation of God’s handmaids has been established in the city of Augustodunum, founded by the bishop of revered memory, Siagrius, and over which you are recognized as presiding:

We decree that no king, no bishop, no person endowed with any dignity, nor anyone else, under any pretext or appearance of a case, may diminish, take away, or appropriate for his own uses any of the things already donated to that monastery by the kings mentioned above, or that may in the future be bestowed upon it by anyone else from his own lawful property, or concede them to others under the guise of pious causes as an excuse for his own avarice. Rather, we wish everything that has been offered there, or that may happen to be offered, to be possessed from the present time intact and without any disturbance, both by you and by those women who shall succeed you in your office and place; nevertheless, all these things must in every way serve the needs of those for whose support and administration they have been granted.

[Note: Other editors thought it sufficient to begin this letter with the words “in the city of Augustodunum,” to which they added “etc.,” as above. Yet many things in the sequence of this letter differ from those read in the preceding [Col. 1266D]. Hence we judged that it should be printed in full, after first collating it with three Vatican manuscripts, the Colbertine, the English, and the Norman.]

We further decree that, when the abbess of the aforesaid monastery dies, no other woman shall be installed there through any device of subterfuge, except one whom the king of that province, with the consent of the nuns, shall have chosen and determined to be installed in the fear of God.

We also append this provision to the present chapter, so that we may exclude an opportunity for avarice: no king, no priest, nor anyone else, either personally or through a substitute, may dare to accept gold or any other kind of advantage in connection with the appointment of that abbess or with any matters pertaining to the monastery itself, nor may the same abbess presume to give anything on account of her appointment, lest on this pretext the offerings made by the faithful to holy places, or already made, be consumed.

[Note: In three Vatican manuscripts: “or offered to the sacred place.”]

And since, as is said, wicked men there seek out many opportunities for deceiving religious women, we decree that the abbess of that monastery may in no way be deprived of her office or deposed, except when the particular cause of a crime requires it. Therefore, if any such complaint should arise against her, not only shall the bishop of the city of Augustodunum examine the case, but, taking six other bishops as his colleagues, he shall investigate it with careful scrutiny, so that, when all have judged concordantly, the severity of canonical discipline may either strike the guilty woman or absolve the innocent.

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts in question read “religious women.”]

[Note: The same codices read “not the bishop alone.”]

We therefore decree that all these things contained in the page of this command and decree of ours [Col. 1266C], both by you and by all those women who shall succeed you in the order and place in which you are, as well as by those to whom it may concern, are to be observed perpetually. But if any king, priest, judge, or secular person, recognizing this page of our constitution, should attempt to act against it, let him lose the dignity of his power and honor, and let him acknowledge that he has rendered himself guilty before the divine judgment on account of the iniquity committed, and so forth, as in the preceding letter.

## LETTER X. TO LUPON, ABBOT

Privilege of the Church of Saint Martin in the suburb of Augustodunum.

**Gregory to Lupon, priest and abbot.**

[Note: Letter X [formerly 12].—In the Colbertine manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts, “to Lupus.”]

When, concerning matters to which the hearts of Catholic kings ought to be urged by episcopal admonitions [Col. 1266D], they are so inflamed by ardent desire through the prevenient grace of God that they themselves spontaneously ask for them, such matters ought to be granted with an eagerness and cheerfulness proportionate to the fact that, even if they had been unwilling to do what they desire, they should nevertheless have been asked to do it. Therefore, in accordance with the written requests of our most excellent sons, the kings Brunhild and her grandson Theuderic, regarding the Church of Saint Martin, which is in the suburb of the city of Augustodunum, etc., we grant the privileges described above.

[Note: In the praised Vatican manuscripts: “Saint Platinus.”]

[Note: This letter is almost identical to the eighth, with only certain words changed. For where the other letter names an abbot and monks, this one reads “priest and clerics.” Moreover, here everything between the words “may absolve” and the final clause, “We therefore decree all these things,” is omitted. This privilege occurs in only a few manuscripts, perhaps because of its similarity to the preceding one. It exists complete in Vatican manuscripts E and F and in the Colbertine manuscript, and in half-length form in Vatican manuscript A.]

As above, Letter 8.

## LETTER XI. TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF SALONA

He will henceforth believe nothing reported by that man’s agents unless they have a legally signed mandate.

**Gregory to Maximus, bishop of Salona.**

We had previously written other letters to Your Fraternity; but, at the time when we wished to release your men whom you had sent to us, we discovered from certain of our people that you had written that you had not at all sent the priest Veteranus and the defensor Optatus at that time in the matter, and that therefore what had been done with them ought not to stand. [Note: See above, Book X, indiction 3, Letter 36.] Thomas also, the defensor of your Church, stated that you had told him this verbally. For this reason we have now judged that even the bearers of the present letters should not be believed, lest the same thing should afterward be said about them.

[Note: Letter XI [formerly 13].—The Rheims manuscript and Vatican manuscript D read: “but at the time when you sent your men to us, we did not wish to quarrel by sending what we had written concerning your having said certain things to some of our people.”]

Since, therefore, this matter has made us very doubtful and has warned us that we ought to be cautious, if you wish to present your case, henceforth send an informed representative with a mandate legally executed and strengthened by the signatures of yourself and of the priests or deacons as testimony, and with the proceedings entered according to custom, so that whatever may be done with that representative may have legal force.

[Note: You will find its form in the Digest, Book III, Title 3, Law 65: “He must send his letter, indicating whom he has appointed as agent against him and in what case, and that he will ratify what has been done with him,” etc. Here, since ecclesiastical matters are at issue, the mandate had to be strengthened by the subscriptions of priests and deacons; yet this practice later fell into disuse when the clerical body was dissolved. AUGET.]

[Note: In four Vatican manuscripts: “and by the signatures of witnesses.”]

For we are ready, with God’s help, to safeguard in every respect what is just and lawful, not only for you but also for everyone; only be careful not to omit what the law requires you to do.

## LETTER XII. TO PASCHASIUS, BISHOP OF NAPLES

Jews are not to be prevented from observing their solemnities, but are to be encouraged toward conversion by admonitions and kindness.

**Gregory to Paschasius, bishop of Naples.**

Those who sincerely desire to lead outsiders from the Christian religion to the true faith (Grat., Distinction 45, Chapter 3) ought to strive by kindness, not harshness, lest hostility drive far away those whose minds a reasoned explanation might have brought to the level ground.

[Note: Letter XII [formerly 15].—Recent printed editions, disregarding the manuscripts, read *extraneos ad Christianam religionem* (“outsiders to the Christian religion”) instead of *extraneos a Christiana religione* (“outsiders from the Christian religion”).]

[Note: That Jews and unbelievers should be treated gently, see above, Book I, Letter 34, now 35, and many other places; nevertheless, he determines something further concerning pagans: their profane rites are not to be tolerated. GUSSANVILLE.]

For whoever acts otherwise, and under this pretext wishes to suspend them from the customary observance of their rite, is shown to be attending more to his own interests than to the causes of God.

The Jews living in Naples have indeed complained to us, asserting that certain people irrationally attempt to prevent them from some of the solemn festivals of their religion, so that they are not permitted to observe the solemnity of their feasts, although until now they and their parents have been permitted, throughout a long period in the past, to keep and celebrate them. If the truth is as they say, they appear to be laboring over a useless matter. For what benefit is there if, contrary to long-established custom, they are forbidden these observances, when this contributes nothing to bringing them to the faith and to conversion? Or why do we establish rules for Jews about how they should observe their ceremonies, if by this means we cannot win them?

We must therefore act so that, attracted rather by reason and gentleness, they may wish to follow us rather than flee from us; so that, with God’s help, by showing them from their own books the truth of what we say, we may bring them into the bosom of Mother Church. Accordingly, let Your Fraternity, as far as possible and with God’s help, kindle them by admonitions toward conversion, and do not again permit them to be disturbed concerning their solemnities. Rather, let them have free permission to observe and celebrate all their festivals and holy days, just as they and their parents have held and celebrated them until now over a long period of time.

[Note: Above, Book III, now Book IV, Letter 21, Saint Gregory had already prescribed many things concerning the Jews. That text is reproduced in the Extravagants, Book V, Title 6, Chapter 2, together with many others whose arguments the brevity of this note does not permit us to include. If you wish to know what the most pious laws are to which Saint Gregory refers in the letter, reader, consult the Code, Book I, Title 9, “Concerning Jews and Worshipers of Heaven.” They appeared so pious that, many centuries later, the pontiffs Alexander III and Clement III issued judgments in accordance with them. In brief, in regions that tolerate Jews, they are allowed to conduct their solemnities, to possess cemeteries and synagogues, to restore those threatened with collapse, and to use Christians as quasi-enrolled dependents; and it is forbidden to compel them to the faith. From the laws—both imperial and pontifical—concerning pagans and heretics, extract for yourself, diligent reader, the foundations of the difference. To assist you, I point out Distinction 45, Chapter 5, “Concerning Jews,” from the Fourth Council of Toledo, and Cause 23, Question 5, Chapters 33, 43, and 44; likewise the Extravagants, Book V, Titles 6 and 7. Historians show that pagans and Jews have scarcely ever lived peacefully together. Yet that the Jews, the most hostile, fiercest, and most implacable enemies of Christians, should be admitted and retained by Christians in their cities is truly astonishing. It is long since Gaul expelled them. GUSSANVILLE.]

## LETTER XIII. TO BARBARUS, BISHOP OF BENEVENTUM

He appoints him visitor of the Church of Palermo according to the customary formula.

[Col. 1268C]

**Gregory to Barbarus, bishop of Beneventum.**

[Note: Letter XIII [formerly 16].—Recent editions read “to the bishop of Beneventum.” We preferred the reading of the old printed editions, supported by the authority of the Rheims manuscript, four Vatican manuscripts, two Colbertine manuscripts, and others. In one Colbertine manuscript, with the title “bishop” suppressed, only “to Barbarus of Carinae” appears. Carinae was formerly an episcopal city among the Bruttians, not far from Rhegium. Rochus Pirrus, volume II, page 461, thinks that another city of this name in Sicily, not far from Palermo, is intended; it was built from the ruins of the town of Hyccara. Yet he says that he is uncertain whether it ever had a bishop. I do not see why Saint Gregory, contrary to custom, entrusted the visitation of the Church of Palermo to a bishop of Beneventum or Carinae situated so far away, unless perhaps he was already detained in those regions by other business, or because he knew the man to be industrious and to have performed that office excellently on another occasion, as when he entrusted him with the visitation of the Church of Hortanum, Letter 39 of Book III, now Letter 41 of Book IV, etc. Partly from GUSSANVILLE.]

A direct report has made known the death of Victor, bishop of the city of Palermo (Grat., Distinction 61, Chapter 16). Therefore, we solemnly entrust to Your Fraternity the visitation of that Church, now left without a bishop, and you must carry it out in such a way that no one presumes to appropriate anything belonging to that Church—whether the advancement of clerics, revenues, furnishings, ministries, or anything else whatsoever in its patrimony.

Accordingly, Your Affection shall hasten to go to the aforesaid Church and shall promptly admonish its clergy and people by frequent exhortations, so that, setting aside factional zeal, with one and the same agreement they may seek to have appointed for themselves a priest who may be found worthy of so great a ministry and who may in no way be rejected by the venerable canons. When he has been requested, he shall come to us to be consecrated with the solemnity of a decree strengthened by the signatures of all and with a letter bearing the testimony of Your Affection.

We also admonish Your Fraternity not to permit anyone from another Church to be elected, unless perhaps—something we do not believe can happen—no one worthy of the episcopate can be found among the clerics of that very city in which you are carrying out the visitation. Above all, take care not to permit a layperson of any manner of life or merit to aspire to this office, lest both their efforts prove fruitless and you, which God forbid, incur danger to your own order.

[Note: The following material to the end of the letter is absent from five Vatican manuscripts, the Tours manuscript, the Rheims manuscript, the Colbertine manuscript, and almost all the others. Nevertheless, it exists in other letters that are entirely similar.]

As for any monasteries established within his diocese, we grant that they shall remain under your care and administration until a bishop of their own has been appointed there.

## LETTER XIV. TO THE PEOPLE OF PALERMO

They are to obey Barbarus, the bishop and visitor.
