[Note: Letter XIV [formerly 19].—This letter is missing from the English and Norman manuscripts. It is found, however, in the Colbertine manuscript, both Rheims manuscripts, the Tours manuscript, and five Vatican manuscripts.]

**Gregory to the clergy, the order, and the people residing in Palermo.**

When we learned of the death of your bishop, we took care to entrust solemnly the visitation of the Church left without a bishop to our brother and fellow bishop Barbarus. We gave him instructions not to permit anyone to usurp anything belonging to the advancement of clerics, revenues, furnishings, or ministries.

You ought to obey his frequent exhortations and, setting aside agitation, with one and the same agreement seek to have appointed for you a priest who in no respect diverges from the venerable canons and who may be found worthy of so great a ministry. When he has been requested, he shall come to us to be ordained with the solemnity of a decree strengthened by the signatures of all and accompanied by a document from the visitor.

Above all, take care that you do not presume to elect a layperson of any manner of life or merit. Know that not only shall such a person in no way be promoted to the summit of the episcopate, but also that you yourselves will be unable to obtain pardon by any intercessions. Moreover, know without doubt that all among you who are found to have sought to elevate a layperson shall be excluded from office and communion.

## LETTER XV. TO VENANTIUS, PATRICIAN OF PALERMO

Urbicus the elected abbot is worthy of the episcopate, but one who resists is not to be compelled. The character of the deacon Crescentius is to be investigated. If they agree neither on this man nor on another, envoys are to be sent to Rome.

[Col. 1270B]

**Gregory to Venantius, patrician of Palermo.**

[Note: Letter XV [formerly 14].—In Vatican manuscript D: “to the clergy and people of Palermo.” In the Norman manuscript: “to the patrician of Palermo.” In three Vatican manuscripts: “to the patrician of Palermo.”]

We inform Your Excellency that your choice of the abbot Urbicus has greatly pleased us, since, as was fitting according to your prudent judgment, you sought for the governance of the Church a man who was watchful and conscientious and who had been formed in knowledge of Sacred Scripture, which is especially to be sought in priests.

[Note: Evangelical knowledge is especially required in bishops. Hence it may perhaps be prescribed in the consecration of bishops that two bishops place and hold the Book of the Gospels over the head and neck of the man being ordained.]

Yet, just as one person ought to be placed before others in such a way that, while he advances outwardly, he does not decline inwardly, we cannot disturb his peace, lest, when we lead him to higher things, we force him, cast amid the waves, to become less than his former self.

As for the person of the deacon Crescentius, because he is entirely unknown to us, our first concern was to inquire how he had governed the hospice over which he had presided, so that from small matters we might learn what he could be expected to be in great ones. But you will learn from the bearers of your letters themselves what they answered us.

[Note: In the printed editions, erroneously: “but this ... to you.” We corrected this error chiefly from the Norman manuscripts.]

Let Your Excellency know, however, that it is altogether difficult for us to provide a priest, because the necessity of persons burdens us considerably when we must appoint pastors to other places left without shepherds.

[Note: As often happens, quite a number were seeking ecclesiastical honors, and were pressing toward them not merely by entreaty but also by payment, as many of Saint Gregory’s letters show. Yet few worthy men were found who could swim in so vast a whirlpool. Hence the holy man’s distress. For he did not wish to confer benefits upon men, but through men to provide for the Church. Read Letter 148, now Letter 21, of Saint Augustine, where it is clear how great was the zeal of the pontiffs in seeking good workers, how carefully good men avoided these dignities, and what worldly people thought of such promotions. GUSSANVILLE.]

And because we know that you fear God and have regard for your souls, after first offering you the greeting of paternal affection, we exhort you, as is fitting, to investigate inwardly, with careful and diligent inquiry, the life, character, and conduct of the aforesaid deacon. If you recognize that he is capable of rising to the governance of the Church, let everyone unite around him at your exhortation.

But if your attentive judgment thinks otherwise and considers that he cannot effectively administer pastoral care, you must act in agreement with everyone so that they may choose another from that very Church whom they judge suitable. Thus, when both the deacon who has already been elected and the one who still must be elected come to us, the one who is pleasing to God may be ordained.

Indeed, if no such person can be found in that Church among the priests or deacons or the rest of the clergy, let them hasten to choose for ordination as bishop from another Church a man who, with watchful care for their external interests and with priestly exhortation for their souls, may, by God’s mercy, prove useful to them.

Moreover, lest there be any delay in this matter, and lest their sins result in none of those elected being suitable, the clergy and people should be exhorted to send word by those who come to us that they have permission to make a choice here, and they should inform us of this very fact in letters confirmed by their own signatures, so that, if someone suitable can be found here, he may be consecrated without any difficulty, with the cooperation of Christ’s grace.

[Note: Thus read the Vatican, Norman, Remigius, and other manuscripts; the printed editions have “and, because of their sins, no one.”]

We say this not because our will has driven us to it, but because necessity has compelled us, since, as far as the judgment of our authority is concerned, we wish them to have a pastor from among their own.

## LETTER XVI. TO PASSIVUS, BISHOP OF FIRMA

He instructs Passivus to consecrate a monastery in honor of Saint Sabinus according to the customary formula.

[Note: Letter XVI [formerly 20].—This letter is also absent from the Norman and English manuscripts, although it is found in four Colbertine manuscripts, five Vatican manuscripts, both Rheims manuscripts, and the Tours manuscript.]

**Gregory to Passivus, bishop of Firma.**

Proculus, deacon of the Church of Asculum, informed us by a petition that, out of his devotion, he had founded on his own property at Gressian a monastery which he desires to have consecrated in honor of Saint Sabinus the martyr.

[Note: Asculum, commonly called Ascoli, formerly called Picenum, to distinguish it from Asculum, which was called Apulum or Satrianum, commonly Ascoli di Satriano. The former belonged to the province of Picenum; the latter to Apulia Daunia. It is still an episcopal city of the March of Ancona, subject to the Roman pontiff. GUSSANVILLE. In the Tours and Colbertine manuscripts it reads “of the Ascularian Church” instead of “of the Asculan Church.”]

Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid building lawfully belongs to your parish and it is established that no body has been buried there, then, after first receiving a lawful donation—namely, one *conduma*, one pair of oxen, five head of cattle, twenty head of sheep and goats mixed together, at the Gressian estate, where the monastery is being founded, eight ounces, at the estate of Stacianus eight ounces, the entire estate of Paternus, ten pigs, bedding, and, with the municipal records attached, etc.—according to custom, you shall consecrate it.

[Note: For the meaning of *conduma*, see again Note b on Letter 20 of Book XI, indiction 4.]

[Note: Four Vatican manuscripts and the Colbertine manuscript read: “five head of bronze objects.”]

[Note: Vatican manuscript D and the Rheims manuscript read: “where the priest of the monastery is founded.”]

Given in the month of December, indiction 6.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads “in the month of January.”]

## LETTER XVII. TO JOHN, SUBDEACON OF RAVENNA

He urges Bishop Marinianus to order the dispute with Bishop John to be settled without litigation. Otherwise, he himself is to press for judgment and execute the sentence. He disapproves of the construction and dedication by Bishop Exuperantius of an oratory in John’s diocese.

[Note: Letter XVII [formerly 21].—This letter is preceded, both in two Colbertine manuscripts and in most Vatican manuscripts, by the date “in December, indiction 6,” and afterward by “in January, indiction 6.” Since those two dates cannot both belong to one and the same letter, perhaps the first belongs to the preceding letter and the second to this seventeenth one.]

**Gregory to John, subdeacon of Ravenna.**

The bearer of this letter, our brother and fellow bishop John, is known to have informed us, through a written memorandum, of certain matters concerning his Church. Once these had become known, we would have had to blame Your Experience if matters brought to your attention had remained unresolved until now. But on inquiry we learned that they had not at all been brought to your notice. Therefore, we have had the very memorandum presented to us appended below.

When everything has been learned and examined, if the truth clearly shows that matters stand with you as has been reported, we wish you to visit our brother and fellow bishop Marinianus and exhort him in every way to appoint people to deal with those matters in which his Church is recognized to have an interest, so that, after everything has been weighed, they may settle among themselves in ecclesiastical peace whatever disputes have arisen with the aforesaid man.

But if they choose to resist, let Your Experience be intent on rendering judgment; and whatever sentence is determined after the matters between them have been investigated, let it be completed through your execution, lest, by prolonged delays, the poverty of his Church—already burdened, as he asserts, by various losses—be aggravated still further.

He has also reported to us (Grat., Cause 16, Question 5, Chapter 3) that a certain bishop, Exuperantius, with rash presumption, built an oratory in his diocese and, without the authority of a command, presumed to dedicate it contrary to custom, and did not fear to celebrate public Masses there. It is your duty to correct this matter with the utmost speed and strictness, and not to permit anything of the kind to be attempted again. If you find that the oratory was built by an incompetent person, then, if the matter is established to be as stated, we wish you, together with its proper bishop, to restore it without any delay.

## LETTER XVIII. TO CERTAIN BISHOPS OF SICILY

[Note: Letter XVIII [formerly 22].—The printed editions, against the English, Norman, and Vatican manuscripts, read “special [assistance].”]

He commends Adrian, administrator of the patrimony. He admonishes the bishops not to burden their subjects excessively when they go out to confirm infants.

**Gregory to Leo, Secundinus, John, Donatus, Lucidus, and Trajan, bishops of Sicily.**

Just as we are admonished to impart spiritual assistance to one another through the prayer of the apostles, so, in matters which the necessity of the government entrusted to us requires us to arrange, with God as our guide, for the administration of the goods of the poor, it is fitting that priestly support should not be lacking.

We have therefore considered it necessary to commend to Your Fraternity the bearer of this letter, Adrian, our chartularius, whom we are sending to administer the patrimony of our Church in the region of Syracuse, so that, whenever practical necessity requires it, you may offer him your assistance, in order that, while he is supported by your physical help in carrying out his duties and by the spiritual assistance of your prayers in accomplishing what he has begun, he may, with God’s cooperation, successfully complete what has been entrusted to him by us.

[Note: Recent editions read incorrectly: “your assistance to them.” The reference here is plainly to Adrian alone.]

You yourselves, however, must display yourselves before the sight of almighty God in good works, so that nothing may be found in your conduct which, with God as judge, could be punished or which any human adversary could accuse. For we have instructed our aforesaid chartularius that, if he discovers anything improperly done by any of our most reverend brothers, the bishops, he should first correct it privately and modestly by exhortation; if it is not thereby amended, he should quickly make it known to us.

Moreover, it has been reported to us (Grat., Cause 10, Question 3, Chapter 9) that, in the time of my predecessor of holy memory, arrangements were made through the deacon Servusdei, who at that time was already administering the ecclesiastical patrimony, that the priests established throughout your various dioceses should not be burdened beyond measure whenever you went out to confirm infants.

[Note: The common editions read “throughout all [the dioceses].” Here the word “priests” means priests, or parish clergy established throughout the dioceses. The term was not so exclusively proper to bishops that it was never applied to priests, as some critics have thought. Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius, chapters 6 and 9, includes priests under the designation “priest.” The same may be seen in his letter to Exuperius, chapter 1. Likewise, in his letter to Decentius of Gubbio, he had said: “For although priests are priests,” etc. So also Siricius in his letter to Himerius. See Letter 13 of Book III.]

A fixed amount had been established, with your consent, as I hear, which those same priests were to give for the labor of the clerics. Yet this arrangement, which was then approved, is now, as is said, not being observed at all. Therefore, I admonish Your Fraternity not to strive to be burdensome to your subjects, but, if there are any burdens, to moderate them, since you ought not to depart from what was once determined. Indeed, you provide for yourselves both in the present life and in the future if you preserve without burden those who have been entrusted to you.

## LETTER XIX. TO JULIAN

He complains that Julian concealed his poverty out of embarrassment. After building a monastery at Catania, he assigns it ten solidi annually.

**Gregory to Julian.**

When I received the letter of Your Glory, I opened it gladly to read it, but after reading it I closed it in sadness. For it said that, out of embarrassment, you had kept silent for a long time about matters that ought to have been told to me. It is certain that the one who is still treated with embarrassment is loved less. I was therefore altogether saddened, because I discovered that I was loved by you less than I had thought.

You greatly support me in this respect if you diligently ask me to make continual provision for the means of your reward. Nor ought you to be ashamed to speak insistently of alms to one who plainly possesses not his own resources, but resources for distributing to the poor. You ought therefore to have spoken freely with the bishop about the causes of reward, even if you did not know what my disposition was toward you in affection.

[Note: This word does not always have the same sense in Gregory; sometimes it means mercy, French *merci*, as in Book III, Letter 16; here it seems to mean a stipend and reward, acquired through the proper distribution and disbursement of the Church’s goods.]

For since we greatly love Your Glory and, as you know, hold the position of steward of the goods of the poor, I confess that your embarrassment was highly blameworthy. I pursue it with so many words of rebuke for this reason: that I may drive it completely from your heart and may find great consolation in your provision in matters of reward.

[Note: Letter XIX [formerly 23].—Thus all the Norman, Vatican, and Colbertine manuscripts, the Regius manuscript, and most of the manuscripts, including the better ones. The Rheims manuscript reads “you honor me.” Here *continere* means “to cherish” or “to assist.” See above, Book V, Letter 30, Note b. In the same sense, among Saint Gregory’s writings *continentia* means a stipend, as is clear from Book V, Letter 52, Note e.]

Therefore, for your monastery, which you have built in the city of Catania, we have assigned ten annual solidi to be given through Adrian, our notary and administrator of the patrimony, after issuing a written command. We ask that you receive them without injury or offense, because this offering is not ours to you, but the blessing of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, that is being offered to you.

[Note: The printed editions add “in the month of February, indiction 6,” which is absent from all our manuscripts.]

## LETTER XX. TO HONORIUS, BISHOP OF TARENTUM

He permits the use of a newly built baptistery.

**Gregory to Honorius, bishop of Tarentum.**

[Note: In one of the Colbertine manuscripts this letter is addressed to Bishop Bonus of Tarentum.]

From a report by Your Fraternity we have learned that, in the city of Tarentum over which you are recognized as presiding, you have recently built a baptistery in the Church of Saint Mary. Therefore, dearest brother, having received this authorization from our present authority, you shall fulfill the object of your desire, so that there the stains of sins may be washed away through the sacred bath.

[Note: In Vatican manuscripts A, B, and E, this letter is preceded by the date “in February, indiction 6.” Two other manuscripts agree.]

In the month of February, indiction 6.

## LETTER XXI. TO PASCHAL AND CONSOLANTIA

He extends the time granted for repayment of money. He consoles them in adversity.

**Gregory to Paschal and Consolantia.**

[Note: Letter XXI [formerly 25].—This is how it is read in the Tours, Colbertine, Norman, and nearly all the other manuscripts, as well as in the old Venetian edition of 1504 and the Paris and Lyons editions. In the Vatican printed edition it reads “to Paschal, consul of Sicily.” In many manuscripts “of Sicily” is added after “Consolantia.” Indeed, in one Colbertine manuscript the entire title appears as in the Vatican edition.]

We received the letter of Your Greatness, delivered by the bearer of this one. Although the time granted for repayment of the money has elapsed, we nevertheless judged that your petition should in no way be met with sadness. We have therefore presently instructed Adrian, our chartularius, whom we sent there to administer the patrimony of our Church, concerning what he ought to discuss with you, so that neither the interests of the Church may be neglected in any respect nor your request fail to obtain its result.

Since you ought to be more concerned for the salvation of your souls than for the advantage of earthly things, we greet you with paternal affection and exhort you not to let your mind, weighed down by the burden of tribulation, murmur against God, lest, after the loss of property, losses to your souls should also follow. Do not hasten to acquire anything through wicked acts or with sin, as though necessity were compelling you; rather, placing your hope in the mercy of our Redeemer, who does not abandon those who trust in him, bear patiently the difficulties you have endured.

Lift up your spirits. Let tribulation not crush your strength. Let patience overcome the adversities of the world. Let a tranquil mind disdain the pomp of the world. Let your conduct occupy itself with the things that belong to God, considering how insignificant is everything subject to chance and everything enclosed by an ending.

Let your heart not afflict itself beyond what is fitting, but strive to trust rightly in the protection of almighty God, who gives what was not possessed, restores what was lost, and preserves what has been restored. For if he knows that you walk in the path of his commandments, he is able both to repair the damages inflicted with manifold compensation and to grant you the eternal life which ought to be sought with every greater effort.

## LETTER XXII. TO RUSTICIANA, PATRICIAN

He indicates that he grieves over her ill health. Weary of his own sufferings, he longs for death. She is to act with the emperors so that they restrain Beator from plotting perversely.

**Gregory to Rusticiana, patrician.**

[Note: Letter XXII [formerly 26].—We have restored the text in this form from five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman manuscripts, the Colbertine manuscripts, the Regius manuscript, and others, as well as from John the Deacon. Most printed editions incorrectly read “Rusticia.” This is the Rusticiana the patrician to whom Gregory sent several letters; concerning her, see what we said in Book II, Letter 21, indiction 10, now Letter 27. GUSSANVILLE.]

[Column 1275D] Whenever someone comes to us from the royal city, it is our concern to inquire about the health of your body; but, because of my sins, I always hear what grieves me to hear, since they report that, amid such frailty and weakness, the pains of gout are still increasing in you. But I beseech almighty God that everything taking place in your body may be directed toward the salvation of your soul, that temporal scourges may prepare eternal rest for you, and that through those pains which have an end he may grant you joys without end.

[Note: [Column 1275D] In the Norman manuscripts: “who directs all things . . .” “May the temporal scourges [Column 1276D] prepare eternal rest for you.” Four of the Vatican manuscripts and both Rheims manuscripts agree as far as the final words: “may he direct. The scourges,” and so forth.]

As for me, I live amid such groaning and burdens that I regret having reached the days I am living, and my only consolation is the expectation of death. Therefore I ask you to pray for me, so that I may be brought more quickly out of this prison of flesh and not be tortured longer by such great pains.

[Column 1276B] Moreover, I report that a certain man named Beator has come here, who wishes to be called, as it were, “count of the private estates,” and who is acting against everyone in many ways, but especially against the men of Your Excellency and against those of your most noble granddaughters, as though he were seeking public property.

[Note: [Column 1276D] Previously, erroneously, “count of the private attendants” was read. On this office, see Cassiodorus, *Book VI of the Variæ*, chapter 8, where it says that this is the *comes privatarum*, from the private substance of the emperors which he administered.]

We indeed do not permit him to act perversely, but neither can we oppose public interests. You, therefore, act with the most devout emperors, as you are able, so that they may forbid him to engage in wrongdoing. For amid all the commotion, neither is any public benefit being achieved, nor is there any substantial advantage in what he appears to be demanding.

I ask that my sweetest son, Lord Strategius, be greeted on my behalf. May almighty God nurture him for himself and for you, and may he always console you through his grace and through that child’s life. As for your return, what should I write, when you know how greatly I desire it? But when I look upon the obligations of the cases, I am driven to despair. Therefore I beseech the Creator of all things that, wherever you are and wherever you may be, he protect you by the extension of his right hand and preserve you from every evil.

## LETTER XXIII. TO BONIFACE, NOTARY OF CORSICA

He urges John the cleric to come to Rome to be examined.

Gregory to Boniface, notary of Corsica.

[Note: [Column 1276D] *Letter XXIII* [Former numbering 27].—Below, letters 38 and 40. Boniface is sent to Constantinople, but is first ordained a deacon. Accordingly, here we do not think *Constantinopolitan* should be read, although it appears in all printed editions and in most manuscripts. It is not found in the Pratellian and other Norman manuscripts.]

We postponed doing what your experience informed us about John, the cleric of Ravenna, because we cannot judge the character of an absent person.

[Note: [Column 1276D] In the same manuscripts and in three Vatican manuscripts: “because, in the person’s absence, or in the absent person, we cannot judge . . . concerning the character of the person . . . but urge him to come to us.”]

But urge him to hasten to come to us, so that, after carefully learning in person both his conduct and his character, we may determine without any uncertainty what should be done concerning the things he requests.

## LETTER XXIV. TO SAVINUS, SUBDEACON

He is to assist Bishop Proculus in restoring what had been neglected during his absence.

Gregory to Savinus, regional subdeacon.

Your experience is not unaware of why our venerable brother Bishop Proculus has been absent from his Church for a long time.

[Note: [Column 1277D] *Letter XXIV* [Former numbering 29].—He was bishop of Nicotera, as appears from Book IX, letter 48, indiction 2.]

Since, by God’s favor, he has now returned to it after making the satisfaction and purification that was required, we do not want the usefulness of his Church to have been neglected in any respect during his absence, or anything belonging to its rights to have been taken away. Therefore, because he wishes to restore or correct these matters, we want you to support and assist him in everything, while maintaining equity, so that, strengthened by your aid, he may neither encounter any difficulty through the obstruction of certain people in the matters he must undertake, nor have to labor longer than necessary.

## LETTER XXV. TO SAVINUS, SUBDEACON

He is to admonish Bishop Palumbus to protect the property of the Churches more diligently; otherwise he himself is to perform the bishop’s duties.

Gregory to Savinus, regional subdeacon.

It has come to our attention that our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Palumbus—something grievous to say—is neglecting the affairs and interests of his Church or parishes, so that he carelessly allows not only certain properties or dependents of theirs, but also their offices, to remain in the hands of various people.

[Note: [Column 1277D] *Letter XXV* [Former numbering 30].—Previously *Proculus* was read, but six manuscripts of excellent quality which we consulted, similar to the editions of 1504, 1508, 1539, and other ancient editions, read *Palumbus*. Palumbus appears to have been bishop of Consentia, who is mentioned in Book VII, letter 4, indiction 1, now Book VIII, letter 3. GUSSANVILLE. Saint Gregory also writes to him in Book IX, letter 47, indiction 2. Hincmar praises this letter in *Opusculum* 33, chapter 43. The same author cites many letters of Saint Gregory: the third letter of Book IX in the capitularies of Charles the Bald, title 7, final chapter; the eighth of that same book in *Opusculum* 33, chapter 17; and, in the same work, letter 108 of the ninth book. Chapter 20 cites letter 107 of the aforementioned book. Chapter 22 cites letter 45 of Book XI, to Theoctista, who had been accused of heresy; chapter 36, letter 13 of that same Book XI; chapter 43, letter 47 of Book IX. Finally, in *Opusculum* 42, or in the letter written in the name of Charles the Bald to Pope Adrian, a notable testimony is cited from Book IX, letter 116.]

This is also suggested and partly confirmed to us by the fact that Gregory, the bearer of this letter, who states that he belongs by right to the Emolita Church, which is situated in your diocese, complains that, in Palumbus’s presence, he is being unlawfully subjected to another’s service.

Therefore, let your experience diligently admonish our aforesaid brother to reclaim and defend, reasonably, the property and offices of his Churches or parishes, and in no way permit them to be held by others. In this matter, lest he perhaps be able to find some excuse, we want you to offer him your assistance, while preserving equity. But if you should find him negligent, as he has been until now, we want you to undertake and carry out in every respect what he ought to have done, so that the interests of the Churches may not suffer any loss on any pretext.

[Column 1278A] But hasten to report to us everything that has been done, so that we may instruct you about what you should do thereafter.

[Note: [Column 1278D] We found this in no manuscripts.]

Given in the month of March, indiction 6.

## LETTER XXVI. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is to rebuke Bishop Paschasius’s negligence before selected witnesses.

Gregory to Anthem­ius, subdeacon of Campania.

It has come to our attention that our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius is so inactive and negligent in everything [Gratian, *Distinctions* 84, chapter 1] that no one recognizes him as a bishop in any respect. Thus neither his Church, nor his monasteries,

[Note: [Column 1278D] *Letter XXVI* [Former numbering 31].—The printed editions read “sons of the Church.” We find the final word in neither the Vatican nor the Norman, Colbert, or other manuscripts; we therefore judged it should be rejected. Yet anyone wishing to retain it may do so. We explain who the sons of the Church are in the notes on Book III, Letter 56.]

nor his sons, nor oppressed poor people experience his devoted care toward them; nor does he grant any assistance of protection to those who petition him in matters where justice requires it. And, what is still more serious, he refuses by any means to accept the advice of wise men who offer sound counsel, so that he might at least learn from another what he cannot attend to himself.

Instead, leaving aside the matters that belong to a pastor’s care, he occupies himself uselessly and with all his energy in building ships. Hence, as it is reported, it has happened that he has already lost four hundred solidi or more. The following is also added to his faults: he is said to descend daily to the sea with one or two clerics in such a contemptible manner that he has become a laughingstock even among his own people, and appears so mean and despicable to outsiders that he is judged to possess nothing episcopal, whether in character or in dignity.

[Note: [Column 1278D] Harsh words are to be conveyed to a bishop by a subdeacon; and what follows is no less severe, being intended to be reproached before others. Let those who disapprove of this correction and of the injury to episcopal dignity write to Saint Gregory—I say, let them accuse the most vigorous defender of that same dignity, if they can. AUGET.]

If this is so, recognize that you are not without blame, since you have delayed rebuking and restraining him as is proper. Because all this not only condemns him personally but is also shown to constitute a disgrace to the priestly office, we want you to confront him about this before other priests or certain noble members among his sons, and exhort him so that, having shaken off the fault of sluggishness, he may no longer be inactive, but may be vigilant in the care of his Church and monasteries; may show fatherly affection toward his sons; may stand ready to defend the poor with discernment, wherever justice demands it; and may willingly accept the advice of wise men.

In this way, that city may be comforted by his solicitude, and he himself may cover over the faults of his inactivity. But if—as we do not believe—after this exhortation of ours he should still attempt to remain negligent in his customary manner, he must by all means be sent to us,

[Column 1279A] so that, placed here, he may learn what a priest ought to do, and how, according to the fear of God.

[Note: [Column 1279D] This sentence is prefixed in three Vatican manuscripts and two Colbert manuscripts.]

Given in the month of March, indiction 6.

## LETTER XXVII. TO ANTHEMIUS, SUBDEACON

He is to summon the bishops of Campania who have forgotten their duty and admonish them to act more vigilantly. If afterward he finds anyone negligent, he is to send him to Rome.

Gregory to Anthem­ius, subdeacon of Campania.

Whenever we hear such reports about our brothers and fellow bishops as both show them to be blameworthy and are capable of causing us sorrow, necessity compels us to think seriously about their correction. Since, therefore, it has been reported to us that the bishops of Campania are so negligent [Gratian, *Distinctions* 84, chapter 2] that, forgetful of their honor and episcopal dignity,

[Note: [Column 1279D] *Letter XXVII* [Former numbering 35].—The holy man repeatedly explains what the honor and dignity of bishops require. Here he mentions four things: devotion toward the Churches; the care of fatherly vigilance toward their sons; solicitude for monasteries; and protection of the oppressed and the poor. In Letter 26, to Anthem­ius, he attributes nearly the same qualities to a bishop and attacks sluggishness and inactivity in both letters. AUGET. See the similar manner of expression above, Letter 25.]

they show neither fatherly vigilance toward their Churches or their sons, nor concern for monasteries, nor devote themselves to protecting the oppressed and the poor, we therefore command you by this authority to summon them and, in our name, admonish them sternly. They must no longer remain inactive, but must demonstrate by their conduct that they possess priestly zeal and solicitude. They must be so vigilant in those matters which they ought rightly to undertake according to God that no further complaint about them may exasperate us.

But if, after this, you discover any one of them to be negligent, send him to us without any excuse, so that he may come to recognize through proper discipline how serious it is to refuse correction in matters that are blameworthy and deserving of severe reproach.

[Note: [Column 1279D] See Saint Peter Damian, Book I, Letter 12, to Alexander II. Saint Chrysostom, Homily 24 on Acts, chapter 11: “They remonstrated with him . . . it happened by a singular dispensation that he [Peter] was rebuked, so that these men might learn . . . But see how far he was from arrogance and vainglory. For Peter, when he began, set the matter before them in order,” and so forth. In his homily *On Bearing Reproofs*, he likewise gives the example of Moses, rebuked by his father-in-law, a barbarian. “He was not puffed up,” he says, “either by the greatness of his authority or by the miracles he had performed; nor was he ashamed because he was corrected before so many people, and those his subjects. Rather, he considered that, although great signs had been wrought by him, he nevertheless shared human nature, from which many things are often hidden; and therefore he accepted the advice with meekness. One may now see some people,” and so forth. AUGET.]

## LETTER XXVIII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF SYRACUSE

He is to restore the priest Cosmas, who had been distressed by the character of the place to which he had been appointed, to his former position.

[Column 1279C]

Gregory to John, bishop of Syracuse.

It has come to us through the report of certain people [Gratian, *Distinctions* 74, chapter 6] that Cosmas, formerly a monk of the monastery of Saint Lucy, made a subdeacon in the Church of Syracuse by your predecessor, Maximian of venerable memory, and afterward, as is said, ordained by you as a priest in the estate called Juliana, has been so afflicted by excessive sorrow and by the character of the place that he considers life itself a punishment,

[Note: [Column 1280D] *Letter XXVIII* [Former numbering 36].—Gratian: “let him seek help by fleeing from his sorrow.” This reading is supported by the Colbert and Regius manuscripts.]

and seeks relief by fleeing from his anguish.

Therefore, since we ought to be toward our subjects the kind of superiors we would have wished our own superiors to be if we had been subjects, it would be an act of great kindness if Your Holiness were willing to bring him back to the Church in which he served as a subdeacon and appoint him there as a cardinal priest. We think you ought to do this, provided there is nothing that justly provokes your displeasure against him. But if there is some fault, let your Fraternity disclose it to us by letter, so that we may know.

[Note: [Column 1280D] In the same Colbert manuscript: “in the month of May, indiction 6.” But shortly before, in that manuscript and in another Colbert manuscript, as also in the Regius manuscript cited immediately afterward, it reads: “in the month of April, indiction 6.”]

Given in the month of April, indiction 6.

## LETTER XXIX. TO PHILIP, PRIEST

He rejoices that Andrew died and reached eternal joys. He asks Philip to obtain the same from God for him. He sends him fifty solidi.

[Column 1280B] Gregory to Philip, priest.

[Note: [Column 1280D] *Letter XXIX* [Former numbering 28].—This is how the ancient editions and manuscript codices read. Other copies incorrectly have “to Philip, bishop.” GUSSANVILLE.]

I have received the letters of your affection, in which you took care to inform me that the venerable man Andrew, the priest, has departed from this light. I rejoiced at his release, because he has reached the eternal joys he always desired.

As for the solidi left by our son Abbot Probus at Jerusalem for the construction of a hospice,

[Note: [Column 1280D] In Vatican manuscripts D and F: “which were left . . . for our son Abbot Probus”; this reading gives the passage a different meaning.]

what had been decided and ought to have been done could not be changed. But I have sent Your Holiness a small gift of fifty solidi. Therefore pray earnestly for me, as I believe you do, so that almighty God may rescue me by his hand from the sea of the present life and grant me rest on the shore of eternal life.

For here I suffer the heavy oppression of swords and the tumult of lawsuits. But if you love me, show it by praying, so that I may feel the intercession of your prayer and no longer be afflicted amid so many evils and disturbances. May almighty God protect you with his hand and grant you, together with your own, to reach the heavenly blessings.

In the month of May, indiction 6.

[Note: [Column 1280D] *Letter XXX* [Former numbering 37].—In three Vatican manuscripts this letter is prefixed with “in the month of April, indiction 6.”]

## LETTER XXX. TO DEUSDEDIT, BISHOP OF MILAN

He is to send Theodore with the Defender to Venantius to investigate Theodore’s complaints.

Gregory to Deusdedit, bishop of Milan.

Our brother and fellow bishop Theodore complains that he is suffering many things contrary to justice and to the promise of Your Holiness, things which we have not readily considered credible. But since we cannot leave these matters without investigation, we have assigned his case to our brother and fellow bishop Venantius for examination, so that he may investigate it carefully and report back to us.

Therefore let Your Fraternity send Theodore, together with the defender of his Church, promptly to the aforementioned brother, so that the latter, once he has learned the truth of the matter, may inform us by his own letters.

## LETTER XXXI. TO PHOCAS, THE EMPEROR

The worst kings are appointed to punish the sins of the people, and the best to console their subjects. He urges Phocas to assist the afflicted commonwealth.

Gregory to Phocas Augustus.

[Note: [Column 1281C] *Letter XXXI* [Former numbering 38].—We have already observed, in Book V, Letter 39, note d, that the hymn *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, formerly customary in times of rejoicing and thanksgiving, was used on such occasions. That the ancient custom of expressing joy by singing this hymn continued until the time of Charlemagne is clear from Anastasius in his account of Leo III: “Then, embracing one another, they kissed with tears”—Leo and Charles—“and when the aforementioned pontiff began the *Gloria in excelsis Deo*,” and so forth. A little later, however, the *Te Deum laudamus* began to be sung in place of this hymn. Thus, when Pope Stephen was received at Rheims by Louis the Pious, the various orders of the Church sang, in such great jubilation, *Te Deum laudamus*, and so forth, as is recorded in the Life of Louis the Pious.

Among the Greeks it had likewise become customary to use the words *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, and so forth, in giving thanks, as Chrysostom explicitly teaches in Homily 3 on chapter 1 of the Epistle to the Colossians.

Everyone knows on what occasion this letter was written. In earlier editions, at the beginning of Book XI, now Book XIII, it appears under the heading of Letter 1: “On Phocas having been crowned,” and so forth. We have judged, however, that this material should be sent to the end.

Some accuse Gregory of having written too harshly about Maurice and flatteringly about Phocas. Yet, to say nothing of the many ways in which Maurice was hostile to Gregory—especially in the controversy with John of Constantinople, who assumed the title “ecumenical,” in the ordination of Maximus of Salona, and in the attempt to make peace with the Lombards, indiction 13, Letter 40—and to say nothing of the fact that Maurice’s notable qualities were then disfigured by extraordinary brutality and a shameful stain of greed, when he preferred to have a great number of captives slaughtered rather than redeem them by paying the very small price that Chagan had set for each one, it is certain that the exarchs sent to Italy to protect the remnants of the empire against the Lombards brought greater damage upon the Italians through their incompetence and avarice than the enemies themselves.

Gregory also complains that the islands adjoining Italy were oppressed by excessive exactions, in Book V, Letter 41. Thus, hoping for more equitable times, he writes to Phocas: “May the crushed and depressed spirits of your subjects be lifted up by your mercy.” In Letter 38: “We owe the Lord praise, because, once the yoke of sorrow has been removed, we have reached an age of liberty under the pious kindness of Your Imperial Clemency.” Finally, in Letter 39: “We owe thanks to God because the heavy burdens of so long a time have been removed from our necks, and the gentle yoke of imperial rule has returned.”

Indeed, at the very beginning of his reign Phocas displayed great clemency and generosity toward his subjects—but falsely, to be sure, so as to win over the minds embittered against him by both the avarice and brutality of his predecessor. Saint Gregory, however, did not foresee that his character would soon change for the worse, and that Phocas would afterward surrender himself to obscene lusts and glut himself with the blood of the best men. Even if he had foreseen that this would happen, he ought in his letters to speak about the present state of affairs, not the future.]

“Glory to God in the highest,” who, as it is written,

[Column 1281B] “changes the times and transfers kingdoms”; and because all have learned what he has deigned to declare through his prophet, saying: “The Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever he wishes” (Daniel 4:14).

For in the incomprehensible ordering of almighty God, the conditions of mortal life alternate. Sometimes, when the sins of many must be punished, one person is raised up, through whose harshness the necks of subjects are bent beneath the yoke of tribulation—as we have experienced during our prolonged affliction. At other times, when merciful God has determined to refresh the sorrowful hearts of many with consolation,

[Note: [Column 1282D] The printed editions, against the manuscripts, read: “to refresh the hearts of the grieving by his bestowal.” With the manuscripts before us, we have changed many other readings in this letter; since they are minor matters, we have not considered it worthwhile to mention them.]

he elevates one person to the summit of rule, and through the compassion of his mercy pours the grace of rejoicing into the hearts of all. We believe that we are quickly strengthened by this abundance of rejoicing, since we rejoice that Your Piety’s kindness has reached the imperial height.

[Column 1281C] Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult (Psalm 95:11), and let the entire population of the commonwealth, hitherto greatly afflicted, rejoice now in your kind actions. Let the proud minds of your enemies be crushed beneath the yoke of your rule. By your mercy let the broken and depressed spirits of your subjects be raised up. Let the power of heavenly grace make you terrifying to your enemies, and piety make you kind to your subjects.

Let the entire commonwealth rest in your most fortunate times, with the plunder of peace advanced under the appearance of legal proceedings. Let the intrigues surrounding wills cease, and the favors in donations that have been extorted by force. Let secure possession of their own property return to all, so that they may rejoice to possess without fear what they have not acquired through fraud. Let the liberty proper to each person under the yoke of a pious empire now be restored.

[Note: [Column 1282D] We noted the same point above, in Book VIII, Letter 51, now Book X. GUSSANVILLE.]

For this is the difference between the kings of the nations and the emperors of the commonwealth: the kings of the nations are lords of slaves, whereas the emperors of the commonwealth are lords of free people.

But we speak these things better by praying than by giving advice. May almighty God hold the heart of Your Piety in every thought and deed by the hand of his grace, and may the Holy Spirit, dwelling in your breast, kindly order whatever must be done justly and mercifully,

[Note: [Column 1282D] Thus the Norman manuscripts, especially the Tours manuscript. The printed editions read: “so that, after the course of many years, Your Clemency may be exalted from the temporal kingdom,” and so forth.]

so that Your Clemency may be exalted in the temporal kingdom and, after the passage of many years, may reach the heavenly kingdoms.

[Note: [Column 1282D] We have found this nowhere except in two Colbert manuscripts, where it nevertheless appears to belong to the following letter.]

Given in the month of June, indiction 6.

## LETTER XXXII. TO EUSEBIA, PATRICIAN

He urges her to think more about the things of the soul than about those of the body.

[Column 1282C] Gregory to Eusebia, patrician.

[Note: [Column 1283C] *Letter XXXII* [Former numbering 39].—She appears to have been the daughter of the patrician Rusticiana, from Book II, Letter 21, now Book II, Letter 27, indiction 10; Book III, Letter 44, now Book IV, Letter 46. GUSSANVILLE.]

Even if your mind, occupied with wealth,

[Note: [Column 1283D] The Rheims manuscript and Vatican manuscript D read “with divine activities,” or perhaps the reading found also in the old edition.]

or perhaps entangled in the tumultuous affairs of the royal city, postpones visiting us by letter, it is nevertheless our duty to pursue the hearts of children who have turned away with sweet affection and to call them back to a kind disposition both by admonition and by prayer.

Therefore, while now offering you the greeting that is your due, I urge Your Excellency to turn your mind away from that city’s needless disturbances and to think more about the things of the soul than about those of the body. Consider that everything here is transitory. Daily, without ceasing, contemplate with fear and tears the dreadful judgment of the Judge who is to come, and bring to mind with dread that day on which everything will be thrown into confusion, so that on that very day you may not fear the Judge’s anger.

May almighty God pour these thoughts into your mind through the inspiration of his Spirit, and may he grant you both to live here in peace with your most noble husband and to rejoice in the health of Lord Strategius,

[Column 1283B]

[Note: [Column 1283D] I think he was the son of the aforementioned Eusebia, and thus the grandson of Rusticiana; I infer this from Book VII, Letter 23, now Book VIII, Letter 22, indiction 1; Book IX, Letter 33, now Book XI, Letter 44; and Book XI, Letter 26, now Book XIII, Letter 22. GUSSANVILLE.]

and, after long ages, to reach eternal rewards.

[Note: [Column 1283D] “In the month of June, indiction 6” could be added, since this is how the beginning of this letter reads in three Vatican manuscripts.]

## LETTER XXXIII. TO SMARAGDUS, EXARCH

He urges him to protect Bishop Firminus, who has returned to the unity of the Church, from Severus’s harassment. Cillanus will observe the thirty-day truce, but the Pisans refused to make an agreement.

Gregory to Smaragdus, patrician and exarch.

Formerly, most excellent son, we knew with what desire and conversion of mind, for the uniting of God’s Church in the regions of Istria, through zeal for our Redeemer and love of eternal reward, the fervor of your devotion had been manifested.

[Note: [Column 1283D] *Letter XXXIII* [Former numbering 40].—Thus the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, Rheims, and other manuscripts read more correctly than the printed editions, which have “for aiding.”]

Since this is so, we have not ceased to bring to your attention what has recently been reported to us from those regions. For our brother and fellow bishop Firminus, bishop of the Tergestine Church,

[Note: [Column 1283D] Tergestum, commonly Trieste, is a city of Istria situated on the border of Carnia, in the innermost recess of the gulf called the Gulf of Trieste after it. It has a capacious harbor and is an episcopal see under the patriarch of Aquileia, or the archbishop of Udine. GUSSANVILLE. We read *Tregestum* in five Vatican manuscripts, in all the Norman manuscripts, and even in the old edition; we are therefore compelled to follow them.]

having, before the arrival of Your Excellency, recovered through sound counsel from the schism to which he had adhered and returned to the unity of Mother Church, was confirmed by our letters so that he might remain firmly and steadfastly fixed in the true bosom of Mother Church, which he had come to recognize.

When Severus, bishop of Grado,

[Note: [Column 1284C] Patriarch of Aquileia after Elias, to whom Pelagius II wrote. When Aquileia was burned by the Lombards, he transferred the see to the Church of Grado, the leader of the schismatics in those regions. See what we said concerning Book I, Letter 16. GUSSANVILLE.]

the head of that same schism, heard this, he first began, if he could, to recall him from his good resolve by various persuasions.

[Note: [Column 1284D] The printed editions have “with various rewards,” and so forth, but at least most manuscripts disagree.]

When, by God’s authority, he was entirely unable to accomplish this, he did not hesitate to stir up a revolt against him among his fellow citizens. You will be able to learn more fully and more reliably, on the spot, how much our aforementioned brother and fellow bishop Firminus suffered from this incitement.

Therefore, by written commands sent to Your Excellency, order those who, by God’s authority, are known to act in your place in the regions of Istria to defend our aforementioned brother from the harassment inflicted upon him and by every means to secure his peace, which will be useful to many as an example to imitate. In this way, your provision will be both the desired security of those who have converted and an appropriate opportunity for those who follow.

Accordingly, while greeting Your Excellency with paternal affection, we ask that the fervor of the zeal you once displayed in this matter now burn more intensely, and that the enemies of God find you all the more their avenger and defender, the more precious the defense of a soul is before God than the defense of the body. Let the uprightness of the faith flourishing in you arm you against the erring; let the torn body of the Church in those regions be restored in your time.

In this matter you have God as the rewarder of your work and the author of uprightness and integrity. For we trust in divine mercy that our external enemies will find you so much stronger against them as the enemies of the true faith perceive you, through God’s love, to be terrifying to them.

Moreover, we sent two letters to Cillanus,

[Note: [Column 1284D] Thus all the Norman, Tours, and Colbert manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts. Other copies read *Varacinallem* or *Vasaccillonem*. We found *Tilquinum*, as in the printed editions, in no manuscript.]

to ask whether he would keep the peace that had been made by Your Excellency for thirty days.

[Column 1284C] He replied that he would keep it, provided it was also observed toward him by the party of the commonwealth. He released all the men whom he had held, together with their property. But he is deeply grieved over the men of his own side who were killed, and he is extremely suspicious of you, since, if he finds an opportunity—which God forbid—there is no doubt that he will overstep the bounds even in time of peace.

[Note: [Column 1284D] Pisa, commonly Pisa, is a renowned city of Etruria, now an archbishopric.]

As for the Pisans, we sent our man to them some time ago in the manner and on the terms we ought to have used, but he could obtain nothing. Hence we have been informed that their *dromones* are already prepared to set out.

[Note: [Column 1284D] On this word, see above, Book VIII, formerly Book X, Letter 37. These ships were also called *Liburnae* or *Liburnicae*, after the Liburnians, peoples of Illyria. Horace, *Epode* 1:

“You will go in Liburnian ships amid the lofty  
battlements of the vessels, my friend.”

Cassiodorus mentions the rowers of dromons in *Variæ*, Book IV, Letter 15.]

## LETTER XXXIV. TO PANTALEON, NOTARY

He praises him for reducing the measure of the *modius* by which the Church’s tenants delivered grain to a just measure. He orders that the money obtained from the unjust measure be secretly distributed among poorer tenants.

[Column 1285A]

Gregory to Pantaleon, notary.

Your experience remembers what kind and what sort of oath you gave before the most sacred body of blessed Peter the apostle. Therefore, trusting in your inquiry, we have also entrusted to you a matter for investigation in the patrimony of the Syracusan district. You must always keep your fidelity and fear of that blessed apostle Peter before your eyes, and act so that you may be found blameworthy neither by human beings in the present life nor by almighty God at the final judgment.

[Note: [Column 1285D] *Letter XXXIV* [Former numbering 41].—Previously *Valerius* was read, but the Norman, English, Vatican, Colbert, and other manuscripts compelled the change. The *modius* mentioned here must have contained only sixteen *sextarii*. See the notes on Book I, Letter 44. From this it is clear how great a fraud was committed by the Church’s administrators, a fraud which the holy pontiff rightly curses.]

For, as our *chartularius* Salerius reported, we learned that you had discovered that the *modius* by which the Church’s tenants were compelled to deliver grain contained twenty-five *sextarii*. We utterly condemned this and regretted that you had conducted this examination so late. Since, therefore, you state that you have broken that *modius* and made it just, we rejoiced.

But because the aforementioned *chartularius* also took care to inform us of the sum that has now been collected through the frauds of the lessees in two territories under your administration, just as we rejoice that you diligently corrected the unjust measure, since we foresee its benefit for us in the future, so we also think about past sins, lest, if what the lessees fraudulently took from the peasants reaches us, the sins committed by them should be transferred to us.

Therefore, with complete faith and purity, with deliberate fear of almighty God and with the strictness of blessed Peter the apostle recalled to mind, we want your experience to draw up, for each estate, a record of the poor and needy tenants. From the money found to have been obtained by fraud, you are to purchase cows, sheep, and pigs and distribute them to the individual poor tenants.

We want you to do this with the advice of the most reverend Lord Bishop John, and of our *chartularius* and administrator Adrian. If advice makes it necessary, our son Lord Julian should also be included, but no one else is to know; the matter must remain entirely secret.

[Column 1285C] You must discuss among yourselves whether the same provision should be given to these poor tenants in gold or, rather,

[Note: [Column 1285D] Three Vatican manuscripts, A, B, and F, read “in livestock.” *Pecunia* means whatever human beings possess on earth; whatever they own is called *pecunia*: a slave, vessel, field, tree, animal—whatever belongs to these categories is called *pecunia*, says Augustine in *On Christian Teaching*, chapter 1, as cited in *Causa* 1, question 3, chapter 6.]

in money. Whatever you jointly decide, first make the record as I have said, and afterward distribute it to each person according to the extent of his poverty.

For, as the Apostle to the Gentiles testifies, “I have all things, and abound”; and I seek not money but a reward (Philippians 4).

[Column 1286A]

Act, therefore, so that on the day of judgment you may show me the fruit you have produced from the matter of benefit entrusted to your charge.

[Note: [Column 1285D] Here “reward” appears to be understood as a benefit. See Book III, Letter 3, note d.]

If you act purely, faithfully, and energetically, you will receive the return for this here in your children, and afterward you will have a full recompense at the judgment of the eternal Judge.

## LETTER XXXV. TO CATULUS AND ROMANUS

He is to assist the Defender Optatus in removing extraneous women from the companionship of priests.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1286D] EPISTLE XXXV [Elsewhere 42].—In the Anglic and Norman manuscripts alone it reads *to Catulus and Romanus*. *Wintharith* is added in five Vatican manuscripts, the Rheims manuscript, and the old Colbert manuscript. In the second Colbert manuscript: *to Romanus in the Cartulary*. In the third: *to Romanus and Winthareth in the Cartulary*. In the fourth: *to Catulus, Romanus, and Wictarith*. In the fifth: *to Catulus and Romanus*. The recent printed editions have *Victor* instead of *Wintharith*.] to Catulus, Romanus, and Vintarith.

It has come to our attention that those who have been constituted in the sacred order within the territory of Nursia [Note: [Col. 1286D] On Nursia, see note b on chapter 1 of Book XI of the *Dialogues*.] [Note: [Col. 1286D] In the Norman manuscript: “sluggish and very indecent.”] are living with unrelated women. Since this is a grave and very [Col. 1286B] indecent matter—indeed, 1243 exceedingly so—we have instructed the defender Optatus to exhort them, so that, if this is indeed the case, none of them may henceforth dare to live with unrelated women.

But if they should perhaps disregard his exhortation, we have also charged him to bring the matter to the attention of our brother and fellow bishop Chrysanthus, provided that through him he correct them, or that the aforesaid defender, with his authority, strive to amend the matter. Therefore let Your Greatness cooperate in this matter, as is fitting for you, and commend the same brother to him in every respect, so that, with your assistance, he may beneficially complete what has been entrusted to him and may not be able to labor at other matters contrary to reason.

## EPISTLE XXXVI. TO CHRYSANTHUS, BISHOP OF SPOLETO

He is to restrain the Nursian priests who live with unrelated women.

[Col. 1286C]

Gregory to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto.

From the report of certain persons we have learned that priests of the territory of Nursia are living with unrelated women. For this reason let your Fraternity know that we have been greatly saddened, since previously your Fraternity did not at all tolerate or restrain such things, if indeed you knew of them.

But since we have instructed Optatus the defender to correct this matter by every means, and, if any one of them should wish to appear obstinate in such a matter, to summon him to the judgment of your Fraternity, we have therefore thought it necessary to write to your Holiness. If you know that any of the priests belonging to your diocese are living with unrelated women—or, at any rate, if the aforementioned Optatus reports to your Holiness that he has found them brazen [Col. 1286D] [Note: [Col. 1286D] EPISTLE XXXVI [Elsewhere 43].—In the Norman, Regius, Colbert, and many other manuscripts, *procaces invenerit* (“has found them brazen”) is omitted.]—let him hasten to correct them henceforth, after first giving priestly admonition and, if the matter requires it, applying canonical discipline also, for we cannot endure hearing of such things for any reason.

Your Fraternity should also admonish or rebuke, as appropriate, the presbyter whom they say inflicts violence on very many people without regard for God. If he refuses to listen to you, suspend him from communion, so that at least in this way he may begin to withdraw from his wicked deeds. [Note: [Col. 1287D] These words are absent from all the manuscripts except the Colbert manuscript, where they seem to belong to the following epistle. Whether or not they occur in the Vatican manuscripts cannot be determined with sufficient certainty from the collection of variant readings that has reached us.]

In the month of July, in the sixth indiction.

## EPISTLE XXXVII. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

He grants the use of the pallium.

Gregory to John, bishop of Panormus.

Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See, we have determined to grant the use of the pallium to your Fraternity, which is known to have undertaken the office of watcher [Note: [Col. 1287D] EPISTLE XXXVII [Elsewhere 44].—He alludes to the name *bishop*, which in Greek signifies “overseer.”] of the Church of Panormus, at those particular times and in that manner in which you do not doubt that other priests of the island of Sicily, or your predecessors, also used it.

We admonish you, however, that the reverence due to the Apostolic See not be disturbed by anyone’s presumption. For the condition of the members remains sound only if no injury assails the head of the faith; and the authority of the canons must always remain safe and inviolate, so that, just as you rejoice to have received from us the use of this distinction for the honor of the priestly office, you may likewise strive to adorn the office you have received by the integrity of your conduct and actions. Thus you will be mutually conspicuous through corresponding distinction, if the goodness of your mind also agrees with this bodily vesture.

## EPISTLE XXXVIII. TO PHOCAS THE EMPEROR

He ingeniously excuses the absence of his deacon. He sends Boniface. He implores aid against the Lombards.

[Col. 1287C]

[Note: [Col. 1287D] EPISTLE XXXVIII [Elsewhere 45].—Amalarius cites this epistle in Book IV *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 25.]

Gregory to Phocas Augustus.

It is pleasant to consider, with joy and great acts of thanksgiving, how much praise we owe to the almighty Lord, because, with the yoke of sorrow removed, we have reached an age of freedom under the pious rule of Your Imperial Benevolence.

For the fact that Your Serenity has not found a deacon of the Apostolic See remaining in the palace according to ancient custom was not due to my negligence, but to the gravest necessity. While all the ministers of our Church were fearfully avoiding and fleeing from these harsh and crushing times, none of them could be compelled to go to the royal city and remain in the palace.

But after they learned that, by the grace of almighty God [Col. 1287D] [Col. 1288A], Your Clemency had reached the summit of imperial power, they too, urged on by joy [Note: [Col. 1288D] A mode of expression signifying both great humility of spirit and reverence. Saint Paulinus, *Epistle* 23, to Severus, p. 147: “While I kiss the divine feet, may I dedicate my impure lips to those holy footprints.” Isaiah 60:14: “They shall adore the footprints of his feet.”], hastened to come to your feet, although previously they had been very afraid to approach that place.

But since some of them are so weakened by old age that they can scarcely endure the journey, while others are deeply involved in ecclesiastical responsibilities, and since the bearer of this letter—who was the first of all the defenders and has become well known to me through long and constant association, approved in life, faith, and conduct [Note: [Col. 1288D] Boniface, who is mentioned in Epistle 49, now numbered 42; Gregory also wrote to him in Book XII, Epistle 3, now Book XIV, Epistle 4. He later became supreme pontiff, called Boniface. GUSSANV.]—I judged him suitable to attend upon Your Piety’s feet.

Accordingly, with God as author, I made him a deacon and hastened to send him, so that, when a suitable opportunity is found, he may be able to report to Your Clemency everything that is happening in these regions. [Note: [Col. 1288D] The text formerly read *propter quod rago*. In many other places we have restored this epistle to the integrity of the manuscripts, from which the printed editions had departed.]

I ask Your Serenity to incline your pious ears to him, so that you may be able to show us mercy all the more quickly in proportion as you learn the truth of our affliction from his report. For how we are oppressed by daily swords and by the many incursions of the Lombards—behold, already for the length of thirty-five years—we cannot express fully in any words of petition. 1245

But we trust in almighty God, because he will complete for us the good things of his consolation that he has begun; and he who has raised up pious rulers in the commonwealth will also extinguish our cruel enemies.

Therefore may the Holy Trinity preserve your life for many years, so that we may enjoy for a longer time the goodness of your piety, which we have received only after delay.

(John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 21.)

## EPISTLE XXXIX. TO LEONTIA THE EMPRESS

He congratulates her on attaining imperial power. He prays that divine grace may be granted to her. He commends the Roman Church.

[Col. 1288C]

Gregory to Leontia Augusta.

What tongue could speak, what mind could conceive, how great is the thanksgiving we owe to almighty God for the tranquility of your reign, since the burdens of such a long and difficult period have been removed from our necks, and the gentle yoke of imperial authority has returned, one that subjects may willingly bear? [Note: [Col. 1288D] Thus the Turon, Rheims, Colbert, Norman, Anglic, and Vatican manuscripts read, differing considerably from the common printed text, which has “it has taken up a light yoke.”]

Therefore let glory be rendered to the Creator of all by the choirs of singing angels in heaven, and let thanksgiving be offered by human beings on earth, because the commonwealth, which has endured many wounds of grief, has now found the remedies of your consolation.

For this reason we must pray all the more earnestly for the mercy of almighty God, that he may always hold the heart of Your Piety by his right hand and govern its thoughts by the aid of heavenly grace [Col. 1288D] [Col. 1289A], so that Your Tranquility may rule those who serve you with greater justice in proportion as you know more truly how to serve the Ruler of all.

May he make those whom he has made our emperors through his kindly work defenders of the Catholic faith. May he pour into your minds both zeal and gentleness, so that you may always be able, with pious fervor, both not to leave unpunished whatever is done against God and to endure with mercy whatever offense is committed against you. [Note: [Col. 1289D] The printed editions have “if anything is done against you.” Here *vobis* means “against you,” as in Psalm 50: “Against you alone I have sinned.”]

May he grant us, through your piety, the clemency of the empress Pulcheria, who, because of her zeal for the Catholic faith, was called “the new Helena” at the holy Council of Chalcedon (Act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon). [Note: [Col. 1289D] The manuscripts differ here. In Vatican D and the Rheims manuscript: “May the clemency of the empress Pulcheria return in your piety.” In A and F: “May the clemency of the empress Pulcheria sit for you in your piety.” Colbert and Turon have a reading which perhaps should be *se dat nobis* (“gives herself to us”) … clemency, as it is read in Audoenus, Lyranus, and Gemeticus. In the Beccensis manuscript: “May she restore to us.”]

May the mercy of almighty God grant you, together with your most pious lord, a longer span of life, so that, the longer your life is extended, the more firmly the consolation of all your subjects may be established.

Perhaps I ought to have asked that Your Tranquility hold especially commended the Church of blessed Peter the apostle, which until now has been suffering under grave plots. But because I know that you love almighty God, I ought not to ask for what you yourselves freely display through the kindness of your piety.

For the more you fear the Creator of all, the more you can love his Church, to Peter, of whom it was said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” And to whom it is said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18). Therefore we have no doubt how strongly you bind yourselves to him through whom you earnestly desire to be loosed [Note: [Col. 1289D] Here we follow the Turon, Norman, Colbert, and two Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions and some manuscripts have: “from all the bonds of sinners you desire to be loosed.”] from all sins.

May he therefore be the guardian of your empire [Col. 1289C], your protector on earth, and your intercessor in heaven, so that, because you make your subjects rejoice in your empire after their harsh burdens have been relieved, you may rejoice in the heavenly kingdom after many years.

(John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 22.)

## EPISTLE XL. TO CYRIACUS, PATRIARCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He urges him, for the sake of peace, to abstain from the proud title “Universal.” He commends the deacon Boniface.

Gregory to Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople.

When we carefully contemplate the power of peace in the words of the Lord, who says, “My peace I give you” (John 14:27), we ought to persist in love of it in such a way that we never provide an occasion for discord.

But since we cannot otherwise live at peace at its root unless we preserve in mind and action the humility taught by the author of peace himself, we urge you with the charity that is fitting to trample under the foot of the heart that profane exaltation, which is always hostile to souls, and to hasten to remove from the midst of the Church the scandal of that perverse and proud title [Note: [Col. 1289D] EPISTLE XL [Elsewhere 47].—Cyriacus had governed the Church of Constantinople for six years and was usurping the title “universal bishop” against the will of Saint Gregory, while communion nevertheless remained intact.] [Note: [Col. 1289D] In the Colbert and Norman manuscripts: “to remove the scandal from the midst of the Church.”], lest you be found separated from fellowship in our peace.

Rather, let there be in us one spirit, one mind, one charity, and one bond of concord in Christ, who willed us to be his members. Let Your Holiness consider how harsh, how indecent, how cruel, and how foreign to the purpose of a priest it is not to possess the peace that he preaches to others, and let him refrain from scandalizing his brothers through pride.

Instead, let him strive all the more to bring down with the sword of humility the author of vain and superfluous exaltation, so that, in such a victory, the grace of the Holy Spirit may claim you as its dwelling place, and what is written may be openly fulfilled in you: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (2 Corinthians 6:17).

We commend to you in every respect the most beloved common son, Boniface the deacon, bearer of this letter, so that wherever necessary he may find the assistance of Your Holiness, as is fitting.

## EPISTLE XLI. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He urges Eulogius to root out simony.

Gregory to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria.

One day, when a discussion had arisen between me and my household about the customs of the Churches, a certain man who had been trained in the medical art in the great city of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 1290D] EPISTLE XLI [Elsewhere 48].—The Norman manuscript had read *medicinam* (“medicine”); the Rheims manuscript, “was skilled in medicine.”] declared that he had had as his collector under his sophist a boy of extreme wickedness, whom he said had suddenly been ordained a deacon. [Note: [Col. 1290D] Vatican B: “a tax-gatherer.”] 1247

He added that the boy had been ordained through payments and gifts, because he admitted that this same practice had become established in the holy Alexandrian Church.

When I heard this, I was astonished and greatly amazed, because the tongue of the most holy and most blessed lord Eulogius—whose teaching recalls so many heretics to the Catholic faith—had not eradicated the heresy of simony from the holy Alexandrian Church.

And whose exhortation or correction will be able to amend this, if his great and admirable teaching has left it uncorrected? Therefore, for the absolution of your soul and for the increase of your reward, so that your works may be perfect in all things before the eyes of the dread Judge, you ought to hasten to tear out and uproot entirely the heresy of simony, which first arose in the Church, from your most holy see [Col. 1290D], which is ours. [Note: [Col. 1290D] On the unity of the three sees of Saint Peter—namely, Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch—see above, Book VII, Epistle 40. Consult Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 55, chapter 16.]

For this reason it has happened that the holiness of ecclesiastical orders has fallen among very many people: persons are brought into those orders not because of their life and conduct, but because of payments. But if moral merit rather than payments is sought, unworthy persons will not come to ordination. And your reward will begin to increase all the more, the more all those who are brought into the sacred orders strive to consider the gain of souls.

## EPISTLE XLII. TO EULOGIUS, PATRIARCH OF ALEXANDRIA

He congratulates him that he has not lost his eyesight and that the Lord’s flock has increased. He reminds him of the eulogiae he received and says that larger timbers have been prepared; if Eulogius needs them, he should write to Boniface.

Gregory to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria.

We give great thanks to almighty God, because, in the mouth of the heart, the taste of charity becomes sweet when what is written is fulfilled: “As cold water to a thirsty person, so is good news from a distant land” (Proverbs 25:25).

Before this time, the letters of Boniface the chartulary, my representative, who resides in the royal city, had greatly disturbed me. They said that your most sweet and delightful Holiness had suffered a loss of bodily sight. From these letters I was struck with profound sorrow.

But suddenly, through the prosperous grace of our Creator and Redeemer, I received a letter from Your Beatitude [Note: [Col. 1291D] EPISTLE XLII [Elsewhere 49].—The Turon, Rheims, Norman, and Vatican D manuscripts read: “and healed from that bodily illness which I had heard of.”], and when I learned that you were well in regard to the bodily illness of which I had heard, I rejoiced exceedingly, because the joy of my heart was as great as the bitterness of sorrow that had preceded it.

For we know that, through the help of almighty God, the life of many depends upon your health. [Col. 1291C] Sailors navigate safely amid the waves when a skilled and experienced helmsman sits at the helm.

In the joy of your health this too has been added to my rejoicing: I have learned that the enemies of the Church have been diminished by your speech and that the Lord’s flocks have multiplied. For heavenly grains grow daily through the plowshare of your tongue and are multiplied in the heavenly storehouses, so that we rejoice that what is written has been fulfilled in you: “Where there are abundant crops, there is evident strength of oxen” (Proverbs 14:4).

From this we plainly conclude that the more you bring his fugitives back to the service of almighty God, the greater your merit with him. And the greater the merit you receive, the more you can obtain what you ask.

Therefore I ask you to pray more earnestly for me, a sinner, because bodily pain, bitterness of heart, and the immense devastation of mortality among so many barbarian swords afflict me severely. Amid all these things I seek not temporal but eternal consolation, which I cannot obtain through myself, but which I trust to obtain through the intercession of Your Beatitude.

In the second year I received no letters from Your Holiness, and I was altogether saddened. Your blessing, which you sent without a letter, was indeed given and received. But because your tongue gives me more joy than a gift, I thought that what was sent was of lesser grace.

I had the common son Epiphanius the deacon write to Alexander and Isidore, deacons of your most holy Church [Note: [Col. 1291D] In most Norman manuscripts it reads “of your glory,” a title by which we do not find Gregory addressing bishops.], so that it might be clear that I had received what was sent.

I wrote that I had prepared large timbers for making arbores and temones, but the small ship that had arrived could not carry them, and you sent me no reply concerning them. Therefore, if they are needed, write to our common son Boniface the deacon, whom we are now sending to the royal city to deliver responses, so that he may write back to me and they may be prepared, in order that, when Your Beatitude sends for them, they may be found ready.

Moreover, we have sent a small cross in which a blessing has been inserted from the chains of your beloved saints, the apostles Peter and Paul. May it be continually placed before your eyes [Note: [Col. 1291D] The reading formerly was *supponatur* (“be placed beneath”); we have corrected it according to the Vatican, Anglic, and Norman manuscripts], since many miracles have customarily been performed through this same blessing.

May almighty God breathe upon the heart of Your Beatitude, so that you may take care to pray for me continually; may he protect you and all your people with his right hand, and, after long years have passed, lead you to the heavenly kingdom.

As for the eulogiae [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Eulogiae* here has the same meaning as *benedictio* (“blessing”), a term Saint Gregory frequently uses for gifts given out of charity. *Eulogiae* is used in the same sense in chapter 54 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. See what we said above on Book VIII, Epistle 29, and consult the observations of our Hugh Menard on chapter 61 of the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 875.] of Saint Mark sent by Your Most Blessed Fraternity, we received them with the same charity with which they were sent, according to their character, and we return thanks for your affection, because from these outward gifts we recognize what you are inwardly toward us.
