(John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 52.)

## EPISTLE XLIII. TO JOHN OF PANORMUS

He very much wished to see him but permits him to remain in Sicily because of the danger of navigation.

Gregory to John of Panormus.

You continually demonstrate by letters and deeds the love you bear toward us, which we wished you to display to us through a bodily visit [Note: [Col. 1292D] The printed editions read *voluistis exhiberi* (“you wished to display”). We have taken our reading from Vatican A and the Remigius manuscript, the only manuscripts in which we found this epistle.], 1249

But what else do you accomplish by displaying this love except that we desire all the more to see the one whom we are taught to love more deeply? And we have already received almost a complaint that we cannot see the one whom we love.

But someone came and told me of the impossibility of your voyage [Note: [Col. 1292D] These words indicate that the title in the printed editions, “To John, bishop of Panormus,” is false. Saint Gregory does not write in this manner to bishops, nor does he show this desire to see John in his other letters addressed to John, bishop of Panormus.], and therefore I retained what I loved and spared what had angered me.

May almighty God guard you with his protection and defend you from all evils by his continual grace. [Note: [Col. 1293D] The common editions have “with continual grace.”]

## EPISTLE XLIV. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

He is to provide what he promised to his clerics when they made just requests.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1293D] EPISTLE XLIV [Elsewhere 51].—In one Colbert manuscript: “to Mariniano, bishop of Ravenna.”] to John, bishop of Panormus.

The wishes of those who make requests must always be fulfilled whenever they ask for things that do not deviate from reason. Therefore, because your clerics have asked us to confirm by our authority certain provisions that you promised to observe for them when they requested them [Note: [Col. 1293D] The common editions read: “which are requested … to be confirmed.”], we exhort your Fraternity in these words to observe, without any resistance, the provisions contained in this letter.

First, from the revenues of the Church you must provide your clerics with a full quarter of your Church’s income, according to each person’s merit, office, or labor, in whatever manner you yourself determine should be given to each, without any delay.

As for what comes in from the offerings of the faithful, do not delay giving them a quarter of it, in coin or in provisions, according to the former custom. You are to retain all the remaining movable property in your power. Immovable property, however, is to be added to the ecclesiastical revenues, so that, through the increase of its amount, the quarter belonging to your clerics may, by God’s generosity, grow. [Note: [Col. 1293D] Thus we have restored the text from the Vatican, Regius, and Colbert manuscripts. In the Corbie manuscript it reads: “so that they may profit from the quarter.” The printed edition has: “so that they may profit, by God’s generosity, for the use of your clerics.”]

You must remember to appoint the chartulary [Note: [Col. 1293D] That is, the administrator of the fourth part of the Church’s revenues and offerings. He distributed portions to the clerics according to their register, which was called the *matricula*. Augustine, Sermon 356: “If anyone is found to have private property, I do not permit him to make a will from it, but I will erase him from the register of the clerics.”] with the consent of the elders and clergy; each year, to remove suspicion of fraud, he must solemnly present his accounts.

At the time of the grape harvest, let that same clergy obtain the means to purchase wine from the possessions of your Church at fair prices, insofar as there is wine to be sold. For it is entirely contrary to reason that what can be sold to outsiders should be denied to clerics when they offer payment.

Therefore, possessions—or any other property belonging by right to the Church—that are being improperly held by outsiders, restore them with every effort, while preserving civility, to the right of your Church [Note: [Col. 1294D] The printed editions have erroneously *praeparare* (“prepare”) instead of *reparare* (“restore”)], so that you may not appear negligent in any matter.

If anything concerning any cleric reaches your ears that could justly offend you (Gratian, *Decree*, distinction 86, chapter 23; cause 15, question 7, chapter 2), do not readily believe it, and do not let an unknown matter inflame you to vengeance. Rather, with the elders of your Church present, the truth must be carefully investigated; and then, if the nature of the matter demands it, canonical strictness must strike the fault of the offender.

Your diligence must therefore preserve all these things with such care and gentleness that you may neither appear to have forgotten your promise nor allow them to find a just occasion for murmuring against you. [Col. 1294A]

[Note: [Col. 1294D] We find these words in no manuscripts except two Colbert manuscripts, where it is unclear whether they belong to the present epistle or to the following one.]

Given in the month of August, in the sixth indiction.

(John the Deacon, Book X, chapter 34.)

[Note: [Col. 1294D] EPISTLE XLV [Elsewhere 52].—This epistle is found in all the Vatican, Norman, Anglic, Colbert, Teller, Turon, Rheims, and Corbie manuscripts. In five Vatican manuscripts it reads: “The capitulary that must be observed by John the defender while going to Spain.”]

## EPISTLE XLV, OR FIRST CAPITULARY. TO JOHN THE DEFENDER

What must be investigated and determined concerning the cases of Januarius, bishop of Malaca, a certain presbyter of his, and Stephen, bishop.

Gregory to John the defender, going to Spain in the name of the Lord.

First of all, an inquiry must be made into the person of the most beloved brother and fellow bishop Januarius’s presbyter (Gratian, 2, question 1, chapter 7). If the truth is as the petition of that bishop states, the same presbyter must by every means be restored to the Church and to his own place.

But if it is said that some case was brought or proved against him, the kind of case and the manner of proof must be carefully investigated, with the man himself present and giving an account on his own behalf, so that from this you may rightly determine whether he must continue in exile or instead be restored to his own Church and office.

Concerning the person of the aforementioned bishop, this must be determined: if no criminal case worthy of exile or deposition was brought or proved against him, the man who, while that bishop was still alive, presumed to be ordained bishop in his Church perversely and contrary to the canons must be deprived of the priesthood and excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry.

He must also be handed over to that most beloved brother and our fellow bishop Januarius, so that either Januarius may keep him in custody or have him sent to us in every respect.

The bishops who ordained him, or who were present and consented to his ordination, must be deprived of communion of the Lord’s body and blood for six months and must be ordered to do penance in a monastery. The aforesaid Januarius must by every means be restored to his place and rank.

If, however, danger of death should threaten those deprived of communion, the blessing of the viaticum must not be denied them.

But if the bishops confess that they consented and acted in such a matter through fear of the judge, to the prejudice of the condemnation or deposition of the bishop mentioned above, and not of their own accord, their time of penance must be shortened and its severity moderated.

If the man who invaded his place has perhaps departed from this life [Col. 1294D] and another has been ordained in his place, because the fault appears lighter—since he seems to have succeeded not a living man, as in the former case, but one who had died—the office of bishop is to be forbidden to him only in that Church, so that, if he is elected, he may be bishop in another Church [Col. 1295A] that has become vacant through the death of its priest. [Note: [Col. 1295D] Malaca, called Malaga by its inhabitants and Malgue by the Gauls, is a maritime city formerly in Baetica in Spain, now in the kingdom of Granada, at the mouth of the river Baetis, commonly called the Guadalquivir. It is a famous commercial center with an episcopal see, formerly under the archbishop of Seville and now under the archbishop of Granada, according to the Roman *Provinciale*. GUSSANV.] He must never return to the Church of Malaca in any way.

The illustrious Comitiolus must be condemned to restore to the same bishop whatever the aforesaid bishop confirms by oath that he expended or suffered as loss through Comitiolus’s violence and persecution.

But if it is reported that matters occurred otherwise than the petition of the aforementioned bishop states, the matter must be carefully investigated; and once the truth is known, judgment must be given with fear of God according to what the order of justice dictates.

Since, then, Bishop Stephen asserts that certain things were fabricated out of hatred against him, that he was accused on the basis of false charges, that nothing was done in a regular manner, and that he was unjustly condemned, it must first be carefully investigated whether the trial was held according to due procedure, or whether the accusers were different from the witnesses.

Next, the nature of the charges must be examined: whether they were worthy of exile or deposition; whether testimony was given against him under oath while he was present [Note: [Col. 1295D] The recent editions read: “while the accused was present”; and below: “of what life and condition.”], or whether it was recorded in writing; and whether he had the opportunity to respond and defend himself.

The persons who accused and testified must also be carefully investigated: what their condition and reputation were; whether they were poor; whether perhaps they had held some enmity against the bishop mentioned above; whether they gave testimony from hearsay or declared that they themselves had specific knowledge; and, if judgment was given in writing, whether the sentence was read aloud in the presence of the parties.

If these things were not carried out solemnly, and no case was proved worthy of exile or deposition [Col. 1295C], he must by every means be restored to his own Church.

Those who condemned him contrary to the fear of God and the statutes of the canons must be excommunicated and sent to a monastery to do penance for six months. It must, however, be arranged that, if the danger of death should threaten any one of them, the blessing of the viaticum not be denied him.

The man who, while Stephen was alive, rashly sought his place must be deprived of the priesthood, excluded from every ecclesiastical ministry, and handed over to our most beloved brother and fellow bishop, so that either he may send him to us or keep him in custody.

The bishops who presumed to ordain him, or who gave their consent to his perverse ordination, must likewise, deprived of communion, be assigned to a monastery to do penance for six months.

If the bishops confess that they consented through fear of the judge, to the prejudice of Stephen’s condemnation or deposition, and that they acted in such a matter not of their own accord [Col. 1295D] [Col. 1296A], their time of penance must be shortened and its severity moderated.

If, therefore, the man who invaded the place of the aforementioned Stephen [1252] has perhaps died and another bishop has been ordained in his Church, the same determination must be made concerning him as we stated above regarding the case of our brother and fellow bishop Januarius.

But if some of the charges brought against the aforementioned Bishop Stephen have been proved while others could not be demonstrated at all, it must be weighed with the utmost care whether the charges proved were lighter or more serious, so that from them you may know how to formulate your decision [Note: [Col. 1295D] The Norman manuscript reads: “how you ought to establish it.”].

If the aforementioned bishop is shown to be innocent, the illustrious Comitiolus must restore to him without any delay whatever he took from his property or from that of his Church. Whatever the same bishop swears that he expended or suffered as loss in consequence of Comitiolus’s persecution and violence, the same illustrious Comitiolus must also repay and make good.

But if it is established that the aforementioned bishop committed such a fault (Gratian, 16, question 6, chapter 3)—which God forbid—and that he was not unreasonably deposed, his deposition must be confirmed, and all the property of the Church that is shown to have been taken away must be restored to it, because the offense of an individual must not be turned into harm for the Church.

For if, as they say, Comitiolus has died, whatever was unjustly taken by him [Note: [Col. 1295D] The Colbert and Vatican A and B manuscripts read “whatever was unjustly taken.”] must be returned without excuse by his heir.

(John the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 28.)

[Note: [Col. 1295D] CAPITULARY II [Elsewhere 56].—It is absent from the Norman, Anglic, and Corbie manuscripts. It exists in five Vatican manuscripts, three Colbert manuscripts, the Turon manuscript, both Rheims manuscripts, and two Teller manuscripts, where it begins as follows: “To John the defender, going to Spain: an exemplar of the law.” In Vatican A the title is prefixed: “Capitulary of the laws,” etc., as in the printed editions. In five Vatican, Rheims, and Colbert manuscripts, only “Exemplar of the law” is prefixed. “Concerning the person …”]

## CAPITULARY II OF THE IMPERIAL LAWS

For the immunity of clerics, addressed to John the defender, going to Spain.

It prescribes more fully what must be done in the cases mentioned above, having collected the laws of the emperors.

[Col. 1296C]

Concerning the person of the presbyter, this must be observed (Gratian, 11, question 1, chapter 38): if he had any case, he ought not to have been held by another person, but his bishop ought to have been approached, as this constitution of the *Novellae* makes clear, which speaks concerning the most holy, God-loving, and most reverend bishops, clerics, and monks.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] The printed editions, contrary to nearly all manuscripts, read “the Emperor Justinian Augustus, to Peter.”] To Peter, the most glorious prefect of the praetorium:

[Note: [Col. 1296D] In the Tours manuscript: “to Peter, the most glorious provost.” Two Vatican, Rheims, and Colbert manuscripts add: “on the day before the Kalends of April.”]

“If anyone has any legal action against a cleric, monk, deaconess, nun, or female ascetic, let him first approach the most holy bishop under whose jurisdiction each of these persons falls. Let that bishop judge the case between them. And if both parties have accepted what has been judged, we order that it be completely carried out by the judge of the place, etc.”

[Note: [Col. 1296D] The particle “not” has been erroneously inserted in recent editions. It is absent from all manuscripts and cannot be read without destroying the sense. [Col. 1297D] Certainly, in the original source one finds: “if he has accepted what has been judged.”]

But lest it be objected that this speaks of a cleric, not of a presbyter, it must be known that in the same constitution, book 1, chapter 1, it is stated that the designation “clerics” also includes presbyters and deacons. The words of the law are these:

“But presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, singers, and readers—we call all of them clerics,” and so forth.

(*Novella* 123, section “If anyone has,” in Julian, chapter 32; Book 1, chapter 1, *Authentic* “Concerning the most holy bishops.”)

Concerning Bishop Januarius, it must be understood that it was a very grave act, and contrary to the laws, that he was violently dragged from the church, since, whenever a bishop has suffered any other injury from anyone in a church, the law strikes the offender with capital punishment and, treating him as guilty of treason, grants everyone permission to accuse him, as the wording of this law states in Book 1 of the *Code*, title 6, constitution 10.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] Two Rheims manuscripts and five Vatican manuscripts read: “title 3, constitution 11.”]

[Col. 1297B]

[Note: [Col. 1297D] The Colbert and Rheims manuscripts read: “The Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Theodorus, presbyter.”]

The Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Theodorus, prefect of the praetorium.

“If anyone should break out into this kind of sacrilege, so as to burst into Catholic churches and inflict any injury upon the priests and ministers, or upon the worship itself and the place, the provincial governors shall take notice of what has occurred; and the governor of the province shall know that the injury done to priests, clerics, and ministers of the Catholic Church, as well as to the place itself and divine worship, must be punished by a capital sentence against those convicted or confessing. And shortly afterward:

“Let it be considered praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute as a public crime the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers, and to obtain vengeance against such offenders,” and so forth.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of May at Milan, in the fourth consulship of Honorius Augustus and the consulship of Eutychianus.

(*Code*, “Concerning Bishops and Clerics,” law “If anyone”; and *Theodosian Code*, Book XVI, title 2, chapter 31.)

The book cited above, title 15, constitution 2:

[Note: [Col. 1297D] Remigius and three Vatican manuscripts have title 12; the Colbert manuscript has title 11.]

The Emperors Honorius and Theodosius, Augusti, to Ionius, prefect of the praetorium.

“By a faithful and devout decree we enact that no one may carry away those who take refuge in the holy churches; with this provision, namely, that if anyone attempts to violate this law, he shall know that he is to be held guilty of treason.”

[Note: [Col. 1297D] The printed edition mistakenly reads “bring [them]” instead of “carry away.”]

Given on the Kalends of April, in the seventh consulship of Honorius and the third consulship of Theodosius.

Likewise, Book 1 of the same title, constitution 5.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] Remigius, together with four Vatican manuscripts, has “constitution 6.”]

The Emperor Leo Augustus, to Eutychianus, prefect of the praetorium.

[Note: [Col. 1297D] Four Vatican manuscripts read: “Under the reign of Leo Augustus, to Eritrius, provost.”]

“By the present law, to be valid everywhere except in this royal city, where, by the favor of God, we reside and, whenever necessity demands and we are summoned, provide immediate decisions for individual cases and persons, we decree that no refugee of any condition whatsoever is to be expelled, dragged away, or forced out of the holy churches of the orthodox faith. And shortly afterward:

“Those who dare to attempt or carry out such an undertaking, or even merely to attempt it in thought or deliberation, are to be punished with capital and final execution. From these places, therefore, and from their boundaries, which the provisions of the earlier laws have established, we never permit anyone to be thrown out or expelled; nor do we permit anyone to be detained or constrained in those venerable churches in such a way that food, clothing, or rest is denied him,” and so forth.

Given on the day before the Kalends of March at Constantinople, in the third consulship of Leo Augustus.

(*Concerning Those Who Take Refuge in a Church*, *Code*, Book 1, laws “By a faithful decree” and “By the present law.”)

[Col. 1298B]

Concerning the person of Bishop Stephen, it must be noted that he could neither be dragged unwillingly to judgment nor be judged by bishops belonging to another council, as the aforementioned constitution of the *Novels* declares, speaking of bishops. It says:

“But we do not permit a bishop to be brought or presented against his will before a civil or military judge, without an imperial order, for any pecuniary or criminal cause whatever; rather, we order that a judge who has presumed to command such a thing, whether in writing or orally, pay a fine of twenty pounds of gold to the church whose bishop was ordered to be brought or presented, after being deprived of his belt; and likewise that the executor, after being deprived of his belt, be subjected to flogging and deported into exile.”

[Note: [Col. 1297D] In the Tours and Colbert manuscripts and in three Vatican manuscripts, with much omitted: “to command, after deprivation of his belt, and to be subjected to flogging.” The same words are omitted in Vatican manuscript D.]

Again, after much else:

“But if an action is brought against a bishop by any cleric or layman, for any cause whatsoever, the case must be judged before his most holy metropolitan, according to the holy canons and our laws. And if anyone contradicts what has been judged, the case is to be referred to the most blessed archbishop and patriarch of that diocese,”

[Note: [Col. 1297D] So that I may remove a scruple from the minds of certain people who find it distasteful when the laws of rulers are brought forward in support of the canons, I shall usefully point out that this is done at the prompting of reason and under the guidance of authority. The reason is drawn from the law of rulers and from the equity of the civil laws—those laws, I mean, which extract, illuminate, and protect natural law, as is customary among jurists. Many canonists take another path, and, while being excessively scrupulous in granting everything to authority, pursue even the minutest points of words and thereby either weaken natural law itself or obscure it through excessive servility. Moreover, that the laws of rulers are commended by the very authority of the canons is obvious even to the blind. Lucius III, *Extra*, Book V, title 32, chapter 1, says: “The statutes of the canons are assisted by the constitutions of rulers.” Innocent III, in the same work, chapter 2, mentions the civil tradition. Nicholas I, distinction 10, chapter 1, says that the laws of the emperors are to be used in ecclesiastical controversies, provided that they do not conflict with canonical enactment. In the same place, chapter 7, a passage from Saint Augustine is cited, but with a different meaning. Gelasius, distinction 54, chapters 9–12, wishes the path of the laws to be observed. I omit many other, much more illustrious examples, which are found even in the principal councils. GUSSANV.]

“and he is to bring the matter to an end according to the canons and laws.”

If it should be said against this that he had neither a metropolitan nor a patriarch, the answer must be that this case ought to have been heard and settled by the apostolic see, which is the head of all the churches, as the aforementioned bishop is known to have requested, since he regarded the bishops of another council as wholly suspect.

Since, therefore, a judgment pronounced by a judge who was not his proper judge has no validity, the text of the following reading makes clear, *Code*, Book VII, title 48, constitution 4.

The Emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, Augusti, to Potitus, vicar.

“And in private cases this form shall likewise be observed, so that no litigant may be bound by a judgment that was not pronounced by his own judge.”

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October at Rome, in the consulship of Ausonius and Olibrius.

(*If by an Incompetent Judge*, *Code*, Book VII, law “And in Private Cases.”)

But concerning the statement that he was accused by his own slaves, and that they ought not to have been heard at all, this constitution makes the matter clear, saying, *Code*, Book IX, title 1, constitution 20.

The Emperors Arcadius and Honorius, Augusti, to Eutychianus, prefect of the praetorium.

“If anyone from the household or slaves of any house should become an informer and accuser of any crime, intending to attack the reputation, life, and fortunes of the person whose household or authority he has served, he shall be struck down by the avenging sword at the very beginning of the charge and accusation, before the production of witnesses and before the examination of the court. For a deadly voice ought to be cut off rather than heard. We except only the crime of treason.”

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.

(*Concerning Those Unable to Accuse*, *Code*, Book IX, law “If Anyone.”)

But if it should be said that he was accused of something relating to the crime of treason, even then he ought not to have been believed if his life or reputation had not previously been of such a character, as Modestinus writes in Book XLVIII of the *Digest*, under the *Lex Julia on Treason*, law “The Notorious,” shortly after the beginning:

[Note: [Col. 1299D] Vatican manuscripts A, B, and F, Remigius, and Colbert have “*Digest* on treason, title 7, Modestinus, Book XII of the *Digest*,” followed shortly by the passage.]

“This crime, however, is not to be considered by judges opportunistically, out of reverence for the emperor’s majesty, but according to the truth of the matter adjudged. For the person also must be considered—whether he could have done it, what he had previously done, and whether he had contemplated it.”

But concerning what the same bishop says, namely, that in his absence some utterly contemptible witnesses were produced: if this is true, it must be recognized by law as entirely without force, according to the Novella constitution that speaks of witnesses, chapter 16:

“We have also frequently learned that certain persons enter before the defenders of the places, or before the most illustrious judges of the provinces, or, as commonly happens, here before the most illustrious master of the census, and complain that they have suffered something contrary to the laws from another person, or have otherwise been injured or damaged, wishing to produce witnesses. But so that they may not later be accused of having had the proceedings conducted by one party alone, the person against whom the complaint is made must also be summoned by the judge or defender, while residing in the very city where the testimony is given, and must be instructed to come and hear the depositions. If he refuses to come and scorns the summons, so that the testimony would otherwise be useless against him because it was given by one party alone, we enact that such testimony shall have the same force as if it had not been given by one party alone but had also been taken in his presence. For if he refuses, declines to come, and declines to hear what is being reported, although the matter is in any event public and he is not prevented from coming by some unavoidable necessity, he shall be treated as though he had come, and his contempt shall bring him no advantage; rather, the proofs shall be regarded as having been made in the presence of both parties.”

[Note: [Col. 1299D] Vatican manuscripts B and D and the Rheims manuscripts differ slightly here, but they appear corrupt at this point.]

Behold, the opposing party must always be summoned to come and hear the witnesses. Since this was omitted here, it is necessary that what was done contrary to the laws have no validity.

(*Authentic*, “Concerning Witnesses,” section “And Here Indeed.”)

[Note: [Col. 1299D] There are two titles concerning witnesses in *Extra*, Book II, followed by another concerning the reliability of documents. In its chapter 2 I read: “Authentic documents, if the witnesses named in them have died, do not appear to us to possess any force of validity unless they were drawn up by public authority, so that they appear to have been made public, or unless they have an authentic seal by which they can be proved.” To counter falsifications, our kings enacted many measures, some of which the reader will find in the great collection of royal ordinances, Book IV, title 5. I transcribe this law of Louis XII: “Notaries shall transcribe no agreement unless they know the contracting parties well, or unless it is clear to them through trustworthy witnesses who attest to their identity that they are the very persons who are contracting; otherwise they shall be expelled from the number of notaries.” Francis I added in 1535: “Notaries shall draw up no contract without witnesses known both to the notaries and to the contracting parties.” As the contrary practice has grown stronger, we have an abundance of forged documents. GUSSANV.]

What sort of witnesses are admissible, and of what reputation they must be to be admitted for testimony, is shown by very many laws, with which almost no one is unfamiliar; these laws also establish that one must not believe the most contemptible witnesses without a physical examination.

As for the statement that nothing was adjudged in writing, one must consult title 44 of Book VII of the *Code*, because judgment ought to have been given in writing. For it is prescribed there, among other things, that a sentence pronounced without writing does not even deserve to bear the name of a sentence.

(*In the same place*, section “Witnesses.”)

[Note: [Col. 1300D] Vatican manuscripts A and F read: “the title is to be read as 19 of Book VI of the Constitutions,” because of the wording. The Tours manuscript agrees, changing 19 to 18. In the Rheims manuscripts it should be read as “*Digest*, Book VI, title 44.”]

[Note: [Col. 1300D] SENTENCE OF JOHN THE DEFENDER [Elsewhere 55].—It exists in five Vatican manuscripts, four Colbert manuscripts, two Teller manuscripts, both Rheims manuscripts, and the Tours manuscript. It is absent from the Norman manuscript.]

## SENTENCE OF JOHN THE DEFENDER

Example of a sentence in favor of Januarius, Bishop of Málaga.

[Col. 1300C]

In the name of the Lord, under that emperor, on that day, in that indiction.

He to whom the office of judge is entrusted must present himself in all things with a pure and undefiled conscience, so that, on account of the judgments he gives concerning others, he may not incur the punishment of the eternal tribunal.

Therefore, when, by the appointment of my most blessed and apostolic lord, Pope Gregory,

[Note: [Col. 1300D] The printed editions, supported by very few manuscripts, add “and by the order.”]

I, John the defender, had taken my seat as judge between Januarius, bishop of the city of Málaga, and those and those bishops,

[Note: [Col. 1300D] The Colbert and Vatican manuscripts read: “had taken my seat as judge.”]

I found it necessary to examine the case of the aforesaid Januarius by inward investigation and to seek the truth carefully from the parties: whether, as his petition states, he had been violently removed from the church by clerics sent by the aforementioned bishops together with the men of the illustrious Comitiolus.

[Col. 1300A] 1256

When they had brought many accusations against one another, as the proceedings testify, both parties eventually came to the conclusion of the case, asking me to judge according to what had been established. Accordingly, carefully rereading the proceedings and seeking the truth through diligent investigation, I found no fault in the aforementioned Januarius that deserved punishment by exile or deposition; rather, I found that he had been violently expelled from the church.

Although the severity of the laws most strictly punishes such presumption, I nevertheless tempered the force of the laws with priestly moderation. In the presence of the holy Gospels, which had been present from the beginning when I took my seat as judge in this trial,

[Note: [Col. 1301C] We have already discussed this matter in Letter 15 of Book VIII. Cassiodorus, Book IV of the *Variae*, Letter 12, testifies that lay judges observed the same procedure: “With the holy Gospels placed between them, together with three distinguished men chosen by agreement of the parties,” and so forth.]

I declare that the measures enacted against him, although they have no legal force

[Col. 1301B]

and are of no effect, are nevertheless unjust and invalid. I condemn those aforementioned bishops who, setting aside priestly consideration, acted unjustly and contrary to the fear of God to the prejudice and condemnation of their brother; I decree and determine that they are to be received into a monastery to perform penance for a time.

But the man who wickedly presumed to invade the place of the aforementioned most holy Januarius, contrary to the provisions of the sacred canons, I condemn and decree shall be deprived of the priesthood and removed from every ecclesiastical order, so that he may lose what he wrongly acquired and may not return to the office that he had previously held unworthily.

I decree that the aforementioned most holy Bishop Januarius, acquitted and restored to his place, shall, by God’s authority, return to the rank of the episcopate and be fully reinstated.

## LETTER XLVI. TO JOHN THE DEFENDER

Let him bring the dissolute and corrupt monks of the island of Capricana back to the right path.

[Col. 1301C]

Gregory to John the defender.

When the nature of offenses calls for canonical strictness against their perpetrators, we must not postpone what needs correction, lest we appear, through concealment, to strengthen evil actions that it is our duty to cut away with the sickle of discipline.

Since, therefore, it has come to our attention that the monks of the monastery on the island of Capricana,

[Note: [Col. 1301C] LETTER XLVI [Elsewhere 54].—Capraria, commonly Cabrera, is an island in the Iberian or Balearic Sea, lying south of Majorca and scarcely two Spanish leagues from it toward the promontory of Salinas. GUSSANV. In all the Norman, Corbie, and Colbert manuscripts and in three Vatican manuscripts, the reading is: “which is situated on the island of Capria near Majorca.”]

which lies near the island of Majorca, are acting so perversely and have subjected their lives to such diverse crimes that they appear to serve not Almighty God but, as we say with grief, the ancient enemy, your Experience, instructed by the authority of this present letter, must go to the aforesaid monastery and diligently investigate the life and conduct of those living there.

Whatever you find deserving correction, you must correct with appropriate punishment, as the canonical order requires,

[Note: [Col. 1301D] The Rheims, Colbert, and Corbie manuscripts read “consideration.” “Canonical order” signifies the laws of the canons. The expression is used in the same sense in Book XIV, Letter 6, and in canon 15 of the Synod of Autun in 674: “Concerning abbots and monks, it is proper to observe this: whatever the canonical order or the rule of Saint Benedict teaches, they must fulfill and observe in all things.” Let no one, therefore, imagine that “canonical order” here means the status of canons, since the subject is the monks of the island of Capraria.]

and instruct them concerning what they ought to observe.

[Note: [Col. 1302D] Vatican manuscript B alone reads “reform them.”]

In this way, the manner of your correction will both bring them back to the path of right conduct and in no way render you blameworthy before us.

## LETTER XLVII. TO THE CURATOR THEODORUS

He lovingly commends Peter and his mother.

Gregory to Theodorus,

[Note: [Col. 1302D] LETTER XLVII [Elsewhere 57].—So it appears in the Victor manuscript. Vatican A reads “procurator.” This letter is found only in these two manuscripts.]

the curator.

Since we have such confidence in the sincerity of Your Glory that we believe you regard as your own those who belong to us, it could have been enough for Peter, the bearer of this letter, a magnificent man, to obtain the favor of your goodness simply by declaring that he is ours.

But since a father’s commendation is accustomed always to kindle the mind of a good son, we greet you with paternal affection and ask that you extend the favor of your protection to our aforementioned son and to our aforementioned daughter, his glorious mother; support them there, where they are, by the remedy of your protection, and assist them with your resources when they come to us.

Thus, while Your Glory provides what it is accustomed to provide from itself, with our more kindly letter intervening, you will appear both laudably to perform your customary duty and to make us, on account of your goodness, wholly indebted to you in gratitude.

[Note: [Col. 1302D] In the cited Vatican manuscript there is added: “in the month of September, in the seventh indiction.” But this letter is contained in Book XII, which belongs to the fifth indiction. Hence it is clear that little weight should be given to this chronological note.]

## BOOK FOURTEEN

In the seventh indiction.

[Col. 1303]

1259

## LETTER I. TO PAUL THE SCHOLASTIC

He congratulates him both on his reconciliation with Bishop Leo and on his zeal against evildoers.

[Col. 1303A]

Gregory to Paul the scholastic

[Note: [Col. 1303D] LETTER I [Elsewhere 58, sixth indiction].—“Of Sicily” is absent from the printed editions, although it appears in all the Norman, Vatican, Colbert, and other manuscripts.]

of Sicily.

As greatly as Your Glory had recently made us sad because, as was being reported, you had certain complaints against our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Leo, so greatly our heart rejoiced when that same brother of ours came to us and testified that, by God’s favor, you had returned together to your former harmony.

Among the other good things he recounted in your praise, he also added that you had shown yourselves very diligent and strict in punishing evildoers, as was truly fitting for noble and Christian men.

Our joy over you therefore increased greatly, because in this way you make him favorable to you against whose enemies you exercise the uprightness of your zeal.

[Note: [Col. 1303D] The printed editions read “for this reason.”]

Moreover, greeting Your Glory with paternal affection, we urge you—since loving peace is sufficiently suited to your character—not to allow any tongue to disturb the harmony restored between you. Rather, let charity burn in you toward one another with such fatherly love that contrary winds, like winds against a flame, may not extinguish it but increase it.

For we have also urged that same brother of ours to show you such fatherly affection that he may always be able to demand, not idly but as a lender demands repayment of a loan, the reciprocal affection of Your Glory.

[Note: [Col. 1303D] The same manuscripts read “not spitefully.”]

## LETTER II. TO VITALIS, THE DEFENDER OF SARDINIA

Concerning neglected hostels for the poor. Concerning protecting the Sardinians before the emperor. Concerning certain men appointed abbots after their fall. Concerning the monastery built in the house of Pomponiana. Concerning recovering the property of churches and monasteries. Concerning the illness of Bishop Januarius during the celebration of the sacrifice.

[Col. 1303C]

Gregory to Vitalis, the defender of Sardinia.

From your report we have learned that the hostels for the poor established in Sardinia are suffering serious neglect.

[Col. 1304A] 1260

Our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Januarius would therefore have deserved the strongest rebuke, had his old age and simplicity, together with the illness that came upon him and that you reported, not restrained us.

Since he is now so situated that he cannot be fit for any administrative action, admonish, by our strict authority, the steward of his church and Epiphanius, the archpresbyter,

[Note: [Col. 1303D] LETTER II [Elsewhere 59, sixth indiction].—The mention of an archpresbyter is rare in these letters. It occurs more often in Gregory of Tours, for example in Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapters 78 and 90, and especially in Book V of the *History*, chapter 5, where Munderic was appointed in place of Tetricus, bishop of Langres, while Tetricus was still alive, on the condition that, while the blessed Tetricus lived, Munderic should govern the fortress of Tornodorum as archpresbyter.]

from our authority, so that they diligently and usefully arrange those hostels at their own risk. For if any neglect occurs there after this, they must know that they will have no possible excuse before us.

Since the landholders of Sardinia have asked us to permit you to travel to Constantinople to provide relief for them, because they are oppressed by various burdens, we grant you permission to go. We have also written to our beloved son Boniface, so that he may endeavor to provide you with his assistance for the relief of that province.

Concerning the churches that you reported to be vacant of priests, we have written to our aforementioned most reverend brother and fellow bishop Januarius that he should arrange for them; but with the provision that not all those promoted to the episcopate be selected from his church. He must arrange the others in such a way that he does not deprive his church of persons from among whom it may be able to advance.

[Note: [Col. 1304D] That is, to be promoted to a higher rank. The verb “to increase” has the same meaning. See Book I, Letter 19; Book VII, Letter 32; and note c to Letter 18 of Book XI, tenth indiction, where “to be increased” has the same meaning.]

You also reported that persons have been placed in charge of certain monasteries who had previously fallen while they were still in the monastic and lower order. They ought certainly not to have undertaken the office of abbot unless their lives had been completely corrected and a worthy period of penance had preceded it.

But since, as you say, they have already assumed the office of abbot, care must be taken concerning their life, conduct, and diligence. If their actions are found not to be contrary to their office, let them remain in the order they now occupy; otherwise, remove them and appoint others who can benefit the souls entrusted to them.

Furthermore, concerning the monastery of Saint Hermes, which our brother built in the house of the religious woman Pomponiana,

[Note: [Col. 1304D] This phrase is omitted by our brother in four Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman and Corbie manuscripts, and most others.]

since the matter should be handled more by kindness than by severity, your Experience should deal gently with that woman, so that she may not, by neglecting the will of her founder, be led into her own sin, and so that you may beneficially provide for the interests of the monastery.

You must in no way permit her girls, whom the aforementioned Pomponiana formerly converted in the monastery after changing their clothing to the religious habit, to be taken away from her or disturbed; rather, with God’s protection, let them remain in the way of life in which they now are.

Concerning the recovery of the property of churches, monasteries, or charitable institutions, as you wrote, those concerned must first be admonished, so that, with you pressing and assisting them, they may seek it by every means. But if they should prove negligent, or if those who ought to seek it cannot be found, then you yourself must search for everything and gather what you find in such a way that you do not appear to inflict judgment upon anyone by force.

Concerning the hostels of Hortulanus and Thomas, we have so far learned nothing of what you reported. Therefore, let your Experience carefully inspect the imperial order issued concerning this matter, arrange everything according to its wording, and inform us of whatever you do.

Concerning what you wrote—that our brother and fellow bishop Januarius frequently suffers such severe distress while celebrating the sacrifice that he can scarcely return to the place of the canon which he has left except after long intervals, and that many therefore doubt whether they ought to receive communion from his consecration—you must admonish them not to fear in any way but to communicate with complete faith and confidence, because bodily illness neither changes nor pollutes the blessing of the sacred mystery.

Nevertheless, the same brother must be privately urged that whenever he feels any discomfort he should not proceed,

[Note: [Col. 1306D] We have explained elsewhere what “to proceed” means; note 471 in the *Sacramentary* explains it at length.]

lest he thereby both make himself appear contemptible and cause scandal in the minds of the sick.

Furthermore, Pomponiana, a religious woman, has complained to us that the inheritance of her former son-in-law Epiphanius—within which Epiphanius had established his wife Matrona, the daughter of the aforementioned Pomponiana, as usufructuary, intending that after the usufruct expired it should benefit the monastery he had decided to establish in his house, along with other things that Matrona is proved to possess by right of ownership—was unjustly taken away from her by your Experience and our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Januarius, and that since then nothing has been restored either to her daughter or to the benefit of the monastery.

If the truth is as she states, and you recognize that you have done anything improperly, restore what was taken away without any delay. Or, if you think the matter is otherwise, so that the opposing party may not appear to be prejudiced, do not postpone submitting the case to the judgment of chosen judges together with her, so that a judicial decision may declare whether her complaint is true and just.

[Note: [Col. 1306D] LETTER III. Elsewhere 60, sixth indiction.]

## LETTER III. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

He grants permission to exchange a house situated at Rome with Epiphanius, a deacon of the Roman Church.

[Col. 1305D]

Gregory to John, bishop of Panormus.

Just as a petition contrary to reason must be rejected far from us, so it is not proper to deny fulfillment in matters that are rightly desired.

Since, therefore, as the petition of Your Fraternity states—a petition endorsed by the signatures of the presbyters, deacons, and other ecclesiastical officials under your authority, who joined you in giving their consent—you wish to exchange with our beloved son Epiphanius, the deacon, a house situated in this city of Rome, with its garden and bath and everything belonging to it, which is known to have come to the right of the Church of Panormus through the inheritance of the former magnificent man Florus; and since the house itself is shown to be partly roofless, partly ruined, and partly consumed by fire, so that, as you testify, it has been unable for many years to provide any advantage to ecclesiastical interests, and you request that our authority grant you permission to carry out this exchange:

Having carefully considered the intention of your provision, and having learned that the house is in the condition you assert,

[Col. 1306B]

and is daily becoming worse through impending ruin, so that it appears likely to be not merely useless but increasingly harmful to your church, we therefore freely grant you, by the full force of this authority of ours, permission to exchange it, together with its bath and garden and everything generally belonging to it, according to your petition, which is supported before us by the order of truth and reason.

Thus, having received this permission, you will not be exposed to blame for rashness or carelessness, nor will the other party incur any uncertainty. For it is prudent and beneficial to secure some advantage where there is no hope of profit but rather fear of loss.

## LETTER IV. TO FANTINUS, THE DEFENDER OF PANORMUS

He must carefully oversee the conduct of Bishop Exhilaratus, so that the bishop shows charity to his clergy and the clergy obedience to him.

[Col. 1306C]

Gregory to Fantinus, the defender of Panormus.

Such things have reached us concerning our brother and fellow bishop Exhilaratus as, you yourself know, deserved to be punished by the utmost severity. But because our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Leo, who also testified that he had been his judge in the case, twice mitigated that punishment, we have decided that he should be sent back to his own church, judging that it was enough to have afflicted him by retaining him here for so long.

Therefore we order Your Experience to take care concerning his conduct and actions, and to admonish him frequently, so that he may show himself kind in extending charity to his clergy, yet, if circumstances require it, diligent in correcting their faults.

We also wish you to admonish his clergy to show him the humility and obedience that the Lord commands, and not to presume in any matter to behave arrogantly toward him.

If any of them—that is, whether bishop or cleric—

[Note: [Col. 1306D] LETTER IV [Elsewhere 61, sixth indiction]. Thus read five Vatican manuscripts, all the Norman and Corbie manuscripts, and others, whereas the printed editions read “that is, whether layman or cleric, or clergy.”]

neglects your admonition, then, by the canonical coercion of our authority, either correct the fault of disobedience yourself, as you deem appropriate, or hasten to report it to us, so that we may determine how the bridle of discipline can prevent those from going outside the proper path whom the spur of an evil mind provokes to excess.

## LETTER V. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

He must investigate carefully the case of Peter with the defender Fantinus and render judgment.

Gregory to John, bishop of Panormus.

Because there are faults in which it is itself culpable to relax punishment (Gratian, *Decretum*, Dist. 28, c. 10), the truth must always be sought, so that inquiry may determine whether guilt condemns the accused or innocence, once revealed, withdraws him from punishment. Thus it has come to us that Fantinus, the defensor, wished to exercise vengeance [Col. 1307B] against Peter, the bearer of this letter, because, as is reported, [Note: [Col. 1307C] EPIST. V [Al. 62, indiction 6].—Concerning the deacon’s widow, see above, Book IV, Letter 36.] during the time when he was a tenant, he had given a certain deacon’s widow to a husband. But since this man asserts that she was not the deacon’s wife, saying that the woman had not come to him as a virgin, [Note: [Col. 1307C] Thus it is read in the Vatican, Norman, Colbert, Rheims, Corbie, and old editions. We read that this obscure passage was altered in the Vatican edition, finally: “nor had she changed her religious habit after he had been promoted to the sacred order.”] and finally that she had not dared to change her religious habit after that man had been promoted to the sacred order, adding also that she had lived in a depraved manner both before he reached the diaconate [Note: [Col. 1307D] In recent editions: “before he reached the diaconate,” against the manuscripts.] and afterward, therefore we exhort your Fraternity in these words: with the fear of God, as is fitting, investigate this case with the utmost care. If it is established that the woman was in the deacon’s marriage, [Note: [Col. 1307D] The printed editions read: “that the woman concerned had been joined to him.”] let the aforesaid bearer be handed over in every way to the aforementioned defensor and rector of the patrimony for punishment, and let those who have been wrongly joined be separated with suitable correction. But if she was not in his marriage, [Col. 1307C] we wish you, by our mandate, to admonish the aforementioned Fantinus not to presume to do anything against them, [Note: [Col. 1307D] The printed editions read: “nor let the accusation against him.” Corbie and Norman have *fallax* (“deceitful”) instead of *falsa* (“false”).] nor let any false accusation weigh against him in any way. [Note: [Col. 1307D] The manuscripts disagree here. In Vatican B, E, F, Corbie, Colbert, Audomar, and Lyra, the reading is: “because he claims to restore what remains … since he possesses it.” Rheims agrees, except that it has *relictam* (“the widow”) instead of *reliquam* (“what remains”). Beccaria and Sagrado read: “some matter.” We have retained the common reading, but rejected *solum* (“only”) before *res suas*, since it destroyed the sense and is absent elsewhere from the manuscripts.] Since, however, the aforesaid Peter declares that his property is being held by the Church’s tenants, we wish him to possess it without anyone’s hindrance, 1264 provided that the right to demand it is indeed so established. For even if he is found guilty, he ought not to lose his property, but to undergo fitting punishment in his own person.

## LETTER VI. TO MARINIANUS, BISHOP OF RAVENNA

He is to restore Fortunatus, an abbot unjustly deposed, and rebuke the bishop for changing without cause what his predecessor had established.

[Col. 1308A]

Gregory to Mariniano, bishop of Ravenna.

Since it is exceedingly improper for anyone to be suspended from an office he has undertaken merely by another’s will, when guilt has not removed him from it, careful provision must be made so that neither a previous appointment is irrationally destroyed nor the things wrongly done afterward are left without correction. Fortunatus, therefore, the bearer of this letter, asserts that in the monastery of Saints Laurence and Zeno, which [Note: [Col. 1307D] EPIST. VI [Al. 1].—Caesena, commonly also Cesena, an Italian city on the river Sapis, between Sarsina and Ravenna. It was an episcopal city under the archbishop of Ravenna, situated in the Senonian territory and in Flaminia, now called the province of Romagna, commonly *la Romagna*, belonging to the Papal States. GUSSANV.] is situated in the fortress of Caesena, the office of abbot had formerly been entrusted to him by Natalis, once bishop, but that he has now [Col. 1308B] been removed from it by Natalis’s successor, Concordius, [Note: [Col. 1307D] The printed editions read: “without any cause or fault existing”; and shortly afterward: “in the presence of certain deacons, with the deacon of the aforesaid bishop Concordius presenting his reasons.”] although he was guilty of no fault, and that another has been appointed in his place. This proved in part to be the case before certain of our deacons, with a deacon of the bishop Concordius present and pleading his bishop’s cause. But since [Note: [Col. 1308C] These words seem to have been taken by Saint Gregory from the letter of the African Fathers to Celestine. It reads as follows: “No decree of the Fathers has detracted from this African Church, and the Nicene decrees have most explicitly entrusted both clergy of the lower orders and the bishops themselves to their metropolitans. For they provided with the greatest prudence and justice that whatever business arose should be concluded in the places where it had arisen, and that the grace of the Holy Spirit would not be lacking to any province … For how will the transmarine—that is, Roman—judgment itself be just, when the necessary witnesses cannot be brought to it because of their sex, the weakness of old age, or many other intervening obstacles? For we find no synod of the Fathers establishing that some persons should be sent as though from your Holiness’s side,” and so forth. Certainly, if there is ever a right of recalling a case home, as the jurists say, *Digest* V, *De iudiciis*, it is especially so in cases in which witnesses are needed. GUSSANV.] more certain proof can be obtained in the region where the matter occurred, your Fraternity should diligently and carefully investigate it. If no manifest cause of deposition existed that would have removed the aforesaid Fortunatus from the office of abbot, hasten to restore him to his place and do not cease to rebuke his bishop with due severity: why did he attempt to destroy his predecessor’s appointment without having been provoked by any misconduct? But if the other party says that the matter is otherwise than we have been informed, the truth must be sought through careful [Col. 1308C] investigation, and whatever the canonical order demands must be settled in such a way that no further complaint remains concerning it. [Note: [Col. 1308D] In one Colbert manuscript this chronological note is prefixed to the letter, while the other manuscripts are silent. In the Remigian manuscript, after this letter, we read “in the month of November, indiction 7.” We believe this belongs to the following letter.] Given in the month of October, indiction 7.

## LETTER VII. TO ALCYSON, BISHOP OF CORCYRA

The fortress of Cassiopi is to remain under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Corcyra; nevertheless, the priests of Euriae are not to be expelled from it.

Gregory to Alcyson, bishop [Note: [Col. 1308D] EPIST. VII [Al. 2].—Corcyra is commonly called Corfu, an island of the province of Nicopolis, adjacent to Epirus. In many Norman manuscripts *Corsicae* is read instead of *Corcyrae*, but erroneously; the error is corrected in what follows. All the manuscripts, together with the Colbert, Rheims, and three Vatican manuscripts, read *Alcysoni*. Vatican B has “to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna.”] of Corcyra.

[Col. 1309A]

It is not without reason that the ambition of an elated heart is required to be restrained when, [Note: [Col. 1309C] The Church is governed by canon law. Yet the canons are weakened, cheapened, and despised by frequent dispensations, as commonly happens. It is remarkable if, whenever we are less favorably disposed toward someone, we invoke the canons, but whenever we wish to favor someone, we disregard them. I offer as an example the Council of Trent, whose discipline we now vigorously defend and now violate with impunity, according to our pleasure. GUSSANV.] setting aside the force of the sacred canons, the excesses of rash presumption unlawfully covet what belongs to another. Such conduct is not only harmful in producing losses, 1265 but is also demonstrably contrary to ecclesiastical peace. Having therefore reread the letters of your Fraternity, we have learned what has happened previously or is now happening concerning the fortress of Cassiopi, which is situated in your diocese, and concerning the bishop of the city of Euriae, [Note: [Col. 1309D] In the printed editions, erroneously, *Isauriae*. All the English and Norman manuscripts and Vatican F read *Euriae*. Colbert, Regius, Rheims, and three Vatican manuscripts read *Eurissae civitatis*, which is the same. The same reading continues in the following letters. The learned Holstenius noted that this is the correct reading in *Sacred Geography*, p. 117. Euria, called San Donato by the Italians, was a city of Epirus and formerly an episcopal see. Its bishop Marcus of Euria subscribed to the Council of Chalcedon, act 1, and Theodore to the Council of Constantinople under Menas. Saint Donatus was its bishop in the time of Pope Honorius, whence the city still bears his name.] and we have been saddened that those who ought to have been indebted to your Church for the charity shown them have not been restrained by any shame from becoming its enemies. Finally, they attempted, contrary to ecclesiastical order, priestly modesty, and the statutes of the sacred canons, to remove the aforesaid fortress from your jurisdiction and subject it to their own [Col. 1309B] power, so that they might in some manner become its lords, although previously they had been received there as strangers.

For this reason, since Andrew, our brother of venerable memory and metropolitan of Nicopolis, acting also with the support of an imperial command, [Note: [Col. 1310C] A “principal command” is a command of a prince, or emperor.] to whom the examination of this case had been assigned, is known to have issued a sentence—as became clear to us—declaring that the aforementioned fortress of Cassiopi ought to remain under the jurisdiction of your Church, as it had always done, we approve the form of that sentence and, with the authority of the apostolic see supporting justice, confirm it and decree that it remain wholly binding. For no principle of equity and no canonical order permits one person in any way to seize another’s parish.

Therefore, although the fault in this dispute seems to demand no small severity against them, because they have repaid good with evil, care must nevertheless be taken that kindness not be overcome by their excess. [Note: [Col. 1310C] Vatican A and F read: “so that kindness may not punish the excess.” [Col. 1310D] Vatican D reads: “so that he may not appear to commit the excess.”] Nor must what is owed to foreign brethren, even when they are suffering hardship, be denied them, lest charity be judged to accomplish nothing in the hearts of bishops if those who deserve great compassion are left without the remedy of consolation.

Therefore the priests or clergy of the city of Euriae must in no way be expelled from residence in the aforesaid fortress of Cassiopi. They must also be permitted, with due reverence, to place the holy and venerable body of blessed Donatus, which they have brought with them, in whichever of the churches of the aforementioned place they choose, whether inside or outside. This, however, is to be done only after security has been provided to your affection, in whose parish the fortress itself is situated, by means of a written guarantee in which the bishop of Euriae promises that he will claim there no power, privilege, jurisdiction, or authority as a [Note: [Col. 1310D] That is, titular or principal, as in the following letter; or proper, as in Letter 8, below. GUSSANV.] cardinal bishop. Rather, once peace has been restored by God’s favor, and, if they wish, the venerable body of Saint Donatus has been removed, they will return in every way to their own place.

Thus, while the memory of this promise endures, they will not afterward dare, on any pretext, to claim anything for themselves there as lords, but will acknowledge at all times that they are guests in that place, and your Fraternity’s Church will suffer no prejudice in any part of its right or privilege. [Note: [Col. 1310D] In the old Colbert manuscript and in Vatican A and F, the beginning of the letter reads: “in the month of November, indiction 7.” In another Vatican manuscript: “in the month of October,” and so forth.] (See also Letters 8 and 13 below.)

## LETTER VIII. TO BONIFACE, DEACON

He is to act with the emperor so that, rescinding the command obtained by deception concerning the fortress of Cassiopi, he orders his own sentence to be observed.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1310D] EPIST. VIII [Al. 3].—Concerning him, see above, Book XIII, Letter 38. Previously the name was not read at Constantinople, but the Norman, Vatican, Regius, Colbert, and other manuscripts persuaded the editors to add it.] to Boniface, deacon, at Constantinople.

Whenever the discord of those who ought to be preachers of peace makes us sad, we must labor with great concern so that, once the cause of the dispute has been removed, those who disagree through differing wills may return to harmony. What happened concerning the fortress of Cassiopi, situated on the island of Corcyra, and how the bishop of Euriae [Col. 1310C] seeks to take it away from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Corcyra and wickedly subject it to his own jurisdiction, would take too long to recount. But so that your affection may understand everything carefully, we have sent you the writings of our brother Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra, and have caused his representative to come there; he can also instruct you verbally and in detail about each point.

We indicate the matter briefly, however. When a command had previously been obtained by deception from the former emperor Maurice, to the prejudice of the Church of Corcyra, and his command—since it had been issued contrary to the laws and sacred canons—had produced no effect, the dispute between the parties remained unresolved. [Col. 1311A] [Note: [Col. 1311D] The same recent editors, with equal freedom, read: “he gave another command to Andrew.” This alteration, made against the Vatican, Norman, and Colbert manuscripts, disturbs the sense.] He therefore gave another command to Andrew, formerly our brother and then metropolitan of Nicopolis, directing that, since both parties were subject to Andrew’s jurisdiction, he himself should hear and canonically conclude the case. After the metropolitan had examined the case and issued a sentence, copies of which we have sent you, he determined that the aforesaid fortress of Cassiopi was under the power and jurisdiction of the bishop of Corcyra, whose diocese it had always been. We approved this sentence and deemed it necessary to confirm it by the authority of the apostolic see.

And lest what we had decreed should be so severe that it seemed to contain no kindness, we took care to arrange the matter for the time being as the text of the sentence we sent you shows: neither the bishop nor the clergy of the city of Euriae would suffer hardship concerning their residence, nor would the privileges of the Church of Corcyra be disturbed in any way.

But because [Note: [Col. 1311D] Above he speaks of the deception practiced against the emperor Maurice. Here Saint Gregory discusses another deception suffered by Phocas at the beginning of his reign.] at the very beginning of the reign of the most serene lord emperor a command was obtained by deception, and the fortress was reportedly handed over to the bishop of Euriae contrary to the judgment of the metropolitan of Nicopolis—a judgment supported by ecclesiastical rectitude and canonical law—which we cannot hear or mention without pain and groaning, and this with even greater injury to the bishop of Corcyra and his clergy, we did not deem it appropriate to send our sentence to anyone, lest we seem to act against the command of the most merciful lord emperor or, God forbid, in contempt of him. For this reason your affection must carefully explain everything to his Piety and firmly assert that this is wholly unlawful, wholly perverse, wholly unjust, and greatly opposed to the sacred canons. Therefore he must not permit such a sin to be introduced during his reign to the prejudice of the Church.

But report what the judgment of the aforementioned former metropolitan contained concerning this matter, and how the things decreed by him were confirmed by us. Strive to arrange that, when our sentence is sent there together with the emperor’s command, we may appear both to have reserved the matter—as is fitting—to his serenity and to have reasonably corrected what had been wrongly attempted.

In this matter every effort must be made so that, if possible, he himself may also issue a command ordering the observance of what we have defined. Once this has been done, every opportunity for further deception is closed off. Therefore hasten, with the help of almighty God, to exercise your vigilance in restraining these prejudices, [Col. 1312A] so that neither now may the will of those who are plotting perversely obtain anything against the ancient order of ecclesiastical custom, nor afterward may this abominable affair serve as an example.

Furthermore, so that you may learn how many evils and how great oppressions our aforesaid brother and fellow bishop Alcyson claims to suffer from the agents of the Church of Thessalonica, we have sent your affection the letter that he sent to us. Therefore arrange for the representative of the aforementioned Church to come to you, examine the case in his presence, and write to our brother and fellow bishop Eusebius concerning those points on which reason moves you, so that he may forbid his men to act unjustly and may instruct them not to oppress their inferiors but rather to assist them whenever justice requires.

We also wish your affection to write to the man who has been appointed metropolitan of the city of Nicopolis, so that he may examine the case concerning the damages that our aforesaid brother Alcyson complains were inflicted upon his Church, and determine what is just. For the matter is recorded as having been left undecided, rather than settled, by his predecessor. [Note: [Col. 1311D] In the recent editions this letter is closed with the words: “Given in the month of December, indiction 7.” These words are absent from our manuscripts and from the old printed editions. In the manuscripts they belong to the following letter, as we shall presently say.]

1268

## LETTER IX. TO JOHN, BISHOP OF PANORMUS

He grants permission to consecrate a basilica.

Gregory to John, bishop of Panormus.

Know that by the tenor of our command authority has been granted to you to consecrate the basilica which, as your affection reports, has been completed in honor of the blessed and ever-virgin Mary through Savinus, our subdeacon and rector of the patrimony. Thus, dearest brother, fulfilling the desire of your devotion, you may rejoice in the completion of its solemn celebration. [Note: [Col. 1311D] EPIST. IX [Al. 4].—We read this wording only in Vatican A and B.] Given in the month of December, indiction 7.

## LETTER X. TO GUDUIN, DUKE

He is to punish the soldier who violated a servant of God.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1312D] EPIST. X [Al. 5].—He is called *Guduin* by the writers of Greek, Γουνδόης (*Goundóēs*). He was commander of the army of Maurice under Priscus, according to Cedrenus, in the seventeenth year of Maurice. Simocatta recounts his distinguished deeds in war, Book VII, chapters 11 and 12, and calls him ταξίαρχος (*taxíarchos*, “commander of a brigade”). He was made ὑποστράτηγος (*hypostrátēgos*, “deputy commander”) by Peter, the brother of Maurice and supreme commander of the army, and performed many notable deeds; see the same author, Book VIII, chapters 5–7. GUSSANV. Colbert, Regius, and Norman read *Guduin*, while Vatican D, E, F, and Rheims read *Guduino*. Corbie has *Gunduino*, Vatican A *Gundino*, and Vatican B *Guidoni*. The old edition corruptly reads “Desiderius, bishop of Gaul.”] to Guduino, duke of Naples.

Although, among the many good reports that are frequently brought us concerning your greatness, it is said that this is especially praiseworthy in you: that you love chastity and observe discipline as is fitting, we have been sufficiently astonished that no very severe punishment has yet been inflicted upon that soldier who, at the devil’s instigation, destroyed a servant of God. For it would have been entirely consistent with your character and goodness that vengeance should reach us before news of the injustice of the crime committed.

But since we believe that punishment for this crime has been delayed not by your will but through the deceptions of others, we exhort you, lest this sin [Note: [Col. 1312D] Recent editions read: “or the shoulder of the undisciplined soldier,” perhaps because they did not understand what the military unit meant in this passage. This is explained at length in the notes to Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 35. See also above, Book VIII, Letter 5. The manuscripts everywhere certainly read “or the number.”] weigh upon either the number of the undisciplined soldier or [Col. 1313A] the places where it was committed, to demonstrate without any excuse or delay what zeal you possess [Note: [Col. 1313C] Vatican B, E, F, the old Colbert manuscript, and Remigian read “toward charity.” The Remigian manuscript has at the beginning of the letter “that you love charity,” whereas the others have “that you love chastity.”] for the preservation of chastity, and to hasten to correct this great crime so severely, as an example to others, that you may make God—against whose honor the man committed this act and whose fear he despised—favorable toward you, and that we may return thanks to you for the uprightness of your zeal. For we cannot in any way tolerate so great an iniquity remaining unpunished.

## LETTER XI. TO JOHN, BISHOP

He is to inquire into the persons, character, and learning of three men elected to the episcopate.

Gregory to John, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1313C] EPIST. XI [Al. 6].—This is found in this form throughout the manuscripts and old printed editions. The more recent editors arbitrarily changed it to: “lest confusion should arise from their careless ordination …” [Col. 1313D].]

Lest the careless ordination of those chosen for the episcopate should occur, their persons must be investigated with vigilant concern. We have indeed been informed that Florentinus, archdeacon of the Church of Ancona, who had been elected to the episcopate, possesses knowledge of sacred Scripture, but is so broken by the old age of his years that he cannot rise to the office of governance. It has also been reported that he is so miserly that no friend ever enters his house out of charity. [Note: [Col. 1313D] Alteserra proves with clear testimonies, in his commentary on this passage, that a bishop’s house ought to be open to everyone; the reader may consult him. We have spoken elsewhere at greater length about episcopal hospitality. GUSSANV.]

Rusticus, a deacon of the same Church, who had likewise been elected, is said to be an alert man, but, as is asserted, does not know the Psalms. We know that Florentinus, a deacon of the Church of Ravenna, who is reported to have been unanimously elected, is diligent, but we do not know at all what he is like inwardly.

Therefore your Fraternity, together with our brother and fellow bishop Armenius, visitor of the aforementioned Church of Ancona, should hasten to go there and inquire carefully into the life and character of each man, and whether any of them is conscious of a crime that would prevent him from undertaking this office. It must likewise be investigated whether what has been said about the aforesaid archdeacon—that no friend has ever entered his house—is true, and [Note: [Col. 1313D] Whether virtue or vice is fixed and rooted in a person must be investigated and subtly discerned with every effort and care, as Saint Gregory here declares, being concerned both about the absence of hospitality and about the reason for that absence. It is not always easy to distinguish the two. It is easy to pretend to virtue but difficult to possess it, as Saint Augustine testifies, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, Book I, chapter 1. “Son, observe carefully the movements of nature and grace, for they move in highly contrary and subtle ways, and can scarcely be distinguished except by a spiritual and inwardly enlightened person,” teaches the author of *The Imitation of Christ*, Book III, chapter 54. If many reflected more deeply upon this, they would walk more cautiously in the ways of the Lord. See also Cardinal Bona, *On the Discernment of Spirits*, chapters 1 and 4. Saint Augustine writes in the same work, chapter 15: “If virtue leads us to the blessed life, I would affirm that virtue is nothing other than the highest love of God … Would that the reality were in people’s minds as the names are on everyone’s lips!” GUSSANV.] whether he is like this from necessity or from miserliness; whether he is so old that he cannot rise to govern; or whether, after touching the most holy Gospels, he has sworn, as we have been informed, never to approach the episcopate.

The deacon Rusticus must also be investigated, to determine in how many Psalms his knowledge is deficient. [Note: [Col. 1314C] *Quanti* (“how many”) is not rarely used for *quot* (“as many as”). Luke 15:17: “How many hired servants are in my father’s house!” Book II of the Code, *On the Prefect of the Praetorian Prefecture of Africa*, section “But if”: “And how many frontier soldiers,” and likewise: “How many soldiers your Greatness may provide there for the protection of the places.” See Antonius Augustinus, Book II of the *Observations*, chapter 5. In any case, ignorance of the Psalms and miserliness exclude a man from the episcopate. For a bishop must be hospitable and a teacher. What Saint Gregory adds concerning the oath is noteworthy. The reader should consult the Gloss on Distinction 85, where many canons are cited on both sides. On the Psalms and the learning of a bishop, see the whole of Distinction 38, especially the chapter *Omnes psallentes*, and Distinction 23, chapter *Qui episcopus*, from the Council of Carthage. Indeed, in Distinction 38, chapter *Quae ipsis*, among the things necessary for priests to learn, I find not only penitential canons but also the Psalter. On knowledge of the Psalms, see further Letter 45 of Book IV, now Letter 48 of Book V. Partly from GUSSANV.]

As for Florentinus, the deacon of Ravenna, if, as we have said, there is no crime that obstructs him, it is necessary to act with his bishop so that the bishop should grant him release. [Note: [Col. 1314D] This was stated above, Letter 19 of Book IV, now Letter 17 of Book V.] Yet this must not be done by our mandate [Note: [Col. 1314D] Recent editions, against the Vatican, Norman, and other manuscripts, read “or decree.”] or instruction, lest he appear to resign against his will. Rather, those who elected him should act on their own, as they know best. You, however, must investigate everything we have written concerning each man with the utmost care and diligence, and strive to report it to us precisely, so that, once we have been made better informed by your report, we may determine, with God as our guide, what should be done thereafter. (Compare John the Deacon, Book III, chapter 12.)

## LETTER XII. TO THEODELINDA, QUEEN OF THE LOMBARDS

He congratulates her on her son’s union with the Catholic faith. He excuses his failure to reply to Secundus on account of gout. He sends the synod held under Justinian. He defends the orthodoxy of the Roman Church. He gives thanks to the king for the peace that has been made.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1314D] EPIST. XII [Al. 7].—Concerning her, see Letter 2 of Book IV.] to Theodelinda, queen.

The letters that you recently sent us from the region of Genoa made us participants in your joy, because by the grace of almighty God we learned both that a son had been given to you and—something highly praiseworthy in your Excellency—that he had been joined to the Catholic faith. For nothing else was to be believed concerning your Christianity except that you would strive to fortify the one whom you had received as a divine gift with the help of Catholic truth, so that our Redeemer might recognize you as his familiar servant, and might happily raise up for the Lombard people a new king in his fear.

Therefore we pray almighty God both to preserve you in the way of his commandments and to cause this same most excellent son of ours, [Note: [Col. 1315B] Fredegar calls him Adaloald; others call him Adoald. Still almost a child, he succeeded his father Agilulf, king of the Lombards, and reigned for ten years under the guardianship of his most wise mother Theodelinda. Through the faction of certain men, however, he and his mother were driven from the kingdom by their own people, and shortly afterward he died by poison. Arioald, duke of Turin, was elected in his place; his wife was Gundeberga, Adaloald’s sister, around the year 624. See more about him in Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*. GUSSANV.] Adulouvaldus, to advance in his love, so that, just as he is already great among human beings, he may also be glorious in good works before the eyes of our God.

As for what your Excellency wrote—that we ought to reply more fully to our beloved son Secundus, the abbot, concerning what he had written—who, knowing that his request and your wishes would benefit many, would have thought them worth postponing if illness had not intervened?
