[Note: [Col. 1315B] Almost all the manuscripts read *Secundo*, while the printed editions have *Secundino*. These writings of Secundus may perhaps have occasioned Letter 54 of Book VII, indiction 2, now Letter 52 of Book IX. Is this the Secundinus, or Secundus, who is sometimes called abbot at Ravenna and is frequently mentioned by Paul the Deacon in his *History of the Lombards*, especially Book IV, chapter 42? Secundus, servant of Christ, died at Trent in the month of March; we have often spoken of him. He wrote a concise history of the deeds of the Lombards down to his own time. GUSSANV.] But so severe an attack of gout held us that we could scarcely rise not only to dictate but even to speak, as your envoys who carried this letter themselves learned: they found us ill when they arrived and left us in the greatest danger and peril of life. But if, by the disposition of almighty God, I recover, I shall reply fully to everything he wrote to me.

Nevertheless, I have sent through the bearers of this letter the synod held in the time of Justinian of pious memory, so that my aforementioned beloved son, reading it, may learn that everything he had heard against the apostolic see or the Catholic Church is false. For far be it from us to accept the opinion of any heretic or in any respect to deviate from the *Tome* of our predecessor, Leo, of holy memory. Rather, we accept whatever has been defined by the four holy synods and condemn whatever has been rejected.

We have also arranged to send to our most excellent son Adulouvaldus, the king, [Note: [Col. 1315C] This word has various meanings; see Menardus, *Harmony of the Rules*, chapter 3, pp. 124–125. Among Christians it is used for sacred relics enclosed in gold, silver, crystal, or any other engraved material. The Greeks also call them ἐγκóλπια (*enkólpia*), and thus Anna Comnena, in the *Alexiad*, calls the cross containing relics of the saints or fragments of the Holy Cross σταυρὸς ἐγκóλπιος (*stauròs enkólpios*). It was worn hanging by small chains from the neck to the breast. Phylacteries are prohibited by the Council of Laodicea, canon 36, and by Chrysostom, Homily 43 on Matthew 23. They understood them to be tablets containing incantations. Saint Gregory, however, speaks of phylacteries believed to possess a certain divine power against various harmful things. Thus Chrysostom writes in his work *On Prayer*: “Prayer is an unconquerable weapon and a secure φυλακτήριον (*phylaktḗrion*, ‘protective charm’).” See the notes on Matthew 23:5, and distinguish religious observance from superstition. The learned Alteserra has much worthy of attention concerning phylacteries, which the diligent student will not regret reading. A recent example is the decree of the Roman Inquisition condemning ἐθελοθρησκεία (*ethelothrēskeía*), or rather ἐθελοδουλία (*ethelodoulía*), by which certain regular and secular persons, by wearing little chains on parts of their bodies, gave themselves into the servitude of the Blessed Virgin. GUSSANV.] phylacteries—that is, a cross containing a piece of the wood of the holy cross of the Lord, together with [Note: [Col. 1315D] It is unclear which Gospel this reading belonged to. Perhaps it was the four Gospels, or the work of one evangelist, or the first chapter of Saint John. It is known that among the Jews sacred Scripture was divided into various sections, each of which was read in the synagogues on a separate Sabbath. Among Christians both Testaments were formerly read in public assembly, not briefly and in fragments as is now done; many have complained about this new practice. What Isidore of Pelusium, Book II, Letter 150, reports about the little Gospels that women carried for religious purposes is especially relevant here: δελτία μικρά … ὥσπερ νῦν αἱ γυναῖκες τὰ εὐαγγέλια μικρά (“small tablets … just as women now [carry] small Gospels”). Clement of Alexandria seems to allude to something similar near the end of the *Protrepticus*, speaking of amulets: Ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐ βούλεσθε τὸν οὐράνιον αὐτὸν περιάψασθαι τὸν σωτῆρα λόγον, καὶ τῇ ἐπωδῇ τοῦ Θεοῦ πιστεύσαντες (“But you are unwilling even to bind around yourselves the heavenly Word himself, the Savior, and, trusting in the incantation of God,” and so forth). Thus this reading of the Gospel would have been a phylactery—not the Jewish kind discussed by Epiphanius, Heresy 15, nor the kind prohibited by the Councils of Agde, canon 68, and of Leptines, canon 5. GUSSANV. Saint Gregory, among the other phylacteries, sends a reading from the holy Gospel, which John Chrysostom teaches was customarily hung around the neck. “Do you not see,” he says, “how women and little children, for great protection, hang the Gospels around their necks?” See also Homily 73 on Matthew. We learn from Augustine, on John, chapter 7, that the Gospel was placed on the head for healing.] a reading of the holy Gospel [Note: [Col. 1316C] Horace, *Odes* 1.38:

“I hate Persian apparatus, boy.”

That is, sumptuous and elaborate equipment. Among the Latins this word is common for receptacles, such as a money-box, pen-case, and so forth. In Greek it is often θήκη (*thḗkē*), equivalent to μνῆμα (*mnḗma*) and σορός (*sorós*), “tomb” or “coffin.” In Saint Augustine and others we read *entechas*, although the Greeks do not seem to have used the word. See *Cause* 12, Question 1, chapter 10, from the sermon *On the Common Life of Clerics*. It is cited in the Council of Aachen, 836, canon 112. GUSSANV.] enclosed in a Persian case.

I have also sent my daughter, her sister, three rings, two [Col. 1316B] with hyacinths, [Note: [Col. 1316D] Here *albula* is counted among precious stones. Perhaps it is the stone mentioned by Epiphanius. In the twelfth place among the twelve gems he discusses the onyx, which he says received its name because of the purity of its whiteness, διὰ τὸ καθαρὸν τῆς λευκότητος (“because of the purity of its whiteness”). Patavius notes that Dioscorides calls the alabaster stone an onyx. Apollinaris Sidonius, in the epithalamium of Ruricius and Iberia, mentions a white stone while enumerating gems.] and one with an *albula*. I ask that you give them to her, so that through your Excellency our charity may be treasured among them.

Paying the duty of greeting with paternal affection, we ask that you return thanks on our behalf to your most excellent son, the king, your husband, for the peace that has been made, and that, as you are accustomed to do, you urge his mind in every way toward peace in the future, so that, amid the many good works you perform, you may find before God the reward of the innocent people who might have perished through scandal.

[Note: [Col. 1316D] He alludes to the peace made in that very year. Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 29, says that Adaloald, son of King Agilulf, was baptized in chapter 28—namely, in the year 603, when Easter fell on the seventh day before the Ides of April; in that same month the seventh indiction began. “Peace was made,” he says, “in the ninth month, lasting until the Kalends of April, in the eighth indiction.” From this we would infer that the peace continued until the year 605, when April fell in the eighth indiction, unless Paul assigns that same eighth indiction in chapter 30, both to the second year of Phocas’s reign and to the year in which Gregory passed to Christ; yet no one doubts that Gregory died in the seventh indiction, whereas Phocas began to reign in the sixth indiction, toward the end of the year 602.]

[Note: [Col. 1317D] In the more recent edition there is added: “Given in the month of January, indiction 7,” which none of our manuscript codices contains. What belonged to the following letter, however, they assigned to this letter. In Paul’s Collection it is corruptly given as: “Given on the second day of the month of March, indiction 2.”]

## Letter XIII. To Alcyson, Bishop of Corcyra

He should allow the body of Saint Donatus to be deposited in the fortress of Cassiopi, while preserving the jurisdiction of his own church.

Gregory to Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra.

Kindness must not be denied to brothers who repent and turn to wholesome counsel, lest guilt appear able to prevail more than charity in the minds of bishops. Accordingly, when Peter, lector of the Church of Euria, came to us bearing letters from our brother and fellow bishop John, we received him in the presence of the representatives of Your Fraternity. After rereading the letters he had brought, we took care to ask him whether he had anything to say against the allegations of those same representatives of yours. Since he stated that nothing else had been entrusted to him and that he had absolutely nothing further to answer beyond what the bishop’s letter contained, we decreed, with God’s authority and without delay, what was consistent with the canons.

After a long interval, however, the aforementioned Peter produced a written memorandum, which he asserted had been given to him by his bishop, and for this reason he had delayed the matter. But because in that memorandum the aforesaid bishop was said to have hoped [Note: [Col. 1317D] Letter XIII [alternative numbering 8].—In the Vatican D and Rheims manuscripts, *petiisse* (“had asked”) was read. In Gussanville and in some manuscripts, *superasse* (“had prevailed”) was read.] that he might have permission to deposit the holy and venerable body of Saint Donatus in the Church of Saint John, [Note: [Col. 1317D] The printed editions read: “which is situated in the fortress of Cassiopi.”] situated within the fortress called Cassiopi, and, he said, that he was prepared, for the sake of Your Fraternity, since it is shown to belong to your diocese, to issue a written guarantee that no prejudice would thereby arise for you, we judged that his petition should not be left without effect. He desires that provision be made for him in this way at a time of necessity [Note: [Col. 1317D] Three Vatican manuscripts, the Bec manuscript, and others from Normandy, together with the Regius manuscript, read *ferri consultum* (“that provision be made”).] while acknowledging that he will preserve in every respect the jurisdiction of your church.

Moved therefore by this consideration, we exhort Your Fraternity by the present letter to grant, without any delay or excuse, permission for the aforesaid holy and venerable body to be deposited in the aforementioned Church of Saint John, [Col. 1318A] provided, of course, that you first secure yourself by a written document, so that he may never, under any pretext, claim in the aforesaid church or fortress any jurisdiction or privilege as though he were its proper bishop, but may inviolably preserve there every right and authority of your church, since it is its parish. Likewise, as our brother himself requested, you should agree to respond that, when by God’s mercy peace has been restored and he has permission to return to his own place, he may lawfully take the aforesaid venerable body away with him without any objection.

For this reason, so that what is being done may not appear to be merely personal, and so that no opportunity may be found for renewed contention to arise, your successors also must be included in every respect in this undertaking, for the preservation of all these arrangements. Thus, with such precaution in place, neither may he thereafter presume to defend anything for himself there in your diocese against equity and the decrees of the sacred canons, nor may the right of your church ever suffer any prejudice on account of this concession. [Note: [Col. 1318C] Vatican B reads: “so that it may appear to be synodal … and no opportunity may be found.”]

[Note: [Col. 1318C] “It could be added: ‘in the month of January, indiction 7.’ For this is read in three Vatican manuscripts and in the old Colbert manuscript, which we regard as preferable to the two Tellerian manuscripts, where one finds: ‘in the month of August, indiction 6.’]

(See above, letters 7 and 8.)

1273

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Letter XIV [alternative numbering 9].—This letter is read on a marble tablet affixed to the wall of the basilica of Saint Peter. John the Deacon mentions the tablet’s being affixed there in book II, chapter 20. From this letter it is clear what sort and how great were the lights in the churches at that time. Cassiodorus, book III of the *Variae*, letter 7, records King Theodoric writing to the bishop of Salona that he should pay the price of sixty *orcae* of oil purchased to fill the lights of his church. We have often discussed the lights of churches in our notes on the *Dialogues*.]

## Letter XIV. To Felix, Subdeacon

He grants substantial revenues to the Church of Saint Paul for maintaining its lights.

Gregory to Felix, subdeacon and administrator of the patrimony of the Appian Way.

Although, by God’s authority, everything that the apostolic Church of the blessed Peter and Paul possesses—acquired through their honor and benefactions—is held in common, there ought nevertheless to be diversity among the persons responsible for administering its affairs, so that more diligent care may be given to the matters assigned to each one.

Since proper concern for the Church of the blessed apostle Paul reminded us that the herald of the faith, who filled the whole world with the light of his preaching, should not be seen to have fewer lights there, [Note: [Col. 1318D] Vatican B and F read: “and that it had become very incongruous and extremely harsh.”] and since it seemed highly improper and extremely harsh that the particular estate in which he won the crown of martyrdom, being beheaded so that he might live, should not serve him, we have judged it useful to assign to its lights the same estate called Aquae Salviae, with all its properties: namely, the wine cellar, Antonianus, [Note: [Col. 1318D] On the marble tablet: “Villa Pertusa.”] Villa Pertusa in the Forum Primianum, [Col. 1319A] Cassianus, Silonis, [Note: [Col. 1319D] There: “Cornelii Tesselata,” and “Cornelianus.”] Cornelius, Tesselata, and Cornelianus, [Note: [Col. 1319D] There is no need here to add a note explaining the meaning of these terms. It is enough to indicate Digest, book III, title 7, entitled *On a Legacy of Equipment or Implements*, where everything by which an estate or house may be equipped is enumerated, and a distinction is established between what is *instructi*, what is *instrumentum*, and what is *instrumenti*. Saint Gregory, in this donation, includes absolutely everything: things, beasts of burden, people. Gussanville.] together with all its rights, equipment, furnishings, and everything generally belonging to it, with the grace of Christ.

We further add to this transfer two gardens between the Tiber and the portico of that church, on the right as one goes from the city gate, divided by the river [Note: [Col. 1319D] Vatican A reads: “Armon.”] Almon, [Note: [Col. 1319D] Vatican B reads: “between the boundaries.”] adjoining the boundaries of the garden of the monastery of Saint Stephen, which is occupied by the servants of God and situated at Saint Paul’s, and extending to the boundaries of the estate of Pissinianus; and also the little plots called the Robbers’ Ditch, situated there beside the same portico as one proceeds; [Note: [Col. 1319D] The printed editions read: *positas*, that is, “beside the same.” It should certainly be read *ibidem* or *itidem*, as in the Regius and Vatican manuscripts. On the marble tablet one reads *idem*, perhaps abbreviated for *ibidem*.] likewise, on the left, toward the gate where vineyards have now been planted. These little plots adjoin on one side the estate formerly belonging to Eugenius the scholar, and on the other the properties of the monastery [Col. 1319B] [Note: [Col. 1320D] On the marble tablet: “of Saint Aristus.” Vatican A and B: “of Saint Hedistus.” Vatican F: “of Saint Edistus.”] of Saint Edistus.

All these we wish to be administered, with God’s help, by the superintendents of the aforesaid church who shall serve from time to time, beginning with the present seventh indiction. Whatever income thereafter accrues is to be spent on its lights, and they themselves are to render accounts of it.

Therefore we command Your Experience to erase from their registers and remove the aforesaid estate of Aquae Salviae, with all its aforementioned properties, as well as the gardens and little plots described above, and to transfer everything in the name of the aforesaid Church of the blessed apostle Paul; so that the superintendents serving there, henceforth having no excuse, may take care of its lights without our supervision in such a way that neglect may never occur there. [Note: [Col. 1320D] The Regius manuscript and Vatican F read: “to the aforesaid monastery.”]

After the transfer of all the aforementioned property has been completed, we wish Your Experience to return this decree to the archives of our church. [Note: [Col. 1320D] On the marble tablet, after *restituat* (“return”), there is added: “Farewell. Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the second year of our lord Phocas, pope, and the first year of his consulship, indiction 7.”]

## Letter XV. To Anthemius, Subdeacon

He should warn the exarch against speaking rashly, and should himself procure through the letter a hoped-for relief for the Romans’ misfortunes.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1320D] Letter XV [alternative numbering 28].—That this heading is false is clear from the words “Your Glory,” as well as from other expressions that do not suit clerics. Gussanville.] to Anthemius, subdeacon.

Because I hear that Your Glory is firmly and steadfastly established in its character, I rejoice greatly, and therefore speak to you with confidence about what displeases me, as to a special son. For the most excellent exarch says certain things capable of provoking all who love him to hostility toward him. Accordingly, through the bearer of this letter I dictated what I thought should be read to him in private; if you wish, let it also be read to you, so that you may know what you ought to write to him concerning the same matter.

[Note: [Col. 1320] This note appears at the foot of column 1320, but the callout letter (a) has not been printed in the text. Letter XVI.—We have found this letter hitherto unprinted in the Corbie, Pratel, Gemet, and Sées manuscripts, which scarcely differ in a single word.]

But how great the necessity is, and what troubles constrain us, you can learn both from the report of our present representative and from the letters of my brother and fellow bishop Mariniani. Therefore it is fitting that Your Glory consider the matter diligently, since we have great confidence in your wisdom in the Lord Almighty, and, where you are present, we do not believe that the cause can in any way be neglected. Act, then, so that our confidence may not prove misplaced. May heavenly grace protect you and grant you success in all your affairs.

## Letter XVI. Felix, Bishop of Messana, to Saint Gregory

He asks about the degrees of kinship within which marriage is permitted, about the harassment of bishops by their subjects, and about churches whose dedications are uncertain.

[Col. 1320B]

To the most blessed and honorable lord, the holy Father Gregory, pope, Felix, lover of Your Health and Holiness.

The rights of Your most blessed Health and Holiness are manifest before God. While the whole earth has been filled with the cultivation of the true faith through apostolic preaching and instruction, the orthodox Church of Christ, founded upon apostolic institution and most firmly strengthened by faithful fathers, is nevertheless built up through instruction in divine words, with your exhortatory admonition guiding it.

To this Church all the most blessed apostles, endowed alike with a share in honor and authority, led the masses of peoples—those whom divine predestination had foreknown—piously and holily from darkness to light, from falling away to the true faith, and from death to life, by saving commands and admonitions. Your venerable fatherhood follows the merits of these holy apostles and more perfectly fulfills their examples; it adorns the Church of God with upright character and holy deeds and, vigorous in sacred faith and Christian conduct, continually undertakes and accomplishes through pontifical zeal whatever it commands to be pleasing to God, preserving the precepts of the divine law, because, as the Apostle says, “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (Romans 2:13).

As we reflected upon these matters, certain people coming from Rome reported to us that you had written to Augustine, our fellow bishop—later ordained through Your Venerable Holiness as bishop for the English people and sent there—and to the English, whom we have learned were formerly converted to the faith through you, that those joined in the fourth generation should not be separated.

That practice formerly did not exist either in those regions or in ours, when I was nourished and instructed with you from childhood. Nor have I read it in any decree of your predecessors or in the regulations, whether general or particular, of the other Fathers; nor have I so far learned that it has been permitted by any wise men. Rather, I have always found that your holy predecessors and the other holy Fathers, both in the Council of Nicaea and in the other holy councils assembled, required this to be observed up to the seventh degree of a person’s ancestry, and I have learned that upright and God-fearing people carefully observe it.

While these matters were being discussed among us, other issues also arose concerning which it seemed necessary for us to consult Your Authority. For there came to us both Benedictus, [Note: [Col. 1321C] There seems to be an error in the name of this Syracusan bishop, for John was still governing that church.] bishop of the Church of Syracuse, and several other brothers of ours, likewise bishops, weeping and saying that they had been excessively disturbed and afflicted in spirit by secular persons and laymen because of their immoderate actions, for which certain unjust accusations were also being brought against them.

There are also certain churches in our province whose consecration is uncertain. Because of their antiquity and the negligence of their custodians, it is not known whether they were dedicated by bishops or not.

Concerning all these matters we ask to be instructed by Your Holiness and by the authority of your holy see. We also ask to be informed by your letters whether what we have heard—that you wrote as described above to our fellow bishop Augustine and to the English people—was written specifically to them or generally to everyone, and we desire to be fully instructed about this and the other matters mentioned.

We do not report to you what we have read and have learned to be observed by the faithful in order to rebuke you—God forbid—but we ask what we ought reasonably and faithfully to observe in these matters. Since considerable murmuring is taking place among us about this question, we seek from you, as from the head, an answer concerning what we should say to our brothers and fellow bishops, lest we remain uncertain about these matters, or that murmuring remain among us or others in your time and afterward, and lest your reputation, which has always been good and excellent, be torn apart by detraction or replaced by it, or—God forbid—your name be blasphemed in times to come.

For our part, faithfully observing what is right, with God as our author, and bound to you by one bond of charity, we ask you for what is right while defending your piety in every respect as faithful disciples. We know that, as the leaders of the holy see—first the apostles and then their successors—have always done, you care for the universal Church, and especially for bishops, who are called the eyes of the Lord because of their contemplation and watchfulness. You constantly reflect upon our religion and law, as it is written: “Blessed is the one who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night” (Psalm 1:2).

This meditation is not perceived merely through reading the forms of letters, but is recognized as immovably implanted in your conscience through the overflowing grace of Christ in you. The sacred law of Christ the Lord never departs from your heart, as the Prophet says in the Psalms: “The mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom, and his tongue shall speak judgment; the law of his God is in his heart” (Psalm 36:30)—written in your inmost being not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, therefore not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart.

We pray that every darkness of ignorance may be extinguished by your wise answers and assistance, so that through you, most holy Father, the morning star may shine upon us, and that doctrinal definition may gladden everyone everywhere, since the glorious Fathers of the holy Church are known to have proclaimed their own devout doctrines as a firm inheritance of eternal life.

[Col. 1322C]

And the subscription:

“May the Lord preserve you, safe and pleasing to God, holy Father of fathers, praying for us, forever. Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 1321D] Letter XVII [alternative numbering 32].—In the Corbie, Vatican D, Rheims, and Gemet manuscripts, the title reads: “Reply of Saint Gregory to the same Felix, bishop,” which presupposes another letter from Felix. Some have doubted that this letter is by Saint Gregory; but John the Deacon’s testimony proves that it was written by him, for John quoted part of it in book II, chapter 37. Hincmar also often mentions it and transcribes nearly a third of it, both in letters 37 and 59 and in the treatise *On the Divorce of Lothair and Theutberga*, question 5 and question 7, and more fully in question 12 near the end. Regino, abbot of Prüm, who flourished around the year 900, and other canonists who followed him, also cited much from it in the first appendix to his book *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 30. This letter is also found in many manuscript codices: the Tellerian, Carnotian, Bigotian, German, Vallombrosan, and English manuscripts. Yet how corrupt and deformed it is becomes clear from the many interpolations and useless repetitions that an attentive and prudent reader will notice while reading. For this reason some rejected it as unworthy of Gregory the Great. Partly from Gussanville.

We do not dare to subscribe to this learned man’s judgment; rather, we consider this letter worthy of Gregory. Certain passages are repeated either from the letters or from the book *The Rule for Pastors*. Such repetitions, however, are characteristic of Saint Gregory. Gussanville thinks that the letter has at least been displaced and believes it should be placed before the eighth letter of book V, now the ninth of book VI, because the Felix to whom Gregory responds concerning the privileges granted to the English people would be the very same man to whom he wrote in book I, indiction 9.

We demonstrate that this Felix was different from him as follows. This letter to Felix presupposes that Augustine had already been sent to Britain and, indeed, that Saint Gregory had already answered his questions concerning the proper governance of the new English Church. Therefore it was written to a different Felix from the bishop of Messana to whom letter 40 of book I is addressed. For Donus had succeeded that Felix, at least at the beginning of indiction 14, as is clear from letter 9 of book VI. If you say that this letter was displaced and belongs to another indiction—a claim contradicted by all the manuscripts and supported by no, even slight, conjecture—what will you say about the many other letters written to Donus? Therefore Felix had succeeded Eucarpus and was Donus’s predecessor. Pelagius II already recognized Eucarpus as an old man in the year 580, writing to him. Thus Felix I had governed the Church of Messana for several years before Gregory’s pontificate. Gregory ordained Donus as his successor; and, not many years before Gregory’s death, Felix II succeeded Donus. I say “not many years,” for at the beginning of the year 603, when Adrian was sent to administer the Syracusan patrimony, he was commended to Leo, Secundinus, John, Donus, and other bishops of Sicily, but not to Felix, in book XIII, letter 18.]

## Letter XVII. To Felix, Bishop of Messana

He responds to questions about the union of relatives, the harassment of bishops by their subjects, and the uncertain consecration of churches. He commands that the incorrigible be separated and that a synod be assembled each year.

To the most reverend brother Felix, bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.

Christ, our Head, willed us to be his members so that through his abundant charity and faith he might make us one body in himself. We ought to cling to him in such a way that, since without him we can do nothing, through him we may be what we are called. Let no thing divide us from the citadel of our Head, lest, if we refuse to be his member, we be abandoned by him and, like branches cast off from the vine, wither away.

Therefore, if we wish to deserve to be the dwelling place of our Redeemer, let us remain in his love with the full devotion of our minds. For he himself says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Your affection, therefore, dearest brother, required that we respond to your questions from the authority of the apostolic see. Although we were eager to do so briefly and concisely, because of certain burdensome circumstances that, through the hindrance of our sins, have fallen upon us, we entrust to your zeal the task of seeking and investigating these matters more extensively through the remaining institutions of the holy Fathers.

For a mind worn down and weighed down by burdens and difficulties cannot accomplish or speak freely about as much good as one that is joyful and released from oppression. We have not set these matters forth, therefore, because we wish to deny Your Holiness these or other things that we recognize as necessary, but so that what is found here in lesser measure may be sought more fully elsewhere.

You believed, following the example of your predecessors, that the apostolic see, in which you were nourished and instructed, should be consulted about three matters: the union of relatives, the harassment of bishops by their subjects, and uncertainty concerning the consecration of churches.

As for what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people and, as you remember, your own disciple, concerning unions among relatives, know that I wrote specifically to him and to the English people, who had recently come to the faith, and not generally to others, so that they might not withdraw in fear from the good they had begun by being confronted with excessive austerity.

All the Roman people bore witness to this. I did not entrust these instructions to them in writing with the intention that, after they had been firmly rooted in the faith, they should not separate if they were found to be related within their own kinship, or that they should unite within the line of affinity, that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, while they were still neophytes, they had first to be taught and repeatedly warned to avoid illicit unions, and those who afterward acted in such matters had to be excluded reasonably and faithfully.

For, in accordance with the Apostle who says, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2), we granted these concessions to them for the present, not for later generations, as was said above, lest the good that had been planted with a still-weak root be uprooted; instead, it was to be strengthened in its beginning and preserved until perfection.

Certainly, if in these matters we acted otherwise than we ought, know that it was done not through obstinacy but through compassion. [Note: [Col. 1324D] In the Corbie and Gemet manuscripts: “not on account of the matter itself.” The printed editions read: “not on account of the matter,” where there is no intelligible sense.]

I call God as witness, who knows the thoughts of all human beings and before whose eyes all things are naked and open. For if I were to destroy what our predecessors established, I would rightly be shown to be not a builder but a demolisher, as the voice of Truth testifies: “Every kingdom divided against itself will not stand” (Luke 11:17), and every knowledge and law divided against itself will be destroyed.

Therefore it is necessary that we all hold in harmony to the statutes of our holy Fathers, doing nothing through contention, but, united in every effort of good devotion, obeying the divine and apostolic constitutions with the Lord’s assistance. [Note: [Col. 1324D] The same words begin letter 53 of book V. A similar encomium of charity is also found in letter 33 of book VIII and letter 108 of book IX.]

(See book XI, letter 64.)

O how good is charity! Through love it presents absent persons to one another as though present, unites what is divided, orders what is confused, joins together what is unequal, and perfects what is incomplete. How rightly the distinguished preacher calls it “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3)! For the other virtues indeed produce perfection, but charity binds them together so firmly that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

Having properly considered these matters, I have now, in charity, yielded to the things just said—not given a command, but offered counsel; not handed down a rule to be observed by any future generations, but shown which of two dangers is easier to avoid. [Note: [Col. 1324D] The printed editions corruptly read: “to your charity.”]

If, therefore, in secular affairs each person’s right and proper order must be preserved, how much more must no confusion be introduced into ecclesiastical arrangements, lest discord find a place where the blessings of peace ought to proceed! This will be preserved if nothing is assigned to power, but everything to equity.

Accordingly, our heart greatly rejoices with Your Greatness because we find you so diligent in your actions that you take care of us and diligently inquire into such matters, so that these things may acquire for you not only glory among human beings but also the reward of recompense from the Lord Almighty.

As for the harassment of bishops, about which you wished to consult us, we know that the lives of prelates ought not to be disturbed by anyone’s excesses, because it is exceedingly unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be troubled by kings or subjects through any agitation. For if David, the most just of kings, did not presume to lay a hand upon Saul, whom it was already certain the Lord had rejected, how much more must care be taken that certain people do not lay the hand of detraction, reproach, indiscretion, or dishonor upon the Lord’s anointed or upon the preachers of the holy Church, since their harassment or detraction concerns Christ, in whose place they exercise an embassy in the Church?

Therefore all the faithful must take the greatest care not to tear apart their bishop—that is, the Lord’s anointed—secretly or publicly by detraction or reproach, considering the example of Miriam. Because she had spoken against Moses, the servant of God, on account of the Ethiopian woman, she was punished with the uncleanness of leprosy (Numbers 12). Let them also consider the Psalmist’s words: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Psalm 104:15).

And in the divine law it is written: “You shall not speak evil of the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people” (Exodus 22:28). Therefore subjects, both clerics and laypeople, must take great care not rashly to criticize the life of their bishops or superiors if they happen to see them doing something reprehensible, lest, in the very matter for which they rebuke evil, they be plunged into deeper things through the impulse of pride.

They must also be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they consider their faults. Rather, they should consider their wrong actions among themselves in such a way that, constrained by fear of God, they do not refuse to bear the yoke of reverence under them. The deeds of bishops or superiors are not to be struck down by the sword of the mouth, even when they appear rightly subject to reproach; for we know that our predecessors and many other holy bishops established that sheep should not readily criticize their shepherds or presume to accuse or charge them with crimes. When we sin against our superiors, we oppose the ordering of the one who gave them to us.

Thus, when Moses learned that the people were murmuring against him and Aaron, he said: “What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against God” (Exodus 16:8). Therefore subjects of both orders must be admonished that, when they see the deeds of their teachers, they should return to their own hearts and not presume to rebuke them, because “a disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his lord” (Matthew 10:24).

Concerning uncertainty about the dedication of churches, about which among other matters you wished to consult us, you ought properly to hold to what we received as handed down by our predecessors: whenever there is doubt either about the baptism or confirmation of certain persons or about the consecration of churches, and no certain basis exists either in written documents or in witnesses for determining whether the persons were baptized or confirmed, or whether the churches were consecrated, such persons should be baptized and confirmed and the churches canonically dedicated, so that such uncertainty may not become a ruin to the faithful. For something is not shown to have been repeated when it is not demonstrated by certain indications that it was rightly performed.

[Note: [Col. 1325D] The same passage reads in the source cited: “When there is doubt about the consecration and dedication of churches.”]

[Note: [Col. 1325D] The printed editions read *haec vos* (“these things you”), against the Vatican, Corbie, Tours, and Gemet manuscripts.]

With the support of divine grace, we wish to hold these principles in this way, and, as you requested, we command you to hold and teach them. We desire not to violate arrogantly what the holy Fathers before us established, but faithfully to preserve it.

Therefore we entreat the mercy of our Redeemer to grant you the support of his grace in all things and to enable you to fulfill what he has allowed you to desire, since the benefits of recompense increase in this matter in proportion as the zeal for labor also increases. [Note: [Col. 1325D] In the Corbie, Gemet, and Vatican D manuscripts, the passage from this point through “his own generation” is omitted, or rather transposed, for it is read between the words “we acted” and “therefore we greet you paternally” in this form: “We acted. Therefore, because in this matter the increase is as great as …, we greet you with paternal sweetness.”]

Concerning his own generation, we decree that each person who has been faithfully instructed in these matters and now stands immovably planted with a firm root should observe the rule up to the seventh generation.

As long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they must not presume to enter into the partnership of this union. Nor is any Christian permitted, or ever will be permitted, to take in marriage a woman whom someone has had as a spouse through his own blood relationship, or whom he has defiled by any illicit pollution, because such intercourse is incestuous and hateful to God and to all good people. We read that the holy Fathers established long ago that incestuous persons are not to be counted under the name of marriage.

Therefore we do not wish to be reproached by you or by other faithful people in this matter, because what we granted to the English people we did not do by laying down a rule, but by taking into consideration the danger that they might abandon unfinished the good of Christianity which they had begun. [Note: [Col. 1326D] Tours reads: “not by giving a rule, but by consideration”; Corbie: “but by consideration.”]

Greeting you, therefore, with paternal affection, we exhort you [Col. 1326C] to labor with the greatest zeal in your effectiveness, taking advantage of the opportunities that have been proposed, and to strive with every effort to accomplish this in whatever ways may be possible, so that, with the Lord’s help, you may fulfill your praiseworthy desire for the assistance of all.

Nor do we leave aside this further aspect of our concern: all incestuous persons are to be separated from the thresholds of holy Church until, through satisfaction and the prayers of priests, they have been canonically reconciled to that same holy Catholic Church. For the wicked must be separated from the good, and the unjust from the just, so that at least through their shame they may recognize their consciences and turn away from their wickedness (Hincmar, *On the Divorce of Lothair and Theutberga*, question 5).

But if they appear incorrigible, let them be separated from the faithful until they have made satisfaction, in accordance with the judgment of the Lord our Savior [Col. 1326D], who, among other things, commanded concerning a brother who sins against another:

“If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that every word may stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses. And if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church. But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector” (Luke XVII, 3; [Col. 1327A] Matthew XVIII, 15 ff.).

By these and many other authorities of the holy Fathers, therefore, the wicked must be separated from the good, lest the just perish for the unjust, as it is written: “The righteous man perishes for the impious” (Isaiah LVII, 1, according to the Septuagint).

A distinction must always be made between the good and the wicked, just as there is between goats and sheep. Manifest sins must not be cleansed by secret correction; rather, those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that, while they are healed by public reprimand, those who have sinned by imitating them may be corrected. For while one person is rebuked, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.

Nor is it surprising that this principle is observed among human beings, since we also know that it is very often practiced among animals: those that appear to have scabies or mange are separated from the healthy, lest the remainder of the healthy animals be condemned or perish through their disease [Col. 1327B]. It is better, therefore, that the wicked be corrected openly than that the good perish on their account.

For this reason we wish all of you bishops to meet together, so that discussion may be held concerning the cases that arise, and a salutary conference may take place concerning ecclesiastical observance; so that, while past matters are corrected through this process and future matters receive a rule, the almighty Lord may everywhere be praised in the concord of the brethren.

Know that his presence will be with you if you observe these things, because it is written: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matthew XVIII, 20). If he deigns to be present when two or three are gathered, how much more will he not be absent where a greater number of priests assemble?

It is indeed well known that the rules of the Fathers have established that a council be held twice each year. But, lest there perhaps be some excuse, we have decreed that you assemble once, so that, in expectation of the council, nothing perverse and nothing unlawful may be presumed. For often, even if not out of love of justice, people nevertheless abstain through fear of an inquiry from doing what everyone knows might incur judgment.

Let us preserve this observance, dearest brother, for our successors [Col. 1328A], and let us keep all the things written in the sacred letters for our instruction, and urge everyone whom we can toward them. For it is certain that, if we devote ourselves wholeheartedly to salutary commandments, we escape every stain of vice: while we rely upon the things by which we are built up, we unquestionably shut out the opportunity for deception.

Therefore you must show yourselves especially zealous in all things toward the brethren and those subject to you.

[Note: [Col. 1327C] Corbie, Vatican D, Gembloux, and Pratelles: “so that you, who have been nourished with us and have learned the holy…”]

Let all those with whom you have been nourished and have learned to obey the commands of the holy Roman Church recognize that they are to multiply the precepts of the apostolic see and make them known most openly; for what we write specifically to you and to your colleagues and to the charity of your brethren, as your letters have made known to us, we command all to observe generally [Col. 1328B].

As for the conduct of those subject to you, let your fraternity be vigilant, so that your example may be their instruction and your life their teacher. By the exhortation of your tongue let them learn what they should fear and be taught what they should love; so that, when the talents entrusted to you have been multiplied with profit, you may deserve, by God’s favor, to hear on the day of reckoning: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew XXV, 21, 25).

Moreover, we wish to know that you are taking every care concerning all the matters that we have written to you, to our other brethren, and generally to everyone, for the prohibition of unlawful things. It is necessary that your fraternity’s vigilance complete these instructions with every zeal and effort, and that everything we have written there for the salvation of souls be faithfully reviewed [Col. 1328C]; so that through this zeal you may show how displeasing unlawful things are to you, and so that we may appear to have made suitable provision, since we have chosen you and your person for this purpose above all others.

[Note: [Col. 1327C] Tours: “and that we have faithfully obeyed, who…”]

May almighty God guard you with his protection and grant that all of you preserve the honor bestowed upon you in your conduct.

[Note: [Col. 1327C] The same codex, together with the Norman manuscript: “to preserve what has been received in your conduct.”]

Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1328C] At the end of the Corbie and Gembloux codexes one reads: “Given on the Kalends of November, in the twelfth indiction,” but this is most erroneous.]

[Col. 1327]

# Appendix to the Letters of Saint Gregory (C, S)

## 1283 I.

[Note: [Col. 1327D] Fragment I.—This is found at the beginning of the Gregorian Register, before all the letters, in nearly all handwritten codices. It is also cited by John the Deacon, Book II of the *Life*, chapter 2, where you will find several variant readings noted by us [Col. 1328D]. We believe that this confession of faith was pronounced by Saint Gregory during the solemn rite of his own ordination and inauguration.]

### The Creed dictated by blessed Pope Gregory

[Col. 1327D]

I believe in one almighty God: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—three persons, one substance. The Father unbegotten, the Son begotten; but the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.

I confess the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with the Father and begotten from the Father without time; creator of all things visible and invisible; Light from Light; true God from true God; the radiance of glory; the exact representation of substance. He, remaining the Word before the ages, was made perfect man at the end of the ages, conceived and born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

He assumed our nature without sin. He was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate; on the third day he rose from the dead [Col. 1329A]. On the fortieth day he ascended into heaven. He sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, setting all the hidden things of each person before the eyes of all. He will give the saints the perpetual rewards of the heavenly kingdom, but to the wicked the punishments of eternal fire. He will renew the world by fire.

I confess one faith, one baptism, and one apostolic and universal Church, in which alone sins can be forgiven.

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

## II. On the deposition of the archdeacon Laurence and the substitution of Honoratus in his place

[Note: [Col. 1329C] Fragment II [Alternatively, Book II, indiction 10, before Letter 1].—This is absent from the English, Norman, and most Vatican manuscripts. It is read in Colbert, Vatican A, B, and C, and in both Tours manuscripts, namely Saint Gatianus and the Greater Monastery.]

In the time of Pope Gregory, in the seventh year of the consulship of Maurice Augustus,

[Note: [Col. 1329C] Justinian Augustus abolished the consulship in the year 541. The emperor Justin attempted to restore this dignity after Justinian, but without success. Nevertheless, emperors commonly assumed the bare title of consul, and the year of the consulship was almost the same as the year of the imperial reign. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under “Consulatus” and “Consul.”]

Laurence, who had previously been first in the order of deacons of the apostolic see, was deposed on account of his pride and his evil deeds, which we have decided should remain unmentioned. Honoratus was made archdeacon before all the priests, deacons, notaries, subdeacons, and the entire clergy in the Golden Basilica [Col. 1329B].

## III. The charter concerning the Greater Litany, in the Basilica of Saint Mary

The annual solemnity of devotion, beloved sons, reminds us that we ought, with anxious and devout minds and with the Lord’s help, to celebrate the litany that is called by everyone the Greater Litany,

[Note: [Col. 1329C] Fragment III [Alternatively, Book II, indiction 10, before Letter 1].—Even now litanies are divided into greater and lesser. The one celebrated on Saint Mark’s day is called the Greater, although it does not seem to differ from the litanies of the Rogations, which are called lesser. Nevertheless, in the very celebrated Basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, a sevenfold litany is held on that day: seven choirs enter the basilica simultaneously through seven gates while chanting the litanies. This practice may also have been customary elsewhere. Hence we suspect that the Greater Litany was the same as the sevenfold litany, contrary to the opinion of Gussanville, whose note is given below. All the copies incorrectly have *letania*. In Greek, λιτή and λιτανεία mean prayer, petition, or supplication. Basil, Letter 63, distinguishes the litany mentioned here from the sevenfold litany discussed in his sermon on the time of pestilence. The Greater Litany mentioned here appears to have been in use before Gregory’s time, whatever Durandus may say, since he failed to notice the words “which is called Greater by everyone.” Speaking of the litanies restored by Mamertus, Sidonius Apollinaris, Letter 14, Book V, acknowledges that they had been in use long before, but were wandering, lukewarm, infrequent, and drowsy—as is now the case among us, whether through the fault of the people or the negligence of pastors. Justinian, in the *Authentics*, Novel 123, chapter 32, forbids litanies to be performed without a bishop, clergy, and sacred crosses. We shall indicate below what difference there is between litanies and processions, in the discussion of public masses. GUSSANVILLE. Saint Ambrose proves that the use of public litanies, or supplications, is extremely ancient, Letter 40, no. 16.]

through which, by imploring his mercy, we may deserve to be cleansed to some extent from our transgressions. For we ought to consider, beloved ones, by how many varied and continuous calamities we are afflicted on account of our sins and offenses, and how, in turn, the medicine of heavenly mercy continually comes to our aid.

When Friday comes, let us go out from the title-church of blessed Laurence the martyr, which is called Lucina’s,

[Note: [Col. 1330C] Above it is said that this litany took place in the Basilica of Saint Mary, whereas here it is said to take place in the church of Saint Peter; this makes the charter doubtful. Moreover, it is absent from nearly all manuscripts, and the few codices that contain it are more recent.]

and hasten to blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, beseeching the Lord with hymns and spiritual songs, so that there, celebrating the sacred mysteries, we may deserve, insofar as we can, to give thanks to his mercy for benefits both ancient and present [Col. 1330A].

## IV.

[Note: [Col. 1330D] Fragment IV.—This privilege was long disputed. We have encountered it in no manuscript except one from Saint Victor. Among those who wrote notes on the Gregorian letters, Alteserra defends it. Gussanville appears to hold a different opinion, although he does not dare to pronounce judgment. It is established that many errors occur in the subscriptions, as is clear from the marginal notes of Philippe Labbe in Volume V of the *Councils*, column 1585. Since this privilege appears in all printed editions of Saint Gregory’s letters, we have judged that it should be preserved in the appendix. See above, Book XIII, Letters 8, 9, and 10, for other privileges granted by Saint Gregory. For the privilege granted to the monks of Subiaco, in which the Rule of Saint Benedict is approved, see Mabillon, Volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 166.]

### The privilege granted to the monastery of Saint Medard

Concerning Gairald, abbot of Saint Medard, and his monastery at Soissons, which he adorns with the most extensive privileges.

Gregory, to all bishops.

To all those members of the holy Church of God who shine, like the most precious stones in Christ’s diadem, with Christ as their universal head: Gregory, although exalted by the pontifical office of the holy Roman see, nevertheless the most humble servant of the servants of God [1285].

When the hearts of Catholic kings are kindled by such ardent desire toward the things that ought to be urged upon them by pontifical admonitions—kindled beforehand by divine grace—so that they ask for them of their own accord, those things must be granted with a spirit as much more eager and joyful as the very things they desire ought to have been requested if they had been unwilling to do them.

Accordingly, in accordance with the letters of our most excellent children, Queen Brunichild and her grandson King Theuderic, we grant by decree of our authority the following privileges to the monastery of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, as well as of Christ’s protomartyr Stephen, situated in the city of Soissons, where Saint Medard rests and the venerable Gairald appears to preside as abbot. We further grant and firmly confirm the privileges previously granted or bestowed upon that place by the late Lord Pope John, with the gracious support of the illustrious kings, namely Chlothar and Sigebert, the husband of our daughter, under the bond of anathema.

We decree that no king, bishop, judge, or anyone invested with any dignity may, under any pretext, diminish, remove, or apply to his own uses the things that have been granted or shall be granted to this place by the most excellent kings or by any other God-fearing persons. Rather, we wish everything that has been offered or may be offered to the monks serving God to be possessed perpetually, intact, and without disturbance, and to be of every possible benefit to those whose support was the reason for its grant.

We also grant that, when the abbot dies, no other person may be installed there through any deceitful maneuver, except one whom the common consent of the monks has chosen or foreseen as worthy of ordination. Let the aforementioned monks beware of the Simoniac heresy, lest, compelled by the power of kings or bishops, they accept a tyrant in place of a shepherd. We altogether forbid this, and we prohibit the same abbot from presuming to give anything on account of his ordination, lest on this pretext the things offered or previously offered by the faithful to pious places be consumed [Col. 1331B].

And because the reputation of the religion of the monks serving God, under whom the venerable man Gairald is known to preside, has reached our ears, and because we favor the just petitions of the most excellent kings Brunichild and Theuderic, out of love for Saint Medard we grant a dignity and security of divine honor that shall remain forever.

Therefore, by divine authority, in the place of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles; with the consent of all Roman pontiffs and the will of the entire Roman senate; at the urging of Anseric, apostolic man and bishop of the city of Soissons; and with the favorable judgment of all the bishops of Gaul, we decree that no archbishop or archdeacon disturb the brethren of the aforesaid basilica concerning the ordination of their abbot or the assumption of ecclesiastical orders. Rather, in accordance with the prerogative of that place recited to you above, decreed in the time of our most blessed predecessor, Lord Pope John [1286], and confirmed by apostolic authority, the brethren themselves shall conduct the ordination of their abbot and receive the dignity of ecclesiastical orders.

Let them also celebrate in that monastery the consecration of fonts and the mysteries of scrutiny. Let them seek from whichever bishop they wish the blessing of the chrism and oil, the altar, the chalice, and the corporal, so that such honor may not be interrupted by any rector for any reason or necessity; so that the place of such great sublimity, consecrated to Saint Mary, Saint Peter, the protomartyr, and Lord Medard, may not be cheapened. We establish it as the head of all the monasteries of Gaul and permit it to be subject to no one’s authority [Col. 1331D].

Just as this Roman see proclaims its watchfulness to the whole world, sends new customs to everyone, and is free from service to every person, so let the aforesaid place, with every utterly wicked custom of kings, bishops, and judges removed, display to the other monasteries an example of divine religion and honesty and rejoice in complete freedom above them. Its rulers and sons, present and future, placed only under the protection of kings, shall proclaim the admonition of Saint Peter and his successors, the pontiffs of this holy Roman see, by their authority. If necessity arises, let them approach them.

For this purpose our daughter Brunichild, queen, granted to the brethren traveling along such a long route twenty freehold estates and an equal number of servile estates, with complete integrity and by an eternal grant, near the end of the Alps [Col. 1332A]. She also assigned many other revenues from lands situated along the same route. She gave the royal estates of Tusiacum and Mortinetum jointly for the support of the brethren. In her grant she enclosed all the estates given or to be given to God and Saint Medard in such a way that anyone who wishes to live or remain on the lands of Saint Medard—whether slave or free, whatever his status—shall be removed from the dominion of another and attached to the service of the holy Mother of God, with no further permission to return.

If anyone flees, let him be regarded as a slave henceforth of that holy Church of God.

Concerning the altars, we also confirm by apostolic authority, according to the institution of Lord Pope John, that whoever is rector of the aforesaid monastery shall also be made superior of the altars and of all the churches belonging to it. From these churches lights shall be provided for the principal altar of the aforementioned saints, and hospitality toward pilgrims shall be carried out with reverence.

We add another decree: if the abbot must be deposed on account of a capital crime, he shall not be deposed before those carrying out the deposition have sought apostolic authority, and until there are three metropolitans with their suffragans and a great many abbots. At the council itself, each accuser shall appear with twelve witnesses and prove by the examination of a true judgment that he saw what he alleges, swearing to it in the hearing of the council.

Finally, the abbot himself shall give the reasons for his defense and, by an oath over the sacred mysteries of the four Gospels, provide satisfaction. If he is then convicted, let him be deposed by correction; but if not, let him be restored to his honor [Col. 1332C], receive the mysteries of ecclesiastical dignity, perform the blessing and preaching amid the sacred solemnities of the Mass in accordance with the regulations of Lord Pope John, and lead the life of his state through better examples [1287].

We also propose this ruling to the monks: none of them is to be oppressed by envy or hatred of the abbot—God forbid—or punished by the judgment of outsiders. If someone has committed an offense arising from a principal vice, he is to be rebuked privately within the cloister of that monastery by the abbot himself and the spiritual brethren, and separated from the body of the holy congregation.

But if, because of persistent stubbornness, he is cut off, we command him, after receiving letters of recommendation, to enter whichever monastery he wishes, or, for the sake of penance, to seek the permission of this apostolic see [Col. 1332D]. After receiving letters from the Lord Pope, he shall return freely to his own monastery.

All these things, therefore, which are contained in the privilege of this apostolic authority and in our grant, we establish under anathema as binding upon the rulers and sons of the aforesaid monastery, present and future, and upon all monasteries subject or attached to that place.

If any king, bishop, judge, or any secular person whatsoever violates, contradicts, or treats negligently the decrees of this apostolic authority and our grant, or disturbs, troubles, or otherwise deals with the brethren—whatever his dignity or rank—let him be deprived of his honor. As a corrupter of the Catholic faith or a destroyer of the holy Church of God, let him be separated from the fellowship of Christians and from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him, together with Judas the betrayer of the Lord, be condemned in the lower hell by the anathema of all the curses by which unbelievers and heretics have been condemned from the beginning of the world until the present—unless by worthy penance he obtains the favor of the aforementioned saints and restores the common harmony of the brethren.

I, Gregory, bishop of the holy Roman see, have subscribed this privilege.
