## V. Decrees of Saint Pope Gregory I

I. On the office of the deacons of the apostolic see.  
II. Who and what sort of persons should attend upon the pope in his bedchamber.  
III. If any ecclesiastic presumes to place titles.  
IV. On not covering the bier of the Roman pontiff.  
V. That nothing be given or received for ordination or the pallium, etc.  
VI. If anyone from the Church’s servants desires to convert to the service of God.

[Note: [Col. 1333C] V. DECREES [Alternatively, 44, Book IV, indiction 13].—Saint Gregory mentions this synod in Book V, Letter 57: “Your fraternity knows that previously the pallium was not given unless a payment had been made. Since this was inappropriate, we forbade by strict prohibition, in a council held before the body of blessed Peter, the acceptance of anything either for this matter or for ordinations.” The acts of that synod survive at the end of the Colbert, Corbie, and many other codices; Bede also seems to recall them, Book II of the *History*, chapter 1: “Except for the book of Responses, which he wrote in answer to the questions of Saint Augustine, the first bishop of the English nation, as we have explained above … and also the Synodical booklet, which he most usefully composed with the bishops concerning necessary ecclesiastical matters,” and so forth. Apart from the manuscript codices of the letters, another book containing forty homilies on the Gospels, which we received from the Bigot Library, presents the same decrees in last place. We have also read them in a parchment manuscript containing decretal letters of the supreme pontiffs from Sylvester onward, now preserved in the library of the Reverend Capuchin Fathers of Rouen [Col. 1333D].

This council was summoned by Pope Gregory in the case of John, a priest of the Church of Chalcedon, who, after having been unjustly condemned for heresy by John, bishop of Constantinople, appealed to the apostolic see. By pontifical authority Gregory caused this synod to be assembled there. Gregory testifies in Book V, Letters 15, 16, and 17, to John, bishop of Constantinople, that after the case had been examined, John was found innocent and was therefore justly absolved, the synodal judgment of Constantinople having been rescinded.

In this same synod, after the six canons preserved above, Saint Gregory ordered that the provision discussed in Book V, Letter 1, indiction 14, be fulfilled: namely, that whatever a bishop had disposed of by testament from goods acquired after obtaining the episcopate should have no force. The rule was otherwise concerning things he had possessed before the episcopate. “We found in a written codex of Subiaco,” says Baronius, year 595, no. 59, “that in the Roman council the same Gregory approved and confirmed the Rule of Saint Benedict.” [Col. 1334C]

SEVERUS BIN. These decrees are exactly the same as the acts of the synod found in Letter 44 of Book IV, except for the few items read after the subscriptions. I do not see where these were taken from, since they are absent from all manuscript codices. Nevertheless, because they occur at the end of certain printed copies of the Register, I did not wish to omit them, lest anyone complain that something was missing from this edition.

GUSSANVILLE.]

During the perpetual reign of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the time of the most pious and serene lords Maurice Tiberius and Theodosius Augustus, in the thirteenth year of the same Lord Maurice’s reign,

[Note: [Col. 1334C] These are two names belonging to the same emperor; accordingly, we have removed the comma that separated them. Maurice Augustus did have a son named Tiberius, but we nowhere read that he was proclaimed emperor or even Caesar, although his father had destined him to rule the old Rome. Moreover, if Maurice’s son Tiberius were mentioned here, he ought not to have been mentioned before Theodosius, the elder of the brothers. Correct “in the thirteenth year of Maurice” to “in the tenth year”; for since the indiction was the thirteenth, Maurice’s tenth year was running, not his thirteenth, as appears at the beginning of Book II of Gregory’s Letters, where he assigns the seventh year of the emperor Maurice to the tenth indiction. SEVERUS BIN.]

in the thirteenth indiction, on the fifth day of the month of July, Pope Gregory, seated before the most holy body of blessed Peter, with all the bishops and the priests of the Roman Church, with the deacons standing by and the entire clergy, said:

[Note: [Col. 1334D] From these chronological notes it is clear that these acts are exactly the same as the decrees printed at the end of the letters in earlier editions. There the same year, whether of the reign or of the indiction, is recorded. The commonly printed text indeed reads “in the fourteenth indiction,” but this is an error that we have corrected from the manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 1334D] As customs gradually changed, priests no longer sat in councils, and indeed neither did the bishops themselves. In assemblies held before the supreme pontiff in the year 1563 they sat, as appears in the French *Life of Bartholomew of the Martyrs*, Book II, chapter 22—a passage worth reading. In ancient times priests sat in councils, gave their judgment, and subscribed, even when the supreme pontiff himself was present, as is clear from this passage and from another under Gregory II in the year 721. To recount many examples would be a light and useless task, since modern writers of the opposing side do not deny the practice but dispute only its legal basis. Few deny that priests sat as judges at the Council of Chalcedon; they claim that this was done unlawfully, in order to diminish the authority of certain later synods—as though elders had not sat in the councils of the apostles, or had sat there mute. GUSSANVILLE.]

[Col. 1335A]

“In the holy Roman Church” (Gratian, Distinction 92, chapter 2), “over which divine providence has willed me to preside, a very blameworthy custom has long arisen: certain men are chosen for the ministry of the sacred altar as singers and, having been placed in the order of deacons, devote themselves to vocal melody, although it would have been appropriate for them to devote themselves to preaching and the care of alms.

[Note: [Col. 1335C] Gregory of Tours provides many examples concerning priests and deacons who sing, in Book VIII of the *History*, chapters 3 and 6. GUSSANVILLE. See note 252 to the *Book of the Sacraments*.]

Thus it commonly happens that, while a pleasing voice is sought for the sacred ministry, a suitable life is neglected; and the singing minister provokes God by his conduct while delighting the people with his voice.

Accordingly, by the present decree I establish that in this see the ministers of the sacred altar are not to sing [Col. 1335C]; they are to perform only the duty of reading the Gospel during the solemnities of the Mass.

[Note: [Col. 1335C] Although in ancient times the Gospel was read by lectors in the public assembly of the faithful, as is especially clear from Cyprian’s Letters 33 and 34, by Jerome’s time this office had begun to belong to deacons, as the holy doctor sufficiently indicates when he writes to Sabinianus: “You used to read the Gospel of Christ as a deacon.” From canon 2 of the First Council of Toledo it appears that in the Spanish Church the ancient custom continued until the fifth century, with lectors responsible for reading the Gospel. Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 19, mentioning those who read the Gospel in church, assigns the duty—according to varying local or temporal rites—to the bishop, archdeacon, and deacons, but does not mention lectors. This first decree is absent from the Capuchin Codex of Rouen.]

I judge that the psalms and the other readings are to be presented by subdeacons or, if necessity requires, by the lower orders. If anyone attempts to act contrary to this decree of mine, let him be anathema.”

And all responded: “Let him be anathema.”

### 2.

[Note: [Col. 1335D] Some printed copies corruptly read this: a modest custom is obscured by the torpor of indiscretion. Ennodius, in Opusculum 7, mentions a certain precept by which it was provided that all bishops should have attendants in their private chambers. Sirmond thinks that this was done either by the pope or by a synod on account of the accusations with which Pope Symmachus had recently been harassed. Gregory of Tours reports that Bishop Aetherius of Lisieux had many clerics’ beds around his own bed, in Book VI of the *History*, chapter 27 [Col. 1336C].]

A shameful custom arose in a time of indiscretion: lay boys and secular persons served the pontiffs of this see in the private services of the bedchamber.

[Note: [Col. 1336C] Although the same arrangement has been established in many other councils, few carry it out. See the Council of Paris of the year 829, chapters 19, 20, and 21. The impious laugh and the devout lament at the sight of such a crowd of household attendants serving certain ecclesiastics, among whom scarcely one or two can be found marked by clerical dress, the tonsure, and the crown, even though, if we listen to the canons, episcopal residences ought to be dwellings of clerics, not palaces of laymen. What if lay boys not only attend upon the private services of the bedchamber but also serve as acolytes at the dread mysteries of the sacred altar? Will custom excuse this? We leave the matter for those who devote themselves to reforming the clergy to examine. GUSSANVILLE.]

And since the life of a shepherd ought always to be an example to his disciples, clerics frequently do not know what the life of their pontiff is like in private, whereas, as has been said, the secular boys do know it (Gratian, Part II, Question 7, chapter 58).

Therefore, by the present decree I establish that some clerics, or even some monks, chosen for this purpose, shall serve in the pontifical bedchamber, so that the person who occupies a position of governance may have such witnesses as see his life in his private conduct and, from their attentive observation, may draw an example for improvement [Col. 1335C].

### 3.

A new and very blameworthy custom has arisen in this Church (Gratian, Part II, Question 6, chapter 1): when its rulers suspect that urban or rural estates belonging to its patrimony may be subject to its legal claim, they imprint titles upon them in the manner of the fisc and defend with their hands, rather than by judgment, what they consider to belong to the poor [Col. 1336A].

[Note: [Col. 1336D] Concerning titles, see Book I, Letter 60.]

Although Truth says through its preachers, “Do nothing through contention” (Philippians II, 3), they even go beyond the evil of contentious litigation; and whenever any property is judged capable of belonging to the Church, it is held by force.

Accordingly, by the present decree I establish that if any ecclesiastic ever presumes on his own initiative to place titles, whether upon a rural or an urban estate, let him be anathema.

And all responded: “Let him be anathema.”

But if the person who presides over the Church either orders this to be done himself or, when it has been done without his order, neglects to punish it with appropriate severity, let him be anathema.

And all responded: “Let him be anathema.”

### 4.

Just as the minds of the faithful venerate us as unworthy in deference to the blessed apostle Peter, so it is fitting that our weakness should always recognize itself and earnestly avoid burdens of veneration directed toward it. For, through the affection of the faithful, a custom has arisen among the rulers of this see beyond what they deserve: when their bodies are carried out for burial, they cover them with dalmatics, and the people tear those same dalmatics into pieces to distribute among themselves out of reverence for their sanctity. Although many coverings from the sacred bodies of apostles and martyrs are available, something is taken from the body of sinners and preserved as an object of great reverence.

Accordingly, by the present decree I establish that the bier on which the body of the Roman pontiff is carried for burial shall be covered with no covering. I judge that the presbyters and deacons of this see must take responsibility for observing this decree. If anyone of their order neglects to enforce it, let him be anathema. And they all answered: Let him be anathema.

[Note: We have already discussed dalmatics in Letter 107 of Book IX. It was the custom of the ancients to bury the dead clothed, and often to adorn them with costly garments. Hence Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Paul*: “Why do you wrap your dead in gilded garments? Why does extravagance not cease amid mourning and tears? Or do the corpses of the rich know how to decay only in silk?”]

### 5.

Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I establish that nothing is ever to be accepted in connection with ordinations—not in exchange for the giving of the pallium, nor for the delivery of documents, nor under that name of *pastelli* which recent ambition has invented.

[Note: *Pastellus* derives from *pastus*, a term expressing a banquet or feast. In the Council of Nantes, canon 15: “But banquets and feasts, which divine authority forbids,” etc. In the Council of Trosle, canon 6: “Let them not exact a tax from the priests themselves, nor oppress presbyters with gifts, banquets, or the fattening of packhorses or horses.” In Hincmar’s capitularies for presbyters, canon 15: “When presbyters have assembled together on the Kalends, after completing the divine mystery, let them sit at the table for necessary discussion, not as though for dinner, and let them not burden one another with such improper little banquets,” etc. It is cited in Distinction 44, canon 9. See the *Extra*, title “On Simony,” canon 1. *Pastellaticum* is the right to a banquet. See Cause 1, Question 3, canon “If anyone should object.” Therefore no one should buy a prebend, a church, or anything ecclesiastical, nor should he pay anything before or afterward for such a banquet or meal. — GUSSANV.]

For when the pontiff lays his hand upon the bishop being ordained, while the minister reads the Gospel and the notary writes the letter of confirmation, just as it is not fitting for the pontiff to sell the hand that he lays upon him, so the minister or notary ought not to sell his voice or pen at the ordination. I entirely prohibit anyone from giving anything for an ordination, or for the pallium, documents, or a banquet, whether he is about to be ordained or has already been ordained. If anyone should nevertheless presume to demand or offer anything under the designation of profit from any of these aforesaid matters, he shall be liable to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God.

If the man who has been ordained, after receiving the documents and pallium, wishes to give something to anyone among the clergy solely as a gift of gratitude—not by agreement, nor because it was demanded or solicited—we in no way prohibit its acceptance, since his offering brings no stain of guilt upon him, having not proceeded from the recipient’s greed.

### 6.

We know that many from ecclesiastical or secular servitude hasten to the service of almighty God, so that, freed from human servitude, they may live more freely in monasteries in divine service. If we dismiss such people indiscriminately, we provide everyone with an occasion to flee the authority of ecclesiastical law. But if we imprudently hold back those hastening to the service of almighty God, we are found to deny something to him who gave all things.

It is therefore necessary that anyone who wishes to turn from servitude under ecclesiastical law or secular service to the service of God should first be tested while still wearing lay clothing. If his character and conduct bear witness to his good desire, he shall be permitted, without reconsideration, to serve almighty God in a monastery, so that the person who seeks a stricter servitude in divine obedience may depart freed from human service.

[Note: In the decrees printed at the end of the letters, the following is added: “But if, in monastic clothing and in accordance with the rules of the Fathers, he has conducted himself irreproachably, then, after the periods prescribed by the sacred canons, he may lawfully be advanced to any ecclesiastical office, provided that he has not been stained by those crimes which in the Old Testament are punished by death.” These words are absent from our manuscripts.]

## VI. Other decrees of Saint Gregory, Pope I

Gregory, bishop by the grace of God, subscribed these decrees, and the bishops and presbyters, fifty-eight in number, confirmed them.

Gregory, most holy apostolic pope, seated in synod before the body of the blessed Peter, said:

“For this reason above all, grieving and sighing deeply, I say that I hear that certain Christians living in the western regions are recklessly acting contrary to the Catholic faith and the statutes of the Fathers, to the extent that they presume to take consecrated women as wives and to marry women related to them. This must be cut away with a spiritual sword and, if it pleases your holiness, uprooted completely, lest the harvest of the good farmer, mixed with the dreadful thorns of the wicked, be defiled.”

The most holy bishops or venerable presbyters answered:

“We truly recognize that, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the heart of your apostolate burns so that you may wipe away the squalor of so great a misery from the minds of the faithful.”

After this unanimous response, Gregory, apostolic pope, before the revered body of the aforesaid blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, pronounced judgment as follows:

I. If anyone takes a presbyter in marriage, let him be anathema.

II. If any presbyter or deacon takes a wife, let him be anathema.

III. If anyone takes into marriage a nun, whom they call a handmaid of God, let him be anathema.

IV. If anyone takes his spiritual godmother in marriage, let him be anathema.

V. If anyone takes his brother’s wife in marriage, let him be anathema.

VI. If anyone takes his niece or granddaughter in marriage, let him be anathema.

VII. If anyone takes his stepmother or daughter-in-law in marriage, let him be anathema.

VIII. If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema.

IX. If anyone takes as a wife a woman from his own kindred, among whom he has female relatives, let him be anathema.

X. If anyone abducts or steals a virgin, let him be anathema together with those who consent to it.

XI. If anyone abducts or steals as a wife a virgin whom he has not betrothed, let him be anathema together with those who favor him.

XII. If anyone consults diviners, haruspices, or enchanters, or uses phylacteries [the manuscript has *filateriis*], let him be anathema.

XIII. If anyone in any respect violates the apostolic Church’s previously issued commands concerning chambers and various places, and does not observe them in all matters, let him be anathema.

XIV. If anyone commits murder, let him do penance for ten years.

XV. If anyone persists in crime, let him be anathema.

XVI. If anyone among the clergy loosens or abandons the tonsure, let him be anathema.

XVII. And they all answered three times, clause by clause: Let him be anathema.

### Signature of the blessed Pope Gregory

“I, Gregory, of the holy Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed this constitution promulgated by you.”

Agnellus, bishop of the city of Ferentis, subscribed this constitution promulgated by us. And the others subscribed. Farewell.

## VII. [Note: Roman Council III]

In the manuscript of the most distinguished Parisian senator Claudius Hardy, the title is: “The privilege of monasteries living under a regular rule, dictated by Saint Gregory, pope of the City of Rome, in a general synod with the consent of all the bishops and Catholic men, and perpetually confirmed with the imposition of anathema and excommunication. Gregory to all the sons of the holy Church. How necessary it is,” etc.

In the manuscripts of Lérins, Angers, and Flavigny, whose variant readings we have written in the margin, and in various others, it is called “Pope Gregory’s Decree on the Freedom of Monks.”

Saint Gregory, having learned through experience how many troubles monks sometimes suffered from bishops, wished, shortly before the end of his life—which he sensed was approaching because of his constant bodily illness—to provide for the peace and security of the monks. Therefore, having assembled twenty bishops, along with cardinal presbyters and deacons, on the Nones of April in the year 601, he issued this synodal decree for the monks, which is customarily called a constitution.

The annals of Baronius have now finally supplied us with the complete and perfect text from the Vatican Library; for in the Venetian edition of the councils the signatures of the bishops—which we have just published in full—are missing. — SEVER. BIN.

### Roman Council III, or Lateran Council, under Saint Gregory, Pope I

In the year of the Lord 601, Gregory issued the following constitution for the monks.

Gregory, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to all the bishops.

How necessary it is to safeguard the peace of monasteries and to provide for their perpetual security is made clear to us by the office we formerly exercised in governing a monastery. Since we know that in very many monasteries monks have suffered numerous prejudices and burdens from prelates, it is fitting that the provision of your fraternity should arrange their future peace by a salutary ordinance, so that those living there in God’s service may, with his grace also assisting them, persevere with a free mind.

But lest anyone presume, on the basis of a custom that ought rather to be corrected, to inflict any trouble upon the monks, it is necessary that the matters we have decided to enumerate below be guarded by the bishops with such fraternal care that no further opportunity for disturbance can arise from them.

Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the authority of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, in whose place we preside over this Church, we forbid and prohibit any bishop or secular person henceforth from diminishing in any way, or on any pretext, the revenues, property, or documents of monasteries, or the cells or estates belonging to them, or from introducing any fraud or interference.

If some dispute should happen to arise between land coming under the jurisdiction of their churches and the monasteries, and it could not be settled peacefully (*potuit*; variant *potuerit*), let it be resolved without voluntary delay before chosen abbots and other fathers who fear the Lord, with the holy Gospels placed between them. (See Book VIII, Letter 5.)

When the abbot of any community has died, no outsider is to be chosen, unless the united fellowship of the brothers itself freely elects someone from that same community. The person elected is to be appointed without fraud or any form of venality. If they cannot find a suitable person among themselves, they should diligently arrange for someone from another monastery to be appointed in the same way. Once an abbot has been established, no other person is to be placed over him on any pretext, unless—God forbid—there are crimes present which the sacred canons declare punishable.

It must likewise be observed that, against the will of the abbot, monks are not to be taken from the monastery to govern other monasteries, to receive sacred orders, or to undertake clerical office.

[Note: In the Flavigny manuscript the following is inserted: “But if there are more monks than are sufficient for celebrating the praises of God or fulfilling the needs of the place, let the abbot offer before God from those remaining as many as he can judge worthy. Whoever proceeds from the monastery to an ecclesiastical order shall thereafter have neither authority nor permission to live there.”]

We entirely forbid [variant: deny, *denegamus*] the making by a bishop of ecclesiastical inventories of the monastery’s property and documents. But if circumstances require it, let the abbot of the place, together with the other brothers, make a record (*causas*; variant *notitiam*) of the property discovered, and let matters be concluded by their counsel and judgment [variant: “let him conclude councils without prejudice,” *concilia sine praejudicio finiat*].

When an abbot dies, the bishop is in no way to interfere in recording and providing for the monastery’s acquired property, or in investigating property given [variant: “acquired as well,” *acquirendisve*].

We also entirely prohibit him from celebrating public Masses in the monastery, lest in the retreats and shelters of God’s servants any opportunity be provided for a popular gathering [variant: “with crowds rushing in,” *popularibus corruentibus*] or for a new entrance of women, neither of which is at all beneficial to their souls. Nor may he dare to set up a cathedra there, exercise however great [variant: whatever, *quamlibet*] an authority to command, or make even the slightest appointment, unless he has been asked by the abbot of the place. Thus the monks may always remain under the authority of their own abbots, and no bishop may retain any monk in any church or advance him to any office without the testimony or permission of the abbot.

We therefore establish that this page of our writing is to be kept firm and inviolate by all bishops for all future time, so that, with the Lord’s help, they may be content with their own Church alone, and so that monasteries may in no way be subjected to ecclesiastical conditions or forced services (*angariae*), or to any secular services, nor serve any canonical rights [variant: cares, *curis*], but, with vexations removed, may complete in all burdens [variant: “and in all burdens,” *ac*] their daily [variant: divine, *divinum*] work with the fullest devotion of spirit.

The bishops all answered:

“We rejoice in the freedom of the monks, and we confirm what Your Holiness now decrees concerning them.”

[The presbyters and deacons said: “We rejoice in the freedom of the monks, and we confirm what Your Holiness now decrees concerning them.”]

### Signatures

“I, Gregory, bishop of the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed this constitution promulgated by us.”

“I, Agnellus, bishop of the holy Church of Ferentinum, have subscribed this constitution promulgated by you.”

“I, Humilis [or Joannes Humilis], bishop of Velletri, have subscribed this constitution promulgated by you.”

And likewise all the other bishops, twenty in number; fourteen presbyters; and four deacons, on the Nones of April, in the fourth indiction [elsewhere, the third].

### Roman Council IV, under Pope Gregory I

Held in the year of the Lord 601 in the case of Andrew, a monastic impostor and forger.

#### Council

Andrew was condemned in this council: a Greek who lived under monastic clothing near the basilica of Saint Paul and was exposed as an impostor and forger. Gregory discusses this matter at greater length in Book IX, Letter 69 [now Letter 74 of Book XI], to Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica.

## VIII. Concerning the case of Maximus the transgressor, and his satisfaction and penance

[Note: Fragment VIII [elsewhere, Book VII, indiction 1, at the beginning of the book]. These passages are absent from many manuscripts. They are found in the Royal Manuscript, formerly belonging to the library of Flavigny, in Colbert Manuscript no. 40, and in two others, at the beginning of Book VII, indiction 2.]

Maximus the usurper was raised up in Dalmatia against the will of the lord Pope Gregory by the soldiers, during the eleventh indiction, and remained in contumacy or presumption for seven years.

After this, following the chastisement and scourging of the most blessed and apostolic Pope Gregory, he left Dalmatia and came to the city of Ravenna to the most blessed Marinianus, archbishop. He stretched himself out in the middle of the pavement within the city and loudly proclaimed: “I have sinned against God and against the most blessed Pope Gregory.”

After he had done penance for three hours, the exarch Callinicus came running, together with Castorius, chartulary of the Roman Church, and the archbishop Marinianus. Maximus was lifted up and began to perform further penance before them.

Then he was led to the holy body of the blessed Apollinaris, and he swore that he had no part in any of the charges brought against him concerning women or the Simonian schism. Castorius, the chartulary, then returned and brought with him a deacon of Maximus named Stephanus, the reporter of everything Maximus had done in satisfaction.

Then the most blessed Pope Gregory, moved to mercy, sent the pallium for the confirmation of that same bishop, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction.

## IX. The privilege of making a will granted to Probus, abbot of Saint Andrew’s.

[Note: [Col. 1343D] IX. Formerly Epistle 22 of Book IX.—This concession of the right to make a will is absent from the English, Norman, and many other manuscripts. In Vatican A and D, and in the Tellerian manuscript, instead of “on the third day before the Nones,” one finds “on the third day before the Kalends.” The manuscripts that assign Maurice’s fourteenth regnal year mark the thirteenth year for his consulship. “Probus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Lucy, desires, if you command it, to be presented before your presence.”

Gregory, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome, said: “Let him come.”

When he had entered, he said: “You ought to tell us why you have wished to be present.”

Abbot Probus said: “I have a petition in hand. I ask my lord’s blessedness to order it to be received and read aloud before you.”

Gregory said: “Let it be done.”

When it had been received, Paterius read as follows:

“In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, while our lord Maurice Tiberius, most pious Augustus, was reigning, in the fourteenth year, after the thirteenth consulship of the same lord, on the third day before the Kalends of October, in the fourth indiction.

“Those matters which I now desire to bring to your blessedness’s attention were long ago well known to my lord, and I know that your conscience bears witness to what I report. For when, some years ago, I had passed from the lay state to a religious office, I had resolved to live alone in my cell and spend there the few days that remained to me. Therefore I had neither previously arranged nor disposed of anything concerning my small property, knowing that a son could succeed me both intestate and by testament. But one day, when I had entered with others to attend upon my lord, you suddenly and unexpectedly ordered me to enter the monastery and assume the burdens of an abbot. Immediately, when we had risen, I was compelled to go with the monks to the monastery, without being granted time for deliberation or consideration. [Note: [Col. 1346D] Four Vatican manuscripts read: “since I had previously neither encountered nor been able to do anything concerning my small property.”]

“Since, therefore, I had previously been able to arrange nothing that occurred to me concerning my small property, I tearfully beseech you to grant me, by the authority of your decree, permission to dispose of all my possessions according to my will, so that neither my obedience may harm me nor my poor son suffer loss. For it is known to all that the legal sanction forbids those who have entered a monastery to dispose of anything from their property after their entrance, although those who have previously had the opportunity to arrange their affairs are granted permission to dispose of them; but this does not apply to those whom the pressure of their superiors compels to obey in a matter they had never considered. For just as the spirit of the law opposes those who do this after deliberation, so [Note: [Col. 1346D] We restore this from the Vatican, Colbert, and other manuscripts. The printed editions read: “with greater foresight it comes to the aid of those who are compelled.”] it comes to the aid, with greater foresight, of those who are compelled.

“I dictated this suggestion and petition of mine to Aemilianus, [Note: [Col. 1346D] Notaries of bishops are frequently mentioned in the Council of Chalcedon. Before that council, Epiphanius, in Heresy 71, p. 830, mentions Eutyches and Theodulus, notaries of Basil, bishop of Ancyra. In Augustine, Against Cresconius, Book III, chapter 29, in the consular acts under Zenophilus, the deacon Nundinarius is called the recorder of Silvanus, the Donatist bishop of Cirta.] a notary of the holy Roman Church and my acquaintance; and I, Probus, your servant, subscribed it in my own hand and presented it to you, my most blessed lord, Pope Gregory. I, Probus, your servant, have subscribed this petition submitted by me.”

Gregory said:

“Now that the text of the petition submitted has become known to us, let Abbot Probus withdraw for a little while, so that with our brothers and sons we may deliberate what ought to be decided concerning the matters he requests.”

When he had withdrawn, after a lengthy discussion of his petition, Gregory said:

“Let Abbot Probus, whom we had ordered to be absent for a little while, come again, so that we may declare what, together with our brothers and sons, we have jointly judged appropriate.”

When he had been presented, he said:

“Where truth agrees with reason, it is no less just than kind to fulfill the desires of the petitioner. Therefore, having carefully considered the sequence of the petition submitted by you, we recall that everything you have stated in it is true. For it had never previously entered our thoughts that we ought to impose upon you the care of an abbacy in any monastery. But one day, while we were discussing with our sons the administration of the monastery over which you are known to preside, and had long been seeking a suitable person for this office, when you unexpectedly entered, it suddenly occurred to our mind and to the minds of those who were present with us for the discussion that, God willing, we ought to appoint you abbot there. Since it is clear that this was imposed upon you against your will, and since our exhortations could scarcely bend the firmness of your will, it was necessary, lest you might perhaps have had the opportunity to return after some time, to send you as an already appointed abbot to that very monastery of which you had not previously even been a monk.

[Note: [Col. 1347D] From John Gerson, Lecture 4, On the Spiritual Life of the Soul, corollary 4 and following: “Ecclesiastical and civil legislators are often known to abuse their power and authority, especially those ecclesiastical legislators who wish whatever they regulate, advise, or command to be regarded as divine laws, and to possess equal force through the threat of eternal damnation. I omit the rest, in which the pious author explains his opinion concerning the obligation of human laws because of their connection with divine law. Many have attacked it as almost erroneous, perhaps because they did not sufficiently understand it. To distinguish in human laws what belongs to divine law from what belongs to human law requires a particularly important branch of theology, which, he says, many either do not know, neglect, or despise.” Gussanvillaeus.]

“Therefore, lest this obedience should bring either sorrow to your affection or loss to others, by the provisions of this our decree we grant you free permission to alienate or otherwise dispose of all your property as you wish. Through this permission, know that you possess the same power of disposing of it as you had before you entered the monastery. Do not fear that the office of abbot—which, as has been said, you are known to have assumed suddenly and unwillingly—may in any way hinder you, since our insistence, as we have said, compelled your affection to ensure that you would not have permission to arrange and dispose of your possessions after returning.

“Accordingly, so that no suspicion may make you uncertain concerning what you wish to arrange, we decree that no one from our Church or from your monastery, or from any other institution or status arising from monastic conversion or the office of abbot, by any device or under any pretext of excuse, shall ever be able to act against the terms of this present decree. Rather, just as though you had never entered the monastery, we establish, God being the author, that everything you shall arrange or dispose of concerning your entire property shall remain inviolate and shall be preserved without any opposition. [Note: [Col. 1347D] The printed editions add: “Given in the month of November, indiction 4,” but this is not found in the Vatican manuscripts or others. Nor can this agree with the other chronological indications assigned above. Certainly this diploma was issued on the same day and at the same time as the synod previously mentioned was held at Rome—that is, in October, not November.]”

## X. The Promise of a Certain Bishop [Note: [Col. 1348D] X [Elsewhere, Epistle 31, indiction 5].—This bishop appears to be Firminus, to whom Epistle 33 of Book XII is addressed.] Anathematizing His Heresy, Which He Caused to Be Discharged [solvi; reading uncertain] in the Name of the Lord Emperor at Constantinople, on the Tenth Day of February, in the Fifth Indiction

Whenever the eye of the heart, covered by the cloud of error, becomes clear through the light of heavenly illumination, we must strive with great vigilance lest the author of schism secretly break in and cut off again from the root of unity, by the weapon of error, those who had returned to it. Therefore I, the bishop of that city, having discovered the snare of division in which I was held, and having considered the matter for a long time within myself, have returned, under the guidance of divine grace, to the unity of the apostolic see with willing and spontaneous resolve.

And lest I be thought to have returned without a pure mind or deceptively, I pledge myself, under penalty of forfeiture of my rank, and by the obligation of an anathema, and I promise you—and through you Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and his vicar, the most blessed Gregory, and his successors—that I shall never, through anyone’s persuasion or by any other means, return to the schism from which I have been rescued by the mercy of our Redeemer. Rather, I shall always remain entirely in the unity of the holy Catholic Church and in communion with the Roman pontiff.

Therefore I swear by almighty God and by these four holy Gospels, which I hold in my hands, [Note: [Col. 1348D] “By the safety and genius.” I think these words were wrongly inserted into this promise, for Catholics did not swear by the genii of emperors. See Tertullian, Apology, chapter 32, and To Scapula, chapter 2: “We swear not by the genii of the Caesars. Do you not know that genii are called demons …? Besides, we are accustomed to adjure demons, that is, genii,” etc. Certainly it was generally acknowledged in antiquity that a genius was nothing other than a demon, as may be read in Lactantius, Book II, chapter 15; since I cite that passage, I advise that it be read cautiously. Many note that even among us in Gaul it was not permitted to swear by the life of the king and his sons. In the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon they frequently swore by the footsteps of the emperor or of the Fathers. Gussanvillaeus.] and by the safety and genius of our illustrious lords who govern the republic, [Col. 1348B] that I shall remain, as I have said, in the unity of the Catholic Church, to which, God being gracious, I have returned, and always and without doubt in communion with the Roman pontiff.

But if—God forbid—I should separate myself from this unity by any excuse or argument, I shall be found guilty of perjury and bound to eternal punishment, and in the age to come I shall share the portion of the author of the schism.

I dictated this written statement of my confession and promise to my notary, with the consent of the presbyters, deacons, and clergy who, binding me to this unity, have followed of their own free will in all the matters written above and will subscribe with their own hands. I subscribed it with my own hand and delivered it to you.

Done in that place, on the day and under the consuls stated above.

Subscription of that bishop:

“I, that bishop of that city, having given an oath to preserve all the matters written above, have subscribed this confession and promise of mine.” [Col. 1348C]

[Note: [Col. 1348D] XI. Elsewhere, Epistle 56, indiction 5.]

## XI. Example of a Concession of the Pallium

To his most beloved brother Peter, Gregory.

We know that it accords with every principle of reason that we should adorn with the pallium those whom the honor of the priesthood, by the inspiration of divine mercy, illumines in those cities in which it is established that this too was granted by those who in former times merited to become pontiffs and by the apostolic see. Therefore, by the authority of this present document, we grant to your charity the use of the pallium, as your predecessors are known to have possessed it, and we wish all that is known to have been preserved for your Church in earlier times concerning the privilege of your honor to remain, so that you may in no way grieve that any of its privileges have been diminished.

And the subscription of the lord pope:

“May God keep you safe.”

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, while our lord Justin [Elsewhere, Justinian] Augustus was reigning. And the lord pope subscribed.

## XII. [Note: [Col. 1349B] FRAGMENT XII [Elsewhere, Epistle 1 of Book IX].—Phocas was crowned by Cyriacus, the patriarch, in A.D. 602. The matter is treated at length by Theophylact Simocatta and the other writers of Byzantine history. Gussanvillaeus.]

### On Phocas Being Crowned and Maurice Being Killed with His Sons

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, in the sixth indiction, on the twenty-third day of November, during the time of our lord and most blessed pope Gregory, Phocas and Leontia Augusta [Note: [Col. 1349B] Greek writers call it ἕβδομον, “the Seventh.” Procopius, On Buildings of Justinian: “In the suburb called the Seventh,” Book I, chapter 14.
