He wanted grain to be sold at the public prices at all times, whether less or more grain was produced, I, 44. Grain was brought to the City chiefly from Sicily, but also from other places, I, 2, 44, 72; X, 33; XII, 49.

## Matters Concerning Saint Gregory as Pontiff
He first considered who he was and the purpose of his office. For the pontiff is chosen as an intercessor for the sins of the people, and his qualifications are that he be familiar and acceptable to the one before whom he has been appointed intercessor, I, 25. He likewise describes the pontiff’s office under the metaphor of steering a rotten ship that has been undertaken for guidance into port. “Now,” he says, “waves rush upon us from ahead; now, from the side, foaming heaps of sea swell up; now, a storm pursues us from behind. Amid all these dangers I am forced, in confusion, sometimes to steer the rudder directly against the adversity [we have emended this passage], and sometimes, when the side of the ship has been bent, to turn aside the threats and force of the waves obliquely,” I, 43.

To feed rightly is to lead the flock entrusted to him to eternal pastures by praying, admonishing, and displaying zeal for good works, XI, 1. He took the greatest care to be pure in thought, lest the hand that ought to cleanse filth should itself defile whatever it touched even more seriously; and he observed how much cleansing was required by one who carried living vessels toward the temple of eternity in the bosom of his own conduct. Nor should anything indiscriminate or useless be entertained by one appointed as an example to others, who must always show through his seriousness how much rational judgment he carries in his heart, I, 25.

He continually kept before his eyes the examples of the Fathers who had gone before, so that he might walk irreproachably, I, 25. He teaches that a ruler must be pre-eminent in conduct, so that by living rightly he may point out the way of life to his subjects, and that the flock which follows the shepherd’s voice and character may advance more effectively by examples than by words. For whoever is compelled by the necessity of his position to say lofty things is compelled by that same necessity to display lofty things. That voice more readily penetrates the hearts of hearers which the speaker’s life commends, because what he commands by speaking, he helps to accomplish by demonstrating, I, 25.

His conduct should be not merely useful but also outstanding: just as he surpasses others in the dignity of his rank, so also should he excel them in virtue of character, I, 25. He should desire nothing belonging to the present life and fear nothing in it. With inward terror in mind, he should despise the world’s flatteries; and, considering the inward sweetness of divine consolation, he should scorn its terrors, I, 25. He should be discerning in silence and useful in speech, so that he neither says what ought to be kept silent nor keeps silent about what ought to be said, I, 25. He should not fear to speak the truth freely through fear of losing human favor, as imprudent rulers do, I, 25.

Whoever ascends to the priesthood undertakes the office of a herald, so that, before the Judge—who follows in terrifying fashion—arrives, he himself may go ahead crying out, I, 25. When a ruler prepares to speak, he should consider with what careful attention he ought to speak, lest, if he is carried away into speaking without order, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error; and lest, when he perhaps desires to appear wise, he foolishly sever the bond of unity, I, 25.

He should devote himself to contemplation and action in such a way that he is near to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation. Thus, through the bowels of mercy, he may take upon himself the weakness of others, while through the height of contemplation he may transcend even himself by aspiring to invisible things. Otherwise, he might either despise the weakness of his neighbors while standing on high ground, or, by adapting himself to their weakness, cease to aspire to higher things. He should follow the example of Moses, who frequently entered and left the tabernacle: within, he is carried away in contemplation; outside, he is pressed by the affairs of the weak. Within, he considers God’s secrets; outside, he bears the burdens of those subject to the flesh, I, 25.

He explains how a ruler ought to occupy himself with external cares, from which he cannot be wholly free, yet ought to attend to them in such a way that the eyes of his mind are not darkened and that he does not entirely abandon concern for them. “But in this place,” he says, “I see that the restraints of this discernment cannot be applied, because so many disasters threaten daily that they overwhelm the mind all at once, while they destroy bodily life,” I, 25. On the disturbances arising in this care, V, 49.

When he is uncertain in doubtful matters, he should, following Moses’ example, return to the tabernacle—that is, to prayers—and consult God within the pages of sacred Scripture, I, 25. He should be compassionate in such a way that he shows himself so sympathetic that none of his subjects is ashamed to disclose even his hidden matters to him, I, 25.

He lifted up the oppressed so effectively that he entrusted the defense of an oppressed woman to her advocate, IX, 62. [Col. 1409] He consoled the afflicted, though absent, by letters, I, 11; and those who were in mourning, IX, ind. II, 33. Because of the misconduct of certain people, he comforted a bishop afflicted by persecutions, III, ind. XI, 2. He also consoled a man who was distressed by harsh words that he himself had spoken against him, X, 68. He consoled one oppressed by the tribulations of the world, lest, after the loss of his possessions, the loss of his soul should follow as well, XIII, 21. He says that there is no need to console a wise man, IX, ind. II, 99.

He sympathized with the sick, especially bishops whom he kept with him, III, ind. XI, 24 and 25. He consoled a bishop suffering from bodily illness, reminding him that, since illness is often granted for correction, thanks should be given to God so that this chastisement might benefit us in that life, V, 3. He summoned to himself a bishop afflicted by a serious illness, wishing to care for him and keep watch over him. He instructed him to come with a few companions, since, while remaining with him in the episcopal residence, he would receive daily services from that bishop’s Church. Thus, if either the bishop himself or Gregory should first be summoned by the Almighty, the responsibility would pass into the hands of whichever one remained, XI, 33. He likewise instructed him not to fast, XI, 40.

To the patrician Rusticiana he said that he was concerned for the health of her body and prayed for her, so that everything taking place in her body might be directed toward the salvation of her soul, and that temporal scourges might prepare eternal rest for her, XIII, 22. He consoled a woman—rather, two virgins still of tender age—who was afflicted by the very serious illness of her father, promising her his protection if her parent should die, XI, 35. He regarded another person’s sadness and injury as his own, II, ind. X, 36.

Humility and zeal belong to a shepherd: with the honor of his rank held in suspension, he should regard himself as equal to subjects who live well, while against the faults of the perverse he should rise up through zeal for justice. Thus Peter treated Cornelius, whose holiness of life merited fellowship in equality, while toward Ananias and Sapphira his zeal for punishment disclosed the force of his authority, I, 25. The highest office is governed well when the one in charge rules over vices rather than over his brothers, I, 25.

The virtue of humility must be preserved in such a way that the rights of government are not dissolved, lest, while a superior casts himself down more than is fitting, he become unable to restrain the life of his subjects under the bond of discipline. The severity of discipline must likewise be preserved in such a way that, while zeal is kindled beyond necessity, gentleness is not entirely lost. For when the knowledge of sacred Scripture in the heart of a good ruler is a rod of severity, it is necessary that there also be a hand of gentleness, I, 25.

It is not a great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored, since any worldly person does this; rather, we ought to be especially humble toward those from whom we suffer something, II, ind. X, 36. He asked Leander, from reading the works of the *Pastoral Rule* and the *Morals*, to mourn over his sins, because from those books he seemed to know precisely what he had failed to do, V, 49.

As an expression of humility, he called his own works bran, but those of Saint Augustine wheat flour, V, 37. He prohibited the reading of his writings at table, lest what he did out of charity should be attributed by others to vain glory, VII, 9. While he was alive, he did not want his book on Job published publicly, and he regretted having issued the *Pastoral Rule* at the emperor’s insistence; the patriarch of Antioch translated it into Greek, XII, 24.

He condemned himself in comparison with King Rechared, who labored for the conversion of unbelievers, saying that he did not know what he himself would say at the dread judgment if he came there empty-handed while that king led the flocks of unbelievers after him, IX, ind. II, 122. He was humble in accepting reproofs with equanimity, VII, 27.

In praising the merits of a companion and lowering himself, he said that he was not only unworthy of the honor of presiding persons but even unworthy to be counted among those standing. He said this to the patriarch of Alexandria, VI, 40. He attributed the conversion of the English to the prayers of others, VIII, ind. I, 30. He professed himself ready to be rebuked and corrected by everyone, II, ind. X, 52. He also imitated his inferiors in good things, although he prohibited them from unlawful acts. “For,” he says, “a person is foolish if he considers himself so superior that he disdains to learn the good things he sees,” IV, 9, ind. II, 12. He declared himself the servant of all priests insofar as they lived priestly lives, V, 20. He said that he bore the sins of all who had been entrusted to him, VII, 32.

[Col. 1410] He displayed zeal in maintaining the authority and dignity of the apostolic see. Thus he asserted that he wished to take action against John, patriarch of Constantinople, who had usurped the title “Universal,” V, 20. Therefore, writing to the empress Constantina, he said: “And if Gregory’s sins are so great that he ought to suffer such things, nevertheless the apostle Peter’s sins are not so great that he should deserve to suffer this in your times,” V, 21. He professed that he wished to avenge the matter through canonical severity, V, 21, 18. Against John of Constantinople he sought the empress’s support, I, 21.

He testified that he was readier to die than to permit the Church of blessed Peter to degenerate in any respect during his lifetime, IV, ind. I, 47. A person should consider himself to have pleased Almighty God in proportion to his awareness that he has displeased wicked people, X, 36. People should not be feared in a matter in which we wish to please God, IX, ind. II, 79.

Zeal should be shown not so much in preserving the rights of the apostolic see as in observing the rights of others. “For,” he says, “just as we demand our rights from others, so we preserve their rights for each person,” III, ind. XI, 29. Just as it is appropriate to be severe toward those who persist in obstinacy, so mercy must not be denied to those who have humbled themselves and repented, IX, ind. II, 81.

Accordingly, in the case of Maximus of Salona, he did not cease pursuing him while he persisted in obstinacy, but did not refuse to embrace him when he returned to repentance. He even wished to write him a letter of consolation, IX, 81. Elsewhere, IV, ind. I, 47, he says: “You know my character well, so long as I endure; but if I once decide not to endure, I go joyfully against every danger.” And in VII, 31, against Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople: “I seek to harm no one in this matter, but to preserve the humility pleasing to God and the concord of the holy Church.” Again, in V, 8, writing to John of Constantinople about the same matter: “Whatever I ought to have done humbly, I have not omitted; but because I am despised when I correct, it remains that I must bring the matter before the Church.”

He exercised great prudence. Thus, on one occasion, while initially concealing a bishop’s fault, he attributed it to a writer close to him, so that the friendship would not be torn apart and the bishop would not become obstinate, III, ind. XI, 53. He received a synodical letter from the new patriarch of Constantinople despite the title “Universal,” saying: “In receiving the synodical letter of our brother and fellow priest Cyriacus, it was not fitting for me to delay over the issue of a profane title, lest I disturb the peace of the holy Church,” VII, 27, 34.

First he dealt with the emperor concerning the abolition of an unjust law; then he explained to the bishops what they ought to do in the matter, IIII, ind. I, 5. The defense of the poor should be moderate and dignified, lest, if anything is done too harshly, people think that he is acting arrogantly. Yet it should be such that the humble feel protected and that oppressors do not easily find anything to criticize from a malicious motive, X, 36.

We must walk with greater caution the more we know that we live among God’s enemies, X, 36. We ought to disregard scandals that entangle us in sins, but in every way mitigate those that we can appease without sin, XI, 44. In calming scandals we must not use authority but reason and kindness, following the example of Saint Peter at the baptism of Cornelius, when he gave an account to those who had been scandalized that he had baptized a Gentile, XI, 45. Consideration must be shown for the weakness of those driven by misguided zeal; they must be appeased by reason and gentleness, XI, 45.

Some matters should be corrected gently; others, which cannot be corrected, should be tolerated with equanimity, XI, 46. He says that it is impossible to cut away everything at once from hard minds, because one who strives to ascend to the highest place is raised by steps or paces, not by leaps. Therefore, in replying to the abbot sent to England to assist Augustine, he instructed him to permit certain practices that the English performed as pagans, provided that they were ordered toward the true worship of God, XI, 76.

His gentleness and kindness were very great. When the emperor called him a fool, he replied gently, explaining how simplicity should be praised and asserting that it is extremely harmful if either prudence is absent from simplicity or simplicity from prudence. He confirmed this by the Lord’s example of the serpent’s cunning and the dove’s simplicity. He asks God to make him pleasing to human beings in such a way that he does not offend God’s eternal grace, V, 40.

He retained no resentment against certain disobedient bishops, but promptly and kindly forgave them. Speaking of one bishop, he said: “I had learned that he had behaved arrogantly, but because he corrected his conduct himself, by conquering myself along with him he consoled my sadness,” I, ind. X, 46. He warned that the pain of no offense should be retained, X, 15. “How we ought to flee anger,” X, 51.

A measured leniency in correction has more power than severity in carrying out punishment. The former sometimes makes a person more faithful and submissive, while the latter makes him a stubborn adversary. This is not so that zeal for righteousness may be withdrawn, but so that we should not be in small matters what we ought to be only in great ones. For if the character of an offense demands severity, action should be taken so that punishment corrects the fault, while grace is not afterward denied to those who have been corrected, X, 15.

He replied kindly to one who said that he had been harshly rebuked by him, X, 52. In cases where he recognized that one ought to act less kindly, he wished not to involve himself but more readily entrusted them to others, III, ind. XI, 60. He maintained that affliction must not be added to the afflicted. “For,” he says, “when divine discipline crushes someone, it is superfluous to add human scourges to him,” II, 34.

He considered it inhuman if one who says that he fears us greatly cannot find us in some respect more restrained, IX, ind. II, 66. He affirmed that he did not wish to be the author of scandal, but preferred that what was to follow should be carried out through others, IX, ind. II, 79. He feared becoming involved in the death of any person so greatly that he spared even the Lombards from destruction, saying: “Because I fear God, I am afraid to involve myself in the death of any person,” IV, 47.

We ought to be toward our subjects what, if we had been subjects, we would have wished our superiors to be toward us, XIII, 3. “It is unjust,” he says, “that those who have loved more should, without cause, feel him harsh toward them,” II, 34. He intended not only to inflict prejudgments on no one but also to bear calmly what had been done, unless perhaps he was reasonably compelled to defend the affairs of the poor, X, 27.

He urges vigilance because of the devil’s snares, V, 58. Following Jacob’s example in tending Laban’s sheep, he teaches that one must watch diligently over the flock entrusted to one’s care, lest either perverse people tearing the sheep of God apart with wicked speech or evil spirits laying the pleasures of vice before them devastate them, IX, ind. II, 48.

He professed that he knew himself to be neglecting the care of the Church unless he left nothing that came to his attention unexamined for God’s sake, XII, 11. He exercised great vigilance in the affairs entrusted to him and demanded an account of them. Thus he rebuked a bishop who had not immediately informed him what he had done concerning the matter committed to him, VII, 2.

He was so constant an administrator of justice that no prayers could persuade him to depart from a sentence once justly pronounced, as in the matter of the pallium for the archbishop of Ravenna, V, 56; VI, 53; IX, ind. II, 74. Concerning the case of Maximus, bishop of Salona, he says: “Maximus, the violator of the Church of Salona, after he was unable to obtain anything through the greater powers of the world, turned to the lesser, and strove to prevail over us by the excessive force of his pleas as well as by the testimony of his good works,” IX, ind. II, 67.

Regarding the preservation of the order of justice, he says: “If in secular offices their proper order and the discipline handed down by our ancestors are preserved, who could tolerate ecclesiastical orders being thrown into confusion by reckless presumption, matters heard being neglected, and matters requiring correction being postponed through a failure to refer them properly?” IX, 41. He declared that he did not know who his friend the bishop was if that bishop did not observe the canons, III, ind. XI, 53.

Against the Jews who had polluted the Christian religion, he wrote to the prefect of Sicily that he should correct everything with the utmost strictness and all speed, so that Gregory might not only thank him for this discipline but also, wherever necessary, provide testimony to his goodness, III, ind. XI, 38. He did not wish to judge anything without hearing both sides, lest anyone be prejudiced, IX, ind. II, 63.

He terrified sinners with the most serious threats so that they might come to their senses. Thus he wrote to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse: “So many evils that are being committed in that province are repeatedly reported to us that, if the Almighty God does not avert them, we believe that it will quickly perish because of its sins,” IV, 12. He pointed out the vices of the province to those who governed it, so that they might take care to eradicate them, V, 56. He foretold that worse things would happen than before, in order to draw them away from sin, X, 36.

He rebuked public sinners even by letters, asserting that the necessity of his office compelled him not to remain silent, I, 34. He taught that strangers should not be trusted indiscriminately, IX, 59. He was very cautious in judging the character of others. Thus, when asked to judge the character of an absent person, he replied that he could not do so, but said that he wished to urge the man to hasten to him, so that, after carefully learning his character and person face to face, they might decide without any uncertainty what should be done regarding his request, XIII, 23.

He did not rashly believe accusations, nor did he investigate them negligently, IX, ind. II, 12. He exercised the greatest circumspection in reports against ecclesiastical persons, so that he did not disclose by letters the wrongs committed by them, lest they should become public, I, ult. He excused those against whom it was difficult to give credence [to the accusations], IX, ind. II, 63. He professed that he said nothing about matters of which he had no certainty, X, 51.

He imposed no delay on just requests, III, ind. XI, 11. Whenever we are asked for what it is appropriate to urge upon others, we must not delay granting it, lest we appear to postpone good desires that ought rather to be encouraged, IX, ind. II, 34. What has been decided he orders to be carried out immediately. Thus he ordered money left for the common good to be distributed without delay. “No reason,” he says, “permits what is known to have been given for the common good to be applied to anyone’s private uses,” IX, 51. If something new was requested, he did not wish to grant it without consultation and precipitously, IX, ind. II, 108.

In adversity, he explains how Peter’s ship should be steered, I, 43. He endured disasters, persecutions, and tribulations with equanimity, II, ind. X, 46. He especially endured those inflicted by people who ought to have relieved burdens; such people must be tolerated all the more because they persecute us not only through a malicious mind but also under the appearance of religious devotion, VIII, ind. I, 2. He showed the same patience toward evils inflicted by barbarian swords and by the perversity of judges, V, 37, 42; XIV, 14.

A sound mind ought not only to bless God in prosperity but also to praise him in adversity, since we do not know what our Creator is accomplishing through it. Perhaps we have offended God in prosperity, and he wishes to cleanse us through merciful bitterness, X, 31. He says that these pains are especially pleasing to him because they do not permit him to take pleasure in anything in this world, V, 42.

The righteous are not promised joys of delight in this life, but the bitterness of tribulation, so that, as by a medicinal treatment, they may return through a bitter drink to the sweetness of eternal salvation. For he suspected that no Abel existed who had not had a Cain: the good cannot be perfect if they are without evils, because they are not cleansed, XI, 45. A letter of consolation in adversity appears at VIII, ind. I, 2, and X, 31, very elegantly.

He urges humility and obedience even in matters unjustly inflicted, II, ind. X, 36. For he says: “The humility of God’s servants ought to appear in the time of affliction.” In adverse circumstances, especially in scourges inflicted by God, he tried to appease the angry God through litanies of all orders: “We beseech his mercy,” he says, “that we may in some measure deserve to be cleansed from our transgressions,” formerly II, ind. X, at the beginning; now at the end of the *Letters*.

During a time of pestilence he urged the people to persist in the litanies of all orders with constant weeping, since the persistence that is displeasing to human beings pleases the Judge of truth, and to lift their hearts with their hands to God. For to lift the heart with the hands is to raise the devotion of our prayer together with the merit of good works, so that we may at least fear the scourges of God that we ought to have feared before they came, now that they are present and experienced, formerly XI, 2; now at the end of the *Letters*.

For the litanies to be heard, one must watch more vigilantly, so that actions may assist the voices, XI, 51. In the same place the cause and remedy of the scourge are set forth: the multitude of our sins gives prosperity to our enemies, ibid. Also, in II, ind. X, 46, and V, 40, he says: “I am a sinful man, and because I sin against Almighty God every day without ceasing, I suspect that I have some remedy at his dread judgment if I am struck every day by unceasing blows.”

Patience and endurance must be maintained in adversity, because we ought to remember the labors of those who came before us, and the hardships we endure will not be difficult, in accordance with Acts XIV: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.” For how can we pass through the heat of this world without labor, we weak sheep, when we know that the rams sweated heavily in it? V, 38.

Adversities must be endured for the sake of the Church, and the foam of the waves must be withstood through the virtue of perseverance, VIII, ind. I, 24. In all adversities, thanks should be given to the Creator, and, trusting in his mercy, we should endure everything patiently, because we suffer far less than we deserve, VIII, 41. Doctrine is consolation for the afflicted, VIII, 41.

He urges good works in adversity, because for those placed under scourges to commit acts worthy of scourges is a particular form of arrogance against the one who strikes and provokes the anger of the one who rages even more fiercely. It is also the first kind of madness to refuse to allow anyone to cease justly from his evils while wishing God unjustly to desist from his punishment, X, 63. His patience and the evils that he endured are described in II, ind. X, 46, and V, 40.

He elegantly urges those enduring tribulations with equanimity to trust in God and not lose heart, lest, after the loss of their possessions, the loss of their souls should also follow, XIII, 21. He receives consolation in adversity and urges compassion and prayer, saying:

“The filth of your sorrow cannot be cleansed unless you also soil the hand of your heart through compassion, just as dirty vessels are usually cleansed with earth so that they may be free from the defilement of earth. But because you do this at once by working and praying, if earthly action soils anything in you on our behalf, the water of prayer immediately washes it away,” V, 16.

He consoled a bishop over the death of his people, VIII, ind. I, 2. He gave a remarkable account of the benefit to be derived from adversity and prosperity: we should neither be elated by prosperity nor broken by adversity, since our whole life is like that of a traveler who sometimes walks over level ground and sometimes over rough places. Thus, humbled, we may learn to mourn whatever we have done wrong; and, exalted again, we may keep the memory of adversity in our minds as an anchor of humility. This should not be attributed to the anger of our Creator but to his grace, through which we learn to preserve his gifts more truly the more humbly we possess them, III, ind. XI, 52.

He patiently endured even the most serious bodily illnesses, being confined to bed for two years by the pains of gout. He says: “Every day I am in death; every day I am driven back from death.” Therefore he urged that prayers be poured out for him to the Lord, so that he might be led out of the body, X, 35; XIII, 22. Because of the pains of gout he could not even rise to speak, XI, 14. Life itself was a punishment to him, and he eagerly awaited death, which he believed could alone be a remedy for his groans, XI, 32. Life amid such great pains seemed to him a most grievous punishment, IX, ind. II, 124.

He taught that bodily illness is God’s mercy and an exercise of his loving providence, because, if present punishment turns the mind of the afflicted person, it is the end of previous guilt. The pains that precede us are intended to terrify us and, when we have been converted to fear of the strict Judge, to hide us eternally from his retribution. Nothing should be done in such circumstances except to recall our sins to mind and give thanks to Almighty God, since we who commit many sins through the delight of the flesh are cleansed through the affliction of the flesh. The sign that God has not abandoned a person is continual chastisement. But if illness does not turn a person toward fear of the Lord, it is the beginning of the punishment that follows. Therefore one must take care, and watch with the whole mind intensely in tears, lest we pass from torment to torment, XI, 30, very elegantly.

Since, when we are rescued from the danger of death, it is uncertain for what purpose we have been spared, the time of reprieve must be turned to the benefit of the soul. We must prepare our case before the coming Judge with tears and works, since we shall have to render an account, so that we may deserve to receive assurance concerning what we have done, XII, 1. Likewise, V, 3, says that illness is granted for correction, and therefore thanks must be rendered to the Creator.

He took no pleasure in human praise. Thus he said that, although iniquity ought to have been punished in him, he was receiving praise instead of punishment, I, 7. And in I, 26, he says: “I consider who I am, and I find nothing in myself corresponding to this sign of goodness.” To a bishop who had announced his good works to many people, he said that he had inferred from this that the bishop was not striving for the sight of God but to please human judgment. “For who are we,” he says, “that we should seek to please human beings? What are we other than dust and ashes?” III, ind. XI, 4.

In the midst of human praise one must always return to one’s own mind, so that, if the good spoken about us is not found there, great sadness should arise, XI, 2. He professed that he took special pleasure in no honor except the honor bestowed upon him as holder of the apostolic see, since he who bestows it also judges its recipient, VII, 40.

He rejected the title “Universal” bestowed upon him, saying: “I know who I am and who you are. In rank you are my brothers; in character, my fathers. I do not seek advancement in words but in conduct,” VIII, ind. I, 30. Detraction caused him no disturbance, because, if we have a witness in heaven—as Job says, Job XVI: “Behold, my witness is in heaven”—and a witness in the heart, as the Apostle says, II Corinthians I: “Our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience,” we should let fools speak outside whatever they wish, XI, 2.

Likewise, in XI, 45, he says: “Those who have fixed their heart in heaven ought not to be shaken on earth by human words, since their firm confidence is especially in the mercy of Almighty God when, in return for good works, something adverse is received in this world, so that the full reward may be preserved in eternal recompense.”

He took no pleasure in glorious titles, but his humility shone forth in everything. He called himself a servant; priests, brothers and fellow ministers; clerics of various orders, dearly beloved sons; laymen, lords; and women, ladies, I, 7; II, ind. X, 12; III, ind. XI, 11; VII, 8, 25, 26. Nor did he permit the patrician Rusticiana to call herself his maidservant, for he says that he had become a servant through the burdens of the episcopate, IX, 44. Among innocent bishops he presented himself as their equal, IX, ind. II, 12.

Honor must be preserved in dignity. He taught how it should be preserved from the Apostle’s words, Romans XI: “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry,” and again from I Thessalonians II: “We became as little children among you.” “Without doubt,” he says, “this example shows us that we should retain humility in our minds and nevertheless preserve the dignity of our rank in honor, so that there may be neither timid humility nor arrogant self-assertion in us,” V, 43.

He rebuked one who had written back to him in a manner unbecoming to him, V, 4. He refused to reply to a Latin who wrote in Greek, IV, 32. In ecclesiastical authority one should seek neither the summit of temporary power nor the adornment of external display, V, 53.

He was entirely free from every appearance of avarice. Thus, what he did not buy he did not wish to sell, VII, ind. I, 29. He was so unaccustomed to accepting what belonged to others that he even rejected payment for certain things of his own, VIII, ind. I, 29.

He ordered the patrimony of the apostolic see existing in various regions to be spent usefully in those places: namely, on clothing the poor and gathering children of unbelievers, so that, once baptized, they might be entrusted to monasteries and make progress in God’s service, VI, 7. What was sent to him for distribution to the poor he ordered to be distributed by the very people through whom it had been sent, VII, 9. He feared giving an account to God for such alms, as for the property of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, VII, 26. He did not disdain to receive alms, VII, 28.

In distributing alms, he asked God to grant him the ability to dispense them without any stain of sin, lest, from the very source by which the donors cleansed their sins, he himself should become defiled, VIII, ind. I, 26. What remained over he ordered to be distributed to the poorest nuns, V, 30.

He took no pleasure in gifts (*xenia*) but rejected them, I, 66. He ordered other gifts not to be sent; when they had been sent, he ordered them to be sold and remitted the proceeds to the senders, I, 66; IX, 2. He declared that other gifts had been sent for the use of the poor, VI, 56. He explains what gifts he would enjoy, VI, 19.

“Because your Holiness refuses to address me with bare words of greeting alone, you have also joined gifts to your letters, which we have received with thanksgiving. Nevertheless, we take greater pleasure in the affection of your mind than in the abundance of your possessions,” VI, 65. “As for the temporal gifts sent by you, although we have no need of such things, we have nevertheless received them with the charity that was due. In due charity, and out of concern for the government entrusted to you, we have deemed it right to congratulate you,” ibid.

To Leontius, a former consul, who had sent him oil of the holy Cross and aloe wood, he replied: “The gifts that you sent were not unlike your character,” VIII, ind. I, 35. He did not refuse gifts from distinguished superiors, such as Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, and called them the blessing of Saint Mark, VII, 40; X, 39.

The gifts that he received from the poor he called blessings. He showed them how things that are small can become exceedingly rich, saying: “What you, a man of God poor in spirit, have sent me—you say, ‘What can a poor person give except what belongs to the poor?’ But if you were not poor through the spirit of humility, your blessings would not have been rich,” VIII, ind. I, 2.

Again, VIII, ind. I, 35: “You ask me to receive these things with a good disposition, but among them recall to mind the widow’s two small coins. If she pleased God, because she offered little with a good intention, why should one who gives much with a humble mind not please human beings?”

He greatly praised rulers for gifts sent to Saint Peter, IX, ind. II, 122; XI, 44. God considers in gifts not what is given but by whom it is given, IX, ind. II, 122. He approved gifts sent to the monastery of Saint Andrew, XI, 44.

He excused himself to the patrician Rusticiana because the curtains she had sent to Saint Peter had not been carried to the Church with litanies, as she wished. “But,” he says, “if human voices were lacking, your offering itself has its own voice before Almighty God,” ibid. He willingly received gifts sent by women, but rebuked them because they had been made through the labor of others and not by the women’s own hands, XI, 78.

The grief and joy of Saint Gregory concerning the actions of bishops, IX, ind. II, 4. He praised prelates and other superiors who conducted themselves well in their office and promoted them, since the goodness of superiors is a salutary rule for their subjects, VI, 56; X, 35. He likewise praised kings who labored for the conversion of unbelievers, IX, ind. II, 122.

He defended a prelate oppressed by false accusations, VI, 2. He congratulated those whom he congratulated, and explains in what manner he congratulated the patriarch of Antioch on his return and the bishops subject to him, V, 39.

He congratulated certain bishops on the new election of the patriarch of Constantinople, saying that, just as the patriarch ought to intercede for everyone, so everyone ought to pray for his conduct and character; thus, through the imitation of him, they might make progress before Almighty God, while he might be helped by their merits, VII, 7. He congratulated those who had ascended to positions of dignity, VI, 5, admonishing them concerning their office and the preservation of the charity, peace, and unity of the holy Church, VII, 4.

He congratulated one who had recovered the emperor’s favor, urging him to maintain humility in prosperity and adversity, III, 52. He likewise congratulated those who had emerged from some danger, IX, ind. II, 33, consoling them concerning illness by saying that God chastises every son whom he receives. And in XII, 14, he instructs one rescued from shipwreck to give thanks to God, so that, just as God had rescued him from external dangers, he might also rescue him from internal ones.

To the bishop of Ephesus: bodily soundness, so that, just as in the present life—which is in a certain sense the shadow of the future—God has granted us joy in the transitory soundness of the body, so also
in the heavenly homeland, in which true life exists, to rejoice with him over the soul’s perfect salvation, and to make him share in the joy of common exultation, VII, 11. He congratulated the bishop of Carthage on the restoration of his health after a very serious illness, showing that the time of respite ought to be converted to the benefit of the soul, XII, 1. He congratulated the patriarch of Alexandria on the restoration of his health, since his life was the salvation of many, XIII, 41. He also congratulated others because, amid the anxieties of the imperial court, their minds were by no means oppressed by them, VII, 26. He congratulated schismatics returning to communion with the Church, IX, ind. II, 97. He congratulated the patriarch of Alexandria because he had shown honor to the holy apostolic see, VII, 40. He congratulated the same patriarch on the conversion of heretics and the growth of the Church, VIII, ind. I, 34. He congratulated the patriarch of Antioch on the steadfastness of his faith, IX, ind. II, 49. He congratulated a bishop—indeed, rather, a monk, namely Secundus, or *Secundinus*, servant of God—because he had asked him for images of the saints and for spiritual things, IX, ind. II, 52. He congratulated the bishop of Jerusalem because he guarded the faith once delivered by the holy Fathers, XI, 46. He congratulated Augustine, bishop of the English, and the queen of the English on the conversion of the kingdom to the faith of Christ, XI, 27–28. He congratulated the emperor on his election, XIII, 31.

[Col. 1416] One ought to devote oneself to the study of Sacred Scripture even amid external business, so that, if such business cannot in every way be avoided, Scripture may not likewise be postponed in every way, III, ind. XI, 67. He retained a religious man with him, with whom he found consolation in the word of God, VIII, ind. I, 16. He did not disdain to answer questions proposed by private individuals. To Gregoria, the empress’s chamberlain, who had asked him to write back if it had been revealed to her that her sins had been forgiven by God, he elegantly replied that she had requested something difficult and useless, VII, 25.

He also treated of the soul of Adam, which died in sin and was saved through repentance, and of how the devil enters the human heart, VII, 34. He addressed the souls of infants who die without baptism, IX, ind. II, 52. He exhorted different people in different ways to love God and their neighbor, to compunction, and to love of the heavenly homeland, VII, 26. He taught that the service of the imperial court should be despised, and that one ought to devote oneself rather to divine contemplation than become entangled in the affairs of the state, VII, 29.

He explained when one should not doubt that divine grace has already been obtained, and when it should be sought, since the desire to seek it is itself God’s gift. He also taught that one should rely upon divine grace in such a way that one does not become negligent in prayer or in action, but asks by praying, seeks by reading, and knocks by working, VII, 36. He exhorted Rustician[a], a patrician woman, to consider how fleeting all temporal things are: for while we are speaking of them, time runs on, the Judge arrives, and the world—which we unwillingly refuse to leave of our own accord—is now, behold, nearly at hand, so that we shall leave it unwillingly, IV, 46.

He explained that, the more the devil perceives a servant of God eagerly longing for the heavenly homeland, the more ardently he seeks the means of deception. Thus a monk who had reached the age of fifty said that he was still subject to youthful desires, because monks suffer stronger assaults of temptation than when they live their life among many others. He also explained that it is impossible for us to devote ourselves to prayer and the praises of God without some interruption of time: for although the intention remains continually ready, human weakness itself nevertheless falls back upon itself, so that at times it lies exhausted and grows sluggish in the exercise of devotion, IX, ind. II, 52.

In the same place he describes the temptations that creep in when we stand idle, calling them the darkness of our heart, which in this life we endure both willingly and unwillingly. Against them, nothing else can be sought [the text reads *quatri*, apparently an OCR error for *quaeri*, “sought”] except a helper in times of need and tribulation, VII, ind. II, 52. He discussed the devil’s temptations and how he must be overcome, since he always desires to invade fortified places. Against him we must cry out to the Lord with the voice of the heart: “Lord, do not put your help far from me; look upon my defense,” V, 58.

He taught that those who cling to earthly affairs should not, whenever a suitable time for helping others presents itself, delay at all what they ought to do, IX, ind. II, 119. He exhorted the illustrious Adeodata to meditate on heavenly things, because whoever loves these temporal things sees a dream while awake, X, 49. To the newly elected patriarch of Constantinople, who was accusing himself of weakness, he replied that it is salutary to recognize one’s own weakness, since the person who is weaker is the one unable to consider his own weakness, VII, 5.

Love for those who are absent is a sign of sincerity, and it is a sign of a good man when he pleases another good man, X, 50. He exhorted people to perform good works, to devote the hours of life more frequently to psalmody and tears, and to chastise the flesh, which, when it has lived in pleasures, has mortified the soul, X, 68. He exhorted them to place their hope in God, and taught that whatever human consolations or adversities may occur are nothing unless God either protects by his grace or disturbs by his displeasure, XI, 78.

He exhorted them to pray for one another, since our prayers are lifted into the ear of the Lord’s compassion all the more swiftly as the ardor of charity intensifies them when they are poured out reciprocally, VI, 19. He exhorted Augustine, bishop of the English, to humility against empty glory in the miracles that God performed through him among the English. He showed that one should glory instead because, as Christ said, “your names are written in heaven,” XI, 28.

Saint Gregory’s intention was to burden no one—not his own soul, nor his own Church, IV, 17. He did not permit anyone to be deprived of the honor due to him, V, 59. He did not neglect a fitting duty; hence he excused himself for not having written back to someone through the same man whom that person had sent, IX, ind. II, 78. He was so careful not to offend anyone and so desirous of encouraging everyone [Col. 1417] that he wondered why Mamilio, former prefect of Sicily, had not informed him of his good health, and exhorted him, whenever an opportunity to write arose, not to refuse to do so, XII, 17.

He asked that the offense against Cyprian be forgiven him, affirming that he had recognized many good qualities in him, XII, 19. He did not permit others to be saddened contrary to equity, IX, ind. II, 3. He did not evade giving an account of his actions, IV, 47. He did not neglect to give an account of certain ordinances that he had established in the holy Roman Church, in order to remove the murmuring of certain people, IX, ind. II, 63.

He did not show partiality. “For,” he says, “we defend no one out of personal affection; but, with God as author, setting aside regard for any person, we preserve the rule of justice,” II, ind. X, 18. The address of a learned man is always useful, because the listener either learns what he knew he did not know, or—what is more—recognizes something that he did not know he did not know, VIII, ind. I, 29.

## On Matters Concerning Secular Princes

He calls the emperor the guardian of ecclesiastical peace, VII, 6. He ordered acclamations to be made at the Lateran for Phocas, the elected emperor, by all the clergy and senate, in these words: “Hear us, O Christ: life to Phocas Augustus and Leontia Augusta.” Then he ordered an icon to be placed in the oratory of Saint Caesarius the Martyr within the palace; for an icon of the emperor and his wife used to be sent to Rome, formerly XI, 1, now at the end of the letter in the appendix.

He congratulates the new emperor on his election and exhorts him to relieve the burdens under which the commonwealth was oppressed; he prays that the power of heavenly grace may make him terrifying to his enemies and his piety gentle toward his subjects, XIII, 31. He explains how one should congratulate those who undertake some office of the commonwealth, X, 37. He explains the difference between the kings of the nations and the emperors of the commonwealth: kings are masters of slaves, whereas emperors are masters of free citizens, X, 51; XIII, 31. He explains how princes should be congratulated on their accession to power, ibid.

He congratulates the king and queen of the English on the conversion of their kingdom, because she imitated Helena and he Constantine, XI, 27. He exhorted the queen to strengthen her husband, ibid. He added that their work would be heard of everywhere and praised by all, on whose behalf the Romans prayed more fervently, ibid.

He softened new princes with praise, so that, hearing what sort of men they ought to be, they might become more gentle, XIII, 38. He explains how one should deal with princes recently converted to the faith, so that a king may pass from one kingdom to another, I, 43.

He spoke freely to princes and the highest magistrates, urging them to abandon their errors, III, ind. XI, 65; IV, 33. Against the exarch, who had given assistance to a certain apostate, he declared that, for God’s sake, he would in no way tolerate such wickedness remaining unpunished, V, 24.

Power was given to princes for this purpose: that those who desire what is good might be assisted, that the way to heaven might be opened more widely, and that the earthly kingdom might serve the heavenly kingdom, III, ind. XI, 65. And in V, 24, he says:

> Sardinia has received such a governor, one who knows how to discharge earthly responsibilities to the commonwealth in such a way that he also knows well how to offer to almighty God the services owed to the heavenly homeland.

He did not fail to recall to princes their origin, however humble, so that, remembering the benefits God had bestowed upon them, he might spur them to act well and justly, III, ind. XI, 65.

The education of her son is presented as evidence of the queen’s integrity. Hence he praised her because she had preserved unimpaired not only the glory of temporal affairs but also provided for the rewards of eternal life, planting her son’s mind, as was fitting, by a motherly and praiseworthy education in the root of the true faith. He admonished her to exhort her son so that his faith might shine forth together with his works, VI, 5. He also prays for the queen’s good disposition, XIV, 12.

He praised the ex-consul for the good and Christian works reported of him: although occupied with earthly affairs, he acted with a gentle spirit, guarded the citadel of humility in every respect, and rendered to each person what was just. He explained this by comparison with serving the heavenly Jerusalem and Babylon, when a good man and a wicked man are appointed to office, VIII, ind. I, 35.

A king should be praised by religion, because being a king is not remarkable; but being a Catholic—something others do not deserve—is sufficient in itself, VI, 6. He exhorts a Catholic king always to show kindness to his subjects, so that, just as he surpasses other kings in faith, he may surpass them in conduct as well, VI, 6. For then he will please the King of kings, that is, almighty God, more fully, when he believes himself permitted to do less than he is able to do, ibid. The piety of his conduct makes the king great before God, ibid.

He advanced and exhorted princes to the propagation and defense of the Catholic faith and the Roman Church, giving thanks for benefits conferred and for goodwill, I, 74. He praised the king of Spain for laboring toward the conversion of the Arians, IX, ind. II, 122. He explained what must especially be guarded against in our works—empty glory—and therefore exhorted the king to humility of heart, to temper royal power by bodily purity, and to avoid anger, ibid.

Princes are bound to concern themselves with the salvation and conversion of their subjects. “They,” he says, “have been entrusted to you so that they too may be able to serve your interests in earthly matters, while you, through your providence, may look to their souls and to what is eternal,” IV, 25.

Many come to the Church through princes who come to it themselves, VII, 8. He frequently set before them the divine judgment at which they would have to render an account of their subjects, III, 23. To make them fear God, he explains the signs preceding that judgment: they are sent beforehand so that we may be concerned for our souls, fearful of the hour of death, and prepared for the coming Judge by good works, XI, 66.

Princes should demonstrate before human beings, by the light of their works, the justice they carry in their minds, I, 48. He exhorted princes and patricians to act well, on the basis of the instability and fickleness of this world, III, ind. XI, 52.

He taught that they must endure adversity, because if we wish to enjoy good things in our own land—that is, in the land of the living—we must bear human evils in a foreign land. For the present life is an exile, and for one who sighs for his homeland, the place of exile is a torment, even if it appears pleasant, XI, 75.

He elegantly exhorted the queen of the Franks to adorn her power with wisdom and to do what belongs to God, because God will do what belongs to him, when the strength of the kingdom consists in zeal against the enemies of Christ. For whatever is gathered together with sin is loss. In earthly affairs, the origin of sin is always the cause of loss; and nothing is unjustly lost if one strives to possess nothing unjustly, XI, 63.

To reign successfully is not to permit crimes in one’s kingdom, XI, 69. The kingdom is then strengthened when a recognized fault is corrected quickly, ibid. Hence he grieved that it might happen that an evil deed should find refuge in the very place from which the censure of discipline ought to proceed, V, 24.

The fault of subjects weighs down the life of their superiors; and when sin in a subject is not corrected, the sentence is turned back upon those who rule, IV, 25.

He did not entrust matters touching the conscience and good reputation of a prince to legates or other agents of the Apostolic See, so that they might discuss them with him. Rather, he entrusted them to pious men among the prince’s household, who, when they found an opportunity, could discuss with him whatever he wished, so that he might appear to be taking thought for their reputation, III, ind. XI, 66.

Princes should be reminded that the scourges of God are averted when they hasten to appease God by correcting wicked people. He declared that war and pestilence are God’s scourges, IX, 11.

He explains how princes can overcome their enemies, IX, ind. II, 9. The army of a prince grows stronger against its enemies when the army of God grows through prayer, III, ind. XI, 65. Victories to come are attained not by worldly prudence but rather through prayers, with God granting them, I, 75.

And in IV, 7, he says:

> Know, most excellent son, that if you seek victories, if you are concerned for the security of the province entrusted to you, nothing else will contribute more to this than zeal for the lives of priests and, as far as possible, the suppression of internal conflicts in the Churches.

He approved the counsel of those who made peace with barbarians in order to bring them to Christ, IV, 23, 24. The king’s prudence is praised because he most willingly accepted what had been reported to him by ambassadors, and because he would negotiate peace with the commonwealth, XIII, 7.

He exhorted a king to eradicate the vices of his kingdom, all of which he pointed out to him, threatening divine judgment. He warned him for this reason because he desired his soul to be saved, V, 55. He set before princes the danger to their own salvation if they neglected to correct offenses, since one who dissimulates or neglects to correct sins becomes a participant in the guilt, XI, 69.

He said that he was astonished that a certain prince had not punished his majordomus when he had committed an offense, IX, ind. II, 9. He refused to absolve princes and the greatest men when he did not see repentance in them, IX, ind. II, 5. Nor did he permit the most distinguished men to commit anything unlawful; instead, he ordered that they first be admonished paternally, X, 26.

He declared that external enemies inflict suffering while internal judges cause disturbance, X, 36. If necessary, he saw to it that sacrilegious persons were punished by the emperor, X, 8.

He praises the emperor’s resolve against heretics, VI, 66. In the same place he exhorted him to avenge and repel the injuries and harms inflicted by heretics upon Catholic bishops. He complains that the emperor’s laws against heretics were not being observed, VI, 66.

He exhorted the queen of Gaul to devote herself to recalling schismatics, converting unbelievers, and punishing wicked and criminal men, so that the kingdom might escape the scourge of God. For if it avoids the scourge of war, it will not escape pestilence. “Wars and pestilence,” he says, “are sent by God because of unpunished sins, when God is appeased by the correction of criminal people,” IX, 11.

He ordered the emperor to be informed that schismatics were voluntarily returning to the unity of the faith, IX, ind. II, 9. He commended those who devoted themselves especially to bringing schismatics back to the bosom of the Church, exhorting them to complete this work with greater determination. “For,” he says, “the benefits of recompense increase in this matter in proportion as the zeal of labor increases,” V, 47.

He commended to princes schismatics who had returned to the bosom of the Church, so that even the stubborn might be induced to return by such an example, IX, ind. II, 94, 95.

He implored the praetor’s help against sorcerers, so that they might be dealt with more severely, V, 31.

At the beginning he conducted himself modestly and kindly toward the emperor and princes when they issued unjust laws contrary to ecclesiastical liberty. Yet he did not cease freely to condemn their evil actions, nor did he permit those laws to be carried out; rather, he worked for their repeal, III, ind. XI, 65.

First he dealt with the princes themselves concerning the unjust commands; afterward he explained to the bishops and other subordinates what ought to be done regarding them, ibid.

He implored the assistance of the magistrates for a delegate of the Apostolic See who was investigating those who did not observe the canons and the decrees of the Fathers. He said that he had undertaken the correction of ecclesiastical matters with all the greater willingness because he trusted in the pious mind of that secular power, IV, 7.

And, so that the bishop would have no excuse for taking action against apostates from the faith, he sought the assistance of the magistrates, VIII, ind. I, 18.

He sent messengers to a queen who was withdrawing from obedience to her bishop, IV, 4.

That the emperor did not interfere in clerical cases, he wrote in reply to Maximus of Salona:

> Since it is known both to us and to everyone that our most pious lords love discipline, observe the orders, revere the canons, and do not interfere in priestly cases, we diligently carry out what benefits both their soul and the commonwealth, and to which the regard of the terrible and awesome Judge impels us, VI, 25.

He did not hesitate to resist the emperor in matters that he judged contrary to the canons, saying:

> We absolutely dare not do otherwise, for fear of almighty God.

And shortly afterward:

> Whatever he himself has done, if it is canonical, we follow; but if it is not canonical, insofar as we can bear it without our own sin, we endure it, XI, 47.

The honor to be shown by the emperor to priests, V, 40.

He attributed it to his own sins that contumacious bishops had recourse to secular authorities, saying:

> If the cases of the bishops entrusted to me are arranged before our most pious lords through the patronage of others, what, unhappy man that I am, am I doing in this Church? V, 21.

Notwithstanding the emperor’s interventions, if a contumacious bishop did not appear, he would in no way cease exercising canonical severity against him, ibid. He did not wish that same bishop to appear before him with honor, despite the emperor’s petitions, ibid.

He exhorted the exarch—more precisely, Venantius the Patrician, not the exarch—to obey the Church, VI, 43. He discusses the mutual charity that ought to exist between a priest and a prince, ibid.

He exhorted the queen of the Franks not to appoint neophytes or simoniacs as bishops, IX, 11. He entrusted the review of the sentence and case of condemned bishops to the justice of the exarch, IX, ind. II, 10.

He excused bishops before princes who complained to him about them, and therefore did not readily believe accusations against them, IX, ind. II, 44. He did not fail to give princes who acted well thanks in his own name, especially for peace, IX, ind. II, 99.

He exhorts tribunes and magistrates to avenge wrongs inflicted against ecclesiastical liberty, IX, ind. II, 101. Prayer should be offered for the life of the emperor, whose life was the reason that orthodox men were advanced to ecclesiastical orders, XI, 46.

He exhorted the king of Gaul to convene a synod against simony, XI, 59–63. He showed him the good things that would come to him from reforming the abuses of his kingdom, and the evils that had proceeded from them, XI, 59–60.

He admonished the king of England to listen to his bishop if he wished the bishop to be heard by God on his behalf, XI, 66. He exhorted the queen of Gaul to provide assistance against the unchastity of priests, saying that wicked priests are the ruin of peoples, IX, ind. II, 109; XI, 69.

He allowed certain sentences he had issued not to be published until he had communicated them to the emperor through a representative, lest he appear to have done anything contemptuously toward him. His predecessor, however, had permitted the contrary of what he decreed, XIV, 7.

He wrote that the prince should come to his judgment, IX, ind. II, 44. The emperor is praised because he preserved priestly unity, VII, 6. The fact that princes love and honor priests and servants of Christ is a sign that they love God, IX, 11.

He was not reluctant to give the emperor an account of something that might cause him astonishment. Thus he informed him why he had not allowed the legates of the new patriarch to remain with him, VII, 6.

He ordered the defensor to inform the provincial praetor of the mandate calling the bishops of the province to the threshold of the apostles, in order to remove every suspicion that their departure was being obstructed, VII, 22.

He informed the queen of Gaul that a reformer was being sent, and that, if it pleased her, she should send him as soon as possible so that, together with the other prelates of the kingdom, he might carefully investigate and correct the abuses, XI, 69. He informed the same queen that he wished to send someone who, in the name of the Apostolic See, would correct what had been perpetrated contrary to the canons after the synod had been held, XIII, 6.

He commended to princes the preachers sent for the conversion of unbelievers, IV, 23, 24. Thanks should be given to princes for the charity they showed to legates of the Apostolic See, IX, 2; XI, 61–62.

He invited princes to the feast of Saint Peter’s nativity, IX, ind. II, 9.

He saw to it that honors were conferred by the emperor upon worthy men. Thus he commended to the representative a man who did not possess all the money necessary to purchase the document of the ex-consulship, so that he might assist him with work and some money—but only if it could be done without difficulty, and so that he would not use the representative’s name before the emperor, since he was a man to whom honor was owed without payment, II, 53.

He exhorted princes not to delay restoring the grain allowance owed to pious institutions. For whatever is given to the poor, if carefully considered, is not a gift but a loan: what is given is undoubtedly received back with multiplied fruit, X, 21.

The love of the queen of Gaul for pious institutions is praised, XIII, 6. He said that he did not wish to commend the Church of Blessed Peter to the empress, since she loved God; for the more she loved God, the more she loved that Church, XIII, 39.

The petition of a Christian king should not be neglected, V, 55. In matters concerning religion, his prayers should be answered, VI, 50. At the king’s request he granted a legate for his kingdom, V, 55. He informed the king of the legate’s instructions and implored his help so that they might be carried out, ibid.

What is not granted to the prayers of princes must not be permitted to others, IX, 11. For the sake of princes, one must sometimes depart from strictness, ibid. Princes must be denied what ought not to be granted, ibid.

He refused to dispense with a bigamist so that he might receive holy orders at the request of the queen of the Franks, saying:

> Far be it from us to allow anything contrary to ecclesiastical discipline to be done in your times, when you perform so many pious and religious works, XIII, 6.

He did not permit them to oppress their secular subjects through forced labor, I, 49.

And in the same letter, 61, he says to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa:

> Therefore, I beg you, with the Lord’s help correct all these matters by the force of our threatening command, so that, if not out of regard for righteousness, at least through fear of our order, the illustrious Theodore and his men may refrain from such actions, [Col. 1421]

He commended the poor to secular princes, I, 48, asserting that, with justice preserved, they should willingly accommodate themselves to pious causes and benevolently order the protection of whatever the law of justice grants to them. And in 76 he says of the bearer of the present letter, among other things:

> In whatever matters he suggests as necessary for him, while justice is preserved, devote your attention to carrying them out.

He exhorted them to remove the burdens and intolerable exactions of the peoples and to relieve their calamities, since the commonwealth is benefited more by the small amount collected justly than by the great amount collected with sin. For this is the reason why such great expenses yield no benefit amid such great calamities.

There is an illustrious letter against those harsh tax collectors from Sardinia, Corsica, and Sicily, V, 41. What is collected must be free from sin. Hence in the same letter he says:

> Perhaps the reason why such great expenses produce so little benefit in this land is that they are collected with some admixture of sin.

He commended provinces to princes, so that they would send good men to govern them and would not permit anyone to oppress those men in any way contrary to justice. Thus he commended the island of Corsica, asking that a governor who would govern it well be sent there; he also praised its previous governor and approved his being sent again to govern the same island, VII, 3.

He wrote in reply to the king of the Franks that he should ensure that a bishop who had been stripped of his possessions was restored to his property and episcopate, IX, ind. II, 116. He informed prefects that, insofar as it lay within his power, he did not deny the afflicted the consolation of his intercession, X, 37.

God brings good men to the government of peoples so that through them he may bestow the gifts of his mercy upon all over whom they have been set, XI, 66. Peoples are happy under the rule of a good king, XIII, 6.

He commended to the emperor the calamities of the provinces, especially those inflicted upon Italy by the Lombards, XIII, 38. He exhorted the Augusta to relieve the burdens of the commonwealth, XIII, 39.

He exhorted the patrician to increase his concern for the causes of the poor before his king, since the good of noble minds appears incomplete when something is left undone that could be added, XI, 14.

He exhorted the nurses of princes’ children to suggest to them things that would later show how good were the lessons they had absorbed from their nurses’ mouths. For the words of those who nurture are either milk, if they are good, or poison, if they are bad, VII, 26.

He praised those who performed their duties outstandingly before their princes in defense of the Catholic faith, IX, ind. II, 121. He exhorted the patrician to consider what concerns the soul more than the body, the fearful judgment of God, and the fact that all things are transitory, XIII, 32.

He describes the duty of a counselor, I, 34, saying that everything should be discussed with friends, but first one should consider the friends themselves, and those should be admitted who love not what is yours but you yourself. And in V, 36, he says that those who attend princes and are bound to them by sincere affection ought to advise them and suggest to them those things that save the soul and do not damage their reputation.

He ordered princes to bring schismatic counselors back to unity, IX, ind. II, 9. He says that it is no wonder if heretics cannot be brought back there, since the counselors are schismatics, ibid.

It is a great consolation for many that prudent men adhere to kings. For when they understand that an opportunity has been granted them for the benefit of their souls, it is certain that, wherever they find grounds for reward, they do not put them aside, XI, 14.

Against counselors who had given a bishop advice contrary to the fear of God and the decrees of the canons, he ordered that they be excommunicated, saying:

> So that those who fall may learn that they must not walk carelessly, IX, 2.

He exhorted prefects and governors of provinces and cities to exercise severity against the enemies of the Christian faith, saying:

> Therefore correct everything with the greatest strictness and all speed, so that we may not only give you thanks for this discipline but also, wherever necessary, bear witness to your goodness, III, ind. XI, 38.

He also asked them to provide the bishops with their assistance for the propagation of the faith, III, ind. XI, 62.

He denounced in letters before their princes those judges whom he could not turn away from their wickedness, V, 41. He admonished certain other high officials at the princes’ courts to advise the princes not to permit magistrates to act wickedly, XIII, 22.

He freely defended the liberties of each person against the insolence of judges, VIII, 51. In what is done unjustly, God is offended, one’s own reputation is burdened, and the times of princes are darkened, X, 51. When God is offended so that a human being may be placated toward us, we in no way placate that human being, ibid.

He says that, if the reports concerning a certain judge were true, he would certainly inform the emperor, since he professed to love people for the sake of justice, not to set justice aside for the sake of people, X, 51.

In the exercise of his office, a magistrate ought first to keep God appeased and then, with every care, fulfill the prince’s interests, ibid. He asserts that anger must be subdued and avoided in a magistrate, ibid.

He exhorted the prefect to correct the very serious burdens, harassments, and acts of violence inflicted by judges, and to relieve those oppressed by taxes, XI, 5.

He admonished a magistrate not to interfere in ecclesiastical cases, since he was defending condemned clerics and nuns who had left their monastery. He assured him that he would not pass over this without due punishment, V, 24.

He commended the conversion of unbelievers to the prefect, so that he might assist the bishop in this work, XI, 22. He did not congratulate a magistrate on his office, but rather shared his grief with him, X, 37.

No one can please God and wicked people at the same time, X, 36. It is a serious matter to appoint men over important places in troubled times. Therefore he exhorted prefects to make such a difficult circumstance an opportunity for reward, X, 37. He says that he rejoiced because the prefect devoted himself to the divine Scriptures, ibid.

He exhorts the master of the soldiers to forgive a certain man his fault, XII, 19. He declares that he did not wish to become involved in arranging for anyone to become prefect, XII, 26. In a letter he severely rebuked Venantius, chancellor of Italy, although he had been a monk, I, 34.

## On Matters Concerning Legates and Other Ministers of the Holy Roman Church

Only deacons were sent as legates from the holy Apostolic See to the emperor, XIII, 38. He sent men who were acceptable to the princes of the province, I, 2; XI, 69. He took care that the proper honor be shown to legates, I, 1.

He commended them to pious men and to those to whom he sent them, VI, 5–6; XIII, 38. He admonished religious men to visit the legate of the Apostolic See frequently:

> So that, after the labors he endures in secular affairs, he may find you in the word of God and, as though with some shining linen cloth, wipe away the sweat of that earthly labor, VII, 30.

To the man who was to undertake the office of legate, he explained the evils from which the province suffered, so that he might eradicate them, V, 48.

He granted the powers of legation while preserving the proper honor of the metropolitans according to ancient custom, V, 54. He granted a legate at the king’s request, V, 54–55.

He wrote to all the bishops of the province to which the legate had been sent that he had decreed the Apostolic See’s legation for them, IV, 54. A legation is necessary so that there may be one person to whom appeal can be made, who may govern through charity and peace, ibid.

The legate should ensure that the integrity of the faith and the four councils are preserved with vigilant devotion, ibid. He should suppress disputes that arise among bishops, ibid. In more serious cases, if necessary, he should assemble the bishops in a suitable number, ibid.

He should examine a question of the faith or an uncertainty concerning some important matter which, because of its magnitude, requires the judgment of the Apostolic See, and refer it to the judgment of His Holiness, ibid.

All the bishops should obey the legate and come when he summons them, unless prevented by a canonical impediment, ibid. Bishops who are prevented should send a priest or deacon in their name, ibid.

No bishop should go to more distant places without the authority of the legate. He declares that this is customary both for a legation and for the Apostolic See, which has been accustomed to issue such orders, ibid.

He wrote to the king concerning the legation decreed for his kingdom, V, 55. At the king’s insistence he says that he wishes to establish a legation for the reform that the king himself had requested, XIII, 6.

He invoked the assistance of the royal arm on behalf of the legate against delinquent bishops and anyone else, V, 55. The legate must not permit vices to persist in the kingdom, since they burden the king’s soul, ibid. He communicated the legate’s instructions to the king, ibid.

He prohibited the legate of the Apostolic See from communicating with the patriarch, VII, 34. He says that whatever the delegates decide pleases him, provided that they take care not to appear to act too leniently or to the injury of the holy Roman Church, IX, ind. II, 67.

He sent John the abbot and Hippolytus the notary as legates to the Lombard queen to persuade her to maintain the unity of the Church and obedience to her bishop, IV, 4.

The reform of the clergy is entrusted to the legate of the Apostolic See together with the ordinary of the place, XI, 68.

## On Matters Concerning the Chapter During a Vacancy of the See

He ordered prayers to be offered for the election of a bishop, saying:

> Pray unanimously and faithfully that whoever is to be ordained may both prove useful to you and offer worthy priestly service to our God, I, 58.

He entrusted the administration of the goods of a vacant Church, especially its movable goods, through an inventory, III, ind. XI, 22.

He appointed a steward in vacant Churches, I, 11, 81, so that the Church might suffer no loss; nor did he permit him to depart from it until the election had taken place.

He decided nothing in that diocese while the see was vacant. Thus he refused to unite a vacant monastery with another until a bishop had been ordained in that city, X, 61. He ordered that a case long delayed should be concluded once the Church had been provided with a bishop, XI, 16.

## On Postulation

He refused to grant the postulation of a monk for ordination as bishop, lest his repose be disturbed, XIII, 15.

He did not permit an archdeacon of one Church to be elected bishop of another Church without the permission of his own bishop, V, 17.

When a deacon was postulated for the episcopate of another Church, he did not permit the resignation to be sought in his own name. Instead, he showed that it was the duty of the electors to seek it from the deacon’s bishop, since he did not wish to appear to grant anything contrary to that bishop’s will, XIV, 11.

## On Election

In the election of bishops, Saint Gregory says that he had adopted the long-established policy of not involving himself on behalf of any individual, but of following their election with prayers, III, ind. XI, 29.

He kept watch so that worthy men would be elected bishops. He ordered inquiries to be made into their morals and integrity, worthy men of this sort to be sought throughout the province, those found to be examined, and finally to be sent to him, I, 18; II, ind. X, 24.

In X, 19, he says:

> Since his life and conduct can be better known in the place where he has lived for a long time, let it be your concern to inquire carefully about him.

And in XIII, 15, he says:

> Because the person of the deacon Crescentius is entirely unknown to us, our first concern was to ask how he had governed the hospice over which he had presided, so that from small matters we might recognize what he might be like in a great one.

He permitted a man to be elected when necessity compelled it because no better man could be found, provided that no canonical impediment stood in the way. Although he considered this man to possess a good mind, he judged him entirely unsuitable to govern; but he wished secretly to indicate someone fit for such a government, V, 17.

Above all, electors must be warned not to consider their own interests in a matter of common concern, III, ind. XI, 29; V, 23. He described to the electors the kind of bishop he desired for them, III, ind. XI, 29; V, 22.

He explained to the electors what should be done in an election, saying:

> Elect one whom you must always obey. For once he has been set over you, he must no longer be judged by you; rather, he must now be judged with all the greater care because afterward he will not be judged by you, III, ind. XI, 29.

The electors must be admonished concerning what they ought to attend to and consider, so that they may place before their eyes the calamities of the world and the fearful judgment of God, ibid.

Electors must not depart from the commendable election that has been designated, III, ind. XI, 47. He exhorts the electors of a bishop to imitate the bishop whom they judged worthy of election and to obey him, VI, 8.

In an election, it is not a place but suitable conduct that is sought. For before God that man holds the first place who pleases him by the instrument of good action, even if here he is despised, VII, 10.

He explains how an election ought to be conducted and what must be observed in it, and says that the man must be elected who does not serve anyone’s improper will, III, ind. XI, 22.

He devoted prolonged consideration to the appointment of bishops, and his mind was not idle in this matter, II, ind. X, 12. An election must be held without delay, because a Church ought not to remain long without its own ruler, VII, 14.

And in III, ind. XI, 35, he says:

> If they should in any way attempt to delay your admonition, exercise ecclesiastical authority against them. For he was zealous that the election should take place as quickly as possible, and he could no longer tolerate that Church’s being without its own ruler.

The sacred canons do not permit a Church to remain vacant for more than three months, VII, 42, lest, when the shepherd has fallen, the ancient enemy—God forbid—should lie in wait and tear apart the Lord’s flock.

He took care that the election of bishops be held quickly, I, 81; II, ind. X, 6; III, ind. XI, 35. He grieved when an election was delayed, because, he says, if the care of a shepherd is lacking to the flock, it easily falls into the snares of the ambusher, I, 80. He was astonished and said that the defender of that province was not without guilt, XI, 77.
