He ordered that the will of those citizens who were outside the city because of barbarian incursions should also be investigated in the election, III, ind. XI, 30. A man from the community itself should be preferred, I, 58; II, ind. X, 25; IX, ind. II, 27.

Bishops should not be elected from among the laity, II, ind. X, 25; III, 41; V, 59; IX, ind. II, 106. He was a vehement opponent and persecutor of this abuse, ibid., 110; XIII, 13.

He praised a layman who was leading a religious life, devoted to the study of psalmody and the love of prayer. He exhorted the same man to become a monk or subdeacon, so that afterward he might be eligible for election as bishop, XII, 12.

Anyone who uses the favor of a layman must be entirely excluded from the election, XIII, 14. An election must not be held at the request of laymen, IX, ind. II, 76.

He did not compel a man elected bishop to accept the election, III, ind. XI, 15. Where a bishop had once been accustomed to serve, he ordered that a bishop be ordained there because of the need for converting unbelievers, IV, 29.

He invited men of outstanding integrity to vacant bishoprics, since the episcopal office should be devoted to works of charity, V, 42.

He took care that primates be established in the provinces where they were to be appointed, according to custom, I, 74. He says that they originated from Blessed Peter, I, 77.

A man is praised who had not rashly elected someone bishop but had proceeded carefully, as was fitting, X, 45. If the electors did not agree on one man but divided between two, he ordered both to be sent to him together with the inquiries, so that the more worthy might be appointed, XI, 77.

If no suitable man could be found, they were to come to him in the name of the clergy and people, supported by their authority, so that an inquiry could be made and a suitable man elected at Rome, XIII, 15.

He sometimes ordered that the election of a bishop be held in his presence, III, ind. XI, 40. He exhorted the metropolitan to provide Churches vacant of priests, but in such a way that not everyone from his own Church would be elected to the episcopate, lest his own Church necessarily be deprived of proper worship, XIII, 47.

## On the Confirmation of the Elections of Prelates
Confirmation of the election of an elected bishop, II, 22. He did not dare lay hands hastily upon the inexperienced and unknown, X, 34. He commissioned an inquiry into the life and conduct of the elected man: whether he had any canonical impediment, whether he had shown zeal in the work of God, and whether he knew the psalms, ibid. He declared it a grave matter when an election was made not by judgment but solely by favor, X, 62. He did not promote anyone incautiously, but ordered an inquiry into the elected man’s life and morals, with watchful care, through the nearest bishop and the visitor of the vacant church, XIV, 11. He judged a man unfit who was excessively old and who had sworn that he did not wish to become a bishop, ibid. He considered unworthy one who had never invited a friend into his house out of charity; therefore he ordered inquiry into whether he had done this out of parsimony or necessity, ibid. Likewise, he judged unworthy one who did not know the psalms, ibid. And in V, 48, he says: “But neither do we presume to ordain John the presbyter, who is ignorant of the Psalms, since this circumstance clearly showed that he had less than proper zeal for himself.” Likewise, he did not confirm a man who was entirely ignorant of what he was inwardly like unless he had first been examined, XIV, 11. He rejected two men elected to the episcopate alike: one because he had a daughter, saying: “For with what presumption does one dare approach the episcopate who is still proved, by the testimony of his little daughter, not to possess a long-standing continence of the body?”; the other because he was simple-minded and, moreover, had lent money at interest, X, 62. He rejected an unworthy man elected bishop and appointed a visitor for a new election, I, 57; V, 48; he elected another worthy man whose life was very well known to him. He suspended in every respect an unworthy man elected bishop until, informed by the responsalis, he should determine what ought to be done, IV, 20. After rejecting the elected man as unworthy, he entrusted the rector of Sicily with the examination for choosing another bishop, VI, 41. He reminded the man elected bishop, whom he himself was to ordain, to have episcopal vestments and silver for his use carried along with him, III, ind. XI, 35. He declares that he will give no consent to the election of one who had not been elected by Catholics, because, he says, “the vicar of Saint Ambrose is plainly shown to be unworthy if one elected by such men is ordained”; the matter concerned the election of the bishop of Milan, XI, 4. He commissioned an inquiry into an elected bishop whom, he says, he knew not by his morals but only outwardly, ibid. He ordered those who had been nominated to come to him, so that he might elect the worthier bishop, V, 22.

## On the Consecration of Prelates

He permits the consecration of one elected as metropolitan to be performed by his own bishops, III, ind. XI, 30; II, 23. In XI, 4, he says that he accepts as valid the consecration of one who had been elected bishop by the bishops throughout Illyricum. Likewise, in VI, 8, he approved the consecration of the bishop of the city of Nicomedia. Bishops came to Rome to be consecrated, VII, 19, 20, 21; IX, ind. II; and elsewhere, concerning elected bishops, as can be seen above in the passages cited under the heading “On Election.”

## On the Authority and Use of the Pallium

The pallium is to be granted when the merits of the case require it and to one who makes a forceful request, IX, 11. At what times an archbishop may use the pallium, III, ind. XI, 56, where he proceeds against the archbishop of Ravenna, who had used the pallium even outside the solemn celebration of Mass. Concerning its use during solemnities and litanies, until something more precise and certain is learned, V, 11. And only during the solemn celebrations of Mass, V, 53, 56; VI, 8, 9, 18. And in IX, ind. II, 108, he says:

“Since the order of reason altogether admonishes us that, together with the use of the pallium, we ought at the same time, as we have said, to grant certain privileges; but since, with an increase of honor, the care of responsibility ought also to increase, so that the ornaments of conduct may correspond to the adornment of vestments, it is necessary that your Fraternity apply itself more earnestly to every endeavor.”

Once the election has been confirmed, the pallium is given, II, 22. After the election of a metropolitan, one of his fellow bishops from the same province is sent for the pallium, V, 57. He decreed by rescript that the pallium should be delivered, provided that the recipient promised to observe the decrees of reform issued in the synod, IX, ind. II, 108, 109. Under strict prohibition he forbade anyone to accept anything for the pallium, V, 57. Concerning the authority of the pallium, IV, 53; IX, ind. II, 109. He granted the defensor of the Apostolic See the authority to deliver the pallium whenever it had been forcefully requested, in accordance with the merits of the person requesting it, IX, 11. On account of the merits of the person, he grants the pallium to a bishop who is not a metropolitan and gives him precedence over the other bishops, while nevertheless preserving in every respect the precedence of his own metropolitan, IX, ind. II, 108.

## On the Translation of Prelates and the Commendation of Churches

He transferred bishops of churches held under occupation by enemies, by incardinating them into vacant churches, I, 79, 80; II, ind. X, 37. He entrusted one church to a bishop from another church, II, ind. X, 16, 38; III, ind. XI, 13, and explained the reason. He decreed that the revenues of the entrusted church should be spent on the repair of the church and the support of the clergy; nevertheless, he entrusted its correction and jurisdiction to that bishop, IX, ind. II, 71. He invited bishops whose sees were vacant to episcopal sees under his authority, V, 42.

## On Resignation

He denied no one who voluntarily resigned his church on account of illness, and he judged that the man should be adequately supported from the revenues of that same church, VII, 19, 20, 21; XIII, 5.

[Col. 1426] ## On Matters Relating to Bishops and Superiors

He admonished a man newly elected bishop concerning his office, II, ind. X, 10. In the same book, letter 23, he says elegantly and at length that the name of pastor ought to be understood as undertaken not for rest but for labor: “Thus what is signified in the name must be displayed in the work.” The superior’s action should be the instruction of the people. “In you,” he says, “let them see what they should love; let them hasten to imitate it; let them be taught by your example how to live; let them not stray from the right path while you lead them; following you, let them arrive at God,” V, 57, where he says much about how he ought to govern God’s flock. He also exhorts him to carry out his proper office, so that each person may be attentive to his own duty and guard the flock entrusted to him with care and prayer, V, 54. In VII, ind. I, 10, he elegantly shows the matters to which a bishop ought to devote himself. Likewise at length in IX, 107, where he says that a bishop is called a guide because he shows the way of salvation to those who walk in it. Likewise, XIV, 17. A bishop should avoid mockery, abuse—which notaries call “manners” [the reading is uncertain], pretense and duplicity, pomp and vanity, so that the honor of his episcopate may not consist entirely in outward display but in the mind; nor should he become angry or, while raging, impose accusations upon his servants and household. He calls the episcopate a burden. Concerning pastoral care, V, 15. There should be nothing disorderly in his dress, V, 11. In our prayers for a bishop we ought to ask God that his divine mercy grant him the gift of preaching what God loves and of following what God has granted him to preach through that bishop, VI, 19. The bishop—although at the passage cited Saint Gregory is admonishing not a bishop but the prefect of Illyricum—should, as one newly elected, regard the dignity bestowed upon him as coming solely from the gift of the giver and, through the administration of the rule granted to him, make his Creator favorable toward him, II, ind. X, 21. He exhorted a bishop to watch over the flock, after the example of earthly shepherds, and spoke elegantly of pastoral office, IV, 35. How a bishop ought to conduct himself in his own church, III, ind. XI, 63. Concerning the gratitude a bishop ought to show toward his electors, IV, 1. That a bishop should be loved and at the same time feared, ibid. He rebuked a bishop who devoted himself only to simplicity, IV, 26. The episcopate consists in devoting oneself to works of charity, V, 42. A bishop is worthy of commendation if he comes to the episcopate unwillingly, IV, 45. A bishop must observe moderation, V, 48. The bishop’s rewards are as numerous as the gains he has achieved for souls, ibid. A bishop must change both his place and his mind, VI, 30. He bears an empty name as bishop if he does not come to the aid of those suffering need and does not regard another’s poverty as his own, ibid. Mere reading, prayer, and sitting apart are not sufficient for a bishop; he must have a generous hand, ibid. A bishop should not devote himself more to money than to souls, since Christ seeks from the bishop’s office not gold but souls, VI, 29. It is astonishing if one who has clothes, silver, and storerooms does not possess what he ought to give to the poor, VI, 30. He sought nothing more in a bishop than holiness, generosity, and wisdom, ibid. A bishop ought to be content with the revenues of his own church and receive nothing from public funds, V, 44. He exhorts a bishop to his office, to peace, charity, and vigilance, to yearn for heavenly things and abandon earthly things, VI, 65. Just as the episcopate should be denied to those who desire it, so it should be offered to those who flee from it, VII, 4. Whoever refuses to feed God’s sheep, though he is able to do so, sins, VII, 4. Feeding his flock is a sign of love for God, ibid. No one can seek serenity of mind in the episcopate, VII, ibid. In what manner serenity of mind is to be sought in the episcopate, ibid. A bishop ought to undertake secular cares, ibid. When and to what extent this is appropriate, ibid. As soon as a bishop has been elected, he should profess his faith and send it to the pope, ibid., 4. A bishop must not depart from the customary form of professing the faith, ibid.

[Col. 1427] A bishop ought to pray for his rulers and his patriarch, VII, 4, 7, 27. A bishop must not fail to do what he can, even if his strength is insufficient, so that his zeal in defending the poor and oppressed may be made known to God, X, 36. In everything he does, a bishop should seek to have the inspector of hearts favorably disposed toward him, ibid. A bishop should omit nothing that may please God, since human terrors and favors are like smoke, which vanishes when carried away by a light breeze, X, ibid. It is a sign that a bishop has pleased God if we discover that he has displeased wicked men, X, ibid. He praises a bishop for his gravity and exhorts him to administer justice, retain the rigor of the canons, and reform the abuses and conduct of priests, VIII, ind. I, 12. The office of pastor is commended, since the light of the flock is the pastor’s flame, VIII, ind. I, 33. The end of a bishop’s office is described: the bishop must recognize that he has undertaken not the care of earthly things but the guidance of souls, IX, ind. II, 2. The solicitude of superiors is useful, and that caution is praiseworthy in which reason governs everything and anger claims nothing for itself, X, 11. It is the bishop’s office to mourn not only his own sins but also those of others, XII, 1. Prayers are to be offered to implore the fulfillment of the bishop’s office, ibid. To feed the flock before the Lord means to reach, together with the flock he feeds, the pastures of eternal life by praying, admonishing, and displaying zeal for good works, XII, 1; XIII, 13. He praises a bishop—more precisely, Maurentius, master of the soldiers—who avoided human gatherings, because often a mind that desires to be renewed in God through the grace of compunction grows old again through wicked conversations, VIII, 17. A bishop should be proved in his conduct by his disposition, just as is evident from his name, II, ind. X, 49. He forbade a bishop to read the books of the gentiles, which he calls “trifles,” saying: “For the praises of Christ and the praises of Jupiter cannot fit within one mouth.” He also rebuked him because he was explaining grammar to certain people, XIII, 54. He praises a bishop—more precisely, not a bishop but a master of the soldiers—who devoted himself to sacred reading, and invites him into fellowship in sacred eloquence, since he had not found anyone who would assist him in this office because of the poverty of the good [or “of goodness,” the text is uncertain], which he deeply lamented, VIII, 17. He congratulates a bishop occupied with secular affairs because he applies himself to Sacred Scripture, and exhorts him to do so, III, ind. XI, 67. He sent the Pastoral Rule to a bishop who had requested it, V, 4. Bishops are rebuked who, in the election of a patriarch, applied to a human person words of Sacred Scripture spoken of Christ: “This is the day which the Lord has made,” and so forth, VII, 7. A bishop should be ambidextrous, V, 39. He provided a remedy against envy: the more one perceives that others envy him, the more vigilantly he should persevere in the interests of the Church and in God’s service, so that they may be unable to harm him, II, ind. X, 15. A bishop is praised for visiting the sick and receiving them into his house, II, ind. X, 35. A bishop is rebuked for taking part in unjust banquets, and a definition is given of just banquets: those at which no absent person’s life is attacked, no one is reproached through mockery, no empty tales of secular affairs are heard, but rather words of sacred reading; and at which the body is not served beyond what is necessary, but only its weakness is refreshed, so that it may be available for the exercise of virtue, II, ind. X, 52. A bishop should have a generous hand, come to the aid of those suffering need, and regard another’s poverty as his own, VI, 30. A bishop is praised for sending alms to Rome, VII, 9. A bishop should have a presbyter whom he can find in his private quarters, where he may rest after the tumult of legal cases, VI, 22. He exhorts a bishop to unity and charity, which is the mother and guardian of all virtues, II, ind. X, 47. Concerning the mutual charity with which he responded to his fellow bishops, inviting them to pray for one another, VI, 19. What can be done for another out of charity without causing scandal, even if the other makes no complaint, is praiseworthy, IV, 32. He judges it improper that one who had shared the table of his predecessor should be driven from it by his successor, ibid. A bishop should provide necessities for a cleric ignorant of letters, VII, 11. He admonished a bishop to act manfully in ecclesiastical cases and to seek nothing except that he should do everything under the consideration of almighty God alone, so that no person might soften him from the rigor of discipline; nor, God forbid, should vehement indignation harden him in rigor into immoderate severity, VII, 9. A bishop is admonished to conduct himself in ecclesiastical cases in such a way that he does not depart from the grace of paternal charity, VI, 44. Priestly zeal consists in settling disputes, VII, 10. A bishop should protect his children, but in such a way that he does not provide an occasion for the curses of his adversaries, IX, ind. II, 23. A bishop should not delay in administering justice, IX, ind. II, 45. Bishops should take particular care to preserve justice toward those who have taken refuge in the Church, X, 38. He exhorts a bishop to take care not only to bring heretics back, but especially to ensure that Catholics live well, lest alien children be nurtured within the bosom of the holy Church, II, ind. X, 52. A bishop is rebuked for being utterly unconcerned about the conversion of his unbelieving subjects, and he threatens to take action against him, IV, 26. He exhorts a bishop to strengthen the faithful, recall apostates, and convert unbelievers, VIII, ind. I, 1. He orders that a bishop hiding out of fear of heretics be sought and commands that he be urged to come to the threshold of the apostles; he also orders that expenses be supplied to him, IX, ind. II, 94. He praises a bishop who investigated the life of his priests and orders him to report what he had discovered to another person acting on his authority, saying: “Let no consideration withdraw you from investigating wicked actions or from reporting them. For the more we now praise your vigilance, the more blameworthy you will be found if you conceal such actions by any dissimulation,” III, ind. XI, 50. A bishop who is ignorant of what is being done against God’s servants can have no excuse, III, ind. XI, 53. Bishops should make their rebukes of priests at the proper time, IV, 1. A bishop should not burden monasteries but defend them, VI, 29. The arrival of bishops at monasteries should take place in such a way that the monasteries desire it, VIII, ind. I, 15. A bishop should approach a monastery only for the sake of visiting and exhorting, ibid. Monasteries should not be burdened by a bishop on the pretext of hospitality, ibid. A bishop’s frequent arrival at a monastery should not be feared but desired, and the manner in which this is to be achieved is explained, ibid. A bishop should not allow the lesser to be oppressed by the greater, X, 38. A bishop should be diligent in choosing the ministers of the Church, because when they offend, he himself offends, X, 24. He wished bishops to be honored in every respect, II, ind. X, 47. He manfully defended bishops oppressed by rulers and, instead of counting those unjustly deposed among the deposed, arranged for them to be restored to their former rank and kept them with him, I, 7, 28. He orders that the cases of bishops be undertaken before the emperor by the responsalis of the Apostolic See, VIII, ind. I, 10, 25; XI, 6, 7, 8. He did not allow a bishop to burden his subordinate clerics, I, 19. He willingly administered justice to laypeople and clerics against bishops and other ecclesiastical persons, III, ind. XI, 36, 44. How he conducted himself in disputes involving bishops, I, 20. In the dioceses of bishops he arranged nothing without consulting them, I, 40, 41; II, 32. He granted a bishop a presbyter belonging to another church, whom that man’s bishop had refused to grant him, but instructed the defensor to persuade him gently and mildly, VI, 20. He refused to grant, against the will of a man’s own bishop, a deacon who might be elected bishop of another church, XIV, 11. He refused to unite a deserted monastery with another monastery in a different diocese when the bishop objected, unless the case had first been examined, XIII, 2. He notified the other bishops of the province that a bishop had been suspended for contumacy, II, ind. X, 19. Out of humanity, he ordered that sustenance be supplied by the church in which a condemned bishop had exercised his office, since it is exceedingly impious that, after punishment, he should be subjected to the necessity of food, III, ind. XI, 55. He came to the aid, with counsel and assistance, of a bishop from whom the queen and other bishops wished to withdraw obedience, IV, 2. Whatever a bishop ought to do by virtue of his office, he should do with much greater zeal when apostolic authority is added, IV, 5. It is harsh and far removed from a priest’s office to neglect a person placed in necessity and improperly to thirst for money under the pretext of gathering it. Therefore he ordered that the ten solidi which the bishop had taken from the archdeacon be restored, V, 33. He informed the people of the wickedness of their bishop, VI, 26. It is utterly detestable in a bishop to take away from the patrimony of Saint Peter what kings preserve for the Church, VI, 53. He elegantly replied by rescript to a bishop who said that he was incurring enmities because of the frequent cases entrusted to him by the Apostolic See. He explained how such things ought to be endured and that one must act and remain vigilant with all the more steadfastness, VII, 2. He admonished a bishop that the more he loved the prefect, the more he should admonish him always to keep God’s judgment before his heart’s eyes in the cases he handled, VII, 8. A bishop is rebuked because, on Sunday, before celebrating Mass, he went to reap someone’s harvest, IX, ind. II, 1. He excommunicated from divine worship for two months the bishop’s advisers, who had advised him badly, ibid. He spared the bishop on account of his gray hair and simplicity, ibid. A bishop is admonished not to delay administering justice, IX, ind. II, 45. He admonished a bishop concerning complaints brought against him, so that he might correct himself, ibid. He excused a bishop before a certain nobleman because that bishop’s agents had occupied the nobleman’s possessions, IX, ind. II, 13. While exhorting the bishops of Sicily to act well, he says that he had instructed the defensor of the Apostolic See first to rebuke their disorderly actions privately, XIII, 22. He ordered that a bishop be admonished privately concerning scandals he had caused, so that, when the illness arrived which was an impediment and scandalized certain people, he might cease from that ministry. Those who had been scandalized were to be admonished that they should in no way fear but communicate with complete security and confidence, because the illness of the person neither changes nor pollutes the blessing of the sacred mystery, XIII, 47. He orders that a bishop who was too hasty in issuing judgments be admonished privately, XII, 32. He not only did not diminish the authority of bishops but strengthened it, IX, ind. II, 64. He forbids the defensor to defend clerics who are contumacious toward their own bishop. But if the merits of the case require it, he should be an intercessor rather than a defender; if they make a just proposal, assistance should not be denied them, lest clerical discipline be dissolved through his defense; rather, the reverence due to each bishop should be preserved, IX, ind. II, 64. The defensor is likewise rebuked for dragging the cases of clerics before himself while disregarding their own bishops. He ordered all of them to approach their bishops, saying: “If jurisdiction is not preserved for each bishop through the Apostolic See, what else is being done except that the ecclesiastical order, which ought to be preserved through them, is being thrown into confusion?” XI, 37. Penitent clerics expelled by the defensor from the place of penance are to be restored without delay by their own bishop, ibid. He decreed nothing against bishops without first hearing them. Thus he instructed the bishop of Naples to send someone to him who could respond in his name to the accusations, IX, ind. II, 104. A bishop is rebuked because he did not reconcile his people, whom his own prejudice had divided into two parties, ibid. He ordered dissolute bishops to come to him so that he might correct their morals. Thus he ordered a bishop whom he had sent to Gaul by his own appointment to return to him on account of his secular conduct, so that, restrained under the discipline appropriate to him, he might strive to convert his secular manners to priestly dignity. “For it is sufficiently harmful and pernicious that, by his example, those things which ought to have been built up should be destroyed. In this matter not only is he found blameworthy, but also the one who did not resist,” IX, ind. II, 115. He supplied bishops with necessities: he sent a horse so that one might ride, calling it the blessing of Saint Peter, VIII, 45. Likewise, to a bishop who had returned from schism to the Church, he provided one set of furnishings, XII, 32. And clothing to bishops in need, XII, 45. He rebuked a bishop who maintained an association with wicked men, because one who receives such people does not correct their crimes but seems rather to give others permission to commit them, XI, 13. He informed a bishop of everything that had happened to his legate and excused the legate, since he had been free of blame in the error into which he had fallen, XI, 74. He ordered the responsalis to admonish the archbishop of Thessalonica to desist from the troubles inflicted upon the bishop of Corcyra, XIV, 8. He did not permit bishops and superiors to be harassed by their subjects, showing the evil that would flow from this, XIV, 17. He sharply rebuked a bishop who avenged a personal injury by excommunicating another, II, ind. X, 49. The cases of bishops must be investigated with great diligence, IX, ind. II, 68. A bishop ought to strive to maintain the good opinion of his clergy, so that nothing wicked or unbefitting the Church may be heard from them, IV, 5. A bishop should be vigilant against heretics and in removing abuses. For, he says, “the one who does not correct what must be cut away commits it,” X, 42. He declares that he wishes to punish a bishop who did not punish wrongdoers if he thereafter leaves them unpunished, IV, 12. He strengthened promises made by bishops to clerics through the authority of the Apostolic See, XIII, 44. A bishop asked Saint Gregory to appoint someone from his side to whom he could carefully report his cases to the pope himself. And against those who saw wrongdoers and remained silent, he wrote as follows: “But if you know that these things are being done, do not be silent; resist earnestly. For if you either neglect to investigate these matters or conceal them once understood, not only will the bond of sin bind those who do these things, but you too will incur before God no slight guilt in this matter,” III, ind. XI, 48.

## On Residence

He did not permit a bishop who wished to come to Rome, but wrote to him that he should pray to God for him, I, 66. He did not allow a bishop sent outside his own church on some business of the Apostolic See to remain away for long, III, ind. XI, 35. He ordered that a presbyter who had been deprived of his position because of a two-month absence from his church be restored to his place if, as he claimed, he had been absent for a just reason, IV, 13. He ordered that a bishop who was not residing in his own church be admonished to reside there under penalty of being thrust into a monastery, VI, 23. Bishops are not permitted to travel wherever they wish, for their own affairs or those of others, without the permission of their metropolitan, except to the Apostolic See against that same metropolitan, IX, ind. II, 8. He rebuked bishops who had gone to the imperial court or to hold a council without letters from their primate, IX, ind. II, 68. Clerics are forbidden to abandon their parishes, IX, ind. II, 65. He compelled a bishop who was serving secular tribunals outside his own church to return to his church, as though he were destroying priestly dignity through secular affairs, X, 10. He ordered the defensor of the Apostolic See that a bishop who had long been absent from his own church should give the required satisfaction of purification, XII, 24. He invited a bishop whom he wished to see to come to him, XII, 43. He invited a bishop to the threshold of the apostles and asserted that he would be his colleague in sacred reading, VIII, 17. He summoned a bishop to Rome on account of bodily illness and sent him one horse from the blessing of Saint Peter, X, 45; and in XI, 33, he wrote to the same bishop what he ought to arrange in his church during his absence. He ordered a bishop to come to him as quickly as possible, so that, after postponing the delay, he might return to his own affairs once his accounts had been presented, II, ind. X, 20.

## On Remedying the Negligence of Prelates

When a superior is negligent, the cesspool of vices grows, I, 44. When bishops were negligent, he wrote to the metropolitan what ought to be done so that he could communicate it to the bishops of his province; above all, he entrusted this to him so that he himself might not appear to diminish the metropolitan’s honor, IV, 26, 34, 35, 39. He rebuked a bishop who was negligent in his office, V, 6. He carefully investigated the negligence of bishops and corrected it through the strictest inquiries, rebuking their negligence in correcting offenses. He asserts that the punishment of so wicked an offense ought to have reached his ears before the offense itself, VIII, ind. I, 8, 9; IX, ind. II, 115. He sharply rebuked the laziness and negligence of Bishop Paschasius, because in no matter was he recognized as a bishop, to such an extent that neither his church, nor the monasteries, nor the children of the Church—whether oppressed or poor—felt his zeal of affection toward them, XIII, 26. He rebuked the bishops of Campania because they were so negligent that, forgetful of their honor, they showed neither paternal vigilance toward their churches or their children, nor concern for the monasteries, nor devoted themselves to protecting the oppressed and the poor, XIII, 27. A bishop is reproved because he did not correct monks living shamefully, X, 22. A bishop negligent in the proper care of monasteries incurs the guilt of reproach, because when monks offend, he himself offends and by his frivolity grieves the pope, X, 24. He exhorts a bishop to be vigilant, cautious in his office, and not sluggish, and rebukes him because he did not correct wrongdoers, XI, 71. He ordered a negligent bishop to appoint for himself a vicedominus (estate steward) and a major domus (head of household), ibid. Bishops should be zealous in correcting their subjects. Thus he says that it is shameful for him to admonish that bishop to bind his cleric under the rigor of discipline, IX, ind. II, 64. He commands the defensor to admonish a bishop to care for his church and not neglect its interests. He commended the church to him so that the defensor might provide his assistance in carrying this out; but if the bishop should also neglect it, the defensor himself was to carry it out, lest the welfare of the churches in any way perish, XIV, 2. The matters in which Gregory considered a bishop worthy of reproach are given there, ibid.

## On Visitation

A bishop is admonished that, if he can, he should visit the diocese, lest baptized persons remain unconfirmed, X, 45. He arranged for the church to be visited in the absence of its own bishop, who was engaged in the service of the Apostolic See, so that whatever the solemnity of Easter required might be fulfilled, XI, ind. X, 26. In the absence of a sick bishop, he entrusted everything to the visitor except the ordination of priests, III, ind. XI, 24, 25. He entrusted the reform of the secular and regular clergy of the city of Luni to the bishop of Milan together with the bishop of that city, who had requested a coadjutor for this work, so that they would not permit people to remain in that city whose conduct did not match what their clothing displayed, IV, 22. He had a church deprived of priests and divine worship visited, so that presbyters and those who would have care of souls might be appointed there, I, 15, 53. He appointed a visitor to a vacant church because he had not approved the election of a certain man as bishop of that church, I, 57. He appointed a visitor to a church because of its prolonged vacancy and entrusted everything to him, including the ordination of priests, I, 80. He charged Bishop Benenatus with the visitation of the church of Cumae, so that he might take part in the election to be held and ensure that no one presumed to take anything from the church—whether the advancement of clerics, revenues, ornaments, ministries, or anything else, II, ind. X, 16, 25, 37, 39. Likewise, I, 4, and that they should not permit a layperson to be elected. Likewise, IX, ind. II, 75, 76, 88, 89; V, 23; VII, 20; VII, 15. Likewise, VI, 21. He permitted the visitor, if no worthy person from within the church could be found, to ordain an outsider as bishop, III, 64, 87. And in XIII, 16, in which passages he also forbids the election of a layperson. He entrusted Bishop Felix with the visitation and care of a church that lacked a pastor, II, ind. X, 43. He admonished the visitor to administer the church’s property more effectively, V, 44. He arranged for one hundred solidi and one orphan boy, whom the visitor himself would choose, to be given to the visiting bishop from the same church as payment for his labor, III, ind. XI, 35. The fourth part which the bishop of that church ought to receive was assigned to the visitor from the day of the visitation for as long as he remained there, V, 12. A visitor is rebuked because he received grain from public funds, V, 44. He ordered the visitors to be supplied with stipends by the churches they visited, IV, 11.

[Col. 1432] ## On Foreign Clerics

He ordered the archdeacon and the other clerics to return to their own church, V, 9. He did not permit bishops summoned by him to travel during inconvenient seasons, I, 72. He also wished the highest prelates, expelled from their sees, to live with him, I, 28. He ordered them to be received by other bishops, where they would live with those bishops on ecclesiastical support until he could incardinate them into other vacant churches, I, 45. At the request of their bishops, he compelled clerics promoted to sacred orders who were wandering among uncertain sees to return to the church in which they had served, IV, 44. He ordered a fugitive bishop who was avoiding the discipline of his metropolitan to return to that same metropolitan, IX, ind. II, 111.

## On Sick Clerics

He praises a bishop summoned by him who did not come because of illness; but after he recovered, he ordered him to come, X, 45. Many things must be done on account of illness which, if we were healthy, we would rightly be considered blameworthy for doing, XI, 40. “For,” he says, “we ought not to be ashamed of what necessity imposes.” He prohibited fasting for a sick bishop, XI, 40, 33. He did not permit a successor to be given to any bishop on account of any illness against that bishop’s will, XI, 47; XIII, 5. At the request of a bishop detained by illness, he granted him a coadjutor, while food and support for that bishop nevertheless remained payable from his own church; but he entrusted the ordinations of the sacred orders to the nearest bishop, XI, 5, 6. He ordered a sick bishop to abstain from vigils, prayers, and the other solemn ministries, XI, 33. He decreed that sick clerics should receive the customary stipends which they earned when healthy, II, ind. X, 8.

## On the Defenders of the Holy Roman Church and Other Ecclesiastical Ministers
Administrators of the patrimony of the Holy Roman Church he sent through the provinces, II, indiction X, 21. He left it to the judgment of their provincial ministers to select the latter’s assistants; nevertheless, he indicated those whom he judged suitable, XIII, 25. A defensor is appointed, and concerning his qualifications: he must not be subject to any condition or corporation, must not be a cleric of another city, and must not contravene the statutes of any canon, V, 29; XI, 38. He granted a privilege to a defensor as remuneration, VIII, indiction I, 14. The affairs of the Holy Roman Church should be entrusted to energetic men, IX, indiction II, 18. He commended to a defensor the faithfulness, skill, and diligence of a certain man in conducting business, free from every kind of duplicity, XI, 39. He ordered that defenders be supplied for their expenses from the revenues of the possessions of the Holy Roman Church, V, 28. The office of a defensor was concerned chiefly with pious works—for example, ensuring that bequests left for pious purposes were distributed as alms to the poor—and with receiving information against bishops acting perversely and correcting the abuses of religious communities, ibid. He instructed his ministers not to burden bishops and ecclesiastical persons with forced services, I, 70. A defensor should conduct diligently and courteously whatever must be done, IX, indiction II, 46. He commended a defensor departing for a province to the bishops of that province, XIII, 17. A defensor should first admonish bishops secretly concerning their disorderly actions, ibid. He ordered false defenders to be restrained by severe correction, X, 41. He directed that energetic and faithful men be presented to him, so that he might appoint them defenders, ibid. He ordered the accounts of an unfaithful defensor to be examined, so that he might no longer administer his office, X, 46. He ordered a false defensor who refused to obey a bishop to be sent into exile, ibid. A defensor should alleviate the burden he has imposed, XIV, 2. A courier is to be chosen with the consent of the elders and clergy; and concerning his office, XIII, 44. He took special care of those who served the apostolic see: he ordered that the property of a notary of the apostolic see be preserved for his wife and children, and that particular account be taken of his servants, XII, 13. He ordered the defensor to care for the property accruing to a notary serving the apostolic see who was absent, IX, indiction II, 46. He prohibited the administration of Church property from being entrusted to laymen, but required that it be entrusted to approved clerics, VII, indiction II, 65. He praised an archdeacon who rebuked his bishop for distributing Church property among his relatives, II, indiction X, 19. [Col. 1433] Concerning vigilance and severity in punishing abuses, he wrote as follows: “If you were a man, or possessed any discernment, you ought to have been so faithful a guardian of regular discipline that you would have corrected by punishment the things unlawfully committed there before their report reached us,” VIII, indiction I, 9.

## On Superiority and Obedience

He urged the people to obey their bishop, III, indiction XI, 14. “How obedience, or rather reverence, ought to be shown to superiors, you yourself do not doubt from your own subjects”; he wrote to Bishop Felix [Read: “to the bishop of Sardica.” The bishop of Prima Justiniana held no authority in Sardinia] in Sardinia, who disdained to obey the bishop of Prima Justiniana, V, 10. Bishops ought to obey their metropolitan, V, 63; and each person his superiors, VI, 25, 43. The order of ranks was established for this purpose: that superiors should not oppress their subjects, nor subjects again rebel against their superiors, VIII, indiction I, 7. The order of ecclesiastical authority is thrown into confusion if unlawful things are rashly presumed, or things not permitted are attempted with impunity, ibid., 27. Those who rise up against their superiors show that they disdain to be servants of God, II, indiction X, 36. “It is no great thing for us to be humble toward those by whom we are honored, for secular people do this as well; but we ought to be especially humble toward those from whom we suffer something,” ibid. Perfect obedience must be rendered to a prelate, since once someone has become a prelate, he is no longer to be judged by his subjects, III, indiction XI, 29. One must not disparage one’s superiors and prelates, since disparagement of them concerns Christ: “For the deeds of our bishops are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even when they seem rightly to require correction,” II, 30.

## On the Life and Moral Conduct of Clerics

He ordered a deacon inflated by the spirit of ambition to be restrained and placed last among the deacons, I, 83. Lawrence, first deacon of the apostolic see, was deposed on account of his pride and other evils. Formerly II, Preface; now in the appendix to the Letters. It is an insult to priests to be admonished concerning divine worship. “For what they themselves,” he says, “ought to demand is shamefully demanded of them; and their office ought to pertain to adornment, not to the ugliness of their actions,” IV, 5. The clergy should not be given relaxation, but compelled with the utmost urgency to pursue the things of God, IV, 5, where more is said about correction. Clerics should satisfy their creditors, IX, indiction II, 101. Clerics should avoid associations and patronage from laymen, III, 27. A priestly order that is falling inwardly cannot stand outwardly, V, 53. Even when oppressed by a false accusation, a bishop should, in the presence of his clergy and people, give an account of the integrity of his faith, VI, 2. Clerics should not be occupied with the services and labors of other Churches, but should serve their own Church, IX, indiction II, 65. It is a serious matter for clerics to fall into the practices of laymen, IX, indiction II, 70. What is often not a fault in laymen is a crime in clerics, X, 4. Clerics who have committed many acts of violence are to be admonished; if they do not listen, they are to be excommunicated, XIII, 36. Those entangled in the affairs of the world are not to be admitted hastily into the clergy. “For when they live in ecclesiastical dress no differently from the way they lived before, they are by no means striving to flee the world, but to change it,” VIII, indiction I, 5. Bad priests are the ruin of the people, XI, 69. The association of the wicked is the purification of the good, XI, 45. Clerics must take care of their reputation and exercise caution, IX, indiction II, 60. “For just as prudent foresight knows how to block the paths of wrongdoing and avoid what is harmful, so neglect leaves an opening for abuses and tends to incur what must be avoided; for the person who has learned even not to use what is permitted wisely overcomes what is unlawful.”

## On the Cohabitation of Clerics and Women

Priests in Corsica are forbidden to associate with women, except only their mother, sister, or wife, who must be governed chastely, I, 52. Bishops who live with women are to be admonished not to cohabit with them in any way, except those whom the authority of the sacred canons permits—that is, a mother, paternal aunt, sister, and others of this kind, concerning whom no improper suspicion can arise. They will do better, however, if they also refrain from cohabiting with such women, as did blessed Augustine, who was not accustomed even to live with his sister, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters,” IX, indiction II, 60; [Col. 1434] XIII, 35, 36. Against those who cohabit with unrelated women. Against immodest priests who cohabit with women, he implores the help of the king [More correctly, “the queen”], XI, 69.

## On Benefices and Dignities

A priest who had been ordained in another’s place after the rightful occupant had been unjustly expelled—if he had attained that order without making any payment, and had therefore not fallen into the simoniacal heresy—he ordered to be ordained in another vacant Church, IV, 13. He did not compel clerics to advance unwillingly, I, 19; II, indiction X, 19, 20. Those violently ordained in another Church he allowed to return to their own, XIII, 28. A cleric of another parish who was suspect but had not committed an offense he incardinated in another Church, out of compassion, to support his poverty, IV, 14; and one expelled from his own Church, VI, 11. He commended a Church that had been destroyed and then recovered, ordering its revenues to be spent on the restoration and worship of the Church, IV, 19. Dignities and offices of the Church are to be entrusted to inferiors when the person who, by order of rank, would ordinarily be entitled to them is unsuitable; for it is usefulness, not position, that must be considered, and it is suitable action, not position, that must be sought, VI, 10. “That person holds the first place before God who, in his sight, even if despised, has pleased him as an instrument of good action,” ibid. A bishop should provide a cleric ignorant of letters with what is necessary for the support of life, VII, 11. He ordered that the pensions owed to clerics be paid, II, indiction X, 44.

## On Religious Communities

“What else does the habit of monks signify except contempt for the world?” XII, 24. Describing the abbot’s care and office, he says: “Let not the reputation of the monastery be stained through his negligence. Let him not frequently go outside. In external matters let him appoint a procurator. Let him devote himself to reading and prayer; let him give generously to the poor as much as he can; let him be diligent in hospitality. Likewise, let the brothers devote themselves to prayer and reading,” III, indiction XI, 3; XI, 12. The deformity of a monastery and the dissolution of monastic discipline arise from the disorderly rule of a superior—when he flatters sinners indulgently and when he becomes angry in a disorderly and excessive manner, XI, 48. He appointed an abbot as visitor to monasteries that had fallen into disorder, where none of the precepts of the monastic rule were observed, I, 51, 52; V, 50. He entrusted the reform of monks to a bishop, VII, 35; and their correction at the request of the abbot of that same monastery, X, 22, 23. He entrusted to a defensor the visitation, reform, and correction of the conduct of monks fighting the ancient enemy, XIII, 46. Boys are not to be received into monasteries before the age of eighteen, I, 50. Monasteries of monks are not to become dwelling places for laymen pretending to live religiously, V, 1. The period of probation is two years, X, 24. An abbot is rebuked because he had admitted someone to profession before the probationary period, ibid. Women are not to be in monasteries of monks, I, 50. Women are not to approach monasteries of monks, and monks must not make them their godmothers [commatres], IV, 42. He recalled wandering monks from one monastery to another to the former rule of their abbot, I, 42. He ordered the defensor to search for those who had been dispersed and to restore those found to their abbot, I, 41, 42; and other fugitives, when found, to be thrust into prison, II, 28. Clerics who have become monks are forbidden to return to their former Church, I, 42. A monk made a priest by a bishop must remain in the Church in which he was ordained, ibid. Monks or abbots who enter the clerical office or sacred order are no longer to have any authority in those monasteries, VII, 43, nor permission to live there, VIII, indiction I, 15. A secular cleric cannot be an abbot; if he wishes to be an abbot, he must cease to be a cleric. “For it is most incongruous that, when someone cannot carefully fulfill one of these offices because of its greatness, he should be judged suitable for both; and thus the ecclesiastical order should hinder monastic life, and the monastic rule ecclesiastical usefulness,” IV, 11. Monks are forbidden to be involved in the tumult of court cases, lest the mind, distracted by various legal concerns, drift away and, weakened, grow sluggish in celebrating its accustomed work, I, 69. The affairs of the monastery are to be conducted through a procurator, III, indiction XI, 3. He ordered an abbot already created to be removed because, through bodily failure, he had fallen from the state of his habit, III, indiction XI, 23. Likewise IV, 6, because one who through his negligence had led so many disciples to hell ought never to have been placed over the others. Therefore, he ordered one of the reformed monastery to be placed in charge of that monastery, so that what was neglected through the former man’s carelessness might be preserved through the latter’s diligence. Because of the priests’ negligence in celebrating the divine Mass for the people, he made a secular Church regular, provided that the abbot had a priest with him to celebrate Mass in that Church and supplied him with the means of support, IV, 18. If an abbot who is a deacon should fall, but afterward his conduct in penance should prove worthy, he is to be appointed prior among the monks, V, 3. In monasteries, a bishop is not to celebrate public Masses with his cathedra except on the day of the monastery’s dedication or anniversary; on other days, Mass is to be celebrated by a priest appointed by him, II, 41; VI, 46; VII, 12. Those wishing to become monks from among the servants of the Church are first to be tested in lay clothing. Formerly IV, 44; now in the appendix, in the Decrees of Saint Gregory. A bishop should watch over monasteries, VI, 11. He permitted monks to be ordained priests at a bishop’s request because of a shortage of clergy, provided they were found worthy, VI, 28. Bishops must not burden monasteries, but defend them, VI, 29; VII, indiction I, 18. Secular priests must not trouble monasteries, V, 28; VI, 40; VIII, indiction I, 15. Secular clerics must not approach monasteries except to pray or when invited to solemn Masses, VII, 43. A bishop must not burden monasteries on the pretext of lodging, VIII, indiction I, 15. A bishop should approach monasteries only for the purpose of visiting or exhorting, so that his arrival may be eagerly awaited, ibid. He permitted a priest to be ordained in a monastery of monks, to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass there, VI, 42. Those coming to the religious life are to be received with charity and strengthened by gentle consolations, so that, with God’s help, they may delight in persevering in every way in the way of life they have chosen, VI, 48. An abbot should answer to his office through good conduct and actions, so that he may remove the occasion of an adverse reputation, VII, 18. Gregory would have judged a monk more worthy of admiration if he had never wished to take charge of others, since he had assumed responsibility for men who retained the appearance of monks but carried on many worldly activities there under the guise of holiness, VII, 32. He urged the abbot to reform his monks and to maintain peace with his bishop, ibid. Bishops must not defend monks disobedient to their abbot, VII, 35. He promised a bishop that he would give him other monks if those who were there did not please him, provided the places were such that they could find there the means of subsistence, VII, 43. He ordered expenses to be supplied from the substance of his mother for a monk who devoted himself to reading and could not work, IV, 47. No bishop or secular person may dare to diminish anything from the revenues or privileges of a monastery, VIII, indiction I, 15. Cases arising between a bishop’s Church and monasteries are to be decided by arbitrators chosen by both parties, ibid. An outsider is not to be chosen as abbot, but someone from the same community; if no suitable person is found there, one is to be chosen from other monasteries, ibid. He ordered that the life of the cellarer be investigated and that, if found worthy, he be appointed abbot, XII, 24. A man who had dared to depart alone on a journey abroad without any of his brothers is excluded from election as abbot; for this shows that the person who walks without a witness does not live rightly, ibid. No one is to be placed over a living abbot in his monastery for any reason, unless definite crimes are present, VIII, indiction I, 15. Monks are not to be transferred, against the will of their abbot, to establish other monasteries; nor are they to be promoted to sacred orders or clerical office, ibid. An abbot may send some of the monks remaining in his monasteries to establish other monasteries; if he refuses, the bishop is to compel him, ibid. The abbot, and no one else, is to make the attestation of the property found in the monastery, ibid. He sent back to the monastery a monk whom he had kept with him for the companionship he enjoyed with him in the word of God, because of the monastery’s need, VIII, indiction I, 16. He ordered a bishop to restore to the monastery everything he had taken from it under the pretext of a gift of hospitality, VIII, indiction I, 34. He ordered the bishop to correct delinquent monks, ibid. He entirely exempted a monastery from the jurisdiction of the bishop, except in the appointment of the abbot, II, 41, 42. He granted a monastery the privilege of exemption from all episcopal jurisdiction, except for the care of discipline, V, 37. Monasteries of religious men and women are not to be disturbed by anyone; their cases are to be heard only by the bishop, IX, indiction II, 64. A monk chosen unanimously by the community is to become a priest because of a shortage of priests, IX, indiction II, 92. A priest is to be requested from the bishop to serve the monastery of monks, and no other is to be appointed, VIII, 2. He sent a monk to Bishop of Naples to govern the monks, whom he then decided should be their superior. If his life pleased the bishop, after some time he would appoint him their father; nevertheless, he did not conceal that he had recognized an evil in him, although he seemed very wise to himself, IX, indiction II, 91. A bishop is rebuked for having appointed as abbot one whom he had not tested, X, 24. He ordered four or five monks to be given to a bishop traveling to an unknown place for his companionship, though this was to be done at the discretion of the ordinary bishop, XII, 1. He ordered that what an abbot acquired after becoming a bishop and being removed from the office of abbot be given to him; but what had been acquired before that time was to belong to the monastery of which he had been abbot; and whatever preceded his office as abbot was to belong to the monastery in which he had entered religious life, ibid. He ordered all troubles to be removed from the monastery, X, 22. He commended one monastery temporarily and permanently united another to the abbot of the other monastery, X, 61. He united one monastery to another as an equal principal establishment, on the condition that divine worship should be adequately maintained in both and that subjection to the bishop within whose boundaries lay the monastery being united to another monastery in a different diocese should be preserved, XI, 72; XIII, 2. He united a Church to a monastery, wishing its revenues to be spent on the Church’s repair, XI, 63. He praised a bishop who did not permit a monastery of monks to be built next to a monastery of nuns, XI, 25. It is more tolerable to place an older brother in charge as abbot than to endure a new and inexperienced one, XI, 48. He refused to grant three monks to an abbot who requested them, especially one whom he knew would be useless because of simplicity and negligence, VII, 45. He invited the abbot to come to him and live with him for some period of time, ibid. He ordered a public slave who had become a monk to be handed over to the defensor Fantinus, XII, 3. He did not permit clerics wishing to become monks to be hindered, even if they were already in sacred orders, XII, 35. He forbade people bound by public duties to be received into a monastery unless they had first been released from them, VIII, indiction I, 5. He granted privileges to monasteries of men and women founded by the queen of the Franks, XIII, 8, 9, 10. Those who fell while wearing the monastic habit when they were still in a lesser order are not to be placed over monasteries as abbots unless their life has been corrected and worthy penance has preceded. If this has otherwise been done, and their actions are not contrary to their office, let them remain in the order in which they are; otherwise, let other worthy men be appointed, XIV, 2. Above all he commended regular observance, concerning which he says: “Therefore be diligent, lest the rigor of the rule be injured either by some delay or by the leniency of those appointed,” V, 35. He prohibited a priest from introducing new customs into a monastery, II, 28. He took care that the construction of monasteries be brought to completion, II, 32. Concerning laymen who wished to be tonsured, he readily permitted them to become administrators under a superior, ibid. Monks are not to possess private property, I, 42. Whatever is said to belong to a monk must all be devoted to the benefit of the monastery, VI, 12. A monk is rejected from the dignity of abbot because he had possessed private property, which indicates a monk’s earthly mind, XII, 24. Private property must be eradicated from monks with the greatest care, and the monastery cleansed of such a plague. For if monks possess individual property there, neither concord nor charity can remain in that community. “What, then, is the habit of a monk except contempt for the world? How, therefore, do those despise the world who, having been placed in a monastery, seek gold there?” ibid. He urged the patriarch of Alexandria to restore the monastery to the monks after expelling the heretics from it, XII, 49. He took particular care of nuns, IV, 9. He did not permit a monastery of holy women to be consecrated unless it was first examined whether a sufficient endowment had been provided for that monastery, X, 66. Concerning an oratory in a monastery of nuns: sacrifices are to be celebrated; their oratory is to be consecrated by the bishop; the bishop is entrusted with care and diligent oversight of discipline among the nuns; a cloister, procurator, and agent are to be appointed, the man chosen being approved in life and conduct, whose age and position give no occasion for improper suspicion. Immunity and privileges were granted to them, III, indiction XI, 40; IV, 9; VI, 12. He entrusted the correction of the conduct of both abbess and nuns to the bishop, VII, 12. He prohibited very young women from becoming abbesses, but approved women of sixty, IV, 11. What should be done with a virgin who left the monastery and married he entrusted orally, but refused to put in writing, IV, 27. He ordered a nun who had unjustly moved to another monastery to return to her own, V, 6. He ordered a nun who had dissipated the monastery’s property to be placed in another monastery until the matter could be investigated by the defensor, ibid. A bishop is rebuked for allowing a physician or any other secular person to enter a monastery of nuns, ibid. The abbess is to be chosen not from outside but from within the community of nuns, VII, 12. Confirmation of her election, or her appointment, belongs to the bishop, ibid. Administration of the property belongs to the abbess, excluding the bishop and all others, ibid. Her care and generosity in times of need, as well as abstinence, numbers, and the tears of the nuns, II, 4; VII, 22. He ordered the defensor to inform him of their condition and needs, VIII, indiction I, 23. Consecration of a monastery of nuns without an endowment is refused, and the endowment is described, VIII, indiction I, 4. He ordered an apostate nun to be shut up again in the monastery and resume the habit, and laymen who opposed this to be excommunicated, VIII, indiction I, 8, 9. He urged a bishop to assist a woman professing the religious life who was being forced to marry, IX, indiction II, 29. He sent a nun to be appointed abbess, X, 43. He praised a secular woman who had built a monastery of nuns, so that, just as she had built earthly places in honor of the saints through religious devotion, she might likewise hasten to prepare dwellings with them in heaven, X, 65. He commended to a notary an abbess going to a newly built monastery of nuns, so that it might be under the notary’s protection, X, 67. Concerning a religious woman who had built a monastery in her own house: because she should be dealt with more by kindness than by severity, he instructed the defensor to strive to act with gentleness, so that she might neither, because of her own sin, be made to disregard the will of her founder, nor be prevented from soundly caring for the monastery’s interests. “Likewise,” he says, “let him in no way permit her girls, whom the aforesaid woman once converted in the monastery after changing their clothing, to be taken away from her or disturbed; but, with God’s protection, let them remain in the conversion in which they are,” XIV, 2.

## On the Good of Chastity and the Conversion of Married Persons

He cared for widows and asserted that this was a priestly duty, V, 37. He entrusted their protection and defense to the defensor of the apostolic see, VI, 38. He took particular care of the welfare of honorable women, IX, indiction II, 26. He permitted a married man to enter the religious life, provided that his wife likewise converted, VI, 48; XI, 45. Marriages are not dissolved for the sake of religion; the same passage also concerns the virtue of continence. [Col. 1438] A betrothed woman may enter the religious life if she wishes, once everything the fiancé had received has been returned to him, VII, 23. He ordered that a husband who had become a monk be restored to his wife, XI, 50.

## On Vows and Pilgrims to Holy Places

To one who was returning quickly from the holy places, he wrote that he did not have a good opinion of him [rather, of her, namely Rusticiana], because she had paid no attention in her heart to what she had seen bodily, IV, 46. He ordered the defensor to inform the provincial praetor of the mandate summoning bishops to the thresholds of the apostles, so that every suspicion might be removed and their departure not be hindered, VII, 22. He invited a bishop to the thresholds of the apostles, IX, indiction II, 74. After commending a priest returning from the thresholds of the apostles, he ordered that his bishop again grant him permission if he wished to return to the same thresholds, IX, 69. He encouraged one who desired to come to the thresholds of the apostles, XI, 74. Whatever pious purpose has been suggested by God to a willing mind ought to be carried out as soon as possible, II, indiction X, 27.

## On the Office of Preaching and Teachers

He rejoiced that a bishop was preaching the Gospel to an unbelieving king, III, indiction XI, 67. He praised a bishop in whose preaching of the word of God the patrician Maria had been converted to the faith, and whose faith he hoped would bring forth great fruit, VII, 8. He ordered the defensor of Gaul to establish, from the patrimony of the apostolic see, a school for English boys, to gather them, and then to hand them over to a monastery to receive the faith and make progress in it, VI, 7.

## On Peace and War

During wartime, while peace had not yet been secured, he was anxious that the city guards should remain vigilant and that watches be kept on the walls, IX, indiction II, 4, 6. He always urged unity of peace with everyone, X, 42. He gave thanks to the king and queen of the Lombards, IX, indiction II, 42, 43. Concerning the preservation of peace with the Apostolic See, VII, 4, 5. In wartime he watched over the safety of the commonwealth, omitting nothing that could help. Thus he instructed the master of soldiers to be with the other masters of soldiers and to do what they had jointly decided, II, 3. He also urged them to act vigorously, II, 29. They were to receive worthy hostages from the enemies for the sake of peace; but if they seemed insufficiently secure, they were to do whatever they judged appropriate for the commonwealth, XII, 30. If they saw the enemies taking the field, he ordered them to disregard the peace and plunder their territories, ibid. He urged obedience to the military tribune, ibid. He gave peace [perhaps: “devoted effort”] to the accomplishment of peace, V, 36. He brought about peace between hostile rulers and proposed just agreements to them, ibid.

## Gifts Sent

To Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, the keys of blessed Peter the apostle, which, placed upon the sick, commonly shine with many miracles, I, 26. To Andrew of Dibiria, a most holy key of Saint Peter the apostle, which contains within it something from his chains, I, 30. To John, former consul, patrician, and quaestor, a similar key, I, 31. He ordered Theodorus the counselor to be given a boy, a slave by status and Sicilian by nation, named Acosimus, III, indiction XI, 18. To Columbus, bishop of Numidia, the keys of blessed Peter, containing something from his chains, as a blessing, III, indiction XI, 48. To Dynamius, patrician of Gaul, a small cross containing a piece of the chains of blessed Peter and, at its extremities, a piece of the grating of Saint Lawrence, III, indiction XI, 33. To the duke of the Barbaricini, a blessing of Saint Peter, IV, 23. To Constantia Augusta, who requested the head of Saint Paul, he says that he would send a half-ounce from his chains if, when a priest passed a file over them, some dust should come away, because, by God’s permission, this is not granted to everyone, IV, 30. To Theodorus, a physician of Constantinople, an anathema [reading uncertain] with two small Attic vessels, V, 41. To Childebert, king of the Franks, keys, VI, 6. To Theotistus, a golden key of Saint Peter, VII, 26. To Theodorus, a physician of Constantinople, a key of Saint Peter, VII, 28. To Narses, a religious man, four shirts, two oraria (stoles), and a boy, VII, 30. [Col. 1439] To Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, six small Aquitanian pallia and two oraria (stoles), VII, 40. To Leontius, former consul, a key, VIII, indiction I, 35. To Secundinus, a servant of God enclosed in seclusion, two books of homilies, a small garment, images of the Savior, the Mother of God, Peter, and Paul, and a Cross, as well as a key of Saint Peter, IX, indiction II, 52. To Arigius, bishop, and his archdeacon, two dalmatics, and permission for them to use them, IX, indiction II, 112. To Reccared, king of Spain, a small key containing iron from the chains, etc.; a Cross containing wood from the Lord’s Cross and some hairs of Saint John the Baptist, IX, indiction II, 122. To Palladius, a priest from Mount Sinai, a cowl and tunic from the blessing of Saint Peter, XI, 2. To the bishop of Clusium, whatever horse he could find, X, 45. To Adilbert, king of the English, he says that he sent gifts, but does not specify what they were, XI, 66. To Savinella, a key of Saint Peter with iron from the chains, II, 7. To Ecclesius, bishop of Clusium, he sent an amphimallum [a woolen garment], a tunic or breastpiece, XII, 46. To Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, a small cross containing a piece from the chains of Saints Peter and Paul, XIII, 42. To Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, and to Adalwald, Theodelinda’s son and king, he sent the acts of the synod held in the time of the emperor Justinian and phylacteries, which he calls a cross containing wood from the holy Cross of the Lord; readings from the holy Gospel enclosed in a Persian case; to the king’s sister, three rings, two with hyacinths and one with a white stone, XIV, 12. To Asclepiodotus, patrician of Gaul, a key containing a piece from the chains, etc., XI, 14.

## On Almsgiving and Care for the Poor of Every Rank

He had various poor people living in various places assisted from the patrimony of the Holy Roman Church through its defenders. He was so ready to help them throughout all the provinces that he ordered departing ministers to inquire and inform him who in those places were in need. If they neglected this, he rebuked them severely, I, 31, 46, 67; IV, 28; X, indiction II, 39. He assisted Cosmas, who was burdened by many debts, III, indiction XI, 58; IV, 45. He ensured that converted Jews would not suffer poverty, IV, 33. He thanked the physician Theodorus for money sent to the poor, IV, 31. He asked Libertinus, former prefect, not to regard it as an offense, saying that gifts from the property of blessed Peter the apostle, however small the offerings might be, should always be received as a great blessing, X, 31. He ordered one thousand measures of wheat to be given to Zeno, bishop, for distribution to the poor of his Church—or, if he could transport more, up to ten thousand, VI, 4. He arranged for food and clothing to be supplied to those doing penance, I, 18. He ordered that holy women be supplied not only with food but also with clothing and bedding, I, 24; VII, 26. He did the same for monks, an abbot, and other religious persons, II, indiction X, 1; V, 32, 38. He ordered properties to be purchased for the support of monks, X, 20. He helped needy noblemen with his alms, II, 32. For the celebration of the dedication of a needy Church, he ordered assistance in various goods to be given every year, I, 56. He ordered slaves to be purchased for the benefit of a parish, XI, 23. He wished necessities to be supplied to hospices through the defenders, XII, 38. To a home for the aged, beds and bedding, XI, 1. He ordered that the building of a very poor monastery be assisted, XI, 1. He ordered clothes to be purchased for those who were to be baptized, V, 3; VIII, indiction I, 1. He ordered assistance to be given to schismatics who had returned to the embrace of the Church, VI, 39; IX, 11. He ordered a slave girl to be redeemed so that she could enter the monastery, as she greatly desired, IV, indiction XI, 40. The faithful are to be preferred to unbelievers in almsgiving, II, indiction X, 46. He refused to burden the interests of the poor, but ordered something to be given to them, II, 32. To orphans who had lost their parents, he remitted the debt owed by their parents, III, indiction XI, 21. He ordered travel provisions to be given to those wishing to come to Rome, III, indiction X, 36. An elegant exhortation to good works and almsgiving: one’s desires should be fixed where whatever is repaid never comes to an end, XII, 7. What is given to the poor is not a gift but a loan, [Col. 1440] because what is given is undoubtedly received back with multiplied fruit, X, 21. Provision for grain is weak if it is not fortified by the help of piety, ibid. Concerning assistance that should be given to a poor orphan, IX, indiction II, 26, 40. What is received from illicit possessions must not be counted as almsgiving. “For whoever accepts wrongly with the intention of distributing it as though it were good is burdened rather than helped.” He speaks at length about almsgiving, IX, indiction II, 106. He ordered a bishop to give alms to poor people whom shame prevents from begging publicly, XI, 34.

## On the Redemption of Captives

He showed care and diligence in redeeming captives from various regions, VII, 26; IX, 17; and from his own funds, not only free persons but also slaves, VI, 35. He showed compassion toward them, V, 30. He ordered Christian slaves belonging to Jews and living at Narbonne, whom he could not free by legal authority, to be redeemed with his own money, VII, 24. He sent a priest for the redemption of captives, II, indiction XI, 16. He ordered a captive cleric to be redeemed by the Church in whose service he had been. “For it is exceedingly harsh,” he says, “if no remedy should come from the Church in which he serves,” IV, 17. A deacon had incurred a debt for his own redemption and was unable to repay it from his property; he entrusted it to the bishop to pay from Church goods, III, indiction XI, 41. He consented to the bishop of Fano, who had borrowed money for the redemption of captives, selling sacred vessels, VII, 13, 38.

## Those Whom Saint Gregory Commended
The poor—especially widows and other persons lacking assistance, afflicted, and burdened by every kind of need—he commended to the emperor, bishops, and all others, I, 50, 62, 64; IV, 15; VI, 17, 40; IX, 54, 69; X, 6, 47; XI, 14, 36, 77; XII, 5, 6, 37, 39. How he commended the defenders of the Holy Roman Church, I, 3; IX, ind. II, 20. And others to them, X, 13; XII, 36. He commended the apostolic responsales to the emperor, bishops, presbyters, monks, nuns, and all religious persons, so that those persons might provide them with help and favor before the emperor in all their affairs and needs, both on behalf of their churches and on their own behalf, I, 45; IX, ind. II, 80. To kings and other eminent rulers he commended bishops, the patrimony of Saint Peter, and various others, VI, 52–59; VII, ind. II, 21; XI, 8, 10, 14. Religious and lay persons to various bishops, VII, ind. I, 16; X, 12; XI, 9, 68, 70. He commended a certain cleric who did not know letters, both in matters pertaining to his spiritual care and in those pertaining to his temporal affairs, VII, 11. He commended noble men who were consular prefects to their superiors, and other illustrious men and women, VII, 3; X, 7, 48, 54, with the four following letters; XI, 17. Jews who had come to the faith, I, 71. Schismatics who had returned to the faith, IX, ind. II, 66. He commended oppressed poor persons to the exarch, I, 61. He says that his commendation is a protection of justice: “For,” he says, “I love people on account of justice; I do not set justice aside on account of people,” X, 51. He was cautious in his commendations, lest the Church’s patronage, through indiscriminate defense, should stain the reputation of the holy Church; rather, intercession was to be employed only to the extent befitting the Church, IX, ind. II, 27. He wished his commendations to be understood in such a way that, on their account, the Churches would not suffer any burden, IX, ind. II, 35. He refused to commend Bonitus, a glorious man, so that the administration of the prefecture might be entrusted to him: “For what is now thought useful,” he says, “will certainly afterward be full of toil and expense,” X, 26. He granted the defensor permission to approach the emperor for the relief of his provincials, asserting that he had commended him to the apostolic responsalis, XIV, 2.

## On Judgments

Not only did he refuse to revive matters that had never been raised, but he also hastened by every means to suppress those wrongful matters which he observed abroad, I, 9. If disputes could not be settled by arbitrators, he ordered them to be brought before him, XI, 11. He entrusted to the defensor the case of a woman harassed contrary to justice, to be settled by the judgment of arbitrators, IX, ind. II, 99. He urged the bishop of Syracuse to strive to ensure that a dispute which had arisen with [Col. 1441] another person should be decided by chosen arbitrators, IX, ind. I, 13. He ordered that the controversy of anyone who had a dispute with a church be settled by chosen judges, X, 27. He intended to inflict no injuries, but to bear even those already inflicted with equanimity, unless perhaps he was reasonably compelled to defend the affairs of the poor, lest he be found guilty before almighty God, ibid. He settled certain cases by means of an oath, ibid. He ordered that a dispute over ecclesiastical property between a bishop and a private person be settled either without quarrelling or through arbitrators, VIII, 58, 59. He entrusted the case between a metropolitan and his suffragan to be settled by the judgment of arbitrators, VIII, 14. He yielded something of his own right in order to settle disputes. “It is burdensome for us,” he says, “to litigate publicly,” III, ind. XI, 3. He confirmed their settlements. “Lest,” he says, “perhaps, under cover of some excuse, a renewed dispute should bring into doubt something that is contrary to religious purpose and equity, and should give rise to litigation out of peace,” VIII, ind. I, 11. Because of the different assertions of the parties, he says that he could not give a subtle response without first examining the truth, since the matter concerned the salvation of souls, not earthly possessions; but he wished to investigate the truth carefully, so that he might provide for the care of souls, VI, 61. He ordered a case that had long been prolonged to be settled without delay once the truth had been ascertained, X, 33; XII, 4. He ordered a dispute between religious persons to be carefully settled by judgment: “For,” he says, “it is a priestly responsibility that, when a dispute over earthly matters arises between religious persons, it should be brought to an end in such a way that contention cannot increase through delay,” XIII, 4. He took a case away from a bishop who was proceeding lightly and rashly, and entrusted it to the defensor, IX, ind. II, 23. He allowed no one to be condemned without a trial, X, 50. Concerning the need to dispose of the affairs of the poor with gentleness, III, ind. XI, 60, where he says: “Let it be known that we do not wish to decide cases concerning the poor with scandal or forensic uproar; but we wish you to know that our silence and patience must not create a precedent for future pontiffs in matters concerning the poor.”

## On the Competent Forum

He reserved the more serious cases to be examined before himself, I, 82. He sent a subdeacon to investigate certain persons committing offenses against a bishop, III, ind. XI, 1. He ordered an inquiry into the life and conduct of the bishop of Pisaurum; if anything were found that had stained the integrity of his priesthood, he wished it to be reported to him, V, 28. He wished cases and complaints against bishops to be examined before himself, III, ind. XI, 12, 36; XIII, 27. Such cases, he said, must be investigated with great care, IX, ind. II, 58.
