He reserved the more serious cases of bishops of the same province to himself; in other matters he wished them to be admonished through their metropolitans, II, ind. X, 35. A defensor is rebuked for bringing clerical cases before himself while disregarding the clerics’ own bishops; and he ordered that all should approach their own bishops. “For,” he says, “if each bishop’s jurisdiction is not preserved, what else is being done except that the ecclesiastical order is being thrown into confusion by us, through whom it ought to be safeguarded?” XI, 37. He entrusted the case of a person unjustly condemned to be reported to him, III, ind. XI, 27. He entrusted a dispute being conducted between ecclesiastical persons to be settled by an ecclesiastical judge; but if it was with others over whom ecclesiastical jurisdiction did not extend, he ordered that evidence be collected and sent to him, so that he might know what answer he ought to give, II, ind. XI, 38. He ordered that a sexual offense committed by a layman be investigated by a notary of the apostolic see, III, ind. XI, 41. He wished a serious crime to be investigated by the bishop and the local praetor, III, ind. XI, 50. He sent a bishop to investigate the irregularity of a fallen bishop, V, 7. A cleric, monk, or other ecclesiastical person could not be summoned, nor could an inquiry be conducted concerning them, except before their own bishop, VI, 11. A boundary dispute between two abbots was entrusted to the bishop, together with the defensor of the apostolic see, to be settled, VII, 39. He entrusted bishops’ cases to his counselors, to be reported back to him, IX, ind. II, 4. He entrusted a dispute between certain ecclesiastical persons to be settled, imposing perpetual silence and removing the possibility of appeal, IX, ind. II, 28. He assigned a tribune to assist the bishop before whom the case had been prepared, and wished the case to be settled by them, XI, 24. He ordered that the defensor not allow clerics to be summoned before laymen, but before their own bishops, XI, 77; XIII, 45. When a bishop was suspected, he ordered the parties to agree on arbitrators, or the defensor to appoint one, XI, 77. He entrusted to a bishop the case of another bishop who had been gravely accused by his own clergy, so that the charges reported to him might not pass unheard, XII, 28, 29. Gregory delivered a judgment concerning occupied Church property, XIV, 8. He protected bishops oppressed by rulers, and ordered that bishops detained by them be released and that their cases be examined before ecclesiastical judges, if they were being detained on account of some crime, I, 33.

## On Judges

“A judge’s action should be strict, and his speech gentle,” VI, 61. No matter and no power of persons should divert one from the pursuit of equity; relying on the Lord’s commands, everything contrary to certainty must be rejected. One must stand firmly in defending the cause of justice, and endure whatever hatred may arise on behalf of truth, so that the reward found at the coming of our Redeemer may be all the greater, in proportion as his commands have not been neglected but employed in favor of justice and its defense, VIII, ind. I, 13.

## On Arbitrators

The judgment of arbitrators must be enforced and treated as a judgment of law, I, 48. For the rest, see above under the heading “On Judgments.”

## On Procurators

He ordered that nothing be done before him without a legitimate mandate, XIII, 11.

## On Delays

He prohibited delay in settling controversies and lawsuits. “And,” he says, “this undoubtedly accords with both equity and vigor,” II, ind. X, 40. He ordered the bishop of Naples not to allow a person acting before his jurisdiction to be harassed by delaying tactics. “Lest,” he says, “we appear to have preserved these privileges for you for the fatigue and harm of another,” VI, 11.

## On the Restoration of Those Dispossessed

He ordered the archbishop of Salona, under penalty first of deprivation of the use of the pallium and then of excommunication, to restore the archdeaconry to the man from whom he had fraudulently taken it; finally, once the latter had been fully restored, he ordered both parties to plead their case before him, II, ind. X, 17, 19. He ordered that ministries taken away be restored to their own Church. “For,” he says, “ecclesiastical property ought to be protected beforehand by due diligence,” II, 23. He ordered a bishop stripped of his bishopric to be restored to his former status, II, ind. XI, 6, 8; VIII, ind. I, 28. He ordered the bishop’s case to be examined in an assembly of bishops, III, ind. XI, 8, 9. And after removing the person who had retained possession, IX, ind. II, 113, 114. When a bishop deposed for a crime invaded and plundered the Church from which he had been deprived, he ordered him, under penalty of excommunication and perpetual confinement in a monastery, to restore everything; and he ordered an investigation into whether he could show that he had possessed those goods before obtaining the bishopric, and, if he had squandered any Church property, that restitution be made from those goods, XII, 28, 29. He confirmed the judgment rendered concerning the property taken away; and he ordered that one church be lent temporarily to those who had carried away relics with them, so that they could store them there, XIV, 7, 13. He restored a person unjustly suspended from sacramental communion, III, ind. XI, 26. He ordered that one unjustly harassed be absolved, XI, 24.

## On Oaths

“Where an oath has been given,” he says, “the agreement must be preserved, and one must not pursue temporal profits by violating it at the cost of one’s soul, lest one incur both the crime of perjury and fail to obtain the advantages wrongly desired,” X, 26.

## On Witnesses

“What sort of witnesses, or witnesses of what reputation, are to be admitted to give testimony, the many laws show,” he says, “laws that are almost unknown to no one; they also decree that the testimony of the most worthless witnesses should not be believed without bodily examination,” XIII, formerly LVI, now Capitular, 2, col. 1252.

## On Prescriptions

The prescription of eleven years is to be observed even against the Holy Roman Church, I, 9.

## On Sentences and Res Judicata

He ordered the sentence of the defensor of the apostolic see to be moderated by the local bishop, VIII, ind. I, 7. [Col. 1443] He entrusted the revision of a sentence against various bishops, VIII, ind. X; IX, 10. Sentences must be executed as soon as possible. Hence he maintained: “Just as we do not wish anyone to be condemned without a trial, so we do not allow what has been decided to be delayed under any pretext,” X, 50. He says, XI, 52: “No end is ever placed upon disputes if the fulfillment of what has been judged is delayed.” A penalty is established for the invader of a bishopric and for the bishops who ordain him, XIII, 45, and in the sentence of John the defensor attached to this letter. The nullities by which a sentence may be rendered void are explained there. He entrusted the revision of the sentence against a condemned deacon, and ordered that, if he were found to have been prosecuted unjustly, his seized property be restored and no further trouble be inflicted upon him. But if he should prove guilty, he ordered not that his property be seized, but that he be punished with a fitting penalty, XIII, 5. He entrusted the revision of the sentence deposing an abbot, so that, if he had been unjustly deposed, he might be restored, and the bishop who had deposed him might be rebuked with appropriate censure, XIV, 6.

## On Appeals

An appeal is made from a bishop’s sentence and from the burden imposed by him to the apostolic see, VI, 24.

## On Settlements

Confirmation of the agreement concerning a dispute between the defensor and a layman over property belonging to the Holy Roman Church. “For,” he says, “it is highly appropriate to ecclesiastical moderation that what has been arranged or decided should not afterward be disturbed by any opposition,” IX, ind. II, 57.

## On Emphyteutic Law

He forbids emphyteuses granted by him from being enforced unless they are clearly to the advantage of the Church, saying to the defensor: “For we do not remember having given anything without reason, nor do we intend to do so,” I, 72.

## On Wills

Bishops are executors of pious intentions, IV, 9; and he urges them to carry this out carefully and diligently, IV, 8. He altered the deceased person’s intention only concerning the place where a monastery was to be built, IV, 15. If the property left for building a monastery should prove insufficient, he ordered that this be reported to him, so that he might know what decision should be made concerning its construction, IV, 9. He entrusted the defensor of the apostolic see with reviewing a bishop’s will and investigating it, lest the Church’s property suffer any loss, V, 27. The defensor was to provide assistance so that gifts left to the poor might be distributed to them as soon as possible, V, 28. He ordered a bishop’s will to be examined, and declared invalid whatever concerned Church property or property acquired during the episcopate, but not property acquired before it, VI, 1. And he ordered that it be restored to the Church, VII, 21. He confirmed a bequest made by a bishop for the construction of a monastery, which he had previously promised him, VI, 1. He entrusted the defensor with carrying out the pious intention concerning the construction of a monastery, whose testator had appointed him and his predecessor as executors of the will, III, 37; ind. II, 24. He pressed that the pious intention be carried out as soon as possible by the person responsible for it, II, 32; X, 3, 5, 13; XII, 10, 37; XIII, 29. The bishop was to protect a monastery according to the founder’s intention and allow nothing to be done contrary to it, VIII, ind. I, 31. Religious persons do not have the power to make wills, but acquire property for the monastery, IX, ind. II, 7. He declared an abbess’s will invalid and void, although it was alleged that she had never wished to put on the monastic habit; this was to be attributed to the bishop’s fault. He assigned her property to the monastery, except for bequests to pious causes, IX, ind. II, 7. Since there was a shortage of monks, he ordered that a monastery for nuns be built instead of the monastery for monks that the testator had intended to construct, III, 37. What had been left for building a monastery that could not, according to the testator’s intention, be completed in that place, he reassigned so that the whole amount might be given to another monastery in need, XI, 25. He ordered a hospice to be built according to the testator’s intention; but if what had been left proved insufficient, he ordered the entire amount to be assigned to another hospice, XII, 10. He ruled that a woman could leave all her property to pious causes, provided that an adequate portion was first preserved for her children, IX, ind. II, 114. [Col. 1444] And he ordered the bishop, in his own name, to commend her children to her, ibid. He granted an abbot permission to make a will concerning the property he had possessed before his profession. Formerly IX, in the privilege or letter 22 to Probus the abbot, now in the appendix. He ordered that a servant of God not be harassed concerning property left to her by a bishop, which the bishop had acquired before his episcopate, XII, 37.

## On the Property Taken from Clerics

He ordered that property clearly inherited from one’s father before the episcopate be restored to the heir, IV, 37. And property acquired after the episcopate he adjudged to the Church of the deceased bishop, XI, 20; XII, 37. He ordered that the revenues of a vacant Church be given to its successor, II, ind. X, 13.

## On Accusations, Penalties, and Correction

He sent away a bishop who had been accused and then cleared, saying: “For just as it was right that, if he were guilty of anything, we should canonically punish his fault, so it was not right that, with innocence assisting him, we should retain him longer or afflict him in any way,” XIII, 6. He did not permit the clergy to come to the apostolic see against their bishop, but entrusted their complaints to the defensor for examination with four bishops, so that he might investigate them thoroughly and carefully and then report to him, enabling him to decide what should be done, IX, ind. II, 47. When something concerning the crimes of bishops had to be examined, he sought the details of each matter with the greatest strictness and caution, and promulgated his judgment with greater difficulty than ease, III, ind. XI, 8, 9. “It is sufficiently serious and improper,” he says, “to pronounce a certain judgment in a doubtful matter,” X, 29. Judgment must be carried out without favor or anyone’s goodwill, lest flattery soften it or shake it from the path of truth, XII, 30. “The head must be cared for if it needs correction, lest—God forbid—the disease begin to invade the whole body. For just as it is praiseworthy and discerning to show due reverence and honor to those who hold precedence, so it belongs to uprightness and fear of God not to postpone, through any dissimulation, whatever correction they may require,” ibid. Just as he scarcely or never left manifest crimes unpunished, so in doubtful matters he never pronounced a certain judgment, III, ind. XI, 45. He restrained laymen who inflicted violence upon vulnerable persons, III, ind. XI, 5. Once crimes had been heard, he never passed them over without investigation, even if the accused had regained the favor of the accuser, III, ind. XI, 29. “For,” he says, “if it is established that this was done not out of charity but for a reward, it must be punished with more severe correction,” V, 28; XII, 30. He declares that he wishes to avenge before the Lord the arrogance of John of Constantinople, V, 20. He rebuked a bishop who delayed inflicting penalties upon idolaters, VIII, ind. I, 18. He took precautions against the smallest offenses, lest greater ones be undertaken with impunity, IX, ind. II, 27. A bishop becomes a participant in guilt if he does not avenge crimes, or does not investigate them, or conceals them, III, ind. XI, 48. He deprived a bishop worthy of death on account of many crimes of his bishopric, II, ind. X, 6. He suspended a bishop for contumacy, II, ind. X, 19. Except in cases of crime, he deposed no one from the priesthood, but deprived them of sacramental communion according to the character of their offenses, III, ind. XI, 6. He entrusted the neighboring bishop with taking action against another bishop, III, ind. XI, 48. He entrusted more difficult offenses, which the bishop himself could not correct unaided, to be determined together with the neighboring bishop, IV, 22. Before condemning a bishop who did not observe the general custom of the Church, he ordered an inquiry into whether a privilege derogating from that custom existed, III, ind. XI, 56. He declared that he would take action against despisers of the canons, even if they were supreme prelates, such as the patriarchs of Constantinople, saying: “If I see the canons of the apostolic see not being observed, almighty God will grant me what I shall do against those who despise them,” III, ind. XI, 67. He ordered a cleric who had often been caught in wrongdoing to be subjected to corporal punishment: “so that,” he says, “according to the apostolic judgment, the spirit may be saved through the affliction of the flesh,” IV, 27. He complains that he cannot punish a bishop implicated in various crimes because of the emperor’s commendation. Nevertheless, he asserts that he will not obey the emperor in opposition to the recklessness of Maximus, the invader of the see of Salona, V, 21. When Maximus of Salona sought forgiveness after abandoning imperial patronage, he spared him, IX, ind. II, 67. And concerning his public penance, when Gregory heard it, he returned to mercy, IX, ind. II, 82. After the completion of his purgation, he wrote the same man a consolatory letter, IX, ind. II, 82. He spared the consecrators of Maximus when they asked forgiveness, VIII, ind. I, 10. Concerning those who seek the commendation of secular persons in order to obtain pardon, V, 34. He showed gentleness in avenging offenses, saying that wounds should first be felt with a light hand before they are cut away, IV, 21. He used gentleness joined with severity: “For,” he says, “it is more fitting for us to devote ourselves to mercy than to strict justice,” V, 52. “In doubtful matters,” he says, “it is better not to carry out strictness, but rather to incline toward gentler measures,” IX, ind. II, 23. Sorrow and joy in correcting one’s neighbor: one should rejoice over the correction of the crime but grieve over the brother’s fall, V, 58. A contumacious bishop was summoned and suspended from office, and he declared that the disobedient man would be punished more severely, VI, 3, 25. He exercised the greatest circumspection in avenging crimes; hence he remitted the punishment for an offense that concerned his own person, lest anyone, when others were punished for different offenses, suspect that he had acted because his authority had been offended, VI, 25, 26. He freed persons harassed by a contumacious bishop from various troubles and restored them to their former liberty, VI, 25. He recalled the clerics Romanus and Dominicus, who had left the city without his blessing, and kindly remitted their punishment, VI, 29. When greater evils are reported, they should not be believed unless proved, but once proved they should be avenged without delay, IX, 14. Proof and investigation are necessary in avenging crimes, following God’s example. “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has risen to me; I shall go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that I have heard, and I shall avenge it—or not, so that I may know”: is this not an example of this principle? VII, 14. A bishop is deprived of his bishopric by an archbishop, ibid. He entrusted the defensor with freeing a woman harassed by a certain Jew, with investigating the Jew, and with ensuring through those concerned that vengeance be exacted, so that God might be appeased and the matter might serve as an example of correction to others, VII, 44. One should deal more mildly with a person who readily confesses the crime committed, VIII, ind. I, 24. When and how an elder is to be rebuked, IX, ind. II, 1. And how the Apostle’s saying is to be understood: “Do not rebuke an elder.” One must also spare his age and simplicity, ibid. He entrusted the deposition of a bishop to be carried out before three or four bishops, IX, ind. II, 63. He ordered the presbyters and deacons who were accomplices to be investigated, and those found guilty to be removed from the rank of their dignity and thrown into a monastery to do penance, ibid. The lay accomplices, however, were to be deprived of communion except at the point of death, and to devote themselves to litanies and prayers, ibid. Just as much as the wickedness of offenders can provoke God to anger, so diligently must one strive to appease him through the strictest correction, IX, ind. II, 63. Not only the person who acts badly and not according to his dignity is found guilty, but also the person who does not resist evil, IX, 113. He was saddened by a bishop who was so negligent in punishing a sacrilegious offender that the report of the wrongdoing reached him before the correction did, X, 8. He ordered that vigorous action be taken against a layman who defended the person holding a nun extracted from her monastery, so that he would have her restored without delay; and if he delayed, he was to issue a public warning, so that he might write to the royal city concerning the punishment, X, 8. He did not allow the cases of the accused to be prolonged indefinitely, because, “just as vengeance appropriate to the accused must be carried out,” he says, “so acquittal must not be delayed for the innocent,” X, 40, 41. He orders that a person burdened by the defensor of the apostolic see be defended, and not allowed to be subjected to burdens or losses contrary to justice, XI, 19. The Church must not be abandoned because of the fault of those serving it, nor its usefulness neglected, X, 22. One ought to love persons and pursue vices, lest, if someone should choose to act otherwise, correction become cruelty and destroy those whom he desires to amend. “For,” he says, “you must cut away the wound in such a way that you cannot ulcerate what is healthy; lest, if you press the iron more deeply than the matter requires, you harm the person whom you hasten to benefit. The gentleness within you must itself be cautious, not lax; but correction must be diligent, not severe,” XI, 12. He ordered a subdeacon who had accused a certain deacon to be deprived of office, then beaten and sent into exile, XI, 71. No inquiry is to be conducted against a cleric without the elders of the Church, XIII, 44. “If anything concerning any cleric,” he says to Bishop John, “comes to your ears that could justly offend you, do not readily believe it,” ibid. Those who could not be punished in their own regions he ordered to be sent to him, V, 32. He rebuked the beating of free persons, X, 58. He ordered that the property of guilty persons not be seized, but that they be punished with a fitting penalty. If the person from whom the property had been taken was found innocent, he ordered everything restored to him, XIV, 5. He did not allow those who had pursued a bishop with hostility to remain unpunished, but entrusted the case and punishment to a judge, together with a subdeacon sent from the court for this purpose, III, ind. XI, 2. On public penance and correction, XIV, 16. It must not be considered lawful for superiors to rage against their subjects; therefore he entrusted the case between a bishop and the clergy who complained of the bishop’s misconduct to another bishop for investigation, XII, 28. He ordered a bishop accused of a very serious crime, and the accusers, to come before him, X, 50. In imposing penalties, he says, one must consider a person’s way of life, advanced age, prolonged illness, and every kind of affliction: for one whom divine discipline crushes, the addition of human scourges is superfluous, II, 34.

## On Calumniators

He ordered the authors of a false accusation brought against a presbyter to be excommunicated unless they proved what they had alleged, and the presbyter to be restored to his position, IV, 27. He deprived a bishop of communion for thirty days because he had condemned another bishop contrary to the laws and canons, III, ind. XI, 6.

## On Simony

The simoniacal heresy first arose against the holy Church, V, 53, 67; IX, ind. II, 106. He asserts that nothing should be accepted for the ordination of clerics, for marriages, or for veiling virgins, except from those who give voluntarily, IV, 27. He entirely prohibited the person being ordained or already ordained from giving anything for ordination, the pallium, or the *charitas* and *pastellum*. Formerly IV, 44; now in the appendix, in the decrees of Saint Gregory, 55, 58. “It is necessary,” he says, “that bishops not allow anyone to be brought to holy orders either for profit, through favor, or through the supplication of certain persons.” Condemnation of simony in holy orders; and concerning its evils, and the fact that what is acquired through simony accomplishes nothing even if it is distributed to the poor, IX, ind. II, 106. Simony was flourishing in ordinations in Gaul and Germany in Saint Gregory’s time, V, 53, where there is an extensive discussion against simony, 55, 58. Detestation of simoniacal greed, XI, 40, 49, 50. What it means to “enter through the door,” XI, 46. In Saint Gregory’s time, in the churches of the East, almost no one was reported to reach holy orders except by giving rewards, XI, 46. Simony must be eradicated: for this caused the holiness of the ecclesiastical order to fall among many. Since persons are brought to orders not on account of their life and conduct but for rewards, XIII, 41. He ordered that a bishop who conferred orders through simony, and the person who received them, be struck by canonical punishment, XII, 28. The ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion and uprightness of life is despised if an unworthy person receives the reward of merit, ibid.

## On Heretics

It is a great grace of almighty God that among heretics themselves there is no unity, because they are divided from the teaching of the holy Church; for “every kingdom divided against itself will not stand,” VIII, ind. I, 2. The holy Church is always instructed more subtly in its teaching when it is attacked by the questions of heretics, so that what is said through the Psalm is plainly fulfilled: “They were divided from the anger of his face, and his heart drew near.” For while they themselves are divided in their perverse error, God’s heart draws near to us; because, instructed by adversities, we discover his meaning more subtly, VIII, ind. I, 2. Heretics strike themselves, because, while they speak against the solidity of truth, they rebound broken, as though the edge of a sword, when it strikes a stone, were shattered and recoiled, ibid. Heresy must be uprooted like weeds, I, 77. It is the bishops’ responsibility to hasten so that the harvest may be made free from every scandal of weeds, in order that the Lord’s field may bear fruit with a more abundant return, ibid. One must not communicate with heretics, X, 42. Heretics must be cut off, so that great profit may come from a small loss: the shepherd must know that he cannot preserve the health of the others except by removing this one, ibid. Heretics are not to be admitted among the household sheep until they have been healed, ibid. Heretics are worse than unbelievers: for it is a lesser offense not to recognize the truth than, after recognizing it, not to remain in it. For one thing is what is committed by someone who is in error, and another what is perpetrated knowingly, I, 16. He ordered the bishop of Aquileia, accused in a matter of faith, to come to him at the emperor’s command, ibid. He had the associates of heretics sought out with great diligence, I, 14. Those whose faith was doubtful, after first giving satisfaction to the bishop, he confirmed in the right belief and restored to the Church, ibid. He maintained that the Catholic Church ought not to use rites which, although good in themselves and containing no error, were used by heretics, lest they boast that they had overcome us in our custom, I, 43. He prohibited bishops who had fallen into heresy and then returned to the unity of the Church from being promoted to a higher rank, I, 77. He ordered a bishop who had been corrupted by a reward from the Donatists because he had permitted another to become bishop to be degraded, XI, ind. X, 48. One must keep watch against heretics, lest anything be lost; or, if anything should perhaps have been captured, it must be brought back to the Lord’s flock by the utterances of divine revelation, so that the Shepherd of shepherds may deign by his judgment to show that we have watched over his flock, ibid. He dedicated places assigned to the execrable errors of heretics to the reverence of the Catholic religion, III, ind. XI, 19. He urges the governor of Africa not to be negligent in restraining heretics, IV, 34. The sheepfolds must be fortified with vigilant protection, so that the lurking wolf may find shepherds opposing him everywhere and have no way to enter, IV, 35. He ordered a bishop from the region to come to him, so that, learning the truth from him concerning heretics springing up again through the negligence of bishops, he might decide what should be done in punishing such a crime, IV, 34, 35. Any good works are nothing if they are not done within the solidity of the faith of blessed Peter, IV, 38. He urges one who refuses to come to the apostolic see on account of the faith to come, IV, 43. He approves the actions taken against heretics and congratulates the bishop on the zeal he exercised against them, V, 5. He wishes the sentence against those who neglect to investigate heretics to be mitigated under penalty of loss of their dignities and of all their property, saying: “It is best, therefore, dearest brother, that in matters requiring correction outside us, internal charity should first be preserved, and that we be subject in mind,” ibid. Those accused of any heretical crime and found innocent he not only received but declared Catholic, VI, 13, 66. He examined matters of faith in a council, I, 16; VI, 15. He absolved a man condemned for heresy by the patriarch of Constantinople who had appealed to the Apostolic See, VI, 66. A man who read and kept a heretical book was condemned as a heretic, ibid. A man who read and kept a heretical book in his possession was absolved from suspicion of heresy after first making a profession of the Catholic faith, condemning the same book himself together with the heresies it contained, promising never again to read it, and asserting that he had read it simply, VI, 66. Formula of the document of profession of faith and abjuration of heresy, ibid. A man suspended on suspicion of heresy first made a general profession of the Catholic faith and then rejected the errors of which he was suspected, VI, 66; X, ind. II, 42. A bishop is censured because, in his synodal letter, he condemned a certain person who was not found to have been condemned by the four general councils, VII, 34. He corrected certain persons who asserted this heresy: that when Christ descended to the underworld, he released all who were held there, both the faithful and the unbelieving, VII, 15. Concerning those who act with misguided zeal, pursuing others as though they were heretics, XI, 45. He urged the bishop of Thessaly to receive a presbyter if he wished to abjure and publicly give satisfaction for everything charged against him, and to profess the Catholic faith; otherwise, he was to be regarded as excommunicated, XI, 74.

## On Schismatics and Apostates
## On Schismatics and Apostates

He first dealt with those who had withdrawn from the unity of the Church by exhortations and reasoned arguments, II, ind. X, 51. He promised to satisfy them if they wished to come to him, granting them safe-conduct; he said that he would receive them with the affection that was fitting and release them graciously, without any harassment, V, 51. Just as schismatics persisting in their perverse zeal are to be rebuked and denounced, so those returning to the bosom of Mother Church are to be consoled and strengthened, VI, 47. For converted schismatics, lest after their conversion they should succumb to some necessity, he provided that something from the Church should be allotted to them annually, VI, 47. Schismatics were not compelled by imperial command to return to unity, IX, ind. II, 10. In the time of Saint Gregory, schismatics, with the help of almighty God and through his own labor, hastened of their own accord to return, ibid. A schismatic bishop was first admonished to return under penalty of deprivation; because he persisted in his obstinacy, he ordered another to be ordained in his place, IX, ind. II, 10, 97. He ordered idol-worshippers, augurs, and diviners to be admonished by the bishop to return, and ordered the most severe penalties to be inflicted on those unwilling to do so, IX, ind. II, 65. He invited schismatics to return to the Church even by granting them property belonging to the Church, saying: “For we do not wish to allow those whom we await with longing to return to the bosom of Mother Church to excuse themselves on any pretext,” IX, ind. II, 53. A written formula of adjuration for a bishop who had fallen into schism. Formerly X, 31; now in the appendix. He took care, by the authority of the exarch, that converted schismatics should not be harassed by other schismatics, XIII, 33. He urged the exarch to devote himself to the conversion of schismatics, ibid. He praised a schismatic bishop who had returned, urged him to persevere, and assisted his needs. “Since,” he said, “Saint Peter, to whom you have returned, must not abandon you,” XII, 32. He commended and praised those who worked especially hard to bring schismatics back to the embrace of the Church, and at the same time exalted their virtues, IX, ind. II, 94–96. He ordered the excommunication of those Catholics who consented to have their children, slaves, or others under their authority baptized into the heresy of the Donatists, VI, 36.

## On Jews and Saracens

Jews were not to be baptized by force, but conquered rather by reasoning and the gentleness of teaching than by violence, I, 47. They were not to be persecuted, but admonished and persuaded with meekness and kindness to the unity of the faith, I, 35. Nor were they to be brought unwillingly; rather, such moderation was to be used toward them that they might be drawn to be willing and not resist. As it is written: “I will sacrifice to you voluntarily,” IX, ind. II, 6.

He recalled expelled Jews to their proper place, I, 35. He prohibited Christian slaves from serving Jews, III, ind. XI, 38; IV, 21. He called this a grave and execrable thing, VII, 24. He wished Jewish male and female slaves who fled to the Church for the sake of the faith—whether they had formerly been Christians or had then been baptized—to obtain freedom, IV, 9. Rustic people persisting in unbelief were to be burdened with so heavy a tax that they would be compelled by the distress of the oppression to come to rectitude, IV, 26. If Jews wished to become Christians, he arranged for something to be remitted from the taxes they owed, II, 32. He arranged through the subdeacon of the apostolic see for food to be supplied to converted Jews, lest they suffer from poverty, IV, 33. He ordered the Manichaeans to be restrained and urged to accept the Christian faith, V, 8.

He permitted something to be deducted from the taxes of Jewish peasants living on Church estates, so that they might be converted to the faith. “For,” he said, “even if they themselves come with less than complete faith, those born from them are already baptized among the faithful; thus we gain either them or their children,” ibid.

Slaves of Jews, whether Jewish or pagan, who became Christians under compulsion were no longer permitted either to be sold or to serve Jews; they were free. Regarding those brought from foreign regions for purposes of trade, he prescribed a definite time limit: if it was established that they had been brought in order to be sold, he wished a price to be paid for them; but not so if they had been brought in order to serve the Jews, VI, 32; IX, ind. II, 36.

He admonished the queen of the Franks that Jews must by no means be permitted to possess Christian slaves. “How contrary it is,” he said, “to honor the head and submit its limbs to be trampled by its enemies! [Col. 1449] For what are Christians if not members of Christ?” IX, ind. II, 109–110. Nor did he permit Christians to serve the Samaritans, VIII, ind. I, 21. Nor did he allow pagan slaves to be circumcised by the Samaritans, VI, 33.

His greatest diligence in the conversion of unbelievers is evident in his appointing Augustine as legate, with his companions, to England for the conversion of the unbelievers, VI, 52–55, 58–59. He ordered a seminary to be established in Gaul from English boys who were being sold, VI, 7. He sent monks to assist Augustine in the conversion of the English and commended them to various persons along the way, XI, 49–56. He sent fifty solidi for the purchase of clothing for those who were to be baptized, VIII, ind. I, 1. For the celebration of their baptism, he permitted, at their own request, that the solemnity of Easter be awaited. But if waiting for the Easter solemnity seemed too long, he ordered them to be baptized after a forty-day period of penance and abstinence, either on a Sunday or, if a highly celebrated feast should occur, VIII, ind. I, 23.

He showed great concern for baptizing Jews and wished to be informed carefully about what had been done concerning those who desired baptism, ibid. He ordered the privileges of the Jews to be preserved, VIII, ind. I, 13. He commanded that their synagogues not be taken from them, IX, ind. II, 6. He wished the bishop to pay them the value of synagogues that had been taken away and to restore their books and ornaments, IX, ind. II, 55. If a synagogue was so close to a church that the voices of those singing psalms, or anything visible in the church, seemed to cause offense, he ordered another place to be given to them for the synagogue, I, 10. He did not permit goods to be taken from Jews or for them to suffer contrary to justice, IX, ind. II, 54–55.

He ordered certain practices performed according to the rite of the pagans to be converted into the worship of the living and true God, lest those converted to the Christian religion be embittered. For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut everything away at once from hard minds. He gives the example of the sacrifices permitted to the people of Israel at their departure from Egypt, so that what they had offered to the devil the Jews might offer to the true God, XI, 77.

He ordered temples, after the idols had been destroyed, to be consecrated to God; oxen intended for sacrifice were to be slaughtered for religious banquets on the day of dedication or on the feast of the birth of the holy martyrs whose relics were placed there, and thanks were to be given to the Giver of all things for their fullness, so that, while some outward joys were preserved for them, they might more easily consent to inward joys, ibid. He permitted tabernacles to be made from tree branches around those same churches that had been converted from pagan shrines, and the solemnity to be celebrated with religious banquets, ibid.

## On the Restoration of Things Taken Away

He ordered a monk, together with the Church property of which he was the servant, to be restored to his master, V, 35. He ordered property that had been taken away and parishes violently occupied by a certain bishop to be restored without delay, VIII, ind. I, 28. He took care that Church silver held by a deacon be restored, IX, ind. II, 16. He ordered an estate of a certain monastery held by the Roman Church to be returned to the abbot, IX, ind. II, 20; XI, 30. He ordered a fugitive slave to be sought and restored, IX, ind. II, 102. He ordered an estate occupied by the bishop’s agents, and a boy unjustly detained by another Church, to be restored immediately, IX, ind. II, 126. He wished things unjustly detained to be returned, X, 1; XI, 18; and things unjustly taken away as well, X, 25. He also ordered a monastery to be returned to its patrons, after the heretics who had occupied it had been expelled, XII, 50. He ordered debts and wages to be paid immediately, VIII, 32; XI, 18, 49. He ordered boundaries taken away by the Church’s agents to be restored to the possession of a certain private individual, XI, 41–43. He instructed that the veils and books of a certain monastery be restored to the abbot, X, 14.

## On Sacrilege

He ordered sacrilege committed against a nun to be punished with the utmost severity, IV, 6, 9: the nun was to be thrust into stricter confinement as penance and devote herself to fasts and prayers; the layman was to be excommunicated; the cleric was to be deposed and confined in a monastery. He had sacrilegious persons pursued with the greatest severity, X, 8. He urged a duke to take strict action against a sacrilegious soldier who had abducted a nun, indicating that he was angry with him because the punishment, rather than the crime, had first reached his ears, XIV, 10.

[Col. 1450]

## On Usury

He did not permit illicit profits and did not spare even men of illustrious rank. Thus he charged the bishop of Naples to urge an illustrious palatine official to cease such illicit profits at another’s expense; if he did not cease, the bishop was to seek the aid of the city prefect, so that the man might be compelled to make reasonable restitution, X, 26. He ordered a nobleman to be urged not to expect profit from another’s loss, but, as befitted a Christian and a nobleman, to be more kind than severe and more merciful than strict, IX, ind. II, 38.

## On the Crime of Falsification and on Lying

He said that it was most disgraceful for a bishop to lie, and worse than failing to abstain from meat and other things, III, ind. XI, 53.

## On Diviners

He praised a notary who pursued enchanters and diviners, whom he ordered to be punished with strict retribution, XI, 53. He did not permit sorcerers to be left unpunished, but entrusted their punishment to the defender of the apostolic see, since the bishop, who had been prevented by death, had been unable to punish this crime, V, 32.

## On a Cleric Who Strikes

When a bishop ordered a certain woman to be cruelly beaten with clubs, he imposed two months of penance involving suspension from office, III, ind. XI, 45. He condemned bishops who wished to be feared through beatings. “It is a new and unheard-of preaching,” he said, “that demands faith by beatings,” III, ind. XI, 53.

## On a Cleric Who Curses, and on Matters Concerning Praise or Blame

A bishop should dispel the rumors of slanderers about himself by the testimony of his good works, VII, 14. It is shown to be extreme frivolity if anyone strives to believe serious evils that cannot be proven, ibid. In all the adversities that occur in this life, only the strict judgment of almighty God is to be weighed, as you know, and one must always return to one’s own heart, lest anyone’s tongue entangle us where conscience does not accuse, VII, 14.

No offense should be taken at slanderers, X, 15. When slanderers report something, they try to accomplish two things: to present themselves as faithful to those concerned and to make those to whom they report harbor wicked suspicions about others, ibid. He speaks elegantly about not troubling oneself over detraction, XI, 2. “In the words of human beings,” he says, “one should neither be saddened nor delighted. One must return to the mind amid the words of those who praise and blame: if the good that is said is not found there, one should be especially sorrowful; and if the evil is not found there, one should be especially glad.

“Slanderers are to be summoned and calmly admonished, and every possible means should be used to satisfy them. Knowing,” he says, “what Truth says about the Jews—‘lest we scandalize them’—if they do not wish to be satisfied by the truth, you have the consolation that you may see in the holy Gospel: ‘Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind,’” ibid. Peace is to be maintained with everyone, ibid. The conversations and murmurs of people are to be regarded as trivial, X, 61.

He excommunicated those who wrote defamatory pamphlets even against him and did not reveal themselves; but those who disclosed their error he absolved, VI, 31. Bishops and other superiors are not to be slandered. “For,” he says, “the deeds of one’s bishops or superiors are not to be struck down by the sword of the mouth, even if they appear rightly deserving of criticism. For when we sin against superiors, we oppose God’s ordering, by which he has placed them over us. Concerning them Exodus XVI says: ‘What are we? Your murmuring is not against us but against God,’” XIV, 17.

## On Canonical Purgation

He imposed canonical purgation on a bishop to remove every doubt concerning the crimes alleged against him and the unfavorable rumor, but only after an inquiry had first been conducted and no fault had been found, II, ind. X, 33. To dispel every suspicion and provide the fullest satisfaction, he absolved an abbot through canonical purgation, VII, 18.

## On Whether Those Who Have Fallen after True Penance May Be Restored to Honor

The property of those who have fallen is to be assigned to the poorest monasteries of religious communities, in which they are to perform penance, or to their legitimate parents, provided that the penitents are not from a clerical family or are not monks; nevertheless, sufficient support is to be given to the penitents, I, 44. Those who fall into sexual sin after receiving sacred orders must lose that order, IV, 26.

He very appropriately denied restoration of rank to those who had fallen, saying: [Col. 1451] “Nor is it fitting for you to petition on behalf of such persons, lest you appear—God forbid—to consent not to rectitude but to indiscipline,” IV, 40. He asserted that a person who had fallen could in no way either remain in or be restored to sacred orders, VIII, ind. I, 24.

He wished a priest who, after falling, had been removed from the order of his priesthood but later presumed to exercise the priestly ministry to be deprived perpetually of communion in the Lord’s Body, except at the point of death, and to remain in penance. If, however, he should be judged worthy of mercy during his penance, he left it to the bishop’s discretion to permit him to receive communion among the laity even before the end of his life, V, 7.

He believed that those who had fallen could return to honor after worthy satisfaction, IX, ind. II, 52. Those who had fallen, whether priests or deacons, were in no way to be restored to sacred orders, V, 16–17. There he gives the reason, saying: “The strength of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken when, in the hope of restoration, anyone is not afraid to conceive desires for wicked action.” And shortly afterward: “Lest it be believed that punishment of this kind is not decreed for them but merely postponed for a time.”

He decreed that fallen subdeacons should receive communion among the laity, V, 3–4. He judged that a fallen deacon who was an abbot, if his conduct in penance deserved it, should hold the first place among the monks, ibid. Gregory’s care and concern for fallen clerics, V, 4. He entrusted him with the care and administration of the monastery but did not restore the exercise of his order, ibid. A bishop who had fallen was deprived of his episcopate, I, 41.

## On the Sentence of Excommunication

He rebuked those who were excommunicated and publicly delinquent, and did not disdain to admonish them by letters and urge them to repent, I, 3. The sentence of excommunication must not be imposed as vengeance for a personal injury, II, ind. X, 49. The sentence of excommunication must not be imposed hastily or in anger, but with great circumspection, II, 34.

He ordered the ministry of sacred office to be forbidden to obstinate priests who refused to come after a second and third admonition, III, ind. XI, 56. No religious person should associate, in accordance with the canons, with those suspended from ecclesiastical communion, IV, 27. He absolved excommunicated penitents, ibid. He absolved a people from excommunication because they had communicated with an excommunicated bishop, VI, 26.

He ordered an excommunicated person who returned after violating ecclesiastical liberty to be absolved; Mass was to be celebrated in his house and his offerings received, VI, 43–44. He admonished those living nearby to avoid an excommunicated bishop, praised those who avoided him, absolved those who had communicated with him, and urged that this not happen again, VI, 27. He ordered bishops and other religious persons who communicated with excommunicated people to come to him for absolution, VII, 17.

He did not permit participation in sacred communion to one who persisted in excommunication, except at the point of death, VIII, ind. I, 7. A person excommunicated by his own superior should not be admitted to communion by another unless the case has been examined and it is found that he was unjustly excommunicated, so that neither injustice may prevail through the prolonged affliction of an innocent person nor the force of discipline be broken or dissolved through indiscreet presumption, IX, ind. II, 37.

He ordered a household deprived of communion because of its mistress to be absolved, X, 32. He ordered the counselors who had unjustly condemned a bishop to be excommunicated, IX, ind. II, 1. Those who are excommunicated are to be expelled from the thresholds of the Church, IX, 64.

He refused to absolve princes and very great men whose penance did not appear genuine, saying: “For if satisfaction has not been made to God, what can our release or favor certainly contribute?” IX, ind. II, 5. Those who say that if someone has been anathematized under compulsion of necessity he is not bound by the bond of the anathema bear witness against themselves that they are not Christians. Therefore they are to be despised in every respect and anathematized, so that precisely where they believe they are deceiving the truth, they may truly be bound in their sins, XI, 45. He calls excommunication separation from the peace of Saint Peter, IX, ind. II, 68.

## On the Primacy of the Roman Church and Obedience to It

The four patriarchs are subject to the correction of the Roman pontiff, IX, ind. II, 12, 59. He says: “I do not know of any bishop who is not subject to him.” A person ordained in the Roman Church does not have permission to depart from it thereafter, V, 38.

[Col. 1452]

The primacy of Saint Peter and the Roman Church is explained in those letters in which Saint Gregory complains about the arrogance of John, bishop of Constantinople, who arrogated to himself the title “Universal,” which had been offered to the Roman Church by the Council of Chalcedon, V, 20. He says: “Certainly, for the honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, it was offered to the Roman pontiff through the venerable Council of Chalcedon; but none of them ever assumed this title of singularity or consented to use it, lest, while something private was given to one, all priests should be deprived of the honor due to them.” See also V, 21, 18–19; VII, 33; IX, ind. II, 68.

Concerning the primacy of Peter and the Roman Church he says: “He himself exalted the see in which he also deigned to rest and to end the present life, and Peter sits in his successors. The see of Peter is in three places—namely, in the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene Churches—which constitute the unity of one Church,” VII, 40.

He says that there can be no doubt that the Church of Constantinople is subject to the apostolic see, IX, ind. II, 12. In cases concerning new heresies that have arisen, appeal is made to the judgment of the Roman pontiff, X, 35. There he says: “Let there be praise in the highest and glory to him by whose gift the voice of Mark still cries out in the see of Peter.”

Concerning a deacon-responsalis of the apostolic see concelebrating with the patriarch of Constantinople, he says: “My deacon ought not to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass with our aforementioned brother Cyriacus, because, through the profane title, he has either committed or is pursuing the fault of pride. Lest, if this proceeds—God forbid—we appear to confirm the vanity of a foolish name in one placed in such exaltation,” VII, 34.

The title “Universal” was offered to the pope by the patriarch of Alexandria, VIII, ind. I, 30. He enumerated the heresies that had arisen from the Church of Constantinople, V, 32; VII, 27. Saint Ignatius is common to the Roman and Antiochene Churches, as is likewise Saint Peter, V, 39; he asserts that we possess writings of Saint Ignatius beginning “Amen, Grace,” and so forth.

Appeal in matters of faith is made to the apostolic see, VI, 15, 66. Recourse is made to the apostolic see in cases against bishops, VI, 24. The patriarch of Alexandria sent someone to visit the pope, who urged him to unity with the Roman Church. “He said,” Gregory reports, “that he was bound by a certain special obligation toward the Church of Alexandria, since blessed Mark the Evangelist had been sent to the Alexandrians by Saint Peter, his teacher”; and he admonished him to read carefully his letters, to which he had not replied, VI, 60.

A synodical letter from a new patriarch is sent to the pope immediately after his election; in it he professes the Catholic faith, VI, 66; VI, 5. It was the custom of the apostolic see not to write to a new patriarch before his synodical letter had been delivered to the pope in his name, VI, 66. Saint Gregory replied eloquently to the synodical letter of the new patriarch of Constantinople concerning pastoral care, the preservation of charity, and the unity of the holy Church, VII, 5. He admonished the patriarch not to depart from the customary formula of the profession of faith, VII, 34.

He says that Saint Peter’s protection in the city is great: “In this city, without a multitude of people and without the aid of soldiers, we have for so many years, by God’s protection, been preserved unharmed amid swords,” VIII, ind. I, 22. He instructed the patriarch of Jerusalem to have a fugitive acolyte sought and, once found, sent to him, VIII, ind. I, 6.

The origin of the priestly order in Africa is from the apostolic see, VIII, ind. I, 33. Asked whether anything had been added to the ordinations of the pontiffs of the apostolic see after the most blessed man Hormisdas, he replied that the published ordinations of prelates extended up to the time of Pope Vigilius, IX, ind. II, 52.

Concerning the truth of the Church, he said to a woman who had married a schismatic: “Since it was not fitting for the wife of such a man to be separated even briefly from the unity of communion, you ought to have considered how great is the multitude of the faithful who remain in the bosom of Mother Church, and with what great virtues the priests who died in this faith have shone; or how many bodies still perform miracles. You ought not to judge them, but to believe such men and priests rather than yourself,” VII, 37. On the unity of the Church, and on the fact that those who stand within it contemplate the joys of the heavenly homeland, IX, ind. II, 52.

## On Bishops Visiting the Thresholds of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul

“It has been the custom,” he says, “for our brothers and fellow bishops from Sicily to come together at Rome once every three years. But, taking account of their labor, we have decreed that they should present themselves here [Col. 1453] once every five years. And since it has now been a long time since they came here, we wish you to urge them to celebrate here with us, God willing, the feast of Saint Peter’s birth.”

He ordered the same defender to inform the provincial governor of his command to summon the bishops of the province to the thresholds of the apostles, so that every suspicion might be removed and their departure not be impeded, XII, 22. He prohibited interference with those coming to the thresholds of the apostles, I, 74.

## On Councils

He ordered a provincial council to be convened against heretics, I, 74. At a provincial council, matters concerning the welfare of the province and the Churches are to be addressed; the needs of the poor and oppressed are to be relieved; those in error are to be admonished; and the excesses of the province are to be corrected. Hatred, envy, and discord must be absent, while concord and charity must be present. Finally, everything is to be conducted with maturity and tranquillity, I, 1; III, ind. XI, 48–49; IX, ind. II, 106.

He says that a council is to be held twice each year: “Just as this is said to have been the custom of your province and is prescribed by the authority of the holy canons, we wish you to celebrate councils of bishops twice a year, so that if anyone among them differs from the form of his profession, conduct, or character, he may be corrected by the fraternal rebuke of the community and, for the security of the flock entrusted to him and the condition of souls, may be dealt with by paternal circumspection,” IV, 9.

He permitted, according to the rules of the Fathers, that a council which was to be held twice a year be convened once a year without any excuse, IX, ind. II, 106; XIV, 17. Concerning compelling a council and its purpose, he says: “We wish the bishops to come together, so that a discussion may be held concerning matters that have arisen and a salutary conference concerning ecclesiastical observance, so that through this both past matters may be corrected and future matters may receive a rule,” ibid.

Concerning the usefulness of a council he says: “For often, even if not out of love of justice, people nevertheless refrain through fear of judgment from what everyone knows could displease the judgment,” IX, ind. II, 106. It belongs to the primate to convene a provincial council, III, ind. XI, 48–49. Once the provincial council has been completed, the primate of the province must inform the supreme pontiff of all its proceedings, III, ind. XI, 49.

Nothing is to be added to or subtracted from the Fourth Synod under penalty of anathema, III, ind. XI, 10; its faith is to be preserved intact, IV, 3; IX, ind. II, 52. He accepted the four synods as he accepted the four books of the holy Gospel, III, ind. XI, 10. A council conducted without the pope’s authority and against his authority is to be annulled, V, 18, 21; IX, ind. II, 68.

At a synod that has been convened, bishops must see to it that nothing is done against the canons, ibid.; there he asserts that he trusts the emperor will permit nothing contrary to the canons to be done in the council. He ordered the bishops of Gaul to celebrate a synod through a bishop and an abbot sent by him, who were to report its proceedings to him, IX, ind. II, 106; and that the proceedings, put into writing, be sent to him through the same bishop, IX, ind. II, 107.

He informed the king and queen of the Franks of everything he had commanded the president of the apostolic see concerning the council that had been convened, and urged them to assist this work of God, IX, ind. II, 109–110. The synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon were corrupted by the Church of Constantinople, VI, 14; VII, 34; IX, ind. II, 48. Copies of the councils are preserved intact at the apostolic see, XIV, 12.

## On Matters Concerning the Sacraments

In baptism all sins are forgiven, as illustrated by the departure from Egypt, XI, 45. Monks are not to receive infants from the sacred font, IV, 42. Those baptized by heretics are not to be rebaptized, but when they return to the bosom of Mother Church they are to be reconciled either by anointing with chrism, as in the East; by the laying on of hands, as in the West; or by a simple profession of faith. If they had not been baptized in the name of the Most Holy Trinity, however, they were to be rebaptized, as in the case of the Cataphrygians; the Nestorians, on the other hand, were not to be rebaptized, XI, 67.

When there is doubt whether someone has been baptized or confirmed, and no certain proof is available either in writing or from witnesses, the person is to be baptized or confirmed, lest such doubt become a ruin to the faithful. For what is not shown by certain indications to have been rightly performed is not shown to have been repeated, XIV, 17.

Priests are to sign infants not on the forehead but on the chest, IV, 9. [Col. 1454] He permitted priests to confirm where bishops were absent, IV, 26. Priests throughout the dioceses were not to burden the bishop by signing infants, but were to observe the agreements made with him, XIII, 16.

In the desert there are other enemies who must be conquered by penance before one reaches the promised land, XI, 45. Penance is to weep over what has been committed and to avoid committing it again, XI, 45.

## On the Age and Qualifications of Those to Be Ordained

Boys are in no way to be admitted to sacred orders, lest they fall all the more dangerously the sooner they hasten to climb to higher things. There must be no venality, influence, or personal solicitation in ordination. God is offended if anyone is advanced to sacred orders not on merit but, God forbid, through favor or purchase, III, ind. XI, 48.

But, so that those who have been ordained may never perish, care must be taken over whom one ordains. It must first be considered whether their life has been continent for many years, whether they have had a zeal for reading, and whether they have loved almsgiving. It must also be investigated whether the person may have been married twice. It must likewise be seen that he is not unlettered or liable to civic obligations that would compel him, after sacred ordination, to return to public service, IV, 26.

No one is to be promoted to the subdiaconate unless he first promises continence, I, 44. Subdeacons are to be celibate; if married, they must either be separated from their wives or deprived of the exercise of their order, IV, 36. He restored to his former rank someone who had been promoted by force, II, ind. X, 17, 19. Those who have been ordained are not to be ordained again, II, ind. X, 46. If someone approaches an order with guilt, penance is to be imposed on him, but the order is nevertheless to be retained, II, ind. X, 46.

He issued a mandate for the promotion of a poor priest, IV, 14. In a church lacking ministers, he ordered clerics to be ordained at the request of the master of the soldiers, IX, II, 34. Men of sound faith are to be advanced to orders, XI, 46.

## On Laws and Constitutions

He declared that an unjust imperial law, although the emperor had caused it to be published, was nevertheless not to be observed, III, ind. XI, 62, 65. He approved a just imperial law, III, ind. XI, 65–66.

He professed that he wished to preserve the statutes of his predecessors and not revoke the good things they had done, which he considered shameful and disgraceful, II, ind. X, 52; III, ind. XI, 60. “If I were to destroy,” he says, “what our predecessors established, I would rightly be judged not a builder but a destroyer,” XIV, 17.

And in VI, 12, he says: “The order of justice and reason urges that those who desire their mandates to be observed by their successors should unquestionably preserve the will and statutes of their predecessor.” It is excessively harsh and especially hostile to the good customs of priests for anyone, under any pretext of reason, to strive to rescind what has been well ordered and, by his example, teach others in time to dissolve what has been established after him, VIII, ind. I, 14.

Concerning Pelagius, his predecessor, against the arrogance of John, bishop of Constantinople, he says: “Clinging in every respect to his rectitude with zeal, we preserve his statutes without opposition, God protecting us. For it is fitting that the one whom the tribunal of the eternal Judge awaits in that same place to render an account should walk with unhindered steps along the straight path of his predecessor,” IX, ind. II, 68. He ordered the civil and imperial laws and constitutions to be observed, XIII, 45.

## On Sacred Scripture

Sacred Scripture is God’s letter to his creature. He urges study of it, saying: “Apply yourself, I beg you, and meditate daily on the words of your Creator. Learn the heart of God in the words of God, so that you may long more ardently for eternal things and your mind may be kindled by greater desires for the heavenly kingdom. Its rest will be all the greater because now it has no rest from love of its Creator,” V, 31.

Concerning its usefulness he says: “I desire that you love reading Holy Scripture, so that, for as long as almighty God joins you to your wives, you may know how you ought to live and how you ought to order your household,” XI, 78.

In understanding Holy Scripture, whatever does not resist sound faith must not be rejected. For just as from a single quantity of gold some make chains, others rings, and others bracelets for adornment, so the various interpreters of knowledge compose from a single Scripture, through innumerable interpretations, ornaments of many kinds; [Col. 1455] yet all of them contribute to the beauty of the heavenly bride, III, ind. XI, 67.

The Roman manuscripts are much more accurate than the Greek, VI, 14. New manuscripts are not to be trusted, ibid. The words of Holy Scripture are not to be appropriated for human use. Thus he reproved certain bishops who applied the words of Psalm 117, “This is the day that the Lord has made,” and so forth, to the election of a new patriarch, VII, 7. He enclosed a reading from the holy Gospel in a Persian case, XIV, 12.

## On Custom

“In one faith,” he says, “a diversity of custom does not harm the holy Church,” I, 43. He ordered customs contrary to the Catholic faith to be uprooted completely like weeds, I, 77. He remitted customs that burdened the Churches, I, 66. He ordered the customs of the clergy, the Church, and the priests to be observed without hesitation, II, ind. X, X; ind. XI, 56. Bishops are to observe the customary practice toward their metropolitans, IX, ind. II, 8. He says that he restored ancient customs and established new and useful ones, IX, ind. II, 12. He prohibited new customs from being introduced against a monastery, II, 28.

## On Privileges

He granted a personal privilege to the bishop of Syracuse: as a delegate of the apostolic see, he was to hear and settle minor cases reserved to that see because of the distance across the sea; but he ordered major and difficult cases to be referred to himself, II, ind. X, 7.

He professes that he preserves the privileges of individual Churches, saying: “Far be it from me to violate in any Church the statutes of my predecessors concerning my fellow priests. For I do myself an injury if I disturb the rights of my brothers,” II, ind. X, 52.

He exempted a bishop from the jurisdiction of his metropolitan and entrusted the responsalis of the apostolic see at Constantinople with hearing his cases, both those already brought and those to be brought; but he reserved difficult cases to the judgment of the apostolic see, III, ind. XI, 7.

Anyone alleging a privilege against the general custom of the Church must explain it, III, ind. XI, 56; VIII, ind. I, 28; IX, ind. II, 112. Despite opposition from the Roman clergy, he granted the use of small handkerchiefs exclusively to the first deacons of the Church of Ravenna, since only the Roman clergy had used them, III, ind. XI, 56.

Because of the insolence of the monks, he ordered the baptistery to be removed from their Church and an altar to be erected there, III, ind. XI, 59. He granted the bishop of Ravenna the privilege of using the pallium in litanies, contrary to customary practice, so as not to grieve him, V, 11.

He ordered the privileges of monasteries to be preserved, VIII, ind. I, 34. He also confirmed them, saying: “We who grant new privileges most willingly restore the old,” IX, ind. II, 111–112. He willingly granted privileges to monasteries of both sexes, to pious places, and to hospitals founded by laymen, especially by kings: “So that,” he says, “I myself might in some measure share in their goods,” XIII, 6, 8.

## On Relaxation and Dispensation from the Sacred Canons

At the request of the queen of Gaul, he refused to dispense a bigamist for sacred orders, saying: “Far be it that in your time you should permit anything contrary to canonical institution,” XIII, 6. He relaxed the degrees of affinity in England because of their coming to the faith, XIV, 17. He most strictly ordered the impediments of kinship to be observed up to the sixth degree, ibid.

## On Rescripts
He ordered all controversies or lawsuits to be concluded according to legal procedure, I, 59. Nevertheless, justice and equity were always to be preserved in everything, III, ind. XI, 34. Because of the difficulty of obtaining proof on account of the distance of the places, he entrusted the investigation of a case to local authorities, III, ind. XI, 36. He warned the person to whom the case was entrusted that, if he did not administer law and justice, he would bear the whole blame before God, ibid. He refused to entrust locally the case of an accused bishop, since the burden of proof rested upon the accusers, VI, 24. He entrusted the case of a bishop appealing to the Apostolic See to the defensor of the Apostolic See, IV, 37. He wished his rescripts to be understood as applying only when the petitions rested upon truth, and he wished to be informed if the facts differed from what had been reported, X, 32.

[Col. 1456] On the building and consecration of churches, and on their sacred vessels and vestments.

He united the Church of Minturnae, completely deprived of both clergy and people and reduced to desolation, to the Church of Formiae, I, 8. Because of the proximity of the churches and the scarcity of the population, he united the Church of Cumae on an equal and principal footing to the Church of Misenum, II, ind. X, 45. Likewise, he united the Church of Carina to the Church of Reate, VI, 10. He united the Church of the Treverenses [the cited letter reads “the Church of the Three Taverns”] to a neighboring church because of its desolation, II, ind. X, 50. He entrusted the Church of Tarracina to the bishop of Fundi, III, ind. XI, 35. Because of the danger of barbarian invasion, he transferred the episcopal seat to a safer place within the same diocese, III, ind. I, 11. He approved the building of a church near its people, VIII, ind. I, 1. He ordered an oratory to be consecrated with an appropriate endowment and a cardinal presbyter, XII, 11. He was concerned about the repair of roofs; accordingly, he ordered timbers to be cut for the churches of Saints Peter and Paul and transported to the sea, promising a generous gift in return, XII, 20, 21, 22, 23. He ordered money to be given for the repair of churches that were in ruins, X, 44. An oratory dedicated by a bishop in another diocese without the ordinary’s permission, in which he had also celebrated public Masses, he assigned to the ordinary of the place, XIII, 17. He established metropolitans and bishops in England, XI, 65. He specified what was to be prepared for the dedication of an oratory, XII, 11. He did not permit a church to be consecrated unless an adequate endowment had first been secured both for worship and for those serving in it, II, ind. X, 5, 12; VIII, ind. I, 4; X, 17, 66. Neither a baptistery was to be constructed nor a cardinal presbyter appointed, IX, ind. II, 70; X, 2. He ordered a church to be built on property belonging by right to the Holy Roman Church, for the benefit of that people, VI, 22. He permitted a church that had been burned and subsequently restored to be consecrated with the relics of the saints, VI, 45. He sent relics of the saints for the consecration of altars, VI, 49. He ordered the bishop who possessed them to give relics of the saints to Gregory, the former prefect, who wished to build a basilica in honor of those saints at his own expense, IX, ind. II, 25. In a similar case he gave the same instruction to the bishop of Spoleto and to others, IX, ind. II, 71, 72, 83; XI, 31.

Concerning the *brandeum*, which is sent in place of holy relics at the dedication of a church, he said as follows, IV, 30:

> Let the most tranquil lady know that it is not the Roman custom, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body. Rather, only a *brandeum* is placed in a small reliquary and set beside the most sacred bodies of the saints; when it is taken up, it is deposited in the church being dedicated with due veneration. Through this, such great miracles occur there as would occur if their bodies themselves were specially brought to that place.

Ministers of the Church were not to use sacred vestments except for Masses, VIII, ind. I, 27. He granted permission for a new church to be consecrated, XIV, 9. He confirmed the construction of a baptistery, XIII, 20. A church was to be consecrated provided that no certain evidence, whether written or testimonial, existed as to whether it had already been consecrated; the same principle applied to someone who had been baptized and confirmed, XIV, 17. He ordered monasteries to be built without delay, II, 32; IV, 15. He entrusted the repair of the churches throughout an entire province to the bishop, IV, 11.

## On the celebration of Masses

He permitted Masses to be celebrated in private houses, VI, 43, 44. He ordered that no mention of Maximus the transgressor be made in the Mass, VII, 17. Concerning the Martyrology used by the Roman Church, he says:

> Apart from what is contained in the books of the same Eusebius concerning the deeds of the holy martyrs, I have learned that there is nothing in the archive of this Church of ours or in the libraries of the city of Rome, except for a few items collected in the volume of a single codex. We, however, possess in one codex the names of almost all the martyrs, collected with their passions assigned to individual days, and every day we celebrate the solemn rites of Mass in their honor. Yet the same volume does not indicate how or in what manner each one suffered; only the name, place, and day of the martyrdom are recorded, VIII, ind. I, 29.

“Alleluia” (“Praise the Lord”) came from the Church of Jerusalem through the tradition of blessed Jerome. Subdeacons, stripped according to ancient custom, were to proceed in linen tunics. “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*) is not said according to the Greeks. The Lord’s Prayer is said in the Mass according to the tradition of the apostles, who consecrated only to this prayer, IX, ind. II, 12. Cantors were not to be chosen for the ministry of the sacred altar. Deacons ought not to devote themselves to modulation of the voice, in the Roman Synod, formerly IV, 44, now in the Appendix among the Decretals of Saint Gregory. During invasions he ordered litanies to be recited, saying:

> Every week, on Wednesday and Friday, you must unfailingly announce the litany and implore the help of heavenly protection against the attacks of barbarian cruelty, XI, 51.

## On feast days

Bishops ought to request the announcement of Easter from the metropolitans according to ancient custom, IX, ind. II, 8. He permitted leafy tents around churches and religious banquets to be held on solemn days, XI, 76. Those who preach that nothing should be done on Saturday are to be regarded as virtually Antichrists. On Sunday, washing the body out of necessity is not forbidden; washing for luxury and pleasure is always forbidden. “For,” he says, “everyone is permitted to nourish and care for his flesh; the contrary applies to lustful desires,” XIII, 1. On Sunday one must cease from earthly labor and devote oneself entirely to prayers, so that if any negligence is committed during the six days, it may be expiated by prayers on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, ibid. Saturday is called “rest”; but the true Sabbath itself is our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, ibid.

## On relics and the veneration of the saints

He took care that the relics of the saints be decently preserved, IV, 30. Where no body had been buried, he ordered that the relics be deposited, IX, ind. II, 15. He sought accounts of the miracles of the holy Fathers in order to write them down, and composed from them the book of the *Dialogues*, III, ind. IX, 51. At the request of the woman who was building a monastery of nuns, he ordered the relics of the saints to be deposited there with due veneration, II, 23.

Concerning the observance and veneration of the holy relics: he permitted the linen cloth of Saint Paul, whose chains could be filed by a priest, to be used so that those requesting a little of the filings might receive this blessing. “When certain people request it,” he says, “the file is drawn for a long time over the chains themselves, yet it is not possible to obtain anything from them,” IV, 30. He was exceedingly careful and guarded with the relics, and did not give them to those who requested them. The relics of the saints in the Roman Church are not touched; rather, only a *brandeum* is placed in a reliquary and set beside the most sacred bodies of the saints. This is regarded as taking the place of relics, and through it such great miracles occur there as if their bodies themselves had been specially brought there, IV, 30.

He sent aloes, incense, storax, and balsam to be offered to the bodies of the holy martyrs, IX, 52. He approved the possession of images of the Savior and of the saints, and sent such images. “Because,” he says, “you love him with your whole heart and your whole mind, you desire to have his image before your eyes,” ibid.

“We do nothing improper if, through visible things, we demonstrate invisible things. We ought not to worship the image of the Savior as though it were God; rather, as he says, let your love for the Son of God grow warm through the image of the one whose likeness you desire to see. We do not prostrate ourselves before it as though before the divine nature; rather, we adore him whom, through the image, we remember either as born or as having suffered, yet seated upon the throne. And while the painting itself, like Scripture, recalls the Son of God to our memory, it either rejoices our mind concerning the resurrection or soothes it concerning the Passion,” ibid.

Concerning the power of Saint Peter’s key he says:

> May you be defended through it from the Evil One, by whose sign you believe yourself protected, ibid.

He praised the zeal of a bishop who had broken and thrown down images of the saints so that nothing made by human hands might be worshiped, but he reproved him for breaking them. “For this reason,” he says, “painting is used in churches: so that those who do not know letters may at least read by seeing on the walls what they are unable to read in books,” IX, ind. II, 105; XI, 13.

Relics of the saints, when carried from one church to another, were not deposited anywhere except in a church, XIV, 7, 13. Saint Paul was beheaded at the Salvian Waters, and concerning his church, XIV, 14.

Concerning the relics of Saints Peter and Paul, he wrote to Brunhild, queen of the Franks:

> So that your praiseworthy and religious devotion may shine more and more brightly, you must see to it that the benefits of the saints are deposited with reverence and due honor, and that those serving there are burdened by no obligations or troubles. Otherwise, if some external necessity should arise, they might be rendered useless and sluggish in the service of God, and—God forbid—they might suffer injury and neglect because of the benefits bestowed by the saints, VI, 50.

When someone requested relics of the saints for the dedication of a church he had built, he delayed granting them, so that, “as miracles taught,” he said, “your love for the veneration of the saints might increase and the exultation of your joy become greater,” X, 65.

## On the immunity of churches

He took care that ecclesiastical liberty not be impeded, I, 61. He warned the bishops of Sicily not to suffer forced services or burdens from the defenders under pretext of the Apostolic See, and not to obey them unless he himself had written, I, 70. He instructed a bishop to promote ecclesiastical liberty, so that the clergy would not be oppressed by laymen, IV, 26. He did not wish anyone to be excused from guarding and keeping watch on the walls, whether for himself or for the church; nor did he consider the clergy exempt from the defense of the city in time of necessity, VIII, ind. I, 18. He ordered that peasants not abandon church holdings in order to undertake the cultivation of private persons’ lands, IX, ind. II, 64.
