He instructed a bishop to defend the property of his Church, which he did not wish to be burdened in any way; for this reason he sent him privileges and promised him the protection of the Apostolic See, XI, ind. II, 100. He said to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks:

> We have heard that the estates of the churches now pay taxes, and we are greatly astonished at this, if unlawful exactions are sought from those to whom even lawful burdens are remitted, IX, ind. II, 110.

He prohibited the sons of a defensor from contracting marriage outside the ecclesiastical estate, X, 27. He promptly entrusted to the defensor whatever was owed to religious places under public law, so that he might bring the persons concerned to court and render judgment concerning it, X, 28. A superintendent of the *Diaconia* was appointed, XI, 27. He acted against violators and invaders of churches, XIII, 6. He urged those residing within ecclesiastical enclosures to leave, X, 50. He ordered the defensor not to allow clergy to be dragged before laymen, but to have them brought before their own bishops, XI, 77.

## On the administration and care of ecclesiastical revenues

Concerning the revenues of the Church, he writes to the visitor of the Church of Ariminum that, according to custom, four portions ought to be made. One is to be provided for the clergy, another for the poor; of the remaining two portions, however, “we wish three portions to be made: one for the repair of the buildings; another to be sent for his support to Castorius, his own bishop; and the remainder to be retained by you,” V, 44.

He ordered that a fourth part of all ecclesiastical property—whether from past revenues or from those that would accrue—be distributed to the clergy according to canonical apportionment, IV, 11; VIII, ind. I, 7; XIII, 42; this also applied to the offerings of the faithful. He ordered the bishop, together with the defensor, to distribute the portion belonging to the clergy and the poor from the revenues of the episcopate, something his predecessor had not observed, XI, 34.

He ordered disputes with the Apostolic treasury to be settled, even to the treasury’s disadvantage. “For,” he says, “we do not wish not only for cases that have never been raised to be revived, but we also hasten by every means to settle those improper matters about which we are warned from outside,” I, 9, 13, 65. When he wrote to the defenders and other agents of the Apostolic See, he said that he had sent them there so that they might act in his place not merely for ecclesiastical interests but also to relieve the needs of the poor, and so that he might protect them more effectively from everyone’s oppression, I, 20, 55; II, 32.

He was so diligent in household administration that he took care that the Church’s purses not be polluted by unjust profits, I, 44, 82. He praised a defensor for breaking a false and unjust measure of grain, XIII, 34. He took care that the peasants be satisfied and that compensation be given to those who had been defrauded by unjust measures, ibid. He watched to ensure that tenant farmers and peasants were not burdened on the Church’s lands. He also took account of their children, treated those left by them kindly, and wished them to pay according to their means and with just weights, I, 44.

He praised an archdeacon who reproved his bishop for distributing Church property among relatives, II, ind. X, 19. He ordered bishops to prepare an inventory of all the property of every Church, movable as well as immovable, III, ind. XI, 41, 50. He ordered the same to be done in all vacant churches, IV, 11, and that the inventories be sent to him, IX, ind. II, 72.

During the vintage season he ordered wine from Church estates to be sold to the clergy, XIII, 44. [Col. 1459] He ordered that peasants be supplied by their own leaseholders with what they needed to borrow from others, so that they would not be burdened by those others, V, 8. He ordered peasants to obey the defensor, IX, ind. II, 19.

Concerning expenses to be given to defenders, he says:

> So that your Experience may suffer no want in meeting expenses, we wish you to meet all your expenses from the revenues of the Holy Roman Church that have been collected there under your supervision; and if anything remains, bring it to us when you come, V, 28.

He ordered that what had been paid for the benefit of the Church be restored to the person who had paid it, V, 52. He prohibited clerics from placing, on urban estates and rural ecclesiastical properties, titles by their own authority. Formerly IV, 44; now in the Appendix among Gregory’s Decretals.

He said that the patrimony of the Apostolic See should be devoted to the expenses of the poor, VI, 5. He ordered an English seminary in Gaul to be established from the patrimony of the Apostolic See, VI, 7. He gave a peculium to persons manumitted by the Holy Roman Church: to the one entering a monastery, so that it would belong to the monastery; and to the one remaining in the world, so that, if he happened to die without legitimate children, it would pass to the patrimony of the same Holy Roman Church, VI, 12.

He did not neglect, with every diligence, to recover the property of the Holy Roman Church. “The holders of it,” he says, “must consider whose property it is and to whom it is to be distributed—namely, to Saint Peter and the poor of Christ.” Concerning these matters he wrote to a certain bishop that it was exceedingly detestable for what had been preserved by kings of the nations to be said to have been taken away by a bishop, VI, 53, 55.

Because of poverty and old age, he remitted half the customary rent owed by a tenant for the duration of his life, XII, 9. He ordered woven chairs to be made and sent to him, XII, 19. He ordered the accounts of the Holy Roman Church to be calculated and settled without loss, XII, 15, 16. He ordered the property of a deserted Church to be preserved and brought to him, and established that the necessary supplies be furnished to any clergy who might have remained there, XII, 40. He wished the revenues of the Holy Roman Church to be collected everywhere outside Rome, but in such a way that whatever was returned would be received, XII, 42. He extended the time for repayment of money, XIII, 21. He ordered the interests of a monastery of nuns to be secured from its foundress by persuasion and gentleness, XIII, 47.

He encouraged the leaseholders of the Holy Roman Church’s estate in Gaul to be faithful and to act well, as befits the servants of blessed Peter, so that they might recognize whom they served. “For,” he says, “just as this title indicates a more illustrious household, so it ought to surpass the rest in the distinction of its morals,” V, 31. He also promised them that he would send to the king a man bearing letters of recommendation who would protect them, ibid.

## On whether ecclesiastical property may be alienated

He ordered ecclesiastical properties unjustly occupied to be restored, I, 73; II, 32. In order to recover Church property, he wrote to a defensor that he should first warn those concerned, X, 1. He took care that churches not be impoverished and ordered the defensor to recover property that had been alienated and sold, I, 64. He punished those who alienated it, ibid.

Because of poverty, he reduced the emphyteutic rent paid by a monastery of monks to a lower rent, II, ind. X, 1. He ordered a monastery of nuns to be established from the property of the Holy Roman Church, III, ind. XI, 17. He gave a servant to a councilor who had served the Church well, III, ind. XI, 18. He did not wish, through his silence, to cause prejudice to his successors in matters concerning the property of the poor. He spoke concerning the property of the Holy Roman Church, III, ind. XI, 60.

He ordered the rector of Sicily to gather up the Church vessels that had been seized and scattered throughout the province and restore them to their proper churches, while retaining with him an inventory of those vessels, IV, 16. He permitted a bishop to sell sacred vessels for the redemption of captives, provided that the transaction was carried out in the presence of the defensor, both for the bishop’s protection and so that the vessels would not be sold improperly beyond the amount necessary, VII, 13, 38; IX, ind. II, 17.

To a bishop who had removed certain things from a monastery under the pretext of a gift, he wrote:

> Your Fraternity has likewise been accused of having removed certain things from the monastery under the appearance, as it were, of a gift. Therefore, if you recall that you have accepted anything improperly from there, you must restore it without delay, lest the guilt of avarice severely condemn you, when priestly generosity ought rather to have shown you to be generous toward monasteries, VIII, ind. I, 34.

He took care that the property of a Church lacking a bishop and clergy be deposited with the defensor, IX, ind. II, 31, 32. He ordered the defensor not to allow any ecclesiastical right to be taken away from certain estates, and for their protection sent imperial privileges, X, 53. He wished Church property squandered by a bishop to be restored from the bishop’s own property, which he had possessed before his episcopate, XII, 29. He gave a small estate to servants of God established in a monastery because of an extremely serious necessity, XII, 44. An exchange was permitted when it was clearly beneficial, XIV, 3. He wished a garden belonging to the Holy Roman Church to be given to a monastery of the servants of God, II, 4.

In retaining or recovering Church property, strict enforcement was not to be observed when the Church was not burdened by relinquishing a wrongful claim and a poor person was mercifully assisted, IX, ind. II, 26, notably. In doubtful matters, it is better not to enforce strictness, but rather to incline toward lenient measures, ibid. He refused to grant possession of ecclesiastical property under the pretext of small leases. Because of dishonest scribes, he did not wish even a trustworthy man to be entrusted with ecclesiastical property, X, 64.

He gave the estate at the Salvian Waters, with all its farms, for the lamps of the church of Saint Paul, XIV, 14. The archdeacons of the churches resisted bishops who squandered and disposed of church property, as shown by the case of the archdeacon Honoratus against Natalis, bishop of Salona, II, ind. X, 19, 20.

## On religious houses

He urges a bishop to care diligently for the xenodochia, their correction, and the administration of their revenues, IV, 27. He was especially concerned with every kind of religious house; accordingly, he ordered the praetor to restore the proper allowance to the Neapolitan *diaconia*, X, 21. He ordered that a possession of the Holy Roman Church previously held by a person who practiced hospitality be returned to him without any rent for the duration of his life, so that he too might share in that good and praiseworthy work, XI, 21.

The immunities granted to a xenodochium built by the queen of the Franks and the bishop of Autun are set out, XIII, 8. He says that the care of venerable places belonged to him and that he ought to consider their welfare, IV, 19. Because the xenodochia were being neglected on account of the bishop’s old age, he appointed an administrator to care for them, XIII, 47. He assisted a home for the aged, XI, 1. A person who devoted himself more to the welfare of the xenodochium than to his own payment was reproved for levity, II, 32. He permitted money left by bequest for alms to the poor to be converted into the purchase of immovable property for the *diaconia*, V, 28. A transfer of citizens was to be arranged with the bishop concerning expenses to be provided for guests, X, 28.

## On burials

In a Roman pontiff’s funeral, he ordered that the body be carried without being covered by any cloth, in the Roman Council. Formerly IV, 44; now in the Appendix among the Decretals of Saint Gregory. Nothing was to be accepted for burials, VIII, ind. I, 3, except what parents, relatives, or heirs might voluntarily wish to offer for lamps, IX, ind. II, 37.

## A

Aaron carrying the breastpiece fastened to his chest by bands: what it signifies, 13. Aaron bearing the judgment of the children of Israel on his breast before the Lord: what this means, 14. *Abbas* means the same as “father,” 724, 997. The election of an abbot entrusted to the monks, 602, 603, 641. He is to be chosen from the congregation, 602, 603. Or, if no suitable man is found, from neighboring monasteries, 603. How carefully Gregory proceeded in choosing an abbot, 1194, 1195. What qualities are required in an abbot, 997, 1294. He is to be ordained by the bishop, 997, 1137. He must obey his bishop, 599. How an abbot should conduct himself in the monastery, 1091, 1098 and following. He must not neglect sacred reading and prayer, 626. Nor hospitality and almsgiving, ibid. He must be concerned for the souls of his brothers, ibid.—An abbot must not be one who, in any clerical church, holds a title belonging to any order, 691, 727. Many abbots are recorded as having been advanced to the priesthood, 496, 691, 729, 730, 1222, 1225. See *Monks*. An abbot advanced to the episcopate: why he ought to be deprived of the office of abbot, 1223. What an abbot acquires, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery, 1042. Whether abbots may make wills: See *Will*. Monks are not to be taken against an abbot’s will either for sacred orders or for the establishment of other monasteries, 604, 815, 906.—An abbot who has fallen from sacred orders is irrevocably deposed, but after penance he retains the first place among the monks, 729, 730. An abbot afflicted with a long penance because of negligence is restored, 732.—Abbates were sometimes required to guard the walls, 988.—In the Eastern Church, distinguished monks are called abbots, 725. Gregory aids an abbot who has been harassed and oppressed, 1048, 1049. The abbot of Mount Praeneste: See *Praeneste*.

What sort of woman should be elected abbess, 692. A virgin under sixty is forbidden to become abbess, 692. The Council of Trent permits a woman of forty to be elected, ibid. Being veiled as an abbess and being veiled as a nun are not the same thing, 692. Certain abbesses in Gregory’s time did not wear monastic dress, 931. They wore the garments of priestesses, ibid. The will of such an abbess is invalid, 931, 932. At the bishop’s request Gregory appoints an abbess over a monastery, 1074.

There was no Abel who did not have Cain as his brother, 1127. In Abel, it was not the gifts but the giver who pleased God, 1029. Abigail commendably concealed Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, but revealed it to him after he had sobered up, 58. What it means for the rejected to be brought back, 23. *Abner* is interpreted as “the father’s lamp,” 58. What figures he represents, ibid. Striking the pursuer with a reversed spear: what it signifies, ibid. An irregular monk is one who takes no care for his rule or for the observances of his state, 529.

Abraham receiving three angels and saluting one: what it signifies, 617. God had predestined Abraham’s seed to multiply through Isaac, 181, 184. Abramius of Alexandria sent by Eulogius to Gregory, 1069. Nothing can be hidden from God, 789. The absent are not considered estranged when their mind does not depart from charity toward either party, 659.

## Absolution

How one canonically purged of the charges brought against him is to be absolved, [Col. 1468] 864. In former times absolution was called the viaticum of penitents, 733. According to the ancient rule, penitents were not to be deprived of this viaticum, ibid. Absolution was also called communion, peace, and reconciliation, ibid. An old custom allowed those who postponed penance until the end of life to be denied communion, or absolution, once penance had been granted, 734. Absolution is of little benefit if satisfaction is lacking, 929.

Those who practice abstinence and who should be admonished, 61, 62. What merit belongs to abstinence, 62. Let the flesh be mortified by abstinence while the mind is directed toward the commandments of charity, 16. Abstinence serves chastity, ibid. Impatience lies in wait for abstinence, 62. And pride as well, ibid. Abstinence is commended only when accompanied by other virtues, 62. What it means to sanctify a fast, 62. Whoever separates abstinence from harmony praises God on the drum but not in the choir, 68, 880. Mercy toward the poor commends abstinence, 63. Abstinence approved by a miracle, 153. The body is worn down in vain through abstinence if the mind is scattered by disordered movements, 62.

## To abstain

Holy men abstain from what is permitted, either to increase their merits or to wipe away their faults, 1130 and following. He overcomes what is unlawful who abstains from what has been permitted, 977.

Abundius: See *Acontius*.

Accellus redeems Stephen for eight solidi, 1210. See *Stephen*.

What a lawful accusation requires, 804. The proofs in criminal accusations must be clearer than daylight, 707. The penalty of the evasive accuser who withdraws from the accusation, 780. If the accuser is not a legitimate one, the accused is not to be harassed, [Col. 1469] 847. Accusers are not readily to be believed, 860, 1238, 1249. What penalties are imposed on accusers who fail in proving their charge, 707. If an accuser does not have his proofs ready, he must suffer the penalties of a slanderer, 805. The persons of accusers must be carefully investigated, 1251.

The Acephali, enemies of the Council of Chalcedon, 615. Condemned by Pope Vigilius, ibid. The Acephali were Semi-Eutychians, 616. The Monophysites were called Acephali, ibid. Who the Acephali monks were, 529.

Acholius, bishop of Thessalonica and vicar of the Apostolic See throughout Eastern Illyricum, 487.

*Acolythus* means the same as attendant or apparitor, 900. Acolytes were sometimes assigned to spiritual offices, 894. Gregory orders that a fugitive acolyte of the Roman Church be apprehended and sent to Rome deprived of communion, 899.

Acontius, mansionarius of the Church of Saint Peter, a man of great humility and seriousness, 333. Called Abundius by some, 334. He heals a paralytic sent to him by Saint Peter, 336.

Acosimus, a Sicilian boy handed over to Theodore as a slave, 637.

*Acroama* is that which is received by the ears, 1031.

Acropolis, formerly an episcopal city in Lucania, 605. Felix, bishop of Acropolis, ibid.

*Actacae* are called the adornments or pleasant features of shores, 713.

*Actio* means the same as administration, 644. Action is signified by Martha, 491.

An *actionarius*, that is, one placed in charge of administration, 644, 1121. Actionarii and actores are the same, 122. Among jurists, an actionarius or actionator is a syndic who conducts the affairs of others before a judge, 595. Perhaps such men were tonsured, ibid. Other actionarii were those who conducted business under rectors, 595. They were for the most part slaves, but by tonsure they were claimed for freedom, 596. Public actionarii, 1183.

The active life signified by Leah, 491. An actor is called a curator of affairs, 497. When the plaintiff fails to prove his case, the defendant is acquitted, 597. See *Actionarii*.

The integrity of good deeds spreads through neighboring places like the light of a lamp, 560.

What blessings Adam enjoyed before the Fall, 372. He was deceived through the woman, 744. He became blind after sin, 372. Yet he did not suffer uncertainty concerning invisible things, 372. Through sin he died in soul, 802, 883. Adam’s descendants are compared to a child born in prison, 372. Through Adam’s sin all human beings died in soul, 883, 970. Through penance Adam returned to life, 883.

A diamond, hard against iron but made soft by the blood of goats: what it signifies, 53.

*Addicere*, that is, to condemn, 503, 570, 571, 726.

Adelphius, a heretic condemned at the Council of Ephesus, 802. The heretical Adelphian monks, 802, 803.

Adeodata complains to Gregory about her mother, Fidentia, 950. The illustrious Adeodata is stirred to despise temporal things and love eternal things, 1077. Relics are sent to her, 1088. She built a monastery on her own property, 1089.

Adeodatus, primate of Numidia, 659, 660 and following. His concern for ecclesiastical order is praised and encouraged, 903.

Adeodatus the priest, released by his bishop because of illness, requests restoration, 693.

Adeodatus, abbot of the monastery in which Romanus lived, 209.

Adeodatus, abbot of Naples, is appointed father of many monasteries, 1085 and following. It is decreed that his monastery be joined to the Craterian monastery, 1215 and following.

Adeodatus, deacon of the Church of Ravenna, 736, 819, 837.

Adeodatus, servant of God, 1216. His donation, made orally before he had undertaken the monastic life, is permitted and confirmed to be set down in writing, ibid.

Adeodatus, citizen of Pisaurum: by what law he appointed a guardian for his children, 756.

Adeodatus, 1186.

Adjacium, an episcopal city of Corsica, 1177, 1178.

Gregory asks that the family of Adorin be released, 571.

In Scripture, adolescence is sometimes called youth, 76. The wise man asserts that adolescence and pleasure are empty, 377.

Who the *ascripticii coloni* are, 700.

What place is called *ad sedem*, 1173, 1174.

Those who delight in flattery are represented by those who wear soft clothing, 1127. Flatterers are called allies of death, 524. They are to be regarded as greater enemies in proportion as they flatter more with praise, 743.

Adulouvaldus, son of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, and Theodelinda, 1270. Saint Gregory sends him phylacteries, 1270. How many years he reigned, ibid. He is expelled and dies by poison, 1271. Arioald succeeds him, ibid.

## Adultery

A rector is guilty of adultery when he strives to please Christ’s bride rather than Christ, 27. Why the fall of the flesh among nuns is called adultery, 688.

What adversity signifies in Gregory, 1049. The usefulness of adversity is compared with the danger of prosperity, 5. Adversity is sometimes useful, like a storm, 519. What adversity teaches us, 662. It is not the Creator’s anger but grace, ibid. Adversities occur by God’s beneficence, 78. Instructed by adversities, we understand God more subtly, 895. Adversity opposed to good intentions is a test of virtue, not a judgment of rejection, 1029. Those who live piously are not free from adversities, 876. How those worn out by the labor of adversity should be admonished, 78. How adversity should be endured, 1062. Those humbled by adversity should rejoice in the hope of the eternal inheritance, 78. We must neither be broken by adversity nor elated by prosperity, 662. Adversity should increase zeal for good works, 876. Confidence in God is then certain when, in return for a good work, some adversity is received in this world, 1128. Exceptional consolation for one who suffers adversity, 1233. See *Affliction*, *The Scourges of God*, *Tribulation*.

The adversary in legal proceedings should be admonished to come to hear the witnesses, 1255.

What the advocate of a case, the patron of a lawsuit, foretold through force and subtlety of mind when death was near, 409. Advocates were formerly not admitted to the clergy, 675.

He commits fraud against edification who conceals the good things he does, 95.

## The sick

What admonitions should be given to the sick, 50, 51. It is a crime to deny the sick the remedy we are able to provide, 74. To the sick person whom the physician despairs of saving, he grants everything he desires, [Col. 1470] 78. But one who is to be healed is prohibited from many things he desires, ibid. Illness is the scourge of God chastising his children, 50. Bodily distress is the health of the heart, ibid. How great a gift bodily distress is, 51. In treating illness, the physician considers the weakness of the patient, 98. Just as with bodily illnesses, so with illnesses of the mind: remedies that act promptly are beneficial, while delayed ones are harmful, 715. Illness is frequently granted for correction, 729. We who have sinned greatly through the indulgence of the flesh are cleansed through affliction of the flesh, 1114. See *Bodily infirmity*.

## Egypt

What it means for breasts to be subdued in Egypt, 82. What it means for the breasts of puberty to be broken in Egypt, ibid.

Aelius, archdeacon of Constantinople: how he was removed from office, 504.

## Bronze

Who is turned into bronze in the middle of the furnace, 52.

Aesina, or Aesis, or Auxima, a city in Picenum, 996. The visitation of the Church of Aesina is entrusted to Bishop Severus, ibid.

No one can desire eternal things without grace, 1077. Those things are to be sought which neither pass away once found nor fail once attained, ibid.

Aetherius was bishop of Lyon, not of Arles, 830. He is praised, 1141. Saint Gregory writes to him about abolishing simony, 1142. Concerning the privileges of his church, ibid. Concerning the writings of Saint Irenaeus, ibid.

Mount Etna in Sicily, 1055.

With what disposition afflictions should be received, 1087. In Christ’s affliction, the commandments should console us, 895. Because we suffer what was foretold, we ought to hope for what was promised, 895. In a time of affliction, the humility of God’s servants must appear, 599. The necessity of grace in affliction, 385. Through impatience, correction itself increases our sin, 385. See *Adversity*, *The Scourges of God*, *Persecution*, *Punishment*, *Tribulation*.

Why Africans are excluded from the orders, 600. Africa is afflicted by plague, 1087. In Africa, the dignity of the primate is attached not to the order of the place but to the antiquity of each bishop’s episcopate, 559. Saint Gregory attempts to abolish this peculiar African custom, ibid. The larger part of the African bishops opposed his effort, ibid. Nevertheless, he later permitted the custom to be retained, 561. Carthage was not subject to this custom, 559. The extortions of the African judges, 1095.

*Agapes*, or religious banquets, in churches, 1176.

An encomium of Pope Agapitus, 1303. When Agapitus was going to the Emperor Justinian in the regions of Greece, after offering the sacrifice of the Mass he healed a mute and a lame man, 284.

Agapitus, abbot, 1172. He complains of the harassment inflicted on his monastery, 498.

Agapitus, subdeacon, asks that oil be given to him as alms, 260.

The worship of Saint Agatha is extremely ancient, 547.

Agatho is elected bishop of Syracuse, 753. Agatho, bishop of Palermo, traveling to Rome, barely escapes a very severe storm, 469. After offering the sacrifice of the Mass, he saves a sailor from shipwreck, ibid.

Agatho, bishop in Sardinia, 932.

Agatho is received into a monastery, 827. He is not the man who later became pope, ibid.

Agathosa obtains the return of her husband, who had become a monk against his will, 1137, 1138.

Agathus, bishop of Lipara, deposed for crimes, 665. Gregory orders that his livelihood be provided from the property of the Church of Lipara, ibid.

What it means for a mound to be carried up, 31.

The conversion of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, to the Catholic faith, 114. On what condition he would not refuse to make a general peace, 762. Gregory foretells that he will not make peace when the truce has ended, 930. Gregory thanks him for the peace that has been arranged, 957. Why Gregory refuses to sign a pact with him, 1002. In what year peace was made with Agilulf, 1272.

Agilegius, notary, 610.

Saint Agileus, or Agilegus, suffered martyrdom at Carthage, 1182, 1183.

Agnella, abbess, 1005. Gregory urges Agnella to good works, 1185.

Agnellus, bishop of Fundi, 947, 1291. Driven from his city by enemies, he is incardinated at Terracina, 634, 635. Gregory writes to him concerning the transfer elsewhere of the synagogue of the Jews, 497. The visitation of the Church of Formiae is entrusted to him, 862. He is rebuked for negligence in punishing idol worshipers, 908.

Agnellus, bishop of Sutrium, 1287.

Agnellus, abbot, 856. He is encouraged to preserve regular discipline, 857.

The death of Agnellus, a monk of the Monastery of Saint Gregory, is foretold, 409.

Agnellus, notary of the Roman Church, 685. He violates Petronilla, a convert, and carries her pregnant from the monastery, 685. Gregory orders that his crime be investigated and punished, 686.

The error of the Agnoitae, 1065. The Agnoitae are called Themistians, ibid. The Agnoitae are a sect of the Theodosians, 1066. They are also Nestorians, 1070. The error of the Agnoitae is refuted by both Greek and Latin Fathers, 1065. And by Saint Gregory, 1065, 1069, 1070.

The Lamb: who sing the canticle to the Lamb, 83.

Ago, king of the Lombards, 683.

Agrigentum, a maritime city of Sicily, episcopal under the archbishop of Palermo, 557. Gregory, bishop of this city, came to Rome to be judged after being accused, 633. A fourth of the revenues of the Church of Agrigentum is granted to Peter, the visiting bishop, 737.

Bishops of Agrigentum: Gregory, 557; Eusanius, 717.

Agrippinus, priest of the Church of Faesulae, 1074.

Aigulfus, bishop of Metz, 1144, 1145.

The Alamanni invade part of Italy, 1061.

Albanum, a city of Latium, 633. One of the six older cardinal bishoprics, ibid.

Albinus, bishop of Formiae, 947.

Albinus, son of Martin the tenant farmer, 707.

Alcisson, bishop of Corcyra, 1261, 1266, 1271.

Alexander, praetor of Sicily, 1096.

Alexander, a magnificent man, 539, 1098.

Alexander, whom Gregory greets, 493, 877.

Alexandra, founder of the Neapolitan monastery, 1050.

Alexandria, a widowed woman commended by Saint Gregory, 823.

A special bond of charity between the Churches of Alexandria and Rome, 836. The Alexandrian see is called apostolic, 836. Why, 764. It is also called the Chair of Peter, 888, 889, 1065, 1069. Peter adorned the Alexandrian see, to which he sent Mark the Evangelist as a disciple, 888.

Bishops of Alexandria: Didymus, 1036; Eulogius, 1288. See *Index of Letters*.

Alfred, king of England, 1149.

Alger, a monk of Cluny: in what year he flourished, 107. He cites Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, ibid.

## Alien

Why evil spirits are called alien to us, 49, 74.

Aligernus, 1104.

In ancient times the Alleluia was not sung in the churches only during the fifty days of Easter, 939. Someone complains that Gregory had ordered the Alleluia to be sung in the Roman Church outside those fifty days, 940. In former times the Alleluia was sung at the funerals of the dead and during Lent, 939.

## To lift up

Who is cast down while being lifted up, 1027.

The soul of the righteous is the altar of God, 43. What the trench of the altar signifies, ibid. Formerly an altar was not consecrated without relics of the saints, 547, 548, 572, 577, 1176. See *Dedication*.

The Greeks have a single altar within each church, 828. The Latins have a different custom, ibid. Altars were the tombs of martyrs, ibid. Altars in private houses in Gregory’s time, 825.

## Height

What it means to be raised above the heights of the earth, 491. Who truly loves lofty things, 1030. Those standing on high should fear a fall, 83.

Alulfus, a monk of Tournai: in what year he flourished, 107. He wrote a book from all the works of Saint Gregory, ibid.

Amalfi, or Amalphis, formerly an episcopal city in Campania, now an archiepiscopal city in the Kingdom of Naples, 808, 809. The bishop of Amalfi was Pimenius, 808.

Amandinus, a priest and deposed abbot, is to retain the first place among the monks but is not to be restored to his former order, 730.

Amandinus, a *domesticus*, 1081. He was forbidden in a dream to write harsh words to Gregory, ibid.

Amandus, bishop of Sorrento, 1052, 1053. He is ordered to come to Rome, 1053.

Saint Ambrose fed consuls and prefects, 580.

Amanrius, a priest and a man of exceptional simplicity, 356. By laying on hands he heals all sorts of sick people, ibid. By the sign of the cross he kills snakes, ibid. He heals a madman, ibid. His name was entered in the martyrology, 356.

What “ambidextrous” means spiritually, 764.

## Ambition

Ambition and avarice are idolatry, [Col. 1472] 30. The mere crime of ambition is condemned by the strictest severity of the canons, 698. Ambitious men must be excluded from the office of shepherd, 3.

## Friend

What it means to go into the forest with a friend, 32. When we are heedlessly joined to friendships with evil people, we are bound by sins, 70. Friends who are at fault should not be humored but admonished, or even freely rebuked, 597, 598. How one should grieve over the loss of friends, 498. Everything should be discussed with friends, but first matters concerning the friends themselves, 524.

Amiternum, a city formerly in the province of Valeria, 164. Castorius, bishop of the city of Amiternum, 168.

Ammonia offered a house to the Roman Church by way of donation, 948.

Ammonius, a monk in Gregory’s monastery, 412. Gregory had learned from him what he reports about Armentarius, ibid.

Love arises from fear, 353. Love and power have a close kinship with each other, 873. See *Charity*, *Affection*.

## Love of neighbor

One must love one’s neighbor in God, and God in one’s neighbor, 540. Those who do good secretly and thereby allow others to form a bad opinion of them sin against love of neighbor, 95. Because of error, let us not hate the person; nor because of the person, love the error, 772. We must not despise our brothers, however poor and degraded they may be, 1129 and following.

Amos, patriarch of Jerusalem, 880. Fifty-eighth in order, 899.

*Amphimalum*, a garment hairy on both sides, 1211.

A glass flask thrown against rocks and not broken, 260.

An *amula* is a wine vessel or a small pitcher, 539, 540. Onyx *amulae* (wine jars), 539.

Anaea, a city of Caria in Asia Minor, 713.

Bishops of Anagni: Pelagius, 1291; Peter, 1287.

*Anagnosticum*, or *anagnosma*, is anything that is read or recited, 1031.

Ananias was punished by death for withholding money that he had vowed to God, 523.

Anas, or Anax, a kind of pitcher, 713.

Anastasius of Antioch must not be confused with the Sinaiite of the same name, 494. Nor with the younger Anastasius, ibid. Why this elder Anastasius was removed from his see by Justinian, ibid. Saint Gregory asks that his honor be restored, not his right, which he had not lost when unjustly deposed, 495. He retained the right, but it was obstructed, ibid. Gregory wishes to keep him at Rome, 495. Saint Gregory writes to him as ex-patriarch, as he does to the other patriarchs, 507. Gregory complains to Anastasius about the burden of pastoral care, 516. After Gregory of Antioch dies, Anastasius is restored, 507, 764. Anastasius is praised, 873. Spiritually, he used both hands in place of the right hand, 764, 765. Anastasius was poor in spirit, 896. Anastasius thought, together with the emperor, that it was not of great importance that the title “Universal” had been assumed by the bishop of Constantinople, 873. Gregory sends Anastasius the keys of blessed Peter, which shine with miracles, 517.

Anastasius, the younger bishop of Antioch: in what year he became bishop, 962. In what year and by what kind of death he died, ibid. Nicephorus’s error concerning this Anastasius, ibid. Anastasius is praised for the orthodox profession of faith, 962.

Anastasius, bishop of Corinth, 517. Saint Gregory, lamenting, informs him of his own ordination, 517, 518. Anastasius was deposed for crimes, 779. The administration of this deceased Anastasius is called the abominable plague of pollution, [Col. 1473] 787.

Anastasius, bishop of Interamna, 570.

Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica and vicar of the Apostolic See throughout Eastern Illyricum, 487.

Anastasius, bishop of Tibur, 1287, 1291.

Anastasius, a priest of Jerusalem, 879. He is praised, ibid. He is encouraged to settle a dispute between a bishop and an abbot, 880.

Anastasius, a religious man near Palermo, 596. Saint Gregory orders six gold solidi to be distributed to him, ibid.

Anastasius, notary of the Holy Roman Church, 180. He was a monk, 181, and governed the monastery with great holiness, 177, 181. He died when called from heaven, ibid. At the request of one of his monks, he obtained the death of that monk, 181.

Anastasius, tribune, 847.

Anastasius the librarian: in what year he died, 107. He is praised, 1192.

Anastasius, a physician, is forbidden to enter a monastery of nuns because of the many evils he had committed there, 733.

What difference there is between anathema and excommunication, 613. Not only a certain and manifest cause but also the consent of the archbishop or fellow bishops is necessary for anathema, ibid. The bond of anathema holds one who, even when compelled by necessity, has anathematized the matter for which he is reproached, 1130, 1132. See *Excommunication*.

Anatholius, a deacon appointed *vicedominus*, 498.

Anatolius of Constantinople deposed Aelius, the archdeacon whom he disliked, by promoting him to the priesthood, 504.

Anatolius, a deacon at Constantinople and Saint Gregory’s *apocrisiarius*, 878, 879, 1096. See *Index of Letters*.

Anatolius of Alexandria, an educated man: in what period he flourished, 1036, 1037. The Scots and Saint Columbanus followed his canons concerning Easter, 1038.

Ancona, formerly a city of suburban Picenum and still an episcopal city, 943. The Church of Ancona, 1269. The bishop of Ancona was Serenus, or Severus, 943.

Angers, 1146. The bishop of this city was Licinius, ibid.

The Monastery of Saint Andochius at Autun, 1219.

The Monastery of Saint Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, built by Saint Gregory in his own house, 902, 903, 1124. There the holy Apostle performs many miracles, ibid. and following. In favor of this monastery Saint Gregory confirms a transaction, 903.

Andreas, bishop of Albano, 1287.

Andreas, bishop of Fundi, 289. By imprudently keeping a nun in the episcopal residence, he is troubled by carnal temptation, ibid. Warned by a Jew who had learned of the matter in a vision, he is freed from danger, 292. He baptizes the Jew himself, ibid.

Andreas, first a muleteer, then a deacon, and afterward bishop of the city of Aquino, 293.

Andreas, metropolitan of Nicopolis, 898, 983, 1265, 1266. Gregory approves his election as metropolitan, 796.

Andreas, bishop of Tarentum, because of suspicion of intercourse with a concubine whom he had had before ordination, must determine what he is obliged to do, 656, 657. He is suspended for two months because a woman was beaten on his orders, 656. Why Gregory received him late, 789.

Andreas, a deacon of Illyricum, 585.

Andreas, an enclosed monk and most wicked forger, 1174. He presents spurious works to Saint Gregory, ibid. He is condemned in a synod, 1296.

Andreas, an illustrious man to whom Gregory laments his own elevation to the episcopate, 519. Gregory sends him a key containing fragments of the chains of Saint Peter, ibid.

Andreas, a magnificent man, importunes Gregory to obtain the use of the pallium for the bishops of Ravenna, 837.

Andreas, a scholar to whom Gregory commends Castorius the chartularius, 775, and Marinianus of Ravenna, 777. Why Gregory refuses to commend him for obtaining secular dignities, 875. Gregory consoles him concerning his illness, 952.

## Dill

Why Christ reproached the Pharisees for tithing dill, 92.

*Angaria*, a Persian word, or a Latin word derived from *angere*, “to oppress,” 725. It signifies exactions, public services, and forced labor, 604, 724, 725, 735, 1003. It is also used for the provision of horses for the public post, 725. Hence *parangariae*, that is, forced services, ibid. *Angariae* sometimes signifies every kind of harassment and injury, 735. It is also used for service and ministry, 923.

The Angelici were formerly heretics who worshiped angels, 673. Who the Angellii were, 672. From where they received their name, 673.

## Angel

Angels are not equal, but one differs from another in power and rank, 784. The Apostle and the ancient Fathers did not condemn every form of veneration of angels, 673. When angels fell in part through pride, the elect stood all the more firmly because they stood more humbly, 308.

England was called transmarine Saxony, 1150. What Saint Gregory prescribed for establishing the English Church, 1150. And throughout the whole of Letter 64 of Book XI, 1163 and following, 1164, 1176. The division of the English bishoprics, 1164.

## The English

Gregory orders that English boys be acquired from the revenues of the Church in Gaul and sent to Rome to be educated in a monastery, 796. The Gallican bishops neglected the conversion of the English, 834, 835. Before their conversion the English worshiped wood and stone, 918. The English converted to the faith, 1110 and following. Miracles performed in this conversion, 1110 and following, 1148. English neophytes joined in prohibited degrees of kinship are not to be separated, 1155.

Angulus is a city of the Vestini in the Abruzzi, 444.

## Corner

What the lofty corners signify, 48.

The soul of the righteous is the altar of God, 43. Why pregnant women are called “souls of Gilead,” 72.—The origin of the soul is uncertain, 970. Errors concerning the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of bodies, 114. They are refuted, 115. Many doubt the immortality of the soul, 369. The soul can be called both mortal and immortal, 452. What it means that the death of human beings and animals is one, 376, 377. The death suffered by the martyrs proves that the soul is immortal, 381. The martyrs’ miracles prove it as well, 384. How the soul is said to have died through sin, 802, 883. The opinion of certain philosophers that one soul informs two bodies, 664. The soul sees through bodily eyes and performs the other vital movements through bodily organs, 381. The nature of the soul is invisible, 380. The soul’s life in the body is perceived from the movements of the limbs, 380. The life of the soul in the body is assessed from below; the life of the soul outside the body, from above, 381. In this visible world nothing can be arranged except through an invisible creature, ibid.—How an undisciplined soul is said to hunger, 55. The soul resembles a ship sailing against the current, 94. In how many ways the soul is led outside itself, 217. In a certain twilight of the mind we now see more concerning souls, 445. How the soul may trust in its own beauty, 1030. How it fornicates in its own name, ibid. How the soul descends from the place where it is more beautiful, ibid.

## The soul at death

The soul leaving the body can be seen by the eye of the mind, but only when purified, 384. Souls leaving the body have been seen, 269, 384, 385, 388. Sometimes the merit of the soul is not revealed at the moment of departure but after death, 404. Sometimes souls about to leave the body learn through revelation what is to come, 409. By their own power and subtlety, those about to depart immediately foresee something that will happen, ibid. Why, at the end of the world, so many things concerning souls become clear that were previously hidden, 445. Sometimes fear alone purifies souls at their departure, 453. Sometimes God strengthens the minds of the trembling through revelations, ibid. After death, souls often ask that the saving sacrifice be offered for them, 464. Souls about to depart can sometimes anticipate the Church not in a dream but while awake, 412, 413. A departing soul generally recognizes those with whom it is to be assigned to dwell, 425, 428. Why a ship appeared to a departing soul, and why it testified that it was being taken to Sicily, 428, 429. Why certain souls return to the body after departing, 429. Examples of some that returned to the body, 432.

## The reward of souls

For souls leaving the body, the reward of blessedness is granted to some and deferred for others, 408. The reason for this difference, 408. How, at the judgment, the souls of the saints will have two robes, 408, 409.

## The punishment of souls

The souls of the wicked are immediately thrust into hell after death to be tormented, 416. Immortal death, unfailing ruin, and the end of the condemned soul in [text uncertain] are one, 453. The condemned soul is called both mortal and immortal, 452.

## Care of souls

The art of arts is the governance of souls, 3. Why the care of souls should not be entrusted to young men, 213. Why it is not permissible to refuse the care of souls, 6. Those who have not learned cannot be guides of souls, 1009, 1014, 1017. What belongs to the soul must be considered more carefully than what belongs to the body, 1240.

What animals within a wall signify, 30. When the mind is divided among many things, it becomes smaller with respect to each individual thing, 172. The mind must be restrained amid miracles, 1112. Unity of minds: See *Charity*.

Anio, count of the fortress of the Abruzzi, 1187.

Anna deserved to obtain what she had asked because, after her tears, she remained in the same strength of mind, 473.

The more recent origin of annates and bulls by which provision is made for bishoprics, 700.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca: in what year he died, 107. He adduces testimonies from Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his collection of canons, ibid.

Ansericus, bishop of Soissons, 1288.

The Church of Saint Anthemius, devastated by enemies, is united to the Church of Nomentum, 638. This appears to be the bishopric of Cures in Sabina, ibid.

Anthemius, subdeacon of Campania, [Col. 1475] 506, 1103, 1210, 1235. He is called a defensor, 867. He is rebuked for neglecting the poor, 528. He is rebuked for not punishing a subdeacon who was a slanderer, 1171. How he should deal with negligent bishops, 1235, 1236. The various duties he performed at Gregory’s command: See the *Alphabetical Index of Letters*.

The Antichrist is called a condemned vessel, 71; the king of pride, 744. He will falsely claim to be God, 881. How harmful is the agreement between the Antichrist’s preachers and attendants, 71. An army of priests is prepared for him, 744. He who calls himself the Universal Priest goes before the Antichrist, 881. When the Antichrist comes, he will make both the Sabbath and the Lord’s Day be kept free from all work, 1213. For what reason, ibid.

*Antigraphus* means chancellor or notary, 519, 630. Greek: **Ἀντιγραφεὺς**, “one who dictates” or “a writer of rescripts,” 519. *Antigraphi* are also called masters of the archives, ibid. What functions the *antigraphi* held among princes, ibid.

## Antioch

Why the see of Antioch is specifically called apostolic, 764. Peter established the see in which he sat for seven years, although he was preparing to depart, 888. The bishop of Antioch holds the See of Peter, 894.

Bishops of Antioch: Anastasius the elder, 494. See *Index of Letters*. Gregory, 507. Anastasius called the younger, 962.

Antiquarii in monasteries, 169. The labor of the antiquarii is especially fitting for monks, ibid. In former times nuns also occupied themselves with the work of the antiquarii, ibid.

Antonia, daughter of the patrician Venantius, 1115. Saint Gregory consoles her concerning her father’s impending death, 1118, and promises his protection, ibid. He commends her to John, bishop of Syracuse, 1119. See Letter 78 of Book XI.

Antoninus, subdeacon and rector of the patrimony in Dalmatia, 639. The various duties he performed at Gregory’s command: See the *Alphabetical Index of Letters*.

Antoninus, defensor, 525, 593, 595.

Antonius, subdeacon in charge of the xenodochium at Rome, 949.

Antonius, a monk who yearned for eternal joys through daily tears, 453. Called again in a nocturnal vision, he died after receiving remission of sins, …

Ibid. The day on which his memory is celebrated, 456. Anysius, bishop of Thessalonica and vicar of the Apostolic See throughout Eastern Illyricum, 487. What it means to expose the wickedness of sinners, 17, 510. It is sometimes useful to disclose the troubles inflicted, 54. The imperial letters are called *apices sacri*, 540. They are also called principal commands and divine commands, 731. Gregory calls letters *apices*, 762, 836, 1096. The *apices juris*, that is, the strict letter of the law, 1097. There were also priestly *apices*, ibid.

Apollonius, commander of the army, 1076.

**Apostates.** A dragon encounters a monk who has left the monastery and is about to devour him, 256. What punishments from God apostate monks should fear, 523. Apostates are to be compelled and chastised to return to their own monastery, 530. See *Fugitive monks*.

The apostles are the first shepherds, 17. Why the Holy Spirit descended upon them in the form of tongues, ibid. The apostles are members of the Church, 743. They are called rams of the flock, 765. Although there are many apostles, the authority of the See of Peter alone grew strong on account of its primacy, 888. In the sixth century the Roman pontiff was already called “Apostolic,” 169. The Greeks likewise call him this, [Col. 1475] 170, 517. Many Churches are apostolic, but above all the Roman Church is called the Apostolic See, 517. In former times all bishops were called apostolic, and their sees apostolic, 764. Apostolic See: see *See*.

What *apparitor* means, 345. The possibility of nocturnal apparitions is established from Holy Scripture, 252. The apparition of Saint Peter, 333. Why those to whom apparitions occur sometimes fall ill afterward, 333.

Appeals to the supreme pontiff, 627, 628, 629, 933, 842, 1072. With what caution the case of those who appealed to the Apostolic See was to be examined, 1061. It belongs by right to the Roman pontiff to revoke the judgments of others, 1061.

Appeals to the emperor, 627, 629.

Apelles, heresiarch, 1168.

**To desire.** Those who desire what belongs to others are deprived more quickly of what is their own, 895.

The Appian Way, 1125.

Gregory greets Appion, 589, 724.

*Applicare* means the same as to accuse someone before a prince or judges, 998.

A chalice set as security, that is, pledged, 537.

Aprutium in Samnium is called Interamna, 1090. Aprutium Castle, 1187, 1188.

What it means to release water, 55. What it means to drink water from one’s own cistern, 73. What it means to divide waters in the streets, 74. What it means for giants to groan beneath the waters, 849.

Water miraculously drawn from a rock, 221, 224, 313. Water used in lamps in place of oil, 173. A river swollen by flooding reached the windows of the Church of Saint Zeno, but nevertheless did not enter, 325.

The use of lustral water, and miracles resulting from its use, 200. It was used in the dedication of churches, 1176.

*Aquae Salvias*, the name of an estate, 1273.

Aquae Sextiae, a city of the Gallic province, 832. The metropolis of the province of Narbonensis Secunda, ibid. Protasius, bishop of Aquae, 832.

Aquileia, formerly the most renowned city of the Carni and the metropolis of Venetia and Histria, 502. The origin of its patriarchate, ibid. Formerly afflicted by various disasters inflicted by the Goths and Lombards, it now lies abandoned, ibid. Its patriarchal see was transferred to Udine, ibid. Severus, bishop of Aquileia, 501.

Aquinum, an episcopal city on this side of Cassinum, 240. After Bishop Constantius and two successors, it was deprived of bishops through the hostility of the barbarians, 293. Bishops of Aquinum: Constantius, 240; Andreas, 293.

**To plough.** Because of the cold, a lazy man is said not to plough, 56. Africa, Sardinia, and especially Sicily ploughed for the Romans, 488.

Cultivators of trees are to be punished, 908.

The ark: whether it was made from incorruptible wood, 1133. What it means for a ruler, following the example of Moses, to consult the Lord concerning uncertainties before the Ark of the Testimony, 19, 512. What the ark containing the tablets, the staff, and the manna together signifies, 23, 514. What it means to carry the Ark by its poles, 34. What it means to coat the Ark with pitch, 850. The ark signifies the priest’s heart, 919. The holy Church is represented by the ark, 33, 850, 1113.

Archelaus, physician, 946. He is commended to the deacon Cyprian, 760.

*Archiater* means either the chief of the physicians or the physician of a prince, 713, 714. The manner of appointing an *archiater*, 714.

An archdeacon who had not yet been raised to the dignity of the presbyterate was called a priest of the second order, 563. He is also called a prelate of the second order, ibid. The custody of sacred things and the administration of ecclesiastical honors belonged to the archdeacon, [Col. 1476] 505. This was so in the West, but not in the East, 581. How the archdeacon was formerly below and above the presbyter, 582. At that time a presbyter was not permitted to perform the duties of an archdeacon, but a deacon was, 504, 581. Why a bishop is said to lower an archdeacon when promoting him to the presbyterate, ibid. An archdeacon in the Church of Salona was compelled to resign his office after completing five years, 1034. The wickedness of a certain archdeacon was punished by death, 288.

The honor of archbishops is called the use of the pallium, 518. Ordinations were attempted or carried out by archbishops in the dioceses of their subject bishops, but contrary to the canons, 578.

Archpresbyters in Gregory’s time, 931. The archpresbyter of Cagliari, 1260, 1161.

What an archive is, 916, 918. The Ἀρκειῶται were custodians of the archive, 918.

Aregius, or Arigius, or Aridius, seventh bishop of Gap, 1011, 1102. He was joined to Gregory by friendship, 1011, 1103, 1142. Aregius, patrician of Gaul, 833. His goodness and gentleness are praised, ibid. Gregory commends Augustine, his companions, and Candidus to him, 834. He also commends Hilary to him, 1024, 1025, and the tenants of estates throughout Gaul, 758.

Arles, an archiepiscopal city of the province, 542. The Church of Arles was never subject to the Church of Vienne, ibid. Paschasius is placed between Virgilius and Licerius, bishops of Arles, 541. The bishop of Arles has received the pallium from ancient times, 1156. Whether the bishops of Arles always exercised in Gaul the office of vicars and legates for the Holy See, 781. The privileges of the monastery of Arles, granted by Vigilius, were confirmed by Blessed Gregory, 1019. Bishops of Arles: Theodosius, 541; Virgilius, see the alphabetical index of the Letters; Paschasius, 541; Liberius, ibid.; Aurelius, 1019; Hilary, 1101.

Arethusa, a noble woman, is commended by Saint Gregory, 1103.

Mount Argentarius in Tuscany, projecting into the sea between the port of Hercules and Telamon, 320. From Mount Argentarius, a monk of venerable life restored life to a dead man, 320. He fled in order to avoid praise, 321.

Argentius, bishop of the Church of Lamia, had permitted Donatists to be placed over Churches, 567. Gregory orders an investigation into him, ibid.

Argentius, a tenant of the Roman Church, praised for his hospitality, 1105. He was rewarded with the gift of a small plot of land, ibid.

“May the Lord multiply silver for us,” 73.

The proportion of silver to gold, 648. In a pound of silver there were six gold solidi, ibid.

What ordinary silver is, 887.

The Arians baptized by two immersions in order to express their error, 532. The sons of the Lombards, baptized in the Arian heresy, are to be brought into the Catholic faith, 502. The Arian Church at Rome was consecrated as a Catholic church with the relics of martyrs, 341. During that dedication a pig was driven out of the Church, 344. Then, amid a tremendous crash, the demons departed, ibid. When the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, God’s presence was manifested, ibid. The Church that was to be handed over to the Arians appeared filled with pigs, 344. Churches occupied by the Arians were consecrated anew, 637, 638. An Arian Lombard bishop who was about to use force against the Church at Spoleto was struck blind, [Col. 1477] 341. The Church doors were opened by divine power, ibid. By what rite the Arians are to be reconciled, 1167, 1168.

What it means to place rams in a circle, 31. The apostles are called rams, and Christians the sons of rams, 765.

Arigis, second duke of Benevento, successor of Zotto, 609.

Arigius, bishop of Lyon and participant in Brunhild’s plans, deposed Desiderius of Vienne at the Council of Chalon, 831.

Arigius, bishop of Vaison: see Aregius.

Arioald, duke of Turin, succeeded Adaloald as king of the Lombards; in what year, 1271.

Ariminum, an episcopal city in the province of Emilia, 549. It is subject to the metropolitan of Ravenna and to the supreme pontiff, ibid. The people of Rimini are accused in connection with the illness of Bishop Castorius, 641. They are ordered to obey Leontius, the visitor, 642. The property of the Church of Rimini is divided into five parts, 774. Castorius, bishop of Rimini, 602. See his entry. A visitation of the Church of Rimini is entrusted to Severus of Ficulinum, 548, 549; to Leontius of Urbino, 641; and to Sebastian, 866.

Aristobulus, former prefect and *antigraphus*, administrator of the royal household under Maurice, 519. Gregory consoles him, ibid. He asks him, when translating his letters into Greek, to render not the words but the sense, ibid.

Ariulphus, duke of Benevento, after Faroald, 607. His savagery, ibid. Gregory orders that he be pursued from behind if he should make incursions into Roman or Ravennate territory, 570, 590, 591. Ariulphus, commander of the armies of Authari and Nordulf, asks that their *precaria* be granted to him, 607. He deceitfully swears peace, 1002.

Armenius, bishop, 943. Visitor of the Church of Ancona, 1269. Armenius, an orphan, is commended to a Roman patrician, 643, 644.

Armentarius, an illustrious man, 317. Armentarius, a boy of exceptional simplicity and humility, 412. Visions at his death, 413. In his vision he received the gift of tongues, ibid. He died after being seized by madness, ibid.

What it signifies when the priest, by divine law, receives the right shoulder and the separated portion for sacrifice, 15, 509. Why the breastpiece is assigned to the priest together with the shoulder, 15, 509.

Aroges, duke of Benevento and commander of the Lombard army, 1002, 1192, 1193.

How the arrogant person is an abomination to the Lord, 73. The affinity between arrogance and impatience, 43.

Arsicinus, duke, 549.

No art is presumed teachable unless it is first thoroughly learned, 2. The art of arts is the governance of souls, 3.

In former times artisans in large cities came together in guilds, 1058. This institution is attributed to Alexander Severus, ibid.

How unrepentant soothsayers are to be treated when they are free, and how when they are slaves, 982. One who observes soothsayers and diviners is excommunicated, 1293.

Asael represents the wrathful, 58.

What it means to ascend from the opposite side, 17, 510.

Asclepiodotus, patrician in Gaul, 1025. He is praised, 1102. Gregory commends the presbyter Candidus to him, ibid.

Asculum, an episcopal city of the March of Ancona, [Col. 1477] 1229. There are two cities of this name, ibid.

The stars are not rational spirits, 622.

Asylums were the enclosures of churches from which no one could lawfully be dragged away, 527, 909. They were called the Lord’s precincts, 527. What they contained, ibid. This immunity ceased because of abuses, ibid. It was not always observed in the same manner, 910. It belongs to bishops to protect these immunities, 1068. Those who had fled to the asylum of the Church did not leave until a promise had been made to them that they would suffer no violence, 1068, 1076, 1078. Anyone who violated the promise was excommunicated, 1079.

Athanasius, a presbyter of Isauria in the monastery of Saint Mile, 441, 842. He was accused of Manichaean heresy, 802, 842. He appealed to the Apostolic See, 842. He was absolved, 843. He was ordered to be received in his own rank, 664, 844. He is commended as orthodox, 852.

The remarkable flooding of the river Athesis, 325. Although its water could be drawn, it could not flow away, ibid.

An importunate bishop of Atella, 1577.

Attic vessels are so called from the region of Attica, where they were made, 713. Why the region of Attica received this name, ibid.

Auctioneers are those who sell publicly under the auctioneer’s spear, 535.

What *auctor* means, 1187. What *auctoritas* means among legal experts, 1044, 1045.

Audentius writes against the Manichaeans and other heretics, 1168.

Saint Augustine occasionally marked his letters with the inscription “servant of the servants of God,” 481. Why he did not wish to live with his sister, 977. What silence Augustine feared, 1051. Gregory praises his works, 1067.

Saint Augustine, a monk, is sent to England with companions, 829, 834, 835. When his companions lost hope and courage in the diocese of Aix, he returned to Rome, 834. Augustine is placed as abbot over his companions, 829. Gregory commends him to many bishops, 830 and following, 1170, as well as to the kings of the Franks and Queen Brunhild, 834, 835. He is ordained bishop by Virgilius of Arles, 782. Why he is said to have been consecrated by bishops of the Germanies, 918, 920. He is ordered to bring presbyters from Gaul to England, 834. He performs many miracles in the conversion of the English, 1110. He is fortified against pride, ibid. He baptized more than ten thousand English on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, 918. He is instructed to establish common life in his Church, 1151. He receives the pallium, 1163. He becomes primate of Britain, 1164. He is praised, 1165. No authority over the bishops of Gaul was granted to him, 1156. Concerning him and his companions, the monks, see the index to the Life of Saint Gregory.

Augustine, delegate of the Soapmakers of the city of Naples, 1058.

Augustodunum, a city of Gaul, 832. Formerly the chief city of the Aedui, ibid. It holds the first place after the Church of Lyon, 1013. From this it became the *protothronus*, 1014. Syagrius, bishop of Augustodunum, 1288. See his entry and the index of the Letters. Three monasteries at Augustodunum founded by Brunhild, 1219.

Augustus, *vicecomes*, 1196. Augustus, 1002.

Aurelia is conjectured to have been in Tuscany, 320.

Aureliana, or Aurelia, sister—not wife—of the patrician Dynamis, 858. Gregory exhorts her, devoted to good works, to perseverance, 885. He also consoles her, [Col. 1478] 1175. She was devoted to hospitality, 1176.

Aurelius, bishop of Arles, 1019. He subscribed to the Council; see the Council of Orléans, ibid.

Aurelius, a presbyter seeking the title of presbyter or abbot, is heard and commended by Saint Gregory, 1171.

What a gold solidus is, 189. A gold coin was sometimes called a solidus, 648. What gold in a priest’s vestment signifies, 15, 16, 509. Gold signifies excellence of holiness, 25. What it means for gold to be darkened, ibid. “May the Lord enrich us with gold,” 73. What proportion gold bore to silver among the Romans and Franks, 648. Gallic gold was of far lower value than Roman gold, 796.

The river Auser, diverted from its own channel, 293.

The Church rejected the austerity of Tertullian and Novatian, 657.

Authari, the Arian king of the Lombards, was struck by God and died, 502, 607. He forbade the sons of the Lombards to be baptized in the Catholic faith, 582.

Auximum, a city of the March of Ancona, 996.

**Avarice.** One whose mind is ravaged by avarice has an itching disease in his body, 12. Avarice, if not restrained in small matters, expands without measure, ibid. Avarice is the service of idols, 30, 1140. It is shameful to care more for money than for souls, 816.

The miser, like a bird, devours the food of earthly things and is strangled by the snare of sin, 65. Riches do not benefit the miser, ibid. The miser will be disinherited from the eternal patrimony, 66. What it means for the miser to weigh down the dirt beneath himself, 65.

What Axa sitting upon the donkey signifies, 353, 871. What her sighing and asking her father for earth indicate, ibid.

Azimarchus, scribe, 1085, 1189, 1190.

## B

**B.** In ancient monuments, the letter B is often changed into V, 977. Babylon treated, yet not healed: what it signifies, 52. The citizens of Babylon generally serve the citizens of Jerusalem, 923. Bacauda, bishop of Firmum, 490, 495. Gregory writes to Bacauda concerning the transfer of the Jewish Synagogue elsewhere, 497. Bacauda recalls to his own Church, in accordance with canon law, the clergy who had been driven from it by war, 723. What the staff signifies, 24. Balaam, rebuked by the Angel threatening the she-ass on which he was riding: what this signifies, 50. Balaam, the insane man, is reproved by a dumb beast subject to him, 51. Balaam changed his voice, not his mind, ibid. Balaam: a brief period of compunction, 87. The visitation of the Church of Populonia is entrusted to Balbinus, bishop of Rosella, 500, 501. Baldinus, bishop of Rosella, 1291.

Cicero’s bath, 164. The city of Balneum Regis, or Royal Bath, an episcopal city of Etruria, 1063, 1064.

Baptism completely removes sins, 1130 ff., 1131. The error of the Messalians concerning the effect of baptism, 802. It is to be believed that infants who die after baptism enter the kingdom of heaven, 400. What it means to touch a dead person after baptism, 87. Peter taught that repentance must precede baptism, 88. The ordinary minister of baptism is the bishop, 521. Formerly presbyters baptized outside the cities, and sometimes in the episcopal city [Col. 1479], but not without the bishop’s authority, 522. Laypeople had the right to baptize in cases of necessity, but did not ordinarily exercise it, 522. The practice of each Church concerning the administration of baptism is to be retained, 532. To express their error, the Arians baptized by triple immersion, ibid. The Fathers before Gregory appear to have taught that triple immersion was required by divine law, ibid. What is signified by triple and single immersion, ibid.

At what seasons of the year baptism was customarily conferred among the Greeks, 911. At what seasons among the Latins, ibid., 918. The constant custom of the Roman Church, 911, 912. The time was sometimes changed when a sound reason required it, 912. Why, and what sort of, repentance was imposed on those to be baptized, 912. Baptism is not to be repeated, 608. The scrutinies of baptism, 735. The ancient practice of baptizing Jews and unbelievers, 543. Formerly people were not admitted to baptism without great caution, 735. Baptism administered in the name of the Trinity even by heretics is considered valid, 822, 1167. Certain Fathers appear to have rejected the baptism of heretics even after the Council of Nicaea, 822. Whether those coming from heresy are to be rebaptized, 823. Baptism was formerly called the catechumens’ viaticum, and they were not to be deprived of it, 733. Baptism may be conferred on a pregnant woman, 1157, and on a newborn infant, 1158. The figure of baptism in the Red Sea, 1131. Baptismal garments, and their use and form, 729, 730, 893, 912. Gregory provides garments for those to be baptized, 729, 912. Baptisteries formerly existed only in cathedral churches, 321, 572. In many places infants are baptized in the cathedral church, 521. The form and decoration of baptisteries, 671, 809. The Eucharist was kept in baptisteries, and the relics of saints were deposited there, 809. A baptistery is not to be established in an oratory, 576, 577, 986, 994. Why it is ordered that a baptistery be removed from a monastery, 671. The blessing of a baptistery is entrusted to the bishop, 808. After constructing a baptistery, Bishop Honorius is permitted to use it, 1232. What it means to be baptized by a dead person, 87, 1132. Those whose baptism is uncertain are to be baptized, 1279.

Baraca, or Varaca, a sailor, is rescued from shipwreck through the sacrifice of the Mass that was offered, 469. Barbara, daughter of Venantius, 1115. Gregory consoles her concerning her father’s imminent death, 1118, and promises her his protection, ibid. He commends her to Bishop John, 1119. See Letter 78, Book XI.

The Barbaricini, inhabitants of Sardinia, 701, 702, 1106, 1108. Hospito, a Christian, ruled these pagans, 701. Barbatianus should be chosen as abbot if he is cautious and humble, 297. He is accused of excessive haste and imprudence, 1056.

Barbarus, bishop of Benevento, is appointed visitor of the Church of Hortae, 721, and of the Church of Panormus, 1227. Some consider him the third bishop of Teanum, 722.

Barce, formerly a city of Africa and the metropolis of Libya, 636. Today it is called Barca, ibid. It is corruptly called Baricis, ibid. Near the city of Baricis, captives were customarily exposed for sale, 636. Peter was bishop of this city, ibid.

The garments called *bardocuculfi* were once very well known among the Aquitani and Santones, 889. Baricis: see Barce. Barjona: what it signifies, 1036.

**Βασιλεὺς.** This name was attributed only to emperors, 278.

A basilica is to be endowed before it is consecrated, [Col. 1479] 571. Formerly Masses and processions were held in basilicas, 572. How a basilica of monks is to be dedicated, 1013. See *Dedication*, *Oratory*. The Basilica of Julius at Rome, 1302. The Basilica of Saint Mary, 1268. Saint Gregory takes care to restore the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, 1192, 1193 ff., 1194.

Basilius, bishop of Capua, 1047. In exercising the office of a forensic advocate, he was becoming degraded, 1048. Basilius: his zeal on behalf of the unity of the Church against schismatics is praised, 775. He was not a bishop, 776. Basilius the Jew, 953, 954. Basilius the magician becomes a monk, 164. His hypocrisy is exposed, ibid. Expelled from the monastery, he is later burned at Rome, 165.

A *batiola*, or *baciola* or *batiolica*, is a certain kind of small vessel, 536, 537.

Eternal blessedness is expressed by the right hand of God, 77. Blessedness gives joy to the elect, 416. There is one blessedness, but unequal recompense, 429. The greater the lack of rest here through love of the Creator, the greater will be the repose in blessedness, 712. Whether the righteous are distinguished from glory, 408. The blessed know nothing of ignorance, since there they know the One who knows all things, 425. *Beatitude* was a title of honor given to bishops, 1064, 1069, and elsewhere frequently.

Beator, count of the private estates, 1233. He is to be restrained when plotting perversely, ibid., 1234.

Bede, author of the ecclesiastical history of the English, 1149. In what year he flourished, 106. He calls Gregory the author of the *Dialogues*, ibid. What he says about a certain letter of Saint Gregory, 1150.

**War.** In war, amid the sin and peril of the parties, the blood of peasants—whose labor benefits both sides—is shed, 958.

The day of death of Saint Benedicta, a nun, is revealed by the Apostle Peter, 392.

In Sacred Scripture, *blessing* is used to mean a gift, 648, 712, 765; and so also in Gregory, 888, 917, 918. Gregory calls the cross in which a particle from the chains of Saint Peter is enclosed a blessing, 648, 659, 702. He calls almsgiving a blessing, 856.

**Saint Benedict.** His homeland and studies, 208. He despises the world, already almost dry like a flower, ibid. Having abandoned his studies, he flees Rome, ibid., 209. At a place called Enfide he performs his first miracle, ibid. He seeks the desert, 209. Clothed in a monastic garment by the monk Romanus, he hides for three years in a very narrow cave, ibid. On Easter Day he is visited by a presbyter divinely warned, 212. Afterwards by shepherds and nearby inhabitants, ibid. How he overcame a grave temptation of the flesh, 213. He becomes the teacher of many disciples, ibid. He is unwillingly chosen abbot, 216. He detects poison offered to him by the sign of the cross, ibid. He lives alone with himself, ibid. What the solitude of Benedict living with himself was, 217. Whether Saint Benedict could abandon the monks whom he had once received, ibid., 220. He builds twelve monasteries, 220. He frees a wandering monk, struck with a rod, from a demon, 221. He brings forth a spring from a rock, 221. He admits uneducated and ignorant people to conversion, 224. Like another Elisha, he draws an iron tool back from deep water, ibid. By divine knowledge he perceives Placidus in danger in the waters, 224. A contest in humility between Saint Benedict and Saint Maurus, 225. The priest Florentius sends Benedict bread infected with poison, 225. Benedict detects the deadly plot by divine revelation, ibid. Benedict yields to Florentius’s envy, 228. He mourns the death of his enemy, ibid. He moves to Cassinum, where, after overthrowing the idols, he builds oratories, 229. At Cassinum he also leads the inhabitants to the faith, 245.

By prayer he drives away the devil sitting upon a stone, 232. He dispels a phantom fire in the kitchen, ibid. By prayer he heals a boy-monk crushed by the collapse of a wall, 233. By the spirit of prophecy he foretells the future and sees absent things as though present, 233, 236, 237, 240, 245. He foretells the future and the time of death to Totila, king of the Goths, 240. He temporarily frees a cleric from a demon, ibid. He foretells the destruction of Cassinum, 244. He knows the hidden thought of a monk, 248. In a time of famine, two hundred measures of flour are found before Benedict’s cell, ibid. In a vision he lays out the regular buildings of the monastery at Tarracina, 249. What power Saint Benedict’s own speech possessed, 252 ff. He excommunicates nuns because of their lack of restraint in speech, 253. After their death he releases them from excommunication, ibid. Through the Eucharist he reconciles a boy-monk whom the earth was casting out, 256. He heals a boy of elephantiasis, 257. By a miracle involving coins, he frees a debtor from his creditor, ibid. He heals a man infected with poison, ibid. Saint Benedict’s generosity poured out upon the needy is rewarded by a miracle, 260. He rebukes a frugal and disobedient cellarer, ibid. He frees a monk from a demon, 261. He subdues Zalla, a savage Goth, 264. By his mere gaze he frees a bound man, ibid. He occupies himself with agricultural work, ibid. He raises from the dead the son of a certain peasant, 265.

Benedict was full of the spirit of all the righteous, 229. He performed miracles either by prayer or by power, 264, 265. His humility in performing miracles, 265. His holy contest with Saint Scholastica, 268 ff. He sees the whole world as though gathered beneath a single ray of the sun, 269, 384. He sees the soul of Bishop Germanus being carried into heaven, ibid., 272. Saint Benedict was distinguished by his teaching, ibid. He wrote a Rule notable for discretion and lucid in language, ibid. Saint Benedict’s Rule is praised under the name “Rule of Monks,” 1137. He taught no differently from how he lived, 273. He instructs the monk Martin to hold him not with a chain of iron but with the chain of Christ, 317. He foretells the day of his death, 273. Standing in prayer, he gives his soul back to God, ibid. At the very moment of his death, he announces his death to the absent brethren, ibid. Where he was buried, 273. After death he shines forth with miracles, ibid.

Benedict, a monk, young in age but advanced in character, 324. The Goths unsuccessfully attempt to burn him in his cell and in an oven, ibid.

Whether it is sometimes permissible to seek a benefice, that is, an ecclesiastical office, 1171. It is fitting that benefices be given not to men, but men to benefices, 857. For what reasons benefices are to be united, 495. Such unions are made in three ways, 495, 496. The union of benefices, except in the case of a bishopric, is permitted to bishops, ibid. Union of benefices: see *Unions*.

Clerics were formerly ordained by their bishop according to the canons, with the right to a stipend granted, 578. In Gregory’s time, minor benefices were conferred in another diocese, ibid. Bishoprics and abbeys were formerly granted to five-year-old boys, 659. What those who confer benefices should consider, ibid.

Benenatus, bishop of Misenum. The visitation of the Church of Cumae is delegated to him, 587. He orders that Cicero, a fallen monk, be restored to him as a servant of his Church, 761. The case of Bishop Benenatus is summoned to Rome, 964. He retains part of the silver given for the construction of a fortress, [Col. 1481] 964.

Benenatus is appointed in place of Peter to oversee the patrimony of the Roman Church at Palermo, 593. The case of Bishop Victor is entrusted to him for examination, 642, 643.

The bishop of Benevento, Barbarus, 721. See his title.

How the well-disposed are to be admonished, 45. A benevolent person should not be an idle praiser of benefactors, ibid., 46. Kindness is the companion of patience, 44. Kindness is not to be denied to one who repents, 1271. The severity of justice is to be tempered with kindness, 1265, 1266.

Berno, abbot of Augia: in what year he lived, 107. In his little book he cites some material from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, ibid.

Bertha, queen of the English, called Adilberga by some, 1112. She contributes greatly to the conversion of the English, 1113 ff. She is compared with Helena, ibid. She is encouraged to secure the king’s conversion, ibid.

Bethel. Concerning the death of the man of God who had been sent to Bethel, 405. Why the lion killed him but nevertheless did not dare touch the slain man, 408.

A bigamist, or one who has not taken a virgin as his wife, is not to be ordained, 704, 1220. Bigamists are excluded from orders so that they may not corrupt the sacrament, 622.

The garments called *bigerrigae* were once in use among the Aquitani and were of the lowest quality, 889. *Birrus* is sometimes used for a cheap garment and sometimes for an expensive one, 530, 929. By some it is used for a shorter cloak, ibid.

Byzacium, a province of Africa in which the kingdom of Tunis is now situated, 977, 1202, 1203. The council of the province of Byzacium is to investigate charges against its own primate, ibid. Crementius, primate of Byzacium, 693.

Blanda, formerly an episcopal city of Lucania, 605. Blandus, bishop of Hortae, is detained by the exarch and is either to be judged in a synod or sent back to his own Church, 521, 522.

Blera, formerly an episcopal city of Tuscia, 1210, 1211. Romanus, bishop of the city of Blera, 1291.

Blidin, one of the three men who always clung to Totila, 237. Bona, a cardinal, is praised, 1167. The abbess Bona is permitted to transfer to another monastery with her congregation, 650, 651.

Boniface, bishop of Ferentum in office and character, 184. While still a boy, he covered the naked with his own garments, 189. Through his prayers wine overflowed from vessels that were nearly empty, 185. He foretells the death of a jester, 188. He was generous toward the poor, ibid. Through prayer he obtains twelve gold pieces, 189. He foretells Constantine’s punishment for avarice, ibid. His humility in concealing miracles, 185. His various miracles, 189.

Boniface, bishop of Rhegium, is warned to keep his clergy in their office, 684, 685. He is reproved for seeking human praise in his good works, 626. Gregory writes to him to restore Stephania’s property, which had been seized by the agents of his predecessor, 655 ff. He is appointed bishop of the Church of Carinum, 799. His case with his clergy, 962.

Boniface, bishop of Piacenza, 1288. Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, 1149. Boniface, superior of the monastery of Saint Lucy at Syracuse, 625. Boniface, a monk of Gregory’s monastery, 341.
