Boniface, notary of the Roman Church, 654, 726. Boniface the defensor is commended to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch, and Anastasius, bishop of Corinth, 517. Boniface, defensor of Corsica, 1177. Notary of Corsica, 1234. He is called the first of the defensores, 1244. He becomes a deacon and is sent to Constantinople, ibid. He is called steward of the Church, 325, and chartularius, 1247. He is commended to the patriarch Cyriacus, 1246.

Boniface, a deacon, 545, 546, 682, 838. Boniface, a treasurer, 1189, 1190. He leaves part of his inheritance to a hospice, ibid., and 1191. Boniface, a distinguished man of Africa, 722. He is ordered to come to Rome to give an account of his faith, 723. Boniface, a man of illustrious rank, complains that he was unjustly deprived of communion by the bishop of Palermo, 643.

Boniface, a boy, fills by prayer with grain a granary that had been exhausted in almsgiving to the poor, 192. Another miracle of his, ibid.

Bonitus, fourth abbot after Saint Benedict; under him the Lateran monastery was built, 208. Bonitus, a defensor, 1206. Why Saint Gregory refused assistance to Bonitus when he was seeking the prefecture, 1198.

What sort of heretics the Bonosians were, 1168. Bonosians are to be rebaptized, ibid.

The good is to be loved for its own sake, not from fear of punishment, 52. Imperfect good does not help, nor does evil that has not been completed harm, 87. How those who do not even begin to do good are to be admonished, 93. How those who publicly do good but secretly do evil are to be rebuked, 95. By what arguments those who secretly do good but allow others to think badly of them are to be deterred, ibid. Many things appear good but are not, 196. He does good who helps those who wish to do good, 1022. It is a fault not to imitate the good that pleases us, 797. We ought also to imitate good things in those beneath us, 941. Good works are to be performed while we live, 472. Why Paul said that good works should be done so that power may not be feared, 98. The good conceived by the gift of the Creator in the heart must be completed with swift devotion, 589. It is a sin when a good deed that can be done is neglected so that it may be done, 1128. Those who misuse the goods of the world are more justly condemned, 78. Temporal goods are consolations in calamity, not rewards, 77. No one can be good unwillingly, 703. The good commonly endure the hatred of the wicked, 816. Why the good are taken away, or why they are so few, 365. Nevertheless, not all the good are taken away, 368. No one can please a good man unless he himself is good, 1078. Like ointment, the reputation of the good gives off fragrance, 1026. If the good were without the wicked, they could not be perfectly good, 1127. The good are always displeasing to the wicked, 1026.

Bonus, a good servant of God and founder of a certain monastery, 1136. Gregory did not consent to make him abbot of the Lucusian monastery, ibid.

The twelve bronze oxen supporting the bronze sea: what they signify, 19, 20, 512.

The cloths called *brandeum*, or *prandeum*, were those applied to the relics of saints and distributed among the faithful, 709, 838. A *brandeum* cut by Saint Leo shed blood, 710.

An inventory is called a *brevis*, or a little document containing a summary of any matters, 655, 889, 890.

The Christian faith had spread through the island of Britain from the earliest centuries, 1111.

Brixia, an episcopal city in Italy, 460. It is also called Brixa, 459. In the vernacular, Brescia, 719.

Brundisium, an archiepiscopal city in the province of Hydruntum, [Col. 1482] 808. The visitation of this Church is entrusted to Peter of Hydruntum, 807.

Brunhilda, daughter of Athanagild, king of the Goths, married Sigibert, king of the Franks, 794, 1218. She is praised for the proper education of her son Childebert, 794. She is praised for other virtues as well, 828, 835, 936, 1024, 1148, 1149, 1219, 1220. By what right Gregory could praise her, 794. Several historians attempt to clear her reputation of crimes, ibid. Gregory commends Augustine, who was going to Gaul, to Brunhilda, 835; and Candidus, administrator of the patrimony, 836; and Hilary, 1024. She received Augustine affectionately, 938. She is admonished concerning the abolition of simony and the exclusion of neophytes from receiving orders, 937, 938, 1149; concerning the restraint of idolaters, 938; and concerning the correction of wicked priests, 1170, 1171 ff. She is asked to convene a synod against the Simonians, 1015. Gregory sends her a book, 939. She builds two monasteries and a hospice at Autun, 1219. She obtains privileges for them, ibid. She asks Saint Gregory to send a legate to hold a synod, 1220, 1221.

The Bruttians, peoples of Italy, 1192. Buccellinus, duke of King Theudebert of the Franks, 157. Burchard, bishop of Worms: in what year he lived, 107. He cites very many testimonies from Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his decrees, ibid.

What *burdatio* is, 535. *Burda*, that is, an estate, ibid.

Sutellius, bishop of Bordeaux, 1288. Burgoaldus, Brunhilda’s legate, 1219, 1220, and Theoderic’s, 1221. The patricians of Burgundy are called governors of the Transjurane district, 493.

Busa, a servant, 757. Buxentum, or Buxentium, formerly an episcopal city in Lucania, 319, 605. *Buxis*, or *pixis*, so called from the boxwood from which it was made, 709.

Twisted byssus joined to crimson dyed twice in the ephod: what it signifies, 16, 510.

Byzacium: see Bisacium.

## C
Cabillonum, a city of Burgundy, 1145. Lupus, bishop of Cabillonum, 1144. Who is called a blind shepherd, 11. What it means to place a stumbling block before the blind, 96. A blind man restored to sight by a miracle, 196. An Arian bishop struck with blindness, 341.

**Celibate.** Admonitions to be given to those living a celibate life, 81. Celibates entangled in earthly anxieties do not escape the burdens of marriage, ibid. Above all, let celibates beware of fornication, ibid. If they cannot overcome the storms of temptation, let them seek the harbor of marriage, ibid. Marriage is permitted to celibates unless they are bound by a vow, ibid.

Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, 616. Caesarius, abbot of the monastery of St. Peter at Baiae, 887. Caesarius, monk of Lérins and bishop of Arles, 1101. The fortress of Caesena, 1264. The bishops of Caesena: Concordius, ibid.; Natalis, ibid.

Cain, stirred by envy, killed his brother, 46. Resentment was the seedbed of fratricide, 46.

**Calabria.** In this province there was a great abundance of building material, 1192. The consolations of calamity are temporal goods, not rewards, 77. Calamities separate us from love of the world, 1175. [Col. 1483]

Calaris. See Caralis. What *calcenterus* signifies, 1036. Shoes were formerly varied according to each person’s rank and condition, 237.

Who the enemies of the Council of Chalcedon were, 615. The Council of Chalcedon gave occasion to the famous controversy over the Three Chapters, ibid. Whatever was decreed at that council concerning persons or other matters beyond or outside the definition of the faith does not belong to it, 632, 720. Whether Gregory believed that judgment had not been passed at that council concerning the Three Chapters, 720, 967. The Chalcedonian faith was not violated at the Fifth Council, 632, 633, 684. Gregory, and the Roman Church, neither subtracts anything from nor adds anything to the definition of faith made at Chalcedon, 633, 683, 684, 718, 938. The Eastern Churches defend and venerate the Council of Chalcedon, 966. Why St. Leo I opposed the Chalcedonian canons, 883. The Council of Chalcedon offered the Roman pontiff the title of universal bishop, 743, 749, 771. This council was falsified in one passage by the Church of Constantinople, 803. What should be done with those who reject this council, 1073.

A *calciarium* is a payment toward the support of food and clothing, 528.

**Caleca.** Emmanuel Caleca, a Greek, used the books of St. Gregory’s *Dialogues* against his fellow Greeks at the Council of Lyons, 104.

A person is called *calidus* who both undertakes and completes good pursuits, 94. Why each person is asked whether he is hot or cold, ibid.

A *caliga* and *caligula* are types of footwear or clothing of monks, 157, 169. *Caligae* refers both to shoes and to leg coverings, 326.

**Chalice.** By the name of the chalice the cup of the Passion is signified, 337. What the proportion of the chalice to the paten formerly was, 897. Calixenus, 948.

Callinicus, exarch of Italy, 876. He compels the inhabitants of the island of Capritana to return to the unity of the Church, 933. He receives an imperial decree that schismatics are not to be compelled to return to the Church, ibid. He is warned no longer to consult Justin, 934. At his prayers communion is restored to Maximus of Salona, 992. Gregory commends to him certain persons restored to the unity of the Church, 999.

Callipolis, an episcopal city of Calabria, 657. It belonged by right to the Roman Church, 1003. See Gallipolis. Bishops of Callipolis: John, 657; Sabinianus, 1003.

Calumny is called unjust harassment and the despoiling of goods, 497. Those whom the ancient enemy cannot drive into sin, he tears apart by fabricating false accusations against their reputation, 596. Calumny is grievous and harsh, even though it may bring a great reward, 861. How calumny is to be endured, 589, 860, 861. When greater evils are alleged, they ought not to be believed unless proved, 860. See Detraction. The corresponding nature of the punishment calls for vengeance upon slanderers, 707. See Accusation. What punishments are to be inflicted on a calumniator, even if he is a subdeacon, 1171, 1172 and following. A calumnious bishop, 1105.

What it means to swallow a camel, 92. Among later Greeks *camisia* means a garment, 878. It signifies an under-tunic, ibid.

The *campagus* is a type of footwear, 915, 916. What its form was, 917. The deacons of Catania wished to use it, 915. Only the deacons of the Church of Messina were permitted to use it, ibid.

Campana, a patrician woman, 539, 636. [Col. 1483] Campanianus, master of the soldiers, 536. Cample, a place six miles from ancient Nursia, 385.

A chancellor was the same as a scribe or notary, 555, 556. Why he was called a chancellor, ibid. The chancellor’s office is called the military service of the chancery, ibid.

Candidus, bishop of Vrbis Vetus, 573, 814. Candidus, bishop of Fulginiae, 1291. Candidus, abbot of the monastery of St. Andrew at the Clivus Scauri, 902. He asks for and obtains relics, 1115. Candidus, a priest and rector of the Roman Church’s patrimony in Gaul, 1140, 1171. He is commended, 794, 795, 830, 836, 1102 and following, 1103. He is ordered to buy boys from the English and clothing for the use of the poor, 796. He is also ordered to redeem four Christians held by Jews, 868. He is warned to give alms to Albinus, who was blind, 707. After a Jew has repaid the sum he had received, Candidus is compelled to return the promissory note, 974.

What it means for a dog to return to its vomit, 86. Who are called mute dogs, 16, 510.

What a canon is, 420. What the grain allowance is, 488. It was established in the time of Augustus, ibid. The Church is governed by the canon, 1265. How great St. Gregory’s zeal was for observance of the canons, 663. The Roman Church did not accept the canons of Constantinople concerning discipline, 882. The Roman Church judged that the Sixth Nicene Canon had been violated by the Third Canon of Constantinople, 883.

Who were formerly called *canonicani*, 420.

**Canonical.** No one is to be counted among the canons unless he knows how to read, speak Latin, and understand it, 858. Canons are the principal members of the Church’s senate, ibid. The canonical order signifies the laws of the canons, 1257. Why canonical solidi were so called, 420. What canonical vengeance is, 1203. Gregory first called the canonical prayer, recited after the *Trisagion* has been completed, the canon, 1262.

*Canterma*, a kind of magical wrongdoing, 759. Virgins sing a song to the Lamb in a unique manner, 83. The song of the angels. See *Glory in the highest*.

Canusium, an episcopal city of Apulia, 240, 546. The revenues of the Church of Canusium were to be spent for the support of the clergy and the future bishop, 537. The visitation of this Church was entrusted to the bishop of Sipontum, 546. Its see was united to the archbishopric of Bari, ibid. Two parish priests were to be ordained in this Church, 547.

Some chapels have roofs, while others among the pagans are without roofs, 435. The hair on the head signifies thoughts in the mind, 27, 514, 849. The hair on the priest’s head is both preserved so that it may cover the skin and cut back so that it may not close the eyes, 850.

A *capisterium* is a winnowing fan or sieve, 209. St. Benedict repairs a broken *capisterium* by prayer, ibid.

What the Three Chapters are, 615. Whether they pertain to the faith, ibid. They were condemned at the Fifth Council, from which the schism arose, 615, 681, 682. The faith of the Council of Chalcedon was not shaken by their condemnation, 682, 694. Whether Gregory believed that judgment concerning the Three Chapters was rendered only after the faith of the Council of Chalcedon had been established, 720. Spain was not divided by schism because of the Three Chapters, 614. A written oath and pledge was used for the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 682. Gregory, while still urban prefect, subscribed this pledge, as did Laurentius, bishop of Milan, [Col. 1484] ibid. The bishop and citizens of Brescia wanted Constantius, bishop of Milan, to swear that he had not condemned the Three Chapters, 719. Gregory forbade this, 720. Gregory attacks the defenders of the Three Chapters, 967.

Capitulana, foundress of a monastery, 1042. A *capitulare* is a memorandum, 525. Or a written document divided into chapters, 530. The First *Capitulare*, 1250. The Second, that is, the collection of imperial laws, 1252 and following.

Capraria, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 729. It is called Capricana, 1256. *Capraria* is better, 1257. St. Caprasius, a monk of Lérins, 1101.

Capris, or Caprea, an island adjacent to Campania, 547. The love of the people of Caprea for ecclesiastical unity, 1001.

The island of Capritana lies in the innermost recess of the Adriatic Gulf, 933, 934. The bishop of Capritana, John, was a schismatic, 935. The island of Capritana returned to the unity of the Church, 933.

Whenever a sacrifice was offered for a certain captive, his chains were released, 469. Captives were transported to Africa to be sold as slaves, 636. The canons and the laws of the world command that aid be given to captives, 696. With what great care the Church arranged for the redemption of captives, 697. How concerned Gregory was for the redemption of captives, 820, 872, 886, 887. He permitted the vessels of the Church to be sold, 859, 886, 887. This was permitted by the canons and laws, 943. Whatever the Church had spent for the redemption of captives was not to be recovered from those who had been redeemed, ibid., 944. Captive clergy were to be redeemed at the expense of their own Church, 654, 696. The price for redeeming a slave did not exceed twelve solidi, 697.

The visitation of the Church of Capua was imposed on Gaudentius of Nola, 737, 738. Gregory writes to the clergy of the Church of Capua residing at Rome, 738. A fourth part of the revenues of the Church of Capua was to be distributed to the Capuan clergy living at Naples, 760. Bishops of Capua: Fuscus, 737; Basilius, 1047, 1215.

Why priests under the Law were forbidden to shave the head, 27, 514. What the head of the faith is, 1244.

A *carabus* is a small boat made of wicker and hide, 470. Caralis, or Calaris, the chief city of Sardinia, 544. Six bishops were subject to the metropolitan of Caralis, ibid., 932. Januarius, bishop of Caralis. See his title and the alphabetical index of the Letters.

The name *cardinal* is ancient, the dignity new, and the purple more recent, 501. *Cardinal* is the same as titular, principal, or proper, 1265, 1266. It also means chief, 501. A cardinal priest is a proper and titular bishop, 501, 563. Cardinal bishops were formerly appointed only for a time, 563, 575. Why and on what condition John, bishop of Lisbon, was incardinated in the Church of Squillace, 600. A cardinal priest and a cardinal deacon were the first of their order, attached to some title, 501, 563, 635. What it means to cardinalize a deacon in the Church, or to constitute him a cardinal, 799. Formerly there were cardinal prefects and cardinal princes, 501. *Cardo* is the same as title, 501.

Carina, formerly an episcopal city of Italy, 698, 1227. The Church of Carina was united to that of Reggio, 597, 799. Bishops of Carina: John, 798; Boniface, 799. [Col. 1485]

Carnal people believe only what they see, 372. What the flesh signifies, 46. What admonitions should be given to those who have experienced sins of the flesh, 81, 82. Let them mourn past sins and avoid future ones, ibid. Those subject to temptations of the flesh are not to preside, but to be subject, 213. In former times the Church dealt severely with those who had fallen through the flesh, 503.

The people of Carseoli in Italy, 639. Carterius marries an abducted nun, 336. His offerings are rejected, 337.

Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena in Spain, 620. Carthage was the center of Africa in ecclesiastical and civil affairs, 559. It was the chief city of the proconsular province, 609, 610. Its bishops were the primates of all Africa, 610. Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, 609, 1288. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

A *casa* was a very modest possession, 534. Hence the distinction between *casati* and *mansuarii*, ibid. What *casales* are, 1105, 1107.

Cassian founded two monasteries outside the walls of Massilia, 858. Another, built under the name of St. Cassian himself, was endowed with privileges, ibid.

The fortress of Cassinum, from which St. Benedict expelled the remnants of idolatry, 229. The location of the fortress of Cassinum, ibid. He built many oratories there, ibid.

Cassiope, a fortress under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Corcyra, 1265, 1266, 1271.

Cassius, bishop of Narni, freed Spatharius of Totila from a demon by the sign of the cross, 289. He celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass every day with the greatest devotion, 468, 674. Foreknowing the day of his death, he died happily, 468. On what day his memory is celebrated, 468.

The monastery of Castellium, founded by Cassiodorus near Squillace, 920. Gregory forbade it to come under lay control, 920. He also forbade its privileges to be violated, 921, 922 and following.

**Chastisement.** Those who chastise others from a sense of duty should take care with what intention they do so, 433.

Chastity is signified by byssus, 16, 510. Abstinence serves chastity, 16. In the practice of good action the purity of the body must be preserved, 1030.

Castorius, bishop of the city of Amiternum, being deceived, commends a certain magician named Basilius to the abbot Equitius, 164. Castorius, bishop of Ariminum, was detained at Rome by Gregory because of illnesses, 641. Gregory attributes the cause of the same illness to the citizens of Ariminum, ibid. Because of his illness Castorius pleads to be relieved of the episcopal burden, 865, 866. He lays it down, 598, 865. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

**Castorius the Deacon.** He is entrusted with examining the life of the bishop of Pisaurum and of the priests of that place, 755, 756. Castorius, notary of the Apostolic See, 668, 778. He is called a *chartularius*, 775. He is commended to Andreas the Scholastic, ibid., and to Basilius, 775. He is ordered to undertake many matters concerning the affair of Marianus, 819, 837, 838. The execution of the sentence against Maximus of Salona is entrusted to Castorius, 983. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Castorius, master of the soldiers, 168. After enduring many hardships during the siege of Rome, he was accused but excused by Gregory, 767. The substance of Castorius the orphan’s father Urbicius, although pledged to the Church, is returned to him, 638, 639. [Col. 1485]

What it means to erect camps against Jerusalem, 31. What it means to pass through the middle of the camps, 75. The fortress commonly called Lamentana succeeded the formerly episcopal city of Nomentum, 638.

**Chaste.** Who are to be admonished when they are ignorant of sins of the flesh, 83. Promises made to those who live chastely, ibid. In Scripture the chaste are called eunuchs, ibid. Castus, a vigorous man and commander of the army of the emperor Maurice, 758. He is commended to the patrician Priscus, 662.

**Fall.** Those standing in a high place should fear a fall, 83. The fall of one person is usually the caution of another, 789.

What the catacombs are, 710. Who the Cataphrygians were, 1168. The Cataphrygians are to be rebaptized, ibid.

Catana, a celebrated city of Sicily, 487, 597. The deacons of Catania were forbidden to use the *campagus*, 915. Bishops of Catania: Elpidius, 1055, 1056; Leo, 557. See his title and the alphabetical index of the Letters.

A *catechumena* is a place suitable for detaining accused persons, 759.

Catella, a widow, is commended by Gregory to the bishop of Caralis, 551, 552. Her case is entrusted to his judgment for final resolution, 552, 553. Catella, the maidservant of a certain Felix, is ordered to be redeemed for the sake of her conversion, 653. Catellus, a monk, 1137. Catellus, a palace official, 726. Catellus, whom Gregory commends to Fortunatus and Anthemius, 867, 868.

A chair ordinarily belongs either to a judge or to one presiding, 91. What it means to sit in the chair of pestilence, ibid. The chairs of those who dared to sell doves in the temple of God fell, 797. What the overthrowing of chairs signifies, 1007. The bishop’s chair, when placed in a given location, is a sign of his jurisdiction there, 827, 859. The Alexandrian see is called the chair of Peter, 888, 889.

The Catholic Church is one, formed from the individual particular churches, 577.

Catulus, 1242.

Cases are to be brought to an end without litigation, or at least without delay, 1230. They are to be concluded where they arose, unless the judges are suspect or the cases themselves are more important, 809, 810, 1053, 1054. Which cases are called major, 574. Private cases are sometimes called major, 574. How cases of faith, or more difficult cases, are to be resolved, 783, 784. How major cases were resolved among the Jews, 783. Formerly the cases of Christians were heard not before lay judges but before bishops, 491. Cases of laypeople against bishops were sometimes entrusted to defenders, 946. The case of Fortunatus against Theodore and Rusticus, 1057. Gregory summoned more difficult cases before himself, 573, 914, 964. Bishops are appointed to restore the Church’s silver, 943. Cases of clergy and bishops. See Clergy, Bishops, Ecclesiastical Judgments.

**Caution.** For the most part, the fall of one person is usually the caution of another, 789. It is altogether weak caution that is not fortified by the help of piety, 1054. *Cautio* is used for a promissory note, 974. There are many kinds of pledges, 682. An oath-pledge, written and subscribed, was used in the condemnation of the Three Chapters, ibid. An oath-pledge, 730.

A *cella* sometimes means a dwelling and sometimes a storeroom, 536. The “cell of the flesh,” that is, a tomb, ibid. The word *cella* is used for a monk’s dwelling or for a monastery, [Col. 1486] 232, 233, 536, 732, 947. Grain given into the cell, that is, allotted as an expense, 536.

The things placed in storerooms are called *cellaria*, 536. Sometimes the term refers to the storerooms themselves, ibid., 924. The person in charge of a cell is called the *cellarius*, 536. The *cellerarius* is called the steward, or also the superior, 155, 1195. A cellarer is rebuked for being stingy toward the poor and disobedient, 260.

A *cellula*, that is, a bedroom, 536. *Celsitudo* is a title of honor by which the pope is addressed by a king, 978.

The Church of Ceneta was transferred to a safer place by the authority of Innocent III, 578.

It is not permitted to avenge personal injuries by means of the Church’s censures, 613.

**Census.** One who owes a head-tax is of servile condition, 757. What the *centenaria* signify, 1032, 1034.

Centumcellae, a town of Etruria on the Tyrrhenian Sea, 463, 464. It belonged to the diocese of Viterbo, 499. Dominicus, bishop of Centumcellae, 499, 1291.

The audacity of the Magdeburg Centuriators in corrupting the testimony of John the Deacon, 482.

Cerbonius, bishop of Populonium, a city of Etruria, venerable in life, 296. He was exceedingly devoted to hospitality, ibid. How he was exposed to bears by Totila and delivered, 297. He foretells the future, ibid. A miracle occurred at his funeral, ibid.

The Paschal candle and the prayers for its blessing, 1117.

**Contest.** Without the labor of combat there is no palm of victory, 325.

What it means to support the head of a person lying down with pillows, 27.

*Cessio* is used for letters of dismissal, 566, 741. The formula of this dismissal, 742.

Cethegus, 1047.

Why the land of Canaan was promised to the Israelite people, 78. Why God left the Canaanites remaining, 308.

*Charaxare* means the same as “to engrave,” 956; “to paint,” 957; “to erase and cancel with transverse lines,” 956, 957.

How charity resembles crimson cloth dyed twice, 16, 510. Charity for unity is the law of Christ, 43, 79. Charity is the mother and guardian of the virtues, 43, 610, 711, 836, 878. When it is least patient, it is not charity, 43. Praises of charity, 780, 839, 1278. The goods of charity are enumerated, 610, 611, 1013. Charity’s praise is perfect in heaven; on earth its form must be displayed more than described, 840. As humility is a part of charity, so charity is a part of humility, 852. Charity cannot be divided by places, 1069.

There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of one’s neighbor, 8. Diverse things flow from the same fountain of charity, 8. The farther charity descends graciously to those below, the more forcefully it returns to those above, 19, 512. Charity alone makes our sacrifice acceptable to God, 44. Charity makes the works of another’s labor our own without labor, 46. Those who are driven by fear should advance toward charity, 52. The effects of charity are reviewed, 780, 781, 839, 921. The efficacy of charity, 268. Charity makes those who do not perform the work share in its labor, 888. Through charity the prayers that we pour out to God for one another reach him more easily, 807. The unity of souls in charity unites more than bodily presence can, 658, 659, 660, 665, 711, 720, 763, 771, 772, 806, 832, 836. Nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love, and nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity, [Col. 1487] 71. We cannot live otherwise at the root of charity unless in mind and deed we hold to humility, 1246.

What *charta paricula* is, 507, 508. Sheets of paper rolled into one volume were formerly called a codex and a tome, 793. A *chartularius* is one who serves documents, 489. There were *chartularii* in the Church, in the palace, and in the army, ibid. Who the chief *chartularius* was, ibid. In the Roman Church the office of the *chartularii* and notaries was the same, 561. What the duties of the *chartularii* of the maritime districts were, 769. The execution of the sentence against a bishop was entrusted to a *chartularius*, 983.

Childebert the Younger, king of the Austrasians, son of King Sigibert and Brunichild, 785. His devotion to the Catholic faith is praised, 795. His achievements in Italy were remarkable, 794. Returning from Spain, he brought back extremely precious vessels, 697. At his request Gregory entrusted his vicariate and the use of the pallium to Virgilius of Arles, 781, 785. Gregory sent him the keys of St. Peter to be worn around his neck, 796. Almost all the Gallican bishops were under his rule, 783. At Childebert’s command a monastery was founded within the walls of Arles, 1019. Childebert asked that it be confirmed by apostolic authority, ibid. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

**Chlamys.** What it signifies when David silently cut the edge of Saul’s cloak, 39.

What chords struck in different ways on a lyre signify, 33.

Chorepiscopi are sometimes signified by priests, 563.

**Choir.** What it means to praise God with tambourine and choir, 68, 80.

What Χρησμός (*chrēsmos*, an oracle) is, 508.

Chrestus, bishop of Syracuse, 486.

The consecration of chrism belongs solely to the bishop, 705, 706. It was sometimes granted to African priests, ibid. To whom the application of chrism was permitted. See Confirmation. Who are reconciled as heretics by anointing with chrism, 1167.

Gregory called Maurice “the most Christian of princes,” 804, 899. *Christianitas* is a title by which Gregory addresses the kings of Gaul, 1024.

**Christian.** Which unbelievers are to be brought to the Christian religion, 525. Christians, subject to their prelates, are called sons of rams, 765.

Christidorus, husband of Theoctista, the daughter of Maurice’s sister, 877.

Christ, through sharing in our nature, is our neighbor, 32. The Lion from the tribe of Judah, 448. The mustard seed, 771. The leaven put into three measures of flour, 772. The small stone cut from the mountain without hands, ibid. The stone rejected by the builders, 854. The day that the Lord made, ibid. The open fountain for the washing away of sins, 869.

Christ is true God and the true Son of God, 1168, 1169. Why Christ came in the flesh, 4. For this purpose he assumed the form of our weakness: so that God, being humble, might teach human beings not to be proud, 744. At Christ’s coming, the darkness of humanity was dispersed through the Holy Spirit, 373. How Christ, the divine Word, became flesh, 1168, 1199. How and when Christ was anointed by the Holy Spirit, ibid. Christ taught us to flee prosperity and not fear adversity, 5. Before the thirtieth year of his life he did not wish to become a teacher of human beings, 76. As a child, Christ sits among the teachers, not teaching but asking questions, ibid. Why Christ wished a miracle he performed to remain secret, but could not make it so, 185. He feeds five thousand people with five loaves, 361. Why Christ devoted himself to prayer on the mountain and performed miracles in the cities, [Col. 1487] 19, 512. Why he did not wish to become king and willingly came to the scaffold of the cross, 4. Standing behind us, God admonished us, 82.

How Christ was ignorant of the day of judgment, 1069, 1070. He could not be ignorant of anything, 1070. Whether he was ignorant of the place where Lazarus had been laid, ibid., 1071. God compels us to patience by enduring so many and such great things from human beings, 51. The minds of the proud and the humble are opposed in relation to the Lord’s Passion, 229. Our redemption was accomplished by God’s humility, 59. Christ humbled himself in order to lead us back to the way of life through humility, 744. Because the pride of the devil offered itself as the origin of our destruction, God’s humility was found to be the instrument of our redemption, ibid.

The will of Christ and the Father is one, 61. Christ does not judge anyone from himself, ibid. By dying, rising, and ascending, Christ opened the book sealed with seven seals, 448. By descending to the underworld, whom Christ freed from there, 861, 862. Christ is our foundation, 1133. For whom Christ is the foundation, 962. He is the head and pontiff of the Church, 773. What we know was done in the head is often done in the members, 348. What Christ did he offered to us as an example, 185. The deeds of truth are set before our action as a rule, 328.

Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto, 674, 942, 1243. The dreadful end of Chrysaorius, a rich man proud and devoted to pleasures, 440.

**Food.** Those who eat forbidden food are handed over to the devil for punishment, 165. Which are the sweet foods of the pious, 269.

A scar is the figure of a healed wound, 966. What it means for a scar to rot, ibid.

Cicero, a fallen monk, is to be restored to the authority of the Church of Misenum, 761.

Cillanes promises that he will observe a truce, 1241.

*Cimelia* are the vessels, ornaments, and possessions of the Church whose care belonged to the archdeacon, 505, 555, 987. Movable property is called *cimelia*, 987. A *cimiliarchium* is the place where such precious movable goods are stored, 661, 1032.

The estate of Cinciana, 538.

What a belt signifies, 1067, 1068. What it means to lay aside the belt, ibid. The honor of the belt, ibid.

Ciridanus, 945, 1204.

Why a person digging a cistern is ordered to open it, 99. What it means for a preacher to drink water from his own cistern, 73.

A person is called *citonatus* whom his mother gave birth to quickly and easily, 488. Hence many are called *citonati*, ibid.

Who the citizens of Babylon and Jerusalem are, 923.

**City.** What the three cities of refuge signify, to which those inadvertently guilty of homicide fled, 32. What fortified cities signify, 48. What it means for fortified cities to fall, ibid. What it means to sit in the city, 76.

**Cry.** How sin with a cry differs from sin with a voice, 89. Why God is said to descend in order to find out whether the cry of Sodom has been completed in action, 860.

The title “most illustrious” is now offered indiscriminately to anyone, but formerly it was not so, 1046.

Classis, a town, or the new harbor, 906. The monastery of Classis was endowed with a privilege, 906 and following.

Claudius, abbot of the monastery of Saints John and Stephen in the city of Classis, 609, 906, 1194. He was very dear to Gregory, 906. Why his case against the bishop of Ravenna was to be examined at Rome rather than at Ravenna, 809, 810. He is strongly commended to the bishop of Ravenna, [Col. 1488] 907. He is ordered to come to Rome, 892. His nocturnal studies, 1195.

Claudius, a man of the highest rank in Spain, 1026. He was dear to Gregory because of his reputation for virtue, ibid.

Who is called a lame shepherd, II. A lame man healed, 284.

To whom the keys of the Church were given, 253. The miracle of St. Peter’s key, 872. Gregory sends the keys of St. Peter, containing enclosed fragments of his chains, to Anastasius of Antioch, 517; to Andreas the Illustrious, 519; to John the former consul, 520; to Bishop Columbus, 659; to King Childebert, 796; to the former consul Leontius, 924; to Secundinus, servant of God, 972; to the patrician Theoctista, 872; to Theodore the physician, 874; to Rechared, 1031. The power of these keys for healing the sick is commended, 517, 520. These keys were worn suspended from the neck for protection and safekeeping, ibid.; 1185, and passim.

What the Lord’s enclosures are, 527. What it signifies to lose the rudder at sea, 90. What the decorative stripes of dalmatics and tunics are, 1012.

Clementina, a patrician woman, was especially dear to Gregory because of her chastity, 1051. Gregory consoles her, 498, and urges her nobly to forgive offenses, 1051. Clementina’s slaves stirred up a revolt against Paul, bishop of Nepi, 623. Clementina kept with her Amandus, a priest elected bishop by the people of Sorrento, 1052, 1053.

Clergy are called the soldiers of the Church, 550, 646, 886, 980. Formerly no clerics were ordained unless attached to a title, 501. They were ordained not from another Church but from their own, unless perhaps no worthy person could be found, 588, 589, 601. Maurice excluded from orders those involved in public administrations, 675. Gregory approved this law, ibid. Advocates, soldiers, officials, actors, and those subject to public accounting were barred from the clergy, ibid. Offenses that invited people to a monastery barred them from the clergy, 675. See Orders.

What distinction there was between clerics who had formerly been Church slaves and freeborn clerics, 538. Among the clergy of one Church, rank and grade were to be derived from no other source than the day of ordination, 565, 566. Clerics were forbidden to transfer their allegiance because of a change of prelate, and a bishop was forbidden to adopt foreign clerics, 566. One who had received a sacred order at Rome did not have permission to leave that Church, 763. The origin of this practice is uncertain, ibid. Gregory ordains an acolyte whom, because of necessity, he sends back to the bishop, 894. Thus formerly clerics were so attached to their own Church that they could not be elected bishops of another Church unless they had obtained release from their own bishop, 741. What the practice was in Gregory’s time concerning each Church’s own clerics, 807. When the clerics of one Church were permitted to be incardinated in another, 799. Clerics who had departed from Rome without a blessing deserved penance, 816. A fugitive acolyte of the Roman Church is to be apprehended and sent to Rome deprived of communion, 899. Clerics who abandon their Church, even in order to take charge of another, are to be restrained, 980, 981.

Formerly clerics were forbidden to be tenants of other people’s possessions, 606. Nevertheless, for just causes, they seem at times to have been granted a dispensation, 606. The apostate Julian ordered clerics to perform the office of senators, 1047. Those clerics are not to be tolerated who do not display in their conduct what they display in their clothing, 701. For the most part, what is a fault in laypeople is a crime in those constituted in sacred orders, [Col. 1489] 1043, 1045. What the life of the clergy ought to be, 685. For a cleric who does not know how to read, the bishop’s tongue should serve as his book, 858. A monk is to be chosen for the clergy if he has acquired literacy; otherwise he can scarcely fulfill the ministry of doorkeeper, 857. Gregory commends to the bishop of Ephesus a cleric who does not know letters, 858. A cleric who loosens his tonsure is excommunicated, 1293.

For the sake of penance or conversion of life, clerics may flee to monasteries, 530. Clerics converted to monasticism are forbidden to return to their own Church unless their bishop summons them, 530, 531. The ecclesiastical order is altogether unsuited to the monastic life, and the monastic rule to ecclesiastical responsibilities, 691, 727. Why clerics are not to be placed in charge of monasteries, 727. At Milan the clergy had a common table, 720.

The goods of the clergy are to be administered by stewards, 640. They are to be divided into four parts, 691, 737. See Church property.

Stipends are owed to clerics who faithfully serve the Church, 828, 1151. The customary stipends are not to be denied to a sick cleric, 573, 574. Captive clerics are to be redeemed at the expense of their own Church, 654, 696. A cleric returning from schism is assigned a stipend, 823. Concerning the property on which clerics may make a will, 791.

Clerics outside the sacred orders may marry, 1151. Sacred clerics are forbidden the companionship of women, 289, 1010, 1011. Nevertheless, they may keep certain women with them, 546, 976, 977, 1010. In former times sacred clerics were ordered to leave their wives, 388, 545, 546. This discipline formerly did not prevail in Italy if disgraceful suspicion was absent, ibid., 977. What the discipline of the Gallican Church concerning clerical celibacy was in the sixth century, 546.

The mutual duties of the clergy and the bishop, 1263. The discipline to be maintained by the bishop among the clergy, 704, 707, 1151. The correction of clerics belongs to the bishop, 668. Gregory entrusts the correction of the clerics of Laon to the metropolitan bishop, 700, 701. Rebellious clerics are to be suspended, 667. They are likewise to be restrained, 980, 981. Clerics are not to flee to the patronage of laypeople, 707. The cases of clerics belong to the bishop, 667, 1071, 1120 and following, 1178. The case of a fallen priest is entrusted to a subdeacon defender for examination, 1044. In the case of a certain cleric, a subdeacon who is rector of the patrimony sits as judge together with his bishop, 1072. Gregory summoned more difficult cases of priests before himself, 667. The cases of priests are to be decided according to the norm of the canons, 713. Women are produced as witnesses against clerics, 650, 651.

Clerics are to be thrown into prison and subjected to severe punishments for wrongdoing, 707, 759. Clerics who had been ordained by a bishop in exchange for abandoning an accusation against him are irrevocably deposed, 780. The ancient canons irrevocably depose sacred clerics who have fallen into sins of the flesh, 704. St. Gregory establishes the same, 503, 704, 729 and following, 730, 890, 914. They were to receive communion among the laity, 720. Clerics were irrevocably deposed not only for public crimes but also for secret ones, 969. A priest who dared to approach the ministry after deposition was deprived of communion until death, 733. Clerics who had committed sexual offenses were deposed and confined in a monastery to perform penance, 654, 688. Why *libellatici*, heretical clerics, and schismatic clerics were not irrevocably deposed, 503. A priest who had fallen into idolatry and sodomy was to be thrust into prison, 1044.

Clerics who had fallen before Boniface VIII were not tormented in workhouses but detained in *decanica*, [Col. 1489] 527. Sometimes a monastery was assigned to them in place of a prison, ibid., 979, 980. They were confined in very poor but regular monasteries, 537, 538. Nevertheless, the monasteries were not to be burdened on their account, 538. The letter numbered fifty-two in Book Nine, which speaks of restoring fallen clerics to their order after satisfaction, is not by St. Gregory, 967, 968. It conflicts with the councils and the Fathers, 968, 969. Gregory nevertheless decreed that after completing his penance a priest could take charge of a monastery, 729. No one against whom no canonical sentence has been issued ought to undergo a canonical penalty, 632.

The continual service of the clergy gave rise to their immunities, 829. The immunities of clerics were violated by imprisonment, 551. For the immunity of the clergy
Collection of imperial laws, 1252 and following. Clerics are not to be summoned before laymen for trial, 799. In this matter the discipline of both Church and Empire differs, 799. Formerly the possessions of clerics were exempt from every tax, 1017. Clerics were sometimes not exempt from watches and guard duty, 909, 910, 998. Clematius, a lector, 780. Clementius, bishop and primate of Byzacena, 693. What *clientelae* means, 1039. Clotharius, king of the Franks, 1147. Who he was, ibid. Saint Gregory writes to him concerning the convocation of a synod and commends to him the monks going to England, ibid. and following. Clusium, an episcopal city in Etruria, 1064. Ecclesius, bishop of Clusium, 1063. What *coccus bis tinctus*—“twice-dyed scarlet”—signifies in a priest’s garment, 16, 509, 510. Gregory accepts the cochlearia and rings offered to him, 833. *Cocus.* What “chief of the cooks” signifies, 61. *Codex.* Gregory requests the ancient codices of the Council of Ephesus, not trusting the newer ones, 803. Why Roman codices are much more accurate than Greek ones, ibid. *Heaven.* In heaven the good recognize the good, and this knowledge is a source of joy for them, 424. They also recognize good people whom they never saw, 425. In heaven there is one blessedness, but unequal recompense, 429. To what animals earthly thoughts are like, 30. Affliction deliberately accepted cleanses the mind, which deliberate iniquity alone had defiled, 86. Whoever is carried too far outside himself by the movement of thought is not with himself, 217. In this age we scarcely ever see one another’s thoughts; it is otherwise in the future age, 445. Among Gregory’s works, *cognata* is used for “a brother’s wife,” 1154. Among the Greeks, *cognatus* means “kinsman,” 1155. What *cognidium* is, 889, 890. Cointius’s opinion concerning the superscription of a certain Gregorian letter is examined, 1143. What *colatum* is, 889, 890, 891. *Conversation.* The mind often desires to be renewed through compunction, but through evil conversations it becomes old again, 909. What it means to anoint the eyes with collyrium, 12. Some colonists are *originarii*, others *ascriptitii*, 700. What colonial tenure (*jus colonarium*) is, ibid. The colonists of Church lands were obliged to deliver annually a fixed number of *modii* of grain, 533. It was also their responsibility to transport this grain-rent to Rome at their own expense and risk, [Col. 1490] ibid. Otherwise, if the grain perished through the fault or negligence of the defender, ibid. Sometimes they paid money instead of grain, 533. Saint Gregory abhors the harassment of the Church’s colonists by unjust exactions, 533 and following, 534. Whatever was used for the rector’s benefit was to be taken from the total rent for the colonists’ relief, 534. The unjust measures used for exacting rents were to be broken, ibid. Nothing beyond certain cheap foodstuffs was to be exacted from the colonists over and above the fair measures, ibid. and 535. What was paid by the colonists of ecclesiastical estates as the *burdatio* tax was to be supplied from that same estate, 535. To colonists from whom the *burdatio* tax had been exacted twice, five hundred and seven solidi were to be restored, 536. The colonists offered their lords a payment for permission to marry; Gregory would not allow it to exceed the sum of one solidus, 535. The Church’s colonists are to be treated humanely by the provosts, 639. A certain colonist of the Roman Church is to be paid wages according to the measure of his labor, 920. What the best color signifies, 25. How the best color is changed, ibid. The simplicity of the dove is to be sharpened by the serpent’s cunning, 47. What the silvered feathers of the dove signify, 896. “To sell doves” means to obtain temporal profit from the Holy Spirit, 782, 788, 790, 797, 1007, 1134. Those who presumed to sell doves in the temple of God had their chairs fall, with God as judge, 782, 788, 790. Gregory exhorts Columba to good works, 1185.

Saint Columbanus. What *Columbanus* signifies according to his name, 1036. Columbanus assumed the name *Barjona*, 1036. At one time he calls himself a dove, at another a wood-pigeon, and at another a “micrologue,” ibid. Whether Gregory wrote to Saint Columbanus, 1035, 1036. Columbanus maintained that the Scots’ custom should be followed in celebrating Easter, 1036, 1037, 1038. He consults Gregory about certain matters, 1038, 1039. He ardently desires to see him, 1039. Columbanus praises Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, 1040. He requests Gregory’s expositions of Ezekiel and the Song of Songs, ibid. He begs him to expound the prophecy of Zechariah, ibid.

Columbus, bishop of Numidia, distinguished for his way of life, 658, 660. Devoted to the Apostolic See, 658. He is praised, 821, 904. He presides over the synod he convened, 659. His zeal against the Donatists is stirred up, 716. He is urged to pastoral vigilance, 846. Because he received Gregory’s letters more frequently, he suffered the hostility of many, 846. He is to depose Maximianus, bishop of Pudentiana, 611, 612. Private affairs are entrusted to Columbus for private settlement, 612. He is to watch that boys not be admitted to holy orders and that no one be ordained through human favor, power, or entreaty, 659. He is to investigate transgressors of the canons, 686. He is not to permit the children or slaves of Catholics to be baptized by Donatists, 822. The case of Peter the bishop is entrusted to him for judgment, 821, 822; and also that of Donadeus the deacon, 1186. Bishop Paul is commended to him, 904. Gregory sends Columbus the keys of Blessed Peter with pieces of the chains, 659. He compels Valention to return the churches he had taken away, 915. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters. Columbus, a presbyter of Luna, 1099. Gregory sends him a copy of the *Pastoral Rule*, 729. A shining dove appeared above Gregory while he was hiding, 505. Why priests are forbidden to grow their hair, 27, 514. [Col. 1491]

A *comes* is one who was sent from the *comitatus*, or court, to govern the principal cities, 413. There were various kinds of counts, 499. The origin of counts is referred to the emperor Hadrian, ibid. and 500. Which senators were made counts, 499. Why there were so many counts, 500. In the time of Gregory the Great, counts were prefects of individual cities, 847. The emperor’s senate was called the *comitatus Caesaris*, 500, 975, 976. Comitiolus, who had deserved well of the Roman Church, is commended to Maurice, master of the soldiers, 909. Comitiolus, a guardsman, 1044. Comitiolus the Glorious, 1251, 1252. *Comitiva* ordinarily means the dignity of a count, 499. It is also a profitable administrative office that could be entrusted to others by the palace, ibid. There were various kinds of *comitiva*, ibid. Whoever takes his spiritual co-mother as wife is excommunicated, 1293. Commissus the scholasticus, 595. *Commodum* is used for a stipend, wage, or reward for labor, 172. The marriage payment is the gift that colonists paid their lords for permission to marry, 535. This ought to benefit not the Church but the tenants, ibid. What *commodalia dispendia* are, 551. Letters of communion were sent by newly ordained bishops to their fellow bishops, 541, 542. This custom was not neglected even by the Roman prelates themselves, ibid. The beginnings and antiquity of this custom, 490. The Roman pontiffs also sent letters to kings as tokens of their communion of faith, ibid. The communion of members of one body is an image of the fellowship of the faithful, 46. By loving the good things we cannot do, we make them our own, ibid. Formerly, *communio* meant the absolution, peace, or reconciliation granted to penitents, 733. Now *communio* is used almost exclusively for the Eucharist, ibid. How the right of communion was formerly acquired, 254. The right of communion which someone had forfeited while alive but recovered after death, ibid. A bishop is deprived of the right of communion because of the crime of simony, 612, and so is one who does not obey the sacred canons, 631. *Communio* used for the Eucharist: see *Eucharist*. What lay communion is, 734. According to Gregory, lay communion is the Eucharist itself, which clerics deposed from their ministries could receive among the laity, 729, 730, 733, 734. Clerics who had fallen after receiving sacred orders and had been deposed from office were reduced to lay communion, 729, 730. A rector ought through compassion to be close to each person, 18. Compassion makes God merciful toward us, 554. Neither devout people on earth nor saints in heaven have compassion on the reprobate suffering in hell, 452. What a compromise is, 960. There are two principal kinds of compunction: one fears eternal punishments; the other sighs for heavenly rewards, 353, 870, 871. Perfect compunction of fear draws the mind toward compunction of love, 353, 871. By what things both kinds of compunction are foreshadowed in Sacred Scripture, 353, 871. With what diligence the grace of tears should be sought, 353. After compunction, with what diligence the mind should be guarded in prayer, 472. In God’s presence no place is secret to the compunctive soul, 870. Those who are affected by the grace of compunction possess the fountain of wisdom, 877. Who were formerly called *compurgatores*, [Col. 1491] 864. Como, an ancient city of Insubria, now in the duchy of Milan, 971.

The necessity and usefulness of councils, 486, 487, 1010. The Holy Spirit is present at councils, 1010. The strength and authority of councils flow from the communion of the saints and catholic consent, 515, 516. Which vices must be avoided in councils, 486. The affairs of the oppressed and poor are to be settled in councils, ibid. Bishops and presbyters sat in councils, but not deacons or the clergy, 1288. Gregory orders councils to be convened twice a year in Sardinia, 688. He determines that councils which ought to have been convened twice a year should be convened once, 1010. Provincial councils, formerly accustomed to meet twice a year, were decreed by the Council of Trent to be convened at least every three years, 688. Virgilius of Arles could convene councils in Gaul as often as he judged necessary, 784. The bishops of Gaul had to attend that council personally or through a presbyter or deacon, ibid. What is called an episcopal council, 487. The emperor Justinian provided by edict that the faith of the four councils should be subscribed by all bishops, 515. Gregory venerates the four general councils as though they were four Gospels, ibid., 632, 718. Whom these councils condemned, he also condemns; whom they absolved, he also absolves, 515, 718, 779. The integrity of the four holy synods must be preserved, 784. The Fifth General Council was convened to condemn the Three Chapters, 615. At this council nothing concerning the faith was overturned or changed, and nothing was established against the four synods; rather, proceedings concerned certain persons, ibid., 632, 633, 694, 720. Nothing concerning these persons is contained in the Council of Chalcedon; but after the canons had been established, proceedings concerning them were debated, 720. In the Fifth Synod nothing else was done concerning the persons than had been done in the Synod of Chalcedon, 633. The Fifth Council followed the Council of Chalcedon in everything, 967. Why, on the occasion of the Fifth Council, many—especially in Africa and Istria—seceded from communion with the Church, 694. Gregory venerates the Fifth Council, 515.

*Concord.* Whoever does not restrain his tongue destroys concord, 55. One does not attain the single hope of the calling unless one runs toward it with a mind united to one’s neighbors, 68. Concord is the greater gift, by which the other gifts become useful, ibid. Irrational nature, by being in harmony with itself, indicates how great an evil rational nature commits through discord, 69. Concord must not be maintained with wicked people, ibid. How harmful concord among the wicked is, 71. Whoever unites the wicked in peace supplies strength to iniquity, ibid. How concord is to be preserved, 1259. Concord among bishops is necessary; see *Bishops*. Concordius, bishop of Cesena, 1264.

Intercourse with one’s wife before the child is weaned is forbidden, 1158, and also with a menstruating woman, ibid. After intercourse, a man should not immediately enter the church, nor before he has washed with water, 1159, 1160. Intercourse is scarcely free from fault, 1160, 1161. If intercourse occurs solely for the procreation of children, then the married couple are to be left to their own judgment concerning entering the church and participating in the Eucharist, 1161.

*Concupiscence.* As long as we live, the fire of concupiscence must be feared, 388. What should be done for those who sin through sudden concupiscence, 89, 90. The punishment prepared for concupiscence is signified by stench and mist, 432, 433, 436, 437. A man is joined to a woman when the mind, through pleasure in thought, joins itself to unlawful concupiscence, 1160. No one should be condemned without judgment, 1078. What *conditio* signifies, 756, 757. Anyone subject to a condition is to be rejected from sacred ordination, 600.

*Tenants.* Gregory did not wish the succession of deceased tenants to accrue to the use of the Church, 535. It was forbidden to lease the Church’s estates to tenants for profit, 536. *Massa.* Clerics were forbidden to lease possessions, 606. What a *conduma* is, 1105, 1107, 1229. What vicarious confession is, 850. Those who have confessed concerning themselves ought not to be questioned about the consciences of others, 651. Whether confession for venial faults was formerly customary among monks, 997. Confirmation is designated by the term *consignatio*, 1075. The bishop ought to sign baptized infants, 689, 705, 1075. Why bishops are forbidden to sign infants twice on the forehead, 689. Sardinian presbyters are forbidden to anoint the forehead with chrism, 689. Later this is permitted to them in the bishop’s absence, ibid., 705. What the former practice was in Spain and Gaul, and what it now is in the Eastern Churches, concerning the minister of confirmation, 706. Those are to be confirmed whose confirmation is not certain, 1279. When going out to sign infants, the bishop must not burden the subordinate presbyters beyond measure, 1231. Confusion is useful to the insolent, 41.

*Marriage.* Who should be admonished among married people, 79, 80. Let each person strive to please a spouse in such a way as not to displease the Creator, 79. The mind of Christian spouses is both weak and faithful, ibid. What it means to have a wife and to be as though one did not have one, ibid. Spouses should tolerate care for the flesh out of necessity and devote themselves to eternal things out of desire, ibid. Spouses should be patient, ibid. Spouses should remember that they were joined for the sake of receiving offspring, 80. The laws of marriage that are transgressed, ibid. The apostolic indulgence was granted not so much to the healthy as to the weak, ibid. It is implied that what is said to be permitted is nevertheless a fault, ibid. Those who use marriage as a remedy for concupiscence are worthy of pardon, ibid. By frequent prayers spouses should wipe away what they defile with pleasures mingled into the beautiful appearance of intercourse, 80. Earthly anxieties arise from marriages, 81. Once the spouses have become one body, it is incongruous for one part to be converted while the other remains in the world, 827. A husband is obliged to receive back a wife whom he had cast off because of her servitude, once her freedom has been established, 845. Different practices in different ages concerning the prohibition of marriage among blood relatives, 1153, 1154 and following. Whether marriage should be dissolved: see *Matrimony*. Who were formerly called *conjuratores*, 864. Cono, abbot of Lérins, 1098, 1099, 1100. Marriage among blood relatives: see *Marriage*.

*Conscience.* Whoever is defended by conscience is free amid accusation; whoever is accused by conscience alone is not free, even without accusation, 860. Conscience alone is sufficient against calumnies, 1093, 1126, 1127. Consecration performed by excommunicated persons is invalid, 699. Consentia, formerly a city of the Bruttii in Italy, 961, 962. Palumbus, bishop of Consentia, 896, 962. Who a true counselor is, 524. Evil counselors must be avoided, 743, 744. [Col. 1493] What a prince’s counselor is bound to do, 762. *Counsel.* Who sits in the seat of perverse counsel, 91. The counsel of life is sometimes sought from those who favor death, 524. From whom counsel for salvation should be heard, ibid. In matters of the highest importance, counsel ought not to be hasty, 574. *Consolantia*, 1232. Consolation for one suffering adversity, 1233. The sole consolation is the expectation of death, ibid. What *conspersio* is, 37, 97, 288, 392.

*Constancy.* The heart of the wise is steadfast; the heart of fools is otherwise, 60. Love of peace must not bend zeal and constancy, 69. Constantina Augusta, daughter of the emperor Tiberius, 708. Her death, ibid. Gregory deters her when she requests the head of Saint Paul, ibid. and following. He sends her pieces of Saint Paul’s chains struck off with a file, 711. What she ought to do on behalf of the unjustly oppressed Corsicans and Sicilians is suggested, 768, 769. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters. Constantina, abbess of the monastery of Saint Lawrence, 800. Constantina, a girl rescued from the allurements of this world before she married, 875.

*Constantinople.* The Constantinopolitan Church falsified the synods of Chalcedon and Ephesus in some passage, 803. The Roman clerics could not endure the bishop of Constantinople’s sphere of authority being enlarged, ibid. Heretics and heresiarchs emerged from the Church of Constantinople, 873. What was accepted by the Roman Church from the First Council of Constantinople, and what was rejected, 882, 883. The Constantinopolitan Church is subject to the Apostolic See, 941. The Second Council of Constantinople: see *Fifth Council*. The bishop of Constantinople appears formerly to have been appointed by the emperor, 853. Bishops of Constantinople: Anatolius, 504; John, 489—see his title; Cyriacus, 354. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters. Whether in Gregory’s time there was a bishop of Constantinople named Eusebius, 941.

*Constantine the Great.* The account of that emperor’s baptism celebrated at Rome had not yet been disseminated in Gregory’s age, 177. Constantine’s reverence toward bishops, 767. Constantine abolishes the worship of idols, 1165. Constantine, bishop of Scodra, 1201. Why Pope Constantine was deposed from his rank, and the ordinations performed by him were invalidated, 608. Constantine, the first abbot of Monte Cassino after Blessed Benedict, 208.

Constantius, bishop of Aquino, 240. Endowed with the spirit of prophecy, 293. He is venerated by the Church, 240, 293. Constantius of Milan, at first a deacon, 565. He is elected bishop by the votes of all, 644, 645, 646, 681, 1288. An irreproachable man, 644. Joined to Gregory by familiarity, 646, 683. The pallium is sent to him, 682. Why schismatic bishops separated themselves from his communion, 682, 683. What he ought to swear and what he ought not to swear in the affair of the Three Chapters, 719. Gregory warns him to urge Bishop Venantius to correct his clergy, 701. Why Constantius did not wish to transmit Gregory’s letter to Theodelinda, 685, 720. Many are scandalized because he names the name of John, bishop of Ravenna, at the altar, 719. The case of Maximus of Salona is entrusted to him for judgment, 983. The death and virtues of Constantius, 1094. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters. [Col. 1493]

Constantius, or Constantius of Narni, bishop, 1288, 1291. He is assigned the visitation of the Church of Interamna, 987. Constantius, presbyter and nephew of Boniface, bishop of Ferentium, 184. His avarice was punished, 189. He was preparing money to obtain the episcopate, ibid. Constantius the Monk was elected abbot; why Gregory rejected him, 1194. Constantius, deacon of the Church of Pudentiana, 611. Constantius, *mansionarius* of the Church of Saint Stephen near Ancona, venerable for his holiness, 173. He uses water instead of oil in the lamp, ibid. His humility, 176 and following. Constantius, prefect, 856. Constantius, tribune, 592. Constantius, defender, 951.

*Custom.* What custom is, 553. Which customs are to be preserved and which abolished, ibid. Many practices have been introduced into the Church that justice, prudence, or the canons now forbid to be exacted, ibid. In doubtful matters one should adhere to the ancient custom, 719. The force of custom, 822. In one faith, diversity of custom does not harm the holy Church, 532. The differing customs of the Churches are not to be rejected; rather, the better ones should be chosen, 1152. Justinus attempted in vain to restore the consulship, which Justinian had abolished, 489, 620, 1283. Consulars and consuls were sometimes appointed by *codicilli*, 489.

The contemplative life is signified by Rachel, 491, and by Mary, ibid. A rector should be elevated through contemplation, 18, 511. It is unworthy of religious people to have prolonged disputes over earthly things, 949. Disputes are not brought to an end if completion of what has been adjudged is delayed, 1139. A dispute between two abbots concerning the boundaries of fields: how it is to be settled, 887. How a controversy concerning earthly matters is to be settled, 1216, 1217, 1261. Among patriarchs, the token of the same faith and communion was formerly fostered as a custom, 490. What *contestari* signifies, 1046, 1047. *Contestatio* is called a defamatory libel, 817. Unless the author of such a libel proves the truth or confesses the fault, he is to be deprived of communion, ibid. Continence is necessary for those approaching the temple, 193. See *Intercourse*. Those who have professed continence must abstain from cohabitation with women, 289. Subdeacons already ordained in Sicily are not to be compelled to continence, but those to be ordained henceforth are to promise and observe it, 538. The life of the continent is for the most part confused with the conduct of secular people, 83.

*Continence.* This word has various meanings: it is used for a person's tenure or condition, 490, 491; for love, goodwill, and favor, 490, 749, 763; for assistance, 502, 539, 644, 763, 1242; and for clerical stipend and *sportula*, 780, 781. Annual *continentia*, that is, an annual pension for support in life, 538. *Continere* means the same as to cherish, assist, or sustain; *contineri* means the same as to be supported by assistance, 540, 640, 757, 1231, 1232. To contain someone means to make him content, 596. Controversy: see *Dispute*, *Lawsuits*. According to the canons, contumacy is sufficient for depriving someone of communion, 811, 812.

*Insult.* The cunning enemy wages war against one who suffers and patiently endures insults, 45. An insult proves what sort of person each one conceals within himself, 176. An insulting bishop, 501.

*Agreements and assemblies.* Gregory’s assent was often required in agreements, 974. The difference between an assembly and a small gathering, 577. What an ordinary and lawful assembly is, ibid. A public assembly of all the faithful to celebrate the principal feasts with their bishop in the mother church, 579. *Conversatio* means the same as conversion, 209.

*Conversion.* What is required for true conversion, 93. Whoever desires to be converted must be overturned by the hand of correction, so that afterward he may be raised to the condition of right action, 94. *Converti* means the same as to put on the habit of conversion, 653, 677, 678. The conversion of a sinner is a greater miracle than the resurrection of the dead, 321. Which banquets are praiseworthy, 617. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, 377. Copiosus, brother of Justus the monk, was a physician, 465. He cared for his brother and sought to correct him of the vice of proprietorship at the end of his life, ibid. The deceased brother appeared to Copiosus, 468. Intercourse is permitted solely for the sake of receiving offspring, 80. Formerly, even after lawful intercourse, it was forbidden to enter churches, 193, and to receive the Eucharist, 194. See *Intercourse*.

The heart slips away amid human words, 33. Nothing in us is more fleeting than the heart, 53. The heart of the wise is steadfast; that of fools is otherwise, 60. The heart must not only be crushed but also humbled, 88. Those pure in heart are readily heard by God, 312. What hinders a return to the heart, 491. Whoever denies that the devil enters the human heart is a Pelagian, 884. Carnal hearts are signified by the world, 1093.

Corcyra, an island of the province of Nicopolis, adjacent to Epirus, 1264, 1265. The Church of Corcyra, 1266. Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra, 1264, 1266, 1271. Corinth, a city situated on an isthmus, 517. It is called “between two seas” and *Bithalassus*, ibid. Bishops of Corinth: Anastasius, 517; John, 779. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters. Cornelium, or the Forum of Cornelius, a city of Italy under the jurisdiction of the supreme pontiff, 872.

*Horn.* What it means to exalt the horn of delinquents, 88. A *corona* is a lampstand in the shape of a crown, 555. *Corona* was a title of honor by which supreme pontiffs and bishops were formerly addressed, 622. The body receives movement from the soul, 381. The resurrection of the body is a lesser miracle than that of the mind, 321. What it means to be subject to the body, or to be a person “of the body,” 756, 757. Bodily purity must be carefully guarded, 1030.

*Fraternal correction.* Its usefulness is twofold, 54. Whoever loves his neighbor as himself does not remain silent about how he may rightly rebuke him, ibid. Whoever neglects the correction of his neighbor is the author of that neighbor’s death, ibid. One must see that love of human peace does not separate us from the peace of our Creator, 69. How great a fault it is to keep peace with the worst people, 70. Whoever rushes forward with words of correction must preserve inner peace, ibid. A bitter cup is gladly accepted when it is offered with the intention of salvation, 1022. It is characteristic of a wise man both to weigh more extensively what he has heard briefly and to correct quickly what displeases God, 1081. How serious it is to refuse correction, 1236, 1237.

*Correction and reproof.* The word of reproof is the key that opens, 17, 510. With what frame of mind correction should be given, 22. Vehement reproof must be circumspect, 32. In correcting, the pastor should imitate the Samaritan, 514. In reproving, he should pursue the fault in such a way that he loves the person, 524. In outward matters requiring correction, inward charity must first be preserved, 732. Wounds that must be cut away should first be touched with a gentle hand, 742. Some things must be corrected mildly, others patiently tolerated, 1135; discrimination must be observed in correcting evils, 1177. One should rejoice over the correction of a crime but grieve over a brother’s fall, 789. Usually discreet leniency in correction has more strength than strictness in carrying out punishment, 1051. If the nature of the excess requires severity, punishment should correct the fault, and grace should not be denied to those who have been corrected, ibid. When and from what circumstances we are bound to correct, 617, 618. Whoever does not correct what needs correction seems to consent to the one who is erring, 1020. In correcting faults, anger must not precede the mind but serve after reason has led the way, 1030, 1080. Whoever does not correct what must be cut away sins, 1074, 1263. A superior owes correction to an inferior not only by the duty of charity but also by that of justice, 618. The more delayed discreet indignation against faults is, the more it must be feared, 681. For one whom divine discipline crushes, the addition of human scourges is superfluous, 597. How greater vices may be recognized through correction of lesser ones, 29. Those who offend through ignorance or weakness are to be gently corrected, 30. Who must be rebuked vehemently, 31. Whoever strives to do evil and wants others to remain silent about it desires to be loved more than he desires truth, 28. Even unjust correction must be endured most patiently, 665. See *Punish*, *Rebuke*.

A *correus* is called a guarantor, 1108. Corsica, an island of the Tyrrhenian Sea, 561, 562. Corsica, joined to Sardinia, was subject to the prefect of Africa, 848. Corsican priests are forbidden to associate with women, 546. A monastery is to be built in Corsica, ibid. The Corsicans, oppressed by exactions, were forced to sell their children, 768, 769. Leo, bishop of Corsica, 562. A raven received its daily food from Saint Benedict’s hand, 228. It is ordered to throw outside bread infected with poison, ibid.

Cosmas, from monk became subdeacon and then presbyter, 237. Cosmas, a Theban deacon, was deposed because of frauds committed concerning Church property, 629. Cosmas, oppressed by debt, for which Gregory orders payment from the Church’s patrimony, 670. Gregory sends sixty solidi to be paid for him, 724. Every creature is narrow to one who sees the Creator, 272. What can be seen cannot be believed, 381.

*Creditor.* Other people’s property must not be unjustly withheld from creditors, 537. The creditor’s right over a debtor was established differently by different laws, 670, 724. The laws forbid a debtor’s son to be held by creditors, 724. Creditors must not press the children of a debtor whose inheritance they have undertaken to possess, 821. What punishments await creditors who retain a free person for debt, 724.

Crementius, primate of Byzacena, accused and to be judged by the council of Byzacena, 1203. Crescens, deacon of Palermo, 1228. [Col. 1495] Crescentius, a cleric, was assigned penance for having sold the sacred furnishings of the Church to a Jew, 554, 555. Crescentius, vicar of the prefect of the City, 1075, 1077. No one is compelled to advance against his will, 504. John, bishop of Crete, 898. See his title.

*Crime.* Associates in crimes cannot testify, 651. Those to whom it pertains are bound to punish crimes, at the risk of their own salvation, 668. Investigation of a crime through punishments: see *Torture*. Just accusers should dread the strictness of the law, 631. *Criminor* is sometimes used passively by authors, 631, 632. Crisconius Afer, bishop, complains about churches and goods taken from his parish, 916. Crispus, son-in-law of Phocas, 663. Crotona, or Croto, a city formerly of the Bruttii in Magna Graecia, 601, 602. There are two cities of this name, 358. The visitation of the Church of Crotona is entrusted to John, bishop of Squillace, 600, 602. Crotona on the Adriatic Sea, captured by the Lombards, 872. Why the apostate angel is called cruel, 49. Who is said to hand over his years to the cruel one, 49.

*Cross.* The sign of the cross was very frequently used by ancient Christians, 196. By the sign of the cross, sight was restored to a blind man, ibid. A glass vessel was broken, 216. Poison that had been drunk caused no harm, 288. Serpents were killed, 356. The sign of the cross was miraculously impressed upon bread, 204. The efficacy of the sign of the cross, 197, 202. A small cross with pieces of Saint Peter’s chains is sent, 618. A piece of the wood of the Lord’s cross is sent to Rechared, 1031. Oil formerly flowed from the wood of the Lord’s cross and was sent as relics, 924.

A *cubicularius* is one who attends the bedchamber or the threshold, 868. It is sometimes called the secretary of secrets, ibid. A *cuculla* is called a *melotes* and a *cappa*, 225. What a *cuculla* is, 1093. From what *culcitra* derives its name, 1092. What it means to “strain out a gnat,” 92. The power of high office is a storm of the mind, 10.

*Fault.* There are three modes of fault: suggestion, pleasure, and consent, 85. What it means to weep over a fault, 87. Which faults are remediable and which irremediable, 472. Lesser faults that are denied are not to be punished, 667. A son must not be burdened by his father’s fault, 717. Faults are to be avenged not in substances but in persons, without hope of profit, 535. Fault is signified by blood, 1027. It is a fault not to punish certain faults, 1263. Nature produced all human beings equal, but fault places some below others, 20.

Cumae, formerly a city of Campania, 587, 588, 606. The visitation of the Church of Cumae is entrusted to Benenatus, bishop of Misenum, 587, 588. The Churches of Cumae and Misenum are united, 606. Liberius, bishop of Cumae, 587. Cumquodeus, abbot in Africa, 884. Desire is the root of all evils, 1007.

*Care.* The mind occupied with external cares forgets on the journey where it was heading, 5. The mind knows how to think many things without knowing that it does so, ibid. The anguish and anxiety of minds occupied with secular business, 152. The more someone advances in the care of secular affairs, the more he declines in the love of God, 520. Rivers overwhelm those whom the activities of this age confuse through disturbance of mind, [Col. 1496] 849, 875. How harmful care for secular affairs is to a pastor, 24. With what caution a pastor should attend to temporal matters, 514. What a city curator is, 1001, 1257. Cures, the principal city of the Sabines, 638. The punishment of a certain unchaste *curialis*, 421. Who the *curiales* are, 421, 675. *Curiales* are called the lesser senate, 421. Those subject to the curia are not to be ordained, 704.

*Cumin.* Why Christ reproached the Pharisees for tithing cumin, 92. *Cypriana* or *Cyprianica* is the name given to Saint Cyprian’s feast, 594. *Cypriana* also signified either a terrible storm or winter, ibid. Cyprian, a deacon and rector of Sicily, 670. He is ordered to gather and preserve the Church’s vessels scattered throughout Sicily, 695, 696. The property of the Church of Lilybaeum is entrusted to him for examination, 755. Various affairs were entrusted to him by Gregory; see the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

Cyriacus, abbot, 925, 928. He was sent to Sardinia to convert the Barbaricini, 702, 703. He is ordered to introduce monks into the monastery built by Theodosius, 727, 728. Cyriacus is sent to Syagrius and commended to Serenus, bishop of Massilia, 1006. Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople, assumed the government, being more inclined toward the quiet of contemplation, 848. Having become bishop, he sent Gregory the customary synodical letter, 850. He was elected long after John’s death, 853. Gregory rejoices over his election, 847, 851, 853. Cyriacus was exceedingly solicitous in administering ecclesiastical affairs, 853. He is praised, 854, 878. Against Gregory’s wishes, he retains the title “universal bishop,” while communion is maintained, 984, 1246. Gregory urges him to abandon this title, 850, 878, 879, 1246. Gregory admits Cyriacus’s representatives to communion but does not wish his own deacon to communicate with Cyriacus, 881, 882. Cyriacus, through the profane designation “universal bishop,” either commits or follows the sin of pride, ibid. After faithfully performing service for Peter the subdeacon, Cyriacus is appointed defender, 593.

Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, is regarded as catholic at the Council of Chalcedon, 968.

## D

**Dalmatia.** Formerly part of Illyricum properly so called, 528. After the First Dalmatian War it was reduced to the status of a province, ibid. The bishops of Dalmatia are rebuked, 689, 690. They are forbidden to ordain the bishop of Salona without Gregory’s consent, 690. The form of the dalmatic, 1012. By whom the use of dalmatics was granted to deacons, 1011. It is permitted to the bishop of Vapincum and his archdeacon, 1012.

**Pope Damasus.** The fourth letter circulated under his name to Stephen and the bishops of Africa is spurious, 481. Hence it is false that the title *servus servorum Dei* (“servant of the servants of God”) was used by Damasus, ibid.

**The condemned.** How they always live and yet die without end, 376. From the day of their departure they are tormented by fire, 416.

**Daniel.** He is refreshed by a meal in the lions’ den, 252. He sees a terrifying vision, from which he is sick for many days, 333.

**Daratitii.** They are the people of the region of Dara, 560. [Col. 1497]

**To give.** *Dare* is used for transferring ownership, 637.

**Darida.** A Gothic commander, 157.

**Giving.** Ownership is acquired by giving; by delivery, possession alone is acquired, 637.

**Datitii.** Who they are, 560.

**Datianus.** See *Domitianus*.

**Datius.** Bishop of Milan drives demons from a house, 285.

**David.** In persecution he pleased God; in the leisure of peace he sinned, 5. He was more pleasing to God in service than when he attained royal power, 78. He is recalled to repentance by scourges, 5. David is rebuked by Nathan, 37. He humbly hears the correction of his subjects, 28. David signifies the humble life of the saints, 36.
