David plays the harp to cure Saul’s madness, ibid. Why David spared Saul in the cave, 39. What the repentance signifies when he cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak, ibid. David represents good subjects, ibid. Although a prophet, David, deceived, condemns Jonathan’s innocent son, 172. Why David’s sin of pride was punished by the slaughter of the people, 855. He did not maintain concord with the wicked, 69. How David asserted that he knew God’s judgments, 241, 244. He acknowledges that his sins were forgiven him through repentance, 969. Why, unwilling to drink the water brought to him, he poured it out as a libation to the Lord, 1029, 1131.

**To owe.** What it signifies in Gregory, 213, 359.

**Debtors.** Various penalties were imposed on debtors by laws and emperors, 670. The holy Fathers teach that they should be treated more mildly, ibid. Formerly debtors were forbidden the clerical state and every honor, 676. Gregory wished them to be able to become monks, 675. Later he changed his opinion, 676. Debtors of the treasury: see *Fiscus*.

**Decanica.** Appendages of a church are so called, in which clerics were sometimes detained, 527, 759. Decanica must not be confused with ecclesiastical enclosures, 527.

**Tithes.** The Church’s tithes are not to be given on lease only to clerics, 606.

**Decimata.** A cask or measure, 541.

**Decius.** A Forensis priest and bishop of Lilybaeum, 1059, 1089. He attempts to reform his church, 801. His case is entrusted to John, bishop of Syracuse, and Leontius, the former consul, 1077.

**Decrees.** The decrees of the ancestors must be observed, 618, 619, 637. The decrees of St. Gregory, 1288.

**Dedication.** Churches were customarily dedicated with the relics of martyrs, 341, 571, 638, 808, 826, 828, 897, 947. Alms were given to the poor at the dedication of a church, 548. Banquets were formerly customary at a dedication, 549. A basilica is not to be dedicated unless its lawful and secure endowment has first been established, 571, 577, 897, 995. Basilicas occupied by heretics and handed over to Catholics are consecrated anew, 637, 638. If there is legitimate doubt concerning a church’s dedication, it is to be consecrated, 1279.

**To defend.** Nothing is safer for defending oneself than purity, 47. Minds continually surrounded by deceptive defenses are signified by fortified cities, 48.

**Defensor.** Who the defenders of the Church were, and what their office and institution were, 193. Formerly defenders were either civil or ecclesiastical, 247. What the duties of defenders of both kinds were, ibid., 517. A *defensor* is called a procurator or syndicus, 517. Some were judges, ibid. Defenders were requested from the emperors, ibid. Under Gregory, defenders devoted themselves not so much to ecclesiastical interests as to relieving the needs of the poor, 547. Defenders are listed among the lesser ecclesiastical orders, 639. Dignity in the presbyterium was granted to defenders, 593. The formula for appointing a defender, 756, 944, 1120. The office of defender was assigned by letters-patent, 979. Those who usurp the name of defenders are restrained, ibid. Who should be chosen as defenders, 756, 979, 1120. There was a school of defenders, 1121. When the clergy or bishop was lacking, defenders administered the Church’s property, 951, 1059. The sons of defenders were not to marry outside the estate in which they were born, 1197. Gregory honors seven defenders with the rank of regionaries, 905. What their privilege was, ibid.

Various duties performed by defenders at Gregory’s command:

- Concerning the relief of the poor or their defense against oppression, 528, 547, 556, 891, 993, 1178.
- Concerning the distribution of alms, 502, 506, 541, 548, 549, 554, 707, 714, 793, 796, 823, 912, 956, 1105, 1182, 1186, 1210.
- Concerning the defense of the oppressed, 1082, 1104, 1209.
- Concerning the redemption of captives, 654, 820, 868, 1210. Gregory permitted the vessels of the Church of Fano to be sold for the redemption of captives only in the presence of a defender, 859.
- Concerning the administration of hospices, 1187, 1207, 1259, 1261.
- Concerning the defense of widows, 626, 822, 1103.
- Concerning orphans, 1044.
- Concerning those oppressed by debt, 670, 723.
- Concerning the administration of Church property or the defense of its rights, 525 and following, 533, 553, 554, 557, 558, 592, 623 and following, 659, 695, 735, 755, 901, 944, 931, 961, 1004, 1041, 1045, 1088, 1188, 1208, 1234, 1261, 1273.
- Concerning the Church’s tenants, 734, 920, 944, 980, 981, 1241.
- Concerning various ecclesiastical affairs, 637, 746, 807, 819, 837, 866, 926, 978, 991, 999, 1171, 1172, 1234.
- Concerning the election of bishops, 503, 639, 645, 649, 653, 753, 755, 889, 990, 1053, 1094, 1177.
- Concerning bishops, 632, 1261. A defender assists a bishop in reforming the condition of the Church, 801, 1234. He relieves an impoverished bishop, 1105.
- Concerning the correction of bishops, 808, 976, 977, 1047, 1048, 1235, 1236, 1262, 1263.
- Concerning cases involving bishops, whether for discussion or judgment, 649, 650, 946, 961, 1059. A case between a bishop and a defender concerning Church property, delayed in litigation, is entrusted to another defender to conclude, 1059, 1060.
- Concerning clerical cases, 1072, 1171, 1172. Sometimes defenders sat as judges with bishops in clerical cases, 961, 980, 1041. How clerics were to be protected by defenders, 980, 981, 1120.
- Concerning the punishment of criminal clerics, 759.
- Concerning priests, whether to be judged or kept in office, 546, 1044, 1243.
- Concerning monks and nuns, whether to be assisted, corrected, or kept in office, 529, 530, 544, 545 and following, 569, 590, 760, 761, 901, 1046, 1055, 1137, 1182, 1206, 1256.
- Concerning abbots, 640, 1260.
- Concerning monasteries, 555, 571, 590, 685, 686, 761, 867, 946, 947, 950, 981, 1042 and following, 1043, 1050, 1053, 1056, 1061, 1089, 1260.
- Concerning the settlement of lawsuits, 496 and following, 648, 1098, 1121, 1183, 1189.
- Concerning defendants subjected to penalties, 654, 685, 1139.
- Concerning heretics or Jews, 733, 912, 973, 974.
- Concerning wills, 946, 947, 956, 960, 961, 989, 1044.
- Concerning various secular affairs, 619, 955, 964, 1004, 1082, 1104, 1106, 1197, 1212, 1274.

[Col. 1498] A case involving one defender is entrusted to another defender for judgment, 974.

**Defenders:** Boniface in Corsica, called the first of the defenders, 905, 1177. Bonitus, 1206. Candidus, 707. Eugenius the notary, 976. Fantinus of Palermo, 723. Felix the subdeacon, 976. Hadrian the notary, ibid. Hilary the notary, 1089. John, 1252, 1255, 1256. Optatus, 1243. Pantaleo the notary, 1094. Peter, 1197. Sabinus, 649. Scholasticus, 1101. Sergius, 901. Sisinnius, defender of the Church of Messina, 897. Symmachus, 545. Vitalis, 926. Vitus, 1120. See all of these under their individual headings. See also *Rectores patrimoniorum*, under the heading *Patrimonium*.

**To fix one’s hand with an outsider.** What this means, 38.

**The deceased.** Prayers for the dead occur frequently among the ancient Fathers, 464. See *Sacrificium*. It is safer for each person to act for himself while alive than to hope that others will act after his death, 472. The pious wishes of the dead are not to be annulled, 689. Whether the dead should be mourned: see *Mortui*.

**To cast down.** Whoever is raised up is cast down, 1027.

**Delegated judge.** An ecclesiastical delegated judge is a subdeacon, 647. Who may be delegated as judges, ibid. Minor cases may be delegated, 630.

**Dolphins.** Candlestands placed in churches were decorated and supported with dolphins, 555.

**Demetianus.** The property of Demetianus, an orphan, although bound to the Church, is restored to him, 638, 639.

**Demetrianus.** A cleric of the Church of Fermo, 943.

**Demetrias.** A city of Thessaly, 629, 630.

**Demetrius.** Bishop of Epirus, 796. Demetrius, bishop of Naples, 500. He was deposed for serious crimes, ibid., 572. Demetrius, a deacon of the Church of Thebes, was handed over to the proconsul to be tortured, 628, 630.

**Denarius.** Why all the laborers receive only one denarius, 429. In former times six thousand denarii made one solidus, 648. Forty denarii made two ounces of silver, ibid.

**To send down from heaven.** To send down manna, rain, and so forth is a manner of speaking familiar to Gregory, 1111, 1112.

**To depose.** One who invades another’s place must be deposed, 581. One unjustly deposed must be restored, 1264.

**Deposit.** A deposit must be returned, 1044.

**Dertona.** See *Tortona*.

**Desideria.** An abbess, 1217. Good desires should not be postponed, 589. To desire to advance toward what is better is a gift of God, 885. He who granted the will will also grant the strength to obtain it, ibid.

**Desiderius.** Bishop of Vienne, deposed through Brunhild’s agency by episcopal judgment and buried under stones, 831. Gregory commends Candidus to Desiderius, 832. Desiderius asks that the pallium and privileges granted to his predecessors be confirmed, 1019. He is rebuked for teaching grammar, 1140 and following. He is excused, ibid. See the alphabetical index of the letters.

**Idleness.** The effects of mental idleness, 55, 56. The vain excuses for this vice, 55.

**Betrothed women.** When betrothed women enter a monastery, the things taken from them must be restored, 867. Formerly, if a betrothed woman wished to enter a monastery, she was required to return double what she had received, 868.

**Desusceptum.** This signifies a *chirographum*, a record or list of things received—a catalogue, 661, 662, 696, 886, 951, 1047, 1075.

**Detraction.** With what disposition detraction should be heard, 860, 1093, 1126 and following. How greatly God permits detraction for the benefit of the elect, 1128. What detractors gain, 1093. In what manner they ought to make satisfaction, ibid., 1128, 1129.

**God.** What God’s left hand and right hand signify, 77. God’s enemies prosper in his left hand and are broken in his right, ibid. What it means to stand before God, 82. God sometimes speaks in human fashion, 1069. What it means to see God’s back parts, 967. Invisible beings render invisible service to the invisible God, 380. Divine power fills all that he has created, 380. Nothing is hidden from God, 789. Why God is said to descend in order to learn what had been done in Sodom, 860. How God knew that Abraham feared him, 1069. Before God innocence is lost, since sin is committed in desire before his eyes, 52. In God there is one will of the Father and the Son, 61. We ought willingly to submit to God, to whom all adverse things are subjected unwillingly, 329. Almighty God, by breathing upon or fulfilling the things that subsist by reason, both gives life to and moves invisible things, 381. Human will must humbly accommodate itself to God’s providence, 517. God alternately punishes and consoles human beings, 1239. Who belongs to God and who does not, 76. No one can please both God and wicked people, 1066.

The wondrous mercy of God toward sinners, 82, 969. Before sinning, he warned human beings what they should and should not do, 82. After sin, he called them back to the recovery of grace, ibid. How great our hope in God’s mercy should be, 85. God often washes away the sins of the heart more quickly when he does not permit them to emerge in deeds, 86. How easy forgiveness is, 86. We must always trust in God’s mercy and fear because of our weakness, 292. God’s mercy shines forth in scourges and blows, 385. God must not be declared so merciful that he is proclaimed deceptive, 449. Who suppose that God’s justice can be bought, 65. It belongs to divine justice never to leave unpunished the one who in this life never wished to be without sin, 449. The pious God is not nourished by the torment of the wretched, but the just God will never cease forever from avenging sins, ibid.

**Deusdedit.** Bishop of Milan, 1206, 1238. He is elected bishop, 1094. St. Gregory’s concern over his ordination, ibid., 1095. Deusdedit, a venerable old man, very close to Gregory, 420. Deusdedit the shoemaker is rewarded by God for his almsgiving, 436. Deusdedit is restrained for oppressing a widow, 627.

**Δευτεράριος (*Deuterarios*).** What it signifies, 155.

**Right hand.** The right hand signifies eternal blessedness, 77.

**The devil.** He is called the prince of the earth, 679. Devils are incorporeal, 417. The devil sinned through envy, 46. What it means for the devil to creep in the serpent, breast, and belly, 61. Devils are tormented by corporeal fire, 417. The devil’s pride brought about our destruction, 59. The devil has no power over a human being except what has been granted by God, 316, 329. The devil sometimes enters the human heart, 884. The devil attacks secretly, 789. He fights more fiercely against those who are watchful and resisting, 885, 965, 1030, 1099. Under the appearance of piety he seeks to overthrow people, 1008. He deceives human beings through dreams, 456. Nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity, 71. The greater gifts he sees in human beings, the more subtly he seeks to take them away through ambushes, 1030. What must then be done, ibid. He deceived Adam through the woman, 744. He stirred up the woman against Job, ibid. His cunning in temptation, 773. He hinders good intentions as much as he can, 589. He seduces a repentant man with the blandishments of a destructive sense of security, 85. He is always present both in bodily deeds and in our thoughts, 325. Sometimes he foretells many true things so that at the end he may deceive the soul with falsehood, 457. Those whom he cannot drive to sin, he tears apart by pretending that their opinions are false, 596. He attacks the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep so that he may capture the flock more easily, 611. The malignant spirit is continually intent upon our thought, speech, and deed, 325.

The devil, in the form of a blackbird, suggests an impure thought to St. Benedict, 213. In the form of a black child he distracts a monk from prayer, 221. In the form of a serpent he tries to frighten the monk Martin, 316. In the shape of a pig he leaves a church newly dedicated to God, 344. The devil is driven from bodies, 165, 193, 196, 210, 261, 289, 328, 352. The devil is driven from places, 285, 344. He is permitted to enter a pig, 328.

The devil’s sons are those who sow quarrels, 71. They are to be pursued by all who possess zeal, since they become helpers of the malignant spirit, 679.

**Diaconate.** This word signifies the archdiaconate, which belongs exclusively to a deacon, 504. Who were called cardinal deacons, 501. Many deacons were promoted to the episcopate, 644, 645, 646, 653, 657, 1064. Why formerly deacons were for the most part raised to the episcopal office, 681. The authority and arrogance of deacons, ibid. Deacons should devote themselves to preaching and almsgiving, 1288. Deacons are forbidden to sing in church, 1288. When deacons began to sing the Gospel during the solemn celebration of Mass, 1289.

A deacon of the Church of the Marsi, struck down by a Lombard sword, is handed over to the demon by whom he had been struck, 405. A captive deacon is to be redeemed at the expense of his church, 654. A deacon ordained at Rome has no permission to leave and go elsewhere, 763. There were seven regionary deacons at Rome, 937. They were subject to the archdeacon, ibid.

**Diaconiae.** Places in which the regionary deacons maintained the poor, widows, orphans, and others, 756, 937. *Diaconiae* also means almsgiving itself, 1109, 1111. It also means the collection made for the sake of the poor, 1111. The name *diaconia* is given to chapels and oratories of hospital houses, 756. The prefects of the *diaconiae* were called cardinal deacons, ibid. Diaconiae existed not only at Rome but also in other cities, 756, 1054. Gregory orders that the grain withheld from the Neapolitan diaconiae be restored, ibid.

**Diaconicum.** What it is, 504.

**Diatypōseis.** Among the Greeks, definitions of faith are called *diatyposes*, 720. *Diatyposis* also means a mandate or decree, 1054, 1055.

**Didymus.** Why Didymus of Alexandria was called *Chalkenterus* (“Bronze-gutted”), 1036.

**Day.** When the day will be perfect, 1026. Why a day is called joyful, 1070. On Sunday the body may be washed when necessity requires it, 1214. Constantine was the first to enact a law concerning abstention from work on that day, ibid. What work is forbidden on that day, ibid., 1215. See *Antichristus*.

**Dignities.** Dignities should be fled from in one’s heart, although they must sometimes be undertaken unwillingly, 7, 875. What must be done so that one does not deceive oneself in seeking a dignity, 9. Humility is endangered at the summit of dignities, 21. Those who stand on high should fear a fall, 83. Humility must be maintained in the heart, and the dignity of rank preserved in honor, 771. Why the dignities of the world should be despised, 875. It is not places or ranks that bring us near to our Creator, but good merits, 879. See *Honores*.

**Love.** Love is the mother and guardian of the virtues, 610. Love has its own authority, 888. Care for feeding the flock is evidence of love, 6. See *Charitas*. Gregory gave *Dilectio* (“Beloved”) as a title to priests and deacons, 644, 657, 740, 746, and elsewhere; to abbots, 1136, 1137, 1177, and frequently elsewhere; and also to bishops themselves, 1265, 1271, 1272. No one can love those whom he does not wish to see, 911. What things are to be loved, 1077.

**Letters of release.** Formerly letters of release were not in use, 501, 600. Formerly laymen could be ordained by any bishop without letters of release, 566. Clerics appear to have been promoted to sacred orders without letters of release, 723. By privilege, the bishops of Constantinople and Carthage admitted clerics under another’s jurisdiction without letters of release, 566. According to present usage, letters of release are required only from the bishops of the place of origin, ibid.

**To forgive.** If we do not forgive from the heart, even what had been forgiven is required of us, 473.

**Dinah.** A type of the sluggish soul deceived by the devil’s arts, 85. The allegorical and tropological explanation of Dinah’s abduction, 679.

**Diocese.** Sometimes the word denotes that ecclesiastical province of which Rome was the metropolis, 1020.

**Diptychs.** One tablet was for the living and the other for the dead, 719. Names were recited from the diptychs as a sign of communion, ibid.

**Barefooted house.** What it signifies, 7.

**Discipline.** The rights of discipline must be exercised in such a way that piety is not abandoned, 23. The practice of canonical discipline is called the medicine of correction, 657. It is proper to discipline to prohibit what is illicit and beneficially cut away excesses and faults, 954. Discipline must not be neglected, ibid., 957. In preserving discipline against heretics, bishops must not disagree among themselves, 732. The ancient discipline of the Church was almost destroyed when the stewards of the Church had died out, 640. When divine discipline crushes someone, adding human scourges is superfluous, 597.

**Discord.** By what arguments those who do not preserve concord should be opposed, 68, 69. God rejects the offerings of those who are at odds, 69, 473. The evil of discord, 71. Discord is hostile to God, 504. It generates scandals, 572. Discord must be feared especially when outward peace supplies it with an escort, 671. The sacrifices of prayers are stained by dissension, 880.

**Discernment.** Discernment is expressed by the nose, 11, 90. Discernment is greatly necessary to physicians of both bodies and souls, 97, 98. How much discernment is necessary in examining dreams, so that illusions may be distinguished from revelations, 457. Discernment is necessary for a priest in preaching, 511. Discernment must be observed in the virtues, 514. The remarkable discernment of prelates in punishing, 669. Discernment must be observed in correcting the wicked, 1177. See *Correctio*.

**Losses.** *Dispendia commodalia*, that is, losses of temporal advantages or goods, 551.

**Dispensations.** Through frequent dispensations canonical discipline is weakened, 657. The canons are wounded and brought into disrepute, 1265. [Col. 1501] *Dispensatio* sometimes means the same as administration, 992, 993.

**Strict.** *Districtus* has the same meaning as “strict” or “severe,” 739.

**The rich.** What should be said to the rich, 36. A proud rich man should often be gently exhorted, ibid. A rich man should be struck skillfully by his own sentence, ibid., following the example of Nathan rebuking David, 37. It often happens that a rich man is humble and a poor man proud, 36. The dreadful end of the proud and pleasure-loving rich, 440. Why riches and glory are placed on the left, 77. The lover of riches does not obtain their fruit, 65.

**Doclea.** A city, 1201, 1202.

**Docleatinus.** Bishop Paul, 1201.

**Teachers.** Why teachers in Scripture are called prophets, 17, 510. How they are rebuked for seeing false things, 17, 510. What it means for teachers to take bricks for themselves, 31. Why they are ordered to describe Jerusalem on the brick placed before them, ibid. The speech of teachers must be formed according to the capacity of the hearers, 33, 34. Teachers are signified by the poles of the ark, 34. Teachers of souls are called guardians of vessels, 213. Let life commend doctrine, 15. Doctrine is the nurse of the virtues, 43.

**Learned.** Why the address of a learned man is useful, 916. The less patient a person is, the less learned he is, 43.

**Bites of sorrow.** They are signified by wine, 23. Sorrows in this life impel us to love heavenly things, 770.

**Household servants.** There were many kinds of household servants, 1081.

**Dometius.** An abbot and priest, 949.

**Domitius.** A distinguished man, 1197.

**Domna.** Abbess of the monastery of St. Stephen in the territory of Agrigento, 912.

**Domnellus.** An administrator, very dear to Gregory, 988. Gregory consoles him when he is ill, 1032. See the alphabetical index of the letters.

**Dominica.** 493, 714. She is called the superior of a certain monastery, 877. Dominica, the wife of a certain John, returned to the unity of the Church, 886.

**Dominicus.** Bishop of Carthage sends Gregory a congratulatory letter on his ordination through two bishops, a deacon, and a notary, 609. Dominicus was Gregory’s friend, 1181. His zeal against the Donatists, 731. At the African Council he pronounced a stricter sentence against bishops who neglected heretics, 731, 732. Dominicus’s charity and pastoral solicitude are praised, 806, 807. His reverence for the Apostolic See, 921. Gregory asks for Dominicus’s prayers and promises him his own, 806, 807. See the alphabetical index of the letters.

Dominicus, bishop of Centumcellae, 499. Dominicus the priest is sent to preside over a church in the diocese of Atella, 577, 578. Dominicus, a cleric of the Roman Church, 816. Dominicus, a distinguished man, 1057. Dominicus, a secretary, 537. Dominicus appeals to Gregory on behalf of his four brothers, who, although redeemed from captivity, were still being detained, 868.

**Lord.** Which masters are to be admonished, 40. Christian masters who drive sick servants from the house are rebuked, 624. Masters are obliged to provide their servants with the means of salvation, 703. The owner of property differs from its possessor and tenant or lessee, 696. The owner does not consent to a monastery being founded on his estate, lest he be deprived of the revenues of the taxable estate, 695.

**Domitianus.** Bishop of Melitene, of the Church of Arsancia; [the text is materially uncertain here: “Arsanctae Ecclesiae consuetudo diversa, meniae”]; a kinsman of the emperor Maurice, 678. He is praised, ibid. He is appointed guardian of Maurice’s sons, 678. Although occupied with secular affairs, he meditates on the Scriptures, 680. He preached the Christian faith to the Persian emperor, 680. Whether he is the same person elsewhere called Datianus, 740. Gregory asks him to sympathize with Gregory in his distress, ibid. See the alphabetical index of the letters.

Domitianus, a bishop in the East, is rebuked because, at Cyriacus’s ordination, he had shouted, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” 854.

**Domitius.** A priest and abbot of the monastery of Lucusianum, 1136. Domitius, a distinguished man, 1197.

**Donadeus.** A deacon who is guilty of disgraceful conduct is to be thrust into penance, 1186.

**Donation.** A direct donation must be made between living persons, 1211.

**Donatists.** They rage against Catholic priests and rebaptize those who have been baptized, 612, 714, 715, 716. The Donatist faction revived for three hundred years, down to Gregory’s time, 715. Catholic bishops offered Donatist bishops their own chairs and sees so that they might return to the unity of the Church, 972. Gregory arouses the zeal of Pantaleo and the bishops of Africa against the Donatists, 715, 716. He orders a council to be convened against them, ibid. He wishes to learn their crimes more fully so that he may suppress them more securely, ibid. Gregory complains that the laws enacted against the Donatists are being neglected, 841. Bishops must not allow the children of Catholics or their slaves to be baptized by Donatists, 822. Maximanus, bishop of Pudentiana, because he permitted another Donatist bishop to be ordained in his city, must be deposed, 611.

**St. Donatus.** Bishop of Arezzo in Etruria, he is venerated as a martyr, 180. The bishop of Euria is permitted to place the body of St. Donatus in the fortress of Cassiopium, 1265, 1272. Under what condition, ibid. St. Donatus, abbot and disciple of Facundus of Hermiana, goes to Spain, 614. Donatus, an African bishop, 609. Donatus, a priest of Catania, 900. Donatus the archdeacon is judged unworthy of the episcopate because of his faults, 776, 777. Donatus, an official of Theodore, duke of Sardinia, 543. Gregory asks that he be brought to trial with the abbess Juliana over possession of a monastery, ibid. A certain Donatus is commended by St. Gregory, 1104.

**Gift.** The gifts of God bestowed upon us, 73. The work proceeds from the gift, not the gift from the work, 168. In God’s judgment, it is not what is given but by whom it is given that is considered, 1029. In the case of heavenly gifts, one must both rejoice with fear and fear while rejoicing, 1110. We must not take such delight in God’s gifts that we prefer the things given to the giver, 1115.

**Donus.** Bishop of Messina. The pallium is granted to him, 798. He is admonished to restore to his church the things he was unjustly retaining, 806, 877. See the alphabetical index of the letters.

**To sleep and to doze.** How they differ, 38. What it means to sleep in the middle of the sea, 90. What it means for prelates to sleep and doze, 38.

**Back.** Who are called backs in the body of the Church, 3. Whose back is bent, ibid. The sinners who build upon the back of the Shepherd, 29, 1135.

A dragon tries to devour a monk at death but is driven away by the prayers of the monks, 440. Another man is devoured by a dragon, 441.

**Droculfus or Droctulfus.** A Lombard who defected to the Roman side and is commended, 568.

**Dromones.** Ships of great speed; hence their name, 1067, 1068. Who are called *dromonarii*, ibid.

**To be led.** We are led outside ourselves in two ways, 217.

**Dulcidus.** A deacon, 971.

**Dulcinus.** Bishop of Locri, 1063.

**Dulcitius.** Bishop of St. Anchimus, called bishop of Sabina; he subscribed to three Roman synods, 638.

**Double and duplicity.** How great the labor of duplicity is, 47. The duplicity of a person cunningly defending himself is signified by a hedgehog, ibid. What the particular evil of the double-minded is, 48. How great evils threaten the double-minded, ibid. Double hearts are expressed by lofty angles, ibid.

**Durandus.** Abbot of Troarn; in what year he flourished, 107. He cites Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on the body and blood of Christ, ibid.

**Duke.** In St. Gregory’s time, dukes were customarily placed in charge of entire provinces, 847.

**Dynamius.** A patrician of Gaul and rector of the province of Marseille, 493, 647. He administered the Roman Church’s Gallic patrimony, 647, 648. He ceased to care for it, 795. He installed no intruding bishop at Marseille, but installed two at Vence, 647. Whether, after losing his wife, he led a religious life with his brother, ibid. He devoted the remainder of his life to pious acts, 795. Dynamius and his sister Aureliana gave their house for the construction or repair of a monastery at Marseille, 858. Gregory urges Dynamius to persevere, 885. He sends him a cross filled with relics, 648. Why Dynamius was removed from every ministry, 795. Dynamius, 720.

**Dyrrhachium or Epidamnus.** A city of Macedonia, 898. The bishop of Dyrrhachium, Urbitius, 898, 983.

## E
Eboracum is not subject to the city of London, 1164. The Church of Eboracum long disputed the primacy, ibid. The Church is represented by the Ark, 33, 34, 1133 ff., 772, 850. It is signified by Gilead, 72. The woman who pours out the alabaster represents the holy Church, 924. Why the Church is said to dwell in gardens, 75. What it means for friends to heed the voice of the Church, ibid. The Church is the body of Christ, 68. Christ is the essential head of the Church, while the pope is its ministerial head, 773. In the Church’s earliest age, many preachers are recorded as having been sent into the provinces by St Peter, that is, by the Apostolic See, 526. The condition of the Church as the fifth century was declining and the whole of the sixth was passing away, 114. Outside the Church there is no unity, 895. The unity of the Church is called a place with God, 967. Provision is made for the unity of the Church, 577, 784. The unity of the universal Church is the bond of Christ’s body, 610, 772. With what gentleness one must deal with those returning to the unity of the Church, 500. Pagans returning to the Church are received differently from heretics, 503. In one faith nothing causes harm, [Col. 1503] 532. The Church is governed by canons, 1265. What it means to enter the Church through the door, 1133, 1134. Why divine dispensation has established different orders in the Church, 783, 784. Who in the body of the Church are the eyes and who the backs, 3. What the nose of the Church is, and why it is like the tower in Lebanon, 90. The connection of the members of the Church’s body, 610. Whether the Church consists only of the strong, 1133, 1134. All the saints before the Law, under the Law, and under grace together complete the body of Christ, 743. All the Apostles are members of the Church under one head, ibid. Under the bishop, the Church consists of clergy and laity, 666. The clergy are called the Church’s soldiers, 691. See Clergy. The laity are called the Church’s children, 666. See Laity.

The Church is one, formed from particular churches, 577. The mother or matricial Church, that is, the senior and cathedral church, is so called; its baptismal daughters are in a direct line, the others in a transverse line, 572. On the principal feasts, clergy and laity gathered at the matricial Church from the whole diocese, 579. Nothing can be established concerning the dignity of Churches and Sees from the sessions and subscriptions of synods, 1014.

Church property. The Church must not be enriched by shameful profits, 536. It must not covet another’s property, 553. Nor seize it, 655. Nor retain it, 595, 656, 941, 942. Whoever subsists on the Church’s revenues must not pant after private gains, 539. The Church’s property belongs to the poor, 638, 640, 834, 835, 1059, 1232. Those serving the Church ought to be supported from the Church’s resources, 700. The Church’s property must be spent either on repairing churches or supporting the clergy, 987. Or on ransoming captive clerics, 654, 696, 943. Formerly it was spent on receiving guests, 1059. The squandering of this property for the benefit of relatives is prohibited, 582. Ecclesiastical revenues are to be divided into four parts, 691, 737, 900, 1150, 1151. At times they were divided into five parts, 774. The fourth parts of both new and old ecclesiastical revenues are to be distributed according to the canonical division, 691. This distribution was made to the clergy according to each person’s merits, 760. Or according to his labor, 900. The Church’s property which a bishop had retained is to be divided, 1117.

Formerly, the administration of ecclesiastical property in the East belonged to presbyters, and in the West to archdeacons, 505, 581. The Church’s property must be administered by its own clergy, 774. A visitor is assigned to a widowed Church, chiefly to care for its temporal affairs, 564. See Visitor. The property of a deceased bishop is to be reserved for his successor, 564. In preserving and disposing of the Church’s property, the bishop must be diligent, 600. The estates of Churches were formerly exempt from paying tribute, 1017. The private property of clerics was formerly distinguished from Church property, 791. They could give or bequeath their own property, but not the Church’s, ibid. Nevertheless, while they lived, they could distribute their own property in moderation, ibid. The Church alone succeeds to property acquired by a bishop during his episcopate, 1105. The Church must suffer no loss in its property, 943. Whoever takes away Church property is to be punished, 1041, 1042. To retain bequests made to pious places is sacrilege, 1045. Church property that has been taken away must be restored, 696, 951, 982, 1041, 1045. Such restitutions must not be burdensome to those making them, 951. How the Church’s property is to be reclaimed, 1261. It must not be defended by force, 1289. The Church is to receive back what was taken from it without increase, 1153. Donations made to the Church but carrying burdens are to be returned, [Col. 1503] 1060. The law does not permit what has entered into the Church’s rights to be alienated, 947. Nevertheless, this law may sometimes be moderated for the benefit of the poor, 948.

Church unions: what the legitimate reasons are for making them, 495, 606, 607, 799. In how many ways such unions are made, 495, 496. To whom it formerly belonged to unite, divide, or enlarge churches, 607. The union of benefices is permitted to bishops, but the union of bishoprics is reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, 496. The churches of Cumae and Misenum are united, 606. The Church of the Three Tabernae is united to that of Velitrae, 614. The Church of St Anthemius is united to that of Nomentum, 638. The Church of Minturnae is united to that of Formiae, 495, 496. The Churches of Fundi and Tarracina are entrusted to one and the same bishop, 634. The Church of Carina is united to that of Reggio, 597.

No churches in Sicily or Italy were dedicated without Gregory’s consent, 826. No churches are to be dedicated unless a legitimate and secure endowment has been established for them, 571, 577, 897, 995. If there is legitimate doubt about a church’s dedication, it is to be consecrated, 1279. The bishop is given authority to consecrate churches, 1268. See Dedication. Public Masses are prohibited in certain churches, 986, 994. See Oratory. The immunities of churches. See Asylum. After committing a crime, entering a church was formerly prohibited, 421. Entering a church is compared with receiving the Lord’s body, ibid., 1161.

The wretched condition of a Church deprived of its shepherd, 563. A Church must not remain vacant for more than three months, 861, 890. How provision is to be made for a Church whose bishop falls ill, 641, 1217 ff., 1219.

The preservation of ecclesiastical discipline belongs to the bishop, 916, 917. The order of ecclesiastical rigor is confused if either illicit acts are rashly presumed or forbidden acts are attempted with impunity, 915. If, through negligence, one overlooks abuses that have been wrongly appropriated, a path to excess is opened for others, ibid. Order must be maintained in ecclesiastical affairs, 1022. If the entrance to an evil practice is not closed before it remains open for long, continued use makes it wider, 1023. See Discipline. Whoever abandons secular dress and hastens to ecclesiastical offices wishes to change the world, not leave it, 675.

Ecclesiastes, that is, Preacher, 376. In Ecclesiastes Solomon plays many persons, ibid. Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi, 1063. His prudence in choosing a bishop is praised, 1075. Winter clothing is sent to Ecclesius, who was suffering from the cold, 1211. Ecia, a woman, 547. Edancius, master of the soldiers, 544. Edilberht, king of the English, is asked to devote himself to propagating the Christian faith, 1164, 1165 ff. An inquiry is made about his name, 1164. Gregory calls him his son, though he was not yet converted, 1113.

ΕΓΚΛΕΙΣΤΟΙ (‘the enclosed’): what the Greeks call recluses, 966.

Pride. When the mind raises itself in thought, it provokes the judge’s anger, 5. A hidden thought of pride is punished by condemnation, 6. Those who guard against small things are driven by their very pride to commit greater ones, 92. The best remedy against pride is to consider what you are, 101, 102. To recall one’s own evils, 1030, 1110. All pride has nothing but ruin, 668. The devil drives one toward pride, 1030. From pride many branches of sin spring forth, 997. Pride punished in Eleutherius, a man of great holiness, 352. See Arrogance, Vanity.

The proud. The proud are signified by Saul, [Col. 1504] 36. How the proud should be admonished, 58. By what method the proud may usefully be corrected, 59. How they may be driven toward progress, ibid., 60. The proud should not be more freely reproved than is fitting, 59. The devil dominates the proud mind, 101. Under the guise of Jerusalem, the soul that takes pride in its virtue is rejected, 100. What happens to the soul that has swollen with confidence in its virtue, 101. The soul elated by its good works places its confidence in its beauty, 1030. It commits fornication in its own name, ibid. From the very point at which it is more beautiful, it descends, ibid. While the soul is lifted up by hidden swelling, it is deprived of the grace of the one who gave the gift, 1030. See Arrogance.

Election to ecclesiastical offices. See Election of a Bishop.

The elect: why they sometimes die harshly, 405, 408. We do not believe that all the elect are taken away, 368. The elect are promised not joys but bitterness and tribulations, 1127. For the elect, detraction is useful, lest they be lifted up by praise, 1128.

Almsgiving. Who should be admonished among those who give alms, 63. They must not exalt themselves in proud thought above those to whom they give earthly goods, ibid. They should know that the Lord has appointed them stewards of temporal resources, ibid. Let not arrogance lift them up, but fear weigh upon them, 64. What caution must be used in almsgiving, ibid. Against what vices those who give their possessions in alms must be fortified, ibid. Those who have redeemed sins by alms must not repeat them, 65. There are people who give their possessions to God and themselves to the devil, ibid. Who should be admonished: those who neither covet another’s property nor give away their own, 66. Such people engage in the killing of their neighbors, ibid. What we receive from the common Lord, it is just that we share in common with the needy, ibid. One excuse made by those who refuse alms, 67. The rich man was condemned not because he had seized another’s property, but because he had used his own fruitlessly, ibid. We must repay something to God, who gives us everything, in the person of the poor, ibid. Those who do not give what they have received imagine themselves innocent in vain, 66. By what admonition those who give alms from property seized from others are to be restrained, 67. Alms must not be made from theft, ibid. Whoever withholds from the needy what he gives to God is like one who sacrifices a son in his father’s sight, 68. Such a person puts gathered money into a perforated bag, ibid. It is one thing to give alms for sins, another to commit sins for the sake of alms, 1008. It is not to be considered almsgiving if what is acquired from illicit things is distributed to the poor, 1008. What sort of almsgiving pleases the eyes of the Redeemer, 1008. A bishop is rebuked for proclaiming his alms, 626. Nothing is more wretched than those in whom avarice arises from generosity, 67. Exhortation to almsgiving, 1185 ff. What remains is to be distributed as alms, 1152. Almsgiving is an act of justice, not of mercy, 66. Why whatever is given to the poor is not a gift but a loan, 1054.

Almsgiving makes fasting acceptable to God, 63. Through almsgiving a golden house is built for us in heaven, 433, 436. The poor are the workers who build this house, ibid. Almsgiving cries secretly into God’s ears, 874, 1124. Almsgiving is rewarded by God, 248. The fruits of almsgiving, 874. The usefulness of almsgiving on the last day, 433, 1185. Here almsgiving helps its author and, on the day of recompense, brings him both what he desires and a reward, 643.

The distribution of alms must be made wisely, 1117. They are not to be provided equally to everyone, 1148. Whether alms should be given to a sinful poor person, 65. They should first be given to the faithful, then to the enemies of the Church, 609. Alms offered from a desire for empty honor must not be rejected by those in need, 599. Things granted for a time as alms are not to be demanded as a debt, 985, 986.

The elevation of the wicked is ruin, 492. St Eleutherius the martyr appears to Probus, bishop of Rieti, as he is dying, 389. Eleutherius, abbot, 301, 328, 349. He was a man of remarkable simplicity and compunction, 349. By praying, he raises a dead man, ibid. He frees a boy from a demon, 352. The boy is afflicted again by the demon because of Eleutherius’ pride, ibid. He is freed again, ibid. Eleutherius obtains for Gregory, who was ill, the virtue of fasting, ibid. Eleutherius’ name is read in the sacred diptychs, 349. Gregory had learned from Eleutherius many of the things he relates in his Dialogues, 301, 328, 425.

The cult of Elijah was not disapproved, 652. A temple of Elijah was built by the emperor Zeno, ibid. In the Latin Church no feast day had been decreed for St Elijah up to the time of St Bernard, ibid. Elisha divided the waters of the Jordan with the cloak of Elijah, his master, 160. The spirit of prophecy did not always illumine Elisha’s mind, 249. What “eulogy” signifies, 687, 1063. The words of divine eloquence are divine banquets, 617. Elpidius, bishop of the East, is rebuked because at Cyriacus’ ordination he had cried out, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” 854. Elpidius, bishop of Catania and predecessor of Leo, 1055, 1056. “Eminence” is a title with which Gregory addresses judges, but not bishops, 1054, 1067. Emissarius is used for admissarius, 1207, 1208. The Church of Emolita, 1235. Enfide, the place where St Benedict first performed a miracle, 209. Ἐνώσις (‘union’): what it signifies, 495. What it means to place a sword upon the thigh, 90. Ephesus, the metropolis of Asia Minor, 857. The chapters of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus were sent to Gregory by John of Constantinople as genuine, 883, 884. Gregory suspects that the more recent manuscripts of the Ephesian synod were falsified, 802, 803. This corruption was made for the benefit of the Pelagians, 963, 965. Rufinus, bishop of Ephesus, 857. Epidamnus. See Dyrrachium. Epidaurus, a city of Dalmatia, 631. Florentius, bishop of Epidaurus, 631. Gregory was not unfamiliar with the writings of St Epiphanius, 851. Epiphanius, archpriest of Caralis, 931, 1260. Gregory orders that the accused presbyter Epiphanius be sent to him, 650. He is returned innocent, 706. Epiphanius was attached to the Roman Church as a deacon, 763, 764, 1248, 1262. Epiphanius, subdeacon, is sent to investigate the sedition raised against Paul, bishop, 623, 625. Epiphanius, lector of the Church of Caralis, asked that a monastery be built in his own house, 1107. Epirus is twofold, Old and New, 796.

The episcopate. How the episcopate is called a good work, 9. How desiring the episcopate is praiseworthy, 8. Some, in seeking the episcopate, seek not the ministry of a good work but the glory of honor, 9. How great its burden and danger are, 489, 490. More priests perish than are saved, ibid. The burdens of the episcopate must neither be sought presumptuously nor rejected obstinately, 521, 621. Whom the canons reject from the episcopate, 573. “Episcopate” is the name of a work, not of an honor, 621. The union of bishoprics is reserved to the Roman pontiff alone, 496. What distinction there is between the episcopate and the honor attached to it, 495. What an episcopium is, 894. The episcopium is entrusted to the deacon Anatholius, vicedominus, to administer according to his judgment, 498. Formerly a bishop could scarcely obtain permission to change his episcopium or see, 894.

Bishop. What the name “bishop” signifies, 621. What it means for a bishop to have an empty name, 817. A proper and titular bishop is called a cardinal priest, 501, 634, 635. By “priests” bishops are almost always understood, 613. Formerly the same men were called bishops and presbyters, 635. In Gregory, a bishop is scarcely designated by the name presbyter, ibid. Bishops are fathers in name, 613. How bishops in the Church are stars and clouds in heaven, 743. They are called rams, 765. They are members of Christ, 1006. From whom they must not be separated, 1007. They are called strong souls, 1133, 1134. The eyes of the Lord, 1276. Bishops were formerly called apostolic, 764. The dignity of bishops seems to surpass other dignities, 1020. Bishops who profess themselves bishops through the favor of the Apostolic See: what they intend, 526.

Election of a bishop. How election differs from postulation, 602. “To elect,” “to request,” “to postulate,” and “to desire” are used in the same sense, 634. Yet to postulate is more than to request, ibid. The election of a bishop belongs to the clergy, the nobles, the order, and the people, 572, 601, 634, 635, 639, 642, 644, 741, 753, 755, 808, 865, 866, 1064, 1086, 1087, 1094. Whence princes possess a right in the promotion of bishops, 700. In episcopal elections the emperor’s consent was sometimes employed and required, 585, 586, 699. The supreme pontiff’s consent was also employed, 585, 586. The Roman pontiff was formerly confirmed by the emperor, ibid. Whether bishops subject to the Roman pontiff ought to be confirmed by the emperor, 700. At the election and ordination of bishops the people acclaimed, 853, 854. It is neither new nor blameworthy for the people’s votes to be divided into two parties when a bishop is being elected, 1086.

As far as possible, the bishop should be chosen from the bosom of the very Church that has been widowed, 588, 601, 863, 989, 995, 1052, 1229. If no suitable person is present, what must be done, 1229. It is a grave reproach to the clergy when a bishop is not taken from their midst, 1087. Gregory orders that bishops be taken from the clergy or monasteries, 303. An inquiry must be made into the life and morals of those to be chosen as bishops, 1095, 1188, 1228, 1229, 1268, 1269. The examination of those elected as bishops was sometimes entrusted to other bishops before their ordination, 865, 866, 889, 1064. Sometimes it was entrusted jointly to a subdeacon who administered an ecclesiastical patrimony and to a bishop, 1053. Gregory asks that two or three men from the Neapolitan clergy be sent to him to elect a bishop on behalf of all, 649. He asks the Syracusans to send two men whom they had elected to the episcopate, so that he might ordain whichever he judged more useful, 588, 753. The Lilybaean clergy receive permission to elect a bishop, whom they later asked Gregory to consecrate, 801. The election of a bishop must be made at the Church’s expense, 639. A mind bound by desire does not examine with free judgment the person it ought to prefer, 644. Gregory urges the citizens who are about to elect a bishop to repentance, 645. By what revelation a bishop’s election ought to be made, 755. Why every patronage must be excluded from an election, [Col. 1506] 639. Gregory excludes Donatus, recommended by a patrician, from the episcopate, 777. What disposition the electors ought to have, 644, 645. Unanimous agreement is required among them, 565, 572, 573, 585, 586, 639, 642, 646, 690, 1094. In an election, the dignity of life and morals must be considered, 539, 642, 644. According to the merit of the peoples, persons are ordinarily provided as shepherds by divine judgment, 645. Gregory does not dare to solicit the election of a man especially known to him, 644. The electors must not seek their own advantages, 644, 753. The electors must please God in their actions, 645. Rewards must not intervene in an election, 639, 786. Nor venality, 753. Nor favoritism, 643. An elected man becomes unworthy of the priesthood through payment, 786. A bishop is not to be elected for another vacant Church but postulated, 602.

Which bishop should or should not be elected: just as the place of government must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee it, 848, 1007. No bishop is to be given to one unwilling, 573, 700. Who are rejected from the episcopate by the canons, 753. Laymen, whatever their merit, must be kept away from the episcopate, 601, 602, 722, 782, 786, 808, 863, 989, 995, 996. And neophytes as well. See Orders. The one elected must be chosen not for generosity in distributing rewards but for worthiness of merit, 753. Whoever does not possess long-standing bodily continence must not be elected, 1086. Nor one who practices usury, ibid. Nor a simple man, ibid. Nor one whose life is blameworthy, 1064. Nor one subject to crimes, 889. He must know the Psalms by heart, 777, 1064, 1269, 1270. He must possess knowledge of Sacred Scripture, 785, 786, 1228. Ignorance of the canons is blameworthy in a bishop, 585. He must devote himself to psalmody and prayer, 1188. Now the way to the episcopate seems closed to the poor, 649. Whether formerly one was required to ascend to the episcopate through each grade of the orders, 1065.

Ordination of a bishop. Whether a bishop can be ordained by only one bishop, 1155. How many bishops must be present as witnesses at a bishop’s ordination, ibid., 1156. That ordination is legitimate when it has been examined with the approval of all, 573. Why a Gospel book is placed upon the head of the one being consecrated during the consecration of bishops, 1228. The punishment of bishops ordained contrary to the canons, 1250, 1251. The punishments of those who ordain bishops contrary to the canons, 1250, 1251. The elected man is to be ordained if none of the offenses punished by death in the Heptateuch is found in him, 865. Newly ordained bishops used to send letters of communion to other bishops, 541, 542. The anniversary of a bishop’s ordination was formerly celebrated with solemn ceremony, 737. Bishops driven from their sees by barbarians were incardinated in vacant Churches, 563, 600. What was to be done with them if they recovered their first see, ibid. In St Gregory’s time, the bishops of Sicily and of the other provinces of Italy were consecrated by the Roman pontiff, 486, 587, 601, 639. Gregory forbids the bishop of Salona to be ordained without his consent, 690.

The rights, privileges, and dignity of bishops. Obedience is owed to bishops, 645. What kind, 1100, 1102, 1278. All bishops are equal according to the measure of humility, unless guilt requires distinction, 976. In councils, bishops are to sit and subscribe according to the time of their ordination, 1013. Gregory is careful not to injure the rights of bishops, 529. Moved by just reason, he sends a presbyter into another diocese, 577, 578. Gregory so defends his own rights that he wishes the rights of the Churches to remain unharmed, 611. He wishes to honor bishops in every respect, [Col. 1507] ibid. He considers that he would injure himself if he disturbed the rights of his brothers, 619. Other pontiffs defend the rights of bishops, 619. No bishop remains in the Church if one person holds the name of universal bishop, 773. If each bishop’s jurisdiction is not preserved, the ecclesiastical order is confused, 1120. With what mind Gregory wished the privileges of bishops to remain unharmed, 800. Whether it is less fitting for bishops to be judged by a simple cleric, 647. A bishop consecrates a monastery at the command of the metropolitan, 1229, 1268. A bishop is disapproved for consecrating an oratory in another diocese, 1230.

The conduct of bishops. What the irreproachability of a bishop is, 8. A bishop who does not know how to obey the sacred canons, administer at the sacred altars, or receive communion: whether he is worthy, 631. What a bishop’s table ought to be like, 580. The differing opinions of St Martin and St Ambrose concerning banquets, ibid. Reading must not be absent from the bishop’s table, 856. A bishop is rebuked for proclaiming his alms, 626. It is far from the priestly office to pant after money out of a desire to accumulate it, 760, 774, 775. Bishops have much to fear from their familiars, 743, 744. Excessive credulity is harmful to bishops, 860, 1249. Let them beware of duplicity, 739. The sins of bishops are the cause of many evils, 747, 1020. A bishop must remove the scandal he has caused, 1100. A bishop must live as an example to the rest, 610, 1020. Wicked men must be removed from the bishop’s company and household, 1101.

The virtues and duties of bishops, 610, 840. In everything they do, bishops must attend to God, 586. A bishop must show canonical obedience to his primate, 735. Nothing is more splendid on a bishop’s neck than humility, 666. A person is established in the rank of the episcopate for this purpose: to bring the souls of others back to humility, 742, 744. A bishop advances insofar as he does not strive to exalt himself by disparaging his brothers, 742. Through the humility of bishops, the concord of all the brothers and the unity of the universal Church are preserved, 742. Let him hold humility in his mind and preserve the dignity of his order in honor, 771. Humility is the elevation of the priestly office, 665. Injury must neither break a bishop’s steadfastness nor turn him from the path of truth, 625. He must endure even unjust correction with the greatest patience, 665. He must embrace brothers and enemies alike with the heart of charity, 840. He must abound in wisdom, 509. He must possess a twofold charity, toward God and neighbor, ibid. All his virtues must be adorned with charity, ibid. He must flee human favor, 509. What a bishop’s moderation ought to be, 739. He must be innocent and learned alike, 621.

The duties of bishops, 586, 634, 644, 677, 708, 798, 840. Useful admonitions for bishops, 739, 785, 788, 797, 902, 1012, 1014. A bishop assumes the name of shepherd not for rest but for labor, 586, 587. Bishops must prove themselves fathers in affection and in action, just as they are fathers in name, 586, 613. In Scripture they are called not so much rulers as shepherds, 963. A bishop is called not to rule but to serve the whole Church, 1123, 1124. Whoever loves to be first and not to be useful is not a bishop, 621. The Lord’s field has been entrusted to bishops, 840. How they are to labor for the Lord, 610. Bishops are shepherds from whom the Lord expects the multiplied fruit of the flock, 562. The Lord approved bishops not through the prerogative of a higher rank but through the merits of their works, 562. They must provide imperishable gifts of souls for the Judge who is to come, 587. They must attend to the gain of souls, not to the advantages of the present life, 600. They diligently care for their order if they strive to draw others to its author, 618. They must bring not only heretics back to the Church but also those within the Church back to uprightness of life, 618. As honor increases, concern, vigilance, and the merits of life must also increase, 781, 787. The priestly prerogative is an honor to the diligent but a burden to the negligent, 586. It is an insult to priests to have to be admonished about divine worship, 684. A bishop must dispense the ministry of the word assiduously, 575, 576, 610. He should draw his subjects to love rather than fear, 586, 587. He must show priestly affection to the people, 825. He must rescue those who have fallen into guilt, 902. He must show the way of return to those who have gone astray, ibid.

A bishop must strive for the unity and concord of the peoples, 1005, 1073. He must not readily believe evil, 1249. How he should conduct himself in quarrels and disputes, 1135. He must help the afflicted, 527. He owes his neighbor love and compassion in infirmities, 598. He must come to the needs of the people with pious compassion, 681. A bishop must know that he is a father, not a lord, 587. Pride is blameworthy in a bishop, 735. Episcopal consolation must be present for converts, 950. What the honor and genius of bishops require, 1236.

The duties of bishops toward the needy, widows, orphans, and oppressed. It belongs to bishops to console desolate widows and support them with priestly protection, 499, 551, 627, 822. To help the afflicted, 527, 821. Orphans and widows, 551, 638. Bishops have been granted the task of defending before emperors and kings the cases of poor and oppressed widows, 627. The administration of pious resources was formerly entrusted to the care of bishops, 706. A bishop who is sparing toward the needy has an empty name as bishop, 817. He must administer not his own property but the property of the poor, 1232. It is fitting that pontifical assistance be present for those suffering need, 707, 760. A bishop must bring help to the harassed and oppressed, 910, 950, 1034, 1035, 1066, 1068, 1076, 1082, 1084, 1085. How bishops ought to defend the property of the poor, 1059, 1232. By what method they ought to console those struck with lashes, 1087, 1088. They ought to intervene on behalf of defendants, 949. Nevertheless, ecclesiastical patronage must not be extended indiscriminately to everyone, 948. It is execrable that what was preserved by the kings of the nations should be said to have been taken away by bishops, 831. Bishops driven from their sees by enemies are to be received by other bishops for the support of their life, 540. Formerly the care of guests belonged to bishops, 1059, 1116, 1151, 1269.

The duties of bishops toward the Church. For the people’s offenses, a bishop is chosen by the Lord as an intercessor, 507, 813. He must govern the Church according to the canons, 563, 585. How he should conduct himself toward the good and the wicked, 672. He must not lack diligence, 787, 902, 903. He must be diligent in preserving and disposing of the Church’s property, 600, 1235. He must defend the Church’s jurisdiction, 825. And also its children and affairs, 946. A bishop summoned to a synod must come; if prevented by illness, he must send a presbyter and a deacon, 784. What bishops ought to do in synods, 985. They must call those who have gone astray back from the truth of the faith to the Church, 673. The African canons urge bishops to care for heretics, 731, 732. Heretics are more effectively defeated when concord among bishops is preserved, 732. How a bishop should conduct himself toward those who have gone astray, 1073. Toward idolaters, soothsayers, and sacrilegious persons, 982. A bishop who neglects to root out idolatry is said to be guilty of sacrilege, 909.

The mutual duties of bishops and clerics, 1263. A bishop must keep his clerics in office, 981, 982. He must maintain discipline among them, 704, 707, 739, 1151. He must not burden his subordinate clerics beyond measure, 1231. The correction of clerics belongs to the bishop, 668. And their cases as well, 667, 1071, 1120 ff., 1178. How disagreements between a bishop and his clerics are to be settled, 1199, 1200. A bishop must provide what he has promised his clerics, 1249. In clerical cases, he must investigate the truth in the presence of the senior members of the Church, ibid.

The duties of bishops toward monasteries. A bishop must watch over monastic discipline, 780, 1021, 1046, 1055, 1056. A bishop is severely rebuked because he allowed a virgin to leave the monastery and return to the world, 900. A bishop must supervise the conduct of monks, 922. He must not defend wandering monks, 884. He must provide protection for monasteries, 815, 921, 922, 1049, 1055, 1063, 1074. He must administer the cases and interests of monasteries, 981. He must preserve unharmed the privileges granted to monasteries, 1019. He must neither burden monasteries himself nor permit them to be burdened by his clerics, 498, 816. He must have no jurisdiction in a monastery beyond ordaining the abbot who has been elected, 604, 997, 1056. He must not inventory the property of monasteries, 603. He must not celebrate public Masses in monasteries, 604, 826. From there he must not take monks into holy orders or the clergy against the abbot’s will, 604. He must not presume to perform there any ordination, however minor, ibid. See Exemptions of Monks. When a bishop was driven by barbarians from the monastery he governed, another was entrusted with its governance, 528.

The duties of bishops concerning cases. The cases of clerics, monks, and religious persons belong to bishops, 667, 799, 800, 1071, 1072. Whether Gregory appointed a bishop as judge in cases involving his own clerics, 667. A case concerning boundaries arising between two abbots is entrusted to the bishop for settlement, 887. In delivering judgments, a bishop must not be rash, 594, 597. If one of the disputants suspects the bishop, he himself must provide that party with a judge, 780, 897. He must not weary litigants with delaying tactics, 780. In judging cases, no circumstance and no influence of persons should suspend a bishop from the pursuit of equity, 904. He must not refuse to endure hatred for the sake of truth, ibid. He must finish cases without provoking the envy of others, 914, 942. The zeal for equity and uprightness of justice must kindle the bishop, 916. Between guilt and innocence he must show himself careful and strict, ibid. The bishop’s judgment must be obeyed, 1063. Punishments for bishops who judge contrary to the canons, 1251.

The bishop must correct faults and excesses, 585, 732, 904. A bishop who is negligent in punishing crimes is rebuked, 693. Why he is bound to correct those who are near him, 663. Whoever fails to correct what must be corrected seems to consent to the one who is going astray, 1020. Bishops must fear silence, 1051. He must correct vices promptly, 681. Whatever deserves punishment must be brought forward not for imitation but as an example of correction, 1010. Priestly indignation must be mixed with the sweetness of virtue, 681. Bishops are shepherds, not persecutors, 664. A bishop’s novel and unheard-of preaching demands faith through beatings, ibid. Wounds must first be touched with a gentle hand before they are cut away, 742. Let it be far from a priestly mind to be moved by private zeal in another’s case, 812, 814. The priest’s anger, like smoke, envelops all the inner parts it has occupied, 812. Some things he must correct gently; some things that cannot be corrected he must tolerate with equanimity, 1135.

The zeal of bishops when mortality is imminent or raging, 502. A bishop must be strict in zeal for discipline, 586, 856. He must not be silent but cry out, 523. He must diligently watch over the souls entrusted to him, 600. He must imitate earthly shepherds, 612. He must observe the sacred canons, 663, 664. His tongue must contain speech, and his mind the fervor of zeal, 840. His tongue must be fiery, ibid. How grave an evil it is not to resist iniquity at its beginning, 715, 716. The honor that a bishop received for preaching the truth he abandons more securely for that same truth, when necessity demands it, than he retains it, 774. To undo what has been well ordered is hostile to the good morals of priests, 905. The negligence of bishops is censured, 586, 587, 836, 900, 1021, 1235, 1236, 1263.

How harmful to a bishop is concern for secular affairs, 24. Following Moses’ example, they must not serve earthly business, 25. Secular business is to be tolerated out of compassion, never sought out of love, 26. A bishop must withdraw from administering temporal affairs, and many benefits will follow, 640. He must recognize that he has undertaken care not of earthly things but of souls, 928. He must not usurp what belongs to laymen, 985. Secular concerns make a bishop contemptible, 1047, 1048, 1235. Some bishops are recorded as occupied with menial services, 1048. Formerly the cases of Christians were heard before the bishop, 491.

How necessary residence is for bishops, 564. What a bishop’s residence ought to be like, 575. How it is to be secured, 640. Some bishops hated their dioceses and regarded constant residence in them as a kind of exile, 575. A bishop is compelled to reside; if he does not obey, he is to be thrust into a monastery, 809. The bishops of Gaul are forbidden to travel farther without the authority of their primate, 783, 785. The bishops of Sardinia could not cross the sea without letters from their metropolitan, unless they appealed to the Apostolic See against that same metropolitan, 933. Bishops must not go to the imperial court but send deacons there, 556. They could not go to the imperial court without letters from their primate, 975.

The transfer of episcopal sees is to be made only for greater reasons and not without the authority of the supreme pontiff, 578. Nor without the consent of the prince,
ibid. Agnelius of Fundi, expelled by the enemy, was transferred to Terracina, 633. Unless necessity compelled it, formerly a bishop was not permitted to change his lodging or episcopal residence, 894. For what reasons a bishop may be granted permission to exchange houses, 1262.—A bishop who has become involved with a concubine is deposed and assigned to penance, 656. What women bishops were permitted to keep in their homes, 976, 977.—The union of bishops is something the devil fears, 797. The unity of bishops strengthens the unity of the Church in the faith, 850. Concord among priests is necessary, 1010. The peace of the commonwealth depends upon the peace of the universal Church, 747.—The cases of bishops must be investigated with great care and vigilance, 975. They must be brought to an end without delay, 1084. How cases arising between bishops are to be concluded, 783, 784. Gregory appears to assert that the cases of bishops have been entrusted to him, 752. Bishops are to be judged in synod according to the canons, 567, 612, 632. Or certainly by twelve bishops, 631. This was the practice of Saint Gregory and of the Roman and Gallican Churches, 567. Emperors entrust a bishop’s case to another bishop for judgment, 627. [Col. 1509] Even a pecuniary case, 629. But they entrust the examination of a criminal case to a bishop while reserving judgment to themselves, ibid. A bishop is judged jointly by the emperors and legates of the Roman See, 630. Gregory reserves minor cases of bishops for his representatives, but major ones for his own decision, ibid. Gregory orders accused bishops to come to Rome either to clear themselves or to be judged, 557, 650, 793, 811. Whoever refuses to appear is to be judged contumacious, 793. Certain cases of bishops are summoned to Rome by Gregory, 809, 810, 839. Gregory orders the bishops who had communicated with Maximus, an intruded bishop, to come to him so that they may receive absolution, 864. He permits accused bishops to present themselves before the emperor in order to clear themselves, 846. Cases of bishops entrusted to other bishops, 821, 822, 902, 916, 936, 983, 991. Cases entrusted jointly to secular judges and bishops, 623, 975, 976, 1077, 1078. Whether it is fitting for a cleric, subdeacon, or anyone inferior to bishops to be appointed their judge, 647. The case of Victor, bishop, is entrusted to Abbot Marinianus and the notary Benenatus for judgment, 642, 643. If Victor is guilty, he is to be confined in a monastery, ibid. A bishop’s case is entrusted to a subdeacon for examination and decision, 647. The case of another bishop is entrusted to other bishops and to one subdeacon, 961, 962. The conduct of the bishop and priests of the Church of Pisaurum is entrusted to the deacon Castorius for examination, 755, 765. Execution of the sentence against a bishop is assigned to a chartularius, 983. Bishops are permitted to appeal to the Apostolic See against their metropolitan, 933. A bishop is to be judged neither by bishops of another council nor by a secular judge, 1253, 1254. If the metropolitan or patriarch is unavailable, judgment is to be given by the Apostolic See, 1254.—The accusation of bishops. A deacon who has been removed from office cannot testify against a bishop, 629. Clerics who were initiated into sacred orders in order that they might desist from accusing a bishop are to be restored to their former rank, 780. Whether clerics and laymen may accuse their own bishops, 780. Unlawful accusers of a bishop are to be rejected, 846, 1254. The persons accusing a bishop must be investigated carefully, 1251. Whoever insults a bishop in church is to be punished with capital punishment, 1252 and following. Injuries inflicted upon bishops are avenged, 623, 630.—The correction or deposition of bishops. A bishop is suspended from the celebration of Mass for two months because a woman was beaten at his command, 656, 657. A bishop is to be deposed for simony, 612, 1199. If, while constituted in sacred orders, he has intercourse with a concubine, he is to be deposed, 656, 657. A bishop intruded into another’s place is to be removed from every ecclesiastical ministry, 699, 1250, 1256. Those who ordained him are to be deposed, 699. Or, deprived of communion, they are to perform penance in a monastery, 1250, 1251, 1256. How the bishop who is ordained in the place of a deceased intruded bishop is to be regarded, 1250, 1251. How those bishops are to be regarded who, out of fear of a judge, condemn and depose another bishop, 1250. A bishop deposed not by law but by authority is to be recalled from exile, and his case is to be examined by bishops, 631. The case of a bishop to be deposed must be weighed with particular rigor, ibid. A bishop is not to be deposed except for just causes and with the unanimous consent of the bishops, 631. He is to be deposed for crime alone, 1217, 1218, 1219. A bishop ought neither to be promoted nor deposed by a single bishop, 861. Four bishops are to be employed for deposing a bishop, 979. One deposed from the episcopate cannot be recalled, 890. If he dares to aspire again to the episcopate, he is to be confined in a monastery, 1202. A bishop is not to take away the property of the episcopate, 1041. It is exceedingly impious if a deposed bishop is subjected to the necessity of receiving alimony, 665. According to the Council of Chalcedon, deposed bishops retain the dignity of the episcopate and the necessary subsidies, 495. It is one thing for a bishop to be restored to his own see and another for him to be restored to honor, ibid.—A bishop is not to be substituted in another’s place unless that person has been degraded, 522, 572, 980. See above, “The deposition of bishops.” The canons forbid giving a successor to a living bishop, 1022, 1023. A bishop is not to be deposed on account of illness unless he himself wishes it, 1135, 1218. Or unless he has requested it in writing, 1136, 1219. A bishop deposed on account of illness is to be supplied with expenses from the same Church, 1218. What is to be done when a bishop is ill and unable to perform his office, 641, 1135, 1217, 1218, 1219. A bishop is to be ordained as quickly as possible in the place of the deceased, 550, 753, 755, 990. The canons forbid a Church to remain vacant for more than three months, 861, 890. Gregory does not wish a bishop to be ordained in the place of a schismatic unless the schismatic is first admonished to return to his Church, 935.—The property and wills of bishops. After a bishop’s death, an inventory of his property and that of the Church is to be made without charge, 639, 691, 692. An account of the administration of the property of a deceased bishop is to be rendered to his successor, 640. The wardrobe or clothing property belonged not to the bishop but to the Church, 649. Formerly the property of a deceased bishop was plundered by laymen, 738. To whom the inheritance of a dead bishop belongs, 1105. A bishop may make a will concerning hereditary property or property acquired before the episcopate, 717, 791, 990. The opposite is true of property acquired during the episcopate: he can neither bequeath, alienate, nor sell it, 717, 791, 1063, 1206, 1207. If, while alive, a bishop has diminished the property of his Church, it must be restored from his own property, 755. Wills made by a bishop to the detriment of the Church are invalid, 791, 792, 990. If a bishop has children, he cannot make a will in favor of the Church concerning property acquired before the episcopate unless the legitimate portion of the children is preserved, 717. A bishop who, not content with his own stipend, also accepts a grain allowance from the treasury is censured, 774. The bishops who refused to use the lodgings offered them by Augustus at the Council of Ariminum are praised, ibid.—African bishops speak with their tongues cut out in defense of the truth, 348, 349. Two of them are deprived of this favor because of the sin of lust, ibid. Gregory promises a synodical letter to the patriarch of Constantinople, 490. He sends one to Anastasius of Antioch, 517. Formerly, patriarchs who had recently been ordained sent synodical letters concerning their faith to one another and to the other patriarchs, 490, 515. Whence this custom had arisen, 515, 516. What are called letters from equals, 507, 508, 563, 661, 830, 831, 834. What the parts of a letter are, 507. Gregory’s letters: see Gregory’s Works and Preface. Why the rich man in the parable asks that his tongue be cooled with a drop of water, 61. He is said to have been condemned not because he had seized what belonged to others, but because he had used his own property fruitlessly, 67. There he receives evils more fully because here he had not been converted through blessings, 78. Saint Equitius, father of many monasteries, 164. Harassed by severe temptations of the flesh, he obtains continence through prayer, ibid. He keeps monks away from conversation with nuns, 165. By a word he heals a feverish handmaid of God, [Col. 1511] ibid. He frees another woman from a demon, ibid. Not initiated into sacred orders, he preaches after receiving a divine mission, 168. Purity of life accorded with zeal for preaching, ibid. With what equipment he traveled about preaching, ibid. Clerics complain to the supreme pontiff about his preaching, ibid. By whom he is summoned, 169. He cuts iron, ibid. He wears nailed sandals, ibid. He foretells the future, 172. The Roman pontiff, divinely admonished, allows Equitius to preach freely, ibid. His tomb is protected from irreverence by a miracle, 173. Upon invoking the name of Equitius, monks are freed from the Lombards, ibid. Equitius, a Roman citizen, entrusts his son Maurus to Saint Benedict, 220. A rabid horse healed by a miracle, 197. Ericius has a pit for the reprobate, 48. One resembling Ericius who acts deceitfully, 47. Erogatores and Erogatorii: whence they are so called, 608, 998. One must resist error at its birth, 716. Because of error, let us not hate the person, nor because of the person love the error, 772. To blush: “Whoever is still made to blush is loved less,” 1231. Locusts expelled from a garden by a miracle, 189. Esychia, 493, 877. What “to be with oneself” means, 217. Etherius was not bishop of Arles but of Lyons, 839. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. He is called bishop of Arles, 1287. The Eucharist was formerly placed upon the chest of the dead in the tomb, 255, 256. Giving the Eucharist to the dead was prohibited, but not placing it upon their bodies, 256. The custom of preserving the Eucharist and carrying it on journeys, 358. The reality of the Eucharist, 472, 1161. The Eucharist given as viaticum to the dying, 273, 397, 425. It was customary for the kiss of peace to precede reception of the Eucharist, 357. Church law forbade approaching the Eucharist after lawful intercourse, 194. How much bodily purity the Eucharist requires, 1161, 1162. The Eucharist was sometimes used for canonical purgation, 598. Eucherius, a monk of Lérins and later bishop of Lyons, 1101. Who the Euchites, the heretics, were, 802. Gregory greets Eudocia, 493, 877. Eudoxius, bishop of Germanicia, invader of the sees of Antioch and Constantinople, 851, 883. From him came the Eudoxians and Eunomians, 851. What he did on behalf of the Arian heresy, ibid. Why Gregory did not wish to list him among the heretics, 851, 882. How Gregory could have said that the Roman Church had hitherto known nothing about the Eudoxians, 883. Eudoxius refuted by the Fathers, 884, 919. Eudoxius is called “the glorious man,” 589, 912. Eugenius, deacon, 1210. Eugenius, notary, 976. Eugubium, formerly a city of Umbria, 995. Gaudiosus, bishop of Eugubium, 995. Eulogiae, 1137. Eulogia means the same as blessing, 1249. The eulogia of Saint Mark, 1248. Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, a man distinguished for piety and learning, 770, 771. Very dear to Gregory, 836. His zeal in attacking heretics, 888, 918. Gregory attributes the conversion of the English to his prayers, 918, 919. [Col. 1511] Eulogius is called an instrument of God, 1065. A minister of truth and a follower of Peter, 1069. He wrote against the Agnoetae, 1065, 1069. Why he did not reply to Gregory’s letters against John of Constantinople, 837, 990. He requests from Gregory Eusebius’s book on the deeds of the martyrs, 916. Gregory sends him gifts, 837, 888. He requests his prayers, 1064, 1065, 1071. See the alphabetical index of the Letters, and 1288. Eumorphiana, also called Orphiana or Orphiaria, an island of the Tyrrhenian Sea, 544. Why a letter is written to the rector of Campania concerning the monks inhabiting it, ibid. Eumorphius died after the death of another had been foretold, 428. His vision is explained, ibid., 429. Who are called eunuchs in Scripture, 83. Eupaterius, master of the soldiers, 930. Eupator, duke of Sardinia, 1191. Euplus, begotten by a bishop before ordination, is ordered to have his mother’s and father’s property restored to him, 717. Euplus, tenant, 537. Euphemius receives sacred orders in order to abandon an accusation, 780. Why he is permanently deposed from such an order, ibid. Euria, a city of Epirus, 1266. John, bishop of Euria, 1271. Peter, lector, ibid. The calamity of Europe in Gregory’s time, 748. Eusanius, bishop of Agrigentum, 717. Why, after Eusanus’s lapse, all his property ought to remain with the Church, ibid. Eusebia, daughter of the patrician Rusticiana, 911, 1239, 1240. Gregory greets her, 589, 724. Eusebius, an abbot, is excommunicated by the bishop of Syracuse, 594, 597.
