At Gregory’s urging, the bishop restores the abbot to favor and communion, 599. Because he rejected both, Eusebius is accused of pride, ibid. Gregory orders one hundred solidi of gold to be given to him, 596, 599. Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, published a two-volume work on the acts of the martyrs, 918. The first volume has been lost, ibid. In Rome, in Gregory’s time, there were no copies of this book, 916. Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica, 898, 983. He is encouraged to promote peace, 1073 and following. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Eutherius is called “a man of magnificent memory,” a title of honor that is not appropriate for a bishop, 497, 498. Euthymius: why he gave Saint Gregory the surname “Dialogus,” 107. Eutychius, bishop of Tyndaris, 672. He is encouraged to persevere in converting worshipers of idols, ibid. Eutychius, prefect, 1205. Saint Eutychius, a man of holy conduct in the province of Nursia, 308. His zeal in bringing souls to God, ibid. He is elected abbot, ibid. His miracles after death, 313. Several Churches in Italy were consecrated under his name, 313. Among Christians it was formerly customary to hang the Gospel around the neck as a means of protection and safekeeping, 520, 1272. And to place it upon the head, ibid. The Gospel was placed in the midst of judicial proceedings, 906, 907, 961. See “Judgment.” Formerly the Gospel was read in the Church by lectors, 1289. Formerly it was permitted to swear by the four Gospels, 1300. See “Oath.” Evangelus, a captive deacon, is ordered to be freed at the Church’s expense, 654. His daughter was violated by Felix, 654, 655. [Col. 1512] Evasa, an island now called Ivica, 431, 432. Eventius, a deacon of Milan, 972. What it means “to exact the canon,” 420. To pay the exactions, the Corsicans sold their children, 768. Exactions made with sin are of no benefit, 769. Gregory forbids the Church’s tenants to be harassed by unjust exactions, 534, 535. Unjust exactions from the Church’s tenants do not contribute to the Church’s advantage, 536. What an exarch is and what his dignity is, 521. Whether an exarch was the same as the prefect of Italy, ibid. Longinus was the first to obtain the name of exarch, 521. Why he is called the exarch of Ravenna, ibid. Exarchs sent into Italy by Maurice inflicted greater harm upon the Italians through incompetence and greed than the enemies themselves had done, 1238. Which persons were formerly called exarchs among bishops, 548. Monks also had their own exarchs, ibid. Who are said to “exceed with their hands,” 1079. “Excellence” is a title of honor used by Gregory toward kings, queens, exarchs, and other men of the highest rank, 506, 686, 712, 999, 1123, and frequently elsewhere. To whom excommunication pertains, 581. Whether the excommunication of offenses established in the Rule of Saint Benedict is canonical, 253. What distinction there is between excommunication and anathema, 613. Whether excommunication should be employed to avenge a personal injury, 613. Excommunication is to be imposed after a second and third warning, 619. The punishment of excommunication must not be inflicted upon the innocent, 642. Unjust excommunication does not bind, ibid. It is an ancient institution that those excommunicated by one bishop are to be avoided everywhere by others throughout the world, 707. One must not communicate with the excommunicated, 813, 814. Whoever, having been forbidden communion, received the Eucharist was struck with anathema and separated from the body of the Church, 817. Those whom Gregory deprived of communion he did not wish, if the danger of death pressed, to be deprived of viaticum, 899, 926, 980. Provision is made that priests should not release monks from excommunication, 955. “Ex-consul” refers either to one who had held the consulship or to one who had been created ex-consul by a codicil, 489, 520, 557. It was merely an empty name of honor, 620. Who the count of the Excubitors was, 520, 1044. “To be excused on no occasion,” that is, to have no opportunity for an excuse, 972. “Exemplare” means to copy from an authentic original, 507. The righteous owe an example of virtue to their neighbor, 95, 185. Examples move more than words, 152. How useful the examples of the saints are, 153. Let the pastor follow the examples of the saints, 508. The chief reason for exemptions was the oppression of subjects, 498. See “Monks.” “To exhibit” means to present oneself or another person, 1002. Exhilaratus, bishop of Sicily, 1262. Exhilaratus, 726. He is called secundicerius, 880. Exhilaratus, carrying two wooden vessels to Saint Benedict, hides one of them, 245. What happened to him, ibid. Ἔξοδος [exodos], expense, expenditure, income, 406. An outlaw, that is, one who refuses to obey the laws, 929. “Experience” is a title with which Gregory addresses the subdeacons who administer patrimonies, [Col. 1513] 497, 541, 653. And notaries, 1056, 1061, and frequently elsewhere. “To complete” means to explain, 677. Who is called an ex-prefect, 527. “In execution,” that is, in carrying out orders, 789. An executor is one who carries out another’s orders, 169, 897. Exile was formerly decreed against clerics by ecclesiastical judgment, 1172. Now it pertains to royal authority, 1173. Exsuperantius, bishop, 1239. Extranea, a handmaid of God, to whom Gregory orders a pension to be assigned, or the donation she made to be returned, 539. Outsiders are to be gently drawn to the faith, not compelled, 1226. Hezekiah, when showing foreigners the storerooms of his spices, why he incurred the anger of God, 5. Ezekiel represents the person of those set over others, 29, 31. Why Ezekiel is called “son of man” before he is led to contemplate heavenly things, 101, 102.

# F

**Fabius**, bishop of Firmum, predecessor of Passivus, 943.

**Face.** What it means to stand before the face of God, 82. Before sin, God admonished the human race face to face, 82. But by sinning, humanity turned its back on God, ibid.

**I do / make.** *Se fecit*, that is, “he went” or “he departed,” 609. *Facio* and *facesso* have the same meaning, ibid.

**Facundus**, bishop of Hermiana, wrote to Justinian concerning the Three Chapters, 614.

**Falerina**, Bishop John, 1291.

**Good reputation**, good odor, 924.

**During a famine**, God came to the aid of the monastery of Saint Benedict, 248.

**Fantinus**, defensor and administrator of the patrimony of Palermo, 974; defensor of Naples, 1050. He was called Faustinus, 911. Why the monk’s testament in favor of Fantinus was valid, whereas Sirica’s testament in favor of a hospice was not, 539. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

**Fanum.** There were many Italian towns of this name, 609. *Fanum Fortunae*, called simply *Fanum*, a bishop’s town in Umbria, ibid., 610, 827. Bishops of Fanum: Leo, 826; Fortunatus, 859.

**Fanum.** See *Temple*.

**Fasagnates**, patrician: at what time he governed Armenia, 493.

**Fausiana.** See *Phausiana*.

**Saint Faustinus**, martyr: he ordered Valerian, a dissolute patrician [one descriptor uncertain], to be removed from his church, 460.

**Faustinus**, a soldier of the Church of Meria, 886. He complained that his father had left certain properties to the Church of Messana which were subject to another jurisdiction, 896.

**Faustus**, former praetor and chancellor, 555, 1121, 1122.

**Faustus**, magnificent man, 1057.

**Faustus**, son of Constantius the defensor, 951.

**The favor of rulers**: how much is acquired through labors and anxieties, and how it is maintained, 875. Human favors are like smoke, 1066. No one can please both God and wicked people, ibid.

**A feverish girl**, healed by a word, 165.

**Felicianus**, priest, 571.

**Felicissimus**, deacon of the Church of Lami, 566.

**Saint Felix of Nola** leased three meager *iugera* of farmland, which he cultivated with his own hands, violating the letter but not the sense of the canons, 606.

**Pope Felix III**, the great-great-grandfather of Saint Gregory, [Col. 1513] 397. He warned his paternal aunt in a vision of her approaching death, ibid.

**Felix**, bishop of Acropolis, to whom the visitation of three churches was entrusted, 605.

**Felix**, bishop of Messana, 528. He consulted Gregory about many matters, 1274. Gregory replied to him, 1276. This reply is attributed to Saint Gregory, 1275. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

**Felix**, bishop of Pisaurum, 826. Gregory forbade him to celebrate public Masses in the monastery, ibid.

**Felix**, bishop of Portus, 947, 1288, 1291. He was born in the province of Sabina, 460. Gregory had learned many things from him, which he reports in the *Dialogues*, ibid., 464. Gregory gave him John, a servant of ecclesiastical law, 110.

**Felix**, bishop of Sardica: because he was unwilling to obey his primate, he was accused, 735, 736.

**Felix**, bishop of Sipontum, 546. The visitation of the Church of Canusium was entrusted to him, ibid. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

**Felix**, a bishop sent by Gregory to Sardinia to convert the Barbaricini, 702, 703. He was ordered to introduce monks into the monastery founded by Theodosius, 727, 728.

**Felix**, a deacon who returned from the schism to the Church; Saint Gregory commended him to the bishop of Syracuse, 694, 695.

**Felix**, subdeacon and administrator of the patrimony of the Appian region, 976, 1273.

**Felix**, defensor, 653.

**Felix**, abbot to whom Gregory ordered that one thousand five hundred pounds of lead be distributed, 544, 545.

**Felix**, superior of the monastery of Fundi, 161.

**Felix**, a nobleman in the province of Nursia, 168.

**Felix**, a man of consular rank: Saint Gregory commended him, as *chartularius*, to Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, 587. He was a magnificent man in Sicily, 941, 942, 955. He complained about John, bishop of Syracuse, 959, 960.

**Felix**, husband of the noblewoman Viviana, 528.

**Felix**, tenant of the noblewoman Campana, 539.

**Felix of Orticello**, 627.

**Felix**, nephew of Felix, bishop of Sipontum: whether he was a cleric, 654. He was ordered either to marry the deacon’s daughter whom he had violated or to be punished in a monastery, 654, 655.

**Felix**, heir by marriage, appointed by a woman named Rustica, 946.

**Women**: what admonitions should be given them, 35.

**Thigh.** What it means to place a sword upon the thigh, 90.

**Ferentia**, a town in Etruria whose episcopal see was later transferred to Viterbium, 189.

**Ferentium**, bishop Martianus, 1291.

**Ferentinum**, a bishop’s town in Latium, 367. Bishops of Ferentinum: Boniface, 184 ff.; Redemptus, 368; Luminosus, 1291.

**Ferocinatus**, a legate of the Roman Church, 1105.

**Iron**: what it signifies, 32. What iron is made in the furnace, 53. Iron brought back from the depths of the water, 224.

**Festus**, bishop of Capua, despised by his own people because of his greed, 648.

**Fesulae**, formerly a famous town of Tuscany, 1075.

**Stench** signifies carnal desire, 436.

**Golden brooch**, a gift of great value that the emperors used to bestow, 896.

**Fig tree.** What it means for a fig tree without fruit to occupy the ground, 67. What the fig tree in which Christ sought fruit signifies, 1069. [Col. 1514]

**Ficulum**, or **Ficocle**, a town in Italy, 754.

**Ficulinus**, Bishop Severus, 548.

**Surety**: what it is, 1108.

**Fidentia**, a woman, 950.

**The faithful** are members of one body, 46.

**Faith.** What can be seen cannot be believed, 381. Invisible things are seen through visible things, ibid. Faith is to be urged, not extorted, 524. Those who are alienated from the faith ought to be brought to it by admonition and persuasion, 525. Pagans and Jews must be compelled or attracted—not by persuasion alone, but also by indirect force—525, 703, 734. See *Jews*. Gregory ordered that peasants obstinate in their idolatry be burdened with a financial levy so that they might be converted, 704.

The necessity of faith, 373. Just as branches wither without the strength of the root, so good works separated from faith are nothing, 718, 967. Our faith does not rest upon new revelations, 822. How many departed from the faith in the fifth and sixth centuries, 114. That confession of faith must be accepted which is made not by force but by spontaneous will, 842. The unbeliever does not live without faith, 373. We believe with certainty many things that cannot be seen, 380. No one can be saved who holds Christ’s faith but does not possess a life corresponding to faith, 861. He loses the faith who agrees with the term “universal,” 747.

**Confidence** is the simplicity of one’s conduct that brings great security, 48. Confidence and security based on merits are corruptions of the soul, 100.

**The sons of the Church** are called laymen, 666. See *Layman*.

**Known sons** are those born from a lawful marriage, 801.

**Filoxenus**, magnificent man, 1046.

**End.** Whether willingly or unwillingly, we move toward the end every day, 875.

**Firminus**, bishop of Tergestum, 1203. Gregory congratulated him after his return from the schism, ibid. He fortified him against temptations, 1204, and promised him assistance, ibid. Firminus suffered much from the schismatics, 1240. He was commended to Smaragdus the exarch, 1241. The renunciation of heresy found among Gregory’s letters appears to belong to this same Firminus, 1300.

**Firmum**, a town in Italy, 944. Bishops of Firmum: Fabius, 943; Passivus, 1187, 1188.

**Fiscal levies** are called taxes, 687, 688.

**The fisc.** Even in ancient times, the property of debtors to the fisc was claimed for the fisc and kept under its custody once the ruler’s seal had been affixed, 1119.

**Those who fear God’s scourges** and therefore live innocently: how they should be admonished, 52. God’s scourges are softened by mercy, 385. It does not rightly follow from Italy’s scourges that one has sinned, 615. Through scourging we are recalled to penitence, 51. God loves the person who is worthy to endure His scourge, 615. With what disposition God’s scourges and blows should be received, 1114 ff. Scourges prove that we have not been abandoned by God, ibid. What consolation is readily available amid scourges, 1028. To commit deeds deserving scourges while placed amid scourges is to act proudly against the one who strikes, 1088. How those struck by scourges should be consoled, 1087, 1088. See *Adversity*, *Affliction*, *Tribulation*.

**Public scourging**, formerly decreed by ecclesiastical judgments against clerics, is now prohibited, 1172.

**Flaminea**, or **Flaminia Gate**, of ancient Rome, 1125.

**Flame.** In the case of the three boys, the flame had power at one and the same time for consolation but not for torment, 324.

**Flavius**, bishop of Rheims, 1288.

**To weep without weeping**: what this means, 79. [Col. 1515]

**Flora**, abbess: Gregory permanently donated her house with its gardens for the construction of a monastery, 636.

**Florentinus**, archdeacon of Ancona, elected bishop, 1269.

**Florentinus**, or **Florentius**, deacon of the Church of Ravenna, 819, 1096. He was elected to the episcopate of Ancona, 1269.

**Florentinus**, a servant of God: he was ordered to restore six ounces to the monastery of Saint Lucy at Syracuse, 626.

**Florentius**, bishop of Epidaurus. The case of his unjust deposition was to be examined in a synod, 631, 632. The investigation was entrusted to Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, 902.

**Florentius**, priest of the Church of Saint Lawrence at Rome, 420.

**Florentius**, grandfather of the subdeacon Florentius, 225. His hatred and envy toward Saint Benedict, ibid. His scheme for destroying the souls of the monks, 228. He paid the penalty for his wickedness, ibid.

**Florentius**, subdeacon: elected bishop by the Neapolitans, he fled, 635.

**Florentius**, a religious man in the province of Nursia, 308. A bear served him, 309. He cursed the perverse monks because they had killed the bear, and divine vengeance immediately struck them, ibid. He mourned their deaths, ibid. By prayer he cleansed a wilderness of serpents, 312. He is venerated among the patrons of the Church of Foligno, 313.

**Florianus**, 625.

**Floridus**, bishop of Tibur, a lover of truth and distinguished for holiness, 300, 356.

**Florus**, teacher of the Church of Lyon, proves that the fire of hell is corporeal, 111.

**Florus**, magnificent man, 1262.

**Floods of rivers**, calmed by a miracle, 293, 296.

**To channel springs outward**: what this means, 74.

**A hole in a wall**: what it signifies, 30.

**Forms**: what they are, 1196. Who the *comes formarum* was, ibid.

**Formiae**, a town in Italy, 495. The Church of Formiae was united with that of Minturnae, ibid. Finally both were transferred to Gaeta together with the body of Saint Erasmus, ibid.

The visitation of the Church of Formiae was entrusted to Agnellus, bishop of Terracina, 862. Bishops of Formiae: Bacauda, 490, 495—see his title; Albinus, 947.

**Fornication** is counted by Paul among the more grievous crimes, 81. How spouses should be separated because of fornication, 1062. How one should deal with a woman who left her husband because of suspicion of fornication and later returned to him, ibid. Whether a husband is permitted to divorce his wife because of fornication, 1138.

**Fortuna**, a Jewess converted to the faith, 714.

**Fortunatus**, bishop of Fanum, 859.

**Fortunatus**, elected bishop of Naples after the deposition of Demetrius, 673. He subscribed to the Roman Council, ibid., 1288, 1291. How he ought to conduct himself in his Church, 672. His zeal on behalf of Christian slaves is praised, 953. The visitation of the Church of Misenum was assigned to him, 988, 989. He is reproved because the Neapolitans were divided among themselves through his fault, 1005. He is accused of negligence toward the monasteries, 1056. Gregory imposed many duties upon him concerning the administration of the Church. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

**Fortunatus**, bishop of Tuder, very powerful in driving away evil spirits, 192, 193, 196. By the sign of the cross he restored light to a blind man, 196. By the sign of the cross he healed a rabid horse, 197. He restored a dead man to life, 201. A Goth did not despise him with impunity, 197. The repentant Goth, imploring Fortunatus’s mercy, was sprinkled with holy water and healed, 200. Many miracles occurred at Fortunatus’s tomb, 200.

**Fortunatus**, abbot of the monastery called the Baths of Cicero, 164, 173, 201.

**Fortunatus**, abbot of the monastery of Caesena, unjustly deposed and to be restored, 1264.

**Fortunatus**, a nobleman, 185, 188.

**Fortunatus** held a seat at the table of the Church of Milan for many years, 720. His case was to be settled at Rome, 730, 731.

**Fortunatus**, to be removed from the office of defensor, 979.

**The trench of the altar**: what it signifies, 43. Why it was one cubit deep, ibid.

**A fracture.** A bond binds it tightly when discipline suppresses guilt, 23.

**The Franks**: why they were sometimes called Germans, 918, 920. The kings of the Franks are rightly called “Most Christian,” 795. Until now no king of France has departed from the orthodox faith, ibid. Formerly the kings of France gloried in the title “Illustrious Man,” 519.

**A dead brother without children**, with a wife left behind: what this signifies, 7. The surviving brother who refuses to take the dead man’s wife: who he is, ibid. Two brothers may marry two sisters, 1153.

**Saint Frigdianus**, bishop of Lucca, a man of extraordinary virtue, 293. By prayer and command he diverted a river from its own channel, ibid.

**Cold** is the person who neither begins nor completes good works, 94. Why everyone is required to be either cold or hot, ibid.

**The Frontinianists**: who they were, 1067.

**To receive grain from the Lord**: what this signifies, 73. What it means to hide grain, 74.

**The grain canon**: what it is, 488.

**Exactions of grain**, 533.

**Fruniscendus**, a debtor of the Church of Otranto, was to be compelled to pay, 1004.

**To flee.** What it means to be forbidden to flee in winter or on the Sabbath, 523.

**Saint Fulgentius** sometimes authenticated his letters with this inscription: “servant of the servants,” etc., 481.

**Saint Fulgentius**, bishop of Utriculus, 300. At Totila’s command he was enclosed within a circle and miraculously freed, ibid.

**Smoke**: how it denotes the prosperity of the wicked, 492.

**Fundi**, a bishop’s town in Latium, 153, 289, 633, 634. Bishops of Fundi: Andreas, 289; Agnellus, 634, 947, 1291.

**A thief**, detected with the help of a serpent, 161.

**Thieves**, recalled from theft by a miracle, 304, 305, 329.

**The punishment of thieves**, 115.

**Property taken by Furio from churches**: how it is to be restored, 1153.

**Theft in a monk**: how it was punished, 1124.

**Fuscus**, bishop of Capua, died at Rome, 737, 738, 760.

**Fuscus**, abbot of a monastery at Naples: he obtained many things for his monastery, 1049, 1050 ff.

**Fuscus**, chief physician, 554.

Those about to die often know the future through revelation, 409, 413.

# G
St. Gabinus. See Gavinus.

Gairaldus, abbot of St. Medard of Soissons, 1285.

Galaad is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” 72. By Galaad the Church is signified, [Col. 1516] ibid. Who are the pregnant women of Galaad, ibid.

St. Galla, daughter of the consul Symmachus, 392. She is believed to be the same woman to whom St. Fulgentius wrote, ibid. A widow, she rejected a second marriage, ibid. She embraced the monastic life, ibid. She was warned by blessed Peter of her imminent death and that of her two sisters, ibid.

Galla the widow, 428.

Why Gaul was called Germany, 781, 782. Why the Gallican Church is the offspring of the Roman Church, 781. The patricians of Gaul are called the governors of the provinces of Arles and Marseille, 493. Whether a delegation on behalf of the Holy See was always entrusted to the bishops of Arles, 781. What the kingdom of Gaul was like under Childebert, 783. The kings of Gaul. See Franks.

Gallipolis, or Callipolis, an episcopal city of Calabria, 657, 808. The visitation of the Church of Gallipolis is entrusted to Peter, bishop of Otranto, 807. See Callipolis.

What the rooster signifies when, in the deep night, it gives forth loud songs, 100. What the rooster signifies when, before crowing, it shakes its wings and strikes itself with them, ibid.

Garnerus, a regular canon of St. Victor in Paris: in what year he lived, 110. He composed a work called Gregorian, ibid.

The visitation of the Church of Capua is entrusted to Gaudentius, bishop of Nola, 737. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters.

Gaudentius the presbyter, 184.

The visitation of the Church of Tadinum is imposed upon Gaudiosus, bishop of Gubbio, 995, 996.

Gaudiosus the presbyter, 800.

Gaudiosus, master of the soldiers in Africa, 560. His sincerity of mind is praised, ibid. Hilary, administrator of the patrimony, is commended to him, 561.

Gaudiosus, deceased primicerius of the representatives of the province of Ravenna, 667.

Gaudiosus the defensor, 956.

A certain Gaudiosus complained to Gregory about violence inflicted upon him by agents of the Roman Church, 547.

What the joy of truth ought to be for disciples, 1110. What “to rejoice without rejoicing” means, 79.

Gavinia, abbess of the monastery of Saints Gavinus and Luxorius in Sardinia, 931.

St. Gavinus, martyr at Torres in Sardinia, 931.

The fire of Gehenna is corporeal, 417. It is one fire, but it torments all sinners in different ways, 448. It will torment the reprobate without end, 449.

Gelasius, a fallen subdeacon, 596.

*Genius* sometimes signifies ornament, splendor, distinction, or privilege, 914. In antiquity *genius* commonly signified a demon, 1300. Whether it is lawful to swear by one’s genius, ibid.

Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa, 550, 558, 841. He is praised for the victories he won, 558, 559, 560. His zeal for the Church, 686. Various matters about which Gregory asked him to act for the Church. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters.

Gennadius Scholarius, patriarch of Constantinople, used Gregory’s books of the *Dialogues* against the Greeks at the Council of Florence, 104.

Why Gentile is called the Arian Vandal prince, 280.

“I write to Gentio,” 1088.

Genoa, the most celebrated city of Liguria, 461, 646.

George the presbyter of Constantinople, 847, 853. His error concerning those condemned and liberated from hell by Christ, 861.

George, prefect of Italy, 527.

A certain George is commended to Donus, bishop of Messina, 823.

The ancient Church of St. George, 1173, 1174.

## Germany

What is to be understood by the regions of Germany, 781. Lugdunian Germany, 782, 920.

Germanus, bishop of Capua, whose soul St. Benedict saw being carried into heaven by angels, 269.

Gerontius, a monk of the Gregorian monastery, is assured in a vision of his own death and that of his brethren, 409, 412. By his prayers he frees the deacon Paschasius from purgatory, 444, 445.

*Gerontocomia* are hospices for the elderly, 1091. By whom the hospice on Mount Sinai was built, 1092.

Whether *gesta* and *facta* differ, 577.

What a hunchback signifies, 11.

What it means for giants to groan beneath the waters, 849.

Gildas, surnamed “the Wise,” a writer, 1038.

What it means to keep the sword from blood, 75.

What it means to place the sword upon the thigh, 90.

“Attached to the soil,” or subject to the body and of servile condition, 757.

The hymn “Glory to God in the highest,” used in joyful circumstances and acts of thanksgiving, 764, 765, 1029, 1109, 1111, 1237, 1238.

The person eager for vain and empty glory is depicted, 9. Those who swell with the desire for empty glory before others lie prostrate in the eyes of God, 172. He is truly glorious who glories not in temporal power but in the Passion of Christ, 850. The fleeting glory of the world commonly obstructs the pursuit of eternal life, 1077.

“Your Glory,” a title of honor by which Gregory addresses kings and emperors, 543, 684; masters of the soldiers, 909, 985, 988, 998; patricians, 834, 1025; prefects, 1068; advocates or scholastics, 721; *domestici*, 1081, 1083; distributors, 1032, 1033; illustrious women, 1077, 1088; a subdeacon, 1274. It is also the title by which King Reccared addresses Gregory himself, 978.

Gloriosa, wife of the scholasticus Andreas, 952.

Gloriosus, bishop of Ostia, 947, 1288.

Godiscalchus, a most worthy man, 541.

Godiscalcus, duke of Campania, 1048.

Gordia, or Gurdia, sister of Maurice, who was given in marriage to Philip, commander of the East, 877.

Gorgona, or Gorgonia, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 545, 546, 729. Horosius, abbot, is entrusted with visiting the monks living there, 546.

## Goths

Why the Vandals are sometimes understood as the Goths, 115. By the “kings of the nations” are understood the kings of the Goths who occupied part of Gaul, 831. The Goths attempt unsuccessfully to burn the monk Benedict, 324.

Gradus, the island to which Severus of Aquileia transferred his see, 502, 1240.

A higher rank will not be approved before God, but rather the merit of one’s life, 562.

How far the prohibited degrees in contracting marriage extend with respect to generations, 1154 and following, 1275, 1277 and following, 1279. What Roman law permits concerning this matter, 1153, 1154.

The schismatic Greeks corrupted the passage in Gregory’s *Dialogues* concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, 118, 275.

Gregory complains that he lacks interpreters of the Greek language, 1071. [Col. 1517]

A bishop may not teach grammar, 1140, 1141.

The necessity of grace for patiently enduring God’s scourges, 185. All God’s works are preceded by gifts, and through the work that follows the gifts themselves increase, 168. The grace of Him without whom one is nowhere free from guilt, and with whom one is nowhere without justice, must be sought, 849. We must presume upon grace in such a way that we do not become negligent in work or prayer, 885. Without God’s help our enemy cannot be defeated, 790. Without divine grace, human affection does us more harm, 957. Without the grace of divine mercy no one can aspire to eternal things, 1077.

Human favor. See Favor.

Gratianus, or Gratiosus, bishop of Numentum (*Numentanus*), 638, 1291.

Gratianus, deacon of the Church of Venafrum, to be incardinated in the Neapolitan Church, 799.

Gratiosa, abbess, 673.

Gratiosus, subdeacon, 636.

Gratiosus, notary, 1046.

Gravinianus, deacon, 602.

Gregoria, 589.

Gregoria, chamberlain of the empress Augusta, asks St. Gregory for a difficult and useless favor, 869.

Gregoria, a Roman virgin and religious woman, 301.

Gregory Thaumaturgus moves a mountain, 180.

Gregory of Nazianzus. His statement concerning the giving of exhortation, 33.

Whether St. Gregory the Great had a brother, 1002, 1004. He indicates that he had been a monk, 172, 368, 405, 417, 453. What sort of man he was in the monastery, 149, 152, 491.

Gregory fled the pontificate by hiding himself, 1, 517, 849. How much he recoiled from the pontificate, 489, 516, 520. With what disposition he undertook the pontificate, 505, 517, 521, 849. He compares secular affairs to the storms of the sea, but the occupations of solitude to the shore, 152. He mourns that the quiet of solitude was lost through his promotion to the pontificate, 149, 152, 488, 491, 492, 516, 531, 1027. He laments that in the pontificate he is overwhelmed by worldly cares, 494, 516, 519, 520, 531, 1027; that he has been cast down from the delight of contemplation, 491, 492, 493; and nearly separated from the love of God, 519. Nevertheless, he does not disparage hierarchical functions, 491. He complains that he loves his storm-tossed life in the pontificate, 531. He calls the priesthood a heavy burden, 610. Recently ordained, he writes synodical letters to the other patriarchs, 490, 517, and to the primates of the sees, 517, 541. How many years he lived in the pontificate, 478. In what sense he says that he is not the bishop of the Romans but of the Lombards, 520.

Gregory professes to venerate the four earlier councils just as he venerates the four books of the Gospel, 615, 632. He likewise venerates the Fifth Council, 515, 957. He professes to preserve inviolate the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, 683. While serving as urban prefect, he subscribed to the oath of caution concerning the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 682. What he thought concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, 118. His reverence toward the Holy Fathers, 1065.

How much Gregory feared negligence in the care of souls, 500, 522. How concerned he was for the salvation of Venantius the patrician, formerly a monk, 523 and following. His tenacity regarding ancient and ecclesiastical discipline, 529, 721, 793, 915, 916. Gregory’s concern for the observance of the canons, 529, 663, 664, 686, 701, 713. He rejoices at the conversion of a bishop to a better way of life, 609. He is deeply afflicted by another’s fault, 613. He was tormented by the faults of others and rejoiced in good action, [Col. 1518] 928. He considers the correction of bishops to belong to him, 617. He says that he lives if the bishops stand firm in the Lord, 626. He rebukes an imperial law as contrary to the divine law, 676, 677, 678. In the case of John of Constantinople, he says that he fears no one except the omnipotent Lord, 746. He says that he would rather die than allow the Church of blessed Peter to degenerate during his lifetime, 725. He says that gifts are pleasing to him when they have been seasoned with the sweetness of a priestly and pious way of life, 841. He believes that the care of all the Churches has been entrusted to him, 865. He wishes all great men to be such that their honor does not detract from God’s honor, 879. He burns with concern over whatever he knows to harm bishops, 1022. He attempts to inspire a bishop with his own zeal against the Donatists, 612. Gregory’s zeal for recalling schismatics to the Church, 608, 614, 615 and following, 632, 683, 684, 778. He seeks the assistance of the great against the efforts of heretics, 559. He groans that the Donatist heresy is spreading, 612. What he did for the conversion of heretics and Jews. See Agnoites, Manichaeans, Photinians, Jews. He was concerned to call idolaters to the faith, 701, 702, 703. Gregory’s concern for souls straying from the truth, 501.

Gregory’s concern for Churches deprived of pastors, 503, 614, 674, 708. He did not wish the election of bishops to be delayed any longer, 550, 563, 564, 572, 633, 649. His active concern in choosing the prelates of the Church, 579, 645. His utmost caution in ordaining bishops, 1064, 1087. He did not wish to solicit the election of anyone, even of a very close friend, 644. He fearlessly defends the honor and prerogatives of his see, 725. He wishes the rights of all Churches to remain unimpaired, just as those of his own Church, 611, 619, 645. He undertook to govern the Apostolic See in the place of Peter, 611. He wished nothing to be done in another diocese without the knowledge of its own bishop, 529. Gregory’s concern for other dioceses, 685. He urges a bishop, on the occasion of a plague, to exhort the people to repentance and faith, 569, 570. He is distressed when bishops are despised by their clergy, 704. How he conducted himself toward bishops unjustly deposed, 628, 630, 631, 632, 665. How he acted toward bishops who had suffered injury, 623, 624, 625, 839. How he assisted bishops expelled by enemies, 540, 634, 638. How he dealt with delinquent or disobedient bishops and priests, 656, 657, 689, 735, 736, 739, 756. What he was like toward the negligent, 693, 900. What he was like toward repentant bishops, 991, 992. He censures a bishop who seeks human praise for good works, 626. He calls bishops brothers, not sons, 1047.

Gregory calls himself the defender of the property of the poor, 1059, and their steward, 1232. See Patrimony. His various acts of charity, 502, 506, 538, 541, 546, 548, 549, 550, 574, 596, 599, 707, 756, 793, 872, 956, 1062. He assists poor bishops, 554, 1211. He gives two thousand modii of grain to a bishop who has nothing with which to feed the poor, 794. He sends clothing for needy people to be baptized, 893. He orders twenty solidi to be given for the repair of Churches, 1075. For a merchant who had suffered a loss, he orders a bishop and subdeacon to intervene so that the money he had promised would not be demanded from him, 955, 956. He pays debts on behalf of debtors, 670, 724. He redeems captives, 609, 636, 820. He fears that a needy person might reject his charity out of a false sense of honor, 599, 1062, 1232. He orders assistance to be given to the poor in the provinces, lest, if they came to Rome, they should be burdened even more by the journey, 627. He does not wish his representative to become involved in cases that would burden the poor, 993. He cautiously undertakes the distribution of the alms of others, 872, 874, 911. He sends beds and bedding to be placed in the hospice for the elderly for the use of travelers, 1092. See Xenodochium.

Gregory considers himself the father of orphans and widows, 551, 552, 553. He assists widows, 528, 626, 627, 823. He orders that a father’s property pledged to the Church be returned to orphans, 638, 639. He commends the orphan Armenius to a Roman patrician, 643, 644. He protects the oppressed and harassed, 542, 543, 547, 548, 550, 551, 556, 768, 769, 821, 1025, 1035. He does not permit others to be saddened contrary to equity, 973. How concerned he was to settle disputes, 527, 648, 649, 652, 653, 824, 825, 880, 887, 959, 960.

Gregory’s concern for Italy, which the Lombards were devastating, 570, 590, 591; for Rome, which the same people threatened, 607; and for Naples, 609. His concern for the Sardinians, Corsicans, and Sicilians, 768, 769. He labors for peace, 816. He orders that an abundant supply of grain be sent to Rome, 557, 960.

Gregory’s generosity toward monasteries, 913. He takes care that wills made for the construction of monasteries be fulfilled, 687, 689. He wishes assistance to be given to Theodosia, who was planning to build a monastery, 695. He orders monks to be introduced into this monastery, 728. He orders enslaved persons taken from the monastery to be restored, 761. Gregory’s concern that regular discipline be observed in monasteries, 732, 733. See Monks, Monasteries.

Gregory considers it profit if he gathers a reward with God rather than riches, 526. He orders that whatever had been converted to the advantage of the Roman Church contrary to equity be restored, 525. He orders that a donation belonging to a fallen handmaid of God be restored to the monastery, 539. He did not wish the patrimony of the Roman Church to be increased through frauds and thefts, 533, 534, 535, 536, 553, 595, 655, 656. He orders the price of a gift to be restored, 926. Moved by compassion for a poor woman, he wishes a house donated to his Church to be returned, 948, 956. He orders an estate to be restored to a monastery, 650, 951. He orders property bequeathed to Churches unjustly and to the detriment of others to be restored, 896. He does not wish enslaved persons belonging to others to be unjustly retained by Churches, 897.

Gregory takes no pleasure in gifts, 553, 586, 841. He orders clothing given to him as a present by a bishop to be sold and the price returned to that bishop, 554. He refuses to accept payment for gifts sent by him, 917. He does not at all permit those who conduct the affairs of the Church to be deprived of the fruits of their labor, 539, 637. He shows gratitude toward those who have served the Church well, 992, 993. Empty excess does not please him, 526. He prohibits the Sicilian bishops from coming to celebrate the anniversary of his ordination, ibid. He urges a bishop wishing to come to Rome to spare himself the hardships of so long a journey, 554.

Gregory was far removed from litigation, 497, 625, 671, 672. He wishes the goods of the Church to be defended as the goods of the poor, not by force but by reason, 526. He preserved each person’s rights, 645, 646. Just as he did not wish the privileges of laypeople to be disturbed in judgments, so he resisted them by his authority when they prejudiced others, 626, 627. He is pierced by the goads of conscience because he had rejected a servant of God on account of a fault that was not serious, 594. He wished to give no one cause for scandal, 663. From the highest to the lowest, he wished to give no human being an occasion for scandal, 879.

What Gregory’s zeal for justice was like, 957. What equity is, 619. With what equity he wished cases to be examined, 526, 643, 822. He decides nothing without investigating the cases, [Col. 1519] 627, 643, 975, nor against an unheard party, 942, 959, 1061. He wishes matters once decided to be carried out without delay, 1078. He neglects no one’s complaint, 960. In the cases of others he is not moved by private hatred, 812, 813, 814. He defends no one out of personal affection, 581, 582. He never seeks protection for anyone unless justice favors it, 1079. He considers it shameful to defend what he has not first established to be just, 1080. He loves people on account of justice; he does not set justice aside for the sake of people, ibid. No underhanded dealing finds a place with him, 579. He does not consider a person’s status, 644. He never places a person before evangelical precepts, the institutions of the canons, or the interests of his brethren, 746.

Gregory is a prudent physician, 977. In all cases, especially those concerning God, he usually binds people more by reason than by power, 723. He carries out externally what belongs to justice in such a way that he does not at all neglect what internally belongs to love and affection, 852. He does not wish crimes to be concealed and left unpunished, 653. The fact that he corrects the faults of others proceeds not from harshness but from brotherly affection, 928, 1090.

Gregory’s remarkable humility, 1027, 1028. In describing the character of a pastor, he says that he, an ugly painter, has depicted a handsome man, 102. He calls himself a little man, 152. He admits that he is subject to error, 172. He says that he learned from another monk many things of which he had been ignorant, 324. Whether Gregory was the first of all to adorn himself with the title of humility, “Servant of the servants of God,” 481, 482, 525, 1213, 1294. He acknowledges himself unequal to the pontificate, 492, 507, 514. He is distressed when he is praised, 494, 516, 618, 713, 855. He calls himself dust and an unworthy servant of God, 524. He calls himself dust and a worm, 676. He dreads the burden of his own weakness and fears that he must render an account, 610. He says that he is pressed into the depths by the weight of his faults, 680, 879. He says that he is ready to be corrected and amended by everyone, 617, 618. He professes himself unworthy to pray for others, 712, or to receive a revelation from God, 869. He says that he is afflicted less than he deserves, 712. He says that he does not do what he appears to know, 778. He says that he has always been of bad character, 873. He humbles himself before monks, 877. He calls himself inferior to a certain priest, 879. He acknowledges himself unworthy to be among those presiding and among the number of those standing, 888. He says that he is capable of conducting no business, ibid.

Gregory prohibits his writings from being read at table in the presence of outsiders, 856. In comparison with Augustine’s writings, he calls his own writings chaff, 1067. He does not approve of his commentaries on Job being read publicly at the vigils, 1195, 1196. He is prepared to give an account of his faith to the other bishops, 779. He is prepared to imitate his inferiors in good things, 941. He attributes the conversion of the English to the prayers of Eulogius of Alexandria, 918, 919. He says that bishops are his brothers in place but fathers in character, 919. He calls himself the servant of all priests insofar as they live priestly lives, 749. He refuses to be called universal bishop, 919. He says that his honor is the honor of the universal Church and of his brethren, ibid. He professes that through the burdens of the episcopate he has become the servant of all, 1123. He calls himself sluggish and useless, languishing in idle leisure, 1028. He asks Rustician to refrain thereafter from calling herself a handmaid in Gregory’s letters, 1123. He asks for the prayers of others, 806, 807, 874, 971, 1091, 1093, 1116. He complains that Maurice called him simple and foolish, 765, 766. In what sense he is foolish, ibid.

[Col. 1520]

How ready Gregory was to forgive injuries, 618, 817, 818. He not only does not cause prejudices, but bears those inflicted upon him with equanimity, 1059. He did not wish to involve himself in the death of the Lombards, 726. His concern for his friends, 524, 1079, 1080, 1081. His unconquered constancy, 725, 749. His devotion to sacred reading, 908. He loves holy work in others, 1029, and in a certain sense makes it his own, ibid., 1031. He longs for the heavenly homeland, 1032, 1064, 1065. His sole consolation is the expectation of death, 1233.

Unable to fast on Holy Saturday, Gregory obtains the power to fast through the prayers of Eleutherius, 352. He suffers from colic, 707. His illnesses, 352, 965, 990, 1032, 1033, 1064, 1065, 1114, 1115, 1116, 1123, 1124. His various calamities and sufferings, 713, 765, 767, 770, 836. He is prepared to endure any adversity, provided that he endures it with the salvation of his soul, 767. The sufferings of this life drive him toward love of heavenly things, 770. He is troubled by what others suffer, 1066.

Gregory’s eulogy, 484, 621. He is called the most beautiful ornament of the Church, 1036; the most august flower of all Europe in its decline, ibid.; an outstanding watchman, ibid.; the spiritual vein of a living fountain, 1039; a living stream of knowledge, ibid.; the most holy apostolic pope, 1292; one whose heart was kindled by the grace of the Holy Spirit, 1293. Gregory knew neither Greek nor wrote anything in Greek, 714, 879, 1174.

The books on Job that Gregory wrote were first delivered as homilies, 532. He published this work at the request of Leander, bishop of Seville, 532, and sent it to him, 777. He is displeased that these commentaries on Job are read publicly at the vigils, 1195, 1196. Why he wrote the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, 1, 103. The encomium of this book, 620, 1040. Gregory reluctantly received this book, which had been offered to the emperor and translated into Greek by Anastasius of Antioch, 1196. He sent the book to the presbyter Columbus, 729, and to St. Leander, 777. He promises it to Bishop Venantius, 729.

Gregory was called “the Dialogue” by the Greeks because of the books of the *Dialogues*, which were especially dear to them, 103. On what occasion he published these books, 105, 116, 149, 152, 661. At what time, 105, 116. In what place, 116. He composed them with the deacon Peter in the form of questions and answers, 107. Who attributes these books to Gregory, 106, 107, 532. Who rejects them, 113. Who approved them, 108. These books are asserted to be Gregory’s, 105 and following, 113 and following. By whom these books were translated into Greek, 103, 107, 111, 112. Why there is such a difference among the translations of these books, 112. The various interpretations of the *Dialogues*, 116, 117, 118. The Greek version was corrupted by the schismatic Greeks, 118, 275. The Gregorian *Dialogues* contributed substantially to the conversion of the Lombards, 114. They contain notable examples of virtue, 115. Many doctrines of the faith are explained and established in them, ibid. In these books Gregory intended to speak only about saints who flourished in Italy, 116. In narrating miracles, Gregory observes the laws of history, 114. What Gregory narrates in these books he had heard from good and faithful men or learned through his own experience, 152, 153. Something false has slipped into these *Dialogues*, 115. Who converses with Gregory in the *Dialogues*, ibid. With what welcome that work was received, 116. What has been accomplished in this edition of the work, 117, 118, 119.

The excellence of Gregory’s letters, 477. What was removed from and added to the Register of the Letters, 480. Why the subjects of the letters were changed, ibid. The letter to Venerius of Cagliari is entirely rejected, 1303, 1304. Gregory wrote as many books of letters as he lived years in the pontificate, 478, 479. Pope Hadrian I compiled two books of Decretals from Gregory’s letters, 479. Gregory wrote on the *Song of Songs*, 140. His other works, 1195.

In what year and on what occasion Gregory, a monk of Mount Sinai, became bishop of Antioch, 507. He was a man of great virtue, ibid. He governed the see of Antioch for twenty-three years and left it to his predecessor, ibid. What Pelagius II ratified concerning that Gregory at the synod of John of Constantinople, 984.

Gregory, bishop of Agrigentum, is summoned to Rome to clear himself, 557. He awaits his accusers in Rome, 634. Gregory orders that they be sent quickly to Rome, 633.

Gregory, bishop of Porto, 1287.

Gregory, a presbyter and abbot of the monastery of St. Theodore in Sicily, 496. Through his negligence nearly all the monks of this monastery fell, 732. After a long penance he is restored to his position, ibid.

Gregory, a monk of the monastery of St. Benedict near Terracina, 384. He saw the soul of his brother, the monk Speciosus, leaving the body, 385.

Gregory, governor of Italy, 506. Prefect of the city, 521. He is called “the former prefect,” 947, 1193. He built a basilica in honor of the martyrs, 947. After enduring many hardships during the siege of Rome, he was accused by Maurice but defended by Gregory the Great, 767. He took refuge in the Church, 1078. Gregory the Great commended him to various bishops and judges, 1082, 1083, 1084, 1085. His late arrival in Sicily is excused, 1085.

The flock follows its shepherd toward a precipice when he walks along steep and dangerous paths, 4. Whoever, when lawfully called, refuses to feed God’s flock proves that he does not love the supreme Shepherd, 6. A people under a bishop is called a flock, 13. The flock advances better through the shepherd’s example than through his words, 15. The Lord’s flock ought not to remain without a shepherd because of the shepherd’s fall or death, 503, 564, 572. See Shepherd.

Grumentum, a city of Lucania, 1209.

The parish of Grumentum, 1209.

Gregory asks that the family of Grussingi be released, 571.

Guduinus, duke of Naples, 1268.

Guitmundus, archbishop of Aversa, cites Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on the truth of the Eucharist, 107.

Those devoted to gluttony: how they should be admonished, 61, 62, 63. The companions of the vice of gluttony are talkativeness, frivolity in work, and lust, 61, 62.

Gulfar, master of the soldiers, 614, 998. His zeal for recalling schismatics to the Church, 998.

Gummarith, duke of the Lombards, 297.

Gundeberga, sister of Adaloald, married Arioald, 1271.

High whirlpools of rivers are filled by small but countless drops of rain, 91.

## H
To dwell with oneself: what it means, 216, 217. Hadrian I, pope, cites the Dialogues under Gregory’s name in his letter to Charlemagne, 107. He compiled only two books of the Decretals from Gregory’s Letters, 479. Hadrian is terrified by a revelation concerning relics sent to Charlemagne, 708. The emperor Hadrian instituted counts, 499, 500. [Col. 1521] Hadrian of Thebes, a bishop who suffered injury from bishops, fled to Rome, 627, 628, 629. Unjustly deposed, he is restored by Gregory, 628, 630. He is accused before the emperors on many charges by deposed deacons, 629. Although the charges brought against him concerning monetary matters were false, he is compelled to confess them, ibid. Pelagius II had exempted him from the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Larissa, 630. Gregory exempts him again, ibid. Gregory wishes to examine the reconciliation of Hadrian with his accusers, 653. Hadrian, notary of Sicily, 976, 1055, 1137. He is praised for prosecuting enchanters and diviners, 1039. He is called a chartularius, 1231. See the Alphabetical Index of the Letters.

Inheritance. Sons do not attain an inheritance except through the scourges of discipline, 50. Whoever abstains from his parents’ inheritance ought not to bear hereditary burdens, 820. An inheritance is called “lying open” when it has not yet been entered upon, 821. An inheritance is entered upon either by word or by deed, ibid. An inheritance is omitted when the heir allows himself to be excluded by the passage of time, ibid. It is repudiated when the person to whom it has passed refuses to enter upon it, ibid. An heir is compelled to pay if his predecessor has bequeathed another person’s property, 896. What an heir *ex asse* is, 990. Who is called an heir in eight or in four ounces, 990. What an heir in one ounce is, 1189, 1190.

Heresy falsely attributed by Catholics, through an impotent zeal, to other Catholics, 803. Truth is so neglected by such envious people that they do not even know the heresy they impose on others, 803, 804. Gregory did not permit anyone professing the true faith to be afflicted under the pretext of heresy, 803. Not to believe one who professes the truth is not to purge oneself of heresy but to commit it, 805. Whoever refuses to believe a correct profession accuses himself in the matter for which he condemns another, 804. Infidelity is failing to have faith in the faithful, 805. After the orthodox profession of his faith, Gregory declares the presbyter Athanasius Catholic, 843, 844. What those accused of heresy ought to do, 1129. The articles of the heresy recently believed to have arisen at Constantinople, 1130 and following. Refuted by Saint Gregory, ibid. The first heresy in the Church was simony. See Simony. Heretics are represented by pregnant women of Gilead, 72. How heretics turn the law of God into a sacrifice to Satan, 73. They offer to the devil the gifts of God bestowed upon us, ibid. What admonitions should be given to heretics, 73. They create discord concerning the precepts of peace, ibid. God is said not to delight in the vessels of heretics after they have been taken away and offered to the Church, nor in their temples either, 697. Gregory and Honoratus, bishop of Novara, held different opinions on this matter, ibid. The Church is instructed by the questions of heretics, 895. The persecution and wickedness of heretics against the Catholic Church, 559. It is a great grace of almighty God that there is no unity among heretics, 895. The law pursues their depravity, 714. Heretics must always be restrained by Catholic priests through force and reason, 731. Those who attack heretics sometimes become heretics themselves, 1132. Heretics were compelled to fall silent under the emperor Maurice, 1134. Inquiry concerning the baptism of heretics, 1167, and throughout Letter 67 of Book XI. With what gentleness heretics returning to the unity of the Church should be received, 500. Various methods of reconciling heretics, 1167 and following. The form for abjuring heresy, 1300 and following.

Halitgarius, bishop of Cambrai, [Col. 1522] 1149. Harenata, a place so called, to which Gregory transferred the bishopric of Velletri, 578. What *hebdomad* signifies, 1301. Who the dull-witted are who must be admonished, 40. Through the efforts of Helena, Constantine’s mother, God kindled the hearts of the Romans toward the Christian faith, 1113. Helena is commended by Saint Gregory, 1104. Eli’s false affection toward his sons, harmful both to himself and to them, 23. Elias, presbyter and abbot of Isauria, 763. Gregory sends him the Gospels, ibid. Gregory surpasses his modest request for assistance with generosity, ibid. He prays for every spiritual good for him, 764. Hellas, or Helladia, is properly Achaea, 789. The bishops of Helladia were subject, according to ancient custom, to the bishop of Corinth, 790. *Heptaticum*, or *Heptateuch*, signifies the first seven books of Sacred Scripture, 596, 597, 865, 867. What the plants that nourish these animals signify, while other plants kill them, 33. Herculanus, a most holy man taken from a monastery and appointed bishop of the city of Perugia, 300. Totila’s savagery toward the holy bishop, 301 and following. Hericius. See Ericius. The monastery of Saint Hermes, situated in the city of Palermo, perhaps one of the six Gregorian monasteries founded in Sicily, 824, 826. Saint Hermenegild, son of the king of the Visigoths, is converted by Bishop Leander, 345. At the urging of Ingund, daughter of Sigibert, king of the Franks, ibid. Out of hatred for the faith, he is stripped of all his possessions by his father and shut up in prison, ibid. He refuses to receive Communion from the hand of an Arian bishop, 345. His holiness is confirmed by miracles after his death, 345. Herundo, a solitary, led an extraordinary life in the Prenestine mountains, 396. Iberia. See Iberia. Hieracium, an episcopal city of Calabria, 871. Hierarchical—that is, an administrator or visiting bishop—691, 692. Cheerfulness is praised in the saints and in monks themselves, and is reconciled with penitence, 360. Saint Hilary of Lérins, monk and archbishop of Arles, 1101. Hilary whom Gregory commends to Queen Brunhild, 1024. To Vantilus and Arigius, ibid., 1025. Which Hilary this was is uncertain, 1026. He is mentioned again, 648. Pope Hilary sent letters of communion to all the bishops of Gaul immediately after his ordination, 542. Hilary, or Hilary of Africa, a monk and chartularius, 561, 566, 612, 1068, 1185, 1199, 1201. He is called a notary, 1089. As legate of the Apostolic See, he convenes a council over which he presides, 567. He is called administrator of the patrimony and is commended to Gennadius, exarch of Africa, 560. Hilary the subdeacon, a slanderer: what punishments he should suffer, 1172. Hilary from the city of Tauromenium, 821. Hincmar, metropolitan of Reims, delegated visiting bishops to the churches of his province that had been left desolate, 501. He cites very many testimonies from the Gregorian Dialogues in his works, 107. And also from other works of the same Father, 1156, 1235. Hippolytus, a cleric of Milan, 644. Hippolytus, a notary, 683, 684. [Col. 1523] Hispalis, the metropolitan city of Andalusia in Spain, 531. The bishop of Hispalis was Saint Leander. See his title. Spain was formerly called Iberia, 431, 1167. Because of the affair of the Three Chapters, Spain was not divided by schism, 614. The bishops of Istria were schismatics in the affair of the Three Chapters, 608. See Schismatics, the bishop of Istria, Providentius, 778. Actors are excluded from the clerical state, 675. For how many years a homicide ought to do penance, 1293. Gregory sends Secundinus two volumes of his homilies, 971.

Human being. All human beings were created equal by nature, but guilt places some below others, 20. A human being is God’s work; vice is the work of the human being, 772. The human being was so constituted that reason possesses the soul, and the soul possesses the body, 43. The human being was created by God midway between an angel and a brute animal, 373. With the angel he shares immortality; with the brute he shares mortality, ibid. Before sin, God warned the human being to his face, but after the fall, behind his back, 82. How great was the human being’s happiness in paradise before sin, and how great his misery after sin, 372. After sin, the human being is like an infant born and raised in prison, ibid. The human soul died through Adam, 802, 883. By sinning, the human being turned his back on God, 82. In what way the death of human beings and animals is one and the same, 377. What more the human being possesses than animals, ibid. The various orders of human beings, 783. Homobonus, bishop of Alba, ordained by Gregory, 633.

What our honor is, 49. Who gives his honor to another, ibid. The distinction between the right and the honor of a bishop, 495. Here “honor” means the use of the pallium by an archbishop, 518. Gregory cannot tolerate those who seize honor through pride, 739. Whoever wishes to be honored against God deserves no honor, 879. While honor is outwardly bestowed by human beings, the mind is plunged into the depths, 880. Whoever advances in honors but falls in character is raised when he is cast down, 1027. Let life be the reward of honor, 1142. Honorata, a maidservant, is summoned to Rome with her son, 596. Because of a second marriage, she is thrust into a monastery and ordered to be recalled from it, 716, 717. Honoratus, bishop of Novara, converts a temple of idols into a church, 697. Honoratus, the presbyter entrusted with the care of the widowed church of Mevania, 565. Honoratus, archdeacon of Salona, is promoted to the priesthood so that he may be removed from the diaconate, 504, 581, 582, 583. He is ordered to be restored to his own rank, 504, 581, 583, 584. The property of the church of Salona was in his custody, 505. Honoratus is summoned to Rome by Gregory, 581, 583, 584. After Natalis, bishop of Salona, dies, Honoratus, absolved from the charges brought against him, is restored to the rank of his order, 647, 812. He is elected bishop of Salona, 657. But Maximus seizes this see, 658. Honoratus does not enter into communion with him, 812, 813. Honoratus is commended to Maximus, 1034. Honoratus, a deacon of the Roman Church and *apocrisiarius* at the imperial court, 543, 544, 619. Gregory instructs him to act with the emperors on behalf of the Sardians who were being harassed, 543. Venantius is commended to him for obtaining documents concerning the ex-consulship, 619. He is deputed to investigate the case of Bishop Hadrian, 628, 630. Saint Honoratus, monk and abbot of Lérins, [Col. 1523] 1101. From his name the island of Lérins is called Saint Honoratus, ibid. Honoratus was exceedingly devoted to silence and abstinence, 153. His abstinence was confirmed by a miracle, ibid. He built the very large monastery of Fundi, of which he also became abbot, ibid. He saved that monastery from the collapse of an overhanging cliff, 156. He was taught solely by the instruction of the Holy Spirit, ibid. He is honored by his disciple Libertinus, 157. His boy, Caligula, was restored from the dead, 160. Honoratus, a disciple of Saint Benedict, 208, 240. Pope Honorius I founded the church of Saint Pancratius on the Via Aurelia, 697. Honorius, bishop of Tarentum, 1232. Horosius, abbot, under whose obedience and rule Gregory placed the monks living on the island of Monte Christi, 545. The correction of the monks of the island of Gorgonia is entrusted to him, 546. Who the granary-keepers are, 1205. What a granary is, ibid. Hortanum, commonly called Orta, formerly a city of Etruria, now a town belonging to the patrimony of Saint Peter, 521. The bishop of Hortanum, Blandus, ibid. Hortona, a city in Italy, 721. The visitation of the church of Hortona is entrusted to Bishop Barbarus, ibid. A gardener-monk, distinguished for holiness, appoints a serpent as guardian of the garden, 161. How he catches a thief, ibid. His kindness toward the thief, 164. The gardener, founder of a hospice, 1261. Garden. Who is said to dwell in the gardens of the Church, 75. Hospito, duke of the Barbaricini in Sardinia, 701. Gregory urges him to assist Felix and Cyriacus in converting the Barbaricini, 701, 702. In former times the care of guests rested upon the faithful, and especially upon bishops, 1059, 1116, 1151, 1269. The enemies of God prosper in His left hand and are broken in His right, 77. “Enemy” has the same meaning as “army,” 568, 591. Spiritual weapons must be set against hostile swords, 1138 and following. We shall truly be a sacrifice to God when we have made ourselves a sacrifice, 472. We shall not need the saving Host after death if before death we have been a sacrifice to God Himself, 473. What *Hualinus* or *Huelinus* signifies, 1039.

The humble are signified by David, 36. How the humble should be admonished, 58. The humble are imitators of God, 59. They should not be subject to others more than is expedient, ibid. They should desire to remain hidden, but so that they may benefit others, they should be revealed against their will, 185. It is not a great thing for those whom we honor to be humble, 599. Whoever is least in his own eyes is great before God, 21. Just as the proud glory in honors, so the humble glory in their own contempt, 176. Whoever truly loves lofty things does not sever his mind from the root of humility, 1030. Humility is the elevation of priestly office, 665. Humility arises from recognizing those who are better than oneself, 153. God became small even unto the passion of death in order to teach humility alone, 744. The effects of true humility, 7. How powerful humility is in performing miracles, 160. Humility is a sign that the Holy Spirit dwells in the mind, 156. Those who know how to despise themselves are in God’s keeping, 172. Just as the proud glory in honors, so the humble glory in their own contempt, 176. Why Christ wished to rise before the humble, though He had wished to die before the proud, 229. We are as much more powerful than our enemies as we become one with God through humility, 329. What false humility is, 7, 23. Sloth is veiled under the appearance of humility, 59. Why Paul joins the appearance of humility to superstition, 62. The connection between humility and charity, 852. A comparison of humility and pride, 744. Obstinacy is opposed to humility, 7. Poverty guards humility, 184. For the protection of humility, certain reprehensible traits are left in the saints, while great gifts of grace are bestowed upon them, 308. The humility of God’s servants ought to appear in times of affliction, 599. We ought especially to be humble toward those from whom we suffer anything, ibid. Humility is endangered at the summit of dignities, 21. Humility to be preserved in virginity, 83. In prosperity and adversity, 662. Uprightness should season humility, and humility make uprightness gracious, 526. In mind let us be subject even to persons lower in dignity, 731, 732. Humility should not be timid, 771. It should lie beneath charity like a foundation or be added like seasoning, 852. Humility should have confidence joined to it, 1112. We cannot live at the root of love unless we hold humility in mind and deed, 1246. Nothing is more exalted than humility, 59. The humility of Christ. See Christ. The humility of prelates. See Prelate. How necessary humility is for preachers, 1110 and following.

In what year Huneric, king of the Vandals, began to reign, 348. What hyacinth signifies in the dress of a priest, 15, 509. How the hyacinth relates to the carbuncle, 84. Hydruntum, or Hydrus, a city of Calabria in Italy, 807. It belonged by right to the Roman Church, 1003. The people of Hydruntum were harassed by Viator, a former tribune, ibid. Peter, bishop of Hydruntum, 807. What it means to flee in winter, and why it is forbidden, 523. A hypocrite is one who rules subjects by feigning discipline, 23. Hypocrites guard against small things but commit greater sins, 92. Those who do evil secretly and good publicly are whitewashed tombs, 95. Those who do good for human approval sell a thing of infinite worth cheaply, ibid. Some hypocrites live for others and die to themselves, ibid. The dreadful end of hypocritical monks, 441. He made the confession of his hypocrisy, useless to himself, useful to the brothers standing by and to us, ibid.

I

Ibas was declared orthodox at the Council of Chalcedon by the legates of the supreme pontiff, 516. His letter is contrary to that synod, 968. Iberia, a region of Asia, 1167. Iberia was formerly called Spain, 431, 1167. Gregory writes to the bishops of Iberia, 1166. Icon. See Image. In what year Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, flourished, 106. How idolaters returning to the Church should be received, 893. What punishment idolaters formerly received, 909. What kind of idolatry existed in Gregory’s time, 908, 938. Long afterward, remnants of idolatry survived in Gaul, 909. How idolaters should be restrained if they are free, and how if they are slaves, 982. What an idol painted on a wall signifies, 30. Temples of idols consecrated for the worship of God, 229. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, 765. The antiquity of the Letters circulated under his name, ibid. Sloth is veiled under the appearance of humility, 59. [Col. 1525] The name “fire” signifies tribulation, 444. The fire of hell. See Hell. The origin of sins of ignorance, 5. Sins of ignorance continue to weigh upon people even after death, 444. Sins of ignorance are lighter than those committed knowingly, 501. Ignorance of letters excludes a person from the orders, 600, 704. Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, mentions Gregory’s Dialogues in his book on ecclesiastical writers, 106. To avoid illicit things, one must also abstain from things that are licit, 388. *Illustrious*, a title of honor that could not be assumed or bestowed unless authorization had been granted by the prince, 432. *Illustratus*, the formula for granting the title, ibid. To whom the title *illustrious* was given, 519. The Frankish kings were called illustrious by the supreme pontiffs before they were called Most Christian, ibid. Which provinces constituted Eastern Illyricum, 487. Gregory urges the bishops of Illyricum to receive bishops expelled by their enemies and provide them with the necessities of life, 540. Gregory writes to those bishops, 585. Elba, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 297. The legitimate use of images, 971, 1006. A passage of Gregory in Letter 52 of Book IX is cited by many ancient authors, 971. Images of the saints are neither to be broken nor worshiped, 1006, 1099, 1100 and following. How they are to be honored, ibid. Various synods held concerning the veneration of images, 1005, 1006. Antiquity admitted images, 1100, 1101. The doctrine of Saint Gregory concerning images is defended, 1101, 1102. How images, or icons, of the emperors are received at Rome, 1302. To abridge—that is, to reduce to a brief form—655.

To imitate. He praises the rightly performed deeds of others in vain if he does not imitate them, 45. It is exceedingly shameful not to imitate what we are, 46. Among human beings it is a fault, and before God a punishment, to refuse to imitate the good that pleases us, 797. In Gregory, *imminere* means “to press upon” and “to be urgent,” 440, 632, 639, 911, 1059. It also means “to take pains,” 645. What *immission* signifies, 906, 907. The immunity of clerics. See Clerics. How the impatient should be admonished, 42. Charity, the mother and guardian of the virtues, and doctrine, which nourishes the virtues, are lost through impatience, 43. Good works are scattered by impatience, ibid. The kinship between impatience and arrogance, 43. How great the fault of impatience is, ibid. When impatience drives it, the whole spirit is brought outward, 44. The disturbance of impatience is a splinter, ibid. Some people do not succumb to impatience immediately but only long after injuries have been inflicted, 44. How the impatient differ from the angry, 57. Impatience lies in wait for abstinence, 62. Through impatience, the correction of sinners itself increases our sin, 385.

Gregory calls the emperor “lord of all things,” 501, 502. The emperors’ letters. See Sacred Letters. There were formerly eleven principal schools of imperial officials, 905. What distinction existed between the Roman emperors and the kings of the nations, 1079. The emperors’ icons received at Rome, 1302. Imperial sacred rescripts, or simply “sacred” documents, are the rescripts or commands of the emperors, 544. The ignorance of shepherds is rebuked by the voice of truth, 3. What *impetigo* signifies, 12. Its nature, ibid. The impious would wish to live without end so that they could sin without end, 449. The happiness of the impious is compared with smoke, 492. And with a wheel, ibid. Why the impious will be punished forever, 449. Importunus, bishop of Atella, 577. What was decreed concerning his will, 989. Importunus, a Palatine, 1108. Who the shameless are who must be admonished, 41. Impunity nourishes license; excessive leniency fosters the relaxation of discipline, 657. How the impure or deceitful should be admonished, 47. They are represented by the hedgehog, ibid., 48. Enchanters are punished, 1139. Whoever consults enchanters is excommunicated, 1293. To incardinate means to establish a bishop, abbot, presbyter, or deacon in a particular church, 501, 634, 635, 1188. See Cardinate. The mystery of the Incarnation is proved, 1168 and following. See Christ. *Incedere* is used of kings walking with majesty, 669. A fire extinguished by a miracle, 177.

Incestuous. Paul’s great indulgence toward the incestuous man of Corinth, 503. There is no marriage for incestuous persons, 1279. Incestuous persons are to be excommunicated, 1280. What *inclusus* signifies, 964, 966. The soul of a certain enclosed person was seen leaving the body and being carried to heaven, 385. Unharmed. See Sound. Who the fickle are who must be admonished, 60. Fickleness arises from levity, ibid. Remedies for fickleness, 61. Why incontinence was formerly called a fall among senior clerics, 640. An abbot deprived of his rank because of incontinence, 641. An incontinent bishop is deposed, 656, 657. Whoever is guilty of incontinence ministers at the peril of his soul, ibid.

To rebuke. How great a fault it is to cease rebuking vices, 70. Peace must be preserved inwardly during rebuke, ibid. See Correction. What an indiction is and who originated it, 485. Its use among ecclesiastical and secular writers, 486. The origin of the term *indiction*, ibid. Indictions are sometimes called taxes, ibid., 488. How many kinds of indiction there are, 486. Gregory uses the Constantinopolitan indiction in his letters, ibid. *Indifferenter*, that is, without delay, 505, 555, 944. What *indisciplinatus* signifies, 930. The reprieves granted to us for repentance, 1181. Baptized infants who die in infancy enter the kingdom of heaven, 400. Not all little children who can speak are saved, ibid. A five-year-old child accustomed to blaspheme, when his father failed to correct him, was handed over to the devil as a blasphemer, 401. For some little children, access to the kingdom of heaven is closed by their parents, 400. How infants should be raised, 871. The words of those who nourish infants are either milk, if they are good, or poison, if they are bad, ibid. Why infants formerly often died without baptism, 521.

Where hell should be believed to exist, 448. The upper and lower hell, ibid. What it means for the dead or the living to descend into hell, 89. Who descend alive into hell, ibid. The fire of hell is corporeal, 109, 110, 111, 416, 417. Nevertheless, it does not require wood in order to be fire, 421. How an incorporeal soul is tormented by corporeal fire, 417, 416. The souls of the wicked descend into hell immediately after death to be tormented, 446. The punishment of the wicked in hell will be eternal, [Col. 1526] 449, 452. Why a fault finite in itself is punished without end, 449. Why sinners will be assigned to eternal punishments, 449. The fire of hell is one, but it torments sinners in different ways, 448, 449. Those who are guilty of the same sins are to suffer the same punishments, 429. In hell, the wicked recognize the wicked, and this contributes to their punishment, 424. God wished the places of torment to be shown for the correction of the living, 429. The punishments of hell are shown to some for their assistance and to others as testimony, 433. To some for their own edification, and to others for the edification of others, 437, 440, 441. To others as an example of fear, 421. The heresy of those who said that Christ, in His descent to the underworld, freed from it all who had confessed Him, 862.

An unbeliever does not live without faith, 373. How unbelievers are to be summoned to the grace of faith, ibid. Infidelity is failing to have faith in the faithful, 805.

Weakness. We must always fear because of our weakness and trust in God’s mercy, 292. The first virtue is knowledge of one’s weakness, 852. The weaker person is the one unable to consider his own weakness, ibid. Bodily weakness sometimes occurs as punishment, 573. In weakness, thanks must be rendered to the Creator for grace, 729. Weakness is a pledge of divine love, 952. Whoever visits the sick makes God his debtor, 598. One must diligently avoid becoming a stumbling block to the weak, 96. *Ingenium* sometimes means an invention or any contrivance, 818, 819, 1197. *Ingratitude* is used for an offense, 582, 929, 958, 992, 1120. Ingund, daughter of Sigibert, 345. She draws her husband Hermenegild toward the faith, ibid.

Love of enemies. It is a virtue before human beings to tolerate adversaries, and before God also to love them, 44. What it means to hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred, 69. To provide bodily assistance not only to brothers but also to enemies is the command of the eternal Prince, 540. Unjust. Whoever joins the unjust in peace supplies strength to iniquity, 71. Injury. Some people do not seek vengeance immediately after injuries have been inflicted on them but only long afterward, 44, 45. Who these people resemble, 45. Whoever first forgives what is done against him rightly asks pardon for his own offense, 473. Whoever disturbs the rights of his brothers does injury to himself, 619. The greater reward is to remain on the path of truth even after suffering injuries, 625. Injuries are to be forgiven, 1051. It is not unworthy to suffer injuries for Christ, 1128.

Disobedience punished by death, 408. The innocent must not be punished, 643. They must be defended against the powerful, 904. Just as punishment properly belongs to the guilty, so acquittal must not be delayed for the innocent, 1072. Innocence is lost before God, before whose eyes sin is committed even in desire, 52. Fervent repentance is to be preferred to sluggish innocence, 83, 84. Whether Pope Innocent I denied reconciliation to the lapsed who sought it at the end of life, 733. Innocent, a bishop in Sardinia, 932, 1217. Innocent, prefect of Africa, 1067. Gregory thanks him for the protection he provided for the patrimony of the Roman Church, 1068. Gregory also writes to him concerning the restraint of unjust judges, 1095. [Col. 1527] What a legitimate inscription ought to contain, 805. Inspiration. Wisdom abandons those whom it called after they had long refused, 49. What it means to be urgent opportunely and importunately, 18. What *institution* signifies, 800. The education of children. See Infants. Some islands are washed all around by the waves; others are situated in cities, 1082. How intention should be directed, 542. From a perverse intention follows nothing but a wicked deed, even if it appears to be right, 196. Interamna, a city of Umbria in Italy, 987, 1090. In what year Totila ordered Interamna to be destroyed, and in what year it was rebuilt, 570. The visitation of the church of Interamna is entrusted to Constantius, bishop of Narni, 987. Anastasius, bishop of Interamna, 570. An intercessor should not approach God if he displeases Him through guilt, 10, 11, 507. Nor should one approach as an intercessor if he does not recognize himself as God’s friend through the merit of his life, 507. No intercessor should be permitted to become bishop of the church to which he has been assigned as intercessor or visitor, 575. How the death of human beings and animals is one and the same, 377. An interpreter ought to render not word for word but sense for sense, 519. When the literal precision of words is observed, the force of the meanings is lost, ibid. Intervals. See Orders.

How the envious should be admonished, 46. How great the blindness of the envious is, ibid. They are tormented by the happiness of others, ibid. The envious resemble the devil, ibid. Envy prepares the way for the gravest crimes, 46. It kills all virtues, ibid. Who is called “rottenness of the bones,” ibid., 47. Invisible things. Because carnal people cannot know invisible things through experience, they doubt whether they exist, 372. Whoever does not believe in invisible things is an unbeliever, 373.

The angry are often deceived by zeal for righteousness, 57. The angry should condemn their disturbance, ibid. The difference between an angry person and an impatient one, ibid. The angry must be corrected with great caution, 58. The stimulus of anger is sometimes thought to be zeal for justice, 57, 812. Two kinds of anger, 57. Patience brings those disturbed by anger back to a sounder mind, 57. To an angered mind, whatever is said to it rightly appears wrong, ibid. The fist signifies anger, 62. How much the anger of the righteous is to be feared, 188. The saints should guard themselves against anger, 597. In seeking vengeance, anger ought to follow reason, not precede it, 1030, 1080. Why anger should be avoided in prelates and superiors, 1048. How much judges should beware of anger, 1080. Saint Irenaeus’s writings and acts were long sought by Gregory, but he could not find them, 1142. Whether Saint Irenaeus was a martyr, ibid. Who are irregular and therefore barred from receiving the orders, 600, 704. See Orders. What the upper and lower irrigation signify, 353, 871.
