Isaac. Why, when the multiplication of Abraham’s descendants was predestined through Isaac, he received a barren wife, 184. What Isaac blessing his son after the meal signifies, 616, 617. Isaac, a servant of God, came from Syria to Italy, 301. His constancy in prayer, 304. Exceedingly devoted to poverty, ibid. Distinguished by the spirit of prophecy and by miracles, 304, 305. Some reprehensible trait was mixed with his virtues and gifts, 305. Isacius, patriarch of Jerusalem, had sent Saint Gregory a synodal letter, to which Gregory replies, 4133 and following. Isaiah commendably seeks the office of preaching after first being cleansed by the altar coal, [Col. 1527] 8, 848. He fell silent from the ministry of the word, but rebuked himself with the voice of repentance, 75. Why he says that he is unclean in his lips, 312. The monks of Isauria, accused of heresy and condemned by John of Constantinople, are acquitted by Saint Gregory, 883. Isidore, deacon of Alexandria, 837, 1248. Isidore, a man of illustrious rank, excommunicated by Januarius of Cagliari, 613. His case against the church of Cagliari is to be examined and concluded at Rome, 650. Isidore, a man of illustrious memory, 1187. Israelites. Why, after the powerful adversaries of the Israelites had been exterminated, the Philistines and Canaanites were preserved longer, 308. Italy formerly had both exarchs and prefects, 521. Whether the prefect and exarch of Italy were at that time the same person, ibid. Gregory commends the affairs of Italy to Philip, count of the bodyguard, 520. Italy captive under the Lombards, 740, 746, 766, 767. It is afflicted by plague, 1087. Italica, the patrician Venantius’s wife, 671, 672.

J
Jacob seeing angels ascending and descending: what it signifies, 19, 512. Jacob’s sons are censured for their vengeance against the Shechemites, 679. James son of Zebedee died in the Passion, 337. Jadera, an archiepiscopal city of Illyricum, 813, 815. Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, 863. Gregory summons him and others adhering to Maximus to appear for examination, after security had been given, 864. Gregory writes to the people of Jadera, 813. Jamnus the Jew, 974.

Januaria is aided when she implores ecclesiastical protection, 993. She built an oratory on her own estate, 994. Januarius, metropolitan of Caralis, pleads before Gregory on behalf of his people, 543. The case of the widow Catella is entrusted to his judgment for settlement, 551. The affairs of the religious woman Pompeiana are commended to his protection, 552. Januarius, accused of crimes, is summoned to Rome for canonical judgment, 650. He is reproved because he excommunicated Isidorus for no reason other than a personal injury, 613. His negligence in converting rustic idolaters is censured, 704. He disturbs a monastery through his avarice and turbulence, 727, 728. He is rebuked for violence inflicted upon another, 925, 928. His advisers are deprived of communion, 925, 926. He is despised by his own clergy, 704. Very many duties are imposed upon him for the discipline of the Church and the good of his subjects, 687–689, 705 and following. He is forbidden to accept anything for a burial, 927. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

Januarius, bishop of Malaca, whose case is entrusted to the defensor John for examination, 1250, 1252. He is acquitted, 1255, 1256 and following. Januarius, subdeacon of the Church of Messana, built a basilica in honor of the holy martyrs, 571.

To sanctify a fast: what it means, 62. To fast not for God but for oneself: what it means, 63. In Gregory’s time even little children customarily observed the fast on Holy Saturday, 352. All clerics should begin the fast at Quinquagesima, 1302. Fasting is harmful to those suffering from vomiting blood, 1117, 1121.

Jeremiah commendably shrank from the office of preaching, but did not wholly resist it, 8, 848. *Jericomia* are lodgings for priests and clerics, 1091. The citizens of Jerusalem generally serve the citizens of Babylon in forced labor, 923. Jesus Christ is the true Sabbath, 1214.

Jethro’s wise counsel to Moses, 25. Moses sought Jethro as a guide on the journey, so that he might lead him to life, 60.

Joanna, the wife of Cyriacus, a Christian from Judea, is commended to Peter the subdeacon, 556, 557.

Saint John the Baptist, taught solely by the instruction of the Holy Spirit, 156. His body was burned after his death, 1128. Saint John is held in great veneration by the Lombards, 364. The Lombard queen Theodelinda builds a basilica in honor of Saint John, ibid. Sanctulus, placed beneath the executioner’s axe, is freed after invoking Saint John, ibid. Relics of Saint John are sent, 709, 1031.

Saint John the Evangelist: how he drank the cup of martyrdom, 337. At Gregory’s command, his tunic is brought to Rome and shines with miracles, 625.

Saint John Damascene: why he called Gregory “the Dialogist,” 107.

Pope John I, 281. The horse on which the holy pontiff was riding refuses to carry a woman who had mounted it, 284. He restores sight to a blind man, ibid. John, killed by Theodoric, was seen with the patrician Symmachus leading Theodoric to eternal punishments, 420.

Pope John III: in what year he began to sit on the episcopal throne, 293. In what year he died, 244.

John of Callipolis, bishop, 657. John, bishop of the island of Capritana, a schismatic, 935. John, bishop of Carinensis, subscribed to the Lateran Council under Martin I, 798.

John called the Faster: in what year he became bishop of Constantinople, 489. John, a man celebrated for great virtues and learning, ibid., 490, 507. A man of great humility and abstinence, 743, 773. Gregory calls him “most holy,” 842. Gregory complains to him that he had arranged for his election to be confirmed by the emperor, 489. Gregory asks for his prayers, 490. John is accused of striking and of feigned ignorance, 662. His familiarity with a wicked young man is censured, 663. He is urged to observe the canons, ibid., 664. John’s dispute with Gregory concerning certain priests, 713. Gregory asks John that the priests Athanasius and John be received in their orders, 664. John wrote to Gregory concerning the same men, 746. Gregory commends the deacon Sabinianus, his apocrisiarius, to John, 664. He also commends the priest John, 804.

John avoided the episcopate, but after becoming a bishop ambitiously assumed the title “universal bishop,” 741, 984. Pelagius II annulled the acts of the synod at which he had assumed the name “universal,” 741, 751, 771, 984. The same Pelagius prohibited his apocrisiarius from celebrating the solemn Masses with John at Constantinople, 742, 771, 984. Gregory likewise forbade the deacon Sabinianus, 742. By this title of universal bishop John attempted to subject all the members of Christ to himself, 742. By this rash presumption the peace of the whole Church was disturbed, ibid. The Church was divided, 745. The pious laws, venerable synods, and commands of Christ himself were disturbed by John’s ambition, 748, 751. John imitates the proud angel, 742, 743, 751, 773. Through arrogance he claims for himself what belongs solely to Christ, 773. No human being, not even a saint, had dared to assume that name before John, 743, 748. To agree to that wicked title is nothing other than to lose the faith, 747, 873. John’s hypocrisy is described, 747. John precedes the Antichrist, 773. He indicates that the time of the Antichrist is near, 751, 984. John craftily persuaded the emperor Maurice to urge Gregory to maintain peace with him, 746. Gregory calls his case against John the cause of God and of the Church, 748. Gregory wishes that affair to be judged by the emperor, 749. Gregory urges Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius to oppose John’s pride, 772, 773.

John, archbishop of Corinth, 779, 983. He is granted the use of the pallium, 788. His zeal is aroused to eradicate simony from the places subject to him, 788. Gregory gives him various admonitions, 787, 788. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Crete, 898, 983. John, bishop of Euria, 1271. John, bishop of the city of Falerina, 1291. John of Jerusalem, 507. John, bishop of the First Justiniana of Illyricum, 983. He is elected bishop by unanimous consent, 585, 586. Gregory confirms this election, ibid. He sends him the pallium and entrusts him with the functions of the Apostolic See, 585, 586. John acts in Gregory’s place, 1201. Although the case of Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, had been entrusted to him and had not been examined, he produced witnesses against the deacon Demetrius for the bishop’s condemnation, 627. He degraded Demetrius from his order and handed him over to the proconsul to be tortured, 628. He unjustly deposed Hadrian, 628, 630. For this reason Gregory deprived him of communion for thirty days, 628.

Felix, bishop of Sardica, refused obedience to John, 735. John is instructed what he should do concerning Paul, a bishop who had fallen into a bodily offense, 1201, 1202 and following. The emperor requested that John be deposed because of a head illness, but Gregory disagreed, 1135. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Larissa, 789, 983. He unjustly condemns Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, 629. He does so without any jurisdiction, 630. He accepts the testimony of deacons degraded from their order against Hadrian, 629. He compels Hadrian to confess the crimes charged against him, ibid. John is compelled to restore the property of the Church of Thebes that he held, 631. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Laurina, 596. John, bishop of Palermo, 1243. The pallium is granted to him, ibid. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Ravenna. Why Gregory dedicates his book *Pastoral Rule* to him, 1. John professes that he was nurtured in the bosom of the Roman Church, 668. He says that he incurred the hatred of many in order to preserve the authority of the Roman Church, 669. He defends the privileges of his church and requests that they not be diminished, 669 and following. He is displeased that the use of the pallium has been forbidden to him in litanies, and requests that it be restored to him through the nobles of his city, 736. Five faults by which he dishonors the episcopate are censured in him, 738, 739. Under Gregory he presumes to use the pallium in a way that he had not previously dared, 739. He built and endowed a monastery near the Church of Saint Apollinaris, 791. What in John’s testament should be valid and what invalid, 791, 792, 815. For more about him, see the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Squillace, 599. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John V, bishop of Sorrento, 530, 947, 1288, 1291. In what year he was elected bishop and in what year he died, 530. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Syracuse, 1288. The archdeacon of Catania is designated by Gregory as bishop of Syracuse, 741. John, heir to the virtues of his predecessor Maximianus, 806. Gregory sends him the pallium, ibid. John is praised, 824. He is called a priest of mature and prudent counsel, 975. His love for the Roman See, 976. He administered the Roman patrimony, 979. See the alphabetical Index of Letters.

John, bishop of Velletri, 1287, 1291. He is transferred from the Church of Velletri to another place because of imminent enemies, 578. He is placed in charge of the desolated Church of Tres Tabernae, 614. John, bishop and visitor of the Church of Nepi, 588. John, bishop of the Old City, 498. John, bishop, 1268.

John, priest of the Church of Chalcedon, was regarded as a heretic by his opponents, 803. Judges assigned to him in a case of faith refused to believe him when he made a strict profession, ibid. His accusers admitted that they did not know the heresy of which they accused him, ibid. John was declared orthodox in a Roman synod, 804, 805, 1292. Gregory commends him as orthodox to John of Constantinople, 804; to the emperor Maurice, 805; to Theotistus, Maurice’s kinsman, ibid.; and to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople, 852, 883. Gregory orders that he be received in his order, 664.

John the priest is prevented from becoming bishop of the Church of Ravenna because of his ignorance, especially of the Psalms, 777. John, a priest of the Roman Church, built and endowed an oratory at Rome, 650. Gregory wishes his intention to be fulfilled, ibid., 651. John the Neapolitan deacon is not to be elected bishop because he is unchaste, 1086. John, deacon of Sicily, 734. John, deacon of Thebes, was removed from office because of bodily lust, 629. John the deacon, writer of the life of Saint Gregory: in what period he flourished, 106. He mentions the Gregorian *Dialogues* in several places, ibid.

John, subdeacon of Ravenna, 1230. He is sent to Sicily to administer the patrimony of the Ravennate Church, 1097. See the alphabetical Index of Letters. John the subdeacon is sent to Genoa to investigate the wishes of the Milanese concerning the election of a bishop, 645, 646. He returns to Rome, 681. John, cleric of Ravenna, 1234.

John the abbot, 683, 684. John, abbot of Reggio, is sent to the monastery of Saint Andrew to restrain vicious monks, 778. John, abbot in Sardinia, 1108, 1217. John, abbot of Mount Sinai, 1091. His holiness and humility, ibid. John, abbot of Saint Lucy at Syracuse, 555, 887. He is accused of negligence, 625. He is urged to solitude, hospitality, and almsgiving, 626. John, abbot in Sicily, 1211.

John, the monk and brother of Eleutherius, is warned of the day of his departure, 425. At the very moment of death he summons a monk of another monastery, who dies at that same moment, 425, 428. John, a monk in Gregory’s monastery, 456. He is forewarned of his future death, ibid. Two years later he dies after being called from the grave by his deceased brother, 456. He is venerated, ibid. John the monk left Fantinus the defensor as his heir, 539.

John the surveyor, 887. John the banker, 1108. John, a most eloquent man and adviser of the prefect Georgius, 527. John, defensor and notary of the Roman Church, 613, 650. He is sent to Spain, 1250. His judgment, 1255. John, duke of Berry, the third son of King John, 116. John, ex-consul, patrician, and quaestor, through whose efforts Gregory attained the papacy, 520. John, founder of the monastery near Pisaurum, 826. John, notary of Campanianus, master of the soldiers, 537. John, notary of Milan, 730. John, prefect of the city of Rome, 1045. John, deputy of the city prefects, 296, 460. John acting in place of the prefecture at Milan, 953. John, governor of Italy, 1054. John the Palatine, 1058. He harasses the soap-makers greatly, ibid. He was their defensor, ibid. John the regional official, 1019. John is placed in charge of a deaconry, 1109. John, a schismatic who returned to the Church, 823, 826. John, servant and agent of Venantius, 1115. John the tribune, 324, 1106. Joatha, a woman, 554.

Job. Why, after the devil had killed Job’s children, he left him a feeble woman, 744. Gregory does not allow his commentaries on Job to be read at the vigils, 1195. A certain passage of this commentary is corrected by Saint Gregory, 1196.

Jobinus, deacon and abbot, after falling irreversibly is deprived of his office, 730. Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum, 540, 584. The punishment of a jester is foretold by Saint Boniface, bishop of Ferentino, 188.

Jehoshaphat, about to perish because of his friendship with King Ahab, is rebuked, 70. Joseph the patriarch, who was a citizen of Jerusalem, is compelled to serve Babylon, 923. Joseph the Jew in Gregory’s time, 524. Jovinus, a fuller of the city of Aquinum and later bishop of that city, 293.

Judas, a citizen of Babylon, serves Jerusalem, 923.

Jews were permitted to live under Roman laws and were not to be burdened contrary to reason, 497, 498. The Jews are permitted to transfer elsewhere the synagogue they have at Terracina, 497, 498, 525. A synagogue taken from the Jews must be restored, 930. If confiscated synagogues have been consecrated, they are not to be restored, but their value is to be paid, 973, 974. Jews are forbidden to erect new synagogues, but are permitted to retain the old ones, 930. Jews are not to be subjected to any disadvantage in matters granted to them, 914. They are not to be prevented from celebrating their festivals, 1226. Why the treatment of pagans and heretics was different, ibid.

It is unlawful for Christians to be held in servitude by Jews, 498, 652, 700, 868, 1016, 1018. This was also prohibited by human laws, 652, 910. Christian slaves purchased by Jews at the order of judges are either to be handed over to the judges themselves or sold to Christians within forty days, 953, 954. Christian slaves are not to remain in a Jew’s household, 954. Nevertheless, Jews were sometimes permitted to possess Christian slaves, 1018. Slaves of Jews who flee to the Church are to be claimed for freedom, 688, 689, 910. This practice did not, however, prevail everywhere, 688. If Jews either perverted their Christian slaves or harassed them out of hatred for the faith, they were punished by losing them, ibid. Christians who had long cultivated Jewish lands are to continue cultivating them, 700. Slaves of Jews who wish to convert to the faith are to be claimed for freedom after their price has been paid, 818. The laws forbid Jews to circumcise pagan slaves, 819. These are to be claimed for freedom without payment of their price, ibid.

Jews are to be brought to the faith not by force but by the gentleness of preaching, 542, 930; by admonitions and kindness, 1226. Many Jews were forcibly compelled to baptism by Chilperic, king of Neustria, 542; and by Childebert, 543; and by Sisebut, king of Spain, 543. The Fourth Council of Toledo forbade this, 543. Whether Dagobert and the emperor Heraclius compelled Jews to baptism, 543. What Gregory and the other Fathers thought concerning the conversion of such persons, 525, 703, 734. Gregory wished that the burdens imposed on those who became Christians from Judaism should be somewhat relaxed, 592, 734. What the ancient custom of baptizing Jews had been, 543. They were not admitted to baptism without great caution, 735. The Church provides converts from Judaism with food, lest they suffer want, 714. Gregory commends Joanna, a Christian from Judea, to Peter the subdeacon, 556, 557. He orders that the written acknowledgment of debt be returned to Jamnus the Jew after the debt has been paid, 974. Jews are forbidden to imitate Christian rites, 652. The false conversion of Jews to the faith: from what it proceeds, 525.

A vision of a certain Jew spending the night in the temple of Apollo, 289, 292. He is baptized, ibid. Whoever observes the day of the Sabbath is Judaizing, 1213.

Judge. Who are the contemptible persons in the Church who should be appointed to judge, 25. Formerly, as now, ecclesiastical and lay judges jointly heard the same case and inflicted punishment deserving of vengeance, 623. Excellent admonitions concerning salvation are given to judges, 487, 488. They must display before human beings the justice they carry in their minds, 542. Whatever they recognize as being wrongly committed, they must restrain by swift prohibition, 550. They should refer the dignity bestowed upon them back to the glory of God, its giver, 584, 585. In the presence of judges, the audacity of the wicked should find the goads of correction rather than the comfort of defense, 754. Judges who are influenced by favor become infamous and are liable to the injured party for the value of the lawsuit, 505. In judging cases, God alone must be considered, 856. In doubtful matters it is better not to enforce strictness, but rather to incline toward kindness, 948. What one who conducts God’s causes on earth deserves, 998. He must leave nothing unpunished in the Church of God, 1007. How judges should deal with those who have committed fraud in public affairs, 1079 and following, 1081. Negligent judges are not without sin, 1080. How greatly they must beware of anger, ibid. Nevertheless, anger must sometimes be displayed but not exercised; at other times it must be exercised but not followed, 1080. Among just judges, recommendation is unnecessary, 1083. Judges must not assent to the words of wicked men, 1082. What those who assist judges ought to advise and suggest to them, 761, 762. A judge must show himself impartial toward both litigating parties, 959. The punishment of judges who unjustly judge bishops, 1251. The discernment of judges, 1263. Delegate judge: see *Delegatus*.

The violence of African judges, 1095. A judgment in ambiguous matters should not be conclusive, 656, 1060. What has been adjudicated must be fulfilled, 1139. In former times judgment was entrusted to arbitrators whom the parties could choose, 932, 941, 942, 1261. In ecclesiastical trials, the sacred Gospels were placed in the midst, 906, 907, 961, 962, 1004, 1045, 1060, 1256. Whether ecclesiastical judges use any other formula, 1046. See *Judico*.

The judgment of God is not to be investigated but feared, 413, 517. How the saints recognize the judgments of God, 241, 244. How they are incomprehensible and how they are not, ibid. The judgments of God are uncertain and very different from ours, 768.

The Last Judgment. As each person departs from this life, so he is presented at the judgment, 441. How great is the trembling of the soul that fears the sentence of condemnation, 453. At the Last Judgment the saints will receive a new increase of glory, 408, 409. The strict Judge will approve each person not according to the prerogative of a higher rank but according to the merits of his works, 562. In the examination of the just Judge, the quality of actions changes the merits of ranks, 84. Who will stand secure at the judgment, 645, 656. How Christ did not know the day of judgment, 1069, 1070. Consideration of the Last Judgment is necessary for those who hold public offices, 487.

Human judgments are vain and to be despised, 95.

*Judico.* An absent person cannot be judged, 1234. What precautions must be taken in delivering judgment, 1250–1252, 1263. What laws must be followed, 1252–1255.

Juliana, abbess of the monastery of Saint Vitus in Sardinia, 542. Julian the Apostate, by a law he enacted, prohibited soldiers from becoming monks, 678. He ordered xenodochia to be built in each city, 706. Out of hatred for the Christian religion, he ordered clerics to perform the office of senators, 1047. In danger he took refuge in the sign of the cross, 196.

Julian, defensor of the Roman Church and later bishop of the Church of Sabina, 169, 193, 417. Julian, bishop of Toledo, published a prognostication of the future age in which he reports many passages from the Gregorian *Dialogues*, 106. Julian the Jew, converted to the faith, 714. Julian the scribe, 957. Gregory complains of his wickedness, 1066. Julian, 1231, 1242.

Juliomagus, an episcopal city of Celtic Gaul, 1146.

Beast. How the death of human beings and of beasts is one and the same, 377. What more human beings possess than beasts, ibid.

An oath upon the Gospels or relics: why it was introduced for canonical purgation, 597. Oaths upon the body of Saint Peter, 597, 864, 1241. Upon the body of Saint Apollinaris, 837, 838. What it means to swear by one’s hand, 864. An oath by the four Gospels, 1300. It is not lawful for Catholics to swear by the genius, ibid. Nor by the life of the king or his sons, ibid.

What admonitions should be given to those who sow quarrels, 71. These are disciples and children of the devil, 71. Why a person who sows quarrels is called an apostate, ibid. In one evil he commits countless others, ibid. He serves as a soldier against God, ibid.

The jurisdictions of laymen and clerics are distinct and each must be confined within its own boundaries, 627. Those who usurp another’s jurisdiction are condemned, 1265.

What *juritheum* is, 890.

The strictest law is the greatest injustice, 638. Each person’s rights must be preserved, 645. How right and honor differ, 495. Right and usage are sometimes separated, 522. Right and force are opposed, 693.

Imperial letters, or sacred rescripts, are called “principal commands” or “divine commands,” 731.

Justiniana Prima, formerly a city of Macedonia, 585, 627. It was endowed with metropolitan rights and with the vicarial dignity of the Roman See, 585. Why it was called Prima, ibid. John, bishop of Justiniana Prima, 983. See his title.

Emperor Justinian: in what year he began to reign, 348. He pressed for the convocation of the Fifth Council and the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 615. By an edict he ordered that the faith of the four holy councils be subscribed throughout the world by the bishops, 515. The Franks did not obey his Novels before the middle of the fifth century, 1021. Justinian’s chartophylacium had already been burned in Gregory’s time, 1031.

Why the emperor Justin was called “the Elder,” 281. Justin, praetor of Sicily, 487, 594. Led by avarice, he neglected to punish a most wicked Jew, 652.

A judge must demonstrate by his works the justice he carries in his mind, 542. To practice justice is the highest virtue in kings, 1023. The just are often tested without guilt, 87. Why the anger of the just is so greatly to be feared, 188. After the just have conquered great enemies, they are wearied even by lesser adversaries, lest they become exalted, 308. The wicked in certain good deeds and the just in their trials are compared with respect to evil, 87.

Justus, a cleric of Sorrento, 530. Justus, a monk severely punished by Saint Gregory because of the vice of proprietorship, 465 and following. By what means he is freed from the punishments of purgatory, 468. *Jutum* and *Jutus* mean *adiutum* (“aided,” neuter) and *adiutus* (“aided,” masculine), 642.

Saint Juvenalis, martyr, appears to Probus, bishop of Rieti, as he is dying, 389. What young men should be admonished, 35.

K

*Kyrie eleison* is said differently in the Roman Church and among the Greeks, 940. In former times it was sung at Matins and Vespers, 939.

L
Laban, an image of the watchful shepherd, 963. The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, 510. What polluted lips are, 312, 313. Labina, a religious woman, had built a monastery in Corsica, 545. Milk. One must abstain from milk during a fast, 1303. Tears. What it means to draw divided waters from the eyes, 84. The tears of one who mourns sins yet does not abandon them are filthy, 86. With what diligence the grace of tears is to be sought, 353. Tears are signified by the upper and lower irrigation channel, ibid., 356. The punishment of a nun who ate lettuce, 165. What a *laena* (cloak) is, 1092. Who the cheerful are to be admonished, 37. Cheerful people have luxury close at hand, ibid. Self-will pertains to cheerfulness, 62.

A layman of whatever merit must not presume to aspire to the episcopate [Col. 1533], nor may he be elected, 588, 601, 602, 989, 995, 996, 1227, 1228. Gregory calls laypeople sons of the Church, 666, 787, 793, 889, 987. The more honored among the laypeople are called by him the *ordo*; the rest, the plebs, 550, 576, 634. Nowhere did Gregory call laypeople men of God, 295. The violence of laypeople is to be restrained, 626, 627. Laypeople are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical services, 1289.

Lamigia, a city of Numidia, 566, 567. There was a twofold bishopric of this name, ibid. Argentius, bishop of Lamigi, 567. The use of lamps in churches, 341, 344. A glass lamp is restored whole by a miracle, 180. Our lamps are good works, 1126. What it means to take oil in vessels together with lamps, 1126, 1127.

Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, takes an argument from Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on the body and blood of the Lord, 107. Gregory’s *Dialogues* contributed not insignificantly to the conversion of the Lombards, 114. The Lombards, while persecuting the monks of Saint Equitius, are tormented by unclean spirits, 173. They kill forty peasants who refused to eat forbidden foods, 337, 340. They put to the sword a very great multitude of captives because they refused to worship a goat’s head, 340. A Lombard Arian bishop, about to use force against the Catholic Church, is struck with blindness, 341. Sanctulus miraculously escapes a Lombard sword, 364. After a vision appeared to Bishop Redemptus, the Lombards invade Italy, 368. Their violence and savagery, ibid. They hang two monks from the branches of a tree; after their death they were heard singing psalms, 404. A Lombard who killed a deacon is handed over to an unclean spirit, 405. Abbot Suranus is killed by the Lombards, ibid. Gregory wishes the sons of Lombard Arians, baptized in heresy, to be reconciled to the Catholic faith, 502. Gregory says that he is a bishop of the Lombards, not of the Romans, 520. Something was given to them daily by the Roman Church so that it might be permitted to live among them, 751. Italy held captive under the Lombards, 766, 767, 836. Peace with the Lombards on fair terms, which they themselves accept, is not to be refused by the exarch, 762. From what time they occupied Italy, 1244. A truce is made with the king of the Lombards, 1067.

The small stone cut from the mountain without hands is Christ, 772. The stone rejected by the builders is Christ, 854. What the stones of the sanctuary signify, 25, 26. They are scattered at the head of every street, 25. Why they are said to be scattered not in the streets but at the head of the streets, 26.

Those are called the fallen who fall into idolatry, heresy, schism, or adultery, 503. The heavier punishment of fallen clerics: the higher the rank, the more disgraceful the fault, ibid. Fallen priests and other lower clerics are to be confined in monasteries where discipline is flourishing, 538. The property of the fallen should benefit poor monasteries, or be given to the parents of the fallen, with an allowance assigned to them, ibid. When a maidservant of God has fallen and been confined in a monastery, her property should promptly be gathered for her support, 539. Gregory is always consistent when he speaks of fallen ministers of the Church, 729. Fallen clerics are irrevocably deposed. See *Clerics*.

Larissa, a city of Thessaly in Greece, 627, 628. John, bishop of Larissa, is deprived of jurisdiction over Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, 630, 631. Concerning the same John, 789, 983. See his title.

The Lateran monastery was built under Abbot Bonitus after the Cassinian monastery had been destroyed, 208. The Latin Way, 1125. Side. Sent “from the side,” that is, from the retinue and household; a very ancient expression, 758, 928. See *Legate*.

To wash. The custom of washing bodies before burial, 400, 416. Whether the body may be washed on the Lord’s Day, 1214. Various customs of washing, 1159. This practice of washing was disapproved by certain Fathers, 1160. A man sleeping with his own wife must not enter the Church unless he has washed with water, 1160. Why Jews today do not wash the body, 1159.

Lauda, a city. See *Laus Pompeia*. To praise. He praises the deeds of others in vain who does not imitate them, 45. How those who praise the unlawful things they themselves do are to be rebuked, 88. A voice that belongs solely to the Creator must not be uttered in praise of a creature, 854. With what disposition those who praise and those who blame are to be heard, 1093.

When the tomb of Saint Lawrence was opened, all who saw his body died within ten days, 709. Fragments from Lawrence’s gridiron are sent to Dynamium, 648. And fragments of his relics to Bishop Palladius, 828. The monastery of Saint Lawrence, 1264. Laurence, antipope, 444. Laurence, bishop of Milan, 1103. Childebert calls him “Patriarch” in a letter, 565. How the dispute between Laurence and the Roman Church is to be settled, ibid. Laurence unjustly deprives Magnus, a priest of his Church, of communion, 642. He sends to Rome a signed guarantee condemning the Three Chapters, 682. He kept the oaths attached to that guarantee, 719. Laurence the priest, one of Saint Augustine’s companions, is commended, 1140. Laurence, archdeacon of the Roman Church, is deposed, 1283. Laurence, a man of illustrious rank, 1190, 1191.

John, bishop of Laurinum, 596. Laurio, a monk, 177. Laus Pompeia, now Lauda, a city of Insubria, 701. Lazarus raised from the dead, 321.

Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, was especially close to Gregory, 345, 531, 532. Gregory’s letter to him is supported by testimonies, 531. Through Leander’s efforts, Saint Hermenegild was brought from Arian error to the Catholic faith, 345. And his brother Reccared, 531. Leander had been grievously afflicted by Liuvigild, 348. Leander’s great charity shines forth in his letter, 1027. From the humility of his speech the elevation of his heart is apparent, ibid. He suffered from gout, 1028. Gregory sends him several books, 532. Likewise the *Exposition on Job* and the book of the *Pastoral Rule*, 777. And a pallium, 1028. Gregory asks for his prayers, 1027.

By whom the lessons in the Church ought to be sung, 1289. What *lectisternia* (ceremonial couch-banquets) are, 1091, 1092. In former times readers read the Gospel in the Church, 1289.

There are three kinds of legates, 928. In former times legates *a latere* were sent not only by the supreme pontiffs but also by emperors and kings, 758, 928. Hilary the monk was appointed legate of the Apostolic See throughout Africa, 567. Two Cistercian monks were legates of that same see against the Albigensians, ibid.

Ecclesiastical and civil legislators generally abuse their power, 1299. Gentleness must be combined with severity, 23. See *Mildness*.

Saint Leo the Great cut a *brandeum* (relic-cloth), from which blood flowed, 710. Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian is called a *tome*, 793. The Churches of the East defend Saint Leo’s faith, 966.

Leo, bishop of Catania, 1097. Accused, he is ordered to come to Rome, 557. He returns to Catania completely cleared, 597, 633. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Leo, bishop in Corsica, 562. The visitation of the Church of Saona is entrusted to him, ibid., 564. The Corsicans are ordered to obey him, 564. Leo, bishop of Fano, 826. Leo, archdeacon of the Church of Myra, 735. Leo, an acolyte entrusted with the care of the Church of Saint Agatha in the Subura, 698. Leo, a *chartarius* (record-keeper), 1062. Leo, former consul, 489, 557. Leontia Augusta, 1301. Gregory congratulates her on having obtained the empire, 1245. Leontius, bishop of Urbino, 641, 774. Later bishop of Rimini, 825. Gregory appoints Leontius prefect of the city of Nepi, 576. Leontius, former consul, 946. His virtues are praised, 923 and following. He is called “most glorious,” 1190, 1191. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Leuparicus, priest of Saintes, 828, 829. The Levites are said to have consecrated their hands to God, 70. What it signifies that Levites serve from the age of twenty-five and become guardians of the vessels from the age of fifty, 213. The lightness of the mind is to be healed and fickleness overcome, 61. Lightness of work and mind is the companion of gluttony, 61, 62. It is extreme frivolity to believe serious evils that cannot be proven, 860.

Liuvigild, king of the Visigoths, deprives Hermenegild of his kingdom and kills him because he had embraced the Catholic faith, 345. As he was dying, he commends his son Reccared to Saint Leander the bishop, 348.

The law of God was given for this reason, that it might prohibit sacrifices to Satan, 73. The law of Christ is charity, 43, 79. How the law of Christ is fulfilled, ibid. When God wished to recall man from sin, he gave him a law, 82. The figurative precepts of the Jewish Law cannot be observed according to the letter, 1213. Ecclesiastical laws are cheapened by excessive dispensations or favors, 657. Things done contrary to the laws are not merely useless but are to be regarded as null and void, 932. Human laws joined with divine laws are binding, 1299. The laws of princes are sometimes rightly brought forward in support of the canons, 1253. And they are commended by the authority of the canons themselves, 1254. A collection of the imperial laws to be observed in ecclesiastical judgment, 1252 and following.

Leah, a symbol of the active life, 491. *Libellatica* are so called from the *libelli* on which leases of fields were written, 536, 1088. They are used for the leases themselves, 536. Under the name *libellarius*, 569. Why the *libellatici* were formerly not punished according to the stricter discipline, 503.

The notorious libel. See *Contestatio* (formal complaint). What the book sealed with seven seals in the Apocalypse signifies, 448. The power to prohibit books belongs to the supreme pontiffs, 843. Liberatus, a deacon whose ambition is restrained, 566. Liberatus, a merchant, 538. Liberius, bishop of Cumae, 587. Liberius Patricius, founder of a monastery in Campania, 269, 946. He was praetorian prefect of Gaul under Theoderic and Athalaric, 988.

Freedom. The question of freedom—whether someone is free or a slave—requires higher judges, 910. Libertinus, bishop in Sardinia, 932, 1217. Libertinus, superior of the monastery at Fundi, 155, 156. His patience, 157, 160, 161. The efficacy of his prayer, 157. Sought by the Franks, he is not found because of a miracle, 157. A remarkable conflict between his humility and devotion to his mother, 160. He brings a boy back from the dead, ibid. His humility, ibid.

Libertinus, prefect of Sicily, 651. Whether he was a praetor, 652, 759. In what year he was praetor of Sicily, 946. He is called a former prefect, 945; a former praetor, 1061. Gregory consoles him while he endures adversity, 1062. When Libertinus assumed the prefecture of Sicily, the entire province rendered thanks, 1079. Libertinus, a magnificent man, 867.

A pound is made up of seventy-two solidi, 570, 648. Licinianus, bishop of Cartagena in Spain: at what time he flourished and by what kind of death he died, 620. He praises the book of the *Pastoral Rule* enthusiastically, 620 and following. He argues that the less experienced should sometimes be promoted to the orders, 622. He asks for Gregory’s books on Job and the other moral works, ibid. Licinius, bishop of Angers, 1144. His lineage, 1146. At what time he flourished, ibid.

To whom the power of binding and loosing was given, 253. What it signifies to cut down trees in a forest, 32. Lilies, ornaments of crowns, 555. Lilybaeum, a city of Sicily, 661. The clergy of Lilybaeum receive permission to elect a bishop, whom they later ask Gregory to consecrate, 801. Bishops of Lilybaeum: Paschasinus, 661; Theodorus, 660; Decius, 801. See his title.

The thresholds of the Apostles, 1205. Why the basilicas of the saints were called thresholds, ibid. The tongue must be restrained with discretion, not always tied, 54. Whoever does not restrain his tongue destroys harmony, 55. Intemperance of the tongue reconciles enemies, 1274. Saint Benedict strikes intemperance of the tongue with excommunication, 253. It is very difficult for the tongue of secular people not to defile the mind that it touches, 313. The remarkable knowledge of all languages in an uneducated boy, 413. What fiery tongues signify, 840. Bishops speak in defense of the truth with their tongues cut out by the roots, 348, 349.

Lipara, an episcopal city on the island of the same name, 580. Agathus, bishop of Lipara, 665. Lippia or Lupia, a town of Calabria, 808. The Church of Lippia is entrusted to Peter, bishop of Otranto, for visitation, 807. What *lippus* (blear-eyed) signifies, 12.

Lérins, an island of Gaul, 1099, 1100. Why Lérins is called the island of Saint Honoratus, 1101. The monastery of Lérins, a nursery of bishops and holy men, ibid. Lissus, a city of Illyricum, 660. John, expelled by enemies from the Church of Lissus, is placed over the Church of Squillace on the condition that he return to the former see if he is liberated, [Col. 1535] 599.

Why the litany is so called and what it signifies, 1138. It is incorrectly written *letania*, 1284. Among ancient authors, litanies are called solemn processions of the clergy and people to an appointed place, 736, 819. How many solemn litanies there were in antiquity, 819, 837. Whether the greater and lesser litanies differ, 1283. What the septiform litany is, ibid. The greater litany is the same as the septiform litany, 1284. Mamertus restored the litanies, ibid. The ancient use of litanies, ibid. Litanies are proclaimed against barbarian incursions, 1138.

Saint Gregory forbids litigating, 1122, 1139, 1183. He prefers to leave good legacies rather than litigate, 1190. Lawsuits are to be ended by elected judges or arbitrators, 1122. Gregory settles by his authority a dispute between an abbot and a subdeacon, 949. Letters of dismissal. See *Dismissal*.

Liturgy. See *Mass*.

Locri, a city of the Bruttians in Greece, 891. Bishops of Locri: Dulcinus, 1063; Marcianus, 962, 1063.

What one’s place is before God, 967. Why different ranks of places have been established, 899. Hidden places cannot save the soul without God’s grace, 849. Neither places nor orders bring us near to our Creator, 879.

Expression. In the mind of the hearer, the quality of the expression heard is the seed of the thought that is to follow, 18. What Λογάριν or λογάριον signifies, 187. Λόγειον or λόγιον is an oracle or divine response in prose, 508. Λόγιος, that is, articulate, eloquent, a prophet or poet, ibid.

London, the principal city of England, 1163. What is decreed concerning the bishop of London, ibid. Mellitus, bishop of London, 1287. Longinus was the first to bear the name of exarch; he was sent to Italy by the emperor Maurice against the Lombards, 521. Longinus, *strator* of the emperor Maurice, 675.

Talkativeness must be avoided by rulers, 18. How great the evils of talkativeness are, 55. The justice of the mind is laid waste when there is no restraint from excessive speech, 55. Talkativeness is the companion of gluttony, 61, 62.

To speak. Who speaks from God and before God, 73. He speaks well who lives perfectly, 873. Bishops speak in defense of the truth with their tongues cut out by the roots, 348, 349. To one of them this ability was taken away because of luxury, ibid.

What Lot, fleeing from burning Sodom and finding Segor, signifies, 80. Why he did not proceed directly to the mountains, ibid. Lot was righteous in the very perverse city but sinned on the mountain, 849.

Lucca, a city of Etruria, now a republic, 293. Saint Frigdianus, bishop of Lucca, 293. Lucania, a province of Italy, 685. Lucas, a priest of Thessalonica, rejects the Council of Chalcedon, 1073. What a person suspected of heresy does, 1174. Lucianus, a monk devoted himself to writing sacred books, 169. Lucidus, bishop of Leontini, 1211, 1230. Lucifer, cellarer of the monastery of Lucusianum, 1137. Later its superior, 1136. Lucillus, bishop of Malta, 605. He is to be deposed in an assembly of four bishops, 979. He is ordered to restore the property of his Church that he had taken away, 1041. Pope Lucius III received schismatics returning to the Church through a repeated ordination, 608. Lucius, bishop of Reggio and predecessor of Boniface, 656.

Profit. What profits are to be sought in this life, 487, 488. Mourning. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, 377.

Lucullanum, a fortress on an island of Campania, 506. In this fortress the monastery of Saint Severinus, apostle of Noricum, was built, 624. The Lucusianum monastery, founded by Saint Gregory, 1136. He complains about the relaxed rule of this monastery, ibid. Its abbot was Domitius the priest, ibid.; and its superior, Lucifer, ibid. What that monastery is called today, 949, 950.

Saint Louis did not wish to involve himself in the cases of priests, 699. Bishops of Lyons: Eucherius, 1101; Etherius, 830, 1217, 1219. Lights customarily used in churches, 333, 341, 344, 1273 and following. And at the funerals of the dead, 927. Luminosa, the widow of the tribune Zemarchus, 499. Luminosus, bishop of Ferentinum, 1291. Luminosus, abbot of the monastery of Saints Andrew and Thomas at Rimini, 602, 603, 604. Luminosus, a servant of the Church of Grumentum, 1209. Luna, a city of Etruria, 700. Venantius, bishop of Luna, 293. Lupus, abbot of Saint Martin of Autun, 1225. May the wolf lying in wait for the sheep find a shepherd watchful and resisting on every side, 715. Lupus, bishop of Chalon, 1144. Saint Lupus, a monk of Lérins and bishop of Troyes, 1101.

Mud. What it means for a miser to heap up dense mud against himself, 65. The light of the flock is the shepherd’s flame, 921. Saint Luxorius, martyr in Sardinia, 931.

Luxury. Stench and mist signify carnal desire, 436. Cheerful people have luxury close at hand, 37. Luxury arises from gluttony, 61. Through luxury the virtues of the soul are destroyed, ibid. What admonitions those conscious of sins of the flesh require, 81. Let them mourn past sins and avoid future ones, 82. Why those who mourn the fault of luxury should not have to feel the severity of discipline, 679. Those whom the stench of the flesh still delights here are surrounded by the mist of stench, 436.

Lycaonia, a region of Asia Minor, 482. Lycaonia was subject to the patriarch of Constantinople, ibid.

M
Macedonius. His heresy, 748. The Roman Church accepted from the Council of Constantinople only what was defined against Macedonius, 882. Machines formerly used for raising immense weights aloft, 381. The Church of Maguelonne transferred to Montpellier by papal authority and with the consent of King Francis I, 578. Mary Magdalene, Lazarus’s sister and the sinful woman, 869. How her sins were forgiven, 869. The resurrection of Christ announced to the disciples from her mouth, ibid. One who has not been a disciple ought not to become a teacher, 156. The dignity of *magister* was the highest among the patricians, 726. Among several, the *magister officiorum* was the chief, ibid. The dignity of *magister* was called *magisteria*, ibid. [Col. 1537] By whom the teaching office is believed to be a light burden, 2. The inexperienced should not dare to undertake the teaching office, ibid. Adversity is a useful teacher, 5. There are those who are taught inwardly by the teaching of the Spirit, 156. Who is suited to the teaching of virtue, 213. *Magnitudo*, a title with which Gregory sometimes addresses judges, 975, 1032, 1033, 1085. And dukes, 1048, 1097, and elsewhere. Magnus, priest, 644, 1095. Unjustly excommunicated by Laurentius, bishop of Milan, he is absolved, 642. The estate of Magulianum, 651. The title *Majesty*, by which kings now rejoice, was not in use in Gregory’s time, 684. The *major domus* is to be appointed by the bishop, 1172. Or by all the clergy if the bishop is negligent, ibid. What his office was, ibid. See *Vicedominus*. Who the *major populi* was, 1005, 1057. The island of Majorca, 1256. Málaga, a city of the kingdom of Granada, 1251. Januarius, bishop of Málaga, 1250. Malchus, bishop of Dalmatia, administered the patrimony of the Apostolic See in Dalmatia, 527. He is summoned to Rome to give an account of his administration, 584, 609, 640. He is forbidden to interfere in the affairs of the Church of Salona, 640, 658. He suddenly dies at Rome, 726. Maximus slanders Gregory as being implicated in his death, 726. Cursing is a grave sin, even when it is uttered through carelessness of the tongue, 312. Sorcerers are to be punished, 759, 891, 1139, 1259. Malice is the mother of vices, 44. Malice in the heart is a beam in the eye, ibid. Gregory asks that the household of Maloin be released, 571. Pomegranates signify the unity of faith, 18, 511. Uncompleted evil deeds do no harm, 87. How those who secretly do evil and publicly do good are to be reproved, 95. They are whitewashed tombs, 95. How greatly those sin who, secretly doing good, permit others to form an evil opinion of them, 96.

The wicked. Friendship joined with the wicked is harmful to the good and rejected by God, 70. Agreement among the wicked is harmful, 71. The good are always displeasing to the wicked, 1026. They are always mingled with the good, 1127, 1128. The company of the wicked is a purification for the good, 1127. The wicked, when gathered together, are to be borne patiently by the shepherd if there are some good people whom he can help, 217. In hell the wicked see the wicked undergoing the same punishments, and the good in the kingdom, 424. Mamertus (Saint) restored the solemn litanies, 1284.

*Mamma*. In Egypt, what it means for the breasts of puberty to be broken, 82. A Christian slave cannot be owned by a pagan, a Jew, or a heretic, 652, 700, 868. A slave who leaves his master and passes to ecclesiastical ownership is to be returned to his master, 526. A slave may justly complain against his master and take refuge with the Church, 624. For the sake of the faith, slaves were claimed for freedom against their masters’ wishes, without any price being paid, 688, 818. This privilege did not prevail everywhere, ibid. A slave is redeemed for the price of twelve solidi, 689. A pagan slave circumcised by Jews is to be claimed for freedom without any redemption price, 819. Slaves unjustly detained by a bishop are to be returned, 897. In former times monasteries made use of slaves, [Col. 1537] 898. Slaves manumitted on the condition that they become monks may not leave the monastery, 955. Why slaves were formerly sold in the presence of ecclesiastics or judges, 1015. *Mandator*, a term with various meanings in law; here it means the judge who ordered the sale, 954. *Manduco*. In what sense Paul said, “Let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats,” 617. *Mane*, or at matins, meaning “early” or “promptly,” 895. Manfredonia, the Italian city formerly called Sipontum Novum, 546. The various insanities of the Manichaeans, 734. The Manichaeans are to be recalled to the Catholic faith by punishments, 734. The use of the *maniple* replaced *mappulae*, or linen napkins, around the tenth century, 668. What manna signifies, 24. The *mansionarius* of a church is its custodian who ministers there continually, 174, 333, 336, 709. There are many dwelling places in heaven, 429. How the gentle are to be admonished, 56. They should embrace solicitude, 57. Torpor is near gentleness, 56. Gentleness should be joined with justice, 514. *Mansus*. See *Massa*.

What the broken hand of the Shepherd signifies, 11. The hand that works to cleanse stains should be clean, 13, 508. What it means to “fix one’s hand upon a stranger,” 38. What it means to purge oneself by a third, fifth, or seventh hand, 864. The hand has always been a symbol of faith, ibid. What it means to use both hands in place of the right hand, 764, 765. The various forms of manumission of slaves, 757, 800. To manumit slaves was to make them free and Roman citizens, 800. Manumission of slaves, as favoring human liberty, ought not to be revoked by the Church, 548. Constantine the Great granted that manumissions might take place in the Church, 576. By a law he likewise granted all clerics permission to set their servants free, 800. Formerly it was extremely difficult to grant slaves their freedom, ibid. The form of manumission, with associated gifts and conditions, 800, 801. Saint Benedict knew by the Spirit that *mappulae*, received from a monk and hidden away, had been concealed, and he reproved the guilty man, 245. The use of *mappulae* is granted only to the chief deacons of Ravenna when they minister with their bishop at the celebration, 668. The *maniples* replaced the *mappulae* at Mass, ibid. Marato, the name of an estate, 590. Marbodus, author of the Life of Saint Licinius, 1146. Petrus de Marca. His opinion concerning the inscription of a certain letter is approved, 1166. Marcellinus, bishop of Ancona, extinguished a fire, 177. Marcellus or Marcellinus, proconsul of Dalmatia, 640, 929, 993. He rendered good service to the Roman Church, 993. He is censured for the favor shown to Maximus, bishop of Salona, 929. Why, when summoned by the emperor, he did not immediately obey, 993. Marcellus the scholastic, 720, 914. Marcellus, a monk of the Gregorian monastery, 409. Marcellus, a citizen of the city of Todi, restored to life, 201. Marcellus the freedman, 1044. What *marcha* signifies, 1015. The Marcianists or Marcionists, heretics, 803, 804. [Col. 1538] Marcianus, a priest of the diocese of Tauriana, designated bishop of Locri, 889. He became bishop of Locri, 962, 1063. Mark the Evangelist (Saint) founded the Church of Alexandria, 889. The blessing of Saint Mark is called the blessing of Saint Peter, 917. Marcus Scribo, sent by the emperor Maurice to Sicily to exact accounts, 1078.

*Sea*. What the depth of the sea signifies, 4. How Sidon is brought to shame by the word “sea,” 83. Who sleeps in the midst of the sea, 90. What the waters of the sea gathered together as in a wineskin signify, 1134. What the bronze sea before the doors of the Temple, for washing the hands of those entering, indicates, 19, 512. The “sea of crystal,” that is, the glassy blue sea, 1039.

Mary: how she is both the handmaid and the Mother of the Lord, 1169. Mary appears to Musa, a virgin soon to die, 400. Mary sitting at the Lord’s feet signifies the contemplative life, 491. See *Magdalene*. Maria the patrician, 856. Marianus, 1060. Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, 1230, 1287, 1291. Having long lived with Gregory in the monastery, he is elected bishop of Ravenna by common agreement, 777, 787. He comes unwillingly to the episcopate, 777. Gregory commends him to Andrew the scholastic, ibid. How the use of the pallium is granted to him, 787. His faith, 792, 793. He is reproved for unjustly burdening the monastery, or permitting it to be burdened by his clergy, 815, 816. His lack of mercy toward the poor, 816. He refuses to read Gregory’s admonitions, 817. The case of Maximus, bishop of Salona, is entrusted to him for judgment, 936, 983, 991. See more about him in the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Marinianus, bishop of the city of Turris in Sardinia, 550, 932. Marinianus, abbot of Palermo, 548, 595, 1173. He is entrusted with examining the case of Bishop Victor, 642, 643. Marinianus, defender of the Church of Milan, 861. Marinus, husband of Gordia, the sister of Maurice, 877. Gregory greets him, 493. The province of the Marsi is the same as Valeria in Latium, 405. Martha signifies the active life, 491, 869. Martia, a religious woman unjustly transferred from her monastery to another, is ordered to be recalled, 732. Martianus, bishop of Ferentum, 1291. Why Martianus the defender should be driven into exile, 979. Martianus the monk, 1055, 1056. Martianus the *tabularius*, 1122. How far Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, kept away from banquets, 580. The monastery of Saint Martin at Autun, 1219. Its privilege, 1225. Martin, bishop of Tainat, because his church had been destroyed, was incardinated in the Church of Saône, 563, 564. Martin, deacon and abbot, defamed by accusations and canonically cleared, is declared innocent, 864. Martin the scholastic, 975, 976. Martin the solitary, 313. By his prayers he obtains water from a rock, ibid. He lives for three years with a serpent into which the devil had entered, 316. He avoids the company of women, ibid. Through his prayers a child thrown over a precipice is not injured, 316. When the rock is torn away, his cell remains unharmed in the collapse, 317. [Col. 1539] He had fastened a chain to his foot, which he loosened at Saint Benedict’s command, 317. Martin the tenant farmer, 707.

It is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr, 615. The worship of one whose martyrdom is by no means certain is to be prohibited, 1157. Who should be called martyrs in a time of peace for the Church, 337. Very many became martyrs under the Lombards. See *Lombards*. There are two kinds of martyrdom, 337. The merit of martyrdom is hidden when virtue, ready for suffering, burns in the soul, ibid. Martyrdom is signified by the name of the cup, 337. The path of a harsher life leads to martyrdom, 340. The palm of martyrdom belongs not to human will but to divine election, ibid. Martyrius, one a monk of Valeria and the other of Lycaonia, 201. By that Martyrius the sign of the cross was divinely impressed on bread, 204.

*Martyrology*. Whether the martyrology read at Rome in Gregory’s time was what we now call the ancient Roman Martyrology, 916, 918. The martyrology published under the name of Saint Jerome is not by that saint, 918. What was contained in the martyrology read at Rome under Gregory, 916, 917. How greatly the death of martyrs benefits the Church, 348. Sometimes those who seemed contemptible in the Church’s peace undergo martyrdom, 340. Sometimes those believed to stand bravely in the Church’s peace abandon the faith during persecution, ibid. Mascator, grandson of Armentarius, a man of distinction, 317. *Massa*, or *mansus* or *mansum*, is land of a definite extent and measurement, 534, 758. *Massa* corresponds to an estate or farm, 534. The distinction between *massa* and *casa*, ibid. Tenants of Church estates are not to be appointed for profit, 536. The sons of tenants of estates are not to marry outside the estate in which they were born, 1197. Tenants of estates throughout Gaul are admonished to live irreproachably, 758. And to obey the patrician Arigius, ibid.

Massilia. At Massilia, or in that city, there were four monasteries in the sixth century, 858. Bishops of Massilia: Theodorus, 541; Paschasius, ibid.; Serenus, 830. Mastalo, exceedingly zealous for the unity of the Church against schismatics, 776. What a *matricula* is, 656. Who are called *matricularii*, ibid., 657. Marriage is not a sin, 1160. In marriage the will must be free, 693. Marriage is to be dissolved if one of the spouses is of servile condition, 845. Marriage is not to be dissolved under the pretext of religion, 1130 and following, 1131. The indissolubility of marriage, ibid. What worldly law is contrary to this indissolubility, 1130, 1138. From where impediments to marriage arise, 1154. Within what degrees of blood relationship and affinity marriage may be contracted, 1153, 1154. The marriage of incestuous persons is null, 1279. Whom men and women may not take in marriage, 1293 and following. The English neophytes joined in prohibited degrees are not to be separated or deprived of communion, 1155.

Matthew, a man of distinction, supported by the alms of Saint Gregory, 1182. Maurentius, bishop of Africa, is praised for his concern for the ecclesiastical order, 903. Maurentius the *chartularius*, 505, 506, 838. He is called “a magnificent man,” 489. Maurentius, master of the soldiers, 903, 956. Very dear to Gregory, 908, 1184. [Col. 1539] He is praised for his study of sacred reading, 908. Having a lawsuit, he is commended by Gregory, 1183. And requesting a *precarium*, 1184. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

The emperor Maurice is called “the most Christian lord of the world,” 501, and “the most Christian of princes,” 804. His lineage and qualities of mind, 675. Gregory calls him “the most serene Lord,” 494, 495. Maurice is addressed more freely, 1188. The virtues of Maurice, 677, 678. He was not accustomed to interfere in priestly cases, 699. Exceedingly devoted to the peace of the Church, 747. His charity toward the poor, 757. The correctness of his faith, 804. His zeal in defense of the faith, 841. In his time heretics were compelled to fall silent, 1134. Maurice prohibited anyone involved in public administration from becoming a cleric, 675. Nor were such men to be received into monasteries, ibid. Likewise he enacted a law forbidding soldiers to become monks, 675, 676, 677, 678. Gregory asks that this law be moderated or changed, 677. He orders that schismatics not be compelled to return to the unity of the Church, 934, 935. He won a notable victory over the Persians and restored Chosroes, king of the Persians, 677. He calls Gregory foolish and simple, 765, 766. The monstrous avarice of Maurice, 1238. How many evils Gregory suffered from him, 766, 767. Saint Gregory was not unjust toward the emperor Maurice, 1238. Maurice was killed together with his entire family, 1301, 1302. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Maurice the monk, 1056. Maurilius, former prefect, 1191. Gregory wishes aid to be given him while he resides within ecclesiastical precincts, 527. Maurilius, master of the soldiers, 570, 571. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Maurus is brought to Saint Benedict, 220. Walking over the waters on dry feet, he rescues Placidus, 225. Because he seemed to rejoice at the death of Florentius, he is reproved, 228. Whether this Maurus is the same as Maurus, son of Equitius, ibid. Maurus is placed in charge as abbot of the monastery of Saint Pancratius at Rome, 697. Maurus the slave, 1035, 1036.

Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Pudentiana, is to be deposed because he permitted a Donatist bishop to be ordained in his city, 611, 612. Maximianus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Gregory and afterward bishop of Syracuse, 105, 357, 421, 573, 1237. One of Saint Gregory’s companions sent by Pelagius to Constantinople, 357. He is miraculously saved from a shipwreck, ibid. Gregory appoints him vicar of the Roman See in Sicily, 487, 573. At that time Gregory entrusted his functions not to a place but to a person, 574. From him Gregory learned certain matters that he inserted into his *Dialogues*, 105, 177, 661. Many matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline are entrusted to him, 690, 691, 692. In what year he died, 105, 573. Gregory grieves over his death, 741. After his death, the Syracusans give him distinguished testimony, 753. He threw certain clerics into prison for sorcery, but, overtaken by death, was unable to punish them, 759. He is called a bishop of holy memory, 897. He is venerated by the Church, 357. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Maximianus the Illyrian priest, 585. Maximilla, a false prophetess, 1168.

Maximus of Constantinople. Why his ordination, and the ordinations conferred by him, are null, 608. Maximus, a monk of Lérins and afterward bishop of Riez, 1101. Maximus was forcibly intruded into the see of Salona, 698, 699. He is called an usurper of the Church of Salona, 793; a seizer, 810; and a transgressor, 983. Gregory prohibits his ordination, 690. The emperor does not consent, 725. Maximus and those who ordained him are removed from every office, especially from the altar, 699, 721. In contempt of excommunication he celebrates Masses, 752, 812. He publicly ordered Saint Gregory’s letter to be torn up, 725. How many vices afflicted him and his ordination, 699, 725, 752. He slanders Gregory by claiming that Bishop Malchus was murdered while in custody, 726. He is summoned to Rome, 793, 811. He refuses to come, 813, 814. If he persists in defiance, he is deprived of communion in the Lord’s Body and Blood, 812, 863. The emperor orders that Maximus, when coming to Rome, be received with honor, 752. Few abstain from communion with him, 813. Gregory exhorts the people of Zadar to suspend communion with Maximus, 814. His case is entrusted to Constantius, bishop of Milan, for judgment, 983, and to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, 991. His devices for obtaining pardon, 983. He gives humble satisfaction and submits himself to penance, 992, 1296. Under what conditions communion is restored to him, 991, 992. Gregory congratulates him on his full satisfaction, 1033. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Maximus the subdeacon, 539. Maximus the monk, son of the wealthy Chrysaorius, 440. Maximus the *palatinus privatarum*, 1047. Maximus, father of Probus, bishop of Rieti, 389. A privilege granted to the monastery of Saint Medard, 1284. Medicine, whether of body or mind, when applied indivisibly ought to serve in a divisible manner, 98.

*Physician*. The rashness of certain people who, ignorant of the wounds of souls, claim to be physicians, 3. One who bears a wound on his face should not be a physician of another, 10. A physician who does not know his own wound but wishes to cure another’s is inexperienced, 73. A physician gives a sick person whom he despairs of everything he desires, 78. Bishops of Milan: Datius, 285; Laurentius, 565, 1103. See his title. Constantius. See his title. Deusdedit, 1206, 1238. The bishops of Milan were not ordained without the consent of the Roman pontiff, 645, 646, 1094, 1095. The bishop of Milan was a metropolitan, 646. Gregory rejects the election of the bishop of Milan made by the Lombards and Agilulf, 1095. The common table of the Milanese clergy, 720. The revenues of the Milanese Church in Sicily and elsewhere, 1095. Megalis, a woman, 960. Melania the Younger devoted herself to copying sacred books, 169. Melantius, bishop of Rouen, 1144. He is substituted for Praetextatus when the latter is driven into exile, 1145. But when Praetextatus is restored, Melantius himself is expelled, 1146. Bishop Meletius, deposed at the Council of Nicaea, retains only the name of his dignity, 495. Melita, an island in the Mediterranean Sea, 605. Lucillus, bishop of Malta, ibid. See his title. Trajanus, 1042. Melitene, a city of Lesser Armenia, 678. Domitianus, bishop of Melitene, 678. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. [Col. 1541] Mellitus, abbot, sent to England, is commended, 1140 and following. He likewise became bishop of London, 1287. The vision of the monk Mellitus at death, 412. *Melotes*, or *cuculla*, a kind of monastic garment, 225. As the members of one body, so also the members of one society, though differing in function, become one through mutual harmony, 46. Menas, a solitary monk in Samnium, 336. His strict poverty and remarkable power over beasts, ibid. His zeal against vices, 336. He possesses the spirit of prophecy, 337. He rejects the offerings of a sacrilegious robber, 336. Menas of Telesia, bishop in Campania, accused before Gregory, returns to Rome, 1020, 1220. At the body of Saint Peter he gives satisfaction by oath, is cleared, and sent back to Gaul, 1219. Telling a lie is worse than eating meat, 663. Menna, bishop of Toulon, 1144. The mind is signified by the name “belly,” 51. The human mind is compared with water, 54. The mind knows how to think of many things without knowing itself, 5. The person whose mind sleeps through care for his own affairs is beaten without pain and dragged without feeling it, 90. In treating illnesses of the mind, discretion is needed so that weakness and debility may be confronted at the same time, 98.

*Table*. At the bishop’s table, sayings of the ancient Fathers are to be read, 856. A menstruating woman. See *Woman*. *Measure*. By the measure of wheat, the mode of speech is expressed, 99. What it means to tithe mint, 92. The hired shepherd flees when the wolf comes, 510. *Merces* is sometimes opposed to loss, 625. Sometimes it is taken to mean a benefit, 625, 646, 1242. Sometimes it means a reward and stipend, 1232. Sometimes it means mercy, French *mercy*, 636. Religious persons assigned to the redemption of captives are called *de mercede*, ibid. Midday sleep granted by the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1125. The Church of Meria in the diocese of Consentia, 886.

*Merit*. In the judgment of a righteous judge, the quality of actions changes the merits of ranks, 84. Immersion. See *Baptism*. Merula, a place near Rome, 297. Merulus, a monk devoted to tears and prayers, 453. He is warned of his death, ibid. He is venerated by the Church, 456. The privileges of the Church of Messina are confirmed, and a pallium is sent to its new bishop, 798. Only the deacons of the Church of Messina are permitted to use the *compages*, 915. Bishops of Messina: Felix, 528. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Donus, 798, 1230. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. What the errors of the Messalians were, 802. Who their leaders were, and what synods were held against them, ibid. Messianus, a Salona cleric, 1034. The Porta Metronia at Rome, 1125. The rights of metropolitans are established by the canons, 933. Bishops must obey the metropolitan, 797. Bishops who avoid discipline by flight are to be sent back to the metropolitan, 1020. How many cities are required to establish a metropolitan see, 1163, 1164. Ordinations performed by metropolitans in the dioceses of their suffragan bishops are recorded, 578. It was the duty of the metropolitan of Cagliari to announce the feast of Easter and to give letters to bishops leaving the island, 933. According to ancient custom, the vicariate of the Apostolic See in Gaul is delegated to the metropolitans of Arles, 783. See *Primate*. Metz, a city of Lorraine, 1145. Aigulfus, bishop of Metz, 1144, 1145. *Fear*. Those held by fear should advance toward charity, 52. See *Timor*. Mevania, an episcopal city of Umbria, 564, 674. Gregory exhorts the people of Mevania to be unanimous in the election of their bishop, 564, 565. The care of the Church of Mevania is meanwhile entrusted to the priest Honoratus, 565, 674. Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto, is sent to ordain priests in the Church of Mevania and to confirm infants, 674. Michaelius, defender of the Roman Church, who served as *responsalis* of the province of Ravenna, 667. *Migrare* sometimes means “to transfer,” 732. A soldier of the Roman Church is the subdeacon who serves in its clergy, 646. See *Clerics*. Soldiers were marked with brands, 676. The six necessities of soldiers, ibid. The conversion of soldiers in a monastery is generally sincere and complete, ibid. The emperor Maurice forbids soldiers to become monks, 675, 676, 677, 678. Soldiers who wish to become monks are to be tested for three years, 898. Gregory forbids soldiers to be received into monasteries without their consent, 1057. Formerly soldiers were excluded from the clergy, 665. The resurrection of a certain soldier after seeing the places of punishments and blessedness, 432, 433. The Church’s *ministeria*, that is, vessels and sacred furnishings, 555, 605, 695, 696, 697, 735, 951. Minturnae, a city of Latium, 495. The Church of Minturnae was united with Formiae, and both were eventually transferred to Gaeta, 495. Minulfus the Lombard, a man devoted to prayer and almsgiving, 872.

*Miracles*. The power of miracles is claimed for the Church from the Old and New Testaments, 109, 113, 114. The miracles recorded in Holy Scripture surpass all belief, 113. The certainty of miracles performed before the army of the Lombards, 114. The holy Fathers relate miracles similar to those narrated by Saint Gregory, 115. The necessity of miracles in the fifth and sixth centuries, 114. The saints perform miracles either by prayer or by power, 261. Those who serve God more familiarly sometimes perform wonders by power, 264. Why more miracles occur through relics than through bodies, 276. The life of the soul after death in the saints is to be considered from the power of miracles, 380, 384. The frequent miracles at the tombs of martyrs prove that their souls live, 384. What miracles performed in humble matters teach us, 192. Miracles are sometimes performed by the reprobate, 1111. How much humility avails in displaying miracles, 160. Why the mind should be restrained amid miracles, 1112. Examples of virtues are to be preferred to miracles, 115. By the miracles of the Fathers may be understood both astonishing works of virtue and signs, 116. The Christian life is to be judged not from signs but from deeds, 205. The conversion of a sinner is a greater miracle than the resurrection of the dead, 321. Miracles performed at the death of certain servants of God. See *Lombards*. The furnishings of the Church of Miriensis, having been taken away, are to be restored to that Church’s bishop, 735. Misenum, a city of Campania in Italy, 606, 988. The visitation of the Church of Misenum is assigned to Fortunatus of Naples, [Col. 1542] 988. Benenatus, bishop of Misenum, 587.

By what reward mercy toward one’s neighbor is repaid, 1025. A twofold mercy is shown when care is taken for the soul and bodily need is relieved, 823. Mercy and discipline must not be separated, 514. The mercy of God. See *God*.

*Mass*. The sacrifice of the Mass offered for the dead frees them from punishments, 464, 465, 468. The origin of the thirty Masses customarily celebrated for the dead, 468. The sacrifice of the Mass effectively offered for the living who are in distress, 469. The unbloody sacrifice of the Mass imitates the bloody sacrifice of the cross, 472. With what disposition of heart we ought to hear or celebrate Mass, ibid. When nocturnal pollution prevents the celebration of Mass and communion, 1161, 1162. Why Mass is so called, 1152. What it means for Mass to be celebrated, ibid. Formerly the Roman and Gallican Churches had different customs in celebrating Mass, 1152. What is called a public Mass, 577, 827. Public Masses are not to be celebrated in oratories, 576, 577. See *Oratory*. Nor in monasteries, 1295. Nevertheless, they were sometimes celebrated in churches that lacked the honor of titular churches, 698. In former times several days in monasteries were without liturgy, 674. Daily attendance at Mass was not customary in the seventh century, ibid. Nevertheless, some who celebrated Mass daily at that time are praised, ibid. Why bishops were sometimes forbidden to celebrate public Masses in monasteries, 827. How the people are said to celebrate Mass, 697, 698. Formerly, during the solemn celebration of Masses, the names even of outsiders who were alive were customarily recited as a sign of communion, 719. What this recitation was called, ibid. In antiquity, lengthy prayers were recited during the celebration of the liturgy, 940. At what point in the Mass the Lord’s Prayer was formerly said. See *Lord’s Prayer*. Private Masses in private houses in Gregory’s time, 825.

The mission said to have been made by Saint Peter of preachers into various provinces is understood to have been made from the Apostolic See, 526. A person’s modesty moves others to love him, 487. Modestus (Saint), martyr. When his translation took place, 709. A *modius* was twenty-four Roman pounds, or twelve ounces, 533. It also contained sixteen *sextarii*, 533, 1241. The *modii* of grain to be received from the Church’s tenants must not exceed eighteen *sextarii*, 533. The amount obtained from an unjust *modius* is distributed among poor tenants, 1242. Those who love flattery and praise are said to be clothed in soft garments, 1127. What *momentum* and *proprietas* are, 959, 960. What a *momentaria possessio* is, ibid. What *momenti causa* is, 960. What the millstone turned by an ass signifies, 4. It is sometimes useful to disclose hardships that have been inflicted, 54.

Monks are called “Fathers,” 393, 724. This title for monks is found among Greek and Latin writers, 724, 725. Saint Jerome disapproved of this custom, 725. One who seeks a possession on earth is not a monk, 304. Excessive love of parents is harmful to a monk, 256. The monk’s habit signifies contempt for the world, 1195. The repose of monastic life, 152, 1091. Monks who do not devote themselves to sacred reading are reproved, 626. It is a great sin for monks to live on another’s offering while neglecting God’s commandments, 626. For many, the profession and life of a monk are necessary for salvation, [Col. 1543] 676. Monks are to live according to the prescription of their rule, 693. Monks are to ascend to the completion of the perfection they have begun, 857. Monastic vows. See *Vow*. Humility is especially fitting for monks, 599. Woe again to the proud poor, ibid. The horrifying end of hypocritical monks, 441.

In the island of Palmaria and the neighboring islands, boys are not to be received into monasteries before their eighteenth year, 545. According to Gregory, monks were to be tested for two years, 1056. Whether it follows from this that they were not Benedictine monks, 1057. Monks are to be tested in lay clothing, 1290. Slaves are not to be admitted to the monastic habit without their masters’ consent, 653, 654, 676. Justinian enacted a contrary law, 676. A slave of the Church escaped his master’s yoke through monastic profession, 761. Gregory disapproved of excluding from monastic life those involved in public administrations, 675. But after changing his view, he wished them first to be released from public offices, 676, 898. Julian the Apostate forbade soldiers to be admitted to conversion, 676, 678. So did the emperor Maurice, 675, 676. Gregory entirely disapproved of this, 676, 677. Soldiers must not put on the monastic habit unless they have first been tested for three years, 898. Gregory forbids their reception without their consent, 1057. A man is not to be received into a monastery if his wife refuses to convert, 827. Those who come to conversion with compunction are to be received kindly, 827. Slaves manumitted on the condition that they become monks may not leave the monastery, 955.

A certain monk, leaving the monastery through fickleness of mind, encountered a dragon on the road, 256. Struck with fear of it, he returned to the monastery, 257. Cicero, an apostate monk, is to be restored to the Church of Misenum, 761. Fugitive monks are to be sought out and brought back to the monastery, 590, 761, 884. Such monks are not to be defended by bishops, 885. Monks who have escaped from the monastery by flight are discovered through a miracle, 1125 and following. Unstable monks are to be restrained, 530. Likewise the acephalous and irregular, 529. Vicious monks are to be restrained, 545, 538, 778, 1256, 1257. A fallen monk is not to become an abbot, 1260. If he has become one, what should be done, ibid. Formerly monks were excommunicated for faults, 954, 955. Such persons are not to be given communion by the priests of the diocese, 954, 955. To prevent monks from sometimes being excommunicated unjustly, the bishop could investigate the cause of excommunication, 955.

Equitius the abbot kept monks away from conversation with nuns, 165. Those who dedicate their bodies to continence should not presume to live with women, 289. Monks who have taken wives are excommunicated, 522. A monk’s marriage is invalid, ibid. Married monks are sent back to their monasteries for punishment, 531. They are to be corrected with appropriate amendment, 1055, 1056. Women are expelled from the island of Eumorphiana so that they may no longer live with monks, 544. Monks are not to introduce women into the monastery, 604, 722. Nor are they to make them their *commatres*, 722. Monks are not to be held back from divine services by the management of business, 555. The monastery’s lawsuits and affairs are to be entrusted to an experienced layman, ibid. Monks are not to be dragged before lay judges, 556. How monks’ lawsuits are to be settled, 603. It is entirely blameworthy for persons serving God to quarrel over secular affairs, 949.

Formerly monks were permitted to make wills and accept inheritances, 539, 1217. For what reason their wills are valid, [Col. 1543] 1297 and following. Under Gallic law monks are not heirs, 1217. See *Will*. How a monk guilty of proprietary possession is to be punished after death, 465. Monks are not permitted to possess anything as their own, ibid. Monks who have personal property are to be reproved, 530. With what penalty they are to be fined, ibid. A monk is reproved for accepting *mappulae*, 245. How a monk was punished for theft, 1124.

The labor of copyists especially befits monks, 169. Monks commonly devoted themselves to this labor, ibid. From the beginning of the Benedictine order, monks obtained their food neither by begging nor by manual labor, 265, 304. Why Nonnosus did not wish monks to work outside the monastery, 180.
