Monks were supported by the offerings of the faithful, 336, 337. Monks were not exempt from guarding the walls, 988.

Monks must always remain under the authority of their abbots, 604, 1295. No one is to be promoted to any rank without the abbot’s consent, ibid., 1223, 1294. Churches of monks are to be dedicated without public Masses, a baptistery, or a cardinal priest, 1043. If monks request Masses, they are to ask the bishop for a priest, ibid.

Monks attached to the offices of clerics, and more suited to the clerical state because of their monastic life, 727. Monks as legates of the Apostolic See, 567. Monastic life was considered suitable for the minor orders and the subdiaconate itself, or at least for the intervals between orders, 727, 1188. See the Index of the Life. Gregory orders that bishops be chosen from the clergy or monasteries, 503. A bishop is permitted, with the abbot’s consent, to take monks and raise them to the priesthood, 815. Whether formerly monasteries had no priest, or only one, and he an outsider, 697, 698. In Gregory’s time there were several priests and deacons in monasteries, 824, 833, 834, 891, 997. A monk made a priest for the benefit of the monastery should remain there permanently, ibid. He is to be chosen by the congregation, ibid. Dometius, abbot and priest, 949. Clerics were nowhere forbidden to pass over to the monks, 691. Why monks who became clerics ought to have no authority in the monasteries from which they came, 890, 906, 907. How dangerous it is for monks to pass to the manner of life of clerics, 530. A cleric who has become a monk should not return to the clergy unless, promoted to the priesthood by his own bishop, he is placed over a church, ibid.

Monastic discipline is to be observed in monasteries, 529. When this has collapsed, it is to be restored according to the canons, 692,
693. Monks easily deviate from the right path if vigilance in maintaining discipline does not keep watch, 857. In a monastery, no one can maintain strict discipline if he is compelled to remain daily in ecclesiastical ministry, 727. Monks ordinarily do not go outside without a companion, 1124. Nor ought they to do so, 1195. Why monks returning from outside would proceed to prayer, 1124. Monks who had eaten outside the monastery contrary to the rule are rebuked, 236. — Why the earth repeatedly cast out a little monk after he had been buried, 256. A certain monk restores life to a dead man by using dust from the altar, 320. That monk fled in order to avoid praise, 321. Two monks hanged from a tree by the Lombards were heard singing psalms after death, 404. At the very moment of death, a certain monk of Gregory’s monastery sees three prophets, 425. A monastery formerly served as a prison for delinquent clerics, 527. A bishop withdraws into a monastery as a penitent, 902. Monasteries are open for conversion not only to criminals but also to clerics and priests, [Col. 1544] 530. Distinguished men, in place of public penance, are to be confined in monasteries on account of their crimes, according to the custom concerning clerics, 643, 654, 979. Some responsibility for monasteries was entrusted to visiting bishops, 601, 808. A monastery cannot be founded on another’s estate against the owner’s will, 695. Gregory unites very many monasteries under one abbot, 1085, 1086, 1136, 1172. This union is to be carried out without prejudice to the bishop’s authority, 1113. Monasteries of nuns ought not to adjoin men’s monasteries, 1107 and following. He orders the baptistery to be removed from the monastery, so that the monks may celebrate the Work of God more securely, 671. Gregory wishes the monastery to be freed from the disturbance caused by visitors, 1049. At Rome, the church of Saint Pancratius is joined to a monastery, 697. Gregory prevents the Castellian monastery from coming under lay control, 920. At the very beginning of the Order of Saint Benedict, monasteries were endowed with very extensive estates and revenues, 265, 922. Monks to whom possessions have been assigned for the necessities of life are not to be blamed, 304. By the common law, the property of converts is acquired by the monastery at the very moment of the monk’s profession, 685, 686, 1021. Monks ceded their property to the monastery, together with the debts they were owed and those they owed, 675, 676. Whatever has once been joined to the monastery’s ownership escapes the right of another acquisition, 1042, 1051. Money received for purchasing possessions for a monastery is not to be spent for other purposes, 1053. How a dispute concerning a possession said to have been granted to a monastery is to be judged, 1061. A monastery is not to be consecrated unless a lawful donation has first been assigned, 1089, 1229. The possessions of a woman who has entered a monastery are not to be withheld by her fiancé, 867, 868. Laws and canons forbid monastery property to be separated under any title whatsoever, 922. The wish of a rustic woman, long neglected, is to be fulfilled in favor of the monastery, 946, 947. Property taken from a monastery is to be restored to it, 950, 951, 981. Property common to a monastery and a hospice is ordered to be divided, 1050. Bishops or others must not diminish the property of monasteries, 1294. Whatever an abbot acquires, he acquires not for himself but for the monastery, 1042. When an abbot has become a bishop, he is given back what he acquired after being removed from the office of abbot, but not what he acquired while he was abbot, ibid. Gregory transfers a possession of a certain church to a monastery, 636, 637. He orders ten solidi to be given annually to the Catanian monastery, 1232. He orders a ship sent for the support of a monastery to be exempt from every compulsory service or burden, 1089. Whatever the faithful offer to monasteries is to benefit them, 763.

— Exemption of monasteries. The principal reason for exemptions was the oppression of subjects, 498, 906, 1294; or the greed of prelates, 728. Exemptions of monasteries are much older than Gregory the Great, 499. They were frequent in Africa, ibid. Monasteries must in no way be subject to secular services of any kind, 604, 1295. The bishop is to regulate the affairs and revenues of monasteries, 981. A bishop is to inflict no inconvenience upon a monastery apart from careful attention to discipline, 674. A monastery’s exemption from the bishop’s jurisdiction should favor regular discipline, not impunity for vices, 605. When an abbot has died, bishops are neither to inventory nor administer the monastery’s property, 602, 603, 504, 1294, 1295. If any disputes arise, they are to be referred to elected abbots and God-fearing Fathers, 603. If an inventory of the monastery’s property must be made, the local abbot, accompanied by other abbots, is to make it, 604, 906, 1294. A bishop is not to celebrate public Masses in the monastery, 603, 604, 1295. Why this was forbidden to him, 603, 604, 605, 826, 827, 1295. A bishop may not place his episcopal chair in a monastery, ibid. A bishop is to have no power in monasteries to command or to make even the slightest appointment, unless requested by the abbot, 604, 1295. This statute is to be observed by all bishops, 604, 1295. A bishop should not visit monasteries too frequently, lest they be burdened, 907. The ordination of an elected abbot was reserved to the bishop, 604. Monasteries must not be burdened by clerics, 815, 816. Clerics are not to enter monasteries unless they have been invited to perform the sacred mysteries, 890. The Neapolitan priests are ordered to celebrate Masses in the monastery of Saint Martin; but they are forbidden, whether they or the bishop, to inflict any inconvenience upon the monks, 763. Concessions made for the monks’ peace are not to be violated, 1018. New customs are not to be introduced into monasteries, 590. The monastery of Saint Cassian at Marseilles is exempted from the bishop’s administration, 858, 859. Nevertheless, he is to watch over the life and conduct of the women servants of God living there and correct their faults, 859. The Classitan monastery is exempted from all episcopal jurisdiction, 906 and following. That privilege was extended to all monasteries in the Roman council, 906. The privileges granted by Pope Vigilius to the monastery of Montmajour outside the walls of the city of Arles are confirmed by Gregory, 1019.

Monastriae and Ascetriae are what the Greeks call nuns, 872. In former times, nuns were not veiled immediately after making their vow of virginity, 692. In former times, nuns devoted themselves to copying sacred books, 169. Some possessions were assigned by parents to virgins dedicated to God, 328. Monks preached the word of God to neighboring nuns, 245. Gregory calls nuns, especially those of advanced age, “Mothers,” 393. A proven and industrious man is to be assigned to the monasteries of nuns to manage their affairs, 688. Gregory takes care that the nuns suffer no want, 571. He considers Rome to have been preserved through their holiness, 872. Soldiers are not to live in their monasteries, 1005. Their monasteries must not adjoin men’s monasteries, 1107 and following. Nuns are excommunicated for lack of restraint in speech, 253. How they are restored to communion after death, ibid. A certain virgin of Spoleto, against her father’s will, assumes the habit of holy religious life, 328. By her example, many more vow virginity to God, ibid. By a mere command she drives a demon out of a man and permits it to enter a pig, 328. Whether she ought to have surrendered a pig to an unclean spirit, ibid. Why a certain religious woman appeared half burned, 460. Nuns are not to marry, 1293. Their marriages were forbidden under threat of excommunication and sometimes the penalty of death, 686. If nuns marry, they are to be punished, 754. They are regarded as adulteresses, 688. Those who have married a nun are admitted to communion after performing a suitable penance, 707. Wandering nuns are to be restrained, 688. Those who have returned to secular life are ordered to be brought back to the religious habit and strictly guarded in a monastery, 901. If anyone resists, he is to be deprived of communion, ibid.

Mons-Christi, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 545. Gregory orders the irregular monks inhabiting this island to obey Abbot Herosius, ibid. By what rite Monophysite heretics are to be reconciled, 1167, 1168. Those converted from their error are commended, 1212. Montana, a servant of the Roman Church, is granted her freedom, 800. Montanus came from Phrygia, 1168. A boy suffering from elephantiasis is healed, 257. Nearly the whole world was afflicted by diseases in Gregory’s time, 1032. What is to be done in illnesses, ibid. Morena, a woman, 547.

To die. The dying foretell the future, 409, 425. The Author of life appears to a dying man, 397. Sometimes a soul’s merit is revealed not at the moment of death but after death, 404. A dying monk sees three prophets coming to meet him, 425. Why the elect sometimes die with difficulty, 405, 408. The death of the saints is often celebrated with heavenly praises, 393. Death occurs in two ways: either through the absence of life or through the quality of one’s life, 802, 882. As each person departs from this life, so is he presented at the judgment, 441. Miracles performed at the death of certain servants of God. See Lombards. Expectation of death was Saint Gregory’s sole consolation, 1233, 1238. Joy concerning death, 1237. The dead restored to the living, 160, 201, 204, 233, 265, 320, 349. Signs involving the dead occur for the instruction of the living, 301. The dead are not to be mourned by Christians for long, 1011. The dead returning to the body, 429, 432. The disposal of the dead is to be observed in every respect, 1107.

Moses did not wish to preside over the multitude, and yet he obeyed, 8. Within, he contemplates the secrets of God; outwardly, he bears the burdens of the fleshly, 19, 512. By always returning to the tabernacle concerning doubtful matters, he left an example for rulers, 19, 512. Although Moses speaks with God, he is judged by Jethro’s reproof because he is occupied with earthly business, 25. He follows the same man’s advice, ibid. By what art of charity he converted Jethro, his kinsman from among the Gentiles, to the people of God, 60. Seeing God angry with the people, what he did, 75. What it signifies that Moses came forth from God’s secrecy and spoke to the people with veiled face, 99. He was taught by an angel in the wilderness, 156. He performs many miracles, 1111 and following. And yet he is forbidden to enter the Promised Land, ibid.

A pregnant woman may be baptized, 1157, 1158. A woman undergoing menstruation is not to be excluded from entering the church, 1158, nor from communion, 1159. Nevertheless, those who abstain are praised, ibid. Women who do not nurse their newborn children are disapproved, 1158. Even very holy women are to be kept away from the company of holier men, 289. Likewise, unrelated women are to be kept away from priests’ households, 1242, 1243. Women are brought forward as witnesses against clerics, 650, 651. In criminal cases, women’s testimony is not accepted, ibid. Under canon and Gallic law, women are admitted to give testimony, ibid. A mad woman is healed, 273. Gregory forbids sins to be punished by a monetary fine, but orders punishment to be inflicted on offenders, 535.

Censure of excessive speech, 54. Excessive speech exposes us naked to the enemy, ibid. One subject to excessive speech cannot maintain the rectitude of justice, 55.

World. After the washing, one should not neglect to be clean, 87. World. The foolish wisdom of the world, 40. The form of this world passes away, 79, 875. The world itself deters us from loving it, 369. In this world nothing is stable, but all prosperity is confounded with adversity, 662. We are recalled from the waves of the world [Col. 1546] to the shore of Christian peace, 875. What the vicissitudes of this world teach us, 662. Whoever loves the pomp of the world sees a waking dream, 1077. Whatever ends in a conclusion should not be loved as something great, ibid. Let the mind despise the pomp of the world, 1233. The world signifies carnal hearts, 1093. In this visible world nothing can be ordered except through a creature, 381. Why we do not yet perfectly understand the things of this world, 445. The world’s wretched condition in Gregory’s time, 744. The world’s collapse is demonstrated in the very effects of events, 498. From the disasters of the earth, Gregory believed that the end of the world was approaching, 445, 645, 703, 744, 875, 879, 984, 1032, 1166.

What municipal records are, 577. In former times, municipalities or towns had their own notary, ibid. What it means to build fortifications around a brick, 31. What it means for a creditor to give a debtor a complete security, 724. What *munitio* signifies, 1109, 1111, 1272.

God accepts our gift in place of our fault if we first appease through humility a brother who has something against us, 473. Gifts (*munera*) are more than guest-gifts (*xenia*), 587. Gifts are not all to be accepted, nor at every time, nor from everyone, ibid. To accept nothing from anyone is inhuman; to accept indiscriminately is contemptible; to accept everything is greed, ibid. God does not regard the gifts but the heart, 1029.

What it means to set a shepherd as a wall before the house of Israel, 17. The walls of Jerusalem signify the virtues of a soul desiring heavenly peace, 61. By whom the walls of Jerusalem are destroyed: by the chief of the cooks, ibid. Clerics were not exempt from guarding the walls, 909, 910. Nor were monks or abbots, 988.

The Blessed Virgin calls the girl Musa to heaven in a vision, 400. Musicus, abbot of the Agilitan monastery, 728. Mustellus, deacon of the Church of Pudentiana, 611. Mutability. All creatures are subject to mutability, 661, 662.

# N

**N.** Why the letter *N* was formerly inserted in the words *totiens*, *quotiens*, etc., 564, 565. Why Abigail concealed Nabal’s guilt, 57, 58. Nebuchadnezzar transformed into a beast because of his pride, 6. Narbonne, or Narbo, a city of Gaul, 868. Narnia, a city of Umbria, 288, 570. Bishops of Narnia: Cassius, 289; Praejectus, 569; Constantius, 1288, 1291. Narses, a vigorous general who, in the time of the emperor Justinian, defeated the Goths in Italy, 412. He later summoned the Lombards, ibid. Narses the patrician, whose valor shone against the Persians under the emperor Maurice, 492. Summoned by Phocas to the court, he was burned to death, ibid. He is called a *comes*, 802, and religious, 876. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Nasas, a most wicked Jew, builds an altar under the name of Elijah and deceives Christians, 652. The nose signifies discernment, 11, 90. A large and crooked nose signifies an immoderate subtlety of discernment, 11. Natalis, bishop of Cesena, 1264. Natalis, bishop of Salona, is rebuked for continual banquets and neglect of pastoral care, 580, 581, 616. How he attempts to excuse his banquets, 616, 617. He improperly defends his negligence of sacred reading by the testimony of Scripture, [Col. 1547] 618. He promotes the archdeacon Honoratus to the priesthood in order to remove him from his rank [as archdeacon], 581, 582, 618. He is ordered to be restored to his former rank, 503, 581, 583, 384. He despised the judgment of Pelagius II and Gregory, 618. The subdeacon Antoninus is entrusted with carrying out the punishment imposed against Natalis, 583. Gregory asks Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum, not to favor Natalis’s party, 585. Natalis later returns to his rank, 618. Natalis is ordered to recall from exile Florentius, a bishop deposed without a council’s judgment, 631.

Nathan skillfully reproves David by means of his own judgment, 37. He had come to a sick man as a physician; he saw that the wound required cutting, but doubted the patient’s endurance, ibid. Nathan first agrees that the king should build the Temple, and afterward forbids it, 249. *Nativitas parva*, that is, “a small harvest,” 557. Nature created all human beings equal, 20. A soul is like a ship climbing against the current, 94. A ship full of water reaches the harbor, 357. Naples belonged by right to the Roman Church, 592, 1003. The privileges of that city are confirmed, 986. Gregory protects the rights of the citizens of Naples, 1082. How the property of the Neapolitan Church which the bishop had detained should be divided, 1117. The Neapolitans are to choose a bishop without delay or dissension, 572, 573. The visitation of the Neapolitan Church is assigned to Paul, bishop of Nepi, 575. The Neapolitans request that this Paul be incardinated as their bishop, 574. Two or three members of the Neapolitan clergy are to be sent to Rome to choose a bishop, 649. The custody of the city of Naples is entrusted to a tribune, 592. Bishops of Naples: Demetrius, 500; Fortunatus—see his heading; Paschasius, 1115.

Neas, a church, 1134. It is in dispute with the Jerusalem Church, 1135. Fog and stench signify carnal desire, 436. The neglected person is exposed to excesses and is accustomed to fall into the very things that must be avoided, 976. Negligence of ecclesiastical solicitude harms souls, 957. What it means to trade for the Lord, 610. Merchants excessively desirous of profit are reproved, 723. Nemesion, bishop of Doclea, ordained in place of Paul, the deposed bishop, is expelled by him, 1201, 1202. Formerly a *neophyte* was one newly planted in the faith; now the word denotes one who is new in holy conduct, 782, 1009. Neophytes are excluded from the orders. See *Laity*, *Orders*. Nepa, more properly Nepet, a city of Etruria, 576. This city appears to have belonged to the patrimony of the Roman Church, for which Gregory appointed a prefect, ibid. The visitation of the Nepi Church is entrusted to John, the bishop, 588. Paul, bishop of Nepi, 575, 1291. A man who marries his niece is excommunicated, 1293. Nereida, a woman, 926.

“I do not know.” Those who do not know the things that belong to the Lord are not known by the Lord, 3. Nestorius, the heresiarch, and his heresy, 748. He is refuted, 1168, 1169. Nestorius is to be anathematized, 1174. By what rite Nestorians are to be reconciled, 1168. They are to be received in their own orders, 1169. Nestorians are like the Jews, 1168. Nicopolis, a city of Epirus, 796. Andrew, bishop of Nicopolis, 898. See his heading. Nicotera, a city of Calabria, 823, 825. Proculus, bishop of Nicotera, 962.

[Col. 1547] *Nisi* sometimes signifies “but only,” 790. Why nobility of birth is rarely joined with nobility of mind, 252. Nobility imposes this law upon itself: to consider itself obliged to give what it gives voluntarily, 1102. Unless it has increased in its benefactions, it considers that it has accomplished nothing, ibid. Nola, an episcopal city in Italy, 277, 506. Bishops of Nola: Paulinus, 115. See his heading. Gaudentius, 737.

**Name.** Names taken from God were familiar among the Africans, 884. What it means to fornicate “in his own name,” 1030. Nomentum. See *Numentum*. Nonnosus, superior of the monastery on Mount Soracte, 177. Later, perhaps, abbot of the same monastery, 663. His virtues, 177, and miracles, 180. Why he is called *domnus*, 661, 663. Nonnosus, 505. Nordulphus, 607.

A notary is a scribe, so called from *notes*, 553. There were different ranks of notaries, ibid. In the Roman Church, notaries and chartularies performed the same office, 561. Notaries are listed among the minor orders, 639. Bishops had their own notaries, 1299. *Notitia* signifies an index, catalogue, or inventory, 696, 697, 820. It is also used for a specimen of a deed of donation inserted in polyptychs, 956. Novas, a city or fortress of Italy, 935. *Novellae*. See *Justinian*. What the error of the Novatians was, 733. A man who marries his stepmother is excommunicated, 1293. According to the Rule of Saint Benedict, novices kept their hair and secular clothing, 225. Night signifies the blindness of our weakness, 90. What the clouds driven by winds signify, 55. The attacks of wicked people are designated by the name “clouds,” ibid. What it means for someone who is considering clouds never to reap, ibid. Nuceria, a city of Campania, 653. Primaerius, bishop of Nuceria, 947. Numentum, or Nomentum, an episcopal city of Valeria, 538. The Church of Saint Anthemius is united to the Church of Nomentum, ibid. Gratianus, bishop of Nomentum, 1291. What a *numbrarius* is, 1189, 1190. Numerius, a deacon, 653.

**Number.** To be “in the number” is the same as to be in a cohort, 428. What it means to serve in the ranks, 720. Military numbers are cohorts and squadrons, 898. Numidia, a province of Africa, 559. No one who wishes to come from the Council of Numidia to the Apostolic See is to be prevented, ibid. Gregory exhorts the bishops of Numidia to peace and zeal for the salvation of souls, 562. Under Constantine, the gold coin acquired the name *solidus*, 648. *Nuper* (“recently”) is sometimes used of a more distant period of time, 244. Spiritual marriages begin in mourning and lead to joys; carnal marriages do the opposite, 392. The advantage connected with marriage is the payment that was required to make marriage permissible, 535. A man who marries his daughter-in-law is excommunicated, 1293. Nursia, formerly an episcopal city situated among the Sabines, 208. Primaerius, bishop of Nursia, 1288. The priests of Nursia lived with foreign women, 1242.

# O

[Col. 1548] Those who are hardened are to be pierced with harsh words, 52. At times they should be soothed with gentle admonition, 53. One should not command obedience from subordinates when one does not know how to show it to superiors, 156, 735, 736. The miracle of obedience in Saint Maurus, 225. The hardness of disobedient people is confounded, 296. The astonishing obedience of subordinates in enduring suffering, 669. The offerings of the faithful, formerly frequent and established by the canons, have almost fallen into disuse, 826. How communion was formerly obtained through offerings, 254. The offerings of excommunicated persons were not received, 825. Offerings made for the sustenance of solitaries, 336, 337. What the “crowns” of offerings are, 464. A sacred offering is of great help. See *Mass*. God rejects the offerings of those who are at variance, 69. *Obreption* and *subreption* occur when something is extorted through a false account, 579.

Among certain authors, *observare* means to perform one’s office, 899, 997. It also means to serve someone continually, 899, 900; likewise, to be present to a case, 927, 1048. *Observatio* is used for a forensic proceeding, 1048, 1060. What it means to arrange a siege around a brick structure, 31. “He kills his brother and friend”: the person who does not spare even those whom he loves with the sword of correction, 75. Occilianus, tribune of Hydruntum, 1003. Ocleatinus is not to be chosen bishop of Rimini, 548, 549.

What the eyes are in the body of the Church, 3. Who is meant by “may bend his back with eyes darkened,” ibid. What eyes are bleary and what they signify, 12. What it means to anoint the eyes with collyrium, ibid. The eyes do not see by themselves, 381. But through the eyes the soul itself sees, ibid. What it means to hate God’s enemies with perfect hatred, 69. Odo, abbot of Cluny, abridged Gregory’s *Dialogues*, 110, 116. How Paul was the good odor of Christ, 924.

The office of *oeconomus*—the steward—was so necessary to the Church and to bishops that it had been established by ancient canons, but is now entirely suppressed, 640. How many and how great scandals have arisen from this, ibid. Whether the *officialis*, the ordinary ecclesiastical judge, should be a priest, 647. Those devoted to public offices are excluded from the sacred orders unless this is done with the consent of the ruler, 675. Innocent I approved this law, the emperor Maurice restored it, and Gregory praised it, ibid. The novelty of any office is very burdensome to everyone, 777. Saint Gregory called the divine office the work of God, 697, 1086. In the sixth century, in places where relics of the saints were kept, the divine offices were performed by their own clergy or by clergy from nearby places, 697, 698.

Oil signifies the softness of piety, 23. May the Lord grant us his oil, 73. Oil multiplied by divine power, 180, 260, 360. What it means to take oil in vessels together with lamps, 1126, 1127. The Latins interpret *omophorium* as *pallium*, 518. The *omophorium* represented the figure of a lamb, ibid. One *omophorium* was patriarchal and another episcopal, ibid.

What *oniromancy* is and what judgment should be made concerning it, 453. Burdens are to be borne for one another, 79. The person who remembers that his own burden is borne by another carries another’s burden more lightly, 80. [Col. 1549] How fearful the pastoral burden is, 507.

He who seeks to increase his wealth neglects to avoid sin, 65. Opilio, a deacon, is assigned penance because he sold the sacred furnishings of the Church of Venafrum to a Jew, 554, 555. Opilio the patrician, 619. Opportunus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Leontius, 838. Opportunus, 1090. Opportunus is praised and proposed for election to the episcopate, 1188. Optatus, defender in the territory of Nursia, 1243. Optatus, defender of the Church of Salona, 1225.

An *optio* is one who acts as the deputy of a military commander or is assigned as an assistant to a centurion, 428, 677, 720. What *opus mortuum* (“dead work”) is, 1132. When the time for good works is anticipated, merit is lost, 56. He who does not now labor in good works asks in vain for entrance into the kingdom, ibid. Christian life consists in the virtue of works, not in the display of signs, 205. No works are good if they are separated from the firmness of faith, 718. The faithful are not saved without good works, 862. One must devote oneself to good works while there is time, 1067. The outward works of virtue establish us as eminent in this life, 560. Perseverance in good work is praised, 903. He who gives assistance to good works shares in the reward, 1106. Those who do good works for human favor sell something of infinite value cheaply, 95, 626. Good works are to be concealed so that we may not be praised, but revealed so that God may be praised, 96. A good work is both hidden when it is done publicly and public when it is done secretly, ibid. The righteousness held in the mind is to be demonstrated by the light of works, 542. Good works are scattered through impatience, 43. What counsel should be given to those who mourn over evil works, 84. What the work of God is, 772. What the work of the sinner is, ibid.

*Oraculum* is the same as *oratorium*, 229, 230. **To pray.** Neither the saints in heaven nor those living on earth pray for the reprobate and the damned, 452. One must pray for emperors, 874, 963. What an *orarium* is, 878. Because of its oblong form, the stole was called an *orarium*, ibid.

**Prayer.** What it means to repeat a word in prayer, 87. The hour of prayer after the completion of the psalmody in the assembly, established by Saint Benedict, 221. Those who are pure of heart, simple, and devoted to silence are readily heard by God, 312. The efficacy of the brothers’ prayer when they pray together with greater intensity for the salvation of the soul, 440. The usefulness of prayer made for one another, 515. How predestination is obtained through prayers, 181, 184. The power of prayer, 268. The wondrous effects of prayer, 316, 352, 364, 440. Why God hears the prayers of those who trust in him even in trivial matters, 192. Prayer becomes empty where conduct is wicked, 1138. God must be asked through prayer with great persistence, 1181. The devil was seen dragging a monk out of the oratory during prayer, 221. Idle or harmful speech is a great impediment to prayer, 312, 313. He who does not hear the Lord commanding is not heard by the Lord, 313. Because of human weakness, we cannot devote ourselves continually to prayers and praises of God, 965. Prayer for faithful departed persons is frequently found among the ancient Fathers, 464. A bishop’s devotion to prayer is praised, 1188. The Lord’s Prayer was customarily said during the Mass before Gregory, 940. Gregory established that it should be said after the canon, ibid. Amalarius believed that it sufficed for the consecration of the Eucharist, [Col. 1549] but later changed his opinion, ibid. Among the Greeks that prayer is recited one way in the liturgy, and among the Latins another way, 941.

An oratory is sometimes called an *oraculum*, 229, 230. Everyone is permitted to have private oratories at home, 577, 825. Public Masses are not to be celebrated in them, 577. Nor is a priest to be incardinated in them, ibid. Nevertheless, with the bishop’s permission, Masses may be celebrated there outside the principal festivals, 577, 825. Private oratories are to be dedicated under five conditions, 576, 577, 986, 994, 1187. A monastery oratory is to be consecrated without public Masses, 898. For Masses celebrated in an oratory, a priest is to be requested from the bishop, 577, 986, 994. Oratories were customarily dedicated with relics, 577, 986, 987, 994.

What the Spanish word *orca* signifies, 548. The Romans used to preserve ashes deposited in *orci*, 549. Ordination is designated by the laying on of hands, 1064.

**Orders.** The name “sacred order” sometimes includes both the major and minor orders, 240, 704. In Gregory’s time the subdiaconate was not counted among the sacred orders, 538. Orders must not be repeated, 608. Whether ordinations given or received from heretics, schismatics, or even Catholics contrary to the canons were formerly considered valid, ibid. Why divine providence established different orders in the Church, 783, 784. Men in sacred orders must not serve earthly affairs out of desire for them, 26. Those established in sacred orders who fall into sexual sin are to be irrevocably deposed, 704. This is done not out of despair of indulgence, but with disciplinary severity, 703. Nevertheless, that severity may be lessened somewhat because of circumstances that arise, ibid. Whoever has received a sacred order in the Roman Church no longer has permission to leave it, 763.

With how much deliberation and caution, and concerning what matters, those who are to be placed in sacred orders must be examined, 501, 547, 562, 660, 704. No one is to be admitted to sacred orders unless he is of mature age and blameless in conduct, 660. Nor those whose life can be criticized, 690. What principal conditions Gregory required in those to be ordained, 600, 704, 798. What conditions the councils formerly required, 704. What matters they are now to be examined on, 704.

—Who must be excluded from the orders, 600, 1118. Bigamists, or those who have not taken a virgin as wife, are to be excluded, 600, 622, 704, 1220. Those physically defective, 600. Those bound to the curia or to any civil condition, 600, 704, 898. The ignorant, 600, 704. Penitents, 600. Africans, because they are Manichaeans or have been rebaptized, ibid. Children, 659. Neophytes, ibid. Laymen are not to be promoted immediately to sacred orders, 588, 589, 782, 783, 786, 938, 1008, 1009, 1014, 1015, 1017. A man who is unchaste and a usurer is rejected from the episcopate, 1086. The poor are not to be excluded from sacred orders, 1017. Each person is to be promoted not through favor or venality, but according to merit, 659, 660, 790, 798, 964, 1007. Although a man may be blameless in merit, he must nevertheless first be exercised in ecclesiastical offices through the distinct orders, 1009. One must ascend through the orders in due sequence, ibid. Whether the canons formerly commanded that one reach the episcopate through each individual rank of the orders, 1065.

A man ordained by violence, and those who ordained him, are suspended from office, 699. Those ordained as a reward for crime are permanently deposed from the order they have received in such a manner, 780. Those ordained simoniacally: see *Simony*. Definite intervals between the ranks of the orders must be observed, [Col. 1550] 659. Because the canonical intervals between orders had not been observed, Pope Constantine was cast down from his rank and the ordinations performed by him were declared null, 608. In former times many were ordained by bishops who were not their own, without letters of release, 566. Today, to receive any order, only letters of release from the bishop of one’s own diocese are required, ibid.

Gregory commonly calls the more distinguished among the laity “the order,” 550, 576, 634. By an order distinguished from the nobility, he means the more distinguished citizens or magistrates, 571, 572, 601. In the examination of a righteous judge, the quality of one’s actions changes the merit associated with one’s rank, 84. Some are worse in a better order, and some better in a worse order, ibid. It is not orders or places that bring us nearer to our Creator, but good merits, 879.

The Eastern Churches, troubled by no heretics under the emperor Maurice, 1134. Nevertheless, they suffer from simony, ibid. Why Origen was called *calcenterus*, 1036. Who are called *originarii*, 700. Whoever gives help to orphans and widows makes the Lord his debtor, 551. He acquires the greatest praise and reward for himself, 644. God is the governor and protector of orphans, 1118. The island of Orphiaria. See *Eumorphiana*. Ortona. See *Hortona*. Orvieto, a city of Etruria, 498.

Why a door, rather than a wall, should be placed at the mouth, 54. The kiss of peace precedes reception of the Eucharist, 357. What bones signify, 46. What it means for bones to rot through envy, 47. Dead bones live in miracles, 329. Why Tiberine Ostia is so called, 948. Gloriosus, bishop of Ostia, 947, 1288. What a door signifies, 30. A door is to be placed at the mouth, which may be opened and closed, 54. What it means to enter through the door, 953, 1134. What an idle word is, 55. From idle words one proceeds to harmful ones, 54, 55. What it means for sheep to drink water disturbed by the feet of shepherds, 4. **Egg.** On which days one must abstain from eggs, 1303.

# P
Pacatus: who are to be admonished, 69, 70. The peaceful: by what admonitions they are to be fortified, 71, 72. Bishop Sabinus restrains the overflowing Po, 296. If the pagans refuse to convert, they are to be burdened with a much heavier load, 525, 704. Provision is made for the salvation of pagan children, 796. Palacenis, a place in the city of Rome, 651. The Palatine woman Urbica is supported by alms from St. Gregory, 528, 549, 550. The Palatini are counts of the lower order, 550. The Palatini are divided into the largitionales and the privationes, 1047. Palladius, the tenth bishop of Saintes, 828. Why he was harassed by King Guntram, ibid. He built a church in which he placed thirteen altars, 828. Palladius, priest of Monte-Sina, 1092. Palls are priestly and sacred vestments, which were also precious in monasteries, 555. Palls are frequently mentioned among the sacred furnishings, ibid. How the pallium differs from the Greeks’ omophorion, 518. Whether the material and form of the pallium were the same in East and West, 586. Which Roman pontiff first gave the pallium, 936. To whom it was formerly granted [Col. 1551], 518, 936. At times it was not granted without the emperor’s consent, 518, 936, 937. It was given only to those whose merits demanded it and who petitioned forcefully, 937. And after an oath of fidelity had been given, 518. Gregory refuses to send the pallium to Syagrius because the man who had come to receive it was a schismatic, 937. Gregory gave the pallium to some, but not all, Greek bishops, 586. The Greek patriarchs granted it to their subjects, Rome not objecting, ibid. Formerly the pallium was not given unless a payment had been made; this is forbidden from being done any longer, 788. The pallium signifies humility, 682. And other virtues, 1034. A bishop is reproved for using the pallium proudly, 666. In sending the pallium, Gregory instructed the recipient how he ought to live, 1028, 1034, 1244. With what disposition it ought to be received, 781, 787, 798, 806, 1014. In Gregory’s time the necessity of the pallium had not yet been introduced, nor did ecclesiastical authority depend upon it, 781. In the time of Gregory VII no archbishop was allowed to perform his duties without the pallium, 518. Why a bishop customarily wears the pallium at Mass only until the reading of the Gospel, 665, 783. Why it must not be worn during the litanies, 666, 739. Formerly no one wore the pallium outside the solemn celebration of Mass, 666, 1013. The bishops of Ravenna did not use the pallium outside the church except during translations of relics, 739. The pallium is to be put on in the secretarium, 737. The formula for granting it, 1301. Gregory sends the pallium to Constantius, bishop of Milan, 682; to Virgilius of Arles, 781, 783, 785; to John of Ravenna, 737; to Marianus of Ravenna, 787; to John, archbishop of Corinth, 788; to Andrew of Nicopolis, 797; to Donus of Messana, 798; to John of Syracuse, 806; to Maximus of Salona, 992. The pallium had been granted to the bishop of Arles since ancient times, 1156.

Palmaria, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea, 545. On that island and on neighboring islands, boys under eighteen years of age are forbidden to be received into monasteries, ibid. What the *palmatianae vestes* are, 553. The *palmata* garment was formerly held in esteem among the Romans, 554. Baronius thinks that by *palmatianae* grapes or Palmatian wine are meant, ibid. What is signified by the unfruitful branch being removed and the fruitful branch being pruned, 952. What it means for the eyelids to droop in sleep, 38. What steps precede the eyelid, 56. Palumbus, bishop of Cosenza, 896, 962, 1234. The Church of St. Pancratius in Rome, founded by Honorius and entrusted to priests, was later united to a monastery, 697. That monastery later passed to the Discalced Carmelites, ibid. Why this church did not possess the honor of a title or a cardinal priest, 698. In this church the work of God is to be performed daily, 697. Gregory sends the relics of St. Pancratius to Bishop Palladius, 828. The deacon Pancratius must not be recalled from monastic life, 1205. Square bread, 201. Breads customarily marked with the sign of the cross, ibid. Bread divided into three parts in memory of the Holy Trinity, 202. Bread multiplied miraculously for ten days, 361. Palermo, a city of Sicily, 557. Bishops of Palermo: Agatho, 469; Victor, 557, 1227; John, 1243. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. Pantaleo, notary of the Roman see, 654, 960. He is ordered to recover the church vessels sold by Sicilian clerics, 915. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. [Col. 1551] Pantaleo, prefect of Africa, 714. Pope. See Roman pontiff. What papyrus is, where it comes from, and for what use it is employed, 173.

Paradise. What the fountain rising from the midst of paradise and watering the face of the earth signifies, 877. A paralytic woman healed, 336. What *paratura* is, 1204. *Parangariae*. See *Angaria*. “Parent” extends also to relatives, 582. Parents sometimes close the entrance to the kingdom of heaven to little ones, 400. How greatly parents sin who do not correct their sinning children, 401. Equals. What letters from equals are, 507, 508, 563, 831, 834, 661, 830. It is unbecoming for an equal to do otherwise, 661. What *pariculae* or *pariclae* letters are, 507. A wall signifies the hardness of subjects, 29. What it means to dig through a wall, ibid. *Parochia* or *paroecia* and diocese are used interchangeably among the ancients, 577, 578, 808, 1265. How the district of a bishop or parish priest came to be called a parish, ibid. Gregory called village and rural churches parishes, 367. In one city there were several parishes in Gregory’s time, 674.

Easter. The question concerning Easter was debated for a long time and at great length, 932. The announcement of Easter was entrusted to the Roman pontiff, 933. This announcement was made on the day of Epiphany, ibid. In Sardinia, the announcement of Easter belonged to the metropolitan, 932, 933. In assigning the date of Easter, the Scots dissented from the Church, 1036, 1037 and following, 1038. The Gallican churches first embraced the Paschal Cycle of Anatolius, 1037. Pope Victor forbade Easter to be celebrated with the Jews, 1037. But the Easterners did not obey, ibid. Paschalis, an orphan, 638. Paschalis, 1232. Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, legate of Pope St. Leo at the Council of Chalcedon, 661. Paschasius, bishop of Marseilles, placed between Virgilius and Licerius, 541. Paschasius, bishop of Naples, 1115, 1172. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. He is ordered to appoint a *vicedominus* and a chief steward, 1172. Paschasius, deacon of the apostolic see, a man of extraordinary holiness, 444. He wrote two exceptionally lucid books on the Holy Spirit, ibid. He was a lover of the poor and despised himself, ibid. Deceived by error, he supported the party of the antipope Laurentius, ibid. After death he was subjected to punishments because of his error, but was freed by Germanus, bishop of Capua, 445. A demoniac is healed at his body, 444. Why his holiness was proved by a miracle and his fault cleansed by punishment, 445. Paschasius Radbertus, monk of Corbie, praises Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on the body and blood of the Lord, 107. Paschasius, a distinguished man, 1209. Passivus, bishop of Fermo, 943. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. Passivus, 589. What *pastellus* is, 1290. Nothing is to be accepted for a *pastellus*, 1290.

Shepherd. Gregory orders that an annual provision be supplied to a shepherd whose eyes are diseased, 554. Shepherds are called heralds, 17, 511. What it means for a shepherd to drink the clearest water, 4. The entire order of shepherds is signified by the twelve oxen carrying the sea, 19, 512. Humility must not flee from access to pastoral care when necessity requires it, 1. The ambitious are to be excluded from the office of shepherd, 3. Let no one, through desire for high office, undertake leadership toward destruction, 4. Let one who is unoccupied not seek pastoral care, and let one who has sought it fear after attaining it, 1. The pastoral office must not be stubbornly avoided, 8, 621. It must be undertaken with fear, even when God commands it, 8, 507. Whoever desires it hastens toward a fall, ibid. When it is permissible to abandon it, 217, 220. Whoever is able to feed God’s sheep but refuses shows that he does not love the supreme Shepherd at all, 6, 848. The care of feeding is evidence of love, 6. How harmful to the flock it is when the election of a shepherd is delayed too long, 564. A shepherd must not be placed over unwilling subjects, 573, 645. Just as a position of government must be denied to those who desire it, so it must be offered to those who flee from it, 848. What it means for the shepherd to enter through the door, 963, 1134.

—The image of the good shepherd, 13, 508. The image of the watchful shepherd in Laban, 963. If he places himself before the flock, he sets himself as a wall before the house of Israel, 17, 510. What fears and flatteries of the world a good shepherd should despise, 509. The good shepherd is compared with the helmsman of a ship, 849. The shepherd’s flame is the light of the flock, 921. The shepherd is chosen as intercessor for the people’s sins, 507, 550. His life should commend his teaching and instruction, 2, 15. In his breast there should be the rod and manna, 23. Let him not oppose in conduct what he preaches in words, 3. Let him be free from vices, 11. Let his eyes not be bleary, 12. Let him fix his eyes on the footsteps of the holy Fathers, 14, 508. Let him surpass others in integrity of conduct, 15. Let him meditate on the precepts of sacred eloquence, 33. In doubtful matters let him consult the pages of sacred eloquence, 19, 512. Let him resemble those heavenly creatures that were full of eyes all around and within, 39. Let him be distinguished in action, 15, 508. Why holy shepherds, having overcome greater vices, are left subject to lesser ones, 102.

—By what virtues the shepherd should shine, 6, 10, 15, 509, 510, 840. Let him walk with an upright step, 11. Let him possess discernment, ibid. Let him display gravity, 14, 508. Let him not be a physician to others while bearing a wound on his own face, 10. Let no one approach God as intercessor who is displeasing to him through guilt, 10, 11. Let him who wipes away the stains of others’ hearts be pure in thought, 508. Let him teach by word and example, 17, 511. Let him be so discerning in silence that he may be useful in speech, 16, 510. Let him season his sermons with the salt of discernment and wisdom, 17, 511. Let him present neither wrong things in any way nor even right things excessively or disorderly, 18. Let him surpass his subjects in the virtue of conduct, 509, 511. Let him not abandon truth, 622. Let him burn with zeal, 31. Yet let it not be immoderate, but circumspect, 32. Humility is necessary for shepherds, 852. Good shepherds rejoice when their subjects accuse them, 28. Let all the shepherd’s virtues be adorned with charity, 16. Let him exercise the pastoral office out of charity, 840. The devil attacks the shepherds of the Lord’s sheep in order to seize the flock more easily, 611.

—The name of shepherd is not assumed for rest but for labor, 586. Who are called shepherds carrying the vessels of the Lord, 508. Our Redeemer seeks not gold but souls, 816. In many places the pastoral care of souls is slight or nonexistent, 834, 836. If pastoral care is lacking, the flock travels through trackless places and falls into the snares of its enemies, 550, 564. It is the shepherd’s task to climb up from the opposite side and stand in battle, 17, 510. It is the shepherd’s task to gather the sheep and the wolf’s to scatter them, 580. [Col. 1553] The shepherd must preserve humility in his heart and discipline in his work, 22. For the shepherd to be able to pour in what is inward, he must also provide what is outward, 26. Concern for subjects should be bestowed according to a fixed measure, 27. Greater grace is acquired if the shepherd’s concern offers the Lord gain from the sheep entrusted to him, 1074. Let the shepherd be close to each person through compassion, 18, 511. Let him rise to God through contemplation and descend to the sick through compassion, 18, 19, 511, 512. Toward those who act well let him be a companion through humility; against offenders let him stand upright through zeal for justice, 20, 21, 22, 513. Let humility not hinder pastoral zeal, nor zeal humility, 514. With what intention he should strive to be loved by his subjects, 28. Let him be a mother to his subjects, not their master, 513. Let him rule vices rather than brothers, 22, 513. In him let mercy advise justly and discipline strike piously, 514. Let him summon subjects to love rather than fear, 586. However rightly a shepherd may denounce something, if he is not loved he is not willingly heard, 28. Let the people recognize that the shepherd’s life is different from what is on his tongue, 586. Let the shepherd’s teaching be for his subjects a welcome goad toward correction, and his life an example for imitation, ibid. Let his speech disclose what his subjects should love and what they should fear, ibid. Let the shepherd not use one exhortation for everyone, 33.

—The shepherd who enters in order to see abominations, 30. What it means for a shepherd to carry up a rampart and build fortifications, 31. What it means for him to erect camps against Jerusalem and place battering rams around it, ibid. Let the shepherd teach which battles against vices are open and which hidden dangers must be feared, 31. What the iron frying pan and the iron wall placed between shepherd and subjects signify, 32. Let the shepherd carry out what he teaches, 38. Let him teach by his deeds before his voice, 100, 508. Let him neither doze nor sleep, ibid. Let gentle shepherds possess zeal for justice, and let the irascible add gentleness to their zeal, 57. Let the concerned shepherd apply remedies contrary to the wounds of each person, 96. Let him know how to admonish one subject to the vices contrary to those of another, 97. Let supreme discernment govern his instruction of individuals, ibid. Let subjects find in the shepherd’s tongue and conduct the pasture of divine exhortation, 644. The shepherd is inexcusable if, while he is unaware, the wolf devours the sheep, 663. Whether shepherds may fulfill their duties personally or through substitutes, 694. Often the life of subjects becomes worse through the fault of their superiors, 855.

—The shepherd should be a companion to subjects who live well, but should fearlessly exercise the rights of rectitude toward the perverse, 20, 27. Let the humble shepherd know how to rise above faults, 21, 22, 31. Whoever is less inflamed against faults is himself held guilty of them, 31. If the shepherd keeps silent, he deserves the wrath of God, 17, 511. Woe to shepherds who keep silent, 75. Whoever neglects to reprove offenders kills them by keeping silent, 523. When sin in a subject is not corrected, the sentence is turned back upon those who preside, 702. The wickedness of sinners must be exposed by reproof, 17. Let the shepherd pursue faults but love persons, 524. Let him exercise the rights of discipline in such a way that he does not lose the bowels of compassion, 23. Gentleness must be mingled with severity, 23. If the rod is strictness that strikes, let the staff be consolation that supports, 24. If he has gone too far in reproving, let him return to the tears of repentance, 32. Some vices of subjects are to be prudently overlooked, 29. Some things, though openly known, are to be tolerated, ibid. Others, though hidden, are to be investigated, ibid. Let the shepherd learn from himself how corrections of offenders arising from ignorance or weakness are to be moderated, 30.

—What the shepherd must avoid, 1, 509. Let not the swelling of pride extinguish his good works, 2. Let him not be blinded by pride, 12. Domination is forbidden to shepherds, 23. Let him beware lest, while satisfying the poverty of his subjects, he kill himself with the sword of ambition, 26. Let him flee domination and arrogance, 594. The incompetence of shepherds is rebuked by the voice of truth, 3. Let him abstain from excessive subtlety in questioning, 11. What it means for a shepherd to have a broken foot or hand, 11. Let him not have his sight dimmed by carnal works, 12. Let him not suffer from the wantonness of the flesh, ibid. Let him not take delight in shameful thoughts, 13, 14. Let him not suffer from avarice, 12. Let him not be weighed down by the burden of earthly anxiety, 11. How harmful concern for secular affairs is to a shepherd, 24. Let worldly dust not obscure his eyes, 25. Secular affairs are to be tolerated out of compassion, never sought out of love, 26. Let the shepherd fear lest, while he manages external concerns, he be submerged away from his inward intention, 26, 27. The multiplicity of cares devastates the shepherd’s mind, 172. The more widely he is occupied with many matters, the more is taken away from him in every individual matter, ibid. With what caution he should attend to temporal affairs, 514, 849, 850. When the wolf comes, let the shepherd not flee by keeping silent, 16. Shepherds must beware of elation and flattery, 21. Let the shepherd keep watch lest the desire to please people drive him, 27. Let him so temper the care of government that the subject may express himself freely, yet freedom may not burst into pride, 28. Let shepherds be ashamed to learn what they should answer only when they are consulted, 34. Let the shepherd beware lest, while helping his subjects, he abandon himself, 99.

—Let hidden sins and temptations be disclosed to the shepherd, 19, 20, 512, 513. When the little ones endure the waves of temptations, let them return to the shepherd’s mind as to a mother’s bosom, 19. Even when struck by what he hears, the shepherd is not defiled or overthrown, but rather freed from his own temptations, 20. When the head languishes, the limbs flourish in vain, 24. Subjects do not willingly receive the word of preaching from a shepherd who does not relieve their outward need, 26. Let the minds of subjects express themselves freely, but not burst into pride against the shepherd, 28. Subjects must not rashly judge the lives of shepherds, 39. If they see anything wrong in the shepherd, let them diminish nothing of the reverence and obedience owed to him, ibid. David’s reverence for Saul signifies excellent subjects, ibid. It is sometimes useful to disclose the troubles one has suffered, 54. Closed wounds cause greater pain, ibid. The flock advances better by examples than by words, 508. Subjects owe obedience to the shepherd, 645. Persons are ordinarily provided as shepherds according to the merit of the peoples, by heavenly judgment, ibid. The shepherd’s incompetence and vices are attributed to the faults of his subjects, 3. Often the lives of shepherds offend in consequence of the merit of their peoples, 855. Peoples are bound to pray for their shepherds, ibid.

—Bad shepherds are signified by Saul, 39. What it means for a shepherd to disturb water with his feet, 4. Bad shepherds offer the sheep mud instead of water, 4. Bad shepherds neither enter the kingdom themselves nor permit others to enter, 10. Let the shepherd beware lest, while delighting in the glory of his position, he become the cause of ruin to his subjects, 11. The bad shepherd sees false and foolish things for the flock, 17, 510. Mute and timid shepherds are censured, 16, 17, 510. The hypocritical shepherd turns the ministry of government, under the pretense of discipline, to the use of domination, 23. Carnal shepherds flatter others, 27. They terrify others by domination, 28. How many deaths the perverse examples of shepherds deserve, 38. More concerning shepherds [Col. 1554]. See Bishop, Prelate, Rector.

Pastoral. See Rule. Why patens were larger in the first centuries, 897.

Father. A priest must continually contemplate the examples of the Fathers, 14. Our ancient fathers were not kings of men but shepherds of cattle, 20. The name “Father” is divine, 1080. A fatherly address always adds something to good minds, 1025. Pateria, St. Gregory’s aunt, whose need was relieved by generous almsgiving, 528. Paterius, notary and *secundicerius* of the Roman Church, published a book of Testimonies from Gregory’s works, 106, 757.

To suffer. We suffer less than we deserve, 1087. The patient person chooses to endure evils rather than have his hidden good works recognized through display, 43. The patient man is better than one who captures cities, 43. By what counsels the patient are to be fortified, 44, 45. Let those who endure strive to love those whom they tolerate, 44. To whom the patient are like, 45. What they must beware of, ibid. Patience is the guardian of our condition, 43. How we possess our souls through patience, ibid. The patience of the good is signified by the ditch of the altar, 43. How worthy of a man is the victory of patience, ibid. Kindness is the companion of patience, 44. It is a virtue to tolerate adversaries before men, but before God it is a virtue to love them, ibid. God compels us to patience by making us suffer so many and such great things from our enemies, 51. Patience recalls those disturbed by anger to a sounder mind, 57. Patience is to be preferred to miracles, 160. How great is the need for patience in usefully enduring scourges, 385. Patience knows how to lighten what is heavy, and steadfastness to overcome what rages, 913. Patience overcomes the adversities of the world, 1233.

Those who consider the heavenly homeland their own must endure labors in this world as though it were foreign, 50. For one who sighs for his homeland, the place of pilgrimage is torment, 1175. What order the patriarchs maintain among themselves in the Church, 507. Honor is denied to all patriarchs when one usurps the title “universal patriarch,” 773. Newly ordained patriarchs formerly used to send one another a synodical letter of their faith, 490, 515, 516, 844, 850, 962, 966.

The patriciate is the highest dignity, dissolved only by death, 492. The *chlamys* and Roman shoes are numbered among the insignia of the patriciate, 493, 520. By whom the patricians were instituted and what their origin was, 492, 493, 686. What dignity the patricians possess, 493. Governors of provinces are often called patricians, ibid. Patricians were often called consuls, ibid. The patricians of Gaul were prefects of the province and supreme commanders in war, 647. Patricians had their own *strator*, 675.

The patrimonies of the Roman Church were located in various provinces, 487. There were two stations of that Church’s patrimony in Sicily, one at Palermo and the other at Syracuse, 593. The care of the patrimony in Sicily is entrusted to Peter the subdeacon, 486. Before the body of Blessed Peter he assumes the care of that patrimony, 558. St. Peter’s patrimony in Gaul consisted chiefly of landed possessions, 758. That patrimony was commended to the kings of Gaul, 1102. Gregory wishes the revenues of this patrimony to be spent on the purchase of English boys and clothing for the poor, 796. Gregory asks that the revenues of the Gallican patrimony be sent to him, [Col. 1555] 648, 831, 832. That patrimony was used for the expenses of the poor, 794. The property of the Church is called the property of the poor, 834, 835. The care of the patrimony was sometimes entrusted to bishops, 979. The Church’s patrimony must not be entrusted to laymen, 982. Why the Church’s property must not be leased to Gentius Scribo, 1088. The patrimony of the Church of Ravenna in Sicily, 1097.

Administrators of the patrimony of St. Peter: in the Appian district, Felix the subdeacon, 976, 1273. In Campania, Peter, subdeacon of Campania. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. In Calabria, Sergius, 901, 960, 976, 1004. In Corsica, Boniface the notary, 976, 1234. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. In Dalmatia, Antoninus, 583, 632, 639. In Gaul, Candidus the priest, 796. See his title. At Palermo, Benenatus, 593. See his title. Fantinus, 973, 976, 1263. Savinus, 1268. At Salona, Antonius the subdeacon, 647. In Sardinia, Vitalis, 926. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. In Sicily, Peter, subdeacon of Sicily. See the same index. Cyprian the deacon. See the same index. Romanus, 944, 956, 976. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. Sabinus, 976. Hadrian the notary, 1055, 1231, 1232, 1242. In Tuscany, Eugenius the deacon, 1210. Certain things that had to be received from the total amount of the pension were converted to the administrator’s use, 534.

Ecclesiastical patronage granted to laymen, 933. Clerics must not have recourse to the patronage of laymen, contrary to Church discipline, 707. By the patronage of the saints, their relics are often meant, 276. Paula, a woman, 891. Paulinus of Nola, a bishop, was captured not by the Vandals but by the Goths, 115, 277. How he came into the power of the Vandals, 115. His alms were rewarded, 248. He distributed everything to the needy, 277. He handed himself over so that he might ransom a captive, 280. How he was freed, ibid., 281. Paulinus was baptized by Delphinus at Bordeaux and ordained by Lampius at Barcelona, 566. He was bound to no Church by his ordination, 763. Paulinus asks St. Augustine whether it benefits anyone that his body is buried in the earth, 457. Paulinus, bishop of Tauriana, 962. He is placed over the monastery of St. Theodore in Sicily, 528, 529. He is placed over the Liparitan Church by the bishop of Syracuse, 580. The visitation of the Church of Tauriana is entrusted to him, 580. Paulinus, a pilgrim in Sicily, 580. Paulinus, bishop of Tegessis, raging against the clergy and selling holy orders, must be restrained, 1198 and following, 1199, 1200 and following. Paulinus, bishop, does not communicate with Maximus, the intruder into the see of Salona, 812, 813. Paulinus, priest of the monastery of St. Erasmus, 506.

The apostle St. Paul, an outstanding ruler of souls, 9. Why Paul was called by the Areopagites “a babbler” (*seminiverbius*), 18. Paul was close to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation, 18, 321, 511. Joined to the highest and lowest alike by the bond of charity, 19, 321, 512. He became as a Jew to the Jews, not by abandoning faith but by extending compassion, 19, 512. When Paul sought to please everyone and when he did not, 28. Paul was a debtor to the wise and the foolish, so that he might teach both, 40. How he confounded the insolent Corinthians, 41. He raised the fainthearted Thessalonians by praise, 42. Why he commended to Timothy and Titus patience and zeal for emulation, 57. Paul was a great cultivator of the Church he had undertaken, ibid. The virtue of Peter and Paul differs in the miracle, but their merit does not differ in heaven, 205. Paul asked God three times but did not obtain what he requested, 265. The knowledge of Paul was Christ crucified, 321. Why the Lord did not immediately tell Paul, after he had fallen and been rebuked, what he must do, 93. The savage persecutor had to lie destroyed for a long time, so that afterward he might rise more solidly in good works, 94. How many miracles followed Paul’s conversion, 321.

—Out of charity Paul represented in himself the person of unbelievers, 19, 512. Among brothers who acted well, Paul, without knowing himself to be superior, remembered himself to be supreme among those who sinned, 22, 513. Paul was as though fried in a pan by burning zeal, 32. His prudent concern, 57. His steadfastness arising from the conquered fickleness of his mind, 61. In the shipwreck, the ship of his heart remained intact, 1029. Paul’s prudence in moderating the preaching of the word according to the weakness of his hearers, 99. Though caught up into heaven, he still fears lest he become reprobate, 869. His indulgence toward the incestuous Corinthian, 503. He did not wish the members of the Lord’s body to be partially subjected to the apostles themselves, 742. How he was the good fragrance of Christ, 924. Why Paul said that good works should be done so that the power of the world might not be feared, 98. How he said that God’s judgments are incomprehensible, 241, 244. Oppressed by the united Pharisees and Sadducees, Paul dissolved their evil concord, 71, 72. Why he said that he was pure from the blood of all, 75, 523. Made stronger in goodness through temptation, 87. Why he secretly fled persecution at Damascus, 220. He was beaten with rods for Christ, whom he had pursued with swords, 321. He would have called his entry among the peoples fruitless if he had not endured insults, 876. A certain man wishing to lift the bones that lay near Blessed Paul’s tomb died suddenly, 709. The body of Blessed Paul shines forth with miracles and terrors in his own church, 708, 709. When the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul were transferred, 710. Particles filed from the chains of St. Paul are sent as relics, 711. A wholly singular miracle that sometimes occurred in their distribution, ibid. Paul of Samosata, a heretic, 1168. Paul, an African bishop, is summoned to Rome by St. Gregory, 715, 716. He is forbidden by the exarch of Africa to depart, 839. Gregory wishes to learn his case, ibid. He suffered much both from the Donatists and from Catholics in defense of the Catholic faith, 839. He is permitted to present himself to the emperor in order to clear himself, 846. Paul is commended by Gregory, 904. Paul, bishop of Doclea, is to be punished for crimes, 1201 and following, 1202 and following. Paul, bishop of Nepi, 1291. He is sent to Naples to carry out the office of visitor, 575. The Neapolitans ask for him as their bishop, 574. Gregory judges that he must first be tested, 574, 575. Gregory urges him, as he is planning to return to his own Church, to remain in Naples, 579. But later permission is granted him to return, 649. See the Alphabetical Index of Letters. Paul, a bishop confined in a monastery for the sake of penance, 661. Paul, a Corinthian deacon, deceived by a promise, withdraws his accusation against his bishop, 779. Why Gregory spares him, 780. He is ordered to receive his customary stipend, ibid. [Col. 1556] Paul the deacon, writer of St. Gregory’s life: in what year he lived, 106. In many places he attributes the *Dialogues* to Gregory, ibid. Whether he could have collected only the letters Gregory the Great sent to Abbot Adhelard, 965, 966. Paul, a Sardinian cleric caught in acts of sorcery, is assigned to penance, 707. Paul the scholastic, 1259. Gregory complains that he had congratulated him on the pontificate, 488.

The poor: who are to be admonished, 36. The poor are to be consoled, ibid. It often happens that the rich are humble and the poor proud, 36, 599. Whether alms should be given to a sinful poor person, 65. Alms must not be made from the spoils of the poor, 68. The bishop has the poor’s property to distribute, 1232. The Church’s goods are called the goods of the poor, 638, 640. Larger shares are to be distributed to respectable and modest poor people than to beggars, 1117. The poor’s property is to be administered with gentleness, 672. Poverty is the guardian of humility, 184. The security of poverty is to be preferred to riches, 304. Those who pretend to poverty are deceived, 305. Victor, bishop of Phausiana in Sardinia, 932.

Peace. Whoever does not care to preserve peace refuses to bear the fruit of the Spirit, 68. What admonitions are to be given to lovers of peace, 69. Love of peace must not bend zeal and steadfastness, 69. There are two kinds of peace: one that the Lord leaves, and another that he gives, ibid. How we ought to use present peace, 69. Transitory peace is a footprint of eternal peace, ibid. Why Christ came not to send peace but a sword, 70. How great a fault it is to maintain peace with the worst people, 70. How peace may be maintained while correcting one’s neighbor, ibid., 772. The wickedness of the perverse, joined together in peace, is strengthened in its evil actions, 71. The evil of simulated peace, 671. Why our Redeemer left peace to his disciples as a great gift, 1073. Peace is to be maintained with everyone if possible, 1093. The excellence of peace, 1246. Humility is necessary for preserving peace, ibid. Cillanes promises peace, 1241. The Pisans refuse, ibid. Peace with the Lombards. See Agilulf.

To sin is to flee from God, 877. What is committed by one who errs differs from what is perpetrated knowingly, 501. What it means for a sinner to exalt his horn, 88. No human being in this world is without sin, 877. How great a fault it is to keep peace with sinners by concealing their vices, 70. The wondrous mercy of God, who calls the sinner back to himself, 82. The sinner’s present prosperity is compared with smoke and a wheel, 492. By what admonitions those who sin after being overcome by sudden desire are to be helped, 89. What must be placed before the eyes of those who sin deliberately, 91. Those who sin deliberately are often driven to despair, ibid. What shamelessness it is to seek darkness not even for the purpose of sinning, 89. The Lord pursues not so much wrong acts as the deliberate pursuit of wrongdoing, 91. Those who have sinned in spirit and flesh, remaining alive essentially forever, will die forever in spirit and flesh, 376. The conversion of a sinner is a greater miracle than the resurrection of the dead, 321. What those who have experienced sins must fear, 81. Let them recall past faults to memory, so that they may be ashamed to be defiled by future ones, 82. The sins of the heart are hidden from human beings but not from God, 6. [Col. 1557] God washes away the sins of the heart all the more quickly because he does not allow them to pass into deeds, 86. How sins arising from weakness differ from sins arising from deliberate malice, 91. Sins of rashness are lighter than sins committed deliberately, ibid. The reproach of those who avoid small sins but commit greater ones, 92. The way from lesser righteousness through pride becomes a pit of graver guilt, ibid. Sin is completed in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent, 85, 1162, 1163. The first is perpetrated by the enemy, the second by the flesh, and the third by the spirit, 86. How sins of thought arise and how deeds are overlooked, 5. By what they are to be admonished who have sinned by thought alone, 85. Let them consider whether they have transgressed through pleasure or also through consent, ibid. It is not the fault of thought but of deed when the will has fulfilled itself inwardly through the act of consent, ibid. Whoever loses innocence before God through desire for sin, 52. We recognize sin through suggestion, are overcome by pleasure, and are bound by consent, 85, 86. Those who praise the unlawful things they do offend more by mouth than by deed, 88. What such people must do, ibid. What it means to sin with a voice and to sin with a cry, 89. How sinning in deeds differs from sinning in intention, 91. Whoever consents to others’ sins is guilty, 659.

Original sin. Through the first human being, the entire human race was condemned to the punishment of death and corruption; through the second human being, we trust that we are freed first from the death of the soul and afterward from all corruption of the flesh, 883. Before baptism every soul is bound by the chains of original sin, 970.

Venial sin. How those subject to the smallest but frequent faults are to be admonished, 91, 92. How great a danger threatens from the multitude of slight sins, 91. Whoever neglects to avoid the smallest sins falls wholly from the state of righteousness, not suddenly but little by little, 92. Why we often sin worse in a small fault than in a greater one, ibid. Small and very minor sins can be remitted in the age to come, 444. Venial sins are signified by wood, hay, and straw, ibid. The deacon Paschasius was freed after death from the sin of ignorance, 445. The punishment of sin in hell is eternal, 449, 452. Why sin, which is finite in itself, is punished with an eternal penalty, 449. Those who are guilty of the same sins must be afflicted with the same punishments, 429. In the punishments of sins God weighs human hearts, not deeds, 449. Sins redeemed by alms must not be repeated, 65. One must not return to sins after penance, 1131. Not only all sins together but also each individual sin must be mourned, 84.

—How sins of deeds are to be lamented, 84, 85. Likewise sins of thought, 85. It does not benefit anyone to abandon sin unless it is cleansed by tears, 87. What must be said to those who confess sins but do not guard against them, 89. The better they see the evil they do, the worse they perish, ibid. They are to be condemned by their own testimony, ibid. A sin that is also strengthened by counsel is dissolved more slowly, 91. Some sins can be remitted in the age to come, 441. But not even the smallest will be remitted there unless a person, while still here, earns this by good works so as to obtain it there, 444. See Venial sin. Other people’s sins must be remitted so that ours may be remitted, 473. Remitted sins sometimes return, ibid. If sins are not punished, they provoke God’s anger, 642. They must not be left [Col. 1557] unpunished, lest from this …

…so that the others may take courage, 1201. Manifest sins are not to be cleansed by secret correction, 1280. A person ought not to become secure about sins that have been forgiven, 869. Peculiarity in a monk is to be condemned, 1194, 1195. *Peculium* (“private property”) is derived from *pecunia*, as though “small money,” 800. What private property is, and whose it is, ibid. What “servile” or “lordly” private property is, 800. *Pecunia* (“money”) is called whatever people possess on earth and of which they are owners, 1242. What it means to tie money in a napkin, 10. Money obtained from God by prayers, 189. Pope Pelagius I, newly ordained, sent the confession of his faith to King Childebert according to ancient custom, 490; to Sapaudus of Arles, 542. He was disliked by the Western bishops because he accepted the Fifth Synod, 682.

Pope Pelagius II. Gregory had learned from him what he relates about the monk Martin in his *Dialogues*, 313. The book sent by St Gregory to the schismatics of Istria is Pelagius’s seventh letter, 616. Pelagius’s efforts to extinguish the schism were unsuccessful, 682. When he wished to move the silver that was above the body of blessed Peter, he was terrified, 708. He dissolved the acts of the synod in which John had assumed the title of universal bishop, 741. Pelagius, bishop of the city of Anagni, 1291. Pelagius, bishop of Turni, 830. Pelagius the deacon and Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, were the cause of the scandal that arose from the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 616. Pelagius the heretic, condemned at the Council of Ephesus: because he asserted that we had been redeemed by Christ in vain, he denied that through Adam we had died in soul, 802. A Pelagian is one who denies that the devil enters the human heart, 884. Peltrasius, 896. “Silvered wings of a dove,” 896.

*Pensio* (“rent”) is what is given for the use of something belonging to another, 606. *Merces* (“payment”) is the rent for inhabiting another’s house, ibid. It also means any annual income, 606. It is called the burden of a possession, 734. Rents were approved at the Council of Chalcedon, 1218. Great caution is needed so that they may be collected with a clear conscience, ibid.

*Per.* Some wish this preposition to mean the same as *durante* (“during”), etc., 743, 749, 750. The striking of a cleric for the sake of correction on account of more serious faults was formerly permitted, 664. By whom it was to be carried out, ibid. A cleric assigned by the bishop to public flogging, 664. A bishop who had ordered a woman to be beaten was suspended from his office for two months, 656, 657.

Pilgrimage is the present life, 1175. For whom the place of pilgrimage is a torment, ibid. Annual pilgrimages undertaken for religious reasons, 320. A pilgrim-priest is one who is not a cardinal or titular priest, 697, 698. Peregrinus, a disciple of blessed Benedict, 257.

*Perfection.* The other virtues produce perfection, but charity also binds them together so that they cannot be loosened from the mind of the one who loves, 781. The soul is like a ship climbing against the current, 94. Why God does not wish anyone to be perfect in this life, 308. The *περιοδεῦται* (*periodeutai*) were visitors who were not bishops, 501.

How the empire of the Persians was subject to the emperor Maurice, 678. The emperor of the Persians was not converted to the faith through the preaching of Bishop Domitian, 680. *Perscrutari* (“to investigate”) is sometimes used in the passive sense, 975, 976.

Schismatics boast in vain that they are suffering persecution, 615. Persecution, when it is not endured reasonably, contributes nothing whatever to salvation, ibid. Persecutions belong to those who live piously, 876. The less piously a person lives, the less persecution he has endured, ibid. Persecution for the faith. See *Martyrdom*.

*Perseverance.* What should be preached to those who do not complete the good they have begun, 94. Whoever does not carry out strictly the good he has begun imitates the undoing caused by a hand that destroys what it has made, ibid. It is better not to begin good works than to turn backward in thought from those already begun, 829. Uncertainty about perseverance keeps the saints anxious and humble, 854.

What a Persian case is, 1270. Partiality in judges is evil, 582. Partiality is forbidden, 643. Public persons are magistrates, officials, and messengers, 687. What the Thessalian persuasion is, 735. Obstinacy is opposed to humility, 7. Who are to be admonished when obstinate, 60, 61. Obstinacy is generated by pride, 60. Its remedies, 60.

*Perverse.* Not all the good are taken away in such a way that only the perverse remain in the world, 368. Those devoted to divine works are accustomed to be torn apart by the adversities of the wicked, 846.

Perusia, a city of Etruria, 300, 550. In this city Marcus Antonius was besieged by Augustus and, compelled by hunger, surrendered, ibid. This same city was captured by the Goths in the seventh year of the siege, 300. Bishops of Perusia: Herculanus, 300; Venantius, 1211.

What a broken foot signifies in a shepherd, 11. A man with a broken foot was formerly excluded from the priesthood, 11. The plague was seen under the appearance of an arrow striking the Romans, 432. With what spirit the scourge of plague should be received, 1087 and following. By what method those struck by this scourge should be consoled, 1087, 1088.

*Peti*, *postulari*, *desiderari*, and *eligi* (“to be sought, requested, desired, and chosen”) are used with the same meaning, 634. Yet *postulare* (“to request”) is stronger than *petere* (“to ask”), ibid.

Petronilla transferred everything she possessed, by way of a donation, to the monastery in which she had become a religious, 685. She was violated by the notary Agnellus and carried away from the monastery, ibid. She was ordered to be sent back to the same monastery to perform penance, 686. Petronius, notary of the holy Roman Church, 553.
