The apostle St Peter was called Peter from *petra* (“rock”), 888. Peter, holding the primacy of the Church, was raised up against the wicked alone, 21. Peter, chief of the apostles, 202, 743. Who should be called a soldier of blessed Peter, 526. “Peter” and “the apostolic see” are used reciprocally, ibid., 831, 832. To go to blessed Peter is the same as to go to the Roman supreme pontiff, 619. The primacy of Peter and of the Roman Church, 668, 669, 743, 748. The care of the Church was entrusted to Peter, 748. The Church was established upon the firmness of the chief of the apostles, 888. In the primacy, only the see of the chief of the apostles grew strong in authority, ibid. Peter himself still sits in his chair in his successors, ibid. The See of blessed Peter is one in three places, and the see of one person, 888, 1247. The prerogatives of Peter, 1129.

Peter’s humility toward Cornelius and his zeal against the fault of Ananias and Sapphira, 21, 22, 513. Peter gladly accepts Paul’s rebuke, 28. He who had received the power of the heavenly kingdom answered the complaints of the faithful not on the basis of power but of reason, 1129 and following, 1130. The power of Peter and Paul was unequal in the miracle, although their merit in heaven is not unequal, 205. Peter, released by an angel: what is meant by his coming to himself, 217. Why he first rebuked the Jews for what they had done before admonishing them concerning what they should do, 93. Peter raised Tabitha by praying, but delivered Ananias and Sapphira to death by rebuking them, 261. The power of St Peter’s keys for healing the sick, 517, 519, 520, 872. A small cross containing fragments of Peter’s chains is sent, 648, 1248. Its power, ibid. Sometimes fragments of St Peter’s chains cannot be removed with a file, 711. When Pelagius II wished to move the silver that was above blessed Peter’s head, he was terrified, 708. The body of St Peter shines forth in his church through miracles and terrors, ibid. The Easterners cannot lift the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul; but the Romans are deemed worthy to lift them through the Lord’s mercy, 710, 711. When the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul were transferred, 710. Gregory sends their relics to Bishop Palladius, 826, and to Queen Brunichild, 829. The various apparitions of St Peter, 333, 389, 392.

Peter, bishop of Aleria in Corsica, 808. He labors to convert the Corsicans, 893. Peter, bishop of Anagni, 1287. Peter, bishop of Baricis, 636. Peter, bishop of Istria, 778. Peter, bishop of Hydruntum, 807. He is assigned the visitation of three churches, 808. He was visitor of the Church of Brundisium, 838. Peter, bishop of Numidia, on whose account the matter was entrusted to Columbus for settlement, 821, 822. Peter, bishop in the East, 853. What he had shouted at the ordination of Cyriacus—“This is the day which the Lord has made”—is criticized, 854. Peter, bishop of Terracina, 524, 634. Peter, bishop of Tricala, 1137. Visitor of the Church of Agrigento, 737.

Peter, a Neapolitan deacon, was not to be chosen bishop because he was a usurer, 1086. Peter, a deacon and representative of the province of Ravenna, deceased, 667. Peter the deacon, 579. Whether Peter the deacon, Gregory’s interlocutor in the *Dialogues*, had been a monk, 115. He seems to have been the Peter the subdeacon to whom Gregory often wrote with great familiarity, ibid. Peter the subdeacon was appointed vicar of the Roman see and administrator of St Peter’s patrimony in Sicily, 486, 488, 489. He was appointed moderator of the synods to be held annually in Sicily, 486. Gregory employed him in numerous ecclesiastical and secular matters, both in Sicily and in Campania. See the *Alphabetical Index of the Letters*.

Peter, notary in Reggio, 569, 735. Peter the defensor, 1197. Peter the acolyte, servant of the deacon Sabinianus, the apocrisiarius at Constantinople, 899. Peter, a Neapolitan cleric accused of wrongdoing, appealed to the apostolic see, 1072. Peter, lector of the Church of Euria, 1271. Peter the abbot, 453. Peter the monk, one of the companions of St Augustine, 1113. Peter the Iberian monk, conspicuous for holiness, 432. Why Peter, the chief of the ecclesiastical household, was seen bound and weighed down in hell by a great weight, 433. Peter, founder of a certain monastery, 689. Peter, a most distinguished man, *vicedominus* of Rusticianus, 1122. Peter of Sicily, 944. Peter the farmer, 536. Peter, son of Lucillus, bishop of Malta, is ordered to restore the Church’s property that he had taken away, 1041. Peter the Jew, having become a Christian, occupied the Jews’ synagogue on the day after his baptism, 930. Peter, 1263.

*Phanum.* See *Fanum*.

The Pharisees accepted the resurrection of the dead, 71. Why Paul sought to divide the Pharisees and Sadducees, ibid., 72. The Pharisees strained out a gnat and swallowed a camel, 92. Phausiana, a city of Sardinia under the archbishop of Torres, 708. In this city, which had long been vacant, a bishop was to be ordained, 708. Victor, bishop of Phausiana, 1095.

*Φελόνιον* (*phelonion*), a sacred vestment for the use of a bishop and a priest, 190. It is also the same as a *paenula*, a kind of cheaper garment, ibid. Philagrius, deprived of his sight and greatly tormented, is highly commended, 1034, 1035 and following. Philaster wrote a book on heresies, 862. Philippus, commander of the palace guard, 520. Philippus, bishop of Epirus, 796. Philippus the priest, 1237.

Why God preserved the Philistines for so long, 308. How greatly the zeal of Phinehas pleased God, 70.

*Phocas.* When Phocas assumed the empire, Gregory hoped that all would go well for the state, 1239. Gregory does not flatter Phocas, 1239. Phocas initially pretends to clemency and generosity, 1239. Gregory excuses the absence of the deacon apocrisiarii before Phocas, 1244. He sends Boniface, ibid. He implores Phocas’s aid against the Lombards, ibid. Phocas is crowned, 1301.

The Photinians were so called from Photinus, 1066. They were also called Bonosians, 1168. How Gregory conducted himself toward them, 1066. Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, praises Gregory as the author of the *Dialogues*, 107. He is thought to have corrupted the passage in Gregory’s *Dialogues* where the procession of the Holy Spirit is discussed, 118.

A maniac was healed, 356. *Phylacteria* are understood as sacred relics set in gold, silver, or carved crystal, 1270, 1271. Which phylacteries were prohibited by the councils, 1271.

The province of Picenum, 1194, 1195. Painting provides for uneducated people who look at it what writing provides for readers, 1100. What false piety is and whose it is, 23. Discipline should be exercised in such a way that piety is not abandoned, ibid. The softness of piety is signified by oil, 23.

*Lazy.* Who are to be admonished as lazy, 55. The empty excuses of the lazy, 56. Who is called lazy because he will beg uselessly in summer, ibid. The evil effects of laziness, 55. What is meant by saying that laziness induces sleep, ibid. Laziness is understood under the name of cold, 56.

Pimenius, bishop of Amalfi, must be compelled to reside in his see, 808, 809. Pisa, a city of Etruria, 1241. Pisaurum, a city of Umbria in Italy, 755. The bishop of Pisaurum is rebuked because he disturbed the monks’ peace by placing his cathedra in their monastery, 826. Felix, bishop of Pisaurum, 826.

[Col. 1560]

A fish discovered by a miracle, 153. During a fast, smaller fish are permitted for the relief of illness, but larger ones are forbidden, 1303. Piacenza, an episcopal city under the archbishop of Bologna, 295, 296. Bishops of Piacenza: Sabinus, 296; Boniface, 1288.

One must please God alone, 626. Placidus, a little boy, was handed over by his father Tertullus to St Benedict, 220. He accompanied Benedict when he brought forth a spring from the rock, 221. After falling into the water, he was rescued by Maurus, 225. At what time he suffered martyrdom, 239. Placidus, a magnificent man, 1139.

*Placitum* is a legal and judicial term with several meanings, 606. Plancho, a most distinguished man, 1209. The breadth of the present life is represented by the word “streets,” 23. They are called streets from their breadth, ibid.

*People.* Why the consent of the people was required for the election of a shepherd, 573. In accordance with the merit of the peoples, persons are usually appointed as shepherds by heavenly judgment, 645. What kind of lead is found in a furnace, 53. Rain divinely withheld from certain places, 297, 300. What is signified by a cup of bitter drink tempered by the sweetness of honey, 59.

*Punishment.* An equal punishment cannot absolve those whose cause is unequal, 617. How present punishment is the end of a preceding fault and how it is the beginning of a subsequent punishment, 1114. Penitents should have confidence in hope without becoming sluggish through security, 85. By what deceptions the devil attempts to deceive a penitent soul, 85. Harsher discipline is not to be applied to penitents who mourn their sins, 679.

*Penance.* We are recalled to penance when scourged, 51. God’s wondrous mercy toward sinners is an incentive to penance, 82. Fervent penance is preferred to sluggish innocence, 83, 84. What it means to give drink in tears according to the measure of penitents, 84. The more a person does not cease to regard his sins, the less God regards those sins, ibid. The measure of penance should equal the measure of sin, 86. By what admonitions those should be stirred who do not mourn the sins they abandon, 87. Just as a writer who ceases writing has not thereby erased what he wrote, so one who ceases sinning but does not erase his sins with tears has not erased them, ibid., 88. Peter believed that penance should precede baptism, 88. No one ought to be secure concerning sins until the time for mourning them has passed, 869.

Penance without amendment is empty, 86. Who are to be admonished—those who mourn sins they do not abandon, ibid., 87. Whoever mourns what he has committed but does not abandon it subjects himself to the guilt of a heavier punishment, 86. The wicked are often pricked with remorse to no purpose, 87. Penance is not merely cessation from sins, 87. To perform true penance is to mourn what has been committed and to avoid what ought to be mourned, 1132. The heart must not only be contrite but also humbled, 88. After the bath, the person who does not preserve innocence of life after tears neglects to remain clean, 87. What should be said to those who confess their sins but do not avoid them, 89. They are condemned by their own testimony, ibid. They descend alive into hell, ibid. The penitent will stand secure at the judgment, 645, 656. Penance merits forgiveness, 969. What kind of penance is effective against sin, 1132. A period of reprieve is granted to us for penance, 1181. After performing penance for three years, one may not live perversely, 1130, 1131, 1132. Distinguished men and bishops were sometimes shut up in monasteries in order to perform penance, 643.

Penance as a sacrament. To whom the power of binding and loosing was given, 253.

*To repent.* What those should do who lament sins of action, 84. They should consider each offense individually so that they may cleanse themselves wholly with tears, 84. Concerning what those who have sinned only in thought should be admonished, 85, 86. When nocturnal pollution prevents communion and the celebration of Mass, 1161 and following.

A *polypticum* is a register in which acts are recorded, 593. It is also a tablet having several folds, 956.

The pomp of the world. See *World*. Pompeiana, a religious woman, 543, 1107. She is called Pomponiana, 1260, 1261. Pompeianus, abbot of one of the monasteries built by Benedict, 221. Pompeius, unjustly condemned bishop, 1060. Pomponiana. See *Pompeiana*.

What the fault of heaviness is, 13. What *ponderosus* (“heavy”) means, 13.

*Bridge.* Why, in a vision, the just were seen crossing a bridge to pleasant places, 432, 433, 436.

*Pontiff.* See *Bishop*. Roman pontiff. See *Roman*.

Populonium, a city of Etruria with various names, 296, 500. The visitation of this Church was entrusted to Balbinus, bishop of Rosella, 500. In it, almost entirely deprived of priests and deacons, priests and deacons were to be ordained, 501. Cerbonius, bishop of Populonium, 296 and following.

*Pig.* The devil is permitted to enter a pig, 328. Under the figure of a pig, the devil abandons the Church newly dedicated to God, 344. The Church that was to be handed over to the Arians was seen filled with a multitude of pigs, ibid.

*Gate.* What it means to go from gate to gate, 75. The Flaminian Gate at Rome, 1125. The Metronian Gate at Rome, ibid.

*To carry.* Burdens are to be carried for one another, 79. He carries more lightly who remembers that he is being carried, 80.

*Portitor* (“carrier”). This is a very ancient word, 1121. The Roman Portus, or Portus Augusti, a city of Etruria, 947. Bishops of Portus: Felix, 947, 1288, 1291; Gregory, 1287. Portus Venetus, a city of Liguria, 729.

The burden of a possession is the rent owed by a tenant, 734. Possession for thirty years suffices in secular matters and formerly had force in ecclesiastical matters, 496. It appears that St Gregory first extended this to forty years for ecclesiastical matters, ibid. See *Prescription*. How possession is interrupted, 497. By what arguments possession is proved, 666. What emphyteutic possession is, 536, 1088. Property belonging by right to the Church is not to be granted in emphyteusis except for the greater advantage of that same Church, 557. A monk who seeks possession of land is not a monk, 304. Nevertheless, monks to whom possessions have been assigned for the necessities of life are not to be blamed, ibid. Some possessions were formerly assigned by parents to virgins dedicated to God, 328. A possessor is not an owner but has a right in the thing, 695. There is a distinction between an owner and a possessor, 696.

When the desires of those who request something should be fulfilled, 1249, 1262. A person is said to be “requested” (*postulari*) when he is chosen for the episcopate by a common decree of the clergy and people, 601, 808, 866, 996. How *postulation* differs from election, 602, 634. *Postulare* (“to request”) is stronger than *petere* (“to ask”), 634. *Postulari*, *peti*, *eligi*, and *desiderari* (“to be requested, asked, chosen, and desired”) are used with the same meaning, ibid. What postulation means among canonists, 808, 809. What must be done if postulation coincides with election, 809.

*Power.* Even when temporal power lifts up the just, it often catches them, as though in a snare, in the guilt of sin, 78. He rules power well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it, 21.

*Authority.* How many storms there are at the summit of authority, 10. The royal authority of the saints, 16. What Christian authority is like, 509. Authority is given to rulers by God so that the way to heaven may be opened more widely to all, 676, and so that they may restrain the internal wars of the Churches, 686. Authority and love have a great kinship with one another, 873. Authority must be restricted according to reason, 1048. The reverence of secular powers toward the Christian religion, 3. God’s commandments are greater than the commandments of rulers, 540. The Lord’s commandments must be observed by kings, 1150. *Praeceptio* and *praeceptum* signify commands delivered in writing by kings and distinguished persons, 956, 957.

Who are to be admonished as rash, 55, 56. Nothing should be decided by rash judgment, 597. Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, 17, 510.

How predestination is obtained through prayers, 181. Predestination is then fulfilled through prayers when it has been predestined that what was predestined should be obtained through prayers, 184.

*To preach.* Some oppose by their conduct what they preach in words, 4. Those who fear to preach through excessive humility are to be admonished, 74 and following. Those who rush prematurely into the office of preaching are to be admonished, 76 and following. It is difficult to preach amid earthly cares, 491. St Benedict used to send his brothers to preach to the neighboring nuns, 245. Some laudably desire the office of preaching, while others are laudably compelled and drawn into it, 7, 848. It is a crime to deny the bread of the word to the hungry and medicine to the sick, 74. To hide grain is to keep the words of preaching within oneself, ibid. It is also a crime not to heal the wounds of minds by cutting with words, ibid. To keep a sword from bloodshed is to withhold the word of preaching from killing bodily life, 75. The person who refused to distribute his talent lost it with the sentence of condemnation, ibid. When the eternal voice makes itself known to someone, he should draw others by crying out to the place toward which he himself is being carried, 75. The knowledge of preaching is promised to increase in the person who is not held by the fault of sluggishness, ibid. Whoever refuses, insofar as he is able, to rebuke the life of carnal people denies that he belongs to God, 76. Those who do not know letters should be instructed through preaching, 634. The same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, 33. How great the variety should be in the art of preaching, 34, 35 and following. High matters should not be preached to weak minds, 99. The measure of wheat expresses the measure of the word, ibid. Those who keep watch over the office of preaching should not withdraw from the study of sacred reading, 33, 34. The preacher is like a cock crying in the night with a different voice, 99, 100. Preachers are compared with oxen, 856.

Who is and who is not a preacher of God, 76. What a holy preacher builds as a fortification, 31. Who carries the earthwork, ibid. Who raises the camp and places the battering rams around it, ibid. The preacher who speaks from God and before God, 73. What it means for the preacher to drink water from his own cistern, 73. What it means for him to channel his springs outward, 74. What it means to divide waters in the streets, ibid. And what it means to drink from the streams of his own well, ibid. A preacher who has been called should call others, 75. What it means for a preacher to be clothed with power from on high, 76. What it means for future preachers to sit in the city, 76.

How difficult and laborious the preacher’s office is, 96, 97. It is a heavy labor for a preacher when he is compelled to preach to someone enslaved to one of two opposing vices, 97. What he should do and what he should avoid, ibid. He should cure the disease in such a way as to take account of the sick person’s weakness, 98. Sometimes he should leave lesser vices untouched in order to remove greater ones, 98. The preacher should pursue more ardently that plague which presses more dangerously, 98. He should not draw the mind of his hearer beyond its strength, 99. He should beware lest, while raising others up, he himself fall, 99. Whoever, out of charity, assumes the role of the infirm imitates the conduct of an excellent preacher, 380. Who ought to climb upon the high mountain as a preacher, 509. When he ought to rebuke elders, 925.

A preacher who admonishes those who practice abstinence, 61, 62; those who endure adversity, 78; the sick, 50. A preacher who admonishes the benevolent, 45; those who do evil secretly and good publicly, 95; what arguments he should use to frighten those who do good secretly but permit others to think certain evil things about them, 95; what evidence he should give to those who do not even begin good works, 93, 94; what he should say to those who do not complete the good they have begun, 94.

A preacher who admonishes the unmarried, 81; the married, 79, 80.

A preacher who admonishes those at odds, 68, 69; the rich, 36; masters, 40.

What a preacher should say to the proud, 58, 59; to those who give alms, 63, 65; to those who neither seize what belongs to others nor distribute what is their own, 66; to those who give away what is their own but do not cease seizing what belongs to others, 67.

How a preacher should admonish women, 35; those who fear scourges, 52; those whom scourges do not restrain, 52.

How a preacher should admonish those devoted to gluttony, 61, 62.

With what words a preacher should admonish the dull, 40; the humble, 58, 59.

A preacher who admonishes the impatient, 42; the shameless, 41; those who are uninjured, 49; the fickle, 60, 61; the poor, 36; the envious, 46; the angry, 56, 57; those who sow quarrels, 71; the young, 35.

How a preacher should admonish the cheerful, 37; those who do not rightly understand the words of the sacred Law, 72.

A preacher who admonishes the meek, 56, 57; those who do evil secretly, 95; those who allow others to think evil of them, ibid.

A preacher who admonishes the peaceful, 69, 70; the peacemakers, 71, 72; the patient, 44, 45; those who have experienced sins of the flesh, 81, 82; those ignorant of sins of the flesh, 83; those who mourn sins of action, 84, 85; those who mourn sins of thought, 85, 86; those who mourn what they have committed but nevertheless do not abandon it, 86, 87; those who abandon sins but nevertheless do not mourn them, 87. What a preacher should say to those who praise their own sins, 88; to those who confess sins but do not avoid them, 89. A preacher who admonishes those who sin after being overcome by sudden desire, 89. What the preacher should place before the eyes of those who sin deliberately, 91. How he should admonish those subject to small but frequent sins, 91, 92. How he should admonish those who avoid small sins but commit greater ones, 92. How he should admonish the obstinate, 60, 61; the lazy, 55; the powerful, 36, 37; the rash, 55. How he should admonish those who refuse the office of preaching through excessive humility, 74. How he should admonish those whom rashness drives into the office of preaching, 76. How he should admonish prelates, 37, 38. How he should admonish those who prosper in this world, 77; the insolent, 41, 42; the fainthearted, 41, 42.

How a preacher should admonish those who seize what belongs to others, 65, 66; those who give away what is their own but nevertheless do not cease seizing what belongs to others, 67.

A preacher who admonishes the wise, 40; the old, 35; slaves, 40; the simple, 47; subjects, 37, 39.

How a preacher should admonish the silent, 53, 54; the sad, 37.

How a preacher should admonish the talkative, 54; the bashful, 41; the deceitful, 47; men, 35.

Holy preachers should teach which battles against vices are open and which are to be feared as hidden, 31. The preacher should return to his own heart, 73. The greatest discretion is necessary for him, 97. He should teach by his works before teaching by his voice, 100. The voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more readily when the speaker’s life commends it, 509. He should surpass his subjects in the virtue of his conduct, 509. Preachers must be fortified with humility against arrogance, 1110. What the preacher’s knowledge should be, 785. The seed of the word germinates easily when the piety of the preacher waters it in the hearer’s breast, 26. What fruit the person gains for himself who diligently performs the office of preacher, 75. Even if a preacher does not achieve conversion, he does not lack the reward of his preaching, 680. The power of preachers is revealed when a harvest of souls arises, 856.

Bad preachers are like an inexperienced physician who, ignorant of his own wound, wishes to cure another’s, 73. Those who understand sacred Scripture correctly but do not preach humbly are to be admonished, 73. Whoever seeks his own glory in the word of God usurps the right of the one who gives it, ibid. Preachers should beware lest through arrogance they serve Satan, 74.

Those who wish to preside flatter themselves with a fictitious promise of good works, 9. All who preside are the head of their subjects, 25. No one should dare to preside who has not learned to be subject, 156. Some, however, are exempted from this rule, ibid.

Which official was formerly called a cardinal prefect, 501. One who holds the place of prefects, that is, a deputy of the prefects, 460. A prefect, a magistrate distinct from an exarch, 521. The prefect of the city demanded accounts from the prefect of the grain supply, ibid.

Why the pregnant women of Gilead signify souls, 72. Which clerics are *praejacentes*, 1117. Praejecta, a distinguished woman, 974. Praejectus, bishop of Narni, 569. *Praejudicium* signifies loss or disadvantage, 959, 973, 974, 1077.

Fear should moderate the desire for prelatehood, 2. Every prelate should be appointed not on the basis of age, lots, or chance, but on the basis of what is more excellent, 692. How important election or nomination is for prelatehood, 853. The common advantage must always be considered, not private advantage, 857.

How a prelate should come to the summit of governance, 1, 10. He should not approach the teaching of humility through arrogance, 3. A prelate’s action should surpass the action of the people by as much as the shepherd’s life differs from the flock, 13. A prelate occupied with divine matters should leave earthly affairs to be managed by his subjects, 25. He should tolerate secular business out of compassion, never seek it out of love, 26. Frequently, in the occupation of governance, the practice of good works is lost—what had been maintained in tranquillity, 9. The density of cares devastates the mind of a prelate, 24, 172. In any one matter he loses as much as he is occupied more widely with many matters, ibid.

Prelates should preside temperately, 37. They should carry out what they teach, 38. Those who preside over others should consider not the power of rank but equality of condition, 20. At the summit of dignities humility is endangered, 21. A prelate should know how to rise above faults, 21. How much he ought to fear arrogance and flattery, 21. He must preserve humility in his heart and discipline in his conduct, 22. What punishment awaits the prelate made proud by the governance he has undertaken, 23. Good prelates rejoice when subjects rebuke them; bad ones hate it, 28. After greater vices have been conquered, God leaves holy prelates in lesser matters for the sake of humility, 102. Every prelate ought to confess that he is liable to error, 172. Humility should not hinder pastoral zeal, nor pastoral zeal humility, 514. In prelates, neither should humility be lax nor authority rigid, 526.

A prelate who assumes care of the people approaches them as a physician approaches a sick person, 10. A prelate is said to carry the vessels of the Lord, 13, 508. He should rejoice not in presiding over people but in benefiting them, 20. When he ought to inspire terror in his subjects, 20, 31. Freedom of speech toward prelates should be granted to subjects in such a way that they do not lose humility of life toward them, 28. Prelates have pledged themselves on behalf of their subjects, 38. A prelate is ensnared by the words of his own mouth, ibid. It is not enough for a prelate to keep watch if he does not separate his subject from the torpor of sin, 38. What it means for a prelate to sleep or doze, ibid. He should have wakeful eyes within and all around, 39. Gentle prelates should embrace solicitude; angry ones should condemn disturbance, 57. Prelates should strive to be loved more than feared, 586. They should prove themselves fathers in name and in the affection shown in their conduct, 613. For this reason they correct their subjects: to make them better, 669. When sin is not corrected in a subject, the sentence is turned back upon those who preside, 702. The peoples entrusted to the great are entrusted for this purpose: while serving them in earthly matters, they may receive from them what is eternal, 703.

A prelate easily considers himself wiser than all those whom he sees himself able to surpass in power, 21. A prelate ought to rule over vices, not over people, 22. The worst effects of prelates’ anger, 57. Rash fury is despised in prelates, 681. How many deaths the perverse examples of prelates deserve, 38. In prelates, indolence is concealed under the appearance of humility; pride pretends to love rectitude, 59. The merits of rulers are joined with those of their peoples, 855. How great an evil credulity is in prelates, 860.

*Battle.* What it means to stand in battle on the day of the Lord, 17, 510.

Praeneste, an episcopal city of Latium, 331, 332, 396. The abbot of Mount Praeneste, venerable in life, 332. He foreknows the day of his death, ibid. Bishops of Praeneste: Sergius, 1287; Proculus, 1291.

A *praepositus* is one who holds second place, either in spiritual or temporal matters, in a monastery, 155, 625, 732. What is neglected through the abbot’s carelessness should be preserved through the diligence of the *praepositus*, 732. The goodness of *praepositi* is the salvation of their subjects, 797, 833. What the *praepositus* of a monastery should care for, 857. With what virtues he should be adorned, ibid. In appointing a *praepositus*, the place should not be considered but the advantage foreseen, 857. Every office is completed beneficially when there is one *praepositus* to whom recourse may be had, 784. Anger must be avoided by *praepositi*, 1048. What kind of person a *praepositus* should be toward his subjects, 1237. Those who sin against the *praepositus* sin against God, 39. Those who rise up against their *praepositi* scorn being servants of God, 599.

*To foreknow.* Those whom God foreknew would be gathered within the bosom of the Church cannot be snatched from his hand, 1000, 1001.

*Prescription* is one of the exceptions derived from the passage of time, 496. Whether a hundred-year prescription is reserved solely to the Roman Church, ibid. A forty-year prescription prevails in a dispute over the boundaries of fields between two abbots, 887.

*Presumption.* Those who are improperly secure through confidence in their own strength die unexpectedly through negligence, 99. Whoever presumes himself strong because he has been helped recognizes his weakness when abandoned, 101. What incautious presumption is, 977. A presumptuous person, that is, an invader and usurper, 793.

Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, 1145. In ancient usage, *praetor* meant any commander of soldiers, 1048. What a praetor should avoid when administering a province, and with what integrity he should render justice, 487. The various meanings of *praetorium*, 1048.

*To foresee.* Things foreseen as future become less remarkable when they have become present, 90.

*Precarium*, according to its etymology, signifies what, 607. It seems to be the same as *roga militaris* (“military pay”), or money, ibid., 1054, 1184. What a *precaria* contract is in canon law, 607. *Precariae* are to be renewed every five years, ibid.

*Prayers.* Why God hears prayers concerning small and worthless matters, 192. The less God hears our mouth in prayer, the more it is defiled by foolish speech, 313. Our prayers are lifted more quickly to the ear of the Lord’s mercy insofar as the ardor of charity intensifies the prayers poured out for us in return, 807.

A priest is called a man of the second see, or of the second throne, or a priest of the second order, 486, 563. In earlier centuries bishops were called priests; this is not so in Gregory’s usage, 635. Why formerly such great…

If there should be a scarcity of presbyters in the Church, 500. In former times no one was ordained presbyter unless attached to some church or title, 501, 694. Who were called cardinal presbyters, 501. A presbyter substituted for another’s place out of necessity, not through fault, is to be removed from that church and ordained in another that is vacant, 694. The former scarcity of presbyters was useful; their present multitude harms discipline, 694. In Gregory’s time several presbyters were assigned to one title, 697, 698. A cardinal presbyter ought not to be established in an oratory, 576, 577. Nevertheless, in certain oratories it was permitted to have a cardinal presbyter, 1188. A peregrine presbyter is one who is not a cardinal or titular presbyter, 697, 698. Who are to be ordained presbyters, 547. Why in former times very few were chosen from among the presbyters for the episcopate, 681. Whether formerly there was no presbyter in monasteries, or only one, and whether this one was an outsider, 697, 698. The wives of presbyters were called *conversae*, 388. Many councils of Gaul forbid presbyters ordained after marriage to live with their wives, 546. Nevertheless, in Gregory’s time this was not yet altogether prohibited in Italy, ibid. After ordination presbyters should love their wives as sisters, but beware of them as enemies, 388. Sardinian presbyters are forbidden to chrism on the forehead, 689. Nevertheless, they were later permitted to do so, 705. Presbyters who bring accusations, if they fail to establish them, are to be excommunicated, 706, 707. Provision is made that they should not absolve monks from excommunication, 955. In former times presbyters sat in synods, 1288, 1297. Presbyters sat as judges at the Council of Chalcedon, 1288. Presbyters are called “sons” by Gregory, 1297. A presbyter who takes a wife, and a woman who takes a presbyter, are excommunicated, 1293. The cases of presbyters. See *Clerics*. Presbyters ought to reside. See *Residence*. A certain presbyter in the province of Valeria brings a thief before his tomb, 329. A certain presbyter of Nursia lived with his wife after his ordination, 388. At the point of his death he orders her to withdraw from him, ibid. Thereupon, refreshed by a vision and conversation with the holy apostles Peter and Paul, he dies, 389. A *presbytera* is the wife of a presbyter, 388, 931. She was also called a *conversa*, 388. So too elderly widows, ibid. and 932. What garments they wore is not clear, 931. *Presbyterium* sometimes signifies a clerical office, 593. Often it means a body of clerics, and sometimes the dignity of the presbyter, ibid. To convene the *presbyterium* means to convene a synod, ibid. Sometimes *presbyterium* signifies a share in the governance, honor, office, and care of the Church, 593. By *presbyterium* Gregory understands the customary stipend of the clergy, 593, 760. It also signifies the gift, or money, that a newly created pontiff distributed to each member of the clergy and senate, 593. It also signifies that distribution of money made on certain solemn occasions throughout the year, ibid. The dignity granted to *defensores* in the *presbyterium*, 593.

Pretiosus, superior of the monastery of which St. Gregory was abbot, 465. At Gregory’s command he celebrates a thirty-day series of Masses for the soul of the monk Justus, 468. Pretiosus, servant of God, 594.

The primate, or metropolitan, in Africa was, according to ancient custom, the senior bishop of the province, 559. Hence both the bishop and the place were often less suitable for the dignity, ibid. Gregory attempts to abolish this custom, ibid. Later he permits it to be retained, 561. One who had been a Donatist could not attain the primacy, ibid. What duties the primate has concerning those to be ordained, 660. Without letters from the primate, bishops could neither travel to the imperial court nor hold assemblies, 975. According to the canons, the primate is to be judged by the Roman pontiff, 976. Or by a provincial council, 1203. See *Metropolitan*.

Primaerius, bishop of Nuceria, 947. Primaerius, bishop of Nursia, 1288. The *primicerius* was the first of any order, recorded on a waxed tablet or entered in a catalogue, 639, 640. Primogenitus, notary, 1188. He leaves the Roman Church as his heir, ibid.

*Primus.* He is foolish who considers himself first in such a way that he disdains to learn the good things he sees, 941.

*Princeps.* In former times cardinals were called princes, 501. For what purpose heavenly power was given to princes over all human beings, 676. “Principal command” and “the command of the prince,” 540, 1266. [Col. 1565] *Principia* is used for the prince’s tabernacle, 1048.

Priscilla, a false prophetess, 1168. Priscus, patrician of the East, that is, commander of the Eastern army, 661, 663. He performed notable deeds in the Persian war, 663. He was not Phocas’s son-in-law; rather, Phocas was Priscus’s *strator*, ibid.

*Privilege.* The Roman pontiffs profess that they preserve the privileges of all churches inviolate, 561, 611. Which privileges are equitable and which are unjust, 611. What sort of privilege is suspect, 666. St. Gregory grants privileges to the monasteries of Autun, 1219, 1221, 1223, 1225. He orders this grant to be entered in the public acts, 1220. Whether those privileges are spurious, 1221, 1223. Penalties for those who act contrary to the privileges, 1223, 1225. Why St. Gregory threatens such severe penalties, 1222. Examples of very serious threats against violators of privileges, ibid. and 1225. The privilege granted to the monastery of St. Medard, 1284 ff. Another privilege granted to all monasteries, 1294 ff.

*Probabilis*, that is, approved, good, praiseworthy, 633. *Probatio.* Who become bronze, tin, iron, and lead in the process of testing, 52. Proof is more certain in those regions where the matter was conducted, 1264. Probinus, presbyter of Seville, 777, 1209. Probus, bishop of Rieti, was honored at the point of death by a visitation from the holy martyrs Juvenal and Eleutherius, 389. His name is read in the Martyrology, ibid. Probus, the abbot from whom Gregory learned many of the things he relates in his *Dialogues*, 389, 400, 401, 440. The same Probus, 958, 1237. Why he was granted the power to make a will, 539, 1297 ff.

What *procedere* means among the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers, 193, 421, 669, 882, 1262. A procession is a gathering of the people, an assembly of peoples, 577. In Gregory it sometimes signifies advancement and promotion, 505. Solemn processions of clergy and people are often called litanies by authors, 736.

Prochisus, 596. Gregory commends the affairs of the island of Prochita to Maurentius, 986. Proculus, bishop of Nicotera, 962, 1234. Proculus, bishop of the city of Praeneste, 1291. Proculus, deacon of the Church of Ascoli, 1229.

Who is called prodigal and said to have come to his senses, 217.

*Proficere.* Not to advance on the way of virtue is to fall short, 94. To advance means to be promoted to a higher rank, 1260, 1261.

*Profligari*, that is, to be arranged, 562. Or to be propagated, 995. Pronulphus, count, 324.

The prophet sent against Samaria is killed by a lion because of his disobedience, 408. His disobedience is purged by his death, ibid. The lion killed the sinner’s life but guarded the righteous man’s corpse, ibid. Why prophets are sometimes called teachers in sacred Scripture, 17, 510. The gift of prophecy is asserted to belong to the Church, 115. Why the spirit of prophecy does not always illuminate the minds of the prophets, 248, 249. In this age the one who prophesies something about God is in darkness, 617. Those possessing the spirit of prophecy, 233, 236, 237, 240, 245, 297, 304, 305, 337, 420, 425, 428.

One who is received as another’s dependent or client is called that other’s *proprius*, [Col. 1566] 1123, 1124. The vice of private property and the penalty with which it is punished in a monk, 465. See *Peculiarity*. What *proprietas* and *momentum* are, 959, 960.

Prosper, representative of Dominicus, bishop of Carthage, 731. The losses of prosperity are compared with the fruits of adversity, 5. Who are to be admonished when they enjoy prosperity, 77. They must beware lest they love their sojourn as their homeland, ibid. Those who have given themselves wholly to prosperity are rebuked, ibid. Prosperous things should be used, not enjoyed, ibid. Prosperity is signified by God’s left hand, 77. Prosperous circumstances should urge us toward a better life, ibid. They strengthen hope of a better good, 78. Those who abuse them are more justly condemned, ibid. By the very things through which they advance outwardly, they fall inwardly, ibid. Temporal prosperity is exposed to many dangers, ibid. We ought neither to be lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity, 662. What punishment it is either to be wearied by desire for prosperity or to tremble from fear of adversity, 875. What prosperity teaches us, 662. However great prosperity may be, it has its end and limit in death, 998.

Protasius, formerly *vicedominus* of the Church of Arles, became the tenth bishop of Aix, 832. His love for the Roman Church is praised, ibid.

Who are to be admonished among the insolent, 41. Shame is useful for the insolent, ibid. What are the ways of the insolent, ibid.

Advancements are promotions of clerics, 588. Others understand by advancements the stipends of clerics, ibid.

Providentius, bishop of Istria, 778. How many cities an ecclesiastical province ought to have, 1163, 1164.

One must devote oneself to securing the salvation of one’s neighbor, 7. Whoever sees his neighbor’s evil and neglects it becomes the author of his death, 54. Let us relieve our neighbor’s distresses with at least some supports, if not with all, 541. Whoever assists his neighbor’s needs finds the merciful Lord in his own needs, 549, 545.

Why Christ wished his servants to be prudent and simple, 766. Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, cites several testimonies from Gregory’s *Dialogues* in his book on predestination, 107.

*Psalms.* In certain places formerly no one was advanced to the episcopate or to any other rank unless he knew the Psalter by heart, 777. The ancient custom of singing the psalms by heart long remained in force in the Church, and still remains so in certain churches, ibid. Gregory recommends that commentaries on the Psalms be read at the vigils, 1196. The psalms are to be sung in the Church by subdeacons and the minor orders, 1289. Zeal for psalmody is praised in a bishop, 1188.

What a *psiathium* is, 233. Πτώκεια, a house intended for feeding the poor, 1107.

Publicans, or public men: whence they received their name, 1097, 1098. Pudentiana, an episcopal city of Numidia, 611. Maximianus, bishop of this city, was to be deposed at the provincial synod of Numidia on account of simony, 612.

A certain boy driven headlong from a mountain is miraculously saved, 316. In the case of the three Hebrew boys, the flame exercised its power for consolation but not for torment, 324. Mutual charity and gentleness toward subjects are to be instilled in royal children, [Col. 1567] 871. The words of those who nurture them will be milk if they are good, but poison if they are bad, ibid.

A fist pertains to anger, 62. Pulcheria Augusta is praised, 1245. Beauty delivered into the hands of an enemy, 101. When the mind is lifted up by confidence in its own beauty, 100. What it means to place confidence in one’s beauty, 1030.

What it means to sew little cushions beneath every elbow of the hands, 27. What a pupil suffering from a white film signifies, 12.

What it means to purge oneself with a third, fifth, or seventh hand, 864. What canonical purgation is and how many kinds there are, 597, 864. The holy Eucharist formerly used for purgation, 598. Examples of canonical purgation, 597, 991, 1219. Formerly a presbyter had to purge himself by taking an oath while touching the Gospels, 864. See *Oath*.

Purgatory is affirmed by testimonies and arguments, 115, 441. The deacon Paschasius was freed from the punishments of purgatory by Germanus, bishop of Capua, 445. The holy sacrifice offered for the dead frees them from the punishments of purgatory, 464, 468. For which souls suffering in purgatory that sacrifice is beneficial, 472. It is safer to do good while we are alive, which we hope others will do for us after death, ibid. It is more blessed to leave this life free than to seek freedom after imprisonment, ibid. Only the smallest sins are expiated by purgatorial fire, 444, 445. The purification of those minor sins is obtained only through good works, 444.

What the purple mixed with gold and hyacinth in the priest’s clothing signifies, 16, 509.

Who among the fainthearted are to be admonished, 41. What disposition the fainthearted possess, ibid. Sometimes they are to be encouraged by praise, 42.

Puteoli, formerly a well-cultivated city of Campania, 1085.

Q

Quadra is a piece of bread, 201. How Lent is to be observed, 1303. From Quinquagesima clerics should undertake the resolve to fast, 1302. Gregory disapproves of laymen gorging themselves on meat on Sunday, 1302, 1303. Quadragesimus, a subdeacon of the Church of Buxentum, was tending the flock, 320. *Quanti* used for *quot*, 1169. Quertinus, former prefect, 1297. Rest is to be desired, but is sometimes to be postponed for the benefit of many, 848. Monastic and pastoral repose are not compatible with care for the laity, 727. Quintianus, bishop, 693. Quiricus, bishop of Toledo, 106. He is called a bishop of Iberia, 1166, 1167. Quodvultdeus, an African bishop, 609. Formerly *quotiens* was said, not *quoties*, 564. Hence the change, ibid.

R

What *Racana* or *Rachana* are, 1092, 1179, 1180. Rachel signifies the contemplative life, 491. Why priests were forbidden to shave the head, 27, 514. Ravagers are those who, not called by God but inflamed by their own desire, approach the summit of government, 3. What admonitions should be given to ravagers of others’ property, 65. Those who do not distribute their own possessions are worthy of eternal punishment; how much more those who seize what belongs to others, ibid. The scriptural testimonies by which these men should be pressed, ibid. [Col. 1567] By what admonition those who give away their own and seize what belongs to others should be restrained, 67. The opportunity for seizure is removed if the rightful ownership of property is properly arranged beforehand, ibid. How the greed of ravagers is to be corrected, 66. The ravager of another man’s wife must be strictly punished, 693. He who abducts a virgin, and those who favor him, are excommunicated, 1293. Reason, however evident, is usually an obstacle to an unwilling mind, 723.

The breastpiece of Aaron: what it signifies, 13, 14, 508, 840. What the names of the twelve Patriarchs inscribed upon it signify, 14, 508. Why it is called the breastpiece of judgment, 14.

Ravenna was the seat of the exarchs of Italy, 521. The arrogance of the bishop of Ravenna concerning the use of the pallium is censured, 666. A privilege granted by Pope John to the Church of Ravenna concerning the use of the pallium, 669. Formerly the bishops of Ravenna did not use the pallium outside the church except during translations of relics, 739. Gregory orders an inquiry into how many solemn litanies there had formerly been at which the bishop of Ravenna wore the pallium, 819. Gregory wishes the faithful and reputable men to swear what had formerly been observed by the bishops of Ravenna in using the pallium, and that it should thereafter be observed, 837, 838. The form of that oath, 838. The use of *mappulae* is granted only to the first deacons of the Church of Ravenna, 668. But the bishop of Ravenna contends that all the priests and deacons of his Church used them on those solemn occasions, 669, 670. Gregory desires to honor the Church of Ravenna, 739. He confirms the privileges of that same Church, 787. The visitation of the Church of Ravenna is entrusted to Severus, bishop of Ficulinum, 754, 755. It is to be examined and concluded there, 810. In the election of the bishop of Ravenna, Gregory orders that five of the senior priests and five of those next in rank, together with certain clerics, be sent to him, 753. A case between the bishop of Ravenna and an abbot is lawfully summoned to Rome, ibid. It is to be examined and concluded, 810. The patrimony of the Church of Ravenna in Sicily, 1097. Bishops of Ravenna: John. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Marinianus, 1230. See his entry and the same index.  

Reate, a city of Umbria in Italy, 943. Bishops of Reate: Albinus, 168. Probus, 389.

Recharedus followed not the example of his father but that of his brother, the martyr Hermenegild; having renounced the Arian perfidy, he converted to the faith, 348. He led the Visigoths to the same faith and allowed none of his subjects to remain an enemy of God, ibid., 1028. The conversion of Recharedus was the fruit of Hermenegild’s martyrdom, 348. Gregory rejoices with him over his conversion, 532. Recharedus sends abbots to Gregory, 978. And a golden chalice, ibid., 1029. The excellence of Gregory’s letters to Recharedus, 1028. Recharedus rejected money offered him by the Jews to repeal the law, 1029. How he ought to flee the snares of the ancient enemy, 1030 and following. Gregory sends him relics, 1031. Why Recharedus did not obtain the documents of agreements that he had requested from the imperial archive, 1031.

Among legal experts, *rector* denotes one who governs a province under whatever title, 595. The ruler of souls should be pure in thought, 13, 508. He should pursue the interests of others, not his own, 14. He should suffer no human weakness, 14. He should govern his subjects not without fear, [Col. 1568] ibid., 15. He should be outstanding in action, 15, 508. He should beware of loquacity, 18. He should be near to each person through compassion, ibid. Through humility he should be a companion to those who act well, 20, 513. Through zeal he should rise against the vices of offenders, 20, 31, 513. A ruler, when he hears of the temptations of others, is not defiled even though he is struck by them, 20, 513. Toward his subjects the ruler should display both the tenderness of a mother and the discipline of a father, 23, 513. When a ruler is surrounded outside by immense favor, he is emptied of truth within, 21. He should not seek to be loved by his subjects more than truth is loved, 27, 28. He who seeks to please Christ’s bride rather than Christ is guilty of adultery, 27. Self-love in a ruler is destructive, ibid. Carnal rulers flatter the powerful and are harsh toward weak sheep, 28. How good rulers ought to please people, 28. A ruler should distinguish virtues and vices with vigilant care, 29. He should meditate daily on the precepts of sacred eloquence, 33. What it means for a ruler to doze or sleep, 38. Why God, although he perfects the minds of rulers to a great extent, nevertheless leaves them imperfect to a great extent, 102. The merits of rulers and of their peoples are linked together, 855. A Church should not remain long without its own ruler, 861. The rulers of the patrimony of the Roman Church should not, on their own initiative, stamp titles in the fiscal manner, 1289. See *Patrimony*.

Redempta, a nun distinguished for holiness, 396. What it means to pay the price of redemption, 696. The sanction of the sacred canons and secular laws has decreed concerning the redemption of captives, 696. See *Captive*. Redemptus, bishop of Ferentinum, 368. Redemptus, a defender, 926, 927. Redemptus, a Jew converted to the faith, 714. Redemptus, 595.

*Redhibere* means to return what one owes, 537. It is sometimes used absolutely for “to return,” 565, 1004. How the revenues of the Church are to be collected, 1209. One quarter of them is to be distributed to the clergy, 1249. See *Church property*.

The government of souls is the art of arts, 3. The ambitious do not attain the summit of government but seize it, 3. No one should undertake the leadership of perdition through desire for the summit, 4. Occupation with government often dissipates stability, 5. The danger of those who are called by God to govern souls but refuse to come, 6, 848. Let one strong in virtues be compelled to assume government; let one lacking virtues not approach it even under compulsion, 10. What sort of person each one should be when coming to government, 10. Let him approach government free from vices, 11. Discipline and mercy must not be separated from each other in government, 23. What the virtues of pastoral government are, 24. A position of government should be denied to those who desire it and offered to those who flee it, 848. God punishes many people by elevating one person to rule, 1239. Since no human being can stand equally by himself, one person is governed by another, 20.

Regino, abbot of Prüm: in what year he died, 107. In his books on ecclesiastical disciplines he relates a history taken from Gregory’s *Dialogues*, ibid.

The *regionarii*: notaries and subdeacons were honored with the dignity of *regionarius* before Gregory, 905. Ten defenders were granted the same honor under Gregory, 905, 937. There were seven *regionarii* deacons in Rome, 937. They were subject to the archdeacon, ibid. [Col. 1569]

What the *Registrum* or *Regestum* is, 484. An ancient word, 485. Some derive *regestum* from the verb *regero*, that is, “I enter into the records,” ibid. *Regestum* is also sometimes used for a private chamber, ibid.

May the earthly kingdom serve the heavenly one, 676. A kingdom is then well governed when the glory of ruling does not dominate the mind, 1030. See *King*. God transfers kingdoms, 1238.

*Rego.* When the highest position is governed well, 22, 513. Servants are governed more rightly in proportion as they serve the ruler of all more truly, 1245.

The Rule of Saint Benedict is praised by Saint Gregory under the title *Rule of the Monks*, 1137.

*Pastoral Rule.* The antiquity and usefulness of the books of the *Pastoral Rule*, Preface, p. 1. When it was conceived, ibid. and p. 2. When it was published and on what occasion, ibid. and p. 2. It was highly esteemed by Greeks and Latins, ibid. Especially by the Gauls, ibid. It was commended by many councils celebrated in Gaul, ibid. Which councils, ibid. It was translated into Greek at the command of the emperor Maurice, ibid. And into the Saxon language by Alfred himself, king of the West Saxons, ibid. From what time the Greek translation was lost, ibid. It was published many times previously in French, and recently appeared again in the same language, ibid. Saints Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom wrote on the same subject and on a similar occasion, ibid.

Maximus, bishop of Riez, 1101.

*Relaxare*, that is, “to release,” 490. The practice of remissions was formerly not frequent; now, with remissions flowing abundantly, sin overflows, 657.

*Relicta*, that is, “widow,” 1363.

The Christian religion. Outsiders should be brought to the Christian religion by gentleness, not harshness, 1226.

*Religious.* This word was attributed not only to monks but also to clerics and other faithful, 551, 701, 707, 782, 822. *Religiosus*, that is, “a pious man,” 1140. Taxes must also be paid by religious persons, 1059.

Relics. Why the holy martyrs display more miracles through their relics than through their bodies, 276. By the patronage of the saints, their relics are understood, ibid. Rain is obtained when Saint Eutychius’s tunic is reverently lifted and carried through the fields, 313. The veneration of relics is extremely ancient, 547. Formerly scarcely any altar was consecrated without relics, 577, 695. The relics of saints were customarily placed in baptisteries, 809. Altars were formerly erected over the tombs and relics of martyrs and confessors, 828. At the beginning of the sixth century, wherever relics were present, divine offices were celebrated there, 697. Relics must not be placed where other bodies lie buried, 547, 548, 571, 572, 577, 897, 943, 986, 994. With what disposition relics should be received, 826, 829, 1088. Reverence for the relics of Saints Peter, Paul, and Lawrence is confirmed by terrifying signs, 708, 709. To touch the bodies of the saints is sacrilege, and the rashness of those who touch them does not remain unpunished, 710. Under Gregory’s pontificate the Latins scarcely dared to touch the bodies of the saints, 829. Instead, they sent *brandea*, 709, 711, 829, 838. Yet at that time not only *brandea* were sent, but also relics of the saints, 625, 638, 709, 828, 829, 943, 994, 1031. Pope Hadrian was terrified in a vision when he sent relics to Charlemagne, 708. Certain Greek monks dig up the bodies of the dead in Rome, as though they intended to carry them to Greece as relics of saints, 710. False relics were sometimes used in place of genuine ones, [Col. 1569] 709. In certain places relics were tested by applying fire, 709. Pieces from Saint Peter’s chains and Saint Lawrence’s gridiron were enclosed in a cross and to be worn around the neck, 648. Pieces chipped from Saint Paul’s chains with a file were sent in the manner of relics, 741. Relics are called shrines, 1115, 1188. See *Shrines*.

*Remunero.* God prepares the rewards of eternal recompense for temporal acts, 750.

Reparatus, a man of rank, 420. His vision concerning the punishment of a certain priest, ibid. and 421.

A person guilty of extortion must be punished in his property, not in his liberty, 1079.

*Reprehendere.* Good rulers rejoice when reproved by their subjects, 28. He who reproves is a friend, 617, 618. When we are reproved, we ought to appease our reprovers with humble reason, 1130.

The reprobate. The hedgehog has a burrow among the reprobate, 48. From the very things by which the reprobate outwardly advance, they fall inwardly, 78. Among the punishments, the flesh of the reprobate does not completely perish but continues to exist while continually perishing, 376. The reprobate receive power to rage against the saints for their own greater condemnation, 408. From the day of their departure the reprobate are tormented by the fire of hell, 416. The reprobate sometimes perform miracles, 1111.

What the creeping things between the wall signify, 30.

Our rest in heaven will be greater in proportion as, through love of the Creator, we now have no rest, 712.

*Res.* The Count of Private Estates, 499. The emperor is called “lord of things,” 501, 502. Imperial rescripts or commands are called “sacred writings,” “sacred imperial documents,” or simply “sacred documents,” 544.

Residence. A priest who is absent from his Church for two months is excluded, and another is substituted in his place, 692. But because he had been absent solely on account of illness, he is ordered to be restored, 694. Hence the frequent absence of priests from their Churches, 694. Unless priests were formerly continually present, the people complained that they had been abandoned, ibid. Whether pastors may fulfill their duties personally or through substitutes, ibid. See *The residence of bishops*.

Kindness must not be denied to one who repents, 1271.

Respecta, an abbess, 858. Respectus, a deacon of Salona, 640.

“To answer” or “to give a response” is the same as to pay what is owed, 1059. A *responsalis* is a messenger or courier who carries letters and brings back replies, 533, 611, 619, 731. A *responsalis* of the Church of Thessalonica, 1267.

The state. “To enter public life” is the same as to pursue the affairs of the state, 568.

How restitution of Church property stolen by theft is to be made, 1035, 1153. Restitution should be made promptly, 536. Restitution must also be made to schismatics, 972.

*Resultare*, that is, “to recoil, to resist,” 505, 576.

The resurrection. In Gregory’s time many doubted the resurrection of bodies, 114, 369. Gregory himself also doubted it, 114. The resurrection of bodies is a lesser miracle than the soul’s resurrection from sin, 321. By adhering to the spirit, the flesh is preserved forever; by adhering to the flesh, the spirit is preserved in God, [Col. 1570] 376. Several resurrections, 432.

*Reverendissimus*, formerly *reverentissimus*, as the customary form, 573. *Reverendissimus* is a title of honor with which Gregory sometimes addresses bishops, 846, 1063, 1095.

What it means to return to oneself, 217. In what ways we are led outside ourselves and return to ourselves, 217.

The accused. The ancient distinction between palace and Church in punishing the accused, 759.

The king. Kings should be admonished concerning matters pertaining to salvation, 678. They ought not to interfere in priestly cases, 699. Subjects ought to pray for kings and their families, 853, 855. The correction of wicked people belongs to kings, 939, 1018. Those whom they govern outwardly by counsel, they should not allow to perish inwardly, 1014. The highest good in kings is to preserve each person’s rights, 1023. They should maintain equity toward priests, 1024. In the government of a kingdom, virtue requires justice and power requires equity, ibid. Whether all things are just and honorable for kings, 1025. What those who adhere to earthly kings ought to do, ibid. The reins of government must be tempered toward subjects, 1030. Kings must flee anger, 1030. A kingdom is then well governed when the glory of ruling does not dominate the mind, ibid. The title “father” suits kings, 1080. Barbarian kings treat their subjects almost as slaves, ibid. The qualities of kings are zeal and gentleness, 1245. By “the kings of the nations” the kings of the barbarians are understood, 831, 1079, 1080. The kings of the nations are lords of servants, 1239.

Ρὴχ (“king”). What that name signifies among the Greeks of the Middle Ages, and to whom it was given, 278.

Rhegium, a city of the Bruttii in Italy, 626. Bishops of Rhegium: Lucius, 656. Boniface, 684. See his title.

Flavius, bishop of Rheims, 1288.

Rhisinium, a city of Dalmatia, 517, 518. Its episcopal see was transferred to Castelnuovo and is subject to the archbishop of Ragusa, 517. Sebastianus, bishop of Rhisinium, 518.

Riggo, Totila’s sword-bearer, who pretended to be Totila, 237.

Why *rimarii* are so called, 1036.

*Roga* signifies a gift, honorarium, or stipend, 608, 757, 1032. It also signifies the stipend of those serving in the Church, and alms, 608. *Rogalia* were days on which *rogae* were distributed, ibid. *Rogatores* are stipendiaries, ibid.

Rogatianus, a deacon in Numidia, 821.

The Roman pontiff is the ministerial head of the whole Church and the center of ecclesiastical unity, 773. The head of the faith, 1244. He was called “Ecumenical” at the Council of Chalcedon, 743, 749, 771. Because he is the successor of Saint Peter, he is by divine law placed over the four patriarchs, 618. He must preserve each bishop’s jurisdiction, 619. What his care toward bishops should be, 983. Formerly bishops came from Sicily to Rome to celebrate the birthday of the Roman pontiff; Saint Gregory forbids this, 526. His election was formerly confirmed by the emperor, 699. Immediately after his election the Roman pontiff sent the synodical statement of his faith to kings, 490. And to the other patriarchs, 844. He ordained the bishops of Italy, Sicily, and the neighboring provinces, or they were ordained with his permission, 587, 601, 722, 1053, 1087. In Gregory’s time many cities were subject to the dominion of the Roman Church, [Col. 1571] 592, 1003. When Churches were deprived of their own pastor, the Roman pontiff appointed visitors not only in provinces subject to him as metropolitan but sometimes also in others, 562. At the Lateran Council he was declared the ordinary of ordinaries, 578. “To come to Blessed Peter” is the same as to come to the Roman supreme pontiff, 619, 723. Boniface, a distinguished man of Africa, and several others are ordered to come to the threshold of blessed Peter to give an account of their faith, 723. The Roman pontiff possessed an ancient power to prohibit certain books, which even Easterners were obliged to obey, 843. He ought to judge cases concerning primacies according to the canons, 976. The authority of the Roman pontiff in granting privileges, 1019. He has the right to revoke the decisions of others, 1061.

*Corona*, a title of honor by which formerly the supreme pontiffs and other bishops were addressed, 622. *Celsitudo* was also a title of honor given to the supreme pontiff, 978. For the private services of the supreme pontiff, not laymen but clerics or monks should be admitted, 1289. The body of a deceased Roman pontiff was formerly covered with dalmatics, which the people tore apart out of reverence for his sanctity, 1290. Saint Gregory forbids this, ibid.

Romanus, bishop of the city of Blera, 1291.

Romanus, a monk, met the holy boy Benedict as he was fleeing the world, 209. He clothed him in the monastic habit, ibid. And in the cave where he was hiding he fed him for three years, ibid., 212.

Romanus, a deacon of the Roman Church, 816. Romanus, a defender, 592, 593. He was appointed defender of the patrimony of the Roman Church in Sicily, 944. The various things he did at Gregory’s command: see the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Romanus, a patrician and the third exarch of Italy, was substituted for Smaragdus by the emperor Maurice, 521, 643, 646. In what year he died, 521. Gregory complains about this Romanus, 607, 608, 770. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Romanus, a man of distinguished memory, built a monastery in his house at Naples, 1043.

Romanus, a distinguished man, 555. Romanus, 1242.

Various calamities were foretold for Rome by Saint Benedict, 240. Rome is preserved among the swords of the apostles Peter and Paul, 911. Rome is worn down by various afflictions, 1032, 1033.

The Roman Church is called, by antonomasia, the Apostolic See, 517. It is sometimes understood under the name of Saint Peter, 831, 832. The primacy of the Roman Church, 668, 669. Peter exalted the see in which he deigned to rest and bring his present life to an end, 888. The Roman Church receives what has been defined by the four holy synods and rejects what they condemned, 1270.

The Roman synod, 1287. In it bishops and priests sit, while deacons and the clergy stand, 1288.

Romula, a nun. Her virtues, 396. Her wondrous death, ibid., 397.

Romulus made the one hundred men elected from among the elders, called senators, into a kind of public council, 493.

Rosellae or Rusellae, a city of ancient Etruria, long ago destroyed, 500. Bishops of Rosella: Balbinus, 500. Baldinius, 1291.

How the wheel signifies the sinner’s happiness, 492.

The rust of vices, not cleansed by the fire of tribulation, is a sign of a hardened mind, 53. [Col. 1571]

Ruderic, one of the three who were accustomed always to adhere to Totila, 237.

Who the unlearned in sacred doctrine are who should be admonished, 72.

Ruferius, a count, 847. Rufinus, bishop of Ephesus, 823. Rufinus, bishop of Viviers, 857.

Rupes is compelled to yield his place, 177.

Rustica, of patrician memory, founded a monastery of servants of God, 673. Her intention concerning the construction of this monastery was long neglected, 946.

Rusticiana, a patrician, 589, 1119. Who ought to endure calumny, ibid. She is criticized for returning too hastily from Mount Sinai, 724. Her charity in redeeming captives, 911. When she calls herself Saint Gregory’s servant, he does not allow it, 1123. She offers gifts to Saint Peter, ibid. Saint Gregory asserts that he is her own, as though a vassal, ibid., 1124. She gives alms to the Roman monastery of Saint Andrew, 1124.

Rusticianus, 539. In what year Rusticula’s funeral was conducted, 541.

Rusticus, a deacon, was rejected from the bishopric of Ancona because of his ignorance of the Psalms, 777, 1269. Rusticus, a man of illustrious rank, 1057. Rusticus: see *Colonus*.

Peasant farmers of the patrimony of the Roman Church in Sicily, 533. Gregory forbids a *burdatio* paid by peasants to a certain Theodosius—whose property was insufficient to pay the Church—from being demanded again from the peasants themselves, 536. Why Gregory orders loans of solidi to be given to the peasants of Sicily, 734, 735. The care of peasants has been entrusted by God to the nobility, 703. Pagan peasants who refuse conversion are to be burdened with a rent, 704. Forty peasants were slaughtered by the Lombards because they refused to eat forbidden foods, 337. A peasant bound and grievously tormented by a Goth is freed through Saint Benedict, 264. A peasant is freed from a demon, 328.

S
Sabanum is a linen cloth used for receiving and drying those baptized from the sacred font, 320, 463, 464, 730. Sabbatius, Armenian patrician under Justinian Rhinotmetus, 493.

**Sabbath.** The Sabbath day is not to be observed according to the letter, 1213, 1214. See Antichrist. How a Christian observes the Sabbath and how he violates it, 1214. When observance of the Christians’ Sabbath, or Sunday, was prescribed by the Church or by the emperors, 1214. What things were forbidden on that day, 1215. What it means to flee on the Sabbath, and why this is forbidden, 23. On Holy Saturday even small children fasted in Gregory’s time, 352.

Sabina, a province of Italy, 459, 460. The boundaries of the Sabine peoples, 460. The Sabine region formerly extended farther than present-day Sabina, 638. The Sabine bishop Julian, 169, 193, 417.

Sabinianus, bishop of Callipolis, 1003. Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera, 863, 1034. He communicates with Maximus of Salona, 863. Later separating from him, he is summoned to Rome to receive absolution, 863, 864. Retiring to a monastery for the sake of penance, he is admitted to communion, 902. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Sabinianus, bishop of Tudertum, 1288. Sabinianus, deacon and apocrisiarius of St. Gregory before the emperor, whom he succeeded in the pontificate, 725, 740, 742, 746, 837. Gregory commends him to the patrician Priscus [Col. 1572], 662; to John of Constantinople, 664; and to the physician Theotimus, 665.

Sabinianus, a most illustrious man and defender of the Church of Lilybaeum during the thirteenth and first indictions, 1059.

Sabinus or Savinus, bishop of Canusium, 240. St. Benedict foretells to him Rome’s future ruin, ibid. Sabinus, endowed with the spirit of prophecy, 285. He safely drinks wine infected with poison after making the sign of the cross, 288. His archdeacon, the author of the crime, dies at the very moment when the holy bishop drinks the poisoned cup, ibid.

Sabinus, bishop of Piacenza, of extraordinary virtue, 296. Having written a letter, he restrains the overflowing Po, ibid. and following pages.

Sabinus, defender of Sardinia, 649.

Sabinus or Savinus, regional subdeacon, 1043, 1192, 1193, 1194. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

**Saccus.** What it means to put money into a pierced bag, 68. St. Gregory does not wish the Church’s purse to be defiled by dishonest profits, 536. *Sacculus*, *saccellus*, *sacellarius*, *saccellarius*, *saccularius*, *sacco*, and *saccarius* are used throughout for purses, the treasury, the storehouse, and so forth, 535. The words *sacella* and *sacellarius* are derived from *saccus*, 535, 620. *Sacellarius* and *saccellarius* mean the same thing, 535. If *sacellarius* is derived from *sacrum*, it has another meaning, 535, 620. Some *sacellarii* were called greater, others lesser, 535. To offer customary payments to the *sacellum*, that is, to make the customary payment to the public treasury, 619, 620. *Saccellarius* is the Quaestor placed in charge of the treasury, 751, 752.

Priests are those who preside over the faithful, 27. By “priests,” bishops are almost always meant, 613, 614, 635. Nevertheless, Gregory sometimes calls an ordinary presbyter a priest, 204. Some priests belonged to the first order, others to the second order, that is, to the greater or lesser order, 563. Who the cardinal priests were, 501, 563. What it means for a priest to wear upon his breast the judgment of the children of Israel before the Lord, 14. Why the Law assigns the shoulder and breast-piece of the sacrifice to the priest, 15. The priest is covered on both shoulders by the shoulder-piece, ibid. A priest entering or leaving the sanctuary dies if no sound is heard from him, 17. Why priests are forbidden to shave their heads and are commanded to grow their hair, 27, 514, 850. The priestly heart must not be possessed by wandering thoughts, 14, 508. Why the priestly heart is the ark of the covenant, 919. Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, 17, 511. A priest ignorant of preaching is a mute herald, ibid. If he is silent, he deserves God’s anger, 17, 511. The priest’s works must proclaim along with the sound of his tongue, 511.

Priests are the stones of the sanctuary, 25. For what purpose, 25. Those who are scattered at the head of the streets, ibid., 26. The priest’s garments are good works, 17, 511. With what salt his sermons should be seasoned, 511. He must teach by word and example, 17, 508. He must possess together both moral innocence and knowledge for teaching and preserving the faith, 621. Humility alone is the elevation of priestly office, 665. Pride is not to be tolerated in priests, 668. It is a grave insult to a priest who serves the truth to be considered deceitful, 766. Priests are to be honored by kings, ibid. Even pagan princes honored the priests of idols, 767. In Scripture priests are called angels and gods, 766. The virtues and miracles of holy priests summon people to faith, 886. A priest ought to shine in conduct and life, 921. It befits a good priest to do nothing that would rightly incur reproach, 930.

—Bad priests are the cause of the people’s ruin, 4, 1171. How great the punishment with which they are tormented, 4. What sort of priest the people is, 25. Bad priests are not the stones of the sanctuary in the pontiff’s ornament, 26. Some serve the neck of pride, though they were appointed to provide leadership in humility, 744. A priest who commits the same sins as his subjects will suffer not the same but much heavier penalties, 1045. Priests living with strange women: a very grave and improper matter, 1242. How such inhabitants are to be corrected, 1243.

**Priesthood.** Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, 17, 511. What those who confer priesthoods and their patrons must consider, 659.

**Sacrament.** The effect of the sacraments does not depend on ministers, whether good or bad, 254. “Sacrament,” or oath: see Oath.

Our sacrifice is made acceptable to God by charity alone, 44. The sacrifice of the New Law is offered for the living and the dead, 115, 464, 465, 468, 472. Prisoners’ chains were loosed in prison through a sacrifice offered for them, 469. A sailor is divinely rescued from shipwreck through the power of a sacrifice offered for him, ibid. A sacrifice offered for the dead on the seventh, thirtieth, and fortieth day, 464. Which dead persons benefit from that sacrifice, 472. How great its power is, ibid. Those who offer this sacrifice must imitate what they perform, ibid. What should be done if the celebrant of the sacrifice frequently suffers illness, 1261.

The error of the Sadducees concerning the resurrection of the dead, 71. Why Paul sought to divide the Sadducees and Pharisees, 71, 72.

How harmful the company of secular persons is to the servants of God, 313.

**World.** In this world we do not see one another’s thoughts, but in the future we shall see them, 445.

**Sagona.** See Saona.

Salt signifies the wisdom of the word, 17, 511, 880. Salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but an indication of condemnation, 68.

The Via Salaria, 1125.

Salerius, notary of the Roman Church, 973, 1137. He is called a *chartularius*, 1242.

Who the *salgamarii* were, 651. The Council of Chalcedon complains that *salgamarii* had been ordained bishops, ibid.

**Salgamum.** By the name *salgami* are understood all things preserved with salt or with other substances having the power of salt and kept in vessels for food, 651. The *salgamaria* chamber is also meant, ibid.

Solomon, using prosperity badly, falls into idolatry, 78. Wisdom abandoned him whom no discipline of tribulation had guarded, 78.

Salona, the metropolis of Dalmatia, 504. Spalatum grew from its ruins, ibid. The people of Salona are reproached because scarcely two of them abstained from communion with Maximus the intruder, 813. Why the bishops of Dalmatia are forbidden to ordain the bishop of Salona without Gregory’s consent, 690.

The bishops of Salona: Natalis—see his title; Maximus, 698—see his title.

Salpingus the Jew, 537.

**Salvation.** One must devote oneself to procuring one’s own salvation and that of one’s neighbors, 7. We must use bodily health for doing good works, 49. What losses befall the person who does not devote bodily health to the practice of virtue, ibid. Weakness of the body is the salvation of the mind, 50.

[Col. 1573] Salustius, a most illustrious man, 1209.

A *salutatorium* is the place where the bishop received the greetings of the faithful before Mass, 504, 787. There were lodgings in the *salutatoria*, 504.

No one can be saved who does not possess a life of faith, 861.

Who the Samaraeans were: whether Samaritans or rather Jews, 819, 910.

Pastors should follow the example of the Samaritans who treated wounds with wine and oil, 23, 514.

Gregory promises that he will expound allegorically certain acts of Samson, 1208.

**Sanctimonialis.** See Nun.

**Holiness.** Formerly a title of honor commonly given to bishops, presbyters, and deacons, 531. Gregory applies it to bishops, 532, 608, 680, 831, 976, 1055, 1075. Sometimes also to abbots adorned with the priesthood, but never to monks or to abbots who were not presbyters, 967, 968. It is now reserved for the supreme pontiff, 531.

**Sanctuaries.** The relics of holy martyrs are called sanctuaries, 547, 548, 572, 577, 808, 826, 943, 994, 1115, 1188. A veil or *brandeum* is also called a sanctuary, 838.

Sanctulus, a presbyter venerable in life and faith, 308, 360. He was cheerful in face and spirit, 360. His miracles, ibid. and 361. His extraordinary charity, 361, 364, 365. He refused to accept gifts made from Lombard booty, 365. Although a presbyter, he scarcely knew the elements of letters, ibid. How learned his ignorance was, ibid.

**Saint.** The royal power of the saints, 16. The prudent discernment of the saints is expressed by the nose of the Church, 90. Why small vices are mingled with the great virtues of the saints, 308. Cheerfulness is praised in the saints, 360. Even the smallest faults of the saints are sometimes punished by death, 405, 408. Sometimes the wicked receive power to rage against the lives of the saints, for their own greater condemnation, 408. The saints are neither exalted by prosperity nor broken by adversity, 662. The benefit they derive from both, ibid. How useful it is to transmit the lives of the saints in writing, 121. How useful the examples of the saints are, 152, 153. How dangerous it is to despise the admonitions of the saints, 197, 200. How the saints share in God’s counsels, 241. The counsels God has proclaimed in Scripture can be known by God’s saints; hidden counsels cannot, 241, 244. Whether the saints obtain everything they ask, 265. Even the holiest men should not live with women, however holy, 289. Many saints led a continent life with their wives and were taken into the governance of the Church, 1130. Why good people are taken away, or why they are so few, 365. The saints sometimes perform wonders by authority, 264.

—The souls of perfect saints, when they leave their bodies, are immediately received into heaven; but the souls of the imperfect are delayed, 408. What single or paired stoles of the saints signify, 409. In heaven the saints know the good who remain with them in the kingdom, 424; and also the wicked in hell, ibid. This vision is granted to the blessed as an addition to their joys, ibid. The saints in heaven know nothing that the One who knows all does not know, 425.
