The hearts of the saints in heaven are mutually open to the saints, 445. They give thanks to God not only for the eternal joy they enjoy but also for the eternal punishment of the wicked from which they have escaped, 449. Why the saints do not pray for the reprobate suffering in hell, 452. Saints whose memory is uncertain are not to be honored, 710.

[Col. 1574] Blood signifies guilt, 1027. How blood is said to touch blood, ibid. Fasting is harmful to those suffering from vomiting blood, 1117, 1121; and also irritation, 1121.

Who the healthy are who must be admonished, 49.

**Santon(es),** or Mediolanum Santonum, an episcopal city of Gaul, 828. Palladius, bishop of Santones, ibid.

**Saona** or **Sagona**, in the Middle Ages a city of Corsica, now destroyed, 562. Gregory entrusts the visitation of the Church of Saona to Bishop Leo, ibid. He appoints Martin bishop, 563, 564.

Who the wise are who must be admonished, 40. Let them learn the foolishness of God, ibid. The heart of the wise is steady in itself; the heart of fools is otherwise, 60. How the wise person remains like the sun, 854. It belongs to a wise man both to weigh at greater length what he has heard briefly and to correct quickly what displeases God, 1081. Wisdom abandons those whom it called while they long refused, 49. The wisdom of God is foolishness, and the wisdom of the world is foolishness, 40. What the wisdom from above is like—chaste and peaceable, 69.

The soap-makers of the city of Naples were already forming a guild in Gregory’s time, 1058.

Sardica, formerly the metropolis of New Dacia and now the capital of Bulgaria, 735, 736. Felix, bishop of Sardica, 735.

Sardinia, a large Italian island under Spanish rule, 542, 543. Sardinia was the seventh and last diocese of the African province, 543, 848. Sardinia was subject to the prefect of the African prefecture, 550. When the Vandals occupied Africa, Sardinia, Corsica, and the other islands obeyed them, 847, 848. After their defeat, Sardinia was attached to Africa, 848. The nobles of Sardinia are rebuked because they do not turn their peasants away from the worship of idols, 702, 703. Gregory sends a bishop to Sardinia to convert the idolaters, 768. The Sardinians paid money to the judge for permission to sacrifice to idols, and after receiving baptism they were compelled to make the same payment, 768. Gregory orders precautions against a renewed incursion into Sardinia, 928, and certain places to be fortified, 930. At last the inhabitants of Sardinia were converted to the faith of Christ, 1166.

The bishops of Sardinia: Agatho, 932; Vincentius, ibid.

The Church of Sardis. Why the angel commands this Church to strengthen the good things it had done, 94.

A frying pan signifies the frying of the mind, 32. What it means to place an iron frying pan as a wall between the prophet and the city, ibid.

Sarzana, a city under Genoese rule, succeeded Luna in episcopal dignity, 700.

He satisfies God and human beings who brings deviations back to rectitude and presumption back to the rule of humility, 929.

Among jurists, *satisfactio* means the provision of a pledge or surety, 821.

Saturninus, a presbyter forbidden to enter the ministry of sacred orders and entrusted with the care of certain monasteries, 729, 730. Because he presumed to minister after deposition, he was deprived of communion until death, 733.

Saturninus, 539.

Saul fled in humility from the summit of government, but, placed in government, swelled with pride, 5. Because Saul did not wish to be publicly reproved, God tore his kingdom apart, 5. Saul was promoted through humility and rejected through pride, 21. David calmed with the harp the madness of Saul, who was driven by an evil spirit, 36. Saul signifies the exaltation of the powerful, [Col. 1575] ibid., and bad shepherds, 39. What Saul’s emptying his bowels signifies, ibid.

**Saulus.** See Paul.

**Sava.** What heresy it had, 802.

Savinella is encouraged to good works, 1185.

The monastery of St. Sabinus, 1229.

Savinus, abbot of St. Stephen on the island of Capri, 547.

Savinus, subdeacon: see Sabinus.

Savona, an episcopal city of Liguria, 1297.

Transmarine Saxony, or England, 1150.

A huge rock, while falling, is miraculously fixed in place, 156.

What scabies signifies, 12.

Giving the weak occasion for scandal must be avoided altogether, 96. How grave an evil scandal is, 851. Gregory swears that he wishes to give no human being occasion for scandal, 879. Some scandals are to be disregarded, others not, 1128, 1129.

Scandinavia, from which the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards emerged, is called the workshop of peoples and the womb of nations, 368.

A *scevophylacium* is a place used for detaining accused persons, 759.

**Schism.** Why good works perish in schism, 718, 967. The formula for renouncing schism, 1300 and following pages.

What the schismatics in the affair of the Three Chapters were contending, 937. What their end was, 938. They understood neither what they defended nor what they followed, 938. Schismatics are recalled to the Church, 615, 718. Those returning to the Church from schism are to be assisted, 823, 826, 827, 999, 1000. What Gregory considered appropriate to do to recall them to the unity of the Church, 972. Schismatics who had returned to the Church were harassed by schismatic bishops, 982. Gregory wishes assistance to be brought to them, 983. Felix, a deacon who returned from schism, is incardinated in the Church of Syracuse, 694, 695. Schismatic bishops returning to the Church are received in their own orders, 1001.

**Schola** means the same as college, order, or body, 905, 1121, 1122. There were eleven principal schools of imperial officials, 905.

St. Scholastica, sister of St. Benedict, consecrated to God from childhood, 265. Her holy conversations with her brother, 268. The great efficacy of her prayer, ibid. Her soul left her body in the form of a dove, ibid.

A *scholasticus* was any eloquent person educated in more refined literary studies, 488, 721, 940. An advocate, judge, and assessors of a judge were called *scholastici*, 488, 977. Gregory grants *scholastici* the title “Glory,” as he does prefects, patricians, exarchs, and kings, 721. A *scholasticus* is called the assessor and counselor of an exarch, 761. The cases of bishops were sometimes entrusted jointly to *scholastici* and bishops, 975, 976. The scholasticus defensor, 920, 1105. He claims for himself the property of the bishop whose son he was, ibid. He is ordered to restore it to the Church, ibid.

The *scholasticus*, judge of Campania, 635. The case of Bishop Paul is entrusted to him, 623, 625.

The Sclavi or Sclavini, or Slavs, peoples spread through the north and east and forced into servitude, 933, 934. The Slavs invade Italy, 1065.

Scodra, formerly an episcopal city and later the metropolis of the province of Praevalitana, 528, 898. Bishops of Scodra: Stephanus, 527; Senecius, who signed the Council of Ephesus, 528; Constantinus, 1201.

The Scots differed from the universal Church in fixing the date of Easter, 1036. There is no vanity in writing when necessity compels it, 1036.

A *scribo* is the prefect or commander of the household troops, cavalry, and infantry, 757. The term is also used for a palace guard, ibid. The duty of the *scribones* in the provinces was to select and approve recruits, 594.

*Scrinia* are chests, boxes, and cupboards in which the records of the Church are kept, 662. A *scriniarius*, or *chartophylax*, that is, a *chartularius*, ibid. There were various *scrinia*, ibid.

**Sacred Scripture.** Who must be admonished—those who do not correctly understand Sacred Scripture, 72. Sacred Scripture is a lamp in the night of the present life, ibid. When misunderstood, it is turned into darkness, ibid. The pride of those who do not correctly understand Sacred Scripture, ibid. Heretics turn it into a sacrifice to Satan, 73. It is a book sealed with seven seals, 448. Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, opened this book, ibid. The words of sacred speech are divine banquets, 617. Those afflicted should seek their consolation in reading Sacred Scripture, 618. In interpreting Sacred Scripture, nothing that does not resist sound faith should be rejected, 680. From a single understanding of Scripture, interpreters compose innumerable interpretations as varied ornaments, 680. Sacred Scripture is a kind of letter from God to his creature, 712. It must be read fervently, ibid. One must learn the heart of God in the words of God, ibid. Passages of Scripture are not to be bent to persons or to unusual or profane meanings, 854. St. Gregory often uses the meaning of Sacred Scripture rather than its words, 869. He urges noble girls to read it, 1180. Sacred Scripture was anciently divided among the Jews into various sections, 1271.

**Scruple.** There were four scruples in a solidus, 648. What the baptismal scrutinies are, 735.

The *sculeae*, that is, guards or watchmen, 591, 592.

Sebastianus, bishop of Rhisinum, 518, 769. Sebastianus, bishop, 866. Sebastianus, *antigraphus*, appointed to examine the case of Bishop Hadrian, 630.

What it means to cut pregnant women of Gilead, 72.

Among jurists, a *secretarium* is the place in which judges hear cases, 503. Among ecclesiastical writers, it is a secluded part of a church, 504. It is also called a *diaconium* and a *salutatorium*, ibid. Why the *secretarium* was called a *salutatorium*, 787.

The *Secundianae*: palace or tribunal, 1301.

*Secundicerius*, or *secundocerius*, 880, 881. See *Primicerius*.

Secundinus, bishop of Tauromenium, 558, 1291. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Secundinus, bishop, 789. His fairness and diligence in investigating and settling a case are praised, 779.

Secundinus, having become an abbot after his lapse, is to be deposed, 640, 641.

Secundinus or Secundus, a servant of God at Ravenna, 816. He is called an enclosed solitary, 964; a monomachus, 965. Perhaps he is the one called an abbot, 1270, 1271. His writings are praised, 964. Why Gregory did not answer them, 1270. Secundinus’s humility, 965. Gregory sends him incense, 970, two codices of the Homilies, a garment, and images, 971.

What it means for an axe to fly from the hand and the iron to spring from the handle, 32.

The careless security of penitents must be avoided, 85. The evil of security, 99. Security concerning one’s merits corrupts the soul, 102. A human being from paradise and an angel from heaven fell, although secure, 849. Security is usually the mother of negligence, 869, 870. No one should be secure about his sins while he can still mourn them, 869.

**To sit.** What it means for future preachers to sit in the city, 76.

The apostolic see and St. Peter are spoken of reciprocally, 526, 832. Many preachers are read to have been sent into various provinces by St. Peter, that is, by the apostolic see, 526. It is right for the apostolic see to take care that unity be preserved in the minds of priests, 683. All bishops are subject to the apostolic see if any fault is found in them; otherwise they are its equals, 976. Without the authority of the apostolic see, matters undertaken in synods have no force, 984. The apostolic see is the head of all Churches, 1254. See Roman Pontiff.

To seduce is to lead aside, 686.

Segor, a city that saves the weak fugitive, 80. How married couples are protected from the fires in that small city, ibid.

**Seed.** What a man suffering from an emission of seed signifies, 18. What seeds of crops covered by winter and sprouting more abundantly signify, 876.

The narrow path is the one that leads to life, 436.

Senator, presbyter and abbot of the hospice of Autun, 1221.

Senecius, bishop of Scodra, signed the Council of Ephesus, 528.

**Old age.** Who the elderly are who must be admonished, 35. Conversations with old men were always pleasing to Gregory, 197. When an older man must be rebuked, 925. An old or sick man must not be reprimanded, 1260. Whether in Africa, apart from metropolitans, any bishop was called an old man, 559.

A judgment pronounced without writing does not deserve to bear the name of a judgment, 1255. An example of an ecclesiastical judgment for a bishop, ibid., 1256.

A bilge that secretly rises does what a storm raging openly does, 91.

**Seventh.** See *Hebdomus*.

**Enclosure.** Ecclesiastical enclosures: see Asylum.

**Tomb.** Hypocrites are like whitewashed tombs, 95. The pious custom of preparing one’s own tomb, 273, 332. Laws did not permit human bodies to be moved from their place, 547. To whom the right of burial in churches formerly belonged, 253. The burial of laypeople in churches, 409, 457. The custom of washing bodies before burial, 400, 416. Whether it benefits souls if their bodies are buried in churches, 457. Those weighed down by grave sins are buried in the church to increase the accumulation of their condemnation, 460, 461. A sanctimonious woman buried in a church appeared half burned, 460. Because he had buried the dissolute patrician Valerian in a church, a bishop was punished by sudden death, 460, 461. Demons dragged from the church at night the body of Valentinus, defender of the Church of Milan, which had been buried in the church, 461. The body of a certain dyer, buried in a church, was divinely exhumed and not found in the tomb at all, ibid. It is forbidden to demand a fee for burial, 897, 927. If something is nevertheless offered for lamps, it is permitted to accept it, 927.

[Col. 1577] Lamps used at burials, 927. The ancient custom of burying the dead clothed, 1290.

**Serenity.** A title of honor by which Gregory addresses the emperor Maurice and his son Theodosius, 494, 495, 804, 805, 841.

Serenus, bishop of Ancona, 943. He is called Severus, 996. The visitation of the Church of Aesis is entrusted to him, ibid.

Serenus, bishop of Marseille, 830. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. With what intention Serenus broke images, 1006. He is rebuked for those he broke, 1100 and following pages, and for admitting corrupt persons into fellowship, 1141. Monks traveling to England are commended to him, 830, 1144.

Serenus, deacon of Ancona, 943.

Sergius, bishop of Praeneste, 1287.

Sergius, defender: see the alphabetical index of the Letters.

**Speech.** The sermons of priests should be seasoned with the salt of discernment and wisdom, 17. The speech of teachers must be formed according to the capacity of their hearers, 33. A punitive speech is one that lacks the goodness of usefulness, 312. What it means to speak with God, 48.

*Seronatus* is said of one whom his mother gave birth to late and with difficulty, 488. Hence many were called *Seronati*, ibid.

The serpent’s cunning must be tempered by the dove’s simplicity, 47. A serpent was miraculously appointed guardian of a garden, 161. Serpents attacking servants of God in the wilderness are miraculously killed, 312. In the form of a serpent the devil attempts to frighten Martin the monk, 316. Serpents killed by the sign of the cross, 356.

Servandus, deacon and abbot, a friend of St. Benedict, 269. He presided over the monastery of St. Sebastian, ibid.

Servandus, deacon of the Church of Fiesole, 1074.

A *servator loci* is a rank of office, 460. One who holds the place of the prefects, that is, a deputy of the prefects, ibid. *Servatores* were deputies or substitutes, 593, 594. The *servator* of the praetor is his deputy, 661, 663.

**Servitude.** Free-born children must not be compelled into slavery, 547. Slavery is an impediment to marriage, 845.

Servulus, a paralytic poor in worldly goods but rich in merits, 393. His charity, ibid. His marvelous death, ibid.

**Servant.** Who the servants are who must be admonished, 40. Slaves may justly complain against their masters, 624. Sometimes, for a just reason and against their masters’ wishes, they can be granted freedom or sold to others, ibid. Christians must not drive sick slaves from their homes but must provide them with necessities, ibid. Slaves abandoned in illness enjoy freedom under the law, ibid. Natural, canonical, and civil laws forbid slaves to be admitted to the religious habit against their masters’ wishes, 653, 654, 676. Nevertheless Justinian permitted them to be received unless it was established that they were guilty of theft or some crime, 676. It was lawful to redeem slaves wishing to convert by payment, 654. Formerly slaves were branded on the hand, 676. A slave of the Church is set free through monastic profession, 761. But if he abandons his profession, he is to be restored to his former condition, ibid.

Slaves under public law, 1183. Whether in Gaul long ago there were no slaves properly so called, 1197. Gregory calls himself “servant of the servants,” 1213. See Gregory.

Slaves of the Jews: see Jews, 539, 716, 1231.

“Servant of God,” a deacon of the Roman Church, 539, 1231.

[Col. 1577] Severianus, bishop of the Gabali in Syria, wrote much, 1071.

Severinus, St., apostle of the Norici, whose body was transferred to the fortress of Lucullanum, 624, 638. A celebrated monastery was built there in his honor, 623. Gregory asks that the relics of St. Severinus be sent to him for consecrating a church in Rome, 637, and for dedicating an oratory, 1115.

Severinus, bishop of the Church of Mirus, brought the ministry’s vessels with him, 735.

**Severity.** Gentleness must be mixed with severity, 23.

Severus the heretic, 1174.

Severus, bishop of Ancona: see Serenus.

Severus, schismatic bishop of Aquileia, is ordered to come to Rome, 501. He is called the head of the entire schism, 1240. Why he was called bishop of Grado, 502. When Aquileia was burned, he transferred the see to Grado, 609, 1240.

Severus, bishop of Ficulinum, is appointed visitor of the Church of Rimini, 548, 549, and of the Church of Ravenna, 754, 755.

Severus, presbyter of the province of Valeria, 204. He attributes to himself and mourns the death of a sick man whom he had delayed visiting when summoned, ibid. Through his tears God restores the dead man to life, ibid.

Severus, *scholasticus*, or assessor of the exarch, 761.

Severus, a magnificent man, 1097.

The *sextariaticum* was an impost exacted from colonists on each *sextarius*, 533. Hence it is called an additional burden, ibid. Gregory forbids this burden, as unjust, to be exacted from the colonists of the Roman Church, ibid.

What a gentle whistle calming horses and urging puppies signifies, 33.

Shechem, son of Hamor, violating Dinah by force, is a type of the devil corrupting the negligent soul, 85.

**Sicily.** In Sicily certain places vomit flames and fires, 429. The places of torment seem to be opened in those locations, ibid. Every three years the Sicilian bishops were required to come to Rome; Gregory grants that they may come once every five years, 469, 867. The same bishops were required to come to the Roman council either annually, every three years, or every five years, 486. Gregory commands them to meet once a year with the subdeacon Peter, 486. It was likewise customary for them to gather in Rome every year for the celebration of the pope’s birthday, 526. Gregory abolishes this custom as vain and foolish superfluity, ibid.

In Gregory’s time there was no metropolitan in Sicily, 486, 487, 867, 898. Why Gregory entrusted his authority in Sicily to a subdeacon, 487. Sicily supplied grain to the Romans above all, 488, 557. From the time Sicily was joined to the Roman Empire, Sicilian farmers paid the Romans a tenth of the grain they harvested, 533. They often paid its value in money instead of grain, and were thereby burdened, ibid. Provision is made that nothing similar be done by the Church’s agents toward farmers on the patrimony of Sicily, 533. How Sicilian bishops should protect themselves from the exactions of fictitious defenders, 536. The Sicilian bishops are not to come to Rome for St. Peter’s birthday because of the unfavorable season, 557. Gregory orders prayers because enemies threaten Sicily, 1138. In Gregory’s time there were many sorcerers in Sicily, 1259.

Sidon, which is brought to shame through the voice of the sea, 83.

The sign of the cross was used very frequently by ancient Christians, 196. Its efficacy, ibid. See Cross.

Disasters and massacres to be inflicted on Italy by the Lombards are foretold by signs in the heavens consisting of spears and fiery armies, 368.

**Silence.** The forcible observance of silence is sometimes harmful, 53. Whoever restrains his tongue but not his mind sins all the more dangerously because he sins with greater security, ibid. If he were to disclose the troubles inflicted upon him calmly with his tongue, pain would flow out from his conscience, 54. The tongue must be restrained with discretion, not always bound, ibid. A city of the mind that lacks the wall of silence lies open to the enemy’s arrows, ibid. Those devoted to silence, simple and pure in heart, are readily heard by God, 312.

What a golden siliqua is, 1105, 1107. There are twenty-four siliquae in a solidus, 648, 955. St. Gregory takes care that the peasants not be charged siliquae beyond the pound of just weight, 534. What the *siliquaticum* is, 534.

Tiberius, bishop of Silva Candida, 1287.

**Simony.** Simony is called a heresy, 586, 587, 782, 786, 788, 790, 793, 798, 1007, 1247. How grave a crime it is, 937, 1015, 1016. It inflicts a lethal wound, 1017. Simoniacs are to be kept from sacred orders, 659, 753, 786, 788, 789, 790, 798, 937, 963, 1007. The ordination of Maximus as bishop of Constantinople was null, and his ordinations invalid, because he had been ordained for money, 608. A presbyter ordained through simony is to be deprived of his order, 694. In what sense a Simoniac is not counted as a priest within the priesthood, 1134, 1135.

Simony was condemned by Christ, 1007, 1134; by the apostles, 1008, 1016, 1134, 1148; and by the Fathers, 937, 1007. Simony is rampant in the East, 1134, and in Gaul and various other provinces, 781, 782, 788, 790, 797, 1007, 1140 and following pages, 1141, 1142, 1143. How many and how great Gregory’s efforts were to remove the stain of simony from Gaul, 782. He demands that a synod be convened in Gaul against it, 1010, 1012, 1014, 1015, 1018, 1141, 1142, 1143, 1145, 1146, 1148, 1149. He himself also suppresses it in a synod, 788. He attempts to turn kings away from simony, 1007.

He who, corrupted by a payment, permits someone to become a bishop is said to sell Christ after receiving money, 612. It is forbidden to accept anything for ordinations, marriages, or veiling virgins, 707. Likewise for burial: see Burial.

Every form of simony is condemned, 1290. Simony is sometimes committed under the appearance of piety, 1008. An almsgiving made from money received for orders has no benefit, 1008.

**Simple.** Who the simple are who must be admonished, 47. They must never speak falsehoods, but sometimes they should keep silent about truths, ibid. The great security of the simple, 48. What God’s speaking with the simple means, ibid. The simple and pure in heart are readily heard by God, 312. Why Christ wishes his servants to be simple as doves, 766. Prudence must be joined to simplicity, 47. In Sacred Scripture simplicity is often joined to prudence and uprightness, 766.

Simplicius, bishop of Paris, 1144. Simplicius, the third abbot after St. Benedict, 208. Simplicius, 1092.

*Simultatio* means the same as *simultas*, 487.

Mount Sinai, where there is a celebrated monastery, 1091. Frequent pilgrimages to that monastery, ibid. A famous hospice for the elderly was located there, 1092.

Sincerus is harassed by his father-in-law’s creditors, 821.

[Col. 1579] **Left.** Why riches and glory are placed on the left, 77.

Sipontum, formerly an episcopal city of Apulia but destroyed, was succeeded by Manfredonia, 546. Bishops of Sipontum: Felix, 546—see the alphabetical index of the Letters; Vitalianus, 900; Vitulinus, 1287.

Sirica, abbess, 931. Her will is declared invalid although she had not adopted the monastic life, ibid.

Sirica, wife of Gaudiosus, 547.

Sisinnius, a presbyter accused of idolatry and sodomy, is to be thrust into prison, 1044.

Sisinnius, defender of the Church of Messina, 897.

Sisinnius, a judge whom Gregory assists with an annual subsidy when he is suffering from poverty, 596.

*Sitonicum* sometimes signifies a definite measure of grain and sometimes a public granary, 488, 1204. The curator of the *sitonici*, 1205.

Augustine, apostle of the English, seeks the relics of St. Sixtus the martyr and obtains them, 1157.

Sixtus of Siena believed with Gregory that the fire of hell is corporeal, 111.

Smaragdus, exarch, burning with zeal for ecclesiastical unity, 1240. Gregory kindles his zeal, 1241.

No society exists in which there are not bad people among the good,
1127, 1128. What it means to flee from burning Sodom, 80. Sodom proclaimed its own sin, 89. Why the Sodomites perished through fire and stench, 437. Why the Lord is said to descend in order to learn what had been done in Sodom, 860.

*Solarium* (a sun-terrace), what it is, 228.

Solatium means the same as help or assistance, 558, 646, 980, 1206. It is sometimes used for a pension or revenue paid to the owner on account of a holding, 922.

Solidus, what the gold coin is, 189, 569. The gold coin acquired the name *solidus* under the reign of Constantine the Great, 648. How many solidi there are in a pound, ibid. Six solidi in an ounce, ibid. In a solidus there are four scruples and twenty-four siliquae, ibid. Forty denarii, 570. The difference between the Gallic solidus and the Roman, 648. The Roman solidus was one quarter smaller than our gold coin of Louis, 707. Why Gallic solidi could not be spent at Rome, 796. Solidi returned to a debtor by a miracle, 257.

Why solitaries are attacked more especially by the ancient enemy, 965, 966. What solitude means for one who dwells with himself, 217. Charity of truth seeks holy leisure; necessity of charity undertakes just work, 621, 848. No secluded places whatever can save the soul without the grace of God, 849.

Σωματοφυλαξ (*sōmatophylax*), a bodyguard, guardian of the body, 1045.

Whether dreams should be heeded, 456. Six kinds and causes of dreams, ibid., 457. The more difficult it is to discern from what impulse dreams come, the less readily should they be believed, 457. Holy men distinguish between illusions and revelations by an inward perception, ibid. A certain man, deceived in a dream and having received a promise of long life, died soon and suddenly, ibid.

What it means “to give sleep to the eyes,” 38. Midday sleep permitted by the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1125.

Mount Soracte, now called Mount Saint Sylvester, 177. Mount Soracte in Etruria, 506.

How sorcerers are to be restrained when they are slaves, and how when they are free, 982. Sorcerers punished by Hadrian the notary, 1139. At that time there were very many sorcerers, ibid. [Col. 1579]

Why the Roman Church rejects the history of Sozomen, 883. This history contradicts the Fifth Synod concerning the Three Chapters, ibid.

Spalatum, a city that grew from the ruins of the city of Salona; an archbishopric, 504.

*Spatha*, that is, a sword, 237, 288. The swords of the Lombards are called *synthiciae spathae*, 520. Gregory asks that the sword left at Ravenna be sent to him, 810, 838.

What the office of the sword-bearers is, 237. The count of the sword-bearers was the prefect of the king’s bodyguards, 500.

*Species* is sometimes contrasted with coined money; sometimes it signifies any more valuable item of household equipment, 692.

Speciosus, Gregory’s fellow presbyter, from whom Gregory himself learned what he reports concerning Romula’s passing, 396. Speciosus the presbyter resists his own bishop, relying on the authority of the Roman Exarch, 754. Speciosus the monk, a disciple of Saint Benedict, 384. His brother sees his soul leaving the body, 385. Speciosus the subdeacon of Catania refrains from his ministry so that he may use a wife, 716. He performs the office of notary, ibid.

*Spectabilis* was a title of honor, 420. It was not conferred upon just anyone, 1043, 1044. The *spectabiles* were counted among the first-ranking counts, 420. The formula by which this title was conferred, ibid., 1045.

Hope. We are drawn not only by hope toward realities but also by realities toward hope, so that we may be strengthened more securely in faith in eternal things, 78. Hope must not be placed in a human being, 1178. Spes the abbot, blind for forty years, 385. He recovers his sight, 388. He dies while singing psalms with the brethren, and all see his soul depart in the form of a dove, ibid.

Spesindeus, governor of Sardinia, 1106.

Spiridion, bishop of the Cypriots, detects a thief by a miracle, 161.

There are three vital spirits, created by God, 373. Spirit is of a more mobile nature than the body, 252. Why the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove and of fire, 57. Whoever is filled with the Holy Spirit joins zeal to gentleness, ibid. The procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, 118, 276. The schismatic Greeks corrupted the passage in the *Dialogues* where the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son is discussed, 118, 275. Why the Son says that he will depart so that the Holy Spirit may come, although the Holy Spirit never departs from the Son, 276. Because we have received the Holy Spirit, we do not doubt the life of invisible things, 373. Why the Holy Spirit settled upon the first shepherds in the form of tongues, 17, 511. Virtue and humility are signs that the Holy Spirit dwells in the mind, 156. The Spirit lifts the hearts that he fills, 870. Amid the tumult of human beings he creates solitude in the mind, ibid. In his presence no place is hidden from a repentant soul, ibid. What it means to sell the Holy Spirit, 937, 1007, 1015. See *Dove*.

Why evil spirits are called “alien,” 49, 74. An evil spirit, received as a guest in the guise of a traveler, attacks and kills his host’s son, 196.

Spoletum, an episcopal city of Umbria and capital of the duchy of Spoleto, 942. Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto, 674, 942, 1243.

What it means to guarantee for a friend, 38.

*Sponsalia*, that is, a dowry, 801.

*Sportula*, that is, the stipend by which the ministers of the Church are honored according to each one’s merits, 760, 781.

Squillacium, formerly a city of the Bruttians, [Col. 1580] 600. It bears the title of a principality, ibid. Because its bishops were repeatedly killed in former times, it was deprived of its episcopal see, ibid. John, bishop of Squillace, 599. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

What *stannum* (“tin”) signifies, 53. Who was made tin in a furnace, ibid.

No one can remain stationary on the way of virtue; if he does not advance, he must necessarily fall back, 94. Those standing on high places should fear a fall, 83.

*Statio* is sometimes used by Gregory for a shop or tavern, 1108, 1109.

The statutes of the ancestors should not easily be violated, 618, 619.

The property of Stephania, seized by the agents of the Church of Reggio, is to be restored, 655, 656. Stephania complains that her house was unjustly given to the Church by her mother-in-law, 948.

The monastery of Saint Stephen in the territory of Agrigento, 911, 912.

Stephen, bishop in Spain, 1251, 1252, 1253. Stephen, bishop of Scodra, 527. Bishop Stephen is praised for his constant preaching, 855. Stephen the bishop, 1052, 1194. Stephen, presbyter of the province of Valeria, 325. The devil pulled the leggings from his shins, ibid. Stephen, abbot of the monastery of Lérins, whose vigilance is praised, 833. He is stirred to greater watchfulness and concern, 833. Stephen, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mark near Spoleto, 950. Stephen, deacon of Salona, 1033, 1034. Stephen, a Theban deacon whose life was extremely disgraceful, 629.

Stephen, a man of God who possessed or sought nothing in this world except the one God, 401. His virtues, ibid. He bears the loss of the harvest with an even and cheerful spirit, ibid. His death, 404. From him Gregory had learned what he reports concerning the death of a certain presbyter, 388.

Stephen, an illustrious man recalled from the dead to the living, 432. But without benefit, 433. In him the vices of the flesh contended with almsgiving, ibid.

Stephen, a magnificent man, 820.

Stephen the *chartularius*, 589, 625. He harshly oppresses the Sicilians, 769.

Stephen the *optio*, whose death had been foretold to him by his dying friend Eumorphius, dies, 428.

Stephen the *primicerius*, 640.

Stephen, a citizen of Caralis, orders a monastery to be built as he is dying, 687, 695.

Stephen, returning from error to the Church, is to be received gently, 500.

Stephen Ferrarius dies, 432.

Stephen, a citizen of Naples, is compelled to restore the property he had taken from the woman betrothed to him after she entered a monastery, 867.

Stephen, redeemed from captivity, 1210.

Στιχαριον (*sticharion*, a tunic), what it signifies, 190.

*Stimulus*, that is, a hostile and ill-disposed mind, 1051.

Stipends are called provisions for sustenance, 828. A minister of the Church subsisting on stipends should not aspire to private gain, 539, 755. The customary stipends must not be denied to an ailing cleric, 573. They are to be given only to those serving in the Church, or at least to those desiring this so earnestly that it is not through their fault that they do not serve, 574. Stipends are to be distributed according to each person’s merits, 760, 828.

Stole. What the single or double stoles of the saints signify, 409.

Stopaulus, a freedman, 1044. [Col. 1581]

Strategius, 912. Son of the patrician Eusebia, 1240.

Who are called *stratiotae*, and what the term signifies, 195.

A *strator* was one who lifted the emperor onto a horse and saddled the horse for him, 675. Each patrician had his own *strator*, ibid.

The fool. “The heart of fools is unlike itself,” 60.

The violator of a virgin is ordered either to marry her or to be physically punished in a monastery, 654, 655. What punishment he would have deserved, 655. The violator of a handmaid of God is to be punished with the utmost severity, 1268. Among the laity, sexual violation is punished by excommunication; among clerics, by deposition, 688.

Suana, commonly called Soana, an episcopal city of Etruria, 591.

Whether the monastic state supplies for the subdiaconate, 1188, 1189. See the index to the *Life*.

Subdeacon. The subdeacons of the Roman Church observed continence, 538. The contrary custom prevailed in Sicily, 716. A constitution of Pelagius II decreed that they should abstain either from marital relations or from their ministry, ibid. Gregory moderates this constitution of Pelagius, 538. Nevertheless, he subsequently forbids any subdeacon to be ordained in Sicily who does not promise continence, 538, 717. He makes the same provision concerning the subdeacons of the Church of Reggio, 685. When the law of celibacy was imposed on subdeacons, they came closer to the sacred orders, and were permitted to enter the sacristy and touch the sacred vessels, 538. Subdeacons who have fallen are to be deposed irrevocably and receive communion among the laity, 729, 730. That subdeacons should proceed stripped was an ancient custom of the Roman Church, which Gregory restored after it had fallen into disuse, 940. The Sicilian subdeacons proceeded in linen tunics, 940. Let the subdeacons sing the psalms in the Church and read what is to be read, 1289. Cases concerning bishops, and even the punishment of a bishop, were entrusted to subdeacons, 584, 1230. A subdeacon sits as judge with the bishops of another bishop, 961. A cleric likewise sits as judge with the bishop, 1072. The case of fallen presbyters is entrusted to the regional subdeacon for examination, 1043. A subdeacon is delegated as judge in the case of an archdeacon, 647.

Subject. The faults of subjects are attributed to the inexperience and vices of the pastor, 3. Subjects are to be admonished to submit humbly, 37. The astonishing obedience of subjects in enduring suffering, 669. The fault of those subject to them weighs down the life of their superiors, 702.

Sublacus, a deserted place into which Benedict withdrew as a boy, 209.

*Subreptio* occurs when something is extorted through a false account, 579. Rescripts obtained by deception are wholly invalid, ibid. An imperial command obtained by deception must be rescinded by the emperor himself, 1267. It is difficult for the great to guard against deception, 579.

*Substantia*, that is, sum, quantity, totality, 820. What “mode of substance” signifies in Gregory and among the jurists, 689, 690.

In Gregory, *subtiliter* means “more inquisitively” or “more carefully,” 653, 654.

There were ten suburban provinces, 1076.

The Subura is a district of the city of Rome, 699. The Church of Saint Agatha is situated in the Subura of Rome, 341, 698. The present Church of Saint Agatha is not situated in the ancient Subura, 699. In this church the Arian Goths held their assemblies, ibid. The temporal administration of this church is entrusted to Leo the acolyte, 698.

Anserius, bishop of Suessio, 1288.

*Suffragium* signifies money given to courtly supporters for the purpose of obtaining an office, 768. What “despotic suffrages” are, ibid. *Suffragium* is used for maintenance and support, 828. By transference, *suffragor* means “I favor” or “I assist,” 828.

Pride turns a human being into a beast, 6. It falsely claims to love rectitude, 59. It lays traps for abstinence, 62. What the elevation of pride has wounded, let the abasement of a humble life heal, 88. Pride is more blameworthy in one of humble condition, 599. How culpable pride is in a bishop, 735, 736. Heavenly judgments keep watch against the swelling of exaltation, 745. The devil first used pride above all in the first human being, and now places it at the end of the virtues for human beings, 773.

To be proud. Whoever is proud while lying on the ground cannot learn humility when exalted, 9. It is contrary to nature to wish to be feared by one’s equal, 20. The proud are imitators of the devil, 59. Why Christ wished to die before the proud and to rise again before the humble, 229.

The *superhumerale* with which the priest is adorned, and what it signifies, 15, 509, 840. The meaning of the elements from which the *superhumerale* is woven, 15, 509, 510.

Who is understood by “writing upon the earth,” 1197, 1198.

Why Paul joins the appearance of humility to superstition, 62.

Suppentonia, the place where a monastery stood, 177, 181. Why it was so called, 181.

*Suppositorium* or *suppostorium*, a twofold thing, 537. A *suppostorium* given in place of a pledge is to be returned, ibid.

Sura or Sora, a city of Latium, distinct from Surrentum, the city of the Picentines, 405. Gregory calls it a province, ibid.

Suranus the abbot distributes all that he and his own possess to the poor, 405. After he was killed by the Lombards, the neighboring mountain was shaken by a tremendous movement, ibid. He is honored by the Church, ibid.

What it means to curse a deaf person, 96.

Surrentum, an episcopal city in Campania, 530. John, bishop of Surrentum, 530, 947, 1288, 1291.

*Surtaria*, a kind of garment, or a shield bearing painted images, 971.

What “a washed sow returning to the mud” signifies, 86.

*Susceptus*, that is, a client, 712. Physicians call their patients *suscepti*, 712. Advocates call their clients *suscepti*, 713.

*Suspendere* sometimes signifies “to turn away,” 953.

What it means to be lifted above the heights of the earth, 391.

Sutellius, bishop of Bordeaux, 1288.

Agnellus, bishop of Sutrium, 1287.

Syagria, after professing the religious life, was forcibly joined to her husband, 1021. She desires to devote her property to pious causes, ibid.

Syagrius, formerly a citizen of Autun and made a bishop, a man of the highest virtues, 831. Summary of his deeds, ibid. He fulfills the name of priest by his works, 937. Whether he was a relative or brother of Queen Brunhilda, 1015. Gregory sends him the Pallium, 937, 1015. On what condition, 1012, 1013. Why he did not send it earlier, 937. Syagrius is praised for the work he undertook for Augustine, 1013. He is ordered to convene a synod against simony and the ordination of neophytes, 1012, 1014, 1015. He is accused of negligence, 1021. He subscribed the privilege granted by Gregory to the monastery of Saint Medard, 1288. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

The Creed of Saint Gregory, 1283.

In what year Pope Symmachus was elected, 444. The patrician Symmachus was slaughtered by Theodoric, 420. He and Pope John I were seen to lead the condemned King Theodoric of the Goths away to punishment, ibid.

Symmachus, a magnificent man, 1123.

Symmachus, a defensor in Corsica, 545.

Synodical letter. See *Letter*.

Synod. In synods, innovation in doctrine is to be suppressed, morals corrected, and disputes among bishops judged, 487. Whence the authority of synodal acts derives, 515, 516. Whatever statutes were established in synods convened by the vicar of the Apostolic See are to be observed with unshaken firmness, 784. Without the authority of the Apostolic See, proceedings conducted in synods have no force, 984. How bishops are to conduct themselves in synods, 985. The usefulness and necessity of synods, 1280. Nestorians returning to the Church are to profess that they accept the synods accepted by the universal Church, 1169. Why nothing may be determined concerning the dignity of sees from the sessions and subscriptions of synods, 1014. Synods were convened by the authority and command of rulers, 1015, 1018, 1145, 1146, 1148, 1149.

The *synthiciae* are agreements and conventions, 520.

Syracuse, an episcopal city of Sicily, 487. The election of the bishop of Syracuse was entrusted by the Syracusans to Gregory, 752. Gregory asks that two men elected by the Syracusans to the episcopate be sent to him, so that he may ordain whichever he judges more useful, 588, 753. The privileges of the Church of Syracuse are confirmed, 806.

Bishops of Syracuse: Chrestus, 486. Maximianus. See his title. John, 1288. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

## T

The “tablets” (*tabulae*) were the straps of dalmatics and tunics, 1012. *Tabularius*, 1122. Various kinds of *tabularii*, 1123. *Tabularius*, the same as *numerarius*, 1190. *Tabularius*, administrator of the Church’s revenues, 1249, 1250. Who are to be admonished among the taciturn, 53, 54.

Tadinum, formerly a city of Umbria, 996. The visitation of its Church is enjoined upon Gaudiosus, bishop of Gubbio, 995.

Taius, or Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, published a collection drawn from the works of Saint Gregory, in which he reports several matters concerning Gregory’s *Dialogues*, 106.

The punishment of one who hides his talent, 75.

Talitanus, administrator of the public patrimony, 1097.

Tanate, or Tainate, an episcopal city of Corsica, destroyed in Saint Gregory’s time, 563. Its bishop was Martinus, ibid.

Tarentum, formerly a city of the Salentines, now in the kingdom of Naples, 655. Bishops of Tarentum: Andreas, 656; Honorius, 1232.

Tarracina. See Terracina.

Taurianum, the place where the Church of Blessed John stands, 464.

Turin, a city of Italy, 1022. Most of the parishes of the diocese of Turin, having been destroyed, are assigned to the Church of Maurienne, 1022. Ursicinus, bishop of Turin, ibid.

[Col. 1583]

Taurominium, formerly an episcopal city of Sicily, 558, 820. Bishops of Taurominium: Victorinus, 558; Secundinus, 1291.

Taurus, formerly an episcopal city of the Bruttians, 529. The Taurian monks were dispersed by the barbarians, ibid. The visitation of the Church of Taurianum is entrusted, 1052. Paulinus, bishop of Taurianum, 528. See his entry.

Tecla, abbess of the monastery of Saint Mary at Naples, 1098.

Tegessis, a city in Africa, 1198–1200.

Telesia, a city of the Samnites, 1297. Menas, bishop of Telesia, 1219, 1220, 1297.

Telo, an ancient city of Gaul, 1144.

### Temple

What the stones dressed elsewhere during the construction of Solomon’s Temple signify, 50.

The self-control necessary for those who enter a temple, 193.

Some disapproved of converting the temples of heretics and idols into churches, while others approved, 697. Gregory judged that these should be destroyed, but changed his opinion, 1165, 1176. What Augustine thought about this, 1175. How such temples are to be consecrated, 1176.

Temporal goods are consolations in calamity, not rewards, 77. They are to be used, not enjoyed as an end in themselves, ibid., 875.

The grasping, like the fig tree occupying the ground without fruit, uselessly preserve what could have benefited many, 67.

*Tenor*, or *Regestum*: a book in which expenses were recorded, 595. By *tenor* some understand a holding or possession subject to specified obligations; others understand a testament, 595.

### Temptation

It is human to endure temptation in the heart; it is demonic to be overcome in the struggle of temptation, 12.

The devil wages war against two kinds of people: the one who inflicts insults and the one who suffers them, 45. Those who are victorious in the open field are sometimes captured within the walls, 45.

The devil’s temptations are signified by the wind, 55.

Temptation is resisted sometimes by reasoning, sometimes by deliberation, 85.

The righteous are often tempted without harm, 87. They are tempted so that, through recognizing their weakness, they may be strengthened in goodness, 87.

Let holy warriors have the sword upon the thigh, 90.

Temptations foreseen as future are of less force when they arrive, 90. An anticipated enemy is weakened, 91.

To sleep amid temptations is to lose the ship’s rudder amid storms at sea, 90.

As virtue increases, the battles of temptation generally increase, 31.

In youth, the temptation of the flesh burns fiercely, 213. From the fiftieth year onward, the body’s heat grows cold, ibid.

The order and degrees of temptations arising through the flesh are reviewed, 1162, 1163. Those subject to temptations of the flesh ought not to preside but to be subordinate, 213. Saint Benedict overcame a temptation of this kind, ibid.

When the devil cannot break into a strong heart, he ascends against its lofty walls by bringing weak persons alongside it, as though ladders had been placed there, 744.

As soon as he finds a mind at leisure, he approaches it in order to speak to it through various occasions, 965, 966.

No place is free from temptation, 1093.

The devil is not to be feared if we attribute our protection not to ourselves but to grace, 328. He cannot be overcome without God’s help, 790.

We are more powerful than our enemies in proportion as, through humility, we become one with God, 329.

Everyone ought to be vigilant against all the enemy’s snares, 789. The mind should be watchful, suspicious on every side, and always alert, so as to avoid the traps of the one lying in wait, 885. Prayer is to be employed against our enemy, 885. In temptations, God is to be sought as helper, 966.

[Col. 1583]

### Tepid

From heat one returns through lukewarmness to coldness, 94. Just as, before lukewarmness, coldness lies beneath hope, so after coldness lukewarmness lies in despair, ibid. One must be either hot or cold, lest one be vomited out as lukewarm, ibid.

Tergestum, or Tregestum, a city of Istria, 1240. Firminus, bishop of Tergestum, 1203. See his entry.

### Back

How God admonished sinful humanity “behind the back,” 82. What it means to turn one’s back to God’s face, 82.

What it means to extend one’s boundary, 72. It is a grave matter to cross the boundaries fixed for us by our fathers, 668.

The earth is common to all human beings and provides food for everyone in common, 66.

What it means to be lifted above the heights of the earth, 391.

Whether the “land of life” is distinguished from the “land of the living,” 1175. Whoever seeks good in the land of the living must bear the evils of human beings in a foreign land, ibid.

Terracina, formerly called Anxur, a city of Latium, 249, 524. In a vision, Saint Benedict arranged the construction of the monastery at Terracina, 249. That monastery was ruined and united with Monte Cassino, ibid.

The Church of Terracina is entrusted to Agnellus, bishop of Fundi, in such a way that the rights and authority of the Church of Fundi are not taken away from him, 634.

Agnellus, bishop of Terracina, 524, 634, 1291.

The care of earthly matters is to be avoided by those who govern souls, 24, 25. We ought to be more concerned for the salvation of the soul than for the usefulness of earthly things, 1233.

When prelates ought to inspire fear in their subjects, 20. Human terrors are like smoke, 1066.

Tertulus, a Roman citizen, handed over his son Placidus to Saint Benedict, 220.

### Testament

The word *testamentum* is sometimes used for a written document confirmed by witnesses, 1075.

Monks have no permission to make wills, 931. Nevertheless, human laws sometimes allowed them to do so, 539, 931. They may also make wills by dispensation from the supreme pontiff, 931.

When he died, the monk John left Fantinus the defender heir to six twelfths (*unciae*), 539.

A certain abbess’s testament is declared invalid, although she had not put on the monastic habit, 539, 931, 932.

How Syagria could have made a will after making her profession, 1021.

A bishop may make a will concerning property acquired before his episcopate, but not concerning what he acquired during his episcopate, 1206, 1207. See Bishop.

Testaments made to the detriment of the Church are declared invalid, 791, 792.

By what law the testament of a priest made in favor of someone was confirmed, 801.

Gregory arranged for the long-neglected wishes of a rustic woman who had made a will to be fulfilled, 946, 947.

The disposition of the dead is to be observed in all respects, 1107.

Who are sacramental witnesses, 864. They were called *conjurators* and *compurgators*, ibid.

What witnesses in court ought to be like, 1255.

Whoever walks without a witness does not live rightly, 1195.

Partners in crimes cannot give testimony, 651. Whether women can do so. See Woman.

Thalassia, abbess at Autun, 1219, 1223.

Tharsilla, Saint Gregory’s paternal aunt, 397. Her virtues, ibid. She was warned in a vision by Pope Felix III of her approaching death, ibid. At the very moment of death she saw Jesus coming, ibid. After her death, marks indicating a prolonged prayer were seen on her body, 400.

Thebes, a city of Thessaly in Greece, 627, 628. Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, 627. Unjustly condemned, he was restored to his see, [Col. 1584] 628.

He was exempted from the jurisdiction of the bishop of Larissa, 630.

What a Persian *theca* was, 1270, 1172. Among the Greeks, θεκή (*theke*) means the same as μνῆμα (*mnēma*), “tomb,” and σορός (*soros*), “coffin” or “sarcophagus,” 1272.

Themistius, leader of the sect and discipline of the Agnoetae, 1066.

Theoctista, sister of the emperor Maurice, 490. Her virtues, 870, 1132. Her generosity toward captives, 872. Gregory sent her a key of Saint Peter, 872. Gregory wrote to her about enduring slander bravely and calming murmuring, 1126 and following. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Theoctista, daughter of the sister of the emperor Maurice, 877.

Theodebert, king of the Franks and brother of Theoderic, 834, 1146. His zeal in bringing his subjects to the faith is praised, 834. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians, 683. Wife of Authari, king of the Lombards, ibid. After Authari’s death, she married Agilulf, ibid. A woman of remarkable piety, ibid.

Gregory dedicated his *Dialogues* to her, 106. She used them to persuade both the king and his subjects to embrace the Catholic faith, 114.

Having been deceived, she temporarily suspended herself from communion with Constantius, bishop of Milan, 683, 684, 718.

Gregory sent her relics, 709. He thanked her for having labored to establish peace, 958. Gregory congratulated her on her son’s adherence to the Catholic faith, 1270. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Theoderic, king of the Franks, 834, 1145. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Theodora Augusta, condemned by Pope Vigilius, 615, 616.

Theodora, widow of Petronius the notary, 553.

Theodora, widow of Sabinus the defender, 1103, 1104.

Theodoretus. Judgment was rendered concerning him at the Council of Chalcedon, 719.

Theodoric, king of the Goths in Italy, died, 420. His condemnation was revealed to a solitary on the island of Lipari, ibid. A certain place was called Theodoric’s hell, 419, 420.

The hospice of Saint Theodore at Palermo, 1187.

Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, and Pelagius the deacon were involved in the scandal arising from the condemnation of the Three Chapters, 616. Theodore was condemned by Vigilius, ibid.

Theodore, bishop of Epirus, 796.

Theodore, bishop of Lilybaeum, 660, 755, 801.

Theodore, bishop of Marseille, distinguished for holiness, 541. Why he suffered many things from the rulers of Marseille, 542. When he heard of Gregory’s ordination, he wrote him a congratulatory letter, 541.

Theodore, bishop of the diocese of Milan, avoided the discipline of the metropolitan, 1020. He had brought his complaints before Gregory, 1238.

Theodore of Mopsuestia was rightly condemned at the Fifth Synod, 615. Sozomen praises Theodore as a teacher of the Church until his death, 883. He renewed the impious doctrines of Photinus, 1066.

Theodore, bishop of Tropaeum, subscribed to the fourth session of the Sixth Council of Constantinople, 569.

Theodore, a deacon of Constantinople, 847, 853. He is accused of having said that Christ Jesus, when he descended into hell, freed from punishment all who confessed him, 861.

Theodore, a counsellor, 929. Gregory made him a written donation of a slave, 637.

[Col. 1585]

Thoedorus, a man of consular rank, 579.

Theodore, curator at Ravenna, most devoted to peace, 1001. Gregory consoled him, 1002. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Theodore, master of the soldiers, commander or prefect of Sardinia, 542. He oppressed the islanders subject to him, 543, 544, as well as the poor and the Church, 550, 551.

Corrupted by money, Theodore prevented the primate of Byzacena from coming to Rome to conduct a judgment, 976.

Theodore, *major populi*, 1005, 1057.

Theodore, physician to the emperor Maurice, a man of keen intelligence and eloquence, 677. Chief physician and former prefect, 713. Gregory addressed him with magnificent titles of glory and excellence, 711, 712.

Theodore was sent by the patrician Priscus to the king of the Avars and succeeded in his mission, 677. He sent Gregory money for the redemption of captives, 712. Constantly bound up in secular affairs, he neglected reading Sacred Scripture, 712. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Gregory sends greetings to Theodore, 493, 877.

Theodore Palatinus, 499.

Theodore, mansionarius of the Church of Saint Peter at Rome, 333. Blessed Peter appeared to him at night, ibid.

Theodore, lector of the Church of Thessalonica, 1173.

Theodore, an unruly boy and brother of a monk, lived in the monastery of Saint Gregory, 437. How he was converted at the moment of death, recovered, and died after a religious life, 437, 440.

Theodore the Jew, a sorcerer, 891.

Theodosia, a religious woman, was admitted to a petition against Januarius, the bishop, 650, 727. Since she wished to fulfill Stephen’s wishes concerning the construction of a monastery, Gregory desired that she be assisted, 695, 728.

Theodosian soldiers belonged to the legion that had taken its name from Theodosius, son of the emperor Maurice, 608.

Theodosianus, a deacon of Catania, 900.

Theodosius, bishop of Arles, 541.

Theodosius was elected abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin in Campania, 641. He pursued three fugitive monks, 761. He demanded that the slaves taken from his monastery be restored, ibid. He requested that a monastery be dedicated in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Michael, 762. He complained that he was being severely distressed by the watches on the walls, 987, 988.

Theodosius, son of the emperor Maurice, 1302. When he was admitted to partnership in the empire, 676.

Theodosius, collector of the *burdatio*, 536.

Theodosius, 539, 776.

Theodulfus, a deacon of Paris, repeatedly raised the question of the resurrection, 114.

Theophanius, count of Centumcellae, devoted to hospitality and other works of mercy, 413. He was occupied with earthly concerns more from the obligations of his office than from personal inclination, ibid. Miracles occurred at his death and after it, 416.

Theoprobus, a monk, was close to Saint Benedict because of the merit of his life, 244. Saint Benedict instructed Theoprobus to inquire what was happening to Bishop Germanus, 269.

Theotimus, a physician and a very close friend of Gregory, 664.

Theotistus, a relative of the emperor Maurice, 805.

Thessalonica, a city of Macedonia, 898. Bishops of Thessalonica: Acholius, Anastasius, Anisius, 487; Eusebius, 898, 1267. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

*Thia*. In Greek, θεῖας (*theias*), it means “aunt,” 528.

Thomas, a bishop, 695.

Thomas of Corinth was initiated into sacred orders in order to abandon his accusation, 780. For this reason he was permanently deposed from such an order, ibid.

Thomas, founder of a hospice, 1261.

Thomas, defender of the Church of Salona, 1225.

Thomas, a servant of the Church, was granted freedom by Gregory, 800. He was made a notary and permitted to enjoy the legacies made to him, 801.

Thomas was appointed guardian of Adeodatus’s children in the city of Pisaurum, 756.

In what year the flooding of the Tiber occurred, 116.

The overflowing Tiber flowed over the city walls, 324. It overturned the Church’s granaries, 488. An inundation of this kind occurred more than once, 324.

Tiberius, bishop of Silva Candida, 1287.

Tiberius, one of the sons of the emperor Maurice, 841, 1302. He was not proclaimed emperor, 1287.

Tibur, an episcopal city in Latium, 356. An episcopal city of Roman Campania, 638. Bishops of Tibur: Floridus, 300, 356. See his entry. Anastasius, 1287, 1291.

Tiburtius, a Roman presbyter devoted to carnal vices, was seen after death placed upon and consumed by an enormous pyre, 420.

Timarchus, an excubitor, 1081.

Fear of human beings is directed not toward human beings but toward irrational animals, 20. It is contrary to nature to be proud and wish to be feared by one’s equal, ibid.

The mind does not recognize the grace of freedom when the slavery of fear binds it, 52.

What nocturnal fears are, 90.

Love arises from fear, 353.

Sometimes fear alone purifies souls at the moment of departure, 453.

In this life we ought always to fear, 870.

It is rash presumption when the strong person is afraid while the weaker does not fear, 977.

One must be fearful concerning the good works one performs, 1110.

Timothea wishes the oratory she founded to be consecrated in honor of the Holy Cross, 576.

Paul moderates Timothy’s zeal, 57.

The body of a dyer, buried after death in a church, was miraculously dug up, 461.

What the bells with which the priest was surrounded as he entered the tabernacle signify, 17, 511, 1065. Why bells were inserted into the priest’s garments, 17, 511. Why pomegranates were added to the bells, 18, 511.

The devil broke the bell that the Roman used to warn Saint Benedict, 212.

### Recruits

The assessment of recruits was a burden imposed on the provinces because of their possessions and estates, 594.

### Titles

Titles are wooden tablets affixed to estates or urban or rural properties as a sign of possession, 553, 769. What it means to place titles, 1289.

In Gregory’s time, several presbyters were assigned to one title, that is, to one church, 697, 698. Titles were not assigned to basilicas outside the walls, 698.

Titles of abbots: “Charity,” 1177.

Titles of abbot-presbyters: “Holiness,” 531, 698.

Titles of advocates: “Glory,” 721.

Titles of defenders: “Experience,” 1209 and elsewhere.

Titles of deacons, formerly: “Holiness,” 531.

Titles of deacon-administrators: “Charity,” 740, 746.

Titles of commanders: “Glory,” 543; “Greatness,” 975, 1032, 1048, 1268.

Titles of bishops: “Beatitude,” 1064, 1069 and elsewhere; “Crown,” 622; “Charity,” 1265, 1271, 1272; “Brotherhood,” 1055, 1056, [Col. 1586] 1209; “Most Reverend,” 846, 1063; “Holiness,” 531, 532, 608, 680.

Titles of exarchs: “Excellence,” 1240.

Titles of emperors: “Clemency,” 1239, 1244; “Piety,” 1244, 1267; “Serenity,” 494, 495, 804, 805, 841.

Titles of judges: “Eminence,” 1054, 1067.

Titles of magistrates: “Excellence,” 506, 686; “Illustrious,” 519; “Greatness,” 975, 1032, 1048 and elsewhere.

Titles of masters of the soldiers: “Glory,” 909, 985 and elsewhere.

Titles of notaries: “Experience,” 1056, 1061.

Titles of the pope: “Highness,” 978; “Crown,” 622; “Holiness,” 531.

Titles of presbyters: “Charity,” 1237; formerly, “Holiness,” 531.

Titles of prefects: “Glory,” 1068.

Titles of kings and queens: “Excellence,” 506, 786, 795, 1146; “Glory,” 684; “Illustrious,” 519.

Titles of subdeacon-administrators of the Church’s patrimony: “Experience,” 497, 541, 653 and elsewhere.

Titles of all persons of distinguished rank: “Glory,” 834, 1032, 1081, 1088, 1257–1259.

Titus. Paul spurs Titus’s gentle spirit with a goad, 57.

*Tomus* means a volume or codex, 793. *Tomus* also means a trunk and a stem, or a branch cut from a tree, ibid. The *tomus* of Saint Leo, that is, the letter of Saint Leo, ibid., 1270.

Clerical tonsure differs from the rite of solemnly cutting the hair, 576. Clerical tonsure was customarily conferred separately before the seventh century, ibid. Many are formerly recorded as tonsured without letters of dismissal, 566. Who are called *tonsuratores*, 978, 979.

Torpor is close to gentleness, 56.

Tortona, an episcopal city of Italy, 1035. It was called Dertona, ibid.

### Torture

Who by written law are exempt from torture, 629. In Gaul, few were exempt from it, even in the ecclesiastical court, if the crime was atrocious, ibid.

Gregory disapproved of investigating crimes through infliction of suffering, 1060, 1061.

Totila, king of the Goths, experienced the prophetic spirit with which Saint Benedict was endowed, 237. Saint Benedict rebuked Totila for his evil deeds and announced what would happen to him, 237, 240. In what year Saint Benedict’s encounter with Totila took place, 239.

He ordered Bishop Cerbonius to be exposed to bears, 297, and Bishop Fulgentius to be bound in chains, 300. Totila was softened by a miracle, ibid. Totila and the ferocity of the Goths, 301.

Gregory ordered beams to be brought to Rome for the Churches of Saints Peter and Paul, 1193.

*Traditio* is the delivery of possession, 637. The recipient of a transfer acquires no right, 637.

Trajan, made bishop of Malta after being an abbot, 1042, 1230. Monks were granted to him for consolation, but with the permission of the diocesan bishop, 1042.

Trajan was a man of good character, but was not judged suitable for the episcopate of Syracuse, 741.

### Tranquility

Because of temporal tranquility, people are often pleased with present things and do not seek eternal things, 69.

It is a sign of great courage not to have been disturbed amid the turmoil of lawsuits, 854.

The rulers of the Transjurane district and of Scutingi in Burgundy, now called dukes, were often called patricians, 493.

The transfer of the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul was carried out by Pope Cornelius, 710.

Transfer of relics. See Relics.

How a translation from Latin into Greek ought to be made, 877.

Translations of episcopal sees, 495, 578.

Trecala, or Tricala, or Triocala, formerly an episcopal city in Sicily, 737. Peter, bishop of Trecala, 737, 1137.

[Col. 1587]

Tregestum. See Tergestum.

A *tremissis* is one-third of a gold solidus, 570, 707, 734. It was approximately equivalent to our silver *scudo*, 708.

Tres-Tabernae, formerly a city of Latium, 614. Its see was united with the Church of Velletri, 614.

### Tribulation

The fire of tribulation, when it does not cleanse the rust of vices, shows that the soul has become hardened, 53.

For those placed in the greatest tribulation, the only consolation is the mercy of the Creator, 1062.

God did not promise his elect joys of delight in this life, but the bitterness of tribulation, 1127.

Tribulation must not overwhelm one’s strength, 1233.

The Council of Tribur, held in 895. A history taken from Gregory’s *Dialogues* is reported, 107.

There were various orders of tribunes, 499. A clerical tribune, 696.

Tributes produce less benefit when collected with sin, 769. Formerly the possessions of ecclesiastics were exempt from every tribute, 1017. Religious persons must also pay tributes, 1059.

Tricala. See Trecala.

The origin of the thirty Masses, 468.

Baptism is to be conferred in the name of the Trinity, 1167. Otherwise it is no baptism, 1168.

What a *tripedica* is, 261. The devil appeared to Saint Benedict equipped with a *tripedica*, ibid.

Who are to be admonished among the sad, 37. Sadness is closely related to anger, ibid.

### Wheat

By the measure of wheat, the proper measure of speech is expressed, 99.

Wheat multiplied by a miracle, 192.

What Τροπάριον (*troparion*) means, 426.

Tropaea, a city of Calabria, 569. The monks of Tropaea are to be assisted if they live religiously, ibid.

Tudertum, an episcopal city in Umbria, 192. Fortunatus, bishop of Tudertum, 190. See his entry. Sabinianus, 1288.

Tullianus, master of the soldiers, 900.

*Tultus*, that is, “taken away” or “removed,” 608, 973, 974, 1035, 1107, 1108.

### Tunic

Roman orders were distinguished by the tunic, 1012. How tunics differ from dalmatics, ibid.

Pelagius, bishop of Turni, 830.

Turris, an episcopal city in Sardinia, 550. The visitation of its Church is entrusted to another, 1052. Marinianus, bishop of Turris, 550, 932.

What it means to praise God with the drum but not in the choir, 68. What it means to praise God with the drum and in the choir, 880.

Tyndaris, formerly an episcopal city in Sicily, 672, 994. Eutychius, bishop of Tyndaris, 672.

What Τζαγγάριος (*tzangarios*) means, 435.

## U

What it means for breasts to be subdued in Egypt, 82.

*Ulna* sometimes means a cubit, and sometimes the span measured by both hands extended, 671.

### Vengeance

Some do not seek vengeance immediately after injuries have been inflicted but only after a long delay, 44, 45. To whom these people are similar, 45.

Moderate leniency in correction has greater force than strictness in carrying out vengeance, 1051.

[Col. 1587]

The mutual unanimity of the Church’s prelates ought to be cultivated with particular care, 879.

An ounce consists of 576 grains, 708. There are six ounces in a solidus, 648, 708.

Nine ounces—that is, three quarters of something, 537.

An heir to six ounces, that is, heir to half of an inheritance, 537, 539, 626.

An heir to eight ounces is one who receives two of the three parts, 577, 990.

An heir to four ounces is one who receives only one of the three parts, 673, 990.

An heir to one ounce, 1189, 1190.

The reason for uniting Churches is the usefulness or necessity of the Church, 495. How many reasons there are for one Church to be united to another, ibid. Churches are united in three ways, ibid.

The Church of Carinensis was united to that of Rhegium, 597, 799. Cuma was united to Misenum, 606. Formiae was united to Minturnae, 495. The Church of Tres-Tabernae was united to that of Velletri, 614.

With what zeal unity is to be pursued, 972.

Gregory calls the title “universal bishop” a name of error, 742. A foolish and proud designation, ibid. A perverse designation, 742, 743. An abominable designation, 745, 850. A wicked designation, 747. A blasphemous name by which the honor of all priests is taken away, 749, 771. A word of pride through which grave scandal is generated in the churches, 878.

Gregory says that by this title the entire faith of the Church is corrupted, 873. He is found opposing this title, 749, 881, 984. Gregory is wrongly accused, as though he would give place to scandal for no reason, 873, 881.

At the Seventh Synod, Pope Hadrian disputed this title with Tarasius, 749. Gregory rejected it when it was offered to him, 771, 919.

In what sense the Greeks bestowed the title “ecumenical” upon their patriarch, 749, 772.

What ὐποκαμίσιον (*hypokamisio[n]*) means, 190.

Urbanus, abbot of the monastery outside Caralis, 1107.

Urbicus, provost, 596, 732. He is called abbot of the monastery of Saint Hermes at Palermo, 824. Who he was, 1136. He is accused of imprudence, 1136 and following. Gregory rebuked him rather harshly, 1137. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

The election of Urbicus as bishop of Palermo is approved, 1228. Why he was not compelled when he resisted, ibid.

Urbicus, a defender, 639.

Urbicus, husband of Domna Palatina, 528.

Urbinum, a city of Umbria, 641. Leontius, bishop of Urbinum, 641, 774.

Urbitius, bishop of Dyrrachium, 898, 983.

Urbs Vetus, an episcopal city of Etruria, 498. John, bishop of Urbs Vetus, 498.

Among secular authors, *urgere* sometimes means “to threaten” or “to be imminent,” 440.

Ursicinus, bishop of Cahors, whose right was preserved after his deposition, but in mutilated and restricted form, 495.

Ursicinus, bishop of Turin, 1022. Gregory requested that the parishes taken from Ursicinus be restored, 1022, 1023.

Ursicinus, who wrote against John, bishop of Ravenna, was to be restrained, 720.

Ursus, a monk, was summoned by another monk who was dying, although he was far away, and died, 425, 428.

Ursus ministered to Florentius, a servant of God, [Col. 1588] 309. He tended sheep, ibid.

Ustica, an island of Sicily, one of the Aeolian Islands, 469.

Usury is prohibited by divine and canon law, 955. What exactly constitutes usury, and for whom, is not so certain, ibid.

Gregory approved of money being lent without interest to the Church’s tenants in their need, 734, 735.

Use and right are sometimes separated, 522.

*Utilitas* is used to mean occupation, 591, 592.

Udine, a city in the province of Forum Julii whose patriarchal see had been transferred to Aquileia, 502.

Utriculum, a town in Umbria, 299. Its various names, ibid. Dominicus, bishop of Utriculum, 1291.

What it signifies when a brother refuses to take his deceased brother’s wife, 6.

What it means to spit in the face of a woman whom one refuses to take, 7.

What it means to have a wife as though one did not have her, 79.

## V
Valdarichus, 1191. Valentinian, first abbot of the Lateran monastery, 208. Valentinian, a monk of the Gregorian monastery, whose death is foretold, 409. Valentinus, the abbot under whom Gregory professed the monastic life, 172. Valentinus, abbot, 722. Valentinus, defender of the Church of Milan, a very unreliable man, 461. His body, buried in the church of Blessed Syrus the martyr, was exhumed by demons at night and dragged outside the church, ibid. Valentinus, a priest of the monastery, 954. Valentio, an African bishop, 916. Valentio, first abbot of a monastery in the province of Valeria, then of the monastery of Saint Gregory at Rome, 404. From him Gregory learned what he reports in his *Dialogues* about a certain priest, 329, 404. On what day his memory is celebrated, 404.

Valeria, a region of Latium, 164. Why it was so called, 1042. It was called the province of the Marsi, 405.

Valerian, a Roman priest sent to Barca in Africa to ransom captives, 636. Valerian, a cleric of the Church of Firmum, 943. The notary of that same Church built an oratory on his own estate, 986. Valerian, a monk, 756. Valerian, an advocate at Rome, 412. Valerian, a patrician, scorned to put an end to his evil ways, 460. Because the bishop of Brescia had buried him after his death in a church, he was punished by a sudden death, ibid., 461.

Health. See *Salus*.

Vanga, what it is, 304.

Vanity. What those who do evil secretly and good publicly should consider, 95. They are whitewashed tombs, 95. They sell a thing of infinite value cheaply, ibid. They live for others and die for themselves, 95. How Christ said that our works should be seen, and how they should not be seen, 96. If the desire to please people insinuates itself, all the labor of a good work is rendered fruitless, 626.

Vantilonus, 1024. Vapincum or Vapingum, a city of Gaul, 1011. Aregius, bishop of Vapincum, ibid. Varmaricarius, Brunhild’s envoy, 1219, 1220; and of Theuderic, 1221. See *Burgoaldus*.

The Varronian mass, 537.

Those who are said to carry the vessels of the Lord, 13, [Col. 1589] 508. Who are the guardians of the vessels, 213. The sacred vessels are the minds of the faithful, ibid. Clerics of the Church of Venafrum sold sacred vessels to a Jew, 554. Laws and canons permit sacred vessels to be sold for the redemption of captives, 859, 886.

Vectanus, a count, 985. What the gilded poles of acacia wood and the rings to be inserted into the ark signify, 34. Why the poles are ordered to be overlaid with gold, ibid. Why they must always remain in the rings, ibid.

*Vel* has the force of the coordinating conjunction “and,” 702.

Velia, formerly an episcopal city of Lucania, 605. Velitrae, a city of Campania in Italy, 578. The see of Velitrae was transferred by Saint Gregory to a safer place, 578, 579. The Church of the Three Taverns was united to the Church of Velitrae with all its rights and revenues, 614. John, bishop of Velitrae, 1287, 1291. See his title.

Velox, master of the soldiers, 570.

The Veil. In former times virgins did not receive the veil immediately after making their vow of virginity, 692. The blessing of the veil belonged to the bishop, 693, 754. Formerly the veil used to be solemnly given to virgins at the altar, 693. The abbess’s blessing of the veil was more solemn than that of the other nuns, 692. The most ancient custom of veiling virgins, 754. To lay aside the veil is unlawful, 754. Veils suspended in churches, 1123, 1124.

Venafrum, a city of Campania in Italy, 554. The clerics of this Church sold its sacred furnishings to a Jew; Saint Gregory orders that these be restored and that the clerics be subjected to penance, 555.

Let there be no venality in ordinations, 659, 660. See *Simony*.

Venantius, bishop of Luna, 293, 296, 297, 461. See the alphabetical index of the Letters. Venantius, bishop of Perugia, 1211. Venantius, bishop, 1238. Venantius, a patrician and former monk, 153. He was not a chancellor, 522. Gregory urges him to return quickly to the monastic life, 523. Venantius married and had two daughters by her, Barbara and Antonia, 522, 1033. As Venantius lay close to death, Gregory tried to bring him back to the monastic habit, 522. Gregory offered to convene a council at which his case could be judged, 524. Gregory despaired of his salvation unless he withdrew from marriage and put on the monastic habit, 523. How concerned Gregory was for his salvation, 1119 and following. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Venantius, a Panormitanian patrician, 1183, 1208, 1228. Venantius, grandson of the patrician Opilio, 619.

Poison swallowed after the sign of the cross does no harm, 288. Saint Benedict heals one infected by poison, 257.

Gregory sometimes uses *venerari* passively, 379, 380.

Venerius, bishop of Cagliari, 1303. Whether the Letter of Gregory circulated as addressed to him is genuine, 1304. Venerius, bishop of Vibo, 962. The visitation of the Church of Tauriana was entrusted to him, 1052.

The forgiveness of sins of thought is easy, 86. He rightly asks pardon for his offense who first forgives offenses committed against himself, 473. The ease of granting pardon is harmful, 657.

To come into public life, what it means, 766.

Vennianus, 1039. [Col. 1589]

The Belly. By the name “belly” the mind is signified, 51. The belly is designated by the title “chief of the cooks,” 61. One who serves the belly is bound by the snares of vices, 62.

The Wind, what it signifies, 56. What it means to observe the wind and not sow, ibid.

Who among the verbose should be admonished, 54.

The word of God is partly written and partly handed down; both forms are equally to be venerated by the faithful, 515. How the divine Word became flesh, 1168. In the midst of human words the heart slips away, 33. What it means to be ensnared by the words of one’s own mouth, 38. From idle words one proceeds to harmful ones, 34, 35, 313. What an idle word is, 55.

Who among the bashful should be admonished, 41.

Truth. Nothing is easier to say than the truth, 47. It is a lesser transgression not to know the truth than not to remain in the truth once it has been known, 301.

Who should be warned against being fickle, 47, 48.

Vitalis, bishop of Vesontio, 1288.

*Vestiarium* means either a wardrobe or the clothing itself, 650. A *vestiarius* is one who manages the wardrobe, ibid. The term also denotes the official second in rank under the wardrobe-master, and the chief prefect of the wardrobe, ibid.

Footprint. To remain at the footprints of emperors, 1130.

What the priest’s garments signify, 17, 511. Why bells are inserted into the priest’s garments, ibid.

Veteranus, a priest of the Church of Salona, 1065, 1225.

Those who follow the narrow way in the peace of the Church are prepared for martyrdom, 340. The course of the righteous, represented by a bridge in a vision, 432, 433, 436.

*Viaticum* is used for Eucharistic communion, 397, 733; for absolution, 397. The ancients called everything *viaticum* that helped toward a safe departure from this life, 733, 926. Viaticum must not be denied to those who are doing penance when death is near, 1250.

Viator, a deacon of Catania, 900. Viator, formerly a tribune, 1003.

Vibo, formerly an episcopal city of the Bruttii, now a fortress in the province of Further Calabria, 825.

*Vicar* sometimes has the same meaning as “successor,” 1095, 1300. Other meanings of this word, 1104, 1105, 1106. Formerly the pope used to appoint his vicars—metropolitans or bishops—in distant provinces outside Italy, 487. In Sicily he entrusts his functions to a subdeacon, ibid. The image of the great vicars, 565. Priests and bishops of the second order were so called, ibid. The vicariate of the Apostolic See is sometimes assigned to a place, not a person; sometimes to a person, not a place, 573. Which bishop of Arles was formerly given this vicariate, 781. Gregory entrusted his functions in Gaul to Virgilius of Arles, 781. What his authority was, 783. He decided nothing alone except in minor cases, 784. Who was to act in matters of faith or more important affairs, ibid. Vicars, or those holding another’s place, were formerly called senators, 593, 594. The prefect was distinct from the Vicar of the City, 1076. Ten provinces were under the Vicar of the City, ibid.

Vice-count, what it is, 909.

The Vice-dominus. The duties of the vice-domini were various, 498. Their dignity, ibid. Today the vice-dominus is called the major domus, ibid. The vice-domini were sometimes distinguished from the stewards, ibid. What their care involved, 498, 832. [Col. 1590] A vice-dominus is to be appointed by the bishop, 1172; or by all the clergy if the bishop neglects to do so, ibid.

Victor, primate of Numidia, 715, 915, 1198, 1199, 1200. Victor, bishop of Palermo, is ordered to come to Rome to clear himself, 557. His case was entrusted for examination to Marinianus the abbot and Benenatus the notary, 642, 643. If guilty, he was to be deprived of communion and confined in a monastery, 643.
