He is accused of negligence concerning the monastery, 732. He is ordered to pay for the Jewish synagogues that had been unjustly seized and rashly consecrated, 973, 974. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Victor, bishop of Phausiana in Sardinia, 932, 1095. He labors to convert the idolaters of Sardinia, 1106. Victor, a deacon of Carthage, 609.

Which victors are seized in the field within the walls, 45.

Victory. Without the labor of combat there is no palm of victory, 325. Victory is to be attributed not to the valor of soldiers but to the will of God, 678. A more excellent victory arises from the desperation that has been won through excessive toil and sweat, 776. Victoria, having scattered the property of the monastery of Saint Martin in Sicily, sought first the position of prioress and afterward that of abbess, 732. Gregory orders that she be examined and, after the things she had given had been reported, be sent to another monastery, ibid.

Victorianus, a priest, 1044. Victorinus, bishop of Taormina, 558. Victorinus, a deacon of Numidia, 699, 660. Victorius composed the Paschal cycle in the middle of the fifth century, 1037. The Scots and Saint Columbanus rejected this cycle, 1037. Columbanus requested that it be rejected by the Roman Church, 1038.

The care of widows belongs to bishops, 499. Emperors and kings have granted bishops the right to defend their cases, 627. The canons forbid the widows of clerics to marry again after their husbands’ deaths, 716. This law does not bind a widow whose husband had withdrawn from his ministry, 717. Why second marriages are forbidden to widows of clerics, 716.

Vienne, a city of Gaul, for a time a rival of the Church of Arles, 831.

When the breast stripped of the breastplate of vigilance is exposed to arrows, 89, 90. The vigilant mind is like the pilot of a ship, 90. The mind sleeping amid the care of its own vigilance is beaten but does not feel it, 90. It is dragged along and does not perceive it, 90. One must keep watch under God’s protection, 328. How useful careful prevention of faults is, 976.

Gregory asks that Vigildus’s household be released, 571.

Pope Vigilius was uncertain about the Fifth Council and the Three Chapters to be condemned, 615. He gave occasion to the schism, or increased its strength, 682. He condemned the Empress Theodora and the Acephali, 615, and Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, 616. Before John, Vigilius acted as deputy of the prefecture at Milan, 953.

Vincentius, a bishop of Sardinia, 932. Vincentius, a deacon of the Church of Lamigis, complained to Gregory about his bishop, Argentius, 566, 567. Vincentius of Lérins, a monk, 1101. Vincomalus was appointed defender of the Church, 756, 823. Vintarith, 1242.

Wine, what it signifies, 23. May the Lord provide us with his wine, 73. What the wine mixed with oil and poured by the Samaritan into the wounds signifies, 514. How wine is to be used on days of fasting, 1303. Wine increases through prayers, 185, 189.

“Violently,” that is, with difficulty or unwillingly, 693. To restrain violent men is not to act against the laws but to support the law, 627.

Man. How men should be admonished, 35.

The Rod, what it signifies, 23.

Virgilius, made bishop of Arles from either the abbacy of Lérins or that of Autun, 541. After hearing of Gregory’s consecration, he wrote him a letter of congratulations, 541. The use of the pallium and the vicariate of the Apostolic See were granted to him according to ancient custom, 781, 783, 784, 785. The cases of bishops, even the more important, were entrusted to him in the first instance, 783, 784. He was permitted to convene councils whenever he considered it necessary, 784. He is accused of negligence, 1021. See the alphabetical index of the Letters.

Virginity. Humility must be preserved in virginity, 83. Virginity is a word that not everyone understands, 83. Some are worse in a better order, and some better in a worse order, 83. What the foolish virgins, who did not take oil, and the wise virgins signify, 1126.

Virgin. Virgins are called eunuchs, 83. Virgins sing the song to the Lamb in a distinctive way, ibid. Who should be admonished after experiencing sins of the flesh, 83. One who abducts a virgin, and those who favor him, are excommunicated, 1293. How ravishers of virgins are to be treated. See *Ravisher*.

Virigantinus, a monk whom Gregory orders to be assisted, 726.

Virtue. What defenses of virtue are necessary, 31. The virtues of the soul are destroyed by lust, 61. Vices must be uprooted before virtues are implanted, 93, 94. If virtue does not grow, it must diminish, 94. On the path of virtue, to go backward is most dangerous, ibid. The memory of virtue is a pitfall of the mind, 99. Virtue struggles against vices, 99. How virtue is handed over into captivity, 101. Examples of virtue are to be preferred to miracles, 115. Those who pursue virtue do not acquire profit for themselves alone, 121. It is easy to pretend to virtue, difficult to possess virtue, 1269. Virtue is nothing except the highest love of God, ibid. Vices often pretend to be virtues, 28, 59, 514.

Force and right are opposed, 693. Things done by force are legally considered invalid, 842. Visible things are seen through invisible things, 381. Why most of the righteous enjoy visions at death, 389. Which visions must be examined, ibid. The visions with which certain saints were honored at the moment of death, 389, 392, 393, 396, 397, 400, 404, 409, 420, 425, 432. The night visions with which monks of holy life were honored, 453, 456.

Visitor. It belonged to metropolitans to delegate visitors—bishops—to deserted Churches, 501. There were also visitors who were not bishops, ibid. When a bishop died or otherwise became unable to serve, another bishop assumed the burden of visitation in the same Church, 501, 562, 823, 824. Visitors were sometimes appointed by the king, 562. A visitor of a Church must not be elected bishop of that same Church, 575. Without a special mandate, a visitor could not interfere in the promotion of clerics, 588, 600, 601, 1227. Visitors were granted permission to ordain priests and deacons in the Churches entrusted to them, 501, 562, 575, 605, 721, 824. The same permission was denied to Leontius, visitor of the Church of Ariminum, [Col. 1591] 641; afterward it was granted to him, 774. A visitor was permitted to celebrate manumissions, 575.

It was the visitor’s duty to seek out someone worthy to succeed a deceased bishop, 588, 722, 808, 862 and elsewhere. He had to confirm the election by his testimony, 601, 720, 808, 1052, 1227 and elsewhere. He was not to permit anyone from another Church to be elected unless perhaps no worthy person could be found, 588, 601, 1227 and elsewhere. It was the visitor’s duty to guard and defend the property of the bishop and of the widowed Church, 588, 600, 737, 738, 755, 774, 808, 862, 987, 988, 995, 1052. The visiting bishop also cared for the monasteries, 601, 808, 1227. The visitor’s office in spiritual matters, 737, 738, 808, 987. The people had to obey visitors as their own bishops, 642, 738, 755, 989, 996, 1228 and elsewhere. Stipends were to be provided for visitors and their clerics, 692. Gregory orders that one hundred solidi and one servant be given to Paul of Nepi when he withdrew from the visitation, as payment for his labor, 649. One quarter of the property assigned to the bishop of a Church was to go to the visitor in place of a stipend, 737.

Visitation was imposed on the Churches of: Agrigentum, 737; Ariminum, 548, 549, 641; Brundisium, 807; Capua, 737; Croton, 600; Cumae, 587; the Three Churches, 605; Formiae, 862; Gallipoli, 807; Hortona, 721; Interamna, 987; the Lipari Islands, 807; Naples, 575; Nepi, 588; Palermo, 1227; Populonia, 500; Ravenna, 754; Saona, 562; Tadinum, 995, 996.

Life. Christian life is to be judged not by signs but by works, 205. Burdened by the weight of human miseries, people in this life ought rather to groan than rejoice, 854. Our life is like that of a sailor, 875. The present life is a pilgrimage, 1175.

Common life in the Church of Canterbury, 1151. By what law the practice of common life was prescribed, ibid. and following.

The exercises and tranquility of the spiritual life, 875.

The active and contemplative life. Through the contemplative life we devote ourselves to God; through the active life, to the salvation of our neighbor, 8. Isaiah commendably desired the former, Jeremiah the latter, ibid. and 848. The contemplative life is signified by Rachel, the active by Leah, 491; likewise by Mary and Martha, ibid. Mary Magdalene, absorbed in the contemplative life, had already surpassed the active life, which Martha still held, 869. Charity for truth seeks holy leisure; the necessity of charity undertakes just work, 621.

Vitalianus, bishop of Sipontum, 900, 1107. He is severely rebuked for having allowed a virgin, after casting aside her religious clothing, to return to the world, 900. Vitalianus, a former priest, was sent to Sicily to perform penance, 730. Vitalianus, master of the soldiers, 570, 590, 591. Vitalis, bishop of Vesontio, 1288. Vitalis, third abbot of Cassino after Saint Benedict, 208. Vitalis, defender of Cagliari, 926, 980, 1106, 1259.

Viterbium, a city in Etruria that succeeded the city of Ferentia as an episcopal see, 189.

Vice. Those who do not abstain from vices surrender themselves to the devil, 49. Certain vices generate others from themselves, and arise from others, 60. Certain vices are prudently to be concealed by a pastor, but, because they are concealed, they are to be indicated, 29. Some things, though openly known, are to be tolerated, ibid. Others, although hidden, are to be investigated, 29. Some are to be rebuked more harshly, [Col. 1592] 30. How great a fault it is to cease rebuking vices, 70. To go from gate to gate means to move from vice to vice in rebuking them, 75. He belongs to God who is roused by zeal for divine love to strike down vices, 76. He denies that he belongs to God who refuses to rebuke the life of the carnal, ibid. In rebuking vices, inward peace must be preserved with the vicious, 70. Vices must be cured with opposing remedies, 88. Vices must be uprooted before virtues are implanted, 93, 94. The vice in which we are most endangered must be attacked more fiercely, even when other vices are concealed, 98. Vices must be treated in such a way that the pastor does not bend the subject toward the opposite extreme, 97, 98. Vices often pretend to be virtues, 28, 514. When vice is believed to be virtue, guilt accumulates without fear, 57.

A glass vessel broken by the sign of the cross, 216.

Vitula built the monastery of Saint Vitus in Sardinia, 543. Vitulinus, bishop of Sipontum, 1287. In what spirit those who criticize are to be heard, 1093. By whom the monastery of Saint Vitus in Sardinia was built, 542, 543. Vitus was appointed defender, 1120.

To live. To live happily is one thing; to live essentially is another, 452.

Viviana, widow of Felix, for whom Gregory orders that generous assistance be provided, 528. Viulandus, 602.

Long vowels were formerly distinguished from short vowels, 564.

To call. Wisdom abandons those whom it has called after they have long refused, 49. How God warned the human race before sin, 82. How he calls it after sin, 82.

Self-will belongs to joy, 62. The pious wishes of the dead are not to be violated but fulfilled, 687, 689, 947. The final wish of the deceased can sometimes be changed, 1107. In marriages, consent must be free, 693. Pleasure and youth are fleeting, 377.

*Votive*, that is, desired or desirable, 589, 590. A vow of chastity makes marriage illicit for the one who takes the vow, 81. One who intended to undertake the greater good made the lesser good, which had been lawful, illicit, ibid. Formerly monks did not vow chastity and poverty in explicit words, although these were essential to the monastic state, 1021.

The living voice usually draws the heart more tightly than a reading delivered in passing, 858.

Wound. Wounds of the soul are more difficult to cure than wounds of the body, 3. The discoloration of a wound wipes away evils, 51. Closed wounds cause greater pain, 54. Those who recognize wounds of the mind but neglect to heal them by cutting words commit sin, 74. Whoever does not feel the pain of a wound does not seek remedies for health, 93. It is better to resist the infliction of wounds than to cure those already inflicted, 716.

A fox is compelled by a miracle to return a hen it had carried off, 192.

Vult, one of the three men who always adhered to Totila, 237.

Volturnum, a city of Campania in Italy, 951.

The Vandals. The persecution of Catholics in Africa by the Arian Vandals under Hunneric, 348. They cut out the tongues of bishops, ibid. They ravage Campania, 277.

Warnilfrida, Ariulf’s secretary, 1002.

The Visigoths were converted to the Catholic faith under King Reccared, 347, 348.

The island of Vulcano, 778.

[Col. 1593]

X

Xenia are gifts sent, 300, 328. *Xenia* is a gift given to guests, 587. In legal usage, *xenia* means small gifts, ibid. Gregory does not consider every *xenium* to be rejectable, 586, 587, 807. What kinds of *xenia* were pleasing to him, 841.

The administration of hospices traditionally belonged to bishops, 706. Hence hospices are called Churches’ institutions, ibid. Gregory orders that the care of hospices be entrusted to clerics of recognized integrity, 706. It was sometimes entrusted to subdeacons, 949. What those who preside over hospices should be like, 706. Gregory does not allow hospices to be neglected, 1259, 1260. A hospice was to be established at Jerusalem, 1237. The privilege of the hospice of Autun, 1221, 1222, 1223.

[Col. 1593]

Z

Zabarda, duke of Sardinia, 702. At what time Pope Zacharias governed the Church, 111, 118. Why he translated the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory into Greek, 107, 111, 121. Perhaps he translated them twice, 112.

Zalla, an Arian Goth, the most bitter enemy especially of Catholics and churchmen, 261. Saint Benedict tames this savage man, 264.

How great the zeal of a good pastor should be, 31. The zeal of God torments the mind of a good pastor, 32. Zeal must not be immoderate but circumspect, ibid. Love of peace must not bend zeal and constancy, 69. Humility must not obstruct pastoral zeal, [Col. 1594] nor zeal humility, 514. Zeal for God’s honor in punishing the guilty of the gravest crime, 759. Far be it from a priestly mind to be moved in any case by private zeal, 812. Certain priests are censured because they are moved by no zeal for the souls whom they see perishing in heresy or vices, 834.

Zemarchus, a tribune, 499.

Zeno. There is doubt concerning the martyrdom of Saint Zeno, 325. The overflowing Athesis reached the windows of the church of Saint Zeno but did not enter it, 325. The monastery of Saint Zeno, 1264. Zeno, a bishop, 794. Zeno, bishop of Epirus, 796.

Zittanus, master of the soldiers, 1059.

What it signifies that the weeds are to be tied into bundles, 429.

[Col. 1593]

ORDER OF THE SUBJECTS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME.

Preface to the Book of the Pastoral Rule. 9

## PART ONE OF THE BOOK OF THE PASTORAL RULE. 13

**Chapter I.**—That the inexperienced should not dare to undertake the office of teaching. Same page.

**Chapter II.**—That those who do not perfect by their way of life what they have learned through reflection should not assume a position of governance. 15

**Chapter III.**—On the burden of governance; and that every adversity should be despised and prosperity feared. 16

**Chapter IV.**—That the activity of governance generally dissipates the mind’s stability. 17

**Chapter V.**—On those who could benefit others by the example of their virtues at the summit of governance, but avoid it by pursuing their own quiet. 18

**Chapter VI.**—That those who flee the burden of governance through humility are truly humble when they do not resist divine judgments. 19

**Chapter VII.**—That some rightly desire the office of preaching, while others are rightly compelled and drawn into it. 20

**Chapter VIII.**—On those who desire to preside and seize the instrument of apostolic speech for the use of their own lust. 21

**Chapter IX.**—That the mind of those who wish to preside generally flatters itself with a fictitious promise of good works. Same page.

**Chapter X.**—What sort of person should come to governance. 23

**Chapter XI.**—What sort of person should not come to governance. 23

## PART TWO OF THE BOOK OF THE PASTORAL RULE. 25

**Chapter I.**—How one who has come to governance in an orderly manner ought to conduct himself in governance itself. Same page.

**Chapter II.**—That the ruler should be pure in thought. 27

**Chapter III.**—That the ruler should always excel in action. 28

**Chapter IV.**—That the ruler should be discerning in silence and useful in speech. 30

**Chapter V.**—That the ruler should be near to each person through compassion and raised above all through contemplation. 32

**Chapter VI.**—That the ruler should be a companion through humility to those who act well, but through zeal for justice stand firm against the vices of wrongdoers. 34

**Chapter VII.**—That the ruler should not lessen his care for inward matters amid outward occupations, nor abandon his provision for outward matters amid concern for inward ones. 38

**Chapter VIII.**—That the ruler should not seek to please people through his own efforts, but should nevertheless direct himself toward that by which he ought to please. 42

**Chapter IX.**—What the ruler must diligently know: that vices often pretend to be virtues. 44

**Chapter X.**—What discernment the ruler’s correction and concealment, fervor and gentleness should have. Same page.

**Chapter XI.**—How devoted the ruler should be to meditation on sacred law. 48

## PART THREE OF THE BOOK OF THE PASTORAL RULE. 49

**Chapter I.**—How great the diversity should be in the art of preaching. 50

**Chapter II.**—How the poor and the rich should be admonished. 52

[Col. 1594]

**Chapter III.**—How the joyful and the sad should be admonished. 53

**Chapter IV.**—How subjects and prelates should be admonished. 54

**Chapter V.**—How servants and masters should be admonished. 56

**Chapter VI.**—How the wise and the dull should be admonished. Same page.

**Chapter VII.**—How the shameless and the modest should be admonished. 57

**Chapter VIII.**—How the insolent and the fainthearted should be admonished. 58

**Chapter IX.**—How the patient and the impatient should be admonished. 59

**Chapter X.**—How the benevolent and the envious should be admonished. 62

**Chapter XI.**—How the simple and the deceitful should be admonished. 64

**Chapter XII.**—How the healthy and the sick should be admonished. 66

**Chapter XIII.**—How those who fear punishments and those who despise them should be admonished. 70

**Chapter XIV.**—How the taciturn and the talkative should be admonished. 71

**Chapter XV.**—How the sluggish and the rash should be admonished. 74

**Chapter XVI.**—How the gentle and the hot-tempered should be admonished. 75

**Chapter XVII.**—How the humble and the haughty should be admonished. 77

**Chapter XVIII.**—How the obstinate and the fickle should be admonished. 79

**Chapter XIX.**—How those who use food too immoderately and those who use it more sparingly should be admonished. 81

**Chapter XX.**—How those who distribute their own possessions and those who seize what belongs to others should be admonished. 83

**Chapter XXI.**—How those who do not desire what belongs to others but retain their own, and those who give away their own yet seize what belongs to others, should be admonished. 87

**Chapter XXII.**—How the quarrelsome and the peaceful should be admonished. 89

**Chapter XXIII.**—How those who sow quarrels and those who make peace should be admonished. 92

**Chapter XXIV.**—How the uneducated in sacred doctrine, and the learned but not humble, should be admonished. 93

**Chapter XXV.**—How those who decline the office of preaching through excessive humility, and those who seize it through rash haste, should be admonished. 96

**Chapter XXVI.**—How those to whom everything turns out as they wish, and those for whom nothing does, should be admonished. 99

**Chapter XXVII.**—How married people and celibates should be admonished. 101

**Chapter XXVIII.**—How those who have experienced sins of the flesh, and those who have not, should be admonished. 104

**Chapter XXIX.**—How those who mourn sins committed in action, and those who mourn only sins of thought, should be admonished. 107

**Chapter XXX.**—How those who do not abstain from the sins they lament, and those who abstain from them but do not lament them, should be admonished. 109

**Chapter XXXI.**—How those who praise the sins of which they are conscious, and those who condemn them but nevertheless take no care to avoid them, should be admonished. 112

[Col. 1595]

**Chapter XXXII.**—How those who sin through sudden impulse and those who sin deliberately should be admonished. 113

**Chapter XXXIII.**—How those who fall into minor but frequent offenses, and those who avoid minor offenses yet sometimes plunge into serious ones, should be admonished. 115

**Chapter XXXIV.**—How those who neither begin good works and those who do not complete what they have begun should be admonished. 117

**Chapter XXXV.**—How those who perform evil secretly and good publicly, and those who do the reverse, should be admonished. 119

**Chapter XXXVI.**—On exhortation addressed to many, so that it may assist the virtues of individuals in such a way that through it vices contrary to the virtues do not grow up. 121

**Chapter XXXVII.**—On exhortation addressed to one person struggling with contrary passions. 122

**Chapter XXXVIII.**—That sometimes lesser vices must be left alone so that more serious ones may be removed. 123

**Chapter XXXIX.**—That nothing else at all should be preached to weak minds. 124

**Chapter XL.**—On the work and voice of preaching. Same page.

## PART FOUR OF THE BOOK OF THE PASTORAL RULE

How the preacher, when everything has been properly accomplished, should return to himself, lest either his life or his preaching exalt him. 125

Argument of the four books of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great. 127

Vindication of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great, by Peter Gussanvillaeus. 129

Preface to the Books of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory. 137

## FOUR BOOKS OF THE DIALOGUES. 149–431

Preface to the Letters of Saint Gregory the Great. 431

## BOOK ONE OF THE LETTERS. 441

**Letter I** *(to all the bishops of Sicily).*—He declares that his responsibilities in Sicily have been entrusted to Peter the subdeacon. He decrees that the bishops of the province meet once a year. He advises them what must be guarded against and what must be done in council. 441

**Letter II** *(to Justin, praetor of Sicily).*—He urges Justin, both amicably and seriously, to strive for peace with the priests and justice toward everyone, and to ensure that the full grain allowance is sent. 443

**Letter III** *(to Paul the scholasticus).*—He rebukes Paul for congratulating him on the pontificate. He commends Maurentius and Peter the subdeacon to him. 446

**Letter IV** *(to John, bishop of Constantinople).*—He complains that he had arranged for his own election to be confirmed by the emperor. He commends himself to John’s prayers. He promises a synodical letter. 447

**Letter V** *(to Theoctista, the emperor’s sister).*—He laments that he has been snatched from the repose of contemplation into the tumult of affairs. He compares the contemplative life to Rachel and Mary, and the active life to Leah and Martha. 448

**Letter VI** *(to Narses the patrician).*—He grieves that he has been cast down from the delight of contemplation. 450

**Letter VII** *(to Anastasius, bishop of Antioch).*—He is distressed that he is weighed down by many occupations, and by Anastasius’s praise. 452

**Letter VIII** *(to Bacauda, bishop of Formiae).*—He unites the desolated Church of Minturnae to that of Formiae. 454

**Letter IX** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That a dispute concerning the boundaries of estates may be settled by forty years of possession. 455

**Letter X** *(to Bacauda and Agnellus, bishops).*—Concerning the transfer of the Jews’ synagogue if it impedes the services of the church. 457

**Letter XI** *(to Clementina the patrician).*—He consoles her over the death of Eutherius. Same page.

**Letter XII** *(to John, bishop of the Old City).*—He admonishes him not to continue harassing the monastery. 458

**Letter XIII** *(to Dominicus, bishop of Centumcellae).*—He commends Lumino­sa, the widow of Zemarchus, so that her comitiva may be preserved. 459

**Letter XIV** *(to Demetrius, bishop of Naples).*—That he receive certain people who were formerly doubtful in the faith but now seek again Catholic communion. Same page.

**Letter XV** *(to Balbinus, bishop of Rosella).*—He orders him to visit the Church of Populonia and ordain priests and deacons. 460

**Letter XVI** *(to Severus, bishop of Aquileia).*—He orders him to come to Rome with his followers to be judged in synod. 461

**Letter XVII** *(to all the bishops of Italy).*—That the sons of the Lombards baptized into the Arian heresy be reconciled to the Catholic faith. 462

**Letter XVIII** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he provide Marcellus with what is necessary for food and clothing, and arrange for shepherds to be substituted in the place and stead of those who have fallen. 463

**Letter XIX** *(to Natalis, bishop of Salona).*—That he restore the archdeacon Honoratus to his rank; then, if the dispute remains, let them plead the case at Rome. 464

[Col. 1596]

**Letter XX** *(to Honoratus, deacon of Salona).*—Concerning his dispute with his bishop, and concerning the custody of the Church’s property. 465

**Letter XXI** *(to Natalis, bishop of Salona).*—He opens his heart to Natalis, who has congratulated him on the pontificate, and asks for the support of his prayers. 466

**Letter XXII** *(to Nonnosus).*—He says that he will hear Maurentius concerning the possession he requested. 467

**Letter XXIII** *(to Gregory, superintendent of Italy).*—He attests their mutual affection. Same page.

**Letter XXIV** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That he distribute a fixed sum of solidi to certain servants of God, to the priest Paulinus, and to two monks. Same page.

**Letter XXV** *(to John, bishop of Constantinople, and the other patriarchs).*—He discusses at length the burden, qualities, and duties of a pastor, and finally professes the faith according to the standard of the councils. 468

**Letter XXVI** *(to Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch).*—He complains about the pastoral burden. 479

**Letter XXVII** *(to Anastasius, archbishop of Corinth).*—He sorrowfully announces his ordination and commends Boniface the defensor. 480

**Letter XXVIII** *(to Sebastian, bishop of Rhisinum).*—That he ascertain the mind of Anastasius, the patriarch expelled from his see, whom Gregory wished to live with him in honor. 481

**Letter XXIX** *(to Aristobulus, former prefect and antigraphus).*—He consoles him and asks that, when translating Gregory’s letters from Latin into Greek, he render not the words but the meaning. 482

**Letter XXX** *(to Andreas the illustrious).*—He grieves over his elevation to the episcopate; he sends a key from the body of Saint Peter. 483

**Letter XXXI** *(to John, former consul, patrician, and quaestor).*—He sends a key of Saint Peter and a relic from his chains. Same page.

**Letter XXXII** *(to Philip, count of the Excubitors).*—He explains why he finally consented to the episcopate and commends the affairs of Italy. 484

**Letter XXXIII** *(to Romanus, patrician and exarch of Italy).*—That he either allow Blandus the bishop to be judged in synod or let him return to his own Church. Same page.

**Letter XXXIV** *(to Venantius, former monk and Syracusan patrician).*—He rebukes Venantius for abandoning the monastic habit and urges him to recover himself as quickly as possible; he teaches him whose counsels he ought to heed. 486

**Letter XXXV** *(to Peter, bishop of Terracina).*—That he restore the place previously granted to the Jews. Those who disagree with the Christian religion are to be attracted kindly. 489

**Letter XXXVI** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—He continually rereads the memorandum given to him. He adds certain admonitions breathing the utmost justice and prudence. Same page.

**Letter XXXVII** *(to John, bishop of Ravenna).*—That he assist Maurilio, the former prefect. 492

**Letter XXXVIII** *(to Malchus, bishop of Dalmatia).*—That he compel Bishop Stephen to face judgment and carry out whatever is adjudged. Same page.

**Letter XXXIX** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—He rebukes him for neglecting the poor. He orders generous and liberal assistance to be offered to the ladies Pateria, Palatina, and Viviana. 493

**Letter XL** *(to Felix, bishop of Messana).*—That Paulinus, a foreign bishop, govern the monastery of Saint Theodore. Same page.

**Letter XLI** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he gather the monks dispersed throughout Sicily into the monastery of Saint Theodore at Messana. 494

**Letter XLII** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That he restrain wandering monks devoted to their own property and monks who have wives; and that he not allow those converted from the clergy to monasticism to return to the Church in which they served. 495

**Letter XLIII** *(to Leander, bishop of Seville).*—He groans over the episcopal burden. He rejoices at the conversion of King Reccared. He approves the custom introduced by the Spaniards, on the occasion of the Arians, of a single immersion in baptism. He sends several books. 496

**Letter XLIV** *(to Peter the subdeacon of Sicily).*—He orders numerous acts contrary to law to be corrected. He rules concerning the celibacy of subdeacons. 498

**Letter XLV** *(to all the bishops throughout Illyricum).*—That they receive bishops expelled by enemies and supply them with what they need. 508

**Letter XLVI** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—He orders him to provide what is necessary for the sustenance of Godiscalchus’s poor and blind son. Same page.

**Letter XLVII** *(to Virgilius of Arles and Theodore, bishop of Marseille).*—The Jews are not to be compelled to baptism, but gently encouraged to embrace the faith. 509

**Letter XLVIII** *(to Theodore, duke of Sardinia).*—That he order his official and the abbess Juliana to undergo judgment. He protects Pompeiana in a pious cause, without prejudice to her rights. 511

[Col. 1597]

**Letter XLIX** *(to Honoratus the deacon).*—What should be suggested to the emperors on behalf of the inhabitants of Sardinia. 512

**Letter L** *(to Authemius the subdeacon).*—That women not live with monks. That boys not be received into the monasteries of certain islands before the age of eighteen. 513

**Letter LI** *(to all the monks established on the island of Christ’s Mountain).*—He orders those irregular monks to obey Horosius the abbot. Same page.

**Letter LII** *(to Symmachus the defensor).*—Concerning the construction of a monastery in Corsica; the correction of the monks in Gorgona; and priests’ association with women. 514

**Letter LIII** *(to Felix, bishop of Sipontum).*—He orders him to visit the Church of Canusium and ordain two parish priests there. 515

**Letter LIV** *(to John, bishop of Surrentum).*—That he solemnly place the relics of Saint Agatha in the monastery of Saint Stephen. Same page.

**Letter LV** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That he allow neither the poor to be oppressed nor the son of a free woman to be forced into servitude. 516

**Letter LVI** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—What he should give for the celebration of a dedication, to be distributed among the poor. 517

**Letter LVII** *(to Severus the bishop).*—Concerning the election of the bishop of Ariminum. Same page.

**Letter LVIII** *(to Arsicinius the duke, the clergy, the council, and the people of Ariminum).*—That they not elect Ocleatinus as bishop. 518

**Letter LIX** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That he grant Palatina thirty solidi annually for her support. Same page.

**Letter LX** *(to the clergy, council, and people residing at Perusia).*—That they not delay the election of a bishop any longer. 519

**Letter LXI** *(to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa).*—That he order Theodore, master of the soldiers, to desist from harassing the poor and the Church. Same page.

**Letter LXII** *(to Januarius, archbishop of Caralis in Sardinia).*—That he protect Catella from the harassment of certain persons, without prejudice to justice. 520

**Letter LXIII** *(to Januarius, bishop of Caralis in Sardinia).*—He commends Pompeianus, so that he not be burdened contrary to equity. 521

**Letter LXIV** *(to Januarius, archbishop of Caralis).*—He commends Catella, a religious woman. Same page.

**Letter LXV** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That the house of Petronius, titled unjustly, be restored to that widow, Theodora. 522

**Letter LXVI** *(to Felix, bishop of Messana).*—He amicably advises which customs should be preserved and which abolished. He tells him not to send him gifts or come to Rome. Same page.

**Letter LXVII** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he provide Pastor, whose eyes are infirm, with an annual allowance for food. 523

**Letter LXVIII** *(to Anthemius the subdeacon).*—That he arrange for the sacred vessels of the Church of Venafrum, which the clergy had sold to a Jew, to be restored, and compel the guilty to do penance. 524

**Letter LXIX** *(to Peter the subdeacon of Sicily).*—All the disputes and business of the monastery are to be entrusted to an experienced layman. 525

**Letter LXX** *(to all the bishops throughout Sicily).*—How they should protect themselves against the exactions of false advocates. Same page.

**Letter LXXI** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he protect Cyriacus and his wife Joanna, a Christian woman of Jewish origin. 526

**Letter LXXII** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That all the Sicilian bishops not come to Rome before winter. Peter should procure more grain than usual and send it to the City at the proper time. Same page.

**Letter LXXIII** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—Concerning the restoration of the possessions and funds of the Church of Tauromenium. 527

**Letter LXXIV** *(to Gennadius, patrician and exarch of Africa).*—He incites him to suppress the attempts of heretics against the Church. That the primate not be elected according to rank of place. That he not reside outside the city. That Numidian bishops who wish to come to Rome not be prevented. 528

**Letter LXXV** *(to Gennadius, patrician and exarch throughout Africa).*—He praises Gennadius highly because he conquers peoples not for earthly advantage but so that the Christian religion may spread. He gives thanks for the inhabitants granted to the patrimony of the Roman Church. He commends Hilary, administrator of that patrimony. 529

**Letter LXXVI** *(to Gaudiosus, master of the soldiers in Africa).*—After formal greetings, he commends Hilary. 530

**Letter LXXVII** *(to all the bishops of Numidia).*—What he formerly refused, he now grants out of reverence for ancient custom: that the senior bishop be elected primate by that very fact. He receives a Donatist. He exhorts the Numidian bishops to peace, to the defense of the Church, and to concern for the souls of their neighbors. 531

**Letter LXXVIII** *(to Leo, bishop in Corsica).*—He assigns him the visitation of the Church of Sagona. 532

**Letter LXXIX** *(to Martin, bishop in Corsica).*—He permits him to transfer from the Church of Tainata to that of Sagona. 533

**Letter LXXX** *(to the clergy and nobles of Corsica).*—Because they had delayed the election of a bishop too long, he himself appoints Martin. Meanwhile, until Martin arrives, he entrusts Leo with the care of the visitation. Same page.

**Letter LXXXI** *(to the clergy, council, and people of Mevania).*—He urges them finally to agree on the election of a bishop. Meanwhile, he entrusts the care of the Church to the priest Honoratus. 534

**Letter LXXXII** *(to Laurence, bishop of Milan).*—That he appoint someone by whom the dispute that had arisen over the money requested may be settled. 535

**Letter LXXXIII** *(to Januarius, archbishop of Caralis).*—That the ambition of the deacon Liberatus be restrained, and that he not be incardinated in any way without the solemn release of his own bishop. 536

**Letter LXXXIV** *(to Hilary, a monk of Africa).*—That a council be convened as soon as possible and an investigation be made into Argentium, bishop of Lamigium. 537

**Letter LXXXV** *(to Gennadius, patrician of Africa).*—He commends Droculfus, returned from the enemy. 538

## BOOK TWO OF THE LETTERS. 539

**Letter I** *(to Peter the notary).*—The monks of Tropaeum are to be assisted in every way if they live religiously. Same page.

**Letter II** *(to Praiectus, bishop of Narnia).*—On the occasion of the deadly plague, the citizens are to be exhorted to penance and faith. Same page.

**Letter III** *(to Velox, master of the soldiers).*—That he pursue Ariulf, duke of the Lombards, from behind if he makes an incursion toward the Roman or Ravennate territories. 540

**Letter IV** *(to Sabinus the subdeacon).*—The garden of Felicianus is to be given to the monastery of the servants of God. Same page.

**Letter V** *(to Felix, bishop of Messana).*—That the basilica be consecrated after a lawful and secure endowment has first been received. 541

**Letter VI** *(to the Neapolitans).*—In place of Demetrius, deposed for unspeakable crimes, they are to elect a bishop without delay or discord. 542

**Letter VII** *(to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse).*—That he act as Gregory’s representative in Sicily, while reserving the more important cases. 543

**Letter VIII** *(to Bishop Candidus).*—That the customary stipends not be denied to a sick cleric. 544

**Letter IX** *(to the Neapolitans).*—Let them test Paul for a longer time and join themselves to him in humble charity; eventually, if he produces fruit among souls and God so inspires, they will obtain him as bishop. 545

**Letter X** *(to Paul, bishop of Naples).*—Meanwhile let him perform his episcopal duties in such a way that the testimony and votes of the Neapolitans may be confirmed. 546

**Letter XI** *(to the Nepesines).*—Concerning Leontius, sent there, that they obey him. 547

**Letter XII** *(to Castorius, bishop of Ariminum).*—Concerning the consecration of the oratory of the Holy Cross. 548

**Letter XIII** *(to Importunus, bishop of Atella).*—He admonishes the suffragan bishop concerning the priest whom he had appointed to preside over a certain church in that bishop’s diocese. 549

**Letter XIV** *(to John, bishop of Velletri).*—The bishop’s seat is to be transferred to a safer place. Same page.

**Letter XV** *(to Paul the bishop).*—He urges Paul, to whom he had entrusted the Church of Naples, who was already thinking too soon about returning, to persevere there. He replies concerning the deacon Peter that Peter has nothing to fear and that there will be no place with Gregory for underhanded action. 550

**Letter XVI** *(to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse).*—He places Paulinus, bishop of Tauriana, over the Church of Lipari. 551

**Letter XVII** *(to Paulinus the bishop).*—He is to reside in the Church of Lipari but visit Tauriana at a suitable time. 552

**Letter XVIII** *(to Natalis, bishop of Salona).*—After rebuking Natalis for his constant banquets, he orders him to restore the archdeacon Honoratus to his place. Same page.

**Letter XIX** *(to all the bishops of Dalmatia).*—He explains what was done in the case of Natalis and Honoratus. 554

**Letter XX** *(to Antoninus the subdeacon).*—After again setting out the same case, he orders Antoninus to urge Natalis to restore Honoratus to his place: if Natalis does not comply, he is first to be deprived of the use of the pallium and then of communion. Once Honoratus has finally been restored, the bishop is to send a representative, while the archdeacon himself is to come to Rome, so that both may state their case. A guarantor is also summoned on behalf of Bishop Malchus. 555

**Letter XXI** *(to Jobinus, prefect of Illyricum).*—He rejoices that the province devastated by barbarians is being revived under Jobinus’s administration. He commends the administrator of the patrimony. He urges Jobinus not to assist Bishop Natalis against justice. 557

**Letter XXII** *(to all the bishops of Illyricum).*—He confirms the ordination of Bishop John. Same page.

**Letter XXIII** *(to John the bishop).*—He congratulates him on having been elected by unanimous consent. According to custom, he gives him the pallium and the vicariate of the apostolic see. He urges him to fulfill the pastoral office with the highest prudence and charity. 558

**Letter XXIV** *(to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse).*—That he carefully examine the priest commended by Felix and send him to Rome if he finds him worthy of the episcopate. 560

**Letter XXV** *(to Benenatus the bishop).*—He delegates to him the visitation of the Church of Cumae, both to protect that Church and to arrange for a suitable priest to be chosen from its clergy. 561

**Letter XXVI** *(to John the bishop).*—He entrusts him with the visitation of the Church of Nepete. 562

**Letter XXVII** *(to Rusticiana, the patrician woman).*—The good conceived in the heart by the Creator’s gift must be completed with swift and steadfast devotion. If anyone contrives slanders against us, the whole hope of the mind must be directed toward God. Same page.

**Letter XXVIII** *(to Stephen the chartularius).*—He is to order two monks who deserted their status to be confined again, and not allow new customs to be imposed on the monastery. 563

**Letter XXIX** *(to Maurilius and Vitalianus).*—If Ariulf proceeds to Rome, they are to pursue him from behind. 564

**Letter XXX** *(to Maurilius and Vitalianus).*—He warns them about the doubtful faith of the Suanenses and the army Ariulf has prepared. Same page.

**Letter XXXI** *(to all the Neapolitan soldiers).*—Concerning the obedience to be shown to the tribune Constantius. 565

**Letter XXXII** *(to Peter the subdeacon of Sicily).*—He gives many orders concerning the administration of the patrimony, in which justice, religion, prudence, and a generous spirit toward the needy shine forth; his personal affection for Peter is also readily apparent. Same page.

**Letter XXXIII** *(to Justin the praetor).*—That, laying aside all suspicion, he show complete charity and appropriate respect to Bishop Leo, who has been fully cleared of false accusations. 571

**Letter XXXIV** *(to Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse).*—That he console Abbot Eusebius, whom he had afflicted imprudently. 572

**Letter XXXV** *(to John, bishop of Ravenna).*—He congratulates him on the charitable services he showed to the sick Bishop Castorius. He asks that Castorius be sent to him through Sicily. He entrusts the Ravennate with responsibility for the suffragan bishops whom intervening enemies kept separated from Rome. 573

**Letter XXXVI** *(to Eusebius the abbot).*—He rebukes him for pride because he rejected the grace and communion restored by Bishop Maximianus. He gives him one hundred solidi. 574

**Letter XXXVII** *(to John, bishop of Squillace).*—He appoints John bishop of Squillace on the condition that he return to the Church of Lissus if it should happen to be freed from the enemies; that he abstain from illicit ordinations; and that he fulfill the pastoral office he has undertaken worthily. 575

**Letter XXXVIII** *(to John the bishop).*—After the death of its bishop, he entrusts him with the visitation and care of the Church of Croton. 576

**Letter XXXIX** *(to the clergy, council, and people of Croton).*—That they obey John, the visiting bishop, and ask for a suitable priest for themselves. 577

**Letter XL** *(to John the bishop).*—That he judge the case of Viulandus against Gravinianus without further delay. Same page.

**Letter XLI** *(to Castorius the bishop).*—Neither Bishop Castorius nor his successors, after the death of the abbot of Ariminum, are to record or administer the monastery’s property; they are not to appoint another abbot except the one requested by the community; and they are not to celebrate public Masses in the monastery. 578

**Letter XLII** *(to Luminosus the abbot).*—He writes concerning all the grievances brought forward by that monastery, so that the divine work may be carried on there with complete tranquility and devotion. 580

**Letter XLIII** *(to Felix the bishop).*—He entrusts him with the visitation of three vacant churches. 581

**Letter XLIV** *(to Lucillus the bishop).*—That he compel his clerics to pay without delay the rent for the lands of the African Church which they held. Same page.

**Letter XLV** *(to Benenatus the bishop).*—He unites the Churches of Cumae and Misenum and appoints Benenatus bishop of both. 582

**Letter XLVI** *(to John the bishop).*—He excuses himself for not having replied to John’s letters, citing illness. He urges him to incline Romanus toward making peace with Ariulf. Concerning the schismatic bishops of Istria, he asserts that he will write to the emperors to compel them to unity. One who has already been ordained is not to be ordained again. The exarch is to be warned about the danger facing the city of Naples. Mercy must first be shown to the faithful rather than to the enemies of the Church. He says that he has been consoled by the correction of Bishop Natalis. He demands accounts from Bishop Malchus, formerly administrator of the patrimony. 583

**Letter XLVII** *(to Dominicus the bishop).*—The delay of the congratulatory letter on his ordination is compensated by exceptional charity. This mother of virtues, which he praises in various ways, must be held with unshaken steadfastness. Just as he defends the privileges of the Roman Church, so he preserves the rights of each individual Church. 586

**Letter XLVIII** *(to Columbanus the bishop).*—Maximianus, bishop of the Church of Pudentiana, is to be deposed by a duly convened council if, corrupted by money, he allowed a Donatist bishop to be made in his city. Certain other private matters are to be settled privately. He grieves that the Donatist heresy is spreading and, so that Catholics may not defect to it, kindles pastoral zeal. 588

**Letter XLIX** *(to Januarius the archbishop).*—After hearing complaints about Bishop Januarius, he sends John the notary to compel the parties to judgment and execute whatever is judged. He rebukes Januarius especially because he excommunicated Isidore for no reason except a personal injury. 590

**Letter L** *(to John the bishop).*—He unites the Church of the Three Taverns, desolated by enemies, to that of Velletri. 591

**Letter LI** *(to all the bishops).*—It is useless for schismatics to boast about persecution. After the Three Chapters were condemned, nothing was changed in the faith. It cannot rightly be inferred from the scourges of Italy that Italy itself had erred. He sends Pelagius’s book; if they read it with a pure heart, he trusts that, since it invites them as sons to return to the Church, they will return. 592

**Letter LII** *(to Natalis the bishop).*—The profane banquets to which Natalis indulged, and his negligence regarding sacred reading, are not properly excused by him. Gregory rejoices in his zeal for exhortation. He is saddened by Natalis’s praise of him. Not only are heretics to be recalled to the Church, but those within the Church are also to be recalled to upright living. He complains that Natalis despised his own judgment and that of his predecessor; nevertheless, he spares him because he has returned to his rank and promises the utmost fairness in judging his case. 595

**Letter LIII** *(to Honoratus the deacon).*—That he favor Venantius, who has requested from the emperors the documents of his former consulship in return for thirty pounds of gold. 598

**Letter LIV.** *([Here begins a letter of Saint Licinianus, bishop, concerning the Book of the Rules, addressed to Saint Gregory, pope of the city of Rome].)*—He praises the Book of the Pastoral Rule; nevertheless, he objects that there will be no one to celebrate the sacred mysteries unless sometimes less experienced men are ordained. He requests the books on Job and the other moral works written by Gregory. 599

## BOOK THREE OF THE LETTERS. 603

**Letter I** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—He sends Epiphanius the subdeacon to investigate the sedition stirred up against Bishop Paul. He urgently orders Peter to assist Epiphanius in prosecuting the guilty, without any delay or partiality toward persons. Slaves are to be recalled to the churches of the city. Same page.

**Letter II** *(to Paul the bishop).*—He consoles him over the injury he received. 604

**Letter III** *(to John the abbot).*—He approves Boniface’s appointment as superintendent. He asks for Saint John’s tunic. In the case involving Florianus, he wishes something to be yielded so that a settlement may be reached. He rebukes the abbot because both he and the brothers neglect sacred reading and prayer. He urges him to take more diligent care of the brothers’ souls, guests, and the poor. 605

**Letter IV** *(to Boniface the bishop).*—The desire for human praise must be avoided in good works. 606

**Letter V** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he protect a widow in all her cases from the violence of the unjust. Same page.

**Letter VI** *(to John the bishop).*—He deprives him of sacred communion because he unjustly condemned Bishop Adrian, whom he orders to be restored to his place and rank. 607

**Letter VII** *(to John the bishop).*—He demonstrates from the order of the trial that Adrian’s unjust condemnation was procured through the machinations of John the metropolitan. He therefore orders John to abstain from all jurisdiction over Adrian and threatens him with deprivation of sacred communion if he does not comply. 609

**Letter VIII** *(to Natalis the archbishop).*—Bishop Florentius, deposed without a council’s judgment, is to be recalled from exile, and his case reconsidered after the bishops have been convened. 611

**Letter IX** *(to Antonius the subdeacon).*—That, if Florentius is acquitted by the assembled bishops, he arrange for all his property to be restored. 612

[Col. 1601]

**Letter X** *(to Sabinus the subdeacon).*—Gregory accepts and venerates the four books of the Gospel just as he accepts and venerates the four councils. He declares that the faith of Chalcedon was not violated in the Fifth Synod. Sabinus must therefore return to the unity of the Church. 613

**Letter XI** *(to the council and people of Alba).*—The bishop ordained for them. Same page.

**Letter XII** *(to Maximianus the bishop).*—That he send to Rome the accusers of the bishop of Agrigentum and the documents relating to his case. 614

**Letter XIII** *(to Agnellus the bishop).*—He places Agnellus over the Church of Terracina without depriving the Church of Fundi of its rights or authority. Same page.

**Letter XIV** *(to the people of Terracina).*—He urges them to obey their bishop Agnellus in everything. 615

**Letter XV** *(to Scholasticus the judge).*—When Florentius the subdeacon, elected by the Neapolitans, avoided the episcopate by flight, they must consider electing another. 616

**Letter XVI** *(to Peter the bishop).*—He commends the priest Valerianus, who has come for the redemption of captives. Same page.

**Letter XVII** *(to Gratiosus the subdeacon).*—That he hand over to Abbess Flora a house with gardens and lodging places for the construction of a monastery. 617

**Letter XVIII** *(to Theodore the counselor).*—He confirms in writing the gift of the boy Acosimus, already made to Theodore. 618

**Letter XIX** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—That he send the relics of Saint Severinus for the consecration of a church. Same page.

**Letter XX** *(to Gratiosus the bishop).*—He unites the Church of Saint Anthemius to that of Nomentum. 619

**Letter XXI** *(to Paschalis, Demetianus, and Castorius).*—He returns to the orphans the property of their father, which had been pledged to the Church, and completely remits the money he owed. 620

**Letter XXII** *(to Antoninus the subdeacon).*—That he arrange for a bishop of Salona to be elected and ordained at Rome. He is to warn that in the election only the distinction of life and character should be considered. He is to entrust the recorded property of the Church to selected men for safekeeping. Bishop Malchus is to abstain from it and hasten to come to Rome finally to complete the accounts of the patrimony he administered. Same page.

**Letter XXIII** *(to Peter the subdeacon).*—The abbot Secundinus is to be deposed for his crimes, and Theodosius, requested by the community, is to be ordained. 622

**Letter XXIV** *(to Leontius the bishop).*—That, while Bishop Castorius is ill and absent, he govern the Church of Ariminum. Same page.

**Letter XXV** *(to the citizens of Ariminum).*—Concerning their bishop’s illness, he orders them to obey Leontius in everything. 623

**Letter XXVI** *(to Magnus the priest).*—He absolves the man whom Bishop Laurence had once excommunicated undeservedly. He urges him to minister to his Church purely and diligently, and to admonish the clergy and people to elect a suitable bishop without dissension. Same page.

**Letter XXVII** *(to Marinianus and Benenatus).*—That they investigate Boniface; if he is found guilty, he is to be deprived of sacred communion and confined in a monastery. 624

**Letter XXVIII** *(to Romanus the patrician).*—That, for Armenius, a needy orphan, ...
and of noble birth, provide him with a position or employment from which he may be supported by daily wages.

**625 EPISTLE XXIX (to the priests and clergy of Milan).**—He does not press for the election of Constantius, although Constantius is very well known and a friend of his. He gives an excellent description of what sort of pastor there ought to be and what the disposition of those making the election should be. From the regions of the earth he indicates that the end of the world and the judgment are near.

**626 EPISTLE XXX (to John the subdeacon).**—He is to investigate at Genoa the votes of the Milanese; if they agree on Constantius, he is to have him consecrated by his own bishops.

**627 EPISTLE XXXI (to Romanus the patrician).**—He commends Constantius, who is very dear to him.

**628 EPISTLE XXXII (to Honoratus the archdeacon).**—He confirms his absolution. The matters about which Honoratus had complained he entrusts to Antoninus for investigation. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXIII (to Dynamius the patrician).**—He states that he has received four hundred solidi from the revenues of the Roman Church. He sends a cross filled with sacred relics.

**630 EPISTLE XXXIV (to Peter the subdeacon).**—He is to reconcile Bishop Festus with his citizens.

**631 EPISTLE XXXV (to Peter the subdeacon).**—Two or three men are to be sent from the Neapolitan clergy to Rome, so that they may elect a bishop on behalf of everyone. The future bishop is to be supplied with what is necessary. To Paul, who is withdrawing, he is to give one hundred solidi for his labor, together with one slave. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXVI (to Sabinus the defensor).**—He is to bring to Rome Januarius the bishop and Epiphanius the priest, who have been accused of crimes. He is also to assist Pompeina, Theodosia, [Col. 1602] and Isidore, who wish to come to Rome.

**632 EPISTLE XXXVII (to Bona the abbess).**—He orders a monastery to be built and confirms everything bequeathed to her by the priest John.

**633 EPISTLE XXXVIII (to Libertinus the prefect).**—He is to punish Nasas, the Jewish seducer, and also free the Christian slaves whom Nasas purchased.

**635 EPISTLE XXXIX (to the bishops of Corinth).**—He sends a deacon to investigate the reconciliation that is said to have taken place between Adrian and the bishops who accused him.

**636 EPISTLE XL (to Peter the subdeacon).**—If he judges the deacon Numerius worthy of the episcopate, he is to send him to Rome for consecration. If the slave-woman Catella sincerely seeks the monastic habit, he is to redeem her from Felix. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLI (to Pantaleon the notary).**—The ravisher of a virgin must either marry her or, after corporal punishment, be thrust into a monastery. A deacon held captive is to be redeemed at the Church’s expense.

**637 EPISTLE XLII (to Felix the bishop).**—The ecclesiastical furnishings, money, and other property of the Church of Sipontum are to be inventoried, and the list is to be sent to Rome.

**638 EPISTLE XLIII (to Felix the bishop).**—He rebukes the bishop for the rape committed by his nephew and imposes upon him the execution of the sentence passed against the offender.

**639 EPISTLE XLIV (to Boniface the bishop).**—He is to restore Stephania’s property, which had been seized by the agents of his predecessor. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLV (to Andrew the bishop).**—He urges him to lay down the priesthood if he is conscious of having sinned with a concubine. Because he ordered a woman to be beaten with clubs, he commands him to abstain from celebrating Mass for two months.

**640 EPISTLE XLVI (to John the bishop).**—Bishop Andrew is to be prohibited from ministry if, while constituted in sacred orders, he has had relations with a concubine. The same man is to be suspended from celebrating Mass because he had a woman beaten with clubs. The complaints of some of his clergy against him are also to be examined.

**641 EPISTLE XLVII (to the clergy of the Church of Salona).**—He approves Honoratus’s election as bishop.

**642 EPISTLE XLVIII (to Columbus the bishop).**—After offering testimony of singular benevolence, he urges him neither to ordain boys nor to confer orders out of favoritism or for money, and to inform him of the state of the council. He sends something taken from the chains of blessed Peter, enclosed within keys. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLIX (to Adeodatus the bishop).**—After a friendly greeting, he urges him to fulfill his office, especially not to ordain anyone except those advanced in age and blameless in conduct, and not to allow venality in ordinations. He is to make use of the counsel of Bishop Maximian. Finally, after the synod has been completed, he is to inform him of the agreement achieved.

**644 EPISTLE L (to Theodore the bishop).**—He praises him for carefully investigating and reporting the lives of priests. He orders Bishop Paul to remain in the monastery for penance. His property is to be inventoried and preserved. An inquiry is to be made into Boniface, who has been gravely accused.

**645 EPISTLE LI (to Maximian the bishop).**—Intending to write about miracles performed by the Fathers in Italy, he asks Maximian to relate those of which he has knowledge.

**646 EPISTLE LII (to Priscus the patrician).**—From the alternation of prosperity and adversity he recommends humility. He congratulates him on having recovered the favor of the emperors. He commends Sabinianus and Castus. Ibid.

**EPISTLE LIII (to John the bishop).**—He attributes the fabricated and foolish response concerning the case of the priests John and Athanasius, wholly unbecoming the holiness of Bishop John, to a wicked young man, whose counsels John was excessively inclined to follow. He presses most vigorously for the case to be concluded according to the canons. He commends his apocrisarius Sabinianus.

**647 EPISTLE LIV (to Theotimus the physician).**—After a most friendly greeting, he commends Sabinianus.

**649 EPISTLE LV (to Maximian the bishop).**—He provides for the support of Bishop Agatho, against whom strict judgment had been exacted.

**650 EPISTLE LVI (to John the bishop).**—He is no longer to wear the pallium in the streets unless he can show that it was granted to him by the Roman pontiffs. Henceforth he is not to sit in the secretarium wearing the pallium. He is to investigate certain of his clergy and forbid the obstinate to exercise sacred ministry. He grants the use of the mappulae only to the first deacons of the Church of Ravenna. Ibid.

**EPISTLE LVII (John, bishop of Ravenna, to Pope Gregory).**—He humbly answers each of the charges brought against him and defends the privileges of his Church on the basis of custom; he asks that these privileges not be diminished.

**654 EPISTLE LVIII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—If Cosmas has no means of paying, he is to come to an agreement with his creditors; and, after paying the agreed sum, he is to free Cosmas’s sons.

**656 EPISTLE LIX (to Secundinus the bishop).**—The baptistery is to be removed from the monastery, so that the monks may celebrate the Work of God more securely.

**657 EPISTLE LX (to Italica the patrician).**—Even in the cases of the poor, he chooses silence so as not to become involved in litigation. He gives Cyprian authority, if Italica herself wishes it, to settle the case without litigation while safeguarding the rights of the poor. Ibid.

**EPISTLE LXI (to Fortunatus the bishop).**—How he ought to conduct himself in his Church.

**658 EPISTLE LXII (to Eutychius the bishop).**—He urges him to persevere in converting worshipers of idols. He asks him for the praetor’s protection.

**659 EPISTLE LXIII (to Fortunatus the bishop).**—Concerning the consecration of the monastery of the abbess Gratiosa.

**660 EPISTLE LXIV (to Chrysanthus the bishop).**—He is to seek a bishop for the Church of Mevania, ordain priests, and there consign infants [to baptism].

**661 EPISTLE LXV (to Maurice Augustus).**—He begs him to moderate or alter the law by which he had prohibited both those involved in public administration and soldiers from being received into monasteries.

**662 EPISTLE LXVI (to Theodore the physician).**—Having demonstrated the injustice of the enacted law, he urges Theodore to present his letter to the emperor and persuade him to revoke the law.

**665 EPISTLE LXVII (to Domitian the metropolitan).**—He defends the interpretation, given earlier by himself, of the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34), according to its spiritual meaning. Gregory congratulates Domitian both because, although occupied with secular affairs, he meditates on the Scriptures, and because he has preached the faith to the Persian emperor.

**666 BOOK IV OF THE LETTERS.**

**667 FIRST EPISTLE (to Constantius the bishop).**—He congratulates him on having been elected by the unanimous agreement of all. He advises him to respond to the affections of his people, assist those in need, and correct vices promptly. He prays for his progress in goodness. He sends the pallium. Ibid.

**EPISTLE II (to Constantius the bishop).**—He hopes that Queen Theodelinda and three bishops, who had separated from Constantius over the Three Chapters, will return to his communion after receiving his letters. Desiring peace with the Lombards, he asks Constantius to inform him about what has occurred between the Franks and the king of the Lombards.

**669 EPISTLE III (to Constantius the bishop).**—Constantius has given no assurance concerning the Three Chapters. The faith of the Council of Chalcedon is preserved intact in the Roman Church. Accordingly, the divided bishops must return to unity.

**670 EPISTLE IV (to Queen Theodelinda).**—He is grieved that she has withdrawn from communion with Constantius. He declares that nothing contrary to the faith of the Council of Chalcedon was done in the time of Justinian. He urges her to accept Constantius’s ordination and join herself to him in communion.

**671 EPISTLE V (to Boniface the bishop).**—He is to take care of the conduct and reputation of his clergy. Concerning his subdeacons he decrees what he previously decreed concerning the Sicilians, Book I, Letter 44.

**672 EPISTLE VI (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to investigate and punish the crime of Petronilla, a convert, and Agnellus, her corrupter, and ensure that what was taken from the monastery is restored. Ibid.

**EPISTLE VII (to Gennadius the patrician).**—He is to support Bishop Columbus, who is investigating the council in Numidia and correcting the wicked. He is to restrain the internal wars of the Churches.

**673 EPISTLE VIII (to Januarius the bishop).**—He is to ensure that the deceased Stephen’s wish concerning the construction of a monastery is fulfilled.

**674 EPISTLE IX (to Januarius the bishop).**—A reputable man is to be assigned to each monastery of the servants of God, by whom their affairs are to be administered so that the nuns may not thereafter be permitted to wander about. Penalties are decreed for their lapses. Councils are to be held twice a year. Jewish slaves fleeing to the Church for the sake of the faith are to be claimed for freedom. Chrismation is not to be repeated on the foreheads of those who have already been baptized: the priests are to anoint only the chest, and then the bishops the forehead. A monastery is to be built according to the wish of the deceased Peter, if a sufficient amount of revenue is available.

**675 EPISTLE X (to all the bishops of Dalmatia).**—They are not to ordain any bishop at Salona without his consent and permission. If, however, they all agree on someone other than Maximus, that man is to be consecrated.

**677 EPISTLE XI (to Maximian the bishop).**—Even a quarter of new revenues is to be distributed according to the canonical allocation. A priest or another cleric is not to become an abbot unless he leaves the care of the Church in which he served. When a bishop dies, the Church’s property is to be inventoried carefully, but without charge. A stipend is to be provided for visitors and their clergy. A virgin not yet sixty years old is not to become abbess.

**679 EPISTLE XII (to Maximian the bishop).**—The crime by which someone’s wife was taken away and sold to another is to be punished.

**681 EPISTLE XIII (to Clementius the bishop).**—If the priest Adeodatus has been absent from his Church solely because of illness, he is to be restored to his position. [Col. 1604]

**682 EPISTLE XIV (to Maximian the bishop).**—He is to receive the deacon Felix into his Church.

**683 EPISTLE XV (to Januarius the bishop).**—He is to assist Theodosia, who intends to build a monastery in her own house.

**684 EPISTLE XVI (to Cyprian the deacon).**—The Church vessels that the Italian priests had scattered and carried into Sicily are to be collected and kept with the greatest care.

**685 EPISTLE XVII (to Felix the bishop).**—He is to repay the redeemer from the Church’s funds the twelve solidi by which the cleric Tribunus was redeemed.

**686 EPISTLE XVIII (to Maurus the abbot).**—He grants the monks in perpetuity the Church of Saint Pancratius, both so that the celebration of Mass may not thereafter be neglected and so that the Work of God may be performed daily at the martyr’s body.

**687 EPISTLE XIX (to Leo the acolyte).**—He commends the Church of Saint Agatha in the Subura.

**688 EPISTLE XX (to Maximus the intruder).**—He removes Maximus, who had been forcibly intruded, and the bishops who ordained him, from every priestly office until the truth of the emperor’s command has been established.

**689 EPISTLE XXI (to Venantius the bishop).**—Jews may not retain a Christian slave; but Christians who have long cultivated Jewish lands are to continue cultivating them under the law of tenant-farming.

**690 EPISTLE XXII (to Constantius the bishop).**—He urges him to assist Bishop Venantius of Luni in correcting his clergy and the other religious persons.

**691 EPISTLE XXIII (to Hospito, duke of the Barbaricini).**—He is to support Felix and Cyriacus, who are laboring to convert the Barbaricini from idolatry.

**692 EPISTLE XXIV (to Zabarda, duke of Sardinia).**—He gives thanks that Zabarda intends to make peace with the Barbaricini on the condition that they serve Christ.

**693 EPISTLE XXV (to the nobles and landowners in Sardinia).**—He rebukes them because they do not turn their peasants away from the worship of idols; if they cannot do this, at least they are to assist Felix and Cyriacus, who have been sent for this work. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXVI (to Januarius the bishop).**—He orders the clerics by whom he was held in contempt to be compelled to submit to discipline. A peasant obstinate in unbelief is to be burdened with a rent obligation. Clerics who have fallen through sexual misconduct are to be irrevocably deposed. They are to be carefully examined before ordination. He grants the priests of Sardinia what he had forbidden: namely, that, when bishops are absent, they may touch on the forehead with chrism those whom they baptize.

**694 EPISTLE XXVII (to Januarius the bishop).**—He is to demand accounts from the hospices; their clerks are to be men of recognized honesty and diligence. If the man who accused the priest Epiphanius in written letters fails to establish his charge, he is to be deprived of communion. The cleric Paul, if caught in criminal acts, is to be assigned to penance. Clerics are to be ordained or joined in marriage without payment; virgins are to receive the veil without payment. Clerics are not to seek the patronage of laymen.

**697 EPISTLE XXVIII (to Candidus the defensor).**—He is to provide Albinus, who has lost his sight, with two tremisses each year.

**700 EPISTLE XXIX (to Januarius the bishop).**—Phausiana, which formerly had a bishop, is to have one now as well. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXX (to Constantina Augusta).**—To dissuade Constantina, who is requesting the head of Saint Paul, he recounts various prodigies. He adds that it is the Roman custom to grant only *brandea* to those who request relics. He responds to the objection based on Greek custom. Finally, he promises that fragments of Saint Paul will be struck off from the chains with a file. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXI (to Theodore the physician).**—He gives thanks for the money sent for the poor. He urges him to read Sacred Scripture. He commends Narses and sends gifts, including tablets.

**705 EPISTLE XXXII (to Narses the patrician).**—He declares that he will examine the case of the priests with John the patriarch entirely according to the rule of the canons. He commends to Narses Theodore, whom he had himself commended. He excuses the brevity of the letter because he is weighed down by tribulations.

**707 EPISTLE XXXIII (to Anthemius the subdeacon).**—He is to give converted Jews three solidi each year.

**708 EPISTLE XXXIV (to Pantaleon the prefect).**—He urges him to suppress the audacity of the Donatists and send Bishop Paul to Rome as quickly as possible. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXV (to Victor and Columbus the bishops).**—After convening a council, they are to resist the Donatists promptly and vigorously. They are to send Bishop Paul to him, so that, once he has disclosed the matter and the crimes of the Donatists are more clearly known, he may decide more safely how they are to be punished and restrained.

**709 EPISTLE XXXVI (to Leo the bishop).**—Subdeacons are not to have sexual relations with their wives. The wife of the subdeacon Speciosus, who had been thrust into a monastery because of a second marriage, is to be released.

**710 [Col. 1605] EPISTLE XXXVII (to Maximian the bishop).**—He orders Euplus’s paternal and maternal property to be returned.

**711 EPISTLE XXXVIII (to Queen Theodelinda).**—He is grieved that she has been led astray by the ignorant. He professes that the faith of the four holy synods, especially the Council of Chalcedon, is preserved intact in the Roman Church. He urges her not to remain outside communion with Bishop Constantius.

**712 EPISTLE XXXIX (to Constantius the bishop).**—He is not to swear to the citizens of Brescia that he has in no way condemned the Three Chapters, but is to profess in a letter the intact faith of the Council of Chalcedon. He is not to name John of Ravenna during the solemn celebration of Mass unless ancient custom requires it, or unless John himself customarily names him. In writing again to Theodelinda, he makes no mention of the Fifth Synod, although that synod established nothing against the preceding four. He is to restrain Fortunatus. He is not to harass Ursicinus in the condition of his status.

**713 EPISTLE XL (to Marcellus the scholasticus).**—To one who is requesting indulgence for Maximus, he states as a friend that this is not permitted by the uprightness of discipline.

**715 EPISTLE XLI (to the clergy, order, and people of Hortona).**—He appoints Barbarus as visitor. Above all, he warns them not to elect a layman as bishop.

**716 EPISTLE XLII (to Valentinus the abbot).**—Monks are not to bring women into the monastery or make them their godmothers.

**717 EPISTLE XLIII (to Boniface, a magnificent man).**—He is to come to Rome and answer for his faith, no longer by letters but in person. Those who share his doubts may come safely, since Gregory will deal with them not by power but by reason. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLIV (to Maximian the bishop).**—He is to send to Bishop Bacauda certain members of his clergy who had been promoted to sacred orders in Sicily, since Bacauda is asking for them back.

**718 EPISTLE XLV (to Fantinus the defensor).**—He sends sixty solidi to be paid on behalf of Cosmas. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLVI (to Rusticiana the patrician).**—He reproves her for returning too quickly from Mount Sinai.

**719 EPISTLE XLVII (to Sabinianus the deacon).**—The pride of Maximus, who had publicly ordered Gregory’s writings to be torn apart, is to be restrained. He indicates how Maximus’s accusation concerning the murdered Bishop Malchus should be answered. He is to warn Romanus about two matters.

**720 BOOK V OF THE LETTERS.**

**721 FIRST EPISTLE (to John, bishop of Ravenna).**—Clerics serving Churches are not to be placed over monasteries. Ibid.

**EPISTLE II (to Felix the bishop and Cyriacus the abbot).**—The servants of God are to be introduced into the monastery founded by Theodosia.

**723 EPISTLE III (to Venantius the bishop).**—Priests, deacons, and subdeacons who have stained themselves with the crime of sexual misconduct are to remain permanently deposed from their rank. After completing penance, they are to receive communion among the laity. He permits Saturninus, a former priest, to take charge of certain monasteries. He sends a garment for a woman to be baptized and the Book of the Pastoral Rule to the priest Columbus. Ibid.

**EPISTLE IV (to Constantius the bishop).**—Concerning those who have lapsed, he decrees what he decreed in the preceding letter. He writes to Constantius that, while punishing John, he must beware of anger. He orders that Constantius’s reputation be safeguarded. The case of Fortunatus is to be concluded at Rome.

**725 EPISTLE V (to Dominicus the bishop).**—He congratulates him because he has striven to restrain the Donatists with pastoral zeal; nevertheless, he does not approve the harsher judgment of the African council against bishops who neglected this duty.

**726 EPISTLE VI (to Victor the bishop).**—He is to restore Gregory the abbot, who has been afflicted by lengthy penance because of negligence. He is to recall Martia, a nun. Victoria is to be handed over to Fantinus for careful examination. Anastasius the physician is henceforth not to enter the monastery of virgins.

**727 EPISTLE VII (to Venantius the bishop).**—If Saturninus, a former priest, has ministered after his lapse, he is to be deprived of communion until the day of his death.

**728 EPISTLE VIII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to prosecute the Manichaeans. The burdens of rent imposed on Jews who have converted to Christ are to be reduced. He is to lend solidi to the peasants.

**729 EPISTLE IX (to Peter the notary).**—The ecclesiastical furnishings of the Church of Myra are to be returned when a bishop has been ordained there.

**731 EPISTLE X (to Felix the bishop).**—He threatens Districta with severe correction unless she obeys the bishop of Prima Justiniana, her primate. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XI (to John the bishop).**—He grants permission to use the pallium during solemn litanies on only four days of the year.

**732 EPISTLE XII (to Peter the bishop).**—He assigns a quarter of the revenues of the Church of Agrigentum as a stipend for visitation.

**733 EPISTLE XIII (to Gaudentius the bishop).**—He entrusts him with the visitation of the Church of Capua.

**734 EPISTLE XIV (to the clergy of the Church of Capua).**—Concerning the visitation of the Church of Capua entrusted to Gaudentius. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XV (to John the bishop).**—He censures five things in him. He desires to honor the Church of Ravenna but does not permit honor to be seized through pride.

**735 EPISTLE XVI (to Datianus the bishop).**—He amicably asks him to sympathize with him in his affliction.

**736 EPISTLE XVII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He grieves over the death of Bishop Maximian. He designates John, archdeacon of Catania, as his successor.

**737 EPISTLE XVIII (to John the bishop).**—He recounts what both he himself and his predecessor Pelagius did concerning John’s usurpation of the title “universal bishop.” He asks him to abstain from it and presses him with many arguments. He warns him to beware of flatterers.

**738 EPISTLE XIX (to Sabinianus the deacon).**—He is to deliver the preceding letter to Bishop John, softened with courtesy out of reverence for the emperor. John had craftily persuaded the emperor to urge Gregory to maintain peace with him. Gregory rouses Sabinianus’s spirit against John’s pride.

**743 EPISTLE XX (to Maurice Augustus).**—He praises the emperor’s zeal for the peace of the Church. He depicts Bishop John’s hypocrisy. He states that, through the ambitious title John had usurped, the whole Church, the venerable synods, the pious laws, and the commands of Christ himself were being thrown into confusion; therefore John’s pride must be restrained by imperial authority. If John does not listen to Gregory admonishing him humbly and gently, Gregory will resist him steadfastly together with God.

**744 EPISTLE XXI (to Constantina Augusta).**—He urges her to continue opposing John’s ambition. He briefly exposes John’s hypocrisy, perversity, and pride. He complains that the emperor and Maximus are giving him their patronage. Out of reverence for the emperor, he forgives Maximus because he was ordained without Gregory’s knowledge, but reserves his other crimes for investigation and judgment.

**748 EPISTLE XXII (to the nobles of Syracuse).**—Since they had entrusted the election of a bishop to Gregory’s judgment, he strives to ordain for them one who will imitate his predecessor Maximian.

**751 EPISTLE XXIII (to Castorius the notary).**—He is to urge the people of Ravenna to elect a bishop as quickly as possible. They are to elect not one who is generous with rewards but one worthy by his merits. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXIV (to Romanus the exarch).**—He is not to protect the priest Speciosus, who is resisting his bishop, nor to offer patronage to nuns who have returned to secular life.

**752 EPISTLE XXV (to Severus the bishop).**—He commends the visitation of the Church of Ravenna.

**753 EPISTLE XXVI (to the people of Ravenna).**—The visitation of the Church of Ravenna has been entrusted to Severus. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXVII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to investigate whether the deceased bishop diminished the Church’s property. He is to urge the clergy and people to elect a successor. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXVIII (to Castorius the deacon).**—He is to investigate the life of the bishop of Pisaurum and of the other priests; if he finds anything reprehensible, he is to report it.
