He is to protect Tutor, so that Tutor may be able to carry out what has been entrusted to him on behalf of the poor.

**754 EPISTLE XXIX (to Vincomalus the defensor).**—He appoints him defensor of the Church.

**755 EPISTLE XXX (to Maurice Augustus).**—He gives thanks to the emperors for the thirty pounds of gold sent as alms. He praises Scribo both for his faithful distribution of that sum and for the generous grants made in response to the soldiers’ requests. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXI (to the lessees of the estates).**—Until the administrator of the Gallic patrimony arrives, they are to obey the patrician Arigius.

**756 EPISTLE XXXII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—After the death of Bishop Maximian, he is to inflict severe penalties on certain clerics whom Maximian had thrown into prison for wrongdoing.

**757 EPISTLE XXXIII (to Gaudentius the bishop).**—He is to distribute a quarter to the Capuan clerics serving at Naples. He is to restore ten solidi to the needy archdeacon.

**759 EPISTLE XXXIV (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to restore the fallen monk Cicero to the Church of Misenum, in which he had been a servant. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXV (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to compel three monks to return to the monastery of Saint Martin, support the administrators of that monastery, and return the slaves to it.

**760 EPISTLE XXXVI (to Severus the scholasticus).**—He is to persuade the exarch to make peace with Agilulf, king of the Lombards. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXXVII (to Fortunatus the bishop).**—He is to dedicate a monastery in honor of Saint Peter and Saint Michael, in which the priests serving there are to celebrate Mass; whatever the faithful happen to offer, however, is to benefit the monks. [Col. 1607]

**761 EPISTLE XXXVIII (to Elias the priest and abbot).**—He accepts his excuse, sends Gospels, binds Epiphanius to the diaconate of the Roman Church, and surpasses his modest request for assistance by his generosity.

**762 EPISTLE XXXIX (to Anastasius the bishop).**—He congratulates him on his restoration to the see of Antioch and briefly recounts his own calamities and those of Italy.

**763 EPISTLE XL (to Maurice Augustus).**—He complains that he has been called a fool, that greater credence is given to others than to him concerning Ariulf’s disposition toward peace, and that Italy is meanwhile being led away captive. He urges the emperor at length to show priests the reverence due to them. He enumerates the blows he himself has suffered. He excuses Gregory the prefect and Castorius the master of the soldiers. Divine judgment will differ from imperial judgment.

**765 EPISTLE XLI (to Constantina Augusta).**—He is to point out to the emperor that the Corsicans and Sicilians are being oppressed unjustly and excessively. Even if there is less money available for Italy’s expenses, the groans of the oppressed must nevertheless be restrained.

**768 EPISTLE XLII (to Sebastianus the bishop).**—He is driven by the pains of this life toward love of heavenly things. He lists what he suffers. He praises Sebastianus because he refused to undertake the governance of the Church offered by Anastasius. If he should ever decide to consent to it, he asks him not to prefer another to Gregory in affection.

**769 EPISTLE XLIII (to Eulogius and Anastasius the bishops).**—He sends them both the letters of his predecessor Pelagius and his own letters to John, who arrogated to himself the title of universal bishop. He earnestly urges them to pursue John’s pride with a common purpose and one spirit.

**770 EPISTLE XLIV (to Leontius the bishop).**—Concerning more effectively arranging the visitation of Ariminum.

**774 EPISTLE XLV (to Andrew the scholasticus).**—He commends Castorius the chartularius.

**775 EPISTLE XLVI (to Basilius).**—He praises his zeal for the unity of the Church. He encourages him not to be deterred from working for the return of the schismatics.

**776 EPISTLE XLVII (to Mastalo).**—He praises his zeal for the unity of the Church. He is not to be deterred from working for the return of the schismatics. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XLVIII (to Andrew the scholasticus).**—With Donatus excluded because of his faults and John because of his ignorance, he states that Marinianus, well known to him, was ordained against his will, and commends him to Andrew.

**777 EPISTLE XLIX (to Leander the bishop).**—He sends books on the exposition of blessed Job and the Book of the Pastoral Rule.

**778 EPISTLE L (to John the abbot).**—He is to proceed to the monastery of Saint Andrew to restrain and punish the vicious.

**779 EPISTLE LI (to Peter and Providentius the bishops).**—He writes that he will satisfy them concerning the faith and promises that he will cause no trouble to those who come to Rome. Ibid.

**EPISTLE LII (to John the archbishop).**—He praises Bishop Secundinus because he properly investigated and concluded the case of Anastasius. He forgives the clerics who had withdrawn from the accusation of Anastasius—Paul and Clematius—but permanently forbids Euphemius and Thomas to exercise the sacred orders they had received as a reward for their crime. He wishes the customary stipends to be distributed to each and whatever Paul had spent for the benefit of the Church to be restored to him.

**780 EPISTLE LIII (to Virgilius the bishop).**—He grants him his vicariate in the kingdom of Childebert. He warns him to prohibit the stain of simony and not to allow laymen suddenly to become bishops. He discusses the use of the pallium and the extent to which he ought to exercise the apostolic vicariate.

**782 EPISTLE LIV (to all the bishops of Childebert’s kingdom).**—They are to obey Virgilius of Arles, to whom he has entrusted his vicariate; when summoned by him, they are to come to the synod; and they are not to go to distant places without his authority.

**785 EPISTLE LV (to Childebert the king).**—He states that, at the king’s request, he has granted Virgilius his vicariate and the pallium. In turn, he urges the king to support Virgilius in prohibiting simony and in preventing laymen from suddenly becoming bishops.

**787 EPISTLE LVI (to Marinianus the bishop).**—He grants him the use of the pallium and confirms the privileges of the Church of Ravenna.

**789 EPISTLE LVII (to John the bishop).**—After the most wicked predecessor Anastasius, he is to govern the Corinthians in such a way as to wipe away all the stains of the preceding contagion. He grants him the use of the pallium. He urges him to restrain simony in the places subject to him.

**790 EPISTLE LVIII (to all the bishops throughout Hellas).**—He congratulates them on the correction of Anastasius, whose downfall should serve them as a warning. They are to obey his successor John. They are not to allow clerics to be ordained or promoted either for a payment or through anyone’s favor or entreaty.

**792 [Col. 1608] BOOK VI OF THE LETTERS.**

**793 FIRST EPISTLE (to Marinianus the bishop).**—What is to be regarded as valid in the testament of his predecessor John. Ibid.

**EPISTLE II (to the clergy and people of Ravenna).**—He testifies that the faith of Bishop Marinianus is entirely orthodox.

**795 EPISTLE III (to Maximus of Salona).**—Maximus, accused of simony and many other offenses, is summoned to Rome. Ibid.

**EPISTLE IV (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to give Bishop Zeno two thousand modii of grain to distribute to the needy.

**796 EPISTLE V (to Queen Brunichild).**—He praises her for the proper education of her son. He commends Candidus the priest, appointed administrator of the patrimony that was in Gaul. Ibid.

**EPISTLE VI (to Childebert the king).**—He praises his devotion to the Catholic faith and commends Candidus, appointed administrator of the patrimony in place of the patrician Dynamius.

**797 EPISTLE VII (to Candidus the priest).**—He orders him to purchase boys from England and clothing for the use of the poor from the revenues of the patrimony.

**799 EPISTLE VIII (to the bishops of Epirus).**—He approves Andrew’s election as metropolitan. He urges them to imitate him, obey him, and be united with him, and each to watch over his own flock. Among them, clerics are to be promoted not for money or anyone’s favor but on the recommendation of their character. Ibid.

**EPISTLE IX (to Donus the bishop).**—He warns that the adornment of character must be added to the pallium with which he honors him. He confirms the ancient privileges of the Church of Messana.

**801 EPISTLE X (to Boniface the bishop).**—He unites the Church of Carina with the Church of Reggio.

**802 EPISTLE XI (to Fortunatus the bishop).**—He permits Gratianus, a deacon of the Church of Venetrana, to be incardinated in the Church of Naples. He forbids clerics to be summoned to court before laymen and forbids him himself to postpone the judgment of cases. He urges him to pastoral vigilance. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XII (to Montana and Thomas).**—He manumits Montana and Thomas, servants of the Roman Church. Since the priest Gaudiosus instituted them as heirs, he permits them to enjoy the legacies.

**803 EPISTLE XIII (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to assist Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum, in reforming the condition of his Church.

**805 EPISTLE XIV (to Narses the count).**—He declares that the priest Athanasius fell into the doctrine of the Manichaeans, but that John is free from heresy; and that the man who denies that Adam’s soul died when he sinned is a Pelagian. He suspects that the more recent copies of the Council of Ephesus have been falsified and advises that ancient copies be sought. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XV (to John the bishop).**—He absolves the priest John, who was unjustly condemned, and declares him free from every taint of heresy. He commends the same man to John, bishop of Constantinople.

**807 EPISTLE XVI (to Maurice Augustus).**—He is not to permit the entirely innocent priest John to be afflicted again as though he were liable to heresy.

**808 EPISTLE XVII (to Theotistus).**—He is to protect the priest John, who was acquitted by a council of the charge of heresy brought against him, from every form of harassment.

**809 EPISTLE XVIII (to John the bishop).**—He grants the use of the pallium and confirms the ancient privileges.

**810 EPISTLE XIX (to Dominicus the bishop).**—So that their mutual affection may obtain heavenly joy, they are to assist one another with mutual prayers. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XX (to Cyprian the deacon).**—He is to persuade Leo, bishop of Catania, to transfer a certain priest to John, bishop of Syracuse.

**811 EPISTLE XXI (to Peter the bishop).**—He commends three Churches deprived of their own bishops.

**812 EPISTLE XXII (to Peter the bishop).**—He is to consecrate the Church and baptistery.

**813 EPISTLE XXIII (to Anthemius the subdeacon).**—He is to compel the bishop of Amalfi to reside in his own Church. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXIV (to Marinianus the bishop).**—He approves the complaints of some who consider it unjust that the case between the Church of Ravenna and the abbot Claudius is being investigated at Rome; he promises an equitable judgment.

**814 EPISTLE XXV (to Maximus of Salona).**—He is finally to obey and, after thirty days, setting aside every excuse, come to Rome, where his case will be concluded according to the canons. Meanwhile, deprived of sacred communion because of his pride, he is to remain in mourning; he is not to trouble either Bishop Paulinus or the archdeacon Honoratus.

**815 EPISTLE XXVI (to the people of Salona).**—He asserts that he is moved against Maximus not by private hatred but solely by zeal for justice; he nevertheless wonders that only very few of them have abstained from communion with Maximus.

**817 EPISTLE XXVII (to the clergy and people of Jadera).**—He asserts that he is moved against Maximus solely by zeal for justice. He urges them to suspend themselves from communion with Maximus and to receive sacred communion from those whom they know not to communicate with Maximus.

**818 EPISTLE XXVIII (to Candidus the bishop).**—With the abbot’s consent, he is to take monks suited to the priestly office and ordain them priests.

**820 EPISTLE XXIX (to Marinianus the bishop).**—He confirms the arrangement concerning his predecessor’s disposition above, Letter 1, and forbids Marinianus to burden the monastery contrary to it. He is not to listen to evil counselors. He is not to pursue money more than the winning of souls. He is not to permit the monasteries to suffer harassment from clerics. Ibid.

**EPISTLE XXX (to Secundus).**—He is to urge Marinianus to hasten to secure peace with King Agilulf and to show mercy toward the poor.

**821 EPISTLE XXXI (to the people of Ravenna).**—The man who posted written accusations against Castorius by night is to be deprived of sacred communion unless he publicly demonstrates the truth of his accusation or confesses his error.

**822 EPISTLE XXXII (to Fortunatus the bishop).**—If a Jew or pagan wishes to be converted to the Christian faith as a slave, he is to be claimed for freedom.

**823 EPISTLE XXXIII (to Leo the bishop).**—If a pagan slave-woman… [the supplied source ends incompletely]

They should free from slavery those whom the Samaritans have circumcised, without returning them to the Samaritans for a price.

**824 EPISTLE XXXIV** (To Castorius, notary).—He is to investigate how many solemn litanies there have been from ancient times in which the bishop of Ravenna wore the pallium.

**825 EPISTLE XXXV** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He sends money for the redemption of captives and orders him to devote himself diligently to this task.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXVI** (To Secundinus, bishop).—If Sincerus has abstained from claiming his father-in-law’s succession, he is not to allow the latter’s creditors to harass him. He is, however, to secure for Sincerus, so that he may find the means of living, unrestricted permission to go wherever he wishes.

**826 EPISTLE XXXVII** (To Columbas, bishop).—He states that he has given written instructions through his deacon Rogatianus to the rector of the patrimony of Sicily, so that a certain case may be concluded more quickly. He sends to Columbas Peter, formerly bishop of Numidia, whom Columbas is to judge canonically, together with those implicated, after examining the case more fully there. He is not to tolerate Catholic children or slaves being infected by the baptism of the Donatists.

**827 EPISTLE XXXVIII** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He commends Alexandria, which has been abandoned, to Vincomalus.

**828 EPISTLE XXXIX** (To Cyprian, deacon).—He commends John, who has returned from the schism, and orders that eight solidi be given him annually.

**829 EPISTLE XL** (To Donus, bishop).—He is to assist in supporting Georgius, provided that Georgius has begun to live more correctly.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLI** (To Rufinus, bishop).—A presbyter is to be ordained in the Church of Massa Nicoterana, who, in place of the bishop assigned to penance, is to baptize and celebrate Masses.

**830 EPISTLE XLII** (To Victor, bishop).—He is to ordain a presbyter in the monastery.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIII** (To Venantius, patrician).—He says that he is distressed by the disagreement between Venantius and Bishop John. Venantius is to show John due reverence, and they are to pursue their cases without injury to charity.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIV** (To John, bishop).—He urges him to show Venantius his former goodwill.

**831 EPISTLE XLV** (To Leontius, bishop).—He grants permission to dedicate the church and confirms the donors’ gifts to it.

**832 EPISTLE XLVI** (To Felix, bishop).—He is to have his cathedra removed from the monastery and is not to celebrate public Masses there again.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLVII** (To Leo, bishop).—He is to protect John, who has returned from the schism of the Istrians, and support him with an annual allowance.

**833 EPISTLE XLVIII** (To Urbicus, abbot).—He is to receive Agathon into the monastery if Agathon’s wife likewise wishes to convert.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIX** (To Palladius, bishop).—He sends relics for the dedication of four altars in the basilica that Palladius had built.

**834 EPISTLE L** (To Brunichild, queen).—He sends the relics she had requested and urges her to provide for the peace of those who will serve them.

**835 EPISTLE LI** (To the brothers going to England).—He urges Augustine’s companions to complete the journey they have begun to England. They are to obey Augustine, whom he has appointed their abbot.

**836 EPISTLE LII** (To Pelagius and Serenus, bishops).—He commends Augustine, who is going to England with his companions, and Candidus, rector of the patrimony.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LIII** (To Virgilius, bishop).—He commends Augustine and, at the same time, the presbyter Candidus; he also warns Virgilius to restore to Candidus the revenues of the patrimony that his predecessor had collected.

**837 EPISTLE LIV** (To Desiderius and Syagrius, bishops).—He commends Augustine and Candidus.

**838 EPISTLE LV** (To Protasius, bishop).—[Col. 1610] He is to press Virgilius of Arles to send the revenues to Rome and keep Candidus in his care.

**839 EPISTLE LVI** (To Stephen, abbot).—He praises him for the order of his congregation and urges him carefully to preserve it. He gives thanks for the spoons and rings.

**840 EPISTLE LVII** (To Arigius, patrician).—He commends Augustine, his companions, and Candidus.

**841 EPISTLE LVIII** (To Theoderic and Theodebert).—He commends Augustine, whom he has instructed to take with him to England some presbyters from the neighboring region, and Candidus, rector of the ecclesiastical patrimony.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LIX** (To Brunichild, queen of the Franks).—He asks her to provide protection and assistance to Augustine as he goes to England and to Candidus, rector of the patrimony.

**842 EPISTLE LX** (To Eulogius, bishop).—He observes that the two of them are bound by a special bond of charity. Therefore he shares in Eulogius’s grief; and, lest he increase his sorrow, he refrains from mentioning the evils he suffers at the hands of the Lombards. He is surprised that Eulogius has not replied to the letter concerning the arrogance of John of Constantinople. He sends mutual gifts.

**843 EPISTLE LXI** (To Castorius, notary).—What serious and trustworthy men of Ravenna swore had formerly been observed concerning the use of the pallium is to be observed at Ravenna.

**844 EPISTLE LXII** (To Peter, bishop).—He is to grant relics to Opportunus, abbot of Saint Leontius.

**846 EPISTLE LXIII** (To Gennadius, patrician).—He complains that Bishop Paul was prevented from coming to Rome. As soon as he has recovered from his illness, he will undertake the examination of Paul’s case.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXIV** (To Dominicus, bishop).—The pastoral office is to be exercised out of charity. He congratulates Dominicus on exercising it in this way and gives thanks for the gifts.

**847 EPISTLE LXV** (To Maurice, emperor).—He sends certain African bishops from Rome to Constantinople, so that they may testify to the emperor Maurice himself that the laws against the Donatists are being neglected. He stirs Maurice’s mind against those who despise his laws.

**848 EPISTLE LXVI** (To Athanasius, presbyter).—He declares him pure from every stain of heresy and promises to write this to the bishop of Constantinople.

**849 BOOK VII OF THE LETTERS**

**851 EPISTLE I** (To Fortunatus, bishop).—He is to restore Unorem, who has been approved as free, to her husband; nor is the husband to consider casting her away again.

**Ibid. EPISTLE II** (To Columbas, bishop).—Bishop Paul has now been sent to the imperial city. Columbas wrote to him later than he should have done. He refutes Columbas’s excuse.

**Ibid. EPISTLE III** (To Gennadius, patrician).—He asks him not to pass judgment with a prejudiced mind concerning Count Ruferius and the fellow citizens summoned before him. He requests that Tribune Anastasius be restored to his position.

**853 EPISTLE IV** (To Cyriacus, bishop).—Quiet is desirable but must sometimes be postponed for the benefit of many. The bishop must take care lest the disturbance of his thoughts—which cannot be driven away completely—overwhelm his mind. The unity of the Church is strengthened by a reciprocal confession of faith and by their mutual charity. He must abstain from the title “universal bishop.” Eudoxius should not have been counted among the heretics.

**Ibid. EPISTLE V** (To Cyriacus, bishop).—He praises Cyriacus because he thinks humbly and modestly of himself; from this he infers that Cyriacus is strong. He urges him most affectionately, now that the occasion of scandal has been removed, to preserve what belongs to peace and love. He commends John and Athanasius to him.

**858 EPISTLE VI** (To Maurice Augustus).—He congratulates him on the election of Cyriacus.

**859 EPISTLE VII** (To Peter, Domitian, and Elpidus).—He rebukes them because, at Cyriacus’s ordination, they shouted: “This is the day which the Lord has made.” The faults of shepherds harm their subjects, and the faults of subjects harm their shepherds.

**860 EPISTLE VIII** (To Stephen, bishop).—Though unwilling, he returns praise for Stephen’s constant preaching, through which Patricia Maria and many others have been recalled to the Church. He urges him to advise the prefect Constantine always to keep God’s judgment before his eyes.

**862 EPISTLE IX** (To John, bishop).—He gives thanks for the alms sent to Rome. In judging cases, John is to consider God alone. He is not to have his letters read at table again.

**863 EPISTLE X** (To Agnellus, abbot).—He is to choose a superior on the basis of the merit of his life and watch over the brothers carefully.

**864 EPISTLE XI** (To Rufinus, Ephesian bishop).—He commends a certain cleric who does not know letters.

**865 EPISTLE XII** (To Respecta, abbess).—He grants the monastery of Saint Cassian privileges.

**866 EPISTLE XIII** (To Fortunatus, bishop).—From the sacred vessels he is to sell only as much as is necessary for the redemption of captives, and only in the presence of John the defensor.

**867 EPISTLE XIV** (To Constantius, bishop).—He is not to be moved by slanders. In place of the bishop whom he has deposed, he is to ordain another [Col. 1611] within three months.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XV** (To Georgius, presbyter).—When Jesus Christ descended into hell, he liberated only those who had believed that he would come and had kept his commandments by their manner of life.

**869 EPISTLE XVI** (To Agnellus, bishop).—He delegates the visitation of the Church of Formiae.

**870 EPISTLE XVII** (To Sabinianus, bishop).—Having set forth Maximus’s contumacy, he summons to Rome Sabinianus, who has now separated from Maximus, and others who adhere to Maximus. He promises them complete security and, if justice permits it, absolution.

**871 EPISTLE XVIII** (To Martin, deacon).—After he has been canonically cleared of the charges brought against him, he restores him to his position and rank.

**872 EPISTLE XIX** (To Marinianus, archbishop).—Because Castorius pleads inability to bear the episcopal burden, another bishop is to be ordained for the people of Rimini. He orders that this man be elected by clergy and people, examined by the bishop of Ravenna, and sent to Rome for consecration.

**873 EPISTLE XX** (To the clergy and people of Rimini).—Because of their bishop’s infirmity, they are to elect another who is worthy.

**874 EPISTLE XXI** (To Sebastianus, bishop).—He is to urge the clergy and people of Rimini to elect a suitable bishop.

**875 EPISTLE XXII** (To Cyprian, deacon).—He is to arrange matters so that the bishops of Sicily, who formerly traveled to Rome every third year and now every fifth year, may assemble for the feast of Saint Peter without giving the praetor any grounds for suspicion. He is also to warn the bishops of Lipara and Reggio and console Libertinus.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXIII** (To Fortunatus and Anthemius).—They are to urge Stephen to restore the property taken from the woman betrothed to him who had entered a monastery. If he refuses, they are to report him so that he may be compelled to restore it.

**876 EPISTLE XXIV** (To Candidus, presbyter).—He is to redeem four Christians who were being held at Narbonne in Jewish service.

**877 EPISTLE XXV** (To Gregoria).—He consoles her, since she has confessed her sins but is anxious about their remission, by adducing the example of the sinful woman whom he supposes to have been Martha’s sister. He shows that God’s revelation of forgiveness is sought in vain.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXVI** (To Theoctista, patrician).—He congratulates her because, amid the tumult of human affairs, she devotes herself to reading and longs for eternal things. He asks whether the empress pursues the same interests. He discusses at greater length the twofold form of compunction. He urges Theoctista to watch diligently over the education of the royal children and to inspire them with mutual charity and gentleness toward their subjects. With half the money Theoctista had sent, he redeemed captives; with the remainder he supports nuns, whose holiness he believes has preserved Rome. He sends a key from the body of Saint Peter and recounts a miracle concerning it.

**879 EPISTLE XXVII** (To Anastasius, bishop).—He had thought that it was not of great importance that the bishop of Constantinople should use the word “universal,” together with the emperor Anastasius. Gregory argues that by this word the faith of the whole Church is corrupted.

**882 EPISTLE XXVIII** (To Theodore, physician).—He praises the alms sent for captives and the poor. In return he sends a key from the body of Saint Peter.

**883 EPISTLE XXIX** (To Andrew).—The dignities of this world are to be despised so that he may devote himself to heavenly pursuits.

**884 EPISTLE XXX** (To Narses, a religious man).—He consoles him in his affliction. He shows that a Christian must not refuse adversity. He explains why he does not write to the inhabitants of the monasteries and to the others living in Constantinople. He rejoices at the death of Hesychius. He explains what should be done regarding Domna Dominica. He sends small gifts and commends Anatolius.

**885 EPISTLE XXXI** (To Cyriacus, bishop).—He writes concerning the removal of the profane title, so that the peace of the Church may be preserved and the scandals of many removed.

**888 EPISTLE XXXII** (To Anastasius, presbyter).—He writes concerning the removal of the dispute that had arisen between the father of the monastery called Neas and the bishop of Jerusalem.

**889 EPISTLE XXXIII** (To Maurice Augustus).—He argues that he was rashly called indiscreet because he rebuked Cyriacus, the bishop of Constantinople, who calls himself universal.

**891 EPISTLE XXXIV** (To Eulogius, bishop).—Cyriacus’s representatives were received at Rome and admitted to communion. His own deacon, however, ought not to have communicated with Cyriacus, whose pride was intolerable to God. Cyriacus’s synodical letter was orthodox, but in it a certain Eudoxius was condemned, although, as Gregory believes, Eudoxius had until then not been condemned. He demonstrates that the monks of Isauria had been unjustly condemned for heresy under John, Cyriacus’s predecessor.

**892 EPISTLE XXXV** (To Dominicus, bishop).—He is to correct monks who evade regular discipline by flight and wander about with impunity. He is to deter bishops from defending them.

**895 EPISTLE XXXVI** (To Dynamius and Aurelia).—Always devoted to prayer, reading, and good works, they are to advance toward better things. [Col. 1612] He promises them a book.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXVII** (To Dominica).—He rejoices that she has returned to the unity of the Church and urges her to come to Rome to her husband.

**896 EPISTLE XXXVIII** (To Donus, bishop).—He is to give Faustinus fifteen pounds of silver, either from the Church’s funds or from sacred vessels, for the redemption of his daughters.

**897 EPISTLE XXXIX** (To John, bishop).—The dispute that has arisen between two abbots over the boundaries of their fields is to be settled in John’s presence with a surveyor.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XL** (To Eulogius, bishop).—The see of Saint Peter at Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch is one and the same; hence there is a singular unity among the bishops seated in those places. He praises Eulogius for opposing heretics, offers him timber, and sends gifts in return.

**898 EPISTLE XLI** (To Cyprian, rector).—He is to arrange for a suitable bishop to be ordained for the Church of Locri.

**901 EPISTLE XLII** (To Marinianus, bishop).—Since the canons neither permit a fallen bishop to be restored to his position nor allow a Church to remain vacant for more than three months, he is to ordain a bishop for Cornelius.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIII** (To Marinianus, bishop).—He writes concerning the removal of clerical control from monasteries.

**902 EPISTLE XLIV** (To Cyprian, deacon).—He is to ensure that Theodore the sorcerer, or any of the clergy of Messina, does not oppose Paula.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLV** (To Claudius, abbot).—He is to come to Rome as quickly as possible.

**903 BOOK VIII OF THE LETTERS**

**Ibid. EPISTLE I** (To Peter, bishop).—He urges him to continue turning the inhabitants away from the worship of idols. He sends fifty solidi for the clothing of those who are to be baptized.

**Ibid. EPISTLE II** (To Anastasius, bishop of Antioch).—He strengthens him against heresies. After praising the bond of mutual charity and recalling his friend’s gifts, he prays for a long life for him.

**905 EPISTLE III** (To Donus, bishop of Messina).—A place for burying a body is not to be sold anywhere. Certain slaves are to be restored.

**907 EPISTLE IV** (To Venantius, bishop).—He grants permission to consecrate a monastery.

**908 EPISTLE V** (To many metropolitans and bishops).—Those bound by public financial obligations are not to be received either into the clergy or into a monastery. Soldiers, however, are first to be tested for three years before assuming the monastic habit.

**909 EPISTLE VI** (To Amos, patriarch of Jerusalem).—He is to order that Peter, an acolyte of the Roman Church who has fled, be arrested and sent to Rome deprived of communion.

**910 EPISTLE VII** (To Leo, bishop).—He is to divide among the clergy, according to the merit of their labor, the fourth part of the Church’s revenues that has been set aside.

**911 EPISTLE VIII** (To Vitalianus, bishop).—He is to recall the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, to the religious habit and force her into a monastery. He is to suspend from communion those who resist.

**912 EPISTLE IX** (To Sergius, defensor).—He writes concerning compelling the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, to resume the religious habit.

**913 EPISTLE X** (To Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera).—He says that, as much as Maximus’s communion had offended him, so much had Maximus’s repentance softened him. He commends the case to Sabinianus’s representative in the imperial city and urges pastoral vigilance. He entrusts him with investigating the case of Bishop Florentius.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XI** (To Candidus, abbot of Saint Andrew).—He confirms the concord and settlement between the monastery of Saint Andrew and Maurentius, master of the soldiers.

**914 EPISTLE XII** (To Adeodatus and Maurentius, bishops).—He praises their concern for ecclesiastical order and rectitude and urges them to persevere. He commends Bishop Paul.

**915 EPISTLE XIII** (To Columbas).—He commends Bishop Paul.

**916 EPISTLE XIV** (To Boniface, chief defensor).—He decrees that seven defensores are to be honored with the rank of regional officials.

**917 EPISTLE XV** (To Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He grants many privileges to the monastery of Saints John and Stephen.

**918 EPISTLE XVI** (To Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He strongly commends Abbot Claudius, who is returning from Rome.

**920 EPISTLE XVII** (To Maurentius).—He congratulates him on his devotion to sacred reading. He mourns the rarity of such students and promises to be his companion.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XVIII** (To Agnellus, bishop of Terracina).—He is to punish idol worshipers when they are discovered and is not to allow anyone to be excused from keeping watch on the walls.

**921 EPISTLE XIX** (To Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He is to show his former favor to Comitiolus, who has served the Roman Church well.

**922 EPISTLE XX** (To Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends [Col. 1613] John’s wife, whose status was being called into dispute.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXI** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He is to free Felix, born of Christian parents, from Samaritan service.

**923 EPISTLE XXII** (To Rusticianus, patrician).—He urges her to come to Rome and gives thanks for the ten pounds of gold to be spent on the redemption of captives.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXIII** (To Fantinus, defensor).—He is to continue to Agrigentum to assist Jews who are approaching the Christian faith.

**924 EPISTLE XXIV** (To Sabinianus, bishop of Jadera).—He congratulates him because he obeys where obedience is required and resists where resistance is required. He strengthens his resolve against hatred of Maximus. He declares that a presbyter cannot, under any circumstances, remain in the sacred order after a fall or be restored to it.

**926 EPISTLE XXV** (To Victor, bishop of Palermo).—The Jews are not to be subjected to any inconvenience in matters granted to them.

**927 EPISTLE XXVI** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—The notary Pantaleo is to investigate which sacred vessels the clerics had sold.

**928 EPISTLE XXVII** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He is not to allow the deacons of Catania to presume to go about wearing campagi.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXVIII** (To Victor and Columbas, bishops).—They are to compel Bishop Valentinus to restore to Crisconius the churches occupied from his parishes and the property taken from the deceased bishop of that parish.

**929 EPISTLE XXIX** (To Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria).—He does not know the book of Eusebius on the deeds of the martyrs that Eulogius had requested. He explains why he sent short pieces of timber, promises longer ones, and refuses payment.

**930 EPISTLE XXX** (To Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria).—He congratulates him on the conversion of the heretics in Alexandria and on the concord of the faithful. In return he writes about the conversion of the English. Regarding Eudoxius the heretic and others, he admits that Eulogius has fully satisfied him. He rejects the title “universal pope,” which the Council of Chalcedon had offered to his predecessors but which they had refused.

**931 EPISTLE XXXI** (To Secundinus).—He is not to allow the monastery to come under the control of a lay person.

**934 EPISTLE XXXII** (To Scholasticus, defensor).—He is to pay the Church’s tenant a wage proportionate to his labor.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXIII** (To Dominicus).—He praises Dominicus’s modesty, charity, and reverence for the apostolic see.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXIV** (To John, bishop of Scillium).—He is to preserve unimpaired the privileges of the monastery of Castellum. He is to return certain things taken under the pretext of a gift. He is to watch over the monks’ conduct and defend the monastery’s rights. He is to restore the field that the abbot had given him. (See above, Epistle 31.)

**935 EPISTLE XXXV** (To Leontius, former consul).—The citizens of Jerusalem sometimes serve Babylon, and the reverse also occurs. He praises Leontius’s gentleness, humility, and justice. He thanks him for the gifts and gives him, from the chains of Saint Peter, a shaving enclosed in a key.

**937 BOOK IX OF THE LETTERS**

**939 EPISTLE I** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—He rebukes him because, on the Lord’s Day, before the solemn Mass, he had plowed up someone’s field, and, after the sacred service, had himself dug up the boundary stones.

**Ibid. EPISTLE II** (To Vitalis, defensor of Sardinia).—He is to carry out the excommunication decreed against Januarius’s advisers. He is to restore the full value of the gift.

**940 EPISTLE III** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—Nothing is to be demanded for a burial place granted without charge. If something is offered for lamps, however, it may be accepted.

**Ibid. EPISTLE IV** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—Until the peace arranged with Agilulf is confirmed, another incursion into Sardinia must be avoided. Out of fraternal affection he again rebukes Januarius for the field he had plowed.

**941 EPISTLE V** (To Marcellus, proconsul of Dalmatia).—He rebukes him for the favor he showed Maximus. He explains how Marcellus may return to Gregory’s good graces.

**943 EPISTLE VI** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—The synagogue occupied by Peter, recently baptized, is to be restored to the Jews; they are not to be compelled to accept the faith. He urges reconciliation between hostile citizens and stronger fortification of the city.

**944 EPISTLE VII** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—Although the abbess did not put on the monastic habit, her testament is nevertheless invalid under imperial law; therefore what Sirica gave unlawfully to others must be returned to the monastery.

**945 EPISTLE VIII** (To the bishops of Sardinia).—They are to receive the Paschal announcement from the metropolitan according to custom and are not to leave the island without his permission.

**947 EPISTLE IX** (To Callinicus, exarch of Italy).—He rejoices that the schismatics are returning to the Church. The emperors are to be advised about this. The one thing forbidden by them is that the schismatics be compelled to unity. He complains of Callinicus’s greater abuses. He asks Callinicus not to summon Justin, a schismatic, to his [Col. 1614] council again.

**948 EPISTLE X** (To Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He is to ordain a bishop for the island of Capritana unless John, after being admonished by Marinianus, returns to the unity of the Church and to his own people. He is to examine and settle Maximus’s case, involving Constantius of Milan if necessary.

**950 EPISTLE XI** (To Brunichild, queen).—He grants the pallium to Bishop Syagrius. He warns her that sacred orders must not be conferred as a reward or favor, and that laymen must not suddenly be made bishops. He praises her charity toward Augustine and urges her to work at recalling the schismatics to concord and at suppressing the remnants of idolatry and other vices in her kingdom. He discusses the book sent to her.

**951 EPISTLE XII** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He says that, as some complained, he had not imitated certain customs of the Church of Constantinople in arranging the rites of the Mass.

**955 EPISTLE XIII** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He is to choose judges without delay, together with Felix, from among the agents of his Church.

**958 EPISTLE XIV** (To Felix in Sicily).—He says that he wrote to Bishop John instructing him to appoint agents of his Church who would enter judgment without delay together with Felix himself.

**959 EPISTLE XV** (To Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto).—He is to place the relics of the martyrs in the basilica at Rieti.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XVI** (To Serenus, bishop of Ancona).—He is to admonish his deacon Severus concerning the restoration of the silver belonging to the Church of Fermo.

**960 EPISTLE XVII** (To Demetrianus and Valerianus).—He decrees that the Church’s money spent on their redemption is never to be reclaimed from them.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XVIII** (To Romanus, defensor).—He commends the Church’s patrimony in Sicily.

**961 EPISTLE XIX** (To the tenants of the Syracuse patrimony).—They are to obey Romanus, the defensor.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XX** (To Peter in Sicily).—He is to assist Romanus as Romanus undertakes the administration of the Syracuse patrimony.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXI** (To Libertinus, former prefect).—He is to aid the new defensor Romanus with his advice.

**962 EPISTLE XXII** (To Ciridanus).—He is to support Romanus, the defensor.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXIII** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He writes concerning the cases of Leontius against Bishop Leo and the physician Archelaus, which have been entrusted to Romanus, the defensor.

**963 EPISTLE XXIV** (To Romanus, defensor).—He is to ensure that the wishes of the testatrix Rustica, neglected for many years, are finally fulfilled.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXV** (To John, bishop of Sorrento, and others).—They are to grant relics to Gregory, former prefect, who wishes to build a basilica.

**964 EPISTLE XXVI** (To Romanus, defensor).—He is to return to Calixenus, Ammonia’s grandson and Stephania’s son, the house that Ammonia had donated to the Roman Church.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXVII** (To Romanus, defensor).—Ecclesiastical protection is not to be extended indiscriminately to everyone.

**965 EPISTLE XXVIII** (To Antonius, subdeacon, and Dometius, abbot).—By his authority he is to bring about reconciliation and concord between the hospice and the monastery.

**966 EPISTLE XXIX** (To Venantius, bishop of Luni).—He is to persuade Fidestia either to satisfy Adeodata, her recently converted daughter, or to assist Adeodata before the judges.

**967 EPISTLE XXX** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to ensure that Massa Veneris is restored to the monastery of Saint Mark.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXI** (To Faustus).—He is to deposit the furnishings of the Church of Volturnus with Anthemius without hesitation.

**968 EPISTLE XXXII** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to receive the furnishings of the Church of Volturnus from Faustus, keep them secure, and make an inventory of them.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXIII** (To Andrew).—To console him in his illness, he shows that the illness itself is a pledge of divine love and a pruning of the fruitful vine.

**969 EPISTLE XXXIV** (To Venantius, bishop).—He is to ordain presbyters or deacons in the city of the Aldiones and urge them to convert the unbelievers.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXV** (To Constantius, bishop of Milan).—He commends John, who will act as deputy prefect, but on the condition that the Church not thereby be burdened, as had happened under Vigilius.

**970 EPISTLE XXXVI** (To Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—When Jewish merchants return from Gaul, the Christian slaves they have brought are either to be handed over to those who had commissioned their purchase, or sold to Christians within forty days. He is to beware of Basil, a Jew who gives slaves to his Christian sons.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XXXVII** (To Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto).—He is not to allow communion to be restored indiscriminately to monks who flee to his diocese. A slave who was manumitted on the condition that he become a monk must not leave the monastery.

**971 [Col. 1615] EPISTLE XXXVIII** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to deal with Felix so that Felix is content with the portion of the price received from Maurus.

**972 EPISTLE XXXIX** (To Romanus, defensor in Sicily).—He is to give six solidi each year to the poor Gaudiosus.

**973 EPISTLE XL** (To Romanus, defensor).—He is to set aside every delay and excuse and carry out what had been ordered above, in Epistle 26.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLI** (To Julianus, scribe).—He says that human considerations do not turn him away from zeal for justice. He will therefore investigate Maximus and deliver sentence according to the canons.

**974 EPISTLE XLII** (To Agilulf, king of the Lombards).—He gives thanks for the peace that has been arranged and asks him to order his dukes not to disturb it.

**975 EPISTLE XLIII** (To Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards).—He gives thanks because she has devoted herself diligently to making peace.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIV** (To Felix in Sicily).—He complains that Felix unjustly accuses him of avoiding judgment concerning Bishop John, since Felix himself postponed it. He urges him to bring the dispute quickly to an end by judicial decision.

**976 EPISTLE XLV** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—Having set forth Felix’s bad faith, he urges John to order without delay that the dispute Felix has raised be ended.

**977 EPISTLE XLVI** (To Sergius, defensor).—While John is occupied with the Church’s business, he is to make an inventory of the inheritance from Pantaleo’s mother-in-law that has fallen to John. He is also to investigate most carefully the sacred furnishings left with John.

**978 EPISTLE XLVII** (To Sabinus, subdeacon).—Together with five bishops, he is to investigate the complaints of the clergy of Reggio against their bishop, so that, informed by their report, Gregory himself may decide the matter at Rome.

**979 EPISTLE XLVIII** (To Paulinus, bishop of Tauriana, and others).—They are to proceed to Reggio together with Sabinus to investigate the clergy’s complaints against their bishop.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLIX** (To Anastasius, bishop of Antioch).—He congratulates him on his orthodox profession of faith. Thanks are to be given to God that only the orthodox are promoted to sacred orders. Prayer is to be offered for the emperor, who is suppressing the heretics. Anastasius is to investigate the authentic copy of the Ephesian synod. Simoniacs are to be excluded from sacred orders.

**980 EPISTLE L** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to send Benenatus, who denies the crime, to Rome together with his accuser and other persons.

**982 EPISTLE LI** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to seek out from Benenatus the remainder of the money given for building the fortress and ensure that all of it is spent on that fortress itself.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LII** (To Secundinus).—He praises his writings, which breathe truth, charity, and humility. Solitaries, like isolated monks, are attacked more intensely by the ancient enemy. The Eastern Churches follow, with one accord, the complete faith of Saint Leo and the Council of Chalcedon. He attacks the defenders of the Three Chapters. He proves that Ibas’s letter is opposed to the definition of the holy synod. The origin of the soul is uncertain, but it is certainly held under original sin until baptism. He sends images and explains their legitimate use.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LIII** (To Constantius, bishop of Milan).—He is prepared to grant the disputed property to the clerics of Como if they return to the unity of the Church.

**992 EPISTLE LIV** (To Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople).—He commends the men of Bishop Constantius.

**993 EPISTLE LV** (To Fantinus, defensor of Palermo).—Bishop Victor is to pay the price for the synagogues of the Jews that were unjustifiably occupied and consecrated.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LVI** (To Fantinus).—He is to compel Candidus, the defensor, to return to John the Jew the written acknowledgment that the debt owed from the price of a ship has been paid.

**994 EPISTLE LVII** (To Praiecta, illustrious woman).—He approves the proceedings conducted between her and Fantinus, the defensor.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LVIII** (To Martin, Scholasticus).—He says that, having received too little information from Martin concerning the bishops’ cases, he cannot pronounce a judgment. Martin is to deal with John, bishop of Syracuse.

**995 EPISTLE LIX** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He reports what the primate of Byzacena did so that he would not be judged by the Roman bishop. Regarding his case, John is to discuss whatever he wishes with Martin Scholasticus.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LX** (To Romanus and the other defensores of the ecclesiastical patrimony).—Women are not to live with bishops or clerics established in sacred orders, on the condition that these men do not abandon their wives but live chastely.

**996 EPISTLE LXI** (Beginning of a letter from Reccared, king of the Goths, addressed to blessed Gregory, bishop of Rome).—He excuses himself for not informing Gregory of his conversion until four years had passed. He sends a golden chalice and testifies to his highest veneration and goodwill. He commends Leander of Seville.

**997 EPISTLE LXII** (To Romanus, defensor).—He is to restrain those who usurp the name of defensores. He is to remove Fortunatus from the Church’s business. He is to compel Martianus, who is disobedient to Bishop John, administrator of the Roman Church’s [Col. 1616] patrimony, to go into exile.

**999 EPISTLE LXIII** (To John, bishop of Syracuse).—He is to employ four bishops to depose Bishop Lucillus. He is to remove priests or deacons who are accomplices in the crime from their rank, deprive laymen of sacred communion, and urge the people of Malta to elect a bishop.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXIV** (To Vitalis, defensor of Sardinia).—He is to protect the clerics in such a way that neither reverence for the bishop nor their discipline is undermined. He is not to allow the Church’s rural properties to be abandoned by their cultivators or the monasteries, which are subject only to bishops, to be disturbed by others.

**1000 EPISTLE LXV** (To Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—Rebellious clerics are to be kept in office. The property left to a monastery by a widow is to be restored by the cleric who possesses it. Worshipers of idols, diviners, and sorcerers are to be restrained both by admonitions and by corporal punishments. The Church’s property is to be entrusted not to laymen but to proven clerics.

**1001 EPISTLE LXVI** (To Anatolius, deacon).—He is to favor those who have returned from the schism of Istria to the unity of the Church.

**1003 EPISTLE LXVII** (To Constantius, bishop of Milan).—He is to judge together with Marinianus of Ravenna the case of Maximus of Salona.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXVIII** (To Eusebius of Thessalonica and others).—They are not in any way to consent to the bishop of Constantinople arrogating to himself the title “ecumenical.” Nor, if other matters are under discussion at the synod, are they to allow the ancient decrees to be overturned.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXIX** (To Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He rebukes him because he does not restrain the bishop of Naples, who is usurping things that belonged to the city’s patrons. He urges him not to allow an alms granted for several years to be demanded afterward as though it were a debt. He commends the privileges of Naples and the case of the island of Prochyta.

**1005 EPISTLE LXX** (To Passivus, bishop of Fermo).—He is to consecrate the oratory of Saint Sabinus.

**1007 EPISTLE LXXI** (To Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto).—He is to grant the sanctuaries of Saint Sabinus to Valerianus, notary of Fermo.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXXII** (To Constantinus, bishop of Narni).—He entrusts the entire administration of the Church of Terni to the visitor already appointed.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXXIII** (To Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He commends Abbot Theodosius, asking that he not be burdened too severely with keeping watch on the walls.

**1008 EPISTLE LXXIV** (To Domnellus, distributor).—He testifies to his exceptional goodwill and excuses himself for not writing when Castorius came to him.

**1009 EPISTLE LXXV** (To Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He entrusts him with the visitation of the Church of Miseno.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXXVI** (To the people of Miseno).—They are to obey Fortunatus, the visitor, and elect a suitable bishop for themselves.

**1010 EPISTLE LXXVII** (To Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to investigate the will of Importunus, bishop of Atella. He is to arrange as quickly as possible for a suitable bishop to be elected both at Atella and at Cumae.

**Ibid. EPISTLE LXXVIII** (To Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria).—He says that the affairs of the man whom Eulogius commended have been concluded more quickly. He complains concerning the arrogance of the bishop of Constantinople.

He should write nothing in reply. Why did he not send longer timbers?

**1011 EPISTLE LXXIX** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends to him and Castorius the judgment concerning Maximus, prescribing its procedure.

**1012 EPISTLE LXXX** (to Castorius, notary).—He should give Maximus his letter as proof of restored communion and favor, provided that, once purified and repentant, he receives Sabinianus and the others in charity. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXXXI** (to Maximus, bishop of Salona).—To the obedient, repentant, and purified man he restores favor and communion, and grants him the use of the pallium.

**1013 EPISTLE LXXXII** (to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople).—He should favor Marcellinus, who has served the Roman Church well, and excuse him before the emperor. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXXXIII** (to Fantinus, defensor of Palermo).—He should protect Januaria from the harassment of Anastasius and Boniface.

**1014 EPISTLE LXXXIV** (to Benenatus, bishop of Tyndaris).—That he consecrate an oratory in honor of Saints Severinus and Juliana.

**1015 EPISTLE LXXXV** (to Fortunatus of Naples).—He orders that the relics of Saints Severinus and Juliana be given to Januaria. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXXXVI** (to Constantius, bishop of Milan).—He grants the relics on the condition that provision first be made for the maintenance of the servants before the place is dedicated. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXXXVII** (to Gaudiosus, bishop of Gubbio).—He delegates the visitation of the Church of Tadinum.

**1016 EPISTLE LXXXVIII** (to the people of Tadinum).—They should obey Bishop Gaudiosus, the visitor, and choose for themselves a suitable priest. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXXXIX** (to Severus, bishop of Ancona).—He entrusts him with the visitation of the city of Aesis [Col. 1617].

**1017 EPISTLE XC** (to the people of Aesis).—They should obey Bishop Severus, the visitor, and choose for themselves a worthy bishop. **Ibid. EPISTLE XCI** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He should appoint Barbatianus abbot, provided that he is prudent in administration and humble in his judgment.

**1018 EPISTLE XCII** (to Victor, bishop of Palermo).—He should ordain as priest for the Praechoritan monastery one of the monks themselves. **Ibid. EPISTLE XCIII** (to Gulfare, master of the soldiers).—After praising his zeal in bringing schismatics back to the Church, he urges him to persevere and to protect those who return.

**1019 EPISTLE XCIV** (to Romanus, defensor).—He should assist certain Istrians so that they may quickly reach their bishop in Sicily. He should urge the bishop himself to come to Rome and provide his travel expenses.

**1020 EPISTLE XCV** (to Callinicus, exarch of Italy).—He commends certain persons who have been restored to the unity of the Church and are returning from Rome to Istria. **Ibid. EPISTLE XCVI** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends the same persons mentioned above.

**1021 EPISTLE XCVII** (to the inhabitants of the island of Capri).—He congratulates them on their undisturbed love of ecclesiastical unity. He gives Marinianus instructions to appoint for them a bishop hostile to the schism. **Ibid. EPISTLE XCVIII** (to Theodorus, administrator at Ravenna).—He praises his devotion to peace. He warns him about the peace deceitfully sworn by Ariulfus. He refuses to sign the agreement with his own hand. He orders that the case of Augustus be settled according to the laws of justice. He consoles the grieving Theodorus, to whom he is preparing to send a representative.

**1022 EPISTLE XCIX** (to Occilianus, tribune of Hydruntum).—He urges him to relieve the city of Hydruntum, which has been burdened by Viator, a former tribune.

**1024 EPISTLE C** (to Sabinianus, bishop of Callipolis).—He should not allow the people of Callipolis to be oppressed by forced services.

**1025 EPISTLE CI** (to Sergius, defensor).—If Fruniscendus, a debtor of the Church of Hydruntum, does not pay voluntarily, he should compel him to appear in court. **Ibid. EPISTLE CII** (to Sergius, defensor).—He should arrange for a slave who has fled from Gregory’s own Germanus to Hydruntum to be apprehended and transported by ship to Rome.

**1026 EPISTLE CIII** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—Soldiers should not be quartered in the monastery of virgins. **Ibid. EPISTLE CIV** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—To restore the citizens of Naples to harmony, he should hasten to send to Rome a man exceptionally well instructed. **Ibid. EPISTLE CV** (to Serenus, bishop of Marseille).—He commends Abbot Cyriacus, who is going to Syagrius, and warns that images are to be preserved in churches.

**1027 EPISTLE CVI** (to Syagrius, Aetherius, Virgilius, and Desiderius, bishops).—He sharpens his censure against simoniacs and neophytes, against forbidden unions with women, and against neglect of synods, which ought to be held annually; and he orders that synods be held every year. He commands that all these matters be treated in the synod and reported to him through Abbot Cyriacus.

**1028 EPISTLE CVII** (to Aregius, bishop of Gap).—He consoles him for the death of his relatives and urges him to discharge his office diligently. He permits him and his archdeacon to use the dalmatic and orders him to attend the synod that is to be convened through Syagrius.

**1033 EPISTLE CVIII** (to Syagrius, bishop).—He praises him for the assistance he rendered to Augustine; grants him the use of the pallium; decrees that the Church of Autun should hold first place in that province after Lyon; and again discusses the synod.

**1035 EPISTLE CIX** (to Brunhild, queen of the Franks).—Concerning men who are suddenly made bishops from the laity or are ordained through simony. He asks her to order a synod to be convened to eradicate these abuses and to establish by edict that Jews may not hold Christian slaves.

**1037 EPISTLE CX** (to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks).—Because many are ordained through simony, taxes are exacted from ecclesiastical estates, and laymen suddenly become bishops, they should arrange for a synod to be held to correct these abuses and should decree that Jews may not hold Christian slaves.

**1039 EPISTLE CXI** (to Virgilius, bishop of Arles).—He confirms the privileges granted by Pope Virgilius to the monastery of Arles.

**1041 EPISTLE CXII** (to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul).—He says that nothing concerning the pallium granted to his predecessors is found in the archives of the Roman Church. He should therefore send anything he finds in the records of his own church.

**1043 EPISTLE CXIII** (to Syagrius, bishop of Autun).—He should compel Bishops Menas and Theodorus to return to Italy. **Ibid. EPISTLE CXIV** (to Virgilius and Syagrius, bishops).—Concerning the case of Syagria, who, although she had professed religious life, was said to have been forcibly joined to her husband [Col. 1618].

**1044 EPISTLE CXV** (to Syagrius, bishop of Autun).—Concerning the parishes taken from the bishop of Turin and another bishop installed in them: he should see that they are restored to him.

**1045 EPISTLE CXVI** (to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks).—That the parishes of the bishop of Turin situated in the Frankish kingdom, in which a new bishop had been ordained, be restored to him.

**1047 EPISTLE CXVII** (to Brunhild, queen of the Franks).—He commends Hilary, asking her to protect him under her protection.

**1048 EPISTLE CXVIII** (to Vantilo and Aregius).—He commends Hilary, asking them to extend their patronage to him. **Ibid. EPISTLE CXIX** (to Asclepiodotus, patrician).—He commends Hilary, asking him to undertake his protection.

**1049 EPISTLE CXX** (to Claudius in Spain).—He praises him, loved by him because of his reputation for virtue. He urges him to advance in the light of truth and in love of the heavenly homeland. He commends Abbot Cyriacus, his legate.

**1050 EPISTLE CXXI** (to Leander, bishop of Seville).—He says that Leander’s letter, written with the pen of charity, reveals the greatness of his heart through the humility of its language. He declares himself unworthy of praise, since burdensome honor depresses his character; overcome by its weight, he joins fault to fault; and, torn from the tranquility of the monastery, he has suffered shipwreck of mind. He piously consoles him concerning the pains of gout. He sends him the pallium. **Ibid. EPISTLE CXXII** (to Reccared, king of the Visigoths).—He praises the king for the conversion of the Gothic people to the faith, for the gifts offered to blessed Peter, and for despising the money of the Jews, with which they sought to have the law enacted against them rescinded. He reminds him that these things should be attributed to God’s praise, and that the snares of the ancient enemy must be guarded against through humility of heart, purity of body, and gentleness of spirit. He sends relics.

**1052 EPISTLE CXXIII** (to Venantius and Italica).—He consoles them, afflicted by illnesses, both for their own troubles and for the general affliction of the whole world, which indicates that the end of the world is near.

**1056 EPISTLE CXXIV** (to Donellus, administrator).—He consoles him in his illness. He rejoices that the military cloak has again been placed upon him. He warns him to repay the money that the exarch had borrowed. He urges him to give especially careful assistance to the city of Rome.

**1057 EPISTLE CXXV** (to Maximus, bishop of Salona).—He congratulates him on complete satisfaction. He sends the pallium. He tells him to express by his conduct what the pallium signifies. He instructs him to deal with Bishop Sabinianus, Archdeacon Honoratus, and the cleric Massianus no longer out of hatred but out of charity.

**1058 EPISTLE CXXVI** (to Constantius, bishop of Milan).—He should not allow Philagrius to be unjustly oppressed either by the people of his church, by the collectors of the levy, or by the bishop of Tortona.

**1059 EPISTLE CXXVII.**—For the celebration of Easter, rejecting Victor’s cycle, the custom of the Scots should be followed, which Anatolius, praised by Jerome, supported. He consults Saint Gregory about bishops ordained through simony or after falling during the period of their diaconate, and about monks abandoning their monasteries; he greatly desires to see him. He praises his *Pastoral Book* and asks for commentaries on Ezekiel and the Song of Songs.

## BOOK X OF THE LETTERS

**1065 EPISTLE I** (to Romanus, defensor in Sicily).—He orders that the property of the Church of Malta, taken both by Lucillus, formerly its bishop, and by Peter, his son, be restored. To Trajan, now bishop, he grants monks for his consolation, but in such a way that the matter remains subject to the discretion of the diocesan bishop. He declares that what Trajan acquired while he was abbot belongs not to him but to the monastery. He permits certain other matters to be removed.

**Ibid. EPISTLE II** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He should consecrate a church for the monks, without public Masses, a baptistery, or a cardinal priest.

**1068 EPISTLE III** (to Fantinus, defensor).—He should collect the slaves belonging to Romanus and send the proceeds of their labor to the monastery built by Romanus himself. **Ibid. EPISTLE IV** (to Savinus, regional subdeacon).—He should investigate most carefully Sisinnius, accused of idolatry and sodomy. If evidence exists, he should cast him into prison. He should also compel him to return the deposit belonging to the orphans, the children of the priest Victorianus.

**1069 EPISTLE V** (to Savinus, subdeacon).—He should admonish Maria finally to fulfill her father’s wishes and, whether willingly or unwillingly, pay what had been left to the freedmen and to the Church of Saint George: two ounces of the estate.

**1070 EPISTLE VI** (to Theodorus, administrator).—He commends the wife of the prefect John. **Ibid. EPISTLE VII** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends the wife of the prefect John.

**1071 EPISTLE VIII** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He says that he is deeply saddened because Marinianus neglected to bring back a nun who had again been removed from her monastery. He urges him earnestly to do so even now [Col. 1619].

**1071 EPISTLE IX** (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—For Basil, bishop of Capua, he should pay ten pounds of gold through Maximus on behalf of Cethegus and Flora.

**1072 EPISTLE X** (to Romanus, defensor).—He should not allow Bishop Basil, who is conducting secular lawsuits, to remain in Sicily for more than four days.

**1073 EPISTLE XI** (to Godiscalc, duke).—He rebukes him for having, in anger, ordered the monastery doors to be broken and its goods plundered. The monks’ flight to the enemy is not to be charged against the abbot. He urges him to cease opposing the monastery and the abbot, and indeed to extend his protection to them. **Ibid. EPISTLE XII** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He commends Abbot Fuscus and his monastery.

**1075 EPISTLE XIII** (to Romanus, defensor).—He should assist Abbot Fuscus so that he may receive without delay what belongs to his monastery. **Ibid. EPISTLE XIV** (to Fantinus, defensor).—He should arrange for the books and curtains of Fuscus’s monastery to be restored to him.

**1076 EPISTLE XV** (to Clementina, patrician).—He declares that he has no scruple of hatred or anger toward her, but rather wholly paternal affection. He urges her nobly to forgive offenses. **Ibid. EPISTLE XVI** (to the people of Turris and Tauriana).—They should obey Bishop Venerius, the visitor, and choose for themselves a suitable priest.

**1078 EPISTLE XVII** (to Bishops Venerius and Stephen).—He entrusts them with the task of visitation according to the customary formula. **Ibid. EPISTLE XVIII** (to Clementina, patrician).—She should not detain Amandus, who had been elected by the people of Sorrento to the episcopate. **Ibid. EPISTLE XIX** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He should investigate the life of Amandus, the man elected bishop, and send him to Rome as soon as possible.

**1079 EPISTLE XX** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—The monks of Sorrento should not spend for other purposes the money received for purchasing estates. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXI** (to John, prefect of Italy).—He complains that the grain allowance of the Neapolitan diaconia has been withheld.

**1080 EPISTLE XXII** (to Leo, bishop of Catania).—He should protect the monastery of Saint Vitus from the harassment of certain people, but correct with worthy discipline the monks who are joined to women.

**1081 EPISTLE XXIII** (to Adrian, notary of Sicily).—He should act both so that the crime of the monks mentioned above is punished and so that no one invades their property. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXIV** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He rebukes his negligence toward the monasteries. He grieves over the flight of Mauricius and other monks. He forbids monks to be tonsured henceforth unless they have been tested for two years, and forbids soldiers to be received into monasteries without his own consent.

**1082 EPISTLE XXV** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He should at last restore the gates to Theodorus and the aqueduct to Rusticus. He may then bring an action against them if he wishes.

**1083 EPISTLE XXVI** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—He should urge John the Palatine neither to oppress the soap-makers nor to favor some of them when they withdraw from a pact confirmed by oath. If John does not heed the admonition, the prefect’s authority should be invoked.

**1084 EPISTLE XXVII** (to Zitanus, master of the soldiers).—He acknowledges that taxes must also be paid by religious persons.

**1085 EPISTLE XXVIII** (to Fantinus, defensor).—He should decide according to his judgment the cases between Sabinianus and Bishop Theodorus, both concerning expenses for guests and concerning other matters. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXIX** (to Constantius, bishop of Milan).—The doubtful case of Bishop Pompeius cannot yet be concluded by a definite judgment.

**1086 EPISTLE XXX** (to Castorius, notary).—He again warns him to do what is just concerning the property said to have been granted to the monastery.

**1087 EPISTLE XXXI** (to Libertinus, former praetor).—He urges him to endure adversity patiently and willingly accept clothing for the use of his people.

**1088 EPISTLE XXXII** (to Secundinus, bishop of Taormina).—He should act more kindly toward the wife of Leo, who, after leaving her husband because of suspicion of adultery and putting on religious dress, had returned to him without consulting Secundinus. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXXIII** (to Secundinus, bishop).—If Bishop Dulcinus truly left six ounces of his estate to the Church of Locri and six to the monastery of Saint Christopher, he should not allow the said monastery to suffer any further harassment.

**1089 EPISTLE XXXIV** (to Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi).—He should investigate carefully John the Deacon, elected bishop by the people of Bagnoregio.

**1090 EPISTLE XXXV** (to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria) [Col. 1620].—He explains that the reason he did not reply sooner was a two-year attack of gout. The Palestinian monks who asked about the error of the Agnoetists went not to Rome but to Constantinople. He says that he wrote to Anatolius against the Agnoetists from the Latin Fathers precisely what Eulogius had written to him from the Greek Fathers.

**1091 EPISTLE XXXVI** (to Maximus, bishop of Salona).—He says that he is afflicted by the incursions of the Slavs. He should vigorously but moderately defend the poor and oppressed against unjust judges. He should continue bringing the Photinianists back to the bosom of the Church.

**1092 EPISTLE XXXVII** (to Innocentius, prefect of Africa).—He rejoices in Innocentius’s prefecture out of affection, but grieves at the burden of the office, which he fervently wishes might become for him an occasion of eternal reward. He reports that a truce has been made with the king of the Lombards. In response to his request concerning Job, he praises Augustine’s books. He gives thanks for the protection of the patrimony of the Roman Church.

**1094 EPISTLE XXXVIII** (to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—He should ensure both that those who take refuge in a church suffer no violence and that those who have hitherto been oppressed suffer no losses.

**1095 EPISTLE XXXIX** (to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria).—He refutes individually the arguments that the Agnoetists drew from Scripture and argues against them at greater length. He complains that he lacks competent interpreters of the Greek language.

**1096 EPISTLE XL** (to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples).—At Peter’s own request, he should investigate more carefully the truth of the charge brought against Peter by boys accusing him of an attempted crime.

**1099 EPISTLE XLI** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—Together with Bishop Fortunatus, he should investigate most diligently the truth of the charge brought against Peter.

**1100 EPISTLE XLII** (to Eusebius, archbishop of Thessalonica).—After commending his devotion to peace, he urges him not to allow the minds of the orthodox to be offended by certain people who reject the Council of Chalcedon. **Ibid. EPISTLE XLIII** (to Venantius, bishop of Luni).—At his request, he sends a servant of God whom he should place over a monastery and for whom he himself should provide the greatest care.

**1101 EPISTLE XLIV** (to Venantius, bishop of Luni).—He should contribute twenty solidi, or even more, for the repair of the churches at Fiesole.

**1102 EPISTLE XLV** (to Ecclesius, bishop of Chiusi).—He expresses sympathy for his illness. He congratulates him on the prudent election of a bishop. He sends him a horse. He should approach the churches in order to confirm those who have been baptized. **Ibid. EPISTLE XLVI** (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He should ensure that Crescentius, the vicar, suffers nothing unjust at the hands of Leontius, the former consul.

**1103 EPISTLE XLVII** (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He commends Apollonius, master of the soldiers. **Ibid. EPISTLE XLVIII** (to Leontius, former consul).—He commends Apollonius.

**1104 EPISTLE XLIX** (to Adeodata, illustrious lady).—He strengthens her mind to despise temporal things and love eternal things. He says that the case of Bishop Decius has been entrusted to John and Leontius. **Ibid. EPISTLE L** (to Domitianus, metropolitan).—Leontius has not yet come to Rome. He says that he supported him in carrying out the emperors’ orders. The case of Bishop Theodorus has been entrusted to him and to Bishop John.

**1105 EPISTLE LI** (to Leontius, former consul).—He says that he has never requested protection for anyone without the support of justice. Even if Libertinus committed fraud in public affairs, his property ought to have been punished, not his liberty. Anger should follow reason in punishing evils, not precede it.

**1106 EPISTLE LII** (to Amandinus, domesticus).—He says that, at Amandinus’s request, he both accepted the offerings and wrote to the exarch on behalf of the prefect John. What he wrote to him concerning Libertinus should not have been received with displeasure, but as something written frankly by a friend.

**1109 EPISTLE LIII** (to Romanus, defensor).—He should warn Leontius not to heed the words of wicked men against the rights of the citizens of Naples.

**1110 EPISTLE LIV** (to Donus, bishop of Messina).—He commends Gregory, the former prefect. **Ibid. EPISTLE LV** (to Leontius, former consul).—He commends Gregory, the former prefect.

**1111 EPISTLE LVI** (to Amandinus, domesticus).—He commends Gregory, the former prefect. **Ibid. EPISTLE LVII** (to Bishops Secundinus and John).—He commends Gregory, the former prefect. **Ibid. EPISTLE LVIII** (to Boniface, bishop of Reggio).—He should settle Gregory’s case with his church without delay, or else regard Gregory’s people as commended to him.

**1112 EPISTLE LIX** (to Bishops John and Fortunatus and Anthemius, subdeacon).—He commends Gregory’s people and possessions. **Ibid.** [Col. 1621] **EPISTLE LX** (to Azimarchus, military secretary).—He says that Gregory’s delayed arrival in Sicily was caused not by lack of diligence but by bodily illness.

**1113 EPISTLE LXI** (to Adeodatus, abbot of Naples).—He unites the monastery of Gazarus to his monastery until a bishop is ordained at Naples, but unites the monastery of Puteoli to it permanently. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXII** (to the people of Naples).—John should not have been chosen bishop, since he was unchaste; nor Peter, if he is careless and a moneylender. They should therefore provide another suitable man from their own clergy.

**1114 EPISTLE LXIII** (to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage).—He teaches with what attitude the scourge of pestilence should be received, what fruit should be gathered from it, and how those who are struck by it should be consoled.

**1115 EPISTLE LXIV** (to Romanus, defensor).—Although Scribonius is a good man, an ecclesiastical estate should not be leased to him; rather, each year he should offer to Gentius whatever profit he had made from the lease.

**1116 EPISTLE LXV** (to Adeodata).—He excuses the delay in giving the relics, which he finally sends. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXVI** (to Decius, bishop of Lilybaeum).—After taking the customary precautions, he should consecrate the monastery built by Adeodata.

**1117 EPISTLE LXVII** (to Hilary, notary).—He orders that the ship sent for the support of the monastery be protected in every respect. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXVIII** (to Opportunus).—He soothes him, saddened by harsh correction, and urges him toward complete conversion.

## BOOK XI OF THE LETTERS

**1118 EPISTLE I** (to John, abbot).—He commends himself to his prayers, praying eternal blessings for him. He sends beds and bedding for the use of pilgrims. **Ibid. EPISTLE II** (to Palladius, priest).—He consoles him, saddened by the words of those who speak against him. He teaches what should be done toward detractors. He asks for prayers and sends clothing.

**1119 EPISTLE III** (to Pantaleon, notary).—He should arrange for the deacon Deusdedit to be ordained bishop of Milan and should diligently administer there the interests of the Roman Church.

**1121 EPISTLE IV** (to the people of Milan).—After praising Constantius after his death, he congratulates them on having chosen Deusdedit as bishop. He rejects another man elected by the Lombards.

**1122 EPISTLE V** (to Innocentius, prefect of Africa).—He brings to him the complaints of Victor, bishop of Fausiana, so that he may restrain the harassment inflicted by the African judges.

**1123 EPISTLE VI** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends Florentius, his deacon, to Anatolius, his own deacon at Constantinople. He approves the proposed ordination. He reproaches him for negligence in a certain case. **Ibid. EPISTLE VII** (to Anatolius, deacon).—He commends the deacon of Bishop Marinianus.

**1124 EPISTLE VIII** (to Alexander, praetor of Sicily).—He commends John, deacon and rector of the patrimony of the Church of Ravenna in Sicily. **Ibid. EPISTLE IX** (to Leo, bishop of Catania).—He commends Severus.

**1125 EPISTLE X** (to Talitanus).—He urges Talitanus, administrator of the public patrimony, to defend the patrimony of the Roman Church from the harassment of the tax collectors. **Ibid. EPISTLE XI** (to Romanus, defensor).—He should act before Alexander so that his case with the abbess Thecla may be settled without delay or contention.

**1526 EPISTLE XII** (to Conon, abbot of Lérins).—He explains with what care and diligence he ought to govern the monastery entrusted to him. He commends the priest Columbus. **Ibid. EPISTLE XIII** (to Serenus, bishop of Marseille).—The images of the saints should not have been broken; they are not to be worshiped, but may be used for instruction. By this reasoning, he should soothe the minds of the faithful whom the breaking of the images had alienated. Wicked men are to be removed from his company and association.

**1128 EPISTLE XIV** (to Asclepiodotus).—He commends the Gallic patrimony of the Roman Church and sends a key together with relics.

**1130 EPISTLE XV** (to Aregius, bishop of Gap).—After a most friendly greeting, he commends the priest Candidus.

**1031 EPISTLE XVI** (to the people of Milan).—As Arethusa returns to Milan, they should show her affection and ensure that her case is soon settled once a bishop has been ordained. **Ibid. EPISTLE XVII** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He commends Theodora, a widow, so that she may not suffer poverty because of the ingratitude of her son, to whom she had given all her property when he married.

**1032 EPISTLE XVIII** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He should not allow the people of Helena to be unjustly detained by the agents of the Roman Church. **Ibid. EPISTLE XIX** (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He commends Donatus [Col. 1622].

**1133 EPISTLE XX** (to Scholasticus, defensor).—He should lease a small vineyard to the poor Bishop Calumniosus, in addition to the conduma already granted. He should restore the bishop’s residence to him, without removing from it what the former bishop, his father, had acquired. Finally, he should hand over to him part of the legacy. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXI** (to Romanus, defensor).—To Argentia, a hospitable woman, he should grant the use and fruits of a small ten-modii plot, so that she may practice more generous hospitality.

**1134 EPISTLE XXII** (to Spesindeus, governor of Sardinia).—He should cooperate with Bishop Victor in converting and baptizing the Sardinians. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXIII** (to Vitalis, defensor of Sardinia).—He should assist Boniface in acquiring slaves among the Barbaricini.

**1135 EPISTLE XXIV** (to John, tribune of Sipontum).—He urges him to decide, together with Bishop Vitalianus, concerning the freedom of the bearer of this letter. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXV** (to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—He praises him for refusing to build a men’s monastery in the house adjoining the monastery of the servants of God. Nevertheless, he orders that monks be established either in the place abandoned by the women or in some deserted monastery, and he commends the matter to Januarius. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXVI** (to John, subdeacon).—He should act before the prefect on behalf of John the silversmith.
