**1136 EPISTLE XXVII** (to John, religious).—He declares John, who is in charge of the table of the poor and of supplying the diaconia, exempt from rendering accounts to men; but he urges him to remember that he will render an account to God, so that he may fulfill his work more diligently.

**1137 EPISTLE XXVIII** (to Augustine, bishop of the English).—All Romans rejoice over the conversion of the English. Augustine too should rejoice in God’s gift, but beware that the performance of miracles does not produce pride of heart. Miracles were performed both by Moses before he was freed from guilt and by the reprobate themselves. In these things he should seek not his own glory but God’s glory and the salvation of souls. We should rejoice in one sign within us, namely, love.

**1138 EPISTLE XXIX** (to Bertha, queen of the English).—He congratulates her on the conversion of the English. He earnestly urges her not to neglect any longer to kindle the king’s heart toward perfect love of the Christian faith.

**1141 EPISTLE XXX** (to Venantius, former monk and patrician of Syracuse).—Taking occasion from both his own gout and that of Venantius, he teaches that the sufferings of this life are God’s blows, by which he mercifully corrects sinners. Accordingly, sins must be recalled to mind in such circumstances, thanks must be given to God, and God’s judgment must be anticipated through repentance.

**1143 EPISTLE XXXI** (to Paschasius, bishop of Naples).—He should grant Venantius the relics of Saint Severinus for the consecration of an oratory.

**1144 EPISTLE XXXII** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He speaks of the relics granted to Abbot Candidus. He says that he is afflicted by so many and such great illnesses that living is a punishment. He asks for prayers before God, that God may moderate his scourges and grant him patience. **Ibid. EPISTLE XXXIII** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He urges him, after arranging the affairs of the Church, to hasten to Rome, where, under Gregory’s own care, he may be cured of vomiting blood in peace. Meanwhile, he should abstain from fasts, vigils, and sermons.

**1145 EPISTLE XXXIV** (to Paschasius, bishop of Naples).—Whatever portion of the clergy or the poor his predecessor had withheld from the Church’s funds, he should distribute according to the procedure prescribed in this letter.

**1146 EPISTLE XXXV** (to Barbara and Antonina).—He consoles them, deeply distressed by their father’s imminent death.

**1147 EPISTLE XXXVI** (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He expresses his grief over Venantius’s desperate illness. Above all, action should be taken so that Venantius may return to the monastic habit, even at the end of his life. Gregory says that he is greatly hindered because Venantius is now commending his daughters to the emperor himself. John should protect them as far as he can. He permits John, as a friend, to come to Rome at a suitable time.

**1148 EPISTLE XXXVII** (to Romanus, defensor).—Cases involving clerics should be brought before bishops, so that episcopal jurisdiction is not violated.

**1149 EPISTLE XXXVIII** (to Vitus, defensor).—He appoints him defender of the Church.

**1150 EPISTLE XXXIX** (to Romanus, defensor).—He commends Vitus, who has been appointed defensor. **Ibid. EPISTLE XL** (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).— **EPISTLE XLI** (to Romanus, defensor).—Concerning the boundaries of Faustus’s estates, which had been unjustly seized. **Ibid.** Because of the outbreak of blood, he should moderate his fasting and avoid every form of aggravation.

**1151 EPISTLE XLII** (to John, bishop).—Concerning the boundaries of Faustus’s estates, which had been unjustly seized. **Ibid.** [Col. 1623] **EPISTLE XLIII** (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He should finally settle the long-delayed case of Rusticiana concerning the seizure of the boundaries of her estate.

**1152 EPISTLE XLIV** (to Rusticiana, patrician).—He asks her not to keep calling herself his servant in letters. The curtains she had offered to blessed Peter have now been suspended. He both grieves and rejoices over her gout. He proves from various miracles that the monastery of Saint Andrew, to which she too had sent alms, is most diligently guarded by that apostle.

**Ibid. EPISTLE XLV** (to Theoctista, patrician).—He shows by many arguments that her mind should not be disturbed by slanders, although the murmur of detractors must be calmed by a tranquil and humble response. He also shows: first, that marriages should not be dissolved for the sake of religion; second, that all sins are completely forgiven in baptism; third, that after three years of repentance there is no license to sin; and fourth, that even the person who, compelled by necessity, anathematized the matter for which he is reproached remains bound by the anathema. Many people, he says, have been falsely accused through ignorant zeal on those four points; nevertheless, the accusers must be appeased by reason and gentleness, and Theoctista herself should act in this way toward her own people.

**1156 EPISTLE XLVI** (to Isaac, bishop of Jerusalem).—In reply to his synodical letter, he compares the Church to the ark, outside which there is no salvation. He praises Isaac’s faith, which he professes to share. He rejoices that, under a most Christian emperor, the mouths of the heretics have been silenced. He urges Isaac to restrain simony in his churches and to mitigate quarrels by restraining some practices and tolerating others.

**1164 EPISTLE XLVII** (to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople).—Neither John nor any other bishop should be deposed on account of bodily illness.

**1167 EPISTLE XLVIII** (to Urbicus, abbot).—He rebukes his fickleness and rashness. He himself orders who should be abbot and who should be superior in the Lucusian monastery. **Ibid. EPISTLE XLIX** (to Urbicus, abbot).—From the money of the Lucusian monastery he should give forty solidi to Peter, bishop of Tricala.

**1168 EPISTLE L** (to Adrian, notary).—He orders that Agathosa’s husband, who had been tonsured and made a monk against her will, be restored to her.

**1169 EPISTLE LI** (to all the bishops of Sicily).—In anticipation of an imminent invasion by the enemy, they should order two litanies each week and exhort the faithful to abandon worldly perversity. **Ibid. EPISTLE LII** (to Donus, bishop of Messina).—The judgment rendered between Placidus and the agents of the Church of Messina should be carried out.

**1170 EPISTLE LIII** (to Adrian, notary).—He should continue pursuing enchanters and practitioners of divination.

**1171 EPISTLE LIV** (to Desiderius, bishop of Gaul).—A bishop ought not to teach grammar. He commends the monks whom he is sending to Britain with Laurentius and Mellitus. **Ibid. EPISTLE LV** (to Virgilius, bishop of Arles).—He should insist that a synod be convened to eradicate simony. He should restrain Bishop Serenus from the company of wicked men. He should regard the monks going to Augustine as commended to him.

**1172 EPISTLE LVI** (to Aetherius, bishop of Lyon).—He should insist on convening a synod. He should send copies concerning the privileges of his church. The writings of Irenaeus cannot be found. He commends the monks sent to Augustine in England.

**1173 EPISTLE LVII** (to Aregius, bishop of Gap).—He should work for the condemnation of simony in council. He should favor the monks going to Augustine.

**1174 EPISTLE LVIII** (to various bishops of Gaul).—He commends the monks going to Augustine in England.

**1176 EPISTLE LIX** (to Theuderic, king of the Franks).—He urges him to convene a synod and commends those same monks.

**1179 EPISTLE LX** (to Theudebert, king of the Franks).—He urges him to convene a synod and commends the same monks.

**1180 EPISTLE LXI** (to Chlothar, king of the Franks).—He commends the monks going to Augustine. He urges him to convene a synod against the simoniacs. **Ibid. EPISTLE LXII** (to Brunhild, queen of the Franks).—He commends the monks going to Britain.

**1181 EPISTLE LXIII** (to Brunhild, queen of the Franks).—That she order a synod to be convened to uproot simony.

**1182 EPISTLE LXIV** (to Augustine, bishop of the English).—He answers various questions on which Augustine had consulted him:

1. Concerning the fourfold division of ecclesiastical goods.
2. Concerning clerics who marry after entering the clergy.
3. Concerning the differing customs of different churches, which should not be condemned.
4. Concerning the repentance of thieves and the restitution of ecclesiastical property.
5. Two brothers may marry two sisters.
6. Which degrees of consanguinity and affinity prohibit marriage.
7. Neophytes joined in a prohibited degree are neither to be separated nor deprived of holy communion, but are to be admonished to abstain.
8. How many bishops are required for the consecration of a bishop.
9. How a metropolitan should conduct himself in another province.
10. That a pregnant woman and a newborn child may be baptized. A woman undergoing menstruation is not barred from entering the church, but after intercourse married couples ought to abstain from entering the church.
11. When nocturnal emission prevents the celebration of the liturgy and communion.

**1183 EPISTLE LXV** (to Augustine, bishop of the English).—He grants him the use of the pallium. He makes the same promise to the bishop of London, whom he orders to be ordained by his own synod. He wishes the bishop of York to enjoy the full dignity of a metropolitan. He appoints Augustine primate of all Britain.

**1200 EPISTLE LXVI** (to Æthelberht, king of the English).—He urges him to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to him. He should willingly listen to Augustine and assist him. He explains why, as the end of this world approaches
May God send signs in advance. He sends gifts and pours out prayers to God.

1201 LETTER LXVII (to Quiricus, bishop, etc.).—Those who were baptized in heresy with an invocation of the Trinity are not to be baptized if they return to the Church; rather, they are to be reconciled either by the laying on of hands, by anointing with chrism, or by a profession of faith. Nestorians who return are to be instructed in the true faith concerning the incarnate Word, which he himself here confirms from the Scriptures; and, if they anathematize Nestorius and venerate the synods accepted by the Church, they are to be received in their own orders.

1204 LETTER LXVIII (to Virgilius, bishop of Arles).—He commends Bishop Augustine if he should come to him.

1208 LETTER LXIX (to Brunichild, queen of the Franks).—On correcting priests who order their lives wickedly.

1209 LETTER LXX (to Candidus, presbyter and rector of the patrimony).—He commends the presbyter Aurelius, asking that he entrust to him an oratory or some other place.

1210 LETTER LXXI (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He rebukes him and the others appointed as judges in the case of John the Deacon because they had inflicted no punishment on Hilary the subdeacon, the false accuser. He orders that Hilary, deprived of his office and publicly punished with blows, be exiled. A vice-manager and steward are to be chosen for Bishop Paschasius.

Ibid. LETTER LXXII (to Agapitus, abbot).—He unites to that man’s monastery another monastery, completely deserted by the monks because of hostilities.

1211 LETTER LXXIII (to Marinianus, abbot).—He entrusts the Church of Saint George to Marinianus and his successors.

1212 LETTER LXXIV (to Eusebius, bishop of Thessalonica).—He says that the letter of that bishop was falsified by Andrew, a most wicked monk. Some sermons were likewise falsely attributed to Gregory himself by the same man. A confession of faith is to be required from Luke, a presbyter whose faith is suspect.

1212 LETTER LXXV (to Aurelius).—He consoles him over the death of his brother and the tribulations he was suffering.

1214 LETTER LXXVI (to Mellitus, abbot).—He gives him instructions to present to Augustine, whom he was visiting, in order to facilitate the conversion of the English.

1215 LETTER LXXVII (to Boniface, defensor in Corsica).—He is to see that bishops of Aleria and Ajaccio are elected as soon as possible. He is neither to allow the poor to be oppressed nor clerics to be held before lay judges.

1217 LETTER LXXVIII (to Barbara and Antonina).—He prays for divine protection for them. He rejoices that they wish to come to Rome. He commends their cases to Bishop John and the Roman defensor. He gladly accepts their gifts.

1218 BOOK XII OF THE LETTERS.

1219 LETTER I (to Dominicus, bishop of Carthage).—He congratulates him on recovering from a serious illness. He reminds him that postponements of life are often granted to us so that we may come more prepared to judgment.

Ibid. LETTER II (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to give twelve solidi to Matthew, a most distinguished man, for his support.

1220 LETTER III (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—Concerning a certain boy brought from Sicily to Misenum, where he had received the monastic habit.

Ibid. LETTER IV (to Fantinus, defensor).—He is to urge Bishop Victor to bring to an end the case of Maurentius against the Church of Palermo.

1221 LETTER V (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He commends the men of Maurentius.

1222 LETTER VI (to Theodorus, curator).—He commends the men of Maurentius.

Ibid. LETTER VII (to Savinella, Columba, and Agnella).—Writing the same to each individually, he urges them to acquire heavenly treasures through more generous almsgiving.

1223 LETTER VIII (to Columbus, bishop of Numidia).—He is to investigate diligently the serious complaint of Donadeus against his bishop Victor, so that the guilty party may receive an appropriate punishment.

1224 LETTER IX (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—If Adeodatus the old man is truly poor, he is to remit one of the two annual solidi owed to him.

Ibid. LETTER X (to Fantinus, defensor).—He is to press Isidore’s heirs either to build a hospice or to assign a legacy to one already built.

1225 LETTER XI (to Passivus, bishop of Firmum).—He orders him to consecrate an oratory, after first receiving a lawful donation, and to establish there a cardinal presbyter.

Ibid. LETTER XII (to Passivus, bishop of Firmum).—He is to urge Opportunus to grow in good pursuits; then he is to become a monk or subdeacon, and finally pastor of the Aprutine territory.

1226 LETTER XIII (to Fantinus, defensor).—He is to place without delay in safe custody the property of the deceased notary Primogenitus, lest it perish for the Roman Church or other heirs.

1227 LETTER XIV (to Azimarchus, the Scribo).—Having been rescued from the danger of the sea, he is urged never to cease remembering divine mercy.

Ibid. LETTER XV (to Romanus, defensor).—He is to assist Laurentius in completing the accounts of Boniface, the former accountant.

1228 LETTER XVI (to Azimarchus, the Scribo).—He is to favor Laurentius as he presents to Leontius the accounts of the late Boniface, the accountant.

1229 LETTER XVII (to Maurilio, former prefect).—He kindly urges him to write to him more often.

Ibid. LETTER XVIII (to Eupator, duke of Sardinia).—He commends Valdarichus.

1230 LETTER XIX (to Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He requests twenty-four wicker chairs.

Ibid. LETTER XX (to Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He is to send to Arogus his letter concerning assistance to the subdeacon Sabinus in transporting beams to the sea.

Ibid. LETTER XXI (to Arogus, duke).—He is to order that Sabinus be assisted as he drags to the sea the beams he has cut for the churches of Saints Peter and Paul; he promises a gift.

1231 LETTER XXII (to Gregory, former prefect).—He is to lend Sabinus twenty of his men and oxen for transporting the beams.

Ibid. LETTER XXIII (to Stephen, bishop).—He is to send men with oxen to assist Sabinus.

1232 LETTER XXIV (to John, subdeacon of Ravenna).—He orders that, after Constantius has been rejected, Maurus be ordained abbot if he is found worthy; that the monastery be cleansed of the plague of private ownership; and that the writings of Abbot Claudius, taken down from his own mouth but in many respects alien to his meaning, be sent to him. He does not approve of his commentaries on Job being read publicly at the vigils. It is more expedient that commentaries on the Psalms be read. He does not wish his works to be readily published while he remains in this body. He commends Albinus and Augustus.

1233 LETTER XXV (to Romanus, defensor).—The sons of the defensor Peter are not to be joined in marriage outside the social class in which they were born.

1235 LETTER XXVI (to Maurentius, master of the soldiers).—He is not to retain the son of Domitius after dismissing the others.

1236 LETTER XXVII (to Quertinus, former prefect).—He explains why he does not wish to act on behalf of Bonitus, who is seeking the administration of the prefecture.

Ibid. LETTER XXVIII (to Columbus, bishop of Numidia).—Bishop Paulinus is to be restrained: he had acted savagely toward his clergy and was selling sacred orders through sacrilegious traffic.

1237 LETTER XXIX (to Bishop Victor).—So that Paulinus’s brutality toward the clergy and his simony may be punished and suppressed, he is to convene a council, summoning Hilary if necessary.

1239 LETTER XXX (to Constantine, bishop of Scodra).—He is to carry out himself, if he can, what is decreed in the following letter to John against Paul’s disgraceful conduct; if he cannot, he is to press John to carry it out.

1240 LETTER XXXI (to John, bishop of Prima Justiniana).—After setting out the disgraceful conduct of Paul, bishop of Doclea, he prescribes remedies.

1241 LETTER XXXII (to all the bishops of the council of Byzacena).—They are to investigate vigorously and carefully the serious accusations brought against Clementius, their primate.

1242 LETTER XXXIII (to Firminus, bishop of Istria).—He congratulates him on his return to the unity of the Church. He urges him to oppose the darts of Satan with the shield of steadfastness and to recall others with him. He promises assistance. He sends supplies.

1243 LETTER XXXIV (to Ciridanus).—Since what he himself had ordered has been done on behalf of Sitonicus, the Church is no longer to suffer that loss.

1244 LETTER XXXV (to Desiderius, bishop of Vienne).—He is not to recall his deacon Pancratius from the monastic life.

1245 LETTER XXXVI (to Bonitus, defensor).—He is to assist the monks who are collecting their fugitive slaves.

1246 LETTER XXXVII (to Romanus, defensor, and the subdeacons Anthemius and Sabinus).—He commends the men and possessions of Romanus, the former praetor.

Ibid. LETTER XXXVIII (to Deusdedit, bishop of Milan).—A bishop may make a will concerning property acquired before his episcopate; therefore, on account of a legacy in his predecessor’s will, Luminosa, a female servant of God, is not to be harassed.

Ibid. LETTER XXXIX (to Fantinus, defensor).—From the inheritance of the deacon Servideus, he is to give ten mares to the hospice and four to Luminosa, a female servant of God.

1247 LETTER XL (to Venantius, patrician).—He promises that, once he has recovered, he will explain allegorically certain deeds of Samson.

1248 LETTER XLI (to Pantaleon, notary).—Concerning the surviving funds, clergy, and other property of certain churches.

Ibid. LETTER XLII (to Romanus, defensor).—He is to warn Salustius not to trouble Luminosus, a servant of the Church, any further.

1249 LETTER XLIII (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He says that revenues should be collected in such a way that neither the debtors are distressed nor the Roman Church suffers loss.

Ibid. LETTER XLIV (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to repay Accello the price he paid—eight solidi—to ransom Stephen from the enemy.

1250 LETTER XLV (to Eugenius, deacon).—He grants two portions of land for thirty-six years to needy servants of God.

Ibid. LETTER XLVI (to Felix, bishop of Porto).—He gives John as a servant.

1251 LETTER XLVII (to Venantius, bishop of Perugia).—He is to send winter clothing without delay to Bishop Ecclesius, who is suffering from the cold.

Ibid. LETTER XLVIII (to Lucidus, bishop of Leontini).—Whomever Abbot John has selected from his congregation, he is to ordain presbyter for the monastery.

1252 LETTER XLIX (to Romanus, defensor).—He is to support before Leontius the palace officials of the city of Rome who are requesting the grain allowance granted by the emperor.

Ibid. LETTER L (to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria).—He commends those converted from the error of the Monophysites.

Ibid. BOOK XIII OF THE LETTERS.

1253 LETTER I (to the citizens of Rome).—The Sabbath day is not to be observed according to the letter. For reasons of necessity, the body may be washed on the Lord’s Day.

Ibid. LETTER II (to Adeodatus, abbot).—He unites the Craterian monastery to his monastery.

1255 LETTER III (to Adeodatus, monk).—He permits a donation made verbally before its donor had undertaken the monastic life to be committed to writing and held valid.

1256 LETTER IV (to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari).—He is to settle the dispute between Abbess Desideria and Abbot John with the assistance of two bishops.

1257 LETTER V (to Etherius, bishop of Lyon).—On the arrangements to be made when a bishop falls ill and cannot perform his office.

1258 LETTER VI (to Brunichild, queen of the Franks).—Concerning the privileges granted to a monastery and hospice, after hearing her envoys and absolving Bishop Menna. Concerning a bishop who was suffering from an illness of the head. Concerning not ordaining a twice-married man. He will send someone to Gaul to attend the synod. The privileges he sends are to be inserted in the public acts.

1259 LETTER VII (to Theoderic, king of the Franks).—He praises the king’s piety and prudence. He deals with the same privileges, with the king’s envoys, and with establishing peace with the emperor.

1262 LETTER VIII (to Senator, abbot).—The privilege of the hospice.

Ibid. LETTER IX (to Thalassia, abbess).—The privilege of the monastery of Saint Mary in the city of Augustodunum.

1265 LETTER X (to Lupon, abbot).—The privilege of the Church of Saint Martin in the suburb of Augustodunum.

1266 LETTER XI (to Maximus, bishop of Salona).—He will no longer trust that bishop’s men unless they have a legally signed mandate.

1267 LETTER XII (to Paschasius, bishop of Naples).—Jews are not to be barred from their celebrations; rather, through admonitions and gentle persuasion, they are to be stirred toward conversion.

Ibid. LETTER XIII (to Barbarus, bishop of Benevento).—He appoints him visitor of the Church of Palermo according to the customary formula.

1268 LETTER XIV (to the people of Palermo).—They are to obey Bishop Barbarus, the visitor.

1269 LETTER XV (to Venantius, patrician of Palermo).—Abbot Urbicus has rightly been elected bishop, but he is not to be compelled if he resists. The conduct of the deacon Crescentius is to be investigated. If they agree neither on this matter nor on another, envoys are to be sent to Rome.

1270 LETTER XVI (to Passivus, bishop of Firmum).—He orders Passivus, according to the customary formula, to consecrate the monastery in honor of Saint Sabinus.

1271 LETTER XVII (to John, subdeacon of Ravenna).—He is to urge Bishop Marinianus to order that the case between him and Bishop John be settled without litigation. Otherwise, he himself is to press for judgment and execute the sentence. He disapproves of the construction and dedication of an oratory carried out by Bishop Exuperantius in John’s diocese.

1272 LETTER XVIII (to certain bishops of Sicily).—He commends Adrian, rector of the patrimony. He warns the bishops not to burden their subjects beyond measure when they go out to confirm infants.

1273 LETTER XIX (to Julianus).—He complains that Julianus concealed his poverty out of embarrassment. After the monastery at Catania was built, he grants him ten annual solidi.

1274 LETTER XX (to Honorius, bishop of Tarentum).—He permits the use of a baptistery once it has been built.

Ibid. LETTER XXI (to Paschal and Consolantia).—He extends the time granted for repaying the money. He consoles those placed in adversity.

1275 LETTER XXII (to Rusticiana, patrician).—He indicates that he grieves over her poor health. Weary of his own sorrows, he longs to die. She herself is to petition the emperors to restrain Beator, who is plotting wicked things.

Ibid. LETTER XXIII (to Boniface, notary of Corsica).—He is to urge John the cleric to come to Rome to be examined.

1276 LETTER XXIV (to Sabinus, subdeacon).—He is to assist Bishop Proculus as he repairs what had been neglected during his absence.

1277 LETTER XXV (to Sabinus, subdeacon).—He is to warn Bishop Palumbus to protect the affairs of the churches more diligently; otherwise, he himself is to perform Palumbus’s duties.

Ibid. LETTER XXVI (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to rebuke Bishop Paschasius’s negligence before chosen witnesses.

1278 LETTER XXVII (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to summon the bishops of Campania who are forgetful of their duty and warn them to act more vigilantly. If afterward he finds anyone negligent, he is to send him to Rome.

1279 LETTER XXVIII (to John, bishop of Syracuse).—He is to restore the presbyter Cosmas, who had been afflicted because of the character of the place to which he had been assigned, to his former position.

Ibid. LETTER XXIX (to Philip, presbyter).—He says that he rejoiced at Andrew’s death because Andrew had attained eternal joys. He asks Philip to obtain the same from God for him. He sends Philip fifty solidi.

1280 LETTER XXX (to Deusdedit, bishop of Milan).—He is to send Theodorus with the defensor to Venantius to investigate Theodorus’s complaints.

Ibid. LETTER XXXI (to Phocas, emperor).—The worst kings are appointed to punish the sins of the people, and the best to console their subjects. He urges Phocas to aid the afflicted state.

1281 LETTER XXXII (to Eusebia, patrician).—He urges her to think more about the things concerning the soul than those concerning the body.

1282 LETTER XXXIII (to Smaragdus, exarch).—He urges him to protect Bishop Firminus, who has returned to the unity of the Church, from Severus’s harassment. Cillanus will observe a thirty-day reprieve, but the Pisans refused to make an agreement.

1283 LETTER XXXIV (to Pantaleon, notary).—He praises him for reducing the measure of the modius by which the Church’s tenant farmers delivered grain to the proper standard. He orders that the money received from the unjust measure be distributed to the poorer tenant farmers.

1285 LETTER XXXV (to Catulus and Romanus).—He is to assist the defensor Optatus in removing foreign women from the company of priests.

1286 LETTER XXXVI (to Chrysanthus, bishop of Spoleto).—He is to restrain the priests of Norcia who live with foreign women.

Ibid. LETTER XXXVII (to John, bishop of Palermo).—He grants the use of the pallium.

1287 LETTER XXXVIII (to Phocas, emperor).—He cleverly excuses the absence of his deacon. He sends Boniface. He implores assistance against the Lombards.

Ibid. LETTER XXXIX (to Leontia, empress).—He congratulates her on attaining the empire. He prays for divine grace for her. He commends the Roman Church.

1288 LETTER XL (to Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople).—For the sake of peace, he urges him to abstain from the proud title “Universal.” He commends the deacon Boniface.

1289 LETTER XLI (to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria).—He urges Eulogius to eradicate simony.

1290 LETTER XLII (to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria).—He congratulates him both on not having lost his eyesight and on the increase of the Lord’s flock. He reminds him that the eulogies he had received have arrived, and that larger timbers are ready; if he needs them, he should write to Boniface.

1291 LETTER XLIII (to John of Palermo).—He permits the man whom he very much wished to see to remain in Sicily because of the danger of the voyage.

1292 LETTER XLIV (to John, bishop of Palermo).—He is to provide what he promised to his clerics when they made a lawful request.

1293 LETTER XLV (to John, defensor).—He gives instructions about what is to be done concerning Januarius, bishop of Malaca, one of that bishop’s presbyters, and Bishop Stephen.

1294 LETTER XLVI (to John, defensor).—He is to bring the dissolute monks of the island of Capraria back to the proper path.

1301 LETTER XLVII (to Theodorus, curator).—He affectionately commends Peter and his mother.

1302 BOOK XIV OF THE LETTERS.

1303 LETTER I (to Paul the scholasticus).—He congratulates him both on his reconciliation with Bishop Leo and on his zeal against evildoers.

Ibid. LETTER II (to Vitalis, defensor of Sardinia).—Concerning neglected hospices. Concerning protecting Sardinians before the emperor. Concerning certain men appointed abbots after their fall. Concerning the monastery built in the house of Pomponia. Concerning the recovery of the property of churches and monasteries. Concerning the illness of Bishop Januarius at the time of the sacrifice.

Ibid. LETTER III (to John, bishop of Palermo).—He permits him to exchange the house located at Rome with Epiphanius, a deacon of the Roman Church.

1305 LETTER IV (to Fantinus, defensor of Palermo).—He is to supervise the actions of Bishop Exhilaratus, so that the bishop shows charity toward his clergy and the clergy offers obedience to him.

1306 LETTER V (to John, bishop of Palermo).—He is to investigate carefully the case of Peter with the defensor Fantinus and render judgment.

1307 LETTER VI (to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna).—He is to restore Abbot Fortunatus, who was unjustly deposed, and rebuke the bishop for changing without cause what had been established by his predecessor.

1308 LETTER VII (to Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra).—The fortress of Cassiopium is to remain under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Corcyra; nevertheless, the priests of Euria are not to be expelled from it.

Ibid. LETTER VIII (to Boniface, deacon).—He is to act before the emperor so that, by rescinding the order secretly obtained concerning the fortress of Cassiopium, the emperor orders his own judgment to be observed.

1310 LETTER IX (to John, bishop of Palermo).—He grants permission to consecrate the basilica.

1312 LETTER X (to Guduinus, duke).—He is to punish the soldier who violated a female servant of God.

Ibid. LETTER XI (to John, bishop).—He is to investigate the persons, conduct, and learning of the three men elected to the episcopate.

1313 LETTER XII (to Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards).—He congratulates her on her son’s joining the Catholic faith. He excuses the fact that he did not reply to Secundus on account of the gout. He sends the synod held under Justinian. He defends the orthodoxy of the Roman Church. He thanks the king for the peace that has been made.

1314 LETTER XIII (to Alcyson, bishop of Corcyra).—He is to allow the body of Saint Donatus to be buried in the fortress of Cassiopium, without prejudice to the jurisdiction of his Church.

1317 LETTER XIV (to Felix, subdeacon).—He grants ample revenues to the Church of Saint Paul for maintaining its lights.

1318 LETTER XV (to Anthemius, subdeacon).—He is to warn the exarch against speaking rashly, and he himself is to seek by letter the hoped-for relief for the Romans in their troubles.

1319 LETTER XVI (from Felix, bishop of Messina, to Saint Gregory).—He asks about the degrees of consanguinity within which marriage is permitted; about the harassment of bishops by their subjects; and about churches whose dedications are uncertain.

1320 LETTER XVII (to Felix, bishop of Messina).—In response to his questions, he answers concerning the union of relatives, the harassment of bishops by their subjects, and the doubtful consecration of churches. He orders that the incorrigible be separated and that a synod be convened every year.

1322 APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF SAINT GREGORY.

1327 Various tables of the Letters of Saint Gregory.

1351
[Col. 1627] **END OF THE SEVENTY-SEVENTH VOLUME.**
